## Volume Front Matter

### Series Title Page

The Complete Course of Patrology, or universal, complete, uniform, convenient, economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared according to the most accurate editions, compared most diligently with one another and with several manuscript codices; continuously illustrated with dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; augmented by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority and influence in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers, and in what places in their works, commented on the individual texts of the books of Scripture.

The most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if the following matters are weighed: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the exceedingly convenient format of the volumes, uniform and consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection—single, methodical, and chronological—which for the first time in our library brings together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

### Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the universal library of the clergy, or of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

Patrology has been printed in two editions, one Latin and the other Greek-Latin. The volumes of the Latin edition are sold for 1,200 francs; those of the Greek-Latin edition for 1,300. The purely Latin edition embraces all authors, both Western and Eastern; the Eastern authors, however, are presented in it only in Latin translation.

**In the year of the Lord 888. Anastasius, Roman abbot, priest and librarian of the Roman Church.**

[Col. 0009]

# Historical and Bibliographical Notice Concerning Anastasius

*(From Oudinus, Ecclesiastical Writers, vol. II.)*

[Col. 0009A] Anastasius, Roman abbot, priest and librarian of the Roman Church, was of an order unknown to me, but, insofar as one may conjecture, of the order of Saint Benedict. He was librarian of the Holy Roman Church, an office that in this ninth century was customarily conferred upon highly learned men.

Which monastery he was abbot of is now established by John Mabillon’s *Italian Literary Itinerary*, part II, p. 82, where this Anastasius begins his prologue to certain miracles of Saint Basil the bishop as follows:

> “To the venerable Ursus, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, physician and household officer of our most sacred lord Pope Nicholas, Anastasius, humble abbot of the monastery of the holy Virgin Mary, Mother of God, situated across the Tiber, where once, around the Nativity of the Lord, a fountain of oil flowed, sends greetings in the Lord,” and so forth.

Thus, as the ninth century passed, he flourished under the supreme pontiffs Nicholas I, Adrian II, and John VIII. According to the distinguished Spanheim, in his *Historical Inquiry Concerning the Female Pope*, §55, p. 271:

> “Some papal historians, by a forced argument, insist that he had already flourished under Leo IV, to whom he had been secretary, and under several pontiffs who followed.”

What Onuphrius says, on p. 126, in his notes to Platina—that Anastasius himself reports that he was present at the elections of Sergius II, Leo IV, Benedict III, Nicholas I, Adrian II, and John VIII—we do not find in this Anastasius at all.

John Launoius is more accurate in his letter to Michael Morollius, part III, letter II, p. 170:

> “He flourished under the pontiffs Adrian II and John VIII.”

Peter Lambecius likewise says in his *Commentaries on the Imperial Library of Vienna*, book II, p. 277:

> “He flourished under Pope Nicholas I, Adrian II, and John VIII.”

Certainly, he dedicated to Adrian II his translation of the anti-Photian synod, commonly called the Eighth Council, whose final sessions he attended in 869. He was sent to Constantinople that year by the emperor Louis II to Basil the Macedonian, concerning the arrangement—such are his words—of a marriage between the emperor Basil’s son and the daughter of Augustus Louis.

Some add that this same Anastasius, who witnessed more than one papal election, was specifically present at the election of Benedict III, immediately after the death of Leo IV, on the basis of these words:

> “They also sent those who conveyed to the emperor our decree concerning the gracious election of Benedict.”

Such, therefore, was the man who committed nothing to writing unless he had examined and observed it, and who cannot be accused of bad faith in recording the events of his own time. Launoius says the same in his letter to Charles Maurice Le Tellier, part IV, p. 155:

> “Vossius, and others if there are any, confuse him with Anastasius, cardinal-priest of Saint Marcellus and librarian under Pope Gregory IV. The latter was deposed by Leo IV in the Roman synod of 850 because he had abandoned his church for five years contrary to the canons.”

This is what Labbe wrote against Vossius. Yet although I have carefully gone through Vossius’s work *On Latin Historians*, I have found nothing of this kind written by him.

The opinion, however, belongs to the Jesuit Antonio Possevino, vol. I of the *Sacred Apparatus*, p. 71, where he writes:

> “Anastasius the Roman, a monk and abbot of the order of Saint Benedict, of the congregation of Subiaco, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellinus, and librarian under Pope Gregory IV. But in the Roman synod of 850 he was deposed by Pope Leo IV because he had abandoned his church for five years contrary to the decrees of the canons. A very learned man, he left monuments of his intellect: a continuation of the *History of the Popes* of Saint Pope Damasus, from his death to Pope Adrian II. He translated from Greek into Latin the Lives of Saints John the Almsgiver, Demetrius the Martyr, and other Fathers. He translated one of the Hierarchies of Dionysius, the Seventh Council, and other works.”

This is Possevino.

Anastasius was not unlearned, considering the character of his age. He possessed no ordinary knowledge of both Greek and Latin, and, finally, he maintained a sufficiently close friendship with the leading men of the century, Photius and Hincmar.

If Cardinal Baronius’s chronology is correct, he lived until about 886, although no one has yet discovered in what year he died.

Bellarmin briefly discusses his writings in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 858. More fully after him, Philip Labbe did so in his *Historical Dissertation on the Ecclesiastical Writers Listed by Bellarmine*, vol. I, p. 63; and William Cave in his *History of the Writers of the Church*, under the year 870, p. 559. Although they report much omitted by Bellarmine, they do not list all of Anastasius’s minor works. This has given us the occasion to discuss here all the works of Abbot Anastasius known to us.

He therefore became famous both through his own works and through his various translations into Latin of Greek works or works written in Greek, by which he commended his name immortally to posterity.

## I

He himself attended in Constantinople in 869, under Basil the Macedonian, the Eighth General Council, or Fourth Council of Constantinople. He wrote part of it in Latin and translated part from Greek, dedicating it to Pope Adrian II. It is found in volume VIII of the Councils, columns 961–1175, of the final Paris edition of 1672, commonly called the Labbean edition.

He translated it from Greek into Latin—a rather harsh and less polished Latin—and added and altered material with considerable freedom. The following works are of the same kind.

## II

The Seventh General Council, or Second Council of Nicaea, which he presented to Pope John VIII, with the inscription:

> “To the lord, co-angelic John, supreme pontiff and universal pope, Anastasius the humble. From what has recently been translated,” and so forth.

It too is found in volume VII of the said Councils, in the cited edition, columns 29 and following.

Labbe adds—something others failed to observe—that Anastasius also translated the Sixth General Council, or Third Council of Constantinople. Labbe, however, ought to have indicated the grounds or authority on which he asserted this. Was it because of the similarity of style between his translation of this Sixth Ecumenical Council and his translations of the Seventh and Eighth? Or did he rely on some ancient writer who attested it? This is unknown to me.

## III

He translated into Latin the Life of Saint John the Almsgiver, patriarch of Alexandria. Sigebert says of it in chapter 103 of his *Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “Anastasius, at the command of Pope Nicholas, translated into Latin the Life of John the Almsgiver, written in Greek by Leontius the bishop.”

John Trithemius says nearly the same.

You have it in Anastasius’s translation in Heribert Rosweyde’s *Lives of the Fathers*, repeatedly printed at Antwerp and Lyons, as everyone knows.

Lambecius says of it in volume VIII of his *Commentaries on the Imperial Library of Vienna*, p. 271:

> “Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, Roman abbot of the order of Saint Benedict and cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Marcellus, translated this Life from Greek into Latin at the command of Pope Nicholas I, who was elected in the year of Christ 858 and died in 867. After various other printed editions, this Latin translation was most excellently published by Heribert Rosweyde of the Society of Jesus in book I of his *Lives of the Fathers*, and by Bollandus and Henschenius in volume II of the saints of the month of January, on the twenty-third day.”

## IV

He likewise translated from Greek into Latin the Life of Saint Demetrius the Martyr, as well as many Acts and Passions that occur in manuscript codices.

A Passion of Saint Demetrius the Martyr translated by the same Anastasius is found in volume I of John Mabillon’s *Ancient Analecta*, dedicated to the most pious emperor Charles, always Augustus, p. 65.

## V

Among the many works that he translated from Greek into Latin is the Life of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite. He sent its translation to the emperor Charles the Bald in 876.

This minor work has been lost, except for its preface, which we have in Surius, volume V, under 11 October, at the end of the Areopagitic works. John Mabillon reprinted the same preface in his *Analecta* according to manuscript authority.

In it Anastasius says that he did not translate everything *κατὰ πόδας*—“step by step,” literally—but nevertheless expressed the sense in good faith.

## VI

Gerardus Johannes Vossius writes in book II, chapter 35, p. 319, of the final edition of his *On Latin Historians*, that the library of the University of Cambridge in England possesses, in manuscript, Dionysius’s works *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, *On the Divine Names*, and *Mystical Theology*, in codex III, together with Anastasius’s preface to King Charles the Bald.

This he reports on another’s authority, namely from Thomas James’s account in the *Oxford–Cambridge Catalogue*. Labbe himself replies to him in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, under “Anastasius the Librarian,” p. 67:

> “In a manuscript codex of our college at Bourges, belonging to the Society of Jesus, written in a most elegant hand approximately eight hundred years ago on parchment, four minor works of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite are read:
>
> “I. *On the Celestial Hierarchy*.
>
> “II. *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*.
>
> “III. *On the Divine Names*.
>
> “IV. *On Mystical Theology*.
>
> “They are from the translation of John Erigena Scotus, whose preface, together with certain verses addressed to Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, is also present.
>
> “Before them, however, Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, prefixed a letter addressed to the same King Charles, dated 23 March, in the eighth indiction—that is, as I believe, in the year 875. In it, concerning the scholia that he translated into Latin and that are written in the manuscript in the margin, he says:
>
> “‘Rightly anxious, I began diligently to seek,’ and so forth.
>
> “If these should please anyone, it will not be laborious to make them available, for the benefit of the learned public.”

Two manuscript codices of this kind are also found in the Imperial Library of Vienna, among the Latin theological manuscripts numbered 20 and 496, as Lambecius notes in book VIII of his *Commentaries on that library*, pp. 183 and 186.

Another such codex is found among the manuscripts of the Bodleian Library, codex 3614; and in the Codices Hyperoi of the Bodleian, codex 148.

Finally, these same works of Dionysius the Areopagite, together with Anastasius the Librarian’s preface to the scholia translated by him into Latin, are also preserved in manuscript in the Paulina Library at Leipzig, as is shown by the *Catalogue of the Manuscripts of this Library*, printed at Leipzig in 1686 under the care and supervision of Joachim Feller, the librarian, p. 102, nos. 2 and 3.

## VII

An *Ecclesiastical History*, or *Tripartite Chronology*, in which he translated into Latin the *Chronicle* of Saint Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople, together with its arrangement and the greater part of the chronicle brought down from the beginning of the world to the reign of Leo the Armenian by George Syncellus, Theophanes the Confessor, and the very celebrated Abbot Agri.

He explains this himself at greater length in his preface to John, deacon of the city of Rome.

From these Greek excerpts many materials were incorporated into the history called the *Miscellany*: either by John the deacon himself, who had obtained them by his requests; or by Landulf Sagax; or by some other compiler of that work. That compiler must have been an entirely different person from Paul Warnefrid the Lombard, deacon of Aquileia and later monk of Cassino, to whom almost everyone has until now attributed this *Miscellany*.

## VIII

A collection of materials concerning the history of the heretical Monothelites, and the martyrdom of Pope Saint Martin, as well as of Saint Maximus the abbot and others, was published by Jacques Sirmond in octavo at Paris in 1620, by Sebastian Cramoisy, on the Jacobin Street, under the sign of the Storks.

It contains accounts of those who, under Constans, the emperor of the East, suffered bonds, prisons, and various afflictions. Two Anastasii are included among them: one, an envoy of the Holy Roman Church; the other, a disciple of Saint Maximus. Their letters are read in the same *Collection*, which Anastasius translated from Greek and arranged into one work for the benefit of the aforementioned John the deacon, when he was preparing an ecclesiastical history.

That the author of the *Collection* and of the *Ecclesiastical History* is the same person may be learned from the preface, in which he openly declares this and explains several of the minor works that he had rendered into Latin and inserted into the collection. If you lack them, they will at least henceforth be most familiar to you from the following list:

1. A letter of Anastasius the Librarian to John, deacon of the city of Rome.

2. An apology of Pope John IV for Pope Honorius I, addressed to Constantine, son of Heraclius.

3. An excerpt from a letter of Saint Maximus to the presbyter Marinus, in which, among other things, he makes an apology for Honorius.

4. An excerpt from another letter of Saint Maximus to the illustrious Peter, in which he mentions Pyrrhus, Sophronius of Jerusalem, and Pope Honorius.

5. An excerpt from another letter of Saint Maximus to Marinus, a Cypriot presbyter, concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit.

6. A synodal letter of Pope Theodore to Paul, patriarch of Constantinople.

7. A proposition of the same, sent to Constantinople.

8. A letter of the same to the bishops who consecrated Paul patriarch of Constantinople.

9. An account of what the Roman legates did at Constantinople, drawn from a letter of Saint Maximus to Abbot Thalassius.

10. A letter of Anastasius the Librarian to Martin, bishop of Narni.

11. A letter of Pope Martin to Theodore.

12. A second letter of the same to Theodore.

13. An account of what was done against Saint Martin at Constantinople, drawn from a letter of someone to the Westerners.

14. Two letters of Pope Martin written from exile.

15. An account of the proceedings brought against Saint Maximus and his companion before the authorities in the secretariat.

16. A letter of Saint Maximus to Anastasius the monk, his disciple.

17. A letter of Anastasius the monk to the monks of Cagliari.

18. An account of the doctrinal issues debated between Saint Maximus, Theodosius, bishop of Caesarea in Bithynia, and the leading men who were with him.

19. A letter of Anastasius, priest and envoy of Rome, to Theodosius of Gangra, together with the testimonies and syllogisms appended below.

20. A *Hypomnesticon* explaining the deeds of Saints Maximus, both Anastasii, and Pope Martin, as well as of Theodore, Euprepius, and others.

Bernard de Montfaucon, the learned Benedictine monk of the congregation of Saint Maur in France, says in his *Italian Journal*, published in Paris in quarto in 1702, chapter 21, p. 309, that these *Collections* of Anastasius the Librarian exist in Greek manuscript in Italy, in the library of Saint John of Carbonara belonging to the Augustinians.

## IX

He also translated from Greek into Latin the *Passion of the 1,480 Martyrs*. This translation is preserved in Rome in the library of Santa Croce in Jerusalem. John Mabillon supplied us with its prologue in his *Italian Itinerary*, part II, p. 80, where, in this preface, Anastasius also mentions that he had undertaken the following work:

> “After translating, at the request of the same person, the Passion of the outstanding teacher and martyr Peter, bishop of the city of Alexandria…”

That work still lies hidden somewhere in those innumerable legendary collections that lie covered with dust in libraries.

## X

He likewise rendered from Greek into Latin the Life of Saint Basil, archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia. John Mabillon published the complete preface to this work in the same *Italian Literary Itinerary*, part II, p. 82.

Baronius praises this work in his notes to the *Roman Martyrology*, under 1 January, and there indicates a preface by Ursus, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, to the Life of Saint Basil translated by him into Latin.

You also have it in Heribert Rosweyde’s *Lives of the Fathers*, book I, p. 116, and in the notes on p. 125, under the word “Ursus.”

In fact, that preface, together with the Life that follows, is not different from Anastasius’s version found in this *Italian Itinerary*, except for the heading, which in Rosweyde and others has been shortened and mutilated.

From the complete form of the text it is clear that Anastasius is the translator of the commonly received Life, which in printed editions is wrongly attributed to Ursus. Henceforth, therefore, the translation of this Life should be attributed to Anastasius the Librarian, who undertook it at the prompting of Ursus.

## XI

He likewise undertook a translation of the *Passion of Saints Cyrus and John*. Its prologue is reproduced in the same *Italian Itinerary*, p. 83, and it exists together with the text of the Passion in a very old codex of the library of Saint Peter at Chartres, belonging to the order of Saint Benedict.

The name of Anastasius, which had been erased from a defective and displaced manuscript exemplar, was restored conjecturally by John Mabillon at the place cited, because the date and style agree with Anastasius.

The manner of expression is certainly the same, as is the method of the preface, as in Anastasius’s preface to the *Passion of the 1,480 Martyrs*. The same is true of the preface to the *Life of Saint John the Almsgiver* in Heribert Rosweyde’s *Lives of the Fathers*, p. 137 of the Lyons edition of 1617.

## XII

Finally, he published a translation from Greek into Latin of the Life of Saint Donatus, bishop at Eurias in Syria. The same author mentioned above supplies its prologue in the same *Italian Itinerary*, p. 85, without doubting that this translation is Anastasius’s, although his name is absent from the Cassinese codex from which he copied the preface.

He did not think it worthwhile to publish the entire little book, since the very text found in the Cassinese codex had already been published by Mombritius, although the April volume of the Bollandists, under 30 April, gives no Acts of Donatus other than those drawn from the Greek *Menaea*.

## XIII

A letter of Anastasius, priest, abbot, and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, to Ado, archbishop of Vienne, is found in the Councils of the final Labbean Paris edition of 1672, volume VIII, column 568. It concerns the death of Pope Nicholas I and the election of Adrian II and appears among the letters of Pope Nicholas I, in the year 867, fifteenth indiction.

You may also see his letter to Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, dated 5 January 876, ninth indiction, in volume III of the Councils of Gaul, p. 423. Jacobus Sirmond published it from the Reims Codex; it had previously been unknown to Binius and the other collectors.

Photius, patriarch of Constantinople, also wrote a brief letter to Anastasius the Librarian, in section 170, p. 244. From it it is easy to conclude that Anastasius then possessed great authority at Rome.

## XIV

There is also a sermon of Saint Theodore the Studite, abbot of Constantinople, on Saint Bartholomew the Apostle. Theodore flourished among the Greeks around the year 820, eminent in learning and piety. Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, translated the sermon from Greek into Latin; Lucas d’Achery arranged for it to be published from a manuscript codex.

It appears in volume III of the *Spicilegium*, p. 13, published by Lucas d’Achery, Benedictine monk of the congregation of Saint Maur in France.

## XV

After Adrian II, Roman pontiff, had died—Anastasius having served as his librarian or referendary, or, as we now say, secretary and secretary of correspondence—he held the same office under Adrian’s successor John VIII, as the aforementioned Pope John VIII’s librarian or secretary, attached to his person and correspondence.

Under John’s name he published six letters, Greek and Latin together, concerning the affairs of the Eastern Church. They are found in volume VIII of the Councils in Labbe’s edition, in the appendix to the Eighth Council of Constantinople, from a Vatican manuscript codex, columns 1451, 1461, 1473, 1477, 1479, and 1485.

Had he lived longer, he would also have left to posterity other letters of that pontiff in both Greek and Latin.

After Anastasius died during the pontificate of John VIII, Zacharias was appointed his successor in the office of librarian or referendary, in a year unknown to me.

[Col. 0013]

# Second Bibliographical Notice

*(From Fabricius, Library of Medieval and Late Latin Literature, vol. I.)*

[Col. 0013D] Anastasius, Roman librarian, abbot and priest—indeed, cardinal-priest—was prominent from the year 848 during the times of Nicholas I, who held the pontificate from 858; Adrian II, who held it from 867; and John VIII, who held it from 872 to 882, and perhaps also during the period of those who followed.

He translated many works from Greek into Latin, “usually in a rather rough and semi-barbarous style, although,” as Combefis rightly judges in the *Preaching Library*, “not useless even in itself; for many Greek authors of the middle period of that age would be exceedingly obscure to us unless he, more skilled in knowledge than in language, had shed light upon them, or had at least rendered them for us in this way.”

From Anastasius’s translation we possess:

1. The *Chronology* of Nicephorus of Constantinople, who died in 828, followed by a stichometry of the sacred books.

2. An *Ecclesiastical History*, published among the Byzantine historians, abridged around the year 872 from the works of the same Nicephorus, George Syncellus, and Theophanes the Confessor.

3. The Acts of the Sixth Synod, held at Constantinople in the Trullo in 680.

4. The Acts of the Seventh Synod, or Second Council of Nicaea, in 787.

5. The Acts of the Eighth Council of Constantinople in 869, which he himself attended.

6. A collection concerning the controversy and history of the Monothelites, published by Sirmond and by Combefis, and also found in volume XII of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*.

I discussed each of these in volume IX of the *Greek Library*, pp. 337 and following, and the *Chronology* also in volume VI, p. 153.

The *Passion of the 10,000 Martyrs* under Adrian and Antoninus Pius is found in the *Acts of the Saints*, 22 June, volume IV, p. 182.

The *Life of John the Almsgiver*, patriarch of Alexandria, is found in Rosweyde, book I of the *Lives of the Fathers*, and in the same *Acts of the Saints*, 23 January.

The *Passion of Saint Demetrius the Martyr* is found in John Mabillon, volume I of the *Analecta*, p. 65, and in the new edition, p. 172.

The encomium of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, from the Greek of Theodore the Studite, is found in d’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, volume III, and in the new edition, volume II, p. 123, as well as in Combefis’s *Preaching Library*, volume VII.

The letter to Charles the Bald prefixed to the scholia of Saint Maximus and John of Scythopolis on Dionysius the Areopagite, translated by Anastasius, was published by Ussher in his *Irish Letters*, p. 45.

A letter to the same Charles, prefixed to the Life of Dionysius written by Methodius, is found in Surius under 8 October, and in Peter Francis Chifletius’s work *On One Dionysius*, among others.

For the Life translated by Anastasius, see Mabillon, volume I of the *Analecta*, pp. 59 and following, and the new edition, p. 212, where he supplies Hincmar’s letter concerning it to the emperor Charles.

The same Mabillon, in volume I of the *Museum Italicum*, pp. 80 and following, published Anastasius’s prologues to the following works translated by him: the *Passion of the 1,480 Martyrs in Palestine under Khosrow*—concerning whom see the *Acts of the Saints*, 22 June, volume IV, p. 188—the *Miracles of Saint Basil of Caesarea*, the *Passion of Saints Cyrus and John*, and the *Life of Saint Donatus, bishop at Eurias in Syria*.

The translation of the *History of Josaphat and Barlaam* among the works of John of Damascus is also attributed to him, as are the letter of Saint Cyril of Alexandria to Gennadius, the Life of Peter of Alexandria, the Passion of Saint Agathius and his companions, and the account of the miracle at Berytus concerning the image of Christ pierced by the Jews in the year 765.

Moreover, Anastasius is said to have written the *Lives of the Pontiffs*,

[Note: [Col. 0015D] Not all of them by any means, but perhaps those of certain pontiffs from Gregory IV to Nicholas I. Learned men reasonably point out that he could have been the author of the lives of those pontiffs whom he lived near. See, above all, Frederick Spanheim’s works, vol. II, pp. 649 and following, and the material collected by Oudinus, vol. II, pp. 258 and following.]

from Peter to Nicholas I. John Busaeus first published them, together with William the Librarian’s Life of Adrian II and Stephen VI, under Anastasius’s name, from the library of Marcus Welser, at Mainz in 1602, quarto.

Afterward Charles-Annibal Fabrot published them together with Anastasius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, Paris, 1649, folio, among the Byzantine historians, which are known to have been most recently reprinted at Venice.

The notes and observations of Antonio Dadini Alteserra were printed separately at Paris in 1680, quarto.

After Busaeus and Fabrot, the learned men Francis Blanchinus and John Vignolius began, under the auspices of Pope Clement XI, to prepare a splendid edition of this *Book of the Pontiffs*, illustrated with notes and observations, at Rome in 1718, 1724, and 1728, folio.

[Note: *Giornale de’ Letterati d’Italia*, vol. XXXI, p. 441 and following; *Acta Eruditorum*, 1719, p. 425; 1725, p. 153; 1631, p. 349.]

The work is not completed even in the third volume, which already ends with Gregory the Great.

After Fabricius completed this Latin *Library*, a fourth volume of the Roman edition appeared. Fabricius indicated its first three volumes.

Several prolegomena precede it, containing seven epistolary dissertations by Joseph Blanchinus of Verona, priest of the Congregation of the Oratory of the City, followed by a minor work on the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs, from the blessed Apostle Peter to Saint Paul, drawn from a Veronese codex.

Another minor work contains an old sacramentary codex of the Roman Church, composed by Pope Saint Leo. We shall discuss it when we come to Saint Leo.

The third minor work presents the decree of Gelasius I, taken from a Florentine codex and compared with two others.

The fourth contains a fragment of the *Pontifical Catalogue* ending with Vigilius, reprinted more fully than it was read in volume III of the same Anastasius edition.

The fifth presents a fragment of an invective against Rome on behalf of Formosus.

The sixth contains an appendix, or variants, to Bede’s *Martyrology*, printed at the beginning of volume II of Bollandus’s *Acts of the Saints* and compared with a Veronese codex dating approximately from the tenth century.

The seventh presents a Psalter with Canticles according to the Old Vulgate and the Itala version, together with variants and a collation made with other very ancient Psalters.

All this is followed by the imperial-papal chronology of Cajetanus Cenni, priest of Pistoia, in volume IV, from the year of Christ 590 to 768.

The entire work was carefully reviewed and published in a new edition by Vignolius at Rome in 1724, in a large quarto format.

[Note: *Acts of the Learned*, 1727, p. 52; *Journal des Savants*, June 1726, p. 248; *Mémoires de Trévoux*, 1727, p. 89.]

At nearly the same time, it was included through the work of the distinguished Muratori in volume III of the *Italian Historical Works*, Milan, 1723, folio, with the continuation of other ancient authors concerning the Lives of the Pontiffs from Leo IX to John XXII.

[Note: See my survey of the *Literary Treasury of Italy*, p. 27 and following, and the *Acts of the Learned*, 1724, p. 377 and following, which also discusses the manuscript notes on Anastasius by Peter Boerius, bishop of Orvieto, around the year 1380.]

A brief Cassinese chronicle ending in the year of Christ 857, attributed to Anastasius, was published by the aforementioned Muratori in volume II of that great collection, which will always bring honor to the Italians, volume II, p. 249. Yet Muratori scarcely, if at all, persuades himself that Anastasius was its author.

A letter to Ado, archbishop of Vienne, another concerning the death of Pope Nicholas I and the election of Pope Adrian II, and a third to Hincmar, are found in volumes XXXIII of the Royal Councils, VIII of Labbe, V of Hardouin, and X of Coleti of the Venetian edition.

Binius, volume II of the 1618 edition of the Councils, publishes letters XIV, XV, XVI, XVII, and XVIII of Pope Martin I translated by Anastasius, and mentions his preface to Martin, bishop of Narni. Others derive the same information from him.

[Col. 0017]

# Eulogies in Praise of Anastasius

[Col. 0017A] William, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, in the Life of Adrian II.

[Note: It is found in this work.]

The legates of the Holy Roman Church, fearing that Greek frivolity might have inserted something false into the text of the synod—namely, the Eighth General Council held at Constantinople—entrusted it to Anastasius, librarian of the apostolic see, for careful investigation before they signed it.

At that time Anastasius had come to Constantinople after them, together with Suppo, chief minister, on the business of Louis, our most serene Augustus, through what was believed to be a divine dispensation.

Because he was most eloquent in both languages, he examined the text with the greatest care. They found that everything which the most holy lord Pope Adrian had added in his letter to Bishop Arsenius concerning the praise of our most serene Caesar had been disclosed.

## John Trithemius, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*

Anastasius, most discerning guardian and restorer of the apostolic library, learned in the divine Scriptures and nobly educated in secular literature, highly skilled in Greek and Latin expression, is said to have composed several minor works, but none of them has reached our hands.

He translated many volumes of the Greeks into Latin. At the command of Pope Nicholas I, he translated the Life of John the Almsgiver; one of the Hierarchies of Saint Dionysius; the Seventh Universal Synod; the Lives of many holy Fathers; and many other works.

He also wrote an *Ecclesiastical History* down to his own times, at the request of Charles II, who was especially fond of him.

He flourished under the emperor Louis II, in the year of the Lord 860.

[Col. 0018A] Blessed Platina, *Lives of the Pontiffs*, under **John IX**.

Emperor Charles, receiving the king of the Normans into favor, raised him from the baptismal font, as Anastasius records. At that time Anastasius was held in esteem as librarian of the Roman Church, a man thoroughly learned in both languages, who elegantly and learnedly translated from Greek into Latin, for Charles’s sake, both the Seventh Ecumenical Synod and the *Hierarchy of Dionysius the Areopagite*, as well as the Lives of many others.

Onuphrius Panvinius, annotating Platina, under Nicholas I

The monk Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, wrote the Lives of the Roman pontiffs down to Nicholas I, which are still in my possession; under Nicholas and his successors, Adrian II and John VIII, he flourished in the City. [Col. 0018B] A certain William, another librarian, arranged what follows; these works survive in the book circulated under the name of Damasus.

Sigebert of Gembloux, *On the Illustrious Writers of the Church*, chapter 104

At the command of Pope Nicholas, Anastasius translated into Latin the Life of John the Almsgiver, written in Greek by Leontius, bishop.

Caesar Baronius, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, volume IX

Although Anastasius the librarian narrated the history of events in a rough style, he did so with the utmost fidelity. Indeed, in the account of the events of his own time, we have no more faithful or better writer, one with whom truth prevailed more through simplicity than falsehoods through disguise.

# LIVES OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS, FROM THE BLESSED APOSTLE PETER TO NICHOLAS I, PRODUCED THROUGH THE CARE OF ANASTASIUS, LIBRARIAN OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH, WITH THE LIVES OF ADRIAN II AND STEPHEN VI ADDED, BY WILLIAM THE LIBRARIAN

First published at Mainz, printed by Albinus, in the year 1602, from the library of Marcus Welser, duumvir of the Commonwealth of Augsburg; afterward at Paris by Charles Hannibal Fabrotus, Doctor of Civil Law, in the Royal Press, 1647.

With various readings drawn from the manuscript codices of the Vatican Library, from the volumes of the Councils of Crabbe and Binius, from the *Ecclesiastical Annals* of Cardinal Baronius, and from other manuscript codices of Germany and France, especially the Freherian, Royal, Mazarin, and Thuanean codices.

NOW APPEARING FOR THE THIRD TIME

With an appendix of variant readings previously described from the most ancient exemplars and from the manuscript catalogues of the Vatican, Florence, Monte Cassino, the Royal Library, the Farnese Library, the Imperial Library of Vienna, the Library of Queen Christina of Sweden, and the Colbert Library, by Lucas Holstenius and Emmanuel a Schelstrate, prefects of the Vatican Library.

Also added are numerous materials collected from the old manuscript codex of Cava by Francesco Penia, auditor of the Roman Rota, previously unpublished.

The division into sections established by Benedict Millini, librarian of Queen Christina of Sweden, has been preserved everywhere; all the readings listed above are assigned individually beneath them.

With a preface and a fuller index, prepared through the work and study of Francesco Bianchini of Verona, subdeacon in the Apostolic Chapel and chamberlain of the sacred bedchamber of that same most holy lord of ours.

[Col. 0019]

# DEDICATORY LETTER

To our most holy lord Clement XI, supreme pontiff, from Giovanni Maria Salvioni, Vatican printer.

Since the useful and necessary disciplines in a well-ordered commonwealth acknowledge you, Most Blessed Father, as one given for the support and advancement of the liberal arts, printing—by no means the least of them—likewise perceives itself restored by your favor and generosity; indeed, it also glories in your judgment, because you earnestly foster it as the servant, so to speak, of all the arts, and especially of those which, in carrying out the duties of religion, refer their benefits to eternity.

Thus I discover that the modest labors—small, indeed, but not to be regretted—that I have hitherto devoted under your auspices to its cultivation have returned to me, received so kindly by your clemency and so generously adorned by your munificence, that, in the residence of the Roman University called the Sapienza, where a very spacious workshop has been furnished, I have been appointed printer in that Archigymnasium and, shortly afterward, by your grant, Vatican printer.

This distinction of name makes me anxious, since I cannot adequately repay the favor of a prince who has been so generous toward me; I must at least strive, according to my ability, to answer the expectations of the most holy Father. I have therefore thought it my duty humbly to explain to you, Most Blessed Father—not only as my most indulgent master, but also as my most gracious judge and patron—for what reason and by what plan I intend to make this edition of the work of Anastasius; and, under your auspices, to disclose it to others, so that all who hereafter use our little work may know especially by what undertakings I wish the presses of our workshop to be occupied, now that I have been endowed by the supreme priest with the office of Vatican printer.

[Note: [Col. 0021] From R. P. Bonanni, at the conclusion of the reverse of the coin of Sixtus V.]

When Pope Sixtus V, of immortal memory, established the Vatican Press, he declared that it had been founded for this purpose: namely, to restore the works of the saints and to propagate the Catholic religion throughout the world. How zealously all who administered the care of its book workshop prepared themselves to fulfill the duty of the office entrusted to them is sufficiently demonstrated by the outstanding works printed at the Vatican Press during those years: the text of both Testaments corrected with the greatest possible accuracy; the Acts of the General Councils transcribed from the most trustworthy manuscripts; the writings of the holy Fathers carefully emended in accordance with ancient exemplars; the *Annals of the Church*, begun at that time by Baronius; and works of this kind, which will never cease to be produced.

Indeed, those celebrated Vatican editors joined Aldine elegance with the usefulness and majesty of subject matter of the highest importance. After such an abundant harvest has been gathered from every direction and brought so successfully into the barn of the Church, what gleaning worthy of the name with which Your Holiness has chosen to honor my efforts will remain for me to collect, when you have revived the Vatican Press after one or two centuries?

Nevertheless, the harvest of sacred things that the great master of the household keeps ready for the laborer’s industry does not at all permit us to lose heart—just as he keeps ready the fruits of the vineyard and the proceeds of wages for vine-dressers called at the ninth and eleventh hours. For what province, Most Blessed Father, will not prove fruitful for you, if even from the remotest Syria and from the deserts and solitudes of Nitria and the Thebaid you gather fruits that had been denied or concealed for many centuries before us?

The Acts of the Martyrs, collected by Eusebius and so carried away and scattered by a certain tempest of the barbarous age that, not quite three hundred years later, they were sought in vain in the archives of the Church, you have recently brought from the East, together with two hundred distinguished codices acquired by your command and generosity to equip the Vatican Library with new resources.

What breadth of territory for cultivation by our labors is opened before our eyes by this one prospect! Since, under an excellent prince devoted with the utmost zeal to sacred letters, there will certainly be no lack of material for editions, it will be worthwhile, as I believe, to offer a specimen of the diligence that your Vatican Press can promise to students of the more serious disciplines, both in the selection of works to be published and in the correction and elegance of the edition.

Although I have dared to promise these three things, I have also tried to fulfill them in printing these *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, which are customarily attributed to Anastasius. The usefulness of the selection should certainly be considered its first merit, since it embraces the principal deeds of your predecessors in the chair of Peter and their uninterrupted succession; all these matters are recorded in authentic notices drawn from the diptychs and festal calendars of the nascent Church.

The illustrious writer himself acknowledges that these were the first beginnings of Baronius’s greatest work, the *Annals*, [Note: [Col. 0021] Baronius, volume I of the *Annals*, in the dedicatory epistle to Sixtus V] in his dedicatory letter to Pope Sixtus: the Lives of the saints and the examples of the Fathers. From these, gathering notes for the use of familiar sermons, which he customarily delivered every day according to the practice of his Oratory, he saw an enormous tree grow from a small seed.

But although the Lives of the greatest pontiffs are expressed with that brevity in which truth chiefly rejoices, how much weight and importance they possess in their subject matter will, I hope, be sufficiently indicated in the preface to the Reader.

The careful correction—which was the second thing I promised and had to fulfill—will reveal itself at first sight on every page. The Reader will see that the emendation of this work has been prepared through the combined studies of almost all the cultivated nations of Europe. The variant readings of the more excellent codices, supplied by the libraries most celebrated above all others—the Vatican, the Imperial Library of Vienna, the Royal Library of Louis the Great, the Royal Library of Christina, the Florentine, Farnese, Barberini, Ottoboni, Cava, and Colbert libraries—will appear alongside the individual readings.

From Upper Germany, Welser and Freher, as well as Binius and Surius; from Lower Germany, Lucas Holstenius and Emmanuel a Schelstrate; from France, Labbe and Fabrotus; from Spain, Penia; from Italy, Baronius—who alone is equal to all the others—have contributed their respective portions.

I call upon this company of first-rank writers as guarantors of the selection of the work I have undertaken and of the promised correction. This also pertains to the dignity of the Church, the mother of all, which will gladly approve the devoted piety toward herself happily employed in faithfully recording the deeds of the greatest pontiffs by the sons of so many nations.

The third thing I promised, prompted by the auspice of your command and benevolence, Most Blessed Father, is the elegance of the edition; experience has taught that this contributes greatly to the permanence of a work. I have pursued it at no small expense, with the advice of distinguished men and by comparing editions that, by the consensus of experts, are regarded as especially distinguished.

I shall consider myself fortunate if I obtain what I desire: that Your Holiness may be convinced that the faithfulness, obedience, and diligence of your printer [Col. 0023] will always be so ready that, as he often falls at the feet of the Apostolic See and, drawing strength from God through the sign of our salvation extended by the pontifical hand—for all our sufficiency comes from him—he may seem, from this specimen of whatever quality, offered to you with the greatest reverence, never to cease advancing toward the goal appointed for the Vatican printer.

[Col. 0023]

# POPE CLEMENT XI, FOR A PERPETUAL RECORD

Since, as has become abundantly clear to us, our beloved son Giovanni Maria Salvioni, as soon as he magnificently opened his own printing house in the buildings of the university called the Sapienza of our beloved City—buildings assigned to him for that purpose by our command and enlarged at our expense—and since, with still greater zeal and alacrity after we appointed him, by a special document signed by our own hand on 28 August of the past year, to preside over the Vatican Press transferred by us to the aforesaid buildings, and appointed him Vatican printer with the customary honors, privileges, prerogatives, and faculties, together with a suitable stipend, has devoted himself unceasingly to the care, sparing no expense, that books printed in the finest characters and examined and corrected with the greatest diligence and fidelity should be issued to the public from that same press;

and since he has certainly not been disappointed in this praiseworthy purpose, for many volumes that he has hitherto published—especially works of sacred and ecclesiastical writers—have appeared so carefully prepared, adorned, and corrected that they have been received with common applause by learned men and by all who hold the liberal arts in esteem;

and since, most recently, as the same Giovanni Maria has lately explained to us, he has resolved to commit to his presses, for the public benefit of all, and especially of students of ecclesiastical history, the celebrated book entitled *Anastasius the Librarian, On the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs, from the Blessed Apostle Peter to Nicholas I, with the Lives of Adrian II and Stephen VI, by William the Librarian*;

but since he fears that, once it has been published, others who seek profit from another’s labor may arrange for a book of this kind to be printed again, to the prejudice of the same Giovanni Maria;

we, wishing to protect the indemnity of the same Giovanni Maria, so that he may suffer no loss from such a printing, and wishing to favor him with special privileges and graces, and absolving him, solely for the purposes to which these present letters relate, from any excommunications, suspensions, interdicts, or other ecclesiastical sentences, censures, and penalties imposed by law or by an ecclesiastical authority, on whatever occasion or for whatever cause, if in any way he is bound by any of them, and declaring him absolved;

moved by the petitions humbly presented to us on his behalf, grant and concede by apostolic authority, through the tenor of these presents, to the same Giovanni Maria, that for the next twenty years, reckoned from the first printing of the aforesaid book, provided nevertheless that the book has been approved by our beloved son, the Master of the Sacred Apostolic Palace, no one either in the aforesaid City or in the rest of the ecclesiastical State directly or indirectly subject to us may print the aforesaid book without the special permission of the aforesaid Giovanni Maria or of those who derive their right from him, nor sell, keep for sale, or offer for sale a copy printed by another person or persons.

Accordingly, we prohibit the faithful of either sex, especially printers of books and booksellers, under penalty of five hundred gold ducats of the Camera, together with forfeiture of the books and all the type—one part to be irrevocably assigned to our Apostolic Camera, another to the aforesaid Giovanni Maria, and the remaining third part to the accuser and the judge carrying out the sentence, penalties incurred by that very fact and without any declaration—from daring or presuming, during the aforesaid twenty years, to print the said book or any part of it, either in the City or in the rest of the aforesaid ecclesiastical State, without such permission, or in any way to sell or keep for sale a copy printed by others.

We therefore command our beloved sons, the legates of the Apostolic See, or their vice-legates, and the presidents, governors, magistrates, and other ministers of justice of the provinces, cities, lands, and places of our aforesaid ecclesiastical State, that, whenever the aforesaid Giovanni Maria shall request it, they assist the aforesaid Giovanni Maria or those deriving their right from him in these matters with the effective protection of justice and irrevocably enforce the aforesaid penalties against all disobedient persons.

Notwithstanding apostolic constitutions and ordinances, and any statutes and customs, even those strengthened by oath, apostolic confirmation, or any other form of ratification; and notwithstanding privileges, indults, and apostolic letters granted, confirmed, or renewed in any way contrary to the foregoing; and all other contrary provisions whatsoever.

We also will that transcriptions of these presents, already printed in the book itself, signed by the hand of any public notary and authenticated by the seal of a person holding ecclesiastical dignity, be everywhere given precisely the same faith as would be given to these original letters themselves if they were produced or displayed.

Given at Rome, at Saint Mary Major, under the Fisherman’s Ring, on the first day of June 1718, in the eighteenth year of our pontificate.

F. Cardinal OLIVERIUS

# PREFACE TO THE LIVES OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS, BY FRANCESCO BIANCHINI OF VERONA, CANON OF THE LIBERIAN BASILICA AND SUBDEACON OF THE PONTIFICAL CHAPEL

## OUTLINE OF THE PREFACE

[Col. 0027]

1. The usefulness of investigating the authors of the Lives of the Roman pontiffs contained in this book called the *Pontifical Book*, and the discussions of those authors’ date, style, and excellence by the learned prelates Holstenius, Ciampini, and Schelstrate in works published at Rome.

2. Holstenius’s labors greatly enhance the dignity of the work in Schelstrate’s distinguished Dissertation, which lists the principal exemplars of the Italian libraries consulted by both prelates.

3. A complete edition of that Dissertation is reserved for the second volume, which will contain the notes of various scholars on this *Pontifical Book*.

4. In the meantime, the more important reflections of both prelates—Holstenius and Schelstrate—are selected from it, insofar as they concern the criticism of this book, and are enlarged with new observations in this preface. Here the proposed subjects are the book’s name, its date, its authors, its origin and growth, and also the reliability of its history and its documents.

5. The older names of this book are: *Pontifical Book*, or *Book of Pontifical Deeds*, or *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*. Although Velser most recently called it *The Book of Anastasius the Librarian on the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, nevertheless the greater part of it was composed a full century before Anastasius. The exemplars of the book older than Anastasius are enumerated.

6. Holstenius proves that the first part of the book, containing the Lives of the supreme pontiffs from Saint Peter to Gregory III, [Col. 0028] was published in Gregory’s time, around the year of Christ 730, on the basis of the incomplete Life of Gregory preserved in ancient manuscript codices, where they end.

7. Schelstrate confirms Holstenius’s opinion from the testimony of the book in the Life of Leo II and in the Life of Conon. These indicate that their author wrote before the year 750.

8. Two appendices, added by different writers, were attached to this first collection of Lives extending to Gregory III. The first contains the Lives of Zachary and Stephen III; the later one contains the remaining Lives down to Hadrian II. Among these, Anastasius the Librarian wrote only that of Pope Nicholas I, while William, Anastasius’s successor, wrote the final two.

9. Although this *Pontifical Book* was compiled by authors of the eighth and ninth centuries, in a large part it was drawn from two catalogues of the Roman pontiffs. The first of these was composed in the fourth century under Pope Liberius, and the second under Pope Felix IV, in the age of Justinian. But some impostor of a later age appended two fictitious letters to the genuine first catalogue: a letter of Jerome to Damasus and one of Damasus to Jerome. These led careless writers into error when they called this book by the name of Damasus.

10. After these points have been summarized from Schelstrate’s Dissertation and from half of Holstenius’s work, this preface proposes to discuss the origin, authority, and reliability of the history expressed in these Lives, together with its documents or proofs.

11. Its original source is owed to the two catalogues mentioned: the first under Liberius and the other under Felix IV. The author of the second catalogue, in the sixth century, transcribed the words of the first, which had already been composed in the fourth century; and from other documents he added several details not expressed in the catalogue of the Liberian age, which was shorter. The writer of the first part of the *Pontifical Book*, in the eighth century, reproduced in the Lives of the pontiffs the words of the second catalogue and likewise added many details learned from elsewhere.

12. The additions made by the *Pontifical Book* beyond the second catalogue are for the most part explanations, as it were fuller notes, more clearly setting out what had been indicated more briefly and obscurely in the second catalogue.

13. On the authority of the matters stated in both catalogues. The first subject is the date, exemplars, and edition of both catalogues.

14. The earlier catalogue, composed under Liberius around the year 354, was published by Bucherius together with other remains of works from that fourth century, which are held in very high esteem by the learned. It had been transcribed from ancient parchment manuscripts once examined by Cuspinianus. From this source, and after being transcribed and again collated with other exemplars, it was published in a more corrected form by Schelstrate.

15. The other catalogue, composed under Felix IV in the age of Justinian, around the year of Christ 530, was published by Schelstrate from a manuscript written in the age of Charlemagne, formerly kept in the Royal Library of Queen Christina of Sweden and now preserved in the Vatican Library. It was published with the assistance of Stephen Baluzius, who supplied the variant readings of a Colbert manuscript from the same age of Charlemagne.

16. On the authority of the matters expressed in the catalogues. These are, in the earlier catalogue, the pontiff’s name, the years of his rule, and the pairs of consuls under whom he entered office and under whom he ended it. In the second catalogue there are added the name of his father, the district of the City if he is a Roman, or his homeland if he is a foreigner, and the number of ordinations, as well as certain decrees or constitutions of the pontiff in question.

17. The practice of giving the pontiff’s name together with his father’s name is shown to have belonged to the customs of the periods in which the catalogues were written. The district name, observed for pontiffs who were Roman by nation, seems to derive from the institution of Clement I and indicates that the catalogue was compiled from the Acts of the Martyrs, written by seven notaries appointed in the City by that same Saint Clement.

Those Acts, which had been destroyed during the persecutions of Decius and Diocletian, were sufficiently supplemented by the surviving history of Hegesippus, extant in the age of Eusebius, as well as by the testimony of Irenaeus and the writings of others. From these sources Eusebius was able to set forth the succession of the Roman pontiffs; and therefore the author of the catalogue, writing in the century of Eusebius, could likewise exhibit that succession.

18. The chronology of the Roman pontiffs, recorded by the consulships in both catalogues, could also have been obtained in the fourth and sixth centuries partly from the inscriptions of martyrs buried in the suburban cemeteries, and partly from the acts of those same pontiffs and martyrs, which necessarily mentioned the emperors and magistrates under whom they suffered martyrdom.

19. The genuine Acts of the passion of Saint Ignatius prove that, in the age of Saint Clement, it was customary for such Acts to be dated by the emperor and the consuls. Other Roman Acts, when they name the urban prefect, and provincial Acts, when they mention the governor or prefect of a province, contain sufficiently definite chronological markers for composing, in the fourth and sixth centuries, the first and final catalogues.

20. The ordinations mentioned in the second catalogue are shown to have been necessarily recorded in the Roman Church from the original institution of the priestly hierarchy, following the preserved example of the ancient priesthood, which recorded the dates of ordinations in the sacred writings.

21. In the City, the priesthood—even the pagan priesthood among the Gentiles—was held in such esteem that they carefully recorded their cooptations and initiations in bronze and marble documents and in the records of the colleges, which reported through consuls and the years of the City the successions even of the lesser priests. In calendars publicly displayed in the age of Augustus and Claudius, they also noted the day on which the supreme pontificate had been assumed by those same emperors.

22. Among the Romans, the practice of engraving priestly acts on marble tablets flourished from the first century of Christ to the fourth, as is proved by the surviving testimony of the stones.

23. Therefore the Roman bishops, the successors of Peter in the supreme pontificate instituted by Christ, and the first faithful—who formed a worthy conception of so great a priesthood and of the degrees of its hierarchy—following the custom of the sacred writings and likewise the practice of their own times, also took care, in the earlier centuries of the Church, to preserve carefully tablets recording priestly ordinations.

Indeed, during the persecutions they left us decrees impressed upon marble—as we see on the marble seat of Saint Hippolytus—concerning Easter and fasting, which are to be referred to the Acts of the pontiffs.

24. When peace was restored to the Church under Constantine, many more documents were engraved on marble tablets by the successors of Peter in the Roman Apostolic See, as the genuine inscriptions of Pope Damasus and others that still survive prove.

25. From the two classes of inscriptions—those composed during the persecution and those composed in the peace of the Church—were compiled, in the fourth century of Christ for the use of the Roman Church, lists of the depositions of bishops and martyrs. Bucherius published some of them together with the earlier catalogue of the Roman pontiffs under Liberius.

26. The custom preserved in the Roman Church of recording the dates of pontiffs by consulships and of compiling from them diptychs, lists, and successions appears to have been transmitted to other nearby episcopal sees, which were subsequently founded in Italy by the authority of the supreme pontiff.

Examples are brought from the Church of Nola, whose bishops were recorded in this way on ancient stones; they belong to the period lying between the two catalogues. Hence the uninterrupted custom of this chronology was preserved with much greater care in the Roman Church, the mother of all, established through the blessed Peter.

27. The Christian supreme pontiffs of the fourth and fifth centuries, who generally celebrated sacred ordinations in the Vatican Basilica—as is clear from the sermons of Leo the Great—rightly took care to celebrate through so many publicly engraved monuments the dignity of the supreme priesthood received from Christ the Lord and communicated to blessed Peter and his successors.

They did so especially in this place on the Vatican Hill, which pagan Rome had polluted with the priestly records of its profane religions or superstitions.

28. The marble records of the college of the Arval Brothers, the cooptations of the pagan priesthood, and the initiations of the priests of Isis, Mithras, Serapis, the Great Mother, and the Sun are reviewed. These were discovered on the very base of the hill around the Vatican Basilica and show that such superstitions had been frequently practiced there by the pagans.

As Leo the Great says, Peter the Apostle was happily appointed to abolish them: under the emperors Claudius and Nero, he fixed in the City the seat of truth, in that City which was then the teacher of every error, and made it a disciple of the truth.

29. From an ancient altar inscribed in the year 160 of the Christian era, discovered at Lyon and explained by the Reverend Father Dominicus de Colonia, a theologian of the Society of Jesus, we learn that in the second century of Christ the pagans introduced the practice of transmitting from the Vatican Hill to the Roman colonies the superstitious rite of the Mother of the Gods, whom they called Idaean Mother.

The devil, as Tertullian says, was imitating us in the mysteries of idols, making a vain attempt to overthrow our sacred rites through sacrilegious imitation.

30. The futile attempts of the pagans, like the statue of Dagon before the Ark of the Covenant, fell to the ground. Our Roman prelates, raising the trophy of the cross upon the ruins of shattered idolatry and displaying the records of Christian priesthood as ever more illustrious and firm, likewise recorded them on marble tablets and publicly fixed them for the perpetual remembrance of the matter, especially in the Vatican Basilica, even in the age of Saint Gregory III, when this *Pontifical Book* was being published.

Thus the reliability and authority of the matters mentioned in both catalogues, from which the *Pontifical Book* was drawn, are sufficiently established.

31. We now pass from the documents of the catalogues to the documents of the rest of the history added to the catalogues in the same *Pontifical Book*. It is shown that, in the age of Saint Gregory III, many documents still survived concerning the events narrated in the *Pontifical Book*, not only in the archives but also in public inscriptions. These confirm this very history according to the three principal categories of events stated in the book.

They are:

1. The chronology and succession of the pontiffs.

2. Their sacred ordinations, which constitute the hierarchy of the Church, and their decrees or constitutions.

3. The foundations, restorations, gifts, and other deeds of the pontiffs concerning sacred buildings.

32. When the *Pontifical Book* was being composed under Gregory III, the first category, concerning pontifical chronology, possessed—besides the resources of the two catalogues—support from the diptychs of the Churches; from the Acts of the Councils; from the history and chronicles of Eusebius and of the other writers of the Latin and Greek Churches and of other Eastern writers; and from the genuine inscriptions of the cemeteries of the holy martyrs, especially those in Rome, which still survive in our own age, a thousand years after the publication of the *Pontifical Book*.

33. The second principal matter, concerning decrees and ordinations, could be gathered from the same sources, and also from the rites of the liturgy observed in the Roman Church, as well as from the letters of the Roman pontiffs.

34. Some fragments of these letters, reproduced in the *Ecclesiastical History* of Eusebius, contain indications of decrees of the bishops of the Apostolic See that preceded the same letters reported by Eusebius.

[Col. 0031] 35. The ordinations of bishops, presbyters, and deacons mentioned in the Catalogues, and from them transcribed by the author of the *Liber Pontificalis*, are wonderfully confirmed by authentic records of the consecration of churches and altars, which began to be committed to marble even in the earlier centuries of the Church. A consecration of a sacred building, entrusted to marble by Pope St. Damasus, is produced; as are other records of the foundations of churches, dated in the same century and carved in marble even in the western provinces.

36. The sacred fountains constructed or enlarged by Saints Damasus, Sixtus III, and Hilary, as well as other church structures, are known from the authentic inscriptions of those same pontiffs.

37. In the time of St. Gregory III, even the Acts of the Roman Council mentioned in this *Liber Pontificalis* were read, carved in marble and preserved in the crypts of the old Vatican basilica.

38. In the Basilica of St. Paul on the Ostian Way there may be read, carved in the time of that same St. Gregory III, his diploma, or *Breve* as it is called, concerning the daily number of Masses and offerings established there. Thus numerous authentic documents of the decrees of the bishops of the Apostolic See, from the beginning of the third century to the ninth, were not only read on marble tablets in the age of the writers of the *Liber Pontificalis*, but are still read by us today.

39. These same monuments, inscriptions carved in a barbarous style, reveal the age of the *Liber Pontificalis*: the work was first composed shortly after the beginning of the eighth century, when the barbarism introduced into Italy by the Lombards and spread widely during the two hundred years of their rule had so disfigured the cultivation of the Latin language that even the royal masters of diplomacy and notaries neglected all the rules of Latin speech.

40. Examples are produced of two diplomas of Desiderius, the last king of the Lombards, and of his son Adelchis, from the original documents preserved at Brescia in the archive of the monastery of St. Julia.

41. The same barbarism had infiltrated the coastal part of Gaul nearest Italy, then troubled by the Saracens, as the Massilian inscription, carved around the time of Gregory III, shows.

42. During the same period the notaries of the Lombard princes at Capua and Spoleto treated the Latin letters no more gently; their successors later imitated them down to the tenth century. Accordingly, it is proved everywhere, from the style characteristic of the age in public monuments, that the writers of the *Liber Pontificalis* dictated it in the eighth and ninth centuries.

43. The third principal category of matters mentioned in the Lives of the Pontiffs comprises the movable and immovable goods donated to the churches, which constitute no small part of the *Liber*. Numerous documents of these donations, likewise public documents, were available to the writers of the *Liber Pontificalis*: the church archives, which had to be supplied with registers and authentic documents of this kind of donation in accordance with the laws of the sacred canons and the decrees of the pontiffs.

44. Besides the parchment documents in the archives, the churches’ marbles were also inscribed, often with the names of estates and the records of donations.

45. The donation of St. Gregory the Great for furnishing the lights in the Vatican basilica can still be read, carved in marble in his own time; it is now visible affixed to the wall in the portico of that same basilica.

46. In the Basilica of St. Paul there may be read a diploma of the same pontiff, committed to a marble tablet for a similar purpose. It was given to Felix, subdeacon and rector of the province of the Patrimony on the Appian Way, in the first consulship of Phocas Augustus, in the seventh indiction, on 8 February—that is, in the year of Christ 604. From this marble it is evident that the pontifical order required the original directive to be deposited in the apostolic archives.

47. On another marble in the Liberian basilica, under Gregory IV, there is read not only a list of the estates donated to the church, but also the reason for the donation; and the practice, customary in that period, of carving public donation documents in marble after the authentic records had been entered into the archive is confirmed. Hence it may be inferred that in the age of the writers of the *Liber Pontificalis* documents of donations abounded both in the archives and on the walls of sacred buildings.

48. There may also be read, carved on ancient stones, formulas of prayers engraved by the supreme pontiffs, especially by St. Gregory III; these survive in the Vatican crypts.

49. Besides the patriarchal basilicas of the City, the presbyteral titular churches, deaconries, other sacred buildings, and monasteries preserve marble documents concerning estates belonging to those sacred places. We see an example in the title of Pammachius, that is, of Saints John and Paul; in the deaconry of St. Mary in Cosmedin, also called the Greek Schola; and in the nearby church, now destroyed, of St. Valentine. There is another example in the Greek inscription of the destroyed Monastery of St. Erasmus near the title of St. Stephen on Mount Caelius, and in the endowment of a tomb dated to the year of Christ 577, preserved in the sacristy of St. Angelo in the Borgo.

50. This common practice and urban custom, observed in Rome from the sixth to the tenth century in basilicas, titular churches, deaconries, even smaller churches, monasteries, and indeed in donations connected with tombs, was also extended to the episcopal sees nearest the City, as the inscriptions of the cathedral churches of Anagni and Tibur confirm.

51. An inscription carved in the time of St. Gregory III near Ravenna, in the celebrated church of St. Apollinaris in Classe, shows that this custom penetrated even into the churches and regions of Italy more remote from the City.

52. Most of these monuments, produced in Rome and outside Rome and belonging to the period of the writers of the *Liber Pontificalis*, abundantly demonstrate the special interest of that age in publicly displaying lists of the movable and immovable goods belonging to the churches. For this reason the authors of the Lives mentioned above devoted such great effort to recording them, following the custom and character of their contemporaries. Taken together, these monuments show that at that time an abundance of documents remained by which everything embraced in the text and history of the *Liber* could be corroborated.

53. These documents are illuminated by a coin of Crispus Caesar, published by Cardinal Baronius, now rediscovered among the treasures of the most illustrious Prince Borghese and prefixed to this preface. The coin is described.

54. The coin, already identified by Fulvio Orsini, prince of antiquarians, and acquired and vindicated by him, is cited by Cardinal Baronius under the year 324 as testimony of unquestionable antiquity and as evidence of the public observance of the Christian religion, adopted in the City by Constantine.

55. It also bears witness to the gifts offered by that same prince in the Lateran basilica of the Savior, since on the reverse there appears a seated statue either of Christ the Lord or of the Apostle Peter, of the kind that Constantine is said to have placed in the same basilica, made of silver for each of them, as mentioned in this *Liber Pontificalis*.

56. Since these princely gifts still survived in the age of the writers of the *Liber Pontificalis*, they show that numerous public documents concerning the matters recorded in it were available to everyone.

57. Thus far concerning the observations collected in this book that generally relate to the Lives of the Pontiffs. The second volume will present what must be said specifically about each individual Life. The method of the notes to be observed in the edition is now proposed.

58. Since in this volume the printer has gathered what concerns the authentic reading of the *Liber*, its use, and the benefits to be derived from it, he promises that in the second volume the more important Variorum Notes on the Lives of the Pontiffs will be collected. Some will be transcribed from the works printed by Altaserra, Binius, Ciacconius, and Labbe; others will be supplied by additional students of ecclesiastical history, whose names, prefixed individually in alphabetical order, will assign each person his own notes.

59. The chronological observations will be omitted from the second volume, since they are to be published in the third; the entire system of restored chronology, or the reconstruction of the sequence of time from the beginning of the Christian era, is also reserved for that volume.

60. Epilogue concerning the matters discussed in the preface about the work and the edition.

[Col. 0033]

## PREFACE

[Col. 0033A] 1. Perhaps some will judge it entirely unnecessary, in introducing the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs* and the name of Anastasius prefixed to them, to investigate more carefully in our own age the true author, or authors, of these Lives, together with their period, style, and excellence. In this age, the distinguished judgments of eminent critics have been committed to the press and are passing through everyone’s hands, not only among writers for libraries but also among those who have published dissertations or books specifically on this subject in the City. For who does not know that an examination of the *Liber Pontificalis*—the name given to this collection of Lives—was published in Roman type in 1688 by the learned prelate Giovanni Ciampini, and that four years after that edition, in the first volume of *Illustrated Ecclesiastical Antiquity*, another most celebrated prelate, Emmanuel [Col. 0033B] de Schelstrate, Prefect of the Vatican Library, published a third Dissertation, especially learned and weighty, bearing this title: *On the Ancient Catalogues of the Roman Pontiffs, from which the Liber Pontificalis was composed, and on the Author and Excellence of the Liber Pontificalis*?

2. I judge this Dissertation, certainly divided into nine chapters, to be so valuable that I consider it worth the effort to publish it in full when the notes on Anastasius appear. It contains mature judgments and observations both of Schelstrate himself and of his illustrious predecessor as Prefect of the Library, Lucas Holstenius. How much we owe to Holstenius’s labors, devoted assiduously over many years, for everything of importance that has reached us concerning this distinguished monument of ecclesiastical [Col. 0033C] history, will be sufficiently demonstrated by a testimony signed in Holstenius’s own hand in the Anastasius copy in which he recorded variant readings collated by him from the manuscripts of the most excellent codices throughout Italy, drawn from the Vatican, Royal Christina, Florentine St. Mark’s, Cassinese, and Farnesian libraries. It is worthwhile to transcribe in full the third section of chapter five of Schelstrate’s Dissertation, so that from Holstenius’s words reported there it may be understood what dignity belongs to a book that occupied so great a man for a considerable part of his life in restoring its true reading; and so that the antiquity of the manuscripts from which he gathered it may also be recognized—some surpassing the age of Anastasius and showing that the writers of the earlier Lives were older than Anastasius:

> “Since it clearly appears from the words of Hannibal Fabrotius mentioned above,” says Schelstrate in section 3, “that editions of the *Liber Pontificalis* were filled with errors down to his time, and that a better edition could be prepared from manuscript codices, my learned predecessor Lucas Holstenius had undertaken this task. He collated Anastasius’s *History of the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, in the Mainz edition, with the finest codices throughout Italy, in order to publish it more correctly and accurately.
>
> “I placed Holstenius’s autograph, purchased from the books of Moroni, in the Vatican Library. On its first leaf, Holstenius’s hand records the following:
>
> “‘Concerning the manuscript codices with which we collated Anastasius. The readings marked in ink in the margin from the beginning of the book through page 53 are variant readings from the Vatican manuscript codex, formerly belonging to the sacred Monastery of Cassino, or from Mombritius’s *Sanctuarium*, or also from the collection of Canons of Anselm of Lucca; these manuscripts are held in the library of the Most Eminent Cardinal Barberini. The readings marked in red from the beginning through the same page 53 are variant readings of the finest Florentine manuscript codex from the library of the convent of St. Mark.
>
> “‘Beginning on page 54 are the collations of the Farnesian manuscript, written in capital letters; I believe that nothing older of this kind exists, and the codex was certainly written before Anastasius was born, or at least during the period in which Anastasius lived. Since the collations of the Farnesian codex are written in red through page 63—that is, through Boniface IV—I marked the collations of the Florentine codex in ink from pages 54 through 63, to distinguish the readings of the different codices.
>
> “‘From page 63 through page 72, at the Life of St. Eugenius, the Farnesian collations are in ink and the Florentine in red. Again, from page 72 through page 107, where the Life of Pope Zacharias begins, the Farnesian collations are in red and the Florentine in ink. On page 107 the Life of Zacharias is missing from the Farnesian codex. The collations from the Florentine codex, marked in red, continue through page 115, where the Farnesian begins again. From there the Florentine readings are marked in ink through page 136, and from there in red through the middle of page 138. From that point they are again marked in ink through the beginning of page 143; from there through page 158 the readings of the Florentine codex are marked in red, ending there in the Life of Hadrian.
>
> “‘I subsequently possessed another very ancient Lombard manuscript codex from the same library of the convent of St. Mark, much older than the first. I marked its readings in ink.
