Where it agrees with the Farnesian and Florentine I underlined the readings of those codices with a black line, by which the agreement of this excellent codex is indicated. But where it has something distinctive, I marked it in ink and added the note “Fl. 2,” that is, “Florentine codex 2.” This codex ends with Leo II, on page 80; moreover, it is defective from page 47 through page 58. In nearly everything this Florentine codex 2 agrees with Vatican Codex 5269, which ends with Gregory II. The marks for this codex are “Vatic. Minor,” or “V. M.”’”

3. Since I hold such opinions concerning the plainly admirable labors of Holstenius and Schelstrate, and concerning the polished judgment they brought to bear upon the *Liber Pontificalis*, I might perhaps be accused of merely repeating what has already been done by attaching a new preface; I might seem not to enlighten the Reader with the reflections of distinguished men but to burden him with my own useless additions, if I postpone transferring Schelstrate’s entire Dissertation to the volume of notes and instead impose this one, which I hope will not be judged objectionable.

I would certainly have refrained from treating a subject attempted and advanced so successfully by such men, if Holstenius’s reflections had reached us intact and many of the matters he intended to add had not been taken away by his premature death, as Schelstrate observes; or if this second Dissertation of Schelstrate’s had dealt entirely with Anastasius. It was chiefly written *On the Ancient Catalogues of the Roman Pontiffs* and contains several chapters published to elucidate those Catalogues, which preceded the work of the Anastasian collection by several centuries.

4. Since, therefore, I saw that those portions of that Dissertation which more closely concern the *Liber Pontificalis* could be excerpted, and that many further observations could be added to the valuable surviving observations of Holstenius—observations that would more strongly confirm what he correctly established and would render the history, criticism, and documents of these Lives almost present and demonstrable—I hoped that I would not be laboring uselessly if I condensed the more important matters treated and proved at greater length by those same writers. By linking and joining them with more recent observations, I would strive to present a judgment, sound on every side, concerning the origin, development, use, documentation, and excellence of this *Liber Pontificalis*.

[Col. 0036B] 5. Everyone agrees that this work was called the *Liber Pontificalis* before Velser’s edition; it contains the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs from St. Peter to Nicholas I. Velser was the first to attribute it to Anastasius, monk and Librarian of the Holy Roman Church, with Bellarmine and Panvinio agreeing, though without offering any reason for the assertion. Baronius opposed Velser’s preconceived opinion and declared that Anastasius should be regarded as a compiler rather than the author of these Lives before Hadrian II (Baronius, under the year 867, no. 139). Holstenius adopts this opinion, and with him Schelstrate, who offers three reasons for holding it (Schelstrate, Dissertation 3, chapter 7, section 1).

6. The first reason is found in the testimony of writers who lived before Anastasius and who explicitly refer to the *Book of the Deeds of the Pontiffs*. Among them is Bede, who preceded the age of Anastasius by an entire century. Later writers, however, called this book the *Pontifical Book* and the *Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs*; they never called it the *Book of Anastasius*. The second reason is drawn from the age of the codices, as observed by Labbe and Lambecius, excellent judges of the writing of books. Labbe, in his book *On Writers*, under Damasus, asserts that Anastasius cannot be the author of the first part: “For,” he says, “I have seen a manuscript codex of the finest quality, written in the time of Charlemagne, in which those Lives were already attributed to Damasus before Anastasius had either been born or had at least emerged from the toys of early childhood.” Lambecius identifies another distinguished codex belonging to the time of Louis the Pious, [Col. 0036D] which concludes the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs with Stephen II, called Stephen III by others. His election falls in the year 752 and his death in 757. Schelstrate produces three other codices: Vatican 5269, ending with the Life of St. Gregory II, who died one hundred years before Anastasius; the Royal Christina codex and the Florentine St. Mark’s codex, both of which end with Hadrian I, before Anastasius had yet been born. “From these,” he says, “it is sufficiently and more than sufficiently clear that the *Liber Pontificalis* is older than Anastasius, and therefore that he cannot be its author.” Holstenius and Schelstrate gather a third reason from the difference of style observed in the Lives of the successors of St. Gregory III, namely Zacharias and those who followed him, since the preceding Lives, through Gregory III, exhibit the same style and the same author. They enumerate the differences among the individual sections in chapter 7, section 7, and chapter 8, sections 5 and following.

After carefully considering these matters, they define the age and author of the *Liber* as follows (Schelstrate, chapter 8, section 2):

> “It therefore appears that the *Liber Pontificalis* was written after the death of Pope Constantine, who died in 714. This is confirmed by the authority of Vatican manuscript codex 5269, which, although written approximately five hundred years ago, was copied from an older exemplar, since the Catalogue of Pontiffs prefixed to the *Liber Pontificalis* in the codex ends with Gregory II, the successor of Constantine.
>
> “The *Liber Pontificalis* itself, which follows the Catalogue in the codex, ends with these words: ‘Gregory, a Roman by nationality, son of Marcellus, held the see for sixteen years, eleven months, and eleven days. He lived in the times of the Augusti Anastasius, Theodosius, Leo, and Constantine.’ Here it merely reports the duration of his pontificate, without any deeds. From this it is inferred that the author began the Life of Gregory but did not complete it by the time the *Liber Pontificalis* appeared.
>
> “I would therefore judge that the *Liber Pontificalis* appeared after Constantine’s death. This agrees entirely with what we noted above concerning the Venerable Bede, who is the first of all to be found citing the *Liber Pontificalis*. Bede lived from the year 673 to the year 735; and since, after the pontificate of Gregory II—which began in 714 and ended in 731—the Venerable Bede survived, he could have seen and cited the *Liber Pontificalis*.
>
> “To disclose my opinion concerning the time when the *Liber Pontificalis* first came to light, I shall conclude briefly. I believe it was made public before the year 732 and that an appendix was later added to this collection by the same author, comprising the Lives of Gregory II and Gregory III. This is confirmed by what Lucas Holstenius observed. After carefully reading through all the Lives of the Pontiffs, he noted that the deeds of the pontiffs from the Apostle Peter through Zacharias, the successor of Gregory III, were written in exactly the same style and therefore by the same author.”

7. Schelstrate derives the same date from the words of the book itself in the Life of Leo II. Leo “received the Sixth Holy Synod, which, by the providence of God, was recently held in the Royal City.” “Since,” he says, “the author testifies that the Sixth Synod was recently held in the city of Constantinople, and since the Sixth Synod was held under Agatho, the predecessor of Leo II, in the year 681, the author must have written this not long after the end of the seventh century, and so forth.”

He adds a similar indication from the Life of Conon. Concerning Conon’s accession to the pontificate, which occurred in the year 686, the author writes: “And they sent messengers together with the clergy and the people to the most excellent Theodore the exarch, **as is customary**.” “These words,” he says, “as is customary, deserve attention. The author did not say ‘as was customary’ or ‘as used to be done,’ but ‘as is customary,’ thereby indicating that this Life was written at a time when the election of a new pontiff was reported to the exarchs—and therefore at a time when exarchs were still at Ravenna. They existed for approximately two hundred years. Longinus, the first, was appointed exarch by Justin the Younger in the year 567; the last, Eutychius, was expelled by Aistulf, king of the Lombards, in the year 752. From this passage it is clear that the author of the Life of Conon must have written before the middle of the eighth century, when the exarchs, or prefects, of the Constantinopolitan emperor ceased to exist in Italy. He could have written around the beginning of the eighth century, when exarchs had not yet ceased to reside at Ravenna and when it was customary to refer the election of a new pontiff to them, as is evident from the *Liber Diurnus*.

It is therefore sufficiently clear, both from the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* himself and from writers of the same period and of the immediately following age, that the Lives of the Pontiffs extending from St. Gregory to Pope Constantine were written and published by a man living in the City under St. Gregory II, who administered the apostolic archive or was in charge of the library. The Lives of Saints Gregory II and Gregory III were added by him after their deaths.

8. The Lives of the Roman Pontiffs from St. Peter through Saints Gregory II and III—which constitute the more important and original part of this collection—were enlarged by two appendices added later, which may also be called the second and third parts of the same collection. Schelstrate attributes the second part to some anonymous member of the Roman clergy who had access to the archive. It comprises the Lives of Zacharias and Stephen III. He assigns the third or final part, that is, the appendix, to several authors, most of them living in the times of the pontiffs whose Lives they wrote. Thus this third [Col. 0038C] part may properly be subdivided into several parts, if it is to be divided according to the number of writers. He does not deny that the Life of Nicholas I should be assigned to Anastasius, monk and librarian of the Apostolic See, as Panvinio calls him. The librarian William added the final two Lives, recorded in Fabrotius’s codex, since the Velserian codex ended with the Life of Nicholas composed by Anastasius. For this reason, Velser chose to attribute the name of Anastasius to the entire collection, although it properly belonged only to its final section.

9. After the individual parts of the work we are reprinting have been assigned to authors of the eighth and ninth centuries, someone may reasonably ask why Damasus’s book is mentioned by many and why the work containing the Lives of his predecessors is regarded as his, although the style reveals that an author under Gregory II wrote both those Lives and the remaining Lives of the first part, as we have called it.

The frequently praised Schelstrate explained the cause of this error. He showed that the material found in the indicated Lives of the Pontiffs, which constitutes the first part of this collection, was copied at the beginning of the eighth century in almost exactly the same words from two much older Catalogues of the bishops of the Roman See, still surviving on parchment. The first of these two Catalogues, which indicates the age of Pope Liberius, whose immediate successor was Damasus, provided an opportunity for some idle man of a later age to refer the Catalogue to Pope Damasus as its author or approver. On his own initiative this man forged two letters: one from St. Jerome to Damasus, asking that the Catalogue be communicated to him, and one from Damasus to Jerome, sending him the Catalogue he had requested.

The impostor’s fraud easily infiltrated the unlearned centuries, when letters had declined after the Lombard invasion. For this reason, in the Carolingian age, both letters—although fictitious—were prefixed to the Lives in a parchment codex then belonging to the Colbert Library, and in another codex of equal antiquity from the books of Queen Christina, acquired by Alexander VIII and given to the Vatican Library, where it is now preserved.

What is more astonishing is that even in our own century, or at least in the immediately preceding one, when the study of history and criticism, cleansed of neglect and squalor, had not merely flourished again but had also reached maturity, there were people who read so carelessly both those letters and a seventh letter with its response, published by Martius Milesius among the works of St. Damasus, that they failed to notice that the context, chronology, and opinions of Damasus and Jerome were plainly contrary to what the letters stated. Hence Labbe, in volume II of the *Councils*, seals their judgment with these words: “They are regarded by learned men as spurious, apocryphal, and utterly foolish; and they are as far removed from the style of Damasus and Jerome as heaven from earth and the Antarctic Pole from the Arctic.”

Schelstrate adds in this Dissertation, chapter 3, section 4: “These matters require no further proof, since the same conclusion is immediately apparent to anyone examining the writing, as I showed so clearly from the letters published by Martius Milesius in the first edition of *Ecclesiastical Antiquity* that the distinguished Papebrochius, in the *Propylaeum* to the fourth volume of May, page 3, judged that he ought to retract the opinion of his predecessor Henschenius, adding that, convinced by my arguments, he preferred to have those letters removed from the first volume of April.”

The spurious letters of Pope Damasus to Jerome and of Jerome to Damasus—fabricated by an inept man of a later age and prefixed to the older Catalogues, namely, the one compiled under Liberius and the other immediately subsequent to it, which must be assigned among the ancient Catalogues to the middle of the sixth century—were fraudulently attached to the Catalogues when they were copied in the age of Charlemagne. Because later generations observed them inattentively, these letters caused Martin of Poland and a few others to believe that Pope Damasus should be named the author either of the Catalogue or of the book containing the deeds of the Pontiffs.

In truth, however, neither was this *Liber Pontificalis* written by Blessed Damasus—since it was first composed approximately three hundred and forty years after Pope Damasus, under Gregory II, from authentic documents of public authority preserved in the pontifical library or in the archives of the City’s principal churches—nor can either of the Catalogues be attributed to Damasus. The older Catalogue appeared under Liberius, Damasus’s predecessor, with whom it ends; consequently, it does not enumerate the years of Damasus’s pontificate, which had not yet been completed. The other Catalogue belongs to the sixth century, since it extends to Felix IV, under Justinian.

10. Since, therefore, neither Damasus should be regarded as the author of the earlier Lives in this collection nor Anastasius as the author of those Lives or of the more recent ones—for he added only the single Life of Pope Nicholas I to the preceding works composed under Gregory II—the writers of all the Lives surviving from Gregory III through Nicholas I are anonymous. It may perhaps be doubted whether the deeds they describe possess authority and credibility. Or, if the Reader prefers to proceed more equitably, he will at least ask why we confidently assert that everything narrated in this *Liber* was collected from authentic documents of public authority, accessible to anonymous writers in the pontifical library, in the archives, or in the monuments of the City’s principal churches, from which they gathered the Lives and deeds of the Roman Pontiffs.

I readily acknowledge that this is the principal subject of our preface. I neither evade the task nor conceal its difficulty; rather, I undertake to show plainly that these anonymous authors of the Lives derived from authentic documents [Col. 0040C] of public authority the material they transferred into this codex. To prove this separately for each case is not suitable to the form of a preface, since that belongs rather to the notes. But I believe that I can show generally, as though presenting a catalogue of the source from which those writers irrigated their little plots, that this can be demonstrated with the greatest clarity.

11. First of all, it is certain that those two Catalogues, or Lists of the Roman Pontiffs, published in the fourth century under Liberius I and in the sixth century under Felix IV, constitute the principal texture of those Lives in the *Liber Pontificalis* that reach to those periods. This is established with such obvious evidence that Schelstrate, who deserved the next place after the often-praised Holstenius, very prudently submitted it to judgment by the eyes. [Col. 0040D] He divided the pages into several columns. He used three columns to display the history of the Life of each pontiff according to the threefold text of the first Catalogue, the second Catalogue, and the *Liber Pontificalis*, as anyone will be able to perceive and compare in this specimen.

[Note: [Col. 0039] In Migne, the sections titled “Words of the first Catalogue … VII and Titus,” “Words of the second Catalogue … the days of the episcopate XXI,” and “Words of the *Liber Pontificalis* … the days of the episcopate XXII” are printed in parallel.]

**Words of the first Catalogue**

[Col. 0039D]

Clement: nine years, eleven months, twelve days. He lived in the times of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus through the seventh consulship of Vespasian and Titus.

**Words of the second Catalogue**

[Col. 0039D]

Clement, a Roman by nationality, from the district of Caelian Mount, son of Faustinus, held the see for nine years, two months, and ten days. He lived in the times of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Trachalus [Col. 0042] and Italicus through the ninth consulship of Vespasian and Titus. He was crowned with martyrdom. He established seven districts and assigned them to the faithful notaries of the Church, so that each of them might diligently and carefully investigate the deeds of the martyrs throughout his own district. He wrote two Letters. He held three ordinations: ten presbyters, two deacons, and five bishops for various places, in the month of December. He died a martyr in the third year of Trajan; he was buried in Greece on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, and the see was vacant for twenty-one days.

**Words of the *Liber Pontificalis***

[Col. 0040D]

Clement, a Roman by nationality, from the district of Caelian Mount, son of Faustinus, held the see for nine years, two months, and ten days. He lived in the times of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Trajanus [Vatican, Florentine, and two Cassinese codices: Trachalus] and Italicus through the ninth consulship of Vespasian and Titus. While he was composing many books out of zeal for the Christian religion, he was crowned with martyrdom. He caused seven [Col. 0041] districts to be divided [Cassinese codex: “and he divided them”] among the faithful notaries of the Church, so that each of them might diligently and carefully investigate the deeds of the martyrs throughout his own district.

He wrote two Letters, which are called Catholic. By the command of Blessed Peter he assumed the Church and undertook the administration of the pontificate, just as the chair had been handed over or entrusted to him by the Lord Jesus Christ. Nevertheless, in the Letter written to James, you will find how the Church was entrusted to him by Blessed Peter. For this reason Linus and Cletus are written before him, because they had been ordained bishops by the very prince of the Apostles to exercise the episcopal ministry.

He held two ordinations in the month of December: ten presbyters, two deacons, and fifteen bishops for various places. He died a martyr in the third year of Trajan, and he too was buried in Greece on the eighth day before the Kalends of December; and the see was vacant for twenty-two days.

[Col. 0041A] 12. In the first column are displayed the words of the earlier Catalogue published under Liberius, in the rounded characters, as they are called; in the second, the same words of the more ancient Catalogue, which were incorporated into the other Catalogue when it was published under Felix IV, are rendered in slanting characters, which they call italics, so that at a glance one may perceive whatever the writer under Justinian retained from the Index published under Liberius, and whatever he added from other documents not expressed in the earlier Catalogue. The third column, which is intended to receive the text of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, reports, by the same method, in italic or slanting characters, whatever was written in precisely the same words from the Catalogue composed under Justinian; but in rounded letters it gives other material which the writer of the Life added to the text, not expressed in the aforesaid Catalogues, [Col. 0041B] but learned from elsewhere.

It may nevertheless be observed in this specimen of the life of Saint Clement that the additions inserted into the text by the writer of the *Book of the Pontiffs* are scarcely anything other than notes or explanations of the same matters which were contained in abbreviated and, in a certain sense, concealed form in the Catalogue. In this example the *Book of the Pontiffs* exhibits two additions: the first concerning Clement’s martyrdom, the second concerning the order of succession and the authority by which he presided over the Church after the blessed Peter.

The Catalogue had expressed the martyrdom in these words: “He died a martyr in Trajan’s third [year].” The *Book of the Pontiffs* rendered it thus: “He died a martyr in the third year of Trajan.” But the author of this book thought that the occasion of Clement’s martyrdom should be reviewed: namely, that when the blessed pontiff was writing many books [Col. 0041C] out of zeal for the Christian religion, and was carefully arranging for the Acts of the martyrs to be collected by faithful notaries, assigned individually to the seven regions, he was crowned with martyrdom.

Both Clement’s writings and those of the notaries are also mentioned in the Catalogue. In the addition the author of the Life seems to suggest that Clement’s martyrdom resulted from the opportunity afforded by such writings to defend and disseminate our religion. For it is established from Suetonius’ *Life of Domitian*, chapter 12, that under Domitian the Jewish tax was exacted with the utmost severity; those were reported to it who, as though professing the Jewish way of life, lived within the City. No one doubts that in that period Christians were commonly confused with those professing the Jewish way of life. Hence Clement’s profession of our religion, published in writing, could more easily have caused him trouble through informers.

Indeed, since it was later discovered that under the emperors of milder disposition, Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, writings in defense of Christian doctrine brought capital punishment upon Justin, Quadratus, Athenagoras, and Apollonius, the Senate or magistrates decreeing the ultimate penalty, while the pagan priests for the most part exerted themselves so that even the milder Augusti, as vindicators of their ceremonies and especially as guardians of the rites of the gentiles, might decree and inflict the same penalties upon us Christians as impious violators of their superstition—it is not surprising that under Trajan the first, or at least the foremost after the apostles and evangelists, author of so many volumes protecting the Christian rites should have received from those works the occasion of undergoing martyrdom. This seems to be indicated by the first addition which the *Book of the Pontiffs* made to the second Catalogue. [Col. 0042B]

The second addition concerns the order of succession by which Clement was substituted for the blessed Peter, with complete authority to govern the whole Christian Church. This passage does not differ greatly from an annotation and, as it were, an interpretation of the text of the Catalogue. For in the earlier Catalogue Clement is placed before Cletus, whereas in the second Catalogue and in the *Book of the Pontiffs* Clement is placed afterward. The author [Col. 0042C] added the reason for this difference.

How much authority should be assigned to this addition may be gathered from the words of Pope Saint Leo II, reported by Vendelinus in Labbe’s *General Councils*, volume I, page 190. After reporting, from an anonymous Greek writer, that the blessed Peter, when departing from Rome, ordained Linus as a kind of coadjutor in the exercise of episcopal duties, and that when he returned to the City in the twelfth year of Nero he found Linus removed from life by martyrdom, and therefore substituted Clement in his place, who shortly afterward succeeded Peter when Peter had been crucified, he adds [Col. 0043A] the testimony of Leo II, who indicates the same thing concerning Cletus.

Vendelini’s words are these:

> “Behold, while Peter was still alive, Linus sat as bishop; for this reason Marianus and others called him a chorepiscopus, among whom was Leo II, successor of Agatho. ‘Peter,’ he says, ‘took Linus and Cletus as assistants for himself, but did not transfer pontifical authority to them; rather, he transferred it to Clement.’ Thus it was always held certain that Linus presided over the Roman faithful together with Peter, and that the pontificate was transferred by that same Peter to Clement. Thus this chronology begins to flow more clearly in the following manner.”

Here I do not undertake to settle the question of the supreme pontificate of Linus and Cletus; we shall recall it for examination among the notes on the *Book of the Pontiffs*. I wish only to demonstrate what I proposed: namely, that the text of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, from Saint Peter down to Felix IV, was for the most part drawn from the Catalogue of the supreme pontiffs composed during that period; and that the additions made by the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* were taken from documents of authority not unlike the statements expressed in the first and second Catalogues. [Col. 0043B]

13. But the order of the argument requires us to investigate somewhat more carefully the authority of the matters stated in both Catalogues. Since the principal texture of this book was taken from the Catalogues, we should certainly not know how much confidence could be placed in the compilers of the Lives unless we had first examined the reliability of both Catalogues, the foundation of the entire work. Let us therefore first examine the reliability and antiquity of the copies from which the Catalogues were transcribed; then we shall consider the genuine documents from which the writers of the Catalogues may have drawn what they transmitted to us. [Col. 0043C]

14. The earlier Catalogue, composed under Liberius around the year 354, was first published by Father Aegidius Bucherius in his distinguished *Commentary on the Paschal Canon of Victor of Aquitaine*, together with four other short works assignable to the same period. This is clear from the enumeration of the Roman consuls expressed in the first short work, concerning the urban prefects, and in the second, which contains a fragment of the ancient *Fasti*, together with the Feriae, Epacts, and the Latin Cycle extending over eighty-four years. Cardinal Henry Noris also wrote a celebrated book about this in our own age.

These five short works, among which the Catalogue under discussion holds the principal place, were contained in ancient parchment manuscripts given by John Brenner, royal secretary and recorder in the Luxembourg senate, to Ansovillius, a councillor to the Catholic King in the private councils at Brussels. From these manuscripts Cuspinian had transcribed the names of several consuls, as he frequently testifies in his book of the *Fasti*. Bucherius likewise observes this (chapter 14, page 244):

> “These parchments contained several short works of an unknown but extremely ancient writer, who seems to have lived under Constantine, the son of Constantine the Great; Cuspinian indicates in several places of his *Fasti* that he had these works in his hands.”

Cardinal Noris adds, in the name of scholars, a common wish [Col. 0044A] (*Dissertation on the Consular Fasti*, part I): that Cuspinian had published the same parchments rather than fragments of them.

> “He inserted throughout his volume the consular lists excerpted from the celebrated anonymous manuscript; learned men would certainly have preferred him to publish them complete from that same source.”

Two copies of the Catalogue in question survive today, transcribed from some more ancient autograph, whose apographs the parchments themselves must be considered to have been; those parchments, once handled by Cuspinian, are now lost. One copy is preserved in the Imperial Library of Vienna among the historical manuscripts, numbered 56, according to Lambecius, book IV of the *Commentaries*, and Schelestratius, dissertation 3, chapter 2, number 1, of the *Antiquity of the Church*. The other is found in the Antwerp library of the Reverend Fathers of the Society of Jesus; Bucherius used it in his edition, while lamenting that the Brenner parchments had not survived to his day. [Col. 0044B]

Schelestratius (*Antiquity of the Church*, dissertation 3, chapter 2, no. 1) arranged for the reading of the imperial Viennese copy to be compared with Bucherius’s, or Antwerp, copy by Father Janning: both to fill the lacunae in the latter from the Viennese copy and also to provide the variant readings of both copies, just as Bucherius had noted in the margin those places in which his manuscript differed from Cuspinian’s reading.

From the collated labors of these distinguished men, we have therefore discovered that the Catalogue was composed under Pope Liberius, but that its autograph no longer survives. Of the several copies transcribed from it, one parchment copy seen by Cuspinian is now missing; two paper copies of lesser antiquity survive; and in them several scribal errors are found, which Schelestratius took care to remove by collating both codices with Cuspinian. Thus, in Schelestratius’s edition, we possess a sufficiently corrected version of the work. [Col. 0044C]

15. The second Catalogue is assigned to the age of Justinian, since it ends with Felix IV, around the year 530 of Christ. It was first published from a parchment codex of square format, written around the age of Charlemagne. Queen Christina bought this codex in Paris and transferred it to Rome; after her death, Pope Alexander VIII purchased it from her heirs for the Vatican Library and donated it, together with the other manuscript codices. From this codex of Queen Christina, the Reverend Fathers Henschenius and Papebrochius first published the Catalogue in the *Prolegomena* to the first volume of April.

But the distinguished prelate Schelestratius discovered that it had not been copied with sufficient accuracy, after obtaining from the illustrious queen, who was then residing in Rome, permission to examine it and keep it in his possession for several months. Moreover, when he learned that another copy of the same Catalogue was found in an ancient codex of the Colbert Library (no. 1868), of the same antiquity, namely from the age of Charlemagne, he obtained from the distinguished man Étienne Baluze that it be faithfully transcribed from there.

He rejoiced greatly when he discovered that the readings of the two copies—the codex of Queen Christina, or the Vatican copy, and the Colbert copy—agreed completely, except that at times there was a slight difference of one letter in written forms or one unit in numbers. Through both codices he also saw that an orderly series of the earlier Roman pontiffs was provided, corresponding to the Canon; this was the reading that Henschenius’s edition had disturbed.

The writing and age of the codices, contemporaneous with Charlemagne, are established beyond doubt by the form of the characters and of the book, as well as by the addition of the subsequent pontiffs: in the Colbert copy, down to Adrian I and Leo IV; in the Vatican copy, that is, the Christina-Alexandrian copy, down to Paschal I. In the latter there is also testimony to its age in a passage expressed in these words:

> “From the passion of our Lord Jesus Christ to the see of the blessed Pope Marcellinus there are 276 years and 8 months. From the completed apostleship of Christ’s martyr Marcellinus to the time of Lord Charles the king, in the twenty-fifth year of his reign—that is, to the eighth day before the Kalends of April—there are 490 years and 13 months.”

This brief account of the antiquity of the Catalogues, and of the age and authority of the codices from which their edition was taken, will suffice. Whoever desires more should consult the aforementioned dissertation of Schelestratius. [Col. 0045B]

16. From this point we must proceed to inquire into the authority of the matters stated in both Catalogues. We must deal summarily with the documents on which the fourth-century author under Liberius relied in order to recover and transmit to us whatever he recorded in the first Catalogue. By the same method, inquiry must be made concerning the author of the other Catalogue under Justinian: from what sources did he draw both what he added to the first Catalogue concerning the pontiffs mentioned in it down to Liberius, and what he continued in the remaining entries after Liberius down to Felix IV? [Col. 0045C]

To satisfy a proper investigation, I ask the reader to attend to the fact that in the earlier Catalogue, from Saint Peter to Liberius, the following are recorded for each pontiff: his name; the years, months, and days of his rule; the pairs of consuls by which the beginning and end of his pontificate are marked; and, in some places, certain decrees, as in the case of Fabian; as well as several buildings in the case of Julius, whom Liberius, the last pontiff of that Catalogue, follows.

In the second Catalogue, the father’s name is added, together with the place in the City or province where the man who later became pontiff was born. Decrees and institutions of sacred rites are also added, especially those introduced for the celebration of the Mass or concerning the public discipline of the Church. Ordinations are likewise added, celebrated by various pontiffs in the two hierarchical orders of this holy Roman Church—namely, presbyters and deacons—as well as bishops sent outside the City. During those periods from which the aforesaid Catalogues begin and at which they end, it was customary to commit all these matters to memory, especially when composing lists of priests. Each point must be examined carefully. [Col. 0045D]

17. Joining the pontiff’s name with an indication of his parent was customary among Christians and Hebrews, indeed even among the pagan Romans, as is clear from the Life of the blessed Peter. No more illustrious document can be cited than the truth recorded in the sacred Gospels.

When Jesus Christ, the eternal pontiff, was called by Simon with an indication of the true Father, “the Son of the living God,” he named that same Simon as his designated vicar: Simon Bar-Jona, Simon son of John; then Cephas, Peter (Matthew 16). John the Forerunner of Christ is said to be of priestly descent, John son of Zechariah. John the Evangelist and James, his brother, called to the apostleship, are said to be sons of Zebedee.

These examples make sufficiently clear the custom of the period and region. We learn that this custom was commonly retained by the Hebrews at that time from their priest and historian Josephus, who records his own name in this way in the preface to his book on the Jewish war:

> “I, Josephus, son of Matthias, a Hebrew, a priest from Jerusalem.”

What could be more similar to this custom than what is preserved in the second Catalogue?

> “Anicetus, Syrian by nationality, son of John, from the village of Amisa, etc.”
>
> “Pius, Italian by nationality, son of Rufinus, brother of Pastor, from the city of Aquileia, etc.”
>
> “Soter, Campanian by nationality, son of Concordius, from the city of Fundi, etc.”
>
> “Eleutherus, Greek by nationality, son of Abundantius, from the town of Nicopolis, etc.”

Among the Romans, especially in the composition of Catalogues, this practice was commonly maintained, as the inscriptions show. Since in many matters of civic life it was necessary to take account of age and of plebeian or patrician family, that necessity of remembering parents, fatherland, and age introduced among the Romans the custom of recording such matters, generally not only in the censorial registers—from which the greater part of their history flowed, as Marcus Tullius testifies—but also on marble tablets set up by public or private authority.

What deserves attention, however, [Col. 0046C] especially in the second Catalogue, is that in the case of Roman pontiffs born in the City, the tribe to which they were enrolled as citizens is not mentioned, but rather the region. In my opinion this indicates that the information found in the Catalogues was collected from tablets and registers written by the seven notaries of the Roman Church. Clement I, the disciple and successor of Peter, assigned these notaries to an equal number of ecclesiastical regions of the City, into which he reduced the fourteen regions established by Augustus, so that they might collect the deeds of the martyrs.

Among the martyrs are all the Roman pontiffs down to Sylvester. These are the words of the second Catalogue concerning Clement:

> “He established seven regions and divided them among faithful notaries of the Church, who, each one diligently in his own region, carefully and attentively investigated the deeds of the martyrs.”

[Col. 0046D] This custom continued into the eighth century, when, under Adrian I, we find that Paul I had appointed a regional notary (no. 291).

Thus in the second Catalogue we read:

> “Cletus, Roman by nationality, from the region of Caelian Mount, son of Faustinus, etc.”

The indication of the urban region is omitted in the case of Zephyrinus, the immediate predecessor of Callistus. The reason is presumably that the Acts, which had been preserved sufficiently intact under the Antonines, when those emperors treated the Church more mildly, were so disrupted in the persecutions of Severus and Decius that under Decius, through Fabian’s foresight, it became necessary to address the matter again, lest they perish entirely, and to provide for the restoration of the ancient Acts and the security of those to come by a new division of the City into seven regions, assigned to the same number of deacons, with nearly the same number of subdeacons to urge the notaries to collect the deeds of the martyrs.

Both Catalogues testify to this in the entry on Fabian, no. 21:

> “He divided the regions among the deacons.”

So the first Catalogue reports it. The second Catalogue adds:

> “And he appointed six subdeacons to supervise the seven notaries, so that they might faithfully collect the deeds of the martyrs.”

But these more recent deeds, collected after Fabian and for the most part destroyed by fire during the savage persecution of Diocletian, have transmitted to us very few remains of that distinguished work. Schelestratius notes this at the passage:

> “Very few martyrs are mentioned,” he says, “in the more ancient Catalogue; and it does not describe their Acts, but indicates only the kind of their martyrdom in a word.”

Hence I think that the Acts of the martyrs, written down by the notaries and subdeacons of the primitive Church, perished together with the other parchments of the Church in the persecution of Diocletian. Or, if some survived the fire intact, they did not come into our hands, but almost all were consumed by the antiquity of the ages.

More Acts were preserved of the martyrs who had preceded them in the first and second centuries of the Christian era, since they had already been written down under the Antonines with little or no danger. Thus Hegesippus, living in Rome, was able in that period to compose five books of ecclesiastical history under Pope Eleutherus, as Jerome and Eusebius testify. Eusebius writes that they were still extant in his own time, book IV, chapter 22.

From those same commentaries of Hegesippus, since he admits that he had included several things that embraced the most truthful history of apostolic preaching, and since he gathers the Catalogue and succession of the Roman pontiffs in more than one place (*Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 22), we may infer that the Acts of the notaries had survived, recording the name, fatherland, region, and years of the pontiff who suffered martyrdom.

Cyprian also gives this instruction in book III, letter 6, addressed to the Roman presbyters and deacons: they should not omit recording the day of death of those who, dying in prison for Christ, were to be numbered among the martyrs. [Col. 0047C]

18. Moreover, the burial place was often marked by indicating the day and year of deposition through the ordinary consuls. This is frequently found even in the case of private believers who had suffered neither martyrdom nor priesthood, when we inspect the suburban cemeteries and read the inscriptions either in the crypts of the martyrs or in the books of subterranean Rome, which record the tablets and inscriptions excavated from those places. [Col. 0047D]

From this Eusebius was able to compare the beginnings and succession, as well as the end, of the Roman pontiffs with the years of the emperors—as he often does—on the basis of the consulship in which each had been elected to undertake the government of the Church and in which he had completed his priesthood and life.

Let us give an example from Telesphorus and Hyginus. Eusebius writes in *History*, book IV, chapter 10:

> “After Hadrian had completed his life, when he had reigned twenty-one years, Antoninus, surnamed Pius, assumed the administration of the empire. In his first year, when Telesphorus had departed this life in the eleventh year of the episcopate he had undertaken, Hyginus obtained the pontificate of the City of Rome.”

The Greek and Latin writers of the *Historia Augusta* record the year of Hadrian’s death and the first year of the reign of Antoninus, surnamed Pius, under the consulship of Niger and Camerinus. This is confirmed by a stone in Gruter, page 256, no. 4, marked on its reverse with the college of the same consuls, as the most eminent Noris observes in his *Consular Letter*, page 85.

The second Catalogue refers the beginning of Hyginus’s pontificate to the consuls Camerinus and Magnus. Through the error of unlearned copyists, this has been made to read “Magnus” instead of “Niger”; it should be Camerinus and Niger. Although in the first Catalogue a lacuna prevents the names of the consuls from being read, they can easily be supplied from what precedes and follows, where the end of the predecessor’s life and the beginning of the successor’s episcopate are assigned.

The last consuls whom the same Catalogue numbers for the seat of Telesphorus are Caesar and Balbinus. The copyist corruptly rendered Balbinus as Albinus, with one letter omitted. These are L. Aelius Caesar II and P. Caelius Balbinus, as they are inscribed on the Auximate marble in Gruter, page 445, no. 10, set up on the sixth day before the Ides of July.

These consuls are immediately followed in the *Consular Fasti* by Camerinus and Niger. The *Fasti* were written in the fourth century of Christ—hence they are of the same age as the first Catalogue—and were published together by Bucherius, but illustrated by Cardinal Noris in his dissertation following the epochs of the Syromacedonians.

Therefore the last consuls assigned to Telesphorus are correctly given as Aelius Caesar II and Balbinus, and the first assigned to Hyginus as Camerinus and Niger. This is again confirmed by other preceding colleges listed in both Catalogues together with the years of the pontiffs and matched with the years of the emperors.

For both Catalogues assign to Telesphorus eleven years and three months of episcopate, and to his immediate predecessor Xystus ten years and two or three months. Their beginning is the consulship of Niger and Apronianus, and their end the consulship of Verus and Ambibulus. The sum of the episcopates of Xystus and Telesphorus gives approximately twenty-one years and six months.

Hadrian spent twenty years and eleven months in imperial power, according to Dio in his Life; coins and stones support this if we apply Noris’s observations in his *Consular Letter*, page 85. Dio says that he received the information he wrote from his father Apronianus, who was governing Cilicia at the time when, after Trajan’s death in that province, Hadrian’s adoption and accession to the empire were brought about through Plotina’s faction.

The ordinary consuls, therefore, when Trajan died at Selinus on 10 August, were Niger and Apronianus, as all the monuments and historians, together with Dio, confirm. These same consuls must be acknowledged to have coincided with the beginning of Xystus. Both Catalogues, however, match the beginning of Xystus with the same consuls, Niger and Antonianus.

In the Fasti, Verus and Ambibulus follow them in the tenth position; the equal calculation of the eleven years assigned to Xystus likewise shows that they correspond. Thus the agreement between the total years both of the emperors’ reigns and of the Roman pontiffs’ episcopates, corresponding to the consular lists inserted in both places—in the Catalogues mentioned, as well as in Eusebius’s *Chronicle* and *History*, written in the same century in which the earlier Catalogue was published—demonstrates that at that time there still survived the lists and documents of the notaries of the Roman Church. From these the writers of the Catalogue composed a chronology and succession of pontiffs no less certain than that of Eusebius. [Col. 0049A]

19. Who, indeed, could doubt that in the age of Eusebius and of the earlier Catalogue extending to Liberius there existed in the Roman Church lists of the years and consulships assigned to each pontiff? The Acts of the martyrs, especially those who suffered in Rome in the age nearest to the apostles, very often express the names of the consuls, the urban prefects, or the emperors, as well as the day of the passion.

In the Acts of Saint Ignatius, numbers 2 and 8 of Ruinart’s edition, we also read the imperial year matched with the consuls:

> “These things happened on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, when Sura and Senecio were presiding among the Romans for the second time”—so number 8 reads, while number 2 has a different form—“after the fourth year of Trajan” [Ruinart corrects this to “the ninth”], after his victories over the Scythians and Thracians [understand: the Dacians].

C. Sosius Senecio III and L. Licinius Sura II proceeded to the consulship in Trajan’s fourth year. After an intervening period of five years, when the ninth year of the same reign was passing, the same consuls, Senecio IV and Sura III, opened the Fasti.

Trajan’s Dacian victory occurred in the sixth year of his reign, while his tribunician power was expiring, as the most eminent Noris has clearly demonstrated from coins in his *Consular Letter*, page 66. Ruinart therefore correctly warned that after “the fourth year of Trajan” there was a copyist’s error, by which the numeral IX had been turned into IV. This agrees perfectly with the epoch of the Dacian victory mentioned three years earlier, and with the expedition undertaken against the Parthians and into Armenia, which is likewise mentioned in the same Acts.

Indeed, the context of the words seems to require this, since Senecio and Sura, “presiding for the second time,” that is, being colleagues in the consulship again—carelessly expressed by the words “Syria and Senecio for the second time”—recur in the ninth year of Trajan.

In sepulchral inscriptions, too, the deposition of martyrs is often found marked by the names of the consuls. We could demonstrate this repeatedly from fragments of stones which are daily excavated from the sacred cemeteries. In the Acts of martyrs who suffered in the City, the name of the urban prefect is sometimes expressed. Although this magistracy was not annual, when it is related to other indications of expeditions, victories, the deaths of emperors, or something similar occurring in the same period and expressed in the Acts of martyrdom, it becomes a sufficiently suitable marker for comparison with the consulship.

In the Acts of Justin the Martyr, the urban prefect Rusticus interrogates him and his companions and puts them to death. Publicus is read as the urban prefect in the Acts of Saint Felicitas under Antoninus.

If today we possessed an intact series of the urban prefects throughout the first two centuries of the Christian era, just as an intact series of their successors in that office is read from the year of Christ 254 to 354—in a fourth-century work published by Bucherius from the same parchments in which he found the first Catalogue—we would know that the epochs of the martyrs, and consequently those of the pontiffs, could be established from the indication of the prefects just as from the indication of the consuls.

That a series of prefects was available in the fourth century, when the earlier Catalogue was composed, is suggested by that fragment preserving a succession of individual prefects for a full hundred years. I have said that this custom, or even historical necessity, of mentioning the same magistrates in the deeds of the Church prevailed in the age nearest to the apostles.

No one should think that I begin this custom too early, since the evangelical oracles teach us that the rule for determining the epochs of the notable deeds of Christ and his disciples was dictated by the divine Spirit.

The birth of the Lord is dated by Saint Matthew [Matthew 1] through the final years of the reign of Herod the Great, and by Saint Luke through the first census, carried out by order of Augustus when Quirinius was governor of Syria [Luke 2].

The baptism of Christ and the preaching of John are referred to the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governing Judaea, Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip was tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias was tetrarch of Abilene, under the high priests Annas and Caiaphas [Luke 3]. Matthew, Mark, and John also designate the year of the Lord’s Passion by the annual high priesthood of the latter [Matthew 26:3, 37; Mark 14:61; John 11:49; 18:14].

The deeds of the apostles, written by Saint Luke at Rome, contain so many chronological indications through the succession of the governors of Syria and the magistrates listed both in the provinces and at Rome during Paul’s activity there that Saint Jerome concludes that the history extends through the two years of Paul’s residence at Rome, that is, to the fourth year of Nero [Saint Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, in the entry on Luke]. [Col. 0050C]

Instructed by these examples, the learned writers of ecclesiastical history, especially those working in Rome and associated with the apostles or with apostolic men—as Hegesippus was—did not omit, among the other criteria of truth by which they confirmed their works, to refer the times of the events to established epochs.

Eusebius produced a passage from Hegesippus concerning the martyrdom of James, the brother of the Lord. He indicated the epoch of that martyrdom by the siege of Jerusalem, which followed shortly afterward:

> “Not long afterward,” he says, “the siege under Vespasian and the captivity of the Jews followed.”

These are Hegesippus’s words, agreeing with Clement (*Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 23). These are the words of Eusebius, who in the same place brings forward Josephus’s testimony, recording the killing of James the Just as occurring within an interval of three months, counted from the death of Festus to Albinus, who was appointed procurator by Nero. During that three-month period Ananus the younger held the high priesthood.

This confirms the custom of the people and age, as well as of the historians writing at Rome, not to omit repeatedly recording the epochs of the events they described and not to deny their history the light supplied by the Roman archives concerning provincial affairs and by public inscriptions.

Those same archives, marbles, lists, and still-intact histories, as the fourth century of Christ was passing—when Eusebius and Jerome flourished—clearly displayed this same light of chronology to the author of the Catalogue under Liberius. It is therefore appropriate not to omit an inquiry into the chronological documents available to him. [Col. 0051A]

20. From here I shall proceed to establish and corroborate by other evidence the certainty and authority of the remaining matters recorded in both Catalogues. The ordinations of the presbyters and deacons of the City, as well as of the bishops sent from here to other churches, whether to found or govern them, hold the more prominent place, since they are found under each individual pontiff.

We must therefore see how it could have happened that the authors of the second Catalogue, belonging to the age of Felix IV and Justinian, discovered and counted so carefully the ordinations in the Roman Church during the first three centuries after the Passion of Christ the Lord. [Col. 0051B]

No one will deny that from the beginning of the Mosaic law the year and day of the erection of the tabernacle and its consecration, as well as of Aaron the high priest and his priestly sons, were recorded. Exodus, chapter 40, says:

> “And the Lord spoke to Moses, saying: ‘On the first month, on the first day of the month, you shall erect the tabernacle of the testimony, and place the ark in it, etc. You shall bring Aaron and his sons to the door of the tabernacle of the testimony, and, after washing them with water, clothe them in the holy garments, so that they may minister to me, and their anointing may advance them to an everlasting priesthood.’ And Moses did everything that the Lord had commanded. Thus, in the first month of the second year, on the first day of the month, the tabernacle was set up. And Moses erected it, etc. Moses, Aaron, and his sons washed their hands and feet whenever they entered the tent of the covenant and approached the altar, as the Lord had commanded Moses.”

Not only is the day of the consecration of Aaron, the first high priest, recorded in the sacred writings; the day, month, and year of his death are also given, and the succession and inauguration of his son Eleazar to the supreme priesthood are expressly mentioned in Numbers, chapter 33, verse 38:

> “Aaron the priest went up Mount Hor at the Lord’s command, and there he died in the fortieth year after the children of Israel had gone out from Egypt, in the fifth month, on the first day of the month, when he was 123 years old. From that point the pontificate of Eleazar, son of Aaron, begins.”

For at the Lord’s command Moses stripped Aaron of his garments and clothed Eleazar in them, as is related in Numbers 20. Then Aaron departed from life, gathered to his fathers. [Col. 0051D]

When our Christian pontiffs observed that the epoch of the high priesthood under the Mosaic law had been carefully recorded in the divine Scriptures, they judged that the dedication of the chair corresponding to the erection of the tabernacle should be recorded with no less care in the registers of the Church. They established that the day of each bishop’s ordination should be celebrated in annual remembrance, corresponding to Aaron’s consecration.

Moreover, in the most ancient ritual books and in the Canons of the Councils we see that certain prayers were assigned to each priest of the second order, namely the presbyter, so that by an annual sacrifice he might commemorate the day of his ordination. Cardinal Thomasius published these prayers in book III of *The Sacraments of the Roman Church*, page 211, under the title:

> “Prayer for the anniversary of a presbyter, concerning how he ought to celebrate Mass for himself.”

Since, then, it was an extremely ancient custom of the priests of the first covenant to record publicly the day of inauguration and death; since at the beginning of the priesthood of the new covenant the anniversary of the chair was recorded no less than the anniversary of martyrdom in the case of Peter; and since this practice was observed among Peter’s successors and extended to the bishops of the lesser cities, indeed being found employed even in the consecration of a presbyter, who could doubt that these documents above all were committed to writing by the notaries of the Roman Church and kept in the Archives, from which the Catalogues, diptychs, and lists [Col. 0052B] were later compiled?

### 21.

Who would deny that at Rome the ordinations of the Christian and truly divine priesthood were more carefully recorded and authenticated, when he observes that even the profane dignitaries of the pagan superstitions were held in such high esteem among the Romans that their co-optations were engraved on coins, marble monuments, and altars—both when the emperors governing the whole empire assumed the highest priesthood of their gods, and when private individuals obtained some lesser priesthood?

I omit the fact that the annals of the pontiffs and their linen books were the first source of Roman history, as Marcus Tullius records in the second book of *De Oratore*:

> History was nothing other than the compilation of annals. For this reason, and in order to preserve the public memory, from the beginning of Roman affairs down to Publius Mucius, the pontifex maximus committed to writing all the events of each year, entered them on a white board, and displayed the tablet at home, so that the people might have the power to know them. These are still called the *Annales Maximi*.

It will be sufficient to inspect the tablets of co-optations into the priesthoods that survive, described by Gruterus on folio 300, and by Panvinius in the *Fasti* under the year 943 from the foundation of the City. Besides the indication of the year, given through the consular colleges, there is also engraved the era reckoned from the foundation of the City. I shall give a fragment from the collection of His Excellency Lord Alessandro Albani:

> [lacuna] COELIUS APOLLINARIS BEING CONSUL, IN THE 922ND YEAR FROM THE FOUNDATION OF ROME, QUINTUS CLODIUS MARCELLINUS WAS CO-OPTED; TITUS AELIUS CILO BEING CONSUL FOR THE SECOND TIME AND FLAVIUS LIBO [being consul] [lacuna].  
> [lacuna] IN THE 450TH YEAR FROM THE FOUNDATION OF ROME, MARCUS VALERIUS PAETUS AQUIL[la] [lacuna] WAS CO-OPTED, GAIUS JUNIUS ASPER BEING CONSUL FOR THE SECOND TIME AND GAIUS JULIUS ASPER [being consul] [lacuna].  
> [lacuna] IN THE 960TH YEAR FROM THE FOUNDATION OF ROME [lacuna] FAUSTINIANUS WAS CO-OPTED [lacuna], AUGUSTUS BEING CONSUL FOR THE THIRD TIME AND COMA[zius] [being consul] [lacuna].  
> [lacuna] IN THE 920TH YEAR FROM THE FOUNDATION OF ROME [lacuna].

Anyone wishing to see coins as witnesses to this practice should examine the silver and gold coins struck by the Senate for Nero Caesar under his father Claudius, bearing the inscription:

> CO-OPTED PRIEST INTO EVERY COLLEGE BEYOND THE NUMBER, BY DECREE OF THE SENATE.

The same co-optation is recorded on an ancient marble inscription published by Gruterus on folio 300, belonging to the fifth consulship of Claudius Caesar, with Orfitus as his colleague, in the year 804 from the foundation of Rome.

Augustus engraved the day on which he entered upon the supreme pontificate in this manner in the marble calendar formerly kept by the Maffeians and now preserved in the Farnese palace near the Campus Florae:

> ON THIS DAY CAESAR WAS MADE PONTIFEX MAXIMUS,

under the day before the Nones of March. On another fragment of a calendar recently excavated at Antium, at the expense and under the care of the illustrious Alexander Albani, the celebrated defender of learned antiquity and nephew of our Most Holy Lord, the date is recorded as the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November:

> ON THIS DAY CAESAR ASSUMED THE MEN’S TOGA.

[lacuna] The break in the marble having removed what followed, Nicolaus of Damascus and Suetonius supply the missing information. From their testimony Cardinal Norisius concluded in *Cenotaphia Pisana*, dissertation II, p. 115, that on this same day Augustus put on the pure toga, laying aside the boyhood *praetexta*, and was appointed pontiff in the place of Lucius Domitius.

On another stone published by Gruterus, p. 228, no. 8, not only is the day recorded on which Tiberius Caesar was created pontifex maximus, but it is expressly stated that the same day had been chosen for dedicating the statues of the Caesars and Augustae:

> We have declared and testified that we shall observe forever the day of his dedication, which will be kept because it is more frequently celebrated each year: the sixth day before the Ides of March, because on this day Tiberius Caesar was most auspiciously created pontifex maximus.

Thus, as the stones show, it was customary among the Romans during the first, second, and third centuries of the Christian era to record in the calendars of the priestly colleges—not to mention the pontifical books—the co-optations of new priests and the elections of lesser and greater pontiffs.

Indeed, the monuments of the college of the Arval Brothers, which adorn the Alban Museum and which we have often had occasion to consult, show that the precise day of co-optation into the college of the Arval Brothers was likewise engraved. This priesthood, it should be noted, was said to have been conferred upon Romulus by Acca Larentia and must therefore be counted among the most ancient institutions of the City. I shall give the portion of the inscription relevant to our subject; the remainder may be seen transcribed from the same marble by Sponius, *Miscellanea*, p. 5, and by Fabretti, *Inscriptiones*, p. 442:

> [lacuna] In the same consulship—that is, of Lucius Ceionius Commodus and Decimus Novius Priscus—on the Kalends of March, in the Temple of Concord, with the Arval Brothers present, from a tablet sent by the Emperor Caesar Vespasian Augustus, we co-opted Gaius Salvius Liberalis Nonius Bassus into the college in place of the deceased Gaius Matidius Patruinus. The following were present: Lucius Veratius Quadratus, Gaius Vipstanus Apronianus, Lucius Maecius Postumus, Gaius Salvius Liberalis Nonius Bassus.  
> In the same consulship, the master Gaius Salonius Matidius Patruinus—on whose vacancy a successor entered office—died while holding the mastership.  
> In the same year, under the same consuls, on the Kalends of March, Publius Sallustius Blaesus [lacuna].  
> In the same consulship, on the fifth day before the Ides of March, in the Temple of Concord, Lucius Sallustius Blaesus, having been co-opted in place of Gaius Matidius Patruinus into the college of the Arval Brothers, summoned the college and [lacuna].

### 22.

Several marble tablets, engraved with the records of this college and mentioned in Gruterus’s collection after folio 118—formerly in the possession of Fulvius Ursinus and now surviving in the Farnese palace—demonstrate that later generations, down to the fourth and fifth centuries of Christ, likewise preserved the custom of engraving the day on which public vows were undertaken for the safety of the Caesars and the day on which those vows were fulfilled. The rites of pagan superstition are carefully explained in other marbles belonging to the same college. These were excavated about twenty years ago at the sixth milestone outside the City and subsequently published by the late Bishop Philippus a Turre of Adria, whose memory is worthy of honor and who, while alive, was my very dear friend. The same inscription is now preserved in the museum of His Excellency Alessandro Albani, mentioned above:

> Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus for the fourth time consul, Gaius Aufidius Victorinus for the second time consul, in the Capitol, etc. In the same consulships, [lacuna], on the seventh day before the Ides of January, in the pronaos, [lacuna], the Arval Brothers announced the sacrifice of the goddess Dea Dia. Quintus Licinius Nepos, the master, with veiled head and facing east, [lacuna], “May it be good, auspicious, favorable, fortunate, and salutary for the Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus Pius, Sarmaticus and Germanicus Maximus, pontifex maximus, father of his country, consul for the fourth time, the best and greatest prince, son of the divine Marcus Antoninus, grandson of the divine Antoninus, great-grandson of the divine Hadrian, great-great-grandson of the divine Trajan; for the Senate and Roman people, and for the Arval Brothers.”  
> The sacrifice of the goddess Dea Dia will take place this year on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June at Rome, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June in the grove and at home, and will be completed at home on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June. The following were present in the college: Quintus Licinius Nepos, the master, etc.  
> [After several intervening passages, the completion of the superstitious sacrifice is described:] In the same consulships, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June, at the house of Quintus Licinius Nepos, the master, the Arval Brothers, wearing the *praetexta*, performed the sacrifice of the goddess Dea Dia with incense and wine. There, reclining on couches decorated with embroidered coverings and served by freeborn boys who were sons of senators, Aelius Aviola and Acilius Severus, etc.  
> In the same consulships, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the grove of Dea Dia, Quintus Licinius Nepos, the master, sacrificed at the altar. [lacuna] He sacrificed the expiatory piglets in the grove for the purification and performance of the work, and there sacrificed a white honorary heifer at the altar. The priests sat in the tetrastyle and feasted upon the sacrifice. Then, having taken up their *praetextae* and crowns bound with ears of grain, they ascended the grove of Dea Dia after it had been cleared, and through Quintus Licinius Nepos and Catilius Severus, the *proflamen*, they sacrificed a large and choice victim. When the sacrifice had been completed, they all performed the rites with incense and wine. Then, with crowns placed upon their heads and the standards anointed, they appointed Petronius Priscus, from the first Saturnalian [college], to the second Saturnalian [college], as master, and Flavius Sulpicianus as flamen.

I have reported so many verses of this inscription, though it consists of many more, to show that under Commodus, near the end of the second century, the custom prevailed of engraving in the public records of the priestly colleges among the Romans the year and day on which their sacred rites were undertaken and completed, as well as the names of the college masters and the flamines who had been created.

Another inscription of the same college, under Caracalla, belongs to the third century. It was discovered together with the preceding inscription and may be read in the aforementioned book of Bishop de Turre, published after his dissertations on the ancient monuments of Antium and on Mithras.

Marbles of similar character belong to the fourth century of the Christian era, although they concern Mithras, since the same superstitions were still retained by pagans in the City. In these inscriptions are recorded the consulships and the days of initiation of those enrolled among the Mithraic priests, according to the rite described by Prudentius. The stones that bear witness to this, mentioned by Gruterus on folio 1087, may still be seen in the Barberini palace on the Quirinal.

Although the opening of the inscription contains what are called the Persian, Solar, and Cryptic rites, these are rather words belonging to the sacred ceremonies than proper designations of initiation, as the author cited in the dissertation on Mithras explains in chapter 5, p. 203. Nevertheless, the day and year of the consecration are expressly stated on the same stone. It took place in the first consulship of Valens and the younger Valentinian, when Aurelius Victor Augentius presented the *coracica* to Aemilianus Corfonius, his son, after he had been consecrated priest of the Sun.

> Under the consulship of Datianus and Cerealis, Nonius Victor Olympius, clarissimus vir, and Publius Aurelius Victor Augentius, clarissimus vir, the father, presented the Persian rites on the day before the Nones of April, Felix and Constantius being consuls.  
> They presented the Solar rites on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of May, Felix and Constantius being consuls.  
> They displayed the Cryptic rites on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, Felix and Constantius being consuls.  
> In the first consulship of our lords Valens and Valentinian the Younger, Augusti, on the sixth day before the Ides of April, Aurelius Victor Augentius, clarissimus vir, father, presented to his son Aemilianus Corfonius Olympius, clarissimus puer, in the thirtieth year of his consecration, the *coracica*. Felix and Constantius being consuls, they displayed the Cryptic rites on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

### 23.

Other consecrations marked by a specific day are displayed by Gruterus on folio 28 and the following pages. Among them is the remarkable inscription in which Sextilius Agesilaus Aedesius says that he was reborn for eternity after receiving the *taurobolium* and *criobolium*, in the consulship of our lords Valens for the fifth time and Valentinian the Younger, Augusti, on the Ides of August. From this it may be determined that it was set up near the end of the fourth century, together with several inscriptions of the same period recorded there.

Since, therefore, the priestly colleges of pagan superstition that flourished at Rome from the first century of Christ to the end of the fourth not only committed to writing the calendars and records of their members, their initiations, rites, decrees, and dedications in linen books, or engraved them on ivory tablets, but also carved them in marble and displayed them in the atria and pronaoi of their temples, and even inserted them into calendars set up in the forum in order to secure authority and permanence for their institutions, the practitioners of the Christian profession—no less provident, and instructed by far holier examples in the divine writings of both Testaments—rightly judged it appropriate to issue pontifical registers and to adorn the passions of the martyrs, as triumphal calendars of the Church, with chronological indications of the year or consulship, month, and day on which they had borne witness to the truth by blood and confession.

For they understood that it would be especially pleasing to God and most useful to posterity if the public record were established by written acts, and if an annual memory could preserve the day of their entrance into glory, especially in those suburban cemeteries where martyrs and pontiffs were buried.

That decrees of pontiffs or councils, issued even in earlier centuries before Constantine the Great, were sometimes expressed on tablets or marble pillars is plainly shown by the inscription of the Paschal Canon on an ancient marble monument displaying the pontifical chair of Saint Hippolytus, bishop and martyr, under Severus Alexander, together with the statue of Hippolytus seated upon it. This monument was transferred from the cemetery of Lucina in the Veran district to the Vatican Library, where it has been illuminated by the books of many scholars, led by Baronius and Boucher.

The title is inscribed as follows:

> ἔτους Α etc., that is: In the first year of the reign of Alexander the Emperor, Easter fell on the fourteenth day of April, on a Saturday, when there had been an intercalary month. In the following years it will occur as set out in the table below. In past years it occurred as indicated. The fast, however, must be ended when it falls on Sunday.

On this stone, therefore, engraved in the year 222 of Christ, the sacred law proposed for observance in celebrating the chief feast of the Christian Pasch contains the institution of ending the fast on Sunday. This practice had been handed down by apostolic tradition to the Eastern and Western Churches and confirmed by the decrees of the Roman pontiffs Pius, Eleutherus, and Victor, especially after councils had been summoned at the command of the last of these by Theophilus in Palestine and elsewhere, as will be explained in its proper place.

There thus remain unmistakable traces, engraved on ancient Roman marbles even during the period of persecution, of pontifical constitutions and sacred laws concerning the observance of festivals and the ending of the fast. Already at that time the hierarchs of this Church, the foremost of all, might learn that marbles inscribed with Christian sacred matters ought to be erected like a triumphal pillar above the shattered tablets of pagan superstition.

Those earlier tablets had been dedicated by the Arval Brothers and by other devotees of demonic mysteries, and by the priests of Isis, Serapis, Mithras, the Sun, and the Great Mother, under the deceptive hope that the eternity promised to them would be theirs, as though the defenses of profane worship and vain gods would never perish. Yet in that same century they were given over as spoils and transformed into monuments of the victory won by the truth of the Christian religion over conquered errors.

But this belongs elsewhere. At present we direct attention to it only so that the authority of the statements found in the ancient catalogues of the Roman pontiffs may become clear, especially those of the fourth and sixth centuries. From these periods the composition of this *Liber Pontificalis* under Gregory II and Gregory III is recognized. During those ages the old custom prevailed at Rome, among Christians as well as pagans, of recording on marble tablets, just as in the pontifical books, the acts and decrees of colleges, the initiations and priesthoods, and especially those of persons who presided over the assemblies.

### 24.

The acts and ordinations of the Roman Church are found recorded more splendidly after the freedom of divine worship had been secured by the great Constantine. The blessed Pope Damasus, who arranged for the atria of churches, the entrances to cemeteries, and the tombs of martyrs to be covered with marble tablets—tablets later called *Platoniae*—also composed elegant verses for their inscriptions, incorporating numerous historical records of his predecessors and of the martyrs.

Some of these survive intact in our own age in the underground chamber of the Vatican basilica, in the church of Saint Sebastian outside the walls, and in the title of Equitius. Others are read in Gruterus and in volume IV of Mabillon’s *Veterum Analecta*, having been transcribed in the time of Charlemagne. Still others were collected by Martius Milesius in his edition of the works of the blessed Damasus.

### 25.

Since in the cemeteries of the martyrs the year and day of burial also frequently appear—usually carved with a chisel on the marble tablets closing the burial place, and not rarely written in plaster or painted with vermilion on the cement joining the marble slabs around the edge of the tomb—who cannot see that from these original records were compiled the tablets, lists, and registers of burials, as well as those early materials of the Roman Martyrology discovered by Boucher in manuscripts of the fourth or fifth century and published by him after Victor’s Paschal Canon, in his third booklet, p. 276?

#### Burial of the Bishops

That is, of the Roman bishops from Lucius to Julius.

- On the sixth day before the Kalends of January: Dionysius, at Callistus.
- On the third day before the Kalends of January: Felix, at Callistus.
- On the day before the Kalends of January: Sylvester, at Priscilla’s.
- On the fourth day before the Ides of January: Miltiades, at Callistus.
- On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February: Marcellinus [or Marcellus, at Priscilla’s].
- On the third day before the Nones of March: Lucius, at Callistus.
- On the tenth day before the Kalends of May: Caius, at Callistus.
- On the fourth day before the Nones of August: Stephen, at Callistus.
- On the sixth day before the Kalends of October: Eusebius, at Callistus.
- On the Nones of October: Marcus, at Balbina’s.
- On the sixth day before the Ides of December: Eutychianus, at Callistus.
- On the day before the Ides of April: Julius, on the Via Aurelia at the third milestone, at Callistus.

### 26.

No one who has observed the diligence with which the bishops of the neighboring cities of Italy, with almost equal zeal, preserved the memory of their predecessors for posterity can rightly doubt the careful work of the notaries of the Apostolic See, both in engraving the dates of burial in the tombs of the supreme pontiffs and in compiling diptychs and catalogues from the original inscriptions and records.

Permit me to produce an illustrious document from the Church of Nola. I collected it there fifteen years ago when, having been appointed by our Most Holy Lord Clement XI to the retinue of those whom His Eminence Cardinal Carlo Barberini, legate *a latere* to the Catholic King of Spain, Philip V, then residing at Naples, had selected as assistants to the legation, I went to Nola with the cardinal’s permission to investigate the sacred antiquities of that church and of the cemetery of Saint Felix called “in Pincis.”

Several portions of the basilica survive there, decorated with mosaics and inscriptions by Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola. Although I could publish many monuments of that great sanctuary that are fully worthy of public attention, I shall content myself with those relevant to the subject I have undertaken in this preface: namely, several sarcophagi and funerary tablets of bishops, engraved with the day and year of their burial, the year being indicated by the consuls.

In the mosaic work of the *zophoros* there is an epigram of Saint Paulinus, an equivalent testimony to the sacred building enlarged by him:

> The space before was small, cramped for sacred rites,  
> And refused to open its hands to suppliants.  
> Now spacious, it offers the people altars  
> For pious services in the lap of the middle martyr.  
>   
> All things renewed by God are pleasing. Christ  
> Always renews all things and enlarges them into a mass of light.  
> So also, honoring the throne of his beloved Felix,  
> He advanced it alike in splendor and in space.

On a marble chest beside the altar:
