> BURIAL OF THE HOLY FELIX, BISHOP, ON THE FIFTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF FEBRUARY, IN THE CONSULSHIP OF FAUSTUS AND VALERIUS.

[Note: The year of Christ 438.]

Since the death of Saint Paulinus is assigned to the year 430, Saint Felix, buried eight years later, was of the same age.

On another nearby marble chest:

> BURIAL OF BISHOP PAULINUS THE YOUNGER, ON THE THIRD DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF SEPTEMBER, FLAVIUS DIOSCORUS BEING CONSUL, CLARISSIMUS VIR, CONSUL.

[Note: The inscription is wrongly carved; the consulship of Flavius Dioscorus falls in the year of Christ 442.]

On another sarcophagus the letters of the inscription have been worn away, so that it is uncertain whether a bishop is buried there. The names of the consuls, however, survive intact and indicate the year 359:

> Always, because of your merit, may you live [in] proclamations of praise, and may your good offspring [lacuna] [lacuna] relics [lacuna] [lacuna] [lacuna] you will always be [lacuna] Lord, leader [lacuna] [lacuna] Felix, Eusebius, and Hypatius being consuls. Burial in peace, on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

On another marble:

> Burial of Theodosius, bishop, on the seventh day before the Ides of December, Flavius Faustus the Younger being consul.

[Note: That is, in the year 490.]

The inscription of Bishop Aurelian must not be omitted, although it lacks the indication of the consuls. I do not know whether he was the Aurelian who is counted as the fifth of the bishops of Nola. His years in that see are recorded as follows:

> + Burial of the holy lord Aurelian, bishop, in peace. He lived more than eighty years; he sat [as bishop] for thirty-eight years. He was buried on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.

On the following marble Bishop Leo is commemorated. The inscription seems to belong to the year 547, the sixth year after the consulship of Basil:

> + Here rests Apollonia, a holy virgin,  
> The lord bishop Leo’s sister. She lived more than seventy-five years.  
> She was buried on [lacuna], in the sixth [year] after the consulship [lacuna].

The name of Leo III, bishop, is read on a funerary marble set in the pavement before the apse of the basilica:

> LEO THE THIRD, BISHOP. I BELIEVE THAT HE WILL RISE AGAIN.

There follows the funerary epigram of another Leo, a bishop who had been a monk, set in the pavement:

> Here lies Leo, a holy man, joined [to Christ],  
> Powerful in piety [lacuna]; here he [lacuna],  
> Who, from a monk, in life [lacuna],  
> Restrained himself so greatly and so much  
> That he was almost angelic [lacuna].

The marble inscription of Bishop Lupercus is also visible in the structure, which he himself ordered to be decorated around the year of Christ 555, during the period in which he governed the Church of Nola:

> + Learn what you see: Bishop Lupercus composed and adorned this work in this church. Lupercus, bishop, ordered it to be made for the love of God and of the saints Felix and Paulinus, Rufus, Laurentius, and Patricius.

Saint Patricius, nephew of the blessed Tartinus, bishop of Tours, was a disciple of Saint Paulinus Maximus, bishop of Nola.

The funerary stones of priests, deacons, subdeacons, and sacred virgins that survive in the same church must likewise be considered. Some record the years of their priesthood, the day of their burial, or the consulship.

The marble epitaph of Adeodatus, archpriest, is as follows; a dove is also carved upon it, according to a custom familiar among Christians:

> Adeodatus, an unworthy archpriest of the holy Nola Church, rests here.

These words appear to have been carved on the stone at his own command when he was preparing his tomb. The following words were added by his fellow priests after his death:

> Beloved by God and by men. In the priesthood he was indeed truthful in speech, just in judgment, faithful in what was entrusted to him, gentle, and persuasive for good. In his verses he always led [people] onward. He was generous in his gifts. When he entered Saint Felix, at a time when no one was more esteemed, he lived as a priest all the days of his life. Before his ordination he [lived] thirty years; he sat in the priestly order for fifty years; and he was buried [lacuna].

An ancient marble tablet now fastened to the wall in the apse bears witness to the burial of the priest Uranus, who is known to have been secretary to Saint Paulinus, bishop of Nola. Several letters of Saint Paulinus were also addressed to Uranus:

> Burial of Uranus, priest, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.

The burials of the priest Patricius, the priest Honoratus, and the priest Florentius are also read there.

The burial of the deacon Reparatus includes chronological indications of the nineteenth day of October and the year 553:

> Burial of the holy martyr Reparatus, deacon, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the twelfth year after the consulship of Basil, clarissimus vir.

The burial of the subdeacon Filicellus is recorded on marble, on which the name of Januaria—perhaps his mother, a relative, or a relation by marriage—and the date of the year 536 are visible:

> + Here rests in peace Januaria [lacuna], who lived more than twenty-nine years. With her husband she completed fifteen years, eleven months, and ten days. She was buried on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth year after the consulship of Basil, clarissimus vir, under the first indiction.  
> + Here rests in peace Filicellus, subdeacon, who [lacuna].

Two burials of sacred virgins belong to the fifth century. The first is assigned to the consulship of Aetius, that is, to one of the years 431, 437, 446, or 454:

> Burial of the sacred virgin [lacuna], on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March, Aetius and [lacuna] being consuls, and Paulinus the priest [lacuna].

When I read the name of the virgin Justa together with the consulship of Flavius Severinus, which occurs twice in the calendars, in the years 461 and 482,

> Burial of the sacred virgin Justa, on the fifth day before the Ides of November, Flavius Severinus, clarissimus vir, being consul,

the pious priest in charge of this church, who pointed out these sacred monuments to me, informed me that this last marble tablet had been found inscribed beneath a church column while the wall was being repaired. It closed a burial place hollowed out in the *tophus*, where the intact bones of the virgin Justa were visible, laid there with her hands crossed, with a lead plate placed at her feet. On the plate were visible letters indicating the virgin’s name and status beneath the monogram of Christ the Lord:

> Α Ω JUSTA, VIRGIN.

He also related that a coin of Licinius had been found there.

When I consider all this—how, after Nola had been captured and devastated by the Goths, there still survive within the circuit of a single church, restored and enlarged by the blessed Paulinus, so many remains; and how on the marbles of the fifth and sixth centuries I see the names, ages, and burials of bishops recorded by consulships, while the ordinations of priests are also mentioned, and deacons—as well as subdeacons and sacred virgins—are recorded as having been buried there, without neglecting chronological indications; and when I see that everything was ultimately arranged on the model of the cemeteries of the City, I must draw two conclusions.

The first is that the blessed Paulinus, restorer of that basilica, who was Roman by origin although born in Gaul and who spent most of his life in the City—where he was also enrolled among the senators and held the consulship in the year of Christ 375—having observed the custom of the Roman Church, which carefully maintained such records through its regional notaries, introduced the same custom into the Church of Nola, or confirmed it after it had already been introduced.

The second is that in the age of Paulinus and the period immediately following, namely the fourth century, when that earlier catalogue of the Roman pontiffs was being compiled under Liberius, the history of this Roman Church abounded in so many genuine and public documents that from the mere inspection of the brief inscriptions read in the Christian cemeteries a sufficiently complete chronology of the Roman pontiffs could be gathered. At the very least, the chronology of the pontiffs could not have been transmitted in so distorted a condition that its correction would not have been easy for those who carefully consulted the funerary inscriptions of the Roman Church, especially if they also used the Acts of the martyrs, enclosed in verses by Damasus and engraved on their memorials, comparing them with the inscriptions of the Caesars and magistrates by whose public judgment the martyrs had been condemned and killed for Christ.

### 26.

I now return to the comparison, interrupted earlier, of the records that the bodies or associations—as Cato calls them in Cicero’s *De Senectute*—enrolled in the worship of pagan divinities in the City, namely the Arval Brothers, the greater pontiffs, augurs, Epulones, Sodal Brotherhoods of the Titians, Augustales, devotees of Isis, worshippers of Hercules, the Sun, Mithras, and other such cults, usually divided into decuries, as Fabretti observes in *Inscriptiones*, chapter 6, pp. 429 and 449, customarily engraved and affixed on marble tablets in the inner sanctuaries and vestibules of temples.

Against these records, publicly displayed by pagan superstition, the power and constancy protected by God of our religion appears to have set up a singular contest through the supreme hierarchs of the Church militant of Christ. Thus the records of the true priesthood of the Christian law, engraved in our basilicas, titles, and colleges more enduringly than bronze, offered triumphal calendars, as it were, against the profane initiations and mysteries of pagan impiety in Peter’s Capitol.

For the pontiffs of the Roman Church, in order to preserve memory for all time, establish the trustworthiness of history, and transmit a record to posterity of the eternal priesthood bestowed upon Christ by the Father and communicated by him to Peter and his successors, who exercise his office on earth, displayed there, engraved in marble and bronze, the trophies of the apostles, the sacred laws, the rights of succession, and the observable sequence of events. Meanwhile the priests of idols had collected there, with the utmost superstition, whatever had anywhere been devised for vain errors, as Saint Leo the Great observes in Sermon 1, *On the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul*.

It was therefore fitting that every kind of document should make evident that Christ—God, King, and Priest according to the order of Melchizedek—also rules through his servants in the midst of his enemies (Psalm 110).

To understand this more clearly—a matter of great importance for asserting the historical reliability of the events recorded in the *Liber Pontificalis*—it is useful to observe where the records mentioned shortly before of the co-optations of priests belonging to pagan professions were found: those of the Arval Brothers and of the worshippers of Isis, Attis, the Great Mother, Mithras, and the Sun. The leaders of our religion judged that the records of the true Christian priesthood ought to be set against them.

### 28.

Gruterus, p. 300, affirms that the co-optations of the decuries of that pagan priestly college to which Nero Caesar is recorded as having been enrolled under the emperor Claudius were found at Rome, in the new church of Saint Peter in the Vatican, in June 1596.

Fabretti, *Inscriptiones*, p. 443, states that the records of the college of the Arval Brothers under Domitian were preserved in the archive of the Vatican basilica. The fragment discovered in his own time and published on folio 494 was also kept there.

Initiations of the priests of Mithras, after the *criobolium* and *taurobolium* had been completed, were carved on several altars, together with the names of the consuls and the day of dedication. They were excavated near the bend of the Vatican Circus while the foundations of the southern side of the transept of the basilica were being laid, at the place where the altar of the holy apostles Simon and Jude was later erected.

Jacopo Grimaldi, a notary appointed for this task so that he might carefully commit to writing everything discovered day by day during the demolition of the old basilica and the construction of the new one, reports this. He performed the task diligently in publicly authorized tablets secured with the impression of a seal. The original of these documents is still preserved in the canonical archive of the same chief basilica of the apostles.

Grimaldi therefore lists on folio 43 several marble altars found around the basilica in the same manner and examined by Pompeo Ugonio, a devoted student of antiquity. They indicated that the pagans had worshipped Isis there as the mother of their gods. I shall give Grimaldi’s words:

> In the place where the chapel of the apostles Simon and Jude now stands, in the apse of the new temple facing south, the mausoleum called by writers that of Saint Petronilla, etc. It is written that this place was sacred to Mars. But the learned man and most devoted investigator of the antiquity of the churches of the City, Lord Pompeo Ugonio, a beneficed cleric of the said basilica and an outstanding orator, believes that it was dedicated not to Mars but rather to the Mother, the word having been corrupted from its original form, *Matrem*.  
>   
> Among other considerations, he chiefly draws this conclusion from the fact that in our own time, when, by order of Pope Paul V, the corner of the front façade facing the Campo Santo was being founded, many altars sacred to the Great Idaean Mother of the Gods were excavated there. They were engraved with sacrifices of the *taurobolium* and *criobolium*, belonging to the times of Constantius and Maximian, the most noble Caesars; of Gratian Augustus and Merobaudes in the consulship; and of Valentinian Augustus and Neoterius in the consulship. Other similar altars had formerly been thrown together here and there in contempt and broken by Christians. They are now visible in Cardinal Borghese’s vineyard outside the Salarian Gate.

He presents the inscriptions transcribed from the originals on folio 164. Although some are said to have been published by Martinello in his booklet *On the Image of the Blessed Virgin Mary among the Nuns of Saints Sixtus and Dominic*, and a few occur in Fabretti, *Inscriptiones*, chapter 9, folio 665, neither author publishes them all. It is therefore preferable to present here, from Grimaldi’s manuscript, both the printed and the unpublished inscriptions.

#### 1.

> M. D. M. I. To our lords Constantius and Maximian, most noble Caesars, being consuls for the fifth time, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May: Julius Italicus, clarissimus vir, one of the fifteen men for sacred rites, received the *taurobolium*. Favorably.

[Note: The year of Christ 305.]

#### 2.

[Note: Published by Fabretti, *Inscriptiones*, p. 665. It belongs to the year of Christ 350.]

> Antonin[us] [lacuna], clarissimus vir, pontiff and decemvir for sacred rites, after the *taurobolium* had been completed, on the third day before the Kalends of May, Flavius Anicius and Nigrinianus being consuls, happily consecrated the altar.

#### 3.

> To the all-powerful Mother of the Gods and to Attis, holy Menotyrannus, his preservers, Caelius Hilarianus, clarissimus vir, duodecemvir of the city of Rome, P. S., and hieroceryx, I. M. S. D. L. S. D. Hecate, on the fourth day before the Ides of May, in the consulship of Gratian Augustus and Merobaudes.

[Note: The year of the Lord 377.]

#### 4.

[Note: Taken from Fabretti, no. 2; Grimaldi transcribes it in this manner.]

> Antonin[us] [lacuna], clarissimus vir, pontiff and decemvir for sacred rites, after the *taurobolium* had been completed, on the third day before the Kalends of May, Flavius Anicius and Nigrinianus being consuls, happily consecrated the altar.

#### 5.

> To the all-powerful gods, Lucius Ragonius Venustus, clarissimus vir, public augur of the Roman people, chief pontiff of Vesta, having received the *taurobolium* and *criobolium* on the tenth day before the Kalends of June, in the consulship of our lord Valentinian Augustus for the fourth time and Neoterius, consecrated the altar.

[Note: The year of Christ 390.]

#### 6.

> To the Mother of the Gods and to holy Attis, Menotyrannus, Quintus Clodius Flavianus, clarissimus vir, chief pontiff, one of the fifteen men for sacred rites, one of the seven Epulones, pontiff of the god Sun, having received the *taurobolium* and *criobolium*, dedicated the altar on the Nones of April, Flavius Merobaudes and Flavius Saturninus being consuls.

[Note: The year of Christ 383.]

#### 7.

> The clarissimus vir [lacuna], chief priest of the Great Mother of the Gods, having repeated the *laurobolium* and *criobolium*, dedicated the altar to the all-powerful gods, the Mother of the Gods and Attis, on the Nones of April, Flavius Merobaudes, clarissimus vir, for the second time, and Flavius Saturninus, clarissimus vir, being consuls.

[Note: The year of Christ 383.]

#### 8.

> To the Great Idaean Mother of the Gods, the supreme parent, to Herma and to Attis, Menotyrannus, the unconquered, Claudius Hermogenianus Caesarius, clarissimus vir, proconsul of Africa, prefect of the City of Rome, one of the fifteen men for sacred rites, having received the *taurobolium* and *criobolium* on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, dedicated an altar to the guardians of his soul and mind, in the consulship of our lord Gratian Augustus for the third time and [lacuna] Aequit[ius].

[Note: Grimaldi adds in the margin: “I copied this inscription with great labor because the lettering was already nearly obliterated.”]

#### 9.

The interpretation of the Greek inscription is as follows:

> To the Mother of the Gods: Crescens, priest and crown-bearer of Phoebus, one of the fifteen men, and Leontius, noble and wise men—the one from the East, the other from the West—having performed the sacred rites together for the all-mother goddess Rhea, set up an altar as ministers of the mysteries with the blood of the criobolic initiation and of the taurobolium [the final ritual term is uncertain].

[Note: The text as transmitted reads ΑΕΔΡΙΩΝ, but this is erroneous for ΑΝΔΡΩΝ, “men.”]

To the Mother of the Gods, the quindecemvir, priest crowned for Phoebus, Crescens, and the divine Leontius, wise men—one indeed from the East, the other from the West—performing the rites together, erected an altar to the almighty goddess Rhea, with the sacred blood of the finest victims of the Criobolium and Taurobolium.

[Col. 0065B] “From these,” adds Ugonius, “two verses are hexameters and two pentameters. On the sides it had Cybele with a pine tree, and Attis with the heads of oxen. It is exceedingly astonishing how the enemy of the human race had intruded beside the holiest basilica of the whole world in order to celebrate so great an abomination of idolatrous sacrifices in the times of Christian emperors. Nor is it astonishing if the very altars were found broken with a hammer by some excellent man and buried in a heap.”

29. This final conjecture of Ugonius, confirmed by so many stones, which recommended the view that the rites of the Great and Idaean Mother had customarily been performed in the Vatican, has in our age acquired the force of a demonstration from another very celebrated inscription, discovered on the summit of the hill of the colony of Lugdunum [Col. 0065C] in Gaul. The most reverend Father Dominicus de Colonia, S.J., a theologian whom I esteem highly for many reasons and whom, because of his singular benevolence no less than his learning, I must revere above all, published it and explained it with the exceptionally refined erudition of which he is possessed. Five years ago, when I was inspecting Roman antiquities that were frequently encountered at Lyon, he showed me an altar of the Taurobolium, engraved with its signs and excavated on that hill, and wished to present me with a copy of his commentary on it as a most precious token of our hospitality. Above all, he then pointed out that the following words could be clearly read in the inscription of that altar:

**VIRES EXCEPIT, ET A VATICANO TRANSTULIT**

“He received the strength, and transferred it from the Vatican.”

For he expressly teaches that this must be understood of the Vatican Hill of the City of Rome, since no place of that name is found in the colony of Lugdunum. When I had returned to Rome, and the book of Grimaldi had been given to me, recalling the inscriptions already reported concerning the Mother of the Gods and the Taurobolium and Criobolium received, and indicating the place of excavation in the Vatican, I understood that by this single Lugdunian altar the use of the others found near the Vatican basilica was demonstrated. Moreover, this Lugdunian altar shows that the practice of which he speaks—the transfer of the superstitious worship of the Idaean Mother, the Taurobolium, and the Criobolium from the Roman Vatican Hill to the colonies—was in force under the Antonines.

**VIRES TAVRI**, that is, as Father de Colonia wisely explains with Salmasius, the horns of that animal, or of the victim slaughtered in the Taurobolium at the Vatican Hill of Rome, were transferred together with the **ARA** and **BUCRANIUM** to the colony, where it had been decreed that the rites of the Great Idaean Mother of the Gods should be performed according to the Roman rite by priests adorned with the *occabus* and crown by the quindecemvirs charged with sacred rites. It is preferable to borrow from the cited book of Father de Colonia the inscription of that Lugdunian altar, which agrees exactly with the original that I myself examined:

> **TAVROBOLIO MATRIS D M I D QVOD FACTVM EST EX IMPERIO MATRIS D DEVM PRO SALVTE IMPERATORIS CAES T, AELI HADRIANI ANTONINI AVG. PII PP LIBERORVMQVE EIVS ET STATVS COLONIAE LVGVDVN L. AEMILIVS CARPVS IIIIII VIR. AVG. ITEM DENDROPHORVS**

“For the Taurobolium of the Mother of the Gods, the Great Idaean Mother, which was performed by command of the Mother of the Gods for the welfare of the emperor Caesar Titus Aelius Hadrianus Antoninus Augustus Pius, father of his country, and of his children, and for the well-being of the colony of Lugdunum: Lucius Aemilius Carpus, Augustal sevir, likewise dendrophorus.”

Here is carved the head of a bull, or bucranium, [Col. 0066D] crowned. Beneath it one reads:

> **VIRES EXCEPIT EX VATICANO TRANSTULIT ARA ET BVCRANIVM SVO INPENDIO CONSECRAVIT SACERDOTE Q. SAMMIO SECVNDO AB XV VIRIS OCCABO ET CORONA EXORNATO CVI SANCTISSIMVS ORDO LVGVDVNENS PERPETVITATEM SACERDOTI DECREVIT APP. ANNIO ATILIO BRADVA T. CLOD. VIBIO VARO COS**

“He received the strength; he transferred it from the Vatican. At his own expense he consecrated the altar and bucranium, with Quintus Sammius Secundus as priest, adorned by the quindecemvirs with the *occabus* and crown. To him the most sacred council of Lugdunum decreed perpetual priesthood, during the consulship of Appius Annius Atilius Bradua and Titus Clodius Vibius Varus.”

On the left side of the same altar is carved a ram’s skull, indicating the Criobolium.

On the right side there is the figure of a knife, with the letters:

> **CVIVS MESONYCTIVM FACTVM EST V. ID. DEC**

“Whose midnight rite was performed on the fifth day before the Ides of December.”

The learned interpreter of this monument aptly observes, [Col. 0067B] from Tertullian, Ambrose, Firmicus Maternus, and other ancient writers, that it was instituted by the devil—whose role is to invert the truth—so that he might imitate even the realities of the divine sacraments, to use Tertullian’s words, in the mysteries of idols. “He too certainly washes his believers and faithful ones and promises purification from the bath.” From the words of Firmicus he likewise shows that, among the errors of profane religions, a belief was slyly introduced by the spirit of falsehood that crimes could be cleansed through the blood of a victim poured out before the altars of idols. In the rite described by Ausonius in the Taurobolium and Criobolium, they were sprinkled in such a way that, as though dew were falling, the limbs and garments of the priest undergoing initiation—who lay hidden beneath a trench—were drenched with that blood.

By such deceits the teacher of impiety [Col. 0067C] and rebellious spirit against God sought to mock the holier mysteries of both Testaments, transferring to the abuse of superstition the sprinkling of blood that had been employed by divine command through Moses in the consecration of the high priest Aaron and his sons; and by sacrilegious daring attempting to oppose those foul imitations of washing to the doctrines of our hope and faith, which teach that through Christ’s precious blood we are cleansed and that his children are consecrated in the saving bath of baptism, while priests are dedicated in that same blood through the anointing of the order and sign instituted by the eternal high priest.

But inspection of the aforementioned marbles reveals how far advanced, though futile, were the arts and the malice of the evil spirit. For he proceeded to such madness that he imagined he could overturn the hierarchy of the Church, and hoped to accomplish this if he inspired his followers to disseminate from the Vatican—where Peter, by Christ’s authority, had established the center of Christian communion—the mysteries of the Idaean Mother of the Gods throughout the Roman world under the authority of the quindecemvirs.

The enemy of the human race saw that, after Peter’s death, bishops were sent out by his successors, just as Peter himself had been accustomed to send them throughout the whole world; he saw that the unity of the Church was preserved through the bond of the supreme priesthood instituted by God; and he perceived that, at the command of the chief bishop, all the members were gathered in councils and directed by laws, while the Roman bishop, successor and helmsman seated on Peter’s chair, governed the whole Christian order as Christ’s vicar, as though at the helm of the commonwealth of Christ.

The enemy of truth and religion therefore devised [Col. 0068A] the plan of sending his own hierarchs from the vicinity of Peter’s chair into the provinces and colonies of the Roman people. In the Vatican—at the very foot of Peter’s throne—he began to establish altars of Mithras, Isis, and the Great Mother, together with Taurobolia, Criobolia, and similar monstrosities of gods and mysteries, so that from there he might spread his impious worship in both directions, to the East and to the West. This is suggested not obscurely by the Greek inscription above, no. 28.

Nor does the date of the transfer of the sacred rites recorded on the Lugdunian marble encourage any other conclusion. Father de Colonia aptly observes, together with several learned men, that before the reign of Antoninus Pius no Taurobolium, or its rite transferred from Rome, is found; nor is any performed or received at Rome or in the provinces mentioned in ancient monuments or histories. We may therefore conclude that, around the period when Hadrian and Antoninus were occupied with organizing the provinces of the empire, and when Peter’s successors were similarly occupied with arranging the episcopal sees, while they were gathering the clergy at the recently constructed shrine of the apostles’ trophies established by Evaristus in the Confession of Blessed Peter, and sending out bishops, priests, and deacons initiated into the sacred orders to perform Christian rites in the suburban sees, in the urban titular churches, and in the provinces—even among the Britons, who were separated from the rest of the world—in that period, I say, when the chief bishops of our religion were thus administering the sacred principate and priesthood of Christ, the quindecemvirs charged with sacred rites and the other initiates of demons, raising the idol Dagon [Col. 0068C] against the ark of the Lord, established at the foot of the Vatican Hill the Taurobolia and Criobolia of the Great Mother, and sent to the colonies priests adorned and crowned with the *occabus*, together with the altar, strength, and bucranium received there, in order to spread the contagion of their superstition through the provinces.

30. But just as once Dagon, cut into pieces and thrown down before the standing ark of the Lord, was found as a mere trunk, so too those monuments of the Mother of the Gods, Mithras, the Arval Brothers, and the quindecemvirs were found broken and scattered in disorder by Christians, and thrown down to serve as a footstool for the Fisherman’s feet. While they lay before his basilica, they became future signs of the victory won by our faith over the nations and their superstitions.

These fragments reveal [Col. 0068D] the empty imitation of declining idolatry, identified by Tertullian in the mysteries of idols: an imitation that transferred even the realities of the sacraments to the abuse of superstition. Through the sprinkling of blood, the observance of the midnight rite, and the selection of the Vatican area and the month of December, it sought to pervert the holier institutions of our religion, and through altars, tablets, and marble and bronze plaques to transmit its profane mysteries to posterity.

But our prelates, displaying amid the ruins of prostrate superstition the standing ark of God and the rock, never to be overthrown by the powers of hell, upon which the Church has been built, have steadfastly continued for more than sixteen hundred years, with Leo the Great and his predecessors and successors, to impose fasts on the fourth and sixth days of the week according to the custom of the fathers, and to celebrate vigils on Saturday at Blessed Peter’s. On these occasions, especially in December, they carry out the ordinations of ministers and priests, both of the minor and the major orders. Nor have they neglected to inscribe upon the basilica’s *platonias* monuments that would never perish, commemorating the Christian priesthood. From these the pontifical history could be gathered and confirmed when the Catalogues were compiled under Liberius and Felix IV, and when the Lives of the pontiffs were collected under Gregory II and Gregory III.

31. It will be pleasant to examine how abundant a supply of documents remained from that period, not only in the codices of the apostolic archive but also on the walls and marbles of sacred buildings—documents that would corroborate most of the matters stated in this *Pontifical Book*. The material found in the Lives of the pontiffs attributed to Anastasius can be reduced approximately to three headings.

The first is chronological, indicating the period of each pontiff’s tenure on Peter’s chair and the consuls corresponding to the beginning and end of each pontificate. The second consists of decrees and ordinations of priests and ministers. The third includes grants of estates, the construction of basilicas and titular churches, and the ornaments and valuable furnishings offered to the Church by Roman pontiffs, emperors, and other rulers.

The documents relating to these three headings were so openly available under Gregory III, when this *Pontifical Book* appeared publicly, that many of them could be read on genuine marbles. We may judge the abundance of the documents [Col. 0069C] from those that, after a thousand years have elapsed since the age of Gregory III, can still be seen in the urban titular churches, cemeteries, basilicas, and archives.

32. As regards the first heading, the pontifical chronology properly verified by the consuls, we have shown that in the Acts of the Martyrs, on the *platonias* engraved by Blessed Damasus, and in Christian cemeteries, tomb niches, and other places, so many documents of the custom of that age still survive that in the fourth and sixth centuries of the Christian era indexes, catalogues, diptychs, and martyrologies could abundantly have been compiled from them.

A book printed at Rome in 1654, containing the ancient inscriptions surviving in the Basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, is in everyone’s hands. As an experiment, it pleased me to count how many consulships they contain. I read more than eighty-two among those belonging to Christians, extending to the number 436. There are, moreover, numerous inscriptions whose fragments do not preserve enough of the wording of the names of the consuls indicated for it to be understood to which consuls they refer; I therefore thought these should be excluded from the aforementioned total.

If, then, in a single Roman sacred building, after a thousand years from the compilation of the *Pontifical Book*, so many pairs of consuls survive that they can fill almost a seventh of the consular Fasti from Tiberius to Justinian, or from the year of the Lord’s Passion to Felix IV, how much more do we suppose was open to everyone’s eyes under Liberius and Damasus, while the catalogues were being written [Col. 0070A] and the deeds of the martyrs were being celebrated in poems engraved on the *platonias*, before the City had been captured and plundered by the Goths, Vandals, and Huns?

If the pagan Delphinius arranged the Roman Fasti from Brutus and Collatinus to Julius Caesar, collecting the Capitoline marbles from the remains of the Roman Forum and from fragments that had been rashly transferred to a few of the City’s churches, as Panvinius relates, fifteen hundred years after they had been placed in the Forum, how many resources for chronology do we believe the authors of the pontifical Catalogues under Liberius and Damasus possessed? Especially since, at that time, after the Chronicle of Eusebius had been arranged by consuls from public records supplied by all the provinces of the empire at the command of the Great Constantine, the consular and pontifical Fasti did not so much need to be reprinted [Col. 0070B] as compared with the Latin registers of notaries, cemeteries, indexes, and diptychs, against which the Catalogues were tested as against a Lydian stone.

The anonymous compiler of the Fasti under Constantius, first discovered by Cuspinianus and soon afterward by Bucherius—who, as a more impartial evaluator of that distinguished monument, left it to the more fortunate care of Cardinal Norisius for elucidation—this anonymous compiler, I say, sufficiently shows how many aids supported the consular epochs in the West, to which the pontifical ones could easily be attached, even without the assistance of the Eusebian Chronicle.

I therefore consider it less necessary to dwell longer on the foundation of this first heading, since the resources of pontifical and consular chronology were readily available to anyone who exercised moderate care in the fourth Christian century in observing the Roman monuments, before they were displaced by the Goths and Vandals. At the beginning of the fifth Christian century, although the flood of barbarians poured over the City declared war on the liberal arts and destroyed many ornaments, it was nevertheless quite unable to abolish the greater part of the documents or to leave chronologists and historians without witnesses to the times and events.

For just as, before the Gothic invasion, Jerome extended the Fasti and Chronicle of Eusebius, and Prosper that of Jerome, to the sixth consulship of Valens and the second of Valentinian, that is, to the Christian year 378, so in the fifth century Victor of Aquitaine continued to arrange the Paschal Canon and the period of 532 years by consuls from the two Gemini, in the year of Christ 28, to Constantine and Rufus, in the year of Christ [Col. 0070D] 457. An anonymous writer of the sixth century extended this to the end of the Victorian period, after the eighteenth consulship of Basil, in the year of Christ 559; it is still read in Bucherius.

Moreover, the marble Fasti discovered in the colonies, fragments of which were published by Gruterus, folio CCIC, and Fabrettus, *Inscriptiones*, folio 485, besides other unpublished material that we shall publish in due time, list the ordinary consuls of Rome together with the magistrates of the colony or municipality. They show that documents of public works in which the succession of the Roman consuls could be recognized could be observed not only at Rome but also in the provinces.

With regard, therefore, to the first heading, the consular chronology to be reconciled with the pontifical chronology, I believe it sufficiently clear that documents were preserved in the fourth and sixth centuries for the authors of the Catalogues under Liberius and Felix IV.

33. I shall now turn to the second heading of the matters set out in these Lives of the pontiffs, which includes certain of their decrees and the number of sacred ordinations that each performed.

The decrees generally concerned discipline, the ministries of the liturgy, and the rite of the sacraments. For the doctrines of our faith, if heretics happened to attempt to overthrow any of them, the pontiffs defended against their audacity through the recitation of the apostolic Creed, the traditions of the fathers, and the prohibition of sacred rites.

Although these safeguards of the faith were for the most part covered by the discipline of secrecy and therefore were not to be openly engraved on marbles in that period, but were to be preserved in the archives of the Church together with the divine Scriptures and the genuine works of the Fathers, they are nevertheless indicated to the faithful on the marble of Hippolytus, bishop and martyr. There, the catalogue of his writings indicates that the apostolic traditions had already been collected at that time, in the words:

> **ΑΠΟϹΤΟΛΙϹΗ ΠΑΡΑΔΟϹΙϹ**  
> “Apostolic tradition”

and in the dogmatic treatises:

> **ΠΕΡΙ ΘΥ ΚΑΙ ϹΑΡΚΟϹ ΑΝΑϹΤΑϹΕΩϹ**  
> “Concerning God and the resurrection of the flesh,”

and:

> **ΠΕΡΙ ΤΟΥ ΑΓΑΘΟΥ ΚΑΙ ΠΟΘΕΝ ΤΟ ΚΑΚΟΝ**  
> “Concerning the good and whence evil comes.”

When necessity demanded that more serious cases be judged in councils held at the apostolic see and that the decisions of the Fathers be confirmed by the authority of the Roman pontiff, the pontiff’s letter and the acts of the council were transmitted to the principal Churches. A celebrated example occurs in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 43:

“Letters of Cornelius, bishop of the Romans, sent to Fabius, bishop of the Church of Antioch, still exist,” he says, “in which the proceedings of the Roman synod, and the decisions of all those throughout Italy, Africa, and the other provinces of those regions, are declared.”

The letters that the successors of Peter sent to the Churches were received with such reverence and held in such esteem that the same History of Eusebius teaches us that the letter which Clement had written in the name of the Roman Church to the Corinthians was accustomed to be publicly read in many Churches, both in his own time and in the preceding generation (Eusebius, *History*, book III, chapter 16). It was regarded as so close in authority to the Epistle of Paul to the Hebrews that it appears to have been included among the other writings of the Apostle for good reason (ibid., chapter 38).

But, as I was observing, in these Lives of the pontiffs [Col. 0071D] the decrees generally concern discipline, and the greater part relates to the liturgy. This part of pontifical history therefore rested on the evidence of the daily ministry, carried out according to the rite of the apostolic see and subsequently arranged in the Gelasian Sacramentary, or in what is called the Roman Order. Thus a monument of such rites and decrees, more enduring than bronze, was consecrated in the daily practice of the Roman Church.

34. Moreover, in the letters of the pontiffs of the Roman Church that I mentioned shortly before—letters transmitted to and carefully preserved in the archives of the principal sees—the practice of the discipline of the sacraments and of other rites shines forth. This practice both confirms and illuminates the decrees issued by their predecessors.

[Col. 0072A] In the celebrated letter of Pope Cornelius to Fabius of Antioch, around the year of Christ 255, while it is related that three bishops had been suborned and summoned by the presbyter Novatian so that they might confer the episcopate upon him by the laying on of hands, it is wonderfully confirmed that this rite must be traced back to the age of the apostles. Morinus concludes that it was also observed in the Greek Church fifteen hundred years ago (*On Sacred Ordinations*, part II, p. 21), from the order first published by Clement of Rome at the command of Blessed Peter and soon enlarged by later generations.

Hence the author of these Lives did not assert without usefulness or authority in the Life of Clement:

“Therefore Linus and Cletus are recorded before him, because they were ordained bishops by the prince of the apostles himself to perform the priestly ministry.”

For when the prince of the apostles established the model by which the other Churches were to be ordered and governed, he did not fail to designate two bishops who would remain at his side, with whom he might lay hands upon bishops to be ordained in various places in the City, in order to provide that ministry of the greater priesthood which required three bishops. Hence among the canons called apostolic there is held to be the first, which establishes that a bishop is to be ordained through the ministry of three bishops.

In the same letter of Cornelius, Novatian is rightly censured because, after recovering from the illness during which he had received baptism, he had not taken care of the remaining matters that ought to be received according to ecclesiastical regulation, nor had he been confirmed by a bishop.

Who would not see that this clearly proves that ecclesiastical regulations concerning the rites of baptism had been established before Cornelius and were to be observed even by those who, under the pressure of necessity, had received the sacrament’s abbreviated benefit, in accordance with the definition of Pope Victor’s decree, enacted sixty years earlier and expressed in his Life as follows?

“He decreed that, when necessity required it, wherever a person was found—whether in a river, in the sea, or in springs—anyone coming from paganism to be baptized should receive baptism once his confession of Christian belief had been made clear.”

Who would not understand that this proves the apostolic discipline of chrism, to be administered by a bishop and not by an ordinary presbyter, which Cornelius rightly censures Novatian for having neglected?

Again, Cornelius exercises judgment against the bishops secretly summoned by Novatian’s supporters for his consecration, rebuking them for having been gathered clandestinely. This was contrary to the decrees of Sixtus and Zephyrinus, recorded in this *Pontifical Book* concerning the letters of authorization to be obtained from the patriarch, under which a bishop, leaving his own see and coming to Rome, was to have the right to return.

Indeed, Cornelius declares that they had conferred upon Novatian an invalid and shadowy consecration after they had been shut in, **συγκλεισθέντας**, at the tenth hour, **ὡρᾷ δεκάτῃ**, drunk and overcome by excess, **μεθύοντας καὶ κραιπαλόντας**. These vices in the ordination clearly indicate the contrary canons of the former bishops of the Roman see—namely, the canon of Telesphorus, who assigned the celebration of Mass from the third hour, at which our Lord ascended the cross, to the ninth hour, at which he expired on the cross, as is explicitly read below in his Life, except on the night of the Nativity of the Lord; and that of Zephyrinus, who ordered that an individual be ordained, whether deacon or priest, in the presence of all the clergy and the faithful laity (Eusebius, p. 245, *History*, book VI).

This also becomes clear in another passage of the letter, where it is said that Novatian had been honored with the dignity of the presbyterate by a bishop who had dealt indulgently with him, even though the entire clergy and many of the people opposed it, because no one who, under the pressure of severe illness, had been washed in bed as Novatian had been was permitted to be admitted to the clergy.

Tertullian confirms these matters in his book *On Fasting against the Psychics*. Although he attacks the practice of the Roman Church, he nevertheless illuminates it by showing that the fast, extended to the ninth hour at which the Lord expired, then permitted the taking of food. Therefore Pope Cornelius rightly censures those bishops who, not fasting but bloated with food and wine, exercised the laying on of hands at the tenth hour.

Finally, in the catalogue of Novatian’s offenses, when the most serious charge is recited concerning the sacrilegious oath he exacted from those to whom he was to distribute the Lord’s Body, the contrary discipline proscribed by the decrees of Zephyrinus, recorded in this *Pontifical Book*, emerges.

“The following regulation concerning the Church,” says the author in the Life of Zephyrinus, “was established: ministers were to carry glass patens before the priests into the church until the bishop celebrated Mass, with the priests standing before him, and Mass was thus to be celebrated. The bishop’s right was excepted, so that only the clergy should support it, while all present at that consecration received from the hand of the bishop the consecrated crown, already prepared, and the presbyter was to deliver it to the people.”

This discipline had been established by Zephyrinus. We learn from Pope Cornelius’s letter what Novatian attempted against it:

“After the offering had been made, while dividing a portion among each person and handing it over, he compels wretched men to swear in place of a blessing, holding the hands of the person receiving the portion clasped in both his own and not releasing them until those who had sworn had said the following”—I shall use his own words—“‘Swear to me by the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ that you will never abandon my party or return to Cornelius.’ Thus the wretched man is not permitted to taste until he has invoked evil upon himself. And when he ought to say ‘Amen’ upon receiving that bread, he says instead: ‘I shall not return again to Cornelius.’”

[Col. 0073D] 35. It is astonishing to say how many supports for the history of the pontificate of this *Book* are contained in the brief fragment of one of the letters of Saint Pope Cornelius preserved for us by Eusebius. How many aids, then, remained for the notaries of the Roman Church, contemporaries of Eusebius, when they were collecting the Acts and Lives of the pontiffs from the archives that preserved the rescripts concerning each one’s affairs?

Let me repeat one further observation drawn from the same fragment of the letter of Cornelius, which will wonderfully illuminate the documents concerning both decrees and ordinations so carefully recorded in those Lives.

Concerning Novatian’s stupidity, Pope Cornelius writes:

“Thus that defender of the Gospel did not know that there ought to be one bishop in the Catholic Church. Yet in that Church he knew—for how could he have failed to know it?—that there were forty-four presbyters; seven deacons and just as many subdeacons; forty-two acolytes; and fifty-two exorcists and readers together with doorkeepers.”

In the Life of Hyginus we shall find the following written out:

“He organized the clergy and distributed it into grades.”

Evaristus is said to have assigned the number of seven deacons. Here we read that an equal number of subdeacons was established by Fabian, the immediate predecessor of Cornelius. From Zephyrinus we have learned that the ordination of clerics was to be celebrated in the presence of the clergy and the people.

Cornelius therefore rightly wonders that Novatian, a presbyter of the Roman Church and one aspiring to its episcopate, did not know the number of those ordained. Indeed, he asks how it could have happened [Col. 0074B] that he alone was ignorant of a matter so well known. Certainly, since the times for exercising the orders had been defined by regulations, and letters of authorization were to be given to those departing from the bishop, the indexes and diptychs of all the clergy and the dates of their ordinations ought to have been carefully written and preserved by the pontiffs’ assistants and the notaries of the Roman Church. Therefore these public documents from the Church’s archives, to be produced repeatedly for frequent use, could certainly not have been lacking from the written sources of the Lives of the pontiffs.

Closely related to the ordinations of clerics is the record of the consecrations of a titular church, a font, and an altar, and of the offering of gifts that the bishop distributed on that occasion. It is enough to touch on this lightly and indicate how abundant a supply of documents was available for the work of Anastasius, especially in those periods when the Catalogues and Lives were being written. I confidently state that much remained not only on the parchments and papyrus sheets of the archive but also on the marbles, metals, and ornaments of the Church.

We still see a consecration of a titular church from the fourth century engraved on a marble tablet by Saint Damasus, surviving among those distinguished inscriptions once collected by Fulvius Ursinus and, after his death, rescued from destruction through the generosity of Cardinal Alessandro Farnese. He left them, placed in a very secure location in the palace of his most illustrious house near the Campo dei Fiori and enclosed with iron bars, to be arranged for the care of posterity.

As I write this, the most illustrious Duke of Parma and Piacenza, Francesco, born for the singular purpose of pursuing learned antiquity, defending ancestral glory, and advancing the commonwealth and letters, cherishes and protects them. Because of his exceptional devotion to antiquity, he has ordered them to be affixed in a more distinguished place in the same palace and displayed before everyone’s eyes.

The tablet of which I speak is very short, as befits its title. It is made of a marble crust half a palm in thickness and engraved with these letters:

> **T. I. X. N. EGO DAMASI VS. VRB ROME EPS AN C DOMV COSECRAVI . . N. R. Q. S. M. S. PA. S.PE**

The meaning of these words seems to be:

“Title in the name of Christ. I, Damasus”—for I find both *Damasium* and *Damasum* written indiscriminately in ancient monuments—“bishop of the city of Rome, consecrated this house.”

I do not understand the meaning of the following sigla, unless perhaps the final ones, **S. PA. S. PE.**, should be interpreted as “Saint Paul, Saint Peter,” as a seal proper to this Roman Church and preserved by its successors in the public documents of decrees and letters. I am happy to believe that this is the case.

On the reverse side of the same tablet are read the names of the saints whose relics were enclosed beneath that seal of the title and dedication, according to a rite transmitted even to our own times:

> **HIC REQVIESCIT CAPVT SCI CRESCENTINI. M. ET RELIQVIE. S. SVANT**

“Here rests the head of Saint Crescentinus, martyr, and the relics of Saint Suant.”

Together with the title thus engraved, the front face [Col. 0075B] of a Christian sarcophagus is visible, on which is carved a monogram of the name of Christ the Lord within a crown with ribbons, in the familiar style of the age of Blessed Damasus.

It is not unlike another tablet in form or size, which Cardinal Francesco Barberini, vice-chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, substituted in more distinguished marble for the principal altar of his titular church of Saint Lawrence in Damaso, imitating, as I believe, the ancient front of the altar. This tablet was perhaps transferred to the Farnese buildings when Cardinal Farnese adorned the same titular church and principal altar with various ornaments, as the family insignia testify on the ceiling and walls, rendered in gold and colors by Taddeo Zuccaro. The cardinal also commissioned him to have the deeds of the life and martyrdom of Blessed Lawrence elegantly painted.

The Ritual and Pontifical Books of the Roman Church [Col. 0075C] prescribe, according to ancient custom, at the dedication of a church and altar, that the date of the consecration be committed to writing and deposited with the relics of the saints beneath the altar table by the consecrating bishop, for the perpetual remembrance of the event.

The devout and learned collectors of the sacred rites also observe—especially the most reverend Father Edmund Martène, in volume three of his celebrated work *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, book II, chapter 12—that both in the East and in the West, from the age of Constantine the Great onward, it became customary for the dedications of churches and altars generally to be performed in an assembly of bishops, who were customarily invited for that purpose.

There still survive in the Acts of the Council of Tyre, in Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book IV, chapter 43; of Constantinople, book II, chapter 39, in Socrates; of Orange in 441, chapter 10; of Arles II, chapter 37; and in the letters of Blessed Ambrose, letter 22 to Marcellinus, and several others, records of the day chosen for the dedication. Thus the dates of dedications were included not only in public acts but also in synodal acts.

Moreover, from letter 9 of Gelasius I, chapters 4 and 25, and from Saint Gregory the Great, book V, letter 45, they infer that the ministry of dedicating a church was regarded as so distinguished that in Italy diocesan bishops in the fourth and fifth centuries did not presume to perform it unless they had first obtained permission from the supreme pontiff.

Furthermore, the custom of marking the date of the foundation stone when laying it in the foundation of churches was also established in the provinces, as the Massilian marble teaches us. It was published by the distinguished man Stefano Baluzius in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the commentary on Lactantius, and by the illustrious historians of Marseille, the Ruffi, book X, p. 46. It records that the foundation stone of that church, restored from its foundations, was laid during the sixth consulship of Valentinian Augustus, namely in the year of Christ 445, [Col. 0076C] on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the nineteenth year of the episcopate of Rusticus. The names of the bishops who collected contributions for the construction of the sacred building are also recorded, together with the sum of solidi that each contributed.

It is expressed in abbreviated letters in the following manner, just as the inscription of Damasus recited shortly before:

[Col. 0075]

> **+ DO. ET XPO MISERANTE. LIM. HOC. C. L. K. T. E. ANNO IIII. C. S. VALENTINIANO. AVG. VI. III. KL. D. XVIIII. ANNO EPTVS RVSTI. . . . . . .**

“By the mercy of God and Christ, this threshold was laid in the fourth year, in the sixth consulship of Valentinian Augustus, on the third day before the Kalends of December, in the nineteenth year of the episcopate of Rusticus.”

[Col. 0075C] In the ancient mosaic of the church of Saint Sabina on the Aventine, the clergy of that titular church similarly expressed the date of the pontificate of Saint Celestine, under whose governance that sacred building was being erected on a more magnificent scale:

> **+ Culmen apostolicum cum Caelestinus haberet**  
> **Primus et in toto fulgeret episcopus orbe**  
> **Haec quae miraris fundavit presbyter urbis**  
> **Illyrica de gente Petrus, etc.**

“While Celestine held the apostolic height, and as the first bishop shone throughout the whole world, Peter, a presbyter of the City, of Illyrian stock, founded this building that you admire, and so forth.”

We can therefore easily understand what monuments of the dedications of sacred buildings must then have survived in so many marbles and mosaics, in the letters of those who dedicated and authorized them, in synodal acts, and in the diptychs and calendars of the churches, which recalled the day of the dedication each year.

### 36

Ancient epigrams, printed in Gruter’s work, p. 1163, no. 11, and p. 1164, nos. 2 and 4, commemorated the sacred fonts constructed through the care of Popes Damasus, Hilary, Boniface, Celestine, and John. Elegant verses carved by Sixtus III in the octagonal Lateran baptistery, reported by Panvinius in his book *On the Seven Churches of Rome* and by Cardinal Rasponi in book III, chapter 1, of *On the Lateran Basilica*, can still be read on the Constantinian architraves. In the same way, the verses of Ambrose were read on the font of the Church of Blessed Thecla, of the same octagonal form—whose symbolism the holy bishop explains there—and were published by Gruter from an ancient manuscript, p. 1168, no. 8, together with the other epigrams of the blessed teacher. These indicate the dedications that he himself carried out and the ritual mysteries employed in them.

Under Pope Siricius, we see, in the *platonia* of Saint Pudentiana, or the Title of Pastor, an epochal inscription—contemporary with Saint Ambrose—recording the restoration of the presbytery:

> **With Bishop Siricius, and Felix and Leopardus, of the holy church, safe [the inscription’s syntax is elliptical]:**

The remainder is missing. Hilary the archdeacon, later Roman pontiff, had an inscription engraved for the oratory of Saint Lawrence, which he had restored. This inscription, discovered among the ruins of that same building near Saint Eusebius, is preserved in the collection of ancient marbles of the Albani Museum:

> **With the Lord God assisting and the blessed martyr Lawrence interceding, Hilary, archdeacon, made this.**

At these celebrations of consecrations, many gifts were offered and dedicated through the generosity of emperors or bishops—both movable and immovable property, which the *Book of the Pontiffs* frequently records. We shall present the documents of these gifts, which constitute the third division of our subject, more suitably if we may first finish briefly indicating what remains to be said in this chapter concerning the decrees of the pontiffs: decrees embracing the dedication of sacred buildings and the ordination of priests and ministers.

### 37

The decrees of the pontiffs and councils must be considered—those concerning the anniversaries of martyrs and churches that we read as having been written even during the continuing persecution in Cyprian, book III, letter 6:

> “Record the days on which they departed, so that we may celebrate their commemorations among the memorials of the martyrs.”

These correspond to the laws enacted through Clement and Anterus concerning the writing of the acts of the martyrs and their deposition in the church, as well as to those enacted in the same century by Pope Felix, which are indicated in his *Life* as follows:

> “He established that Masses should be celebrated over the tombs of the martyrs.”

They are confirmed by the diptychs and martyrologies of the following centuries, and by that established custom which Tertullian commends in *On the Crown of the Soldier* when he reviews it.

Finally, in the age of Saint Gregory III, when the lives of the pontiffs were being collected and compiled into this Book, the acts of the Roman council and the decrees of that same pontiff, which the author of his life mentions toward the end, were carved on marble tablets displayed in the Vatican basilica. They may still be read, preserved after ten centuries and carefully kept in the hypogeum of the same basilica together with the other ancient memorials of the old basilica discovered under Paul V:

> **With Peter, Theophanes, Sergius, Jordan, and John present, together also with the deacons Moschus the archdeacon, Zachariah, John, Theophylact, and Gemmulus, or the entire clergy, the aforesaid lord Gregory, apostolic pope, said: “I recall to mind, my most holy brothers …”**

The remainder may be read in Torrigius, *On the Vatican Crypts*, p. 70, and in Ciampini, *On the Sacred Buildings Constructed by Constantine the Great*, chapter 4, section 15, p. 101.

### 38

We therefore learn that the Roman Church did not neglect to record the acts of its pontiffs and councils on marble tablets and to affix, in the most celebrated place of Christian assembly—that is, at the threshold of the Apostles—documents for posterity concerning our laws and trophies of victory over the pagan superstitions of the ethnic peoples whom Rome had conquered. Thus, where the decrees and rites of the Arval Brothers and the Quindecemvirs concerning the annual renewal of profane sacrifices for the safety of the Caesars were once read—those decrees that we produced above under numbers 21 and 22—there could be seen the responses of our bishops and the acts of councils decreeing that a divine service should be performed in memory of the martyrs and confessors of Christ and that sacred hymns should be sung.

A document of the pontifical law of that same Gregory III concerning daily sacred offerings to be brought above the Confession of Blessed Paul must be produced. It is still visible in the same basilica, carved in ancient marble in the following sense and published with the other ancient inscriptions of that basilica by the Moneta press in Rome in 1654. It is also found in Baronius, at the end of volume X, p. 963. Since, however, Baronius’s edition removed the sculptor’s errors and restored the reading to the rules of Latin speech, I prefer to give it here according to Moneta, with the numerous mistakes in the marble, in order to preserve the evidence of the original. These mistakes indicate the barbarism of the age, which lacked a more accurate sculptor. Perhaps, in order to shorten Gregory’s diploma, the sculptor dared, on his own initiative—or at the dictation of some incompetent person—to carve and deform the holy pontiff’s constitution in this manner. I have no doubt that it had been properly composed in the original, both because Gregory III is described in his *Life* as learned in Greek and Latin and because his surviving letters, published by Binius and Labbe together with the councils, show that he dictated in a sufficiently cultivated, if not fully polished, style.

> **In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ the Savior. A brief written by me, Gregory III, pope, concerning the offerings that ought to be offered each day in the Church of Blessed Paul the Apostle. I have determined that the following offerings be made: at the first Mass, at the body, one offering; at the second Mass, at Saint Timothy, one offering; at the third Mass, at the image of the Savior, which is also of the Apostles, one offering; at the fourth Mass, at Saint Gregory, at the door, one offering; then, at the fifth Mass, at the major altar, two offerings. Since these are made together each day, there shall be six daily offerings, which the church shall offer in your basilica, my blessed lord Paul the Apostle, whose brief title we confirm by apostolic authority for all time …**

There consequently remain not a few ancient marble monuments in the Roman Church, from the age of the martyr Hippolytus to Gregory III, under whom this collection of lives was being compiled before Anastasius. They provide genuine and public evidence of many acts conducted in councils held at the apostolic see, as well as of decrees of the supreme pontiffs and laws enacted by them. They enumerate the priests and deacons of this Church who took part in synods. It can therefore be established that many events reported in this *Book of the Pontiffs* could already at that time have been refuted as false by public testimony, had they been written contrary to the evidence of these monuments.

### 39

It may be permitted here to indicate incidentally how much these monuments contribute to the authority of the history of the *Book of the Pontiffs*. They display the barbarism of style proper to the age in which, under Gregory II and Gregory III, the lives of the pontiffs were being collected from the catalogues and archives of earlier periods.

One inscription that we have just reported was handled so carelessly by the person responsible for its carving—whether a notary, the superintendent of the building works, or another administrator of the basilica—that, while it frequently and seriously violates the rules of grammar in almost every line, it vividly expresses the unhappy character of that age. After the Lombards had completed nearly two centuries of rule in Italy, they had become so alien to the Latin mode of expression that the recorders of public acts, and even the notaries and diploma-writers of the kings themselves, dictated no more correctly.

I shall give an example from the archive of the monastery formerly called of the Savior, now named Saint Julia, founded at Brescia by Queen Ansa, wife of King Desiderius and mother of Adelchis, or Adelgis.

### 40

I copied from the originals the beginnings and subscriptions of two diplomas, which read as follows. The first belongs to the year 771 of the Christian era:

> **… rius [Flavius Desiderius], illustrious man, king. To the monastery of our Lord and Redeemer, situated within our city of Brescia, which we, with Christ’s help, together with our most reverend wife, Queen Ansa, built from its foundations and [granted to] the holy Lady Anselperga, abbess, our beloved daughter; the following transmitted syntax is defective: “you have brought to the excellence of our kingdom, because” our most excellent king Adelchis, your full brother and our son, and our glorious wife Ansa, your mother, have transferred by royal commands various properties in that holy monastery, within our territories of Austria and Neustria, Spoletium and Tuscany—estates with their dependent holdings, etc. I, Peter the notary, wrote this. Done at Brescia, on the day of July, in the year of our most fortunate reign …, in the ninth indiction, happily.**

A second diploma follows, belonging to the year 772:

> **Flavius Adelchis, illustrious man, king, to the monastery of our Lord the Savior, situated in the city of Brescia, which our most excellent mother, Queen Ansa, and the dedicated Lady Anselperga, abbess, our beloved sister, etc. From the statement of the lord king, for Adwald the notary, I, Ermoald the notary, wrote this from his dictation. Done in the city of Brescia, on the eleventh day of November, in the year of our most fortunate reign, in the name of God, the fourteenth, in the tenth indiction.**

### 41

In Gaul, too, in the same and the preceding century, one reads several royal diplomas dictated with no greater success in R. P. Mabillon’s *On Diplomatics*, book VI, until letters revived under Pepin and Charlemagne. Even there they had been disfigured and almost destroyed by the incursions of the Saracens, as we shall read below in the *Life of Saint Gregory*, no. 182, and as Ruffus laments in his *History of Marseille*, book XI, chapter 1. He produces the epitaph of Eusebia, a religious woman of Saint Cyriacus, p. 128; on p. 58, from ancient documents, he proves that this virgin, together with eleven other holy virgins whom she led, disfigured herself by cutting off her nose so that she would not be violated by the barbarians who devastated Provence around the years 725 and 730—that is, in the age of Saints Gregory II and III. The epitaph is carved in no better grammatical style:

> **Here rests in peace Eusebia, a religious woman, a great servant of the Lord, who in the world lived thirteen secular years from her earliest age; and when she was chosen by the Lord, she served in the monastery of the saints Cyriacus for fifty years. She departed on the day before the Kalends of October, in the sixth indiction.**

He also gives another inscription of the same style on p. 55.

Even in the royal archives of the Franks, the autograph diplomas of King Chlothar II, written on bark or papyrus, have been published by the Reverend Father Félibien in his *History of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*. They were dictated around the year 620:

> **… to the illustrious men Chrodegarius … going through the basilicas from his own properties, if he should wish legally to delegate by the page of a testament through our authority, the testament … our Dodo, abbot of the Basilica of the Lord Saint Dionysius, the martyr, our special patron, etc. Chlothar, in Christ’s name king, have subscribed this command.**

If anyone wishes to contemplate the barbarism of these ages even in brief inscriptions placed within Italy, I shall produce, from Panvinius’s *Antiquities of Verona*, book V, chapter 11, and from Count Moscardo’s *History of Verona*, book IV, p. 70, an inscription carved on a small column. Formerly it stood beneath the principal altar; it is now set into the side altar of the Church of Saint George in the Valpolicella, together with three similar columns, to support the altar table. The date of the carving and construction is given under King Liutprand, that is, shortly before the year 743.

I shall not hesitate to print this inscription again, although Panvinius and Moscardo have already published it, since it may appear that neither of them examined it directly, but that it was copied less carefully from the work of others. When I happened to ask Count Ottolino Ottolini, who has served our studies most excellently, to apply moistened paper to the marble so that each stroke of the letters could be reproduced with complete fidelity, he—owing to his exceptional learning and the care he devotes to cultivating the more serious disciplines in our homeland and illuminating the foundations of history—undertook to send me the inscription published by both historians, copied directly from the original, and also to provide the inscription on the other column, which Panvinius and Moscardo had not noticed.

In both inscriptions it is especially worthwhile to observe the numerous letters carved in the form of the Greek alphabet, particularly D and L. The first inscription, therefore, as published by the praised writers, is as follows:

> **In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, by the gifts of Saint John the Baptist, this ciborium was built under our lord King Liutprand and under the venerable Bishop Paternus Domnicus, and his custodians, the venerable men Vitalianus and Tancor, priests, and Refol, the gastald. Gondelme, an unworthy deacon, wrote this.**

On another column of the four supporting the table of the altar are read the names of Ursus the master and his disciples, by whom the ciborium was constructed. The urgency of the present undertaking prevents us from imitating the barbarous form of each individual letter by casting types after their model:

> **Ursus the master, with his disciples Iuventinus and Iovianus, built this ciborium. Verecundus, Tegodal [or Theobald], Foscar.**

I could also demonstrate the same style from Lombard diplomas of Insubria. As an example, there is the donation of Theopertus, by which he bestowed all his movable and immovable property on the Basilica of Saint Ambrose in the thirtieth year of King Liutprand, and in the seventh year after Hilderprand had been taken by Liutprand into partnership in the kingdom, on the eighth day before the Ides of May, in the thirteenth indiction—that is, in the year 740—at the request of the notary Protasius. John Peter Puricellus indicates that its autograph was preserved in the same basilica in *Monuments of the Ambrosian Basilica of Milan*, p. 10.

### 42

In another part of Italy, far removed from Insubria, namely in the Capuan territory, which the Lombard princes possessed, notaries left behind precisely similar barbarism of writing up to the eleventh century. This is shown by the charter of Pandulf IV, prince of Capua, in Camillus Peregrinus, *History of the Lombard Princes*, p. 229, under the year 1034.

Nor did the other regions of Italy that had obeyed the Lombards depart from these examples. This is demonstrated by the public acts produced in book XV of Count Campello’s *History of the Duchy of Spoleto*, composed from genuine monuments: under Duke Hildebrand, p. 494, around the year 779; under Duke Guy, p. 496, in the year 849; and in other similar documents to be sought in the same author.

No one, therefore, will reasonably doubt that in the age of Gregory, when the lives of the pontiffs were being written, documents concerning the reported events were available not only in archives and registers but also on the marbles of churches. Even in our own century, inscriptions survive that confirm both deeds and decrees and the characteristic style of the age in which those decrees were written.

To this subject—namely, the monuments of offerings, elections, ordinations, and pontifical chronology carefully and faithfully transferred from Roman stones into the catalogues and lives of the supreme leaders of the Church—belongs the marble tablet recording a gift offered by Severus, a priest of the Roman Church of the Title of Saint Peter in Chains, under the patronage of the same prince of the Apostles, after the election of Pope John II. Cardinal Baronius, of eminent memory, took care to insert it as an illustrious document of ecclesiastical history in volume VIII of his *Annals*, under the year 531.

The marble may be seen in the same Title of Eudoxia, or Saint Peter in Chains. In our own age it is preserved and affixed to the wall of the left-hand side aisle, for worshippers approaching the altar of the Most Holy Sacrament. It is carved as follows:

> **With Pope John, surnamed Mercury, safely reigning, ordained from among the priests of the holy Roman Church, promoted from the Title of Saint Clement to pontifical glory, Severus, a priest, offers [a gift] to Blessed Peter the Apostle, his patron, at [Saint Peter] in Chains; and likewise, P.C., for the lamp of Orestes, VV CC, etc. [the abbreviations are uncertain].**

From this one stone we learn the election and ordination of the pontiff and the offering of the priest Severus; and we see the pontifical chronology illustrated by consular notices, supported by the authority of contemporary marbles down to the last consuls of the West.

It is pleasing to observe that, two full years after the death of Pope John II, in the year 534, the consular lists were marked by Justinian Augustus for the fourth time and by Decius Theodorus Paulinus, whom the chronologists observe to have been the **last of the Western consuls**. The authority of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, just like that of the praised catalogue, is therefore founded under Justinian upon the solid testimony of publicly erected stones. These matters, however, will be examined more carefully in their proper place, in the notes to the *Life of John II*.

### 43

I now come to the final category of documents, concerning the donation of estates and the ornaments bestowed upon churches and recorded in the *Book of the Pontiffs*.

Every sensible person will easily understand that the public documents of emperors and private individuals, by which urban or rural properties were donated, were not carelessly maintained in the archives of the basilicas and titles of the City. Even during the heat of persecution, the movable goods of the Church were entrusted to archdeacons, as Pope Lucius entrusted them to Stephen, Stephen to Xystus, and Xystus to Lawrence, for distribution as alms to the poor and for sacred uses.

The learned correctly infer that immovable property also belonged to the Church even then, from whose annual revenues the poor or ministers were supported. This follows from the law of Constantine cited by Eusebius in his *Life*, book II, chapter 39, by which he commands that property seized by the treasury during the persecution be restored to the churches:

> “We therefore order that everything which appears rightly to belong to the churches—whether it be a house or an estate, fields, gardens, or anything else—be restored without any diminution of the right pertaining to ownership, with all things remaining safe and intact.”

On this subject, Thomasinus, *On Benefices*, part III, book I, chapter 3, should be consulted. From the *Acts of Blessed Abercius*, cited by Baronius under the year 163, he proves that even pagan emperors had donated certain churches to Christians together with annual revenues. Marcus Aurelius is said to have donated three thousand measures of grain to the Church of Hierapolis, whose bishop had healed his daughter, who was afflicted by a demon. Nor was that gift withdrawn except by Julian the Apostate.

It was therefore necessary for lists of estates to be written by the Church’s notaries and advocates, especially since the same Augustus Constantine had decreed that the property of martyrs and confessors seized by the treasury should be restored to their heirs; if there were no heirs, it was to be assigned to the church of the place, as Eusebius testifies in chapters 36 and 37 of the same book.

Thus, in the *Life of Sylvester*, no. 43, this *Book of the Pontiffs* reports that Constantine bestowed public gifts upon the Church of Saint Lawrence that he had built in the Veran field, and among its immovable property assigned to it the estate of a certain religious woman, Cyriaceti, which the treasury had occupied during the persecution.

Scarcely had peace been restored to the Church, and basilicas founded and endowed under Constantine, Sylvester, and Mark come into view, when Mark’s immediate successor, Pope Julius, established that information concerning matters and acts relating to the Church should be collected by notaries and recorded with the authority of the chief of the notaries and the archivist of the holy see.

The *Book of the Pontiffs*, in the *Life of Julius*, no. 50, says:

> “He established that no cleric should conduct any case in public except in the church; that the records, which are necessary for ecclesiastical good faith, should be collected by notaries; and that all documents concerning the Church, prepared through the chief of the notaries, should be formally recorded—whether lawsuits, instruments, donations, exchanges, transfers, wills, allegations, or manumissions. Clerics were to record these matters in the Church through the archivist of the holy see.”

From this arose the canonical laws enacted by apostolic authority under Sylvester at the Second Council of Gangra, chapters 7 and 8, as Pope Symmachus testifies at the Roman council, where he observes that Hosius, the legate of Sylvester, had attended the council in the year 324, no. 44. Other laws were enacted under Pope Julius in his fifth year, that is, in the year 341, at the First Council of Antioch, canon 24. Although several of the bishops who had assembled secretly supported the Arian party in the case of Athanasius, they nevertheless decreed with the Catholics concerning the property of the Church, imitating Pope Julius in his laws:

> “It is rightly established that the things belonging to the church should be preserved for the church with a completely good conscience and faith before God, the ruler and judge of all. They should also be administered with the judgment and authority of the bishop, to whom the entire people and the souls of those who assemble in the church have been entrusted.
