The things belonging to the church should be made known in the presence of the priests and deacons who are around him, so that they may know and not be ignorant,” etc.

The apostolic laws of Julius were illustrated far more excellently by the Council of Chalcedon, held in 451 under Leo the Great, in session XV, canon 26:

> “It has been determined that every church possessing a bishop should also have an administrator from its own clergy, who shall dispense the church’s property according to the judgment of its own bishop, so that the administration of the church may not occur without testimony, and so that the church’s resources may not be scattered and the priesthood exposed to the insult of a curse.”

That this discipline already pertained to the universal Church before the canon of the Council of Chalcedon, following Julius’s constitution, is declared by a letter of Cyril of Alexandria. He complains that the bishops were required to render accounts not only of the expenditures that the foresight of the praised law had established in order to preserve the integrity of the goods dedicated to God, but also of matters beyond the limits of the law and contrary to the dignity and rights of bishops.

Cyril’s letter—he died in the year 444, seven years before the Council of Chalcedon—was published in volume V, part II, p. 211, where the following is read:

> “It is an evil and causes great sorrow to the most holy bishops throughout the world that an account of the administration of the expenses incurred by them should be demanded, whether these come from ecclesiastical revenues or from produce received from elsewhere. Each of us will give an account of all his own evils to the Judge of all. Precious vessels and immovable possessions ought to be preserved for the churches. The administration of the expenses incurred should safely be entrusted to the bishops who at that time exercise the divine priesthood.”

### 44

Since, therefore, according to the laws of the apostolic see applying to the universal Church, and according to the regulations of councils and Fathers, such great care had to be exercised in protecting movable goods and preserving the precious vessels of sacred buildings under the custody of an administrator, and since the administration of revenues and offerings had to be arranged at the bishop’s discretion but under the testimony of the clergy, it was necessary to compose a record of the goods, prepare an inventory and catalogue of the sacred furnishings and gifts that were dedicated, and produce accounts of disbursements and receipts by the administrators.

It is therefore not surprising that the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* records and counts the gifts of bishops and emperors in such minute detail in almost every basilica and title. It is our task to show that documents remained from that age not only in archives and on parchment but also on walls and marbles, documents that confirmed the inventories of the things described.

### 45

If anyone should doubt the possessions and estates of the churches and their annual revenues, he should be led around the basilicas and titles of the City, where one can still see engraved not only the names of estates and revenues but also the custom of our ancestors, who, in the Roman manner, displayed before the eyes of the people the census of the Church itself, just as Augustus once displayed the register of the empire.

In the portico of the Vatican basilica, one of seven marble tablets survives—Ciampini counts that many from Alpharanus, who had seen two remaining in his own age—inscribed with the names of the estates and properties belonging to that basilica. This tablet was carved by Blessed Gregory the Great concerning estates donated by him for the preparation of the lamps:

> **To the holy and most blessed lords Peter and Paul, princes of the Apostles, Gregory, an unworthy servant. Whenever [something is done] to your praise, etc., I establish and decree that it be observed by me and by my successors without any opposition: that the places or estates with olive groves listed below, which I have recovered from various persons by whom they were held, and which I have dedicated to you for the preparation of your lamps, remain unaltered—namely, in the patrimony of Appia: the estate of Victoriolas, with its olive grove; in the estate of Rumellianus, in full, an olive grove; in Octavianus, in full; the estate of Trabatiana, with its olive grove; in the estate of Burreianus, as above, an olive grove; in the estate of Appianus, as above, etc.**

Another forty-four names of olive groves and estates included in this donation follow. They may be read in Paul de Angelis, *Description of the Vatican Basilica*, p. 81; in Ciampini, *On the Sacred Buildings Constructed by Constantine the Great*, pp. 81–82; and in the Paris edition of the works of Saint Gregory the Great, as well as in other authors.

### 46

In the Basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, before the steps of the presbytery, there is read an ancient letter of the same pontiff, Gregory the Great, carved in marble. It was addressed to Felix, subdeacon and administrator of the Patrimony of Appia. It is best to give it in full, since it alone can suffice to confirm the documents preserved in the apostolic archive: both the documents concerning donations of this kind belonging to the titles and basilicas of the Roman Church and those concerning the administration of property by superintendents supplied with brief records or inventories of the possessions and estates entrusted to their care.

The pontiff orders that the superintendents of the aforesaid Church, who were to serve successively from the date of the donation—that is, from the seventh indiction, the second year of the reign of Phocas and his first consulship, namely from the year 604—should administer them successively from the date of the donation, so that thereafter they themselves would render accounts.

He orders Felix, the subdeacon and administrator of the Patrimony of Appia, to delete and remove from his inventories the estate and properties, gardens, and small plots listed among the donations, and to transfer everything to the name of the aforementioned Church of Blessed Paul the Apostle. Finally, he commands that the original donation be restored to the apostolic archive:

> **We wish you, through your experience, to restore this command to the archive of our Church.**

These three commands, already carved in marble, express for us the entire discipline and practice of the administration of the Church’s property that prevailed at that time. They show that public documents, recorded both in archives and on the marbles of sacred buildings, supplied writers of the *Pontifical History*—in accordance with the custom of earlier ages—with precise information concerning such minute matters, which could not escape the careful attention of a bishop and his minister even in that age.

Such, then, is the letter of Gregory the Great that we see carved on a marble tablet in the basilica of the Doctor of the Nations on the Ostian Way:

> **Gregory, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to Felix, subdeacon and administrator of the Patrimony of Appia. Although everything possessed by this apostolic Church of Blessed Peter and Paul, acquired through their honor and benefits, is, with God as its author, held in common, there must nevertheless be diversity among persons in the administration of affairs, so that more diligent care may be given to the matters assigned to each person.**
>
> **Since our proper concern for the Church of the Apostle Paul admonished us that the herald of the faith, who filled the whole world with the light of his preaching, should not be seen to possess fewer lamps there, and since it seemed very unfitting and harsh that no possession should serve him specially in the place where, having won the palm of martyrdom, he was beheaded so that he might live, we have judged it useful to assign to his lamps, with the grace of Christ, the same estate called Aquae Salviae, with all its properties: the wine cellar of Antoniana, Villa Portusa, Bifurcum, Priminianus, Cassianus of Silon, Cornelius Tessellata, and Cornelianus, together with every right belonging to it, its instruments, and everything generally pertaining to the property.**
>
> **We further add to this transfer two gardens situated between the Tiber and the portico of that church, for those travelling toward it from the right-hand side of the city gate. They are divided by the river from the boundaries of the garden of the monastery of Saint Stephen, which belongs to the women servants of God and is situated at Saint Paul’s, and from the boundaries of the possession of Pisinianus. Likewise, we add the small plots called the Robber’s Ditch, situated there beside the same portico, for those travelling toward it on the left-hand side, where vineyards have now been made. These small plots adjoin on one side the possession of Eugenius, formerly a scholar, and on the other the possession of the monastery of Saint Arista.**
>
> **Since, with God’s help, we wish all these things to be administered through the superintendents of the aforesaid Church who shall serve successively from the present seventh indiction, and whatever accrues from them to be expended on its lamps, and since we wish those superintendents thereafter to render accounts, we therefore command your Experience to delete and remove from your inventories the estate of Aquae Salviae, with all the properties named above, together with the gardens and small plots mentioned earlier, and to transfer everything to the name of the aforesaid Church of Blessed Paul the Apostle. Thus, the superintendents serving it, no longer able to plead any excuse, may thereafter devote themselves to caring for its lamps without requiring our supervision, so that no neglect may ever occur there.**
>
> **After the transfer of all the things written above has been completed, we wish your Experience to restore this command to the archive of the Church. Farewell.**
>
> **Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the second year of the emperor our lord Phocas, pious and august, and in the first year of his consulship, in the seventh indiction.**

### 47

I shall give another ancient marble inscription, carved under Gregory IV around the year 843 and belonging to the Liberian Basilica of Saint Mary Major, where it may be seen affixed in the portico.

From this we shall understand the singular foresight of that age, from which Anastasius and William the librarians, the authors of the final lives, are separated by only a few years. The inscription shows how carefully the Church’s estates were protected and preserved in perpetual memory, since it records that Rado, the regional notary of the holy Roman Church, testifies that everything written on that stone had been copied from authentic writings and had it carved in marble as a precaution and safeguard for future times.

The beginning of the inscription is missing.

[Col. 0087] [lacuna] … “I dictated this to be written by Noto, my notary, and beneath it I subscribed in my own hand with Greek letters; and I presented it to the witnesses whom I had summoned for subscription, granting permission also for it to be alleged in whatever proceedings they might wish, and at whatever time you wish, without any further appearance, after my declaration had again been read according to custom. I grant permission concerning all these matters, with the stipulation and solemn undertaking duly interposed. Done at Rome, on the day, consulship, and indiction stated above. + Flavia Xanthippe, daughter of the late Egistus, imperial secretary, to this charter of usufructuary donation, concerning the entire estate called Paganicense, with its estates and farmsteads, namely:

the estate Arturianus; the estate Garganus; the estate Mattianus; the estate Viarus; the estate Criscianus; the estate Turita; the estate Solinianus; the estate Casa Porcinaria; the estate Calvisianus; the estate Rubianus; the estate Sipicianus; the estate Bubianus, six unciae; the estate Ucupia; the estate Casauita; the estate Eruttianus; the estate Ferratula; the estate Casularius; the estate Calgianus, four unciae; the estate Pistore; the estate Petrociana; the estate Casabili; the estate Optavianus; the estate Arbuscianus; the estate Gurgus; the estate Casaginus; the estate Turanus; the estate Rubianus; the estate Felianus; the estate Manilius; the estate Oglata; the estate Cottianus, six unciae; the estate Filipianus; the estate Orcianus; the estate Triscasa; and gardens and vineyards within the city of Signia; likewise the estate Candigianus, in its entirety, and everything generally belonging to them.

Made by me for all the tenants who are present and who shall perpetually enter the basilica of the holy Mother of God, Mary, which is at the Manger, for the offering of our soul, as is written above. Having read all these matters, I consented and subscribed, and summoned the witnesses who were to subscribe. + Flavius Anastasius, tribune of Saint Peter. + Theodatus, custodian of the Theodosian treasury. + I, Georgius, keeper of the military treasury of Sermisianus. + Flavius Epiphanius, goldsmith. + Theodorus, acolyte of the holy Roman Church.

To this charter of usufructuary donation, concerning the entire estate called Paganicense, with its estates and farmsteads, and likewise the entire estate Candianus, and everything generally belonging to them, except slaves and movable property, and including the mills: the donation of Xanthippe, daughter of Egistus, was made for all the tenants who are present and who shall perpetually enter the basilica of the holy Mother of God, which is at the Manger, as is written above. At the request of the holy donor, we wrote this; while she herself was present, we witnesses subscribed, and we saw this charter of donation delivered at the present time. + I, Theodorus, seventh notary, urban Roman scribe, completed and finalized this charter of usufructuary donation after the subscription of the witnesses and after the delivery had taken place. +

In the time of our most holy lord Gregory IV, pope, at the request of Rado, regional notary of the holy Roman Church, this was copied from authentic documents and engraved on marble for the protection and security of future ages.

[Col. 0087B] 48. If anyone compares the inscriptions of Saints Gregory the Great and Gregory III given above under numbers 38 and 45 with this last one, made under Saint Gregory IV, transferred from genuine charters onto marble tablets and set before the eyes of present and future generations on the walls of churches, he will readily understand what an abundance of documents from the sixth to the tenth century the archives and marbles preserved for the writers of the *Liber Pontificalis*, especially when they were reviewing and enumerating the decrees of the pontiffs and the possessions of the churches.

I should certainly be excessive for the scope of a preface [Col. 0088B]—although, considering the sequence of my subject, I might perhaps appear a not unwelcome admonisher—if I wished to review all the monuments of that age, recorded on marble tablets, which assisted those writers and sharpen our own efforts to establish the history, style, and authority of works of this kind. We shall read, under numbers 523 and 524, in the Life of Saint Leo IV, prayers composed by him, both at Ostia on repelling the Saracens from the shore and at Rome for the dedication of the Leonine City, so named after him:

“God, whose right hand caused blessed Peter to walk upon the waves”; [Col. 0089A] and: “God, who … to your apostle Peter,” etc.

In the Lateran dining hall, however, which was called the Leonian Hall after its founder Leo III and still preserves his likeness, the mosaic and inscription of the *zophorus* of that apse which was called the Greater House, and which was destroyed in the new construction of Sixtus V, contained, according to Panvinius in his book *On the Seven Churches of the City* and Cardinal Rasponi in book IV, chapter 6 of *On the Lateran Patriarchate*, an inscription by which that earlier prayer formula was adapted, invoking the apostles’ protection over guests and pilgrims, that they might be preserved from dangers on their journey and there received at table:

“God, whose holy right hand delivered blessed Peter and his fellow apostle Paul, shipwrecked three times, from the depths of the sea: may your holy right hand protect this house and all the faithful who feast here and rejoice in the gifts of your apostle,’” [Col. 0089B] etc.

The oratory of Saint Gregory III in the old Vatican basilica displayed marble tablets affixed and engraved by that pontiff with formulas of prayers established by him. We read most of them, still surviving, in fragments of those same tablets, transferred to the crypt of the aforementioned basilica and printed by Ciampini in *On Sacred Buildings Constructed by the Emperor Constantine*, chapter 2, page 104, and by Torrigius in *On the Vatican Crypts* and by other writers:

“Hear us, almighty and merciful Lord,” etc.

Thus, even today, there are found and survive, anciently engraved on the marbles of the principal basilicas of the City, not only the names, chronology, and decrees of numerous Roman pontiffs before the tenth century, but also the formulas of prayers established by them [Col. 0089C] themselves.

[Col. 0090A] 49. Nevertheless, so as not to depart farther from the proposed discussion of marbles engraved with the names and information concerning the Church’s estates—since inscriptions brought to the principal Roman basilicas and surviving even in our own age have testified to it—I shall also point out examples of the same practice in the titles and deaconries preserved in the City during the same periods of which we are speaking, and observed outside the City in the neighboring cathedral churches.

The title-church of Saints John and Paul, which the most eminent and most reverend Cardinal Paulutius, following the example of Our Most Holy Lord, has magnificently restored—being the nearby title-church of Saint Clement—and which he arranged to have illuminated by a learned commentary from the distinguished man Philippus Rondininus, canon of the Church of Faenza, preserves for us an example of ancient diligence in reviewing the Church’s estates [Col. 0090B]. For it displays marble tablets anciently engraved from a charter of Saint Gregory the Great, listed among his letters as book IX, number 22, addressed to Deusdedit, cardinal, and John, archpriest of that title. There one reads not only the names of the estates, with their location indicated on the Roman road, and Gregory the Great’s confirmation, but also the name of Pope Constantine, placed opposite in the margin. This shows that the information concerning the estates of that title, confirmed by his predecessor Gregory in the preceding century, was reviewed and strengthened again in his own age—that is, in the eighth Christian century—by the words expressed in letters descending on both sides: on the reader’s left,

“+ REGISTER OF THE ESTATES BELONGING BY RIGHT TO THIS TITLE,”

and on the right,

“+ CONSTANTINE, SERVANT OF THE SERVANTS [OF GOD].”

[Col. 0089] “+ Territory of Beltrus, 22 miles. The estate Mucianus in its entirety; the estate Cosconis in its entirety, where the Praetorian estate lies above; the estate Casacatelli in its entirety, where it lies above; the estate Proclis in its entirety.

On the Appian Way, two miles: the estate Cumpantanus. On the Appian Way, thirteen miles: the estate of the Virgin in its entirety. On the Ardeatine Way, three miles: the estate Capito. On the aforesaid way, five miles: the estate Fonteianus in its entirety. On the aforesaid way, twelve miles: the estate Fausianus in its entirety. On the aforesaid way, [lacuna] miles: the estate Lausianus in its entirety. On the Sacred Way, seven miles: the estate of the Carbonarii in its entirety. On the Latin Way, eleven miles: the estate Publica in its entirety. On the Latin Way, eleven miles: the estate Casa Quinta in its entirety. On the Lavican Way, fifteen miles: the estate Lacitianus in its entirety. The estate Sergianus in its entirety, where it lies above. The estate Septeminus in its entirety. On the Via Funis Caesarianus, five miles: the estate in its entirety. On the Praenestine Way, thirty miles: the estate Stagnis in its entirety. On the Latin Way, thirty miles: the estate Casaluci in its entirety, where it lies above. On the Appian Way, thirteen miles: the estate Casacellense.

We confirm these things as belonging to your Church, and we likewise confirm them, so that if anyone should prove to be a violator, he may be subject forever to the bond of anathema.”

[Col. 0089D] The celebrated deaconry of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, restored to its former splendor by our most holy lord and by his brother’s son, the most eminent and most reverend Cardinal Albano, and which the distinguished Giovanni Mario Crescimbeni, canon, undertook to illuminate after being cultivated in the more elegant letters at the most flourishing academies of Italy, preserves for us, in a commentary filled with solid learning, an illustrious document engraved in the year of Christ 901 under John IX. It shows the diligence of that same age in listing even the movable gifts and ornaments of the Church. The marble is ancient; it was transferred from the ruins of the nearby church of Saint Valentine, now destroyed, into the portico of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, as the title placed by the canons beside the inscription explains [Col. 0091A], and it was printed together with that title on page 81, book II, chapter 10, of the aforementioned work [Col. 0092A].

[Col. 0091]

“An ancient monument dating to the year 902 from the Incarnation, or 901 from the Nativity, under John IX, Supreme Pontiff. Concerning the donation made by Theobald to the Church of Saint Valentine, which stood opposite this holy deaconry. Found in the destroyed sacristy of that church and placed here by the archpriest and canons. Under Urban VIII, Supreme Pontiff, in the first year of his Jubilee, 1625.”

“Receive, O Valentine, blessed martyr, these gifts which the craftsman Theobald, generous in heart, brings to you. These, therefore, are what the same Theobald has granted to you, most blessed martyr, so that they may be used by the clergy as a perpetual gift:

Here, for those who serve you, are two adjoining houses with roofed courtyards in the neighborhood of your church; a cell beside the same church; a small garden with olive trees behind the church of Saint Nicholas; a vineyard at Antonianus; one mass-book; two antiphonaries, one for the day and the other for the nocturnal office; two weekday books of Genesis with canonical histories; a passionary; the *Dialogue* with the *Scintillarium*; two hymn-books; a book from the *Moralia*; a gilded silver chalice with its paten; a silver thurible; one manual.

If anyone, O most blessed martyr, should rashly remove, sell, alienate, or defraud anything of these things granted to you by the aforementioned Theobald, or of anything that shall be granted by him or by others, let him be separated from the assembly of all Christian people, forever struck by anathema, joined to the devil and all the impious, and burned in eternal fire, in the time of the ninth pontiff, the supreme John. This hall was consecrated on the last day of November, when the eleventh indiction was running toward its end.”

[Col. 0091B] A list of estates engraved in Greek characters was published by the distinguished Fabrettus in *Inscriptions*, chapter 10, number 629, page 757. He stated that it had been excavated at Saint Stephen in the Borgo—I believe one should read “at Saint Stephen on the Caelian,” and that it was thereafter transferred to the German College. For on the Caelian Hill the German College possesses the church of Saint Stephen and a vineyard, from which ancient monuments were also extracted a few years ago. The inscription belonged to the church of Saint Erasmus, or to its monastery, as may be inferred from the first line of the surviving fragment.

[Col. 0091]

“[lacuna] … estate(s) … of the glorious holy hieromartyr Erasmus, *cornificis* [an official title; reading uncertain] … estates … Opianus; the African estate and that at Palombara; [lacuna] … the Merlian estate; the estate of Anticus; Pompinianus; Longianus; the small [lacuna] … estate of Ontianus with Marmoratula; Lacume[g]ianus; Buxitula; the estate of Atregianus; Mucianus; Quartilianus; Maximianus; Casa Ferrata; [lacuna] … the estate of Mucianus; Tesserarorum; Aripus; Casteius; the estate of Gerphis; [lacuna] … the estate of Calcellatula; the estate of Strumaciana.”

[Col. 0091C] The celebrated monastery of Saint Erasmus was situated near the title-church of Saint Stephen on the Caelian Hill, as Martinellus observes together with Fulvius and Ugonius. It is frequently mentioned in this very *Liber Pontificalis*, especially in the Life of Adeodatus, number 138; in that of Leo III, number 405; and in that of Gregory IV, number 471. When Adeodatus had been elected pontiff in the year of Christ 669 from among the monks of that monastery, he bestowed many estates upon it. “In the monastery,” he says, “of Saint Erasmus situated on the Caelian Hill, where the aforementioned most holy man appeared to have grown up, he enlarged many new buildings; he also acquired farmsteads [another reading: ‘and acquired many estates there’], and during his life established an abbot or congregation there.”

Finally, in the endowment assigned to the sacred building on the occasion of the tomb, for offerings and lights, Boethius was deposited on the eighth day before the Kalends of November, in the eleventh indiction, under the Emperor Our Lord Justin, eternal Augustus, in his twelfth year, and under Tiberius Constantine Caesar in his third year—dates corresponding to the year 577 of the common Christian era. Boethius and his mother, named Argentea, assigned estates and engraved them on marble placed in the sacristy of Saint Angelo in the Borgo, as published by Fabrettus in *Inscriptions*, chapter 3, number 447:

“+ We have assigned in this our burial-place, according to the deed, for offerings or lights, six unciae of our garden across the Tiber, outside the walls, beside the Porta Portuensis, which belonged to Micinus Camelus, in the city, from our father.

+ But four [Col. 0092D] unciae of the estate Eucarpianus, which is situated beside Saint Cyprianus on the Lavican Way, between the boundaries of the estate Capitinus, belonging by right to the holy Roman Church; and also the estate Flavianus, belonging to the public treasury, beside Sabinianus. Here it ends.”

50. We thus see in the City basilicas, title-churches, deaconries, monasteries, and tombs showing us—especially from the age of Blessed Gregory the Great, that is, from the end of the sixth and beginning of the seventh century through the time of Leo IV and other pontiffs of the tenth century—lists of estates and properties customarily engraved, and sometimes also movable goods belonging to those sacred places, so that succeeding ages might provide for the preservation of those same things.

Examples of this provident policy of the Roman Church extended to the bishoprics near the City. From their marbles I have transcribed what follows.

In the cathedral church of Anagni, Bishop Grimaldus ordered an inscription to be engraved containing a list of estates, of which this fragment survives:

[Col. 0093] “[lacuna] … holy Mother of God, Mary, who deemed it worthy to possess … Bishop Maldus, we shall prepare … within your church … books … we shall plant … or endow … The estates which are placed here, which our lord Pope Leo will embrace and grant to us … We shall match them for you, my Lady, with gifts:

two unciae in the estate of the deacons’ garden, with its houses, or half the estate of Peregrinus, two unciae in the vineyard itself, in the estate which is called Eubarbaricum … at the bath, or likewise the vineyard which is in the district of Ge … in the estate Quorianus, as much as ought to be held there … by the command of our lord, the most reverend apostolic … the estate Macerata … two unciae in the estate Prinianus, and nine unciae in the estate Ilarianus; one uncia … three unciae of the estate Balnearea, or likewise the estate [lacuna] in its entirety, with houses and vineyards, forests, lands, and in the same farmstead … holy Mother of God … and vineyard.”

[Col. 0093B] In the church of Tibur, Suaresius described a donation of movable and immovable goods, anciently [Col. 0094B] engraved on marble in the year 930, and published it in book II of *Praenestine Antiquities*, chapter 7, page 146, under Gregory IV, in the year of Christ:

[Col. 0093]

“+ Behold the light, all you who see this house of Fullius, which the distinguished military commander and cultivator of churches, generous to the poor, took care to repair. The more savage the age had passed, the more this ancient building seemed likely to collapse by accident and to become a burden to many. Now Vigil, together with his sons, enlarged it from the ground to the summit, for the redemption of his offenses and also for the soul of his wife Agatha, and adorned it with varied paintings.

Therefore I earnestly ask you, O Christ, and Virgin Mother, and blessed Paul, vessel of election, together with your companions Romula, Redempta, and Erundus, whose bodies he took care to place in three sacred altars: may you deign to receive this small gift which he presented for the benefit of the temple. It consists of a paten, a chalice, curtains, candelabra, a thurible, and a silver basin; a bronze basket; vestments, curtains, books, and images with three seals for sounding the praise of God, which I caused to be set above the vault of this temple.

The houses and the estate Valvianus; likewise a vineyard at Laureto, and a wood; at Baruatiana, a parcel of land and an enclosure; one pergola; and in the meadow, a meadow.

If anyone should presume to remove anything from these gifts, which I have taken care to offer—whether bishop or person of high or low rank—may he hold my heirs under his power. But whoever should rashly presume to do anything of this kind, let the kingdom of God be alienated from him, and let him be subject to the bond of anathema by the sentence or decree of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers, and have his portion with Judas, the betrayer of the Lord.

Blessed are you who will enter here; I ask you to pray for me. May the Lord grant that you may rejoice for many years, so that with a ready heart you may be able to pray to him. M. Amen.

Done in the time of our lord Gregory IV, pope, at Rome, in the third indiction.”

[Col. 0093C] 51. An ancient marble inscription belonging to the year of Christ 731 should not be separated from this discussion. I copied it at Ravenna in the church of Saint Apollinaris in Classe. For it shows that the Roman practice of recording on stones placed in public the donations made to churches and monasteries, and of listing in them the names of estates, had, as the eighth century was drawing to a close, also reached the neighboring regions of Italy [Col. 0094C].

[Col. 0093]

“In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Under our most devout lords Leo and Constantine, crowned by God, peaceful and great emperors—Leo, most clement emperor, in the sixth year of his imperial rule, and Constantine, crowned by God, in the eleventh year of his imperial rule—while Our Lord Eutychius, excellent patrician, governed Italy,

and while the fourth exarch was in office, on the fourth day before the Kalends of February, in the fourteenth indiction.

This inscription displays a praiseworthy work, conceived by the pious counsel of the mind of Bishop John, the kindly pontiff, the younger, who was fifth by name. In faithful watchfulness, that he might possess the rewards of the eternal kingdom, he placed this monument for himself; bands of needy people pray at the sacred thresholds. He commended to Saint Apollinaris his dust-covered limbs, which he believes will rise when the vigor of the flesh has been restored.

He bestowed a gift beneficial to the servants of God who pour forth continual praises: the estate Cammillaria, surrounded on every side by farmsteads, with its boundaries as the text of the donation specifies. It is a suitable, fertile, productive land for the servants of the Lord at Ravenna, rich in firewood for use and in pasture for animals, producing acorn-bearing fruits. To the holy church he assigned, in exchange, the estate Trecintula in Faenza territory, and he transferred the estate Pitulis, lying in the same territory, together with fourteen pounds of silver which had lawfully come to him by the rights of his parents.

This gift shall remain secure and shall never be revoked. He ceded it to this college of monks as a yearly allowance, so that from its revenues agreeable meals might be prepared, and so that they might observe the right of his name annually. When, by the command of the Lord who rules, he shall have departed to the heavenly kingdoms, he established and confirmed this before this assembly:

If anyone, successor of the see, administrator of the church, abbot, or provost of this venerable temple, should presume by any device to alienate or exchange any part or the whole of the aforementioned estate of Miliaria from the use of the servants of the Lord serving here, or to grant it perpetually by deed or charter, let him suffer eternal condemnation with Judas, the betrayer, and with those who have asked for it and those who have attempted to grant it, bound by the chains of anathema of the three hundred and eighteen Fathers. +”

[Col. 0095A] 52. In all these monuments which I have produced, I ask the reader to observe that they belong to the period between Gregory II and Gregory IV, that is, the period in which the Lives of the *Liber Pontificalis* were being written. From this it may be understood why those authors devoted such assiduous and, so to speak, excessive labor to enumerating the gifts of the pontiffs, which were offered through them to God in sacred buildings, especially those established at Rome.

Wherever the pious writers turned, inscriptions of donations, lists of estates, and inscribed offerings came before their eyes, together with the practice of their age, which was occupied with reviewing such things. What, then, could they have preferred to do in writing than to provide precisely what they knew would most please their contemporaries? What could they pursue more diligently to commend the credibility of their history than to gather things which, as everyone could see, were confirmed by so many public documents?

The authors of the catalogues had arranged chronology, successions, and sacred ordinations from monuments of the fourth, fifth, and sixth centuries. They produced few decrees, since these scarcely belonged to the purpose of a catalogue. Nevertheless, writers of the following period could gather them from the acts of councils, from the archives of the Roman patriarchate, and from the papal library. That these places were open to the writers of the eighth and ninth centuries, who bring this collection to a close, is clearly inferred from their words, as examined by Luca Holstenius and Emmanuel Schelestratius.

The same is evident from their detailed enumeration of small gifts: it is clear that they preserved these for us from direct inspection of the things, usually inscribed, and from the donor’s remembered account; likewise from the inventories of movable and immovable property then preserved and often transferred to public marbles. I trust that this has been made abundantly clear by so many monuments, happily preserved for our age after a long succession of ten centuries.

All these things, therefore, sufficiently commend, as I believe, the authority of this *Liber Pontificalis*, which produces for each successive age the material that, in accordance with the practices and documents of those times, was committed to writing by the Church’s notaries, historians, and librarians.

53. I shall bring the preface to an end and, if I may say so, place a seal upon it by observing a coin which was deliberately set at its front—not so much to imitate Fabrotti’s edition, which began its first page with a sacred coin and displayed there the faces of the holy apostles Peter and Paul [Col. 0095D–0096A], as to indicate the genuine documents which, by direct inspection alone, safeguarded the credibility of history during the periods in which these Lives were written.

The coin is a large bronze coin of Crispus Caesar, and it may be considered the most distinguished of all those that Christian Rome struck in antiquity. Although it was wonderfully illustrated in the previous century by Cardinal Baronius in both editions of his *Annals*, we would not have seen the noble original had it not first been preserved at Rome through the kindness of Fulvius Ursinus and thereafter through that of the most illustrious Borghese family. It had long been preserved among the latter’s choicer treasures and enclosed in a special container, together with another distinguished coin of Constantine the Great, when the eminent Prince Marcus Antonius recently displayed it.

By this singular example, which he had inherited together with the blood of his ancestors, his devotion to religion, and his learning, he teaches children like himself to prefer, from the entire and truly royal treasure of their forefathers, that portion which advances the cultivation of the mind in both branches of learning. It was especially opportune that the coin was once again shown, as though reserved for this edition, so that readers might in some sense contemplate in it the contemporary testimony of the Constantinian age, and the corroboration of events arranged from public documents in catalogues during that same century, and subsequently transferred from the Church’s catalogues into the Lives of the pontiffs. The figure of the coin may be repeated.

On the obverse of Crispus’s coin, Crispus Caesar is shown from the chest upward, laureate—although the artist employed by Baronius did not render the laurel leaves very clearly—and wearing the toga. He holds in his left hand an ivory scepter, upon which an eagle rests according to custom, while he raises his open right hand as though a peacemaker and triumphant victor. Around the bust are the customary letters: “CRISPUS NOBILIS CAESAR.”

The reverse is much more remarkable. It displays a bearded man seated between two standing Caesars, both adorned in military dress and holding spears. The seated man’s hair is cut short to the ears; his beard is not long but fuller and more curly, like that seen in ancient images of Saint Peter, especially mosaics, and in the sarcophagi and sacred vessels of the same fourth century. The right hand of this figure is raised in blessing, with the joints of the fourth and fifth fingers slightly bent, according to the practice of the Latin Church. In his left hand he holds a spear, on the upper part of which the venerable sign of the cross is fixed [Col. 0096D]. A circular halo surrounds his head; his body is clothed in a tunic and pallium.

Baronius believes that one or another image of our Savior is represented here [Col. 0097A], from the two images which Constantine the Great set up in the Lateran basilica, made of silver, weighing 120 and 140 pounds respectively and standing five feet high, as this *Liber Pontificalis* records in the Life of Sylvester, number 36:

“During his time Constantine Augustus made these basilicas, and also adorned them. In the Constantinian basilica, where he placed these gifts, there was a repoussé silver canopy which had on its front the Savior seated on a chair, five feet high, weighing 120 pounds. The twelve apostles were each five feet high and each weighed ninety pounds, with crowns of the purest silver. Likewise, at the rear, facing into the apse, there was the Savior seated on a throne, five feet high, made of the purest silver, weighing 140 pounds.”

54. In the first edition of the *Annals*, published in 1592, volume III, page 215, Cardinal Baronius, discussing Crispus’s profession of the Christian religion at baptism, stated that he had found a distinguished proof of it in this coin. To most antiquarians of his age it appeared ancient; but since some regarded it with suspicion, he then preferred to refrain from publishing it, lest he introduce into his *Annals* anything tainted by a suspicion of falsehood.

Three years later, when preparing a second edition of the work, he published and illustrated the same coin in volume III, as though it had been vindicated from every danger and suspicion of fraud by the authority of all the antiquarians, and especially of Fulvius Ursinus, easily the foremost of them at that time. Ursinus, without reducing the price set by the owners, purchased this exceptionally fine coin at the highest possible price and placed it in his celebrated museum. He also compelled the few antiquarians of doubtful reliability who had deliberately called the coin’s antiquity into question, so that they might make it their own at a lower price, to give sincere testimony in favor of the monument’s unquestionable authenticity.

As a concluding statement, it is worthwhile to quote the words of that eminent writer on page 233 of the third volume of the second edition, number 13, after he had reported what he had written in the first edition three years earlier:

“‘These were the statements we made in the first edition,’ he says, ‘while the question of the coin’s genuineness was being debated. In that matter we considered the safer course to be the one that entirely removed every suspicion, however slight, of forgery. Since, therefore, in that edition of this volume we omitted the noble Roman coin of Crispus (in the margin he adds: “The bronze coin existed while he was alive in the possession of Horatius Tigrinus de Mariis”), because some people doubted its authenticity, now, as though every particle of doubt had been brushed away and the case had been proved, we thought it worthwhile to replace it here in the second edition.

We were moved especially by the fact that my good friend Fulvius Ursinus, the most diligent investigator of ancient things—one to whom, as to a Lydian stone, all ancient monuments that need to be tested and elucidated are brought, and whose authority carries very great weight with me—was repeatedly consulted on this matter. After carefully inspecting the coin, examining and testing it with all the resources of his intelligence and every applicable method, and doing so in the presence of those who, because of the coin’s unusual character, seemed inwardly disturbed by some suspicion of forgery, he affirmed that it contained absolutely no fraud.

Just as he vindicated the coin from every suspicion of forgery by known and proven arguments, so he exposed the hidden motives of its opponents: they had rejected it for the very reason that they might purchase it at a lower price. Having thoroughly recognized, examined, tested, and approved it in every respect, he bought it from the owner’s heirs for the price they requested and judged it worthy of adorning his museum, which was filled with the noblest monuments.’”

[Col. 0098B] Baronius then proceeds to explain the inscription on this reverse side:

“Salvation and hope of the state: Christ—SALUS ET SPES X REIPUBLICAE.”

It contains the name of Christ in abbreviated form in the Greek letter chi, Χ, which in that century and in later periods was used to express it, as he recalls having shown earlier from Julian’s *Misopogon*:

“‘Later it became customary,’ he says, ‘for the letter X, which earlier people used to place above Christ’s head to signify the name of Christ, subsequently to be placed in the diadem for the same reason, and arranged in such a way as to express the form of a cross. Otherwise, in the earlier images of our Savior, a small diadem without any sign is found represented in the form of a sphere, with the name of Christ added beside it [Col. 0098C]. If that addition is absent, then the sign is found placed in the diadem by means of the letter X (X).’”

55. We have willingly presented all these matters from Baronius, the restorer of ecclesiastical history, so that it might be evident, not only from his testimony but also from his example, how much authenticity and weight genuine monuments add to historical truth when writers consult them.

From this it necessarily follows how faithfully the authors of the Lives wrote during the centuries in which both writers and readers could compare nearly every individual point of their subject with surviving public documents. It is pleasing, from this same coin, to confirm how readily they could at once form an accurate judgment through the inspection of contemporary documents.

[Col. 0098D] The coin of Crispus produced by Baronius has been preserved for our age through the beneficence of the Burghese family. Its examination taught us that the figure seated on the reverse, between two standing Caesars, adorned with a nimbus, blessing with his raised right hand and holding in his left a cross fixed upon a spear, must be referred either to Christ the Lord, as Baronius thought, or, as some prefer, to the prince of the apostles, constituted his vicar in the Church. Whichever figure it represents, this testimony on the coin to the public exercise of the Christian religion under Constantine is indisputable, before Crispus, his son, was put to death through the accusation of his stepmother Fausta.

As we have said, Baronius believes that the image of Christ the Lord stamped on the coin represents the silver statue of that same Savior, God, and Lord of ours, erected by Constantine in the Lateran basilica, as the *Liber Pontificalis* relates. Those, however, who recognize in that figure a likeness of the apostle Peter observe that its bodily appearance, and especially the tonsure of the head and the form of the beard, resembles the most ancient images of the apostle Peter rather than those of Christ the Lord. For in marble sarcophagi sculpted in the fourth and fifth centuries and brought from the Vatican cemetery, in *Roma Subterranea* of Aringhi, volume I, plates, page 293 and following, whenever Christ the Lord is represented—whether beardless or bearded—he is always given long hair, with a beard tapering to a point. But in the apostle Peter, those same ancient marbles, folios 293, [Col. 0099B] 295, 297, 299, 301, and 307, together with all the paintings, reliefs, and ancient mosaics, display hair cut to the ear, a stiff and not particularly long beard, such as is seen on the coin.

In the reliefs mentioned, Saint Peter also carries a cross, just as on the coin. The engraver of the type printed by Cardinal Baronius represented the face of the seated man as beardless, contrary to the evidence of the coin, although he faithfully showed the hair cut to the ear. The images of the holy apostles Peter and Paul preserved in the sacristy of the Vatican basilica—which are said to have been presented to Constantine the Great by Blessed Sylvester, and whose history Adrian I related to Charlemagne in a letter published with the acts of the Second Council of Nicaea—show the apostle Peter with abundant hair, but cut short at the ear, [Col. 0099C] and Paul bald, as he is described by Lucian, with Baronius likewise observing this at the year 69, no. 14, and Spondanus, the author of his epitome, nos. 6 and 8.

In a small bronze image of Saint Peter, formerly in the museum of Bellorius and also seen by me, and published by Pietro Santo Bartoli together with the ancient lamps, part III, plate 27, the same style of hair tonsure and beard appears as that reported by Spondanus in the words of Nicephorus: the hair of the head and beard is curly and thick, but not particularly prominent.

The reliefs mentioned, in the Vatican sarcophagi of the fourth and fifth centuries—especially that occurring on folio 294 of Aringhi, where Christ the Lord is represented four times and Saint Peter three times—declare much more clearly that it was the custom of the Constantinian age, when images of the apostles, nearly contemporary with them, were preserved, which Eusebius says he himself saw (*Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 18), to assign long hair flowing over the shoulders to Christ the Lord, but hair cut short in the manner of a clerical tonsure to blessed Peter, since the two figures are sculpted with this consistent distinction in those same marbles.

The same facial appearance is also observed on silver vessels of sacred service made before Constantine the Great, as we perceive from their elegance and antiquity, and found among the ruins of older sacred buildings and cemeteries. We shall present them among the notes to the *Lives of the Pontiffs* under Urban I. There Christ the Lord hands the keys to Peter. The same form was also shown by later believers in the older mosaics of the City: in the titular church of Saint Prudentiana, built under Pope Siricius and restored by Adrian I; in the dining hall of Leo III at the Lateran; in the church of Saint Constantia under Honorius I; and everywhere in reliefs, paintings, and mosaics.

Since these works show Peter’s face to be plainly similar to that represented on this coin, they leave us no reason to doubt that, in the age of Constantine the Great, the image of Peter proposed by this coin corresponded to the other images derived from it, in accordance with the history related by Pope Adrian in the letter mentioned above.

The letters S. P. appearing on the same coin beneath the image we have described of the prince of the apostles either indicate *SANCTUS PETRUS*, with the capital letters of both words—as the letter X enclosed above in the inscription *SALVS ET SPES X. REIPVBLICAE* [Col. 0100B] contains the name of Christ—or signify *SIGNUM PETRI*. For here, as I suppose, *SIRMII PERCVSSA* is not indicated, since it is unusual on Latin coins to express the location of the minting workshop in large bronze.

If this figure indicates the apostle Peter, and his image has been placed upon a square seat, I think it should be referred to the statue of that same apostle, erected with the others by Constantine in the basilica of the Savior, five feet high and weighing ninety pounds, with a crown of the purest silver, which the *Liber Pontificalis* reports under Sylvester, no. 38.

Since the same apostle displays a cross, he may perhaps indicate the upright cross which Constantine placed in the Vatican basilica above the Confession of blessed Peter, weighing one hundred and fifty pounds [Col. 0100C] of the purest gold. On the measure of the place where this was written:

> Constantine Augustus and Helena Augusta:  
> This house, shining with a royal splendor like theirs, surrounds the hall.

This was written in black letters on the cross.

What we strive to conjecture from the indication of the coin, and cannot determine with sufficient certainty even after prolonged examinations, the authors of the *Liber Pontificalis* could have recognized clearly at a glance. In the Constantinian cross, still surviving in their time, they could read the names of the donors; and in the silver statues of Christ the Lord and the apostles they could see the image assigned to each in the age of Sylvester.

If those same monuments still existed, perhaps comparison with the coin would establish that, following the model of the image of blessed Peter proposed under Sylvester and Constantine for the veneration of the Lord’s cross [Col. 0100D] and of the one bearing it by the standing Caesars, later successors of Sylvester fashioned two statues of blessed Peter: one marble statue, preserved in the subterranean chamber of the Vatican basilica; and another bronze statue, set up in the upper church to receive the kisses of the faithful as a sign of veneration—a custom descended from the beginnings of the Church to our own age.

**56.** We were not reluctant to dwell somewhat longer upon the contemplation of the coin, the sacred image, and the inscription represented upon it under Constantine. Indeed, we took care to place all these matters before the preface, since they are indications of the documents that lay ready and available to the authors of the *Liber Pontificalis*. [Col. 0101A] For these examples, as it were, or surviving fragments of monuments that were then accessible to everyone and displayed publicly, sufficiently show that the authors of the older *Catalog* did not lack chronological documents; that the author of the second *Catalog* did not lack records of ordinances and papal laws; and that the narrators of the later *Lives* did not lack lists of churches from which they could obtain information about patrimonies, large estates, rural and urban properties, movable and immovable gifts, sacred furnishings, and every minor treasure offered to the basilicas, titular churches, deaconries, monasteries, and all the sacred buildings of the City.

As for the deeds of the pontiffs that they narrate, after the age of the second *Catalog* the historians of the *Lives* either saw most of them themselves, since they were nearly contemporary, or borrowed them from public archives, where they had been written down shortly before, [Col. 0101B] and collected them from the consistent testimony handed down to them by elders who had taken part in the events.

Thus, with the best of rights, each author of this book deserves the encomium bestowed by Baronius, the founder of the *Annals* and a seasoned judge of historical truth, upon Anastasius, volume IX, under the year of Christ 752, no. 19: “Although he wrote in an unpolished style, he nevertheless recorded the history of events with the utmost fidelity.”

**57.** These, dear Reader, are the general matters we had to place beforehand concerning the authority of the manuscripts and the documents of the events stated in the *Liber Pontificalis*. For the observations that must be brought forward in their proper place concerning its individual parts will set out below the notes of the various authors.

**58.** Since, in the printing of the *Liber*, everything was carefully provided that could best preserve its genuine reading and most promote the uses and advantages that Readers might derive from it, it necessarily follows that equal care for diligence and public benefit must also be taken in the edition of the notes. Therefore the printer has decided to select, from authors approved by the unanimous consent of all—Binius, Ciacconius, and Labbe—the more important notes and those most suited to explaining the text, which they themselves placed after the *Lives of the Pontiffs*.

The notes of Alteserra on Anastasius, published in a separate book, will be given in full, both because of their commendable brevity and because of their exceptionally choice learning. And so that no words, deeds, or documents of this history may remain unexplored through which the labors of our age could shed new light, since several students of ecclesiastical history [Col. 0101D] and Christian sacred antiquity have undertaken to contribute their own share toward explaining or confirming what earlier notes left untouched or did not sufficiently clarify, we shall gladly communicate the annotations they have generously supplied.

They will not be given in a confused mixture. Each interpreter will be credited with what is his own. Whether the author of a note belongs to the older or the more recent writers, he will occupy the place assigned by the first letter of his family name according to the alphabetical order. Alteserra, Bencinius, Binius, and all the others will individually show what they have contributed after reflection, according to the custom already established in commentaries by various authors.

**59.** The chronological observations, however, are so interconnected that individual points cannot be examined apart from the structure of the entire system. For this reason, the method seems to require that the matter as a whole be reserved for a particular place, where the reckoning of time from the birth of Christ to all the chronological documents will be set out. We have attempted to collect these documents through the study of many years and through investigations based both on carefully compared movements of the heavenly bodies [Col. 0102B] and on examination of ancient stones and coins, in which the sequence of the times that we must reckon and the chronological markers issued by public testimony are known.

**60.** With these aids prepared, make good use of them, diligent and kindly Reader; and regard the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs* as the chief part of universal ecclesiastical history, the sources of the annals, and precious remains of sacred antiquity. They were first collected in the Liberian *Catalog* from the Acts of martyrs and councils, as well as from the letters of pontiffs and confessors, the history of Hegesippus, the Eusebian chronicles and those of others, and from the diptychs of the Churches.

After another century they were enlarged by the same resources in the *Catalog* under Justinian, and at a later time under Gregory II and III were transferred into the *Liber Pontificalis*, [Col. 0102C] and more fully extended with the assistance of the records office and the apostolic library, as well as the archives, marbles, and treasuries of nearly all the churches of the City.

Finally, through the common efforts of nations distinguished for learning—the Belgian, French, German, Spanish, Illyrian, and Italian—these materials have in our age been cleansed of their squalor and rescued from the injury of time, as the lords and prefects of libraries everywhere supply older manuscripts.

As for our little work, however small it may ultimately be, judge it fairly and favorably; and, when you can, help it either by suggesting new documents for the chronology and history of the pontiffs that could be inserted in the second or third volume, or by healthfully and amicably correcting anything that may perhaps have inadvertently escaped us [Col. 0102D] as we composed the preface and notes. Know that I shall be most grateful to a well-intentioned admonisher, since I have nothing more at heart than, under the guidance of more learned men and accompanied by the support of many, to approach as closely as possible the truth sought by minds devoted to its worthy remembrance.

[Col. 0103]

# PREFACE OF FRANCESCO BLANCHINI TO THE SECOND VOLUME OF THE ROMANO-VATICAN EDITION

[Col. 0103A] **1.** In the preceding volume we published the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, attributed to Anastasius after the compilation of his collection. There we took care faithfully to reproduce the earlier editions and to enlarge them with the abundance of variant readings drawn from the finest manuscripts sought out everywhere, both within and beyond Italy.

We now undertake the edition of the second volume, which we have decided should contain prolegomena and notes especially suited to illuminating the text of the work. The Reader will readily understand from what follows how we shall carry this out, in accordance with the judgment of those who contributed counsel and assistance to this work.

**2.** In the preface to the first volume, no. 11, we considered, with Schelestratius, whom we have often praised, that the original formation of the *Liber Pontificalis*, or of the *Lives* bearing the name of Anastasius, [Col. 0103B] was owed to the ancient *Catalogs* of the Roman pontiffs, especially to that most ancient one collected under Pope Liberius. For this reason we judged it necessary to place it first as the basis and foundation, or at least the beginning and rudimentary form, of pontifical history.

P. Aegidius Bucherius was the first to publish it, in his celebrated work on the Paschal Cycle of Victorinus. From that work it must be copied in full.

**3.** Several *Catalogs* are also presented by Schelestratius, the more important of which, because of the antiquity of their manuscripts, I have decided to publish entire. They are the following, produced by him in the Appendix to his *Chronological Work*, namely:

**I.** No. 22, p. 611. From an ancient manuscript codex of 865 years in the Palatine-Vatican Library, a *Catalog of the Roman Pontiffs* under this title: “The Names of the Bishops of the City of Rome.”

**II.** No. 27, p. 626. From Vatican manuscript Codex 1353, which was copied under Paul II from an ancient codex of 800 years belonging to the church of Pergamum.

This *Catalog*, already impressive because of the antiquity of the codex from which it was transcribed, is made more commendable by its chronological arrangement, which corresponds to the numbers of years, months, and days of each pontiff’s episcopate assigned in an ancient painting surviving on the walls of the Basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way. That painting is no less ancient than the aforementioned *Catalog* of 800 years, copied from the codex of the church of Pergamum, and perhaps is even contemporary with the mosaic work constructed in the same basilica by Saint Leo the Great.

Thus it may be conjectured that either the painters drew from the scribes, or the scribes from the painters, or that both drew from the same sources for this kind of chronology. I shall propose that this be observed more carefully before the survey of the [Col. 0103D] *Catalogs*, when it will be necessary to examine the mutual support these monuments provide one another, together with the testimony of churches and libraries in their paintings and codices.

**III.** No. 31, p. 644: a *Catalog of the Pontiffs and of the Decrees Issued by Them*, from a six-hundred-year-old codex, Vatican 638, preceding the *Decretum* of Anselm, bishop of Lucca.

It is also worth observing here that the series and succession of the Roman pontiffs, and the chronological ordering of their episcopates, have always been held in such high regard in the Church that the ancient Fathers—including Irenaeus and others belonging to the earliest centuries of Christianity—wove it into their accounts amid the fury of the persecutions, while later ages, after the freedom of divine worship had been secured, displayed it [Col. 0104B] not only in the Roman basilicas but also in several places far from Rome. I have seen two such examples in Etruria: the metropolitan church of Siena and an ancient church dedicated to God in the name of Saint Peter, in the diocese of Pisa, which they call Saint Peter in Vado.

**4.** To the principal *Catalogs* edited by Schelestratius must be added others of no lesser note, especially two produced by the Reverend Father Jean Mabillon from the autographs of the library of the monastery of Corbie, in volume III of the *Analecta*, p. 426. The first ends with Vigilius, and its writing is assigned to the age of that pontiff, around the middle of the sixth century of the Christian era. The other confirms an age toward the end of the seventh century under Conon and at the beginning of the eighth under Sergius II and John VI. It is contemporary with that most ancient exemplar of the Farnesian *Pontifical Codex*, so often commended by Luca Holstenius and Schelestratius.

I shall therefore present a specimen of it, so that it may be compared with the specimen of the second Corbie *Catalog*, published by Mabillon in book V of *De Re Diplomatica*, table VIII, p. 359. It seemed to me that these two specimens should be joined, so that the nearly equal antiquity of the two codices might be recognized more clearly, an antiquity confirmed by the illustrious men Mabillon and Schelestratius, who are especially competent judges in this field.

**5.** This will be followed by the complete dissertation of that prelate on the *Ancient Catalogs of the Roman Pontiffs*, which I promised in the preface to the first volume, no. 2, would be published before the notes of the various authors on the work of Anastasius. It is the safest guide and, in a sense, a perpetual commentary for recognizing the truth of pontifical history in these *Lives*.

**6.** I have also thought it appropriate to append another Dissertation [Col. 0105A] on the *Ancient Catalogs of the Roman Pontiffs*.

Although the prelate just mentioned wrote so many distinguished works on this subject in the dissertation referred to that he brought forth a rich harvest of selected learning in nearly every chapter, he nevertheless left us some not insignificant gleanings. This is especially so because his inquiry dealt principally with two *Catalogs* rightly regarded as the more important: the first collected under Liberius, the second under Vigilius, both preserved in ancient parchment manuscripts. In passing, however, he touched upon other *Catalogs*, and scarcely indicated the history and chronology of those formerly visible in paintings in the patriarchal basilicas of the City—the Lateran, the Vatican, and Saint Paul on the Ostian Way. Of the last there still survives a sufficiently conspicuous fragment, extending from Fabian to Innocent I.

I thought it worthwhile to dwell on these matters, since they appear to have been publicly displayed by the Roman Church, not without the authority of the pontiffs. It is therefore surprising that, so far as I know, none of the writers has undertaken to compare them with the other writings from the most remote antiquity.

I certainly think it will be exceedingly agreeable to observe that the *Catalog* surviving in the Basilica of Saint Paul displays indications of an age belonging either to Saint Leo the Great himself or not far removed from his century; and to see there assigned to the Roman pontiffs the same numbers of years, months, and days that are read in the 800-year-old codex of the church of Pergamum mentioned above in no. 3, II, and in other documents of equal antiquity to be set out below in our Dissertation, no. 12.

That Dissertation considers not merely the two more important *Catalogs* but also the others, institutes a comparison among several of them, and, unless I am mistaken, explains the causes of the variation found in their chronological numbers.

**7.** To these Prolegomena of the Notes we have attempted to add an appendix: certain short works useful for illustrating many of the *Lives*, and worthy of attention no less for their brevity than for their antiquity, since we shall often have to point to them in collecting documents concerning the events mentioned in the *Lives*.

The first short work bears the title *Description of the Regions of the City*. It is a survey of the principal memorable places occurring on the right and left, both within the walls of the city of Rome and in the suburbs, along the routes of the roads. The author commended these places in writing in the manner of a brief itinerary or topographical map, in the ninth century of Christ, around the age of Charles the Bald.

From this, the location of many sacred buildings and cemeteries of the holy martyrs can be inferred, as well as the names and arrangement of the City’s famous monuments. Since these had not yet been damaged in that age but are now partly destroyed and partly preserved, some obscurity would remain in Anastasius’s text unless it were illuminated with the aid of this itinerary.

The often-praised Mabillon, defender of ancient manuscripts, found the work in the library of the monastery of Einsiedeln in Switzerland, bound into a single codex together with a most ancient collection of Roman inscriptions copied in the City from both sacred and profane buildings. He published it in volume IV of the *Analecta of Learned Antiquity*, p. 506.

I undertake the preparation of a new edition of this brief work all the more willingly because I see that it is necessary to reconnect and articulate its parts, which were separated and torn apart from one another by the binder of that codex and placed in the wrong order—as is clear from the half-words whose letters correspond to the complete wording on the neighboring pages of Mabillon’s edition.

The second short work, dealing with nearly the same subject, must be taken from the *History of the English People* by William, a monk of Malmesbury, written about two hundred years later. On the occasion of the holy expedition undertaken by the crusaders under Urban II in the year of Christ 1096, this writer listed the suburban cemeteries of the holy martyrs according to the number and sequence of the gates of the City and according to the principal roads, recording them in their proper order. It may be called a *Notice of the City*.

**8.** In publishing both of these short works, I have as my authority an eminent writer, equally venerable for the holiness of his life and renowned for his study and writings, through which he illustrated the ancient books and sacred monuments of the Church with exceptional distinction: namely, Joseph Maria Cardinal Thomasius.

In his notes on the ancient Books of Masses, especially on the *Capitularium of the Gospels*, he often produces testimonies from both of the works mentioned: from the Einsiedeln codex, containing the *Description of the Regions of the City* and the collection of Roman inscriptions visible in the City in the ninth century of Christ; and from the *Notice of the City* inserted by William of Malmesbury in book III of his *History of the English People*.

The materials derived from these works should not be regarded as minor aids for clarifying many parts of the work of Anastasius. Since the cemetery in which nearly every pontiff was buried is assigned in each entry, these testimonies teach us the precise location of their tomb and burial.

If anyone considers how closely linked are the ages of the individual monuments—that is, the codices, paintings, and inscriptions collected to protect and preserve the sequence and deeds of the pontiffs—from the fourth century of Christ, when the Liberian *Catalog* was composed, to the sequence carried through the fifth century in the paintings of the Basilica of Saint Paul, extending to the immediate predecessors of Saint Leo the Great; then to the second *Catalog* under Justinian around the middle of the sixth century; and to the Corbie codex *Catalog* contemporary with Vigilius; then from there to the other Corbie *Catalog*, written at the end of the seventh century under Conon and at the beginning of the eighth under Sergius II and John VI; and finally to the notice in the Einsiedeln codex, which displays the age of the ninth century; and if he considers the description of the City produced around the end of the eleventh century by the historian of Malmesbury—if, I say, he attends to these successive ages and codices of corresponding date, everyone can see that these monuments, contemporary with the authors of the *Lives* surviving in this *Liber Pontificalis*, solidly support and elegantly illuminate the work of Anastasius [Col. 0107A]: whether it records the burials of the pontiffs, the foundations of cemeteries and churches, the gifts bestowed upon those sacred buildings by the pontiffs, or the repairs subsequently added. In recording these matters, the authors of the *Lives* generally devoted no small part of their care to them.

**9.** Indeed, I judge that a considerable abridgment could be made from these materials if a topographical map were drawn from the short works. It could display both the more celebrated roads of the City and the principal roads leading into the suburbs, at their proper intervals and dimensions, as far as the cemeteries encountered within two or three miles of the City. Thus, following the indications of both works, the more important memorials and monuments encountered on the right and left along each road would come into view. This would certainly be a kind of note especially commendable for its brevity and usefulness.

**10.** With these explanations, applicable to the work as a whole, now placed beforehand, the individual *Lives* will be furnished with the Notes of the Various Authors in sections attached to the text published in the first volume, and arranged according to the method that I understand most people approve.

To show that the author of the second *Catalog* under Justinian took most of his material from the earlier Liberian *Catalog* published by Bucherius, and that the authors of the *Lives* of Anastasius later borrowed from both, the individual *Lives* of the pontiffs from Saint Peter to Liberius will be reproduced verbatim, as Schelestratius did. [Col. 0107C] We gave a specimen of this in the preface to the first volume, no. 11.

He arranged the material in columns to make room for a review of the succession of the pontiffs collected from the writings of the Fathers and to facilitate comparison of the variant readings. All this harmonizes very well with his purpose and undertaking.

Our purpose here, however, is to show the words transferred from the *Catalogs* into the *Lives of the Liber Pontificalis*; since we included the variant readings in the preceding volume, we shall be content to place the texts of the *Catalogs* and the *Lives* next to one another for comparison.

In this way, the sequence and number of the lines to which the notes refer can be preserved in reproducing the text of the *Lives* of Anastasius, whether they are read in the first volume or in this second volume of the work that we are undertaking. This arrangement by lines could scarcely be preserved if the material were organized in columns.

**11.** The Notes of the Various Authors whom the printer promised to include in this volume will follow, with the names and observations of each produced in alphabetical order.

Schelestratius will be placed before the others, not so much because of the initial letter A of the alphabet, which precedes the complete word of his family name, as because of the nature of his notes. Since they demonstrate the words transferred from the *Catalogs* into Anastasius, they must not be separated from the text of those writers.

Alteserra will come next. Bencinius will follow him. [Col. 0108A] Binius will be joined with Labbe—though their notes will be assigned separately to each—because, in the edition of this *Liber Pontificalis*, the care of both authors comes together as a single undertaking in the material placed under the *Lives* of the pontiffs before the councils held under each pontiff.

If Blanchini has anything to contribute, it will be presented after Binius and Labbe.

He will treat chronological matters rather sparingly in the Notes included in this volume, both because responsibility for the whole of Christian chronology has been assigned to a separate volume, which, God willing, will be the third of this edition, and because the Dissertation he composed on the *Ancient Catalogs of the Roman Pontiffs*, inserted in these Prolegomena as no. 11, will sufficiently present the observations relevant to the chronological ordering of the pontiffs—especially since, at the end of this volume, the said dissertation is accompanied by a consular and pontifical chronology extending across the whole work of Anastasius.

Thus it can readily be understood which *Catalog*, and on the basis of what indications and proofs, should be given preference for each pontiff. More extensive and firmer chronological notes and demonstrations will then be set out year by year in that chronological volume, which will fully treat the Christian era and will also include the sequence of years from Julius Caesar to the beginning of the common Christian era, so that nothing may be lacking in this subject of chronology or in anything necessarily connected with it.

He gives advance notice that he has reserved for the indicated third volume the demonstrations of chronology collected through prolonged labor over more than thirty years, during which he has worked to establish and illuminate chronology; the corrections of the Consular Fasti derived from genuine monuments, marble inscriptions, and ancient coins; and also the corrections or clearer explanations of both pontifical and consular chronology, which are gathered day by day from documents not previously examined, should any such materials come to light while the edition is being prepared.

Ciacconius will receive the place next in alphabetical order. Yet not all of Ciacconius’s observations concerning the *Lives* of the pontiffs are to be included, any more than all the notes of Binius or Labbe, lest the work grow to an immeasurable size.

The more choice observations from their commentaries, and those most useful for explaining the work of Anastasius, have been selected by distinguished men in such a way as to preserve the proportions of a proper volume. Nor will selections be made otherwise from the learned work recently published by the Reverend Father Francesco Pagi, entitled *A Critical Historical-Chronological Breviary Containing the More Illustrious Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs, etc.*

Likewise selections will be made from the distinguished writings of the most illustrious man, Doctor of Sacred Theology, Abbot Jean-Claude Sommier, privy counselor to the most serene Duke of Lorraine and envoy to our most holy lord, published at Nancy in 1716, in which he presents a dogmatic history of the Holy See.

Only a little, however, will be drawn from the chronological material in the notes, since, as was said shortly before, a fuller treatment of chronology is reserved for the third volume of this edition.

[Col. 0109]

# PREFACE OF THE SAME FRANCESCO BLANCHINI TO THE THIRD VOLUME OF THE ROMANO-VATICAN EDITION

[Col. 0109A] **1.** In the preface placed at the beginning of the work, no. 10, I had declared that I would treat in general the origin, authority, and reliability of the history expressed in these *Lives*, as well as its documents and proofs.

I stated that its first origin must be sought in the *Catalogs*, especially in those two which surpass the others in antiquity. The first is assigned to the fourth century of the Christian era under Pope Liberius; the other, under Felix IV, to the first third of the sixth century, approximately the year 530.

We treated both *Catalogs* sufficiently—briefly in the preface to volume I and more fully in the prolegomena to the second volume, where we disclosed the sources and documents of the *Catalogs* in the genuine monuments of the Roman Church and produced the more reliable ancient examples of both, as well as of other *Catalogs*, together with corrections and supplements to them all.

It would therefore seem that this volume too had been adequately provided for by the prolegomena of the second volume, which illuminate the age defined by both *Catalogs*, if the *Lives* included in this third volume did not proceed beyond Felix IV. But since they extend beyond the limits of the Felician *Catalog* nearly to the end of the sixth century, they require us here to bring forward whatever particular material is available after the *Catalog* of Felix IV for illuminating the chronology, history, and documents of the deeds of the pontiffs of the succeeding age.

I shall arrange this material partly in the preface, partly in the prolegomena, and partly in the notes, as was done in the preceding volume.
