**2.** I observe, then, first of all, that under Felix [Col. 0109C] IV the concern of several ministers of the Roman Church did not cease: they continued to collect and abridge the *Lives* of the pontiffs, as they had learned to do from the authors of both the Liberian and Felician *Catalogs*, down to the year 530.

The subsequent *Lives*, composed in due course by the librarians of the Holy Roman See, and the later *Catalogs*, extended into the tenth and eleventh centuries of Christ, abundantly reveal that this custom continued without interruption.

I shall nevertheless produce two particular documents that prove that men devoted to that ancient practice continued repeatedly to observe it—not only down to Gregory the Great, at whom this third volume ends, and even to the twelfth century of Christ, which some of the *Catalogs* published in the earlier volumes reach, but also into later times, indeed down to our own age [Col. 0109D]. Whether through private study or public testimony, they embraced in a document displayed before all eyes [Col. 0110A] a summary of the acts issued by the supreme pontiffs.

### 3

I must not defraud the thirteenth century of Christ of its share in this praise. I shall gladly present a particularly excellent monument of it, and one especially suitable to my subject, recently unearthed on a marble tablet from the suburban ruins of a vineyard situated not far from the city walls on the Vatican hills. An epitaph of Pope Nicholas III, engraved on that marble in capital letters, so closely approaches the style of the concise compilation of Lives employed in the catalogues that it might seem to be a portion of a catalogue—unless the appearance of the stone and the Gothic form of the letters, characteristic of that age, showed that it was an inscription once affixed to the wall of the City, in that part of the Vatican pomerium which, as we read also in Ptolemy of Lucca, Jordanus, and Platina, had been founded or restored by Nicholas III.

I suspect that it was thrown down together with the ancient walls and recklessly carried into the neighboring vineyards by the masons when the new fortifications, with their bastions, were constructed according to the principles of modern military architecture under Urban VIII, and when the old walls with their towers—which had formerly defined the circuit of the Leonine City and the Vatican palace—were demolished. When the marble was fortunately pointed out to me, and was being removed from the chisels of the stonecutters, who were just about to cut it into pieces or consign it miserably to the lime kiln, I redeemed it as quickly as possible for a cash payment. I judged that it ought to be offered [Col. 0110C] to the Roman magistracy, so that it might henceforth be preserved in the Capitoline buildings together with the other monuments of the supreme pontiffs that may hereafter be found torn from their original places.

For the memories of our pontiffs have a stronger claim to be preserved there and rescued from the injuries of time than the names and records of the ancient or recent princes and magistrates of the City, inasmuch as the royal priesthood of Christ, consecrated in the city that rules all things through the see of blessed Peter, surpasses the heights to which human affairs are subject.

Yet I should wish that this might serve as an incentive to the care imposed upon me of rescuing Roman antiquities from destruction and oblivion, and to my most obedient devotion toward the City, which has deserved the love of all nations by so many titles, since it kindly embraces, nourishes, cherishes, and honors them. As a unique mother and fatherland, she offers foreigners not only the gifts of her own commonwealth, even the highest, but whatever is most precious in heaven and on earth, which God Almighty has granted to the human race to be distributed through her. I say, I should wish this grateful and dutiful devotion toward our common mother to serve as an incentive, so that whatever she brings forth from her own entrails—especially ancient works and writings conveying to posterity the memory of events, of her rulers and citizens, above all of the holy martyrs and supreme pontiffs, and then of Caesars, kings, dictators, consuls, city prefects, and other magistrates, as well as of laws, triumphs, and distinguished achievements—may be preserved for that most benevolent mother and teacher of truth.

But these matters, though belonging elsewhere, have nevertheless been brought forward here by the piety owed to my most beloved mother and by the close connection and bond between her monuments and the public good, which compelled me to make this prayer. [Col. 0111B]

It was therefore a fortunate circumstance that this tablet displayed to us a document of the best pontiff preserved for our age: Nicholas III, from the illustrious family of the Orsini. For this very age in which we happily live boasts that the most holy Father and lord, our own Benedict XIII, was born from the same stock and divinely given as pontiff for the good of the Church; and it earnestly prays that he may long remain safe and flourishing in office, so that he may transmit richer and lasting examples of his virtues to late posterity. [Col. 0112A]

Yet it was especially fitting that the revived memory of Pope Nicholas should be preserved for this work—namely, of that prelate who, being zealously devoted to transmitting the monuments of his predecessors to posterity, ordered the series of Roman pontiffs in the patriarchal basilicas of Saints Peter and Paul to be repeated, together with the chronology of the years, months, and days assigned there to each pontificate. This series had been depicted above from ancient exemplars under Leo the Great, and he ordered it to be repeated with images of the same pontiffs beneath the entablatures of the columns. I explained this in the prolegomena to the second volume, from folio 72 to folio 80; the very form and shape of the letters also demonstrates it.

For the letters of those ancient Leonine series, both in mosaic and in paintings and [Col. 0112B] inscriptions of the pontiffs, are square, just as in the epigrams carved in marble in the fourth century under Damasus, or toward the end of the fifth under Celestine, Sixtus, Leo the Great, Hilary, and others. In the series added by Nicholas III, however, the form of the letters is no longer straight, square, or circular, but elongated and curved with a Gothic inflection. Such is what we see in the marble tablet engraved under the pontificate of Nicholas himself, which I reproduce here faithfully.

[Col. 0111]

**Inscription of Nicholas III, Pope, discovered in this year 1727 and transferred to the Capitoline buildings, with the following epigraph by decree of the Senate.**

[Col. 0112B]

**Ancient inscription of Nicholas III, Supreme Pontiff—who deserved exceptionally well of the increase of divine worship, the peace of the Christian commonwealth, the liberty and security of the ecclesiastical dominion, its rights, and the tranquil condition of the City—formerly affixed to the walls of the Vatican pomerium and recently found on a suburban estate on the Via Aurelia.**

**While our most holy lord Benedict XIII sat as pope, Paul, Marquis de Maccaranis, Councillor; Camillus Capranica, Councillor; Prosper, Marquis de Caffarellis, Councillor; and Lothaire, Marquis de Lotteriis, Prior Cap. Reg., caused it to be added to the Capitoline Fasti, as destined to be an ornament not so much to the glory of the Orsini family as to the fatherland. On the Ides of December 1727. Francis Blanchinus of Verona, Domestic Prelate of His Holiness the Pope, presented it to the Capitol.**

[Col. 0111C]

### 4

Everyone can easily understand that the author of this inscription had before his eyes the style of the ancient catalogues and biographers of the Anastasian age [Col. 0112C] when he dictated it with unpolished skill, as the condition of that unhappy age allowed. For just as they, and indeed still older writers, were accustomed to write:

“Vigilius, a Roman by nationality, son of the consul John; Pelagius, a Roman by nationality, son of Vicarianus; Gregory, a Roman by nationality, son of Gordianus; Nicholas II, a Roman by nationality, son of Theodore the regionary,”

so the author of our inscription thought it necessary to record that Nicholas III was a Roman by nationality, the son of Lord Matthew, to whom the surname Rubeus was additionally given, of the house of the Orsini.

Those earlier writers had written of Felix IV:

“He built the basilica of Saints Cosmas and Damian, and rebuilt from the ground the basilica of Saint Saturninus.”

And of Leo III he records that the city named after him, the Leonine City [as its founder], began to be built in the second year of his pontificate, while in the sixth year he completed the work with great and marvelous buildings. [section 33]

So too the more recent eulogist of Nicholas III wrote:

“He caused larger palaces, a hall, and a chapel to be built, and enlarged other ancient houses in the first year of his pontificate; and in the second year of his pontificate he caused the circuit of the walls of this pomerium to be built.”

It is therefore clear that for many centuries, even after the two catalogues of Liberius and Felix IV had been composed, imitation of the style of the ancient catalogues and biographers of the apostolic see remained vigorous. These writers recorded the homeland and father of each pontiff, together with a summary of his deeds, just as the Roman clergy were accustomed to recite in the morning lessons of the holy pontiffs. I am easily persuaded that the inscription of Nicholas III which we have reproduced was dictated by someone from the clergy accustomed to such lessons.

From this it may also be understood that the ancient titles and inscriptions of works constructed or restored by the supreme pontiffs sometimes supplied posterity not only with material but also with wording, when later writers produced their catalogues and brief Lives for their own age. [Col. 0113C]

### 5

Another source was available to the biographers and abbreviators, immediately after the Liberian Catalogue, from which they could obtain reliable and public evidence for the concise chronology, genealogy, and history of each pontiff. Blessed Damasus, the immediate successor of Liberius, adorned in verse many memorials of martyrs and other saints, and sometimes even embellished the ashes of private faithful, out of the charity with which that most devout Father cared for the children of the Church entrusted to him.

He thus introduced examples of a practice that continued thereafter: namely, the placing at the tombs of succeeding pontiffs of epigraphs bound by meter, in which the more important deeds and usually the chronology of those prelates were indicated. Examples of such epigraphs are read everywhere in the Annals of Baronius and in the appendix to Gruter’s *Thesaurus*, as well as in the description of the Vatican basilica by Benedict the Canon, published by Pietro de Angelis.

Many of these were transcribed by the retinue of Charlemagne, and even by Charlemagne himself. He not only brought learned men with him, but also composed with his own hand that elegant epigraph for the tomb of Pope Hadrian I, as we learn from the collection of an old codex in the library of Einsiedeln, in the fourth volume of Mabillon’s *Analecta*, and from the learned notes on that same collection. [Col. 0114A]

A considerable harvest of documents was therefore available to writers who continued the catalogues and Lives of the supreme pontiffs, as they examined such titles in order to gather their gleanings from them. Much fuller sources of history, however, were opened to them in the letters of those same pontiffs and in the Acts of the councils, as was observed long ago in the prefaces to the first and second volumes of our edition.

### 6

Having briefly indicated these matters, I must not pass over another category of concise documents, which were used not only in past ages but remain in use in our own, and which reproduce the brevity and order of the catalogues and biographers.

At the funeral of a Roman pontiff, the physicians and surgeons receive the deceased body, washed by the penitentiary priests of the Vatican basilica, in order to embalm it with balm and spices; when it has thus been prepared and cleansed, they hand it over to the sacred ministers to be clothed in pontifical vestments. It is then carried by the canons and clergy of the Vatican for the customary nine-day funeral rites. After it has been exposed for three days to the pious devotion of the people, who flock to it and reverently offer their final kisses to the feet of the apostolic man, they place it in a cypress coffin, over which they fit another leaden case.

On the lid of this they arrange a short inscription, composed of raised bronze letters. Each letter is fixed by sharp projecting points, like nails, and firmly secured to the sheet of lead so that the letters may not fall out or be displaced. Through them one reads distinctly the name, homeland, age, and dates of the life and pontificate of the deceased prelate.

Nearly forty-four years have now passed since, by God’s favor, I happily came to the City, while Pope Innocent XI, of venerable memory, occupied the Roman chair. When he was taken from human affairs on the day before the Ides of August 1689, a Friday, I saw the following inscription, in raised bronze characters, affixed to the lid of the leaden case prepared to enclose his body. The inscription was reported in his *Diary* by Candidus Cassina, master of pontifical sacred ceremonies and canon of the basilica of Saint Mary across the Tiber.

[Col. 0114D]

**+ To God, the Best and Greatest. Innocent XI, Supreme Pontiff, formerly Benedict Odescalchi of Como, died on the 12th day of August 1689. He was 78 years, 2 months, and 24 days old. He lived in the pontificate for 12 years, 10 months, and 21 days.**

The venerable servant of God was succeeded by Alexander VIII, Innocent XII, and Clement XI. If I were to try to repay in writing the benefits they bestowed upon me, I would plainly be charged with arrogance and with undertaking a task beyond my powers. Yet I shall not be blamed if, as an eyewitness, I testify that the custom observed in their burials was the same as in the case of Innocent, since by their gracious favor I had been chosen for domestic service to Alexander and Clement and ought not to have failed in my final duties toward them.

I therefore add that, besides the inscription fixed to the leaden coffin, another special inscription on a bronze tablet was enclosed in the coffin of Pope Alexander by His Eminence and Most Reverend Nephew, Cardinal Pietro Ottoboni, Vice-Chancellor of the Holy Roman Church and now also Bishop of Sabina, when he transferred the body of his great-uncle, who had deserved so well of him, to the cell of the magnificent monument which he had erected at his own expense and which we admire among the chief ornaments of the Vatican basilica.

On that bronze tablet too the restraint of the ancient catalogues was preserved. It briefly indicated the name, homeland, lineage, and principal dates of his life and offices in the Roman Church, in a concise arrangement, with the customary sign of the Lord’s cross placed at the beginning.

[Col. 0115B]

**+ To God, the Best and Greatest. To Alexander VIII, Supreme Pontiff, formerly Pietro Ottoboni, son of Marco, knight and grand chancellor of the Venetian Republic, born at Venice on 22 April 1610 of his wife Vittoria Torniela; admitted among the cardinals in 1652; raised to the Roman See on the day before the Nones of October 1689; resting in Christ on the Kalends of February 1691. Pietro Cardinal Ottoboni, Vice-Chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, grandson of his brother, placed this for his most excellent great-uncle and prince, in the Jubilee Year 1700.**

For Clement XI, His Eminence and Most Reverend Lord Cardinal Annibale Albani, Camerlengo of the Holy Roman Church and Archpriest of the Vatican basilica, placed in the underground chamber of the basilica choir—which was opened solely to his devoted diligence so that he might adorn with appropriate dignity and zeal the tomb of so great a pontiff—this brief marble tablet in the ancient manner, in addition to the inscription customarily affixed to the leaden coffin. Clement himself had forbidden that a magnificent monument be erected for him after his death.

[Col. 0115D]

**To Clement XI, Supreme Pontiff, formerly Giovanni Francesco Albani, son of Carlo. Cardinal Annibale Albani, Camerlengo of the Holy Roman Church and Archpriest of the Vatican basilica, placed this for his most beneficent uncle. In the year of salvation 1722.**

Other very brief inscriptions are also placed for Roman pontiffs who close their final day in the City, when their hearts, removed from the body during the preparation and embalming of the corpse with spices, are honorably deposited in a sacred place.

If the pontiff happens to die in the Vatican palace, they are placed in the pavement of the sacristy of the basilica of Saint Peter, near the altar, in a small shrine or chapel constructed for preserving the relics of the saints. If he dies at the Quirinal—which has happened to most of them since they began to inhabit the palace founded there by Paul V—the hearts are carried to the parish church of Saints Vincent and Anastasius. There, near the high altar on the Gospel side, they are buried in the pavement beneath very brief marble inscriptions expressing the following sense. I shall transcribe two of the several inscriptions that can be read there.

**To God, the Best and Greatest. The heart of Clement X, Supreme Pontiff, who died at the Quirinal on 22 July 1676.**

**To God, the Best and Greatest. The heart of Innocent XIII, Supreme Pontiff, who died at the Quirinal on 7 March 1724.**

[Col. 0116B]

### 7

We therefore see that neither in the age of Liberius nor in the time of Felix IV did the practice cease of preserving the style of the catalogues in brief and public monuments of this kind. Rather, it was consistently transmitted in the Roman Church down to our own age, partly in sacred diptychs, partly in catalogues and brief Lives, and also in marble tablets and metal inscriptions.

It must therefore be accepted by all that the reliability of the chronology and history of the Roman pontiffs is established not only by these documents collected after the catalogues of Liberius and Felix IV, but also by monuments of a similar kind—diptychs, inscriptions, and publicly authenticated Acts—through the record of their lives in councils, ordinations, dedications, and numerous deeds performed during their pontificates, as well as through the record of their funerals and burials.

### 8

The preface therefore had to touch upon these customs still practiced among us, which in general establish the origins and sources of the later Anastasian work after the two catalogues published under Liberius and Felix IV. They show that the pious practice of recording the name, lineage, and times of each successor to the chair of blessed Peter had never been interrupted.

I say “in general,” because our preface was bound to address these proofs only in general terms. The other particular matters that demonstrate, one by one, the chronological characteristics of each pontiff and indicate his more important deeds are reserved for the notes customarily supplied for the individual sections.

### 9

Having completed this prior task in our preface—which, as we said, concerns the indication of the origins of the later work from the endpoint of the period defined by the two ancient catalogues—it proceeds to another duty, namely, to present the short works that I judged should be included in the Prolegomena. I decided that three would suffice for this volume.

In the long succession of pontiffs extending over nearly three centuries, from blessed Sylvester to Gregory the Great, who are presented in this volume, the Church, flourishing in peace under Christian rulers for the most part, seemed to offer the ministry of its government more easily to the supreme pontiffs, who governed it with the authority of Christ’s vicar on earth. The open force of persecutors no longer attacked men of the priestly order as it had under Decius and Diocletian.

But when the storm of that tenth persecution had subsided, and no longer sought to swallow Peter’s ship together with its helmsman, an internal disturbance of heresies and schisms shook the sailors and attempted to drive the helmsman himself from the helm. The authors of that turmoil, cast out from the assembly of the faithful by a just expulsion, as was fitting, degenerated from fellow travelers into pirates.

The heresiarchs, expelled from the Church, displayed hostile intentions. They were often thrust forward by princes who had themselves been led into error, in order to seize the very thrones from which they had been deposed. From there they thundered against the Roman faith and see. This happened more than once among the Constantinopolitans: relying on secular power, they attempted to overturn the dogma of the Catholic religion and tear down and destroy apostolic rights.

Meanwhile, the unbroken courage of Peter’s successors defended the authority entrusted to them, strengthened the other bishops in preserving constancy of faith and maintaining the order of unity and discipline. Through the changing circumstances of different ages, the equal and consistent vigor of the Roman prelates manifested the power divinely promised to them, and the firmness of that rock against which the gates of hell shall not prevail.

This equal solidity amid such a variety of dangers throughout those three centuries, from the fourth to the sixth of the Christian era—centuries that miserably tore apart and overthrew the Roman Empire—would strike the reader’s mind less clearly if it were divided limb by limb, so to speak, and displayed piecemeal only in the text [Col. 0117C] and notes. It had to be gathered into a continuous delineation, as it were into a single body of history.

Since the illustrious and most reverend Lord Archbishop of Caesarea, Jean-Claude Sommier, had done this in the preface to the second volume of his *Dogmatic History of the Holy See*, we arranged for it to be printed first among the short works in the prolegomena to this volume, as number 1. The distinguished gentleman Don Gaetano Cenni translated it from French into Latin, thereby relieving me of this labor, since I was otherwise occupied with rendering into Latin the notes from the same prelate’s book and with continuing the chronology, which occupies the final place in the prolegomena.

### 10

That first short work therefore serves to clarify the general view of the History. The remaining works collected in the prolegomena concern the confirmation of the deeds mentioned in that History or in the Lives of the pontiffs.

The principal deeds concern either the establishment of rules of faith and morals or the enactment of laws governing the accurate performance of divine worship, together with the causes and judgments pertaining to that worship. Under this heading come the elections, ordinations, and consecrations of major and minor priests and ministers; the foundations, endowments, and dedications of sacred buildings; and the canon and order of the entire divine ministry by which these matters are carried out.

Those matters that concern the rules of faith and morals, whether established in councils summoned and approved by the supreme pontiffs or outside councils in their decretal letters, require no clarification or proof in the prolegomena. The ancient collections of canons, especially the Latin ones, are available to everyone. Most writers of our age date the beginnings of these collections to the fifth century of Christ and find their growth in the sixth century through Dionysius surnamed Exiguus, or in the immediately subsequent ages through the work of Cresconius and Isidore.

More recent scholars of canon law have also abundantly surpassed the diligence of the ancients in extensive works subjected to keen judgment and correction. The same is true of the collection of decretal letters and of the separation among them of genuine and authentic letters from apocryphal and spurious ones. Thus this part of the pontifical deeds seems to need no separate short work.

[Col. 0118B]

### 11

The other part of the pontifical office, however, concerns the proper practice of divine worship through the foundation of sacred places and communities, their endowments and dedications, as well as through the institution and ordination of priests and the orderly sequence of the ministry suitably performed by them. All these matters usefully invite the selection of several short works to be inserted into these prolegomena for the illustration or confirmation of the history arranged in the Lives.

For during the nearly three hundred years counted from the age of Constantine and Sylvester to Gregory the Great and, very nearly, the reign of Phocas—the period covered by this volume—there occurred the principal foundations and endowments of churches, the kinds of sacred furnishings brought into buildings dedicated to God, and the other instruments of divine worship. These are here recorded under ancient names by the librarians of their respective times, terms which writers of the Latin language had not previously admitted and which later generations did not retain down to our own age.

This obscurity therefore needed to be illuminated with the aid of a learned nomenclator who could appropriately carry a torch before us. The prudent restorer of history, Panvinio, had already done this when he composed a short work transmitted to Laurentius Celsus and printed together with Platina’s *Lives of the Pontiffs* at Cologne by Scholinus in 1574. Its title is: *Interpretation of Ecclesiastical Words That Appear Obscure or Barbarous*.

I had resolved to reprint this work of Panvinio here as the primary source of the *Hierolexica*, and as sufficiently suitable for elucidating the vocabulary of Anastasius, especially since it was not readily available because of the scarcity of copies. But since much more extensive dictionaries, filled with the learning of every age, have now appeared—especially those of Macri and Du Cange—which can no longer be obtained only with difficulty because of repeated printings, I refrained from including Panvinio’s work and similar works among the prolegomena.

I thought it preferable to present several public documents from the age under discussion, in which the foundation and endowment of churches are associated with descriptions of sacred furnishings, the obscure and barbarous terms used by the librarian being also expressed in the text itself.

### 12

Of these, the document from the archive of Tivoli called by diplomatic writers the Cornutian Charter was to be preferred above the others. It was first brought to light by the distinguished Joseph Suaresius, then a learned young man and later most illustrious Bishop of Vaison. It was subsequently reprinted by Mabillon, the most authoritative of all experts in diplomatic matters, and rightly placed at the beginning of the other charters collected in that entirely incomparable work.

It will be sufficient, then, to show from this document of the period under discussion, entered into the public records under the fourth consulship of Leo Augustus and that of Probianus—that is, in the Christian era 471—the practice of donations and endowments made to sacred buildings, as well as several terms for kinds and categories of sacred furnishings, which occur equally in the text of the Librarian and in the Cornutian Charter.

We shall be content to use this as a specimen with which to illustrate the prolegomena to this third volume, since other examples have been brought forward from ancient inscriptions in the preface to the first volume, number 45 and following.

### 13

Having furnished our prolegomena with these short works, we shall complete them by adding the pontifical, imperial, and consular chronology of the three centuries entrusted to this volume. I arranged it in imitation of that set out in the preceding second volume, year by year, with the documents of ancient monuments that confirm it, so that afterward the way may lie open for entering, as usual, into the sections of the librarian’s text and their notes, and so that the royal road may be secured.

[Col. 0119]

## Catalogue of the Roman Pontiffs

[Note: This catalogue is more confused and corrupt as far as Callistus; after him it becomes somewhat clearer, especially after Lucius.]

Cuspinianus transferred the whole of it into his *Fasti*.

From the commentary of Aegidius Bucherius on Victor of Aquitaine’s *Paschal Canon*, p. 269 of the Plantinian edition, Antwerp, 1634, with the marginal notes of Bucherius himself. (C)

[Col. 0119B]

Under the reign of Caesar Tiberius, our Lord Jesus Christ suffered, when the two Gemini were consuls, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. After his Ascension, the most blessed Peter assumed the episcopate. From that time the succession was arranged: who each bishop was, how many years he presided, and under which emperor.

**PETER**, for twenty-five years, one month, and nine days. He lived during the times of Tiberius Caesar, Caius, Tiberius Claudius, and Nero, from the consulship of Vinicius and Longinus to that of Nero and Vetus [Note: My manuscript has Nerva and Verus]. He suffered with Paul on the third day before the Kalends of July, when the consuls were SS., under the emperor Nero.

**LINUS**, for twelve years, four months, and twelve days. He lived during the time of Nero, from the consulship of Saturninus and Scipio to that of Capito and Rufus.

**CLEMENT**, for nine years, eleven months, and twelve days. [Note: Eusebius and Baronius place Clement after Cletus.] He lived during the times of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus to the sixth consulship of Vespasian and that of Titus.

**CLETUS**, for six years, two months, and ten days. [Col. 0119C] He lived during the times of Vespasian and Titus and at the beginning of Domitian’s reign, from the eighth consulship of Vespasian and the fifth of Domitian to the ninth of Domitian and that of Rufus.

**ANACLETUS**, for twelve years, ten months, and three days. He lived during the time of Domitian, from the tenth consulship of Domitian and that of Sabinus to the seventeenth of Domitian and that of Clement.

**EVARISTUS**, for thirteen years, seven months, and two days. [Note: The manuscript has Aristus.] He lived during the final years of Domitian, and during the reigns of Nerva and Trajan, from the consulship of Valens and Verus to that of Gallus and Bradua.

**ALEXANDER**, for seven years, two months, and one day. He lived during the time of Trajan, from the consulship of Palma and Tullus to that of Velianus [Note: Perhaps Aelianus] and Vetus.

**SIXTUS**, for ten years, three months, and twenty-one days. He lived during the time of Hadrian, from the consulship of Niger and Apronianus to the third consulship of Verus and that of Ambibulus.

[Col. 0120B]

**TELESPHORUS**, for eleven years, three months, and three days. He lived during the time of Antoninus Macrinus, from the consulship of Titianus and Gallicanus to that of Caesar and Balbinus.

**HYGINUS**, for twelve years, three months, and six days. He lived during the time of Verus, from the consulship of Gallicanus and Vetus to that of Praesens and Rufinus.

**PIUS**, for twenty years, four months, and twenty-one days. He lived during the time of Antoninus Pius, from the consulship of Clarus and Severus to the two Augusti. During his episcopate, his brother Hermes wrote a book containing and setting forth the command given to him by the angel when the angel came to him in the guise of a shepherd.

[Note: Anicetus is missing here; they assign him nearly eight years.]

**SOTER**, for nine years, three months, and two days. He lived during the times of Antoninus and Commodus, from the consulship of Verus and Erennianus to that of Paternus and Bradua.

[Note: Eleutherius is again missing; they maintain that he occupied the see for fifteen years.]

**VICTOR**, for nine years, two months, and ten days, from the consulship of Saturninus and Gallus to that of Praesens [Col. 0120C] and Extricatus.

[Note: Zephyrinus is likewise missing; they assign him eighteen years.]

**CALLISTUS**, for five years, two months, and ten days. He lived during the times of Macrinus and Heliogabalus, from the consulship of Antoninus and Adventus to the third consulship of Antoninus and that of Alexander.

**URBAN**, for eight years, eleven months, and twelve days. He lived during the time of Alexander, from the consulship of Maximus and Aelianus to that of Agricola and Clementinus.

**PONTIANUS**, for five years, two months, and seven days. He lived during the time of Alexander, from the consulship of Pompeianus and Pelignianus. At that time Bishop Nepotianus [Note: Cuspinianus reads Pontianus; I believe that is better.] and the presbyter Hippolytus were deported as exiles to the harmful island of Sardinia, when Severus and Quintianus were consuls. On that island he was stripped of his office on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, and Anteros was ordained in his place on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, when the consuls were SS.

**ANTEROS**, for one month and ten days. He fell asleep on the third day before the Nones of January, when Maximus and Africanus were consuls.

[Col. 0121A]

**FABIAN**, for fourteen years, one month, and ten days. He lived during the times of Maximinus, Gordian, and Philip, from the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus to the second consulship of Decius and that of Gratus. He suffered on the twelfth day before the Kalends of February.

He divided the regions among the deacons and ordered many buildings to be constructed in the cemeteries. After his suffering, the presbyters Moses and Maximus and the deacon Nicostratus were arrested and thrown into prison. At that time Novatus came from Africa and separated Novatian and certain confessors from the Church, after Moses had died in prison. He had been there eleven months and eleven days.

**CORNELIUS**, for two years, three months, and ten days. From the consulships of Decius IV and Decius II to those of Gallus and Volusianus. During his episcopate, Novatus ordained Novatian outside the Church in the city of Rome, and Nicostratus in Africa. After this had happened, the confessors who had separated themselves from Cornelius, together with the presbyter Maximus, who had been with Moses, returned to the Church; afterward they were expelled to Centumcellae. There he received a glorious falling-asleep.

[Col. 0121B]

**LUCIUS**, for three years, eight months, and ten days. He lived during the times of Gallus and Volusianus, to the third consulship of Valerian and the second of Gallienus. He was an exile; afterward, by the will of God, he returned unharmed to the Church [Note: It appears that “he died” is missing here], on the third day before the Nones of March, when the consuls were SS.

**STEPHANUS**, for four years, two months, and twenty-one days. He lived during the times of Valerian and Gallienus, from the consulship of Volusianus and Maximinus to the third consulship of Valerian and the second of Gallienus.

**SIXTUS**, for two years, eleven months, and six days. He began with the consulship of Maximus and Glabrio and continued to that of Tuscus and Bassus. He suffered on the eighth day before the Ides of August, from the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus to the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, when Aemilianus and Bassus were consuls.

**DIONYSIUS**, for eight years, two months, and four days. He lived during the time of Gallienus, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, when Aemilianus and Bassus were consuls, to the seventh day before the Kalends of January, when Claudius and Paternus were consuls.

**FELIX**, for five years, eleven months, and twenty-five days. He lived during the times of Claudius and Aurelian, from the consulship of Claudius and Paternus to the second consulship of Aurelian and that of Capitolinus.

**EUTYCHIAN**, for eight years, eleven months, and three days. He lived during the time of Aurelian, from the third consulship of Aurelian and that of Marcellinus to the seventh day before the Ides of December, when Carus II and Carinus were consuls.

[Col. 0122A]

**CAIUS**, for twelve years, four months, and seven days. He lived during the times of Carus and Carinus, from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, when Carus II and Carinus were consuls, to the tenth day before the Kalends of May, when Diocletian VI and Constantius II were consuls.

**MARCELLINUS**, for eight years, three months, and twenty-five days. He lived during the times of Diocletian and Maximian, from the day before the Kalends of July, beginning with the consulships of Diocletian VI and Constantius II and continuing to the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII. At that time there was a persecution, and the episcopate ceased for seven years [Note: Three should apparently be read here, according to the sequence of the consuls, although that sequence is confused], six months, and twenty-five days.

**MARCELLUS**, for one year, seven months, and twenty days. He lived during the time of Maxentius, from the tenth consulship and Maximian [Note: The seventh appears to be missing here. Others read “the ninth and Maximian”] to after the tenth and seventh consulships.

**EUSEBIUS**, for four months and sixteen days, from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September.

[Col. 0122B]

**MILTIADES**, for three years, six months, and nine days, from the sixth day before the Nones of July, beginning with the consulship of Maximian VIII alone—which occurred in September, when Volusianus and Rufinus were consuls—to the third day before the Ides of January, when Volusianus and Annianus were consuls.

**SYLVESTER**, for twenty-one years and eleven months. He lived during the time of Constantine, from the consulship of Volusianus and Annianus, beginning on the day before the Kalends of February, to the Kalends of January, when Constantius and Albinus were consuls.

**MARCUS**, for eight months and twenty days. He too lived during the time of Constantine, when Nepotianus and Facundus were consuls, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February to the day of the Nones of October, when the consuls were SS.

JULIUS: fifteen years, one month, eleven days. He was [bishop] in the time of Constantine, from the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus, from the eighth day before the Ides of February until the day before the Ides of April, when Constantius V and Constantius Caesar were consuls. He constructed many buildings: a basilica on the Via Portuensis at the third milestone; a basilica on the [Col. 0122C] Via Flaminia at the second milestone, which is called Valentini [Note: [Col. 0122C] Perhaps it is Valentinus, to whom the following Calendar is inscribed.]; the Basilica Julia, which is in the seventh region, beside the Forum of the deified Trajan; a basilica across the Tiber, in the fourteenth region, beside Callistus; and a basilica on the Via Aureliana, at the third milestone, at Callistus.

LIBERIUS was [bishop] in the time of Constantius, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of June until the day . . . ., when Constantius V and Constantius Caesar were consuls [Note: [Col. 0122C] Almost all these little works end with these consuls; from this it appears that they were written in this year of Christ 354, or approximately then.].

[Col. 0121]

## THE DEPOSITION OF THE BISHOPS

[Note: [Col. 0121D] Namely, of the Roman bishops from Lucius to Julius.]

(From the same Bucherius.) (C)

[Col. 0121D] On the sixth day before the Kalends of January: Dionysius, at Callistus’. On the third day before the Kalends of January: Felix, at Callistus’. On the day before the Kalends of January: Sylvester, at Priscilla’s. On the fourth day before the Ides of January: Miltiades, at Callistus’. On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February: Marcellinus, at Priscilla’s. On the third day before the Nones of March: Lucius [Note: [Col. 0121D] Lucius is the oldest of these twelve pontiffs, Julius the most recent. Two intermediate names are missing, [Col. 0122D] Sixtus and Marcellus. Sixtus is among the martyrs.] at Callistus’.

[Col. 0122D] On the tenth day before the Kalends of May: Caius, at Callistus’. On the fourth day before the Nones of August: Stephen, at Callistus’. On the sixth day before the Kalends of October: Eusebius, at Callistus’. On the Nones of October: Marcus, at Balbina’s. On the sixth day before the Ides of December: Eutychianus, at Callistus’. On the day before the Ides of April: Julius, on the Via Aurelia, at the third milestone, at Callistus’.

[Col. 0123]

## THE DEPOSITION OF THE MARTYRS

(From the same Bucherius.) (C)

[Col. 0123A] On the eighth day before the Kalends of January, Christ was born at Bethlehem of Judea.

### IN THE MONTH OF JANUARY

On the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February: Fabianus, at Callistus’, and Sebastianus, in the Catacombs. On the twelfth day before the Kalends of February: Agnes, on the Nomentan Way.

### IN THE MONTH OF FEBRUARY

On the eighth day before the Kalends of March: the commemoration of Peter of the Chair.

### IN THE MONTH OF MARCH

On the Nones of March: Perpetua and Felicitas of Africa.

### IN THE MONTH OF MAY

On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June: Parthinus and Calocerus, at Callistus’, in the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximianus VIII.

### IN THE MONTH OF JUNE

On the third day before the Kalends of July: PETER, in the Catacombs, and [Col. 0123B] PAUL, on the Ostian Way, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus [Note: [Col. 0123B] I do not know what these consuls are doing here; perhaps they have been displaced from another place.].

### IN THE MONTH OF JULY

On the sixth day before the Ides [Note: [Col. 0123B] There are seven sons of Saint Felicitas. The cemeteries of the Jordani, Maximus, and Praetextatus were in Rome.]: Felix and Philippus, at Priscilla’s; and, at the Jordani, Martialis, Vitalis, and Alexander; and, at Maximus, Silanus (this martyr Silanus [Note: [Col. 0124B] Perhaps Novatianus.] the followers of Novatus stole); and, at Praetextatus, Januarius. On the third day before the Kalends of August: Abdon and Sennen, at Pontianus’, which is at the Bear with the Cap.

### IN THE MONTH OF AUGUST

On the eighth day before the Ides: Sixtus, at Callistus’, and Praetextatus, Agapitus, and Felicissimus.

[Col. 0124A] On the seventh day before the Ides of August: Secundus, Carpophorus, Victorinus, and Severianus, at Albano and on the Ostian Way. On the sixth day before the Ides: Ballistaria [Note: [Col. 0124B] Perhaps the Salarian Way.], Cyriacus, Largus, Crescentianus, Memmia, Juliana, and Smaragdus. On the fourth day before the Ides: Laurentius, on the Tiburtine Way. On the Ides of August: Hippolytus, on the Tiburtine Way, and Pontianus, at Callistus’. On the eleventh day before the Kalends of September: Timotheus, on the Ostian Way. On the fifth day before the Kalends: Hermes, at Bassilla’s, on the old Salarian Way.

### IN THE MONTH OF SEPTEMBER

On the Nones of September: Acontius at Porto, and Nonnus, Herculanus, and Taurinus. On the fifth day before the Ides: Gorgonius, on the Labican Way. On the third day before the Ides: Protus and Hyacinthus, at Bassilla’s. On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October: Cyprianus of Africa. He is celebrated at Rome, at Callistus’. On the tenth day before the Kalends of October: Bassilla, on the old Salarian Way, in the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximianus VIII.

[Col. 0124B] ### IN THE MONTH OF OCTOBER

On the day before the Ides: Callistus, on the Via Aurelia, at the third milestone.

### IN THE MONTH OF NOVEMBER

On the fifth day before the Ides: Clemens, Sempronianus, Claudius, and Nicostratus, at the Comitatum. On the third day before the Kalends of December: Saturninus, at Thrason’s.

### IN THE MONTH OF DECEMBER

On the Ides: Aristo, at Pontus [Note: [Col. 0124B] Perhaps Pontianus.].
