## FRANCESCO BLANCHINI’S BRIEF NOTES

### On the chronology of the Catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, reckoned from the epoch of the Passion of Christ our Lord, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the two Gemini

[Col. 0123C] So many vigils have been devoted to adorning this celebrated little work by Bucherius, its first editor, and by other learned men, that adding new studies might seem superfluous. It is enough, indeed, to consult the dissertation of Schelestratius, reprinted below, in order to understand its value, defend its authority, clarify obscure passages, and uncover and supply its lacunae.

I shall append only brief notes to the chronology of this same little work, reckoned from the epoch of Christ’s Passion, established on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the two Gemini. If you desire fuller documentation concerning this, I hope that ample and reliable material will be produced by me [Col. 0124C] in a dissertation on the same subject, which I reserve for printing below, since it is devoted to Christian chronology, whose key and hinge is the epoch of the Passion of Christ our Lord. This epoch is to be established, with Victorius of Aquitaine, in the twenty-eighth year of the common era, a leap year, in the consulship of the two Gemini.

In that year, the twenty-eighth of the common era—but the thirty-third year of the life of Christ our Lord—the reckoning begins on the day before the eighth day before the Kalends of January. For no one now doubts that he was born a full five years before the common era, if he has examined the coin of Herod Antipas, felicitously explained by Cardinal Norisius after the epochs of the Syro-Macedonians: it was struck under Gaius Caligula and marked as belonging to the forty-third year of that same HEROD THE TETRARCH, on the eighth day before the Kalends of [Col. 0125A] April, a Thursday, but on the first day of Unleavened Bread. Our Lord Jesus Christ, dining with his disciples, after revealing the sacraments of his body and blood, proceeded to the Mount of Olives, as the holy Gospels testify, and there was seized by the Jews, when a disciple handed him over. Thereafter, on the following Friday, that is, the seventh day before the Kalends of April, he was crucified and buried; on the third day, that is, the fifth day before the Kalends of April, a Sunday, he rose from the dead. These are the words of Victorius to Hilary, then archdeacon of Saint Leo the Great and later his successor, in the preface to the Paschal Feast, published by Bucherius, p. 9.

So that I may not delay in offering some evidence of the solidity of this chronology, from which the reckoning of the times of pontifical history takes its beginning, I shall bring forward, [Col. 0125B] or at least indicate in summary, the principal proofs upon which the Victorian chronology and our own securely rest, and by which they are demonstrated as far as the nature of historical inquiry permits.

In establishing the epoch of Christ’s Passion, two signs have been handed down to us by divine authority and must necessarily be observed: namely, the day of the Jews’ Passover, or the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month, on which the lamb had to be sacrificed; and Thursday, the time of the Lord’s Supper and the beginning of the Passion. That Passion was then to be completed on the following day, Friday, on the cross, so that, after the Sabbath had been granted to rest, Christ would rise from the dead on the third day, which was Sunday.

To these two chronological indications, confirmed by divine authority in the Gospel, two others are added. These were not received through revelation, [Col. 0125C] but were transmitted by the common testimony of the Fathers, especially of those who were more exact in calculating chronology and closer in time to the age of Christ. They are the consulship of the Gemini—namely, Fufius and Rubellius—which is the first; and the eighth day before the Kalends of April, consecrated by the Lord’s Passion, which is the second.

Hippolytus the martyr established that the Paschal feast, falling on the same evening on which, after the Last Supper, Christ our Lord went into the Garden of Gethsemane to begin his Passion, was to be correlated with the fourteenth day of the moon and with the eighth day before the Kalends of April. He left the order of the preceding Passovers inscribed in his Cycle in the year 222 of the common era:

Η ΚΑΛ . ΑΠΡΕΙ ΠΑΘΟΣ ΧϹ  
[Col. 0125D] THE EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF APRIL, THE PASSION OF CHRIST.

I have brought together further material concerning that Cycle in my dissertation on the Cycle of Saint Hippolytus the Martyr, chapter 2, p. 107. Tertullian, a contemporary of Hippolytus, assigns the same day to Christ’s final Passover, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, and the same consuls, the two Gemini, in his book Against the Jews. The Fathers and writers who flourished shortly after them, and especially those who examined chronological matters thoroughly, correlate the same consuls, the Gemini, and the same day, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, with Christ’s Passion.

Among the Latin Fathers, Saint Augustine may stand for all, in Book IV, chapter 5, of On the Trinity: “Receiving what has been handed down by our ancestors, the authority of the Church [Col. 0126A] preserves it: he is traditionally said to have been conceived on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, on which he also suffered.”

Although a later age confused the Passion begun on the eighth day before the Kalends, Thursday, in the Garden of Gethsemane, with the Passion completed on the cross on the seventh day before the Kalends, Friday, on Mount Calvary, nevertheless Victorius, as we have seen, and with him the more careful chronologists distinguish the eighth day before the Kalends, the beginning of the Passion in the garden, from the seventh day before the Kalends, the completion of the Passion at Golgotha.

The more carefully corrected editions of Lactantius—such as the two Lyons editions, that of Jean de Tournes, 1587, and that of Thomas Soubron, 1594, said to have been corrected on the basis of the fidelity and authority of manuscript books—have the following in Book IV, chapter 10, of the Divine Institutes: “From that time they had tetrarchs [the Jews] up to Herod, who lived under the rule of [Col. 0126B] Tiberius Caesar.” In his fifteenth year, that is, in the consulship of the two Gemini, before the seventh day before the Kalends of April, the Jews fastened Christ to the cross.”

Betuleius, as well as other writers, also observes that the better editions of Lactantius read “before the seventh day before the Kalends,” although others prefer those in which “the tenth day before the Kalends” is written.

Among the Greek Fathers, Saint John Chrysostom, speaking of the Annunciation of the Virgin Mother of God in his homily on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, says: “It was therefore when the angel announced these things to Mary, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the month of March, which is the day of the Lord’s Passover and of his conception. For on the day on which he was conceived, on that same day he also suffered.”

Saint Proterius of Alexandria, in his Paschal Letter written to Saint Leo the Great [Col. 0126C] and published by Bucherius on p. 83, correlates the day on which the divine Word assumed flesh with the day of the Supper celebrated by him toward evening before the Passion, in these words: “The Lord, being the fullness of the law, when he deigned to become man, on Thursday, the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month, eating the Passover in the upper room with his disciples, shortly afterward is handed over by Judas; and on the following day, the fifteenth day of the moon, he is crucified, that is, on Friday, and so forth.”

I refrain from citing more, since they are indicated by La Barre in his notes on the passage of Tertullian’s book Against the Jews, p. 110 of that edition, and by R. P. le Nourry in his notes on the book of Lucius Caecilius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors, chapter 4, p. 159. I discuss and examine these matters more fully and carefully in my dissertation on the correct establishment of the epoch of the Lord’s Passion begun on the eighth day before the Kalends [Col. 0126D], and of the Passion completed, or the crucifixion, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the two Gemini, in the twenty-eighth year of the common era, but the thirty-third year of the age of Christ our Lord.

Chronologists therefore attempt to reconcile four signs of the day and year of the Lord’s Passion and death: two certain by divine revelation, and two received from the tradition and opinion of the Fathers, both in the East and in the West. But their attempt has so far been unsuccessful since they departed from Victorius in correlating the two Gemini with the leap year 28 of the common era.

Although he correctly assigned them to that year, they place them in the following year, the year immediately after the leap year, the common era 29, [Col. 0127A] and retain the epoch of the Passion on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. That date cannot in any way be reconciled with the four signs mentioned if the consuls are placed in this manner.

For if they assign the Passion to the leap year 28—in which the fourteenth day of the Jews’ Paschal moon properly corresponds to the seventh day before the Kalends of April and to the preceding evening, the eighth day before the Kalends, as I shall show below—they then abandon the sign of that consulship, asserted by Tertullian, Lactantius, Lucius Caecilius, Augustine, Sulpicius Severus, Victorius, and other Fathers and chronologists. Moreover, they fail to preserve Friday, which is a certain sign of the Lord’s crucifixion, recorded in the Gospel, if they assign the fastening of the Only-Begotten Son of God to the cross to the eighth day before the Kalends of April in the leap year 28, which was Thursday.

But if they postpone this [Col. 0127B] to the eighth day before the Kalends of April in the following year, 29, which they mark as the year of the two Gemini, they preserve the consuls and the sign of Friday, but they remove from the day of 25 March—and exclude from the entire month—the other equally certain sign in the Gospel, namely, the Jews’ Passover.

For the tables of lunisolar motions show that, fully eleven days before the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the fourteenth day of the moon had already passed in March of the Julian year 29, and that it was not therefore Paschal, since that moon preceded the equinox by more than ten days. Consequently, the Paschal fourteenth day must be sought in the year 29 around the Ides of April.

They therefore cannot retain the eighth day before the Kalends under those consuls whom they place in the Fasti in the year 29 of the common era. It thus becomes altogether impossible to reconcile those four signs with the consulship of the Gemini when it is postponed in this way.

[Col. 0127C] But when the same Gemini consuls are restored to the preceding year, the leap year 28 of the common era, with Victorius, everything proceeds neatly and consistently, and each of the four signs retains its validity.

For since in the year 28 Thursday fell on 25 March, that is, the eighth day before the Kalends of April; and since the fourteenth moon of the month Nisan in that year fell exactly on 26 March, that is, the seventh day before the Kalends of April, Friday, as I shall shortly show, the day of the Lord’s Supper and of the Passion begun in the garden rightly falls on Thursday evening, 25 March, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, as the Paschal Canon of Saint Hippolytus sets forth, enumerating the fourteenth moons of the preceding Passovers [Col. 0127D] during his lifetime, namely the year 222 of the common era, when he was writing. Likewise, the day of the Passion completed on the cross rightly belongs to the following Friday, which in the year 28 was 26 March Julian, or the seventh day before the Kalends of April, as Victorius teaches and the editions of Lactantius mentioned above prefer.

I must therefore demonstrate first that the fourteenth day of the moon of the month Nisan, or the Jews’ Paschal month, fell in the year 28 of the common era on 26 March. Since the preceding evening belonged to 25 March—according to the institution of the Law, which reckons Sabbaths from evening to evening—the Supper, properly celebrated on Thursday evening, 25 March, was the occasion on which Christ our Lord instituted the sacraments of his body and blood, the perpetual sacrifice [Col. 0128A] and memorial of his Passion.

Beginning the Passion in the garden on that same night of 25 March, he continued it in the praetorium as Friday dawned and on the 26th. Hanging on the cross from the sixth to the ninth hour and declaring, “It is finished,” he completed it by undergoing death, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, as the Romans reckoned the date, in the Julian leap year 28 of the common era of Christ.

It must be shown, secondly, that the two Gemini consuls do not belong to the year 29, as chronologists commonly think, but to the year 28, as Victorius placed them.

I shall summarize both this assertion and its proofs from the more extended demonstration that I presented in the dissertation mentioned above, on correlating the epoch of Christ’s Passion with the year 28 of the common era, in the consulship of the two [Col. 0128B] Gemini.

I demonstrate the former assertion in that same dissertation, section 3, number 4, as follows.

The calculations of the fourteenth Paschal moon in the year 28 of the common era are so clear that those who have prepared tables on the subject, both ancient and modern, do not disagree with one another concerning the feast of Passover, whether Jewish or Christian, in that year.

Victorius’ Paschal Canon, beginning the Period from this point, assigns to Sunday, 28 March, the age of the moon as sixteen days, and consequently assigns the fourteenth moon to Friday, 26 March. On that day the Lord, having been led to the cross, completed his Passion in death, which had begun on the preceding evening and had been dedicated by him through the mystery of the unbloody sacrifice.

Although, according to the Roman custom of reckoning days from midnight [Col. 0128C] to midnight—as Macrobius, Saturnalia, chapter 3, and Aulus Gellius, Attic Nights, Book III, chapter 2, attest, and before them Pliny, Book II, chapter 77—that evening belonged to the 25th, nevertheless, according to the laws of the Hebrews, it belonged to the beginning of the following day, as the Lord commanded in Leviticus 23:32: “From evening to evening you shall celebrate your Sabbaths.”

Among more recent writers, Father Francesco Bordonus, General of the Third Order of Saint Francis, in his Paschal Tables arranged from the year of the Lord’s Incarnation for the following two thousand years, according to the Julian year before Gregory’s correction and according to the Gregorian year after that pontiff’s reform, gives exactly the same figures: the epact 16 and Christian Easter on Sunday, 28 March, in the year 28 of the common era of Christ.

[Col. 0128D] These same calculations correspond perfectly to the motions of the heavenly bodies, as the computations will show. Drawn from astronomical tables, they yield the following result for the beginning of the Jewish year: the new moon of Tishri, or the first month of the Jewish civil year, occurred in the year 27 of the common Christian era. From that new moon, the 177th day immediately following demonstrates the new moon of Nisan—six lunations distant from it and the beginning of the sacred year, or the start of the first month so named in the sacred writings—as falling on 13 March Julian, extending into the leap year 28 of the same Christian era. Let us consult the lunisolar figures in the Tables of D. de la Hire, approved by the Royal Academy of Sciences and widely accepted elsewhere, which are to be gathered as follows.

[Col. 0129]

[Col. 0129A] The true conjunction of the heavenly bodies therefore occurred in the year 27 of the common Christian era, on 18 September Julian, at 8 hours and 24 minutes after noon in Paris; in Rome, at 9:05 p.m.; and in Jerusalem, at 10:40 p.m., since Jerusalem is farther east than Paris by 34 degrees 40 minutes of longitude, or by 2 hours and 16 minutes of time.

The Jews ought to have begun from this conjunction the month of Tishri and their Rosh Hashanah, or “Head of the Year” of the lunar civil year, which they used, following the example of the Syro-Macedonians, who likewise began from autumn.

Since, therefore, according to the true lunisolar motions, the new moon of Tishri occurred on 18 September Julian in the year 27 of the common Christian era, it is necessary that the new moon of the Paschal month in the year 28 fall on the 177th day counted from 18 September [Col. 0129B]. For six lunations must be counted from Tishri to Nisan, and they require that many days.

Add the twelve remaining days of September after the day of the new moon, 18 September, to the end of the month; then the 31 days of Julian October, 30 of November, 31 of December, the same number for January, 29 days of the leap February, and 13 of March: the total will be 177 days, which completes six civil lunations, alternately hollow and full.

The first assumption has therefore been demonstrated: the true motions of the heavenly bodies in the year 27 of the era of Christ show the new moon of Tishri on 18 September Julian at 10:40 p.m. in Jerusalem. For this reason, that same day, 18 September, was the beginning of the Jewish year as the year 27 of the common era was coming to an end.

Therefore the 177th day counted from that point—which falls on 13 March of the leap year 28 [Col. 0129C]—was the first day of the moon of Nisan, or of the Paschal month. Add thirteen complete days to this 13 March, and you arrive at the beginning of the fourteenth lunar day, or the legally determined day of the Jews’ Passover.

Its terminus shows that the day was 26 March, on which Christ our Lord, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world, was sacrificed for us on the cross on Friday, the seventh day before the Kalends of April, according to the opinion of Victorius and our own. On the preceding evening—which, according to the rite of the Mosaic Law, must be referred to this same day, but according to Roman custom to the eighth day before the Kalends of April, or 25 March—he had celebrated the Passover itself with his disciples and begun his Passion, whose sacraments he had instituted.

From the calculations presented you may also gather why some have said that certain Jews postponed the sacrifice of the Lamb in that same year until the evening of 26 [Col. 0129D] March [Col. 0130A] Julian—hence John says that on Friday they did not enter the praetorium, so that they might eat the Passover—although others had eaten the Paschal lamb with Christ our Lord on the evening of Thursday, the Roman 25th.

The reason for both opinions cannot be obscure if one considers the twofold reckoning and measurement either of the Paschal day alone or of both the day and the hours in which they fell, according to the true motions of the new moons of Tishri and Nisan.

The new moon of Tishri, occurring on 18 September at 10:40 p.m., produced, after 177 days, the new moon of Nisan on 13 March of the Julian leap year and civil calendar, if only complete days are taken into account, as happens in civil reckoning, in calculating the years and months.

But if we also take account of the addition of four hours and twenty-four minutes—which, beyond the 177 complete days, are required by the six mean lunations [Col. 0130B] from Tishri to Nisan—then, when these four hours and twenty-four minutes are added to the hourly epoch of the Tishri lunation, 10 hours and 40 minutes after noon on 18 September, the result is 3:04 p.m. on 26 March for the beginning of the Paschal fourteenth day. It therefore extends beyond midnight, which according to Roman custom closes 26 March and opens 27 March.

It is thus clear why some Jews could properly refer the fourteenth Paschal day, from the true new moon of Tishri and the civil reckoning of complete days alone, to Friday, 26 March, and the preceding evening, Thursday, 25 March, with Christ our Lord and his disciples.

Others, however, along with the Jews who did not enter the praetorium on Friday, 26 March, in order to eat the Passover that same evening, referred that evening [Col. 0130C] to the 27th. They took account of the three hours after midnight, by which the beginning of the fourteenth day, so calculated, was postponed to the 27th according to Roman reckoning in the leap year that we are discussing, the year 28 of the common Christian era, in the consulship of the two Gemini.

The second assertion—that the consulship of Fufius Gemini and Rubellius Gemini is to be correlated with the year 28 of the Christian era—is the other point that I proposed to demonstrate. I have followed the chronology of Victorius, who likewise assigns these consuls to leap year 28, whereas the other chronologists postpone them to the following year, the year 29 of the common Christian era. I judge that I have demonstrated this in the dissertation mentioned above.

It is established that the two Sexti, Sextus Pompeius and Sextus Apuleius—in whose consulship all historians record the death of Augustus, namely Velleius, [Col. 0130D] [Col. 0131A] Tacitus, Suetonius, Dio, and the others—are separated by a period of fifteen years from the two Gemini consuls, Fufius Gemini and Rubellius Gemini.

For an uninterrupted series of these fifteen years is found in the collections of the Fasti, and also emerges from the historians of the Augustan age. Velleius, who dedicates his work to the consul Marcus Vinicius, the year immediately following the two Gemini, when in Book II, chapter 123, he had related the death of Augustus in the consulship of Pompeius and Apuleius, and in chapter 126 of the same book had explicitly counted sixteen years from that point to the consulship of Vinicius, thereby establishes fifteen years from the two Sexti to the two Gemini, whom Vinicius follows continuously.

Therefore, if the two Sexti belong to the fourteenth year [Col. 0131B] of the common Christian era, the two Gemini must necessarily be correlated with the year 29 of that same era, as almost all chronologists do.

But if the two Sexti are clearly to be moved back, together with the death of Augustus, to the year 13 of the common era, it follows that the two Gemini belong to leap year 28, as Victorius established.

That the two Sexti consuls and the death of Augustus must indeed be moved back to the year 13 of the Christian era becomes evident from the chronological sign reported in the History of Dio.

Dio, in Book LVI, among the prodigies that were believed, through popular prejudice and superstition, to foretell the death of Augustus, enumerates a total eclipse of the sun in the consulship of Sextus Apuleius and Sextus Pompeius:

[Col. 0131C] “In the following year, when Sextus Apuleius and Sextus Pompeius were consuls, Augustus went to Campania, presented a spectacle at Naples, and at Nola surrendered to death. The prodigies that foretold this for him were neither insignificant nor obscure. THE SUN HAD FAILED ENTIRELY. Ὅτε γὰρ ἥλιος πᾶς ἐξέλιπε [For the whole sun was eclipsed],” and so forth.

The investigation of this eclipse in the fourteenth year of the Christian era perplexes the ingenuity of chronologists and astronomers alike, since no such eclipse could have been observed in that year according to any tables of the heavenly motions.

But if they investigate it according to the same tables in the thirteenth year of the common Christian era, they will recognize clearly from the calculations that an eclipse of the sun visible in several provinces of Europe occurred on 28 April while the sun was approaching setting.

From the calculation and diagram reported in our dissertation they will learn that a total obscuration of the disk, seen as the sun was setting, was visible from the small islands west of Britain, around the northern region of the Scots [Col. 0131D]—similar to another eclipse visible on 22 May 1724, likewise at sunset, to observers situated on the western coast of Etruria around Livorno.

From the same Cassinian, Hirian, Bolognese, and British tables, both eclipses are likewise calculated as total. The eclipse would necessarily have been partial in the regions nearby—Britain, Lower Germany, Gaul, and Lusitania—but the phases of the partial eclipse observed in those regions demonstrate that it must have been visible as total in the nearby climate and meridian [Col. 0132A] indicated, namely in the Orkney Islands.

Who, then, could deny that this sign of the heavenly motions, expressly recorded by Dio in his History, clearly indicates that the consulship of the two Sexti must be correlated with the thirteenth year of the common era, and that the two Gemini must be correlated with the leap year 28 of that same era, as Victorius established?

You may ask whether, once the two Gemini consuls have been moved back by one year, the series of preceding consuls must likewise be moved back by the same amount all the way to the Caesarian period. We assert precisely this.

[Col. 0132B] Indeed, we bring forward a new argument and demonstration that this backward displacement must necessarily be employed in arranging the consulships of Gaius Julius Caesar. His inseparable companion in the Spanish campaign, Aulus Hirtius, who was also a most careful historian, provides the evidence. In counting day by day the sieges of towns and the military operations of his commander, he records that the army encamped near Hispalis on the third day before the Nones of March, at approximately the sixth hour of the night, when the moon was visible. This supplies a manifest indication of the year commonly called the Year of Confusion and of its correlation with this Spanish campaign, and of the year of Caesar’s death with the first Julian year before the Christian era, 45.

It follows that the two Sexti occupy the year 13 and the two Gemini the year 28 of the common era. You will read a fuller discussion of these matters, cleared of every difficulty, in our dissertation mentioned above, in which I shall present, as I hope, accurate calculations of these heavenly motions and eclipses [Col. 0132C].

Thus, in the chronology of Victorius and our own, the Lord’s Supper and the beginning of the Passion are assigned to Thursday, 25 March Julian, in the year 28 of the common era, a leap year, in the consulship of the two Gemini; and the crucifixion and death of the Lord to the following day, Friday, 26 March. The four signs are thereby harmoniously reconciled.

Chronologists had vainly sought them in the consulship of the Gemini postponed to the year 29: two signs firmly established by divine faith in the holy Gospels, namely the Passover and the Passion, with the Supper and the weekdays Thursday and Friday, the fifth and sixth days of the week, to be correlated with its beginning and completion; and two signs recorded by Fathers close to the apostolic age and by the more expert chronologists together with Victorius, namely 25 March, to be correlated with the Lord’s Supper and the beginning of the Passion, and 26 March [Col. 0132D], to be correlated with the fastening of our Redeemer to the cross and the completed Passion.

By these observations, we trust that the chronology of our Catalogue, likewise reckoned from the epoch of the Passion, has been illustrated and confirmed.

Notes should also be added concerning several pontiffs listed there and concerning the establishment of the era of those omitted. But these matters will be placed or arranged more appropriately in their proper places in the dissertation on the ancient Catalogues of the Roman pontiffs, which I shall append shortly below, after the one to be obtained from Bishop Schelestratius.

[Col. 0133]

## ANOTHER CATALOGUE OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS

Taken from an ancient manuscript codex of 865 years in the Palatine-Vatican Library, reported by Schelestratius under this title, no. 22, p. 611:

### NAMES OF THE BISHOPS OF THE CITY OF ROME (C)

[Col. 0133A] 1. Blessed Peter the apostle and prince of the apostles, an Antiochene, son of John, of the province of Galilee, from the village of Bethsaida, brother of Andrew, first occupied the episcopal chair in Antioch for six years; and, having entered Rome under Caesar Nero, he sat there for twenty-five years, two months, and four days. He wrote two Epistles, which are called Catholic, and the Gospel of Mark; and he ordained three bishops, Linus, Cletus, and Clement, ten presbyters, and eight deacons.

2. Linus, Italian by nationality, of the region of Tuscia, son of Herculanus, sat for eleven years, three months, and eleven days. He ordained fifteen bishops and eighteen presbyters.

3. Cletus, a Roman by nationality, from the region of the Vicus Patricius, son of Aemilianus, sat for twelve years, one month, and eleven days. At the command of blessed Peter, he ordained twenty-five presbyters in Rome. In another hand: Under the emperor Vespasian and Titus.

4. Clement, a Roman by nationality, from the region of Caelian Hill, son of Faustinus, sat for nine years, two months, and ten days. He ordained fifteen bishops, ten presbyters, and [Col. 0133B] two deacons. In another hand: Under the emperors Domitian, Nerva, and Trajan.

5. Anacletus, a Greek by nationality, from Athens, son of Antiochus, sat for nine years, two months, and ten days. He ordained six bishops, five presbyters, and three deacons. In another hand: Under the emperor Trajan.

6. Evaristus, a Greek by nationality, son of a Jew named Juda, from the city of Bethlehem, sat for nine years, ten months, and two days. He ordained five bishops, six presbyters, and two deacons. In another hand: Under the emperor Trajan.

7. Alexander, a Roman by nationality, son of Alexander, from the region of the Bull’s Head, sat for ten years, six months, and two days. He decreed that water for sprinkling should be blessed with salt. He ordained five bishops, six presbyters, and two deacons. In another hand: Under the emperor Trajan and under the emperor Aelius Hadrian.

8. Xystus, a Roman by nationality, son of Pastor, from the region of the Vialata, sat for ten years, two months, and one day. He decreed [Col. 0133C] that sacred ministries should be touched only by ministers. He ordained four bishops, nine presbyters, and four deacons. In another hand: Under the emperor Hadrian.

9. Telesphorus, a Greek by nationality, formerly a hermit, sat for twenty-one years and three months. He decreed that a fast should be observed for seven weeks before Easter, and that on the night of the Nativity of the Lord Masses should be celebrated and the Gloria in excelsis Deo sung. He ordained twelve presbyters and eight deacons. In another hand: Under the emperor Antoninus Pius.

10. Hyginus, a Greek by nationality, formerly a philosopher from Athens, whose genealogy I have not found, sat for four years, three months, and four days. He organized the clergy and distributed the ecclesiastical ranks. He ordained six bishops, fifteen presbyters, and five deacons. In another hand: Under the emperor Antoninus Pius.

11. Pius, an Italian by nationality, son of Rufinus, brother of Pastor, from the city of Aquila, sat for eighteen years, four months, and three days. At the prompting of an angel, he ordered Easter to be celebrated on Sunday [Col. 0133D]. He ordained twelve bishops, nineteen presbyters, and twenty-one deacons. In another hand: Under the emperor Antoninus Pius.

12. Anicetus, a Syrian by nationality, son of John, from the village of Umisa, sat for ten years, four months, and three days. He decreed that a cleric should not grow his hair long. He ordained nine bishops, seventeen presbyters, and four deacons.

[Col. 0134A] 13. Soter, a Campanian by nationality, son of Concordius, from the city of Fundi, sat for nine years, six months, and twelve days. He decreed that no nun should touch a consecrated pallium or place incense in the holy church. He ordained eleven bishops, eight presbyters, and nine deacons.

14. Eleutherus, a Greek by nationality, son of Abundius, from the town of Nicopolis, sat for fifteen years, three months, and two days. He decreed that Christians should reject no food that was rational and humanly appropriate. He ordained fifteen bishops, twelve presbyters, and eight deacons.

15. Victor, an African by nationality, son of Felix, sat for ten years, two months, and ten days. He decreed that Easter should be celebrated on Sunday, as Pius had also done. He ordained twelve bishops, four presbyters, and seven deacons.

16. Zephyrinus, a Roman by nationality, son of Abundius, sat for eight years, seven months, and ten days. He ordained thirteen bishops, four presbyters, and seven deacons.

17. Callistus, a Roman by nationality, son of Domitius from the district of the Ravennates, held office for 6 years, 2 months, and 10 days. He ordained 8 bishops, 16 priests, and 3 deacons. [Col. 0134B] In another hand: Under the emperor Marcus Aurelius.

18. Urbanus, a Roman by nationality, son of Pontianus, held office for 4 years, 10 months, and 11 days. He ordained 8 bishops, 6 priests, and 5 deacons. In another hand: Under Aurelius Alexander the emperor.

19. Antherus, a Greek by nationality, son of Romulus, held office for 12 years, 1 month, and 12 days. He diligently sought out the acts of the martyrs; he ordained 1 bishop. In another hand: Under the emperor Maximus.

20. Pontianus, a Roman by nationality, son of Calpurnius, held office for 9 years, 5 months, and 2 days. He ordained 6 bishops and 5 deacons. In another hand: Under the emperor Maximus.

21. Fabianus, a Roman by nationality, son of Fabius, held office for 14 years, 11 months, and 11 days. He ordained 11 bishops, 21 priests, and 7 deacons. In another hand: Under the emperors Gordian, Philip, and Decius.

[Col. 0134C] 22. Cornelius, a Roman by nationality, son of Castinus, held office for 2 years, 2 months, and 2 days. He removed the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul from the catacombs. He ordained 7 bishops, 4 priests, and 4 deacons. In another hand: Under the emperor Decius, and under the emperors Gallus and Volusianus.

23. Lucius, a Roman by nationality, son of Porphyrius, held office for 3 years, 3 months, and 3 days. He prescribed that two priests and three deacons should not leave the bishop anywhere. He ordained 7 bishops, 4 priests, and 4 deacons. In another hand: Under the emperors Valerian and Gallienus.

24. Stephanus, a Roman by nationality, son of Jobius, held office for 7 years, 5 months, and 2 days. He decreed for priests and Levites that they should not use sacred vestments in daily life, but only in the church. He ordained 3 bishops, 6 priests, and 5 deacons. In another hand: Under the emperor Valerian and Gallienus.

[Col. 0134D] 25. Xistus, a Greek by nationality, formerly a philosopher, held office for 1 year, 10 months, and 23 days. He ordained 3 bishops, 4 priests, and 7 deacons. In another hand: Under Valerian and Gallienus the emperors.

26. Dionysius, formerly a monk, whose lineage we were unable to discover, held office for 6 years, 2 months, and 4 days. He gave churches to priests and established parishes [Col. 0135A] and dioceses. He ordained 8 bishops, 12 priests, and 6 deacons. In another hand: Under Valerian and Gallienus the emperors.

27. Felix, a Roman by nationality, son of Constantius, held office for 4 years, 3 months, and 25 days. He decreed that Masses should be celebrated over the memorials of the martyrs. He ordained 5 bishops, 8 priests, and 5 deacons. In another hand: Under the emperors Claudius and Aurelian.

28. Eutychianus, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Marinus from the city of Luna, held office for 1 year, 1 month, and 1 day. He decreed that fruits, beans, and grapes should be blessed upon the altar. He ordained 9 bishops, 14 priests, and 5 deacons. In another hand: Under the emperor Aurelian.

29. Caius, a Dalmatian by nationality, of the family of Diocletian, son of Gaius, held office for 11 years, 4 months, and 12 days. He arranged the ecclesiastical orders. He ordained 5 bishops, 26 priests, and 8 deacons.

[Col. 0135B] 30. Marcellinus, a Roman by nationality, son of Projectus, held office for 9 years, 4 months, and 6 days. He ordained 5 bishops, 4 priests, and 2 deacons.

31. Marcellus, a Roman by nationality, son of Benedictus from the district of Vialata, held office for 5 years, 7 months, and 21 days. He established titular churches in the city of Rome for baptism and penance. He ordained 12 priests and 2 deacons.

32. Eusebius, a Greek by nationality, formerly a physician, held office for 2 years, 1 month, and 3 days. In his time the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ was discovered, and Judas was baptized. He ordained 14 bishops, 14 priests, and 3 deacons.

33. Mathiadis, an African by nationality, held office for 4 years. He decreed that no member of the faithful should fast under any circumstances on Sunday or Thursday. He ordained 12 bishops, 7 priests, and 5 deacons.

34. Sylvester, a Roman by nationality, son of Rufinus, held office for 23 years, 10 months, and 11 days. He assembled [Col. 0135C] 318 bishops, who set forth the catholic faith, decreed that chrism be prepared by a bishop, and that the baptized be confirmed. He ordered that dalmatics be worn. He ordered the entire sacrifice to be wrapped in linen cloth. He ordained 65 bishops, 42 priests, and 26 deacons.

35. Marcus, a Roman by nationality, son of Priscus, held office for 2 years, 8 months, and 21 days. He decreed that the bishop of the city who consecrates the host should wear the pallium. He ordained 27 bishops, 25 priests, and 6 deacons.

36. Julius, a Roman by nationality, son of Rusticus, held office for 15 years, 2 months, and 6 days. He decreed that no cleric should conduct a lawsuit in public except in the church. He ordained 9 bishops, 27 priests, and 4 deacons.

37. Liberius, a Roman by nationality, son of Augustinus, held office for 6 years, 3 months, and 4 days. He ordained 19 bishops, 18 priests, and [Col. 0135D] 5 deacons.

38. Felix, a Roman by nationality, son of Anastasius, held office for 1 year, 3 months, and 2 days. He ordained 19 bishops, 21 priests, and 5 deacons.

39. Damasus, a Spaniard by nationality, son of Antonius, held office for 18 years, 3 months, and 11 days. He was maliciously accused of adultery and cleared by 44 bishops. He decreed that the psalms should be sung in the church day and night. He ordained 62 bishops, 31 priests, and 11 deacons.

40. Siricius, a Roman by nationality, son of Tibustius, held office for 15 years. He ordained 32 bishops, 31 priests, and 16 deacons. He prescribed that penitents should not be denied viaticum at the end of life.

41. Anastasius, a Roman by nationality, son of Maximus, held office for 3 years and 10 days. He decreed that, when the Gospel is read, the priests should not stand upright but should remain bent over. He ordained 11 bishops, 8 priests, and 5 deacons.

[Col. 0136A] 42. Innocentius, an Albanian by nationality, son of Innocentius, held office for 15 years, 2 months, and 21 days. He decreed that whoever was born of a Christian woman should be born again through baptism. He decreed fasting on Saturday, because the Lord lay in the tomb on Saturday and the disciples lay there on Saturday. He ordained 54 bishops, 30 priests, and 11 deacons.

43. Zosimus, a Greek by nationality, son of Ebramius, held office for 1 year, 3 months, and 11 days. He established many things in the Church. He ordained 8 bishops, 10 priests, and 3 deacons.

44. Bonifacius, a Roman by nationality, son of the priest Jocundius, held office for 3 years, 8 months, and 7 days. He decreed that no woman or nun should wash the sacred cloth (*palla*) or place incense in the church, except a minister. He ordained 36 bishops, 13 priests, and 3 deacons.

45. Coelestinus, a Roman by nationality, son of Priscus, held office for 8 years, 10 months, and 17 days. He decreed [Col. 0136B] that an antiphon should be sung before the sacrifice—a practice that had not previously been followed, except that the Epistle of blessed Paul and the holy Gospel were read. He ordained 46 bishops, 32 priests, and 12 deacons.

46. Xistus, a Roman by nationality, son of Xistus, held office for 8 years and 19 months. After a year and eight months he was accused by a certain Bassus; he cleared himself with 57 bishops, and Bassus was condemned. He ordained 52 bishops, 28 priests, and 12 deacons.

47. Leo, born a Tuscan, son of Quintianus, held office for 21 years, 1 month, and 13 days. He assembled 1,200 bishops, who set forth the catholic faith: two natures, God and man, in one Christ. He ordained 185 bishops, 81 priests, and 31 deacons.

48. Hilarius, a Sardinian by nationality, son of Crispinus, held office for 6 years, 3 months, and 10 days. He disseminated letters on the catholic faith throughout the Eastern world and confirmed the three synods: Nicaea, Ephesus, and [Col. 0136C] Chalcedon. He ordained 25 bishops and 5 deacons.

49. Simplicianus, a Tiburtine by nationality, son of Castinus, held office for 15 years, 1 month, and 8 days. He decreed that priests should remain at Saint Peter’s, Saint Paul’s, and Saint Lawrence’s on account of penitents and baptism. He ordained 37 bishops, 58 priests, and 11 deacons.

50. Felix, a Roman by nationality, son of the priest Felix of the titular church of Fasciola, held office for 8 years, 11 months, and 19 days. He ordained 31 bishops, 18 priests, and 5 deacons.

51. Gelasius, an African by nationality, son of Valerius, held office for 4 years, 8 months, and 19 days. He delivered the city of Rome from the danger of famine. He composed tracts and hymns, like blessed Ambrose. He ordained 67 bishops, 32 priests, and 2 deacons.

52. Anastasius, a Roman by nationality, son of Peter [Col. 0136D] from the fifth district, Caput Tauri, held office for 1 year, 11 months, and 24 days. He ordained 16 bishops and 13 priests.

53. Symmachus, a Sardinian by nationality, son of Fortunatus, held office for 11 years, 7 months, and 27 days. Symmachus and Laurentius were ordained on the same day, each with a claim to the office: Symmachus at the Lateran, Laurentius in the church of Blessed Mary. Symmachus was confirmed in the see according to the judgment of King Theodoric, and afterward Symmachus, having been accused, cleared himself with 115 bishops. He decreed that “Glory to God in the highest” should be sung every Sunday and on the feasts of the saints. He ordained 117 bishops, 92 priests, and 16 deacons.

54. Hormisda, a Campanian by nationality, son of Justus from the city of Frisinone, held office for 9 years and 14 days. He established the clergy and instructed them in the psalms. He ordained 55 bishops and 21 priests.

55. Joannes, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Constantius, [Col. 0137A] held office for 2 years, 8 months, and 16 days. He died afflicted in custody. He ordained 15 bishops.

56. Felix, a Somman by nationality, son of Castorius, held office for 4 years, 2 months, and 13 days. He himself was ordained into rest. He ordained 19 bishops, 55 priests, and 4 deacons.

57. Bonifacius, a Roman by nationality, son of Sigibaldus, held office for 2 years and 26 days. He and Dioscorus were ordained as rival claimants; Dioscorus died at that same time, and Bonifacius held the see.

58. Mercurius, also called Joannes, a Roman by nationality, son of Projectus, from the Caelian Hill, held office for 2 years, 4 months, and 6 days. He ordained 16 bishops and 15 priests.

59. Agapitus, a Roman by nationality, son of the priest Gordianus, held office for 11 months and 19 days. He ordained 11 bishops and 4 deacons.

[Col. 0137B] 60. Silverius, a Campanian by nationality, son of Hormisda, bishop of Rome, held office for 1 year, 5 months, and 11 days. He ordained 81 bishops, 46 priests, and 16 deacons.

61. Pelagius, a Roman by nationality, son of Joannes Vicarianus, held office for 11 years, 10 months, and 18 days. He was ordained by two bishops and one priest. He ordained 49 bishops, 26 priests, and 9 deacons.

62. Joannes, a Roman by nationality, son of Anastasius, held office for 12 years, 11 months, and 26 days. He loved and restored the cemeteries of the holy martyrs and decreed that offerings and lights should be provided there every Sunday. He ordained 61 bishops, 26 priests, and 13 deacons.

63. Benedictus, a Roman by nationality, son of Bonifacius, held office for 4 years, 1 month, and 28 days. He ordained 21 bishops, 15 priests, and 3 deacons.

[Col. 0137C] 64. Pelagius, a Roman by nationality, son of Ungildus, held office for 10 years, 2 months, and 10 days. At that time there were such great rains that everyone said that the waters of the Flood were overflowing, and that no one remembered there having been such a calamity in an age. He ordained 48 bishops, 28 priests, and 8 deacons.

65. Gregorius, a Roman by nationality, son of Gordianus, held office for 13 years, 6 months, and 10 days. He composed forty Homilies, the Moralia on Job, the work on Ezekiel, the Pastoral Rule, and the Dialogues, and produced many other works. He added to the Canon “and our days,” up to the end of the Mass, and converted the English to our Lord. He arranged that Mass should be sung over the body of blessed Peter. He ordained 62 bishops, 39 priests, and 5 deacons.

66. Sabianus, a Tuscan from the city of Blera, son of Bonus, held office for 1 year, 5 months, and 8 days. He added lights in the church of blessed Peter. He ordained 26 bishops.

[Col. 0137D] 67. Bonifacius, a Roman by nationality, son of Joannes, held office for 8 months and 28 days. He ordained 21 bishops.

68. Bonifacius, a Marsian by nationality, from the city of Valeria, son of Joannes the physician, held office for 6 years, 8 months, and 13 days. He ordained 35 bishops and 8 deacons.

69. Deusdedit, a Roman by nationality, son of Stephanus the subdeacon, held office for 3 years and 33 days. He greatly loved the clergy. He ordained 39 bishops, 19 priests, and 5 deacons.

70. Bonifacius, a Campanian by nationality, from the city of Naples, son of Joannes, held office for 5 years. He decreed that no one should be dragged out of the church. He ordained 28 bishops, 25 priests, and 4 deacons.

71. Honorosius, a Campanian by nationality, son of Petronius the consul, held office for 12 years, 11 months, and 18 days. In his time the beam was raised in the church of blessed [Col. 0138A] Peter. He ordained 88 bishops, 13 priests, and 11 deacons.

72. Severinus, a Roman by nationality, son of Abienus, held office for 2 months and 4 days. He ordained 4 bishops.

73. Joannes, a Dalmatian by nationality, son of Venantius, held office for 1 year, 9 months, and 18 days. Throughout Dalmatia and Istria he sent large sums of money for the ransom of captives who had been taken. He ordained 4 bishops.

74. Martinus, from the city of Todi in the province of Tuscia, held office for 6 years, 1 month, and 26 days. He assembled a synod of 105 bishops and condemned Cyrus of Alexandria, Sergius, Pyrrhus, and Paul, the patriarch of Constantinople, who had revived innovations at night against the undefiled faith; and, composing the Sixth Synod, he confirmed 1 bishop. He ordained 28 bishops and 11 priests.

75. Theodorus, a Greek by nationality, son of Theodorus [Col. 0138B] the bishop of the city of Jerusalem, held office for 6 years, 5 months, and 18 days. He ordained 46 bishops, 21 priests, and 4 deacons.

76. Eugenius, a Roman by nationality, son of Rufianus, held office for 2 years, 9 months, and 24 days. He ordained 21 bishops.

77. Vitalianus, from Signia in the province of Campania, son of Anastasius, held office for 14 years and 6 months. He preserved the ecclesiastical rule and discipline in their entirety, as was customary. He ordained 27 bishops, 22 priests, and 1 deacon.

78. Adeodatus, a Roman by nationality, from the monks, son of Cobianus, held office for 4 years, 2 months, and 5 days. He ordained 47 bishops, 14 priests, and 2 deacons.

79. Donus, a Roman by nationality, son of Mauricinus, held office for 1 year, 5 months, and 10 days. He ordained 6 bishops, 10 priests, and 5 deacons.

80. Agatho, a Sicilian by nationality, held office for 2 years, 6 months, and 4 days. He ordained 18 bishops, 9 priests, and 3 deacons.

[Col. 0138C] 81. Leo the Younger, a Sicilian by nationality, son of Paulus, held office for 10 months and 17 days. He established that whoever had been ordained archbishop should pay nothing from the church treasury, under any customary obligation, for the use of the pallium or for any other ecclesiastical office. He ordained 21 bishops, 9 priests, and 3 deacons.

82. Benedictus the Younger, a Roman by nationality, held office for 10 months and 12 days. He ordained 12 bishops.

83. Joannes, a Syrian by nationality, from the province of Antioch, son of Cyrianus, held office for 1 year and 9 days. He ordained 13 bishops.

84. Sergius, a Syrian by nationality, born in the region of Antioch, son of Tiberius at Parmomum in Sicily. He decreed that, at the time of the Lord’s body, “Agnus Dei” (“Lamb of God”) should be sung by clergy and people. He decreed that on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, of holy Mary, and of Saint Simeon—called in Greek *Ypapanti* (“Meeting,” or the Presentation)—the litanies should go forth. He ordained 97 bishops, 18 priests, and 4 deacons. He held office for 13 years, 7 months, and 23 days.

[Col. 0138D] 85. Joannes, a Greek by nationality, held office for 3 years, 2 months, and 12 days. He ordained 15 bishops, 9 priests, and 2 deacons.

86. Joannes, a Greek by nationality, son of Plato, held office for 2 years, 6 months, and 17 days. He ordained 19 bishops.

87. Sisinnius, a Syrian by nationality, son of Joannes, held office for 7 years and 15 days. He ordained 64 bishops, 10 priests, and 2 deacons.

88. Constantinus, a Syrian by nationality, son of Joannes, held office for 7 years and 15 days. He ordained 64 bishops, 10 priests, and 2 deacons.

89. Gregorius, a Roman by nationality, son of Marcellus, held office for 5 years, 9 months, and 11 days. He decreed that on Thursdays during Lent fasting and the celebration of Masses should take place, which had not previously been done. He ordained 150 bishops, 25 priests, and 4 deacons.

90. Gregorius, a Syrian by nationality, son of Joannes, [Col. 0139A] held office for 10 years, 8 months, and 25 days. Learned in Greek and Latin, he retained all the psalms in order by heart and was refined by the most subtle discernment of their meanings. He ordained 80 bishops, 24 priests, and 4 deacons.

91. Zacharias, a Greek by nationality, son of Polychronius, held office for 10 years, 3 months, and 14 days. He ordained 85 bishops, 30 priests, and 5 deacons.

[Col. 0140A] 92. Stephanus, a Roman by nationality, son of Constantinus, held office for 5 years and 24 days. He ordained 15 bishops, 2 priests, and 2 deacons.

93. Paulus.

94. Adrianus.

95. Leo.

96. Stephanus.

97. Paschalis.

[Col. 0139]

## HERE BEGIN THE NAMES OF THE POPES OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH IN ORDER

(From Vatican manuscript codex 1353, which was copied under Paul II from an ancient codex of the Pergamene church, 800 years old.)

[Col. 0139B] The Lord Peter held office for 25 years, 2 months, and 8 days. Linus held office for 15 years, 3 months, and 11 days. Cletus, 12 years, 1 month, and 11 days. Clemens, 9 years, 2 months, and 10 days. Anacletus, 12 years, 10 months, and 6 days. Evaristus, 13 years, 7 months, and 2 days. Alexander, 10 years, 7 months, and 2 days. Xystus, 10 years, 7 months, and 21 days. Telesphorus, 11 years, 3 months, and 22 days. Hyginus, 4 years, 3 months, and 8 days. Anicetus, 9 years, 3 months, and 3 days. Pius, 11 years, 3 months, and 21 days. Soter, 9 years, 3 months, and [lacuna]. Eleuther, 15 years, 6 months, and 5 days. Victor, 10 years, 2 months, and 10 days. Zepherinus, 17 years, 2 months, and 10 days. Callistus, 5 years, 2 months, and 10 days. Urbanus, 8 years, 11 months, and 12 days. Antherus, 1 month and 15 days. Contianus [Pontianus], 5 years and 11 months. [Col. 0139C] Fabianus, 13 years, 1 month, and 10 days. Cornelius, 3 years and 10 days. Lucius, 3 years, 3 months, and 3 days. Stephanus, 4 years, 2 months, and 11 days. Xystus, 2 years, 11 months, and 6 days. Dionysius, 2 years, 3 months, and 7 days. Felix, 2 years and 10 months. Eutichianus, 8 years, 10 months, and 4 days. Caius, 10 years, 4 months, and 9 days. Marcellinus, 8 years, 2 months, and 25 days. Marcellus, 5 years, 7 months, and 21 days. Eusebius, 2 years, 1 month, and 25 days. Melchiades, 2 years, 7 months, and 8 days. Sylvester, 23 years. Marcus, 2 years, 7 months, and 20 days. Julius, 11 years, 2 months, and 6 days. Liberius, 10 years, 7 months, and 3 days. Felix, 1 year, 3 months, and 2 days. Damasus, 18 years, 2 months, and 10 days. [Col. 0139D] Siricius, 15 years, 11 months, and 25 days. Anastasius, 2 years and 28 days. Innocentius, 15 years, 2 months, and 20 days. Zosimus, 1 year, 7 months, and 25 days. Bonifacius, 3 years, 7 months, and 13 days. Coelestinus, 8 years, 2 months, and 24 days. Xystus, 8 years and 24 days. Leo, 21 years, 1 month, and 28 days. Hilarius, 6 years, 3 months, and 18 days. Simplicius, 15 years and 28 days. Felix, 8 years, 11 months, and 28 days. Gelasius, 3 years, 8 months, and 9 days. Anastasius, 1 year, 11 months, and 24 days. Symmachus, 15 years, 7 months, and 27 days. [Col. 0140B] Hormisda, 9 years and 17 days. Joannes, 2 years, 9 months, and 16 days. Felix, 4 years, 2 months, and 13 days. Bonifacius, 2 years, 1 month, and 27 days. Joannes, 2 years, 4 months, and 6 days. Agapitus, 3 months and 18 days. Silverius, 8 months. Vigilius, 17 years, 6 months, and 26 days. Pelagius, 4 years, 10 months, and 28 days. Joannes, 12 years, 11 months, and 26 days. Benedictus, 4 years, 1 month, and 28 days. Pelagius, 10 years, 2 months, and 10 days. Gregorius, 13 years, 6 months, and 10 days. Fabianus, 4 years, 5 months, and 9 days. Bonifacius, 6 months and 23 days. Deusdedit, 3 years and 20 days. Bonifacius, 5 years, 10 months, and 11 days. Honorius, 12 years, 11 months, and 17 days. Severus, [lacuna] months and 4 days. Joannes, 1 year, 8 months, and 18 days. [Col. 0140C] Martinus, 6 years, 1 month, and 26 days. Eugenius, 2 years, 9 months, and 24 days. Vitalianus, 13 years, [lacuna] months, and 6 days. Adeodatus, 4 years, 2 months, and 5 days. Donus, 1 year, 5 months, and 10 days. Agatho, 2 years, 6 months, and 4 days. Leo, 10 months and 17 days. Benedictus, 10 months and 12 days. Joannes, 1 year and 9 days. Conon, 11 months. Sergius, 12 years, 8 months, and 14 days. Joannes, 3 years, 2 months, and 13 days. Joannes, 2 years, 7 months, and 17 days. Sisinnius, 20 days. Constantinus, 7 years and 15 days. Gregorius, 15 years, 7 months, and 24 days. Zacharias, 10 years, 3 months, and 14 days. Stephanus, 5 years, 5 months, and 27 days. Paulus, 10 years and 1 month. [Col. 0140D] Stephanus, 3 years, 5 months, and 27 days. Adrianus, 23 years, 10 months, and 17 days. Leo, 20 years, 10 months, and 16 days. Stephanus, 7 months. Paschalis, 7 years and 16 days. Eugenius, 3 years, 7 months, and 23 days. Valentinus, 1 month and 10 days. Gregorius, 15 years. Sergius, 3 years. Leo, 8 years, 3 months, and 5 days. Benedictus, 2 years, 6 months, and 11 days. Nicolaus, 9 years, 6 months, and 20 days. Adrianus. Joannes.

[Col. 0141]

## CATALOGUE OF THE POPES AND OF THE DECREES ISSUED BY THEM

From the six-hundred-year-old Vatican codex 6381, preceding the Decree of Anselm, bishop of Lucca.

## ORDER OF THE ROMAN POPES

(The material enclosed in brackets was added in another hand in the codex.)

[Col. 0141A] Blessed Peter held office for 25 years, 2 months, and 7 days. He was crowned with martyrdom together with Paul after the Lord’s Passion, in the year 38.

Linus: 11 years, 3 months, and 12 days. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October; at the command of Blessed Peter he decreed that a woman should not enter the church with her head uncovered.

Cletus: 12 years, 1 month, and 11 days. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of May. At the command of Blessed Peter he ordained 25 priests in the city of Rome.

Clemens: 9 years, 2 months, and 10 days.

Anacletus: 11 years, 1 month, and 7 days.

Evaristus: 13 years.

Alexander: 11 years, 7 months, and 1 day; vacancy, 35 days. He introduced into the preaching of priests, when Masses are celebrated, material concerning the Lord’s Passion. A Roman by nationality.

Xistus: 10 years, 3 months, and 21 days; vacancy, 11 days. A Roman by nationality. He decreed that sacred ministries should be touched only by ministers.

[Col. 0141B] Telesphorus: 11 years, 2 months, and 22 days; vacancy, 7 days. A Greek by nationality. He decreed that Masses should be celebrated at night on the Nativity of the Lord, together with the angelic hymn, that is, “Glory in the Highest to God.”

Hyginus: 4 years, 3 months, and 7 days; vacancy, 3 days. A Greek by nationality. He organized the clergy and distributed the grades.

Anicetus: 8 years, 3 months, and 6 days; vacancy, 17 days. He died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May.

Pius: 11 years, 4 months, and 3 days; vacancy, 14 days. He decreed that holy Easter should be celebrated on Sunday.

Soter: 9 years, 3 months, and 20 days; vacancy, 22 days. He decreed that no nun should touch the sacred cloth (*palla*) or place incense in the holy church.

Eleuther: 15 years, 6 months, and 5 days; vacancy, 6 days. He died on the seventh day before the Kalends of June.

Victor: 10 years, 2 months, and 10 days; vacancy, 12 days. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.

Zepherinus: 16 years, 2 months, and 10 days; vacancy, 6 days. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of September.

[Col. 0141C] Callistus: 7 years, 2 months, and 10 days; vacancy, 6 days. He decreed that fasting should take place three times a year on Saturday.

Urbanus: 8 years, 11 months, and 12 days; vacancy, 30 days. He died on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

Pontianus: 5 years, 2 months, and 2 days; vacancy, 10 days. He died on the Kalends [the third day before the Kalends] of November.

Antherus: 12 years, 1 month, and 12 days; vacancy, 13 days.

Fabianus: 14 years, 11 months, and 7 days; vacancy, 13 days.

Cornelius: 3 years, 2 months, and 10 days; vacancy, 66 days.

Lucius: 3 years, 3 months, and 3 days; vacancy, 33 days. He prescribed that two priests and three deacons should not leave the bishop anywhere, for the sake of ecclesiastical testimony. He died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September.

Stephanus: 4 years, 2 months, and 15 days; vacancy, 22 days. He decreed that ecclesiastical vestments, with which service is rendered to God and which ought to be sacred and honorable, should not be used for any other purposes than ecclesiastical and God-worthy services; nor should they be touched or carried by anyone except holy men.

Xistus, a Greek by nationality: 2 years, 11 months, and 6 days; vacancy [Col. 0141D] 25 days.

Dionysius: 2 years, 3 months, and 7 days; vacancy, 5 days.

Felix: 2 years, 10 months, and 25 days; vacancy, 5 days. He decreed [Col. 0142A] that Masses should be celebrated over the memorials of the martyrs. He died on the fourth day before the Kalends of June.

Eutychianus: 8 years, 10 months, and 4 days; vacancy, 8 days. He decreed that only grapes and beans among the fruits should be blessed upon the altar. He died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of August.

Caius: 11 years, 4 months, and 9 days; vacancy, 11 days.

Marcellinus: 9 years, 2 months, and 25 days; the episcopate ended after 7 years, 6 months, and 25 days.

Marcellus: 5 years, 7 months, and 21 days; vacancy, 20 days.

Eusebius: 2 years, 2 months, and 25 days; vacancy, 7 days. In his time the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ was discovered on the fifth day before the Nones of May. He died on the sixth day before the Nones of October.

Melchiades: 3 years, 7 months, and 21 days; vacancy, 16 days. He died on the Ides of December.

Sylvester: 23 years, 10 months, and 11 days; vacancy, 15 days. He decreed that a priest should anoint the baptized with chrism after he had been lifted from the water, because of the danger of death; and that no layman should dare to bring an accusation against a cleric. He also decreed that the sacrifice of the altar should not be celebrated on silk or dyed cloth, but only on linen produced from the earth and blessed by the bishop. Just as our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean linen shroud, so should Mass be celebrated.

Marcus: 11 years, 7 months, and 20 days; the episcopate ended after 20 days. He died on the third day before the Nones of October.

Julius: 11 years, 2 months, and 5 days; vacancy, 25 days.

Liberius: 10 years, 3 months, and 4 days; vacancy, 6 days.

Felix (2): 1 year, 3 months, and 2 days; vacancy, 38 days. He suffered on the third day before the Ides of November.

Damasus: 18 years, 2 months, and 10 days; vacancy, 31 days.

Siricius: 15 years, 11 months, and 25 days; vacancy, 20 days.

Anastasius (1): 2 years and 26 days; vacancy, 20 days. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends of May.

Innocentius: 15 years, 2 months, and 21 days; vacancy, 33 days. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of August.

Zosimus: 1 year, 8 months, and 23 days; vacancy, 11 days. He decreed that a wax candle should be blessed by the Levites. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of May.

[Col. 0142C] Bonifacius: 3 years, 5 months, and 13 days; vacancy, 9 days. He died on the ninth day before the Kalends of November.

Coelestinus: 7 years, 10 months, and 9 days; vacancy, 21 days. He died on the eighth day before the Ides of April.

Xistus (III): 8 years and 19 days; vacancy, 22 days.

Leo (I): 22 years, 1 month, and 26 days; vacancy, 7 days. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of April.

Hilarius: 6 years, 3 months, and 10 days; vacancy, 10 days.

Simplicius: 15 years, 1 month, and 7 days; vacancy, 6 days. He held ordinations in the city of Rome in December and February: 63 priests, 11 deacons, and bishops in various places.

Felix (3): 8 years, 11 months, and 17 days; vacancy, 5 days.

Gelasius: 4 years, 8 months, and 18 days; vacancy, 8 days. He held two ordinations in the city of Rome, in February and December: 32 priests, 2 deacons, and bishops in various places. He composed tracts and hymns, like blessed Ambrose. He died on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December.

Anastasius: 1 year, 11 months, and 24 days; vacancy, 4 days. Many clerics and priests separated themselves from communion with him because he had communicated with the deacon Photinus and because he wished secretly to recall Acacius but was unable to do so. He died on the fourth day before the Kalends of December.

[Col. 0143A] Symmachus: 15 years, 8 months, and 27 days; vacancy, 7 days. He decreed that every Sunday, or on the feast of a martyr, “Glory in the Highest” should be said. He held four ordinations in the city of Rome, in December and February: 92 priests, 16 deacons, and 117 bishops in various places.

Hormisda: 8 years and 17 days; vacancy, 6 days. He died on the eighth day before the Ides of August.

Joannes: 2 years, 8 months, and 17 days; vacancy, 58 days. He was captured by King Theodoric, tortured, and died as a martyr in custody at Ravenna on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June.

Felix (4): 4 years, 2 months, and 13 days; vacancy, 3 days. He held two ordinations in the city of Rome, in February and March: 55 priests, 4 deacons, and 28 bishops in various places. He died on the fifth day before the Ides of October.

Bonifacius (2): 2 years and 26 days; vacancy, 1 month and 15 days. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

Joannes (2): 2 years, 4 months, and 6 days; vacancy, 6 days. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

Agapitus: 11 months and 18 days; vacancy, 24 days. He died on the tenth day before the Kalends of May.

[Col. 0143B] Silverius: 1 year, 5 months, and 11 days. He was captured by deceit, clothed in a monastic garment, and sent by Vigilius the archdeacon to the Pontian Islands. Sustained by the bread of tribulation and the water of distress, he died in weakness as a confessor and was buried in the same place on the twelfth day before the Kalends of July. He signed his condemnation of Vigilius in the following manner:

“Thus the faith of the holy Fathers ought to be preserved in the Catholic Church: that he should lose what he possessed who, with irreproachable rashness, assumed what he had not received.”

Vigilius: 17 years, 6 months, and 26 days; vacancy, 3 months and 5 days.

Pelagius: 11 years, 10 months, and 18 days; vacancy, 2 months and 25 days.

Joannes (3): 12 years, 11 months, and 26 days; vacancy, 10 months and 3 days. He died on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August.

Benedictus: 4 years, 1 month, and 29 days; vacancy, 11 days. In his time the people of the Lombards invaded Italy.

Pelagius (2): 10 years, 2 months, and 10 days; vacancy, 3 months and 25 days. He died on the seventh day of February.

Gregorius: 13 years, 6 months, and 10 days; vacancy, 5 months and 23 days. He added to the Canon: “And our days in your peace.” [Col. 0143C] He decreed that Mass should be celebrated over the body of Blessed Peter.

Fabianus: 1 year and 5 months, and 8 days; vacancy, 11 months and 26 days. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of March.

Bonifacius (3): 8 months and 22 days; vacancy, 10 months and 6 days. He died on the eleventh day before the Ides of November.

Bonifacius (4): 6 years, 8 months, and 13 days. He obtained from Phocas the Pantheon temple, in which he established a church of Saint Mary and all the martyrs. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.

Deusdedit: 3 years and 24 days; vacancy, 13 days. He died on the sixth day before the Ides of November.

Bonifacius (5): 5 years and 13 days. He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of November.

Honorius: 12 years, 11 months, and 17 days; vacancy, 1 year, 7 months, and 18 days. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of October.

Severinus: 2 months and 4 days; vacancy, 4 months and 29 days. He died on the fourth day before the Nones of August.

Joannes (4): 1 year, 9 months, and 19 days; vacancy, 1 month and 13 days. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of October.

Theodorus: 6 years, 5 months, and 18 days; vacancy, 42 days. He died on the second day before the Ides [Col. 0143D] of May.

Martinus: 6 years, 1 month, and 29 days; vacancy, 28 days.

[Col. 0144A] Eugenius: 2 years, 9 months, and 29 days; vacancy, 28 days. He died on the fourth day before the Nones of June.

Vitalianus: 14 years and 6 months; vacancy, 2 months and 13 days. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of February.

Adeodatus: 4 years, 2 months, and 5 days; vacancy, 2 months and 5 days and 4 months and 90 days. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of June.

Donus (I): 5 years, 5 months, and 10 days; vacancy, 2 months and 15 days.

Agatho: 2 years, 6 months, and 4 days; vacancy, 1 year, 7 months, and 5 days. He died on the fourth day before the Ides of January.

Leo (2): 10 months and 25 days; vacancy, 2 months and 15 days. He died on the fifth day before the Nones of July.

Joannes (5): 1 year and 9 days; vacancy, 1 month and 19 days. He died on the fourth day before the Nones of August.

Conon: 11 months; vacancy, 13 days. He died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October.

Sergius (I): 13 years, 8 months, and 24 days; vacancy, 1 month and 20 days. He decreed that “Agnus Dei” should be sung at Mass. He died on the sixth day before the Ides of September.

Joannes (6): 3 years, 2 months, and 12 days; vacancy, 1 month and 18 days.

Joannes (7): 2 years, 7 months, and 17 days; vacancy, 4 months. He died on the fifth day before the Kalends [Col. 0144B] of November.

Sisignius: 20 days; vacancy, 1 month and 18 days.

Constantinus: 7 years and 15 days; vacancy, 40 days. He died on the sixth day before the Ides of April.

Gregorius (2): 16 years and 9 months; vacancy, 1 month and 10 days. He added to the Canon: “Whose solemnity is in the presence of glory.” He died on the fourth day before the Ides of February.

Gregorius (3): 10 years, 8 months, and 25 days; vacancy, 8 days.

Zacharias: 10 years, 3 months, and 13 days.

Stephanus (2): 5 years and 29 days; vacancy, 1 month and 5 days. He went to Francia and anointed Pippin. When Pippin came into Italy, he took Ravenna and twenty other cities from the hand of Aistulf and restored them under the jurisdiction of Saint Peter. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of May.

Paulus: 10 years and 1 month; vacancy, 1 year and 1 month.

Stephanus (3): 3 years and 5 months; vacancy, 29 days.

Adrianus (I): 23 years and 10 months; vacancy, 17 days. He caused King Charles to come to Rome against Desiderius, king of the Lombards. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.

[Col. 0144C] Leo (3): 20 years, 5 months, and 17 days. He was blinded by his own men and placed in strict custody; after a few days he recovered his sight, and the use of his tongue for speaking was restored to him. He decreed that litanies should be celebrated before the third day preceding the Lord’s Ascension. He crowned Charles.

Stephanus (4): 7 years.

Paschalis: 7 years and 16 days.

Eugenius (2): 4 years, 7 months, and 23 days.

Valentinus: 10 months and 40 days.

Gregorius (4): 16 years.

Sergius (2): 3 years. He crowned Louis.

Leo (4): 8 years, 3 months, and 5 days.

Benedictus (2): 2 years, 6 months, and 10 days.

Nicolaus (1): 9 years, 6 months, and 20 days.

[Col. 0144D] The remaining popes up to Paschal II, at whom the catalogue ends, are not added, since they do not pertain to the history of Anastasius. See Schelestrus, p. 644.

# Francis Bianchini’s notes on the preceding catalogues, as well as on specimens of the script of the second Corbie manuscript and of the Farnesian manuscript of the *Book of the Pontiffs*

[Col. 0147A] An explanation must be given of the principle guiding our decision—namely, why, from among the several ancient catalogues of the Roman pontiffs presented by learned writers, I judged those that I have inserted here to be selected: three from Schelestratius and two obtained from Mabillon. Many more could indeed have been collected, had I preferred multiplicity to selection. From Schelestratius’s appendix to his chronological work, eight different catalogues were available, distinguished by him with the numbers 6, 18, 22, 26, 27, 29, 31, and 32, from Vatican manuscripts of the Palatine, Urbinate, Alexandrine, and other libraries that he himself identified. Nor were notable catalogues lacking in the libraries of Gaul. In addition to the two transcribed by Mabillon, the single Colbert Library supplied Pagius with eight different ones, printed in the second edition of the *Critique of Baronius*,

[Col. 0147B] together with two completing the number ten: one from the Royal manuscripts and another from the manuscripts of Thou. The English collections likewise offered series of Roman pontiffs, especially the one from the Bodleian Library that we see published in the posthumous work of Pearson.

I judged, however, that quality rather than abundance had to be considered. I therefore selected three of the eight catalogues published by Schelestratius, whose antiquity and sources were not obscure and whose use for illuminating Anastasius was especially appropriate. For the three principal features that our text brings forward in each pontificate—at least for the most part—are an account of the chronology of the see in years, months, and days; enumerated ordinations of bishops, presbyters, and deacons;

[Col. 0147C] and, finally, a record of numerous decrees and various deeds. These three features, I say, I undertook to confirm individually from three of Schelestratius’s catalogues. The catalogue published by him from a manuscript of the Palatine-Vatican Library, which was 865 years old when he wrote—and now is nearly 900 years old—contains all three. Another catalogue is merely an index of chronology, but it must be regarded as among the most reliable. It was copied by order of Paul II from a manuscript of the Church of Bergamo that bore the appearance of being 800 years old. I shall show in my dissertation on the ancient catalogues of the Roman pontiffs that those catalogues deserve preference over the others which are known to have been copied from genuine records of the Roman Church, especially records placed in a public and more sacred location, and [Col. 0147D] from the period that was rich in more exact chronologists. I shall present sufficiently intact traces of such records from the walls of the patriarchal churches, especially Saint Paul’s on the Ostian Way. Thus I shall conclude that the ancient Italian manuscripts deserve confidence, and specifically this Bergamo manuscript, which corresponds exceptionally well to those Roman archetypes of such authority—where the agreement of manuscripts copied so many centuries ago with the surviving numbers of the distinguished monuments of the Roman Church, erected in the period I have mentioned, is evident. Our selection will be splendidly confirmed by the astonishing agreement of two Italian manuscripts and catalogues related to this one in antiquity and proximity to the City. One of them I already published in the first volume, page 4, from a manuscript of Cava carefully copied by Francesco Penia; the other I shall publish below from the distinguished manuscript of the abbey of Farfa, to which an antiquity of seven hundred years or more must be assigned.

[Col. 0148A] The agreement of these three manuscripts, outstanding in such antiquity and in their complete agreement both with one another and with the genuine monuments of the Basilica of Saint Paul that I have mentioned, wonderfully confirms the superiority of Italian manuscripts for deriving pontifical chronology from authentic sources, especially when the numbers in these catalogues are compared with the numbers of other foreign manuscripts—which may be commended either for equal or even greater antiquity—and are found to differ greatly both among themselves and from the genuine indications of public records, gathered from councils, letters, and reliable diplomas of pontiffs and other rulers.

For this reason, among Schelestratius’s catalogues I selected that catalogue transcribed from the Bergamo manuscript as an especially trustworthy and suitable index of pontifical chronology, and it ought to be regarded as such.

[Col. 0148C] Finally, the third catalogue reveals an antiquity of approximately 650 years. It is added to our selection because, besides certain decrees and deeds of the pontiffs, it also indicates several sacred ordinations and the customary chronology of the years, months, and days assigned to each pontificate; it also records the periods during which the see was vacant, or, as these catalogues ordinarily express it, during which the episcopate ceased. Although the periods between pontificates, or periods of vacancy, are not attested by documents so certain as to leave no room for doubt—for the period is calculated according to the varying practice of the reckoners, beginning sometimes from the day of a predecessor’s death, sometimes from his deposition, and extending now to the day of election, now to ordination, while in cases of schism

[Col. 0148D] or persecution it is interrupted in various ways, as will become clear in detail at the appropriate places—nevertheless, so that I might not deprive the Anastasian text of whatever light or support the catalogues can provide for history,

[Col. 0149A] I thought this third catalogue should be borrowed from Schelestratius.

Several reasons moved me to add the two catalogues collected by Mabillon from the most ancient manuscripts of the monastery of Corbie’s library. The first is the antiquity of the manuscripts, for which both the editor—an exceptionally skilled student of diplomatic matters—and all learned men hold them in high esteem. The earlier catalogue must be assigned to the sixth century, as I indicated from Mabillon’s own notes in the preface, no. 4; the later catalogue is recognized as having been written around the end of the seventh century. While examining a specimen of its script in *De re diplomatica*, book V, plate 8, no. 5, and while I had before me a specimen sent to me by the illustrious Mauritius, Marquis de Sanctis, of the script of the Farnesian manuscript containing the Anastasian *Lives of the Pontiffs*,

[Col. 0149B] I detected such a similarity in the strokes of the letters and in the graphic delineation of the two scripts, each carefully executed in accordance with its archetype,

[Col. 0150A] that I could not doubt that the same indication of antiquity appeared in both. This, then, was the second reason for adding this second Corbie catalogue: not merely to illuminate the chronology of the pontiffs, but also to establish the age of the Anastasian manuscript, which, in the judgment of the foremost authorities in this field—Holstenius, Schelestratius, and Mabillon—must be regarded as the most ancient of all. Indeed, so that anyone who cultivates diplomatic studies and the art of calligraphy may be able to judge the antiquity of each, I took care to insert here specimens of the script of both manuscripts. Let the reader therefore have, from Mabillon’s specimen, an example of the script of the second Corbie catalogue, belonging to the seventh Christian century,

[Col. 0150B] which is as follows.

[Col. 0149]

[Col. 0149C] Mabillon demonstrates, for two reasons, that the script of this second Corbie catalogue must be assigned to the end of the seventh century. First, because it ends with John VI, who began to sit in the year 701 and held office for three years. The years of this pontiff and of his immediate predecessor Sergius are not given; only those of the preceding pontiffs are expressed. The last of these, Conon, is said to have held office for eleven months, reckoned from the day of his consecration, Sunday, 21 October 686, to 21 September 687, as we shall say in its place with Anastasius. Therefore the catalogue appears to have been written while Sergius was still alive, after Conon’s death; someone subsequently added the name of John, his successor.

Mabillon again demonstrates that the same date must be assigned to the script of this catalogue by comparing its letter forms

[Col. 0149D] with a completely similar specimen of the Beauvais manuscript, expressed on the same plate 8, no. 2, where the date of the writing is indicated by this testimony:

> “The work was completed, with the Lord’s favor, at the monastery of Luxeuil, in the twelfth year of King Chlothar, in the thirteenth indiction, the fortieth year of our Father having been happily completed.”

Mabillon explains the date in these words:

[Col. 0150C]

> “The time when the manuscript was written is expressed at its end, as it is read here: at the monastery of Luxeuil, in the twelfth year of King Chlothar, in the thirteenth indiction, the fortieth year of our Father having been happily completed.
