I have interpreted this as referring to Saint Columban and to Chlothar II, whose twelfth year in Burgundy coincides with the year of Christ 625, marked by the thirteenth indiction; and perhaps the fortieth year of Columban’s arrival in Burgundy was likewise reckoned by the people of Luxeuil. If, however, anyone insists that this should be referred to the reign of Chlothar III and to the administration of Waldebert, who governed Luxeuil for forty years, it would have to be said that Waldebert exceeded the year 665, which is ordinarily assigned as his last, and reached the year 670, which under the rule of Chlothar III was marked by the thirteenth indiction.”

[Col. 0150D]

Since, then, these documents establish the age of the Luxeuil manuscript and of the Corbie catalogue, both of which were written in a script entirely similar, I judged that a specimen of the script of the Anastasian manuscript should be added here. In antiquity it deserves preference over the others, according to the judgment of the two prelates Holstenius and Schelestratius, who compared the Farnesian manuscript—then preserved at Rome—with the others with such care.

[Col. 0151A] Inspection and comparison of the specimens, each executed with the utmost care according to the fidelity of its prototype, will show how solidly Holstenius argued concerning the antiquity of the *Lives* of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, which exceeds the age of Anastasius, since the script of the Farnesian manuscript alone demonstrates it. I have reproduced Holstenius’s words from no. 2 of the preface to the first volume, which I shall not hesitate to repeat here:

[Col. 0152]

> “On page 54 the collations of the Farnesian manuscript begin. It was written in large letters, and I do not think anything older survives in this genre. The manuscript was certainly written before Anastasius was born, or at least during the period in which Anastasius lived.”

[Col. 0152]

[Col. 0153A] To this testimony of Holstenius I added, in the preface indicated, no. 6, similar observations by Labbe and Lambecius, affirming the judgment of the finest manuscripts of antiquity. They had seen manuscripts of excellent quality written in the time of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious. In one of them, the *Lives* were attributed to Damasus before Anastasius had been born—or at least before he had emerged from the trinkets of early childhood; in others, the ending of the *Lives* showed that they had been written a hundred years before Anastasius was born. The force of these arguments becomes more evident from direct inspection of the script of the Farnesian manuscript and its comparison with the similar script of the Corbie catalogue, belonging to the end of the seventh Christian century.

As for the similarity of this specimen

[Col. 0153B] engraved by us to the Farnesian original, the same carefulness of the Marquis de Sanctis stands as guarantor. Through his generosity the manuscript was found, preserved, and restored for the benefit of the republic of letters—a manuscript long desired and unsuccessfully sought by many, until the perseverance of that distinguished man, who deserved so well of pontifical history, brought it back from obscurity in a corner and almost from the darkness of death into the light.

After the death of the prelate Schelestratius, when the most serene Farnese princes ordered several ancient manuscripts from the library they possessed at Rome to be transferred to Parma, that Anastasian manuscript was sent along with the others included in this selection. But the man entrusted with arranging the books placed it—mutilated in a considerable portion, just as Holstenius and Schelestratius had seen it at Rome—

[Col. 0153C] with the entire fifty-eight *Lives* of the pontiffs from Saint Peter to Saint Agapetus missing, and nearly consigned it to oblivion with bundles of unbound leaves. Perhaps he had postponed a more careful inquiry into what work the surviving portion belonged to; perhaps he was waiting to see whether other fragments might be sent from Rome that could belong to this very manuscript.

When responsibility for the library subsequently passed into other hands through the succession of the princes, no one suspected that Anastasius should be sought among these discarded materials. We, however, suspecting that the book was concealed at Rome, urgently requested that it be diligently sought in the shelves of the Farnesian household’s archive in its celebrated palace near the Campo dei Fiori.

The illustrious and German brothers de Sanctis—namely, Ignatius, Marquis and superintendent of the affairs of the most serene household in Rome, and Mauritius, Marquis, employed with the highest praise as a privy councillor and in other trusted positions by his prince—were distressed, in view of their humanity and their eagerness to benefit everyone, that the Farnesian manuscript so highly commended by Holstenius could be found neither here nor in the prince’s palace at Parma, although they had repeatedly attempted, at my request, to discover this important monument among the precious treasures of the most serene household.

[Col. 0153D] They searched the Roman archive and the Parma library. At last, through the shrewd care of Marquis Mauritius, who examined every corner, the long-desired manuscript was found: written in square or large letters, as they commonly call them,

[Col. 0154A] and mutilated in precisely that portion which had already been missing in Holstenius’s time. It was the very copy from which that prelate had transcribed the variant readings, declaring that all other manuscripts were surpassed in antiquity by this single Farnesian one.

After Marquis Mauritius communicated this to his brother in a letter dated 15 September 1719—about a year after the publication of the first volume of our edition—and Marquis Ignatius shared the letter with me, he offered the efforts and care of both brothers in having a specimen of the script accurately prepared by a skilled calligrapher. They chose to transcribe the *Life of Saint Eugenius*. Since it is brief, begins at the front of the leaf in the first column, and is completed in the second column, it can display the form of the capital letters, the entire arrangement of the text,

[Col. 0154B] and the form of the final verses of the life. After he had carried this out obligingly, I had each letter of the *Life of Saint Eugenius* engraved at Rome according to the model of the specimen sent to me, and I arranged for the impression of our edition to be returned to him so that it could be compared with the prototype. He found them so consistent that he judged it safe to publish the specimen, with the support of his exact imitation and his testimony, on 29 April of the present year, 1720. He wrote to me as follows:

> “You may confidently include the impression in your work, assuring yourself that the script is very similar to the original and that it could not have been imitated better by the engraver. I am very glad of it.”

[Col. 0154C] The care that he himself required of the calligrapher in copying the specimen proposed as the model for this Roman engraving

[Col. 0154D] is attested by a letter sent to me from Piacenza on 20 November 1719. I reproduce it as well, since it makes the antiquity of the Farnesian manuscript evident:

> “The copies mentioned above—the *Life of Saint Eugenius* and a fragment of the *Life of Sergius*—were not transcribed on the Chinese paper you sent me for two reasons. One reason was that, because of the antiquity of the original, the blackness of the ink on the parchment had greatly diminished, so that it would not show sufficiently through the Chinese paper to permit the form of the script to be imitated exactly. The other was that the copyist’s experience with the Chinese paper showed him that, when using a pen, however fine, its point made the ink appear very thick; when the ink dried,

[Col. 0155A] it became thin again, and, shrinking, distorted the resemblance of the script. It was therefore necessary to use ordinary paper. He made an alphabet with the utmost care, containing all the letters in the likeness of those of the Author; by means of this alphabet and by inspecting the original, he imitated the script so well, both in the width of the lines and in the shape of each letter, that there is not the slightest difference. I regret that Your Most Illustrious Lordship cannot make the comparison with Anastasius’s text with your own eyes; you would in fact see something miraculous. I compared the copy with that same text and found it faithful. You may therefore be assured that the work has achieved the perfection and refinement you desired.”

Let no one reproach me for appearing to have pursued these matters at excessive length. Since we have undertaken the task of illuminating the *Book of the Pontiffs*, it requires us to show, with the praised prelates, that the work attributed to Anastasius must be referred to earlier writers. That assertion, supported by several arguments in the preface to the first volume and in Schelestratius’s dissertation, which will be presented shortly, ought not to be deprived of this further demonstration, supplied by the antiquity of manuscripts exceeding the age of Anastasius.

This discussion was reserved for the present place because, when the subject of the Corbie catalogues arose, it demanded that specimens of their script be presented, so that we might judge with equal certainty the antiquity of the Farnesian manuscript,

[Col. 0155B] which was opportunely preserved to furnish an argument of this kind for this Vatican edition of the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*. I offer my heartfelt congratulations to the princes of the most serene Farnese household, truly Roman princes. Through their efforts we owe the preservation both of the chronology and history of pagan Rome in the marble records excavated from the Forum and placed on the Capitoline nearly two centuries ago, and of a document on the chronology and history of the supreme pontiffs, no less worthy than the others for illuminating Christian Rome, which we have received in our own age.

The first reason, then, was the publication of both Corbie catalogues together with specimens of their script, so that their antiquity might be established.

A second reason was added, no less important than the first:

[Col. 0155C] namely, to show how much preference should be given to catalogues commended by the ancient Italian libraries over the pontifical catalogues of foreign archives, even when the latter possess great antiquity. The Italian catalogues both originated from and were corrected by genuine documents of the Roman Church, in the manner that we shall discuss below in our dissertation on the ancient catalogues of the Roman pontiffs and on their selection and authority. For the moment we shall summarize it in advance by noting the following.

Let the numbers assigned to the see of each pontiff in the two Corbie catalogues be compared with one another. Although the antiquity of the script and manuscript appears in one catalogue to be eleven centuries old and in the other ten—and therefore the ages of the scribes who copied them do not differ by more than one or two centuries—

[Col. 0155D] nevertheless, the difference between the two chronologies is incredible. For the most part, neither the years nor the months agree, to say nothing of the differences in days, which may be regarded as the smaller matter. For the seven pontiffs nearest to Saint Peter, we see the following numbers assigned.

[Col. 0156A] It must seem remarkable that not a single number of years agrees in the two catalogues; that all the months likewise disagree, except for those of one Xystus; and that the days agree only in the cases of Linus and Xystus. When critics considered this disagreement, observing it in manuscripts of the sixth and seventh centuries, they were almost driven to despair of establishing pontifical chronology in the first and second centuries of Christianity. Heterodox chronologists reproached us with the same difficulty. Since it was attested by manuscripts of such great antiquity, they called into question most of the deeds and even the martyrdom of many of those counted among the pontiffs in our catalogues who had suffered death for Christ’s name.

Pearson, in dissertation II, chapter 6, although he was not the most aggressive among the non-Catholics, nevertheless seemed to advise that we should admit the historical account to have been irretrievably lost, as well as the assertion of the martyrdoms, decrees, and rites entrusted by these most holy men to the archives of the Church—as anyone can perceive in the three published dissertations of his posthumous works.

Among our own writers, some were uncertain what course to take in establishing pontifical chronology. For, guided by preconceived opinions, once they had decided to take account only of the antiquity of the manuscripts, they considered it unnecessary to investigate the differing sources of the catalogues or to become better informed about their origin and authority.

[Col. 0156B] We, however, agreeing with Tertullian (*On the Crown of the Soldier*, page 344 of della Barre’s edition) that historical conceptions—and especially chronology, which must be regarded as the basis and foundation of events—must be traced back to their origins, judged that it would be safer to derive chronology from those catalogues that proceeded from genuine documents of the Roman Church, especially documents publicly displayed, and from the period that was richer than any other in diligent and skilled chronologists. Everyone agrees that this period must be identified with the fourth and fifth Christian centuries, and the facts themselves show it, as I shall demonstrate more fully in the dissertation mentioned on the ancient catalogues of the Roman pontiffs.

It follows that, if an older series of pontiffs and a chronology existed that had been publicly displayed in the patriarchal basilicas of Rome—such as I shall show survives in considerable part at Saint Paul’s on the Ostian Way—and if it were found to agree both with the other records of deeds preserving the marks of unquestionable authenticity, whether in councils or in letters, and with the oldest catalogues preserved in Italian libraries and archives, such a series would be the touchstone against which the reliability of all catalogues would be tested.

[Col. 0156C] Whenever several catalogues, especially very ancient ones, were found in the Italian libraries of cathedral churches and distinguished monasteries that agreed with the series and chronology just mentioned, they would rightly deserve preference over those that differed. For the proximity of the Italian churches, which more frequently provided the opportunity for comparison, reasonably leads us to presume that the written catalogues and copies were more accurately transcribed from the prototypes of the patriarchal basilicas when they agreed closely with these Roman sources.

The writers and copyists of distant regions and provinces, who had less opportunity to approach the City and compare their copies with the genuine monuments of the Roman basilicas, could not correct with equal confidence the errors and divergences found in the numbers of the manuscripts they had copied.

[Col. 0158A] The difficulty is demonstrated above all by those two Corbie catalogues, which differ so greatly in their chronological eras despite their close relationship and similarity in antiquity.

It is sufficient to have indicated these matters briefly, in connection with the notes to be applied to the Corbie catalogues, so that we may weigh the other considerations favoring the three ancient Italian catalogues, which agree both with one another and with the genuine documents of the Roman Church. In the dissertation we shall undertake after the one by Schelestratius, I shall do my utmost to establish this.

# Dissertation

[Col. 0157]

## Emmanuel Schelestratius’s dissertation on the ancient catalogues of the Roman pontiffs, from which the *Book of the Pontiffs* was compiled, and on the author and excellence of the *Book of the Pontiffs*

### Chapter One. On the ancient Fathers and writers who included the succession of the Roman pontiffs in their works or chronicles

[Col. 0157B]

Among the ancient Fathers and writers who composed a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs are the very ancient Saint Irenaeus, who came to Rome under Eleutherius; Saint Optatus of Milevis, whose catalogue ends with Siricius; and Saint Augustine, whose catalogue ends with Anastasius.

**II.** Victor of Tunnuna followed them. Isidore of Seville’s testimony concerning him is cited. Victor’s *Chronicle* was published by Scaliger, and its final words, into which a chronological error had crept, are corrected.

**III.** Eusebius inserted another series of pontiffs into his *Chronicle* and his *History*. The *Chronicle* translated into Latin by Saint Jerome was enlarged and supplemented in various places; Marcellinus’s testimony to its excellence is cited. A few observations are made concerning the *History* translated and supplemented into Latin by Rufinus.

**IV.** The years of Christ were inserted into the Eusebian *Chronicle* by another hand, and in several places it requires correction.

**V.** Greek copies of this *Chronicle* are lacking;

[Col. 0157C] nevertheless, Jerome’s Latin versions survive. He added a supplement, not, as some think, in his youth, but in the forty-seventh year of his life, as may be deduced from the year in which Jerome died.

**VI.** Next follows the *Chronicle* of Saint Prosper, which Philip Labbe published complete; he adduces the testimonies of Victor of Aquitaine and Gennadius of Marseille concerning it. Consuls from the Incarnation of Christ to the consulship of Valentinian VIII and Anthemius are appended to this *Chronicle*. It nevertheless retains the errors of the Eusebian *Chronicle* and added some others concerning the consuls.

**VII.** Marcellinus Comes followed Prosper. Cassiodorus mentions his *Chronicle* and asserts that it continued to the time of the Emperor Justinian; this is likewise confirmed by Marcellinus’s own testimony.

**1.** Many people in our own time and in that of our parents have written the lives of the Roman pontiffs, but among the earlier writers few are found to have devoted their effort and industry to this historical field. Nevertheless, some included in their works and chronicles either the succession of the pontiffs or the years and months of their pontificates. Since we must present their catalogues here, it seemed appropriate first to preface them with a few remarks about the authors themselves and briefly to investigate when and with what degree of accuracy each wrote.

[Col. 0157D] First, then, we must discuss the holy Fathers and those authors who recorded the succession of the Roman pontiffs. The most ancient of these is Saint Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons in Gaul, who, in book III, chapter 3, composed a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, concluding it with these words:

[Col. 0158B]

> “Now Eleutherius holds the episcopate as the twelfth in succession from the apostles.”

Eleutherius lived before the middle of the second century, by which time the succession of the Roman pontiffs must have been known to everyone in the City; for not yet had eighty-five years elapsed since Peter’s death. Since, therefore, Irenaeus was in Rome during the pontificate of Eleutherius and composed a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, his testimony on this matter must not be dismissed but should be highly valued as an outstanding monument of antiquity.

To Irenaeus we add the catalogues of two African Fathers. One was published by Saint Optatus, bishop of Milevis, under Siricius; the other by Saint Augustine under Anastasius, the successor of Siricius. Those Fathers followed Saint Irenaeus’s judgment: they omit Cletus and recognize only Anacletus, as will become clearer below from their catalogues.

## 2.

Furthermore, since the catalogues of the earlier Fathers extend only to the pontificate of Anastasius, while we must continue the chronological sequence down to John III, who outlived Justinian, we shall supplement the catalogue of those Fathers from the *Chronicle* of Victor, who was bishop of Tunnuna in Africa and who, according to Isidore’s testimony in Book I, the final chapter, “completed the deeds of the succeeding ages down to the consulship of the emperor Justin the Younger.” [Col. 0158D]

Isidore also says in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 38, concerning this same Victor of Tunnuna, that he began his history from the beginning of the world. For there he reports as follows:

> “Victor, bishop of the Church of Tunnuna in Africa. From the beginning of the world down to the first reign of Justin the Younger, he published, arranged according to the successive annual consulships, a brief history of the most distinguished military and ecclesiastical affairs, illustrious for its praise and critical judgment, and highly worthy of remembrance. For defending the Three Chapters, he was transported by Augustus Justinian into exile in Egypt. Summoned thence again to Constantinople, when he resisted the detractors of those same Three Chapters—namely, the emperor Justinian and Eutychius, bishop of the city of Constantinople—he was again sent to be kept under guard in a monastery of that same city, and, remaining, as they say, under that condemnation, he died there.”

This testimony of Isidore concerning Victor of Tunnuna is outstanding. From it we learn not only about the *Chronicle*, but also about the person and activities of Victor, who, as a defender of the Three Chapters, is believed to have inserted certain material into his history out of partisan zeal.

Joseph Scaliger published Victor’s *Chronicle* in his *Thesaurus temporum*. In Scaliger’s edition it begins with these words:

> “In the eighteenth year, during the consulship of Theodosius the Younger, Victor, bishop of the Church of Tunnuna in Africa, continues the history where Prosper left off.”

These words do not belong to Victor of Tunnuna, but to another writer who collected the chronicles of Eusebius, Jerome, Prosper, and Victor into a single work, and who added to what was lacking in the chronicle of the earlier writer from the history or chronicle of a later one. [Col. 0159C]

He ends his *Chronicle* with these words:

> “All the years from Adam, the first man, down to the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ according to the flesh—which took place in the year 5199—are counted; and from the birth of our Lord Jesus Christ, which took place in the forty-third year of the reign of Augustus Octavian Caesar, down to the first year of Justin, the first Roman ruler who succeeded Justinian in the empire, there are 527 years. Altogether, from Adam down to the first year of the aforesaid Roman ruler, there are 5726 years.”

It is certain that these words contain an error concerning the years said to have elapsed from the birth of Christ to the accession of Justin. For from the forty-third year of the emperor Augustus, in which Victor places Christ’s birth, to the first year of Justin, 567 years elapsed, not merely 527 years, as the words cited above state. I would suppose that this error entered through the fault of copyists, with the numeral L having been changed into X.

Although the final number of years added by Victor for the period from Adam to Justin’s first year seems to indicate that the above-mentioned error ought to be attributed to Victor, this need not be of great concern, since, once the first number had been corrupted, the later number appears to have been adjusted by the copyists to match the earlier one.

That this error entered the *Chronicle* through the fault of the copyists, and not of Victor of Tunnuna, is made clear by the final two numbers, 17 and 16. These numbers correspond exactly to the true chronology, which counts 567 years from the forty-third year of Augustus to Justin’s first year. If 567 years are added to the year of the world 5199, in which, according to Victor, Christ was born, the year of the world 5766 is obtained; this must be Justin’s first year according to Victor’s reckoning. [Col. 0160A]

This, then, is what may be said about the error that entered Victor’s *Chronicle*. It ends in Justin’s first year, in which the consular fasti also end and the emperor Justinian completed his mortal life. Accordingly, we too shall bring our chronological treatment of matters relating to antiquity to an end in that same year.

## 3.

To the earlier chronology, which was carried from Peter down to Pelagius I, we add a second one, composed in Greek by Eusebius of Caesarea, bishop in Palestine, and continued by Saint Jerome and others. [Col. 0160B]

As I have already indicated, Eusebius occupies the first place among these writers. He was born in the third century of Christ, when many writings of apostolic men had not yet perished; from them the facts concerning the earliest pontiffs and their deeds could be known with great clarity.

That Eusebius wrote a comprehensive history from these sources in his *Chronological Canons* is attested by Saint Jerome, who admits in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* that he translated it into Latin and enlarged it in various places. In the preface to Eusebius’s *Chronicle* he says:

> “For it must be understood that I have performed, in part, both the task of a translator and that of a writer: I have rendered the Greek with the greatest fidelity, and I have added certain things that seemed to me to have been omitted—especially in Roman history, which Eusebius, the author of this work, did not so much fail to know, being a most learned man, as, since he was writing in Greek, seem to me to have touched upon rather briefly what was less necessary for his own readers. Thus, from Ninus and Abraham down to the capture of Troy, the translation is purely Greek. From Troy down to Constantine’s twentieth year, much has now been added and now intermixed, which we most carefully excerpted from Tranquillus and the other distinguished historians.” [Col. 0160C]

Count Marcellinus calls this work wholly remarkable and says that not only Eusebius but also Saint Jerome should be regarded as its author. His words should be heard:

> “After the remarkable work in which Eusebius of Caesarea, from the creation of the world down to the emperor Constantine, recorded in Greek the origins, times, years, kingdoms, and virtues of mortals of this age, the inventors of various arts, and the monuments of almost all the provinces—and in which our Jerome translated it into Latin and extended it in Roman language down to the emperor Valens—both are therefore authors of this work.”

This, then, is what may be said about the excellence of the Eusebian *Chronicle*. We shall add more on that subject after making a few observations concerning Eusebius’s *History*, in which a succession of the pontiffs is also found.

There exists in the archive of the principal basilica of the Apostles in Rome an ancient manuscript codex bearing this title:

> “In the name of Christ begins the Ecclesiastical History, which Saint Jerome translated from the Greek of Eusebius of Caesarea in Palestine into Latin for Chromatius the bishop.”

Yet, as a certain possessor of the book noted in the margin, the translation is not by Saint Jerome but by Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia, who made it at the command of Chromatius, bishop of Aquileia, as is clear from the preface. Rufinus also continued the same history. After Book IX, where Eusebius ends, the manuscript adds:

> “Thus far Eusebius has handed down the memory of events that took place in the Church. The remaining events, which are to follow in order down to the present time, whether we have found them in the writings of our ancestors or whether our own memory has supplied them, we shall add, obeying the instructions of our religious Father, and in this also following him, with whatever brevity we can.”

This is Rufinus, who added two books and brought the ecclesiastical history down to the death of Theodosius the Elder. [Col. 0161B]

So much for the *History* of Eusebius; let us now return to his *Chronicle*.

## 4.

There are very many editions of the Eusebian *Chronicle* in which the years of Christ are recorded. It is certain, however, that these were neither supplied by Eusebius nor added by Saint Jerome, since this method of numbering was first introduced by Dionysius Exiguus after the fifth century, during the time of the emperor Justinian. Hence the years of Christ are nowhere recorded in the Amandine manuscript codex.

The years of the emperors, however, are displayed in the manuscript codices. It is so certain that events were recorded according to them by the ancients that Eusebius himself, throughout his *Ecclesiastical History*, assigns the periods of the Roman pontiffs by the years of the emperors, together with the more notable events that occurred in the Church under them.

Therefore, if we were presenting Eusebius’s *Chronicle* according to the years of the emperors, we could establish a fixed epoch for the Roman pontiffs in accordance with Eusebius’s reckoning—provided that we could obtain a certain and reliable copy of the Eusebian *Chronicle*.

But the manuscripts we have seen in Rome are more recent, while the older ones preserved elsewhere also differ in their recording of the imperial years. Aubert Miraeus observes the same thing concerning the Aquicinctine, Ortelian, and Lipsian manuscript codices. Moreover, the edition prepared by Arnoldus Pontacus, bishop of Bazas, from several manuscript copies differs greatly from Scaliger’s edition. It is therefore perfectly clear that the authority of the codices and editions is unstable, and that nothing certain can be established from them.

This is shown by Miraeus’s own edition, which states that Victor assumed the episcopate while Aelius Pertinax was reigning. Yet Eusebius himself, in Book V of his *History*, chapter 20, relates that Eleutherius died in the tenth year of the emperor Commodus, three years before Aelius Pertinax attained the imperial power, and that Victor succeeded Eleutherius at that time. [Col. 0161D]

The *Chronicle* of Eusebius contains many similar statements that conflict with what is transmitted in his *History*. It also contains other matters requiring correction, such as what it reports concerning Marcellinus and Marcellus, who flourished in those periods but whom Eusebius, in a serious error, treated as one and the same pontiff.

It eventually ends the pontificate of Melchiades in Constantine’s third year, although it is certain that the Roman council in the case of Donatus was held under Melchiades in Constantine’s seventh or eighth year.

Finally, it places the Council of Nicaea in the fifteenth year of the emperor Constantine, although it is evident from other sources—and also from Eusebius himself, in Book III of *The Life of Constantine*, chapter 14—that it was held in the twentieth year of his reign.

Thus, from all these considerations it is clear that the *Chronicle* of Eusebius has reached us in a very corrupt form, and that even Saint Jerome, who added much of his own, did not completely purge it of errors or restore it everywhere to its original truth. [Col. 0162A]

## 5.

Indeed, nearly all the manuscript *Chronicles* of Eusebius that now exist in libraries are Latin, deriving from the translation of Saint Jerome, who continued the work from Constantine’s twentieth year, in which Eusebius’s *Chronicle* ends, down to the sixth consulship of Valens and the second consulship of the emperors Valentinian.

Some believe that Saint Jerome wrote the supplement to the Eusebian *Chronicle* in his youth, and that it should therefore not be considered a work of such great authority.

They may support their opinion with the arguments that led Baronius, under the year 420, to state that Jerome died in the seventy-eighth year of his age. Since everyone agrees that Saint Jerome died around the year 420, and since Jerome brought his *Chronicle* to an end in the fourteenth year of Valens, which coincides with the year 377, it would follow that Jerome completed the *Chronicle* around the thirty-fifth year of his life.

But, apart from the fact that the thirty-fifth year of life cannot be called youthful, others point out that what Baronius undertook to prove—namely, that Jerome died in the seventy-eighth year of his age—is not so certain.

Indeed, the common opinion of more recent scholars rejects it, chiefly for three reasons. The first is drawn from Jerome’s own words, from which we learn that Jerome more than once called himself old, while calling Augustine younger.

Since it is certain that Saint Augustine died at Hippo in Africa in the year 430 of the common era, in the seventy-sixth year of his age, if Saint Jerome died in 420 at the age of seventy-eight, Jerome would have been only twelve years older than Augustine. Yet Jerome would never have called himself old and Augustine young on account of a difference of only twelve years. [Col. 0162C]

The second reason is drawn from the testimony of Saint Prosper, a disciple of Saint Augustine, who records in his *Chronicle* the time of Jerome’s birth and death. According to the Lodunensis codex in Pontacus, it reads:

> “In the consulship of Bassus and Ablavius, Jerome is born.”

And in all the manuscripts and printed editions:

> “Jerome the presbyter dies in the ninety-first year of his age, on the day before the Kalends of October, during the consulship of Theodosius IX and Constantius III.”

Theodosius and Constantius held that consulship in the year 420, while Bassus and Ablavius held theirs in the year 331. From the year 331 to the year 420 there are more than seventy-eight years, since ninety years intervene. Thus Saint Prosper came very close to the truth when he stated that Jerome died in the ninety-first year of his age.

This agrees perfectly with what is read in Count Marcellinus: that Jerome brought his life to an end at a very advanced age; and with what is found in Saint Augustine, Book I *Against Julian*, chapter 7, namely, that he reached decrepit old age. [Col. 0163A]

Since these statements can scarcely be applied to a man of seventy-eight but fit a man of ninety much better, it follows altogether that, when Saint Jerome completed the *Chronicle*, he was in his forty-seventh year.

For this reason the ancients never regarded it as a work of youthful age, but valued it as an exceptional work of Jerome.

When Idatius, in the preface to his *Chronicle*, had said certain things about the *Chronicle* of Eusebius, he continued:

> “After him, Jerome the presbyter, a successor and perfected recorder of all deeds and sayings—himself another Eusebius in name—translated this work of Scripture from Greek into Latin and, beginning with the twentieth year of the aforesaid emperor, wove the history that follows down to the fourteenth year of Valens Augustus.”

Thus writes Idatius, bishop of the province of Gallaecia, who testifies that he saw Jerome in the East during his own youth.

It should be noted that word “perfected” (*perfectus*) is significant, since Idatius uses it to indicate that Saint Jerome’s *Chronicle* must be held in the highest esteem because of the completeness of its composition, and therefore must not be despised as incomplete or carelessly published. [Col. 0163B]

## 6.

There follows the *Chronicle* of Prosper, formerly the most faithful and distinguished disciple of Augustine. Its supplement, after the *Chronicles* of Eusebius and Saint Jerome, was frequently published in print.

Hence most people believed that Saint Prosper had written nothing more than a supplement to the Eusebian and Hieronymian *Chronicles*.

Labbeus notes that they were seriously mistaken. In Volume I of the *New Library of Manuscript Books*, in the catalogue of writers, he says:

> “Very many, including highly learned men, were deceived, believing that Prosper had merely attached an appendix to Jerome’s *Chronicle*. For it is certain, and is confirmed by many testimonies of the ancients, that he carried a chronological epitome from the beginning of events down to his own times as though by a single thread and continuous course.

> “Victor of Aquitaine testifies to this in the preface to the Paschal Canon addressed to Hilary, archdeacon of Rome and later pope: ‘The venerable Prosper followed the course of this Eusebius and composed these same matters in the same *Chronicles* with the same excellent brevity, so that their beginning might commence from the origin of the world.’”

Gennadius adds his testimony in his *Catalogue of Illustrious Men*:

> “Prosper, a man of the region of Aquitaine, learned in language and forceful in argument, is said to have composed many works. Among them I have read *Chronicles* bearing his name, containing, in accordance with the faith of the divine Scriptures, the period from the creation of the first man down to the death of the emperor Valentinian and the capture of the city of Rome by Genseric, king of the Vandals.”

Philip Labbeus published this *Chronicle* of Saint Prosper in the volume cited above, at Paris in the year 1657. From it one may see that Saint Prosper generally presented his *Chronicle* according to the accounts of Eusebius and Jerome in the same words, except that he added the consuls from the death of Christ down to his own times:

> “We begin,” he says, “the consuls from the manifestation of the Lord, that is, from the consulship of Rufinus Geminus and Rubellius Geminus.”

And in the *Chronicle*:

> “The record of the consuls begins with the history, with Rufinus Geminus and Rubellius Geminus as consuls.”

It ends:

> “With Valentinian VIII and Anthemius.”

Saint Prosper’s *Chronicle* also contains Eusebius’s errors concerning Cletus and Anacletus, and concerning Marcellinus and Marcellus, although it is established that these were two pontiffs only.

He likewise retained ecclesiastical events that had sometimes been incorrectly assigned to particular consuls, as well as an obvious lacuna after the pontificate of Soter, assigned to the consulship of Apronianus and Paulus. The pontificate of Eleutherius is missing there—not omitted through any fault of the author, but eroded by the ravages of time, as is suggested by the order of the Roman pontiffs. The eleventh pontiff is written there as Soter, while Victor is the thirteenth, with no mention of the twelfth pontiff. [Col. 0164B]

So much for the *Chronicle* of Prosper. From it we presented a complete catalogue of the Roman pontiffs in the first edition of our work on antiquity. Here, however, so as not to multiply the chronological schemes of the ancient writers, we shall provide only the supplement concerning the pontiffs.

## 7.

Other writers followed Prosper, carrying ecclesiastical history down to their own times. Among them the foremost place belongs to Marcellinus Comes of Illyricum. Cassiodorus the senator writes of him in Book 17 of *Divine Readings*:

> “Marcellinus of Illyricum followed Jerome. He is said still to have served as secretary to the patrician Justinian, but, devoted to better expression, he brought his work, with the Lord’s help, from the time of the emperor Theodosius down to the threshold of the triumphant reign of Augustus Justinian.”

Marcellinus himself should be heard concerning his *Chronicle*. In the preface, after mentioning the *Chronicles* of Eusebius and Jerome, he speaks as follows of the supplement he added to them:

> “But I, following the Eastern empire with a simple reckoning only, counting 150 years by indictions and by the consuls listed below—from the seventh indiction and from the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius [during whose consulship Theodosius the Great was also created emperor], and bringing the count down to the consulship of Magnus—inserted them as a continuation into the work of those authors. I likewise supplied another seventeen years, from the first consulship of Justin Augustus down to the fourth consulship of Justinian Augustus. Altogether these make 156 years.”

Thus far Marcellinus, who inserted into his *Chronicle* all the Roman pontiffs who held office during that span of 156 years and recorded the years of their pontificates with sufficient accuracy.

# CHAPTER II. On the most ancient catalogue, which ends with Pope Liberius.

I. The most ancient catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, drawn up in the time of Pope Liberius, was once known to Cuspinian, but unknown to Onuphrius Panvinius; it was finally printed by Bucherius and is preserved in manuscript in a codex of the Imperial Library.---II. The codex of the Imperial Library does not contain the autograph, but a more recent copy written 300 years ago.---III. From the aforesaid codex I obtained variant readings which agree with Bucherius’s edition, not with Henschenius’s edition; this difference, however, does not impair the antiquity of the work, but rather commends it.---IV. Henschenius’s opinion is that the earlier part of the catalogue, down to Urban, was written by Pope Antherus, and the latter part, down to Liberius, was added by Saint Damasus.---V. Papebroch agrees with Henschenius concerning the author of the first part, but assigns four authors to the second part.---VI. It is shown that Pope Antherus was not the author of the first part of the catalogue.---VII. This is proved from two errors committed in this catalogue concerning the order in which the pontiffs succeeded one another: for it places Clement before Cletus, and Pius after Anicetus, although it is established that Clement succeeded Cletus and Anicetus succeeded Pius.---VIII. Concerning the authors of the second part, it is shown that the pontiffs down to the pontificate of Felix were by no means added by a third-century author; this is proved from chronological errors, for avoiding which recourse to a vicariate is of no help, as is clear from the period during which Stephen held the pontificate.---IX. It is likewise shown that the pontiffs following Felix were not added by three different authors, but by one and the same author.---X. Nevertheless, despite these facts, it is proved by various reasons that the author of this catalogue is most ancient and lived about the time of Liberius’s pontificate.---XI. This has been admitted not only by Catholics but also by heretics, with the exception of Dodwell, whose opinion is rejected.

## 1.

The most ancient catalogue of the Roman pontiffs still surviving today appears to be that which extends to the pontificate of Liberius. From it Cuspinian drew the consuls which he inserted into his commentary on the *Fasti* of Aurelius Cassiodorus, as we shall demonstrate from that commentary itself at the end of this chapter. Nicholas Fabricius, lord Peiresc and senator of Aix, had the same catalogue among ancient parchments, as Antonius Cappellus testifies in chapter 5 of *On the Supper and Passion of Christ*. And, if we believe Henschenius, Onuphrius Panvinius had this same catalogue, since in his commentary on Book II of the *Fasti* he begins to cite Damasus’s *Lives of the Pontiffs* from the consulship of Saturninus and Scipio, under whom Saint Linus is said in the aforesaid catalogue to have been created bishop. [Col. 0165C]

But that learned man is mistaken. For there survives in the Vatican Library, after Onuphrius Panvinius’s book on the *Fasti*, an index of manuscript books and records which Onuphrius Panvinius had seen or possessed concerning the lives of the pontiffs. In this index the aforesaid catalogue does not appear at all; only the lives of the Roman pontiffs by Pope Damasus, Anastasius, William, librarians of the Holy Roman Church, Pandulf of Pisa, and more recent authors are cited. From these Onuphrius thought that the *Liber Pontificalis*, of which we shall speak below, had been compiled. Onuphrius therefore never saw the most ancient catalogue which ends with Pope Liberius and which some believed to have been lost, until Aegidius Bucherius published it in his commentary on the Paschal Canon, noting that Cuspinian had possessed the autograph. Lambecius likewise testifies to this in Book IV of his *Commentaries on the Imperial Library*:

> “The excellent manuscript codex which Bucherius praises and seeks, but almost laments as lost, still survives, equally intact, in the most august Imperial Library at Vienna, as Cuspinian himself once used it; and it holds the fifty-sixth place among the Latin historical manuscripts.”

## 2.

From these words of Lambecius I began to doubt whether the autograph of the aforesaid catalogue, written on very ancient parchments in the time of Liberius, might still survive in the Imperial Library. Therefore, led by a great desire to learn the truth, I wrote to the distinguished Conrad Janning, who in 1688 was visiting the libraries of Germany in order to compile the *Acts of the Saints*, and who was travelling as far as Vienna. I asked him to examine the fifty-sixth Latin historical manuscript, and not merely to extract the variant readings of the older catalogue, but also to send me a specimen of its script, so that I might judge the age of the writing. That gentleman, with his usual kindness, did what I asked; and in a letter sent to me from Vienna on 29 July 1688, he not only supplied the variant readings of that codex, but also stated:

> “From these things it is plain that neither was this catalogue of the Imperial Library copied from Henschenius’s catalogue, nor Henschenius’s catalogue from the codex of the Imperial Library; rather, each was drawn from a different exemplar, though both mediately had one and the same more ancient prototype, because of certain precisely identical defects in each. As to antiquity, however, it seems probable to me that the age of its first author may be referred to the time of Pope Liberius. Thus I would venture to affirm that this Imperial copy is, at most, no older than five hundred years. This is suggested, if not demonstrated, by a little work attached in the same codex, entitled *Chronicle of the Poles*, which mentions Pope Alexander III—not to mention marks of later times, which those prevented from investigating them are unable to examine—and therefore the codex cannot exceed that age. Now this little work is indeed written in a script different from that of the catalogue, but its paper—for this codex is not made of parchment, nor is it the same as that which our Bucherius mentions in Lambecius, Book IV—is so similar that not even one egg is more like another; nor does the script of the catalogue itself indicate greater antiquity, if not rather less. I add, however, a specimen of it,” etc.

Thus he wrote. From the specimen itself which he sent me, I inferred that he had judged the age of the writing correctly; for I judged that it could scarcely exceed three hundred years.

## 3.

Since, therefore, these letters establish that the autograph of this older catalogue has perished and that only more recent transcripts survive, which are known to differ greatly from one another, I thought I should perform a useful service by publishing the aforesaid catalogue below with its variant readings. Accordingly, I shall add here only that the catalogue as edited by Henschenius in the *Acts of the Saints*, and by us in *Antiquity Illustrated*, is far more complete than that still found in the Imperial Library. For the Imperial codex lacks the pontiffs Anicetus, Eleutherius, and Zephyrinus, who occur in our edition. Since these same three pontiffs are also wanting in Bucherius’s edition, it seemed highly probable to me that the parchments possessed by Bucherius had been copied from the Imperial codex. [Col. 0167A]

I was especially confirmed in this view when, on comparing the readings of the Imperial codex, I observed that almost all of them, except two or three, occur in Bucherius’s edition. Bucherius, therefore, used one exemplar, and Henschenius before us another. These facts, however, do nothing against either the genuineness or antiquity of this catalogue, since it could easily have happened—as frequently happened with other works of the ancients—that scribes and copyists did not copy the codices accurately, but transmitted them to posterity with many errors and lacunae. Hence I venture to affirm that errors and lacunae are a sign that works have issued from ancient writers. Since manuscript codices everywhere teach us that this is so, it remains briefly to inquire concerning the authors of this catalogue and the times at which they wrote.

## 4.

Henschenius, indeed, in the first volume of the *Saints for April*, thought that this catalogue has two parts and that each was written by a different author:

> “The first part,” he says, “is completed with Saint Urban, the pontiff martyred in the year 230. In this earlier part no consuls are repeated twice, even though, under the same consuls in whose term some began to sit, their predecessors may have died or been crowned with martyrdom. . . . The author of this part seems capable of being identified as Saint Antherus, pope, who diligently sought out the acts of the martyrs from the notaries and deposited them in the church. He sat only one month in his pontificate, and appears to have sought out the acts of the martyrs, especially of the supreme pontiffs, while not yet pope, under Saint Pontian, successor of Saint Urban; indeed, we shall say on 25 May, when Saint Urban is commemorated, and on 10 May, when the priest Saint Calepodius, the consul Palmatius, the senator Simplicius, and other martyrs are commemorated, that the Acts of Saints Urban and Callistus, Urban’s predecessor, seem to have been written by Saint Antherus. The second part, then, would begin with the said Pontian; and in it fuller eulogies of the pontiffs are frequently related, the same consuls are repeated, and the days of the ordination and death of the pontiffs are assigned. This part is carried almost to the end, where the eulogy of Saint Julius, contrary to the practice with the others, has an exact account of the basilicas built by him. From this account we establish on 12 April, in the life of this Saint Julius, the eminent soundness of this catalogue. Liberius succeeded Saint Julius, and Dionysius Petavius, in Book V, chapter 5 of his *Rationarium temporum*, asserts that this old list of Roman pontiffs was composed in Liberius’s time; he had it in his possession. After Liberius’s death Saint Damasus was made Roman pontiff. Asked by Saint Jerome, he sent him the acts of the pontiffs which he could find through diligent inquiry at his see. We judge that these words of Damasus are to be understood of the catalogue already indicated, carried down to Liberius, his predecessor. We prefix from manuscript codices the letters of both men on this matter, both Saint Jerome’s and Saint Damasus’s. The same Saint Jerome, in chapter 15 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, makes Saint Clement the fourth Roman pontiff after Peter, since, he says, Linus was second and Anacletus third, although most Latins think that Clement was second after the apostle Peter. Here we suppose that by the name ‘Latins’ is indicated this catalogue sent by Saint Damasus to Saint Jerome. Jerome also, in Book I *Against Jovinian*, calls Clement the successor of the apostle Peter; and, writing on Isaiah, chapter 52, says that Clement ruled the Roman Church after Peter—namely, after Saint Linus had intervened for a short time. Optatus of Milevis, Book II, and Saint Augustine, Letter 165, state that Clement succeeded Linus.”

## 5.

Thus far Henschenius on the older catalogue. Concerning his opinion, the distinguished Papebroch made certain observations which he thought required correction. Henschenius makes two authors of the catalogue, namely Antherus of the first part and Damasus of the latter; but Papebroch thought that the latter part had been composed by four different authors. Accordingly, in the *Propylaeum* to the *Acts of the Saints for May*, he observed as follows:

> “The second part, then, would begin with the said Pontian; and in it fuller eulogies of the pontiffs are frequently related, the same consuls are repeated, and the days of the ordination and death of the pontiffs are assigned. This part seems to have had four successive authors, distinguishable by a certain diversity of style. The first ended with Saint Felix; the second added his three successors, Eutychianus, Caius, and Marcellinus; the third joined Marcellus and Eusebius; the fourth continued the writing from Melchiades down to the beginning of Liberius, and flourished under Liberius’s predecessor Julius, in whose eulogy, contrary to the practice observed in the preceding eulogies, there is an exact account of the basilicas built by him.”

I omit the rest, because it coincides with Henschenius’s opinion indicated above, so that, according to Papebroch, nothing need be corrected in his words except that five authors in all must be substituted for the two authors of the most ancient catalogue. It must now be investigated whether he proceeded more successfully in this correction than Henschenius. For I consider that none of the things said by these two distinguished men concerning the authors of the first and second parts can stand.

## 6.

To begin with the author of the first part: Saint Antherus, pope, is said to have been its author. Of him the second catalogue, which ends with Felix IV and was written in the sixth century, says:

> “He diligently sought out the acts of the martyrs from the notaries and deposited them in the church.”

Another catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, drawn up in the time of Charlemagne and preserved in the Palatine-Vatican Library, says of Antherus:

> “He diligently sought out the acts of the martyrs.”

The *Liber Pontificalis*, as it now survives, repeats the words of the catalogue composed in the sixth century. Thus, by the consistent tradition of the catalogues and the *Liber Pontificalis*, it is established that Pope Antherus deposited in the church the acts of the martyrs, diligently sought out from the notaries. But, I ask, what have these things to do with the earlier part of the catalogue, in which, from the apostle Peter to Pontian, only the names of the Roman pontiffs are set forth and no mention of their acts or martyrdom is found, except that Peter is said in one word to have suffered under Nero and Pontian to have been sent into exile? [Col. 0169A]

If this part contained the matters mentioned by the ancient catalogues, would not the acts of those pontiffs and the manner of their martyrdom have been recorded in it? These are the things which Pope Antherus is said to have diligently sought out from the notaries and deposited in the Church, not the bare names of Roman pontiffs with the consuls under whom each began and ended, as in the earlier part of the older catalogue now under discussion. It must further be observed that Antherus sought out the acts of martyrs not only of the supreme pontiffs, but of all other faithful persons whatever who daily underwent martyrdom for Christ’s faith; so that the acts which he deposited in the Church must rather have had the form of a martyrology than of a catalogue. The author of the *Liber Pontificalis* further says of Fabian:

> “He appointed seven subdeacons to supervise the seven notaries, so that they might collect in full the acts of the martyrs.”

This manner of speaking indicates that all the proceedings, tortures, words, and deeds of the martyrs were likewise carefully recorded by the notaries at Fabian’s command.

### 7

To make it still clearer that Pope Antherus was not the author of the earlier part of the catalogue, the catalogue’s author places Clement before Cletus, contrary to the perpetual tradition of the Roman Church, which in the most ancient canon of the Mass has, from as early as the third or fourth century, commemorated Linus, Cletus, and Clement—an order that represents the first pontiffs according to the Roman Church. [Col. 0169C] It is therefore impossible that the Acts of the martyrs, carefully written down by the Roman notaries and deposited by Pope Antherus in the archives of the Roman Church, should have had a different order and placed Clement before Cletus.

Nor did the blessed Jerome have this catalogue’s author in mind when he wrote, under Clement, that Clement had been fourth in order, although most Latin writers thought him to have been second after the apostle Peter. By “most Latin writers,” indeed, the blessed Jerome did not mean the Roman Church or its pontiffs, but Saint Optatus, certain Latin writers, and perhaps the author of this catalogue, who lived in the time of Liberius and was not Damasus but a private writer. Hence the blessed Jerome departed from the opinion of this author and of Saint Optatus [Col. 0169D] and maintained that Clement had been not the second but the fourth pontiff after Peter.

Second, the earlier part of the catalogue places Anicetus before Pius. That this is another error of the catalogue is shown by two writers of those times who are beyond all exception: namely, Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons in Gaul, and the historian Hegesippus, who came to Rome under Anicetus and Eleutherius. The testimonies of both were reported more than 1,350 years ago in his books on Ecclesiastical History by Eusebius of Caesarea, bishop in Palestine. Both Irenaeus and Hegesippus certainly state that Anicetus came after Pius. The blessed Jerome also transmitted this view, in agreement with the common judgment of the Roman Church, as can easily be gathered from what we demonstrated in Dissertation II, *On the Roman Pontiffs*. [Col. 0170A]

Third, the catalogue assigns years and consuls to the beginning and end of the pontificates, but in so many places contradicts itself that the stated number of years and months conflicts with the consuls, while the periods of the consuls indicate either fewer or more years than those presented by the catalogue. One example among many will suffice. Concerning the eighth pontiff, this older catalogue states:

> “Sixtus: ten years, three months, twenty-one days. He lived in the time of Hadrian, from the consulship of Niger and Apronianus until that of Verus III and Ambibulus.”

Ten years and three months are counted, although Niger and Apronianus were consuls in the common era 117. Verus III and Ambibulus, however, held the consulship in the common era 126. From the year 117 to the year 126, it is impossible to count ten years [Col. 0170B] and three months; there are only nine years. For this reason Godefridus Henschenius, in his chronological table, also extended Sixtus’s pontificate to the year 127. The same thing appears to have been done elsewhere, contrary to the custom of the catalogue, which ordinarily gives the last consuls under whom the pontiffs died. These points, if I am not mistaken, are sufficient to prove that the earlier part of the catalogue could not have been written by Pope Antherus.

### 8

Let us now examine the second part, which Henschenius thought had been written by a single author, namely Pope Damasus, whereas Papebrochius believed it had been composed by four different authors who wrote from the time of Antherus to that of Damasus.

To discuss the first of these four, Papebrochius believed that this author had ended with Saint Felix. Since Felix, the successor of Dionysius, lived around the year 272, he therefore thought that the author of this part had flourished before the end of the third century. But if an author of the third century had composed the part of the catalogue extending from Antherus to Felix, he would certainly have known the pontificates and consulships of his own time and would have assigned the pontiffs to their proper consuls. Yet even in this part of the catalogue we see the consuls of one pontificate repeatedly mixed with those assigned to another pontificate.

This results in the frequent necessity of resorting to a vicariate: while the predecessor was still seated as the true pontiff, the successor was assigned a vicariate, so that in this way he could somehow be regarded as having been pontiff. Thus, concerning the twenty-fourth pontiff, the catalogue states:

> “Stephen: four years, two months, twenty-one days. He lived in the time of Valerian and Gallienus, from the consulship of Volusianus and Maximinus until that of Valerian III and Gallienus II.” [Col. 0170D]

Volusianus and Maximinus were consuls in the year 253. The catalogue assigns that year as the beginning of Lucius’s pontificate. Henschenius therefore writes that Saint Stephen was then Lucius’s vicar, and assigns Stephen only five months after Lucius’s death, under the same consuls, Valerian III and Gallienus II—that is, in the year 255.

Yet although this general notion of a vicariate might suitably remedy many defects in the catalogue, it could scarcely be applied to Stephen’s pontificate, since not merely two or three years but a longer period is demanded by the facts, as all earlier and modern writers alike attribute to him. Cyprian testifies that Saint Stephen acted as the true pontiff for more than five months against those who rebaptized, implying that in this matter he acted with pontifical authority as “the bishop of bishops.” Firmilian likewise indicates the same thing when he speaks of the foundational rock of the Church, about which he expressly declares that Stephen was accustomed to boast.

I would add more here in confirmation of this matter, had Papebrochius himself not admitted in his notes on Stephen’s life, which he presents in the *Chronological-Historical Attempt*, that I had correctly observed these facts. He himself also noted that Firmilian’s letter was written when nearly the twenty-second year had passed since the death of the emperor Alexander, as Baronius observes in the *Annals*; this occurred in the year 235. Therefore Firmilian’s letter must have been written around the year 257. At that time the controversy was still being debated between Stephen and Cyprian of Carthage, Dionysius of Alexandria, and others concerning the validity of baptism conferred by heretics. Stephen therefore could not have died in the year 255, as the consuls assigned by the catalogue would indicate. [Col. 0171B]

This is essentially what Papebrochius says. Yet in the notes mentioned above he tried in vain to restore to his own chronology the period of Stephen assigned in the older catalogue from the consuls.

### 9

Nor do the statements concerning the second, third, and fourth authors of the second part rest on any firmer foundation. Without a single witness, writer, or monument of antiquity, it is asserted that the second part of the catalogue was written by so many authors; and it is entirely gratuitously maintained that one author added Eutychianus, Caius, and Marcellinus; another added Marcellus and Eusebius; and a final author added all the rest, from Melchiades to Liberius. [Col. 0171C]

To begin with the first of these: what is found in the Acts of Eutychianus, Caius, and Marcellinus that is not also found in the records of earlier pontiffs? Concerning Eutychianus, the catalogue states:

> “Eutychianus: eight years, eleven months, three days. He lived in the time of Aurelian III and Marcellinus until the seventh day before the Ides of December, under the consulship of Carus II and Carinus.”

Concerning Dionysius, one of Eutychianus’s predecessors, it states:

> “Dionysius: eight years, two months, four days. He lived in the time of Gallienus, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, under the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus, [Col. 0171D] until the seventh day before the Kalends of January, under the consulship of Claudius and Paternus.”

What, I ask, is there in these two pontiffs that indicates different authors? The style is exactly the same, as is the method of recording the period during which each pontiff sat, so that every word indicates that there was one and the same author, not several.

The same must plainly be said of Marcellus and Eusebius, whom Papebrochius believed had been added by another author. Concerning Marcellus, the catalogue states:

> “Marcellus: one year, seven months, twenty days. He lived in the time of Maxentius, from the consulship of [lacuna] X and Maximian VI until after the consulship of X and VII.”

And concerning Eusebius:

> “Eusebius: four months, sixteen days, from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May until the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September.”

There is absolutely no difference in style, method of writing, or notation of time. The only omission in the entry for Eusebius is the consulship. This should not seem surprising, since he did not sit for several years under different consuls but only for a few months in the same year. The author omitted adding the consulship to that year because its consulship had to be cited under Eusebius’s successor, Melchiades.

Thus the catalogue states:

> “Miltiades: three years, six months, nine days, from the sixth day before the Nones of July, from the consulship of Maximianus VIII alone—which was in the month of September, under Volusianus and Rufinus—until the third day before the Ides of January, under the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus.” [Col. 0172A]

Maximianus was sole consul in the year in which he died; then Volusianus and Rufinus were appointed in his place. Thus all these consuls fall within the year in which the death of Marcellus was assigned above by the author of the catalogue. It is therefore plainly evident that the catalogue’s author deliberately omitted the names of the consuls under Marcellus’s pontificate, so that they would not be repeated under Melchiades.

This certainly would never have happened if Marcellus’s period had been inserted into the catalogue by a third author and Melchiades’s by a fourth, as, for example, Papebrochius believed. The second part of the catalogue was therefore written by one and the same author. So far from it being possible to infer from the catalogue that it was woven together by different authors, the continuous sequence of its chronological material rather shows that it was composed by one and the same author.

Unless someone wishes to say that the author of this catalogue took the years, months, and days from some earlier document, because they regularly disagree with the consular dates.

### 10

Cuspinianus judged that this older catalogue had been composed not by different authors but by one and the same author. He was the first to extract it from a manuscript codex and to include it in his commentaries on the consuls of Cassiodorus. Writing under the consulship of the two Gemini, he states:

> “An extremely old little work by an anonymous author was brought to me, in which the supreme pontiffs are listed together with the consuls under whom they lived. It reads as follows: ‘While Tiberius Caesar was emperor, the Lord Jesus Christ suffered under the two Gemini, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April. After his ascension, the blessed Peter undertook the episcopate,’ etc.”

From the opening words of this little work—which are exactly the same as the opening words of the catalogue we are discussing—it can easily be concluded that it is the same catalogue that Cuspinianus once possessed and attributed to an anonymous author. He continued to attribute it to that author as his work proceeded, whenever he mentioned the catalogue, especially under the consulship of Saturninus I and Venuvi, when discussing Peter:

> “I discovered in a certain library a most ancient little work by an anonymous author, containing the Roman pontiffs together with the consuls under whom they lived, from Saint Peter to Marcellinus, who lived under Diocletian, as we shall relate hereafter.”

Cuspinianus consistently and correctly asserts that this little work is an ancient work by an anonymous writer. He seems, however, to have suffered a lapse of memory when he reports that it contains the Roman pontiffs only up to Marcellinus. For after Marcellinus, from the same little work, he lists Marcellus again under “after the consulship of X and VII”; Melchiades under the consulship of Maximus VIII and Licinius; Sylvester under the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus; and Julius under the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus. Concerning Julius he writes:

> “That uncertain author mentions the pontiffs under these consuls as follows: ‘Julius: fifteen years, one month, eleven days. He lived in the time of Constantine, from the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus, from the eighth day before the Ides of February, until the day before the Ides of April, under the consulship of Constantius V and Constantius Caesar.’ Thus far the author whom I cited advances concerning the supreme pontiffs; I encountered nothing further, as long as they were called popes.”

Here Cuspinianus expressly states that the pontiffs, together with their consuls, continue beyond Marcellinus to Julius, just as they still continue in our edition of the catalogue. In our edition Liberius is also added, but without a consular notation, because the author reached the beginning of Liberius’s pontificate but not its end, having died before Liberius.

### 11

This is not merely our judgment but also that of others concerning the age of this author. Bucherius, who was the first to publish the complete catalogue, writes:

> “Up to this point—that is, to Liberius—the catalogue of the Roman pontiffs was composed before the death of Liberius, which the parchment expresses only by dots.” [Col. 0173C]

He refers to the parchment on which three other little works were found, written at the same time and under the same consuls.

The first was a fragment of the *Fasti*, extending from the year of Christ 205 to 354, when Constantius VII and Constantius III were consuls. There was also a little work on the Urban Prefects, with this title: “From the time of Gallienus: who administered the prefecture of the City and for how long.” In it the same prefects are listed from the year 254 to the year 354. The work ends with these words: “Under Constantius VII and Constantius III, Vitrasius Orfitus was prefect of the City.”

Finally, there was an ancient calendar dedicated to a certain Valentinus under Constantius, whom it lists as the last of the emperors and calls not “divine,” as it calls all the others, but “lord.” This is a most unmistakable sign that the author wrote under Constantius and that he was the same person who carried the aforementioned works down to the seventh consulship of Constantius and ended the catalogue of the Roman pontiffs under Constantius with these words:

> “Liberius lived in the time of Constantine, and from the eleventh day before the Kalends of June until [lacuna], from the consulship of Constantius V and Constantius Caesar.”

Neither the consulship in which Liberius died nor the day of his death is added because, as Bucherius correctly observes, the catalogue was composed before Liberius’s death.

The learned Petavius holds the same view in book V, chapter 5, of his *Rationarius temporum*, where he writes:

> “An old list of the Roman pontiffs composed in the time of Liberius, which we possess.”

After Petavius, Pearson—although alien to the Catholic faith, yet a man of exceptionally sharp intellect and sound judgment—frankly admits in Dissertation I, *On the Succession of the First Bishops of Rome*, chapter 13, section 2:

> “This catalogue was written under the pontificate of Liberius, whose successor was Damasus. Its author was therefore somewhat earlier than Jerome himself.” [Col. 0174A]

Dodwell of Dublin published this dissertation among Pearson’s posthumous works in London in 1688. Although Dodwell sometimes attempts to illuminate antiquity through his lengthy notes and commentaries, and also tries to do so with the present catalogue, he nevertheless detracts from its antiquity without any foundation or reason.

## CHAPTER III  
### Whether the older catalogue was written by Pope Damasus, and whether the two letters of Damasus and Jerome published on this subject should be regarded as spurious

I. The older catalogue is attributed to Pope Damasus on the authority of two letters, one written by the blessed Jerome to Damasus and the other by Damasus to the blessed Jerome.

II. Godefridus Henschenius proves the authenticity of these letters from similar letters published among the works of Damasus by Martius Milesius.

III. Henschenius adds several arguments by which he attempts to prove that the two authors of the *Book of the Pontiffs* were Antherus and Pope Damasus.

IV. Henschenius’s first argument, drawn from letters published by Martius Milesius, is refuted because those letters are spurious, as Erasmus and Labbeus correctly noted in their censures.

V. The letters of Damasus and Jerome concerning the *Book of the Pontiffs* are also spurious, as is first proved from Jerome’s style, which differs greatly from the style of the spurious letter.

VI. The same is confirmed by certain statements inserted into the spurious letter that conflict with the truth—especially the claim that Jerome, after becoming a presbyter, learned of Damasus’s elevation to the pontificate and wished to know which of the Roman pontiffs was recognized as having transgressed against the canons.

VII. Nor does it help to say that Jerome wished to know this because he was working on a martyrology. For that purpose it was sufficient for him to know which men had won the palm of martyrdom for the Christian religion.

VIII. That Damasus’s letter is also spurious is shown by its uncultivated and crude style.

IX. We show that the older catalogue was neither written by Damasus nor published as approved by his authority, nor transmitted to the blessed Jerome.

### 1

In the preceding chapter we investigated whether the older catalogue had been published by several authors in the third century. We showed that its author wrote in the fourth century, in the time of the emperor Constantius, although his name has until now remained unknown.

We must now inquire about Pope Damasus, who occupied the see in the fourth century, and ask whether the catalogue can perhaps be attributed to him. Two letters gave rise to this question. One is said to have been written by the blessed Jerome to Pope Damasus, and the other by Damasus to the blessed Jerome, in the following words:

> **Jerome to the most blessed Pope Damasus**
>
> Our humility beseeches the glory of your holiness that, in accordance with the authority of the apostolic see, which we have learned is governed through your holiness, you would deign briefly to recount for us, in order, the acts and records from the primacy of the blessed apostle Peter down to your own times—namely, what was done in your see—so that our humility, perceiving and recognizing the matter, may know which of the bishops of the aforementioned see deserved to be crowned with martyrdom, or whether anyone is recognized as having transgressed against the canons of the apostles. Pray for us, most blessed pope.

> **Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, to Jerome the presbyter**
>
> The Church rejoices, already satisfied by your fountain, yet curiosity about priestly times thirsts for more, so that what is worthy may be known and what is unworthy rejected. Nevertheless, the records of the pontiffs that we were able to discover through the diligence of our see we have gladly sent to your charity. Pray for us at the holy resurrection, brother and fellow presbyter. Farewell in Christ God and our Lord.  
> Dated the tenth day before the Kalends of June, and received on the Kalends of October; sent from Rome to Jerusalem.

### 2

Godefridus Henschenius was the first to have these letters printed. In the first volume of April, before the catalogues of the Roman pontiffs, he published them from ancient manuscripts and considered them genuine. He praised Martius Milesius Sarazanius, a Roman jurist, because in 1638 he had published at the Vatican Press, among the works of Saint Damasus, other letters exactly like these. On page 121 and the following pages he includes a letter from Damasus to Jerome, from which the aforementioned Henschenius excerpted the following:

> **Damasus, bishop, to his brother and fellow presbyter Jerome, greetings in the Lord**
>
> When many books had been brought under my authority, it happened that I hastened to learn that the Book of Psalms was being held in my mind, and I considered filling the capacity of my memory, dearest brother and always a priest in Christ, in order to find traces according to the Seventy Interpreters … I also ask your charity that your fraternity may be pleased to send us the Greek chanting of the Psalms … Therefore, through our brother and fellow presbyter Boniface, I ask that your fraternity order the traces of this matter to be disclosed to us. Sent on the fifth day before the Kalends of November.

He appends the presbyter Jerome’s reply to Damasus:

> **The suppliant Jerome to the most blessed Pope Damasus of the apostolic see of the city of Rome**
>
> I have read the letter of your apostleship, asking that, according to the simplicity of the Seventy Interpreters, I hasten to translate the Psalm-book for chanting [lacuna]. Your servant therefore begs that this voice of those singing psalms may be sung day and night in your Roman see, and that your apostolic office order the following to be joined at the end of every psalm: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, as it was in the beginning,” etc.

### 3

After publishing these two letters, Henschenius adds:

> “It does not seem that Saint Damasus himself wrote the earlier catalogue of the lives of the pontiffs; rather, he merely approved these materials, collected from various sources down to Liberius, his predecessor, and sent them to Saint Jerome. Therefore, when Ptolemy of Lucca, in Milesius on page 21, says that down to Damasus the chronicles of the supreme pontiffs receive their authority, we understand this to mean that Damasus wrote, approved, or subscribed to them; and we approve even less the fact that the lives of the pontiffs themselves are commonly attributed to him as their first author by Sabellicus, Panvinius, and others.”

Thus Henschenius himself admits that Damasus was not properly the author of this older catalogue [Col. 0176A] but only its approver. The author, however, lived under Liberius, as Henschenius confirms through the testimony of Petavius:

> “After Saint Julius, Liberius, in whose time this old list of the Roman pontiffs was composed, as Dionysius Petavius asserts in book V, and which he possessed himself, Saint Damasus was appointed Roman pontiff. When asked by Saint Jerome, he sent him the records of the pontiffs that he had been able to discover through the diligence of his see. We believe that Damasus’s words should be understood of the catalogue already mentioned, carried down to Liberius, his predecessor. We place before it the letters of both men on this subject, Saint Jerome’s and Saint Damasus’s, from manuscript codices.

> “The same Saint Jerome, in chapter 15 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, places Saint Clement fourth after Peter as Roman pontiff. He says: ‘Linus was second, Anacletus third, and although most Latin writers think Clement was second after the apostle Peter…’ Here we believe that by ‘Latin writers’ this catalogue, sent by Saint Damasus to Saint Jerome, is indicated. Jerome also calls Clement the successor of the apostle Peter in book I *Against Jovinianus*.
