And, writing on Isaiah 52, he says that Clement ruled the Roman Church after Peter—that is, with Saint Linus intervening between them, Linus whom Optatus of Milevis, in book II, and Saint Augustine, in Letter 165, report Clement succeeded.”

### 4

Thus far Henschenius. From the letters published by Martius Milesius he attempts to prove an exchange of correspondence between Pope Damasus and the blessed Jerome on similar subjects, so that he may more easily persuade us that the letters concerning the deeds of the Roman pontiffs, which he himself first published, are both genuine and attributable to Pope Damasus and the presbyter Jerome.

Yet in the first edition of *Illustrated Antiquity* I was surprised that Henschenius had not observed that the letters concerning psalmody had been published at Basel in 1516 by Erasmus. Erasmus made the following judgment concerning the earlier letter about psalmody, said to have been written by Damasus to Jerome:

> “It is clearer than needs to be pointed out that this letter is by the same author as the one that follows immediately, and that both suffer from the same fever. Good God! What impudence it was to attribute this to Damasus!”

Concerning Jerome’s reply to Damasus he adds:

> “It is astonishing that anyone could have been found who hoped that this letter—than which nothing could have been fabricated that was more tasteless, ignorant, or childish—would be read by anyone as Jerome’s.”

And lest we seem to wish to rely on the judgment of Erasmus, an author considered suspect, Philippus Labbeus most recently confirms his censures in the marginal notes to the two letters published by Milesius in volume II of the *Collection of Councils*:

> “They are regarded by learned men as spurious, apocryphal, and utterly foolish, and they are as far removed from the style of Damasus and Jerome as heaven is from earth, and the Antarctic Pole from the Arctic.”

These letters need no further proof, since the same facts plainly present themselves to anyone who examines them. I had demonstrated this so clearly from the letters published by Martius Milesius in the first edition of *Ecclesiastical Antiquity* that the distinguished Papebrochius, in the *Propylaeum* to the fourth volume of May, page III, thought it necessary to retract the opinion of his predecessor Henschenius. He added that, convinced by my arguments, he preferred to have those letters removed from volume I of April.

### 5

Papebrochius recognized how elegant and flowing was the style used by the blessed Jerome and Saint Damasus. Many of their works, about which there is no room for doubt, have come into our hands.

To prove this first of all concerning the works of the blessed Jerome: there are the *Epitaphs* of Paula, Fabiola, Lucinius, Marcella, and Nepotianus, published by that holy teacher. There are also several works composed against Helvidius, Jovinianus, Vigilantius, the Pelagians, Montanus, Rufinus, and other opponents of Jerome himself or of the Catholic religion. There are numerous treatises on the virtues, countless commentaries on the sacred Scriptures, and, to conclude, among his various letters, two notable ones written to Pope Damasus.

The first, numbered 57, begins as follows:

> **Jerome to Damasus**
>
> Since the ancient East, convulsed by the fury of its peoples against one another, tears apart piece by piece the undivided and seamless tunic of the Lord, woven from above, and foxes destroy Christ’s vineyard, so that amid broken cisterns that hold no water it is difficult to discern where the sealed fountain and that enclosed garden may be, I have decided to consult Peter’s chair and the faith praised by the apostolic mouth. From there I now ask for food for my soul, from the place where once I received Christ’s garments, etc.

The second, numbered 58, begins as follows:

> **Jerome to Damasus**
>
> The importunate woman in the Gospel finally deserved to be heard; and when the door had been shut with the servants, even at midnight a friend received loaves from a friend. God himself, who cannot be overcome by any forces opposed to him, is conquered by the prayers of a tax collector. The city of Nineveh, which perished through sin, stood through weeping. Why have I repeated these things at such length in my opening? Clearly, so that you, though great, may look upon one who is small, etc.

From these passages, if I am not mistaken, it is abundantly clear how elegant and ornate was Jerome’s style in the letters he wrote to Pope Damasus, and how greatly the letter concerning the deeds of the pontiffs presented above differs from his manner of writing.

### 6

Whenever the blessed Jerome asked something of Pope Damasus, he was accustomed to entreat Damasus in ornate language and with a lengthy repeated exordium, as can be gathered from the two fragments of the letters mentioned above. But the letter attributed to Jerome concerning the deeds of the Roman pontiffs, written in a humble and debased style, immediately states what is requested, without any ornament of an introduction, as is evident from its opening:

> “Our humility beseeches the glory of your holiness.”

It immediately continues:

> “That, in accordance with the authority of the apostolic see, which we have learned is governed through your holiness, you would deign briefly to recount for us, in order, the acts and records from the primacy of the blessed apostle Peter down to your own times—namely, what was done in your see.”

Here we must also note the words:

> “Which we have learned is governed through your holiness.”

These words indicate that the letter was written when the blessed Jerome, in Syria, learned that Pope Damasus had been placed in charge of the apostolic see. This conflicts with what is assumed in Damasus’s second letter. For there it is implied that the blessed Jerome was a presbyter when he wrote this letter.

But Jerome was made a presbyter by Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, after he had departed from the Syrian desert, from which he had written the two letters mentioned above to Pope Damasus. It is therefore entirely false that the blessed Jerome, already a presbyter, first learned of Damasus’s elevation to the pontificate. It is evident that the letter in question was composed by someone ignorant of Jerome’s deeds. [Col. 0178A]

Not only this chronological error, but also the following barbarism—“so that our humility, perceiving, may recognize”—shows that the letter must be denied to the blessed Jerome. He would never have concluded it with these words:

> “Or whether anyone is recognized as having transgressed against the canons of the apostles.”

The meaning of these words is obscure, contrary to Jerome’s manner of writing. He would have explained which apostolic canons were meant and what kind of transgression was under discussion.

### 7

Even if it could be supposed that Jerome was then working on a martyrology and therefore requested a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs from Pope Damasus in order to learn which of them had won the palm of martyrdom, it may nevertheless seem strange that the blessed Jerome should have asked Damasus to indicate whether any pontiff, having violated the apostolic canons, had departed from this world.

Jerome had written to Damasus that he consulted Peter’s chair and the faith praised by the apostolic mouth because that chair is the Gospel rock upon which he knew the Church to have been built, and because he believed the Roman faith to be the faith praised by Paul and destined never to fail. He professed that the incorrupt inheritance of the Fathers was preserved only among Peter’s successors.

Since Jerome made these statements in his letters to Damasus, with what purpose or reasoning would he have written to Damasus himself that he was uncertain about the transgression of some of Peter’s successors? Could it perhaps have been relevant to Jerome’s martyrology if one of the Roman pontiffs had committed some offense?

The blessed Jerome ought to have been concerned, for the composition of his martyrology, with holy pontiffs and their martyrdoms. Since he had studied in Rome in his youth and had often visited the martyrs’ crypts and the apostles’ churches, where the bodies of holy pontiffs were buried, it is scarcely credible that the martyrdoms of the Roman pontiffs were unknown to him.

It is much more improbable that Pope Damasus would have enumerated only three or four pontifical martyrdoms in the older catalogue if he had sent it to the blessed Jerome with the letter presented above. We shall address this matter immediately after showing, from its style, that Damasus’s letter is spurious.

### 8

The inept manner of writing found in this letter is far removed from Damasus’s style and alien to purity of expression. The letter begins with these words:

> “The Church rejoices, already satisfied by your fountain, yet curiosity about priestly times thirsts for more.”

These words alone should be sufficient to deny the letter to Damasus. Apart from the fact that the blessed Jerome, when he had first obtained the office of presbyter, had not written so many works that he could have filled the Church with his writings—and therefore it is untrue that the Church was already satisfied by his fountain—the letter adds:

> “Yet curiosity about priestly times thirsts for more.”

These words produce an inept meaning and can in no way be attributed to Damasus. For what do “priestly times” mean? Were priests then holding imperial power, or did they first begin to exist in the Church at that time, although they had not existed before?

Did not emperors reign in the time of Pope Damasus, just as his predecessors had held the reins of empire? If emperors ruled before Damasus, and if pontiffs and priests existed in the Church before that time, what, I ask, can “priestly times” mean? How did curiosity thirst for priestly times?

Or were priests driven by curiosity to hear Jerome’s interpretations of Scripture, as the Athenians, eager for novelties, once were driven to hear Saint Paul? If Pope Damasus had wished to express this eagerness of the priests, he would have said “the curiosity of the priests,” not “curiosity about priestly times,” as we observed in the first edition of *Antiquity*.

To this we may add that the whole of Damasus’s letter is written in a style so crude and uncultivated that it contains no sentence worthy of so learned and eloquent a pontiff. Jerome testifies of Damasus in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* that he possessed an elegant talent for composing verse.

His letters written in an elegant style were published by Martius Milesius and Lucas Holstenius. Many of his poems are also still found in the published *Library of the Fathers*, while others are inscribed on marble tablets. If we compare these with the construction of the letter published above, it will easily be evident that the phrases “through the diligence of our see” and “we have gladly sent” were produced by an author other than Damasus.

The author also gives himself away in the closing formula:

> “Dated the tenth day before the Kalends of June, and received on the Kalends of October; sent from Rome to Jerusalem.”

This formula is found in none of Damasus’s other letters. It was fabricated by the person who attributed the entire letter to Damasus.

9. And let this suffice concerning the spurious attribution of the letters. It remains only to show that the older Catalogue cannot even be attributed to Damasus, although those letters were genuine. This is easily demonstrated if we consider what Jerome requests in the first letter and Pope Damasus answers in the second.

For Jerome asks that “the Acts of the deeds” from the principate of blessed Peter the Apostle down to his own time be sent to him, so that he may know which of the bishops of the aforesaid see had deserved to be crowned with martyrdom, or whether anyone was known to have transgressed against the canons of the apostles. Damasus replies that the Catalogue of pontiffs requested by Jerome and sent by him contained the Acts of their deeds, or the deeds of the pontiffs, to which their deaths and the manner of their deaths had been appended.

Yet scarcely anything of all this is found in the older Catalogue. For hardly any deeds of the pontiffs are mentioned in it; and among all the pontiffs who sat from the holy Apostle Peter down to Pope Damasus, only four martyrdoms are enumerated: namely, those of the Apostles Peter and Paul, of whom it says, “Peter suffered with Paul on the third day before the Kalends of July”; of Pontian, concerning whom it reports, “On that same island [Sardinia] he was deprived of his belt on the fourth day before the Kalends of October”; of Fabian, of whom it relates, “He suffered on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February”; and of Cornelius, concerning whom it asserts, “Driven out to Centumcellae, there he received the sleep of death with glory.”

Thus the Catalogue commemorates only the martyrdoms of these pontiffs. If it had been written by Pope Damasus, or approved by him, and if it were the work that is presumed to be mentioned in his letters, can one believe that Damasus was ignorant of the other martyrdoms of the pontiffs? Was he perhaps unaware of Clement’s martyrdom, famous throughout the whole world? Was absolutely nothing left of the deeds of the martyrs that, at Antherus’s command, had been faithfully written down by the notaries and deposited in the Church? Had he forgotten what the Acts of Pope Stephen testified concerning his martyrdom? Could he have been unaware of what the Roman clergy had reported concerning the death of Xystus, what Cyprian had written, and what the Church read on the feast of Saint Laurence, who followed Xystus three days later? Could it have been hidden from him what the Canon of the Mass, composed in the third century, contained? These matters, unless I am mistaken, are too clear to be called into question by anyone.

## CHAPTER IV. Concerning the second Catalogue, which ends with the Acts of Felix IV of that name

I. The Catalogue was published from the manuscript codex of Queen Christina of Sweden and corrected from the same codex after the first edition; Clement was restored to his proper place.  
II. Dodwell’s quibbles on this subject are refuted, and all agree that the Catalogue was composed in the sixth century.  
III. In the manuscript codex, twelve pontiffs’ names are added after Felix IV, together with a chronological note. That these additions were made by some incompetent person is shown by the errors that have crept into this appendix.  
IV. The codex of Queen Christina of Sweden containing this appendix does not preserve the autograph Catalogue, but was written after the sixth century, around the pontificate of Paschal I.  
V. The Catalogue was copied from another, older codex; it is also contained in the Colbertine codex, written in the time of Charlemagne, as the Most Illustrious V.-C. Baluzius testified in a letter sent to me.  
VI. Readings are cited from both codices that differ from the Henschenian edition but nevertheless agree with one another.  
VII. From these observations it is inferred that both manuscript codices were copied from one and the same older codex.  
VIII. The Catalogue took from the older Catalogue the consuls whom it supplies at the beginning and end of the pontificates from Peter to Liberius.  
IX. The author of the second Catalogue took the Acts of the pontiffs partly from the older Catalogue and partly from elsewhere, as various examples demonstrate.  
X. The same is confirmed by other deeds of the pontiffs that he mentions.  
XI. The Acts of the martyrs used by the author of the Catalogue are older than the sixth century. He seems to have taken the ordinations and their number from a register of the Apostolic See that ended with Hormisdas.  
XII. That the author was a Roman, and perhaps director of the archive, is confirmed by many expressions in the Catalogue.

### 1.

The Catalogue with which we are presently concerned was first published in our own time from a codex of the library of Christina, Queen of the Swedes, by Godefridus Henschenius and Daniel Papebrochius in the prolegomena to volume I of April. From this edition I too, in the first edition of my *Illustrated Antiquity* in 1678, copied the portion extending to Sylvester, with the same fidelity with which those most distinguished men had brought it to light.

When I reached Rome, however, and suspected that some errors had crept into the edition, I asked the most wise queen for permission to inspect the codex and compare it with the printed text. In keeping with her benevolence toward me, she readily granted this request. I therefore had the manuscript codex in my possession for many months, carefully compared the Catalogue in question with the printed edition, and observed how greatly they differed from one another.

For not only are many words omitted from the printed edition that are found in the manuscript, but several pontiffs are also presented in the printed edition in the wrong order, whereas they are correctly read in the manuscript. The order of the first five pontiffs, as published in the first volume of April, provides evidence of this. There Peter is listed first, Linus second, Clement third, Cletus fourth, and Anacletus fifth. In the manuscript codex of Queen Christina of Sweden, however—which after her death, together with the other manuscripts of her library, was transferred to the Vatican—the order of the pontiffs is explicitly given as follows:

1. Peter, 2. Linus, 3. Cletus, 4. Clement, 5. Anacletus.

The Roman Church also lists those pontiffs in this order in the Canon of the Mass, when it mentions Linus, Cletus, and Clement. Cletus is placed between Linus and Clement, not after Clement.

### 2.

This correction of the Catalogue also refutes Henry Dodwell, who, in a separate dissertation on the early succession of the Roman pontiffs, chapter 9, section 1, complains that the author of the Catalogue altered the order and that those who followed the author of the second Catalogue placed the spurious Cletus before the genuine Clement. We have already shown that this is false from the manuscript codex itself, which we possess in the Alexandrian Library, and which we can show to anyone.

For the author of this Catalogue placed Cletus before Clement already in the time of Felix IV, under whom Dodwell admits that he wrote, in these words: “For in the year 530, according to the Catalogue, an uncertain author collected it under Justinian, at the end of Felix IV.” Pearson agrees in Dissertation I on the succession of the first Roman pontiffs, chapter 12, number 6, where he asserts that the Catalogue was written in the sixth century. Before Pearson, the distinguished men Papebrochius and Henschenius had also noted, before the preface to this Catalogue, that it was composed in the time of the emperor Justinian.

On this matter I agree with the learned men, since it can be deduced from the Catalogue itself that it was compiled under Justin and Justinian, whose reigns we assign indiscriminately to it in this work. For it ends with Felix IV, who died during the consulship of Orestes, in the fourth year of the emperor Justinian and in the year 530 of the common era.

### 3.

Nor should the fact that twelve other pontiffs’ names are added after Felix IV in the codex of Queen Christina of Sweden be an obstacle. They are added without any Acts, in the following manner:

57. Boniface sat for 2 years and 25 days.  
58. John sat for 2 years, 3 months, and 25 days.  
59. Felix sat for 4 years, 2 months, and 12 days.  
60. Boniface sat for 2 years and 27 days.  
61. John sat for 2 years, 3 months, and 5 days.  
62. Agapitus sat for 11 months and 17 days.  
63. Silverius sat for 1 year, 5 months, and 11 days.  
64. Vigilius sat for 16 years, 6 months, and 25 days.  
65. Pelagius sat for 4 years, 10 months, and 28 days.  
66. John sat for 12 years, 11 months, and 26 days.  
67. Benedict sat for 4 years.  
68. Pelagius sat for 10 years, 2 months, and 10 days.

From blessed Peter until now there are 444 years and six months, excluding the interval of the vacant pontificate.

These additions were plainly made by an unskilled hand after the time of the emperor Justinian, since neither the years correspond to the Catalogue nor is the order of the pontiffs observed in this appendix.

To begin with the final matter: here the three pontiffs Felix, Boniface, and John are divided into six pontificates, their names being repeated. This is evident from the fact that between Felix IV, with whom the Catalogue ends, and Silverius, whom the appendix lists as the seventh after Felix IV, only three pontiffs—Boniface II, John II, and Agapitus—appear in the genuine succession of pontiffs.

Three pontificates are therefore superfluous in the appendix, through an entirely inexcusable error. To this is added an erroneous chronological note, which we undertook to discuss in the second place. That note signifies that from blessed Peter to the pontificate of Pelagius II, excluding the time of the vacant see, 444 years are to be counted. Whether one counts from the beginning of Peter’s pontificate or from its end, this departs astonishingly from the true chronology.

For Pelagius II held the pontificate before Gregory the Great, toward the end of the sixth century, so that more than sixty years are missing from the computation. Not only did 444 years elapse from Peter until the time when that appendix was written, but even if we count the pontiffs from Peter’s death, which occurred in the year 68 of the common era, 522 years intervene before the pontificate of Gregory, which began in the year 590. After subtracting the interval attributable to the vacant see, more than five hundred years will still remain between the times of Peter and Pelagius II.

### 4.

Nor should anyone be surprised that such ugly errors are found in the appendix to this Catalogue. The codex of Queen Christina of Sweden, from which we published the Catalogue in print, does not contain the autograph of the Catalogue itself, but a transcript written many centuries later.

The codex containing this Catalogue includes, on page 1, a brief chronicle from the year 815, when Charlemagne died and his son Louis assumed the empire, down to the year 1000. I would consequently say that this codex was written in that year, except that from the year 918 to the year 1000 only the years themselves have been written down, and whatever historical event is noted appears to have been added by another hand. From this it may be conjectured that the author of the chronicle lived before the year 918.

Some chroniclers customarily set down years in manuscript codices in an uninterrupted series, including years after their own lifetime; if anything worthy of record occurred during their lifetime, they noted it in their own hand, whereas events that occurred after their death were left for posterity to record.

These observations could indeed allow us to judge the age of the manuscript codex, if it were certain that the aforesaid chronicle had been written by the same copyist who wrote the other material contained in the work. On this point, however, there is reasonable cause for doubt. As far as I can judge from the script, this chronicle, placed at the beginning of the codex, together with the account of the provinces and the genealogy immediately following it, was added by a more recent hand. The same is true of some material added at the end after the age of the codex.

The codex is in folio, square in format, and written in characters used in the age of Charlemagne. I would therefore readily believe that it was written in the period when the Catalogue of the Roman pontiffs found on page 10 was written. That Catalogue ends with Paschal I, beneath whom a chronological note is placed in these words:

“From the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ to the see of the blessed Pope Marcellinus there are 276 years and 8 months. From the apostolate already accomplished of Christ’s martyr Marcellinus to the time of the most glorious Lord King Charles, in the twenty-fifth year of his reign—that is, to the eighth day before the Kalends of April—there are 490 years and 13 months.”

The codex formerly belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden, now in the Alexandrian Library of the Vatican, therefore appears to have been written around this time—that is, shortly after the beginning of the ninth century. From it we published the second Catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, which the copyist of this codex transcribed from another, older codex.

### 5.

A firm argument for this truth was recently supplied by a letter from the distinguished Antonius Pagius, in which he reported that another manuscript copy of this Catalogue was found in the Colbertine Library:

“In the Colbertine Library,” he wrote, “there exists a Catalogue from which the most distinguished Baluzius believes that the Catalogue of Queen Christina of Sweden was copied.”

During the several occasions when I was in Paris, I had heard nothing about this codex, nor had I learned anything before Pagius’s letter, which he sent to me toward the end of the year 1680. Therefore, driven by a great desire to learn the truth, I wrote to Paris to the distinguished Joannes Harduinus, asking him to obtain from Baluzius both the variant readings of that codex and his judgment concerning the age in which it had been written.

The most distinguished Baluzius, with his customary humanity, supplied both, and Harduinus sent everything to me as quickly as possible. I therefore owe to their kindness—and the republic of letters owes—the knowledge of the Colbertine codex. This will contribute substantially to determining the source from which the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* drew the Acts of Peter’s successors, as we shall see in its proper place.

I therefore append the words of the distinguished Baluzius, in which he gives his judgment concerning the Colbertine manuscript codex and the variant readings of our Catalogue:

“Codex 1868 of the Colbertine Library, which is known to be similar to the one formerly held in the library of Queen Christina, was written under the rule of Charlemagne. The Catalogue of the Roman pontiffs begins with Saint Peter and bears this title: ‘Here are the pontiffs of the holy Roman Church of blessed Peter the Apostle.’ It ends with Hadrian I in this manner: ‘97. Hadrian sat for 23 years, 10 months, and 17 days.’ Afterward an old hand added: ‘98. Pope Leo.’”

These are Baluzius’s first words. They establish the antiquity of a manuscript codex containing a Catalogue similar, as I believe, to the one that we have said is preserved in the Alexandrian Library of the Vatican, which ends with Paschal I.

### 6.

Concerning the second Catalogue with which we are here dealing, Baluzius notes that various readings are found in the deeds of the pontiffs. With a few exceptions, we shall report them here, since I have observed that those variant readings concern the Henschenian edition rather than our manuscript codex.

Thus the distinguished scholar notes that in Peter one should read: “In the territory of the Triumphal Way, on the Aurelia, on the third day before the Kalends of July.” This is also how it is read in the Alexandrian-Vatican manuscript codex, although the Henschenian edition has: “Between the Zetarian and Triumphal Ways, on the third day before the Kalends of June.”

Baluzius next notes from his own codex: “Cletus is placed before Clement.” The Alexandrian-Vatican codex has the same reading, although the Henschenian edition, I do not know for what reason or on what basis, places Cletus after Clement.

Baluzius further notes from the Colbertine codex: “In Victor I read: ‘with Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, concerning the moon.’” The same is read in the codex of Queen Christina of Sweden, although the Henschenian edition places “of Caesarea” instead of “of Alexandria,” and Theophilus was bishop not of Alexandria but of Caesarea.

Baluzius next gives from the Colbertine codex, under Pope Lucius: “He was beheaded on the sixth day before the Nones of March.” The same is found in the Alexandrian codex, although the Henschenian edition reads: “on the third day before the Nones of March.”

Again, from the Colbertine codex, Baluzius reads under Damasus: “He sat for 17 years, 3 months, and 11 days. He lived in the time of Julian and built two libraries.” The same is read in our codex, although the Henschenian edition omits the words “He lived in the time of Julian.”

Finally, under Pope Felix, Baluzius reads from his own codex: “The episcopate was vacant for one day.” The same is found in ours, although the Henschenian edition has: “The episcopate was vacant for three days.” With these words Henschenius brings the Catalogue to an end. In our manuscript codex, however, from which he arranged for the Catalogue to be copied, the names of the twelve pontiffs follow, together with the note concerning the 444 years that had elapsed from blessed Peter until that time. The same names and note follow in the Colbertine codex, as the distinguished Baluzius testifies in the variant readings he sent to me.

### 7.

From these facts it is plainly evident that both manuscript codices—the Colbertine and the Alexandrian-Vatican—present exactly the same Catalogue. Either the second was copied from the first, as Pagius reported, or both codices were taken from another, older one. The latter could easily have happened, since both the Colbertine and the Alexandrian-Vatican codices are extremely old, written in Carolingian characters, and contain some variant readings, although very few, from one another.

Thus the Colbertine reads under Peter, “Territory” and “the Aurelia,” where the Alexandrian-Vatican has “Terretory” and “the Aurilia.” Under Telesphorus the Colbertine has: “And the episcopate was vacant for seven days,” whereas the Alexandrian-Vatican has “six days.” Under Hyginus the Colbertine has: “Seven bishops in various places,” while the Alexandrian-Vatican has “six in various places.” Under Anicetus the Colbertine has “in various places, nine”; the Vatican has “in various places, eight.” Likewise, the first has “the episcopate was vacant for seven days,” the second “six days.”

Under Zephyrinus the Colbertine has: “Episcopus interest, tantum clericus sustinerit” (“Let the bishop be present; let a cleric alone support [him]”), while the Alexandrian-Vatican has: “Episcopo interest, tantum Clerus sustineret” (“Let [one] be present to the bishop; let the clergy support [him]”).

These and other variant readings readily prove that older codices existed from which the Colbertine and Alexandrian-Vatican Catalogues were copied, and that all of them derived their origin from the autograph written under the emperor Justinian after the death of Felix IV.

We have shown that the addition of the names of twelve pontiffs after Felix, together with the years, months, and days during which they sat, in both the Colbertine and Alexandrian-Vatican manuscripts was made by some incompetent copyist. We think that this happened in the time of Pelagius II, when that copyist, transcribing the Catalogue from the autograph, added the pontiffs after Felix and appended the erroneous chronological note concerning the 444 years from Peter to Pelagius II, who obtained the pontificate in the year 577.

So much, then, for the manuscript codices from which the Catalogue is published. We must now say a little about the contents of the Catalogue.

### 8.

This Catalogue supplies the consuls under whom each pontiff was created and died, beginning with Peter, prince of the Apostles and first Roman pontiff, and continuing to Liberius, with whom the earlier Catalogue ends. The author of the second Catalogue copied the names of the consuls from the earlier Catalogue up to that point, as is proved chiefly in three ways.

First, the names of the consuls are the same everywhere. Second, the errors concerning the names of the consuls are nearly identical in both. Third, after Liberius the author placed no consuls beside the succeeding pontiffs, because, when the earlier Catalogue failed, he had no source from which to obtain information about the consuls.

Thus in this second Catalogue the consular information fails from Liberius down to the time of John I and Felix IV. The author gives the dates of those two pontiffs individually because he lived and wrote under them; consequently he also ends the Catalogue with them.

### 9.

It appears that the author of the second Catalogue took not only the names of the consuls but also some of the Acts of the pontiffs from the first Catalogue, though he nevertheless considered himself free at times to disregard them and report Acts from elsewhere.

Thus, although the first Catalogue says of Peter: “He suffered with Paul on the third day before the Kalends of July, under the consuls named above, while Nero was emperor,” and although the author of the second Catalogue has from the earlier one: “Here he is crowned with martyrdom together with Paul,” he nevertheless adds:

“He was also buried on the Aurelia, in the temple of Apollo, near the place where he was crucified, near the Neronian palace in the Vatican, between the Zetarian and Triumphal Ways, on the third day before the Kalends of June.”

These details were taken from elsewhere and contain an error concerning the Kalends of June, since one should read “the third day before the Kalends of July.”

The same is proved by the Acts that the first Catalogue reports under Pius in these words:

“Under his episcopate his brother Hermes wrote a book containing the command that the angel gave him when he came to him in the guise of a shepherd.”

The author of the second Catalogue copied these words in full, but added:

“And he commanded him that holy Easter should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day.”

This too he took from elsewhere.

It is also confirmed by what the first Catalogue presents under Pontian:

“At that time Pontian, the bishop, and Hippolytus, the presbyter, were deported as exiles to the harmful island of Sardinia, under the consulship of Severus and Quintianus. On that same island he was deprived of his belt on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, and Anterus was ordained in his place on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, under the consuls named above.”

The author of the second Catalogue partly copied this, partly reported it in other words, and partly omitted it. For under Pontian he has:

“At that time Pontian the bishop and Hippolytus the presbyter were deported into exile by Alexander to the island of Sardinia, called Bucina, under the consulship of Severus and Quintianus. On that island, afflicted and tormented with blows, he died on the third day before the Kalends of November.”

Although most of this was copied from the earlier Catalogue, the name of the emperor Alexander and the manner in which he suffered martyrdom have been added; the name of the place has also been changed, and the eleventh day before the Kalends of December has been changed to the third day before the Kalends of November.

Moreover, the author of the second Catalogue makes no mention of Anterus under Pontian. It is therefore readily apparent that the author of the second Catalogue did copy some Acts from the older Catalogue, but did not follow it in every respect; he also took material from elsewhere.

### 10.

These observations can be confirmed by what the author of the first Catalogue has under the supreme pontiffs Fabian, Cornelius, and Lucius. For the author of the second Catalogue partly copied and partly omitted what the first Catalogue reports under Fabian. What the first Catalogue presents under Cornelius, the second Catalogue omitted entirely and did not report even a word of it. What the author of the first Catalogue reports under Lucius, the author of the second copied almost entirely word for word, as will be plainly evident to anyone who compares the two Catalogues.

In addition to these Acts, the older Catalogue has under Marcellinus:

“At that time there was a persecution, and the episcopate was vacant for 7 years, 6 months, and 25 days.”

The second Catalogue reports this as follows:

“At that time there was a great persecution . . . and the episcopate was vacant for six years, six months, and twenty-five days, while Diocletian was persecuting the Christians.”

In these words, the material concerning the persecution was copied from the earlier Catalogue; the material concerning the years of the vacant see was altered; and the persecutor’s name was taken from elsewhere.

Finally, some Acts follow under Julius I. The author of the earlier Catalogue lists his sacred buildings, but not a word of them appears in the second Catalogue.

From the Acts themselves, therefore, we believe it has been abundantly confirmed what we undertook to prove: that the author of the second Catalogue copied some Acts from the earlier Catalogue, but considered himself free at times to omit them and take Acts from elsewhere, reporting very many such materials under the individual pontiffs.

### 11.

For he introduces many matters taken from ancient Acts of the saints. Although some of them may not have been written down in the very periods in which the events occurred, all are nevertheless older than the sixth century, and for the most part they appear to have been derived from the proconsular records of the martyrs and from genuine Acts of the saints.

This should be said of what the author of this Catalogue transmits under Alexander I concerning Eventius and Theodulus; of what he reports under Urban concerning Valerian, the husband of Saint Cecilia; of what he relates under Cornelius concerning blessed Lucina; and of what he narrates under Xystus concerning blessed Laurence, whose Acts of martyrdom were found in the time of Saint Ambrose.

The author presents not only Acts of martyrs but also statutes issued for the discipline of the Church under the individual pontiffs. Thus under Linus he reports that Linus decreed that a woman should enter the church with her head covered; under Xystus, that he established that sacred ministries should not be touched except by ministers; under Anicetus, that he ordered that a cleric should not grow his hair long; under Victor, that he established that Easter should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day; under Lucius, that he commanded that in every place two presbyters and three deacons should not abandon the bishop; and similarly under the other pontiffs.

It would be too long to enumerate them individually, and they can readily be seen in the Catalogue itself. I shall add only this: under each pontiff it reports how many ordinations he performed and how many bishops, priests, and deacons he consecrated.

Beginning with Clement I, it reports:

“He performed three ordinations: 10 priests, 2 deacons, and 5 bishops in various places.”

Under Evaristus:

“He performed four ordinations: 17 priests, 9 deacons, and 15 bishops in various places.”

And so under the other pontiffs down to Hormisdas. Under him the author does not note the number of ordinations, deacons, priests, or bishops, but simply reports:

“He performed ordinations: priests and bishops in various places.”

Under John, the successor of Hormisdas:

“He performed ordinations in various places.”

Under Felix, John’s successor, with whom the Catalogue ends, he again gives the number in these words:

“He performed two ordinations: 55 priests, 4 deacons, and 29 bishops in various places.”

From this I infer that the author took his information about the ordinations from some register or record of the Roman Church written before the time of Hormisdas. He noted nothing under Hormisdas or John, but only under Felix IV, because once the register or record ended, he had no other information on this subject than what had reached his ears during the time of Felix IV, under whom he was living.

### 12.

This is sufficient concerning the second Catalogue. Since we shall observe many other matters in the following chapters, it remains here to inquire by what author and in what place this Catalogue was composed.

I know nothing about the author’s name, since the Catalogue was written in the sixth century, and no one among the ancients is remembered as having collected the Acts of the Roman pontiffs at that time. Yet, as seems to be inferred from the Acts themselves, the author flourished at Rome and was perhaps placed in charge of the Apostolic Archive.

That he wrote at Rome is indicated by his extensive knowledge of the City and the Roman territory. He knew all the cemeteries, even those situated at a very great distance from the City; all the tombs of the martyrs, even those located in crypts and caves; all the churches and districts of the City; all the relics and titles; all the roads and the distances between them; and, finally, everything else.

That he may have been director of the Apostolic Archive seems to be inferred from what he says about Leo the Great:

“He wrote many letters setting forth the correct Catholic faith, which are today kept in the archive of the Roman Church.”

The same is suggested by the Acts of Hormisdas, in which the author reports that, at Justin’s command, all the bishops signed a booklet of the Catholic faith:

“The text of this booklet,” he says, “is kept today in the archive.”

How could the author have cited the Roman archive unless he had seen it and perhaps been placed in charge of it? What he consistently asserts concerning the decrees of the individual pontiffs, their deeds, and the ordinations of bishops, presbyters, and deacons clearly indicates that he took all these things from the archival registers. Thus, even if he was not the librarian of the Apostolic See, he must be regarded as having had access to the pontifical library.

# CHAPTER V. Concerning the *Book of the Pontiffs*

I. The *Book of the Pontiffs* was first inserted by Peter Crabbe into the volumes of the Councils; it was subsequently cited frequently by Baronius in his *Annals*, and was finally printed in its entirety at Mainz in 1602.  
II. After the Mainz edition there appeared the Paris edition of Annibal Fabrottus, who appended variant readings from five manuscript codices, two of which are preserved in the libraries of Germany and three in the libraries of Gaul.  
III. The work, which Annibal Fabrottus admits that he left uncorrected, was undertaken for correction by Lucas Holstenius from Vatican, royal, Medicean, Cassinese, and Farnesian codices, the last of all being the most ancient; his words concerning the manuscript codices he used are cited.  
IV. From the Farnesian codex a previously unpublished fragment of the life of Sergius II is cited, and variant readings from Holstenius’s autograph are presented.  
V. Several pious donations made to the basilicas of the City have been added to the *Book of the Pontiffs*.  
VI. Several Acts of martyrs are also included. Although some of them may have been taken from doubtful records, it is nevertheless certain that they existed from an earlier age and sometimes from the earliest centuries of the Church.  
VII. The Acts of the pontiffs from the Apostle Peter to Pope Constantine are shorter; from Constantine to Stephen VI they are more extensive, so that they encompass almost the whole of ecclesiastical history.

### 1.

After treating the two older Catalogues of the Roman pontiffs, we must now discuss the *Book of the Pontiffs*. The first person who seems to have extracted it from manuscript codices was Peter Crabbe, who inserted it into his Cologne edition of the Councils of 1538 under this title:

*Book of the Pontiffs, from Pope Peter to Pope Nicholas I, in which their deeds are described: those of the first pontiffs by Pope Damasus, and those of the others by other ancient and trustworthy authors.*

He cites the lives of the first pontiffs, from Peter to Liberius, from the *Book of the Pontiffs of Damasus*; those of the others, from Damasus to Leo III, he cites from the *Book of the Pontiffs*.

Following in his footsteps, Laurentius Surius and the compilers of the Councils who followed Surius inserted the lives of the Roman pontiffs sporadically into the collection of the Councils. Baronius likewise inserted many fragments of the *Book of the Pontiffs* into his *Annals*. Since he frequently corrected the readings of this book from manuscript codices, he gave the author of the preface placed before the Mainz edition of the book, printed by Johann Albin and published in 1602, an opportunity to assert:

“The variant readings have been taken either from the two volumes of the Councils in the Surian edition or from Baronius’s *Annals*, in which the words of Anastasius are cited throughout under the individual pontiffs, with only a few omissions.”

He mentions Anastasius because he had published the *Book of the Pontiffs* under that name, with this title prefixed:

*The History of Anastasius, Librarian of the Holy Roman Church, concerning the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs, from the Apostle Peter to Nicholas I, never before printed.*

Then follow the life of Hadrian II and that of Stephen IV, by William the Librarian, from the library of Marcus Welser, a leading man of the Augsburg commonwealth.

### 2.

If anyone asks why the Mainz edition of 1602 is called the first edition of this *Book of the Pontiffs*, when Crabbe had published it so many years earlier in his Cologne edition of the Councils, the answer is easy: Crabbe had published this *Book of the Pontiffs* neither in its entirety nor as one continuous text; it appeared from the manuscript codex of Marcus Welser, a leading man of the Augsburg commonwealth, with the name of the author added, who is supposed to have been Anastasius the Librarian.

Under that name Annibal Fabrottus published the same *Book of the Pontiffs* in 1648 in folio, from the royal press, appending to the work most of the variant readings that he had taken from various manuscript codices.

First he used two manuscript codices belonging to Marquard Freher, one of which ends with Leo IV and the other with Stephen VI. He then added further variant readings from two codices, namely the royal codex and the Mazarin codex. The latter bears this title:

*Here begins the succession of the Roman pontiffs who have sat in the see of blessed Peter the Apostle, from him down to the present time.*

Among other things, from these two codices he reports under Sylvester a fairly extensive fragment of the Donation of Constantine, which I have so far found in no other codices of the *Book of the Pontiffs*. I therefore conjectured that the book had been interpolated in those codices and that they had been written by a more recent hand.

I was confirmed in this judgment by what Annibal Fabrottus noted near the end of these readings from the lives of the Roman pontiffs, which they contain down to Martin V. The Thuanus codex is therefore older; he appended its variant readings to those mentioned above, with this title for the codex:

*Here begins the episcopal book, containing the Acts of the blessed pontiffs of the City of Rome.*

It is mutilated and ends with Stephen IV, as Annibal Fabrottus admits at the end. At the beginning of the works of Anastasius he had prefaced the statement that this *Book of the Pontiffs* was riddled with errors:

“I do not deny that this author is riddled with errors,” he says, “and perhaps it would have been preferable for him to be handled only by a few people rather than to appear again with so many errors. But it is altogether better to enjoy even uncorrected authors than to lack them entirely. Meanwhile, until a better edition can be prepared, we have added variant readings excerpted from three old codices, with the help of which a more accurate edition can undoubtedly be produced.

“We used the royal codex and the Mazarin codex, by which Gabriel Naudé, a man of outstanding learning, enriched the library of the most eminent cardinal. Both, however, seem to have descended from the same exemplar, since they differ from one another in only a few places. I also compared them with the Thuanus codex, certainly a most ancient one, but in many places insufficiently corrected because of the ignorance of its scribal copyist.”

### 3

Since it clearly appears from the foregoing words of Annibal Fabrottus that editions of the *Liber Pontificalis* had remained filled with errors down to his own time, and that a better edition could be prepared from manuscript codices, this task had been undertaken by a most learned man, my former predecessor, Lucas Holstenius. He collated Anastasius’s history, *On the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, in the Mainz edition with the most distinguished manuscripts in all Italy, so that he might publish it in a more correct and emended form.

I deposited Holstenius’s autograph, purchased from Moroni’s books, in the Vatican Library. On its first folio, Holstenius’s own hand records the following:

> “Concerning the manuscript codices with which we collated Anastasius. The readings marked in ink in the margin from the beginning of the book through page 53 are variant readings from a Vatican manuscript codex, formerly belonging to the sacred monastery of Cassino, or from Mombritius’s collection, or also from the Collection of Canons of Anselm of Lucca, a manuscript preserved in the library of the most eminent Cardinal Barberini. The readings marked in vermilion from the beginning through the same page 53 are variant readings from an excellent Florentine manuscript codex, from the library of the convent of St. Mark.

> “From page 54 onward begin the collations of the Farnesian manuscript, written in capital letters; I believe that nothing older exists in this class, and the codex was undoubtedly written before Anastasius was born, or certainly during the time in which Anastasius himself lived. Since the collations of the Farnesian codex are written in vermilion through page 63—that is, through Boniface IV—in order to distinguish the readings of the different codices, from page 54 through page 64 I marked the collations of the Florentine codex in ink. From page 63 through page 72 … to the *Life of St. Eugene*, the Farnesian collations are marked in ink and the Florentine in vermilion.

> “Again, from page 72 through page 107, where the *Life of Pope Zacharias* begins, the Farnesian readings are marked in vermilion and the Florentine collated in ink. On page 107 the *Life of Zacharias* is missing from the Farnesian codex; the collations from the Florentine codex are marked in vermilion through page 115, where the Farnesian begins again. From there the Florentine readings are again marked in ink through page 136, and thereafter in red through the middle of page 138. From that point they are again marked in ink through the beginning of page 143, for from there through page 158 the readings of the Florentine codex are marked in red; there the codex ends in the *Life of Hadrian*.

> “I subsequently obtained another, extremely ancient Lombard manuscript codex from the same library of the convent of St. Mark, much older than the former. I marked its readings in ink. Where it agrees with the Farnesian and Florentine codices, I underlined the readings of those codices with a black line, by which the agreement of this excellent codex is indicated; but where it has something distinctive, I marked it in ink, adding the notation ‘Fl. 2,’ that is, ‘Florentine codex 2.’

> “This codex ends with Leo II, on page 80. Moreover, it is mutilated from page 47 through page 58. Codex Vaticanus 5269 agrees with this Florentine codex 2 in almost everything; it ends with Gregory II. The notation for this codex is ‘Vaticanus minor,’ or ‘V. M.’”

### 4

I have faithfully reproduced what Lucas Holstenius recorded at the beginning. From this everyone can see what an immense labor a man worthy of eternal remembrance had begun, using the excellent codices of the Vatican, Royal, Florentine library of St. Mark, Cassinese, and Farnesian libraries; prevented by death, he left it unfinished for us.

Therefore, so that such great labor may not perish, after this dissertation we shall publish the *Liber Pontificalis* from blessed Peter through Felix IV, leaving the rest to those who devote themselves to publishing the complete *Liber Pontificalis*. For there are many passages after Felix IV that can contribute to correcting that work.

There are also certain fragments in the *Life of Sergius II*, which Holstenius reproduced at the end from the most ancient Farnesian codex. As a specimen, we reproduce the following. In the *Life of Sergius II*, after the words:

> “Which none of the pontiffs, throughout so many cycles of years, had thought to bring to such a degree of splendor.”

the Farnesian manuscript continues:

> “This most holy prelate, observing the structure called the Jovia, which, after the passage of many years, had been destroyed and stood full of ruins, restored it anew, like a kind and pious shepherd; and water shone forth in such abundance that it almost satisfied the whole city. In his time the river called the Tiber left its channel and spread across the plains. It likewise swelled with a great inundation of waters in the eighth indiction, on the twenty-second day of November, which was observed as the Saturday of the Nativity of St. Cecilia the martyr, and entered the city of Rome through the postern called St. Agatha at the first hour of the day.

> “Meanwhile, in some places it rose above the walls of the City and entered the church of Blessed Lawrence, called Lucina’s; from there it entered the church of the Blessed Ever-Virgin, Mother of God, situated on the Via Lata; and from there it passed to Blessed Mark. It spread through the streets, devastated the fields, and uprooted the shrubs. At that hour of the night the water subsided, and the river returned to its own channel,” etc.

### 5

From these examples it is clear how highly those variant readings and fragments extracted by Lucas Holstenius from manuscript codices ought to be valued. Since publishing everything does not at all belong to our purpose, we shall refrain from reviewing the remainder and, returning to the *Liber Pontificalis* itself, shall note several matters more directly relevant to our subject.

First of all, we consider it worthy of notice that the *Liber Pontificalis* contains many additional materials beyond the deeds of the pontiffs presented in the second catalogue, as can be seen, among other places, in the accounts of the pontiffs Clement, Cornelius, and Marcellus. The additions under Sylvester, however, show much more clearly what we have undertaken to prove. For the *Acts of St. Sylvester* are three times more extensive than those presented by the second catalogue. They consist chiefly of pious donations made by Constantine for the churches of the City and its suburban territory.

After Sylvester, the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* frequently added what was offered by the Roman pontiffs to the churches and basilicas of the City. Thus in the accounts of Pope Damasus, Innocent, Boniface I, Sixtus III, Leo I, Hilary, Simplicius, Symmachus, and the remaining pontiffs and their successors, as anyone can easily see from the *Liber Pontificalis* itself.

### 6

Besides donations, the *Liber Pontificalis* contains numerous acts of martyrs. Although some of them may be spurious, they nevertheless appear to have been composed in antiquity and during the earliest centuries of the Church.

Thus, in the account of Clement, his letter to James is cited. Although it is not Clement’s, it was attributed to him before the time of Eusebius. In the account of Marcellinus, mention is made of his lapse and repentance. Although these materials were taken from the ancient acts of the Council of Sinvessa, those acts themselves were composed before the age of Isidore Mercator.

In the account of Eusebius, mention is made of the discovery of the holy cross through the agency of the Jew Cyriacus. Although this was taken from acts rejected by Pope Gelasius, it is nevertheless older than the time of Gelasius.

A few other matters are related concerning the martyrdoms of pontiffs. Although they may have been excerpted from interpolated acts, the acts themselves will nevertheless always be found to have been composed by authors of an earlier age, as with the material concerning the acts of Pontius and several other martyrs cited above.

All the remaining material is drawn either from genuine and wholly uninterpolated acts of martyrs, from the public records of the notaries of the Apostolic See, or from the works of approved writers.

### 7

I set aside the acts themselves of the Roman pontiffs, in which the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* usually dispatches his account briefly from the apostle Peter through Pope Constantine. From Pope Constantine through Stephen VI, however, he is so expansive that it may rightly be said that he has included the whole of ecclesiastical history in the lives of these pontiffs.

For he presents whatever was done at Rome, in Italy, throughout Europe, and in the East itself in ecclesiastical affairs by the emperors. Thus, under Constantine, he relates what occurred at Constantinople. Under Justinian and Philippicus, and in the account of Gregory II, he relates what was done against the Agarenes, in Spain by the Gauls, and at Constantinople by the emperor Leo.

He describes the invasions of the Lombards, the wars of the Franks on behalf of the Church, and many other matters that can scarcely be found elsewhere described with such accuracy and clarity.

He ends with Stephen VI, with these words: “that they ought to seek help from heaven against the impending scourge, and soon joyful …” The rest is missing. Hence it is clear that this *Life* is mutilated and that something is missing from the *Liber Pontificalis* which could be supplied from a more complete exemplar.

# CHAPTER VI  
## Whether the *Liber Pontificalis* Was Written by Pope Damasus

**I.** Two letters, one from Pope Damasus and one from the presbyter Jerome, are placed before the *Liber Pontificalis* in manuscript codices. Hence some attribute the *Liber Pontificalis* to Pope Damasus.

**II.** That Damasus was not the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* is demonstrated by the authority of St. Jerome and confirmed by all the testimonies of writers who cited the *Liber Pontificalis* after Bede without any mention of Damasus.

**III.** Passages cited from the deeds of Damasus by St. Anselm of Lucca and Cardinal Deusdedit are brought forward. Yet these passages were taken not from the *Liber Pontificalis* attributed to Pope Damasus, but from the special deeds of Damasus published by Mombritius, and they have no bearing on the present question.

**IV.** Nor could the Vatican manuscript codices containing the *Liber Pontificalis* have Damasus as their author, since they contain the lives of several successors of Damasus. Accordingly, the scribe of the third codex expressly noted that Damasus could have written only up to his own time.

**V.** The opinion of Peter Lambecius is presented: that the earlier part of the *Liber Pontificalis* was written by notaries of the Apostolic See at different times but in the same style, and that Damasus found it in the Vatican records and transmitted it to Jerome.

**VI.** Lambecius’s opinion is examined, and it is shown that the earlier part of the *Liber Pontificalis* cannot be attributed to the notaries of the Apostolic See as its authors.

**VII.** Nor was it approved by Pope Damasus, as is shown by the numerous errors with which it abounds and by the crudeness and uniformity of its style, from Peter through those who occupied the see in the seventh century.

### 1

Since in the preceding chapter we demonstrated that the earlier catalogue is not the one mentioned in the letters of Jerome and Pope Damasus, it must now be investigated whether those letters perhaps concern the *Liber Pontificalis*. The reason for doubt is supplied by many manuscript codices in which these two letters are placed before the *Liber Pontificalis*.

Thus, in Book II of his *Commentaries*, Lambecius reports that, under number 277, there is preserved in the Imperial Library:

> “A very old parchment volume, of great value, in quarto, containing the history of the Roman pontiffs, which is commonly attributed to Anastasius the Librarian but which in this and four other manuscript codices of the Imperial Library is attributed to St. Damasus the pope, because of the letters placed before it in the manner of a preface. One of these begins: ‘To the most blessed Pope Damasus, Jerome. Our humility beseeches the glory of your holiness.’ The second begins: ‘Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome, to Jerome. The Church rejoices, satisfied from your fountain.’

> “Because of these two letters,” Lambecius continues in the same place, “which are prefixed not only in the manuscripts already mentioned of the most august Imperial Library but also in certain manuscript codices of other distinguished libraries, to this history of the lives of the Roman pontiffs, some have believed that St. Damasus himself was the author of all the lives contained in that work, from St. Peter, prince of the apostles, through St. Damasus.”

### 2

Although Lambecius proposes this opinion of certain persons, he correctly observes that many contradict it, both for other reasons and especially because St. Jerome, when listing the works of Pope Damasus in his book *On Illustrious Men of the Church*, makes no mention of the *Liber Pontificalis*:

> “Damasus,” he says, “bishop of the city of Rome, possessed an elegant talent for composing verse. He published many brief works in heroic meter and died almost eighty years old under the emperor Theodosius.”

Moreover, no one among all those who cited the *Liber Pontificalis* from the time of the Venerable Bede through the later centuries attributed it to Damasus.

Leaving aside the intervening period between Pope Damasus and the Venerable Bede, during which no mention of the *Liber Pontificalis* is found in any writer, Bede was, so far as I know, the first human being to cite it. In his *Martyrology*, under the eighth day before the Ides of August, he cites certain material concerning the death of Sixtus from the *Gesta Pontificalia*, but attributes it neither to Damasus nor to any particular author.

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, who wrote in the ninth century, mentions this book in Letter 28 to Nicholas I under the title *Liber Episcopalis*, but attributes it to no author whatsoever.

The presbyter Rodulphus, who lived at the same time as Hincmar of Rheims, cited certain material concerning the relics of the saints from the *Gesta Pontificalia* in the *Life of Abbot Rabanus*, published by Browerus in Book III of the *Fuldensian Antiquities*; yet he nowhere said that this material should be attributed to Damasus.

St. Ivo, bishop of Chartres, frequently cites the *Liber Pontificalis* in Part IV of the *Decree*, but nowhere indicates that it was written by Damasus as its author. The title of chapter 94 is:

> “Concerning the books of Gelasius, from the *Liber Pontificalis*.”

The title of chapter 124 is:

> “Likewise, concerning the confirmation of the Sixth Synod, from the *Liber Pontificalis*.”

Romualdus, whom Lucas Holstenius calls a presbyter and others call bishop of Salerno, simply calls this book the *Pontifical* in his history, preserved in manuscript at Rome:

> “As it is read,” he says on page 80, “in the *Pontifical*.”

Finally, Cardinal Laborans, in his compilation of decrees—which has not yet been published and is preserved in the archive of the Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles in Rome, over which I have been appointed—mentions this book twice and gives it the title *Gesta Pontificalia*. In Part II, chapter 10, he cites the *Gesta Pontificalia*; and in Part XI, chapter 6, he cites “from the *Acts of the Roman Pontiffs*: Agatho, a Sicilian by nationality,” and so forth.

Here it can be seen that Cardinal Laborans attributed to no author the book containing the *Acts of the Roman Pontiffs*.

### 3

For some time I believed that these materials had been attributed to Pope Damasus by St. Anselm of Lucca, because Book III of the *Decree*, preserved in manuscript in the Barberini Library, reads:

> “Concerning Pope Liberius and his admonition: from the deeds of Pope Damasus, title 120. The emperor Constantius became extremely angry with Liberius and ordered him to live outside the city. He lived three miles from the city of Rome, like an exile, in a cemetery [lacuna] on the Salarian Way. When Easter Day arrived, he summoned all the Roman presbyters and deacons, sat in that same cemetery, and said: ‘Do not be afraid, because although I do not live with you in the city, you have as our representative our brother and fellow presbyter Damasus, whose testimony you have given to me.’”

A little later it continues:

> “Holy lords and fellow presbyters, do not concern yourselves with tomorrow, for thus our teacher said.”

Cardinal Deusdedit has exactly the same material in the manuscript *Collection* now called that of Victor III, of which, as I believe, the only copy is preserved in the Vatican Library. In Book II, chapter 26, when the compiler had written in the margin “from the deeds of Pope Damasus,” he gives the text in the same words as Anselm of Lucca:

> “The emperor Constantius was extremely angry with Liberius and ordered him to live outside the city,” etc.

When I first read these passages, I believed that the two writers were citing testimony from the *Liber Pontificalis* and that they attributed that book to Pope Damasus. But when I could find the cited testimony nowhere in the *Liber Pontificalis*, I recognized my error and learned that they were citing here not the *Liber Pontificalis*, but the *Life*, or deeds, of Pope Damasus, which Mombritius published from ancient manuscript codices.

Thus blessed Anselm did not attribute the deeds of the Roman pontiffs to Pope Damasus, nor did he cite the *Liber Pontificalis* there. This is made clear by title 121:

> “Concerning the exile of Pope Liberius and Felix, ordained on his advice, from the *Pontifical*.”

The testimony that he presents on this subject is found in the *Liber Pontificalis*. As the titles themselves show, he distinguishes that book from the deeds of Damasus. Cardinal Deusdedit likewise made the distinction: in Book II, number 75, he cites several decrees of the pontiffs from the Roman *Pontifical*, all of which are found in the *Liber Pontificalis*, and he emphatically does not attribute that book to Damasus.

### 4

Since it is sufficiently established from the foregoing that ancient writers by no means attributed the *Liber Pontificalis* to Pope Damasus, we must now examine the manuscript codices of that same book to see whether they identify Damasus as its author.

Three copies of this book are found in the Vatican Library. One of them is preserved under number 3762. After the letters of Damasus and Jerome cited above have been presented on folio 1, the following title is appended:

> “In the name of the Lord begins the series of the Roman pontiffs who have occupied the see of Blessed Peter the apostle, from him himself up to the present time.”

This copy presents the lives through Honorius III, who died in the year 1131. Thus it contains pontiffs who occupied the see for 700 years after the death of Damasus, and consequently Damasus cannot possibly be the author of this *Liber Pontificalis*.

The second copy, numbered 5269, on page 49, after the letters mentioned above, gives the catalogue of the Roman pontiffs from Peter through Gregory II and appends their lives without any title. The scribe had understood very well that Damasus could not have been the author of this *Liber Pontificalis*, which adds so many pontiffs from the death of Damasus through Gregory II.

The third copy, numbered 3763, continues the lives of the Roman pontiffs from Peter through Martin V. On its first folio it does indeed place the two aforementioned letters, but with this title prefixed to them:

> “This book is entitled ‘Damasus, On the Deeds of the Pontiffs.’ But since he could have written only up to his own time, what has been added belongs to another author, whose name I do not know.”

The words of the codex deserve attention. Although its author expressly affirms that the *Liber Pontificalis*, which contains the lives of the Roman pontiffs from Damasus through Martin V, cannot be attributed to Pope Damasus, he nevertheless seems to indicate that the lives of the pontiffs from St. Peter through Liberius, the predecessor of Damasus, were written by Damasus himself.

Peter Lambecius adopted this opinion to some extent in Book II, chapter 8, of his *Commentaries on the Imperial Library*, where, under number 277, he explains his view in the following words:

### 5

> “It seems probable to me,” he says, “that the first origin of this history of the lives of the Roman pontiffs is not merely much older than St. Damasus, but must also be derived from and traced back to the original establishment of the notaries of the Holy Apostolic See by St. Pope Clement.

> “Since the principal duty of these notaries was carefully and diligently to investigate the deeds of the holy martyrs and to deposit their careful records in the Church, at the same time they necessarily began to write the lives of the Roman pontiffs in the form of a simple catalogue, in which the name, homeland, father, time of pontificate, ordinations, constitutions, death, burial, and termination of each episcopate up to the succession of a new pontiff would be briefly indicated.

> “After the freedom of the Christian Church was proclaimed by the emperor Constantine the Great, just as the splendor and wealth of the Roman Church gradually increased, so that catalogue also became more extensive and elaborate. For, besides the matters already described, there began to be inserted into it, as into a kind of register, the construction, restoration, and adornment of churches and other sacred places, together with a detailed inventory of all sacred furnishings and of all donations, both movable and immovable, along with their revenues.

> “This catalogue, although composed at different times and by different authors, was nevertheless everywhere similar to itself in arrangement and style, as commonly happens in the continuation of other official records. It lay hidden in storage, in the record office or archive of the Vatican Basilica of St. Peter, prince of the apostles, until the pontificate of St. Damasus.

> “When St. Jerome, in the letter quoted above, asked him to relate to him the deeds of the Roman pontiffs from St. Peter through his own time, Damasus had that ancient pontifical history copied from the Vatican records and sent from Rome to Jerusalem. For this reason, in his reply to St. Jerome’s letter, he does not call it his own work but the work of the Apostolic See.

> “For these words must truly be interpreted in this way: ‘Nevertheless, what was done, and what we were able to find as the work of our see, we have gladly sent to your charity.’

> “Therefore St. Damasus himself did not compose that history of the Roman pontiffs. Rather, he merely made public and shared with St. Jerome the work of the Holy Apostolic See, which had gradually been assembled from the records of different persons beginning in the time of St. Clement the First.”

### 6

There are several points in this opinion of Lambecius that deserve careful examination, so that the authorship of the *Liber Pontificalis* may be made perfectly clear.

Although Lambecius correctly asserts that the first origin of the history of the lives of the Roman pontiffs is much older than St. Damasus and must be derived from and traced back to the establishment of the notaries of the Holy Apostolic See, I cannot prove what he adds in these words:

> “Since the principal duty of these notaries was carefully and diligently to investigate the deeds of the holy martyrs and to deposit their careful records in the Church, at the same time they necessarily began to write the lives of the Roman pontiffs in the form of a simple catalogue, in which the name, homeland, father, time of pontificate, ordinations, constitutions, death, burial, and termination of each episcopate up to the succession of a new pontiff would be briefly indicated.”

Since, as Lambecius admits, the principal duty of these notaries was carefully and diligently to investigate the deeds of the holy martyrs and to deposit their careful records in the Church, it follows entirely that these notaries devoted their chief labor to recording the martyrdoms of the Roman pontiffs and deposited those acts in the Roman Church.

Accordingly, at the beginning of the Church there must have been written not a simple and brief catalogue, but a complete history of the pontiffs who were martyrs. This history was perhaps lost under Diocletian, for scarcely any memory of it remained among later generations. Yet among them there survived a brief catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, written not by Damasus but by a private individual during the time of Pope Liberius, the predecessor of Damasus, as we clearly demonstrated in the preceding chapter.

That catalogue—and no other—is the one that was enlarged over time with various notices and, during the reign of the emperor Justinian, grew into the little work that we discussed under the title of the second catalogue.

I therefore cannot prove what Lambecius says: that the catalogue of the notaries began to be enlarged under Constantine the Great with various acts and deeds and was deposited in the archive of the Basilica of the Prince of the Apostles in Rome, from which Pope Damasus took and copied it, extending it through the pontificate of Liberius by means of various authors, and sent it from Rome to Jerome in Jerusalem.

### 7

Certainly, among the evident considerations that Lambecius himself recognized as obstacles to his view, the first is that the history itself is filled with many chronological errors and several uncertain assertions. This can easily be proved from what we said in the preceding chapter about the earlier catalogues, which the author of the *Pontifical* followed so clearly that he is known to have copied them and taken them up for his own use.

Thus the same argument by which we assigned the earlier part of the ancient catalogue to Antherus and the later part to Damasus demonstrates that the *Liber Pontificalis* must be attributed to Pope Damasus as author or approver.

The second reason why we cannot accept Lambecius’s opinion is drawn from the style and its uniformity. Since the style is uncultivated, crude, and unpolished, it does not at all seem to reflect the age of the first centuries of the Church, when the Latin language excelled in elegance. Since, moreover, the style is uniform in all the lives of the pontiffs from the apostle St. Peter through those who occupied the see in the sixth or seventh century, it must be concluded entirely that the work was composed not by different authors but by one and the same author, who lived and wrote in later centuries.

This was precisely the reason why the common opinion of modern scholars attributed the *Liber Pontificalis* to Anastasius the Librarian, a ninth-century writer, as we shall immediately see.

Nor may I accept what Lambecius adds in these words:

> “This catalogue, although composed at different times and by different authors, was nevertheless everywhere similar to itself in arrangement and style, as commonly happens in the continuation of other official records.”

The same style may indeed be preserved in records that contain scarcely more than one or two words, such as consular fasti, registers of patriarchal sees, catalogues of the Roman emperors, diptychs of the dead, and similar records that display hardly anything besides names.

In records, however, that present many deeds beyond the names of the pontiffs, as the *Liber Pontificalis* does, it is scarcely possible for different authors to preserve the same style. I believe this will be clearer to every expert than anything I could establish by spending time on the proof of this truth and wearying readers with a lengthy discussion.

# CHAPTER VII  
## Whether the *Liber Pontificalis* Should Be Attributed to Anastasius the Librarian

**I.** The opinion of Velser, Bellarmine, and Onuphrius Panvinius that the *Liber Pontificalis* should be attributed to Anastasius the Librarian.

**II.** The opinion of Baronius and Holstenius, according to which the *Liber Pontificalis* appears capable of being assigned to Anastasius as its author in three ways.

**III.** First, from the testimonies of those who either wrote during Anastasius’s lifetime or before him and nevertheless mention the *Liber Pontificalis* without Anastasius’s name, such as the presbyter Rodulphus, Hincmar of Rheims, the author of the *Ritual Book* attributed to Charlemagne, and the Venerable Bede.

**IV.** The same is confirmed by the testimonies of those who wrote after Anastasius and cited the *Liber Pontificalis* without mentioning Anastasius, such as Anselm of Lucca, Cardinal Deusdedit, Ivo of Chartres, Romualdus, Cardinal Laborans, and Bernard of Pavia, the provost.

**V.** Finally, from the fact that although some have attributed the earlier part to Pope Damasus, no one before these most recent centuries is found to have attributed the later part to Anastasius, as is proved by the testimonies of Martin of Troppau and Zeno, bishop of Padua.

**VI.** Second, this is proved by the authority of manuscript codices which, by their antiquity, predate Anastasius’s lifetime and nevertheless contain the *Liber Pontificalis*.

**VII.** Third, it is proved by the diversity of style, from which Lucas Holstenius rightly concluded that the final part of the *Liber Pontificalis* was written by different authors and therefore cannot be attributed to Anastasius alone, although some more recent scholars have thought otherwise.

### 1

Since it is clear from what we said in the preceding chapter that the *Liber Pontificalis* cannot at all be attributed to Pope Damasus, it must be investigated in this chapter whether it should be attributed to Anastasius the Librarian.

Marcus Velser writes as follows in the preface to the *Liber Pontificalis*, which he published in 1602 under the name of Anastasius the Librarian:

> “Because of the style and the entire manner of writing found in the earlier lives, hitherto ascribed to Damasus—something that any reader of sound judgment will easily be able to smell out and recognize—we are altogether inclined to the view that Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, was the true and legitimate parent of all those lives, although in certain places they have been corrupted by the adulterous additions or omissions of others, owing to the extreme ignorance of earlier centuries. Therefore we did not hesitate to adorn the whole work with his name.”

Bellarmine agrees with Velser in his book *On Writers*, under Damasus:

> “A book on the lives of the pontiffs, which is found in the first volume of the Councils, is attributed to St. Damasus. But that book is by Anastasius the Librarian, not Damasus, as is well known.”

Under Anastasius the Librarian he writes:

> “He wrote the lives of the Roman pontiffs from St. Peter through Nicholas I.”

Before Bellarmine, Onuphrius Panvinius wrote in his notes on Platina, under the *Life of Nicholas I*:
