> “Anastasius, a monk and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, wrote the lives of the Roman pontiffs from St. Peter through Nicholas I, which are still in my possession. Under him and under his successors Hadrian II and John VIII he flourished in the City. What follows was compiled by a certain other librarian, William; it is found in the book circulated under the name of Damasus.”

These are the statements of those learned men, whose opinion is by no means accepted by everyone else.

### 2

The most eminent Cardinal Baronius, writing about Anastasius the Librarian under the year of Christ 867, says:

> “We affirm that he was rather a compiler than the writer of the lives of the former Roman pontiffs.”

The learned Holstenius, who wrote after Baronius, examined this work of Anastasius against the most distinguished codices of the Vatican, Royal, Medicean, Farnesian, and Cassinese libraries. Commenting on this passage of Baronius, he observes in his manuscript notes:

> “Under the year of Christ 867, number 139, Baronius affirms that Anastasius was rather the compiler than the writer of the lives of the pontiffs through Nicholas I. He considers the subsequent *Life of Hadrian* to have been written by him, and in my judgment quite rightly.”

Lucas Holstenius expressed this briefly. His opinion may be established chiefly by three arguments.

The first rests on the testimony of writers who either cited the *Liber Pontificalis* before the time of Anastasius or, after Anastasius’s death, did not attribute it to Anastasius at all.

The second is drawn from the antiquity of the manuscript codices, since this demonstrates that the *Liber Pontificalis* existed before Anastasius’s time.

The third is derived from the diversity of style. For this shows that several lives were added to the *Liber Pontificalis* by different authors and consequently that Anastasius was its compiler rather than its author.

### 3

To begin with the first argument, the testimonies of certain persons must be brought forward—men who either lived at the same time as Anastasius the Librarian or wrote long before Anastasius was born.

In the *Annals of the Franks*, published from the library of P. Pithoeus, under the year 865 there is mention of Rudolph, a priest of the monastery of Fulda, who was then flourishing and was regarded as an outstanding and most distinguished historian. King Louis, brother of Louis the Pious and king of Germany and the Eastern Franks, praises him highly in a charter of donation for the scholars of Fulda. This Rudolph, in the *Life of Abbot Rabanus*, published by Brower in book III of the *Fuldensian Antiquities*, writes as follows:

> Theodorus “also brought the bones of Saints Agapitus, Januarius, and Magnus, deacons of the blessed Pope Sixtus, who were beheaded with him under Decius, as is read in the *Gesta Pontificalia*.””

Here Rudolph the priest cites not, indeed, Anastasius’s work on the lives of the popes, but the *Gesta Pontificalia*. It follows that Rudolph, who lived at the same time as Anastasius, already had the *Liber Pontificalis* in his possession.

Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, likewise mentions the *Episcopal Book* in letter 26 to Pope Nicholas. This can be no other book than the *Pontifical Book*. From it he relates, in volume II, page 305, concerning Ebbo, summoned by Sergius to the synod:

> “That he did not attend it, as the previously mentioned letters of Your Authority demonstrate. Such was he held by the Apostolic See and by Pope Sergius, in whose case it was well known that litigation was being pursued by others—that is, as the *Episcopal Codex* shows, he had been deprived of his honor on account of his crimes and expelled from the Church.””

A little farther on he says:

> “As Saint Gelasius says of Acacius, who, having been condemned by the Apostolic See and not restored, ended his life, although Pope Anastasius, as we read in the *Episcopal Book*, wished to receive him.”

This last matter concerning the second Anastasius is found in the *Pontifical Book*, so that there can be no doubt that Hincmar of Rheims understood “Episcopal Book” to mean the *Gesta Pontificalia*.

To this may be added the ritual book which Onuphrius Panvinius attributes to Charlemagne in his manuscript notes on Cencius Camerarius.

[Note: [Col. 0199D] Vatican manuscript.]

In this book, under the Purification of Saint Mary, we read:

> “Concerning this feast and the other feasts of Saint Mary, it is read in the *Gesta Pontificalia* that Pope Sergius ordered litanies to be performed on the day of the Presentation of the Lord in the Temple. For it is written that on the days of the Annunciation of the Lord, the Dormition and Nativity of the holy Mother of God Mary, and of Saint Simeon—which is called *Hypapante* in Greek—when they go out with litanies from Saint Adrian’s, the people should meet them at Saint Mary’s.”

This material was published under the name not of Charlemagne but of an unknown author, after the fragments of Charlemagne.

But why should we hesitate over the testimony of this *Ritual*, when we have the very clear passage of the Venerable Bede, who died more than a hundred years before the time of Anastasius and nevertheless cited the *Gesta Pontificalia*? In his *Martyrology*, under the eighth day before the Ides of August, he writes:

> “At Rome, Saint Sixtus, bishop, and Felicissimus and Agapitus, deacons, who were beheaded under Decius. With him, four other subdeacons—Januarius, Magnus, Vincentius, and Stephen—were also beheaded, as is read in the *Gesta Pontificalia*.”

Thus Bede writes in his *Martyrology*, which Henschenius published in a more accurate form from several ancient manuscript codices and which is found in two eight-hundred-year-old manuscript codices of the Palatine-Vatican Library.

Therefore it is certainly established that, before Anastasius, the *Liber Pontificalis* had already been written in Bede’s time, and consequently Anastasius cannot have been its author.

### 4

The same conclusion is confirmed by those authors who, although they wrote after Anastasius the Librarian and cited the *Liber Pontificalis*, never nevertheless mentioned Anastasius.

Anselm, bishop of Lucca under Gregory VII, when discussing the exile of Pope Liberius and the ordination of Felix with Liberius’s consent, cites in book III, chapter 120 of his *Decree* the book from which he took his passage in these words: “From the *Pontifical*.” In book I, chapter 77, he gives this heading: “On the obedience and humility which King Pepin showed to Pope Stephen, from the *Pontifical*.” There he makes no mention whatsoever of Anastasius, because in Anselm’s time the *Liber Pontificalis* had not yet been attributed to Anastasius.

[Col. 0201B] Cardinal Deusdedit, in his *Collection of Canons*, which he dedicated to Victor III, cites in book II, number 75, several passages concerning Pope Conon from the Roman *Pontifical*. The *Liber Pontificalis* is called “Roman” because it contains the deeds of the Roman pontiffs. Yet the cardinal mentioned it without any author’s name, because in his time that book had not been attributed to any author.

The same is evident from Ivo, bishop of Chartres, part IV, chapter 79, where he writes:

> “Pope Sergius, because certain chapters had been added contrary to ecclesiastical rite, did not subscribe to the synod which the emperor Justinian had assembled in the imperial city. From the *Liber Pontificalis*.”

From chapter 94:

> “Concerning the books of Gelasius, from the *Liber Pontificalis*.”

From chapter 124:

> “Likewise, concerning the confirmation of the Sixth Synod, from the *Liber Pontificalis*.”

Romuald, archbishop of Salerno, does exactly the same in his manuscript *History*, citing the *Liber Pontificalis* in these words:

> “This same Leo IV, as is read in the *Pontifical*, having been maliciously accused concerning certain crimes, convened a synod and demonstrated by oath that he was innocent.”

Cardinal Laborans, who wrote in 1182, gives the book almost the same title, as can be gathered from his compilation, preserved in manuscript in the archive of the Basilica of Saint Peter. In part II, chapter 10, and part XI, chapter 6, he cites simply the *Gesta Pontificum* and identifies none of their authors.

To this may be added Bernard, first provost of Pavia and later bishop of Faenza, in the *Collection of Decretals* which Antonius Augustinus, archbishop of Tarragona, published first among the ancient collections of Decretals. In book III, title 4, chapter 2, he writes:

> “From the *Gesta of the Roman Pontiffs*. Leo III, Roman by nationality, in the council of the emperors Lothair and Louis, assembled in the church of Saint Peter a holy and venerable synod of seventy-seven bishops.”

And in book V, title 5, chapter 2:

> “From the *Gesta of the Roman Pontiffs*. In the time of Zacharias, Greek by nationality, it happened that…”

And in title 7, chapter 1:

> “From the *Gesta of the Roman Pontiffs*. In the time of Pope Stephen, Sicilian by nationality…”

Here the *Gesta of the Roman Pontiffs* are cited but attributed to no author. This is because, as we have already indicated above, in those times the *Liber Pontificalis* was not yet circulating under the name of Anastasius the Librarian.

[Col. 0202A] ### 5

Although ancient writers have been found who attributed the lives of the popes from Peter to Liberius to Damasus, I have found no one who attributed the lives of the later popes—from Pope Damasus to Nicholas I, under whom Anastasius the Librarian wrote—to Anastasius.

Martin of Poland, in the preface to his *Chronicle*, lists all the authors from whom he drew his history of the emperors and Roman pontiffs:

> “I have compiled this little work,” he says, “from the writings of Titus Livius; likewise from the *Chronicles* of Orosius; likewise from the *Chronicles* of Pope Damasus concerning the deeds of the pontiffs; likewise from the deeds of Bovo, bishop of Sutri, concerning the deeds of the pontiffs; likewise from the *Chronicles* of Paul the Roman cardinal-deacon concerning the deeds of both; likewise from the *Chronicles* of Gilbert concerning the deeds of both; likewise from the *Chronicles* of Richard, monk of Cluny,” and so forth.

Thus Martin of Poland, who nowhere mentions Anastasius the Librarian, although he enumerates all those whom he had read concerning the Roman pontiffs, and considered Pope Damasus one of them.

In the same way, Jacobus Zeno, bishop of Padua, in his book on the lives of the pontiffs, which has not yet been printed, indeed regards Pope Damasus as the author of the first part of the *Liber Pontificalis*, but by no means recognizes Anastasius the Librarian as the author of the second part. For, in order to demonstrate that Felix II was a true pontiff, he first confirms this by the authority of Damasus.

[Note: [Col. 0201D] In a manuscript codex of the Vatican Library.]

> “Damasus,” he says, “appears to deserve more credible trust concerning his Roman predecessors, the pontiffs, and especially those who held office during his own lifetime.” For if Damasus himself was the author of this work, as the letters placed at the beginning of the work indicate, who could doubt that he had a more certain knowledge of those who, during his own times, presided as the greatest pontiffs?”

This is what Zeno of Padua says concerning the first part of the *Liber Pontificalis*, from the apostle Peter to the pontificate of Damasus, on the basis of the two letters which we have shown to be spurious.

Let us now hear what he says concerning the lives of the pontiffs who succeeded Pope Damasus. At the end of the *Life of Felix II* he writes:

> “Although there were many other writers who, after Damasus, attempted to add the deeds of the succeeding pontiffs, nevertheless, since the name of those writers is obscure and their authorship quite uncertain, while their language is uncultivated and exceedingly harsh, smelling of barbarism, they were of little or no use to us,” and so forth.

From this it is clear that Zeno of Padua regarded as true what we have undertaken to prove: that the *Liber Pontificalis* was composed not by Anastasius the Librarian, a well-known author, but by several authors whose names were unknown.

[Col. 0202D] ### 6

The second argument establishing that the *Liber Pontificalis* should not be attributed to Anastasius the Librarian rests upon the authority of manuscript codices whose antiquity exceeds the lifetime of Anastasius.

On this subject we must hear Philip Labbe, in his book on writers, under Damasus, where he asserts that Anastasius cannot be the author of the first part:

> “For,” he says, “I have seen a manuscript codex of the highest quality, written in the time of Charlemagne, in which those lives were already attributed to Damasus, before Anastasius had either been born or at least emerged from the first toys of infancy.”

Lambecius repeats these words of Labbe in book II, chapter 8 of the *Imperial Library*, concerning codex 277, which he calls membranous and extremely ancient and declares to be of the same kind as the one Labbe says he saw:

> “Of the same kind,” he says, “is also that outstanding and most worthy-to-be-collated Ambrosian manuscript codex of which we are now speaking, since it is certain from both its script and other circumstances that it belongs to the time of the emperor Louis the Pious. In it the history of the Roman pontiffs extends only as far as Pope Stephen II—or, according to the reckoning of others, Stephen III—who was elected in 752 and died in 757.”

Finally, there are three manuscript codices, one of which is found in the Vatican Library under number 5269. In this codex the lives of the Roman pontiffs end with Gregory II, who died a hundred years before Anastasius the Librarian. The other two are preserved in the library of the Queen of Sweden and in the Library of Saint Mark at Florence; these codices end with Adrian I, at whose time Anastasius had not yet been born.

From all this it is more than sufficiently clear that the *Liber Pontificalis* is older than Anastasius, and therefore he cannot be the author of that book.

### 7

The third argument, by which it is proved that the final part of the *Liber Pontificalis* must be attributed not to Anastasius the Librarian alone but to several authors, is drawn from the diversity of style. On this subject there is an exact judgment by Lucas Holstenius in his manuscript notes on Anastasius’s *Lives of the Pontiffs*. He observes that the section containing the lives from Zacharias to Nicholas I was written by various authors in different styles.

Thus, concerning the *Life of Zacharias*, he notes:

> “Written in a somewhat purer and more vigorous style, it encompasses the whole history of the pontificate, whereas in the case of the preceding pontiffs, whose deeds display the same style and author, the situation was otherwise.”

Concerning Pope Paul, the successor of Stephen III, Holstenius likewise notes:

> “This life is extremely meager; it contains nothing historical and has the same style as the preceding lives.”

According to Holstenius’s view, therefore, the same author added the three lives of the pontiffs mentioned above.

Concerning Stephen IV, however, he writes:

> “The life of Pope Stephen is written in a style different from that of the preceding lives, and has peculiar modes of expression, or barbarisms, which seem—I do not know why—to suggest some kind of Africanism.”

Concerning the *Life of Adrian*, which contains the whole history of his pontificate, he makes no observation except at the end, where he writes in the margin:

> “Here ends the Florentine codex of Saint Mark and the manuscripts of the most serene queen.”

As we shall see below, this indicates that this life may have been written or added by the author who gathered into one volume the *Liber Pontificalis* from which the codices of the Queen of Sweden’s library and of the Library of Saint Mark were copied.

Of Adrian I’s successors—Leo III, Stephen V, Paschal I, and Eugene II—Lucas Holstenius makes no observation at all. Concerning Valentinus, however, Eugene’s successor, he noted in the margin:

> “This life is recognized as adorned with a distinctive style.”

After Valentinus, omitting his notes on the lives of the next three successors, he writes concerning Benedict III:

> “Observe here the affected and most inept outpouring of exaggeration, and the poetic rhythms.”

And concerning the *Life of Nicholas I*:

> “That this life was written by the librarian of the Apostolic See is shown by the frequent mention of the ecclesiastical archive.”

These are Lucas Holstenius’s notes concerning the lives of the pontiffs from Gregory III, under whom the Venerable Bede lived, to the time of Nicholas I, when Anastasius the Librarian flourished. We have reproduced these notes here all the more willingly because that most learned man spent a large part of his life collating manuscript codices with the published work of Anastasius, and because he possessed exceptionally keen judgment in distinguishing differences of style.

From these observations it will readily be apparent to everyone—as I certainly believe—that the final part of the *Liber Pontificalis* ought to be attributed not to Anastasius alone but to several different authors, as we shall show in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER VIII  
### By Which Authors and at What Time Was the *Liber Pontificalis* Written?

I. As regards its first part, which contains the lives of the pontiffs up to Pope Constantine, the *Liber Pontificalis* was written after the Sixth Synod, at the time when the Exarchs were seated at Ravenna.

II. After the death of Pope Constantine, around the beginning of the eighth century, the first appendix appeared; by the same author the lives of Gregory II and Gregory III were added to it. This is proved by the Vatican manuscript codex and by Bede’s testimony, and is confirmed by Holstenius’s judgment, who shows that all the lives of the Roman pontiffs from Saint Peter to Zacharias were written in one and the same style.

III. The testimony of the legates of Agatho, cited by Cardinal Humbert, is dealt with by showing that it is spurious.

IV. That earlier part of the *Liber Pontificalis* had a Roman author, perhaps someone placed in charge of the papal library or of the Apostolic archive.

V. The lives of Zacharias, Stephen III, and Paul I were added by another author. They form the second appendix and were written in the same style by a member of the Roman clergy, who cites the Apostolic archive in the *Life of Stephen III*.

VI. The *Life of Stephen IV* does not have an African author, as Holstenius thinks, but a Roman contemporary. This is proved from the *Acts* and confirmed by the *Life of Adrian I*, which is shown to have been written by the same author, a cleric of the Lateran or Vatican basilica. This is the third appendix added to the *Liber Pontificalis*, with which the two manuscript codices—the Royal codex and the Florentine codex of Saint Mark—come to an end.

VII. The *Life of Leo III* has an entirely different author, perhaps attached to the Basilica of Saint Paul, who also added the *Life of Stephen V* to the *Pontifical*. Thus this would constitute the fourth appendix to the *Liber Pontificalis*.

VIII. The *Life of Gregory IV* has a Roman author and was written in an elegant style. The lives of Eugene II, Valentinus, and Gregory IV differ somewhat from that style.

IX. The *Life of Sergius II* differs in style from the preceding lives, and it was added to the *Liber Pontificalis* by the same author who wrote the *Life of Leo IV*. The *Acts* themselves testify that this author held a position of high dignity at Rome.

X. Anastasius the Librarian was not the author of the lives of Sergius II and Leo IV, and still less of Benedict III, who succeeded Leo IV; Benedict’s life was written in an affected and peculiar style. The opinion is therefore proved correct which makes Anastasius the author of the *Life of Nicholas I*.

### 1

After it has been shown in the preceding chapters that the *Liber Pontificalis*, which contains the lives of the pontiffs from Peter to Nicholas I, is older than Anastasius and was composed not by one but by several authors, it remains in this chapter to inquire who those authors might have been and when they wrote.

It should be noted that the *Liber Pontificalis* is rightly divided here into two parts: the first, written in one style by the same author; and the second, which appears to have been composed in different styles by several authors.

Concerning the first part, which contains the lives of the pontiffs in a single style, the *Life of Leo II* first supplies an indication of the time when it was written. In that life we read of this pontiff:

> “He accepted the holy Sixth Synod, which, through God’s providence, had recently been celebrated in the imperial city.”

Since the author testifies that the Sixth Synod had recently been celebrated in Constantinople, and since the Sixth Synod was celebrated under Agatho, the predecessor of Leo II, in the year 681, the author must have written this not long after the end of the seventh century. Otherwise, what he said—that the Sixth Synod had recently been celebrated—could not be true.

A second indication is found in the *Life of Conon*. There we read concerning his accession to the pontificate, which occurred in the year 686:

> “And they sent messengers together with the clergy and the people to the most excellent Exarch Theodore, as is customary.”

The words “as is customary” deserve attention. The author did not say “as was customary” or “as used to be done,” but “as is customary.” By these words he indicates that this life was written at a time when reports concerning the election of a new pontiff were being made to the Exarchs, and thus at a time when the Exarchs were still at Ravenna.

They existed for nearly two hundred years. Longinus, the first, was appointed exarch by Justin II in the year 567; the last, Eutychius, was expelled by Aistulf, king of the Lombards, in the year 752.

From the passage just cited it is therefore clear that the author of the *Life of Conon* must have written before the middle of the eighth century, when the Exarchs, or prefects of the emperor of Constantinople in Italy, ceased to exist. He could, however, have written around the beginning of the eighth century, when the Exarchs had not yet ceased to sit at Ravenna and reports concerning the election of a new pontiff were still customarily made to them, as is clear from the *Liber Diurnus*.

### 2

It therefore appears that the *Liber Pontificalis* was written after the death of Pope Constantine, who died in the year 714. This is confirmed by the authority of Vatican manuscript codex 5269. Although it was written approximately five hundred years ago, it was copied from an older exemplar, since it ends the catalogue of pontiffs placed before the *Liber Pontificalis* with Gregory II, the successor of Constantine.

The *Liber Pontificalis* itself, which follows the catalogue in the codex, ends with these words:

> “Gregory, Roman by nationality, son of Marcellus, sat for sixteen years, nine months, and eleven days. He lived in the times of the emperors Anastasius, Theodosius, Leo, and Constantine.”

Here only the length of his pontificate is reported, without any deeds. From this it may be inferred that the author began the *Life of Gregory* but did not complete it when the *Liber Pontificalis* was published.

I would therefore suppose that the *Liber Pontificalis* appeared after the death of Constantine. This agrees entirely with what we noted above concerning the Venerable Bede, who is the earliest person found to have cited the *Liber Pontificalis*.

Bede lived from the year 673 to the year 735. Since he survived the pontificate of Gregory II, which began in 714 and ended in 731, the Venerable Bede could have seen and cited the *Liber Pontificalis*.

To summarize my view briefly concerning the time when the *Liber Pontificalis* first appeared, I believe that it was made public before the year 732 and that an appendix was later added to this collection by the same author, containing the lives of Gregory II and Gregory III.

This is confirmed by what Lucas Holstenius observed. Since he had carefully read through all the lives of the pontiffs, he noted that the deeds of the pontiffs from the apostle Peter to Zacharias, the successor of Gregory III, were written entirely in the same style and therefore by the same author.

“The deeds of the preceding pontiffs,” Lucas Holstenius says in his notes on the *Life of Zacharias*, “display the same style and author.”

Since this is evident from reading the book itself, I do not think it requires any proof.

### 3

An objection may nevertheless be raised against our opinion from the authority of Cardinal Humbert of Silva Candida. In his little work against Nicetas Pectoratus, published by Heinrich Canisius in volume VI of the *Ancient Readings*, he reports that, at the Sixth Synod, the legates of Pope Agatho cited a passage from the *Gesta Pontificalia*. It would therefore follow that the *Liber Pontificalis* was written before the time of Pope Constantine, since Agatho died nearly thirty years before Constantine.

Before answering this objection, however, the passage itself must be presented. In Canisius it reads as follows:

> “Then the most pious prince Constantine asked them how the Roman Church observed the order concerning the sacrifice of the body and blood of Our Lord Jesus Christ. They replied: In the Lord’s chalice not only wine ought to be offered, but wine mixed with water.”

And afterward:

> “The offering, however, which is offered as a sacrifice on the altar must contain no mixture or corruption of leaven, just as the blessed Virgin Mary conceived and bore Christ without any corruption. Hence the custom was established in the Church that the sacrifice of the altar should be celebrated not on silk or dyed cloth but on linen of the earth, just as the Lord’s body was buried in a clean shroud. Thus the offering also must be clean of leaven, according to what we read as having been established by the blessed Sylvester in the *Gesta Pontificalia*.”

Thus far the legates. The *Acts* continue:

> “Then it pleased the most pious prince Constantine that this tradition of the Apostolic See…” and so forth.

Pearson cited part of this passage, beginning with the words “Hence the custom was established in the Church,” as evidence for the antiquity of the *Liber Pontificalis* in his posthumous works, dissertation I. He entirely failed to notice that the *Acts* reported by Humbert are completely apocryphal and had been fabricated by some Latin writer not long before Humbert’s time. The speech of the emperor Constantine mentioned above, or the response of the legates of the Apostolic See, is not found in the Sixth Synod.

Nor could the legates have cited the *Gesta Pontificalia*, since the relevant material is not found there. It is likewise not found in Anastasius the Librarian’s account of Sylvester, nor in the account of the second catalogue in the same author. There we read only that Saint Sylvester established:

> “That the sacrifice of the altar should not be celebrated on silk or dyed cloth, but only on linen; and just as the body of Our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a linen shroud, so the Mass should be celebrated.”

These are the words of the author of the second catalogue. No comparison is made there between the conception of the blessed Virgin Mary without any corruption and the offering of the sacrifice without leaven. Indeed, there is no mention at all of leaven. The author of the aforesaid *Acts* added that word to the passage taken from the *Gesta Pontificalia* after the time of Anastasius the Librarian, since Anastasius reports the final words in this form:

> “Just as the body of Our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean linen shroud, so the Mass should be celebrated.”

Everyone can see that these words signify that, just as Christ’s body was buried in a linen shroud, so the sacrifice of Christ’s body should be offered on clean linen. Yet they were twisted into another meaning and transferred to the question concerning leavened and unleavened bread that arose between the Greeks and Latins after the time of Photius, in these words:

> “Thus the offering also must be clean of leaven.”

The author of the testimony cited by Cardinal Humbert therefore lived after the controversy concerning unleavened and leavened bread had arisen between the Greeks and Latins. Consequently, nothing at all can be established from his words concerning the antiquity of the *Liber Pontificalis*.

It remains true, therefore, as we have already noted, that Bede was the first to cite it, because the *Liber Pontificalis* was published in his time.

### 4

Since the time at which the *Liber Pontificalis* was written has now been established, it remains to inquire into its author. Pearson discusses him in dissertation I, chapter 12, number 8:

> “Its author was an anonymous and uncertain writer of the sixth century, ignorant of the condition of the primitive Church; hence the work teems with numerous and disgraceful errors and is full of fabricated narratives.”

This was the judgment of a learned man, but one alien to the Catholic religion. He therefore disliked the antiquity of the rites and doctrines which this book attributes to the Catholic religion, and which we shall discuss in the following chapters.

Let us return, then, to the author of the *Liber Pontificalis*. Pearson incorrectly called him an author of the sixth century, but rightly called him anonymous. The author of the *Liber Pontificalis* did not live in the sixth but in the seventh century, and is a full century later than Pearson believed. He was nevertheless anonymous because he himself chose to conceal his name, while others either did not know it or omitted to preserve it in memory.

This seems in no way to diminish the authority of the same writer, since it is sufficient for that authority that he recorded the place and office which he held. From this anyone can readily conclude that he was a man thoroughly informed about the condition of the Church and that no one had a more complete knowledge of ecclesiastical affairs.

To confirm what we say by the testimony of the author himself, in the account of Sisinnius he writes:

> “He was steadfast in spirit and concerned for the inhabitants of this city.”

Holstenius adds this reading from a Vatican-Roman manuscript codex.

Thus it is clear that the author wrote at Rome, as can be plainly confirmed from the deeds recorded under each pontiff. Just as we showed in chapter 2 that the author of the second catalogue had extensive knowledge of the City and the Roman territory—having a detailed understanding of all the regions and churches of the City, all the relics and titles of the churches, all the roads of the Roman territory, and all the distances along those roads—so it seems that the same must be said of the author of the *Liber Pontificalis*, since the book itself shows that he knew all those places exceedingly well.

He sometimes cites public documents preserved in the archive of the Apostolic See. This is evident from the *Life of Leo II*, where, speaking of the ordination of the archbishop of Ravenna, he writes that a decree concerning the nonpayment of the pallium had been issued and was preserved in the archive of the Church.

It is also evident from the *Life of John V*, who was elevated to the pontificate in the year 685. Concerning the restoration to the Apostolic See of the ordination of Novellus, bishop of Sardinia, he states:

> “His signed document is kept in the archive of the Church.”

From these passages it may be inferred without much difficulty that the author was in charge of the papal library or of the archive of the Apostolic See—unless one prefers to say that he had access to the archive or library and thus cited from the archive what he had seen or learned was preserved there.

### 5

Thus far we have discussed that part of the *Liber Pontificalis* which appears to have been written in the same style by the same author and which contains the pontiffs from the apostle Peter to Gregory III.

We must now discuss the other part of the aforesaid book, which was written in a different style and begins with the *Life of Zacharias*, who succeeded Gregory III in the year 742. Concerning his deeds, Lucas Holstenius judged in his manuscript annotations:

> “The life of Pope Zacharias is written in a somewhat purer and more vigorous style, and the whole history.”

This life evidently contains the entire history of the pontificate, and a different author added it to the *Liber Pontificalis*. Its style appears to differ somewhat from the preceding style.

I say “somewhat,” because although this applies in many passages, in others the style appears debased and low, as in the following, even though these passages too were written in the purer style:

> “Returning no evil for evil and not inflicting vengeance according to merit, but having become pious and merciful toward everyone from the time of his ordination,” and so forth.

The rest bears the mark of the barbarism of that age:

> “Having gone out from this Roman city, he proceeded with the priests and clergy confidently and boldly to travel to the place of the Interamnans of the City.”

And farther on:

> “He took food [lacuna] he feasted [lacuna] they were attempting to make an impediment [lacuna] he might restore to him [lacuna] he released him to return [lacuna] in which he also solemnly professed under oath that his own life would rightly end.”

These passages occur in the *Life of Zacharias*, which was nevertheless written at Rome, as is clear from the passage already cited, where the author says, “from this Roman city.” By these words he indicates that he wrote at Rome. He indicates the same thing in what follows:

> “And thus, with God’s favor, he returned with the palm of victory to this city of Rome.”

And farther on:

> “Finally, in his time our great Lord God deigned, through the same beneficent pontiff, to reveal a great treasure in this Roman city. In the venerable patriarchate, this most holy pope found, deposited in a chest, the head [lacuna] of the blessed martyr George…

And:

> “In the venerable deaconry bearing his name, situated in this Roman city, in the second region at the Golden Veil, he ordered it to be brought.”

In all these passages the author indicates that the Roman city is the place in which he wrote the present life. There too he wrote, in the same style, the *Life of Stephen III*, who succeeded Zacharias. He states that Stephen restored four hospices situated in this Roman city since ancient times, repeatedly calls it “this Roman city,” and adds near the end, concerning the cities restored to the Church through the aid of Pepin:

> “He sent a written donation to blessed Peter and to the holy Roman Church, and for possession in perpetuity by all the pontiffs of the Apostolic See; it is preserved to this day in the archive of our holy Church.”

Here the author states that he was not only a Roman but also a cleric of the Roman Church, and he indicates that he was in charge of the Apostolic archive when he wrote the *Life of Stephen*.

He adds the words “to this day” because the author survived Paul, Stephen’s successor, whose life he also wrote in the same style.

Thus the lives of these three pontiffs were written in the same style and were added to the *Liber Pontificalis* by one member of the Roman clergy.

6. There follows in the *Pontifical Book* the Life of Stephen IV, concerning which Lucas Holstenius judged as follows: “The Life of Pope Stephen was written in a style different from those preceding it, and has peculiar modes of expression, or barbarisms, which seem—I do not know why—to suggest some Africanism.” [Col. 0209C] Thus far he wrote, indicating nothing else; hence one must conjecture which peculiar modes of expression he himself had noticed. Whether the following should be counted among them, let the prudent reader judge:

“They were going to assume the monastic habit. Likewise, after all their affairs had been concluded . . . . . they ordered them to be shut up in the monastery of the Clivus Staturius, where, burning with hunger and thirst and crying out for water, he thus breathed out his spirit . . . . . . . under the prescription of rashness . . . . . . they rose up against Michael . . . . . the cases concerning the rights of blessed Peter . . . . and perceiving themselves to have been placed in great deceit,” and so forth.

I have submitted these expressions to the judgment of the prudent reader; for I do not know by what reasoning Holstenius asserted that they suggested Africanism, or from where he inferred this. They seem to me rather to indicate the barbarism of those times, which had also taken possession of Roman ears, [Col. 0209D] especially since it is clear from many passages of this Life that its author wrote it at Rome. For whenever he speaks of the city of Rome, he uses the following form of expression: “Into this Roman city.” A little before the middle he says: “And they brought him here to Rome,” or, as another reading has it, “they brought him here, to Rome.” In the same place: “Afterward, however, certain wicked Campanians, who had come here to Rome.” And below: “While the Tuscans and Campanians had gathered here at Rome.” Later: “He pretended that, for the sake of prayer, he was going to hasten to Rome, to blessed Peter.” From these words everyone can see that the author wrote at Rome.

The following words also deserve notice: “Confounding and anathematizing that abominable synod which had recently been held in the regions of Greece.” These [Col. 0210A] must be understood of the synod held at Constantinople under Constantine Copronymus in the year 754. Since the author writes that it had recently been held, he must necessarily have written at Rome around that time. This will become clearer from what follows.

The Life of Adrian I follows in the *Pontifical Book*. Although Lucas Holstenius made no annotation concerning it, I think that it was written by the same author, both because of the similarity of style and because of the same phrases and the same barbarisms interwoven with those phrases. Everywhere he calls Rome “this Roman city.” In one place he says: “He would bring him back with him here to Rome.” From these modes of expression it may be inferred that the author wrote at Rome, as is readily confirmed by what he records at the beginning of this Life about Adrian’s father: “His father Theodatus, formerly consul and commander, but afterward [Col. 0210B] first officer of our holy Church.”

From this it is perfectly clear that the author belonged to the Roman clergy, and perhaps was attached to the Lateran or the Vatican basilica. Hence I would readily suppose that the Lives of Stephen IV and Adrian I formed a third appendix to the *Pontifical Book*. In confirmation of this may be adduced two very ancient manuscript codices, namely the Florentine codex of St. Mark and another belonging to Queen Christina of Sweden. Both end after the Life of Adrian I, because they were copied from those codices of the *Pontifical Book* which had been written before Leo III, the successor of Adrian I.

7. The Life of Leo III follows. It was composed in another style and by another author. None of the phrases cited above occurs in it; and whenever it mentions the city of Rome, [Col. 0210C] it nowhere adds the pronoun “this.” The author does not say that the pontiff, returning from Gaul, came “here” to Rome, but simply mentions the city of Rome:

“The Franks,” he says, “sent him back to Rome, to his apostolic see, with due and very great honor. They escorted him through every city, receiving him as though he were the apostle himself, all the way to Rome. Then the Romans, receiving their shepherd with immense joy . . . . . . .”

And below:

“Entering Rome with great joy and gladness, he entered the Lateran patriarchium.”

From this mode of expression it is easily understood that the author of this Life was not only different from the preceding author, but that it may even be questioned whether he wrote at Rome. Nothing in the whole Life permits such a suspicion except [Col. 0210D] these words:

“In the ninth indiction, while our sins were bringing calamities upon us, an earthquake suddenly occurred on the day before the Kalends of May; and the church of the blessed apostle Paul, shaken by that earthquake, had all its roofing and structures collapse.”

From this someone might infer that the author was attached to the church of St. Paul outside the City, which he everywhere calls “the basilica of the teacher of the world, the blessed apostle Paul.” I note this because perhaps he wished to distinguish St. Paul, as the patron of his basilica, from the other apostles, whom he habitually calls simply “apostles” when he names them.

The Life of Stephen V, who succeeded Leo III, was perhaps composed by the same author. For after briefly recounting his deeds, he devotes almost the whole account to describing the gifts that Stephen presented to various [Col. 0211A] churches. The same practice may be observed in the Life of Leo III.

8. Concerning the Life of Paschal I, it is clear that it was written by a Roman author, for he mentions the city of Rome as the city in which he was writing. Thus he relates the translation of the body of St. Cecilia with great honor within the walls:

“In the church of this Roman city dedicated to that holy martyr, for the praise and glory of almighty God, he placed the body of the same virgin together with her most beloved husband Valerian, and with the martyrs Tiburtius and Maximus, as well as the pontiffs Urban and Lucius, beneath the most sacred altar.”

From these words it is clear not only where this Life was written, but also the elegance of style with which the author adorned the history of Paschal. This may certainly be gathered from [Col. 0211B] what he relates about the burning of the Leonine city:

“But we think that this too must not be passed over in silence,” he says: “At the same time, through the devil’s cunning, because of a dissension among certain members of the Anglo people, their entire habitation—which in their language is called *Burgus*—was so consumed by the overflowing flame of fire that no traces of the former settlement could be found in that place. Through the force of that conflagration, the fire destroyed nearly the whole portico that leads to the basilica of the prince of the apostles.”

Here and elsewhere the author writes in a sufficiently elegant style. The style of the Lives of the successors of Eugene II, namely Valentine and Gregory IV, appears somewhat different from it. From the deeds of Gregory IV it may be inferred that its author wrote after Gregory’s lifetime. For, speaking of the monastery of [Col. 0211C] St. Callixtus across the Tiber, he writes:

“In it he also gathered canonical monks, who would perform the office there and, day and night, offer thanks and praises to almighty God, singing them with the innermost breath of their hearts; and, as we see at the present time, the distinguished shepherd greatly enlarged and firmly strengthened this work with great exertion and zeal.”

From these words it is plainly inferred that the author lived at Rome, but wrote after the time of Gregory IV.

9. From the opening words of the deeds of Sergius II, who succeeded Gregory IV, it may readily be inferred that his Life was composed by another author. For at the beginning all the years of the Roman pontiffs from Leo III to Sergius II are repeated—something that would certainly not have been done if one and the same author had added to the *Pontifical Book* the Lives of the pontiffs missing from Leo through Sergius II.

The author of the deeds of Sergius II is therefore different from those who wrote the Lives of the preceding pontiffs. This is clearly shown by his style, which appears distinctive because numerous words are inserted everywhere between nouns and adjectives. Thus, at the beginning of the deeds, we read:

“He began with great zeal . . . . to seem to flourish in pious deeds before all, and to begin to shine in the customs of noble forebears . . . . he was committed to ordinary letters, that he might be instructed by the honey-sweet melodies of song . . . . he took up the whole capacity of literary discipline.”

I omit the rest. Nothing particularly noteworthy presents itself, except that in many places the account is [Col. 0212A] mutilated. Lucas Holstenius supplied these passages from the outstanding Farnese codex in the various readings and notes that he added in the margin and at the end of his copy.

The Life of Leo IV appears to have been written in the same style. It contains phrases similar to those mentioned above and indicates that its author wrote at Rome in these words:

“The monastery of the blessed Martin, confessor of Christ, which is situated outside the walls of this Roman city beside the church of the blessed apostle Peter.”

Elsewhere the author is shown to have been a contemporary, as when the slaughter of the Agarenes is recounted. When, by a divinely sent wind, the ships of the Agarenes were scattered and could not reach the harbor, the author says:

“Concerning these new and mysterious miracles, which divine [Col. 0212B] clemency has deigned to display and demonstrate in our times, although we are not worthy of them . . . .”

Here everyone can see that the author testifies that the events he narrates occurred in his own time. He also indicates the authority he possessed when he reports that, together with the Roman nobles, he ordered the captured Saracens to be bound. He adds:

“Afterward, through the various works of craftsmen, whatever he saw to be necessary, we ordered everything to be brought by them.”

Who, however, was the author of this Life and the preceding one is nowhere stated or indicated.

10. Some people indeed thought that the author was Anastasius the Librarian, who added the aforementioned Lives of Sergius II and Leo IV, as well as the subsequent Lives of Benedict III and Nicholas I, to the *Pontifical Book*. But the Life of Benedict III stands in the way of this attribution. It can in no way be assigned to Anastasius the Librarian because of the affected and utterly inept [Col. 0212C] outpouring of exaggeration and the poetic rhythms found in it, as Lucas Holstenius observed.

It is enough to read the beginning of this Life to confirm the point:

“This blessed man, born from most beloved entrails, endowed with starry dew, and growing more swiftly through devotion to the divine letters, is handed over to his father’s discretion for instruction.”

The Life of this pontiff is similarly filled with an inept flood of exaggeration. The succession of the Roman pontiffs Gregory IV and Sergius II, which had been presented in the Life of Leo IV, would certainly not have been repeated in it if one and the same author had composed the Lives of Leo and Benedict.

The opinion of learned men that assigns the Life of Nicholas I to Anastasius the Librarian therefore appears more worthy of approval. This was the opinion of Lucas Holstenius, who noted at the beginning of the Life of Nicholas [Col. 0212D]: “That this Life was written by the librarian of the apostolic see is shown by the frequent mention of the ecclesiastical archive.”

One example of this truth will suffice. Speaking of the deeds of Lothair, the author writes:

“As is demonstrated in those badly composed deeds deposited in the archive of this see.”

§ He then mentions the Aemilian Apostolic Library: “Whoever investigates will be able to find it in the deeds that lie in the library.”

By these words the author clearly indicates that he was in charge of the apostolic archive and library. Hence the most eminent Cardinal Baronius, in volume IX of his *Annals*, quite properly [Col. 0213A] attributes the deeds of Nicholas I in many places to Anastasius the Librarian, who flourished at Rome under Nicholas I. Bellarmine, however, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, improperly attributes to Anastasius all the Lives of the Roman pontiffs contained in the *Pontifical Book*:

“He wrote the Lives of the Roman pontiffs,” Bellarmine said, “from St. Peter to Nicholas I.”

If so many authors wrote the Lives of the pontiffs before Anastasius, then, with Lucas Holstenius, we should say that Anastasius may have been a compiler rather than the author of the pontiffs’ Lives.

For this reason Velser could have proceeded in no other way when he first published the *Pontifical Book* in print under the title:

“Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church: *History of the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs from the blessed apostle Peter to Nicholas I*, never previously printed.”

Although in his preface [Col. 0213B] to the reader he gives his reason:

“Because the style, and the whole manner of writing, order, and method of those Lives that appear in this codex after the Life of blessed Damasus seem entirely to agree with the phrasing and the whole manner of writing found in the earlier Lives attributed up to this point to Damasus, as any reader of sound judgment may easily perceive and recognize, we are altogether inclined to the opinion that Anastasius, librarian of the Holy Roman Church, is the true and genuine parent of all those Lives—although in some places they have been corrupted by the additions or omissions of others, owing to the extreme ignorance of earlier centuries. Therefore we have not hesitated to adorn the whole work with his name.”

Although, I say, the author indicates by these words that all the Lives of the pontiffs [Col. 0213C] were composed by one and the same Anastasius, he nevertheless departs from the truth in a most remarkable manner, as may easily be inferred from what has been said above.

Let this suffice concerning the *Pontifical Book* and its author. It remains for us to see from what monuments of antiquity that book was compiled, and what confidence a judicious man may or ought to place in it.

# CHAPTER IX. From what monuments of antiquity the *Pontifical Book* was compiled, and what confidence may be placed in it

I. The author of the first part of the *Pontifical Book*, from Peter to Zacharias, used a Catalogue composed in the sixth century, as is shown especially by the various passages that he copied from the Catalogue.—II. This is established secondly by the consular notices, which the author of the *Pontifical Book* took from the second Catalogue, since he assigns no consuls other than those assigned in the second Catalogue.—III. Concerning the deeds that the author of the *Pontifical Book* obtained elsewhere, it is partly known and partly unknown from where they were taken.—IV. Among those whose source and origin are known are certain deeds of Pope Cornelius, copied from the older Catalogue; the deeds of Stephen, Marcellus, and others were collected from their Lives, or from the acts of their martyrdom.—V. The material added concerning the donations under Sylvester and Mark came from the instruments of the churches and from the archive of the apostolic see; hence the excellence of the *Pontifical Book* is evident.—VI. From the second part of the *Pontifical Book*, from Zacharias to Nicholas I, its excellence is evident because it was composed by contemporary authors.—VII. Moreover, because it was compiled from authentic records of those times.—VIII. From what has been said it is clear with what veneration the material concerning history, discipline, rites, and faith found in the *Pontifical Book* should be received.—IX. Even heretics have not dared to deny this, as is shown by their testimonies.

[Col. 0214A] 1. Concerning the first part of the *Pontifical Book*, which contains the Lives of the Roman pontiffs from Peter to Gregory II, described by one and the same author, there appears to be no doubt, first of all, that the author used a Catalogue of the Roman pontiffs compiled under the rule of Justinian. In the Lives of the individual pontiffs there occur so many and such clear examples of this truth that the author of the *Pontifical Book* often seems to have copied the words of the Catalogue.

Concerning Pope Simplicius, the Catalogue says:

“He established weekly stations at St. Peter, St. Paul, and St. Lawrence, so that the priests might remain there for the sake of baptism and for those seeking penance: from the first region at St. Paul, from the third region at St. Lawrence, and from the seventh region at St. Peter.”

The author of the *Pontifical Book* reports this in the following words:

“He established at St. Peter the apostle, at St. Paul the apostle, and at St. Lawrence the martyr a weekly station, so that the priests might remain there for the sake of penitents and baptism: the third region at St. Lawrence, the first region at St. Paul, and the sixth or seventh region at St. Peter.”

No one can fail to see that the author of the *Pontifical Book* took this from the passage of the Catalogue cited above.

The Catalogue also says concerning Pope Hilary, the predecessor of Simplicius:

“He composed a decretal and sent it throughout the whole East, together with letters concerning the Catholic faith.”

The author of the *Pontifical Book* transmits this in these words:

“He composed a decretal and scattered letters concerning the catholic [Col. 0214C] and apostolic faith throughout the whole East, confirming the three synods, Nicaea, Ephesus, and Chalcedon.”

These words are evidently taken from the aforementioned passage of the Catalogue, in which, however, nothing is said about the three synods. Therefore the author of the *Pontifical Book* must be later than that Catalogue, since he added certain details to it—perhaps from the same source from which the author of another Catalogue, composed in the time of Charlemagne before the year 850, took the following passage concerning Pope Hilary:

“He scattered letters concerning the Catholic faith throughout the Eastern world and confirmed the three synods, Nicaea, Ephesus, and Chalcedon.”

These statements appear to have been taken first by the author of the *Pontifical Book*, and then by the author of the Catalogue composed in the time of Charlemagne, from the deeds of Pope Hilary.

[Col. 0214D] 2. Secondly, the same point is established by the consular notices that occur under each pontificate in the *Pontifical Book*. The author of the second Catalogue took them partly from the older Catalogue, composed in the time of Liberius, and partly added them himself. Thus, I think, it may be established that all the consuls from the pontificate of Linus to that of Pope Mark are precisely the same as those assigned in both Catalogues and in the *Pontifical Book*. Accordingly, the author of the second Catalogue is believed to have taken the consuls from the older Catalogue, while the author of the *Pontifical Book* took them from the second Catalogue.

To offer a particularly clear example, the older Catalogue says concerning Mark:

“He was pope in the time of Constantine, with Nepotianus and Facundus as consuls, from the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February until the Nones of October, under the aforementioned consuls.”

The author of the second Catalogue reports this as follows:

“He was pope in the time of the consuls Constantine and Nepotianus for the second time, from the Kalends of February until the Kalends of October.”

Here the error lies with the copyists in the names of the consuls, and some alteration also appears to have been made in the dates on which Mark began and ended his pontificate. The author of the *Pontifical Book* retained these errors, for he says:

“He was pope in the time of the consuls Constantine, Nepotianus, and Secundus, from the Kalends of February until the Kalends of October.”

From this it appears to be confirmed that the author of the *Pontifical Book* took the consuls and the dates of Mark’s pontificate from the second Catalogue, which had been composed in the sixth century and had by then been corrupted through the carelessness of copyists.

Moreover, no one will doubt that the older Catalogue was the source from which the author of the second Catalogue derived the names of the consuls who considers that, after the pontificate of Liberius—where the older Catalogue ends—no further consuls are assigned in the second Catalogue. For concerning Damasus, the successor of Liberius, the author of the second Catalogue says:

“He sat for seventeen years, three months, and eleven days. He was pope in the time of Julian.”

The author of the *Pontifical Book*, however, says:

“He sat for eighteen years, two months, and ten days.”

And after recounting the matters concerning the intrusion of Ursicinus, he adds:

“He was pope in the time of Julian,”

without any mention whatever of the consulship in which Damasus began or ended his pontificate.

The same may be observed in Siricius, Anastasius, Innocent I, Zosimus, and the other successors of Damasus, down to John. Since the author of the second Catalogue lived near the time of John, he assigned the beginning and end of John’s pontificate to definite consuls:

“He sat,” he says concerning John, “for two years, eight months, and fifteen days, from the consulship of Maximus to the consulship of Olibrius.”

The author of the *Pontifical Book* repeats the same account for this pontiff, as also for Felix IV, with whom the author of the second Catalogue ends:

“From the consulship of Aburtius to the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes, from the fourth day before the Ides of July to the fourth day before the Ides of October.”

In place of Aburtius, the author of the *Pontifical Book* reads Mamortinus. The remaining words are exactly the same. Hence the author of the *Pontifical Book* appears to have taken them from the second Catalogue.

A clear sign of this is also to be judged from the fact that after Hormisdas and Felix, who are the final two pontificates presented by the author of the second Catalogue, no other pontificate is designated by consuls in the *Pontifical Book*.

3. Since it is therefore clear from what has been said where the author of the *Pontifical Book* obtained the consular notices and most of the deeds, we must examine where he obtained the remaining acts, which are not found at all in the second Catalogue.

There is indeed more in the *Pontifical Book* than in the second Catalogue, as is shown especially by the following words, which occur under St. Peter:

“He died thirty-eight years after the Lord’s Passion.”

This information concerning the time of Peter’s death is found not in the second Catalogue but in St. Jerome’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, from which the author took it.

The Life of Pope Pius contains the following:

“At the request of blessed Praxedis, he dedicated the church of the Baths of Novatus in the district of Patricius in honor of her sister, St. Potentiana. There he also offered many gifts; there he frequently ministered while offering sacrifice to the Lord. Indeed, he had a baptismal font constructed, blessed and consecrated it with his own hand, and baptized many who came to the faith in the name of the Trinity.”

Yet these words, as Lucas Holstenius noted, are absent from the Florentine manuscript codices and from the Royal codex. Since they are placed out of order at the end of the Life, they are thought to have been added to the *Pontifical Book* at a later time.

The following passage found in the *Pontifical Book* under Victor was likewise added:

“He established a decree, at the request of the priests, concerning the cycle of Easter, after a conference had been held with priests and bishops and Bishop Theophilus of Alexandria had been summoned and an assembly convened, so that holy Easter might be observed on Sunday from the fourteenth moon of the first month through the twenty-first.”

This passage occurs there out of order, after the discussion of ordinations. It should also be noted that what is said there about Theophilus of Alexandria is false, since he was Theophilus of Caesarea, to whom Victor wrote on this matter, as Bede testifies.

The following passage, however, was not added; rather, it appears always to have existed in the *Pontifical Book*, although it is not found in the second Catalogue:

“He established a decree concerning the Church, that ministers should carry glass patens before the priests into the church until the bishop celebrated Mass, with the priests standing before him. Thus Masses are celebrated, except that the bishop’s right should be present, so that only the clergy, with everyone present, might receive from the hand of the bishop that already-consecrated crown from that consecration, and the priest might receive it to hand over to the people.”

From where this was taken, I confess that I do not know.

4. It is by no means unknown, however, from where the passage concerning Pope Cornelius was taken. The author of the *Pontifical Book* has it in these words:

“During his episcopate Novatus ordained Novatian outside the Church, and Nicostratus in Africa. After this had been done, the confessors who had separated from Cornelius with the presbyter Maximus, who had been with Moses, returned to the Church, and became faithful confessors. After this, Cornelius the bishop was driven out to Centumcellae. There he received a letter concerning his confirmation, sent by Cyprian, which Cyprian had written in prison and which he received from Celerinus the lector.”

These statements were taken partly from the older Catalogue and partly from Cyprian himself, as the author indicates clearly enough.

The remaining material found after the translation of blessed Peter, concerning the reason for which blessed Cornelius was crowned with martyrdom, was taken from the Acts of this holy pontiff. The same is true of the Acts of Stephen, which the author of the *Pontifical Book* includes from the words “In his time” up to “He carried out ordinations.” All of this is absent from the second Catalogue.

Very little was added in the Lives of Caius and Marcellinus, but much more in the Life of Marcellus, in which we read:

“He asked a certain matron named Priscilla, and established cemeteries on the Salarian Way. In the city of Rome he established fifteen titular churches, as though dioceses, for the sake of the baptism and penance of the many who were being converted from paganism.”

To pass over the rest, much more concerning Lucina’s house—consecrated as a church and converted by Maxentius into a stable—is found in the Acts of Marcellus, which still survive in manuscript. Thus it is clear that the material was taken from those Acts, or from similar ones.

5. Just as the author of the *Pontifical Book* used the Acts of the pontiffs for the Lives of those who lived during the first three centuries, so in the Life of St. Sylvester he appears to have used various pious donations and the instruments of the churches preserved in the archive of the apostolic see.

The additions in the *Pontifical Book* consist for the most part of donations made by the emperor Constantine, by the heirs of his piety, and by the Roman pontiffs themselves. I omit the very numerous donations contained in the Life of Sylvester. It will be sufficient to give a brief selection from the Life of St. Mark, where we read:

“He built two basilicas, one on the Ardeatine Way, where he rests, and another in the city of Rome near the Palatine. At his suggestion, the emperor Constantine offered to the basilica that he established as a cemetery on the Ardeatine Way the estate called ‘of the Roses,’ with all its cultivated land, yielding forty solidi.

“To the basilica in the city of Rome he offered the following: a silver paten weighing thirty pounds; two silver urns weighing twenty pounds; a silver cup weighing ten pounds; three silver ministerial chalices weighing two pounds each; a silver crown [Col. 0217C] weighing ten pounds; the Antonian estate on the Claudian Way, yielding thirty solidi; the Vacean estate on the Appian Way, yielding forty solidi and two tremisses; the Orrean estate on the Ardeatine Way, yielding fifty-five solidi and one tremissis.”

The author of the *Pontifical Book* wrote all this at Rome. Even if he was not in charge of the apostolic library or archive, he at least had access to them and appears to have obtained knowledge of the donations from there, using it to enlarge the accounts of the pontiffs.

Hence we may infer how highly the material contained in the *Pontifical Book* concerning this subject deserves to be valued, since it was taken either from the archives of the apostolic see or from Catalogues compiled in the fourth and sixth centuries.

This concludes what concerns the first part of the *Pontifical Book*, which was composed by one and the same author from St. Peter to Pope Zacharias.

6. We shall deal more easily with the deeds of Zacharias and the succeeding pontiffs down to Nicholas I, since it has already been shown above that they were written by contemporary authors who lived at Rome.

Thus the deeds of Zacharias, Stephen III, and Paul were written by an author attached to the clergy of the Roman Church and perhaps in charge of the apostolic archive. Likewise, the Lives of Stephen IV and Adrian I were published by a contemporary author who was attached either to the Lateran basilica or to the Vatican basilica, as we showed in chapter 6, section 5.

The author of the Life of Leo III was perhaps from the clergy of the basilica of St. Paul, as is suggested in the same chapter, section 6. From section 7 it is clear that the Lives of Paschal and his three successors—Eugene II, Valentine, and Gregory III—were written by Roman authors around the times of those pontiffs.

In section 8 we showed that the deeds of Sergius II and Leo IV were described not only by a Roman and contemporary author, but by a man of great authority and an eyewitness.

Although it is unknown who wrote the Life of Benedict III, it must nevertheless have been published by a contemporary author, since it was composed before Anastasius the Librarian, who added that Life, together with the Life of Nicholas I, the successor of Benedict, to the *Pontifical Book*, as may readily be inferred from what we often related in section 9 of the aforementioned chapter.

7. The pontifical history of this second part was composed not only by contemporary authors, but also [Col. 0218B] from the authentic records of the Roman Church. For if we examine the Lives of the Roman pontiffs who occupied the see from the year 742 until after the middle of the ninth century, we shall certainly find that the authors of those Lives took from the registers of the Roman Church and from the archives of the apostolic see what they reported.

They all wrote at Rome. They were either in charge of the archives of the Lateran basilica, the Vatican basilica, and St. Paul’s, or were attached to the clergy of those basilicas and therefore able to consult their documents and archival registers.

Thus, in the Life of Stephen III, the successor of Zacharias, the author writes:

“Of all the cities that had been recovered, he sent a written donation to blessed Peter and to the holy Roman Church, and to all the pontiffs of the apostolic see forever, to be possessed; it is preserved to this day in the archive of our holy Church.”

Likewise, in the Life of Adrian I, the author cites the donation made by Charlemagne to blessed Peter:

“As,” he says, “is shown to be contained in that same donation.”

He adds that a copy of that donation was placed over the body of blessed Peter:

“And other copies,” he says, “of that same donation, transcribed by the archivist of this holy Church of ours, his Excellency carried away with him.”

By these words the author indicates that he was not the archivist of the Vatican archive, but that he was attached to that same church and had seen copies of the donations written out by the archivist.

What more is needed? In the Lives of the remaining pontiffs down to Nicholas I, the archive of the apostolic see is mentioned so often that for this reason alone Onuphrius Panvinius, Ciaconius, and other learned men have declared Anastasius the Librarian to be the author of them all.

8. From all this it is clear how great the authority that should be attributed to the later part of the *Pontifical Book*, since it was composed by contemporary authors from ancient records of the Roman Church preserved in its archives.

Although the first part was not written by contemporary authors, it was likewise compiled from ancient records of the Roman Church. Consequently this book may rightly be cited for discerning the rites of the Roman Church and for learning its discipline and doctrines, since knowledge of all these matters may be extracted from it.

If we examine the rites of sacrifice that began from the earliest times; the ordinations of bishops, priests, deacons, subdeacons, and the lower clergy, together with their offices; the relics of the martyrs; the invocation of the saints; the psalms and prayers customarily recited in the Church; the various methods of electing the supreme pontiff; and six hundred other matters concerning ecclesiastical discipline, rites, and doctrines, we shall certainly find in this *Pontifical Book* material capable of satisfying everyone.

We shall gain a clear view of the errors of heretics and learn when and by whom they were condemned. We shall observe the acts of general councils, the decrees of the pontiffs, and the statutes of national and provincial synods. We shall readily infer the ways in which the government of the Church was constituted throughout the first eight centuries.

Thus I scarcely know whether any other work from the whole of antiquity can be found from which so much may be learned as from the *Pontifical Book*.

9. Let this suffice concerning the excellence and authority of the *Pontifical Book*, which even the heretics themselves have declared not to be despised.

Blondel, writing against Turrianus concerning the decretal letters of the early pontiffs, observes in the prolegomena, chapter 12, that the author of the *Pontifical Book* lived before the year 700 [Col. 0220A] and was cited by “Bede, Amalarius Fortunatus, Walafrid Strabo, and others older than Anastasius the Librarian.” He adds in chapter 16: “The author may perhaps not be a bad one.”

Elsewhere he admits that the ancient records of the Roman Church are contained in this work, and that nothing more incorrupt has been published, nor anything more free from suspicion of falsehood.

Salmasius followed Blondel’s judgment. He admits with Blondel that the author wrote as though by the light of the sun. When Pearson attempts to refute their view in his posthumous works, *Dissertation I on the Succession of the Roman Pontiffs*, chapter 12, he gives the following reason in section 12:

“Because its author was anonymous and uncertain, a writer of the sixth century, and ignorant of the condition of the primitive Church.”

He adds certain remarks that breathe the signs of a prejudiced mind and reveal hostility toward the opposing religion. Hence no one will find it surprising that the narratives contained in the *Pontifical Book* displease him, that he despises the rites of the Roman Church presented there, and that he attacks and rejects the doctrines or teachings of the primitive Church expressed in it.

We have shown from what sources the material transmitted in the *Pontifical Book* was taken. From this everyone may easily recognize that Pearson suffered a human lapse when he rose up against the author of the *Pontifical Book*. Although he admits that the author wrote in the seventh century, he ought to have acknowledged that the author was better instructed concerning the Roman Church, its discipline, rites, and faith than those born in these most recent times.

Such is my judgment concerning the *Pontifical Book*.

[Col. 0219]

# FRANCIS BLANCHINI’S BRIEF APPENDIX TO EMANUEL A SCHELESTRATE’S DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENT CATALOGUES OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS

## SECTIONS OF THE APPENDIX

[Col. 0219C]

## Sections of the Appendix

**I.** This Appendix serves two dissertations: both the Schelestrian dissertation already mentioned and our own, soon to be presented, entitled *On the Catalogues of the Roman Pontiffs*.

**II.** The authority of the *Liber Pontificalis* is drawn chiefly from autograph documents, not yet lost at the time when this book, or the Lives collected in it, were compiled by eyewitnesses of those times.

**III.** Ancient copies of the *Liber Pontificalis*, being close in date to those same autograph documents, in some manner take their place.

**IV.** Our edition includes the variant readings of the older manuscripts.

**V.** The antiquity of the manuscripts is established from specimens of their script.

**VI.** For this reason these specimens ought to have been presented before the notes.

**VII.** Concerning both specimens of the Farnese manuscript: the first already cited, and the second soon to be presented.

**VIII, IX, X.** A specimen of the donation of Charlemagne from the Farnese manuscript, nearly contemporary with the donation, is presented here; for the reason indicated, it must be held in the highest esteem.

**XI.** Specimens of the script of two Florentine manuscripts from the library of Saint Mark are added to the preceding ones.

**XII. [Col. 0219D] XIII, XIV.** The earlier date of the older of the two Florentine manuscripts mentioned is also established from a catalogue of the bishops of Naples, which ends at approximately the period to which the last Lives of this *Liber Pontificalis* belong.

**XV.** That catalogue, highly useful for confirming the chronology of the pontiffs, is presented here.

**XVI.** It is said to have been taken from the History of John the Deacon.

**XVII.** A specimen of the letters of that Catalogue.

**XVIII.** A specimen of the script of the second [Col. 0220C] of the Florentine manuscripts.

**XIX.** The antiquity of the Farnese manuscript is also established from several images of pontiffs depicted in it, especially the image of Pope Saint Paul I, very similar to the paintings displaying the succession of the Roman pontiffs in the basilica of Saint Paul.

**XX.** What is missing from the Farnese manuscript can be supplied from other genuine documents, as the following dissertation will show.

### I

I shall not hesitate to append this Appendix to the learned prelate’s dissertation on the Ancient Catalogues of the Roman Pontiffs. It will also be useful for our own treatise on the same subject, which has been written and will be presented immediately afterward. For just as the material that we refer to in this supplement suitably answers the final chapter of the aforementioned dissertation, so it also prepares a no less convenient path toward a clearer understanding of what we have collected in the work that will follow shortly. [Col. 0220D] For this reason, the principle of common usefulness—which concerned both dissertations—recommended that this Appendix be inserted between them.

### II

In the ninth chapter of his dissertation, from the first paragraph through paragraph 6, Schelestratius teaches that what is narrated in the *Liber Pontificalis* from Saint Peter to Zacharias was drawn by the author, or authors, of the Lives from ancient Catalogues, from the Acts of martyrs and councils, and from documents in the archives, especially those of the Apostolic See and of the basilicas of the City. Then, from paragraph 6 to the end of the chapter, he demonstrates that what is recorded from Zacharias to Nicholas I was either personally witnessed as it occurred by various contemporary authors—most of them attached to the clergy and offices of the Roman Church—or collected from authentic documents deposited or preserved in their own age throughout the registers, libraries, and archives of that same Church, and published before witnesses who could easily have challenged and censured the credibility of the writings, had those authors dared to commit to writing anything contrary to what had happened.

Therefore he concluded that the authority [Col. 0221B] and excellence of this *Liber Pontificalis* are so great that in paragraph 8 he expressly declares: “He scarcely knows whether any work can be found in all antiquity from which so much can be learned as from the *Liber Pontificalis*.” In paragraph 9 he also adduces the candid testimonies of critics who, although otherwise not attached to the Catholic religion, readily acknowledged the excellence of the *Liber Pontificalis* by comparing the history of the Lives with genuine monuments contemporary with them.

In particular, he cites Blondel, who says that “the ancient records of the Roman Church are contained in that Book, and that nothing more incorrupt has been published in writing, nor can anything be found more free from suspicion of falsehood.” He also reports a judgment very similar to this from Salmasius, who, together with Blondel, admits that “the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* wrote as though by the rays of the sun.” [Col. 0221C]

### III

Fabrotti, Holstenius, and Schelestratius likewise understood that this Book, collected with complete faithfulness and a concern for truth from genuine, mostly public documents, would be as useful to posterity as we now recognize it to be, since it in some manner takes the place of those documents which were still visible in autograph form when the later Lives—those of Anastasius and of William the Librarian—were issued and added to the earlier ones.

For this reason they judged that the oldest existing manuscripts should be consulted, and that their variant readings should be extracted and published, so that in the editing of this work nothing should be withheld from our age that might serve that supreme zeal for truth [Col. 0221D] which the authors of the Lives had so solemnly professed when composing them.

### IV

Our edition has advanced this same undertaking further by presenting variant readings from several other manuscripts, all those whose antiquity we have found to be especially noteworthy. Nor will this be the end of our efforts, undertaken for the demonstration of historical truth. If possible, we wish to place the documents themselves before everyone’s eyes.

For this reason, in the preface to the first volume, we identified ancient monuments that are genuine testimonies preserved for our age, in order to open the sources of this history. Now we also display specimens that establish the credibility and, in a sense, convey the presence of the autographs. These are carefully drawn specimens [Col. 0222A] of older manuscripts, from which the age of the *Liber Pontificalis* can be inferred.

### V

This was the one thing lacking from the celebrated dissertation of Schelestratius. Since, with Holstenius, he assigns the Farnese manuscript an age earlier than, or at least contemporary with, Anastasius, and gives both Florentine manuscripts of the library of Saint Mark precedence immediately after it, he would have fully established his case if he had placed a specimen of its script before the eyes of experts—especially since very few people are able to investigate the truth of his assertion by a long journey and considerable travel expenses, or because the duties of their offices prevent them from setting out.

### VI
