Below, after the Catalogues of the supreme pontiffs, I have done what I could while absent from the illustrious library of the Most Serene Duke of Parma, assisted by the outstanding patron of letters whom I must frequently mention, Marquis Maurizio de Sanctiis, councillor in the most private and confidential matters of His Highness.

He sent me an extremely accurate transcript of page 16, on which the complete Life of Pope Eugene I was contained. I published it engraved on copper on page XXIII (cols. 149, 150), as evidence of the specimen. It remained for me also to make the learned reader’s mind and eyes more certain concerning the Florentine manuscripts so highly commended by Holstenius.

### VII

What was denied to me—and to you, kind reader—in the notes to the works mentioned above, this Appendix will now abundantly provide, offered under favorable divine auspices. You should attribute it to the benevolence of our excellent prince, lord, patron, and most holy Father, Clement XI. Although he had successfully arranged for literary resources, especially sacred ones, to be brought into the City from Egypt, Arabia, and Syria, he did not allow these nearer aids to pontifical history to be lacking in this Vatican edition.

Since it pleased him to choose me, in continuation of the twenty years of clemency by which he has shown himself a most indulgent patron of our studies, he granted me—through the eminent Cardinal Giovanni Francesco Barbarigo, who energetically exercises his patronage of letters and, since being appointed bishop of Verona and then transferred to Brescia, has in both places awakened distinguished talents—the opportunity not only to visit Parma and Florence, where those manuscripts of the pontiffs, remarkable for their antiquity, are preserved, but also to examine autograph documents in numerous archives and churches. Since these deserve to enjoy the use of public light no less than the Lives of the Pontiffs, I trust that they will soon receive it from editors of my own country.

I therefore judged that I ought to devote as much labor and diligence to this undertaking as the Most Holy Father had bestowed support for obtaining these defenses of the history of the pontiffs and for preparing its edition. I resolved to inspect the Farnese and Florentine manuscripts and to copy at least those portions that would offer the clearest evidence to students of antiquity and truth.

The generosity poured out upon me by the Most Serene Duke of Parma, Francesco I, in fostering and adorning our work rivalled the benevolence of the supreme pontiff. He ordered that all the monuments of his antiquarian and literary treasury be opened to me, both at Parma and at Colorno, where he had received the Most Eminent and Most Reverend Lord Cardinal Gozzadini as a guest with his customary royal magnificence. He even graciously summoned me to go there voluntarily and, during a full three days, overwhelmed me with every kind of generosity.

Accordingly, I ordered the Farnese manuscript to be handed over to me, through the previously mentioned Marquis Maurizio de Sanctiis, so that I might examine and copy it at will. I devoted all the zeal within my power to consulting the book and comparing the specimen of its script already sent in the Life of Saint Eugene, as well as to copying other pages from that celebrated exemplar. I saw that a more splendid and firmer support for diligence and truth had been placed in the presence and testimony of the eminent cardinal, whose disposition toward the best arts was an inheritance from his ancestors, while his habit of assisting our studies was a virtue practiced with me for more than thirty years. [Col. 0223B]

### VIII

Yet, so that my grateful eagerness toward my patrons and my candid desire to acknowledge through whom I have advanced may not divert me from the purpose of the Appendix [the reading of the source is uncertain here], I shall briefly state the more important matters that I judged should be extracted from the Farnese manuscript in order to illuminate Schelestratius’s dissertation.

I remembered that the aforementioned prelate, in the final chapter of his dissertation, paragraph 7, while commending the authority of the second part of the *Liber Pontificalis* as well, had written:

“History of the second part of the pontifical work—from Zacharias to Nicholas—was composed not only by contemporary authors but also from the authentic monuments of the Roman Church.”

To establish this, he refers to a particularly distinguished document: the donations of Pippin and Charlemagne, copied by the authors of the Lives from the autographs.

“Thus,” he says, “the author in the Life of Stephen III, successor of Zacharias, writes: ‘Concerning all the cities received, he issued a written donation to be possessed in perpetuity by blessed Peter and by the holy Roman Church, or by all the pontiffs of the Apostolic See; it is kept to this day deposited in the archive of our holy Church.’ Likewise, in the Life of Hadrian I, the author cites the donation made by Charlemagne to blessed Peter: ‘As is shown to be contained in that same donation.’”

He adds that a copy of that donation was placed above the body of blessed Peter, and then continues: “His excellence carried away with him other copies of the same donation, written by the archivist of this holy Church.”

### IX

Reflecting on these matters and recognizing the antiquity of this manuscript, only slightly later than the age of the Carolingian donation and almost contemporary with it, I judged that, above all else, I ought faithfully to copy from it a specimen of that same donation.

For it must be acknowledged that nothing more excellent could be selected from those parchment leaves, bearing an age of nearly nine hundred years, for establishing the truthfulness and historical authority of the Lives from genuine monuments.

The matter is obvious to every sensible person who considers that Charlemagne arranged for several copies of his donation to be written from the autograph by the archivist of the Roman Church, and that he carried those copies, thus written, with him into Gaul in the same year in which he himself had offered the autograph above the body of blessed Peter. The autograph was signed not only by him but also by all the bishops, abbots, dukes, and counts, with their judges likewise cooperating in the common undertaking, as we read in section 319 of the *Liber Pontificalis*, in the Life of Saint Hadrian.

The Farnese and Florentine manuscripts, which contain the second part of the *Liber Pontificalis*, plainly demonstrate that in the same century in which Charlemagne carried several such copies of his donation into Gaul, copies of the second part of the *Liber Pontificalis* also began to be made and circulated in the provinces.

Before Charlemagne’s donation, the earlier part of the *Liber Pontificalis*, extending from Saint Peter to Saint Zacharias, had already become known through the Venerable Bede and others older than Charlemagne, and had been cited and handled by the Gauls, English, and other Western peoples. [Col. 0224A]

Nothing more distinguished or more certain could therefore be produced to establish the credibility of this history and the truth of those monuments than manuscripts contemporary with the century of the donation, which were then circulated in the very regions where Charlemagne, the author of the donation, had deposited copies of his autograph.

For the copies of the donation written by the archivist from the genuine document establish its credibility in precisely the same way as the words of the donation, copied by the librarians and scribes of the Roman See in the History of the Lives, establish the credibility of the *Liber Pontificalis*—the latter having been circulated in the provinces during the same century of Charlemagne, among the judges, dukes, abbots, and bishops of the Carolingian kingdom and empire who had taken part in the donation and subscribed its autograph.

The script of so old a manuscript is therefore evidence both of the history [Col. 0224B] and of the donation. For this reason, since Schelestratius rightly cited it above all others, Holstenius observed it, and Charlemagne circulated it in Gaul, I judged that it should be faithfully copied by me and inserted into this Appendix as a second genuine exemplar in support of the truth. It demonstrates the truth of the second part of the *Liber Pontificalis*, just as, for illuminating the first part and the Catalogues, we presented in the notes the Life of Saint Eugene and the specimens of the Mabillonian Catalogues.

### X

Thus it is read on page 60 of the Farnese manuscript.

[Col. 0225] [Col. 0227]

[Col. 0229A]

I have therefore judged that these passages from the Farnese manuscript, the oldest of all, should be copied and presented, in order to complete the force of the demonstration in the arguments of Holstenius and Schelestratius, which indicate the genuine sources of pontifical history.

### XI

No slight additions to the firm foundations of truth must also be drawn from the two Florentine manuscripts of the library of Saint Mark. While I was examining, comparing, and transcribing them during the constrained period in which I was hastening my return to Rome, the Most Reverend Fathers of the Order of Preachers most kindly contributed their assistance. They were impelled by as much zeal to serve learning as we also experience in Rome, when they make the Casanatense Library accessible to those who visit it, in keeping with the constant character of that sacred family, which was born to cultivate the minds of men through piety and learning. [Col. 0229B]

### XII

Of the two manuscripts that Holstenius saw and identified above the others in the Florentine library of Saint Mark as nearly equal in excellence to the Farnese manuscript, he called one older and said that it was written in Lombard letters.

It is a parchment manuscript in the format commonly called an octavo portion of a folio. It displays evidence of its antiquity not only in the script of the text of the *Liber Pontificalis*, but also in the Catalogue of the bishops of the Neapolitan Church, which is placed before the Lives of the Roman pontiffs. This indicates, unless I am mistaken, that the book once belonged to the Neapolitan Church, or that it was copied from a similar manuscript belonging to that Church.

### XIII

That Catalogue of the Neapolitan bishops contributes greatly to confirming the chronology, history, and antiquity of the work of Anastasius. For it assigns to each Neapolitan bishop the years of his episcopate, and usually also the months and days. It then adds the names of the Roman pontiffs and emperors who lived during those same years.

For this reason it is a testimony of the greatest importance for pontifical chronology, especially since I noted in paragraph 26 of the preface to the first volume of this edition that in the Nolan Church and its most ancient basilica and cemetery of Saint Felix, called *in Pincis*, richly adorned with mosaics and verses by blessed Paulinus, so many ancient inscriptions still survive—so many that I recorded them there—bearing the names of the Nolan pontiffs, the years of their episcopates, and also the consuls in whose years they were deposited. [Col. 0229D]

The proximity of the two Churches, Neapolitan and Nolan, and the cemeteries similar to those of Rome that can be seen at Naples, abounding in genuine ancient inscriptions—which I myself saw through the kindness of the Most Eminent Cardinal Canteloni, then archbishop, illustrious alike for his most holy character and sacred learning, and commended to eternal memory by his vigilance, constancy, prudence, and every pastoral virtue—demonstrate that the epochs of the bishops of that province were recorded in writing with no less care.

Another document of this survives in the cemetery of Saint Gaudiosus, as the most learned cardinal demonstrated. [Col. 0230A] There are still preserved there very ancient circular images of bishops, beginning with Saint Aspren, the first bishop of Naples, and forming a succession of his successors; each is marked with the name of the individual. These paintings, once colored at the entrance of the cemetery, as in the suburban cemeteries of Rome and in the crypts and chambers of the martyrs, are visible where fragments of the later coating have fallen away from the first and second layers of plaster applied over them after several centuries.

The circles enclosing these images of the bishops imitate the appearance of those that preserve the succession of the pontiffs in the basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way. Similar circles were observed in the frieze of the old Vatican basilica before it was demolished under Paul V. If you seek examples of them in Rome from the eighth and ninth centuries, it will be enough to observe, in the title of Saint Praxedes, the oratory or chapel of Saint Zeno, likewise decorated on its façade by Saint Paschal I, and in the underground chapel of each of the two deaconries—Saint Mary in Via Lata and Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison—the images of prophets enclosed in such circles and formed in colors, with the names of each added.

In volume II of *Veterum Monumentorum*, the prelate Ciampini reproduces most of these on copper plates. In volume I, chapter 21, he also shows how this custom was maintained in the fourth and fifth centuries of the Christian era: in the mosaic of the title of Saint Sabina under Celestine I, and in the triumphal arch and mosaic of the Liberian basilica under Sixtus III.

For our fifth-century mosaic in the Liberian basilica, constructed by Sixtus III, displays according to the ancient custom colored images of the holy apostles Peter and Paul in circular medallions, placed upon the altar. [Col. 0230C]

Earlier centuries also testify to this custom at Rome. For our suburban cemeteries very often offer sacred images, drawn in the glass medallions of the age of the martyrs with gold scratched into them: images of Christ our Lord and his virgin mother, of the apostles, martyrs, and other saints, together with their names.

Aringhius in *Roma Subterranea*, Fabretti in the volume of inscriptions, and most elegantly of all the Florentine senator Filippo Buonarroti—who often earned a place in the annals of antiquarian study—have illustrated these images. Most recently, this sacred tradition was also touched upon by the most devout guardian, devotee, and interpreter of the martyrs, M. Antonius Boldetti, canon, in book I, chapter 39, of his *Observations on the Cemeteries*, by which he richly adorns both the Roman cemeteries and those far distant from Rome. [Col. 0230D]

### XIV

That Catalogue of the bishops of the Neapolitan Church, whose images and succession were, according to ancient custom, displayed in sacred cemeteries and entrusted to circular medallions, is presented complete in the older of the two Florentine manuscripts. It must be held in such high esteem that I judge it necessary to give it in full.

For it approaches the testimony of a witness exactly contemporary with the age of Anastasius’s work, since it ends with the forty-seventh bishop, Stephen. Before him comes Athanasius, the forty-sixth among the Neapolitan bishops, with the following chronological notice:

“Athanasius the bishop sat for 37 years, 6 months, 2 days. He built the basilica of Saint Julian the martyr, situated outside the City. He lived in the times of John, Marinus, Hadrian, Stephen, and Formosus the popes, and of Basil, Leo, and Alexander, his sons, as emperors.”

The *Liber Pontificalis*, continued after Anastasius by William the Librarian, reaches those same pontiffs, Hadrian II and Stephen VI, the immediate predecessors of Formosus.

I shall therefore give the Neapolitan Catalogue as a contemporary witness to the *Liber Pontificalis*, and I shall give it complete, together with the errors with which it is sprinkled. The errors themselves and its barbarous language establish its date, just as does the specimen of its script, as we showed in the preface to the first volume, paragraph 39 and following.

Here is the Catalogue itself and a specimen of the Lombard script so called by Holstenius. (See above, cols. 227–228.) [Col. 0231B]

### XV

“These are the names of the bishops who were at Naples, and whose periods were as follows:”

“**Aspren**, bishop, sat for 23 years. He lived in the times of Clement, Anacletus, and Evaristus, the popes, and of the emperors Trajan and Hadrian.

**II. Epitimitus**, bishop, sat for 17 years. He lived in the times of Sixtus and Telesphorus, the popes, and of the emperor Hadrian.

**III. Maron**, bishop, sat for 24 years. He lived in the times of Hyginus and Pius, the popes, and of the emperor Antoninus Pius and his sons.

**IV. Probus**, bishop, sat for 24 years. He lived in the times of Anicetus, Soter, and Eleutherus, the popes, and of the emperors Antoninus Verus, Lucius Commodus, Aelius Pertinax, and Severus.

**V. Paul**, bishop, sat for 31 years. He lived in the times of Victor, Zephyrinus, and Callistus, the popes, and of Antoninus Caracalla and the emperor Macrinus.

**VI. Agrippinus**, bishop, sat for 12 years. He lived in the times of Urban and Pontian, the popes, and of the emperors Aurelius and Alexander.

**VII. Eustachius**, bishop, sat for 17 years. He lived in the times of Anterus and Fabian, the popes, and of the emperors Maximinus, Gordian, and Philip.

**VIII. Ephebus**, bishop, sat for 9 years. He lived in the times of Cornelius, Lucius, and Stephen, the popes, and of the emperors Decius, Gallus, Volusian, Aemilian, Valerian, and Gallienus.

**IX. Fortunatus**, bishop, sat for 21 years. He lived in the times of Sixtus, Dionysius, Felix, and Eutychian, the popes, and of the emperors Claudius, Aurelian, Tacitus, and Probus.

**X. Maximus**, bishop, sat for 22 years. He lived in the times of Gaius, Marcellinus, and Marcellus, the popes, and of the emperors Carus, Carinus, Aurelian, Diocletian, and Maximian.

**XI. Zosimus**, bishop, sat for 14 years. Under him Saint Restituta was made by the emperor Constantine. He lived in the times of Eusebius, Miltiades, and Sylvester, the popes, and of the emperor Constantine.

**XII. Severus**, bishop, sat for 47 years, 2 months, 11 days. He built four basilicas: one outside the City near Saint Susanna and bearing his own name; another within the city, which some call the Severian basilica and others Saint George’s. He also built the monasteries of Saint Martin and Saint Potitus. He lived in the times of Sylvester, Mark, Julius, Liberius, and Felix, the popes, and of the emperors Constantine, Constantius, Constantine, and Constans, his sons, and of Julian and Jovian, or Valentinian.

**XIII. Ursus**, bishop, sat for 4 years. He lived in the times of Damasus, the pope, and of the emperors Valens and Gratian.

**XIV. John**, bishop, sat for 27 years. He lived in the times of Damasus, Siricius, and Anastasius, the popes, and of the emperors Theodosius, Arcadius, and Honorius, his sons.

**XV. Nostianus**, bishop, sat for 17 years. He built the bath of Nostianus. He lived in the times of Innocent, Zosimus, and Boniface, the popes, and of Theodosius.

**XVI. Timasius**, bishop, sat for 31 years. He lived in the times of Celestine, Sixtus, and Leo, the popes, and of the emperor Theodosius.

**XVII. Felix**, bishop, sat for 9 years, 3 months, 6 days. He lived in the time of Leo the pope, and of the emperors Marcian and Valentinian.

**XVIII. Soter**, bishop, sat for 21 years. He built the church of the blessed Apostles. He also made a baptistery with the greater font inside the episcopal residence. He lived in the times of Hilary, Simplicius, and Felix, the popes, and of the emperor Leo.

**XIX. Victor**, bishop, sat for 11 years, 10 months. He built two basilicas outside the city: one before the church of Saint Januarius the martyr and Saint Agrippinus the confessor, dedicated under the name of Saint Stephen; the other dedicated to Saint Euphemia the martyr. He lived in the time of Gelasius the pope and of the emperor Zeno.

**XX. Stephen** sat for 15 years, 2 months. He built a basilica dedicated to the Savior, joined to the episcopal residence, which is commonly called the Stephania. He lived in the times of Anastasius and Symmachus, the popes, and of the emperor Anastasius.

**XXI. Pomponius**, bishop, sat for 28 years and 10 days. He built a basilica dedicated to the holy Mother of God, ever-Virgin Mary, which is called the Major Basilica. He lived in the times of Hormisdas, John, Felix, and Boniface, the popes, and of the emperors Anastasius and Justin.

**XXII. John Mediocris**, bishop, sat for 20 years, 11 days. He restored the apse of the Stephania church, which had fallen because of a fire. He built the basilica of Saint Lawrence the martyr. He lived in the times of John, Agapetus, Silverius, and Vigilius, the popes, and of the emperor Justin.

**XXIII. Vincent**, bishop, sat for 23 years. He built a splendid church dedicated to the most blessed forerunner, John the Baptist. He also built a baptistery with the lesser font inside the episcopal residence. He lived in the times of Pelagius and John, the popes, and of the emperors Justinian and Justin.

**XXIV. Redux**, bishop, sat for 3 years and 24 days. He lived in the times of Benedict, the pope, and of the emperor Tiberius Constantine.

**XXV. Demetrius**, bishop, sat for 4 years. He lived in the times of Pelagius, the pope, and of the emperor Maurice.

**XXVI. Fortunatus**, bishop, sat for 7 years and 11 days. He lived in the time of Gregory the pope and of the emperor Maurice.

**XXVII. Paschasius**, bishop, sat for 14 years and 6 days. He lived in the times of Sabinian, Boniface, and another Boniface, the popes, and of the emperor Phocas.

**XXVIII. John**, bishop, sat for 20 years, 6 months, 14 days. He built a dressing room for the white-robed baptizands between the greater font and the Stephania church. He lived in the times of Deusdedit, Boniface, and Honorius, the popes, and of the emperor Heraclius.

**XXIX. Caesarius**, bishop, sat for 4 years and 4 days. He lived in the time of Severinus the pope and of the emperor Heraclius.

**XXX. Gratiosus**, bishop, sat for 7 years. He lived in the time of John and Theodore, the popes, and of the emperor Heraclius and his son.

**XXXVI. Eusebius**, bishop, sat for 6 years. He lived in the time of Martin the pope and of the emperor Constantine.

**XXXII. Leontius**, bishop, sat for 4 years. He lived in the time of Eugene the pope and of the emperor Constantine.

**XXXIII. Adeodatus**, bishop, sat for 18 years. He lived in the time of Vitalian the pope and of the emperor Constantine.

**XXXIV. Agnellus**, bishop, sat for 21 years and 15 days. He built a basilica dedicated to Saint Lawrence the martyr, which is called a deaconry. He lived in the times of Adeodatus, Donus, Agatho, Leo, Benedict, John, Conon, and Sergius, the popes, and of the emperor Constantine Justinian.

**XXXV. Julian**, bishop, sat for 7 years, 3 months. He lived in the time of Sergius the pope and of the emperors Leontius and Tiberius.

**XXXVII. Faustus**, bishop, sat for 15 years, 8 months, 26 days. He lived in the times of John, another John, and Constantine, the popes, and of the emperors Justinian, Philippicus, Anastasius, and Theodosius.

**XXXVII. Sergius**, bishop, sat for 28 years, 4 months, 4 days. He lived in the times of Gregory, another Gregory, and Zacharias, the popes, and of the emperors Leo and Constantine.

**XXXVIII. Cosmas**, bishop, sat for 1 year, 2 months, 3 days. He lived in the time of Zacharias the pope and of the emperor Constantine.

**XXXIX. Caldus**, bishop, sat for 12 years, 4 months, 3 days. He built the church of Saint Sossius not far from the city. He lived in the time of Stephen the pope and of the emperor Constantius.

**XL. Paul**, bishop, sat for 4 years, 2 months, 6 days. He built a marble baptistery in the monastery of Saint Januarius outside the City. He lived in the time of Pope Paul and of the emperor Constantine.

**XLI. Stephen**, bishop, sat for 33 years, 5 months, 27 days. He built the church of Saint Peter inside the episcopal residence. He also built monasteries dedicated to Saint Festus, Saint Pantaleon the martyr, and Saint Gaudiosus the confessor. He further added, in the monastery of Saint Gaudiosus, the basilica of Saint Susanna, in which he himself placed the body of that martyr. He restored the Stephania church, burned by fire, and there placed the bodies of Saint Eutyches and Acutius, the martyrs. He lived in the times of Stephen and Hadrian, the popes, and of the emperors Constantine and Leo.

**XLII. Paul**, bishop, sat for 20 years, 4 months, 6 days. Under him the lady Euphrasia made the monastery of Saint Mary called *ad Albini*, and Anthimus the consul built the basilica of Saint Paul the Apostle and the monastery of Saints Quiricus and Julitta, the martyrs. He lived in the times of Leo, Stephen, and Paschal, the popes, and of Irene, Nicephorus, Stauracius, Michael, Leo, and Constantine, the emperors.

**XLIII. Tiberius**, bishop, sat for 20 years, 4 months, 11 days, in the days of Theodenand. In the days of Theodenand, the widow of [lacuna] Duke Anthimus founded in the praetorium a monastery dedicated to Saints Marcellinus and Peter the martyrs. He lived in the times of Eugene, Valentine, and Gregory, the popes, and of Michael and Theophilus, his son, the emperors.

**XLIV. John**, bishop, sat for 7 years, 9 months, 22 days. He lived in the time of Sergius the pope and of the emperor Michael.

**XLV. Athanasius**, bishop, sat for 22 years, 6 months, 24 days. He restored the church of Saint Januarius the martyr inside the episcopal residence. He lived in the times of Leo, Benedict, Nicholas, and Hadrian, the popes, and of Michael and Basil, the emperors.

**XLVI. Athanasius**, bishop, sat for 22 years, 6 months, 2 days. He built the basilica of Saint Julian the martyr, situated outside the City. He lived in the times of John, Marinus, Hadrian, Stephen, and Formosus, the popes, and of Basil, Leo, and Alexander, his sons, the emperors.

**XLVII. Stephen**, bishop, sat for 8 years, 10 months, [days missing].”

### XVI

Permit me to append to the Catalogue the brief summary prefixed to it in the same manuscript, written in red letters, perhaps in the hand of Holstenius. It reads:

“This is an epitome of John the Deacon, whose short work on the bishops of Naples is held in the Vatican Library.”

Sigebert, in his *Chronicle* under the year 873 and in chapter 107 of his Catalogue, mentions John the Deacon of the Roman Church under Pope John VIII, to whom he also dedicated a Life of Saint Gregory the Great, and under the emperors Louis the Younger and Charles the Bald. From him Vossius also speaks in book II, chapter 36, of *On Latin Historians*.

Labbe, in more than one place, affirms that this same John the Deacon was not only contemporary with Anastasius the Librarian but also his friend and intimate associate. Therefore nothing could be more closely related to this work to bind together in a single manuscript, nor anything more closely related to this edition for us to present, either as evidence of its date or as confirmation, through contemporary documents, of the testimony of the collection of Lives.

This is especially so because in the same ninth century, with which this Catalogue ends, the illustrious deacon Paul Warnefrid had preceded it under Charlemagne. Some people observe in Labbe and Vossius that his works were confused with the *Miscella* of John the Deacon. Paul had written the succession and deeds of the bishops of Metz at the request of Bishop Angilram—just as this John the Deacon perhaps wrote the succession and deeds of the bishops of Naples at the request of some bishop of that Church, following the custom of that age, which began to imitate the librarians of the Roman See in collecting the succession and deeds of its own prelates.

This is clear from the work of Agnellus on the archbishops of Ravenna and from other works that belong approximately to this period. [Col. 0233D]

We may also mention another John the Deacon of Saint Januarius, from whom, as we read in Vossius, *On Latin History*, p. 708, the Acts of that blessed bishop and martyr, and of Sossius and his companions, were copied. He was present at their translation, although Vossius lists him among writers of uncertain date. The translation of Saint Januarius took place in the ninth century, as is known from the Cassinese Chronicle.

Whether, therefore, this second John the Deacon of Saint Januarius, or the earlier Roman John joined in friendship with Anastasius the Librarian—the latter I would attribute it to with greater confidence—compiled this remarkable Catalogue in the Florentine manuscript, whose great antiquity is shown by its specimen of script and its succession of pontiffs, historians of the Neapolitan Church frequently use the testimony of that John the Deacon. Among them is Ughelli, in volume VI of *Sacred Italy*, although, as far as I know, no one has until now produced the Catalogue itself, hidden in the library of Saint Mark.

### XVII

In the second plate of this Appendix, engraved on copper, after imitating the Farnese manuscript, I presented a specimen of the aforementioned Catalogue and the first verses of the *Liber Pontificalis*, written in the older of the two Florentine manuscripts in letters that Holstenius calls Lombardic.

### XVIII

The other Florentine manuscript of Saint Mark is somewhat later in date, though not so far removed from the preceding one that it reaches the tenth century. This can be established from the specimen added on the same plate.

The leaves of this manuscript, likewise written on parchment, carry the Lives of the Pontiffs to approximately section 323 of our edition, in the Life of Hadrian I. Some leaves and quires of an exposition by blessed Ambrose, bishop, on the *Song of Songs* follow.

XIX. So that nothing on our part might be omitted that could illuminate either the documentary evidence contemporaneous with Anastasius’s collection of Lives, or the observations of our Appendix concerning the three codices commended in Schelestratius’s dissertation, I placed on the specimen plate of the Farnesian codex’s script the beginning of the Life of Saint Paul I, pope. In it, the initial letter [Col. 0234C] displays a portrait of that pontiff, graphically drawn within a circular frame, very similar to the shield-like images of the Roman pontiffs visible in the basilica of Saint Paul on the Via Ostiensis and in other Roman churches, indicated in this Appendix at no. 13 and to be discussed more fully in the forthcoming dissertation. I could also have presented other images from the same codex, showing a pontiff giving a blessing; these are seen at the end of Saint Leo III, before the beginning of the Life of Saint Adrian, and closely resemble those visible in the mosaics of the churches of the City built during the same period. I judged, however, that those were sufficient which could conveniently be included on the bronze plate intended to display the specimen of the script.

XX. It is regrettable that the Farnesian codex lacks the Lives of the earlier pontiffs, from Saint Peter to [Col. 0234D] Saint Silverius. Had they survived, the epochs of each could have been compared with other copies of the Lives and with the surviving chronological numbers among the portraits of the pontiffs in the aforesaid Pauline basilica on the Via Ostiensis, from Saint Peter to Saint Innocent I—materials reserved for illustration in our forthcoming dissertation. Nevertheless, I shall try to remedy the losses of this outstanding codex through other genuine monuments of pontifical history and through other codices of approximately the same period. These materials ought to have been preceded by an account of the Farnesian and Florentine codices, which has been presented in this Appendix.

[Col. 0235]

# FRANCIS BLANCHINI’S DISSERTATION ON THE ANCIENT CATALOGUES OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS

And on establishing their comparison and selection, from genuine documents of the Roman Church, for the use of history and chronology.

## CHAPTER ONE

On the rules to be observed in examining correct chronology, especially pontifical chronology.

[Col. 0235A]

## SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

I. The Lives of the Roman pontiffs derive their origin from catalogues and contain three principal kinds of information, namely, the succession, chronology, and deeds of those same pontiffs.—II. The uninterrupted succession of the supreme pontiffs, which is the most important and necessary of all these kinds of information, is indeed gathered from the Catalogues, but is also abundantly confirmed by the holy Fathers.—III. The discrepancies in pontifical chronology have generally arisen from the ignorance or negligence of copyists and transcribers. For this reason, the abundance of transcribers should be regarded as harmful rather than useful to the proper establishment of pontifical chronology, unless the use and evaluation of so many transcribers and codices are referred, according to definite rules, to the investigation of truth.—IV. Such rules will be brought forward in the next chapter and confirmed from the axioms and discipline of critical scholarship.

[Col. 0235B]

1. It is now as certain and established as anything can be that the Lives here being elucidated owe their origin to ancient Catalogues. For since the Lives contain three things—the succession, chronology, and deeds of those who, succeeding Peter, the Prince of the Apostles, undertook to administer the governance of the universal Church attached to the Roman episcopate—the succession is displayed in all the Catalogues, the chronology in most of them, and part of the deeds in some. It was therefore rightly done that those who undertake to elucidate the Lives of the pontiffs should first discuss the Catalogues.

2. Of the three kinds of information—succession, chronology, and deeds—the first is both the principal and the most necessary: it displays the uninterrupted series of the supreme pontiffs, exercising on earth the power of Christ’s vicariate for the administration of the universal Church. We see that, by the design of divine providence, this succession was preserved without interruption both through the Catalogues and through the writings of the Fathers transmitted to us from the very beginnings of the Church. This consideration persuaded Schelestratius, often praised above, to show from Irenaeus and other Fathers that the same series and succession which they had drawn from the diptychs and other documents of periods close to their own was preserved in the Catalogues and in the *Liber Pontificalis* through the constant tradition of their predecessors. If some slight difficulty should arise concerning the numbering of one or another pontiff, whether among successive pontiffs or among vicars and coadjutors of absent pontiffs, or even concerning the exclusion or admission of someone in the register of legitimate pontiffs on account of a schism then arising, that difficulty is sufficiently resolved and dispelled by documents received and approved by the Church, as will be demonstrated in its proper place in the case of Felix II and a very few others.

3. Since, then, sufficient provision has been made for the uninterrupted succession—which was the principal concern and purpose of the writers in compiling the Catalogues—it remains that the second kind of information, namely the chronology and epoch of each pontiff, should be derived from those same Catalogues. Here someone might apply the familiar saying: “Abundance has made me poor.” For the abundance of authors who everywhere thrust forward catalogues of the Roman pontiffs without selection, or at least without identifying the sources and documents from which the epochs assigned to them are taken, causes the frequent disagreement of numbers—which has entered through years, months, and days, either because of the carelessness of copyists or because of information collected rashly and disorderly—to hinder rather than assist students of chronology in establishing the true reckoning of times. The judgments of critics are especially confused in defining these periods by the appearance and mutual comparison of ancient Catalogues that display ten or even more centuries of antiquity. We cannot conceal the fact that the Liberian Catalogue is commonly regarded by learned men as the oldest of all, yet is accused of having a corrupted reckoning of the consuls in more than one place, contrary to the evidence of the Fasti; and, as necessarily follows from this, of having wrongly reckoned the intervals of time in the same pontifical chronology through the erroneous pairs of consuls derived from it. The second Catalogue in antiquity, next after the first, and composed during the reign of Justinian, is observed not to agree with the others published in various places by Schelestratius, who printed the first two, nor with those published by Sirmond, Mabillon, and Pagi, who edited several from codices of distinguished libraries, written in the sixth, eighth, and ninth centuries of the Christian era.

4. Nevertheless, so that we may not lose heart in extracting the true chronology from so great a variety of writings, transcriptions, and copyists, we accept the rules to be set forth and established in the next chapter, so that they may be placed before our examination as certain laws of judgment, to be applied and observed by every prudent person in evaluating historical truth.

# CHAPTER II

Rules are handed down for investigating chronological truth from the more ancient Catalogues, which record times in different ways within the given series of Roman pontiffs and also of other princes and illustrious men.

## SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

[Col. 0237B]

I. Rules of critical judgment are to be established, by which we may proceed in preferring the opinions of chronologists and the testimonies on which they rely.—II. First rule. In asserting dates, it is preferable to consult public monuments, if any exist; and those should be preferred which, having been established by suitable persons, are closest in place and time to the period chiefly under consideration.—III. Writers especially distinguished in sacred history and chronology, even those divinely inspired, confirm the rule by examples.—IV. The same rule is followed by the authors of secular history and chronology who surpass the others of their kind.—V. Second rule. Among public documents, and among those close both in time and place, which were established under the care and authority of magistrates, preference should be given to those which, once established by suitable and legitimate custodians of the public will, remained so complete and carefully preserved that they show no sign of erasure or alteration, and which in fact cannot be shown to have been rashly violated.—VI. Corollary of the second rule. Corrections of copies, when no autograph exemplars exist from which they can be taken, should be sought from public documents of the same or a nearby period.—VII. Third rule. Among documents supplied from a place other than that where the events most immediately occurred, the privilege of giving decisive evidence should belong to the one whose author’s opportunity for investigation of time and events was enlarged by his access to information, expertise in the discipline, and devotion to truth.—VIII. Two corollaries of the third rule. First corollary. The agreement of several writers or documents close in place and time, especially when they are supported by public authority, should be regarded as an indication of historical and chronological truth. Second corollary. From such agreement, copies written later may reasonably be corrected if they differ from it and from the more ancient witnesses.—IX. Fourth rule. The agreement of the times indicated by historical documents with the legal days established by law for carrying out the events recorded is an indication of correctly established chronology.—X. Examples of this rule are given.—XI. Fifth rule. The demonstration of correctly established chronology will be some characteristic of an observed celestial motion that exactly corresponds to the interval of time required for completing those motions of the heavenly bodies.—XII. An illustrious example of this fifth [Col. 0237D] rule is offered in assigning the year of the consulship [and death] of Jovian Augustus, with Varronianus his colleague, to the year 364 of the common Christian era, and in assigning to that same year the celestial motions recorded in an ancient inscription then set up.—XIII. From that consulship, thus established, the epoch of the pontificate assumed by Saint Damasus is fixed in the year 366 of the common Christian era.

## [RULE]

1. When discrepancies among the totals gathered in the chronological series for the age, life, and administration of the Roman pontiffs, or of any princes and illustrious men, extending especially across many centuries, cannot at all be reduced to the rules of arithmetic—provided that the rules of the Julian years have been properly observed, being established in the Julian period or in any other period accepted by all chronologists among the adherents of each opinion—it follows that the discrepancies must arise from the rules of critical judgment employed by differing chronographers and biographers in comparing, preferring, and selecting the testimonies from which each takes the separate portions of periods that are subsequently brought together into a complete reckoning and total. Therefore, one calculation and opinion must be preferred to another to the extent that the rules governing the selection by which each calculation and total, together with the testimonies supporting it, is to be preferred come closer to the indications most likely to represent historical truth. These rules of selection must therefore first be established: through them we seek, among conflicting opinions, to choose and follow the one which the method of critical judgment demonstrates [Col. 0238B] to approach the truth more closely. Our rules of critical judgment will be briefly explained, and their foundations will be sought in the necessary connection which reason shows them to possess with truth.

## FIRST RULE

2. The first rule of selection is that, in examining, comparing, and preferring any chronology, we should consult public documents, if any exist, established by suitable persons, and especially those which are closer in time and place to the men and events about whom the chronology and history are being composed and ordered.

Our rule therefore considers two features in documents that establish chronology: first, that they be public; second, that they be nearer.

3. Writers of historical scholarship who excel and are regarded as leaders in that genre of writing, especially those devoted to truth, which is history’s highest merit, lend authority to both parts of this rule. For if the rule is to be sought from those writers whom Truth itself instructed, these too, divinely inspired, direct attention to public documents so that they may display the markers of the times they designate. Luke records the edict of Caesar Augustus, when the earlier census under Quirinius is used to indicate the year of Christ’s birth. To state and free from all obscurity the beginnings of Christ’s baptism and ministry, he then lists both the sacred and civil magistrates [Col. 0238D] who at that time exercised public authority in the region where the events that he knew he had to describe in his Gospel took place:

“In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judaea, Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, and his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, under the chief priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came upon John the son of Zachariah in the wilderness.”

When the ancient Fathers observe these matters, in addition to the mysteries always inherent in the sacred writings, they also find reasons why the minds of human beings are led by public and proximate documents to perceive truth more attentively and retain it more firmly. Concerning the earlier epoch of Quirinius, mentioned by Saint Luke, Ambrose expresses himself as follows [Note: [Col. 0239D] *On Luke*, chapter 2]:

> “Under the governorship of Quirinius,” he says, “this first registration was made, so that the evangelist may seem to have inserted into this book, as a kind of consul for the sake of identification. For if consuls are entered in bills of sale, how much more ought a time to have been entered for the redemption of all? You therefore have all the things that are customarily found in contracts. They ordinarily include the name of the person exercising supreme authority, the day, the place, the cause, and witnesses as well. Christ also employed these as witnesses to his birth and generation according to the flesh, saying: ‘You shall be my witnesses in Jerusalem.’”

Saint Gregory discusses the chronological markers of the second period at length [Note: [Col. 0239D] Homily 20, *On the Gospel*], producing many things from the mystical sense but explaining this principal point from the literal sense: namely, that the evangelist, following the custom of the ancient prophets, preserved so careful an account of the times that no authority of an instrument was lacking—though it was strengthened far more solidly by divine faith—through the indications which rational care ordinarily records in public and most solemn acts. Long before Gregory, Tertullian had foreseen this and understood it from the apostolic age. In his *Apologeticus* against the Gentiles he professed this discipline: that, as witnesses to the truth which constantly accompanies the writings of Christians, he should summon certain chronological marks expressed in public documents of antiquity and in archives. Thus he writes in chapter 19 [Note: [Col. 0240D], chapter 19]:

> “First, these documents” (he is speaking of the divine books of the ancient covenant, which are displayed at the Serapeum, in the library of Ptolemy, together with the Hebrew letters themselves, and are publicly read by the Jews) “are defended by the authority of their great antiquity. Among you also, it is almost a matter of religion to establish faith concerning dates.”

He therefore concluded that the genuine practice of establishing faith concerning dates was to open the archives of all nations that excelled in antiquity and compare them with the genuine indications of the times and books of the Christians.

> “To explain,” he says (chapter 20), “by what order these things may be proved is not so difficult for us as it is vast and arduous. But for the moment it would take a long time to sit with many documents and count upon our fingers. The archives even of the most ancient nations must be opened—the Egyptians, Chaldaeans, Phoenicians,” and so forth.

[Col. 0239D] It is therefore clear that the divine Scriptures, as teachers of all truth, also hold out a lamp for this investigation, so that, when the chronology of events is being vindicated, genuine documents from all antiquity—documents carefully preserved for them by public authority—may be eagerly sought.

4. But so that we may bring forward guarantors of a humbler rank for this first rule, within the boundaries of human scholarship, history, and chronology, all those whom the consensus of the ages has included among the outstanding Latin or Greek writers will not refuse to be its defenders and champions as we investigate the most reliable guides. For them, as for us, it was established that the chronological documents and records of events they narrated should be taken from the most reliable public monuments and from those closest in time and place to the events proposed for historical treatment. They openly declare that they learned the things they narrate from the annals of the pontiffs, the censorial books, the public acts and archives, and the linen and ivory books written under the authority of the magistrates and deposited by order of those who governed the state in libraries, or even in shrines and temples. I discussed these matters more fully in the Preface to the *Universal History*, chapter 4, drawing on Marcus Tullius in book 2 of *On the Orator*, where he says:

> “History was nothing other than the compilation of annals; and for the sake of preserving the memory of this matter, from the beginning of Roman history down to the pontificate of Publius Mucius, the chief pontiff committed all the affairs of individual years to writing, published them on a white tablet, and displayed the tablet at home, so that the people might have the power of knowing them. These are the annals which are still called the Great Annals.”

Macrobius also confirms this in *Saturnalia*, book 2, chapter 2. Before him should be placed Livy, book 4, no. 20, who mentions the ancient annals and the linen books of the magistrates kept in the temple of Moneta, which Macer Livineius repeatedly cites as authorities to prove that Aulus Cornelius Cossus did not become consul with Titus Quinctius until the ninth year thereafter. Concerning the censorial commentaries, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, close in time to Livy, says in book 1, page 60 of the edition of G. L. Sylburgius, that fathers customarily handed these down to their sons from hand to hand, so that the sons might transmit them to their descendants with equal care, no differently from their ancestral and family rites. Roman historians therefore repeatedly appeal to these public monuments when the truth, circumstances, or date of an event must be determined. The most distinguished Greek writers likewise recognized that these sources had to be approached and drawn upon, such as Diodorus Siculus, book 1, section 4; Dionysius of Halicarnassus; Appian of Alexandria; and others.

Euhemerus recognized that the entire structure of chronology and history, extended even to the most remote ages, had to be built upon this solid foundation of publicly established documents. Lactantius followed him in *The Divine Institutes*, book 1, chapter 11 [Col. 0240D], after the example of Tullius and Varro in establishing a matter of the greatest importance; Arnobius likewise imitates them. For in order to show that the beings whom pagan superstition impiously worshiped as gods were human beings—I mean Jupiter, Saturn, Neptune, and the rest—they present their history and dates, carefully collected by Euhemerus from funerary inscriptions and sacred inscriptions that were publicly displayed in the most ancient temples. Lactantius’s words are:

> “The ancient author Euhemerus, who was from the city of Messana, collected the deeds of Jupiter and the others who are thought to be gods from the sacred inscriptions kept in the most ancient temples, especially in the temple of Jupiter Triphylius, where an inscription indicated that a golden column had been erected by Jupiter himself. On it he had inscribed all his deeds, so that it might be a memorial for posterity of the things accomplished.”

He then adds:

> “Ennius followed this history and interpretation.”

Since, then, the documents publicly established by an entire people, a whole community, or the magistrates are regarded as the most suitable testimonies for confirming events, they must provide their evidence with much greater distinction and effectiveness in determining the times outside which events could not possibly have occurred. Since the division of time has varied among different nations, and has sometimes changed within the same nation, it follows that, among public monuments capable of confirming the sequence of times, preference should be given to those found closest in place and time to the periods chiefly under consideration. Just as a judge who prudently seeks the basis of knowledge in a claimant more readily admits testimony close to a recent event, perceived through immediate and living experience, and prefers what was placed before trustworthy eyes to what has entered the witness’s mind through the languid insinuation of reports heard by ear, so too, in admitting monuments concerning events and times, a stronger force is rightly attributed to proximity. It ensures that the makers of the monuments cannot be regarded as having lost their memory, nor as boldly lying or rashly putting forward false indications of events and dates before the eyes of those in whose presence the events took place, since any sensible person would have been free to accuse and correct them.

Let this, then, be the principal rule of our chronological critical method: In asserting dates, we should consult public monuments, if any exist, and among public monuments prefer those established by suitable persons that are closest in place and time to the period chiefly under consideration.

## SECOND RULE

5. The second canon will be this: Among public documents close both in time and place, established under the care and authority of magistrates, preference should be given to those which, once established by suitable and legitimate custodians of the public will, remained so complete and carefully preserved that they display no sign of erasure or alteration [Col. 0241D], and which in fact cannot be shown to have been rashly violated.

The following follows from this second canon.

## COROLLARY

6. Corrections of ancient codices—if the writings in those codices are not autographs but copies—should be sought by inspecting and comparing them with the public documents of the same or a nearby period indicated above.

For an old copy by a private writer introduces a solitary person as guarantor and defender of the history and truth. Public documents, however, bring forward as witnesses to their assertion either peoples or magistrates. It is therefore just that the public faith entrusted with judging both private and public matters should be preferred to the statements of individual writers—or, more accurately, individual transcribers. This is done by testing the codices of copyists against documents to which the authority of the people and the magistrates has added as many witnesses as there are observers who vindicate their assertions.

## THIRD RULE

7. Let the third rule be this: Among documents supplied from a place other than that where the events most immediately occurred, the privilege of giving decisive evidence should belong to the one whose author’s opportunity for investigating times and events was enlarged by his access to information, expertise in the discipline, and devotion to truth.

All who have led the way in arranging periods of time, whether historians [Col. 0242B] or chronologists, have handed down this rule. Among the ancients these included Fabius Pictor, Lucius Cincius, Marcus Cato, Gaius Licinius Macer, Marcus Terentius Varro, and Titus Pomponius Atticus; among more recent writers, Cuspinianus, Sigonius, Panvinius, Baronius, Petavius, and Norisius, all highly commended, gather testimonies from every direction in order to establish and correct their knowledge of dates and events. To each of them may be applied what Nicolaus Gerbelius records about Cuspinianus in the preface to his *Fasti*:

> “After comparing the most ancient authors of both languages,” he says, “whenever he detected errors in them, he corrected them with the greatest moderation. Then, with incredible care and industry, he showed by what reasoning and in what manner discrepancies and disagreements between them should be reconciled: what should be added to one and what taken away from another. You will read with singular pleasure that whenever some of them agreed with one another and finally set out the matter in the same words, he gathered them all into a single class, as it were, and collected them with the greatest diligence. Everyone who possesses even moderate literary judgment understands how much this diligence brings light to obscure and dark passages, clarity to tangled matters, and transparency to confused ones. In short, he left nothing unexamined and investigated everything he thought would be useful to him. He searched through very many libraries: nothing so recent, nothing so ancient, escaped his investigation conducted with the greatest vigilance. He omitted no stone or rock, no triumphal arch, no imperial edict, no marble base, no wall or building from which he could not extract titles, inscriptions, and epitaphs and transfer them into these learned commentaries.”

From this third rule, approved in this way by the most learned men, two corollaries descend that will be highly useful for our purposes.

## FIRST COROLLARY

8. The agreement of several persons—whether of writers more expert and closer in place and time, or of documents similarly connected with the events—especially when both those writers and those documents are supported by public authority, is a clear indication of historical truth.

[Col. 0243A]

## SECOND COROLLARY

The indications and agreement mentioned above have the greatest power reasonably to correct and amend copies written later, whenever they depart from the agreement just mentioned.

In my judgment, neither corollary, any more than the rule itself, requires arguments for proof, but only examples for explanation. Hundreds of examples will occur, as Gerbelius indicated, in Cuspinianus, who attends to the agreement of witnesses closer in place and more expert in order to reconcile or correct more remote and less competent authorities, whether authors or scribes who disagree. Nor will examples be lacking in the other writers praised above, if one wishes to run through a single consular letter in the works of Norisius. But from these Prolegomena of ours I prefer to borrow an example, so that the sensible reader may judge whether it is necessary to assent to this third rule and its corollaries.

Under the direction of this third rule, I have therefore attempted above, in the notes on the chronology of the Catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, to reconcile with Victor of Aquitaine the ancient Fathers and contemporary documents concerning the dating of Christ’s Passion to the year 28 of the common Christian era and to the consulship of the two Gemini. Why should I not follow, in Roman chronology—consular, Caesarean, and pontifical—the Roman or provincial authorities who, in the judgment of their contemporaries, surpassed the others in collecting and arranging the markers of time? Or why should I not defer to Victor of Aquitaine over his contemporaries in establishing the era of Easter and the Lord’s Passion, when we see that he himself was selected by the judgment of two Roman pontiffs, Hilary and Leo the Great, to arrange and restore the reckoning of time?

## FOURTH RULE

9. The fourth rule for arranging chronology will be the agreement of the times indicated by historical documents with the legal days established by law for carrying out the events recorded. Let an example clarify the rule.

The lawful day for sacred ordinations, especially episcopal ordinations, was also in the earlier centuries of the Christian Church Sunday, after the fast and vigils of Saturday, as we learn both from the teaching of the canons and from the sermons of Leo the Great. If, therefore, there is a discrepancy among Catalogues that establish the epoch of a pontiff in different ways, I would prefer, on the evidence of this rule, all other things being equal, the chronology that connects the ordination with the lawful time. I would place no confidence in the others, which overturn the times established by our predecessors for ordination, unless it were established from elsewhere by clear documents that the custom and the laws of the canons had been set aside for a reasonable cause by those who possessed the authority to set them aside.

10. Let two opinions, differing from one another in establishing the epoch of the pontificate of Saint Damasus, be presented to me as I investigate it. Let one opinion, together with the most ancient inscriptions and paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul and with almost all the Catalogues, historians, and chronologists, assert that Blessed Damasus sat for eighteen years, two months, and eleven days. Let another opinion, perhaps relying on that single Catalogue which Schelestratius calls the second among those he published in the first volume of *Ecclesiastical Antiquity*, assign twenty-two years, three months, and eleven days; or, with Baronius’s support, two months and twenty-seven days beyond seventeen years. Baronius prefers to shorten the eighteen full years assigned by Saint Jerome and Prosper, contemporaries of Damasus, so that the year in which Maximus entered the prefecture would fall within the beginning of Damasus’s pontificate. He would have judged otherwise if he had observed—as others later noted in the membranes of the city prefects edited by Bucherius and belonging to the age of Damasus—that the prefects of the City did not exercise their office from the Kalends of January for a full year, as ordinary consuls did, but from any day of the year for a period determined at the emperors’ discretion, for more or fewer months, within or beyond the limits of a year.

These two opinions, or even more, although they disagree so greatly in their totals, must nevertheless agree in one of the termini enclosing the total, namely in the day and year of the death of Blessed Damasus: that day was 11 December, in the consulship of Recimer and Clearchus, in the year 384 of the common Christian era. The date is confirmed by the archives of the Church, by ritual books, and by the martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, and Ado; Baronius agrees in the Roman martyrology, although he moves one or another entry back to 10 December in the Florentine manuscript. Prosper, who was writing at that time, recorded the year and the consuls, Recimer and Clearchus, in his *Chronicle*. Therefore, counting backward from 11 December of the year 384 of Christ through eighteen full years, two months, and ten days, according to the first opinion, which rests on Roman monuments, we arrive at the day on which Damasus assumed the pontificate: the Kalends of October in the year 366 of Christ, in the consulship of Gratian and Daglaiphus.

The Dominical Letter A of that same year shows that the Kalends of October, to which it was attached, coincided with a Sunday. Since this was suitable for episcopal consecration according to the laws of the sacred canons, it supplies support for this fourth rule, which we employ in directing pontifical chronology. The rule in turn gives mutual support for preferring the earlier chronology of Damasus’s pontificate to the second, which assigns him seventeen years, three months, and eleven days: the former assigns a lawful day to the ordination, whereas the latter assigns Friday, a day wholly unsuitable for consecration. That date was the Kalends of September in the year 367; from it one would count seventeen years, three months, and eleven days to 11 December 384.

Moreover, if Liberius died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October—as Faustinus and Marcellinus testify in their *Letter to Theodosius*—then certainly the lawful day for electing his successor could not have preceded that death by twenty-three days. Again, that letter records the death of Liberius in the consulship of Gratian and Daglaiphus, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October; and Jerome records the ordination of Damasus, his successor, in the same consulship in his *Chronicle*. It is certain among chronologists that these consuls opened the year 366 of the Christian era, and this will be clearly proved by us in the example of the fifth rule with which we shall conclude this chapter. Thus the period to be counted from October of the year 366 to December of the year 384, including two months, is eighteen full years, not merely seventeen, and these years are to be assigned to the administration of Blessed Damasus by the aid of this fourth rule, which we employ in the chronological critical method for the succession and see of the Roman pontiffs.

## FIFTH RULE

11. The fifth rule—or rather, the demonstration of correctly established chronology—will be some characteristic of an observed celestial motion [Col. 0245B], such as a solar or lunar eclipse, or the relative position and configuration of other fixed stars, that exactly corresponds to the interval of time required for completing those same motions of the heavenly bodies.

Among chronologists, this rule has the force of an axiom. No one so lightly versed in chronology and history that he does not know that the chief demonstration of the date of the Peloponnesian War is supplied by the eclipses recorded by Thucydides. The years of the Assyrian kings are likewise rendered certain in the era of Nabonassar by the eclipses that Ptolemy recorded in the *Almagest*. The same method applies equally to historians and chronologists in determining the periods of every age and region, since the wisest Creator of all things declared that the heavenly bodies had been so balanced and set in various motions by him that they might serve as documents for precisely measuring time by years, months, and days.

12. I shall not allow an example of this rule, both to explain and to confirm it, to be lacking. A striking example survives on an ancient stone excavated from the suburban Christian cemeteries in the Roman countryside and generously given to me by the distinguished man Antonio Boldetti, canon of Santa Maria in Trastevere. You may read it in his learned *Commentary on the Sacred Cemeteries of the Martyrs*, recently published, book 1, chapter 19, page 84. The words, faithfully reproduced from the marble itself, are:

[Col. 0245D]

> **A BOY, NAMED SIMPLICIUS, WAS BORN UNDER THE CONSULS [A W] OF THE DEIFIED AUGUSTUS JOVIAN AND VARRONIANUS, AT THE FOURTH HOUR OF THE NIGHT; HE LIVED UNTIL THE EIGHTH DAY BEFORE THE IDES OF MAY, ON SATURDAY, WITH THE MOON IN ITS TWENTIETH DAY, UNDER THE SIGN “API ORNO.”**

> *The readings “A W,” “IN VXIT” (apparently* vixit, “he lived”), *and “SIGNO API ORNO” are materially uncertain; no zodiacal sign has been supplied.*
So many chronological indications, showing the year and day, are contained in this inscription that it may serve as an example of ancient documents confirming dates. I shall review them briefly one by one, but shall dwell especially on the movements of the heavenly bodies, which attach the other indications to a definite time and turn them into demonstrations.

The year opened by the consulship of Jovian Augustus and Varronianus [Col. 0246A] is shown to have been the year of Jovian’s death, before 8 May, since Jovian is called “divine” (*divus*) in the inscription. Eutropius confirms this admirably: in this very consulship and with Jovian’s death he brings his history to a close, writing as follows about Jovian:

> “He died in the seventh month of his reign, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of March [16 February], at the age of—according to those who report the highest and lowest figures—thirty-three years. Through the benevolence of the emperors who succeeded him, he was enrolled among the gods. Such was the condition of the Roman state when Jovian and Varronianus were consuls, in the 1119th year from the foundation of the City.”

The consular fasti likewise assign the same college of consuls and the same death to the year 364 of the common Christian era, which was a leap year. [Col. 0246B] That Valentinian’s death occurred in a leap year is attested by another contemporary historian, Ammianus Marcellinus. Near the end of Book XXV and the beginning of Book XXVI he recounts the consular procession of Jovian Augustus with Varronianus, his son, who was crying and stubbornly resisting being carried in the chair according to custom; Jovian’s death followed shortly afterward. Ten days after that death, during which no one held the reins of imperial government, Valentinian arrived, summoned by the unanimous vote of all to assume command. Nevertheless, he postponed his advance to the nearest leap-day, “so that, avoiding the leap-day of the month of February then dawning—for he had learned that it had several times been disastrous to the Roman state”—he might reach the following day:

> “When he advanced into the field and was permitted to mount the tribunal, which had been built higher, he was proclaimed ruler of the empire amid the most favorable appearance of the election and the unanimous will of those present. Soon, surrounded by imperial dress and a crown, he was named Augustus,” etc.

The leap-year indication asserted by the historians would indeed identify the year’s place within the four-year cycle, but it would still leave us uncertain in which four-year cycle the leap year avoided by Valentinian was to be found. The decisive evidence is supplied by the character of the Saturday falling on 8 May, and by the moon’s position in the sign of Capricorn as it was carried toward the eastern horizon around the fourth hour of the night—the same hour at which the child Simplicius, represented on the marble, was born. These details establish that the consuls mentioned, and Valentinian’s succession, belong to the year 364 of the common Christian era.

[Col. 0246D] The tenth Latin cycle, consisting of eighty-four Julian years, published by R. P. Bucherius and explained by Cardinal de Noris, had begun in the year 298 of the common Christian era, when Faustus II and Gallus were consuls. Consequently, in the year 364 of the Christian era, the sixty-fourth year of that cycle was running, and on the Kalends of January it had Thursday, that is, weekday V, and the twelfth lunar day, as recorded in the ancient manuscripts elucidated by Noris and Bucherius. Therefore the day of the Kalends of May, which in a leap year is the 122nd day, fell on Saturday; and the eighth day of that month—called 8 May—was likewise assigned to Saturday.

Again, if on the Kalends of January of that year, according to the Latin cycle—which was proceeding with sufficient accuracy in that century, as Cardinal Noris shows—the moon was twelve days old, then after 121 complete days had elapsed, or 120 in a leap year where one day is suppressed, the moon was thirteen days old; and after another seven days it was twenty days old, as the inscription reckons it.

Finally, in order to test the demonstration of the time by astronomical tables through the moon’s position in Capricorn at the fourth hour of the night, we should proceed as follows. In the year 364 of the common Christian era, on 8 May, the sun was in the eighteenth degree of Taurus; and at noon on the seventh day it was traversing the seventeenth degree of Taurus. Thus, at sunset on the seventh day, the seventeenth degree of Scorpio was rising. Four hours later—that is, at the fourth hour of the night mentioned in the inscription—approximately the eighteenth degree of Capricorn was rising. At that time the moon was near the same degree of the same sign according to its mean motions, as anyone may see from the astronomical tables.

To leave nothing lacking in the test of these eminent chronological indications, attached to the consuls Jovian Augustus and Varronianus and to the year of Jovian’s death, all of which are collected in this memorable stone, it is worthwhile to verify, by any lunar tables, even tables of mean motions (to accommodate convenience, since there is no need to pursue one or another degree of correction, by which the true positions are derived from mean motions), the moon’s position in the zodiacal circle at the time marked on the marble, namely at the fourth hour of the night following sunset on the seventh day of May. After an hour and a half from the fourth night-hour, midnight dividing—according to Roman practice—the seventh day from the eighth, the eighth day of May dawned, called 8 May, at the beginning of Saturday, which the Romans called Saturn’s day.

On 7 May the sun was in the seventeenth degree of Taurus. For the Roman latitude this produces a semi-nocturnal arc of five equal hours. Therefore the fourth hour of the night after that sunset, among the Romans who divided every night into twelve hours, corresponds to ten astronomical hours and twenty hourly minutes after noon on the seventh day.

[Col. 0247D] [Col. 0248A] The root of the mean lunar motions, at the Roman meridian on the Kalends of January at the beginning of the common Christian era, gives Capricorn; and at that same hour that degree of Capricorn rose with the moon from the eastern horizon under the consuls Jovian the divine and Varronianus—namely, in the year 364 of the common Christian era, also a leap year, when the child Simplicius was born.

The demonstrations of dates derived from these observed characteristics of the heavenly motions, corresponding so precisely to the intervals of years, months, and days by which they are separated from our own age, constitute the fifth rule of the chronology proposed here.

### 13.

I shall briefly show how much this same consulship of Jovian and Varronianus, together with Jovian’s death, clearly assignable to the year 364 of the common Christian era, contributes to establishing the dates of the Roman pontiffs.

Saint Jerome, then in the vigor of age, assigns in his continuation of the *Chronicle* of Eusebius the death of Jovian, while he was consul with Varronianus, to the fourth year of the 284th Olympiad, together with Valentinian’s succession. Two years later, namely in the second year of the 285th Olympiad, he records the death of Pope Liberius and the succession of Damasus, to whom Jerome himself served as secretary during his apostolate. According to Cassiodorus and the other compilers of the fasti, the consuls Gratianus and Daglaiphus were likewise two years removed from the consulship of Jovian and Varronianus; Liberius’s death is assigned to their consulship in the petition of Faustinus and Marcellinus to Theodosius, cited above in the fourth rule.

Once it has therefore been demonstrated that the year of Jovian’s consulship and death, and of the consulship of his colleague and son Varronianus, coincides with the year 364 of the common Christian era, and that Pope Liberius’s death followed two years later according to the testimony of contemporary writers, the election of Damasus must necessarily be assigned, together with the consuls Gratianus and Daglaiphus, to the year 366 of the common Christian era.

Having proposed, explained, and proved these five rules of chronological evidence, we may safely proceed in the following chapters to arrange and demonstrate individually the dates of the Roman pontiffs.

## CHAPTER III

The succession of the Roman pontiffs and its chronology are set out, to be derived and established from a public monument of the Roman Church, still surviving in the patriarchal basilica of Saint Paul the Apostle on the Ostian Way, placed there by Saint Leo the Great together with the mosaic, or by Pope Symmachus when he adorned it with paintings in the fifth century of Christ.

[Col. 0248D]

## SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

I. The succession and catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, expressed in painting and writing in the basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, must be attributed either to Saint Leo the Great or to Pope Symmachus and referred to the fifth century of Christ.—II. It has been mentioned by several writers of our own age, but until now published by no one, nor carefully observed or compared with written catalogues; it is now edited for the first time. It appears similar to another catalogue, with a succession of pontiffs and paintings likewise representing the histories of both Testaments, placed or restored in the Vatican basilica during the time of Pope Formosus. In both basilicas a more recent succession of pontiffs was also added beneath the earlier one under Nicholas III; this still survives in the basilica of Saint Paul, though greatly damaged, above the architraves of the columns.—III. That older succession, painted in the fifth century in the basilica of Saint Paul, extends from Saint Peter to Saint Innocent I on the southern wall of the central nave; while the images and inscriptions that followed immediately on the western wall are now indistinct.—IV. The more recent succession, painted at the command of Nicholas III, as Veggius, Grimaldi, and Ciampini relate, is distinguished from the higher and much older succession, as may be observed in Ciampini’s plates, which show the Vatican series and are inserted here.—V. Besides the two ordered successions painted in the time of Leo the Great and Nicholas III, certain repeated images of pontiffs are visible on the opposite, northern wall of the central nave of Saint Paul’s, carelessly painted in confused order. They are works of uncertain date and therefore must not be taken into account in arranging the chronology.—VI. The two ordered successions once colored in the Vatican basilica—the older under Pope Formosus, the more recent under Nicholas III—are described; Grimaldi inserted them in public plates before the old basilica of the Prince of the Apostles was demolished under Paul V.—VII. The authority of both the ancient successions painted in the basilicas of Saints Peter and Paul in the centuries of Leo the Great, Symmachus, and Formosus, and of the more recent one added there by Nicholas III. As for the succession formed under Nicholas: since the chronological numbers expressed in it were taken from the older succession, it derives its authority from that same source. The pontifical ornaments, however, added by the painter’s discretion to the images of the pontiffs from Saint Sylvester onward, contrary to the evidence and usage both of the older upper succession surviving there and of the mosaics and paintings of Rome, as well as of coins struck in Rome down to the ninth and the beginning of the tenth century of Christ, indicate only the usage of Nicholas’s age, in which they were painted.—VIII. The square ornament or insignia observed by Grimaldi in the single image of Liberius in the Vatican series was not merely derived from ancient painting and custom; it also indicates that a succession was once painted in antiquity, ending in Liberius’s time, just as in the most ancient Bucherian Catalogue. Such a square insignia is consistently asserted, on the testimony of ancient and recent writers alike, to be an indication of a living pontiff.—IX. It is shown, from the unanimous statements of historians, that the succession of Roman pontiffs painted in the three patriarchal basilicas within and outside the City—namely, the Lateran, Vatican, and Pauline basilicas—was repeated in antiquity by Nicholas III, while the old succession remained untouched; from that older succession he arranged and reproduced the order of the individual pontiffs and the chronological numbers in his more recent series, placed beneath the images and inscriptions of the older one.—X. The authority of that ancient succession, which must be called the archetypal Catalogue and the source of the others, is still sufficiently observable and preserved in the basilica of Saint Paul.

### 1.
