I have wondered that, among so many writers who investigate the catalogues and dates of the Roman pontiffs so diligently in libraries, both Greek and Latin, and illuminate them with learned commentaries, no one, so far as I know, has applied himself to publishing and comparing with the written catalogues the succession that has been publicly displayed since the age of Leo the Great or Pope Symmachus—as I shall show shortly—in the most celebrated basilica of the Doctor of the Nations on the Ostian Way, at the second milestone from the City, where it is visible to everyone. All the conditions and rules of examination and evidence explained and defended in the preceding chapter agree in favoring this monument above others of the same subject.

From where could we obtain more probable evidence concerning the pontiffs of the Roman Church than from its principal basilicas? Where should we seek indications both older and more evident, possessing public authority and testimony, than in this basilica erected in the name of the Doctor of the Nations? Here the zeal of Leo the Great in providing for it is conspicuous, as is his care in selecting and arranging its ornaments, visible in the mosaic still surviving above the great arch of the central nave. Its completion through the piety and generosity of Galla Placidia and through the zeal of the holy pontiff Leo is attested by the inscription, still read today, which expresses the following thought in verse:

> “Placidia’s pious mind rejoices that the entire beauty of her father’s work shines through the zeal of the pontiff Leo.”

Adjacent to this mosaic are paintings representing the history of the Old Testament. They adorn the southern wall of the central nave of the same basilica, from the presbytery to the façade facing the setting sun. Opposite them, on the northern wall, are the events of the New Testament expressed in color. Each wall rests upon twenty columns, supplied with bases, capitals, architrave, frieze, and cornice.

Above the cornice a stylobate is painted, extending along the entire length of the nave, as though separating the second gallery from the lower one. On this stylobate one sees the succession and catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, together with their individual images, counted from the bust of Blessed Peter, which occupies the more honored position nearest the altar. Each image is colored within a circular space, which is why the ancient Romans called them shield-images (*clypeatae*). Between the images and the circles an equal amount of space was left, so that an equal number of brief inscriptions, painted in large letters, could be placed in the field. These give the names of the pontiffs to whom they belong, together with the numbers of years, months, and days during which each held the Roman see, recorded in numerical letters according to Roman usage.

### 2.

I therefore wondered that this catalogue and chronological succession, so conspicuous, so ancient, and placed in so distinguished a location—either by Blessed Leo the Great together with the mosaic, or by Symmachus together with the paintings—should not yet have exercised the calculations of any chronologist, nor even stirred any writer to reproduce it accurately and insert it into the history and description of a basilica celebrated in so many volumes. Serranus did not include it in his account of the seven churches of Rome; nor did Panvinio, in his book on the same subject, do more than state, on page 73, that the whole basilica was adorned with ancient paintings of the Old and New Testaments.

Ciampini devoted an entire chapter, Chapter 24 of the first volume of *Ancient Monuments*, to describing the mosaic of the great arch constructed by Leo the Great, since he chose to explain only the mosaic works. He does indeed mention the paintings in his book on the Sacred Buildings constructed by Constantine the Great. They were arranged in precisely the same manner in the Vatican basilica, where they remained preserved until the beginning of the seventeenth century, when the walls were demolished under Paul V in the construction of the new basilica. He also engraved images of them in Plate X, where he presents an orthographic drawing of the wall forming the central nave of that church, decorated with exactly the same division and ornament that we see on the surface of the walls belonging to the central nave in the basilica of Saint Paul.

The order of columns rising from the pavement supports the architraves, frieze, and cornice, as Ciampini’s Plates X and XI show in the Vatican basilica. Since I have obtained these plates, I think they should be shown here again, so that the matters which must be retained concerning the most ancient succession of the supreme pontiffs painted in the basilica on the Ostian Way in the fifth century of Christ, and concerning the other, much more recent succession painted under Nicholas III, may be placed more faithfully before the eyes and minds of readers. Thus anyone wishing to observe the archetype in the basilica of Saint Paul may compare the surviving chronological inscriptions of the older succession with the catalogues.

In the frieze supported by the columns of the old Vatican basilica, several circular fields—G H, Plate X—contained images of the Roman pontiffs, produced under Nicholas III. They were dressed in head coverings adopted much later for pontifical ornament: namely, a raised mitre or even one adorned with a crown, and so forth, as Ciampini shows more clearly in Plate XI, in the same succession above the letter E.

We see similar images, painted at the command of Nicholas III in the basilica of Saint Paul, in the lower succession, placed above the capitals of the columns. Besides the images of the pontiffs, these also give their names and the chronology expressed in letters, and they display the characteristic form of the script belonging to Nicholas’s own age.

Painters and engravers who first issued the faces of the Roman pontiffs in bronze or wooden impressions imitated this succession. They paid no attention to the much older succession placed above, both in the Pauline and in the Vatican basilica, above the cornice of the columns on the parallelepiped, or stylobate, marked by the letters A B in Ciampini’s Plate XI. Those craftsmen, finding their labor shortened by drawing the images nearer to the viewer, were little concerned with the antiquity of the older succession. Yet in it the age and customs of those times are clearly expressed, as I shall observe shortly.

### 3.

In the basilica of Saint Paul, therefore, this older succession of the supreme pontiffs is read without interruption on the wall situated on the southern side of the central nave. It contains forty-two circular fields and an equal number of images of pontiffs, one in each field, from Saint Peter to Saint Innocent I. It also contains an equal number of brief inscriptions, painted in large letters on the stylobate, as I have said, giving the name of the pontiff attached to each and indicating the years, months, and days assigned to him in the see of Peter.

The last of the forty-two, belonging to Saint Innocent, was composed as follows:

> “Innocentius: he held the see 15 years, 3 months, 20 days.”

The inscriptions that followed came immediately after the bend of the corner on the western wall. There, however, both the images and the inscriptions have perished through the ravages of time, the coating of plaster on which they had been painted having fallen away. Nothing remains of that painting except certain portions of the circles that once contained [Col. 0252A] the images of the Roman pontiffs who succeeded Saint Innocent.

Moreover, that Saint Innocent must be counted as the forty-second among the successors of Peter is attested by the Palatine-Vatican codex of Bede, written 865 years ago, from which the Catalogue was taken. Schlestratius published it as number 22 in his book *Illustrated Ecclesiastical Antiquity*, and we cited it above. He also appears in the forty-second place in the second Catalogue of the library of Queen Christina of Sweden, now the Alexandrian-Vatican Library. Many of the words of the Lives in the work of Anastasius were taken from that Catalogue and published by Schlestratius and by us together with the text of the *Book of the Pontiffs* and its variant readings.

### 4.

Above the succession of pontiffs thus painted on the stylobate, and above the other paintings representing the histories of the Old Testament in quadrangular fields, broad windows admit light. Their intervening spaces are filled with images of prophets, almost of colossal stature, just as we recently see—or see restored in accordance with the ancient custom preserved in the three principal basilicas of Rome—in the Lateran basilica.

In the old Vatican structure, too, a similarly colored succession of Roman bishops, with the histories of both Testaments placed above it and figures of prophets above those, is explicitly recalled by the notary Jacobus Grimaldus. He was charged with examining and describing the arrangement and ornaments of that old building and inserting them in public plates before it was demolished by the masons during the enlargement of the new basilica under Paul V.

Moreover, in the Vatican crypts one can still see a graphic drawing, rendered in colors, both of the ground plan and of the elevation of the old basilica. Bishop Ciampini later reproduced it on copper plates in the aforementioned book on the sacred buildings constructed by Constantine the Great.

To these authors, Grimaldi and Ciampini, we also owe the preservation of the memory both of the date of the paintings and of the double succession of Roman pontiffs arranged there. I shall not hesitate to append their testimonies, so that the antiquity and authority of such monuments may be established, as well as the evidence for pontifical chronology preserved in them through the uncorrupted testimony of so many centuries. For this reason I have decided to examine and observe these matters with particular care.

[Col. 0252D] Ciampini, therefore, in *Sacred Buildings*, Chapter 4, pages 34 and following, describes the individual parts and ornaments of the walls of the old Vatican basilica. When he reaches the succession of pontiffs already mentioned and drawn in Plates X and XI, he indicates that the paintings were added or restored by Pope Formosus in the following words:

> “The remaining paintings, one part of which represented the history of the Old Testament—some of them having been erased by the ravages of time, as can easily be inferred from the same Plate X—and the other part representing images of various saints above, were very ancient and, already almost consumed by age, were made by order of Formosus, the first supreme pontiff, who flourished in the year 890. In the frieze, moreover, which projects above the architraves of the columns, namely in those circular signs indicated in Plate X, letters G and H, there were painted the heads of the Roman pontiffs, just as in the other circular signs placed above them, indicated there by the letters I and L and shown more clearly in another plate, Plate XI, drawn on a larger scale under the letters A, B, C, D, and so forth.”

This is Ciampini’s account.

From the public plates prepared on this matter by the aforementioned Jacobus Grimaldi, appointed by Paul V as the notary responsible for the task, whose autograph I was permitted to consult and copy in the archive of the most sacred basilica, with the assent of the most eminent and reverend Lord Cardinal Albani, archpriest, and with the consent of the entire most reverend chapter—from which Ciampini had also drawn his material—it is useful to present a survey of the ancient paintings that were visible there.

It will establish that the succession of pontiffs painted above the architraves and cornice of the columns, on the higher stylobate beneath the colored paintings of the Old Testament, indicated by the letters I L in Ciampini’s Plate X, was older and belonged to the age of Pope Formosus. The other succession of the same pontiffs, placed within the cornice and architrave of the order of columns in the frieze, where the letters G and H appear in Ciampini’s Plate X, was a work of a much later age, since it had been painted there by order of Nicholas III nearly four hundred full years after the succession arranged above by Formosus.

### 5.

The same difference of age is still clearly discernible in the double succession of Roman bishops visible in the basilica of Saint Paul. The only difference is that in the Pauline basilica the succession above the cornice, accurately reproducing the order and chronology of the same pontiffs, on the southern wall and on the stylobate beneath the paintings of the Old Testament, appears to belong to the fifth century of Christ, as I shall show below.

The mosaic of the triumphal arch, immediately adjacent to that wall in the same central nave of the basilica, unquestionably belongs to that century. It still bears the names of Leo the Great and the Empress Placidia, who ordered the work to be completed.

On the opposite wall, however, the northern wall, the succession of pontiffs was disorderly arranged by some incompetent caretaker who, in a later century, wished either to fill the vacant circular fields or to imitate the damaged pigments of the opposite wall. In a thoroughly unsuccessful attempt, he mixed everything together without observing any order or chronology. He placed near one another pontiffs separated by several centuries and repeated several who were already represented in their proper places in the same fifth-century succession painted on the southern wall.

For example, after Hadrian I, to whom the eighth circle on the northern wall belongs when counted from the front of the basilica, the next pontiff occupying the ninth circle is inscribed MARCELLUS—namely, the martyr under Diocletian, five hundred full years older than Hadrian I. Then AGATHO follows, approximately 280 years more recent than Marcellus and nearly a full century earlier than Hadrian.

Nor did that painter of the northern wall express the chronology more successfully or carefully than he could have done by borrowing it at least from the pontiffs repeated on the opposite wall. He would have seen that five years and seven months were assigned to Marcellus’s tenure of Peter’s see—as they are also assigned in the ancient and more reliable Catalogues—and that it was not extended to eight years and two months, as he painted it.

It is therefore established that the paintings on the northern wall were added later, in a subsequent age, as is also indicated by the marble inscription on that same northern side, which deforms in barbarous style a brief letter of Gregory III, brought forward by us in the preface to the first volume, number 38.

When, therefore, I call the older succession, placed higher in the basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way, I mean that genuine succession, not hitherto corrupted, which on the southern wall counts forty-two pontiffs from Blessed Peter to Saint Innocent I.

The added section, placed at a later date and plainly corrupted, painted on the opposite northern wall with disordered sequence and erroneous chronological indications, is an undigested rhapsody. Its author, source, and indeed any model are unknown; it must be considered worthless according to the second rule of the preceding chapter.

### 6.

Beneath that older succession, assigned to the southern wall in the fifth century, another, more recent succession was added by Nicholas III in the basilica of Saint Paul. It proceeds in suitable order from Saint Peter to the succeeding pontiffs, with chronological indications added in what are called affixed letters, distorted in a barbarous style according to the conditions of that age.

Most of the paintings and letters, however, have fallen away, because the fresh plaster applied over the old walls and worked with gypsum did not adhere sufficiently well. Nevertheless, no loss occurred to the history or chronology in so recent a monument, where the ancient work, belonging to the age of Leo the Great, remains intact in its most important part.

The two successions of the Pauline basilica—the most ancient Leonine one above the cornice, and the more recent one added by Nicholas III below the cornice on the architraves—were imitated by the two remarkable successions in the Vatican. The upper is attributed to Pope Formosus and the lower to Nicholas III, also in the public plates of the notary Grimaldi, folio 161, where they are described as follows.

[Col. 0255]

[Col. 0257A]

> “In this year [1610], the little boat in the atrium, executed in mosaic by the excellent painter Giotto, for which work Cardinal Jacobus Stefaneschi, the great-grandson of Nicholas III, had spent 2,200 florins from his own funds, was enclosed with wood and strongly protected. It was transferred over the ruins, which had formed a hill,” etc.

> “On the walls above the principal columns of the central nave were paintings of Pope Formosus. On the right-hand side when leaving the basilica were scenes from the New Testament; but because the wall was leaning and dust easily adhered to it there, they could scarcely be seen. I noted several: ‘He appeared to the eleven apostles’; ‘The descent into limbo’; ‘The baptism in the Jordan’; and above the fourth and fifth columns the Crucified One was likewise painted with the two thieves. Beneath him were visible the very ancient painted heads of the apostles Simon and Jude; lights used to be lit before them on the feast of those same apostles.
>
> “On the other wall, which was likewise leaning but which dust could not strike, were: ‘The ark of the Flood’; ‘The inundation of the waters’; ‘Lot goes out from Sodom’; ‘Abraham saw three and worshiped one’; ‘The sacrifice of Isaac’; ‘Moses and Aaron speak to Pharaoh, asking him to let the people go’; ‘Moses and Aaron turn the rod into a serpent,’” etc.

He then continues by listing other scenes from Exodus painted there in the square fields shown in Ciampini’s Plate X. He adds the following concerning the older succession of pontiffs there, marked I L:

> “Beneath these paintings were the heads of the pontiffs, with a mantle in the manner of the ancients, together with their names; for example: ‘Siricius held the see 15 years, 5 months, 20 days’; ‘Anastasius held the see … years’; ‘Felix held the see 1 year, … months’; ‘Julius held the see … years’; ‘Eusebius held the see … years’; ‘Hormisdas held the see … years.’”

Finally, descending to the lower succession of the same pontiffs, arranged by order of Nicholas III in the frieze and on the architraves, he writes as follows:

> “In the frieze of mosaic work above the architraves of the columns were circles with images of the supreme pontiffs, which, as Mapheus Veggius says, Nicholas III had painted. On the left-hand side when leaving the basilica were Pius, Soter, Eleutherus, Victor, Zephyrinus, Callistus, Urban, Anterus, Pontianus, Fabianus, and Cornelius. Above the architrave of the African column were Lucius, Stephen, Sixtus, Dionysius, Felix, Eutychianus, Caius, and Marcellinus. These eight pontiffs were on the wall of the front of the church.
>
> “Marcellus was above another African column, followed by Eusebius and Miltiades. Sylvester had a tiara with only one crown. Those before him had diadems with a pallium in the Greek manner. After Sylvester, those who are saints had round diadems and a tiara with one crown: Mark and Julius. Liberius had only a square diadem. Then came Felix, Damasus, Siricius, and Anastasius.
>
> “Above the paintings of Formosus were standing prophets (see Ciampini’s Plate X, letters C and D). The entire painting of Formosus was quite inept, barbarous, and faded.”

These passages, copied by us from Grimaldi’s codex, are sufficient to perceive that the method of ornamentation in the old Vatican basilica was plainly similar to that of the Pauline basilica, and they provide indications for demonstrating the date and authority of both successions.

From Grimaldi’s narratives and descriptions, and from Ciampini’s drawings, we understand clearly that almost the same method of ornamenting the central nave was preserved in both basilicas: columns and paintings displayed images of the pontiffs both above and below the cornice, together with their ordered succession marked by chronological indications. The other paintings represented biblical history above the older succession of pontiffs; and images of prophets, extended above to colossal size and filling the spaces between the windows beneath the ceiling, were arranged as they still survive in the basilica of Saint Paul.

### 7.

It is part of our subject to pursue more carefully the authority of both of these ordered successions: the more recent one made by Nicholas III in both basilicas, and the ancient ones made by Formosus in the Vatican basilica and by Leo the Great or Symmachus in the Pauline basilica.

To begin with the nearer one, undertaken by Nicholas III, which nearly all more recent writers after the painter and engraver Tempesta have reproduced, abandoning the upper and older one as being farther from view: it is regrettable that the artists employed by Nicholas, although they rendered with sufficient accuracy the chronological numbers expressed in the older series, did not imitate with equal fidelity and diligence the ornamentation of the images that still survives intact in the ancient series. They would certainly have seen that neither Saint Sylvester nor his successors down to the tenth century of Christ had been fitted by our ancestors with those enormous tiaras, either bare or crowned—whether they painted them in colors, joined them from mosaic tesserae, or even struck the likenesses of the pontiffs on coins—which the artists themselves forged on their own authority and added contrary to the evidence of the paintings and mosaics of the City that still survive, transferring the usage of their own age, separated by eight hundred years from the Leonine age and by more than nine hundred from the age of Saint Sylvester, to those earlier times. It would have been better to inspect the image of Honorius I, placed in a mosaic of the apse of Saint Agnes Outside-the-Walls and belonging to his own age, or that of Leo III in the Leonine Triclinium at the Lateran patriarchate, or that of Paschal I, represented by him in mosaic in three sacred buildings—namely, in the titular churches of Saint Praxedes and Saint Cecilia, and in the deaconry of Saint Mary in Domnica—as well as in other works engraved by Ciampini. [Col. 0258D] They would then have seen that both the predecessors of Sylvester and his successors down to the end of the ninth century after Christ were depicted bareheaded, showing as their only ornament the clerical tonsure, or crown, in their own hair. Such are the genuine and untouched images painted in the basilica of Saint Paul in the fifth century and extending from Saint Peter to Innocent I.

The pontifical ornaments of the age of Nicholas III, therefore, transferred by prolepsis and superimposed upon the age of Sylvester, contribute no ancient authority to that same series. The chronological notes, however, which count the years, months, and days assigned to each pontiff’s tenure and still survive in the ancient series, since they faithfully reproduce it—insofar as this can be determined from the numbers that remain—transfer to Nicholas’s series the authority of the older one, just as publicly authenticated copies borrow their authority from their exemplars. Accordingly, wherever the numbers of the upper series have been so effaced by the injury of time that they do not appear complete, they may be supplied from this series of Nicholas, which repeats them, according to the rule of chronological criteria established by us above, in chapter [III], sections 6 and 7.

As I reported above, however, most of these paintings added by Nicholas III to the ancient ones on the walls, over lime plaster worked with gypsum by inexperienced masons, have fallen away because they adhered insufficiently firmly. They therefore provide little assistance in supplying the few missing numbers. The chronological supplements of the older series are nevertheless completed from another source, namely from ancient copies derived from the same archetype and faithfully reproduced in codices and Catalogues that surpass our own age by eight hundred and nine hundred years, as we shall explain below.

8. What I stated above concerning the merely clerical crown represented on the heads of the Roman pontiffs, both in mosaics and in other ancient paintings down to the beginning of the tenth century after Christ, in no way conflicts with that square sign or insignia represented behind the heads of those same pontiffs. Learned writers have not merely indicated it but also explained it: it was used to show that the man to whom such an ornament was attached was still alive when his image was painted.

In the aforementioned mosaics of Leo III and Paschal I, and in several others constructed at Rome and still surviving above the apses of the titular churches of Saint Mark and Saints Cosmas and Damian, that square insignia is used for pontiffs who were living. That it was an indication of the living is also attested by John the Deacon in his *Life of Saint Gregory the Great*, book IV, chapter 84. Alamannus adds, in his explanation of the Lateran mosaic, page 65, that the sign was both an emblem of enduring life and of virtues handed down (*retradis*, reading uncertain), attributed chiefly to priestly prelates and sometimes also to princes exercising royal or even imperial dignity. This is clearly demonstrated by the very ancient inscription accompanying the image of Charlemagne, ornamented in this way, in which four principal virtues—those we call the cardinal virtues—are said to have been conspicuous in him while he was still alive.

This square insignia, therefore, customarily attached to images of living pontiffs and observed in most mosaics constructed before the tenth century after Christ, is not merely compatible with the indications of the ancient pontifical series; it contributes remarkably to confirming the equal authority of such an ancient painted pontifical series in the Roman basilicas and of the old Catalogues, especially that most ancient one ending with Liberius. With the agreement of all learned scholars, we have seen this Catalogue, in Bucherius, Schelestratius, and the other writers on the subject, preferred in authority and antiquity to all the others.

The diligence Grimaldi employed in describing the series of supreme pontiffs, repeated by Nicholas III in the Vatican basilica, expressly warned us that among the pontiffs of the fourth century only Liberius had been adorned with this square insignia, while the others before Sylvester had been ornamented with the crown of the clerical tonsure and those after Sylvester with the tiara painted by Nicholas’s artist. Since the artist did not dare to alter this singular square insignia, taken from an ancient exemplar, in the case of Liberius, or to attach it to the others, it indicates that an ancient series once existed which, like the Bucherian Catalogue, had been set out while Liberius was still alive; and for that reason it had placed this square insignia—an indication, namely, of a living person—on his head. Thanks are therefore due to Grimaldi, who preserved even in Nicholas III’s series these records of earlier ages and of the Liberian Catalogue.

[Col. 0260B] 9. Moreover, that this more recent series was painted at the command of Nicholas III four hundred and forty years ago, both in the basilica of Saint Paul, where it is still seen, and in the other two patriarchal basilicas, the Lateran and the Vatican; and that the number and order of the pontiffs were taken from that more ancient series placed earlier on the walls—in the Paulina in the age of Leo the Great and in the Vatican in the age of Formosus—this is attested by all the historians who are counted from the age of Nicholas to our own. Let those whom I list here for the sake of brevity stand for all the others.

Benedict Platina recounts the matter in this way in the *Life of Nicholas III*, as does Ptolemy of Lucca in Raynaldus under the year of Christ 1280, section 25. I shall transcribe Ptolemy’s words from Raynaldus, for they indicate that in the three patriarchal basilicas that older series had been visible, and that from it, by Nicholas’s command, the order and number of the supreme pontiffs had been taken—an order which he himself had proposed for immediate inspection in the lower and more recent series:

> “Nicholas III,” he says, “made many innovations. First, because at Saint Peter’s he built a very splendid pontifical palace, etc. He almost entirely renewed the church of Blessed Peter, and had the number of the supreme pontiffs written according to the images in the church of Blessed Peter in an elevated place, and in that of Blessed Paul and of Saint John Lateran.”

10. It is therefore necessary to return to that archetypal series which Nicholas, separated from us by five centuries, proposed for imitation and continuation, since it was genuine and had been displayed by his predecessors for so many centuries in those same patriarchal basilicas, which the entire Christian people, hurrying to the thresholds of the Apostles, endeavored to visit, observe, and copy.

It is certainly astonishing that those concerned with the Catalogues and chronology of the pontiffs—who consulted so many codices and archives in order to bring forth the most ancient and especially the most genuine monuments—did not turn their eyes to that archetypal series indicated by Nicholas to later generations as an exemplar and surviving in at least two basilicas down to the age of Paul V; for only the Lateran series had been consumed by fire after Nicholas.

So far as I can determine by reflection, [Col. 0261A] and by following the rules established in the preceding chapter for discovering and confirming the truth of chronology, Nicholas’s judgment guides the studies of all learned men toward the truth they so urgently seek. For that older and genuine series, so large a part of which is still preserved and visible on the walls of the basilica of Saint Paul, surpasses the others so greatly in authority and antiquity that, by the testimony of every age, it has been regarded as the source and origin of the more accurate Catalogues. I trust that I shall demonstrate this in the following chapter.

# CHAPTER IV

**On the antiquity and authority of the series and chronology of the Roman pontiffs, which is seen painted together with the mosaic of Saint Leo the Great in the central nave of the basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way.** It is shown that the older and more faithful Catalogues of the pontiffs took their origin from this source, and that, by the uninterrupted testimony of succeeding centuries, the chronology painted here was always preferred to the others with public authority.

[Col. 0261B]

## SYNOPSIS OF THE CHAPTER

I. The series and chronology of the Roman pontiffs painted in the basilica of Saint Paul still survives sufficiently clearly preserved for most pontiffs from Saint Peter to Saint Innocent I, so that it can be compared with the older and more reliable Catalogues, especially those preserved in the archives of Italy.

II. Why it ought to be compared with the codices of Italy, and especially with those nearer to the City, according to the rules of chronological criteria established in the preceding chapter.

III. Great and precise diligence was required to copy this chronology faithfully from the images and inscriptions [Col. 0261C] of the supreme pontiffs, painted on the southern wall of the central nave approximately in the fifth century after Christ. Instruments were employed so that each surviving letter might be made clearly visible at that distance.

IV. The ancient copyists of the Catalogues, especially those who lived in distant provinces outside Italy, even when they visited Rome and observed these paintings, images, and inscriptions, could easily have transcribed many things incorrectly, since they lacked in their observations the aids that we were fortunate enough to employ. Moreover, when the numbers represented in Roman letters in the prototype shine forth in colors that have faded, and are viewed from the floor at so great a distance from the eye, the observer requires exceptionally sharp sight—or assistance from optical instruments—lest he be deceived when passing over them hastily.

V. Italian copyists, especially those living in the suburban region and in Campania, had more frequent opportunities and greater leisure to observe and copy those paintings and inscriptions. They could therefore leave us a more accurate exemplar from the same prototype than foreigners visiting Rome but hastening their return to their own libraries and monasteries.

VI. The series of the Roman pontiffs and their chronology, painted in large letters on the southern wall of the basilica of Saint Paul, is recognized as belonging to the fifth century after Christ. First, this is shown by the style of the painting, compared with the mosaic constructed in the age of Leo the Great and Galla Placidia. [Col. 0261D]

VII. Second, this is confirmed by the account in the *Book of the Pontiffs*, from which it is clear that the paintings were added together with the mosaic in the basilica of Saint Paul by Saint Leo the Great, and repaired or enlarged in the same century by Pope Symmachus; nor is any successor mentioned who commissioned these paintings.

VIII. Third, it is established by the testimony of Pope Adrian, who wrote to Charlemagne in defense of the veneration of sacred images, in a letter recited and published in the Acts of the Second Council of Nicaea. There the mosaic work and the paintings of histories and images in the basilica of Saint Paul are expressly attributed to Saint Leo the Great.

IX. The fourth argument demonstrating that this series and chronology were placed there in the fifth century is derived from the point at which the same ordered series of images and chronology of the supreme pontiffs ends. The remaining colored images on the northern wall are repetitions [Col. 0262A] and transpositions both of the same pontiffs and of their successors, with no order preserved according to age or succession, but added indiscriminately by some inept custodian in a later and uncertain age.

X. That ordered series and chronology, painted in the fifth century in the basilica of Saint Paul, as well as a similar series once existing under Pope Formosus in the Lateran and the Vatican, are reported by the older and more reliable codices of the archives of Italy.

XI. The authority of this chronology is confirmed by the uninterrupted agreement of twelve centuries, from the Leonine age to our own, consistently expressing the same chronology in public documents. In the following chapter it will be shown that these documents agree, for each pontiff and his respective dates, with the Paulina mentioned above.

[Col. 0262B]

1. It would be a sign of the indolence and intolerable negligence of our age if it failed to bring forward those precious remnants of the archetypal Catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, which alone now survive on the inner southern wall of the basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way. All the other images and inscriptions of a similar pontifical Catalogue have been completely erased and scattered—the Catalogue that had been painted for the instruction of posterity both there and in each of the two patriarchal basilicas within the City, the Lateran and the Vatican, as we mentioned shortly before on the authority of Ptolemy of Lucca, Platina, Veggio, Raynaldus, Grimaldi, and other historians.

When I call those surviving images and inscriptions of the Roman pontiffs “remnants of the Catalogue,” I do not wish them to be regarded as so few, or their colors and letters as so faded or worn away, that most of them are not visible from Saint Peter to Saint Innocent I. On the contrary, of the forty-two images of as many supreme pontiffs covering this same period, most are intact, especially after Saint Anterus. Of an equal number of inscriptions expressing the name and chronology of each bishop, there is only one whose letters have all disappeared. Many of the others are intact, especially from Saint Fabian to Saint Innocent. Among the twenty upper images, from Blessed Peter to Fabian, so many letters are clear both in the names and in the numbers formed according to Roman usage that the chronology painted here can easily be compared with the more reliable and ancient Catalogues, with which it agrees remarkably.

2. There are, however, three Catalogues superior in authority and antiquity among those obtained from the archives of Italy, against which I judged that the reliability of the chronology painted in the Paulina should be tested: the Farfensis, the Cavensis, and the Bergomensis. [Col. 0262D] The reason why I considered it preferable to select them from the archives of Italy rather than from documents of foreign regions follows from the first and third rules, together with their corollaries, established in the preceding chapter while we were pursuing the method for discovering chronological truth, sections 2, 7, and 8.

In section 2 it was shown that, for establishing true chronology, we ought to consult public monuments, where any exist, and that those should be preferred which, having been produced by suitable men, are nearer in place and time to the age and events principally under investigation. Again, in section 7 it was established that, among documents supplied from elsewhere than the place where the events occurred most directly, precedence in evidentiary value belongs to the document whose author’s knowledge, expertise in the discipline, and devotion to truth gave him greater capacity to investigate the times and events in question. Finally, in section 8 I inferred that the agreement of several writers or documents nearer in place and time, especially when supported by public authority, should be regarded as an indication of historical and chronological truth.

3. Everyone will understand why these conditions had to be sought in the codices of Italy, especially those nearer to Rome, of which the Farfensis should be regarded as first, the Cavensis as second, and the Bergomensis as third by virtue of their proximity. For I considered that the writers and custodians of the libraries and archives nearer to Rome had a ready opportunity to visit the City frequently and to compare their Catalogues and documents of pontifical chronology, recorded in their own codices, more often with the archetypal monuments of the patriarchal basilicas within and around Rome. In those monuments the series and inscriptions of the pontiffs, embracing their successions and dates, lay open to everyone’s eyes.

Learned men who had to cross seas or climb mountains and travel through several provinces before finally reaching Italy and Latium had extremely rare opportunities to go to Rome, remain there for a long time, and prepare the necessary means for carefully examining the paintings and inscriptions through repeated inspection. Such preparation was necessary even for me, although I had been living in the City for thirty-seven years and wished to leave nothing unexplored in matters that appeared doubtful. A monk, for example, from a monastery situated in Gaul or Britain could not inspect everything with the same ease as a monk of the abbey of Farfa or of Cava, whom the studies of all his friends and fellow provincials could assist, so that they might help me investigate and distinguish these matters with greater exactitude.

Everyone will also concede that the eyes are frequently deceived when numbers are being copied, especially when a visitor, observing from a low position—from the floor of the church—inscriptions and letters indicating numbers that are painted in a higher place, and not very brightly illuminated, has the entire distance of usually two hundred palms between the paintings and his eyes. This is the distance confronting those who observe from the floor of the basilica of Saint Paul. I shall not hesitate briefly to indicate what we accomplished in the preceding year, 1720, through repeated examinations over several days, so that we might ascertain the true form of the letters and their number.

4. Although the Latin characters of the alphabet forming the inscriptions—names and chronology of the pontiffs—in the series mentioned on the central nave and southern side of the basilica of Saint Paul are large, they can nevertheless scarcely be distinguished at a distance of nearly two hundred palms from an observer standing on the floor, unless they are flooded with full light from the sun’s rays admitted through the larger windows in the western front of the church during the afternoon. These windows distribute sufficiently vivid light to the nearer images, but weaker light to the more distant ones.

Moreover, in many places and paintings, especially those displaying images near Blessed Peter, water once falling through cracks in the roof or windows had caused damage, while adhering dust had covered the wall so thoroughly that the strokes of the letters were less distinct. To counter this difficulty of sight and access, we arranged as many aids as possible when we met by agreement in the preceding year, 1720, especially on 12 March, 29 April, and 10 May, to inspect the images and inscriptions painted there.

When the basilica was illuminated by a very clear sun around midday and in the hours immediately following noon, we strained our eyes, assisted not only by that light but also armed with optical tubes to enlarge the angle formed by even the smallest parts of the object, so that they might be perceived more clearly. We directed several tubes, on the one hand, toward the mosaic marked with the names of Saint Leo the Great and Placidia, and, on the other, toward the histories of the Old Testament painted above the images of the pontiffs on the southern wall, so that we might observe and compare the style of the painting in both places.

We clearly discovered that the faces of the twenty-four elders of the Apocalypse, depicted in Saint Leo’s mosaic, were so similar to the faces of Aaron and Moses represented in the paintings of the aforementioned histories of the Exodus—especially where the painter displayed the plagues inflicted upon Egypt—that the hand of the same artist, or at least the work of the same school, revealed itself in both places. The same method of arranging the garments and the same treatment of the bodies are found throughout; everything, in short, indicates the skill of the same craftsman.

Nor is the treatment of the faces different in the images assigned by the painter to the supreme pontiffs, arranged in that series from Saint Peter to Innocent I. Each displays the bust of an individual, dressed in a white tunic marked with purple bands (*in futuris*, reading uncertain) and covered over the shoulders by a white pallium. These images, or busts, are individually enclosed within a circular field or shield—hence the ancient designation *imagines clypeatae*, “shield-images.” Each circle is accompanied by a brief inscription, written in large letters, indicating the pontiff’s name and the number of years, months, and days assigned to his tenure.

I maintain that these inscriptions constitute the most excellent archetype of the pontifical Catalogue, derived from genuine documents of the Roman Church and recorded there in the age of Leo the Great. They deserve to be observed and copied by us with no less care than students of refined literature devote to collecting fragments of Ennius, Cato, and other distinguished writers of secular learning. For this reason we sought everywhere every possible aid for clearly distinguishing and faithfully copying these inscriptions.

Those who lacked these aids—especially the optical instruments of telescopes—and who before their invention observed from the floor with the naked eye could easily have been mistaken in distinguishing the letters used for numbers. They could readily substitute the sign for five, V, in their copies for the complete sign for ten, X, if half of the exemplar were hidden beneath dust, insufficiently illuminated, or deprived of the clarity of its color by the damage caused by falling rain. They encountered the same difficulty in determining the number of units when several followed one another; consequently, where the sight was obstructed by such external concealment of the characters, they could write VII for VIII just as easily as VIII for VII.

To remove these obstacles, we obtained permission both from the Most Holy Father Clement XI, under whose authority this had to be attempted in the patriarchal basilica, and from the Most Reverend Abbot and the Cassinese monks, who were most devotedly overseeing the matter, to bring near longer ladders. We arranged for them to be brought from the City, [Col. 0265B] and through suitable assistants we not only had the walls swept with brooms and cloths and the dust removed, so that the letters and colors might appear more clearly, but also arranged for the same capable men who had climbed the portable ladders, after wiping away the dust, to touch the individual letters with their fingers and call them out to us by name. We, observing from the floor through optical tubes, could thus determine whether the same indication appeared faithfully to our sight as was being spoken aloud by the person touching the letters.

For those ancient students of pontifical chronology who visited Rome before the invention of the telescope and attempted to copy this series and its chronological notes, wooden platforms had to be employed and brought close to each image and inscription, at great expense and with considerable labor, if they were to ascertain with equal success the numbers colored in Roman letters in this archetype. Anyone who considers the height of the walls and the distance of the paintings from the floor can easily imagine how difficult it would be for visitors coming to Rome, after completing a long journey, to think about transporting platforms and machinery from the City to the basilica and erecting them there, so that, after the dirt had been removed from the walls, they might copy the letters more clearly from close at hand.

It is therefore not surprising that so many Catalogues, even those copied in ancient times from these same paintings and inscriptions of the City’s basilicas by visitors and pilgrims of foreign nations who came to Rome out of devotion or on account of a vow, differ from one another by such a diversity of numbers, even if they perhaps derived from the same source. Since ancient exemplars of the same series and chronology had been painted in the three Roman basilicas—the series that Nicholas III, 450 years ago, judged should be repeated in the lower position in each of them—some numbers might be less distinct in the Lateran, for example, than in the Vatican, or less distinct in the latter than in the Paulina. If a copyist observed only one basilica, and that hastily, as travelers generally do, or if he had weaker eyesight, he could easily turn them into different numbers. Another copyist, finding clearer numbers in a different basilica, which he perhaps more willingly visited because it was nearer his lodging, might reproduce them accurately in his copy, yet err in other numbers of that same basilica that appeared less distinctly than in the other two basilicas, which he had no leisure to visit in order to compare their inscriptions.

I believe this was the principal cause of the diversity introduced into so many Catalogues. Later copyists compounded it with new errors, both when they carelessly corrupted the numerical signs and when they boldly supplied letters or numbers that had been obliterated in the codices, or passed over them inattentively. Nor was there anyone to think of sending his codex to the City so that its numbers might be compared with the prototypes of the basilicas, since an antiquarian or librarian living in distant provinces, who had never been in the City, had learned very little about their paintings and chronology.

5. These aids for comparison and inspection, extremely difficult for visitors arriving in Rome from a distant region to arrange, could easily be available to writers and librarians living in Latium, the Sabine territory, and Campania. Their easy access to the City, while the basilica was being maintained and repaired, could provide them with a more convenient opportunity to compare their Catalogues at close range with these paintings. The same could also be achieved without difficulty by others established elsewhere in Italy and summoned to Rome several times.

This consideration therefore moved us to prefer the older codices of the Italian archives in arranging the pontifical chronology and comparing it with these paintings, over others perhaps equal to them in antiquity but deposited, preserved, or copied long ago in libraries and archives far removed from Italy [Col. 0266C] by persons who had made no effort to visit Rome and compare them with ours.

6. The aids available to writers and librarians living in the suburban region were far more abundant and comprehensive in our case, since we inhabit the City. We were therefore able at will to employ many means in carefully examining the letters, comparing the style of the painting and images with Saint Leo’s mosaic, using ladders and telescopes, and choosing bright days for observation. We may confidently assert, with good reason, that the series of pontiffs and the chronology painted on the inner southern wall of the central nave of the basilica of Saint Paul, extending from Saint Peter to Saint Innocent I, belongs to the fifth century after Christ, to which the mosaic of Leo the Great belongs. This was sufficiently detected through direct examination of the similar style of the mosaic and the images.

7. Authority of the most weighty authors further strengthens the confirmation of this Leonine date, common to the mosaic of the great arch and to the paintings adorning the inner face of the southern wall along the entire length of the central nave of the same basilica, as well as to the series of pontiffs painted beneath and together with them. I mean that the authority of these authors contributes to asserting the Leonine date for both elements: they attribute to Leo the Great both works preserved in the basilica of Saint Paul, namely the mosaic of the great arch and the painted histories [Col. 0267A] of the Old Testament, together with the images of the venerable Fathers and his predecessors in the Roman See.

First, the *Book of the Pontiffs* attributes the renovation of the basilica of Saint Paul, which had burned, to no one other than Saint Leo the Great. The inscription of the Leonine age, visible in the same mosaic, likewise ascribes all its restoration and ornament to him, when it says:

> Placidia’s pious mind rejoices in all the glory of her father’s work,  
> through the zeal and splendor of Bishop Leo.

What the ornament added by Leo after the restoration was like is sufficiently shown by the mosaic and by the paintings already mentioned, which are very similar in style. We shall shortly see Adrian I refer these paintings [Col. 0267B] to the same Saint Leo.

The *Book of the Pontiffs* mentions paintings added by Pope Symmachus after the confessio in the same basilica in these words, section 79:

> “Likewise, at the basilica of Blessed Paul the Apostle, he restored the apse, which was threatening to collapse, and adorned with painting the space beyond the *confessio*.”

If this is to be understood of the paintings colored from the steps of the presbytery to the western front—imagine the writer viewing them from the presbytery after passing beyond the confessio—that is precisely what we maintain: that the paintings belong to the fifth century of the Christian era. For Pope Symmachus, the sixth successor of Leo the Great, also belongs to the Leonine century, since he was elected in the year of Christ 498.

But if it is the apse of Saint Paul that is understood to have been restored by Symmachus—Leo having made no restoration there, since it did not yet require one, although he is reported to have adorned the vault or apse of the Lateran and Vatican basilicas in section 67, while he renewed the basilica of Saint Paul, burned by divine fire—that is, struck from heaven or by lightning—and consequently set ablaze, from the great arch along the length of the nave, and adorned it with every form of cult and ornament—and if the church was decorated with paintings here and there beyond the vault or apse, in the senatorial and matronal galleries that Symmachus constructed (section 79), then the painted histories and images, together with the mosaic of the great arch, still belong to Leo.

In succeeding centuries, the Lives of the pontiffs relate quite carefully several restorations of this basilica, concerning its roofs, its pavement, and its walls. But no mention is made of any paintings except those that Leo III commissioned in the presbytery. Adrian I is said to have replaced fifteen roof beams (section 340). When the basilica of the teacher of the nations was so shaken by an earthquake that all its timbers and fittings collapsed, as we read in section 380, Leo III immediately began to restore it and, as he says:

> “He brought it into a better condition, making it as spacious and exceptionally strong as it had existed in ancient times; and he adorned it with marble in a better form, covered both the presbytery and the whole church with marble, and renewed its porticoes.”

In this restoration he says nothing significant about paintings, but mentions only the marble placed in the pavement, the presbytery, and the porticoes. He certainly would not have omitted paintings that had been added, had any been added, since in the *Life* of the same pontiff, section 360, he records that an image of the Savior, together with the others, had been painted by his command in the gable beneath the great arch of the Vatican basilica, after the model of those images that had been arranged in the Lateran and the Paulina by Saint Leo the Great.

As for the Paulina, paintings are recorded as having been executed by Leo III only around the altar. Section 416 says:

> “Above the marble columns that stand around the altar of that teacher of the world, where wooden beams had once been placed and had already decayed through excessive age, this holy bishop had lilies placed upon the columns, and above the lilies he placed *platonias* made of marble and metal, and adorned the work with paintings of marvelous magnitude.”

But he says nothing then about anything having been painted beyond the circuit of the altar.

Finally, under Sergius II, section 495:

> “The churches of the most blessed princes Peter and Paul were utterly plundered by the Saracens.”

Benedict III, his second successor, says in section 568:

> “In the basilica of the teacher of the world, Blessed Paul the Apostle, he richly adorned the tomb, which had been destroyed by the Saracens.”

There is no mention here of paintings established in the same basilica, nor is there any such mention in the Lives of his successors.

Moreover, that the custom of displaying images of patriarchs in churches had already been introduced before the age of Leo III is abundantly attested by this *Book of the Pontiffs* in its account of Agatho (section 145), where it records that similar images of the Eastern patriarchs were removed when those patriarchs, by decree of the holy synod, incurred a sentence of condemnation:

> “They removed,” it says, “from the diptychs of the churches the names of the patriarchs, and from the paintings of the church their figures, removing them also from the doors where they might have been, namely those of Cyrus, Sergius, Paul, Pyrrhus, Peter,” and so forth.

The same *Book of the Pontiffs* records in the Life of John VII, section 167, that in the church of Blessed Peter in the Vatican, images of the venerable Fathers—that is, of the supreme pontiffs—had been painted a full century before Leo III.

8. But what more is needed to prove that this series, together with the paintings displaying the history of Genesis and Exodus and with the mosaic of the great arch, [Col. 0268D] depicting the twenty-four elders of the Apocalypse worshiping our Savior by offering their crowns, is a work executed at the command and under the direction of Leo the Great? For Saint Adrian I explicitly states this in his letter to Charlemagne, presented at the Second Council of Nicaea and published, together with the Acts of that council, by Labbe, *General Councils*, vol. VII, col. 955. He clearly enumerates three classes of sacred paintings lavishly added by Leo the Great in the churches he built or restored—a threefold class that the Basilica of Blessed Paul still retains: the mosaic work representing the Savior of the world and the twenty-four elders; the histories formed in colors, that is, those of the Old Testament; and the images, namely the shield-shaped ones [Col. 0269A] that represent the series of the Roman pontiffs beneath the biblical histories just mentioned.

I shall reproduce the words of the letter, first stating its purport. In that letter Adrian had undertaken to prove the veneration of sacred images, received from the tradition of the ancestors and consistently defended by his predecessors, especially in the six general councils over which they had presided in person or, as was customary, through their legates. He therefore lists the mosaics, paintings, and works of that kind which, after the defeat of the heresies, Silvester, Mark, and Julius had dedicated to God in the Roman basilicas at the time of the Council of Nicaea; Damasus after the Council of Constantinople; Sixtus III after the Ephesian synod; and Leo the Great after the Council of Chalcedon.

Everywhere he records that threefold kind of ornament: mosaics, histories, and images painted in color. Thus he presents the Lateran and Vatican basilicas as they were adorned under Silvester, Mark, and Julius. “And from that time,” he says, “until now, the holy churches of extraordinary size belonging to the supreme pontiffs—namely, Silvester, Mark, and Julius—have been painted among us both in mosaic, on the apse and great arch, and in the other histories, that is, the colored histories of both Testaments on the walls of the central nave, as the Ciampini panel printed above as Plate X displays, and with sacred images, namely, the images of the venerable Fathers or pontifical predecessors, adorned.”

He then continues his survey through the succeeding councils. When he reaches the Fourth Ecumenical Council, celebrated at Chalcedon under Leo the Great, he specifically mentions the mosaic, histories, and images established by that pontiff in the Basilica of Saint Paul according to the example of his predecessors—works that we still see surviving today:

“Likewise, with regard to the fourth holy council, the outstanding and munificent preacher, Saint Leo the pope, himself also built churches, which he adorned by painting them in MOSAIC and with various HISTORIES or IMAGES. But especially in the BASILICA OF SAINT PAUL THE APOSTLE, constructing there the great arch and depicting in mosaic our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and the twenty-four elders, he adorned them with verses bearing his own name; and from that time until now they have been faithfully venerated by us.”

Two points must be observed here in Adrian’s testimony. First, the churches adorned by Saint Leo were decorated with mosaics, histories, and images, especially the Pauline basilica, in whose mosaic he placed his own name and verses. Second, the particle *seu*—the conjunction “or”—has the force of “and” here, as was generally customary in that period and is often repeated in the *Liber Pontificalis*. This is evident in the description of the mosaic work dedicated by Leo the Great in the Basilica of Saint Paul. Adrian asserts that our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the Savior of the world, was depicted there, “or” the twenty-four elders, since both the face of our Redeemer and the figures of the twenty-four elders were displayed together, arranged on either side.

It is therefore established, also from the testimony of Adrian I, that both the mosaic and the paintings of the histories of the Old Testament, as well as the images of the Roman pontiffs, were installed in the Basilica of Saint Paul by Saint Leo the Great.

[Col. 0270A] 9. In addition to these testimonies of Adrian I and the *Liber Pontificalis*, and to the evidence derived from the style of painting, which assigns both the mosaic and the paintings of biblical history and the images of the supreme pontiffs to the age of Leo the Great, the compartments themselves—or the circular areas—demonstrate that this older series, proceeding without interruption in its order, did not extend beyond the age of Saint Leo and Symmachus, the fifth century of the Christian era.

For the circular spaces opposite the image of Saint Innocent I, intended for the continuation of the series of pontiffs on the northern wall after that century, ought, in accordance with the order of succession consistently observed on the southern wall from Saint Peter to Saint Innocent I, in the circular panel or shield that appears first when one proceeds from the western front of the church toward the presbytery, [Col. 0270B] to have displayed the image of Symmachus, who closed the fifth century and opened the sixth. Ten pontiffs are counted between Innocent and Symmachus, and an equal number of circular panels or shields intervene on the western wall between the southern and northern sides. From these, the plaster, lime, and colored images and inscriptions fell away in flakes.

In the second circular panel or shield of the northern side, the image of Hormisdas, elected after Symmachus, should have followed. In the third came John I; in the fourth, Felix IV; and so the series of pontiffs should have continued in the next panels. But the evidence plainly shows that the series came to an end while it was being painted. For, leaving aside the first and second circular panels or shields, and their inscriptions, where the damage caused by fallen lime and plaster does not allow us to determine which pontiff the painter had colored, the third and fourth circular panels, together with the inscriptions attached to them, show that the ordered series is not continued there.

For Saint Eusebius is repeated in the third circular panel or shield, as if he were to be regarded as the fifty-fifth pontiff from Saint Peter, whereas on the opposite southern wall, in the old and orderly series, he is represented in his proper place, occupying the position corresponding to him between Marcellus and Melchiades—the thirty-second pontificate from Saint Peter. The fourth after this repeated Eusebius—for the three immediately following him are missing along with their lost inscriptions—is Anastasius, who in the ancient and orderly series of the southern wall is ninth after Eusebius. Anastasius is followed by Marcellus, although Marcellus precedes Eusebius in the true series, which is still visible on the opposite wall. Adrian is placed after Marcellus, despite being separated from him by nearly five hundred years; then comes Agatho, who preceded Adrian and sixteen other predecessors of his.

It is therefore perfectly clear from the third circular panel of the northern side that the series was not continued, but that the spaces were arbitrarily filled by a painter hired at an uncertain date to fill the circular areas and the spaces for inscriptions—which had been left vacant in the Leonine period for successors who would later be elected and painted and adorned there in their proper order with chronological notices of the years, months, and days of their pontificates. These spaces were rashly filled with figures of pontiffs gathered by the painter wherever he happened to choose, sometimes repeated from the old series, sometimes inserted from a catalogue of successors, placed out of order, mixed together, and accompanied by chronological inscriptions no more accurate than the patchwork of images he had selected.

10. Since, then, that older series and genuine chronology of the southern wall have been assigned to the Leonine age both by the clear indication of the style of the paintings—which corresponds to that of the mosaic—and by the numerous testimonies of Pope Adrian I and the *Liber Pontificalis*, we may rightly affirm that the origin of the older and more accurate catalogues is to be sought here. Their Italian, and especially suburban, copies, preserved in archives and manuscripts and repeatedly compared with this archetype, will be shown to derive from it wherever the agreement of the more distinguished catalogues found there is manifest with the surviving paintings cared for by Saint Leo in the Basilica of Saint Paul. In the following chapter I shall present, pontiff by pontiff, the agreement between the oldest Italian manuscripts and the paintings of this Leonine series.

11. Finally, on the basis of the rules of chronological criticism set forth and established in the preceding chapter, I shall add that this papal chronology, collected from the genuine and public monuments of the Roman Church, installed, preserved, and repeated by the same pontiffs in its principal basilicas, and confirmed by the agreement of the more distinguished manuscripts, can again be strengthened by the constant testimony and approval of all the periods intervening between the age of Leo and our own, through documents equally public. These chronological numbers so clearly take precedence over other methods that the clergy as a whole was instructed to preserve and recite them in the divine offices until the end of the fifteenth century of the Christian era.

I owe the support of this invincible argument to the diligence, learning, and benevolence of the most reverend Father, Dom Giovanni Marangoni. He had been joined, as a companion, to the piety and expertise of the most distinguished Marcantonio Boldetti, canon of the Transtiberine basilica, in the care of the sacred cemeteries of the martyrs and the elucidation of ecclesiastical history. In the preceding year, 1720, he worked with me for several days, faithfully copying from the Leonine-age archetype in the Basilica of Saint Paul the catalogue and chronology of the pontiffs of which we are speaking.

As the year 1721 was drawing to a close, he had been appointed to minister the word of God during the Lenten fast in the collegiate church—formerly the cathedral—of the town of Ocriculum. He had scarcely arrived there and begun to exercise his apostolic ministry when he was led to the archive to spend his spare hours profitably. There he found a collection of ancient manuscripts written on parchment, as well as a considerable number of printed books produced before the end of the fifteenth century, gathered for the celebration of the divine offices in the former cathedral.

He observed in the manuscripts and printed books—especially in the edition printed at Venice in 1594 by Andrea de Torresanis of Asola, on 20 June—that the readings appointed for recitation on the feasts of the holy supreme pontiffs not only displayed chronological notices [Col. 0272A] of the years, months, and days of their respective pontificates, but also distinguished those years, in the case of pontiffs who had ruled the Church while the office of consul continued, by the names of the consuls.

The age of the manuscript codices can be determined both from the specimen of their script and from a section found in one of them, extending into the thirteenth century of the common era. He therefore judged that all this material ought to be communicated, and most opportunely so, since this dissertation had not yet been committed to the press. He sent me transcripts of the readings both from the parchment manuscripts and from the printed books. When I compared them with the Liberian Catalogue and with the other Lives of the pontiffs that assign consular colleges, and with the chronological numbers painted in the Basilica of Saint Paul, I was extraordinarily impressed, [Col. 0272B] gathering from them a plainly consistent agreement among these documents, supplied by the city of Rome, by the suburban regions, and by other ecclesiastical archives of Italy through nearly every century of the Christian era.

For the Acts of the martyrs, generally marked by consular colleges throughout the period of persecution, are followed by the Catalogue collected in the age of Liberius, to which the Vatican paintings correspond, adorning the image of the living Liberius with an identifying sign. This is followed by the Leonine catalogue, painted and preserved in the Basilica of Saint Paul, whether it ends with Leo or extends to Symmachus, the pontiff of the fifth and sixth centuries. Nearly contemporary with it, therefore, is the second catalogue, produced under Felix IV and Justinian, which Henschenius, Papebrochius, Holstenius, Schelestratius—who corrected it from the archetype—and all scholars have held in such high esteem.

In the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth centuries there follow the older and more distinguished catalogues of the Italian archives, namely the Bergomensis, Cavensis, and Farfensis, the latter transcribed around the eleventh century from a more ancient exemplar. These are followed immediately by the parchment manuscripts of the divine offices found in the archive of the Ocriculan church, and by the repetitions of the old papal series and chronology undertaken by Nicholas III in the thirteenth century in three patriarchal basilicas within and outside the City, until, at the end of the fifteenth century, the recently invented art of printing repeated the same chronology in books of divine prayers offered to the clergy for recitation—a chronology publicly dedicated in the churches and in the Roman patriarchium from the Leonine age, indeed from the Liberian age.

[Col. 0272D] Unless this uninterrupted series of proofs and documents is to be regarded as a historical and chronological demonstration of the truth, according to the rule established above in chapter 2, section 8, I confess that I entirely fail to understand what can ever be called certain on human testimony in historical and chronological matters.

# CHAPTER V

The surviving series and chronology of the Roman pontiffs, painted in the fifth century of the Christian era in the Basilica of Saint Paul, is presented; and its agreement is demonstrated through the distinct epochs of the individual pontiffs, compared with the more reliable catalogues of every period, arranged in order, so that their agreement may appear with the celebrated archetype of the Pauline basilica from Saint Peter to Saint Innocent I.

[Col. 0273A]

## SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTER

I. The method to be followed here in setting out and comparing individually the epochs of the supreme pontiffs preserved in the Basilica of Saint Paul with their chronology recorded in the most trustworthy manuscripts of every period.

II. First, the surviving letters of that painting’s archetype will be faithfully reproduced, together with the lacunae whose supplements will be sought from catalogues once copied from those same archetypes of the basilicas of the City.

III. The catalogues collected in the fourth, fifth, and sixth centuries of the Christian era from diptychs, the Acts of the Roman martyrs, and similar documents, having been composed during periods flourishing with men distinguished in chronological matters, are to be preferred to the others and used before all others for comparison. Two among them are especially famous: the Liberian Catalogue, first published by Bucherius, and the other extending to the age of Felix IV and Justinian, which also illuminates the years of the epochs by means of the consuls. These are to be compared [Col. 0273B] with the chronological series presented in the paintings of the basilicas of the City during the same centuries, under Liberius, Leo the Great, and the pontiffs of the apostolic see who immediately followed them.

IV. These will then be followed by catalogues drawn from the archives of the suburban region and from elsewhere within Italy. Four are selected above the others: the Farfensis, Cavensis, Bergomensis, and Lucensis, since they appear not only to have been compared from the sixth to the eleventh century, but also to have been copied from the same archetypes of the basilicas of the City.

V. Nor should catalogues preserved in archives outside Italy be omitted, if any are considered close in date and more accurate, such as the Belgic catalogue of Papebrochius, copied from an eleventh-century parchment from older exemplars, and several published by Pagius from the Colbert Library. The numbers in these, too, are to be compared, since they agree almost everywhere with those given above.

VI. As the catalogues proceed in succession from the fourth to the eleventh century, the same epochs will next be compared with the epochs of the pontiffs recorded in manuscripts of the divine offices intended for the use of churches near the City, both handwritten and printed, from the twelfth century to the end of the fifteenth. Three parchment manuscripts written for the use of the ancient cathedral of Ocriculum will be produced, [Col. 0273C] together with one printed shortly after the beginnings of the art of printing, namely at Venice in 1492. All of them agree sufficiently precisely with the preceding catalogues.

VII. Authority is added to the Ocriculan manuscripts by their derivation from Roman origins.

VIII. After setting forth the method that we have decided to observe in comparing the epochs, and giving information about the manuscripts selected for comparing the written chronology with the painted chronology in the Basilica of Saint Paul, we shall present that painted chronology itself, together with the others collected from the manuscripts indicated, so that they may be compared with one another at a glance.

1. Everything stated above relates to the foundation and demonstration of this fifth chapter, in which the entire usefulness of our dissertation and investigation lies. The demonstration of the argument to be treated in this chapter requires nothing else at all except exposition and arrangement. We shall therefore expand the individual epochs painted on the southern wall of the Basilica of Blessed Paul, and arrange comparisons between that archetype and all the documents of later periods, provided that we complete the procedures that establish the method of our expansion, arrangement, and comparison.

2. First, I have decided to assign one column on each page separately to each pontiff from Saint Peter to Innocent I, where the Pauline series is interrupted. At the top of each column I shall faithfully reproduce the epoch assigned there to one of the Roman pontiffs, following the order in which their images were painted and attached to the shield-shaped portraits of those same Roman pontiffs.

The Roman letters surviving in the archetype will be indicated by me in an initial rounded typeface. Both the letters constituting the pontiff’s name [Col. 0274A] and those expressing the chronology of his pontificate, consisting of years, months, and days, will likewise be printed in Roman capitals in that older series, painted in colors in the Basilica of Saint Paul. We call this series painted in the fifth century, around the age of Leo the Great, when the mosaic was also being made and displayed the style of the same workmanship and school.

Therefore, all letters still visible in the archetype will be printed by us in rounded capitals, preserving the order and number of the verses or lines in which the painter arranged the inscription next to the image of the pontiff to whom it refers. Lacunae caused to the verses and letters by the injury of time, if there are any, will be shown by the different typeface that we shall use for the supplements there.

Moreover, wherever the supplements to the older series of the Leonine age can be found in the same basilica and borrowed from the more recent series repeated there under Nicholas III, as we have said, in imitation of the earlier one, they will be marked in capitals, though not rounded capitals but slanted letters, or, as they are called, italics.

But if those supplements to the letters and lacunae have also disappeared from the paintings of Nicholas III—which certainly suffered greater damage, because the lime, plaster, and color applied to the old walls so many centuries after their construction adhered less firmly—the missing letters and words must be supplied from the older and more accurate catalogues, especially those deposited in the archives of the suburban region. These were closer to the archetype in place and time, according to the rules of criticism established in chapter 2, at the end of section 4, since it may and should be believed that they were either derived from those prototypes or compared with them in antiquity, through the patriarchal churches of Rome where the originals could be viewed.

The indications of the legitimate reading to be restored from the catalogues in these lacunae will be represented in our edition by lowercase rounded alphabetic letters, as they are commonly called, not capitals, since capitals alone are used for the letters surviving from the Leonine archetype.

Thus the reader will have before his eyes almost the archetype itself of the Basilica of Saint Paul and the inscriptions painted there in the fifth century of the Christian era, with the number of lines and letters preserved. In this example he will also clearly see the lacunae and the supplements taken both from the series of Nicholas III and from the written catalogues.

3. Above all other catalogues and lists of papal chronology, therefore, I shall insist that those be especially observed and compared which are closer to the Leonine archetype in age and place, and which appeared during the centuries abundant in more experienced writers on chronology. This is required by the first and third rules confirmed above in chapter 2, sections 2 and 7, where we stated that the following principle must be accepted:

Among public documents from the periods in question, if any exist, preference should be given to those established by competent men who were close to the period about which inquiry is principally being made. Among documents supplied from elsewhere than the place where the events were conducted, precedence in evidentiary force belongs to the work whose author was given, by the grounds of his knowledge, expertise in the discipline, and devotion to truth, the greater capacity for investigating the period and the matters under examination.

When selecting catalogues, therefore, we take into account both their proximity in place and time to the events and men they represent, and the expertise and grounds of knowledge possessed by the authors who compiled them.
