It becomes clear that, for this reason also, the chronology appearing in those catalogues must be preferred to the others that were compiled and publicly displayed in the Roman basilicas during the age of Liberius, in the fourth century of the Christian era, and during the fifth century of Leo the Great, and the sixth century of Symmachus, Felix IV, and the emperors Justin and Justinian.

For those ages and centuries were more abundant than others in writers skilled in chronological matters, and these men were employed by the Roman pontiffs to calculate and arrange the times, on the occasion of the controversies then prevailing concerning the celebration of the feast of Easter.

During the lifetime of Liberius, the learned were diligently handling the *Chronicle* of Eusebius. Jerome, who had been secretary to the blessed Damasus, Liberius’s successor, not only translated it into Latin so that it might come into general use throughout the West, but also extended it to his own times. In this century Latin chronologists likewise completed and clarified the Paschal cycles. More accurate lists of consuls were attached to them, as is demonstrated by the celebrated works of this kind published by Bucherius after the cycle of Victorinus. These include a collection of consular and urban-prefect lists belonging to the fourth century of the Christian era, [Col. 0275C] together with the names and depositions of the Roman pontiffs of the same age, written on parchment. Some of these are also inserted above in these Prolegomena.

The age of Pope Liberius was therefore extraordinarily fertile in diligent and skilled chronological writers. I also indicated shortly before, in chapter 3, section 8, that the older series of Roman pontiffs painted in the Vatican basilica displayed an indication that Liberius was alive only in the image of Liberius, through the distinctive square object attached to his head. From this it may be inferred either that this portion of the Vatican series was painted during Liberius’s lifetime and was later extended to Hormisdas, or that a model from the older series of the Liberian age was used, one that was adorned with such an emblem in the Vatican.

Whichever possibility we accept, it is certain that in the same age of Liberius, when the older series from the written catalogues and the older series painted on the walls of the basilicas of the City were being produced together, a considerable number of outstanding chronologists was to be found.

The times of Leo the Great were no less abundant than the Liberian age in learned chronologists. The investigation of the Paschal question had encouraged them in these studies, and the same pontiffs had appointed them from among the ministers of the apostolic see, as is demonstrated by the letters of Victor of Aquitaine and by the Paschal cycle that he sent to Hilary, then archdeacon of Pope Leo and later his successor.

I believe that the extent of Hilary’s expertise in chronology can be abundantly inferred from the exceptionally exact correspondence of his chronology of the Passion of Christ the Lord [Col. 0276A] with the fixed chronological markers of the years indicated above, and from the other considerations that I have shown to be preferable in these Prolegomena, p. XII (above, col. 129). Leo the Great therefore had every right to paint and display in the Basilica of Saint Paul, as a series complete in every numerical respect, the chronology to which we owe whatever the Roman documents, through catalogues copied from it, have consistently and faithfully handed down to posterity concerning papal chronology.

Finally, in the following century, under Felix IV and the emperor Justinian—the period to which the catalogue called by Schelestratius the second belongs—the study of chronology had not yet declined. Ammianus Marcellinus was flourishing among the writers of the Eastern Empire, while in the West Prosper and Cassiodorus were reviving the same studies. They provided ample assistance in arranging the times of the pontiffs and recording them in consular lists.

Dionysius Exiguus, a Roman abbot, appeared in the years immediately following. He was an accomplished student both of the Paschal question and of the Christian era. His cycle pleased the supreme pontiffs so much that they judged it should be published for the use of the universal Church. His chronology likewise appeared so convenient to later generations that from the age of Charlemagne onward they wished the years of Christ to be expressed through it, and in every subsequent century they used it both in private administration and in recording public acts, as it is used today.

4. Since I have demonstrated that the catalogues of these periods, and the papal chronology contained in them, received from Roman documents, are to be preferred to the others, it follows that I should place them here for comparison and to indicate their agreement with the archetype of Saint Paul.

I therefore diligently investigated their genuine exemplars in the older manuscripts and archives of the suburban region or of churches nearer to the City, provided at least that they were located within Italy and could consequently have been repeatedly compared by our ancestors with the Roman prototypes. I arranged for the numbers of the Farfensis, Cavensis, and Bergomensis catalogues to be printed immediately after the catalogues of Liberius, Leo, and Felix IV, written on ancient parchment or painted on the walls of the patriarchal churches of the City. [Col. 0276D] I add a fourth, which I call the Lucensis, since it is attached to the collection of Canons, or to the Decree of Anselm, bishop of Lucca.

5. Nevertheless, so that we might not fail to investigate the agreement of foreign catalogues as well, if any more accurate ones existed, it seemed appropriate, after the Italian catalogues just mentioned, to append the exemplar published by the reverend Father Daniel Papebrochius in his *Chronhistorical Endeavor concerning the Catalogues of the Roman Pontiffs*, p. 75, preceded by the following notice:

“Moreover, so that I may not withhold anything from our collection of antiquarian materials that might illuminate the history of the pontiffs, I add a parchment manuscript apparently copied six hundred years ago from another, still older one. It ends with Pope Vigilius; there also end the NAMES OF THE APOSTLES, copied and found among Mabillon’s *Analecta*, vol. III, p. 426, after a certain collection of decretal letters and canons that does not extend beyond the year 571. But just as many names are written incorrectly there, so the numbers also differ greatly from those of our parchment manuscript. No less diversity appears in another Corbie parchment, which begins in the same volume of the *Analecta*, p. 429, with *On the Bishops of the Roman Church*, and extends to John VI, ending in such a way that it omits recording the years and days of him and of his predecessor, Sergius I.”

I mentioned both Corbie manuscripts above and gave a specimen of them in the Notes on the Catalogues of the Pontiffs, from section 5 to section 9. There it was also observed [Col. 0277B] that the discrepancy in the chronology of the two manuscripts was almost incredible, both between themselves and in comparison with the other catalogues. Thus, among the first seven pontiffs counted from Saint Peter, not even the total of the years agrees, and the total of the months agrees in only one case.

But when I noticed that the pontiff Anacletus was missing from both Corbie catalogues, I seemed able either to understand or to suspect the reason why they so frequently disagreed both with one another and with the others. For the omission of his name among the other Roman pontiffs shows that neither of these catalogues was copied from Roman sources or from the source and archetype established by the supreme pontiffs in the patriarchal basilicas of the City.

This confirms the axiom stated above in chapter 2, sections 1 and 2, and repeated so often in this dissertation, namely:

Those who study the true chronology and series of the Roman pontiffs, if they wish to attain it, must consult the genuine and public documents of this Church, in which the successors of Peter not only sat, but also left to posterity a clear memorial of their own apostolate and of their predecessors.

From the other catalogues produced by libraries and archives outside Italy, I thought it preferable to publish this distinguished one, rightly esteemed and collated by Papebrochius with the older Corbie manuscripts, whose chronologies contradict one another. This will show how far it departs from their numbers, which are supported by no probable authority and indeed oppose one another, and how closely it approaches agreement with the chronological calculations recorded in the Basilica of Saint Paul and written in the oldest exemplars nearest to the City. In those exemplars the series and chronology remained expressed in colors from the age of Liberius, Leo, Felix, Hormisdas, and even Formosus in other patriarchal basilicas within and outside the City.

Nevertheless, to show that there were also in provinces outside Italy certain diligent and prudent collectors of chronological material who repeatedly transcribed, compared, and corrected their catalogues in accordance with the authority of these documents, which were accessible to everyone in the basilicas of the Roman Church, and with a similar care to that employed by some of them in transcribing ancient inscriptions at Rome—a care confirmed by the manuscripts published by Gruterus in the *Thesaurus* and by Mabillon in the *Analecta*, vol. IV, p. 483—I shall append in their proper place, in the notes compiled for the Lives of the individual pontiffs, several catalogues from the more distinguished catalogues outside Italy.

Among these must first be counted those published by Pagius in the second edition of Baronio’s *Criticism*, vol. I, most of them drawn from the Colbert Library. Their agreement with the series and chronology of the Basilica of Saint Paul, confirmed by the Italian exemplars, follows these Roman and Italian documents so closely that it departs from them very little.

6. I shall also call upon the same catalogues of provincial libraries as supplementary evidence for the concordant testimony that I have taken pains to elicit from the Lectionaries, [Col. 0278B] as they are called, of the divine offices, found in the suburban region, where they were commonly used by the clergy of the churches to which they belonged.

I shall append information about them so that it may appear that I have rightly undertaken this recension and comparison and placed it immediately after the agreement of the Italian catalogues with the series and chronology of the Basilica of Saint Paul. My principal purpose is to prove that the same numbers were preserved so consistently and regarded as so firmly established by public documents even after the centuries of the more distinguished chronologists—from the tenth through the fifteenth century—that they were used in the sacred offices recited for the feasts of the supreme pontiffs in the region near the City.

For other pontiffs whose feasts were not celebrated, chronological evidence and comparisons cannot be obtained from these books. I therefore judged that supplements must be sought from the catalogues written during the same centuries after the tenth or copied from more reliable and accurate exemplars. I thought it preferable, however, to reserve these supplements for the notes to the Lives, lest the dissertation grow into a book if it were filled with so many comparisons, or depart from its intended purpose of placing before the eyes, at a single glance, the agreement of those monuments whose proximity to the City caused them to be preserved in more accurate form through each century of the Christian era.

There are three manuscripts of readings of this kind, written on parchment four hundred years ago and used in the church formerly the cathedral and now collegiate at Ocriculum. The distinguished Father Giovanni Marangoni recently informed me that he had found them there while I was publishing these Prolegomena. When I subsequently asked him to transcribe an exemplar of the readings containing the papal chronology, he immediately, with his customary courtesy, carefully extracted it from them and sent it to me in a letter. I shall provide a Latin version of that letter, so that the character of the manuscripts’ script, which he accurately observed, may be evident.

He writes to me as follows:

“In this collegiate church, where I am engaged in preaching during Lent, I found various sacred manuscripts formerly collected for the use of the old cathedral and written in the Gothic form of letters. [Col. 0279A] Among them is a Breviary, as it is called, written, as far as I can determine, approximately four hundred years ago.

“In it I immediately noticed the readings of the holy pontiffs, which are marked not only by the years of their respective pontificates, but also by references to the consuls who designated those years. Therefore, remembering the diligence that you applied several months ago in the Basilica of Saint Paul, when I had the opportunity to go there with you twice for the purpose of observation, I judged that this information might perhaps be useful for the notes you are preparing on Anastasius.

“Accordingly, receive the readings carefully copied by me, especially the letters indicating the numerical entries and the names of the consuls, even though the script of the manuscripts from which I copied them is extremely old and does not distinguish punctuation by commas [Col. 0279B] or capital letters, that is, majuscules, as they are called,” and so forth.

At the end of the second codex he observed that an epact, the Dominical Letters, and the numbers of the solar cycle had been added for twenty-eight years, running from the year 1307, in order to announce the Sunday of Septuagesima and the other movable feasts. He therefore rightly argues that the writing of the codex is older than the year 1307.

> “At the end,” he says, “of this codex (the second), there are noted the days on which the Sunday of Septuagesima was to fall during twenty-eight years, as follows:
>
> `M. l. ccc. vii — xvi a. x. stante Januario`
>
> `M. l. ccc. viii — xxvii g. f. xi. intrante Februario,` [Col. 0279C] etc.
>
> These characters are not by the same hand by which the codex was written, nor were they formed with the same ink. It may therefore be believed that the codex was written before the year 1307.”

There is no room for doubt concerning the age of the third codex, since the distinguished man observed that, after the offices for the season, the following colophon was to be read:

> “Here ends the breviary according to the rubric of the Friars Minor, written in the own hand of Lord James John of Narni in the year of Our Lord 1354, on May 29. Thanks be to God.
>
> “Amen. Amen.”

Besides these codices containing the written divine offices, he found there an old Breviary, printed in Gothic characters, [Col. 0279D] as they are called, at Venice by Andrea de Torresanis of Asola on 20 June 1494, in folio. Since in it the years, months, and days of the pontiffs’ reigns are assigned, and the consulships are also usually recorded, without differing from those expressed in the Catalogues of the Roman Church, I judged that this printed codex too had to be taken into account and that its testimony should be added to those already given. Thus it may clearly be seen that the chronology in question was consistently employed, inserted in public monuments, and confirmed by ecclesiastical authority—for such authority is applied above all to codices prescribed and printed for divine use—from the fourth century of Christ to the end of the fifteenth.

[Col. 0280A]

**7.** I use these codices all the more willingly because it is reasonable to judge that they were copied with greater accuracy from the exemplars of the Roman Church: first, because codices already formed for the use of a cathedral church situated in the suburbicarian region are still preserved at that same collegiate church; and secondly, because the second of the manuscripts is said to have been arranged according to the rubric of the Friars Minor in the year 1354, while the rule of that order instituted by its seraphic Father and founder was in force—a rule also confirmed by his testament, so that those professing it might observe with the greatest care the customs and rites of the Holy Roman Church.

**8.** Having set out the preliminary considerations concerning the method, the expansion, and the order that I shall follow in presenting the archetypal Catalogue, the succession and chronology of the Roman pontiffs [Col. 0280B] drawn from the Leonine paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul, and in adding the confirmation of that succession taken from the more reliable Catalogues preserved within and outside Italy and transmitted to us through twelve successive centuries; and having also produced information about the codices through which this system of dates has been handed down to us, I shall now undertake to expand the basilica’s succession itself.

I shall assign one of the two columns forming each page to each pontiff. In the upper part of it I shall place the inscription of that pontiff from the Pauline basilica, transcribed in rounded or sloping capital letters. The rounded capitals indicate characters still surviving in that basilica, and indeed in the ancient Leonine prototype; the sloping capitals, which are called Italic characters, indicate [Col. 0280C] supplements to that older inscription, taken from the surviving letters of the more recent series painted there under Nicholas III.

The lacunae whose supplements cannot be obtained from either series—Leon’s or Nicholas’s—when characters have fallen away in both, are to be supplied from the Catalogues of the suburbicarian region. By this name I may call the four Catalogues which have been found in the churches of Farfa, Cava, Lucca, and Bergamo, where their inscriptions agree in full with the Pauline series. I judged that these supplements should be indicated by rounded lower-case characters, so that it might more clearly be shown that the space of the lacuna still survives there where that same space declares that letters once existed, and that the authority of the other Catalogues, agreeing in the remaining details and assigning letters corresponding to this space, supports their insertion.

To the archetypal document of the succession and chronology of the pontiffs, therefore, drawn from the walls of Saint Paul, supplemented and revised, will be added other supports from the suburbicarian region: namely, the chronology expressed in books of the divine offices, both manuscripts from the thirteenth century and printed books from before the end of the fifteenth, given by the number of years, months, and days and by the consuls. Whenever, however, we encounter a pontiff whose readings or feast is not found in those codices, or whose years are not recited, testimonies to the chronology collected from other, older and more carefully corrected Catalogues will be substituted—especially from those which Pagius produced from [Col. 0281A] the Colbert Library, written around the age of Charlemagne; and also from those which Schelestratius published from the Vatican, written in the centuries immediately following the Carolingian empire, together with the older materials brought forward by him and reproduced above among these prolegomena.

# CHRONOLOGICAL SUCCESSION OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS, FROM THE APOSTLE SAINT PETER TO SAINT INNOCENT I, FAITHFULLY DRAWN

Both from the most ancient images and inscriptions, together with the mosaic work painted by Saint Leo the Great in the basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way; and from the more recent images placed beneath them in the same church by order of Nicholas III.

# CONFIRMED

From the codices and Catalogues of the foremost archives and libraries both within and outside Italy.

[Col. 0281B]

## BLANCHINI’S NOTICE

So that I may not be compelled to repeat in each column of this succession the information concerning the codices and Catalogues, and to provide evidence of their age and writing, I shall supply it all here in advance once for all. I have assigned to each codex and Catalogue a letter of the alphabet, which, wherever it occurs in the individual columns, will always indicate the same codex or Catalogue and its age, as I list them here.

**a** The Catalogue of the fourth century, under Pope Liberius, published by Bucherius and Schelestratius, and likewise printed above among these Prolegomena.

**b** The Catalogue of the sixth century, under Felix IV, published by Schelestratius from the library of the King of Sweden, now the Vatican Alexandrian Library.

**c d e f.** Codices and Catalogues of the libraries and archives of Italy.

**c** The Bergamo Catalogue, published by Schelestratius and reprinted above here, described under Pius II from an old codex eight hundred years old belonging to the Church of Bergamo.

**d** The Cava Catalogue, from an eleventh-century codex ending with Gregory VII, published by us below.

**e** The Farfa Catalogue, from a codex transcribed during the eleventh century from an older one, to be published below in these Prolegomena.

**f** The Lucca Catalogue. This is what I called above on page XIX (col. 141), from a Vatican codex containing the Decree of Anselm of Lucca, written six hundred years ago, according to the testimony of Schelestratius, who first published it.

Codices of archives and libraries outside Italy.

**g** The Belgian codex and Catalogue of Papebrochius, copied six hundred years ago from an older one ending with Pope Vigilius of the sixth century; concerning it see above, page XXXVII (col. 180), no. 1, and chapter 5 of this dissertation, no. 5.

**h i k l m n o.** Seven Catalogues published by Pagius from the Colbert Library in the second edition of the first volume of the *Critica on Baronius*, page L and following, of which:

**h** is from the ninth century and ends with Benedict II, at the year of Christ 858.

**i** is from the eleventh century and extends to the year 1073, under Alexander II.

**k** is from the eleventh century and extends to the year 1099, under Paschal II.

**l** is from the twelfth century and extends to the year 1134, under Honorius II.

**m** is from the same century and extends to the year 1130, under Innocent II.

**n** is from the same century and extends to the year 1191, under Celestine III.

**o** is from the thirteenth century and extends to the year 1245, under Innocent IV.

[Col. 0282A]

Other codices of the suburbicarian church.

**p q r s.** Four codices for the use of the choir of the church now collegiate, formerly cathedral, of Otricoli, dating from after the twelfth century.

**p** A parchment Lectionary written around the end of the thirteenth century.

**q** Another parchment Lectionary, whose writing predates the year 1308.

**r** A third Lectionary of similar age and writing.

**s** A Breviary printed at Venice by Andrea de Torresanis of Asola on 20 June 1494.

I shall refrain from bringing forward other codices, especially printed ones, so that I may confine myself to those used by churches near the City.

## XI. SAINT PIUS

[Note: [Col. 0289D] Although Irenaeus, a contemporary of these times, in book III, chapter 3, places Pius before Anicetus, as we have also done, the reversal of the order in later ages nevertheless renders the Catalogues confused. Their copyists could scarcely have been able to establish their reliability against this painting, which occupies the place of an autograph, if the names were already then worn away or damaged, as they are today. From so many Catalogues, especially the Italian ones, a total of either twenty or nineteen years, together with seven months and twenty-four days, is gathered for distribution between the two pontiffs. We distribute this total according to the paintings of Saint Paul as follows: Pius, eight years, three months, three days; Anicetus, eleven years, four months, three days. From the consulship of Severus and Priscinus, Christian Era 141, to the consulship of Orfitus and Priscus: Christian Era 149. From the consulship of Gallicanus and Vetus, Christian Era 150, to the consulship of the two Augusti: Christian Era 160. The pairs of consuls agree with the calculations of the years if they are taken from the older Catalogue of the Imperial Library, according to the manuscript exemplar, and from Cuspinian’s edition corrected according to Schelestratius; and if the consulship of Severus and Priscinus—not Severus and Clarus—is assigned to Pius, who preceded Anicetus, extending to the consulship of Orfitus and Priscus in the year of Christ 149; while to Anicetus are assigned Gallicanus and Vetus, recorded there in the same source, as also in the second Catalogue, extending to the two Augusti, incorrectly mentioned under Pius, as the chronological calculation and the total number of years demonstrate. See the notes on Saints Pius and Anicetus.]

All the codices from **a** to **o** number fourteen.

All assign Victor ten years | 10 |

Twelve of them assign the months | 2 |

All but one number the days | 10 |

The surviving numeral X in the paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul from the Leonine period, placed beside the years, denotes the first part of the number XII, and no month, together with the ten days assigned to Victor. But the copyists, imprudently inserting the siglum M for months between X and the binary numeral II, formed from the number XII the entry “10 years, 2 months,” which must not be assigned to Victor, as is proved in the notes to his Life.

## XIX. St. Pontian.

In the ancient paintings of St. Paul’s Basilica, Pontian’s inscription has been so obliterated that no letters remain except the initials, which constitute the first syllable of his name and indicate his place with certainty, written as follows:

### Consular pairs in the Christian Era

Only one consular pair is assigned to Anterus, both in the Catalogues of Liberius and Felix IV and in St. Prosper. The Acts of St. Pontius and Eusebius likewise assign Anterus only one month of governance of the Church. Therefore the catalogues a, c, i, and o must be followed, and the others corrected accordingly: one month and 10, 12, or 15 days should be assigned to him under the consulships of Maximinus and Africanus, in the Christian Era 236.

[Col. 0296C] As is demonstrated by the following epoch of St. Fabian.

### Consular pairs in the Christian Era

From the consulships of Volusianus and Annianus, under whom he was elected Roman pontiff on the Kalends of February | 314 |

to the consulships of Constantius and Rufius Albinus | 335 |

and to the beginning of Nepotianus and Facundus | 336 |

so that, as in Marcus, who follows, there are 21 years, 11 months | |

But from 10 February, on which he was ordained bishop | 312 |

to the same endpoint, 31 December | 335 |

there are 23 years, 10 months, 20 days. | |

In the ancient paintings of St. Paul’s Basilica, as also in most of the catalogues, the epoch is reckoned from the ordination—which can also be observed in Melchiades and Marcus. In the Liberian Catalogue, however, the epoch appears to be recorded from his assumption of the Roman pontificate after the death of his predecessor.

### Consular pairs in the Christian Era

The testimonies of contemporaries, together with the Acts of St. Felix, pope and martyr, produced by Schelestratius in *Dissertation* 2, chapter 9, demonstrate, along with the older catalogues, that Felix’s legitimate pontificate must not be extended beyond one year, three months, and two days—namely, part of Liberius’s three-year exile—from the year of Christ 357 [Col. 0309C] to the year 358. | |

All the manuscripts from a through o number fourteen. | |

Of these, eleven count the year | 1 |

The same number also mention the months | 3 |

Ten likewise assign the days | 2 |

As they are displayed in the paintings of St. Paul’s Basilica. The first and second Ocriculan manuscripts must be added to these. In the first we read, reading 5:

“His head having been cut off, he is crowned with martyrdom on the fourth day before the Ides of November; and thereafter his body, taken away by the presbyter and clergy, was buried in the basilica that he himself had built on the Aurelian Way, at the second milestone, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December. His natal feast is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.”

### Consular pairs in the Christian Era

The First Council of Toledo was celebrated under Pope Anastasius, with Stilicho as consul, in the year of the Christian Era 400.

Sulpicius Severus writes as follows in Book II of his *History*: “While Herod was reigning, in the eighteenth year of his reign, the Lord was crucified under the consulship of Julius Geminus (Fufius Geminus) and Rubellius Geminus; from that time until the consulship of Stilicho there are 372 years.”

Add to these 28 years of the common Christian era, from the beginning of that era to the consulship of the two Gemini. The total is 400 years from the beginning of the common Christian era to the First Council of Toledo under Pope Anastasius and the consulship of Stilicho, as our chronology reckons it.

# CHAPTER VI. On continuing the chronology of the Roman pontiffs from the Catalogues and other documents after St Innocent I

## Synopsis of the chapter

I. Summary of the documents for pontifical chronology concerning the first four centuries of Christ, thus far established. — II. Indication of the monuments that demonstrate the subsequent periods in the succession of the Roman pontiffs after the fourth century of the Christian era.

1. Having set out the rules of the criterion for correctly gathering the calculations of pontifical chronology from genuine documents, and having extended and confirmed their use through the individual successors of Peter, carrying the evidence from the Roman patriarchal basilicas beyond the beginning of the fifth century and down to Innocent I, it remains only to show that the periods of the succeeding pontiffs can be established with equal certainty, even though the series of ancient images in the Basilica of St Paul breaks off after Innocent, is scattered in the Vatican, and was consumed by fire in the Lateran, so that the Catalogues cannot be compared with them.

There are many aids that restore our knowledge of periods nearer to our own time, when the Church’s peace allowed them to flow more freely, after we see safely established those things which the fury of persecutors, amid storms of persecution raised on every side, vainly attempted to envelop and submerge beneath enormous waves. For we have seen that, despite the edicts of Decius and Diocletian and the futile attempts to eradicate Christian memories everywhere, while the fury of pagan authorities raged against the noblest members of Christ—as Leo the Great says [Note: [Col. 0313D] St Leo the Great, sermon on St Lawrence]—and especially attacked those of the priestly order, the bravest watchmen and leaders of the Christian army, the bishops of the Catholic Church and successors of Peter, not only did not abandon their station so long as life remained, but even, after dying for Christ, in a certain manner came to life again through the zeal of their successors.

Following the example of that same Peter, who promised that he would take care that we should have frequent remembrance of him after his death [Note: [Col. 0314D] II Peter 2:15], almost every century saw their years and deeds recorded in public documents: in diptychs and registers of depositions, during the persecution under Cornelius; in catalogues under Liberius and Felix IV; in the paintings of the basilicas under Leo I and Hormisdas; and in the writers of Lives and the Church’s Lectionaries and codices, in an unbroken succession through the ages that followed down to our own.

To our age it has been granted to gather from all those earlier witnesses a cloud of testimony against the envy of those who declaim that the documents of that golden age of bishops were taken from us either through negligence, discord, or tales foolishly woven by ordinary writers, who boldly impose everything unexplored as truth. No history or chronology that has been placed in the public light for several centuries has escaped the efforts of writers and copyists, in both cultivated and barbarous ages.

Consequently, none has been exempt from the necessity of separating—especially in chronological figures—the genuine reading of a competent author, supported by the public authority of his approved codices, from the divergent reckoning of private exemplars, commentators, and copyists. To say nothing of that famous controversy in the Churches which St Augustine, in Book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 11, calls most notorious, arising from the discrepancy between the Greek codices and the Hebrew in the addition or subtraction of hundreds of years from the lives of several patriarchs, let us confine ourselves to works written solely through human industry.

The Latin compilers of the fasti, after being harassed by the judgment of so many critics in restoring the series of consuls—which they had corrupted either through their own fault or that of incompetent copyists—and after our own age has purged them of almost all errors, sufficiently and more than sufficiently prove that effort is usefully expended in bringing truth out of darkness, when the royal road of method leading to it is cleared, by means of documents placed in the public record, of the prejudices of private opinions, like an overgrown thicket of brambles and thorns.

2. Since, then, in the first four centuries of the Christian Church we seem to have gathered so many testimonies of public authority, especially from the Roman territories and the suburbicarian region, where they had to be sought according to the rules of prudent criticism, sufficient to establish correctly the era of each pontiff in the notes to Anastasius, it remains for us to indicate with how much stronger a right we may confidently assert that, in the succeeding centuries also, the periods of the bishops who followed can be restored.

No one should doubt this if we consider that, from the fourth century of Christ onward, the frequent Acts of councils already appear, confirming the periods of the Roman pontiffs. Moreover, their letters have been preserved for posterity, no longer in parts and fragments, as in the history of Eusebius, but for the most part complete after Siricius, as the consensus of scholars now makes clear.

To these must be added the testimonies of contemporary authors: the origins of Churches, or their growth under the care of those pontiffs; sacred buildings founded, adorned, or restored with genuine inscriptions; laws enacted and privileges granted; journeys undertaken for reasons of public necessity; their Lives committed to writing, for the most part by contemporary authors; and every kind of evidence that connects the head of the Christian community, the vicar of Christ on earth, with the rest of the Church, spread throughout all nations.

Nor are sepulchral titles and inscriptions lacking in considerable number; some of them were even written by kings and emperors in their honor. This was done for Hadrian by Charles, surnamed the Great. If anyone should lose heart amid such an abundance of documents and despair that we can continue the epochs of the Roman pontiffs, he must plainly refrain from attempting any chronology of rulers and kingdoms, since no series of presidents of any state over seventeen centuries is displayed whose individual deeds and annals are confirmed by as many documents as those that are demonstrated and read in the open light of the Church concerning the successors of the Apostle Peter [Col. 0314D] and those who preside over the Christian world from the Roman See.

# [CATALOGUES]

# FRANCESCO BLANCHINI’S OBSERVATIONS ON THREE FOLLOWING CHRONOLOGICAL OPUSCULA

First published from the Farfa Archive.

[Col. 0315A]

Just as much assistance as the use of municipal fasti, preserved in the colonies—especially those nearest the City and Latium—has contributed to restoring Roman chronology, both consular and imperial, so much support for restoring the ordering of pontifical periods is supplied by the churches and monasteries of the suburbicarian region. With no less attentive diligence, they recorded in their codices the annals, or at least the epochs, of the chief pontiffs, just as the record-keepers of those colonies entered into public registers, together with the colleges of Roman consuls, their own duumvirs and magistrates.

I shall provide a specimen of this support in the three following opuscula, suitably copied from the Farfa Archive in the previous year, when I had gone there to complete certain geographical observations that would present a more accurate chorography of Italy. A meridian line from the Upper Sea to the Lower Sea had already been marked and magnificently adorned through the Baths of Diocletian, under the auspices of Clement XI, of holy memory. This was undertaken with precisely the same zeal and diligence with which our colleagues in the flourishing kingdom of Gaul, from the Royal Academy of Sciences and at the command of Louis the Great—a prince destined to illuminate the century and letters forever—arranged for a meridian line to be extended from the Paris Observatory, on one side to the shore of the Mediterranean near Marseilles, and on the other to the Ocean near Calais. They are preparing to publish it shortly.

[Col. 0315C]

Guided by this purpose, when I had gone to the Sabine hills and had been received with the greatest kindness by the most reverend and most religious abbot, Dom Archangelo Piccioni, a Roman, who, approaching his hundredth year and living in good health, was a model and exemplar of regular discipline, he and the monks of that monastery—who showed me, among the other services of hospitality which they generously extended to me, the innate benevolence of that sacred order, and who resembled their prelate in his good service to all, especially to sacred studies and those devoted to them—offered me several of its monuments for examination. Above all were the most reverend Fathers Dom Vincentius Manenti, the prior, and Dom Bernardus Cretonius, prefect of the archive and exceptionally experienced in its documents.

When they had brought me two codices, famous both for their antiquity and for the excellence of the matters described in them, so that I might examine and copy them at will, I selected from them three chronological opuscula to publish in these Prolegomena, as being especially suitable for illuminating the Lives of the pontiffs in the Anastasian collection.

The first codex, written on parchment around the end of the eleventh century, is called the *Chronicle of Farfa*. It initially contains the epochs of the emperors from Julius Caesar to Leo IV, also inserting the Gothic, Vandal, and Lombard kings who ruled Italy, as well as the dukes of the same Lombard people, both before and after King Desiderius. It then contains the Western emperors from Charlemagne to Henry III, together with a recension of the dukes of Benevento, Spoleto, and Sabina, and also the names of the marquises and counts encountered in the same Sabine region down to the year 1084.

The second codex, likewise on parchment and of larger format, is called the *Register of Gregory of Catino the monk*. It extends from the year of Christ 661 to the year 1140 and is drawn from genuine charters, donations, and privileges of the supreme pontiffs, Caesars, Lombard kings, dukes of Spoleto, counts of Sabina, and other princes and illustrious men, whose portraits are sometimes inserted.

Prefixed to this second codex is a prologue by Dom John the Grammarian, with an acrostic poem marking the name of Gregory of Catino. I shall expand the prologue’s abbreviated notes into complete words.

> **IN THE NAME OF CHRIST GOD ALMIGHTY, HERE BEGINS THE PROLOGUE OF DOM JOHN THE GRAMMARIAN ON THE BOOK OF THIS WORK.**
>
> **IN THE NAME OF THE HOLY AND UNDIVIDED TRINITY, FOR THE HONOR AND PRAISE OF THE HOLY MOTHER OF GOD, EVER-VIRGIN MARY, OUR MOST GLORIOUS LADY.**
>
> In the reign of Dom Henry IV, patrician and emperor of the Romans, from the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ in the year 1092, in the fifteenth indiction, on 16 April.
>
> By divine grace inspiring him, it pleased Dom Berard, most reverend abbot of this church, born of a noble family of the city of Florence, to collect into one volume all the privileges and decrees of this sacred monastery, as well as the books and legal charters, already almost consumed by excessive age, and to leave them most diligently explained and most truthfully transcribed for the memory of posterity.
>
> This was undertaken by the wisest counsel, lest what we have already known to happen very often—whether through the negligence of custodians or because excessive age consumed them—the aforesaid decrees, books, charters, and privileges should be handed over to oblivion. In truth, after painstaking labor, we added or subtracted nothing from them, nor did we alter them; but, with the corrupt portions corrected rhetorically, and according to the form in which they had been written, we legally transferred them through the hand of our confrater Gregory, a man of great acuteness, born in the county of Sabina, descended from most noble parents in the castle of Catino, and nourished almost from infancy on the milk of our Church.

> **GREGORY, SERVANT AND SLAVE OF HOLY MARY,**
>
> Desiring to attain the life of the eternal kingdom,
>
> Ever renewed the writings of the blessed one.
>
> Burning to leave behind a famous vow after death,
>
> His father Donadeus likewise offered him as a gift,
>
> Restoring a hundred pounds, and nine tens,
>
> To the brothers of the Mother of God, ΘΕΟΤΟΚΟϹ (*Theotokos*), in the kindly temple,
>
> So that they might receive the rewards of the sacred Farfa rule.
>
> Thus the first pastor Berard made both men monks.
>
> Shortly afterward, he migrated to heaven in the greater order.
>
> Sixty-eight years after the thousand years of Christ,
>
> At last the younger brother Gregory was advanced.
>
> From that point, exceeding thirty years, more or less,
>
> For after he had received the monastic habit according to the rule,
>
> Having completed ten years twice and again four,
>
> After our first pastor Berard had departed,
>
> Berard, the second abbot, ordered these sheets of the nourishing Virgin’s charters
>
> To be neatly written.
>
> For he wrote freely, since he seeks the rewards of life.
>
> From these verses you will recognize Gregory of Catino,
>
> If you read again the letters that are the beginnings of the poem.
>
> May Christ grant the writer to ascend to heaven.

Beneath the image of the Virgin Mother of God of Farfa, depicted here, the following couplet is written:

> These are the beginnings of the book of the priest Peter;
>
> For he himself offered ten solidi for the charters.

I have thought it appropriate to render the prologue of the *Register* faithfully here, so that the antiquity and sincerity of the documents from which it was compiled might be evident, as well as the diligence of Gregory of Catino in describing each item accurately and faithfully.

Nor do I think it will be useless to produce evidence of the expertise of that earlier chronicler by whom the *Chronicle of Farfa* was compiled from the same documents of the archive and library. When he was writing in the eleventh century of the Christian era and illustrating the origin of the monastery, he explained and distinguished, with sufficiently successful effort, the otherwise confused and obscure period of the Goths, so that he seems to have excelled his contemporaries in the art of chronology.

Therefore, according to the first and third rules of chronological criticism established shortly before in chapter 2 of the preceding opusculum—namely, that among documents closer to us in time and place, preference must be given to those supplied by suitable men who are skilled in the discipline of chronology—it follows that all who, from the specimen of his intellect that will shortly be reported, have perceived his force and solidity in suitably gathering and establishing the correspondence of periods, should agree with us that the author of this *Chronicle* must not be lightly regarded. He displays prudent evidence of hesitation wherever certain arguments fail him for exact assertion and definition.

Thus he writes of the first foundation of the monastery of Farfa:

> We nevertheless read in the preface to its authentic foundation that, before Italy was handed over to be ravaged by the sword of the pagans in the time of the Romans, three men came from Syria, namely Isaac, John, and Laurence, together with their sister Susanna.
>
> Of the first two, blessed Pope Gregory, who was the sixty-sixth after blessed Peter and was taken up into the pontificate in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 603, in the tenth month and twentieth day, in the second indiction, on the third day before the Nones of October, under the emperor Tiberius Augustus, makes mention in Book III, chapter 14, of the *Dialogues*, saying:
>
> “In the earliest times of the Goths there was near the city of Spoleto a man of venerable life named Isaac, who lived almost to the latest times of the Goths. Many of our people knew him, and especially the holy virgin Gregoria, who now dwells in this Roman city near the church of blessed Mary, ever-virgin.”
>
> And shortly afterward:
>
> “I learned many things about the same man from the venerable Father Eleutherius, who had known him intimately and whose words gave credibility to his life. This venerable Isaac was not born in Italy, but first came from the regions of Syria to the city of Spoleto.”
>
> Let the prudent reader observe what were the earliest times of the Goths, or what were the Roman times, before Italy was handed over to be ravaged by the sword of the pagans.
>
> It is therefore established that this monastery was founded a considerable time before the aforementioned most glorious pontiff, because he described Isaac, of venerable memory, the companion, namely, of this most holy monk Laurence the abbot, not as having seen him in the times of the saints, but clearly stated in his account that Isaac lived in the earliest times of the Goths.
>
> For the earliest times of the Goths, as may be more accurately conjectured and as is found in the written chronicle of the history of Orosius the priest, were those when the emperor Arcadius was reigning, at the time when Ambrose was shining at Milan, while Martin—whose glorious death occurred 322 years after the Lord’s Passion, in the eighty-first year of his age and the twenty-sixth of his episcopate—was in Gaul at Tours, and Jerome, who migrated to Christ after completing ninety-one years of life, was radiating like a star at Bethlehem.
>
> Radagaisus, king of the Goths, barbarous in character and nature, having with him 290 men of Scythian stock, first devastated Italy. Then, under his brother Honorius, Alaric, king of the Goths, invaded Rome and burned part of it with fire, on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, in the 164th year of its foundation. On the sixth day after he had entered it, he departed from the plundered City, when the year of the Lord’s Incarnation was 413.
>
> At that time also, at Hippo Regius, Augustine, the most brilliant and flourishing teacher of the whole Church, was living. In the third year of that city’s siege, in the sixth month, and in the seventieth year of his life, he rested in Christ.
>
> Then, while Leo was presiding over the Roman Church, Rome was captured by Genseric, after Alaric had first invaded it; this was now the second time, forty-four years having been completed from that event, 208 years from the foundation of the City, and 457 from the Incarnation of Christ.
>
> After these events, in the time of Pope Agapitus, in the year 529 of the Lord’s Incarnation, the Goths possessed the City and consumed everything around it by plunder and fires. At that time Witigis was reigning. In the East Justinian was emperor.
>
> Finally, after Witigis was captured, the Goths made Hildebad king. He too was killed in the same year, and Eraric received the kingdom; before a year had been completed, he was slaughtered. Then they set up Baduila, who was called Totila, as king. Having gathered an army from every side, he again invaded all Italy, and they entered the besieged City after thirteen days, in the time of Pope Vigilius and the emperor Justinian, namely, after 540 years from the Lord’s Incarnation and in the thirteenth indiction.
>
> From King Arcadius, therefore, down to Justin the Younger, under whom Narses, the patrician of the Romans, fought against Totila, the last of the Goths, defeated him, and drove him into flight, there are approximately 529 years.
>
> The earliest period of the Goths also began under the emperor Valens, when the Goths, expelled from their own homes by the nation of the Huns, crossed the Danube and, as fugitives, were received by the aforesaid ruler. For in the time of the emperor Valentinian, while they were living together within the boundaries of Thrace, they were divided there: Fridigern, with the aforementioned Ostrogoths, called the eastern [people], held the eastern region; while Alicern, with his army, whose name was the Visigoths, held the western region, R.P.
>
> We have recounted these matters at greater length so that we might set out, as best we could, both the earliest and the latest times of the Goths, which we inserted because of the narrative of blessed Laurence, the abbot of this monastery, the companion, namely, of Isaac, whom the most holy Pope Gregory mentioned.
>
> We have likewise included the Roman period before Italy was handed over to be ravaged by the sword of the pagans. Since, as was stated above, the three men were in Syria, we believe that this occurred when all Italy was free from the yoke or oppression of every people and was governed by the command of the Eastern Empire, R.P., as in the times of the emperors Julian the Apostate, Jovian, Valens, Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius.
>
> The apostolic pontiffs Damasus, Siricius, Anastasius I, Innocent, Zosimus, and Boniface I were presiding; Placidia Augusta with her son Valentinian Augustus were residing at Ravenna, and Honorius Augustus at Milan, together with the other pontiffs Celestine and Sixtus III.
>
> In the time of Leo I, the Vandal catastrophe was pressing upon Italy. Then, in the times of the pontiffs Hilary, Simplicius, and Felix III, it was ruled by King Odovacer. He came from the borders of Pannonia with a most powerful multitude of Heruli, relying also on the aid of the Turcilingi or Syrrians, and ruled Italy for fourteen years.
>
> Then, while Gelasius, Anastasius II, Symmachus, Hormisdas, John I, and Felix IV were presiding, Theodoric was reigning. After him, while Boniface II and John II were presiding, Athalaric was reigning. Thereafter, while Agapitus I and Silverius were presiding, Theodahad was reigning. When Vigilius was also presiding, Witigis was already reigning over the Goths.
>
> For from the time of Felix III, who was the fiftieth pontiff after the blessed Apostle Peter, and thereafter, Italy endured the sword of pagan domination. These, therefore, were not Roman times; for although Italy was sometimes governed by patricians, chamberlains, or exarchs of the Eastern Empire, R.P., nevertheless the whole of Italy was oppressed by the sword of the Gothic, Herulian, or Lombard people.
>
> For the emperor Zeno gave the whole of Italy to King Theodoric by a pragmatic sanction.
>
> For the rest, we leave it to the prudent reader to choose for himself the period of the aforementioned Laurence that seems more truthful.

As for the time when this monastery was first destroyed, just as it was founded, we have no fuller or clearer knowledge, except for what is read in the same book of the foundation:

> After the death of the blessed and most holy man Laurence, when the inhabitants had been killed or driven away on every side by the Lombards, the place itself was desolated and reduced to solitude. It remained without an inhabitant through many cycles of years, namely until a venerable man of life, the priest Thomas, came from the province of Maurienne in Gaul and stayed at the Lord’s sepulchre. There he was admonished by blessed Mary, ever-virgin and Mother of God, to return to Italy. He found this holy monastery and restored it.

Of the fortunate and glorious period of this most blessed Thomas, the aforesaid sacred abbot of this monastery, we have made a more precise and clear collection through the years of the pontiffs, the periods of the kings, the successions of the abbots, and also the indictions of the charters written below, according to the thirty-five years, seven months, and five days during which he presided over this monastery after reconstructing it.

We find that this occurred approximately in the year 680 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the eighth indiction, and in the times of the emperors Constantine, son of Constans; Justinian, his son; and Leo and Tiberius. Tiberius seized the emperor Leo, who had overthrown Justinian Augustus, and invaded his empire. But afterward that same Justinian Augustus had them captured and slaughtered, and recovered the principate.

From the time, therefore, of the first pontiff Damasus and the emperor Julian the Apostate—namely, approximately the year 382 of the Lord’s Incarnation—to the time of Leo I, the apostolic pontiff, and of Theodosius, son of the emperor Arcadius, when Genseric captured Rome in the year of Christ 462, we judge that there were Roman times, approximately 131 years. Within that period, according to the assessment of our ancestors, this holy monastery was built by blessed Laurence.

[Col. 0320A]

Then, from this Bishop Leo down to the time of the pontiff Adeodatus, who lived around the year 677 of Christ, and of the emperor Constantine, also called Constans, son of the emperor Heraclius, there were approximately 226 years. It is believed that in their time the most holy Thomas found and restored this holy monastery.

How, however, we are to estimate the time when the inhabitants of this place were killed or driven out by the Lombards, we cannot know fully, because, in the time of the emperor Tiberius, who reigned for seven years after Justin the Younger, Isidore reports that the Lombards seized Italy, while Pelagius II was presiding as pontiff.

From the year of Christ 593 until the time of Pope Adeodatus, who lived around the year 677 of Christ, when we have said that the most holy Thomas found and restored this monastery, there are approximately eighty-four years. Thus, when it is read in the preface to the *Foundation* that the monastery remained desolate through many cycles of years—

[Col. 0320B]

Finally, when the envoys of Duke Faroald consulted the neighboring inhabitants—he had sent considerable funds there at the prompting of Holy Mary, Mother of God—the neighbors stated that they did not know at all, nor did they remember, the intact condition of this monastery. Yet they had heard from the fathers mentioned above that those fathers, or their fathers, remembered having said that in the estate called Acutianus, beside three cypresses, there stood a church of blessed Mary constructed with marvelous beauty.

Can it be supposed that so famous and distinguished a place was given over to oblivion for only eighty-four years? For that is the number of years from the first devastation by the Lombards until Thomas, the servant of God, found it. Therefore, as may be more truly conjectured, it should be called not the destruction of the Lombards but rather that of the Goths or Vandals—or that destruction which occurred in the time of Pope Leo I, or the other, 136 years later, which occurred while Agapitus was presiding. From either of these events until the time of Pope Adeodatus there were 226 years. It should therefore rightly be judged [Col. 0320C] that its desolation occurred then and that this place remained surrendered to oblivion or ignorance through so many cycles of years.

We have recorded all these things for this reason: so that we might not state anything false about the time of the foundation or destruction of this place, nor appear to be deceived by writing doubtful matters as certainties. In all things we humbly ask those who read or hear this that, if we have offended in any matter of style, we not be condemned, since, with Almighty God as witness—whom no one can deceive—and with his most blameless Mother, whose cause this is, we knowingly state absolutely nothing false and desire to transcribe nothing incorrectly.

And so that we may write only what is true in this work, I beg the Truth itself, which is Christ, to pray most devoutly for us.

Since, therefore, we have hitherto endeavored to investigate the periods of the most holy Laurence with greater precision, we have lingered over their narration.

[Col. 0320D]

The reason for the aforesaid author’s chronological examination was supplied by the preface to the *Chronicle* that he himself indicated, and by what is written at the foot of folio 10 and on the facing page of the preceding leaf in the same hand, in these words:

> It remains intact in year 72. It was desolated by the Goths in the year of Christ 457; it was abandoned for approximately 223 years, and was rebuilt by Dom Thomas after the year of Christ 680.

Concerning this first author, therefore, who investigated the preface to the *Chronicle of Farfa* so cautiously and prudently, I believe that we should judge him not to have been the least among the chroniclers of his century.

Whether the same author should be assigned both the shorter and older *Chronicle* itself and the two earlier chronological opuscula prefixed to it, or whether they should be attributed to different authors, is not clear to me; nor do I think that discovering this is of great importance for our purposes.

It is certain that the author of the *Register*, and of the second *Chronicle* prefixed to the *Register* in the larger codex, was Gregory of Catino, from his name prefixed both in the title and in the acrostic poem, and from the testimony of John the Grammarian.

Since, however, no indication of Gregory is attached to the two aforementioned chronological opuscula, the smaller and older ones prefixed to the *Chronicle*—namely, the *Catalogue of Emperors*, etc., and the *Catalogue of Roman Pontiffs*—just as no such indication is attached to the shorter and older *Chronicle* itself, I would more willingly attribute them to an author earlier than Gregory of Catino.

This is especially so since the first of the two opuscula seems to have been completed around the year 1056, a full forty-four years before Berard, the second abbot of that name, charged Gregory with compiling the *Register*, as is confirmed by the prologue of John the Grammarian. Only the death of Henry III, recorded in the year 1084, was added in the final verse, and no count is mentioned after the year 1040.

The second of the two opuscula, bound together with the shorter and older *Chronicle of Farfa*, contains the chronology of the Roman pontiffs from St Peter to Benedict VII, that is, to the year 984. It therefore precedes the *Register* of Gregory of Catino by more than an entire century, up to the *Chronicle*—the second one—prefixed to the *Register* and to be presented below, which extends to the year 1099.

[Col. 0321C]

I considered it necessary to observe the different ages of the two preceding opuscula in the smaller codex and of the third opusculum found in the larger codex, in order to investigate why, in the *Chronicle of the Register*—which I shall now call the second—several antipopes are listed toward the end, while several legitimate Roman pontiffs of the same periods are omitted.

I consider it necessary to observe this fact and to propose that others observe it as well. For it will reveal the corrupt origin of several *Acts* which factional men, with criminal audacity, then arranged to be completed in the courts and tribunals, even those of the lowest bench, against the rights of the Apostolic See; while writers of our own age, through imprudent judgment, arranged to publish them from this archive as though they were evidence that the supreme power of the highest pontiffs had already been subverted and brought under their own dominion.

The examination depends upon the epoch recorded in the second *Chronicle*, that is, in that of Gregory of Catino, under the year 1082 [the supplied text reads 1532], where we read: “King Henry IV came to this monastery.” Immediately after two years follows the deteriorated entry, worded thus: “Pope Clement III. Emperor Henry.”

Who that Clement was, and who that Henry was, the *Annals of Baronius* teach us. To begin with Henry: he is that most bitter enemy of the Apostolic See, so often struck with anathema and deprived of communion and kingdom by repeated judgments of the supreme pontiffs and councils. He dared to bring charges against St Gregory VII; by the greatest crime he caused Guibert, the antipope, to be imposed under the name of Clement III; and in the year 1083, after besieging and capturing Rome, he arranged for him to be consecrated in the Vatican Basilica by schismatic and deposed bishops. In the following year, 1084, he wished the emperor to be crowned by him in the Lateran.

This obstinate and rebellious man, equally against Gregory VII, Victor III, and Paschal II, the successors of Gregory, by whom he was condemned again and a third time together with his heresy, held the Farfa monastery and the Sabine region under his tyranny so completely that no one dared to enter the names of the legitimate pontiffs in its registers. Instead, in place of Victor III and Paschal II, who are suppressed, these records place the pseudopontiff Clement, who styled himself Clement III, from Henry’s attempted coronation to the end of the century.

We added a brief note marked with an asterisk to this year in our edition of the *Chronicle* [Col. 0322B], so that readers might remember who this Clement was. He was that Guibert of Parma, chancellor of Henry, king of Germany, who arranged for the antipope Cadalus to be promoted in 1061, already foreshadowing the criminal schemes that he himself later devised against Gregory after obtaining the See of Ravenna by evil arts, while he coveted the Roman See.

At last, having attained his wish and having remained always hostile to the true pontiffs, he paid the penalty for his impiety: first, while alive, expelled everywhere by the faithful; then, when he died around the year 1099 or 1100, his body was exhumed after death and scattered into running water in 1105.

As Rome herself groaned under the oppression of these tyrants and was compelled to keep her legitimate prince and shepherd imprisoned in the fortress of St. Angelo under criminal custody, while she watched the leaders of the schism, Guibert and Henry, crowned in the Lateran patriarchate and at the Vatican and overthrowing sacred and secular rights—until faithful citizens of St. Peter, mindful of the Roman name and of virtue, were found to avenge the public majesty and drive these monsters from their necks—who could wonder that, in the second Chronicle of the Register of the monastery of Farfa, where Henry had established his strongholds and tyranny, the names of the legitimate pontiffs were suppressed and the invader Guibert alone, under the name of Clement III, together with his partner in crime Henry, filled the final page?

It is also worth observing that the second Chronicle ends at the same point as the eleventh century, although the Register contains later acts extending through forty years of the succeeding century. From this we may infer that Gregory of Catino did not mark these final periods, but rather some partisan copyist of Peter, abbot of Farfa. Concerning this abbot, it is sufficient to consult Spondanus’s Epitome of Baronius, which gathers the following from the Bibliothecarius under the year 1108:

> “In the year of Christ 1108, indiction 1, Pope Paschal—as the Bibliothecarius relates—again restrained certain Romans who were causing disturbances, whose leaders were Ptolemy, count of Tusculum, and Peter of Colonna, abbot of Farfa, usurpers of ecclesiastical property, together with others who were inciting the people to revolt. This was accomplished chiefly through the agency of Peter Leo and Leo Frangipani, most noble Roman citizens who were faithfully acting on Paschal’s behalf.”

I am astonished that that anonymous writer, who in 1689 published at Paris, together with a historical dissertation on certain coins of Charlemagne and his successors struck at Rome, also produced an Act from the Farfa archive, chapter 8, concerning the year 1105, by which he thought that he could undermine the rights of the supreme dominion of the supreme pontiffs over his own territory. He should have realized that he was borrowing these materials from the archives of Peter, abbot of Farfa, the leader of rebels against the Holy Roman Church in those days when the antipope and heresiarch Guibert had filled churches and monasteries with men of this sort. Leo of Ostia writes of him in the Cassinese Chronicle, book III, chapter 70:

> “That Guibert, after expelling Catholic bishops and abbots who presided over the churches and were distinguished alike in learning and religion, substituted for them in the individual cities and monasteries or churches wicked and ignorant men—one at a time, and sometimes two or several—by means of the condemned traffic of his former master Simon Magus. In the plundering of holy places and of Christians who did not support him, indeed even of those who did support him, since there was no one to resist him by force of arms, he spread himself far and wide, with the will of Nero and Decius, though with less power.”

Something similar occurred in this same second Chronicle around the middle of the tenth century, in the periods that followed, when factions arising in Italy and especially at Rome were tearing the Church apart through frequent schisms. During these same years the codex appears to have been corrupted by the erasure of names and the transposition of legitimate pontiffs, but especially by the insertion of schismatics and intruders, whose names I judged should be accompanied in the margin by asterisks and brief notes, so that they might more easily be distinguished.

For these reasons also, I warn that the chronology of this second Chronicle, since it does not distinguish such matters, should be regarded as less reliable from the year 1050 onward. In the earlier period, several pontiffs’ reigns occur twice, after an interval of two or three years: namely those of Eugenius II, under the years 820 and 823; Sergius II, under 838 and 841; Leo IV, under 830 and 833; and Anastasius III, under 906 and 908. In one place they had been erased so that they could be transferred to the other. I have restored them in both places, since it is not sufficiently clear which of the two entries was first written by the author of the Chronicle; nor is it apparent whether he himself altered the earlier reading in a subsequent revision, or whether some more recent librarian changed it after discovering later documents.

As was my duty, I have faithfully indicated even the defects and erasures, so that no one may attribute to these chroniclers, or think that I have attributed to them, more authority than is appropriate. In the earlier chronology of the Roman pontiffs, which you have below in these prolegomena and which was copied from another earlier codex called the Farfa Chronicle, we found no erasures. But when we encountered, in the penultimate line, the antipope Boniface, and four places before him Leo, likewise an intruded false pontiff under the name of Leo VIII, we suspected that they may have been added by an ignorant person from an older Catalogue that ended in the preceding material. There, through the fault of a copyist, as I believe, three pontiffs were omitted before Marinus—who is placed fourth before the Leo mentioned: John XI, Leo VII, and Stephen IX.

The remaining material in that earlier Chronicle proceeds correctly.

[Col. 0324C]

Having therefore prefaced this information about the codices and authors, we can now safely publish those three chronological booklets, accurately transcribed from them, since even with their defects and indications of schisms they will contribute to historical truth.

[Col. 0323]

## Catalogue of the Emperors, from Julius Caesar to Henry III

Here is also read the succession of the Gothic and Lombard kings, together with the dukes of Spoleto and Benevento and several counts of the Sabine district.

*(From the Farfa Chronicle.)*

[Col. 0323D]

**Julius Caesar.** He ruled first in the year 699 from the foundation of the City.

**Octavian**, son of Octavius the Senator; he ruled for [the manuscript reads] 56/46 years and lived 77 years. In the forty-second year of his reign Jesus Christ, Son of God and our Lord, was born according to the flesh, in the sixth age of the world. According to the Hebrews, 3,952 years had passed from the beginning of the world; according to the Greeks, 6,508 years; according to the City, 751. He died.

**Tiberius**, Augustus’s stepson, son-in-law, and adopted son, ruled 23 years and lived 83 years. In the fifteenth year of his reign Christ was baptized; in the eighteenth He suffered and died.

In this Chronicle numbers are always expressed by the numerical letters of the Latin alphabet. For the sake of brevity, we shall render the following numbers in Arabic numerals.

## Catalogue of the Supreme Pontiffs

From the same Farfa Chronicle, written around the end of the eleventh century but apparently excerpted from an older codex, since it extends from St. Peter to Benedict VII of that name, namely to the year of Christ 984. In this Catalogue are expressed not only the years, months, and days during which each pontiff sat, but also the years, months, and days of the intervals between pontificates, or vacancies of the see, down to Benedict III.

[Col. 0329C]

**Blessed Peter** first sat in the chair at Antioch for 7 years; then, having entered the city of Rome in the year 45 of the Lord’s Incarnation, he sat in its chair for 25 years, 2 months, and 7 days, in the second year of the emperor Claudius, during the times of Tiberius Caesar, Gaius, Claudius, and Nero. After the Lord’s Incarnation, in the year 70, but in the thirty-eighth year after his Passion, he was crowned with martyrdom together with his fellow apostle Paul.+

**Linus:** sat 11 years, 3 months, and 12 days, during the time of Nero.

**Cletus:** sat 12 years, 1 month, and 11 days, during the times of Vespasian and Titus.

**Clement:** sat 9 years, 2 months, and 10 days, during the times of Galba and Vespasian. The episcopate was vacant for 22 days.

**Anacletus:** [sat] 11 years, 1 month, and 7 days, during the time of Domitian; the see was vacant 13 days.

[Col. 0330C]

**Evaristus:** 13 years, 7 months, and 2 days, during the times of Domitian, Nerva, and Trajan; vacancy 19 days.

[Col. 0330D]

## Register of Gregory of Catino, or Chronicle

Collected by Gregory of Catino, a monk of the same sacred monastery of Farfa, from the diplomas of the Roman pontiffs, emperors, kings of the Lombards, dukes, counts, and other public records preserved there, from the year of Christ 661 to the year 1098. It presents the succession of the Roman pontiffs, emperors, kings, dukes, and others, as well as the abbots of the same monastery, distinguished year by year according to the Christian era, together with notes of the indictions.

*(From a codex of the Farfa archive, written around the end of the eleventh century.)*
