# DESCRIPTION OF THE REGIONS OF THE CITY

## FRANCESCO BLANCHINI’S PREFACE TO THE TWO FOLLOWING SHORT WORKS

The next two short works will, as I hope, illuminate the Lives of the popes in more than one place. For since it has been observed that the writers of these Lives, especially the earlier ones, customarily—following the practice of public records—not only carefully enumerated the times of individual events by consulates, but also noted the places where the beginnings of their Lives occurred and where their final acts and duties were completed; and since those places consequently seemed noteworthy to them and worthy of being indicated to posterity, the plan of our undertaking appears to require that, after assembling the resources pertaining to chronology, we should also consider clarifying the topography of this history.

In almost every Life, moreover, the place of birth and the place of burial are recorded. If the man who subsequently attained the chair of Peter was born at Rome, the biographer generally adds the name of the region, and sometimes identifies a notable part of the region by some distinctive designation. Nor is the writer less careful in indicating the place of burial. For he mentions the cemetery, basilica, or titular church where the mortal remains of that pontiff were buried. Therefore, so that we should not be compelled to repeat in each Life an explanation of the region or cemetery thus indicated, we thought it more concise to present two short works that would somewhat clarify this topography.

Antiquity gives authority to both, and identifies the parts of the City or of the suburban territory discussed in the account of the region or cemetery. For, because these works were composed several centuries before us, the ruins of the same buildings had not yet disappeared in their time; those buildings were later destroyed and almost leveled with the ground, and the courses of the roads and the divisions of the regions had not yet been altered by new constructions so as to make their names more obscure to posterity.

The first of these topographical works was brought forth by the Reverend Father John Mabillon from a ninth-century parchment manuscript found in the library of the monastery of Einsiedeln, and was published among the *Vetera Analecta*, volume four, page 506. It was rightly given the title *Description of the Regions of the City*. For it is an ordered enumeration of the principal buildings, either within the bounds of the City of Rome or outside the City, visible on the right and left as a traveler proceeds from some gate of the City to a fixed destination.

After those descriptions of the regions of the City which Publicus Victor and Sextus Rufus composed in the time of Valentinian and Valens—one first published by Aldus Manutius, the other by our Panvinio—I have encountered none older than this. How greatly they benefited ancient history and antiquarian studies is shown by Panvinio in his preface to P. Victor, where he writes:

> “This is the one little book whose assistance has, above all, wonderfully supported everyone who has hitherto written about the antiquity of the City of Rome. Because it was either misunderstood or abridged, many errors have also been committed here and there throughout Roman antiquity.”

The utility and richness of those older descriptions by Rufus and Victor under Valentinian—when the City had not yet been destroyed by the Goths—cannot be compared with those of this Anonymous, whom we understand to have written after the many disasters inflicted on Rome by barbarians. It is clear that this work belongs approximately to the eighth or ninth century of the Christian era, since it is later than the age of Belisarius; for it mentions mills (page 509 of Mabillon’s edition), or structures for grinding, and appears to be older than the circuit of Leo IV and the City called Leonine after him, by which that prudent pontiff protected the Vatican basilica and its adjoining estates against the frequent attacks of the Saracens. No one, therefore, can fail to understand that this work is so far removed from the others that it cannot even be compared with them.

The account of Rufus and Victor is full, elegant, and carefully revised, enumerating in each region streets, small buildings, temples, lakes, bathhouses, thermal baths, and, finally, noteworthy public and private buildings. This description, by contrast, is more meager and runs through only a very few indications of important monuments. Yet it is useful because of its ordered, though sparse, indication of the places situated on the right and left along the course of a road and facing the person who proceeds from one gate of the City to another, or to a fixed destination on his route within or outside the City, as is indicated in the headings of such itineraries.

Would that this incomplete and confused survey had reached us in a less abrupt form. At least we would know something of the trace of all the principal roads used in the City after the Gothic and Vandal disasters and the pillaging of the Lombards and Saracens. But by an unfortunate fate of letters, this collection was written carelessly by its author, in the manner of notes or memoranda made solely for recollection, as circumstances offered, and entered day by day into a codex. He proceeded sometimes from one gate of the City and sometimes from another—as visitors and pilgrims usually do—to some destination either fixed by prior agreement for his journey or offered by chance, observing on the way whatever seemed worthy of note.

To these notes, written so casually that they sometimes call the right side the left, a new confusion was added through the negligence or, as I believe, the carelessness of the binder. For someone cut those parchment sheets, each divided into two columns of verses—as is apparent from the half-words expressed in some verses by capital letters, to which the syllables and letters completing the same word correspond and occupy the neighboring column of the same page, to which they must be joined—into two parts, and then bound them as though the columns followed one another rather than being joined.

This damage was nevertheless not difficult to repair, since the words themselves indicated the syllables that followed them, as anyone may observe who compares the pages of Mabillon’s edition in the way that, as he will recognize, we have done. For example, the last verse on page 507 of Mabillon’s edition, continuing the journey from the Flaminian Gate into the City on the left, indicates the following verses on page 508, together with the title of Saint Sylvester—now called *in capite*—and then: “through the portico as far as the Column AN” (read “AN” rather than “AR”). Soon, as those proceeding along the same Flaminian road into the City, the “Virgin’s Forma”—that is, the aqueduct of the Virgin—appears likewise on the left, broken; then the titular church of Saint Marcellus. “Again through the portico as far as the Apostles.”

Who, then, does not see that this account of the buildings situated on the left of a person proceeding from the Flaminian Gate to the Twelve Holy Apostles along the Flaminian Road—now called the Via del Corso—inside the City must be joined to the other section, which indicates on page 508 the things seen on the right along the same road, but which was placed afterward in a disordered sequence and written out in that form?

### Via Lateranensis

Saint Lawrence in Lucina; TONINI; the Obelisk; the Column of Antoninus

From this it follows that the preceding verses on page 507 must be joined to the following and postponed verses on page 508 in this way:

### From the Flaminian Gate as far as the Lateran Road

**On the left:** the *Pariturium*, Saint Sylvester, and then through the portico as far as the Column of Antoninus; Saint Marcellus; again through the portico as far as the Apostles.

**On the right:** Saint Lawrence in Lucina; the Obelisk; the Column of Antoninus; the Lateran Road.

The Anonymous’ itinerary indicates that he was stationed at the Flaminian Gate and proceeded straight to the titular church of Saint Marcellus and to that of the Twelve Holy Apostles. On the left he saw the *Pariturium*—some think that *Periturium* should be read, that is, the circuit of the towers visible from the Flaminian Gate to the Pincian, on the walls and slope; page 514 enumerates twenty-nine of them. Then he saw the titular church of Saint Sylvester, from which he proceeded through the portico—among those remaining in the Campus Martius—as far as the Column of Antoninus, namely the spiral column of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus. He passed on the left by the titular church of Saint Marcellus and again through the portico reached the titular church of the Holy Apostles and the Lateran Road, which, as appears from the title of the section, had been established as the destination of this journey.

On the right, he evidently noted the titular church of Saint Lawrence in Lucina and then the obelisk, namely the famous obelisk of the Campus Martius, still lying in our own time near that same titular church. Most of it is still visible in the wine cellar of a private house, and Nardini describes it in book VI, chapter 6, page 354. He reports that near this obelisk, which Augustus erected in the Campus Martius in place of a gnomon, as Pliny relates in book XXXVI, chapter 9, to detect the shadows of the sun and indicate the length of days and nights on a horizontal sundial, gilded bronze fragments of rods indicating the hours and shadow were found.

After the obelisk, on the right, stood the Column of Antoninus, that is, another column which remained standing there on the hill commonly called the Quirinal until the year 1702. At that time, it was discovered from its pedestal and inscription that it was the famous column dedicated to Antoninus Pius at his deification and represented on coins. It was therefore moved to adorn the nearby forum, in front of the palace recently constructed for the administration of justice and the preservation of public records.

After that Column of Antoninus Pius, we reach the Lateran Road, namely the road that leads from there to the Lateran, turning to the right through the places listed in the following verses:

> The Alexandrian Baths; Saint Eustachius; the Rotunda;  
> The Commodian Baths; the Minervium; and Saint Mark.

After the itinerary’s describer had led us from the Flaminian Gate to the Lateran Road and listed the more important buildings on the right and left, he again stops at the gate and, reversing his route outside the walls, adds this:

> On the Flaminian Road, outside the wall:  
> **On the right:** Saint Valentine.  
> **On the left:** the Tiber.

With this observation applied, the displaced sections of this itinerary are restored to their proper order and the separated parts are joined. If these Einsiedeln parchments had remained intact, we would have a sufficiently convenient ground plan of the City and a fuller topographical catalogue of the cemeteries. Yet from the enumeration of the gates that it provides, it is apparent that several sections are missing. Nevertheless, it is better to produce whatever documents of that age survive, even if mutilated, than to deprive the history of Anastasius of them altogether.

I shall also add a confirmation of the truth to be drawn from the disordered arrangement of the itinerary’s sections and from its errors. It should be observed that the author of this itinerary takes his position at each of the gates of Rome and directs his journey either from one gate of the City to another or from a gate to the Forum, as is clear from the section headings.

His plan, as I have often said, was to place in one column the more noteworthy things situated on the left, prefixed by the letter **S**, an index of the left side, or with the complete word written on the left; and to place in another column those situated on the right, prefixed by the letter **D**, signifying the right side of the person proceeding, or by the complete word written on the right.

It is astonishing that our Anonymous sometimes exchanged the same sigla, **D** and **S**, and carelessly presented as things on the left those that faced him on the right; or conversely inscribed on the right in his notes what he had seen on the left. These examples show how easily visitors of that age, which was not highly cultivated, could go wrong when copying ancient inscriptions and their numbers, which served as chronological indices from the autograph catalogues of basilicas, arches, and monuments of emperors and magistrates; such mistakes could render the entire course of a road incorrectly as left instead of right.

For this reason I have judged, not without cause, that greater trust should be placed in the readings of the manuscripts kept in libraries near the City, which were often compared with the original monuments, than in those of the manuscripts kept far from Italy, whose texts could scarcely have been compared with the originals by someone who was copying them hurriedly, in the manner of a traveler, not sufficiently learned or impatient of delay and eager to hasten his return.

Having been warned of this, the Reader will allow me to arrange the Einsiedeln notes and their sections in an order that restores the method of the itinerary, without any mutilation of words or verses, preserving each word of Mabillon’s edition. I have taken care to indicate the pages of that edition by numbers placed alongside on the right and left wherever they must be joined.

# DESCRIPTION OF THE REGIONS OF THE CITY, OR THE ANONYMOUS’ ITINERARY THROUGH AND AROUND THE CITY

With indications of the noteworthy buildings surviving there around the eighth century of Christ

[Note: This description of Rome represents the walls of the City in the condition in which they were after the restoration by Belisarius, and in which they have, for the most part, remained even to the present day.]

From page 514 of Mabillon’s edition there is prefixed an enumeration of the gates of the City, together with the circuit and description of its walls. (C)

## From the Gate of Saint Peter

[Note: The Gate of Saint Peter. This gate stood on the nearer bank of the Tiber, at the entrance to the Aelian Bridge—now the Bridge of Saint Angelo—which led to the Mausoleum of Hadrian, situated on the farther bank and now called the Castle of Saint Angelo. The author of this itinerary calls the mausoleum the Hadrianium, and from there the road continued to Saint Peter. He therefore calls the gate itself the Gate of Saint Peter at the Hadrianium.

It was demolished after Leo IV extended the city’s perimeter beyond the Tiber and enclosed the Vatican basilica and its neighboring estates within walls, thereby establishing the Leonine City. In front of the same gate there could be seen the Arch of Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, with an inscription published both in the very ancient collection of the Einsiedeln manuscript joined to this description and in Gruter, folio 172, no. 1, as well as by Mazochius and others whom he cites. Marlianus, book VI, chapter 8, relates that fragments of the arch were found near the church of Saint Celsus; they now remain opposite that same church.

That inscription records great porticoes extending from this point along the Triumphal Way and across the Vatican Bridge to the Basilica of Saint Peter, and from there to the Theater of Pompey and the Flaminian Circus. The Einsiedeln parchment in Mabillon, folio 487, no. 15, agrees with Mazochius’ edition, folio 6, even in the arrangement of the imperial title. In the Carpensis notes, Metellus placed the title after the sigla **D. D. D. N. N. N.**; but while the arch still stood, the Anonymous copied it as Mazochius reproduced it after its destruction:]

> IMP. CAESSS. D. D. D. N. N. N. GRATIANVS. VALENTINIANVS ET THEODOSIVS PII FELICES SEMPER AVGGG. ARCVM AD CONCLVDENDVM OPVS OMNE PORTICVVM MAXIMARVM AETERNI NOMINIS SVI PECVNIA PROPRIA FIERI ORNARIQVE IVSSERVNT.

> The emperors and Caesars, our lords, Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, pious, fortunate, ever august, ordered that this arch, to complete the entire work of the great porticoes bearing their eternal name, be made and adorned at their own expense.

From this same Gate of Saint Peter the Anonymous begins several stages of his itinerary, as I shall soon show. In one of them, since he mentions the arch on the left while proceeding toward Saint Apollinaris, it is clear that the arch meant is this very arch of the three Augusti, Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius.]

From the gate itself as far as the Flaminian Gate: sixteen towers, 782 battlements, three posterns, four necessary openings. Larger windows on the outside, 107; smaller, 66.

[Col. 0348D] From the Flaminian Gate, including the gate itself, as far as the closed Pincian Gate: twenty-nine towers, 644 battlements, three necessary openings; larger windows on the outside, 75; smaller, 117.

[Col. 0349A] From the closed Pincian Gate, including the gate itself, as far as the Salarian Gate: twenty-two towers, 266 battlements, seventeen necessary openings; larger windows, 200; smaller, 160.

From the Salarian Gate, including the gate itself, as far as the Nomentan Gate: ten towers, 199 battlements, two necessary openings; larger windows on the outside, 71; smaller, 65.

From the Nomentan Gate, including the gate itself, as far as the Tiburtine Gate: fifty-seven towers, 806 battlements, two necessary openings; larger windows on the outside, 214; smaller, 200.

From the Tiburtine Gate, including the gate itself, as far as the Praenestine Gate: nineteen towers, 302 battlements including the Praenestine Gate, one necessary opening; larger windows on the outside, 80; smaller, 108.

From the Praenestine Gate as far as the Asinarian Gate: twenty-six towers, 904 battlements, six necessary openings; larger windows on the outside, 180; smaller, 150.

[Col. 0349B] From the Asinarian Gate as far as the Metrovan Gate: twenty towers, 342 battlements, four necessary openings; larger windows on the outside, 130; smaller, 180.

[Note: The Metrovan Gate. In Letter 69 of Saint Gregory the Great, book IX, it is called the Metronian Gate, as Nardini observes in book I, chapter 9. It therefore seems that it should be called Metronia rather than Metrovia. His words are: “Having mounted their horses, they went out through the Metronian Gate, so that he might follow them onto the Latin or Appian Way.” Its location indicates that it was not far from the entrance of the Aqua Crabra—now called the Marrana—into the City, where a closed gate is still visible, once called the Gabian Gate, from Gabii, to which it led.]

From the Metrovan Gate as far as the Latin Gate: twenty towers, 294 battlements, seventeen necessary openings; larger windows on the outside, 100; smaller, 183.

From the Latin Gate as far as the Appian Gate: twelve towers, 174 battlements, six necessary openings; larger windows on the outside, 80; smaller, 85.

From the Appian Gate as far as the Ostian Gate: forty-nine towers, 615 battlements, twenty-four necessary openings; larger windows on the outside, 330; smaller, 284.

[Note: The Ostian Gate. Mabillon noted on page 518, no. 73, that in this Einsiedeln manuscript *Ostensem viam*, “Ostian road,” and *Ostensem portam*, “Ostian gate,” are consistently read. Everyone knows that in both places the error must be corrected as a barbarism originating either in the usage of the age or in the scribe, since the name derived from the colony of Ostia, to which the road led, is formed in exactly the same way as *Praenestina* from Praeneste and *Tiburtina* from Tibur. The same should be said of the Portuensian Gate, which he calls the Portensian Gate.

The remaining gates are sufficiently well known, since their names are preserved with little variation among all antiquarians. Concerning the Asinarian Gate, which no longer survives, Nardini doubts whether it is the same as the Coelimontan Gate, now called Saint John’s, which Anastasius, in the Life of Silverius, indicates was near the Lateran; or whether it was opened somewhat lower down, since Festus appears to place the Asinarian Way between the Ardeatine and Latin Ways.

Antiquarians also dispute the location of the Aurelian Gate: whether it should be sought at the Triumphal Bridge on this side of the Tiber—fragments of which bridge can be seen near the Aelian Bridge—or whether it was established on the elevated Janiculum, at the Severan walls, toward the church of Saint Pancratius.

The Einsiedeln Anonymous indicates from the number of towers and battlements that the circuit of the City and its walls between the Praenestine and Latin Gates was divided into approximately three equal parts, thereby showing us the locations of the Asinarian and Metrovan Gates, the former nearer to the Praenestine Gate and the latter nearer to the Latin Gate.

From the same indication, namely the number of towers and battlements between the Portuensian Gate and the Gate of Saint Peter at the Aelian Bridge, we can also determine without difficulty that the Aurelian Gate was situated approximately there, where we proceed from the walls of the City in the Transtiberine region, on the summit of the Janiculum, toward Saint Pancratius. The rest requires no explanation.

I shall add one point to illuminate the circuit of the City from this description: the number of towers can still be seen surviving in many places. I counted twenty-two from the Pincian Gate to the Salarian Gate, precisely the number described by the Anonymous—thirteen within the Ludovisi Gardens and nine in the adjoining vineyards as far as the next Salarian Gate.

They stand at nearly equal distances, 120 Roman feet from the center of one tower to the center of the next, which is twenty-five *passus*, of the kind of which one thousand make the Roman mile marked by milestones in the age of Vespasian and in our own. The width of a tower is approximately twenty feet. The curtain walls between the towers are generally one hundred feet long and usually divided into six equal arches, so that from the number of towers one can easily calculate the total number of paces constituting the circuit of the walls.

Assigning twenty-five paces to the distance from each tower to the next, and calculating 383 towers from the Anonymous’ figures, the circuit of Rome defined by the walls of Aurelian and Belisarius amounts to 9,575 paces—that is, 75 above 9,500. Today, including the Leonine City and the Janiculum, it is said to equal 15,330 paces.

Having prefaced the description and order of the City’s gates, from which the Anonymous begins his journeys, we think that the itinerary’s sections should be referred to the order of the gates in this way, beginning with the Gate of Saint Peter, which he establishes as the first. (Page 502, no. 72, of Mabillon’s edition, arranged by us into sections.)]

From the Ostian Gate as far as the Tiber: thirty-five towers, 733 battlements, seventeen necessary openings; larger windows on the outside, [Col. 0349C] 338; smaller, 211.

From the Tiber River as far as the Portuensian Gate: four towers, fifty-nine battlements; larger windows on the outside, ten; smaller, fifteen.

From the Portuensian Gate as far as the Aurelian Gate: twenty-nine towers, 400 battlements, two necessary openings; larger windows on the outside, 137; smaller, 163.

From the Aurelian Gate as far as the Tiber: twenty-four towers, 327 battlements, eleven necessary openings; larger windows on the outside, 160; smaller, 131.

From the Tiber River as far as the Gate of Saint Peter: nine towers, 489 battlements; larger windows on the outside, twenty-one; smaller, seven; two posterns.

The Gate of Saint Peter at the Hadrianium.

There are six towers, 164 battlements; larger windows on the outside, fourteen; smaller, nineteen.

There are altogether 383 towers, 7,020 battlements, six posterns, 106 necessary openings, and 2,066 larger windows on the outside.

[Note: The Anonymous begins his route under the auspices of Christian piety, setting out on the journey he had planned to the threshold of the Apostles. This follows the ancient custom of religious people, from the age of Tertullian and Gaius—nearly contemporary with the apostolic age—who first visited those monuments that they already called the trophies of the Apostles, as one reads in Eusebius, book II, chapter 25:

> “But I can show the trophies of the Apostles. For whether you wish to go to the Vatican or to the Ostian Way, you will encounter the trophies of those who founded that Church.”

Beginning, therefore, at the Gate of Saint Peter, he proceeds to the Basilica of Saint Paul, turning his route through the more celebrated cemeteries and memorials of earlier popes and martyrs, from Saint Paul to Saint Sebastian, and then returning to the City by the Appian Way.

From the Gate of Saint Peter, therefore, proceeding through the so-called Lesser Campus, described by Nardini in book VI, chapter 5, where one will find its ground plan, he sees on the left the titular church of Saint Lawrence in Damasus, near the Theater of Pompey, which he leaves on the right.]

## SECTION I. From the Gate of Saint Peter to Saint Paul

**On the left:** Saint Lawrence [in Damasus] and the Theater of Pompey, and through the portico [or perhaps *posticum*] as far as Saint Angelo and the Temple of Jupiter.

[Note: From there, through the portico—for several porticoes had been erected for walking, among them the one located here, the Portico of Philippus, drawn by Nardini at this point— as far as Saint Angelo, namely in the Piscarian Forum, where the same deaconry still survives today.]

[Note: The Temple of Jupiter. That is, the Capitoline Temple, likewise situated on the left of the person proceeding.]

In the right-hand direction [*In dextera*]: the theater. [Note: “Theater.” I understand this as the Theater of Marcellus, rising on the right opposite the Capitoline slope and the Temple of Jupiter.] Again through the portico to the Elephant. [Note: “Elephant Herbarium.” That is, a statue of an elephant erected by Augustus near the Fish Market, as Nardini sensibly conjectures on p. 323, indicating that it is mentioned in this eighth region of the Roman Forum by Publius Victor and the *Notitia Imperii*.]

From there through the Greek School. There is an aqueduct beneath the Aventine hill, with a stairway ascending the Aventine hill, and the Baths of Mercury. From there to the Ostian Gate. [Note: “To the Ostian Gate.” To the gate of the Ostian Way, where a portico first appears outside the City, extending to the church distinguished by the name of the martyr Menna. In the age of this Anonymous, the remaining portion of the portico as far as Saint Paul’s seems to have been demolished. Pope Saint Adrian later restored it as far as the basilica, as Anastasius records in his *Life*, section 342: “He restored anew the portico that leads to blessed Paul the Apostle, from the gate, together with the church of Saint Euplius, as far as the aforesaid basilica of Saint Paul.” Concerning the church of Saint Euplius, see what the distinguished Giovanni Maria Crescimbeni learnedly assembled in *The History of Saint Mary in Cosmedin, or the Greek School*, book VII, chapter 29; he performs the office of its archpresbyter with great distinction. In chapter 36 Martinelli likewise mentions the church of blessed Menna, notable for its collection, when the station was held at Saint Paul’s on the Fourth Sunday of Lent, and appearing in these Einsiedeln itineraries between the Ostian Gate and Paul’s basilica. It was restored by Saint Leo III, as Anastasius records in his *Life*, section 361, and, as he relates, also by Saint Paschal I, section 444, who presented gifts to the same church of blessed Menna.]

From there through the rear passage to the church of Menna; and from Menna to Saint Paul the Apostle; from there to Saints Felix, Adauctus, and Emerita. [Note: “To Saint Felix, Adauctus, and Emerita.” This notable cemetery was discovered a few years ago precisely at the place indicated by the Itinerary: namely, after leaving Saint Paul’s church, once the nearby hill on the road leading to Saint Sebastian has been crossed. It is first encountered beyond that slope at Villa Mandosia, recently identified through ancient paintings found in a chamber of the cemetery; these clearly displayed the names of the three saints beneath their respective images. The same paintings were drawn and communicated by the frequently praised Reverend Father Giovanni Marangoni, as the canon Boldetti, mentioned above with equal praise, clearly described them in his *Observations on the Cemeteries of the Martyrs*, book II, chapter 18, p. 541. Thus the Librarian, no. 361, not without reason calls this place, marked by a church and cemetery of Felix and Adauctus, “near Saint Paul the Apostle.” The antiquity of the cemetery is understood from the same book of Anastasius, section 89, in the *Life of Saint John I*, where it is said to have been renewed by him: “Likewise he renewed the cemetery of Felix and Adauctus.” But concerning this cemetery and the others mentioned in this section, see the Notes to Opusculum XVI, which is to follow immediately.]

Then to Saint Petronilla, and Nereus, and [Col. 0351D] Achilleus. From there to Saint Mark and Saint Marcellianus. From there to Saint Soter; from there to Saint Sixtus; there also are Saint Fabian, Anterus, and Miltiades. From there to Saint Cornelius. From there to Saint Sebastian. From there, returning by the Appian Way, to the church where Saint Sixtus was beheaded together with his deacons. From there to the Appian Gate. There is the aqueduct called Jopia, which comes from the Marcia and runs as far as the bank. [Note: “The Jopia aqueduct, which comes from the Marcia.” One should read *forma Julia*, or *Appia*, “which comes from the Marcia.” For the three aqueducts—the Marcia, Julia, and Tepula—were the highest of all those supplying the City before the Emperor Claudius brought in the Claudia and the New Anio; they carried channels to the higher hills of Rome through a triple conduit, still visible outside the walls before the Praenestine Gate, commonly called Porta Maggiore, as the distinguished Fabretti described it on p. 18, no. 29, of the first dissertation *On Aqueducts and Watercourses*. But, as Fabretti himself observes there, no. 49, drawing on Frontinus, the Marcia, after the gardens of Pallantius, descends through the Caelian into the channel called the Herculaneus. Since its conduit supplied nothing to the uses of the hill, being lower, [the measure (*modus*, editorial supplementation)] was taken above the Capenian Gate. Frontinus prefaces this with the following words: “The Marcia also, which, after the Tepula had been intercepted, had joined the Julia by the channel, as we demonstrated above, now receives its measure from the reservoir of that same Julia; it comes by its own channel and under its own name, and from the reservoirs both are received into the same arches.” From this it can be gathered why this aqueduct, carried above the Capenian Gate from the Caelian, is called Julia, coming from the Marcia. Since the two waters, the Marcia and the Julia, joined in such a way that one received its measure from the reservoir of the other and was received into the same arches, it was very easy to apply both names to it and to call the aqueduct “Julia, coming from the Marcia”: it descended through the Caelian, and its measure was taken above the Capenian Gate.

“I know that Fabretti, highly skilled in matters concerning water, taught us in the cited place, nos. 43, 49, and 58, that the old Capenian Gate and the Appian aqueduct must be placed farther within the City, beneath the gardens of the Mattei, and that the present Gate of Saint Sebastian, after the time of Aurelian, was regarded as the Capenian Gate. This led antiquaries of our own time to believe that the aqueduct arch overhanging the recent Gate of Saint Sebastian was the Appian, although it is a branch of the Old Anio, brought here through the Octavian conduit.

“Yet this same occasion for the common error—which indiscriminately assigns three names, Julia, Marcia, and Appia, to the neighboring waters and conduits—could more easily, in the age of this Anonymous, when barbarism was everywhere apparent, have confused the names and changed *Appia*, or *Julia*, into *Jopia*. To this obscure name he prudently added ‘coming from the Marcia,’ so that we might understand that, whatever its name, it was an aqueduct bringing water here over the arches of the Marcia, whether the water had been drawn from the Old Anio, from the Julia, or even from what was then believed to be the Appia.”]

From there to the broken spiral staircase. From there to the Arch of Remembrance. [Note: “The Arch of Remembrance.” I interpret this as the Arch of the Memory of Drusus, erected by Augustus in accordance with a decree of the Senate. Fabretti proved that it survived before the Gate of Saint Sebastian, based on the form represented on coins, in no. 72 of his frequently cited dissertation. His conclusion is supported by the fragments of a bronze tablet discovered at the same place, recording decrees passed by the most distinguished order in honor of another Drusus, namely the son of Tiberius Caesar. These are the same decrees mentioned by Tacitus in *Annals* IV.9, namely those resembling the decrees made for Germanicus under Augustus, *Annals* II.83: “For the memory of Drusus, the same decrees as those made for Germanicus.”

“From these unpublished fragments of bronze tablets belonging to the Claudian family, adopted into the Julian family, and from several other inscriptions of the Julian family found around this arch and published by the distinguished Giovanni, Abbot Aignolio, after his dissertation *On the Column of Antoninus Pius*, there is no remaining room for doubt that the arch belonged to Drusus, the father of Claudius Augustus and the paternal uncle of Drusus, the son of Tiberius. Above all, however, this is demonstrated by three inscriptions found in the Einsiedeln manuscripts together with this itinerary. They are described at the Appian Gate—corruptly called the Papian Gate—and were published by Mabillon, *Ancient Annals*, vol. IV, pp. 504–505.”]

**76. At the Papian Gate**

**NERONI IVLIO. D. F. GERMANICO**  
To Nero Julius Germanicus, son of the deified [one]; to Tiberius Caesar, grandson of Germanicus Augustus; to Julius, son of Augustus, great-grandson; to the deified pontiff Caesar, grandson of Augustus, grandson of the deified [one], pontiff Caesar, great-grandson of the deified [one], consul three times, imperator three times, augur, holding tribunician power for the eighth time. [The printed sequence conflates inscriptional segments.]

**77. Likewise there**

**IMP. CAESARI. LIVIA [that is, LIVIAE]. I. DIVI F. AUGUST. DRUSI F. PONTIFIC. MAXIMO, UXORI CAESARIS AUG. COS. III. IMP. III. TRIBUNIC. POT. VIII. PATRI PATRIAE AUG. XV. VIR. S. F. VII. VIR. EPULON. COS. XIII. IMP. XVII. TRIBUNIC. POTEST. XXX.**

To Imperator Caesar; to Livia; to the son of the deified [one], Augustus; to the son of Drusus; to the chief pontiff; to the wife of Caesar Augustus; consul three times; imperator three times; holding tribunician power for the eighth time; Father of the Fatherland; augur; one of the Fifteen for Sacred Rites; one of the Seven Banqueters; consul thirteen times; imperator seventeen times; holding tribunician power for the thirtieth time. [The headings and titles are conflated in the transmitted text.]

**78. Likewise there**

**CAESARI I. CAESARI DRUSO. JULIO TI. CLAUDIO AUGUSTI F. AUGUSTI F. GERMANICI F. DRUSI GERMANICI F. DIVI NEPOT. DIVI NEPOT. AUG. PRONEPOT. NERONI GERMANICO PONTIF. COS. AUGURI. COS. DESIGN. GERMANICO IMPERATORI PRINCIPI JUVENTUTIS.**

To Caesar; to Caesar Drusus Julius; to Tiberius Claudius, son of Augustus, son of Augustus, son of Germanicus, son of Drusus Germanicus, grandson of the deified [one], grandson of the deified [one], great-grandson of Augustus; to Nero Germanicus, pontiff, consul, augur; consul designate; to Germanicus, imperator, leader of the youth. [The names and filiations are interwoven in the printed transcription.]

“I have judged that the three inscriptions of the Einsiedeln manuscript should be reproduced here as Mabillon published them, both to show that this Drusian arch on the Appian Way, erected by the Senate and dedicated to the memory of Drusus Germanicus—hence the Anonymous calls it the Arch of Remembrance—was everywhere adorned with many inscriptions dedicated to the honor of the Claudians, or Neros, adopted by Augustus into the Julian family, and to demonstrate that this anonymous recorder of the epigrams or inscriptions of the City was no more successful in dealing with these than in the sections of his Itinerary, which he mixed together rather than arranged.

“For those inscriptions mention several members of the Julian family and the principal members of the Claudian family individually, persons granted affiliation with the Julian clan after their adoption by Caesar Augustus, the husband of Livia. They may perhaps have been engraved in the same order as the four inscriptions in Gruter, fol. CCXXVI, no. 9, which identify men and women of the same period and family: Drusus and Antonia, the parents of the Emperor Claudius, and Agrippina, his wife, and Nero, his son.

“But the Anonymous copied them from the arch in such a way that he believed the continuous lines to be segments of the individual inscriptions extended along the same straight line. Thus those segments are extraordinarily entangled and confused, just as happened on a similar arch, built of square stones at Spoleto near the church of the Canons Regular. There, Germanicus and Drusus, the sons of Tiberius and members of the Claudian family adopted into the Julian family, had once been commemorated in this manner. The surviving letters make this clear, although others have produced an entangled reading because they did not distinguish the portion of the verses belonging to Germanicus from the adjacent portion referring to the inscription of Drusus:

**GERMANICO CAESARI TI. AVG. F. DRVSO CAESARI TI. AVG. F. DIVI AVGVSTI N. D. IVLI. PRONEP. DIVI AVGVSTI N. DIVI IVLI PRON. IMP. II. AVG. FLAMINI AVG. COS. II. T. R. POT. II. PONT. . . . . S. C.**

[The inscription should be divided as follows:]

First, to be read separately:

“To Germanicus Caesar, son of Tiberius Augustus, grandson of the deified Augustus, great-grandson of the deified Julius, imperator twice, augur, priest of Augustus.”

Then:

“Drusus Caesar, son of Tiberius Augustus, grandson of the deified Augustus, great-grandson of the deified Julius, consul twice, holding tribunician power for the second time, pontiff, by decree of the Senate.”

“But those who continued the individual lines without interruption, as though they extended across both inscriptions, read them rashly in this form:

‘To Germanicus Caesar, son of Tiberius Augustus; to Drusus Caesar, son of Tiberius Augustus; grandson of the deified Augustus, great-grandson of the deified Julius, grandson of the deified Augustus, great-grandson of the deified Julius, victorious commander twice, Augustus, priest of Augustus, consul twice, holding tribunician power twice, pontiff, by decree of the Senate.’

“The Anonymous was evidently preoccupied by the same error, mixing together sections of the itinerary and portions of ancient inscriptions, as is clear from the passages quoted above. For who would not see that in the item numbered 77 on p. 504 of Mabillon’s edition, three distinct inscriptions—that of Augustus, that of Livia, and that of Tiberius—have been confused into one?

“The letters belonging to Augustus are:

**IMP. CAESARI DIVI F. AUGUSTO PONTIFICI MAXIMO PATRI PATRIAE COS. XIII. IMP. XVII. TRIBUNIC. PO. TEST. XXX. III.**

‘To the Emperor Caesar Augustus, son of the deified one, chief pontiff, Father of the Fatherland, consul thirteen times, victorious commander seventeen times, holding tribunician power for the thirtieth time, three times.’

Thus the number XXX must be supplied.

“To Livia belong these words:

**LIVIAI UXORI CAESARIS AUG.**

‘To Livia, wife of Caesar Augustus.’

“To Tiberius belong several titles contained in these same words and lines, although the numbers were carelessly copied and altered contrary to the evidence of other inscriptions. They should therefore be restored as follows:

**TI. CAESARI AUG. F. DIVI N. COS. II. IMP. III. TR. P. VIII. AUGURI VII. VIRO EPULON.**

‘To Tiberius Caesar, son of Augustus, grandson of the deified one, consul twice, victorious commander three times, holding tribunician power for the eighth time, augur, one of the Seven Banqueters.’

“These titles and numbers were assigned to Tiberius in the fifth year of the common era, when Lucius Valerius Messala and Gaius Cornelius Cinna were consuls and he had conquered several peoples in Germany. In any event, they continued to be arranged in this way even after he had assumed the empire following the death of Augustus, as is clear from the Gruterian inscription, fol. CCXXXV, no. 10, and from this inscription from Antium, transferred to the Alban Museum:

**TI. CAESARI DIVI AUGUSTI F. DIVI IVLI NEPOTI AUG. PONTIFICI MAXIMO COS. V. IMP. VIII. TR. POT. XXXVIII. AUGURI. XV. VIR. SACR. FACIEND. VII. VIR. EPULON. L. SCRIBONIVS L. F. VOT. CELER. AEDIL. EX D. D. PRO LUDIS.**

‘To Tiberius Caesar, son of the deified Augustus, grandson of the deified Julius, Augustus, chief pontiff, consul five times, victorious commander eight times, holding tribunician power for the thirty-eighth time, augur, one of the Fifteen for Sacred Rites, one of the Seven Banqueters. Lucius Scribonius Celer, son of Lucius, aedile, by decree of the decurions, for the games.’

“We could easily identify here the remaining princes of the Claudian family—Drusus, Germanicus, Nero the son of Germanicus, Tiberius Claudius Drusus, who later became emperor, and Drusus the son of Tiberius—by assigning to each the segments of inscriptions 76, 77, and 78 that the Einsiedeln Anonymous confused. But it is not worth pursuing this at greater length. I have touched on it here only to elucidate the Arch of Remembrance, described in the Itinerary near the Appian Gate, and to confirm from the inscriptions of the Julian and Claudian families, found there even in our own time but much more evident in the age of that recorder, who transferred into his Einsiedeln manuscript what he himself had seen at the Appian Gate, which he called the Papian Gate.

“All these documents confirm the defective patchwork of visitors who came here from distant regions and hastily entered in their diary what they saw. They frequently made mistakes when copying numbers, even when they had before their eyes inscriptions carved in marble in large letters, placed in the open air, illuminated by the full sun, and exposed to them at will. We should therefore rightly accept what we have so often indicated: that the external catalogues of the supreme pontiffs must be tested against the older Italian catalogues and those nearer to the City, which correspond much more faithfully to the originals of all such examples once displayed in the Pauline basilica and in the other urban and suburban patriarchal churches.

“But let us return from this digression to the road. Let us therefore follow the route of the Anonymous, who records in his Roman Itinerary the sections and neighboring paths from the Gate of Saint Peter in the following manner.”

The Arch of Remembrance. On the left, the Antonine Baths. On the right, Xystus. Saint Nereus and Saint Achilleus. From there through the portico to the aqueduct. From there to the Seven Ways. There are Saint Lucia and the Septizonium. On the left, the Circus Maximus. On the right, the Palatine. And thus through the great portico as far as Anastasia, and from there continually—

## SECTION II. From the Gate of Saint Peter to the Asinarian Gate

[Col. 0356B]

**THROUGH THE ARCH.** [Note: “Through the arch.” Namely, the arch of Gratian, Valentinian, and Theodosius, which he describes as near the bridge of Saint Peter, together with its inscription, copied by the Einsiedeln manuscript among the inscriptions in his collection, no. 15 of Mabillon’s edition, p. 487; we mentioned it shortly before in the notes on the Gate of Saint Peter.]

On the left:

The Flaminian Circus. There is Saint Agnes. [Note: “The Flaminian Circus.” Here he confuses the Flaminian with the Agonal Circus, in which Saint Agnes was located.] The Alexandrian Baths. Saint Eustachius. The Rotunda. The Commodian Baths. Minervium. [Note: “Minervium.” That is, the *Minervium*, formerly a temple of Minerva, now the church of Saint Mary above Minerva.] There is Saint Mary. At Saint Mark’s: Trajan’s Forum and its column.

On the right:

Saint Lawrence in Damaso. Pompey’s Theater. [Note: See section III, letter e, below.] The Cypress. Saint Lawrence in Minerva. The Capitol. [Col. 0356C] Saint Sergius. There is the navel of Rome. [Note: “Saint George.” In the Velabrum.] Saint George.

**RETURNING THROUGH THE ARCH OF SEVERUS**

On the left:

The Tiber. [Note: “The Tiber.” Perhaps a notable statue representing the river Tiber, now transferred to the Capitol from the Vicus Corneliorum, situated near Saint Agatha in the Subura—above the hill now called Monte Bagnanapoli, near the Baths of Paulus Aemilius—as Nardini observes from Rufus and Victor, book IV, chapter 6, p. 188.] Saint Hadrian. The Roman Forum. The Subura. Saint Lucia in Orthea. Saint Silvester and Saint Martin. The Palace near Jerusalem. Jerusalem. [Note: “The Amphitheater.” The Castrense Amphitheater near the title of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.] The Amphitheater. [Note: “The Lateran aqueduct.” This carried water from the Claudian aqueduct between the title of Santa Croce and the Praenestine Gate, now Porta Maggiore, up the Caelian hill to the Lateran.] The Lateran aqueduct. The monastery of Honorius. The Praenestine Gate. [Note: “Saint Helena. Saint Marcellinus and Saint Peter.” Outside the Praenestine Gate, at the second milestone, the foundations of the church still survive above the cemetery celebrated under the names of those same saints.]

Saint Helena, Saint Marcellinus, and Saint Peter.

On the right:

Saint Mary Antiqua. Saints Cosmas and Damian. [Col. 0356D] The Palace of Nero. The Church of Saint Peter in Chains. The Arch of Titus and Vespasian. [Note: “The Palace of Trajan.” The Baths of Trajan.] The Palace of Trajan. The Amphitheater. At Saint Clement’s. [Note: “The monastery of Honorius. The Claudian aqueduct. The Lateran patriarchate.” Near the Claudian aqueduct, after the aqueduct of the Lateran patriarchate, the *Life of Paschal I* records a monastery of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. In the *Life of Leo III* it is called the monastery of Saints Andrew and Bartholomew and is attributed to Honorius. It is not sufficiently clear whether there were two monasteries, one for men and the other for women, situated near the Lateran patriarchate and the Claudian aqueduct—just as two hospitals were established there for the separate treatment of the sick of each sex, a location which Cardinal Rasponus also attributes to the monastery of Honorius in book III, chapter 13, of *On the Lateran Patriarchate—or whether the same monastery bore two names.

“Rasponus shows from Anastasius that the monastery for men was founded by Pope Honorius and restored by Adrian I under the invocation of Saints Andrew and Bartholomew. We know from the *Life of Paschal I* that the monastery situated after the aqueduct of the Lateran patriarchate was distinguished by the title of Saints Sergius and Bacchus. There we read that the congregation of handmaids of God residing there, because of poverty and want, was unable to sing any praises to the almighty Lord and his saints. But the provident Pontiff supplied the handmaids of God not only with necessities but also added a monastery of monks, enriching it with estates, households, farms, vineyards, and houses. He bestowed these resources on their congregation, just as his predecessor Adrian had bestowed them on the monks of Saints Andrew and Bartholomew, so that they might chant praises and hymns to God and his saints night and day, with melody, in the venerable church of Our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ situated beside the Lateran.”]

The monastery of Honorius. The Claudian aqueduct. The Lateran patriarchate.

## SECTION III. From the Gate of Saint Peter to Saint Lucia in Orthea

[Note: “On the right” [*in dextera*; note: “that is, LIVIAE”]. This is an obvious error. The letters D and S must necessarily be exchanged. In this progression, as one advances toward the left, one sees the Agonal Circus—which in section II and here he incorrectly calls the Flaminian Circus—the Rotunda, the Commodian Baths, and so forth; while on the right are Saint Lawrence in Damaso, Pompey’s Theater, and so forth.]

On the right.

On the right:

The Flaminian Circus. The Rotunda. The Commodian Baths. Trajan’s Forum and its column.

On the left. [Note: “On the left: Saint Lawrence.” Read “on the right,” *in dextera*, as I said shortly before, letter a.] The Church of Saint Lawrence in Damaso. Pompey’s Theater. The Cypress. [Note: “Saint Lawrence.” This was a church called Saint Lawrence in the Palatine district under Adrian I, situated opposite the houses of the Mattei, where Saint Catherine of the Funari is now seen. Martinelli says on p. 364: “Adrian I newly restored Saint Lawrence in the Palatine district and the monastery of Pallacini, and joined it to another monastery of Saint Stephen situated beside it, called Baganda; and he appointed monks there to sing the office at the title of Saint Mark.” Concerning the same church, Grimaldus says in the *Bibliothecarius* under Leo III, Gregory IV, and Benedict III: “This church stood opposite the palace of the Mattei and perished in the construction of the monastery of Saint Catherine. It is mentioned in a bull of Celestine III, in which it is called ‘in the Golden Castle,’ that is, in the Flaminian Circus. It is also called the Enclosure.”

“In section II of this Itinerary Saint Lawrence in Minerva is also mentioned, from which it is clear that the place there called the Cypress was also identified. It seems to correspond to the street which, a few years ago, was called *l’Olmo*, perhaps because an elm tree had at some time been substituted there for a cypress near the sacred building and monastery of Saint Lawrence.”] The Capitol. Saint Sergius, where the navel of Rome is located.

**THE ARCH OF SEVERUS**

[Col. 0358A]

On the right:

The Tiber. Saint Hadrian.

On the left. [Note: “That is, LIVIAE.”]

The statue of Constantine’s horse. [Note: “The horse of Constantine.” Nardini observes that the *Notitia Imperii*, in the eighth region called the Roman Forum, indicates a horse of Constantine in the Forum itself. Yet he is mistaken, and too optimistic, on p. 253 when he thinks that in a later period the equestrian statue of Domitian, celebrated in the poems of Statius, was called by this name. Perhaps it was dedicated to Constantine as well, after Domitian’s name had been erased or the base changed, just as the triumphal arch erected for him, which we see, was built by the Senate and Roman people from the dismantled arch of Trajan.]

The Roman Forum.

On the right:

Saint Cyriacus. [Note: “Saint Cyriacus.” That is, Quiricus and Julitta, near the Forum of Nerva. Anastasius, no. 471, has the title of Saint Cyriacus. It was in the Baths of Diocletian, as in the Roman synod under Pope Gelasius. Sixtus IV, when the building had nearly collapsed from age, transferred the cardinal’s title to the church of Saint Cyriacus near the Forum of Nerva, of which we are speaking. Its antiquity is so great that Cardinal Alexander Medici learned from an inscription found upon it that its marble altar-table had been consecrated by Pope Vigilius. See Carlo Piazza, *On the Cardinal Hierarchy*, under the title of Saints Quiricus—or Cyriacus—and Julitta, and under the now antiquated or suppressed title of Saint Cyriacus in the Baths.] Saint Cyriacus. Saint Agatha. There are images of Paul and Saint Mary.

**THE SUBURA**

On the right:

The Baths of Constantine. [Note: “Saint Vitalis . . . where there are excellent horses.” Understand two statues discovered in the Baths of Constantine and set up beside the fountain on the Quirinal; they give the hill its name, Monte Cavallo.] Saint Vitalis in the Long Street, where there are excellent horses. [Note: “Saint Euphemia in the Vicus Patricius.” In the Vicus Patricius there was an ancient church and monastery of Saint Euphemia and of the Archangel Michael, according to Anastasius, no. 338, and indeed near the title of Pudentiana, no. 407, in the *Life of Saint Leo III*, as Floravantes Martinelli observed in his *Sacred Rome*, p. 357. Saint Pius V bestowed the honor of a cardinal’s title on the church of the martyr Eugenia. His successor Sixtus V, however, leveled it to the ground when he opened the broad road from the Liberian Basilica to Trajan’s Column. Near Trajan’s Forum Clement VIII, a provident father, established a monastery of mendicant girls, so that the patronage of that virgin and martyr, especially revered by the Roman people, might be made manifest through a sacred building and a college devoted to her praises. On this matter see the aforementioned Piazza under the suppressed title of Saint Euphemia, p. 699.] Saint Euphemia in the Vicus Patricius.

On the left:

The virgin Pudentiana in the Vicus Patricius. [Note: “Saint Lawrence at Formonso.” The same spelling occurs in the Vatican Virgil: “the handsome [one], the shepherd Corydon,” and so forth. At the end of this section the Subura must also be added, for the route stated in the title of the section will then be clear: it leads from the Nomentan Gate to the Roman Forum. When one has reached the church of Saint Euphemia, then near Saint Pudentiana in the Vicus Patricius—as you read above in section III, letter c—one enters the adjacent Subura and from there proceeds to the Roman Forum.]

The Subura. Saint Isidore. Saint Eusebius. The road beneath the monastery. Saint Vitus. Saint Mary in the Manger. Again Saint Vitus. Saint Euphemia.

## SECTION VIII

[Note: “Another Tiburtine Way.” The City is entered from the Tiburtine Way not, as previously, through the Gate of Saint Lawrence, but through the Naevian Gate, now Porta Maggiore, where the Claudian aqueduct, with its surviving channels and inscriptions, also displays the arch mentioned here. Proceeding through it, one sees the church of Saint Bibiana on the right and the Nymphaeum; on the left are the churches and monasteries of Saint Agatha and Saint Eusebius.

“Saint Agatha is now missing from this part of the City. I think it is the church that Martinelli says was called Saint Agatha at the Entrance of the City, at the lying hills, on Pine Hill, in the Lardarium, and in the monastery. Several monasteries of Saint Agatha occur within the City in Anastasius. Most famous, however, is the one that Saint Gregory II built after the death of his mother Honesta in his paternal house, assigning rural and urban estates to it, no. 183. From this it perhaps acquired the name Saint Agatha in the Monastery.

“The Librarian relates that the holy Pontiff began to adorn and restore this part of the City with buildings more than any other, no. 177, although adverse changes in the times prevented him from carrying the work farther. For he had decided to begin by restoring the walls of the City from the Gate of Saint Lawrence; after completing a portion, he was hindered by various untimely disturbances. In no. 178 he relates that the Pontiff completed several repairs at Saint Lawrence outside the walls and established two monasteries around the Liberian Basilica. From this it can be understood that the chief benefits of his construction belonged to the Esquiline Hill, where the church of Saint Agatha is designated by the author of the Itinerary.”]

Likewise another Tiburtine Way as far as Saint Vitus.

The Claudian aqueduct. **THROUGH THE ARCH.** Saint Bibiana. The Nymphaeum. On the Tiburtine Way, outside the wall. On the left, Saint Hippolytus. On the right, Saint Lawrence. Saint Agatha. Saint Eusebius.

## SECTION IX. From the Seven Ways to the Asinarian Gate

[Note: “From the Seven Ways, and so forth.” Martinelli correctly notes from several passages of Anastasius that the Seven Ways, the Septodium, Septisolium, and Septizonium gave their name to the church of Saint Lucia, which is mentioned here on the right, opposite Saints John and Paul.

“The deaconry of Saint Lucia, which is said to be ‘in the Seven Ways,’ is found in no. 404; it is distinct from another deaconry mentioned in the same no. 404 as situated near the Orphaea, elsewhere called Orthea—today surviving under the name Saint Lucia in Silice, mentioned above in section II—near the Subura and close to the title of Saints Silvester and Martin.

“Whether the Seven Ways were near the Septizonium of Severus, situated at the foot of the Palatine Hill opposite Saint Gregory on the Clivus Scauri, or whether the corrupted name of the Septizonium changed into Septodium and Septisolium, this progression makes it clear that the deaconry of Saint Lucia must be placed opposite Saints John and Paul and Saint Gregory on the Clivus Scauri. The Seven Ways, which even now extend more or less toward the Palatine, the Arch of Constantine, the Caelian by the Clivus Scauri, and below the Caelian toward the old Capenian Gate beneath the gardens of the Mattei and toward the new Gate of Saint Sebastian, as well as toward the Aventine and both sides of the Circus Maximus, indicate the location of the Septizonium.

“From there the Einsiedeln Anonymous began this section, proceeding toward the Asinarian Gate, which stood open near the Lateran buildings. Some think that it ought to be identified more or less with the present Gate of Saint John and that it received its name from the nearby gardens and estates of the Asinii.”]

The Asinarian Gate.

On the left: John and Paul [Col. 0362A]. The Lateran Forma [Note: [Col. 0362C] At Saint Erasmus. Opposite the church of Saint Mary in Domnica, the titular church of Saint Stephen Rotundus on Mount Caelius, and the monastery of Saint Erasmus adjoining it, were discussed in the preface to the first volume, no. 49. There, too, the estates assigned to it seem to be mentioned in a Greek inscription.] At Saint Erasmus. Saint Mary in Domnica [Note: [Col. 0362C] On the Via Latina, inside the city. The location agrees with the statement of V. C. Fabretti, *On Waters and Aqueducts*, nos. 43, 48, and 58, who places the old Porta Capena beneath the Gardens of the Mattei; from there, outside the City, the Via Latina branched off from the Via Appia before Aurelian enlarged the *pomerium*. Therefore our Anonymous rightly represents the Via Latina as already incorporated within the City.] On the Via Latina, inside the City.

On the left: the Oratory of Saint Mary. Saint Gordianus. On the right: Saint Lucy [Note: [Col. 0362D] The Palatine. Turning to the right, the route follows the course of the Palatine westward toward Saint Anastasia. Soon, as though taking up the route again from the Seven Ways, it proceeds to the right, eastward, toward the churches and cemeteries outside the City along the Via Appia and the Via Ardeatina. The cemetery of Saint Petronilla and of Saints Nereus and Achilleus is indicated by Bosio and Aringhi, from manuscript Acts preserved in the Vatican, as lying outside the walls of the City on the Via Ardeatina, one and a half miles away. It must be said that both the cemetery and the church of Saint Petronilla stood at the old Porta Capena—where the City walls then were—somewhat beyond the Almo River. Aringhi, in the place cited, proves from the Bibliothecarius that a station was held there on a fixed day under Leo III. The same cemetery, and the other places that follow, also occur in Section I of this Itinerary, where the route proceeds from the Basilica of Saint Paul along the Via Ostiensis to Saint Sebastian; see that section.] The Palatine, as far as Saint Anastasia. Saint Petronilla. Nereus and Achilleus. Marcellus and Marcellianus at Saint Soter. Saints Cornelius, Xystus, Fabianus, Anterus, and Miltiades. To Saint Sebastian.

## SECTION X. From the Porta Metrovia to the Forma by the Seven Ways

[Note: [Col. 0363B] Porta Metrovia. It was said in the notes on the gates of the City that Metrovia is called the Porta Metronis in the letters of Saint Gregory the Great. Fulvio calls it the Porta Metrodii, but it is not clear on whose authority.] On the right: the Clivus Taurus (Scaurus) [Note: [Col. 0363B] The Clivus Taurus. Mabillon correctly emends this, adding in the margin “Clivus Scauri,” where Saint Gregory the Great built the monastery of Saint Andrew, called the monastery in his maternal house on the Clivus Scauri.] From Saint Stephen on Mount Caelius.

Another road from the Porta Metrovia [Note: [Col. 0363C] Porta Metrovia. We therefore understand this gate to have stood approximately where the Aqua Crabra, now called the Marrana, passes through the City walls and is received on the eastern slope of Mount Caelius beneath the church of Saint Stephen Rotundus and the Gardens of the Mattei.] On the right, toward Saint Sixtus. On the left, the church of Saint John.

Outside the City, on the right: Saint Januarius [Note: [Col. 0363C] Saint Januarius. The Bibliothecarius, in his account of Sixtus II, no. 25, records that the body of Januarius, a subdeacon who suffered martyrdom with Sixtus II and his companions, was buried on the Via Appia in the cemetery of Callistus. From the Acts, they infer that the place of his passion was at the Temple of Mars. Therefore, outside the City, between the second and third milestones, the memorials of Pope Sixtus, his subdeacon Januarius, and the other martyrs listed here are to be placed near the Porta Metrovia, or Metronis, from which a road branched equally toward the Via Latina and the Via Appia. The authors of *Subterranean Rome* agree, as does Canon Boldetti in his *Observations on the Cemeteries of the Holy Martyrs*, book II, chapter 18 [Col. 0363D], where he likewise discusses the cemetery of Saint Eugenia.] On the left, the Circus Maximus, Mount Aventine, the Septizonium.

Again, on the same road, outside the City. And so, through the portico, as far as [Note: [Col. 0363C] To Saint Januarius, where Sixtus was martyred. The Bibliothecarius, in his account of Sixtus II, no. 25, records that the body of Januarius, a subdeacon who suffered martyrdom with Sixtus II and his companions, was buried on the Via Appia in the cemetery of Callistus. From the Acts, they infer that the place of his passion was at the Temple of Mars. Therefore, outside the City, between the second and third milestones, the memorials of Pope Sixtus, his subdeacon Januarius, and the other martyrs listed here are to be placed near the Porta Metrovia, or Metronis, from which access lies equally open toward the Via Latina and the Via Appia. The authors of *Subterranean Rome* agree, as does Canon Boldetti in his *Observations on the Cemeteries of the Holy Martyrs*, book II, chapter 18 [Col. 0363D], where he likewise reaches the same conclusion concerning the cemetery of Saint Eugenia.] Saint Januarius, where Sixtus was martyred. The Oratory of Saint Sixtus.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] You will read about the church of Saint Eugenia outside the Porta Latina, near the cemetery of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr, in the work to be published below, in the tenth section, “The Porta Latina”; consult it. I think that what follows on page 512 of the Mabillon edition can be assigned to this tenth section, although it may also be joined to the final words in the context of the first section, which read as follows: “On the right, the Palatine. And so, through the great portico, to Anastasia, and from there continually.” The continuation of the journey from the Basilica of Saint Paul to Saint Sebastian, and from there, after returning into the City, along the Via Appia toward Saint Anastasia and to the end of the Claudian Forma above the Palatine, so that from Saint Anastasia, turning around the Palatine, one proceeds through the Arch of Titus and the Meta Sudans to the other end of the Claudian Forma at the Lateran, will be as follows. The sentence, joined to the preceding words as far as Saint Anastasia, is: “and from there continually through the portico to Saint Theodore,” with the places that are enumerated in this Itinerary on page 312 appearing on the right.

“The Palatine; the Testament; the Arch of Constantine; the Meta Sudans; the Head of Africa; the Four Crowned Ones; Saint John at the Lateran.” I say that this route agrees with the heading of Section X, which proposes a journey to the Forma—the aqueduct of the Aqua Claudia—by the Seven Ways. Above, it brought the traveler to the end of the Claudian Forma on the Palatine Hill, so that from there it could carry him to the other end of the same Claudian Forma within the City, namely to the Lateran aqueduct, where the Lateran Forma is conducted from the Claudian’s enormous conduit at the Porta Naevia [Col. 0364A] onto Mount Caelius. Thus, in order to bring him here from the title of Saint Anastasia near the Circus Maximus, he enters through the portico first at Saint Theodore, that is, the deaconry situated near the Forum of the Money-Changers and Saint George. On the right appears the Palatine Hill, which he circles until he reaches the Arch of Titus, called by the Anonymous the Testament because it represents in relief the vessels of the Old Testament carried into the City in Titus’s triumph: the candlestick, the table of the showbread, the altar of incense, and the priests’ trumpets. Then, proceeding to the Arch of Constantine and the Meta Sudans, near the southern part of the Amphitheatre, he finds the Head of Africa beneath the gardens of the monastery of Saints John and Paul. There a stone was found, set up by the tutors of the boys “from the Head of Africa,” indicating that this was a celebrated place in the City’s second region. Sponius reports it on page 227 of his *Miscellanies of Learned Antiquity*, and Fabretti in *Inscriptions*, folio 296, no. 257; Nardini is corrected on folio 99, where he introduces the Head of Africa against the texts of Victor and Rufus. From here the traveler is brought directly to the Four Crowned Ones and to Saint John at the Lateran, where the Lateran Forma—the aqueduct—and the goal of this section had been established, thus completing the journey to the Forma by the Seven Ways.] Saint Eugenia. To Saint Theodore.

[Note: [Col. 0363D] You will read about the church of Saint Eugenia outside the Porta Latina, near the cemetery of Saint Stephen, pope and martyr, in the work to be published below, in the tenth section, “The Porta Latina”; consult it. I think that what follows on page 512 of the Mabillon edition can be assigned to this tenth section, although it may also be joined to the final words in the context of the first section, which read as follows: “On the right, the Palatine. And so, through the great portico, to Anastasia, and from there continually.” The continuation of the journey from the Basilica of Saint Paul to Saint Sebastian, and from there, after returning into the City, along the Via Appia toward Saint Anastasia and to the end of the Claudian Forma above the Palatine, so that from Saint Anastasia, turning around the Palatine, one proceeds through the Arch of Titus and the Meta Sudans to the other end of the Claudian Forma at the Lateran, will be as follows. The sentence, joined to the preceding words [Col. 0364A] as far as Saint Anastasia, is: “and from there continually through the portico to Saint Theodore,” with the places that are enumerated in this Itinerary on page 312 appearing on the right.

“The Palatine; the Testament; the Arch of Constantine; the Meta Sudans; the Head of Africa; the Four Crowned Ones; Saint John at the Lateran.” I say that this route agrees with the heading of Section X, which proposes a journey to the Forma—the aqueduct of the Aqua Claudia—by the Seven Ways. Above, it brought the traveler to the end of the Claudian Forma on the Palatine Hill, so that from there it could carry him to the other end of the same Claudian Forma within the City, namely to the Lateran aqueduct, where the Lateran Forma is conducted from the Claudian’s enormous conduit at the Porta Naevia Lateranensis [Col. 0364B] onto Mount Caelius. Thus, in order to bring him here from the title of Saint Anastasia near the Circus Maximus, he enters through the portico first at Saint Theodore, that is, the deaconry situated near the Forum of the Money-Changers and Saint George. On the right appears the Palatine Hill, which he circles until he reaches the Arch of Titus, called by the Anonymous the Testament because it represents in relief the vessels of the Old Testament carried into the City in Titus’s triumph: the candlestick, the table of the showbread, the altar of incense, and the priests’ trumpets. Then, proceeding to the Arch of Constantine and the Meta Sudans, near the southern part of the Amphitheatre, he finds the Head of Africa beneath the gardens of the monastery of Saints John and Paul. There a stone was found, set up by the tutors of the boys “from the Head of Africa,” indicating that this was a celebrated place in the City’s second region. Sponius reports it on page 227 of his *Miscellanies of Learned Antiquity*, and Fabretti in *Inscriptions*, folio 296, no. 257; Nardini is corrected on folio 99, where he introduces the Head of Africa against the texts of Victor and Rufus. From here the traveler is brought directly to the Four Crowned Ones and to Saint John at the Lateran, where the Lateran Forma—the aqueduct—and the goal of this section had been established, thus completing the journey to the Forma by the Seven Ways.] Saint Eugenia. To Saint Theodore.

## SECTION XI. From the Porta Appia as far as the Greek School on the Via Appia

[Note: [Col. 0364D] The Greek School. In the heading of the Mabillon edition one reads *usque Sancto*. I think that the first syllable, *sco*, of the complete expression *scola Graeca* was extended, the editor supposing that *sco* had been written above for *Sancto*, just as below *sci* stands for *Nerei* and *sci* for *Xysti*. But the syllables and lines must be joined as we have presented them; this is demanded by the matter itself, by the context of the sentence, and by the course of the road.] The Greek School on the Via Appia.

[Note: [Col. 0364D] The Broken Screw. I think that some hydraulic machine had once been constructed here, which, by the Archimedean device of a screw, raised the waters of the old Appian aqueduct—lower-lying as they were—to higher ground, before the higher conduit of the Marcia, or of the New Anio, was brought here across the Caelian, as I indicated above. Alternatively, the Anonymous may have indicated a hydraulic screw constructed for auxiliary use in raising the lower water to higher levels after those conduits had been broken by the barbarians, and which by his own time had itself been damaged.] The Broken Screw. The Baths of Antoninus [Note: [Col. 0364D] The Arch of Remembrance. The Jobian Forma, and so forth. I have already explained these in the preceding sections.] The Arch of Remembrance. The Jobian Forma. Saints Nereus and Achilleus. Saint Sixtus.

## SECTION XII. From the Porta Aurelia to the Porta and Via Praenestina

[Col. 0365A]

[Note: [Col. 0366B] The Fountain of Saint Peter, where his prison is. For those proceeding from the Porta Aurelia to the title of Saints John and Paul, no fountain of Saint Peter or prison, so far as I know, is encountered. Antiquarians place the fountain and prison of Saint Peter, made famous by the chains and by the baptism of Saints Processus and Martinianus, at the Mamertine Prison at the foot of the Capitoline. I think that our Anonymous, whose memory had failed, confused the fountain of Saint Peter at Saint Prisca on the Aventine—where they report that baptism was administered by the prince of the apostles—with the other fountain at the Mamertine, where, by common agreement, his prison is asserted to have been and where the spring of the fountain confirms it. The route undertaken in this section from the Porta Aurelia to Saints John and Paul can scarcely indicate any fountain of Saint Peter other than the one at the title of Saint Prisca, where the blessed apostle is said to have been received as a guest. From there the route proceeds across the Aventine to the eastern side of the Circus Maximus and to the title of Saints John and Paul, then to Saint George, the Capitol, and the other places described in the Itinerary. Besides the roads within the City defined in the preceding sections, the Itinerary of the Anonymous, in the Mabillon edition, page 513, contains fragments indicating memorials of martyrs and cemeteries outside the circuit of the walls. They are so mutilated that it would not be worthwhile to supplement them, since they are distinctly listed in the work that follows immediately afterward. The indicated fragments of the Einsiedeln manuscript are rendered as follows:

On the Via Portuensis, outside the City.

On the Via Aurelia, outside the City, on the right, Saint … On the Via Salaria, outside the City, on the right, Saint … On the Via Pinciana, outside the City, on the right, Saint … Protus and Hyacinthus. Saint Hermes.

Again, on the right:

Abdon and Sennen; of Pancratius, Processus, and Martinianus; of Saturninus; of Saint Felicity with her seven sons; of Saint Basilissa; of Saint Pamphilus; the head of Saint John.]

The Fountain of Saint Peter, where his prison is. Saint John and Paul. Saint George. Saint Sergius. Across the bridge, the Capitol, the Umbilicus, through the Arch. Saint Hadrian. The horse of Con[stantine]. Saints Cyriacus and the Baths of Constantine. The Roman Forum. The Claudian Forma.

Again, the Baths of Diocletian. Saint Agatha. Saint Vitalis. [Col. 0365B] Saint Pudentiana. Saint Lawrence in Formonso, where he was roasted. The Monastery of Saint Agatha.

[Note: [Col. 0365C] The Mills. The route crosses the Transtiberine region from the Porta Aurelia and reaches the Forum either by the Senatorial Bridge or by the Cestian Bridge, then proceeds toward the Via Praenestina. The mills first seen are either those on the Golden Hill, turned by the Trajanic water, concerning which Fabretti, *On Waters and Aqueducts*, no. 247, cites Procopius, beginning: “τούτου δὲ”—“Opposite Trastevere rises a great hill, and there all the mills have long since been built; for a great quantity of water, conducted by a built channel to the summit of the hill, then rushes down the slope with violent force”—or river mills, which Belisarius devised under the pressure of necessity, after the Goths had cut the aqueducts during the siege of the City. Fabretti, in the same work, nos. 348 and 350, describes them from Procopius as follows: “For the bridge, beneath the Janiculum, he fitted ropes and stretched them with great strength from either bank of the river; he fastened two boats together, leaving a space of two feet between them, through which the water descended with greater force from the arch of the bridge. Then, placing two millstones upon each boat, he suspended in the middle a machine by which the millstones could be turned. He continually joined other boats to those behind in the same arrangement and inserted machines in the same manner; all of them, driven in order by the force of the flowing water, turned the millstones placed upon them and ground as much as the City required.”] The Mills.

[Note: [Col. 0365D] The Golden Mica. Sextus Rufus places the Golden Mica in the second region, between the Alban Mansions and the Armamentarium. Therefore the Golden Mica mentioned by our Anonymous in this region—the fourteenth, Transtiberine region, as he is still proceeding from the Golden Hill to Saint Chrysogonus—was a different place. Nardini observed that the Mica mentioned by Martial, book II, epigram 59 [Col. 0366A], was a dining room, from which the poet says that he can see the Caesarean dome:

“I am called Mica; you see what I am: a little dining room;

From me, look—there you see the Caesarean dome.”

He thinks it was called Golden because of the elegance of its decoration, and on that account interprets it as one of Domitian’s dining rooms. But when I consider that Martial, in book IV, epigram 64, celebrates the villa of another Martial situated on the Janiculum, which he vividly describes in these verses:

“The few acres of Tullius Martial

Lie along the long ridge of the Janiculum,” and so forth,

I am led to think of the Golden Mica mentioned here in this way: that it was a dining room on the Golden Hill, or Janiculum, called Golden Mica either from the name of the hill or after that Augustan dining room which Nardini, because of its elegant decoration, believed to be the same Golden Mica placed by Rufus in the second region.] The Golden Mica.

[Note: [Col. 0366A] Saint Mary. Across the Tiber; from there, proceeding to Saint Chrysogonus, the route crosses by the Cestian Bridge, or by the Senatorial Bridge, or even by the Sublician Bridge, and travels through an arch—perhaps the four-faced arch of Janus, visible near the deaconry of Saint George, and the Arch of the Money-Changers—to the Palatine and Saint Theodore. There stood Saint Mary Antiqua and the other buildings already explained in the preceding sections.] Saint Mary. Saint Chrysogonus and Saint Cecilia. The Palatine. To Saint Theodore. Saint Mary Antiqua. Saints Cosmas and Damian. The Palace of Trajan. The Monastery of Saint Agatha.

The Subura. Saint Lawrence in Formonso. Saint Vitalis. Saint Pudentiana and Saint Euphemia.

[Note: [Col. 0366B] The Palace of Pilate. Unless this name is to be attributed to a popular fantasy of the sort that foolish common people invent in our own day, calling surviving buildings near the Senatorial Bridge the Palace of Pilate without the testimony of any writer—buildings which they say were once inhabited by Nicolaus, son of Laurentius—I would readily believe that the Baths and Palace of Novatus had been transformed by our Anonymous, or by his eighth- or ninth-century copyist, into the Palace of Pilate.] The Palace of Pilate. Saint Mary Major. Saint Vitus. The Nymphaeum. Saint Bibiana. [Col. 0365C] The Claudian Forma. On the Via Praenestina, outside the Wall: the Claudian Forma.

[Col. 0367]

# APPENDIX TO THE PRECEDING WORK: ON THE REGIONS OF THE CITY OF ROME

[Col. 0367A] Since this little work describes the routes within the City from the seventh or eighth century through the fourteen regions that had been described four centuries earlier by Rufus and Victor, the editors of the *Analecta* thought it appropriate to place before it the title “Description of the Regions of the City.” For that reason, we judged that it might be useful for clarifying Anastasius and the *Lives*, in which the regions of the City are frequently mentioned.

The regions listed by Anastasius and the bibliographers, however, are those seven regions that sometimes also occur in the ritual books of the Roman order.
