The supreme pontiffs reduced to these seven the ancient fourteen regions established by Augustus and individually enumerated on ancient stones, especially on the Capitoline marble published under Hadrian by Gruter, folio 248, [Col. 0367B] no. 8. In their place came the fourteen regions of the City, now called *rioni*, with somewhat different boundaries.

We therefore seem likely to serve the exposition of the *Lives* and the convenience of readers more successfully if, in addition to the indications of the roads, we give a brief account both of the fourteen regions established by Augustus and described under the emperor Theodosius by Victor and Rufus, identifying the principal buildings included in them, and of the seven ecclesiastical regions, as they are called, which our pontiffs entrusted to an equal number of deacons for administration, together with subdeacons and notaries for writing down and collecting the acts of the martyrs.

Both systems would be more clearly understood if they were drawn on a single map together with the roads, with an additional portion of the suburban countryside showing the principal cemeteries of the martyrs within the second or third mile from the City walls [Col. 0367C]. Anyone could readily accomplish this by combining a single figure engraved by Nardini at the end of his first book with two or three drawn by Fabretti in his learned work on waters and aqueducts, numbers 1, 238, and 248. From Nardini’s figure he would obtain the fourteen civic regions. From Fabretti’s he would borrow the roads and the measurements of the suburban Roman countryside, which Fabretti carefully surveyed and engraved. It would therefore not be difficult to assign the cemeteries along the individual roads, with Bosio, Aringhi, *Subterranean Rome*, and Boldetti’s *Observations on the Cemeteries* also consulted.

If the printer permits it, we shall arrange for a topographical map to be appended at the end of the *Prolegomena*. In the meantime, we shall use Nardini’s indication of the fourteen civic regions established by Augustus’s decree, and the figure he drew on page 50, though it must be corrected somewhat from Fabretti in the first region because of the position of the old Porta Capena, which Fabretti more accurately places beneath the Gardens of the Mattei.

We shall also set out in Latin Nardini’s opinion concerning the seven ecclesiastical regions, which we understand to be approved by the most learned men, especially Mabillon, who writes as follows in his commentary on the Roman Order, page 18:

> “The division of the City into seven ecclesiastical regions is established, since by Augustus’s decree it had been divided into fourteen; but that ecclesiastical division, although much later and now obsolete, is far more obscure than the civic division, which has survived to the present. Nardini has assigned the position and boundaries of each ecclesiastical region better than anyone, on the basis of Anastasius, who places Mount Aventine in the first, the Mamertine Road in the second, the Basilica of Saint Lawrence above Saint Clement in the third, and the Head of Taurus in the fifth. The same author identifies the others conjecturally. To these add, in the fourth region, the title of Vestina, [Col. 0368B] from an ancient inscription read in the second volume of *Subterranean Rome*, or book IV, chapter 25, where Abundantius, an acolyte of the fourth region, title of Vestina, is mentioned. This title was later called that of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, or of Saint Vitalis.”

I shall therefore render Nardini’s opinion concerning the ecclesiastical regions, which he set out in chapter 4 of his second book, as follows.

He first remarks that Augustus decided to increase to fourteen, for the sake of more convenient administration, the number of the City’s regions, which according to the ancient division had not exceeded four. He attempted to show us their boundaries by dotted lines in the figure on page 50, using the more important buildings and places listed by Victor, Rufus, and the *Notitia of the Empire*, many of which are still known today. He then adds:

[Col. 0368C] “A greater difficulty arises in assigning boundaries to the regions during the early period of the Church, when the regions were distributed by our pontiffs among notaries and deacons. Anastasius writes of Clement I: ‘He established seven notaries, to whom he divided the regions, so that they might record the acts of the martyrs,’ and so forth.

Since the fourteen ancient regions are here being distributed among seven notaries, it is credible that Clement placed each notary over two regions. The small number of Christians in each region—distributed fairly evenly throughout the City—did not require more than that. Alternatively, according to the greater or smaller number of Christians, which differed from one region to another, Saint Clement may have assigned one region to one notary, two to another, and three to another.

The same Anastasius records that Evaristus established seven deacons [Col. 0368D]. Fabian, who governed the Church around the year 238, divided the fourteen urban regions among them. ‘He divided the urban regions among seven deacons and also created seven subdeacons, who were to supervise the seven notaries,’ and so forth.

Up to this point, although only seven notaries and deacons are mentioned, the regions appear to have been just as numerous, and to have been the same among the Christians as among the pagans; nor are they said to have been reduced from the number fourteen. Therefore Ciaconius is mistaken when, in the *Life of Hyginus*, he writes:

> ‘To advance the religion of Christ, to administer preaching, baptism, and the Eucharist, seven deacons were first appointed, placed over seven regions—the only ones out of fourteen to survive the fire of Nero intact and unharmed, as Tacitus testifies when he says: “Rome is divided into fourteen regions, of which four remained whole, three were demolished to the ground, and in the remaining seven only a few traces of buildings survived, damaged and half-burned.”’

For Tacitus neither asserts that only seven remained inhabited, but merely states that four were untouched, three destroyed, and seven partly damaged and still visible; nor was Rome after the fire less cultivated or less crowded with inhabitants than it had been before. Tacitus says that it was restored and rebuilt more elegantly.

It can also be gathered from an inscription preserved in the building of the Capitoline Conservators that the City was still divided equally into fourteen regions even in Hadrian’s time. It is as follows, in the form in which Panvinius and Gruter report it, although Nardini’s edition differs:

> IMP. CAESARI DIVI TRAIANI PARTHICI FIL. DIVI NERVAE NEPOTI TRAIANO HADRIANO TRIBVNIC. POTESTAT. XX. MP. II. COS III. P. P. MAGISTRI VICORVM VRBIS REGIONVM XIIII.
>
> To the Emperor Caesar Trajan Hadrian, son of the deified Trajan Parthicus, grandson of the deified Nerva, holder of tribunician power for the twentieth time, consul three times, father of his country: the magistrates of the districts of the City’s fourteen regions.

Moreover, Anastasius states that Saint Clement distributed fourteen regions among the notaries, not seven.

Many centuries later, when the Roman Empire had received no increase in extent and the number of inhabitants in the City of Rome had greatly declined after Constantinople had been built as the capital of the eastern empire, Victor described not merely the seven regions supposedly surviving Nero’s fire, but the entire number of the ancient fourteen.

I agree that among the Christians it later became customary for the regions to be called seven. If, in the *Life of Blessed Caius*, Anastasius writes that they were likewise divided—‘He divided the regions among the deacons’—and if, in the second Roman council, second session, we read of Saint Sylvester, ‘He made seven regions and divided them among the deacons,’ it is necessary to conclude that the ancient fourteen had been variously divided by several pontiffs, sometimes among notaries and at other times among deacons. That is, one region was made larger or smaller than another according as it had a greater abundance or a greater lack of Christians, until Blessed Sylvester, after the persecutions had been abolished, reduced them to seven regions that were no longer subject to change.

In the *Life of Pope Simplicius*, around the year of the Lord 464, Anastasius writes as follows:

> “He established weekly stations at Saint Peter the Apostle, Saint Paul the Apostle, and Saint Lawrence the Martyr, so that priests might remain there for penitents and baptism. The third region at Saint Lawrence; the first region at Saint Paul; the sixth and seventh regions at Saint Peter, and so forth. But these weekly ministers were appointed for four regions, although there were seven, because the other three regions were occupied by the Heruli, who did not communicate with the Catholic Church, since they were heretics of the Arian sect.”

Here only seven regions are mentioned. I could hardly be persuaded to believe that Blessed Sylvester introduced seven new regions without regard for any of the ancient ones; there would have been no reason for Christians to undertake such a difficult task contrary to the City’s established practice.

I would rather believe that in the course of time two neighboring regions entrusted to one person gradually coalesced, as it were, into one for purposes of administration, and that when Saint Sylvester decreed that this arrangement should thereafter be maintained, they were permanently regarded as seven paired regions.

But no one tells us what these seven paired regions were, and no one could easily explain them. Nevertheless, I am pleased to attempt the task step by step.

First, the words of Anastasius just quoted provide us with a guiding light. Since Saint Simplicius assigned to the Basilica of Blessed Paul the first pagan region of the Porta Capena—namely, the tract extending outside the City as far as the church of Saint Sebastian beyond the walls—and since it was close to that basilica, it seems that the thirteenth, Aventine, region ought above all to have been joined with that first region because of its proximity.

The same Anastasius makes this conjunction not merely probable but certain when he writes the following in the *Life of Eugenius*:

> “Eugenius, a Roman by birth, from the first Aventine region.”

This is confirmed [Col. 0370C] by letter 19 of book XII of Saint Gregory the Great:

> “We order that a certain garden belonging to the priest Politianus, situated in the first region before the steps of Saint Sabina, be placed beyond excuse,” and so forth.

Other words of Anastasius in the *Life of Simplicius*, “the third region at Saint Lawrence,” show with equal ease that the third region—called by the pagans the region of Isis and Serapis, but extending over the Esquiline from approximately the place where today stand the churches of Saint Peter ad Vincula and of Saints Silvester and Martin in the Mountains, to the other slope of the Caelian where the title of Saints Peter and Marcellinus was erected, and including everything lying on the lower part of the hills between the title of Saint Clement, the Flavian Amphitheatre, and the Subura—was joined to the fifth. The latter comprised the remaining parts of the Esquiline together with the Viminal, since no region was nearer to the church of Saint Lawrence outside the walls. [Col. 0370D]

This conjunction is confirmed by a letter of Pope Gregory I, Book II, Letter 58, in which the Merulana house, where today the title of Saint Matthew is seen, is assigned to the third region although it lay at the boundary of the fifth: “Since, therefore, the church situated beside the Merulana house in the third region …”

Anastasius likewise supports this in the *Life of Hadrian*, saying that the church of Saint Clement stood in the ruins of the third region: “The title of the blessed Clement, which was also destined to fall and was situated in the ruins of the third region”—that church, of course, lies at the extreme boundary of the second region but belongs to the third, around which these ruins could have fallen. [Col. 0371A]

It is perceived even more clearly from the same Anastasius in the *Life of Stephen III*: “He restored the basilica of Saint Lawrence above Saint Clement in the third region.”

There is likewise no difficulty in identifying the fourth, if we consider the words of Saint Gregory in Book II, Letter 5: “A house situated in this city, in the fourth region, beside the place called the White Hens.” This was the place listed by Rufus and Victor in the sixth region called *Alta Semita*, situated on the Quirinal and adjoining the fourth region at the Temple of Peace, but extending from the place now called *li Pantani* toward the Subura of later times.

The two regions that Anastasius indicates as having been nearest to the Vatican basilica in the *Life of Simplicius*—namely, the sixth and the seventh—seem manifestly identifiable. No part of the city, except the Transtiberine region, was more closely connected by its situation than the plain of the Campus, which in antiquity was divided into two regions: the seventh, called Via Lata, and the ninth, named Circus Flaminius. When these were joined, the designation of the seventh ecclesiastical region was, I believe, assigned to them. [Col. 0371B]

The name of the sixth, since the sixth pagan region has already been said to have been joined to the fourth ecclesiastical region, must have been assigned to the fourteenth region, the Transtiberine, in which the church of Saint Peter rises. This could easily have been joined to none of the other urban regions, since the Tiber separates it far from all the rest; and its considerable extent is sufficient to occupy a notary and a deacon of its own.

There remain, among the Christian regions, the second and the fifth; and among the fourteen pagan regions, five: the second, eighth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth. That the eighth pagan region, called the Roman Forum, belonged to the second Christian region is shown by Anastasius. Zacharias, when describing the deaconry of Saint George in the Velabrum—namely, in the place belonging to the eighth ancient region—lists it under the second: “In the venerable deaconry of the name of Saint George, situated in this Roman city in the second region, at the Golden Veil.” [Col. 0371C]

In the same way, in the *Life of Anastasius* he says: “He built the basilica called Crescentiana, in the second region, on the Mamertine Way in the city of Rome.” It is almost certainly established that this road lay near the prison beneath the Capitoline, called the Mamertine, in the region of the Roman Forum. It is reasonable to assert that the eleventh region, called the Circus Maximus, was joined to the eighth, or at least that part of it which extended along the Tiber in a longer and narrower strip. [Col. 0371D]

The second region may have received its name because it adjoined the first beneath the Aventine.

Nor should the Acts of Saint Martina be brought against me, where that church is called part of the sixth region. Anastasius says that the Mamertine Way and the deaconry of Saint George at the Golden Veil belonged to the second region; and, according to the same witness, Simplicius places the sixth region near the basilica of Saint Peter. All this proves that the number in the Acts of Saint Martina was wrongly copied by a scribe, who substituted the numeral V for the numeral I and changed “from region II” into “VI.”

Finally, what other region could the fifth ecclesiastical region have been than the tenth ancient region, called the Palatium; or the second, called the Caelian Mount; or the twelfth, called the Public Pool? [Col. 0372A] From the *Bibliothecarius* in Anastasius II it appears that the surname *Thauma* belonged to it, as did the other name *Caput Tauri*: “Anastasius, a Roman by nation, son of Peter, from the fifth region, Thauma, Caput Tauri.” Earlier, in the *Life of Alexander*, he had also said: “A Roman by nation, son of Alexander, from the region Caput Tauri.”

Both names point to the tenth region. For *Thauma*, which in Latin means “the wondrous” or “the admirable,” could scarcely be more appropriately applied to the Palace of the emperors, which occupied the greater part of the region. *Caput Tauri* either was the particular district of the Palatine called *Capita Bubula* (“Ox Heads”), or the part overlooking the Forum Boarium, perhaps deriving its name from a bronze bull.

The tenth region must therefore have been joined to the second, which was called the Caelian region, and perhaps also to the twelfth, lying beneath it in a very short circuit—unless the latter was joined to the first, which included the Capena Gate and the Aventine. [Col. 0372B]

These, then, are the conjectures that I thought should be set out concerning the seven ecclesiastical regions of the city of Rome.

Thus far we have heard Nardini. Since he admits that in many matters he follows Martinelli, we must necessarily transcribe either the whole of his fourth chapter of *Sacred Rome* or part of it, since it will provide a list and brief summary of the divisions mentioned above.

> “Following the established order,” he says, “we shall explain briefly a few matters concerning the regions of the sacred City. Suetonius, chapter 30, reports that the city of the pagan Romans was divided by Augustus Caesar into fourteen regions. Tacitus writes that most of it was burned in Nero’s fire, in these words: ‘Rome is divided into fourteen regions, of which four remained intact; three were razed to the ground; over the remaining seven only a few traces of buildings survived, broken and half-burned.’ [Col. 0372C] And although historians testify that in the tenth year of Nero’s reign the city rose again from the flames, nevertheless the sacred writers speak only of seven regions, perhaps because two were joined together and the pontiffs decreed that through these the ministers of the Roman Church should exercise their offices, as we shall say below. We find them listed in the following manner by Anastasius the Bibliothecary.
>
> “Region I, Aventine, under Pope Eugenius I and under Simplicius I. Region II, in which the Mamertine Way lies, under Pope Anastasius I; and the deaconry of Saint George at the Golden Veil under Zacharias I. Region III is noted under Simplicius I. The basilica of Saint Lawrence lies in this region, under Stephen III; and the title of Saint Clement is also there, under Hadrian I. Region IV, in which Sergius II was born, the son of Sergius. Region V, Thauma Caput Tauri, under Alexander I and Anastasius II. Region VI under Pope Simplicius. In it are the church of Saint Martina and the triumphal arch of Septimius Severus, as in the Acts of that saint. Region VII under the same pontiff. [Col. 0372D]
>
> “Into these regions, therefore, as into larger members, the pontiffs divided the city, if we are not mistaken; and for each region notaries, subdeacons, deacons, priests—who by another name are called bishops—and defenders were appointed.” [Col. 0373A]

From these observations of Martinelli and Nardini, the division of the ecclesiastical regions, which ought to have been prefixed in order to illuminate Anastasius, cannot remain obscure.

At the end of his fourth chapter Nardini adds that the fourteen regions now existing in the city have nothing in common with the fourteen established by Augustus. He says that these later regions ought to be referred to those unfortunate times when the Roman people, stirred up by the ambition of factions and the tumult of rebels, attempted to throw off the lawful rule of the chief pontiff and to introduce the consular title and the senate, under a certain appearance of popular government.

Whether or not the origin of the later regions should be referred to those times matters little for explaining the text of Anastasius, which is completed much earlier. I must not, however, omit the fact that the number and situation of the fourteen civil regions were still preserved and designated in public records in the eleventh century. [Col. 0373B]

Among other documents, folio 539 of the register of the Farfa Archive—often mentioned in the notes to *Opuscula* XII, XIII, and XIV—records a transfer of houses entered in the public registers by the clergy of the deaconry of Saint Eustachius in the fifth year of Benedict VII’s pontificate, and in the third year of the Emperor Henry II, in indiction 15, on 23 January—that is, in the year of Christ 1017. The houses are said to have stood in Rome, in the ninth region, in the *scorticlari*, between the Alexandrian Baths and the following boundaries: on one side, the property of Benedict the priest, who belongs to our deaconry of Saint Eustachius, and the oratory of the Saviour, and so forth. [Col. 0373C]

Thus the ninth region was then designated—the region now called Saint Eustachius—and in it stood, together with the aforementioned deaconry, the Alexandrian Baths and the oratory of the Saviour, all of which still survive today. [Col. 0374A]

One further point from Martinelli must also be retained: ecclesiastical authors use the term “regions” in a less precise sense for the smaller parts of the city, or districts, formerly named after their more prominent feature, such as Aventine, Caelian Mount, Fellonia, Piri, Via Lata, Merulana, Patricius, and Porta Metodii; or after some notable building in the district, such as Colosseus, Naumachia, *Ad Duos Adamantes*, Caput Tauri, Thauma, and Orthea, as well as Gallinae Albae.

Sometimes a region took its name from churches situated in the district, such as Saint Theodore and Saint Hadrian. Finally, he says that he found the region called Bibaretica in an epitaph still surviving at Saint Lawrence outside the walls. To this region, he says, the monastery of Saint Andrew behind the basilica of the Twelve Apostles should be assigned. [Col. 0374B]

I think that this region, now called Monti, was called *Vivarium* from a notable building and from part of the Praetorian Camp. For inscriptions and manuscript leaves from the fifth and sixth centuries, numbering in the hundreds, teach us that *BIBARIVM* was written, to be pronounced *VIVARIVM*. The word was corrupted by the Goths, just as happened in Spain.

So that the many names of the same region should not entangle the text of Anastasius, we thought it appropriate to add the following, briefly collected from the authors cited above. From the observations thus far set out, the seven ecclesiastical regions can be matched with the fourteen regions designated by Augustus in the city of Rome, as the following table shows. [Col. 0374C]

| Names of the ecclesiastical regions of the city | Ancient regions of Augustus corresponding to them |
|---|---|
| Region I | Region I, Porta Capena; Region XIII, Aventine |
| Region II | Region II, Caelian Mount; Region VIII, Roman Forum |
| Region III | Region XI, Circus Maximus; Region III, Isis and Serapis |
| Region IV | Region V, Esquiline; Region IV, Sacred Way |
| Region V | Region VI, *Alta Semita*; Region X, Palatium |
| Region VI | Region XII, Public Pool; Region XIV, Transtiberim |
| Region VII | Region VII, Via Lata; Region IX, Circus Flaminius |

[Col. 0375]

# Enumeration and Topographical Description of the Cemeteries of the Holy Martyrs near the City, Taken from the History of Malmesbury

*From the History of Malmesbury, toward the end of the eleventh century.* (C)

[Note: [Col. 0378A]]

I said that scarcely any notes needed to be attached to this little work, since both the matters that William attempts to enumerate and the faulty method of writing that had crept into several names through the ignorance of that age are sufficiently clear. I have therefore retained these forms in our edition so that we might reproduce the text literally from the exemplar from which the little work was taken.

Such forms do not disturb an understanding of the subject: for example, when *porta* and *via Flaminea* are written for *Flaminia*, *Assenarica* for *Asinaria*, *Metrosa* for *Metrovia* or *Metronia*, and the martyr *Xenon*, who ought to have been called *Zenon* or *Zeno*, and so forth. Passing over these minor errors, I thought that one or two passages should be explained.

The first concerns the first, Cornelian, gate and the Cornelian Way. With Panvinio, we identify the Cornelian Way from Victor. From ancient inscriptions we infer that it lay between the Triumphal Way and the two Aurelians, the old and the new. Panvinio, page 118, writes: [Col. 0378B]

> “The Cornelian Way, of which I have found mention only in marble inscriptions and in Publius Victor, I infer from these inscriptions to have lain in this region between the two Aurelians and the Triumphal Way.”

At Rome, in the house of Caesius:

> “To Gaius Sallius Aristaenetus, clarissimus vir, one of the seven Epulones, a member of the Augustal college, juridical officer for Picenum and Apulia, curator of the roads—the Aurelia, Cornelia, and Triumphal …”

Likewise at Tibur, on the wall of the church of Saint Paul:

> “To Gaius Popillius Caropedon, son of Gaius, of the Quirina tribe, consul, one of the seven Epulones, a member of the Hadrianic college, legate of the Emperor Caesar Antoninus Augustus Pius for Upper Germany and the army serving there, curator of public works, prefect of the Saturnian treasury, curator of the roads—the old and new Aurelia, the Cornelia, and the Triumphal …” [Col. 0378C]

Gruter likewise reported these inscriptions: the first on folio 457, no. 6, and the second on folio 465, carved on two bases, one belonging to the people of Asculum and the other to the people of Ancona, distinguished by numbers 5 and 6. In each, the roads are listed in the same order: Aurelia, Cornelia, Triumphal.

As for the Cornelian Gate, since Victor and the other writers before him are completely silent about it, and since it has not yet been named in any stones discovered, we may infer that the neighborhood later transferred that name to the gate leading from the city toward it. This is especially likely if the Cornelian Way received its name only from the second milestone from the city, where the New Aurelia divided into two branches, as will be seen shortly from Fabretti’s maps. [Col. 0378D]

Learned writers on Roman antiquities disputed whether the Cornelian Way should be placed between the Aurelia and the Portuensis, or rather between the Aurelia and the Triumphal. Some preferred the latter view and inferred it from the consistent order assigned to these roads in the inscriptions quoted above. Others preferred the former, following the authority of Bosius and Aringhi, *Subterranean Rome*, Book II, chapter 11, no. 8. They thought that it agreed more closely with the Acts of the holy martyrs.

The Acts brought forward by these authors, I believe, are those that they present in chapter 16 of the same book: the holy virgins and martyrs Rufina and Secunda, and also the martyrs Marius, Martha, Audifax, and Abacum. Those Acts assert that they were killed for Christ on the Cornelian Way at the thirteenth milestone, in the estate of *Cata Bassi*, where there were also Massa Candida and Silva Candida. Since the popes assigned these places to the Cardinal Bishop of Portus, the cited authors were led to direct the Cornelian Way between the Aurelia and the Portuensis.

But if the cited Acts are examined carefully, and the sites of Massa Candida and Silva Candida are compared with the neighboring estates—especially with the name of Saint Rufina, which they still retain today—and with the more accurate chorographic maps of the Roman countryside published both by Fabretti, a man of distinguished authority and, in the judgment of all, the most skilled investigator of that territory and the most expert judge of its antiquities, in his book *On Aqueducts*, and by Domenico de’ Rubeis, who had them carefully engraved in the form of a larger map with the support of outstanding antiquarians, then, I say, if all these things are compared, everyone will clearly understand that the Cornelian Way turned rightward from the fork of the Aurelia at the inn called *del Pidocchio*, near the Carpine vineyard, at the second milestone from the city, beside the channel of the Trajan-Sabatine or Braccian aqueduct—called the Aqua Paola after its restorer Paul V—and proceeded toward the Triumphal Way and the Caeretan territory. [Col. 0379A]

It nevertheless ran so near the Aurelia that the same sand-pits, martyr shrines, and cemeteries could be assigned to both roads, the Cornelian and the Aurelia, just as in the Acts of Saints Eusebius and his companions, cited by Aringhi, Book II, chapter 15, no. 3. There the blessed martyrs are said to have been buried not far from the city of Rome, at the sixth milestone, in a sand-pit between the Aurelia and Triumphal Ways. [Col. 0379B]

Consult Fabretti’s map, inserted in his book *On Aqueducts* after no. 283, at the end of the second dissertation. It will be clear that from the Aurelia Gate of Procopius—which William calls the Cornelian Gate—and from Saint Peter’s, by way of the valley adjoining the Vatican basilica called *Fornaces*, the New Aurelia was reached. This road, rising toward the western hills beyond the basilica of Saint Peter, led to the remains of the old road, part of which can still be seen paved with stone between the Carpine vineyard and the Aqua Paola fortress in the Burana vineyard.

At the inn called *del Pidocchio*, the New Aurelia divided into two roads. The right-hand branch, approaching the Triumphal and Cassian Ways for a short distance, took the name Cornelian; the left retained the name New Aurelia. Continuing through the estate called *del Porcareccio*, according to the map of Domenico de’ Rubeis, it reached the estate still called Saint Rufina. From there it extended on the right toward the Cornelian Way and on the left toward Silva Candida, thirteen miles from the city near ruined Lorium. From there the New Aurelia curved leftward toward the old Aurelia and joined it near the estate called *della Bottaccia*, about three miles from Saint Rufina and Porcareccio. At that place the New Aurelia was only slightly separated from the Cornelian Way, which turned rightward toward Caere. [Col. 0379C]

Fabretti had promised, at no. 100 of the cited work *On Aqueducts*, that, God willing, he would explain these matters more fully in his already promised work *On the Suburban and Suburbicarian Territory*. Since learned men eagerly await this work, they ask the heirs of that distinguished man, who deserved so well of learning, to bring it to public light if it should happen to be found among his unpublished writings. [Col. 0379D]

From the Acts of the martyrs produced by Bosius, Severanus, and Aringhi—those of Saints Rufina and Secunda, and of Saints Marius, Martha, Audifax, and Abacum—if they are compared with the maps of the Roman countryside and with the published writings of the learned Fabretti, who devoted himself with exceptional diligence and attention to surveying the suburbicarian territory, it seems to me that the position of the Cornelian Way is confirmed: the ancient inscriptions place it midway between the Triumphal Way and the two Aurelians, old and new. The indication of the martyrdom and cemetery of the saints described here is also suitably established. This will likewise appear from the following notes on William’s text concerning the Aurelia Gate and Way.

[Col. 0380A]

> “The fourteenth gate and the Aurelia Way, now called the Way of Saint Pancratius, etc. And at the fifth [milestone] Saint Basilides. At the twelfth milestone within the city, on the Caelian Mount, Saints John and Paul.”

In this text of William, the punctuation has plainly been corrupted, disturbing both the meaning and the topography. Yet the genuine reading can readily be restored; the Frankfurt edition, or the manuscript from which it was taken, has overturned it through a very gross error.

The writer’s intention was to proceed from the Aurelia Gate along the road of that name toward the Roman countryside and to enumerate, after four nearer churches, a fifth among the principal churches encountered along the Aurelia Way and distinguished by the memory, cemeteries, or relics of martyrs. Accordingly, after listing the first four, he adds: “and at the fifth, Saint Basilides, at the twelfth milestone outside the city”—or “within the city,” as that age commonly expressed it.

After completing his list of the gates and roads outside the city that were distinguished by cemeteries, he turned to the enumeration of the sanctuaries which, as he himself calls them, were situated inside the Roman city, within the circuit of the walls and the *pomerium*. [Col. 0380B] The words “On the Caelian Mount are the martyrs John and Paul in their own house, which was made into a church after their martyrdom” therefore begin a new period. The text had wrongly included them in the preceding sentence. The Caelian Mount and the title of Saints John and Paul, erected on the Clivus Scauri and lying almost at the center of the city, could never be said to be twelve miles within the city.

It is also clear that the reading can be completely restored merely by placing the punctuation correctly, if we observe the distance of the cemetery of Saint Basilides on the Aurelia Way. Bede and Ado list it in their martyrologies at the thirteenth milestone from the city, as the cited authors of *Subterranean Rome* observed when reporting the same evidence in Book II, chapter 15, no. 5.

With Bede, they enumerate two Basilides who suffered martyrdom on the Aurelia Way. One was Basilides under Aurelian, whose feast is celebrated on the fourth day before the Ides of June, together with his companions Tripodes, Mandale, and twenty others. [Col. 0380C] The other was Basilides, crowned with Cyrinus, Nabor, and Nazarius during the persecution of Diocletian on the day before the Ides of June.

The passion of this second Basilides and his companions is recorded at the fifth milestone from the city. Bede writes:

> “At Rome, on the Aurelia Way, at the fifth milestone, the passion of the holy martyrs Basilides, Cyrinus, Nabor, and Nazarius. Nabor and Nazarius, together with the martyr Gorgonius, were transferred from Rome to Gaul by Grodegand, bishop of Metz, with the permission of Paul, Roman pope, in the year 765 of the Lord’s Incarnation, etc.”

The martyrologies of Rabanus and Notker, along with other writers, agree with this.

But the feast day and place of combat of the earlier Basilides and his companions are reported by the same Bede and Ado under the fourth day before the Ides of June:

> “At Rome, on the Aurelia Way, at the thirteenth milestone, the feast of the saints Basilides, Tripodes, and Mandales under the emperor Aurelian, with Plato as governor, and of twenty other martyrs.”

At the same distance from the city, on the nearby Cornelian Way, we read that there was a sand-pit where Marius, Audifax, and Abacum were beheaded and buried. Bosius, Severanus, and Aringhi, in Book II, chapter 16, no. 7, note this from the codices containing their Acts: the Lateran, Vatican, and Saint Cecilia manuscripts:

> “On the Cornelian Way, at the thirteenth milestone, at the Nymphs of Cata Bassi.” [Col. 0380D]

Where the place called the Nymphs of Cata Bassi should be sought, we learn from the maps of the Vatican basilica’s archive. When Grimaldus examined them, he found that in the donations of Saint Leo IV the large estate of Catabassi was situated in the castle called Bucceia. Martinelli, in his *Sacred Rome*, page 327, writes:

> “The Nympha of Catabassi was the castle of Bucceia, donated by Saint Leo IV to the monastery of Saint Martin, which belonged to the Vatican basilica and is today a wealthy estate of 750 *rubbia* of land, as Grimaldus says.”

And on folio 124, speaking of the church of Saint John Calybita, he says:

> “From the estate of the Vatican basilica called Bucceia, situated on the Cornelian Way at the thirteenth milestone from the city, the bodies of the holy martyrs Marius, Martha, and her sons were transferred here,”

as James Grimaldus, one of the canons of the aforementioned basilica, wrote, and so forth. [Col. 0381A]

No one is unaware of the location of the castle of Bucceia and of the large estate lying between the New Aurelia and Triumphal Ways, and also between two places four miles apart—Saint Rufina and Galera, or Careiae, as it was called in antiquity. Thus the Bucceia estate almost touches both places, as the map of Latium demonstrates.

We can also infer that the Nymphs of Cata Bassi should be sought here from Frontinus, who asserts that at Careiae the supply of the Alsietine Aqueduct was increased by acquisitions from the nearby Sabatine or Braccian Lake:

> “The quantity of the intake of the Alsietine [Aqueduct] is recorded neither in the commentaries nor could it be established with certainty at the present time, since from the Alsietine Lake, and then near Careiae from the Sabatine Lake, as much as the water-measurers have regulated, it receives no more than two thousand *quinariae*.”

The distances of these places agree with the Acts of the martyrs: Saint Rufina at the tenth milestone, between the New Aurelia and Cornelian Ways, but nearer to the Aurelia; and the large estate of Cata Bassi, or Bucceia, diverging two or three miles away and including the Cornelian Way as far as the thirteenth milestone from the city. At that point too there were the Nymphs—that is, the accessions and intake channels flowing into the Alsietine Aqueduct from the Sabatine Lake near Careiae, now Galera. [Col. 0381B]

The arrangement of the Cata Bassi estate at the Nymphs is therefore sufficiently clear. It occupied almost the entire space of roughly three miles from the New Aurelia to the Cornelian Way. Within it lay Saint Rufina at the tenth milestone, Bucceia at the twelfth between Careiae and ruined Lorium, and Silva Candida, together with the cemetery of Saint Basilides, who suffered under Aurelian. The latter lay nearer the twelfth than the thirteenth milestone. The cemetery of Saints Marius, Martha, and their companions, being nearer the Cornelian Way at the thirteenth milestone than the Aurelia, is rightly assigned to the Cornelian Way by Bede and Ado, by William of Malmesbury, by the archivist of the Vatican basilica and its inspector Grimaldus, as reported by Martinelli, and by the more skilled topographers of the Roman countryside. [Col. 0381C]

The two roads, Cornelian and Aurelia, were so close to each other from the second milestone, where they divided, that they approached one another again near the tenth milestone. Thus the same church of Saint Rufina, when it was begun by Pope Julius and completed by his successor Damasus, is said to have stood on the Cornelian Way at the tenth milestone; but when the same church, together with the adjoining estates, was donated by Saint Hadrian I to the Lateran patriarchate, it is said to have stood approximately at the tenth milestone but is assigned to the Aurelia.

In the same way, the estates of the Colonna family, situated at the eleventh milestone outside the city between the Latin and Appian Ways, which touch them on either side, could be called estates situated at the eleventh milestone on the Latin Way and at the eleventh milestone on the Appian Way.

The interchangeable attribution of the estates and church of Saint Rufina at the tenth milestone from the city, both to the Cornelian and to the Aurelia, is demonstrated as follows. From the Acts cited in *Subterranean Rome*, Book II, chapter 16, no. 3, Bosius proves that the basilica of Saints Rufina and Secunda was completed by Blessed Damasus. Julius, successor of Mark, had begun it in the territory of Silva Candida, where the bodies of Saints Marcellinus and Peter had been buried. [Col. 0381D]

Saints Rufina and Secunda were led away and beheaded on the Cornelian Way at the tenth milestone, in the estate called Buxus or Buxetum, in the territory of Silva Candida. The holy martyrs Peter and Marcellinus were also beheaded in the same Silva Candida and subsequently buried there, where shortly afterward the church mentioned above was built over the place of the martyrdom of Saints Rufina and Secunda by order of the pontiffs Julius and Damasus.

Yet at the tenth milestone outside the city on the Aurelia stands the cultivated estate of Galeria—or Careia, now Galera—situated approximately ten miles along the Aurelia. According to Anastasius in the *Life of Hadrian*, section 328, the same church of Saint Rufina was donated by Hadrian I to the Lateran patriarchate for the support of the poor. [Col. 0382A] The Lateran Hospital of the Holy of Holies still possesses this church of Saint Rufina, together with the estates assigned to it, for the relief of the poor.

The name of the church of Saint Rufina, as well as of the estates and cemeteries at the tenth milestone, was therefore used interchangeably for both the Cornelian and the New Aurelia, between which they lay. Consequently, the cemetery of Saint Basilides at the twelfth and thirteenth milestones on the Cornelian Way is rightly restored through the corrected punctuation of the text.

So that I may omit nothing in this little work that could illuminate the history of the martyrs or the topography of the city and the suburban countryside, the final verse of the cited text must also be clarified.

> “On Mount Nola,” he says, “Saint Tatiana rests.” [Col. 0382B]

I would be extremely grateful to William if he identified the sacred body and tomb of this Roman virgin and martyr, so illustrious under Severus Alexander, whose heroic struggle the Greeks and Latins alike celebrate—as Baronius observes both in his notes to the *Martyrology* on 12 January and in volume II of the *Annals* under the year 227, and Gallonius in his *Lives of the Holy Roman Virgins*, together with other writers—unless William’s benefit were lost through his own carelessness or through the fault of scribes.

I simply do not know of any Mount Nola, either within the city or near it, such as the Frankfurt edition gives. William is speaking there of Roman sanctuaries within the city, after he had surveyed the suburban cemeteries according to the order of the gates and roads. Inside the city he had begun with the Caelian Mount; he continued through the Aventine, where he had mentioned the martyr Boniface, still preserved in the title of Saints Alexius and Boniface.

The order of his undertaking required that, if he wished to add anything he had observed among the sanctuaries of that same Aventine Mount, he should describe it there. But Mount Nola has so far appeared neither on the Aventine nor, so far as I know, in any place within or near the city. [Col. 0382C]

It would be worthwhile if some more fortunate interpreter could either identify the modern name of the place or restore the genuine reading of the corrupt text. Gallonius, laboring to collect the life of this celebrated virgin and martyr from Greek and Latin sources, laments that he could not discover where her sacred body or parts of her body had been deposited.

Nevertheless, Bollandus produced from Greek manuscripts part of the Acts, expressly stating that her relics had been buried in the twelfth region. From this we can confirm the emendation that we suspect should be applied to William’s text in this verse.

Certainly, if conjecture is permitted, I would readily believe that William, or a scribe, wrote in the autograph in abbreviated syllables:

> *In mon. ce. noba sancta Tatiana pausat*

From these an inexperienced copyist may have produced:

> *In monte nola sancta Tatiana pausat*

when the author intended to express:

> *In monasterio Cella Nova sancta Tatiana pausat*—

“Saint Tatiana rests in the monastery of Cella Nova,” or *Cella Noba* if the consonantal *v* was written barbarously. [Col. 0382D]

The monastery of Cella Nova, mentioned in this *Pontifical Book* in the *Life of Stephen IV*, sections 272 and 273, belonged to the part of the thirteenth region adjoining the twelfth, in which the Acts cited by Bollandus report that Blessed Tatiana was buried.

Cella Nova was the oratory of Saint Silvia, the mother of Blessed Gregory the Great, situated near the church of Saint Sabas, as John the Deacon describes it in Book I, chapter 9, of the *Life* of that pontiff. This monastery later became famous as Saint Sabas and continued to be called Cella Nova in subsequent centuries. Thus Panvinio, in *The Seven Churches of Rome*, page 143, lists the Abbot of Saint Sabas of Cella Nova among the twenty principal men who assisted the Roman pontiff when he celebrated the sacred rites with solemn ceremony. John the Deacon, edited by the Reverend Father Mabillon in the *Appendix to the Roman Order*, page 574 of the *Museum Italicum*, also lists them.

That the monastery of Saint Sabas, or Cella Nova, belonged to the thirteenth region, in the part where it touched the twelfth region called the Public Pool, is clear from the topography of the city. [Col. 0383A] Among other buildings of the twelfth region, Victor lists the Baths of Antoninus. The slope of the hill and the precinct of the monastery and church of Saint Sabas adjoin these baths so closely that some topographers of the city call the nearby title of Saint Balbina—although it is established on the Aventine and on the same slope as Saint Sabas—“at the Baths of Antoninus.”

Moreover, numerous tombs, and indeed magnificently constructed ones, have been found near these baths, especially in the vineyard of the noble Marquises Cavalieri. It can therefore clearly be inferred that before the city was newly enlarged under the emperor Aurelian, this part of the twelfth region, not yet included within the *pomerium*, could receive corpses. [Col. 0384A] Thus the body of Blessed Tatiana could have been buried in the twelfth region under Severus Alexander, as the Acts record, and from there transferred to the nearby monastery of Cella Nova, or Saint Sabas, where our emendation of William’s text places it.

I would make these assertions more confidently if I had been able to inspect ancient manuscript copies of Malmesbury’s works. If anyone should find such copies anywhere, he will be able to judge our conjectures with greater security.

[Col. 0375A] William of Malmesbury, writing about the deeds of the kings of the English in Book IV, where he continues with the deeds of King William II, when, around the year 1096, he brings to Rome men of his nation preparing themselves for the eastern expedition through the duties of religion and undertaking a sacred pilgrimage for that purpose to the mother and mistress of all the Churches, so that there they might venerate the prince of the apostles, deposited there, and the innumerable companies of martyrs, first provides a description of the cemeteries in which the memory of those same martyrs was celebrated; for those buried there gave their names to the same sacred crypts and to the churches or oratories founded above them. In the preceding work, only brief extracts from the seventh or eighth century had been given by an anonymous author in his *Itinerary*. Here, however, since they are read as more carefully investigated and enumerated by an author of the eleventh century, I judged them to be of very great value for illustrating the *Lives of Anastasius*, in which references to the cemeteries where the pontiffs were buried, and to the repairs and gifts continually offered by their successors for the decent administration of divine worship in these sacred underground burial places or in the churches built above them, frequently occupy both pages. This William likewise proceeds according to the number of the gates of the City and of the roads in his *Itinerary*. Almost no notes need to be added to it, since he explains his meaning clearly enough and in an orderly fashion. I have therefore taken care merely to transcribe his words from folio 134 of the Frankfurt edition printed in 1601. They are as follows:

[Col. 0375C] “But so that nothing may be lacking to the honor of the subject, I shall add both the number of the gates and the multitude of the sacred ashes; and so that no one may complain that, because of the obscurity of the words, he is excluded from knowledge of the facts, the style will be ordinary and plain.

“The first gate is the Cornelian Gate, now called the Gate of Saint Peter, and the Cornelian Way. Near it stands the church of blessed Peter, in which his body lies, furnished with gold, silver, and precious stones; and no one knows the number of martyrs who rest in that same church. On the same road is another church, in which the holy virgins Rufina and Secunda rest. In a third are Marius, Martha, and Audifax and Abachus, their sons.

“[Col. 0375D] The second gate is the Flaminian Gate, now called [Col. 0376A] that of Saint Valentine, and the Flaminian Way; but when it reaches the Milvian Bridge, it is called the Ravenna Way, because it leads to Ravenna. There, at the first mile outside the city, Saint Valentine rests in his own church.

“The third gate is the Portinian [alternative: Porcinian], and the road is called by the same name; but when it reaches the Salarian Way, it loses its name. Nearby, in the place called Cucumeris, rest the martyrs Festus, John, Liberalis, Diogenes, Blastus, and Lucina—240 [alternative: 260] in one tomb and 30 in another.

“The fourth gate, and the Salarian Way, is now called that of Saint Sylvester. There, beside the road, Saint Hermes rests, as do Saint Vasella, Protus, Hyacinthus, Maximilian, Herculanus, and Crispus. In another place nearby rest the holy martyrs Pamphilus and Quirinus, seventy steps deep beneath the earth. Next comes the basilica of Saint Felicitas, where she rests, together with Silanus, [Col. 0376B] her son, and, not far away, the martyr Boniface. In another church there are Chrysanthus, Daria, Saturninus, Maurus, Jason, and their mother Hilaria, together with countless others. In another basilica are Saint Alexander, Vitalis, and Martial, the sons of Saint Felicitas, and the seven holy virgins Saturnina, Hilarina, Dominanda [alternative: Dunanda], Rogantina, Serotina, Paulina, and Donata. Next comes the basilica of Saint Sylvester, where he lies covered by a marble sarcophagus; and the martyrs Caelestinus, Philip, and Felix, together with 365 martyrs, rest there in one tomb. Nearby rest Paul, Crescentianus, Prisca, Demetrius, Praxides [alternative: Praxedis], and Potentiana.

“The fifth gate is the Nomentan Gate. There Saint Nicomedes, a presbyter and martyr, rests; the road too is called by the same name. Beside the road are the church and body of Saint Agnes; in another church are Saint Emerentiana and the martyrs Alexander, Felix, and Papias. At the seventh mile of the same road, Saint Alexander the pope rests with Eventius and Theodulus.

“The sixth gate and road are the Tiburtine, now called that of Saint Lawrence. Beside this road Saint Lawrence lies in his own church, together with the martyr Abundius. Nearby, in another church, rest the martyrs Cyriaca, Romanus, Justinus, and Crescentianus. Not far away is the basilica of Saint Hippolytus, where he rests with his household, eighteen persons in all. There also rest blessed Tryphaena, the wife of Decius, her daughter Cyrilla, and her nurse Concordia. On the other side of the road is the church of the martyr Agapitus.

[Col. 0376D] “The seventh gate, now called Major, was formerly called Sirucrana [alternative: Syracusana], and the road is called the Lavican, leading toward blessed Helena. Nearby are Peter, [Col. 0377A] Marcellinus, Tiburtius, Geminus, Gorgonius, forty soldiers, and countless others; and not far away are the four holy Crowned Martyrs.

“The eighth gate is that of Saint John, which among the ancients was called Asseranica [alternative: Assenarica].

“The ninth gate is called Metrosa. In front of these two gates lies the Latin Way.

“The tenth gate, and the road, are called the Latin Gate and Latin Way. Beside it, in one church, rest the martyrs Gordianus, Epimachus, Sulpicius, Servilianus, Quintinus, Quartus, Sophia, and Tryphaenus. Nearby, in another place, is Tertullinus; and not far away is the church of blessed Eugenia, in which her mother Claudia also lies, together with Pope Stephen and his clergy, nineteen in number, and the deacon Nemesius.

[Col. 0377B] “The eleventh gate and road are called the Appian. There rested Saint Sebastian and Quirinus, and formerly the bodies of the apostles rested there. A little nearer Rome are the martyrs Januarius, Urbanus, Xeno, Quirinus, Agapetus, and Felicissimus. In another church are Tiburtius, Valerianus, and Maximus; and there are buried Stephen, Sixtus, Zephyrinus, Eusebius, Melchiades, Marcellus, Eutychianus, Dionysius, Anteros, Pontianus, Lucian the pope, Optatus, Julianus, Calocerus, Parthenius, Tharsicius, and the martyr Politanus [alternative: Policamus]. There is also the church of Saint Cornelius and his body. In another church is Saint Soteris; and not far away rest the martyrs Hippolytus, Hadrian, Eusebius, Maria, Martha, Paulina, Valeria, and Marcellus. Nearby is Pope Mark in his own church. [Col. 0377C] Between the Appian and Ostian Ways is the Ardeatine Way, where are Mark and Marcellianus; and Pope Damasus lies there in his own church. Not far away are Saint Petronilla, Nereus and Achilleus, and many others.

“The twelfth gate and road are called the Ostian [alternative: Ostense]; the gate is now called Saint Paul’s, because he rests in his church beside it. There also is the martyr Timothy; and not far away, in the church of Saint Thecla, are the martyrs Felix, Adauctus, and Nemesius. At the Salt Works is the head of the martyr Anastasius.

“The thirteenth gate and road are called the Portuensian. Nearby, in a church, are the martyrs Felix, Alexander, Abdon and Sennes, Symeon, Anastasius, Polion, Vincentius, Milex, Candida, and Innocentia.

[Col. 0377D] “The fourteenth gate and road are the Aurelian, now called the Gate of Saint Pancratius, because he rests in his church beside it; there are also the martyrs Paulinus and Artemius, and Saint Sophia with her three daughters, Faith, Hope, and Charity. In another church are Processus and Martinianus; in a third, two Felixes; in a fourth, Calixtus and Calepodius; and in a fifth, Saint Basilides. At the twelfth mile within the city, on Mount Caelius, are the martyrs John and Paul, in their own house, which became a church after their martyrdom, together with Crespinus, Crespinianus, and Saint Benedicta. On the same mountain is the church of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr, and there are buried the martyrs Primus and Felicianus. On the Aventine Hill is Saint [Col. 0378A] Boniface, and on Mount Nola Saint Tatiana rests.”

[BLANCHINIAN CHRONOLOGY.]

[Col. 0383]

ON PONTIFICAL, CAESAREAN, AND CONSULAR CHRONOLOGY

[Col. 0383B] I must now present that brief consular and pontifical chronology which I promised would follow, covering the first four centuries of the Christian era, to which the *Lives of the Pontiffs* included in this first volume extend—from Saint Peter to Saint Sylvester I of that name. In the following volume the remainder will be given [Note: [Col. 0383D] For the reader’s convenience, we present this later chronology after the earlier one. EDITOR], from Saint Sylvester to Stephen VI, together with the corresponding sequence of years. Yet, why I judged that fifty years immediately preceding the same Christian era should be prefixed to this summary of its first four centuries, let the reader learn from the matters which I judge should be stated beforehand, so that the rationale of our plan may be explained more clearly; from this the method will become evident, and the use of this chronology, arranged for the fuller elucidation of the *Book* and of pontifical history, will be understood.

[Col. 0383C] It might seem that the sequence of this chronology, adapted to the *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, ought to begin with the first foundation of the Roman see, or at least with the beginning of the life of the apostle Peter, its first bishop, which nearly coincides with the beginning of the Christian era. Earlier times do not fall within the subject of the book. But when our purpose in the notes and observations—both chronological and historical—on these *Lives* is carefully considered, namely, to clarify the times and deeds of each pontiff not only from the assertion of the librarian from whom the life was compiled, but also from other genuine documents and proofs that confirm and explain the chronological indications recorded there and the historical pointers lightly touched upon, [Col. 0383D] it will become clear that we had to recover solid evidence for the times and deeds from at least the fifty years immediately preceding the common Christian era. These have a particular connection with the chronology and history of the supreme pontificate of the Church of Christ, and with the deeds and chronological markers stated by the authors of these *Lives* within those same four hundred years.

As far as chronology is concerned, it is obvious that the epochs of the individual pontiffs are recorded both in the text of Anastasius and in the catalogues older than Anastasius [Col. 0384B] by means of consulships and the reigns of Roman rulers. If these were not placed in their proper setting, it would necessarily be impossible to retain those matters that are linked to the consulships and the years of the Caesars. I leave it to those versed in antiquarian matters to decide whether a consular and Caesarean chronology can be considered sufficiently sound if it does not correspond to the measures and enumerations of the epochs publicly established and begun in the cities and provinces under Roman rule in Asia, Africa, and Europe during those fifty years, from the age of the dictator Caesar to the beginning of the Christian era. The Antiochene and Laodicean eras in Syria begin the era of the dictator Caesar before his Julian reform. How many eras were established in that same province of Syria, how many in Asia Minor and Pontus, how many in Africa and Europe, beginning from Augustus’s victory at Actium, engraved on coins [Col. 0384C] and continued under the succeeding emperors? The Alexandrian and Coptic era of the Egyptians, the Spanish years of the Augusti, the Roman quinquennial games, besides the sequence of Olympiads and the years from the founding of the City, all contribute to strengthening the consular and Caesarean chronology to which the pontifical chronology is attached. It is therefore necessary to ascend to their origin, which falls within these fifty years, so that the chronological markers may be tested against the evidence, whether they are stated in consulships and imperial reigns or in the deeds of the pontiffs. In this way, the periods, confirmed from every direction, may lay an unshaken foundation for history.

As for the history itself, everyone can judge how much light the history of the supreme pontiffs of the New [Col. 0384D] Testament receives from those final annals of the priests of the Old Law that precede the epoch of Christ by half a century, by comparing the deeds of Hyrcanus and his successors, as transmitted by Josephus under the various dominations of the different rulers who possessed Judaea and the neighboring regions during that period, with what happened shortly afterward to the great priests of the Christian Church, who, through legitimate succession, obtained Peter’s place and apostolate in the Roman chair. I would have the reader attend to this point: in the shadow of the Levitical priesthood, such a great majesty of royal dignity continued to shine until the final times of Aaron’s successors, within those same fifty years, proclaiming Christ’s truth in figure. Thus it is evident that Hyrcanus the high priest, although held captive by the Parthians, was nevertheless regarded by the Jews who were held with him in the same captivity on both sides of the Euphrates not otherwise than as a king, as Josephus explicitly records in Book XV, chapters 1 and 2, of the *Antiquities*, cited in our *Chronology* under the year 38 of Christ. This appears even more clearly from the rights and titles of ethnarch among his people, and from the treaty and alliance with the Roman Republic granted to him both by the Senate and by the dictator Caesar, as reported under the year 49 before the Christian era from the same Josephus. Thus the high priest of the Jews [Col. 0385B] possessed the power of a king among the allies of the Roman people, until the times fixed by the prophets, when, after the kingdom had been transferred to the foreigner Herod, this very sign of the coming Christ was to be produced. I would also have the reader consider that the rights of judging his nation, of taxation, tithes, and succession were asserted to belong to Hyrcanus the high priest and his children in the Capitol, and were attested on bronze tablets publicly displayed both in the City, mistress of all, and in the two cities nearest to that dignity—Alexandria in Egypt and Antioch in the East. The reason for this honorable grant was explicitly stated: the Jews, both those living in Palestine and those living in Egypt, had supported Caesar in the siege of Alexandria because they obeyed the authority of the priest Hyrcanus.

[Col. 0385C] These matters certainly could not be omitted without diminishing the light they shed upon the pontifical history of the Christian Church. For when we read in that history that the Roman see was established by the prince of the apostles to take precedence over the others, and that Alexandria and Antioch were founded in his name in such a way that they were regarded as next in dignity after Rome, while to the successors of Peter alone he entrusted the governance of the universal Church—as we read in Clement—it immediately occurs to us that in the high priesthood of Hyrcanus we see the same arrangement: colonies led forth from the people chosen to practice the true worship of God obeyed the supreme hierarch in all the laws of sacred matters. Nor does an unlike appearance of imitation present itself to the mind of one who observes the first Christian emperor, Constantine, honoring in the life of Sylvester, with royal endowments and insignia, the royal priesthood of the new law in its supreme pontiff and in the Roman see proper to him, while seeing that the rights of jurisdiction, tithes, and rule over their own people had been granted and confirmed by the first founders of the Roman Empire, Julius and Augustus, although pagan rulers, to the supreme moderator of the Jewish Church and the chief hierarch of the entire Levitical order.

It is also useful to observe that in our pontifical catalogues, from which the *Lives* derive their origin, the beginnings of the pontiffs are recorded by consulships, and the years of those same pontiffs are numbered even throughout these first four centuries of the Christian era. We note that this practice was preceded by a similar custom in the Jewish Church, gathered from the annals of Josephus, himself both a priest and a historian living in the very age of the apostles. For he records the pontifical epoch of Hyrcanus, belonging to the period we have mentioned, by consulships in Book XIV, chapter 1, of his history, as follows: “When Hyrcanus had therefore received the pontificate in the third year of the 177th Olympiad, in the consulship of Quintus Hortensius and Quintus Metellus Creticus, Aristobulus immediately made war upon him.”

I do not know whether those more recent writers paid attention to these matters who imagined that the names of the consuls had been added to the catalogues of the Roman pontiffs by later editors. In the preface to my first volume I pointed out that, throughout the first four centuries of the Christian era, the Romans too were accustomed to record the epochs of priests enrolled in their colleges, just as Josephus, writing in the City, distinguished the beginning of Hyrcanus’s pontificate. Elsewhere also he counts the successions of the entire series of high priests and the years of each down to the destruction of the Temple and of Jerusalem under Vespasian. It would rather be astonishing if those earlier disciples of the apostles, who had lived with Peter and Paul at Rome and knew well the practice of sacred writers, had not done this. The careful numbering of years had been indicated by Moses and the prophets, employed by Stephen in his sermons, retained by Paul in his letters, and preserved by Luke in his Gospel and in the Acts of the Apostles. In the City they saw Josephus, writing his history of his people only a few years after the martyrdom of the prince of the apostles, [Col. 0386C] assigning the age of the supreme priests individually to the years of their own rulers and of the Romans. They saw every college of chief priests in the City marking the enrolment of its individual members by the consuls and by the epoch of the founding of the City, just as the many ancient marbles preserved from that age before our eyes in fasti, calendars, and the records of the colleges attest to us. These will often be brought forward in our chronology to demonstrate the same consulships and their definite date and documentation. The seven notaries instituted by Clement to write and collect the deeds of the martyrs, and the same number of deacons and subdeacons appointed by Fabian after the administration of Anterus for this task—among whom the Roman pontiffs of that age, almost all crowned with martyrdom, stand out in dignity and example—would have been almost senseless if they alone had failed to follow so celebrated, so universal, and so well-established a custom. But, lest we return to the evidence for pontifical chronology already established by so many arguments, we turn to the historical proofs that we have deliberately collected from those same fifty years.

It can by no means be denied that the events related in the first section concerning the first and second arrivals of the prince of the apostles in the City from Syria, and concerning the plan divinely inspired in him for establishing the chair of the supreme pontificate, are in a certain sense prepared for by the events belonging to the year 45 before the Christian era. At that time, after Caesar’s death, the consuls Antonius and Dolabella were responsible for the Senate and Roman people renewing for the Jews, who requested them through ambassadors sent by their high priest Hyrcanus, the same privileges that Caesar had previously granted. Among these, Josephus mentions the right to maintain associations in the City for the practice of their own religious rites, even if such associations were forbidden to other foreign nations. Through this indulgence of the Romans, and especially of Caesar, granted to the Jews above all other nations, Caesar’s successors were prepared by a special providence of God to foster the first associations of our people at Rome. At the first and second arrivals of Peter in the City, the pagans did not yet know how to distinguish these associations from the gatherings of the Jews, especially when they saw the apostles, their fellow countrymen among the Jews, proclaiming the faith of Christ among them first.

In the same way, one may observe that a path was smoothed for founding, before Nero’s persecution, the most celebrated episcopal sees of the Christian Church after Rome, at Antioch and Alexandria. In both places the Jews possessed the same privileges of the earlier kings, confirmed by Julius Caesar and by the Senate and Roman people, and by Caesar’s successors throughout these fifty years and the years that followed down to Titus: namely, the right of citizenship and the right to practice the ancestral rites according to the custom of their forefathers. By a similar beneficence of divine assistance, so many other episcopal sees had been prepared before Nero’s persecution among the chosen newcomers of the dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, and on the islands adjacent to Asia and Europe. In those regions, as in Greece and Macedonia, the synagogues of the Jews had, so to speak, pledged open access to the apostolic men who would carry through the tabernacle of Moses into the inner sanctuary beyond the veil the tablets of the new covenant and the ark of the New and eternal Testament. Saint Ambrose observes this [Book VIII on Luke, near the end], that Christ the Lord came in such a way that he passed through the Jews to the Gentiles. The captivity of Hyrcanus among the Parthians, and the reverence shown to him by the Jews living in Mesopotamia, displayed the path opened by God’s will for bringing the sons of Christ’s free bride beyond the boundaries of the Roman Empire, since the children of her slave woman, who gives birth into slavery, had penetrated there with him.

Although the persecutions of the pagans—stirred up by the examples and plots of the Jews against Christ the Lord and against his Church as soon as it was founded through the apostles—attacked it like the waves of the great abyss driving against the ark from every side, as soon as its structure had been completed and, within it, Noah had gathered the living race to be preserved from the common disaster, nevertheless the Church of Christ experienced the stages of her elevation amid those same waves, wonderfully laid beneath her by God. He who was to bring salvation from our enemies had deliberately willed that synagogues should first be founded in those places where the sons of the synagogue would drive against the Church the whirlwinds of the Gentiles, so that, when both were dashed against it, they might fall together and, their waves being gathered, raise the saving ark to higher ground.

This foundation, therefore, laid in the East and in the West for raising up a living temple of Christian worship upon the crushed and confused ruins of the Jews and Gentiles, who were striving by their own collapse to overwhelm us, must be studied through the history and examination of the events of these fifty years preceding the epoch of Christ. In them the great force and extent of both peoples, striving against our pontiffs, become apparent. Consider either the elevation of the later Temple, whose destruction the Lord foretold, although Herod restored it with such magnificence that to the inexperienced it seemed likely to surpass the glory of the earlier Temple; or consider the expansion and strength of the Roman Empire, and the abundance of all the superstitions flourishing within it, already preparing in their priestlings just as many enemies against the bishops of the Roman see, to whom, above all others, the care of the prince of the apostles was transmitted, together with the priesthood of proclaiming the Gospel of Christ to all nations.

This apparatus of the world, prepared to strive against the Church and to be most beneficially overcome through the Church, had to be unfolded in all its grandeur through the fifty years observed before the Christian era, so that it might shed light upon pontifical history. For those abbreviated lives of Peter’s earlier successors, which compress their great deeds into one or two verses with the familiar and simple formula of sacred ordinations—“He ordained N presbyters and N bishops in various places”—will be shown to be pregnant with immense achievements, namely, the acquisition of provinces, the founding of sees, and the conversion of regions, by the additional knowledge of the East and West within this interval of half a century preceding the Christian era. [Col. 0388C] In this way the condition of nearly the entire world is displayed as destined to be brought by those same apostolic bishops into the fellowship of the Catholic Church.

I have taken care to present this according to the following method in this chronology, although the overview itself can sufficiently teach the method; nevertheless, I do not hesitate to explain it briefly.

A double column divides each page into two parts, so that one contains the chronology and civil history of the pagans, and the other that of the priestly people called by God to carry out divine worship correctly: namely, the Church of the Jews before the Lord’s coming, and the Christian Church after God and Man, and the cornerstone who makes the two one, had been given to the world.

In the first column, assigned to the chronology and history of the nations, especially of the Roman Republic and the empire of its rulers, with which the history of the Church has an especially continuous connection, the events of the western region have been arranged both chronologically and historically.

A general indication of chronology, comprising the individual year-markers from the cycle now received by Western chronologists—as it distinguishes any year, and its distance from the present, without any danger of confusion—is visible in the marginal line of the column, occupying the first position on the left and descending in sequence. Above it is placed the heading: “Years of the Julian Period.” The Julian period, invented by Scaliger, arranges the individual years, adding the markers of the solar and lunar cycles and of the Dominical letters. A secondary series descending alongside it assigns to the same year of the Julian period the Roman civil years from the founding of the City. Since the beginning of the years of Scaliger’s Julian period falls on the Kalends of January—whether the actual date after Caesar’s reform or the proleptic date before the arrangement of the Kalends by Julius Caesar—whereas the first day of the years from the founding of the City is the day that had been the festival of the Parilia for the Romans, assigned in Caesar’s calendar to the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, it follows that the portion of the year of the Julian period from 1 January to 21 April belongs to the completion of the year from the founding of the City, while from 21 April of that same Julian period a new year is reckoned, following the completed year in the sequence from the founding of the City. Consequently, a double number is attached to each individual year in this column: one belonging to the year being completed before the Parilia, the other designating the new year after the Parilia, as the heading prefixed at the top of each page shows.

Within these two descending series of epochs proceeds the line of a broader column, indicating the principal evidence for the date belonging to the same year, derived from the Roman magistrates who marked the year with public authority, such as consuls and emperors. Several men who have labored to present the fasti correctly have attempted to give the praenomen, nomen, and cognomen of the ordinary consuls. Those who know Cuspinian, Sigonius, Manutius, Panvinio, Pighius, Gruter, Goltzius, [Col. 0389C] and other authors of the preceding century need not be reminded how much remained to be accomplished after the labors of so many distinguished men had been exhausted. How greatly the most learned men of our own age have advanced consular chronology by supplying documents from stones and coins successfully discovered, and by carefully comparing and explaining them, can be made abundantly clear by a single letter of our Norisius on consular matters to the celebrated chronologist Pagius. Almeloveen and Reland have added excellent contributions to it in the volumes of their *Fasti*, recently printed. In reconciling Caesarean chronology with consular chronology, how much C. Mediabarbus labored after Occonius is attested by the excellent work on coins that he published in advance of the edition of the *Fasti* that he was planning. [Col. 0389D] Several uncertainties, especially concerning the names of the consuls, which had not yet been resolved because of the lack of documents that would establish reliable testimony to the truth, prevented him from completing it.

We too have contributed a small effort to the adornment of this branch of learning in this column. Since the zeal and favor of Clement XI, the pontiff of eternal memory, in promoting the disciplines—and especially those that provide from genuine antiquity reliable assistance for clarifying the history of the Church—had made it clear that a rich harvest of Roman monuments was growing daily, allowing the ancient crop to be gathered into no contemptible sheaves, he took care that ancient marbles inscribed with letters should not be moved from their places, either within or outside the City, during the excavations of ruins that take place every day, unless, before that occurred, the arrival of those whom he himself had appointed to inspect them and to record them for the support of history had secured whatever learned antiquity had preserved for us, late descendants, in safety. It pleased that most beneficent Father to entrust this duty to my humble self, through a decree proposed by the Most Eminent Cardinal Spinola, chamberlain, which prudently confirmed the old commands of his pontifical predecessors on 30 September 1704, in the fourth year of his pontificate.

Throughout these twenty years, both the natural concern attached to the responsibility entrusted to me—as Frontinus experienced in the office assigned to him by the emperor Nerva, concerning whom he hesitates whether to call him more diligent or more devoted to the commonwealth—and faithful diligence have urged me not merely toward carefulness but also toward love for the charge entrusted to me. Whatever ancient stones I happened to excavate—and there were very many of them—or coins that confirmed or corrected the principles of consular and Caesarean chronology, I reserved for this work. In this column, therefore, where the names of the consuls are given in full with their praenomina and cognomina whenever they could be known with certainty, you will find individual years marked with an asterisk indicating places where the same colleges of consuls, whether in giving the praenomen, nomen, or cognomen, are corrected, as far as I have been able to determine, from monuments of certain authority during this twenty-year period since I was entrusted with the task of examining and preserving these valuable documents for the use of sacred and secular history. In each college of consuls, or list, I have chosen to indicate the authority of the document by which the names are confirmed.

Although Almeloveen and Reland received many of these recently discovered monuments at this very time and published a large number of them, to the great praise of the learned public, I nevertheless judged that I should not abandon the undertaking I had begun. For a separately published *Fasti*, if God grants me leisure and the opportunity, I have accumulated numerous materials—especially from coins and stones bearing epochs, and from celestial observations—which will provide fuller light for the restoration of the chronology.

I shall be content to offer a single specimen of this addition of inscriptions to our corrected *Fasti*: namely, an unpublished inscription on a marble tablet excavated on the coast of Antium, together with other distinguished ruins, through the care and expense of the Most Eminent Prince Cardinal Alexander Albani, who, following the exhortation and example of his learned uncle Clement XI, undertook the protection and patronage of learned antiquity.
