On that marble tablet is read an engraved fragment of the Julian Calendar, comprising the latter half-year beginning with the Kalends of July, similar to the Farnesian calendar in the letters of the lunar cycle assigned to individual days and in the other accompanying indications of the days, sufficiently explained in our dissertation on the Cycle and Calendar of Caesar. But this marble is enlarged by several epochs referring the more illustrious deeds of Caesar and Augustus and of the members of their imperial family to specific days. Among these it records the day of the victory at Pharsalus, the fifth day before the Ides of August, hitherto unknown; and—what contributes to our purpose of confirming the consular fasti and presenting them in a more accurate form—it contains seven colleges of consuls under the emperors Tiberius, Gaius Caligula, and Claudius. I shall provide a faithful typographical reproduction of this most distinguished fragment at the end of these Prolegomena, and reserve the interpretation and notes that I have attached for a fuller illustration of the monument, either for the edition of the *Fasti* or for the *Unpublished Analecta of Antiquity*.

Nor did I wish the Prolegomena to lack the other astronomical indications that demonstrate the exact place and day of the year no less clearly than this marble does. I have therefore appended to them a *Brief Chronology*, serving this volume, from Julius Caesar to the end of the life of [Col. 0391B] blessed Pope Sylvester. I have noted the eclipses of the sun and moon observed during these four centuries and recorded in writing by authors, marking them in the same chronological tables by the customary sign of the sun if they are solar, or by the sign of the other luminary if they are lunar. Wherever these signs occur, the year and its position—that is, its distance from the present year—are confirmed by the phases of the eclipse. I demonstrate in the treatise *On the Restoration of Time* that the calculations correspond equally with the tables and with the observations. Among these notable eclipses, some may be seen that had not been found by chronologists, such as that belonging to the year 13 of the Christian era.

For the stabilization of this demonstration of the dates, the beneficence of the most holy Father and never sufficiently praised prince, Clement XI, provided support. At the beginning of his administration of the Church, he caused an astronomical gnomon to be erected for the use of the Calendar in the Baths of Diocletian. Since later generations would be able there to investigate the movements of the luminaries with the greatest care, and since what was necessary for preserving the benefits of Gregory XIII and for the ecclesiastical provision of the Paschal matter had to be prepared at the proper time, he also prudently added the more solid supports needed for confirming and restoring chronology in every respect.

Having given these general preliminary remarks about the chronological documents arranged in these tables, I shall briefly explain what remains to be said about their arrangement and use, so that their use may be more readily understood.

That five-year period of Caesar’s years, [Col. 0391D] before the form of the year introduced by the dictator, required that the column’s arrangement display a different beginning of the Roman civil year, then falling approximately one quarter of a year before the winter solstice in the proleptic regular series of Scaliger; this solstice is followed, seven days later, by the beginning of the Julian year on the Kalends of January. We have shown this in that five-year period by inserting lines for that interval which display the Roman civil years, completed from the Founding of the City at the Parilia and renewed from the Parilia.

When the five-year period had been completed, through the year called the Year of Confusion, in which the dictator gave the Roman citizens the new civil year of the Julian form, lines indicating the end of the Roman civil year are indeed to be placed both in the column of the Scaligerian period and in the column of the Roman civil years. Alongside these, however, it is appropriate to use a double number: the first should indicate the year from the Founding of the City completed in that same civil year and, in the Scaligerian reckoning, on 21 April at the Parilia; the second should count the new year from the Founding of the City beginning from the Parilia, or 21 April. It was necessary to mark each year with this double number so that our demonstration of chronology would not lack the evidence preserved among the ancient Capitoline marbles and the records of the Arval Brothers, which assign the same consuls before the Parilia with the first number, and after the Parilia with the second number of the years from the Founding of the City.

[Col. 0392B] These few remarks concerning the first column, which encompasses Western affairs, and its adjacent chronological strips concerning the West, should suffice. The remaining matters relating to them can be adequately understood from the table itself.

The second column, containing pontifical and Eastern history, is likewise enclosed on either side by two descending lateral columns. One of these serves for the chronology of the Olympiads; the other serves for counting the years both before the common era of Christ—through fifty Julian years, including the preceding five-year proleptic Caesarian period—and from the common era of Christ, which begins with the forty-sixth year of the new Julian arrangement. It seemed appropriate to add to the column of the history of the Eastern region the epoch of the Olympiads, which was generally [Col. 0392C] in use there. I placed the years of the common era of Christ in the other column, so that the pontifical chronology—which is the principal purpose established for this table and work—might be displayed and related more clearly to that eternal Pontiff according to the order of Melchizedek, who, for the sake of our salvation, willed to be born in time, and who willed the years of his coming and preaching to be distinguished by the years of the pontiffs whom he established in both Testaments.

Therefore, in this column, in the middle between the two lateral columns, before the coming of Christ the Lord are placed the years of the Hebrew pontiffs then holding the supreme priesthood of the Church of God. After the Lord’s coming, the principal place in the column is rightly occupied by the reckoning of the years of the age of Christ the Lord, according to our view—which is now being confirmed by the near-universal agreement of all—that precede the vulgar era by five years; for the years of the common era are marked in the lateral series under the heading “common era” prefixed to it.

When the year 33 of Christ’s age, the common era 28, has been reached, in which, after completing the work of our redemption, the Lord ascended into heaven and established on earth the new supreme pontificate of his Church in the apostle Peter and his successors, this column counts the years of the pontificate of the apostle Peter before the Roman see was founded. From the fortieth year of the common era, in which our chronology endeavors to prove that the Roman episcopate was founded by that same prince of the apostles, it counts the years of the Roman see, [Col. 0393A] both under Peter and under his successors.

Besides the years of the pontiffs of the New Law, this column also counts the Jewish pontiffs up to the destruction of the Jerusalem Temple under Vespasian. For although, when the priesthood had been transferred to the Christian Church by that Pontiff who, through his own blood, entered the Holy of Holies once for all, eternal redemption having been found, the shadow of the legal ordinances ceased and the Jewish pontificate fell; nevertheless, since the Jewish history collected by Josephus—and contributing greatly to the elucidation of Christian history—lists the successors of Annas and Caiaphas, it ought not to have seemed inappropriate, for the purpose of distinguishing and verifying the chronology, that these too should be listed up to the [Col. 0393B] destruction of the Temple.

For the same reason, we admitted into the same column the names and epochs of the kings of the Jews, so that we might neglect nothing that could usefully be employed to correct, complete, or verify the chronology.

Among these, the eras of many Eastern cities, marked on their coins and repeatedly paired with the years of Roman emperors, are especially important. We recognize sufficiently how much assistance this fact has contributed to the perfection of chronology from the work especially celebrated for this purpose by Cardinal Noris, *On the Syromacedonian Epochs*: perhaps our age has produced nothing more finely polished, and future ages will scarcely find anything comparable. Had I not added the evidence of these eras, I would certainly have deprived the demonstration of these times of an authority superior to that supplied by so many public monuments dating from the same periods—monuments rightly preferred to written works whose pages are not autograph but have been transmitted to us by copyists. The narrowness of the tables does not permit us to add illustrations of the coins or explanations; these must be sought in the books of the eminent Noris, Vaillant, and others, which were used to assign the origin of the epochs to their respective years and are therefore cited there.

With the series of individual years thus verified from the Roman consuls, the years of the emperors, and the epochs of cities—which, by joining the two reckonings, are marked in both East and West in public acts and monuments—the epochs of the individual Roman pontiffs are assigned. Their evidence, connections, [Col. 0393D] and determination must be sought in our chronological notes, which I appended individually to their Lives. I did not omit to distinguish ordination to the episcopate from election to the Roman pontificate in those who are shown to have already been marked by episcopal rank: either because they were to serve as vicars, as assistants to a Pontiff in need of such help—for Peter the Apostle is recorded to have enrolled Linus, Cletus, and Clement for this purpose—or because they were destined to be bishops of foreign peoples and, while being trained as if through an apprenticeship in pastoral office, were to exercise their duties in the City in the name of the Roman pontiff who had destined them to be sent out shortly afterward to found new Churches. If the Roman see became vacant through the death of the pontiff while they were carrying out this service, they could then be elected as the legitimate successors of that deceased shepherd.

For the sake of distinction, when I refer to ordination to the episcopal office, I print their names in the ordinary type in these tables, and I do not count their years in the column, but rather those of the Roman pontiff who was then governing the Church. When, however, they duly succeed to the Roman see, having been elected to it by the votes of the Roman clergy, I display their names in capital letters and count their pontifical years from that point, so that the eyes may readily run through the chronological table and see whatever I seem to have presented in the notes as verified concerning the epochs of each.

The events relating to individual years, collected from reliable authors and contained in both columns—Western and Eastern—belong to pontifical and universal ecclesiastical history, or are so connected by chronological purpose or by the affinity of the events themselves that they cannot be separated or passed over without loss of clarity. Whenever there was insufficient space in the Western column for events belonging to it, while there was room in the other, Eastern column, we sometimes included Roman affairs there as well. Our table was not to be burdened with more than these selected documents, lest it seem to unfold the display of universal history and chronology—which I have not undertaken here—rather than to furnish the pontifical apparatus with all, or at least the principal, evidence, which the purpose of the work assigned to me taught me to be my responsibility.

Having prefaced these remarks concerning the subject, construction, authority, and scope of the tables, let us now present the tables themselves.

So that the documents of the epochs engraved on ancient coins and stones may be more easily compared with the tables of our chronology, we give here, arranged in order, the more notable eras appearing on coins or celebrated by authors, and relate them, according to our reckoning, to the year of the Julian period. We first set out the chronological markers of the Christian era and its principal divisions, for the sake of which we compare the others.

The common era of Christ coincides, at the Kalends of January, with the year beginning in Julian period 4714, solar cycle 10, lunar cycle 2, and Dominical Letter B; with the Founding of the City, according to the marble Fasti that we follow, 753 before the Parilia and 754 from the Parilia; with the 195th Olympiad, the first year before the summer solstice and the second beginning from the summer days.

The birth of Christ the Lord precedes the common era by five full years and seven days. The era of his baptism and Gospel, begun around the beginning of the thirtieth year of his age, falls in Julian period 4738, common era 25. His passion, death, resurrection, ascension, and supreme pontificate of the New Law, which he conferred upon Peter and his successors, fall in the thirty-third year of his age, common era 28, Julian period 4741. The foundation of the Roman see falls in Julian period 4753, common era 40.

## Establishment of the Other Epochs

The Actian era of Augustus: Julian period 4682, from autumn.  
The era of the Aegeans in Cilicia: 4666, from autumn.  
The Alexandrian era of Augustus: 4683, from 29 August, the first of the fixed Thoth.  
The era of Anazarbus in Cilicia: 4694, from autumn.

The era of Apamea, also that of the Seleucids: 4402, from autumn.  
The era of the Aradians: 4455, from autumn.  
The era of the Ascalonites: 4610, from autumn.

The Hispanic era of the Augusti: 4675, from the Kalends of January.  
The era of the Augusti, from the time when Augustus was called Caesar Octavianus: 4686.  
The era of Caesar the dictator, or of the new Julian arrangement: 4669, from the Kalends of January.  
The era of the Chalcidenians: 4806, from autumn.  
The Coptic Julian era: 4689, from the first of Thoth, 29 August.  
The era of the Damascenes: 4402, also that of the Seleucids, from autumn.  
The era of the Edessenes: 4402, also that of the Seleucids, from autumn.  
The era of the Emesenes: 4402, as above.  
The era of the Gadarenes: 4650, from autumn.  
The era of the Gazans: 4652, from autumn.  
The era of the Laodiceans: 4666, from autumn.  
The era of the Neapolitans of Samaria: 4682, from autumn.  
The era of the Palmyrenes: 4402, from autumn, also that of the Seleucids.  
The Pompeian era of the Philadelphians: 4650, from autumn.  
The era of the Sebastenes of Samaria: 4688, from autumn.  
The era of the Seleucids: 4402, from autumn.  
The era of the Sidonians: 4602, from autumn.  
The proconsular era of the reign of Tiberius: 4723, common era 10.  
The era of the Tripolitans, also that of the Seleucids: 4402, from autumn.

The era of the Founding of the City: 3961, from 21 April at the Parilia.

# Chronology for Volume I of the Roman-Vatican Edition

## Consular and Caesarian Chronology of the Romans, and Pontifical Chronology of the Jews

From the fifty years immediately preceding the era of Christ up to Saint Sylvester, the first of that name.

[Note: [Col. 0396] The following texts, headed “Roman Civil Years” and “Proleptic Julian Years,” are printed in parallel in Migne. Two columns of dates, headed “Completed years of the Founding of the City at the Parilia and beginning after the Parilia” and “Completed years of the Olympiads at the summer solstice, and beginning through the solstice,” have been incorporated as notes to these texts. Two further columns, headed “Years of the Julian period and cycle” and “Years before the Era of Christ,” have been omitted. This pattern has been followed throughout the *Chronology*, which ends at column 797.]

## Consular and Caesarian Chronology of the Romans

Roman civil years, and their correspondence with the common Era of Christ and with the Julian period of Scaliger, distinguished by consulships and the events carried out in them, with evidence assigned everywhere.

[Col. 0395B]

The fifth Roman civil year before the new Julian institution of C. Caesar the Dictator consists—according to the old arrangement of King Tarquinius in Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 8—of 378 days, since it contains an intercalary month, Mercedonius, of 23 days after February.

The Kalends of January of this Tarquinian year—that is, the Roman civil year then in use—preceded the Kalends of January of the proleptic Julian year 50 before the common Era of Christ by 84 days [Note: [Col. 0395C] Before the Parilia: 703; after the Parilia: 704]. Accordingly, they fell on 9 October of the declining year 4663 of the Julian period, taken proleptically as 51 before the common Era of Christ, and preceded the Kalends of January of the new Julian arrangement by 1,910 days.

This year is marked in the Capitoline marble Fasti by the following consuls, published by Sigonius, Pighius, Panvinius, and Gruter [Col. 0397A] from those same marbles; Caesar’s first dictatorship is also carved there:

**C. Claudius, son of Marcus, grandson of Marcus, Marcellus**

**L. Cornelius Lentulus**

**IN THE SAME YEAR: C. Julius, son of Caius, grandson of Caius, Caesar, Dictator**

It is also marked by a solar eclipse, seven digits in magnitude and visible at Rome after sunrise on 21 August at the end of Julian-period year 4664, as can be inferred from the astronomical tables of de la Hire and others [Col. 0397B], that is, in the proleptic year 50 before the common Era of Christ. In the Tarquinian calendar this date was called the fourth day before the Kalends of November.

## Events

On the Kalends of January, the new consuls, Marcellus and Lentulus, by decree of the Senate, initiated war by demanding the dismissal of Caesar’s army. Caesar crossed the Rubicon and occupied Ariminum, then the City and Italy, after Pompey had been driven out [Cicero, *Letters to Friends*, book XVI, letter 11]. He set out for Spain and compelled Pompey’s legates to surrender [Col. 0397C]. Returning to Rome, he was created Dictator for the purpose of holding the elections. Within eleven days, he resigned the dictatorship and was created consul for the following year together with P. Servilius [Caesar, *Civil War*, book III].

The fourth Roman civil year before Caesar’s new arrangement consists of 355 days.

Its Kalends of January preceded the beginning of the new arrangement of Caesar the dictator by 1,532 days and fell on 22 October of Julian-period year 4664, or the proleptic year 50 before the Era of Christ [Col. 0397D]. This year is marked by the consuls recorded in the Capitoline marble Fasti and in Gruter, folio 295; Panvinius, Pighius, and Sigonius:

**C. Julius, son of Caius, grandson of Caius, Caesar II**

**P. Servilius Vatia Isauricus**

This is immediately followed by Caesar’s first dictatorship. Since it lasted for most of a year, it belongs chiefly to the following year. Thus [Note: [Col. 0397D] 704 A.U.C. after the Parilia, 705.] it is read on the Capitoline marble:

**C. Julius, son of Caius, grandson of Caius, Caesar, Dictator**

**M. Antonius, son of Marcus, grandson of Marcus, Master of the Horse**

## Events of the Romans and Their Evidence

[Col. 0399A]

After resigning the dictatorship, Caesar was created consul for the second time [Caesar, *Civil War*, book III]. He departed from the City for Brundisium, then set sail for Epirus on the day before the Nones of January [same source]. He fought in the plains of Pharsalus in mid-summer [Plutarch, *Life of Brutus*], on 9 Sextilis:

**V. EID. AVGVSTI D. IVLIVS PHARS. VICIT**  
“On the fifth day before the Ides of August, D. Julius conquered at Pharsalus.”

This is read in an ancient marble calendar discovered among the ruins of Antium and transferred to the museum of Cardinal Alessandro Albani [Col. 0399B]. The date corresponds to 9 June in the Julian calendar. After defeating Pompey, he sailed to Alexandria, suspecting that Pompey had withdrawn there into Egypt. But the treacherous attendants slaughtered the great guest on the day before his birthday, that is, on the day before the Kalends of October of the Tarquinian year; this date corresponds to 25 Quinctilis of the present Julian year [Velleius, book II, chapter 53]. Caesar received the head brought to him with tears and arranged for it to be buried in a shrine of Nemesis erected in the suburbs [Appian; Plutarch, *Life of Caesar*; Livy, book 112]. At Rome, Pompey’s death was believed only later, after his ring had been brought there.

Then the highest honors and power were conferred upon Caesar: that he should have authority over war and peace for all peoples, even though he had referred none of these matters to the people; that he should hold the consulship for five consecutive years; that he should be named Dictator not merely for six months, as formerly, but for a full year; and that he should possess tribunician power for life [Dio, book XLII].

After receiving these honors, Caesar, although he was outside Italy, immediately assumed the dictatorship [Dio, same passage]. Usserius, [Col. 0399D] reporting these matters, also aptly observes that Josephus rightly derived the beginning of Caesar’s principate from this point, assigning him three and a half years [book XIV, chapter 17]. In Syria, therefore, the Antiochenes appear to have counted the Caesarian era from his first dictatorship, and the Laodiceans from this second dictatorship. Eusebius indicates in his *Chronicle*, under the second year of the reign of Probus, that the Laodicean era was only one year later than the Antiochene.

Thus, toward the end of the Tarquinian year, [Col. 0401A] or around the autumnal equinox, when the news of the honors decreed for Caesar had been brought to him at Alexandria, Caesar immediately assumed the dictatorship for a full year. It therefore extends through the greater part of the following year, so that the consuls mark only one or two of the final months of the year.

## Why the Antiochene Era of Caesar Begins in Autumn

Julian period 4665. See column 2 of the following year.

[Col. 0401B]

The third Roman civil year before Caesar’s new arrangement consists of 377 days because an intercalary Mercedonius of 22 days was inserted according to the Tarquinian institution. Its Kalends of January preceded the beginning of Caesar’s new arrangement by 1,177 days and fell on 11 October of Julian period 4665, that is, in the year 49 before the common Era of Christ.

This year is marked by:

**C. Julius, son of Caius, grandson of Caius, Caesar, Dictator**  
**M. Antonius, son of Marcus, grandson of Marcus, Master of the Horse**

and, toward the final months,

[Col. 0401C]

**IN THE SAME YEAR, IN THE SECOND DICTATORSHIP OF CAESAR** [Note: [Col. 0401C] 704 A.U.C.; after the Parilia, 706.]

**Q. Fufius, son of Quintus, grandson of Caius, Calenus**  
**P. Vatinius**

The names of the dictator’s Master of the Horse and of the consuls of the same year survive in the Capitoline marble Fasti, published by Gruter, Sigonius, Pighius, Panvinius, and others.

## Events

Caesar, created Dictator II at Rome although absent, after news of Pompey’s death had been brought to the City—that is, about the beginning of autumn—immediately assumed the dictatorship at Alexandria toward the end of the year [Col. 0401D], contrary to the examples of his ancestors, intending to hold it for a full year. Hence this year is marked by Caesar’s dictatorship rather than by the consuls.

During the winter he engaged in a difficult war and several battles with the Alexandrians [Suetonius, *Life of Julius*, chapter 35]. At last, on the sixth day before the Kalends of April of the Tarquinian year—that is, 14 January of this proleptic Julian year, 48 before the Christian Era and Julian period 4666—he gained possession of Alexandria:

**CAESAR RECOVERED ALEXANDRIA ON THIS DAY**

as it is recorded in the ancient Farnese calendar [Col. 0403A] and in Gruter, page 133. King Ptolemy, having been miserably drowned during the fighting, he assigned the kingdom to the younger Ptolemy and to Cleopatra, his sister, whom he betrothed to him as a wife while he was still an eleven-year-old boy, according to Egyptian custom [Strabo, book XVII, page 796; Dio, book XLII; Hirtius; Suetonius, *Life of Julius*, chapter 35].

Caesar remained in Egypt for nine months [Appian, book II, *Civil War*]. Around the beginning of spring he departed from Alexandria [Col. 0403B] for Syria. News of his departure reached Italy on the third day before the Nones of Quinctilis, or 23 April in the Julian calendar [Cicero, *Letters to Atticus*, book II, letter 19]. John Malalas, *Chronicle*, book IX, shows that on that day he was at Antioch. After spending a few days in the province of Syria, he appointed Sextus Caesar over it and over the legions [Dio, book XLVII].

He sailed in the fleet by which he had arrived to Cilicia [Hirtius and Josephus, book XIV, chapter 16] [Note: [Col. 0403B] The Egyptian and Laodicean eras in Syria: from autumn; Vaillant, edition 25], and arranged the affairs of the regions and of the neighboring kingdoms. He granted autonomy to the principal cities, [Col. 0403C] including **LAODICEA BY THE SEA**, from which the Era of Caesar derives its beginning.

Summoned to the Pontic war against Pharnaces, he came, saw, and conquered [Plutarch, *Life of Caesar*, etc.] within five days [Suetonius, *Life of Julius*, chapter 35]. He appointed Mithridates king of the Bosporus. Passing through Greece, he came to Rome as the year revolved from the time when he had again been designated dictator [Plutarch, *Life of Caesar*]. Having been designated consul III for the following year, he created, during the final months of this year, the consuls recorded in the Capitoline marble Fasti [Col. 0403D]:

**Q. Fufius Calenus**

**P. Vatinius, for the final three months of the year**

[Suetonius, *Life of Claudius*, chapter 15].

The Laodicean Era of Caesar begins here, from autumn, when Caesar granted autonomy.

The second Roman civil year before Caesar’s new arrangement consists of 355 days.

Its Kalends of January preceded the beginning of the new arrangement of the Julian years by 800 days and fell on 23 October of the proleptic Julian year 48 before the [Col. 0405A] Era of Christ, or Julian period 4666. This year is marked by the consuls expressed in the Capitoline marbles as follows:

**C. Julius, son of Caius, grandson of Caius, Caesar III**

**M. Aemilius, son of Marcus, grandson of Quintus, Lepidus**

**C. Julius, son of Caius, grandson of Caius, Caesar III, Dictator**

**M. Aemilius, son of Marcus, grandson of Quintus, Lepidus, Master of the Horse**

Sigonius, in his commentary on the Fasti for this year, A.U.C. 707 [Col. 0405B]—beginning from the Parilia—observes that the view of the person who arranged the Capitoline Fasti in this manner seems different from that of those who wrote the Roman Annals. The former assigns only the second dictatorship to the preceding year, whereas the latter assigns to this year both the third consulship and the third dictatorship, and to the immediately following year the fourth consulship and fourth dictatorship, and to the next year after that the fifth consulship. Others inquire about a fifth dictatorship, which is nowhere read.

Sigonius reconciles the accounts—and with him we remove the entire controversy—by adducing the words of Dio. In the following year, [after the year which he had completed as Dictator II,] [Col. 0405C] he held the dictatorship together with the consulship, both for the third time, with M. Lepidus substituted as his colleague in both offices.

## Events

Caesar undertook an expedition against P. Cornelius Scipio, father-in-law of Pompey the Great, M. Cato, and Juba, king of Mauretania. On the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January [6 October of Julian period 4667] he arrived at Lilybaeum, and twelve days later he was in sight of Africa [Hirtius, *On the African War*]. On the Kalends of January—that is, 23 October of the proleptic Julian year [Col. 0405D]—he had his camp at the town of Ruspina [same source].

He took the field on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April [8 January in the Julian calendar], after reviewing the army. On the day before the Nones of April [22 January], he defeated Juba and Scipio in a memorable battle, while Cato took his own life [Hirtius, same passage]. After the African war had been completed, he landed at the port of Calaris on the Ides of June [5 April in the Julian calendar], and fifteen days later came to Rome [Hirtius, at the end of *On the African War*].

In this year he celebrated four triumphs at Rome, in the same month but with intervening days [Suetonius, *Life of Julius*, [Col. 0407A] chapter 37; Velleius, book II, chapter 37]: the Gallic, Pontic, Alexandrian, and African triumphs.

He instituted the correction of the year, employing the services of Sosigenes in astronomical matters and of Flavius the secretary in arranging the Fasti [Dio, book XLIII; Macrobius, *Saturnalia*, book I, chapter 14].

The immediately preceding Roman civil year before the new arrangement of the Julian years of Caesar the dictator—the year also called the Year of Confusion—consists of 445 days. By its 445 days it precedes the Kalends of January of the first year in the Julian sequence, that is, the year 45 before the common Era of Christ.

Its Kalends of January fall on 13 October of Julian period 4667 and precede by 80 days the Kalends of January of Julian-period year 4668, or 46 before the common Era of Christ.

Besides the twelve Tarquinian months, which together contain 355 days, there were three intercalary months: Mercedonius of 23 days between February and March, and two [Col. 0407C] intercalary months between November and December, each of 34 days. The total number of days in this Year of Confusion was 445 [Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 8].

It was marked by Caesar’s fourth consulship without a colleague and by his dictatorship [Note: [Col. 0407C] A.U.C. 707; after the Parilia, 708], partly III and partly IIII, as the Capitoline marble Fasti show:

**C. Julius, son of Caius, grandson of Caius, Caesar III, Dictator**

**M. Aemilius, son of Marcus, grandson of Quintus, Lepidus, Master of the Horse**

**IN THE SAME YEAR C. JULIUS, SON OF CAIUS, GRANDSON OF CAIUS, CAESAR IIII, WITHOUT A COLLEAGUE**

**IN THE SAME YEAR Q. FABIUS, SON OF QUINTUS, GRANDSON OF QUINTUS, MAXIMUS, DIED IN OFFICE**

In his place was substituted:

**C. Caninius, son of Caius, grandson of Caius, Rebila**

And in the Colotian tablet, in Gruter, folio 298:

**C. JULIUS CAESAR IIII, WITHOUT A COLLEAGUE, DICTATOR**  
*(designated for the third time, for the fourth time)*

**Substitutes:** Q. Fabius Maximus, C. Trebonius, C. Caninius; C. Julius Caesar, Dictator IV; M. Aemilius, Master of the Horse.

The completed year of the third consulship had passed when Caesar entered his fourth consulship, but the year of his third dictatorship had not yet been completed [Col. 0409A]. Therefore, since it was the same year in the third dictatorship but not the same year in the third consulship, he is said to have entered his fourth consulship without a colleague. Alternatively, the two words **IN THE SAME YEAR**, which properly belong after the fourth consulship, may have been carved by the sculptor’s negligence in the Capitoline tablets before the words “Caesar IIII without a colleague.” This Year of Confusion, I believe, confused the sculptor or compiler when the Capitoline tablets were engraved [Col. 0409B]: the words “in the same year” are abundant and placed in the earlier position, while the fourth dictatorship is lacking, though it is attested both on the Colotian marble and on Caesar’s coins bearing the fourth consulship; these coins are to be trusted as contemporary evidence.

## Events

C. Julius Caesar, having entered his fourth consulship at Rome without a colleague and being at the same time Dictator—thus named in the Colotian tablet, namely, Dictator III and designated for the fourth time, as Hirtius writes at the beginning of his book on the Spanish War—after completing great forced marches, hastened to Spain to bring the war to an end [Col. 0409C] against the sons of Pompey.

In Spain, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March [22 December of Julian period 4667 in the Julian calendar], Caesar captured the town of Ategua and was hailed as **Imperator**. On the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, at the festival of the Liberalia—called the **Dionysia** (festival of Dionysus) in Plutarch’s *Life of Caesar*—a memorable battle was fought at Munda. Approximately 30,000 Pompeians fell in it. In the proleptic Julian year, the date was 17 January.

Twelve days before that battle, Hirtius, an eyewitness who followed Caesar in his *Journal of the Spanish War*, writes that on the third day before the Nones of March [which in the proleptic Julian year corresponds to 5 January], when Caesar was moving camp, the moon shone upon him auspiciously at the sixth hour of the night [Col. 0409D]. This could not have happened in the first year of Caesar’s new style—which chronologists commonly assign this expedition—since, according to everyone’s view, that year had its new moon on the Kalends of January, and on 5 March the moon would have descended below the horizon three days after conjunction with the sun [Col. 0411A] at the second hour of the night.

In our chronology, however, which assigns the Spanish expedition against Pompey’s sons to the Year of Confusion, on the third day before the Nones of March—361 days before the new Julian style and the new moon—the age of the moon was 23 days. The moon, being near quadrature with the sun, rose around the sixth hour of the night, exactly as Caesar and Hirtius saw it.

[Col. 0411B] Victorious in Spain, Caesar entered Rome in October and celebrated a Spanish triumph. For the remaining three months of the year—namely, for the two intercalary months after November and for December—he resigned the consulship and appointed substitute consuls, Q. Fabius Maximus and C. Trebonius; after Fabius died, he substituted C. Caninius for the final day of the year.

Many great honors were decreed to Caesar by the Senate. Above all, that he should be **Dictator in perpetuity**, and that he should bear the praenomen **Imperator** [Suetonius, *Life of Julius*, chapter 76], by which was signified not merely a successful military action [Col. 0411C] but supreme authority in the republic [Dio, book XLIII; Appian, book II, *Civil War*, page 494].

# Proleptic Julian Years before the Common Era of Christ

[Col. 0396B]

## 51

As the proleptic year 51 before the common Era of Christ was passing—the year occupying position 4663 in the Julian period of Scaliger—a central solar eclipse visible at Rome occurred at midday on 7 March.

The Kalends of January of the civil year then counted by the Romans according to the arrangement of King Tarquinius, as described by Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 8, fell on 9 October of this year, Julian period 4663, or 51 proleptic years before the common Era of Christ [Col. 0396C].

[Note: [Col. 0396C] Olympiad 182, year III before the summer solstice; after the solstice, year IV.] Dio’s testimony in book XLIII, page 159, G. L., refers to the solar eclipses of this and the following year.

## 50

This is the fifth proleptic year of the Julian style and the year 50 before the common Era of Christ. It precedes Caesar’s new arrangement of the years by a full five-year period, or 1,827 days. Its Kalends of January coincide [Col. 0398A] with the 85th day of the Tarquinian year, or civil year then used by the Romans. It consists of 365 days. It is marked by the consuls:

**C. Claudius Marcellus**

**L. Cornelius Lentulus**

Velleius, book II, writes that under these consuls the civil war broke out, in the 703rd year after the founding of Rome and 78 years before the consulship of Vinicius, who had Cassius Longinus as his colleague, in the common Era of Christ according to our reckoning, year 29.

## Events of the Jews and Neighboring Regions, Especially in Matters Concerning the Sacred Institutions and the Hebrew Pontiffs

Hyrcanus, the high priest, fifty-fourth in descent from Aaron and of the Hasmonean [*Assamonaean*] line of princes, who had assumed the pontificate in the third year of the 177th Olympiad, when Q. Hortensius and Q. Metellus Creticus were consuls [Josephus, book XIV, chapter 1], had also succeeded his mother in the kingdom before the Era of Christ, year 69 [Josephus, book XV, chapter 9]. Having been expelled by his brother Aristobulus, he was restored by Pompey the Great after Jerusalem was captured [Josephus, same passage, and Dio, book LIII]. In the immediately preceding years he was defended by the Roman proconsuls Gabinius, Crassus, and Bibulus against the restless character of Aristobulus and his sons [Col. 0398C].

[Note: [Col. 0398C] Olympiad 182, year IV; and from the summer, Olympiad 183, year I.]

The Kalends of January of the Tarquinian, or Roman civil, year fell on 22 October of this proleptic Julian year 50 before the Era of Christ.

## 49

The fourth proleptic year of the Julian style before Caesar’s arrangement [Col. 0398D], and year 49 before the common Era of Christ, occupying Julian-period position 4665, has its Kalends of January on the 72nd day of the Tarquinian year of the Romans. In the City this day was called the Ides of March according to the civil calendar then in use before Caesar’s reform. It is marked by the consuls:

**C. Julius Caesar II**

**P. Servilius Vatia Isauricus**

Since it is a leap year, it consists of 366 days.

Its Kalends of January preceded the beginning of the new Julian arrangement by 1,461 days.

[Col. 0400A]

## Events of the Jewish Pontiffs, Their People, and Neighboring Regions

While Caesar was staying at Alexandria and was intent on exacting the money owed to him by Ptolemy Auletes, the father of the boy king, and on settling the dispute between the king and his sister Cleopatra, who were contending for the kingdom according to their father’s will, a disturbance was stirred up through the counsels of the eunuch Pothinus, and Caesar was placed in danger [Dio, book XLII, and Plutarch, *Life of Caesar*].

Caesar believed that the disputes of kings concerned the Roman people, who were their guardians, and himself, since he was consul [Col. 0400B]. He therefore declared that it was his wish that King Ptolemy and his sister Cleopatra should dismiss the armies they possessed and should settle their disputes legally before him rather than by arms against one another [Caesar, book III].

Caesar’s power was increased by the Senate and People of Rome, which, toward the end of the year, conferred upon him the dictatorship and other honors and rights destined to continue through the following years. This encouraged him to undertake that adjudication more securely, but at the same time it inflamed the Egyptians against him, since Pothinus carefully incited their feelings against the foreign guest whom they saw becoming judge of their kings.

He assigned the kingdom of Egypt to Ptolemy and Cleopatra, and bestowed Cyprus upon their younger brother and sister, the younger Ptolemy and Arsinoe [Caesar, same passage; Livy, book 112; Plutarch, *Life of Caesar*].

When, therefore, the repeated disturbance brought the Egyptians and Romans into open war, that famous library of King Philadelphus, containing 400,000 books, was burned in the harbor together with the ships [Seneca, *On Tranquility of Mind*, chapter 9; Orosius, book VI, chapter 15; Plutarch, *Life of Caesar*; Dio, book XLII].

Although Caesar had been drawn into this battle with only a small number of his own soldiers, and had not expected the outcome, he nevertheless managed the affair successfully with the timely assistance of his allies and friends of the Roman people. The Jews, both Alexandrian and Palestinian, rendered him vigorous assistance at the urging and under the authority of Hyrcanus the pontiff and Aristobulus [Josephus, book XIV, chapter 14]. Thus, after a bloody battle, he was victorious on the sixth day before the Kalends of April [as it is read in the ancient calendar in the Farnese Palace, published by Gruter, folio 133]:

**ON THIS DAY CAESAR RECOVERED ALEXANDRIA**

This date corresponds to 14 January of Julian period 4666, the year 48 before the Era of Christ, which began immediately afterward. While Caesar was in Egypt, he assumed a second dictatorship around the autumn of this year and spent nine months there, as Appian reports in book II of the *Civil War*, page 484.

[Col. 0402B]

Besides sending auxiliary forces to Caesar while he was staying at Alexandria, Hyrcanus the pontiff and king of the Jews also organized an embassy. Through it he obtained that he should be registered as ethnarch of his people and should retain the pontificate for life according to ancestral custom, together with alliance and friendship with the Roman people, judicial rights, and other privileges recorded by Josephus from bronze columns and tablets set up in the Alexandrian forum and at Rome in the Capitol, book XIV, chapter 17.

## 48

[Col. 0402C]

The third proleptic year of the Julian style before Caesar’s arrangement, and year 48 before the common Era of Christ, Julian period 4666, has its Kalends of January on the 83rd day of the Tarquinian year, or Roman civil year, in which it was called the fourth day before the Nones of March. It is marked by:

[Note: [Col. 0402C] Olympiad 183, year I; and from the summer, year II.]

**C. Julius Caesar, Dictator II,**

**M. Antonius, Master of the Horse;**

and, around autumn,

**Q. Fufius Calenus,**

**P. Vatinius, consuls.**
Around the beginning of spring, Caesar, dictator for the second time, sailed from Egypt and was in Antioch in Syria [Col. 0402D] around 6 May in the Julian calendar [from Cicero, Letters to Atticus, Book II, Letter 19; Ussher, p. 351]. There, on the twelfth day of the month Artemisium, or May, an edict was published concerning the right of metropolitan status, sacred privileges, asylum, autonomy, and primacy over the whole East, granted to Antioch by Caesar’s dictatorial authority [John Malalas, Chronicle, Book IX]. Hence:

## THE ANTIOCHENE ERA OF CAESAR

was established in this year. Nevertheless, it is reckoned from the preceding autumn, from which the beginning of the civil year was derived [Col. 0404A] by the Antiochenes, as Cardinal Noris demonstrates in *Epistle on Syrian Chronology*, Dissertation III, chapter 4. He demonstrates from the coins of Galba, struck under Mucianus with era-year 117, and from those of Tiberius Augustus, struck under Flaccus in the first year of his reign and Antiochene year 82, that its beginning was taken from the autumn of Julian Period 4665, 49 years before the common Christian Era. From the autumn of this year, Julian Period 4666, begins there the **LAODICEAN ERA OF CAESAR**, ibid., chapter 8, § 2.

Three years earlier Aristobulus [Col. 0404B], the brother and would-be assassin of Hyrcanus, the Jewish high priest, had been detained at Rome because of complaints against his brother. He was later released through the favor of Caesar’s party and sent back to his homeland, but was killed by poison by the Pompeians; his son Alexander was beheaded at Antioch by Scipio on Pompey’s orders [Josephus, Book XIV, chapter 13].

This year Antigonus, son of Aristobulus, came to Caesar, who was staying at Antioch, recalling the misfortunes of his father and brother and accusing Hyrcanus the high priest [Col. 0404C] and Antipater, governor of the Jews, of exercising the leadership of the nation by force under Hyrcanus’s mandate. Antipater prevailed when the case was argued before Caesar. The authority of Hyrcanus the high priest was confirmed; a dynasty of whatever kind he might wish was offered to Antipater, and the administration of Judaea was entrusted to him by Caesar [Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XIV, chapter 15, and *The Jewish War*, Book I, chapter 8].

Moreover, Caesar confirmed for Hyrcanus the high priest and his children the perpetual retention, according to ancestral custom, of the ethnarchate and the high priesthood of the Jews, judicial authority in matters of Jewish [Col. 0404D] religious discipline, the rights of tithes, and the other priestly privileges. On this subject he ordered bronze tablets, inscribed in Roman and Greek letters, to be set up both in the Capitol at Rome and at Tyre, Sidon, and Ascalon [Josephus, Book XIV, chapter 17].

Antipater, governor of Judaea, observing that Hyrcanus was dull and inactive, brought his own sons into the public administration under Hyrcanus in such a way that Phasael, the eldest, was commander of Jerusalem and the surrounding region [Col. 0406A], while Herod, then an adolescent of fifteen or certainly a young man of twenty-five years [as Ussher emends the manuscripts of Josephus from Nicolaus of Damascus, annals, fol. 353], administered Galilee.

## 47

The second proleptic year of the Julian style, before Caesar’s reform, and the year 47 before the common Christian Era, of Julian Period 4665, places its Kalends of January on day 71 of the Tarquinian, or Roman civil, year [Col. 0406B], which was called 14 March, or the day before the Ides of March. It consists of 365 days. It is marked by the third consulship of Caesar and his third dictatorship, with Lepidus as colleague.

[Note: [Col. 0406B] Olympiad 183, years II and III.]

C. Julius Caesar, consul for the third time and dictator for the third time; M. Aemilius Lepidus, consul and Master of the Horse.

## EVENTS

Herod gave proof of vigilance in his office by apprehending Hezekiah, leader of the brigands. But because he put him to death without consulting the high priest Hyrcanus, he was accused of rashness by the Jewish nobles [Col. 0406C] and summoned to judgment before that same Hyrcanus. They also charged that Phasael, following his brother’s example, was becoming insolent, although Antipater, the father of both, displayed obedience to the high priest. Nevertheless, Hyrcanus was honored, though without the royal title, just as if he himself were ruling.

Herod had so greatly won over Sextus Caesar, proconsul of Syria, by gifts [which Hyrcanus had supplied, although Herod offered them in his own name] that Sextus became the cause of Hyrcanus’s acquitting Herod. Hyrcanus did this to his own disadvantage, as Sameas had foretold in the [Col. 0406D] council. For Sextus Caesar, after receiving the money, appointed Herod governor of Coele-Syria. This office supplied him with the means of taking up arms against Hyrcanus and besieging Jerusalem, unless his father and brother had opposed him. Josephus, Book XIV, chapter 17.

Sextus Caesar was rebuked by Caecilius Bassus because he improperly retained the legion entrusted to him by C. Caesar. While he was ordering Bassus to be dragged before him, he was killed in a riot by the legionaries. The mutinous soldiers conspired [Col. 0408A] for their own immunity and on behalf of Bassus, who protected himself by claiming to have been appointed praetor at Apamea. C. Antistius Vetus and other Caesarians besieged him.

Antipater supplied assistance to the Caesarians through his sons. Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book I, chapter 8, and *Antiquities*, Book XIV, chapter 17; Dio, Book XLVII.

## 46

[Note: [Col. 0408A] Olympiad 183, years III and IV.]

The first proleptic year of the Julian style before Caesar’s reform, and the year 46 before the common Christian Era [Col. 0408B], of Julian Period 4668, places its Kalends of January on day 81 of the Roman civil year, which was called the Year of Confusion and contained 445 days: specifically, on the twenty-first day of Mercedonius, intercalated between February and March, or the fourth day before the Kalends of March. It consists of 365 days. The beginning of the year is marked by:

C. Julius Caesar, consul for the fourth time, alone, and dictator for the third time, designated for a fourth consulship.

As the year progressed, for its final three months [namely, the two intercalary months after the completion of November, which contained 34 days, and December], the following consuls were substituted:

Q. Fabius Maximus.

C. Trebonius.

On the last day of the year, Q. Fabius Maximus having died in office, the following man was substituted in his place for a few hours:

C. Caninius Rebilus.

Pliny, Book VII, chapter 53; Suetonius, *Claudius*, chapter 15; Macrobius, Book VII, chapter 3.

## EVENTS

While the war in Syria was being prolonged against Caecilius Bassus, L. Statius [Col. 0408D] Murcus, a former praetor, was sent by Julius Caesar as the successor of Sextus, with three divisions from Italy, but was bravely repulsed by Bassus [Josephus, *The Jewish War*, Book I, chapter 8, at the end, and *Antiquities*, Book XIV, chapter 17, at the end; Velleius Paterculus, Book II, chapter 69; Appian, etc.].

In Josephus, Murcus is incorrectly written Marcus. Bassus was supported in the war by Arab tribal chiefs, especially those of the Emesene nation, and by Alchaudonius, king of the Rhambaean nomads living beyond the Euphrates [Col. 0410A], an Arab [Strabo, Book XVI, p. 753, and Dio, Book XLVII]. Toward the end of the year, the Parthians also arrived, having been summoned by Bassus to Syria, but because winter intervened they did not remain long [ibid.]. Nevertheless, Caesar foresaw the war threatening the republic and himself from the Parthians so clearly that, after returning from the Spanish expedition around October of this year, he prepared for a Parthian campaign in the following summer. He sent C. Octavius ahead to Apollonia for the sake of his studies [whom he had taken as his companion in the Spanish war because, through Accia, daughter of Julia, he was his nearest relative] and designated him Master of the Horse.

He later became emperor, having been named Caesar’s heir in the final will, which Caesar deposited this year, on the Ides of September, with the chief Vestal Virgin for safekeeping. Suetonius, *Julius*, chapter 83.

Hyrcanus the high priest sent an embassy to Caesar, whom he heard had been permanently invested with the greatest authority in the Roman republic, requesting confirmation of the decrees that Caesar had issued in Egypt and Syria, honorable and advantageous both [Col. 0410C] to himself and to the entire Jewish nation. The impending Parthian war and the Syrian war against Bassus, together with the ancient services of the high priest Hyrcanus and the Jews to Caesar, secured a most generous favor.

Josephus, *Antiquities*, Book XIV, chapter 17, recites the letters and decrees of Caesar, bearing the titles “consul for the fifth time” and “dictator in perpetuity”:

“By these decrees, the priesthood and high priesthood of Jerusalem and of the entire nation are assigned to Hyrcanus, the high priest of the Jews, and to his children, with the same right by which their ancestors held this priesthood [Col. 0410D]; he is to possess and fortify the city of Jerusalem, and Hyrcanus, son of Alexander, the high priest and ethnarch of the Jews, is to govern it according to his own will. In the second year of the lease they may deduct from their revenues, and they are to be exempt from forced labor and taxes, and so forth. They are to pay tithes to Hyrcanus and his sons, as they have hitherto paid them to their ancestors.

“No governor, commander, or legate is to gather auxiliary forces within the borders of the Jews; nor may soldiers demand money from them, whether for winter quarters or under any other name. They are to be exempt from all such burdens, and so forth. The rights that existed from the beginning between the Jews and their high priests are also to remain, as are all privileges granted by the Senate and People of Rome.

“Moreover, they are to enjoy the same rights at Lydda. The places, lands, and dwellings that the kings of Syria and Phoenicia had possessed by donation of the Roman people are approved by the Senate for Hyrcanus, ethnarch of the Jews, to possess. Hyrcanus, his sons, and his envoys sent by him are to have the right to watch games and gladiatorial shows while seated among the senators. Whenever they request it, they are to be introduced into the Senate by the dictator or Master of the Horse, and within ten days a reply is to be given to them concerning whatever the Senate has decreed,” and so forth.

After the Year of Confusion had been completed, the civil years of the Romans, newly organized by C. Julius Caesar, now correspond with the Julian years and are henceforth to be continued on equal calculations as follows.

[Col. 0411]

## Emperors, Roman consuls, events, and documents

[Col. 0411C]

On the Kalends of January:

Mean new moon at Rome, 5 hours and 41 minutes after noon.

True new moon at Rome, 15 hours and 26 minutes after noon on the Kalends of January.

[Col. 0411D] From the astronomical tables of de la Hire.

Consuls: C. Julius Caesar, consul for the fifth time; M. Antonius, son of Marcus. Substituted consul: P. Cornelius, son of Publius.

The Colotian Tablet, in Gruter, fol. CCXCVIII, and in the Capitoline marble tablets.

C. Julius Caesar, son of Gaius, grandson of Gaius, Caesar, consul for the fifth time.

Ancient gold and silver coins in Vaillant, Occon, Mediobarbus, and others: “C. Caesar, consul for the fifth time, dictator in perpetuity.”

[Col. 0413A] C. Julius Caesar celebrated his sixth triumph, in an ovation from the Alban Mount, on 26 January.

“C. Julius Caesar, son of Gaius, grandson of Gaius, Caesar, consul for the sixth time and dictator for the fourth time, celebrating an ovation, in the 709th year from the foundation of Rome, from the Alban Mount, on the seventh day before the Kalends of February.” Capitoline triumphal Fasti, in Gruter.

On the Ides of March, C. Caesar was stabbed in the Senate house by the conspirators with 23 wounds. The substituted consul was P. Cornelius Dolabella.

C. Octavius, Caesar’s heir, adopted into the Julian family, was thereafter called C. Julius [Col. 0413B] Caesar. Returning from Apollonia to Rome around the Kalends of May [for on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May he was at Naples, and the following day at Cumae with Cicero [Book XIV, Letter 10, to Atticus]], he began to be surrounded by such a great crowd of friends and strengthened by popular favor, having been commended to the Senate by Cicero, that around the month of August [then called Sextilis] he undertook to gather an army from the colonies at his private expense. [Livy, Book CXVII; Florus, Book IV, chapter 4; and the Ancyran Tablets.]

The Macedonian war against the Getae and the Parthian war, together with the legions prepared by C. Caesar, were assigned to M. Antonius, with whom Octavius had been reconciled. Provinces were assigned. Most of Caesar’s acts were confirmed. The assassins of Caesar, Brutus and Cassius, abandoning hope of preserving the popular republic, withdrew voluntarily into exile at Athens. Velleius, Book II, chapter 62; Dio, Book XLVII.

Cicero, intending this year to undertake a journey to Greece before the Olympic Games [to Atticus, Book XV, Letter 24, and Book XVI, Letter 7], indicates that the beginning of the 184th Olympiad should be assigned chiefly to this year, the year of C. Caesar’s assassination.

Antonius, having received authority from the Senate and People of Rome to investigate and execute whatever Caesar had ordered concerning his acts, was selling everywhere freedom, Roman citizenship, and exemptions to peoples and dynasts. Tablets recording all these matters were posted throughout the Capitol. Cicero, *Philippics*, 2, and Book II, *Letters to Friends*, Letter 1; Paterculus, Book II; Plutarch, *Antony*; Dio, Book XLIV. All these confirm Josephus’s history.

[Col. 0415A]

C. Vibius, son of Gaius, grandson of Gaius, Pansa.

A. Hirtius, son of Aulus.

[Note: [Col. 0415A] 709 from the foundation of Rome, and after the Festival of Pales, 710.]

C. Carrinas, son of Gaius.

P. Ventidius, son of Publius.

On the Kalends of January, Cicero, in the Fifth Philippic, urged that Antony be pursued by war. On the following day extraordinary command was conferred upon C. Caesar [Col. 0415B] Octavian. [Cicero, *Philippic* XI.] Lepidus, Antony, and Caesar, reconciled, assumed the triumvirate for reorganizing the republic on the fifth day before the Kalends of December. M. Aemilius Lepidus, son of Marcus, grandson of Quintus, for the second time; M. Antonius; P. Sulpicius. Consuls. The lustrum was not completed.

The Colotian marble Fasti, in Gruter, fol. 298.

At Philippi in Macedonia a battle was fought. The twenty-one legions of Brutus and Cassius, together with an equal number belonging to M. Antonius [Col. 0415C] and Caesar, were engaged. Cassius, having been driven from the camp, killed himself. Brutus, defeated in a second battle, likewise killed himself. Livy, Book CXXIV; Velleius Paterculus, Book II, chapter 70; Plutarch, *Brutus*; Appian, Book IV.

Antony departed for the eastern provinces, Caesar for the western, their forces having been divided between them; meanwhile Antony wintered at Athens. Plutarch, *Antony*.

L. Antonius; P. Servilius, son of Publius.

[Note: [Col. 0415C] 711, 712.]

Rauricus. The Colotian Stone.

Antony demanded rewards from the Asians for the twenty-eight victorious legions [Col. 0415D] [which, together with the auxiliaries, amounted to 170,000 men], requiring nine years’ tribute within two years. Appian, Book III, p. 673. He then departed for Syria.

Octavian Caesar, having arranged that the question of distributing among the Caesarian soldiers the lands of citizens who had favored Brutus and Cassius should be settled by the soldiers themselves, won the soldiers’ favor and Fulvia’s hatred. Hence the war between Caesar and Antony, Fulvia’s husband. Dio, Book XLVIII; Suetonius, *Octavian*, chapter 62.

The Perusine War.

[Col. 0417A]

Cn. Domitius, son of Marcus, Calvinus, for the second time.

C. Asinius, son of Gnaeus, Pollio.

Inniani Carinani, *Agricultural Affairs*; Noris, *Pisan Censorinus*, p. 139.

Substituted: L. Cornelius, son of Lucius.

Substituted: P. Cassidius, son of Publius.

The Fasti of the Colotian Stone, Gruter, p. 298.

[Col. 0417B] The emperor Caesar, having compelled L. Antonius to surrender, entered Perusia as victor and brought all Italy under his power, partly by voluntary agreement and partly by force. Antony, one of the triumvirs, [Note: [Col. 0417B] 712 from the foundation of Rome; 713 by the Pisan reckoning], after the death of his wife Fulvia, was reconciled with Caesar and divided the Roman Empire with him.

All the eastern regions beyond the Ionian Gulf, together with the islands and provinces as far as the Euphrates, obeyed Antony. The western regions—Dalmatia, Spain, and Gaul—belonged to Caesar, who had already assigned Africa to Lepidus. Appian, p. 709; Dio, p. 374; Plutarch, *Antony*. [Col. 0417C] In the month of October. Noris, *Pisan Chronology*, p. 140.

L. Marcius Censorinus.

[Note: [Col. 0417C] 714 from the foundation of Rome, 715 by the Actian reckoning, 715 by the Pisan reckoning.]

C. Calvisius Sabinus.

On the Kalends of January, L. Marcius Censorinus, son and grandson of Lucius, consul, celebrated a triumph from Macedonia. The Capitoline triumphal Fasti, Gruter, p. 296.

Ventidius first expelled Labienus, and then the Parthians, defeated in battle, from Cilicia and Syria. Dio, Book XLVIII. He also recovered Palestine and, at Rome, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, triumphed as proconsul over Mount Taurus and the Parthians in the following year. The Capitoline triumphal Fasti, in Gruter, fol. 296.

App. Claudius Pulcher.

[Note: [Col. 0417C] 714 from the foundation of Rome, 715 by the Actian reckoning, 715 by the Pisan reckoning.]

C. Norbanus Flaccus.

From this point the **HISPANIC ERA** is reckoned.

Domitius Calvinus, as proconsul, had brought Spain under Caesar’s authority in the preceding year and ordered it to pay tribute beginning on the Kalends of January of this year; hence the Hispanic Era begins.

“P. Ventidius, son of Publius, proconsul, from Mount Taurus and the Parthians, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, in the 715th year from the foundation of Rome.”

[Col. 0419A] Capitoline triumphal Fasti.

Orodes, king of the Parthians, appointed his son Phraates to the kingdom. Dio.

M. Vipsanius Agrippa, son of Lucius.

[Note: [Col. 0419A] 715 from the foundation of Rome, 716 by the Actian reckoning, 716 by the Pisan reckoning.]

L. Caninius Gallus, son of Lucius.

Dio, Book XLIX.

When the five-year term of the triumvirate for reorganizing the republic had been completed, the triumvirs, on the day before the Kalends of January, again declared themselves triumvirs for another five-year term, to begin on the Kalends of January of this year. Capitoline Stone, above, under year 710 from the foundation of Rome.

M. Agrippa undertook the Sicilian War against Sextus Pompey and opened the harbor of Baiae. Dio, Book XLVIII, p. 388.

L. Gellius Publicola, son of Lucius.

[Note: [Col. 0419B] 716 from the foundation of Rome, 718 by the Actian reckoning, 718 by the Pisan reckoning.]

M. Cocceius Nerva. Dio, Book XLIX.

Cn. Domitius Calvinus, son of Marcus and grandson of Marcus, proconsul of Spain, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of Sextilis, in the 717th year from the foundation of Rome.

“Emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, grandson of Caesar, for the second time, triumvir for reorganizing the republic for the second time, celebrating an ovation from Sicily on the Ides of November, in the 717th year from the foundation of Rome.” Capitoline triumphal Fasti.

[Col. 0419C] The triumvirate was taken away from Lepidus, with his life spared; he himself was banished to Circeii.

L. Cornificius, son of Lucius.

Sextus Pompeius, son of Lucius.

Dio, Book XLIX.

In their consulship, Sextus Pompey, son of Gnaeus Magnus, informed of Antony’s unsuccessful expedition against the Parthians, was encouraged by the hope of joining them and crossed into Asia. There he was compelled to surrender by Amyntas, ruler of Galatia, Lycaonia, and Pamphylia, appointed by Antony [Note: [Col. 0419C] 717 from the foundation of Rome, 718 by the Actian reckoning, 718 by the Pisan reckoning], [Col. 0419D] and was killed at Miletus. Appian, Book V; Dio, Book XLIX, p. 403, and elsewhere.

M. Antonius, son of Marcus, for the second time. He abdicated on the Kalends of January; L. Scribonius Libo was substituted in his place.

[Note: [Col. 0419D] 718 from the foundation of Rome, 719 by the Actian reckoning, 719 by the Pisan reckoning.]

L. Sempronius Atratinus. Municipal Fasti Stone, in Gruter, fol. CCIC.

In their consulship occurred the Illyrian War and the Marsic War. There:

C. Sosius, son of Gaius, grandson of Titus, proconsul, from Judaea, on the third day before the Nones of September, in the 719th year from the foundation of Rome.

C. Norbanus Flaccus, son of Gaius, proconsul, from Spain, on the fourth day before the Ides of October, in the 719th year from the foundation of Rome.

Capitoline triumphal Fasti.

The emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, for the second time, on the same day as the Kalends, abdicated. In his place was substituted:

L. Volcatius Tullus, son of Lucius.

The same stone of the municipal Fasti, in Gruter, fol. CCIC, and Frontinus, records that in this consulship the year from the foundation of Rome was 719; and thirteen years later it records C. Sentius and P. Lucretius as consuls. After Bocchus, king of Mauretania, died, Mauretania was reduced to a province. Dio, Book XLIX. Hostilities grew between Caesar and Antony.

Cn. Domitius Ahenobarbus.

[Note: [Col. 0421B] 720, 721.]

C. Sosius.

The same stone, which also lists the substituted consuls.

On the Kalends of January, a dispute between the consuls provided the occasion for civil war between Caesar and Antony. Dio, at the beginning of Book L.

In their consulship, Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in the preface to his history, places the beginning of the 187th Olympiad, as can be inferred from the following two-year period, in which he counts the midpoint during the summer days.

The emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, for the third time.

M. Valerius Messala Corvinus, son of Marcus, grandson of Marcus.

[Note: [Col. 0421C] 721.]

The same stone, and the Acts elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0421C] 722.] The Battle of Actium was fought on the fourth day before the Nones of September. Velleius Paterculus, Book II, chapter 84. See Noris, *Pisan Cenotaph*, p. 159.

After this victory Augustus went to Asia, the province of Asia being immediately assigned to him as proconsul. From the nearest part of Africa to Egypt, Pinarius Scarpus, one of Antony’s prefects, defected to him. Didius, Caesar’s legate, occupied Syria. Hence the **ERA OF AUGUSTUS IN SYRIA**, reckoned from autumn. See Noris, *Syrian Epistle*, p. 251, Leipzig edition.

The emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, for the fourth time.

M. Licinius Crassus, son of Marcus, grandson of Marcus.

[Note: [Col. 0421D] 722.]

## THE ALEXANDRIAN WAR

[Note: [Col. 0421D] 723.]

The same stone, which also names the substituted consuls [Col. 0423A], among them M. Tullius, son of the orator Cicero, who publicly read Augustus’s letter concerning Antony’s defeat. Plutarch, *Cicero*; Appian, *Civil Wars*, Book IV; Dio, Book LI; and others.

Antony, abandoned after Cleopatra’s betrayal, when the fleet and troops defected to Augustus, killed himself in the Alexandrian battle, and Cleopatra did so shortly afterward. After Egypt had been reduced to submission, Augustus appointed C. Cornelius [Col. 0423B] Gallus as its governor.

From this begins the **ALEXANDRIAN ERA OF AUGUSTUS**, from which Censorinus, in the year of Christ 238, reckons 268 years.

The emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, for the fifth time.

Sex. Appuleius.

[Note: [Col. 0432B] 723, 724.]

The same stone, the Ancyran stone, and Gruter.

On the Kalends of January, while Caesar was staying at Samos, an oath was sworn to him at Rome, and his acts were confirmed. Dio, Book LI, p. 456.

Caesar was called “Imperator.” Dio, p. 458. There he also closed the temple of Janus, p. [Col. 0423C] 457, and increased the number of the patricians. The Ancyran Stone, in Gruter, p. CLXXXI, when he was censor with M. Agrippa, ibid.

The emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, for the seventh time.

[Note: [Col. 0423C] 724, 725.]

M. Vipsanius Agrippa, son of Lucius, for the second time.

The Cantabrian War [Ancyran Stone] and the Gallic War, in which Messala subdued the Aquitanians.

Quinquennial games were instituted in honor of the Actian Victory; Dio, Book [Col. 0423D] LIII, asserts that they continued in his own time. See *Pisan Cenotaph*, p. 295.

Augustus, by a law enacted for ten years concerning the retention of the power that he appeared about to relinquish, divided the provinces. He assigned the pacified provinces to the Senate and People, but retained for himself those exposed to war. Dio, Book XIII. On the Ides of January. Ovid, *Fasti*.

The emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, for the seventh time.

[Note: [Col. 0423D] 725, 726.]

M. Vipsanius Agrippa, son of Lucius, for the third time. A stone in the Farnese Palace, in Gruter, CCXXIV, 1.

In their consulship Caesar was called **Augustus**, on the motion of Munatius Plancus. [Col. 0425A] Dio, Book 53.

Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 21. From this Vaillant believes that Augustus alone possessed the authority to strike gold and silver coinage, in Table XX, *Julian Family*.

This year Messala Corvinus celebrated a triumph from Gaul on the seventh day before the Kalends of October, in the 726th year from the foundation of Rome. Triumph Fasti. See Noris, *Pisan Cenotaph*, p. 288.

The emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, Augustus, for the eighth time.

[Note: [Col. 0425A] 726, 727.]

T. Statilius Taurus, son of Titus, for the second time.

The same stone in the Farnese Palace, in Gruter 234, 1.

Augustus, having undertaken an expedition to Britain [Col. 0425B], was appeased by the arrival of envoys from the Britons and remained in Gaul; then he went to Spain and subdued the Cantabrians. There he received envoys sent by King Pandion of India, as well as envoys of the Scythians. Horace, *Carmen Saeculare*, and Book IV, Ode 14.

The emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, Augustus, for the ninth time.

[Note: [Col. 0425B] 727, 728.]

M. Junius Silanus, son and grandson of Decimus. The same stone.

Augustus entered his ninth consulship at Tarragona [Suetonius, *Octavian*, chapter 26], toward the end of the third year of the 188th Olympiad. Eusebius, *Chronicle*. In this year he received the envoys from India; see also Syncellus and Florus, Book IV, final chapter. Suetonius, *Octavian*, chapter 21.

He closed the temple of Janus for the second time. Dio, Book 53.

Augusta Emerita was founded in Lusitania by Augustus. The Pantheon at Rome was built by Agrippa. Dio, Book 53.

[Col. 0425] From this point begins the **COPTIC ERA** in Egypt and the **ERA OF THE SEBASTENI** in Syria.

The emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, Augustus, for the tenth time.

[Note: [Col. 0425C] 728, 729.]

C. Norbanus Flaccus.

[Col. 0425D] The same Farnesian stone.

Aelius Gallus, the third Augustal prefect of Egypt, undertook an expedition against the Arabs, intending also to test the boundaries of the Ethiopians and the Troglodytic region. Strabo, Book II, p. 118, and Book XVII, p. 816.

The Egyptians called Copts reckon their era from this point, accepting the Julian year, with Thoth falling on 29 August. Petavius, Book X, chapter 71.

[Col. 0427A] The emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, Augustus, for the eleventh time.

Cn. Calpurnius Piso, son of Gnaeus, grandson of Gnaeus.

[Note: [Col. 0427A] 729, 730.]

The same Farnesian stone.

Augustus abdicated [the same stone], went to Alba [Dio, Book 53], and substituted L. Sestius in his place around the beginning of April. From the fifth day before the Kalends of July he received tribunician power, although he had previously and consistently refused the dictatorship when it was offered. Patin, on Suetonius, fol. 139.

Phraates III, restored to the kingdom with the aid of the Scythians, sent envoys to Caesar, demanding that his son, held hostage, be returned to him and that Tiridates be handed over. Augustus retained the latter and surrendered the former; but he demanded the standards lost under Crassus and Antony. Justin, Book 42; Dio, Book 53.

[Col. 0427] From this point the periods of the Roman emperors are distinctly numbered by the annual tribunician powers.

The emperor Caesar Augustus, tribunician power I and II.

L. Arruntius.

C. Claudius Marcellus Aeserninus.

Vignoli, from an ancient Puteolan stone, in his book on the Column of Pius, p. 192.

Gold and silver coins struck for Augustus: “Son of the deified one, consul for the eleventh time, tribunician power II, imperator VIII”; on the reverse, three globes, containing Europe, Asia, and Africa, with “S. P. Q. R.” around them, and M. Cocceius Nerva, triumvir.

In their consulship Augustus departed for Sicily in order to organize that province and all the others as far as Syria. Dio, Book 54. See Noris, *Pisan Cenotaph*, p. 292.

[Col. 0427D] The emperor Augustus, tribunician power II and III.

[Note: [Col. 0427D] 731, 732.]

Consuls:

Q. Aemilius Lepidus.

M. Lollius.

The Colotian Stone, in Gruter, fol. CCXCVIII.

Augustus appointed Agrippa prefect of the city.

Dio, Book 54. See *Pisan Cenotaph*, p. 292. He also gave him Julia in marriage. He established a colony at Syracuse and crossed into Greece. Dio, ibid.

[Col. 0429A] The emperor Caesar Augustus, tribunician power III and IV.

[Note: [Col. 0429A] 732, 733.]

Consuls:

M. Apuleius, son of Sextus, Nepos.

P. Silius Nerva.

The same stone.

At Samos Augustus received envoys from Candace, queen. From there he proceeded to Asia. To the people of Greater Armenia, who accused Artabazus and requested Tigranes as a hostage at Rome, he granted a king and ordered Tigranes to be installed in the kingdom through Tiberius [Col. 0429B]. Dio, Book 54; Tacitus, *Annals*, Book II, chapter 3; and coins.

The Tyrians and Sidonians were deprived by Augustus of their freedom because of their factions. Dio, p. 525.

M. Cicero, son of the orator, was legate of Syria. Appian, Book IV.

The emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, Augustus, tribunician power IV and V.

[Note: [Col. 0429B] 733, 734.]

Consuls:

Q. Lucretius [Vipsalius].

In their consulship Agrippa brought the Aqua Virgo into the city. Frontinus. The poet Virgil died in their consulship. Donatus, in his life of Virgil.

Augustus returned to Rome. See Cardinal Noris, *Pisan Cenotaph*, p. 293, concerning M. Cicero, son of the orator, legate of Syria, p. 294.

The emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, Augustus, tribunician power V and VI.

[Note: [Col. 0429C] 734, 735.]

Consuls:

Cn. Cornelius Lentulus Augur.

The same stone, and the Ancyran Stone, in Gruter 231.

Censorial power was conferred upon Augustus.

The emperor Caesar, son of the deified one, Augustus, tribunician power VI and VII.

C. Junius [Silanus].

[Note: [Col. 0433B] 742, 743.]

Consuls:

Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, tribunician power XIV and XV.

Herod, intending to send him to Caesar after convicting him of the impious plot, detained him for a long time; finally, ordering him to be killed five days before his own death, he sent him ahead to the tomb. [Col. 0439] Ancient coins, on the evidence of the Fathers, elucidating the year of Christ’s birth.

Coins 1 and 2 were issued at the colony of Caesaraugusta in Spain by Johann Vaillant; the remainder were issued in Syria:

1. Under Augustus, tribunician power after XIX, consul XI, designated consul XII, in the year of Christ’s birth.

2. In the following year, tribunician power XX.

3. Under Saturninus, governor of Syria, in year EA. 35, under whom Tertullian reports that the census was conducted in Syria. From our museum, together with the following coins.

4. Under Quinctilius Varus, governor of Syria, in the twenty-sixth year of Augustus in Syria.

5. In year XXVII.

6. Of Herod Antipas, under C. Caligula, in year 43 from the death of Herod the Great. From the Rigor Museum.

From this point the **COMMON CHRISTIAN ERA** begins.

Ancient Antiate Calendar in the Museum of Cardinal Albani, at the end of the prolegomena. Claudius extended the pomerium. Ancient inscription at the Cloaca of Saint Lucia, published [Col. 0463A] by Panvinio in the *Fasti*. Tacitus, *Annals* XII, 23. Frontinus, *On Aqueducts*, section 102.

**Emperor Tiberius Claudius, Pontifex Maximus, tribunician power 9 and 10.** [Note: [Col. 0463A] 802, 803]

Consuls: Gaius Antistius Vetus; Marcus Svillius Nervillianus.

Ancient Antiate Calendar in the Museum of Cardinal Albani, at the end of the prolegomena. Tacitus, *Annals* XII, 25. [Col. 0463B] Inscription in the Villa Mattei, in Gruter, p. 113, no. 3, and Fabretti, p. 726: “Tiberius Claudius, etc., tribunician power 10, Imperator 18, consul 4, designated consul 5.”

The colony of Camalodunum was established in Britain. See the notes below, pp. 142 and 146.

**Emperor Caesar Tiberius Claudius Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, tribunician power 10, 11.** [Note: [Col. 0463B] 803, 804]

Consuls: Tiberius Claudius Augustus Germanicus, for the fifth time; Servius Cornelius Orfitus.

[Col. 0463C] Tacitus, *Annals* XII, 41.

Antiate Calendar at the end of the prolegomena, from the Museum of Cardinal Albani; inscription from the same museum in Fabretti, p. 472.

A stone inscription in Gruter, p. 300, under these consuls, counts the year of Rome 804—namely, after the Palilia—as is clear from another inscription below for the year of the Christian Era 92.

On a stone in Panvinio: “Tiberius Claudius, tribunician power 11, Imperator 24, consul 5.”

**Emperor Caesar Tiberius Claudius Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, tribunician power 11, 12.** [Note: [Col. 0463C] 804, 805]

Consuls: Publius Cornelius Sulla Faustus; Lucius Salvius Otho Titianus.

[Col. 0463D] Tacitus, *Annals* XII, 52. Frontinus, *On Aqueducts*, section 13, counts the years from the founding of the City, which are written variously in the manuscripts; the reading 805 is to be retained.

**Emperor Caesar Tiberius Claudius Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, tribunician power 12, 13.** [Note: [Col. 0463D] 805, 806]

Consuls: Decimus Junius Silanus; Quintus Haterius Antoninus.

Tacitus, *Annals* XII, 58.

He writes that, under these consuls, Nero married Octavia at the age of sixteen. [The printed *natum* is uncertain in this construction.] [Col. 0465A] Nero had been born ten months after the death of Tiberius, namely on the eighth day before the Kalends of January in the year 36 of the Christian Era.

The Parthians expelled Rhadamistus from Armenia; then they withdrew.

Tacitus, *Annals* XIII, 6–7.

**Emperor Caesar Tiberius Claudius Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, tribunician power 13, 14.** [Note: [Col. 0465A] 806, 807]

Consuls: Marcus Asinius Marcellus; [Col. 0465B] Marcus Acilius Aviola.

Tacitus, *Annals* XII, 64.

With these consuls Claudius died on the third day before the Ides of October, aged sixty-four, after fourteen years of rule. Suetonius, chapter 45. He had been born on the Kalends of August, when Julius Africanus and Quintus Fabius Maximus were consuls.

**NERO succeeds, Pontifex Maximus, tribunician power 1.**

**Emperor Caesar Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 1, 2.** [Note: [Col. 0465B] 807, 808]

Consuls: Emperor Caesar Nero Claudius Augustus; Lucius Antistius Vetus.

[Col. 0465C] Tacitus, *Annals* XIII, 11.

After the Parthians had been driven from Armenia, Nero entered the City in an ovation. He killed Britannicus. Tacitus, *there*.

**Emperor Caesar Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 2, 3.** [Note: [Col. 0465C] 808, 809]

Consuls: Quintus Volusius Saturninus; Publius Cornelius Scipio.

Tacitus, *Annals* XIII, 25. Peace abroad, disgraceful luxury at home. *There.*

[Col. 0465D] **Emperor Caesar Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 3, 4.** [Note: [Col. 0465D] 809, 810]

Consuls: Nero Claudius Augustus, for the second time; Lucius Calpurnius Piso.

Tacitus, *Annals* XIII, 31.

The colonies of Capua and Nuceria were strengthened by the addition of veterans. *There.*

[Col. 0467A] **Emperor Caesar Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 4, 5.** [Note: [Col. 0467A] 810, 811]

Consuls: Emperor Nero Claudius Augustus, for the third time; Marcus Valerius Messalla.

Tacitus, *Annals* XIII, 34.

The war between the Parthians and Romans over the possession of Armenia, which had been prolonged, was resumed with violence at the beginning of this year. Corbulo’s valor opposed Tiridates’ cunning with arms. Artaxata was devastated by fire.

**Emperor Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 5, 6.** [Note: [Col. 0467B] 811, 812]

Consuls: Lucius Vipsanius Apronianus; Lucius Fonteius Capito.

Tacitus, *Annals* XIV, 1.
