Nero made his way to an adulterous marriage with Poppaea through the murder of his mother. An eclipse of the sun was observed in Campania between the seventh and eighth hours, but in Armenia between the tenth and eleventh. Pliny, book II, chapter 70. At Rome, during this eclipse, stars were seen in the daytime. Tacitus XIV, 12, and Xiphilinus from Dio. It occurred on 30 April according to the astronomical tables.

**Emperor Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 6, 7.** [Note: [Col. 0467C] 812, 813; Quinquennial games were instituted in the City.]

Consuls: Emperor Nero Claudius Augustus, for the fourth time; Cossus Cornelius Lentulus.

Tacitus, *Annals* XIV, 20. Frontinus, *On Aqueducts*, section 102. Gruter, p. 108, from an ancient stone now preserved [Col. 0467D] in the Farnese Palace.

A quinquennial spectacle was established at Rome according to the manner of a Greek contest. Ancient coins and Tacitus, *there*.

**Emperor Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 7, 8.** [Note: [Col. 0467D] 813, 814]

Consuls: Caesonius Paetus; Publius Petronius Turpilianus.

Tacitus, *Annals* XIV, 29.

[Col. 0469A] A great disaster was inflicted upon the Romans in Britain. Camalodunum was made a colony, but 70,000 citizens and allies were killed there. *There*, and Dio, book 92. See the notes below, p. 142.

**Emperor Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 8, 9.** [Note: [Col. 0469A] 814, 815]

Consuls: Publius Marius Celsus; Lucius Asinius Gallus.

Tacitus, *Annals* XIX, 48.

Nero filled the City with accusations and massacres. Corbulo bravely checked Vologaeses, who was invading Armenia. But Caesonius Paetus concluded a shameful treaty with the enemy. Tacitus, *there*.

**Emperor Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 9, 10.** [Note: [Col. 0469B] 815, 816]

Consuls: Lucius Memmius Regulus; Lucius Verginius Rufus.

Tacitus, *Annals* XV, 23, and Frontinus, *On Aqueducts*, section 102.

Corbulo once again checked Vologaeses and compelled Tiridates to lay down [Col. 0469C] the royal insignia before Nero’s image, from whose hand he was to receive it back. The peoples of the Maritime Alps were admitted to Latin rights. Tacitus, *there*.

**Emperor Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 10, 11.** [Note: [Col. 0469C] 876, 877]

Consuls: Lucius Lecanius Bassus; Marcus Licinius Crassus.

Tacitus XV, 43, and Frontinus, *On Aqueducts*, section 102.

Nero engaged in acting. Tacitus, *there*. The fire of the City began on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of Sextilis. *There*, section 42. The Eleans, at Nero’s command, transferred the Olympic games to the following year. Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*, book V. Hence the reckoning of the Olympiads varies from year to year.

**Emperor Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 11, 12.** [Note: [Col. 0469D] 817, 818]

Consuls: Aulus Licinius Nerva Silianus; Marcus Vestinus Atticus.

Tacitus, *Annals* XV, 48. Noris, *Epistola consularis*, p. 43, from Gruter’s inscription 8, no. 3, and from the authorities.

Year 1 of the 211th Olympiad, postponed from the preceding year to this one together with the Elean Games (Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*) [Col. 0471A] at Nero’s command. He perhaps wished the second quinquennial games of his own contest, which fell in this year (Tacitus, *Annals* XVI, 2), to be made equal to the course of the Olympiads.

[Col. 0471B] **Emperor Caesar Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 12, 13.** [Note: [Col. 0471B] 818, 819]

Consuls: Lucius Suetonius Paulinus; Gaius Pontius Telesinus.

Tacitus, *Annals* XVI, 19, and Frontinus, *On Aqueducts*, section 102.

Tiridates, approaching Nero’s knees in a servile manner, received the royal insignia from him in the City. Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 13; Tacitus, *Annals* XVI; Dio, and others.

Nero closed the temple of Janus, only to open it again shortly afterward when the Jewish war arose. Soon afterward he sailed to Greece. Dio, book 63.

[Col. 0471C] **Emperor Caesar Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 13, 14.** [Note: [Col. 0471C] 819, 820]

Consuls: Gaius Fonteius Capito; Gaius Julius Rufus.

Marble Fasti of the colony of Casinum in the Albani Museum. See the notes on the bridge of Saint Clement, p. 47.

Flavius Vespasianus, while staying in Achaea with Nero, was placed in command of the war against the Jews. Josephus, book III of the *Jewish War*, chapter 1; Tacitus, book V of the *Histories*. See Cardinal Noris, *Cenotaphium Pisanum*, p. 335.

**Emperor Caesar Nero Claudius Augustus, tribunician power 14; he took his own life on the fourth day before the Ides of June.** [Note: [Col. 0471C] 820, 821] [Col. 0471D] See Cardinal Noris, *Epistola consularis*.

Consuls: Tiberius Catius Silius Italicus; Valerius Trachalus.

In the year 821 of Rome. Gruter, folio 300, records the same consuls. Frontinus, section 102, *On Aqueducts*, and the Casinati Fasti in the Albani Museum, below in the notes on the bridge of Saint Clement; see the suffect consuls in Gruter, p. 238, no. 12.

Julius Vindex, usurping the imperial power in Gaul, was killed. Galba accepted the empire offered to him in Spain. [Col. 0473A] In Africa Macer, and in Germany Capito, were hailed as emperors, but with unsuccessful results.

**Emperor Sergius Sulpicius Galba** [Note: [Col. 0473A] 821, 822] was killed on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, aged seventy-three. Suetonius, *Galba*, chapter 23.

Consuls: Emperor Servius Sulpicius Galba, for the second time; Titus Vinius.

Casinati stone inscription, below in the notes as above, and Tacitus, *Histories* I, 1. Burning of the Capitol.

[Col. 0473B] **Salvius Otho**, frustrated in his adoption, plotted a rebellion; proclaimed emperor, he was killed on the ninety-fifth day of his reign. Suetonius.

Vitellius, hailed as emperor by the German legions, was killed on 20 December, after completing his fifty-seventh year. Suetonius and Tacitus. See Petavius XI, 16.

**Emperor Caesar Flavius Vespasianus Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, tribunician power 1.** [Note: [Col. 0473B] 822, 823]

Consuls: Emperor Caesar Flavius Vespasianus; Augustus Titus Caesar, son of Vespasian.

Casinati Fasti inscription in the notes on the bridge of Saint Clement.

The new foundations of the Capitol were laid on 21 June. Tacitus. Civilis the Batavian, having joined friendships with the Gauls, besieged the Romans [Col. 0473C] and compelled their legions to swear allegiance to him, as well as the colony of Agrippina. Cerealis, sent against him, strengthened Vespasian’s cause. Tacitus, *Histories* V.

**Emperor Caesar Flavius Vespasianus Augustus, tribunician power 1, 2.** [Note: [Col. 0473C] 823, 824]

Consuls: Emperor Caesar Vespasianus Augustus, for the third time; Marcus Cocceius Nerva.

Marble Casinati Fasti in the Museum of Cardinal Albani, below in the notes on the bridge of Saint Clement. Gruter, folio 300, no. 1, gives these [Col. 0473D] consuls in an ancient inscription with the era of the founding of the City, 824.

The temple of Janus was closed. Orosius, book VII, chapter 9. Vespasian laid the foundations of the Temple of Peace. See the notes on the bridge of Saint Clement. Inscription in Gruter, p. 573. It joins Vespasian’s tribunician power 2 with the titles Imperator 6 and consul 3, designated consul 4.

**Emperor Caesar Flavius Vespasianus Augustus, tribunician power 2, 3.** [Note: [Col. 0473D] 824, 825]

Consuls: Emperor Vespasianus Augustus, for the fourth time; Titus Caesar, son of Augustus Vespasian, for the second time.

[Col. 0475A] Casinati Fasti in the Albani Museum, in the notes on Saint Clement. Pliny records two eclipses within twelve days—more correctly, fourteen—under these consuls, book II, chapter 13.

**Emperor Caesar Vespasianus Augustus, tribunician power 3, 4.** [Note: [Col. 0475A] 825, 826]

[Col. 0475B] Consuls: Domitianus Caesar, son of Vespasian Augustus, for the second time; Valerius Messalinus.

Casinati Fasti as above, and Frontinus, section 102. All philosophers except Musonius were expelled from Rome. Xiphilinus from Dio, book 66. See the notes on the bridge of Saint Cletus.

Petilius Cerealis subdued the Brigantes in Britain. Tacitus, *Life of Agricola*.

**Emperor Caesar Vespasianus Augustus, tribunician power 4, 5.** [Note: [Col. 0475B] 826, 827]

Consuls: Emperor Vespasianus Augustus, for the fifth time; Titus Caesar, son of Augustus, for the third time.

[Col. 0475C] Frontinus, *On Aqueducts*, section 102, and the Casinati marble Fasti as above. The emperor Vespasian and his son Titus were made censors and conducted the seventy-fifth lustrum, the last of all. Pliny, book VII, chapter 49; Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 6.

**Emperor Caesar Vespasianus Augustus, tribunician power 5, 6.** [Note: [Col. 0475C] 827, 828]

Consuls: Emperor Vespasianus Augustus, for the sixth time; Titus Caesar, son of Vespasian, for the fourth time.

The same marble Casinati Fasti in the Albani Museum.

Vespasian dedicated the Temple of Peace at Rome [Col. 0475D] and minted coins commemorating the dedication with the notation “consul for the sixth time.”

From the same Colossus he removed Nero’s head and placed the sun’s head upon it. Xiphilinus from Dio. Saint Jerome also mentions the same Colossus.

**Emperor Caesar Vespasianus Augustus, tribunician power 6, 7.** [Note: [Col. 0475D] 828, 829]

Consuls: Emperor Vespasianus Augustus, for the seventh time; Titus, son of Vespasian Augustus, for the fifth time.

Coins in Occon and Mediobarbus.

Spartianus, in the *Life of Hadrian*, asserts that the same prince was born on the ninth day before the Kalends of [Col. 0477A] February under these consuls.

Julius Frontinus subdued the Silures in Britain. Tacitus, *Life of Agricola*.

**Emperor Caesar Vespasianus Augustus, tribunician power 7, 8.** [Note: [Col. 0477A] 829, 830]

Consuls: Emperor Vespasianus Augustus, for the eighth time; Titus, son of Vespasian Augustus, for the sixth time.

From the Kalends of July, the suffect consuls were Titus Flavius [Col. 0477B] Domitianus, for the sixth time, and Gnaeus Julius Agricola.

Ancient stone inscription in Panvinio and coins in Occon.

After completing his magistracy, Agricola, as suffect consul, was sent to Britain, which soon afterward he subdued almost entirely. Tacitus, in his *Life*.

**Emperor Caesar Vespasianus Augustus, tribunician power 8, 9.** [Note: [Col. 0477B] 830, 831]

Consuls: Lucius Ceionius Commodus; Decimus Novius Priscus.

Inscription in Spon, section 1, article 2, in the vineyard [Col. 0477C] of Montalto, now in the Museum of Cardinal Alessandro Albani.

A great plague at Rome, so that ten thousand people were carried out every day. Suetonius and Eusebius in the *Chronicle*.

**Emperor Caesar Vespasianus Augustus, tribunician power 9, 10.** [Note: [Col. 0477C] 831, 832]

Consuls: Emperor Caesar Vespasianus Augustus, for the ninth time; Titus Caesar, son of Vespasian Augustus, for the seventh time.

Coins in Occon and Mediobarbus, and inscription in Fleetwood, p. 78, where the tribunician power 9 is to be corrected from the coins.

Vespasianus Augustus died on the eighth day before the Kalends of [Col. 0477D] July, in the sixty-ninth year of his life, plus one month and seven days. Suetonius, chapter 24. Titus ruled from the seventh day before the Kalends of July.

The eruption of Vesuvius on the Kalends of November, in which Pliny perished, according to the letter of Pliny the Younger.

**Emperor Titus succeeded his father, tribunician power 9, 10.** [Note: [Col. 0477D] 832, 833]

Consuls: Emperor Titus, son of the deified Vespasian, Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, tribunician power 9, consul 8; Domitian Caesar, consul 7.

Coins in Occon and Mediobarbus, and Gruterian inscriptions [Col. 0479A] 172, no. 10; 316, no. 1; and 943, no. 1. A great fire at Rome, in which the Temple of Capitoline Jupiter, the Temple of Neptune, the temples of Isis and Serapis, the voting enclosures, and the Baths of Agrippa were destroyed. Dio, book 66.

**Emperor Titus Caesar, son of the deified Vespasian Augustus, tribunician power 10, 11; he also died this year on the Ides of September.** [Note: [Col. 0479A] 833, 834] [Col. 0479B] Suetonius, chapter 11 of his *Life*.

Consuls: Lucius Flavius Silva Nonius; Asinius Pollio Verrucosus.

These consuls are recorded in the marble Fasti of the Arval Brothers in the Museum of Cardinal Alessandro Albani, published in *Monumenta veteris Antii*, pp. 99 and 387, by Filippo della Torre, bishop of Adria. They are also recorded on another stone below in the notes on the bridge of Saint Pius I.

Titus was succeeded by **DOMITIAN (another Nero)**, beginning shortly before the 214th Olympiad and in the year 829 of Nabonassar. According to Ptolemy and Lvdiat, in the *Fasti* [Col. 0479C] he has 215, Pontifex Maximus, tribunician power, consul 7, designated consul 8. Coins.

**Emperor Domitianus Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, tribunician power 1, 2.** [Note: [Col. 0479C] 834, 835]

Consuls: Emperor Domitianus Augustus, for the eighth time; Titus Flavius Sabinus.

Gruter, 68, no. 18, and 314, no. 3.

Agricola discovered the Orkney Islands and added them to the empire. Tacitus, in his *Life*, in which he also writes that Agricola penetrated as far as Ireland.

**Emperor Domitianus Augustus, tribunician power 2, 3.** [Note: [Col. 0479C] 835, 836]

Consuls: Emperor Domitianus Augustus, for the eighth time; Quintus Petilius Rufus * II.

[Col. 0479D] From an ancient Smyrnaean stone in Cardinal Noris, *Epistola consularis*, p. 53.

Gaius Valerius Messalinus was suffect in place of Rufus. Gruter, 314, no. 3.

**Emperor Domitianus Augustus, tribunician power 3, 4.** [Note: [Col. 0479D] 836, 837]

Consuls: Emperor Domitianus Augustus, for the tenth time; Titus * Aurelius Sabinus.

From an ancient stone in Almeloveen [Col. 0481A] in the preface to the *Fasti*, no. XIV.

Domitian is shown by coins bearing tribunician power 4 or consulship 10 to have departed for Germany with an army; they bear the inscription “Victory of Augustus,” together with the title Germanicus and Imperator 2, 3, or 4, in Occon and Mediobarbus.

**Emperor Domitianus Augustus Germanicus, tribunician power 4 and 5.** [Note: [Col. 0481A] 837, 838]

[Col. 0481B] Consuls: Domitianus Augustus, for the eleventh time; Titus Aurelius Fulvus.

In the *Life of Antoninus Pius*, Capitolinus records that the victories over the Germans brought back this year by Domitian, either personally or through his generals, are demonstrated by coins bearing tribunician power 4 and Imperator 8 and 9. See Occon and Mediobarbus. Domitian celebrated a triumph over the Quadi, Dacians, Getae, Sarmatians, and Germans. *There.*

**Emperor Domitianus Augustus Germanicus, tribunician power 5, 6.** [Note: [Col. 0481B] 838, 839]

Consuls: Domitianus Augustus, for the twelfth time; Servius Cornelius Dolabella.

[Col. 0481C] Ancient stone in Gruter, p. 8, no. 2, in which Domitian’s name has been erased, now in the Museum of Cardinal Albani. Capitolinus, in the *Life of Antoninus Pius*, records the birthday of this prince in this year on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October.

**Emperor Domitianus Augustus Germanicus, tribunician power 6, 7.** [Note: [Col. 0481C] 839, 840]

Consuls: Emperor Domitianus Augustus, for the thirteenth time; Aulus Volusius Saturninus.

[Col. 0481D] Stone in Cuperus’ letter prefixed to Almeloveen’s *Fasti*, no. XXI. Eusebius reports that, through the emperor’s flattery, the names of the months September and October were changed into “Germanicus” and “Domitianus” in this, the seventh year of Domitian.

[Col. 0483A] **Emperor Domitianus Augustus Germanicus, tribunician power 7.** [Note: [Col. 0483A] 840, 841]

Consuls: Emperor Domitianus Augustus, for the fourteenth time; Lucius Minucius Rufus.

Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 5, places these consuls in the year 841 from the founding of the City.

The Dacian war against Decebalus, in which the Suebi are mentioned. Dio, book 67.

**THE SEVENTH SECULAR GAMES** were celebrated this year, according to Censorinus [Col. 0483B] above, with the coins and Tacitus, *Annals* XI and XII agreeing; Tacitus himself, as one of the fifteen men for sacred rites, took part in them. See Pagius on this year.

**Emperor Domitianus Augustus Germanicus, tribunician power 8, 9.** [Note: [Col. 0483B] 841, 842]

Consuls: Titus Aurelius Fulvus, for the second time; Aulus Sempronius Atratinus.

Capitolinus, in the *Life of Pius*, reports Fulvus’ repeated consulship.

Marcus Cocceius Nerva, driven into exile, was recalled and designated consul. Apollonius of Tyana is said by Philostratus to have foretold the empire to him. From Dio, book 67.

**Emperor Domitianus Augustus Germanicus, tribunician power 9, 10.** [Note: [Col. 0483B] 842, 843] [Col. 0483C]

Consuls: Emperor Domitianus Augustus, for the fifteenth time; Marcus Cocceius Nerva.

Ancient inscription in Fabretti, *Inscriptiones*, p. 274, no. 158, where Domitian’s name has been erased.

The second Capitoline Contest.

**Emperor Domitianus Augustus Germanicus, tribunician power.** [Note: [Col. 0483C] 843, 844]

Consuls: Marcus Ulpius Trajanus; Marcus Acilius Glabrio.

Dio, book 67, Greek edition, pp. 765–766.

Emperor Domitian Augustus Germanicus, tribune [Note: [Col. 0483C] 844–845], pp. 11–12.

Consuls: Emperor Domitian Augustus XVI.

[Col. 0483D] Quintus Volusius Saturninus.

These consuls are associated with the era from the founding of Rome, year 844 (before the Parilia), in an ancient inscription preserved by Gruter, fol. 300. See Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 57, where it is observed that Domitian’s name has been erased. In another inscription likewise, in which Domitian is called tribune with tribunician power XXII, perpetual censor.

Emperor Domitian Augustus Germanicus, tribune [Note: [Col. 0483D] 845–846], pp. 12–13.

Consuls: … Pompeius Collega.

… Cornelius Priscus.

From Tacitus, *Life of Agricola*, chapter 44.

[Col. 0485A] Suffect consuls before the Ides of July: Marcus Lollius Paulinus;

Valerius Asiaticus Saturninus;

Gaius Antistius Julius Quadratus. Gruter, p. 189.

Emperor Domitian Augustus Germanicus, tribune [Note: [Col. 0485A] 846–847], pp. 13–14.

Consuls: Lucius Nonius Torquatus Asprenas;

—Lateranus.

[Col. 0485B] The fourth-century Anonymous Fasti in Bucher and Noris. An ancient inscription formerly in the Villa Bosia, now in the Villa Cesarina, likewise has:

“Consuls Lucius Nonius Torquatus Asprenas [and] Lucius Sergius Paulus.”

Perhaps Sergius Paulus was substituted for Lateranus.

Emperor Domitian Augustus Germanicus, tribune with power [Note: [Col. 0485B] 847–848], pp. 14–15.

Consuls: Emperor Domitian Augustus XVII;

—Flavius Clemens.

The Anonymous Fasti, as above, and Dio, p. 766, Gelenius edition: he adds that in the following year Domitian killed Clemens, his paternal cousin, whom he had taken as his colleague in the consulship in this year.

Domitian’s seventeenth consulship. Coins also associate it with tribunician power XIV and XV.

Emperor Domitian Augustus Germanicus, tribune [Note: [Col. 0485C] 848–849], pp. 15–16.

Consuls: Gaius Antistius Vetus;

Gaius Manlius Valens.

A stone excavated near Saint Paul’s, published by Vignolius in his book on the Column of Pius. It gives the praenomen Gaius. Dio, p. 766.

Domitian was killed on 18 September, at the first hour before noon [Col. 0485D]. Suetonius also reports that the Moon was then situated in Aquarius, which agrees with the astronomical tables.

Marcus Cocceius Nerva is chosen emperor.

Emperor Nerva Caesar Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, tribune [Note: [Col. 0485D] 849–850], 1–2.

Consuls: Marcus Cocceius Nerva Augustus III;

Publius Virginius Rufus III.

An ancient inscription in Cuper’s *Letter to Cardinal Corradini*, and Frontinus, section 102. See also Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 65.

[Col. 0487A] Trajan’s adoption, together with the tribunician power, was conferred upon him around the beginning of November. Noris, in the same place.

Emperor Nerva dies on 28 January. [Note: [Col. 0487A] 850–851] Trajan succeeds, as Pontifex Maximus, tribune 1 and 2.

Consuls: Emperor Nerva Augustus IV;

Marcus Ulpius Trajan Caesar II.

Cuperus, in the letter prefixed to Almeloveen’s Fasti, no. XVII.

[Col. 0487B] An eclipse of the sun is reported by Aurelius Victor for this year. Calvisius assembles his calculations for 21 March at the fifth-and-a-half hour after noon.

Emperor Trajan Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, tribune 2–3 [Note: [Col. 0487B] 851–852].

Consuls: Aulus Cornelius Palma;

Gaius Sosius Senecio.

A stone cited by Panvinius in the *Fasti* of Tacitus, at the beginning of the *Histories*.

Emperor Trajan Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, tribune [Note: [Col. 0487B] 852–853].

Consuls: Trajan Augustus III;

Sextus Julius Frontinus III.

A stone cited by Cardinal Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 61. The suffect consuls may be seen on a stone in the Albani Museum [Col. 0487C], published by Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 203, and *On Trajan’s Column*, chapter 9, p. 273, where Trajan is called, on 29 December, Pontifex Maximus, tribunician power IV, consul III, designated consul IV.

Emperor Caesar Nerva Trajan Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, tribune [Note: [Col. 0487C] 853–854], 4–5.

Consuls: Emperor Trajan Augustus IV;

Sextus Articuleius Paetus.

Gruter 35.2 and 190.2. Spartianus, *Life of Hadrian*, chapter 3. A stone in Gruter, fol. 246, following Manutius, assigns to Trajan tribunician power IV and consulship IV. [Col. 0487D] Coins likewise, in Occon and Mediobarbus, have tribunician power V and consulship IV, as do inscriptions in Gruter 198.3–4.

Hadrian was quaestor in this year. Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 65, citing Spartianus.

Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus, tribune, power 5 [Note: [Col. 0487D] 854–855] and 6.

Consuls: Gaius Sosius Senecio III [perhaps II];

Lucius Licinius Sura II.

Tribunician power 6, Trajan’s consulship IV, in Fabretti, *On Trajan’s Column*, p. 228. The fourth-century Anonymous Fasti have, for this year, Servilius II and Sura.

[Col. 0489A] Trajan’s departure for the first Dacian war against Decebalus. Cardinal Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 65, citing Spartianus.

Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus, tribune [Note: [Col. 0489A] 855–856], 6–7.

Consuls: —Sura III;

Publius Neratius Marcellus.

The fourth-century Anonymous Fasti have Suranus II and Marcellus. Spartianus, in the *Life of Hadrian*, says that this man was appointed praetor by Trajan under the consulship of Sura II and Servianus. Some think that these were suffect consuls. In an ancient inscription of Gruter 190.3, now in the Albani Museum, Trajan is called *Dacicus*: tribunician power VII, imperial acclamation IV, consulship IV, designated consul V. [Col. 0489B] Cardinal Noris adduces supporting coins in his *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 66.

Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus [Note: [Col. 0489B] 856–857], tribune, power 7–8.

Consuls: Trajan Augustus V; coins: … Maximus. Panvinius’s inscription.

On this, see Cardinal Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 67.

[Col. 0489C] Gruter’s inscription 246.8 calls Trajan tribunician power V, imperial acclamation VII, consulship V.

Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, tribune [Note: [Col. 0489C] 857–858], power 8–9, imperial acclamation 4.

Consuls: Tiberius Julius Candidus II;

Gaius Actius Quadratus II.

Pagi, from an inscription cited by Spon. Another inscription in Panvinius’s *Fasti* and Gruter 184.5; Spartianus, *Life of Hadrian*, chapter 3.

Hadrian, having served as tribune of the people in this year, is appointed by Trajan legate of a legion and is taken with him to the second Dacian war, according to Spartianus. See Cardinal Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls* [Col. 0489D], p. 67.

Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0489D] 858–859] 9–10, imperial acclamation 5.

Consuls: Lucius Cejonius Commodus Verus;

Lucius Tutius Cerealis.

For the first, Spartianus and Capitolinus, *Life of Aelius Verus*, section 2; Pliny the Younger, *Letters*, book XI, letter 2; Panvinius in the *Fasti*. Decebalus was defeated and driven to death.

Dacia was made a province. Coins and Dio; and from these, Mediobarbus.

[Col. 0491A] Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, tribune [Note: [Col. 0491A] 859–860] 10–11, imperial acclamation 5.

Consuls: Lucius Licinius Sura III;

Gaius Sosius Senecio III.

An ancient inscription cited by Boldetti, *Observations on the Cemeteries*, p. 79, who correctly remarks that Ignatius suffered martyrdom in this year.

[Col. 0491B] Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0491B] 860–861] 11–12, imperial acclamation 6.

Consuls: Appius Annius Trebonianus Gallus;

Marcus Atilius Metellus Bradua.

Gruter, pp. 23.7–9, 65.7, and 1082.15. In Gruter 190.4 Trajan is called tribunician power XII and imperial acclamation VI, as Fabretti observes in *On Trajan’s Column*, p. 290.

[Col. 0491C] Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, tribunician power 12 [Note: [Col. 0491C] 861–862] and 13, imperial acclamation 6.

Consuls: Aulus Cornelius Palma II;

Gaius Calvisius Tullus II.

Capitolinus in the *Life of Marcus Aurelius*, and the fourth-century Anonymous in the Fasti preserved by Bucher and Noris.

The Trajan Way was constructed from Beneventum to Brundisium [Col. 0491D]. A circus is said to have been built. Mediobarbus, from coins.

Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, tribunician power 13 [Note: [Col. 0491D] 862–863] and 14, imperial acclamation 6.

Consuls: Servius Salvidienus Orfitus;

Marcus Peducaeus Priscinus.

From an ancient stone excavated near the Porta Capena, printed in the *Notae*, p. 122, where *Peducaeus* should be read; and from brick stamps in Fabretti, p. 509, and in our Museum.

[Col. 0493A] Trajan accepted the surname *Optimus*, decreed to him by the Senate, in this year. Mediobarbus, from historical sources. See Pagi, critical notes on Baronius, for this consulship and the following ones.

Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, tribunician power 14 [Note: [Col. 0493A] 863–864], 15, imperial acclamation 6.

Consuls: Gaius Calpurnius Piso;

Marcus Vettius Bolanus.

An inscription in the house of the Marchese de’ Massimi near the Agonal Circus, formerly at Saint Stephen’s on the Caelian Hill, according to Manutius and Gruter 128.5. Fabretti, *Inscriptions* 696.173. Boldetti, *Observations on the Cemeteries*, p. 78; and Cuperus’s letter prefixed to Almeloveen’s Fasti, no. X, incorrectly read: “M. Calpurnius Pisona and L. Junius Rusticus Junianus Bolanus as consuls.”

Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, tribunician power 15 [Note: [Col. 0493B] 864–865], 16, imperial acclamation 6.

Consuls: Emperor Trajan Augustus VI;

Titus Sextius Africanus.

Cardinal Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 71, citing Julius Obsequens, *On Prodigies*, and Gruter’s inscription 1029.6.

[Col. 0493C] Trajan’s departure for the Armenian and Parthian war is recorded on coins bearing his sixth consulship, in Occon and Mediobarbus. On these, see Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 72, and Fabretti, *On Trajan’s Column*.

Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0493C] 865–866] 16–17, imperial acclamation 6.

Consuls: Lucius Publicius Celsus II;

Gaius Clodius Crispinus.

An ancient inscription in the Farnese Palace, published by Gruter, p. 214.

[Col. 0493D] Emperor Trajan Augustus Dacicus, tribunician power 17–18 [Note: [Col. 0493D] 866–867], imperial acclamation 6–7.

Consuls: Quintus Ninnius Hasta;

Publius Manilius Vopiscus.

The inscription mentioned above, in the Farnese Palace, in Gruter, p. 214. The Column in Trajan’s Forum was dedicated; on its pedestal is inscribed that Trajan held tribunician power XVII, was acclaimed emperor VI, and was consul VI. Gruter 247.8 calls him *Dacicus*, but not yet *Parthicus*. The arch at Beneventum [Col. 0495A] was erected for Trajan; on it he is called “Optimus Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, Pontifex Maximus,” with tribunician power XVIII, imperial acclamation VI, consulship VI, and *Pater Patriae*.

Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus, tribunician power 18 [Note: [Col. 0495A] 867–868] and 19, imperial acclamation 7.

Consuls: Lucius Vipstanius Messalla;

Marcus Vergilianus Pedo.

Gruter’s inscription 74.1, today in the Villa Mattei on the Caelian Hill, and inscriptions 1066 and 1070.

[Col. 0495B] Under these consuls, another inscription in Gruter, p. 300, numbers the year from the founding of the City as 867. Baronius discusses it in the appendix to volume X of the *Annals*, as does Noris in his *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 75.

Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus Parthicus, tribunician [Note: [Col. 0495B] 868–869] power 19–20, imperial acclamation 7, 8, and 9.

Consuls: Lucius Aelius Lamia;

… Aelianus Veter.

Phlegon, in Cardinal Noris’s *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 76.

[Col. 0495C] Emperor Trajan Augustus Germanicus Dacicus Parthicus, tribunician power XX, imperial acclamation VIII, died at Selinunte in Cilicia on 10 August, having adopted Hadrian on the preceding day through the influence of his wife Plotina. HADRIAN, who succeeded him, celebrated the anniversary of his accession on 11 August [Col. 0495D]. Dio, Spartianus, and others.

Consuls: … Quintius Niger;

Gaius Vipstanus Apronianus.

Gruter 578.1, 1008.7, and 1009.2. Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 77. Spon, *Miscellanies*, section 1, article 2.

Hadrian’s first year, and from 11 August his second year, as tribune, power 1–2 [Note: [Col. 0495D] 870–871].

[Col. 0497A] Consuls: Emperor Caesar Trajan Hadrian Augustus II;

Tiberius Claudius Fuscus Salinator.

Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 677, no. 33. Panvinius in the *Fasti*, and the letters of Trajan and Pliny, confirm the name Salinator.

Hadrian carried through the City, in a triumphal chariot, an image of Trajan as though he were celebrating a triumph over the Parthians. Spartianus, *Life of Hadrian*.

[Col. 0497B] The Britons cannot be held under Roman rule. Dio and Spartianus, *Life of Hadrian*. Baebius Macer was urban prefect. In the same place.

Hadrian went to Moesia, made peace with the Sarmatians and Roxolani. In the same place. See Petavius, *Chronology*.

Emperor Hadrian Augustus, tribunician power 2 and 3 [Note: [Col. 0497B] 871–872], and from 11 August his third imperial year.

Consuls: Emperor Hadrian Augustus III;

Quintus Junius Rusticus.

Spon, *Miscellanies*, p. 278. Ancient coins.

Spartianus, *Life of Hadrian*, chapter 8.

Emperor Hadrian Augustus, tribunician power 3 and 4 [Note: [Col. 0497B] 872–873], and from 11 August his third imperial year.

Consuls: Lucius Catilius Severus;

[Col. 0497C] Lucius Aurelius Fulvus.

Gruter 499.9; Capitolinus, *Life of Pius*, chapter 1.

Emperor Trajan Hadrian, tribunician power 4 and 5 [Note: [Col. 0497C] 873–874], at the beginning of his fifth imperial year, on 11 August.

Consuls: Lucius Annius Verus II;

Lucius Aurelius Augurinus.

An Arician inscription cited by Cuperus, no. 2, in the letter prefixed to Almeloveen’s Fasti.

Marcus Aurelius the Philosopher was born this year [who later became emperor], at Rome, on the Caelian Hill, on 26 April, under these consuls. Capitolinus in his life [Col. 0497D].

Hadrian returned to Rome and distributed a *congiarium*; he restored the Circus. “In the year 874 from the founding of the City.” Ancient coins.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 5 and 6 [Note: [Col. 0497D] 874–875].

Consuls: Manius Acilius Aviola;

Gaius Cornelius Pansa.

Gruter 337.

Hadrian visited Gaul, Germany, and Britain, from which he crossed back into Gaul. Occon and Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

In Britain he constructed a wall eighty miles long [Col. 0499A]. Spartianus.

In Gaul, at Nemausus, he erected a basilica of Plotina.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 6 and 7 [Note: [Col. 0499A] 875–876].

Consuls: Quintus Arrius Paetinus;

Gaius Ventidius Apronianus.

Gruter 1079.10 and 1082.16. Brick stamps in Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, pp. 503 and 509, and in the Albani Museum.

Hadrian, on his way to Spain, wintered at Tarraco, where he restored the Temple of Augustus. Occon and Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources [Col. 0499B].

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 7 and 8 [Note: [Col. 0499B] 876–877].

Consuls: Manius Acilius Glabrio;

Gaius Bellicius Torquatus.

Gruter, p. 337. Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 505.

Hadrian sailed through Asia and the islands to Achaea, wintered at Athens, bestowed many benefits upon the Athenians, and was initiated into the Eleusinian rites. Occon and Mediobarbus, from coins and historical writers, including Spartianus.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 8 and 9 [Note: [Col. 0499B] 877–878].

[Col. 0499C] Consuls: Cornelius Scipio Asiaticus II;

Quintus Vettius Aquilinus.

Gruter 1082.16; Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 804.

Hadrian crossed from Greece to Sicily and afterward returned to Rome. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 9 and 10 [Note: [Col. 0499C] 878–879].

Consuls: Marcus Annius Verus III;

Lucius Varius Ambibulus.

Noris, from an ancient stone, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 79.

Hadrian crossed into Africa and bestowed many benefits upon the African provinces. Mediobarbus, from coins [Col. 0499D] and historical sources.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 10 and 11 [Note: [Col. 0499D] 879–880].

Consuls: Titianus;

… Gallicanus. Gruter, p. 302.

Ciampinus, *On Sacred Buildings*, from an ancient brick stamp, has “M. Attilius,” etc. From another inscription in my possession, the following seem to be established:

Consuls Titus Attilius Titianus;

Quintus Villius Gallicus. “T. ATIL. TITIAN.”

For thus it is read: “SQUIGA COS. EX PR. Q. SER. PUD. FM. M. V.”

[Col. 0501A] Ptolemy’s observation of Saturn at 13° Libra is recorded in Hadrian’s eleventh year, on 7 Pachon, 874. The Nabonassarian year fell on 26 March, according to Calvisius.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 11 and 12 [Note: [Col. 0501A] 880–881].

Consuls: Lucius Nonius Asprenas Torquatus II;

Marcus Annius Libo.

[Col. 0501B] Gruter, p. 337, and an ancient brick stamp in Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 510, and in our Museum. Capitolinus also, *Marcus Antoninus*, chapter 1.

Hadrian accepted the title *Pater Patriae*. Eusebius; and Sabina is called Augusta. Mediobarbus, for this year.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 12 and 13 [Note: [Col. 0501B] 881–882].

Consuls: Quintus Junius Balbus;

Publius Juventius Celsus Marcellus II.

Under these consuls, on 18 February, Hadrian is called tribunician power XII and consul III on a bronze tablet in Gruter 573 [Col. 0501C].

See Noris, *Syrian Epistle*, p. 498, and Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 506. “Juventius II and Marcellus II.” Another brick stamp in Fabretti, p. 508, and in the Albani Museum has:

“Marcus Pompeius Macrinus, Publius Juventius Celsus, consuls.”

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 13 and 14 [Note: [Col. 0501C] 882–883].

Consuls: Quintus Fabius Catullinus;

Marcus Flavius Aper.

Gruter 108.6; Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, from a brick stamp, p. 503; Panvinius in the *Fasti*.

[Col. 0501D] Calvisius assigns Hadrian’s departure for Egypt through Greece and Asia, and his initiation into the Eleusinian rites [customarily performed at the beginning of the second year of an Olympiad, according to Plutarch], to this year. He also refers to this year the observation of Mars in 21° Gemini, in agreement with the astronomical tables, on 26 Tybi [Ptolemy, book X, chapter 7], corresponding to 15 December.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 14 and 15 [Note: [Col. 0501D] 883–884].

Consuls: Sextus Octavius Laenas Pontianus;

Marcus Antonius Rufinus.

[Col. 0503A] Gruter 179.6 and 337 [“Annius” is an error], and Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 509, from an ancient brick stamp.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 15 and 16 [Note: [Col. 0503A] 884–885].

Consuls: Sentius Augurinus;

Arrius Severianus II [or, according to another reading, Sergius].

For the first consul, Panvinius in the *Fasti*, from Pliny’s *Letters*, book IV.

For the second, the same source, which had earlier shown that he was a suffect consul [Col. 0503B].

Almeloveen lists Arrius Severianus as consul with Titus Aufidius Fronto as suffect consul in the year 129, from the *Digest*, “On the Petition for an Inheritance,” book 20, section 6.

Hadrian wintered at Athens, where he built several temples and a library and held a contest. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 16 and 17 [Note: [Col. 0503B] 885–886].

Consuls: —Antonius Hiberus;

—Nummius Sisenna.

An ancient stone in the Albani Museum: on it, from the day before the Ides of May under these consuls to 26 December under the consulship of Orfitus and Priscus [Col. 0503C], Lucius Balbillus Numitorianus is said to have lived sixteen years, seven months, and twelve days. Another stone in Panvinius’s *Fasti*, now in the Albani Museum, reads “Hibero consul.”

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 17–18 [Note: [Col. 0503C] 886–887].

Consuls: Gaius Julius Servianus III;

Gaius Vibius Varus.

Gruter 108.7, now in the Albani Museum; also 431.9. Ciampinus, *On Sacred Buildings*, chapter 4, p. 30, from a brick stamp now in the Albani Museum, and Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 509; Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, who points out an error [Col. 0503D] introduced in Gruter 115.1, where “Servianus III and Gaius Juventius Verus” are read as consuls.

Hadrian returned to Rome, according to an inscription in Gruter and Mediobarbus.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 18–19 [Note: [Col. 0503D] 887–888].

Consuls: —Pontianus;

—Atilianus.

A brick stamp in Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 509, and *On Trajan’s Column*, p. 197; the brick stamp is now in the Albani Museum. Cardinal Noris also discusses it in his *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 83.

The fourth-century Anonymous, in the Fasti [Col. 0505A], marks this year under Lupercus and Atticus.

Lucius Aelius is adopted by Hadrian. Mediobarbus.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 19 and 20 [Note: [Col. 0505A] 888–889].

Consuls: Lucius Cejonius Commodus Verus;

Sextus Vetulenus Civica Pompeianus.

Panvinius in the *Fasti*, and Gruter 99.5, now in the Capitol, and 874.5.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 20 and 21 [Note: [Col. 0505B] 889–890].

Consuls: Lucius Aelius Verus Caesar II;

Publius Caelius Balbinus Vibullus Pius [Col. 0505C].

Gruter 23.12 and 445.10; Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 513, no. 180, from a brick stamp now in the Albani Museum.

Phlegon, Hadrian’s freedman, brought his work on the Olympiads in book VIII down to this time. Petavius, citing the *Suda*.

Emperor Hadrian, tribunician power 21, dies [Note: [Col. 0505C] 890–891] on 10 July. Antoninus Pius succeeds him, having been adopted on 25 February, after Lucius Aelius Caesar had died on 2 January of this year. See Mediobarbus, fol. 189, and Noris, whom he cites.

Consuls: … Camerinus;

… Niger. Gruter 256.5; Fabretti.

In Fabretti 508, no. 132, from an ancient brick stamp, which is also in the Albani Museum. Hadrian died on 10 July, having ruled twenty years and eleven months, according to Spartianus. Eutropius incorrectly gives twenty-one years. Coins and inscriptions make no reference to a twenty-second year. See C. Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 85.

[Col. 0507A] Emperor Antoninus Pius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0507A] 891–892] 1 and 2, from 25 February.

Consuls: Emperor Antoninus Pius Augustus II;

… Bruttius Praesens II.

Spon, *Miscellanies*, p. 352. Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 21.

In place of Antoninus Pius, who abdicated, Aulus Junius Rufinus was substituted as consul. Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 726.

The autumnal equinox observed by Ptolemy [Col. 0507B] in Nabonassarian year 887, Athyr 9, or 26 September, at the seventh hour after noon, and so forth.

Emperor Antoninus Pius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0507B] 892–893] 2 and 3.

Consuls: Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius III;

Marcus Aelius Aurelius Caesar [who at that time was also called Verus]. Almeloveen in the *Fasti*, Cuperus’s letter no. VIII incorrectly gives Antoninus Pius’s seventh consulship and Marcus Aurelius’s second.

Panvinius, from an inscription in the Farnese Palace, where Antoninus [Col. 0507C] is called tribunician power III and consul III, and also from another Greek inscription published by Gruter 316.1. Likewise Gruter 126, which is in the Capitol, and a brick stamp in the Albani Museum.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribune [Note: [Col. 0507C] 893–894], power 3 and 4.

Consuls: Marcus Peducaeus Syloga Priscinus;

Titus … Hoenius Severus.

Gruter, from an ancient inscription 182.4.

Antoninus Pius assumed tribunician power IV on 19 February; shortly afterward his wife Faustina died. Calvisius, from Capitolinus, who nevertheless writes that Faustina died in the third year of the reign [Col. 0507D].

In Antoninus’s fourth year, Nabonassarian year 888, on 19 Phamenoth before sunrise, Ptolemy observed Mercury at 13° 30′ Capricorn. Calvisius assigns the observation to this year and to 2 February, in the month when Antoninus assumed tribunician power IV, shortly afterward.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribune [Note: [Col. 0507D] 894–895], power 4 and 5.

Consuls: Lucius Cuspius Rufinus;

Lucius Statius Quadratus.

[Col. 0509A] Panvinius, from an inscription, and Gruter 1082.18.

The fifteenth Capitoline contest was celebrated this year, toward the end of Antoninus Pius’s tribunician power V, as Lydiatus observes in Panvinius’s stone. He nevertheless wrongly concludes that Trajan’s reign lasted only eighteen and a half years and that one pair of consuls must be removed from the Fasti around this period. Calvisius refers the sacred Iselastic contest established at Puteoli to this year, from an inscription counting Antoninus’s tribunician power IV [Col. 0509B].

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribune [Note: [Col. 0509B] 895–896], power 5 and 6.

Consuls: Gaius Bellicius Torquatus;

Tiberius Claudius Atticus Herodes.

Panvinius in the *Fasti*, and Gruter 172.10, 316.1, and 943.1; Montfaucon, *Italian Diary*, pp. 389–390, correcting Gruter. Gellius mentions this Herodes Atticus, a consular man, in book I, chapter 2. Capitolinus and an inscription in the Albani Museum also mention him.

[Col. 0509C] Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribune [Note: [Col. 0509C] 896–897], power 6 and 7.

Consuls: Publius Lollianus Avitus;

Gaius Gavius Maximus.

Gruter’s inscription 301, more correctly given by Montfaucon, *Italian Diary*, pp. 389–390, correcting Gruter.

Around this time Antoninus conquered the Britons through his legate Lollius Urbicus and kept the barbarians out by another turf wall [Col. 0509D]. Calvisius, from Capitolinus.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribune [Note: [Col. 0509D] 897–898], power 7 and 8.

Consuls: Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius IV;

Marcus Aelius Aurelius Caesar II.

Brick stamps in Fabretti, p. 513, inscription no. 183, also in the Albani Museum.

Mediobarbus, from coins, assigns to this year the third and fourth largesses of Antoninus Pius and the restoration of the Temple of the Deified Augustus [Col. 0511A]. See also Pagi for this year [Note: [Col. 0511A] 898–899].

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribunician power 8 and 9.

Consuls: Sextus Erucius Clarus II;

Gnaeus Claudius Severus. Gruter 314.2.

Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 614, no. 146, and p. 504, no. 115. Spon, *Miscellanies*, p. 70. Reland, from book I of the *Codex* “On Minors” and book III, section 2, *Digest*, “On the Office of the Prefect of the Night Watch.” Fontanin, *Hortan Antiquities*, book II, chapter 1, p. 202, from an ancient inscription, reads *Eruccio*. Spon had read *Erucio*.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribune [Note: [Col. 0511B] 899–900], power 9 and 10.

Consuls: … Largus;

… Messalinus. Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 401, no. 296.

In this year tribunician power was conferred upon Marcus Aurelius Caesar on 25 February; from that date to 1 April 180, when he died, it counts as tribunician power 33 completed and 34 begun.

[Col. 0511C] In this year Antoninus celebrated the Secular Games, as Cardinal Noris proves in his *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 88, against Pagi, p. 46 of his critical notes on Baronius.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribune [Note: [Col. 0511C] 900–901], power 10 and 11.

Consuls: Lucius … Torquatus III. Almeloveen incorrectly has II.

Gaius … Julianus Vetus.

An inscription of Gudius, reported by Reland in the Fasti for this year. Fabretti, from a brick stamp, p. 510, inscription no. 151. “Torquatus and Julianus as consuls.” Reland, from book V of the *Digest*, “On Manumission by Vindication,” who does not think that Fabretti’s brick stamp belongs to this year [Col. 0511D], since the numeral 3 is omitted in Torquatus’s consulship. But that numeral is sometimes omitted on brick stamps because of lack of space. The vows for Antoninus’s tenth anniversary were undertaken. Mediobarbus, from coins.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribune [Note: [Col. 0511D] 901–902], power 11 and 12.

Consuls: Servius Cornelius Scipio Orfitus, alternatively Orphitus;

Quintus Nonius Priscus, alternatively Quintus Sosius Priscus.

Panvinius, from an ancient inscription also found in Aldus and Gruter 32.9 and 48.1 [Col. 0513A]. Fabretti, p. 473. Gudius, cited by Reland, advises from a stone on the Ardeatine Way that Quintus Sosius should be read; likewise Spon, *Miscellanies*, p. 85, and Fabretti, *On Trajan’s Column*, p. 248, who also correct *Orphitus*. Others say that both Orfitus and Nonius are clearly expressed on stones reviewed by Fabretti, who found both Nonius and Sosius on p. 474. See Reland in the Fasti.

From the consuls of the year 133 to these consuls, an inscription in the Albani Museum counts sixteen years [Col. 0513B].

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribune [Note: [Col. 0513B] 902–903], power 12 and 13.

Consuls: Quintus Romulus Gallicanus;

… Antistius Vetus, or Veter.

From an ancient inscription, Gruter 108.7; Spon, p. 302; Fabretti, pp. 505 and 511. Reland, from several inscriptions, says that the law in book I of the *Codex* “On Procurators,” assigned to the consulship of Gallicanus and Venustus, should be corrected to Gallicanus and Vetus.

[Col. 0513C] Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribune [Note: [Col. 0513C] 903–904], power 13 and 14.

Consuls: … Condianus, alternatively Gordianus;

… Maximus.

The fourth-century Anonymous Fasti and the Alexandrian Chronicle incorrectly have *Cordianus*. Cassiodorus, Idatius, and Prosper have *Gordianus*. [Col. 0513D] See Reland in the Fasti and Pagi for this year. No stones have yet been found that settle the dispute.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0513D] 904–905] 14 and 15.

Consuls: Manius Ancilius Glabrio;

Marcus Valerius Homullus.

Gruter 1077; Spon, *Miscellanies*, p. 278; Fabretti, p. 506; Reines 230; Gruter 344.4, cited by Reland in the Fasti. See also Cardinal Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 91.

At Rome, 340 apartment blocks were destroyed by fire. From Julius Capitolinus, as calculated by Calvisius.

[Col. 0515A] Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribune [Note: [Col. 0515A] 905–906], power 15 and 16.

Consuls: Gaius Bruttius Praesens;

Aulus Junius Rufinus. Gruter, fol. 301, where this consulship is associated with the year 906 from the founding of Rome. Spon, *Miscellanies*, p. 52; appendix to the Oxford Marble, p. 305; Reland; Cardinal Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 93.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0515A] 906–907] [Col. 0515B] 16 and 17.

Consuls: Lucius Aelius Aurelius Commodus;

Titus Sextius Lateranus.

A Roman inscription which Reland cites from Gudius in the Fasti, to be compared with Spon, *Miscellanies*, p. 74; Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, pp. 338 and 510; Gruter 1021; the Oxford Marble, p. 282; and Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 94.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0515B] 907–908] 17 and 18.

Consuls: Gaius Julius Severus;

Marcus Rufinus Sabinianus.

[Col. 0515C] Suffect from 1 November:

Antius Pollio Opimianus. See Reland’s Fasti, and there book I of the *Codex*, “On Publishing,” under the consulship of Sabinus II and Severus; Gruter 607.1; Bernardino Butil, *Lives of the Ancient Jurists*, p. 159; Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 96.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0515C] 908–909] 18–19.

Consuls: Marcus Cejonius Silvanus;

Gaius Sentius Augurinus.

An ancient inscription in the house of the Marchese de’ Massimi near the Agonal Circus, formerly on the Caelian Hill, which Gruter cites from Manutius, 128.5. [Col. 0515D] There *Sentius* is read. Another, Gruter 126, is in the Capitol. Another, also 128.5, requires correction. Cuperus, in the letter prefixed to Almeloveen’s Fasti, no. VII, gives different names for the consuls but does not indicate where in Rome they are found.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0515D] 909–910] 19 and 20.

Consuls: … Barbarus;

… Regulus.

Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 139, no. 138, in the Justinian Gardens. A brick stamp in the same author, p. 504, no. 112 [Col. 0517A], also in our Museum. Spon, *Miscellanies*, p. 20.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0517A] 910–911] 20 and 21.

Consuls: … Tertullus;

… Sacerdos.

Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 359, from an ancient stone in the Alterian house on the Pincian Hill, where it can still be seen.

[Col. 0517B] Reland, together with Hotomanus, and following Cujacius on section 2 of the Institutes, “On the Senatus Consultum Tertullianum,” holds that the *Senatus Consultum Tertullianum* was enacted this year and named after the consul Tertullus.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0517B] 911–912] Pius, tribunician power 21 and 22.

Consuls: … Plautius Quintilius;

… Statius Priscus.

Gruter 68.3; Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 509, no. 143, from a brick stamp. The vows of the second decade were fulfilled and those of the third decade undertaken. The Temple of the Deified Augustus was restored. Mediobarbus, from coins.

[Col. 0517C] Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius [Note: [Col. 0517C] 912–913], tribunician power 22 and 23.

Consuls: Appius Annius Atilius Bradua;

Titus Clodius Vibius Varus.

A stone in the Albani Museum, discussed by Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 128; Spon, p. 120; and the Lyon Inscriptions in the *Acts of Trivolt*, 1705, article 95. Antoninus’s eighth largess. Mediobarbus, from coins.

Emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0517C] 913–914] 23, and from 25 February tribunician power 24, consul VI, in the second year of his reign. He dies on 7 March [Col. 0517D]. Marcus Aurelius succeeds him, with tribunician power 15, begun on 25 February; shortly afterward he assumes his adoptive brother, or son, Lucius Verus as colleague in the empire and soon designates him his son-in-law.

The era of the two Augusti begins from 7 March.

Consuls: Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus III;

Emperor Caesar Lucius Aurelius Verus Augustus II.

An inscription from Puteoli, published by Vignolius, *On the Column of Pius*, p. 323; Fabretti, pp. 513 and 684, no. 179. See also [Col. 0519A] our dissertation on the Caesarian cycle, p. 75.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0519A] 914–915], tribunician power 15 and 16, and Lucius Aurelius Verus Augustus, tribunician power 1 and 2.

Quintus Junius Rusticus.

Consuls: Gaius Vettius Aquilinus. Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 101; suffect from 1 July in place of Aquilinus.

Titus Flavius Tertullus. Gruter, pp. 131.3 and 286.7. Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 101. Reland, from book III of the *Codex*, “On the Support of Children by Their Parents.” See the notes, p. 139, column …

An inundation of the Tiber. War against Vologeses was decreed. Mediobarbus, from coins.

Emperors Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus [Note: [Col. 0519B] 915–916] Augustus, tribunician power 16 and 17, and Lucius Aurelius Verus Augustus, tribunician power 2 and 3.

Consuls: Lucius … Aelianus;

… Pastor.

Gruter, *Inscriptions*, p. 116, now in the Capitol.

[Col. 0519C] Statius Priscus invaded Armenia and captured Artaxata. Mediobarbus, from historical sources.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus Armeniacus [Note: [Col. 0519C] 916–917], tribunician power 17 and 18, and Lucius Aurelius Verus Augustus Armeniacus, tribunician power 3 and 4.

Consuls: Marcus Pompeius Macrinus;

Publius Juventius Celsus.

From an ancient brick stamp in the Albani Museum, discussed by Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 507.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0519C] 917–918] Armeniacus, tribunician power 18 and 19, and Lucius Ceionius Commodus Verus Augustus Armeniacus, tribunician power 4 and 5.

[Col. 0519D] Consuls: Lucius Arrius Pudens;

Marcus Gavius Orfitus.

Gruter 1032.6 and 751.3; Spon, *Miscellanies*, p. 33; Reland.

Emperors Caesar Marcus Antoninus Augustus Armeniacus [Note: [Col. 0519D] 918–919] Parthicus Maximus, tribunician power 19 and 20, imperial acclamation 3, and Lucius Verus Augustus Armeniacus Parthicus Maximus, tribunician power 5 and 6, imperial acclamation 3.

Consuls: Quintus Servilius Pudens;

Lucius Fufidius Pollio.

Gruter 1009.12; Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 106; Spon, *Miscellanies*, pp. 33–34.

Under these consuls Commodus was called Caesar on 12 October. Lampridius, *Life of Commodus*, chapter 12.

[Col. 0521A] Emperors Caesar Marcus Antoninus Augustus Armeniacus [Note: [Col. 0521A] 919–920] Parthicus Maximus, tribunician power 20 and 21, imperial acclamation 4, and Lucius Verus Augustus Armeniacus Parthicus Maximus, tribunician power 6 and 7, imperial acclamation 4.

Consuls: Lucius Verus Augustus III;

—Quadratus.

Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 501, from an ancient brick stamp now in the Albani Museum.

Marcus Aurelius is called *Sarmaticus*. The plague delayed the expedition against the Marcomanni. Mediobarbus, from coins and [Col. 0521B] historical sources.

Emperors Caesar Marcus Antoninus Augustus Armeniacus [Note: [Col. 0521B] 920–921] Parthicus Maximus, tribunician power 21 and 22, imperial acclamation 4 and 5, and Lucius Verus Augustus Armeniacus Parthicus Maximus, tribunician power 7 and 8, imperial acclamation 4 and 5.

Consuls: Titus Junius Montanus;

Lucius Vettius Paullus.

Ferretti, *Lapidary Museum*, p. 27, cited by Reland in the Fasti.

Emperors Caesar Marcus Antoninus Augustus Armeniacus [Note: [Col. 0521B] 921–922] Parthicus Maximus, tribunician power 22 and 23, imperial acclamation 5, and Lucius Verus Augustus Armeniacus Parthicus Maximus, tribunician power 8 and 9, imperial acclamation V, who died during the Marcomannic expedition.

Consuls: Quintus Sosius Priscus;

Publius Caelius Apollinaris.

Under these consuls, the year 922 from the founding of Rome is numbered in an inscription in Gruter, p. 300.1. The same consuls are recorded in another inscription, Gruter 330.2, and in another in the Albani Museum, published by Fabretti, p. 494; the same consuls are there given with the year 922 from the founding of Rome. Reland cites this from the same Fabretti.

The Marcomannic expedition, during which Lucius Verus died in December or in January of the following year, in midwinter.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Antoninus Augustus Armeniacus Parthicus [Note: [Col. 0521B] 922–923] Maximus Sarmaticus, tribunician power 23 and 24, imperial acclamation V and VI.

[Col. 0521D] Consuls: Marcus Cornelius Cethegus;

Gaius Erucius Clarus. Noris.

From an ancient stone, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 108. Gruter, p. 126; it is in the Capitol.

A Germanic victory, from which Marcus Aurelius is called emperor VI.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, etc. [Note: [Col. 0521D] 923–924], tribunician power 24 and 25, imperial acclamation VI.

Consuls: Lucius Septimius Severus;

Lucius Alfidius Herennianus.

Fabretti, p. 510, from a brick stamp, gives “Severus II and Herennianus.” Cardinal Noris thinks, from Gruter’s inscription 6, p. 1045, that this Herennianus belonged to the Alfidian family [Col. 0523A].

The vows of the tenth anniversary were fulfilled and those of the twentieth anniversary proclaimed. Mediobarbus, from coins. See also Fabretti, p. 625.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, etc. [Note: [Col. 0523A] 924–925] [Col. 0523B], tribunician power 25 and 26, imperial acclamation VI.

Consuls: —Orfitus;

—Maximus.

Gruter’s inscription, p. 126, now in the Capitol; also pp. 419.5, 1014.1, and 1072.3. Spon, *Miscellanies*, p. 172. Germany was subdued. Marcus Aurelius destroyed the Marcomanni as they crossed the Danube.

Under these consuls Commodus was called *Germanicus* on 15 October. Lampridius, *Life of Commodus*.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0523B] 925–926] Germanicus, etc., tribunician power 26 and 27, imperial acclamation 6.

[Col. 0523C] Consuls: Marcus Aurelius Severus II;

Tiberius Claudius Pompeianus.

Gruter 1025.6; Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls*, p. 109.

Pertinax, Marcus Aurelius’s legate, recovered Raetia and Noricum from the enemy. The Marcomanni were received into surrender, and many were transferred to Italy. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0523C] 926–927] Germanicus, etc., tribunician power 27 and 28, imperial acclamation 6.

Consuls: —Gallus;

—Flaccus.

Gruter 108.5, an inscription which Reland observes was reported somewhat differently by Gruter and by Castalio in his notes on Rutilius’s *Journey*.

A great victory over the Quadi, from which Marcus Aurelius was called emperor VII.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0523D] 927–928] Germanicus, etc., tribunician power 28 and 29, imperial acclamation 7 and 8.

Consuls: —Calpurnius Piso;

Marcus Salvius Julianus.

The fourth-century Anonymous, Idatius, Prosper, and Cassiodorus in the Fasti.

Commodus, brought into Germany by [lacuna], there put on the *toga virilis* and was granted tribunician power. A *congiarium* was therefore given to the Roman people. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources. See also Pagi for the year 192, note V.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, etc. [Note: [Col. 0525A] 928–929], tribunician power 29 and 30, imperial acclamation 8.

Consuls: Titus Vitrasius Pollio II;

Marcus Flavius Aper II.

Gruter 30.4. Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 213, today in the Institute of Science at Bologna. Noris, *Epistle on the Consuls* [Col. 0525B], p. 142. Marcus Aurelius returned from the East to Rome; after his son Commodus had been named emperor Augustus, on 26 November he triumphed together with him over the Marcomanni, Quadi, Suevi, Sarmatians, and Germans. Lydiatus, from coins and historical sources.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, etc. [Note: [Col. 0525B] 929–930], tribunician power 30 and 31, imperial acclamation 8 and 9, consulship 3.

Consuls: Emperor Caesar Lucius Aurelius Commodus Augustus;

—Quintillus.

Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, p. 213, now in the Institute of Science at Bologna.

[Col. 0525C] Marcus Aurelius gives Crispina to Commodus as wife. Thereafter he sets out for Germany and is called Emperor for the ninth time. From coins and historical sources, according to Mediobarbus.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, etc.; tribunician power 31 and 32, ninth imperial acclamation, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0525C] 930–931]

Consuls: Julianus Rufus; Gavius Orfitus.

Fabrett and Noris, from the same stone mentioned above.

A Germanic victory over the Quadi and Hermunduri. From coins and historical sources, according to Mediobarbus.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, etc.; tribunician power 32 and 33, ninth and tenth imperial acclamations, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0525C] 931–932]

[Col. 0525D] Consuls: Emperor Lucius Aurelius Commodus Augustus, for the second time; Titus Annius Aurelius Verus, for the second time.

From the same stone mentioned above, cited by Noris and Fabrett.

Paternus, Marcus Aurelius’ legate, defeats the barbarians in a battle lasting an entire day. Hence Marcus Aurelius is called Emperor for the tenth time.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, etc.; tribunician power 33 and 34, tenth imperial acclamation, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0525D] 932–933]

Consuls: Lucius Fulvius Bruttius Praesens, for the second time; Sextus Quintilius Condianus.

[Col. 0527A] Noris selected the names of the first consuls from Gruter, p. 1095, no. 1; he thinks this is the same man who is there called consul for the second time.

During the consulship of these men, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, Marcus Aurelius died, having ruled for nineteen years and eleven days, at the age of fifty-nine [Victor, *Epitome*]; he was born in the year 121.

His son Commodus succeeds him, with tribunician power for the fifth year and, from the month of August, for the sixth; he is acclaimed emperor for the fourth time and designated consul for the second time and for the third.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Aurelius Commodus Augustus Germanicus Sarmaticus; tribunician power 6 and 7, fourth imperial acclamation, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0527A] 933–934]

Consuls: Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, for the third time; Lucius Antistius Burrus.

Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, p. 440; another inscription in Reland, *Fasti*, formerly in the vineyard of the Reverend Fathers of the Society of Jesus near the Praetorian Camp; also a Gades inscription cited by the same Reland in the *Fasti*.

Commodus triumphs over the Germans and is called Pius. Mediobarbus.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Antoninus Commodus Augustus, etc.; tribunician power 7 and 8, fourth imperial acclamation, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0527A] 934–935]

[Col. 0527C] Consuls: Gaius Petronius Mamertinus; Cornelius Rufus.

Because affairs had gone well in Sarmatia and Perennis had been killed, Commodus is called Felix. From coins and historical sources, according to Mediobarbus.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Antoninus Commodus Pius Felix Augustus, etc.; tribunician power 8 and 9, third imperial acclamation, fourth consulship. [Note: [Col. 0527C] 935–936]

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus.

Consuls: Augustus, for the fourth time—that is, Commodus; Gaius Aufidius Victorinus, for the second time.

From a stone in the museum of Cardinal Albani, belonging to the Arval Brothers, cited by de la Torre in *Monumenta Veteris Antii*, p. 388; another is cited by Fleetwood, p. 194.

The inscription “Commodus Augustus Pius Felix IV and Victorinus II, consuls” occurs in Gruter 35.1 and in Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, p. 115.

He is said this year to have been acclaimed Emperor for the sixth time, after defeating the Germans and Dacians, who were refusing to recognize his rule. Mediobarbus.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Antoninus Commodus, etc.; tribunician power 9 and 10, sixth and seventh imperial acclamations, fourth consulship. [Note: [Col. 0527D] 936–937]

Consuls: Lucius Eggius Marullus; Annius Papirius Aelianus.

[Col. 0529A] A stone cited by Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, pp. 367–368, and Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, p. 116; also by Gruter from another stone, 35.12, 30.2, and 49.5. Fabrett examined it and published corrections. Reland.

The rebellious Britons are defeated through the legates. Hence Commodus is called Emperor for the seventh time and Britannicus. Grain is distributed at Rome. The vows for ten years are undertaken. From coins and other sources, according to Mediobarbus.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Commodus Antoninus Augustus Pius Felix Britannicus Germanicus Sarmaticus, etc.; tribunician power 10 and 11, seventh imperial acclamation, fourth consulship. [Note: [Col. 0529A–B] 937–938]

Consuls: Marcus Atilius Bradua; Maternus.

A stone in Gruter 192.13, Spon, *Miscellanea*, p. 80, and Almeloveen, from Cuper’s letter prefixed to the *Fasti*, no. 11.

Cleander designates twenty-five consuls for this year. Mediobarbus and Calvisius, from Dio. Pagius, however, argues that so many consuls should be assigned after the year 186; he himself assigns them to 189.

[Col. 0529C] Emperor Caesar Marcus Commodus Antoninus, etc.; tribunician power 11 and 12, seventh and eighth imperial acclamations, fifth consulship. [Note: [Col. 0529C] 938–939]

Consuls: Emperor Commodus Augustus Felix, for the fifth time; Manius Acilius Glabrio, for the second time.

Gruter 94.2 and 364.1, and Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, p. 117.

Commodus’ expedition against the enemy—whether Pannonians or Moors. His address to the army, the army’s victory, his return, and the establishment of an African fleet. From coins and historical sources, according to Mediobarbus.

Commodus is called Emperor for the eighth time.

Emperor Caesar Commodus Antoninus, etc.; tribunician power 12 and 13, eighth imperial acclamation, fifth consulship. [Note: [Col. 0529D] 939–940]

Consuls: Crispinus; Aelianus.

Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, 575.3, and Cuperus in the preface to Almeloveen’s *Fasti*, no. 3.

Commodus worships the rites of Isis, carries Anubis, and commits numerous acts of cruelty under the pretext of restoring religion; hence he is styled “Author of Piety” on the coins cited by Mediobarbus. Perennis, the praetorian prefect, is killed after conspiring.

Thereafter two praetorian prefects are appointed. Petavius, from Herodian.

Emperor Commodus Augustus, etc.; tribunician power 13 and 14, eighth imperial acclamation, fifth consulship. [Note: [Col. 0531A] 940–941]

Consuls: Gaius Allius Fuscianus, for the second time; Duillius Silanus, for the second time.

Gruter 1006.9; Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, p. 117; Gale, *Itinerary of Britain* of Antoninus, p. 38; Lampridius, *Life of Commodus*.

The Capitol is struck by lightning from heaven; the libraries are burned.

Petavius, from Eusebius. Mediobarbus referred it to the preceding two-year period.

Emperor Caesar Commodus Augustus, etc.; tribunician power 14 and 15, eighth imperial acclamation, fifth consulship. [Note: [Col. 0531B] 941–942]

Consuls: Junius Silanus; Sextilius Silanus, or the two Silani as consuls. Reines, p. 551, and Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, p. 77.

Severus is consul suffect for this year; Geta was born during his consulship, as Calvisius infers from Spartianus.

Cleander, once bought from the slave-market, and another minister of Commodus’ tyranny after Perennis, are handed over to the fury of the people and dragged to death by a hook. Lydus. In the following year plague rages in Italy. Mediobarbus.

Emperor Commodus Augustus, etc.; tribunician power 15 and 16, eighth imperial acclamation, sixth consulship. [Note: [Col. 0531C] 942–943]

Consuls: Emperor Commodus Antoninus, for the sixth time; Marcus Petronius Septimianus.

Gruter, folio 300.2, where these consuls are joined on the Kalends of December with the year 943 from the founding of Rome.

[Col. 0531D] The vows for twenty years are undertaken for Commodus’ rule, together with vows for the safety of the Roman people [because of the plague]. Rome is called the Colony of Commodus. From coins and historical sources, according to Mediobarbus.

Emperor Commodus Antoninus Augustus, etc.; tribunician power 16 and 17, eighth imperial acclamation, sixth consulship. [Note: [Col. 0531D] 943–944]

Consuls: Cassius Apronianus; Bradua.

Reines, p. 171, from an ancient stone; Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, p. 118; Spon, *Miscellanea*, p. 114.

A second fire at Rome burns the Temple of Peace near the Forum and the Temple of Vesta, among others. Herodian, Xiphilinus, and Lampridius.

Emperor Commodus Antoninus Augustus, etc.; tribunician power 17 and 18, eighth imperial acclamation, seventh consulship. [Note: [Col. 0533A] 944–945]

Consuls: Emperor Commodus Augustus, for the seventh time; Publius Helvius Pertinax, for the second time.

Gruter 184.1.

At the end of this year, on the day before the Kalends of January, the Emperor Commodus was strangled, having ruled twelve years, nine months, and a half; in the Egyptian calendar it was the year 222, 236 years after the murder of Julius Caesar, and 107 years after Domitian’s first Capitoline contest, according to Clement of Alexandria and Lydus.

Emperor Caesar Publius Helvius Pertinax [Note: [Col. 0533B] 945–946] is created Augustus on the Kalends of January. On the preceding day he had completed the second year of his consulship, while Commodus, his colleague, was killed on the final day of that year and consulship. Pertinax himself, however, is handed over to death in the third month of his reign by soldiers impatient of his discipline, while Didius Julianus buys the empire; after a reign of seven months Julianus is likewise killed, as also happened to Niger.

Consuls: Quintus Socius Falco, for the second time; Eruccius Alarus.

Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, p. 688, now in the museum of Cardinal Albani, and reproduced in the notes, p. 157.

See the suffect consuls in Reland.

The emperor elected is Septimius Severus.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus; tribunician power 1 and 2, second, third, and fourth imperial acclamations, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0533C] 946–947]

Consuls: Emperor Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus, for the second time; Lucius Postumius Albinus, for the second time.

Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, 367; Almeloveen in the *Fasti*, from Cuper’s letter, no. 17. Reland [Col. 0533D] also cites Book 2 of the *Digest*, title “On Publication,” and Book 1 of the *Code*, title “On Sureties,” etc.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus; tribunician power 2 and 3, fourth and fifth imperial acclamations, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0533D] 947–948]

Consuls: Scapula Tertullus; Tineius Clemens.

Gruter 1027 and 4, together with other inscriptions among the Gudian collection, cited by Reland.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus; tribunician power 3 and 4, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth imperial acclamations, consul for the second time. [Note: [Col. 0533D] 948–949]

Consuls: Aulus Domitius Dexter; Lucius Valerius Messalla Thrasea Priscus.

[Col. 0535A] Gruter 444.2. Reland reproduces several laws dated by these consuls in the *Fasti*.

Caracalla is called Caesar when Severus begins the war against Albinus.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus; tribunician power 4 and 5, eighth, ninth, and tenth imperial acclamations, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0535A] 949–950]

Consuls: Lateranus; Rufinus. Gruter 46.9, 51.1, and 300, where these consuls are joined with year 949 of the Roman people.

[Col. 0535B] After Byzantium was captured and Albinus defeated in Gaul on the twelfth day before the Kalends of March, Severus immediately returned to Rome. Mediobarbus, from historical sources and coins.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus; tribunician power 5 and 6, tenth imperial acclamation, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0535B] 950–951]

Consuls: Tiberius—[name missing]—Saturninus; Aulus—[name missing]—Gallus.

Gruter, p. 99.1 and p. 300, where these consuls are joined with year 750 of the Roman people. Also Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, 296; Spon, p. 227. Reland adds four laws and [another beginning with] S, in which causes of infamy are imposed, etc.

[Col. 0535C] On the Nones of March Severus names Geta Caesar, and before the Kalends of April grants tribunician power to Marcus Antoninus Caracalla, his elder son. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus; tribunician power 6 and 7, tenth and eleventh imperial acclamations, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0535C] 951–952]

Consuls: Publius Cornelius Anullinus, for the second time; Marcus Aufidius Fronto.

Gruter 263.1 and 672.12; Panvinius, *Roman History*, Book 1, p. 90, cited by Reland, who also provides several Gudian inscriptions and laws enacted under these consuls, including Book 1, title “On the Management of Affairs,” etc.

[Col. 0535D] Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus; tribunician power 7 and 8, eleventh imperial acclamation, Parthicus Maximus, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0535D] 952–953]

Consuls: Titus Claudius Severus; Gaius Aufidius Victorinus.

Gruter 269.2, where it says: “Dedicated before the Nones of April, under the emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Caracalla, tribunician power 3”; another inscription in Gruter, p. 300, where this consulship is joined with the year 952 from the founding of Rome, on the Ides of April.

Reland indicates laws dated under these consuls, Severus and Victorinus, which are wrongly assigned to Severus Augustus III, consul for the second time, as in Book 1 of the *Code*, title “On Agreements,” etc.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus [Note: [Col. 0537A] 953–954] Augustus; tribunician power 8 and 9, Parthicus Maximus, second consulship, designated for the third time, eleventh imperial acclamation. Emperor Antoninus, son of Severus; tribunician power 3 and 4.

Consuls: Lucius Annius Fabianus; Marcus Nonius Mucianus.

An old inscription in the Roman Museum; Gruter 32.6, 310.6, 313.6, etc. Laws in Reland, Book 4 of the *Code*, title “On the Management of Affairs,” and Book 1, title “On Dowry Rights,” etc.

[Col. 0537B] Caracalla is presented with the *toga virilis* by his father and designated consul. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources. The Septizonium is constructed at Rome, as are the Severan Baths. Lydus.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus, Parthicus Maximus; tribunician power 9 and 10, third consulship, eleventh imperial acclamation. Emperor Antoninus, son of Severus; tribunician power 4 and 5, consul.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus, for the third time; Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus.

A lead pipe in our museum. [Col. 0537C] Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, p. 230.

Gruter 300.1, where this consulship is associated with the year 954 from the founding of Rome.

Severus and Antoninus return to Rome, celebrate Severus’ decennalia, and restore the Pantheon.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus, Parthicus Maximus; tribunician power 10 and 11, third consulship, eleventh imperial acclamation. Emperor Antoninus, son of Severus; tribunician power 5 and 6, consul.

Consuls: Publius Septimius Geta; Lucius Fulvius Plautianus, for the second time.

Pagius, from Cardinal Noris. Reland cites Book 2, §47 of the *Digest*, title “On the Senatus Consultum Tertullianum,” and other laws, as well as Fontanini, *Antiquities of the Garden*, Book 1, chapter 3.

An arch is erected in the Roman Forum for Severus and Antoninus. The vows for twenty years are undertaken. Mediobarbus, from inscriptions, coins, and historical sources.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus, Parthicus Maximus; tribunician power 11 and 12, third consulship, imperial acclamation; Emperor Antoninus, son of Severus; tribunician power 6 and 7, consul. [Note: [Col. 0537D] 956–957]

Consuls: Lucius Fabius Septimius Cilo, for the second time; Marcus Flavius Libo.

A stone formerly in the Vatican, now in the museum of Cardinal Albani, published by Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, 494; this consulship is joined with [Col. 0539A] year 956 from the Roman foundation. Also Gruter 406.9; Boldetti, p. 83; Reland, from Book 3 of the *Code*, title “On Procurators,” etc.; and Gruter 386.1, 397.13, and the Gudian inscriptions.

The eighth Secular Games are held by decree of the Senate, and the sixth *Liberalitas* is celebrated. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources. Plautianus, the praetorian prefect, is killed as though he had conspired against the emperor. Petavius, from Herodian, Spartianus, and Xiphilinus.

[Col. 0539B] Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus, Parthicus Maximus; tribunician power 12 and 13, third consulship, eleventh imperial acclamation. Emperor Caesar Antoninus, son of Severus Augustus; tribunician power 7 and 8, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0539B] 957–958]

Consuls: Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, for the second time; Publius Septimius Geta Caesar.

A stone in the Villa Carpinea, published by Boldetti, *Observations on Cemeteries*, p. 442. Reland cites Book 1 of the *Code*, title “On the Limitation of Fines.”

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus, Parthicus Maximus; tribunician power 13 and 14, third consulship, eleventh imperial acclamation. Emperor Caesar Antoninus, son of Severus Augustus; tribunician power 8 and 9, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0539B] 958–959]

Consuls: Nummius Albinus; Fulvius Aemilianus.

[Col. 0539C] Panvinius in the *Fasti*, from a stone now in the Villa Medici outside the Porta Flaminia; Gruter 115.9 and 175.8; Reland cites Book 4 of the *Code*, title “On Agreements,” etc.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus Augustus, Parthicus Maximus; tribunician power 14 and 15, third consulship, twelfth imperial acclamation. Emperor Caesar Antoninus, son of Severus Augustus; tribunician power 9 and 10. Imperial acclamation 2, consulship 2, designated for the third time. Panvinius in the *Fasti*. [Note: [Col. 0539C] 959–960]

Consuls: Aper; Maximus.

Gruter 103.6; Reland, Book 1 of the *Code*, title “On Litigious Matters,” etc.

A British victory is won through Severus’ commanders. Hence the twelfth imperial acclamation and Caracalla’s second. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

The vows for Antoninus’ tenth year are undertaken. Mediobarbus, from coins.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus, Parthicus Maximus; tribunician power 15 and 16, third consulship, twelfth imperial acclamation. Emperor Caesar Antoninus, son of Severus Augustus; tribunician power 10 and 11, third consulship, second imperial acclamation. [Note: [Col. 0539D] 960–961]

Consuls: Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, for the third time; Publius Septimius Geta Caesar, for the second time.

Panvinius in the *Fasti*; Gruter 45.13 and 1017.3; Reland, Book 2 of the *Code*, title “On the Release of Pledges,” etc.

The vows for Antoninus’ tenth year are paid. He sets out with his father for Britain. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

Geta is advanced by his father through tribunician power and the title of Augustus. In the same source.

Emperor Caesar Lucius Septimius Severus, Parthicus Maximus; tribunician power 16 and 17, third consulship, twelfth imperial acclamation. The two Caesars, Antoninus and Geta, sons of Severus: Antoninus, tribunician power 11 and 12, third consulship, second imperial acclamation; Geta, tribunician power 1 and 2, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0541A–B] 961–962]

Consuls: Claudius Civica Pompeianus; Lollianus Avitus.

A stone in the house of Prince Altieri on the Pincian Hill. Vignoli, *Selected Inscriptions*, p. 310; Spon, *Miscellanea*, p. 40; Reland from another stone of Gudius; and Book 1 of the *Code*, title “On Private Dowries.”

The Caledonians and other barbarians are defeated in Britain. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

Severus, tribunician power 17 and 18, third consulship, twelfth imperial acclamation, divides Britain by a wall 130 miles long and defeats several other barbarians; he is called Britannicus, together with his sons, and Emperor for the thirteenth time. The two Caesars, sons of Severus Augustus: Antoninus, tribunician power 12 and 13, and Geta, tribunician power 2 and 3, etc. Mediobarbus, from coins and other sources.

[Col. 0541C] Consuls: Manius Acilius Faustinus; Gaius Caesonius Macer Rufinianus [or Rufinus].

Gruter 300.1 and 344.4, from Panvinius. Reland also cites Book 1 of the *Code*, title “On the Property of Freedmen,” etc.
