Emperor Severus Augustus, tribunician power 18, dies at York on the day before the Nones of February, in his third consulship and thirteenth imperial acclamation. [Note: [Col. 0541C–D] 963–964] His ashes are brought to Rome by his sons, his successors in the empire, who call him divine.

The emperors Antoninus Augustus, Parthicus Maximus, Britannicus: tribunician power 13 and 14, third consulship, second imperial acclamation; and Geta Augustus Britannicus: tribunician power 3 and 4, second consulship.

Consuls: Quintus Elpid Rufus Lollianus Gentianus; Pomponius Bassus.

After peace is made with the barbarians in Britain, the Augustan brothers Antoninus and Geta return to Rome.

[Col. 0543A] The emperors Caesar Antoninus Pius Augustus, Parthicus, Britannicus, Pontifex Maximus: tribunician power 14 and 15, third consulship, *pater patriae*; and Publius Septimius Geta Pius Augustus Britannicus: tribunician power 4 and 5, second imperial consulship. [Note: [Col. 0543A] 964–965]

Consuls: Gaius Julius Asper; Gaius Julius Asper, or the two Aspri as consuls.

Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, 51 and 494, from a Vatican stone now in the museum of Cardinal Albani, where these consuls are joined with year 964 or, after the Parilia, 965 from the founding of the city. Panvinius, *Fasti*, and Gruter 132.1. Reines, p. 476, in his letter to Rupert, p. 337. Spon, *Miscellanea*, p. 84, assigns this to the consuls of the preceding year. Reland cites Book 4 of the *Code*, title “On Publication,” etc.

Antoninus kills his brother Geta in their mother’s lap on the fifth day before the Kalends of March. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

Emperor Caesar Antoninus Pius Augustus, Parthicus, Britannicus, Pontifex Maximus; tribunician power 15 and 16, fourth consulship, second imperial acclamation. [Note: [Col. 0543B–C] 965–966]

Consuls: Emperor Antoninus Augustus, for the fourth time; Decimus Caelius Balbinus, for the second time.

Suffect from the Kalends of March: Marcus Antonius Gordianus; and from—[lacuna]—May, Helvius Pertinax. Gruter 49.2, 208.1, 1117.8, and 1075.10.

Reland establishes the suffect consuls from Capitolinus and Spartianus. He likewise lists the ordinary consuls from several laws, including Book 2 of the *Code*, title “On the Right of Dowry,” etc.

Caracalla’s departure for the Germanic war, where, because he has won a victory, he is called Germanicus. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

[Col. 0543D] Emperor Caesar Antoninus Germanicus, etc.; tribunician power 16 and 17, fourth consulship, second and third imperial acclamations. [Note: [Col. 0543D] 966–967]

Consuls: Silius Messalla; Sabinus.

Gruter 4.6, 122.1, and 1108.6; Reland cites Book 2 of the *Code*, title “If a Definite Sum Is Claimed,” etc.

The eighth and ninth *Liberalitas* of Caracalla, who makes a circuit of Macedonia and Asia. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

Emperor Caesar Antoninus, etc.; tribunician power 17 and 18, fourth consulship, third imperial acclamation. [Note: [Col. 0543D] 967–968]

Consuls: Laetus, for the second time; Cerealis.

[Col. 0545A] Gruter 312.2; Reland cites Book 3 of the *Code*, title “On the Arbitration of Guardianship,” etc.

Antoninus sets out from Antioch and reaches Alexandria. There, after being received with honor, he sends in his troops and kills the crowd indiscriminately because they had once hurled insults at him.

He returns to Antioch. Petavius, from Spartianus and Herodian.

[Col. 0545B] Emperor Antoninus, etc.; tribunician power 18 and 19, fourth consulship, third imperial acclamation. [Note: [Col. 0545B] 968–969]

Consuls: Gaius Atius Sabinus or Catius Sabinus; Sextus Cornelius Anullinus.

Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, and Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, p. 681, correct Gruter 183.4 and Panvinius, who read Aurelius in the second consul’s name instead of Cornelius and Gaius Atius in the first. But the inscription reported by Spon, no. 271, has “Catius Sabinus II and Anullinus.”

Reland cites Book 1 of the *Code*, title “On Petitioning,” etc.

A Parthian war is waged by stratagem against Artabanus. Many barbarians are killed. Antoninus returns to Mesopotamia.

Emperor Antoninus, etc.; tribunician power 19 and 20, fourth consulship, third imperial acclamation; on the sixth day before the Ides of April he is killed at Edessa by a plot of his own men. Marcus Opellius Severus Macrinus is chosen as his successor. Macrinus makes his son, Diadumenianus—or Diadumenian—Caesar and Augustus, as shown by coins and historical sources. [Note: [Col. 0545C] 969–970]

Consuls: Gaius Bruttius Praesens; Titus Messius Extricatus.

Gruter 300.1, where these consuls are joined with year 770 of the Roman people; Reland cites Book 9 of the *Code*, title “On Unlawful Transactions,” etc. Coins of the Aegian towns in Cilicia were struck for Diadumenian, according to Vaillant. Era 264, which began in the year 706 from the founding of the city, indicates that this is the year beginning in autumn.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Opellius Severus Macrinus Augustus; tribunician power 1 and 2; he calls his son Diadumenian Caesar Augustus. [Note: [Col. 0545D] 970–971]

Consuls: Emperor Caesar Marcus Opellius Severus Macrinus Augustus; Marcus Coclatinus Adventus.

Elagabalus erased the former name from the *Fasti* [Col. 0547A] but retained Coclatinus Adventus as consul, after Macrinus had been defeated and killed by him on the seventh day before the Ides of June, together with his son. Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, p. 131.

On a stone in the Villa Fonseca on the Caelian Hill the consuls are read as—[lacuna]—Augustus, evidently. Macrinus has been erased and Oclatinius Adventus remains.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus [Elagabalus] [Note: [Col. 0547A] 971–972] Augustus, Pontifex Maximus; tribunician power 1 and 2, second consulship, designated for the third. [Col. 0547B]

Consuls: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus, for the second time;—[lacuna]—Tineius Sacerdos.

An inscription on an old lead pipe in our museum. Another in Gruter, p. 300.1, joins this consulship with year 972 from the founding of Rome. Another, Gruter 87.4, adds the mark “II” of the consulship also to Sacerdos. Reland produces a third from Reines and others, which does not repeat the second consulship. Heliogabalus enters Rome after an image of himself has been carried before him and serves as priest of the Sun; he also strikes coins bearing the inscription: “PRIEST OF THE GOD ELAGABAL, THE SUN.” [Col. 0547C]

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, etc.; tribunician power 2 and 3, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0547C] 972–973]

Consuls: Emperor Antoninus, for the third time; Eutychianus Comazon.

A stone formerly in the Vatican, now in the museum of Cardinal Alexander Albani, joins these consuls with year 973 from the founding of Rome.

Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Pius Augustus, son; tribunician power 3 and 4, third consulship, designated for the fourth. [Note: [Col. 0547C–D] 973–974]

Consuls:—[lacuna]—Grafus;—[lacuna]—Claudius Seleucus.

Antoninus adopts Alexander, the son of Mamaea and his paternal cousin, and names him Caesar. Petavius, from Herodian, Book 5, Xiphilinus, and Lampridius.

Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus; tribunician power 4 and 5, fourth consulship, designated for the fifth. He is killed on the sixth day before the Ides of March, in the eighteenth year of his age. Valesius, *On Elagabalus*, tribunician power. [Note: [Col. 0547D] 974–975]

Consuls: Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, for the fourth time; Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander Caesar, who succeeds the emperor.

Gruter 75.2, 1082.9, and 508.1; Reland, Books 2 and 3 of the *Code*, title “On Actions Concerning Pledges,” etc.

In the first year of Severus Alexander the fourteenth Paschal [cycle] occurred on the Ides of April, a Saturday. The marble of Saint Hippolytus, transferred from the cemetery of Saint Lawrence in the Veran field to the Vatican Library, was published in the notes, p. 160. In the same year the jurists begin a persecution against the Christians; they are discussed in the following year.

Emperor Caesar Aurelius Severus Alexander [Note: [Col. 0549B] 975–976] Pontifex Maximus; tribunician power 1 and 2, consul.

Consuls: Gaius Marius Maximus, for the second time; Lucius Roscius Aelianus.

Gruter 1005.2.

Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, from a bronze tablet; Spon 261; Fabrett 599. Alexander employs Papinian, Paulus, Pomponius, Celsus, Modestinus, and Venuleius, highly expert jurists, as advisers. But these men are hostile to the Christian name and begin a persecution against the Christians. Petavius, on the preceding year, from Lampridius.

[Col. 0549C] Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander, etc.; tribunician power 2 and 3, consul. [Note: [Col. 0549C] 976–977]

Consuls: Julianus, for the second time; Crispinus.

Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, p. 695, no. 260, from which Cardinal Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, p. 137. Reland cites Book 11 of the *Code*, title “On Undutiful Wills,” etc.

Ulpian, the distinguished jurist and praetorian prefect, is killed by the praetorian soldiers.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander, etc.; tribunician power 3 and 4, consul. [Note: [Col. 0549C] 977–978]

Consuls:—[lacuna]—Fuscus, for the second time;—[lacuna]—Dexter.

[Col. 0549D] Gruter 9.2 and 21. This inscription is now in the Farnese Palace at Rome. Another stone of Gruter, no. 493, was kept in the house of the Caesarian family; I myself inspected it, and read: “Dedicated on the Kalends of December, under the consulship of Lucius Turpilius De—[lacuna]—rus and Marcus Mecius Rufus.” These consuls, however, are thought to have been suffect. See Reland, and in him Book 2 of the *Code*, title “On Wills,” etc. Alexander constructs baths at Rome, enacts laws, and institutes instruction in mathematics, according to Lampridius.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander, etc.; tribunician power 4 and 5, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0549D] 978–979]

[Col. 0551A] Consuls: Emperor Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander Augustus, for the second time; Gaius Marcellus Quintilianus, for the second time.

Gruter 84.5; Fabrett 279, now in the third museum of Cardinal Albani. Reland, from the Gudian inscriptions and from Books 8 and 9 of the *Code*, title “On Agreements,” etc.

Alexander is called Pius. The Alexandrian Baths are dedicated. The third *Liberalitas*. Eusebius. Mediobarbus, from coins.

[Col. 0551B] Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander, etc.; tribunician power 5 and 6, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0551B] 979–980]

Consuls: Marcus Nummius Albinus;—[lacuna]—Maximus.

Gruter 7.3; Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, p. 139; Reines 524. Reland cites Book 5 of the *Code*, title “On Transactions,” etc.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander, etc.; tribunician power 6 and 7, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0551B] 980–981]

Consuls: Tiberius Manilius Modestus; Sergius Calpurnius Probus.

Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, p. 141, from Gruter 300; Reland cites Book 2 of the *Code*, title “On Moderating Fines,” etc.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander, etc.; tribunician power 6 and 8, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0551B] 981–982]

[Col. 0551C] Consuls: Emperor Severus Alexander Augustus, for the third time;—[lacuna]—Cassius Dio, for the second time.

The beginning and end of Dio’s history. Gruter 1079, where it should be corrected to “Dio Cassius,” which is presented as “Dionysius.” See Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, p. 146; Reland cites Book 11 of the *Code*, title “On Procurators,” etc.

Mediobarbus thought the coins struck this year, bearing tribunician power 8 and third consulship, should be referred to an expedition against the Germans undertaken by Alexander’s commanders: “On the Germans” and “Germany Conquered.”

Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander, etc.; tribunician power 8 and 9, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0551C] 982–983]

[Col. 0551D] Consuls: Lucius Virius Agricola; Sextus Catius Clementinus.

Noris, *Epistola Consularis*, p. 146, and Gruter 300.1; Reland cites Book 12 of the *Code*, title “On Transactions,” etc. Alexander Augustus’ departure for the Persian war. Mediobarbus, from coins.

[Col. 0553A] Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Severus Alexander, etc.; tribunician power 9 and 10, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0553A] 983–984]

Consuls:—[lacuna]—Civica Pompeianus;—[lacuna]—Pelignanus.

A Gudian inscription cited by Reland in the *Fasti* and Book 3 of the *Code*, title “On Proofs,” etc.

The vows for ten years are paid and those for twenty years are proclaimed. A Persian victory. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

[Col. 0553B] Emperor Caesar Severus Alexander, etc.; tribunician power 10 and 11, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0553B] 984–985]

Consuls:—[lacuna]—Lupus;—[lacuna]—Maximus.

Fabrett, *Inscriptions*, p. 676; Cuperus, *Ancient Monuments*, p. 230; and the laws listed by Reland, such as Book 3 of the *Code*, title “On Wills,” etc.

Alexander returns to Rome from his Persian triumph, where he is called Felix. [Col. 0553C] The fifth *Congiarium*. Mediobarbus, from coins.

Successful actions are carried out in Mauretania Tingitana by Furius Celsus, in Illyricum by Varius Macrinus, and in Armenia by Junius Palmat(t)us. Lydus, from historical sources.

Emperor Caesar Severus Alexander, etc.; tribunician power 11 and 12, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0553C] 985–986]

Consuls:—[lacuna]—Maximus;—[lacuna]—Paternus.

Reland, from the Gudian inscriptions and from Book 4 and the senatus consultum on suspected guardians; several of these attach the second or third consulship to Maximus, contrary to the evidence of the inscriptions.

[Col. 0553D] Emperor Caesar Severus Alexander, etc.; tribunician power 12 and 13, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0553D] 986–987]

Consuls:—[lacuna]—Maximus, for the second time; Gaius Caelius Urbanus.

Fabrett, p. 565, and Aringhi, Book 3, *Subterranean Rome*, chapter 37, p. 327, have Maximus and Urbanus, as does Reines, p. 658; but on p. 407 he observes that Gaius Caelius Urbanus, a former consul, is thought by Pagius to be the consul of this year. Reland adds the laws in which Maximus II and Urbanus are consuls, namely Book 14 of the *Code*, title “On Transactions,” etc.

Emperor Caesar Severus Alexander, etc.; tribunician power 13 and 14, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0555A] 987–988]

Consuls:—[lacuna]—Severus; Lucius Rangonius Urinatius; Lartius Quinctianus.

Gruter 45.9, 463.1, and 1029.1; Boldetti, p. 79. Reland adds Book 2 of the *Code*, title “On the Office of the Prefect of the East”; on this see also Pagius in the *Critical Commentary on the Baronius*.

During the consulship of these men, Emperor Severus Alexander and his mother Mamaea are killed in a military disturbance at Mainz on 18 March, after he had ruled thirteen years and nine days, according to Lampridius, following Elagabalus’ death on 6 March. MAXIMINUS is chosen as successor.

Emperor Caesar Gaius Julius Maximinus [Note: [Col. 0555B] 988–989] Augustus; tribunician power 1 and 2.

Consuls: Emperor Maximinus Augustus;—[lacuna]—Julius Africanus.

Reland cites Book 13 of the *Code*, title “On Agreements,” and Book 6, title “On the Right of Dowry.” Sponius, *Antiquities*, p. 283, thinks that Maximinus’ sixth consulship, attested in a Ravenna charter of a Christian woman, should be assigned to this year; but it may perhaps belong to Maximianus’ sixth consulship.

Maximinus lays waste Germany for 400 miles and is called Germanicus. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

Emperor Caesar Maximinus Augustus Germanicus; tribunician power 2 and 3, consulship of the two Gordians, father and son. [Note: [Col. 0555C] 989–990]

Consuls:—[lacuna]—Perpetuus;—[lacuna]—Cornelianus.

The old *Fasti*, Cassiodorus, Idatius, Prosper, and Bucherius correct Gruter 23.10, which incorrectly reads “Coriolanus.”

Around 12 April in Africa, the two Gordians, father and son, assume imperial power after being acclaimed by the Senate on the sixth day before the Kalends of June. Valesius, *On the Tribunician Power of Elagabalus*, p. 34. The Senate elects twenty men to preserve the republic [Petavius, from Lampridius and Herodian], after hearing of the Gordians’ death; shortly thereafter it elects Pupienus and Balbinus as Augusti.

Emperor Caesar Maximinus Augustus, etc.; tribunician power 3 and 4. [Note: [Col. 0555D] 990–991]

He is killed while unsuccessfully besieging Aquileia in March. Meanwhile the aged Augusti Pupienus and Balbinus are murdered by a military uprising at the Capitoline Games before the end of May. After them Gordian alone rules, surnamed Pius. From Herodian. See Pagius on the year 238.

[Col. 0557A] Consuls: Marcus Ulpius Crinitus;—[lacuna]—Proculus Pontianus.

This consulship is made famous by Censorinus in many chronological eras and by historians through the solar eclipse that occurred at Gordian’s election.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Antonius Gordianus Pius [Note: [Col. 0557B] 991–992] Felix; tribunician power 1 and 2, consulship.

Consuls: Emperor Gordianus Augustus; Manius Acilius Aviola.

Gruter 8.7 and 30.4; other inscriptions of Cuperus and Gudius cited by Reland; and many laws, namely Book 3 of the *Code*, title “On the Moderation of Fines,” etc.

Emperor Caesar Gordianus Pius, etc.; tribunician power 2 and 3, consulship. [Note: [Col. 0557B] 992–993]

Consuls: Sabinus, for the second time; Venustus.

[Col. 0557C] Gruter 309.6; Capitolinus, *Life of Gordian*, chapter 23. Reland adds laws, namely Book 12 of the *Code*, title “On Legacies,” etc.

Sabinianus, rebelling against Gordian in Africa, is suppressed by the governor of Mauretania. Petavius, from Capitolinus. The second *Liberalitas*. Mediobarbus, from coins.

Emperor Caesar Gordianus Pius, etc.; tribunician power 3 and 4, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0557C] 993–994]

Consuls: Emperor Caesar Gordianus Augustus, for the second time; Civica Pompeianus.

Gruter 29.13–14 and 30.1, 3, 5; a stone cited by Fabrett, p. 682, no. 65, now in the Albani Museum; Reines 663. Reland cites Book 14 of the *Code*, title “On Agreements,” etc., and the Gudian collection; Cuper, in the letter prefixed to Almeloveen’s *Fasti*, no. 19.

Gordian marries the daughter of Misitheus, whom he makes praetorian prefect. Hence the third *Liberalitas*. Coins.

Emperor Caesar Gordianus, etc.; tribunician power 4 and 5, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0557D] 994–995]

Consuls: Gaius Vettius Atticus; Gaius Asinius Praetextatus.

Capitolinus, *Life of the Gordians*, chapter 26; Gruter 443.6 and 1006.8; several Gudian inscriptions cited by Reland; and Book 1 of the *Code*, title “On Property Taken by Force,” etc.

[Col. 0559A] After the Twin Janus is opened, Gordian sets out for the Persian war through Moesia and there defeats whatever enemies were in Thrace. Capitolinus.

Emperor Caesar Gordianus, etc.; tribunician power 5 and 6, second consulship, second imperial acclamation. [Note: [Col. 0559A] 995–996]

Consuls: Arrianus; Papus.

Gruter 168.7; Fabrett 699, no. 210. Reland cites Book 15 of the *Code*, title “On Excusing Guardians,” and Capitolinus in Gordian’s biography. Misitheus, Gordian’s father-in-law, dies through Philip the Arab’s treachery. Philip, appointed in his place, makes Gordian unpopular with the soldiers by causing a shortage of provisions there.

Emperor Caesar Gordianus, etc.; tribunician power 6 and 7, second consulship, second imperial acclamation. [Note: [Col. 0559B] 996–997]

Consuls: Peregrinus; Aemilianus.

Fabrett 279, no. 171, and another inscription in the Museum of Ciampino, now in the Museum of Cardinal Albani; another in the Barberini Gardens, which appears in 279. Fabrett’s correction of Aurelianus to Aemilianus is supported. Reland adds Book 6 of the *Code*, title “On Contributions,” etc.

Gordian is killed through Philip’s treachery around May or June, after Philip had been made his colleague in the empire and, as it were, tutor by the army. See Pagius.

Emperor Caesar Julius Philippus Augustus; tribunician power 1 and 2, consulship. [Note: [Col. 0559C] 997–998]

Consuls: Emperor Marcus Julius Philippus Augustus;—[lacuna]—Junius Titianus.

Fabrett gives Junius as consul in no. 119, whereas the inscription calls him Gaius Maesius Aquilius Fabius Titianus, *vir clarissimus*, consul; another inscription is in Fabrett, p. 610. Spon, *Miscellanea*, p. 98. Laws in Reland under “Philippus Augustus and Titianus as consuls,” such as Book 7 of the *Code*, title “On Vindication of Property,” etc.; and the Gudian collection, also in Reines 425.1, where Junius Didianus is incorrectly given instead of Junius Titianus. Philippus returns to Rome and brings the philosopher Plotinus there. Calvisius.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Julius Philippus Augustus; tribunician power 2 and 3, consulship. [Note: [Col. 0559D] 998–999]

Consuls:—[lacuna]—Praesens;—[lacuna]—Albinus.

[Col. 0561A] The *Fasti* and the laws cited by Reland, such as Book 8 of the *Code*, title “On Vindication of Property,” etc.

Philippus the father makes Philippus his son Caesar. Calvisius, from coins.

The emperors Caesar Marcus Julius Philippus Augustus: tribunician power 3 and 4, second consulship; and Marcus Julius Philippus [son] Augustus: tribunician power and consulship. [Note: [Col. 0561A] 999–1000]

Consuls: Emperor Marcus Julius Philippus Augustus, for the second time; Marcus Julius Philippus Caesar, or the two Philippi as Augusti.

[Col. 0561B] Reland, citing Book 2 of the Gregorian *Code*, title “On Vindication of Property,” the *Fasti*, and supporting coins. Add Gruter 273, as Pagius observes.

The millennium of the city’s foundation is celebrated with Games; at them Philippus Caesar is called Augustus, since tribunician power has been conferred on him. Mediobarbus, from coins.

Emperor Caesar Marcus Julius Philippus Augustus; tribunician power 4 and 5, third consulship; and Emperor Caesar Marcus Julius Philippus [son] Augustus; tribunician power 1 and 2, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0561B] 1000–1001]

Consuls: Emperor Marcus Julius Philippus Augustus, for the third time; Marcus Julius Philippus Augustus, for the second time.

[Col. 0561C] Coins and an inscription, such as the bronze one in the Picchiati Museum at Naples, discussed by Bellori in *Vestiges of Ancient Rome*, plate 3; Fabrett, p. 687; and Reland.

The Secular Games are celebrated this year, according to the same coins and the historians. Pompey’s Theater is burned, as is the Hecatostylon. Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*.

Emperor Caesar Philippus Augustus, etc.; tribunician power 5 and 6, third consulship; and Emperor Caesar Philippus Augustus [son]; tribunician power 2 and 3, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0561C–D] 1001–1002]

Both are killed this year: the father at Verona, the son at Rome. Decius succeeds, a native of Lower Pannonia.

Consuls: Marcus—[lacuna]—Aemilianus, for the second time;—[lacuna]—Junius Aquilinus.

Gruter 74.6 and 103.2; Fabrett 434, now in the museum of Cardinal Albani, and 6.35. Reland cites Book 1 of the *Code*, title “On Revoking Gifts,” etc.

In Pannonia, around February, the army demands Decius for the imperial power. Philippus, already in mature age, marches against him. He dies in battle at Verona in June. Decius becomes emperor. See the notes, p. 199.

Emperor Caesar A[nnius] Messius Quintus Trajanus Decius Augustus; tribunician power 1 and 2, second consulship. [Note: [Col. 0563A] 1002–1003]

Consuls: Emperor Decius Augustus, for the second time;—[lacuna]—Maximus Gratus.

Gruter 273.6 and a coin on which Trajanus Decius has tribunician power 3 and consulship 2. See Cardinal Noris, *Syro-Macedonian Eras*, p. 350. Reland cites Book 9 of the *Code*, title “On Dowry Rights,” etc.

Julius Valens attempts to seize the empire in Italy while Decius is occupied with the Scythian war. See the notes, p. 201. Valerian, sent against him, destroys him; Valerian is soon afterward chosen censor by the Senate, with Decius’ approval. The Senate’s acts are signed by the two Decii as consuls, after he had made his son Quintus Herennius consul suffect. See the notes.

[Col. 0563C] Emperor Caesar Trajan Decius Augustus; tribunician power 2 and 3, third consulship. [Note: [Col. 0563C] 1003–1004]

Consuls: Emperor Trajan Decius Augustus, for the third time; Quintus Herennius Etruscus Messius Decius Caesar, for the second time—or the two Decii as ordinary consuls, as Trebellius Pollio says in the *Life of Valerian*.

After Decius and his son are killed around June, Trebonianus Gallus and Hostilianus, the other son of Decius, are proclaimed Augusti; and Volusianus, Gallus’ son, is called Caesar. Victor, *On the Caesars*, and the coins. See the notes, pp. 200 and 205.

Lucius Priscus usurps the empire in Macedonia but soon falls. Mediobarbus, from coins.

Caesar Gaius Vibius Trebonianus Gallus Augustus, in the first and second years of tribunician power; consul for the second time; and Valens Hostilianus Messius Quintus Augustus, in the first and second years of tribunician power; and the emperor Vibius Volusianus Augustus, proclaimed from the rank of Caesar, in the first and second years of tribunician power.

[Note: Col. 0563D; 1004–1005.]

Consuls: the emperor Trebonianus Gallus Augustus, for the second time.

Volusianus, first Caesar and soon Augustus.

Gruter 995.9 and 1981.1; and—

Reland, Book XVI of the *Code*, “On the Conduct of Business,” etc.

[Col. 0565A]

Gallus returned to Rome after purchasing peace from the barbarians by an annual payment; he adopted Hostilianus and soon killed him. Zosimus, Book I, chapter 25. Others think that he died of plague.

The emperor Caesar Gaius Vibius Trebonianus Gallus Augustus, in the second and third years of tribunician power; consul for the second time; and the emperor Caesar Gaius Vibius Volusianus Augustus, in the first and second years of tribunician power; consul for the second time.

[Note: Col. 0565A; 1005–1006.]

Consuls: the emperor Caesar Gaius Vibius Volusianus Augustus, for the second time.

[Col. 0565B]

Marcus Valerius Maximus.

The Anonymous Fasti of the fourth century, etc.

AEMILIANUS, a consular, is proclaimed Augustus by the Moesian army against Gallus and Volusianus because of the vigorous service he had rendered against the Scythians. Gallus dispatches VALERIANUS to bring up the Gallic and German legions. In a battle near Interamna, Gallus and Volusianus fall. Aemilianus rules from June until September, when he is butchered by his own men at Spoletium, who defect to Valerianus. Histories and coins. See the notes.

[Col. 0565C]

The emperor Caesar Publius Licinius Valerianus Augustus, in the first and second years of tribunician power; consul for the second time; and the emperor Caesar Publius Licinius Gallienus, son of Valerianus, Augustus, in the first and second years of tribunician power; consul for the first and second times.

[Note: Col. 0565C; 1006–1007.]

Consuls: the emperor Publius Licinius Valerianus Augustus.

The emperor Publius Licinius Gallienus Augustus.

Reland, from ancient inscriptions in the Gudian collection and Gruter 275.1.

[Col. 0565D]

The urban prefects are counted annually from these consuls for nearly the following hundred years in fourth-century manuscripts, together with the consuls, published by Bucherius and others down to the year 352. In that year Lollianus was urban prefect.

The emperor Caesar Publius Licinius Valerianus Augustus, in the second and third years of tribunician power, consul for the third time; and the emperor Caesar Publius Licinius Gallienus Augustus, in the second and third years of tribunician power, consul for the second time.

[Note: Col. 0565D; 1007–1008.]

Consuls: the emperor Valerianus, for the third time.

The emperor Gallienus, for the second time.

Reland, from Book III of the *Code*, “On Witnesses,” etc. Aurelianus defeats the Goths in Illyricum. Mediobarbus, from coins and history. Valerius Maximus, urban prefect.

[Col. 0567A]

The emperors Caesars Publius Licinius Valerianus and Gallienus Augusti, in the third and fourth tribunician powers; consuls for the third and second times.

[Note: Col. 0567A; 1008–1009.]

Consuls: Valerius Maximus, for the second time.

[lacuna] Glabrio.

An old inscription in the house of Count Carandini. Published by Bolognetti at Saint Mark’s through Fabretti, p. 723, *Inscriptions*.

Nummius Albinus, urban prefect, from Bucherius’s *Opuscula*.

[Col. 0567B]

Gallienus is sent to Postumus in Gaul with an army, to be guarded and trained. The Goths are defeated by Aurelianus. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

The emperors Caesars Publius Licinius Valerianus and Gallienus Augusti, in the fourth and fifth tribunician powers; consuls for the fourth and third times.

[Note: Col. 0567B; 1009–1010.]

Consuls: the emperor Valerianus Augustus, for the fourth time.

The emperor Gallienus Augustus, for the third time, according to coins.

Reland, from Book III of the *Code*, “On Inofficious Gifts,” etc.

Junius Donatus, urban prefect. Anonymous Fasti of the fourth century.

Valerianus, advancing against the Persians and leaving Gallienus in the City, remains with the army at Byzantium. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

[Col. 0567C]

The emperors Caesars Valerianus Augustus, in the fifth and sixth years of tribunician power, consul for the fourth time; and Gallienus Augustus, in the fifth and sixth years of tribunician power, consul for the third time.

[Note: Col. 0567C; 1010–1011.]

Consuls:

[lacuna] Memmius Tuscus.

[lacuna] Bassus.

Reland, from Book XV of the *Code*, “On Inofficious Wills,” etc. Cornelius Saecularis, urban prefect. After Valerianus entered Persian territory, Ingenuus is proclaimed emperor by the Moesian legions; but he is defeated and killed by Gallienus. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

[Col. 0567D]

The emperors Caesars Valerianus Augustus, in the sixth and seventh tribunician powers, consul for the fourth time; and Gallienus Augustus, in the sixth and seventh tribunician powers, consul for the third time.

[Note: Col. 0567D; 1011–1012.]

Consuls:

[lacuna] Aemilianus.

[lacuna] Bassus, for the second time.

Reland, from Book I of the *Gregorian Code*, “If Gifts Are Made Contrary to Law,” etc. Cornelius Saecularis, urban prefect.

[Col. 0569A]

Valerianus is captured by the Persians, among whom he grows old in miserable servitude.

Regilianus is proclaimed Augustus in place of Ingenuus; Gallienus returns to Rome. Postumus rebels in Gaul. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

The emperor Caesar Gallienus Augustus [while his father was being held captive among the Persians], in the seventh and eighth years of tribunician power; consul for the third time.

[Note: Col. 0569A; 1012–1013.]

Consuls:

[lacuna] Cornelius Saecularis, for the second time.

[lacuna] Junius Donatus.

Book II of the *Code*, “On Fires,” etc. Reland: Saecularis for the second time and Donatus as consuls. Cornelius Saecularis, urban prefect. Bucherius’s *Opuscula*.

[Col. 0569B]

The chronologists prove that these and the preceding consuls, removed from the annals, should be restored. See Pagius, year 280. Macrianus is proclaimed Augustus with his sons by the armies of the East; he is defeated by Aureolus and killed together with his children and Quietus. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

The emperor Caesar Gallienus Augustus, etc., in the eighth and ninth years of tribunician power; consul for the fourth time.

[Note: Col. 0569B; 1013–1014.]

[Col. 0569C]

Consuls: the emperor Caesar Gallienus Augustus, for the fourth time.

Lucius Petronius Taurus Volusianus.

Gruter 1028.2; Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 356.

Under the fourth consulship of Gallienus and Volusianus, Nummius Albinus was urban prefect. Cassius Postumus, formerly prefect of the Rhine frontier, after Valerianus, Gallienus’s third son—whose guardian he had been—was killed, assumes imperial power in Gaul with his own son Postumus and holds it for seven years. Calvisius, from Aurelius Victor, Pollio, etc.

[Col. 0569D]

The emperor Caesar Gallienus Augustus, etc., in the ninth and tenth years of tribunician power; consul for the fifth time.

[Note: Col. 0569C–D; 1014–1015.]

Consuls: the emperor Caesar Publius Licinius Gallienus Augustus, for the fifth time.

[lacuna] Faustinus.

Book II of the *Code*, “On the Ordering of Proceedings.” Reland.

Under the fifth consulship of Gallienus and Faustinus, Nummius Albinus was urban prefect.

A great earthquake occurred at Rome, in Libya, and in Asia. Plague occurred at Rome and in Achaea. Peace with the gods was sought from the Sibylline Books, etc. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

Gallienus celebrated his decennalia. Ancient coins.

[Col. 0571A]

The emperor Gallienus Augustus, in the tenth and eleventh years of tribunician power; consul for the fifth time.

[Note: Col. 0571A; 1015–1016.]

Consuls:

[lacuna] Albinus, for the second time.

[lacuna] Maximus Dexter.

An inscription in the Barberini gardens, published by Valesius in his notes on Eusebius, Book IV of *The Life of Constantine*, p. 240, and by Reland, who observes, following Cardinal Noris, that the stone belongs to the consuls of the year 227. Pagius considers the same consuls to have been ordinary in both years. Nummius Albinus, urban prefect.

[Col. 0571B]

Trebellianus in Isauria and Celsus in Africa seize the imperial power for themselves, but are killed shortly afterward. Calvisius, from Pollio.

The emperor Caesar Gallienus Augustus, in the eleventh and twelfth years of tribunician power; consul for the sixth time.

[Note: Col. 0571B; 1016–1017.]

Consuls: the emperor Gallienus Augustus, for the sixth time.

[lacuna] Saturnius.

Pollio, *On Gallienus*, chapter 10. Vaillant, *On the Silver Coins of Gallienus*, tribunician power XII, consulship VI.

Gallienus’s Persian triumph. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

[Col. 0571C]

The emperor Gallienus Augustus, etc., in the twelfth and thirteenth years of tribunician power; consul for the sixth time.

[Note: Col. 0571C; 1017–1018.]

Consuls: Publius Licinius Valerianus, for the second time.

Lucius Caesonius Macer Lucillus Rufinianus.

Under these consuls, the dedication of the walls of Verona is recorded on the gate called Bursarea. Gruter 166.2 and Panvinius, *Antiquities of Verona*. Reland, from Book VII of the *Code*, “On the Excuses of Guardians.” Paternus, urban prefect.

Gallienus wages war against Postumus in Gaul and defeats him several times. The Scythians are defeated and return to their own territory. Mediobarbus.

[Col. 0571D]

The emperor Gallienus Augustus, in the thirteenth and fourteenth years of tribunician power; consul for the seventh time.

[Note: Col. 0571D; 1017–1018.]

Consuls: the emperor Gallienus Augustus, for the seventh time.

[lacuna] Sabinillus.

Gruter 274.6. Reland, from Book VII of the *Code*, “On Proofs.” Paternus, urban prefect.

Under these consuls, Servilius Lollianus is proclaimed emperor in Gaul against Postumus. Moeonius, however, is killed as a tyrant. Lydiatus, for this year.

The emperor Caesar Gallienus Augustus, in the thirteenth and fourteenth years of tribunician power; consul for the seventh time.

[Note: Col. 0571D; 1018–1019.]

[Col. 0573A]

Consuls:

[lacuna] Paternus.

[lacuna] Arcesilaus.

Reland, from Book IV of the *Code*, “On the Giving of Suits to Guardians and Curators.” Petronius Volusianus, urban prefect.

After the tyrants Postumus had been killed, Marcus Aurelius Victorinus is proclaimed emperor, and Pomponius Aelianus in Germany. Lydiatus.

[Col. 0573B]

The emperor Caesar Gallienus Augustus, in the fifteenth year of tribunician power; consul for the seventh time.

[Note: Col. 0573A; 1019–1020.]

Consuls:

[lacuna] Paternus, for the second time.

[lacuna] Marinianus.

Boldetti, from an ancient stone, *On Sacred Cemeteries*, p. 80. Petronius Volusianus, urban prefect.

Gallienus is killed near Milan by the plots of the generals Martianus and Cecropius after slaughtering the Goths in Illyricum and routing the Scythians. Petavius and Mediobarbus, from history and coins.

CLAUDIUS succeeded him around the ninth day before the Kalends of April [Petavius, from Trebellius], defeated and killed Aureolus, according to Zosimus. Tetricus, father and son, seize the imperial power.

The emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Claudius Gothicus Augustus, in the first and second tribunician powers; consul for the second time.

[Note: Col. 0573B–C; 1020–1021.]

Consuls: the emperor Marcus Aurelius Claudius Augustus, for the second time.

[lacuna] Nonius Paternus.

An old stone in the Alban Museum. Reland, from Book VI of the *Code*, “On Servitudes and Water.”

Under the consulship of Claudius for the second time and Paternus, Flavius Antiochianus was urban prefect.

The emperor Caesar Flavius Claudius Pius Felix Invictus Augustus, Pontifex Maximus, in his second tribunician power and second consulship, proconsul, etc. Rupert, *Universal History*, from Salmasius. Claudius routs the Goths in various battles and wins several victories over them. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

[Col. 0573C]

The emperor Caesar Claudius Gothicus Augustus, in the second and third years of tribunician power; consul for the second time.

[Note: Col. 0573C–D; 1021–1022.]

Consuls:

[lacuna] Antiochianus.

[lacuna] Furius Orfitus.

Reines, p. 443.

Under the consulship of Antiochianus and Orfitus, Antiochianus was urban prefect.

Reland, from Book II of the *Code*, “On Various Rescripts,” previously cited by Cardinal Noris in *On the Decennial Vows*, who observes that it can be inferred from this that Claudius lived at least until 25 October of this year.

At the end of October Claudius dies of plague. His brother QUINTILLUS, who had previously also been Augustus, succeeds him; and he dies on the twentieth day. AURELIANUS becomes emperor. Mediobarbus, etc.

[Col. 0575A]

The emperor Caesar Domitius Aurelianus Augustus, in the first and second years of tribunician power; consul.

[Note: Col. 0575A; 1023–1024.]

Consuls:

* the emperor Caesar Valerius Aurelianus Augustus, for the second time;
* Lucius Cejonius Virius Bassus, for the second time.

Postumius Varus, urban prefect.

Reines, p. 384, to be corrected from the Gudian manuscripts apud Reland. The Alamanni and Marcomanni harass the Roman Empire. A great defeat was also inflicted by them at Placentia. For this reason there was alarm at Rome, and, at Aurelianus’s command, the Sibylline Books were consulted. Petavius, from Vopiscus, who adds that the Goths were later defeated and that Aurelianus returned to the City and enlarged the *pomerium*.

[Col. 0575B]

The emperor Caesar Aurelianus Augustus, in the second and third years of tribunician power; consul for the second time.

[Note: Col. 0575B; 1024–1025.]

Consuls:

[lacuna] Quietus.

[lacuna] Voldumianus.

Metius Falconius and Nicomachus, suffect consuls, from Vopiscus. Reland.

Flavius Antiochianus, urban prefect.

Aurelianus advances against Zenobia and the Palmyrenes; in Thrace, Illyricum, and beyond the Danube he defeats the barbarians.

From this he is called Gothicus and Sarmaticus.

[Col. 0575C]

The emperor Caesar Aurelianus Augustus Gothicus Sarmaticus, in the third and fourth years of tribunician power; consul for the second time.

[Note: Col. 0575C; 1025–1026.]

Consuls:

* Marcus Claudius Tacitus;
* [lacuna] Placidianus.

From an old inscription at Firmum, in Rupert’s *Universal History*. Reland.

Under the consulship of Tacitus and Placidianus, Virius Orfitus was urban prefect.

[Col. 0575D]

The emperor Caesar Aurelianus Augustus Gothicus, Sarmaticus, Carpicus, Armeniacus, Parthicus, Adiabenicus, and so forth, in the fourth and fifth years of tribunician power; consul for the second time.

[Note: Col. 0575D; 1026–1027.]

Consuls:

* the emperor Aurelianus Augustus, for the third time;
* Gaius Julius Capitolinus.

Gruter 1082.12, where Reland notes that “III” should be read. Gruter 276.5 likewise gives the fifth tribunician power of Aurelianus with his third consulship and represents the same consulship with the numeral 3.

Virius Orfitus, urban prefect.

Tetricus the Tyrant of Gaul surrendered himself to Aurelianus, who celebrates a magnificent triumph from East and West. Having proceeded to Gaul, he frees the Vindelicians from the siege of the barbarians. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

[Col. 0577A]

The emperor Caesar Aurelianus Augustus, etc., in the fifth tribunician power; consul for the fourth time.

[Note: Col. 0577A; 1027–1028.]

Consuls: the emperor Aurelianus Augustus, for the fourth time. (Postumus; Syagrius.)

Titus Nonius [otherwise Avonius]. Marcellinus, urban prefect.

Under these consuls, Aurelius Gordianus and Vettius Cornificius were suffect consuls, according to Vopiscus, in *Aurelianus and Tacitus*. Gruter 276.4 and 338.3.

Fabretti, p. 747. The Felsinean Marble, p. 534. Contelorius, *On the Urban Prefect*, 39, where Reland notes that Aurelianus’s first suffect consul was neglected.

[Col. 0577B]

Aurelianus, having returned to Illyricum in order to advance against the Persians, is killed between Heraclea and Byzantium in January of this year. Marcus Claudius TACITUS is chosen by the Senate after an interregnum of six months. Mediobarbus, from Vopiscus and coins.

The emperor Caesar Tacitus Augustus, in the tribunician power; consul for the second time.

[Note: Col. 0577B; 1028–1029.]

Consuls: the emperor Tacitus Augustus, for the second time.

[lacuna] Aemilianus.

Under the consulship of Tacitus Augustus for the second time and Aemilianus, Ovinius Paternus was urban prefect.

The Anonymous Fasti of the fourth century, Severus, and others who edited the Fasti.

Tacitus drives the barbarians from the Roman borders. Hence the Gothic Victory. But on the tenth day before the Kalends of May he gives up his life. Mediobarbus, from coins and history. FLORIANUS holds his brother’s empire and kills himself on the sixth day before the Ides of July. PROBUS is proclaimed Augustus and peacefully obtains the empire on the fifth day before the Nones of July. The same is reported by Mediobarbus and Petavius from Vopiscus.

[Col. 0577D]

The emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Probus Augustus, in the first and second tribunician powers; consul.

[Note: Col. 0577D; 1029–1030.]

Consuls: the emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Probus Augustus.

Marcus Aurelius Paulinus.

An old inscription seen by Sponius at Rome and published by Cardinal Noris in *Cenotaphs of Pisa*, p. 325, and in *On the Decennial Vows*, from Book II of the *Code*, “On the Revocation of Gifts.”

Ovinius Paternus, urban prefect.

Probus goes to Gaul, recovers one hundred and ten cities from the barbarians, and kills nearly seven hundred thousand of them. From Vopiscus, through Petavius.

[Col. 0579A]

The emperor Caesar Probus Augustus, in the second and third tribunician powers; consul for the second time.

[Note: Col. 0579A; 1030–1031.]

Consuls: the emperor Probus Augustus, for the second time.

[lacuna] Lupus.

Under these consuls, Virius Lupus was urban prefect.

Reland, from the *Code*, “That No One May Be Summoned without Judicial Authority,” etc.

In Thrace Probus receives the Getic peoples into friendship. Petavius and Mediobarbus, from Vopiscus.

[Col. 0579B]

The emperor Caesar Probus Augustus, in the third and fourth tribunician powers; consul for the third time.

[Note: Col. 0579B; 1031–1032.]

Consuls: the emperor Probus Augustus, for the third time.

[lacuna] Nonius Paternus, for the second time.

An ancient stone in the Museum of Cardinal Albani.

Under these consuls, Virius Lupus was urban prefect.

The emperor Caesar Probus Augustus, in the fourth and fifth tribunician powers; consul for the third time.

[Note: Col. 0579B; 1032–1033.]

Consuls:

[lacuna] Messala.

[lacuna] Gratus.

The Felsinean Marble, p. 353, and Reland, from Book IV of the *Code*, “On Gifts.”

Under these consuls, Virius Lupus was urban prefect.

[Col. 0579C]

The emperor Caesar Probus Augustus, in the fifth and sixth tribunician powers.

[Note: Col. 0579B; 1033–1034.]

Consuls: the emperor Probus Augustus, for the fourth time.

[lacuna] Tiberianus.

Reland, from the Gudian inscriptions and from Rupert’s *Universal History*, p. 388, where Probus Augustus is said to possess the fourth tribunician power.

Under these consuls, Ovinius Paternus was urban prefect.

Probus defeats the Gallic tyrants Proculus and Bonosus. He comes to Rome, where he triumphs over the Germans and Blemyes. He distributes a largess, etc. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

[Col. 0579D]

The emperor Caesar Probus Augustus, in the sixth and seventh tribunician powers; consul for the fifth time.

[Note: Col. 0579C–D; 1034–1035.]

Consuls: the emperor Probus Augustus, for the fifth time.

[lacuna] Victorinus.

The Anonymous Fasti of the fourth century.

Under these consuls, Pomponius Victorianus was urban prefect.

This year, according to Pagius, Probus celebrates a triumph over the Germans and Blemyes. Then, while preparing war against the Persians, he is killed in a military mutiny at Sirmium in November. Marcus Aurelius CARUS succeeds him. All the chronologists, from Vopiscus and Aurelius Victor.

[Col. 0581A]

The emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Carus, in the first and second tribunician powers; consul for the second time.

[Note: Col. 0581A; 1035–1036.]

Consuls: the emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Carus Augustus, for the second time.

Marcus Aurelius Carinus, Caesar.

Reland, from Book IV of the *Code*, “On Witnesses.”

Under these consuls, Titurius Roburrus [also Robustus] was urban prefect.

After his father’s death around December, both sons, CARINUS and NUMERIANUS, are proclaimed Augusti. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

[Col. 0581B]

The emperors Marcus Aurelius Carinus and Numerianus, in tribunician power; consuls for the second time.

[Note: Col. 0581B; 1036–1037.]

# Beginning of the Empire of Constantine the Great

Maxentius usurps the empire on 25 September.

From this point, for six years, the empire is divided among several Augusti: some consuls are found in Italy, where Maxentius ruled, and others in the rest of the Roman world. See the notes.

[Col. 0599D]

With this fortunate epoch—the RESTORATION OF PEACE TO THE CHRISTIANS—achieved through the repeated edicts of Constantine Maximus and Licinius, after the persecutors of the Church had been overthrown by the just judgment of God and their stock had been destroyed, we consider the chronology of this volume appropriately concluded. Concerning this epoch Pagius writes, under the year 314, no. 13:

“After Maximinus was defeated in the year 313, the celebrated epoch defined by THE RESTORATION OF PEACE TO THE CHURCH was established. Eusebius mentions it in the *Chronicle*, as does the author [Col. 0601A] of the Alexandrian chronicle, when he speaks of the death of Constantius Augustus, the son of Constantine the Great. Churches were afterward dedicated in the individual cities, and assemblies of bishops were held, as Eusebius records in Book X, chapter 3.”

Cardinal Baronius should also be consulted for this year, no. 7, where, from Eusebius, he records decrees issued for the Christians by Maximinus before the end of his life.

## High Priests, kings, achievements, and documents of the Jews and neighboring peoples

[Col. 0412C]

### The twenty-fifth year of Hyrcanus the high priest

[Note: Olympiad 183.4, from the summer days; Olympiad 184.1.]

Hyrcanus’s envoys, sent to Caesar near the end of the preceding year, obtain from him, this year, when he was consul for the fifth time and perpetual dictator, that the privileges recounted from Josephus at the end of the preceding year be brought before the Senate and confirmed.

[Col. 0412D]

To this must be added the edict concerning Jewish associations, which Gaius Caesar, as consul, permitted only to the Jewish people in the City, after he had forbidden everything else. Josephus discusses it in the same chapter, Book XIV, chapter 17. Then follow these words:

[Col. 0414A]

“After Caesar’s death, when Marcus Antonius and Publius Dolabella were consuls, they convened the Senate, introduced the envoys of Hyrcanus, reported on their requests, renewed the friendship with them, and granted whatever they asked. It was decreed for them by senatorial decree. Dolabella also, after receiving a letter from Hyrcanus, wrote throughout Asia, and to Ephesus, the foremost city of that province, as follows:

‘Dolabella imperator to the magistrates of Ephesus, and to the Senate and People of Rome. Alexander, son of Theodorus, envoy of Hyrcanus, high priest and ethnarch of the Jews, has reported to me concerning his fellow citizens that they are unable to serve in the army because it is neither permitted for them to bear arms nor to travel on the Sabbath days, nor can they obtain their food for themselves according to their ancestral custom. Therefore I too, just as the commanders before me have done, wish them exempt from military service, and I permit them to live according to their ancestral customs, to assemble for religious purposes as their laws require, and to contribute offerings for sacrifices in the temple. I also wish you to write these same instructions to each of the cities of the province, etc.’

[Col. 0414B]

Lucius Lentulus, consul, then spoke in favor of the resolution concerning the Jews: ‘The Jews, Roman citizens who possess Jewish temples and conduct their affairs at Ephesus before the tribunal for the sake of religion, are declared exempt from military service on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October.’ Josephus, in the same place, relates that these decrees were fixed on bronze tablets in the Capitol.

[Col. 0414C]

The historians of Rome indicated in the adjoining column support Josephus; they confirm that, in various places, Antonius also sold many other privileges of this kind, under the pretext of Caesar’s acts, and that they were engraved on bronze tablets and fixed in the Capitol.”

[Col. 0414D]

After Ptolemy’s death, Cleopatra alone rules in Egypt. Josephus, Book XV, chapter 4.

[Col. 0416A] C. Cassius, formerly quaestor under Crassus, having occupied Syria, advanced into Judaea and made it subject to himself in the name of the Republic. From Judaea he exacted 700 talents of silver. [Note: [Col. 0416A] Olympiad 184, years I–II.] History of the Jews in the Paris Polyglot Bible: Herod of Galilee [paid] 100 talents; Hyrcanus sent an equal amount, Josephus, *War* I, chapter 9, and *Antiquities* XIV, chapter 18.

Antipater is removed from the world by the treachery of Malichus through poison. Phasaelus and Herod, his sons, postpone vengeance for their father. Herod, with Cassius’s permission, stabs him through his agents, Josephus, *Antiquities* XIV, chapter 20, and *War* I, chapter 9.

[Note: [Col. 0416B] II–III.] Hyrcanus sends a golden crown to M. Antony through ambassadors, requesting, on behalf of the liberty of his people, that the lands taken away by Cassius be restored. Antony, judging their requests equitable, not only granted them but, by publishing an edict at Tyre, wrote to the Tyrians, Sidonians, Antiochenes, and Aradians in the same sense: that the Jews sold under the spear by C. Cassius or by the Cassians should be released as free persons; that all places similarly taken away from those same Jews should be restored; and that the privileges and rights granted to the Jewish people through the favor of Dolabella and himself should remain valid. Josephus, *Antiquities* XIV, chapter 22.

[Note: [Col. 0416C] III–IIII.] Antigonus, son of Aristobulus [who had been the brother of the high priest Hyrcanus], raises the arms of the Parthians against his uncle, whose kingdom and priesthood he coveted. He had made an agreement with the Parthian leader Parbro, whose arms had already been stirred up against the Romans by Labienus: he promised 1,000 talents and 500 women if they would transfer the kingdom from Hyrcanus to him and kill Herod together with his sons.

For Antony had appointed Herod and Phasaelus tetrarchs; they were accused before him by the leading Jews at Daphne, near Antioch, where he was staying that year. When, however, he heard Hyrcanus, who had betrothed his daughter Mariamne to Herod and declared him superior in administering the state, Antony, disregarding the accusation, created both brothers tetrarchs. Josephus, *Antiquities* XIV, chapter 23.

The Parthians, stirred up by Labienus, had occupied Syria; incited by Antigonus, they seized Jerusalem. They led away Hyrcanus the high priest as a captive and, at Antigonus’s instigation, mutilated his ears so that he could not recover the high priesthood; they installed Antigonus in his place, from Aaron 58. Herod, having tried in vain to fight for Hyrcanus and his own people, withdrew first to the Arabs and then to Cleopatra. His brother Phasaelus, taken with Hyrcanus into Galilee and thrown into chains, dashed his head against a wall and died. Herod hurried to Rome, where Antony and Caesar received him so favorably that, through their influence and by decree of the Senate, he obtained the kingdom of Judaea beyond his expectation. He was conducted to the Capitol, between Caesar and Antony. Dio, and Josephus, *Antiquities* XIV, chapters 24–26.

[Col. 0418C] HERE BEGINS THE REIGN OF HEROD BY DECREE OF THE SENATE.

[Note: [Col. 0418C] Olympiad 185, year I before the summer, and from the summer year II.] Hyrcanus the high priest, 30; Antigonus, intruded [into the high priesthood], I; Herod the king, 1–2.

Herod, returning from Italy with instructions to Ventidius that he should help Herod against Antigonus—a command that he also gave to C. Sosius, governor of Syria and Cilicia—renders distinguished service to Ventidius in the Parthian expedition. Thus, after the Parthians had lost their leader Pacorus and 20,000 of their men had been killed, they were driven back within Media and Mesopotamia. Velleius Paterculus II, chapter 78; Josephus XIV, chapter 27; Dio XLIX, and elsewhere.

[Note: [Col. 0418C] II–III.] Hyrcanus 31; Antigonus 2; Herod 2–3.

At the beginning of spring Herod brings two legions and C. Sosius eleven to besiege Jerusalem. They capture it in the third month, during the solemnity of the fast, Josephus XIV, at the end. At the beginning of a sabbatical year. Cardinal Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 145, from Dio. In the consulship of these men, Antigonus is brought before Antony, bound to a cross, beaten with scourges, and then beheaded. With him, the rule of the Hasmonaeans ended, [Col. 0420A] after 126 years, beginning with Judas Maccabaeus. Dio and Josephus, in the same place.

Hyrcanus 32; Anan 1; Herod 3–4.

Hyrcanus the high priest, detained by the Parthians, learned that Herod was reigning. Although he was honorably detained at Babylon and was revered by the Jews living there as both high priest and king [with Phraates, king of the Parthians, permitting this], he preferred to obtain permission to go to Herod. Herod received his father-in-law courteously, but appointed Ananiel high priest, from Aaron 58, Josephus XV, chapters 1–2, since Hyrcanus’s ears had been mutilated and Herod was careful not to appoint a nobleman high priest, Josephus, in the same place.

[Note: [Col. 0420B] Olympiad 186, year IV, and 186 according to the Parthian era, year 1.] Ananiel 2; Herod 4.

Antony, persuaded by Artavasdes, king of Armenia and son of Tigranes, undertakes war against the king of Media, who favored the Parthians, and takes Polemon, king of Pontus, as an ally in the war. Alexandra, wife of Alexander, the son of King Aristobulus, arranges through Cleopatra that Herod be approached so that he might confer the high priesthood upon her son Aristobulus, at the urging of M. Antony, Josephus XV, chapter 2. He is the one numbered 59 from Aaron.

Aristobulus 1; Herod 5.

Herod removes Ananiel from the high priesthood and confers it upon Aristobulus, a youth of seventeen. During the Feast of Tabernacles, while he was officiating in the sacred rites, Herod deliberately invited him to swim and contrived that he should be secretly drowned, from Aaron 59.

Ananiel is again appointed high priest after the drowning. [Note: [Col. 0420C] I–II.] Formerly from Aaron 58, now 60. Antony, returning to Syria from his unsuccessful expedition, is appeased by Herod’s gifts when accusations concerning Aristobulus’s death are brought before him. Josephus XV, chapter 4.

Ananiel 3; Herod 6.

[Note: [Col. 0420D] II–III.] Herod, irritated on his return from Antony by the accusations of his womenfolk, rages against his relatives. Josephus XV, chapter 4. Cleopatra, having entangled Antony in her love, induces him to assign several neighboring regions to her. She demanded that Judaea and Arabia [Col. 0422A] be given to her, after they had been taken from their kings. Antony resisted, however, though he granted her the coastal lands from the river Eleutherus to Egypt, except Tyre and Sidon, in the same place.

When the Jewish high priest died, Jesus, son of Phabes, succeeded him, from Aaron 61.

Jesus, son of Phabes, 1; Herod 7.

[Note: [Col. 0422A] III–IIII.] Herod leads out the auxiliary forces Antony had sent him after the war with Media against the Arabs and engages them in battle with varying success.

Antony had joined an alliance of war with the king of Media: the latter was to fight against the Persians, Antony against Caesar, because Caesar had appropriated Lepidus’s provinces for himself. Antony also captured the king of Armenia by treachery, led him bound in triumph to Alexandria, and divided kingdoms among Cleopatra’s sons. Dio XLIX.

[Note: [Col. 0422B] Olympiad 186, year IV, and 187, year I.] Jesus 2; Herod 8.

Hillel the Babylonian, of Davidic descent, flourishes. From the numerous company of his disciples, Jonathan, son of Uzziel, is regarded as the most distinguished author of the Chaldaic Paraphrase. When a dispute arose between this Hillel and Shammai, the schools of the scribes and Pharisees arose. Jerome, *Commentary on Isaiah* III, chapter 8; and from him, Ussher, *Annals*.

Jesus 3; Herod 9.

[Note: [Col. 0422C] I–II.] Herod takes up arms against Aretas, king of the Arabs, on account of tribute. Josephus XV, chapter 6.

Judaea is shaken by a violent earthquake, chapter 7.

Herod, fearing the danger that had come upon him because he had favored Antony after the victory at Actium, deliberates about the death of Hyrcanus, lest, while he still lived, he should be restored to the kingdom. In the same place, chapter 9.

[Note: [Col. 0422D] II–III.] Jesus 4; Herod 10.

After intercepting letters from Hyrcanus to Malchus, king of the Arabs, written at the urging of his daughter Alexandra to obtain hospitality and protection, Herod has Hyrcanus killed by the Sanhedrin as though he were guilty of treason. Josephus, in the same place. He then hastens to Augustus in Cyprus, laying aside his diadem and approaching as a suppliant. Augustus, the victor, increased the kingdom Antony had given Herod beyond expectation. Tacitus, *Histories* I, chapter 9; Josephus XV, chapters 9–10; and *War* I, chapter 15. When Augustus was advancing through Syria against Antony, Herod gave him gifts amounting to 800 talents. Josephus XV, chapter 10.

Jesus 5; Herod 11.

[Note: [Col. 0424B] III–IV.] M. Valerius Messala is sent to Syria with extraordinary authority, Dio LI, but is soon recalled so that he may command in the Aquitanian war. Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 289, from Dio. Q. Didius was governor of Syria, in the same place.

Augustus entered the City in the month of Sextilis and celebrated a triple triumph: first, over the Pannonians, Dalmatians, and Iapydes; second, a naval triumph over the victory at Actium; third, over the conquest of Egypt. Macrobius, *Saturnalia* I, chapter 12. On the fifth day before the Kalends of September, an altar of Victory was dedicated in the Curia. Ancient Calendar in the Farnese collection, in Gruter, CXXVI.

[Note: [Col. 0424C] Olympiad 187, year IV, and Olympiad 188, year I.] Jesus 6; Herod 12.

Herod, inflamed by denunciations and driven on by suspicions, kills his wife Mariamne and his mother-in-law Alexandra. Josephus XV, chapter 11.

Mariamne’s unjust condemnation [her innocence having been discovered after her death] [Col. 0424D] torments Herod. The Jews interpret the punishment for this crime as the pestilence that raged in Jerusalem and carried off many of the leading men. Josephus XV, chapter 11.

[Note: [Col. 0424D] Olympiad I–II.] Jesus 7; Herod 13, by decree of the Senate, ten years from the death of Antigonus.

Herod had given his sister Salome in marriage to Costabarus the Idumaean. After Costabarus had been spared from Salome’s first accusation through her entreaties, Herod now kills him when he is denounced again and repudiated by his wife. Then Herod, turning away from ancestral rites, introduced foreign institutions: he constructed a theater and amphitheater and brought athletic contests, held every five years in honor of Augustus, into Jerusalem. Josephus XV, chapter 11.

[Note: [Col. 0426A] II–III.] Jesus 8; Herod 14, by decree of the Senate.

Herod puts ten conspirators from among the Jewish nobility to death because of their violation of religion; they had openly confessed that they had tried to kill him. Josephus, in the same place.

After Cornelius Gallus was condemned by decree of the Senate and anticipated his execution by killing himself, Petronius was appointed his successor in the prefecture of Egypt. Dio LIII.

[Note: [Col. 0426B] III–IV.] Jesus 9; Herod 15, by decree of the Senate.

To secure himself against popular uprisings, Herod begins to fortify Samaria and to call it Sebaste, from the name of Augustus; he also establishes another fortress at Strato’s Tower and soon names it Caesarea. In Galilee he establishes Gabala, and in Peraea, Esthmonitim. Josephus XV, chapter 11. After King Amyntas’s death, Galatia was reduced to a province together with Lycaonia and entrusted to Lollius. Rufus.

[Col. 0425] HERE THE COPTIC ERA IN EGYPT AND THE ERA OF THE SEBASTENIANS IN SYRIA BEGIN.

[Col. 0426C] [Note: [Col. 0426C] Olympiad 188, year IV, and 189, year I.] Jesus 10; Herod 16, by decree of the Senate, and 13 from the death of Antigonus.

[Col. 0426D] The Samaritans, now called Sebastenians, begin their era from this point, as Cardinal Noris demonstrates from their coins, *Syrian Epistles*, p. 534, Leipzig edition. This was the year of sterility and pestilence in Judaea, Herod’s thirteenth year, reckoned from the death of Antigonus as indicated in Josephus XV, chapter 13. Terentius Varro was Augustus’s legate in Syria and proconsul, Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 290, from Josephus. Aelius Gallus was the third prefect of Egypt. The Nabataean Arabian king was Obodas. Strabo XVI, p. 780; and Aretas, who received Gallus amicably.

[Col. 0428A] [Note: [Col. 0428A] I–II.] Jesus 11; Herod 10 by decree of the Senate and 14 from Antigonus.

Simon, son of Boethus, year 1, from Aaron 62.

After removing Jesus, son of Phabetes, from the high priesthood, Herod substitutes Simon, son of Boethus of Alexandria, whose daughter Mariamne he marries. Josephus XV, chapter 12, and XVIII, chapter 7. He is numbered 61 from Aaron. P. Petronius advances the Roman arms beyond Syene, 870 miles, against the Ethiopians [Pliny VI, chapter 29]. [Col. 0428B] Their queen Candace was compelled to return the statues of Caesar that had been carried away. Strabo XVII, p. 820; Dio LIV, p. 524.

Agrippa, sent to Syria because of his disputes with Marcellus, stops on the island of Lesbos. Dio, in the same place.

[Col. 0427] HEREAFTER THE PERIODS OF THE ROMAN PRINCES ARE DISTINCTLY NUMBERED BY THEIR ANNUAL TRIBUNICIAN POWERS.

[Col. 0428B] [Note: [Col. 0428B] II–III.] Simon 1–2; Herod 18 by decree of the Senate.

Herod magnificently constructs the harbor of Caesarea, equal to the Piraeus. Many of the stones laid in the foundations were 50 feet long, 18 feet wide, and 9 feet high. He also establishes a temple to Caesar, as well as a stone theater and amphitheater; finally, he seeks Caesar’s favor by giving the city the name Caesarea. Josephus XV, chapter 13.

[Col. 0428D] [Note: [Col. 0428D] III–IV.] Simon 2–3; Herod 19 by decree of the Senate.

Herod, contemplating the restoration of the Temple, brings in building materials. Josephus XV, chapter 14. From this point the 46 years are reckoned to the first Passover of Christ’s preaching. John 2:20.

The same Herod sends his sons Aristobulus and Alexander to Rome to greet Caesar and to become accustomed to Roman customs. Augustus, moved by these services, enlarges his kingdom by adding Trachonitis and Batanaea, while Varro governs Syria. Josephus XV, chapter 13. See C. Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 290.

[Note: [Col. 0430A] Olympiad 189, year IV, and 190, year I.] Simon 3–4; Herod by decree of the Senate 20, 17 from the death of Antigonus. Josephus XV, chapter 13.

Herod, accused by the Gadarenes before Augustus of administering the kingdom tyrannically, was not only acquitted by Caesar but was also rewarded with the addition of the region around the sources of the Jordan. He erected a temple there in honor of Augustus, where there was a cave of Pan beneath Mount Hermon, called Panium by the peoples; hence the nearby city is called Paneas. Caesarea Augusta beneath Panium was founded by Herod the tetrarch, the son of this Herod, about twenty years later. See Cardinal Noris, *Syrian Epistles*, p. 450.

Simon 4–5; Herod by decree of the Senate 20, 18 from the death of Antigonus.

In this year, the eighteenth of his reign from the death of Antigonus, Herod, the material having already been brought together, begins the new construction of the Jerusalem Temple, from white stones 25 cubits long, 12 wide, and 8 high. Josephus XV, chapter 14. He fortified the tower erected by the Hasmonaeans as a citadel, where the high-priestly vestment was kept, and called it Antonia. He also fortified the underground passage leading from it to another tower at the eastern gate of the Temple. Josephus XV, final chapter.

Simon 5–6; Herod by decree of the Senate 22, 19 from the death of Antigonus.

Herod sails to Rome and receives his sons from Augustus. He brings them home, instructed in good practices, and gives wives to both: to Aristobulus, Berenice, the daughter of his sister Salome; and to Alexander, Glaphyra, daughter of Archelaus, king of the Cappadocians. Josephus XVI, chapters 1–2.

Simon 6–7; Herod by decree of the Senate 23, 20 from the death of Antigonus.

Alexander and Aristobulus, the sons, return to Palestine with their father and are attacked by the plots of Salome and Pheroras. Josephus XVI, chapter 1.

[Col. 0432A] [Note: [Col. 0432A] Olympiad 190, year IV, and Olympiad 191, year I.] Simon 7–8; Herod by decree of the Senate 24, 21 from the death of Antigonus.

Herod honorably invites Agrippa, who was living in Asia, after the Actian games celebrated by the XV-men in September of this year under his presidency, as Agrippa was departing for Syria, the province assigned to him. Josephus XVI, chapter 2.

Agrippa sacrifices a hecatomb to God in Jerusalem. In the same place.

Simon 8–9; Herod 25, 10 from the decree of the Senate.

[Col. 0432B] [Note: [Col. 0432B] I–II.] Asander, king of the Bosporus, dies. A certain Scribonius attempts to succeed him, Dio, and Calvisius from him. As Agrippa seeks to deal with the disturbances of the Bosporans, he gives Herod the king an opportunity to attach himself to Agrippa’s retinue and to obtain from him further benefits for the Jews. Josephus XVI, chapters 4–5.

Simon 9–10; Herod by decree of the Senate 26, 23 from the death of Antigonus.

Herod accompanies Agrippa when he marches against the Bosporans until Agrippa, having conquered them, hands them over to King Polemon. He appeases Agrippa, who was angry with the Ilians, and obtains from him exemption for the Jews of Ionia. Josephus XVI, chapters 3–4. Domestic disputes and accusations trouble Herod. Josephus, in the same place, chapter 6.

Simon 10–11; Herod by decree of the Senate 27, 24 from the death of Antigonus.

[Note: [Col. 0432C] III–IV.] After Agrippa had administered the Asian diocese and Syria for ten years, he is recalled to Italy to conduct the Pannonian war with M. Vinicius; M. Titius is appointed in his place in Syria. Strabo; Josephus XVI, chapter 6, at the end. See Noris, *Syrian Epistles*, p. 254, and Paterculus II. Herod commends his son Antipater to Agrippa so that he may take him with him to Rome. Josephus, in the same place.

[Note: [Col. 0432D] Olympiad 191, year IV, Olympiad 192, year I.] Simon 11–12; Herod by decree of the Senate 28, 25 from the death of Antigonus.

Herod dedicates Caesarea, Josephus XVI, chapter 9. Soon afterward, sailing again to Italy, he presides at the Olympic games of Olympiad 192 at Elis and is declared perpetual director of the games because of the generosity he displayed there. Josephus, *War* I, chapter 16, and *Antiquities* XVI, chapter 9. See Cardinal Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 154.

[Col. 0434A] Simon 12–13; Herod by decree of the Senate 29, 26 from the death of Antigonus.

[Note: [Col. 0434A] I–II.] Herod visits Augustus at Aquileia. After accusing his sons, he is reconciled with them through Caesar. He gives Caesar 300 talents, or 180,000 pieces of money [Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 154, from Josephus], who distributed 400 coins per person in the third year of his tribunician power. The Ancyran inscription. Herod dedicates Caesarea, completed by him in twelve years, in the twenty-eighth year of his reign. Olympiad 192. Josephus and Noris, in the places cited above.

[Note: [Col. 0434B] II–III.] Simon 13–14; Herod by decree of the Senate 30, 27 from the death of Antigonus.

Phraates, king of the Parthians, sends four sons as hostages to Augustus, after Titius, who at that time governed Syria, has been summoned to a conference. Strabo XVI, p. 515; and from him Cardinal Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, dissertation 2, §9. There he corrects the names of two men from an inscription preserved in the Medici Gardens on the Pincian Hill, where Seraspadanes and Rodaspes, Parthians, are called sons of Phraates, king of kings. Josephus XVIII, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0434C] III–IV.] Simon 14–15; Herod by decree of the Senate 31, 28 from the death of Antigonus.

Herod searches for treasures in the tombs of David and Solomon. From this point Josephus XVI, chapter 11, and the following chapters, asserts that the royal household was turned into a seedbed of accusations because of Pheroras’s disordered loves and the ambition of the sons.

[Col. 0434D] [Note: [Col. 0434D] Olympiad 192, year IV, Olympiad 193, year I.] Simon 15–16; Herod by decree of the Senate 32, 29 from the death of Antigonus.

After Obodas, king of the Nabataean Arabs, dies, Aretas succeeds him; previously he had been called Aeneas. Josephus XVI, chapter 15.

Dionysius of Halicarnassus, in the preface to his history, states that he began writing this year, 22 years after the end of the civil wars imposed by Augustus. He reckons the middle of Olympiad 187 in the year that brought the civil wars to an end, when he immediately sailed to Italy.

[Col. 0436A] [Note: [Col. 0436A] I–II.] Simon 16; Herod by decree of the Senate 33, 30 from the death of Antigonus. Matthew 1. Syria under Saturninus; Judaea under Volumnius.

Simon Boethus, the high priest, is deprived of the high priesthood because he knew of the poisoning imputed to his daughter, Herod’s wife. Matthias succeeds him [from Aaron 63]. Josephus XVII, chapter 15, and XVIII, chapter 3. C. Sentius Saturninus, legate and propraetor, comes to Syria with Volumnius the procurator. Coins struck according to the Augustan era. See Cardinal Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 306, from Josephus XVI, chapter 16.

Aretas the king is confirmed there by Augustus after gifts have been given.

[Note: [Col. 0436B] II–III.] Joazar I; Herod by decree of the Senate 34, 31 from the death of Antigonus.

After Matthias is compelled to resign, Joazar [or Gozar] is appointed high priest, Josephus, in the same place, from Aaron 64.

Herod’s sons, condemned at the council of Berytus, are strangled at Sebaste. Josephus XVI, chapter 17. While Saturninus presided [over] Syria, in the same place, he pronounced sentence together with Volumnius and others, up to the number of 150. Antipater, after his brothers had been removed, impiously plans to remove his father as well. In the same place, book XVII, chapter 1.

[Note: [Col. 0436C] III–IV.] Joazar 1–2; Herod by decree of the Senate 35, 32 from the death of Antigonus.

In this year, when the world had been settled in peace,

THE WORD OF GOD BECAME FLESH.

Christ was conceived in the womb of the Blessed Virgin Mary, when the angel announced it, by the HOLY SPIRIT, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, according to the holy fathers and the Gospel of Luke. His forerunner, John the Baptist, was born in June. On the eighth day before the Kalends of January, OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST WAS BORN OF THE VIRGIN MARY IN BETHLEHEM OF JUDAEA, IN THE DAYS OF HEROD THE KING, when an edict had gone out from Caesar Augustus that the whole world should be registered. In the same place.

[Note: [Col. 0436D] Olympiad 193, year IV, Olympiad 194, year I.] THIS FIRST REGISTRATION WAS MADE BY QUIRINIUS, GOVERNOR OF SYRIA. Luke 2.

After Tigranes’s death, Armenia rebels. See *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 185.

Joazar 2–3; Herod by decree of the Senate 36, 5 (bissextile), [Col. 0438A] 37, from the death of Antigonus 33.

ON THE KALENDS OF JANUARY, THE CIRCUMCISION OF THE LORD, at which his name was called JESUS.

Quintilius Varus is sent to Syria as Saturninus’s successor. Josephus XVII, chapter 17.

In the same year occurred THE ADORATION OF THE MAGI, THE FLIGHT OF THE LORD INTO EGYPT, and THE MASSACRE OF THE INNOCENT CHILDREN. Judas and Matthias, with their companions, were burned at Jerusalem on the night when a total eclipse of the moon was observed at its rising, on 23 March, according to the astronomical tables. Josephus XVII, chapter 10.

Herod suffers a more serious illness and dies on 25 November, in the thirty-seventh year of his reign. From this point Archelaus is declared his successor by decree of the Senate at Rome. He visits Augustus.

[Note: [Col. 0438B] I–II.] Joazar 3–4; Archelaus 1–2.

The return of the child JESUS from Egypt. Matthew 2.

Caesar confirms Herod’s will, appointing Archelaus ethnarch over Judaea, Idumaea, and Samaria; to Herod Antipas, the region beyond the Jordan and Galilee; to Philip, Batanaea, Trachonitis, and Gaulanitis; and certain cities of Greek institutions are attached to Syria. Josephus XVII, chapter 13.

[Note: [Col. 0438C] II–III.] Joazar 4; Eleazar 1; Archelaus 2–3.

Archelaus, having returned to Judaea as ethnarch, removes Joazar from the high priesthood and confers it upon his brother Eleazar. Josephus XVII, chapter 15.

Caius Caesar sets out for the Parthian war while Augustus is called Father of his Country. See C. Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 188, and Ovid, book I *On the Art of Love*, and elsewhere. In this same year Augustus gave a naumachia. In the same place. Tiberius sails to Samos to visit Caius. Velleius.

[Note: [Col. 0438D] III–IV.] Eleazar 1–2; Archelaus 3–4.

Armenia is recovered [again]. Previously it had been recovered through Tiberius in the year 732 from the foundation of the City, when he was called Augustus Imperator VII on the coins; now it is recovered through Caius, when he is called Imperator XIV. See Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 185.

[Note: [Col. 0438D] Olympiad 194, year IV, Olympiad 195, year I.] Eleazar 2–3; Archelaus 4–5.

Caius Caesar begins his consulship in Syria on the Kalends of January; and in the East he completes it. C. Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 243. In the same place.

[Col. 0440A] After Artavasdes, recently established by Caius in the kingdom of Armenia, dies, Tigranes offers gifts to Augustus so that the kingdom may be given to him. Augustus refers the petition to Caius and orders him to remain hopeful.

[Col. 0439A]

Ancient coins illustrating the year of Christ’s birth from the fathers. The first and second were issued at the colony of Caesaraugusta in Spain by Jo. Vaillant; the rest in Syria:

1. Under Augustus, after the nineteenth year of his tribunician power, consul eleven, designated consul twelve, in the year of Christ’s birth.

2. In the following year, tribunician power twenty.

3. Under Saturninus, governor of Syria, in the year 35 of the Augustan era, under whom Tertullian reports that the census was conducted in Syria. From our museum, together with the following two.

4. Under Quinctilius Varus, governor of Syria, in the twenty-sixth year of Augustus.

5. In the twenty-seventh year.

6. Of Herod Antipas under C. Caligula, in the year 43 from the death of Herod the Great. From the Rigor Museum.

HERE THE COMMON ERA OF CHRIST BEGINS.

[Col. 0440B] [Note: [Col. 0440B] Olympiad 195, year I, and from the summer days, year II.] CHRIST THE LORD, HIGH PRIEST FOREVER ACCORDING TO THE ORDER OF MELCHIZEDEK.

The third and fourth years of Eleazar, high priest of the Jews; the fifth and sixth years of Archelaus, king.

Caius Caesar, son of Augustus, placed in command of the East and preparing for war against the Parthians, makes peace after a conference with Phraates, the king’s son. See Cardinal Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 317.

[Col. 0442A] [Note: [Col. 0442A] II–III.] The seventh year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Eleazar, Jewish high priest, 4–5; Archelaus, king, 6–7.

While Caius Caesar was besieging Artagera, a traitor inflicted a wound upon him. While he lay incapacitated by the wound, his attendants plundered the province out of greed. Lollius, anticipating accusation, killed himself. Quirinius, who had conducted the census in Judaea at the birth of the Lord, was appointed in his place as guardian of the young prince. See the authors cited in *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, pp. 317 and 341.

[Note: [Col. 0442B] III–IV.] The eighth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Eleazar 5–6; Archelaus 7–8.

Caius Caesar dies in the consulship of these men, on the ninth day before the Kalends of March. C. Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 342. Augustus was then counting his twenty-sixth year of tribunician power. In the same place, from the same Pisan inscription.

[Note: [Col. 0442B] IV, Olympiad 195, and Olympiad 196, year I.] The ninth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Eleazar 6; Archelaus 8–9.

Jesus, son of Sias, I. Josephus XVIII, chapter 3. Eleazar is ordered by Archelaus to withdraw from the high priesthood [Col. 0442C] and receives as successor Jesus, son of Sias [from Aaron 65]. Josephus XVII, chapter 15; he is also called Joazar.

[Note: [Col. 0442C] I–II.] The ninth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Jesus, son of Sias, or Joazar, 1–2; Archelaus 9–10.

Archelaus, accused by the leading Jews before Augustus, is summoned to Rome and condemned to exile. He is banished to Vienna, and Judaea with all his dominion is assigned to the province of Syria. It receives Quirinius as governor, who conducts a census there. Josephus XVII, chapter 15. JUDAEA WAS REDUCED TO A PROVINCE in the thirty-seventh year from the victory at Actium. Josephus XVIII, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0442D] II–III.] The eleventh year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Jesus, or Joazar, 2–3. [Lacuna.]

Quirinius, governor.

Coponius, procurator.

Under this second census of Quirinius in Judaea, Judas the Galilaean [the one mentioned in Acts 5:37], together with Saddoc the Pharisee, founder of the fourth sect of the Jews, raises a revolt on account of the census and fills everything with slaughter. Josephus XVIII, chapters 1–2.
