[Note: [Col. 0442D] III–IV.] The twelfth year of the age of Christ the Lord, when, at the age of twelve, he disputes in the Temple among the teachers. Luke 2. Jesus, or Joazar, 3; Anna, or Ananus, 1.

Quirinius, after removing Joazar from the priesthood, confers the high priesthood upon Ananus, or Annas. Josephus XVIII, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0444A] Olympiad 196, year IV, and 197, year I.] The thirteenth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Roman governors and procurators.

Annas 1–2.

Governor Quirinius.

Procurator Coponius.

[Col. 0444B] M. Ambivius.

M. Ambivius, the second procurator, succeeds Coponius, the first procurator of Caesar sent to Judaea, while Quirinius is still governing Syria. Josephus XVIII, chapter 3.

See Cardinal Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, pp. 323 and 327.

[Note: [Col. 0444B] I–II.] The fourteenth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Annas 2–3.

Quirinius, governor, 4.

Ambivius, procurator, 1–2.

Salome, the wife of King Herod, dying, leaves the toparchy of Jamnia in Judaea [Col. 0444C]. Josephus XVIII, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0444C] II–III.] The fifteenth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Annas 3–4.

Quirinius, governor, 5.

Ambivius, procurator, 3.

In Syria also, as in the other provinces, since Tiberius had this year been made the colleague of Augustus in proconsular authority over the empire, his era is reckoned from this point, as in Luke, chapter 3.

[Col. 0444D] [Note: [Col. 0444D] III–IV.] The sixteenth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Annas 4–5; Tiberius’s proconsular authority over the empire, 1–2.

Quirinius, governor of Syria, 6.

Annius Rufus, successor.

M. Ambivius, procurator.

[Col. 0446A] [Note: [Col. 0446A] Olympiad 197, year IV, and 198, year I.] The seventeenth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Annas, high priest, 5–6, bissextile [year].

Tiberius’s proconsular authority over the empire, 2–3.

Quirinius, governor of Syria, 7.

Annius Rufus, procurator of Judaea, 2.

Herod Antipas not only restores the city of Sepphoris, formerly destroyed by fire by Quinctilius Varus, during these years, but also makes it the principal fortress of Galilee, [Col. 0446B] where he himself would reside. See Pezelius, *History of the Gospel*, volume I, p. 303, from Josephus XVIII, *Antiquities* 5, 3. Philip calls Paneas Caesarea, and Bethsaida, Julias. In the same place.

[Note: [Col. 0446B] I–II.] The eighteenth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Ananus 6–7.

Tiberius’s imperial proconsular authority, 4–5.

Quirinius, governor of Syria, 8.

Rufus, procurator of Judaea, 3.

In the common era of Christ, day 18 of April.

A total eclipse of the sun is reported in the consulship of these men, before Augustus’s death, by Dio LVI; and a [lacuna] eclipse in Pannonia after Augustus’s death, by Tacitus.

A lunar eclipse was observed in Pannonia after Augustus’s death by the mutinous legions under Germanicus.

According to the astronomical tables, a total eclipse could have been observed this year, with the sun setting in the western part of the British islands, year 13.

The nineteenth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0446C] II–III.] Ananus 7–8.

Tiberius’s imperial proconsular authority, 5–6.

Silanus, governor of Syria, 1.

Coins of Valerius Gratus, procurator [Col. 0446D] of Judaea, 1.

Silanus, in the first year of Tiberius and Augustus in Syria, 45.

He strikes coins at Antioch. C. Noris, *Syrian Epistles*, p. 252.

In the Medici Museum and in ours. This is Caecilius Silanus Creticus, related by marriage to Germanicus. Tacitus II; and Valerius Gratus, procurator of Judaea, replaces Annius Rufus. Josephus XVIII, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0446D] III–IV.] The twentieth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Ananus 8–9.

Tiberius’s imperial proconsular authority, 6–7.

Silanus, governor of Syria, 10–11.

Valerius Gratus, procurator of Judaea, 1–2.

[Col. 0448A] In the consulship of these men, the kingdoms of the East were disturbed. The Parthians, having expelled King Vonones into Armenia—he had been a hostage at Rome—had accepted Artabanus. Vonones implores the aid of Tiberius. Suetonius, *Tiberius*, chapter 49; Tacitus, *Annals* II, chapter 4.

[Note: [Col. 0448A] Olympiad 198, year IV, and 199, year I.] The twenty-first year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Ishmael, high priest, from Aaron 68.

Tiberius’s imperial proconsular authority, 7–8.

Calpurnius Piso, governor of Syria, 1.

Valerius Gratus, procurator of Judaea, 2–3.

[Col. 0448B] After Ishmael is removed from the high priesthood, Ananus becomes high priest, 69 from Aaron. Josephus XVIII, chapter 3.

Cappadocia is reduced to a province after the death of King Archelaus. Cn. Piso becomes governor of Syria after the removal of Silanus Creticus. Tacitus, *Annals* II.

[Note: [Col. 0448B] I–II.] The twenty-second year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Eleazar, son of Ananus,

high priest, from Aaron 70.

Piso, governor of Syria, 2.

Valerius Gratus, procurator of Judaea, 3–4.

The era of Tiberias, from coins. Noris, *Syrian Epistles*, p. 558.

Commagene is reduced to a province after the death of King Antiochus, [Col. 0448C] and Tiberius appoints Q. Severus as its governor. Tacitus, *Annals* II.

[Note: [Col. 0448C] III–III.] The twenty-third year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Simon, son of Camithus; Piso, governor of Syria, 3.

From Aaron 71. Gratus, procurator of Judaea, 4–5.

Valerius Gratus, having removed Eleazar from the high priesthood, substitutes Simon, son of Camithus, as high priest, 71 from Aaron. Josephus XVIII, chapter 3. Decree of the Senate concerning the expulsion of Egyptian and Jewish rites from Italy. Tacitus, *Annals* II, chapter 85.

[Note: [Col. 0448C] III–IV.] The twenty-fourth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Simon, high priest, 1, [Col. 0448D] and after his removal,

Joseph Caiaphas, high priest, 1, 72 from Aaron.

Piso, governor of Syria, 4.

Gratus, procurator of Judaea, 5–6.

Tiberius’s imperial proconsular authority, 10–11.

The body of Germanicus, who died in Syria, is brought to Rome by Piso. Accused of poisoning, Piso anticipates his condemnation by death. Tacitus, *Annals* III, 15. Saturninus. See Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, [Note: [Col. 0448D] Olympiad 199, year IV, Olympiad 200, year I] p. 328.

The twenty-fifth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Caiaphas, high priest, 2–3.

Saturninus, governor of Syria, 1–2.

[Col. 0450A] Tiberius’s imperial proconsular authority, 11–12.

Gratus, procurator of Judaea, 6–7.

Valerius Gratus, procurator of Judaea under Tiberius Augustus, changes the high priests annually during these years, until he completes the eleventh year of his administration, at which point he is recalled to Rome. Josephus XVIII, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0450A] I–II.] The twenty-sixth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Caiaphas 3–4, or Annas 73.

For Gratus, procurator of Judaea, appointed the high priests annually. Saturninus, governor of Syria, 2–3.

From this point we shall mark, through Gratus’s eleventh year, the alternating annual high priests, Annas and Caiaphas, who took office near the beginning of the Jews’ civil year, according to the authorities, especially Josephus XVIII, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0450B] II–III.] The twenty-seventh year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Annas and Caiaphas,

alternating, 4–5.

Flaccus, governor of Syria, 1.

Gratus, procurator of Judaea, 8–9.

L. Pomponius Flaccus holds the governorship of Syria. Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, chapter 16, p. 329, from Tacitus. He dies there after eleven years, under the consuls Galba and Sulla, p. 330.

[Note: [Col. 0450C] III–IIII.] The twenty-eighth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

Caiaphas and Annas,

alternating, 5–6.

Flaccus, governor of Syria, 1–2.

Gratus, procurator of Judaea, 9–10.

Sejanus harasses the Jews, as he does many others, in the city through denunciations and slanders. Philo, *Embassy to Gaius*. See Ussher, *Annals*, p. 564. Pontius Pilate is designated as Gratus’s successor for the following year. See *Cenotaphia Pisiana*, p. 326.

[Note: [Col. 0450D] Olympiad 200, year IV, Olympiad 201, year I.] The twenty-ninth year of the age of Christ the Lord.

The eleventh and twelfth years of Tiberius’s reign, from the death of Augustus; but the fourteenth and fifteenth years of his imperial proconsular authority over Syria.

In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governing Judaea, Herod was tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of the region of Ituraea and Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, under the chief priests Annas and Caiaphas, the word of the Lord came to John. Luke 3.

[Note: [Col. 0452A] I–II.] Jesus Christ, beginning at about thirty years of age, is baptized by John in the Jordan. He opens THE ERA OF THE GOSPEL and illuminates Galilee first, then Judaea also, when he had gone up to Jerusalem for Passover (John 11), and baptizes in Judaea (John 3). Returning to Galilee, he converts the Samaritan woman (John 4) and is acknowledged as the Savior of the world. In the same place. John is imprisoned.

[Note: [Col. 0452B] II–III.] The thirty-first year of the age of Christ the Lord, and the second year of his preaching begins. As he was about to depart for the Feast of Passover and had performed miracles everywhere, he was received badly only in his homeland. Returning to Galilee, he chooses twelve Apostles from among his disciples. Luke 6. John is beheaded. The Pharisees conspire against him together with the Herodians. Matthew 10 and 13; Mark 3; Luke 4 and 9. In the desert near Bethsaida, he feeds 5,000 men with three loaves, and again 4,000 with four loaves. In the same place.

[Note: [Col. 0452C] III–IIII.] The thirty-second year of the age of Christ the Lord, and the third year of his preaching.

As he is about to depart for Jerusalem, he is not received by the Samaritans. He appoints and sends ahead seventy-two disciples. He is received as a guest by Martha and Magdalene, Luke 10; he teaches the disciples to pray, chapter 11. Peter’s confession is repeated at Caesarea, Matthew 16. John 6, when some of the disciples withdraw from him.

He remains in Galilee and avoids the plots of the Pharisees, whom he nevertheless refutes in John 8 and 9, confirming his divinity and teaching by miracles.

[Note: [Col. 0452D] Olympiad 201, year IV, and Olympiad 202, year I.] The thirty-third year of the age of Christ the Lord, and the fourth year of his preaching.

The man blind from birth is healed. Lazarus is recalled to life by the Lord. After the Paschal Supper had been completed on Thursday, the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the evening he begins THE PASSION, and on the following day, Friday, 26 March, he completes it, CRUCIFIED.

He rises on Sunday, 28 March. He appears to the Apostles for forty days before the Ascension. [Col. 0454A] During this time he appoints Peter, prince of the Apostles, supreme pontiff of his Church.

[Note: [Col. 0454A] I–II.] Peter’s pontificate, year 1, and from the Paschal season, year 2. See below in the notes, p. 16, the Acts of the Apostles for this year: the first persecution of the Church by the Jews. The martyrdom of Stephen, Acts 8. Philip evangelizes Samaria, Acts …

[Col. 0454B] **Pontificate of Peter 2, 3.**

[Note: [Col. 0454B] III] The conversion of Paul. Acts 19. See the notes below. He preaches in the synagogues; he departs for Arabia and returns to Damascus [cf. Gal. 1]. Syria is under the administration of Flaccus, years 8 and 9. Since Sejanus, according to Orosius (book 7, chapter 4), opposed Tiberius when he proposed that the Lord Christ be enrolled among the gods, it follows that the Lord’s Passion occurred before Sejanus’s year of death. See Schelestratus, *Antiquitates Ecclesiasticae*, discourse I, chapter V, article II, numbers 3 and 4.

[Col. 0454C] [Note: [Col. 0454C] III IV] Peter 3, and from the Paschal season 4.

Peter and John, returning to Jerusalem, evangelize many regions of the Samaritans, Acts 8:25.

[Col. 0454D] [Note: [Col. 0454D] Olympiad 202 IV, Olympiad 203 I] Peter 4, 5.

“Those who had been scattered because of the persecution that arose on account of Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews.” Acts 11:19. “Meanwhile, throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria, the Church had peace.” Acts 9:31.

[Col. 0456A] [Note: [Col. 0456A] I II] Peter 5, 6; first year of the See of Antioch.

Peter baptizes Cornelius the centurion. Soon afterward the See of Antioch is founded, where the disciples were subsequently called **Christians**. Acts 9 and 10. See the notes below.

A coin of Pomponius Flaccus, propraetor of Syria, struck in the preceding year, Antiochene Era 82; after his death there, Syria remained for two full years without a consular legate. Tacitus, *Annals* 6:27; Suetonius, *Life of Tiberius*, chapter 41. See Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisana*, p. 330.

[Note: [Col. 0456B] II III] Peter 6, 7; See of Antioch 1, 2; Syrian administration of Vitellius 1.

After Peter had baptized Cornelius in the preceding year, he returns to Jerusalem this year and speaks in the council about the calling of the Gentiles, Acts 11.

L. Vitellius is appointed consular legate of Syria. Tacitus, *Annals* 6, and from him C. Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisana*, p. 330. Pilate, the procurator, is denounced by the provincials after completing ten years [Col. 0456C]; [Note: [Col. 0456C] III IV] Marcellus is appointed by Tiberius in his place.

Peter 7, 8; See of Antioch 2, 3; Syrian administration of Vitellius 1, 2.

Men from Cyprus and Cyrene, who had been scattered after the martyrdom of Stephen, announce Christ also to the Greeks. For this reason Barnabas is sent by the Jerusalem Church to Antioch, so that he may investigate the matter. Acts 11.

After Caiaphas had been reduced to ordinary rank, Jonathan, son of Ananus, is appointed high priest of the Jews. Josephus 18:5. Vitellius restores custody of the high-priestly vestments to the priests. Josephus, book 7.

[Col. 0456D] [Note: [Col. 0456D] Olympiad 203 IV and 204 I] Peter 8, 9; See of Antioch 3, 4; Vitellius’s Syrian administration 2, 3; Marcellus’s procuratorship 1.

Barnabas converts many to Christ at Antioch. Acts 11.

Marcellus succeeds Pilate as procurator. Josephus, book 7, chapter 5. Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, visits Vitellius. Herod Agrippa, grandson of Herod the Great through his son Aristobulus, is called king by Gaius Caligula and receives the tetrarchies of Philip and Lysanias.

[Note: [Col. 0456D] I II] Peter 9, 10; See of Antioch 4, 5; Syrian administration of Vitellius 3, 4. [Col. 0458A] [Note: [Col. 0458A] II] Marcellus 1; procuratorship 1, 2; Herod Agrippa 1, 2.

Barnabas travels to Tarsus, finds Paul, and brings him to Antioch. They remain there for a year and convert many. There the disciples are called **Christians**. Acts 11. Matthew writes the Gospel. See the note concerning the pontificate of Saint Peter.

Vitellius transfers the high priesthood of the Jews from Jonathan to Theophilus, [Col. 0458B] his brother. Josephus 18:7.

[Note: [Col. 0458B] II III] Peter 10, 11; See of Antioch 5, 6; Vitellius’s Syrian administration 4, 5; Theophilus’s priesthood 2; Herod Agrippa 2, 3.

The prophets at Antioch predict a future famine under Claudius. Acts 11. See the notes below concerning the pontificate of Saint Peter.

Herod Antipas travels to Rome and tries to obtain from Gaius the kingdom of Agrippa. He is deprived of his own tetrarchies [Galilee and Perea] and sent into exile. Josephus 19:6.

[Note: [Col. 0458B] III IV] Peter 11, 12; See of Antioch 6, 7; Petronius’s administration 1, who is appointed successor when L. Vitellius is summoned to Rome. Josephus 18, chapter 11; Herod Agrippa 3, 4.

Peter takes advantage of the legions being summoned from Syria to the West in order to bring the faith here. See the notes concerning the pontificates of Saints Peter, Clement, and Eleutherius. When Herod Agrippa returns to Rome, Gaius assigns him the kingdom of his uncle Antipas. He orders a colossal statue of himself to be erected at Jerusalem. Philo of Alexandria is sent as envoy to Gaius. Josephus, book 19, chapter 9.

[Note: [Col. 0458C] Olympiad 204 IV and 205 I] Peter 12, 13; See of Antioch 7; Roman See 1.

[Col. 0458D] **FOUNDATION OF THE ROMAN SEE.**

On his first arrival in the City, Peter founds the Roman episcopal see in January. See the notes concerning the pontificate of Saint Peter; during the Paschal season he renews the thirteen years of his pontificate on 25 April. See the notes there.

Petronius, governor of Syria, 1, 2; Herod Agrippa 3, 4.

Agrippa makes Gaius more favorable toward the Jews by delaying the dedication of his colossal statue at Jerusalem. Josephus, book 19.

[Col. 0460A] [Note: [Col. 0460A] I II] Peter 13, 14; Roman See 1, 2.

Mark brings to Egypt the Gospel written by him and approved by Peter, and in Peter’s name founds the Alexandrian See. Claudius grants to Herod Agrippa, who had rendered him excellent service, the kingdom of Jerusalem, Samaria, and Judea. Josephus 19:4. Petronius’s administration 2, 3.

[Col. 0460B] His coin is reproduced in Noris, *Epistola Syriaca*, p. 178, with the Antiochene Era.

[Note: [Col. 0460B] II III] Peter 14, 15; Roman See 2, 3; King Agrippa 1, 2.

The Jews are forbidden to hold assemblies in Rome because of their large numbers, though they are permitted elsewhere. Dio, p. 669. Peter returns from Rome to Palestine to assist the Church there, which is endangered under the new King Agrippa. Agrippa has James killed; Peter, thrown into prison, is freed by an angel. Acts 12. He visits Antioch and Asia Minor. See the notes concerning the pontificate [Col. 0460C] of Saint Peter. Soon afterward he returns to Italy.

[Note: [Col. 0460C] III IV] Peter 15, 16; Roman See 3, 4; King Agrippa 2, 3.

The British expedition of the emperor Claudius provides Peter with the opportunity to go to Britain, or to send ministers of the Gospel there. See the notes mentioned above.

Paul returns to Antioch, then sails to Cyprus, and is called Paul by Sergius the proconsul. Acts 13.

Marsus succeeds Petronius as governor of Syria. Josephus 19:6; Tacitus 11.

[Col. 0460D] [Note: [Col. 0460D] Olympiad 205 IV and 206 I] Peter 16, 17; Roman See 4, 5; King Agrippa 3, 4; Vibius Marsus’s administration 1, 2.

Claudius grants the Jews, at their request, the right to preserve the high-priestly vestments. Josephus, book 2, *Bellum*, chapter 1. King Agrippa dies in the seventh year of his reign and the fourth year of Claudius’s reign, which had already begun. While Agrippa the Younger, his son, is still growing up, Cuspius Fadus is appointed procurator over the kingdom. Josephus 19, final chapter; Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisana*, p. 332.

[Note: [Col. 0460D] I II] Peter 17, 18; Roman See 5, 6; Vibius Marsus’s Syrian administration [Col. 0462A] 2, 3; Fadus’s procuratorship 1, 2.

King Herod, having obtained from Claudius Augustus the right to appoint the Jewish high priest, and securing it for himself and his heirs until the destruction of Jerusalem, removes Simon Cantharus and gives the high priesthood to Joseph, son of Camus. Josephus, book 20.

[Note: [Col. 0462A] II III] Peter 18, 19; Roman See 6, 7.

Helena, queen of Adiabene, and her son Izates embrace the Jewish religion. The remains of Noah’s Ark are said to have been found in their territory. Josephus 20, chapter 2.

C. Cassius Longinus is appointed successor to Vibius Marsus as governor of Syria. Josephus 19, final chapter, and Tacitus, books 11 and 12 of the *Annals*. C. Noris reconciles these accounts in *Epistola Syriaca*, p. 181, correcting *Cenotaphia Pisana*, p. 332.

[Note: [Col. 0462B] III IV] Peter 19, 20; Roman See 7, 8.

In succession: Cuspius Fadus, procurator of Judea; Tiberius Alexander; C. Cassius Longinus, governor of Syria, 1, 2.

[Col. 0462C] Famine in Judea, formerly predicted by Agabus, Acts 11; concerning it, Josephus 20, chapter 3.

[Note: [Col. 0462C] Olympiad 206 IV and 207 I] Peter 20, 21; Roman See 8, 9.

C. Cassius Longinus 2, 3; Tiberius Alexander, procurator 1, 2; King Agrippa 1.

King Herod of Chalcis removes Joseph son of Camus from the high priesthood of the Jews and appoints Ananias in his place, concerning whom see Acts 23:2. Josephus 20:4.

Claudius expels the Jews from Rome. For this reason Peter returns to Judea; Aquila and Priscilla go to Corinth. Acts 18:2.

[Note: [Col. 0462D] I II] Peter 21, 22; Roman See 9, 10; C. Cassius Longinus 3, 4; Tiberius Alexander, procurator 2, 3; King Agrippa 1, 2.

Claudius orders C. Cassius Longinus, governor of Syria, to bring Mithridates, the king held hostage at Rome, into his own Parthian kingdom against the usurper Gotarzes. [Col. 0464A] Mithridates is nevertheless defeated and killed by him. Tacitus 12.

Tiberius Alexander is replaced as procurator of Judea by Vervidius Cumanus. Josephus 20:3–4.

[Note: [Col. 0464A] II III] Peter 22, 23; Roman See 10, 11; King Agrippa 2, 3.

This year, or very shortly before it, according to Petavius, book 11, chapter 12, at the end, the **Council of the Apostles** is held at Jerusalem, after an embassy from the Church of Antioch, as described in Acts 15 [Col. 0464B]. Returning from the council, Paul remains at Antioch with Barnabas. Soon afterward he traverses Syria and Cilicia with Silas as his companion. At Lystra he takes Timothy. He proceeds to Macedonia, then to Achaia and Corinth, where he finds Priscilla and Aquila, expelled from Rome by Claudius three years earlier. Acts 20, 17, 18. See Petavius, book 11, chapter 12.

[Note: [Col. 0464B] III IV] Peter 23, 24; Roman See 11, 12; King Agrippa 3, 4. Longinus’s administration 5, whose successor is appointed this year: C. Ummidius Durmius [Col. 0464C] Quadratus.

See this man’s inscription and coins in Noris, *Epistola Syriaca*, p. 182, and *Cenotaphia Pisana*, p. 332. Tacitus 12, chapter 54. Judea is assigned to Felix, freedman of Pallas, and the nation of the Galileans to Ventidius Cumanus, after an uprising had arisen in Galilee. Josephus 20.

[Note: [Col. 0464C] 207 IV, 208 I] Peter 24, 25; Roman See 12, 13; Agrippa the Younger 4, 5; Cumanus’s procuratorship 1, 2; Quadratus’s administration 1, 2; Felix 1, 2. Ananias, Jewish high priest 4, [Col. 0464D] is sent to Rome in chains with the other defendants in the sedition. Josephus 20:5.

Cumanus is likewise summoned to Rome. There.

Paul, having spent eighteen months in Corinth from the year 50, comes to Ephesus. Acts 18 and 19:1, where he remains for two years. Acts 19:10.

[Note: [Col. 0464D] I II] Peter 25, 26; Roman See 13, 14; Quadratus’s administration 2, 3; King Agrippa 5, 6; Felix’s procuratorship 2, 3.

Saint Paul, from the house of Aquila and Priscilla, with whom he was staying in Asia Minor, sends his First Epistle to the Corinthians, as appears from the final chapter of that Epistle. [Col. 0466A]

In the twelfth year of Claudius’s reign, Claudius grants King Agrippa the tetrarchy of Philip, Batanaea, and the territories formerly belonging to Lysanias, Trachonitis, and Abilene. He takes Chalcis away from him, which Agrippa had governed for four years. Josephus 20:5.

[Note: [Col. 0466A] II III] Peter 26, 27; Roman See 14, 15; Quadratus’s administration 3, 4; Felix’s procuratorship [Col. 0466B] 3, 4; King Agrippa the Younger 6, 7.

After completing two years at Ephesus, Paul visits Macedonia and sails through Asia toward Syria. Acts 20.

When news of the Parthians reaches Rome, Nero, recently chosen, orders the allied kings Agrippa the Jew and Antiochus of Commagene to join their arms with his against the Parthians under Domitius Corbulo, whom he places in charge of retaining Armenia. Tacitus 13:6–8.

[Note: [Col. 0466B] III IV] Peter 27, 28; Roman See 15, 16; Quadratus’s procuratorship 4, 5; Felix’s procuratorship 4, 5; King Agrippa 7, 8, who has Jonathan, the Jewish high priest, killed by assassins. Ishmael, son of Phalai, succeeds him.

Paul goes to Jerusalem for the fifth time, around Pentecost. He is seized by the Jews and brought before Felix. Acts 24.

[Note: [Col. 0466C] 208 IV, 209 I] Peter 28, 29; Roman See 16, 17; Quadratus’s administration 5, 6; King Agrippa 8, 9.

Blessed Peter, having returned to Rome, sends his First Epistle to the elect of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, and elsewhere.

Portius Festus succeeds Felix in the procuratorship of Judea. Paul is brought before Felix’s tribunal. Acts 24. After presenting the case for the faith before Felix, his successor, and the king, he appeals to Caesar and is sent to Rome. Acts 25–26.

[Note: [Col. 0466D] I II] Peter 29, 30; Roman See 17, 18; Quadratus’s administration 6, 7; King Agrippa 9, 10; Festus’s procuratorship 1, 2; Ishmael’s high priesthood 1.

Peter appoints Linus as vicar, visits the western provinces, and establishes bishops in the cities.

As Paul approaches Rome, having reached Malta after the shipwreck [Col. 0468A], and then Syracuse and Puteoli, Roman believers meet him at the Forum of Appius and the Three Taverns. Acts 28.

[Note: [Col. 0468A] II III] Peter 30, 31; Roman See 18, 19; Quadratus’s administration 7, 8; King Agrippa 10, 11; Ishmael’s high priesthood 2.

For these two years [from his arrival in Rome], Paul remains in the City in a rented house and freely preaches Christ. From there he writes Epistles to the Galatians, Ephesians, Philippians, and Colossians; around this time he also writes the Acts of the Apostles. Luke likewise writes in the City.

Coins struck by Quadratus, governor of Syria, in Nero’s fourth year bear the inscription **ΕΠΙ ΚΟΥΑΔΡΑΤΟΥ ΕΥ. Δ.**—“under Quadratus, year 4.” See Noris, *Epochs of the Syro-Macedonians*.

[Note: [Col. 0468B] III IV] Peter 31, 32; Roman See 19, 20; Quadratus’s administration 8, 9; King Agrippa 11, 12; Ishmael’s Jewish high priesthood 2, 3.

The Apostle Peter, traversing the western provinces and appointing bishops in them, is also said to have penetrated as far as the Britons, as is related in the notes on p. 53 from ancient writers observed by Vendelinus.

[Note: [Col. 0468C] Olympiad 209 IV and, from the summer days, Olympiad 210 I] Peter 32, 33; Roman See 20, 21; Quadratus 9, 10; King Agrippa 12, 13. After removing Ishmael, Agrippa appoints Simon, son of Cabi, who had formerly been high priest, and soon afterward Ananus, or Ananias. Josephus 20:7–8. Ishmael the high priest was being detained at Rome by Caesar as a hostage, having been sent as an envoy to Nero concerning the dispute between the Jews and Festus the procurator.

[Note: [Col. 0468D] I II] Peter 33, 34; Roman See 21, 22.

After Quadratus has governed the province of Syria for ten years, Corbulo succeeds him.

After Festus has administered the procuratorship of Judea for six years, Albinus succeeds him.

King Agrippa, years 13, 14. At Ananus’s command, James the apostle is stoned to death [Col. 0470A]. Josephus 20:8. Jesus son of Damnaeus succeeds Ananus. There.

For the succession of Corbulo and Albinus, consult Cardinal Noris, *Cenotaphia Pisana*, p. 334.

[Note: [Col. 0470A] II III] Peter 34, 35; Roman See 22, 23; Corbulo 1, 2; King Agrippa 14, 15; Albinus’s procuratorship 1, 2; Jesus son of Damnaeus, high priest, Josephus 20:8.

Martyrdom of Saint Mark at Alexandria [Col. 0470B], with Anianus succeeding him, in Nero’s eighth year. Saint Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. After Evodius is killed at Antioch, Ignatius succeeds him.

Saint Peter returns to Rome to oppose Simon Magus. Theophilus in Malalas.

[Note: [Col. 0470B] III IV] Peter 35, 36; Roman See 23, 24; Corbulo 2, 3; King Agrippa 15, 16; Albinus’s procuratorship 2, 3; Jesus son of Damnaeus 2, 3.

Simon Magus, as blessed Peter prays, falls headlong to the ground.

Some attribute Paul’s journeys to Spain to the preceding two-year period [Col. 0470C], others to the present year. See the notes concerning the pontificate of Saint Clement.

[Note: [Col. 0470C] Olympiad 210 IV and, from the summer days, Olympiad 211 I. The Games transferred to the following year] Peter 36, 37; Roman See 24, 25; Corbulo, governor of Syria, 3, 5; King Agrippa 16, 17; Albinus’s procuratorship 3, 4.

Jesus son of Gamaliel becomes Jewish high priest and succeeds Jesus son of Damnaeus. Josephus 20:8.

In the consulship of these men, on the occasion of Nero’s fire in the City, the **FIRST PERSECUTION OF THE CHURCH**, undertaken by the Gentiles, rages cruelly. Tacitus, *Annals* 14:44.

The ordination of Saint Clement to the episcopate. See the notes concerning the pontificate of Saint Clement.

[Note: [Col. 0470D] Olympiad 211, postponed to this year I, from the summer days.] Peter 37, 38; Roman See 25.

The year ends on 25 April, and the martyrdom follows two months later, on 29 June, when Peter is crucified at the Vatican. Counting from 21 April, from which the years of the City are numbered, Peter is assigned 25 years, 2 months, and 7 days of the Roman See. See the notes concerning the pontificate of Saint Peter, and elsewhere.

[Col. 0472A] **YEAR 1 OF POPE LINUS.**

After the martyrdom of Blessed Peter, Linus is chosen as his successor on the following day, 30 June.

The Apostle Paul is beheaded on the same day on which Peter was crucified, in the thirty-seventh year after the Lord’s Passion. Saint Jerome.

King Agrippa removes Jesus son of Gamaliel and appoints Matthias son of Theophilus Jewish high priest. Josephus [Col. 0472B] 20:8.

[Note: [Col. 0472B] I II] Linus 1 and 2, beginning on 30 June.

C. Caestius Gallus, governor of Syria, year 1; King Agrippa, years 17, 18.

Gessius Florus, procurator of Judea, by his plundering and cruelty provides the occasion for the Jewish war. Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book 2, chapter 13. Matthias, Jewish high priest, years 1, 2.

Coins of this Caestius, struck in Antiochene Era ΡΙΔ 114, are published by Cardinal Noris in *Epochs of the Syro-Macedonians*.

[Col. 0472C] [Note: [Col. 0472C] II III] Linus 2, 3. After Linus is crowned with martyrdom on 23 September, Clement succeeds him beginning on 24 September.

From the episcopal ordination that he received in the year 59, on Sunday 23 June, under the consuls Saturninus and Scipio, Linus is assigned—according to the catalogue and the *Book of the Pontiffs*—12 years, 3 months, and 12 days. See the notes concerning the pontificate of Saint Linus.

C. Caestius Gallus 1, 2; King Agrippa 18, 19; Matthias, Jewish high priest, 3, 5.

[Note: [Col. 0472C] III IV] Clement 1, 2.

After Caestius Gallus dies in the province of Syria [Col. 0472D],

P. Licinius Mucianus is appointed successor, around autumn, as propraetor of Syria. He strikes a coin bearing Galba’s imperial title, dated in the Antiochene Era 117. See Noris, *Epochs of the Syro-Macedonians*, p. 165. King Agrippa 19, 20.

Matthias, high priest, 3, 4.

[Col. 0474A] [Note: [Col. 0474A] Olympiad 211 IV and, from the summer days, Olympiad 212 I] Pope Clement 2, 3; Mucianus, propraetor of Syria, 1, 2; Matthias, Jewish high priest, 4, 5.

This year, on the Kalends of July, T. Flavius Vespasianus, commander of the war against the Jews, with the support of the prefect of Egypt, Tiberius Alexander, and of Mucianus, legate of Syria, is hailed as emperor in Syria. When Mucianus advances against Vitellius with the army, Titus, Vespasian’s son, conducts the war in Judea, while Vespasian the father first heads to Egypt and then to Rome to receive the insignia of imperial power.

[Note: [Col. 0474B] I II] Pope Clement 3, 4.

A coin of Titus preserved in our museum, dated by two Antiochene eras—Caesarean 120 and Augustan 102—belongs to this year, during which all Syria had entered Vespasian’s allegiance before the Ides of July. Tacitus. After Jerusalem was captured, the Temple was burned 107 years after Herod’s reign had begun there [Josephus 20:8], on Saturday, the Kalends of September. Philostratus, *Life of Apollonius*. Phananus is appointed high priest of the Jews by the rebels in place of Matthias. Josephus, book 20, chapter 8, counts 84 high priests from Aaron to Phananus.

[Note: [Col. 0474C] II III] Pope Clement 4, 5.

Titus preserves the privileges of the Jews, although they had been defeated by him, despite the Alexandrians and Antiochenes pleading in vain that he abolish them. Josephus. See the notes, p. 11.

The triumph of Vespasian the father and Titus the son over conquered Judea takes place on the Kalends of July; on that occasion the tribunician power is conferred upon Titus by his father. Caesarea Maritima, where Vespasian had first been hailed emperor, becomes a Roman colony. See the coins of the colony in Vaillant and Reland, *On the Cities of Palestine*, book 3, p. 500.

[Note: [Col. 0474D] III IV] Pope Clement 5, 6.

Several buildings are constructed at Antioch. Malalas. Caesonius Paetus expels Antiochus, the last Seleucid king of Commagene, from his kingdom. [Col. 0476A] Antiochus flees to Cilicia, while his son flees to the Parthians. After both are reconciled with one another, Vespasian restores the kingdom to them. The Alans, a Scythian people near the Tanais, ravage Media while King Pacorus flees. When they invade Armenia, Tiridates resists them. Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book 7, chapter 27.

[Note: [Col. 0476A] Olympiad 212 IV and, from the summer days, Olympiad 213 I] Clement 6, 7.

Within this five-year period, from the year 71 to 75 of the Christian Era, while the Temple of Peace is being built at Rome, flatterers attribute to Vespasian, together with Josephus, book 7, chapter 12, the things foretold by the prophets concerning the Lord Christ, Prince of Peace. Clement, in the exercise of his pastoral office, correctly interprets the prophecies of Christ and thereby incurs the hatred of the pagans. See the notes concerning the pontificate of Saint Cletus.

[Note: [Col. 0476B] I II] Clement 7, 8.

Achaea, Greece, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium, Samos, Thrace, Cilicia, and Commagene, which had previously been under kings, are reduced to provinces. Eutropius and Rufus.

Europe is separated from Thrace. Heraclea is made the metropolis. Antioch and Caesarea are embellished. A magnificent odeum is built at Caesarea where the synagogue of the Jews had stood. John Malalas.

[Note: [Col. 0476C] II III] Clement 8, 9.

The occasion for Pope Clement’s exile arises from his declaration that the prophecies concerning Christ, the Prince of Peace, had been impiously distorted by flatterers and applied to Vespasian. See the notes cited above. The philosophers are likewise expelled from Rome. [Col. 0476D]

The expedition of Domitian, suffect consul for the fifth time, against the Sarmatians is attested by coins in Mediobarbus and by Josephus, *The Jewish War*, book 7, chapter 24.

[Note: [Col. 0476D] III IV] These consuls are assigned as the final consuls of Pope Clement in the Liberian Catalogue; under them he celebrated the final Passover of his pontificate. See the notes cited above. Clement abdicates the Roman pontificate on 3 December, having held it for 9 years, 2 months, and 10 days. See in the *Prolegomena* the chronological series of the Roman pontiffs and the notes concerning the pontificate of Saint Cletus, where the vacancy of the Roman See until 15 February of the following year is also discussed.

[Col. 0478A] [Note: [Col. 0478A] Olympiad 213 IV and, from the summer days, Olympiad 214] Cletus is elected and placed in the Roman See as Clement’s successor on Sunday, 16 February. From that day he held it for 6 years, 2 months, and 10 days, through the consuls of the year 83. See the *Prolegomena* and the notes cited above.

[Note: [Col. 0478B] I II] Cletus 1, 2.

Three cities of Cyprus collapse in an earthquake. Eusebius; Orosius.

[Col. 0478C] [Note: [Col. 0478C] II III] Cletus 2, 3.

A Temple of the Winds is built at Antioch by Vespasian near the theater.

John Malalas, p. 339.

[Col. 0478D] [Note: [Col. 0478D] III IV] Cletus 3, 4.

While the pagans restore their superstitious rites, which were destined to collapse, at the Capitol, Cletus, following the command of the Apostle Peter, fortifies the Roman Church with a permanent presbytery of twenty-five titular priests. The dedication of the Amphitheater and the Baths takes place under Titus and bears his own name. Dio, book 66.

Under these consuls, on 7 December, vows are made for the restoration and dedication of the Capitol by the emperor Titus Caesar Vespasian Augustus, and so forth. An ancient inscription in the Albani Museum, published by Bishop Filippo della Torre of Adria at the end of *Monumenta Veteris Antii*, p. 385.

[Note: [Col. 0480A] Olympiad 214 IV and, from the summer days, Olympiad 215 I] Cletus 4, 5.

Cletus opportunely takes advantage of Titus’s peaceful times [Col. 0480B] to organize the presbytery of the Roman Church, consisting permanently of twenty-five titular presbyters by command of the Prince of the Apostles, representing the universal Church through an equal number of priestly offices, as is explained more fully in the notes, pp. 37 and 232.

If, with Petavius, Suetonius is read as saying that Titus died in his forty-first year of life—not his forty-second, as nearly all manuscripts have it—the calculation is consistent. He is said to have been born on 30 December in the notable year of the death of Gaius, that is, two days before the Kalends of the January in which Gaius was killed.

[Note: [Col. 0480C] I II] Cletus 5, 6.

The philosophers are expelled from Italy by Domitian. Xiphilinus, excerpting Dio. Christians too, professing a virtue far superior to that of the philosophers, and for that reason confused by the pagans with the philosophers, experience Domitian’s harsher times. See the notes concerning the pontificate of Saint Cletus.

[Note: [Col. 0480C] II III] Cletus 6, 7; Anacletus, year 1, beginning on Sunday, 7 September. See the notes.

Cletus completes his martyrdom on 26 April, according to the Church Table, having held office for 6 years, 2 months, and 10 days, according to the Liberian Catalogue. The Roman See remains vacant until 7 September. See the notes concerning the pontificate of Saint Anacletus.

These consuls, under whom Cletus celebrated the final Passover of his administration, are assigned as the final consuls in the Catalogues and manuscripts. See the notes and the *Prolegomena*.

[Note: [Col. 0480D] III IV] Anacletus 1, 2.

These consuls are assigned as Anacletus’s first consuls in the Liberian Catalogue and the manuscripts cited in the *Prolegomena* [Col. 0482A] folio VII and in the notes mentioned above; under them he celebrated the first Passover of his pontificate.

[Note: [Col. 0482A] Olympiad 215 IV and, from the summer days, Olympiad 216 I] Anacletus 2, 3.

At Antioch, by the order and at the expense both of Domitian and of his freedman Paris, baths and magnificent buildings are constructed. John Malalas, *Chronography*, book 10.

[Note: [Col. 0482B] I II] Anacletus 3, 4.

The Capitol, which had burned during Titus’s reign, is restored and dedicated this year by Domitian. Plutarch, in *Publicola*, writes that it was gilded at a cost of 12,000 talents; Calvisius reckons this sum as twelve million.

In the same year Domitian establishes the Capitoline **AGON**, a quinquennial festival modeled on the Olympiads, recurring every four years in each fifth year. See Noris, *Epochs of the Syro-Macedonians*, pp. 328, 330, and the inscription in Gruter, p. 314, where it is indicated.

[Note: [Col. 0482C] II III] Anacletus 4, 5.

Anacletus erects a monument more enduring than the Capitol of the pagans, namely the Apostles’ Trophy, or a small shrine in the Vatican at the site of the martyrdom of Blessed Peter—the beginning of a Christian structure to be enlarged by his successors for the praise of God and in honor of the Prince of the Apostles.

Domitian orders himself to be called god and lord. Eusebius assigns this to the sixth year of his reign.

This may perhaps have provided the occasion for the second persecution against Christians, who reserved supreme worship for God alone.

[Col. 0484A] [Note: [Col. 0484A] III IV] Anacletus 5, 6.

Do not refer the consulship of Domitian and Rufus, which the Roman catalogues assign as Cletus’s final pontifical consuls, to this Rufus or to Domitian’s fourteenth consulship, but to Domitian’s ninth, in which he had Q. Petilius Rufus II as colleague, in the year 83 of the Christian Era, as is clear from the immediately following consuls assigned to his successor. See the notes concerning the pontificate of Saint Cletus.

[Col. 0484B] [Note: [Col. 0484B] Olympiad 216 IV and, from the summer days, Olympiad 217 I] Anacletus 6, 7.

Eusebius assigns to this eighth year of Domitian the slaughter of nobles and the expulsion of the philosophers from the City by the same prince. After returning to Rome, Domitian celebrates a ridiculous triumph over the Dacians, according to Xiphilinus’s excerpts from Dio, book 67. Coins.

Domitian mocks Apollonius of Tyana by having his beard cut off. Philostratus, in his *Life*.

[Note: [Col. 0484B] I II] Anacletus 7, 8.

[Col. 0484C] Apollonius of Tyana travels to Antioch and increases the superstitious rites there; soon afterward he heads to Egypt. Malalas, *Chronology*, book 10.

[Note: [Col. 0484C] II III] Anacletus 8, 9.

The era of Capitoliadis [Claudia] in Coele-Syria begins in this year or the next, according to the coins. See Cardinal Noris, *Epochs of the Syro-Macedonians*, p. 331.

[Note: [Col. 0484C] III IV] Anacletus 9, 10.

The mathematician Agrippa in Bithynia observed the Moon in conjunction with the Pleiades on 29 November, at the third hour, at the beginning of the night, five equal hours before midnight. Ptolemy, book 7, chapter 3, correlating it with the 811th year of Nabonassar. Second of Tybi.

[Note: [Col. 0484D] Olympiad 217 VI and, from the summer days, Olympiad 218 I] Anacletus 10, 11.

**SECOND PERSECUTION OF THE CHURCH**, concerning which Tertullian writes *Against the Jews*. He also asserts that Saint John the Apostle was cast into a cauldron of boiling oil [Col. 0486A], escaped unharmed, and was thereafter banished to the island of Patmos; Jerome and Eusebius likewise affirm this.

The era of Anazarbus is to be reckoned from this point, according to coins of Trajan and Hadrian, era 25.

[Note: [Col. 0486A] I II] Anacletus 11, 12.

Around this time Blessed John the Apostle is banished to the island of Patmos and writes the Apocalypse, which Justin Martyr [Col. 0486B] and Irenaeus interpreted shortly afterward. See the notes concerning the pontificate of Saint Anacletus, near the end.

[Note: [Col. 0486B] II III] Anacletus 12, 13.

Amid the dangers of the persecution, Bishop Evaristus is ordained on Sunday, 25 March, the anniversary of the Incarnation, and is appointed vicar by Anacletus. See the notes concerning the pontificate of Evaristus himself.

[Col. 0486C] [Note: [Col. 0486C] III IV] Anacletus 13. In this year the blessed pontiff completes his martyrdom on 13 July, having held office for 12 years, 10 months, and 8 days. See the *Prolegomena* and the notes.

Evaristus is chosen as successor; he had been appointed vicar by Anacletus and ordained bishop in the preceding year.

[Col. 0486D] Clement is killed this year; he had held the consulship with Domitian in the immediately preceding year. Flavia Domitilla also suffers martyrdom, as did that Clement, a relative of Domitian.

[Note: [Col. 0486D] Olympiad 218 IV and, from the summer days, Olympiad 219 I] Evaristus 1, 2.

John the Apostle returns to Ephesus and governs the churches of Asia. Eusebius in the *Chronicle*; according to Baronius, he also protects those churches against the heresies that arose there.

[Col. 0488A] [Note: [Col. 0488A] I II] Evaristus 2, 3.

Menelaus the astronomer observes at Rome that Spica of Virgo, having been occulted by the Moon for five hours, reemerges at the sixth hour after midnight. Ptolemy, *Almagest*, book 6, chapter 7.

From the astronomical tables it is gathered that this occurred on the 11th [Col. 0488B] of January, in the morning. He calls this the 845th year of Nabonassar, day 16 of Mechir.

[Note: [Col. 0488B] II III] Evaristus 3, 4.

Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist dies at Ephesus. Saint Jerome and Eusebius in the *Chronicle*.

[Note: [Col. 0488B] III V] Evaristus 4, 5.

Saint Clement, exiled at Chersona, dies a martyr this year, in the third year of Trajan’s reign, according to Eusebius and Saint Jerome in the *Chronicle*. See the notes concerning the pontificate of Saint Clement.

[Col. 0488C] Pliny the Younger, in January, when he had been designated consul for the Kalends of September, accuses Marius Priscus before Trajan, who was consul for the third time. Pliny, *Letters*, book 2, letter 11; book 6, letter 20. See Noris, *Epistola Consulares*, p. 69.

[Note: [Col. 0488C] Olympiad 219, year IV and, from the summer days, Olympiad 220 I] Pope Evaristus 5 and 6, after 13 July.

According to a coin of Trajan bearing the sign **TIGRIS**, with the titles IMP. III, TR. P. IV, Mediobarbus argues that some victory was won by Trajan through his legates this year in the region of Mesopotamia or Parthia. John Malalas, [Col. 0488D] *Chronography*, book 11, reports several Parthian uprisings under Trajan but assigns them to his twelfth year.

[Note: [Col. 0488D] I II] Evaristus 6, 7.

In the City of Rome, Evaristus distributes the titular churches among the presbyters and the regions among seven principal deacons, whom he orders to be present when the bishop preaches. The Bibliothecarius.

[Col. 0490A] [Note: [Col. 0490A] II III] Evaristus 7, 8.

**Trajan’s Dacian Victory**

Decebalus comes humbly before Trajan. Trajan brings his envoys, who had been sent to seek peace, to Italy before the Senate. After peace is established, Trajan triumphs and is called **Dacicus**. See Fabretti, *On Trajan’s Colony*, p. 275.

[Note: [Col. 0490B] III IV] Evaristus 8, 9.

Decebalus violates the peace treaties and is again declared an enemy.

[Col. 0490C] [Note: [Col. 0490C] Olympiad 220, year IV and, from the summer days, Olympiad 221 I] Evaristus 9, 10.

The second Dacian war.

At the same time Palma, governor of Syria, reduces the Arabs of Bostra to the power of the Roman people. Mediobarbus, from coins, and Dio. Hence Trajan is called Emperor V. See Fabretti, *On Trajan’s Colony*, p. 290.

[Col. 0490D] [Note: [Col. 0490D] I II] Evaristus 10, 11.

At the beginning of the persecution under Trajan, Evaristus ordains Alexander bishop on Sunday, 27 September, to serve as vicar. See the notes, p. 81, column 1, where the error in the final line should be corrected and one should read: “in the year 106, on Sunday, 27 September.” From that day until the martyrdom of Pope Alexander, the paintings of Saint Paul assign him ten years, seven months, and three days of episcopate. Perhaps “six days” should be read; for that is the number that elapses from 27 September 106 to 3 May 117, the day on which his feast is celebrated.

[Note: [Col. 0492A] I III] Evaristus 11, 12.

The *Acts of the Martyrs, Genuine and Selected*, by R. Father Martène, pp. 11 and 696, state that Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, suffered martyrdom this year, the ninth year of Trajan’s reign. Others, following Pagius, place it in the year 112.

Arabia is acquired, and Trajan obtains the title Emperor VI through Palma. Coins in Fabretti, *On Trajan’s Colony*, p. 290.

[Note: [Col. 0492B] III IIII] Evaristus 12, 13; Alexander I.

These consuls are assigned as Evaristus’s final consuls. He is crowned with martyrdom on 26 October and, from his ordination, is credited with thirteen years, six months, and two days of episcopate, including the final days, according to the Catalogue and the paintings. See the *Prolegomena*, folio LXXXIX, and the notes, p. 76. Counting from Anacletus’s death, he is credited with thirteen years, two months, and twelve days of Roman pontificate. Around this time Alexander is chosen as Evaristus’s successor [Col. 0492C] and placed in Peter’s chair on Sunday, 3 December of this year. From that date he holds the Roman See for nine years and five months, until his martyrdom on 3 May 117.

[Note: [Col. 0492C] Olympiad 221 IIII and, from the summer days, Olympiad 222 I] Pope Alexander 1, 2.

These consuls are assigned as Pope Alexander’s first consuls, under whom he celebrated the Passover of his administration, according to the established Paschal rule. See the notes, p. 76. Around this time the Bithynian legation of C. Pliny the Younger is to be placed, on the basis of documents published by Cardinal Noris, *Epistolae Consulares*, p. 70. From there he writes to Trajan concerning the regulation of punishments for Christians, book 10, letter 97.

[Note: [Col. 0492D] I II] Pope Alexander 2, 3.

In Bithynia the number of Christians increases astonishingly. Pliny, *Letters*, book 10, letters 97–98.

[Col. 0494A] [Note: [Col. 0494A] II III] Pope Alexander 3, 4.

Pope Alexander greatly advances the Christian religion in the City, bringing a large part of the Roman nobility to Christ. The Bibliothecarius in his *Life*. See the notes, p. 82.

[Note: [Col. 0494B] III IIII] Pope Alexander 4, 5.

Idatius writes in the *Fasti* concerning this year: “Under these consuls there was a persecution of the Christians.”

Trajan’s expedition for the Parthian and Armenian war, because the king of the Armenians had received the diadem not from Trajan but from [Col. 0494C] the king of the Parthians. Dio, book 68. See Cardinal Noris, *Epistolae Consulares*, p. 72.

[Note: [Col. 0494C] Olympiad 222 IV and, from the summer days, Olympiad 223 I] Pope Alexander 5, 6.

Armenia [formerly “of Armenia”] and Mesopotamia were reduced to the power of the Roman people. Ancient coins and Dio, book 68. John Malalas presents different names of the Armenian and Parthian—or Persian—kings with whom Trajan waged these wars. After departing from Antioch, he occupied Samosata and Commagene within two years and extended the boundaries of the Roman Empire into Mesopotamia.

[Note: [Col. 0494D] I II] Pope Alexander, years 6 and 7.

Assyria was reduced to Roman control. Ancient coins. When Trajan advanced into Armenia, he expelled Parthamasaris and made the country a Roman province. After entering Mesopotamia, he was splendidly received by King Abgar, and confirmed him in his kingdom. Then, after conquering Nisibis and Batnae, cities between the Tigris and Euphrates held by the king of the Parthians, he was called *Parthicus* by the army, though not yet by the Senate. See Cardinal Noris, *Epistola consularis*, p. 73.

[Note: [Col. 0496A] II III] Pope Alexander, years 6 and 7.

A large part of the Roman nobility was converted to the faith of Christ through Pope Alexander. See the notes, p. 82.

Antioch was shaken by an earthquake. Dio and Malalas, who also gives the date: 13 December of the Antiochene era, year 164.

The island of Rhodes was likewise shaken. The consul Pedo was crushed beneath the ruins at Antioch while accompanying Trajan. Dio, book 68.

The Jews, rioting in Mesopotamia and Egypt, suffered an enormous slaughter. See also Eusebius, book 4 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 2.

[Note: [Col. 0496B] III IV] Alexander, years 7 and 8.

These were the last consuls assigned to Alexander. See the *Prolegomena*, fol. XC.

As the persecution by the magistrates intensified during Trajan’s absence from the city, Sixtus was marked out for episcopal ordination by Alexander on Sunday, 14 December. See the notes, p. 89. He was appointed vicar while Alexander, detained in prison, was prevented from performing several duties. There.

[Note: [Col. 0496C] Olympiad 222, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 223, first year] Pope Alexander, year 9; Pope Sixtus, year 1.

Saint Alexander, in the ninth year of his pontificate, but after ten years, seven months, and three days—or, more accurately, six days—from his episcopal ordination, was crowned with martyrdom on 3 May. See the notes, pp. 80 and 85, based on the paintings and catalogues. Saint Sixtus was elected as his successor and placed in the apostolic see on Sunday, 7 June. These consuls are assigned to him as his first.

Coins of the Tripolitans in Syria, struck under both Trajan and Hadrian, with the same era, 428, marked “HKY,” confirm Hadrian’s succession in this year. See Cardinal Noris, *Epistola Syriaca*, p. 99. The greatest slaughter of the Jews. Spartianus.

[Note: [Col. 0496D] I II] Sixtus, years 1 and 2.

Petavius assigned the fourth persecution of the Church to this year in his *Chronology*.

Hadrian appointed Catilius Severus governor of Syria. Spartianus.

The same emperor granted Cosdroes, king of the Persians, three provinces beyond the Euphrates, previously acquired by Trajan: Greater Armenia, Assyria, and Mesopotamia.

[Note: [Col. 0498B] II III] Sixtus, years 2 and 3.

Petavius, drawing on Eusebius, reports that the rioting Jews were suppressed in this year by Tinius Rufus, governor of Judaea.

[Note: [Col. 0498B] III IV] Sixtus, years 3 and 4.

War was waged against the Sarmatians. Advancing against the Sarmatians, Hadrian went to Moesia and made peace with the king of the Roxolani. Occo and Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

[Note: [Col. 0498C] Olympiad 224, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 225, first year] Sixtus, years 4 and 5.

When Nicomedia and the neighboring cities had been overthrown by an earthquake, Hadrian contributed generously from the public treasury for their restoration. Eusebius, *Chronicle*.

[Note: [Col. 0498D] I II] Sixtus, years 5 and 6.

Hadrian ordered colonies to be settled in Libya, which had been devastated by the Jews. Occo and Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

[Note: [Col. 0500A] II III] Sixtus, years 6 and 7.

Saturninus of Antioch, Basilides of Alexandria, and Carpocrates were heretics and founders of the abominable Gnostic sect. Epiphanius and Eusebius, book 4 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapters 7 and 8.

[Note: [Col. 0500B] III IV] Sixtus, years 7 and 8.

Quadratus, a disciple of the Apostles, and Aristides of Athens, a philosopher, presented works in defense of the Christian religion to Hadrian. Serenus Granianus sent the same emperor a letter on behalf of the Christians. Hadrian himself wrote to Minucius Fundanus, proconsul of Asia, that Christians were not to be condemned without charges being brought against them. Petavius, from Eusebius’ *Chronicle* and *Ecclesiastical History*.

[Note: [Col. 0500B] Olympiad 225, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 226, first year] Sixtus, years 8 and 9.

[Col. 0500C] The moon was eclipsed in Nabonassar year 872, Pachon 17, at 8:24 in the afternoon at Alexandria—that is, 5 April, Wednesday. Petavius, from Ptolemy, book 4, chapter 9.

[Note: [Col. 0500C] I II] Sixtus, years 9 and 10.

While Hadrian’s persecution had not yet ceased, Sixtus ordained Telesphorus bishop this year, on Sunday, 16 September. These were the last consuls assigned to Sixtus, under whom he celebrated the final Easter of his pontificate. See the *Prolegomena*, p. XC, and the notes, p. 86 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0500D] II III] Sixtus, year 10; Telesphorus, first year from 5 April.

Sixtus was crowned with martyrdom on 3 April, in the tenth year of his see, which had not yet been completed; but the catalogues and paintings assign him ten years, three months, and twenty-one days from his episcopal ordination. Telesphorus was elected as successor on 5 April and raised to the chair on Sunday, 7 April. Therefore these consuls, under whom he celebrated the first Easter of his pontificate, are assigned to him in the catalogues and manuscripts. See the notes, p. 96.

Hadrian, setting out again for the East, erected a temple to Olympian Jupiter at Athens and an altar to himself. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

[Note: [Col. 0502A] III IV] Telesphorus, years 1 and 2.

Hadrian invited the kings of Asia to friendship, among them Cosrhoes of the Parthians, returning his daughter, whom Trajan had captured. Mediobarbus, in his discussion of the coins for this year.

Nicopolis and Caesarea collapsed in an earthquake. Eusebius.

Aquila of Pontus, a proselyte who had changed from Christian to Jew, translated the Scriptures into Greek. Petavius for this year, from Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*.

[Note: [Col. 0502B] Olympiad 228, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 229, first year] Telesphorus, years 2 and 3.

Hadrian is said to have set out from Asia for Egypt in this year, which Eusebius numbers as the first year of Olympiad 227 and the thirteenth of Hadrian’s reign. See C. Noris, *Epochs of the Syro-Macedonian Era*, p. 498.

[Col. 0502C] Hadrian attempted to separate Syria from Phoenicia, out of hatred for the Antiochenes. Mediobarbus for this year.

[Note: [Col. 0502C] I II] Telesphorus, years 3 and 4.

After restoring Jerusalem, Hadrian gave it the name Aelia Capitolina and settled a colony there. The Jews, distressed that Gentiles were being placed in their city, began at first to stir secretly. Petavius for this year, from Spartianus. The same emperor, setting out for Arabia, came to Pelusium and there built a more magnificent tomb for Pompey. There; from Dio, book 69.

[Note: [Col. 0502D] II III] Telesphorus, years 4 and 5.

Petavius and Mediobarbus, from coins, as well as Calvisius, assign to this year Hadrian’s arrival in Egypt, the drowning of Antinous, and the foundation of the city of Antinoopolis, named after him. See Spartianus and Dio, book 69.

[Note: [Col. 0504A] III IV] Telesphorus, years 5 and 6.

Hadrian returned from Egypt to Syria and then to Greece. Meanwhile the Jews rebelled under the leadership of Cocheba, or Barchocheba, who, because the Christians refused to provide him assistance against the Romans, tortured them in various ways. Eusebius, *Chronicle* and book 4 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 6; and Petavius from him. Severus was sent from Britain against them. Dio, book 69. The autumn equinox was observed by Ptolemy in Nabonassar year 870, Athyr 7. *Prologue*, book 3, chapter 8.

[Note: [Col. 0504B] Olympiad 228, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 229] Telesphorus, years 6 and 7.

Julius Severus, a Roman commander, attacked the Jews one by one and, though belatedly, crushed them with less danger. Petavius, from Dio, book 69.

A lunar eclipse was recorded in Hadrian’s seventeenth year, Nabonassar year 880, Payni 30, at 15:16 after noon—namely, 6 May, Tuesday.

Petavius, from the *Prologue*, book 4, chapter 6, and Calvisius, who also adds observations of Jupiter and Saturn for this year. He found the observations marked in the *Prologue* to agree with the tables.

[Note: [Col. 0504C] I II] Telesphorus, years 7 and 8.

The moon was eclipsed in Nabonassar year 882, Choiak 2, at 11 o’clock after noon—that is, 20 October, Tuesday.

Petavius, from Ptolemy at that place; Calvisius adds observations of Venus and Mercury from the same Ptolemy.

Marcion began to publish his heresy around this time, as we showed in the annotations on Epiphanius, p. 83. The same is stated by Petavius.

[Note: [Col. 0504D] II III] Telesphorus, years 8 and 9.

The Romans besieged Bethar and finally captured it. Thus, after the leaders of the faction had been killed and 580,000 Jews had been slain, the war was brought to an end, so that Judaea was almost entirely deserted. From then on, Jews were forbidden access to the territory of Jerusalem. Dio, book 69; Eusebius, book 4 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 6.

[Col. 0506A] When all those of the circumcision had perished, the first bishop of Jerusalem from the Gentiles was Marcus. Eusebius, *Chronicle* and book 4 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 6; Petavius.

[Note: [Col. 0506A] III VI] Telesphorus, years 9 and 10.

Pharasmanes, king of the Iberians, incited the Alans against the Romans. But Flavius Arrianus, governor of Cappadocia, restrained them. At last Pharasmanes came to Rome and had his authority increased. Petavius, from Dio.

Calvisius reports from Ptolemy the observations made in this year: a lunar eclipse, “XX, Hadr. no. 5” [uncertain], on 19 Pharmuthi—or 6 March—at the fourth hour after midnight at Alexandria, of six digits; Saturn at 14° Capricorn on 24 Mesori—or 8 July; Jupiter at 8° Pisces on 13 Paophi—or 31 August; Venus at 19° Aquarius on 9 Mechir—or 25 December.

[Note: [Col. 0506B] Olympiad 228, year 3, and from the summer days of Olympiad 229, first year] Telesphorus, years 10 and 11.

These consuls are assigned as the last to Telesphorus in the Liberian catalogue; under them, as the year-marker, he celebrated the final Easter of his pontificate.

Hyginus was marked out for episcopal ordination on Sunday, 30 September; from that date until his martyrdom, four years, three months, and eight days of episcopate are counted, as they are to be assigned to him from the paintings of Saint Paul and the manuscripts. See the notes, p. 105, and the *Prolegomena*, fol. XC.

[Note: [Col. 0506C] I II] Telesphorus was crowned with martyrdom on 5 January, in the eleventh year of his pontificate, which had not yet been completed; but from his episcopal ordination he had completed eleven years, three months, and twenty days.

Hyginus was chosen as his successor and began to sit on Sunday, 6 January. See the notes, p. 96.

The catalogue of Felix IV names Magnus and Camerinus as the first consuls of Hyginus’ pontificate, in the year in which he celebrated the first Easter of his pontificate. See the *Prolegomena* and the notes on Felix IV.

[Col. 0508A] [Note: [Col. 0508A] II III] Hyginus, years 1 and 2.

At the beginning of Antoninus’ reign, Justin Martyr published his first apology for the Christians, which is commonly numbered as the second. Petavius’ *Chronology* and annotations on Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 46, p. 85, should be consulted. Ptolemy, book 9, chapter 9, observed Mercury this year on 17 May at 17°30′ Gemini; he calls it Antoninus’ second year, Nabonassar year 886, Epiphi 2. Ten days later he observed Mars at 1°33′ Sagittarius, agreeing with the table, according to Calvisius and others.

[Note: [Col. 0508B] III IV] Hyginus, years 2 and 3.

The arrival of Valentinus, the heresiarch, in Rome in the third year of Antoninus Pius. Ptolemy’s observations, compared by Calvisius with the astronomical tables, belong to this year: Venus at 13°45′ Aries on 18 February, and on 30 July at approximately 18°30′ Gemini. The spring equinox occurred on 21 March at one hour after noon, where Calvisius thinks there is some error; likewise, he thinks there is a slight error in the summer solstice on 25 June.

[Note: [Col. 0508C] Olympiad 229, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 230, first year] Hyginus, years 3 and 4.

The final consuls of Hyginus’ pontificate, from the documents cited on pp. 101, 105, 110 and following, are discussed in the notes, which should be consulted. Since Hyginus was to suffer martyrdom at the beginning of the following year, he celebrated his final Easter under these consuls. The lacunae of the Liberian catalogue, wrongly supplied by copyists, are to be restored as on p. 112 of the notes. There, too, the names of the consuls in the catalogue lacunae—confused because of the similarity of words and family names—are restored from epigraphic evidence.

On Easter Day, 10 April, Pius was ordained as the future vicar of Hyginus. See the notes, p. 121.

[Note: [Col. 0508D] I II] Hyginus, year 4; Pope Pius, year 1.

Hyginus completed his martyrdom around 8 January; he was buried in the Vatican cemetery on 11 January, in the fourth year of his see, completed with five days. But from the episcopal ordination he had received, he had completed four years, three months, and eight days, which the catalogues and Anastasius assign to him, as we have shown there, pp. 101 and 112 of the notes.

Calvisius observes from Eusebius that the beginning of Pius’ pontificate is also assigned to these consuls. For Hyginus’ successor was elected on Sunday, 9 April, and placed in Peter’s chair. See the notes.

[Note: [Col. 0510B] II III] Pius, years 1 and 2.

Marcion, who had come to Rome during the vacancy of the Roman see in the preceding year, sowed the seeds of his heresy around this time, according to Tertullian’s testimony against him. See the notes on Pius I. Valentinus, the heresiarch who had come to the city in the third year of Antoninus Pius, had preceded him. See above, under the year 140. Antoninus prohibited the reading of the Sibylline poems and of Cicero’s books *On the Nature of the Gods*, *On Divination*, and others, because they seemed to undermine the fictions of their gods. Calvisius, from Justin’s *Apology* and Arnobius.

[Note: [Col. 0510C] III IIII] Pius, years 2 and 3.

Valentinus of Egypt, Cerdo, and Marcion, through their blasphemies, provided the occasion for Potitus, Blastus, Synerotus, Prepon, and Python, who followed shortly afterward. Theodoretus; see Pagius under the years 143 and 144.

[Col. 0510D] [Note: [Col. 0510D] Olympiad 230, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 231, first year] Pius, years 3 and 4.

Taurus of Beirut, a Platonic philosopher, is said to have flourished in this year according to Eusebius in the *Chronicle*.

[Col. 0512A] [Note: [Col. 0512A] I II] Pius, years 4 and 5.

The worship of Serapis is said to have been restored in the city under these consuls, according to Calvisius, on the testimony of an ancient inscription identifying this year.

[Col. 0512B] [Note: [Col. 0512B] II III] Pius, years 5 and 6.

Arrianus, a philosopher of Nicomedia; Maximus of Tyre; Apollonius of Chalcis, a Stoic; and Basilides of Scythopolis were distinguished philosophers who had been teachers of Caesar Verissimus; Sextus of Chaeronea, the nephew of Plutarch, should also be included among them. Volusianus Martianus, a jurist, also flourished. The Latin grammarians were Aper, Pollio, Eutychius, Proculus, and Siccensis. Fronto Cornelius was also an orator. Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Time*, from Capitolinus and Eusebius.

[Note: [Col. 0512C] III IV] Pius, years 6 and 7.

Anicetus was ordained bishop on Sunday, 14 December. See the notes, p. 121.

Because the lacunae of the Liberian catalogue had been wrongly supplied by copyists, these consuls are wrongly transferred to the summary of Hyginus; they must be restored to the ordination of Anicetus. See the notes, pp. 104 and 120.

[Col. 0512D] [Note: [Col. 0512D] Olympiad 231, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 232, first year] Pius, years 7 and 8.

Anicetus was ordained bishop under these consuls, on Sunday, 15 December. Since this date is expressed according to Roman practice as the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January, which Gallicanus and Veter were about to open as consuls, the names of the consuls Gallicanus and Veter appear in certain catalogues. They were confused with the beginning of Hyginus and transferred to his summary in the wrongly supplied lacunae of the Liberian catalogue; in fact they belong to the indication of Pius’ ordination. See the notes and the *Prolegomena*.

[Col. 0514B] [Note: [Col. 0514B] I II] Pius, years 8 and 9; Anicetus, year 1.

Saint Pius completed his martyrdom on 11 July, after sitting for eight years, three months, and three days from his election to the Roman pontificate; but from his episcopal ordination, nine years, three months, and two days, including the terminal days. See the notes.

Anicetus, Pius’ successor, was elected two days after his death, on Sunday, 13 July. From that date to the day of his martyrdom, 17 April 161, eleven years of his see are counted. See the notes, pp. 95, 112, 113, 117, and 121. There it is shown that from his ordination on 15 December 149 to his martyrdom on 17 April 161, the eleven years, three months, and three days expressed in the catalogues and the paintings of Saint Paul are correctly calculated.

[Note: [Col. 0514C] II III] Anicetus, years 1 and 2.

Crescens, an impure man and adherent of the Cynic sect, flourished. Since he was hostile to Justin, he eventually brought about Justin’s martyrdom at a later time. Calvisius, who also assigns Justin’s *Apology* to the immediately preceding year.

[Col. 0514D] [Note: [Col. 0514D] III IV] Anicetus, years 2 and 3.

Calvisius writes from Justin that persecution was prohibited by Antoninus in this year and that the accusers of Christians were ordered to suffer punishment. The reason added was that Christians could not be destroyed by punishments, since they themselves preferred death to life.

[Col. 0516A] [Note: [Col. 0516A] Olympiad 232, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 233, first year] Anicetus, years 3 and 4.

After peace had been restored by Antoninus, the Christian Churches flourished. Tonsure was prescribed for the clergy. Inquiry was made concerning the observance of Easter. See the notes, p. 114.

[Col. 0516B] [Note: [Col. 0516B] I II] Anicetus, years 4 and 5.

The gap in Roman history under Antoninus Pius clearly suggests that it was deliberately suppressed because of the zeal of the pagans, so that his equitable decrees and examples toward the Christians would not be exposed to posterity.

[Note: [Col. 0516B] II III] Anicetus, years 5 and 6.

Cassianus is said to have succeeded Marcus at Jerusalem in this year, according to Eusebius, as noted by Calvisius.

[Col. 0516C] [Note: [Col. 0516C] III IV] Anicetus, years 6 and 7.

Under Antoninus Pius, the only senator proscribed at Rome was Attilius Titianus, punished by the Senate because he was accused of aspiring to tyranny. Capitolinus, in Calvisius’ account of this year. It therefore becomes clear why, under Antoninus Pius, long after the first *Apology*, Justin was preserved—although Crescens the Cynic was indignant—and why Anicetus was pontiff while Antoninus was still alive, as were Polycarp, Irenaeus, and other distinguished Christian men known for their deeds and writings.

[Note: [Col. 0516D] Olympiad 233, sixth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 234, first year] Anicetus, years 7 and 8.

Nothing certain is known about these consuls or about what was done in their year. Lydiatus in the *Fasti*. But something concerning the consuls is certain from the clay tablets and inscriptions reported by Fabretti and Sponius; from them we have already learned something about what occurred in their year. Suarez, *Ancient Praeneste*, p. 51, should also be consulted.

[Note: [Col. 0518A] I II] Anicetus, years 8 and 9.

Saint Polycarp came to Rome because of the questions concerning Easter, according to Eusebius and the Alexandrian *Chronicle*. When Marcion met him and said, “Recognize us,” Polycarp replied, “I recognize you as the firstborn of Satan.” Saint Irenaeus, in Eusebius.

[Note: [Col. 0518B] II III] A council concerning the celebration of Easter was held at Rome around this year, with Saint Polycarp and ten other bishops attending. From the *Synodicon*, cited by Pagius. See the notes on Anicetus.

[Col. 0518C] [Note: [Col. 0518C] III III] Anicetus, years 10 and 11.

Around this time the Bactrians, Hyrcanians, and Indians are said to have sent ambassadors to the emperor Antoninus. Lydiatus in the *Fasti*, from the epitome of Sextus Aurelius Victor.

[Note: [Col. 0518C] Olympiad 234, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 235, first year] Anicetus, year 11. After the death of Antoninus Pius,

Anicetus completed his martyrdom on 17 April, in the eleventh year of his Roman pontificate, which had not yet been completed; but from his episcopal ordination, eleven years, three months, and twenty days—or, according to other catalogues, eleven years, four months, and three days. See the notes, p. 112. Soter was elected as his successor toward the end of the year.

The coins of Orthosia, in Cardinal Noris, p. 104, and of Capitoliades, *Syro-Macedonian Era*, p. 325, are dated to year 92.

[Col. 0520A] [Note: [Col. 0520A] I II] Soter, year 1, from the Kalends of January.

Soter, elected Anicetus’ successor toward the end of the year 161, was ordained bishop and placed in Peter’s See on the Kalends of January, the eighth day of the Lord’s Nativity, or on the Sunday immediately preceding the Kalends of January. His era of the see, calculated from the Kalends of January as the beginning of the Roman civil year, amounts to nine years, three months, and twenty-one days up to the day of his martyrdom, 22 April 171, as indicated in several catalogues. See the notes, pp. 132 and 137.

Vologaeses, king of the Parthians, devastated Syria and occupied Armenia. Lucius Verus set out for the Parthian and Armenian war.

[Note: [Col. 0520B] II III] Soter, year 2.

Armenia was captured through the legate Priscus.

The Parthians were driven back beyond the Euphrates. Vologaeses was defeated by Cassius. Marcus Aurelius was called *Armeniacus*, according to Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

[Col. 0520C] [Note: [Col. 0520C] III IV] Soter, year 3.

The martyrdom of Saint Polycarp must be assigned to this year. See the notes, p. 133.

A king was appointed for the Armenians. From coins and historical sources.

[Note: [Col. 0520C] Olympiad 235, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 236, first year] Soter, year 4.

The legate Cassius penetrated into Mesopotamia and Assyria, captured Seleucia, and ravaged Ctesiphon. Hence both Augusti were called *Parthicus Maximus* and were styled *Imperator* for the third time. Mediolanum, from coins and historical sources.

[Note: [Col. 0520D] I II] Soter, year 5.

Under the city prefect Urbicus, several martyrdoms are reported in this year by Ruinartius. See the note, p. 138.

Marcius Verus invaded the Medes. Lucius Verus again set out for the Euphrates and successfully conducted the campaign against the barbarians through his legates; both Augusti were called *Imperator* for the fourth time. From coins and historical sources, Mediobarbus.

[Col. 0522A] [Note: [Col. 0522A] II III] Soter, year 6.

The martyr Pionius received the crown in this year.

According to Ruinartius, Justin’s martyrdom should also be assigned to this year. See the notes on Soter.

[Col. 0522B] [Note: [Col. 0522B] III IIII] Soter, year 7.

Avidius Cassius defeated the Arabs and the Bucolic people in Egypt.

Hence both Augusti were styled *Imperator* for the fifth time. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

[Note: [Col. 0522B] Olympiad 236, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 237, first year] Soter, year 8.

Melito, bishop of Sardis, published an apology on behalf of the Christians. Eusebius, *Chronicle* and *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 25. At the same time Apollinaris of Hierapolis and Miltiades wrote on behalf of the Christians; Praÿtus, bishop of Gnosia; Philippus, bishop of Gortyna; and Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, also wrote. Petavius, for the following year, from Jerome’s account of the Church.

[Note: [Col. 0522B] I II] Soter, year 9.

These were the last consuls assigned to Soter. See the *Prolegomena*, fol. XCIII, and the notes, p. 132.

Eleutherius was ordained bishop as the future coadjutor of Soter during the fourth persecution, which began under Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus. The day of his ordination was Sunday, 22 January, according to the catalogues. See the notes on Soter.

[Note: [Col. 0522D] II III] Soter, year 10, who was crowned with martyrdom on 22 April after sitting eight years, three months, and twenty days.

After his death, Eleutherius was elected as his successor. He had been ordained bishop to assist Soter in the crisis of the persecution on Sunday, 22 January of the preceding year. He sat for fifteen years, four months, and five days.

In the badly sewn fragments of the Liberian catalogue, these consuls were dragged by the copyists to the entry for Soter; they belong to Eleutherius, whose entry has been lost and must be restored, as indicated in the notes on Eleutherius.

[Note: [Col. 0524A] III IV] Eleutherius, years 1 and 2.

[Col. 0524B] Concerning the partial relaxation of the persecution in this year, after Soter’s martyrdom, see the notes, pp. 132 and 139. In particular, the persecution was less severe in Asia Minor after the letter of Marcus Aurelius, which must be assigned to this same year on the grounds established there, since it is said to be in the twenty-fifth year of the tribunician power and is joined to the title *Armeniacus*. See the annotations there.

Rain was obtained through the prayers of Christian soldiers when the Roman army was suffering from thirst, and the enemy camp was thrown into confusion.

[Note: [Col. 0524B] Olympiad 237, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 238, first year] Eleutherius, years 2 and 3.

Saint Felicitas suffered at Rome with her seven sons: she herself on 24 November, and her children on 10 July. Petavius for this year.

[Note: [Col. 0524C] I II] Eleutherius, years 3 and 4.

Petavius, for this year, reports that rain was obtained from God through the prayers of the Christian soldiers for the Roman forces, and that victory was consequently won over the Quadi, on the authority of Eusebius, Xiphilinus, and Dio.

[Note: [Col. 0524D] II III] Eleutherius, years 4 and 5.

Avidius Cassius rebelled in the East and was killed in July. Marcus set out for the East. Lydiatus and Petavius for this year, from historical sources.

[Col. 0526A] [Note: [Col. 0526A] III IV] Eleutherius, years 5 and 6.

Faustina died at the Taurus Mountains and was enrolled among the deified women by her husband. Coins and historical sources.

[Col. 0526B] [Note: [Col. 0526B] Olympiad 238, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 239] Eleutherius, years 6 and 7.

The martyrdom of Saint Pothinus, bishop of Lyons. See p. 136.

Athenagoras of Athens, a philosopher, undertook an embassy to the emperor on behalf of the Christians. Petavius for this year; he also records that Irenaeus was sent by the martyrs of Lyons as an envoy to Pope Eleutherius around this time, from Eusebius.

Persecution raged in Gaul. See p. 136.

[Note: [Col. 0526C] I II] Eleutherius, years 7 and 8.

Saint Irenaeus became bishop of Lyons in this year. Petavius, from Eusebius and Jerome.

[Note: [Col. 0526C] II III] Eleutherius, years 8 and 9.

Montanus, together with Priscilla and Maximilla, deranged women, gave rise to the Cataphrygian heresy.

The same is stated by Petavius, from Epiphanius.

[Note: [Col. 0526D] III IV] Eleutherius, years 9 and 10.

Pantaenus, the teacher of Clement of Alexandria, a Christian converted from Stoicism and inflamed by the desire to propagate the religion, went to India. Petavius, from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 10.

[Note: [Col. 0528A] Olympiad 239, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 240, first year] Eleutherius, years 10 and 11.

Theodosius, a native of Pontus and a Jew converted from Marcionism, lived at this time and translated the sacred Scriptures into Greek. Petavius, from Saint Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*, p. 340.

[Note: [Col. 0528A] I II] Eleutherius, years 11 and 12.

The temple of Serapis at Alexandria was burned. Eusebius. Julius Pollux flourished at this time. Petavius, at the place cited above.

[Note: [Col. 0528C] II III] Eleutherius, years 12 and 13.

Around this time, after requests had been sent by Lucius, king of Britain, to Pope Eleutherius to obtain heralds of the Gospel, and after the restoration of Roman colonies and the transfer of legions had taken place under the Antonines, the Christian religion appears to have been expanded there and the first episcopal sees established. Consult the notes, pp. 143 and 149.

[Note: [Col. 0528D] III IV] Eleutherius, years 13 and 14.
