The Goths, bursting forth from the regions of Noricum or Sweden, inflicted many great disasters on various provinces. Establishing their homes on both banks of the Weser, they were called by their neighbors Ostuali and Westuali (eastern and western dwellers). Calvisius, from the Frisian annals.

[Note: [Col. 0530A] Olympiad 240, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 241, first year] Eleutherius, years 15 and 16; Victor, year 1.

[Col. 0530B] Eleutherius suffered martyrdom on 26 May. Victor was elected as his successor and ordained supreme pontiff on Sunday, 18 July.

These consuls are assigned as the last to Eleutherius in the Liberian catalogue, although the copyists, failing to notice the lacuna, placed them with the first consuls under Soter. The number of years—nine—assigned to Soter in the same catalogue indicates that both groups, separated from one another by fifteen years—that is, by the date assigned to Eleutherius in all the catalogues—belong to the successor. [Col. 0530C] See the *Prolegomena*, fol. XCIII, and the notes, pp. 112, 120, and 157.

[Note: [Col. 0530C] I II] Victor, years 1 and 2.

In this year Victor celebrated the first Easter of his pontificate.

Pagius shows that the speech of Apollonius the senator in the Senate on behalf of the Christian religion, and his martyrdom, ought to be assigned to the year before this one; Petavius assigns them to the following year.

[Col. 0530D] [Note: [Col. 0530D] II III] Victor, years 2 and 3.

Apollonius the senator, accused of adherence to the Christian religion, delivered a speech before the Senate; by its sentence he was beheaded. Petavius, from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 5, chapter 20, and the *Roman Martyrology*.

Baronius assigned the prefecture of Philippus, the father of the virgin and martyr Eugenia, to this year, and Calvisius followed him.

[Col. 0532A] [Note: [Col. 0532A] III IV] Victor, years 3 and 4.

Pagius assigns the beginning of Demetrius’ episcopate at Alexandria to this year; Petavius assigns it to the immediately following year.

[Col. 0532B] [Note: [Col. 0532B] Olympiad 241, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 242, first year] Victor, years 4 and 5.

Demetrius was made the eleventh bishop of Alexandria and presided for forty-three years. Petavius, from Eusebius.

[Col. 0532C] [Note: [Col. 0532C] I II] Victor, years 5 and 6.

Serapion, whose writings Eusebius cites, was made bishop of Antioch. Calvisius, from Eusebius.

[Col. 0532D] [Note: [Col. 0532D] II III] Victor, years 6 and 7.

The *Mishnah* of the Jews was compiled by the rabbis Adda, Judah, and others. Calvisius for the preceding year, from their books.

[Col. 0534A] [Note: [Col. 0534A] II IV] Victor, years 7 and 8.

Pagius observes that in this year, the year of Commodus’ death, the Alexandrian era counted from the Incarnation or Nativity of the Lord begins in Julian year 43, whereas the Latin era begins in year 46. Therefore he does not think that Clement’s passage, which counts 194 years at the death of Commodus from the Lord’s Nativity, can serve to confirm the Dionysian era.

[Note: [Col. 0534B] Olympiad 242, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 243, first year] Victor, years 8 and 9.

After Julian was killed, C. Pescennius Niger was proclaimed emperor by the Syrian army; shortly afterward he was killed by Severus’ army.

L. Septimius Severus was proclaimed emperor by the Illyrian and Pannonian armies before the Ides of May, and by the Senate before the Kalends of July. He set out for the East against Pescennius.

[Col. 0534C] Victor, years 9 and 10.

[Note: [Col. 0534C] I II] Severus waged war against Niger in the East and defeated him. Niger fled to Antioch; after it was captured, he hurried toward the Euphrates and was killed. Petavius and Mediobarbus, from historical sources and coins.

[Col. 0534D] [Note: [Col. 0534D] II III] Victor, years 10 and 11.

Severus’ expedition against the Osrhoenians, Arabs, and Adiabenians. Several cities were captured, including Nisibis. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

[Note: [Col. 0534D] III IV] Victor, years 11 and 12.

Councils concerning the celebration of Easter were held at Rome by Victor, at Caesarea by Theophilus at Victor’s command, and elsewhere.

Severus was called *Parthicus Arabicus* and *Parthicus Adiabenicus* because he had devastated Arabia and defeated the Parthians and Adiabenians in the preceding year. The war was then turned against Albinus. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

[Note: [Col. 0536A] Olympiad 243, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 244, first year] Victor, years 12 and 13; Zephyrinus, year 1.

These consuls are assigned as the last to Victor by the catalogue of Felix IV and others in the *Prolegomena*, p. 94. Under them he was crowned with martyrdom after sitting twelve years and ten days. After his death, Zephyrinus was elected as successor on Sunday, 25 September. Having been ordained on that day, he sat for eighteen years and ten months, until 26 June of the year 217, when he completed his martyrdom. See the notes on Victor.

[Note: [Col. 0536B] I II] Zephyrinus, years 1 and 2.

These consuls are assigned as Zephyrinus’ first by all the catalogues and manuscripts in the *Prolegomena*, fol. 94. Under them he celebrated the first Easter of his pontificate.

The magnificent games exhibited by Severus, during which a Christian refused to place a crown on his head, gave Tertullian occasion to write the book *On the Crown of the Soldier*. Petavius, from Herodian, Xiphilinus, Spartianus, and Tertullian.

[Note: [Col. 0536C] II III] Zephyrinus, years 2 and 3.

The Augusti’s departure for the Parthian war and their successful operations in Syria; hence a Jewish triumph was decreed for Antoninus. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

[Col. 0536D] [Note: [Col. 0536D] III IV] Zephyrinus, years 3 and 4.

There was a certain outbreak of persecution in Africa under the governor Saturninus. Petavius, from Tertullian, *To Scapula*, chapter 2.

Seleucia, Babylon, Ctesiphon, and Parthia were captured and devastated. Hence Severus Augustus was called *Parthicus Maximus*. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

Abgar, king of the Osrhoenians, submitted to Severus. The king of Armenia made a treaty with him. Lydiatus.

[Col. 0538A] [Note: [Col. 0538A] Olympiad 244, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 245, first year] Zephyrinus, years 4 and 5.

A Parthian triumph was decreed for Severus, but he refused it. Antoninus, the son of Severus, celebrated a triumph over the Jews and was granted the *toga virilis*. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

[Col. 0538B] [Note: [Col. 0538B] I II] Zephyrinus, years 5 and 6.

The fifth persecution against the Christians was stirred up, especially at Alexandria and in Egypt, while Laetus held the prefecture. Becoming a Jew or a Christian was prohibited. Petavius, from Spartianus.

At Antioch Severus, consul for the third time, and Antoninus, his son and colleague, proceeded. After traversing Egypt, Severus entered Rome in triumph; together with his son he was called *Parthicus Arabicus* and *Parthicus Adiabenicus*. Mediobarbus, from coins and historical sources.

[Note: [Col. 0538C] II III] Zephyrinus, years 6 and 7.

As Severus’ tenth year of reign was passing, the persecution in Egypt made Leonides, the father of Origen—who was then seventeen years old and burning with a desire for martyrdom—a martyr. In Gaul it likewise made Irenaeus and countless others martyrs, as Pagius demonstrates against Dodwell from Eusebius, Gregory of Tours, and others.

[Note: [Col. 0538D] III IV] Zephyrinus, years 7 and 8.

At the end of the summer of this year, in Antiochene year 252 according to Eusebius’ *Chronicle*, Severus celebrated the secular games. Lydiatus. Noris contends in his *Epistola consularis* that these were improperly called the eighth games by Censorinus. Pagius disagrees with Noris; see their works.

[Col. 0540B] [Note: [Col. 0540B] Olympiad 245, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 246, first year] Zephyrinus, years 8 and 9.

Tertullian in Africa and Clement of Alexandria in Egypt were regarded as distinguished men. Petavius.

[Note: [Col. 0540B] I II] Zephyrinus, years 9 and 10.

Origen castrated himself. Petavius for this year, from Eusebius, book 6, chapter 7.

[Col. 0540C] [Note: [Col. 0540C] II III] Zephyrinus, years 10 and 11.

Tertullian wrote against Marcion. Petavius, from the same book, *Against Marcion*, book 1, chapter 15.

Minucius Felix, practicing law at Rome, published a dialogue in defense of the Christian religion. Petavius, at the same place.

[Col. 0540D] [Note: [Col. 0540D] III IV] Zephyrinus, years 11 and 12.

Tertullian’s book *On the Pallium* is understood to have been written in this year, from chapter 3 of that work. Petavius.

[Col. 0542A] [Note: [Col. 0542A] Olympiad 246, fourth year, and from the summer days of Olympiad 247, first year] Zephyrinus, years 12 and 13.

Minucius Felix, the celebrated author of the dialogue entitled *Octavius*, flourished. Calvisius.

[Note: [Col. 0542B] I II] Zephyrinus, years 13 and 14.

Severus’ expedition to the farthest [Col. 0542C] boundaries of the island of Britain secured a route for the heralds of the Christian faith into regions previously inaccessible to the Romans, in order to bring them under Christ. From Tertullian. See the notes on Zephyrinus.

[Note: [Col. 0542C] II III] Zephyrinus, years 11 and 15.

Before this year—the first in which Caracalla ruled, when he withdrew from part of Britain, added to the empire by his father—it is necessary to recognize the establishment on that island of three bishoprics: the Eboracensian [York], the Londinian [London], and that of Lindum Colonia [Lincoln]. See the discussion above.

[Col. 0544A] [Note: [Col. 0544A] III IV] Zephyrinus 15 and 16.

Asclepiades is appointed the ninth bishop of Antioch. Eusebius, in the year after Severus’s death.

[Col. 0544B] [Note: [Col. 0544B] O. 240 IV and, from the summer days, O. 241 I] Zephyrinus 16 and 17.

Alexander is ordained the thirty-fifth [Col. 0544C] bishop of Jerusalem while Narcissus is still living, and governs the Church together with him. Eusebius in the *Chronicle*. But the letters of the former, preserved by Baronius under the year 199, no. IX, prove that Alexander was bishop of a neighboring church and was summoned, with Alexander’s consent, while he was in his 116th year, at the prompting of divine revelation, to administer that Church.

[Col. 0544D] [Note: [Col. 0544D] I II] Zephyrinus 17 and 18.

Around this time Tertullian fell into the doctrine of Montanus. Petavius adds that, after this lapse, he wrote the book *On Monogamy* 160 years after Saint Paul had written his First Epistle to the Corinthians, as appears from chapter 3 of that same book of Tertullian.

[Note: [Col. 0544D] II III] Zephyrinus 18 and 19.

Antoninus, angered against the Alexandrians, slaughters them in a massacre. Mediobarbus, from the history of those same events, whence Petavius.

[Col. 0546A] [Note: [Col. 0546A] III IV] Zephyrinus 19 and 20.

[Col. 0546B] Caracalla keeps Abgar, king of Osrhoene, whom he had summoned to himself under pledged faith, in chains. He marches against the Parthians, having unsuccessfully summoned the king of Armenia to him. He covets the kingdom of the Parthians and overturns the tombs of those same kings in the fields of Arbela. From Dio Xiphilinus.

[Col. 0546C] [Note: [Col. 0546C] Olympiad 248 IV and Olympiad 249] Zephyrinus 19 and 20. Callistus I.

Zephyrinus wins the palm of martyrdom on 26 July. The see is vacant for six days. Callistus is elected on Saturday, 2 August, and on the following day, 3 August, which was also a Sunday, he is ordained. He remains in office for five years, two months, and ten days, until 13 October, on which day he suffers martyrdom; he is buried on the 14th, the day on which he is commemorated, in the cemetery of Calepodius. See the notes, p. 175. From the day of Zephyrinus’s ordination, Sunday, 25 September 197, to the day of his martyrdom, 26 July, his tenure amounted to nineteen years and ten months. See the *Prolegomena* and the notes on Zephyrinus.

[Col. 0546D] [Note: [Col. 0546D] I II] Callistus 1 and 2.

Through the money and schemes of Julia Maesa, the mother of Elagabalus, who was the sister of Julia Pia, the wife of Septimius Severus Augustus, the Syrian army, and soon also the remaining legions, defect from Macrinus to Elagabalus.

[Col. 0548A] [Note: [Col. 0548A] II III] Callistus 2 and 3.

On his return to Rome, Elagabalus introduced his namesake god and built a temple for him. Petavius, from Herodian and Lampridius.

[Col. 0548C] [Note: [Col. 0548C] III IV] Callistus 3 and 4.

Among the Jews flourishes Rabbi Samuel, who moved the day called *Te kuphas* in the Julian Calendar from 7 October back to 24 September. Calvisius, from the Talmudists.

Julius Africanus undertakes an embassy to the Emperor on behalf of the restoration of Nicopolis in Palestine, which was also called Emmaus. Petavius. Calvisius thinks this Africanus was the author of the *Chronicle of the Olympiads*.

[Note: [Col. 0548C] Olympiad 249 IV and Olympiad 250 I] Callistus 4 and 5.

Saint Urban is ordained bishop on Sunday, 10 June. From that date to his martyrdom on 23 May 230 there are reckoned eight years, eleven months, and sixteen days, and to his burial on 20 May, fifteen days. See the notes on Callistus.

[Col. 0548D] [Note: [Col. 0548D] I II] Callistus 5 and 6. Urban I.

Callistus completes his martyrdom on the 12th and is buried on 14 October, having held office for five years, two months, and ten days from his episcopal ordination on Sunday, 3 August 217. Urban is elected as his successor; [Col. 0550A] he had been his vicar during the preceding year and had been ordained bishop. See the notes, p. 178, and the *Prolegomena*, fol. XCV.

This year the Paschal fourteenth fell on the Ides of April, a Saturday. From the marble inscription of Saint Hippolytus preserved in the Vatican Library, excavated from the cemetery in the Veran field, p. 160, where the Paschal cycle is arranged according to the *Heccaedecaeterides*.

[Col. 0550B] [Note: [Col. 0550B] II III] Urban 1 and 2.

Saint Urban first celebrated Easter of his Roman pontificate in the consulship of these men, on Sunday, 6 April, as in Saint Hippolytus’s cycle above, p. 160. Therefore these consuls are also assigned to him as his first consuls. See the notes, p. 178.

The Jews were granted by Alexander permission to have their own prefect and to dwell in Palestine. Calvisius, from Eusebius.

[Col. 0550C] [Note: [Col. 0550C] III IV] Urban 2 and 3.

Alexander places in his private shrine, among the images of illustrious men and of his gods, also an image of Christ the Lord. Lampridius, in his *Life* of Alexander.

[Note: [Col. 0550C] Olympiad 250 IV and Olympiad 251 I] Urban 3 and 4.

The 251st Olympiad was celebrated. It is the 1001st Olympiad year. Calvisius.

[Col. 0550D] [Note: [Col. 0550D] I II] Urban 4 and 5.

Artaxerxes the Persian revolts from the Parthians and makes war upon Artabanus in the fourth year of Alexander, as Agathias reports. Calvisius.

[Note: [Col. 0552A] II III] Urban 5 and 6.

Geminus, a presbyter of Antioch whose writings are mentioned by Eusebius and Jerome, flourishes at this time. Calvisius.

[Col. 0552B] [Note: [Col. 0552B] III IV] Urban 6 and 7.

In the third battle Artaxerxes at last kills Artabanus the Parthian and occupies his entire kingdom. Dio.

[Note: [Col. 0552B] Olympiad 251 IV and Olympiad 252 I] Urban 7 and 8.

Artaxerxes invades Armenia, [Col. 0552C] entering Roman territory. Alexander writes to him not to do this but rather to cultivate peace in his new kingdom; he replies arrogantly. Therefore, since the Roman armies, having been treated too leniently, possessed no strength, military discipline began to be cultivated. Calvisius, from Dio.

[Col. 0552C] [Note: [Col. 0552C] I II] Urban 8 and 9. Pontian I.

Saint Urban suffers martyrdom on 23 [Col. 0552D] May; he is buried on the 25th, reckoning from his episcopal ordination to the day of his burial eight years, eleven months, and twelve days.

Saint Pontian, elected as his successor, is ordained on Sunday, 29 August. From that date to his martyrdom on 30 October 235 there elapse five years, two months, and two days. See the notes, p. 181.

The martyrdom of Saints Cecilia, Valerian, and their companions. See the notes, p. 179. Origen is harassed at Alexandria by Demetrius the bishop. Petavius, from Eusebius, Book 6 of the *History*.

[Col. 0554A] [Note: [Col. 0554A] II III] Pontian 1 and 2.

In the tenth year of Alexander, Origen flees to Caesarea, abandoning the Alexandrian school over which he had presided. When Demetrius the bishop died, Heraclas succeeds him there. At this time Origen is believed to have composed the *Hexapla* and also the *Octapla*, since he had obtained bishops who were especially devoted to his studies: Firmilian of Caesarea in Cappadocia, Alexander of Jerusalem, [Col. 0554B] and Theoctistus of Caesarea in Palestine. Petavius, from Epiphanius, *On Weights and Measures*, and from Eusebius, *History*, Book 6, chapter 20.

[Col. 0554B] [Note: [Col. 0554B] III IV] Pontian 2 and 3.

Theodorus flourishes; he was also called Gregory Thaumaturgus, a disciple of Origen, together with his brother Athenodorus. Eusebius, in the same work, chapter 23, and also Africanus. Petavius, from Eusebius.

Ammonius the Christian teaches Platonic philosophy at Alexandria. His pupil was [Col. 0554C] Porphyry of Lycopolis. Petavius, from Porphyry.

[Col. 0554C] [Note: [Col. 0554C] Olympiad 252 IV and Olympiad 253 I] Pontian 3 and 4.

Around this time, news having been received of the invasion by the Germans who had crossed the Rhine and Danube and had overrun Roman territory, the emperor Severus Alexander, recalled from the East, triumphed over Artaxerxes, king of the Parthians, in the month of October. The corrupt figures in Herodian [Col. 0554D] seem to have led most people into error regarding the chronology of the deeds of the Roman emperor Alexander in the East, which are otherwise uncertain and disputed. Lydiatus.

Pontian 4 and 5.

[Note: [Col. 0554D] II] *Hippolytus of Porto, a contemporary of this period, in excerpts preserved by Canisius, Volume II, reckons from Christ’s Passion to this thirteenth year of Alexander 206 years, which likewise corresponds to our chronology, assigning the Lord’s Passion to the year 28 of the common era.*

[Col. 0556A] [Note: [Col. 0556A] II III] Pontian 5 and 6. Anterus I.

Pontian dies in exile on 30 October, having held office for five years, two months, and the same number of days. Shortly afterward he is buried, and not long thereafter his remains are brought to Rome. His feast [Col. 0556B] is celebrated on 19 November. Anterus is elected as his successor and ordained on Sunday, 22 November; from that date he held office for one month and two days, until 3 January of the following year. See the notes on Pontian.

[Note: [Col. 0556B] III IV] Anterus 1. Fabian I.

Anterus, made a martyr scarcely at the beginning of the second month of his pontificate, is buried on 3 January. After his death the see remains vacant for a long time. [Since Maximinus was raging especially against the clergy,] Fabian is elected, as indicated by the passing dove, [Col. 0556C] and is ordained on Sunday, 11 December. From that date he held office for thirteen years, one month, and ten days. See the notes on Anterus.

[Col. 0556C] [Note: [Col. 0556C] Olympiad 253 IV and, from the summer days, Olympiad 254 I] Fabian 1 and 2.

The sixth persecution began under Maximinus. It was, however, more local in character and was carried out especially in Cappadocia. It was mitigated when Maximinus’s power was curtailed through the election of the Gordians, and after they were killed, through the subsequent election of Pupienus and Balbinus. See Pagius under the year 235.

A total eclipse of the sun was observed at Rome this year, so that it was thought to be night [Capitolinus]. It corresponds in the astronomical tables to 12 April in the afternoon.

[Col. 0556D] [Note: [Col. 0556D] I II] Fabian 2 and 3.

Another eclipse of the sun was observed at Rome on 2 April, which the astronomical tables likewise show to have occurred in the morning.

This year, whose consulate of Ulpius and Pontian is, as it were, a kind of index and title [as Censorinus says in *On the Day of Birth*, chapter 8], is, according to Varro, the year 1014 from the Olympiad, reckoned from the summer days, and from the founding of Rome 991, specifically from the Parilia, and so forth. See the notes on Fabian.

[Col. 0558B] [Note: [Col. 0558B] II III] Fabian 3 and 4.

When Zebinus, bishop of Antioch, died, Babylas succeeded him. Eusebius, *History*, Book VI, chapter XXIII; Petavius; Calvisius.

[Col. 0558B] [Note: [Col. 0558B] III IIII] Fabian 4 and 5.

Origen travels to Athens to furnish his library. Calvisius.

[Col. 0558C] [Note: [Col. 0558C] Olympiad 254 IIII and Olympiad 255 I] Fabian 5 and 6.

The Persian War breaks out. When Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, dies after fifteen years of rule, Sapor succeeds him, a most cruel man, who this year invades Mesopotamia and Syria. Calvisius, from Agathias.

[Col. 0558D] [Note: [Col. 0558D] I II] Fabian 6 and 7.

Gordian, setting out for the Persian War, crosses through Moesia into Asia [whence the phrase *TRAIECTUM AUG* on coins struck this year is explained by Mediobarbus]. He proceeds to Antioch; through the efforts of Misitheus he recovers Carrhae, Nisibis, and other towns from the Persians, whom he drives back into their own territory. Julius Capitolinus. Hence he was acclaimed imperator for the second time.

[Col. 0560A] [Note: [Col. 0560A] II III] Fabian 7 and 8.

Around this time Beryllus, bishop of Arabia, was condemned by the bishops for holding an incorrect opinion about Christ’s divinity; Origen [Col. 0560B] brought him back to a sounder understanding. Petavius, from Eusebius, *History*, Book VI, chapter 25.

[Col. 0560B] [Note: [Col. 0560B] III IV] Fabian 8 and 9.

Philip, formerly prefect of the praetorian guard, is made Gordian’s colleague in the empire by force of the army. Having accused the emperor in an assembly, he arranges for him to be killed by soldiers whom he had suborned. The Senate, indignant at this, creates Marcus emperor and then Hostilian. [Col. 0560C] After both have died, it accepts Philip. Calvisius, from the history. Philip makes an ignoble peace with the Persians, to whom he leaves Assyria and Mesopotamia. Mediobarbus.

[Col. 0560C] [Note: [Col. 0560C] Olympiad 255 IV and Olympiad 256 I] Fabian 9 and 10.

In Arabia Philip restores Bostra, and, having settled colonists there, names it Philippopolis. Calvisius, from Zonaras, supported by the coins. He places his brother Priscus in command of the Syrian armies [Col. 0560D] and his son-in-law Severianus over Moesia and Macedonia. Petavius, from Zosimus.

[Col. 0560D] [Note: [Col. 0560D] I II] Fabian 10 and 11.

Philip, having revoked the peace, declares war on the Persians; this is settled by a promise to restore the provinces. Mediobarbus, from the history.

[Col. 0562A] [Note: [Col. 0562A] II III] Fabian 11 and 12.

The games celebrated at Rome this year and the next by both emperors named Philip [father and son] abundantly prove that they were not yet Christians. See Pagius under this year and the notes of the younger Pagius below, pp. 190–192.

[Col. 0562B] [Note: [Col. 0562B] III IV] Fabian 12 and 13.

When Donatus died, Saint Cyprian was made bishop of Carthage, and Saint Dionysius of Alexandria began his episcopate this year; he held it for seventeen years. Petavius, from Eusebius.

[Col. 0562C] Aurelius Victor, from this year of Philip’s Secular Games to the consulship of Philip and Salia in the year of Christ 348, when he wrote, reckons one hundred years, as Calvisius and others observe.

The Scythians cross the frontier and carry off booty. Marinus is sent against them and defeats them. Hence the victory over the Carpi. Soon Marinus is chosen emperor by the army against Philip; Decius is sent by Philip against him. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

[Col. 0562C] [Note: [Col. 0562C] Olympiad 256 IV and Olympiad 257 I] Fabian 13 and 14.

[Col. 0562D] Decius initiates the seventh persecution against the Christians. Eusebius, *Chronicle* and *History*, Book VI, chapter 22; Orosius, Book VI, chapter 21.

[Col. 0564A] [Note: [Col. 0564A] I II] Fabian 14, who completes his martyrdom and is buried in the cemetery of Callistus on 20 January, having held office for thirteen years, one month, and ten days. The see remains vacant until 1 June. See the notes, p. 201.

[Col. 0564B] Cornelius is elected and ordained on Sunday, 2 June. From that date to his martyrdom on 14 September 252 there are reckoned two years, three months, and ten days in the Liberian Catalogue, and twelve days in the Lucens Catalogue. See the *Prolegomena*, p. 97, and the notes, pp. 197 and 205.

While the persecution was raging and was directed especially against the clergy, Lucius was ordained by Cornelius as a bishop-vicar on Sunday, 1 December. From that date to his martyrdom on 3 March 254 there are reckoned three years, three months, and three days, assigned to him in the Catalogue and the *Pictures*.

[Col. 0564C] [Note: [Col. 0564C] II III] Cornelius 1 and 2.

Saint Cornelius is driven into exile at Centumcellae by the censor Valerian. See the notes, pp. 201 and 205. Undaunted, he governs the Church, sending letters back and forth to Cyprian.

Novatus, having arrived at Rome from Africa in the preceding year while the see was vacant, stirs up trouble this year against Pope Cornelius’s indulgence toward the lapsed. See the notes on Cornelius.

[Col. 0564D] [Note: [Col. 0564D] III IV] Cornelius 2 and 3. Lucius 1.

Saint Cornelius is summoned from his place of exile to Rome and beheaded at the tribunal of Valerian Augustus and Maximus, prefect of the city, a martyr of Christ on the Appian Way, on 14 September. See the notes, p. 205. On Sunday, 18 October, Lucius, previously his vicar, is elected by the clergy in his place and occupies the Roman see after his martyrdom. See the notes on Cornelius.

[Col. 0566A] A plague arising in Ethiopia invades almost the entire Roman world. Victor, *On the Caesars*.

[Col. 0566A] [Note: [Col. 0566A] Olympiad 257 IV and Olympiad 258 I] Lucius 1 and 2.

While the persecution was still raging, especially against the clergy, Lucius ordains Stephen, chosen from among the archdeacons, as bishop-vicar this year, on Pentecost, 23 May. At this time Lucius was compelled to go into exile, though he would soon return to the city. See the notes on Lucius.

The people of Aegae in Cilicia mark on coins struck for Aemilian this year the era 299, reckoned from the founding of the city in 706, beginning in autumn. Anazarbus struck coins for Valerian this year marked with the epoch 272, reckoned from the founding of the city in 733, beginning in autumn. See the notes on Lucius.

[Col. 0566C] [Note: [Col. 0566C] I II] Lucius 2. Stephen 1.

Lucius’s martyrdom is to be assigned this year to 3 March, after three years, three months, and three days had elapsed from his episcopal ordination, as attributed to him in the *Pictures* of Saint Paul and in the Catalogues.

Stephen is elected successor by the clergy on Sunday, 9 April, the Sunday of the Passion. See the notes on Stephen.

[Col. 0566D] [Note: [Col. 0566D] II III] Stephen 1 and 2.

Stephen celebrates Easter for the first time during his pontificate this year; therefore the consuls of this year are recorded as the first in his era.

Sixtus is ordained Stephen’s coadjutor bishop during the persecution on Sunday, 2 September. From this date to his martyrdom there are two years, eleven months, and five days—namely, to 6 August 258. See the notes, p. 225.

[Col. 0568A] [Note: [Col. 0568A] III IV] Stephen 2 and 3.

During Stephen’s absence, after he had been driven into exile, his vicar Sixtus [according to the letters of Cyprian cited in the notes, p. 216, I] is said to have celebrated the pontifical offices at Easter this year. For this reason some Catalogues assign the first consuls of the year to him. See the notes on Stephen.

[Col. 0568B] [Note: [Col. 0568B] Olympiad 258 IV and Olympiad 259 I] Stephen 3 and 4. Sixtus I.

Stephen is beheaded at his own see at the Catacombs on 2 August, having held office, both as vicar and as pontiff, for four years, two months, and fifteen days, according to the Catalogues and the *Pictures*. See the notes cited above. After his martyrdom,

Sixtus, formerly his vicar, is elected by the clergy as successor. See the notes at the indicated place.

Sapor, king of the Persians, devastates Syria, [Col. 0568C] Cilicia, and Cappadocia. Valerian sets out against him.

[Col. 0568C] [Note: [Col. 0568C] I II] Sixtus 1 and 2, scarcely begun; and his martyrdom on 6 August, after two years, eleven months, and six days from his episcopal ordination. See the notes on Sixtus. The eighth persecution.

At the instigation of Macrianus, chief of the synagogue at Antioch, and of the Egyptian Magi [Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 9], Valerian unleashes a savage persecution against the Christians everywhere. He sends letters to the Senate and to the provincial governors ordering that bishops, presbyters, [Col. 0568D] and deacons be immediately punished. See Cyprian, Epistle 82.5, who is beheaded on 14 September, just as Saint Lawrence is burned at Rome, and so forth.

[Col. 0568D] [Note: [Col. 0568D] II III] During the vacancy of the see, the presbyters presided until 17 July. The ancient Catalogues. See the notes.

Dionysius is elected Roman pontiff and ordained on Sunday, 19 September. From that date he held office until 27 December 268, for nine years, three months, and seven days, as appears from the Catalogue and the *Pictures*. See the notes on Dionysius.

[Col. 0570A] After Valerian was captured by the Persians, several men usurp imperial power in various provinces; Pollio mentions them in the thirtieth book, *The Thirty Tyrants*. Petavius.

[Col. 0570A] [Note: [Col. 0570A] III IV] Dionysius 1 and 2.

The persecution ceased under Gallienus. Eusebius, Book VII, chapters 14 and 17.

When the Scythians invaded, the temple [Col. 0570B] of Diana at Ephesus was burned, Nicaea was captured, Chalcedon was taken, Trapezus was plundered, and so forth. Petavius and Eusebius, from Zosimus and Trebellius.

Paul of Samosata becomes bishop of Antioch. Pagius under the year 261, no. v.

[Col. 0570B] [Note: [Col. 0570B] Olympiad 259 IV and Olympiad 260 I] Dionysius 2 and 3.

Aemilianus, prefect of Egypt, having seized the granaries during the revolt which he had vigorously suppressed, assumes imperial power; but he is captured alive by Theodorus, a commander of Gallienus, and sent to Gallienus. Calvisius, from Aurelius.

After the death of Macrianus [whose rebellion in Egypt was the reason that the Egyptian Christians did not receive the benefit of the remission of persecution granted elsewhere], Gallienus issues a rescript this year.

[Col. 0570C] [Note: [Col. 0570C] I II] Dionysius 3 and 4.

Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, having been reported to Pope Dionysius on account of writings that were obscure and later used by the Arians, clears himself of suspicion by sending him a letter. Petavius.

[Col. 0570D] The Goths, having occupied Thrace, ravage Macedonia and soon withdraw after being defeated. The Scythians devastate Asia and plunder the temple of Diana. Pagius under this year, from Pollio.

Porphyry the Platonist, hostile to the Christians, a writer from Tyre, comes to Rome this year.

[Col. 0572A] [Note: [Col. 0572A] II III] Dionysius 4 and 5.

Regilianus in Pannonia and Saturninus in Egypt, usurping tyranny, are killed. From Trebellius. Petavius and Calvisius assign the former to the preceding year and the latter to the following year.

[Col. 0572B] [Note: [Col. 0572B] III IV] Dionysius 5 and 6.

Odenathus, king of the Palmyrenes, drives Sapor, king of the Persians, from the Roman frontiers, occupies Nisibis and Carrhae, and sends Persian captives to Gallienus. Gallienus, who has called him Augustus, grants him authority over the whole East. Pollio, *The Two Gallieni*, chapter 10.

[Col. 0572C] [Note: [Col. 0572C] Olympiad 260 IV and Olympiad 261 I] Dionysius 6 and 7.

A synod is convened at Antioch against Paul of Samosata. Petavius and Pagius, from Eusebius, Book 7 of the *History*, chapter 22.

[Col. 0572D] [Note: [Col. 0572D] I II] Dionysius 7 and 8.

Because of the energetic service he had rendered against the Persians, Odenathus, king of the Palmyrenes, is called Augustus by Gallienus; shortly afterward he is killed by a plot. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

[Col. 0572D] [Note: [Col. 0572D] II III] Dionysius 8 and 9.

After Odenathus, king of the Palmyrenes, was killed, his wife Zenobia [Col. 0574A] obtained the supreme power. Gallienus sends the commander Heraclianus against the Persians, but he is defeated by the Palmyrenes. Petavius, from Trebellius. Zenobia, a most warlike woman, not only repels the Persians but also extends her power into Egypt. Calvisius, from the same Trebellius.

[Col. 0574A] [Note: [Col. 0574A] III IV] Dionysius 9 and 10.

Zenobia administers the Eastern empire in the name of her sons Herennianus, Timolaus, and Vaballathus. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

[Col. 0574B] [Note: [Col. 0574B] Olympiad 261 IV and Olympiad 262 I] Felix, five days after the death of Dionysius, [Col. 0574C] is elected and ordained Roman pontiff on Sunday, 3 January, in the consulship of Claudius and Paternus—as the Liberian Catalogue states—and, according to the *Book of the Pontiffs*, holds office for five years, eleven months, and twenty-five days, until 3 January of the year 274, as in the *Short Work on Episcopal Burials*. See the notes on Felix.

[Col. 0574C] [Note: [Col. 0574C] I II] Felix 2.

[Col. 0574D] Paul of Samosata, reviving the heresy condemned in the first council of Antioch, is condemned again in the second Synod of Antioch and expelled from his see. But when he refused to yield to the Churches, Aurelian was appealed to, and Paul was forcibly removed. Eusebius, Book 7 of the *History*, chapters 23 and 24. Athanasius, *On the Synods*, who also indicates that a synod was held at Rome concerning this matter by Pope Dionysius. Petavius.

[Col. 0576A] [Note: [Col. 0576A] II III] Felix 3.

Petavius, under this year, reports from Vopiscus Aurelian’s rescript to the Senate concerning consultation of the Sibylline Books: “I am amazed, holy Fathers, that you have hesitated so long about opening the Sibylline Books, as though you were dealing with them in the Church of the Christians and not in the temple of all the gods.” [Col. 0576B] “The reason,” says Petavius, “was that Christians utterly shrank from reading such profane books in the churches.” He adds from Vopiscus that many nobles were killed after Aurelian’s arrival in the city. That hesitation indicates the presence of many Christians among the Roman nobility. Hence the ninth persecution.

[Col. 0576B] [Note: [Col. 0576B] III IV] Felix 4. The ninth persecution.

Aurelian renews at this time the persecution against the Christians that had previously been attempted. Petavius, from Saint Leo the Great, *Sermon 2 on Pentecost*.

An expedition against Zenobia, queen of the Palmyrenes.

[Col. 0576C] [Note: [Col. 0576C] Olympiad 262 IV and Olympiad 263 I] Felix 5.

Aurelian engages Zenobia, defeats and captures her. Having restored the East, he crosses into Europe, where he crushes the forces of the Carpi; the Senate gives him the titles Carpicus, Armeniacus, Parthicus, [Col. 0576D] and Adiabenicus. Mediobarbus, from coins and history.

[Col. 0576D] [Note: [Col. 0576D] I II] Felix 6.

Saint Felix, having held office for five years, eleven months, and twenty-five days, dies in this consulship on 30 December, according to the Catalogue, which states that the see was vacant for five days. See the notes, p. 238.

Firmus rebels in Egypt but is defeated by Aurelian. Mediobarbus, from the history.

[Col. 0578A] [Note: [Col. 0578A] II III] Eutychianus is ordained bishop of Rome on Sunday, 3 January, in the consulship of Aurelian and Marcellinus, as the Catalogue states. He holds office for eight years, eleven months, and four days, until 8 December, in the consulship of Carus II and Carinus, in the year of Christ 283. See the notes on Eutychianus.

[Col. 0578B] [Note: [Col. 0578B] III IV] Eutychianus 2.

In the East, when the death of Tacitus is heard, Probus is elected emperor. He holds Syria, Phoenicia, Palestine, and all Egypt; Florianus holds the remaining territories. Zosimus, cited by Pagius under this year. Pagius begins Probus’s reign in the month of April, when Florianus was also elected at Tarsus.

[Col. 0578D] [Note: [Col. 0578D] Olympiad 263 IV and Olympiad 264 I] Eutychianus 3.

Eusebius writes in the *Chronicle* that in this second year of Probus, in the 325th year of the Antiochenes, the 402nd of the Tyrians, the 324th of the Laodiceans, the 588th of the Edessenes, and the 380th of the Ascalonites, the insane heresy of the Manichaeans erupted to the common destruction of the human race. Petavius, Pagius, and others derive this from him.

[Col. 0580A] [Note: [Col. 0580A] I II] Eutychianus 4.

Anatolius, bishop of Laodicea, is regarded as distinguished. Eusebius.

[Note: [Col. 0580A] II III] Eutychianus 5.

Probus, having set out for the East, [Col. 0580B] liberates Isauria, subdues the Blemyes, occupies Coptos and Ptolemais, and makes peace with the Persians. Petavius, Mediobarbus, and Vopiscus.

[Col. 0580B] [Note: [Col. 0580B] III IV] Eutychianus 6.

Probus defeats Saturninus, proclaimed Augustus at Alexandria, through his commanders and, although reluctantly, kills him. Mediobarbus, from Vopiscus.

Baronius’s *Annals* restore the consuls of this year to their proper place in the common Dionysian era.

[Note: [Col. 0580B] Olympiad 264 IV and Olympiad 265 I] Eutychianus 7.

On his return to Thrace from the East, Probus settles one hundred thousand Bastarnae there to protect the empire. Petavius.

[Col. 0580C] [Note: [Col. 0580C] I II] Eutychianus 8.

[Col. 0580D] The emperor Carus makes his sons Carinus and Numerian Caesars; he leaves the former in Gaul and takes the latter with him to the Persian War.

[Col. 0582A] [Note: [Col. 0582A] II II] Eutychianus 9. Caius I.

Carus captures Mesopotamia and reaches Ctesiphon. Hence he is called “the Persian.” He dies, struck by lightning, around December. Vopiscus, Eutropius, and Zosimus.

In this consulship Eutychianus dies and is buried in the cemetery of Callistus on 8 December [*Prolegomena*, *Short Work* II, p. 9], having held office for eight years and eleven months. See the notes, p. 243. The episcopate is vacant [Col. 0582B] for eight days. Caius is elected pontiff and ordained on Sunday, 16 December; from that date he holds office for eleven years, four months, and nine days. See the notes, pp. 143 and 252.

[Note: [Col. 0582B] III IV] Caius 1 and 2.

Here begins the Era of Diocletian, also called the Era of the Martyrs, from the fixed new moon of Thoth, that is, 29 August. Petavius and the other chronologists.

The lunar cycle begins among the Egyptian Christians this year; among the Latins, from the following Easter. Calvisius, Pagius, and others.

[Col. 0582C] [Note: [Col. 0582C] Olympiad 265 IV and Olympiad 266 I] Caius 2 and 3.

In the Alexandrian *Chronicle*, under the consuls of this year, it reads: “From these consuls the Diocletian years are arranged according to the Paschal reckoning.” On this matter, what we said in the preceding year, no. IV, should be consulted. Pagius under this year, no. 3.

[Col. 0582D] [Note: [Col. 0582D] I II] Caius 3 and 4.

Saint Sebastian, commander of the first cohort of the Praetorians, is crowned with martyrdom. So too Tiburtius, son of Chromatius, and others. From the *Acts*, Petavius.

Diocletian, advancing from Nicomedia against Narseus, king of the Persians, forces him to withdraw from Syria, which he had occupied; he recovers Antioch and drives the enemy beyond the Tigris.

[Col. 0584A] [Note: [Col. 0584A] II III] Caius 4 and 5.

On the Kalends of January, Maximian wins a notable victory over the Germans, while Diocletian is pursuing his operations in the East. A triumphal coin was struck for this victory, explained with great erudition by Cardinal Noris, from Gaza Medicus.

[Col. 0584B] [Note: [Col. 0584B] III IV] Caius 5 and 6.

Egypt defects to Achilleus, [Col. 0584C] who assumes the purple there, while the Quinquegentiani also rebel in Africa near Cyrene. Calvisius writes that he has referred this event to this year from Eusebius. But Eusebius placed it under Olympiad 169 and Diocletian’s thirteenth year; Petavius and Pagius, following him, assign it to the years 290 and 296. See below.

[Note: [Col. 0584C] Olympiad 266 IV and Olympiad 267 I] Caius 6 and 7.

Cassiodorus writes under these consuls [Col. 0584D] that Maximian was admitted by Diocletian into partnership in the kingdom. But genuine monuments, inscriptions, and coins show that this occurred three years earlier. See above.

[Col. 0584D] [Note: [Col. 0584D] I II] Caius 7 and 8.

Alexandria defected to Achilleus this year or immediately afterward. From Eusebius, Pagius under the year 296, no. 6, proves this from coins and

[Col. 0586B] [Note: [Col. 0586B] II III] Caius 8 and 9.

In this consulship there was darkness during the day, and in that year Constantius and Galerius Maximian were raised to the rank of Caesars on the Kalends of March. Idatius, in the *Fasti*.

Petavius infers that a nearly total eclipse of the sun occurred at Carthage on 15 May, at the third hour of the afternoon.

Eusebius in the *Chronicle* reports that Narseus brought war against the East in the preceding year, before the creation of the Caesars Constantius and Galerius Maximian. But the war, victory, and Persian triumph had already occurred before the year 288. See above.

[Col. 0586C] [Note: [Col. 0586C] III IV] Caius 9 and 10.

Lydiatus refers to this year the victory over the Carpi won by Galerius Maximian.

[Col. 0586C] [Note: [Col. 0586C] Olympiad 267 IV and Olympiad 268 I] Caius 10 and 11.

The vows of the tenth anniversary were fulfilled; vows for the twentieth were now proclaimed. Mediobarbus, from coins.

[Col. 0586D] Lydiatus writes that Diocletian completed the Egyptian War this year after defeating Achilleus; likewise, that he transferred the Nabataeans, removed from their territory, to the Nile; and that he began to consider the persecution of the Christians.

[Col. 0586D] [Note: [Col. 0586D] I II] Caius 11 and 12.

Diocletian’s first limited persecution, before the edicts. See Bencini’s notes under Caius below. He assigns to this year, or to the preceding year of the Decennalia, the report from Eusebius [Col. 0588A] that Diocletian ordered himself to be worshiped as a god and used jewels in his clothing and footwear; Pagius confirms this under the year 301, no. 3.

[Col. 0588A] [Note: [Col. 0588A] II III] Caius 12. Marcellinus 1.

Caius completes his martyrdom on 22 April, having held office for six years, [Col. 0588B] four months, and eight days. See the notes, p. 252. The see remains vacant until 20 December.

In this consulship the nation of the Carpi surrendered in Romania. Idatius. The Carpi were a people in European Sarmatia, between the Carpathian Mountains and the Vistula River. See Cluver and Pagius under this year. Marcellinus is elected as Caius’s successor and ordained bishop on Sunday, 22 December. From that date he holds office for eight years, two months, and twenty-five days, until 16 March of the year 304. See the notes on Caius.

[Col. 0588C] [Note: [Col. 0588C] III IV] Marcellinus 1 and 2.

Alexandria, together with all Egypt, is recovered this year, according to Eusebius, in the sixth year after it had defected to Achilleus. See Pagius under this year, no. 6. He also reports that the Persian War was renewed this year, Galerius Caesar having been sent there from Egypt. See Pagius under the year 297, no. 4.

[Col. 0588D] [Note: [Col. 0588D] Olympiad 268 IV and 269] Marcellinus 2 and 3.

In this consulship the Persians were defeated, says Idatius, and with him Petavius and Pagius, who also adds the testimony of the Alexandrian *Chronicle*.

John Malalas, in his *Chronography*, records that Diocletian built enormous structures at Antioch while advancing toward the Persian War; and that, after the war had been completed, Diocletian constructed camps everywhere along the frontiers, from Egypt to the Persian borders, stationing frontier soldiers there and appointing commanders in each province to guard the camps and so forth.

[Col. 0590A] [Note: [Col. 0590A] I II] Marcellinus 3 and 4.

Veturius, master of the army, persecutes Christian soldiers; from that time the persecution against us gradually begins. Eusebius in the *Chronicle*, according to Pontacus’s edition. See Pagius under the year 297, no. 6, and under the year 298, no. 2.

Arnobius writes *Against the Pagans*, as he himself states in Book 2, in the year 1050 from the founding of the city. See Pagius under the year 302, no. 14.

[Col. 0590B] [Note: [Col. 0590B] II III] Marcellinus 4 and 5.

Eusebius, in the same edition of the *Chronicle*, writes that Hermione presided this year over the Church of Jerusalem as its twentieth bishop, Tyrannus over Antioch as its nineteenth, and Peter was ordained at Alexandria as its sixteenth bishop after Theonas. [Col. 0590C]

[Col. 0590C] [Note: [Col. 0590C] III IV] Marcellinus 5 and 6.

The author of the history of the Coptic patriarchs reports that this year Theonas, bishop of Alexandria, died in the eighth year of Juba, on Wednesday [Col. 0590D] [that is, 3 January, which Pagius observes was a Wednesday in this year, under this year, no. 5], and that Saint Peter succeeded him three years before the persecution; Pagius confirms this from Eusebius.

[Col. 0590D] [Note: [Col. 0590D] Olympiad 269 IV and Olympiad 270 I] Marcellinus 6 and 7.

Pagius concludes from the Encyclical Letter of Saint Athanasius against the Arians that the epoch of the Meletian schism must be assigned to this year; see him under the year 306, no. 24.

[Col. 0592A] [Note: [Col. 0592A] I II] Marcellinus 7 and 8.

Diocletian, returning from the Persian triumph celebrated at Rome and wintering in Bithynia, is stirred up by Maximian, whom his mother had inflamed against the Christians, and by the opinions of the judges and the response of Apollo of Miletus; he decrees a persecution against the Christians for the following year. From Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. See Pagius under the year 302, no. 3.

[Col. 0592B] [Note: [Col. 0592B] II III] Marcellinus 8 and 9.

The tenth persecution of the Church.

[Col. 0592C] An edict issued by the senior Augusti at Nicomedia on the day of the Terminalia, that is, 23 February, in the consulship of Diocletian for the eighth time and Maximian for the seventh [Lactantius], and in the month of March, during the days of Easter, the churches were overthrown, according to the Antiochenes in their year 351 [Eusebius]. Idatius agrees with this under these consuls. The edict read: “That all the leaders of the Churches everywhere should be bound and thrown into prison.” Eusebius, *History*, Book VIII, chapter 6.

[Col. 0592C] [Note: [Col. 0592C] III IV] Marcellinus 9, Marcellus 1. Persecution 2.

Marcellinus, having held office for eight years, two months, and twenty-five days, completes his martyrdom on 16 March this year. From the Lord’s Passion, 276 years are correctly reckoned, less nine days. See the notes, pp. 257 and 258.

Marcellus is elected as successor and ordained bishop on Sunday, 21 May. From that date he holds office until 16 January of the year 310, for five years, seven months, and twenty-five days. See the notes on Marcellus.

[Col. 0594A] [Note: [Col. 0594A] Olympiad 270 IV and Olympiad 271 I] Marcellus 1 and 2. Persecution 3.

During these times the emperor Galerius showed himself harsh and cruel, while Constantius, by contrast, showed himself mild and benevolent. Lydiatus under this year.

[Col. 0594B] Marcellus 2 and 3. Persecution 4.

[Note: [Col. 0594B] I II] In the fourth year of the persecution, Constantine [Col. 0594C] began to reign. Eusebius in the *Chronicle*.

Galerius Maximian creates Severus Caesar in the East. See the notes on Marcellus.

The schism of Majorinus in Africa and that of Meletius in Egypt are assigned to this year by Petavius.

[Col. 0594D] [Note: [Col. 0594D] II III] Marcellus 3 and 4. Persecution 5.

Severus Caesar is killed around the month of May by Maximian Herculius, who was attempting to recover the empire. Lydiatus, from Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. See, however, Pagius under the year 306, no. 9, from Caecilius, *On the Death of the Persecutors*, chapter 25, [Col. 0596A] who explains the matter more clearly and assigns it to its proper time, with coins bearing witness, while Mediobarbus [assigns] Alexander, the tyrant of Africa [to this year]. Mediobarbus.

Licinius is made partner in the empire by Galerius Maximian at Carnuntum in Pannonia on 11 November. Pagius, no. 14, and Mediobarbus.

[Col. 0596B] [Note: [Col. 0596B] III IV] Marcellus 4 and 5. Persecution 6.

Six Augusti were in office in this year: Herculeus, Galerius, Constantinus, Maximinus, Maxentius, and Licinius. See Pagius, on the year 307, no. VI.

On Sunday, 23 May, Eusebius was ordained bishop, to serve as Marcellus’s vicar. From that time until the day of his death, 17 August of the second year after the consulship of X and VII, that is, A.D. 310, there elapsed two years, two months, and twenty-five days, as marked in the paintings of Saint Paul [Col. 0596C]. See the notes on Marcellus.

[Note: [Col. 0596C] Olympiad 271 IV and 272.] Marcellus 5 and 6. Persecution 7.

In the East the persecution raged. Eusebius reports, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VIII, chapter 25, that an entire city in Phrygia was denounced because of the Christian faith. Petavius, on this year.

[Col. 0596D] [Note: [Col. 0596D] I II] Marcellus 6. Persecution 8. Eusebius and Melchiades I.

Marcellus completed his martyrdom on 16 January, the day on which he is commemorated, having sat for five years, seven months, and twenty-five days. See the notes on Marcellus.

[Col. 0598A] Eusebius, who had been vicar, was chosen as successor at Easter, on 2 April; shortly afterward, namely on 17 August, he died, according to the *Liberian Catalogue*, having sat for four months and sixteen days, according to the same catalogue, and for two years, two months, and twenty-five days from his episcopal ordination. See the notes on Eusebius.

Melchiades was ordained bishop by Eusebius on Sunday, 4 June [Col. 0598B], and appointed vicar; after Eusebius’s death he was chosen Roman pontiff. See the notes on Melchiades.

[Note: [Col. 0598B] II III] Melchiades 1 and 2. Persecution 9.

Galerius Maximianus died after his genitals had been consumed by a pestilential wound, having shortly before his death restrained the persecution by an edict. In it he is called *Tribunicia potestate XX* and consul VIII. Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* VIII, chapter 17; Petavius. Pagius maintains that this occurred at Sardica [Col. 0598C], on this year, no. XII. Maximianus and Licinius divide among themselves the provinces of the deceased Galerius. See there, no. XIV and following.

Around this year the persecution came to an end in Africa. See the notes cited above.

[Note: [Col. 0598C] III IV] Melchiades 2 and 3. Persecution 10.

The salutary sign of the cross was shown from heaven to Constantine as a prediction [Col. 0598D] of the victory which he won over Maxentius, who was thrown into the Tiber. Eusebius, Lactantius, and Baluzius in the notes on the same author, together with Pagius on this year, no. IV.

**PEACE RESTORED TO OUR CHURCHES BY CONSTANTINE.**

Eusebius, in the *Chronicle*. Nevertheless, while persecution was still raging at Rome under Maxentius, on Sunday, 10 February, Pope Melchiades ordained the bishop **SILVESTER**, who was to become vicar. See the notes cited above. From that day until [Col. 0600A] his death, on 31 December of the year 335, there elapsed twenty-three years, ten months, and twenty days of episcopate, the period assigned to him in the paintings of Saint Paul. See the notes cited above.

[Note: [Col. 0600A] Olympiad 272 IV and 273 I.] Melchiades 3 and 4.

A Roman synod was held in the house of Fausta at the Lateran against the Donatists, with Melchiades presiding, on 2 October. See the notes cited above [Col. 0600B], from a letter of Saint Augustine.

Maximinus, advancing from Syria against Licinius and Constantine, promised Jupiter the extinction of the Christian name if he should emerge victorious. Licinius, instructed by an angel to offer prayers to the supreme God, encountered him; Maximinus was driven out of Europe on 1 May, and, in a second battle, was defeated at Cybalum on 8 October. The victors, Constantine and Licinius, promulgated at Milan a second edict of **PEACE FOR THE CHURCH**. See Baronius and Mediobardus, and above all Pagius, who, from Lactantius’s *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, reviews each event in its proper order [Col. 0600C] for this year, no. 4 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0600C] I II] Melchiades 4. Silvester I.

Melchiades died and was deposited on 10 January in the cemetery of Callistus, as stated in a fourth-century work in its prologue and on an ancient stone. The inscription of Saint Silvester’s title records that he had sat, from his episcopal ordination as vicar and as pontiff, for three years, seven months, and seven days. See the notes cited above.

Silvester, already ordained bishop at the end of the persecution, in the year 312, on Sunday, 10 February, remained in office after the see had been vacant for sixteen days [as in the catalogue and the books], namely until 25 January. On 26 January he was chosen as successor, and on the following Sunday, 31 January, he was enthroned in the apostolic see. He held it for twenty-one years and eleven months, as expressed in the *Liberian Catalogue*, until 31 December, under the consuls Constantius and Albinus [namely, until the final day of the year 335, which, by the common agreement of all chronologists, belongs to that same year], and, counting from his episcopal ordination, for twenty-three years, ten months, and twenty days, preserved in the paintings of Saint Paul [Col. 0602A]. See the notes on Silvester.

The Synod of Arles was held, as were also those of Ancyra and Neocaesarea. Petavius on this year, and Cardinal Baronius on the same year.

The same Rufus, or Rufius Volusianus, was urban prefect from 20 August, in the *Laterculus Bucherianus*. Pagius thought that he had been consul a second time because of a wrongly transcribed stone in Spon 2, 76, in the Justinian gardens; there *ITERUM* is not read, but *ET FRVM*.

The *Paschal Chronicle* places the beginning of the Indiction in the preceding September, under the third consulship of Constantine and Licinius; it calls this Constantine’s eighth year, whereas the others, and we, place it one complete year earlier. Thus, under the consuls Volusianus and Anianus, the Indiction II runs from 1 January to 1 September, and from 1 September the Indiction III begins.
