and Constantius Gallus Caesar, consul II.

The same consuls: the Emperor Constantius Augustus VI and Constantius Gallus Caesar II.

Book 7 of the Theodosian Code, “On Veterans,” and others in Reland, where Gallus is also called Constans.

[Col. 0627C] After Cerealis, on 8 December, Vetrasius Orfitus became urban prefect.

Magnentius killed himself in Gaul on 11 August, and Caesar Decentius hanged himself on 18 August. Jerome and Idatius.

Constantius, victorious and master of the entire Roman Empire, celebrated magnificent games at Arles for the beginning of his thirtieth year. See Petavius.

The Emperor Caesar Constantius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0627C] 1106, 1107] 17 and 18; consul VII.

[Col. 0627D] And Constantius Gallus Caesar, consul II.

The same consuls: the Emperor Constantius Augustus VII;

Constantius Gallus Caesar III.

Book 1 of the Theodosian Code, “On the Property of Shipowners.”

Urban prefect: Vetrasius Orfitus.

Here ends the *Laterculus of the Urban Prefects* edited by Bucherius.

Constantius, advancing from Arles against the kings of the Alemanni, Gundomadus and Vadomarius, afterward made a treaty with them. Ammianus.

[Col. 0629A] The Emperor Caesar Constantius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0629A] 1107, 1108] 18 and 19; consul VII.

Flavius Claudius Julianus is called Caesar; he was the brother of Gallus Caesar, on 8 November.

Consuls: Flavius … Arbetio;

… Lollianus.

Gruter 1055, 4; Aringhi, volume 2, p. 287; book 12 of the Theodosian Code, “On Bishops” [Col. 0629B] etc., in Reland. Flavius Julianus was made Caesar, placed in command of the transalpine regions, and married Helena, Constantius’s sister. Ammianus; Zosimus III; Idatius; Jerome.

The Emperor Caesar Constantius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0629B] 1108, 1109] 19 and 20; consul VIII.

Julianus Caesar.

The same consuls: the Emperor Constantius Augustus VIII;

Flavius Julianus Caesar.

The Theodosian Code, book 6, “On Pagan Sacrifices and Temples” (and others in Reland), where the death penalty is decreed against those sacrificing to images.

[Col. 0629C] On 29 May Constantius departed from the City and proceeded into Illyricum. He kept Hosius there in hardship for a year in order to force from him the condemnation of Athanasius. Socrates, book 2.

The Emperor Caesar Constantius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0629C] 1109, 1110] 20 and 21; consul IX.

Julianus Caesar, consul II.

The same consuls: the Emperor Constantius Augustus IX;

Flavius Julianus Caesar II.

[Col. 0629D] The Theodosian Code, “On the Public Post,” book 10; and others in Reland; also book 1, title 3, law 2, of the Justinian Code; and Gruter 303, 1.

The *Paschal Chronicle* records that Constantius’s Vicennalia were celebrated under these consuls.

Julianus fought successfully against the Germans invading Lyons. He defeated the Alemanni in a bloody battle at Strasbourg and sent their king Chonodomarius, bound, to Rome to Constantius. He wintered at Paris. Ammianus VI; Zosimus III.

[Col. 0631A] The Emperor Caesar Constantius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0631A] 1110, 1111] 21 and 22; consul IX.

Julianus Caesar, consul II.

Consuls: … Datianus;

Neratius Cerealis.

Gruter 303, 2 and 1087, 4 and 5; Contelorius, *On the Urban Prefect*, p. 57; Reines, p. 929; Fabretti, p. 707. See also the laws of both codes [Col. 0631B] in Reland.

Constantius came from Sirmium to Rome on 28 April, in his thirty-fifth year, as Idatius records. He erected an obelisk in the Circus Maximus. Ammianus. He abolished gladiators by law 2 of the Code, “On Gladiators.”

Julianus struck the Salian Franks and received them into submission.

[Col. 0631C] The Emperor Caesar Constantius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0631C] 1111, 1112] 22 and 23; consul IX.

Julianus Caesar, consul II.

Consuls: … Eusebius;

… Hypatius.

Urban prefect Junius Bassus, who, while holding that prefecture under these consuls, went to God on 25 August, as stated on his sarcophagus in the Vatican Basilica beneath the Confession of the Holy Apostles. See Aringhi, Gruter, and Fabretti. Other inscriptions are also in Gruter 1087, 5, and [Col. 0631D] the laws of both codes in Reland. Urban prefect: Anicius Tertullus.

Julianus again subdued the Alemanni and compelled them to seek peace. Constantius defeated the Limigantes, a Sarmatian people. Petavius, from Ammianus, books 18 and 19. Gratianus was born. Jerome, *Chronicle*.

The third formula of Sirmium was issued under these consuls, on 22 May, according to Socrates and Epiphanius. See the notes there.

[Col. 0633A] The Emperor Caesar Constantius Augustus, tribunician [Note: [Col. 0633A] 1112, 1113] power 23 and 24; consul X.

Julianus Caesar, consul III. On the Ides of August, tribunician power [fragment; the source is incomplete].

The same consuls: the Emperor Constantius Augustus X;

Flavius Julianus Caesar III.

Book 3 of the Code, “On Bishops and Clergy,” and others in Reland. * Also an inscription in Boldetti, p. 86, dated 28 August, Monday. A total solar eclipse occurred in Mesopotamia [Col. 0633B] shortly after sunrise, according to Ammianus. See Pagius on this year, no. VII.

Julianus was acclaimed Augustus against Constantius, although he sent envoys to him. At Vienna he celebrated his Quinquennalia.

Urban prefect: Anicius Tertullus II.

The Emperor Caesar Constantius Augustus, tribunician [Note: [Col. 0633B] 1113, 1114] power 24 and 25; consul X; he died this year on 5 October [Col. 0633C]. See the notes, p. 29.

The Emperor Flavius Claudius Julianus Augustus, tribunician power 1 and 2; consul III; from 5 October he alone held the government.

Consuls: Flavius … Taurus;

Flavius … Florentius.

Reines, p. 997, from Aringhi; and law 7 of the Code, “On Dignities,” with others in Reland.

Constantius, returning from the Persian war, advanced against Julianus and died on the journey near Tarsus on 3 October. Ammianus, book XXI. See the notes, p. 29; Socrates at the end of book II; and Zosimus, book III, chapter 10. Julianus alone [Col. 0633D] ruled and entered Constantinople on 13 December. There he appointed Sallustius prefect of the Praetorian Guard.

Urban prefect: Anicius Tertullus III.

The first monastery in Gaul was constructed at Poitiers. Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book II, chapter 2, p. 173.

The Emperor Caesar Julianus Augustus, tribunician power 2 [Note: [Col. 0633D] 1114, 1115] and 3; consul III.

* Consuls: … Mamertinus;

… Nevitta.

* An ancient stone from Holstenius, in Vignoli, *On the Coloniae of Pius*, p. 328, and Fabretti, p. 695.

[Col. 0635A] Also law 1 of the Theodosian Code, “On Domestic Officials and Protectors,” and others in Reland.

Urban prefect: Anicius Maximus.

When Julianus came to Antioch, he excluded Christian grammarians and rhetoricians from the schools. He also became the author of a persecution that led people to apostasy by enticements rather than by slaughter. Nevertheless, many suffered martyrdom, among them Artemius. Jerome, *Chronicle*; Ammianus, book XXII; Malalas, who begins Julianus’s reign with these consuls.

The Emperor Caesar Julianus Augustus, tribunician power 3 [Note: [Col. 0635A] 1115, 1116] and 4; consul IV.

Consuls: Julianus Augustus IV;

… Sallustius.

An ancient inscription in Saint Martin of the Mountains; also in Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 113, and Gruter 185, 2; and laws of both codes in Reland, such as law 2 of the Theodosian Code, “On Dowries,” etc.

[Col. 0635C] Urban prefect: Lucius Turcius Apronianus. Contelorius, from Panvinius and an ancient inscription from Fanum, together with several others.

After Julianus departed this life from his wound, according also to the *Paschal Chronicle*, on 26 June, **JOVIANUS**, formerly commander of the household troops, was chosen emperor by the army. He made peace with the Persians for thirty years. Idatius; Ammianus; Jerome. He also ordered the temples of the idols to be closed and sacrifices abolished. Socrates, book 3, chapter 25.

[Col. 0635D] The Emperor Caesar Jovianus Augustus, tribunician power 1; consul; he died on 19 February. In his place **VALENTINIANUS** was chosen on 25 February, with the bisextile day omitted. At Constantinople he named **VALENS** Augustus on 29 March. Idatius.

* Consuls: the Emperor Caesar Jovianus Augustus;

Varronianus Caesar Augustus, son.

* An ancient stone in our Museum, reproduced in volume 2 of the Prologue, folio LXVIII, and in Boldetti, *On the Cemeteries*, p. 84, where the age of the Moon and the weekday are correctly given. See the laws in Reland dated under these consuls, such as book 2 of the Code, “On Those Involved in the Same Suit,” etc.

Sallustius was restored by Valentinianus to the urban prefecture. *Paschal Chronicle* [understand: at Constantinople].

Valentinianus, retaining the government of the western empire, entrusted the care of the East to Valens. Ammianus, book 25; Socrates IV, chapter 1; Zosimus IV.

At Rome, the urban prefects were Gaius Cejonius [Col. 0637A] Rufus Volusianus, according to an inscription, and Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, according to the laws cited by Contelorius.

The Emperor Caesar Valentinianus Augustus, tribunician [Note: [Col. 0637B] 1117, 1118] power 1 and, from 1 March, tribunician power 2; consul.

The Emperor Caesar Valens Augustus, tribunician power 1 and, from 29 March, tribunician power 2; consul.

* The same consuls, the Augusti Valentinianus Augustus and Valens Augustus.

* An ancient stone excavated from a cemetery in 1720, and many laws in Reland, book 5 of the Theodosian Code, “On Jurisdiction,” etc.

After Symmachus, the urban prefect was Gaius Cejonius Rufius Volusianus. Panvinius and the inscriptions.

[Col. 0637C] Festus Rufus, under this year, counts 243 years under the kings, 467 consuls, and 407 emperors. The total is 1117.

The Emperor Caesar Valentinianus Augustus, tribunician [Note: [Col. 0637C] 1118, 1119] power 2 and 3; consul.

The Emperor Caesar Valens Augustus, tribunician power 2 and 3; consul.

* Consuls: … Gratianus;

… Daglaiphus.

* An ancient stone from the cemetery of Callistus in Boldetti, p. 80; Gruter 1162, 5; and many laws in Gothofredus and Reland, namely book 9 of the Theodosian Code, “On Veterans,” etc.

Urban prefect: Viventius, according to Ammianus. [Col. 0637D] Valentinianus defeated the Alemanni. Idatius. A son, Valentinianus the Younger, was born to him on 18 January by Justina, who had been Magnentius’s wife. Zosimus, book 4; the edition concerning the Franks. See Petavius.

The Emperor Caesar Valentinianus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0637D] 1119, 1120], tribunician power 3 and 4; consul; and Gratianus Caesar.

The Emperor Caesar Valens Augustus, tribunician power 3 and 4; consul.

Consuls: Flavius … Lupicinus;

Flavius … Jovinus.

[Col. 0639A] Inscription in Reines, p. 906; Mabillon, *Supplement to Diplomatic Matters*, p. 15; and many laws in Gothofredus and Reland, such as book 3 of the Theodosian Code, “On Remission of Crimes,” etc.

It is also said that this year is designated as “after the consulship of Gratianus N. P. and Daglaiphus” in Law 16 of the Theodosian Code, concerning the annona and tribute, and on an inscription in Fleetwood, p. 501, cited by Reland.

Urban prefect: Vettius Praetextatus, as appears from an old inscription at Rome, in Panvinio and Contelori, and from Ammianus.

Emperor Caesar Valentinian Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0639B] 1120–1121] 4 and 5, consul 2; and Gratianus Caesar Augustus, also with tribunician power granted on the ninth day before the Kalends of September.

Emperor Caesar Valens Augustus, tribunician power 4 and 5.

The same Augusti as consuls:

- Valentinianus Augustus II
- Valens Augustus II

The Theodosian Code, Book 9, title 36, law 19, in Gothofredus; and other laws in Reland, such as Laws 29 and 30 of the Theodosian Code, concerning the public post, etc.

Inscription in Fabretti, p. 584.

Urban prefect: Quintus Clodius Hermogenianus Olybrius. An old inscription in Contelori; and the laws of the Code indicated by him and by Almeloveen.

Emperors Caesars Valentinianus [Note: [Col. 0639C] 1121–1122] Augustus, tribunician power 5 and 6, consul 2;

and Valens Augustus, tribunician power 5 and 6, consul 2;

and Gratianus Augustus, tribunician power 1 and 2, consul.

Consuls:

- Valentinianus, our young prince
- Sextus Aurelius Victor

An old inscription in Fabretti, p. 419, and laws cited by Reland, such as Law 10 of the Theodosian Code, concerning veterans, together with others there.

Urban prefect: Hermogenianus Olybrius, for the second time.

Anicius Probus, Praetorian Prefect, entrusted Ambrose—who had been invested with consular insignia—with the government of Insubria, Liguria, and Aemilia. Paulinus, in the Life of Ambrose.

Emperors Caesars Valentinianus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0639D] 1122–1123], tribunician power 6 and 7, consul 3.

[Col. 0641A] And Valens Augustus, tribunician power 6 and 7, consul 3.

And Gratianus Augustus, tribunician power 2 and 3, consul.

Consuls:

- Valentinianus Augustus III
- Valens Augustus III

An old inscription reported by Reland from Boissard attributes to both of them the titles: Pontifex Maximus, Germanicus Maximus, Alamannicus Maximus, Francicus Maximus, Gothicus Maximus, tribunician power 7, imperatorial acclamation 6, consul 2, Father of the Fatherland four times.

But the inscription that survives at Rome [Col. 0641B] on the Fabrician Bridge attributes the same titles also to Gratianus, with tribunician power 3, imperatorial acclamation 2, and first consulship, as it is read in Panvinius; indeed, it shows that the bridge was erected under Gratianus’ name.

Both codices read the same consuls, as in Law 6 of the Theodosian Code, concerning recruits, and in other passages cited by Reland.

Urban prefect after Olybrius: Ampelius of Antioch. Valentinianus defeats the Sarmatians and the Alamanni.

Emperors Caesars Valentinianus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0641B] 1123–1124], tribunician power 7 and 8, consul 3, imperatorial acclamation 6.

[Col. 0641C] And Valens Augustus, tribunician power 7 and 8, consul 3, imperatorial acclamation 6.

And Gratianus, most noble youth (N. P.), tribunician power 3 and 4, consul.

Consuls:

- Emperor Flavius Gratianus Augustus II
- Sextus Anicius Petronius Probus

Inscription: Gruter 164.4; Fabretti 271–272, 476, and 73.7; and Law 7 of the Code, concerning fugitive slaves, together with other material in Reland.

Urban prefect: Ampelius of Antioch. Panvinius and Contelori, from an old document. See the notes, p. 44.

Valentinianus puts the Alamanni to flight through the general Severus. Ammianus, Book 29. With his permission, the altar of Victory stands in the Capitol and sacrifices are performed. [Col. 0641D] Symmachus, to Valentinianus; and Ambrose, Letter 89.

Emperors Caesars Valentinianus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0641D] 1124–1125], tribunician power 8 and 9, consul 3, imperatorial acclamation 6.

And Valens, tribunician power 8 and 9, consul 3, imperatorial acclamation 6.

And Gratianus, tribunician power 4 and 5, consul 2.

Consuls:

- […] Modestus
- […] Arintheus

An inscription in Boldetti, p. 808, where it should be read: “Gratianus Augustus II and Probus, consuls,” in peace.

Also Law 1 of the Theodosian Code, concerning the Praetorian and Urban Prefects, and other laws in Reland; and from the Acts of Saint Saba, where the Easter calendar indicates that, after Ampelius, Claudius was Urban Prefect.

Theodosius the Younger, commander in Moesia, restrains the Sarmatians. Ammianus, Book 27.

About 80,000 Burgundians descend to the Rhine. There Melania, [Col. 0643B] daughter of the consul Marcellus, while intending to go to Jerusalem, sails to Egypt. Jerome, Chronicle; he was then living in the Syrian desert.

Rufinus of Aquileia, Melania’s companion, introduces her to the errors of Origen. Rufinus, History, Books 2 and 7.

Emperors Caesars Valentinianus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0643B] 1125–1126], tribunician power 9 and 10, consul 4, imperatorial acclamation 6.

And Valens Augustus, tribunician power 9 and 10, consul 4, imperatorial acclamation 6.

And Gratianus Augustus, tribunician power 5 and 6, consul 2.

[Col. 0643C] Consuls:

- Emperor Valentinianus Augustus IV
- Emperor Valens Augustus IV

An old inscription: Gruter 1061.7; Fabretti, p. 507; Vignoli, On the Column of Pius, p. 332; and laws collected by Reland, such as Law 11 of the Theodosian Code, concerning veterans, etc.

Urban prefect: Claudius II.

Theodosius the Elder, father of the younger Theodosius, who later became emperor, twice defeated Firmus, the African usurper, and drove him to the noose. Gildo, Firmus’ brother, renewed the usurpation and, favoring the Donatists, persecuted the Catholics. Ammianus, Books 28 and 29; and Claudian, On the War against Gildo.

[Col. 0643D] Emperors Caesars Valentinianus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0643D] 1126–1127], tribunician power 10 and 11, consul 4.

And Valens Augustus, tribunician power 10 and 11, consul 4.

And Gratianus Augustus, tribunician power 6 and 7, consul 3.

Consul: Gratianus Augustus III.

C. Equitius Valens.

An old inscription in Fabretti, p. 666, and from the Gudian manuscripts Reland; he also cites laws enacted under these consuls, such as Law 18 of the Theodosian Code, concerning public works, etc.

Urban prefect: Euphraxius. Panvinius.

Peace with Macrianus, king of Alamannia, established by Valentinianus on the banks of the Rhine. Military preparations against the Sarmatians; the vows for ten years fulfilled, and vows for twenty years undertaken. Ammianus and Zosimus; and Mediob., from coins.

The Council of Valence was held in Gaul, where the five provinces of Gaul are mentioned. See Pagi the Elder.

Emperors Caesars Valentinianus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0645A] 1127–1128], tribunician power 11 and 12, consul 4.

[Col. 0645B] And Valens Augustus, tribunician power 11 and 12, consul 4.

And Gratianus Augustus, tribunician power 7 and 8, consul 3.

“After the consulship of Gratianus Augustus III and Equitius.” Boldetti, p. 808; Gruter 1018.8. Thus this year is designated on inscriptions in Reinesius, p. 997; Cringius, vol. 2, p. 169; and in the laws of the Theodosian Code concerning recruits, and elsewhere in Reland.

Urban prefect in the second year: Euphraxius.

Valentinianus attacked the Sarmatians, who were ravaging the Pannonias. Exasperated by the speech of envoys sent by the Quadi, and seized by apoplexy, he died at Bregitio in Pannonia on 17 November, after ruling for eleven years and nine months. Six days later, namely on 22 November, Flavius Valentinianus the Younger, a four-year-old boy, the son of Justina, Gratianus’ stepmother, was created emperor Augustus through her efforts. Gratianus granted him Italy, Africa, and Illyricum, while retaining the remaining provinces of the Western Empire for himself. Ammianus, at the end of Book 30; Zosimus, Book 4, chapter 19.

Emperors Caesars Valens Augustus [Note: [Col. 0645C] 1128–1129] [Col. 0645D], tribunician power 12 and 13, consul 5.

And Gratianus Augustus, tribunician power 8 and 9, consul 3.

And Valentinianus the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 1, and from 22 November, 2, consul.

Consuls:

- Emperor Valens Augustus V
- Emperor Valentinianus Augustus

An old inscription: Gruter 17.4, 28.2, 192.3, and 1080.4; and many laws in Reland, such as Law 3 of the Theodosian Code, concerning theatrical performers.

Urban prefect after Euphraxius: Probianus.

[Col. 0647A] Emperors Caesars Valens Augustus [Note: [Col. 0647A] 1129–1130], tribunician power 13 and 14, consul 5.

And Gratianus Augustus, tribunician power 9 and 10, consul 4.

And Valentinianus the Younger, tribunician power 2 and 3, consul.

Consuls:

- Gratianus Augustus IV
- Flavius Merobaudes

An old inscription in Saint Cecilia’s and [Col. 0647B] in Almeloveen, fol. 121, correcting Gruter, p. 28.2.6, from the same Gruter, p. 370.3, and Fleetwood, p. 409 and p. 432.

Urban prefect in the second year: Probianus.

Emperors Caesars Valens Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0647B] 1130–1131] 14 and 15, consul 6.

And Gratianus Augustus, tribunician power 10 and 11, consul 4.

And Valentinianus the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 3 and 4, consul 2.

Consuls:

- Valens Augustus VI
- Valentinianus the Younger Augustus II

Book 11, title 19, law 9 of the Theodosian Code, and law 35 concerning the public post, together with other material in Reland.

Urban prefect: Hypatius.

Fourth Roman synod under Damasus, in which the heresy of Marcellus and Photinus was condemned; that heresy was later revived by Bonosus. See the younger Pagi on Siricius, no. 7; his notes below on Damasus; and Sommier, in the same place.

Emperors Caesars Gratianus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0647C] 1131–1132], tribunician power 10 and 11, consul 4.

And Valentinianus the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 4 and 5, consul 2.

And Theodosius Augustus, tribunician power 1, and from 19 January, 2.

Consuls:

- Decimus Magnus Ausonius
- Quintus Clodius Hermogenianus Olybrius

Gruter 353.2; Reinesius 983; and Laws 3 and 4 of the Theodosian Code, concerning the imperial household and the sacred largesses, together with other material in Reland.

Urban prefect: the sequence is interrupted.

Emperor Caesar Gratianus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0647D] 1132–1133] 11 and 12, consul 5.

And Valentinianus the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 5 and 6, consul 2.

[Col. 0649A] And Theodosius Augustus, tribunician power 1 and 2, consul.

Consuls:

- Gratianus Augustus V
- Theodosius Augustus

Inscription of Boldetti, from a cemetery, p. 85; and Book 3, title 5, law 6 of the Theodosian Code, together with other material in Reland.

Theophilus of Alexandria, then a cleric and later bishop, begins his computation of the hundred-year Paschal cycle from this year. Leo the Great, Letter 64. See Petavius.

Gratianus sends highly experienced commanders against the Goths and compels them to withdraw from Macedonia and Pannonia; soon afterward he establishes peace with them. From Prosper.

Justina, mother of Valentinianus the Younger, an Arian woman, strives to promote the heresy; Ambrose resists her most vigorously. Paulinus, in his Life of Ambrose.

[Col. 0649C] Emperors Caesars Gratianus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0649C] 1133–1134], tribunician power 12 and 13, consul 5.

And Valentinianus the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 6 and 7, consul 2.

And Theodosius Augustus, tribunician power 2 and 3, consul.

Consuls:

- […] Syagrius
- […] Eucherius

An old inscription from the Gudian manuscripts in Reland; and laws such as Law 6 of the Theodosian Code, concerning various rescripts, together with other material there.

Urban prefect: Flavius Annianus Eucharius Epiphanius. Panvinius and Contelori.

The Council of Aquileia was held on the Nones of September, at which Palladius and Secundianus, Arian bishops, were condemned. In Spain likewise, at Saragossa, the Priscillianists were condemned in a synod, together with Priscillian himself, a layman, whom the heretical bishops appointed bishop of Ávila. But through the agency of Idacius and Ithacius, Catholic bishops, he was expelled by decree of Gratianus. The Priscillianists, rejected at Rome by Damasus and at Milan by Ambrose, stirred up disturbances in Spain, to which they had returned by another rescript obtained through the bribery of the Master of Offices. Sulpicius Severus, Book 2. See the notes below on Damasus.

Emperors Caesars Gratianus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0651A] 1134–1135], tribunician power 13 and 14, consul 5.

And Valentinianus the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 7 and 8, consul 2.

And Theodosius Augustus, tribunician power 3 and 4, consul.

Consuls:

- […] Antoninus
- […] Syagrius

An old inscription in Saint Agnes Outside the Walls; and laws of both codes in Reland, such as Book 6 of the Theodosian Code, concerning various rescripts, and in the letter of Paschasinus to Leo the Great.

Maximus seized supreme power in Britain and, establishing his seat at Trier, named his son Victor as his partner in the empire. Zosimus 4; Socrates; and Victor.

Emperors Caesars Gratianus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0651B] 1135–1136], tribunician power 14 and 15, consul 5; he was killed on the eighth day before the Kalends of September.

And Valentinianus Augustus, tribunician power 8 and [Col. 0651C] 9, consul 2.

And Theodosius Augustus, tribunician power 4 and 5, consul.

Consuls:

- […] Merobaudes II
- […] Saturninus

An old stone inscription in Saint Martin in the Hills, inscribed by Pope Damasus under these consuls; Fabretti, pp. 659 and 666; and the single law of the Theodosian Code concerning imperial officials, together with other material in Reland.

The tyrant Maximus killed Gratianus Augustus, abandoned by his own men, through the agency of the general Andragathius, at Lyons on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. Marcellinus Comes; Socrates, Book 5, chapter 11.

[Col. 0651D] Emperors Caesars Valentinianus the Younger [Note: [Col. 0651D] 1136–1137] Augustus, tribunician power 9 and 10, consul 2.

And Theodosius Augustus, tribunician power 5 and 6, consul.

And Arcadius Augustus, tribunician power 1 and 2.

Consuls:

- Flavius Recimer
- Flavius Clearchus

An old inscription of Boldetti, from a cemetery, p. 82; and of the Alban Museum; Fabretti, p. 270; Fleetwood, p. 442; and laws of both codes in Reland, such as Law 3 of Book 6, title 2, of the Theodosian Code.

Symmachus, Urban Prefect, presents Valentinianus with a petition concerning the restoration of the worship of the gods; Ambrose refutes it. His Letter 30.

Emperors Caesars Valentinianus the Younger [Note: [Col. 0653A] 1137–1138] Augustus, tribunician power 10 and 11, consul 2.

And Theodosius Augustus, tribunician power 6 and 7, consul.

And Arcadius Augustus, tribunician power 2 and 3, consul.

Consuls:

- Emperor Caesar Flavius Arcadius
- […] Bauto

A letter of Pope Siricius was issued under these consuls. See the notes, p. 55; and many laws in Reland, such as Book 6 of the Theodosian Code, concerning jurisdiction, etc.

The Council of Bordeaux against the Priscillianists, in which Justantius and Salvianus were deposed. Prosper; Sulpicius Severus, Book 2. Priscillian, the heretic, appealed from the synod to Maximus and was condemned to the sword. There.

Emperors Caesars Valentinianus the Younger [Note: [Col. 0653B] 1138–1139] Augustus, tribunician power 11 and 12, consul 2.

And Theodosius Augustus, tribunician power 7 and 8, consul.

And Arcadius Augustus, tribunician power 3 and 4, consul.

[Col. 0653C] Consuls:

- Flavius Honorius, son of Theodosius Augustus, most noble boy (*filius nobilissimus puer*)
- Flavius Evodius

Book 2 of the Theodosian Code, concerning the curators of the Kalends, and other material in Reland.

The sister of Valentinianus the Younger marries Theodosius. Marcellinus.

Valentinianus the Younger, at the instigation of his mother Justina, an Arian woman, issues a law in favor of the Ariminian confession—Law 4 of the Code, concerning the Catholic Faith—and persecutes Ambrose. When Auxentius challenged Ambrose to a disputation, Ambrose requested before the people that it be held, and resisted the emperor lest he surrender the basilica [Col. 0653D] to the Arians. Saint Ambrose, Letter 14, and On Not Handing Over the Basilica.

Emperors Caesars Valentinianus Augustus [Note: [Col. 0653D] 1139–1140], tribunician power 12 and 13, consul 3.

And Theodosius Augustus, tribunician power 8 and 9, consul.

And Arcadius Augustus, tribunician power 4 and 5, consul.

- Eutropius

Maximus restores sacrifices to the pagans and the altar of Victory, with Symmachus praising him. Socrates, Book 5, chapter 4.

Emperors Caesars Valentinianus the Younger [Note: [Col. 0655A] 1140–1141] Augustus, tribunician power 13 and 14, consul 3.

Theodosius abolishes at Milan all dignities conferred by Maximus—Law 8 of the Code, concerning the invalidation of acts done under tyrants—and entirely removes the assemblies of heretics—Law 19, concerning heretics. With his son Honorius he enters Rome on the Ides of June and, having given a largess to the Roman people, departs on the Kalends of September. Idacius.

Urban prefect of Constantinople: Pancratius. Almeloveen, from the Theodosian and Justinian Codes.

Urban prefect: Albinus, in the law *servos* of the Code concerning public violence under the Julian law, etc.; the Code in Contelori and Almeloveen.

An obelisk was placed in the circus by Theodosius, and a silver statue of him was erected above a column near the Church of Constantinople. Ammianus Marcellinus.

Emperors Caesars Valentinianus the Younger [Note: [Col. 0657A] 1143–1144] Augustus, tribunician power 15 and 16, consul 4.

Fabius Tatianus as the regular consul, as in Contelori, p. 55; and the laws of both codes in Reland have Tatianus and Symmachus, in Book 6 of the Theodosian Code, concerning contracts of sale, and Book 4, concerning shipwrecks, etc.

Urban prefect: Proculus of Constantinople. Almeloveen; at Rome, Alypius; Faltus; Probus. There.

[Col. 0657C] Emperors Caesars Valentinianus the Younger [Note: [Col. 0657C] 1144–1145] Augustus, tribunician power 16, consul 4 [who was killed on the Ides of May].

Laws 2 and 3 of the Theodosian Code, concerning the defense of cities, Book 1, title 10, and other material in Reland.

Valentinianus the Younger, a catechumen, is buried at Milan. Saint Ambrose, On His Funeral, and Letter 34.

Reinesius, in the appendix to his Inscriptions, p. 1021, no. 16, presents an inscription reading “Theodosius Augustus III and Eugenius, our Lords, consuls.” He notes that Eugenius served as Western consul, but that, according to a subsequent law issued after his death in the year 395—found in Book 15, title 14, of the Theodosian Code, concerning the invalidation of acts done under tyrants, law 9—both his name and those of others were suppressed and the names of the Eastern consuls substituted.

Gruter, inscriptions 352.5–6 and 350.2–3, in the museum of Cardinal Albani. Also laws of the Theodosian Code, Book 6, title 24, concerning domestics and protectors, law 6, together with other material in Reland.

Urban prefects at Rome: Basilius, and shortly afterward Andromachus, then Florentinus. At Constantinople, Theodorus, and afterward Africanus. Almeloveen, from the laws.

Arcadius prohibits the assemblies of heretics. Theodosian Code, Book 16, title 5, concerning heretics, law 26 and following. He likewise enacted several measures against the pagans, Law 13, concerning pagans.

[Col. 0661B] Emperors Caesars Arcadius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0661B] 1148–1149] 13 and 14, consul 4.

Fritigil, queen of the Marcomanni, having heard of Ambrose’s fame, believed in Christ and asked him for a rule of faith. Then she persuaded her husband to surrender himself to the Romans; when she came to Milan the following year to see him, she found him dead. Petavius, from Paulinus’ Life of Saint Ambrose.

Emperors Caesars Arcadius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0661C] 1149–1150] 14 and 15, consul 4.

And Honorius Augustus, tribunician power 4 and 5, consul [Col. 0661D] 3.

Urban prefect: R. Florentinus, from Book 14, title 2, law 3 of the Theodosian Code; and at Constantinople, Africanus, from Book 4, title 4, law 4 of the Theodosian Code.

[Col. 0663A] Under these consuls Quintus Hilarion wrote, calculating that 369 complete years had elapsed from the Passion of the Lord in this year. Therefore our chronology is correct in placing the Passion of the Lord in the year 28

of the common era: to which, when 369 years are added,

the total is 397.

See Schelestratius, Ecclesiastical Antiquities, dissertation 1, at the end, and Reland in the Fasti under these consuls.

Emperors Caesars Arcadius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0663B] 1150–1151] 15 and 16, consul 4.

And Honorius Augustus, tribunician power 5 and 6, consul 4.

- Eutychianus

Urban prefect at Rome: Felix, Theodosian Code, Book 6, title 2, law 10; but see Gothofredus. At Constantinople: Optatus, Theodosian Code, Book 12, title 26, law 13; and Romulianus, there, Book 7, title 1, law 17.

Emperors Caesars Arcadius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0663C] 1151–1152] 16 and 17, consul 4.

And Honorius Augustus, tribunician power 6 and 7, consul 4.

He was killed while in office (*in Mag.*) and removed from the Fasti. See Baronius. Therefore, in Book 3, title 1, law 8 of the Theodosian Code, only Theodorus is named consul; likewise in other laws of the same Code issued at Verona and Altinum, as Gothofredus observes, and with him Almeloveen, in the Fasti and Reland. Moreover, an old inscription—Gruter 192.12—names only Theodorus as consul. Saint Augustine, City of God, Book 18, chapter 54; and the African Council held this year under Pope Anastasius [see Binius, p. 795] is entitled: “After the consulship of Honorius Augustus IV and Eutychianus.”

Urban prefects: at Rome, Flavianus, Theodosian Code, Book 14, title 10, law 3; at Constantinople, Severinus, there, Book 6, title 12, single law, and Clearchus, there, Book 13, title 1, law 16.

Sulpicius Severus, Book 2, counts 372 years from the Crucifixion of Our Lord Jesus Christ under the two Gemini as consuls down to the consulship of Stilicho; this total agrees entirely with our chronology.

Urban prefects: at Rome, Andromachus, Theodosian Code, Book 11, title 28, law 3; at Constantinople, Clearchus, Book 6, title 26, law 12.

The first Paschal letter of Theophilus of Alexandria, in which Easter is prescribed for this year on 19 Pharmuthi, or 14 April. See below in the notes on Innocent, and Noris, History of the Pelagians, Book 1, chapter 2, and Pagi under this year, no. 2.

Laws of the Theodosian Code in Reland, such as Book 7, title 13, law 15, concerning recruits, and Book 14, title 17, law 14; and in the corrected Code under these consuls in the same Reland. The Council of Milevis was also held under these consuls, on the sixth day before the Kalends of September.

The twentieth anniversary of Arcadius and the tenth anniversary of Honorius were celebrated. Pagi. Theodosius the Younger is called Augustus by his father Arcadius on 17 January. Marcellinus and the Alexandrian Chronicle.

Stilicho frees Honorius, who was besieged by the Goths at Asti, and again defeats the Goths near Verona. Mediobarbus, from Jordanes, chapter 9, On the Affairs of the Goths.

Under these consuls there was a solar eclipse on the third day before the Ides of November, according to Idacius; it occurred on a Monday at the first hour before noon at Constantinople.

And Honorius Augustus, tribunician power 10 and 11, consul 5.

- Flavius Rumorides

An old inscription: Gruter 1052.10; Fabretti 387, now in the Alban Museum; and laws of both codes in Reland, such as the Code concerning judges and the worshippers of heaven, Law 10, etc.

From this year Honorius began to reside at Ravenna, as Dufresne infers from his constitutions in the notes on Zonaras, p. 45. There.

Emperors Caesars Arcadius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0667C] 1156–1157] 21 and 22, consul 6.

And Honorius Augustus, tribunician power 11 and 12, [Col. 0667D] consul 6.

On the Kalends of January, Honorius, returning to Rome [from *vecadio*, reading uncertain], celebrated a triumph over Alaric. Claudian.

Gladiatorial games were entirely abolished everywhere by Honorius in this year [see Pagi, no. 3], although previously they had been prohibited by Constantine and other emperors but had not been abolished everywhere.

Emperors Caesars Arcadius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0669A] 1157–1158] 22 and 23, consul 5.

An ancient stone in the Alban Museum; another in Fabretti, inscription fol. 734; and another formerly in Saint Martin in the Hills, reported by Martinello, Sacred Rome, p. 256, and by Gruter 1053.4. On it the boy Helias Argentarius is buried on the seventh day before the Kalends of November, a Friday, at the fourth hour. The dominical letter A, on 26 October, shows that it was a Thursday. [Col. 0669C] See Lydiat under this year.

Other stones are also found in Gruter 1054.5 and Boissard; and laws cited by Reland, such as Law 18 of the Theodosian Code, concerning the sacred largesses of the imperial household, etc.

Rhadagaisus, after many thousands of Goths had been killed in Tuscany, was defeated and captured while Stilicho commanded the army. Prosper and Orosius. See Baronius and Pagi.

Emperors Caesars Arcadius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0669C] 1158–1159] [Col. 0669D] 23 and 24, consul 6.

And Honorius Augustus, tribunician power 13 and 14, consul 6.

And Theodosius the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 4 and 5, consul.

Laws of both codes in Reland, such as the Theodosian Code concerning notices of sale, Book 6, etc.

The Vandals and Alans, having crossed the Rhine, enter Gaul on the day before the Kalends of January. Others give September. Prosper, Cassiodorus, and Zosimus, Book 6; he adds the Suevi. But see Pagi under this year, nos. 12 and following, and no. 10, etc.

Emperors Caesars Arcadius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0671A] 1159–1160] 24 and 25, consul 6.

And Honorius Augustus, tribunician power 14 and 15, consul 7.

And Theodosius the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 5 and 6, consul 2.

The Vandals and Pannonian peoples [see Pagi, no. 10] ravage far and wide the provinces nearest the Rhine. They overthrow Mainz; they plunder the Rhine districts, Amiens, Arras, Thérouanne, Strasbourg, etc. Zosimus [Col. 0671C] and Saint Jerome, Letter 11.

In Britain, a military uprising chooses Marcus as tyrant. Zosimus, Book 6, chapter 2.

Emperors Caesars Arcadius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0671C] 1160–1161] 25 and 26, consul 6; he died on the Kalends of May, having ruled after his father’s death for 13 years, 3 months, and 15 days.

And Honorius Augustus, tribunician power 15 and 16, consul 7.

And Theodosius the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 6 and 7, consul 2.

Consuls:

- Anicius Bassus

An old inscription in Saint Agnes Outside the Walls, reported by Aringhi, vol. 2, p. 168; Reinesius, p. 943; and laws in Reland, Law 19 of the Theodosian Code, concerning recruits, etc.; Fabretti, p. 268.

Urban prefects: at Rome, Hilarius, Theodosian Code, Book 14, title 4, law 1; at Constantinople, Monaxius, Theodosian Code, Book 14, title 17, law 15.

Emperors Caesars Honorius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0671D] 1161–1162] 16 and 17, consul 8.

And Theodosius the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 7 and 8, consul 3.

Consuls, the same Augusti:

- Honorius Augustus VIII
- Theodosius Augustus III

Gruter 1058.2, whose number for the consulship of Theodosius must be corrected, since it gives V [unless it is Honorius IX, which is correctly joined with Theodosius V below, in the year 411]. The same Gruter 1052.6 presents an epitaph at Trier joining the eighth consulship of Honorius with the first of Constantine [namely, that British tyrant who had established himself at Arles in this year]. On this, see Noris, Syro-Macedonian Era, dissertation 4, chapter 1, near the end. Olympiodorus, in Photius, says that Honorius sent him the purple. The same consuls, Honorius VIII and Theodosius III, are read in the laws of both codes in Reland, such as Book 6 of the Theodosian Code, concerning decurions of the city of Rome, and Book 14, title 1, etc.

Urban prefects: at Rome, Bonosianus, and Attalus, according to Zosimus; at Constantinople, Monaxius, Theodosian Code, Book 15, title 1, law 47, etc.

The Alans, Vandals, and Suevi enter Spain. Idacius and Orosius. Constans, son of the tyrant Constantine, is sent into Spain after peace had been made with Honorius [Col. 0673C]. Zosimus, Book 6, chapter 4. But Maximus exercises tyranny in Spain.

Emperors Caesars Honorius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0673C] 1162–1163] 17 and 18, consul 8.

And Theodosius the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 8 and 9, consul 3.

Consul: Flavius Varanes alone; for Tertullus, appointed by Attalus, is regarded as a shadow consul. Orosius, Book 7, chapter 42.

The Theodosian Code has Varanes alone, Book 9, title 28, laws 11 and 12, etc., in Reland; and Book 7, title 13, law 20, which show that the sack of the city occurred in the preceding year.

Marcianus was appointed Urban Prefect by Attalus. Zosimus, Book 6, chapter 7.

Emperors Caesars Honorius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0673D] 1163–1164] 18 and 19, consul 8.

And Theodosius the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 9 and 10, consul 4.

Theodosius the Younger Augustus was consul 4 without a colleague, according to Law 48 of the Theodosian Code, concerning public works, issued under the post-consulship of Varanes, and Book 7 of the same Code, title 17, single law, concerning the games of the Danube. On this see Gothofredus, who assigns it to Theodosius IV, and identifies the one who was announced [the text incorrectly assigns it to V]. Theodosius the Younger celebrated his decennalia, and Honorius his vicennalia, at Rome. Marcellinus, Chronicle.

The barbarians who had poured into Spain divide the provinces among themselves. The Vandals occupy Gallaecia; the Suevi and Alans, Lusitania and the provinces of Carthage; the Vandal Silingi, Baetica. Idacius.

[Col. 0675B] Urban prefects: at Rome, Bonosianus, Theodosian Code, Book 15, title 1, law 48; at Constantinople, Isidorus. Reland and Gothofredus, from the Register of Dignities.

Emperors Caesars Honorius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0675B] 1164–1165] 19 and 20, consul 9.

And Theodosius Augustus, tribunician power 10 and 11, consul 5.

Consuls:

- Honorius Augustus IX
- Theodosius Augustus V

Laws of both codes in Reland, such as Laws 22, 23, 24, and 25 of the Theodosian Code, concerning the imperial exhortation to prefects, etc. Under these consuls Jovinus and Sebastianus, brothers exercising tyranny in Gaul and [Col. 0675C] Spain, were killed. Marcellinus, Chronicle.

Honorius, after the conference, punishes the obstinate Donatists with various penalties and orders their churches and property to be restored to the Catholics. Law 52 of the Code, concerning heretics. Jovinianus the heretic is banished by the same emperor to the island of Boa. Theodosian Code, same title, law 51.

Emperors Caesars Honorius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0675C] 1165–1166] [Col. 0675D] 20 and 21, consul 9.

And Theodosius the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 11 and 12, consul 5.

Consul: Lucius alone, for Heraclianus, governor of Africa, who had been appointed Lucius’ colleague in the consulship, was struck from the Fasti, as appears in Book 15, title 14, law 13 of the Theodosian Code, and in Prosper and Marcellinus, Chronicle.

Thus the laws of both codes designate the consulship of Lucius alone, as in the single law of the Code concerning the comites and the tribunes of the scholars, etc., in Reland.

Pelagius the Briton, with Caelestius and Julian as his hearers, puts forward a doctrine bearing his name against the grace of Christ. Prosper.

The Burgundians, a people of Germany, occupy the part of Gaul near the Rhine. Prosper.

The twentieth anniversary of the reign of Honorius. After the Gothic devastation, the city’s desolation gradually comes to an end; 15,000 citizens are counted. Olympiodorus.

Emperors Caesars Honorius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0677A] 1166–1167] [Col. 0677B] 21 and 22, consul 9.

And Theodosius the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 12 and 13, consul 5.

Consuls:

- Flavius Constantius
- Flavius Constans

Law 38 of the Theodosian Code, concerning shipowners, addressed to Albinus, Urban Prefect, and Laws 54 and 55, concerning heretics, together with other material in Reland; and Letter 22 of Pope Innocent, issued on the Ides of December under Constantius’ consulship.

Constantius, Count, stationed at Arles, a city of Gaul, drives the Goths from Narbonne and compels them to go to Spain. Athaulphus, who had been considering the destruction of the Roman name, abandons war at the advice of his wife Placidia and after learning, through experience, how incapable his own people were of obeying laws; he seeks glory by restoring the Roman Empire through Gothic strength. Orosius, Book 7, chapter 43.

Emperors Caesars Honorius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0677C] 1167–1168] 22 and 23, consul 10.

And Theodosius the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 13 and 14, consul 6.

The same consuls:

- Honorius Augustus X
- Theodosius Augustus VI

Laws 36, 57, and 58 of the Theodosian Code, concerning heretics, and other material in Reland.

Urban prefects: at Rome, Gracchus, Theodosian Code, [Col. 0677D] Book 8, title 7, law 20; at Constantinople, Ursus, Theodosian Code, Book 6, title 23, law 1.

Attalus, neglected by the Goths migrating toward Spain and left without protection, is captured and handed over alive to Constantius the Patrician.

Athaulphus dies after being wounded by one of his own men, and Vallia seized his kingdom. Prosper.

Vallia undertakes war against the Alans and the Vandals, the Silingi. Idacius.

[Col. 0679A] Emperors Caesars Honorius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0679A] 1168–1169] 23 and 24, consul 10.

And Theodosius the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 14 and 15, consul 7.

Consuls:

- Theodosius the Younger Augustus VII
- Junius Quartus Palladius

[Col. 0679B] Panvinius, from an old stone inscription, and Reinesius, p. 422; and letters of Innocent issued on the sixth day before the Kalends of February, where these consuls are mentioned. See Reland and the laws cited by him, Books 8 and 9 of the Theodosian Code, concerning domestics and protectors, etc.

Urban prefects: at Rome, Probianus, Theodosian Code, Book 14, title 20, law 4; at Constantinople, Ursus, Theodosian Code, Book 12, title 1, law 180, etc.

Vallia makes peace with Honorius, and Placidia is restored; she marries Constantius. Orosius and Prosper.

Emperors Caesars Honorius Augustus, tribunician power 24 and 25, consul 11.

And Theodosius the Younger Augustus, tribunician power 15 and 16, consul 7.

Consuls:

- Honorius Augustus XI
- Constantius II

Law 12 of the Theodosian Code, Book 6, title 2, addressed to Monaxius, Urban Prefect, etc., in Reland; and in the letter of Paschasinus and the letter of Pope Zosimus to Aurelius.

The Siling Vandals in Baetica were all destroyed by King Vallia. Idacius. He likewise reports that the Alans, who ruled over the Vandals and Suevi, were so thoroughly slaughtered by the Goths that, after their king Atax had been killed, the few survivors, abandoning the name of their kingdom, submitted themselves to the Vandals who had remained in Gaul. Petavius.

Controversy concerning Easter between the Westerners and the Alexandrians. See Paschasinus’s letters to Leo the Great.

Honorius entered Rome in triumph, with Attalus preceding his chariot; Attalus was mutilated by the cutting off of two fingers and banished to the island of Lipara. Prosper, from the chronicle, and Philostorgius.

Emperors and Caesars Honorius Augustus, in the 25th and 26th years of tribunician power, consuls for the twelfth time. [Note: [Col. 0679D] 1669 1160] [Col. 0681A]

And Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 16th and 17th years of tribunician power, consul for the eighth time.

Consuls: the same Augusti—Honorius XII; Theodosius VIII.

Theodosian Code, book X, title 10, law 38, and elsewhere in Reland; the African council; and in the most ancient copy of Justellus’s *Code of the Canons of the African Church*, now preserved in the Bodleian Library at Oxford. [Col. 0681B] See the notes on Zosimus.

An eclipse of the sun, eleven and a half digits [according to Petavius’s calculations], occurred at Rome on 19 August, a Friday, at the eighth hour; concerning it, see the Alexandrian Chronicle, Idacius, and Marcellinus. See the notes above.

Valentinian Junior was born at Ravenna to Constantius and Placidia, on 2 July. Prosper.

Urban prefect of Rome: Palladius. Theodosian Code, book IV, title 4, law 6.

Emperors and Caesars Honorius Augustus, in the 26th and 27th years of tribunician power, consuls for the twelfth time. [Note: [Col. 0681B] 1171 1172]

And Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 17th and 18th years of tribunician power, consul for the eighth time.

[Col. 0681C] Consuls: Monaxius; Plinta.

Gruter, inscription p. 1050, no. 7; the Theodosian Code, book VI, title 30, law 22; other sources in Reland; and Aurelius’s letter to all the Byzaceni. Noris, *History of Pelagius*, p. 115.

Urban prefect of Constantinople: Aetius. Theodosian Code, book XIV, title 6, law 5. At Rome, Symmachus, as is clear from the circumstances of the schism.

This year Easter was celebrated on 30 March. Saint Augustine, *On Seven Questions to Dulcitius*. See Noris, *History of Pelagius*, book I, chapter 17, p. 107, and the Paschal Table below, p. [Col. 0681D] 146.

Emperors and Caesars Honorius Augustus, in the 27th and 28th years of tribunician power, consul for the twelfth time. [Note: [Col. 0681D] 1172 1173]

Consuls: Theodosius Augustus IX; Constantius Augustus III.

Theodosian Code, “On Bishops, Churches, and Clerics,” law 44, and elsewhere in Reland, where only the two Augusti, Honorius and Theodosius, are mentioned, while Constantius is called *vir clarissimus* but not Augustus.

Urban prefect of Rome: Palladius. Justinian Code, book I, title 3, law 19.

[Col. 0683A] From this point, according to Petavius, the Frankish kingdom begins. Pharamund, the first king of the Franks, began his reign this year. Prosper, in the chronicle edited by Pithoeus.

Idacius affirms that Constantius was created Augustus this year, but Prosper assigns it to the following year, consistently with the laws.

Emperors and Caesars Honorius Augustus, in the 28th and 29th years of tribunician power, consul for the twelfth time. [Note: [Col. 0683A] 1173 1174]

[Col. 0683B] And Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 19th and 20th years of tribunician power, consul for the ninth time.

And Constantius Augustus, in the year of tribunician power not stated, consul for the third time, was admitted to a share in the Empire on 8 February; he died on 2 September of that same year. Theophanes.

Consuls: Eustathius; Agricola.

Theodosian Code, law 45, “On Bishops and Churches,” where Illyricum is placed under the bishop of Constantinople; but the Roman pontiffs did not abandon their rights through their apostolic vicars. See the notes on Boniface.

[Col. 0683C] Other laws of both Codes in Reland also give these consuls. The laws of the Theodosian Code issued under these consuls—namely, book II, title 27, “If a Definite Thing Is Claimed,” issued on 28 July, and the preceding laws issued on 12 March, 10 March, and 8 July—published by Noris, *History of Pelagius*, book I, chapter 20, demonstrate that Constantius was Augustus this year. He also died seven months after his adoption, as Olympiodorus, a contemporary witness, writes, and Theophanes.

Urban prefect of Rome: Volusianus. See Noris, *History of Pelagius*, book I, chapter 20, p. [Col. 0683D] 126.

Emperors and Caesars Honorius Augustus, in the 29th and 30th years of tribunician power, consul for the thirteenth time. [Note: [Col. 0683D] 1174 1175]

The Romans in Spain were defeated by the Vandals under Castinus, Master of the Soldiers. See Ruinart, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, part 2, chapter 2, no. 3, and Idacius.

The thirtieth anniversary of Honorius and the twentieth anniversary of Theodosius.

Urban prefect of Constantinople: Florentius. Theodosian Code, book XV, title 1, law 8.

The emperor Honorius died at Rome on 16 or 29 August. See the notes on Celestine and du Cange, *History of the Byzantine Imperial Family*, p. 72.

Under these consuls Eudoxia was created Augusta on 2 January. Alexandrian Chronicle.

[Col. 0685C] Among the Lombards, Lamissus, the second king, reigned for three years. John, formerly a notary, usurped the Empire in the West. Socrates, book VII, chapter 25.

Emperors and Caesars Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 22nd and 23rd years of tribunician power, consul for the tenth time. [Note: [Col. 0685C] 1176 1177]

Valentinian Caesar.

Consuls: Castinus; Victor.

Theodosian Code, book XV, title 5, “On Public Spectacles,” law 4, where only the emperor Theodosius is named, with Victor, *vir clarissimus*, as consul on 22 April; and book X, title 20, “On the Mureleguli,” law 14, issued on 16 October under Victor’s consulship, where Theodosius Augustus and Valentinian Caesar are named.

Urban prefect of Constantinople: Severinus. Theodosian Code, book XV, title 1, law 52.

And Flavius Placidius Valentinianus Junior Caesar, soon also called Augustus, on 23 October. Du Cange, *Byzantine Families*, from Olympiodorus and Silvius.

Theodosian Code, book VI, title 10, “On Primicerii and Notaries,” law 4, where Theodosius is Augustus and Valentinian Caesar on 22 September, as also in other preceding documents in Reland. Near the end of the year, the seven-year-old Valentinian appeared at Rome as emperor, as Noris proves from Idacius and Olympiodorus, who were then living. [Col. 0687B] Noris, *History of Pelagius*, book I, chapter 24, p. 152. He also shows that the title Augustus appears in the second law of the Theodosian Code, book X, title 26, “On Conductores,” issued on 3 January of the following year, under the consuls Theodosius XII and Valentinian II.

Gunderic, king of the Vandals, after capturing Hispalis, extended impious hands against the city’s church and, seized by a demon, perished. His brother Genseric succeeded him, falling into Arian perfidy. Idacius, in the chronicle.

Ruinart, *History of the Vandals*, part 2, chapter 3, no. 6, and in the preface to Victor of Vita’s history, no. 8.

Consuls: Valentinian Augustus V; Anatolius.

[Col. 0697C] Old inscription in the title of Saint Martin at the Monti; two inscriptions in Gudius, printed by Reland; and several laws, such as book VII of the Code, “On Laws,” and others in the same Reland.

Emperors and Caesars Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 39th and 40th years of tribunician power, consul for the seventeenth time. [Note: [Col. 0697C] 1193 1194]

And Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 16th and 17th years of tribunician power, consul for the fifth time.

Consul: Cyrus alone, promoted to the consulship through Eudocia’s favor because of his poetic skill. Petavius, from Suidas.

An old inscription in San Martino ai Monti has “After the consulship of our lords Valentinian and Anatolius,” and displays Cyrus in law 10 of the Code, “On the Defense of Cities,” with other sources in Reland.

This year the First Council of Orange was celebrated, from the provinces of Narbonensis and Lyon. Petavius.

Emperors and Caesars Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 40th and 41st years of tribunician power, consul for the seventeenth time. [Note: [Col. 0697D] 1194 1195]

And Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 17th and 18th years of tribunician power, consul for the fifth time.

Consuls: Eudoxius and Dioscorus, both in the East.

[Col. 0699A] Ancient inscriptions in Fabretti, p. 112; Aringhius, p. 109; Reines, pp. 985 and 988; the Acts of the Council of Vaison; and law 9 of the Code, “On Legal Proceedings,” with other sources in Reland.

Emperors and Caesars Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 41st and 42nd years of tribunician power, consul for the seventeenth time. [Note: [Col. 0699A] 1195 1196]

And Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 18th and 19th years of tribunician power, consul for the fifth time.

Consuls: Petronius Maximus II; Paternus.

[Col. 0699B] Letter 1 of Saint Leo, issued on 10 October under the second consulship of Maximus and the consulship of Paternus, in a manuscript of Santa Croce; law 4 of the Code, “On the Office of the Master of Offices,” and other sources in Reland.

The Maffei papyrus, formerly at San Bonifacio, in Mabillon, *Italian Diary*, and in Marchese Maffei, *History of Diplomatics*, p. 132.

Africa was divided with the Vandals under Valentinian. Ruinart, *History of the Vandal Persecution*, part 2, chapter 6, no. 4.

[Col. 0699C] Emperor and Caesar Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 42nd and 43rd years of tribunician power, consul for the eighteenth time. [Note: [Col. 0699C] 1196 1197]

And Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 19th and 20th years of tribunician power, consul for the fifth time.

Consuls: Theodosius Augustus XVIII; Albinus.

On an ancient papyrus in Mabillon, *Supplement to the History of Diplomatics*, p. 88, and in Maffei, *History of Diplomatics*, p. 134.

Letter of Saint Leo, issued on 11 February under these consuls, in an old manuscript of Santa Croce.

Also laws in Reland, such as law 4 of the Code, “On Statues,” etc.

Theodosius Junior Augustus completed his eighth quinquennalia. [Col. 0699D] Noris, *On the Coin of Licinius*, p. 80.

Emperors and Caesars Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 43rd and 44th years of tribunician power, consul for the eighteenth time. [Note: [Col. 0699D] 1197 1198]

And Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 20th and 21st years of tribunician power, consul for the sixth time.

Consuls: Valentinian Junior Augustus VI; Nonius.

Narbonese inscription in Golnitz, *Belgian Journey*; in Pagius under this year; in our *Prolegomena*; and in the Ruffi, *History of Marseille*. See the notes on Leo the Great and [Col. 0701A] the third title of Valentinian’s Novels, together with other sources in Reland.

Victor of Tunnuna begins his chronicle at this point.

Emperors and Caesars Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 44th and 45th years of tribunician power, consul for the eighteenth time. [Note: [Col. 0701A] 1198 1199]

And Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 21st and 22nd years of tribunician power, consul for the sixth time.

Consuls: Aetius III; Quintus Aurelius Symmachus.

Law 8 of the Code, “On Laws,” and other sources [Col. 0701B] in Pagius, Reland, etc.

The Picts and Scots invaded Britain, after the Britons had unsuccessfully sought Aetius’s aid. Gildas; Usserius, *British Antiquities*, pp. 198, 211, and 218.

Emperors and Caesars Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 45th and 46th years of tribunician power, consul for the eighteenth time. [Note: [Col. 0701B] 1199 1200]

And Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 22nd and 23rd years of tribunician power, consul for the sixth time.

Consuls: Callippius, or Alypius, as in the Paschal Chronicle; Ardaburius.

The fourth letter of Saint Pope Leo to Januarius, bishop of Aquileia, in a manuscript of Santa Croce, is dated 30 December under the consulship of Alypius and Ardaburius. [Col. 0701C]

Valentinian’s Novels and other monuments in Reland have “under the consulship of Callippius and Ardaburius, *viri clarissimi*.”

Emperors and Caesars Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 46th and 47th years of tribunician power, consul for the eighteenth time. [Note: [Col. 0701C] 1200 1201]

And Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 23rd and 24th years of tribunician power, consul for the sixth time.

[Col. 0701D] Consuls: Rufus Pretextatus Postumianus; Flavius Zeno.

Stone inscription in Gruter, 464, no. 8; letter 48 of Saint Leo the Great to Eutyches, dated 1 June under these consuls; the Acts of the Council of Constantinople; and Valentinian’s Novel, title 13, in Reland.

The third king of the Franks, Meroveus, began his reign this year after Clodio’s death; he reigned for approximately twenty years. Petavius.

Rechila, pagan king of the Suevi, died at Mérida. His son Rechiarius, a Catholic, succeeded him and was the son-in-law of Theodoric, king of the Goths, who ravaged the province of Zaragoza. The same from Idacius.

Emperors and Caesars Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 47th and 48th years of tribunician power, consul for the eighteenth time. [Note: [Col. 0703A] 1201 1202]

And Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 24th and 25th years of tribunician power, consul for the sixth time.

Consuls: Flavius Protogenes, in the East; Flavius Asterius, in the West, or Flavius Astyricus.

[Col. 0703B] The Leodiense diptych. The dogmatic letter of Saint Leo the Great and many others, from 8 to 30. Letter 6 of Sidonius Apollinaris; book VIII, chapter [of the Code], “On Repudiations”; and other sources in Reland, who writes that Publius Annaeus Silvius said: “After 1,200 years had been completed from the foundation of the City, with Postumianus and Zeno as consuls, and Asterius as consul, he begins as though first.” In the most ancient manuscripts of the Church of Verona, in Saint Leo’s letter to Flavian, it is written: “Asturius and Protogenes, *viri clarissimi*, being consuls.” [Col. 0703C]

Saint Hilary, bishop of Arles, and Eucherius of Lyon died on the same day. See Noris, *History of Pelagius*, book II, chapter 2, and book XI, chapter 13, from Prosper of Aquitaine.

Emperors and Caesars Theodosius Junior Augustus, in the 48th and 49th years of tribunician power, consul for the eighteenth time; he subsequently died this year after falling from a horse on 28 July, and Marcian succeeded him. [Note: [Col. 0703C] 1202 1203]

And Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 25th and 26th years of tribunician power, consul for the seventh time.

Flavius Marcianus, a Thracian or Illyrian, married Pulcheria, sister of Theodosius Junior, and was created Augustus on 25 August, in the first year of tribunician power. [Col. 0703D]

Consuls: Valentinian Augustus VII; Avienus.

Old inscription in the Basilica of Saint Paul, in Aringhius, *Roman Sacred Antiquities*, p. 500; and Sirmond on letter I, 9. Sidonius Apollinaris reports another. A third is in Fleetwood, p. 402. Letter 32 of Pope Leo. Acts of the Council of Chalcedon, volume IV of the General Councils, p. 62.

The Scots, together with the Picts, ravaged the northern regions of the island of Britain. King Vortigern summoned soldiers from Germany to drive them out; this became the occasion for idolatry to be brought back into the island. See Pagius Senior, no. 16.

Emperors and Caesars Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 26th and 27th years of tribunician power, consul for the seventh time. [Note: [Col. 0705A] 1203 1204] And Marcian Augustus, in the first and second years of tribunician power.

Consuls: Marcian Augustus; Adelphius.

Old inscription in the Basilica of Saint Paul. Aringhius, volume II, p. 419; Severanus, p. 151; Reines, p. 977; and book VII of the Code, “On Pagans,” etc., with other sources in Reland. Also letters 35, 38, etc., of Saint Leo.

This year Attila ravaged Gaul. The Parisians were saved through the prayers of Geneviève. At last he was defeated by Aetius in the Catalaunian Fields; concerning this victory, see Idacius. See Petavius on this year, who also reports, from Idacius, that a lunar eclipse was observed on 26 September.

Emperors and Caesars Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 27th and 28th years of tribunician power, consul for the seventh time. [Note: [Col. 0705B] 1204 1205]

And Marcian Augustus, in the second and third years of tribunician power.

[Col. 0705C] Consuls: Flavius Herculanus, in the West; Asporacius, or Sporacius, in the East.

Letters 52–55 and 91 of Saint Leo; book II of the Code, “On the Consulship”; and book X, “On Advocates in Various Courts,” etc., in Reland.

Old inscription in the Basilica of Saint Paul at Rome, subterranean section, volume II, p. 416; Gruter 1054, no. 8; and Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 757, where the consulship of Herculanus is compared with the first consulship of Our Lord Severus Augustus.

The Church of Carthage, which had lacked a bishop for thirteen years since its capture, this year appointed Deogratias bishop. Victor of Utica.

Emperors and Caesars Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 28th and 29th years of tribunician power, consul for the seventh time. [Note: [Col. 0705D] 1205 1206]

And Marcian Augustus, in the third and fourth years of tribunician power.

Consuls: Vincomalus, in the East; Opilio, in the West.

Council of Angers. Old inscription in the cemetery of the Five Names at Rome, subterranean section, volume II, p. 174; another Gudian inscription in Reland; and letters 56 and following of Saint Leo. Also, from volume IV of the Councils, and Noris, *On the Consular Fasti*, dissertation, p. 51, the Augusti Valentinian and Marcian.

Emperors and Caesars Valentinian Junior Augustus, in the 29th and 30th years of tribunician power, consul for the seventh time. [Note: [Col. 0707A] 1206 1207]

And Marcian Augustus, in the fourth and fifth years of tribunician power.

Consuls: Aetius, in the West; Studius, elsewhere Asterius, in the East.

Letter of Saint Leo to Julian of Cos, his legate. See Bucher, *On the Paschal Cycle of Victor*, p. 81.

[Col. 0707B] Also letters 70, 71, and 72 of the same Leo; and book XII of the Code, “On Holy Churches,” with other sources in Reland.

Valentinian was driven by Maximus’s violation of his wife to the murder of Aetius and Boethius. Marcellinus; Idacius.

Attila perished by vomiting blood because of his intemperance. Pagius Senior, no. 8, assigns this to the preceding year.

Emperor Valentinian Augustus, in the 30th and 31st years of tribunician power, consul for the eighth time, was murdered by Maximus in the Campus Martius. [Note: [Col. 0707B] 1207 1208] Maximus, invading the Empire, violated Eudoxia. This summoned Genseric from Africa; after taking possession of Rome, he plundered it and transferred to Africa the Jewish vessels brought here from Jerusalem and formerly carried away by Vespasian and Titus. From Prosper, Idacius, Theophanes, etc. See Pagius.

Avitus was acclaimed Augustus by the Gallic army.

Consuls: Valentinian Augustus VIII; Anthemius.

Old inscription in the garden of Santa Sabina, in Gudius and Reland. [Col. 0707D] Letters 112 and following of Saint Leo, concerning which see Pagius Senior under this year, no. 13; Victorinus, in the preface to the Paschal Feast of Festus.

Emperors and Caesars Marcian Augustus, in the sixth and seventh years of tribunician power, consul; [Note: [Col. 0707D] 1208 1209]

and Avitus Augustus, in the first and second years of tribunician power, whose consulship with Eparchus survives in two Roman stones. See Reland.

Consuls: Varanes; John.

* An old inscription in Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 738, placed after these consuls on Sunday, 10 May, in the following year; law 25 of the Code, “On Bishops and Clerics,” etc., in Reland.

Childeric, the fourth king of the Franks, succeeded Meroveus after his death. Theodosius, king of the Goths, entered Spain at the urging of the emperor Avitus and drove Rechiarius to the farthest limits of Galicia. He captured Braga, plundered all sacred things, and, with Rechiarius’s death, extinguished the kingdom of the Suevi in Spain. [Col. 0709B] Idacius.

Emperor and Caesar Marcian Augustus, in the seventh and eighth years of tribunician power, consul; he died on 30 April, and Leo succeeded him. With Leo’s consent, Majorian was acclaimed Augustus at Ravenna. [Note: [Col. 0709B] 1209 1210]

Consuls: Constantinus; Rufus.

Laws 8 and 9 of the Code, “On Heretics”; letters 7 and following of Saint Leo; and a stone in Fabretti, p. 577, where it is noted that Paschasius was born under these consuls during the Paschal days, on Thursday, 4 April. Under these consuls Victorius of Aquitaine published his Paschal Canon, calculating 430 years, including the endpoints, from the two Gemini to these consuls, Constantinus and Rufus.

The Suevi entered Lusitania and occupied Lisbon. Idacius.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the first and second years of tribunician power. [Note: [Col. 0709C] 1210 1211]

And Majorian Augustus, in the first and second years of tribunician power.

Consuls: Leo Augustus; Majorian Augustus.

Majorian’s Novels, title 7; law 15 of the Code, “On Military Affairs”; and other sources in Reland. Letters 77 and 131–132, etc., of Saint Leo. [Col. 0709D]

A solar eclipse on 28 May, reported by Idacius as occurring on a Wednesday from the fourth to the sixth hour; Petavius calculates it at eight digits at Rome.

Childeric was expelled by the Franks, who acclaimed the Roman Count Aegidius, Master of the Army, as king. From Gregory of Tours and Aimoinus.

[Col. 0711A] Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the second and third years of tribunician power; consul. [Note: [Col. 0711A] 1211 1212]

And Majorian Augustus, in the second and third years of tribunician power; consul.

Consuls: Flavius Ricimer, in the West; Patricius, in the East.

Old Roman inscription, subterranean section, volume II, p. 693; Reines, p. 976; and law 4 of the Code, “On the Supreme Trinity,” etc., in [Col. 0711B] Reland. Letter 80 of Saint Leo; concerning it, see the notes on Leo the Great.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the third and fourth years of tribunician power; consul. [Note: [Col. 0711B] 1212 1213]

And Majorian Augustus, in the third and fourth years of tribunician power.

Consuls: Apollonius, in the East; Magnus, in the West.

Law 11 of the Code, “On Advocates in Various Courts,” in Reland; and letters 99–103 of Saint Leo.

Maldias, ruling the Suevi, was slaughtered. [Col. 0711C] Frumarius and Remismundus succeeded him. In Spain, Theodoric appointed Nepotianus Master of the Soldiers and Sunericus count. Idacius.

Emperor and Caesar Leo Augustus, in the fourth and fifth years of tribunician power; consul. [Note: [Col. 0711C] 1213 1214]

And Majorian Augustus, in the fourth and fifth years of tribunician power; consul.

Consuls: Flavius Severinus, in the West; Daglaiphus, in the East.

Old Nolan inscription in the preface, volume I, no. 26, near the end; letter XI, book I, of Sidonius Apollinaris; and the First Council of Tours. See Pagius Senior under this year.

Majorian Augustus was killed by Ricimer. In the preceding year, while preparing war against the Vandals, he had gone to Genseric in Spain in disguise, under the appearance of an envoy. Procopius, *Vandalic War*, book I.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the fifth and sixth years of tribunician power; consul for the second time. [Note: [Col. 0711D] 1214 1215]

[Col. 0713A] And Libius Severus, in the first and second years of tribunician power.

Consuls: Leo Augustus II; Libius Severus Augustus.

Old inscription in Fabretti, p. 757; letter V of Saint Hilary; and the letter of Leontius of Arles to Pope Hilary.

A lunar eclipse on 2 March, a Friday. Idacius.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the sixth and seventh years of tribunician power, consul for the second time. [Note: [Col. 0713A] 1215 1216]

And Libius Severus Augustus, in the second and third years of tribunician power; consul. [Col. 0713B]

Consuls: Vivianus; Basilius, also Flavius Caecina Basilius.

In Sidonius Apollinaris, book I, letter 9.

Paschal inscription in Fabretti, p. 577, and Noris, *On the Consular Fasti*, p. 53, from which it appears that Easter was celebrated this year on 21 April. See above, under the year 457, law 12 of the Code, “On Advocates.”

Victorius of Aquitaine, at the request of Pope Hilary, issued a Paschal cycle of 532 years. See Petavius.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the seventh and eighth years of tribunician power, consul for the second time. [Note: [Col. 0713B] 1216 1217]

[Col. 0713C] And Libius Severus Augustus, in the third and fourth years of tribunician power; consul.

Consuls: Rusticus; Olybrius, also Flavius Anicius Olybrius.

Old inscription in Santa Sabina, Fabretti, p. 567.

An eclipse of the sun on 20 August at Constantinople, nearly nine digits, mentioned by Idacius; concerning it, see Petavius.

Childeric, having been expelled by the Franks for eight years, was restored to his kingdom. See Pagius Senior under this year, no. 6.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the eighth and ninth years of tribunician power, consul for the second time. [Note: [Col. 0713C] 1217 1218] [Col. 0713D]

And Libius Severus Augustus, in the fourth and fifth years of tribunician power; he was killed by Ricimer the Patrician through treachery. An interregnum followed his death, lasting one year and several months, according to Cassiodorus.

Consuls: Flavius Basiliscus; Herminericus.

Old inscription in Fabretti, p. 567; Montfaucon, *Italian Diary*, p. 161; the Roman Council; and the letter of Pope Hilary. See the notes on Leo the Great.

Genseric ravaged the coasts of Italy and Greece with a powerful fleet. He even reached Alexandria. Procopius, book I.

Emperor and Caesar Leo Augustus, in the ninth and tenth years of tribunician power, consul for the third time. [Note: [Col. 0715A] 1218 1219]

The Western emperor is vacant.

Consul: Leo Augustus III, at first alone; toward the end of the year Tatianus was added as his colleague in the consulship.

Old Roman inscription, subterranean section, volume II, p. 418; Reines, p. 967; and law 6 of the Code, “On Those Who Take Refuge in Churches.”

Theodoric, king of the Goths, died; his brother Euric succeeded him. After devastating Spain, Euric descended into Gaul and besieged Auvergne. Petavius, from Isidore and Sidonius. Pagius Senior assigns this to the immediately following year.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the 10th and 11th years of tribunician power, consul for the third time. [Note: [Col. 0715A] 1219 1220]

And Anthemius Augustus, in the years of tribunician power beginning in August.

Consuls: Busaeus; John.

Law 17 of the Code, “On Contributions.”

[Col. 0715C] Coimbra was occupied and ravaged by the Suevi through treachery. Idacius. Heraclius, son of Florius the former consul, and Marsus the Isaurian, sent by the emperor Leo against the Vandals, captured Tripolis and other cities. Therefore Genseric sought and obtained peace. Theophanes; Procopius, book I.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the 11th and 12th years of tribunician power, consul for the third time. [Note: [Col. 0715C] 1221 1222]

And Anthemius Augustus, in the first and second years of tribunician power; consul for the second time.

[Col. 0715D] Consul: Anthemius Augustus II, alone.

A Neapolitan inscription in Fabretti, p. 757, has “Anthemius III, consul.” It seems that “Anthemius I, again consul” should be read. Perhaps worn letters gave rise to the error in copying.

“Anthemius Augustus II, alone” is read in law 15 of the Code, “On Bishops,” and in several other sources in Reland.

Arvandus, prefect of Gaul, was condemned at Rome for treason and sent into exile. Cassiodorus, *Chronicle*; Sidonius, letter 7, book I.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the 12th and 13th years of tribunician power, consul for the third time. [Note: [Col. 0717A] 1222 1223]

And Anthemius Augustus, in the second and third years of tribunician power; consul for the second time.

Consuls: Zeno; Flavius Marcianus.

Law 31 of the Code, “On Bishops and Clerics,” and other sources in Reland.

[Col. 0717B] Isidore, after recounting in his history of the Suevi that Remismund, king of the Suevi, plundered Coimbra and occupied Lisbon, reports that, through a certain Ajax, a Galatian by nationality, the Suevian kings were infected with Arian perfidy until Theodemir, who, having renounced his errors, became Catholic. Therefore the successors of Remismund are passed over in silence until the year 560 in the history of Spain. See Pagius Senior.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the 13th and 14th years of tribunician power, consul for the third time. [Note: [Col. 0717B] 1223 1224]

And Anthemius Augustus, in the third and fourth years of tribunician power; consul for the second time.

Consuls: Severus, in the West; Jordanes, in the East.

Law 14 of the Code, “On Sacred Churches,” and chapter [of the Code], in Reland.

The chronographer inserted into Victor of Tunnuna’s work incorrectly assigns to this year the capture of Arles and Marseille by the Goths. From Jordanes under the year 477, Pagius, no. 20 of the year 477, shows that Euric’s domination must be assigned elsewhere.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the 14th and 15th years of tribunician power, consul for the fourth time. [Note: [Col. 0717C] 1224 1225]

[Col. 0717D] And Anthemius Augustus, in the fourth and fifth years of tribunician power; consul for the second time.

Consuls: Leo Augustus IV; Probanius.

The Cornutian charter from the Tibur archive. See the *Prolegomena*, p. XXXII, and law 13 of the Code, “On the Office of the Rectors of Provinces,” with other sources in Reland.

Also a stone excavated in 1724 at Saint Paul’s.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the 15th and 16th years of tribunician power, consul for the fourth time. [Note: [Col. 0717D] 1224 1225]

And Anthemius Augustus, in the fifth and sixth years of tribunician power; consul for the second time.

[Col. 0719A] Consuls: Maximus, in the East; Faustus, in the West.

Old inscription at Saint Paul’s in Rome, *Roman Sacred Antiquities*, p. 419; Reines 982; Gruter 1057, no. 5; letter of Pope Simplicius to John, bishop of Ravenna, in a manuscript of Santa Croce, p. 174; and the Code, “On Advocates in Various Courts.”

The emperor Anthemius was killed at Rome by Ricimer, his son-in-law, on 11 July. Flavius Anicius Olybrius, previously proclaimed emperor, was confirmed, but [Col. 0719B] perished in the seventh month, according to Marcellinus. Ricimer also died on 18 August. Cassiodorus.

Ashes erupted from Mount Vesuvius and were carried as far as Byzantium. Marcellinus.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the 16th and 17th years of tribunician power, consul for the fifth time. [Note: [Col. 0719B] 1225 1226]

And from 5 March Glycerius, according to the chronographer Cuspinianus, was raised to the imperial office at Ravenna; according to Marcellinus, he became Caesar more through presumption than election. See Cangius, *Christian Constantinople*, and Pagius Senior.

And from the month of March Leo Junior, grandson of Leo Senior through Zeno, was declared Caesar. [Col. 0719C] Others think this occurred after the elder Leo’s death. See Pagius.

Consul: Leo Augustus V, without a colleague.

Law 5 of the Code, “On Property That Is Liberated,” etc.

Emperors and Caesars Leo Augustus, in the 17th year of tribunician power, consul for the fifth time. [Note: [Col. 0719C] 1226 1227]

And Glycerius, in the first and second years of tribunician power; and Zeno, as below; and Julius Nepos from 4 June.

And Leo Junior, who succeeded his grandfather Leo Senior, who died in January—Cangius, from Greek history—and crowned his father Zeno, [Col. 0719D] but died of illness. Leo Junior died in the same year. Theophanes Malalas and the Alexandrian Chronicle.

Consul: Leo Junior, without a colleague.

Law 11 of the Code, “On Laws”; other sources in Reland; an old inscription in Mabillon, *On the Cult of the Saints*, unpublished, Utrecht, p. 44; another in Fleetwood, p. 342; and the Roman subterranean inscription, volume II, p. 419, at the Basilica of Saint Paul.

Emperors and Caesars Zeno Augustus, in the first and second years of tribunician power, consul for the second time, expelled by the tyrant Basiliscus and soon restored. [Note: [Col. 0719D] 1227 1228]

And Julius Nepos, whom Orestes, after expelling him on 28 August, [Col. 0721A] replaced with his own son Augustulus as emperor on 31 October. Cuspinianus’s Chronicle.

Consul: Zeno Augustus II, without a colleague.

Law 29 of the Code, “On Inofficious Wills,” etc., in Reland; and a letter of Saint Pope Simplicius to Florentius, etc., issued after the consulship of Leo Augustus, an ancient copy of which is in a manuscript of the monastery of Santa Croce at Rome.

[Col. 0721B] Augustulus, promoted to the imperial office by his father Orestes, is also called Momyllus. Jordanes.

Emperor and Caesar Zeno Augustus, in the second and third years of tribunician power, consul for the eleventh time. [Note: [Col. 0721B] 1228 1229]

And Augustulus, in the tenth month of his reign, was expelled by ODOACER, who ordered that he be called king of Italy.
