**Consuls:** Flavius Basiliscus II.

Armatus.

Law 28 of the *Code*, “Concerning Dowry,” etc., in Reland.

Odoacer, king of the Heruli, was invited into Italy by the supporters of Nepos [Col. 0721C] and seized Rome. He condemned Augustulus to exile in the Castle of Lucullanum in Campania. Thus the Western Empire collapsed. Petavius, from Marcellinus.

Geiseric appears to have died this year, having reigned thirty-nine years from the capture of Carthage, according to Procopius. He was succeeded by Huneric. Same source. But Pagius the Elder thinks these events should be assigned to the following year.

**Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 3, [Note: [Col. 0721C] 1229 1230] 4, consul 11.**

Odoacer’s kingship in Italy, years 1 and 2, beginning on 23 August.

[Col. 0721D] **Consul:** none.

A letter of Pope Simplicius to Zeno, 18 October; and an old inscription, Gruter 1051.6, reads: “After the consulship, again, of Armatus.” Perhaps it should be read: “After the consulship [with the name of Basiliscus deleted], again, and of Armatus”; Fleetwood, p. 378, marks it in the same way, book 9 of the *Code*, “Concerning Violence,” etc., in Reland.

After Basiliscus had been reduced to the rank of a private citizen, about the month of August, Zeno recovered the imperial city and the empire. From Theophanes and the letters of Pope Simplicius quoted by Baronius. Pagius, no. 6 for this year. Theodoricus Amal, king of Italy, is said to have aided Zeno in Ennodius’s *Panegyric*, no. 7.

**Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 4, [Note: [Col. 0723A] 1230 1231] 5, consul 11.**

Odoacer’s kingship, years 2 and 3.

**Consuls:** Illus in the East, without a colleague.

Law 11 of the *Code*, “Concerning Insults,” etc., in Reland; and a letter of Pope Simplicius to Acacius.

Saint Lupus of Troyes died on 1 August, according to Petavius, after having governed his church for fifty-two years.

**Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 5, [Note: [Col. 0723B] 1231 1232] 6, consul III.**

Odoacer’s kingship, years 3 and 4.

**Consuls:** Zeno Augustus III, without a colleague.

Law 11 of the *Code*, “Who May Seek Guardians,” and a letter of Simplicius, marked “after the consulship of Illus.” Pagius nevertheless thinks it should be read “after the consulship of Placidius,” evidently written in the year 481.

The energetic Sabinianus, commander of the Illyrian army, frightened King Theodoricus while he was raging through Greece, according to Marcellinus. According to Theophanes, he was born of the brother of Aspar’s wife and had defected from Zeno.

**Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 6, [Note: [Col. 0723C] 1232 1233] 7, consul III.**

Odoacer’s kingship, years 4 and 5.

**Consul:** Basilius the Younger, without a colleague.

Law 22 of the *Code*, “Concerning Wills,” etc., in Reland.

Nepos, whom Orestes had forced to abdicate the empire, was killed near Salonae through the treachery of his own companions. Marcellinus.

In this year, or in the following one, Clovis V, king of the Franks, began his reign, according to Petavius.

Saint Benedict was born. Same source, from Leo of Ostia.

**Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 7, [Note: [Col. 0723D] 1233 1234] 8, consul III.**

Odoacer’s kingship, years 5 and 6.

**Consul:** Placidius, without a colleague.

This consulship is mentioned, according to Pagius, in a letter of Pope Simplicius dated in the following year, after the consulship of Placidius.

[Col. 0725A] Huneric raged against the Catholics, but much more fiercely against his own people. Victor of Vita, book 2.

Chilperic, king of the Franks, died, according to Pagius the Elder, this year, no. 6.

**Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 8, [Note: [Col. 0725A] 1234 1235] 9, consul III.**

Odoacer’s kingship, years 6 and 7.

**Consuls:** Severinus; Trocondus.

Letter 14 of Pope Simplicius, whose ancient copy is in the library of the monastery of Santa Croce in Rome; and the Council of Tours, book 1. See Pagius for this year, no. 27.

Saint Severinus, apostle of Noricum, died this year. Pagius, no. 29.

[Col. 0725C] **Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 9, [Note: [Col. 0725C] 1235 1236] 10, consul III.**

Odoacer’s kingship, years 7 and 8.

**Consul:** Faustus, without a colleague.

An old inscription, Gruter 1062.5, and the Nolan inscription in the preface to volume 1 of this edition, no. [illegible], also in Fleetwood, p. 400.

King Theodoricus of the Goths, nearly reconciled through the generosity of Augustus Zeno, was made Master of the Soldiers of the Presence and designated consul. He held the parts of Ripuarian Dacia and Moesia entrusted to him. Petavius.

[Col. 0725D] **Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 10, [Note: [Col. 0725D] 1236 1237] 11, consul III, who creates Basiliscus Caesar.**

Odoacer’s kingship, years 8 and 9.

**Consuls:** King Theodoricus; Venantius.

An old inscription in Aringhius, p. 419, in the Basilica of Saint Paul; Fleetwood, p. 456; a letter of Felix III to Acacius; and book 1, law 10 of the *Code*, “Concerning Violence,” in Reland.

Evarix, king of the Goths in Gaul, died, and was succeeded by his son Alaric, after having reigned twenty years. Petavius, from Victor and the Council of Agde.

Huneric’s edict of persecution was issued six days before the Kalends of March; in that year there was a solar eclipse on 13 January. See Noris, *History of Pelagius*, book 2, chapter 21.

[Col. 0727B] **Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 11, [Note: [Col. 0727B] 1237 1238] 12, consul III.**

Odoacer’s kingship, years 9 and 10.

**Consul:** Symmachus, without a colleague.

An old inscription in Aringhius, volume 2, p. 419; Gruter 1057.5; and Reines, p. 982.

Zeno’s son, destined for the hope of the empire but very badly educated, died. Petavius, from Suidas.

In the fifth year of his reign, Clovis defeated in battle Syagrius, who ruled at Soissons; and when Syagrius fled to Alaric, king of the Visigoths, Clovis obtained his surrender and had him killed. From Gregory of Tours and Aimoinus. Petavius.

**Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 12, [Note: [Col. 0727C] 1238 1239] 13, consul III.**

Odoacer’s kingship, years 10 and 11.

**Consuls:** Decius; Longinus.

[Col. 0727D] An old inscription in Saint Martin in the Mountains, of which only fragments now remain in the pavement. It is read complete in Fleetwood, p. 458; in Reland under the years 472 and 486; and in law 14 of the *Code*, “Concerning Witnesses,” along with other sources there.

**Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 13, [Note: [Col. 0727D] 1239 1240] 14, consul III.**

Odoacer’s kingship, years 11 and 12.

**Consul:** Flavius Boethius alone.

Aringhius, book 4; *Roman Subterranean Antiquities*, p. 169; Reines, p. 920; Fleetwood, pp. 410 and 514; the Council of Rome for this year; and book 5 of the *Code*, “Concerning Fruits and Litigation Expenses.”

[Col. 0729A] Guntabundus, king of the Vandals, recalled Saint Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, from exile. Appendix to the chronicle of Prosper; Noris, *History of Pelagius*, book 2, chapter 21.

**Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 14, [Note: [Col. 0729A] 1240 1241] 15, consul III.**

Odoacer’s kingship, years 12 and 13.

**Consuls:** Dynamius; Sifidius.

[Col. 0729B] They are read in a letter of Felix III in the monastery codex of Santa Croce in Rome. Dynamius is read in Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 528. Claudius Julius Edesius reads “Dynamius, clarissimus man”; Reinesius reads “Aedesius Dynamius, perfectissimus man” in an old inscription. See Reland.

King Theodoricus, having gathered the whole multitude of his Goths, marched into Italy. Marcellinus says that Zeno persuaded him to fight against Odoacer. Procopius, book 1, from which Petavius draws this account.

**Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 15, [Note: [Col. 0729B] 1241 1242] 16, consul III.**

[Col. 0729C] Odoacer’s kingship, years 13 and 14.

**Consuls:** Eusebius in the East; Probinus in the West.

An old inscription in the Basilica of Saint Paul, in Aringhius, p. 419; Fleetwood, p. 457; Reines, p. 982; the Gudian collection in Reland; and from book 6 of the *Code*, “Concerning the Trebellian Senate’s Decree.”

Odoacer, king of the Heruli, was defeated at the Isonzo near Aquileia; and in a renewed battle in the Veronese plain he was destroyed with great slaughter. Cassiodorus and Jordanes. But see Pagius the Elder for this year, no. 3.

[Col. 0729D] **Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 16, [Note: [Col. 0729D] 1242 1243] 17, consul III.**

Odoacer’s kingship, years 14 and 15.

**Consuls:** Longinus II; Faustus the Younger.

An old inscription in Aringhius, *Roman Subterranean Antiquities*, book 4, chapter 25; Spon, *Researches into the Antiquities of Lyon*, p. 202; Mabillon, from a Venetian charter, p. 201; Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 757; Fleetwood, pp. 397 and 494; and letters of Pope Felix.

Theodoricus, at the Abdua or Adda, defeated Odoacer in a third battle and forced him to shut himself up in Ravenna, where he was besieged for three years.

**Emperor Caesar Zeno Augustus, tribunician power 17, [Note: [Col. 0731A] 1243 1244] 18, consul III. Anastasius, emperor, from 18 April.**

Odoacer’s kingship, years 15 and 16.

**Consul:** Olybrius the Younger, without a colleague.

Law 4 of the *Code*, “Concerning Prescription of Thirty or Forty Years,” etc., in Reland; and the Council of Carpentras. See Pagius the Elder for this year, no. 21.

[Col. 0731B] This year is also said to be dated “after the second consulship of Longinus and Faust[inus]” on an old Lyonese stone in Fleetwood, p. 483.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius** was taken as husband by Ariadne, widow of Augustus Zeno, and was crowned emperor.

Theophanes counts this year as 5999 from Adam, 5983 according to the Alexandrians, 207 according to Diocletian, and 483 from the Incarnation. Petavius. Evagrius counts 532 from the reign of Augustus. But the numbers are corrupt. Lydiat.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius, tribunician power 1, [Note: [Col. 0731B] 1244 1245] and from 18 April 2, consul.**

[Col. 0731C] Odoacer’s kingship, years 16 and 17.

**Consuls:** Anastasius Augustus; Rufus.

Law 3 of the *Code*, “Concerning the Office of the Quaestor,” and an old Lyonese inscription in Spon, *Antiquities of Lyon*, p. 48; Fleetwood, *Sylloge*, p. 341; Gruter 1049.2; Pagius, *Dissertation on Hypotheses*, p. 296; and another stone placed in the impluvium of the Vatican. Emperor Anastasius, belonging to the sect of the Acephali and Hesitants, allowed everyone to embrace whatever he wished. Petavius, from Evagrius, book 3, chapter 30. See also Baronius and Pagius the Elder for this year.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0731C] 1245 1246] 2, 3, consul.**

[Col. 0731D] Odoacer’s kingship, year 17; he was killed near the beginning of March by Theodoricus, who ruled in Italy from 10 March onward.

**Consuls:** Eusebius II; Albinus, or Albinus alone.

Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 758. The consulship of Albinus, and letters of Pope Gelasius to Albinus, a clarissimus man and consul. According to Marcellinus, however, both were consuls.

Odoacer, besieged at Ravenna, made an agreement with Theodoricus that both should rule Italy with equal rights; but [Col. 0733A] he was killed by the treaty-breaker at a banquet. Procopius, Cassiodorus, and Jordanes.

Theodoricus, king of Italy, sought the friendship of Emperor Anastasius and of the neighboring kings Clovis the Frank, Alaric the Visigoth, and Sigismund the Burgundian. Cassiodorus, Letter 1, from Jordanes.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0733A] 1246 1247] 3, 4, consul.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 1 and 2.

[Col. 0733B] **Consuls:** Asterius, also called Turcius Rufus Apronianus; Praesidius.

An old inscription in the title-church of Saint Cecilia, in Fabretti, p. 758; another in Saint Paul; and a letter of Pope Gelasius dated under the same consuls. Asterius’s autograph as consul appears in the Medicean Virgil, discussed by Cardinal Noris in *Cenotaphian Dissertation*, dissertation 4, section 1.

Clovis extended the Frankish kingdom as far as the Seine. Petavius, from Sigebert.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0733B] 1247 1248] 4, 5, consul.**

[Col. 0733C] Theodoricus’s kingship in Italy, years 2 and 3.

**Consuls:** Flavius Viator, in some sources alone; Aemilianus.

Both names are given in book 2 of the *Code*, “Concerning Possession of Goods Contrary to the Table of Freedmen,” as Reland notes. The Acts of the Second Roman Council under Gelasius: “Flavius Viator, clarissimus man, consul”; and the letters of Gelasius.

Clovis, king of the Franks, victorious over the Alamanni, was baptized by Saint Remigius at the urging of Queen Clotilde, together with three thousand soldiers. Gregory, book 2, chapter 3; and Aimoinus, book 1, chapter 19, in Petavius for this year.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0733D] 1248 1249] 5, 6, consul.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 3 and 4.

**Consul:** Paulus alone, who was the emperor’s brother, etc.

Law 16 of the *Code*, “Concerning Military Wills,” etc., in Reland. Some designate this year “after the consulship of Viator,” as on a stone found at Saint Peter’s and reported by Schelestr in the *Fasti* (*Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, volume 1), and in Fleetwood, *Sylloge*, p. 421.

The four sons of Gunderic, king of the Burgundians, fought among themselves. See Petavius for this year.

[Col. 0735A] Guntabundus, king of the Vandals, died on 24 September. From the appendix to Prosper’s chronicle; Noris, *History of Pelagius*, book 2, chapter 21. He was succeeded by Trasamundus, who reigned twenty-six years, eight months, and four days. Same source.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0735A] 1249 1250] 6, 7, consul II.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 4 and 5.

**Consul:** Anastasius Augustus II, without a colleague.

Law 9 of the *Code*, “Concerning Repudiations,” etc., in Reland.

In this consulship a solar eclipse appeared, and the Isaurian War was settled in its sixth year. Athenodorus, or Antenodorus, the first of the Isaurians, was captured in Isauria and beheaded. Marcellinus, and Lydiat from him. But see Pagius the Elder for the following year, 498, whom Petavius makes a witness from Marcellinus for dating the solar eclipse.

Saint Eleutherius, bishop of Tournai, baptized more than eleven thousand people converted to Christ this year, following the example of Clovis. Pagius for this year, no. 4.

Ambrosius Aurelius, king of the Britons, died through the treachery of his son. His brother Uther succeeded him, according to the *Florilegium*. Pagius there, no. 5.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0735C] 1250 1251] 7, 8, consul II.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 5 and 6.

**Consuls:** John the Scythian in the East; Paulinus in the West.

Law 4 of the *Code*, “Concerning Legitimate Guardianship,” in Reland.

A certain Roman senator, Festus, sent by King Theodoricus to Emperor Anastasius [Col. 0735D] after secretly promising the emperor that he would arrange for Pope Anastasius to subscribe to the *Henoticon*, learned on his return to Rome that the pontiff had died. By bribing several members of the clergy, he arranged for Laurentius to be elected against Symmachus, the legitimate successor. For the sake of peace the matter was referred to Theodoricus, from which the origin of secular usurpations is said to derive. See the notes on Symmachus.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0735D] 1251 1252] 8, 9, consul II.**

[Col. 0737A] Theodoricus’s kingship, years 6 and 7.

**Consuls:** John the Hunchback, in some sources alone; Aselepius.

Law 25 of the *Code*, “Concerning Excuses of Guardians,” and law 5, “Concerning Silentarii,” present both consuls, although Reland gives only John, as do the Paschal Chronicle and Marcellinus. The Council of Rome and Letter 1 of Pope Symmachus date this year “after the consulship of Paulinus.”

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0737A] 1252 1253] 9, [Col. 0737B] 10, consul II.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 7 and 8.

**Consuls:** Patricius; Hypatius.

Law 43 of the *Code*, “Concerning Transactions,” etc., in Reland. Both consuls were Eastern. Therefore in the West the year is dated “again after the consulship of Paulinus.” An old inscription in the pavement of the Basilica of Saint Paul, reported by Aringhius, *Roman Subterranean Antiquities*, volume 1, p. 417; Reines, p. 964; and Reland.

Theodoricus, eagerly desired by everyone, came to Rome, where he earned the generosity of the Senate and Roman people and assigned a fixed sum of money for repairing the walls. Cassiodorus. Many roof tiles in the churches of Rome and other buildings bear the mark “under the reign of Our Lord Theodoricus. Happy Rome.” See Ciampini, *On Sacred Buildings*, chapter 9, p. 129.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0737C] 1253 1254] 10, 11, consul II.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 8 and 9.

**Consuls:** Pompeius in the East; Avienus in the West, also called Rufus; Magnus Faustus Avienus.

An old Lyonese inscription in Reland and Fleetwood, p. 495; the Acts of the Roman Synod for this year; and the letters of Pope Symmachus under the same consuls.

The code of Burgundian laws was promulgated this year by King Gundobad, according to Pagius, no. 3. He also assigns to this year, from Procopius, the restoration of Cabades to the Persian kingdom and the incursion of the Bulgarians [a previously unheard-of name] into Illyricum and Thrace.

[Col. 0739A] **Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0739A] 1254 1255] 11, 12, consul II.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 9 and 10.

**Consuls:** Probus; Avienus the Younger, also called Rufius Magnus Faustus; Avienus Junior.

Law 18 of the *Code*, “Concerning Collations,” and other sources in Reland, including a letter of Pope Symmachus to Probus, clarissimus man and consul; the Acts of the Roman Synod under Avienus, clarissimus man and consul; and an inscription in Reines, p. 961, previously published by Aringhius, volume 1, *Roman Subterranean Antiquities*, p. 338. Pagius, no. 10, assigns Symmachus’s letter to Probus to the year 513.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0739B] 1255 1256] 12, 13, consul II.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 10 and 11.

**Consuls:** Dexicrates in the East; Volusianus in the West.

An old inscription in Fabretti, p. 757; Fleetwood, p. 500; and Reines, p. 991.

These consuls are omitted in the chronicles of Cassiodorus and Tunnunensis, as is their year in the annals of Jordanes. Lydiat.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0739C] 1256 1257] 13, 14, consul II.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 11 and 12.

**Consul:** Cethegus alone.

In an ancient charter from Ravenna, in Lambecius, *Imperial Library*, volume 8, and Mabillon, *Diplomatic Works*, p. 458.

Theodoricus, after defeating the Bulgarians, subjected Sirmium and Pannonia to himself. Cassiodorus.

[Col. 0739D] **Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0739D] 1257 1258] 14, 15, consul II.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 12 and 13.

**Consuls:** Sabinianus in the East; Theodorus in the West.

Law 19 of the *Code*, “Concerning the Hearing of Bishops,” etc., in Reland, along with old inscriptions from the Gudian collection there.

At about this time Clovis, at the urging of his wife, began to construct a church in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, which is now called Saint Genevieve. Petavius, from Hincmar.

[Col. 0741A] **Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0741A] 1258 1259] 15, 16, consul II.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 13 and 14.

**Consuls:** Areobindas, the Younger, in the East; Messala in the West.

Law 4 of the *Code*, “Concerning Advocates in Various Courts,” and the *Theodosian Code*, book 5, chapter 3, single law. Alaric issued a code of Roman laws in February, called the *Breviary of Anianus*. Pagius, from Gothofredus in the preface to the *Theodosian Code*. Alaric was then killed in battle by Clovis, king of the Franks, and the greater part of his kingdom fell under the victor’s control. Gregory of Tours, etc., in Petavius.

Hispania obeyed Amalaric, Alaric’s son. Same source, and from Aimoinus and Cassiodorus, book 3.

Petavius, following Gregory, counts the Gothic kingdom of Toulouse as belonging to this year.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0741B] 1259 1260] 16, 17, consul III.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 14 and 15.

[Col. 0741C] **Consuls:** Anastasius Augustus III; Venantius in the West.

Marcellinus gives Anastasius without a colleague. Cassiodorus gives Venantius in the West.

A law issued by Theodoricus at Ravenna, under Venantius, clarissimus man, as consul [volume 4 of the *Councils*, p. 1042].

Clovis, following up his victory, subjected all Aquitania to his rule, acquiring the metropolitan city of Tours and the territory of Poitiers; while Theodoricus, his son, under his father’s auspices, likewise subdued and held the Padurci [perhaps Cadurci], Albigeois, Ruthenian, and Auvergne territories. [Col. 0741D] See Pagius for this year, no. 8. Gisalaric, an illegitimate son of Alaric, became ruler at Narbonne. Chronicle of Isidore.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0741D] 1260 1261] 17, 18, consul III.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 15 and 16.

**Consuls:** Celer in the East; Venantius the Younger in the West.

He is also called Basilius Venantius Decius, who may be the person mentioned by Reines, p. 980, in the final inscription.

King Theodoricus of the Goths inflicted a great defeat on the Franks and administered the territory of the Visigoths, brought under his power, in the name of Amalaric, his ward, through prefects, just as he administered Hispania. From Cassiodorus, book 3, letters; Petavius.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0743A] 1261 1262] 18, 19, consul III.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 16 and 17.

[Col. 0743B] **Consul:** Importunus, without a colleague.

Some, with Pagius, call him Basilius Importunus; others call him Decius Importunus, and others Opportunus. Some assign to him the inscription of Reines cited for the preceding year and, by Reland, to this year, from Fleetwood, p. 452, or to the consuls of the year 529.

Clovis, king of the Franks, raged against his relatives. Gregory of Tours, book 2, chapter 44. See Petavius and Pagius for this year.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0743B] 1262 1263] 19, 20, consul III.**

[Col. 0743C] Theodoricus’s kingship, years 17 and 18.

**Consul:** Boethius alone, namely Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, distinguished for his studies of philosophy, mathematics, and the other sciences. His consular diptych, reported by Nobilius Barbisonus from Brescia in *Italian Scholarly Journal*, volume 28, p. 39, bears the inscription:

“Nar[?] Mun[?] Boethius, clarissimus and illustrious man, former praetorian prefect, ordinary consul, and patrician.”

Regarding Euthericus, added as his colleague in book 10 of the *Code*, “Concerning Heretical Error,” Pagius for this year considers it a copyist’s error.

[Col. 0743D] **Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0743D] 1263 1264] 20, 21, consul III.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 18 and 19.

**Consuls:** Secundinus in the East; Felix in the West.

An old inscription in Reines, p. 511; Fleetwood, pp. 348, 446, and 514; and other sources in Reland. The Council of Orléans is dated with “Felix, consul”; Amalaric, son of Alaric, king of the Visigoths, married Clotilde, daughter of Clovis. Gregory of Tours, book 3, chapter 1. Pagius assigns Clovis’s death to this year. See the year 514.

Pagius demonstrates that the Council of Orléans was held this year, against Cointius, from the consular note. See him for this year, no. 14, and for the year 507, nos. 10 and following.

Count Vitalianus, having engaged Patricius, Anastasius’s nephew and master of the soldiers, captured him alive and tore him to pieces. Lydiat.

[Col. 0745B] **Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0745B] 1264 1265] 21, 22, consul III.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 19 and 20.

**Consuls:** Paulus in the West; Muscianus in the East.

Law 32 of the *Code*, “Concerning Donations.” See Pagius for this year. This year is also called “after the consulship of Felix” in a letter of Pope Symmachus.

The nation of the Heruli was received into Roman lands and cities by Anastasius’s order. Marcellinus, who records that a solar eclipse occurred this year. Petavius denies that the eclipse could have occurred in our hemisphere. Calvisius’s calculation assigns it to the eleventh digit, 29 June, at the first hour before noon at Constantinople.

The Danes, harassing Theodoricus’s kingdom, were defeated by his son Theodebertus, their king himself being killed. Gregory, book 3, chapter 3.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0745C] 1265 1266] 22, 23, consul III.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 20 and 21.

**Consuls:** Clementinus; Probus the Younger.

Law 14 of the *Code*, “Concerning the Office of Provincial Governor,” and an old inscription in the Basilica of Saint Paul, Aringhius, p. 420; Reines, p. 981; Fleetwood, p. 453; and Reland. Pagius, no. 6 for this year, shows that Symmachus’s responses to Saint Caesarius and his letters to the bishops of Gaul concerning the division of the provinces of Vienne and Arles were dated under Probus’s consulship.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0745D] 1266 1267] 23, 24, consul III.**

[Col. 0747A] Theodoricus’s kingship, years 21 and 22.

**Consul:** Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator, without a colleague.

The letter of Pope Symmachus, the letters of Cassiodorus himself, and the chronicle.

Pagius reports that those who assign Clovis’s death to this year postpone it by three years, namely to 27 November 511, under Felix, clarissimus man, as consul. From the chronicle of Saint Vincent of Metz. See Pagius for the division of his kingdom among his sons.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0747B] 1267 1268] 24, 25, consul III.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 22 and 23.

**Consuls:** Anthemius in the East; Florentius in the West.

Two letters of Emperor Anastasius to Hormisdas under these consuls. See Reland; and other letters of Hormisdas to Anastasius under the same consulship. See Pagius.

King Theodoricus gave his daughter Amalasuntha in marriage to Eutharic. Cassiodorus.

[Col. 0747C] Augusta Ariadne died; she had more than once rebuked Anastasius.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0747C] 1268 1269] 25, 26, consul III.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 23 and 24.

**Consul:** Petrus, without a colleague.

An old inscription in Saint Martin in the Mountains at Rome; and letters of Hormisdas from the ninth and tenth years through the twenty-fifth.

The Council of Tarragona is dated under this consul and in the sixth year of King Theodoricus in Hispania, on 6 November.

[Col. 0747D] **Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0747D] 1269 1270] 26, 27, consul III.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 24 and 25.

**Consuls:** Flavius Anastasius in the East; Agapitus in the West.

An old inscription of Agapitus as consul in Rome, in the deaconry of Saint Nicholas in the Tullian Prison. Fabretti, p. 561. As for Anastasius, an inscription at Aix-les-Bains, in the metropolitan church, in Gruter 1049, from which Cardinal Noris, in his *Letter on the Consuls*, p. 150, proves that Anastasius was not Augustus but consul this year. A double consular diptych of the same man was published by Wilthemius. We gave an image of one in the *Prolegomena*, folio XXVII.

The Synod of Epaon was held under this consul. See Noris, *History of Pelagius*, book 2, chapter 23.

**Emperor Caesar Anastasius Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0749A] 1270 1271] 27, 28, who died on 11 April.** [Col. 0749B] **JUSTINUS the Thracian** assumed the imperial purple on 9 July, indiction 11, in the year 566 of Antioch. Paschal Chronicle.

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 25 and 26.

**Consul:** Magnus, without a colleague.

A letter of Emperor Justinus to Hormisdas, dated 1 August. Volume 4 of the councils, p. 1469.

Vitalianus, who had opposed Anastasius on behalf of the Catholics, and was Justinus’s close friend, pressed the emperor to have the tongue of the impious Severus of Antioch cut out by imperial order. Severus fled to Egypt and infected that province with the contagion of his error.

[Col. 0749C] Paulus was elected bishop of Antioch in his place.

**Emperor Flavius Caesar Anicius Justinus Augustus, [Note: [Col. 0749C] 1271 1272] tribunician power 1 and from 9 July tribunician power 2, consul.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 26 and 27.

**Consuls:** Justinus Augustus; Eutharic Cillica, a Goth.

Law 7 of the *Code*, “Concerning Natural Children,” etc., in Reland. An old inscription formerly in the pavement of Saint Clement’s in Rome, now in the museum of Cardinal Alessandro Albani, in Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 207; Gruter 1053; Reines, p. 900. Forty letters of Hormisdas and his legates, nos. 62 and 68.

[Col. 0749D] Pagius, no. 22, asserts from English history that in this year the kingdom of the West Saxons, or Western Saxons, was established in Britain by Cerdic.

**Emperor Justinus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0749D] 1272 1273] 2 and 3, consul.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 27 and 28.

**Consuls:** Vitalianus in the East; Rusticus in the West.

An old inscription in the pavement of the Basilica of Saint Paul. Justinus’s letter to Hormisdas, 15 days before the Kalends of February, under these consuls. See the notes, p. 240, and the letters of Hormisdas, nos. 66–84.

Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, an exile for the sake of the faith in Sardinia, wrote the book *On the Faith to Peter*, which they count among the works of Saint Augustine under Fulgentius’s title. See Noris, *History of Pelagius*, book 2, chapter 19.

**Emperor Justinus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0751A] 1273 1274] 3, 4, consul.**

[Col. 0751B] Theodoricus’s kingship, years 28 and 29.

**Consuls:** Justinianus; Valerius.

An old inscription of Fabretti, chapter 10, no. 454, at Ticinum. Letters of Hormisdas through no. 89, and of Emperor Justinus. See the notes, p. 235, column 2.

Justinianus made this famous consulship magnificent through his generosity. For he spent 289,000 solidi on the people and the staging of spectacles. He exhibited twenty lions and thirty leopards in the amphitheater, apart from other wild animals. Marcellinus.

[Col. 0751C] **Emperor Justinus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0751C] 1274 1275] 4, 5, consul.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 29 and 30.

**Consuls:** Symmachus and Boethius, sons of Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius, consul in 510.

An old inscription in the Basilica of Saint Paul, discussed by Severanus, p. 152, and Fleetwood, p. 476. See another inscription in Fleetwood, p. 455, at Saint Pancras.

Petavius assigns the death of Trasamundus, king of the Vandals in Africa, to this year. Pagius postpones it to the following consulship. [Col. 0751D] From Victor of Tunnuna and others.

Dunaan, king of the Homerites [the Ethiopians in Africa], having been made a Jew from Christianity, persecuted the faithful, putting Saint Arethas and his companions to death.

**Emperor Justinus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0751D] 1275 1276] 5, 6, consul.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 30 and 31.

**Consul:** Maximus alone.

An old inscription in the Vatican Basilica, discussed in the notes, p. 229, column 1.

Marius of Aventicum begins in this year to insert indictions after the names of the consuls in his chronicle. See Pagius.

Trasamundus, king of Africa, died; and the Orthodox bishops were recalled from exile by his successor Hilderic. See Pagius for this year and for the preceding year, no. 2.

**Emperor Caesar Justinus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0753A] 1276 1277] 6, 7, consul II.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 31 and 32.

**Consul:** Justinus Augustus II.

[Col. 0753B] Opilio.

A fragment of an old inscription in the Basilica of Saint Paul; laws 7 and 8 of the *Code*, “Concerning Advocates in Various Courts,” and other sources in Reland for this year.

Around this time the Lombards occupied Pannonia. Paul the Deacon, [lacuna], book 2, chapter 7.

The Council of Arles was held this year, under these consuls. Petavius and Pagius.

**Emperor Caesar Justinus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0753B] 1277 1278] 7, 8, consul II.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 32 and 33.

**Consuls:** Philoxenus in the East; Probus the Younger in the West.

[Col. 0753C] An old inscription in Reines, pp. 446 and 981; Sirmond on Sidonius, book 8, letter 6; and on Ennodius, p. 1817.

Law 7 of the *Code*, “Concerning Prescription of Thirty or Forty Years.” The Council of Carthage was held this year, on 5 February. Volume 4 of the councils.

**Emperor Caesar Justinus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0753C] 1278 1279] 8, 9, consul II.**

Theodoricus’s kingship, years 33 and 34; he died at the beginning of September.

**Consul:** Olybrius, without a colleague.

Law 6 of the *Code*, “Concerning Violation of Tombs.”

[Col. 0753D] After Pope John had been martyred, King Theodoricus ordered Boethius and Symmachus to be beheaded. Then, terrified by the appearance of a fish’s head at dinner—as though he had seen Symmachus’s head—he himself died shortly afterward. Procopius, book 1, *On the Gothic War*. Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, book 4, relates that a hermit saw him thrust into a fiery abyss. After Theodoricus died, Athalaricus, son of Amalasuntha, succeeded him; he was eight years old. Procopius, same place. Pagius says that the deaths of Symmachus and Boethius should be assigned to the preceding year, no. 6.

**Emperor Caesar Justinus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0755A] 1279 1280] 9 and 10, consul II, who on the Kalends of April crowned Augustus JUSTINIANUS, the son of his sister and his colleague, and on the Kalends of August departed this life.**

**Emperor Justinianus Augustus, tribunician power 1, [Col. 0755B] from 1 April, according to the Alexandrian Chronicle.**

Athalaricus’s kingship, year 1, and from 2 September, year 2.

**Consul:** Flavius Mavortius, without a colleague.

Law 5 of the *Code*, “Concerning the Office of the Master of Offices,” and an old inscription in Reines from Cujas and others, p. 412; and the diptych of Saint Maximin in Wilthemius, in Liège, p. 5, where this year is combined with 13 January of indiction 5.

**Emperor Flavius Justinianus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0755B] 1280 1281] 1, 2, consul II.**

Athalaricus’s kingship, years 2 and 3.

[Col. 0755C] **Consul:** Justinianus Augustus II, alone.

Preface to the first *Constitution*, and other sources in Reland for this year. A letter of Pope Felix to Caesarius of Arles, dated 3 February, calls it “after the consulship of Mavortius.” See Noris, *History of Pelagius*, book 2, chapter 22. Marcellinus correctly counts the year as 198 from the foundation of the royal city.

**Emperor Caesar Justinianus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0755C] 1281 1282] [Col. 0755D] 2, 3, consul II.**

Athalaricus’s kingship, years 3 and 4.

**Consul:** Decius alone, also called Decius the Younger.

Preface to the second *Constitution*, and law 44 of the *Code*, “Concerning Bishops and Clergy,” which see also in Reland and Pagius. See the Second Council of Vaison and the Second Council of Orange, dated under the consulship of Saint Caesarius. At the Council of Orange, doctrines concerning grace and free will were sanctioned against the Pelagians and Semi-Pelagians, in accordance with the Chapters transmitted by Felix IV and signed by Saint Caesarius under this consulship, approving Saint Augustine’s teaching. Thus an end was imposed on a long controversy of many years. Baronius and Sirmond, etc., in Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book 2, chapter 23. See the notes on Felix IV.

**Emperor Caesar Justinianus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0757A] 1282 1283] 3, 4, consul II.**

Athalaricus’s kingship, years 4 and 5.

[Col. 0757B] **Consuls:** Lampadius; Orestes.

An old inscription in the Basilica of Saint Paul, in Aringhius, volume 2, p. 414; another in Saint Agnes Outside the Walls; law 26 of the *Code*, “Concerning Holy Churches”; other sources in Reland; and a letter of Pope Boniface. See the notes on Felix IV.

Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, nos. 327 and 398; Gruter 459; Spon, *Miscellanies*, p. 160.

Mundus, prefect of Illyricum, defeated the Getae in the same province and the Bulgarians in Thrace. Marcellinus.

[Col. 0757C] **Emperor Justinianus Augustus, [Note: [Col. 0757C] 1283 1284] tribunician power 4, 5; consul II.**

Athalaricus’s kingship, years 5 and 6.

“After the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes.”

This year is so dated in an ancient Veronese inscription of Saint Valentinus, bishop, reported by Panvinius in the *Fasti*; and in other inscriptions in Fabretti, p. 757; Fleetwood, p. 499; the Gudian collection in Reland; and book 48 of the *Code*, “Concerning Bishops and Clergy,” along with other sources there.

Amalaric, king in Hispania, was killed by the Franks after five years of rule. Petavius, from Gregory of Tours, book 3, chapter 10, and Procopius, book 1 of the Gothic War.

Theudis succeeded Amalaric. See Petavius for this year.

**Emperor Caesar Justinianus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0757D] 1284 1285] 5, 6; consul II.**

Athalaricus’s kingship, years 6 and 7.

This year is again dated “after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes” in an old inscription at Saint Peter in Chains, which see in the notes on Boniface. Also laws 50 and 53 of the *Code*, “Concerning Bishops and Clergy,” and other sources in Reland.

[Col. 0759A] Ado of Vienne, in his chronicle for this year, which he counts as 248 of Diocletian, says that the end of the Dionysian cycle was promulgated and that Justinianus’s code was issued, perhaps following the calculations of Victor of Capua against Victorius of Aquitaine.

Clothar and Childebert, kings of the Franks, after defeating Gundemar, obtained Burgundy. Their brother Theodoricus devastated the Auvergne. [Col. 0759B] Petavius, from Gregory of Tours, book 4, chapter 11.

**Emperor Caesar Justinianus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0759B] 1285 1286] 6, 7; consul III.**

Athalaricus’s kingship, years 7 and 8.

**Consul:** Justinianus Augustus III, without a colleague.

Laws 6 and 7 of the *Code*, “Concerning the Holy Trinity,” and other sources in Reland and Gothofredus.

Having completed the entire Dionysian cycle in the common era of Christ, the phoenix of chronologers here places the end of his work. Petavius.

Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, died this year on the Kalends of January. See Noris, *History of Pelagius*, book 2, chapter 24, and the notes on John II.

**Emperor Justinianus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0759C] 1286 1287] 6, 7, consul IV.**

Athalaricus’s kingship, years 8 and 9; he died.

**Consuls:** Emperor Flavius Anicius Justinianus IV; Flavius Decius Theodorus Paulinus the Younger, who was the **last of the Western consuls**.

Law 33 of the *Code*, “Concerning the Hearing of Bishops,” etc., in Reland; and a letter of Pope John to Justinianus. See the notes on John II.

[Col. 0759D] The final revision of the code was made under these consuls, with laws concerning the constitution of the province of Africa added. See Pagius for this year.

Athalaricus, king of the Goths, died consumed by disease. His mother, Amalasuntha, placed her cousin Theodahad on the throne; at his order she was strangled within a few days on the island in Lake Bolsena. Jordanes, *On the Gothic Affairs*, chapter 59; Marcellinus, chronicle for this year.

Pagius asserts that the kingdom of Burgundy was extinguished this year with the death of King Theodoricus.

[Col. 0761A] **Emperor Justinianus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0761A] 1287 1288] 8, 9, consul IV.**

Theodahad’s kingship, years 1 and 2.

**Consul:** Belisarius alone in the East.

Novels 1, 3, 4, 7, 9, etc., of Justinianus, in Reland. In the West this year is also called “after the consulship of Paulinus the Younger, clarissimus man,” as in the Acts of the Council of Auvergne, concerning which see Pagius here and under the year 541.

[Col. 0761B] Beginning of the Gothic War for the recovery of Italy. See Noris, *On the Synod of V*, p. 26. Belisarius, who had been sent to recover Sicily, entered Syracuse in triumph on the last day of his consulship. Procopius, *On the Gothic War*, book 1, no. 4. See the notes on John II.

**Emperor Caesar Justinianus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0761B] 1288 1289] 9, 10, consul IV.**

Theodahad’s kingship, years 2 and 3; he was killed and succeeded by Vitiges.

[Col. 0761C] “After the consulship of Belisarius.”

This is how the year is dated in Act 1 of the Council of Constantinople and in Novels 16 and 18 of Justinianus, etc., in Reland. It is also called “again after the consulship of Paulinus” in an ancient stone reported by Aringhius, volume 2, p. 693.

The Goths elected Vitiges king and killed Theodahad. Procopius, *On the Gothic War*, book 1, no. 12. See Pagius for this year, no. 2.

Belisarius, passing through Campania, devastated Naples. Marcellinus. In December he recovered Rome. [Col. 0761D] See Pagius for the following year, no. 4.

**Emperor Caesar Justinianus Augustus, tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0761D] 1289 1290] 10, 11, consul IV.**

Vitiges’s kingship, years 1 and 2. Again, “after the consulship of Belisarius.”

Justinian, *Authenticum*, Collection V, title 2, Novel 47, in the second year after the consulship of Belisarius, which he declares to be the eleventh year of his reign, and he ordains that from the Kalends of April the twelfth shall begin. [Col. 0763A] In chapter 1 he orders that henceforth, wherever official acts are drawn up, they must begin in this manner in the public documents of that most sacred emperor’s government: “In the year so-and-so”; after this they are to add the name of the consul who holds office in that year; in third place, the indiction, and then the month and day. In chapter 2 he orders that in Latin documents the numbers be written in letters, which everyone who is not wholly ignorant of Latin syllables may read. [Col. 0763B] He subscribes this constitution as follows: “Given on the Kalends of … at Constantinople, while Justinian, perpetual Augustus, was reigning, in the second year after the consulship of Belisarius, illustrious man.”

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0763B] 1290, 1291], years 11 and 12, consul for the fourth time.

Years 2 and 3 of King Vitigis.

* Consul: Flavius John, Eastern consul, without a colleague.

An ancient inscription. *Fabretti*, p. 418 [Col. 0763C], and the Gudian inscription in Reland, as well as Justinian’s Novel 57 and Pope Vigilius’s letter to Caesar, bishop of Arles, and the Acts of the Third Council of Orléans. See Pagius, no. 6 for the year 540, and Vigilius’s letter, discussed in the notes on Agapetus.

Rome, afflicted by famine and plague, is liberated in March after a year of siege. Pagius, from Procopius, with his text corrected from the observations of Cardinal Noris in *De Synodo V*, chapter 6. See Pagius.

Datius, bishop of Milan, undertakes an embassy to Belisarius, imploring aid [Col. 0763D] against the Goths. There, no. 22, from Procopius.

Childebert the Younger begins to reign in Gaul. Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book 4, no. 7.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0763D] 1291, 1292], years 12 and 13, consul for the fourth time.

Years 3 and 4 of King Vitigis, and the first of Ildebald.

Consul: Appion, Eastern consul, without a colleague.

An ancient Greek inscription, published by Montfaucon, in which Appion’s consulship is read together with the second indiction; consequently the version in Reland is to be corrected. Likewise several of Justinian’s Novels, from 89 to 96.

[Col. 0765A] The Romans’ plan was to drive the Ostrogoths out of Picenum. After crossing the Alps and devastating Liguria, Theudebert, king of the Franks, brought assistance; but, persuaded by Belisarius’s letters, he returned to Gaul. Pagius, from Procopius.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0765A] 1292, 1293], years 13 and 14, consul for the fourth time.

The first year of King Araric and the first [Col. 0765B] of King Totila.

Consul: Justin the Younger, Eastern consul, without a colleague.

Justinian’s Novel 98, the *Pragmatic Sanction*, and letters of Pope Vigilius dated in this consulship on 17 September; Noris, *De Synodo V*, p. 8. This year is also called six times “after the consulship of Paulinus the Younger.” Not “January” in the Vatican papyrus published by Maffei, *Diplomatic History*, p. 158.

Under the consulship of Justin the Younger, in the third indiction, the *Paschal Chronicle* counts the 330th Olympiad.

Hildebald is killed in the first year of his reign. Araric is called king.

[Col. 0765C] Solomon, sent by Justinian into Africa against the Moors, fights successfully and suppresses rebellions. The Continuator of Marcellinus. See Pagius for this year, no. 13.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0765C] 1293, 1294], years 14 and 15, consul for the fourth time.

The first year of King Totila.

* Consul: Basil the Younger, Eastern consul without a colleague, and the last private individual to hold the consulship. See Panvinio.

* An ancient inscription of Sedaignuchus, chamberlain of King Theodoric, found at Ravenna [Col. 0765D]: “On the fourth ides of March, under the consulship of Basil the Younger, illustrious man, in the fourth indiction.” Also the Fourth Council of Orléans, concerning which see Pagius under the year 545, no. 9.

Likewise Justinian’s Novels from 107 through 146, in Reland. From his Novel 105, Pagius infers the reason why thereafter the consulship was not so readily conferred upon private persons, because of the expenses indicated by Procopius in *Secret History*, chapter 26.

The Goths [Col. 0767A] refuse Araric, elected king by the Rugians who were among the Goths, and kill him. Then they elevate Braduila, surnamed Totila, to the kingship. The Romans and Goths fight with varying success. Verona becomes the theater of war, now within, now outside the walls. See Procopius, book 3 of the Gothic War, chapter 6; Panvinio, *History of Verona*, book 4, chapter 23.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0767A] 1294, 1295], years 15 and 16, consul for the fourth time.

[Col. 0767B] Years 1 and 2 of King Totila.

For lack of consuls this year is entered after the consulship of Basil the Younger, illustrious man—that is, “after the consulship of Flavius Basil, illustrious man”—and so the following years are entered down to 586.

In this year, after the Frankish kings Childeric and Chlothar entered Spain, they ravage the province of Tarraconensis and capture Vasconia and Cantabria. See Pagius for this year, nos. 6 and 7.

King Arthur of the Britons, mortally wounded in battle, granted the diadem of Britain to his kinsman [Col. 0767C] Constantine. There, no. 7.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0767C] 1295, 1296], years 16 and 17, consul for the fourth time.

Years 2 and 3 of King Totila.

* Again, “after the consulship of Basil the Younger, illustrious man”; * Pope Vigilius’s letter to Caesarius,

bishop of Arles, and to Auxanius. See Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book 2, chapter 22.

Totila captures Naples and treats it more mildly, having been rendered gentler by his meeting with Saint Benedict, abbot of Cassino. See Baronius and Pagius for this year.

Saint Caesarius of Arles dies on 6 September. See Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, book 2, final chapter.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0767D] 1296, 1297], years 17 and 18, consul for the fourth time.

Years 3 and 4 of King Totila.

* “After the consulship of Basil the Younger, illustrious man, for the third time.”

* An ancient inscription in Boldetti, *Cemetery*, p. 86, and Justinian’s Novels 118, 147, and 149.

Because the Arians had been expelled from the city by Roman commanders, Totila, angered, advances against Rome. Belisarius, having been restored to the emperor’s favor in this year, [Col. 0769A] is sent again to Italy. See Pagius for this year, no. 2.

Saint Benedict dies. There, no. 12.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0769A] 1297, 1298], years 18 and 19, consul for the fourth time.

Years 4 and 5 of King Totila.

* Four times “after the consulship of Basil the Younger.”

Justinian’s Novels 130 and 148, *and an ancient inscription in the presbytery of Saint Michael at Ravenna, published by [Col. 0769B] Agnellus in the edition of Bacchini, p. 94; also Vigilius’s letters to Auxanius of Arles, published by Baronius, on 21 May.

Totila captures several cities in Picenum and Umbria and presses Rome with famine; Bessas was residing there.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0769B] 1298, 1299], years 19 and 20, consul for the fourth time.

[Col. 0769C] Years 5 and 6 of King Totila.

Five times “after the consulship of Basil the Younger.”

Justinian’s Novels 115.

The Councils of Lérida and Valencia were held in Spain in this year, as Pagius shows, no. 10.

Pagius, after weighing the words of Marius of Avenches and Procopius, places Totila’s entry into Rome near the end of this year, namely on 17 December; hence others assign it to the following year.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0769C] 1299, 1300] [Col. 0769D], years 20 and 21, consul for the fourth time.

Years 6 and 7 of King Totila.

* Six times “after the consulship of Basil the Younger.”

* An inscription at the apse of Saint Vitalis at Ravenna, in Agnellus, edited by Bacchini, p. 95, and one from Nola transcribed by me.

King Theudebert of the Franks dies. Theudevald reigns. Pagius under the year 552, no. 21.

Totila, having gained possession of Rome through the treachery of the Isaurians near the end of the preceding year, begins to devastate it; moved by Belisarius’s letters, he refrains and leads the Roman captives away into Campania. [Col. 0771A] Belisarius repairs the walls of the city after recovering it. Procopius, book 3, chapter 13. See Noris, *De Synodo V*, p. 27, and the notes on Vigilius.

Alboin, king of the Lombards, is attacked in war by Cunimund, king of the Gepids. Sigebert.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0771A] 1300, 1301], years 21 and 22, consul for the fourth time.

Years 7 and 8 of King Totila.

* Seven times “after the consulship of Basil the Younger.”

[Col. 0771B] * An ancient inscription in Fabretti, p. 758, and another transcribed by me at Terracina. Also in Reines, p. 996, and Reland under this year, where Justinian’s Novels 38 and 127 are also cited.

The Heruli raid all Illyricum; the Gepids capture Sirmium and other places in Dalmatia. The Lombards fight the Gepids and capture certain forts in Noricum. Marcellinus.

In this year the sixth kingdom of the Anglo-Saxon Heptarchy, namely Northumbria, began. Pagius, from Malesinus and other historians [Col. 0771C], no. 13.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0771C] 1301, 1302], years 22 and 23, consul for the fourth time.

Years 8 and 9 of King Totila.

* Eight times “after the consulship of Basil the Younger.”

* An ancient inscription at Saint Apollinaris in Classe near Ravenna, dated 9 May in the twelfth indiction, transcribed by me.

Totila recovers Rome near the end of this year. See Pagius under the following year, no. 3.

After Theudis, king of the Visigoths, is killed, Theudisclus reigns. The Spanish Era is 86, in Justinian’s 23rd year. Isidore, according to the editions of Grotius and Labbe; but according to Pagius, no. 7, it belongs to the preceding year, the 22nd.

The Fifth Council of Orléans, in the 38th year of Childebert’s reign and the 13th indiction. Pagius.

Justinian assigns to the Franks the part of Gaul that the Goths had possessed, in order to detach them from their alliance with the Goths. Pagius, from Procopius.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0771D] 1302, 1303], years 23 and 24, consul for the fourth time.

[Col. 0773A] Years 9 and 10 of King Totila.

* Nine times “after the consulship of Basil the Younger.”

An ancient inscription of the dedication of the Basilica of Saint Stephen at Ravenna: “On 11 December, nine times after the consulship of Basil the Younger.” See Agnellus, Bacchini’s second part, p. 89; and Vigilius’s letter of 3 May, “under Emperor Justinian in the twenty-fourth year, in the ninth year after the consulship of Basil, illustrious man.” Baronius under this year, no. 4.

The Slavs cross the Danube, capture cities [Col. 0773B], and cruelly rage against them. Procopius. Lech, a Slav, is said to have occupied Poland around this time. Calvisius, from Polish history.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0773B] 1303, 1304], years 24 and 25, consul for the fourth time.

Years 10 and 11 of King Totila.

Ten times “after the consulship of Basil the Younger.”

Justinian’s edict on the Three Chapters, and the petition of the Roman clergy written to him in this year on behalf of Vigilius. See Noris and Pagius.

[Col. 0773C] Freed from fear of Germanus, whom Justinian had first sent against the Slavs—and who died during that expedition, intending afterward to come to Italy against the Goths—Totila acts freely, sets out for Sicily, devastates it, and returns to Italy enriched by enormous booty and an abundance of grain. Procopius, and from him Calvisius under this year.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0773C] 1304, 1305], years 25 and 26, consul for the fourth time.

Years 11 and 12 of King Totila, who is killed in June, with Teja succeeding him.

Eleven times “after the consulship of Basil the Younger.”

[Col. 0773D] Vigilius’s encyclical, issued on 5 February, “while the Lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, was reigning, in the twenty-fifth year; after the consulship of Basil, in the eleventh year.” See Noris, *De Synodo V*, p. 49.

Narses, sent into Italy against the Goths, fights successfully near Ravenna, routing and killing Totila. Teja succeeds him, when the Goths withdraw to Ticinum, but Teja soon dies; with him the Ostrogothic kingdom in Italy came to an end. Narses restores the recovered city. See the notes on Vigilius.

[Col. 0775A] While the Romans recover Cumae and the remaining towns. Procopius. See Pagius for this year, nos. 10, 11, and 16.

Agathias begins his account of Persian affairs from this year, where Procopius ended. There, no. 13.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0775A] 1305, 1306], years 26 and 27, consul for the fourth time.

The first and last year of Teja, both of his own reign and of the Ostrogoths in Italy.

[Col. 0775B] Twelve times “after the consulship of Basil the Younger.”

The Acts of the Fifth Ecumenical Council, the Second Council of Constantinople, and Justinian’s Novels 145 and 146.

Teja, after Theudebald, king of the Franks, had been unsuccessfully invited to join the war, is routed and killed by the Romans near Cumae around February. Procopius, at the end of book 3 of *The Gothic War*, and Agathias.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0775B] 1306, 1307], years 27 and 28, consul for the fourth time.

After the consulship of Basil the Younger, for the thirteenth time.

[Col. 0775C] Vigilius’s *Constitutum* for the condemnation of the Three Chapters and the approval of the Council, issued on 23 February: “Under the emperor, our Lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus, in the twenty-seventh year, and in the thirteenth year after the consulship of Basil, illustrious man,” from Baluzius’s edition. See Pagius for this year, no. 4.

Theudevald, king of the Franks, dies. His uncle Chlothar, his father’s brother, takes both his kingdom and his wife, whom he later dismisses at the priests’ urging. There, nos. 7 and 8.

After King Agila is killed, the Visigoths in Spain create Athanagild [Col. 0775D] king. Isidore.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0775D] 1307, 1308], years 28 and 29, consul for the fourth time.

After the consulship of Basil the Younger, for the fourteenth time.

Ancient coins in Cangius, *Constantinople Christian*, table 26, and in Mediobarbus, mark this year as Justinian’s twenty-ninth.

At this time the Saxons again rebel against Chlothar. When he attacked them and they offered him half their property as compensation, the Frankish army rejected the offer and, having fought unwillingly, was routed with great slaughter by the Saxons and sought safety in flight. [Col. 0777A] Marcellinus, *Chronicle*.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0777A] 1308, 1309], years 29 and 30, consul for the fourth time.

After the consulship of Basil the Younger, for the fifteenth time.

Several letters of Pelagius were issued in this year, in Baronius, Binius, Labbe, and Pagius; see Pagius.

The duchy of Bavaria is established in this year [Col. 0777B], and Garibald becomes its first duke. Gregory of Tours, book 4, chapter 9. Garibald is also called king of the Bavarians by Paul the Deacon, book 3 of *The History of the Lombards*. See Pagius for this year, no. 17.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0777B] 1309, 1310], years 30 and 31, consul for the fourth time.

After the consulship of Basil the Younger, for the sixteenth time.

Letters of Pelagius to Childebert, king of the Franks, issued in this year, in the sixteenth year after the consulship of Basil. See Pagius. A papyrus in Marchese Maffei, *Diplomatic History*, p. 163.

Sinduald, king of the Heruli, a rebel, is defeated and killed by Narses [Col. 0777C]. Aimoinus, book 2, chapter 34. Thus Narses recovered all Italy for Justinian. Mediobarbus, under Occho, for this year.

The beginning of Theodemir’s reign in Spain, who restored the Catholic religion there. See Pagius under the year 560, nos. 3 and 4.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0777C] 1310, 1311], years 31 and 32, consul for the fourth time.

After the consulship of Basil the Younger, for the seventeenth time.

An ancient inscription of the church at Narni, in Baronius under this year, and in Gruter [Col. 0777D] 1161, 8, and Fabretti 167; A. and Fleetwood, p. 376.

King Childebert dies, according to Pagius under this year, after reigning 47 or 48 years. Marius of Avenches.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0777D] 1311, 1312], years 32 and 33, consul for the fourth time.

After the consulship of Basil the Younger, for the eighteenth time.

Justinian’s Novel 141 … and Edict 11.

In this year Victor of Aquitaine’s Paschal Cycle of 531 years is completed, beginning from the 28th year of the Christian era, in which he asserts that Christ the Lord suffered; and from this point we also reckon.

[Col. 0779A] See Pagius under this year.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0779A] 1312, 1313], years 33 and 34, consul for the fourth time.

After the consulship of Basil the Younger, for the nineteenth time.

Pagius proves that a war was conducted in Armorica in Britain in this year, no. 3 under the year 564.

The Council of Braga is held in Spain. See Pagius under this year, no. 4; under the year 563, no. 4; and Baronius [Col. 0779B] under the following year.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0779B] 1313, 1314], years 34 and 35, consul for the fourth time.

After the consulship of Basil the Younger, for the twentieth time.

Pagius, no. 1, infers from the circus games recorded by Theophanes that the eighth quinquennial celebration of the empire, undertaken by Justinian while Justin was alive, was held.

Chlothar, king of the Franks, dies. Pagius, no. 11, and Henschenius, *On the Three Dagoberts*, p. 13.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0779B] 1314, 1315] [Col. 0779C], years 35 and 36, consul for the fourth time.

After the consulship of Basil the Younger, for the twenty-first time.

The Frankish kingdom is divided four ways among Chlothar’s sons. Sigebert obtains Austrasia, and Guntram Burgundy.

Cassiodorus, around this time, furnished notable libraries in the monasteries he founded at Scyllacium and Vivarium. See Baronius and Pagius under this year.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0779C] 1315, 1316], years 36 and 37, consul for the fourth time.

After the consulship of Basil the Younger, for the twenty-second time.

An ancient inscription in the Vatican crypt, which appears below in the notes, p. 299: “The site of Marcellus, subdeacon of the sixth region, granted by the most blessed Pope John, and so forth, under the twenty-second year after the consulship of Basil, illustrious man; the eleventh indiction [to be read: twelfth], on 22 December.” Torrig, p. 93, and Ciampini, *On Sacred Buildings*, p. 104.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0779C] 1316, 1317], years 37 and 38, consul for the fourth time.

After the consulship of Basil the Younger, for the twenty-third time.

An ancient inscription at Rome in Panvinio’s *Fasti* under this year and in Reines, p. 975 [Col. 0781A], and a charter concerning full security at Ravenna in the supplement to Mabillon’s *Diplomatic History*: “Under Flavius Justinian, perpetual Augustus, in the thirty-eighth year, after the consulship of Basil, in the twenty-third year, on 14 July, in the twelfth indiction.”

Gildas publishes his book *On the Ruin of Britain* in this year, in which he writes the history of the preceding 44 years. See Pagius, no. 6, under this year.

Emperor Caesar Justinian Augustus, with tribunician power [Note: [Col. 0781A] 1317, 1318] [Col. 0781B], years 38 and 39, consul for the fourth time; he dies on 14 November, and Justin Augustus succeeds him with tribunician power from 14 November.

After the consulship of Basil the Younger, for the twenty-fourth time. See Cardinal Noris, *On the Fifth Ecumenical Synod*, p. 86, from a Roman inscription, and the laws by which he demonstrates this. Pagius also, under this year, nos. 3 and 7, shows that Justin, made Augustus by the palace chamberlain and crowned by John, patriarch of Constantinople, assumed the empire on 14 November.

[Col. 0781C] Justin the Younger, emperor Augustus, years 1 and [Note: [Col. 0781C] 1318, 1319] 2, consul. Since the title of tribunician power had fallen out of use at this period both on coins and in inscriptions, and the years of the reign were counted in its place in both, whether under the perpetual consulships of the Augusti or otherwise, we shall likewise designate their years by the years of their reign.

A Novel of Justin Augustus on divorce, issued on 14 September at Chalcedon, “while our Lord Justin, perpetual Augustus, was reigning, in his first year, in the fifteenth indiction,” according to Pithaeus’s edition. See Pagius under this year, no. 7.

[Col. 0781D] Emperor Justin Augustus, years 2 and 3 [Note: [Col. 0781D] 1319, 1320], consul.

* After the consulship of Justin the Younger Augustus.

* An ancient inscription excavated on the Esquiline: “Flora, who lived five years and twenty-eight days, was buried on 11 August, in the fifteenth indiction, after the consulship of our Lord Justin, perpetual Augustus.” This year is also called Justin’s second year of consulship by Marius of Avenches, and is called year II on the coins of Constantinople. Christian, table 27.

By Justin’s very bad decision, Narses, the restorer of Italy, is recalled to Constantinople. Consequently courage increased not only among the barbarians [Col. 0783A] but also among the Venetians, the schismatics; and shortly afterward that most noble province was ruined, afflicted both by the Lombard war and by the dissensions of the schismatics. Noris, *De Synodo V*, p. 89.

Emperor Justin Augustus, years 3 and 4 [Note: [Col. 0783A] 1320, 1321], consul.

Ancient coins in Cangius and Mediobarbus marked “YEAR III” and “YEAR IV.”

[Col. 0783B] The *Paschal Chronicle*: first indiction, after the second consulship of Justin the Younger Augustus, alone.

The migration of the Lombards from Pannonia toward Italy under Alboin is assigned to this year by Paul the Deacon, book 2, chapter 7. He relates that they departed from Pannonia in April, in the first indiction, on the day after Holy Easter; according to the calculation, the feast fell that year on the Kalends of April, when 568 years from the Lord’s Incarnation had already elapsed.

Emperor Justin Augustus, years 4 and 5 [Note: [Col. 0783B] 1321, 1322], consul.

[Col. 0783C] As shown above from coins marked with both years.

In this year Alboin enters Liguria, at the beginning of the third indiction, on 3 September, during the episcopate of Honoratus, archbishop of Milan. Paul the Deacon, book 2 of the *History of the Lombards*, chapter 25; and Noris, *De Synodo V*, p. 90.

Leovigild, having obtained the rule of Spain, determines to enlarge his kingdom by war. Isidore, *Chronicle*.

Emperor Justin Augustus, years 5 and 6 [Note: [Col. 0783C] 1322, 1323], consul.

[Col. 0783D] As above, from coins.

A Novel of Justin on the children of free women, issued on the Kalends of March at Constantinople: “Under our Lord Justin, perpetual Augustus, in the fifth year, after the second consulship of the same our Lord.” Baluzius discusses it in the notes on the Frankish royal capitularies, p. 1255, without any correction, for Justin’s fifth year was running from his second consulship in this year.

In the province of Gallaecia, Miro becomes king of the Suevi after Theodemir. Biclarensis. See Pagius, no. 8.

Emperor Justin Augustus, years 6 and 7 [Note: [Col. 0783D] 1323, 1324], consul.

[Col. 0785A] From coins marked “YEAR 6” and “YEAR 7.”

In this year Saint Gregory the Great was urban prefect. See Cardinal Noris, *De Synodo V*, pp. 90 and 95.

THE BEGINNING OF ALBOIN’S REIGN IN ITALY.

The bubonic plague in Gaul and Italy. Marius of Avenches.

Alboin occupies Pavia and establishes the seat of his kingdom there. From Paul the Deacon, book 2, chapter 13. Pagius [Col. 0785B] under this year, no. 2.

Laurentius, bishop of Milan, sends a written declaration concerning the Fifth Synod to Pope John. Noris, *De Synodo V*, p. 90.

Emperor Justin Augustus, years 7 and 8 [Note: [Col. 0785B] 1324, 1325], consul.

From coins inscribed “YEAR 7” and “YEAR 8,” in Mediobarbus and Cangius at Constantinople. A chronological charter on parchment: “In the seventh year of Justin, perpetual Augustus, and after his second consulship, in the fourth year, in the fourth indiction, on 3 June,” among the heirs of Decianus, jurist of Imola, now in the possession of the illustrious archbishop of Ancyra, Fontanini; also discussed in the learned Venetian journals and by Marchese Maffei, *Diplomatic History*, p. 163.

Charibert, king of the Franks, dies in this year. He is succeeded in Austrasia by Sigebert, in Neustria by Chilperic, and in Burgundy by Guntram. Cointius, in Pagius under this year, no. 4.

Emperor Justin Augustus, years 8 and 9 [Note: [Col. 0785C] 1325, 1326], consul.

Ancient coins on which “YEAR 8” and “YEAR 13” are engraved, in Mediobarbus and Cangius.

The prefecture of the city was administered by Gregory the Great in this year, according to Pagius under this year and under the year 581, no. 3.

A dispute arises among the kings of Gaul, which Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, strives to avert through Queen Brunhild. Pagius, there, no. 7; he holds that the Fourth Council was celebrated at Paris. See the year 576, no. 5. The Spaniards disagree about the celebration of Easter. There, no. 4.

Emperor Justin Augustus, years 9 and 10 [Note: [Col. 0785D] 1326, 1327], consul.

From ancient coins marked “YEAR 10.”

[Col. 0787A] Justin’s decennalia are celebrated. Since the same Augustus was suffering from mental weakness, at the urging of the empress Sophia, on 7 September, according to Mediobarbus, he creates Tiberius Constantine Caesar and Augustus and entrusts the government of the state to him. From an ancient Vatican stone at Saint Angelo. Cardinal Noris, *De Synodo V*, p. 91, and Pagius under this year, no. 6 and following.

[Col. 0787B] Emperors Justin Augustus, years 10 and [Note: [Col. 0787B] 1327, 1328] 11, consul.

From ancient coins marked “YEAR 10” and “YEAR 11.”

And Tiberius Constantine, Caesar Augustus.

Various Lombard raids throughout Italy, beginning in the year 570 and continuing into this one, disfigure and plunder sacred buildings, killing priests. See Pagius, from Gregory of Tours; he also indicates under this year, no. 2, that the death of Sigebert, king of the Franks, should be placed here.

[Col. 0787C] Emperor Justin Augustus, years 11 and [Note: [Col. 0787C] 1328, 1329] 12, consul.

From coins marked “YEAR 11” and “YEAR 12.”

And Tiberius Constantine Caesar, whose coins are marked with years II and III.

While the empire’s forces are weakened by the Persian war, the Lombards devote themselves to new acquisitions and plunder throughout Italy. See the notes on Benedict I.

Emperors Justin Augustus, years 12 and 13 [Note: [Col. 0787C] 1329, 1330], consul.

And Tiberius Constantine Caesar, years 3 [Col. 0787D] and 4.

A Vatican stone, published after Aringhi by Cardinal Noris, *De Synodo V*, p. 86, contains, as he himself observes, several chronological notations. The year is given in the deposition of Boethius: “On 15 October, on the Kalends of November, in the eleventh indiction, under our Lord Justin, perpetual Augustus, in the twelfth year, and Tiberius Constantine Caesar in the third year,” and so forth.

Emperor Justin Augustus, year 13, consul [Note: [Col. 0787D] 1330, 1331]; he dies on 5 October, according to the Alexandrian Chronicle.

Tiberius Constantine succeeds Justin [Col. 0789A] and is crowned Augustus on 26 September by Eutychius, patriarch, at Justin’s command. See Cangius, *On the Byzantine Families*, under Tiberius Constantine.

This is also called Tiberius Constantine’s years 4 and 5 from the time when he obtained the rank of Caesar. During this period one hundred thousand Slavs invade Thrace. Menander Protector, p. 124. See Pagius under this year, no. 7.

[Col. 0789B] Emperor Tiberius Constantine Augustus, years [Note: [Col. 0789B] 1331, 1332] 5 and 6.

Consul: Tiberius Junior Constantine Augustus, who distributed the extensive consular office among the people. Theophanes.

The schismatic Aquileians celebrate the Council of Grado in this year, on 3 November. It bears these chronological formulas: “Under the reign of the lord Tiberius Constantine Augustus, in the fifth year of his reign, with the same man consul, on 3 November, in the thirteenth indiction.” See Noris, *De Synodo V*, pp. 97 and 100, where he discusses the transfer of the see [Col. 0789C] of Aquileia to Grado.

Emperor Tiberius Constantine Augustus, consul [Note: [Col. 0789C] 1332, 1333], years 6 and 7, as marked on coins.

This is also called the second year of the consulship of Tiberius Constantine Augustus, and otherwise “the second year after the consulship of Tiberius Constantine,” and so forth.

Around this time the Lombards established in Italy three duchies, two marquisates, and 36 city governorships. See Panvinio, *Antiquities of Verona*, book 5, chapter 5; and Campelli, *History of Spoleto*, book 11, p. 324, where, from Paul the Deacon, book 3, chapter 15, he mentions Faroald as the first duke of Spoleto [Col. 0789D]; and Camillo Pellegrini, book 2, where he discusses Zotto, the first duke of the Beneventans, from Paul the Deacon; and Panvinio, who gives Gisulf as the first duke of Friuli.

Emperor Tiberius Constantine Augustus, consul, year 7 [Note: [Col. 0789D] 1333, 1334] and 8, from coins.

This year Peter the Notary of the Neapolitan Church, correcting a codex at the command of Bishop Reductius, indicates that it should be emended as follows: “On the ides of December, under our Lord Tiberius, Augustus at Constantinople [perhaps it should be read: Tiberius Constantine [Col. 0791A] Augustus], in the seventh year, after the consulship of the same Augustus, in the third year, in the fifteenth indiction, while the Lombards were besieging the city of Naples.” Mabillon, *Analecta*, vol. 2, p. 11, from a manuscript codex of the Library of Saint-Germain.

[Col. 0791B] Emperor Tiberius Constantine Augustus, consul [Note: [Col. 0791B] 1334, 1335], year 8; he dies on 14 August, having first elevated Tiberius Maurice to the rank of Augustus and given him his daughter Constantina as wife.

The *Pragmatic Sanction* of Tiberius is dated as follows: “Given on 11 August at Constantinople, in the eighth year of the emperor, our Lord Tiberius Constantine Augustus, and in the third year after his consulship, and in the first year of the most noble Caesar Flavius Mauritius Felix.”

Emperor Tiberius Maurice, years 1 and 2. [Note: [Col. 0791B] 1335, 1336]

[Col. 0791C] Although this year lacked consuls, who are designated on coins, the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle relates that it was inscribed: “After the consulship of the divine memory of Tiberius Constantine, in the fourth year.” Pagius under this year, no. 1. Yet the following year is designated in the same Chronicle: “After the consulship of Tiberius Maurice Augustus, alone, for the first time.” Therefore Maurice was consul after the autumn of this year. See Noris, *De Synodo V*, p. 93, from Theophylact Simocatta.

After the decade had been completed under dukes, the Lombards create Authari, duke of Verona, as king in March [Col. 0791D]. Panvinio discusses him from Paul the Deacon, *Antiquities of Verona*, book 5, chapter 8.

Smaragdus, the second exarch, is sent into Italy. Panvinio, *Fasti*, from Paul the Deacon.

Emperor Caesar Tiberius Maurice, years 2 [Note: [Col. 0791D] 1336, 1337] and 3, from coins; the same man is consul.

The present year is designated in the Alexandrian Chronicle as after the consulship of Maurice, as Cardinal Noris observes, *De Synodo V*, p. 93, although it was marked by his consulship. There, from Simocatta, a fact confirmed by Pagius from Theophylact.

Chilperic, king of the Franks, is killed in this year. There, no. 16.

[Col. 0793A] Emperor Tiberius Maurice Augustus, year 3 [Note: [Col. 0793A] 1337, 1338] and 4, after his second consulship.

This year is designated in Candida’s epitaph, on 10 September: “Under our Lord Maurice, perpetual Augustus, in the fourth year, after his consulship in the second year, in the fourth indiction.” Baronius, *Roman Martyrology*, under 4 September; Reines, p. 960, from Capaccio and Summontius. See Pagius under this year, no. 1.

Ebaric, son of Miro, king of the Suevi in Gallaecia, and his successor, is deprived of the kingdom by Audica, who usurps the tyranny. But Leovigild, king of the Goths, campaigns against Audica in this year, and thus the Suevian rule in Spain, which had begun in the year 409 of the Christian era, comes to an end. See Pagius, from no. 12, under the year 582.

Emperor Caesar Tiberius Maurice Augustus, years [Note: [Col. 0793B] 1338, 1339] 4 and 5 marked on coins, after his third consulship.

Pagius seeks to establish the election of Authari, king of the Lombards, in this year, the fourth of Maurice, from the abbot of Biclaro [Col. 0793C], under the year 585, nos. 2 and 3.

King Leovigild dies, with Reccared succeeding him. From Biclar, in Pagius, no. 14. Reccared sends envoys concerning peace to Guntram, king of the Franks. Pagius, there, no. 11.

Childebert, who had descended into Italy against the Lombards after being invited by gifts from Flavius Smaragdus, the exarch, is likewise induced by the Lombards to make peace with them and to return to Gaul. From Gregory of Tours and Paul the Deacon. Pagius, no. 4.

[Col. 0793D] Emperor Caesar Tiberius Maurice Augustus, years [Note: [Col. 0793D] 1339, 1340] 5 and 6 marked on coins, after his fourth consulship.

Severus, bishop of Aquileia, who had succeeded Elias and was no less vigorously fighting for the Three Chapters, is captured with his fellow bishops and brought to Ravenna by Smaragdus. In the presence of John, bishop of Ravenna, he condemns the Three Chapters with his companions and is released. See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, p. 102.

Romanus succeeds Smaragdus as the third exarch. Panvinio, *Fasti*, from Paul the Deacon.

[Col. 0795A] Emperor Caesar Tiberius Maurice Augustus, years [Note: [Col. 0795A] 1340, 1341] 6 and 7 marked on coins; in public acts this year is called “after his fifth consulship.”

Panvinio, *Antiquities of Verona*, book 5, chapter 8, reports that in this year Childebert, king of the Franks, sent an army into Italy against the Lombards; but, compelled to return after three months by famine and disease, Authari also died shortly afterward. Agilulf, formerly duke of Turin, is chosen as the fourth king of the Lombards in Italy; he was the father of Aodald, who succeeded him in the twenty-fifth year of his father’s reign. But see the year 590.

Emperor Caesar Tiberius Maurice Augustus is designated [Note: [Col. 0795B] 1341, 1342] on coins as years 7 and 8; in the acts it is also called “after his sixth consulship,” while others call it the fifth.

The army sent by Guntram, king of the Franks, under the leadership of Boso, is defeated in Narbonensian Gaul by Claudius, commander of Reccared [Col. 0795C], and, after its camp is captured, is put to flight. Biclar, *Chronicle*. See Pagius under this year, no. 9.

In the same year, the seventh of Maurice, which was the third of King Reccared, Uldila conspires against Reccared and lays ambushes for him; he is driven into exile. Biclar, there, no. 12.

The Third Council of Toledo is held in this year. There, nos. 4 and 6: the Goths and Suevi are converted to the Catholic faith. There, no. 8.

Emperor Caesar Tiberius Maurice Augustus is designated [Note: [Col. 0795C] 1342, 1343] on coins as years 8 and 9; historians also call this “after his seventh consulship” [Col. 0795D], while others call it the sixth.

The First Council of Seville, held in this year, gives the era as follows: “On 5 November, in the fifth year of the reign of our most glorious lord Reccared, king, era 628.” See Pagius under this year, no. 6.

In this year, according to Gregory of Tours, book 10, chapter 3, the army of Childebert, king of the Franks, in his fifteenth year, harassed the Lombards in Italy for three months. Authari sends an embassy to Guntram, Childebert’s maternal uncle, asking him to obtain peace from his uncle.
