But before the envoys had returned from Gaul, Authari died at Ticinum on 5 September, not without suspicion of poison, after reigning six years; Agilulf succeeded him. From Paul the Deacon. Pagius under this year, no. 17; and from Gregory the Great’s letter 17, book 1. Panvinio assigns these events to the year 598. See above.

Christians, Jews, and neighboring peoples: pontiffs, kings, events, and documents.

[Col. 0602B]

[Col. 0602C] [Note: [Col. 0602C] Olympiad 273, year 1, and year 2 from the summer days.] Fourth year of Melchiades. First of SYLVESTER. Melchiades dies, being buried on 10 January.

SYLVESTER is elected successor, after a vacancy of the apostolic see of sixteen days (as in the catalogues and the Library), and on Sunday, 31 January, is installed in the Roman see. He holds it for 21 years and 11 months, as stated in the Liberian Catalogue, until 31 December 335. Constantius and Albinus being consuls.

The Synod of Arles was held under these consuls, as were also those of Ancyra and Neocaesarea. Baronius and Petavius under this year.

The Donatists are condemned in Africa. Saint Augustine, Letters 68 and 162.

Maximinus, breaking the treaty and making war on Licinius, is stripped of his camp; scarcely escaping from the hands of the enemy, he withdraws into Asia and dies at Tarsus at the beginning of spring. From this Noris proves, confirming Baronius’s opinion, that Licinius’s reign in Asia is to be reckoned after the month of March; *Dissertation on Two Coins of Diocletian and Licinius*, pp. 64 ff. [Col. 0604A]

Constantine at Milan gives his sister Constantia in marriage to Licinius.

[Note: [Col. 0604A] II III] First and second years of Sylvester.

Constantine attacks Licinius in war and, after defeating him in battle at Cibalae, a town of Lower Pannonia, on 8 October, and again on the Campus Mardienus, deprives him of Illyricum, adding seventeen of Licinius’s provinces, together with Raetia and Pannonia, to his own empire. He permits Licinius to retain Asia and the Diocese of the East together with Thrace, Lower Moesia, and European Scythia. See Noris, *On the Coins of Licinius*, ch. 2, p. 68; Lydiat and Petavius. [Col. 0604B]

[Note: [Col. 0604B] III IV] Second and third years of Sylvester.

Arius is discovered spreading his heresy in popular discourses; at the same time Colluthus, a presbyter of Alexandria, was likewise instilling the poison of his doctrine. Petavius, from Epiphanius, *Heresies* [Col. 0604C] 69.

Caecilianus is acquitted before Constantine, and the Donatists are sent into exile. Pagius, no. 17, with Noris.

[Note: [Col. 0604C] Olympiad 273, year 4, and 274, year 1] Third and fourth years of Sylvester.

Under these consuls three Caesars—Crispus, Licinius, and Constantine—are elevated on the Kalends of March. Idatius; and Noris proves it from other documents, p. 84, in *On Two Coins of Diocletian and Licinius*. [Col. 0604D]

An eclipse of the sun, seven digits, at Paris on 20 December: Petavius, from Idatius (who assigned it to the following consuls) and other writers. But see the following year.

[Note: [Col. 0604D] I II] Fourth and fifth years of Sylvester.

Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, expels Arius, who goes to Palestine and throws everything into confusion. Petavius, from Socrates, Severus, and Epiphanius.

Metrophanes, bishop of Byzantium, [Col. 0606A] after sitting for three years, arranged for Alexander to be substituted for him. For the latter held the see for 23 years, according to Socrates, book 2, chapter 4, and Sozomen, book 3, chapter 3. Petavius.

Idatius assigns the eclipse of the sun to three years earlier. See Valesius’s notes on Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book 2, chapter 6. Crispus is instructed in sacred letters by Lactantius. Eusebius.

[Note: [Col. 0606A] II III] Fifth and sixth years of Sylvester.

[Col. 0606B] On the death of Philogonius, bishop of Antioch, Paulinus succeeds him. Petavius, from Nicephorus’s *Chronicle*.

Licinius begins a persecution against the Christians, in which Theodorus, a distinguished military commander, undergoes martyrdom. From his Acts in Surius; Noris, *On Two Coins of Licinius*, etc., p. 90. He expels Christians from his palace and forbids them to hold councils. Petavius, from Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, book 1, chapters 44–45.

Constantine attacked the Sarmatians, inhabitants of the Maeotis, who had crossed the Danube; shortly afterward he utterly defeated them in their own territory, killing their king Rausimodus. This is recorded there from Zosimus, book II.

The same emperor issued a rescript against the haruspices: laws 1 and 2 of the Code, *On Sorcery*; law 2 of the Code, *On the Immunity of Clerics*; and law 2 of the Code, *On Bishops*.

[Note: [Col. 0606C] III IV] Years 6 and 7 of Sylvester.

The Paschal Chronicle frequently indicates that Christian churches were dedicated under these consuls.

Constantine abolished the penalties imposed upon the childless and celibate, Code, book 1, *On the Penalty for the Childless and Celibate*. Petavius.

[Col. 0606D] [Note: [Col. 0606D] Olympiad 274 IV and 275 I] Years 7 and 8 of Sylvester.

About this time one should apparently place the baptism received at Rome by Constantine Augustus together with his mother Saint Helena and many of his children and household members, administered to them by Pope Saint Sylvester, according to the evidence cited in our notes on Sylvester from John Malalas and from the more ancient chronographer preserved by the same author.

Under these consuls Constantine Augustus issued a law concerning observance of the Lord’s Day, Code, book 3, *On Holidays*.

The Second Synod of Alexandria was held against Arius, according to the evidence presented by Pagius under the year 315, section V and following.

[Col. 0608B] [Note: [Col. 0608B] I II] Years 8 and 9 of Sylvester.

Constantine the Great declared war on Licinius. Preparations for war were made everywhere. Licinius halted at Hadrianopolis. Crispus was taken by his father Constantine as a partner in the expedition.

Hormisdas, of the royal Persian line, escaped from prison and fled to Constantine through an extraordinary device devised by his wife. Zonaras, book II, chapter 27.

[Note: [Col. 0608B] II III] Years 9 and 10 of Sylvester.

Licinius engaged Constantine and, defeated by land and sea, was driven first to Byzantium, then to Chalcedon—where he created Martianus Caesar—and finally withdrew to Nicomedia. Zosimus, book II, chapter 26.

Constantine issued a decree against people of the various religions who compelled clerics to celebrate the sacrifices of the lustral rites. Code, book V, *On the Church and Clergy*. Petavius.

[Note: [Col. 0608C] III IV] Years 10 and 11 of Sylvester.

Licinius, besieged by Constantine at Nicomedia, surrendered himself and the city to the victor and laid aside the purple in the eighteenth year of the empire conferred upon him by Galerius. The Asians, however, reckon it as the eleventh year. Noris, *Dissertation on the Two Coins of Licinius*, p. 101. Licinius was killed shortly afterward, and before him Martinianus. Zosimus, book II, chapter 28.

When Paulinus, bishop of Antioch, died, consideration was given to substituting Eusebius of Caesarea. But Eustathius, a Catholic and highly praised bishop, was elected. Petavius, from Eusebius and Theodoret, book I, chapter 7.

[Note: [Col. 0608D] Olympiad 275 IV and 276] Years 11 and 12 of Sylvester.

The Council of Nicaea was held by 318 Fathers. It affirmed the creed, made a ruling concerning the feast of Easter, and, judging Arius, condemned his heresy. It began on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of July and was concluded on the eighth day before the Kalends of September.

Sylvester, having received the council’s decrees, approved at a synod convened at Rome what had been done there. Baronius under this year, sections 171 and 199; and Petavius near the end of his account of the Council of Nicaea. Constantine the Great celebrated his Vicennalia at Nicomedia. Eusebius, book IV, chapter 11 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, and in the *Chronicle* and *Life of Constantine*, book III, chapter 14.

[Col. 0610B] [Note: [Col. 0610B] I II] Years 12 and 13 of Sylvester.

Saint Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, died on 26 February. See Baronius and Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 2, p. 8. Athanasius succeeded him. See Petavius.

Crispus Caesar, though innocent, was killed on suspicion of an illicit relationship with his stepmother. See Baronius and the authors cited by him under the year 324, section V and following.

In the same year Licinius Junior, son of Licinius Augustus, was killed. Eusebius [Col. 0610C] and Zosimus, book II.

A severe persecution against the Christians was stirred up in Persia by Sapor. Petavius, from Theophanes and Cedrenus.

Constantine enacted several laws against heretics of various sects. See Baronius, section 16 and following. At his urging Saint Helena, his mother, set out for Jerusalem, built many basilicas, and discovered the Lord’s Cross. Ibid., sections 31, 42, and elsewhere; and John Malalas, book XIII, p. 5.

[Note: [Col. 0610C] II III] Years 13 and 14 of Sylvester.

Arius, who had until then concealed his heresy, attempted through Eusebius of Nicomedia to return to Alexandria. But neither Eusebius nor the emperor could force this from Athanasius. From Athanasius, *Apology* II; Petavius under this year.

The Gospel was brought to the Indians by Frumentius of Tyre, whom Athanasius appointed bishop for them. Rufinus, book I, chapter 9; Socrates, book I, chapter 15; Theodoret and Sozomen, in Petavius under this year.

At the same time the Iberians accepted the faith of Christ through the agency of a Christian captive woman. Ibid.

[Note: [Col. 0612A] III IV] Years 14 and 15 of Sylvester.

While touring his diocese, Athanasius deposed Ischyras, who was acting as a bishop in Mareotis and who fled to the Meletians. Athanasius, *Apology*. During this journey he visited Saints Antony and Pachomius. Petavius, from Saint Athanasius.

About this time Constantine, having surveyed the site and advantageous position of Byzantium, began to restore and fortify it and to establish the imperial seat there. Petavius and Zosimus, book II.

Constantine defeated the Taiphali and the Goths and built a stone bridge over the Danube. Mediobardus, from the Alexandrian Chronicle and from inscribed coins commemorating the Gothic victory.

[Col. 0612C] [Note: [Col. 0612C] Olympiad 276 IV and 277 I] Years 15 and 16 of Sylvester.

Constantine summoned men of the highest nobility from the city of Rome and other cities to frequent his own city. He removed the forts, garrisons, and frontier troops stationed along the banks of the Danube—[since their removal would soon bring about the destruction of the Roman Empire]. Lydiatus, from the history of Zosimus, book II, chapters 34–35, and from Eusebius and others; John Malalas should be added.

[Note: [Col. 0612C] I II] Years 16 and 17 of Sylvester.

Under these consuls Constantinople was dedicated on the fifth day before the Ides of May, according to Idatius and John Malalas, part II, p. 5. Malalas assigns the year to the Antiochene Era 378, while the author of the Paschal Chronicle assigns it to 301 after Christ the Lord’s Ascension into heaven, on a Monday, in the third indiction, and 1080 years from the founding of Rome.

Under the same consuls, Lydiatus says—not under the following consuls, as Onuphrius, Golzius, and others maintained—that Constantine established a new arrangement of the provinces, magistracies, and armies. Instead of two praetorian prefects, he instituted four prefectures, [Col. 0614A] described by Zosimus, book II, chapter 33, with the limits of each man’s authority. See also Pagius under the year 332.

[Note: [Col. 0614A] II III] Years 17 and 18 of Sylvester.

The Meletians, on the authority of Eusebius of Nicomedia, brought false charges against Athanasius: the breaking of a chalice and the murder of Arsenius. Petavius, from Socrates I, chapter 20, and Sozomen II, chapter 22.

By Constantine’s edict the temples of the Gentiles were overthrown. Ibid., from Jerome’s Chronicle and Theophanes; add John Malalas, part II, pp. 3 and 10, and the authors cited by Pagius under the year 333, section IV.

[Note: [Col. 0614B] III IV] Years 18 and 19 of Sylvester.

When the Sarmatians appealed for aid against the Goths, Constantine came to their assistance. Consequently nearly one hundred thousand of them perished from hunger and cold at Constantine’s hands. At that time he also received hostages, among them the son of King Ariaricus. The Anonymous Valesianus, in Petavius and Pagius under this year; Idatius and Jerome in their chronicles support the account.

[Col. 0614C] [Note: [Col. 0614C] Olympiad 277 IV and 278 I] Years 19 and 20 of Sylvester.

Under these consuls Constans was raised to the rank of Caesar on the eighth day before the Kalends of January. Idatius under this year. See Noris, *On the Coins of Licinius*, p. 77.

The consuls of this year are displaced in the Paschal Chronicle and confused with those of the preceding and following years.

[Note: [Col. 0614C] I II] Years 20 and 21 of Sylvester.

In the case of Bishop Athanasius, they were ordered to assemble at Tyre and to dedicate a basilica at Jerusalem. Socrates, book I, chapter 20. It was dedicated on 17 September, according to the Paschal Chronicle. Constantine gladly received the Sarmatians’ slaves, who had been driven out by the masters against whom they had rebelled, and distributed more than 300,000 of them through Thrace, Scythia, Macedonia, and Italy. The Anonymous, Idatius, and Jerome’s Chronicle, in Petavius; from which also—

[Note: [Col. 0614D] III] A solar eclipse at Rome, at the eleventh hour, seventeen minutes after midnight on 17 July, is reported from Firmicus, book I, chapter 11; magnitude 10½.

[Note: [Col. 0614D] II III] Years 21 and 22 of Sylvester.

Under these consuls the letter of the Mareotic people is dated, volume II of the *General Councils*, p. 458: namely, under Julius Constantius, most illustrious patrician and brother of the most religious Constantine Augustus, and Rufinus Albinus, men of illustrious rank, on the tenth day of the month Thoth. Reland.

Under these consuls—Julius Constantius and Albinus, whom the copyist of Malalas incorrectly transcribed, writing “Illus and Albinus” instead of “Julius and Albinus,” p. 4—Constantine granted the dignity of second-ranking *comitatus* at Antioch in the Antiochene Era 383. He left Rufinus there as prefect, by whom a basilica was built.

Under these consuls Pope Saint Sylvester, on 31 December, completed the years of his pontificate in a holy death: twenty-one years and eleven months, counted in the catalogue of Liberius from the Era of Enthronement after his election on 31 January; and twenty-three years, ten months, and twenty days from his episcopal ordination, received when he was chosen as the deputy of Miltiades on Sunday, 10 February 312, as recorded in the painting of the basilica of Saint Paul. See our notes on Sylvester.

[Note: [Col. 0616C] III IV] Saint Mark occupied the see from 18 January and died on the Nones of October of this year, after eight months and twenty days. Since 18 January was a Sunday—the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter at Rome, as we established above in the series of the Roman Pontiffs and in the notes on Saint Peter—Mark is placed in the Roman see as Sylvester’s successor, having previously been his deputy. Hence the Liberian catalogue says that he occupied the see for eight months and twenty days [from 18 January to 6 October of this year], while in the paintings of Saint Paul’s Basilica he is said to have occupied it [as deputy, that is, as pontiff] for two years, eight months, and twenty-one days. See the notes on Saint Mark.

At the Synod of Constantinople, Marcellus of Ancyra was deposed and Saint Athanasius was ordered into exile. See the notes on Saint Mark.

[Note: [Col. 0618D] Olympiad 278 IV and 279 I]

JULIUS was ordained bishop under these consuls, on Sunday, 6 February [according to the Liberian catalogue]. He occupied the see for fifteen years, two months, and six days, until the consuls of the year 352, Constantius V and Constantius Gallus Caesar. See the notes below on Julius.

While preparing an expedition against the Persians, Constantine died.

Sapor, king of the Persians, had invaded Mesopotamia to ravage Nisibis. After besieging it for sixty-three days, he withdrew, having abandoned the attack. Paschal Chronicle.

Dalmatius Caesar was given the title of “Most Noble,” and Hannibalianus that of “King,” by Constantine, out of respect for their family relationship. Zosimus, book II, chapter 29. But they were killed shortly afterward by Constantius. A council was celebrated at Rome by Pope Julius, at which the acts of the Council of Nicaea were approved and the Arian heresy condemned. Petavius, from Baronius, section LXVII, and Isidore Mercator, from the *Tripartite History*. But see Pagius, section VIII under this year.

The Synod of Milan was held this year in the case of Photinus, in the presence of legates of the Holy See. See Pagius’s notes on Julius.

[Note: [Col. 0618B] I II] Years 1 and 2 of Julius.

[Col. 0618C] Athanasius was sent back to Alexandria by Constantius the Younger with letters and was received there with great honor. Petavius and Theodoret, book II, chapter 1; Athanasius, *Apology* II.

Constantius undertook an expedition against the Persians and was cured of an illness at Antioch by Saint Spyridon. Ibid., from the *Menologion*.

Sapor, king of the Persians, pressed Nisibis with a fierce siege for two months, but was repelled by Saint James, its bishop. Ibid., from Jerome’s Chronicle, Theodoret, and Julian.

In the first year of the reign of Constans, Lidorius was ordained the second bishop of Tours. He built the first church within the city of Tours. Saint Gregory of Tours, book X of the *History of the Franks*.

[Note: [Col. 0618D] II III] Years 2 and 3 of Julius.

Eusebius of Nicomedia and his supporters sent legates to Julius, Constantine, and Constans with a complaint against Athanasius. His legates refuted them and demanded a general council. Athanasius, *Apology* II [Col. 0620A] and *To the Solitaries*. Petavius. See the notes on Julius.

Pagius assigns the Roman synod concerning Photinus to this year. See the notes there.

[Note: [Col. 0620A] III IV] Years 3 and 4 of Julius.

Julius summoned a synod at Rome concerning Athanasius. Athanasius came to it and remained at Rome for one year and six months. Meanwhile he published the *Life of Antony*. Letter of Pope Julius in Athanasius, *Apology* II. Petavius.

Eusebius of Caesarea died, as Socrates indicates, book II, chapter 3. Ibid.

Alexander, bishop of Constantinople, died after occupying the see for twenty-three years. Paul, an orthodox bishop, succeeded him, but Constantius drove him into exile. Eusebius of Nicomedia was substituted in his place. Socrates, book II, chapter 4; Sozomen, book III, chapter 4; Athanasius, *To the Solitaries*. Eustathius of Antioch was deposed through calumny. Ibid.

[Col. 0620C] [Note: [Col. 0620C] Olympiad 279 IV and 280] Years 4 and 5 of Julius.

At Antioch a dedication was held for the Lord’s church, begun by Constantine the Great and completed by Constantius, who was present. At the council held there Athanasius was deprived of office, and Gregory the Cappadocian was forced into his place.

Pope Julius, after waiting in vain for the Eusebians at the Roman Synod, acquitted Athanasius, who set out for Alexandria. Socrates and Sozomen, and Athanasius, *On the Synods*. Petavius.

In his notes, p. 9, Pagius assigns the Roman Synod to the following year and the Synod of Sirmium to this year.

[Note: [Col. 0620D] I II] Years 5 and 6 of Julius.

Gregory the Cappadocian was brought into Alexandria by the prefect Philagrius, on the order of Constantius; a great massacre was carried out there. Athanasius secretly escaped and fled to Rome. Athanasius, *To the Orthodox*. Petavius.

Eusebius of Nicomedia, bishop of Constantinople, died. The Catholics restored Paul, who had formerly been expelled; the Arians substituted Macedonius. The commander Hermogenes expelled Paul on Constantius’s order. Paul fled to Rome with other Catholic bishops who had been expelled. Socrates, book II, chapter 10; Sozomen, book III, chapter 5.

Macedonius was elected by the Arians as bishop of Constantinople in place of the deceased Eusebius of Nicomedia, the same usurper. See the notes on Julius.

[Col. 0622B] [Note: [Col. 0622B] II III] Years 6 and 7 of Julius.

Saint Paul the First Hermit died at the age of 113. Jerome, in his *Life*.

A terrible persecution arose among the Persians against the Christians. Simon, bishop of Seleucia and Ctesiphon; Ustazanes, chief of the eunuchs and tutor of the king; and many others were killed. Baronius and Sozomen, and Saint Jerome in his *Chronicle*.

Constans moved his camp into Gaul against the Franks. After defeating them in a most serious battle, he compelled them, upon renewal of the treaty, to return to their own territory. Lydiatus.

[Note: [Col. 0622C] III IV] Years 7 and 8 of Julius.

Another council was held at Antioch by the Arians. At it a new form of faith was composed, longer than the others, and published under the title of the martyr Lucian. Sozomen, book III, chapter 5; Athanasius, *On the Synods*. The profession of the Eusebians was rejected at Rome. Baronius. The persecution among the Persians against the Christians raged particularly against bishops and clergy. Ibid.

Several acts of martyrs from this period are preserved in a sixth-century Syriac codex brought to the Vatican Library in 1717 and written in the year 563.

[Note: [Col. 0622D] Olympiad 280 IV and 281 I] Years 7 and 8 of Julius.

Constantius kept watch in Mesopotamia against Sapor, king of the Persians, and at Seleucia of Syria, situated on the Tigris, built a bridge at great expense. Lydiatus, from Theophanes. Pagius, in his letter to Hypatius, p. 254, postpones this to the following consuls, together with Jerome in his *Chronicle*.

Gallus and Julian, sons of Constantius, the brother of Constantine the Great, were made clerics this year. Petavius, from Gregory of Nazianzus, *Oration on Julian*.

[Note: [Col. 0624A] I II] Years 9 and 10 of Julius.

This year is described in the acts of the Council of Cologne as “after the consulship of Amantius and Albinus,” and in the Latin book of Buch.

Athanasius [*Apology* I], summoned by Constans to Milan concerning the convocation of the Council of Sardica, was informed of it. Petavius also reports a solar eclipse at Constantinople on 6 June, at the sixth hour, magnitude 8.

[Note: [Col. 0624B] II III] Years 10 and 11 of Julius.

The Synod of Sardica was held under these consuls, attended by 370 bishops, most of them Catholic. Athanasius was acquitted there. The Arian bishops withdrew and convened a conciliabulum at Philippopolis, where they decreed that the word “consubstantial” should be abolished. Petavius, from Saint Hilary, Socrates, and Sozomen. See the notes below on Julius.

[Col. 0624C] [Note: [Col. 0624C] III IV] Years 11 and 12 of Julius.

A nocturnal Persian war was fought near Singara. Of the nine very serious battles fought by Constantius against the Persians, none was more severe; in it he lost a certain victory through the soldiers’ stupidity. Nisibis was besieged, and Bezabde and Amida were captured. Jerome, in his *Chronicle*.

Maximus, the fortieth bishop of Jerusalem after Macarius, died. After him the Arians seized the church—namely Cyril, Eutychius, and others. Ibid., in Jerome’s *Chronicle*. Also, the First Council of Carthage under Gratus the bishop.

[Note: [Col. 0624D] Olympiad 281 IV and 282 I] Years 12 and 13 of Julius.

Constantius, compelled by his brother’s letters and threats, summoned Athanasius to him after Gregory had been killed by the Alexandrians. He received Athanasius, who came to Antioch, kindly. Indeed, he ordered all proceedings against him to be annulled and sent him back to Alexandria with honor. Petavius, from Theodoret, book II, chapter 12, and Socrates, book II, chapter 1.

[Col. 0626A] [Note: [Col. 0626A] I II] Years 13 and 14 of Julius.

Constantius stripped Vetranio of imperial power at Sirmium in Pannonia. As he was preparing to take up arms against the tyranny of Magnentius, he created Flavius Constantius Gallus, his cousin, Caesar, gave him his sister Constantina as wife, and entrusted him with the administration of the Eastern Empire, while he himself set out westward against Magnentius. Panvinius, from Victor, Eutropius, Socrates, Zosimus, and Saint Jerome’s *Chronicle*.

While Athanasius was traveling through Jerusalem, a synod was held there at Alexandria. Petavius, from Socrates and Sozomen.

Ursacius and Valens, professing repentance, presented petitions of repentance at Rome as suppliants to Pope Julius. See the notes below on Julius.

[Col. 0626C] [Note: [Col. 0626C] II III] Years 14 and 15 of Julius.

Constantius set out for Italy against Magnentius and sent Gallus Caesar eastward against the Persians. Lydiatus and Ammianus Marcellinus; Petavius, from Victor, Eutropius, Zosimus, and others.

A synod was held at Sirmium, at which Photinus was condemned, chiefly through the action of Basil of Ancyra, bishop. It is praised by Hilary and Vigilius. Petavius, in the same place.

The designation “pagans” is thought to have arisen about this time, when Constantius ordered all soldiers to be Christians and dismissed those who refused. Ibid.

Paul, bishop of Constantinople, was deposed by Constantius and driven into exile and killed; Macedonius was substituted for him, and from him persecution was launched against the Catholics. Ibid., from Theodoret, Socrates, and Sozomen.

[Note: [Col. 0626D] III IV] Years 15 and 16 of Julius, who died on 12 April after occupying the see for fifteen years, two months, and six days, counted from 6 February 337. See the notes on Julius.

[Col. 0628A] LIBERIUS was ordained bishop on the ninth day before the Kalends of June, according to the Liberian catalogue—that is, on 24 May, which was a Sunday. From that date to 24 September 366 there are fourteen years and four months, interrupted by the pontificate of Felix II. See the notes on Liberius.

Magnentius, defeated by Constantius in battle at Mursa in Pannonia, fled into Italy. Decentius Caesar was defeated in Gaul by Chnodomarius, king of the Alamanni. Gallus Caesar suppressed the rebellious Jews in the East. Aurelius Victor and Jerome.

[Note: [Col. 0628B] Olympiad 282 IV and 283 I] Years 1 and 2 of Pope Liberius.

Because of the massacre of several nobles at Antioch, Gallus was recalled to Italy. But he allowed Domitian, the count of the treasury, who had been sent to him and who addressed him in an overbearing manner, to be killed by the soldiers whom he had incited. Ammianus XIV.

Constantius convened an Arian synod at Arles, by which Athanasius was condemned and Paulinus of Trier was sent into exile. Sulpicius Severus II. Magnentius’s permission for nocturnal sacrifices throughout the cities was abolished by the Theodosian Code, book 16, title 10, and Constantius ordered that throughout Italy the temples of the Gentiles be closed everywhere and access to them and the use of their sacrifices be prevented, book 16, title 10, law 4.

The legation of Pope Liberius to Constantius concerning the convocation of a council, p. 17.

[Note: [Col. 0628C] I II] Years 2 and 3 of Liberius. Liberius sent legates to Constantius, who was at Arles.

Gallus Caesar was deceitfully drawn, on Constantius’s order, into Illyricum and killed on the island of Flanona. Constantina, Gallus’s wife, was likewise summoned and died through the violence of illness. Ammianus XIV; Socrates II, chapter 27; and Idatius.

Saint Augustine was born this year, on the Ides of November. See Petavius under this year.

Holstenius believes that the first author of the Paschal Chronicle carried his work this far and considers what follows to have been added by a continuator. See Charles du Fresne’s preface, section X, where he thinks that the continuator lived under Heraclius, around the twentieth year of his reign.

[Note: [Col. 0630A] II III] Years 3 and 4 of Pope Liberius.

Liberius, refusing to subscribe to the condemnation of Athanasius, was sent into exile on the Ides of August. See the notes, pp. 16 and 18. Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; Rhodanus, bishop; and others were likewise exiled and celebrated throughout the world for their steadfastness. Sulpicius Severus II and Jerome in his *Chronicle*. Donatus, from whom the Donatists derive their name, was expelled from Carthage. Some of his followers were called Montenses because at Rome they had first begun to maintain a church on the Mountain. Ibid.

[Note: [Col. 0630B] III IV] Years 4 and 5 of Liberius.

Constantius entered Rome on the third day before the Kalends of May, almost in triumph. There, when appealed to by the matrons, he promised that he would recall Liberius. Ammianus XVI; Theodoret II, chapter 17.

Felix was forced into the Roman see. See the notes.

George was forced into the Alexandrian see, and Athanasius was compelled to flee. Lucifer of Cagliari resisted splendidly in defense of the Catholic faith. Eusebius of Vercelli was harassed in exile for the same faith; worn out by their hardships, Dionysius of Milan and Paulinus of Trier died for it. See Petavius and the notes below on Liberius.

[Note: [Col. 0630C] Olympiad 283 IV and 284 I] Years 5 and 6 of Liberius.

On the fourth day before the Nones of August Liberius returned from his first exile. See the notes, p. 16. Compelled by the terror inspired by Constantius and by the fraud of the Arians, he subscribed to the condemnation of Athanasius and at the same time issued a profession of faith in which, for the sake of concord, the term τοῦ ὁμοουσίου—“consubstantial”—was suppressed, although it defined the Son as like the Father in all things. Having obtained this ἔκθεσις, or “exposition,” Ursacius and Valens published another formula of faith under Liberius’s name, full of treachery. Because of it great disturbance arose throughout the East and Syria. Petavius. See the notes, p. 17 and following, and Sulpicius Severus II. The privileges of the clergy of the Roman city’s churches were confirmed on the fourth day before the Kalends of November, law 13, Code, *On Bishops*.

[Note: [Col. 0632A] I] Years 6 and 7 of Liberius, and year 1 of Felix.

After seven months and nine days from his return to the city, Liberius was again compelled to go into exile and voluntarily withdrew from the pontificate. Felix, previously an intruder, was elected, after Liberius’s resignation, as the legitimate Roman pontiff by the votes of the clergy on 9 August. See the notes.

The Persian legates sent to Constantius reached Constantinople on the seventh day before the Kalends of March. Idatius. Three terrible earthquakes occurred throughout Asia, and Nicomedia was destroyed. One hundred and fifty cities were afflicted. Constantius ravaged the Quadi and Sarmatians and acquired the name “Sarmaticus.”

The Synod of Ancyra was held by Basil and other bishops. The convocation of a general synod was also discussed. See Petavius under this year. The third Synod of Sirmium according to Pagius. See the notes.

Saint Antony the monk died at the age of 105. Jerome, in his *Chronicle*.

[Note: [Col. 0632C] II III] Years 1 and 2 of Felix II, and year 7 of Liberius.

Felix was either secretly killed on Constantius’s order on 11 November, or resigned the pontificate; the see then remained vacant until 21 December, on which day Liberius, elected again by the clergy, resumed the pontificate. See the notes.

Macedonius, deposed as bishop of Constantinople, founded a new heresy. See the notes on Liberius and Felix II.

[Col. 0632D] Two synods were held on Constantius’s order. The first was at Seleucia on 27 September, where the semi-Arians resisted Acacius when he produced a new ἔκθεσις, or “exposition,” plainly contrary to the Nicene faith. The second was at Ariminum. It had a good beginning but an unfortunate end, with the prefect Taurus wearing down the bishops so that they would subscribe to the deceitful profession of faith offered by Ursacius and Valens. See the notes.

The Persians began a war against the Romans [Col. 0634A] and captured Amida.

[Note: [Col. 0634A] III and IV] Years 7 and 8 of Liberius.

Valens, traveling through the cities on Constantius’s order, compelled people to subscribe to the faith of the conciliabulum of Ariminum and expelled those who refused. Among them Liberius was compelled to go into exile again. Sozomen, book IV, chapter 18. Nevertheless, when Saint Hilary of Poitiers had presented a book to Constantius, he returned to Gaul and was received by the Catholics [Col. 0634B] with rejoicing, as though he were returning in triumph.

The Paschal Chronicle records under this year the deposition of Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, in whose place the utterly depraved heretic Eudoxius was substituted.

There were three factions at Antioch: the Meletians, Eustathians, and Arians. See Petavius and the notes below.

The Persians invaded Mesopotamia and captured Singara.

[Note: [Col. 0634B] Olympiad 284 IV and 285 I] Years 8 and 9 of Liberius.

After the death of Constantius, Julian entered Constantinople on the third day before the Ides of December. He summoned the Christian bishops into the palace and ordered each to adhere to his own sect, with the intention that they should not be united among themselves. Ammianus, book XXII. Liberius was therefore able to return freely to Rome. Julian also recalled the exiled bishops. Ammianus, in the same place, and Socrates, book III, chapter 4.

Julian, having renounced all the sacraments of the Christian religion, was consecrated as pontifex maximus by profane rites. Baronius, from Prudentius. But see Pagius under this year, section VI.

[Note: [Col. 0634D] I II] Years 9 and 10 of Liberius.

Various embassies arrived from every direction to Julian. He set out against the Persians, visited Nicomedia, Pessinus, and the temple of the Mother of the Gods on the journey, and then wintered at Antioch. There he investigated the burning of the temple and statue of Apollo of Daphne, suspecting that Christians had set them on fire. Ammianus, book 22.

George, the pseudo-bishop of Alexandria, was killed by the aroused populace. The legitimate bishop Athanasius returned, but when the Arians pressed the matter, he was again expelled on Julian’s order. Socrates III; Theodoret III; Sozomen V.

The schism of the Luciferians arose at Antioch. The Donatists obtained from Julian the relaxation of their exile and the restoration of their basilicas, and threw everything into disorder. Optatus II.

[Note: [Col. 0636A] II III] Years 10 and 11 of Liberius.

Julian unsuccessfully attempted to restore the temple of Jerusalem through the Jews. Setting out against the Persians, he besieged Ctesiphon. While withdrawing from it, he died from a mortal wound [it is uncertain whether it was inflicted from heaven or by an unknown man], blasphemous and apostate. Theodoret III, chapter 2. He had reigned after Constantius’s death for approximately one year and seven months.

JOVIAN was chosen emperor by the soldiers, who immediately proclaimed themselves Christians, since he had said that he was unwilling to rule with Gentiles.

At the Council of Antioch the Acacians joined themselves to Meletius and embraced the Nicene faith, according to Socrates, book III, chapter 25. Saint Jerome writes that he accepted a middle position, the *Homoiousion*, between the *Homoousion* and the *Anomoion*.

[Col. 0636D] [Note: [Col. 0636D] III IV] Years 11 and 12 of Liberius.

The Macedonians obtained from Valens authority to convene a council.

Valens went to Antioch, expelled Meletius, and compelled the Catholics to communicate with Euzoius. Socrates IV.

The Macedonians and semi-Arians assembled at Lampsacus against the dreadful blasphemies issued at the Constantinopolitan conciliabulum by Acacius and other Anomoeans. They condemned the profession of Ariminum and approved the Antiochene formula. They rejected the divinity of the Holy Spirit. They sent legates to Liberius so that, with his authority, those bishops who had been expelled might be restored to their sees, after accepting the Catholic profession. Pagius maintains that these events belong to this year, although others assign them to the following year. See Pagius under the year 363, section IV.

[Col. 0638B] [Note: [Col. 0638B] Olympiad 285 IV and 286 I] Years 12 and 13 of Liberius.

Together with Baronius, Petavius assigns to this year the events concerning the Macedonians that Pagius, in the immediately preceding year, decides should be placed there.

Procopius, a Cilician by birth and a kinsman of Julian, seized the tyranny at Constantinople on the fourth day before the Kalends of October. Idatius; Ammianus 26; Zosimus 4.

The earth was shaken by an earthquake. Over a large part of the Roman world the sea rose beyond the shore, and many cities in Sicily [Col. 0638C] were overwhelmed. Jerome, *Chronicle*.

[Note: [Col. 0638C] I II] Years 13 and 14 of Liberius and of DAMASUS.

Liberius died under these consuls, on 24 September, as appears from the little book of petitions of Faustinus and Marcellinus. See the notes, p. 15, and the Prologue to volume 2, folio CVI. DAMASUS, elected as his successor, was ordained bishop on the Kalends of October. See the notes, p. 33. The factions introduced a schism by intruding Ursicinus. A massacre took place in the Basilica Siciniana. See the notes.

Procopius the tyrant was overthrown by Valens; after him, Marcellus. Ammianus, book 27; Zosimus 4 and 8. Valens, baptized by Eudoxius, the Arian bishop, persecuted our people. Jerome, *Chronicle*.

[Note: [Col. 0638D] II III] Years 1 and 2 of Damasus.

A synod was held at Rome against Ursicinus. See the notes on Damasus below.

Under these consuls an enormous hailstorm fell at Constantinople, in the form of stones, on the fourth day before the Nones of July. Gratian Augustus was raised by his father Valentinian at Amiens in Gaul, upon the tribunal, on the ninth day before the Kalends of September. Idatius. The British war against the Picts and Saxons was also successfully completed by Theodosius, and he named the province Valeria after the emperor. From Ammianus 27, Lydiatus, and Mediobardus.

Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, died this year. Jerome, *Chronicle*. But Petavius thinks it should be postponed by two years.

The emperor issued a rescript that, on account of the day of Easter, prisoners should be released, except those guilty of treason, adultery, murder, sorcery, and so forth. Code, chapter 3, *On Indulgence*.

[Note: [Col. 0640B] III IV] Years 2 and 3 of Damasus.

The followers of Ursicinus were forbidden access to or residence in the city of Rome, although they were permitted to live elsewhere. See the notes.

Valens, invading the lands of the Goths, compelled them to negotiate peace.

The king of the Persians, after subduing Armenia, prepared to wage war against the Romans. [Col. 0640C] Ammianus 27.

[Note: [Col. 0640C] IV of Olympiad 286 and Olympiad 287 I] Years 3 and 4 of Damasus.

Damasus convened a synod of ninety bishops against Auxentius. Auxentius was condemned there, and the formula of the faith of Ariminum was rejected. The schism of Ursicinus and its advocate were condemned again. See the notes [Col. 0640D] on Damasus.

Valens drove Athanaric, king of the Goths, into flight and soon afterward granted him peace. Ammianus 27. Agon, after seventeen years, was restored by Valens. Idatius and Jerome, *Chronicle*.

Cedrenus says that Valens permitted sacrifices to the Gentiles. Petavius.

Saint Basil, after the death of Eusebius, became bishop of Caesarea on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of July. Gregory of Nazianzus, letter XX and following, and the encomium of Basil in the same place.

[Note: [Col. 0640D] I II] Years 4 and 5 of Damasus.

When Valens had gone to Antioch and was staying at Nicomedia, Eudoxius, bishop of Constantinople, died after occupying the see for nineteen years. The Catholics breathed again, and Eustathius of Antioch ordained Evagrius in his place. The Arians, however, ordained Demophilus. Valens exiled both Evagrius and Eustathius. From then on the persecution began to grow more severe. Eighty men of the ecclesiastical order were put on a ship and burned in the middle of the sea. [Col. 0642B] Socrates, book IV, chapters 13 and 14. Eusebius of Vercelli and Lucifer of Cagliari died. Jerome, *Chronicle*.

Many orthodox bishops were expelled. Athanasius himself was harassed, but when the people rose in tumult he was permitted to remain in his see. Eusebius of Samosata, exiled to Thrace, traveled through the churches of Syria, Phoenicia, and Palestine in military dress. Petavius, from Theodoret, book IV, chapter 13.

[Note: [Col. 0642B] II III] Years 5 and 6 of Damasus.

Basil, created bishop this year, and other Eastern bishops wrote to the Western bishops and implored their aid. Basil himself was supported by Athanasius, as appears from his letter. Gregory was ordained bishop of Sasima, according to the poem on his life. Athanasius held a synod and wrote to Damasus. See the notes, p. 40. According to Petavius and Socrates IV, chapter 19, Athanasius died; Peter succeeded him. Valens, however, ordered Lucius to be ordained there. Thus Peter was bound by Palladius, the prefect; the clergy were exiled; and then extraordinary violence was inflicted upon the Catholics and monks, as appears from the same Socrates, chapter 20. These events, however, belong to the following year.

The Mauritanian war was successfully completed by Theodosius, the master of the soldiers. Ibid., from Ammianus 29.

[Note: [Col. 0642D] III IV] Years 6 and 7 of Damasus.

The Second Roman Synod was held under Damasus against Auxentius. See the notes, pp. 40 and 47.

Noris proves that the death of Saint Athanasius and the persecution against the Catholics should be assigned to this year, *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 2, p. 8; Pagius placed them under the following year. In the eighth year of Valens and the third of Valentinian, Saint Martin was ordained the third bishop of Tours. Gregory of Tours, book X, where he adds that Martin occupied the see for twenty-six years, four months, and twenty-seven days, and ceased to be bishop on the twentieth day. The same author dates Saint Martin’s ordination to the fourth day before the Nones of July, *History of the Franks*, book I, chapter 46, and book II, chapter 14.

Mauvia, queen of the Saracens, having embraced the Christian faith, made peace with the Romans on the condition that she be granted Moses the anchorite as her bishop. Brought to Alexandria, after repudiating Lucius the Arian, Moses wished to be ordained by a Catholic bishop. Socrates IV, chapter 29, and Theodoret IV, chapter 21. The death of Saint Hilarion the anchorite, from Saint Jerome.

[Note: [Col. 0644B] Olympiad 287 IV and 288 I] Years 7 and 8 of Damasus.

At Rome, in a synod convened by Damasus, Apollinaris and his disciple Vitalis were condemned. Vitalis had traveled from Antioch to Rome to Damasus and was sent back to Paulinus of Antioch with a written statement to which he was to subscribe. When he had done this deceitfully and the fraud was discovered, Damasus proscribed him. Sozomen VI, chapter 25; Gregory of Nazianzus, letter XI, to Cledonius. See the notes below.

At this synod several anathemas were issued against various heresies. Petavius. See the notes below.

Para, king of Armenia, was captured by deceit and unjustly detained by Valens; finally, on Valens’s order, he was killed at a banquet. Ammianus 28 and 29.

[Col. 0644D] [Note: [Col. 0644D] I II] Years 8 and 9 of Damasus.

After Auxentius died, Ambrose was ordained bishop of Milan in his place, on the eighth day after he had been baptized, on the seventh day before the Ides of December. Jerome’s Chronicle; Paulinus in his Life. St. Epiphanius, asked by the magistrate and clergy of the Soudians in Pamphylia, writes the *Anchoratus*. Petavius.

Valens was concerned about the Gothic war. For the Goths, driven out by the Huns—a barbarian people originating from the remotest regions of Sarmatia—asked the emperor for new settlements within the borders of Thrace [Col. 0646A] (Ammianus, book 31), and were permitted to cross the Ister and establish settlements near Thrace, to the ruin of the Roman Empire.

[Note: [Col. 0646A] II and III] Damasus, years 9 and 10.

The third Roman Synod under Damasus. [Col. 0646B] See the notes on Damasus.

St. Simplicianus, a presbyter of the Roman Church, a man of recognized holiness and learning, was given by Pope Damasus as instructor to Blessed Ambrose, who had shortly before been elected bishop. St. Augustine, *Confessions* 8.2. See the notes. He later succeeded Ambrose in the episcopate.

St. Martin, according to Petavius’s chronology and Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks* 2.14, was ordained bishop of Tours in this year.

Valens acted more harshly toward the Christians and, among other measures, enacted by law [Col. 0646C] that monks should serve as soldiers. He was soon appeased by Themistius. Jerome’s Chronicle and Sozomen, book 6, chapter 25.

St. Epiphanius began to write the *Panarion* in this year, according to Petavius.

Valens was assailed by many wars. The Isaurians devastated the towns of Lycia and Pamphylia; to confront them, he settled matters with the Persians. Zonaras, book 4, chapter 20.

[Note: [Col. 0646C] III and IV] Damasus, years 10 and 11.

[Col. 0646D] Gratian, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, prohibited a gathering of heretics at Trier and confiscated their places for the treasury, *Codex Theodosianus*, book 4, title “On Heretics.” In book 23, title “On Bishops,” he ordered that cases concerning religion arising among clergy should be settled by the bishops together with the diocesan presbytery. Criminal matters, however, were to be heard by the city judge.

Theodosius the Elder, father of that Theodosius who later ruled, was killed in Africa by order of Valens [as appears], after receiving baptism. His son escaped the danger. [Col. 0648A] Jerome’s Chronicle; Orosius 7.23; Ambrose, *Funeral Oration for Theodosius*.

[Note: [Col. 0648A] Olympiad 288, IV and 289, I] Damasus, years 11 and 12.

The Goths rebelled against the Romans. Valens opposed them with an army, which won a grievous victory over them, not without much bloodshed. Idacius and Ammianus 31.

Valens departed from Antioch and, moved by belated repentance, ceased the persecution. Jerome’s Chronicle.

[Col. 0648B] [Note: [Col. 0648B] I and II] Damasus, years 12 and 13.

The fourth Roman Synod under Damasus. See the notes on Damasus.

Valens, returning to the East, engaged the Goths in Thrace on the fifth day before the Ides of August and died. Idacius. See Noris, *History of Pelagianism* 2.4.

THEODOSIUS the Great, as he was later called, and who was raised to the imperial office in the following year, entered Constantinople on the eighth day before the Kalends of December, having been made Augustus at Sirmium by Gratian, his wife’s brother, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February. Throughout the entire year the Goths plundered the dioceses of Thrace, Moesia, and Scythia, even to the gates of the imperial city. Idacius. Here Jerome’s Chronicle ends.

[Note: [Col. 0648C] Olympiad 289, II and III] Damasus, years 13 and 14.

Theodosius was proclaimed Augustus by Gratian on 19 January and, fighting successfully against the Goths, drove them out of Thrace. Zonaras; Idacius; Prosper. Theodoret, however, records these deeds as having been performed by him before he obtained the imperial office. See Petavius on this year.

The Lombards, having left the island of Scandia, first defeated the Vandals. Prosper.

St. Basil died on the Kalends of January.

Maximus the Cynic was intruded as bishop of Constantinople. See the notes on Damasus.

[Note: [Col. 0648D] Olympiad 289, III and IV] Damasus, years 14 and 15.

Theodosius, seized by illness at Thessalonica, was baptized by Acholius, the Catholic bishop. Socrates, book 5, [Col. 0650A] chapter 6. He then issued the law numbered 11, *Codex Theodosianus*, “On the Catholic Faith,” on the third day before the Kalends of March at Thessalonica, decreeing that, after the condemnation of the heresies, only the Catholic faith should prevail—namely, the faith received from Peter and held by the Roman Church and Damasus, and by Peter of Alexandria. See Pagius the Elder on this year, no. 3 and following.

After Peter, bishop of Alexandria, died, his brother Timothy succeeded him. Nicephorus, *Chronicle*.

Around this time Illyricum was divided into Eastern and Western Illyricum. Therefore Theodosius, to whom dominion over the Eastern Empire had fallen, also held Eastern Illyricum. See Pagius the Elder on this year.

Theodosius entered Constantinople on the eighth day before the Kalends of December and deprived the Arians of the churches they had held for forty years. Demophilus withdrew from the city. Gregory of Nazianzus was introduced into the church on the sixth day before the Kalends of December. Petavius.

[Col. 0650C] [Note: [Col. 0650C] Olympiad 289, IV and 290, I] Damasus, years 15 and 16.

The Constantinopolitan Synod was held on the occasion of the ordination of Maximus and the heresy of Macedonius. The agreement of Damasus, who had announced at Rome that an ecumenical synod should be held, later made this synod ecumenical. See the notes below. All the decrees of that synod concerning faith were confirmed by Damasus; but among those relating to discipline, the jurisdiction of the See of Constantinople was not confirmed to the same extent. See the notes on Damasus.

[Col. 0650D] On the third day before the Kalends of August, Theodosius wrote to Auxonius, proconsul of Asia, that the churches should be handed over to Catholic bishops. He brought into the Basilica of St. Paul at Constantinople the relics of those who had suffered under the Arians. Against the Arians, Manichaeans, and others, he enacted the measures contained in book 16, title 3 of the *Codex Theodosianus*. Petavius.

[Col. 0652A] [Note: [Col. 0652A] I and II] Damasus, years 16 and 17. In this year Prosper records the arrival of Athanaric, king of the Goths, at Constantinople and his death in January, which others assign to the preceding year. Lydiat. The entire Gothic nation surrendered to the Roman Empire in October. Marcellinus; the *Chronicle*; and Idacius.

[Col. 0652B] Jerome, according to Petavius, remained at Rome with Damasus and wrote against Helvidius, Jovinianus, and the Luciferians. See the notes on Damasus.

Paulinus of Antioch, Epiphanius of Cyprus, Acholius of Thessalonica, and Ambrose also came to Rome.

[Note: [Col. 0652B] II and III] Damasus, years 17 and 18.

Ambassadors were sent by Maximus to Theodosius, and Ambrose was dispatched by Valentinian as ambassador to Maximus. [Col. 0652C] Theodosius arranged for a synod to be held at Constantinople in June, so that the decrees against the heretics might be carried out. Theodosius added new laws against the disobedient, *Codex Theodosianus*, “On Heretics,” book 9 and elsewhere. See Pagius the Elder on this year.

ARCADIUS was proclaimed Augustus by his father Theodosius on 19 January. Pope Damasus sent Arsenius to educate him. Petavius, from the Life of Arsenius.

[Col. 0652D] [Note: [Col. 0652D] III and IV] Damasus, years 18 and 19.

After Damasus had occupied the See for eighteen years, two months, and ten days, he died on 11 December. See the notes on Damasus.

Persian ambassadors came to Constantinople asking Theodosius for peace. A son, Honorius, was born to him on the fifth day before the Ides of September. Idacius; Marcellinus. Artaxerxes, king of the Persians, died after reigning four years. His son Shapur succeeded him and sent ambassadors to Theodosius. Agathias.

[Col. 0654A] [Note: [Col. 0654A] Olympiad 290, IV and Olympiad 291, I] Year 1 of Pope Siricius, beginning with the Kalends of January.

After the Roman See had been vacant for twenty-one days following the death of Damasus, SIRICIUS was elected as his successor on the Kalends of January. See the notes on Siricius.

In the letter sent to Himerius of Tarragona on the third day before the Ides of February, during these consulships—an exemplar of which is preserved in an ancient manuscript, codex 800, in the monastery of Santa Croce in Rome—the matters that may be read in the notes are contained.

St. Jerome sailed to Syria and entered Jerusalem in midwinter. His Letter 99 and *Apology against Rufinus*. St. Augustine was converted to the Catholic faith. *Confessions* 8.1 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0654B] I and II] Siricius, year 2.

Siricius held a council at Rome of eighty bishops concerning the discipline of the African Church. See the notes. A synod was also held at Trier [Col. 0654C] concerning bishops who accused one another before the emperor. Severus, in the Life of Blessed Martin, who attended the council.

St. Jerome went to hear Didymus and visited the monasteries of Egypt. *Apology against Rufinus*. St. Paula was also making a pilgrimage there. Jerome, Letter 27. St. John Chrysostom was ordained presbyter. St. Cyril of Jerusalem died, and John, contaminated by communion with heretics, succeeded him. St. Jerome, Letter 61.

Theodosius, triumphing over the Greuthungi with his son Arcadius, entered Constantinople on the fourth day before the Ides of October. Idacius; Marcellinus; Zosimus 4.

[Note: [Col. 0654D] II and III] Siricius, year 3.

Arcadius celebrated the quinquennalia with his father Theodosius by public entertainments and games. Idacius; Marcellinus.

Justina harassed St. Ambrose with increasing severity and arranged for him to be driven into exile, but he was retained by the resistance of the people. Ambrose discovered the relics of Saints Gervasius and Protasius, which became renowned for miracles. He was also sent as ambassador to Maximus, who, when he came to him, permitted him to communicate neither with himself nor with the Ithacians. Letters 33 and 85.

When Maximus invaded Italy, Valentinian fled to Theodosius, who undertook an expedition into Italy. Zosimus 4.

[Note: [Col. 0656A] III and IV] Siricius, year 4.

Theodosius, commending himself to the prayers of the saints (Augustine, *City of God* 5.26; Rufinus 2.32), marched into Italy against Maximus and defeated him. Maximus was killed at Aquileia on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August. A few days later, his son Victor was also killed by Arbogastes in Gaul. Theodosius restored to Valentinian the whole empire that he had recovered from Maximus. Idacius; Marcellinus; Zosimus.

[Note: [Col. 0656B] Olympiad 291, IV and 292, I] Siricius, year 5.

At the Council of Capua, Siricius entrusted the case of Flavianus and Evagrius to Theophilus. The schism at Antioch was ended.

The temple of Serapis at Alexandria was destroyed by order of Theodosius. Marcellinus; Socrates 5.16. [Col. 0656C] At Rome also the statues of the idols were broken and the ceremonies abolished. From Prosper, *On the Promises* 3.38; St. Augustine, *City of God* 5.26. Pagius, however, from the law in the *Codex Theodosianus* “On the Pagans,” proves that the Serapeum was destroyed in the year 391.

St. Gregory of Nazianzus died. From St. Jerome, *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*.

St. Monica, mother of St. Augustine, died. Augustine returned to Africa. *Confessions* 9.8.

After the death of their dukes, the Lombards first created a king for themselves, Agilmund, son of Aio, who reigned thirty-three years. Prosper, *Chronicle*.

[Note: [Col. 0656D] I and II] Siricius, year 6.

Pope Siricius condemned Jovinianus the heretic. See the notes on Siricius.

At the Council of Milan, the Fathers followed the judgment of Siricius. See the notes.

The head of St. John the Baptist was found and carried to Constantinople.

The Second Council of Carthage, presided over by Genethlius. Petavius. See the notes on Siricius.

[Col. 0658A] The massacre of the Thessalonians was carried out by order of Theodosius. Because of it, the emperor was excluded from the church doors by Ambrose and performed penance. Rufinus 2.18; Sozomen 7.24; Theodoret 5.17; Paulinus, *Life of St. Ambrose*.

[Note: [Col. 0658A] II and III] Siricius, year 7.

During these consulships Theodosius, having completed his Italian campaign, departed and returned to Constantinople. Arbogastes, however, began revolutionary activity in the West against Valentinian; supported by Arbogastes, Eugenius usurped the empire. Prosper and Zosimus 4.

During these consulships, Law 11 of the *Codex Theodosianus*, book 16, title 10, “On the Prohibition of the Use of Sacrifices,” was issued to Evagrius, prefect of the praetorium, and to the count of Egypt. Pagius with Gothofredus.

[Col. 0658C] [Note: [Col. 0658C] III and IV] Siricius, year 8.

Valentinian the Younger was killed by Count Arbogastes, while Eugenius usurped the empire. Zosimus 4.54. Theodosius prepared an expedition against him.

A disagreement arose between John, bishop of Jerusalem and an Origenist, and Epiphanius. St. Jerome, Letter 60.

In this year St. Jerome completed his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, as appears from his preface addressed to Dexter the Praetorian Prefect.

During these consulships, the use of pagan sacrifices was everywhere abolished by Law 12 of the *Codex Theodosianus*, “On the Pagans.”

[Note: [Col. 0658D] Olympiad 292, IV and 293, I] Siricius, year 9.

Honorius was proclaimed Augustus by his father Theodosius on the fourth day before the Ides of January, as Pagius demonstrates with Petavius on this year, no. 11, and shows that Socrates was mistaken: there was a solar eclipse on 20 November of this year, but not on the day when Honorius was proclaimed Augustus.

A solar eclipse, lasting nearly eleven digits, occurred at Constantinople on 20 November. Prosper and Marcellinus. See Petavius.

The Theodosian Forum was dedicated. [Col. 0660A] Alexandrian Chronicle.

A council was held at Hippo concerning discipline; Schelestrius learnedly explains its canons, *On the African Church*, dissertation 3, chapter 6. Pagius.

Theodosius celebrated the fifteen-year anniversary of his reign. Same source.

Aurelianus was prefect of the city of Constantinople. Alm., from both manuscripts.

[Col. 0660B] [Note: [Col. 0660B] I and II] Siricius, year 10.

Theodosius, taking his son Honorius with him, fought against Arbogastes and Eugenius. On the first day, which appears to have been 5 September, victory belonged to the tyrant. But at night, having fallen prostrate in prayer and having been informed by the apostles, he defeated the tyrant, God fighting on his behalf. Eugenius was captured and killed on 6 September. Arbogastes took his own life. Petavius, from Prosper and Marcellinus.

The Arcadian Baths were so called from their founder. Same source.

[Col. 0660C] The Donatists held the Council of Bagai in Numidia, consisting of 310 bishops. After Parmenianus, bishop of the Donatists at Carthage, died and Primianus succeeded him, Maximianus had been ordained by others; he was condemned. Same source; Augustine, Letters 255 and 265.

Another synod was held at Constantinople concerning a similar schism in the election of the bishop of Bostra. Same source, from Balsamon.

[Note: [Col. 0660C] II and III] Siricius, year 11.

Theodosius, having completed the sixteenth year of his reign, died at Milan, [Col. 0660D] leaving his two sons as emperors, to govern the two empires jointly, with only their residences divided: Arcadius in the East and Honorius in the West. Rufinus, wishing to give his daughter to Arcadius—unless Eutropius had forestalled him by arranging another marriage—aroused the indignation of Stilicho. Stilicho, guardian of the Western Empire (indeed, of both empires and of the princes, appointed by their father), exposed Rufinus’s treachery and punished his disloyalty with death. For, with a fleet equipped against him and against the Goth Alaric, whom Rufinus had summoned into Greece, he drove Alaric away and had Rufinus killed by Gainas and the soldiers. Rufinus’s property was assigned to Eutropius, who was attached to Stilicho.

St. Augustine was ordained bishop of Hippo while Valerius was still bishop. Augustine, Letter 5; Letter 110; Prosper in his *Chronicle*; Possidius, chapter 8. [Col. 0662B] Others defer his ordination until the following year; see Pagius, no. 10 on this year.

[Note: [Col. 0662B] III and IV] Siricius, year 12.

Count Gildo, appointed by Theodosius commander of both armies in Africa, this year attempted a revolution and seized the tyranny around autumn; he had been appointed nine years earlier (from Claudian, *On the Gildonic War*). He afflicted the city of Rome with famine, according to other authorities cited by Pagius on this year.

Eutropius ravaged the Eastern Empire with avarice and cruelty. Timasius, formerly commander of the army, was banished to the Oasis, and Abundantius, a former consul, to Sidon. Petavius, from Zosimus 5.

The relics of St. John the Baptist were transferred to Alexandria on the second day of Payni, which Theophanes calls the sixth day before the Kalends, in the year 5890 from the Incarnation, 390. Same source.

The Paschal Chronicle counts 335 years from the martyrdom of the holy apostles Peter and Paul to these consulships; we, however, begin the count with 331.

[Note: [Col. 0662C] Olympiad 293, IV and 294, I] Siricius, years 13 and 14.

Eutropius, in order to recall Stilicho from his expedition to the East, arranged for Stilicho himself to be denounced by the emperor and Senate as an enemy. He won over Count Gildo, a pagan, whom Theodosius had placed in charge of Africa. Thus Africa, defecting from Honorius, was joined to Arcadius. Petavius, from Zosimus 5 and Marcellinus.

St. Ambrose died shortly before dawn on Holy Saturday, on the day before the Nones of April. Paulinus.

Nectarius died in this year, around 27 September, and by common consent John Chrysostom was elected bishop of Constantinople, with Arcadius sending ambassadors to him at Antioch. Same source.

The Third Council of Carthage, presided over by Aurelius, to which Augustine subscribed.

Flacilla, daughter of Arcadius, was born on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July. Alexandrian Chronicle.

Rufinus of Aquileia, having returned from Rome, attempted to disseminate the errors of Origen in the city. See Noris, *History of Pelagianism* [Col. 0664B] chapter 2, p. 9, and Pagius.

[Note: [Col. 0664B] I and II] Siricius, years 14 and 15.

Gildo, son of a certain Moorish ruler, who had resisted his brother Firmus, the tyrant, was made Count of Africa and commander of both armies by Theodosius. When he prohibited the transport of grain to Rome, war was waged against him. Mascezel, his brother, who had fled to Italy, was sent against him by Stilicho and killed 70,000 of his army. Gildo strangled himself. When Mascezel returned to Italy, Stilicho threw him from a bridge into the river. Petavius, from Jordanes.

Honorius, the emperor, married Maria, daughter of Stilicho and Serena, the daughter of Theodosius’s brother.

[Note: [Col. 0664C] II and III] Siricius, years 15 and 16. Siricius died on 19 September. ANASTASIUS was elected as his successor and ordained bishop on Sunday, 9 October. See the notes on Siricius.

The pagans had claimed that the Christian religion would be destroyed before this year, since they asserted that only 365 years would remain after the martyrdom of Blessed Peter. St. Augustine shows that those 365 years had already been completed and adds that, in this very year, the pagan temples at Carthage had been overthrown. See the notes on Siricius and Pagius on this year.

The Fourth Council of Carthage was held on the sixth day before the Ides of November, under the presidency of Aurelius.

[Col. 0666A] [Note: [Col. 0666A] III and IV] Anastasius, years 1 and 2.

Gainas, who had rebelled in the preceding year and had obtained permission to have Eutropius killed, secured from Arcadius the delivery to him of Saturninus, the former consul, and Eutropius, the consul. He could not, however, obtain the churches of Constantinople for the Arians, because St. John Chrysostom resisted.

During these consulships, Eudoxia was proclaimed Augusta, [Col. 0666B] and Arcadia was born on the third day before the Nones of April. The church of the Goths burned on the fourth day before the Ides of July. Paschal Chronicle.

Alaric, king of the Goths, descended into Italy through the Julian Alps. Noris, *History of Pelagianism* 2, p. 12.

[Note: [Col. 0666B] Olympiad 294, IV and 295, I] Pope Anastasius, year 2, and, from 9 October, year 3. He died on 3 November; the See was vacant for twenty days.

INNOCENT was elected as his successor and ordained on Sunday, 24 November. See the notes on Anastasius.

Two African councils were held in this year: one on the fourth day before the Kalends of July, during the consulship of Stilicho, and the other on the Ides of September at Carthage, during the consulship of Vincentius and Fravitta, according to Binius’s edition, identified as the second and third councils under Anastasius. In the latter, letters of Pope Anastasius were read, and an embassy was appointed to him. See the *Code of the Canons of the African Church* from Justellus’s library, the oldest copy of which we saw preserved in the Bodleian Library.

Gainas’s head, fixed upon a spear, was brought to Constantinople on the Nones of January. Marcellinus and the Paschal Chronicle.

[Col. 0666D] Theodosius, son of Arcadius, was born on the fourth day before the Ides of April. Same source.

[Note: [Col. 0666D] I and II] Anastasius, years 1 and 2.

The First Council of Milevis was held in Africa. There the dispute over the primacy of Numidia between Xantippus and Victorinus was discussed and adjudicated in favor of Xantippus. See Noris, *History of Pelagianism* 2.8, and Pagius on this year, no. 21 and following.

St. Jerome wrote his second *Apology against Rufinus*. [Col. 0668A] Pagius on this year, no. 12, from Jerome himself.

Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, was accused at Constantinople by the Origenist monks whom he had expelled. (Baronius, no. 3, from Palladius.) Consequently, serious disputes arose among Saints John Chrysostom, Theophilus, and Epiphanius, who died either around the end of this year or at the beginning of the next. See Pagius [Col. 0668B] no. 7, with John of Jerusalem also involved. See Noris, *History of Pelagianism* 2, p. 19.

[Note: [Col. 0668B] II and II] Innocent, years 2 and 3.

The assembly at the Oak, instigated by Eudoxia against John Chrysostom, expelled the holy bishop; but shortly afterward, when a popular tumult arose, Chrysostom was recalled by Arcadius. See the notes on Innocent. A synod was also held at Carthage in this year, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, concerning the Donatists; St. Augustine mentions it in *Against Cresconius* 3.45.

Marina, daughter of Arcadius, was born on the third day before the Ides of February. Marcellinus and the Alexandrian Chronicle.

[Note: [Col. 0668C] III and IV] Innocent, years 3 and 4. Letter of Innocent to Victricius. See the notes on Innocent.

[Col. 0668D] Around the Easter festivals, St. John Chrysostom was deposed from his See by the sentence of Theophilus and appealed to Pope Innocent at Rome; Theophilus also sent an embassy to him. Three months after Chrysostom’s expulsion, Augusta Eudoxia died. Arsacius was intruded into the See of Constantinople. A group of clergy fled to Rome. Petavius, from George’s Life of Chrysostom. Innocent rescinded the sentence of Theophilus. See the notes on Innocent. Innocent wrote to Arcadius [Col. 0670A] that a synod should be held in this matter at Thessalonica, because of the danger of schism. See Pagius the Younger, no. 7.

A council was also held at Carthage concerning the restraint of the Donatists. Felix the Manichaean, convicted by Augustine, condemned his heresy. Augustine, *Disputation against Felix*.

[Note: [Col. 0670A] Olympiad 295, IV and 296, I] Innocent, years 4 and 5. The second decretal of Innocent to Exuperius. See the notes.

The bishops of Italy assembled at Rome and asked the emperor Honorius to write to Arcadius and order that a synod be held at Thessalonica. After receiving letters from him, together with letters from Pope Innocent, the ambassadors departed for Constantinople. Petavius, from Palladius’s *Dialogue*.

Honorius issued various sanctions against the Donatists, under the pressure of which many returned to the Church. *Codex Theodosianus* 16.6; Augustine, Letter 48.

Arsacius died on 11 November, after having occupied the See for fourteen months. Petavius, from Socrates 6.18 and George’s Life of Chrysostom.

St. Chrysostom, while at Cucusus and nearly overcome by the extreme severity of winter, was transferred to Armenia. Same source, from Palladius’s fourth letter.

The Isaurians, ranging through Mount Taurus, inflicted enormous damage on the commonwealth. Lydiat, from Zosimus 5.25.

[Note: [Col. 0670C] I and II] Innocent, years 5 and 6.

[Col. 0670D] The legates sent by Innocent, carrying letters from Honorius and from Innocent himself, suffered terribly on the journey and returned. Theodorus in Palladius and Georgius.

Four months after the death of Arsacius, Atticus, formerly a monk, was ordained bishop of Constantinople. Socrates 6.18; Sozomen 8.17.

The quinquennalia of Theodosius the Younger. The relics of the prophet Samuel were brought to Constantinople on 19 May, with Arcadius Augustus, Anthemius the prefect and former consul, Aemilianus, prefect of the city, and the entire Senate leading the procession. Alexandrian Chronicle and St. Jerome, *Against Vigilantius*, a treatise he published in this year.

[Note: [Col. 0672A] II and III] Innocent, years 6 and 7. Theodosius the Younger celebrated the quinquennalia. Marcellinus and the Alexandrian Chronicle add that this occurred on the third day before the Ides of January.

St. John Chrysostom died at Comana on the Pontus Euxinus on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December, after having occupied the See for nine years, six months, and twenty days. Socrates 6.19.

After his death, Pope Innocent and the Westerners refused to communicate with his opponents until his name had been restored to the diptychs and that of Arsacius erased. Theodoret 5.34. See the notes on Innocent.

A Council of Carthage was held, in which an embassy was decreed to Honorius for the defense of the Catholics against the Donatists.

[Col. 0672C] [Note: [Col. 0672C] III and IV] Innocent, years 7 and 8.

Arcadius died on the Kalends of May. Socrates, final chapter of book 6.

Honorius, wishing to go to the East after his brother’s death, was detained by Stilicho because the tyrant Constantius had gone from Britain to Gaul and was residing at Arles. Stilicho, who had been designated for the East, was denounced to Honorius as an aspirant to imperial power. After he had betrothed his two daughters, Maria and Thermantia, as virgins, and had been accused of stirring up Alaric, the Alans, Suebi, and Vandals against the emperor’s rule, he was killed at Ravenna by imperial order. Zosimus 5; Philostorgius 12.2, in Photius.

[Note: [Col. 0672D] Olympiad 296, IV and 297, I] Innocent, years 8 and 9.

When the Romans were in great distress, certain people urged that some pagan sacrifices be performed. Zosimus falsely writes that Innocent permitted this; on the contrary, Innocent himself went as an ambassador to Honorius [Col. 0674A] and advised him, while the emperor issued several laws in this year against various superstitions. See Baronius, Petavius, Pagius, and, among the ancient authors, Orosius.

The city of Rome, besieged by Alaric in the preceding year, was invaded again after his withdrawal in this year; it was captured and plundered for seven days, beginning on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. Three thousand pounds of gold and thirty thousand pounds of silver [Col. 0674B] were carried away, in addition to other goods stipulated by the Senate. Zosimus 5; Marcellinus; Orosius, and others. See Pagius on this year, who shows that certain ancient chronologists and historians wrongly postponed the sack of the city to the following year or two years later. See Philostorgius 12.3.

Attalus was proclaimed emperor by order of Alaric; he had been prefect of the city.

Placidia, the emperor’s sister, was captured and married Ataulf, a relative of Alaric.

St. Honoratus, after visiting the monasteries of Italy, founded the monastery of Lérins around this year, initially under the rule of St. Pachomius. Noris, *History of Pelagianism* 2, pp. 173, 176.

[Note: [Col. 0674C] I and II] Innocent, years 9 and 10.

Alaric persuaded Attalus to send troops against Heraclianus, who was supporting Honorius’s cause in Africa. Ignoring Alaric’s advice, Attalus marched against Honorius, who was at Ravenna. Jovius created distrust between Alaric and Attalus. Alaric stripped Attalus of the imperial office (Zosimus 6) and handed him over to Honorius, with whom Alaric made peace. Alaric died while preparing to cross into Africa. Ataulf succeeded him. Jordanes, chapter 30.

[Note: [Col. 0674D] II and III] Innocent, years 10 and 11.

A conference was held at Carthage between the Catholics and the Donatists, in which the Donatists were completely overthrown. See Noris, *History of Pelagianism* 1.3 and 2, p. 222.

Antiochus the Persian, sent by Isdegerd—who had been appointed guardian of Theodosius by Arcadius’s testament—to regulate the guardianship of Theodosius, was removed from office, and Augusta Pulcheria alone administered the empire. Theophanes.

The head of Constantine, borne on a pole, was brought to Honorius on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October. Idacius. Constans was also killed at Vienne by Gerontius, and Maximus was substituted for him; later stripped of the purple, he lived obscurely in Spain. Zosimus 6; Marcellinus.

[Col. 0676B] Synesius, after convening a council, removed Andronicus, governor of Pentapolis, from the communion of the Church; he was received back into grace after repenting. Synesius, Letter 58.

[Note: [Col. 0676B] III and IV] Innocent, years 11 and 12.

After Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, died on 15 October, Cyril succeeded him. Noris, *History of Pelagianism* 1.4 and 2.1. The Council of Carthage condemned Caelestius, who appealed to the Roman See. Mercator.

St. Augustine began in this year to write against the Pelagians. Same source, book 1, chapter 4, and book 2, chapter 10, p. 238.

[Col. 0676C] Cassianus, having founded a monastery at Massilia, became famous. At the request of Castor, bishop of Apt, he wrote twelve books on the institutions of the Egyptian monks. In them he introduced the Semi-Pelagian doctrine, asserting that good works can be begun by human powers but cannot be completed without divine grace. See Noris, *History of Pelagianism* 2.1, p. 162.

A council was held at Cirta in Numidia in June against the Donatists.

[Note: [Col. 0676C] Olympiad 297, IV and 298, I] Innocent, years 12 and 13.

[Col. 0676D] Heraclianus, having performed vigorous service against the rebels, was made Count of Africa and consul. He himself then became a rebel, sailed to Italy with a fleet of seven hundred ships, and led troops against Rome. He was defeated by the approach of Count Marinus at Utriculum and put to flight. Carried back to Africa, he was captured and killed at Carthage, and Marinus succeeded him. By Marinus’s order, the tribune Marcellinus, who had labored courageously for the Catholic faith, was killed by an ambush of the Donatists; the Church honors him as a martyr [Col. 0678A] on the eighth day before the Ides of April. Petavius, from Idacius and Orosius 8.42.

See Cardinal Noris, *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 5.

[Note: [Col. 0678A] I and II] Innocent, years 13 and 14. In Letter 22, sent on the Ides of December during the consulship of Constantius, he confirms the decrees of the Macedonian synod. [Col. 0678B]

Pulcheria, sister of Theodosius, was proclaimed Augusta on the fourth day before the Nones of July. Marcellinus and the Alexandrian Chronicle.

A Gothic fleet attempting to cross into Africa was sunk by a storm in the Strait of Cádiz. Orosius.

On the tenth day before the Kalends of July, Honorius struck the Donatists with a new sanction and confirmed the acts against them enacted under Marcellinus, a man of illustrious memory, in book 16 of the *Codex Theodosianus*, title 5, “On Heretics,” laws 54 and 55. [Col. 0678C] He entrusted their execution to Dulcitius, the tribune and notary, to whom St. Augustine wrote, just as he had dedicated his books *On the City of God* to Marcellinus.

[Note: [Col. 0678C] II and III] Innocent, years 14 and 15.

The relics of St. Stephen, the Protomartyr, were discovered, according to the letters of St. Lucianus and others. See Baronius and Pagius.

Orosius, present at the Synod of Jerusalem held on the occasion of the Encaenia, described the proceedings against Pelagius, who was likewise residing there. The Fathers decreed that brothers and letters should be sent to Blessed Innocent, the Roman Pope, and that all should follow whatever he decided. See Cardinal Noris, *History of Pelagianism* 1.7, and Pagius on year 2, no. 6.

The Jews were expelled from Alexandria by Cyril because they had committed a nocturnal massacre of Christians, having been falsely roused by a report that a church had been burned. Socrates 8.13–14.

Isdegerd, king of the Persians, had been close to conversion to the Christian faith because of the examples of the holiness of Maruthas, bishop of Mesopotamia. After Maruthas died, however, because of the untimely zeal of Bishop Abda, who had burned a fire temple, Isdegerd afflicted the Christians with a severe persecution lasting five years. Theophanes.

[Note: [Col. 0680A] Olympiad 298, III and IV] Innocent, years 15 and 16.

A synodical letter of sixty-seven African bishops condemned the errors of Pelagius and asked Pope Innocent himself to condemn them by apostolic authority. The Council of Milevis in Africa likewise condemned the same errors and referred the case for judgment by Innocent. Augustine, Letters 94 and 178. See Pagius the Elder on this year, no. 8.

Because of the victory over Attalus, games were held at Constantinople, and Theodosius, coming from Heraclea to Constantinople, was presented with a golden crown by Ursus, the prefect of the city, and the Senate. Alexandrian Chronicle.

[Note: [Col. 0680B] Olympiad 298, IV and 299, I] Innocent, year 16, died on 14 February after having occupied the See for fifteen years, eleven months, and twenty days. See the notes [Col. 0680C] on Innocent. The See was vacant for twenty-two days. ZOSIMUS was elected as his successor on the ninth day and ordained on 11 March; he celebrated Easter on the day mentioned in Paschasinus’s letter, the eighth day before the Kalends of April.

Before his death, Innocent answered the synodical letter of the Council of Milevis and condemned the Pelagian heresy. See Noris, *History of Pelagianism* 1.11, pp. 70, 73, 74.
