When the supreme judgment of the Apostolic See had been added to the decrees of the two councils, Carthage and Milevis, against the Pelagian and Caelestian heresies, the case was finished, says St. Augustine, *Sermon on the Words of the Apostle*. See Noris, *History of Pelagianism* 1.17, p. 104.

Nevertheless, when Caelestius came to Rome and, through clever dissimulation, offered Zosimus a written statement of faith, just as Pelagius had done, composed as a deceptive defense, he was considered innocent. Shortly afterward, however, both were ordered to undergo a fuller examination; they lost their case, and at Zosimus’s insistence both were expelled into exile as heretics. [Note: [Col. 0680D] I and II] See the notes on Zosimus.

Zosimus, years 1 and 2; BONIFACE.

[Col. 0682A] Zosimus sent legates to Africa to deal with the matter of appeals. Meanwhile he died on 13 December. His successor Boniface was elected and ordained on the third day before the Kalends of January. See the notes on Zosimus. Another part of the clergy, during the schism, elected Eulalius, who was supported by Symmachus.

A Council of Carthage was held with 214 bishops present and legates of the Apostolic See. Its decrees were sent to Pope Zosimus; after their approval, the Pelagian heresy was condemned throughout the world. Prosper.

The Council of Telepte was held in this year in the province of Byzacena.

[Note: [Col. 0682B] II and III] Boniface, years 1 and 2.

The schism of Eulalius, supported by Symmachus, caused those who had been promoted to be summoned to Ravenna.

After losing his case, Eulalius was banished to Campania after the Easter festivals. See the notes on Boniface.

A Council of Carthage was held on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, with 217 bishops, among them St. Augustine and Alypius; it met again on the sixth day before the Kalends of December and transmitted the synodal proceedings to Boniface. See Noris, *History of Pelagianism* 1.17, and the notes on Boniface.

[Col. 0682D] [Note: [Col. 0682D] III and IV] Boniface, years 2 and 3.

Persecution raged in Persia, having begun five years earlier. Socrates 7.18; Theodoret 5.39; Marcellinus.

The Romans besieged the Persians and Nisibis. Vararanes, son of Isdegerd, came against them with Alamundar the Saracen as his ally and was defeated. Socrates 7.18. But see Pagius, no. 15.

St. Jerome died at the age of ninety. Prosper gives his age as ninety-five, through a scribal error. Pagius on this year.

[Note: [Col. 0684A] Olympiad 299, IV and Olympiad 300] Boniface, years 3 and 4.

Boniface endeavored, through letters and embassies sent to Honorius, to nullify the usurpations of the Greeks in the provinces of Illyricum. See the notes on Boniface.

Theodosius married Eudocia. He erected and dedicated a statue of his father Arcadius in the Forum, upon a column. The Romans fought the Persians and won a victory on 8 September. Marcellinus and the Alexandrian Chronicle.

Theodotus, bishop of Antioch, was appointed in this year and expelled the exposed Pelagius by synodal sentence. Noris, *History of Pelagianism* 2.4, [Col. 0684C] p. 186.

Caelestius, associate of Pelagius, was expelled by Volusianus, prefect of the city. Same source, book 1, chapter 20. He attempted in vain to draw Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, and Rufus, vicar of the Apostolic See at Thessalonica, to his side. See Noris, at the cited place, where he shows that Theodosius himself revoked a law obtained by stealth from bishops of Illyricum who were contemplating defection from the Roman See to Constantinople. Same source, book 1, *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 20, p. [Col. 0684D] 131.

Alypius, sent by St. Augustine to St. Pope Boniface with his writings, was received with honor. Same source, chapter 21, p. 133.

[Note: [Col. 0684D] I and II] Boniface, year 4, died and was buried on the fourth day of September, according to an old Florentine manuscript. The See was vacant for nine days after his death. Library. See the notes on Boniface. Coelestine was elected as his successor on 13 September and ordained on the following Sunday, the seventeenth.

Pope Boniface boldly suppresses the audacity of Patroclus, the invader of the episcopate of Arles and usurper of the rights of Narbonne, as well as the audacity of the Illyrian prelates. [Col. 0686A] See the notes on Boniface.

A daughter, Eudoxia, is born to Theodosius. Marcellinus: the Persians make peace with the Romans. See there.

The tyrant Maximus and Jovinus are defeated by the sword, brought from Spain, and executed during Honorius’s tricennalia. See there.

[Col. 0686B] [Note: [Col. 0686B] II III] **The first and second years of Celestine.**

From this year and throughout the following three-year period, St. Augustine completed his fifteen books *On the Trinity* and his twenty-two books *On the City of God*. See Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book I, chapter 24, p. 152.

The empress Placidia, expelled by her brother Honorius together with her sons, travels to Theodosius, with the count Boniface supplying the expenses. Olympiodorus and Prosper.

Pope Celestine expels the Pelagians from Italy. Prosper, *Against the Collator*, chapter 41. During this period Julian [of Eclanum] writes eight books in Cilicia against St. Augustine, where he visits Theodore of Mopsuestia, a Pelagian.

See Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book I, chapter 9, and Pagi on this year, no. 15.

[Col. 0686C] [Note: [Col. 0686C] III IV] **The second and third years of Celestine.**

Theodosius makes Valentinian, the son of his aunt, Caesar and sends him to recover the empire against John (Prosper); he was created Augustus at Rome after the tyrant John was killed in the following year, as Hydatius and Marcellinus write. Meanwhile, in this year, once created Caesar, he betroths to himself Eudoxia, the daughter of Theodosius. See there.

The monks of Hadrumetum in Africa, disputing about grace and free will, are brought back into agreement after receiving Augustine’s books. Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book I, chapter 23.

[Note: [Col. 0686D] Olym. 300 IV and 301 I] **The third and fourth years of Celestine.**

The empress Placidia, showing great concern for the Catholic religion and the churches, has several laws issued against heretics and schismatics after the tyrant John had been put to death. See Noris, [Col. 0688A] *History of the Pelagians*, book I, chapter 24, p. 152.

The island of Lérins, in the monastery founded by St. Honoratus, becomes a nursery of holy bishops. There Saints Eucherius, Maximus, Hilary, Faustus, and Lupus were trained in this period under Honoratus, the monastery’s abbot. See there, book II, chapter 1, p. 163. Nevertheless, among those monks the doctrine of the Semi-Pelagians begins to creep in. See there, book II, chapter 2.

[Col. 0688B] Theodosius restores the schools of Constantinople and their professors to better condition and grants them privileges: law 3 of the *Theodosian Code*, “On Liberal Studies,” and law 1, “On Professors.”

**The fourth and fifth years of Celestine.**

[Note: [Col. 0688B] II] After Atticus, bishop of Constantinople, died on the sixth day before the Ides of October of the preceding year, according to Socrates, book VII, chapter 25, Sisinnius is elected bishop on the day before the Kalends of March, according to Socrates and Marcellinus. Honoratus, formerly abbot of Lérins, succeeds Patroclus of Arles. [Col. 0688C]

St. Augustine undertakes a critical review of his writings, after the Pelagians had been overthrown everywhere throughout the world. He also designates the presbyter Eradius as coadjutor of the episcopate, in a public act bearing these consuls’ names. See Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book I, pp. 153 and 155.

[Col. 0688D] [Note: [Col. 0688D] II III] **The fifth and sixth years of Celestine.**

Sisinnius, bishop of Constantinople, dies near the end of this year, on 24 December; in the following year Nestorius is given as his successor. Socrates, book VII, chapter 28.

St. Augustine completes two books of his *Retractions* this year, in which the Vandals, Alans, and Goths invade Africa from Spain. Possidius, *Life of St. Augustine*. See Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book I, chapter 23, p. 155.

This year he also completes four volumes [Col. 0690A] against Julian’s final books. See there, p. 204. Theodore, bishop of Mopsuestia—the patron of the Pelagian sect and the source of Nestorianism—dies around this time according to Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 4, but two years later according to Pagi.

[Note: [Col. 0690A] II IV] **The sixth and seventh years of Celestine.**

Nestorius is ordained bishop of Constantinople on the Kalends of April of this year. Liberatus the Deacon, *Brief Account of the Case of Nestorius* [Col. 0690B], chapter 4. But Socrates, book VI, chapter 24, says the fourth day before the Ides of April.

Nestorius attempts to introduce a new error into the churches, and so forth. The principal opposition to this impiety comes from the energetic action of Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, and the authority of Pope Celestine. Prosper, *Chronicle*. See Noris, book II of the *History of the Pelagians*, chapter 7, p. 204. See the notes of Pagi and Sommier below, under Celestine.

[Col. 0690C] [Note: [Col. 0690C] Olympiad 301 IV and 302 I] **The seventh and eighth years of Celestine.**

While Nestorius of Constantinople was troubling the Church with new heresies and extending patronage to the Pelagians, Marius Mercator presents to the emperor Theodosius Augustus and to the clergy a memorandum against the Pelagians. See Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 6.

St. Augustine writes book XVIII of *The City of God* this year, as appears from chapter 54, where he states that the thirtieth year is running since the consulship of Manlius Theodorus. St. Celestine, informed that Nestorius’s writings have been disseminated through Egypt and other provinces [Col. 0690D], instructs St. Cyril to investigate their author carefully. Nestorius responds arrogantly to Cyril’s most courteous letter. Petavius, from the Acts of the Council of Ephesus.

Juvenal is made bishop of Jerusalem after Praylius’s death, according to Baronius and Petavius; but Pagi, no. 27, proves from the *Life of St. Euthymius* that Juvenal governed that church already in the preceding year.

[Col. 0692A] [Note: [Col. 0692A] I II] **The eighth and ninth years of Celestine.**

A Roman synod is held by St. Celestine at the beginning of August against Nestorius. See Pagi, June, no. 15, under Celestine, and the notes below.

St. Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, reports to St. Celestine the heresy of Nestorius and his patronage of the Pelagians. In his reply Celestine encloses a letter to be transmitted to Nestorius, in which [Col. 0692B] he prescribes a deadline for repentance. Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 7.

While the Vandals had already been besieging Hippo for a third month, St. Augustine dies. See there and p. 183, where he proves that the Augustinian rule of the coenobite monks was brought to the Jurenses and others shortly after the holy Father’s death.

[Note: [Col. 0692B] II III] **The ninth and tenth years of Celestine.**

Celestine, after holding another synod, sends legates to the East [Col. 0692C] with a memorandum, dated the eighth day before the Ides of May under these consuls, for the holding of a synod at Ephesus, so that the decisions made at Rome against Nestorius might be carried out. See Pagi, no. 4.

The ecumenical Council of Ephesus, consisting of 200 holy Fathers, is celebrated in the year 431 of the Lord, on the twenty-third year of the reign of Theodosius Augustus, on the feast of the Ascension into heaven, according to the *Paschal Chronicle*. St. Cyril presides, to whom St. Celestine entrusts his authority. On 22 June Nestorius is deposed, and the Pelagian and Nestorian heresies are condemned. See Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 9, pp. 233 and 256, and the notes on Celestine below. Maximus is placed over the Church of Constantinople. Noris, there. John of Antioch holds a synod against the Ephesian council, yet does not support the Pelagians. Noris, there.

[Note: [Col. 0692D] III IV] **The tenth year of Celestine**, who dies on 21 July. See the notes cited above.

St. Xystus III succeeds him on 10 August. See there and p. 104. St. Celestine’s letter to the holy Synod of Ephesus was given under these consuls on the Ides of March, together with other letters of the same pope, in Binius’s edition of the councils, volume [Col. 0694A] I, pp. 739–742: the Synod of Antioch.

The faction of the Semi-Pelagians, which was increasing daily throughout Gaul against the teaching of St. Augustine, is restrained by St. Celestine’s letters. According to Cardinal Noris, he dies on the fifth day before the Ides of April; according to our reckoning, on 21 July. See Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 10.

St. Prosper of Aquitaine continues the struggle against the Semi-Pelagians in succession to St. Augustine and writes against Cassian. See there.

[Note: [Col. 0694B] Olympiad 302 IV and 303 I] **The first and second years of Xystus III.**

A Roman synod is held by Pope Xystus, at which the Pelagians and Nestorians are discussed. See Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 12, p. 255.

This year Faustus, appointed abbot of Lérins, becomes the leader of the Semi-Pelagians after Cassian. See there, book II, chapter 2.

St. Peter Chrysologus is given as bishop to the people of Ravenna [Col. 0694C] at the recommendation of St. Apollinaris. See Pagi, June, under St. Xystus, no. 8.

The appeal of the Easterners to the Roman pontiff. See Pagi.

[Note: [Col. 0694C] I II] **The second and third years of Xystus.**

Vincent of Lérins wrote his short treatise this year after the Council of Ephesus. Petavius, Noris, Pagi, and others.

Honoria, the sister of the emperor Valentinian, violated by her procurator Eugenius, [Col. 0694D] expelled from the palace, and sent to Theodosius, incited Attila against the Western Empire. See there. After Maximianus, bishop of Constantinople, died, Proculus was appointed in his place. See there, from Socrates, book VII, chapter 39.

[Note: [Col. 0694D] II III] **The third and fourth years of Xystus.**

The Theodosian Code is promulgated this year, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of March. There, in the final law of the title “On Heretics,” Nestorius’s books are prohibited and condemned to burning.

Proclus of Constantinople replies this year to the bishops [Col. 0696A] of Armenia, who were consulting him about the books of Theodore of Mopsuestia. See Noris, dissertation on the fifth ecumenical synod, chapter 11, p. 150.

Basil publishes a book in which he teaches that the blasphemies of Theodore and Diodore must be avoided. After this, Armenian monks come to Constantinople and urge everywhere that both men must be condemned. Petavius, from Liberatus, chapter 10.

[Col. 0696B] [Note: [Col. 0696B] III IV] **The fourth and fifth years of Xystus.**

Nestorius is deported to the Oasis by an edict of Theodosius. From the Acts of the Synod of Ephesus and from Evagrius, according to Petavius. After John of Antioch had died following thirteen years in office, Domnus is appointed in his place. See there, from Cyril.

Aetius, commander of both military forces, is called patrician, a vigorous defender of the Roman Empire. See there, from Jordanes.

[Col. 0696C] [Note: [Col. 0696C] Olympiad 303 IV and 304 I] **The fifth and sixth years of Xystus.**

The beginnings of the Vandal persecution initiated by Geiseric in Africa. See Ruinart, in his history, part 2, chapter 4, no. 2.

The marriage of Valentinian to Eudoxia, daughter of Theodosius. Marcellinus and Prosper.

War is waged against the Goths with the assistance of the Huns. Petavius.

The first cycle of Cyril begins this year; it lasted ninety-five years. [Col. 0696D] Petavius.

[Note: [Col. 0696D] I II] **The sixth and seventh years of Xystus.**

The relics of St. John Chrysostom are brought to Constantinople. Socrates, book VII, chapter 44. The relics of Ignatius are also transferred to the temple of Fortune. Petavius, from Evagrius, book I, chapter 16; and the bodies of the Forty Holy Martyrs are discovered. The same author, from Sozomen, book IX, chapter 2.

Eudocia travels to Jerusalem to fulfill a vow and obtains the relics of St. Stephen and the chains [Col. 0698A] of St. Peter, one of which she sends to Rome to Eudoxia. See Petavius on the following year and our notes on Xystus.

[Note: [Col. 0698A] II III] **The seventh and eighth years of Xystus.**

Julian of Eclanum, the Pelagian, is prevented from recovering his see by Blessed Pope Xystus, at the urging of St. Leo, then a deacon and soon afterward his successor. Prosper, *Chronicle*.

[Col. 0698B] The *Paschal Chronicle*: this year Geiseric, king of the Vandals, entered Carthage in the month Hyperberetaeus, and in the same year attempted to ravage Sicily. After violating the peace, he occupied Carthage on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November. See Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 21, from Prosper and Hydatius.

[Note: [Col. 0698B] III IV] **St. Xystus dies on 22 July.** The see is vacant for forty-two days. St. Leo is elected and ordained on the Kalends of September, after he had been summoned back from Gaul by an official embassy. See the notes on Xystus.

[Col. 0698C] A disputation or legal proceeding is held before the death of Pope Xystus in the Basilica of Heleniana, or Sessoriana, under these consuls. See the councils in Binius, volume I, part II, p. 488.

[Note: [Col. 0698C] Olympiad 304 IV and 305 I] **The first and second years of Leo I.**

Theodosius launches war against the Vandals, with Areobindus, Anavilla, and Germanus as commanders, but the expedition with its great fleet has little success. Prosper. The Persians, Saracens, Zani, Isaurians, and Huns ravage the Roman provinces. Anatolius and Aspar are sent against them and make peace. The *Alexandrian Chronicle*, and Petavius from it.

[Col. 0698D] Sirmium is destroyed, together with many towns of Illyricum, by Bleda and Attila, kings of the Huns. From Marcellinus’s chronicle. See Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book I, chapter 20, where he writes that Paul the Deacon, book XIV, says that Theodosius had agreed to annual payments of one thousand pounds of gold. See Petavius on the following year.

[Note: [Col. 0698D] I II] **The second and third years of Leo.**

The Council of Vaison, in Narbonese Gaul, is celebrated. Petavius.

Peace with Geiseric is confirmed by Valentinian, and Africa is divided between them into specified territories [Col. 0700A]. But the nobles conspire against Geiseric; when discovered, they are put to death with extreme cruelty. Petavius, from Prosper.

[Note: [Col. 0700A] II III] **The third and fourth years of Leo.**

Pope Leo rises against the Manichaeans hiding in Rome and burns their books. Prosper, *Chronicle*. The same Leo overthrows the Manichaeans and converts the Pelagians. [Col. 0700B] Prosper, *On the Promises of God*, chapter 6. See Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 12, p. 255.

Theodoret, frequently attending synods at Antioch, incurs suspicion of Nestorian heresy with Theodosius, who orders him to remain within his own city. Petavius, from Theodoret’s letters 81, 90, and others.

The emperor Theodosius, returning from an expedition in Asia, dedicates the Baths, according to Marcellinus; Petavius argues, from the *Alexandrian Chronicle*, that they had been dedicated earlier. See there.

[Col. 0700C] [Note: [Col. 0700C] III IV] **The fourth and fifth years of Leo.**

Petavius, from Leo’s ninth letter to Turibius, mentions a council held at Rome by Leo the Great against the Manichaeans.

The Council of Arles is held concerning the deposition of Celidonius. Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 12.

St. Cyril of Alexandria dies. See there, p. 256. Dioscorus succeeds him and was hostile to Theodoret. Petavius.

When consulted about the date of Easter for this year, Paschasinus replies to St. Leo that it should be celebrated on 23 April [Col. 0700D], in a letter following Leo’s sixty-third.

Attila subjugates the peoples of his brother Bleda after having killed him. Arcadia, the sister of Theodosius, dies. See there.

[Note: [Col. 0700D] Olympiad 305 IV and 306 I] **The fifth and sixth years of Leo.**

When Pope Leo, in a council held at Rome, issued a decision against the ordinations of St. Hilary in another province, the law of Valentinian was enacted: *Novels*, book VI, title 24, “On the Ordination of Bishops.” Petavius.

St. Prosper brought his chronicle down to this point. Vitus, master of both military forces, was sent to Spain to harass the Carthaginians [Col. 0702A] and the Baetici. After defeating the Suebi and Goths who had come to their aid, he fled. The Suebi ravage those provinces. See there, from Hydatius.

[Note: [Col. 0702A] I II] **The sixth and seventh years of Leo.**

A severe famine occurs at Constantinople, and the Temple of the Imperial City is burned. Marcellinus in his chronicle; Bede; Gildas. Pulcheria is removed from the administration of affairs. See Pagi the Elder on this year, no. 11.

[Col. 0702B] [Note: [Col. 0702B] II III] **The seventh and eighth years of Leo.**

Proclus, patriarch of Constantinople, dies and is succeeded by St. Flavian. Pagius. Constantinople is shaken by a great earthquake. Marcellinus, *Chronicle* [26 January; Malalas, p. 66; Nicephorus, 25 September].

Attila, the king, inflicts a great war this year and ravages nearly all [Col. 0702C] Europe, destroying and plundering cities and fortresses. This year King Attila advances as far as Thermopylae, bringing devastation. Marcellinus, *Chronicle*.

Leo the Great, writing to Januarius of Aquileia and Septimius of Altinum, overthrows the Pelagian heresy. See also Pagi the Elder on this year, no. 5 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0702C] III IV] **The eighth and ninth years of Leo.**

The Council of Constantinople begins on the sixth day before the Ides of November, as in the first act of Chalcedon. At it Eutyches is convicted of heresy, accused by Eusebius, [Col. 0702D] bishop of Dorylaeum. See the notes on Leo. In the same year Ibas of Edessa is twice brought to trial and twice acquitted: first at Tyre in February, then at Berytus in September. Petavius, from the Acts of the Council of Chalcedon. See the notes on Leo.

The province of India sends the emperor Theodosius a tamed tiger as a gift. Marcellinus, *Chronicle*.

St. Germanus, bishop of Auxerre, dies at Ravenna. See Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 12.

[Col. 0704A] [Note: [Col. 0704A] Olympiad 306 IV and 307 I] **The ninth and tenth years of Leo.**

This year the predatory Synod of Ephesus is held through the fraud of the eunuch Chrysaphius. At it Eutyches is restored to communion by Dioscorus. Flavian is condemned; and when he appealed to the Roman pontiff, he was driven into exile [Col. 0704B], where he died. Anatolius, Dioscorus’s presbyter and *apocrisiarius*, is appointed in his place, as Nicephorus says in his chronicle, and Petavius after him. The legates of the Roman pontiff are mistreated; Hilary escapes and comes to Rome. There Leo, the pope, holds a synod and annuls that Ephesian council. Acts of the Council of Chalcedon; Liberatus. See there. See the notes on Leo the Great. Sebastian is killed by Geiseric. See there, from Hydatius.

[Col. 0704C] [Note: [Col. 0704C] I II] **The tenth and eleventh years of Leo.**

A council is held at Constantinople at which Eutyches is condemned by Anatolius. Placidia dies. Prosper, *Chronicle*, and St. Peter Chrysologus. See Noris, *History of the Pelagians*, book II, chapter 12, p. 260.

The *Alexandrian Chronicle* reports that this year Attila [Col. 0704D] ordered Valentinian to prepare a palace for him. It also says that Aetius, having gone to Gaul, incited Alaric against him. Then Attila’s forces were defeated near the Danube, but Alaric died. Petavius. But see the following year.

Cyrus, formerly prefect of the praetorian guard and of the city, becomes a cleric and then bishop of Smyrna. See there.

[Col. 0706A] [Note: [Col. 0706A] II III] **The eleventh and twelfth years of Leo.**

The holy Council of Chalcedon, consisting of 738 Fathers, is celebrated on the eighth day before the Kalends of October. See its Acts below in the notes on Leo.

Although St. Leo wished to be present, he sent legates, lest Italy, because of his absence, be made [Col. 0706B] more vulnerable to Attila’s invasions. Attila, accompanied by a crowd of kings, as Jordanes says, was ravaging the Roman provinces, especially in Gaul and along the Rhine. A battle was fought in the Catalaunian Fields, where 200,000 were killed. See Pagi on this year, no. 26.

After being driven from Gaul, Attila turned his arms toward Italy.

[Note: [Col. 0706B] III IV] **The twelfth and thirteenth years of Leo.**

When Attila was advancing toward Rome after ravaging Aquileia, Ticinum, and Milan, Leo the Great met him [Col. 0706C], and at his persuasion the victorious barbarian withdrew. On this occasion the Italians, fleeing to the lagoons, founded Venice. Marcellinus; Cassiodorus, *Miscellany*. See Petavius and Pagi, June, under St. Leo, no. 37, from Prosper.

The emperor labors on behalf of the Council of Chalcedon and abolishes what had been done against Flavian. Acts of the Council of Chalcedon.

The monk Theodosius infects Eudocia in Palestine with the pestilence of heresy, occupies the see of Jerusalem, drives out the Catholic bishops, and kills others. When Marcian ordered him to be brought before him, he fled. Theophanes.

[Note: [Col. 0706D] Olympiad 307 IV and 308 I] **The thirteenth and fourteenth years of Leo.**

The *Alexandrian Chronicle* reports that the head of St. John the Baptist was found at Emesa under these consuls, in the month Peritius, that is, February, assigning it to the Syro-Macedonian era 763 and the Antiochene era 501. But see Pagi the Elder and Du Cange, who assign it to the preceding year.

The empress Pulcheria dies on 10 September, a martyr at Rome. Marcellinus, *Alexandrian Chronicle*.

After Dioscorus is deposed from the bishopric of Alexandria [Col. 0708A] at the Council of Chalcedon, Proterius succeeds him. See Pagi, June, under St. Leo, no. 33.

[Note: [Col. 0708A] I II] **The fourteenth and fifteenth years of Leo.**

The controversies concerning the date of Easter that arose in the present year, the immediately preceding year, and the following year. See the letters of St. Leo and Bucherius, as well as Pagi, and our Paschal table, p. 146, in the notes on Leo the Great.

Juvenal, bishop of Jerusalem, [Col. 0708B] admonished by St. Leo, proposes to all, in a synod he has gathered, that the Catholic faith be embraced. Appendix to the Council of Chalcedon.

Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, raising himself too high, is restrained by St. Leo and yields his claim to primacy. Letter 71 of St. Leo. Petavius.

Jordanes assigns Pannonia to the Goths and Dacia to the Gepids. See Pagi the Elder on this year, no. 9.

Dioscorus the heretic dies this year. See there, no. 15.

[Note: [Col. 0708B] II III] **The fifteenth and sixteenth years of Leo.**

The emperor Marcian, in the fifth and sixth years of his tribunician power, [Col. 0708C] unsuccessfully prepares an embassy to Geiseric for the security of Italy and the freedom of the empresses. Concerning Geiseric’s booty collected at Rome over fourteen days, with St. Leo pleading against the disaster and still more severe losses, see Procopius, *On the Vandalic War*; Evagrius, book II, chapter 7; Ruinart, *On the Vandal Persecution*, part 2, chapter 6, no. 9; Pagi the Elder on this year; and the notes below, p. 161.

Marius, bishop of Aventicum, begins his chronicle this year.

[Col. 0708D] [Note: [Col. 0708D] III IV] **The sixteenth and seventeenth years of Leo.**

Marcian acknowledges Avitus as emperor and partner in the empire. Hydatius, *Chronicle*.

Geiseric, after Valentinian’s death, invades and ravages not only Africa and Sicily but also several provinces of the Eastern and Western empires. Victor of Vita.

Geiseric persecutes the Catholics in [Col. 0710A] Africa. After Victor, bishop of Antioch, dies, Basil the Orthodox succeeds him, according to the letter of the Syrians to St. Leo.

Jordanes, cited by Petavius for this year, reports that Theodoric permitted the Suebi to choose a king from their own people; they chose Remismund.

[Col. 0710B] [Note: [Col. 0710B] Olympiad 308 IV and 309 I] **The seventeenth and eighteenth years of Leo.**

Geiseric sends back Eudoxia together with her daughter Placidia, the wife of Olybrius. Theophanes; Evagrius, book II, chapter 7.

In the third year after Avitus had been made emperor by the Gauls and Goths, he was deprived of empire and life after being abandoned by the Goths. Hydatius. Yet Hydatius and others do not assign even a full year to his reign. The *Miscellaneous History* relates that, after abdicating the empire, he was made bishop of Placentia. Petavius.

[Col. 0710C] The Egyptian heretics riot after Marcian’s death. Their leader, Timothy the Cat, formerly a monk and then a presbyter of Alexandria, stirs up the monks against Proterius by his tricks and persuades them to install Timothy the Cat. Theophanes; Liberatus. See Pagi in the notes on St. Leo, no. 34.

[Note: [Col. 0710C] I II] **The eighteenth and nineteenth years of Leo.**

The emperor Leo receives letters from the bishops of the world agreeing concerning the Council of Chalcedon. Marcellinus; Evagrius.

When Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, dies, Gennadius succeeds him. [Col. 0710D] Theodoret; Baronius and Pagi the Elder, no. 8.

Anastasius becomes bishop of Jerusalem. Cyril and Euthymius, cited by Petavius.

Timothy the Cat kills Proterius in the baptistery on Easter Day and corrupts Cyril’s writings. See there, from Theophanes and Evagrius, book II, chapter 8.

Euthalius, first a deacon and then bishop of Sulci, whose work was published by Laurentius Zacagnius, completes his work on the Epistles of Paul during this consulship. For its chronology he counts 462 years from the coming of the Savior. Pagi.

[Note: [Col. 0712A] II III] **The nineteenth and twentieth years of Leo.**

After learning of Proterius’s murder, Leo sends Caesarius and punishes him, as a participant in that killing, by cutting out his tongue; but he leaves Timothy to the judgment of the bishops. Petavius, from Theophanes.

A council is held at Constantinople at which the Council of Chalcedon [Col. 0712B] is confirmed and ecclesiastical discipline established. Balsamon, in the *Nomocanon*.

After Acacius of Antioch dies, Martyrius is appointed in his place. Nicephorus, *Chronicle*.

[Note: [Col. 0712B] III IV] **The twentieth and twenty-first years of Leo.**

Timothy the Cat, the murderer of Bishop Proterius, is banished to Cherson. Five months later Timothy Solofaciolus, a defender of Chalcedon, is appointed in his place in the bishopric of Alexandria. Victor of Tunnuna; Letters 99 and 100 of St. Leo; Theophanes. See Pagi, June, under St. [Col. 0712C] Leo, no. 36.

Eudocia, widow of Theodosius, dies at Jerusalem after she had recovered from the Eutychian heresy into which she had temporarily fallen, through the efforts of Saints Euthymius and Simeon Stylites. Cyril and Nicephorus.

[Note: [Col. 0712C] Olympiad 309 IV and 310 I] **The twenty-first and twenty-second years of Leo; the first of Hilary.**

St. Leo the Great dies on 3 November and is buried on 10 November. The see is vacant for seventeen days; St. Hilary succeeds him and is ordained on Sunday, 12 November. See the notes on Hilary.

The emperor Majorian is killed by the patrician Ricimer near Dertona [Col. 0712D] on 7 August, according to the chronographer published by Cuspinian and noted by Onuphrius. See Pagi the Elder on this year, no. 2. In his place, the emperor **Libius Severus** is elevated at Ravenna on 19 November. See there.

This year, sixty-four years after the death of St. Martin of Tours, Perpetuus is ordained bishop. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book X, chapter 31, says that he organized fasts and vigils throughout the year.

[Note: [Col. 0712D] I II] **The first and second years of Hilary.**

The patrician Studius founds at Constantinople a celebrated monastery [Col. 0714A], into which he transfers the Acoemete monks; afterward they are called Studites. Theophanes.

Antioch in Isauria is swallowed up when the earth splits open, though some pious people are left alive. Hydatius.

[Note: [Col. 0714A] II III] **The second and third years of Hilary.**

Petavius, noting that Theophanes dates this year to the year 5956 of the world [Col. 0714B] and 456 of Christ, which is 463 of the common era, reports that Peter the Fuller, having won over Zeno, commander of the East, stirred certain Apollinarists against Martyrius, bishop of Antioch. Martyrius is honorably received by Gennadius at Constantinople; while returning to Antioch, he sees the people in revolt and resigns his see. Peter, the usurper of that see, is driven into exile by the emperor.

[Note: [Col. 0714B] III IV] **The third and fourth years of Hilary.**

Olybrius is sent to Rome by the emperor Leo. After marrying [Col. 0714C] Placidia, he is unwillingly crowned by the Romans. The *Paschal Chronicle* reports this together with the consulship. But Olybrius’s three-month reign must be assigned to the year 472. See below.

Beogor, king of the Alans, is killed by Ricimer near Bergomum. Cassiodorus. With him the principate of the Alans between the Loire and the Rhône came to an end.

The death of St. Simeon Stylites is recorded this year by the *Paschal Chronicle*.

[Note: [Col. 0714C] Olympiad 310 IV and Olympiad 311 I] **The fourth and fifth years of Hilary**, who holds a council at Rome [Col. 0714D]. See the notes below on Hilary.

A fire at Constantinople, according to the *Alexandrian Chronicle*.

Aegidius, count of the Goths, dies by ambush; after his death they occupy Roman cities. Hydatius.

Childeric fights at Angers. Odovacar comes to Angers with the Saxons and devastates the people with a great slaughter. From the histories of the Franks; see Pagi the Elder on this year, no. 10, for their evaluation.

[Col. 0716A] [Note: [Col. 0716A] I II] **The fifth and sixth years of Hilary.**

Vortigern, king of the Britons, dies in the western part of Britain. By the vote of the clergy, the leaders, and the people, Aurelius Ambrosius is chosen in his place; a Council of the Cymri is held for his inauguration. From the English councils. Pagi on this year, no. 7.

Clovis is born this year, begotten by Childeric from Basina, the wife of the king of the Thuringians, whom Childeric married after her divorce. See Petavius.

[Note: [Col. 0716A] II III] **The sixth and seventh years of Hilary.**

The emperor Leo sends Anthemius, the patrician, to Rome and makes him emperor. Marcellinus and the *Paschal Chronicle*.

Ricimer, the patrician and master of the soldiers, persuaded Leo to send a Greek [Col. 0716C] to Rome as Augustus, whose daughter Ricimer would marry. The Senate likewise sent legates to request Anthemius, and in August hailed him as emperor eight miles from the city. Petavius, from Sidonius’s panegyric and history, and from Evagrius, book II, chapter 18.

A plague rages in the city while the Lupercalia are being celebrated there. Pope Gelasius, in his letter to Andromachus.

[Note: [Col. 0716C] I IV] **The seventh year of Hilary; the first of Simplicius.**

When Hilary ended his life on 21 February, after a vacancy of three days, Simplicius succeeded him and was ordained on Sunday, 24 February [Col. 0716D]. See the notes on pp. 165 and 174.

Victor of Tunnuna places the beginning of Simplicius’s pontificate under the consulship of Leo IV and Anthemius II, but, according to the laws cited here, only “Anthemius II” should be read, without a colleague.

Leo places Basiliscus, the brother of the empress Verina, in command of a fleet of a thousand ships sent against the Vandals. After Geiseric’s ships had been defeated, Basiliscus is said to have been corrupted by a bribe, in the hope of gaining the empire, by the Arians Aspar and Ardaburius, so that he fled to Constantinople as though defeated. He is freed by the empress Verina and banished to Perinthus. Procopius; Nicephorus, book 15, chapter 17.

[Note: [Col. 0718A] Olympiad 311 IV and 312 I] **The first and second years of Simplicius.**

The head of Denzic, son of Attila, king of the Huns, is brought to Constantinople. Marcellinus.

Aspar’s son Patricius, called Caesar by Leo, is sent to Alexandria to recall Aspar from the corrupt doctrines of Arius [Col. 0718B]. Zeno, the emperor’s son-in-law, is sent by the same ruler with an army into Thrace and successfully escapes Aspar’s ambushes. As a result Aspar becomes suspect to Leo. See Pagi the Elder, who recounts these events from Theophanes, and who assigns to this year, from other chronographers, the defeat of Geiseric reported under the preceding year.

[Note: [Col. 0718B] I II] **The second and third years of Simplicius.**

Pagi records Leo’s fifteenth anniversary this year [Col. 0718C], although, with others, he assigns his fourth consulship to the following year.

Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, commented on the prophet Daniel in its entirety, word for word, and composed many homilies; he also expounded all the Epistles of Paul. Marcellinus, and Petavius with him.

[Note: [Col. 0718C] II III] **The third and fourth years of Simplicius.**

Aspar, together with his sons Ardaburius and Patricius—the former a patrician, the latter Caesar and son-in-law of the emperor Leo—is wounded in the palace by the swords of eunuchs and dies, an Arian together with his Arian offspring. [Col. 0718D] From the chronicle of Marcellinus and the history of Evagrius, book II, chapter 15. Petavius, Pagi, and the other chronologists.

When Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople, dies, Acacius succeeds him. Evagrius; Nicephorus.

[Note: [Col. 0718D] III IV] **The fourth and fifth years of Simplicius.**

Theophanes marks this as the year 5964 of the world. He reports that Constantinople was besieged by the faction of Aspar [Col. 0720A], but that the besiegers were repulsed by Basiliscus and Zeno. Leo designates Olybrius, the husband of Placidia, as emperor; he nevertheless dies of illness.

Acacius of Constantinople extorts from the emperor Leo a privilege of the second see. See the notes, p. 173.

Eudoxia, after living with Honorius for sixteen years and bearing him a son, Hilderic, secretly flees to the holy places [Col. 0720B], where she dies. Theophanes. Sidonius Apollinaris is made bishop of the Arverni this year, according to Baronius and Petavius, from Sidonius’s first letter, book VI, and others. Pagi the Elder assigns this to the following year.

[Note: [Col. 0720B] Olympiad 312 IV and 313 I] **The fifth and sixth years of Simplicius.**

The Ostrogoths, who lived under King Valamir and his brothers Theodemir and Vidimir, divide after Valamir is killed. Some of them, led by Vidimir, make for Italy, where Glycerius was. But Vidimir dies there, leaving behind his son Vidimir, who is sent to the neighboring Visigoths—that is, the western Goths. Joining themselves to them, they defend Gaul and Spain as their rightful possessions. Theodemir attacks Illyricum and dies, leaving Theodoric as his successor. Jordanes.

[Note: [Col. 0720C] I II] **The sixth and seventh years of Simplicius.**

The emperor Zeno, from 19 January.

The Saracens raid Mesopotamia, and the Huns raid Thrace. Theophanes and Cedrenus.

Glycerius, driven from the empire by Nepos, the son of the sister of Marcellinus, formerly a patrician, is ordained bishop at the Port of the City of Rome. Marcellinus.

[Col. 0720D] Through the mediation of Epiphanius of Ticinum, the emperor Julius Nepos—called emperor by Leo Augustus and sent to Italy to expel Glycerius, which he accomplished—obtains peace from Evagrius. See the history in Pagi on this year, no. 8 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0720D] II III] **The seventh and eighth years of Simplicius.**

Theophanes reports that, after Leo’s death, Zeno fled to Syria because of the faction of Basiliscus. Basiliscus [Col. 0722A] is acclaimed Caesar in the camp and, at his wife’s urging, recalls Timothy the Cat and Peter the Fuller. He presses Acacius of Constantinople to condemn the Council of Chalcedon, but is prevented by the people. Evagrius, book III, chapter 4. Timothy Solofaciolus withdraws from Alexandria.

The Ostrogoths ravage Illyricum, with King Theodemir leading them together with his illustrious son Theodoric. Pagi the Elder, from Jordanes and others [Col. 0722B], on this year, no. 6 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0722B] III IV] **The eighth and ninth years of Simplicius.**

Simplicius writes to the emperor concerning the restraint of Timothy the Cat. See the notes on Simplicius.

Zeno reduces Peter the Fuller, a supporter of Basiliscus, to clerical order and banishes him to Pityus, from which he later escapes. Nevertheless, after Basiliscus was betrayed by the treachery of Armatus, he is banished to Cappadocia and shut up in a tower, where he dies of hunger. Procopius, book I, *Vandalic War*.

[Col. 0722C] Timothy the Cat, installed on the throne of Alexandria, is driven out by the monks. Theophanes. Liberatus, chapter 16, asserts that he brought about his own death by poison. The Alexandrians substitute Peter Mongus for the Cat; Zeno expels him, according to Liberatus and Pope Felix, letter 2. Petavius. Pagi the Elder judges that most of these events should be assigned to the following year.

[Note: [Col. 0722C] Olympiad 313, 14] **The ninth and tenth years of Simplicius.**

The body of the apostle Barnabas is discovered in Cyprus together with the Gospel of Matthew placed upon his breast [Col. 0722D]. On this occasion Cyprus is removed from the Antiochene patriarchate and assigned to Constantinople. Zeno, after expelling the bishops installed by Basiliscus, restores the Catholics who had been expelled or has new ones ordained. In particular, Peter the Fuller is expelled from Antioch, and Stephen is appointed in his place. Petavius, from Cedrenus and Theophanes, who adds that Stephen was declared innocent at the Synod of Laodicea, after having been accused of Nestorian heresy by the supporters of the Fuller. Pagi the Elder thinks that Stephen’s ordination should be postponed to the following years; see him [Col. 0724A]. See also the notes of Bencini, p. 171, and of Pagi, p. 177.

[Note: [Col. 0724A] I II] **The tenth and eleventh years of Simplicius.**

A Roman synod is held by Simplicius and a Constantinopolitan synod by Acacius. Peter the Fuller is condemned at both. See Pagi the Elder on this year, no. 6 and following, and the notes of Pagi the Younger on Simplicius.

[Note: [Col. 0724B] II III] **The eleventh and twelfth years of Simplicius.**

Stephen of Antioch [who was also called “the Elder”] is said by Petavius and Evagrius, book III, chapter 10, to have been stabbed this year with sharp pens by followers of the Fuller. Pagi the Elder, on this year, no. 3, contends that Stephen the Elder lived until 480 and was not stabbed by the Fullerians, but that the victim was Stephen the Younger; likewise, he teaches that the ordination of the younger Stephen, appropriated by Acacius, should be assigned to the year 481 [Col. 0724C].

[Note: [Col. 0724C] III IV] **The twelfth and thirteenth years of Simplicius.**

The imperial city is shaken by an earthquake for eleven continuous days, beginning on the eighth day before the Kalends of October. Marcellinus. But Pagi thinks that this should be transferred to the year 477, from Theophanes. See there, no. 9.

Huneric, with Zeno and Placidia arranging it, permits the Africans of Carthage [Col. 0724D] to choose a bishop. Eugenius is ordained. Victor of Vita, book II.

[Note: [Col. 0724D] Olympiad 314 IV and 315 I] **The thirteenth and fourteenth years of Simplicius.**

Stephen the Younger succeeds Stephen the Elder in the see of Antioch. Pagi, in the notes below, p. 177.

Theodoric, king of the Goths and son of Triarius, had approached to within four miles of Constantinople with his forces. He dies after being pierced by the point of a weapon while lying on a wagon [Col. 0726A]. Marcellinus.

Perozes, king of the Persians, dies around this year during an expedition against the Nephthalites, or White Huns. Pagi the Elder, no. 5, from Agathias and Procopius. Stephen the Elder, bishop of Antioch, dies there. See there, no. 6.

[Note: [Col. 0726A] I II] **The fourteenth and fifteenth years of Simplicius.**

The rites and decrees of Simplicius this year. See the notes of Pagi on Simplicius.

After Stephen the Younger of Antioch is killed, Calendion, an orthodox bishop, is appointed in his place. From a letter of Pope Simplicius, according to Pagi; he is ordained at Constantinople.

Theodoricus Volamer [or Amalus] lays waste to both Macedonias and Thessaly, and plunders Larissa, the metropolis. Marcellinus.

When Timothy Solophaciolus, bishop of Alexandria, died, John the Catholic succeeded him. The emperor Zeno ordered John expelled and published the Henoticon.

[Col. 0726C] [Note: [Col. 0726C] II III] Simplicius 15, 16. FELIX III, 1.

Saint Simplicius died on 2 March. The see remained vacant for five days. Saint Felix, third of that name, was elected and ordained on Sunday, 6 March. See the notes on Simplicius.

According to Bencini’s notes, he also held a synod at Rome, p. 182, in which Peter Cnapheus, usurper of the see of Antioch, was condemned as a Eutychian and Theopaschite.

Peter Moggus, bishop of Alexandria, wavered in the faith after accepting the Henoticon and became the occasion for the sect of the Acephali.

Stirred up by letters from the empress Verina, the Easterners accepted Leontius as emperor. Petavius, from Theophanes.

[Col. 0726D] [Note: [Col. 0726D] III IV] Felix III, 1 and 2.

The Third Roman Synod was held under Felix. See the notes, pp. 187, 189, 191, column 2. He appointed John Talaja to the church of Nola. Petavius, from Liberatus, ch. 18.

The Paschal Chronicle records that in this year the emperor Zeno made Basiliscus, son of Armatus, Master of the Soldiers Present, Caesar.

On 27 June, Indiction VII, Leontius entered Antioch as emperor and appointed Lilialus praetorian prefect. Zeno Augustus sent John the Scythian against him and his associate; defeated by John, they withdrew into a fortress. Petavius, from Theophanes.

A dreadful persecution was stirred up in Africa against the Catholics by King Huneric in February; more than 334 bishops were driven into exile. Huneric died on the Ides of December. Guntabudus succeeded him. Noris, *Historia Pelagiana*, book 2, ch. 21.

[Col. 0728B] [Note: [Col. 0728B] Olympiad 315 IV and 316] Felix 2 and 3.

The Fourth Roman Synod was held under Felix against the Fuller and Acacius. See the notes, pp. 187 and 191.

On the island of Cyprus, the body of Saint Barnabas the Apostle was discovered when he revealed its location; the Gospel of Saint Matthew was found at his breast and carried to Constantinople. Petavius. But the year is uncertain, within a period of three years. See Pagius for this year, no. 2.

After the Catholic Callandion was expelled from the throne of Antioch, Peter the Fuller occupied the see and appointed Xenaias, a Persian slave, bishop of Hierapolis; he was the first to teach against the sacred images, according to Theophanes in the *Miscellany* and Anastasius the Deacon in the Second Council of Nicaea. After Martyrius, bishop of Jerusalem, died, Sallustius succeeded him. Petavius. Pagius assigns this to the following year.

Felix 3 and 4.

[Col. 0728C] [Note: [Col. 0728C] II] John, a presbyter of the church of Antioch, wrote against the Eutychians. Marcellinus; Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 93, considers him suspect of Nestorianism, as Petavius observes.

Clovis married Clotilde, daughter of Chilperic of Burgundy, although he had already fathered Theodoric by a concubine. From Gregory of Tours.

[Col. 0728D] [Note: [Col. 0728D] II III] Felix 4 and 5.

The Fifth Roman Council was held under Felix III, during the consulship of Boethius, vir clarissimus. See the notes on Felix III.

Theodoric, king of the Goths, never satisfied with the favors of Zeno Augustus, advanced menacingly close to Constantinople and, after burning several places with fire, returned to Moesia. Marcellinus and Suidas.

Odoacer defeated Pebanus, king of the Rugians, in battle near the banks of the Danube and brought him captive on 17 November. Cassiodorus. See Pagius for this year, no. 3.

[Col. 0730A] [Note: [Col. 0730A] III IV] Felix 5 and 6.

Acacius died, according to Petavius, this year; according to Pagius, who follows Victor of Tunnuna, he died in the following year. Flavitta succeeded him but died after three months. Wishing to appear Catholic, Flavitta wrote to Felix; but Felix, having learned of his communion with Moggus, did not admit his envoys. Petavius.

Callandion transferred the relics of Saint Philip, bishop and martyr of Antioch, from Philippi to Antioch and brought his church’s schism to an end after one hundred years. Theophanes.

[Col. 0730B] [Note: [Col. 0730B] Olympiad 316 IV and Olympiad 317 I] Felix 6 and 7.

After Flavitta of Constantinople died, Euphemius was appointed in his place. He detested Peter Moggus but refused to erase Acacius, and therefore did not deserve communion with Pope Felix. Nicephorus, book XVI, ch. 19; Theophanes. See the notes below, p. 201.

Nevertheless, Pagius teaches from Victor of Tunnuna that Acacius’s death, and therefore also the succession, should be assigned to this year.

[Col. 0730D] [Note: [Col. 0730D] I II] Felix 7 and 8.

[Col. 0730D] Pope Felix commends a book written by Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, on grace and free will. Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 86. Petavius for this year.

After the Council of Arles, the Council of Lyon was recorded by the same author in this year. See Pagius Senior for this year, where he recounts the origin of the Predestinarian sect.

Peter Moggus died in this year, according to Baronius, Pagius, and Petavius, from Theophanes. Athanasius, likewise a heretic, succeeded him. There.

[Col. 0732A] [Note: [Col. 0732A] II III] Felix 8 and 9.

The Paschal Chronicle records under this consulship: “In this year, in the month Xanthicus, or April, seized by a flow of blood, Zeno died on the ninth day, aged sixty-five.”

He had reigned forty-five years. ANASTASIUS DICORUS was crowned in April, on Friday of Holy Week, Indiction XIV, according to the era of Great Antioch, year 537. The same is reported from Malalas.

The Council of Carpentras. See Pagius Senior for this year, no. 21.

Saint Patrick, the first bishop of Ireland, died in this year, according to Petavius. But see Pagius Senior.

[Col. 0732B] [Note: [Col. 0732B] III IV] Felix 9, who died on 25 February. See the notes on Felix III. GELASIUS was elected as his successor and ordained on 1 March. See the notes there.

Longinus, brother of the deceased Zeno, rebelled against Anastasius; he was nevertheless captured and banished to Alexandria, where he was ordained a presbyter.

The Isaurians, who were still in rebellion, were subdued by John the Scythian, John the Hunchback, and Diogenes, after a war prolonged for six years. Petavius, from Theophanes and Marcellinus.

Gelasius wrote to the bishops of Dardania that they should avoid communion with heretics. See the notes on Felix III.

[Col. 0732C] [Note: [Col. 0732C] Olympiad 317 IV and 318 I] Gelasius 1, and from 1 March, 2.

[Col. 0732D] Gelasius, through Faustus, Master of Offices, sent by King Theodoric to Constantinople, sought to recall the Greeks to their duty, but in vain. He dealt with Euphemius, bishop of Constantinople; he refuted the Greeks’ objections in writing and defended the faith against the Pelagians in Letters 5, 6, and 7.

A sedition broke out at Constantinople, during which the statues of the emperor Anastasius and his wife were thrown down and dragged through the city. Marcellinus.

Zamasphes, son of Perozes, king of the Persians, expelled Cabades and seized the kingdom for four years. There.

The commanders sent by Anastasius fought successfully against the Isaurians; only Conon was killed, a soldier who had been made a bishop. Petavius, from Theophanes.

[Col. 0734A] [Note: [Col. 0734A] I II] Gelasius 2 and 3.

A Roman synod at which Gelasius, together with seventy bishops, decreed which books were to be received by Catholics and which rejected. He also condemned Pelagius, Celestius, and Julian of Eclanum, together with their books, and rejected the writings of the Semi-Pelagians [Cassian and Faustus of Riez] as apocryphal. Baronius and Noris, *Historia Pelagiana*, book 2, ch. 17. But compare the notes added by Cardinal Noris to *Cenotaphium Pisanum*, dissertation 4, § 1, p. 445, and by Pagius for this year. In an ancient codex of the monastery of Santa Croce it is designated: “The Decree, under the consulship of Asterius and Praesidius, most illustrious men.”

[Col. 0734B] [Note: [Col. 0734B] II III III] Gelasius 3 and 4.

[Col. 0734C] The Second Roman Synod was held on the Ides of May. Misenus, formerly legate of the Apostolic See and tainted by communion with Acacius, was reconciled after doing penance.

Saint Eugenius, bishop of Carthage, died in exile in Gaul for the faith. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, ch. 3.

Euphemius, prelate of Constantinople, was reduced to lay status by the emperor Anastasius and driven into exile. Macedonius was substituted for him; he subscribed to the Henoticon. Marcellinus; Theophanes; Theodore the Reader; and Cedrenus, cited by Petavius for this year.

[Col. 0734D] [Note: [Col. 0734D] III IV] Gelasius 4 and 5. Gelasius died on 19 November, having held office for four years, eight months, and eighteen days, as stated in several codices, from Anastasius and others cited by Pagius Junior. He was buried at Saint Peter’s on 21 November. His successor, ANASTASIUS, second of that name, was elected and ordained on Sunday, 24 November. See the notes on Gelasius.

India sent the emperor Anastasius an elephant and two giraffes as gifts. Marcellinus.

Saint Epiphanius, bishop of Ticinum, died. Ennodius. Pagius assigns the conversion of Clovis to Christ to this year; Petavius assigned it to the preceding year and Baronius to three years later. See the notes on Gelasius.

[Col. 0736A] [Note: [Col. 0736A] Olympiad 318 IV and 319 I] Anastasius II, 1 and 2.

While Anastasius II was pope, the political situation was unfortunate: the rulers of the principalities were heretics—Anastasius the emperor, as he was later recognized; Theodoric in Italy; Alaric the Visigoth in Gaul; Gundebald among the Burgundians; the Arians; the Suebi; and any others in Spain. In Germany and Britain, however, the people were still pagan. Anastasius could rejoice only over the baptized Clovis. See the notes on Anastasius. Nevertheless, he sent as legates to the emperor Saint Germanus, bishop of Capua, and Cresconius of Todi, so that Acacius’s name might be abolished. Petavius for this year.

After Athanasius, the heretical bishop of Alexandria, died, John, infected with the same stain, succeeded him. There, from Liberatus. See also Pagius for this year, no. 3.

Anastasius II, 2 and 3. He died on 17 or 18 November. [Col. 0736C] [Note: [Col. 0736C] II] His successor, Symmachus, was ordained on 22 November. See the notes on Symmachus.

A great sedition broke out at Constantinople, and many were killed in it. Petavius, from the Alexandrian chronicle. The emperor struck coins called *folles*, which the Romans call *teruntiani*, for popular use. There, from Marcellinus.

Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, tried unsuccessfully, by order of the emperor, to bring into his communion the city’s monasteries that had withdrawn from communion with him because they refused to subscribe to the Henoticon. The constancy of the virgins, matrons, and Sophia prevailed. There, from Theophanes.

After Palladius, bishop of Antioch, died, Flavian succeeded him. There.

[Col. 0736D] [Note: [Col. 0736D] II III] Symmachus 1 and 2.

The First Roman Synod under Symmachus was held on 1 March against canvassing for the papacy.

Anastasius abolished several taxes, among them the *chrysargyrum*; he abolished amphitheatrical hunts; and he forbade magistracies to be bought and sold. Petavius, from Theophanes and Evagrius, book II, ch. 39, and also from Cedrenus.

[Col. 0738B] [Note: [Col. 0738B] III IV] Symmachus 2 and 3.

Pagius shows from Theodore the Reader and the Anonymous Valesianus that the Second Roman Synod under Symmachus was held in this year; at it peace was made between Symmachus and Laurentius before Theodoric came to Rome.

Saint Fulgentius came to Rome to the thresholds of the Apostles. Petavius, from the Acts preserved by Surius. The Saracens raided Phoenicia and Syria. The same from Theophanes.

[Col. 0738C] [Note: [Col. 0738C] Olympiad 319 IV and 320 I] Symmachus 3 and 4.

A synod was held at Rome concerning the schism stirred up by Laurentius; Petavius describes it briefly and clearly for this year. Theodoric, with the agreement of Symmachus himself, who was voluntarily willing to submit to judgment, decided that it should be convened. But the Fathers, apparently prevented by the faction of the schismatics from deciding anything concerning the bishop of the First See, finally, under pressure from the king, condemned Laurentius on 23 October and pronounced judgment in favor of Symmachus. See the notes on Symmachus. Pagius assigns the synod to 503.

Three thousand citizens were killed at Constantinople during a disturbance arising from theatrical games. Marcellinus.

Peace was made with the Arab Saracens by Anastasius, and tranquility was restored to the state. Theophanes.

[Col. 0740A] [Note: [Col. 0740A] I II] Symmachus 4 and 5.

The Fourth Roman Synod under Symmachus, called the Palmary Synod, was held at Rome. In it, the enactment of Odoacer, formerly king of the Heruli, was annulled; that enactment had been issued against the freedom of election of the Roman pontiff. See the notes on Symmachus, where Pagius Junior follows the opinion of his uncle, distinguishing the synod of this year, which he calls the Third, from the Fourth, the Palmary Synod under Symmachus, which he assigns to the following year. He pays no attention to the consular designations by which they are dated, believing that these resulted from scribal errors.

[Col. 0740B] [Note: [Col. 0740B] II III] Symmachus 5 and 6.

A synod was held at Rome, which Petavius calls the Fifth and Pagius the Fourth Palmary Synod.

The emperor Anastasius sent a huge army against the Persians, entrusting supreme command of the war to four commanders: Patricius, Hypatius, Celer, and Areobindus. Their discord, after earlier victories, so harassed the state that it was forced to purchase peace from the barbarians. Procopius, *Persian War*, chs. 8 and 9; Marcellinus; Theophanes.

[Col. 0740C] [Note: [Col. 0740C] III IV] Symmachus 6 and 7.

The Sixth Roman Synod, also the last under Symmachus, was held against those who occupied ecclesiastical property. See the notes on Symmachus.

The persecution by Thrasamund in Africa intensified. While the exiled bishops endured it, Pope Symmachus sent them annual assistance for their livelihood. See the notes there.

[Col. 0740D] [Note: [Col. 0740D] Olympiad 320 IV and 321 I] Symmachus 7 and 8.

In this year an end was declared to the Persian war through a truce concluded for seven years. King Cabades had been afflicted with various defeats by Celer, and Amida and other towns were restored. From Theophanes.

After John, bishop of Alexandria, died, John the Nicotaean succeeded him. Liberatus calls him Machaeotes; Petavius [does so as well].

The consul Sabinianus suffered a disgraceful defeat while fighting Mundon the Getan. Marcellinus.

[Col. 0742A] [Note: [Col. 0742A] I II] Symmachus 8 and 9.

The Council of Agde was held in Gaul on 3 September, during the consulship of Messala, in the twenty-second year of our lord King Alaric [the Visigoth]. See Noris, *Historia Pelagiana*, book I, ch. 19, p. 121.

The emperor Anastasius, having unsuccessfully tried to draw Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, into his heresy, harassed him because he resisted. He also brought Xenaias, leader of the Manichaeans, into the city; but when Macedonius rejected communion with him and the people rioted, he secretly removed him by night. Petavius, from Theophanes.

Pagius derives the publication of the Jewish Talmud, which they call the Babylonian Talmud, from the Jewish calendar in this year, and for the year 476, no. 19.

[Col. 0742B] [Note: [Col. 0742B] II III] Symmachus 9 and 10.

After learning of Clovis’s achievements, Anastasius sent him letters of consulship. At Tours, in the basilica of Saint Martin, Clovis put on a purple tunic and a cloak and placed a diadem on his head. He also scattered gold and silver among the people with his own hand; from that day he was called consul and Augustus. Evidently, he received the insignia of the consulship. Later, when he came to Paris, he established his royal seat there. Gregory, book 2, ch. 28, and Aimoinus, in Petavius for this year. Pagius interprets the insignia as those of the patriciate.

Anastasius fortified Daras, a town of Mesopotamia on the frontier of the Persian and Roman empires, and called it Anastasiopolis. There, from Theophanes and Evagrius, book III, ch. 37.

[Col. 0742D] [Note: [Col. 0742D] III IV] Symmachus 10 and 11.

Anastasius unsuccessfully attempted to have his Henoticon subscribed by Elias, bishop of Jerusalem. He also drew Flavian of Antioch partly over to his side, but not completely. See Evagrius, book III, ch. 31; Petavius for this year; and Pagius for 510, no. 2.

Gundebald, king of the Burgundians, driven from every side by Clovis, fled into Italy and died miserably. His son Sigismund retained what remained of the Burgundian kingdom and embraced the Catholic faith through the agency of Saint Avitus of Vienne. There, from Gregory, book III, ch. 5. But Pagius proves that Gundebald lived until 516.

[Col. 0744A] [Note: [Col. 0744A] Olympiad 321 IV and 322 I] Symmachus 11 and 12.

Two hundred heretical monks came from the East to Constantinople with Severus, the impious heretic. Received honorably by the emperor Anastasius against Macedonius and the Council of Chalcedon, they stirred up riots, with the support of John, bishop of Alexandria. Catholic monks then arrived from Palestine and defended the faith. Macedonius condemned Flavian of Antioch and the others who had risen against the synod. Petavius and Pagius, from Theophanes, Alexandrian year 501.

[Col. 0744B] [Note: [Col. 0744B] I II] Symmachus 12 and 13.

New disturbances were stirred up at Constantinople and throughout the East by Anastasius to promote acceptance of the Henoticon and abolish the Council of Chalcedon. Petavius warns, however, that Theophanes’s account should not be trusted in every respect. Pagius begins correcting the chronology in this year and in 512.

Vitalian, son of Patriciolus, fearing the suppression of the Catholic faith through the condemnation of the Council of Chalcedon and the expulsion of Catholic bishops, gathered a force of brave men and rose against Anastasius. Victor of Tunnuna and Jordanes, *On the Succession of the Kingdoms*, ch. 109. Pagius. See the notes on Symmachus.

[Col. 0744D] [Note: [Col. 0744D] II III] Symmachus 13 and 14.

When the Theopaschite *Trisagion* stirred up new disturbances at Constantinople, Anastasius was forced to approach Macedonius while preparing to flee and to pretend that he agreed with the Catholics. But shortly afterward, dropping the mask, he fabricated accusations against Macedonius—who had openly professed that he accepted the Council of Chalcedon together with the Catholic clergy—drove him from the episcopal throne, and sent him into exile. Macedonius refused to return the documents of the Catholic faith that Anastasius had signed at his coronation and placed upon the altar. Anastasius therefore arranged for Timothy to be intruded in his place and received back from him the deposited documents. From Theophanes and Evagrius. See Petavius for this year and Pagius, nos. 3 and following.

[Col. 0746B] [Note: [Col. 0746B] III IV] Symmachus 14 and 15.

The emperor Anastasius ordered that a pseudo-synod be held at Sidon against Chalcedon (see the notes, p. 225), but his expectation was frustrated. Elias, patriarch of Jerusalem, induced Flavian of Antioch and others to abstain from the impious undertaking. The emperor was angered at this and was appeased by an embassy from Saint Sabas. The Orthodox stirred up new disturbances against the emperor, who, after removing his diadem, addressed the people and won them over.

Areobindus, acclaimed emperor, fled. Vitalian too was called to the empire. See Pagius, who arranges these events from Marcellinus, Theophanes, and other writers; he also reports that in this year Flavian was driven into exile and Severus intruded in his place.

[Col. 0746C] [Note: [Col. 0746C] Olympiad 322 IV and 323 I] Symmachus 15 and 16. He convened the Council of Heraclea. See the notes, p. 227.

Severus was intruded into the see of Antioch after Flavian was driven into exile. Elias of Jerusalem was likewise exiled because he refused to anathematize the Council of Chalcedon, despite a renewed imperial decree (see the notes, p. 225). John, a partisan of Severus, was intruded in his place; through the agency of Saint Sabas, he later returned to publicly profess the Catholic faith. Cyril, in the *Life of Saint Sabas*, and from him Petavius. Pagius and others.

Cabades, king of the Persians, admiring the Christians’ power over demons, granted our people freedom to act in his kingdom.

[Col. 0746D] [Note: [Col. 0746D] I II] Symmachus 16. He died on 19 July of this year. See the notes, p. 213.

[Col. 0748A] HORMISDAS was elected successor on the 26th and ordained on 29 November. See the notes, p. 229; with this election the schism was removed and peace restored to the Church. See the notes on Hormisdas.

Petavius teaches for this year, from Marcellinus, that Count Vitalian, appointed leader and champion by the allied Orthodox, stood at Hebdomon with sixty thousand armed men; but he withdrew within eight days, deceived by Anastasius’s pretenses and perjuries.

[Col. 0748B] [Note: [Col. 0748B] II III] Hormisdas 1 and 2.

Vitalian rose more vehemently against Anastasius, who, through envoys sent to him, negotiated the restoration of peace to the Catholics. Theodoric, supporting Vitalian, did not cease urging Hormisdas to send envoys to Constantinople. Ennodius of Ticinum and others were sent.

The Huns, having crossed Armenia, devastated Cappadocia and Lycaonia.

[Col. 0748C] Macedonius, bishop of Constantinople, died in exile.

[Col. 0748C] [Note: [Col. 0748C] III IV] Hormisdas 2 and 3.

Anastasius prepared an embassy to Hormisdas and offered hope of convening a council. But since the emperor’s envoys were estranged from the Catholic faith, Hormisdas dismissed them.

The Illyrian bishops were restored to communion with the Roman Church. Baronius; Petavius; Pagius, from the letters of Hormisdas.

Elias, bishop of Jerusalem, died in exile, according to Pagius. Petavius writes that he died two years later.

[Col. 0748D] [Note: [Col. 0748D] Olympiad 323 IV and 324 I] Hormisdas 3 and 4.

Hormisdas’s embassy to Anastasius was renewed. Anastasius unsuccessfully tried to draw the envoys over to his view by gifts. They remained steadfast not only when expelled and placed on a frail ship, but also arranged for the Apostolic letters to be carried everywhere by faithful monks. See the notes on Hormisdas.

[Col. 0750A] A dreadful persecution was launched in Syria against the Catholics, especially the monks, by Severus of Antioch. The Maronites, more steadfast than the rest, suffered martyrdom. Baronius; Petavius; Pagius.

John, bishop of Alexandria, died. Dioscorus Junior was elected. Noris, *On the Synod*, book V, p. 7, from Victor’s Chronicle.

[Col. 0750A] [Note: [Col. 0750A] I II] Hormisdas 4 and 5.

[Col. 0750B] The impious emperor Anastasius died on Thursday of Holy Week, terrified by a vision or, as others maintain, struck by lightning. Timothy, bishop of Constantinople, also died. John the Cappadocian, a supporter of the Catholic faith, was elected in Timothy’s place and on the third day of Easter was invested with the pontifical ornaments. He convened a synod at Constantinople and held it; in it, the Holy Council of Chalcedon and the names of Pope Saint Leo and Macedonius were inserted into the sacred diptychs.

A synod was likewise held in Palestine to receive the doctrinal letter of Saint Leo and the Council of Chalcedon. See the notes [Col. 0750C] on Hormisdas.

[Col. 0750C] [Note: [Col. 0750C] II III] Hormisdas 5 and 6.

Hormisdas sent five envoys to Byzantium to settle the affairs disturbed by Anastasius. See the notes, pp. 235 and 237, and Noris, *Historia Pelagiana*, book 2, ch. 18.

The Scythian monks brought a dispute with Victor the Deacon concerning “one of the Trinity who suffered” and concerning Eutychian and Pelagian heresy. The matter was brought before the tribunal of Hormisdas. See the notes below.

Pagius assigns the death of Dioscorus and the succession of Timothy in the Catholic Church of Alexandria to this year, but Noris, *On the Synod*, book V, p. 7, shows that it occurred two years later.

[Col. 0750D] [Note: [Col. 0750D] III IV] Hormisdas 6 and 7.

Justinian, Master of the Soldiers, violating the faith that he had sworn by the Lord’s sacrament, out of ambition to rule, killed the consul Vitalian. Procopius, *Secret History*, p. 30. Some, with Theophanes, attribute the slaughter to the citizens of Constantinople; others, with Evagrius, book 4, ch. 3, attribute it to the deceit of Justin. See Petavius.

After John the Cappadocian died, Epiphanius succeeded him this year in the church of Constantinople.

[Col. 0752A] [Note: [Col. 0752A] Olympiad 324 IV and 325 I] Hormisdas 7 and 8.

John Malalas, p. 140. The same emperor, Justin, also prohibited the Olympic contests, so that thereafter they would not be celebrated at Antioch from Indiction XIV onward. From Afranius to the year 568 [of the Antiochene Era], when those games were prohibited, seventy-seven *alytarchs* are counted.

Victor, in Noris, *On the Synod*, book V, p. 7, assigns the succession of Dioscorus after the death of Timothy of Alexandria to this consulship.

After Paul of Antioch died, Euphrasius succeeded him. Theophanes.

[Col. 0752C] [Note: [Col. 0752C] I II] Hormisdas 8 and 9.

Tzathius, king of the Lazi, defected from the Persian king and came to Justin at Constantinople. After being initiated into the Christian rites and receiving royal insignia from Justin, he incurred the anger of Cabades, king of the Persians. Cabades stirred up against Justin Ziligbin, king of the Huns; Ziligbin later broke faith with both sides and was killed by Cabades, after which the Persian restored friendship with the Romans. Alexandrian Chronicle; Theophanes.

Cabades asked Justin to adopt his son Chosroes, but Justin refused after Proclus dissuaded him. Procopius, book 3, *Persian War*; Theophanes.

[Col. 0752D] [Note: [Col. 0752D] II III] Hormisdas 9 and 10. Hormisdas died on 6 August. See the notes, pp. 229 and 246. His successor, JOHN, was elected and ordained on Sunday, 13 July. See the notes, p. 246.

Elesbaan, king of the Ethiopians, or Axumites, embraced the Christian faith and entered into treaties with the new Christian king of the Homerites and with the emperor Justin. See Pagius, no. b and following.

Justin issued edicts against heretics and unbelievers and ordered the Manichaeans to be executed by beheading. Book 12, title *On Heretics and Manichaeans*.

[Col. 0754A] [Note: [Col. 0754A] III V] John 1 and 2.

Justin rebuilt Anazarbus, which had been destroyed by an earthquake, and named it Justinopolis after himself. Theophanes.

He also arranged for the churches of heretics, especially the Arians, to be dedicated according to the Catholic rite; as a result he experienced threats from Theodoric and incurred his anger. Petavius for this year.

John, bishop of Jerusalem, died on 22 April. Peter succeeded him. See Noris, *On the Synod*, book V, p. 21.

[Col. 0754B] [Note: [Col. 0754B] Olympiad 325 IV and 326 I] John 2 and 3.

Pope John, to prevent the harassment of Catholics, was forced by Theodoric of the same name to undertake an embassy to Justin. He was received by Justin with exceptional honor. See the notes on John I. But on his return he was received inhumanely by Theodoric. There.

Marcellinus, in his *Chronicle*, counts 475 years from the year of the chair of blessed Peter to this consulship. This is perhaps a scribal error, since the number is 485.

[Col. 0754C] [Note: [Col. 0754C] I II] John 3. After holding office for two years, eight months, and twenty-three days, he died at Ravenna in custody on 18 May and was buried in the basilica of Saint Peter during the consulship of Olybrius. The episcopate was vacant for fifty-eight days. [Col. 0754D] Saint FELIX IV, his successor, was ordained on 10 July. See the notes on John I and Cassiodorus, book 8, Letter 15.

John Malalas reports that a tremendous earthquake struck Antioch this year; 250,000 people perished on 29 May, a Thursday. Petavius and Cardinal Noris, *On the Synod*, book V, Oecumenical section, p. 20, likewise report from Evagrius that Euphemius, prefect of the East, was sent to Antioch to repair the ruins and was chosen as its bishop after Euphrasius died.

[Col. 0756A] Dionysius Exiguus composed his cycle in this year. Petavius for this year and book XII, ch. 3.

[Col. 0756A] [Note: [Col. 0756A] II III] Felix IV, 1, and from 12 July, 2.

Justin, dying after completing nine years, one month, and several days of his reign on 1 August, left Justinian alone as Augustus. Justinian ruled for thirty-eight years and eleven months, according to the Alexandrian Chronicle.

Nevertheless, the beginning of Justinian’s reign is reckoned from the day on which he shared the empire, 1 April, as is shown by his *Novella*. Cardinal Noris, *On the Synod*, book V, p. 85.

He governed the state with excellent laws, promoting the Catholic faith and the dignity of the Church. See Petavius and the letters of Cassiodorus cited by him for this year. Athalaric obtained peace from Justinian. There.

[Col. 0756B] [Note: [Col. 0756B] III IV] Felix 2 and 3.

On 1 January, Indiction VI, Justinian scattered such a quantity of money that no other emperor had distributed as much during his consulship. See the Paschal Chronicle for this year and Malalas, p. 153. He also sent assistance to Tzathius, king of the Lazi, who was being attacked by the Persians.

Gethes, king of the Heruli, went over to the Romans. Boazes, widow of the king of the Huns, likewise allied herself with them, accompanied by about one hundred thousand warriors. Cordas, king of the Huns who inhabited the Bosporus, likewise cultivated the Roman religion and alliance.

[Col. 0756C] [Note: [Col. 0756C] Olympiad 326 IV and 327] Felix 3 and 4.

[Col. 0756D] In this year Justinian’s Code was completed and ordered to have force from 16 April of the present Indiction VII. Code of Justinian; Paschal Chronicle. John Malalas, at the second consulship of Justinian, completed in Indiction VII, p. 156, counts 1,280 years from the founding of Rome and 199 from the founding of Constantinople. See the notes on that same Malalas.

Justinian also rebuilt Antioch and called it Theopolis. Alamundarus, petty king of the Saracens, devastated First Syria; when the Roman commanders moved against him, he fled as far as India. Petavius, from Theophanes, who also writes that Belisarius advanced successfully against the Persians, intercepted their envoys after their treachery had been discovered, and killed them after they confessed their crime.

[Col. 0758A] [Note: [Col. 0758A] I II] Felix 4 and 5. He died on 25 September. The see remained vacant for three days. BONIFACE was elected as successor on 28 September and ordained bishop on 29 September. See the notes on Felix IV.

The Persians were twice defeated in battles with the Romans this year. Rufinus was finally sent to negotiate peace with them but returned without accomplishing his mission. Narses and Ararius, brothers, defected from the Persians; the former proved to be a most capable commander.

Hilderic, king of the Vandals in Africa, was deprived of his kingdom by his cousin Gelimer. Gelimer, refusing his restoration, which Justinian demanded, threatened war. Procopius, book I, *Vandalic War*.

[Col. 0758C] [Note: [Col. 0758C] II III] Boniface 1 and 2.

Boniface approved the synodal acts of the Second Council of Orange in the sixth month after the council had been completed. See Noris, *Historia Pelagiana*, book 2, ch. 23, pp. 331 and following.

Boniface also held a Roman synod at which, contrary to the canons, he designated the deacon Vigilius as his successor. Shortly afterward, however, at another synod, the pontiff himself rescinded his written act. See the notes, where the Third Roman Council is also mentioned as having been held in the case of Stephen, bishop of Larissa, in this year.

[Col. 0758D] [Note: [Col. 0758D] III IV] Boniface 2 died on 8 November. JOHN, surnamed Mercurius, succeeded him.

At Constantinople, a violent sedition broke out in January because of the factions of the Circus. Hypatius was acclaimed emperor by the people, but on the following day he was captured, brought before the emperor, and killed. Procopius, book I, *Persian War*, and the other historians cited by Petavius.

The Origenists again rose up in Palestine, and their leader Nonnus stirred up disturbances. See the histories cited by Petavius and Cardinal Noris, *On the Synod*, book V, Oecumenical section, p. 4.

[Col. 0760B] [Note: [Col. 0760B] Olympiad 327 IV and 328 I] John II was ordained bishop on Sunday, 23 January. See the notes.

Embassies came to Pope John in the case against the Akoimētai, on behalf of the Scythian monks; judgment was rendered in their favor at the Roman council. See the notes on John II.

Peace with the Parthians was negotiated by Rufinus the patrician and Hermogenes, Master of Offices, envoys sent by Justinian. Marcellinus’s *Chronicle* and others cited by Petavius.

[Col. 0760C] [Note: [Col. 0760C] I II] John I and 2.

Pope John approved the profession of faith sent by Justinian together with an edict in which “one of the Trinity crucified” was declared; he deprived of communion the Akoimētai monks who denied the Ascension. See the notes on John II.

After Carthage was captured by Belisarius and Gelimer, the last king of the Vandals, who shortly before had killed Hilderic, was defeated and sent to Constantinople for the triumph; Africa, together with the Mediterranean islands formerly occupied by the Vandals, was restored to the empire. See Ruinart, *Chronology of the Vandal Persecution*, and Pagius for this year, with the notes on John II.

[Col. 0762A] [Note: [Col. 0762A] II III] John 2 and 3. John died on 27 May, after holding office for two years, four months, and six days. From the Lucensian Catalogue, volume II, prologue, folio XIX, and others cited by Pagius for this year. The episcopate was vacant for seven days.
