On 3 June, AGAPETUS, his successor, was ordained. He had come to Constantinople this year as an envoy sent by Theodahad, king of the Goths, as Marcellinus records in his *Chronicle*.

[Col. 0762B] Epiphanius, bishop of the imperial city, died before the arrival of the Roman prelate. Anthimus invaded his episcopate contrary to the canons, abandoning the church of Trebizond. There.

Boniface, bishop of Carthage, died. Reparatus succeeded him and held a general council of Africa, to which Agapetus sent congratulations. See Ruinart.

[Col. 0762B] [Note: [Col. 0762B] III IV] Agapetus 1. After Anthimus was removed, Mennas was appointed bishop on 14 March. See Cardinal Noris, *On One of the Trinity Who Suffered*, ch. 10. Agapetus died at Constantinople on 22 April, the day on which he is venerated. His body was brought back to Rome and buried on 20 September. Liberatus in the *Breviary*, Anastasius, and Marcellinus. The see remained vacant for twenty-eight days. SILVERIUS, his successor, was ordained on Sunday, 8 June. See the notes on Agapetus.

At the Constantinopolitan Synod, Severus, Peter of Apamea, Zoras, and Anthimus were condemned on 21 May. See Noris, *On the Synod*, book V, Oecumenical section, ch. 2.

Fifteen thousand Saracens under Alamundarus entered the Euphrates frontier. Because of the lack of pasture caused by the drought experienced in Persia, they were repelled by the skill of the frontier commanders from the war they desired. Marcellinus.

[Col. 0762D] [Note: [Col. 0762D] Olympiad 328 IV and 329 I] Silverius 1 and 2.

By order of the emperor, Silverius was deposed from the episcopate on 19 November (Pagius assigns it to the 22nd), and the deacon Vigilius was intruded in his place; Vigilius was ordained bishop on 22 November. *Bibliotheca*, in the section on Vigilius, §104.

Pagius Senior observes that Justinian’s decennalia were completed this year and places the dedication of the Church of Saint Sophia on 27 December, from the continuator of Marcellinus.

After Timothy, bishop of Alexandria, died, first Gajanus and then Theodosius succeeded him. Pagius for this year, from the history of the Coptic patriarchs; Cardinal Noris assigns it to the following year in *On the Synod*, book V, Oecumenical section, p. 8, from Victor’s Chronicle.

Vitiges besieged Rome around the spring equinox. There, no. 7, from the continuator of Marcellinus.

[Col. 0764B] The political settlement of Gaul: when Vitiges ceded to the Franks the part that had been subject to the Goths, the Franks began to possess the whole of Gaul, except Septimania, where the Visigoths remained, and except Britain and Armorica, which had their own counts. See Pagius for this year, no. 3.

[Col. 0764B] [Note: [Col. 0764B] I II] Silverius 2. Since he died in exile in June of this year, he made way for the succession of VIGILIUS. Vigilius, who had been an usurper, became the legitimate pontiff after Silverius’s death by the consent of the clergy; from this point he ought to date the beginning of his see. See the notes on Vigilius.

The Origenists, under the leadership of Nonnus, caused disturbances in Palestine. See Pagius for this year, no. 12 and following, and Noris, cited by him, in his dissertation on the Fifth Synod.

The disturbance of the Alexandrian Church after Timothy’s death, when, through a perverse election by the two factions, Theodosius and Gajanus were ordained bishops on the same day, is assigned to this year by Cardinal Noris, *On the Synod*, book V, p. 8; Pagius assigns it to the preceding year.

[Col. 0764D] [Note: [Col. 0764D] II III] Vigilius 1 and 2.

Chosroes, king of the Persians, moved by an embassy from Vitiges, set out to wage war against the Roman Empire. Procopius, book 2, *Persian War*, chs. 2 and 5; from this source Pelagius for this year, no. 5, and for the following year, no. 12.

Nevertheless, Vitiges, besieged at Ravenna with his wife and children, is captured by Belisarius and sent to Constantinople [Col. 0766A] to Justinian. Procopius, Book II of *The Gothic War*, chapter 28. See Pagius, under the year 540, no. 11. The Goths establish Hildebad as their king. Procopius and Pagius, at that place.

Hildebad, after Vitiges, was called king of the Goths, having previously been commander of Verona.

[Note: [Col. 0766A] III IV] Years 2 and 3 of Vigilius.

The Parthians enter Syria and destroy many cities. Great Antioch [Col. 0766B] is demolished by the Persians. Marcellinus. Malalas adds that Antioch was captured in June, indiction 3.

Theodosius, bishop of Alexandria, because he refused to receive the Council of Chalcedon, is struck with an anathema by Pope Vigilius and driven into exile by Justinian. Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, p. 8.

[Col. 0766C] [Note: [Col. 0766C] Olympiad 329 IV and 330 I] Years 3 and 4 of Vigilius.

In these consulships, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April, according to Justinian’s Novella 131, and in accordance with what had been defined by the most holy Pope Vigilius, a new metropolis, the Church of Justiniana Prima, is established, while the Primate of Thessalonica is deprived of his ancient jurisdiction. See [Col. 0766D] Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, chapter 4, p. 31.

Paul, superior of the monks of Tabennisi, is ordained bishop of Alexandria by the defenders of the Council of Chalcedon, after Theodosius and Gajanus had been driven into exile. There, p. 8, from Victor of Tunnuna and others.

Recalled from Italy by the Emperor, Belisarius comes to Byzantium. After wintering there, at the beginning of spring Augustus sends him against Chosroes and the Persians with supreme command of the war, together with the commanders who had followed him when he returned from Italy [Col. 0768A]. Procopius, Book II of *The Persian War*, chapter 14.

Pagius teaches that Totila’s reign must be dated from this point—namely, from the eighth year of the Gothic War—together with the conquest of the places in Emilia and Samnium, concerning which see Procopius, Book III of *The Gothic War*, chapters 6 and 7. See Pagius under the year 543, no. 2.

[Note: [Col. 0768A] I II] Years 4 and 5 of Vigilius.

Chosroes’ third expedition against the Romans [Col. 0768B], concerning which see Procopius, Book II of *The Persian War*, chapter 20, and, following him, Pagius under this year, no. 3.

Although Belisarius had driven back the Persians with distinction, he nevertheless incurred Justinian’s displeasure through Theodora’s intrigues and was recalled to Constantinople. See Pagius there, from Procopius’ *Secret History*, chapter 3, indicating these matters, no. 4.

A very severe plague rages in Egypt and Constantinople. See Calvisius under this year, from Procopius.

[Col. 0768C] [Note: [Col. 0768C] II III] Years 5 and 6 of Vigilius.

Paul, bishop of Alexandria, is deposed, and Zoilus is placed over that Church. Noris, *On the Fifth Ecumenical Synod*, p. 9, from Liberatus and others.

At the urging of Pelagius, representative of the Roman See, and of the Palestinian monks, Justinian publishes an encyclical against Origen, which he sends to the patriarchs so that Origen may be condemned by them again. See Noris there, chapter 2, where the subsequent condemnation and its subscription are established.

[Col. 0768D] [Note: [Col. 0768D] III IV] Years 6 and 7 of Vigilius.

Vigilius departs from Rome around the end of November, having been summoned to Constantinople by Justinian, who had been stirred up by the deceptions of the Acephali. See the notes below. Arator, subdeacon of the Holy Roman Church, had presented to Vigilius the *Acts of the Apostles* in verse in this year, in the third year after the consulship of Basilius, in April, indiction 7. See Pagius, no. 3, from Baronius.

Chosroes undertakes a fourth expedition [Col. 0770A] against the Roman Empire. There, no. 4.

[Note: [Col. 0770A] Olympiad 330 IV and 331 I] Years 7 and 8 of Vigilius.

In the preceding year the Origenists, having enticed Justinian with an empty hope, had induced him to expunge the Three Chapters from the Council of Chalcedon. The papal representative, acting [Col. 0770B] at Constantinople, refused to subscribe to this expunction [although the Easterners had been compelled to subscribe], as did others; but Vigilius, together with the Westerners, refused much more firmly. For this reason the Emperor had decided that a Council should be convened. Summoned to it in this year, Vigilius delays in Sicily. [See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, p. 23.] From there he sends grain ships to Rome, loaded with grain to relieve the hunger of the besieged city; the Goths intercept them. Noris, there, p. 26. See Pagius under the year 546, no. 1.

[Note: [Col. 0770B] I II] Years 8 and 9 of Vigilius.

On the day before the Ides of October, in the fifth year after the consulship of Basilius, in the tenth indiction [Col. 0770C], at Patras in Achaea, Maximianus is consecrated bishop of Ravenna by Pope Vigilius.

A popular revolt almost broke out at Constantinople, both because of the edict concerning the Three Chapters and because the abstinence from meat before the Paschal feasts had begun earlier than usual. See Agnellus, *Life of Maximianus*, p. 85, Bachini’s edition; Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, pp. 24–25; and the notes to Vigilius.

[Note: [Col. 0770C] I II] Years 9 and 10 of Vigilius.

[Col. 0770D] Vigilius entered Constantinople on the eighth day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth year after the consulship of Basilius, according to the author of Marcellinus’ continuation. A few days later he excludes Mennas, the bishop of Constantinople, from the sacred rites and publishes a Decree against the Acephali, although they were supported by the patronage of the Empress Theodora. See the notes below, p. 280. He promises that he will condemn the Three Chapters. He restores peace with Mennas on the Feast of the Apostles. See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, p. 27; the notes to Vigilius; and Pagius under this year, nos. 5 and following.

[Col. 0772A] [Note: [Col. 0772A] III IV] Years 10 and 11 of Vigilius.

In January, the name of the Patriarch of Constantinople was removed from the first place, Vigilius being placed above him. [Col. 0772B] Theophanes, under this year. See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, chapter 4. Vigilius convenes and opens the Council at Constantinople and issues a Judgment in which he condemns the Three Chapters, while preserving in every respect the reverence due to the Council of Chalcedon. The Africans, Illyrians, and nearly all the Westerners oppose this Judgment. See Noris there, the notes below, and Pagius under this year and 547.

The Empress Theodora, patroness of the Acephali and author—or occasion—of the entire tragedy of the Three Chapters, dies in June. Noris, there.

[Col. 0772C] [Note: [Col. 0772C] Olympiad 331 IV and 332 I] Years 11 and 12 of Vigilius.

After the eighth year following the consulship of Basilius, the Emperor Justinian compels all the bishops throughout the provinces of his realm to condemn the Three Chapters. Victor of Tunnuna. See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, chapter 4.

The Persian war proceeds with less success for the Romans, who are forced to withdraw from the siege of Petra and make a five-year truce with the Persians. See Pagius under this year, no. 3.

[Col. 0772D] The Illyrian synod writes to Justinian in defense of the Three Chapters and condemns Bishop Benenatus as their detractor. See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, chapter 4, and Pagius under this year.

[Note: [Col. 0772D] I II] Years 12 and 13 of Vigilius.

Vigilius condemns Rusticus and Sebastianus, [Col. 0774A] deacons of the Holy Roman Church, as adversaries of the holy Council of Chalcedon. See Baronius, Noris, and Pagius under this year, nos. 4 and 5, and the notes below.

The African bishops, with the greatest rashness, excommunicate Vigilius by synodal judgment. Victor of Tunnuna. Both they and the Illyrians are struck down by the decree of Vigilius and by Justinian’s rescript. There, the question concerns the convening of an ecumenical synod. Meanwhile, a synod is held at Mopsuestia in this year. See Noris and Pagius under this year, nos. 9 and 10. Vigilius recovers his Judgment from the hands of Mennas. See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, at the end of chapter 4.

[Note: [Col. 0774B] II III] Years 13 and 14 of Vigilius.

When the Western bishops were approaching Constantinople for the synod, Vigilius decided to celebrate it without them. Justinian condemns the Three Chapters by his edict. Vigilius, having summoned the bishops, declares anyone who gives assent to the condemnation suspended from communion with the Apostolic See [Col. 0774C]. The indignant Emperor orders him to be kept under guard; but, escaping, he reaches Chalcedon with the bishops who adhered to him. See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, pp. 40–48.

[Note: [Col. 0774C] III IV] Years 14 and 15 of Vigilius.

Vigilius’ steadfastness, tested by so many trials, persuades Justinian to recall him to Constantinople by sending a delegation to him with an oath of indemnity. For he understood that nothing could be firmly established without the consent of the Roman pontiff [Col. 0774D]. Vigilius returns, and receives Mennas, Theodore, Andrew of Ephesus, and other bishops, who were asking pardon, back into favor and communion. Justinian revokes the edict. Mennas dies. Eutychius succeeds him in the see of Constantinople. See Noris there, pp. 49–51, and the notes to Vigilius.

The royal remains of the slain Totila are sent to Constantinople.

[Col. 0776A] The Armenian era now in use began this year on 9 July, a Tuesday. See Pagius under this year, no. 23.

[Note: [Col. 0776A] Olympiad 332 IV and 333 I] Years 15 and 16 of Vigilius.

The first session of the Fifth Ecumenical Synod is held on 5 May. Vigilius publishes his Constitution on 14 May. See [Col. 0776B] the notes, pp. 284–285. The eighth and final session is held on the fourth day before the Nones of July. See Noris, from pp. 65–69.

After hesitating for a short time over the approval of the acts of the Council, Vigilius finally signed it in the following year. See the notes to Vigilius.

[Note: [Col. 0776B] I II] Years 16 and 17 of Vigilius.

Although Vigilius had not been present with the other patriarchs, he approves the acts of the Council, condemns the Three [Col. 0776C] Chapters, and is permitted to return to Italy. But when he reached Sicily, he was brought to the end of his life by the pain of a calculus at the beginning of the following year. See the notes below on Vigilius.

While the Persians were at rest, Justinian entrusts to Justin, the son of Germanus, the regions of Colchis and Armenia with full authority; Justin oppresses them through John the African with harsh exactions. Agathias.

[Col. 0776D] [Note: [Col. 0776D] II] Year 17 of Vigilius and the first of Pelagius.

Vigilius dies at Syracuse in Sicily on 11 January. On Sunday, 18 April, Pelagius is ordained bishop as his successor. See the notes to Pelagius, where the usurpation attempted and introduced by Justinian is discussed—following the example of the Goths—in the election of the Roman pontiff, from which the Church was certainly liberated under King Pippin.

[Col. 0778A] [Note: [Col. 0778A] III IV] Years 1 and 2 of Pelagius.

Pelagius replies to the legates and to the letters sent to him by Childebert, king of the Franks, concerning the dogmatic teaching of St. Leo and the faith of the Council of Chalcedon, pronouncing an anathema against those who thought differently about the faith [Col. 0778B] from what was contained in the letters of St. Leo and in the Council of Chalcedon. See Pagius under this year, no. 7. Peace is established with the Persians.

[Note: [Col. 0778B] Olympiad 333 IV and 334 I] Years 2 and 3 of Pelagius.

Pelagius grants Childebert’s customary request for a pallium for the bishop of Arles, together with apostolic authority.

Around this year the schismatics of Aquileia held a synod against the Fifth Ecumenical Council. Pelagius asks Narses [Col. 0778C] to restrain the schismatics and to send Paulinus, their principal leader and bishop, as a captive to Justinian. See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, p. 82.

Years 3 and 4 of Pelagius.

[Note: [Col. 0778C] II] A plague rages at Constantinople from February to July. The Bulgars, or Huns, and the Slavs invade the region around Thrace and the Tauric Chersonese; Belisarius is sent against them. [Col. 0778D] Theophanes and Agathias.

[Note: [Col. 0778D] II III] Years 4 and 5 of Pelagius.

The Bulgars are driven back across the Danube by Belisarius. Agathias.

In this year the holy virgin Sira, born at Seleucia in Mesopotamia, is crowned with martyrdom in Persia by a certain prefect. Pagius, from her life, under this year, no. 10.

In the see of Antioch, Anastasius succeeds Domninus. See Pagius [Col. 0780A] under the year 561, no. 2, from Theophanes.

[Note: [Col. 0780A] III IV] Pelagius 5, who dies on 2 March; JOHN III is ordained as his successor on the Kalends of August. See the notes, p. 294 and following.

Mediob [reading uncertain], at or in Occon [reading uncertain], writes that the Huns crossed from Moesia into Thrace in this year and were driven back by Belisarius. See Malalas.

[Col. 0780B] [Note: [Col. 0780B] Olympiad 334 IV and 335 I] Years 1 and 2 of John.

Victor of Tunnuna reported in his *Chronicle* that, after the twentieth year following the consulship of Basilius, the Bulgars’ invasion of Thrace, their raid near Constantinople, and their capture of Sergius Patricius occurred in this year, and that they were driven back across the Danube by Belisarius.

A fifty-year peace is established with the Persians in this year. Menander Protector, in the excerpt *On Embassies*. See Pagius under this year, nos. 9 and 10.

[Note: [Col. 0780B] I II] Years 2 and 3 of John.

[Col. 0780C] The body of St. Antony the Hermit is discovered and, with the greatest honor, brought to Alexandria, where it is reverently placed in the Basilica of St. John the Baptist. Victor of Tunnuna.

The Great Church of St. Sophia at Constantinople is dedicated this year on 24 December. Theophanes and Agathias, from whom Pagius and other historians draw their accounts.

[Note: [Col. 0780C] II III] Years 3 and 4 of John.

A conspiracy arises against Justinian at Constantinople, concerning which Theophanes brings even many innocent men into danger, among them Belisarius. But when Belisarius’ innocence was subsequently recognized, he was restored to the honors from which he had fallen. See Pagius under the year 561, no. 1, where he demonstrates, from the chronological indications given by Theophanes, that the conspiracy should be assigned to this year.

[Note: [Col. 0780C] III IV] Years 4 and 5 of John.

On 19 July, Patricius Belisarius, restored to all his former honors, is also received back into the Emperor’s favor [Col. 0782A]. Theophanes. See Pagius there, no. 5. Eustochius, bishop of Jerusalem, who had been ordained while Macarius was still alive, is expelled; Macarius is restored once again—that is, reinstated. Victor of Tunnuna and Evagrius, in Pagius; see him under the year 561, no. 3.

[Note: [Col. 0782A] Olympiad 335 IV and 336 I] Years 5 and 6 of John.

[Col. 0782B] In March of this year, indiction 13, Patricius Belisarius dies at Byzantium. Theophanes. See Pagius, no. 5, under the year 561.

At the beginning of this year Justinian issued his edict concerning the incorruptibility of Christ’s body. Pagius under this year, no. 2. Because of it, Eutychius, Patriarch of Constantinople, was expelled when he refused to subscribe to a heretical opinion, and John Scholasticus was intruded into his place. See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, p. 91, and Pagius, no. 2, under the year 563.

[Col. 0782C] [Note: [Col. 0782C] I II] Years 6 and 7 of John.

Envoys of the Avars, received by Justin near the end of the preceding November, are sent away without those gifts which they had been accustomed to demand arrogantly. Pagius, from Menander in the excerpts, and from Corippus, under this year, nos. 4 and 5.

The Turks also prepare an embassy to Justin, so that he would not receive the Avars.

[Col. 0782D] [Note: [Col. 0782D] II III] Years 7 and 8 of John.

In the second year of Justin’s consulship, June, August, first indiction: “In this year Narses, after so many tyrants had been overthrown—namely, Baduila and Teia, kings of the Goths; Bucelinus, commander of the Franks; and also Sindaral, the Herul, as well as Milan and the remaining cities which the Goths had destroyed and which had been laudably restored—was removed from Italy by the aforementioned Augustus.” Marcellinus Aventicensis.

The Emperor Justin and Chosroes break the treaties established between the Romans and Persians at the end of the second year of the Empire. Pagius under this year, no. 6, from Theophanes.

[Note: [Col. 0784A] III IV] Years 8 and 9 of John.

Narses, terrified by the threats of Sophia Augusta, the wife of Justin, and recalled from the exarchate of Italy, in which Longinus had succeeded him, invites the Lombards into Italy. See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, p. 89, and Pagius under the preceding year, no. 5 and following. They rightly warn that two different men named Narses must be distinguished, and produce ancient historians as witnesses of this event. Pagius places the entry into Italy one year earlier than Noris, chiefly on the basis of the edict of Rothari, or the beginning of the Lombard laws, which he cites under this year, no. 5.

[Note: [Col. 0784B] Olympiad 336 IV and 337 I] Years 9 and 10 of John.

The Emperor Justin, through Tiberius, Count of the Excubitors, brings war in Thrace against the barbarian people, the Avars, and the victorious Tiberius returns to Constantinople. The Abbot of Biclaro, noted by Pagius under this year, no. 4.

According to Pope John, as Gregory the Great testifies, Book III, Letter 2, those who were consecrated as bishops of cities were required to swear, orally and in writing, to the Fifth Synod. See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, p. 89.

[Note: [Col. 0784C] I II] Years 10 and 11 of John.

Baronius assigned to this year the death of Apollinaris, bishop of Alexandria [Col. 0784D]; Pagius assigns it to the preceding year, together with the ordination of John, his successor. See both authors. The Emperor Justin makes Armenia and Iberia Roman provinces, although they had belonged to the Persians. Hence the Persian war began. Calvisius, from the Arabic historian Gerundus, refers in this year to the birth of Muhammad the Saracen, on 5 May, a Monday. There.

[Note: [Col. 0784D] II III] Years 11 and 12 of John.

Macarius II, Patriarch of Jerusalem, dies around this year [Col. 0786A]. John succeeds him. Pagius under this year, no. 4.

Pagius dates the beginning of the twenty-year Persian war to this year, on the basis of Theophylact, Book III, chapter 8, because the Persarmenians surrendered themselves to the Romans in the first year of the pontificate of Gregory—the patriarch of Antioch, namely, the man who was appointed by Justin in place of the deposed Anastasius. Others also refer the causes of the broken peace to the embassies sent by Justin to Arethas [Col. 0786B], king of the Ethiopians, and to Justin by the Turks. There, and under the following year, no. 11.

[Note: [Col. 0786B] III IV] Years 12 and 13 of John.

Marcianus, Master of the Eastern Forces and related by blood to the Emperor, is sent against the Persians. Though advanced in age, he reaches Osrhoene; after crossing the Euphrates, he drives the barbarians back into the region of Arzanene and puts them to flight in terror. From Evagrius, Book V, chapter 8, and Theophanes of Byzantium, in Photius [Col. 0786C]. Pagius shows that this event should be assigned to the preceding year, no. 7.

Justin, while ill, behaves insultingly toward his own brother Badua. Baronius and Pagius under this year, no. 15, from Theophanes.

[Note: [Col. 0786C] Olympiad 337 IV and 338 I] John 13, who dies on 23 July after having sat for 11 years, 11 months, and 27 days. The See is vacant for 10 months and 3 days. See the notes to John III.

Marcianus advances from the town of Dara against the Persians who were moving toward Nisibis, defeats them, and returns once more to Dara. Theophylact, Book III, chapter 10, in Pagius under this year, no. 6.

Chosroes, on the other hand, burns Apamea in Coelesyria and returns again to Persia. There, no. 7.

[Note: [Col. 0786D] I II] Benedict I, from 27 May.

After the See had been vacant for 10 months and 3 days since John’s death, BENEDICT is elected and ordained on Sunday, 27 May [Col. 0788A]. See the notes to Benedict I.

The Persians capture Dara, and the Romans lift the siege of Nisibis. Evagrius, Book V, chapter 10, and others in Pagius under this year, no. 3.

The privileges granted to the Samaritans by Justinian are taken away. There, no. 10.

[Col. 0788B] [Note: [Col. 0788B] II III] Years 1 and 2 of Benedict.

A three-year truce is established with the Persians throughout the East, Armenia excluded; in Armenia the forces of both the Roman and Persian Empires clash. Chosroes is defeated by the Romans, who advance into Persia itself, ravage it, and send twenty-four elephants among the Persian spoils to Constantinople. See Theophylact and the Abbot of Biclaro, cited on this matter by Pagius under this year, nos. 6 and 7.

[Col. 0788C] [Note: [Col. 0788C] III IV] Years 2 and 3 of Benedict.

Contrary to the agreed three-year truce, the Persians attack Constantina and Theodosiopolis and ravage the neighboring parts of Armenia. From Theophylact and Menander, Pagius under this year, nos. 6 and 7.

[Note: [Col. 0788C] Olympiad 338 IV and 339 I] Years 3 and 4 of Benedict.

Eutychius is recalled from exile to Constantinople on 3 October, after the death of John Scholasticus, who had been intruded into his see by the Emperor Justinian. See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, p. 91 and following. Pagius confirms this, no. 5, under the year 578.

[Note: [Col. 0788D] I II] Years 4 and 5 of Benedict.

Benedict, after having occupied the see for 4 years, 1 month, and 28 days, dies on 25 July of this year and is buried on the 30th [from the Library] [Col. 0790A]. The episcopate was vacant for 3 months and 10 days (the Catalogue of Lucca gives 3 months and 25 days). PELAGIUS II, elected as his successor, is ordained on Sunday, 27 November. See the notes, p. 305.

Mauricius, a commander [later Emperor], sent against the Persians, ravages their territory. Pagius under this year, no. 6, from Theophanes.

[Col. 0790B] [Note: [Col. 0790B] II III] Years 1 and 2 of Pelagius.

While peace between the Romans and Persians is being negotiated, Chosroes dies, having reigned for 48 years. Hormisdas succeeds him in the kingdom and, receiving the legates arrogantly, replies that he will grant peace on no other condition than that all the sums annually contributed by Justinian be paid. From Theophylact and Menander, Pagius under this year, no. 3 and following.

[Col. 0790C] [Note: [Col. 0790C] III IV] Years 2 and 3 of Pelagius.

Tiberius Mauricius undertakes an expedition against the arrogant Hormisdas. He pitches camp on the bank of the Tigris and sends Martinus and Theodoricus into enemy territory, which they devastate. Theophylact.

Eulogius, Patriarch of Alexandria, succeeds John. Pagius under this year, no. 8.

[Col. 0790D] [Note: [Col. 0790D] Olympiad 339 IV and 340 I] Years 3 and 4 of Pelagius.

The Persian war again intensifies. In it the Romans win a splendid victory, capturing Hormisdas’ camp and equipment, together with his elephants; these are reserved solely for the Emperor, while the rest is given to the soldiers. Calvisius, from Zonaras. To this add Theophylact [Col. 0792A] and Evagrius, cited by Pagius under this year, no. 14.

Sirmium is surrendered to the Avars by the Romans. There, no. 15, from Menander Protector, p. 175.

Marius, bishop of Aventicum, or Lausanne, who subscribed the Second Council of Mâcon in 585, completes his *Chronicle* in this year, continuing Prosper’s *Chronicle*. Pagius there, no. 17.

[Col. 0792B] [Note: [Col. 0792B] I II] Years 4 and 5 of Pelagius.

St. Eutychius, Patriarch of Constantinople, dies on 6 April, and six days later John the Deacon, called the Faster, is consecrated as his successor. See Pagius, no. 6 and following, under this year.

The *Alexandrian Chronicle* reports that Mauricius was raised to the dignity of Caesar on 5 August, indiction 15, was crowned Augustus on the 13th, and that Tiberius Constantine died on the following day. See Pagius under this year, no. 9.

[Note: [Col. 0792B] II III] Years 5 and 6 of Pelagius.

[Col. 0792C] A terrible earthquake occurs at Constantinople on the tenth day of May [reading uncertain] in the first year of Tiberius Mauricius; it is recorded by Theophylact, Book II, chapter 12, and by Theophanes. They add that the envoys of the Avars asked Mauricius that 80,000 be added to their annual payment, along with another 20,000. When the Emperor refused this addition, the Avars declared war and captured Singidunum, Augusta, and Viminacium. See Pagius under this year, nos. 14 and 15.

Persecution of the Catholic Church by Leovigild, king of the Goths, in [Col. 0792D] Spain. There, no. 9.

[Note: [Col. 0792D] III IV] Years 6 and 7 of Pelagius.

Around the end of this year, or the beginning of the next, St. Gregory, papal representative of Pope Pelagius at Constantinople, returns to Rome. Pagius under this year, no. 13; a letter of Pelagius is extant there, issued by Baronius as no. 15, dated on the fourth day before the Nones of October, indiction 3. Pagius, no. 13.

The Persian war continues. There, no. 15.

[Col. 0794A] [Note: [Col. 0794A] Olympiad 340 IV and 341 I] Years 7 and 8 of Pelagius.

Theodosius, son of the Emperor Mauricius, is born. Theophanes, in Pagius under the year 588, no. 9.

Pagius proves that the martyrdom of St. Hermenegild occurred in this year, no. 2 and following, under the year 584.

Around this year St. Columbanus, promoter of monastic discipline, left the island of Ireland and came to Gaul, as Mabillon argues from an ancient codex; Pagius agrees with him under this year, no. 5.

Childebert, king of the Franks, intending to avenge the death of St. Hermenegild, whose sister he had married, sends an army into Spain; but it is repelled by Reccared, Leovigild’s commander. Isidore.

[Note: [Col. 0794B] I II] Years 8 and 9 of Pelagius.

Pelagius sends a letter to the bishops of Istria who were persisting in schism over the matter of the Three Chapters, and establishes a legation to bring them back to the unity of the Church. He seeks the assistance of Flavius Smaragdus, the exarch, with whose support the Lombards had made a truce, fearing the arrival of Childebert, king of the Franks, with strong forces to aid the Romans. From both Gregorys—Gregory the Great and Gregory of Tours—and from Paul the Deacon, Noris and Pagius under this year, nos. 4 and following.

[Col. 0794D] [Note: [Col. 0794D] II III] Years 9 and 10 of Pelagius.

The Romans ravage parts of Persia. The Avars harass Thrace. From Theophylact, Book II, chapter 10. Pagius under this year, nos. 3 and 4.

From an epitaph of Caesaria in the diocese of Avignon, sent to Baronius, in which the middle of the night is said to have dawned on Sunday, the sixth day before the Ides of December, in the fortieth year, and in the sixth post-consular year of Basilius Junior, *vir clarissimus*, consul, in the twelfth year of the reign of Lord Childebert, king, in the fifth indiction, Pagius shows that several chronological eras are established for this year.

[Col. 0796A] [Note: [Col. 0796A] III IV] Years 10 and 11 of Pelagius.

John, Patriarch of Constantinople, holds a synod in the case of Gregory, Patriarch of Antioch, accused of incest; Gregory is declared innocent and returns to his bishopric. At that time the Roman army, fighting against the Persians, was in turmoil because of the reduction of the grain supply, fraudulently suggested by Philippicus. Once the tumult had been calmed, [Col. 0796B] the Romans won a notable victory over the Persians and sent rich spoils to Constantinople. Pagius under this year, from Theophylact and others, nos. 3 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0796B] Olympiad 341 IV and 342 I] Years 11 and 12 of Pelagius.

Although the Romans had defeated the Persians in the preceding year, they did not cease fighting them near Martyropolis. Philippicus was reluctantly accepted as commander by the army, through the persuasion of Gregory, Archbishop of Antioch. But after fighting unsuccessfully, he was recalled, and Mauricius appointed Comentiolus in his place [Col. 0796C]. From Theophylact and Evagrius, Pagius under this year.

The Tiber floods at Rome in November; this is followed immediately by a disaster, or bubonic plague. Gregory of Tours, Book X, chapter 1.

[Note: [Col. 0796C] I II] Pelagius II, who dies on 7 February. See the notes to Pelagius and Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, p. 105.

[Col. 0796D] Theodosius, son of Mauricius, in the fourth year and sixth month of his age, is crowned Augustus. The *Alexandrian Chronicle* and Theophanes. See Pagius under the year 588, no. 8, and under this year, no. 3.

After a lengthy vacancy of the Roman See, GREGORY, later called the Great, is ordained as successor on 3 September of this year, indiction 9. See Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*, p. 93.

From the death of St. Sylvester to the beginning of Gregory the Great, the years are correctly counted according to the Anastasian codices as 246. Sylvester died at the end of the year 335. Gregory was ordained [Col. 0798A] on 3 September 590. See the notes to Gregory the Great.

[CONTINUATION OF THE CHRONOLOGY.]

[Col. 0797]

PREFACE OF CAJETAN CENNI, PRIEST OF PISTOIA, TO THE CONTINUATION OF THE BLANCHINIAN CHRONOLOGY

SUMMARY OF THE SECTIONS

[Col. 0797B] The Blanchinian Chronology is continued from the year of Christ 590, or from St. Gregory the Great, through three complete centuries. — II. The organization of this fourth volume. — III. The obscure affairs of Italy receive much light from the Milan edition of the *Italian Writers*. — IV. They have been made still more obscure by the disputes of recent scholars. — V. For these matters buried under the weight of antiquity, the monuments of the ancients would be the sole support. — VI. Once the obsolete private consulships are set aside, the safer chronological markers are the post-consular years, which are correctly counted up to 668; thereafter they function rather like tribunician powers. — VII. The years of the Lombard kings and exarchs, who succeeded the consuls, were little attended to by ancient writers. — VIII. The former counted them in public acts, while the latter did otherwise. — IX. The varying opinions of writers concerning both systems. — X. Frankish affairs were carefully recorded, but in the Merovingian period they were only loosely connected with our own affairs. — XI. After the Hegira, Olympiads and years from the foundation of the City were rarely used; nevertheless, all the Blanchinian eras are continued. — XII. The cycle of Victorius was still in use among Italians and Gauls throughout the seventh and eighth centuries. — XIII. The era of the Lombards’ descent into Italy, neglected by Blanchinus, is omitted, although it is mentioned more than once by ancient writers. — XIV and XV. The condition of the Spanish Church up to St. Gregory the Great, while the Gothic kings, who were Arians, held power. — XVI and XVII. The condition of the British Churches up to the same pontiff, when they had reverted to idolatry introduced by the Anglo-Saxons. — XVIII. Both kingdoms, after undergoing comparable reversals of fortune, return to the faith with equal success at the end of the sixth century. — XIX. At that time a new misfortune befalls Spain when the Saracens invade it, while the Gospel is proclaimed throughout all Germany. — XX. On the occasion of praising the munificence toward the Holy See of King Pippin and of the Emperors Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, the organization of the entire Anastasian work is set forth. — XXI. The ecclesiastical territory, emerging from the defection of the Italians when the impious Emperors began persecuting the sacred images, is enlarged by King Pippin. — XXII. The era of the ecclesiastical territory is distinguished from Pippin’s donation. — XXIII. The Roman Duchy, first of all, defecting from the Eastern Emperor together with the whole of Italy, is granted to the jurisdiction of the Church. — XXIV. By divine providence it comes about that, when the impious Leo profanes the sacred revenues of the Church from its patrimonies, richer revenues succeed them from the ecclesiastical territory. — XXV. In matters relating to the Holy See, the opinion of Cardinal Baronius is to be preferred to all others. — XXVI and following. The chronological account of Theophanes concerning the three Emperors—Anastasius, Theodosius, and Leo the Isaurian—is defended against Pagius and more recent writers. — XXXI. Catalogue of the Lombard kings. — XXXII and following. Notes and observations on the catalogue of the Lombard kings. — XXXIX. Catalogue of the exarchs of Ravenna. — XL. Notes and observations on the catalogue of the exarchs of Ravenna. — XLI and XLII. Two kinds of patricians, imperial and papal. Imperial patricians. — XLIII. Papal patricians.

[THE FASTI.]

[Col. 0797C] 1. I have received an assignment in which no fuller opportunity for work and risk could have been allotted to me. For I have been ordered to complete the pontifical Caesarean chronology undertaken for the *Book of the Pontiffs* by the most distinguished prelate of every branch of learning, Francis Blanchinus of Verona, and successfully carried through the first year of Gregory the Great, the ninth year of Tiberius Mauricius, and his seventh post-consular year, [Col. 0797D] but, such is the condition of human affairs, left unfinished midway through its course.

To speak frankly, I have received an assignment when the parent of the *Annals of the Church* died with scarcely a third of it completed. “With justice,” he says, “we rest, and indeed fatigued by the journey, since at times, through the vast solitude of ignorance of events, the road had to be laboriously sought where there was no path; at other times, like Jonathan amid the mountain heights, we had to crawl on hands and feet, so that we might overcome the immense obstacles confronting us everywhere; while amid all these circumstances we were very often hindered by barriers of dense thorns [Col. 0798C]—that is, violently carried away by the manifold and diverse affairs pressing in from every side—and were obliged, at almost every step, to turn aside from the route we had undertaken in order to attend to other matters.” (*Baronius, Annals*, vol. VIII, year 714.)

Nevertheless, I am glad to have obtained it. For how could I better honor his immortal name, whose companionship I enjoyed in his declining years, whose instructions I heard, and whose immense cares I helped to lighten in some measure? Or how could I better begin my apprenticeship than by undertaking an assignment that would bear witness both to the memory of so great a prelate and to my own duty for future generations?

For this reason neither arduous labor nor constant reflection—which I understood to be necessary for completing the work—ever deterred me; rather, duty and affection persuaded me that these same things were pleasing. Accordingly, after carefully traversing the three centuries left untouched by the Blanchinian chronology, I accurately arranged, according to my ability, whatever I judged useful for illuminating the *Book of the Pontiffs* [Col. 0799A], and I have presented nearly two complete centuries for consideration in this volume; what remains I intend to exhibit in the fifth and final volume [Note: [Col. 0799D] This fifth and final volume, of which Cenni speaks, never saw the light of day. EDIT. PATROL.].

But since, as chronologists commonly do, while attending to the reckoning of time I had to indicate piecemeal the events narrated in the *Book of the Pontiffs* itself and in the historical notes, I must therefore offer some preliminary remarks on them, so that these events, even when merely sampled and reduced to summary, may pave the way for a safer passage through antiquity, which is enveloped in darkness on every side.

2. The history of this volume therefore comprises the deeds of thirty-one supreme pontiffs, from St. Gregory the Great to Stephen III, otherwise IV [Note: [Col. 0800D] In our edition, near the middle of the second volume. EDIT. PATROL.]. Some of these men are worthy of immortal remembrance for their outstanding virtues, others for the renown of their holiness. Through their labors, faith, and steadfastness they protected all Italy, the city of Rome, and the Apostolic See from the savagery, tyranny, and impiety both of the Lombard kings, most of whom were Arians, and of the [Col. 0799B] Eastern Emperors, who very rarely showed reverence toward the Holy See and the vicar of Christ. Many of them, amid great hardships, deportation, exile, and death, defended the Catholic faith and the rights of the Holy See.

Moreover, all Italy, and Rome itself more than once, fought for life, home, possessions, and children. At the same time, utterly depraved men violated and overthrew everything divine and human, or stretched out impious hands against the visible head of the Church, the vicar of Christ. A new heresy harassed the Church, new persecutions afflicted her, and new martyrs and confessors adorned her. Finally, the rise of empires and the destruction of kingdoms form the subject matter of this fourth volume.

I have arranged by years this most mournful history, which ought to be set forth with tears and which is narrated for the most part in the *Book of the Pontiffs*, so that the age of these calamities might be established with certainty. Yet, so that the beginning, course, and end might not all be tragic, I carried the sequence of events forward until Christ himself, the invisible head of the Church, fighting for her with a strong hand, overthrew and almost crushed the power of the Lombards [Col. 0799C]; completely destroyed the remaining strength of the Eastern Empire in Italy by expelling the exarchs; extended the territory of the Apostolic See, previously confined within narrow boundaries; brought the Augustan crown, improperly clinging to the heads of the Easterners, back to the West; and through his vicar bestowed it upon the most devout kings of France.

Although the final event—namely, the revival of the Western Empire—is not included in this volume, since it ends with the first year of Charlemagne, king of France, I nevertheless judged that it should not be separated from the account. For Charlemagne, like his predecessors, had vigorously defended the glory of the Apostolic See, whose territory had been extended in every direction, before he became Emperor; and he later received the imperial crown as the reward for this achievement. Thus I thought that mention of so joyful an ending should erase the memory of such mournful events.

### 3

Baronius rightly laments that such a great and varied history is shrouded in darkness; for such ignorance had spread over almost the whole of the West, especially in the seventh century, that letters themselves seemed to have perished. In Italy this calamity was brought about chiefly by the arrival of the Lombards, who possessed it by force and arms for more than two hundred years. Yet our affairs are made more deserving of lament not by the scarcity of ancient writers than by the disagreements of more recent ones.

Indeed, the immense abundance of monuments—the many little works, privileges, charters, donations, and documents of that kind—which the distinguished Ludovico Antonio Muratori, prefect of the Este Library, has brought to light in our own age, proves that, however poor our ancestors may have been in learning, they nevertheless tried to transmit to us the memory of what happened in their own times. I would not dare deny that this greatest champion of Italian glory has produced very rare monuments illuminating the seventh century, which was darker than the others, although those monuments have been disfigured and corrupted either by the injuries of time or by the carelessness of copyists. Yet through them—by employing manuscripts of the best quality, by the acumen of his intellect, and by adding the most distinguished observations—he shows more than once that it is possible to traverse the most remote ages from this point onward with an unhindered step.

Moreover, among the other ancient writers, after restoring to their original splendor the author of the *Miscellany* and Paul Warnefrid, surnamed the Deacon, and after publishing the *Book of the Pontiffs*, commonly attributed to Anastasius, together with four manuscripts containing variant readings from the Ambrosian Library, he undoubtedly offers anyone examining Italian antiquities a much brighter torch than that used by those who preceded our age. For this reason I wished this Vatican edition of ours, enriched by so many excellent manuscripts and by the most learned prelate, to appear still more complete by adding four outstanding Ambrosian manuscripts extracted from the edition of that same illustrious man, so that the dates of the pontiffs and of their deeds might be established more firmly.

For the same purpose I also used the celebrated Farnesian manuscript, transcribed from Blanchini’s papers, and the Veronese Catalogue published by the most learned Father Joseph Blanchini in his *Prolegomena*. He added to it the variant readings of another manuscript, namely the Vallicellian, so that this fourth volume may appear richer than the printed editions through the addition of six outstanding manuscripts.

### 4

What, then? Recent scholars, I say, have brought upon learned men a much graver disadvantage in both our own affairs and those of foreign peoples through so many and such varied opinions than the barbarism of the Lombards itself. To say nothing of the others, with the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* and Paul Warnefrid, whom I have just praised, what access to the truth is open today? Panvinio, Baronius, Papebrochius, and Pagius have extracted the succession of the Roman pontiffs from the *Book of the Pontiffs*; but how rarely are they unanimous!

From Paul Warnefrid, Peregrinus, Sigonius, Panvinio, Baronius, Pagius, and Bacchinus have composed, with the greatest diligence, the history of the Lombard kings above all others. Yet what disagreement do we find among them, and how many divergences have we later discovered? The same is true of the author of the *Miscellany*. Since in his final books he copied Theophanes, Baronius rightly praises him as Theophanes, because he did not see that author’s *Chronography*, published in Greek and Latin after Baronius’s death.

Many things occur in this author that compelled others to adopt a different view. One point especially seemed worthy of notice: from the final year of Phocas he anticipates events by a year, a matter overlooked by Baronius. The most learned Henschenius and Papebrochius were the first to detect this chronological displacement: the former in his *Exegesis on the Chronography of St. Theophanes*, the latter in his *Historical-Chronological Essay* (vol. III of the *Acta Sanctorum*, and 6 May). Both carried it forward to the final year of Constantine Copronymus, A.D. 775.

Antonius Pagius, however, while praising and more rigorously examining the point observed by them, notes that Theophanes correctly records the eclipse of the sun in the year 693, and therefore argues that after an error of eighty-four years he returned to the proper path. Then, when he reaches Constantine Copronymus, rather than admit with those most learned men that Theophanes had returned to the chronological displacement, he says that the *Chronographer* was corrupted throughout the whole period of that emperor. But we shall return to these matters below.

Since this is so, everyone can see that the recent writers themselves, instead of illuminating a history shrouded in darkness, tried to confirm it as being placed in ever greater uncertainty. How much difficulty and danger this creates for a writer need not be explained.

### 5

Therefore those who in our age strive with all their strength to write a reliable history usually reject the observations of others and employ the support of ancient monuments. With their help the most learned prelate Blanchini, the latest illuminator of the consular *Fasti*, enriched the same observations with a greater number and with exceptional learning.

After the private consulships had ended, when the perpetual consulships of the emperors began and the tribunician powers had fallen out of use, less learning is subsequently encountered in the monuments. This is clear from Blanchini’s chronology. From the year 565 of Justin the Younger—that is, the first year of the Curopalates; the twenty-fourth year after the consulship of Basil, a man of consular rank; and the last consulship of private men—to 590, the final year of that same emperor, it presents only two inscriptions establishing a definite date.

The first is from the year 657, recently excavated on the Esquiline, which he displays in fulfillment of his office, since he had been chosen by His Holiness Clement XI, because of his remarkable knowledge of antiquity, as the recognized describer and interpreter of all monuments excavated daily in Rome and elsewhere. The second he gives under the year 577, from Cardinal Noris’s work *On the Fifth Synod*. A third may also be added, namely the epitaph of Candida, whose inscription Blanchini cites from the Martyrology under the year 585, to which it belongs.

Since he did not transcribe this inscription in full, I wish to present it from Baronius. In the *Annals*, volume IX, under the year 715, when he is reciting the inscription of Theodimus, subdeacon and *corrector* of the Roman Church, from the same Neapolitan church of St Andrew at the Nidum, where that inscription stands, he also cites Candida’s epitaph, whose inscription reads as follows:

> **HIC REQVIESCIT IN PACE CANDIDA C. F. QVAE VIXIT PL. M. ANN. L. DIE IIII. ID. SEPT. IMP. D. N. MAURITIO PP. AUG. ANN. IIII. PC. EJUSD. AN. II. IND. QUARTA.**

> Here rests in peace Candida C.F., who lived more or less fifty years; on the fourth day before the Ides of September, in the fourth year of the emperor our lord Maurice, perpetual Augustus, in the second year of his post-consulship, the fourth indiction.

Such inscriptions demonstrate that, once the more customary and more reliable chronological markers—the tribunician powers and the consulships—had fallen out of use (for, once the emperors had assumed the consulship, the subsequent years of their lives were numbered by post-consulships 1, 2, 3, and so on), only the imperial years were recorded in public documents, together with the post-consulships just mentioned. At the same time, they warn us that it would henceforth be pointless to call the chronology “consular,” since, when we call it “Caesarean,” we understand it as displaying at once the Augustan and consular dignities.

### 6

Before I proceed to the other matters that ought to precede the chronology, I must point out a very important distinction which the most learned Antonius Pagius observes both in his *Hypatic Epistle* and in his *Critique* under the year 668, concerning the post-consulships of the emperors.

Some people properly number the post-consulship from the year after the consulship was held; others, however, number the post-consulship from the very year in which the perpetual consulship began, just as they number the tribunician powers. If this distinction is overlooked, the entire calculation of the dates is ruined.

Thus, from the year 566, when Justin the Younger held the consulship, until 668, when Constantine Pogonatus began to administer the supreme power of the empire with his brothers Heraclius and Tiberius, after their father Constans had been killed at Syracuse, coins and documents properly display the post-consulship. From that point, as Pagius says, a new change in the *Fasti* may be observed: scarcely had the emperors proceeded as consuls when they began numbering the first post-consular year.

Examples of both systems are available from public documents and monuments, but not from coins, which display only the years of imperial rule. This is the principal reason why I have not used numismatic learning in the chronology, lest I fill it with irrelevant material.

Moreover, besides the absence of learning, the great scarcity of Byzantine coins that number the years of the emperors is also regrettable. For, as Cangius affirms (*Dissertation on the Coinage of the Lower Empire*, no. 44), apart from a few bronze coins of Justin the Thracian, Justinian, Justin the Younger, Tiberius, Maurice, Phocas, Heraclius, and several others, no gold or silver coins are found engraved with such chronological indications. This is evident from the collections made by Occon, Mediobarbus, and Cangius himself.

Accordingly, in councils, letters of the pontiffs, diplomas, and other public acts, the post-consulships of the emperors before Constantine Pogonatus will be seen always distinguished from the years of imperial rule; after Constantine, however, the post-consulships generally proceed together with the imperial years. For the emperors, scarcely had they appeared with their imperial dignity when they also desired to be distinguished by the consular dignity. Whoever failed to notice this before Pagius must necessarily have fallen into very serious errors.

### 7

Returning now to the point from which I began: when I saw that my chronology would be entirely unequal to Blanchini’s if it lacked the principal indications of time, I considered supporting it with new aids—namely, by numbering the years of the Lombard kings and of the exarchs of Ravenna.

I noticed that nothing is more closely connected with the affairs of the pontiffs and of all Italy than Lombard and exarchal history. Moreover, it has been established that the authors themselves trace the origin of both powers to the very beginnings of the perpetual consulships of the emperors. For in the first year of Justin’s post-consulship, A.D. 567, they report that, after Narses had been dismissed, Longinus became prefect of Italy. Later, he was called “exarch,” a title previously unknown among the Italians and extraordinary even in its insolence.

At the end of the following year, the Lombards, setting out from Pannonia, entered Italy after the Kalends of April. What could have been devised that would be more useful for our purposes than to record the individual years of both Italian powers, which, by God’s will, had been substituted for the consular power? Since these years correspond with the imperial and pontifical years, they would both make the absence of consuls less regrettable and relieve us of a large part of the work that remains when one begins to calculate the dates.

Since I had not seen this done among the ancients, I judged that I would not be performing a worthwhile task if, while passing over the Byzantine coins as something useless, I nevertheless numbered a double series of years that would be still less useful for establishing Italian affairs.

I therefore decided that this one undertaking was not merely useful but necessary. On the basis of private observations and those of others, I prepared the *Fasti* both of the Lombard kings and of the exarchs of Ravenna, to be placed before everyone’s eyes after I have said enough by way of preface.

For the present, I must establish what I asserted shortly before: namely, that the years of the Lombard kings and of the exarchs have been given too little weight in public acts and in other documents suited to illuminating the history of Italian affairs.

### 8

There can certainly be no doubt that many monuments of the Lombard kings exist, such as their charters, donations, and privileges, which number their years. The prologues to the laws enacted by Rothari and several of his successors also mention their years, as is clear.

But what usefulness do these things have for imperial or pontifical history? They would indeed have been useful to both kinds of history if councils, letters of the pontiffs, and even the sacred imperial decrees of the Caesars or Augusti had been accustomed to number the years of the Lombards or of the exarchs.

There is only one monument of this kind: the council held at Rome by St Zachary in the year 743, in which the thirty-second year of Liutprand is mentioned. Baronius and Pagius point out that this was an entirely new example and had never previously occurred. From it Pagius further infers that at that time an alliance was established between the Romans and the Lombards to defend the sacred images against the impious Constantine (Pagius, year 743, no. 16).

If rare and non-public documents display the years of the Lombards, there is, so far as I know, no record at all of the exarchs that indicates their years. This is further established by an ancient marble inscription belonging to the year 731, which the prelate Blanchini, having transcribed it at Ravenna in the church of St Apollinaris in Classe, brought into public view in the learned preface to volume I of this work, no. 51. From it I have extracted the following fragment:

> **IN N PATRIS ET FILII ET SPS SCTI IMP PIISSIMIS DO NN LEONE ET CONSTANTINO A DO. CORONAT PACIF. MAGNIS IMP LEONE QUIDEM CLEMENTISS. IMP. ANNOXIS. CONSTANTINO VERO A DO CORONATO IMP ANNO XI. GVVERNANTEM ITALIA DN EVTVCHIO EXCELL. PATRICIO Et Exarch. IIII. Kal. Februarias Ind. XIIII. etc.**

> In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Under the most pious emperors, our lords Leo and Constantine, [and] under the most peaceful and great emperors crowned by the Lord: Leo, most clement emperor, in the fifteenth year of his empire; Constantine, truly crowned by the Lord, in the eleventh year of his empire. With our lord Eutychius, excellent patrician and exarch, governing Italy. The fourth day before the Kalends of February, the fourteenth indiction, etc.

This makes it clear that Eutychius, the last of the exarchs, who in the year 731 was numbering the fifth year of his exarchate, kept entirely silent about it. It is therefore probable that the same was done by his predecessors, to the great detriment of our history.

This matter certainly filled me with the greatest astonishment when I saw the custom of the highest rulers neglected by the exarchs, who are said to have governed that portion of the Western Empire which remained with supreme authority. Yet antiquity has preserved coins struck by them, the design of which Cangius reproduced; I present it here at the end of the material concerning Maurice.

Cangius testifies that on most of these coins one sees a bust of a woman wearing a mural crown, with the inscription **Felix Ravenna**—“Happy Ravenna”—while on the reverse there is the city’s monogram. He thinks that the eagle visible on others may represent the emblem of the Roman Empire.

### 9

Our history suffered great disadvantage from this circumstance, and for that reason the more recent writers are forgiven. If such disagreement occurs in Lombard affairs, which were recorded in writing by a writer of that people, a native of Forum Julii, where his nation first settled, a contemporary of their kingdom and lacking none of the materials necessary for composing a history—as he himself testifies when he warns his readers whenever he narrates something not established (*Book* IV, chapter 43)—what wonder is it that so many and such varied opinions have been adopted by those who wrote about the affairs of the exarchs of Ravenna, which are reported piecemeal among the ancients?

The Greeks, although these were their affairs, remained silent. The monuments of Ravenna, if any existed, have perished. The exarchs themselves, as we have seen, neglected the years of their office.

Thus, in the time of the most learned Cardinal Baronius, their succession was circulating in an incomplete form, although many had written about them. After Baronius, Antonius Pagius and Benedictus Bacchinus tried to complete the same succession by bringing forward new names of exarchs.

Finally, the Milanese Anonymous, the most recent of all, undertook to adorn this field and subjected both ancient and recent writers to examination (*Scriptors of Italy*, vol. X, chronological table, section 16, nos. 79–80), so that one might expect something substantial from him.

But what happened? While he persists in refuting the writings of others, he compresses their observations into a summary, while bringing forward himself material that is extremely meager and conflicts with the *Book of the Pontiffs*. He speaks of only three exarchs recently discovered, and says that he once wondered that Theodorus Calliopa had completed thirty-six years, from 650 to 686.

The *Book of the Pontiffs*, however, teaches that he ought not to have dated Theodorus’s beginnings so early. In the life of St Martin it speaks clearly about the arrival and killing of Olympius, as well as about Theodorus’s second arrival in Italy, which Sirmondus rightly assigns to the year 653 (*Synopsis of the Collection of Anastasius*).

Similarly, the beginnings of Platys ought to have been shifted by a period of one year; this matter will be discussed more appropriately below.

Since this is so, I am content, I say, to present the *Fasti* of the Lombard kings and of the exarchs separately, so that their periods may be more clearly distinguished. I shall indicate their deeds here and there within the chronology, so that their relationship with the other events may be visible. For this reason I have wished to indicate both of these Italian powers in the main body of the imperial chronology.

### 10

Indeed, whatever support our chronology could vainly desire from the Lombards and exarchs, the kings of the Franks would have supplied. Their history, with the chronological order for the most part preserved, was written by many of the ancients, since distinguished intellects were never lacking in that kingdom, as may be seen in Duchesne’s celebrated collection. More recently, the most learned writers have illuminated it with various and excellent observations.

But just as the civil affairs of the Franks down to Charles Martel, the mayor of the palace, are only slightly connected with our own, and just as the deeds both of Charles Martel himself and of his son, King Pippin, belong to the already advanced eighth century, at whose end the kings of the Franks occupy the principal place in the imperial chronology as Roman emperors, so I did not wish to enumerate the years of the last Merovingians, Charles Martel, or the first of the Carolingians, King Pippin. I have not been silent about their deeds, which brought such splendor to the Holy See.

Nor was this burdensome for me. When the order of events led me from the first year of St Gregory the Great, from which I begin, to the first year of St Gregory II—that is, from 590 to 715—I entered upon a road that was exceedingly pleasant, rich in an abundance of material and marked by stones measuring the route. I found annalists who were extremely accurate; nothing more suitable for a chronologist could be imagined.

I also had as my guide, both for narrating the events and for establishing the calculation of the dates, the Carolingian Codex containing ninety-nine letters of Gregory III, Zachary, Stephen II (also called III), Paul, Stephen III (also called IV), Adrian, and Pseudo-Constantine, addressed to Charles Martel, Pippin, Charlemagne, and his brother Carloman. Gretser published it after Baronius’s death, in the year 1613.

However carefully I may have carried out all these tasks, and however much I may have enriched the chronology with additions of historical material, it will always yield to the consular chronology and will not display the firmness of events and dates that we have become accustomed to admire in Blanchini’s work. If the fault is attributed to the changing nature of the events rather than to negligence of intellect, neither truth will be wronged nor envy directed against me.

### 11

It will not be irrelevant to indicate what additions I have made to the imperial and pontifical chronology. I arranged by years the principal civil and ecclesiastical events of the most flourishing kingdoms of our age: Spain, Great Britain, and Germany, which are either mentioned or narrated in the *Book of the Pontiffs*.

The reason why Blanchini’s chronology speaks sparingly or not at all of these kingdoms is their unfortunate condition before Gregory the Great. The Arian heresy was destroying the kingdom of Spain, while idolatry was ruining the other two.

There is nevertheless this difference among them: Germany at that time first heard the Gospel, whereas Spain and Britain had departed from it. I shall therefore include in a brief narrative the reasons why each kingdom fell away, so that the history of those returning to the faith, and especially of those making progress in it, may be more pleasing.

Before this, however, what remains concerning chronological indications must be set forth. I used Blanchini’s eras down to the end of the *Book of the Pontiffs*. In this respect I may perhaps be criticized. Someone may say, with Pagius: “It was useful and necessary to employ the Julian Period, the solar and lunar cycles, the Dominical Letters, the imperial indictions, and the Dionysian era. But what usefulness or necessity persuaded anyone that the Olympiads and the years of the City before and after the Parilia ought to be continued?”

Indeed, after that new era began—the Hegira, so hostile to the Christian name—Pagius teaches that both of these could be omitted, since they thereafter came into rare use, and he himself truly omits them. I, however, chose to follow other chronographers who may rightly be compared with Pagius, especially since I learned from that eminent chronologist that the Olympiad eras and the eras of the City, which I have mentioned, are necessary for aligning the years of the Arabs, or of the Hegira, and of the Greeks with the Latin years (Cardinal Noris, *On Syrian Epochs*).

For, to tell the truth, no era among Blanchini’s systems is, by the agreement of all learned men, more secure than the two just mentioned. Therefore I also began to number the lunar years of the Hegira from 16 July, a Friday, when the Arabs begin from Muhammad’s flight, before the beginning of the second year of the 350th Olympiad. That year is A.D. 622, the year 1374 from the City before the Parilia and 1375 after the Parilia. I indicated for each year, according to custom, the day of the month and the weekday, so that our affairs would not be confused by the new form of numbering the years. Nevertheless, I have continuously carried the years of the Olympiads and of the City alongside Calvisius and others.

### 12

To make it clearer why I refuse to listen to the most learned Pagius, I wish to point out that the Dionysian cycle itself—whose era is certainly more famous than the Arabian one—did not begin to be preferred among the Gauls to the Victorian cycle until the times of Charlemagne, and, unless I am mistaken, in Italy itself as well, as I shall soon show.

That is why, if the years of the Olympiads and of the City were omitted, our affairs, and those of the Gauls so closely connected with ours in the eighth century, would be deprived of every certain epoch.

For the Gauls used the Victorian cycle in the second year of the 369th Olympiad, the year 1451 from the City before the Parilia, which is A.D. 699, as Scaliger notes from the most ancient manuscript of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, and with him Noris in *On the Ravenna Cycle* and Pagius under the year 699, no. 19. There we read:

> In the fifth year of Childebert, king of the Franks, by order of Pippin, five thousand years have passed from Adam. Easter was on the tenth day before the Kalends of April; the Lord’s Ascension was on the Kalends of May. By the cycle, the number of years was 160. The repetition was from the beginning of the cycle.

Furthermore, the Continuator of Fredegar, completing his continuation at the beginning of the year A.D. 736, says:

> From the Passion of the Lord to this present year, in the Victorian cycle, it is the 177th year; on the Kalends of January, the Lord’s Day, the year was 735.

He counts from the month of March, as is still done today at Florence and elsewhere.

Bucherius also observes that the Victorian cycle was in force among the Gauls in the year A.D. 740, on the basis of the dispute concerning Easter in that year. The Victorians argued that it should be celebrated on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, while the Alexandrians argued for the eighth day before the Kalends. The same dispute was renewed twenty years later, namely in 760. Since the date of Easter was 5 April, the Victorians refused to celebrate Easter with the Alexandrians on the following Sunday, 6 April, and postponed it to the next Sunday, 13 April.

For this reason Pagius rightly observes under that year, no. 6, that the Victorian cycle remained in use among the Gauls until Charlemagne.

It is equally certain that the Italians, who had long celebrated Easter according to the ninety-five-year cycle of Dionysius, did not entirely abandon the Victorian cycle at the beginning of the eighth century. This is sufficiently demonstrated by a monument that I cited in the chronological notes on Constantine:

> In the first year of his pontificate, one hundred and fifty years of the repeated Victorian cycle are completed, indiction VII, the first year of the reign of Tiberius with Justinian his father.

For if, in a contemporary catalogue of those times, the Roman pontiffs were listed according to the Victorian cycle, the Dionysian era was not then valued so highly that I should have thought the more certain eras—such as the Olympiads and the years of the City—could be passed over, lest I allow the chronology to remain dependent on epochs that were still uncertain. Nevertheless, the Dionysian era, which soon became universal throughout the West, rightly deserves preference over all the others.

### 13

It would certainly have been desirable that, since the varying opinions of writers made it laborious to examine the years of the Lombard kings one by one, at least a private epoch of Italian affairs should be carried forward year by year from the Lombards’ arrival mentioned above. For the years since that arrival are more than once numbered throughout the seventh and eighth centuries.

To state what I think, I was greatly surprised that this did not occur to the prelate Blanchini, whom I saw arrange by years the other invasion of Italy, that by the Goths, before the Lombard invasion. He not only arranged it by years but also enumerated the years of the Gothic kings together with those of the emperors, and from the arrival of Odoacer in 476 to the defeat of Totila and Teia by the valor of Narses in the years 552 and 553, he described with the greatest diligence the entire period of their stay in Italy.

But afterward, when I considered the matter more attentively, I saw that this most learned man had been deterred from doing so by the many and varied opinions concerning the arrival of the Lombards—opinions that would have made such an epoch useless. As I said in section 7, it would be pointless to enumerate the years of the kings of that people and of the exarchs, since the ancients had neglected them.

Moreover, he did not devote the same particular care to Lombard history. I see that he adhered especially to the chronology of Pagius, who, following the Frankish writers, sometimes conflicts with the *Book of the Pontiffs* and with Paul the Deacon. Consequently, in compiling the *Fasti* I have promised, I shall be compelled to depart from him slightly in this matter.

I have always proceeded sparingly and with caution when dealing with the opinion of foreigners, even contemporaries. When I saw the abbot of Biclaro, a contemporary of those times, place the murder of Alboin, the first Lombard king, in the seventh year of Justin the Younger, the fifth of Leovigild, and A.D. 572, and then, only eight years later—namely, in the fifth year of Tiberius and the thirteenth of Leovigild—record the beginning of the rule of Antharis, which plainly conflicts with Paul Warnefrid and with the letters of St Gregory the Great, I deliberated with myself that I should not listen to foreigners reporting our affairs.

Who could endure that the eighteen-month reign of Cleph and the ten-year interregnum after Alboin’s murder, before Autharis was raised to the throne, should be compressed by a contemporary writer into eight years?

Therefore the most learned prelate will grant me permission to depart from him in composing the succession of the Lombards—or, to speak more accurately, to compare Antonius Pagius’s opinion with the writings of our own authors, lest others be deceived along with Blanchini.

### 14

Having considered these principal chronological indications—for I have no need to speak of certain astronomical indications that appear under their proper signs—I now come to give a brief account of the departures of Spain and Great Britain from the Catholic faith, so that what is scattered through the chronology concerning their return to it may more easily be understood.

First, Spain. From the very times of the apostles it had the Church, and afterward bishops and metropolitans. During the three centuries of persecution it was distinguished by the number of its martyrs. When peace was restored to the Church through Constantine, and sacred buildings and holy institutions were established, it gloried that the Catholic faith and the discipline of the Church were being spread far and wide.

First by Hadrian and then by Constantine himself it was divided into five provinces—for Mauretania Tingitana and the Balearic Islands lie outside the mainland: Baetica, Lusitania, Gallaecia, Tarraconensis, and Carthaginensis. It had an equal number of metropolitans, under each of whom several bishops were subject.

In a short time all these things were ruined. In the eighth consulship of Honorius and the third of Theodosius, A.D. 409, the Alans, Vandals, and Suebi invaded Spain and threw everything into confusion. Later they were defeated by the Goths, who took control; all were barbarians and all were hostile to the Catholic faith.

The Goths in particular, who for nearly two centuries before King Reccared—who rejected the heresy—harassed the Catholics, professed Arianism. This was the religion of the Goths, whose origin must now be explained.

When the Gothic people, driven out by the Huns, obtained permission from Valens to settle first in Thrace, they soon revolted and were defeated, not without Roman bloodshed. Finally, under the emperor Gratian, they made a treaty with the Romans and had Ulphilas as their bishop.

They made him the leader of their embassy when, needing land to cultivate, they asked the Romans to allow them to remain wherever the Romans wished. Thus the Gothic bishop, residing at Constantinople, attended the Second General Council in the year 381 and adhered to the position of the Nicene Fathers, who were defending their doctrine.

Afterward, on returning to *Apolim* [place-name uncertain], whether he was seeking supporters for his embassy or wishing to show gratitude for the favor he had received, he entered into communion with the Arians. Not long afterward all the Goths, instructed in Ulphilas’s teachings, were torn away from the Catholic Church as Arians.

They were divided only by different names: the Visigoths and the Ostrogoths. The latter invaded Italy, while the former invaded Gaul and Spain.

### 15

The Visigoths who occupied Spain were able to establish their heresy more deeply there than the others had done among the Italians. They immediately attempted, by force and arms, to impose Gothic liturgy everywhere and then gradually to overturn all sacred things.

The Catholic bishops struggled in vain either to preserve ecclesiastical discipline or at least to save the Catholic religion, which was in danger. The Arian kings defended their error with the utmost constancy and were never restrained by piety, kinship, or blood relationship from deporting, exiling, or putting to death its opponents.

The many bishops expelled from their sees bear witness to this; the countless martyrs who died with the utmost steadfastness for the faith bear witness; and finally Hermenegild himself bears witness, the son of King Leovigild, who fought bravely with his followers for the faith but was defeated and killed by the Arians.

Some bishops, inflamed by zeal for the Catholic religion, are recorded to have defended the sacred canons while the barbarian factions were tearing apart the Spanish provinces and violently persecuting the Catholics.

For this reason, when matters had reached the utmost misery, the Roman pontiffs, lest whatever jurisdiction existed among the bishops be thrown into confusion, repeatedly honored one of them—one whose zeal surpassed that of the others—with an apostolic vicariate. Thus zeal for the faith and discipline would not be confined within any limits, but wherever the Church of the Catholics existed, it would be preserved there unharmed.

We read that this honor was first given by Leo the Great to Turibius, bishop of Astorga. Simplicius and Hormisdas conferred the same honor on one or another bishop of Seville, and Hormisdas granted it also to John, bishop of Tarragona.

Moreover, Spain, always most steadfast in righteousness and faith, held several Catholic councils even during these extremely turbulent times and carried out many other undertakings that should perpetually be counted to the glory of its inhabitants.

But what happened? The Spanish Church as a whole remained miserable for nearly two centuries, down to King Reccared. We do not read that it ever emerged from this condition except in the final year of the pontificate of Pelagius, when the Third Council of Toledo was held and both the king and his entire people rejected Arianism, as Leander of Seville and the monk Eutropius preached.

The remaining matters must be sought from the chronology and from the notes below. For from the beginning of St Gregory the Great to St Gregory II—that is, from the end of the sixth century to the beginning of the eighth—no diocese of the Western patriarchate was more fortunate or more flourishing than the Spanish. Afterward, however, the invasion of the Saracens made it miserable and much more wretched than before.

### 16

From Spain I now proceed to Great Britain. In the second century of the Church, through the piety of King Lucius, it obtained from Pope Eleutherius the illumination of evangelical preaching. Later, however—as is the fate of that kingdom—it departed from the faith.

Knowledge of this great island, both ecclesiastical and civil, must be drawn from the most learned description of the prelate Blanchini in his historical notes on St Eleutherius. He has impressed both aspects of its condition so deeply upon his mind that I confess I have never seen so skillfully executed an image of any province during the first three centuries of the Church.
