Then, in order to proceed as though by a single continuous line toward the preaching of the monk Augustine, it is necessary to recall the principal points of this more extended history.

When Constantine restored the form of government devised by Hadrian after the Council of Nicaea and divided the Roman world among four praetorian prefects, the territory of the three dioceses of Gaul, Spain, and Britain was assigned to the prefect of the Gauls.

Constantine established four provinces of Britain; afterward Valentinian made them five: three governed by presidents—Britannia I, Britannia II, and Flavia Caesariensis—and two governed by consulars—Maxima Caesariensis and Valentia.

Thus divided, the diocese remained subject to an illustrious vicar until the seventh consulship of Honorius Augustus and the second of Theodosius Augustus, that is, until the year 407. Then it assumed the form of a tyranny. After Marcus and Gratian were elevated and soon killed, the more successful Constantine succeeded them. Crossing into Gaul, he drew the entire Gallic and Aquitanian army over to his side.

The barbarians seized the opportunity and invaded Gaul; republics arose everywhere. The Britons themselves, while Alaric was attacking Rome in A.D. 410, asserted their independence.

Thus the great island, torn away from the Empire by a sudden revolt, became first unfortunate and then miserable. Stripped of Roman soldiers and exposed to the plunder of overseas peoples, its native inhabitants could scarcely defend it.

Accordingly, in the year 421, they sent envoys to Honorius and promised submission, provided they were freed from the invading Picts and Scots. A legion was sent from Rome; they were freed from the attacks and were warned about the defense of the wall.

Nevertheless, they requested fresh assistance from the Romans the following year. But the Romans, exhausted by their campaigns, bade them farewell. The overseas peoples therefore became fiercer and more destructive to Britain through plunder and slaughter until the year 446, when Wortigern, king of the Britons, having again attempted in vain to obtain Roman aid from Aetius, commander-in-chief under Valentinian III, deliberated with an assembled council about seeking assistance from the Saxons.

### 17

Therefore, in the following year, following the rash counsel of the nobles, he sent an embassy to invite the Saxons, who had long been eager for his kingdom. After two years, the stronger peoples of Germany—the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes—brought aid to the Britons under the leadership of Hengist, soon to bring danger instead. Scarcely had they entered the island and established themselves in its eastern region when they fought against the Picts and Scots and put them to flight.

Later an agreement was made between the Britons and the Anglo-Saxons—this is the name by which those three nations were called after being united—that the latter should thereafter fight on behalf of the Britons’ homes, receiving military pay. In the year 450 Wortigern fought against the enemy and won a notable victory over them with the aid of the allied forces; for this reason he granted Kent to Hengist as a reward.

Meanwhile Hengist, plotting rebellion, summoned his brother Horsa and a new force from Germany, together with his daughter Rowen. He greeted Horsa as king of Kent; but Wortigern was so bewitched by the girl’s beauty that, after repudiating his wife, he married her. Wortigern had a son of great promise named Wortimer. He informed his father and the Britons that Hengist’s treachery had been discovered. The guests were treated as enemies, and a battle took place. Through Wortimer’s valor Horsa was killed, and Hengist was put to flight—he had succeeded his brother in the kingdom of Kent.

The fugitive withdrew to the Isle of Thanet and from there returned to Germany. Having gathered large forces, he came back the following year and, finding Wortigern ruling alone after the premature death of his son, invaded the kingdom through the intrigues and devices of his daughter. Wortigern was captured once and again; first he was compelled to redeem his freedom by surrendering three provinces, and then his life by handing over fortified places.

Then the barbarians ran wild against everything sacred and against the priests; with fire and slaughter they cast down everything connected with religion. Wortigern himself escaped in flight to Cambria, or Wales, and fortified himself in the town of Genorium [possibly an OCR corruption]. Those who followed him brought there the remnants of the British faith; all the rest miserably returned to idolatry.

The barbarians subsequently established the Heptarchy, or seven kingdoms, at different times. The kingdom of the Jutes was Kent, whose capital was Durovernum, or Canterbury. The Saxons possessed three kingdoms, called those of the East, South, and West Saxons; the Angles likewise possessed three: those of the East Angles, the Middle Angles, or Mercians, and the Northumbrians.

It was into this political arrangement of Britain that the monk Augustine came, sent to that people by Saint Gregory the Great. Although I have set out elsewhere how those kingdoms returned to the faith after various intervals, I wish here to survey in a single account the kingdom of Kent, whose principal city was Durovernum, or Canterbury. From there Bede calls the inhabitants Cantuarians and Vectuarians, of Jutish origin. This kingdom was the first of all to be enlightened by the evangelical light through the monk Augustine, and its king Aedilbert, or Aethelbert, was the first of all the kings of the Heptarchy to reject idolatry and embrace the Catholic faith, in the year 597.

Seven years later, namely in 604, East Saxony—which today is called the region of Essex and Middlesex—was enlightened by the baptism of its king Sigebert, also called Seberetus. Northumbria, which in former times, according to Bede, was divided into the two provinces or kingdoms of Bernicia and Deira, gloried in the baptism of its king Edwin in the year 627, on 12 April, the holy day of Easter, at York, by the bishop Paulinus. The king rewarded him by giving him the city itself as an episcopal see, and during six years of preaching many thousands were baptized by the holy bishop.

The kingdom of the East Angles, which included the provinces of Norfolk, Suffolk, and Cambridge together with the Isle of Ely, as Pagius states on the authority of Spelman (year 627, no. 25), saw its king Carpwald, or Erpenwald, become a Christian in the year 628. But because he was lamentably killed in that same year, it was not until 629, or later in 630, when Sigbert succeeded him, that the bishop Felix undertook the task of instructing that people.

The West Saxons, also called the Gewissae, became Christians in 635, when their king Cynigils was baptized, through the preaching of the bishop Birinus, whom Pope Honorius had sent without assigning him to any particular see. The same king Cynigils, together with Oswald, who received him from the sacred font and married his daughter, gave Birinus the city of Dorchester, which he established as an episcopal see; today it is called Dorchester in the counties of Cobuinus [an uncertain reading] and Oxford.

The kingdom of the Mercians, which until the year 626 had been administered by leaders appointed from the establishment of the Heptarchy, then had the name of king assumed by Penda. In the year 653, while Peada was king, it embraced the faith through the efforts of Oswiu, king of the Northumbrians, and his son Alcfrid.

Finally, the South Saxons, or West Saxons, last of all the kingdoms of the Heptarchy, gave their name to Christ in the year 661, when their king Edilwalch embraced the Catholic faith.

Thus, within the space of sixty-four years, that vast island embraced the laws of the Gospel. Previously, its smallest part alone—Cambria, or Wales, where the Britons had withdrawn—had preserved the faith, although in the observance of Easter and certain other matters it disagreed with the Roman Church.

### 18

How rightly I have joined together the vicissitudes of both kingdoms is evident from the fact that both present to us a less dreadful aspect of the Western Church, especially in the seventh century, when Italy’s difficult circumstances were being produced by the madness of the Lombards and the audacity of the emperors.

Moreover, there is such great similarity and connection between the two that, at almost the same time, Spain suffered the Catholic religion and the Church’s sacred laws to be trampled underfoot by the Arians, while Britain suffered the same from idolaters. At almost the same time, too, the former began to be watered by the abundant stream of the Gospel through Saint Leander of Seville, and the latter through the monk Saint Augustine. Each, casting off impiety or error respectively, restored the beauty of the Bride of Christ by a return from exile.

Although one great difference separates them—Britain, gradually enlightened, retained its splendor for a longer time, whereas Spain, boasting that Catholic voices had penetrated like lightning to every extremity, soon experienced a more serious and more lamentable disaster because of the Saracen invasion—nevertheless, just as Wortigern and his few companions suffered the calamities of flight into Wales, Pelagius and his followers suffered the same when they fled into Asturias.

Yet because this new calamity, which imposed three centuries of silence upon the churches of Spain, occurred in the eighth century, nothing prevents us from viewing both kingdoms together throughout the completed seventh century as exceedingly fertile in the broadest harvest of religion, after we have considered together the horror that afflicted both during nearly the two preceding centuries.

Would that Britain had again been subject to a similar misfortune, so that the similar condition of both might always have been remembered down to our own age! For the Spaniards who had fled to the mountains of Asturias and had carried with them the remnants of the faith preserved it there unharmed. As they were gradually permitted to enlarge the narrow boundaries of their kingdom, they had many bishops in order to maintain everywhere the Church’s discipline intact and sound. This is attested by the Council of Oviedo, held in the year 882, at which twenty-two bishops subordinate to Oviedo took part.

Therefore, later, when the valor of the last kings of the Gothic people, weakened by indolence, gradually returned to the Spaniards, and they began to defeat the barbarians in battle and drive them from cities and entire provinces, they advanced religion step by step with the victorious arms they brought against them. Although the sacred canons had received great wounds, there was no need for new preachers of the faith to proclaim again the Gospel from which the Spaniards had not departed.

### 19

For the rest, this new calamity of Spain was largely alleviated by the renowned German nation, which during the same period was led out as a whole from the darkness of idolatry by Saint Boniface, later called the apostle of that nation.

The preaching of Saint Willibrord had prepared the way for this universal conversion of the Germans before the end of the seventh century. He was the first of all to proclaim the Gospel in Frisia and in part of Germany, to establish the Church, and to cement it with the blood of native martyrs.

What did this preaching of the Gospel, spread so far and so widely throughout the West, portend? It portended first the diminution and then even the destruction of the Eastern Empire and Church, always frivolous and always inconstant. For when the emperors, ever devoted to the boldest heresies and finally persecutors of the sacred images, began at last to act with audacity, they saw the Church daily sinking and the tottering empire first wavering and then completely ruined.

And if, as Baronius said,

> “It was done by God’s counsel that, when the emperors rose against the Roman pontiffs, the soldiers of Italy should rebel against them, preferring to expose themselves to danger for the pontiffs’ safety rather than leave them defenseless in Greek hands. From this time the power of the exarchs began to be greatly weakened; whereas the power of the Roman pontiffs, for whom the soldiers stood, increased. And what is written in the Books of Kings then occurred: after a long struggle, the house of Saul diminished day by day, while David advanced more and more.”

(Baronius, year 701.)

But when those same emperors reached such a degree of audacity that they crushed the images of Christ, the most holy Virgin, and all the saints, and ordered them everywhere to be trampled underfoot by public edicts, then, deprived of the greater part of their empire, they retained the empty name of Roman emperors and preserved nothing beyond the image of imperial power, down to the capture of Constantinople.

For this reason, the civil and ecclesiastical affairs of the East, which formed the larger part of Blanchini’s chronology, will occupy only a small portion of ours. For the three flourishing kingdoms of Europe mentioned above will take the place of the affairs of the East and, so to speak, clear the broadest path for the account, in the fifth volume of this work, of the earliest Western emperors after the restoration of the empire: the most pious kings of France, who deserved so well of the Apostolic See and the Roman pontiffs. What their predecessors Charles Martel and Pippin accomplished gloriously for that same see will be set out below year by year.

### 20

The intention of Charles Martel, mayor of the palace, is praised more than his deeds. But when death overtook him, his son Pippin, the first Carolingian king, both freed the Apostolic See from Lombard tyranny and from the wicked efforts of the iconoclasts, and enriched it first with the Exarchate and the Pentapolis, then with many other regions, cities, and fortresses.

These final matters are narrated at great length in the Pontifical Book in the final part of this volume, and I have examined them individually in the final part of the chronology. The munificent generosity with which Charlemagne and his successor Louis the Pious, more than their other successors, treated the Holy See has persuaded me to defer both the extended narrative and the bulk of the volume to another book.

What? Are you surprised that the chronology promised in two parts by Bishop Blanchini (preface to volume II) should be divided into four? Let me warn you that the learned man, having surveyed the abundance of material, adopted another plan when the third volume of his work did not carry the account as far as the age of Pelagius II. Worn out by the immense efforts of his other labors, to which he soon surrendered his life, he published a very meager Prolegomenon.

Therefore Joseph Blanchini, a distinguished man and nephew of the bishop, rightly devoted to his uncle’s glory, having obtained three codices of the finest quality and extraordinary antiquity that illuminate the same third volume—the Decree of Gelasius, the Sacramentary of Saint Leo the Great, and the Psalter of the ancient Italian version—prefaced them to this fourth volume, so that they might be published neither less opportunely nor less usefully.

His plan certainly was to publish separately both the three works mentioned above and many others gathered together by the same distinguished author. But, so that those awaiting the continuation of Anastasius with the notes of various scholars would not be disappointed, it seemed best to preface the surviving Lives of the Pontiffs, divided into two parts, with a corresponding two-part set of prolegomena, as has begun to be done.

Thus the fourth volume will extend from Saint Gregory the Great to the beginning of the reign of Charlemagne, namely from the year 590 to 768; the fifth will complete the whole work. Nor does this seem to have been imprudently done. The fourth volume will represent the pontiffs and Italy oppressed by the tyranny of the Lombards and the exarchs; the fifth will display the dominion of the Apostolic See, greatly enlarged through the Franks, whose kings, by that very benefaction, were raised to the highest summit of imperial power.

### 21

I return to Pippin, the first enlarger of the dominion of the Holy See. Everyone admits that the principal glory for enlarging the ecclesiastical dominion belongs to him, for the memory of that achievement is preserved in an ancient tablet at Ravenna, cited by Papirius Masson in book II:

> PIPPIN THE PIOUS, THE FIRST, OPENED THE WAY TO ENLARGING THE CHURCH AND THE EXARCHATE OF RAVENNA WITH THE MOST EXTENSIVE … [the rest is worn away].

But several more recent and highly learned scholars, especially Antonius Pagius, bring the beginning of the civil administration of the Holy See back to this point. After examining with Baronius Pippin’s second arrival in Italy and the very extensive donation made to the Holy See, which the Pontifical Book narrates at length under Stephen II, also called III, Pagius interprets the inscription cited above (year 755, no. 6) as though the pontiffs’ certain civil rule had begun at that time. Following the Continuator of Fredegar, he fixes its beginning in the aforementioned year 755.

I shall pass over the small difference of one year between the Continuator of Fredegar and the Fulda Annals, which record Pippin’s donation in the following year. But I wish to ask Pagius whether to institute something and to enlarge it are one and the same thing. Without lingering over grammatical questions, I press the matter at once.

The two restorations of the Cottian Alps before Pippin’s donation—one by Aripert to John VII (Anastasius, no. 168; Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 28), the other by Liutprand to Gregory II (Anastasius, no. 179)—ought not to be disregarded, as though the Cottian Alps had the same status as the Patrimonies and Durtium. But did the fortress of Gallienum, which Saint Gregory III redeemed from Trasamund, duke of Spoleto, resemble Durtium and the Patrimonies?

Let Anastasius be heard:

> “Giving no small sums of money to Trasamund, their duke, so that wars and disputes might cease, he was able to bring the matter to an end and ordered that it be joined to the structure of the Holy Commonwealth and to the body of the Roman army beloved by Christ.”

(Chapter 203.)

Does Pagius perhaps think that “the Holy Commonwealth” and “the body of the Roman army” refer to the dominion of the impious Leo, from whom all Italy had defected in order to protect the Roman pontiffs, and that all Italy would undoubtedly have passed into the pontiffs’ dominion had it not been oppressed by such a mass of armed forces?

Let him hear an even clearer testimony from Anastasius himself, where he discusses the four cities restored by Zacharias:

> “He restored to that holy man the aforementioned four cities, which he himself two years earlier had taken by siege from the aforesaid Trasamund, duke of Spoleto, together with their inhabitants.”

After this, when Anastasius records the Sabine, Narnian, Auximan, and other Patrimonies, another argument becomes apparent, which I shall examine below.

### 22

I was astonished that Pagius, who correctly argues against Dointius for falsely claiming that the city of Rome itself remained under the dominion of the emperors of Constantinople until the year 796, should later, after distinguishing with Doinius the Patrimonies and rights of the Holy See, conclude that:

> “The rights, places, boundaries, and territories of the cities belong to the Pippinian donation; but the Patrimonies exist both within and outside that donation.”

For this is to make Pippin the author of the ecclesiastical dominion, which plainly conflicts with the Ravenna inscription cited above. That inscription calls him not its author or founder, but its enlarger.

In this matter, having no personal interest to defend, as befits a historian, he speaks neither for the dignity of the Frankish kings nor for that of the Apostolic See. For he presents the dominion of the Holy See in civil affairs as arising from donations, although it derives its origin from the will of peoples who voluntarily surrendered themselves. He wrongly teaches that the most pious kings of the Franks, who successively enlarged the ecclesiastical dominion, Pippin having happily begun the undertaking, established its principate. This is manifestly false.

Indeed, so that no scruple might remain for him, Anastasius, under Stephen II, also called III (nos. 246 and 247), before mentioning Pippin’s donation, twice calls the cities and places invaded by Aistulf the rights of the Holy Church of God and of the Roman Commonwealth.

Then, when he comes to the donation after the second siege of Pavia (no. 252 and following), he first states that the cities were restored and then that they were donated by Pippin to be possessed perpetually by the Roman pontiffs.

What cities were these, first restored and then donated? Of all those which Anastasius lists there, none except Narnia belonged to the Roman duchy; he expressly mentions this:

> “And also the city of Narnia, which for a long period of years had been seized from the duchy of Spoleto on the Roman side.”

Therefore, none of the four cities previously restored to the holy pontiff Zacharias with their inhabitants was included in Pippin’s donation. But all the cities of Ravenna, Aemilia, and the Pentapolis were included; and there is no controversy that Pippin donated those regions to the Supreme Pontiffs.

The only point that could be disputed is whether those same regions—whose cities are called the rights of the Roman Commonwealth and of the Holy See—had earlier voluntarily surrendered themselves to the pontiffs when they defected from the Eastern emperors and were later invaded by the Lombards, or whether they were captured by the Franks under the law of war and donated to the pontiffs. But since developing this controversy would exceed the limits of a preface, I think it better to leave it untouched.

### 23

I must not pass over one point, which will show that Pippin is rightly called an enlarger in the inscription cited above, but wrongly called by Pagius and others the founder of the ecclesiastical principate.

Among the changes introduced into Italy by the exarchs, one was especially significant: Longinus reduced it to the form of duchies. Whether the urban praetors continued to exist is of little importance; several of them are mentioned in the letters of Saint Gregory. Certainly the city of Rome and its duchy were governed by a duke sent from the imperial city.

This administration of both remained in place until approximately the year 726, when the impious Leo, so that he might persecute the images more effectively and securely, attempted by every means to kill Saint Gregory II. Of those who were preparing to commit so great a crime, Anastasius says:

> “Marinus, the imperial spatharius, who held the Roman duchy and had been sent from the imperial city, approved this at the emperor’s command.”

(Anastasius, no. 183.)

Hence came the previously mentioned defection of all Italy; hence the yoke of the empire was shaken off when dukes were created everywhere; hence, finally, the certain origin of the Church’s dominion.

For the people of Ravenna themselves were divided: some adhered to the pontiff, others to the emperor. The exarch Paul himself was killed, and Peter, duke of the Romans, was afflicted. Many fortresses and towns in Aemilia and the Pentapolis surrendered to the Lombards.

Eutychius, the last of the exarchs, was sent from Constantinople to replace the slain Paul and to renew the impious crime against the Roman pontiff. Finding the affairs of Italy in ruins, he humbly implored the aid of that same pontiff, who defended him. The Roman duke Stephen, successor of Peter, was no longer dependent upon the empire but upon the Roman pontiff. At the command of Gregory III he defended the city when it was besieged by Liutprand. Obeying the commands of Saint Zacharias, while that pontiff went to Ravenna to protect the exarch, he governed the city.

Anastasius narrates this entire history; I have explained it, not invented it. As we have seen, the Supreme Pontiffs Gregory III and Zacharias introduced no new form of government. Nevertheless, they possessed control of a large part of the territory, and for that reason they reclaimed from the Lombard invaders what belonged to them. The Lombards, in turn, restored to the pontiff as his own both cities and towns.

Thus the royal priesthood—than which nothing is holier and nothing more firmly established throughout the world—had an origin more illustrious than that of the other kingdoms. The zeal and piety of the peoples first established it; afterward, with the munificence of the Frankish kings added, they gave to the Apostolic See, secured by a deed of donation for perpetual possession, those territories which they had taken from the hands of barbarians and from the most wicked emperors of the East by courage and arms.

For greater confirmation of what has been said, see below, column 225, the example of the Carolingian Donation from the Farnese codex, copied in the age of Charles.

### 24

If anyone, following Pagius, interprets with him the letter of Gregory III to Charles Martel, mayor of the palace of France, in which the holy pontiff laments that whatever remained in the territories of Ravenna for the support and nourishment of Christ’s poor, or for the provision of lamps, was being devastated by the Lombards (Pagius, year 760, no. 4), he will certainly have adopted the common opinion that he learned from ecclesiastical history: that the civil administration of the Holy See did not begin in the age of Constantine the Great.

He will also have absorbed such a slight notion of that emperor’s donations of the Patrimonies, and of the Patrimonies themselves, that I think it necessary to say something—or rather to recall something—for their vindication.

I say “to recall,” because the most learned Bishop Blanchini, in his notes on Saint Sylvester, discussed the matter at length with Nicolaus Alemannus concerning the Lateran ruins. He enumerates them individually and shows that, from their revenues combined into one sum, thirty-five thousand solidi were produced. Nicephorus and Theophanes affirm that this amount was customarily paid every year by the governors of the provinces before Leo the Isaurian.

According to Blanchini’s calculation, those solidi amounted to seventeen thousand gold coins, commonly called doppie. Consequently, an equal amount was brought every year into the treasury of the Apostolic See in the name of the Patrimonies. A tenth part of their revenues, itself a considerable sum, was customarily spent on the officials responsible for collection.

If these facts are properly considered, they will first remove all our astonishment at the immense generosity of the pontiffs, the restoration of basilicas, and other great expenditures that recall our own age, as well as at the repeated plundering of the Lateran patriarchal residence by barbarians and the immense sums they ordered to be paid for the recovery of what had been taken.

They will also cause us to marvel greatly at the plan of divine omnipotence. No sooner had the impious Isaurian ordered that the Patrimonies of the holy princes of the apostles—which once contributed half a talent of gold and three talents of silver to the churches—be paid into the public treasury (Theophanes, under Leo), something none of his predecessors had dared to do, than he saw the Church exalted while he himself was increasingly humbled.

We have said that the same thing happened with the Lombards, who did not fear to extend their wicked hands against holy things. Countless other examples of this kind could also be brought forward, from which it would become evident that Christ has always fought for the Church with a strong hand, whenever irreverent princes have attacked it with the two-edged sword of his vicars.

For when the Supreme Pontiffs vindicate the Church’s property, they have always used and will always use that sword, since they do not rely solely upon the right of the Patrimonies, as Blanchini said, but upon another and higher right deriving from divine laws. According to that right, things sacred to God are to be administered, possessed, retained, and reclaimed by the supreme priest of God from sacrilegious usurpers whenever they are occupied.

See Blanchini’s notes on Saint Sylvester below.

### 25

I could not refrain from presenting these few observations, so that the reader might clearly understand that, as far as the affairs of the Holy See are concerned, one ought to follow Baronius’s opinion, not Pagius’s.

Although Pagius enriched the Ecclesiastical Annals with many new discoveries, using monuments that came to light after his death, and arranged the chronological calculations more accurately, it would have been more useful had he remained silent about several points that he brought against the learned cardinal.

Anyone who takes the trouble to compare the two authors carefully will readily discover this. I have perhaps recalled the opinions of the most learned Pagius for examination more boldly than was proper, and I myself regret doing so. The author in question had won such esteem and admiration among all people that he is everywhere proclaimed easily the foremost of all annalists.

Moreover, although one may always refute another’s opinion in order to defend one’s own, a person’s character, position, or age sometimes prevents him from exercising such license. Nature did not fashion all minds for the purpose of examining the writings of others and diminishing their authority.

This will make me liable to still more serious criticism: I consulted this author at almost every step where difficult points arose, yet I have departed from him more than once—a fault that someone may now call ingratitude.

But how else could I have acted, when at times I saw the most learned Cardinal Baronius unjustly criticized, and at other times observed that Bishop Blanchini’s opinions were being rightly challenged?

Take, for example, the ordinations of the Roman pontiffs. Blanchini’s doctrine conflicts with Pagius’s opinion. Pagius teaches that the pontiffs were ordained or consecrated on Sundays or on more solemn feast days. To prove this, he repeatedly counts among the feast days certain occasions that were not festivals in antiquity, such as the Feast of All Saints and the Roman Chair, as I have shown in the notes.

Blanchini, on the contrary, states that not only Roman pontiffs but bishops themselves were customarily ordained, after peace had been restored to the Church, only on Sundays. This could be established by many examples of bishops, especially in England, which had recently been converted—or, better said, reconverted—to the Catholic faith.

Thus, in a work of such great learning, I may sometimes appear to attack Baronius’s criticism, although in reality I always follow and increasingly admire its most learned author.

### 26

Moreover, however much freedom I have used against Pagius, there is only one reason for which I am compelled to ask pardon: the conjecture by which I dared to establish the chronology of the three emperors Anastasius, Theodosius, and Leo the Isaurian in opposition to Pagius’s conjecture.

For Pagius himself preferred, by conjecturing, to hand down a history obscured by antiquity rather than to narrate it together with Theophanes. Therefore, so that the events arranged by years may be more easily understood, I think I should state what I conjectured against Pagius.

I observed that Anastasius’s accession is certain in everyone’s judgment, but Leo’s is uncertain. More recent writers, compelled by the difficulties of the chronology, differ from Baronius by a year, postponing Leo’s beginning to the year 717. I would have followed their opinion completely if the letter of Saint Gregory II had not shown me that Leo began to reign in the fourteenth indiction, which indicates the year 716.

Therefore, thinking that I had to adhere to one of the two opinions while nevertheless not departing from the authority of Theophanes, I fixed Leo’s beginning, with Baronius, in the aforementioned year 716. And because I thought that the beginning of Constantine Copronymus ought to be measured from Leo’s end, I said in the notes that the beginnings both of Leo and of Copronymus had to be brought back to the time of Gregory II.

But afterward, after considering the matter more carefully and examining the letters of the pontiffs at leisure, I discovered that, while avoiding Pagius’s error, I had become entangled in another error no less serious when I removed the beginning of Copronymus—a beginning that, as will soon be clear, cannot be removed.

I also understood that the periods of the three emperors mentioned above should not be separated from one another but joined together. Accordingly, while retaining Theophanes’s chronology, I present the several periods interwoven in such a way that it is clear that Anastasius and Theodosius, and Theodosius and Leo, ruled the empire simultaneously. For Theophanes himself clearly relates that Theodosius was acclaimed while Anastasius was still alive, and Leo while Theodosius was still living.

### 27

Artemius, therefore, after Philippicus had been reduced to the rank of a private citizen—he had ruled for one year and six months, as Paul Warnefrid correctly states (book VI, chapter 34)—began to reign on the very Saturday of Holy Pentecost, in the eleventh indiction, toward evening, according to Agatho the Deacon in his peroration (in Combefis, *Auctarium Bibliothecae Patrum*, cited by Pagius under the years 711 and 713). That is, he began on 3 June 713.

According to Theophanes, corrected by Pagius (year 714, no. 3), he ruled for two years and nine months, and rightly so. For, apart from the fact that the *Pontifical Book* attests that Saint Gregory II, who was ordained on 19 May 715, lived in the times of Anastasius, Theodosius, and Leo—Artemius, when he received the crown, was called Anastasius—there survives in the editions of the Councils a letter of Gregory II to Bishop Martinian and the priest George as they were setting out for Bavaria. It was dated on the Ides of March, in the third year of Anastasius and the third of the pontificate (post-consulate).

From this it is clear that Anastasius’s abdication, which had occurred ten days earlier, was still unknown at Rome.

Theodosius, the successor of Anastasius, reigned, according to the same Theophanes and in accordance with Pagius’s cited correction, for one year and three months. Thus the two Augusti together completed exactly four years—two months and nine days beyond the date fixed by Theophanes, 25 March, for Leo’s inauguration. This overturns both Baronius’s and Pagius’s opinions.

Moreover, as we have seen, the certain beginning of Anastasius is separated from the equally certain end of Copronymus by sixty-two years, three months, and eleven days. For that same period elapses from 3 June 713 to 14 September 775, when Copronymus is certainly known to have died.

But Theophanes assigns to Leo twenty-four years, two months, and twenty-five days, and to Copronymus thirty-five years, two months, and twenty-six days. Added together, these yield fifty-nine full years, five months, and twenty-one days. If the aforementioned four years of Anastasius and Theodosius are added, the total becomes sixty-three years, five months, and twenty-one days—one year, two months, and eleven days more than the limits allowed by the stated beginning of Anastasius and the end of Copronymus.

Furthermore, the number of fifty-nine years, five months, and twenty-one days to be divided between Leo and Copronymus cannot be reduced without great damage to Theophanes’s chronology. This ought not to be done at the discretion of modern writers unless the authority of antiquity, preferable to that of Theophanes, supports it.

Theophanes connects Leo’s beginning with the Alexandrian year 709, which corresponds for us to 716, and Copronymus’s death with the year 768, which corresponds for us to 775. These two endpoints are separated by fifty-nine years, while the months are counted from 25 March to 14 September.

Nor is there any refuge in the month of March of the Alexandrian year 710, or Dionysian year 717. Pagius repeatedly observed that Theophanes counts the years of the Augusti according to the civil year beginning in September, even though some of them had begun several months earlier.

### 28

Since this is so, a new chronology must therefore be established in view of the sequence of events.

In the year 715 Anastasius sent a fleet against the Saracens (Anastasius the Librarian; Theophanes, *Miscellany*). But his soldiers rebelled, turned aside in the middle of their journey, and, having acclaimed Theodosius emperor, returned to Constantinople under that same leader, which they had besieged.

When Anastasius heard this, he arranged matters as the urgency of the circumstances permitted and fled to Nicaea, where he fortified himself. Meanwhile Constantinople endured a six-month siege and surrendered to Theodosius. He entered the city and was crowned; afterward, at the beginning of March 716, as may be gathered from the foregoing, he reduced Anastasius to the rank of a private citizen.

At that time Leo, governor of the East, who had defended Anastasius’s cause as vigorously as he could, was living at Amorium, a city of Phrygia Salutaris. In that same year 716 Suliman, caliph of the Saracens, arrived there. He was leading an army by land, while he sent Umar with a fleet against Constantinople, where the Saracens were carrying on the war.

The Saracens immediately acclaimed Leo emperor. The soldiers of the governor within the walls, joining in their acclamations, also acclaimed him emperor.

Soon afterward, Musalma, the Saracen commander, unsuccessfully tested the loyalty of the people of Amorium. He “had planned to take it in the summer, await the fleet, and then descend into Asia and winter there” (*Miscellany*, author uncertain). An agreement was reached between him and Leo: Musalma went into Asia to winter, while Leo, seeing the Roman provinces free, went to Nicomedia and brought with him to Constantinople Theodosius’s son, who was living there, together with all the royal equipment.

Therefore Theodosius, after consulting Saint Germanus and the nobles, surrendered the empire to Leo; he himself and his son became monks. These events occurred in the year 716, as will be made clear by what follows.

In the following year, 717, Musalma, who had wintered in Asia and realized that Leo had deceived him, again moved his forces into Thrace. He sent a letter to Suliman and summoned him with the fleet. That famous siege of Constantinople began on 15 August, by which the Blessed Virgin delivered the city (Theophanes; the author of the *Miscellany*).

On the Kalends of September Suliman himself arrived with the fleet. Shortly afterward, on 8 October, Suliman died, and Omar succeeded him in the caliphate, in the second year of Leo’s reign and the Dionysian year 717, according to Theophanes and Elmacinus, whose authority Pagius uses. Pagius criticizes Baronius for differing by a year (Pagius, year 717, no. 1; 718, no. 2).

Furthermore, in the third year of Leo, his son Copronymus was born, and his wife Maria was crowned on 21 October, according to Theophanes, or on 25 December, according to the author of the *Miscellany*. Pagius, criticizing Baronius in a similar manner, assigns these events to the year 718 (Pagius, year 719, no. 9).

I now ask: if on 8 October of the year 719 Leo’s second year was in progress, and on 21 October of the following year his third year had begun, then which Leo was inaugurated on 25 March of the year 717? Let modern writers be believed.

29. From this alone everyone sees that Leo began to reign before October of the year 716. The frequently cited letter of Gregory II, however, suggests that his reign must be dated from before September of that same year. For my part, to state what I think, Leo was acclaimed at Amorium at the beginning of the Saracen expedition, and Theophanes counts the years from that event; he also indicates the day, namely 25 March. Pagius falsely attacks Baronius for teaching this, while adhering to the authority of the same Theophanes, who counts Leo’s first year from the fifteenth indiction and the year 709 of the Alexandrian era. Everything is in fact consistent: [Col. 0817B] both the fifteenth indiction and the year 709 begin on the Kalends of September in the Dionysian year 716. Theophanes’ only error was to indicate the month and day within the waning year. I should suppose that this persuaded Pagius to believe that the chronographer, forgetting his customary practice, no longer counted the emperors’ years according to the civil year, but had adopted a unique method in Leo’s case—unless Pagius himself had written so explicitly concerning Leo’s beginning (year 727, no. 1):

> “Theophanes, who correctly joined Leo’s beginning with the Dionysian year 717, began his first year of reign, as usual, with the Kalends of September, together with the civil year.”

But, with Pagius’ permission, if Theophanes customarily begins Leo’s years with the civil year 709, would not all his reasoning collapse—both his claim that Theophanes returned to the correct path after a prolonged chronological displacement, contrary to the very learned Henschenius and Papebrochius, and his account of Theophanes’ method of reckoning—if he had joined the month of March in the year 717 with the beginning of the Alexandrian year 709?

[Col. 0817C] It is also worth noting that Theophanes does not attach the fifteenth indiction to the beginning of Leo’s reign except when speaking of his death and of Copronymus’ succession. He could not have associated any other indiction with the Dionysian September of the year 716, from which the Alexandrian year 709 begins. In the same place he correctly gives the ninth indiction, because the matter concerns the very day of his death, 18 June 741, when the ninth indiction was in progress. For the same reason he begins the reign of Copronymus from that same day of death and indiction, which he associates with the Alexandrian year 733, of which two months and twelve days still remained. Neglecting this minor point, Henschenius and Papebrochius maintained that the chronological displacement continued to the end of Copronymus’ reign.

[Col. 0817D] Moreover, Theophanes once and again counts those two months and twelve days of the Alexandrian year 733 as a full year in the case of Copronymus, whom he says reigned for thirty-five years, plainly contradicting himself, since in the case of Leo he had taught that he reigned only thirty-four years. Accordingly, I reconcile the age of both Augusti with the Dionysian years, without conflict with Theophanes’ chronology, as follows:

- Leo the Isaurian, acclaimed at Amorium on 25 March 716, reigned 25 years, 2 months, and 25 days; he died on 18 June 741.
- Constantine Copronymus reigned from the same year and day of his father’s death for 34 years, 2 months, and 26 days; he died on 14 September 775.

30. Thus, after disregarding the final years of Leo, which have been joined to false indictions, and carefully considering the sequence of events, I have supplied the period omitted by Theophanes in the age of this impious Caesar and restored the number of Copronymus’ years, which Theophanes himself began inconsistently. It is therefore clear that, of the 62 years, 3 months, and 12 days extending from 3 June 713, when Anastasius was inaugurated, to 14 September 775, the day of Copronymus’ death, these two most wicked Augusti—the son and his father—reigned for 59 years, 5 months, and 20 days. Only [Col. 0818A] 2 years, 9 months, and 21 days remain to be divided between Anastasius and Theodosius.

Accordingly, once Anastasius has been placed in order at the beginning of March 716, after two years and nine months of his reign, Theodosius has only the aforesaid twenty-one days remaining until Leo’s acclamation, although Theophanes testifies that he reigned for one year and three months before putting on the monastic habit. Therefore, in accordance with the sequence of events that I have set out, the periods of Anastasius, Theodosius, and Leo must be woven together, lest so many and such varied opinions of recent writers be preferred to Theophanes’ chronology.

Some may perhaps object that so many papal letters take away from Leo the year that I restore to him—the same year that the very learned Baronius had previously restored to him on the authority of the *Basilian Menologion*. To dispel this objection, two beginnings of Leo’s reign must apparently be distinguished: the time when he was acclaimed by the soldiers and the time when he received the crown. Hence Leo’s years are not counted in the papal letters from the acclamation made at [Col. 0818B] Amorium, but from the coronation carried out at Constantinople, after Theodosius had embraced the monastic life.

The sequence of events given above, together with the letters of both Gregory II and Gregory III, shows that the coronation took place in December, and indeed late in the month. Thus, when Leo sent a letter to Gregory II in the fourteenth indiction, he had not yet received the imperial crown. If this distinction between Theophanes and the letters of the popes were ignored, we would repeatedly be forced onto the rocks. In Leo’s case, therefore, acclamation and coronation must be distinguished.

31. Having, as I think, sufficiently prefaced my treatment of the imperial and papal chronology, I now present the fasti of the kings of the Lombards and of the exarchs of Italy, or Ravenna. I place the kings first, even though the exarchs preceded them; for just as an effect follows its cause, so the exarchs sent into Italy to resist the Lombards must necessarily be listed after their kings.

## FASTI OF THE KINGS OF THE LOMBARDS

[Col. 0818C]

### 1. ALBOIN

After spending forty-two years in Pannonia, the Lombards set out for Italy under Alboin on 2 April 568. They first invaded Forum Julium. Leaving his nephew Gisulf there, Alboin occupied Liguria the following year, on 3 September, and entered Milan. Soon afterward he attacked Ticinum; after completing a three-year siege, he captured it in 573 and established his royal seat there.

After reigning for three years and six months from his entry into Milan at the beginning of September 569, Alboin was murdered at Verona at the beginning of March through the plotting of his wife Rosemunda (Paul the Deacon, *History of the Lombards*, book II, chapters 7, 9, 25–28).

### 2. FLEPHO

When the royal offspring of the Lombards had perished together with Alboin, Clepho, the most distinguished man of his nation, was unanimously chosen king. He afflicted the Romans with exile and slaughter, and was finally murdered by his own people [Col. 0818D] after reigning for one year and six months—namely, from the same month of March in which Alboin died in 573 until September 574 (Paul the Deacon, book II, chapter 31).

### 3. AUTHARIS

After the ten-year interregnum lasting until 584, during which thirty-five dukes ruled everything tyrannically, amid great suffering for Italy (Paul the Deacon, book II, chapter 32; Saint Gregory, *Dialogues* and letters), Autharis, an Arian whom Clepho had begotten by Messana, was elected at a general council of the Lombards. The dukes contributed half of what they possessed for royal purposes.

After reigning for six years, from 584 to 590, he is said to have died at Ticinum from poison on the Nones of September. In that same year he had enacted that children should not be baptized according to Christian rite at Easter (Paul the Deacon, book III, chapters 16 and 34; Saint Gregory, book I, letter 17).

[Col. 0819A]

### 4. AGILULPHUS, ALSO CALLED AGO

After Autharis’ death, Queen Theudelinda, with the consent of the Lombards, chose a husband for herself and made Agilulphus, duke of Turin, king at the beginning of November 590. In the following year he was elevated at Milan by the entire people.

After a long reign of twenty-five years, he died in November 615 (Paul the Deacon, book III, chapter 34; book IV, chapter 43).

### 5. ADALOALDUS

He was first summoned by his father into a partnership in the kingdom in 605 and acclaimed in the circus at Milan. He was betrothed to Theodebert’s daughter, and peace was established with the Franks. He began to reign with his mother Theudelinda when he was thirteen years old. After ten years, however, he was poisoned in the bath and driven from the throne as though insane; his mother had already died. This occurred in 625 (Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapters 32 and 43; Baronius, year 616).

### 6. ARIOALDUS

He invaded the Lombard kingdom in 624, apparently while Adaloaldus was still alive, and reigned for twelve years, namely until the beginning of 636 (Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 43 and following).

### 7. ROTHARI

By birth an Arodus and by religion an Arian, Rothari was the first of his nation’s kings to give the Lombards written laws, which they had previously preserved by memory. After reigning for sixteen years and four months, from the beginning of 636 until May 652, he died, leaving behind a son whom he had made his partner in the kingdom (Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapters 44, 47, and 49).

[Col. 0819B]

### 8. RODOALDUS

Rodoaldus, Rothari’s son, was killed a few days after his father’s death. Therefore his five years and seven days of reign are counted together with Rothari’s reign (Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapters 49 and 50).

### 9. ARIPERTUS

Aripertus, the son of Gunduald, Theudelinda’s brother, began to reign in the same year in which Rothari died, toward the end of 652. He reigned for nine years and died at the end of 661 (Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 53).

### 10. BERTARIDUS AND GODEBERTUS

The sons of Aripertus divided the kingdom between themselves. Godebertus reigned at Ticinum and Bertaridus at Milan until the beginning of 663, for one year and three months. At that time Godebertus was killed by the usurper Grimoaldus, while Bertaridus fled to Gaganus, king of the Avars (Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 53; book V, chapter 33).

[Col. 0819C]

### 11. GRIMOALDUS

While the brothers were fighting over the kingdom they had divided, Grimoaldus, duke of Beneventum, was summoned to Godebertus’ aid. Believing Godebertus to be a traitor to his own people, he killed him, invaded the kingdom, and held it for nine incomplete years, from 663 to 671 (Paul the Deacon, book V, chapter 33).

### 12. BERTARIDUS

When he heard of the usurper’s death, Bertaridus returned from Saxony within three months. He expelled the young Garibaldus, Grimoaldus’ son, and held the ancestral kingdom for eighteen incomplete years, from 671 to 688 (Paul the Deacon, book V, chapters 45 and 47).

### 13. BUNIBERTUS

Bunibertus, Bertaridus’ son, was admitted by his father into a partnership in the kingdom in the eighth year of his reign. After his father’s death, he reigned for twelve years, namely from 688 until the end of 700 (Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 17; Sigebert, 687).

### 14. LIUTBERTUS

Liutbertus, still a very young child, reigned under the guardianship of Ansprandus. In the eighth month of the following year, 701, he was expelled by the usurper Ragumbertus (Paul the Deacon, in the same place).

[Col. 0819D]

### 15. RAGUMBERTUS

Ragumbertus, the son of Godebertus, who had been killed by the usurper Grimoaldus, was duke of Turin. Taking advantage of the young king’s situation, he returned to the throne and died in the same year (Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 18).

### 16. ARIPERTUS II

Aripertus II, Ragumbertus’ son, was immediately made his father’s partner in the kingdom. He had a powerful rival in Ansprandus, who was living in exile in Bavaria. In the tenth year of his exile, Ansprandus came to Italy with the assistance of Theodebertus, duke of the Bavarians, and fought Aripertus with uncertain fortune.

Believing himself defeated and preparing to depart for Francia, Aripertus, weighed down with gold, was drowned at Ticinum after reigning for twelve years, from 701 to 712 (Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapter 35).

### 17. ANSPRANDUS

Ansprandus was an outstanding man, greatly loved by the Lombards. Hardly had he obtained the kingdom when he died on the Ides of June 712, after reigning for only three months (the same author, in the same place; the *Ticinian Epitaph*).

[Col. 0820A]

### 18. LIUTPRANDUS

Liutprandus was Ansprandus’ son, whom the Lombards acclaimed out of gratitude while his father was still alive. He reigned for thirty-one years and seven months, and died on 13 January 744 (Paul the Deacon, book VI, final chapter; Herempertus; Dnastus; the Roman Council held in 743; Baronius; Pagius, no. 16, 743).

### 19. HEILDEBRANDUS

When Liutprandus was falling into a sickness and was believed to be dying, the Lombards elevated his nephew Heildebrandus. When Liutprandus later recovered, Heildebrandus became his partner in the kingdom.

After Liutprandus’ death, Heildebrandus was deposed by the Lombards themselves, who had been frightened by an omen: while he was being elevated, a cuckoo settled on the royal spear. He reigned, sometimes alone and sometimes with Liutprandus, for more than eight years (Paul the Deacon, book VI, chapters 55 and 58; Herempertus; Anastasius; charters).

### 20. RACHIS

After Heildebrandus was deposed by the Lombards, Rachis was raised to the throne in July 744. At the urging of Pope Zacharias he became a monk in 749, after reigning for four years and nine months (Herempertus, *Epitome of the Chronicle*; Anastasius, in Zacharias, nos. 217 and 223; Sigebert; Baronius, year 750; Pagius, in the same place, no. 1).

### 21. AISTULPHUS

Aistulphus administered the kingdom left to him by his brother. He was always hostile to the Roman pontiff and reigned for seven years [Col. 0820B], from 749 before July until after 5 April 756 (Sigebert, *Chronicle*; Anastasius, in Stephen II, also called III; Bacchinius, in *Peter the Elder*).

### 22. DESIDERIUS

When Aistulphus came to a bad end, Desiderius, duke of Tuscany, was elected king. He reigned for eighteen years, from 756 to 774. He was defeated by Charles the Great, then king of the Franks, and was carried with his wife into Francia, while his son Adalgisus escaped to Constantinople.

Thus the kingdom of the Lombards, by which Italy had been afflicted for 206 years, lay extinguished by the valor of the Franks (Anastasius, in Adrian; Herempertus; the *Annals of Fulda*, Metz, Bertin; and all the better recent authorities).

32. [Col. 0820C] With the catalogue of the kings completed, I must now explain both the observations of others and my own. Carefully preserving Paul the Deacon’s chronology, I associate the death of Autharis with the Nones of September 590, on the authority of Saint Gregory the Great (book I, letter 17). Counting backward from there, I assign to Autharis six years, to the interregnum ten, to Clepho one year and six months, and to Alboin three years and six months. When these are added together, I find that I have moved backward twenty-one years and reached the Nones of September 569. At that time Alboin, having invaded Liguria two days earlier, seems to me to have entered Milan, the metropolis of Liguria and formerly the royal seat where the praetorian prefect of Italy resided. The city had been almost destroyed by the Goths and was restored by Narses, as Marius of Avenches says.

Accordingly, with Sigonius, I date the beginning of the Lombards’ kingdom in Italy from this year, as Benedictus Bacchinius does, although I differ from him by several months. He begins not with the entry into Milan, but with the siege of Ticinum, which he places on 29 December, compelled by Bignelli’s authority, who records Alboin’s death on 28 June. This is certainly improbable, since it would make the Lombard kingdom in Italy begin with the opening of the siege of Ticinum, although the city was not captured until three years later and the origin of its siege is uncertain and unattested.

From the year and day of Autharis’ death—590, on the Nones of September—to the beginning of Rothari the legislator, Paul the Deacon’s chronology is certain. [Col. 0820D] He assigns twenty-five years to Agilulphus, ten to Adaloaldus, and twelve to Arioaldus. Taken together, these amount to forty-seven years and bring us to 637, while 22 November was the second year of Rothari, as is clear from the preface to his laws:

> “In the eighth year of my reign, with God’s favor, and in the thirty-eighth year of my age, in the second indiction, and in the seventy-sixth year after the Lombards’ arrival in the province of Italy, from the time when, under the king Alboin, they were assisted by divine power, this was favorably given at Ticinum in the palace.”

These chronological markers indicate the year 643; at the conclusion, however, 22 November is also mentioned. Therefore, lest we extend the indiction in order to gain a year, as Bacchinius does, Rothari’s beginning must be moved back to 636, and the excess year in Paul’s chronology must be doubled by joining Adaloaldus’ tenth year with the first year of the usurper Arioaldus.

[Col. 0821A] That Adaloaldus was still alive after the invasion of his kingdom is testified by the letters of Pope Honorius concerning the restoration of the legitimate king. Honorius, however, was ordained pope on 27 October 625. Thus, in that same year the usurper was reigning as well as the legitimate king, who had been driven insane by the criminal administration or drinking of a poisoned liquid at the usurper’s command and was counting the tenth year of his reign.

Pagius falsely believes that Adaloaldus returned to the kingdom, having been misled by two documents (in the *Cassinense Bullarium*, vol. II) that bear a corrupted date. They have, namely, the fifteenth and first indictions joined to Adaloaldus’ sixteenth and seventeenth years in the month of August, whereas another document from the same month teaches that the ninth indiction was in progress (Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, vol. IV). Accordingly, the indictions mentioned above must indicate the twelfth and thirteenth years.

I am surprised that this escaped Pagius’ notice, for the documents cited from the same *Bullarium* are preceded by an equally corrupted donation of Agilulphus, which joins Agilulphus’ eighteenth year with the fifth indiction in August, although it should have been joined with the twelfth indiction, as is sufficiently clear from what has been said in the catalogue.

33. [Col. 0821B] It is somewhat more difficult to work through Paul the Deacon’s chronology from the beginning of Rothari’s reign to Grimoaldus’ invasion. We have already seen that Rothari began in 636. That the kingdom was invaded by Grimoaldus in 663 is plainly shown by the preface to his laws:

> “In the sixth year of my reign, with God’s favor, in the month of July, in the eleventh indiction…”

This indicates the year 668. Thus, between 636 and 663, before the month of July, twenty-seven complete years are counted, whereas Paul the Deacon gives thirty-one years, seven months, and seven days. He assigns sixteen years and four months to Rothari, five years and seven days to Rodoaldus, nine years to Aripertus, and one year and three months to his sons Bertaridus and Godebertus.

I have therefore adopted Bacchinius’ opinion, according to which Rodoaldus’ period is measured together with his father’s reign, so that the deaths of both occurred in the same year, only a few days apart. Nor is this unprecedented among the Lombards, whose practice it was, following the example of the Augusti, to associate their sons with themselves in the kingdom while dying.

Agilulphus did this before Rothari. Paul the Deacon explicitly counts the ten years of Agilulphus’ son Adaloaldus with his mother Theudelinda after his father’s death (book IV, chapter 43). He likewise does not distinguish the five years and seven days of Rothari’s son from the years of his father (book IV, chapter 50).

[Col. 0821C] I nevertheless differ from Bacchinius by one year because of the later beginning that he, following Sigonius, assigns to Rothari. This forced him to extend the second indiction of Rothari’s edict to the Kalends of January, a practice condemned by many examples in the history of the Lombard kingdom. Its very beginning, in 569, on 3 September, is marked by the third indiction, a sure indication that the Lombards used the Caesarean indiction, which begins on 1 September.

The rest proceeds consistently. But what follows, from Grimoaldus’ invasion in 663 to the beginning of Liutprandus, must be considered only after first examining the beginning of Liutprandus’ reign.

Nothing seems capable of being more certain than this beginning, since it is derived from the death of his father. [Col. 0821D] His memory survives at Ticinum in the following inscription beneath his tomb:

> “Given at Pavia on the Ides of June, in the tenth indiction,”

namely, in the year 712. Horatius Blanchus, an eminent man, cites it in his notes on Paul the Deacon.

The preface to Liutprandus’ laws agrees with this inscription:

> “In the first year of my reign, with God’s favor, on the day before the Kalends of March, in the eleventh indiction,”

namely, in the year 713.

The same is true of a document concerning the convent of nuns of Saint Mary and Saint Aurelia, founded by Senator:

> “The son of the honorable Albinus and of Theodolinda, while Liutprandus was reigning, in the third year of his reign, on the fifth day before the Kalends of December, in the thirteenth indiction,”

that is, in the year 714. Mabillon records this (*Italian Journey*).

I take this opportunity to warn that Mabillon should not be followed when he reports the following document from the Augustinian monastery of Saint Peter in the Golden Heaven at Ticinum:

> “All these things that we have mentioned above we adjudge to the venerable monastery of Saint Peter in the Golden Heaven, in which we have brought Saint and Venerable Augustine. Given on the fourth day before the Nones of April, in the first year of Liutprandus’ reign, in the tenth indiction.”

Apart from its betraying a later composition, Liutprandus had not yet ascended the throne in April 712, nor had the church of Saint Peter in the Golden Heaven been founded, nor, finally, had Saint Augustine’s body been brought there from Sardinia.

Liutprandus’ reign must therefore be associated either with the very day of his father Ansprandus’ death, 13 June, or dated a few days earlier, when the Lombards, to gratify the sick man, raised his son—who was still alive at that time—in the third month of Ansprandus’ reign. Nevertheless, rather than leave the matter uncertain, I establish the beginning of Liutprandus’ reign on the very day of Ansprandus’ death, 13 June.

34. [Col. 0822A] For this reason the beginnings of the reigns of Grimoaldus and Liutprandus are separated from one another by forty-nine years and several months, for that is the period from 663 to 712. Paul the Deacon, however, gives fifty-two years and several months. He assigns nine years to Grimoaldus; eighteen to Bertaridus, who was created three months later; twelve to Cunibertus; eight months to Liutbertus; twelve incomplete years to Aripertus, together with an uncertain number of months for Ragumbertus; and finally three months to Ansprandus. Taken together, these amount to approximately fifty-two years and two months.

Everything will nevertheless fit if we take the years of the first three kings as incomplete, with Sigebertus and more recent writers, as I indicated in the catalogue. Paul the Deacon himself acknowledges this concerning Bertaridus (book V, chapters 35 and 37). Nor should we extend Cunibertus’ death beyond the year 700.

[Col. 0822B] I shall now explain the chronology of the four kings who followed, according to the sequence of events already proposed. Cunibertus, dying at the end of 700, entrusted the kingdom to his son Liutbertus under the guardianship of Ansprandus.

Ragumbertus, duke of Turin, who thirty-eight years earlier had escaped after his father Godebertus was killed, with the connivance of the usurper Grimoaldus, rose in hope of his paternal kingdom and made war upon Ansprandus. Eight months passed while arms were prepared on both sides. Around May of the following year, 701, they fought near Novara. Ansprandus and Rotharit, duke of Bergomum, were defeated. Ragumbertus ascended the throne and soon died; his son Aripertus became king.

The war was renewed. A more violent battle took place, and the allies were defeated. The boy Liutbertus was captured and killed, Ansprandus was put to flight, and Rotharit was driven into exile. Ansprandus then escaped by flight to the island of Comacina, where he was pursued by troops. Once he learned of this, he withdrew to the Bavarians toward the end of 702, as Pagius learnedly observes, moved by Paul’s authority (book VI, chapters 22 and 35) and by reconciling the years of Theodebertus’ tetrarchy.

[Col. 0822C] He spent nine years in exile. At the beginning of the tenth, which was 712, he appeared with the tetrarch Theodebertus and the Bavarians and fought a battle of uncertain outcome not far from Ticinum. Aripertus, thinking himself defeated, fled toward Francia and was drowned at Ticinum around 13 March. This is suggested by Ansprandus’ three-month reign; as stated, Ansprandus died on 13 June of the same year, leaving his son Liutprandus, whom the Lombards had raised as king before his father’s death.

[Col. 0822D] Once this beginning had been established, and since Paul the Deacon assigns Liutprandus a reign of thirty-one years and seven months, I associated his death with 13 January 744, contrary to Bacchinius, who placed both Liutprandus’ death and the beginning of Rachis’ reign in the preceding year. In my view he interpreted the history of the *Book of the Pontiffs* incorrectly, although it will be necessary to follow it hereafter. With Liutprandus’ death, Paul’s *History of the Affairs of the Lombards* comes to an end.

Having considered with Paul the chronology of the eighteen kings, it remains to determine what can be established concerning the period of their successors with the aid of the *Book of the Pontiffs* and the documents.

35. The four final kings of the Lombards—Heildebrandus, Rachis, Aistulphus, and Desiderius—fill exactly thirty years after Liutprandus. Since their history lacks the support of Paul Warnefridus, who, lest he recount the destruction of his nation as an imprudent historian, ended his work with Liutprandus, one might think it necessary to follow Herempertus, lest, assailed by so many and such varied opinions of recent writers, we seem to be restoring a contest rather than the chronology of the Lombard kings.

Yet because the documents show that Herempertus was not a very exact chronologer, I must turn elsewhere. I shall first establish the period of Heildeprandus’ joint reign with Liutprandus. Then, after setting out the sequence of events, I shall explain the beginning of Rachis, who succeeded Heildeprandus after his expulsion, associate his abdication with the beginning of his brother Aistulphus, and explain Aistulphus’ end together with the creation and captivity of Desiderius.

[Col. 0823A] That Heildeprandus reigned jointly with Liutprandus is certain. This is shown by a document—although its chronological notation has been corrupted—which Johannes Pusterla, prefect of the Ambrosian Library, communicated to Mabillon:

> “Manigulda, servant of God, living in the habit of nuns according to Lombard law, while Liutprandus and Heildeprandus were reigning, in their twenty-third year, in the fifth indiction” (*Italian Journey*).

Fiorentinius published a clearer document from the Lucchese archive, famous among learned men:

> “While the lord Liutprandus, most excellent king, was reigning, in the twenty-fourth year of his reign, and his most excellent nephew, Lord Hilprandus, king, in the first year, in the month of March, in the fourth indiction.”

It is therefore clear that in March 736 Liutprandus had already admitted his nephew as a partner in the kingdom. The Lombards had raised him while Liutprandus was ill, and Liutprandus, having later recovered, had retained him in that position.

[Col. 0823B] Finally, another document preserved by the same Mabillon (*Italian Journey* and *Benedictine Century II*) confirms that Heildeprandus began to reign jointly in March of that year, 736, and was still alive on the day before the Kalends of April in the year of Liutprandus’ death, 744. The document reads:

> “Enacted at Ticinum on the second day before the Kalends of April, in the ninth year of our fortunate reign, in the twelfth indiction.”

Accordingly, apart from eight complete years, Heildeprandus reigned for several months, the number of which cannot be investigated because the events are buried in antiquity. I therefore entirely reject the new chronology of Abbot Bacchinius (in the excursus to the *Chronicle* before John of Senigallia) and retain only the six months that he assigns to Heildeprandus after Liutprandus’ death. On this reckoning Heildeprandus was not driven from the throne until July, six months after Liutprandus’ death on 13 January 744.

But lest I appear to assert contradictory things at once, here are the contemporary history of the *Book of the Pontiffs* and the documents on which I rely.

36. [Col. 0823C] While Liutprandus was pressing Ravenna, the exarch Eutychius and the Ravennates begged Pope Saint Zacharias to bring aid. After arranging an embassy to the king without success, Zacharias himself went to meet Liutprandus. He departed from Rome for Ravenna and from there for Ticinum, arriving on 28 June 743. On the following day he celebrated the sacred rites at Saint Peter in the Golden Heaven.

Negotiations then began concerning the liberation of the Ravennates and the restoration of what had been taken from them. At last the king’s harshness was overcome, and it was agreed that, after the other things had been restored, the king would retain for himself a third part of the territory of Cesena, to be returned after the Kalends of June—namely, in the year 744—while royal envoys were meanwhile sent to Constantinople and returned.

After these arrangements, the holy pontiff returned to Rome and again celebrated the feast of the Holy Apostles, whose feast day he had celebrated at Ticinum. Not long afterward he learned that King Liutprandus had died before the appointed day for the complete restoration, on the Kalends of June 744.

The *Book of the Pontiffs* recounts these events in its life of Zacharias. Without adding any chronological indication, it then relates the expulsion of King Heildeprandus, whom Liutprandus had left behind, the election of Rachis, and the peace established with him by the pontiff for twenty years. All these events occurred in 744, as will become clear from what follows.

[OCR: “B”] I proceed to the remaining events narrated by the *Book of the Pontiffs* at the end of the life of Saint Zacharias and in the life of Stephen II, also called III.

[Col. 0823D] King Rachis, contemptuous of the peace that had been established, was attacking Perusia and other cities of the Pentapolis when the holy pontiff approached him, appeased him with gifts, and converted him to better purposes by the sweetness of his exhortation. Rachis therefore abandoned the throne, went with his wife and sons to the sacred threshold, and from there proceeded to Cassinum, where he put on the monastic habit.

Aistulphus, having obtained his brother’s scepter, was always hostile to the holy pontiff Stephen. He regarded Pippin, king of the Franks, who was fighting for the Holy See, as an enemy. Twice tested in close combat, he feared Pippin’s valor at close quarters and eluded it at a distance. At last, having broken his treaty and with God as his avenger, he died while hunting, after seeing the territory of the Church enlarged by Pippin’s donation through the Exarchate, the Pentapolis, and Emilia.

[Col. 0824A] Aistulphus was succeeded by Desiderius, duke of Tuscany, with the assistance of the pontiff and against the wishes of the Lombards. At first mild toward the Holy See, Desiderius later dared to inflict the greatest injuries upon it. He was defeated by Charles the Great, then king of the Franks, and carried with his wife into Francia in 774. He thereby brought the Lombard kingdom in Italy to an end, in the 206th year from their entry into Italy.

37. It remains for me to confirm the periods of Rachis, Aistulphus, and Desiderius by documentary evidence. As I have said, after Heildeprandus was expelled, Rachis immediately began to reign—approximately on 13 July 744. Two documents confirm this:

1. The preface to his laws, bearing the following chronological notation:

> “In the second year of my reign, on the second day of the Kalends of March, in the fourteenth indiction.”

2. A privilege issued by him at Ticinum in the palace:

> “On the fourth day of the month of March, in the second year of our most fortunate reign, in the fourteenth indiction, successfully.”

(Ughelli, *Sacred Italy*, vol. II; concerning the bishop of Piacenza.)

Since these two documents refer to the year 746, they most certainly show that Rachis was raised to the throne after 4 March 744. Pagius admits this (year 736, no. 9; 744, no. 5; 750, no. 1).

[Col. 0824B] What uncertainty, then, remains concerning his beginning—a matter rendered certain both by Herempertus’ authority and by Bacchinius’ observations? Bacchinius notes that six months after Liutprandus’ death must be assigned to Heildeprandus. As I said above, these extend to the end of the aforesaid month. Herempertus, however, fixes Rachis’ period at four years and nine months, which, beginning on approximately 13 July, extends to approximately 13 April 749.

That Rachis abdicated in this year and that his brother Aistulphus began to reign is testified by a document of approximately that period, which reads:

> “In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 749, and in the one hundred and eightieth year from the Lombards’ entry into Italy, the most glorious man AISTULPHUS—his brother Rachis, having conquered the Pentapolis, having at the urging of Lord Pope Zacharias been made a cleric at Rome—vigorously ruling the scepter of the Lombards…”

(*Italian Writers*, vol. I, part 2, concerning the foundation of the monastery of Nonantola.)

Pagius elsewhere takes note of this monument (year 750, no. 1), but wrongly argues against it as though it curtailed the years of the Lombard era. The Ligurian writer began counting from the arrival in Liguria, or from the beginning of the Lombard kingdom; the 180th year of both was still in progress until the first days of September in the Dionysian year 749.

[Col. 0824C] The month, however, remains uncertain. Two documents, namely, restrict the beginning of Aistulphus’ reign to the interval between March and July of that same year. The preface to his laws compelled Pagius to place it after the Kalends of March, for it reads:

> “In the fifth year of our most fortunate reign, in the name of God, on the day of the Kalends of March, in the seventh indiction,”

which corresponds to the year 754.

A confirmation of the possessions of the monastery of Farfa, however, reads:

> “Given at Ravenna in the palace, on the fourth day of the month of July, in the third year of our most fortunate reign, in the fourth indiction,”

that is, in 751. This compelled Bacchinius to place the beginning of Aistulphus before July (Pagius, year 750, no. 1; Bacchinius, in Agnellus; *Italian Writers*, vol. II, part I, p. 168).

But another document concerning the same monastery of Farfa reads:

> “Given at Ticinum in the palace, on 5 April, in the seventh year of our most fortunate reign in the name of God, in the ninth indiction, successfully,”

namely, in 756. This shows that Aistulphus did not begin to reign until after 5 April, since his seventh year was still in progress.

[Col. 0824D] In view of these facts, I do not think we should depart here from Herempertus in order to follow the opinion of Ostia, together with Baronius, Pagius, Bacchinius, and other learned men who were unaware of this latest document. Although only a difference of a few days appears in Herempertus, we are led still farther away from the Ostiensian opinion unless we rely on the false monuments of the ancients.

38. To this may be added the fact that Pagius, while attacking Sigonius and Angelus de Nuce for deriving from documents the conclusion that Desiderius’ reign began at the end of 756, and while accusing the documents themselves of having corrupted chronological markers, uses no other authority against them except a letter of Stephen II, also called III, in the *Codex Carolinus*, which reads:

> “For in those very days in which he [Aistulphus] set out to devastate this Roman city, after the cycle of a year had passed he was struck by the divine sword, so that, certainly, at the very time when, testing his faith, he had committed various crimes that seemed pleasing, he also ended his impious life.”

[Col. 0825A] But although Pagius correctly argued concerning the Roman siege, against Cardinal Baronius, that it began on the Kalends of January rather than on the Kalends of June 755 (year 755, no. 1 and following), this certainly does not prevent the pope’s letter from using that expression with a margin of several days, if the siege lasted three months, as the *Book of the Pontiffs* reports, or even several months, if it was shorter, as in Pippin’s letter cited by Baronius (year 755).

The substance is the same, and Stephen causes no difficulty for chronologers, since the year he indicates for Aistulphus’ death agrees with the Frankish Annals, except for the Annals of Fulda and Lambecius, which extend his death to the year 757.

Therefore Sigebert’s *Chronicle*, defining Aistulphus’ period as seven years, is wrongly corrected by Pagius. For, beginning from the year 749 around the Ides of that same month, Aistulphus completed exactly seven years.

[Col. 0825B] Perhaps even Herempertus himself should be followed when he adds five months. He counted Rachis’ years until Rachis’ departure for the city of Rome, so that after his conversion Rachis remained for another five months, as though wintering, on the Lombard throne, while Herempertus assigned those same months to Aistulphus, as though he had truly become king after Rachis’ abdication.

However the matter may stand, the last Lombard king began to reign after April in the aforesaid year 756. According to the common judgment of the Annals, after holding the kingdom for eighteen years he brought about the certain destruction of the Lombard kingdom. For Charles,

> “having obtained the entire kingdom of Italy, returned to Francia, taking with him Desiderius and his wife. His son Adalgisus fled to Constantinople”

(*Annals of Fulda and Lambecius*, year 774).

39. Having completed the fasti of the Lombards, I now turn to the exarchs of Italy. I shall compile their catalogue by comparing the observations of others, for the most part, with the *Book of the Pontiffs*.

[Col. 0825C]

### 1. LONGINUS
