After Narses, famous for so many outstanding achievements, was deprived of office by Justinus through the envy stirred up against him by his rivals, Longinus was sent to Italy as prefect in the year 567.

Later Narses withdrew to Naples and summoned the Lombards from Pannonia through envoys. Consequently, Longinus acquired an unprecedented title and new dignity among the Italians, that of exarch, and protected the portion of the Western Empire that had not been invaded by the Lombards.

He ruled Italy for fifteen years, counting from his arrival from the imperial city in 567 (Paul the Deacon, book II, chapter 5; Noris, *On the Fifth Synod*; Pagius, year 567, no. 4, citing Marius of Avenches).

2. **SMARAGDUS**, illustrious *chartularius* of the sacred palace. He was sent to Italy in 583 with this dignity, but soon recalled for an uncertain reason after three years (*Booklet on the Schism*; in Noris, *On the Synod* V; Pelagius II, letters).

3. **ROMANUS**, patrician. After Smaragdus was recalled to Constantinople in 586, Romanus succeeded him in the exarchate and died at Ravenna after eleven years, namely in 598 (Anastasius, no. 113; John the Deacon, *Life of Gregory*, book III, chapters 44 and 48; Henschenius there; Noris, *On the Synod* V, chapter 9, § 5).

4. **CALLINICUS**, or **GALLICINUS**. He was sent as Romanus’s successor in 598 and recalled after four years (Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 26; Noris, cited above; Panvinio, *Chronicle*).

5. **FLAVIUS SMARAGDUS**, again. After Callinicus was recalled, Maurice again sent Smaragdus with the dignity; Panvinio says that he governed Italy for nine years, from 602 to 611 (Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 26; Noris, cited above; Panvinio, *Chronicle*).

6. **JOANNES LEMIGIUS**, judge of the Republic. He was killed in the fourth year of his office, when John, prefect of Naples, was in revolt (Anastasius, no. 117; Panvinio, *Chronicle*).

7. **JOANNES ELEUTHERIUS**, patrician and chamberlain, or eunuch. After Lemigius was killed during the interregnum following Boniface IV, before 19 October 615, Eleutherius was sent as his successor. After three years and several months, while aspiring to imperial power, he was killed, meeting the same fate as Lemigius, during the interregnum following Saint Deusdedit, before 24 December 618 (Anastasius, nos. 117 and 118).

8. **ISAACIUS**, patrician. As soon as Heraclius heard of John’s death at the end of 618, he appointed Isaacius to govern Italy. Isaacius arrived in the following year, 619, and held the dignity for a very long time—twenty-three years. Together with the chartularius Maurice, he plundered the Lateran patriarchium in 639. He died at Ravenna after seeing the chartularius Maurice beheaded; Maurice had aspired to imperial power in Italy against Isaacius in 643 (Anastasius, nos. 121 and 126; Panvinio, *Chronicle*; Baronius and Pagi, under the year 643).

9. **THEODORUS CALLIOPA**, patrician. While governing Italy, he was recalled in his second year for an uncertain reason (Anastasius, no. 126).

10. **PLATO**, illustrious patrician. He began to govern Italy in 645 and governed it until 649 (Saint Martin, letter 16; Anastasius, no. 131; Baronius and Pagi, 649, no. 7).

11. **OLYMPIUS**, chamberlain. He departed from Constantinople and came to Rome with the dignity in 649, while the Lateran council was being held. He governed Italy for four full years and several months and died of illness in 653 (Anastasius, nos. 131–133).

12. **THEODORUS CALLIOPA**, patrician, a second time. When Constans heard of Olympius’s death, he sent Theodorus as his successor, ordering him to take Pope Saint Martin captive. The duration of his office is uncertain (Anastasius, no. 133; Muratori, *Italian Historical Records*, vol. I, part II, p. 303; Muratori casts doubt on the existence of two offices held by Theodorus).

13. **GREGORIUS**. Abbot Bacchinius conjectures that Gregory was sent as exarch around the year 658, on the basis of the privilege of Constans at Syracuse in 666.

14. **THEODORUS**, most excellent exarch. Later writers wrongly identify him with Calliopa because of the silence of Paul and Anastasius. The period of his office is likewise uncertain; but, according to Bacchinius, it extended from 668 to 687 (Anastasius, no. 156; Bacchinius, *To Peter the Elder*).

15. **JOANNES PLATYS**, patrician. He began to govern Italy in 687. Since no other exarch appears until Theophylactus, he may be believed to have governed it until 702, approximately fifteen years (Anastasius, nos. 157 and 159; Pagi, 687).

16. **THEOPHYLACTUS**, chamberlain and patrician. He was sent from Constantinople to Ravenna in 702. He governed Italy for eight years, until 710 (Anastasius, no. 165; Panvinio, *Chronicle*).

17. **JOANNES RIZOCOPUS**, patrician. Sent to Italy in 710, he received Pope Constantine at Naples when the pope was setting out for Constantinople. He then came to Rome and committed many disgraceful acts there; finally, he died at Ravenna by a most shameful death, in an uncertain year. Panvinio assigns the date 711 and says that the exarchate remained vacant for three years. Scaliger assigns Rizocopus six years, whereas Pagius criticizes him (Anastasius, no. 172; Panvinio, *Chronicle*; Scaliger, *On the Exarchs of Ravenna*; Pagi, 713, no. 4).

18. **FLAVIUS SCHOLASTICUS**, chamberlain and patrician. He was sent to Italy with the dignity at the end of 713 or the beginning of the following year, for he brought with him the imperial letter of Anastasius, who, after Philippicus had been deposed, was hailed as emperor on 4 June 713. Therefore Panvinio and Scaliger wrongly place him two years later, namely in 715 (Anastasius, no. 176; Baronius, 713).

19. **PAULUS**, patrician. He was sent to Italy by Leo the Isaurian in 726. He renewed the conspiracy against Saint Gregory II and was himself killed at Ravenna the following year (Anastasius, nos. 183 and 185; the Deacon, book VI, chapter 49).

20. **EUTYCHIUS**, patrician and eunuch. On hearing of the killing of Paul, Leo the Isaurian—who had sent Paul after the spatharius Marinus, so that Paul too might plot against the pope—likewise ordered Eutychius to come to Italy in order to complete the crime begun by the exarch Paul and the two spatharii. Of all the exarchs, Eutychius held Italy the longest, from 727 to 751—at one time hostile to the Roman pontiffs, at another protected by them against the Lombards. Finally, when their king Aistulf captured Ravenna before 4 July, Eutychius departed for Greece and brought the exarchate to an end. The year was 751 in the Dionysian era: the tenth year of Zacharias, the thirty-second of Constantine Copronymus, the tenth of the post-consulate of Constantine, and the third of Aistulf.

Thus the exarchate of Italy, or of Ravenna, whose beginnings I have placed in the first year of Longinus, 567, lasted approximately 184 years and had exactly twenty exarchs, counting the repeated offices of Smaragdus and Calliopa (Anastasius, nos. 183, 185–187, 194, 213; later writers generally, especially Benedict Bacchinius in Agnellus).

40. This epoch—the ending of the exarchs, at a time when almost all Italy had defected from the impious Greek emperors—will properly be joined with the destruction of the Greek Empire. For although its restoration was attempted more than once, divine providence nevertheless brought it about that all the emperors’ efforts were in vain. The exarchate, which for so many years had been secured by Greek forces for the enlargement of the dominion of the Holy See against the most warlike Lombards, finally fell into the hands of the latter. Afterwards, however, when King Pippin of the Franks had defeated the usurpers, it passed into the dominion of the Holy See together with the Pentapolis and Emilia; nor has it since been open to barbarians in our own age.

This office, already renowned both by its origin and by its dignity, later became more illustrious when three most eminent legates of the Apostolic See began, in the name of the supreme pontiffs, to administer it in three divisions and preserve it under sacred laws, as we see done in our own age.

As for the exarchs whose catalogue I have presented, it is difficult to arrange their chronology by months and days. History reports that some were sent immediately after their appointment at Constantinople, while others arrived late in Italy because they were detained either by the will of the emperors or by the length of the journey. For this reason, following the practice used elsewhere, I have been content to indicate the years and have neglected to investigate in which particular month they were appointed at Constantinople or arrived in Italy.

I have observed, however, that the succession of exarchs is certain down to Theodorus Calliopa, who, sent in 653, took Pope Saint Martin captive. From that point down to Joannes Platys, who came to Italy in 687, it rests on the conjectures of the learned Pagius and Bacchinius. The five exarchs who follow Platys seem to me certainly historical; yet among them are three whose succession is not so certain as to leave no room for doubt—Theophylactus, Joannes Rizocopus, and Paulus. The other two, Flavius Scholasticus and Eutychius, unquestionably succeeded Rizocopus and Paulus respectively, as may be seen in the authors whom I cited in the catalogue.

Therefore, if the passage of time should bring to light some new exarch, he must necessarily be placed, according to the chronology, either between Theodorus Calliopa and Joannes Platys, or between Platys and Rizocopus, or finally between Flavius Scholasticus and Paulus. There is neither time nor place to observe more concerning the chronology. With regard to the dignity of the exarch, however, besides what I remarked in passing above (nos. 7 and 8), I have reserved something to indicate here more appropriately.

41. We learn that the dignity of exarch, although new to the Italians, was not unknown to other peoples; Gregory the Great bears witness to this (letters, book I, nos. 59 and 72, to the exarch of Africa). We also learn that it was always joined to palatine offices, since we read that patricians, *chartularii* of the sacred palace, eunuchs, chamberlains, and judges of cities were adorned with it.

It would be tedious for learned readers to examine each of these offices in detail. Concerning the patricians, however, I am determined to recall certain matters, however much I may already have long abused their patience. I recognize two classes of patricians; and I believe that many of the other distinctions reported by Cangius in his general *Glossary* may be included under this division: some were patricians of the emperors, others of the pontiffs—that is, some were created by the emperors, others by the Roman pontiffs.

I present the form of creating imperial patricians, preserved in the Vatican Library and reproduced by Cangius from Paul of Friuli, or the Deacon:

> The dignity of patrician is to be arranged in such a way that it is not granted to an unworthy person or to anyone unknown. He must be very well known to the emperor; he must be faithful and prudent, not arrogant. The protospatharius, coming before the emperor, shall kiss his shoulder and say: “Most exalted of emperors, here is the man whom you summoned.” Then the emperor’s hyparch, whom we call the prefect, shall stand at his left and the emperor shall say to him: “Bring the future patrician with the protospatharius.”
>
> When the patrician has arrived, he shall first kiss the emperor’s feet, then his knee, and finally kiss the emperor himself. He shall then kiss all the Romans standing around, and they shall all say: “Welcome. It seems to us exceedingly burdensome that we alone should administer the ministry entrusted to us by God. Therefore we make you our assistant and grant you this honor, so that you may establish law for God’s churches and for the poor, and thereafter render an account before the Most High Judge.”
>
> Then the emperor shall clothe him with a mantle, place a ring on the index finger of his right hand, and give him a written document in his own hand, containing the following words: “Be a patrician, merciful and just.” Then he shall place a golden circlet on his head and dismiss him.

Senator teaches that this dignity—which, according to Walafrid Strabo, adorned those who were first after the emperors—was perpetual:

> As soon as this honor has been bestowed, it becomes coeval with the man for the remainder of his life.

(*Book VI*, chapter 2.)

Cangius therefore conjectures that perhaps for this reason it was joined to some other, shorter-lived dignity, such as the exarchate or another prefecture. Yet, reading *expatricios* in the Theodosian Code, he agrees with other authorities that among the Goths it signified only that they had held this dignity. Gutherus, however, maintains that this dignity was not perpetual, even though it was among the most eminent palatine offices; rather, like the other offices, it depended on the prince’s will, and when the administration ended its holders were customarily called *expatricii* (*On the Offices of the Imperial Household*, book II, chapter 19).

42. We must therefore accept the opinion of Dufresne. For when the imperial residence had been transferred to Constantinople, two patricians, as Porphyrogenitus says, were customarily sent from there to Italy (*On the Administration of the Empire*, chapter 27). We would call them viceroys today. One governed Sicily, Calabria, Naples, and Amalfi; the other governed Benevento, Capua, Pavia, and the remaining territories, and they paid annual tribute into the emperor’s treasury. I believe that, in dignity, these men were equal to the masters of the soldiers in military expeditions and were accustomed to be removed at the prince’s pleasure, although two inscriptions cited by Gutherus may appear to teach otherwise.

The first, preserved at Trier, reads:

> HERE LIES ELIUS CONSTANTIUS, CONSULARIS, COUNT AND MASTER OF BOTH MILITARY SERVICES, AND PATRICIAN.

The other, at Rome:

> FLAVIUS RICIMER, ILLUSTRIOUS MAN, MASTER OF BOTH MILITARY SERVICES, PATRICIAN.

From these inscriptions we learn both that the patriciate was joined with military command and that the dignity was perpetual. But the case of the patricians who were sent to Italy before the Gothic period must have been different. The patricians who, in the Gothic age, were sent as prefects to Italy, and all the others then created by the Augusti, were perpetual, according to Senator’s doctrine.

The evidence for this is the great number of patricians living at one and the same time in the court at Constantinople. Saint Pope Paul says in his letter to Pippin that six of them, bringing with them three hundred ships and at the same time the fleet of the Sicilians, were released from the imperial city and hastened toward this Roman city (*Carolingian Code*, 24).

Moreover, both in the *Pontifical Book* and in the historians contemporary with the Lombard kingdom in Italy, we frequently read of several patricians in different places, while one of them was administering the exarchate at Ravenna; for this dignity was generally conferred upon patricians. Thus Belisarius and Narses, who retained only the name of patrician, and all the exarchs who joined the most eminent patriciate to the most excellent dignity of exarch, never laid it down once they had been adorned with it. Nor is it found anywhere that, when some of them were recalled to Constantinople, they were called *expatricii* after their administration had ended.

Finally, this dignity, as the first after the emperors, was conferred by the Byzantine Augusti as a mark of the highest honor upon foreign kings and princes, as may be seen in Cangius’s *Glossary*.

43. The Roman pontiffs followed the example of the Augusti when they created the kings of the Franks patricians. There is, however, this distinction between the two classes of patricians: the imperial patricians were the first after the emperors among the palatine offices; the pontifical patricians, on the other hand, possessed the highest dignity and power. As Gutherus observes, they were called “patricians of the Romans,” not “Roman patricians,” because they commanded all the Romans, led the army, and truly shone with the majesty of the emperor. Thus Charles the Great was called “patrician of the Romans,” as the father and protector of the entire Roman Empire (Gutherus, *On the Offices*, book II, chapter 29).

Therefore, as Pagius learnedly explains with Marca (640, no. 6 and following), the Roman pontiffs’ patriciate comprised two things: jurisdiction, by which the Frankish kings exercised authority in the City with the consent of the pontiff and the Roman people; and protection, or defense, which they promised to the Roman Church.

Hence the banner that Roman pontiffs customarily sent to princes bearing arms against pagans or heretics was also sent to the patricians themselves. They did not send it to the emperors, because the protection of the Roman Church was joined to the Empire by a general obligation and a special agreement.

Since this is so, Cangius, and before him many other writers, judged incorrectly that the patriciate of the Romans was nothing other than the prefecture of the City, or even of Italy—a dignity devised by the Romans after the yoke of the Greek Empire had been thrown off. Alamannus agrees with this view (*On the Lateran Walls*, chapter 11), apparently because when Charles the Great acquired imperial majesty he ceased to use the name of patrician. For whatever the title of emperor may seem to confer beyond that of patrician of the Romans, the power was one and the same: namely, that of protector and defender of the Roman Church.

For this reason, when Charles the Great, patrician of the Romans, came to Rome, Adrianus gave him the same honor that Sergius later gave to the emperor Louis. Adrianus went out to meet Charles, his holiness sending venerable crosses—that is, banners—as is customary when receiving an exarch or patrician (Anastasius, no. 315). Sergius did the same for Louis, as Anastasius says: “As is customary when receiving an emperor or king” (no. 484).

Moreover, when the Roman pontiff created Charles Martel patrician, the Greek Empire still existed, as Pagius shows at length (cited above). The dignity of the pontifical patricians was therefore much greater than that of the imperial patricians.

But enough has now been said.

[Col. 0829]

# CHRONOLOGY FOR VOLUME IV OF THE ROMAN-VATICAN EDITION

From Saint Gregory the Great to Stephen III, also called IV.

[Note: The following texts, headed “Roman Emperors …” and “Roman Pontiffs …,” are printed in parallel in Migne. Two columns of dates, headed “Years from the Founding of the City” and “Olympiad Years,” have been incorporated as notes to these texts. Two further columns, headed “Years of the Julian Period and Indiction” and “Years of the Christian Era,” have been omitted.]

Roman emperors, Lombard kings, exarchs, and events.

[Col. 0829C]

**Maurice Tiberius Augustus, regnal years 8 and 9, after the seventh consulate, alternatively the sixth.**  
[Note: 1342; 1343.]

Maurice crowns his son Theodosius emperor at the Paschal festival, on 26 March or 2 April, according to Theophanes and the Alexandrian Chronicle; Pagius and Baronius assign this to the year 593.

The Franks fight successfully against the Lombards (the Deacon, Turonensis, Baronius, and Pagius).

Authari, king of the Lombards, while negotiating peace with the Franks, dies at Pavia on 5 September. Theodolinda chooses Agilulf, duke of Turin, as her husband and king in November; in May of the following year he is acclaimed by the army at Milan (the Deacon, book III, final chapter; Pagius, 616, no. 2).

Hormisdas, prefect of the Romans, is killed at the command of Chosroes, the son of the elected king (Theophylact, book III, chapter 8; Pagius, following year).

**Emperor Maurice Tiberius Augustus, regnal years 9 and 10, after the eighth consulate, alternatively the seventh.**  
[Note: 1343; 1344.]

Narses, Maurice’s adjutant, enters Persia with Domitian, bishop of Melitene, and fights successfully against Varamus. The Persian war, which had lasted twenty years, comes to an end. Chosroes, driven out by Varamus, is restored to the kingdom after entering into an alliance with the Romans (Theophanes and the Alexandrian Chronicle; Pagius, 593, nos. 2 and 4). Baronius places this two years later.

The head of Zadesprates, the deserter who had formerly led Hormisdas, is brought to Chosroes (Pagius, following year, no. 4, with Baronius).

The chronicle of the abbot of Biclaro ends in this year.

**Emperor Maurice Tiberius Augustus, regnal years 10 and 11, after the ninth consulate, alternatively the eighth.**  
[Note: 1344; 1345.]

Maurice marches against the Avars, or Turks dwelling in Thrace (Pagius, following year, no. 10).

An eclipse of the sun on 19 March. Fredegar, chapter 13; Aimoinus, book III, chapter 8; Petavius, *On Theological Doctrine*, book VIII. Parallax of latitude, 46° 29′. Northern latitude, 41° 29′; apparent latitude, 5° 0′. Semidiameter of the sun, 16′ 58″; total semidiameter, 34′ 30″; remaining arc, 29′ 30″; ecliptic digits, 10′ 26″. According to the Prutenic Tables, Calvisius says that it occurred on Friday at the tenth hour after midnight at Constantinople.

**Emperor Maurice Tiberius Augustus, regnal years 11 and 12, consuls tenth, alternatively ninth.**  
[Note: 1345; 1346.]

Chosroes, seeking assistance from Maurice, vowed to Saint Sergius the Martyr and pretended that he wished to become a Christian; he did not, however, do so, as Saint Gregory testifies (letter 62, book II).

Guntram, king of the Franks, dies on 28 March (Fredegar and Herman the Contracted; Pagius, no. 17). Baronius, having incorrectly established the beginning of his reign, wrongly postpones his death to 598.

An expedition against the Avars is entrusted to the patrician Priscus (Pagius, no. 12).

Baronius and others suppose the privilege of Sammedard to belong to this year, but Pagius, no. 8, and Dupin, dissertation 7, show it to be spurious.

**Emperor Maurice Tiberius Augustus, regnal years 12 and 13, consuls eleventh, alternatively tenth.**  
[Note: 1346; 1347.]

Empress Constantina, at the urging of John, patriarch of Constantinople, seeks the head of Saint Paul, but the pontiff eludes her (Gregory, book III, letter 30).

The six books of Evagrius’s history, extending from the end of Theodoret and Socrates, end in this year (Photius). Pagius shows that the work does not extend beyond the preceding August; to prevent Photius’s opinion from collapsing, he supposes that it was published in this year.

An eclipse of the sun on 23 July, Friday, six hours before noon; ecliptic digits, 11′ 28″; the sun in the first degree of Leo. Calvisius follows Aimoinus against Sigebert, who reports it two years later.

**Emperor Maurice Tiberius Augustus, regnal years 13 and 14, after the twelfth consulate, alternatively the eleventh.**  
[Note: 1347; 1348.]

Romanus, exarch of Rome, returning to Ravenna, recovers cities captured by the Lombards; consequently Agilulf invades the Roman Empire (the Deacon, book IV, chapter 7). Sigonius places this two years earlier.

Italy had now groaned under Lombard arms for twenty-seven years—that is, since 568 (Gregory, book IV, letter 34).

Because Maurice treated Gregory with contempt, John of Constantinople seized an opportunity to exalt himself through the title “ecumenical”; Gregory therefore forbade Sabinianus, the apocrisiarius, to communicate with him (Saint Gregory, book IV, letters 32, 34, 36, 38, 39).

**Emperor Maurice Tiberius Augustus, regnal years 14 and 15, after the thirteenth consulate, alternatively the twelfth.**  
[Note: 1348; 1349.]

The imperial prefects repeatedly frustrate peace with the Lombards, which Gregory had often attempted.

Childebert dies, leaving Theuderic and Theudebert as heirs (the *Life of Saint Columbanus*, chapter 18, in Bede, vol. III). Baronius, who wrongly connected the beginning of his reign with 579, assigns him only seventeen years of rule, contrary to the ancient authorities. Pagius, nos. 13 and 14, confirms the date of his death from Gregory, letter 58, book V.

Zotto, duke of Benevento, captures Croton; elsewhere also the Romans suffer many things at the hands of the Lombards (Sigonius).

**Emperor Maurice Tiberius Augustus, regnal years 15 and 16, after the fourteenth consulate, alternatively the thirteenth.**  
[Note: 1349; 1350.]

King Æthelberht of England, who has Bertha, or Adilberga, a Christian wife, grants Augustine permission to preach in his kingdom of Kent. The other six kingdoms of England do not receive the faith in this year. The king of England himself becomes a Christian; Augustine had crossed over into England in this year, according to Bede (Pagius, no. 2 and following).

The testament of the ailing Maurice, by which he divides the Empire among his sons, belongs to this year or the preceding one, not to the following year as Baronius thinks (from Theophylact; Pagius, no. 2, under 598).

**Emperor Maurice Tiberius Augustus, regnal years 16 and 17, after the fifteenth consulate, alternatively the fourteenth.**  
[Note: 1350; 1351.]

Peace is finally concluded with the Lombards through the agency of Probus, and in the following year it is confirmed by the Lombard king (Gregory, book VII, letters 2 and 5).

News is brought to Rome of the victory over the Slavs and of the return of schismatics to the Church (the same book, letter 9; Baronius).

Fredegund, widow of Chilperic, king of Neustria, and mother of Chlothar II, dies.

Gallinicus, or according to others Callinicus, succeeds the exarch Romanus. See Eschen on John the Deacon, chapters 44 and 42, book III, and Panvinio’s *Chronicle*.

**Emperor Maurice Tiberius Augustus, regnal years 17 and 18, after the sixteenth consulate, alternatively the fifteenth.**  
[Note: 1351; 1352.]

Gregory sends letters to Agilulf and Theodolinda, after subscribing to the peace (book VII, letters 41 and 42). He is afraid of Arnulf, duke of Spoleto, who subscribed to the agreement at the counsel of his wife Varnilfrida (the same book, letter 102).

The council at Constantinople is convened, and Gregory suspects that it concerns the title “ecumenical”; hence his letter to Eusebius of Thessalonica (the same source).

Maurice sends thirty pounds of gold to Rome, to be distributed among the poor and as payments to the soldiers (Gregory, book VIII, letter 2).

The khagan, king of the Avars, invades Thrace (Theophylact, book VII, chapter 13; Pagius, no. 2). Baronius postpones the event to the following year and says that it occurred in Lower Pannonia.

**Emperor Maurice Tiberius Augustus, regnal years 18 and 19, after the seventeenth consulate, alternatively the sixteenth.**  
[Note: 1352; 1353.]

The Slavs invade Italy; on this occasion the bishop of Epidaurus transfers the body of Saint Donatus to Corcyra (Gregory, book XII, letters 2, 3, and 8).

Commentiolus is again created duke, and after the Romans return to his favor he fights successfully against the Avars five times (Theophylact, book VIII, chapters 2 and 3).

After Gregory was recalled, Leontius was sent as prefect to the City. Passing through Sicily, he removed the prefect Libertinus from office after having him killed (Gregory, book VIII, letter 31).

Civil war between the Frankish kings: Theuderic and Theudebert are victorious, Chlothar defeated (Aimoinus, book III, chapter 88). Baronius places it in the following year; Pagius, in the same year, no. 16.

A comet had previously appeared in the sky (the Deacon, book IV, chapter 16).

**Emperor Maurice Tiberius Augustus, regnal years 19 and 20, after the eighteenth consulate, alternatively the seventeenth.**  
[Note: 1353; 1354.]

When the period of peace had ended, fighting again took place between the Lombards and the Romans. The Romans were defeated by Arnulf, duke of Spoleto (the Deacon, book IV, chapter 17). Baronius places it in the following year; Pagius, in the same year, no. 2.

Reccared, king of Spain, after reigning fifteen years, one month, and ten days from the year 586, dies toward the end of April (from Vasæus and Valla; Pagius, no. 17).

Maurice gives his son Theodosius in marriage to the daughter of the patrician Germanus in November of the twentieth imperial year (Theophanes; Ducange, *On the Byzantine Families*).

**Emperor Maurice Tiberius Augustus, regnal years 20 and 21, after the nineteenth consulate, alternatively the eighteenth.**  
[Note: 1354; 1355.]

Maurice, who had succeeded Tiberius Constantine in 582, is slaughtered with his household on 27 November of this year, after twenty imperial years, three months, and several days, according to Blanchinus and Pagius. Noris, *On the Synod* V, chapter 9, §§ 3 and 5; Pagius, no. 9. Ducange, *On the Augustan Byzantine Families*, chapter 9, presents a coin inscribed “Year XX” and another “Year XX,” struck at Thessalonica. See Ducange, *On the Byzantine Families*.

Before this, however, on 23 November, Phocas, a centurion raised up by the soldiers, had usurped the tyranny. Theophylact, book VIII, chapter 5 and following. See the year 610. He was crowned by the patriarch Cyriacus on 23 November, Friday.

After Callinicus was recalled, Flavius Smaragdus was sent as exarch for the second time (the Deacon; Noris).

**Emperor Phocas Augustus, regnal years 1 and 2.**  
[Note: 1355; 1356.]

The image of Phocas and Leontia comes to Rome on 25 April and is acclaimed for them in the Lateran by all the clergy (John the Deacon, book IV, chapter 20).

When Chosroes received the letter announcing Phocas’s elevation, he broke the treaty concluded with the Romans and, as avenger of Maurice, sounded the trumpet of war (Theophylact, p. 3).

Phocas rages against the wife and the surviving members of Maurice’s family. From the Alexandrian Chronicle, Theophanes, Theophylact, and Pagius, no. 4. Baronius incorrectly assigns the event to 607 and, after the massacre, sends the legate Lilius to Chosroes as above, five months after the inauguration. Arnulf, with Christmas approaching, prepares the destruction of the city of Rome (Gregory, book XII, letter 22).

Witteric, having seized the tyranny, removes Liuvа from the Spanish kingdom after two years (same source).

An eclipse of the sun (Fredegar, *Chronicle*, chapter 24; Cim, book III, chapter 90). Pagius assigns it to 612, no. 11.

**Emperor Phocas Augustus, regnal years 2 and 3.**  
[Note: 1356; 1357.]

This year is inscribed “Phocas Augustus, first year, sole consul.”

Agilulf, having again made peace with Rome, increases his male offspring; Theodolinda wishes that Adaloald be baptized according to Christian custom (Gregory, book XII, letter 7).

In the East, dignities and honors are for sale (same source, letter 27).

In this year or the following one, Constantina, the wife of Maurice, with her three daughters and the wife of her son Theodosius, is beheaded at the harbor of Eutropius near Chalcedon by order of Phocas. Theophanes places it two years later. Ducange, *On the Byzantine Families*.

**Emperor Phocas Augustus, regnal years 3 and 4, after the first consulate.**  
[Note: 1357; 1358.]

When Adaloald was two years old, his father admitted him to a share in the kingdom and betrothed him to the three- or four-year-old daughter of Theudebert; perpetual peace with the Franks was confirmed (Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 31). Aimoinus places it two years earlier, book III, chapter 89.

After moving every stone to get hold of Narses, Phocas obtained by repeated oaths that he would return to the Romans; then, breaking faith, he ordered him to be burned alive (from Cedrenus and the *Miscellany*; Baronius).

A cold winter follows Gregory’s death; the vines and crops being destroyed, famine arises in Italy (the Deacon, book IV, chapter 30).

**Emperor Phocas Augustus, regnal years 4 and 5, second consulate.**  
[Note: 1358; 1359.]

Agilulf again confirms peace with the Romans for three years in November (Paul the Deacon, book IV, chapter 33). Sigonius adds that in this year Ferrara, which was then a village, was enclosed with walls by the exarch Smaragdus and converted into a fortress. Calvisius wrongly attributes this to the Deacon and, misunderstanding a passage of Aimoinus, book III, chapter 90, postpones to this year an eclipse of the sun that had been seen three years earlier.

At Rome the dearth becomes less keenly felt through the beneficence of Sabinianus. See Baldini’s notes below.

**Emperor Phocas Augustus, regnal years 5 and 6, after the third consulate.**  
[Note: 1359; 1360.]

Phocas gives his daughter Domitia in marriage to the patrician Priscus, commander of the Excubitors; Priscus exercises tyranny (Theophylact, p. 6).

He likewise grants Boniface III, Roman pontiff, who had requested it of him, the decree that—against the audacity of the patriarchs of Constantinople, who called themselves “ecumenical”—the Roman Church was the head of all the churches. Baronius under this year. See the notes on the same Boniface.

The shaking of the Cross at Constantinople during a public procession foretells great evils, according to Theodore of Syceon.

**Emperor Phocas Augustus, regnal years 6 and 7, after the fourth consulate.**  
[Note: 1360; 1361.]

Priscus plots against Phocas. He therefore writes to Heraclius, the prefect of Africa, asking him to send his son Heraclius against the tyrant (from Theophanes; Baronius, *Miscellaneous History*).

Meanwhile the Persians, meeting no resistance, occupy Armenia and Cappadocia. After routing the Roman army, they lay waste everything with fire and sword and advance as far as Chalcedon (Cedrenus).

**Emperor Phocas Augustus, regnal years 7 and 8, after the fifth consulate.**  
[Note: 1361; 1362.]

Phocas, neglecting the administration of the state to men of his own kind, creates Bonosus, a harsh man, count of the East. He makes him master of the circus, and Bonosus cuts down many who insult him (*Miscellaneous History*).

Tassilo, duke of the Bavarians, dies around this year (the Deacon, book IV, chapter 41; Pagius, no. 5).

From this year begins the prochronism of Theophanes, followed by Baronius. Therefore, throughout eighty-four years of the Alexandrian era, eight years must be added to its dates in order to make it agree with the Dionysian era. Pagius, Henschenius, volume III, March, in the *Exegesis on the Chronography of Saint Theophanes*, and Papebrochius, in his *Attempt toward Constantinople*, maintain that it continued to the end of Copronymus, even to the year 775.

**Emperor Phocas Augustus, regnal year 8, after the sixth consulate.**  
[Note: 1362; 1363.]

According to the Alexandrian Chronicle, from 7 October to 13 January the emperor Heraclius’s first year is recorded in the public tables.

Phocas, defeated by Heraclius, is miserably killed on 5 October, after reigning seven years, ten months, and eighteen days, for he had been crowned on 23 November 602 (Zonaras, Cedrenus, Ducange).

Heraclius is inaugurated on 5 October by the patriarch Sergius, and his wife Eudocia is crowned Augusta (Baronius and Pagius, no. 6).

After Witteric was killed by a conspiracy in Spain, having reigned seven years, Gundemar succeeds him (Isidore, *Chronicle*).

**Emperor Heraclius Augustus, regnal years 1 and 2.**  
[Note: 1363; 1364.]

According to the Alexandrian Chronicle, this year is recorded from 14 January through the completion of December, together with the consulate of our most religious prince.

Syria is devastated by the Persians in May (Pagius, no. 2).

Heraclius is given a daughter, Epiphania, by Eudocia on 7 July (same source, no. 4). According to Theophanes and the Alexandrian Chronicle, she was baptized on 15 August and named Eudocia. Ducange, *On the Byzantine Families*.

Joannes Lemigius comes to Italy as exarch at the end of this year.

**Emperor Heraclius Augustus, regnal years 2 and 3.**  
[Note: 1364; 1365.]

This year is inscribed “after the consulate of Heraclius Augustus.”

Heraclius the Younger, called Constantine, is born on 3 May, and Eudocia dies on 13 August. According to the Alexandrian Chronicle and Pagius, no. 2, Epiphania is crowned Augusta on 4 October, according to Theophanes. Ducange, *On the Byzantine Families*.

The Persians, under their commander Raxates, capture Caesarea of Cappadocia (Theophylact, book VIII, chapter 12).

Theudebert, king of Austrasia, defeated by his brother, is forced to become a cleric and soon afterward killed (Fredegar, chapter 38; Aimoinus, book III, chapter 98). Baronius incorrectly places this above.

**Emperor Heraclius Augustus, regnal years 3 and 4, after the second consulate.**  
[Note: 1365; 1366.]

This year is recorded as the third year after the consulate of Heraclius Augustus, and as the second year of the Augusti emperors Heraclius and Flavius Heraclius Constantine, his son, preserved by God, from the beginning of their joint reign.

Heraclius the Younger is crowned on 22 January, not on 25 December as Theophanes says, nor on 22 April as Eleus says (Pagius, from the Alexandrian Chronicle, nos. 1 and 3).

The emperor contracts an incestuous marriage with his niece, who is crowned Augusta by Sergius. Baronius and Pagius, no. 2.

Theuderic, king of Burgundy and Austrasia, dies of dysentery. Fredegar and Aimoinus, book III, chapter 100; or, as Jonas prefers, struck by lightning. He leaves four sons: Sigebert, Childebert, Corbus, and Macroveus, whose life Chlothar spared. Fredegar, chapter 42. In this matter Baronius is mistaken, following Jonas in the *Life of Saint Columbanus*. Pagius, no. 28.

Sigebert reigns for a few months after his father; when he is killed, Chlothar II, king of Neustria, obtains the monarchy of the Franks. Since the death of Chlothar I in 561, several kings had held it for approximately fifty-one years (Aimoinus, beginning of book IV; Pagius, no. 33).

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, regnal years 4 and 5, after the third consulate.**  
[Note: 1366; 1367.]

Heraclius the Younger, regnal years 2 and 3.

In this year, apparently, the city of Damascus is captured (from Theophanes and Nicephorus; Pagius, no. 2 under the preceding year, with Baronius); Jerusalem too is captured, according to Lindebruch.

Sisebut, in Spain, issues an edict against the Jews, requiring all of them to become Christians within a year or to be expelled from Spain after losing all their possessions (from Isidore; Calvisius).

Heraclius marries Martina, his niece by his sister. The canons opposed the marriage, and the patriarch Sergius protested; nevertheless, she bore him sons from the unlawful union, deformed and maimed (Nicephorus; Ducange, *On the Byzantine Families*).

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, regnal years 5 and 6, after the fourth consulate.**  
[Note: 1367; 1368.]

Heraclius the Younger, regnal years 3 and 4.

Heraclius sends ambassadors to Chosroes; they accomplish nothing and are instead detained in prison (Pagius, no. 3 and following; Petavius, Bollandus, and others under the following year).

A second Constantine is born to the emperor by Martina (Pagius, no. 18).

When John, the prefect of Naples, rebelled, John the exarch was killed. During the interregnum, Eleutherius was sent as his successor. While plotting tyranny, Eleutherius went to Naples to avenge John and bind his subjects to himself; after killing John Compsinus, he returned to Ravenna.

Agilulf, king of the Lombards, dies. Adaloald succeeds under the guardianship of his mother Theodolinda, who rules with him for ten years (the Deacon, book IV, chapter 43; Sigonius).

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, regnal years 6 and 7, after the fifth consulate.**  
[Note: 1368; 1369.]

Heraclius the Younger, regnal years 4 and 5.

Chosroes invades all Egypt and extends his march through Libya as far as Chalcedon—not Carthage, as Anastasius reads in his *Ecclesiastical History*, nor as the author of the *Miscellany* reads, whom Baronius follows. They were misled by the similarity of the names Χαλκηδών (*Chalkēdōn*, Chalcedon) and Καρκηδιών (*Karkēdiōn*, Carthage). Baronius above; Pagius, in the same place, no. 2, and in this year, no. 3, shows that Alexandria was captured.

After this, the Persians return home, leaving behind a garrison to besiege Chalcedon. Baronius assigns this to the preceding year; Pagius correctly observes that military expeditions were customarily undertaken in spring and therefore assigns it to this year (Pagius, preceding year, no. 1).

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, regnal years 7 and 8, after the sixth consulate.**  
[Note: 1369; 1370.]

Heraclius the Younger, regnal years 5 and 6; he is said to have held the consulate with his father in this year.

Famine and plague begin at Constantinople this year. Since the Persians had begun to occupy Egypt and Alexandria in the preceding year, no grain was brought from there; hence famine arose, followed by plague (from Nicephorus; Pagius, no. 9, and the following year, no. 11).

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, regnal years 8 and 9, after the seventh consulate.**  
[Note: 1370; 1371.]

Heraclius the Younger, regnal years 6 and 7.

At Constantinople, as the famine increased, distributions of public allowances were abolished.

When the Italian disturbances had spread into Greece, Heraclius appointed Isaac the Patrician to govern Italy in place of Eleutherius. Sigonius. He did not arrive until the following year [Col. 0845D], after Eleutherius had been murdered at the fortress of Luceoli, while the see was vacant—that is, after 8 November. At the same time Rome was suffering from the elephantine plague, which was immediately followed by a great earthquake in August. Anastasius; Calvisius.

John Eleutherius, Exarch, having already governed Italy for four years, on hearing of the Emperor’s difficulties, usurped tyranny while the see was vacant and, following the example of his predecessor, was murdered before 24 December. Anastasius.

**Emperor Heraclius Augustus, years 9 and 10, after the eighth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0845D] 1371–1372].

Heraclius, years 7 and 8 of his June era.

The pragmatic sanction of Heraclius belongs to this year [Col. 0847A]: no one is to be admitted into the clergy of Constantinople unless he is substituted in the place of a deceased cleric; from this arose a considerable reduction in its numbers. Baronius assigns it incorrectly to the preceding year; see Pagius, no. 12.

Following Theophanes and Cedrenus, Sigonius and Baronius assign the arrival of the Avar khagan at the city, together with the ensuing defeat and great plundering, to the preceding year. But since the Alexandrian Chronicle records that these events occurred in June, in the ninth indiction, they belong to the year 612. Therefore the peace was neither concluded in this year, as Baronius maintains, nor requested, as Sigonius says, between Heraclius and the khagan, whatever Theophanes, Cedrenus, and Zonaras may say to the contrary. Pagius, no. 4, under the year 621.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 10 and 11, after the ninth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0847B] 1372–1373].

Heraclius, years 8 and 9 of his June era.

The incursion of the khagan and the Avars into the imperial city. Pagius, no. 4, under the following year.

After Sisebut, king of the Goths in Spain, had died, Suinthila succeeded him and reigned for ten years and some months. Calvisius incorrectly connects the beginning of his reign with the following year, relying on Saint Isidore. For Isidore’s Gothic Chronicle ends with Sisebut, and the World Chronicle places Sisebut’s fourth year, Heraclius’ fifth year—understood as after the consulships—and the era 654. Le Brul notes that one manuscript contains a double concluding clause: the one just mentioned, and another reading, “In the eighteenth year of Heraclius, the seventh of Suinthila, era 665,” which is clearly corrupt. For the eighteenth year of Heraclius corresponds to era 665 with a difference of two years; therefore Pagius, who assigns the complete Gothic Chronicle to the year 625 and Suinthila’s fifth year, is mistaken.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 11 and 12, after the tenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0847C] 1373–1374].

Heraclius, years 9 and 10 of his June era.

Finally, according to the Alexandrian Chronicle, peace was concluded this year between Heraclius and the khagan. The Emperor made preparations to carry the war into Persia, as he did in the following year. Pagius, no. 4; Calvisius.

On this occasion, since the Emperor was short of money [Col. 0847D], he borrowed the treasures of the churches, for whose sake the war was being waged, and used the gold and silver vessels taken from those same churches for striking coinage. Miscellany.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 12 and 13, after the eleventh consulship** [Note: [Col. 0847D] 1374–1375].

Heraclius, years 10 and 11 of his June era.

After celebrating Easter on 4 April, a Monday, Heraclius set out at evening with arms for Persia. Sigonius, from Theophanes; Pagius, under the preceding year, no. 5.

First year of the Persian war, which lasted six years.

He likewise distributed among the soldiers money melted down from sacred vessels. Theophanes; Anastasius, *Ecclesiastical History*; Cedrenus; Miscellany. Incorrectly: Baronius places it two years earlier.

From this point Pagius omits Olympiads and years of the City, since they are of little use thereafter.

Dagobert, son of Clotarius II, began to reign in Austrasia in the thirty-ninth year of his father’s reign, in March of this year, and reigned sixteen years. Petavius; Pagius, nos. 10 and 11.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 13 and 14, after the twelfth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0849A] 1375–1376].

Heraclius, years 11 and 12 of his June era.

Second year of the Persian war.

[Col. 0849B] Heraclius, penetrating into the heart of Persia, laid everything waste with fire and sword. Later, wintering in Albania, he granted freedom to fifty thousand Persian captives whom he had been leading with him. Anastasius, *Ecclesiastical History*; Baronius, under the preceding year.

Sexred and Siward, kings of the East Saxons, who after the death of their father Sebert had returned to idolatry, were killed while fighting against Kinigild, king of the West Saxons. Sigebert, surnamed the Little, succeeded them and restored the faith among the East Saxons. From William of Malmesbury. Pagius, no. 3.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 14 and 15, after the thirteenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0849B] 1376–1377].

Heraclius, years 12 and 13 of his June era.

Third year of the Persian war.

[Col. 0849C] Heraclius defeated, in three battles, three commanders of Chosroes—Sarablanga, Sarbazan, and Sain—and then wintered again in Albania. Anastasius; Baronius, under the preceding year, where Pagius, no. 2.

Adaloald, king of the Lombards, having killed twelve nobles, was driven from the kingdom by the others; Arioald, duke of Turin, was raised in his place. Aimoinus, book 4, chapter 10; from the same source and from Fredegar. Pagius, under the year 626, no. 7, argues that Paul the Deacon was mistaken; but Adaloald survived until the following year.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 15 and 16, after the fourteenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0849C] 1377–1378].

Heraclius, years 13 and 14 of his June era.

Fourth year of the Persian war.

[Col. 0849D] On the Kalends of March Heraclius traversed Syria with his entire army in seven days, reached the Euphrates, crossed the river in the same month, and pitched camp beyond the Sarus, while Sarbar, commander of Chosroes, occupied the opposite bank. Heraclius performed many brave deeds; reaching the city of Sebastea, he crossed the Aly and wintered in that region. Theophanes; Pagius, no. 2.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 16 and 17, after the fifteenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0849D] 1378–1379].

Heraclius, years 14 and 15 of his June era.

Fifth year of the Persian war.

[Col. 0851A] Chosroes sent Sain with a powerful army against Heraclius, while he sent Sarbar to Constantinople with the remaining forces, so that, joined by the Avars, Bulgars, Slavs, and Gepids, he might besiege that city. Heraclius divided his army into three divisions: he sent the first to defend the city, entrusted the second to his brother Theodore to resist Sain, and led the third himself into Lazica, that is, Colchis. Sain was defeated and killed by Theodore. While Constantinople was being besieged, Sarbar attacked Chalcedon, devastating everything around it. Theophanes; Nicephorus; Alexandrian Chronicle; Pagius, under the preceding year, with Baronius.

[Col. 0851B] **Emperor Heraclius Augustus, years 17 and 18, after the sixteenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0851B] 1379–1380].

Heraclius, years 15 and 16 of his June era.

Sixth year of the Persian war.

Heraclius formed an alliance with the Turks, who abandoned him when winter approached. Nevertheless, with the sole aid of God and the blessed Virgin Mary, he won a remarkable victory over the Persians on 21 December. He occupied Nineveh and then, after pitching camp near Jesde, celebrated the Nativity of Christ. The Persian history is supplemented by Antonius Pagius from the Saracen historian Elmacin, since he was unable to obtain from his friend Schelstrat, keeper of the Vatican library, the still unpublished work of George Pisides. Pagius, no. 4.

Theodolinda, seeing that she had been cast down from the throne [Col. 0851C] without any hope of recovering it, wasted away from grief. Sigonius.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 18 and 19, after the seventeenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0851C] 1380–1381].

Heraclius, years 16 and 17 of his June era.

Chosroes was acclaimed king by his son Siroes on 25 February; four days later, on the 28th of the same month, he was strangled in prison, in the thirty-eighth year of his reign, which had begun in 590. Heraclius, after concluding peace with Siroes, entered Constantinople in triumph, with four elephants drawing his chariot and carrying rich spoils with him, especially the most holy Cross. Pagius, under the preceding year, with Baronius, from Elmacin. At the end of this year Siroes died.

Clotarius II died in the forty-fourth year of his reign, aged forty-five. He had held the sole monarchy of all France for sixteen years. He had succeeded his father in 584. Fredegar; Aimoinus; Pagius, no. 8.

The beginning of Dagobert’s reign is taken from Fredegar as beginning in the year 622, when he became king of Austrasia. Therefore he is said here to be in his seventh year, reckoned from that point, not from his father’s death. Petavius, *Rationes temporum*, part 2, book 4, chapter 1, §7.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 19 and 20, after the eighteenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0851D] 1381–1382].

Heraclius the Younger, years 17 and 18.

Heraclius brought the life-giving Cross to Jerusalem to Bishop Zacharias and expelled the Jews from the Holy City. Pagius, two years earlier, with Baronius. Sigonius testifies that he had read in ritual books that the gate of Jerusalem closed of its own accord when Heraclius was divinely warned, as he entered barefoot.

Dagobert compelled all the Jews of his kingdom to receive baptism, as Sisebut, king of Spain, had done in 615. Pagius, under the year 614, with Baronius.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 20 and 21, after the nineteenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0853A] 1382–1383].

Heraclius, years 18 and 19 of his June era.

The Alexandrian Chronicle, called by Pagius the Alexandrian Chronicle and by Ducange the Great Paschal Chronicle, ends in this year [Col. 0853B].

Pagius, who maintains that the deacon erred in correctly establishing the Lombard kings, assigns the succession of Rotharis to the death of Arioald in this year, no. 7, under the year 638. But since the twelve years assigned by Paul the Deacon to Arioald are counted from 624 to 656, it is clear that Arioald had not yet died. It will appear below, under the year 643, whether Pagius’ criticism is sound.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 21 and 22, after the twentieth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0853B] 1383–1384].

[Col. 0853C] Heraclius, years 19 and 20 of his June era.

Heraclius made Heracleonas, that is, Heraclius, his son by Martina, Caesar. Nicephorus; Pagius, no. 20.

Sisenand, after overthrowing Suinthila by tyranny, invaded Spain. Vulsa; Mariana; Calvisius; Pagius.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 22 and 23, after the twenty-first consulship** [Note: [Col. 0853C] 1384–1385].

Heraclius, years 20 and 21 of his June era.

Muhammad died on 17 June, and Abu Bakr succeeded him.

The Persians made Yazdegerd, grandson of Chosroes and son of Shahriyar, who had fled from Siroes, king. From his enthronement on the throne of Cyrus began the Yazdegerdian Era, on an uncertain day, though it begins from 16 June. From Elmacin; Pagius.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 23 and 24, after the twenty-second consulship** [Note: [Col. 0853D] 1385–1386].

Heraclius, years 21 and 22 of his June era.

The origin of the irreconcilable war between the Romans and the Saracens begins in this year, although Baronius, following Theophanes, places it in 631. See Pagius, no. 2.

In the eleventh year of his reign—which begins in March of the preceding year—Dagobert made his three-year-old son Sigibert king of Austrasia. Hence Fredegar begins the reckoning of his reign from that point. Meanwhile another son was born to him, whom he named Chlodoveus after his great-grandfather and appointed king of Neustria and Burgundy. From Fredegar; Pagius, nos. 31 and 32.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 24 and 25, after the twenty-third consulship** [Note: [Col. 0855A] 1386–1387].

Heraclius, years 22 and 23 of his June era.

The Roman commander, fighting with the Saracen commander, was first put to flight as far as Damascus; then he killed the same commander together with many others. These were the deeds of Abu Bakr in Syria in this year, according to Sigebert and Elmacin; Pagius, no. 2, under the preceding year. Abu Bakr was the first of all to collect the Qur’an, previously scattered on tablets, so that nothing might perish. After reigning for two years, he died on 23 August [Col. 0855B], and Umar succeeded him as the third caliph of the Saracens. Umar took several cities from the Romans; consequently Heraclius, abandoning Syria, transferred the Holy Cross from Jerusalem to Constantinople, although shortly before his commander had fought successfully. Sigonius, from Nicephorus; Pagius, nos. 4 and 5.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 25 and 26, after the twenty-fourth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0855B] 1387–1388].

Heraclius, years 23 and 24 of his June era.

After defeating the army of Baanes, the imperial treasurer, the Saracens captured Damascus on 23 July. Baronius, under the preceding year; Pagius, no. 3.

Sisenand, king of Spain, died before completing the fourth year of his reign; Chintila succeeded him. Mariana; Calvisius and Pagius defer Sisenand’s death to the following year.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 26 and 27, after the twenty-fifth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0855C] 1388–1389].

Heraclius, years 24 and 25 of his June era.

The beginnings of Rotharis should be assigned to this year, as is indicated both by Arioald’s twelfth and final year of reign and especially by the prologue to Rotharis’ laws, dated to 643, the eighth year of his reign. Blancus, in his notes on Paul the Deacon, book 4, chapter 44.

**Emperor Heraclius Augustus, years 27 and 28, after the twenty-sixth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0855C] 1389–1390].

Heraclius, years 25 and 26 of his June era.

Jerusalem was conquered by the Saracens, who captured Medain, the city in which the treasures of Chosroes, king of the Persians, were kept. Thus Umar overturned two mighty empires, the Roman and the Persian: from the former he gradually took Egypt and Syria, and from the latter Chaldaea, Media, and Persia. Pagius, no. 3.

Dagobert restored the laws once enacted by Theodoric for the Bavarians, Franks, and Alemanni. The same author, no. 4.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 28 and 29, after the twenty-seventh consulship** [Note: [Col. 0855D] 1390–1391].

Heraclius, years 26 and 27 of his June era.

Rotharis published several laws of his people under the name of an Edict; the general compilation belongs to the year 643. Paul the Deacon, book 4, chapter 44. Sigonius reports that in this same year he invaded the Cottian Alps and seized their patrimony.

[Col. 0857A] Dagobert, king of the Franks, died on 19 January, in the sixteenth year of his reign. Fredegar, chapter 79; Aimoinus, book 4, chapter 43. Six of those years—out of the aforesaid sixteen—are counted as years of his reign in Austrasia while his father Clotarius was still alive, contrary to the more recent opinion of Hadrian Valesius and, following him, Pagius under this year, no. 10, and under 647, with Baronius, no. 2.

The Saracens captured Antioch in Syria. Elmacin.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 29 and 30, after the twenty-eighth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0857A] 1391–1392].

Heraclius, years 27 and 28 of his June era.

[Col. 0857B] Saint Pippin, surnamed of Landen, duke and mayor of the palace of the Austrasian kings, died. The Martyrology gives 21 February. Pagius, no. 14.

Chintila, king of Spain, died before completing the fourth year; his son Tulga succeeded him and reigned two years and four months. Mariana, book 6, chapter 8; Fredegar; Chronicle under the following year.

Isaac the Exarch and Mauritius the Chartularius plundered the Lateran patriarchium.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 30 and 31, after the twenty-ninth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0857B] 1392–1393].

Heraclius, years 28 and 29 of his June era.

Eadwald, king of the Angles in Kent, died after reigning twenty-four years. His son Earcombert succeeded him. Through him, Bede testifies, ecclesiastical affairs advanced more favorably. For he was the first of the English kings to order the destruction of idols and to prescribe observance of the Lenten fast. His daughter Eartongatha also embraced the monastic life. Since monasteries were then rare in England, she went to Gaul and lived in the monastery of the noble abbess Fara. Baronius; Spondanus, from Bede, book 3, chapter 8; Calvisius.

**Emperors Heraclius Augustus, years 31 and 32, after the thirtieth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0857C] 1393–1394].

Heraclius, year 29 of his June era.

[Col. 0857D] Heraclius, after reigning thirty years, four months, and six days from 5 October 610, died on 11 February, a Sunday. He left two sons, Heraclius Constantine and Heracleonas, as equal heirs, so that both honored Martina as empress. From an Oriental Chronicle compared with Nicephorus. Pagius, no. 2; Ducange differs concerning the month.

Heraclius Constantine died after 103 days, on 25 May, believed to have been poisoned by his stepmother Martina through the agency of the patriarch Pyrrhus.

After Heraclius, or Heracleonas, had likewise been deposed six months later, Constans, son of Heraclius Constantine and grandson of Heraclius Augustus, was elevated. Theophanes; Cedrenus; Sigonius, under the following year.

Mauritius, who had conspired against Isaac, was arrested by the treasurer, taken to Ravenna, and strangled on the way. Sigonius.

The Saracens captured Alexandria. Elmacin; Pagius, no. 13.

**Emperor Constans, years 1 and 2** [Note: [Col. 0859A] 1394–1395].

Fredegar’s Chronicle, which was being written in Burgundy around this time, ends in this year; its continuation was composed by another author.

Tulga, king of Spain, whether dead or deposed after two years and four months of reign, was succeeded by Chindaswinth on 2 May. Chindaswinth, having recognized the Goths’ tendency toward expelling kings, punished some by death and others by exile. Fredegar, chapter 82; Pagius, no. 4. Roderic believes that Tulga died at the beginning of this year and that his successor Chindaswinth obtained the privilege of primacy for the see of Toledo from the Apostolic See.

**Emperor Constans Augustus, years 2 and 3, his first consulship** [Note: [Col. 0859B] 1395–1396].

In the seventy-sixth year after the Lombards entered Italy, Rotharis collected all the laws on 10 December and published them at Pavia. They are called *Edictum Rothari*; the Goths call them *Bellagines*, and Lindebrog calls them *Auricabeones*. This occurred in the eighth year of his reign, not the thirteenth, as Pagius thinks. Ludovico Muratori, preface to the Lombard laws, volume 1, part 2, *Scriptura Italica*.

[Col. 0859C] **Emperor Constans Augustus, years 3 and 4, after the consulship of Constans** [Note: [Col. 0859C] 1396–1397].

A solar eclipse occurred on 5 November, a Friday, half an hour after noon. Its ecliptic magnitude was 9.53 digits. From Cedrenus and Zonaras. Calvisius assigns it to the third year of Constans.

Theodore Calliopa, after Isaac had died in the preceding year, came to Italy at the beginning or toward the end of this year.

**Emperor Constans Augustus, years 4 and 5, after the second consulship** [Note: [Col. 0859C] 1397–1398].

Plato was given to Theodore the Exarch as his successor by Constans.

Othman, the fourth caliph of the Saracens, succeeded Umar. Theophanes.

Plato succeeded Calliopa, who had been recalled to Constantinople, while Plato was in the second year of his office [Col. 0859D].

**Emperor Constans Augustus, years 5 and 6, after the third consulship** [Note: [Col. 0859D] 1398–1399].

Gregory the Patrician, having won over the Africans, stirred up a revolt in Africa. From Theophanes; Baronius and Pagius, no. 2.

The first Saracen expedition into Africa took place. Theophanes.

In his Chronicle under this year, Calvisius records Rotharis’ war with the Romans, whom he stripped of various maritime cities, joining this expedition with the famous battle that Rotharis fought at Scultenna against the Romans and the people of Ravenna, killing eight thousand of them and putting the rest to flight. Certainly the Deacon attests that these events occurred after Rotharis’ laws had been enacted—that is, after 643.

**Emperor Constans Augustus, years 6 and 7, after the fourth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0861A] 1399–1400].

Gregory the Tyrant was killed in Africa by the Saracens, and tribute was imposed on the Africans. Baronius, from Elmacin; Pagius, no. 2.

When violent winds were blowing, many Stylite monks were thrown down. Spondanus.

Plato the Exarch, opening a way for Pyrrhus to return to friendship with the Easterners, obtained that Pyrrhus should mock the doctrinal statement presented to Theodore two years earlier. Therefore, although he was deposed in the following year, in 654, when Paul died, he was again installed in the see of Constantinople. Miscellany.

**Emperor Constans Augustus, years 7 and 8, after the fifth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0861B] 1400–1401].

Just as Sergius had promulgated the *Ecthesis* in the name of Heraclius, so Paul published the *Typos* in the name of Constans, by which silence was boldly imposed on Catholics and heretics alike. Pagius, under the preceding year, no. 2. Sirmond, *Synopsis of the Collections*. It is nevertheless established that the work was published before September, from the sixth indiction, as stated there [Col. 0861C].

**Emperor Constans Augustus, years 8 and 9, after the sixth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0861C] 1401–1402].

Constans threatened Martin with letters and even with arms, sending Olympius the Exarch with an army. When Olympius came to Rome while the council was being held, he ordered his *spatharius* to kill Martin while he was performing the sacred rites. But when the soldier was struck with blindness by divine intervention, Martin completed the service unharmed and undaunted, and celebrated the council. Baronius; Spondanus; Pagius, no. 7.

Chindaswinth, king of Spain, admitted his son Recceswinth to a share in the kingdom in February; he himself survived four years and seven months. Vas.

**Emperor Constans Augustus, years 9 and 10, after the seventh consulship** [Note: [Col. 0861D] 1402–1403].

A solar eclipse occurred on 6 February, three hours after noon, on a Saturday, in England. Its ecliptic magnitude was 10.25 digits; the Sun was at 20° 41′ of Aquarius. Bede, volume 2; Calvisius.

Busur, commander of the Saracens, ravaging Isauria, induced Constans through ambassadors to obtain peace for two years. Author of the Miscellany.

[Col. 0863A] **Emperor Constans Augustus, years 10 and 11, after the eighth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0863A] 1403–1404].

The Persian kingdom, which had begun in the year 226 after Christ under Artaxerxes, during the reign of the Emperor Alexander Severus IV, came to an end when Yazdegerd, son of Shahriyar and grandson of Chosroes, died. It had lasted 426 years. The Muslims, or Saracens, succeeded it. From Elmacin, book 1, chapter 4; Pagius, no. 10.

**Emperor Constans Augustus, years 11 and 12, after the ninth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0863A] 1404–1405].

[Col. 0863B] Constans prepared a persecution against Saint Martin and tried to have a successor appointed to him. For he was unwilling to use the sword, lest he be called a persecutor. Baronius. [Uncertain:] Ash fell this year in the East, according to the Miscellany.

Rotharis, king of the Lombards, died in May, leaving his son Rodoald as king. Rodoald was killed a few days later, and Aripert became king of the Lombards, reigning nine years. Paul the Deacon, book 4, chapter 53. He reports that during Rodoald’s time the judicial duel was introduced into Italy to settle disputes. The same, chapters 49 and 50.

**Emperor Constans Augustus, years 12 and 13, after the tenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0863B] 1405–1406].

Constans, having heard of the death of Olympius the Exarch, sent Theodore Calliopa once more with orders against Saint Martin, being deeply offended that Martin had condemned the Monothelites. The persecution began in June. Anastasius.

Clovis II issued the Clichy decree, by which the liberty of the monastery of Saint Denis was confirmed. From this Pagius derives the origin of the Church’s broader immunity. Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, table 17; Pagius, under 662, no. 2, against Baronius.

Mu‘awiya destroyed the Colossus of Rhodes, famous for 1,360 years, and sold it to a Jewish merchant from Emesa, who loaded nine hundred camels with its bronze. Miscellany.

Peada, king of the Mercians, first embraced the faith through the agency of Oswiu, king of Northumbria, and his son Alchfrith. From Bede; Baronius.

**Emperors Constans Augustus, years 13 and 14** [Note: [Col. 0863C] 1406–1407], **after the eleventh consulship** [Col. 0863D].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, year 1.

Constantine Pogonatus was named Augustus by his father Constans, certainly before 26 April of this year. Pagius, no. 15, from the acts of the Sixth Ecumenical Council, whose editors conjecture that he was named Augustus on 13 April.

The Emperor was defeated in a battle fought with the Saracens. Theophanes; Warnefrid; Ducange.

Anna, king of the East Angles, was killed by Penda, king of the Mercians, after his army had been defeated. Penda himself was killed in the following year by Oswiu, king of Northumbria. Bede; Pagius, under this and the following year.

Around this time the monk Marculf published his ancient formulary. Pagius, no. 13.

**Emperors Constans Augustus, years 14 and 15, after the twelfth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0865A] 1407–1408].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 1 and 2.

After Othman, or Uthman, commander of the Saracens, had been killed, Mu‘awiya, or Mavia, became the fifth caliph, elected by the inhabitants of Syria and Egypt. Theophanes; Elmacin; Hegira 35; Pagius, no. 18. Those who lived in the desert elected their own *clim* there.

Through the efforts of Oswiu, king of Northumbria [Col. 0865B], the faith made great progress in England. After Sigebert, king of the East Saxons, had been baptized, they accepted the faith—or restored it after having rejected it following the expulsion of Mellitus. Bede, book 3, chapter 22.

**Emperors Constans Augustus, years 15 and 16, after the thirteenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0865B] 1408–1409].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 2 and 3.

In the sixteenth year of his imperial rule, Constans marched against the Sclavini and, after subduing them, led away many captives. Miscellany.

Sigibert, king of Austrasia, who had begun to reign in 633 and had reigned twenty-six years and seven months, died a holy death on the Kalends of February. Childebert, son of Grimoald, the mayor of the palace, succeeded him. After both had been expelled by the Austrasians, Clovis II, Sigibert’s brother, who was reigning in Neustria and Burgundy, became king. Seven months after his brother’s death he acquired the monarchy and, in August, inflicted the ultimate punishment on the invaders. He too soon died, after reigning eighteen years, counted from the year 638, on the Kalends of January. Clotarius, the eldest of his three children, still a boy, reigned after him. The *Annals*, cited by Pagius, under this and the following year, against Baronius.

**Emperors Constans Augustus, years 16 and 17, after the fourteenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0865C] 1409–1410].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 3 and 4.

After Constans had recalled Saint Maximus and his disciples to Constantinople and saw that all his efforts to draw them into Monothelism were fruitless, he inflicted dreadful punishments on them. Their hands were cut off and their tongues cut out, and he sent them into the bitterest exile. Baronius; Combefis. Pagius maintains that the punishment was postponed for several years.

**Emperors Constans Augustus, years 17 and 18, after the fifteenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0865D] 1410–1411].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 4 and 5.

In the seventeenth year of his imperial rule, Constans concluded peace with the Saracens at the request of Mavia, who was being troubled by internal disturbances. Miscellany. Pagius, following Theophanes, assigns this to the following year, no. 3.

Around this year Gregory the Exarch was sent to Italy; he governed Italy for eighteen years, according to Bacchin, from a privilege granted by Constans at Syracuse in the year 666.

[Col. 0867A] **Emperors Constans Augustus, years 18 and 19, after the sixteenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0867A] 1411–1412].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 5 and 6.

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, year 1.

Heraclius and Tiberius, brothers of Constantine Pogonatus and the elder and younger sons of Constans, were named Caesars by their father between 26 April and 9 August. Pagius, no. 2, from the acts of the Sixth Council.

A great earthquake occurred in Palestine and Syria in June. Miscellany.

Constans killed his brother Theodosius the Deacon, and afterward was terrified in his sleep by the repeated apparition of Theodosius presenting him with a cup full of blood while wearing a deacon’s vestment [Col. 0867B]. From Cedrenus; Baronius.

**Emperors Constans Augustus, years 19 and 20, after the seventeenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0867B] 1412–1413].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 6 and 7; Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 1 and 2.

Ali, the fifth caliph of the Saracens, who had been elected by the Arab faction in 655 together with Mavia, was killed in this year. His son Hasan, or Chasan, succeeded him for six months and five days; for then he abdicated the caliphate, and Mavia ruled alone. Mavia is therefore called the seventh caliph. Theophanes and Elmacin. Pagius, under 659, no. 3.

Queen Bathildis, in order to quiet the rebellious Austrasians, made Childeric, her second-born, their king after 25 July. Clotarius thereafter ruled only the Burgundians and Neustrians. Pagius, under this year, nos. 6 and 7.

Sigebert, king of the East Saxons, was killed. He had embraced the faith in 655. Baronius under 655, and Pagius there.

**Emperors Constans Augustus, years 20 and 21, after the eighteenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0867C] 1413–1414].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 7 and 8.

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 2 and 3.

Aripert, king of the Lombards, died toward the end of this year. His sons Bertarid and Godebert succeeded him for one year and three months. Paul the Deacon, book 4, chapter 53.

King Childeric, in the second year of his reign, granted Saint Amandus, formerly bishop of Tongeren, a village in the diocese of Laon called Barisiacum [Col. 0867D], where Amandus founded a monastery. Diplomatic charter, cited by Miraeus and Pagius, no. 4.

Edilwalch, king of the South or Southern Saxons, the last of the heptarchic kings, embraced the faith. Pagius, under 681, no. 18, from the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle.

**Emperors Constans Augustus, years 21 and 22, after the nineteenth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0867D] 1414–1415].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 8 and 9.

Heraclius and Tiberius, consuls, years 3 and 4.

Childeric, desirous that monasteries be founded everywhere, aided in completing the monastery at Hautvillers. Saint Nivard, bishop of Reims, died this year before the monastery, which he was founding for his friend, the monk Saint Bercharius, had been completed. See Bercharius. Pagius, no. 5; Flodoard, book 2, chapter 27.

[Col. 0869A] **Emperors Constans Augustus, years 22 and 23, after the twentieth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0869A] 1415–1416].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 9 and 10.

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 4 and 5.

Constans, coming to Italy, reached Rome on 5 July and decided to establish the imperial seat there. Theophanes; Warnefrid.

Grimoald, duke of Benevento, after expelling the brothers Bertarid and Godebert, usurped the Lombard kingdom for nine years. Paul the Deacon, book 5, chapter 33.

The Dervense monastery was founded in Gaul by Saint Bercharius, abbot of Hautvillers. Pagius, no. 7 and following, against Coint.

**Emperors Constans Augustus, years 23 and 24, after the twenty-first consulship** [Note: [Col. 0869B] 1416–1417].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 10 and 11.

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 5 and 6.

A solar eclipse occurred on the Kalends of May, a Wednesday, in the seventh indiction, at the tenth hour of the day. Bede and Calvisius’ Prutenic tables give 3:45 in the afternoon, an ecliptic magnitude of 11.48 digits, and the Sun at 12° 39′ of Taurus. A plague followed it in England. While it was raging, Sigher, king of the East Saxons, apostatized from the faith, which his co-heir Sebba preserved. Bede, book 3, chapter 30; Baronius; Pagius.

[Col. 0869C] **Emperors Constans Augustus, years 24 and 25, after the twenty-second consulship** [Note: [Col. 0869C] 1417–1418].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 11 and 12.

Heraclius and Tiberius, consuls, years 6 and 7.

Egbert of Kent and Oswiu of Northumbria sent the priest Wigard to Rome to be ordained by Vitalian as bishop of Canterbury. But when Wigard died of the plague at Rome, the see of Canterbury remained vacant until 668. From Bede; Baronius and Pagius.

**Emperors Constans Augustus, years 25 and 26, after the twenty-third consulship** [Note: [Col. 0869C] 1418–1419].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 12 and 13.

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 7 and 8.

[Col. 0869D] Mavia, caliph of the Saracens, invaded Africa. From Nowairi and Elmacin. Pagius, no. 10, with Theophanes under the first year of Constantine’s reign. From this began a war lasting many years between the Arabs and their proselytes on one side and the Greeks and Africans on the other. The same author, in the same place.

**Emperors Constans Augustus, years 26 and 27, after the twenty-fourth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0869D] 1419–1420].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 13 and 14.

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 8 and 9.

Saborius, commander of the Armenian forces, defected from Constans. Each side sought the aid of Mavia through ambassadors; after deceiving the imperial representatives, the rebel was heard. But God, avenging the Emperor, granted victory. Baronius, from Theophanes.

[Col. 0871A] **Emperor Constans Augustus, year 27, after the twenty-fifth consulship** [Note: [Col. 0871A] 1420–1421].

Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 14 and 15, after the first consulship.

Heraclius and Tiberius, years 9 and 10.

Constans, after reigning twenty-seven years, reckoned from December of the year 641, was killed in a bath at Syracuse on 15 July. Anastasius; Theophanes; Cedrenus and others. Ducange, *Byzantine Families*. Pagius, under this year, no. 3, proves from the Sixth Ecumenical Council that Constans was killed between 16 September and 7 November.

Theodore the Younger, Exarch, came to Italy this year. Bacchin.

Grimoald, king of the Lombards, enlarged Rotharis’ edict with laws promulgated by himself in July, in the sixth year of his reign.

**Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 15 and 16, after the first and second consulships** [Note: [Col. 0871B] 1421–1422].

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 10 and 11.

The Saracens invaded Sicily and, making an incursion from there into Africa, took eighty thousand people captive. The *Annals*, cited by Pagius; Theophanes; Zonaras; Cedrenus; Hermanus the Contractus. Pagius, no. 5. They also seized all the booty that Constans had removed from Rome, after inflicting a great slaughter. Paul the Deacon, book 5, chapter 13.

[Col. 0871C] **Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 16 and 17, after the second and third consulships** [Note: [Col. 0871C] 1422–1423].

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 11 and 12.

Oswiu, king of the Northumbrians, of Roman and Apostolic observance, died on 15 February at the age of fifty-eight. Bede, book 4, chapter 5. Ecgfrith succeeded him; Oswiu had fathered him and three other children by Saint Eanfleda, daughter of Saint Edwin. From Bede; Pagius, no. 3.

Clotarius III, son of Clovis II, who had succeeded him in 656 in November, died toward the end of this year after reigning fourteen years. Pagius, with Baronius, no. 6, under 668, following H. Valesius; and no. 7, under 669. His brother Childeric assumed the monarchy for three years; others, however, allow his brother Theodoric several months in Neustria and Burgundy. Pagius, under 668, no. 8.

**Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 17 and 18, after the third and fourth consulships** [Note: [Col. 0871D] 1423–1424].

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 12 and 13.

The Picts attacked Ecgfrith, king of Northumbria, believing him to be a young and inexperienced ruler. But after being defeated, they furnished an opportunity for the expansion of the Church. Edward Stephens, cited by Mabillon. At the same time, in Gaul, both the civil and ecclesiastical order was collapsing because of internal wars, and a return to idolatry was occurring in more than one place. Pagius, no. 5 and following.

[Col. 0873A] After Grimoald, the usurper of the Lombard kingdom, died, Bertarid returned to the throne and held it for eighteen incomplete years. Paul the Deacon, book 5, chapters 35 and 37.

**Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 18 and 19, after the fourth and fifth consulships** [Note: [Col. 0873A] 1424–1425].

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 13 and 14.

The Saracens began to besiege Constantinople. The siege lasted seven years, not four, as Baronius thinks. Pagius extensively overturns both the older and the more recent opinions, relying especially on the authority of Elmacin.
