Recceswinth, king of the Visigoths, having reigned from 22 January 649 for twenty-three years, seven months, and eleven days, died on the Kalends of September. Wamba succeeded him. Vasconcellos and the *Annals*, cited by Pagius, Baronius, and Mariana, disagree among themselves concerning the months and days. Pagius, no. 16. Wamba undertook a war against rebellious Septimania and completed it in the following year. Julian; Baronius under the following year; Vasconcellos; Roderic of Toledo; Pagius under this and the following year.

**Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 19 and 20, after the fifth and sixth consulships** [Note: [Col. 0873B] 1425–1426].

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 14 and 15.

A dreadful rainbow was seen in the sky and was believed to portend the end of the world; some call it a comet. Sigebert; the Anonymous; *Life of Saint Leodegarius*, cited by Pagius under 671 [Col. 0873C], no. 3.

Three kings died this year: Childeric, king of the Franks, succeeded by Theodoric III before 15 September; Pagius, no. 4 and following. Cenwalh, the second Christian king of the West Saxons, died after reigning thirty-one years, and his wife Sexburga reigned in his place, leaving no son. Pagius, nos. 13 and 14. Ecgbert, king of Kent, who had succeeded his father Earcombert in 664 on 14 July, died after reigning nine years. Bede, book 4, chapter 1; Pagius, under the preceding year, no. 3. After his death, Lothair invaded the kingdom, to the great injury of his sons Eadric and Wihtred, and from this arose very great wars.

**Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 20 and 21, after the sixth and seventh consulships** [Note: [Col. 0873C] 1426–1427].

[Col. 0873D] Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 15 and 16.

Ebroin, mayor of the palace in Austrasia under Chlotarius, emerged from the monastery; Leudesius and Vulfoald likewise, each at a different time, as mayors of the palace, contended together over administering the kingdom and threw it into confusion. All France was disturbed by factions. Pagius discusses this extensively under the present year, while Baronius is silent.

A great comet appeared, followed by drought, plague, and famine. Alsted.

**Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 21 and 22, after the seventh and eighth consulships** [Note: [Col. 0873D] 1427–1428].

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 16 and 17.

Wulfhere, king of the Mercians, died after reigning seventeen years. His brother Æthelred succeeded him; Æthelred’s wife Ermenilda and daughter Werburga were women renowned for holiness, especially Werburga, who presided over monasteries. Bede, book 3, chapter 24, and the Epistle under this year; the *Annals*, cited by Pagius, nos. 5 and 7.

**Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 22 and 23, after the eighth and ninth consulships** [Note: [Col. 0875A] 1428–1429].

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 17 and 18.

The Maronites defected from the Emperor and chose a duke for themselves [Col. 0875B]. In this and the following year they fought against the Saracens with such success that, being unable to match their strength, the Saracens insulted them through a corruption of their name, calling them Mardaites. Baronius and Pagius extensively, nos. 4 and following.

Æthelred, king of the Mercians, ravaged Kent. Bede, epitome; Baronius under the following year. Pagius objects, no. 15.

**Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 23 and 24, after the ninth and tenth consulships** [Note: [Col. 0875B] 1429–1430].

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 18 and 19.

A great war took place in Gaul between Theodoric III, king of the Franks, and Dagobert II, who had been recalled from Ireland to the throne of Austrasia during the factional struggles in 674. Peace was later arranged between them [Col. 0875C] in this year. Pagius, nos. 7 and 8.

**Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 24 and 25, after the tenth and eleventh consulships** [Note: [Col. 0875C] 1430–1431].

Heraclius and Tiberius, years 19 and 20.

The Emperor, concerned for the peace of the Church, sent a sacred letter to Donus; this preceded the Sixth Ecumenical Council and is published by Baronius in the *Annals* under this year.

Peace was concluded between the Saracens and the Bulgars, who had been stirred up against the Emperor. Pagius, no. 3.

A comet appeared for three months, followed by drought and plague. Anastasius; Bede; *British Antiquities*; *Theatrum Cometarum*, part 1, page 421; Riccioli; Rockemb and Eckstorm under the preceding year. Alsted places it two years earlier.

[Col. 0875D] **Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 25 and 26, after the eleventh and twelfth consulships** [Note: [Col. 0875D] 1431–1432].

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 20 and 21.

A solar eclipse occurred on 13 July at the tenth hour of the day, the fourth hour after noon, on a Wednesday. Its ecliptic magnitude was 6.6 digits; the Sun was at 23° of Cancer. Calvisius.

A battle took place between Ecgfrith, king of Northumbria, and Æthelred, king of the Mercians. In it Elphwin, Ecgfrith’s brother, was killed in accordance with the prophecy of Saint Wilfrid. Bede, book 4, chapter 27. See the notes on Donus.

[Col. 0877A] **Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 26 and 27, after the twelfth and thirteenth consulships** [Note: [Col. 0877A] 1432–1433].

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 21 and 22.

Lunar eclipse on 18 June, Monday, beginning half an hour after midnight. Ecliptic digits: 16, 37. The sun was at the end of Gemini. From Anastasius and Ursberg, as cited by Calvisius. A plague followed for three months; it was turned away when the relics of Saint Sebastian were brought into the City. Hence the practice arose of invoking this saint during a plague. Baronius.

Mavias, the first king of the Saracens, died in April. From Elmacin [Col. 0877B] and Pag. with Baronius above, no. 6. He was succeeded by his son Izitus, the eighth caliph.

Wamba, having abdicated the kingdom, entered a monastery, after having reigned in Spain for eight years, one month, and fourteen days. Ervigius administered well the kingdom which he had acquired by evil arts. Vulsa, Mariana, Pag. no. 22.

Theodo, duke of the Bavarians and founder of the monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, died about this year. The same, no. 27.

Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, year 27 [Note: [Col. 0877B] 1433–1434], and 28, after the consulships XIII and XIV.

Heraclius and Tiberius, Caesars, years 22 and 23.

Constantine, suspecting that his brothers were intent on innovations, removed them from participation in the Empire after 16 September [Col. 0877C]. Baronius and Pag., no. 13. He associated with himself his son Justinian, twelve years old; yet no one counts the years of this co-reign, according to Nicephorus and Valesius, in Ducange.

Ebroin, the murderer of Saint Leodegarius, was killed by order of King Theodoric. After his death the mayors of the palace were Warato, Gislemarus, Warato again, and, after the latter’s death, Bertharius. Pag. no. 27, this year, and no. 4 under the year 687.

Emperor Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 28 [Note: [Col. 0877D] 1434–1435] and 29, after the consulships XIV and XV.

King Ecgfrid of Northumbria ordered the monastery of Jarrow, dedicated to Saint Paul, to be founded by Saint Benedict Biscop; Bede later lived in this monastery, which was destroyed by the Danes. From Worcester, Pag. no. 12.

King Centwine of the West Saxons drove the Britons, who still inhabited the mountains and the interior of the island, as far as the sea. Pag. no. 13.

Emperor Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 29 [Note: [Col. 0877D] 1435–1436] and 30, after the consulships XV and XVI.

Izitus, caliph of the Saracens, died on 9 November. After disputes among the Arabs, Abimelech, the ninth caliph, succeeded to the caliphate [Col. 0879A]. From Theophanes and Elmacin, Pag. no. 16.

Lunar eclipse on 16 April, after the Lord’s Supper. It began at the middle of the tenth hour and ended about an hour and a half after midnight, having lasted nearly four hours. Ecliptic digits: 19, 18. The sun was at 29 degrees of Aries. Anastasius, Calvisius.

Saint Ebba, daughter of Ethelfrid, king of the Northumbrians, sister of Kings Oswiu and Oswald, and aunt of King Ecgfrid, abbess of the monastery of Coldingham, died. Pag. no. 17.

Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 30 [Note: [Col. 0879B] 1436–1437] and 31, after the consulships XVI and XVII.

Ecgfrid, king of Northumbria, ravaged Ireland for an uncertain reason. Bede, book 4, chapter 26. In the following year, having rashly led an army to devastate the province of the Picts, he perished with a large part of his men on 20 May, in the fortieth year of his age and the fifteenth of his reign; his illegitimate brother Alcfrid succeeded him. Bede, in the passage cited above.

A star appeared at night beside the Pleiades, in a clear sky, between the Nativity of the Lord and Epiphany, with a dim light like the moon. On 14 February a star appeared in the evening, moving from south to north. Anastasius, Calvisius.

Emperors Constantine Pogonatus Augustus, years 31 [Note: [Col. 0879C] 1437–1438] and 32, after the consulships XVII.

Justinian, June 1, after the first consulship.

Constantine died at the beginning of September. Ducange; Anastasius in John V, section 155. His son Justinian succeeded him at the age of sixteen, as Pag. no. 2 demonstrates from the Greek authorities. He governed the Empire with such instability, however, that he was later thrown from the throne. Ducange, Byzantine Families.

The same year, King Hlothar of Kent and Centwine, king of the West Saxons, died; Cedwalla succeeded Centwine. From Bede and Worcester, Pag. no. 11 and following.

Emperor Justinian Augustus, years 1 and 2, after the first and second consulships [Note: [Col. 0879C] 1438–1439].

Justinian concluded peace with Abimelech, caliph of the Saracens; all historians call it disastrous for the Roman state. From Theophanes and Anastasius, Baronius above, and Pag. no. 3 there.

Emperor Justinian Augustus, years 2 and 3, after the second and third consulships [Note: [Col. 0879D] 1439–1440].

The notable epoch of the rule of the mayors of the palace of France begins this year [Col. 0881A], in June or July, after Pepin’s victory in the battle of Tertry. For Pepin, son of Ansegisel, having defeated and put to flight Berthar, the mayor of the palace, and King Theodoric, and having slain all the nobles, himself seized the supreme authority. Pag. no. 8 and following. Baronius, in his account under the following year, after the death of Theodoric—which he says was followed by Clovis III—explains that the kings thereafter were feeble and that supreme power lay with the commanders of the army, called mayors of the palace. See his fifth volume under the year 691.

John Platys was sent to Italy as exarch. Baronius.

Emperor Justinian Augustus, years 3 and 4, after the third and fourth consulships [Note: [Col. 0881B] 1440–1441].

Bertharitus, king of the Lombards, died. His son Cunibert succeeded him; his father had made him co-ruler in the eighth year of his reign, and he reigned twelve years after his father. Paul the Deacon, book 6, chapter 17; Sigebert, under the year cited above.

Egica, closely related to Wamba, whom Ervigius had previously made his son-in-law by giving him his daughter Cixilo, began to reign in Spain at the beginning of this year and reigned for nearly thirteen years. Vasaeus and Pag., however, following Mariana, argue that Ervigius died in the seventeenth year of his reign, on the first day before the Kalends of December, after reigning seven years and twenty-five days, and that Egica’s reign therefore began from that point [Col. 0881C].

Emperor Justinian Augustus, years 4 and 5, after the fourth and fifth consulships [Note: [Col. 0881C] 1441–1442].

Justinian overturned everything that had been arranged by his father Constantine Pogonatus. He broke the peace with the Bulgarians, first defeated them, and then barely escaped from their hands. From Sigebert and Theophanes, Pag. no. 10.

Baronius produces the monument of King Cedwalla of the West Saxons, baptized this year and deceased at Rome twelve days later. It reads:

> Here lies Cedwalla, also called Peter, king of the Saxons, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, in Indiction 2; he lived scarcely more or less than thirty years, under the most pious Emperor Justinian Augustus, in the fourth year of his consulship, while the apostolic man Lord Sergius, Pope, was pontiff in his second year.

Emperor Justinian Augustus, years 5 and 6, after the fifth and sixth consulships [Note: [Col. 0881D] 1442–1443].

Justinian lightly broke the treaty of peace with the Saracens because the caliph had paid him tribute in a new kind of coin devised by the caliph himself. Baronius and, from Theophanes, Pag. no. 8.

Abimelech, or Abdulmelik, caliph, conquered Mecca, the city of Arabia Felix celebrated for the tomb of Muhammad, and subjected it to himself in October. From Elmacin; Pag., following year, no. 5.

Germany heard the first Christian preaching, when Saint Willibrord, with twelve companions, proceeded to Frisia for this purpose; the region was still entangled in pagan errors. Mabillon, Baronius, and Pag., following year.

Emperor Justinian Augustus, years 6 and 7, after the sixth and seventh consulships [Note: [Col. 0883A] 1443–1444].

Abimelech, caliph of the Saracens, having appointed Hasan commander in the West, entrusted him with the expedition to Africa. Hasan invaded Africa, captured Carthage, stripped it of its walls, and cruelly slaughtered the inhabitants. From Nowairi, Pag. no. 5.

Theodoric III, king of the Franks, died this year; Clovis III, still a child, succeeded him [Col. 0883B]. Annals of Metz; Pag. with Baronius under the year 668, nos. 3 and 4.

Emperor Justinian Augustus, years 7 and 8, after the seventh and eighth consulships [Note: [Col. 0883B] 1444–1445].

Justinian sent Zacharias, the protospatharius, to Rome to bring Sergius to Constantinople in chains. Anastasius; Baronius.

In England, Wictred became king of Kent; Ina, king of the West Saxons, arranged for ecclesiastical laws to be issued by the bishops for the whole province. Consequently, some authorities, on the basis of Bede, attest that a synod was held this year [Col. 0883C] in Wessex. From Bede; Pag. no. 22 and following.

Emperor Justinian Augustus, years 8 and 9, after the eighth and ninth consulships [Note: [Col. 0883C] 1445–1446].

Solar eclipse on 5 October, Monday, nearly four hours before noon. Ecliptic digits: 2, 32. The sun was at 15 degrees of Libra. Calvisius, from Theophanes.

Justinian destroyed the sacred church of the Mother of God, intending to convert it to other uses. Thus, with the additional brutality of his ministers, he incurred universal hatred. Baronius.

Sebbi, king of the East Saxons, became a monk and soon afterward died, having reigned thirty years. His sons Sighard and Suefred succeeded him. From Bede; Pag. no. 6.

Emperor Justinian Augustus, years 9 and 10, after the ninth and tenth consulships [Note: [Col. 0883D] 1446–1447].

Spain was disturbed by a movement of the Jews. All of them, however, were reduced to servitude by a council convened for this purpose. It was decreed that their sons and daughters should be taken from their parents from the age of seven, educated as Christians, and married to Christians. Baronius, from Vasaeus; Calvisius.

Emperors Justinian Augustus, year 10, after the tenth consulship [Note: [Col. 0885A] 1447–1448].

Leontius Patricius, year 1.

Leontius Patricius, commander of the army, seized Justinian, mutilated his nose, and banished him to Cherson. This occurred around the beginning of September, as Pag. notes, no. 1. Ducange, from Nicephorus, Byzantine Families. Thus Leontius, whom Justinian had held in prison for three years and then placed over Greece, proved himself a usurping and cruel emperor. Nicephorus; Pag. above, with Baronius.

Clovis III, king of the Franks, having reigned four years and entering upon his fifth, died before 23 March [Col. 0885B]. The Continuator of Fredegar, Sigebert; Pag. with Baronius under the year 692, no. 18.

Emperor Leontius Patricius, the usurper, years 1 and 2 [Note: [Col. 0885B] 1448–1449].

Since the Gallican Church had begun, from about the year 670, to decline in its rights in eastern Francia, and since heresy and idolatry had gradually been introduced into it from 671 onward, it was almost entirely thrown into confusion around this year, the disorder having increased. Ecclesiastical property was usurped by laymen, and the Church became subject to such great evils that in the year 774 Hadrian I asked Charlemagne to provide some remedy for them. Pag. no. 16.

Emperor Leontius Patricius, the usurper, years 2 and 3 [Note: [Col. 0885B] 1449–1450] [Col. 0885C].

Sergius Patricius, while a revolt had broken out in Lazica, subjected it to the Arabs in Leontius’s second year. Miscellanies.

Osthryth, wife of Æthelred, king of the Mercians, and sister of Ecgfrid, king of Northumbria, was wickedly killed by her own people. Bede, Epistle.

Egica, king of the Goths in Spain, made his son Witiza co-ruler this year or the preceding year, and wished him to establish the royal seat at Tui in Galicia. There Witiza violated the wife of Favila, duke of Cantabria, and killed Favila. Favila’s son Pelagius was made king by the Spaniards who fled into Asturias, as we shall see under the year 712. Vasaeus.

Emperor Leontius Patricius, the usurper, year 3 [Note: [Col. 0885D] 1450–1451].

Tiberius Apsimarus, the usurper, year 1.

Tiberius Apsimarus, acclaimed by the army, confined the captured Leontius, whose nose had been mutilated as Leontius had mutilated Justinian’s, in the monastery of Dalmatos. Ducange, Byzantine Families, around the end of this year.

Constantinople suffered a plague for four months, with enormous loss of life. Nicephorus.

The Greeks, attacked by land and sea in Africa, fled to the island of Crete. Consequently, all the cities, deprived of assistance, surrendered to the Saracens. From Nowairi; Pag. under the year 691, no. 5.

Emperor Tiberius Apsimarus, years 1 and 2 [Note: [Col. 0887A] 1451–1452].

The Romans, traversing Syria, reached Samosata and slaughtered many thousands of Saracens. The Greek Annals in Baronius under Apsimarus’s second year. Pag. therefore correctly refers this event to the present year, contrary to Baronius, who above places it under the preceding year.

Emperor Tiberius Apsimarus, years 2 and 3 [Note: [Col. 0887B] 1452–1453].

Cunibert, king of the Lombards, died; his son Liutbert succeeded him under the guardianship of Ansprand. After eight months, however, he was deprived of both kingdom and life. Paul the Deacon, book 6, chapter 17; Hermann the Contracted, according to the Canisius edition; Baronius under the year 703, and Pag. there, no. 3.

Emperor Tiberius Apsimarus, years 3 and 4 [Note: [Col. 0887B] 1453–1454].

Ragimbert, son of Godebert, returned to the Lombard throne, but died shortly afterward, leaving his son Aripert II, who reigned twelve incomplete years. Paul the Deacon, book 6, chapter 35.

Egica, king of Spain, after reigning fifteen years—ten alone and five with his son Witiza—died. Witiza reigned alone for ten years. He was an impious king, stained by every kind of crime, and deserved that the kingdom of Spain should be invaded by the Saracens. Baronius, extensively, from Tudensis.

Tiberius Apsimarus, the usurper, years 4 and 5 [Note: [Col. 0887C] 1454–1455].

Bavaria, divided into three parts, was organized as a tetrarchy. Theodo II, duke of Bavaria, divided the duchy among his three sons, Theodebert, Theodebald, and Grimoald, retaining a portion of Bavaria for himself. Pag. no. 8 and following.

Theophylact, exarch, was sent from Constantinople to Ravenna; he governed Italy with the dignity of exarch for eight years. Anastasius; Panvinio.

Emperor Tiberius Apsimarus, the usurper, years 5 and 6 [Note: [Col. 0887D] 1455–1456].

Heraclius, the emperor’s brother, fought successfully against the Saracens once and again this year and the preceding one. First, he fought against ten thousand and sent many captives to Constantinople to his brother; then he fought against a much larger force and killed twelve thousand of them. The author of the Miscellanies.

Emperor Tiberius Apsimarus, the usurper, years 6 and 7 [Note: [Col. 0887D] 1456–1457].

Justinian, planning to recover the Empire, fled to Cherson. He sent one of his most trusted men to Terbel, king of the Bulgarians, promising him, among many other things, his daughter in marriage [Col. 0889A]. Terbel therefore gathered Bulgarian and Slav forces and, in the following year, marched to Constantinople. From Theophanes; Pag. with Baronius under the year 702, no. 1.

Æthelred, king of the Mercians, after reigning thirty years, resigned the kingdom to his son Coenred and became a monk. Bede; Baronius.

Tiberius Apsimarus, the usurper, year 7 [Note: [Col. 0889A] 1457–1458].

Emperors Justinian Augustus, restored to the throne, year 1.

Tiberius, son of Augustus, year 1.

After ten years of exile, Justinian recovered the Empire with the assistance of Terbel, king of the Bulgarians. He had Leontius and Apsimarus led through the city and beheaded. Ducange, Byzantine Families; Pag. under the year 703, with Baronius under the years 705 and 711, places the event at the end of this year.

At the beginning of his reign Justinian associated with himself his son Tiberius, in this or the following year. Ducange, in the same place.

Abimelech, caliph of the Saracens, died on 11 October. His son Walid, the thirteenth caliph, succeeded him; after destroying the church of Saint John at Damascus, he built a shrine. Pag. no. 17.

Emperors Justinian Augustus, restored to the throne, years 1 and 2 [Note: [Col. 0889B] 1458–1459].

Tiberius Augustus, years 1 and 2.

As soon as Justinian had taken revenge on his enemies and had been confirmed on the imperial throne, he sent two metropolitans to Rome with the Trullan Canons, so that the pontiff, distinguishing good from evil, might approve or reject whatever he pleased. Anastasius.

Emperors Justinian Augustus, restored to the throne, years 2 and 3 [Note: [Col. 0889C] 1459–1460].

Tiberius Augustus, years 2 and 3.

Muza, sent by Caliph Walid as governor to Africa, acquired Tingitanian Mauretania after capturing Tangier itself. He endeavored to introduce the Qur’an there. He later made war on the Visigoths who held part of that province and attacked their principal fortress, Septa, now Ceuta, which Count Julian defended. When he saw that he was accomplishing nothing, he withdrew after ravaging the countryside. From Arabic authorities; Pag. no. 2.

Emperors Justinian Augustus, restored to the throne, years 3 and 4 [Note: [Col. 0889D] 1460–1461].

Tiberius Augustus, years 3 and 4.

Justinian returned evil thanks to the Bulgarians and, after violating the peace with their king, engaged them in battle. The outcome was unfortunate: after his army had been routed, he himself barely escaped by flight to Constantinople. Baronius and Pag., from Theophanes, under the year 706.

Drogo, son of Pepin, died this year. The pseudo-Marcellinus, cited by Baronius under the year 714, maintains that he survived his father by a long time [Col. 0891A]. Pag. under this year, no. 2, from the Frankish Annals.

Emperors Justinian Augustus, restored to the throne, years 4 and 5 [Note: [Col. 0891A] 1461–1462].

Tiberius Augustus, years 4 and 5.

Two kings of England, Coenred of the Mercians and Offa of the East Saxons, abdicated and came to Rome. With them came Egwin, bishop of Worcester, to seek approval for the monastery of Evesham, which he had founded. From the Bollandists and Mabillon; Pag., no. 6; Baronius.

Emperors Justinian Augustus, restored to the throne, years 5 and 6 [Note: [Col. 0891A] 1462–1463] [Col. 0891B].

Tiberius Augustus, years 5 and 6.

Justinian marched against Cherson and, intending to avenge himself on its inhabitants—whose character he had experienced during his exile—practiced every kind of cruelty against them. From Theophanes and Nicephorus; the Miscellanies; Baronius; Pag. under this year.

John Rizocopus was sent to Italy with the rank of exarch, as successor to Theophylact. Anastasius.

Witiza, who had disfigured the Spanish kingdom with every kind of disgrace, died, leaving his sons Eba and Sisebut. Roderic was elevated over them and reigned for only one year. Pag. no. 4, who refers the Spanish authorities to censure.

Emperors Justinian Augustus, restored to the throne, years 6 and 7 [Note: [Col. 0891C] 1463–1464].

Tiberius Augustus, years 6 and 7.

Philippicus, the usurper, year 1.

Justinian, who had been violently hostile to the people of Cherson in the preceding year because they had secretly planned to hand him over, while he was an exile, to Apsimarus, sent a powerful fleet and ordered all of them to be slaughtered. When the soldiers had spared the children, he sent the fleet back to kill them as well this year. The fleet, enraged by this, proclaimed Bardan, son of Nicephorus of Pergamum, emperor; he was called Philippicus. Philippicus beheaded Justinian and Tiberius at Damalis. From the Greek authorities; Baronius; Pag.; Ducange, Byzantine Families; Anastasius [Col. 0891D] under Constantine.

Childebert III, king of the Franks, died on 14 April; Dagobert III succeeded him. Annals of Metz.

Emperor Philippicus, the usurper, years 1 and 2 [Note: [Col. 0891D] 1464–1465].

Philippicus persecuted the Sixth Synod. He expelled Cyrus, patriarch of Constantinople, and appointed John in his place. John defended the condemnable economy of a large part of the Eastern bishops: in order not to be removed from their sees, they condemned the Sixth Synod and defended Monothelitism, adhering to the emperor. Agathus the Deacon speaks at length in Combefis, *Auctarium to the Bibliotheca of the Fathers*, and Pag. above, no. 4, and under 713, nos. 1 and 3; see Baronius at length.

Ansprand, having defeated Aripert with the assistance of the Bavarians, became king of the Lombards, but soon died, namely on the Ides of June. His son Liutprand succeeded him and, hostile to the Roman Church, reigned thirty-one years and seven months. Paul the Deacon, final book 6; the epitaph at Pavia.

Emperors Philippicus, the usurper, year 2 [Note: [Col. 0893A] 1465–1466].

Anastasius II Augustus, year 1.

Anastasius Augustus began to reign on 4 June, the day of Pentecost, after Philippicus—who had reigned one year and six months, beginning in the middle of December—had been reduced to the status of a private citizen. Pag., from the Greek authorities and from Paul the Deacon and Bede; Baronius preceded him.

Flavius Scholasticus, exarch, sent to Italy, arrived at Rome this year with the emperor Anastasius’s sacred letter, or, later, at the beginning of the following year.

Liutprand, king of the Lombards, issued his laws on the day before the Kalends of March. Prologue.

Walid, caliph, recalled Muza, who had suffered a great defeat in the preceding year, from Africa. Muza sent his son Abdulaziz from Africa into Spain and himself went on to Syria. There, accused by Tarik before the caliph of embezzlement, Muza was condemned to a fine of 1,100,000 solidi and driven into exile, where he died in grief. Roderic; Pag. no. 6.

Emperor Anastasius II Augustus, years 1 and 2 [Note: [Col. 0893C] 1466–1467].

The two mayors of the palace of the Franks, Pepin of Herstal and his son Grimoald, died this year. While Pepin was ill, Grimoald went to pray at the basilica of Saint Lambert for his father’s recovery and was murdered in April. That Pepin, having avenged his son’s murder, fell ill again and died in December is confirmed by the Annals of Metz. Baronius and, from the Continuator of Fredegar, Pag. no. 3. Earlier, however, he had appointed Theudoald, grandson through his son Grimoald, mayor of the palace together with King Dagobert. The same source.

[Col. 0893D] After Pepin’s death, Gaul suffered internal wars for the next three years. Everything was later settled through the aid of Charles Martel. Continuator of Fredegar.

Emperors Anastasius II Augustus, years 2 and 3 [Note: [Col. 0893D] 1467–1468].

Theodosius III Augustus, year 1.

Anastasius sent a fleet against the Saracens. The fleet, however, mutinied, acclaimed Theodosius emperor, and withdrew; under his leadership it returned to besiege Constantinople. Anastasius fortified himself at Nicaea. After Constantinople had endured a six-month siege, it surrendered to Theodosius, who, after reducing Anastasius to private status in March of the following year, ruled as emperor.

The Franks, or Neustrians, resentful that Pepin of Austrasia exercised equal authority in Neustria and Austrasia, revolted against Theudoald after Pepin’s death [Col. 0895A]. A serious war followed, and soon afterward Theudoald himself died. Ragenfrid succeeded in Neustria; in Austrasia, where affairs were in danger, Charles Martel was miraculously freed from the custody of his stepmother Plectrude and restored the situation. From the Continuator of Fredegar; Pag. no. 3.

Dagobert III, king of the Franks, died; Childeric II succeeded him.

When Walid, caliph, died on 23 February, his brother Sulayman, the fourteenth caliph, succeeded him. Arabic authorities in Pag. no. 7.

Emperors Theodosius III Augustus, year 1 [Note: [Col. 0895B] 1468–1469].

Leo the Isaurian Augustus, year 1.

Leo the Isaurian, commander of the eastern forces, having always fought on Anastasius’s behalf and therefore being hostile to Theodosius, conspired against him with the aid of Artabasdes, commander of the Armenian troops. Theodosius, inexperienced in military affairs, abdicated on the advice of his supporters and became a monk with his son. He had not completed one year as emperor. Nicephorus; Baronius. Theophanes, beginning Leo’s reign from 25 March, appears to indicate that the acclamation took place at Amorium. See the preface, nos. 26 and following.

Lunar eclipse on 13 January, Monday, at the seventh hour after noon. Ecliptic digits: 18, 36. It began to grow dark a few minutes after the fifth hour from noon. Anastasius; Calvisius.

Emperor Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 1 and 2 [Note: [Col. 0895C] 1469–1470].

The Saracens under the command of Maslama, who had wintered in Asia, realizing that Leo had deceived them, again marched into Thrace and besieged Constantinople by land and sea. The city was freed by the protection of the Blessed Virgin, while the Saracens suffered an enormous defeat on land and sea. The siege began on 15 August; on 8 October Sulayman, the caliph, died, and Omar, the fifteenth caliph, succeeded him. This was, according to Theophanes and the Miscellanies, Leo’s second year, contrary to more recent writers, who place the beginning of Leo’s reign in this year. Bede; Paul the Deacon; Baronius; Pag., no. 1.

[Col. 0895D] Battle of Vincy, in which King Chilperic and Ragenfrid, mayor of the palace, were defeated by Charles Martel. Annals.

Emperor Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 2 and 3 [Note: [Col. 0895D] 1470–1471].

Constantine Copronymus was born to Leo and his wife Maria, who was crowned on 21 October. Theophanes; Pag., following year, with Baronius, no. 9; the Miscellanies.

Solar eclipse in Spain on 3 June, Friday, one hour and fifteen minutes after noon. Ecliptic digits: 12, 14. The sun was at 15 degrees of Gemini. Isidore; the Pacatian and Toledan authorities; Calvisius; Pag. no. 5.

When an earthquake shook Syria, the impious Umar compelled Christians to abandon the faith. He attracted apostates with rewards, but bitterly persecuted those who remained steadfast under the harsh laws he enacted. Theophanes; the Miscellanies.

Emperor Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 3 and 4 [Note: [Col. 0897A] 1471–1472].

Charles Martel fought for the third time against King Chilperic and Ragenfrid, the mayor of the palace. Ragenfrid was defeated and escaped by flight to Angers. Charles pursued Chilperic, who was fleeing with Eudes, duke of Aquitaine, and the treasures, as far as Paris. From the Continuator of Fredegar, contrary to Paul the Deacon; Pag. nos. 10 and 11.

Radbod, king of the Frisians and a great hater of the Christian name, died shortly after Saint Boniface’s arrival. Baronius and Pag. no. 4.

Emperor Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 4 and 5 [Note: [Col. 0897B] 1472–1473].

Constantine Copronymus Augustus, year 1.

Constantine Copronymus was crowned by his father on 31 March, Easter Day, and made co-ruler of the Empire. Theophanes; the Miscellanies.

Umar, caliph of the Saracens, died on the seventh day before the Ides of February. His brother Izitus, the sixteenth caliph, succeeded him; Izitus had previously been co-ruler. From Elmacin; Pag. no. 2.

Chilperic, king of the Franks, died. Theodoric IV, aged seven, succeeded him; his father Dagobert III had left him in the monastery at Chelles [Col. 0897C]. Pag. nos. 3 and 4.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 5 and 6 [Note: [Col. 0897C] 1473–1474].

Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 1 and 2.

Izitus, caliph, issued a decree against the sacred images of the Christians, as Pag. no. 7 records under the year 723, with Baronius.

Alahor, governor of the Saracens in Spain, had unsuccessfully attempted to attack Narbonese Gaul. His successor Zama, who was in the third year of his governorship, subjected it to his authority this year. Later, when he attempted to attack Toulouse, he was defeated and killed by Eudes, duke of Aquitaine. Ambiza then became governor of Spain. From Isidore, the Pacatian and Roderican authorities; Pag. nos. 4 and following [Col. 0897D].

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 6 and 7 [Note: [Col. 0897D] 1474–1475].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 2 and 3.

Leo compelled the Jews and Montanists to be baptized. Many of them therefore preferred to be burned alive in their own homes. Theophanes; Baronius; Pag.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 7 and 8 [Note: [Col. 0897D] 1475–1476].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 3 and 4.

The Africans who, when the Saracens invaded Africa, had poured into Europe seeking food were discovered to be either Manichaeans or Donatists. By a general decree they were forbidden to be ordained by any bishop. Baronius.

Theodo II, tetrarch of Bavaria, died. His son Grimoald succeeded him, the other son and tetrarch, Theodebald, having died earlier, and perhaps also another son, Theodebert. Pag. no. 9.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 8 and 9, after the eighth and ninth consulships [Note: [Col. 0899A] 1476–1477].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 4 and 5.

Izitus, caliph of the Saracens, after reigning four years and one month, died on 4 February. His brother Hisham succeeded him as the seventeenth caliph. From Elmacin [Col. 0899B]; Pag. under the preceding year, no. 8.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 9 and 10 [Note: [Col. 0899B] 1477–1478].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 5 and 6.

The tetrarchy of Bavaria established by Theodo II ended with the death of Grimoald, the last of the brothers, in the first war fought this year against the Bavarians by Charles Martel. Hubert succeeded to the entire duchy; he was the son of Theodebert, the eldest son of Theodo II. From the Annals; Pag. nos. 6 and following.

The Saracens suffered a great defeat at the hands of Eudes, duke of Aquitaine, who had distributed among his soldiers sacred sponges received from Rome. This occurred in the eleventh year after the invasion of Spain, that is, from the year 714, from which several writers begin their reckoning. Anastasius.

Ambiza, governor of the Saracens in Spain, died; Jahya succeeded him. Isidore; the Pacatian and Roderican authorities.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 10 and 11 [Note: [Col. 0899C] 1478–1479].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 6 and 7.

Leo’s madness against the sacred images began this year. See the year 730, from which the emperor’s hostility toward Saint Germanus, the other bishops, and all Christians began. Gregory himself, who until then had annually received letters from the emperor, received none thereafter; hence, in an uncertain year, he turned to the protection of Charles. Baronius and Pag., from Theophanes and the Miscellanies, under this year and 730 [Col. 0899D].

The Greeks, rebelling over the images, brought a fleet against Constantinople and fought on 18 October. They were defeated, and the emperor’s boldness consequently increased. Theophanes, with Pag. under the following year, no. 1. The author of the Miscellanies gives 18 April and refers the event to the following year; Baronius follows him.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 11 and 12 [Note: [Col. 0899D] 1479–1480].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 7 and 8.

Paul, the exarch sent in the preceding year by the emperor to carry out the crime of murdering the pontiff with the spatharii, was killed by the Italians defending the pontiff. His successor Eutychius was sent for the same criminal purpose.

The Saracens besieged Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia, during the summer, but withdrew without accomplishing anything. The Miscellanies; Baronius; Arabic authorities cited by Pag., no. 2.

Emperor Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 12 and 13 [Note: [Col. 0901A] 1480–1481].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 8 and 9.

Charles Martel defeated the Bavarians, who had rebelled again, in a second battle. From the Annals; Pag. no. 1.

Jahya, governor of the Saracens in Spain, died after governing it for three years. Codoyfa succeeded him for only six months; at the end of this year Othman succeeded Codoyfa and himself died shortly afterward, after four months. Arabic authorities cited by Pag. no. 2.

The fortress of Sutri was occupied by the Lombards for forty days and then restored to the Holy See. Anastasius; Baronius.

Emperor Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 13 and 14 [Note: [Col. 0901B] 1481–1482].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 9 and 10.

Othman, governor of the Saracens in Spain, died after governing Spain for only four months. Haithan succeeded him and held the governorship for ten months. Arabic authorities cited by Pag., under the preceding year, no. 2.

The Saracens invaded Gaul, and a great slaughter of them took place. Bede, book 5, chapter 24; the epitome of Anastasius; Baronius; Pag. no. 3.

Two comets were seen this year, one in the east and the other in the west. The same sources.

Emperor Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 14 and 15 [Note: [Col. 0901C] 1482–1483].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 10 and 11.

Leo openly persecuted the sacred images by publishing edicts. Consequently all Italy defected from him. In particular, the armies of Ravenna and Venice planned to create a new emperor, but the Holy Pontiff intervened, hoping for the conversion of the impious Leo. Anastasius; Pag. no. 8.

Muhammad succeeded Othman as governor of the Saracens in Spain and soon afterward, around March, appointed Abderrahman in his place. Abderrahman governed for nearly three years. Pag. under the year 728, no. 2.

Charles Martel, always victorious, engaged the Suebi in battle and subdued them. The Annals; Pag. no. 16.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 15 and 16 [Note: [Col. 0901D] 1483–1484].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus, years 11 and 12.

Eudes, duke of Aquitaine, broke the peace concluded with Charles Martel twelve years earlier. He was defeated once and again this year. From the Annals; Pag. no. 15.

Abderrahman, governor of the Saracens in Spain, ravaged the monasteries and the cities of Autun and Sens in Gaul. Arabic authorities cited by Pag. no. 13.

The history of the English by the venerable Bede ends here. Bede, at the end of book 5.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 16 [Note: [Col. 0903A] 1484–1485] and 17.

Flavius Constantine Copronymus, years 12 and 13.

Leo arranged the marriage of his son Constantine with Irene, daughter of the khagan. Theophanes; Baronius.

Charles Martel inflicted two great defeats on the Saracens: one this year and the other in 737, the latter near Narbonne at the river Berre, the former in Aquitaine near Poitiers. Eudes, having been twice defeated by Charles in the preceding year, sought his aid this year when the common cause against the Saracens was being pursued; their forces united and won a notable victory. Abderrahman himself, governor of Spain, who had subjected Wasconia and Aquitaine twice to himself, was killed; Abdelmelech succeeded him. The Annals and Arabic authorities cited by Pag. nos. 1 and following [Col. 0903B].

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 17 [Note: [Col. 0903B] 1485–1486] and 18.

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 13 and 14.

Abdelmelech, governor of Spain, seeing that Gaul had often been unsuccessfully attacked by his predecessors, exercised his fury against the Spaniards by persecuting the Christian name. Hence the kingdom of Pelagius was confined to the mountains of Asturias [Col. 0903C]. Pag. under the preceding year, nos. 5 and following, and under this year, no. 2.

Solar eclipse on 14 August, eight hours and thirty minutes after midnight, in England. Ecliptic digits: 2, 1. The sun was at 24 degrees of Leo. From English writers; Calvisius.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 18 and 19 [Note: [Col. 0903C] 1486–1487].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 14 and 15.

Charles Martel completed this year the Frisian war undertaken in the preceding year. The Annals; Pag. no. 9.

As Abdelmelech was approaching his final day, Obeydallah, the caliph’s governor in Africa, entrusted the governorship of Spain to Ocba, so that he would not cease persecuting the Christians, following the example of his predecessor. Arabic authorities cited by Pag. no. 7.

Lunar eclipse in England at approximately the second hour after midnight, Monday, 24 January. Ecliptic digits: 18, 15. The sun was at approximately 8 degrees of Aquarius. Calvisius.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 19 and 20 [Note: [Col. 0903D] 1487–1488].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 15 and 16.

After Eudes, duke of Aquitaine, died, Charles Martel entered Provence and subjected it to his authority. Of Eudes’s two sons, Hunald and Hatto, Hunald became duke after his father. Pag., from the Annals, no. 5, where he learnedly distinguishes the Wascones and Aquitanians, who are confused by ancient writers, although there was a duchy of Aquitaine and another of Wasconia.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 20 and 21 [Note: [Col. 0903D] 1488–1489].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 16 and 17.

Charles Martel, after completing the Aquitanian war [Col. 0905A], subjected Burgundy and Provence to his authority. Pag. no. 7, from the Annals.

Here ends the Continuator of Fredegar, to which two appendices are attached: the first extends to Pepin’s consecration; the second to Pepin’s death.

When Liutprand, king of the Lombards, fell ill, the Lombards raised his grandson Hildebrand to the kingship. After recovering, Liutprand allowed him to be his co-ruler. Privileges of the Lucchese Archives, cited by Florentine authorities.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 21 and 22 [Note: [Col. 0905B] 1489–1490].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 17 and 18.

Charles Martel, who, after Theodoric IV died this year, ruled France until the year 742, when Childeric IV was created king, fought successfully this year in Septimania against the Saracens. Pag. demonstrates this in no. 8 and following, from the Annals and the first Appendix, contrary to Baronius, who makes one war out of two Saracen wars and postpones it to the following year.

Geolwlf, king of Northumbria, died; Eadbert succeeded him. Baronius and Pag. no. 3, and the continuation of Bede’s epitome, which was written for the same Geolwlf.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 22 and 23 [Note: [Col. 0905C] 1490–1491].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 18 and 19.

Charles Martel, who had fought the Saxons beyond the Rhine once in 718 and again in 720, fought them successfully for the third time this year in defense of the sacred things and religion. The Annals; Pag. no. 4.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 23 and 24 [Note: [Col. 0905C] 1491–1492].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 19 and 20.

When the Saracens again entered Gaul and widely ravaged Provence [Col. 0905D], Charles Martel, aided by Liutprand, king of the Lombards, defeated them. The Annals; Pag. no. 6.

Æthelard, king of the West Saxons, died; Cuthred succeeded him. Continuation of Bede’s epitome; Pag. no. 10.

Emperors Leo the Isaurian Augustus, years 24 and 25 [Note: [Col. 0905D] 1492–1493].

Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 20 and 21.

A tremendous earthquake shook Constantinople and other cities of the East on 26 October, Wednesday; it continued for many months. Theophanes.

Liutprand, king of the Lombards, besieged Rome, where Trasamund, duke of Spoleto, was defending himself. Gregory the pontiff, Patricius Stephen, the duke, and the Roman army refused to surrender Trasamund to the king. Liutprand therefore raised the siege and departed, taking four cities from the Apostolic See. Anastasius, in the account of Zacharias.

Emperor Leo the Isaurian Augustus, year 25 [Note: [Col. 0907A] 1493–1494].

[Col. 0907B] Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus, years 21 and 22, year 1.

Leo the Isaurian, having reigned from the acclamation at Amorium for twenty-five years, two months, and twenty-five days—that is, from 25 March 716—died this year on 18 June. Constantine Copronymus alone ruled for thirty-four years, two months, and twenty-six days, until 14 September 775. The beginning of his reign, however, was contentious: for, out of hatred toward him, because he was like his father in overthrowing the sacred images, Artabasdes was made emperor after 27 June. Baronius; Pag. no. 4.

Charles Martel, after having ruled for 25 years from the Battle of Vincennes in 717, died on 15 or 22 October, dividing the office of mayor of the palace between his sons Pepin and Carloman—Austrasia, that is, and Neustria. Pagi, pp. 11 and 19, from the continuation of Fredegar appended to the Annals.

Emperor Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus. [Note: [Column 0907C] 1494–1495] Years 22 and 23, years 1 and 2.

Artavasdus and his son Nicetas fought twice, unsuccessfully, against Constantine. Miscellanies; Baronius; Pagi, from Theophanes, following year.

Francia was troubled by new internal disturbances, both in Aquitaine and in Germany; and after a five-year interregnum Childeric III became king. Annals; Pagi, pp. 15 and following.

Charles, later called the Great and emperor of the West, was born to Pepin this year, not—as some maintain—not until five years later. H. Valesius against Coint and Pagi, from the Annals, no. 22 and following.

Emperor Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus. [Note: [Column 0907D] 1495–1496] Years 23 and 24, years 2 and 3.

Constantine defeated Artavasdus in battle. According to Zonaras, Artavasdus had ruled for two years; Constantine ordered his eyes and those of his son Nicephorus to be put out. Baronius and Pagi, no. 18.

When the Exarch was preparing to besiege Ravenna, he and the archbishop appealed to the pope for assistance. The pope therefore went there and established peace with the king. Anastasius; Baronius; Marca; Pagi, no. 14.

Hisham, seventeenth caliph of the Saracens, died; al-Walid II, eighteenth caliph, succeeded him. From al-Makin; Pagi, no. 4; Baronius, from the supplement to the Miscellanies, following year.

Emperor Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus. [Note: [Column 0909A] 1496–1497] Years 24 and 25, years 3 and 4.

Liutprand died at the beginning of this year. His nephew Hildebrand ruled alone until July, when the Lombards expelled him and raised Ratchis. Rachis, book 6, chapter 58; Herempert.

Al-Walid II, caliph of the Saracens, after ruling for one year, was killed on 16 April. His son Yazid III, nineteenth caliph, succeeded him; he died after five months. Ibrahim then became the twentieth caliph, but was deposed after 69 days by Marwan, or Marwa, the rebel, who was the twenty-first caliph. He favored Christians, especially those in Spain, whom he freed from the taxes payable for the dead. Pagi, from al-Makin, no. 17, above, and no. 1; the latter from Isidore of Pacensis.

Emperor Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus. [Note: [Column 0909B] 1497–1498] Years 25 and 26, years 4 and 5.

Carloman and Pepin, mayors of the palace of the Franks, fought successfully in Saxony and Aquitaine, perhaps also in Germany, with a favorable outcome for religion. Annals and Pagi, no. 11 and following.

Ethelbald, king of the Mercians, who had greatly offended against the laws and customs, was brought back to good conduct at a synod held in Germany this year. The synod deposed Gervil, bishop of Mainz, and replaced him with Saint Boniface. Baronius and Pagi, no. 1.

Emperor Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus. [Note: [Column 0909C] 1498–1499] Years 26 and 27, years 5 and 6.

Dark shadows appeared in Syria while the Saracens were fighting among themselves, an indication of their declining empire. From Theophanes; Baronius; Pagi, no. 1.

A great plague, which had begun above in Sicily and Calabria, reached Constantinople, and the impious emperor was scourged by it. Baronius and Pagi, no. 3.

In Spain, on the third day before the Nones of April, for three days—namely, Sunday, Monday, and Tuesday—three suns were seen; afterward all the inhabitants suffered from a severe famine. Isidore of Pacensis; Pagi, no. 9.

Ratchis, king of the Lombards, issued his laws on the Kalends of March, in the second year of his reign. Prologue to the Laws.

Abulcatar was sent as viceroy of the Saracens to Spain, where civil wars were being waged among them; he reconciled them. From Isidore of Pacensis; Pagi, following year, no. 14.

Emperor Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus. [Note: [Column 0909D] 1499–1500] Years 27 and 28, years 6 and 7.

A great earthquake occurred in Palestine on 18 January, at the fourth hour. Theophanes; Baronius and Pagi, above, no. 2.

Grifo, the brother of Pepin and Carloman, who had been held under guard because he had rashly taken up arms against his brothers, was released this year. Pepin, while Carloman had gone to Rome, renewed the war against the Saxons and defeated them. From the Annals and the continuation of Fredegar appended to them; Pagi, nos. 5 and 6.

At the end of summer, Abulcatar was removed from his office as viceroy of the Saracens in Spain. The rebels raised Thoaban, who likewise died at the end of summer this year; Joseph succeeded him. Pagi, no. 14.

Emperor Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus. [Note: [Column 0911A] 1500–1501] Years 28 and 29, years 7 and 8.

The plague that had begun two years earlier raged widely in Constantinople, especially in the suburbs. Pagi, under the year 746 and following, from Theophanes and Nicephorus.

Grifo went to the Saxons and took up arms against his brother. Pepin, however, after defeating them and devastating their territory extensively, returned home. Annals of Metz.

Eadbert, king of Kent, died; his brother Ethelbert succeeded him. When Odilo likewise died, Tassilo II, still a child, succeeded him this year. Coint; Pagi, no. 8.

Emperor Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus. [Note: [Column 0911B] 1501–1502] Years 29 and 30, years 8 and 9.

Syria was shaken by a great earthquake.

Abdallah became the twenty-second caliph of the Saracens at the end of October, while Marwan was still alive. Shortly afterward Marwan was killed by Abdallah, the uncle of the caliph Abdallah. Theophanes and al-Makin; Pagi, no. 1.

Grifo, having been defeated by his brother with the Saxons in the preceding year, this year incited the Bavarians against him. Annals and Pagi, no. 4.

Aistulf, the brother of Ratchis, became king of the Lombards. Baronius, following year.

Emperor Flavius Constantine Copronymus Augustus. [Note: [Column 0911C] 1502–1503] Years 30 and 31, years 9 and 10.

This year, on 25 January, Constantine had by Irene, daughter of the khagan, king of the Khazars, and the first of his three wives, a son, Leo. Leo was admitted to a share in the empire in the following year and, after his father’s death on 14 September 775, ruled alone. Theophanes; Cedrenus.

According to the annals, Francia was disturbed by no war this year.

The Muslims living in Galicia had long harassed the Christians by war. At last, divided by mutual dissensions, they were expelled from all Galicia this year by the Catholic Alfonso. From the Anonymous of Andalusia; Pagi, under 753, no. 11.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0911D] 1503–1504] Years 31 and 32, years 10 and 11.

Leo IV Augustus, year 1.

On 6 June, on Pentecost itself, Constantine made his son Leo, a child of sixteen months, co-emperor. Theophanes; Nicephorus; Pagi, no. 11.

The famous embassy of Pepin to the Holy See was entrusted to Bishop Burchard and Abbot Fulrad. They were to negotiate the transfer of the Frankish kingdom from the indolent Merovingians to the most warlike Carolingians. By the authority of the Holy See, the latter were declared kings; and in the following year Pepin, the first of them, was anointed. The Annals passim.

At the beginning of July, Aistulf captured Ravenna and brought the Exarchate to an end; it had lasted approximately 184 years.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0913A] 1504–1505] Years 32 and 33, years 11 and 12.

Leo IV Augustus, years 1 and 2.

A lunar eclipse occurred on the day before the Kalends of August, Monday, beginning one hour after midnight; the eclipse measured 20 degrees, 50 minutes. From Roger of Wendover and Calvisius, in England.

Pepin, the first Carolingian king, was recognized in Francia by the authority of the Holy See and was anointed at Soissons by Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz. Baronius and, more fully, Pagi, no. 1 and following. Childeric III, the last of the Merovingians, was deposed and confined in the monastery of Bertin. Pagi, no. 9.

Copronymus strove to spread his impiety and heresy widely. From Theophanes; Pagi, no. 18.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0913B] 1505–1506] Years 33 and 34, years 12 and 13.

Leo IV Augustus, years 2 and 3.

Aistulf besieged Rome. Meanwhile, when the legates sent to Pepin returned and reported that the king’s aid was ready, the legates who had gone to Constantinople returned without accomplishing anything. The pope therefore turned wholly to the kings of Francia, and we no longer read that he sought the emperor’s assistance. Baronius and Pagi, above, no. 16.

Pepin won a notable victory over the Saxons. They appealed to the king’s clemency and obtained peace. On his return, he learned that his rebellious brother Grifo had died in Gascony, where he had sought refuge. From the second appendix to the continuation of Fredegar and the Annals; Pagi, no. 8.

A solar eclipse occurred on 9 January, Tuesday, at the second hour before noon; and a lunar eclipse on 24 January, at the first hour after midnight, at the beginning of Wednesday. Calvisius.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0913D] 1506–1507] Years 34 and 35, years 13 and 14.

Leo IV Augustus, years 3 and 4.

A false synod was held at Constantinople against the sacred images, with the emperor’s patriarch in support. Stephen the Deacon of Constantinople; Pagi, no. 10 and following.

At the assembly of Quierzy, Pepin and the nobles decided to aid the Holy See. Aistulf, who had issued his laws on the Kalends of March this year, attempted in vain, through his legate Carloman, to turn the king away from taking up arms against the Lombards. With the pope’s consent Carloman remained in the monastery of Saint-Denis, while Pepin, with a large army, came to Pavia with the pope. Annals; Anastasius.

Abdallah, twenty-second caliph of the Saracens and the first of the Abbasids, died on 9 June. His brother Abū Jaʿfar al-Manṣūr succeeded him as the twenty-third caliph. From al-Makin; Pagi, no. 23.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0915A] 1507–1508] Years 35 and 36, years 14 and 15.

Leo IV Augustus, years 4 and 5.

A lunar eclipse occurred on 23 November, Monday, in London. From Roger of Wendover and Calvisius.

After Pepin had returned to Gaul, Narbonne, which had endured a three-year siege, was captured by the Franks with the cooperation of the Goths. The Saracens were expelled from Septimania, and the province was restored beyond the Pyrenees. Annals; Pagi, no. 23.

After Aistulf had gone to Francia, he turned back against Pepin, refused to observe the agreements, despised the papal legates, and besieged Rome. Anastasius; Baronius, at length; Pagi, no. 1 and following.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0915B] 1508–1509] Years 36 and 37, years 15 and 16.

Leo IV Augustus, years 5 and 6.

Aistulf, after reigning seven years following his brother and remaining continually hostile to the pope, died badly this year after 5 April. With the pope’s approval, Desiderius became king of the Lombards, the last of their kings, as I shall say under 774.

A new era began for the Saracens of Spain, for from this year their kings begin. Abd al-Rahman fought Joseph, the governor; after defeating him and driving him to Toledo, Abd al-Rahman himself was proclaimed king. Although he was content with the title of emir, he was nevertheless their first king in Spain. He began to reign this year, although Joseph was not killed until three years later. Thus, until this year, they were called governors; from this point until 913, emirs; thereafter, caliphs. From the Anonymous of Andalusia and al-Makin; Pagi, no. 7.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0915C] 1509–1510] Years 37 and 38, years 16 and 17.

Leo IV Augustus, years 6 and 7.

Pepin and Constantine negotiated peace through reciprocal embassies, but the negotiations produced no result. Second Appendix to the continuation of Fredegar; Pagi, no. 7.

Desiderius, having begun to trouble the Church’s territory, came to Rome in the autumn and promised that he would return Imola, Bologna, Auximum, Ancona, and other places that he had occupied, provided that the hostages whom Pepin had taken with him to Francia were returned to him. The pope therefore sent an embassy to Pepin and conveyed one message to him in writing and another orally. Code of the Carolingian Letters, 28, 29, 30, 33. These letters reveal Constantine’s attempt, through his agent Leo, to induce Ravenna and the Exarchate to revolt.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0917A] 1510–1511] Years 38 and 39, years 17 and 18.

Leo IV Augustus, years 7 and 8.

Desiderius likewise came this year, in autumn, to the sacred threshold and promised the pope that he would restore several estates that he had seized in Tuscany. Code of the Carolingian Letters, letter 26; Pagi, no. 9.

Pepin fought the Saxons again. After killing many of them, he compelled them, before returning to Francia, to promise that they would obey all his commands and send three hundred horses every year to the general assembly as a mark of honor. Baronius, above, and Pagi, no. 8, from the Annals.

García, surnamed Arista, the first prince of Navarre, died. His son Eneco Garseanis, or Íñigo García Arista, succeeded him and was the first to assume the title of king this year. Acts of the Saints; Pagi, no. 12.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0917B] 1511–1512] Years 39 and 40, years 18 and 19.

Leo IV Augustus, years 8 and 9.

The county of Aragon, which became a kingdom in the eleventh century, was established this year, and its first count was Aznar. At first Aragon was confined within narrow boundaries, but it began to be held by the kings of Navarre. This happened because the Christians of Spain who did not wish to obey the Saracen king, or emir, Abd al-Rahman, paid allegiance to the counts while awaiting an opportunity to free the kingdom from Saracen servitude. Pagi, no. 13.

A son was born to Pepin, whom he named after himself. The Holy Pontiff wished to receive him from the sacred font. Letter 23 of the Code of the Carolingian Letters. He died two years later.

After Osulf had been wickedly killed by his own people following one year of reign, Ethelwald ruled in Northumbria from August. Annals of Mailros; Pagi, above, no. 11.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0917C] 1512–1513] Years 40 and 41, years 19 and 20.

Leo IV Augustus, years 9 and 10.

A solar eclipse occurred on 15 August, four hours after noon, measuring 8 degrees and 15 minutes; the sun was at 26 degrees Gemini. From the Miscellanies and the Prutenic Tables; Calvisius.

Waifar, duke of Aquitaine, assumed tyrannical power and appropriated the property of the churches. Pepin demanded the ecclesiastical properties belonging to his kingdom and, through legates, urged that their former immunity be restored. Waifar disregarded everything. Hence arose a nine-year war, which the Annals call the Aquitanian War; Pepin completed it in the last year of his life, 768. From the Annals, the second appendix to the continuation of Fredegar, and Einhard; Pagi, no. 1 and following.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0917D] 1513–1514] Years 41 and 42, years 20 and 21.

Leo IV Augustus, years 10 and 11.

Second year of the Aquitanian War; tenth of Pepin. Annals.

Pepin fought successfully against Waifar this year. After killing many Gascons, or Aquitanians, and capturing them together with Blandinus, count of Clermont, he also captured the city itself and devastated the region extensively before returning home. From the Annals and the second appendix to the continuation of Fredegar; Pagi, no. 5.

In the East, the defenders of the sacred images suffered much from the impious Constantine. This year Saint Andrew of Crete suffered martyrdom for the same cause. From Metaphrastes; Baronius and Pagi, no. 2. See Baronius, above, for a full account of this history.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0919B] 1514–1515] Years 42 and 43, years 21 and 22.

Leo IV Augustus, years 11 and 12.

Third year of the Aquitanian War; eleventh of Pepin.

Pepin went against Waifar for the third time and surrounded Bourges with a siege. At last he captured it with siege engines and subjected it to his authority by right of war. He mercifully released the soldiers whom the enemy had sent into the city to defend it; he ordered the counts found there to go to Francia with their wives and children, and replaced them with his own counts. After capturing the fortress of Thouars with astonishing speed, he returned to Francia. Annals; continuation of Fredegar, second appendix; Pagi, no. 6.

Al-Manṣūr built Baghdad, later the seat of the caliphate, at an hour designated by the astrologers, and called it the City of Peace. From al-Makin and Abū al-Faraj; Pagi, no. 7.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0919C] 1515–1516] Years 43 and 44, years 22 and 23.

Leo IV Augustus, years 12 and 13.

Fourth year of the Aquitanian War; twelfth of Pepin.

Pepin descended into Aquitaine for the fourth time and reached Cahors. After devastating the region extensively, he returned to Francia. Annals of Metz.

Constantine fought successfully against the Bulgarians, killed many thousands of them, and, elated by victory, entered the city in triumph. Theophanes.

The Turks left the Caspian Gates this year or the following year—namely, in Constantine’s twenty-third year—and, after killing or capturing many in Armenia, returned home. The same author.

A dreadful winter raged in the East, according to Theophanes, and in the West, according to the Annals of the Franks, Baronius, and Pagi, no. 3.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0919D] 1516–1517] Years 44 and 45, years 23 and 24.

Leo IV Augustus, years 13 and 14.

Fifth year of the Aquitanian War; thirteenth of Pepin. Annals.

A solar eclipse occurred on 4 June, Monday, almost at midday; it measured 7 degrees and 15 minutes, and the sun was at 16 degrees Gemini. From Aimoin, Bunting, and Calvisius.

Pepin held an assembly at Worms, where he negotiated peace with Waifar, duke of Aquitaine, and with Tassilo of Bavaria, who in the preceding year had broken his treaty with his uncle Pepin and fled from Francia to Bavaria. For this reason he led his troops in no direction this year. At the same assembly Pepin’s sons were declared counts. According to the Annals and Pagi, no. 3, he celebrated Christmas and Easter at Quierzy.

Pepin refused to hear the emperor’s legates unless the papal legates were present. He heard both sides disputing about the orthodox faith and the tradition of the Fathers; afterward he reported what had occurred by sending legates both to the pope and to the emperor. Pagi, no. 4.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0921B] 1517–1518] Years 45 and 46, years 24 and 25.

Leo IV Augustus, years 14 and 15.

Sixth year of the Aquitanian War; fourteenth of Pepin. Annals.

Many battles were fought this year between the counts of Aquitaine and the Franks, who defeated them. Pepin celebrated Christmas and Easter at Aachen and did not lead out his forces. He did, however, hold the assembly mentioned above, which is called the Assembly of Attigny after the town where it was held. Assuerus, abbot of Prüm, came to it and obtained from Pepin the cell of Saint Goar, situated above the confluence of the Moselle and Rhine; from this year onward it remained joined to the monastery of Prüm. From the Annals and Wandelbert; Pagi, no. 6.

Ethelwald, king of Northumbria, died; Ealred, the great-grandson of Ida, succeeded him and ruled for eight years, according to the Westminster source. Pagi, no. 7.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0921C] 1518–1519] Years 46 and 47, years 25 and 26.

Leo IV Augustus, years 15 and 16.

Seventh year of the Aquitanian War; fifteenth of Pepin. Annals.

After celebrating Easter at Aachen, Pepin again advanced into Aquitaine. Having crossed the Loire and devastated the entire province so thoroughly that all its inhabitants were subjected to his authority, he returned to Francia with much booty and spoils, having acquired nearly all Aquitaine. From the second appendix to the continuation of Fredegar; Pagi, no. 4.

Paul held a meeting in the presence of Desiderius’s legates and deliberated about sending a new embassy to Pepin. Through it he reported that Desiderius, far from restoring the remaining possessions to the Holy See, had again invaded all those that he had restored. Fearing worse, Paul therefore appealed for Pepin’s assistance. From letter 17 of the Code of the Carolingian Letters; Pagi, no. 5.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0923A] 1519–1520] Years 47 and 48, years 26 and 27.

Leo IV Augustus, years 16 and 17.

Eighth year of the Aquitanian War; sixteenth of Pepin. Annals.

After celebrating Easter at Gentilly, Pepin went with his wife Bertrada to Bourges and held an assembly there. In May he undertook an expedition against Waifar in the same month; in August he undertook another. He was victorious on both occasions and wintered at Bourges. Pagi, no. 8 and following, from the Annals. He sent the army to winter in Burgundy. Appendix to the continuation of Fredegar.

The three Eastern patriarchs, defenders of the sacred images, together with many metropolitans and bishops, wrote synodical letters to the pope, declaring that the veneration of images was flourishing in the East. After Paul’s death, the pseudo-pope received these letters and sent them to Pepin in Greek and Latin in order to win him over. Letter 99 of the Code of the Carolingian Letters. Pepin, however, did not allow himself to be deceived by the usurper, as his silence indicates.

Emperors Flavius Constantine Copronymus. [Note: [Column 0923B] 1520–1521] Years 48 and 49, years 27 and 28.

Leo IV Augustus, years 17 and 18.

Ninth and final year of the Aquitanian War.

Pepin summoned the army from Burgundy and sent his counts with part of the forces to capture Remistagnus, Waifar’s uncle, who had broken faith in the preceding year. After they had captured him together with his wife, Pepin ordered both to be executed. He himself marched with the whole army against Waifar. After bringing all Aquitaine under his authority, he finally captured and killed the duke on the fourth day before the Nones of June, according to the Chronicle of Saint Gall. At last Pepin himself fell ill. After dividing the kingdom between his sons Charles and Carloman, he died on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, having ruled twenty-six years after the death of his father Charles and sixteen years after attaining royal dignity. The kings were crowned on the seventh day before the Ides of October: Carloman at Soissons and Charles—later called the Great and emperor of the West—at Noyon. Annals; Pagi, no. 2 and following.

## Roman Pontiffs and Ecclesiastical Affairs in the East and West

[Column 0830C]

[Note: [Column 0830C] 342 I–II] Saint Gregory the Great was ordained after a lengthy vacancy on 3 September, not on 19 March, as in the manuscripts cited by the Bollandists.

The discovery of the Holy Tunic belongs to this year. From Fredegar and Aimoin; Pagi, no. 6, under 593, with Baronius.

The sevenfold litany was held at Rome before Gregory’s consecration. Pagi, nos. 5 and 16; Sigonius.

The Roman council and two false synods of the Istrian schismatics. Pagi, no. 13.

[Column 0830D] Dispute in Gaul concerning the date of Easter; and there the Council of Metz concerning the case of the rebel Aegidius. From Gregory of Tours; Pagi, no. 2, under 594, with Baronius.

Saint Columbanus founded the monastery of Luxeuil. Pagi, no. 13; also under 612, no. 6.

[Note: [Column 0830D] II–III] Gregory, years 1 and 2.

Gregory sent a synodical letter to the Eastern patriarchs, in which he said that he venerated the four general councils as he did the four Gospels and approved the fifth. He dedicated the church of Saint Agatha in the Subura, which had been profaned by the Goths. From the Dialogues; Baronius. He replied to Leander, bishop of Seville, concerning triple immersion in baptism and rejoiced that King Reccared had embraced the Catholic faith. In letter 41 of book 1 he replied to Saint Leander, bishop of Seville; in letter 72 he wrote against the Donatist bishop who was claiming the primacy in Africa.

Through the agency of Queen Theodelinda the Lombards became Christians, just as the Franks had become Christians through the agency of Clotilda and the Goths through that of Ingundis. Baronius.

The History of Gregory of Tours ends. Baronius assigns it to 595, whereas Pagi, no. 11, asserts that Gregory perhaps died in that year, after having held office for twenty-three years.

[Note: [Column 0832A] III–IV] Gregory, years 2 and 3.

[Column 0832B] When two deacons announced that the Donatists in Africa were gaining strength, Gregory sent Hilary the notary there. In the same year he confirmed the privileges of the church of Carthage, book 2, letter 39; he also wrote to the Irish concerning the schism, book 2, letter 36. Gussanvillaeus, reading from manuscripts, has “to the Istrians”; Noris follows this opinion in On the Fifth Synod, vol. 1, p. 726. Pagius holds the contrary view, no. 2.

This year Gregory delivered a homily on Saint Clement, number 38. From the Deacon; Baronius, who wants all forty homilies to have been completed this year. He also restored Hadrian, bishop of Thebes, who had been unjustly deposed.

Second Council of Zaragoza.

[Note: [Column 0832B] IV and 343 I] Gregory, years 3 and 4.

Gregory sent a protest against the unjust law enacted by Maurice against the Church, book 2, letters 26 and 65.

Gregory sent Sabinian, a deacon and apocrisiarius, to Constantinople; Sabinian later succeeded him in the pontificate. Book 2, letter 52. Gregory returned to solitude in order to devote himself to writing the Dialogues and took with him Peter the Deacon, whom he used as interlocutor. Nevertheless, he did not neglect the care of the Church, as is clear from various letters to various bishops.

Simeon the Younger Stylite and Gregory of Antioch died. Anastasius was restored to the see of Antioch. Pagi, no. 17 and following, under the following year, no. 4, from Evagrius; Lambec likewise asserts this, arguing against the account above by Chrysostom of Alexandria. Baronius, under the following year, gives Gregory of Antioch’s death as two years later.

[Column 0832D] [Note: [Column 0832D] I–II] Gregory, years 4 and 5.

This year Gregory labored greatly because of the schismatics who opposed the confirmation of Constantius, bishop of Milan, unless he condemned the Fifth Synod. He also labored against the Donatists of Africa, who rebaptized converts, book 3, letter 32; over the conversion of the heretics of Sicily, book 4, letter 6; and over the conversion of the pagan Barbaricini in Sardinia, book 3, letters 25 and 27. Procopius, Gothic War, book 2. He separated Maximus of Salona, an intruder, from communion.

Amos became bishop of Jerusalem after John. Baronius, following year, where Pagi, no. 6.

Maximian, bishop of Syracuse, died; John succeeded him, and Gregory sent him the pallium as usual. Gregory, book 5, letter 18.

[Note: [Column 0834A] II–III] Gregory, years 5 and 6.

Gregory ceased interpreting Ezekiel because the Lombards were filling everything with slaughter. Homily 22, at the end. He appointed Virgil of Arles as vicar in Austria and Burgundy. Pagi, no. 3. At the request of the emperor, who favored the intruder Maximus of Salona, Gregory ordered his case to be heard at Ravenna, where a see was granted to him and the pallium was later sent. The Second Roman Council was held; in it John, a priest of Chalcedon, who had been deposed by John the Faster, was absolved. Gregory, book 5, letter 15. He sent the Morals and the Pastoral Rule to Saint Leander of Seville.

John the Faster died after having held office for thirteen years and five months, reckoned from 582, on 12 April. Noris, On the Fifth Synod, chapter 9, section 4; Pagi, following year, nos. 2 and 3. Baronius and Panvinio place John’s death later.

[Note: [Column 0834B] III–IV] Gregory, years 6 and 7.

Legates were sent back and forth by Cyriacus, John the Faster’s successor, and Gregory, concerning communion.

Augustine the monk was sent to England with his companions. On returning from Gaul to Rome, he turned back at the request of his companions in order to dissuade them from the difficult undertaking, carrying letters from Gregory, which are preserved in Bede with their signatures.

Pagius wishes “Maurice’s fourteenth year, after the fourteenth consulship,” to be read as the thirteenth.

The affairs of faith in Africa deteriorated severely through the Donatists. Gregory, book 5, letter 63.

[Note: [Column 0834C] IV and 344 I] Gregory, years 7 and 8.

Gregory received the representatives of Cyriacus with letters of recommendation from the emperor and a synodical letter. After recalling Sabinian, he sent Anatolius to Constantinople. He undertook the care of the Eastern Church. From various letters of this year, and concerning the African Church, book 6, letter 32.

Augustine was ordained bishop of Arles and, after returning to England, baptized ten thousand people. The same author, book 7, letter 30. Henschen, in his notes to the Life of Augustine written by John the Deacon, postpones Augustine’s ordination to the following year; but Gregory’s letter, which he cites, no less clearly testifies that the conversion of the English had taken place by 597 than it testifies to the ordination.

Council of Toledo concerning the chastity of the clergy.

[Note: [Column 0834D] I–II] Gregory, years 8 and 9.

Gregory increased the office of the defenders in honor and dignity; from among them he sent Faustinus to Sicily to convert the Jews. The same author, book 7, letter 24.

Through the efforts of Eulogius of Alexandria, heretics were converted, book 7, letter 30. Other heretics rose up at Thessalonica against the Council of Chalcedon, book 7, letter 7.

Anastasius the Elder, bishop of Antioch, died. Pagi, no. 9; Baronius, following year.

A synod was held at Huesca in Spain, in which nothing relevant to our times is found. Bail, Summary of the Councils, part 2.

[Note: [Column 0836A] II–III] Gregory, years 9 and 10.

The schismatics of Istria returned to the Church through the efforts of Gulfarius, the master of the soldiers, and others. The same author, book 7, letter 97.

Gregory sent gifts to Secundinus, an abbot of great renown among the Lombards, together with two copies of the Homilies. Book 7, letter 53. He sent Cyprian, an abbot, to Gaul and Spain to correct morals by convening synods everywhere and to abolish simony. Book 7, letter 111 and following. He sent gifts to Reccared, king of the Goths in Spain, and sent the pallium to Saint Leander, bishop of Seville, who was suffering from gout, the same disease that was then afflicting the pontiff. Book 7, letters 125 and 126.

The plague raged in Africa. The same author, book 8, letter 41.

[Note: [Column 0836B] III–IV] Gregory, years 10 and 11.

Gregory received from Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, a Commentary written by Eulogius against the Agnoite heretics, so that he might judge it. Gregory praised him as a Catholic. Gregory, book 8, letter 42.

The Third Roman Council was held. In it Andreas the Greek, discovered to be an impostor, was condemned together with his forgeries. Pagi, no. 7; Baronius, following year.

After Constantius, bishop of Milan, died, Deusdedit was appointed in opposition to the king of the Lombards. Book 8, letter 65.

[Note: [Column 0836C] IV and 345 I] Gregory, years 11 and 12.

Gregory replied to the synodical letter of Hesychius, bishop of Jerusalem, who had succeeded Amos after Amos’s death. Book 9, letter 4. He wrote to Virgil of Arles and to the kings of the Franks about extinguishing the stain of simony, which still prevailed in Gaul. The same work, letters 49, 53, and following. He congratulated Augustine, to whom he sent the pallium and instructions concerning the creation of new bishops; King Æthelberht of the English; and Queen Bertha on the progress of the faith. Book 9, letters 58–60. Bede, Ecclesiastical History of the English, book 1, chapter 29.

The Fourth Roman Council, which the collectors falsely call the Third, was held. It decreed a constitution in favor of monks. Pagi, no. 2. Louis Bail calls this the Third Council and places it among the Fourth, or says that the condemnation of Andrew the monk and impostor occurred in the same year. Summary of the Councils.

[Column 0838A] [Note: [Column 0838A] I–II] Gregory, years 12 and 13.

Gregory, grieving over the calamity that had struck Rome in the preceding year and laboring for the African Church, was consoled when the bishop of Trieste, a schismatic, and some Monophysite heretics voluntarily returned to the Church. The same author, book 10, letters 30 and 36.

Gregory restored the collapsing roofs of the churches of Saint Peter and Saint Paul. Book 10, letter 24 and following.

The body of Saint Victor the martyr was discovered. Pagi, no. 10. Baronius assigns this to 608.
