Anatolius, the apocrisiarius at Constantinople, died, and no successor was appointed. Book 11, letter 35.

[Note: [Column 0838B] II–III] Gregory, years 13 and 14.

When Phocas asked about the cessation of the apocrisiarius, Gregory replied, citing the extreme difficulties of Maurice’s times. He sent Boniface with letters to the emperors and to Cyriacus the patriarch, and especially grieved over Phocas. Rome had already been oppressed for thirty-five years by Lombard incursions. Book 11, letter 35. He sent John the Defender to Spain in the case of Januarius, bishop of Málaga, and of Stephen, who had been deposed at the command of Comitiolus. Book 11, letter 57. He sent Vitalis the defender from Sardinia to Phocas, so that that island might be freed from its burdens. The same letter, 57.

Brunhilda, pretending to seek the good of the Church, sent Burgoald and Varmaric, noble Franks, as legates to the pope, ostensibly on account of private boundaries but in reality to form an alliance with Phocas. Baronius.

[Note: [Column 0838C] III–IV] Gregory, year 14; Sabinian, year 1.

Gregory donated a large estate at the Baths of Sylva to the basilica of Saint Paul for the lamps. Book 12, letter 9. Other similar donations appear in Ciampini, On Sacred Buildings, and elsewhere, with uncertain dates.

[Column 0838D] Gregory died on 12 March, as all agree. Sabinian was ordained as his successor on 30 August, after a vacancy of five months and eighteen days.

Baronius assigns Augustine’s death to this year; but Mabillon, Benedictine section 1, places it under 607, as does Pagius. He admits, however, that this chronology rests only on conjecture. The same author, no. 16. Certainly this year Sigebert, also called Seberet, the first king of the East Saxons, brought glory to his kingdom by receiving baptism.

[Note: [Column 0838D] IV and 346 I] Sabinian, years 1 and 2.

Severus, patriarch of Aquileia, whose name Gregory the Great detested, as John the Deacon testifies, died. John the abbot succeeded him, not Marcian, as the Chronicle of Aquileia incorrectly reports. Noris, On the Fifth Synod, chapter 9, section 5.

Candidian, or Candian, as Noris has it, was elected patriarch of Grado with the support of the Exarch, just as the schismatics had elected the patriarch of Aquileia with the support of Agilulf, king of the Lombards. Grado was in the Exarch’s territory, whereas Aquileia belonged to the Lombards. The same author, in the same place; Sigonius.

[Column 0840B] [Note: [Column 0840B] I–II] Sabinian, year 2.

Sabinian died on 2 February, having held office for one year, five months, and four days. The see was vacant for two months and twenty-six days. Baronius and Fleury, who shortened the period of the vacancy, are refuted by Pagi, nos. 3 and 4.

Cyriacus, patriarch of Constantinople, died. The Deacon Baronius also gives the date as 29 October, a Saturday, from the Alexandrian Chronicle. Pagi, no. 3.

Faustus, a monk and disciple of Saint Maurus, returned from Gaul and presented to Boniface in the following year a life of the holy abbot, whose companion he had been, for approval.

[Note: [Column 0840B] II–III] Boniface III, year 1.

BONIFACE III was ordained on 29 January. After holding office for only eight months and twenty-two days, he died on 20 October, not on 10 November as Pagius maintains above, according to a manuscript of the monastery of Saint Vanne at Verdun, which says that he was buried on 12 November of this year, no. 2.

Thomas, the successor of Cyriacus, was ordained at Constantinople on 22 January. The same source, from the Alexandrian Chronicle, above, no. 3.

Saint Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, died this year after holding office for twenty-seven years, not seventeen, as Nicephorus incorrectly states, reckoning from 580. Blanchinus confirms this with Pagius. He died this year, not the following year as Baronius believes; see Pagi, no. 3.

Saint Desiderius, bishop of Vienne, returned from four years of exile and shortly afterward suffered martyrdom by order of Brunhilda. From Fredegar and Aimoin; Pagi under 612, no. 12.

[Column 0840D] [Note: [Column 0840D] III–IV] Boniface IV, year 1.

BONIFACE IV, after an interregnum of ten months and six days, was ordained on 25 August.

During these times Pope Boniface obtained the Pantheon from Phocas. He dedicated it according to Christian rite in honor of the Blessed Virgin Mary and the holy martyrs, on an uncertain day, although the martyrologies assign it to 13 May. Pagi, no. 3; under the same year, Baronius; Sigonius, two years later. Pagius thinks that from this time the feast of All Saints was instituted on the Kalends of November, as it is celebrated today. See the chronological notes under Boniface.

[Note: [Column 0840D] IV and 347 I] Boniface, years 1 and 2.

In the West, ecclesiastical affairs were entirely obscure this year. Baronius.

Theodore the Scrivener, patriarch of Alexandria, was killed; John the Almsgiver succeeded him. From the Alexandrian Chronicle; Pagi, no. 3; Baronius, following year.

Isicius, patriarch of Jerusalem, died after having held office for eight years. Pagi, in the same place and following year, no. 9.

Virgil of Arles died about this time. Florian and Theodosius succeeded him. Pagi, no. 4.

When a sedition broke out at Antioch, the Jews cruelly attacked the Christians. Saint Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, was killed in the tumult. Phocas therefore sent an army and ordered an investigation. Many Jews were condemned and expelled from the city. Miscellanies.

[Note: [Column 0842B] I–II] Boniface IV, years 2 and 3.

A Roman council was held, attended by Mellitus, bishop of London. Two decrees were issued for the English:

1. Those who opposed the monks were restrained.

2. The foundation of the monastery of Dorchester, or Canterbury, was confirmed.

Holstenius, Roman Collection, p. 224; Pagi, no. 10.

Saint Columbanus was sent into exile by Theuderic, king of Burgundy. Mabillon, Benedictine section 2, presents a more accurate text of his Life, written by Jonas, after comparison with manuscripts. Pagi, no. 13.

Thomas, patriarch of Constantinople, died; Sergius succeeded him, at first a very good man, later the head of the Monothelites. Baronius under 608; Nicephorus; Calvisius; Pagi, no. 2.

After Anastasius, patriarch of Antioch, had been murdered, Nicephorus completed the catalogue of its bishops, for those who followed were heretics. Alexandrian Chronicle; Pagi, above, no. 2.

Council of Toledo concerning the primacy of Toledo.

[Note: [Column 0842C] II–III] Boniface IV, years 3 and 4.

The ecclesiastical affairs of the West were obscure this year, as Baronius notes.

Saint Columbanus this year resolved to preach the Gospel among the Slavs. Pagi under 613, no. 5.

This year or the following, when Saint Apollinaris, bishop of Bourges, died, Saint Austregisilus, abbot of Saint-Nicetius, succeeded him. An anonymous writer has comprised his deeds and miracles in three books. Henschen, under 20 May; Mabillon; Pagi, no. 5 and following.

[Note: [Column 0842D] III–IV] Boniface IV, years 4 and 5.

Saint Columbanus came to Italy and, when Agilulf allowed him to choose his place of residence, settled at Milan. Baronius, following year, where Pagi, no. 5. Sigonius adds that, with the king approving in word and writing, Columbanus overthrew the Arians, of whom many still remained.

St Gall, one of the companions of St Columban, fell into a severe fever at the time of their departure for Italy. After recovering from it following St Columban’s [Col. 0844A] departure, he founded a cell in a beautiful forest; after several years, however, he built a very famous monastery beside Lake Constance, which gave distinction to the town of St Gall, in the territories of the Helvetians and Vindelicians. Its abbot today is a Prince of the Empire. From Walfrid; Pagi, note 5, following year.

[Note: [Col. 0844A] IV and 348 I] Boniface IV, 5 and 6.

St Theodore of Syceon died on 22 April; see Henschen and the Byzantine Menologion under that date.

St Columban founded the monastery of Bobbio not far from Pavia, just as he had already [Col. 0844B] founded Luxeuil in France; he died there the following year. Sigonius; Pagi, two years later.

The monastery of Bobbio, whose founder was St Columban and whose first abbot he was, with Saints Attala, Bertulf, and Wandelbert succeeding him, is situated in the Cottian Alps, forty miles from the city of Ticinum, as Paul the Deacon says, book 4, chapter 43, in the diocese of Piacenza. The generosity of Agilulf aided the foundation of this monastery; later kings of the Lombards enlarged it with their donations. Adaloald, and especially Liutprand, became famous for their benefactions.

[Col. 0844C] [Note: [Col. 0844C] I II] Boniface IV, 6 and 7.

About this time St Columban wrote a letter to Boniface IV concerning the Three Chapters; consult no. 7 and following in Pagi, who reports that the holy abbot wrote it from the monastery of Bobbio, at the command of Agilulf, king of the Lombards, to remove the slander by which the pontiff was said to receive heretics, no. 23.

Jerusalem was captured on 26 October. Zacharias the prelate, the Holy Cross, immense booty, and many captives were carried off into Persia. Hence the Jews’ [Col. 0844D] insults against the Christians and their slaughter of them. Baronius and Pagi, no. 38, from the Alexandrian Chronicle. Petavius, however, assigns these events to the following year.

[Note: [Col. 0844D] II III] Boniface IV, 7; Deusdedit, 1.

Boniface IV, after having sat for six years, eight months, and twelve days, died this year on 7 May. After a vacancy of five months and thirteen days, St Deusdedit was appointed in his place on 19 October.

Two councils were held this year. One was the Council of Paris, published by Sirmond after Baronius; fifteen of its canons survive. Pagi, no. 15, perhaps thinks that the council indicated above was meant. The other was the Council of Egara, in the third year of Sisebut. The same author, no. 16. Labbe, above, under this year.

St Columban died in the monastery of Bobbio on 21 November. Baronius and Pagi, no. 14, both drawing on Jonas in Mabillon.

[Note: [Col. 0846A] III IV] Deusdedit, 1 and 2.

After Alexandria was captured by the Persians, John the Almsgiver came to Cyprus, where he died this year. Pagi, no. 6; see the year [Col. 0846B] 620, from no. 3 to 8.

After Zacharias had been taken into captivity, the presbyter Modestus administered the Church of Jerusalem as vicar. From Antiochus the Monk; Baronius and Pagi, from the Anonymous, no. 5.

The beginning of the Monothelite heresy. The same author, no. 6.

Theodelinda built the Basilica of St John the Baptist at Modoetia (Monza), twelve miles above Milan. From that time the Lombards began to invoke St John in all their undertakings. Baronius.

[Note: [Col. 0846B] IV and 149 I] Deusdedit, 2 and 3.

St Eustasius, abbot of Luxeuil, preached first among the Warasci and then among the Boii. [Col. 0846C] Later he was slandered by Agrestius, a monk infected with the schism of the Three Chapters. For this reason the Council of Mâcon is assigned to an uncertain period. Pagi, nos. 4 and 5; Baronius wishes the council to have been held this year.

[Note: [Col. 0846C] I II] Deusdedit, 3 and 4; Boniface V, 1.

After occupying the see for three years and twenty days, counting from 19 October 615, Deusdedit died this year on 7 November and was buried on the 8th, as Anastasius and the Martyrology correctly corrected by Baronius show. Boniface V was appointed in his place after an interregnum of one month and sixteen days and was ordained on 24 December.

[Col. 0846D] The Second Council of Seville, against the Acephali. Baronius, following year.

Sigonius and others maintain that John V was appointed this year in succession to John IV, bishop of Ravenna. Rubeus, however, and with him Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. 2, hold that John IV, surnamed Classianus, had occupied the see from the year of his election, 606, until 630, and that the admission of two Johns is incorrect. See Bacchin, *Chronological Dissertation on Peter of Senigallia*, chapter 6.

[Note: [Col. 0846D] II III] Boniface V, 1 and 2.

At the beginning of this year, or near the end of the preceding one, Eadbald, king of Kent, who in the lifetime of his father St Ethelbert had refused to accept the faith, was converted through the work of St Laurence, bishop of Canterbury, who died this year, as the Chronicle of Sigebert records from Cotselin. Pagi, no. 5, above. Therefore Mellitus and Justus returned after a year, having gone to Gaul. Bede, book 2, chapter 6; Baronius; Pagi, no. 3.

Mellitus, who succeeded Laurence, and Justus, bishop of Rochester, governing the Church of the English with great diligence, received an exhortatory letter from Pope Boniface. Bede, book 2, chapter 7.

[Col. 0848B] [Note: [Col. 0848B] III IV] Boniface V, 2 and 3.

St Anastasius the Persian, who, drawn by love of the Christian faith, had already withdrawn from the army, became a Christian at Jerusalem this year and embraced the monastic life. Herman and Sigebert in their Chronicles; Pagi, following year, with Baronius, no. 7. There Petavius had assigned the martyrdom of this saint to 622; on the authority of Bollandus, Pagi restored it to 628.

[Col. 0848C] [Note: [Col. 0848C] IV and 350 I] Boniface V, 3 and 4.

The monk Agrestius of Luxeuil, having left Abbot Eustasius, came to Aquileia. Finding that church in dissension from the Roman Church because of the Three Chapters, he acted as its defender in that dispute and wrote a poisonous letter on the subject through Aurio, the notary of King Adaloald, to Attala, abbot of Bobbio. [Col. 0848D] From Bede and Sigonius. Baronius, year 618. Noris, *On the Synod* V.

[Note: [Col. 0848D] I II, Hegira year 1, evening of the fifteenth day, beginning on the sixth day of the week of the Jews] Boniface V, 4 and 5.

When Heraclius entered the borders of Armenia, Paul the One-Eyed, otherwise Severianus, came to meet him; he professed Monothelitism. Therefore the emperor appears to have been deceived from that time onward. Pagi, no. 3.

Muhammad, the false prophet, fled from the city of Mecca out of fear of his enemies. From this arose the beginning of the Hegira, or the era of the Arabs, which consists solely of lunar years—namely, twelve [Col. 0850A] lunar months, which they call Muharram, Safar, the first Rabiʿ, the latter Rabiʿ, the first Jumada, the latter Jumada, Rajab, Shaʿban, Ramadan, Shawwal (or Xavel), Dhu al-Qaʿdah (Silcade), and Dhu al-Hijjah (Zilitsche). The odd-numbered months—1, 3, 5, 7, 9, and 11—have thirty days; the even-numbered months have twenty-nine. The Hegira begins on the evening of 15 July, when the sixth day of the Jewish week begins. Calvisius.

[Note: [Col. 0850A] II III, Hegira 2, 15 July, third day of the week] Boniface V, 3 and 6.

Two letters of Boniface to Edwin, king of the Northumbrians, and to his wife Ethelburg, which [Col. 0850B] Bede recites in *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, book 2, chapter 10 and following, were written this year or the next. In them the pontiff says that he had heard that Ethelburg, who shortly before had embraced the Catholic faith, had been betrothed to Edwin, king of the Northumbrians, provided nevertheless that he left both his wife and her retinue free to practise their religion. Pagius incorrectly assigns this to the year 625. See the chronological notes on Boniface.

[Note: [Col. 0850B] III IV, Hegira 3, 24 July, eleventh day of the week] Boniface V, 6.

Boniface V, after having sat from the day of his ordination, 24 December 618, for five years and ten months, died this year on 24 October [Col. 0850C] and was buried on the following day. Pagius incorrectly postpones this to the following year because of the ordination of Paulinus as bishop of York. See the chronological notes on Boniface V.

Mellitus, archbishop of Canterbury, died on 24 April, and Justus, bishop of Rochester, succeeded him. As soon as he had received the pallium and authority to ordain bishops from Pope Boniface, he ordained Romanus bishop of Rochester. Bede, book 2, chapter 8.

[Note: [Col. 0850C] IV and 351 I, Hegira 4, 13 June, fifth day of the week] Year 1 of Honorius.

The fact that the Apostolic See was vacant for more than thirteen days after Boniface, as the manuscripts and catalogues state, is also taught by the calculation itself [Col. 0850D] and by Heraclius’ absence from Constantinople. It is therefore more probable that it was vacant for one year and three days, so that Honorius was ordained on 27 October this year. See the notes on Honorius.

Justus, archbishop of Canterbury, ordained Paulinus bishop for the Northumbrian people on 21 July, that is, the twelfth day before the Kalends of August. Paulinus proceeded to York in the retinue of Ethelburg, the wife of Edwin, their king, and after Edwin had been baptized two years later, he made that city an episcopal see. Bede, book 2, chapter 9.

[Note: [Col. 0850D] I II, Hegira 5, 2 June, second day of the week] Honorius, 1 and 2.

The besieged city of Constantinople was freed by the protection of the Blessed Virgin Mary, according to the Alexandrian Chronicle.

The pseudo-synod of Constantinople, where [Col. 0852A] the question between Cyrus, bishop of Phasis, and Sergius the patriarch—whether there was one will or two, concerning which Heraclius, while staying in Colchis, consulted Cyrus—was resolved in favor of one will. *Synodal Libellus*.

[Col. 0852B] [Note: [Col. 0852B] II III, Hegira 6, 22 May, sixth day of the week] Honorius, 2 and 3.

By a Novella issued on the Kalends of May, Heraclius decreed that the clergy of Constantinople, especially that of St Mary at Blachernae, should be reduced in number. From book 2, canon; Pagi, final note.

Edwin, king of the Northumbrians, was baptized at York on Holy Easter Day, 12 April. He gave that city to his teacher and bishop Paulinus, who made it an episcopal see and converted many thousands by preaching for six years. Bede, book 2, chapter 14.

St Eustasius, abbot of Luxeuil, died on 29 April, and St Attala, abbot of Bobbio, on 10 March. Mabillon, section 2 of the Benedictine *Annals*; Bollandus.

[Col. 0852C] [Note: [Col. 0852C] III IV, Hegira 7, 11 May, fourth day of the week] Honorius, 2 and 3.

St Anastasius the Persian was strangled by Khosrow together with seventy companions because he refused to abandon the Catholic faith. Bollandus, 22 January. His bones, afterward shining with miracles, were brought to Rome and kept their place at the Salvian Waters. Sigonius, year 620.

Asterius, a Roman by birth, succeeded Deusdedit in the see of the Church of Milan. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, and Sigonius.

Carpuald, or Herpenwald, was the first king of the East Angles to be baptized, and was killed in the same year. His successor Sigebert, however, did not begin to reign until three years later; then Bishop Felix immediately devoted himself to preaching to the English. From Bede. Pagi, no. 25, above.

[Note: [Col. 0852D] IV and 352 I, Hegira 8, 30 April, first day of the week] Honorius, 4 and 5.

Baronius places in this year the meeting of Heraclius with Athanasius, patriarch of the Jacobites, and consequently the beginnings of Monothelitism. Pagius considers the event fictitious and instead identifies the following certain stages of Monothelitism: first, Heraclius’ meeting with Paul the One-Eyed, Severianus, in 622; second, Heraclius’ instruction to Cyrus, while residing in Lazica in 626, to consult Sergius [Col. 0854A] and so forth, and Cyrus’ use of testimonies from a libellus falsely attributed to Menas to teach that one will must be maintained; third, Sergius’ letter to Honorius in 634, which shows that from 633 certain decisions had been made by Cyrus, then bishop of Alexandria, in the Alexandrian Council. Pagi, no. 4.

[Note: [Col. 0854A] I II, Hegira 9, 20 April, sixth day of the week] Honorius, 5 and 6.

After George, patriarch of Alexandria, died, Cyrus was chosen as his successor and transferred there from Phasis.

Around this time the Croats, [Col. 0854B] also called Chrobati, came into Dalmatia and accepted the Christian faith. Pagi, no. 14.

Bonus succeeded John as patriarch of Ravenna. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, and Sigonius.

After Cyprian, patriarch of Grado, died, the Arian Fortunatus seized the see. Pope Honorius deposed him and appointed Primogenius, apocrisiary of the Roman Church. On this matter letters of Honorius to the bishops of Venetia and Istria survive in Baronius and Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. 5. Sigonius wrongly makes the usurper Fortunatus the legitimate bishop in 622.

[Note: [Col. 0854B] II III, Hegira 10, 9 April, third day of the week] Honorius, 6 and 7.

This year the Scots celebrated Holy Easter on 21 April, whereas the Romans celebrated it on 24 [Col. 0854C] March. Usserius. Bede, book 3, chapter 19, reports that Pope Honorius refuted among the Scots this error of the Quartodecimans.

[Note: [Col. 0854C] III IV, Hegira 11, 28 March, seventh day of the week] Honorius, 7 and 8.

Justus, archbishop of Canterbury, died on 10 November, the fourth day before the Ides. Honorius succeeded him; Pope Honorius sent him the pallium, just as a papal letter to Paulinus of York also survives in Bede, book 2, chapters 17 and 18.

[Col. 0854D] [Note: [Col. 0854D] IV and 353 I, Hegira 12, 18 March, fifth day of the week] Honorius, 8 and 9.

Cyrus, patriarch of Alexandria, confirmed Monothelitism in a pseudo-synod on 4 May. From St Maximus’ *Disputation*.

After Edwin was killed while fighting for the faith against Cadwallon, king of the Britons, Ethelburg returned to Kent to Eadbald, the king, and died there in holiness in 647. Bede, *Epitome*; Baronius; Pagi, no. 23. Paulinus returned with her and, finding the church of Rochester without a pastor, undertook its governance at the urging of the king and Archbishop Honorius; he died there.

The Fourth National Council of Toledo, [Col. 0856A] with seventy bishops, presided over by the senior bishop St Isidore.

[Note: [Col. 0856A] I II, Hegira 13, 7 March, second day of the week] Honorius, 9 and 10.

This year, or toward the end of the preceding one, after the death of Modestus, bishop of Jerusalem, Sophronius succeeded him. His celebrated *Encyclical* survives, sent according to custom from the Council of Palestine to the patriarchs, bearing witness to two wills and two operations in Christ; it was later read at the Sixth Council, session 2.

The letters of Sergius to Honorius and of Honorius to Sergius belong to this year. Concerning Honorius’ *Economic Letter*, [Col. 0856B] which, by indulging Monothelitism too much, appeared to support it and therefore brought condemnation upon him at the Sixth Council, see the notes on Martin and Agatho.

[Note: [Col. 0856B] II III, Hegira 14, 25 February, seventh day of the week] Honorius, 10 and 11.

While Birinus, assigned to no particular see, was preaching, the West Saxons became Christians. Their king, Cynigils, was received from the baptismal font by King Oswald, who took Cynigils’ daughter as his wife. Later the city of Dorchester was given to Birinus so that he might establish his see there. Bede, book 3, chapter 7.

[Note: [Col. 0856C] III IV, Hegira 15, 13 February, fourth day of the week] Honorius, 11 and 12.

The Fifth Provincial Council of Toledo was held, presided over by Eugene II, bishop of Toledo.

St Isidore of Seville, after having occupied the see for thirty-seven years, died on 4 April. Bollandus, under that date.

[Note: [Col. 0856C] IV and 354 I, Hegira 16, 2 February, first day of the week] Honorius, 12 and 13.

St Sophronius, bishop of Jerusalem, who had succeeded Modestus in 634, died while the Monothelites were disturbing the Church with increasing violence. Martyrology, 11 March. Bollandus gives more details there.

[Col. 0856D] [Note: [Col. 0856D] I II, Hegira 17, 23 January, sixth day of the week] Honorius, 13.

Honorius, after occupying the see for twelve years, eleven months, and sixteen days from 27 October 625, died this year—or was buried at St Peter’s—on 12 October. His death was followed by an exceptionally long interregnum of one year, seven months, and seventeen days. The apocrisarii were not given the prince’s order until they promised that they would ask the [Col. 0858A] elected man to subscribe to the *Ecthesis*.

Sergius published the *Ecthesis* in the name of Heraclius, held a pseudo-synod, and died in December after having sat for twenty-eight years, seven months, and twenty-one days. *Concilium Lateranense Secretum*, book 3. Pagi, no. 2 and following, under no. 8.

The Sixth Council of Toledo, with fifty-two bishops and representatives of the absent bishops, presided over by the senior bishop Selva of Narbonne, was held on 9 January.

[Note: [Col. 0858A] II III, Hegira 18, 12 January, third day of the week; Hegira 19, 31 December, sixth day of the week] The Apostolic See is vacant, although Severinus has already been elected.

After approximately a month, [Col. 0858B] Pyrrhus was elected patriarch of Constantinople in Sergius’ place and immediately held a pseudo-synod in which he confirmed the decrees of Sergius and Cyrus. *Synodal Libellus*. Pagi, no. 9. Sigonius, under the preceding year.

Sirmond, in his *Synopsis* of the collection of Anastasius, wishes the *Ecthesis* to have been published under Heraclius this year.

[Note: [Col. 0858B] III IV, Hegira 20, 21 December, fifth day of the week] Severinus and John IV, 1.

After a long vacancy, Severinus was ordained on 28 May. He condemned the Monothelites, as is clear from the *Papal Formularies* (*Diurnum Pontificum*), chapter 3, title 6, in a synod—as Baronius thinks—by a decree, as Carnerius holds.

After Severinus died two months and four [Col. 0858C] days later, on 2 August, the see was vacant for four months and twenty-four days. On 24 December his successor John IV was ordained. Before his ordination he had answered the Scots’ question concerning Easter. Bede, book 2, chapter 19; Baronius, above, under this year; Pagi, no. 7.

St Maximus the Monk composed the Ecclesiastical Computus, or a brief explanation of the Christian Easter, which survives in the Paduan Chronology.

Cyrus of Alexandria, having been summoned to Constantinople and accused of treason, was deposed.

[Note: [Col. 0858C] IV and 355 I, Hegira 21, 10 December, second day of the week] John IV, 1 and 2.

A Roman council against the Monothelites was held. In it John condemned their doctrines but spared the persons, as the learned Pagius says, [Col. 0858D] no. 3, above, and sent the decrees to the emperors. He also wrote an apology for Honorius to the emperor Constantine; after Constantine’s death, Constans replied to it. Collection of Anastasius in Sirmond.

Pyrrhus, yielding to a popular uprising, abdicated and sailed to Chalcedon. Paul was appointed in his place. Nicephorus, Baronius, and Sigonius assign this to the following year; see Pagi, no. 2.

[Col. 0860A] [Note: [Col. 0860A] II, Hegira 22, 30 November, seventh day of the week] After John IV was buried on 12 October, having occupied the see for one year, nine months, and eighteen days from 24 December 640, as Anastasius establishes, he was followed after thirty-three days by the ordination of Theodore on 24 November. This was done without awaiting the prince’s command at Constantinople, for during this period the authority had been delegated to the exarch of Ravenna, as is evident from the *Papal Formularies* published by Garnerius.

St Sulpitius, bishop of Bourges, died as the successor of St Austregisilus. Bollandus, 17 January.

[Note: [Col. 0860B] II III, Hegira 23, 19 November, fourth day of the week] Theodore, 1 and 2.

The privilege granted this year to Bobulenus, abbot of Bobbio, by Theodore. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. 5, p. 329.

Mauritius the chartularius, who had plundered the Lateran Patriarchate in 639 with Isaac the exarch, aspiring this year to imperial rule in Italy, was beheaded by order of the exarch. The exarch himself died at Ravenna.

A synodal letter of the bishops of Cyprus to Theodore, in which they accuse Paul of Constantinople of Monothelitism. *Concilium Lateranense Secretum*, book 2.

[Note: [Col. 0860C] III IV, Hegira 24, 7 November, first day of the week] Theodore, 2 and 3.

St Paulinus, formerly bishop of York and later bishop of Rochester, died on 10 October; Ithamar succeeded him. Bede, book 3, chapter 14.

[Note: [Col. 0860C] IV and 356 I, Hegira 25, 28 October, sixth day of the week] Theodore, 3 and 4.

A famous disputation in Africa took place between Pyrrhus, patriarch of Constantinople, and St Maximus the abbot, before the prefect and many bishops. Pyrrhus was defeated and recanted his former position. Later, coming to Rome, he offered Theodore [Col. 0860D] a *Libellus of the Catholic Faith* and was therefore received into the Church. Collection of Anastasius, and Sirmond there.

Theodore, 4 and 5.

[Note: [Col. 0860D] II, Hegira 26, 17 October, third day of the week] Paul of Constantinople, previously praised by Theodore for a cleverly composed letter, finally declared himself a Monothelite this year; therefore the pontiff began proceedings to depose him. Collection of Anastasius. Pagi, no. 3.

The four African primates of Byzacena, Numidia, Mauretania, and Proconsular Africa each convened a synod in his own province to confirm the Catholic doctrines which they had seen St Maximus the Monk defend so vigorously in the preceding year. The brothers Theodore and Euprepius, captured in Africa for the sake of the [Col. 0862A] faith, were sent into exile at Cherson. Sirmond.

The Seventh Council of Toledo, with thirty-eight bishops, was held on 18 October, presided over by Orontius, senior bishop of Mérida.

[Note: [Col. 0862A] II III, Hegira 27, 6 October, seventh day of the week] Theodore, 5 and 6.

St Amandus became bishop of Utrecht; after three years, however, he resigned the dignity, shaking the dust from his feet because of the depravity of the priests. Henschen, 6 February, preliminary commentary, no. 87.

Pyrrhus went from Rome to Ravenna, hoping that he could return to his see if he supported the Monothelites, but he returned to his former error. Therefore, in the synod held the following year, the pontiff not only separated him from the communion of the Church but also deposed him from the episcopal dignity, signing the judgment with a pen sprinkled with the blood of Christ. Theophanes.

[Note: [Col. 0862B] III IV, Hegira 28, 25 September, fifth day of the week] Theodore, 6 and 7.

After extremely affectionate letters and services had been ineffectually offered by his apocrisarii, Theodore condemned Paul as well, Pyrrhus already having been condemned in a synod. He condemned both before news of the publication of the *Typos* reached Rome. Anastasius in Martin.

Maurus, formerly steward of the Church of Ravenna, became the successor of Bonus, who died this year, in the Ravennate see. He is said to have been rebellious toward the Roman pontiff throughout his life. Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. 2.

[Note: [Col. 0862C] IV and 357 I, Hegira 29, 14 September, second day of the week] Theodore, 7; Martin, 1.

Theodore, after occupying the see for six years, five months, and eighteen days from 24 November 642, died on 13 May. After an interregnum of fifty-two days, Martin was ordained on 5 July. Not at all frightened by the emperor’s threats, he immediately convoked the Lateran Council, which began on 3 October. One hundred and five bishops assembled there and condemned Sergius, Cyrus, Pyrrhus, and Paul, as well as the *Typos*, full of impiety and audacity. Hence the emperor’s hatred burst into flame.

[Col. 0862D] He sent the acts of the synod throughout the West and East, especially to the Frankish kings Clovis and Sigebert. Baronius; Pagi, no. 6.

[Note: [Col. 0862D] I II, Hegira 30, 3 September, sixth day of the week] Martin, 1 and 2.

Agilbert, a Gaul by nationality, became bishop of the West Saxons and occupied the second see at Dorchester, where St Birinus had first sat. This was done at the command of King Cenwalh, who, rejecting the piety of his father Cynegils, whom he had succeeded around 642, was expelled from the kingdom for that reason. During three years of exile, under Anna, king of the East Angles, he acknowledged the faith and returned to the kingdom this year. Bede, book 3, chapters 2 and 7.

Since the exhortation of St Martin had moved St Amandus not at all, and he had resigned, St Remaclus succeeded him [Col. 0864A] in the bishopric of Utrecht. From Milon. Pagi, no. 15.

[Note: [Col. 0864A] II III, Hegira 31, 24 August, fourth day of the week] Martin, 2 and 3.

Monasteries were founded in Austrasia by King Sigebert, above all Malmedy in the diocese of Cologne and Stavelot, or Stabulaus, in the diocese of Utrecht. St Remaclus became abbot of both. Chronicle of Sigebert. Pagi, no. 9.

[Note: [Col. 0864A] III IV, Hegira 32, 12 August, first day of the week] Martin, 3 and 4.

St Emmerammus, bishop of Poitiers, went down into Bavaria [Col. 0864B] to preach the Gospel there and became a martyr. Baronius, Appendix to volume 9.

The holy virgin Etheldreda, daughter of Anna, king of the East Angles, was compelled to marry Tombert, prince of the Gyrvii, but remained a virgin after the marriage. From Thomas of Ely in Mabillon, section 2 of the Benedictine *Annals*. Pagi, year 660, no. 12.

[Note: [Col. 0864B] IV and 358 I, Hegira 33, 2 August, sixth day of the week] Martin, 4 and 5.

St Martin was impiously captured at the command of Constans, when Theodore Calliopas, the exarch, burst into the Lateran basilica with soldiers. [Col. 0864C] He was taken from Rome, placed on a ship, and reached Messina, then the island of Naxos, in September; there he remained for the entire year. Martin, letter 15.

St Maximus the abbot and his disciple Anastasius of Constantinople were taken away this year and tormented for ten years. Pagi, year 657, no. 8.

The Eighth National Council of Toledo was held with fifty-two bishops, presided over by Orontius, metropolitan of Mérida, as the senior among the others.

[Col. 0864D] [Note: [Col. 0864D] I II, Hegira 34, 22 July, third day of the week] Martin, 5 and 6; Eugene, 1.

After remaining for a year on the island of Naxos, St Martin reached Constantinople in September this year. When his case became known, he was sent to prison like an innocent lamb. Collection of Anastasius.

While St Martin was still staying on the island of Naxos, the clergy and people secretly chose Eugene, so that the emperor would not obstruct them, Martin probably having resigned. Nevertheless, I follow Eugene’s years down to Martin’s death. See the notes on pages 49 and 65. Eugene sent the customary apocrisarii with a synodical letter to Constans. Collection of Anastasius; those same men afterward adhered to Monothelitism. There.

[Col. 0866A] Paul, patriarch of Constantinople, died after having occupied the see for approximately thirteen years.

Deusdedit succeeded Honorius as bishop of Canterbury on 12 December. Bede.

[Note: [Col. 0866A] II III, Hegira 35, 11 July, seventh day of the week] Martin, 6 and 7; Eugene, 1 and 2.

St Martin was led out of prison and deported to Cherson, where, after suffering many hardships, he died on 16 September, after four months. Anastasius, Collection. He was buried at Blachernae. *Hypomnesticon* in the Collection of Anastasius.

The Ninth Council of Toledo was held as a provincial council with sixteen bishops.

The first disputation of St Maximus, called a conference with the authorities in the [Col. 0866B] *secretarium*, took place. After it he was sent into exile at Byzia in the province of Thrace, and his disciple Anastasius to Perberis. Collection of Anastasius. Pagi with Baronius, year 657, no. 2 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0866B] III IV, Hegira 36, 30 June, fifth day of the week] Eugene, 2 and 3.

The second disputation of St Maximus with Theodore, bishop of Caesarea in Bithynia, and with the two consuls, Paul and Theodore of Byzia, occurred at the place of exile on 24 August. Afterward he was recalled to Constantinople and thrown into prison. Baronius and Pagi.

The Tenth National Council of Toledo was held with twenty-one bishops, presided over by Eugene III, metropolitan of Toledo. It established especially that 18 December should be celebrated throughout Spain as the feast of the Expectation of [Col. 0866C] the Blessed Virgin Mary’s childbirth.

[Note: [Col. 0866C] IV and 359 I, Hegira 37, 19 June, second day of the week] Eugene, 3; Vitalian, 1.

Eugene, after having occupied the see for two years, nine months, and twenty-four days—partly while Martin was alive and partly after his death, namely from 10 August 654—died on 2 June this year. After an interregnum of one month and twenty-eight days, his successor St Vitalian was ordained on 30 July.

After Eugene III had died and been buried [Col. 0866D] at St Leocadia, St Ildefonsus succeeded him, famous for an apparition of the Blessed Virgin Mary and for the gift of a sacred garment. Ildefonsus, *On Illustrious Men* III. Pagi, nos. 10 and 11. Baronius at length under this year.

[Note: [Col. 0866D] I II, Hegira 38, 8 June, sixth day of the week] Vitalian, 1 and 2.

St Dalphinus, also called Annemundus, bishop of Lyons, suffered martyrdom at the command of Bathilda, who governed the child Chlothar III. St Wilfrid, later bishop of York, who, returning from Rome in the third year, had been detained through friendship with and devotion to the holy bishop, wishing to die with him, returned to England. Bede, book 5, chapter 20. Pagi, no. 7.

[Col. 0868A] [Note: [Col. 0868A] II III, Hegira 39, 29 May, fourth day of the week] Vitalian, 2 and 3.

John, surnamed Bonus, bishop of Milan, whom Baronius reports as having been harassed by the Arian Lombards, perhaps died this year on 2 January. Martyrology. Pagi, no. 7, from the catalogue in Mabillon, where he is now found from manuscripts of the Capitular Library of Milan, *Scriptors of Italy*, vol. 1, part 2, p. 228. By assigning ten years to John, this shows that he began in early 649, since he took part in the Lateran Council, as the same Pagi notes.

[Col. 0868B] [Note: [Col. 0868B] III IV, Hegira 40, 17 May, first day of the week] Vitalian, 3 and 4.

St Remaclus, who had succeeded St Amandus, after his resignation, in the bishopric of Utrecht in 650, himself resigned this year, obtaining that St Theodore should become his successor. Pagi, no. 8 and following.

The holy virgin Etheldreda, who had married Tombert in 652, was given, after his death, as wife to King Ecgfrith, son of Oswiu, king of Northumbria. She always preserved her virginity and finally obtained from Ecgfrith permission to enter the monastery she had founded. Pagi, no. 13.

This year or the following, the kingdom of the West Saxons, which had possessed only one ecclesiastical province, [Col. 0868C] began to have two, with two bishops established there.

[Note: [Col. 0868C] IV and 360 I, Hegira 41, 6 May, fifth day of the week] Vitalian, 4 and 5.

In the kingdom of Northumbria, St Finan, bishop of Lindisfarne, died after occupying the see for ten years. St Colman succeeded him; through his preaching a large part of the kingdom of the Mercians was converted, together with their prince Peada, son of the great persecutor Penda. Bede, book 3, chapter 26. Pagi, no. 8.

St Gertrude, the first abbess of Nivelles, died on 17 March. Baronius, year 664, there; Pagi, no. 21 and following.

[Col. 0868D] [Note: [Col. 0868D] I II, Hegira 42, 26 April, third day of the week] Vitalian, 5 and 6.

St Maximus the abbot, famous for his disputations against the Monothelites, of whom we have often spoken, and his disciple Anastasius, after suffering ten years of tribulation and three exiles, passed this year to heavenly life. St Maximus died on 13 August, as he had foretold fifteen days earlier. St Anastasius had preceded him on 24 July. *Hypomnesticon* in the Collection of Anastasius.

[Col. 0870A] [Note: [Col. 0870A] II III, Hegira 43, 15 April, seventh day of the week] Vitalian, 6 and 7.

The pontiff went out to meet the emperor and addressed him, although he was contaminated by so many crimes and unworthy of such treatment. He led him into the basilicas and treated him with the greatest moderation and humanity during the twelve days he stayed in Rome, earnestly desiring that the East, divided from the West by a long schism, might be bound with it by Catholic communion. Baronius, together with Anastasius, who says that the emperor came as an orthodox man but afterward, after the sacred buildings had been plundered in barbarous fashion, departed for Sicily on the seventh indiction—that is, after September. [Col. 0870B] The same account from the *Life of St Barbatus* and Cangius, *On the Byzantine Family*.

[Note: [Col. 0870B] III IV, Hegira 44, 4 April, fifth day of the week] Vitalian, 7 and 8.

At the Pharense council in England, the Scots were defeated in the Easter dispute by the English who adhered to the Roman Church. Bucher defends the Scots, assigning the blame to Victor’s cycle. Baronius and Pagi, from Bede, book 3, chapter 26. For, as Baronius observes, during this period the discipline of the clergy and monks flourished greatly in England.

Archbishop Deusdedit, who had succeeded Honorius in the see of Canterbury in 654 as its sixth bishop, died this year. He had occupied the see for nine years, seven months, and two days. Bede, book 4, chapter 1. Theodore succeeded him. Pagi, no. 10; see the year 668.

[Col. 0870C] St Wilfrid and Ceadda were appointed bishops of the Northumbrians. Bede, *Epitome*.

[Note: [Col. 0870C] IV and 361 I, Hegira 45, 24 March, second day of the week] Vitalian, 8 and 9.

St Wilfrid, mentioned above, bishop of York, went to Gaul to be ordained there. He did not immediately return to England, however; therefore Oswiu ordered Ceadda to become bishop of York. According to Bede, book 5, chapter 20, Ceadda occupied the see for three years. Pagius argues that Ceadda was ordained in the following year, no. 16 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0870C] I II, Hegira 46, 13 March, sixth day of the week] Vitalian, 9 and 10.

Peter, patriarch of Constantinople, died as a Monothelite; Thomas, an orthodox man, succeeded him. Pagi, year 656, [Col. 0870D] nos. 5 and 6. Baronius, the preceding year.

The Synod of Mérida was held on 6 November, in the eighteenth year of Recceswinth, in the era 704, which are the chronological characters of this year.

[Note: [Col. 0870D] II III, Hegira 47, 2 March, third day of the week] Vitalian, 10 and 11.

St Ildefonsus, who in 657 had succeeded Eugene III in the see of Toledo, died on 23 January, the tenth day before the Kalends of February, after occupying the see for nine years. Julian, *On Illustrious Men*. Quiricus succeeded him. Bollandus and the Main Life of St Ildefonsus.

John, bishop of Lappa, a suffragan of the archbishop of Crete, appealed to the Holy See and was absolved. Baronius.

[Col. 0872A] [Note: [Col. 0872A] III IV, Hegira 48, 19 February, seventh day of the week] Vitalian, 11 and 12.

Thomas, bishop of Constantinople, died, and John succeeded him. Baronius, year 658 and there; Pagi, no. 1.

St Wilfrid, having returned to Gaul, ordained priests and deacons in the kingdom of Kent. For he was the first bishop of the English people to introduce the Catholic manner of life into the churches, as Bede records, book 4, chapter 2. Theodore, bishop of Canterbury, had not yet come to England, since Vitalian ordained him on 26 March, the seventh day before the Kalends, this year, on Sunday, and sent him to England [Col. 0872B] with letters of recommendation. Bede, book 4, chapter 1. Hence the years of St Wilfrid are not counted from 665, as Pagius wishes. For in the year of his expulsion, 678, he counted ten years, as the same author testifies in the Roman Council of 679.

[Note: [Col. 0872B] IV and 362 I, Hegira 49, 8 February, fifth day of the week] Vitalian, 12 and 13.

Theodore, the bishop of Canterbury ordained at Rome in the preceding year, arrived at his church on Sunday, 27 May, in the second year of his ordination. He governed it for twenty-one years, three months, and twenty-six days, until 22 September 690. Meanwhile, in accordance with the authority granted him by Vitalian, he visited all England. Finding Ceadda illegitimately ordained in the see of York, he canonically ordained him and entrusted another church to him, while St Wilfrid administered York. [Col. 0872C] After Theodore’s arrival, Wilfrid did not exceed the limits of his primacy. Bede, book 4, chapter 2, and book 5, chapter 20.

[Note: [Col. 0872C] I II, Hegira 50, 28 January, second day of the week] Vitalian, 13 and 14.

During this period the English Church flourished greatly, especially through kings and bishops worthy of praise. Baronius and Pagi, no. 4. A large part of England, however, was afflicted by the Quartodeciman heresy. Bede, book 4, chapter 5.

St Leodegarius, counsellor of Childeric, king of the Franks, was torn away from the king through the envy of his rivals and banished to the monastery of Luxeuil, where he spent his days in holiness. Pagi, nos. 10 and 11, year 668.

[Col. 0872D] [Note: [Col. 0872D] II III, Hegira 51, 18 January, seventh day of the week] Vitalian, 14 and 15.

During this period the Gallican Church was being ruined by internal wars. For the dissolution of morals, the collapse of ecclesiastical discipline, and the introduction of idolatry and heresy followed those wars. Eastern Gaul in particular suffered the greatest damage; it was remedied in the eighth century in the time of Carloman. Pagi, nos. 7 and 8.

The death of St Erembert preceded this unhappy age. Having been a monk of Fontenelle under St Wandrille, he became bishop of Toulouse and had again withdrawn to the monastery, where, worn out by old age, he died. The same author, no. 4.

[Note: [Col. 0874A] III IV, Hegira 52, 7 January, fourth day of the week] Vitalian, 15; Adeodatus, 1.

When St Vitalian died on 27 or 29 January, after occupying the see for fourteen years, six months, and one or two days fewer, Adeodatus succeeded him. After an interregnum of two months and thirteen or fourteen days, Adeodatus was ordained in April this year. See the notes on Vitalian.

[Note: [Col. 0874A] Hegira 53, 27 December, second day of the week] Ceadda, bishop of Lindisfarne, died after occupying the see for two years and six months. [Col. 0874B] Bede, book 4, chapter 3. St Etheldreda, who in 660 had entered a second marriage as a virgin, became a nun after obtaining permission from her husband, King Ecgfrith, and was instructed by St Wilfrid. Pagi, no. 8.

[Note: [Col. 0874B] IV and 363 I, Hegira 54, 16 December, sixth day of the week] Adeodatus, 1 and 2.

Theodore, bishop of Canterbury, held the Council of Hertford and settled ten matters concerning ecclesiastical discipline. Baronius, from Bede, under the preceding year; Bede’s *Epitome* under this year. Pagius shows that the council was falsely marked as belonging to the first indiction and assigns it to 24 September, when the second—namely, the Constantinopolitan—indiction began; he likewise demonstrates, with Bede’s *On the Reckoning of Time*, no. 4 above, that this indiction was in use among the English.

The exile of St Leodegarius and the killing of the holy bishop Prajectus of Auvergne, assigned to this year by Pagi, nos. 4 and 5, show the difference between the Gallican Church and the English and Spanish Churches, which at this time especially honored the Sacred Canons and the dignities of the Church.

Adeodatus, 2 and 3.

[Note: [Col. 0874C] II, Hegira 55, 6 December, fourth day of the week] The Venerable Bede was born this year, according to his own testimony, in which he states that he became a deacon at the age of nineteen. Pagi, year 693, no. 8.

Around this year John, bishop of Constantinople, died after occupying the see, according to Nicephorus, for five years and nine months. Constantine, a deacon of the same church, keeper of the vessels and steward, succeeded him. Pagi, year 664, with Baronius, no. 2.

St Benedict Biscop, greatly loved by Ecgfrith, returned to England two years earlier and founded the monastery of Wearmouth. [Note: [Col. 0874D] II III, Hegira 56, 25 November, first day of the week] Pagi, no. 23.

Adeodatus, 3 and 4.

The Eleventh Council of Toledo was held on 7 September, the seventh day before the Ides, with seventeen bishops, presided over by Quiricus, bishop of Toledo. The Hispanic authors report that in it they defined the division of the parishes of Spain, which Baronius thinks was made in a general council that has perished. Pagius also assigns to this year the Council of Mérida, whose date is uncertain, no. 3.

St. Audoin, together with many pious and venerable companions, came to the threshold of the Apostles. Fridegod, in the *Life of St. Audoin, Bishop of Rouen*. Pagi, under the year 672, with Baronius, no. 2.

[Note: [Col. 0876A] III IV Hegira 57, 13 November, feria 5] Adeodatus 4 and 5. Donus 1.

Adeodatus, after having occupied the see for four years, two months, and five days, from 11 April 672, died this year on 17 June. Donus was given as his successor; after an interpontificate of four months and fifteen days, he was ordained on 2 November.

Constantine, Bishop of Constantinople, died after having occupied the see for one year, eight months, and seven days. He was succeeded by Theodore, presbyter, Syncellus, and Keeper of the Vessels, a most wicked Monothelite, who occupied the see for two years and three months, according to Nicephorus. Pagi, under the year 666, no. 2, with Baronius.

[Note: [Col. 0876B] IV et 64 I Hegira 58, 3 November, feria 3] Donus 1 and 2.

Theodore of Constantinople and Macarius, Bishop of Antioch, moved every stone with the Emperor so that the name of Vitalian, which was the only name read after Honorius in the sacred diptychs, might be erased from them. The Emperor, overcome by their earnest entreaties, appeared to connive at this. Baronius; Pagi, no. 2 and following.

[Col. 0876C] [Note: [Col. 0876C] I II Hegira 59, 23 October, feria 7] Donus 2 and 3.

Theodore was expelled from the see of Constantinople by the Emperor for an uncertain reason, and George was substituted in his place. Baronius; Pagi, no. 5.

St. Wilfrid was deposed from the see of York by King Ecgfrith, and two bishops were appointed in his place: Bosa to the see of Lindisfarne and Eata to that of York. At the beginning of winter he reached Frisia, which he enlightened by preaching the holy Gospel; afterward he went to Rome. Bede, book 4, chapter 11. Pagi postpones this to the following year; see the notes under Donus.

St. Leodegarius was killed at Ebroin’s command. From the anonymous author, Pagi, no. 22 under this year and under 685, with Baronius, no. 9.

[Col. 0876D] [Note: [Col. 0876D] II III Hegira 60, 12 October, feria 4] Donus 3; St. Agatho 1.

After Donus had occupied the see for two years, five months, and ten days, from 2 November 676, he died on 11 April of this year. St. Agatho succeeded him and, after an interpontificate of two months and fifteen days, was ordained on 26 June.

St. Wilfrid set out for Rome through Gaul at the beginning of spring. Reaching Rome in autumn, he was heard at the council and acquitted; he was ordered to remain there so that he might attend the council of 125 bishops that was being convened.

St. Amandus, Bishop of Trajectum and Apostle of the Flemings, died. From Milo the Monk, in Mabillon, section 2 of the Benedictines; Baronius, under the year 661, and Pagi there.

[Col. 0878A] [Note: [Col. 0878A] III IV Hegira 61, 1 October, feria 2] Agatho 1 and 2.

This year and the preceding one saw many synods in Italy and elsewhere, especially the celebrated Roman synod of 125 bishops on 27 March, from which a synodical letter was sent to Constantinople, and the general council, begun on 7 November, and the synod of Heathfield in England in September, attended by John the Abbot, sent by Agatho in the preceding year. Thus Pagi correctly opposes Baronius, who was misled by the Indiction, no. 6.

The papal legates arrived at Constantinople on 10 September, as Pagi correctly shows, no. 5 and following, correcting Anastasius, whose numbers are corrupt.

[Col. 0878B] At approximately this time St. Bathildis, mother of Chlothar III and of Childeric, kings of France, who founded and endowed various monasteries, especially those of Corbie and Chelles, died. Baronius, under the year 665; Pagi there, no. 7 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0878B] IV et 365 I Hegira 62, 20 September, feria 6] Agatho 2 and 3.

The Sixth Ecumenical Council, the Third of Constantinople, begun in the preceding year and carried through its sixth session, was completed this year, and the Monothelites were condemned. Pagi treats its acts at length under this year. See the notes of Pagi and Sommier under Agatho.

[Col. 0878C] St. Wilfrid, not restored to his own see, went to the South Saxons and announced the Gospel to them. Bede.

The Eleventh Council of Toledo, a national council, decreed in one of its canons that the bishops of all Spain, appointed by the king, should be examined and ordained by the Bishop of Toledo. No such kind of primacy ever existed in any Spanish see, whatever may be said about the notable Apostolic vicariates of Seville, Tarragona, and Braga.

The Roman pontiffs were exempted, through the generosity of the Emperor Pogonatus, from the payment which the Gothic kings had imposed upon them and which the emperors had continued. Anastasius.

[Col. 0878D] [Note: [Col. 0878D] I II Hegira 63, 10 September, feria 4] Agatho 3; Leo II 1.

After St. Agatho had occupied the see for two years, six months, and fourteen days, from 26 June 679, he died this year on 10 January. Leo II was given as his successor; after a lengthy interpontificate of seven months and six days, he was ordained this year on 17 August.

Before Leo’s ordination, the legates returned from Constantinople with the acts of the Sixth Council, which they had presided over in Agatho’s name. Anastasius.

[Note: [Col. 0878D] II III Hegira 64, 30 August, feria 1] Leo II 1.

Leo died on 3 July, without completing a year of his pontificate. For he had sat from 17 August of the preceding year until 3 July of this year, namely ten months and seventeen days. His death was followed by an interpontificate longer than the preceding one.

George, Bishop of Constantinople, died; Theodore was restored to that see. Nicephorus, Theophanes, Baronius under the preceding year, and Pagi there, no. 7.

The Thirteenth Council of Toledo, attended by forty-eight bishops, was held on 4 November. After its celebration, the letters of Leo II and the acts of the Sixth Council reached Spain. Baronius and Pagi, no. 15.

[Col. 0880B] [Note: [Col. 0880B] III IV Hegira 65, 18 August, feria 5] Benedict II 1.

After the see had been vacant for eleven months and twenty-two days following Leo II, his successor Benedict II was not ordained until 26 June of this year.

The Fourteenth Council of Toledo, begun on 18 November and completed on 20 November, was held for the acceptance of the Sixth Ecumenical Council throughout Spain and Gothic Gaul.

St. Audoin, Bishop of Rouen, worn out by old age, died after establishing peace among the Frankish nobles. He died in November, though on an uncertain day, and was succeeded by St. Ansbert. Pagi under the year 682, no. 8, and under this year, no. 23, against Baronius, who places his death in 677.

[Col. 0880C] [Note: [Col. 0880C] IV et 366 I Hegira 66, 8 August, feria 3] Benedict II 1; John V 1.

After Benedict II had occupied the see for ten months and twelve days from 26 June of the preceding year, he died this year on 8 May. John V succeeded him and, after an interpontificate of two months and fifteen days, was ordained on 23 July of this year.

Benedict II sent a letter to the bishops of Spain ordering Julian, Bishop of Toledo, to correct his apology concerning the three substances; Julian did so. Baronius; Pagi, no. 6.

Theophanes, Bishop of Antioch, died. Baronius and Pagi, no. 8.

[Note: [Col. 0880C] I II Hegira 67, 28 July, feria 7] John V 1 and 2. Conon [lacuna].

John V, after having occupied the see for one year and nine days from 23 July of the preceding year, died this year on 2 August. Conon succeeded him and, after an interpontificate of two months and eighteen days, was ordained on 21 October of this year.

Theodore, Bishop of Constantinople, died. Paul, a layman and imperial secretary, succeeded him. Baronius under the year 684, and Pagi there, no. 14.

Theodore, Bishop of Canterbury, reconciled Wilfrid, who was living in exile among the South Saxons and was especially dear to Cædwalla. The editions of Bede. Pagi, nos. 14 and 21.

St. Julian, Bishop of Toledo, wrote three books against the Jews. The same Julian, book 3, at the end. Baronius; Pagi, no. 10.

[Note: [Col. 0880D] II III Hegira 68, 17 July, feria 4]

Conon 1; Sergius 1.

After Conon had occupied the see for two months, he died on 21 September. Sergius succeeded him and, after an interpontificate of two months and twenty-three days, was ordained on 15 December of this year.

St. Cuthbert, Bishop of Lindisfarne in Northumbria, after governing that church for two years, returned to his monastery on Inner Farne, where he soon died. St. Wilfrid, restored to his see this year, administered the Bishopric of Lindisfarne for one year, until St. Eadbert was chosen as his successor; and St. Aedilwald succeeded St. Cuthbert in the monastery. Bede, in his life and in book 4, chapter 19, and book 5, chapters 1 and 20. Baronius and Pagi, no. 5.

[Col. 0882B] [Note: [Col. 0882B] III IV Hegira 69, 6 July, feria 2] Sergius 1 and 2.

The translation of St. Leo the Great from the hidden place of the lower sacristy of St. Peter’s to a more fitting location in the same basilica took place on 28 June. This was the first of the three translations of the holy body. The second was carried out by Paul V in May 1607; the third by Clement XI in April 1714, in the presence of Bianchini, the prefect, who described it. Anastasius, treating the matter in volume 3, page 159, promises a fuller account, which he had planned but did not complete because death intervened. See Anastasius, book 1, volume 3.

The Fifteenth Council of Toledo was held on 11 May; at it Julian’s book on the three wills was examined. Baronius celebrates at length the virtues of Egica and the most holy discipline preserved by the bishops of Spain.

[Note: [Col. 0882C] IV et 367 I Hegira 70, 25 June, feria 6] Sergius 2 and 3.

Cædwalla, King of the West Saxons, came to the holy threshold. He was baptized by Sergius on Saturday, 10 April, the Saturday before Easter; he died twelve days later, on 21 April. Baronius.

St. Kilian, Bishop and Apostle of the Franks, who three years earlier had come from Ireland to Francia and thence to Rome, suffered martyrdom this year at Würzburg with Coloman the presbyter and Totnan the deacon. Following the example of St. John the Baptist, he told Gosbert, Duke of the Franks, who had been converted to the faith, that he could not retain the wife of his brother Geila. Consequently, the woman’s hatred was turned against him. [Col. 0882D] Baronius gives at length the epitaph and the divine vengeance upon the sacrilegious murderers. See also H. Canisius and Mabillon, cited by Pagi under the year 686, no. 9.

[Note: [Col. 0882D] I II Hegira 71, 14 June, feria 3] Sergius 3 and 4.

St. Theodore, Bishop of Canterbury, the last of those ordained in Rome, who wrote a notable *Penitential*, died this year. Bede, the Saxon Chronicle, Baronius, and Pagi, no. 5.

Julian, Archbishop of Toledo, who had succeeded Quiricus on 29 January 680, died on 6 March after having occupied the see for ten years, one month, and seven days. He was buried in St. Leocadia. Bollandists, 8 March, preliminary commentary.

St. Benedict, Bishop and Abbot of Wearmouth, also died this year. Pagi under the year 703, no. 4, against Baronius, the Bollandists, and others, on the authority of the life written by Bede and preserved by Mabillon.

[Note: [Col. 0884A] II III Hegira 72, 4 June, feria 1] Sergius 4 and 5.

The Council in Trullo, or Quinisext Council, was held this year. Concerning its date [lacuna], Baronius and Pagi discuss the matter under the following year. Pagi, however, no. 7, concludes from the Alexandrian era 6199 that it was certainly held this year, since that year ended in August and 6200 began, during the fifth Indiction. Concerning the Trullan canons, rejected by Sergius and John VII, and partly approved and partly rejected by John VIII, both authors should be consulted, especially Christophe Lupus, volume 2. Petavius places it in the year 707.

The Third Council of Zaragoza was celebrated on 28 October, in the era 729, that is, this year.

[Note: [Col. 0884B] III IV Hegira 73, 24 May, feria 6] Sergius 5 and 6.

St. Wilfrid was again expelled from the see of York by King Ælfred, with several bishops at Westminster. Pagi, no. 20.

Theodore, Bishop of Canterbury, having died two years earlier, was given a successor only this year: Berctuald, who was ordained in Gaul on 25 June of the following year. Bede, book 5, chapter 9.

[Col. 0884C] [Note: [Col. 0884C] IV et 368 I Hegira 74, 13 May, feria 3] Sergius 6 and 7.

Paul, Bishop of Constantinople, died after occupying the see for six years and eight months, according to Nicephorus, or seven years, according to Theophanes. Callinicus succeeded him. Baronius under the year 691 and Pagi there, no. 4.

This year, or at the end of the preceding year, Erkenwald, Bishop of London, died, and Walder succeeded him. Suidbert was also ordained bishop in Britain, though no definite see was assigned to him. Pagi, no. 7.

The Sixteenth Council of Toledo, held on 6 May in the era 731, in the sixth year of Egica’s reign, was a national council. Sisbert, Archbishop of Toledo, was deposed as a rebel, and Felix of Seville was made his successor. Many decrees concerning discipline and reform were also enacted.

[Note: [Col. 0884D] I II Hegira 75, 2 May, feria 7] Sergius 7 and 8.

This year, or at the end of the preceding year, Sergius sent letters to Æthelred, Ælfred, and Adulf, kings of the Angles and Saxons, commending Brihtwald as primate of all Britain. From William of Malmesbury. Pagi, no. 5.

The Seventeenth Council of Toledo was held on 9 November, in the seventh year of Egica’s reign and the era 732. Many matters concerning ecclesiastical discipline were decreed, in addition to those mentioned by Baronius.

Pagi, no. 4, reports that a council was also held at Becanceld, a city of Kent; Bede, William of Malmesbury, and all the ancient writers, except Spelman, are silent about it.

[Col. 0886A] [Note: [Col. 0886A] II III Hegira 76, 21 April, feria 4] Sergius 8 and 9.

St. Begga, mother of Pippin, mayor of the palace of Francia, died this year or at the end of the preceding year, not three years later as Sigebert, Baronius, and others who followed his authority maintain. Pagi refutes them under the year 698, no. 9 and following.

The two priest Ewalds, who followed the example of St. Willibrord and were striving to enlighten the ancient Saxons with evangelical preaching while announcing the faith to the Frisians, suffered martyrdom. Baronius under the year 693, and Pagi there, no. 4.

[Col. 0886B] [Note: [Col. 0886B] III IV Hegira 77, 10 April, feria 2] Sergius 9 and 10.

St. Willibrord, who was still announcing the faith to the Frisians as a presbyter, was ordained Bishop of Utrecht this year. Bede; Pagi, no. 1. Baronius, following the Pseudo-Marcellinus, says much in this and the following years about him and St. Suidbert. The Pseudo-Marcellinus presents himself as one of the twelve companions of St. Willibrord. It is therefore necessary to separate what is true from what is false.

[Note: [Col. 0886B] IV et 369 I Hegira 78, 30 March, feria 6] Sergius 10 and 11.

[Col. 0886C] St. Willibrord, ordained at Rome in the preceding year in the church of St. Cecilia on 22 November, came this year to Pippin, who sent him into the northern parts of the kingdom. He completed the conversion of the Frisians, which had been attempted by Egbert and Wigbert, archbishops of Cologne. From Alcuin. Pagi, under the preceding year, no. 2.

Following the same Pseudo-Marcellinus, Baronius says that the Synod of Utrecht was held this year; Pagi argues that it was fictitious, no. 2.

[Col. 0886D] [Note: [Col. 0886D] I II Hegira 79, 19 March, feria 3] Sergius 11 and 12.

The Synod of Aquileia was held, at which the schism over the Three Chapters was completely extinguished. Paul the Deacon, Anastasius, and Baronius. After considering these matters, Pagi teaches that the schism, begun under Vigilius, although the bishops of Istria had previously come to their senses, was not completely eradicated until the pontificate of Sergius. Pagi, nos. 13 and 14, from Hermannus Contractus and Anastasius, with the observations of Cardinal Noris, volume 4.

St. Claudius, Abbot of Joux in the Diocese of Lyon, who had already become very old and had been Bishop of Besançon, resigned after seven years, returning to his hermitage. He died this year, having presided over the monastery for fifty-five years, both as abbot and as bishop. Pagi, no. 16.

[Col. 0888A] [Note: [Col. 0888A] II III Hegira 80, 9 March, feria 1] Sergius 12 and 13.

St. Aldhelm, Abbot of Malmesbury, should be counted among ecclesiastical writers on account of his various writings, especially his book against the error of the Britons concerning Easter. While he was living in Rome at this time, he freed Sergius from a great slander by means of a remarkable miracle. Henschen, 25 May; Baronius and Pagi call this into question.

St. Adamnan, Abbot of Iona, or of St. Columba’s monastery in Scotland, also flourished, celebrated for various writings. Bede, book 5, chapter 16.

[Col. 0888B] [Note: [Col. 0888B] III IV Hegira 81, 25 February, feria 4] Sergius 13 and 14.

Sergius summoned the Venerable Bede, who was living in a monastery at this time, to Rome; Bede nevertheless did not come. Baronius; Mabillon, section 3 of the Benedictines, calls this letter to Bede into question, as does Henschen on 27 May. Pagi, under the following year, no. 2, thinks that it was issued by one of Sergius’s successors.

[Note: [Col. 0888B] IV et 370 I Hegira 82, 15 February, feria 3] Sergius 14; John VI 1.

After Sergius had occupied the see for thirteen years, eight months, and twenty-three days from 15 December 687, he died this year on 8 September. John VI succeeded him and, after an interpontificate of fifty days, was ordained on Sunday, 30 October.

The Eighteenth and final Council of Toledo was held at Witiza’s command. Its canons, being for the most part contrary to ecclesiastical discipline, have not reached us. Baronius; Pagi, no. 4.

[Note: [Col. 0888C] I II Hegira 83, 4 February, feria 7] John VI 1 and 2.

During this period the pontiff suffered injury from Gisulf, Duke of Benevento, who invaded and plundered Roman territory. The pontiff therefore obtained his return to his own lands after ransoming the captives. Anastasius and the Deacon Baronius.

St. Wilfrid’s case was again heard at the Synod of Onestrefeld, whereupon the holy bishop appealed to Rome. From the editions of Eddius. Pagi, no. 3 and following.

[Col. 0888D] [Note: [Col. 0888D] II III Hegira 84, 24 January, feria 4] John VI 2 and 3.

St. Wilfrid, having left Britain and the church of Leicester, which he administered in Mercia, again sought Rome. There he prayed that the decrees of Saints Agatho and Sergius might be fulfilled, and, for the sake of peace, he renounced the bishopric of York. The opposing party was also present, and the case was not decided until the following year. From Eddius. Pagi, no. 5. Baronius relates this after two years.

[Note: [Col. 0888D] III IV Hegira 85, 13 January, feria 1] John VI 3 and 4.

St. Wilfrid, finally acquitted this year, set out through Gaul for England. At the city of Meaux he fell ill; in the following year he had a vision of St. Michael, who promised him four more years of life. From Eddius; Pagi, no. 8 and following, and under the following year, no. 5.

An unrepentant soldier died in England; Baronius recounts his horrifying end.

At this time Anastasius, Bishop of Jerusalem, died. He was a most ardent defender of the sacred images. Pagi under the following year, no. 21.

[Note: [Col. 0890A] IV et 371 I Hegira 86, 2 January, feria 6; Hegira 87, 22 December, feria 3] John VI 4; John VII 1.

After John VI had occupied the see for three years, two months, and twelve days, he died this year on 11 January. John VII succeeded him and, after an interpontificate of one month and eighteen days, was ordained on 1 March, a Sunday, of this year.

Callinicus, Patriarch of Constantinople, was deprived of his sight by the Emperor in a just judgment of God and sent into exile at Rome because of his rash attempts against the Apostolic See. Baronius under the year 703. Cyrus the monk became his successor.

When St. Wilfrid returned to his homeland, he was harshly received by Ælfred, who afterward fell ill and promised to restore him to his see. This was done in the same year by his son and successor Osred; at the Synod of Nidd, reconciliation was achieved with everyone. Eddius; Pagi, no. 11.

[Note: [Col. 0890B] I II Hegira 88, 12 December, feria 1] John VII 1 and 2.

The pontiff did not correct the Trullan canons at all; rather, through the same legates and metropolitans, he sent them back to the Emperor. Anastasius.

[Note: [Col. 0890C] II III Hegira 89, 1 December, feria 5] John VII 2 and 3.

After John VII had occupied the see for two years, seven months, and seventeen days from his ordination on 1 March 705, he died this year on 18 October. Sisinnius succeeded him, but was pontiff for only a few days and appears to have begun his pontificate in the following year.

St. Lambert, Bishop of Tongeren on the Meuse, completed his martyrdom. St. Hubert succeeded him and transferred the episcopal see to Liège. [Col. 0890D] See Baronius under the year 698 and Pagi there, no. 1 and following.

The Cottian Alps were restored to the Roman See and confirmed by a donation written in letters of gold.

[Note: [Col. 0890D] III IV Hegira 90, 19 November, feria 2] Sisinnius 1; Constantine 1.

Sisinnius is believed to have died after occupying the see for twenty days, on 7 February of this year. His successor was certainly Constantine, who, after an interpontificate of one month and eighteen days, was ordained on Sunday, 25 March of this year.

Felix, Bishop of Ravenna, was ordained by the Roman pontiff and unwillingly made his profession of faith. Anastasius; Baronius.

[Col. 0892A] [Note: [Col. 0892A] IV et 372 I Hegira 91, 8 November, feria 6] Constantine 1 and 2.

St. Wilfrid died before the month of May, after St. Michael had appeared to him again in the eighteenth month. He was seventy-six years old and had been a bishop for forty-five years, according to Eadmer: born in 634 and made a bishop in 665. Eddius, Bede, Eadmer, Baronius, and Pagi.

[Col. 0892B] [Note: [Col. 0892B] I II Hegira 92, 29 October, feria 4] Constantine 2 and 3.

Invited by the Emperor to Constantinople, the pontiff set out and departed from the port of Rome on 5 October. When he came to Naples, he found John Rizocopus coming from Constantinople; he spent the winter at Otranto. Anastasius, together with Pagi, correctly; Baronius follows them.

An unfortunate turning point in the calamities of the Church and of the kingdom of Spain. Julian, governor of Ceuta, for a reason that is not sufficiently certain, entered into an alliance with Musa, governor of Africa. After handing over his towns to him, he urged an invasion of Spain. The same Julian, together with Tarif ibn Malik and one hundred infantry and one hundred cavalry, reached the Strait of Cádiz in mid-July and returned to Africa laden with booty. From al-Nuwayri, the Geography of Nubianus, and Rodrigo of Toledo; Scaliger. [Col. 0892C] Pagi, no. 4.

[Note: [Col. 0892C] II III Hegira 93, 19 October, feria 2] Constantine 3 and 4.

The pontiff reached Constantinople at the beginning of spring and was received with great honor. He approved the Trullan canons, since they were not contrary to the Church—a course John VII had not followed. Lupus Scholasticus on the Trullan canons; Baronius and Pagi under the year 710, no. 1. He returned to Rome on 24 October, bringing with him several donations made by the Emperor to the Church. Anastasius; Pagi, in the same place.

Julian, with Tariq ibn Ziyad and another Saracen commander, reached Mount Jabal Tariq in April with twelve thousand warriors. In July the Spaniards, already unaccustomed to arms, suffered their final defeat. King Roderic perished, and his body was not found. With new troops arriving from Africa, the Muslim Arabs gradually subjected the cities of Spain to themselves. Rodrigo; Pagi, no. 8 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0892D] III IV Hegira 94, 7 October, feria 6] Constantine 4 and 5.

The principal churches of Spain fell into the worst condition. For Musa, governor of Africa, having heard of Tariq’s victories, himself crossed the strait with twelve thousand armed men and stormed Medina-Sidonia, Carmona, and Seville, the metropolitan city of Baetica. The Arabic authorities, cited by Pagi under this year.

After this the kingdom of Asturias began. The Spaniards, having fled to the mountains of Asturias, created Pelagius, son of Favila, Duke of Cantabria, as king. At first confined within narrow boundaries, this new kingdom had been greatly enlarged by the year 882, as is evident from the Council of Oviedo held that year. For at that time twenty-two bishops were subject to the metropolitan of Oviedo, who had then been declared metropolitan, as Pagi observes, no. 17. In this new kingdom both the royal line and the uncorrupted Catholic faith were preserved; the latter later began to flourish again throughout Spain under Urban II in 1088.

[Note: [Col. 0894A] IV et 373 I Hegira 93, 26 September, feria 3] Constantine 5 and 6.

Count Julian and the sons of Witiza were beheaded at Musa’s command, since he believed them to be the leaders of the faction after the defeat inflicted by Pelagius. Thus the author of Spain’s calamity paid the penalty for his crime before Musa was recalled to Syria.

The Spaniards who remained were free to live according to Christian custom. They had judges from among their own people, granted to them by the Saracen governors, and these men were given the ancient dignity of counts, so that, as nobles participating in the commonwealth, they might keep the Christian population in obedience. Marca, *History of Spain*, book 3, chapter 2. This was especially the case under the Saracen caliph Marwan, as will appear under the year 744. Hence the Office of Saints Isidore and Leander and the Mozarabic liturgy continued to flourish, as they still flourish today in six parishes of Toledo. Rodrigo; Pagi, no. 7. See the dissertation prefixed to volume 6 of the *July Acts of the Saints*.

Constantine 6 and 7.

[Note: [Col. 0894C] II Hegira 96, 16 September, feria 1] This year a monastery of nuns dedicated to St. Mary and St. Aurelian at Pavia was founded by a certain senator of clarissimus rank. Mabillon, *Italian Journey*.

[Col. 0894D] [Note: [Col. 0894D] II III Hegira 97, 5 September, feria 5] Constantine 7; St. Gregory II 1.

After Constantine had occupied the see for seven years and fifteen days from 25 March 708, he died this year on 9 April. St. Gregory II succeeded him and, after an interpontificate of forty days, was ordained on 19 May.

Germanus was transferred from the metropolitan see of Cyzicus to Constantinople and ordained bishop on 11 August. He held the Constantinopolitan synod of one hundred bishops mentioned by an anonymous author of a *Synodical Booklet*. The annals and his life, in Henschen, 12 May, are entirely silent about this synod. Pagi, no. 8.

[Col. 0896A] The Lombards took from the Roman Church the fortress of Cumae, which Gregory ransomed for seventy pounds of gold from the Duke of Naples. The duke, together with Theodimus, his subordinate and administrator, had taken it from the hands of the Lombards. Anastasius and the Deacon. Baronius gives Theodimus’s epitaph, without any indication of date, from the church of St. Andrew at the Nidum in Naples, together with another, more ancient epitaph of Candida, which belongs to the year 585.

[Col. 0896B] [Note: [Col. 0896B] III IV Hegira 98, 24 August, feria 2] Gregory II 1 and 2.

A great flood of the Tiber lasted seven days. Anastasius.

The monastery of Cassino, destroyed by the Lombards, was restored after approximately 140 years by St. Petronax, the sixth abbot after St. Benedict. Baronius, Mabillon, and Pagi, no. 7.

St. Boniface, called Winfrid, sailed from England to Frisia with two monks in order to preach the Gospel there. From his life. Pagi, no. 16.

Theodo, Duke of the Bavarians, converted to the faith through the work of St. Rupert, made a pilgrimage to Rome. Baronius under the year 726, and Pagi there, no. 15.

[Col. 0896C] [Note: [Col. 0896C] IV et 374 I Hegira 99, 14 August, feria 7] Gregory II 2 and 3.

St. Rigobert, Bishop of Reims, who before the battle of Vincennes had refused Charles Martel admission, wishing to see the outcome of the war, was expelled from his see by Charles after the victory had been won, and Milo of Trier, already a bishop, was intruded in his place. Rigobert lived in exile in Gascony, where he became renowned for miracles. Baronius and Pagi, no. 5.

St. Wibert, who had been ordained bishop in order to announce the Gospel to the Frisians and neighboring peoples, died this year in March. Baronius; Pagi, from the Chronicle of Saint-Denis, no. 7.

[Col. 0896D] [Note: [Col. 0896D] I II Hegira 100, 3 August, feria 4] Gregory II 3 and 4.

St. Boniface, who had come from England to Frisia two years earlier, had remained there for scarcely half a year before returning to his homeland. This year, having declined the dignity of abbot, he set out for Rome around October with several companions. On 30 November he received from the Holy Pontiff the apostolic commission, as Pagi proves from the authors of his life, Willibald and Othlonus, no. 1 and following under the following year, with Baronius.

[Col. 0898A] [Note: [Col. 0898A] II III Hegira 101, 23 July, feria 1] Gregory II 4 and 5.

St. Gregory sent Boniface to convert the Germans, armed with letters that he gave him this year on the Ides of May. Baronius quotes them from Willibald; their date is given as the third year of Emperor Leo and the second Indiction.

Pagi reports from Hincmar the exceedingly poor condition of the churches of Gaul and Germany during this period, no. 8.

[Col. 0898B] [Note: [Col. 0898B] III IV Hegira 102, 12 July, feria 6] Gregory II 5 and 6.

St. Germanus, Patriarch of Constantinople, crowned the boy Constantine, whom his father had made co-emperor, on Holy Easter Day. Theophanes; Baronius.

[Col. 0898C] [Note: [Col. 0898C] IV et 375 I Hegira 103, 31 June, feria 3] Gregory II 6 and 7.

The First Roman Council under St. Gregory II was held in the sixth year of Leo, the sixth post-consulate, the second year of Constantine, in April, during the fourth Indiction. Baronius therefore correctly says that it was held this year. Pagi, however, because Leo’s accession has been incorrectly established, is compelled to correct all the manuscripts, no. 1.
