St. John, Bishop of York, who four years earlier had resigned the episcopate and returned to the monastery, died this year, following the custom of the holy bishops of England in this period. Bede; Pagi, no. 6 and following.

[Col. 0898D] [Note: [Col. 0898D] I II Hegira 104, 21 June, feria 1] Gregory II 7 and 8.

St. Boniface, who had spent three years in Frisia with St. Willibrord, Bishop of that people, declined the episcopal dignity offered to him and set out for Germany, where he had been sent by St. Gregory. Baronius and Pagi.

[Note: [Col. 0898D] II III Hegira 105, 10 June, feria 5] Gregory II 8 and 9.

St. Boniface, who had preached the Gospel with successful results in Hesse and Thuringia, was summoned to Rome by apostolic letters. There he was consecrated bishop without attachment to any particular see, on the day before the Kalends of December. On the Kalends themselves several letters were issued, so that he might be received everywhere as an Apostolic Legate. Baronius quotes them under this year. [Col. 0900A]

[Note: [Col. 0900A] III IV Hegira 106, 29 May, feria 2] Gregory II 9 and 10.

St. Gregory wrote to Boniface on the day before the Nones of December, in the eighth year of Leo, the eighth post-consulate, the fifth year of Constantine, and the eighth Indiction. After returning, Boniface was announcing the faith in Hesse and Thuringia with extraordinary success. Baronius treats this at length.

The Venerable Bede completed his book on the six ages in the ninth year of Leo, that is, this year, according to Pagi, under the year 725, no. 1.

[Note: [Col. 0900B] IV et 376 I Hegira 107, 19 May, feria 7] Gregory II 10 and 11.

St. Corbinian, reproving Grimoald, tetrarch of Bavaria, because he retained Plectrude, the wife of his brother, in an incestuous marriage, was harassed in extraordinary fashion by this new Herodias. Baronius under the preceding year.

Æthelbert, King of Kent, congratulated St. Boniface on the great conversions he had accomplished and desired that the pious king might maintain an exchange of letters with him. Baronius and Pagi, from the letters of Boniface, no. 12.

[Col. 0900C] [Note: [Col. 0900C] I II Hegira 108, 8 May, feria 4] Gregory II 11 and 12.

An image of Christ in bronze was thrown down by the Emperor from the top of the palace gate; women defended it by suffering martyrdom. Baronius under this year; Pagi under the year 730, no. 9, both from Theophanes.

St. Gregory answered the consultations of St. Boniface in the tenth year of Leo, the seventh year of Constantine, on the tenth day before the Kalends of December. Baronius quotes his letter, as well as another letter of Boniface to his former bishop Daniel in England, written this year, and Pagi agrees with him, no. 16.

Ina, King of the West Saxons, resigned the kingdom which he had assumed in 689 and made a pilgrimage to Rome. From Bede; Pagi, no. 15; from Polydore, Baronius under the year 740.

[Note: [Col. 0900D] II III Hegira 109, 27 April, feria 1] Gregory II 12 and 13.

While the Imperial iconoclasts were laying plots against the Holy Pontiff in Italy, St. John of Damascus, a Syrian prefect of Damascus and minister of the Saracen caliph, published three orations and other short works against the iconoclasts. Combefis, *History of the Monothelites*; Baronius; Pagi, no. 3.

[Col. 0902A] St. Hubert, Bishop of Liège, died this year, not in the following year as Baronius states in the appendix to volume 9. From Cointius. Pagi, no. 4.

[Note: [Col. 0902A] III IV Hegira 110, 16 April, feria 6] Gregory II 13 and 14.

Plots were laid against St. Germanus by the Emperor through Anastasius, who afterward became his successor. Baronius.

St. John of Damascus, likewise a defender of the images, was attacked by plots. A forged letter, by which he was declared a traitor, was sent to the Saracen king, who, believing it genuine, ordered the holy man’s right hand to be amputated. After it was restored to him through the Blessed Virgin, he became dearer to the king than before; nevertheless, after selling all his possessions, he became a monk. Baronius.

Under the governor Jahya, Christians in Spain were treated peacefully, while the Saracens and Moors who opposed them were punished severely. Isidore of Beja.

[Note: [Col. 0902B] IV et 377 I Hegira 111, 5 April, feria 3] Gregory II 14 and 15.

St. Ecgbert, an English monk who had once contemplated converting the Germans but, being unable to carry this out, had crossed into Ireland and taught the monks of Iona to celebrate Easter according to the Catholic Roman Church, died this year on Easter Day itself. He had been divinely delivered from the plague. From Bede. [Col. 0902C] Pagi, no. 7.

[Note: [Col. 0902C] I II Hegira 112, 26 March, feria 1] Gregory II 15 and 16.

St. Germanus, who had occupied the see of Constantinople for fourteen years, five months, and seven days, was compelled to resign on 7 January, a Tuesday, and was sent into exile. Theophanes; Baronius and Pagi.

Two letters of St. Gregory, which Baronius assigns to the year 726, belong here. The first, addressed to the Emperor, is milder, since the pontiff was seeking his conversion; the other, addressed to the intruded patriarch Anastasius, is very sharp. He excommunicates him unless he repents, and so forth. Anastasius; Baronius.

[Col. 0902D] St. Corbinian, the first Bishop of Freising, died. Pagi, no. 13 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0902D] II III Hegira 113, 15 March, feria 5] Gregory II 16; Gregory III 1.

After St. Gregory II had occupied the see for fifteen years, eight months, and twenty-four days from 19 May 715, he died this year on 11 February. St. Gregory III succeeded him and, after an interpontificate of thirty-five days, was consecrated on 18 March of this year.

St. Boniface sent letters to Gregory III, promising due submission to the Holy See and recounting many conversions; they are no longer extant. Baronius and Pagi, from Othlonus in his *Life*.

[Note: [Col. 0904A] III IV Hegira 114, 3 March, feria 2] Gregory III 1 and 2.

A council was held at Rome for the restoration of the sacred images against the Emperor Leo; the images were set up everywhere, especially at Rome, with great splendor. Baronius. The emperor detained the papal legates who were working for their restoration and sent them into exile. Anastasius; Baronius.

A letter of Gregory to Boniface, in which he answered each of the chapters of Boniface’s letter and sent him the pallium, is reported by Baronius under the preceding year; Pagi likewise shows that it belongs here. [Col. 0904B]

Pagi recounts the death of St. Wilfrid the Younger, Bishop of York, under the year 731, no. 9 and following, against the Bollandists, 29 April. He also assigns to this year the exile of St. Eucherius, Bishop of Orléans, ordered by Charles Martel, against Baronius, who places it under the year 725, no. 4.

[Note: [Col. 0904B] IV et 378 I Hegira 115, 21 February, feria 7] Gregory III 2 and 3.

A new and fruitless embassy was sent to the Emperor, both by St. Gregory and by all Italy. Anastasius; Baronius.

In Bavaria a certain schismatic named Eremwulf became the author of heretical depravity, but St. Boniface, by apostolic authority, suppressed both the rising heresy and the heresiarch himself. Baronius. Pagi thinks that this occurred in 736, where he treats it, [Col. 0904C] no. 8.

[Note: [Col. 0904C] I I Hegira 116, 10 February, feria 4] Gregory III 3 and 4.

In this year and the following years Baronius reports many examples of martyrs and confessors on account of the sacred images in the East. Pagi, however, shows from the *Menaea* that all these events belong to the time of Leo the Armenian, as we shall see then. Both authors should be consulted, since they discuss these matters at length.

St. Theodore the Cantor was exiled by the Isaurian because of his defense of the sacred images, as Baronius relates under this year. Pagi distinguishes two learned men named Theodore, no. 1; they must not be confused.

[Note: [Col. 0904D] II III Hegira 117, 30 January, feria 1] Gregory III 4 and 5.

The Venerable Bede died this year on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, on Ascension Day itself, as Baronius and Pagi show under the year 731 from Cuthbert’s letter to his disciple Cuthwin. Pagi nevertheless says that Baronius, in the same place, no. 4, was deceived by a corrupt manuscript and places Bede’s death too late.

[Note: [Col. 0904D] 118, 19 January, feria 5, III IV Hegira] Gregory III 5 and 6.

Pagi assigns to this year the arrival of St. Boniface in Bavaria and the rising heresy condemned by him, concerning which we dealt with Baronius under the year 733.

[Note: [Col. 0906B] IV et 379 I Hegira 119, 8 January, feria 3; Hegira 120, 28 December, feria 7] Gregory III 6 and 7.

Evantius, archdeacon of the Church of Toledo, who had assisted Urban, the archbishop, during the persecution by the Saracens, together with Frederick, bishop of the Church of Écija, died. Isidore of Beja. Pagi, no. 11.

This year St. Ermin, first bishop and afterward abbot of Lobbes, also died on the seventh day before the Kalends of May. Theotuine succeeded him, not Theodulf, as Baronius maintains. Mabillon, and from him Henschen and Pagi, no. 1.

During this period the Dionysian era began to be used in Gaul—that is, the years began to be reckoned from the Incarnation. Pagi, no. 7.

[Note: [Col. 0906C] I II Hegira 121, 18 December, feria 5] Gregory III 7 and 8.

After the Saracens had been expelled, the bishops of Gaul became concerned with restoring the churches. Baronius.

Third journey of St. Boniface to Rome, from which he departs furnished with three letters, which Baron quotes without any indication of their date. The synod mentioned in Boniface’s letter, which he wrote while residing in Rome this year and which was to be convened there—not at Augsburg, as Baron maintains, or elsewhere, according to another opinion which Pagi demonstrates in no. 2.

[Note: [Col. 0906C] II III Hegira 122, 7 Dec., feria 2] Gregory III, 8 and 9.

After returning from Rome, St. Boniface divides Bavaria into four bishoprics: Salzburg, Freising, Regensburg, and Passau. Gregory’s letter, which Baron quotes. Pagi discusses these dioceses at length, no. 1 and following.

St. Willibrord, first bishop of Utrecht, who completed the conversion of the Frisians begun by Saints Egbert and Wigbert and established the bishopric of Utrecht, dies on 6 November. From Alcuin. Pagi, no. 11. Later Paul IV raised this see to an archbishopric.

[Note: [Col. 0906D] III IV Hegira 123, 26 Nov., feria 7]

Gregory III, 9 and 10.

Gaul, which this year is troubled by no wars, as the Annals show, raises a dispute concerning Easter. For according to the Victorian cycle, which was still in use, especially among the Gauls, Easter fell on 17 April, whereas according to the Alexandrian cycle it fell on 24 April, a difference of eight days. Continuation of Fredegar.

[Note: [Col. 0908B] IV and 380 I; Hegira 124, 15 Nov., feria 4] Gregory III, 10 and 11; St. Zachary, 1.

St. Gregory III, after having occupied the see for ten years, eight months, and twenty-four days from 18 March 731, dies this year on 28 November. His successor, St. Zachary, is ordained four days later, on 3 December.

The double embassy of Gregory III to Charles, reported above by Baron under the earlier year, belongs here. Since both men died in the same year, it is uncertain what decision Charles made. This much is certain: he was declared by the holy pontiff to be Patrician, or defender of the Apostolic See. Pagi, no. 4 and following.

As the number of the faithful increased, St. Boniface established three further bishoprics: first, in Eastern Francia, Würzburg, today Herbipolis; second, in Hesse, Büraburg, today destroyed; third, in Thuringia, at Erphesfurt, today Herford. Letter 22 of Boniface to Zachary.

[Note: [Col. 0908C] I II; Hegira 125, 4 Nov., feria 1] Zachary, 1 and 2.

After peace had been made with Liutprand through legates, St. Zachary shortly afterward met him in person and obtained the restoration of the four cities taken from the Apostolic See two years earlier. Anastasius; Baronius; Pagi, under this year and the preceding one. In a letter sent to Boniface on the Kalends of April, he likewise confirms the three bishoprics which Boniface had founded the previous year in Eastern Francia. Baronius and Pagi, no. 6.

A council is held by St. Boniface in Germany. Baron discusses it under the year 740, where Pagi, no. 1, wrongly presents it as divided into two parts; under this year, no. 9, he says that it was the first of the councils celebrated by St. Boniface.

[Note: [Col. 0908D] II III; Hegira 126, 25 Oct., feria 6] Zachary, 2 and 3.

A council is celebrated at Rome in the twelfth indiction, in which, by a new example, Liutprand’s thirty-second year is designated as that of the Langobardic king. From this Pagi, no. 16, infers that a treaty was concluded between the Pontiff and the Langobards for the defense of the sacred images.

A council is likewise celebrated at Liptina this year. Baronius and Pagi, no. 1.

The papal legates sent to Constantine the previous year obtain what they had gone to request: namely, several estates to be held in perpetuity by the Apostolic See, after Artavasdes had been defeated and blinded. Baronius; Pagi, no. 19.

[Col. 0910A] Two letters of Zachary exist, dated on the Kalends of April, one also addressed to Boniface, concerning their age. Pagi, no. 2 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0910A] III IV; Hegira 127, 13 Oct., feria 3] Zachary, 3 and 4.

The Council of Soissons is held under the presidency of St. Boniface; from it the condition of the Gallican Church is recognized. Pagi, no. 7.

Carloman founds the monastery of Fulda, and its first abbot is Sturmius, a Bavarian and disciple of St. Boniface. Pagi, no. 10 and following.

Two letters of St. Zachary—one in the twelfth indiction, on the tenth day before the Kalends of July, and the other on the Nones of November, in the thirteenth indiction—indicate this year. They bear the following subscription: “Artavasdes, in the third year, third post-consulate”; and also “in the third year of the Emperor Nicephorus the Great.” These indications show that Artavasdes prolonged his imperial rule until this year.

[Note: [Col. 0910B] IV and 381 I; Hegira 128, 2 Oct., feria 7] Zachary, 4 and 5.

The second council is held at Rome under Zachary. In it Adelbert, a Gaul, and Clement, a Scot, heretics condemned by St. Boniface in the German synod, are condemned again on 25 October by apostolic authority. Antoninus Pagi, in treating this council and others held during this period, corrects Cointius, who had confused their dates, no. 10.

Cologne, Agrippina, is established as a metropolis; Mainz is later placed above it. Zachary’s letter; Pagi, no. 4.

[Note: [Col. 0910C] I II; Hegira 129, 22 Sept., feria 5] Zachary, 5 and 6.

After the war against the Alamanni had been concluded this year, Carloman, thinking of abandoning the world, sets out for Rome. Pipin, meanwhile, plans to send his brother, who is journeying to the Holy Thresholds, on his way with great honors and gifts. Annals.

About this time St. Virgil becomes bishop of Salzburg; he is the fifth in succession. Pagi, no. 6.

[Col. 0910D] [Note: [Col. 0910D] II III; Hegira 130, 11 Sept., feria 2] Zachary, 6 and 7.

The holy pontiff receives the envoys of the Franks concerning the elevation of the see of Mainz to metropolitan status. Pagi, against Baron, from Zachary’s letters under the following year, no. 3, and under 751, no. 8. But earlier, namely on the Nones of January, he had replied to Boniface’s letters and to various chapters of Pipin: twenty-seven chapters, partly concerning the priestly order, partly the care of souls, and partly unlawful unions. Pagi, 744, no. 4 and following.

Carloman, a vigorous man who had defeated rebellious princes—Homald of Aquitaine, Odilo of Bavaria, and the marauding Saxons—and had suppressed the Alamanni who were attempting a new uprising, now, after all had been pacified, abandons the world and assumes the monastic habit. Baron, from Regino and the Bishop of Ostia. Pagi, no. 1.

[Note: [Col. 0912A] III IV; Hegira 131, 30 Aug., feria 6] Zachary, 7 and 8.

St. Zachary sends letters to Reginfred and twelve other bishops, praising their union with the Holy See and urging them, together with St. Boniface, the apostolic vicar, to devote themselves steadfastly to their ministries. Baronius and Pagi, with Cointius, no. 5.

[Col. 0912B] Toward the end of this year, Mainz is established as a metropolitan see by the holy pontiff. From Zachary’s restored letter; Pagi under 751, no. 8, with Baron.

[Note: [Col. 0912B] IV and 382 I; Hegira 132, 20 Aug., feria 4] Zachary, 8 and 9.

Anastasius, monk and abbot of the monastery of St. Euthymius, stirs up a heresy concerning the Trisagion, asserting that it ought to be understood of the Son alone. But St. John of Damascus is at hand, defending the Trisagion in his writings. Baronius and Pagi, no. 2.

Rachis, king of the Langobards, at the urging of St. Zachary, becomes a monk from being an enemy of the Apostolic See, leaving the kingdom to his brother Aistulf, who for a long time dared to harass the Holy See.

[Note: [Col. 0912C] I II; Hegira 133, 9 Aug., feria 1] Zachary, 9 and 10.

St. Anselm, founder of monasteries, flourishes. Formerly duke of Friuli, he became a monk and first founded the monastery of Fanano; then he founded Nonantola, of which he was the first abbot; afterward he erected the monastery at Vicenza and had 1,149 monks under his authority. Italian Writers, vol. 1, part 2, the work on the foundation of Nonantola. Pagi, no. 2, citing Mabillon, praises the same work as the Life of St. Anselm written by an anonymous author.

[Col. 0912D] [Note: [Col. 0912D] II III; Hegira 134, 29 July, feria 5] Zachary, 10 and 11.

St. Zachary replies to various inquiries of St. Boniface on the day before the Nones of November, in the thirty-second year of Constantine, Emperor II, indiction 5. Another letter also exists, written in the same indiction on the Nones themselves. Codex of Boniface; Pagi, no. 7, with Baron.

Aistulf, after capturing Ravenna, grants, in the very palace of the exarchs—the last of whom, Eutychius, had fled to Constantinople—a privilege confirming the possessions of the monastery of Farfa, on 4 July, in the third year of his reign and the fourth indiction. But four years later the Exarchate and many other territories were transferred to the jurisdiction of the Holy See through the benefaction of King Pipin. Bacchini, in Agnellus. See the preface and notes to Stephen II, otherwise called III.

Theophylact, patriarch of Antioch, dies; Theodore succeeds him. From Theophanes. Pagi, no. 10.

[Note: [Col. 0914A] III IV; Hegira 135, 18 July, feria 3] Zachary, 11; Stephen II, otherwise III, 1.

Since St. Zachary had occupied the see from 3 December 741 for ten years, three months, and thirteen days, he dies this year on 15 March. After an interval of twelve days, his successor Stephen II is consecrated on 26 March; Panvinio and Baronius call him Stephen III because they count among the pontiffs another Stephen who was elected after Zachary but not ordained.

Stephen, having solicited the emperor’s assistance against Aistulf, king of the Langobards, without success, turns to the king of the Franks and asks him for aid. Anastasius; Baronius; Pagi, no. 16. There Pagi says that the Roman pontiffs had not yet rejected the emperor of the East—a remarkable tolerance on the part of Christ’s vicar, following the example of Christ himself.

[Note: [Col. 0914B] IV and 383 I; Hegira 136, 7 July, feria 7] Stephen II, otherwise III, 1 and 2.

Harassed by the Langobards, Stephen implores God’s help through public and private prayers. Setting out for Francia, he leaves Rome on 14 October and departs from Ticinum on 15 November. Upon arriving in Francia, he is received with immense honor, the king’s sons going out to meet him, and so forth. Anastasius.

Anastasius, who had been intruded into the see of Constantinople by Leo in 730 and had been its usurper for twenty-four years, dies this year. Constantine, a heretical monk, succeeds him. Baronius and Pagi, no. 1.

After Lullus has been substituted for him as bishop of Mainz, St. Boniface returns to Frisia, where he governs the bishopric of Utrecht. Baronius under 755; Pagi there, and also under this year, no. 9 and following.

Privilege of Stephen for the abbots of the monastery of Nonantola, granted in perpetuity in the month of January. Italian Writers, vol. 1, part 2, p. 191.

[Col. 0914D] [Note: [Col. 0914D] I II; Hegira 137, 26 June, feria 4] Stephen II, otherwise III, 2 and 3.

On the Epiphany, St. Stephen is escorted by the king to the palace at Ponthion, and from there to Quierzy. At the monastery of St. Denis he falls ill, then recovers and carries out many functions of the pontificate in Gaul. He anoints King Pipin, his wife, and his sons, although it is uncertain whether he was confirming them with chrism or with the anointing of St. Boniface. He sets out with the army; after affairs have been settled by the victorious Pipin, he enters Rome at the close of the year. Anastasius; Annals; Baronius; Pagi, no. 4 and following.

The Chronicle of Isidore of Paz is completed. [Col. 0916A] This is the first of five writers on the kings of Spain published by Sandoval in 1605, and therefore not seen by Baronius. Pagi, no. 26.

[Note: [Col. 0916A] II III; Hegira 138, 15 June, feria 1] Stephen II, otherwise III, 3 and 4.

When Pipin, moved by the pontiff’s urgent prayers, returns to Italy, the audacity of the treaty-breaking Aistulf is suppressed, and the ancient donations made to the Church are restored, with new ones added. [Col. 0916B] Anastasius; Baronius.

Carloman, a monk, dies this year or the preceding one in Francia. Annals.

St. Boniface suffers martyrdom with his companions in Frisia. Thinking that he would find novices in the faith, he instead finds new executioners. From Othlonus; Mabillon and Pagi, no. 15 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0916B] III IV; Hegira 139, 3 June, feria 5] Stephen II, otherwise III, 4 and 5.

After the death of Aistulf and the restoration of peace throughout Italy, the pontiff writes to Pipin, asking him to ensure that what the Langobards had previously taken from the Holy See and the impious Aistulf had not returned be restored by the new king, Desiderius; to work for the Catholic faith of the East, attacked by Constantine; and to attend to many other matters, as may be seen in the Carolingian Code, letter 8, and in Pagi, no. 2 and following.

Theodore, bishop of Antioch, is sent into exile by the Saracens, and the Orthodox are harassed; they are forbidden to dispute with the Arabs concerning Christian doctrine. Theophanes, in Pagi, no. 5.

[Note: [Col. 0916C] IV and 384 I; Hegira 140, 24 May, feria 3] Stephen II, otherwise III, 5 and 6; St. Paul, 1.

After Stephen had occupied the see for five years and twenty-nine days from 26 March 752, he dies this year on 26 April. St. Paul succeeds him and is ordained on 29 May, after an interval of thirty-five—or thirty-two—days from the day of his predecessor’s deposition.

As soon as St. Paul ascends the Apostolic See, in two letters he renews the treaty of his predecessors with King Pipin and the Franks. Letters 13 and 22 of the Carolingian Code.

[Col. 0918A] [Note: [Col. 0918A] I II; Hegira 141, 13 May, feria 7] Paul, 1 and 2.

Paul leaves nothing unattempted in order to separate Pipin from Constantine. He testifies in many ways to every expression of affection toward Pipin and to vehement hatred toward Constantine. He also orders Marinus the priest, by whom he had been betrayed, to become a bishop in Pipin’s kingdom, thereby restoring him to Pipin’s favor. From the Carolingian Code. Pagi, no. 1 and following.

Paul sends an Antiphonary, a Responsorial, and other books of this kind to Francia, in accordance with the custom of the time, so that Roman chant might gradually be introduced into that kingdom. Letter 25 of the Carolingian Code.

Eadbert, king of Northumbria, warned by the pontiff to restore to Abbot Foldred the monasteries he had taken, abandons the kingdom to his son Osulf and becomes a canon of York. Pagi, no. 11.

[Note: [Col. 0918B] II III; Hegira 142, 3 May, feria 5] Paul, 2 and 3.

Sergius, bishop of Ravenna, asks the holy pontiff to order the monastery of St. Hilary at Galiata to be returned to his church. The pontiff therefore issues a diploma for its restoration, which Baron reports from Rubeus; Pagi, no. 1, corrects Rubeus’s chronological indications.

St. Othmar, second abbot of Saint Gall, dies. From Mabillon and other authors; Pagi, no. 2 and following, before him Baron. St. Pirmin also dies this year, on the third day before the Nones of November, the first abbot of Reichenau and founder of its monastery. Pagi, no. 8 and following.

The Christians in the East are harassed by the Saracens and are forbidden to prepare the public records of tax revenues. The Saracens are soon forced to restore this office to them, for they were unable to write down the numbers and totals. Theophanes.

[Note: [Col. 0918C] III IV; Hegira 143, 21 Apr., feria 2] Paul, 3 and 4.

There is an error concerning Easter among the Easterners: the Orthodox celebrate it on 6 April, while the heretics celebrate it on the 13th. [Col. 0918D] Theophanes. Pagi observes, no. 6, that those who followed the Victorian cycle, as the Gauls did, when in this year the lunar cycle had its first day on 1 April and the term of Easter on the 5th, did not wish to celebrate Easter on the following day, the 6th, but postponed it until the following Sunday, the 13th.

Moved by the envoys of King Pipin, Desiderius partly satisfies the pontiff by restoring much of what had been taken and promising to restore the remainder. [Note: [Col. 0918D] IV and 385 I; Hegira 144] Yet the holy pontiff, informing Pipin of this and of the agreement he had made with Desiderius, does not cease urging him to ensure that everything be restored to the Holy See. Carolingian Code, letter 21. Pagi, no. 3.

[Note: [Col. 0918D] 10 Apr., feria 6] Paul, 4 and 5.

The holy pontiff converts his ancestral house into a monastery and church for monks and dedicates it to God in honor of the holy pontiffs Stephen the Martyr and Sylvester the Confessor. It later passed to nuns, as it remains today, commonly called St. Sylvester in Capite. Baronius testifies that a privilege granted by the holy pontiff on that occasion is preserved among those nuns. Pagi, no. 1, corrects the chronological indication.

St. Garibald, the second bishop of Regensburg, dies approximately this year, after having held that see for twenty-two years, namely from 739, when St. Boniface divided Bavaria [Col. 0920B] into four bishoprics. It was customary in the church of Regensburg for monks and canons to succeed one another alternately. Authors, in Pagi, no. 7.

[Note: [Col. 0920B] I II; Hegira 145, 31 Mar., feria 4] Paul, 5 and 6.

The monks of the East, defenders of the sacred images, suffer persecution from the impious emperor. Metaphrastes; Baronius.

Pope Paul gives Pipin four monasteries: namely, St. Sylvester on Mount Soracte, St. Stephen the Martyr, St. Andrew the Apostle, and St. Victor, together with everything belonging to them, for the support of pilgrim monks and the poor of Christ, and so forth. Carolingian Code, letter 12. Pagi, no. 2.

Pipin founds the monastery of Prüm, situated about thirty-five miles from Trier, at the request of his wife Bertrada. It later flourishes with men distinguished both in monastic discipline and in learning; he places over it Assuerus, a holy man. The founding privilege exists, dated 13 August in the eleventh year of Pipin. Pagi, no. 3.

[Note: [Col. 0920C] II III; Hegira 146, 20 Mar., feria 1] St. Paul, 6 and 7.

Pipin sends Abbot Haribert and Count Donon to Rome, so that they might assure the pontiff, who feared the Langobards, of Pipin’s constancy in defending the Holy See. The pontiff, for his part, sends with them to Francia his own legates—John, subdeacon and abbot, and Peter, the first defensor—with congratulations on Pipin’s firm and steadfast disposition toward the Holy See. Carolingian Code, letter 18.

Willisvinda and her son, Count Cancor, found the monastery of Lorsch beyond the Rhine, in the diocese of Worms, and appoint Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, as its first abbot. From a diploma published by Marquard Freher. Pagi, no. 5.

[Note: [Col. 0920D] III IV; Hegira 147, 9 Mar., feria 6] St. Paul, 7 and 8.

As the persecution of the defenders of the sacred images intensifies, St. Stephen, at the age of forty-nine, is sent into exile on the island of Proconnesus in the Hellespont. [Col. 0922A] This occurs in the present year, although he had been condemned to it at Constantinople in the preceding year. Baron, under the preceding year; Pagi there, no. 1.

The three Eastern patriarchs—Theodore of Antioch, Theodore of Jerusalem, and Cosmas of Alexandria—celebrate a council with their suffragans on Pentecost. They subject to anathema the bishop of Epiphany, who had assented to the emperor’s impious position against the images. It is therefore clear that, apart from the patriarch of Constantinople, the other patriarchs of the East were defenders of the sacred images. Baron, under the preceding year; [Col. 0922B] Pagi there, no. 2.

[Note: [Col. 0922B] IV and 386 I; Hegira 148, 27 Feb., feria 4] St. Paul, 8 and 9.

The Langobards had ravaged Senigallia, killing the inhabitants and carrying off the booty. Desiderius, however, had informed Pipin through envoys that the Langobards had done nothing against the Roman Pontiff. When Paul learns this, he reports the truth of the matter to Pipin through his own legates. Carolingian Code, letter 14.

Another letter from this year, letter 24 of the Carolingian Code, announces to Pipin that six patricians, prepared with a huge fleet, were being sent by the emperor to Italy; that, reinforced by the Sicilian fleet, they were hastening to Rome and would proceed from there to Francia. In the same letter he reports the obstinacy of Desiderius, who had restored none of what he had promised to the Holy See and had even terrified him with a threatening letter. Pagi, no. 2 and following.

[Note: [Col. 0922C] I II; Hegira 149, 16 Feb., feria 1] St. Paul, 9 and 10.

Constantine the Monk, the heretical patriarch of Constantinople who had been elected in 753, is sent into exile after occupying the see for thirteen years. On 18 November, Nicetas, a eunuch of Slavic origin, succeeds him, contrary to the canons. Theophanes; Baronius; Pagi, no. 1.

Baronius gives a lengthy account of the cruelty of Constantine Copronymus and of his irreverence toward the sacred images and illustrious men. From the Miscellanies and Nicephorus.

Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, who had been placed in charge of the recently founded monastery of Lorsch in 763, dies this year on 6 March, according to the Martyrology of Metz. Pagi, no. 6. Egbert, archbishop of York, also dies this year, as Pagi agrees with Baron under 761, no. 4.

[Col. 0924A] [Note: [Col. 0924A] II III; Hegira 150, 5 Feb., feria 5] St. Paul, 10 and 11.

Paul, residing at the basilica of St. Paul, is seized by illness during the summer heat and dies on 28 June, after occupying the see for ten years and one month from 29 May 757. Before he breathes his last, Constantine is intruded, and he seizes the Apostolic See for one year and one month, namely until 29 July of the following year. Anastasius calls this period of usurpation an interpontificate. See the chronological notes on Stephen II and Paul.

The Council of Gentilly, near Paris, is held by order of Pipin. It discusses the procession of the Holy Spirit and the sacred images against the Greeks. Pagi does not doubt that the Frankish bishops condemned the Greek errors, but the council is not extant. Pagi under the preceding year, with Baron, no. 3.

[Note: [Col. 0924B] III IV; Hegira 151, 25 Jan., feria 2] Stephen III, otherwise IV, 1.

On 28 July of this year, the priests Sergius and Waldipert, entering Rome with the Langobards, depose Constantine the following day from the Apostolic See which he had seized for one year and one month. [Col. 0924C] Ten days later, namely on 7 August, Stephen III, otherwise IV, is consecrated pontiff. Anastasius.

Stephen II and Paul rightly called Pipin “Most Christian” in their letters: Pipin, the first Carolingian king, whose power had been transferred to him from the Merovingians by the authority of the Holy See; enlarger of the dominion of the Holy See, whose expansion had begun in the age of Charles Martel, when all Italy had fallen away from the impious Leo, the hater of the sacred images; their greatest defender against Constantine; and restorer of the Catholic religion, undermined by the Saracens in a great part of Aquitaine and overthrown by idolaters in Trans-Rhenane Francia. Carolingian Code.

[Col. 0923]

APPENDIX TO THE CHRONOLOGY

[Col. 0923D] I must now present, as I promised earlier, one or two examples of documents offered to us that are genuine and exceptionally illuminating for confirming the sequence and notation of dates—especially in the very distinguished collection of engraved stones belonging to the eminent prince, Cardinal Alessandro Albani, which we have so often presented and shall continue to present. If I call it a second Capitol, for restoring the consular fasti from the birth of Christ through contemporary monuments, the truth of the statement will be evident without any envy of the word. The same thing happened at the Roman Capitol: the munificence [Col. 0924D] and zeal of another prince, Cardinal Alessandro of the most serene Farnese family, recovered the ancient and original fasti that had been excavated in the nearby Forum. To his beneficence, generosity, and care every age owes the chief ornament of Roman history, both sacred and profane.

As an example, therefore, I shall select two stones from the immense number: one Latin, the other Greek. The first was discovered seven years ago on the shore of Antium, through the expense and care of the aforementioned Cardinal Albani, not without the joy and encouragement of the most holy father, who was seeking out these solid supports for history. The second had long been known and had been published more than one hundred and twenty years ago by Gruterus from a sheet sent by Pighius, itself taken from the books of Antiquities belonging to Cardinal Bernardino Maffei. In that copy, however, the transcriber rendered several lines so incorrectly that he completely concealed the precious evidence of the Tyrian era inscribed on that marble together with the consulship of Gallus and Flaccus, and therefore together with all the other epochs of the Eastern and Western peoples of the Roman world. Now, brought intact and preserved in its original form to Rome and deposited in the Albani museum, we see it exquisitely carved, and we present it opportunely in order to illuminate and establish all the eras by this double example, and to confirm them year by year in our chronological tables through the authority of genuine antiquities.

The first marble, therefore, inscribed in Latin letters and discovered among the ruins of ancient Antium, is a fragment of a larger tablet on which a Julian calendar was arranged, divided into twelve columns corresponding to the twelve months of the year. It was furnished day by day with the same letters indicating fasti, nefasti, and comitial days, as well as the age of the moon according to the octaeteric cycle. These features are found in the Farnesian calendar, published and explained by others and by us in the book on the Calendar and Cycle of Caesar.

Besides the principal Roman festivals and notices of games, this Antian calendar contains, assigned to their respective days, [Col. 0925C] the chief events of the emperors of the Julian family and of those adopted into it—their births and deaths—from Julius Caesar the dictator to the age of Claudius. Among these it is worth noting that 20 August is marked as follows: “Funeral rites of Lucius Caesar.” From this Antian calendar the day of Lucius Caesar’s death has now for the first time been established with certainty. Cardinal Norisius had come very close to determining it in his Cenotaphium Pis., p. 265, demonstrating that the death of that prince must have occurred on one of the days between 16 and 21 August, contrary to Salianus and Ricciolius, who extended it to December. The truth and success of the Norisian calculation would not be so important for chronology, as he himself writes, if it concerned only that prince. We regard the consequence that follows from it as far more valuable. It produces an increase of confidence that stimulates our industry in establishing the epochs of our pontiffs. For the dates of the deaths of the holy martyrs and pontiffs, commemorated annually by the Church, can likewise be fixed from the tables of depositions if selected monuments are added and compared. Thus, even before this marble had been seen, the day of Lucius Caesar’s death could rightly be derived from contemporary evidence in stones and coins, which Norisius had carefully examined. We similarly recognize that this method was used in determining the date of the battle of Pharsalus, although it is now declared for the first time in this same calendar fragment at the fifth day before the Ides of August, even though it was not previously unknown.

We regret that only part of this marble could be recovered: it contains the six later months of the Julian year, from July to December, and even these are incomplete, since the tablet, having been cut or broken into pieces in later times, has lost the final decade of days in each month.

The value of this monument, although broken, is increased by that portion of the tablet which extends above the calendar, [Col. 0926A] although that part too has been mutilated at the top. It displays a kind of fasti closely resembling municipal calendars, such as the Casinensis, published in our notes on St. Clement below, and others that can be seen in Gruterus, Fabrottus, and other antiquarians. For just as in colonies and municipalities it was customary, following the example of the Roman people, the Quirites, to have engraved each year the names of the ordinary consuls entering office at Rome on the Kalends of January, from whom the year received its name, and then to list either the names of the duumvirs in colonies, or of the quattuorviri for administering justice in municipalities, or of the quinquennales, as we see in the Casinensis calendar, so on this stone excavated from the ruins of Antium the Roman ordinary consuls are marked in continuous succession. The surviving fragment begins with the consulship of Gnaeus Acerronius Proculus and Gaius Pontius Nigrinus, the year of Tiberius’ death and the thirty-sixth year of the Christian era, and reaches the fifth consulship of Tiberius Claudius, with Orfitus as colleague, in the year 51 of the Christian era. Beneath each pair of consuls are engraved [Col. 0926B] the names of six magistri, or assistant magistri, who were elected each year to oversee or finance the games from among the corporate body of vernae—that is, slaves born in the household—or freedmen of the imperial household residing at the Antian retreat. I have shown in a letter on the Antian stone, on the testimony of ancient writers, that the emperors frequented this retreat from the age of Tiberius to that of Emperor Hadrian. These men were assigned to particular duties and crafts, apparently individually, within the imperial household.

The phrase “Festival Day of the Vernae” (*VERNARUM DIES FESTUS*) is very clearly visible, marked on that marble on 6 October. Among the magistri under the consulship of Tiberius Claudius Caesar and Vitellius II, in the forty-third year of the Christian era, we read: “Lysimachus, doorkeeper of his god Vernus” (*LYSIMACHUS AEDITUUS DEI SUI VERNANI*). The god Vernus was evidently the protective spirit and patron whom these corporate vernae had chosen and whom they celebrated on their special festival day. The crafts and occupations proper to the freedmen and vernae of the imperial household are commonly recorded beside the names of individuals. They include: baker (*PISTOR*), sauce-maker or cook (*JUSCULARIUS*), measurer (*MENSOR*), tile-maker (*TEGULARIUS*), gardener (*TOPIARIUS*), pavement-worker (*PAVIMENTARIUS*), steward (*DISPENSATOR*), under-steward (*SUBVILICUS*), keeper of furnishings (*A SUPELLECTILE*), keeper of Corinthian objects (*A CORINTHIIS*), and others. More distinguished offices also occur: painter (*PICTOR*), atrium attendant (*ATRIENSIS*), physician (*MEDICUS*), and librarian (*A BIBLIOTHECA*). We reserve the consideration of these matters for a special explanation of this monument, to be published in its proper place.

Here we need touch only upon the chronological advantages. The epoch of the battle and victory of Pharsalus is recorded there under the ninth day of the month of August: “The deified Julius conquered at Pharsalus” (*DIVUS JUL. PHARSALIAE VICIT*). Until now this had not been made certain by any monuments, although the highly fortunate genius of the eminent Cardinal Norisius, by comparing the authorities of ancient writers, had approached it very closely in his *Epoch of the Syro-Macedonians*, dissertation 3, chapter 5.

More important than all the chronological evidence recorded on this stone, however, is the succession of consuls, which shows that more than twenty pairs had been engraved on the marble over the half-year extending from July to December. Since the preceding half-year, from January to June, had likewise contained the same number and had been lost, it follows that more than forty consecutive years, with an equal number of pairs of consuls, would have been displayed to us from the first century of Christianity by this single stone, had it reached us intact. If to these could be added the nine consular colleges preserved, fortunately, on the Casinensis marble, from Capito and Rufus in the year 67 of Christ to the sixth consulship of Vespasian and the fifth of Titus in the year 75, and printed below in the notes on St. Clement, we would see the consular fasti for more than half a century of the Christian era confirmed by two marbles in the Albani museum. Several of that number nevertheless survive on the Antian stone, as the bronze tablet demonstrates; they were faithfully copied from the original and are to be inserted here as an example from the collection of Latin marbles relating to chronology.

From the Greek stones of the same museum of the eminent Cardinal Alessandro Albani I now produce another document and support for chronology, joining [Col. 0929A] the Tyrian epoch to the consular era. Once these are connected, all the remaining eras known in the East and West of the Roman world become no less certain.

[Col. 0927]

[Col. 0927] Surviving fragment of an inscription on a marble tablet, discovered in the ruins of ancient Antium through the care and expense of the eminent and reverend prince, Alessandro, Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church. It is preserved in his famous stone museum at Rome.

This Greek tablet contains a letter of the Tyrians residing at Puteoli, written on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Gallus and Flaccus—that is, in the year 174 of the Christian era—to the chief magistrate, senate, and people of their native city, namely the city of Tyre. They honor that city with all the titles of its dignity: “sacred and inviolable,” “living under its own laws,” “metropolis of Phoenicia,” and “Navarchis,” or naval city. Cardinal Norisius had likewise produced these titles ascribed to Tyre from this very marble in his discussion of the Syro-Macedonian eras, dissertation 4, chapter 3. There, as usual, he successfully established the beginning of the Tyrian era and clearly demonstrated it from the acts of the councils. He borrowed only the attribution of the titles from Gruterus’s edition. This was sensible, for the Pighian sheet from which Gruterus made his copy had obliterated the important evidence of the Tyrian era. That evidence likewise remains hidden in the recent edition of Gruterus’s work, although several authors who mention the same stone are cited there. None of them had been able to compare the original with the Pighian sheets. They would certainly have seen the complete and unmistakable evidence that the three-hundredth year of the Tyrian era, beginning in autumn, corresponded to the consulship of Tuscus and Gallus, in the year 174 of the Christian era. It is fitting to make this clear now that, through Cardinal Albani’s generosity, the marble brought to Rome gives illustrious testimony to the epoch of Tyre, so well established by Cardinal Norisius from the acts of the councils, and connects it with the Christian era and the Roman consular fasti. From this the safest correspondence with all the other chronological coordinates among Eastern and Western peoples may be deduced. The following observations, therefore, are found on the Puteolan marble.

The beginning of the inscription is the heading of a letter written on the tenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Tuscus and Gallus, by the Tyrians residing at the station at Puteoli, to the senate and their fellow citizens. It is engraved [Col. 0929C] in larger letters, although both the first and the latest edition of Gruterus prints the heading in small characters, as if it were a note rather than part of the inscription. The letters of the heading are expressed as follows:

**ΕΠΙϹΤΟΛΗ ΓΡΑΦΕΙϹΑ ΤΗ ΠΟΛΕΙ** etc.

“Letter written to the city,” etc.

After this letter, the Tyrians residing at Puteoli ordered the proceedings of the Tyrian senate, convened on this matter after receiving the letter, to be engraved. The meeting took place on the twenty-first day of the month Dios, which was the second month in the year of the Syro-Macedonians and Tyrians, as the aforementioned Cardinal Norisius demonstrates by providing a diagram of the Tyrian year and its months. From this it is known that the twenty-first day of Dios corresponds to 8 December in the Roman Julian calendar. The proceedings belong to the three-hundredth year, at its beginning, of the Tyrian era, reckoned from 19 October in the Roman calendar, since that was the customary beginning of the year.

The marble presents this era, expressed in the proceedings of the senate shortly after the receipt of the letter dated on the tenth day before the Kalends of August in the consulship of Tuscus and Gallus, as follows:

**ΑΠΟΙΚΙΩΝ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ ΑΧΘΕΙΣΗΣ . ΚΑ. ΔΙΟΤ. ΤΟΥ. ΕΤΟΥϹ. Τ.** etc.

[Col. 0930A] These words should be rendered in Latin as follows: “The senate of the colonists having been convened, on the twenty-first day of Dios, of the three-hundredth year,” etc.

In place of these words, preserved most clearly and completely on the marble, that careless transcriber, who had reported the inscription inattentively in the books of Antiquities of Cardinal Maffei’s library, inserted the following words, which provide no indication whatever of the Tyrian era:

**απολλων του λησαχθεισης δι ου ετους** — [materially uncertain Greek: “Apollo … of the … brought/led … through which year”].

It should therefore by no means seem surprising if foreign copyists of the chronology of the Roman pontiffs in the barbarous age—who were transcribing from the three patriarchal basilicas the years, months, and days of the tenure of each, depicted there and set more than sixty palms away from the eyes of those inspecting them—introduced so many errors in the numerals into their hastily copied catalogues, taken from a wall poorly illuminated through narrow windows. For antiquarians of our own highly cultivated age, and of the preceding century, while these studies flourished and still flourish, have corrupted entire words, altered the sequence [Col. 0930B] of expressions, and then reprinted them uncorrected without consulting the archetype, which they could, as we now can, bring not merely close to their eyes but even handle with their hands.

This single specimen sufficiently demonstrates the cause of the errors in catalogues copied in haste, especially by visitors from regions far removed from the City, and the usefulness and necessity of consulting monuments together with their archetype, even after repeated editions by scholars of our own age who have claimed the distinction of presenting antiquities accurately and faithfully. But let our discussion return to the date of the Puteolan inscription.

The year 174 of the common Christian era, marked by the consulship of Gallus and Flaccus, since it introduces the three-hundredth year of the Tyrian era, expressed in the proceedings of the senate summoned on the twenty-first day of the month Dii—that is, on 8 December according to the Julian calendar—in order to give a reply to the letter sent to it that same year by its fellow citizens at Puteoli on 23 July, shows that the beginning of the Tyrian era fell in the autumn of the year 126 before the Christian era. [Col. 0930C] From the proceedings of the Council of Tyre, recited in the ecumenical synod at Chalcedon, session 9, Cardinal Norisius had likewise most accurately inferred this beginning. The character of that era, therefore, confirmed by this clear testimony, is corroborated by the acts of the council and wonderfully illuminates the correspondence of Eastern epochs with Western ones.

Although Gruter’s edition was drawn from faulty transcripts and corrected by no one in later labors, it is nevertheless of the greatest assistance to us in transmitting the integrity of this inscription to posterity. For, within the century completed since Gruter’s first edition, several fragments of this Greek Puteolan marble were rashly cut away. Unless that edition had preceded them, we could not now present the complete inscription from the archetype. We shall indeed present it in full, indicating in square or capital letters—what are called majuscules—the letters preserved on the marble; the rest, on the fragments now lost, which in Cardinal Maffaeus’s time had been transcribed from the then-complete archetype and sent by Pighius to Gruter, we shall show in lowercase, non-capital letters.

[Col. 0929] **Letter written to the city** [Col. 0929] **of the Tyrians, the sacred, inviolable, and autonomous metropolis of Phoenicia and of other cities, and to the naval commanders. The senate, people, and inhabitants of the mother-city living at Puteoli send greetings, through the gods and through the fortune of our lord the emperor.**

Although there are also other *stationarii*—that is, members of a station or association—at Puteoli, all of whom most of you know to be more numerous than we are, our own community is distinguished from the others in wealth and size. In former times the Tyrians living at Puteoli, being numerous and prosperous, took care of this station. Now only a few of us remain, and, as we spend our resources on sacrifices and religious observances to our ancestral gods, whose temples are here being restored, we are unable to provide the annual payment of the station. Moreover, the expenses for the contest held at Puteoli have been added to us.

We therefore ask you to take care that the station always be maintained. It will remain so if, from the annual amounts assigned for its maintenance, you make [the sum of] 50,000 [uncertain] available for its financing. For we have reckoned the other expenses, and those incurred for the repair of the station on the sacred days of our lord the emperor, so as not to burden the city.

We remind you that no revenue is obtained here either from shipowners or from merchants for the station, as in royal Rome. [Note: Thus it is read on the marble, perhaps through an error of the stonecutter; it seems it should read: ΑΠΟΙΚΙΩΝ ΒΟΥΛΗΣ ΑΧΘΕΙΣΗΣ, “the council of the colonists having been convened,” etc.] We therefore entreat you to consider this matter and to take thought for our fortune.

Written at Puteoli, on 23 July, in the consulship of Gallus and Flaccus.

**Proceedings of the senate. The senate having been convened on the twenty-first day of the month Dii, in the three-hundredth year, while Callistratus was presiding, the letter of the Tyrians concerning the *stationarii* was read. It had been delivered by one of them, who had been appointed to take care of their interests: that they should provide 50,000 [uncertain] for sacrifices and religious observances to their ancestral gods, whose temples there were being restored, and that they were unable to pay the annual maintenance of the station, [lacuna], as well as the expenses for the contest at Puteoli, which had been assigned to them. For, after calculating the other expenses incurred for the repair of the station and for the sacred days of the Lord Emperor, they had determined that they should not burden the city, and they reminded the senate that no revenue came to them either from shipowners or merchants.**

In the royal city, Rome, after the reading, Philocles, son of Diodorus, said:

“The *stationarii* in Rome have always had the custom of providing those at Puteoli with 50,000 [uncertain]. They now ask that the *stationarii* at Puteoli enjoy these same benefits; or, if those in Rome are willing to provide them, they undertake to maintain the two stations under the same arrangement.”

They voted: “Well spoken,” said Philocles. “The *stationarii* at Puteoli are making a just request. It was done so before, and it should now be done so again. This is advantageous to the city.”

The decision was confirmed. The resolution was read.

A memorandum was submitted by Lachetes Primogeneia and Agathopolos, his son, Tyrian *stationarii* of the Tyrian station in the colony Augusta Puteoli, in which they declared that their mother-city provided [lacuna] for [lacuna], though it was difficult [lacuna].

[Col. 0931A] If the reader desires a third specimen confirming the chronology of especially important years from genuine documents preserved on stones in the museum of Cardinal Albani, he will find it at the beginning of the notes, where he will encounter a specimen taken from the archetype of the consulship most celebrated among us Christians, namely that of the two Gemini. I shall not repeat it here.

From these specimens several conclusions may be drawn, highly useful both for establishing chronology and for illuminating history. How many corollaries may be extracted from the Antiate Calendar for strengthening the history and chronology from the death of Tiberius to the fifth consulship of Claudius was indicated shortly before. The Puteolan stone, however, the letter of the Tyrians who maintained a station there, and the reply of the senate and decree of their metropolis teach us, among other things, about the use of the terms *station* and *stationarii*: elsewhere these terms are applied to military affairs, but here to an assembly, association, or corporation of members of that nation living in the Puteolan colony, with the right of performing ancestral rites; also about their exchange of official letters with their metropolis, and about the adaptation of the station-house “for the repair of the station” (*εἰς ἐπισκευὴν τῆς στατιῶνος*), for sacrifices and religious duties, “for sacrifices and religious observances” (*εἴς τε θυσίας καὶ θρησκείας*), on sacred days, “for the sacred days” (*εἰς τὰς ἱερὰς ἡμέρας*).

How much all this contributes to explaining the force of the word transferred to signify the custom and rite of the stations of our Christians, a word handed down from the age of the nascent Church to our own time, we readily understand from the idea attached to that word in this inscription. There will be no lack of opportunity to explain and apply it to our subject when we come to speak of stations.

Finally, from the third specimen of the stone marked with the celebrated notation of the consulship of the two Gemini, let each person consider how much support is thereby added to our ecclesiastical diptychs, in which, from the beginning of the Church’s foundation, we say that the days of the burial of the faithful—especially of holy martyrs and supreme pontiffs—were recorded through ministers chosen for that task.

For the sight of that stone makes it clear that, in the very year in which our Redemption was accomplished at Jerusalem, even the pagan Romans carefully arranged the funerals of their own people and entered them so accurately in necrological registers that the names of all who were buried were not only written in family records but also engraved on marble, with the precise consulship, month, and day, together with an indication of the wall and columbarium where the ashes of each were deposited and preserved.

When one has seen such a stone, a contemporary witness to the same practice flourishing at Rome, who would dare detract from the credibility of the registers of our Roman faithful, established in the same century in the City by notaries appointed by Pope Clement; by priests, deacons, subdeacons, clerics, and gravediggers devoted to collecting the Acts of the martyrs; by their successors, who were also employed to care for and deposit their bodies and relics; and by those who were to celebrate their annual sacred rites offered to God in their memory—as the letter of Cyprian and the custom and rite of the universal Church demonstrate everywhere among the nations?

Who, I say, would dare detract from the credibility of the registers of the burials of bishops, of the diptychs, and of the catalogues of martyrs, from which the earliest origin of pontifical history must be drawn, when he sees that it was familiar to all Romans of that same age to record the day, month, and year by means of consular tablets, on which the burial of each deceased person was entered?

Kinsmen, friends, heirs, and descendants, inclined by civic custom toward these acts of piety, when they were instructed in the Christian faith and elevated by the duties of divine charity, raised that natural piety toward their fellow believers—those who had taken the name of Christ together with them—into the faith of the resurrection, and consecrated it in a practice far more enduring than the Roman one.

These and similar conclusions, to be drawn from the specimens, prepare the way for the notes and observations in the Lives of the individual pontiffs.

## BLANCHINI’S NOTICE ON THE FOLLOWING TABLES

[Col. 0931]

I present two brief additions which seem to have been opportunely offered to us for confirming chronology and history. The first of these additions consists of three ancient inscriptions, engraved in the age of Gallienus on three bronze tablets, which were offered for sale this year, 1728, to the most eminent and most reverend prince Alexander Cardinal Albani. With his permission I copied them from the originals, and they are now published for the benefit of scholars.

Much may be drawn from them for confirming chronology and history. In them chronology will find confirmation of the Consular Fasti for the years 260 and 261 of the common Christian era, for which genuine contemporary documents had been lacking, so that both consular tablets could be completed. The reader will have a double monument of the second consulship of Publius Cornelius Saecularis and Gaius Junius Donatus, belonging to the year 260; while the third tablet will demonstrate the consuls of the following year, 261, the Emperor Gallienus for the fourth time and Volusianus.

History, too, will not lack a particular benefit from these tablets, since it will observe that barbarous orthography had already penetrated even into the suburban jurisdiction of Italy, although the style of official documents had not yet been deformed. What seems especially worthy of attention is the second tablet, line thirteen, where the name and use of a *diploma* occur—namely, the co-optation of a patron by means of a *duplomum*. I have found no older example of this matter or of the term recorded in bronze or marble. Students of diplomatics will find here material for their investigations.

Geographers, too, will not be deprived of some fruit for which they have hoped concerning the municipalities of Ostra and Sentinum mentioned in these tablets. Antiquarians will water their own plots from this source, whether they examine the formulas for co-opting patrons or the honorary rite of offering through envoys a bronze tablet after the authority of the diploma had already been granted by public decree.

This observation concerning the barbarous deformation of words and letters, already entering public documents under Gallienus, fits conveniently into our Anastasius work. It should therefore cause no surprise that a later corruption followed in writing, pronunciation, and dictation, which the centuries immediately after Gallienus introduced into public records—for example, in the Cornutian charter, in the donations and concessions of the Goths and Lombards, and in writings of this kind, by which we have attempted to illuminate pontifical history.

Here, then, is the inscription of the three plates that I mentioned.

The first is two Roman palms high and one palm nine ounces wide; to its height is added a raised triangular pediment nine ounces high.

[Col. 0933]

**In the second consulship of Publius Cornelius Saecularis and the second consulship of Junius Donatus, on the Kalends of July.**

At Sentinum, when a numerous body of the guild of the Sentinate craftsmen had assembled in its own hall, with Gaius Julius Martialis and Gaius Casidius Rufinus as *quinquennales*, and with them reporting that in the past the most distinguished body had always acted so that, out of affection for its own distinction, it might bestow honour on each person found worthy and deserving, especially in honour and dignity [in connection with] Memmia Victoria, once [of] the character and memory of a woman, mother of our guild [the text is corrupt]; and that the name of her household had advanced through the order of its lineage, [they proposed] that all should be called into our body as patrons in our college.

It was desirable that all the members of the corporation should appear safe and sound in our number. And since the splendid man Corellius Fuscus ought to be patron of the guild, following the example of the piety of his parents and the honor shown by his mother, therefore, if it seemed good to all, that a bronze tablet should be offered to him—

**Q. F. P. D. E. R. I. C. C.** [traditional abbreviation; expansion uncertain]

“It is glorious that the report of the good and excellent men, the *quinquennales* of the college, has been made, and therefore, since Corellius Fuscus is splendidly born, so that he may understand the measure of our honor and since it is necessary that a bronze tablet decorated with inscriptions be offered to him, we ask that he deign to receive this offering with willing spirit, and that envoys be appointed for this purpose who may honorably escort [it]: Neratius Ampliatus, Orpius Vertalis, Aemilius Victor, Bebidius Istus, Casidius Martialis, Julius Martialis, Casidius Rufinus, Bebidius Januarius, Aetrius Romanus, Casidius Clementinus, Aetrius Verna, Vassidenus Favor, Casidius Justissimus, Satrius Verecundus, Statius Velox, Veturius Celerinus.”

The second is two and a half palms wide and two palms three ounces high, with an added pediment one palm high.

**In the second consulship of Publius Cornelius Saecularis and the second consulship of Junius Donatus, on the fourth day before the Nones of December.**

At Ostra, in the municipality, when the members of the guild of the Centonenses had assembled in their hall and had come together for the purpose of writing, and when there, with Julius Vessidius Fortunatus as *quinquennalis*, the words of the whole body’s agreement had been set forth, [they declared] how much love and generosity Marcus N[?] Carenus Vibianus had shown and how he had adorned the hall; and that, since their resources were unequal to his benefactions, they ought to seek means of rewarding his affection.

But the common vote had found a particularly suitable and praiseworthy plan: that we should honor Corellius Victorinus, belonging to his family and honors, and should present him with a gift, and should enroll him as an enduring patron, already long ago chosen by public testimony.

[Col. 0935] **Prolegomena to Anastasius, Roman–Vatican edition**

If, therefore, it seems good to all, let a bronze tablet be presented containing the testimony of our affection toward him, and therefore [the relevant body] has decreed that it should be pleasing to offer to Corellius Victorinus, our patron, a bronze tablet containing the words of our decree, through Julius Vessidius Fortunatus, Cornelius Tertius, the *quinquennales*, Publilius Maximinus, Aurelius Ursinus, Vacerinus Istus, Cocceius Mercurialis, the chief priest Octavius Clemens, Petronius Felix, Vessidius Philoquirus, Octavius Taurus, Satrenus Superus, Vessidius Verecundus, Statius Faustus, as envoys.”

The third is two palms three ounces wide and two and a half palms high, with a perpendicular pediment one palm high.

*(Where an asterisk has been placed, it indicates that in the original the wording was deformed and barbarously engraved.)*

**In the fourth consulship of the Emperor Gallienus Augustus and the consulship of Volusianus, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of September.**

At Sentinum, in the dining hall of the house of the guild, when the members of the corporation had assembled, with the successors of the same college present and with Casidius Severus, father of our [lord?], and Helbius Peregrinus, kinsman, reporting:

“Since it is appropriate, in view of the frequent benefactions and affection of love which our [lord] has shown, to be present and to reward generosity, just as opportunity has offered testimony, therefore, if it seems good to all, let Corellius Fuscus, a splendid decurion of our fatherland and also patron of three principal guilds, and Vesia Martina, his wife and patroness, and also Corellius Sabinus, their son, who were long ago co-opted as patrons of our corporation by a *duplomum*, now receive from the guild a bronze tablet of patronage, so that the honor may become known according to merit and in return for their merits.

**Q. F. P. D. E. R. I. C. C.**

Because in the past we have received the benefactions which Corellius Fuscus, our patron, Vesia Martina, our patroness, and Corellius Sabinus, their son, have bestowed upon us with affection, we now also hope that in the future similar benefactions, which we now experience, will proceed perpetually from their household with equal affection. And therefore we agree with the report of the good and excellent men, Casidius Severus, father of our [lord], and Helbius Peregrinus, kinsman, and, in order to reward their benevolence, we have resolved that they should deign to accept the honor offered to them more splendidly and handsomely, and that the decree should be written out on a bronze tablet and proceed from us to them. We have also decided that envoys should be appointed to escort this tablet honorably:

Satrius Acilius, Satrius Clemens, Vessidenus Megellinus, Vassidenus Verinus, Casidius Severus, Aelidius Primus, Helidius Peregrinus, Brittius Maximus, Aelius Honoratus, Prolivius Hilarinus, Aetrius Terminalis, Gavius Felicissimus, Satrius Januarius, Casidius Romulus, Aetrius Verna, Satrius Vpsus.”

[Col. 0937]

# ANALYTICAL TREATISE BRIEFLY ENCOMPASSING THE PRE-EMINENCE AND AUTHORITY OF THE HOLY SEE

A dogmatic history of that same Holy See, from its foundation to the pontificate of Saint Leo the Great. Written in the French language by the Caesarean archbishop, the distinguished Sommier, and translated into Latin by D. Cajetan Cenni, priest of Pistoia.

[Col. 0937A] Both Sacred Scripture [Note: [Col. 0937C] Wisdom 6:4; Romans 13:1; 1 Peter 13.] and the constant tradition of the Fathers affirm that the power of kings and princes over the peoples subject to them proceeds uniquely from God. Yet no dominion on earth has its institution and jurisdiction more clearly displayed in the oracles of Scripture, nor its exercise more fully confirmed by the authority of the Fathers, than that of blessed Peter and the Roman pontiffs who succeeded him. Whatever could be drawn from these two sources down to our own times, we shall present here in a condensed form, using both analytical and historical method, so that from it we may complete the dogmatic history of the Holy See.

## ARTICLE I. Arguments concerning the constitution and attributes of the Holy See drawn from Sacred Scripture

Sacred Scripture consists of the Old and New Testaments. The Old Testament foreshadowed the image of the New, and the Synagogue [Col. 0937B] of the Church [Note: [Col. 0937C] 1 Corinthians 10:11; Hebrews 10:1]. Its various ministers prefigured the ministers of the latter; consequently, the high priest of the Jews indicated the supreme pontiff of the Christians. These symbolic correspondences provided by Scripture have been made clearer than light itself by subsequent events.

The Jewish high priest possessed a fixed and supreme tribunal [Note: [Col. 0937C] Deuteronomy 17; 2 Chronicles 19; Sirach 45:8, 11] for passing judgment on all matters concerning religion, for opening up the true meaning of the laws, and for definitively settling every controversy. In the same way, the supreme pontiff of the Christians uses a stable and supreme see, since he exercises the same authority in the Church.

At times, in the Synagogue, that same priest combined temporal administration with spiritual authority. Once the Church had been constituted and strengthened, when the empire of Rome—which had dominated almost all things—had completely perished after being divided among many kings, divine Providence made the successors of Peter absolute and supreme rulers even of temporal affairs in the portion of places and peoples where their see is situated.

Thus the royal priesthood, foreshadowed both by written law and by nature—in which the fathers, and later the elders of the patriarchal family, exercised both priestly and royal office—is found complete in every respect. Moreover, as the head and father of all Christians, freed from the power of all princes of this world, he can exercise his authority with greater dignity and liberty, entirely unsuspected by anyone.

In the New Testament, where the foundation of the Church is discussed, it first appears that Peter and each of his successors are designated as the head and foundation of the Church. He himself, previously called Simon, receives the name Peter [Note: [Col. 0937C] John 1:42; Mark 3:16; Luke 6:14; Matthew 10:2]. He everywhere occupies the first place. Through him the eternal Father reveals Jesus Christ to humanity as the Son of the living God.

The Savior makes Peter and his successors sharers in his own dignity [Note: [Col. 0937C] Matthew 16:13 and following], he himself being the cornerstone of the Church, through whose grace it is established so that the gates of hell may not prevail against it. Finally, he gives to Peter and his successors the keys of the kingdom of heaven—that is, the supreme power of governing the Church.

The Savior himself testifies that he prayed for them, so that their faith might not fail [Note: [Col. 0938C] Luke 22:31–32], and even that they might strengthen their brethren in faith.

After his resurrection, before ascending into heaven [Note: [Col. 0938C] John 21:15 and following], the same divine Savior appointed Peter and his successors as supreme governors of the whole Church, when he commanded them to feed the lambs and sheep, by which the entire body of the Church is constituted.

The lambs are the Christian peoples, and the sheep—the mothers of the lambs—are the various pastors, to whose care different portions of the flocks are entrusted. Therefore, to entrust lambs and sheep, that is, peoples and pastors, to Peter and his successors so that they may guard them is equivalent to declaring them supreme governors of the whole Church, whose one fold depends upon one shepherd [Note: [Col. 0938C] John 10:16].

No sooner had Jesus Christ ascended into heaven than Peter began to perform his office [Note: [Col. 0938C] Acts 1:5; John Chrysostom, Homily 3 on Acts]. While he held a large part of the nascent Church gathered at Jerusalem, preparing it to receive the Holy Spirit, he was able to have another apostle appointed in the place of the traitor Judas, so that all the seats of that sacred college might be filled.

After Pentecost, Peter was the first of all to begin preaching the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0938C] Acts 2 and following], unlocking the mysteries of the Old Testament [Col. 0938C] in which Jesus Christ had been foreshadowed. He was the first to proclaim the word of God and, after announcing it once and again, to cause eight thousand people to be converted to God and baptized. He was the first to demonstrate himself the supreme dispenser of graces by performing miracles, and to show himself the judge of sins by inflicting anathemas [Note: [Col. 0938C] Saint John Chrysostom, Homily 87 on John].

Peter himself created James the Less bishop of Jerusalem; and Paul, not long after his conversion, approached him as the head of the Church [Note: [Col. 0939A] Galatians 1 and 2; Saint Ambrose on the same passage]. When the Gospel had already spread widely throughout Judea and the neighboring provinces, Peter visited the Churches established both by the other apostles and by other heralds of the Gospel, and extended them immeasurably, winning entire villages and districts everywhere for Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0939D] Acts 9; Chrysostom, Homily 21 on Acts].

Moreover, Peter was the first to announce salvation to the Gentiles, just as he had first announced it to the Jews. Since he was to become the common father and supreme shepherd of both peoples, he opened the door of the fold to each and sought the grace of divine adoption for them. Finally, when he was held in prison, bound for the faith, and was scarcely prevented from providing the Jews with a spectacle most pleasing to them through his death, the Church—something recorded as never having been done for any other apostle—became particularly anxious for the safety of him as its head and ordered public prayers for his deliverance [Note: [Col. 0939D] Acts 12:5].

## ARTICLE II. The constitution and jurisdiction of the Holy See under Saint Peter’s pontificate are established by tradition

[Col. 0939B]

Before Peter came to Rome, which he knew had been destined by God to be the supreme see of the Catholic Church, he established his chair at Antioch, the metropolis of the eastern Roman Empire, a city which held the leading place among the other cities of that great empire after Rome and Alexandria.

This visible head of the Church imitated, in establishing the principal sees, the form displayed to it by divine Providence in founding the kingdoms of this world, understanding especially that this would be useful for the doctrine, growth, and permanence of the faith, as well as for the Church’s external government. Accordingly, for the particular oversight of the flock of Jesus Christ, which was to be composed of the peoples of the whole world, he established three superior sees: Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch; besides the general oversight of all, established in one of those three sees, which his successors would occupy.

He raised the patriarchal see of Antioch before the others, since the holy apostle first encountered that renowned city on his journey. Scripture does not speak openly of the establishment of this see, merely omitting it, as Saint Jerome testifies [Note: [Col. 0939D] Saint Jerome, Book 1, Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians, chapter 2]. Nevertheless, tradition confirms it with arguments so firm that it cannot be called into doubt.

Saint Ignatius [Note: [Col. 0939D] Saint Ignatius, Letter to the Antiochenes], Peter’s successor after Evodius in the same patriarchal see, and Saint John Chrysostom [Note: [Col. 0939D] Chrysostom, Eulogy of Saint Ignatius], himself born in that city, committed this fact to writing. All the chroniclers commended the epoch thus established to posterity, as may be seen in the chronicles of Eusebius of Caesarea [Note: [Col. 0939D] Eusebius, Chronicle, years 38 and 44], the Alexandrian chronicle [Note: [Col. 0939D] Alexandrian, year 36], Nicephorus [Note: [Col. 0939D] Nicephorus, at the end], and Ado [Note: [Col. 0939D] Ado, sixth age].

The supreme pontiffs Damasus, Saint Leo [Col. 0939D] the Great, Gelasius, and Saint Gregory the Great show this most plainly. Long before Gregory’s time, the Church consecrated the enduring memory of this event by instituting a feast celebrated every year on the seventh or eighth day before the Kalends of March.

The Great Synod of Nicaea [Note: [Col. 0939D] Council of Nicaea, canon 6] speaks of the authority of the patriarchal see of Antioch over its provinces as of a right attested by all antiquity. Its origin, therefore, should be attributed to nothing other than the foundation of the Church itself. As for the boundaries of its jurisdiction, the ancients acknowledge that it once embraced everything that was called the East of the Roman Empire [Note: [Col. 0939D] Saint Jerome, Letter 61]—namely, fifteen provinces, which afterward obeyed one of the prefects of the praetorium. It is also certain that, as the number of Churches increased over time, it extended its boundaries farther toward the East.

After establishing the see at Antioch, the prince of the apostles founded the Roman Church. The distinction was that, besides founding the patriarchate of the whole West at Rome, he also established there the primacy over all the Churches.

This had been foretold once from the age of Moses [Note: [Col. 0940D] Numbers 23 and 24], and again by the prophet Daniel [Note: [Col. 0940D] Daniel 7:23 and following]. The holy Fathers, especially Augustine, observed certain oracles of the pagans as signs foretelling both the spiritual and temporal empire of the Romans [Note: [Col. 0940D] Cicero, On Divination, 110 and 112]. Such are the passages supplied from Cicero’s books On Philosophy, from the histories of Titus Livy [Note: [Col. 0940D] Titus Livy, decade 1, book 1], and of Dionysius of Halicarnassus [Note: [Col. 0940D] Dionysius of Halicarnassus, book 2], and from the poems of Virgil [Note: [Col. 0940D] Virgil, Eclogue 4].

It should further be observed that Rome, since it lies at the center of the region that is easily the leading one among all the lands of the world, enjoys commerce with every nation [Note: [Col. 0940D] Saint Augustine, City of God, books 5 and 10]; that its empire was then spread far and wide, at the time when the Gospel had to be preached to every creature; and that the mighty genius of the Romans, whenever the matter concerned ruling, was a sure prelude to the religion which God had determined to establish there.

Peter, to whom supreme administration of all matters relating to religion had been entrusted, was not unaware of the plan of divine wisdom. To carry it out, he went to Rome [Note: [Col. 0940D] Saint Leo, Sermon 1, On the Feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul].
