Several years later, the divine apostle Paul, writing to the Romans, briefly embraced what the prince of the apostles had accomplished there and supplied an analysis of the Church founded by him. “Your faith,” he says, “is proclaimed throughout the whole world. Your obedience”—to the Gospel of Christ—“has been spread everywhere” [Note: [Col. 0940D] Romans 1:8, 14, 15, 16, 19]. “You are full of charity and of the knowledge of perfect faith, so that you are able to teach and strengthen one another by example.”

Saint Peter wrote at Rome the first canonical Epistle that survives, which should be regarded as the first of the Decretals [Note: [Col. 0940D] Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 15; Saint Jerome on Mark]. For, besides transmitting the mysteries of the faith and moral precepts, it also prescribes points of discipline appropriate to those earliest times.

In the same Epistle he approves the Gospel book written by his own disciple, Saint Mark, containing what Mark had heard him preach. By proposing this book to the Catholic Church as divinely inspired, he demonstrates through such an act of jurisdiction the authority of the supreme pontiff to define everything that serves as a norm for the faith and for forming the morals of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0940D] Eusebius, cited passage].

[Col. 0940D] He supplied another proof of supreme pontifical authority when he sent Saint Mark to Alexandria, so that in Peter’s name he might establish there another patriarchal see of the Church [Note: [Col. 0940D] Gelasius, Decree on Apocryphal Books]. Alexandria held the leading place in the Roman Empire after Rome; therefore, for the reasons given above, Peter conferred the same place upon its bishop in the ecclesiastical order.

Moreover, he sent other disciples of his into various provinces of the West, so that they might establish metropolitan and suffragan bishoprics there. The ancients recognized that no Church had been founded except those established by Peter and his successors [Note: [Col. 0941D] Innocent I, to Decentius].

He was the first to attend and preside over the council assembled at Jerusalem. After the matters under discussion had been debated, he rose [Note: [Col. 0941D] Acts 15:7 and following] and said that he had been chosen by God before the others so that the Gentiles might hear from his mouth the word of the Gospel and learn their definition of what had to be believed.

Then, pronouncing judgment, he defined that the law of Moses was not necessary in the Church, and that human beings were saved through the faith and grace of Jesus Christ. Then, as Scripture testifies, the entire multitude kept silent: that is, according to Saint Peter’s judgment, no one thereafter dared to argue. Only some of the leading men testified with their own mouths to the truth of the words they had heard and declared how the council’s decrees should be arranged.

Peter and Saint Paul carefully observed what had been decreed in that synod. At times, however, they used certain legal ceremonies so that, by showing some indulgence toward the Jews, they might convert them more effectively to the faith of Christ.

It was not expedient to abolish all the precepts of Moses suddenly, nor were Jews newly converted to be entirely forbidden to follow them. It was enough to declare that those from the Gentiles who were converted to the faith of Christ were not bound by such laws, so that they might gradually grow obsolete and the Synagogue happily come to an end.

When Paul rebuked Peter for observing some of these rites, it happened because the prince of the apostles’ indulgence toward the Jews was harming the Gentiles in their still-new situation, since they drew an occasion of scandal from the very place where the apostle had not suspected that one would arise [Note: [Col. 0941D] Galatians 2:31 and following].

From the synod Peter returned to Rome, both to complete the work he had undertaken and to cement with his own blood the Holy See whose foundations he had laid. Athanasius testifies that this plan, begun by the apostle [Note: [Col. 0941D] Saint Athanasius, Apology for His Flight], was completed with joy.

Here he wrote his final Epistle and sent it to all the faithful of Christ, as a testament and final monument of his paternal love toward all believers, whose father he himself was [Note: [Col. 0941D] 2 Peter 1:20–21]. In it he explains how the interpretation of Scripture ought to be carried out. He commends the Epistles of Saint Paul, acknowledging that they are difficult to understand and can easily be twisted into wicked meanings by the unlearned [Note: [Col. 0941D] 2 Peter 2:15–16].

He records a distinguished victory over Simon Magus, the most deceitful of all men, and a much more distinguished victory over Satan, who had imposed an exceedingly savage yoke upon this city, mistress of the nations, through the greatest disgrace [Note: [Col. 0941D] Saint Augustine, Against Fulgentius the Donatist, chapter 23].

In this city the vicar of Jesus Christ accumulated the fruits of his labors with the same result as the Savior himself had done at Jerusalem, crucified like him outside the city on a mountain [Note: [Col. 0941D] John, final chapter, verses 18 and 19].

Thus, together with the same Savior, he fulfilled Daniel’s prophecy, which said that the stone that appeared so small to human beings, cut from the mountain without hands, struck the great and lofty statue erected at the foot of the mountain and reduced it to something like the chaff of a summer threshing floor [Note: [Col. 0941D] Daniel 2:34–35]. [Col. 0942A] But the stone that had struck the statue became a great mountain and filled the whole earth.

## ARTICLE III. The tradition of the second and third centuries concerning the authority and jurisdiction of the Holy See

The holy Fathers regarded the uninterrupted succession of the Roman pontiffs at every time as the strongest proof of the authority of the Holy See. For witnesses to this matter, see Tertullian [Note: [Col. 0942D] Tertullian, On the Prescription Against Heretics; Saint Irenaeus, books 3 and 4; Saint Cyprian, letter 69; Saint Augustine, Against the Fundamental Epistle], Saints Irenaeus and Cyprian, and others.

Saint Irenaeus reviews all the pontiffs by numbering them, those who governed the Church down to his own time. Eusebius of Caesarea follows the same succession down to his own age, namely, the beginning of the fourth century. Both of them passed over Saint Cletus in silence, while Eusebius also omitted Saint Marcellus.

Many other writers have arranged the following list in this order:

Blessed Peter; Saints Linus, Cletus, Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, Alexander, Xystus, Telesphorus, Hyginus, Pius, Anicetus, Soter, Eleutherius, Victor, Zephyrinus, Callixtus, Urban, Pontian, Anterus, Fabian, Cornelius, Lucius, Stephen, Xystus II, Dionysius, Felix, Eutychian, Caius, Marcellinus, Marcellus, Eusebius, and Melchiades.

Very little, indeed, has come down to us concerning the earliest pontiffs, since the worshipers of idols, while persecuting the Church, seized many of the ancient records that spoke about them. It is said that very many bishops were created by them—on which point there can be no doubt—in order that they might preside over the Churches being established throughout the Western patriarchate by the authority of those same pontiffs [Note: [Col. 0942D] *Liber Pontificalis*, under the name of Damasus, in the entries on Linus and the others]. Saint Linus ordained fifteen bishops. Saint Cletus established twenty-five presbyters at Rome; Evaristus later increased their number and divided them, together with seven deacons whom he had created, into synaxes, which were called *titles* [Note: [Col. 0942D] Saint Irenaeus, Book III *Against Heresies*, chapter 3; Eusebius, Book III of the *History*, chapter 12].

[Col. 0942C] The blessed Clement wrote a letter to the Corinthians, which the Fathers judged to be the most powerful evidence of the authority of the Roman Church: it was intended to preserve peace and concord among the faithful, to strengthen those wavering in the faith, and finally to proclaim openly the things handed down by the apostles. Nothing is advanced concerning the other works attributed to Saint Clement, since some regard them as spurious.

Alexander and Xystus added certain things to the liturgy, as did Telesphorus, who, by a promulgated law, confirmed the forty-day fast, already observed by tradition [Note: [Col. 0942D] Eusebius, *Chronicle*]. Hyginus expelled the heretic Cerdon from the Church and forbade him access to it, since, after he had preached his errors in the provinces, he concealed them at Rome. Once finally exposed, he gave the appearance of rejecting them, while in the meantime he continued secretly to profess them [Note: [Col. 0942D] Irenaeus, Book III, chapter 4]. Pius issued a decree concerning the celebration of Easter on Sunday [Note: [Col. 0942D] Eusebius, *Chronicle*; the same, *History*, 5.24].

During the pontificate of Anicetus, his successor, Polycarp—easily the most distinguished among all the contemporary bishops of Asia for holiness and learning, since he had been a disciple of the blessed [Col. 0942D] John—came to Rome to consult the pontiff about matters relating to discipline. On this matter they agreed that no one should depart from the established practice.

Saint Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, testifies that the Roman pontiffs were always regarded in the Church as the common fathers of all, not only with respect to spiritual life but also with respect to temporal life [Note: [Col. 0942D] The same, ibid., IV.22], since they never failed to provide the faithful with whatever was necessary to sustain life when, wherever they might be in the world, they were harassed by the afflictions of persecution on account of the Catholic faith.

During the pontificate of Eleutherius, Saint Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons, testifies [Note: [Col. 0943D] Saint Irenaeus, Book III, chapter 3] that, in order to reduce to extremity the audacity of heretics and schismatics in the provinces and to prevent them from corrupting morals, recourse was had to the apostolic see as the trustee of the doctrine committed to him, from which an unimpaired tradition flows down to later generations through the succession of the supreme pontiffs. He also testifies that, by the constant judgment of all, that see was established as unique and supreme, like a perpetual and illustrious monument, so that at no time would there be in the Church any other faith than that which the apostles had handed down.

The Montanists, whose plague was spreading through Asia, set out for the same see in order to obtain letters of communion, by which they might defend themselves against various attacks; and, actually pretending to be Catholics, they obtained them [Note: [Col. 0943D] Tertullian, Book *Against Praxeas*]. But when their fraud was finally detected, the pontiff declared the letters that had been granted invalid and inflicted an anathema on those impious men. It is reported that this same pontiff sent two preachers of the Gospel to the king of Greater Britain, through whom he and all the peoples subject to him received the Christian faith.

Pontiff Victor removed Theodorus the leather-worker (*coriarius*) from the communion of the faithful and condemned his teaching [Note: [Col. 0943D] *Liber Pontificalis*; Bede, *On the Six Ages of the World*; Ado, *Chronicle*]. Florinus and Blastus, presbyters of the Roman Church, met with the same fate. Because of their error and schism, and because they contended that Easter ought to be celebrated with the Jews on the fourteenth day of the moon of March, whichever day of the week it happened to fall on [Note: [Col. 0943D] Theodoret, *Heretical Fables*, Book II], Victor decreed that the decree of Pius, his predecessor, should be observed throughout the entire Christian world: Easter was to be celebrated on Sunday, following the fourteenth day of the moon.

Only the bishops of Asia Minor, seeking to preserve the custom tolerated by the pontiff Anicetus, refused [Col. 0943C] to obey this new law of Victor [Note: [Col. 0943D] *Pontifical Book*, under Victor]. Therefore the pontiff would immediately have struck them with an anathema, had Saint Irenaeus not averted the blow. The Council of Nicaea later demonstrated most clearly how rightly the pontiff had resolved to proscribe the discipline of the Asiatics in this matter [Note: [Col. 0943D] Eusebius, Book V of the *History*, chapter 22 and following]. On the same occasion, by the richest authorities of the holy Fathers, it is shown [Note: [Col. 0943D] Rufinus, *History*, Book II, chapter 6], contrary to the opinion of certain more recent writers, that to be excluded from communion with the apostolic see is equivalent to being removed from the unity of the Catholic Church.

Zephyrinus condemned the heresies of Marcion, Praxeas, Sabellius, and other heretics, against whom Tertullian inveighed [Note: [Col. 0943D] Optatus of Milevis, Book [lacuna]]. Tertullian, who shortly afterward professed the ravings of Montanus and became entangled in the same sentence of condemnation that the pontiff pronounced against the madness of that arch-heretic, was likewise condemned. Moreover, when Tertullian had become an excessively rigorous defender of innocence and declared that the crimes of fornication and adultery were more serious than those for which people could be absolved by the Church, and did not withdraw from that opinion, he was condemned again [Note: [Col. 0943D] Tertullian, *On Fasting* and *On Modesty*].

Callixtus instituted the fast of the four seasons of the year [Note: [Col. 0944D] *Liber Pontificalis*]. Fabian confirmed the sentence issued in the African council against the heretic Privatus [Note: [Col. 0944D] Saint Cyprian, Letter 59]. Origen sent him his profession of faith; indeed, as some historians report, he also went to the apostolic see in order to refute in person the errors that were being alleged against him [Col. 0944A] [Note: [Col. 0944D] Eusebius, *History* VI.19]. There are likewise those who maintain that this pontiff imposed penance on the emperor Philip, whom not a few of the ancients count among the Christians.

After Fabian’s death, the holy see remained vacant for sixteen and a half months because of the extreme ferocity of the emperor Decius. According to Cyprian [Note: [Col. 0944D] Saint Cyprian, Letter 55], Decius would have tolerated a rival to the empire less unwillingly than a pontiff at Rome [Note: [Col. 0944D] In the same author, Letter 8]. During this period of widowhood, the Roman see displayed the vigilance, authority, and ardent zeal proper to a common father, governing Christians living both at Rome and in the provinces with the best counsels. Meanwhile, as it awaited its bridegroom, it established salutary laws that were promulgated throughout the Catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0944D] The same, Letter 55].

Nevertheless, although the tyrants left nothing unattempted to prevent the election of the supreme pontiff, Cornelius was raised to the chair of Peter—that is, to use Cyprian’s words, to the sublime height of the priesthood [Note: [Col. 0944D] The same]. Novatian raised a schism against this pontiff; he was the first antipope. As commonly happens, he joined heresy to the schism, teaching that the Church could not reconcile those who had fallen after baptism or admit them to communion in the sacred mysteries, however greatly they might repent, since God had reserved that judgment exclusively to himself and had shared his authority in this matter with no one else.

Cornelius therefore assembled a council against him. After condemning his heresy and schism, he separated Novatian and all who shared his opinion from communion with the Church [Note: [Col. 0944D] Eusebius, *History* VI.35]. The bishops of the universal Church participated in this broadly issued judgment and unanimously approved it.

Cyprian [Note: [Col. 0944D] Cyprian, Letter 55], above all others, sharpened his pen against the false pontiff, demonstrating with the greatest clarity that, since Jesus Christ had established one Church and one wholly united episcopate, whose ministry is exercised by bishops distributed throughout the various provinces entrusted to their care; and since the one whom God had chosen and inaugurated, to whom he had entrusted the governance of this universal Church, was the person through whom the unity and communion of that Church existed, this could not in any way be accomplished by another except through a schismatic association. Since such an association had nothing but a human character, it had to meet the fate ordinarily suffered by schisms: they suddenly cause the greatest disturbances, but soon collapse and dissolve.

After this, Cyprian demonstrates that no one can be joined to the Church by faith and charity if he is separated from the Roman pontiff—that is, if he does not adhere to the pontiff by the indissoluble and enduring bond of those same virtues. Finally, he declares that the Roman Church must be regarded as the root and mother of all Churches, and that no one may depart from it in any way.

That same holy bishop, as human affairs are subject to vicissitude, eventually had to plead his own cause against that most insane leader named Fortunatus, whom a band of wicked men was attempting to elevate in his place to the see of Carthage [Col. 0944D]. Therefore, in a letter of remonstrance to Cornelius, he particularly complains [Note: [Col. 0944D] The same, Letter 59] that that schismatic and criminal association had been so shameless as not to hesitate to send the message of its audacity and impudence to the chair of blessed Peter, to the prince of all Churches, and to the origin of episcopal unity. They paid no attention at all to the fact that they would have to deal with those Romans whose faith the Apostle had proclaimed with such great praise, and to whom no access is granted to treachery [Col. 0945A].

What the same Saint Cyprian later writes in that letter about that most wicked group of men—that, after judgment had been pronounced against them in Africa, they should be heard nowhere—does not in the least diminish the authority of the holy see. The holy doctor evidently acknowledges that authority and defends it with the strongest arguments. How remarkably consistent this holy bishop is in this matter may be seen in our *Dogmatic History* [Note: [Col. 0945D] Book II, chapter 7]. Lucius, the successor of Cornelius, confirmed his decree concerning the reconciliation of those who repented of the crimes they had truly committed [Note: [Col. 0945D] Saint Cyprian, Letter 68].

Stephen, elected pontiff after the death of Lucius, lent an impartial ear to two bishops of Spain who had been expelled from their sees and ordered that the provinces that had deposed them should restore them to their Churches. Nevertheless, when it became known that the rescript of the holy see had been obtained through misrepresentation [Col. 0945B], it was of no benefit to them. What entirely removes every suspicion that the supreme pontiff’s authority in this matter was insufficiently recognized [Note: [Col. 0945D] In Saint Cyprian, Letter 67] is that, at the same time, the Gallican Church, and Cyprian himself, whose advice had been sought in the case of the Spanish bishops, referred a certain bishop of Arles, a follower of Novatian, to the same authority of the supreme pontiff for the purpose of his deposition [Note: [Col. 0945D] Saint Cyprian, Letter 68].

There are those who deny that the blessed Cyprian was that great defender and champion of the authority of the holy see whom we proclaim him to have been [Note: [Col. 0945D] The same, Letter 74], because he opposed the decrees issued by Pontiff Stephen concerning the validity of baptism legitimately administered by heretics [Note: [Col. 0945D] Firmilian, in Cyprian, Letter 72]. I would not deny that both Cyprian and the supporters of his opinion, who contended that all baptism administered outside the Roman Church was entirely without force, provoked the pontiff with writings that were excessively harsh [Note: [Col. 0945D] Likewise, the Council of Carthage concerning the baptism of heretics]. Yet in truth they were persuaded that this controversy concerned only the discipline and administration [Col. 0945C] of the Church. Indeed, they declared most openly that they wished each person to follow his own custom in undisturbed peace.

However the matter may have stood, the causes both of this Stephen and of Victor certainly had the same outcome as they always have in affairs of a similar nature: what the holy see decreed prevailed, and the universal Church afterward embraced it [Note: [Col. 0945D] Saint Vincent of Lérins, *Against Heresies*, chapter 3].

Xystus II received from Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, a denunciation of the heresy of Sabellius [Note: [Col. 0945D] Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 5]. But when the persecution that arose had taken the pontiff from the living before he could proscribe that heresy, his successor Dionysius undertook the task and condemned not only the heresies of Sabellius but also those of Paul of Samosata and others. He likewise settled a case brought from the Pentapolis to Rome against their own patriarch, Dionysius of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0945D] Saint Athanasius, *On the Opinion of Dionysius*; likewise *On the Councils*; likewise *On the Decrees of the Council of Nicaea*]. The Fathers of the Antiochene synod held against Paul of Samosata sent Xystus a synodal letter concerning the deposition of that arch-heretic [Col. 0945D]. The emperor Aurelian, although a pagan, decreed that the buildings of deposed bishops should be assigned to the person whom the Roman pontiff adjudged entitled to them [Note: [Col. 0945D] Eusebius, *History* VII.14].

Pope Felix wrote a letter against the heresies [Col. 0946A] of the same Sabellius and Paul of Samosata. Relying on his authority, both ecumenical councils—the Council of Ephesus and the Council of Chalcedon—confirmed their decrees [Note: [Col. 0945D] Council of Ephesus, Part II, Act 1; likewise Chalcedon, Act 1]. He also decreed that Mass should be celebrated over the memorials and tombs of the martyrs [Note: [Col. 0946D] *Liber Pontificalis*]. Two decrees are attributed to Eutychianus: the first concerning the blessing of the first fruits of the harvest, the second concerning the burial of martyrs [Note: [Col. 0946D] The same]. Caius decreed that throughout the Church everyone should advance by degrees from the minor orders to the greater orders [Note: [Col. 0946D] The same].

## ARTICLE IV. The Tradition of the Fourth Century Concerning the Authority and Jurisdiction of the Holy See

No one rejects the fall of Pontiff Marcellinus, except certain critics of more recent times who, opposing the eminent gifts of the apostolic see, prefer to remove the stain from human weakness rather than acknowledge the authority of a pontiff who alone could impose a penalty upon himself. Whatever these writers assert against the Council of Sinuessa is not weighty enough to invalidate the history of its celebration [Note: [Col. 0946D] See Book II, chapter 11].

Marcellus distinguished several churches at Rome, which even in our own age are the titles of certain cardinals [Note: [Col. 0946D] *Liber Pontificalis*]. Eusebius confirmed Stephen’s decree concerning the validity of the baptism of heretics, reconciling them to the Church by the laying on of hands alone [Note: [Col. 0946D] The same]. Melchiades rendered the final judgment against the Donatists [Note: [Col. 0946D] Optatus, *Book Against Parmenian*; Saint Augustine, Letters 68 and 162]. Whatever was later added to that judgment must, according to Saint Augustine’s opinion, be regarded either as accessory or superfluous, or as having been done improperly.

The same pontiff forbade the observance of a fast on Sundays and ordered that, on those same days [Note: [Col. 0946D] *Liber Pontificalis*], when only the bishop celebrated the sacred mysteries in the episcopal city, the Eucharistic bread should be carried to those who had been unable to attend the sacrifice.

During the pontificate of Sylvester, the Council of Arles was convoked, and legates of that same pontiff presided over it [Note: [Col. 0946D] Letter of the First Synod of Arles]. The Fathers [Col. 0946C] of the council sent all its decrees to him, so that they might be confirmed and then proposed to the Catholic Church as laws.

Here he joined pontifical power with the imperial authority of Constantine [Note: [Col. 0946D] General Council VI, Act 18], so that the great Council of Nicaea might be proclaimed; he himself presided over it through his legates. There the primacy of the holy see over all the Churches was recognized [Note: [Col. 0946D] Eusebius, in Gelasius of Cyzicus], as is demonstrated by the emperor’s encyclical letter to the bishops, by the synodal letter of the Fathers to the Church of Alexandria, and, sixthly, by the sixth canon of that council, as the Council of Chalcedon and the pontiffs Boniface, Gelasius, and Nicholas—each the first of his name—have testified. By that same sixth canon, the patriarchal authority of the holy see throughout the whole of the West is also confirmed.

I would certainly be wasting my effort if I were to examine the carelessness of Rufinus [Note: [Col. 0946D] Rufinus, *History*, Book I, chapter 6], who in his *History* presents this canon so corrupted and mutilated that it displays a jurisdiction of the Roman Church very different from that found in the text of the council itself. Nevertheless, what Rufinus reports will agree with the truth if, in place of the suburban cities whose governance he says belongs to the Roman see, we understand the part of the Western Empire that obeyed the emperor’s vicar at Rome [Note: [Col. 0947D] Felix III, Letter 4]. The most ancient records confirm that this Council of Nicaea was celebrated by Saint Sylvester, who also established many regulations for the Church’s internal and external discipline [Note: [Col. 0947D] *Liber Pontificalis*].

Pontiff Mark instituted the use of the pallium for the bishop of Ostia, thereby confirming his authority to consecrate the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 0947D] The same]. This ornament is properly characteristic of metropolitan sees and of the higher-ranking bishops.

During the pontificate of Julius I, men hostile to Saint Athanasius, after the holy bishop had been expelled from the Alexandrian see in a council held at Tyre [Note: [Col. 0947D] Sozomen, *History*, Book III, chapter 7], set out for the holy see so that, by its authority, both the broad judgment they had issued and the election of the intruder whom they had installed in the holy bishop’s place might be confirmed. Athanasius [Note: [Col. 0947D] Saint Athanasius, *Second Apology*] likewise sent his legates to Rome. The adversaries, convicted and rendered speechless by them, asked that the matter be postponed so that they might explain their case, which, they repeatedly claimed, was not yet ready.

The pontiff convoked a council at Rome [Note: [Col. 0947D] Theodoret, Book II, chapter 4], to which he summoned all the parties. Saint Athanasius [Col. 0947B] [Note: [Col. 0947D] Saint Athanasius, *Second Apology*; likewise *To the Solitaries*; likewise Sozomen, Book III, chapter 7], obeying the command of his judge, arrived as quickly as possible. Likewise, bishops from Constantinople, Adrianople, Ancyra, Gaza, and many other places throughout the East and Egypt came to Rome, as did innumerable priests expelled from their Churches because they were believed to be infected with the Arian taint.

The Arians, however, with the testimony of their own consciousness of injustice, went into hiding. Inventing the flimsiest excuses for this fraud, they delivered to Julius a letter full of insolence and audacity [Note: [Col. 0947D] Saint Athanasius, *Second Apology* and *To the Solitaries*]. The pontiff, after investigating the entire case with the greatest diligence, restored Saint Athanasius and the other bishops who had been expelled by their persecutors to their former dignity. He forbade the adversaries to disturb those who had been restored; condemned their acts and writings; and finally communicated his judgment to them by letter, refuting the absurdities of the letter they had submitted [Note: [Col. 0947D] In the same author, *Second Apology*].

In order to accomplish this and restore tranquility to the Churches of the East, the pontiff appealed to the imperial majesty [Col. 0947C]. Thus, with civil and ecclesiastical power joined together, the Council of Sardica was convoked and held, comprising all the bishops of both empires [Note: [Col. 0947D] Socrates, Book II, chapter 10]. Julius presided over it through legates. Above all, three canons issued there establish the right of the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0947D] Saint Athanasius, *Second Apology], namely, the right of appeal in episcopal cases, which was to be referred from the provinces to that same see [Note: [Col. 0947D] Canons 3, 4, and 7].

It was decreed that the Roman pontiff could receive such appeals; approve the acts that had been performed, or entrust some part of the case to new judges for examination; and appoint judges from his own court who would issue a sentence together with the provincial investigators, from whose sentence an appeal could again be made to Rome. In their synodal letter to the pontiff, the Fathers of the council say that they had instructed their legates to report individually all that had been done and decided in the council to him as the successor of blessed Peter and head of the Church, whose office it is to know whatever pertains to that Church.

[Col. 0947D] The bishops Ursacius and Valens, both celebrated supporters of the Arians, after renouncing their error at the Council of Milan [Note: [Col. 0948D] Letter of the Council of Ariminum], over which the pontiff’s legates presided, went to Rome in order to obtain full pardon from the holy see. This happened according to their wish: they presented Julius with a written profession of faith [Note: [Col. 0948D] Saint Hilary, *Fragments*] and revoked whatever they had dared to do against Saint Athanasius [Note: [Col. 0948D] Socrates, Book II, chapter 18]. Before returning to his Church, to which the emperor Constantius was inviting him, that holy doctor visited Pontiff Julius [Note: [Col. 0948D] Sozomen, Book III, chapter 19] to hear his counsels and receive letters of recommendation for the clergy and people of Alexandria.

Liberius, the successor of Julius, as soon as he ascended the chair of Peter, sent letters of communion to the blessed Athanasius [Note: [Col. 0948D] Letter of Pope Liberius to Constantius Augustus], despite the persistent efforts of his Eastern persecutors to prevent it. He foresaw the great calamity that would befall the Church when Constantius alone held power. Intending to forestall it by an ecumenical council, he earnestly entreated the emperor by letter and finally prevailed, so that the emperor would raise no objection to the convocation of a council.

In one of these letters to the emperor, he showed what secular authorities ought to do in order to convene councils. “Princes,” he says, “ought to provide for public tranquility, so that councils may be celebrated and votes may be free;” [Col. 0948B] then they should employ their authority so that what has been defined may be accepted and what has been decreed may be observed.

Constantius took every measure to assemble the Fathers at Milan. He himself wished to be present with the intention of presiding and deciding [Note: [Col. 0948D] Saint Athanasius, *Letter to the Solitaries*]. Everything was done to please the Arians; the pontiff’s legates and the bishops who supported their cause were ordered into exile. Liberius too had to endure the same storm, because he resisted the emperor, who, as a pagan historian relates, was especially eager to draw the pontiff over to his side because of the supreme authority of his see [Note: [Col. 0948D] Ammianus Marcellinus, Book XV, near the end]. He had no doubt—something the Arians approved—that the entire Church would follow the pontiff’s example [Note: [Col. 0948D] Saint Athanasius, *Letter to the Solitaries*].

The emperor therefore began by offering gifts, then by threatening, and finally, when he realized that these measures were producing no result, turned to force and ordered that the pontiff be dragged to his court. When the emperor saw him, he asked whether the supreme dignity with which he was invested gave him such courage that he could stand alone against everyone. Liberius replied: [Col. 0948C] “So be it; I stand alone for the faith: the cause itself is sustained by no small support” [Note: [Col. 0948D] Theodoret, Book II of the *History*, chapter 16]. The pontiff was therefore driven into exile.

The hardships of exile and the threat of death weakened Liberius’s constancy to such an extent that he subscribed to the condemnation of Saint Athanasius. This alone is counted against Liberius, and it is unjustly asserted that he subscribed to a collection of formularies contrary to the faith. In fact, that document could not have been [Note: [Col. 0948D] See Book III, chapter 12 of our *Dogmatic History*] the first one he signed at Beroea, nor either of those sent to Sirmium, since they contradict the opinion of the bishops who induced Liberius to sign; much less could it have been the third, which had not yet been published when the pontiff was released and sent back to Rome.

It is therefore necessary that it was the first formula drawn up against Photinus and, as Hilary testifies, thoroughly orthodox [Note: [Col. 0948D] Saint Hilary, *Fragment on the Council against the Arians*]. If Liberius subscribed to another profession of faith at Sirmium, where the term “consubstantial” was absent, he nevertheless did not for that reason condemn the term as an Arian expression [Col. 0948D] [Note: [Col. 0948D] Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 14]. He merely forbade its use in certain cases, in which Paul of Samosata and some other heretics had abused it to strengthen their errors.

In any event, it is utterly contrary to the faith that Saint Hilary, that distinguished doctor of holiness, wrote those anathemas against Liberius that were inserted into his fragments. He was composing and publishing his works at the time when Liberius had already returned to Rome and, with the greatest glory to his name, was defending what the Council of Nicaea had established concerning the faith. Jerome likewise says that Liberius subscribed to heresy [Note: [Col. 0949D] Saint Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and *Chronicle*], but in this he follows popular rumor: namely, the rumor that, when Liberius subscribed to the condemnation of Athanasius, the Arians had deposed Athanasius under the pretext of particular crimes, but in reality because of their hatred of the ardent zeal with which he defended the Nicene faith.

When Liberius again took up the reins of ecclesiastical government, which during his exile Felix, appointed in his place, had governed peacefully, he once more fortified himself with apostolic constancy. He condemned the deceitful formula of the council of Ariminum, with the result that, when the persecution of the Arians broke out again, he was forced once more to flee [Note: [Col. 0949D] In Theodoret, Book II, chapter 22] and to remain in hiding as long as Constantius, the supporter of the Arians, lived [Note: [Col. 0949D] Sozomen, Book IV, chapter 18].

When the Church finally regained its former tranquility, the pontiff ordered a public amnesty to be proclaimed for all who had been deceived into subscribing to some deceptive formula [Col. 0949B] [Note: [Col. 0949D] Letter of Liberius to the Pontiffs, in Hilary, *Fragments*], while also ordering the full force of the law to be used against those who had not withdrawn from error [Note: [Col. 0949D] Socrates, Book IV, chapter 11; Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 10].

The Semi-Arians sent three bishops from the East to subscribe in their name to the doctrine of the holy see, where they knew that the faith was perpetually preserved incorrupt and that authority to govern the Church resided [Note: [Col. 0949D] Saint Basil, Letter 74]. They also asked that certain bishops be restored to their sees, from which they had been expelled by several councils in the East [Note: [Col. 0949D] The same, ibid.]. After hearing their profession of orthodox faith, the pontiff received them into communion and ordered that the bishops who had been expelled be returned as quickly as possible to their Churches. This was done [Note: [Col. 0949D] Sozomen, Book VI, chapter 21]. The same pontiff also issued a judgment against the heresy that denied the divinity of the Spirit, the Paraclete; and the records of the ancients show that all the Churches immediately adhered to this judgment of the holy see.

During the pontificate of Damasus, the emperors Gratian and Valentinian II declared by a promulgated law [Note: [Col. 0949D] Rescript of Gratian and Valentinian Augustus to Aquilinus] the authority of the pontiff in episcopal cases and appeals to the holy see, as had already been defined by the Church in the Council of Sardica [Col. 0949C] [Note: [Col. 0949D] Saint Ambrose, Letter 13, to Valentinian]. This was indeed the fruit produced by the calamities inflicted by the antipope Ursicinus upon the legitimate pontiff.

Saint Basil [Note: [Col. 0949D] Saint Basil, Letters 55 and 220], in letters addressed to the blessed Athanasius and to Pontiff Damasus concerning the schism at Antioch and the disorder of the Eastern Churches, testifies that he fled to the Roman pontiff as to the one who possesses authority to decide, to order that crimes be investigated, to punish the guilty, and to distinguish those who ought to be retained in communion with the Church.

Writing to Damasus about the same matters, Jerome [Note: [Col. 0949D] Saint Jerome, Letters 57 and 58] declares that he could be separated and removed from communion with the see of blessed Peter by no one—whether presbyters, monks, bishops, or princes of this world. He says that he knows that no one outside that see can be saved, and that those who do not adhere to the Roman pontiff are called by them “Antichrist,” which is equivalent to sending back a message to Christ Jesus [Col. 0949D] [Note: [Col. 0949D] Saint Basil, Letter 272].

The pontiff condemned that schism [Note: [Col. 0950D] Sozomen VII.11; Socrates IV.30; Theodoret IV.9], as well as others that had arisen in the Churches of Alexandria and Constantinople. At last, those were regarded as the true bishops of those Churches whom the holy see, after their election, had confirmed.

After this, he took every measure to extinguish completely the schism of the Donatists, which had troubled the Churches of Africa for many years [Note: [Col. 0950D] Boniface I, to the bishops of Illyricum]. Indeed, no more distinguished testimony can be desired than that of the contemporary bishop Saint Optatus [Note: [Col. 0950D] Optatus of Milevis, Books I and II *Against Parmenian*]. In commending the faith of his own times in writing, he transmitted his teaching concerning the privileges, primacy, and preeminence attributed to the chair of the Apostle Peter, and concerning the communion by which all the Churches of the entire world are bound to adhere to that same see for the sake of preserving unity. This communion is so necessary that none of them can exist free from it.

“No apostle,” says the holy doctor, “was ever permitted to establish a see that did not depend upon the chair of blessed Peter founded at Rome.” The emperors acknowledged this authority of the Roman Church in their laws. Ancient histories report that the law enacted by Gratian on this matter was an outstanding proof of his devotion to God [Note: [Col. 0950D] Theodoret, Book V, chapters 2 and 3], since, after Valens had died and Gratian alone held power, he offered to God, as it were, the first fruits of the whole empire.

Theodosius the Great, by that most celebrated law, *Cunctos populos*, decreed that Christians who professed the faith [Note: [Col. 0950D] Book II, *On the Catholic Faith*, *Theodosian Code*] whose deposit the blessed Peter had left to his successors to guard should be called Catholics, while all the others should be branded with the utterly disgraceful name of heretics.

Thus divine providence increasingly won greater veneration for the Holy See, also magnifying its temporal power and splendor in the eyes of all. Those devoted to idolatry certainly did not conceal the envy and anxiety by which they were afflicted [Note: [Col. 0950D] Ammianus Marcellinus, book XXVII], just as in our own times do the defenders of heresy and schism. The faithful, like us, likewise extolled to the highest degree the divine plan by which the Church has always stood and still stands today, admiring its infinite wisdom—something which others do not accept without offense.

The Church’s small beginnings offended the Jews and provoked laughter among the Gentiles [Note: [Col. 0950D] 1 Corinthians 1:23]. At the present time its authority offends heretics and wicked Christians. [Col. 0950C] But whoever sets aside motives of mere partisanship admires, with Paul, the divine power and wisdom [Note: [Col. 0950D] Ibid., verse 24]. Wherever one looks, the Fathers say, one finds prodigal sons who squander their inheritance, as well as weeds mixed with good grain [Note: [Col. 0950D] Saint Jerome, letter 57]. Everywhere one sees Lucifers, like flashes of lightning falling from heaven, and likewise wooden and earthen vessels that are broken and cast into the fire.

The Apostolic See, on the contrary, has always preserved its paternal inheritance faithfully; in it the grain has been gathered a hundredfold; the sun of justice rises there daily; and nowhere are vessels seen except golden and silver ones, because the purity of its doctrine has been preserved there, undefiled, at every time. “Such doctrine,” the Fathers continue, “is subject to no deceitful arts” [Note: [Col. 0950D] The same author, letter 8, to Demetrius]. Therefore, however prudent or wise someone may think himself, let him beware—let him beware—lest he accept a foreign doctrine. Its safest and most faithful guardian is the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 0950D] Saint Ambrose, on 1 Timothy, chapter 3; likewise book 1, letter 7]. He is also the ruler of God’s household and the universal shepherd [Col. 0950D] of the Lord’s flock, and finally the master and teacher of bishops and councils: Ambrose calls him this.

“The writings of the pontiffs,” says Saint Athanasius [Note: [Col. 0950D] Saint Athanasius, letter to the Africans], “are sufficient to confirm the faith of the Church.” [Col. 0951A] One must approach him before all others, and the decisions of any synod, however numerous its participants, have no force without the assent of the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 0951D] According to Theodoret, book II, chapter 22, and Sozomen, book VI, chapter 23]. Saint Basil [Note: [Col. 0951D] Saint Basil, letter 74] referred Apollinaris and his heresy to him; and he condemned both. Clergymen who refused to subscribe to the formula sent by Damasus were deposed [Note: [Col. 0951D] Sozomen, book VI, chapter 25]. The same pontiff prohibited the Macedonians, who denied the divinity of the Holy Spirit, and proscribed all the sects of the Arians that rejected the consubstantiality of the divine Persons [Note: [Col. 0951D] Letter of Damasus to Paulinus]. He uprooted the delusions and destructive doctrine of Priscillian; he likewise opposed the most wicked heretic Helvidius, who not only branded virginity with disgrace but also, impiously, dared to attack the virginity of the Mother of God.

The Fathers of the First Council of Constantinople abundantly testify in their synodical letter to the pontiff [Note: [Col. 0951D] Theodoret, book V, chapter 11] that they had assembled at his command. They further acknowledge that they were obliged to attend the Roman synod held by the pontiff [Note: [Col. 0951D] Sulpicius Severus, History, book I], to which they had been summoned by him [Note: [Col. 0951D] Saint Augustine, Retractions, book II, chapter 22]. They sent three bishops to him to render an account of what had been done and decreed in the council, so that the same pontiff might confirm it [Note: [Col. 0951D] According to Theodoret, book IV, chapter 9], and to excuse themselves before him for not having come to Rome in person [Note: [Col. 0951D] Sozomen, book VI, chapter 12].

The emperor Theodosius likewise sent envoys to the pontiff to request confirmation of the Constantinopolitan bishop who had recently been elected in the council [Note: [Col. 0951D] Synodical letter, according to Theodoret, book IV, chapter 9]. The pontiff ratified this election and approved everything that had been decreed in the council concerning faith and doctrine [Note: [Col. 0951D] Letter of Boniface I to the bishops of Illyricum]; for this reason he called the council ecumenical, which is the name it retains in the Church.

He rejected, however, the election of Flavian [Note: [Col. 0951D] Photius, book on the Seven Synods], whom those same Fathers had substituted for Meletius in the see of Antioch, although he himself had always rejected Meletius as bishop of Antioch, to the detriment of Paulinus, to whom he had assigned that see. He certainly disapproved the plan [Note: [Col. 0951D] See book III, chapter 18, at the end] by which the Fathers had undertaken to constitute the Church of Constantinople as patriarchal and to assign it the place immediately after Rome—a place that Alexandria had always occupied. [Col. 0951C]

In the provinces of Eastern Illyricum he established an apostolic vicar who, acting in the pontiff’s place [Note: [Col. 0952D] Innocent I, letter to Anysius and to Rufus], was to examine matters relating to that region, which in the patriarchate of the West were increasing extraordinarily with the number of those embracing the faith of Christ and of the Churches being founded.

Pope Siricius, in a decretal addressed to the bishop of Tarragona, among other disciplinary matters, ordered that bishops, priests, and deacons lead a celibate life, and permitted monks to be admitted to clerical dignity. In another decretal to the African bishops he reviewed the rules of celibate life, established regulations for ordination, and discussed irregularities. In both, however, he prohibited the rebaptizing of heretics returning to communion with the Church, since the legitimate form had been used when baptism was conferred upon them [Note: [Col. 0952D] Council of Turin, canon 5].

He bound by a curse bloodthirsty bishops who were fiercely hostile to heretics even unto capital punishment; nevertheless, he did not forbid appealing to civil magistrates, [Col. 0951D] who would send them into exile [Note: [Col. 0952D] Book XVIII, On Heretics, in the Theodosian Code]. He also issued a decretal to all Catholics, in order, as he himself says, to avert—by the authority he possesses over all the Churches of the entire world—the innovations that some were attempting to introduce on their own authority. He labored with the greatest zeal to settle the Antiochene schism. And just as arbiters had been assigned to the rival parties, Saint Ambrose, writing to them [Note: [Col. 0952D] Saint Ambrose, Letters, book I, letter 9], urged them to give their judgment such a form that it might readily be approved by the Holy See, so that the whole matter could be brought to a settlement.

Although a letter to the bishop of Thessalonica concerning the matter of the heresy of Bishop Bonosus, who had been summoned to account [Note: [Col. 0952D] According to Saint Ambrose, letter 79, among the ancient letters], was attributed to this pontiff, no inference against the authority of the Holy See can be drawn from it. Whoever wrote it speaks with authority concerning the substance of doctrine, and does not refrain from pronouncing judgment except regarding certain facts about which no inquiry can be instituted except in the places where those events occurred.

That same Siricius condemned the heresy of Jovinian at Rome [Note: [Col. 0952D] Letter of Pope Siricius to the Church of Milan] and ordered that it be condemned likewise at Milan. He speaks of his own judgment just as the council held at Jerusalem in the age of the apostles had already done: “It has seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us.” “The divine judgment and our judgment” [Note: [Col. 0952D] Jerome, letter to Pammachius]. John of Jerusalem was referred to him as a defender of Origenism. Maximus, although a tyrant, acknowledged that Rome was first in religion throughout the entire world, just as it was first in imperial power [Note: [Col. 0952D] Letter of Maximus to the emperor Valentinian Augustus].

The pontiff Anastasius proscribed Origenism, and all Christians received that judgment with the deepest submission [Note: [Col. 0952D] Jerome, Apology against Rufinus]. Rufinus, an advocate of this error, sent his apology to the pontiff. Soon afterward, however, the same pontiff summoned him to Rome and, when he remained in hiding, cut him off from communion.

In his letter to John of Jerusalem, Anastasius declares that judgment concerning the soundness or unsoundness of the opinions found in books belongs to the Apostolic See, since, by the special providence of Almighty God, it can neither admit nor tolerate errors; and he declares that it will preserve both itself and the Catholic Church in the faith forever. The African bishops went to Rome [Note: [Col. 0952D] Council commonly called the Second African Council, under Anastasius] to obtain a relaxation of the written law, which prescribed what safeguards of nature and doctrine those who were to be enrolled among the clergy had to possess. [Col. 0952C]

## ARTICLE V. The Tradition of the Fifth Century up to Pope Saint Leo the Great

The following are the acts of Pope Innocent I, who was the supreme head of the Catholic Church.

I. He restored the rights of Saint John Chrysostom, who had been expelled from the see of Constantinople by the faction of Theophilus of Alexandria [Note: [Col. 0952D] Palladius, Dialogue, at the beginning]. News of this matter reached Rome from both sides. Chrysostom [Note: [Col. 0952D] Saint John Chrysostom, letter 1, to Innocent I] asked the pontiff through his legates to annul the judgment pronounced against him, restore him to his see, and punish the unjust judges with canonical penalties [Note: [Col. 0952D] According to Palladius’s Dialogue].

After investigating the case, the pontiff rescinded everything that had been done against Chrysostom and summoned all the parties, intending to establish the matter more fully and extensively. Meanwhile, those hostile to Chrysostom, who enjoyed great influence with the emperor, obtained permission for the bishop to be deported and for the clergy who remained in his communion to be expelled from their Churches. All who had been subjected to this persecution fled to Rome. [Col. 0953A]

Therefore, understanding that an ecumenical synod would be needed to restrain disturbances so numerous and so great, the pontiff induced the emperor Honorius to write to his brother, the emperor Arcadius, urging him to devote every effort to a matter that concerned them both. Honorius sent legates with letters; but after being attacked and turned back on the road by the faction of Theophilus, they carried out a futile and ineffectual embassy.

Meanwhile Saint Chrysostom, overwhelmed by the hardships of exile, died. When Innocent learned of this, he wished to restore the most equitable right to the eternal memory of so holy a man—a right that the urgency of the times had prevented from being restored to him while he was alive and still surviving. He rejected from communion all who had persecuted him [Note: [Col. 0953D] Theodoret, book V, chapter 35] and declared them all unworthy of pardon until they had entered the name of the holy bishop in the sacred diptychs. Without accepting this condition, some of them tried in vain to return to communion with the Holy See. Thus, with the name entirely excepted, they all fulfilled it.

II. Next, Innocent, likewise as head of the Church, condemned Pelagianism [Note: [Col. 0953D] Letter of the Council of Carthage to Pope Innocent]. Coelestius, easily the foremost of Pelagius’s disciples and the most ardent defender and champion of that heresy, had already been condemned in an African council [Note: [Col. 0953D] Likewise Marius Mercator, in the Commonitorium], from which he appealed to the Holy See. Pelagius, however, avoided the canonical penalties by apparently denying his errors in the Palestinian synod.

Later, both Coelestius—who abandoned his appeal—and Pelagius, whose frauds had been brought to light, were condemned in two African councils, together with the most destructive doctrine they professed [Note: [Col. 0953D] Letters 90 and 92 among Augustine’s letters]. The Fathers of these synods sent legates to the pontiff to render an account of the matters they had judged, and humbly asked that whatever they, in their weakness, had decreed might be confirmed by the authority of the Apostolic See.

“For this See,” they say, “has chiefly received the office of teaching others; and, by the authority which Sacred Scripture openly attributes to it in many places, it is able more safely and effectively to restore those who have strayed to the right path than others can do” [Col. 0953C] by any counsel obtained elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0953D] The same, letters 91 and 93].

The pontiff rejoiced at this expression of reverence toward the Holy See. The Fathers declared that they were firmly convinced that certain decisions always proceeded from it, especially when there was controversy concerning a dogma of faith. They also affirmed that their own undertaking followed the tradition and custom of all ages: namely, seeking a judgment by which their own sentence might be strengthened and thereafter prevail throughout the Church. The pontiff therefore ratified the sentence they had pronounced against the heresies and their authors and supporters. Thus, as Augustine testifies, the case was concluded [Note: [Col. 0953D] Saint Augustine, Sermon 2, On the Words of the Apostle].

III. Finally, Innocent [Note: [Col. 0953D] Innocent, chapters 32 and 33], as head of the Catholic Church, threatened the bishop of Jerusalem with his authority unless, by whatever power he possessed, he restrained the audacity of the heretics who were injuring Jerome and the monks of Palestine under his direction with every form of mockery.

That same supreme pontiff, as patriarch of the West, prescribed disciplinary rules for the Churches of Gaul, Spain, Illyricum, Africa, and Italy. He issued two decretals for Gaul, the first containing thirteen canons and the second seven. In the latter he presented a catalogue of the books of Sacred Scripture.

The Churches of Spain had first established certain provisions at the Council of Toledo, with the assent of the Apostolic See; Innocent confirmed them in a decretal addressed to the synod. Three decretal letters of his to the Churches of Illyricum survive; one to the primate of Africa; six to various prelates of Italy; and two to private individuals.

In the decretal addressed to the bishop of Gubbio, he concludes that, since all the Churches of Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, and the neighboring islands had either been founded or had received their first bishops from the Roman pontiff, it was equally proper that they should receive disciplinary rules from him, and that they should not pursue innovations apart from his authority. This must be regarded as the genuine meaning of the decretal in question; one must not lend an ear at all to a certain modern writer who expressed its meaning in mockery.

Likewise, by virtue of his patriarchal authority, Innocent confirmed in the Western Church [Note: [Col. 0953D] According to the Third Roman Council under Boniface] the dignity of apostolic vicar in Illyricum for Anysius, metropolitan of Thessalonica, which he had already held during the time of the preceding three pontiffs. After Anysius’s death, he conferred that same dignity upon Rufus, his successor, assigning to him individually the ten provinces of Illyricum. In addition to the authority proper to his own see, he delegated authority over those provinces to him, since they were exceedingly distant from the Apostolic See. Meanwhile he sent several encyclical letters to the metropolitans of those provinces, so that none of them could be unaware of the pontiff’s will in this matter.

Under Pope Zosimus, the heretic Coelestius again contemplated the appeal that many years earlier he had made from the African council to the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0954D] Saint Augustine, On Original Sin, chapter 6]. He therefore went to Rome and, by a written petition, begged the pontiff to correct him if he had unknowingly fallen into error. The pontiff did not absolve him but postponed the case for two months [Note: [Col. 0954D] Ibid., chapter 8]. Meanwhile he ordered the Africans, during this period of delay, to send accusers to Rome who would charge him, as they asserted, with unsound faith [Note: [Col. 0954D] From an old Vatican codex].

Pelagius had likewise taken precautions for himself before the Holy See. He sent there a profession of faith, accompanied by a formal declaration that, if he proposed anything foolish, it should be judged to have escaped him through ignorance, and that pardon should be granted him—as he earnestly requested—by him who was no less the successor of Saint Peter in the faith than in his chair. When the pontiff and the Roman clergy received this apparently sincere declaration from Pelagius, they could scarcely restrain their tears and wished the Africans to be informed of it [Note: [Col. 0954D] Pope Zosimus, letter 4].

The Africans, however, sent to Rome as quickly as possible everything necessary to expose the cunning of Pelagius and Coelestius. Since Coelestius, whom the Romans were pressing to profess plainly and openly what he believed concerning the faith, had fled, Zosimus pronounced a proper judgment against him and Pelagius, and confirmed it by an encyclical addressed to all the prelates of the Church [Note: [Col. 0954D] Saint Augustine, letters 47 and 157].

By that letter, as Saint Prosper testifies [Note: [Col. 0954D] Saint Prosper, Against the Collation], he armed the right hands of all the bishops with the sword of Peter, for the elimination of the impious. Marius Mercator and the deacon Paulinus of Milan [Note: [Col. 0954D] Marius Mercator, in the Commonitorium; Paulinus the Deacon, in his pamphlet], recounting the proceedings of this case brought before the Holy See and the judgment delivered, present as unquestionable axioms the following claims: that the true faith had never been stained by any blemish in the Apostolic See; that in it there existed the authority to expose sectarians and to punish them with the penalty they deserved; that its judgments were definitive; and that the bishops of the whole world had subscribed to Zosimus’s sentence, since he had ordered them to do so and had threatened the penalty of deposition against those who refused [Note: [Col. 0954D] Mercator, in the same work].

The emperor Honorius reinforced the pontiff’s decree by a law, adding exile to the penalty of deposition. Eighteen prelates from Italy underwent these penalties.

When a dispute arose between the Churches of Arles and Vienne over primacy in several provinces of Gaul, Zosimus [Note: [Col. 0955D] Pope Zosimus, letter 5] gave judgment in favor of the metropolitan of Arles and also appointed him his vicar in Gaul itself. He sent letters on this matter to the bishops of those regions, and likewise to the bishops of Africa, Spain, and the provinces of Vienne and Second Narbonensis; to the metropolitan of First Narbonensis; to Patroclus of Arles; to the clergy and people of Marseille; and he addressed other letters to others.

In a decretal to Hesychius of Salona, he fixed the periods of interstices and granted him authority to act in his province as a delegate of the Holy See, so that he might ensure that the established rules were observed if he believed that the metropolitan’s authority was deficient. In another letter to the bishops of the province of Byzacena in Africa, he rebuked them for admitting laymen together with themselves to give judgment in episcopal cases. He delegated Saint Augustine [Note: [Col. 0955D] Saint Augustine, letter 157, to Optatus] and other African prelates to decide an ecclesiastical matter in the Caesarean province of Mauretania.

Apiarius, a priest of the diocese of Sicca in the same province, having been struck with anathema by his own bishop, [Col. 0955B] appealed to the Holy See. Zosimus absolved him and took the occasion to send legates to Africa to enforce the constitutions delivered to them [Note: [Col. 0955D] Synodical letter of the African council to Pope Boniface], especially concerning appeals, which both custom and the sacred canons permitted ecclesiastics to make from their own judges.

These constitutions of the Holy See were communicated to the national African council held at Carthage under Boniface, the successor of Zosimus. They were supported by the canons of the Council of Sardica, although those canons are attributed to the Council of Nicaea—a matter whose explanation is given in our Dogmatic History [Note: [Col. 0955D] Book IV, chapter 12].

The African Fathers, having examined all the copies of the Nicene Council that could be found there [Note: [Col. 0955D] The synod mentioned above] and not finding those canons among them, resolved to procure other copies from the East. Meanwhile, they decided that the pontiff’s decrees should be observed, hoping that, unless the Nicene canons contained something similar, the Apostolic See would not bind them by other laws than those which prudence and equity suggested ought to bind them. [Col. 0955C]

Meanwhile Antonius, bishop of Fussala in Numidia, appealed from the judgment of the bishops of his province, [Note: [Col. 0955D] Saint Augustine, letter 161] who had expelled him from his own see. He had a letter of recommendation from his metropolitan and was restored by the pontiff to his own see, but only on the condition that there had been no concealment or deception in what he had reported at Rome. [Note: [Col. 0956D] Rescript of the emperor Honorius against the Pelagians to Aurelius and Augustine.]

During the reign of this pontiff, the emperors, in order to suppress the audacity of the Pelagians—who, as is customary with heretics, were declaiming against the Holy See—expelled Pelagius and Coelestius and all their assistants from the entire empire. They also decreed that if any bishops refused, contrary to the decrees of the Apostolic See, to subscribe to the condemnation of the proscribed men, they would suffer the same penalties.

When the clergy of Valencia complained that their bishop Maximus, having been summoned on many charges, had always avoided appearing before the judges whom [Col. 0955D] the Holy See had repeatedly appointed to investigate his case, Boniface announced by a decretal letter that, although he could condemn Maximus as contumacious, he nevertheless wished to postpone his case until a fixed time, appointing new judges of recovery; when the prescribed period had elapsed, judgment would be pronounced against him whether the accused was hiding or not.

In another decretal to the bishop of Narbonne, he took away from the bishop of Arles the dignity of primate that Zosimus had conferred upon him. He confirmed the metropolitan of Corinth, strongly urged to do so by his own apostolic [Col. 0956A] vicar in the provinces of Illyricum [Note: [Col. 0956D] According to the Third Roman Council under Boniface II].

He vigorously defended the rights of the Holy See concerning the Western patriarchate against the efforts of the bishop of Constantinople, who, claiming that Eastern Illyricum belonged to the Eastern Empire, had arranged for jurisdiction over it to be assigned to himself by a law enacted by the emperor Theodosius. The emperor, at the urging of his colleague Honorius, repealed the former law and issued another by which the ancient rights of the Roman pontiff were vindicated.

In several letters sent to Illyricum, Boniface displayed the rights of the pontiff [Note: [Col. 0956D] Ibid.], both as patriarch of the West and as Roman pontiff. Concerning the former, he testified that many documents existed in the archives of the Roman Church proving that the very Churches then being placed in jeopardy belonged to the patriarch of the West.

Concerning the latter, when the bishop of Constantinople was, as he thought, announcing a synod at Corinth, the pontiff wrote that all action and deliberation ceased after the judgment of the Roman pontiff; that until that time no one had ever dared to challenge the supreme authority of the Apostolic See, from whose judgment no appeal was permitted; that he traced his authority to Jesus Christ, not to councils; and that even the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, being fully convinced that whatever honor they might confer upon the Apostolic See would not, even by the greatest interval, attain the prerogatives with which Christ the Lord had honored it, had dared to establish nothing for it.

No one, he declared, could separate himself from the head of all the Churches without at the same time departing from the Christian faith. [Col. 0956B]

Under Pope Celestine, the appeals that Bishop Antonius of Fussala and the priest Apiarius had brought to the Apostolic See were pursued. The judgment delivered in Antonius’s case appeared to be an inquiry based upon his petition; and the people of his own diocese resisted its execution. Antonius threatened them with force, claiming that the pontiff would grant him the means to employ it.

Saint Augustine [Note: [Col. 0956D] Saint Augustine, letter 261, to Pope Celestine], who was extraordinarily concerned for the justice of the people of Fussala—for they had been separated from his own episcopate at Hippo at the urging of the same Antonius—referred Antonius’s case to the Holy See, adding new arguments to prove the justice of the judgment pronounced against him in Africa. A letter of that same holy doctor to Quodvultdeus informs us that he had again undertaken the task of governing the people of Fussala [Note: [Col. 0956D] His letter 224]; from this it may be inferred that the judgment of the Africans had been confirmed at Rome.

The priest Apiarius, having again been struck with anathema in Africa on account of new crimes, once more appealed to the Apostolic See. The pontiff sent him back with the same legate who had previously worked for his restoration, and ordered that he should enjoy the benefit of the absolution that the pontiff himself granted, provided that matters were as he had reported them. But when he was entirely unable to prove what he had reported, he was subjected to the severity of the laws.

The Africans had been furnished with a copy of the Nicene Council from the East [Note: [Col. 0956D] Synodical letter of the African council to Pope Celestine]. Therefore they delivered a letter to the pontiff, earnestly requesting three things: first, that he not lend such ready ears to those who appealed; second, that he not send from Rome someone who, together with judges of recovery appointed by the Apostolic See in each province, would pass judgment, since this had not been established by any synod—the seventh canon of the Council of Sardica was unknown to these Africans; and finally, that secular magistrates not be employed to execute what they had decreed.

In a decretal letter to the bishops of Vienne and Narbonne, after transmitting several disciplinary rules concerning ecclesiastical dress, the rusticity of certain persons in administering the sacrament of penance, and negligence in the election of bishops and lower-ranking clergy, Celestine appointed those same bishops judges in the case of two bishops.

In a decretal to the bishops of Calabria and Apulia, he commended to them knowledge of the sacred canons, as being entirely necessary for bishops. He indicated that, by virtue of the supreme power he possessed to command, he would punish with the penalties prescribed by law those whom obedience to his authority and commands had not brought to the performance of their proper duty.

Finally, in another decretal letter to the Illyrian prelates, he declared that the duties of his apostolic vicar were to deliver definitive judgment in that province, consecrate bishops, convene synods, and hear cases that ought to be referred to the Apostolic See.

The Pelagians, employing solicitations and entreaties everywhere, attempted to persuade the pontiff to hear them [Col. 0957B] [Note: [Col. 0957D] Saint Prosper, Against the Conference, toward the end]. He, on the contrary, refused to lend his ears to their impious propositions, which had been condemned by law, and declared that the one path remaining for them to return to the Church was penance [Note: [Col. 0957D] The same author, in the same work and in the Chronicle].

He sent men to Greater Britain to purge the province of this heresy. He gave the Scots a bishop with the authority of a herald of the Gospel, so that he might travel to Ireland both to preserve those who already worshiped Christ there and to add new worshipers to the Gospel.

The same pontiff condemned the Nestorian heresy after Cyril of Alexandria had reported it to him [Note: [Col. 0957D] Letter of Pope Celestine to Cyril, in the Council of Ephesus, part I, chapter 15]. He likewise imposed the penalty of deposition upon the heresiarch unless he confirmed in writing, within the appointed time, that he had sincerely cast his errors out of his heart.

He appointed Saint Cyril his apostolic vicar, so that Cyril might see to the execution of the sentence he had pronounced against Nestorius. The dignity thus conferred upon him was the reason Cyril presided over the ecumenical synod held at Ephesus [Note: [Col. 0957D] The same source, first session].

That council was summoned at the urgent request of all parties, but especially at the insistence of Nestorius, who maintained that Cyril, his accuser, was himself tainted with heretical corruption. Both powers—the papal and the imperial—were jointly employed, as was customary, in summoning the bishops [Note: [Col. 0957D] The same source, there and at the end; see also book IV, chapter 21].

The Alexandrian prelate, as a delegate of the Apostolic See, presided alone in the first session, which was held before the three legates sent by the pontiff had arrived. In the remaining sessions, up to the completion of the synod, those three presided together with Cyril.

At that synod there was no question whatsoever concerning the matters [Note: [Col. 0957D] Ibid., second session] that had been established and defined by the pontiff regarding the faith of the Catholic Church. The sole matter under discussion was that, since Nestorius opposed that same faith, he should either be compelled to sing a recantation or be deposed in accordance with the judgment pronounced against him by the Apostolic See.

The Fathers did precisely this, as the sentence of deposition that they pronounced against him clearly demonstrates [Note: [Col. 0957D] The same source, first session]. As soon as the pontiff’s legates arrived and his letters had been read to the Fathers, amid acclamations and expressions of gratitude to the Roman pontiff as the best guardian of the deposit of faith, it was heard both in the letters themselves [Note: [Col. 0957D] Ibid., second session] and through the arrival of the legates that the sentence the Fathers had delivered against Nestorius was divinely confirmed, so that no sentence other than the one the Holy See had previously pronounced against him might be carried into execution [Note: [Col. 0958D] Ibid.].

The legates had already subscribed, and everything seemed completed, when the Fathers were compelled to arm themselves against the insulting conduct of John of Antioch. Although he did not approve Nestorius’s doctrine, John had nevertheless arranged for the doctrine of Saint Cyril to be condemned in a conciliabulum convened in the same city of Ephesus [Note: [Col. 0958D] Ibid., fifth session].

After issuing the necessary admonitions, the Fathers therefore, with the best of right, separated those schismatics from communion. Yet they did not depose them, leaving the imposition of such a penalty to the judgment of the Holy See, as they testify in their synodical letter to Celestine. They likewise informed him of the penalties of deposition and exile by which they had condemned Nestorius, and of the other bishop who had been substituted for him.

The emperor Theodosius sent two legates to the pontiff to offer congratulations on the victory [Note: [Col. 0958D] Saint Prosper, Against the Conference, near the end] that the Church had won over the heresies—the most glorious of victories—using the apostolic swords with which the pontiff had armed it.

In his encyclical to the bishops who had celebrated the synod [Note: [Col. 0958D] According to the Council of Ephesus, part III], the pontiff confirmed the sentence of deposition both against the leader of that heretical sect and against the followers whom the Fathers of the council had named individually. He ordered the same penalty to be imposed upon others who, having fallen into the same impious opinions, refused to subscribe to the condemnation of the heresy and its author. As for the others—namely, the bishop of Antioch and his associates, who condemned the heresy but left the heresiarch uncondemned—he first wished them to be admonished fraternally before harsher action was taken against them.

He wrote to the clergy and people of Constantinople concerning their recently elected bishop [Note: [Col. 0958D] Ibid.] that, putting aside every cause for doubt, they should listen to him, since, having been raised and nurtured within the bosom of the Roman Church, he could not have been imbued with any doctrine other than the ancient one. Access to Rome, he said, was closed to innovations; and since the doctrine of that bishop was the foundation and cornerstone of the Church, it was wholly impious to depart from it.

Information was brought to the Holy See concerning a great number of priests from Gaul [Note: [Col. 0958D] According to the letter of Pope Celestine to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 1], and concerning some from the city of Genoa, who had united against Saint Augustine’s doctrine of grace and free will. Therefore, wishing to defend a teacher renowned for holiness who had died shortly before, the pontiff sent an encyclical letter to the Gallic bishops [Note: [Col. 0958D] Ibid.], ordering them to restrain the audacity of those priests and impose silence upon them. For, the pontiff said, it was not proper for ecclesiastics of that rank to raise their voice above the bishops in the Church and decide questions of doctrine [Note: [Col. 0958D] Ibid., chapter 2].

Moreover, he commemorates Saint Augustine with those carefully chosen praises that are especially fitting for a bishop: namely, his ardent devotion to the Apostolic See and the singular esteem in which the supreme pontiffs before him had held him because of the integrity of his doctrine and the great labors he had endured for the Church of God. At the conclusion of this treatise I shall insert a separate article on that ardent devotion and veneration toward the Apostolic See, of which this holy doctor left so distinguished a testimony to the Church.

[Col. 0958D] At the end of the letter we are discussing, one finds a collection of decrees issued by the pontiffs who preceded Celestine concerning grace and free will. The following are established there as axioms: that grace is necessary for thinking about the good, desiring it, and embracing it; that free will is not destroyed by grace but rather perfected; that through grace God works in us both to will and to act, so that we ourselves are his fellow workers, since he cannot tolerate our rendering his grace idle and neglecting it; and finally, that when we feel grace growing weak in us because of our falls, we must flee to God in prayer in order to obtain the strength we need.

Finally, it is declared there that the Apostolic See had decreed nothing further on this matter [Note: [Col. 0959D] See my Dogmatic History, book IV, chapter 23].

Sixtus III, while still a presbyter of the Roman Church, acquired such an eminent reputation by wielding his pen against the Pelagians with the greatest ardor [Note: [Col. 0959D] St. Augustine, Epistle 104] that St. Augustine judged his writings, full of doctrine and wisdom, worthy of being presented to the whole world. Hardly had he ascended the throne of the Church when he confirmed everything that had been done at Ephesus against the Nestorians regarding the heresy [Note: [Col. 0959D] Epistle of Pope Sixtus to Cyril, from the collection of Baluze]. But concerning the schism stirred up by John of Antioch and the Easterners, he did not wish to judge harshly, since he hoped that they might be brought back to their duty by admonitions [Note: [Col. 0959D] Ibid.]. Therefore he wanted a letter written to them—and he did write one—in such a friendly and humane manner that he won them over to himself and promoted concord between the two principal sees, Alexandria and Antioch, [Col. 0959B] whose disagreement was disturbing the whole Church of the East. He exposed the craftiness of certain Pelagians who were attempting to return to the Church under the pretense of conversion, in order to introduce poison into it. In this matter, according to the judgment of St. Prosper [Note: [Col. 0959D] St. Prosper, *Chronicle*, under the year 440], this pontiff won a triumph over the heretics equal in magnitude and glory to that which earlier pontiffs had won over heretics. He maintained the patriarchal jurisdiction in Illyricum, as two letters delivered by him to the bishops of Illyricum, and another to Proclus of Constantinople, make clear. In the first of these he confirmed to Anastasius of Thessalonica the dignity of apostolic vicar, which his predecessor pontiffs had conferred upon the bishops of that diocese. In the second he commands all the provinces of Illyricum to obey the bishop of Thessalonica, as was their custom, and not to be removed from that observance by anything that the Council of Constantinople had decreed contrary to the laws of the apostolic see, which had approved none of the council’s constitutions except those relating to the faith. Finally, in a third letter to the bishop of Constantinople, on whose account all these matters had arisen, he showed him that he could not therefore deviate from the sanctions of the canons, which he knew thoroughly.

## ARTICLE VI. On the authority of the holy see under Pope St. Leo the Great
