St. Leo, rightly and deservedly called “the Great,” as soon as he had been raised to the highest dignity of the pontificate [Note: [Col. 0959D] Sermon on his Assumption], began to confess and proclaim that blessed Peter perpetually governs the Church of God through the Roman pontiffs; that the faith and authority of the prince of the apostles would never fail them; and that Jesus Christ, who chose the same apostle Peter as a sharer in his power, communicates that power through him to the other leaders of his people [Note: [Col. 0959D] Epistle 2 of the old edition, also Epistles 93 and 86]. Leo the Great provided an example of what he taught in his dealings with the Manichaeans in Italy, the Priscillianists in Spain, and the Pelagians in Istria, through the commands he sent to the bishops of those provinces for the extermination of these heretics. He therefore prescribed formulas to which clergy suspected of unsound doctrine were to subscribe.

He issued many decretal letters, some to one bishop and some to another [Col. 0960A] [Note: [Col. 0959D] Epistles 1 and 80]. In the one he wrote to the bishops of Italy, besides other enactments, he forbade usury even to laymen and prohibited the solemn administration of baptism outside the seasons of Easter and Pentecost. He likewise prohibited public confession, affirming that confession to a priest was sufficient. In the decretal addressed to the bishops of Sicily [Note: [Col. 0959D] Epistles 4 and 16], he commands them never to cease sending three bishops from among themselves to the Roman synod every three years, and forbids them to alienate Church property without the consent of the clergy. In another letter, addressed to the bishops of Caesarea in Mauretania, he appointed a bishop [Note: [Col. 0959D] Epistle 87] to visit their province, and ordered them to pass judgment concerning another bishop who had appealed to the holy see; likewise, he wished the sentence issued in Africa concerning the affairs of Churches and bishops to be referred to him, so that it might receive added force. In the decretal to Rusticus of Narbonne, he forbade public penance to be imposed upon priests [Note: [Col. 0960D] Epistle 92, in the Holstein Collection] and extended the law of celibacy to subdeacons [Col. 0960B]. To the metropolitans of Illyricum he demonstrated that the Roman pontiff bears responsibility for the Churches of the entire world, but that his apostolic vicar bears responsibility only for those provinces entrusted to him [Note: [Col. 0960D] Epistle 84]; for he testified that a portion of the care, not its fullness, had been shared with the vicar. He forbids bishops to be transferred from one Church to another, and ecclesiastics to pass from one diocese to another against the wishes of their own bishops [Note: [Col. 0960D] Ibid.]. He indicates various grades of jurisdiction and appeal: from the bishop to the metropolitan, and from the latter to the pontiff. He commands the Church of Alexandria to maintain with the Roman Church, its mother, one and the same rule [Note: [Col. 0960D] Epistles 81 and 46]. He grants Anatolius, bishop of Constantinople, the power to restore to communion with the Roman Church all who have renounced heresy; and he forbids him to pronounce at the altar the names of the three bishops who had persecuted St. Flavian, his predecessor. In the decretal to Theodore, bishop of Fréjus, he demonstrates the necessity and power of the sacrament of penance [Note: [Col. 0960D] Epistle 91], affirming that it should not be denied even to those who are at the end of life and have lost the use of speech, when they seek absolution by some sign or when it is already clear that they had sought it, provided that illness and the shortness of time prevent them from giving any sign.

This holy pontiff personally gave judgment in the case of Celidonius [Note: [Col. 0960D] Epistle 89] and Projectus, bishops of Gaul, who appealed from the sentence of Hilary of Arles. He sustained both in their own sees and prohibited Hilary from every act of jurisdiction outside his own Church of Arles, which he did not take away from him out of indulgence. He replaced him with Leontius of Fréjus [Note: [Col. 0960D] Ibid.], who was to perform the duties of apostolic vicar in Gaul. In a letter to the bishops of the province of Vienne he speaks of appeals to the holy see as a right which no antiquity had ever rejected.

The emperor Valentinian III prepared the execution of the decrees of Leo the Great by a law ordering [Col. 0960D] [Note: [Col. 0960D] Valentinian’s Novel, after the Theodosian Code, title 24, *On Bishops to Be Ordained*] that all sanctions of the apostolic see be reverently and religiously observed throughout the empire; that no bishop be permitted, without the authority of that see, to attempt anything contrary to ancient custom; and that whenever a date had been assigned for appearance before the tribunal of the Roman pontiff, force should be applied by the governors of the provinces if the summons were disregarded. This law expressly made clear that the sentence pronounced against Hilary [Col. 0961A] by the apostolic see did not at all require imperial authority in order to be enforced even in Gaul, because of the supreme power which the pontiff possesses in the Church. Indeed, the sentence itself would have been valid throughout Gaul even without an imperial sanction. For what could the authority of so great a pontiff not permit in the Churches? See our history [Note: [Col. 0961D] Book V, chapter 3], and it will be evident that this law remained in force during the time of the Frankish kings who succeeded the emperors. The same pontiff settled the disputes between the Churches of Arles and Vienne [Note: [Col. 0961D] Epistle 109 to the bishops of the province of Arles], establishing the dioceses that were to be suffragans of one or the other metropolitan see.

Eutyches, condemned as a heretic at Constantinople, fled to Rome [Note: [Col. 0961D] Epistle 7, to Emperor Theodosius], promising in a supplicatory petition that he would correct everything in which his doctrine had been tainted with matters deserving reproach [Note: [Col. 0961D] Also Epistle 8, to Bishop Flavian]. He also sent letters to several bishops of the West, seeking their support, and received from them the reply that he ought to approach the Roman pontiff in order to have the doctrines of the faith judged; for private bishops [Note: [Col. 0961D] St. Peter Chrysologus, letter to Eutyches] declared that, without the consent of the Roman pontiff, they lacked the power to pronounce judgment in such cases. Flavian, bishop of Constantinople, brought all the proceedings against Eutyches before the Roman pontiff, together with the sentence he had pronounced against him [Note: [Col. 0961D] Letter of Flavian to Pope Leo], humbly begging him to cut off the rising heresy by strengthening that sentence, and to prevent the council whose impending convocation had been rumored from taking place; for such a gathering could only stir up disturbances in the Church.

The great pontiff then sent to Flavian that remarkable and unique letter, famously known as St. Leo’s Dogmatic Epistle, in which he defined and explained the faith of the mystery of the Incarnation with outstanding clarity. Wishing, for the sake of Emperor Theodosius, to give his assent to the council being convened at Ephesus [Note: [Col. 0961D] Epistles 12 and 13], he sent three legates to preside over it, and gave them the same letter as the rule for the matters that were to be decided. The pontiff recalls this in all the letters he wrote concerning the matter [Col. 0961C], especially in the one he sent to the fathers of the council, indicating that everything necessary for eliminating errors and establishing the unity of the faith and profession throughout the world was supplied by the letter to Flavian [Note: [Col. 0961D] Epistle 15].

That synod was turned into a robber council. Military forces were stationed at the place of the council, and three great commanders of the empire entered the sacred assembly in order to deprive the votes of their freedom. Dioscorus of Alexandria, the defender of Eutyches, disregarding the most sacred laws of the apostolic see, presided over the council with the utmost audacity. The pontifical letters—the dogmatic letter to Flavian as well as the other to the fathers of the synod—were not read at all. Judgment was rendered according to the plan devised by the supporters of Dioscorus: Eutyches was acquitted, and soldiers bursting in with drawn swords threatened that anyone who divided Christ into two natures would be cut into two parts. No one withstood the violence except the pontifical legates, Eusebius of Dorylaeum, who was the open and principal accuser of Eutyches, and Flavian of Constantinople, his own bishop and chief judge, who appealed to the holy see against everything that had been decreed in that council.

The wise man Theodoret [Note: [Col. 0961D] Theodoret, Epistles 113 and 126], bishop of Cyrus in the patriarchate of Antioch, likewise fled to the apostolic see, appealing from the sentence of deposition pronounced against him. At the same time he bore witness to the superior power of this august see over all the Churches of the entire world, and among its other most illustrious prerogatives confessed this one in particular: that, abhorring the stain of heresy, it had never ceased to do so, since none of the supreme pontiffs had ever held anything contrary to the truth, whereas all of them had always preserved the apostolic deposit intact and pure in every respect.

To remedy these evils, the holy pontiff [Note: [Col. 0962D] Epistle 25] condemned that false synod and declared in a letter to the emperor Theodosius that, since an appeal had been made to the holy see, another council had to be held, in accordance with the provisions of the canons of the Council of Nicaea. But Theodosius, acting according to the will of a certain eunuch who was strongly devoted to Eutyches, refused to lend a gracious ear to the arguments of St. Leo, or to the letters of the emperors of the West, by which they informed him that the Roman pontiff could not be rejected as the supreme judge of cases of appeal concerning the faith and the judgment of bishops [Note: [Col. 0962D] Council of Chalcedon, part I, nos. 25, 26, 27, and 28]. [Col. 0962B] Theodosius placed his confidence in the false acts of the assembly constructed under the direction of Dioscorus, namely, that nothing had been changed there from the decrees of Nicaea and the First Council of Ephesus, and that the bishops deposed there were infected with Nestorian heresy. Meanwhile he begged the pontiff to confirm Anatolius, who had been substituted for the deceased Flavian in the see of Constantinople. Leo the pope understood that this emperor, although he did not profess heresy [Note: [Col. 0962D] Epistle 33], nevertheless protected heretics. Therefore, confident that he could easily recall him from the opinion fixed in his mind, he sent legates to him and again urged the convocation of a synod; at the same time he indicated by letter the conditions under which he himself would confirm the newly elected bishop of Constantinople. Yet the glory of initiating this excellent plan belonged to Marcian, the successor of Theodosius.

When Marcian therefore took possession of the government, the first duties of the emperor which he undertook [Note: [Col. 0962D] Council of Chalcedon, part II, no. 33] were accompanied by an expression of his mind [Col. 0962C]: namely, that he wished a council to be held by the authority of the pontiff, so that error might be proscribed and the tranquility of the Catholic Church restored [Note: [Col. 0962D] Ibid., no. 34]. He begged St. Leo to attend the synod in person; but if that could not be done, he asked him to grant him by letter the authority to convene it, so that the bishops might profess what had been established by the supreme pontiff.

The fathers gathered at Chalcedon. The pontiff sent legates to preside over it and wrote to the emperor, expressing his hope [Note: [Col. 0962D] Epistle 49] that the faith of tradition, whose doctrines the holy see was handing over to him, would close every avenue of access to the error of the sectarians. He also wrote to the fathers of the council, indicating that his desire could not be unknown to them, since they were not at all ignorant of his religion and faith [Note: [Col. 0962D] Epistle 47]: namely, that, setting aside every dispute, they should embrace that full and explicit definition of the faith which he had expressed in his letter to Flavian. He wished bishops to be restored to their own sees if they repented; but much more so those who had been expelled from their Churches because they had defended the better side. They had to be especially careful that, while condemning Eutyches, they did not show indulgence to Nestorius.

The legates presiding over the synod began by declaring that the pontiff’s will was [Note: [Col. 0962D] Council of Chalcedon, action 1] that Dioscorus be excluded from the assembly until he had presented himself before the fathers as an accused man and given an account of his audacity in convening an ecumenical synod without any [Col. 0963A] authority from the apostolic see—a wholly unheard-of act, which until that time had neither been permitted nor undertaken. He was therefore expelled from the assembly of the fathers. Theodoret, by contrast, was admitted, having been restored to his own see by order of the pontiff. Dioscorus was convicted of having maliciously suppressed St. Leo’s Dogmatic Epistle at Ephesus, while all the fathers of the council professed that they received it purely and simply: “We all readily receive it” [Note: [Col. 0963D] Ibid.]. In the second session the fathers testified that they had subscribed to that same letter without any formula or deliberation: “We have all subscribed to the letter.” They recognized that it contained and affirmed the true faith, just as did the Nicene Creed and the tradition of the holy fathers who flourished after that council. When it had been read aloud, the fathers applauded the same letter and shouted that they had already subscribed to it: “We have already subscribed.”

In the third session the pontiff was called “universal archbishop.” Dioscorus was condemned and deposed for various reasons, and especially because he had prevented that letter from being read at Ephesus, to the great scandal of the Catholic Church, which had already suffered much. In the fourth session the fathers were asked by the imperial inquisitors whether St. Leo’s letter agreed with the expositions of faith of the Councils of Nicaea and Constantinople; they again acclaimed the letter. Nothing, therefore, is more certain than the pure and simple acceptance of this letter of Leo the Great at the Council of Chalcedon, whatever those who oppose the supreme authority of the holy see may assert. I have refuted their objections in my *Dogmatic History* [Note: [Col. 0963D] Book V, chapter 9].

The fifth session most effectively confirms our position. The fathers of the council had drafted a definition of faith which the legates rejected because, being incomplete, it did not express everything that the dogmatic letter had defined against the heresy. Therefore, although they defended that definition with stubborn zeal, as soon as they recognized the discrepancy between it and the dogmatic [Col. 0963C] letter, they promptly altered it so that every difference would be removed. The emperor Marcian, who was present at the council [Note: [Col. 0963D] Session 6], declared that he would ensure that no one thereafter dared to teach anything concerning the mystery of the Incarnation other than what the apostles, the Nicene fathers, and Pope Leo had handed down in the letter to Flavian.

Among the canons of the Council of Chalcedon, Canon 28, following Canon 3 of the Council of Constantinople, grants the bishop of that city second place in the Church, together with patriarchal jurisdiction over the exarchates of Pontus, Asia Minor, and Thrace. The legates, who were not present when this canon was proposed [Note: [Col. 0963D] Ibid., session 16, at the end], opposed it vehemently when the question of ratifying it was raised. But when they saw that their efforts to prevent the vote from proceeding were useless, they opposed the decree by means of a formal protest and complaint, and appealed to the apostolic see.

[Col. 0963D] After the synod had ended, the fathers begged the emperor [Note: [Col. 0963D] Ibid., part III, no. 1], in accordance with his piety and power, to support and strengthen by the authority of the apostolic see the profession of faith they had made; that is, they asked him to intercede with the Roman pontiff in order to obtain its confirmation. Later, sending the complete acts of the council to the pontiff, they entreated him by synodical letter not to disdain confirming them [Note: [Col. 0963D] Ibid., no. 2]. Above all, they pressed for the confirmation of Canon 28, presenting whatever arguments [Col. 0964A] they thought most compelling in order to convince the pontiff, and offering recommendations that they believed would be most useful for moving his mind.

The pontiff confirmed the definition with the fullest and most certain faith in letters to the bishops of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0963D] Letter of the emperor, in the Holstein Collection], to the emperor Marcian, to the empress Pulcheria, and to Anatolius of Constantinople [Note: [Col. 0963D] Epistles 52, 53, 54, 55, and 61]; and he confirmed it still more openly in letters to the bishops who had celebrated the synod. He completely rejected Canon 28 insofar as it concerned the see of Constantinople, and informed those distinguished men of the fact in the same letters; in other letters he communicated the matter to the patriarchs of Alexandria and Antioch [Note: [Col. 0963D] Epistles 62, 63, 68, and 105], whose interests were especially affected by this innovation, and also to several of their suffragan bishops.

The authority of the holy pontiff prevented the execution of this canon. Although the bishop of Constantinople was displeased by this [Note: [Col. 0964D] Letter of Anatolius of Constantinople, in the Holstein Collection], he nevertheless remained content, under pressure from the emperor, to fulfill his duty toward the pontiff’s will, and satisfied him by a letter full of obedience.

St. Leo cared above all that the faith concerning the Incarnation of the Word should be established in all the Churches of the world through his dogmatic letter. The Churches of Gaul embraced it with a joy that cannot easily be expressed in words [Note: [Col. 0964D] Letter of the bishops of Gaul after St. Leo’s Epistles 51 and 98]. With unanimous agreement they confessed and proclaimed that the apostolic see, from which the letter had proceeded, was the place from which the same Holy Spirit who had filled the apostles with knowledge uttered oracles; that its doctrine was the doctrine of God; that the Savior himself was conveying the mystery of his Incarnation to human beings through the mouth of the Roman pontiff; and that they owed the faith received by the Gallican Church to true religion and clung to it by the closest and most indissoluble bond of union. The letters of that same holy pontiff show us that the Churches of Spain shared in so great a benefit [Note: [Col. 0964D] Epistle 52]. Leo records that the Italian Churches neighboring the Alps subscribed to his decrees and obeyed them most carefully [Col. 0964C] [Note: [Col. 0964D] After Epistle 52].

The East, being always agitated by storms and tempests more than the provinces of the West, embraced tranquility more slowly. In Palestine it was necessary to resort to force in order to bring the monks back to their duty [Note: [Col. 0964D] See Epistle 83]; almost all of them had become followers of Eutyches, and they had to leave the churches they had invaded and return to their own monasteries. In Egypt, where some corrupted copies of St. Leo’s dogmatic letter had circulated and were introducing Nestorian errors [Note: [Col. 0964D] Epistle 69], authentic copies bearing the imperial seal had to be sent; it was also necessary to instruct the magistrates that the letters be read publicly to clergy and people alike. After the death of Marcian, that most religious prince and especially devoted adherent of the apostolic see, a faction of error again arose [Note: [Col. 0964D] Epistles 75, 78, and 99, to Emperor Leo]. Therefore the pontiff had to write to the emperor once, twice, and a third time, in order to make him secure against the plots which the heretics were preparing against his religion, taking advantage of the ease with which he listened to those condemned by the holy see, for whom nothing remained beyond repentance. “Even now they continue to demand a hearing, although those who have been condemned ought to do penance.” [Note: [Col. 0964D] St. Augustine, *Against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, book I, at the end.]

Thus Augustine thought when the apostolic see gave judgment in cases of the same kind. Those who in our own time boast of being disciples of so great a teacher ought to begin with this position, which he defended with such ardent zeal that he easily attained the foremost place among the other Fathers of the Church. Yet they are far from boasting, with St. Prosper, of using the authority of the holy see to explain and defend St. Augustine’s doctrine; on the contrary, they boast of using St. Augustine’s authority to attack the doctrine of the apostolic see. In order that they may see how greatly they are mistaken, I have resolved to set out briefly here everything that the holy doctor either said or did at other times, affirming it in accordance with the Church’s tradition concerning the preeminence and authority of the holy see.

## ARTICLE VII. Testimonies from St. Augustine concerning the preeminence and authority of the holy see

St. Augustine had three principal opportunities to express his judgment concerning the authority which the holy see exercises and ought to exercise in the Church, when appeals from the Churches of Africa to Rome were under discussion. In this way the holy doctor made his mind clear concerning all the prerogatives of the Roman pontiff and concerning those most powerful supports with which that pontiff is equipped: as the center and bond against schisms, the supreme interpreter of disputes against heresies, and the supreme arbiter of the law against those who rashly violate it.

I. The Donatists, who wanted to repeat baptism, appropriated the authority of St. Cyprian. To frustrate their plans, Augustine compares Cyprian with the prince of the apostles, whom St. Paul rebuked. Nevertheless, he admits that he fears the comparison may be an injury to St. Peter, because the prince of the apostles ought not to be compared with any other bishop. “I must fear,” he says, “that I may be insulting Peter. For who does not know that the primacy of the apostolate must be preferred to every episcopate?” (St. Augustine, *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, book II, [Col. 0965C] chapter 1.)

He then does his best to defend St. Cyprian: “For that question concerning baptism had not yet been carefully examined; nevertheless the Church held a most salutary custom . . . which I believe came from apostolic tradition . . . St. Cyprian says that through Agrippinus, his predecessor, it had, as it were, begun to be corrected. But, as the truth, more carefully investigated, has taught—a truth which, after great waves of doubt, was brought to the confirmation of a plenary council—it is more credible that through Agrippinus it began to be corrupted, not corrected.” (Ibid., chapter 7.)

Cyprian did indeed observe that custom; but “when,” Augustine continues, “the defenses of that custom were not such as could move a mind of that kind, he did not wish to yield to a custom that had not yet been established . . . He preferred to defend it as an invention of his predecessors.” (Ibid., chapter 8.)

Finally, as Augustine observes, Cyprian judged that the substance of the question concerned not faith but discipline, about which different people could hold different opinions without generating schism [Col. 0965D] or heresy: “Judging no one, and removing no one from the right of communion if he held a different opinion.” (Ibid., chapter 2.) “He tolerated colleagues who held another opinion, just as he himself was tolerated.” (Ibid., book IV, chapter 9.)

For this reason he judged that a universal synod ought to be convened, in order to discuss and examine the custom that admitted the baptism of heretics; and meanwhile he held that baptism could be conferred again upon those who had been baptized by heretics: “Before the judgment of a plenary council had confirmed what ought to be held on this matter, it seemed good to him, together with nearly eighty of his fellow bishops of the African Churches, that every person who had been baptized outside the communion of the Catholic Church ought, upon coming to the Church, to be baptized again.” (Ibid., book I, chapter 18.)

St. Augustine himself declares that, in the various provinces of the Church, particular investigations first had to be held [Col. 0966A] before an ecumenical synod could take place, so that the nature of that custom might be fully established—namely, whether it was universal and therefore of apostolic tradition. “For how could this matter, enveloped in such clouds of disputes, have been brought to the clear illumination and confirmation of a plenary council unless it had first been examined for a long time throughout the regions of the world in many discussions and conferences of bishops on both sides?” (Ibid., book II, chapter 4.)

The evident proof that both of these Fathers judged the question to concern discipline is found in the fact that Cyprian, in addition to what we have mentioned, believed that God would supply by his mercy whatever was lacking to one baptized by heretics who had been received into the Church without being washed again in the sacred font: “The Lord,” he says in his own words, “is able in his mercy to grant forgiveness, and not to separate from the gifts of his Church those who, coming to his Church, were admitted simply and fell asleep within the Church.” (St. Cyprian, letter to Jubaianus, [Col. 0966B] chapter 13.)

St. Augustine, however, said that this was a matter concerning which even plenary councils could correct one another: “The plenary councils themselves are often corrected by later ones, when experience of events reveals what had been concealed.” (St. Augustine, *On Baptism, against the Donatists*, book II, chapter 3.) This must plainly be understood only of discipline, for the laws of faith and morals are inviolable.

Moreover, the holy doctor held it certain that Cyprian had withdrawn from that opinion, and that no writing on the matter remained because those who favored such an error may perhaps have suppressed the holy man’s contrary writings, so that they might support their error with his authority: “He is not found to have corrected that opinion; nevertheless, it is not inappropriate to think of such a man that he did correct it, and perhaps it was suppressed by those who were excessively pleased with that error and did not wish to be deprived of such a patronage.” (St. Augustine, Epistle 48, to Vincentius.)

This, however, most firmly proves that St. Augustine regarded the authority of the Roman pontiff [Col. 0966C] as the place of truth, against which no one in the Church could oppose himself: “For who does not know that the primacy of the apostolate must be preferred to every episcopate?” He speaks in this way both of the dispute from which the Donatist schism arose and of a matter already settled by a sentence issued by the apostolic see.

This sentence was issued by Pope Miltiades in the dispute between Caecilianus and Majorinus concerning the bishopric of Carthage. Caecilianus had been lawfully elected and established in that see. Majorinus, however, had been instigated by a faction of men who had drawn a considerable number of African bishops over to their side. Augustine therefore speaks clearly of Caecilianus, saying:

“Caecilianus could have disregarded the conspiring multitude of his enemies, since he saw that he was united by letters of communion both with the Roman Church, in which the primacy of the apostolic chair has always flourished, and with all the lands from which the Gospel came to Africa, and that he was ready to plead his case if his adversaries attempted to alienate those Churches from him.” (Ibid., Epistle 162.)

In fact, it happened at the Donatists’ own request that the case was judged by judges from across the sea—that is, in the language of that age, by the apostolic see. The parties appeared before the pontiff on the appointed day, and after hearing the arguments of both sides, Miltiades pronounced sentence in favor of Caecilianus.

It certainly cannot be denied that the Donatists refused to abide by this judgment and appealed to the emperor Constantine. Nor can it be denied that, when they brought further charges in the case, the emperor appointed new judges—namely, the fathers of the Council of Arles. Yet if the fathers of that synod are to be called new judges, St. Sylvester sent legates who judged the case in the manner of his predecessor and decided the new charges. It is therefore better to call what the emperor granted a review of the case.

But how did the emperor grant such a review [Col. 0967A]? Augustine says that he yielded to their perversity and wished to restrain their shamelessness. For why was a council convened when the case had already been heard and decided at Rome? Detesting their insolent conduct, the holy doctor continues: they had dared to appeal from the judgment of the Church to the tribunal of the emperor.

“The ecclesiastical proceedings show how the case was pleaded and concluded in the city of Rome.” (Ibid., Epistle 68.)

“He granted another judgment at Arles, not because it was already necessary, but yielding to their perversity and desiring above all to restrain such shamelessness. For the Christian emperor did not dare to receive their tumultuous and deceitful complaints in such a way that he himself would judge the decision of the bishops who had sat at Rome . . . In this matter you have heard how he detested them.” (Ibid., Epistle 162.)

The emperor himself had written to Miltiades, indicating that it belonged to him to decide such a case and that he could not tolerate in any way the raising of a schism in the Church or the creation of divisions anywhere:

“Your Gravity will weigh how that dispute may finally be settled . . . I wish you to leave no general schism and no discord anywhere at all.” (Quoted in Eusebius, book X of the *History*, chapter 5.)

Thus he regarded the dispute as already decided by the sentence of the pontiff: “When the matter had been settled in the city of Rome by suitable and highly approved men, the bishops.” (Letter of the Emperor Constantine to Aelaphius.)

When he learned that the Donatists had appealed, he exclaimed: “O unheard-of madness! O audacity worthy of proclamation!” Christian men and bishops were imitating the nations.

“Upon this appeal the emperor Constantine replied: ‘With rabid and furious audacity, they have lodged an appeal, as is customary in cases involving the nations.’” (Optatus of Milevis, book I against Parmenianus.)

By this definitive judgment of Pope Miltiades, Caecilianus was absolved from all the charges that the Donatists had brought against him, and consequently he remained in communion with the Church [Col. 0967C] and suffered no loss of his legal rights. As for his rivals, apart from Donatus, the chief author of the crime, who was deposed, the pontiff ordered all the others to retain their respective dignities and offices, provided that they abandoned their erroneous opinion.

For this reason Augustine says that this excellent pontiff showed himself a son of Christian peace and the father of all Christians:

“The judgment of Miltiades closed the case in these words: ‘Since it has not been established that Caecilianus was convicted by Donatus in any respect, I rightly judge that he must be retained in his ecclesiastical communion with his status unimpaired.’” (Ibid., same work.)

“Miltiades’ final sentence was issued . . . Donatus alone, whom he had found to be the chief author of the whole evil, was held chiefly responsible, while the others were freely offered the opportunity of recovering their soundness, and he was prepared to send free letters of communion to the rest . . . O excellent man! O son of Christian peace, and father of the Christian people!” (St. Augustine, Epistle 162.)

[Col. 0967D] To this judgment of the apostolic see Augustine referred the Donatists in the many and weighty disputes that he had with them. When he undertook to prove to them that their party was nothing other than a schismatic faction separated from the Church of Jesus Christ, he placed before their eyes the fact that they were not in communion with the Roman Church. This argument seemed so compelling to him that he was accustomed to say that, if—by way of hypothesis—one from the holy choirs of angels asserted that one ought to join Donatus’s party and abandon the Catholics, that angel himself would be anathema.

“The Catholic party,” says the holy Doctor, “is found wherever there exists, after blessed Peter, a continuous succession of bishops succeeding one another. To Peter, who represented the figure of the whole Church, the Redeemer said: ‘Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.’ In this perpetual succession of pontiffs it is impossible to find any Donatist prelate. Since their origin in Africa is not legitimate, they strive to imitate the Catholic Church and send one of their own to Rome to govern the small number of Africans there.”

Here are Augustine’s own words:

> “For if the order of bishops succeeding one another is to be considered, how much more certainly and truly for our salvation do we reckon from Peter himself, to whom the Lord, as he represented the figure of the whole Church, said: ‘Upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not overcome it.’ Peter was succeeded by Linus, Linus by Clement, and so forth. In this order of succession no Donatist bishop is found. But, proceeding obliquely, they sent one ordained in Africa, who, presiding over a few Africans in the city of Rome, propagated the name of the Montenses or Cuzipitae.”  
> (The same, Letter 165.)

## II

If, especially on the occasion of the Donatists, Augustine demonstrated the authority of the holy see as the centre of unity against schisms, on the occasion chiefly of the Pelagians he acknowledged in that same see the supreme judge in matters pertaining to the faith and directed against heresy. It is established that the first judgment against the Pelagian heresy was issued in Africa. The Fathers of the council held at Carthage in the year 412 of our redemption condemned this heresy in Caelestius; whereupon that most insane leader appealed to the apostolic see.

But because the heretic did not pursue his appeal, the African bishops, some years later, pronounced against the same heresy and again condemned it, together with its authors, in the Councils of Carthage and Milevis. The Fathers of both councils reported to Pope Innocent I, by synodical letters, the reasons for the judgment they had issued. Those of Milevis, among whom Augustine was numbered, wrote to the pontiff as the common shepherd of all, and as the one possessing supreme and pre-eminent power to eliminate new heresies, correct errors, and suffocate them before they gained strength.

The same Fathers confess that this power was handed down to the Roman pontiffs by Jesus Christ, who deigns to direct their counsels and hear their prayers. “The Lord,” they say, “has placed you in the apostolic see through the special gift of his grace . . . . We ask that you deign to apply pastoral diligence; for a new heresy, and so forth. So that they may be corrected before they spread more widely . . . . With the aid of the mercy of our God Jesus Christ, who deigns both to direct you when you deliberate and to hear you when you pray, we submit to the authority of your Holiness, drawn from the authority of the sacred Scriptures,” and so forth.  
(The same, Letter 92.)

In another letter, which the blessed Augustine and four African bishops sent separately to the same pontiff, they inform him that it belonged to his office to summon Pelagius, who appeared to have abandoned his error, to appear before him, either in person or by letter, and give an account of his teaching. They say that, for this heresiarch, the pontifical authority of the pope would have greater weight than that of all the other bishops throughout the entire world.

At the end of the letter they ask his pardon if the letter should perhaps seem excessively lengthy to him. They confess that they had not intended to add brightness to the light, but wished to learn from his definition whether what they themselves knew derived its origin from that same source from which his highest wisdom flowed.

> “He is to be summoned to Rome by your Reverence, or dealt with by letter . . . . By the authority of the Catholic bishops, and especially by that of your Holiness, which we have no doubt carries greater weight with him . . . . The gentleness of your most mild heart will surely forgive us if we have sent your Holiness a longer letter than you might have wished. For we are not pouring our little stream back into your abundant spring in order to enlarge it, but . . . we wish to have it approved by you whether our stream, although small, flows from the same source from which yours, abundant as it is, also proceeds.”  
> (The same, Letter 95.)

Here, then, are the testimonies supplied by that holy Doctor concerning the pontiff’s rescripts in response to the councils and the letters just cited.

[Col. 0969A]

> “For what,” he says in Book I, chapter 2, Against Julian, “could that holy man have replied to the African councils except what the apostolic see and the Roman Church, together with the others, have steadfastly maintained from ancient times?”

And in Letter 106:

> “He”—Innocent—“replied to us concerning everything in the manner that was right and proper for the bishop of the apostolic see.”

And below:

> “A novel and pernicious error was so crushed by ecclesiastical authority that we are greatly astonished that there are still some who strive, through whatever error, to resist the grace of God—if, at least, they have learned what took place.”

And elsewhere:

> “Bring those who resist before us. For two councils have already been sent to the apostolic see concerning this matter; and rescripts have also come from there. The case is finished—would that the error might at some point be finished as well! Therefore, we admonish them so that they may take notice; we teach so that they may be instructed; we pray so that they may be changed.”  
> (The same, On the Words of the Apostle, Sermon 2, at the end.)

But had the practice of appealing to an ecumenical synod not yet begun? Let us hear Augustine on this matter:

[Col. 0969B]

> “What is it that they say? Was a subscription extorted from simple bishops sitting in their own places without the gathering of a synod? Or was the gathering of a synod really necessary for an obvious evil to be condemned? As though any heresy had ever been condemned only through the gathering of a synod, when in fact exceedingly few are found for whose condemnation such a necessity arose; and when there are many more—incomparably more—which, once they appeared, deserved to be rejected and condemned there, and from there could become known throughout the other lands as things to be avoided.
>
> “Yet these men’s pride is understood to seek even this glory: that a synod of East and West should be convened on their account. Since they cannot corrupt the Catholic world, because the Lord opposes them, they at least try to disturb it, whereas, after a fitting and sufficient judgment has been given against them, pastoral vigilance and diligence require that, wherever these wolves appear, they be dealt with—either so that they may be healed and changed, or so that they may be avoided for the safety and integrity of others.”  
> (The same, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, Book IV, at the end.)

[Col. 0969C]

The same holy Doctor says to Julian on this subject:

> “I think that part of the world ought to suffice for you in which the Lord willed the most glorious martyrdom of his first apostles to take place. If you had been willing to listen to blessed Innocent, who presides over that Church, you would already then have stripped your dangerous youth of the Pelagian snares.”  
> (The same, Book I Against Julian, chapter 2.)

After the sentence had been issued by the apostolic see, therefore, nothing remained for those most wicked men, under those names, except detestation of their crimes and repentance.

> “And although they hold and sow these execrable doctrines, they nevertheless still demand a hearing, when those who have been condemned ought to be doing penance.”  
> (The same, Against the Second Letter of the Pelagians, Book I, at the end.)

## III

Concerning appeals to the holy see for the correction of morals, I shall report whatever was done in Africa on this matter during the age of Augustine under the pontiffs Zosimus, Boniface, and Celestine. This province of the Western Church was greatly troubled by being subjected and, consequently, sought to diminish the rights of its patriarchal position. To put it more accurately: the Africans were disputing rather about the kind of judgment and the execution of the sentence in appellate cases than about the right of the supreme tribunal, which they never called into question as belonging to the holy see.

It is clear that the substance of their consultations and assemblies was to beg the supreme pontiff not to send legates thereafter, but merely to designate investigators who would be present on the spot and settle such cases, and not to permit the execution of the sentence to be entrusted any longer to secular magistrates.

Augustine earnestly begs Pope Celestine that this be permitted in the case of Antony of Fussala, who, having been expelled from his own see by the bishops of his province, had obtained a decree from the apostolic see. Although that decree was only conditional, it nevertheless threatened to be enforced despite the opposition of his adversaries.

Moreover, far from placing the right of the apostolic see in doubt, the holy Doctor rather acknowledges and confirms it by numerous examples of judgments that were either issued or confirmed by that see. I myself present the testimonies to this effect concerning the pontificate of Celestine, from the letter that Augustine wrote to that pontiff, numbered 161 in the older edition and 209 in the more recent one.

For the rest, Saint Augustine not only acknowledged, revered, and defended the supreme rights of the holy see, but, whenever necessary, acted as the most vigorous champion of the pontiffs themselves. Yet he did not fail to distinguish between a man and a pontiff if the wretched condition of their private life had rendered them liable to some fault.

But after he had vindicated the honour of their ministry—most sacred and entirely beyond reproach—he defended the reputation of the minister himself, who was especially exposed to the calumnies of wicked men and heretics. In its proper place we shall state what he himself replied to the Donatists when they objected to the Church that the pontiffs Marcellinus, Marcellus, Melchiades, and Sylvester had succumbed to the persecutions.

In his books against the Pelagians we see how effectively he defends Pope Zosimus from that censorious charge with which those foolish men attempted to brand him concerning the exercise of his authority in support of the heresy they professed.

These are the very words of the holy Doctor:

[Col. 0970C]

> “But if”—which God forbid—“judgment had been passed concerning Caelestius or Pelagius in the Roman Church in such a way that those doctrines of theirs which Pope Innocent had condemned in them and together with them were pronounced worthy of approval and adherence, then the Roman clergy would rather deserve to be branded with the mark of treachery.
>
> “But now, since Zosimus, when Caelestius was attempting to clear himself, compelled him by frequent interlocutions to agree to the aforesaid letters of the apostolic see”—which Innocent had written to the African Churches—“whatever was meanwhile dealt with more leniently in the case of Caelestius, provided only that the firmness of the most ancient and most robust faith was preserved, was a most merciful exhortation to correction, not the most destructive approval of depravity.
>
> “And since Caelestius and Pelagius were later condemned by the same priest with renewed authority, this was the severity that had been briefly interrupted but now necessarily had to be preferred; it was not a betrayal of the truth previously recognized, nor a new recognition of the truth.
>
> “How, then, are the Roman clergy accused by these deserters and enemies of the faith of treachery under Bishop Zosimus, as though they had held one view in the later condemnation of Caelestius and Pelagius and another under Innocent in the earlier condemnation?
>
> “For, since the antiquity of the Catholic faith was clearly expressed in the letters of the venerable Innocent concerning infants who, unless they were baptized in Christ, would remain in eternal death, whoever had departed from that judgment would rather have been a betrayer of the Roman Church. But, by God’s favour, this did not happen; rather, through the repeated condemnation of Caelestius and Pelagius, that faith was preserved. Let them understand that they themselves possess the source from which they accuse others, and let them at last be healed of their betrayal of the faith.”  
> (The same, Against Two Letters of the Pelagians, Book II, chapters 3 and 4.)

# 12. THE CORNUTIAN CHARTER

Or the donation which Flavius Valia Quintus Theudovius offered to the Cornutian Church.

[Col. 0971]

## BLANCHINI’S PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

[Col. 0971A]

This charter is a public document recording the donation which Flavius Valia Quintus Theudovius, a most illustrious man, conferred upon the Cornutian Church, together with an inventory of the furnishings and estates assigned to that sacred building. It was signed in the fifth consulate of Leo, perpetual Augustus, with Probianus as his colleague—that is, in the year 471 of the Christian era—as the learned editors of that distinguished document have observed.

If you compare this charter with the Praenestine inscription carved in the year of Christ 930, under Pope Gregory IV, published by the same Suaresius in Book II, chapter 7, page 146, of Ancient Praeneste, and reprinted by us in the preface to the first volume of this edition, number 50, you will see that throughout the five centuries separating the two monuments it was customary for both movable and immovable goods to be donated to churches, according to nearly the same practice preserved in the Lives of the Pontiffs contemporary with this period by the librarian of the Roman see.

Mabillon adds an observation worthy of a most learned man: among the other gifts conferred upon the Cornutian Church, a *Book of the Comes* is mentioned. It follows that before the year 471 of Christ there existed a completed book of this kind, used for the clergy.

[Col. 0971B]

This single and most ancient document, signed with public authority, would suffice to illustrate and confirm the history and the catalogues of the movable and immovable goods assigned to our churches under nearly every pontiff. It therefore seemed that sufficient provision had been made for the authority of this part of the history of the biographers here listed under the single name of Anastasius if we produced one or another document of this kind recording donations and registers.

Yet it would be an offence to omit the memory of another distinguished monument. In the cemeteries of the holy martyrs situated on the Via Salaria, in the year 1726, the excavators of His Eminence Cardinal Marefoschi discovered a chamber anciently painted with sacred images and filled with the bodies of several holy martyrs. Their blood becomes visible when light is brought near it in glass vessels, customarily fastened with cement to their tombs. The chamber was also furnished with marble inscriptions, one of which indicates, from the consular date belonging to the year 340 of the common era, that a Christian whose tomb it closed had been deposited there four years after the death of blessed Sylvester. The inscription reads:

**SEMVESTINO ALOM D. V. ID IAN ACYNDINO ET PROC. CONSS.**

“Semvestinus Alomnus (Alumnus) was deposited on the fifth day before the Ides of January, in the consulship of Acyndinus and Proculus.”

If anyone thinks that the first syllable **SEM** should be separated from the cognomen Vestinus, and interprets it as consisting of abbreviations expressing *Sem[piternae memoriae]*, “of eternal memory,” or even *SEMno Vestino*—with the word altered from the Greek **ΣΕΜΝΟΣ**, “venerable,” since Greek words are not rarely observed mixed and incorporated into Latin in Christian inscriptions of the fourth century and later—let him use whichever conjectural interpretation he prefers.

**SEM** might also be understood as a Hebrew name belonging to Vestinus, or as the family name Sempronius Vestinus. For in Fabretti, from the cemetery of blessed Castulus, *Inscriptions*, plate 555, number 25, one also reads:

**CARTORI. VESTINO QUI DECESSIT. IN. PACE.** etc.

[Col. 0972B]

However the name Vestinus is explained, I do not concern myself with it. I propose only that one point be observed in this inscription: namely, that the deposition of this Christian man occurred only four years after blessed Sylvester had been buried in the same cemetery of Priscilla on 31 December, in the consulship of Julius Constantius and Albinus—that is, at the end of the Christian year 335, which Constantius and Albinus marked.

For from that date to the Kalends of January in the year 340, opened by the consuls Acyndinus and Proculus, only four complete years are counted, according to all the little tables of the fasti.

Besides this inscription, a fragment of another was found there, coming still closer to the deposition of blessed Sylvester, since it bears the consular date of Felicianus and Titianus, namely, the year 337. It reads as follows:

**CON STANTIE CONSTANTIUS S. DEP. XVI. KAL. DEC. FELICIANO ET XX. TITIANO CONS.**

“Constantius was deposited on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Felicianus and Titianus.”

Completion of the following larger tablet. See Blanchini’s text, col. 977.

[Col. 0973]

[Col. 0975A]

The arrangement, then, of the parts of this chamber, prepared for the celebration of the sacred mysteries there during the last persecutions, since it approaches so closely the age of Sylvester, suggests many things to us that wonderfully confirm and illuminate the writings of the Librarian in the Life of Sylvester and his successors. For this reason it seemed appropriate to present it among the Prolegomena. (Plate I.)

The vaulted ceiling of the chamber opens toward those entering into an arch. Its inner recess, within a narrow area of this kind, somewhat imitates the apses of basilicas. The structure of the arch itself may likewise be compared with the arch placed over the presbyteries of basilicas, which, as we have received it from our ancestors, we call the triumphal arch.

The age contemporary with Constantine was accustomed to adorn this above all with sacred images, especially with the Lord Christ seated among the apostles. This, certainly, is the design of the principal church of all, namely the Basilica of the Saviour founded by the great Constantine in the Lateran under Pope Sylvester, which the Librarian displays for us in number 36:

[Col. 0975B]

> “In his time Constantine Augustus made these basilicas and also adorned them. In the Constantinian Basilica he placed these gifts: a beaten silver gable, which on its front has the seated Saviour sitting on a throne, five feet high, weighing 102 pounds; and the twelve apostles, each five feet high, each weighing ninety pounds.”

The example of Sylvester and Constantine was never forgotten by later ages. Not only in the apse of that same Lateran basilica, but also in the surviving chamber of the dining hall of that patriarchate, built by Saint Leo III, Christ the Lord and the twelve apostles were represented in mosaic work.

During repairs to the basilica, Pope Nicholas IV in the year 1291 represented those same apostles in mosaic beneath the image of the Saviour in the vault of the apse. Most recently, Clement XI, following the footsteps of his predecessors, ordered the blessed apostles—the foundations of the new city Jerusalem—to be fashioned in the nave of the principal church, each beneath a small shrine or niche. These were constructed according to the same design by Innocent X, cut from solid marble on a colossal scale by the foremost sculptors of our age. The pious princes vied in contributing funds to adorn the chief of all basilicas with sacred images of this kind, according to the custom of the Constantinian age.

[Col. 0975C]

We know that the same was done in the Vatican, both in ancient times and in our own. Gregory III placed images of the twelve apostles upon twelve vine-shaped columns to crown the presbytery, as the Librarian testifies in number 194. Sixtus V wished the broad apse founded by him to be adorned with their figures, likewise executed in mosaic. Paul V, also bearing that name, decorated the front of the basilica that he had built with colossal figures representing Christ the Lord and the twelve apostles.

A similar arrangement is read and seen in the Basilica of Saint Paul on the Ostian Way. When blessed Leo III restored it after it had been shaken by an earthquake, the Librarian reports, while preserving its ancient form:

[Col. 0975D]

> “In the canopy above the altar he offered golden images of Christ the Lord and of the apostles Peter and Paul.”

More recently, Pope Honorius III restored in the tribunal, or chamber of the presbytery, the images of Christ the Lord and the twelve apostles, traditionally composed in mosaic.

But so that we do not multiply examples of a custom so widely received and confirmed, it will be more than sufficient to point out that, on the principal solemnities of the year, the worship of the pontifical altar consisted in this single ornament: statues of the holy apostles placed beneath the image of the crucified Lord.

Thus, at the request of blessed Sixtus III, the emperor Valentinian, in number 65, offered above the confession of blessed Peter the apostle a golden image with twelve doors, and twelve apostles and a Saviour adorned with precious gems. Likewise, in the Greek Pontificals, images of Christ the Lord and of the twelve apostles are placed upon the doors of the sanctuary, or **προθύρῳ** (*prothyro*, “vestibule”), and made visible by burning candles and torches.

[Col. 0976A]

It pleased the Catholic Church, in its solemn rites, to display the eternal Priest according to the order of Melchizedek, seated upon a throne in royal majesty, and to represent the apostles as sharing in his kingdom and, in a certain sense, as **συνθεόνους** (*syntheonous*, “co-enthroned with God”), since they sit with him upon twelve thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel—that is, the entire Church of believers. Through the royal priesthood communicated to them, he established fishermen as princes over all the earth.

A more explicit image of the fulfilment of this prophecy in the Christian Church shone forth especially when, after peace had been restored to it and the persecutions had been removed, the bishops of the apostolic sees were permitted under Constantine and his successors to assemble in ecumenical councils upon the thrones of the apostles and to exercise publicly the judgment of the whole world, deciding concerning divine and human affairs.

He presided over the others—the one whom he wished above all to exercise his vicarious authority—so that whatever was pronounced on earth in such a judgment might be ratified in heaven. When, then, the promise of that oracle had become fulfilled and more manifest, having been exposed to the eyes of the regions of East and West, it was especially fitting that its image should also be dedicated in sacred buildings, where our Redeemer, to whom all power in heaven and on earth has been given, deigned to establish among mortals the royal throne of his majesty.

It therefore became customary, from the Constantinian age onward, to depict the apostolic thrones, flanked and crowned on either side by the divine presence, either with images of the apostles by whom they had been founded or with the mystical figures of the elders of the Apocalypse, who, from their own seats, thus adore the throne of the Lamb. This was done both in basilicas erected during the peace of the Church and in cemetery chambers that anticipated those basilicas in their immediate vicinity at the end of the persecutions.

We recognize this from the memorable chamber on the Via Salaria in the crypts of Saint Hermes, or adjoining the cemetery of Priscilla. The inscriptions on the graves of the faithful make clear that it was used and frequented for the burial of Christians for four years after the deposition of Sylvester, for the celebration of their sacred mysteries.

[Col. 0976C]

It is evident from Eusebius’s *History*, Book IX, chapter 2, that while Constantine was ruling together with his colleague in the imperial government, Licinius, Maximinus, no less hostile to both of them than to our faith, declared such a war against the sacred rites of the Christians and everywhere destroyed and levelled their temples that they were forced to take refuge in the cemetery crypts in order to perform the sacred mysteries.

He judged that the edicts of Diocletian and Maximian, by which shortly before the assemblies of our religion and the sacred buildings prepared for the **συνάξις** (*synaxis*, “assembly”) had been savagely attacked, had to be renewed. “The persecution,” he says in Book VIII, at the end, “having begun with the destruction of the churches, subsequently advanced much farther through the attacks of the rulers that followed at different times.”

Indeed, even after he had entered into sham peace agreements with his imperial colleagues, he did not allow the peaceful condition of the Church to remain undisturbed for even half a complete year. “While he was attempting everything possible to overthrow the peace, he first tried, under some pretext or other, to prevent our people from attending the assemblies (**συνόδου**, *synodou*) that customarily took place in the cemeteries.”

Thus, during Maximinus’s constant persecution in the East, Christian assemblies took place in the cemeteries, and during the intervals of peace sacred gatherings were held in the cemeteries of the martyrs—just as they were also held at Rome while Maxentius, his equal and counterpart, was exercising tyranny, as the same Eusebius observes.

[Col. 0977A]

But when the divine power of Christ had destroyed the tyrants and reduced them to nothing—as Eusebius records in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book X, chapter 4, page 374, in connection with the dedication of the church at Tyre after the persecutions had been removed—it raised his friends and intimates not only among mortals but also among the heavenly powers.

Thus the Ruler of heaven and earth, having appointed the apostles as judges’ assessors, as it were, handed over to their successors the judgment of the world in ecumenical councils, in the seats which the apostles themselves had founded on earth at his command. Those who had previously been forbidden by tyrants even to gather secret assemblies beneath the crypts were now invited by the emperors to celebrate publicly the synods of all provinces and nations.

Rightly, therefore, did the piety of Constantine imprint upon the crypts—at whose entrances Christians had shortly before been forbidden to gather—and upon the basilicas which he soon afterward erected with triumphal splendour, a spectacle so delightful and divinely reserved for the age and piety of Constantine.

But let us continue to examine in the image the parts of this sacred chamber, which shed no small light upon the events of those same times.

[Col. 0977B]

In order, then, that we might understand that the thrones of the apostles signify the seats founded by them on earth and handed down to their successors together with episcopal authority, beneath the arch crowned by those same seats there is seen an image of the Good Shepherd feeding the sheep. This is the Lord Christ, Prince of shepherds, after whose example the shepherds of peoples, appointed by him, ought to be formed.

They must preside over the lambs entrusted to them in such a way that they nevertheless remain subject to him who received from the Prince of shepherds the sheep and lambs to govern with vicarious authority, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd.

Beneath the arched covering of the vault, the bodies of Christ’s faithful are deposited according to custom, but especially those of the holy martyrs. The custodian of the sacred relics drew the indications of them from the vessel of blood placed beneath the image of the Good Shepherd.

He also drew them from the lower niche, constructed in the manner of an altar. Above its table, or marble slab closing the niche, Christians were accustomed to offer sacrifice, as countless monuments of the Church prove. Among these is the testimony of blessed Augustine in Book VIII of *The City of God*, chapter 27:

[Col. 0977C]

> “Nevertheless, we do not establish temples, priests, sacred rites, and sacrifices for those same martyrs, because their God, not they themselves, is our God.
>
> “Certainly we honour their memorials as those of holy men of God who fought for the truth even to the death of their bodies, so that the true religion might become known, false and fabricated religions having been exposed; and so that even those who previously held the truth might no longer suppress it through fear.
>
> “But who has ever heard a faithful priest standing at an altar—even one constructed above the holy body of a martyr for the honour and worship of God—say in his prayers: ‘I offer sacrifice to you, Peter, or Paul, or Cyprian,’ when sacrifice is offered at their memorials to God, who made them both human beings and martyrs and joined them to his holy angels in heavenly honour?” and so forth.

This final expression of Augustine corresponds to another painting beneath the image of the Good Shepherd and above the martyr’s niche and altar table, painted on the wall. There the angel of God appears to the three youths in the Babylonian furnace, who steadfastly assert the worship of the one God.

Thus we are to understand that the witnesses of the divinity, or the martyrs of Christ, are honoured by the Church of God in association with the angels. From the sacred writings, together with Augustine, the Church has learned to think and profess this.

Furthermore, it is clear from the letter of blessed Cyprian written to Saint Lucius the pope during the persecution of Decius and Valerian—which the patriarchal basilicas of the City read on the feast of Saint Lucius, pope—how the figure of the three youths was applied to the steadfast confession of the Roman pontiffs. For this reason it frequently appears in the Roman crypts of the martyrs.

The front of the altar is formed by the niche that we have mentioned, in which three figures are painted. The central figure is that of an excavator opening such niches on the slope with his pickaxe; the cemetery crypts have been opened there.

The distinguished gentleman Joannes Marangonius, highly skilled in the sacred cemeteries, observes that these very crypts may belong to that part of the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria which, as we read, was called *Ad Clivum Cucumeris*. On this matter Aringhius, Severanus, and Boldettus should be consulted, the most diligent guides to this sacred topography.

[Col. 0978A]

The second figure shows a woman wearing a long robe and carrying a glass vessel half-filled with blood, collected either from the body of a martyr or with a sponge from the place of martyrdom, as Prudentius describes it, together with other writers of the nearby period, frequently cited by the distinguished authors of the sacred cemeteries.

The third figure represents a woman, decently dressed in a long garment like the second, carrying in her hand several crowns woven from branches and flowers. A basket likewise full of branches and flowers has been placed nearby.

For in the burial and translation of martyrs, besides the *colobia* decreed by blessed Eutychianus, we know from Augustine that branches and flowers were placed beneath them. From him we also learn the reason for this custom, likewise indicated by Prudentius: flowers, branches, and *brandea*—sprinkled with the dew of the blood shed for Christ or touched by the sacred body of one killed for Christ—were intended to stir the minds of the faithful, as pledges of the common faith, to imitate the virtues of the martyrs, seek their patronage before God, and obtain divine assistance.

Augustine relates an example of this kind concerning Bishop Lucillus at the translation of the relics of the protomartyr Stephen, and concerning a devout woman who, after receiving flowers from Bishop Projectus and using them while the relics were being carried, was freed from blindness.  
(Saint Augustine, *The City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 8.)

[Col. 0978B]

Others may observe that very large glass vessels of the kind we have indicated in the hands of the other figure carrying the martyrs’ blood—vessels measuring a palm and a half or two palms—occur more than once in this cemetery. Their traces and impressions remained attached to the plaster closing the niches, together with gilded glass crusts still visible there.

One point, however, should be observed above all: in another chamber excavated not far from the entrance to the crypts, beneath an arched vault and very similar to the one we have described, a vessel was found whose diameter is three palms. This indicates a vessel of very considerable size, equal to broad dishes. Perhaps it was used for serving at the large assemblies of the faithful held there during the last persecutions. This is confirmed by the broad area of the building constructed at the entrance of the same cemetery and graphically described by Aringhius in Book IV, chapter 37, under the name of Saint Silvanus, together with Saint Boniface, who were once deposited there.

These matters we leave for others to observe, so that we may touch only upon what pertains to the argument we have undertaken: namely, that the royal priesthood of Christ, communicated by the eternal Pontiff according to the order of Melchizedek to his apostles and their successors, freely displayed the splendour of its dignity through these signs as well.

The peaceful Solomon had given such signs to his bride, the Church: apostolic chairs erected in the caves of the persecutions and, in the peace of the Church under Constantine, raised more exaltedly into the royal thrones of the basilicas.

[Col. 0978D]

The episcopal thrones, displayed more magnificently to the whole world in ecumenical councils, declared to the delegates appointed by Christ that, just as they had received authority from the Lord Christ, so they had also been enriched by the piety of princes with the addition of royal insignia. They thereby proclaimed his majesty reigning everywhere and, as it were, subjecting the earth as the footstool of his feet.

Thus consular chairs, *trabeae*, and *laticlaves* were eagerly offered by princes to the ministers of Christ, so that they might be placed beneath the humble cloak of shepherds and the garments of fishermen.

The sacred altar tables received gold and silver drinking vessels commonly contributed from the imperial dining rooms, so that every precious furnishing of human grandeur might be dedicated under the New Covenant to the worship of the true divinity, just as under the Old Covenant the profane spoils of the Egyptians were converted into ornaments for the tabernacle.

From this source, then, comes that long series of gifts attached by the pontifical biographers to nearly every Life as its own catalogue and enumeration. Besides vessels of every kind dedicated in basilicas and titular churches, it includes garments woven with gold and silver; portable and hanging crowns; gem-studded brooches; senators’ shoes; the *palmatae* of triumphing generals; and the purple of rulers—attached to the heads, feet, shoulders, chests, and bodies of bishops, priests, and Levites alike—like the spoils of the most distinguished offices in the state, skilfully arranged as a trophy of the cross of Christ and carried upon the shoulders of priests to this stronghold of the heavenly Jerusalem.

Here, then, would be an appropriate place to enumerate individually the Levitical, priestly, and pontifical ornaments properly adapted to our uses—partly by imitation of the divine institution under the Old Testament, partly from apostolic tradition under the New, and partly from the discipline of the successors of the pontiffs and of the councils, which, during the peace of the Church, more fully explained the mysteries of the authority attributed by Christ the Lord to himself and to the Church. Here, I say, would be the appropriate place to enumerate them. But the brevity that must be imposed upon the Prolegomena does not permit us to proceed through them individually, especially since most of the origins and developments of the vesture pertaining to the hierarchical orders of the Church may be sought elsewhere, in the more expert writers on liturgical matters and expositors of sacred antiquity. We have touched upon some of these below, in the notes to Saint Zosimus.

Much also was contributed to their elucidation above all by the learned writer Father Alexander Wilthemius, a Jesuit priest, in his *Dyptichon Leodiense*, concerning the consular diptych transformed into an episcopal one. Further material could have been collected from our studies on the mitre, the pallium or pontifical Phrygium, and the sacred vestments, once prepared for the press in connection with the translation of the sacred body of Blessed Leo the Great, though never published. But since the subject is equal to a work of substantial size, it has no place among the shorter pieces to be inserted in the Prolegomena.

From this material I shall select one item, noted in order to illustrate the history and the indication of the authority signified by the pallium and the pontifical Phrygium. The first account reports that the pontiff Saint Mark granted it to the bishop of Ostia, since he possessed the right of consecrating the [Col. 0985C] Roman pontiff. Other ecclesiastical monuments teach that the Phrygium was sent by Pope Saint Celestine to blessed Cyril, so that he might preside in his name over the Council of Ephesus; and that later successors of Celestine granted the pallium to primates and metropolitans (see Thomassinus, *Vetus et Nova Ecclesiae Disciplina*, Part I, Book II, chapter 45), as a badge of authority conferred over several bishops of a kingdom or province. Others, however, maintain that the pallia of the Alexandrian pontiffs are so close to the foundation of that see that a custom prevailed in that Church of clothing each successor at his consecration with the very pallium of blessed Mark. All these matters subject the episcopal pallium and Phrygium to innumerable questions.

I believe that all these questions can be resolved by considering two ancient images which Cardinal Camillo de’ Massimi formerly collected from the paintings of the ancient Romans. They were bound together in a single codex in his exceptionally choice treasury, and most elegantly drawn by the Apelles of antiquaries, Pietro Santi Bartoli. Two assemblies of Roman magistrates are displayed in these paintings (Tables III and III). Each is presided over by the head of the assembly, with the title of dignity *PRAESES* in one case and *PRAESES CONSILII* in the other.

This president is distinguished from all the others by a peculiar ornament wound around his neck, shoulders, and chest, just like the pallia of sacred prelates, especially the Greek ones. It resembles a broader band—of the sort that among the Romans received the name *laticlavus*—and which, in many shield-bearing images of the age of the Antonines and later, is sometimes represented plain and sometimes embroidered or figured (*phrygiata*). In consular diptychs from the age of Constantine onward it is usually shown embroidered and figured, as may be seen in the image which I append, reproduced from Wilthemius’s Leodiensis (Table IV). In another Biturican diptych, too, the consuls are represented in similar dress. The same is true of the diptych of the royal treasury of the Grand Duke, printed by Senator Filippo Buonarroti in his most learned *Appendix to the Glass Images of the Cemeteries*, and of others cited by him: namely, one from the antiquarian treasury of the kings of France, published by Monsieur du Cange in his dissertation on coins of the lower age, and another from Dijon belonging to Monsieur de Mare, inserted by Monsieur de Partival in his book *On the Usefulness of Travel*.

All these monuments, formed by Roman sculpture or painting, suggest to us that those bands across the chest were originally borders or purple *clavi*, woven into and sewn onto the edges of togas. Hence the toga *praetexta* is said to have been given to the higher magistrates, both under the Republic and under the twelve Caesars. In the following century, that of the Antonines, the practice became established of attaching a broader *clavus* to the toga, especially at the point where the toga, wrapped around the chest and shoulders, was neatly folded into its folds.

As time progressed—perhaps under Trebonianus Gallus and the emperors who followed—bands, borders, and *clavi* of figured work were sewn onto the consular *toga palmata* worn in procession. This is proved by numerous coins struck with such insignia for Trebonianus Gallus, Aurelian, Probus, Carinus, Diocletian, Maximian, and Licinius, especially the exceptionally well-preserved examples kept in the antiquarian treasury of the most eminent Cardinal Alessandro Albani. The diptychs mentioned above also show this practice. These diptychs were distributed by the consuls and sent to their friends as *apophoreta*, that is, commemorative gifts recalling the magistracy held and the public entertainments given.

It has again become clear that our Christian prelates, both in the East and in the West, within the boundaries of the Roman Empire and beyond them, possessed—besides the civil garments of the body, which the common usage of the nations and the moderation appropriate to our profession allowed, garments not unlike those of philosophers, such as ordinary pallia or *homophoria*, also called *mafortes* in the later age, woollen *birri*, and common tunics—certain insignia of the priesthood reserved solely for sacred uses. These were derived for the most part from the divine Scriptures of both Testaments, namely the Pentateuch and the Apocalypse, and were commended by their cleanliness, simplicity, and ease of preparation.

We have touched upon some of these in the notes to Saint Zosimus. Thus the apostle James is said by Eusebius to have used linen garments and a frontal plate or *petalon*; John, too, is said to have worn it in Asia. Pallia or *homophoria*, pastoral *birri*, and dalmatics are mentioned in the Acts of Cyprian. Tunics with bands, or distinguished by certain stripes, are visible in the very ancient images of the sacred cemeteries, made from glass plaques, in which the apostles and apostolic men are represented.

These monuments further demonstrate that the borders of the pallia and the neck-pieces or insertions of the tunics, like Aaron’s shoulder-piece, which was furnished with a woven collar, cords, and priestly ribbons—the latter also being used to fasten to the tiara the frontal plate inscribed with the name of God—formed certain ornaments of Christian pontiffs, especially around the shoulders and chest. When the collar of the priestly *birrus* was drawn back over the head, it also presented something resembling a mitre. I could establish this not only by written testimony but also by ancient images.

Thus, by these brief indications, the insignia of the pontiffs—derived from the institution of sacred Scripture and not inconsistent with the common practice of civilized nations—were established even in the earlier centuries of the Church. Accordingly, in the mosaic images of the Liberian Basilica, executed under Sixtus III around the beginning of the fifth century, whose engravings are displayed in the notes to his Life, Melchizedek, priest of the Most High God, is shown wearing a purple pallium and collar bordered with bands and ribbons, together with a jeweled breast-clasp fastened above the sternum.

The same is true of the images of our pontiffs painted in the Basilica of Saint Paul during the course of the same fifth century under Leo the Great; of the image of Pius I of that name, painted much earlier in the cemeteries of the martyrs, whose likeness we have printed in his Life; and of the blessed Damasus and Sixtus, drawn from the glass plaques of the cemeteries, which we reproduce here. They are shown adorned with tunics, collars, and pallia furnished with *clavi*—whether called a *phylacterium*, border, *clavus*, or band—and fastened across the chest by a clasp resembling the *rationale* in the Mosaic law, and also resembling the clasp which in the Roman Church is still customarily worn by cardinal bishops and by the supreme pontiff, commonly called the *formale*.

[Col. 0987B]

The sewn borders or bands, together with the plate and plaques, attached to cleaner woollen *birri* or apostolic pallia and to priestly collars, which in the course of ministry were generally thrown back from the forehead over the back of the head and neck, constituted in the earlier centuries that simple and easily prepared garment and insignia of the episcopal hierarchy.

When, after the peace had been granted to the Church, the religious generosity of princes wished to offer magnificent insignia of royal majesty in homage to and testimony of the Christian royal priesthood, the apostolic prelates responded to the devout zeal of the donors by wearing precious garments woven with gold threads, such as Constantine the Great also sent to Macarius of Jerusalem, according to Eusebius in his Life of Constantine.
