Yet, never forgetting their ancient garments, whose superiority to all others they knew very well, they always wished the royal sign of the Lord’s cross and their own woollen ribbons—the tokens of the pastoral mystery and authority conferred upon them by God—to remain above the consular *palmata* and imperial *trabeae*.

They also arranged these same ornaments so as to make them more easily intelligible to the Christian people, who, by analogy with the common dress of magistrates, could readily understand the order of our hierarchy. They saw to it that the ornaments were disposed around the edges of the pallia and decently encircled the neck, arms, and chest, so that the manner of wearing them did not differ from the *laticlavus* of the presidents in the case of that prelate who surpassed the others in authority and jurisdiction.

The faculty of wearing such a pallium everywhere therefore belongs solely to the Roman pontiff, who holds the primacy of blessed Peter throughout the entire Church. For the other bishops who exercise patriarchal or metropolitan rights within defined limits of their dioceses, exarchates, and provinces, the wearing of that ornament is confined within the same boundary as the jurisdiction of each.

When, however, it happened that, by delegation of the Roman prelate, someone left the limits of his diocese, exarchate, or province in order to preside, in the name of the one who sent him, over sacred ecumenical councils—as happened with Cyril, who went by delegation of Pope Celestine to preside over the Council of Ephesus—no more fitting insignia could be sent than that pontifical band of the pallium, also called the Phrygium. Although it is known to have been made of wool and simple weave, marked with crosses, it later began to be fitted with gold-woven *stolae*, offered by Christian princes for the adornment of the royal priesthood. Thus, to the eyes of peoples accustomed to recognizing the president of a council, province, or region by similar dress, it immediately indicated that the wearer had been delegated by the pontiff to exercise, beyond his own boundaries, the office of presiding in the name of the one who had delegated him and who presides everywhere.

These observations, made in passing, are sufficient for touching upon the origin, discipline, and development of the sacred vestments, especially the pontifical vestments of the Christian priesthood, insofar as it has been necessary to treat them in the Prolegomena. To follow each of them more carefully and compare Eastern and Western usages, the earlier gifts of princes with those that followed, would provide material for a substantial volume, and would require many additions of ancient images, which cannot be engraved without considerable expense to the printer.

[Col. 0990A]

Nevertheless, since we are dealing with vesture, it will not be burdensome for me to present, at my own expense, both the other material inserted here and a very rare monument from a bronze seal. It was given to me by a prelate of immortal memory, Leone Strozzi, distinguished not less by his praise of learned antiquity and the gentleness and integrity of his character than by the nobility of his lineage. I had a likeness of it most carefully engraved to the scale of the original, not only to enrich the subject of the vesture of the ancients but also to elucidate the history of Constantine the Great and of the Sarmatians, the Lombards, and peoples related to them.

An ancient bronze seal, the size of a palm, excavated in Rome, displaying a soldier or barbarian commander, both in the features of his face and in the dress of his body. The garments, tightly fastened to the torso and limbs, imitate the Sarmatian fashion. They are sewn from bands—such as we see worn today by the Swiss guards—and an undershirt with loose sleeves, still retained by the Hungarian Illyrians and neighboring peoples; these reveal the Lombard usage. Paul the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 23.

The club in the right hand and the handle of an Amazonian double axe in the left are weapons familiar to the Polish nobility, who call them in their own language *Buchecann* and *Bardis*. Formerly, however, they belonged to the Lombard prince or king Authari, according to their history in Paul the Deacon, Book III, chapter 31.

The image of Constantine the Great is seen on the chest; this perhaps indicates the military gifts bestowed by him upon the Scythians and Sarmatians who had been added to the Empire, or upon its allies, after that victory had been won under the auspices of the Lord’s cross, which Eusebius recorded in his Life, Book IV, chapters 5–7. For this reason we reproduce his coin, showing a cross upon an altar crowned with victories.

[Col. 0991A]

This ancient bronze seal, filling the measure of a palm in breadth—if its legs had not been lost—displays a barbarian soldier or commander, both in the features of his face and in the dress of his body. The garments, tightly fastened to the torso and limbs, imitate the Sarmatian fashion represented on the column of Marcus Antoninus. But here they are sewn not from scales, as on the column of Marcus Aurelius, but from bands or strips, such as we see worn today by the Swiss guards. The undershirt, however, with its loose sleeves, is still retained by the Hungarians, Illyrians, and neighboring peoples.

This second form of clothing reveals the Lombard usage described by Paul the Deacon, Book IV, chapter 23, from a painting which Theodoric, king of the Goths, had ordered to be made in the palace he built at Monza:

> “In this painting,” he says, “it is clearly shown how the Lombards at that time cut the hair of their heads, and what their clothing and appearance were. For, shaving the crown of the head as far as the back of the neck, they left it bare; they wore their hair hanging from the face down to the mouth, and divided it on either side. Their garments were loose, and chiefly linen, such as the Anglo-Saxons usually wear, adorned with broader bands woven in various colors.”

In this little image the Sarmatian usage is recognized in the garments tightly fitted to the body, and the Lombard usage in the cutting of the hair, which descends in front as far as the mouth. A similar style among the Goths is noted by the Palatine Academics of Milan, in the edition of Paul the Deacon, at the cited passage of their distinguished collection of Italian matters, volume I, page 460, from Sidonius Apollinaris, Book I, Letter 2. The same Lombard usage is visible in the loose-sleeved linen undershirts or undergarments, and in the multiple bands or strips fastened over the linen undershirts around the entire body.

The weapons displayed on this seal were likewise used indiscriminately by Lombards and Sarmatians, and are still employed by Polish nobles inhabiting Sarmatia. The club in the right hand and the hanging handle of the Amazonian double axe in the left are familiar weapons among the Polish nobility, who call them in their vernacular *Buchecann* and *Bardis*. Authari, king of the Lombards, carried a small axe among his weapons, as Paul the Deacon testifies in Book III, chapter 31 of his *History of the Lombards*.

This barbarian soldier or commander represented on the seal may therefore have belonged to a people neighboring the Sarmatians and Lombards, whom Constantine the Great joined to himself and enriched with gifts after his Sarmatian victory, and whom he led, by his generosity and piety, to embrace the institutions of our religion, as we read in Eusebius, in the passage to be cited shortly.

For this reason I also arranged for another coin of Constantine the Great from our treasures to be engraved on the same plate—besides the one which the little image shows hanging from its neck like a victory token. On it two Victories are displayed, holding a crown and a shield inscribed with the vows of the Roman people above an altar engraved with the saving sign of the cross. This suggests that the campaigns and victories of the religious prince, and the vows of the Roman people, were directed not, as previously, toward spurious gods, but toward the true God and our Savior, and were offered upon altars marked with his cross, so that the worship of the Christian faith might be advanced and propagated even among the nations.

[Col. 0991D]

It would perhaps not be unrelated to an elucidation of pontifical history and of the Christian religion extended more widely through the victories of Constantine the Great to consider the new organization of the provinces established by that prince in the Roman Empire, and to examine whether it brought about any change in the ecclesiastical division of the dioceses of the bishops of the East and West. But this would carry us farther than is appropriate. The invasions of the barbarian peoples that followed immediately, together with the civil division of the kingdoms and the end of the Western Empire, introduced greatly differing changes in dominion, and these would require separate treatises to examine them properly.

It is better to leave this field to more expert scholars, who will be able to illuminate the individual provinces in a work devoted specifically to them. For me, who am merely making these observations in passing, it will be sufficient to offer a specimen in the notes to the Life of Eleutherius, concerning the provinces of Britain. In the age of Constantine a new division occurred there in the civil administration, with the addition of those provinces—or of that province—which it pleased them to name after the emperor: Flavia Caesariensis and Maxima Caesariensis, the latter later subdivided into Valentia.

We must therefore refrain from such an excursion and remain within the shorter course opened to us by the consideration of this seal, which displays the victories of Constantine, the barbarians joined to the Empire, and the clothing and ornaments characteristic of that age.

Moreover, not only Eusebius and other historians and chronologists but also Constantine’s coins testify that the Sarmatians were conquered by Constantine the Great around the year 321. The coins bear the inscription *SARMATIA DEVICTA*, “Sarmatia conquered.” Yet Eusebius testifies that the magnanimous prince shared the chief fruit of his victory with the very enemies whom he had conquered, in Book IV of his *Life of Constantine*, chapters 6 and 7. He received them within the boundaries of the Roman Empire, gave them lands, and enrolled suitable men among the military forces:

> “So much so,” he says, “that they themselves confessed that their calamity had turned out happily for them, since they had exchanged barbarian savagery for Roman liberty. In this way God added very many barbarian nations to his Empire. For from every place ambassadors continually came to him, bringing him whatever they possessed that was most precious as gifts. Indeed, we ourselves have sometimes seen before the doors of the palace various types and appearances of barbarians standing in order; their clothing and ornaments were different, and their hair and beards were very unlike one another. Their appearance was grim and barbarous and inspired terror, and the stature of their bodies was of extraordinary height,” and so forth.

The sight of this little image provides an excellent commentary on Eusebius’s history. The historian goes on to enumerate the kinds of gifts offered by the various nations: golden crowns, diadems filled with jewels, barbarian garments woven with gold and flowers, horses, shields, long spears, arrows, and bows.

> “By these gifts,” he says, “they signified that they offered the emperor their allegiance and alliance in arms, if he wished it. But he accepted and set aside what each brought, and in return gave them so many and such great gifts that in a moment he made those who had brought gifts extremely wealthy. From their number he also honored the noblest with Roman dignities, so that many of them, forgetting their return to their homeland, wished to remain here among us.”

This barbarian prince represented on the bronze seal wears upon his chest a coin bearing the face and name of Constantine the Great, evidently a gift which he had received, and perhaps he should be counted among those nobles whom Constantine honored with Roman dignities.

Others may consider whether the attachment of the coin and of the victory token of the same kind, hanging from the neck like a torque, when compared with the gem of the Odescalchi Museum representing Constantine himself with a pendant disk hanging from his neck and inscribed with the monogram of Christ the Lord—which the distinguished Brachiani Duke published engraved by Pietro Santi Bartoli together with several objects from his treasury, formerly that of Queen Christina of Sweden—and with coins of the sons of the Caesars of the same prince bearing the Labarum and marked with the same letters and guarded by those same Caesars, belongs to the insignia of the fifty men whom Constantine selected from the Protectores to guard and carry that saving sign.

For in the mosaic at Ravenna of Justinian, published by several writers, namely Cangius, Ciampini, and others, those Protectores carry a shield marked with the monogram of Christ. Or does it designate a prince allied with the Empire, since the custom of wearing a hanging image of the Roman emperor around the neck continued even to Justin the Elder? John Malalas, in his *Chronographia*, written under Justinian, his son, records that the king of the Lazi, Ztathius, after throwing off the Persian yoke, went to Constantinople and, having been cleansed in the sacred font and given his name to the Christian religion, was presented with:

> “A royal diadem in the Roman manner; a white *holoseric* cloak, in place of the purple, having a golden royal *clavus*, in the middle of which was a seal, *stēdárion* [στηδάριον], displaying the image of the emperor Justin. He also wore a white *paragaudion* tunic”—*paragaudion sticharion* [παραγαύδιον στιχάριον], which the learned editors of the notes prove, from Symeon of Thessalonica, to be also a priestly garment, and which, from Trebellius Pollio’s account of Claudius, was a Parthian garment bound around with golden bands—“adorned, in accordance with royal custom, with golden *clavi*, which likewise bore the emperor’s image.”

The Church, after the princes’ gifts, attached such golden *clavi* or borders sewn onto the tunics, according to royal custom, to bishops, deacons, and subdeacons. The royal sign of Christ—the cross, through which he reigned—adorns them, rightly taking precedence over the images of the emperors, which Justin and other princes had stamped on the tunic of the king of the Lazi and on their own gifts sent to allied rulers. The emperors themselves, following the example of Constantine, placed the divine monogram of Christ upon their royal robes, as may be seen engraved on the breast ornaments of Justin and Justinian on their coins.

[Col. 0994A]

A consideration of these garments would easily lead us to set out individually the insignia of our priestly hierarchy and to explain many words which seem barbarous in Anastasius but which are derived from the indicated Greek and Roman sources: *Paragaudes*, concerning the *chrysoclavus*; *periclysin* concerning the *starausi*, concerning the Tyrian purple or Byzantine *blatta* (nos. 468, 469); the cross and *gammadia* of *chrysoclavus* (no. 416); *holovera* pallia of *blatta* with panels covered in gold, derived from the *chlamys* or imperial *stola* (no. 85), and many similar terms.

From the garments we would then proceed to the vessels of sacred ministry, which likewise occur in Anastasius: silver and golden *amae*, electrum *gabata* (no. 85), the *pharan* crown before the altar (no. 64), the *Diacopton* cross (no. 366), and similar objects. But the sails must be shortened, lest this little work become an appendix of observations and treatises be hammered out of the Prolegomena.

I shall therefore present the charter of donation, adding within brackets the corrections found in the Barberini Library. Some of these are partly printed, and the printer will represent them in round type; others were added by some learned man, perhaps Suarez himself, and I shall have these rendered in slanted type, or italics, as the Italians call it.

[Col. 0993]

# THE CORNUTIAN CHARTER

[Note: [Col. 0995C]

This charter, first published by Joseph Maria Suaresius from the archive of Tivoli, it seemed worthwhile to print again here and place at the head of all the ancient instruments, as the oldest monument, since it was drawn up under the consulship of Leo, perpetual Augustus, for the fourth time, and of Probianus, *vir clarissimus*—that is, in the year of Christ 471—as is established from Cassiodorus, Marcellinus Comes, and other chronological records.

Among the many matters worthy of observation, one may not lightly pass over what is read concerning the *Book of the Comes*, which is attributed to Jerome and was written eight hundred years ago. Certainly, from this charter, it has an author named Jerome who was contemporary or nearly so.

*Mabillon.*

It seemed worthwhile to interpret several terms concerning the vessels and garments offered in this donation. Since these words frequently occur in the *Bibliothecarius*, the explanations may serve in place of a lexicon for the *Anastasian Lives*. In the text they occur beside the following numbers.

## I. The offering-hamula

*Hamula*, or *amula*, is a diminutive of the word *hama* or *ama*. In writers of the later age it indicates a small pitcher; in our ritual books it is more often used for the vessel in which water, to be mixed with the wine of the sacrifice at the offering, is brought by the subdeacon. It may also be taken for either of the two small pitchers containing the wine and water of the offering.

I have given an image of it in the notes to Saint Urban, taken from an ancient silver vessel decorated with sacred images in relief; see those notes. Altaserra and Bencinius may also be consulted in the notes to Saint Sylvester, as may Cangius in his *Glossary of Medieval and Lower Latin*. Panvinius, in his interpretation of obscure ecclesiastical terms, published together with his supplement to Platina’s *Lives of the Pontiffs*, observes that *amula* and *oma* are also used with the same meaning by the standard translator of the sacred books in translating the Greek word *phialas* [φυάλας] in 3 Kings, chapter VII, verse 40.

Columella likewise uses *hamula* in the cultivation of gardens for a vessel employed to hold water:

> “Or a hamula suitable for water and a flask of Bacchus.”

It should therefore be regarded as a word belonging not only to Middle and Late Latin but also to genuine Latin, and as indicating a vessel for water.

## II. The strainer

“This was a certain small vessel,” says Panvinius in the passage cited, “perforated at the bottom with extremely fine holes, through which the wine was poured from the *hamulae* into the chalice.”

It was therefore made from thin metal plate, as is still done in the shops of apothecaries and similar establishments, so that as the liquid passed through the tiny holes it would leave behind all sediment, lest the substance of the liquid offered in the chalice contain anything turbid.

The Roman Order proves that it was used in antiquity and was then certainly necessary because of the discipline of communicating under both kinds. Since this required a considerable quantity of material for consecration, care had to be taken lest, during such a large pouring of liquid, anything foreign—small animals or the like—slip into the chalice. For the same reason, the larger and smaller chalices mentioned here were used. See the image of the strainer or sieve in our notes to Saint Urban, nos. 3 and 4, reproduced from an ancient treasure.

## III. The *pharus*, and so forth

A lamp from which a broad silver vessel was suspended below by little chains, so that, if the lamp were moved, the oil would not spill onto the pavement. The chains which attached this vessel to the lamp were elegantly supported by finely worked dolphin-shaped ornaments. The same is true of the chains of the lamp-crowns, suspended in the customary manner and fastened by clasps:

> “Four silver crowns with their chains and eight dolphins.”

The suspension of the crowns may be seen in the consular diptychs in Cangius’s dissertation on coins of the lower age, and before the bishop’s throne in the mosaic at Ravenna and elsewhere.

## IV. Silver *cicindelae*

Panvinius recognizes different kinds of lamps in these *phari*, vessels, *cerostata*, crowns, and so forth. Thus he writes in the lexicon contained in his supplement to Platina:

> “Damasus and the *Bibliothecarius* of the Roman pontiffs, especially the Life of Saint Sylvester, use *phara*, *canthara*, *cerostata*, crowns, dolphins, *lychni*, and *lynochi* for lamps and lights of different kinds burning in churches.”

After adducing many learned materials to illuminate the word *pharus*, he adds:

> “Why, however, a *pharus* is called a *cantharus*, I do not know with certainty, unless it was made in the form of a large vessel at its extremity. For the *cantharus* was a drinking cup attributed to Bacchus, just as the *scyphus* was called the cup of Hercules. Pliny, Book XXXIII, chapter 11, reports that Marius, after his victory over the Cimbri, drank from *canthari*, following the example of Father Liber. Virgil writes:
>
> ‘And the heavy *cantharus* hung from its worn handle.’
>
> Ulpian says that *canthari* are vessels from which water spurts.”

So much for Panvinius. Correctly so: in both cases liquid is received in open vessels.

We infer from ancient reliefs, frequently encountered in the friezes of temples, that handled *canthari* placed upon a candelabrum constituted *pharacanthara*. They were used to illuminate buildings not only with wax but also with an aromatic mixture of other substances nourishing the flame, such as spices, balsam, drops of myrrh, and so forth.

Today, vessels filled with a thicker substance and an unpleasant-smelling liquid are commonly used to illuminate the streets during public celebrations; they are popularly called *padellae* and are used in the open air in place of *pharacanthari*.

As for the *cicindelae* mentioned here, Cangius shows, from Festus, that *cicindelae* are the small winged insects resembling flies which shine at night during the summer; they are also called “night-lights.” From their resemblance, the wicks floating in oil inside glass lamps were called *cicindelae*, and the name was transferred to the lamps themselves and to the metal vessel enclosing these glass lamps.

*Stantarea.* According to the same writer, *stantarea*, derived from *stare*, are free-standing candelabra.

*In the confession, oysters.* The same author rightly thinks that a scribal error should be corrected and that we should read *ostia*, namely doors or leaves placed at the confession, or at the entrance to the presbytery, since the words that follow are “with its key.”

*And in the pallia.* From the enumeration of the vessels of sacred ministry, the text proceeds to the garments. It first lists the priestly garments, namely pallia and *mafortes*. Then it lists the veils which are hung before the altar, the royal doors of the basilica, the consistory, the porch, and the secretarium.

A reader can easily establish the differences and names of these garments. Their names may derive from the material of which they were woven—silk, linen, or gold—or from the form of their weave; from an added purple or gold *clavus* or border; from the shape of that *clavus*, whether square or round; or from the regions from which they were brought. Hence the terms Aquitanian pallia, Cassiotian pallia, and Persian veils. They may also derive from the colors with which they were dyed: white, rose-colored or rhodomeline, white-and-rose, *blatteus* or purple—for *blattion* [βλαγτιον] in Greek is a kind of shellfish dye, as Cangius and Macer note—green, green-and-scarlet, scarlet-and-rose, eagle-colored, and similar shades.

I explained above, at column 993, on the occasion of the bronze little image girded with bands or strips, which displays the coin of Constantine the Great fastened to its chest, what *paragaudis* means: namely, a broader band or golden *clavus*, fitted according to royal custom to a tunic, pallium, or other garments and veils. Hence the name *paragaudis* is sometimes applied to them. The lexicographers do not disagree. Macer writes:

> “*Paragaudis*: a kind of band or *laticlavus*, woven of silk and gold, with which the edges of garments were adorned; from the *Codex*.”

The image of Melchizedek, king and priest, represented in the mosaic of the Liberian Basilica under Saint Sixtus III, shows purple *paragaudes* of violet color properly attached to a white pallium and white tunic. We give an engraving of this image below in the notes to his Life.

In the same basilica’s mosaic of the triumphal arch, likewise executed under Sixtus, the Jewish scribes and priests who show Herod the prophetic Scriptures in response to his question about the place where Christ would be born, indicating Bethlehem, wear plain pallia without sewn-on *clavi*. They are fastened only to the chest by clasps, as may be seen in the image of that mosaic which we reproduce there.

These few observations, made on the occasion of the Cornutian Charter, will perhaps be sufficient for understanding those obsolete terms for vessels and garments mentioned in these Lives—or at least for recognizing that hardly any such word will occur in the *Bibliothecarius* whose meaning cannot be found in the lexicons of Cangius and Macer. We therefore do not consider it necessary to reprint Panvinius, nor to dwell longer on these matters.

**Blanchini.**
[Col. 0993B] A copy of the authentic charter from which we were able to gather it, belonging to the church of Cornutiana: namely, so that those subject to the divine ministry may be able to have a suitable income from the place [Col. 0993C] which they serve. Immediately also, we consider it fitting that the temple should every day be adorned with the lamps of divine worship, and that, when repairs are required because of the length of time, the expense for mending and restoring it, supplied by this our gift, should not be lacking. For these purposes we provide suitable expenditures, so that our service may deserve to obtain the favor of the Godhead.

Moved by this consideration, by the tenor of the present document I grant to the Cornutan church the estates of my own right, established and founded by me through the favor and assistance of God: namely, the paternal estate, Maranus; the paternal estate, Monte Paterno; the estate called Casa Martis; the estate called Vegetem, which is Casa Projectici; and the estate called Batilianum—except for Sigillosa, daughter of Anastasius, and Pice (rather, Pica) of the colonists, which we have retained and continue to retain under our own right—situated in the province of Picenum, in the territory of Tibur. They are to be possessed under the title of pure and direct liberality, with everything belonging to them and with all their rights, equipment, and appurtenances, just as I myself possess them, including, of course, every burden of their tenure or obligation which it is certain that *formensia* estates must bear.

We also donate to the same church the ground on which it has been established, together with its area, and separate it from the legal possession of the aforesaid Praetorium; and we grant it to the clergy and custodians for making gardens or dwellings: namely, from the hollow arch which leads to the Praetorium, and then along the walls which, returning opposite the Praetorium, enclose the church’s area, as far as beyond the apse [Col. 0994B]; and from those walls along the hedge which appears to secure the gardens of the tenants who live in the Praetorium. This hedge descends along the path in front toward [Col. 0994C] the hollow road, or toward the Torus (*Torum*), and returns as far as the arch written above, so that between the hedge and the hollow road, behind the apse, the aforesaid clergy may be able to have gardens.

Furthermore, by the same liberality I offer the following estates: the Callician estate, Casa Nova, Casa Prati, Casa Marturi, Casa Crispini, the Boaric estate, and Casa Pressa, situated in the province of Picenum, in the territory of Tibur.

I retain the usufruct during my lifetime, transferring ownership of this property to the same Catholic Church by this gift, under this law and condition: when it has begun to receive and claim the fruits after my death, it must recognize not only the customary fiscal payment, but also the propagation of the *formae* which is customarily paid by all owners of estates of this kind. [Col. 0994D]

I also expend silver for the adornment of the same church and for the celebration of the aforesaid most holy mystery, in the following objects: one large silver paten; one large silver chalice; two smaller silver chalices; one silver pitcher; one offering-hook; one strainer; one *thymiamaterion*; one lamp; one silver *cantharus* with chains and eighteen dolphins; four silver crowns with their chains and eight dolphins; five silver lamps with their chains.

One silver *stantarea* (*στηδάρεα*), and in the confession two silver shells, with their nail. All these objects, when weighed on the city standard, amount to fifty-four ounces of silver.

Seven bronze lamps: two having eight dolphins and *hermoriae*; six larger bronze *canthari* and twelve smaller ones; two bronze lilies; and thirteen bronze *stantaria* (*στηδάρια*). Also, among the hangings: one holoseric, unfulled, gold-clavus-bearing pallium; one four-coloured (*tetraphorum*) holoseric pallium; a *maforte* of *tramosericum*, rose-colored, eagle-patterned. Also a *maforte* of *teleoporphyric* *tramosericum*, with a maritime design; another holoseric pallium, *luricatum* (*luritatum*); a Cassiotic pallium; one Aquitanian linen pallium; and four other linen pallia.

For the border of the altar: two white *tramoseric* hangings with gold *clavi*; two purple hangings with gold *clavi* and *paragaudiae*; two white holoseric hangings with gold *clavi* and *orthopluma*; two *tramoseric* hangings of green-and-purple; two *tramoseric* hangings of white-and-rose; two *tramoseric* hangings of white-and-purple; [Col. 0995B] two holoseric hangings of scarlet-and-green.

Another set of furnishings: two purple hangings with gold *clavi* and *orthopluma*; two *tramoseric* hangings of eagle-patterned scarlet-and-green; two wholly purple *tramoseric* hangings; two hooked hangings, *loricata* (*luricata*), of melon-colored and purple cloth; two wholly purple holoseric hangings; two *apoplacia* (*apoblacia*, or *ad ploblatea*), scarlet-and-green, latticed and rosette-patterned; and five *aploblattea* hangings of scarlet-and-green, *cantharata*.

Another set: two square-patterned linen hangings with gold *clavi*; two linen hangings with gold *clavi*, *paragaudata*, and round *clavatura* patterns; two Persian linen hangings, *paragaudata*, with scarlet-and-melon and green square-patterns; two Persian linen hangings, *paragaudata*, with white-and-rose square-patterns; two linen-and-purple-silk hangings, *paragaudata*; and two linen-and-purple-silk hangings, *orthopluma*.

Fourteen plain linen hangings. Before the basilica’s royal doors, [Col. 0995C] three large divided, embroidered linen hangings. Three plain linen hangings. Before the consistory, one plain linen veil. In the narthex, one plain linen veil; and within the basilica, six rosette-patterned linen hangings for the porticoes; and before the secretarium, or the curtains (*curricula*), two rosette-patterned linen curtains fitted with arches.

Also, books: four Gospels, an Apostolos, a Psalter, and a *Comes*.

Immediately taking every precaution above all, lest—God forbid—the observance and worship of the Cornutian church should appear to perish with me, I established this law and condition for my donation: no bishop or priest succeeding another, nor any cleric, may ever alienate any of these estates, gardens, silver objects, or garments designated above by me, under any title whatsoever, or transfer them on the pretext of divine worship for the adornment of another church on any occasion.

I also wish the same condition to be observed regarding whatever may in future be added through the prompting of our devotion, since I desire the permanent substance of this present liberality of ours to belong to the aforesaid Church.

If anything should perhaps be attempted concerning the alienation forbidden by me, then I, or my heir or heirs, or my successor or successors, or those who succeed them thereafter, shall restore to their own right and ownership everything included in the terms of this donation. For what was offered by us out of reverence for religion, according to the law and condition established, must not be assigned by anyone to any person, another church, or estates belonging to anyone.

I dictated this deed of donation to be written by Felicianus, my notary; after I had reread it, I subscribed it with my own hand, without fraudulent intent, and by my own will ordered it to be entered in the records. I promised all the matters stated above to the venerable presbyter, the deacons, and all the clergy of the aforesaid church, who had stipulated them.

Subscribed on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of May, under Pope Lord Leo Augustus, in the fourth consulship of Probianus, illustrious man, as consuls. Flavius Valia. Quintus Theudovius, illustrious man, and Illustrius, count and master of both military forces, consented to and subscribed this donation of all the estates, silver, and garments written above, dictated by me and reread to me, with the law and condition which I imposed upon the donation preserved and observed forever; specifically, however, reserving the usufruct of the aforesaid lands, which I reserved to myself above in the same document.

[Col. 0999]

Image of Blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, from the age of Saint Sylvester, preserved in the Roman Church, as it is represented in the letter of Hadrian I to Charlemagne; likewise carefully delineated and engraved from the mosaics of the Liberian Basilica by Sixtus III, and of the titles of Saints Praxedes and Cecilia by Paschal I, as well as from ancient images and the seals of the pontiffs, by Pietro Rotari, nobleman of Verona, at Rome in the year 1728.

[Col. 1001A]

Image of Saint Paul the Apostle, preserved in the Roman Church from the age of Blessed Sylvester, whose features are expressed with equal accuracy, as read from the letter of Hadrian I in the Second Council of Nicaea; followed and engraved from the mosaics of the Liberian Basilica under Sixtus III, those of the titles of Saint Praxedes and Saint Cecilia under Paschal I, and other most ancient images and papal seals, by Pietro Rotari, nobleman of Verona, at Rome in the year 1728.

[Col. 1003]

HISTORY OF THE LIVES OF THE ROMAN PONTIFFS, BY ANASTASIUS, ABBOT, PRESBYTER OF THE ROMAN CHURCH, AND LIBRARIAN.

The author of this *Liber Pontificalis* borrows nearly everything from the author of the second Catalogue—the Regina Sueca and Colbertina manuscripts—which we indicate in the text by italic type. Those matters printed in Roman type the author drew from elsewhere, such as what he says concerning the martyrdom of the apostles in the year 38 after Christ’s death and concerning the ordinations performed by Peter and Linus. (Patrologia edition, from the notes of Schelestratus.)

(In the notes collected from the margin of Fabrotti’s edition, an asterisk indicates the Velser manuscript collated with the Vatican; B indicates readings from the manuscripts of Cardinal Baronius; B indicates readings according to the opinion of that same cardinal; C indicates readings from the Councils edited by Surius.) (C)

I. SAINT PETER THE APOSTLE. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 45, IN THE THIRD YEAR OF THE EMPEROR CLAUDIUS.

[Note: [Col. 1005A]

Variant readings added by Fabrotti outside the margin, from the manuscripts of Marquard Freher: A, the first; B, the second.

Number 1, line 4: A, six years. Same line: B, two months and seven days. Line 6: B, “which were canonical.” Line 7: A, “which after every …,” confirmed; B, “formed.” Same line: B, “confirmed.”

“He ordained two bishops, Linus and Cletus, who in person were to provide all priestly ministry in the city of Rome for the people and for those arriving. Blessed Peter, however, devoted himself to prayer and preaching, instructing the peoples. He had many disputations with Simon Magus, both before Nero and before the people. Those whom Blessed Peter gathered into the faith of Christ, Simon separated through magical deceptions. While they continued their dispute for a long time, Simon was killed by divine will.

“He consecrated the blessed bishop Clement and entrusted to him the arrangement of the whole chair and Church, saying: ‘Just as the power of binding and loosing has been entrusted to me by my Lord Jesus [Col. 1005B] Christ, so I entrust it to you: appoint administrators of various matters through whom ecclesiastical activity may be conducted, so that you may not be found occupied with worldly concerns, but may strive to devote yourself solely to prayer and preaching to the people.’

“After this arrangement, he was crowned with martyrdom together with Paul.”

Line 14: A and B, seven deacons.

The same Fabrotti’s readings excerpted from three manuscripts: the Regius, the Mazarin, and the Thuane.

In the letter of Blessed Jerome [ [Col. 1005] Fabrotti presents this letter in his editions; it is absent from the Roman-Vatican edition which we follow. EDITOR.], the superscription is absent: “the things which happened,” namely, “in.” In the same place: “our holiness”; in the margin: “our humility perceiving.” And immediately, “who deserved,” etc. Letter of Damasus to Jerome: “of priestly times.” Nevertheless, “the acts of P.”

Page 1, in the margin, C. Maz.: “This book is entitled: ‘Damasus, On the Deeds of the Pontiffs.’ But since he could have written only up to his own times, what has been added afterward belongs to another author, whose name I do not retain. Indeed, in the Life of Pope Gelasius II, a certain Pandulphus, an usher, claims that he wrote these things. This may be understood either of the entire work up to his own times, or of the Life of Gelasius alone, as may be conjectured from the Life of Paschal II.”

Title in manuscript M.: “Here begins the succession of the Roman Pontiffs who have sat in the chair of Blessed Peter the Apostle, from Peter himself up to the present time.” And in the margin: “Our Lord Jesus Christ, the supreme pontiff, is born in the thirteenth year of the reign of Augustus; he lived in this number [that is, in this period] thirty-three years, three months, and …; he was baptized in his thirtieth year; he preached during the remaining time. After his Passion, in the following year, the Apostle Peter held the chair in the eastern regions for four years; then, in the year of the Lord 38, he came to Antioch, where he sat for seven years and eight days; then he came to Rome, where he sat for twenty-five years, seven months, and eight days.

Number 1, line 1: “and” is absent. Line 2: “The Apostle, a Galilean by nation, from the land of Bethsaida, son of John, brother of Andrew, first sat in the episcopal chair at Antioch for seven years. He lived in the times of Tiberius Caesar, Gaius Caligula, Tiberius Claudius, and Nero.” Line 6: “who … and son in baptism.” After “all,” “which at his questioning,” confirmed by his testimony—that is, “the faith of Peter”—while one agrees in Greek, another in Hebrew, and another in Latin. Line 13:

“He ordained at Rome two bishops, Linus and Cletus, who in person were to provide all priestly ministry in the city of Rome for the people and for those arriving. Blessed Peter, however, devoted himself to prayer and preaching, instructing the people. Earlier in Judaea, and afterward at Rome, he had many disputations with Simon Magus, both before the emperor Nero and before the people. Those whom Peter gathered into the faith of Christ, Simon separated through magical deceptions. But while they continued their dispute for a long time, Simon was killed by divine will.

“Peter, perceiving that the day of his death was approaching, consecrated Clement bishop and entrusted to him the chair and the whole Church to administer, saying: ‘Just as the power of binding and loosing has been entrusted to me by my Lord Jesus Christ, so I also entrust it to you: appoint administrators of various matters through whom ecclesiastical activity may be directed (Mazarin manuscript: conducted), and do not allow yourself to be found devoted to worldly cares, but strive to devote yourself solely to prayer and preaching to the people.’

“After this arrangement, he was crowned with martyrdom together with Paul, his fellow apostle, in the year 39 after the Lord’s Passion. He sat in the Roman episcopate for twenty-five years, two months, and eight days. He was buried on the Via Aurelia, in the Temple of Apollo, near the place where he was crucified, beside Nero’s palace. In the Vatican manuscript: ‘once’; elsewhere: ‘three.’ On the third day before the Kalends of July. He performed ordinations in the month of December: six bishops, ten priests, and eight deacons.”

The same author’s variant readings from another, the Thuane manuscript.

Here begins the episcopal book, in which are contained the acts of the Blessed Pontiffs of the city of Rome.

In the letter of Blessed Jerome: “Here begins the letter of Blessed Jerome the presbyter to the most blessed Damasus, bishop of the city of Rome.” In the same place: “our humility, considering”; “who deserved.” Superscription of the reply of Pope Damasus to Jerome: “to the most blessed Damasus, pope of the city of Rome, sends greetings”; “of priestly time, nevertheless, who …”

Number 1. Line 2: “In the village of Bethsaida.” Line 3: “seven years.” “Here Blessed Peter.” Line 4: “three days.” Line 7: “son from baptism.” Same line: “the font”; “at Peter’s questioning they were confirmed, while one agrees in Greek, another in Hebrew, and another in Latin”; “by his testimony they were confirmed.” “He ordained.” Line 12: “the third day before the Kalends.” Line 13: “in the month of December, ten priests, seven deacons, and three bishops in various places.” “He ordained.”

[Col. 1006C]

Variant readings excerpted through the diligence of the illustrious Luca Holstenius from the most distinguished manuscripts of Italy—two Vatican manuscripts, two Florentine manuscripts, the Cassinese, the Regius, and the Farnesian—published by the illustrious Emmanuel de Schelestratus in volume I of *Antiquity of the Church*, pages 403 and following. He also collated them with the more ancient Catalogues of the Imperial Library of Vienna, the Queen of Sweden, and the Colbertine Library.

Number 1, line 2: two Florentine manuscripts, “the chair.” Line 4: both Florentine manuscripts, “two months, three days.” Line 6: the Florentine and Vatican manuscripts, “canonical.” Line 10: the Florentine manuscript, “39.” Line 12: Vatican and Florentine manuscripts, “the third day before the Kalends.” Line 14: both Florentine manuscripts and the Vatican, “seven deacons.”

Variant readings of the Cavensis manuscript, excerpted by the illustrious prelate Francisco Penia, auditor of the Roman Rota, whose autograph is preserved in the Ottobonian Library, as the following testimony prefixed to the work shows.

“Near Salerno, in the kingdom of Naples, lies the city of Cava, and in it a distinguished monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, of the Cassinese Congregation, under the invocation of the Most Holy Trinity. In that monastery there was an ancient book, written in old characters, concerning the Lives of the Roman Pontiffs. At the urging of Don Antonio de Aquino, who had found the book in that monastery, and at the request of Don Caesar Baronius, Cardinal Montalto, protector of the same order, ordered it to be brought to Rome in the year 1593.

“When I, Francisco Penia, auditor of the Rota, had obtained the same book, I arranged for it to be transcribed for me, preserving the same characters, and I myself collated it with the ancient exemplar, in which there are frequent solecisms, perhaps through the writer’s lack of learning, as appears in this book.”

After this preliminary notice, the text of the book follows. It first contains a Catalogue of the Pontiffs of the Church of Constantinople, perhaps stitched onto the Anastasian codex. Then are read two letters, attributed under the name of Blessed Jerome: one to Blessed Damasus, and one of Pope Damasus to Jerome. After these follow the Catalogues of the Roman Pontiffs listed below, from Saint Peter to Gregory VII; from this the age of the codex may perhaps be inferred. In the final Catalogue, while preserving the reading of the codex, we have noted its obscure passages and its cruder errors for correction from Baronius.

There he caused him to be held in custody; and there John endured severe illness and hunger for four months, died, and, as it is said, was killed.

Boniface himself held office for eleven months after John’s death. He died a sudden death, and his own people hated him so greatly that after his death they beat him and wounded him with spears. They dragged him by the feet, his body naked, as far as the Campus, and threw him down before the horse of Constantine. Sylvester, who was John, bishop of Sabina, unjustly held the pontifical chair for fifty-six days. He was expelled, and the aforesaid Benedict was restored; Benedict held the pontificate for one month and twenty-one days. He himself then gave it to John, archcanon of Saint John at the Latin Gate, his godfather, on the Kalends of May. They gave him the name Gregory. See Baronius under the year 1044.

Gregory, who is called Gratianus, held the pontificate for two years and six months; and through *imprm* [uncertain] he lawfully lost it and was carried away by him into the transalpine regions. This is recorded in the Synod. See Baronius under the year 1046.

Clement the Kindly, who is called Suger, a Saxon by nation, held office nine months, seven days. The aforementioned Benedict again returned to the pontificate and held it for eight months and nine days—that is, from the feast of the Four Crowned Saints to the feast of Saint Alexius.

[Col. 1014A] The following testimony, in the hand of R. P. D. Penia, follows.

> “This distinguished book was lost outside the monastery for many years. At last, through the efforts of the Reverend Lord Nicolaus Antonius, bishop of Muro, it was restored to the sacred monastery of Cava, at the time when Father Chrysostomus of Naples was abbot of that same sacred monastery—indeed, in the fifth year of his administration, namely in the year of salvation 1516, on 18 November.”

From this codex, therefore, we give the variant readings.

Line 2: “in the village Bethsaida.” Line 5: “and Gagi.” Line 8: “which are confirmed concerning the question and by his testimony—that is, Peter’s.” Although one is in Latin, another in Greek, and another in Hebrew, they nevertheless are confirmed by his testimony. “Here by martyrdom,” etc. Line 11: “in the temple of Apollo.” Line 12: “the third day before the Kalends of July.” Line 14: “seven deacons.”]

[Note: [Col. 1013B]

Line 1.—“Blessed.” The older catalogues of the Roman pontiffs, whether published or unpublished, and the codices of the *Liber Pontificalis*, generally give Peter alone the double title “blessed,” or “lord”; in designating the names of the others, although the pontiffs of the primitive Church were distinguished by the honor of martyrdom, they mark them with their bare and simple names. In placing “blessed” before Peter alone, they seem to have had regard to the Redeemer’s praise, by which, after Simon’s confession of the Word of God, he honored him with the title “blessed”: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar-Jonah” (Matthew 16:17). Reflecting on this, Basil wrote that St. Peter (Oration 3, *On Penance*) attained a blessedness far greater than all the others. For in the New Testament two persons are honored by that title: the Mother of God, who, inspired by the divine Spirit, said, “Henceforth all generations will call me blessed” (Luke 1); and Peter, by the voice of the Redeemer. Hence arose the true origin of the terms “blessedness” and “most blessed,” which the Fathers and councils applied to pontiffs, so that, by antonomasia, the Roman pontiff was designated by that title.

Thus the emperor Maurice, in the year 590, wrote to Gregory the Great (in volume 3 of the Councils, p. 528): “In all these matters your blessedness has sent soldiers to them . . . so that they may reach your blessedness.” Optatus frequently uses this title, as does Jerome in his letters to Damasus. The *Liber Pontificalis* likewise says below, under Hadrian: “At the very beginning of his ordination he sent his messengers to his blessedness, King Desiderius of the Lombards.” In the seventh century it was introduced with greater right and customary usage as the title belonging exclusively to the Roman pontiff. Thus Constantine Pogonatus, in his letter to Donus, while writing about the heretics’ attempt to remove the name of Pope Vitalian from the sacred diptychs, says: “so that Vitalian, the most blessed, might be removed from the diptychs” (Hardouin, volume 3 of the Councils, p. 1047); and Anastasius, under Benedict III, no. 556: “His blessedness shone and flourished so far and wide that by everyone he was called most blessed in word and deed.”

The word “lord,” however, is attributed to Peter alone in the catalogue preserved in the preceding volume, p. 40, while his successors are designated by their bare names. The usage is ancient. For in the Roman council under Hilary, successor of Leo the Great, it was repeatedly said among the acclamations: “Through the lord Peter, we ask that they may be preserved forever” (in the synod of Cassino, edited by Lupus, c. 218, p. 473). Stephen II likewise calls Peter “lord” in his encyclical published in Gaul, which Hilduin cites in the *Areopagitica*. The same word is read as applied to the Roman pontiffs from the end of the sixth century, when Gregory of Tours calls Gregory “lord” in book 9 of his *History*, chapter 45, and Gregory of Tours designates Paul, the first of that name, as “lord.” Hence in the most ancient inscriptions the word *domnus*, or *dominus*, is placed before the names of the pontiffs; and in the Lateran Triclinium Charlemagne and Leo III are honored equally by that title, “Lord.” The title “lord” was also applied to martyrs in the age of St. Cyprian, as will be noted below.

**Peter.** The series of the Roman pontiffs and the various older catalogues—whether they present the order of the pontiffs, mark their deaths, or constitute lists and other similar records—without any disagreement begin the order of succession with Peter alone and as a single figure; none associates Paul with Peter as bishop of the Roman see. This also demolishes the recent fiction of a two-headed see belonging to Peter and Paul.

Indeed, in the primitive Church the conviction was so firm that there had been one pontiff, and that the origin and succession had proceeded from Peter alone, that admitting a colleague to the see was considered foreign to evangelical institution. It is not appropriate here to heap up many examples, but three briefly deserve mention, from the threefold schism of the Novatians, the Donatists, and Felix, when Liberius was sent into exile. They illustrate the Church’s and the peoples’ conviction and bring out more clearly the authority of these catalogues, which unanimously derive their origin from Peter alone.

When Novatian, attacking Cornelius and invading the apostolic see, created a schism, among those who undertook the defense of the see and Cornelius’s struggle against the schismatics, St. Cyprian is especially praised. On that occasion he published his golden book *On Unity* and sent letters to various persons; throughout he persistently defended the proposition that, by divine institution, there is one see, delivered to Peter alone and transmitted to his successors; that admitting a colleague is alien and sacrilegious:

“He builds his Church,” he says, “upon one man . . . and, to manifest unity, by his authority he established the origin of that same unity as beginning from one.”

In all his letters written to defend the legitimacy of Cornelius’s pontificate he repeats this (Letter 40): “There is one God, and one Christ, and one Church, and one see founded upon Peter by the Lord’s word. Another altar cannot be built, nor a new priest appointed, apart from the one altar and the one priest . . . It is adulterous, it is impious, it is sacrilegious.”

And in the letter addressed to Antonianus, where he develops the statement more fully, after saying that Cornelius had succeeded the martyr Fabian, “when the place of Peter and the rank of the priestly see were vacant,” he immediately adds: “And since a second cannot exist after the first, whoever was appointed after the one who alone ought to exist is no longer a second, but is nobody.”

Writing to Lucius, the successor of Cornelius, he observes that Cornelius had confirmed the statement by his martyrdom: “Whence has secular power suddenly broken out against the Church of Christ and the blessed bishop Cornelius, the martyr, and all of you” (that is, through the contrivance of the Novatians), “whence God might show, for the confusion of heretics and their refutation, what the Church was and who was its one bishop chosen by divine ordinance.”

In the schism of the Donatists, this truth, the agreement of the catalogues, and the universal conviction of the Church concerning the one see given to Peter alone, with the necessary origin proceeding from Peter alone, were most conspicuously proved by Optatus in his books against Parmenianus. The Donatists agreed with the Catholics on the first mark of the true Church, which they said was Peter’s see; likewise, on the continuing succession in the see, in which one bishop sits. Thus, according to the understanding of both parties, Optatus says of the first mark of the true Church: “Among these the first is the see, without which, unless a bishop has sat there, the other endowment cannot be joined” (book 2, p. 34).

That the see had been established by St. Peter at Rome, that he alone had sat in it, and that the Donatists could not be ignorant of this, just as they could not be ignorant of the succession derived from Peter, he expressed as follows: “It must be seen who sat first in the see and where. If you are ignorant, learn; if you know, be ashamed . . . Ignorance cannot be charged against you.”

So great was the certainty both of Peter’s one see and of the uninterrupted succession that he did not hesitate to address the schismatic in these words: “Therefore you cannot deny that you know that in the city of Rome the episcopal see was first conferred upon Peter, in which Peter, the head of all the apostles, sat . . . in which the unity of the one see was preserved by all, lest the other apostles should each claim one for himself, so that he would already be a schismatic and sinner who established another see against the singular see.”

Then, from the previously established truth of the one Roman see, he proceeds to demonstrate the continuing succession, which he reviews according to the ancient catalogues: “Therefore the one see, which is first among the endowments, was occupied first by Peter, whom Linus succeeded,” and, after assigning the other pontiffs down to Siricius—at whose time he was waging his controversy with the schismatics—he concludes: “With him we agree, through the communication of the whole world, in the one fellowship of communion.”

Seeing that this common conviction of the whole world stood before them, the earlier Donatists, lest they appear to be deprived of the first endowment of the true Church—the Roman see and the one bishop sitting there, whose necessary origin was derived from Peter—invented a fantastic head and a proper Roman bishop. Optatus confronts them with these words:

“Give back to your see its origin, you who wish to claim the holy Church. You also say that you have some portion in the city of Rome. The branch of your error extends from falsehood, not from the root of truth. Finally, if Macrobius were asked where he sits there, could he say that he sits in Peter’s see? I do not know whether he has even seen it with his eyes; and he does not approach its memorial as though he were not a schismatic?”

He then attacks this Roman primacy and Roman see of the Donatists, since it did not derive from Peter but from Victor of Garba, who, after creating a pestilential schism in Africa, was the first to dare establish the seat of the plague at Rome. Optatus therefore continues:

“It remains, then, that your associate Macrobius admit that he sits there where Enclopius once sat. If Enclopius himself could be questioned, he would say that he sits there where Boniface of Bellita sat before him. And if he himself could then have been questioned, he would say where Victor of Garba had sat, who was sent long ago by your people from Africa to a few wanderers. What is this, that your party could not have a Roman citizen as bishop in the city of Rome? What is this, that all the Africans and foreigners are known to have succeeded one another in that city? Is the deceit not apparent? Is there not a fiction, which is the mother of schism? Meanwhile Victor of Garba was sent from there—I do not say a stone to the fountain, since he was not even able to disturb the purity of the Catholic multitude.”

St. Augustine repeatedly developed the same argument. From the one see and the succession derived from one man, Peter alone, he demonstrated that the Donatist Church was schismatic. He treats the matter at length in Letter 165, where, after reviewing the catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, he adds:

“In this order of succession no Donatist bishop is found; rather, from across the sea they had sent one ordained in Africa, who, presiding over a few Africans in the city of Rome, propagated the name of the Montenses or Cuzupitani.”

The people regarded the Roman Donatist bishop with such esteem that at the Carthaginian conference they obstinately tried to avoid beginning the discussion in his absence, as is recorded in the acts of the conference.

That one could be ignorant of the one see in the Church, of Peter alone sitting there with the succession of pontiffs, could not be attributed to ignorance, as Optatus had said. Thus Cornelius, in Eusebius, book 6, chapter 43, p. 244, while acting against Novatian in his letter to Fabius of Antioch, also brands him as guilty of schism on this ground: “Therefore that defender of the Gospel was ignorant that there ought to be one bishop in the Catholic Church.” And in another letter addressed to Cyprian: “For we are not ignorant that there is one God, that there is one Christ the Lord whom we have confessed, one Holy Spirit, and that there ought to be one bishop in the Catholic Church.”

Soon afterward, in this matter, he mocks the Novatian opinion and the fiction of a two-headed see: “By establishing a bishop for himself, he made outside the Church an adulterous and opposing head, against the sacrament once delivered by divine disposition and against Catholic unity.”

The Romans had been nourished by that common conviction of the faithful. While playing in the circus, although divided into factions, when they heard the imperial edict by which either Liberius or Felix was to be given to both parties, they laid aside their quarrels and shouted with one voice, according to Theodoret, *Ecclesiastical History*, book 2, chapter 17: “One God, one Christ, one bishop.”

If nothing else were available, we would owe this one thing to the compiler of the *Liber Pontificalis*: that he preserved the series of the Roman pontiffs and the order of the bishops succeeding one another in Peter’s see, which exhibit the first endowment of the true Church.

If the Fathers sometimes add Paul’s association to Peter’s, this must be understood as association in preaching, not in the see. This was noted by Eutherius of Tyana and Helladius of Tarsus. When they appealed to Sixtus after being deposed by the judgment delivered against them by John of Antioch for contumacy in the schism against St. Cyril, they wrote as follows in the Cassinese synodical record, c. 107, p. 240:

“Imitate also the great herald of piety, the oracle of the world, whom we believe we possess as a pledge of our familiarity with your holiness. For, being our fellow citizen, after the error of the whole world had been extinguished, he became an ornament of that apostolic see and received from blessed Peter the right hand of fellowship, so that it might appear that both preserved an equal exactness of doctrine.”

Gelasius and other Fathers speak in this sense in his decree concerning sacred books.

**Antiochene.** He received this designation from his earlier residence, sojourn, and episcopate at Antioch, just as the Redeemer was called Nazarene from his longer residence there. From this circumstance the Antiochene patriarchs derived the episcopal origin of their see from Peter, according to Fulgentius, book 1, *On the Trinity*:

“We wish to make known to your most sincere mind that faith through which the patriarchs were justified, the prophets, the apostles, and the crowned martyrs, which the holy Church has preserved throughout the whole world down to the present. Through the succession of generations it is preached even now by the bishops themselves in the see of the apostle Peter at Rome, or at Antioch, and in the see of Mark the evangelist.”

From Peter’s residence in the city and his see, Chrysostom and Theodoret derive its preeminence. Chrysostom, in his encomium of St. Ignatius the martyr, adds:

“Although God’s special care for this city was extraordinary, he also made this fully clear in fact. For he commanded Peter, whom he had set over the whole world, to whom he had given the keys of the kingdom of heaven, and to whose judgment and power he had entrusted all things, to remain there for a long time. Therefore our city corresponds, on the other side, to the whole world.”

Theodoret, observing Dioscorus’s ambition, by which he claimed primacy in the East, wrote to Flavian in Letter 14:

“This Dioscorus of Alexandria does not wish to submit to these laws, but again and again points downward to the see of blessed Mark, even though he clearly understands that the great city of Antioch possesses the see of the great Peter, who was the teacher of blessed Mark and the prince and coryphaeus of the apostolic chorus. We know the exalted dignity of the see; we also know and measure ourselves.”

In this sense Innocent I wrote to Alexander of Antioch, who had undertaken to defend Chrysostom’s cause in response to the pontiff’s admonitions:

“The Church of Antioch, like a sister of the Roman Church, did not allow itself to remain separated from it for long. For, having sent ambassadors, it sought and deserved peace in such a way that it gathered and united in one body both the clergy and the laity of John of holy memory.”

Line 3.—“Here Peter entered the city of Rome.” A serious dispute has arisen concerning St. Peter’s arrival in the City and the year of that arrival, as well as concerning whether he was ever in the City at all. Before Lactantius’ celebrated little work *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* was published, heterodox writers rushed into the negative opinion and defended Peter’s arrival in the City as a fiction. But after the work praised by Baluze was published, they can oppose this truth only foolishly, and they do not dare to do so, since Lactantius speaks of the matter as fully established and since both the subject of the work and the labor expended upon it clearly imply the same thing.

Lactantius wished to compose that work with the approval of Constantine the Great in order to review the outstanding struggles arising from the savagery of the persecuting emperors and their pitiable ends, so that from the reported triumphs and punishment of the tyrannical persecutors he might establish the truth of the Christian religion. With public assistance from Constantine he examined and investigated the official records. Thus, when he testifies concerning Peter’s and Paul’s residence in the City and Nero’s persecution of them—and does so precisely in order to demonstrate the truth of the Christian religion—if he speaks of Peter and Paul’s martyrdom as a matter of the greatest certainty, and of the multitude of Christians converted by them, it will rightly be considered absurd to call the matter into doubt later.

Tertullian certainly presupposes that records existed concerning these martyrs who were killed under Nero. In chapter 5 of the *Apology*, he himself undertakes a discussion and defense of the religion, addressing the nations as follows:

“Consult your own records. There you will find that Nero was the first to rage against this sect, then especially flourishing at Rome, with the sword of Caesar. Yet we glory in such a founder of our condemnation.”

Line 4.—“And there he occupied the episcopal see.” The Codex Regius should be read *cathedra*, “the see.” This corresponds to the martyrology for the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, “the see of St. Peter,” that is, the episcopate. Cyprian likewise, who, according to the ancient codices, entitled his work *On Unity*: “On the singularity of the see,” says among other things:

“Primacy is given to Peter, so that the one Church of Christ and the one see may be shown.”

In the same sense he wrote in Letter 51:

“Peter’s see and the principal Church, from which priestly unity arose.”

Optatus agrees:

“By the benefit of unity, blessed Peter—who would have been satisfied if, after denying the Lord, he had obtained pardon alone—deserved to be placed before all the apostles, and alone received the keys of the kingdom of heaven, to be shared with the others.”

Line 6.—“Which are called Catholic.” A title assigned to a written work denoted a dogmatic and authoritative institution. Hence, in the following century, when Themison was proposing the new doctrines of the Cataphrygians, he published a letter and distinguished it with the title “Catholic.” Apollonius, the celebrated opponent of that heresy, writes as follows in Eusebius, book 5, chapter 18:

“Themison, covered over with an attractive greed, who did not bear the sign of confession but, after distributing a great sum of money, cast off his bonds, although for this reason he ought thereafter to have acted more modestly and submissively, nevertheless, presenting himself as a martyr, dared, after the example of the Apostle, to write a catholic epistle, in which he instructed those who had proved more faithful than himself and supported a new doctrine.”

**The Gospel of Mark.** Eusebius speaks of this kind of confirmation in book 2, chapter 15, on the authority of Clement of Rome, Clement of Alexandria, and Papias, when discussing the Gospel of Mark:

“When Peter learned this through the revelation of the Holy Spirit, he is said, delighted by the people’s eager interest, to have confirmed the book by his authority, so that thereafter it might be read in the Church. Clement reports this in the sixth book of the *Institutions*. The bishop Papias of Hierapolis also bears witness to it.”

Line 8.—“His testimony—that is, Peter’s—was confirmed.” With the other codices, one should read *testimonio*, “by his testimony.” Nor is this improperly stated, since we have St. Paul as an indisputable witness to the testimony that was presented. Accused by false brothers, and indeed instructed by a revelation of the Holy Spirit, he went to Jerusalem so that he might compare the Gospel also with Peter, as he writes to the Galatians, chapter 2:

“But I went up according to revelation, and I laid the Gospel before them.”

Regarding this comparison, Theodoret wrote to Leo the Great in Letter 153, after the Ephesian Robber Synod, oppressed by the tyranny of Dioscorus and seeking assistance from the pontiff:

“If Paul, the herald of truth, the trumpet of the Holy Spirit, went to the great Peter so that he might receive from him an explanation for those at Antioch who were uncertain about legal observance, much more do we, humble and insignificant, hasten to your apostolic see, so that we may receive from you a remedy for the wounds of the Churches.”

What Paul did in accordance with revelation when confronted by false brothers, Peter brought to completion; a similar occasion could have arisen from the malice of the Judaizers, compelling Peter to declare which Gospels were to be retained, while they, having rejected the lawful ones, had fabricated a new one, which they called the Gospel according to the Hebrews. Eusebius writes of it in book 3, chapter 27, while discussing the Judaizers:

“They considered observance of the Law altogether necessary . . . There they judged that Paul’s letters should be entirely rejected . . . They embraced only that Gospel which is called according to the Hebrews and paid little attention to the others.”

I think it was from their hatred of Paul that St. Peter likewise wrote in his second letter, chapter 3, verse 15:

“Just as our most beloved brother Paul wrote to you according to the wisdom given to him, speaking of these things in all his letters, in which there are certain matters difficult to understand, which the ignorant and unstable distort, as they do the other Scriptures, to their own destruction.”

Line 9.—“In Latin.” The Syriac and Arabic versions of the Gospel of St. Mark agree with the *Liber Pontificalis*; in the text they have, at the end, the Gospel written in Latin by St. Mark.

Line 11.—“In the temple of Apollo.” The place and occasion of this temple in the Vatican are unknown to the writers of Roman antiquities. Nevertheless, since a Neronian circus is admitted in the Vatican; since Suetonius, *Nero*, chapter 53, establishes with certainty that Nero had even planned to be regarded as one who equaled Apollo in song and in driving a chariot; and since temples were dedicated to Apollo near circuses, as is reported concerning the Flaminian Circus, so that victors might fulfill their vows to the god, there could have been a temple of Apollo in the Vatican field, and its existence is affirmed both here and elsewhere.

Moreover, Neronian gardens certainly existed there, and it was considered sacrilegious to construct such places without a sacred shrine, as appears from Apuleius, *Apology*, p. 496. In criticizing the character of his opponent, he writes among other things:

“This man, however, gives no first fruits of his grain, vines, or flocks to the rural gods who feed and clothe him; in his country estate there is no shrine, no place or grove consecrated.”

It is also clear from Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, who, while discussing the origin of temples, says:

“And since they possessed fields and cities by the gift of the gods, they dedicated a certain portion to temples and shrines in which they might worship them.”

From these considerations, therefore, it must be concluded that Nero dedicated in his gardens a shrine, or even a temple, to Apollo.

Line 11.—“Near Nero’s palace in the Vatican.” The writers who recount Nero’s deeds are completely silent about a palace of Nero in the Vatican. Gardens certainly existed there, where that earlier and monstrous slaughter of the martyrs of Rome took place. Tacitus, in book 15, while recalling the burning of the City carried out at Nero’s command, adds:

“Therefore, to suppress the rumor, Nero substituted as culprits and subjected to the most refined punishments those whom the populace, detesting them for their crimes, called Christians. First, those who confessed were seized; then, on the evidence they supplied, a vast multitude was convicted, not so much on the charge of the fire as because of hatred of the human race. Mockery was added to their deaths: they were covered with the hides of wild beasts and torn to pieces by dogs; or they were fastened to crosses; or, doomed to the flames, they were burned as nocturnal illumination when daylight failed. Nero had offered his gardens for this spectacle and was giving a circus performance, mingling with the people in the dress of a charioteer or standing upon a chariot.”

Thus, if it is established that gardens were constructed there, that processions of games were received, and that splendid banquets were prepared; and since all these things could not have been carried out according to ordinary usage without dining rooms, baths, and other facilities requiring a large mass of buildings, this is why the surviving ruins could have acquired the name of Nero’s palace, near which the bodies of the apostles are buried.

Line 13.—“During the months of December.” Since the *Liber Pontificalis* was formed from ancient catalogues of the apostolic see—both those in which succession is designated and those in which the ordinations performed by each pontiff are listed—it follows that these matters too are recorded in the deeds of each pontiff.

Three points should be noticed in this entry. First, up to Simplicius it was customary for ordinations to take place on the Saturday of the fasts in the tenth month; Leo the Great discusses this custom at length in his sermons for that day. After Simplicius, however, ordination was assigned to other times, as will be explained in its place. Second, this formula, “during the months of December,” designates an ordination repeated each year on a Saturday in December. Third, a determined number of ordinations is sometimes assigned. Whether the consecrations of bishops took place on the same day as clerical ordination will be debated below.]

[Note: [Col. 1019C]

(EX BIN.) Line 2.—“He first occupied the episcopal see of Antioch.” Blessed Peter undertook to establish the Church of Antioch and administered it for seven years, though not complete years. See Baronius, year of Christ 37, no. 9 and following; Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*, book 1, chapter 6.

Line 4.—“Twenty-five years.” The statement that Blessed Peter remained in this Roman see until his death must be understood of the authority, power, and governance by which he ruled all the Churches, not of his local residence. For it is established that, after he had administered this see for seven years, in the year of Christ 51 and the ninth year of Claudius—whose edict expelled all Jews and Christians from Rome—Peter too was expelled and returned to Jerusalem, where he took part in the third Jerusalem council. After Claudius’s death, however, he returned to Rome and there completed his life.

Line 10.—“He was crowned with martyrdom together with Paul.” In the year of Christ 68, the twelfth year of Nero, Peter and Paul were thrown into prison: Peter because he had cast down Simon Magus, who was flying through the air, by invoking the divine name; Paul because he had converted Nero’s mistress to the Christian religion and made her chaste from her immoral condition. In the following year both were beaten with rods and, after giving each other a kiss, were put to death: Peter was fastened to a cross with his head lowered toward the ground; Paul, however, died most gloriously by the sword.

(EX LABB.) Line 10.—“Thirty-eight years.” The material is missing in chapter 4.]

[Note: [Col. 1020A]

**CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES**

I shall preserve this method in presenting my notes: I shall place the chronological notes first and then append the historical ones. We establish the chronology of each pontiff by two indications, drawn both from the *Bibliothecarius* and from the catalogues: namely, from the consuls, which is the first indication, and from the number of years, months, and days, which is the second.

In assigning the consuls, I observe that the writers of the catalogues and Lives generally preferred to assign to a pontiff those consuls who entered office when the sacred year began, reckoned according to the ancient custom of the Roman Church from the Passion of the Lord, or from Easter. This is clear in determining the beginning of the pontificate of the apostle Peter.

It is certain that Blessed Peter assumed the supreme priesthood at Eastertide, between the Lord’s Resurrection and Ascension, when the Lord entrusted to him the keys of the kingdom of heaven and the care of the entire Lord’s flock, so that he might feed it and strengthen his brethren. This occurred under the consuls known as the Gemini, to whom we have repeatedly shown above in *Work* 4, chapter 1, that the epoch of Christ’s Passion, Resurrection, and Ascension must be referred, in the year 28 of the common era.

Peter’s beginning is nevertheless assigned not to those consuls but to the immediately succeeding ones, namely Vinicius and Longinus, in the year 29 of the common era. It was under these consuls that the first Easter was celebrated on earth by Christ’s vicar. The Christian Church retained with far greater willingness the epoch of the sacred year beginning with the month of Nisan among the Hebrews, since it recognized that the mysteries of our restoration were to be derived from and commemorated at that time.

Bede therefore testifies that, when he was at Rome, it was customary to mark on the candles of St. Mary the years from the Lord’s Passion. And since the Fathers likewise assign to that Paschal season the epoch of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, the custom also arose of counting the years from the Lord’s Incarnation. This custom has not yet become obsolete in certain Italian cities, especially Venice and Florence, although the entire Christian world has derived the common era from the Nativity.

Having prefaced this explanation of the custom of the catalogues in assigning to pontiffs the college of consuls under whom they celebrated the Paschal feast, rather than the Kalends of January, we shall set out the consular chronology of Blessed Peter in this first number as follows.

Under the consuls known as the Gemini, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the common Christian year 28, a leap year, on Thursday, the first day of Unleavened Bread, the Lord Jesus Christ, dining with his disciples after revealing the sacraments of his body and blood, proceeded to the Mount of Olives, as the holy Gospels testify. There he was arrested by the Jews, betrayed by a disciple. Then, on the following Friday, that is, the seventh day before the Kalends of April, he was crucified and buried. On the third day, that is, on Sunday, the fifth day before the Kalends of April, he rose from the dead (Victor of Aquitaine, in the *Paschal Canon*).

After his Resurrection he remained with his disciples for forty days, appearing to them and speaking about the kingdom of God—from Sunday, 28 March, to Thursday, 6 May, when, before their eyes, he was lifted up and ascended into heaven. At that time the Fathers and interpreters commonly number ten principal appearances recorded in sacred Scripture.
