In the seventh of these, at Capernaum, Christ the Lord conferred upon Peter the office of the supreme pontiff, that is, the government of the universal Church and the episcopate previously promised to him, saying, “Feed my sheep” (John 21), as is confirmed by Gregory the Great in Letter 37, book 6, and by other Fathers.

These events occurred under the consuls known as the Gemini. Their successors, Vinicius and Longinus, entered office on the Kalends of January in the year 29, while Peter was beginning the ninth month of his administration. Peter’s first year as pontiff was therefore completed around the end of April of that same consular year, in the common Christian year 29.

The last Easter celebrated by Peter as supreme pontiff before his martyrdom is assigned in the catalogue compiled in the age of Liberius to the consuls Nerva and Vestinus. These consuls mark the year 65 of the common Christian era; under those same consuls, on the third day before the Kalends of July, Peter was fastened to the cross and crowned with martyrdom.

Therefore, according to the consular chronology, Peter must be credited with approximately thirty-seven years and two months of episcopate, spent partly at Jerusalem, partly in the see of Antioch, and partly in the Roman see by the prince of the apostles. St. Jerome likewise counts this number in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

He spent twelve of these years in the East organizing the Churches of that region before he came to Rome. Apollonius, a second-century ecclesiastical writer, relates in Eusebius, book 5 of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 18, as though from ancient tradition, that the Lord commanded his apostles not to leave Jerusalem within twelve years—namely, not to go beyond the boundaries of Syria, to which Jerusalem belonged, or to proceed elsewhere to establish episcopal sees.

For the Fathers infer from the Acts of the Apostles that the episcopal see had been established at Antioch within twelve years, indeed within five years, of the Lord’s Passion. They also assert that Peter presided over the see of Antioch for seven years before departing for the City in the twelfth year after the Lord’s Passion to establish the Roman see.

Thus St. Gregory, writing to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria, in book 6, Letter 37, says of the Antiochene see founded by Peter:

“He himself established the see in which he sat for seven years, although he was destined to depart.”

Clement of Alexandria likewise, in *Stromata*, book 6, p. 637, in the Paris edition of G. L., 1629, confirms the tradition of the apostles’ departure beyond Syria twelve years after Christ’s Passion. Schelestratius observes this while restoring the punctuation of the passage in *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, dissertation 1, chapter 5, article 3. Clement writes that Christ had commanded:

“After twelve years, go out into the world, so that no one may say: ‘We have not heard.’”

Henschenius too, in Exercise 4 on the pontifical chronology, no. 28, after showing that Peter founded the see of Antioch in the fifth year after Christ’s Passion, adds:

“After the seven years of the Antiochene see had elapsed, with St. Evodius appointed there in his place, he established the first see of the Christian Church in the city of Rome, the seat of the emperors and the head of the world, in the fortieth year of the common era. From that year the twenty-five years of this see are to be reckoned in the catalogue already cited. These twenty-five years are also found in the other catalogue soon to be presented, as well as in the Palatine manuscript, which we have omitted; likewise in the Roman *Pontifical* and in the handwritten and printed codices of Anastasius the Bibliothecarius, and also in Liutprand, Abbo, and other writers on pontifical affairs.”

Then, in number 35, while discussing the year of the martyrdom of Saints Peter and Paul, he writes:

“Therefore Saints Peter and Paul are correctly said to have suffered martyrdom while Nero was present at Rome, under the consuls Nerva and Vestinus, in the year 65 of the Christian era. If the beginning of Nero’s imperial reign is taken into account, it was his eleventh year, although it is usually reckoned as his twelfth, since it had begun only in the preceding October. Moreover, it is said to have been the thirty-seventh year after the Lord’s Passion, which St. Jerome requires in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the notice on St. Peter, as do also Honorius, Isidore, Nicephorus, and others.”]

All the catalogues, together with the very ancient paintings of the Basilica of Saint Paul reproduced above on folio 87, assign twenty-five full years to Blessed Peter in the Roman see. That he suffered martyrdom with Paul in the thirty-seventh year after Christ’s Passion, during the twelfth year of Nero’s reign, when Vestinus and Nerva were consuls, is clearly demonstrated—apart from the writers already cited—by Schelestratius in the aforementioned dissertation, *Antiquities of the Church*, I, chapter 5, article 5.

Since twenty-five years are thus asserted for Peter from the time when he established the episcopal chair at Rome, it is worth investigating why two months and three days are also assigned to him. If we count backward from the day of his martyrdom, 29 June in the year of Christ 65, by twenty-five years, two months, and three days—the period assigned to him in the Roman episcopal catalogue of Felix IV [Col. 1022A] and in Codex II Colbertinus—the initial point of the reckoning, and the beginning of the Roman episcopate, falls on 25 April of the common-era year 40, to which Henschenius also refers it.

The founding of the Antiochene chair would then have occurred seven years earlier, in the common-era year 33. The Sunday letter D assigned to that year indicates Sunday, 22 February. We commemorate the feast of the Chair of Antioch on that day in the present age; and from manuscripts written under Pope Liberius and published by us above from Bucherius in the *Prolegomena*, as well as from Saint Augustine, we know that it was customarily celebrated in the earlier centuries of the Christian era. I could easily prove by monuments of all the Eastern and Western Churches that the Sunday of the episcopal ἐνθρονισμός, or enthronement, was already customarily assigned to that day.

Everything therefore confirms the proposed dates: the Passion of the Lord in the twenty-eighth year of the common era, on 25 March; his death on 26 March; the founding of the Antiochene chair [Col. 1022B] near the end of the fifth year after the Lord’s Passion, on Sunday, 22 February in the year 33; and, seven years later—that is, in the common-era year 40—the apostles’ departure from Syria, Peter’s arrival in the City, and the establishment of the Roman chair.

It remains to inquire what connection the date 25 April of the year 40 has with the beginning of the Roman pontificate undertaken by the prince of the apostles. From that date the period of twenty-five years, two months, and three days assigned to him is reckoned up to the triumphant day of his martyrdom, 29 June in the year 65, if we follow the catalogue composed in the age of Felix IV. Or should we instead use 21 April of that same year 40, from which to 29 June in the year 65—when Nero and Vestinus were consuls—there intervene twenty-five years, two months, and seven days, as reckoned in the most ancient paintings of the patriarchal basilica and in most of the more reliable catalogues?

Since I see that the litany called the Greater Litanies was appointed for 25 April not only before Gregory the Great but also for many ages before him, and almost from the beginnings of the Church [Col. 1022C]—a litany in which all the titular churches, deaconries, and basilicas themselves, from the Constantinian age onward, attend the assembly of clergy and people in the Campus Martius, formerly at the titular church of Saint Lawrence in Lucina and now at Saint Mark’s, and proceed thence to Saint Peter—I judged that in those days it had already become customary to commemorate the primacy of the Roman see over the others, established by the prince of the apostles himself.

That the feast of the Chair on 18 January was recorded in this way by Bede and others, and that Paul IV therefore restored in his constitution of 1558 the ancient date of the chair founded in the City of Peter to 18 January, does not prevent us from understanding that the episcopate was founded on that day; but that somewhat later—that is, in April, whether of the same year or of the years immediately following—the primacy over the other churches was added to this episcopal see, after the Gospel had been preached in the neighboring cities, churches had been founded, and bishops ordained, so that a certain hierarchical system had coalesced [Col. 1022D]. In its form this system appeared sufficiently suitable to Peter for the dignity of the chief see to be declared and fostered by his ministry and by the submission owed to it.

The sixth canon of the Council of Nicaea, clarified by so many labors of learned men, sufficiently demonstrates how much dignity was expressed by that ancient patriarchal custom whereby several bishops attended the Roman bishop both to perform the sacred mysteries and to represent the unity of the whole ecclesial body under one head. The progression was therefore orderly: first the pontifical chair was erected; then, as its component parts were gradually added and assistants to its authority prepared, the greatest authority was conferred upon its bishop, so that Peter might also exercise the power of sending patriarchs away, a power later to be transmitted to his successors.

It is certain that the Gospel of Christ was first preached at Rome by the prince of the apostles for some period of time (a chair having been established here); afterwards, at the request of the brethren, it was committed to writing by Mark and approved by Peter [Col. 1023A]. Later Mark was sent away from there to lay, in Peter’s name, the foundations of the Alexandrian patriarchate. He obeyed, taking with him the Gospel which, at the insistence of the Roman Church, he had written and received under Peter’s authority to be read, and to be disseminated everywhere as the rule of faith.

For this reason many also believe that Evodius was dismissed so that he might administer the government of the Church of Antioch, which had been entrusted to him by Peter, already bishop of Rome. They are persuaded by the testimony of Eusebius, whose *Chronicle* first records Peter’s arrival in the City and the foundation of the Roman Church under the second year of the 205th Olympiad, in the year of Christ 43, in these words:

> “The apostle Peter, after he had first founded the Church of Antioch, was sent to Rome, where, preaching the Gospel, he remained bishop of that city for twenty-five years.”

In the same year there follows an entry concerning Mark, who was ordained bishop of Alexandria by Peter, whose interpreter he was at Rome. Blessed Jerome renders it into Latin as follows:

> “Mark, the interpreter of Peter, announces Christ in Egypt and Alexandria.” [Col. 1023B]

Then follows the third year of that same 205th Olympiad, but the Christian year 44, according to Eusebius, in which the following is read concerning Evodius:

> “Evodius is ordained the first bishop of Antioch.”

By this testimony of the Eusebian *Chronicle*, therefore, I believe that I can confirm that progression which Peter, the wise architect, maintained at the Roman see: first founding it, then enlarging it, and finally raising it to such dignity above the others that he ordained and sent out from there the first bishops of the two sees nearest to it in dignity. In this he displayed the primacy which the clergy of the Roman City, representing the universal Church, commemorates every year in the Greater Litany on 25 April.

But why that date was chosen, I think should be explained as follows.

The Roman order distributes the fixed solemnities throughout the yearly cycle in such a way that they correspond as closely as possible to the times of those acts chosen for their performance by Christ the Lord, whose mysteries it sets before us for commemoration in those feasts. [Col. 1023C] The sending forth of the apostles, therefore, which took place during the Paschal season between the Resurrection and the Ascension, and the authority of the supreme priesthood bestowed upon Peter, together with the care of all the sheep entrusted to him, belong to the days that immediately follow the Paschal feast and do not extend beyond the Ascension.

Although Easter is movable, it never extends beyond 25 April. Nor does the feast of the Ascension, when it falls at the earliest possible time, ever occur before 30 April. The final week of April, therefore, counted from the twenty-fifth day, will always form part of the forty-day period preceding the Ascension, to which Christ the Lord, departing for heaven, attached the institution of the supreme pontificate of the new law.

There is therefore a reason why 25 April is assigned as the beginning of the supreme pontificate, both as instituted by Christ the Lord and as transferred by blessed Peter to the Roman see; and why the years of the supreme priesthood exercised by the prince of the apostles in the Roman chair are reckoned from that day [Col. 1023D], 25 April of the year 40, to 29 June of the year 65, when he completed his martyrdom. The total is thus twenty-five years, two months, and three days, as the catalogue of Felix IV has it.

Nor am I greatly concerned by the four-day difference whereby the Liberian catalogue, as well as most of those listed above on page 87 together with the ancient paintings of the Basilica of Saint Paul, begins the era on 21 April and consequently reckons twenty-five years, two months, and eight days to the martyrdom. For the era of the Nativity itself, which was introduced later by Dionysius Exiguus and subsequently accepted by public consensus, is deferred by eight days after the feast of the Lord’s Nativity, from 25 December to the approaching Kalends of January, so that it might correspond with the beginning of the civil year established among the Romans.

Besides the Julian dating from the Kalends of January, another no less celebrated Roman era was in use, recorded in public monuments and attached to 21 April: namely, the era of the years from the founding of the City, reckoned from the Parilia. We see it preserved in the marble Capitoline fasti [Col. 1024A], just as in the priestly fasti of the Arval Brothers, likewise carved in marble, part of which we reproduced in the preface to the previous volume, section 21.

By the same right, therefore, the priestly era of blessed Peter, as begun by the Liberian catalogue and by most of the sources mentioned, as well as by the paintings of the basilicas from the age of Leo the Great, begins on the day of the Parilia, 21 April. Although the solemnity of the public supplication and assembly at Saint Peter in the Greater Litany, four days later, recalls his supreme dignity, Peter should accordingly be assigned in the Roman chair the period from the Parilia of the common-era year 40, when he first sat at Rome—that is, from 21 April—to 29 June, consecrated by his martyrdom in the common-era year 65, when Nero and Vestinus were consuls.

I say that the total assigned should be twenty-five years, two months, and seven days, which are the full days intervening between the two termini; or eight days, as found in Bergomensis Codex c and in the three Colbertine codices h, k, and m, which perhaps include both termini.

This practice of reckoning the sacred years of the nascent Church from these Paschal events—whether the Passion, the Resurrection, or the Lord’s Ascension—is supported by a custom equally maintained among the Eastern and Western Churches in the apostolic age. Apart from the Jewish people, who by divine command established the beginning of the sacred year at the Paschal moon, Christians too, although freed from the Jewish law, adapted the Paschal era to the deeds of Christ the Lord.

We have already seen that the Roman Church marked its years from the Lord’s Passion. The works called the Paschal Chronicles, arranged by the Antiochenes who professed the faith of Christ, sometimes reckon the years from Easter and, on more than one occasion, from the Lord’s Ascension.

In what is incorrectly called the Alexandrian chronicle, and in Rader’s Sicilian fasti, the martyrdom of Saint Polycarp is recorded with an era reckoned from Christ’s Ascension, although the martyrdom occurred on the Saturday before Easter. Polycarp is said to have suffered and been burned “on the eve of Easter, on the Sabbath itself, at the eighth hour, in the third year of the two Augusti, Marcus and Verus, when Aelianus and Pastor were consuls, [Col. 1024C] in the year 133 after Christ’s departure into heaven.”

Likewise, Saint Athanasius of Alexandria, in his sermon on the image of Berytus, states that the destruction of Jerusalem took place in the forty-third year after the Ascension of the Lord and Savior into heaven.

We therefore seem to have discovered a probable reason for the reckoning of the months and days, in addition to the full years, of Peter’s tenure in this Roman chair. Whether he enlarged the chair founded on 18 January and subsequently endowed it with primacy over the other churches in the Paschal month, when he himself had received from Christ the Lord the care of the whole flock; or whether he enriched it with that privilege on the very day on which he founded it, both possibilities accord with the practice of deriving the era of the supreme pontificate from the Paschal month, both in the East, where Peter received it, and in the West, to which he transferred it.

For this reason the explanation is supplied for why, although the feast of the Roman Chair has not been moved from 18 January and that of the Antiochene Chair from 22 February, the reckoning of the supreme pontificate established by Peter in the Roman see is brought back to the beginning of the years from the founding of the City [Col. 1024D], 21 April of the common-era year 40, and is then marked in the oldest catalogues and in the paintings of the basilicas as twenty-five years, two months, and seven days, up to the end of his life in the consummation of his martyrdom on 29 June of the common-era year 65.

Let these chronological observations, intended to illuminate Peter’s pontifical era in the Roman see, be concluded by the testimony of a writer held in the highest esteem among historians of the fifth and sixth centuries. From it the beginning of Peter’s Roman pontificate is confirmed as belonging to the fortieth year of the common era, and this according to a reckoning already accepted at that time and disseminated in Rome no less than in the East.

This writer is Ammianus Marcellinus, who, while living at Constantinople, recorded the arrival of Pope John in the imperial City in his *Chronicle* as follows:

> “In the consulship of Philoxenus and Probus”—that is, in the year of Christ 525—“John, pope of the Roman Church, the fifty-third from Peter, the chief of the apostles and of the bishops, in the 485th year of his [Peter’s] tenure, during the reign of King Theodoric, [Col. 1025A] etc., departed from the City and came to Constantinople.”

The common-era year 40 of Christ, which we have assigned from the catalogue and from the genuine documents of the Roman Church to the pontifical see established in the City by blessed Peter, is correctly assigned as the twenty-fifth year before the Apostle’s martyrdom, under the consulship of Vestinus and Nerva. It is likewise 485 years before the consulship of Philoxenus and Probus, at the time of John’s first journey, correctly reckoned both at Rome and at Constantinople.

The ancient catalogues and chronicles therefore confirm, in accordance with the genuine documents of the Roman Church, that the chronology of the Roman see was rightly established for the prince of the apostles and expressed in the paintings of the basilicas as twenty-five years, two months, and seven days.

If it is desirable to confirm this established chronology also from the era of the foundation of the Antiochene chair, as transmitted in writing by the ancient writers of that city, I shall append the following testimony from the Antiochene chronography of John Malalas, page 311 of the London edition [Col. 1025B]:

> Μετὰ δὲ ἔτη τέσσαρα, etc. (“But four years later,” etc.)

“Four years later, under the same Tiberius Caesar, after our Savior Jesus Christ had risen from the dead and been taken up into heaven—which was also the time when Paul had migrated to Cilicia, having left Great Antioch, where he had first preached the word of God with Barnabas, near the Pantheon in the village of Singonion—at that time, I say, Peter departed from Jerusalem and came to Antioch. There, after proclaiming the Gospel, he undertook the office of bishop, etc., as the most learned chroniclers Clement and Tatian have recorded in writing.”

This is an appropriate place to insert an observation by a particularly learned man, which may illuminate the chronology and the foundation of the Antiochene see no less than those of the Roman and Alexandrian sees.

The most reverend Father Abbot Bacchini, in his learned dissertation *On the Origins of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, page 194, perceived that the ancient account of Apollonius concerning the insertion of a period of twelve years [Col. 1025C] between the Lord’s Ascension and the apostles’ departure from Jerusalem into the provinces is more conveniently and accurately explained both from the force of the Greek expression χωρισθῆναι, which Eusebius used, and from a comparison with what the apostle Paul says in his Epistle to the Galatians when discussing his first arrival in Jerusalem.

From both sources he concluded that the apostles had not been commanded never to set foot outside Jerusalem, but rather not to found churches during that period which were independent of the Church of Jerusalem. The phrase χωρισθῆναι τῆς Ἱερουσαλὴμ should therefore be interpreted as “to be separated from Jerusalem,” “to be set apart,” or “to be detached”—that is, to found another church that in no way depended upon the Jerusalem church.

For during the twelve years, the apostolic college, presided over by Peter as the greater synedrium of the new law, was seated only at Jerusalem and exercised jurisdiction over the entire assembly of Jewish believers, and so forth. But to establish another principal church in which one of the apostles would reside could not occur without the jurisdiction of the apostolic college being fully exercised elsewhere as well, and without the Jerusalem Church ceasing to be the sole church presiding over the others. To be separated, detached, and set apart from Jerusalem meant separation from the place where, according to Jewish custom, the fullness and summit of jurisdiction resided.

Although the apostle Peter had given an episcopal chair to the Antiochene converts to the faith of Christ before six full years had elapsed from Christ the Lord’s Ascension, he could nevertheless have refrained from defining the jurisdiction and boundaries of that episcopate at that time, reserving them until the completion of the twelve-year period. At that time, having departed for Rome in the year 40 according to our view, he conferred upon the Roman see the fullness of pastoral office and primacy over all the churches.

In that same year, or shortly afterward, he could have measured the extent of the Antiochene see by assigning it the East, and established the authority of the Alexandrian see over the southern provinces separated from the fifteen Eastern provinces, sending Evodius to the former and Mark to the latter [Col. 1026A], shortly after the establishment of the Roman chair. This accords remarkably with the Eusebian chronicle cited above.

## HISTORICAL NOTES BY THE SAME AUTHOR

### Line 1—“Antiochene”

This is lacking in the Liberian catalogue and is added in the later ones. Some think that the metropolis of the Roman province under which Galilee was counted was substituted for the place of Peter’s birth, which was situated in the tetrarchy of a foreign king. Others suppose that a later age wished to call Peter “Antiochene” because he had administered the episcopate there for seven years, since a bishop is regarded as the foremost among the citizens.

Nevertheless, I prefer a third explanation, which may be gathered from Josephus as follows. In Book XII, chapter 3, the Jewish historian relates that among the various honors decreed to members of his nation through the privileges granted by the Seleucids and Romans was also the right of Antiochene citizenship, bestowed upon them so that they might live there on equal terms with the Greeks and Macedonians.

He further reports that this privilege was so sacredly confirmed and preserved by the Roman emperors that under Vespasian and Titus the Alexandrians and Antiochenes tried unsuccessfully to deprive the Jews of that right. Therefore, not only during Peter’s lifetime but even after his martyrdom—for Josephus, his contemporary, records the matter—Jews were regarded as citizens of Antioch.

Accordingly, no one will deny that the apostle Peter, a Jew by nation and from the village of Bethsaida, could and should in the fullest right be called and regarded as an Antiochene citizen. Josephus’s words must be cited.

He concludes chapter 2 of Book XII as follows:

> “These are the things presented in honor of the Jews by Philadelphus.”

He then begins chapter 3 with these words:

> “They were also honored by the kings of Asia because of their good and faithful service in military affairs. For Seleucus, surnamed Nicator, in the cities which he founded throughout Asia and Lower Syria, and finally in Antioch itself, the metropolis, granted them the rights of citizenship and wished them to live there on equal terms with the Macedonians and Greeks. They still live among them with this right. [Col. 1026C]
>
> “The evidence is that, because the Jews refused to use foreign oil, the gymnasiarchs paid them a fixed sum in its place. When the people of Antioch attempted to abolish this custom during the recent war, Mucianus, who then governed the province of Syria, did not permit it.
>
> “Later, under Vespasian and his son Titus, when the Alexandrians and Antiochenes asked that the Jews be deprived of their civic rights, they could not obtain this. It was a clear indication of the fairness and magnanimity of the Romans, but especially of those emperors, who, although they had endured many hardships in that war and were hostile to those who had obstinately rebelled, nevertheless did not wish anything to be diminished from the Jews’ rights. Nor did they permit either their own anger or the hostility of the two peoples toward the Jews to prevail against them. They placed greater value on the ancient merits of the nation than on its present offense, or on the favor which this action might have won them among those peoples.
>
> “They said that those who had taken up arms against the Roman state had paid sufficient penalties, but that it was not just for those who had committed no offense to be stripped of their privileges and rights.” [Col. 1026D]

### Line 3—“He entered the city of Rome under Nero Caesar”

That is, at the beginning of the reign of Claudius, son of Nero Drusus, whose family had such a close association with the surname Nero—a Sabine word meaning “strong”—as is shown by Suetonius and Gellius. Horace twice calls Nero’s relatives “Neros” in *Odes* IV.4. His son Domitius, adopted into the Claudian family, was called Nero, as he is also named here in line 8. Or, if the reference is to Domitius Nero, the later arrival of Peter is being confused with the earlier one.

We have sufficiently treated, in the chronological notes, the testimonies of the ancients confirming the arrival of the prince of the apostles in the City in the common-era year 40 of Christ. The occasion and reason for the journey, and the apostle’s lodging in the City, seem to require discussion here.

It will also be worthwhile to touch briefly upon whether Peter reached not only the City but also the more remote regions of the West, since some believe that he even went as far as Britain. We shall reserve the remaining matters for the life of Eleutherius.

In the common-era year 40 of the Christian era, which was the twelfth year after the Lord’s Passion, I proved by the testimony of the ancients that Peter came to Rome. If an occasion was ever readily available, it was certainly offered and prepared by heaven in that year.

For it is clear from the Acts of the Apostles that Peter, forewarned by a divine vision to receive the Gentiles, began with Cornelius, a centurion of the Italian cohort—that is, one of the four legions stationed in Syria at that time.

From Tacitus and Dio, our Panvinius counts these legions as the Fourth Scythica, the Sixth Victrix, the Tenth Gemina Pia Fidelis, and the Twelfth Fulminata. Tacitus reports that the Sixth had winter quarters near Laodicea in Syria under Tiberius, *Annals* II.79. Dio names the Sixth Ferrata as stationed in Judaea, Book LV; and Panvinius observes that the emperor Galba in Spain was created by that same legion.

Nearly all chronologists refer the baptism of Cornelius either to an earlier date or to the eighth year after Christ’s Passion, which would be the common-era year 36, when Gaius succeeded Tiberius, under the consulship of Proculus and Nigrinus.

In the third year of this reign, “Gaius was seized by the impulse of a German expedition,” as Suetonius reports in his *Life of Gaius*, chapter 43. “He did not delay, but summoned legions and auxiliaries from everywhere, conducted the harshest levies throughout the provinces, assembled supplies of every kind in quantities never before seen, and began the march.”

This sudden expedition, for which Gaius summoned legions from every quarter, was directed toward Britain. There he received Adminius, the son of the British king Ginobellinus, who had been driven out by his father, although Gaius then turned instead to collecting shells on the shore of the Ocean.

Claudius nevertheless advanced this war at the beginning of his reign. Under him, it is also recorded, both the Second and Twentieth Legions were transferred from Germany, and the Fourth, Sixth, and Tenth from Syria, to the West; some were even transferred to Britain. Several of their coins and inscriptions discovered in Britain can be read in Thomas Gale’s commentary on the *Itinerary of Antoninus through Britain*.

Panvinius likewise concludes that the Sixth Victrix, one of the four legions left by Augustus in Syria, shortly afterward went to Italy and Germany, and inscriptions cited by Gale show that it was subsequently added to the forces defending Britain.

Whether, therefore, the legion in which Cornelius the centurion and the Italian cohort served was summoned by Gaius in haste, or called out when Claudius assumed the imperial power; whether Cornelius himself obtained an honorable discharge after completing his lawful term of service, or attained military rank in another legion guarding the western regions of the empire, as often occurred and is observed in ancient inscriptions—an important gateway was opened to the prince of the apostles, and an opportunity was prepared for him to sail to Italy with the faithful centurion and to lodge among Cornelius’s kinsmen of the Cornelian family or among his friends.

This accords remarkably with the ancient tradition that the apostles lodged in the City with Pudens, near the Vicus Corneliorum, a matter we shall discuss in its proper place in the life of Pius. Ancient monuments preserved at the titular church of Saint Pudentiana confirm it. Among them is an inscription of Pudentianetis, of the Cornelian family, transferred from the martyrs’ cemetery on the Appian Way, between the first and second milestones, where the tomb of the Cornelii is known to have stood from Cicero, *Tusculan Disputations* I.12, to the same church. It is seen marked with these words, together with the figure of a woman in a stole, whose Phrygian-bordered garment indicates the nobility of her family in the customary manner:

> **CORN. PUDENTIANETI** [Col. 1028B]  
> **BENEM. Q. VIXIT. AN. XLVII D. I. VAL. PETRONIUS MAT DULC. IN PACE**

> “To Cornelia Pudentianetis, well deserving, who lived forty-seven years and one day. Valerius Petronius [set this up] for his sweetest mother. In peace.”

The expeditions of Claudius and Nero into Britain, through which the same legions that had served in Syria were transferred to Britain, likewise opened an easy access for the preachers of the Gospel to that island. Once the centurion, or some distinguished legionary soldier, had been brought to the faith of Christ—or once such a man had gradually been promoted to the honors of another legion, or had received an honorable discharge after completing his lawful term of service—Peter, or whoever had been chosen to bring the apostolic mission there, could readily take him as a companion.

I would not dare affirm whether Cornelius’s Italian cohort was ordered by Gaius or Claudius to cross into Britain with its legion. I do know, however, that I myself saw in London a fragment of an ancient inscription recording, as is customary, several centuries of soldiers, together with their names and native cities. It was in the collection of Mr. Kemps near Pall Mall. As many city names as were recorded there, assigning colonial rights to the same soldiers for the completion of their service in the legion, so many showed that those soldiers had been Italians.

Here is the fragment of the stone, on which the Italian colonies serving as the soldiers’ homelands are listed:

> Fulcinium, Mantua, Florence, Ticinum, Patavium, Clusium, Adria, Regium of Lepidus, Ateste, Eporedia, Pausulae, Beneventum, Cremona, Verona, Aquinum, Brundisium—these homelands of the soldiers are Roman colonies established within Italy. [Col. 1029]

[Col. 1029A] It is regrettable that the remaining portions of the inscriptions carved on this stone have not survived. From them we might learn whether the second or third consulship of Titus or Vespasian is intended by the consulships mentioned here, under which an honorable discharge may perhaps have been granted to these veteran soldiers; and whether that centurion Sabinus had anything in common with the surname mentioned by Suetonius in the *Life of Titus*, chapter 1.

Our conjecture would come closer to determining whether the soldiers should be regarded as belonging to the Sixth or the Tenth Legion. Both served under Augustus and Tiberius in Syria and Armenia, according to Tacitus, *Annals* II.79 and XIII.40, and were later transferred to Britain, as shown by the documents published by Gale. Nor would it be far from the question whether both of these centuries, collected from men of our nation, could be counted as part of the Italian cohort.

But let us stop at the threshold, content merely to indicate that, by the plan of divine providence, which orders all things with gentle wisdom, six years before Peter’s arrival in the City the centurion of the Italian cohort was summoned by a heavenly vision to baptism, and the prince of the apostles to announce salvation to the Gentiles. Through the conversion of one man, and through the transfer of one cohort—or its commander—to Italy, both lodging among the Cornelian family in the City and an easy route to the Britons, separated from the rest of the world, could have been opened.

This would have occurred whether Gaius Caligula summoned the legions from every quarter or Claudius assigned to the British expedition those troops which had been serving in Syria and the neighboring provinces and had witnessed the marvelous works and miracles of the nascent Church of Christ.

Nor should we think otherwise concerning the evangelizing expedition of blessed Mark to Egypt, which Eusebius’s chronicle assigns to the second year of Claudius’s reign.

Philo’s embassy to the City at the end of Gaius’s reign, when the arrival of Herod Agrippa occurred at almost the same time, and the increased goodwill shown under Claudius—which made the emperors more favorable toward the Jewish nation—created an opportunity for a relationship to be formed in the City itself between Mark and Philo. This could have occurred through their attending the synagogue and joining one another as traveling companions while Philo returned to Alexandria.

There, “that most eloquent of the Jews,” to use Jerome’s words, “seeing that the first Church at Alexandria was still Judaizing, wrote, as though in praise of his nation, a book about their way of life.”

As a commentary, the complete eulogy of Philo should be used, as Blessed Jerome recorded it in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

> “Philo the Jew, an Alexandrian by nation and descended from the priestly class, is included by us among ecclesiastical writers because, when writing a book about the church of the evangelist Mark at Alexandria, he devoted himself to praising our people. He records that they existed not only there but also in many provinces, and he calls their dwellings monasteries.
>
> “From this it appears that the first church of those who believed in Christ was of the kind that monks now strive and desire to be: nothing belonged privately to anyone; there was neither a rich person nor a poor person among them; estates were distributed to those in need; they devoted themselves to prayer, psalms, teaching, and continence, just as Luke reports that the first believers in Jerusalem did.
>
> “They say that this man was in danger at Rome under Gaius Caligula, because he had been sent as the ambassador of his nation. When he came to Claudius for the second time, he spoke in that same city with the apostle Peter and formed a friendship with him. For this reason he also adorned with praise the followers of Mark, Peter’s disciple, at Alexandria.” [Col. 1029D]

When these matters are considered, and we recognize that entire legions were transferred from Syria to Italy, Germany, and Britain during nearly the same years in which Philo, the Jewish ambassador, had to sail back and forth from Egypt to Italy and return to his homeland, one is compelled to wonder at the difficulty displayed by certain minds. They hesitate to grant the apostle Peter the possibility of making the journey to Italy, although he needed no equipment or supplies and, without shoes or a purse, was sent forth at the impulse of the divine Spirit.

Nevertheless, it is established that he wrote his first epistle from Rome before Mark was dispatched to Egypt. Eusebius, Jerome, and others commonly refer this to the first or second year of Claudius’s reign.

They must be more generous toward the messengers of Christ. While the disciples openly laid at their feet the prices of their lands, their ancestral wealth, and their estates, they could much more easily have provided transport to Italy and to the farthest regions of the West through the household of the centurion Cornelius.

In the notes which we shall give below in the life of Clement, Father Philip Labbe, in the first volume of the Councils, page 190, cites from Vendelinus a Greek codex by an anonymous writer concerning the contests, journeys, life, and death of the apostles Peter and Paul. The chaplain of the Earl of Arundel brought it with him from Greece to England. From it Patrick Junius produced the following distinguished passage in Greek, which Vendelinus rendered into Latin:

> “Peter remained in Britain for several days. After enlightening many by the word of grace, and establishing churches, he also ordained bishops, presbyters, and deacons by the laying on of hands. In the twelfth year of Nero he returned again to Rome.” [Col. 1030B]

Vendelinus adds:

> “Baronius also learned elsewhere of this journey of Peter to Britain; and it has recently been clearly supported,” etc.

Let those busy minds therefore cease their muttering against Peter’s repeated arrivals in the City, and let them not raise an objection concerning the spread of the light of the Gospel to the Britons, to whom entire legions were being transported from Syria—where, under Tiberius, a large part of the Lord’s Passion and of the deeds and contests of the apostles had taken place—by Gaius Caligula, Claudius, and Nero.

Nothing could have been more readily available at that time, after the linen sheet had been lowered from heaven and displayed to Peter at prayer, and after Cornelius, the centurion of the Italian cohort, had been enrolled in the Christian army, than this easy route, divinely opened to the preachers of the Gospel toward the farthest limits of the Roman Empire. As Leo the Great says in Sermon 1, *On the Holy Apostles*:

> “The most blessed Peter, prince of the apostolic order, was destined for the citadel of the Roman Empire, so that the light of truth, which was being revealed for the salvation of all nations, might spread more effectively from the very head throughout the body of the world.”

The adversaries strive to overthrow this rock—the ecclesiastical hierarchy and the primacy of the apostolic see—and to remove it from the foundation of the Christian building. They do so either by virtually denying with Calvin that the apostle Peter was ever in Rome, or, “deterred by the long-established authority and consensus of so many centuries” (to use Petavius’s words, *De doctrina temporum*, book IX, chapter 13), by conceding with him only this: that Peter died in Rome; while declaring that they utterly deny that he was ever bishop of that city or remained there for any length of time. [Col. 1030D]

Petavius continues:

> “Spalato has recently pressed this same question, and the defense of the error, with still greater force. In book IV, chapter 1, he argued at great length and with the utmost painstaking against both sees of Peter. He first declared this knot scarcely capable of being untied, yet nevertheless professed that he would untie it and illuminate the whole matter from the very sources of Sacred Scripture, so that, against the torrent of writers—for this is how he puts it—he might proceed by the royal road. But after making such great and splendid promises, and giving readers hope of a certain recondite and uncommon expertise in these matters, it is incredible to say how incompetently he conducted himself throughout that entire controversy over chronology; indeed, he gave no evidence that he had learned even the first elements of the art which he professed. Since, nearly two years ago, at the pious request and urging of the most reverend Lord Nicholas Coeffeteau, bishop of Marseille, now of blessed memory, I wrote a Dissertation on these matters, which he inserted into that brilliant and excellent work he published against Spalato, and since there we set forth these points more fully and abundantly, we have judged it appropriate here to touch upon them briefly, in this place which is the proper seat of the question.”

I shall not transcribe chapters 13 and 14 of Petavius’s book, since they are in everyone’s hands. I shall merely touch upon their substance. He demonstrates the truth and Spalato’s ignorance—Spalato who reheats Calvin’s stale cabbage and the objections of the Magdeburg Centuriators, objections repeatedly dissolved by Catholics. From Luke he shows that, shortly after Stephen’s death, Christian light was brought to the Jews of Antioch through the disciples who had been scattered. Three years after Paul’s conversion, Peter went to Antioch and established an episcopal see in that city. The number of the Antiochene Church was then increased when news was brought to Jerusalem that the Christian faith had there been expanded. Peter made frequent excursions to visit the faithful; not all of them are individually recorded in Acts, but Luke was content to state the general fact when he reported that Peter passed through all the believers as he visited them. [Col. 1031B]

The patronage of the truth might seem sufficiently secured by these observations of Petavius, easily the foremost of chronologers, as he explains at the beginning of chapter 14. “Once the arguments which heretics ordinarily raise against Peter’s chair from an exact discussion of the years and from the history of Acts have been utterly overturned and refuted,” he says, “nothing can now prevent the ancient tradition received among Catholics from retaining its weight and authority.”

But because it is necessary to reconcile sacred apostolic history with the chronology of secular history—especially in establishing the years of the Jewish kings and Roman Caesars in relation to Peter’s presence at Jerusalem, Paul’s ascent there to see Peter, Herod Agrippa’s imprisonment of Peter, Paul’s subsequent return to Jerusalem after James had been killed by the sword, and Paul’s return there [Col. 1031C] fourteen years after his conversion, or after his first conversation with Peter and the assembled apostles at the council called to answer questions concerning the Law, which interpreters commonly assign to the year 53 of the common Christian era—because, I say, the need to reconcile these histories of the apostles and the Caesars gives rise to complicated questions, the enemies of the Roman see easily seize upon one or another historical passage in order, as they say, to find “a knot in a reed.”

Thus, after setting aside Petavius’s arguments and blunting the edge of his reasoning, they launch new attacks against him through Schelestratius, who took his place in the battle, calling the chronology into question so that our pontifical history might fall with it. This is done not only by Dodwell and Pearson, who are always more vehemently stirred up against us, but also by those who usually deal with us more moderately, such as John Mill, in the preface to his edition of the New Testament, and William Cave, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, under the entry “Peter”; as though, in their pity, they were attending the deathbed of our chronological case. [Col. 1031A]

[Col. 1031D] To make it known that the dates and events we attribute to Peter are consistent with themselves, with Sacred Scripture, and with the documents of reliable—even secular—history, I have thought it fitting to append here, in the manner of annals, a brief chronicle from the beginning of Peter’s pontificate to the foundation of the three principal sees founded by him: Antioch and Rome by his own presence, and Alexandria through the evangelist Mark. But so that I may not interrupt the sequence of the notes belonging to this number, it may be placed at the end of those notes.

### Line 6

“And the Gospel of Mark, because Mark was his hearer and his son from baptism.”

Tertullian, book IV, *Against Marcion*, chapter 5, reported the reason why some attributed the Gospel of Mark to Peter; Blessed Jerome also indicates this in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. His words are:

> “Mark, the disciple and interpreter of Peter, wrote a brief Gospel at the request of the brethren in Rome, according to what he had heard Peter relate. When Peter heard it, he approved it and, by his authority, gave it to the Church to be read. Having therefore taken up the Gospel which he himself had composed, he proceeded to Egypt.” [Col. 1032A]

There is a report that the autograph of the blessed Mark’s Gospel is preserved at Venice in the treasury of the ducal basilica, with letters from princes bearing witness to this. The letters were published by R. P. Montfaucon in his *Italian Journal*, page 55 and following. Through the favor of the most distinguished Lord Foscarini, procurator of Saint Mark, to whose magistracy the care of the sacred treasury is entrusted, I obtained permission to unfold the leaves of the codex while, in the preceding year, 1720, on 2 December, I was venerating the sacred relics preserved there. I also used a magnifying glass to investigate carefully whether the form of the letters, as Montfaucon had depicted them, appeared to be Greek or Latin. I had deliberately brought his journal with me, together with a thin blade by which I could separate the decayed leaves without danger of breaking them.

All of us who were engaged in this undertaking labored in vain. Although we brought several lights close to the manuscript and enlarged the angle of our vision with crystal lenses, we were nevertheless unable to detect any trace whatever of either a Latin or a Greek element. The individual letters had been so worn away by age and eroded—perhaps by the saltiness of the lagoons—that no form of any letter remained. [Col. 1032B]

It is reported in the documents cited by Montfaucon from the Bollandists, volume III of April, page 345, that in the metropolitan Church of Prague the two final quires of this same codex of Saint Mark are preserved, written in Latin letters. The Emperor Charles IV obtained them and gave them to the aforementioned Church of Prague.

No one who carefully examined the leaves of this Venetian codex among those present doubted that they were parchment, not made of *phylira*—as he supposes. The corrosion of the ink and letters visible even in the more recent Gospel codices kept in the same cabinet must be attributed to the acridity of the salty moisture stirred up by southern winds, which make the very marbles of Saint Mark’s Church wet as they blow through, although the antiquity of the writing in those codices does not exceed four hundred years. For when this moisture penetrated with the air itself into the innermost recesses, the result was that the outlines of the letters which had given R. P. Montfaucon clear evidence of Latin writing had entirely disappeared within twenty-two years, leaving no trace of their form. [Col. 1032C]

### Line 7

“After the entire source of the four Gospels, which have been confirmed by his questioning and testimony [the codices of Holstenius and Schelestratius read *formata*, ‘formed’], while one agrees in Latin, another in Greek, and another in Hebrew, nevertheless they have been confirmed by his testimony.”

The texts of the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke display not only confirmation through Peter’s testimony but also formation from his response. The Gospel of John, composed approximately thirty years after Peter’s martyrdom—as we shall say in the discussion of Clement—increased the canon of Scripture, which the Apocalypse closed.

The Mainz and Paris editors rightly observe at this point that these writings, although divinely dictated, were not without the testimony of the prince of the apostles: either Matthew, in a matter of such importance as committing Christ’s deeds and teaching to writing, did not wish to use apostolic authority without the knowledge of the prince of the apostles; or Peter’s testimony was employed to compare the Gospel’s version, drawn from three languages, with the autograph of the Scriptures; and a seal was applied to strengthen the genuine authority of that copy which he handed over to the Roman Church. [Col. 1032D] It is certain that the Roman pontiffs, Peter’s successors, have always possessed this honor and right in the Catholic Church: that they confirm, subscribe, and ratify the decrees of ecumenical councils, both concerning faith and morals, although those decrees are issued by the universal Church under the inspiration of the same divine Spirit and with the authority by which the Gospels were written.

Hence there also arose the ancient custom of that sacred rite which the editors report as handed down in the most ancient liturgy, or *Roman Order*: namely, that the Gospel codex should be sealed by the bishop each time the deacon, after it had been opened by the bishop and read from the ambo, was to carry it back again to the bishop and then to the apostolic archive through the regional subdeacons. [Col. 1033A]

The Mazarin Codex, as we learn from Fabrotus, records the ordination of Linus and Cletus to the episcopate, so that they might assist Peter in fulfilling the priestly office. This refers to the time when the ordination of bishops began to be performed by three bishops, as is established by the first of the apostolic canons. Hence also arose the ancient custom of the Roman Church of employing suburbicarian bishops, who still constitute the principal part of the sacred college of cardinals.

It seems that the Prince of the Apostles increased the number of suburbicarian bishops to six, since at the end of this first number the *Liber Pontificalis* reports that Blessed Peter ordained six bishops, ten presbyters, and eight deacons—or rather seven, as the codices of Surius, Freher, Mazarin, the two Florentine codices, and the Vatican codex more correctly present it.

For the ordinations enumerated in the *Liber Pontificalis* in the Lives of the Pontiffs refer to the Roman Church. It is sufficiently clear from documents concerning the whole of the West—both the continental and island territories subject to the Roman patriarchate—that many bishops were ordained and sent out by Blessed Peter. They may be found in the notes of Ciaconius, Somier, and others. [Col. 1033B]

The Royal, Mazarin, and Thuani codices also report debates held by Peter to dissolve the devices of Simon Magus, and the divinely inflicted death of the Magus, who was attempting to turn the Roman people away from receiving apostolic doctrine. Justin mentions this in *Apology* 2, section 34; Irenaeus, book I, chapter 20; and Eusebius, book II, chapter 13. See Baronius under the year 44, no. 13, and Somier, *Dogmatic History of the Holy See*, book I, page 105.

The ordination of Clement is recorded in the same codices in a special formula:

> “Peter, perceiving that the day of his death was approaching, [Col. 1033C] consecrated Clement bishop and entrusted to him the chair, or the governance of the whole Church, saying: ‘Just as the power of binding and loosing was delivered to me by my Lord Jesus Christ, so I also entrust it to you, so that you may appoint administrators of various matters, through whom ecclesiastical action will be directed,’ etc.”

There will be a more suitable occasion for discussing this matter in the notes to the Life of Clement.

### Line 10

“Thirty-eight years.” Exactly. According to our chronology, the Lord suffered on 25 March in the year 28 of the common era. Thirty-seven years from the Passion were completed on 25 March in the year 65 of the common era. After a period of three months had elapsed in the thirty-eighth year—namely, on 28 June of the year 65—Peter and Paul were crowned with martyrdom.

### Line 11

“He was buried on the Via Aurelia in the temple of Apollo, near the place where he was crucified, near the Neronian palace in the Vatican.”

No ancient writer, so far as I know, ever doubted the place of Blessed Peter’s martyrdom. [Col. 1033D] The consensus of all ages teaches that he was fastened to the cross in the Vatican Circus, between the two turning-posts of that same circus. Near that place Evaristus erected an inscription over the tomb, and Constantine built the Vatican basilica.

The first person, I believe, to indulge in such speculation was Maffeo Veggio. He argued that the phrase “between the two turning-posts,” which is read in the Acts of the martyrdom, ought to be interpreted as follows: one turning-post was the obelisk of Nero’s circus at the foot of the Vatican hill—or the tomb near Hadrian’s mole, now demolished, which the common people called the tomb of Scipio Africanus or of Romulus—while the other was the pyramid of the tomb of Cestius, situated at the full diameter of the city from the Vatican Circus. (Torrigius, *On the Vatican Crypts*, page 195.)

This is plainly a new method of designating a place, one which no surveyor or architect would ever use. Certainly no prudent person would say that Queen Christina of Sweden died in Rome in a house situated between the Vatican obelisk and the pyramid of Cestius, in order to indicate the houses of the Riario family as lying between those two boundaries; for, with the entire city intervening, that description would fit innumerable parts of it. Moreover, who would ever call the tomb of Scipio or the pyramid of Cestius a turning-post?

The reader may rightly laugh at so inept a designation, which ears can scarcely endure, and at the stupidity of those who fail to understand that the two turning-posts of the circus are the two extremities of the same central barrier of the Vatican Circus. Between them Peter was fastened to the cross and erected the trophy of the Christian religion, mentioned by Tertullian and visited in pious pilgrimages by all nations for seventeen centuries, from Peter’s martyrdom to our own age. [Col. 1034A]

### Line 13

“Here he performed ordinations, etc.”

The ordinations mentioned in this book, as we have said, pertain to the Roman Church. Why the conferral of those orders which constitute the Church’s hierarchy—the episcopate, presbyterate, and diaconate—is listed among the principal deeds of the pontiffs, you will gather from the Acts of the Apostles.

Learned men, together with Ciaconius, have observed that Peter’s activity after the Ascension of Christ the Lord began, after the intervening period of nine days, with the completion of the number of the sacred senate, before the coming of the Holy [Col. 1034B] Spirit. For nothing was more urgent for Christ’s vicar, when undertaking the administration of the whole Church, than to address the brethren in the assembly of all Christ’s faithful, convoked at the command of the Lord, and to decree that two outstanding men from the body of the faithful should be proposed by common suffrage, while common prayers sought that divine designation might select one of them to be numbered among the apostles in the place of the traitor Judas. We read that this was accomplished in Matthias, in chapter 1.

The beginning, therefore, of Peter’s pontifical activity, when he assumed the governance of the universal Church at Jerusalem, commenced with the election and consecration of a bishop, or apostle. There we learn that the apostles made daily use of the priestly power they had received—and consequently so did the newly ordained presbyter, bishop, and apostle Matthias—in interpreting the word of God, offering prayers, repeating the unbloody sacrifice, and distributing the Eucharistic bread to the faithful, from verses 42 and 46 of chapter 2:

> “They were persevering in the doctrine of the apostles, and in fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in prayers, etc.”
>
> “Every day they continued unanimously in the temple, and breaking bread in their homes, etc.” [Col. 1034C]

We are also taught from Acts, chapter 15, that presbyters were established at Jerusalem by the apostles, when the Church of Antioch sent Paul and Barnabas and certain others to the apostles and presbyters in Jerusalem concerning the question of circumcision and the other ceremonies of the Law.

After the offices of the apostolate, or episcopate and presbyterate, the election of the seven deacons and their ordination by the apostles through the imposition of hands, as carried out in chapter 6, completed the hierarchy of the nascent Church at Jerusalem in the first year after the Passion of Christ the Lord.

Antioch, when Peter established his see there, imitated this form handed down to it; Rome likewise adopted it and has steadfastly retained it since the Prince of the Apostles transferred the universal chair and primacy to that city. [Col. 1034D]

The letters of the bishops of that Church who were closest to Peter, especially Ignatius the Martyr, who succeeded Evodius immediately after Peter, bear witness to the hierarchy of the Church of Antioch, constituted in these three grades, explicitly mentioning the same orders.

Every age bears witness to the Roman Church; above all, this *Liber Pontificalis*, which, in the case of each pontiff, records the presbyters and deacons of the Roman Church appointed by them, and sometimes suburbicarian bishops, while at other times bishops were established in other cities throughout the Western patriarchate. For this reason, when these are listed, the phrase “bishops in various places, number N” is generally added.

There will be an opportunity below, in the Life of Saint Cletus, to discuss the number of presbyters and deacons of the Roman Church. Here I observe that Peter established three assistant bishops around Rome—Linus, Cletus, and Clement—so that through their ministry the consecration of bishops required in the city might be performed, since apostolic institution and tradition require at least three bishops. [Col. 1035A]

Whether Peter later doubled this number, or whether it was done by his successors—who likewise increased the number of the cardinal presbyters and deacons of the Roman Church, raising the total of presbyters from twenty-five to fifty and the deacons from seven to fourteen—it is certain that in the age of the Council of Nicaea six bishops were, according to ancient custom, recorded as being available to the Roman pontiff.

## Annals of the Pontificate of Blessed Peter

From the Ascension of the Lord to the foundation of the three principal sees—Roman, Alexandrian, and Antiochene—according to the common Christian era.

### Year 28, leap year

Under the consuls the two Gemini.

On 25 March, eight days before the Kalends of April, Thursday, Christ the Lord celebrates Passover with his disciples and begins his Passion in the garden. On 26 March, seven days before the Kalends of April, Friday, he dies hanging [Col. 1035B] on the cross. He rises on Sunday, 28 March, five days before the Kalends of April (Victorius of Aquitaine, *Paschal Canon*, and Saint Hippolytus, *Paschal Table*).

As the month of April was drawing to a close, he entrusted Peter with the care of the entire flock of the faithful and made him supreme pontiff.

Here begins the epoch of Blessed Peter’s pontificate in the Church.

Christ the Lord ascends into heaven on Thursday, 6 May. Saint Matthias is ordained.

Seven deacons are elected.

### Year 29

Under the consuls Vinicius and Longinus; Peter’s pontificate, years I and II.

While the first year of the pontificate was not yet complete, Blessed Peter celebrated Passover. These consuls are assigned to the first year of his pontificate in the catalogues because the catalogues were arranged according to the Oriental practice of sacred, or paschal, years.

The first persecution of the Church, in which Stephen is crowned. Acts, chapter 8. Philip evangelizes Samaria. In the same chapter, Peter and John are sent from Jerusalem to Samaria. [Col. 1035C]

### Year 30

Under the consuls Tiberius Augustus V and Sejanus; Peter’s pontificate, years II and III.

The conversion of Paul (Acts 9), who preaches Christ in the synagogues of Damascus. In the same chapter, verse 22. He departs for Arabia; after returning to Damascus three years later, he is brought by Barnabas to Peter and the apostle James, who were active at Jerusalem. See below on Galatians, chapter 1.

### Year 31

Under the consuls Gnaeus Domitius and Marcus Furius Camillus; Peter’s pontificate, years III and IV.

Peter and John, returning to Jerusalem, evangelize many regions of the Samaritans (Acts 8:25).

### Year 32, leap year

Under the consuls Galba and Sulla; Peter’s pontificate, years IV and V.

“Those who had been scattered because of the tribulation which arose under Stephen traveled as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch, speaking the word to no one except Jews” (Acts 11:19).

Meanwhile, “the Church throughout all Judea, Galilee, and Samaria had peace” (Acts 9:31). [Col. 1035D]

### Year 33

Under the consuls Persicus and Vitellius; Peter’s pontificate, years V and VI, and the Antiochene see.

Paul, rescued from the plot of the Jews in Damascus, comes to Jerusalem. There, according to Acts 9:27, Barnabas brings him to the apostles, Peter and James. He remains with Peter for fifteen days (Galatians 1:19). “He was with them, entering and departing, and acting boldly in the name of the Lord. He also spoke to the Gentiles and disputed with the Greeks” (Acts 9:29).

Peter likewise, sometimes entering Jerusalem, sometimes departing, and visiting the faithful, passed through them all (same chapter, verse 32). In that same year Peter should be said to have come to Antioch and, in the Church gathered there from Jews—not yet admitting Gentiles—to have established a see, since he is said to have held it for seven years before establishing the Roman see in the year 40. [Col. 1036A]

Soon afterward, at Lydda he heals Aeneas, and at Joppa he raises Tabitha from the dead. He remains there for many days with Simon the tanner (Acts 9:43). Having been instructed there concerning the calling of the Gentiles, he is summoned to Caesarea, where he baptizes Cornelius, the centurion of the Italian cohort (Acts 10).

Paul incurs hostility while disputing with the Greeks and is sought for execution. The brethren, to remove him from the plot, lead him down to Caesarea and send him away to Tarsus (Acts 9:30).

### Year 34

Under the consuls Gallus and Nonianus; Peter’s pontificate, years VI and VII, and the Antiochene see, years I and II.

After baptizing Cornelius, Peter goes up to Jerusalem and reveals the mystery of grace, which had also been spread among the Gentiles (Acts 11:2 and following).

### Year 35

Under the consuls Papius and Plautius; Peter’s pontificate, years VII and VIII, and the Antiochene see, years II and III.

Among those who had been scattered after Stephen’s martyrdom were men from Cyprus and Cyrene. When they came to Antioch, they spoke and announced the Lord Jesus to the Greeks (Acts 11:20), and a great number was converted to the Lord.

The report reached the ears of the Church at Jerusalem concerning these events, and they sent Barnabas as far as Antioch (same chapter, verse 22). [Col. 1036B]

### Year 36, leap year

Under the consuls Proculus and Nigrinus; Peter’s pontificate, years VIII and IX, and the Antiochene see, years III and IV.

The emperor Tiberius died on the Kalends of April, as Usserius corrects the account from Dio. Caius, his successor in the empire, names Agrippa king—Agrippa being the grandson of Herod the Great through his son Aristobulus, and having been left by the dying Tiberius in chains at Rome—and assigns to him the tetrarchies of Philip and Lysanias. Herod, the tetrarch Antipas of Galilee, goes up to Jerusalem to offer sacrifice to God (Josephus, book XVIII, chapter 7). Vitellius is governor of Syria.

When Barnabas reached Antioch, he exhorted everyone, and a great multitude was added to the Lord (Acts 11:24). [Col. 1036C]

### Year 37

Under the consuls Julianus and Asprenates; Peter’s pontificate, years IX and X, and the Antiochene see, years IV and V.

In the second year of Caius’s reign, Herod Agrippa obtained permission to return home and arrange his kingdom. Flaccus, governor of Egypt, persecuted the Jews at Alexandria. Soon afterward he himself was arrested and punished with exile by order of Caius.

Barnabas departed from Antioch for Tarsus in search of Paul. When he found him, he brought him to Antioch. They spent an entire year there in the Church and taught a great multitude, so that the disciples were first called Christians at Antioch (Acts 11:26).

Around this year Matthew committed his Gospel to writing. Eusebius asserts that this happened after he had first preached the faith to the Hebrews and before he departed for other nations as well (*Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 24)—that is, before the twelfth year after the Lord’s Passion, to which he assigns the apostles’ departure into the provinces and Peter’s arrival at Rome in his *Chronicle*—and before Mark wrote his Gospel and, taking it with him, departed for Egypt. Eusebius likewise assigned this to the twelfth year after Christ’s Passion. [Col. 1036D]

### Year 38

Under the consuls Caius Caesar and Caesienus; Peter’s pontificate, years X and XI, and the Antiochene see, years V and VI.

The tetrarch Herod, coming to Italy, asks Caius for the kingdom of Agrippa. Caius, suspecting him of defection, drives him into exile and deprives him of the tetrarchy of Galilee and Peraea, which he adds to the kingdom of Agrippa, his rival, although Agrippa was the brother of his wife. Petronius is appointed successor to L. Vitellius, recalled from Syria (Josephus, book XIX, chapter 6).

Prophets come from Jerusalem to Antioch. Among them is Agabus, who foretold the famine that was to occur under Claudius (Acts 11).

### Year 39

Under Caius Caesar III, sole consul; Peter’s pontificate, years XI and XII, and the Antiochene see, years VI and VII. [Col. 1037A]

Caius, seeking divine honors, decrees that a colossal statue of himself should be erected at Jerusalem. The Jews resist. Caius reproaches Herod Agrippa, who was staying with him. Agrippa pleads the injury this would do to the ancestral laws. Caius, appeased, replies more mildly.

Agrippa returns to Rome. Caius adds to his domain the tetrarchy of Herod Antipas, his uncle, who had been driven into exile at Lugdunum.

In the same year a riot arose at Alexandria between Jews and Greeks, giving Philo an opportunity to undertake an embassy to Caius Caesar.

Caius had summoned legions from everywhere for the Germanic and British war which he was planning. Several legions that had until then been stationed in Syria, Judea, and the neighboring provinces were transferred to the West, and shortly afterward served in Britain under Claudius.

Perhaps the Italian cohort of the centurion Cornelius, or Christian soldiers from the garrison at Caesarea, migrated to Italy with that legion. All these circumstances provided Blessed Peter with an opportunity for travel and lodging at Rome. Providence also required him to migrate to Rome for the sake of the Eastern Church, amid this change in the kings and tetrarchs of Judea. [Col. 1037B]

### Year 40

Under the consuls Caius Caesar IV and Saturninus; Peter’s pontificate, years XII and XIII, and the Roman see, year I.

At the beginning of the year the apostle Peter comes to Rome and establishes the Roman Church. From the paschal month, in which the twelfth year of his supreme pontificate was completed, begins the epoch of exercising the pontificate in the Roman see.

The paschal epoch, or sacred year, according to the practice of the Orientals and Jews, fell in the month of April. Since the epoch of the years from the foundation of the City, reckoned at Rome from the Parilia, fell on 21 April, and since in the age of Claudius it was recorded in the priestly calendars of the pagans, as can be seen in Gruter, folio 300, the Romans attached to this same terminus the beginning of the supreme pontificate transferred by Peter to Rome together with the see. Thus, to Peter’s martyrdom on 29 June of the year 65 of the common Christian era, there are correctly counted twenty-five years, two months, and eight days.

In the age of Constantine the Great, when the Christian paschal reckoning was established and the final paschal terminus fell on 25 April, it was decided that on that day the greater litany and the public procession of all orders to Saint Peter should be instituted. Therefore, referring the paschal and pontifical year to this date, some authors count from that day to 29 June of the year 65 twenty-five years, two months, and three days. [Col. 1037C]

Caius Caligula presses for the dedication of the colossal statue at Jerusalem. The Jews resist. Caius reproaches Herod Agrippa for this while Agrippa is staying with him. Agrippa pleads that the act would violate the ancestral laws. Caius is mollified and responds more mercifully.

While Philo was delaying in Rome, he conversed with Peter and formed a friendship with him. For this reason too, it is reported that he adorned with praise the followers of Mark, Peter’s disciple, at Alexandria (Saint Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Philo”).

### Year 41

The year of Caius’s assassination; the ninth day before the Kalends of February. Saint Peter’s pontificate, years XIII and XIV; the Roman see, years I and II. [Col. 1037D]

After the consuls, following two days of interregnum, had reported to the Senate concerning the restoration of the republic and the abolition of imperial rule, they were erased from the official calendars so that all memory of this period might be removed.

John Malalas, in his *Chronographia*, reports that Caius was killed and Claudius elected emperor under the consuls Cassius and Silo, who appear nowhere in the calendars. The names of the ordinary consuls—those appointed on the Kalends of January—survive on a gladiatorial ticket published by Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, chapter 1, number 191, although they are not found in the calendars:

> MARTIALIS MANLII SP. K. IAN TI. CATIO. P. CAELER.

Perhaps the ordinary consuls of this year were Tiberius Cattus [Col. 1038A]—from whom Malalas formed the name Cassius—and Publius Caerellius. This family had produced men of consular rank, including Gaius Caerellius, proconsul of Macedonia (in Reinesius, page 402), unless P. Caeler was one of Caius’s obscure friends whom he made consul with the same ease with which he is said to have designated his own horse as his colleague in the same magistracy.

Perhaps one of these men was succeeded a few days later by Pomponius, the second consul, whom Dio mentions in book LX at the beginning, or Quintus Pompeius, as Josephus calls him in book X, chapter 3.

Whatever the case, it is clear that Claudius considered nothing more urgent, once the empire had been secured, than to remove from memory those two days during which there had been hesitation over changing the condition of the republic (Suetonius, *Claudius*, chapter 11). Josephus adds at the cited passage that the Senate had been abandoned by its defenders and that the consuls had been reduced almost to the rank of private citizens, while everyone was overcome by grief and astonishment and did not know what ought to be done after Claudius had been provoked against them.

For this reason the consuls of this year are missing from the calendars, as is demonstrated more fully elsewhere. [Col. 1038B]

Having obtained the empire, Claudius, not without the prudent counsels of Herod Agrippa, confirms his kingdom, enlarges it with the territory of Judea and Samaria, and honors the king with the consulship. Agrippa then returns to Palestine.

Mark, Peter’s interpreter, writes the Gospel at the request of the brethren and presents it to Peter for approval. By the same prince of the apostles he is sent from Rome to Egypt, so that in Peter’s name he may establish the Alexandrian see and announce the Gospel which he had written (Saint Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Mark”).

### Year 42

Under Claudius Augustus II and Largus; Peter’s pontificate, years XIV and XV; the Roman see, years II and III; the Alexandrian see, year I.

Since the Jews at Rome had become excessively numerous, they were forbidden to assemble (Dio, page 669). Elsewhere, throughout the provinces of the Roman Empire, they were granted permission to live according to their own customs. [Col. 1038C]

Peter returns from Rome to Palestine, both to care for that Church, which was threatened with danger under the new king Agrippa, and to visit the other Eastern Churches—those of Pontus, Cappadocia, Asia, Bithynia, and the remaining regions.

Herod Agrippa began to rage against the Church in order to win the favor of the Jews. First he killed James, and then he cast Peter into prison. From there Peter, rescued by an angel, departs to another place (Acts 12), namely Antioch, and then to the provinces of Asia Minor mentioned above.

Claudius, preparing an expedition to Britain, recalls the Fourth Legion and others from Syria to the West. See our earlier notes on line 5 of this number.

### Year 43

Under Claudius Augustus III and Vitellius II; Peter’s pontificate, years XV and XVI; the Roman see, years III and IV.

Claudius, summoned to Britain by Suetonius Paulinus, receives that island and some of its kings into submission, and celebrates a triumph for it at Rome in the following year. The Senate decrees a triumphal arch for Claudius on account of his successful operations in Britain. Half of the inscription of that monument, still surviving in the Barberini residence, was published among the ancient inscriptions (Fabretti, page 728, with supplements). [Col. 1038D]

Having brought Peter’s annals down to the foundation of the three principal sees, and having returned with him to Judea, where, after the council of the apostles concerning the Law—which interpreters commonly assign, on the basis of the Epistle to the Galatians 2:1, to the eighteenth year after the Lord’s Ascension—he then departed for Antioch (there, verse 11) in order to visit the neighboring provinces, and subsequently returned to Rome, where under Nero he wrote his First Epistle, I shall refrain from distributing Peter’s deeds among the individual years, since the documents for each year are not available.

It will be enough to indicate that he appears to have remained in the East until the end of Claudius, namely until the consulship of Marcus Asinius Marcellus and Marcus Acilius Aviola, in the year 54 of Christ, occupied especially with founding and visiting the Churches in Asia. [Col. 1039A]

We arrange the remaining years as follows.

### Year 55

Under the consuls Nero and Vetus; Blessed Peter’s pontificate, years XXVII and XXVIII; the Roman see, years XV and XVI.

According to the Liberian Catalogue, Blessed Peter came to Rome again.

### Year 56

Under the consuls Saturninus and Scipio; Blessed Peter’s pontificate, years XXVIII and XXIX; the Roman see, years XVI and XVII.

Blessed Peter ordains Linus bishop, according to the same Liberian Catalogue, so that he might exercise the priestly ministry in the City during the absence of the prince of the apostles and assist him when he was present, as we shall say below in number 2.

Around this year, 56 of the common Christian era, or somewhat earlier, Blessed Peter wrote his First Epistle. It is clear that it was written after the disciples had been called Christians and after Churches had been founded in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, and enlarged with elders, or presbyters; and before Nero’s eighth year, marked by the martyrdom of the evangelist Mark. Peter sends greetings in Mark’s name to the churches of the faithful to which he writes. [Col. 1039B]

From that time until the year 65 of the common Christian era he was active partly in the City and partly throughout the provinces of the West. He was occupied with enlarging the boundaries of the Church and especially adorned with bishops those sees which the notes of Somier enumerate below near the end.

### Year 58

Under the consuls Nero III and Messala; Saint Peter’s pontificate, years XXX and XXXI; the Roman see, years XVIII and XIX.

Festus succeeds Felix in governing Judea (Acts 24:27).

Saint Paul, having appealed to Caesar, is sent to Rome (Acts 27) in the fourth year of Nero (Saint Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under “Luke”).

### Year 60

Under the consuls Nero IV and Lentulus; Saint Peter’s pontificate, years XXXII and XXXIII; the Roman see, years XX and XXI.

[Col. 1039C] John Malalas of Antioch, in his chronicle, assigns to these consuls the martyrdom of Saints Peter and Paul at Rome. He confuses Paul’s first imprisonment with his second.
