From his custody Paul writes, according to the Epistle to Timothy, summoning him to come quickly to Rome. When Timothy arrives, Paul sends other Epistles, enumerated by Baronius under the years 59 and 60.

**Year 61.**—In the consulship of Paetus and Turpilianus; the thirty-third and thirty-fourth years of Saint Peter, and the twenty-first and twenty-second years of the Roman see.

Saint Paul is released from custody. Saint Peter visits and teaches in the western provinces (from Saint Innocent I, Letter to Decentius). Saint Luke writes the Acts of the Apostles at Rome. See Baronius under the year 61, no. 6.

**Year 62.**—In the consulship of Celsus and Gallus; the thirty-fourth and thirty-fifth years of Saint Peter, and the twenty-second and twenty-third years of the Roman see.

The martyrdom of Saint Mark in the eighth year of Nero (Saint Jerome, [Col. 1039D] *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Mark). The chronographer Theophilus, in John Malalas, p. 325, likewise reports in that year the death of Saint Mark at Alexandria, with Anianus succeeding him; the death of Evodius at Antioch, with Ignatius succeeding him; and the return of Blessed Peter to Rome, in order to overthrow the deceptions of Simon Magus.

**Year 63.**—In the consulship of Regulus and Rufus; the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth years of Saint Peter, and the twenty-third and twenty-fourth years of the Roman see.

Simon Magus, while Blessed Peter was praying, falls headlong. See Baronius and the authors whom he cites under the year 68, as well as the notes of Sommier below under this number.

**Year 64.**—In the consulship of Lecanus Bassus and Licinius Crassus; the thirty-sixth and thirty-seventh years of Saint Peter, and the twenty-fourth and twenty-fifth years of the Roman see.

The fire at Rome under Nero, and the first persecution of the Christians (Tacitus, *Annals* XV, sections 38 and 44). Saint Peter sends his Second Epistle from this place.

[Col. 1040A] **Year 65.**—In the consulship of Nerva and Vestinus. Nero’s twelfth year, beginning on the third day before the Ides of October. The thirty-seventh year and the beginning of the thirty-eighth year of Saint Peter, and the twenty-fifth year of the Roman see, lasting two months and seven days from 21 April of the fortieth year.

The martyrdom of the holy apostles Peter and Paul on 29 June, thirty-seven complete years after the Passion of the Lord (Saint Jerome, under Peter). Epiphanius assigned it to Nero’s twelfth year. See Baronius under the year 69, no. 2. Saint Linus succeeds to the Roman see and to the universal governance of the whole Church; concerning him, see the following number.

[Note: [Col. 1040A]

**Line 1.**—Blessed Peter the apostle and prince of the apostles. Christ called him Cephas, or Peter—not because Cephas means one thing and Peter another, but because what we call *petra* in Latin and Greek the Hebrews and Syrians, on account of the affinity of their languages, call *Cepha*, as Jerome testifies in book I, commentary on chapter II of the Epistle to the Galatians. [Col. 1040B] Cephas signifies not just any rock, but the most solid kind, like a cliff or crag, which, when placed beneath foundations, is ordinarily the firmest support. Nor does it signify “head” because of its affinity with the Greek word *Kephalís* (Κεφαλίς), as Isidore thought in *Etymologies* VII, chapter 9. The Syriac word *Cephas* is one thing, and *Kephalís*, that is, “head,” another. Christ imposed this name on Simon not without a great mystery and a judgment concerning the deeds he was to perform most conspicuously. The same occurred with James and John, the sons of Zebedee, whom the same Savior named Boanerges—that is, “sons of thunder”—lightning, so to speak, because one was destined to illuminate the western region and the other the eastern.

**Line 2.**—From the village of Bethsaida. Bethsaida was a small and obscure town of the district of Capernaum, situated on the shore of the great lake of Gennesaret, or Sea of Tiberias.

**The same line.**—He first occupied the episcopal chair at Antioch. In the sixth year of his pontificate, as that year was progressing, he reached Antioch, the metropolis of Syria, and there taught the mysteries of the faith of Christ. He first founded and governed the Antiochene church in person, taking possession of its episcopal chair on the eighth day before the Kalends of March—that is, on 22 February—the day celebrated by the Catholic Church, a Saturday, in the year 37 from the Nativity of Christ, twenty-three days before the death of Tiberius. This is established from Clement, Eusebius, Jerome, and others, who gathered it from the more ancient records of that Church and state that he presided over it for seven years, though not a complete seven years. Such is the judgment of the ancient Fathers; such are the ancient ecclesiastical traditions, confirmed by the agreement of all. These should be followed rather than the recent inventions of others who have written that Peter received the Antiochene chair only after receiving the Roman one.

**Line 3.**—Here Peter entered the city of Rome under Nero Caesar. In the year of Christ 44, the twelfth year of Peter’s pontificate, the second year of the emperor Claudius, when Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus II and Lucius Vitellius Nepos II were consuls. After Peter had chiefly instructed the peoples who were of the circumcision, founded the Church of Antioch, and imbued Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia with the laws of evangelical preaching, the prince of the apostles and foremost leader of the world entered the principal city and mistress of the whole world, its chief citadel, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February—that is, on 18 January—which then fell on a Friday, after the second year of Claudius’ reign had ended and six days of the third had begun. This was in the twelfth year of Peter’s pontificate, three months and a few days short of its completion, after the new consuls had been appointed on the nearest Kalends of January. He had spent five years in Jerusalem and nearly seven years in the see of Antioch, while the famine that had begun in the second year of Claudius still continued.

From Peter’s arrival in Rome his pontificate there began. That day was held especially sacred and is commemorated everywhere with an annual festival. The chair in which he sat to teach the people is still preserved intact in his basilica and is held in singular veneration. In the year of Christ 46, the third year of Peter’s Roman pontificate, after the fifth year of Claudius’ reign had elapsed, when Marcus Vinicius Quartinus II and Marcus Statilius Corvinus were consuls, Peter had already spent three complete years at Rome establishing and strengthening that Church and preaching the Gospel. Yet persistent concern for the other eastern Churches occupied him and drew him away from the West to Jerusalem, where at that time a serious disturbance had arisen among the faithful from the circumcision. Therefore, in order to restore harmony to the Church, Peter returned to Jerusalem, leaving at Rome a vicar or vicars who could preserve and daily enlarge the Lord’s flock in his absence.

After the eastern disputes had meanwhile been settled in the council of Jerusalem, Peter remained in the East throughout the whole period of Claudius’ reign, until the year of Christ 56, the first year of the emperor Nero, when Nero Claudius [Col. 1041B] Caesar Augustus and Lucius Antistius Vetus were consuls. Returning to Rome after a long absence, he revisited the Church there and again strengthened and enlarged it by his holy sermons. Earlier he had been unable to reclaim his see because of the edict of Claudius, who had expelled all Jews from Rome; yet that edict had expired with Claudius’ death.

**Line 5.**—Here he wrote two Epistles that are called Catholic. While Peter was at Rome, which because of its idolatry and immeasurable crimes he calls Babylon, he wrote two Epistles. The first was sent through Silvanus, the faithful brother, to the Churches of Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia, in Nero’s second year, while Mark the evangelist remained in Peter’s company. The second was written in Nero’s twelfth year, when God had revealed to Peter that his death and imminent martyrdom were at hand.

These Epistles are called Catholic, that is, universal, because they were written not to one people or nation but to many and diverse ones, as Isidore testifies in *Etymologies* VI, chapter 2. These two Epistles are included among the sacred and canonical Scriptures. [Col. 1041C] Six other books, however—*The Preaching*, *The Gospel*, *The Acts*, *The Revelation*, *The Teaching*, and *The Judgment*—written under Peter’s name, are apocryphal and spurious and are falsely attributed to the prince of the apostles. We also find that the work called the *Apocalypse of Peter*, which the ancients identified as spurious and illegitimate, was nevertheless once customarily read annually on Good Friday in certain churches among the Palestinians (Nicephorus, book XII, chapter 34).

**Line 6.**—And the Gospel of Mark, because Mark was his helper and his son through baptism. Mark, Peter’s disciple and follower, and his son in baptism, wrote in Greek the Gospel that the prince of the apostles himself had preached, at the urging and request of the Romans—or, as others hold, in Latin, whose original they think is preserved in the Marcian treasury at Venice. All the Syrians attest this latter view, and reason suggests that a Gospel intended for Latin speakers would have been written in no language other than Latin.

Whichever of these alternatives is correct, Eusebius, quoting Papias and Clement in book VI [Col. 1041D] (*History* II, chapter 14), reports that, when Blessed Peter learned by revelation of the Holy Spirit that the work had been published by Mark, he approved and confirmed it by his authority, so that it might be read throughout the Church. It is therefore clear that, while Peter was still alive, Mark wrote and published at Rome not so much his own Gospel as Peter’s Gospel. Likewise, in Nero’s fifth year, Luke published there, shortly after being released by Caesar after two years, the book entitled the Acts of the Apostles.

**Line 10.**—Here he is crowned with martyrdom together with Paul. Accordingly, in Nero’s thirteenth year and the year of Christ 68, several days before their execution, Peter and Paul, delivered into prison and chains and brought forward on false accusations, endured the tyrant’s capital sentence. They were first bound and beaten with rods, as had become customary among the Romans, especially in a case involving the impiety charged against them.

Paul, because he was a Roman and of noble status, was beheaded at the Salvian Waters outside the Trigemina Gate, [Col. 1042A] three miles from the city. Peter, because he was considered a commoner and of lower condition, was condemned to death on the cross in the same thirteenth year of Nero, on the same day—namely, the third day before the Kalends of July—which then fell on Wednesday, 29 June, when Gaius Fonteius Capito and Gaius Julius Rufus were consuls.

Christ foretold this kind of death to Peter not only as he was leaving the city but also when he entrusted the Church to his governance: “When you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John 21:18). John adds: “He said this to signify by what death he would glorify God” (ibid., verse 19).

Peter asked the executioners not to crucify him in the same manner as the Lord, but in the opposite and inverted position, fearing, as is plausible, that the same passion might win him the same honor among the foolish. He therefore obtained permission for his hands to be fastened below and his feet above.

**Line 11.**—Near the place where he was crucified. The place of execution, the summit of the Janiculum or Vatican Hill, [Col. 1042B] overlooked Nero’s naumachia, situated below beside the Tiber. A magnificent church now rises there, bearing the title of Peter of the Golden Mountain, where Peter surrendered his pure and immaculate soul into the hands of God.

His disciple Clement, who was a bishop, had first magnificently prepared Peter’s most venerable and holy body in the lower part of the Vatican, where Nero’s gardens and circus with its obelisk stood near the temple of Apollo, and buried it there. There it still rests in the most illustrious basilica founded on that site by the emperor Constantine the Great in his honor, celebrated throughout the Christian world for worship and attendance.

**Line 13.**—Here he performed ordinations during the months of December. Blessed Peter performed several ordinations in the month of December: fifty-three bishops throughout the dioceses, and at Rome ten presbyters and seven deacons. Among them were the bishops Linus, Cletus, Clement, Apollinaris, Mark, Hermagoras, and others; and the presbyters Anacletus and Evaristus, [Col. 1042C] who later became Roman pontiffs.]

[Note: [Col. 1042C]

**Line 6.**—Two Epistles. (Pagius the Younger, nos. 11 and 12.) Saint Peter wrote two Epistles called Catholic. There was never any doubt about the first; concerning the second, some ambiguity existed among certain writers because of the difference in style. But if anyone examines the style of the first Epistle thoroughly, he will easily notice that it does not differ greatly from that of the second; even the Magdeburg Centuriators admit this. The Church has taught in the Councils of Laodicea, Carthage III, Florence, and Trent that both Epistles are canonical and belong to Saint Peter.

The Gospel of Saint Mark is called Saint Peter’s by some because, as Saint Jerome writes, Mark, his hearer and interpreter, wrote it at the request of the brethren, according to what he had heard Peter report. When Peter heard it, he approved it and, by his authority, gave it to the Church to be read: so Jerome in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Mark.

The holy doctor, in the same work under Peter, mentions that many other books had been written under Peter’s name: one entitled *The Supplement*; another, *The Gospel*; a third, *The Preaching*; a fourth, *The Apocalypse*; and a fifth, *The Judgment*. But he states there that all of them are reckoned among the apocryphal Scriptures.

Moreover, in the *Supplement to the Library of the Fathers* there is a liturgy, or apostolic Mass, which William Lindanus, bishop of Roermond, published in Greek and Latin near the end of the sixteenth century from a manuscript codex of Cardinal Sirlet, bearing Peter’s name. Cardinal Bona, however, demonstrates in book I, chapter 8 of *Liturgical Matters*, that it is spurious, since it contains certain prayers from the *Book of Sacraments* of Saint Gregory the Great and has been pieced together from the Latin Mass and the liturgies of James, Basil, and Chrysostom.

After these and other considerations have been properly weighed, [Col. 1043A] he suspects that it was written in that same sixteenth century by some Italian-Greek priest who prefixed Peter’s name to it, either because the canon of the Roman Church, of which Peter was the founder, constitutes its principal part, or because the insertion of so great a name was intended to lend it authority. Concerning the translation of the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul, see what is to be said under Sixtus II.

**Line 6.**—And the Gospel of Mark. (Pagius, no. 6.) While he was at Rome, Saint Peter sent Saint Mark to Egypt, where he founded the Church of Alexandria. Saint Epiphanius writes in *Heresy* 51:

“After Matthew, Mark followed, ordered by Saint Peter at Rome to publish the Gospel; and after he had written it, he was sent by Saint Peter into the region of the Egyptians.”

Eusebius asserts in book II, chapter 24, that Mark was the first bishop of Alexandria, in these words:

“Meanwhile, while Nero was in the eighth year of his reign, Anianus was the first after Mark the evangelist to undertake the administration of the Alexandrian Church.”

The same Eusebius, in the cited chapters 16 and 17, discusses Saint Mark’s establishment of the Alexandrian Church and the conduct of the Christians whom he had formed. In chapter 15 he says that Saint Mark wrote the Gospel at the urging of the believers living at Rome. When Peter learned of this through a revelation of the Holy Spirit, he is said to have been delighted by the people’s ardent zeal and to have approved the book by his authority, so that thereafter it would be read in the Churches.

The Alexandrian Church therefore obtained the first place after the Roman Church because Mark, by Peter’s command, established it. Pope Gelasius testifies to this in his decree on apocryphal books:

“The second see, at Alexandria, was consecrated in the name of blessed Peter by Mark, his disciple and evangelist. For, sent by the apostle Peter into Egypt, he preached the word of truth and completed his martyrdom.”

**Line 10.**—He is crowned with martyrdom together with Paul. (Pagius, nos. 9 and 10.) Justin Martyr in *Apology* 2 and Irenaeus in book I, chapter 20 of *Against Heresies*, report that Simon Magus was at Rome and was held in the highest honor because of his magical arts. [Col. 1043C]

According to Arnobius, book II of *Against the Pagans*, p. 23, Saint Peter overthrew him when he was gravely disturbing the Church:

“When Simon, supported by two demons, had flown up by magical arts in order to prove himself a god, the demons were driven away by the prayers of the apostles Peter and Paul; he fell to the ground and was torn apart before the watching crowd.”

The *Acts of Saints Peter and Paul*, translated from Greek and published by Lippomano and Surius for 29 June, state that the holy apostles instructed two women, mistresses of the emperor Nero, in the Christian faith. Thereafter they resolved to live chastely. Elsewhere, when Nero had ordered Rome to be burned and had thereby incurred everyone’s hatred, Tacitus says in book XV of the *Annals* that, to suppress the rumor, “he fastened the charge upon the Christians” and inflicted on them the most refined punishments.

When this matter—that is, the miracles and conversions taking place through Peter and Paul—was reported to Nero, Lactantius, in the passage cited above, adds: “[lacuna] he was the first of all to persecute God’s servants: he fastened Peter to the cross and killed Paul.”

That martyrdom occurred in the consulship of Nerva and Vestinus, as is read in the *Catalogue of the Ancient Pontiffs*, and therefore in the sixty-fifth year of Christ. Baronius, indeed, places the martyrdom of the holy apostles in the sixty-seventh year of Christ, which he calls the sixty-ninth, and says that his opinion has very weighty supporters—namely, the ancient theologian Caius, Zephyrinus the Roman pontiff, and Dionysius, bishop of Corinth. Metaphrastes, citing them all in Surius under 29 June, supports and agrees with them, affirming that the apostles were killed thirty-six years after the Passion of the Lord.

So Baronius. But this rather confirms our position. For the ancients, as we said above, thought that Christ suffered under the consuls Gemini, and therefore in the twenty-ninth year of the Christian era. From that year to the sixty-fifth, thirty-six years elapsed. Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, both in his eulogy of Saint Peter and in that of Saint Paul, does not differ from this calculation; nor do the Roman Pontifical, Chrysostom, Isidore, Bede, Rabanus, Nicephorus, and others, who hand down that Peter and Paul were crowned with martyrdom thirty-seven years after the Passion of Christ. They count each of the two terminal years as complete, though incomplete, and differ from the earlier writers only in this respect.

They suffered on 29 June, the day on which their memory is commemorated in nearly all the Martyrologies, and indeed during the first persecution of the Church raised by the emperor Nero.]

[Note: [Col. 1044A]

**Line 1.**—Apostle and prince of the apostles. This distinctive designation in the pastoral authority of Blessed Peter embraces two attributes on which his nature rests. The first is extension, which is bounded by no limit and gathers under one shepherd all the faithful throughout the whole world, as Christ the Lord declares: “There shall be one flock and one shepherd” (John 10:16).

The second attribute is the excellence of power and direction belonging to the universal shepherd. Since he includes within his flock even the shepherds themselves, he must possess such vigilance and such strength of governance that the flock can follow him with complete security. For this to occur, his voice and direction must be truth and uprightness. If these were lacking, the care of the flock would have been entrusted to him wrongly; and greater danger would threaten a flock constituted under one shepherd than one left under the direction of several leaders who were not dependent upon one another. For if one excessively authoritative leader became the flock’s source of error, the others could opportunely bring the wandering sheep back to the right path.

Nevertheless, it is certain that the purpose Christ Jesus set before himself in establishing one see superior to all the others and declaring one supreme pontiff in the Church was unity, and consequently truth, without which unity can neither exist nor ever be understood. Many unsubordinated leaders cannot long remain joined to one another. Hence it has resulted that the unity found in the Catholic Church alone has always been regarded as the safest means of preserving that Church itself.

Therefore whoever in this Church is the center of unity must necessarily also be the center of truth; the two amount to the same thing. The characteristic of the supreme and universal shepherd is that he be infallible in feeding the whole flock, since no superior has been appointed over him to direct him except Christ Jesus himself, who says to him without granting any faculty of censure or power to be exercised over him by another: “Feed my lambs; feed my sheep” (John 21:16–17). Earlier he had said to him: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church; and I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:18–19); and: “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail; and you, once converted, strengthen your brethren” (Luke 22:32).

Such are the immovable foundations on which the primacy in the Catholic Church and the other prerogatives of the Roman see are established.

**Line 6.**—Two Epistles. From the words of the first Epistle, Sommier gathers that the order of the Churches had already been established under Peter when he wrote to them. On page 44 he notes the following:

“Saint Peter himself indicates the order and character of the Churches to which he writes his first Epistle, according to the order held by the provinces he names within the Roman Empire: ‘Peter, an apostle of Jesus Christ, to the elect exiles of the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia.’ Amasia was the metropolis of Pontus; Ancyra, of Galatia; Caesarea, of Cappadocia; Ephesus, of Asia; and Nicomedia, of Bithynia.

“The seven Churches to which John directs his Apocalypse—Ephesus, Smyrna, Pergamum, Thyatira, Sardis, Philadelphia, and Laodicea—were metropolises in Asia Minor. And when Saint Paul wrote to Titus, his disciple, whom he had appointed bishop in the island of Crete, one of the provinces of Macedonia under the Roman Empire, whose metropolis was Gortyna, he commanded him to appoint bishops throughout the cities: ‘As I also appointed you’ (Titus 1:5). Scripture itself therefore establishes, among the other rights of the superior sees, that even in the apostolic age they appointed the bishops of the inferior sees.”

**Line 8.**—They were confirmed by his testimony. There, orthodox authors—that is, the holy Fathers and other ecclesiastical writers whom he cited above—adhere to the authority of Jesus Christ, who testified that he had not come to abolish the law but to fulfill it, as well as to the words of his Apostle teaching that everything occurring under the Law was a figure of things to be fulfilled under the Gospel. They accordingly determine that God, by establishing the pontificate of the Old Testament, foreshadowed and sketched out, as it were, the rudimentary form of the pontificate to be erected in the New Testament.

[Col. 1045B] Under the former covenant God disclosed his revelations in several ways: sometimes through the instrument of a voice, whose words were heard although the appearance of the speaker was not seen, as on Mount Sinai and at the place of the tabernacle and later of the temple called the Holy of Holies; sometimes through the ministry of the high priest wearing his distinctive and singular vestment; and sometimes through prophets and other divinely inspired men.

To ensure that the revelations containing the faith and the conduct to be observed by the Israelites would remain free from the corruption that the passage of time and the fluctuation of human opinions usually introduce into other matters, he established in Israel a fixed and supreme see and tribunal. It was to be the arbiter of everything pertaining to religion, to disclose to human beings the true meaning of his laws, and to decide absolutely all controversies:

“If you perceive that a judgment is difficult and ambiguous for you, etc.” (Deuteronomy 17:8ff.).

[Col. 1045C] **Line 4.**—The episcopal chair. In the New Testament the truth of realities corresponds perfectly to these figures of the Old Testament. Just as under that former covenant there was never lacking a tribunal of certain and permanent institution to disclose the true meaning of revelations and pronounce a definitive judgment in matters pertaining to religion, so in this age of the new covenant a supreme see has been erected in the Church, from whose judgments appeal is not permitted: “Whatever you bind”; whose decisions are irrevocable: “Strengthen your brethren”; whose direction is universal and secure: “Feed my lambs, feed my sheep.”

For the readings of the codices of Freher A and B and of Fabrottus’ three codices—Reg., Maz., and Th.—and for the words:

“After his Passion [that is, Christ’s], in the following year, the apostle Peter held the chair in the eastern regions for four years; then, in the year of the Lord 38, he came to Antioch, where he sat for seven years and eight days; then he came to Rome, where he sat for twenty-five years, seven months, and eight days,”

the following notes from Sommier, *Dogmatic History of the Holy See*, pp. 48 and 58, may be used.

The time appointed by divine Providence for the foundation of the Roman Church was approaching. Saint Peter set out for that place. While visiting the Churches he encountered on the journey, he appointed bishops at Caesarea in Palestine, Sidon, Berytus, Byblos, Tripoli in Syria, and Laodicea, as well as in other places recorded by ancient writers in very old monuments.

After this he revisited his Antiochene Church, from which he proceeded to Cappadocia, Galatia, Pontus, and Bithynia, everywhere appointing bishops. He also founded most of the Churches of Thrace, among them Byzantium, which later became famous after assuming the name Constantinople.

We find these things recorded in a letter of Pope Agapetus to Peter of Jerusalem. Its testimony is all the more venerable and firm because it was cited in the fifth ecumenical synod celebrated at Constantinople [Col. 1046A] (Act II, at the end):

“We believe that we should add this to his dignity: from the time of the apostle Peter, the Eastern Church has never received any other bishop ordained by the hands of our see. Perhaps, either to demonstrate his praise or to destroy his enemies, so great a matter has now come to pass that he himself may appear similar to those whom the election of the first of the apostles once appointed in these regions.”

And on page 53 I shall add the following from the author cited above.

Someone may wish to know which Churches Blessed Peter subjected to the Antiochene patriarchate. We say generally that he subjected the East to it, just as he was to subject the West and the North to the Roman patriarchate and the southern part of the earth to the Alexandrian patriarchate. This should not be regarded as an empty supposition but as a true history of the facts, whose clarity was illuminated by subsequent events.

The division derived from the Council of Nicaea confirms this, since it attests its antiquity and demonstrates that it proceeded from the one who founded those three sees. Anyone may challenge all critics to show us a founder other than Peter. No one among the ancients therefore doubted that the Council of Nicaea recognized the territory of the Antiochene patriarchate as the East.

Saint Jerome reproaches John of Jerusalem because, although John was counted among the bishops of Palestine, he had arranged for an ecclesiastical case to be referred to the bishop of Alexandria. That judgment did not belong to the Alexandrian bishop, since it directly concerned the metropolitan of Caesarea, from whom appeal ought then to have been made to the patriarch of Antioch.

“You who seek ecclesiastical regulations,” says the holy doctor in Letter 60, “and use the canons of the Council of Nicaea, answer me: what does Palestine have to do with the bishop of Alexandria? If I am not mistaken, it is decreed there that Caesarea is the metropolis of Palestine and Antioch of the whole East.”

Writing to Alexander, bishop of Antioch, Innocent I declares:

“Therefore, reviewing the authority of the Council of Nicaea, which sets forth the single mind of all priests throughout the world, we find that it judged it necessary for all the faithful, not to say all priests, to preserve the authority of the Church of Antioch, which we recognize as established over its own diocese, not over some other province.” [Col. 1046C]

And on page 54 he says:

“By the name of the East, which is under discussion here, is understood the whole of the fifteen provinces that were later listed under the designation of the Diocese of the East in the register of the Roman Empire. Their government was administered by an official appointed by the emperor to reside at Antioch, bearing the title of prefect of the praetorium of the East.

“These provinces are the two Syrias, the two Palestines, the two Cilicias, the two Phoenicias, Armenia, the island of Cyprus, Arabia, Isauria, Euphratensis, Osrhoene, and Mesopotamia. This division of the Eastern diocese was completed before the age of Honorius and Arcadius.

“Under the authority of the patriarch of Antioch there were also Eastern nations situated beyond the boundaries of the Roman Empire. His jurisdiction extended in proportion to the growth of the Churches that were subsequently founded there. An Eastern writer of the eleventh century reports that the Parthians, Medes, and Persians, as far as the Indians, obeyed his authority. This writer is Nilus the archimandrite, cited by Allatius in his work *On the Agreement of the Eastern and Western Churches*.

“Nor are there lacking those who believe that the exarchates of Pontus, Asia, and Thrace obeyed the jurisdiction of the see of Antioch in the earliest periods of the Church” (Cabassut, *Ecclesiastical Notes*, century II, dissertation 14, no. 3).

Others assert that these dioceses were autocephalous, subject to no patriarchate, since in each of them the chief metropolitan, or primate, had been appointed as an independent prefect and had been granted a certain patriarchal jurisdiction: in Pontus, the metropolitan of Caesarea in Cappadocia; in Asia Minor, the metropolitan of Ephesus; and in Thrace, the metropolitan of Heraclea, before Constantinople was raised to patriarchal status.

These, they say, were the metropolises more illustrious than the others of which the Council of Nicaea speaks in canon 6. After asserting the ancient rights of the three patriarchal Churches—Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch—it declares that in the other provinces each Church’s own honor must be preserved. See Lupus on canon 6 of the Council of Nicaea.

On page 89, concerning the Western Churches founded within the Roman patriarchate by Saint Peter, he writes as follows after relating that Mark was sent to Alexandria:

“At the same time Blessed Peter sent other disciples into various southern, western, and northern provinces, so that they might found Churches there. For it is manifest, as Innocent I says in Letter 1 to Decentius:

‘Throughout all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the islands lying between them, no one founded Churches except those whom the venerable apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests. Let them read, if some other apostle is found or reported to have taught in those provinces.’”

It is nevertheless not clearly established which Churches were actually founded by Saint Peter or founded in his lifetime by his disciples in the provinces of the western Empire. Those whose origin is popularly traced back to him, with greater probability, are the following.

In Italy: Capua, Naples, Anxur, Aequa, Nepete, Fiesole, Lucca, Ravenna, Verona, Padua, Ticinum, and Aquileia.

In Gaul: Limoges, Toulouse, Bordeaux, Reims, Arles, Sens, Le Mans, Vienne, Châlons, Bordeaux, Auvergne, Saintes, Tongeren, Trier, Cologne, and Mainz.

The bishops Torquatus, Ctesiphon, Secundus, and others are attributed to Spain; Eucherius, Aegistus, and Maricanus to Germany; Pancratius, Marcianus, Beryllus, and Philippus to Sicily.

It is also reported that the Gospel reached the British islands under Blessed Peter. This should be considered highly probable, since the conquest of Britain by Caesar Claudius opened free access to those islands for the preachers of the faith.]

**1.** Blessed Peter, apostle and prince of the apostles,

an Antiochene [Note: [Col. 1003] “Antiochene” is absent from T. I, *Councils*.], son of John, of the province of Galilee, from the village of Bethsaida, brother of Andrew [Note: [Col. 1003] See Baronius, vol. I of the *Annals*, under the year 39]. He first occupied the episcopal chair at Antioch for seven years. Here [Note: [Col. 1003] “Hence.”] Peter entered the city of Rome under Nero Caesar [Note: [Col. 1003] C and B read “under Claudius.”], and there occupied the episcopal chair for twenty-five years, one month, and eight days [Note: [Col. 1003] B reads “twenty-four years, five months, and eleven days.”]. He lived during the times of Tiberius Caesar, Gaius, Tiberius Claudius, and Nero [Note: [Col. 1003] B reads “Claudius and Nero.”]. [Note: [Col. 1003] See Baronius under the years 45 and 68.]

Here he wrote two Epistles, which are called Catholic [Note: [Col. 1003] C adds “and canonical.”], and the Gospel of Mark, because Mark was his hearer and his son through baptism [Note: [Col. 1003] “from baptism.”]. After the whole source of the four Gospels—which were confirmed at his questioning and testimony, that is, Peter’s, while one speaks in Latin, another in Greek, and another in Hebrew [Note: [Col. 1003] C reads “writing in Hebrew”—]—they were nevertheless confirmed by his testimony [Note: [Col. 1003] C reads “all of them.”].

He is crowned with martyrdom together with Paul thirty-eight years after the Passion of the Lord [Note: [Col. 1003] Baronius under the year 69]. He was buried on the Aurelian Way in the temple of Apollo, near the place where he was crucified, near Nero’s palace in the Vatican, beside the triumphal territory, on the Kalends [Note: [Col. 1003] C reads “the third day before the Kalends.”] of July.

Here he performed ordinations during the months of December: six bishops, ten presbyters, and eight deacons [Note: [Col. 1003] C reads “three bishops and seven deacons.”]

## Catalogue under Liberius

Peter: twenty-five years, one month, and nine days. He lived during the times of Tiberius Caesar, Gaius, Tiberius Claudius, and Nero—from the consulship of Vinicius and Longinus to that of Nero and Vetus [the manuscript of Bucherius reads “Nerva and Verus”]. He suffered together with Paul on the third day before the Kalends of July, during the consulship of the aforementioned consuls, while Nero was emperor.

## II. SAINT LINUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 69. IN THE THIRTEENTH YEAR OF THE REIGN OF NERO.

[Note: [Col. 1047A]]
