[Note: [Col. 1047B]]

Line 4.—“By the command of blessed Peter, he established that a woman should enter the church with her head veiled.” Peter is here said to have instituted that women should be in church with veiled heads, so that due regard might be shown to the modesty of the sex. Paul likewise commanded this (1 Corinthians 11), that a woman should pray with her head veiled, as though nature itself were giving the instruction, since it gave the woman hair “ἀντὶ περιβολαίου”—“in place of a covering.” It was an institution of the apostles that women should have a place in the church separated by a partition of boards from the men. John Chrysostom, *Homily 74 on Matthew*: “Ἐχρῆν μὲν οὖν ἔνδον ἔχειν τὸ πεῖχος τὸ διεῖργον ὑμᾶς τῶν γυναικῶν”—“It was indeed necessary to have within a wall separating you from the women.”

Augustine, *City of God*, Book XXII, chapter 8: “In a dream, as Easter approached, he was instructed that, while keeping watch in the women’s section at the baptistery, he should mark with the sign of Christ’s cross the place where the first baptized woman should meet him.”

Anastasius, under Sergius: “He made an image of blessed Peter the Apostle, which is in the women’s section.” The same author, under Gregory III: “He made an oratory within the same basilica, beside the principal arch, in the men’s section.” The same, under Hadrian I: “And curtains in the presbytery, on the men’s and women’s sides, of the purest silver.” The same, under Leo III: “Likewise, he made turned columns both at the entrance of the body of the church, on the right and left, on the men’s and women’s sides.”

There was also a distinct place in the church for consecrated virgins. Ambrose, *To the Fallen Virgin*, chapter 6: “Should you not also have remembered that place separated by boards, where you stood in the church, toward which devout matrons and noblewomen eagerly ran, seeking your kisses—women who were more holy and better than you?”

[Note: [Col. 1049A]]

Line 1.—LINUS. There is a serious controversy concerning Peter’s successor; more observations on it will occur in the chronological work. For the present, unless an evident reason persuades us otherwise, this succession must be taken from the *Pontifical Book*, through which the memory of the most ancient catalogues has been preserved.

The catalogues, specifically those that represented apostolic origin, foundation, and uninterrupted succession, were carefully preserved in the primitive Church, since they were an argument for the truth. If other churches took pride in such a register, this must be asserted much more strongly of the Roman Church, where the episcopal chair had been established, together with the necessary origin, which was regarded as the prior endowment of the true Church, and where the chair persisted through successors. For, according to Optatus—and even the Donatists agreed on this point—a chair cannot exist where no bishop has sat.

Accordingly, among their other records, the churches preserved with the greatest care the registers [Col. 1049B] of bishops, so that they might bring them forward in support of the truth; but the Roman chair preserved them in order to demonstrate its necessary origin. Thus Cyprian, writing to Cornelius about the constancy of the African churches, their zeal in rejecting the attempts of schismatics, the letters of Novatian, and the recognition of a legitimately established pontificate, joins two things together: the recognition of legitimate ordination and the necessary origin.

Ordination referred to the continuing succession of the chair; necessary origin referred to the chair of Peter, then universally regarded as the prior endowment of the true Church. Thus he writes in Letter 68:

“So now also your episcopate, and the truth and dignity alike, have been founded in the clearest light and established by the most open, firm, and conclusive proof, so that from the replies of our colleagues who sent letters to us from there, and from the report and testimony of your fellow bishops Pompeius, Stephanus, Caldonius, and Fortunatus concerning your ordination, both your necessary origin, your just claim, and your glorious innocence might be known to all.”

[Col. 1049C] A little earlier, speaking of certain bishops who had been ensnared by the Novatians, he had said: “We know that we exhorted them to recognize and hold fast to the root and mother of the Catholic Church.”

The root and necessary origin were to be recognized and retained in the chair of Peter, together with communion with his successor Cornelius. From this it is clear that the Roman Church had to preserve the succession of bishops with the greatest diligence, since the true Church was recognized from it just as from its origin.

The other churches, especially those that took pride in an apostolic foundation, brought forward these registers; and uninterrupted succession was regarded as an argument for the truth. Irenaeus refers to such registers in Book III, chapter 3:

“Thus the tradition of the apostles, manifested throughout the whole world, is present for all who wish to hear the truth to see in every church; and we can enumerate those who were established as bishops in the churches by the apostles, and their successors down to our own time, who taught nothing of this kind.”

Tertullian also attacks the assemblies of heretics [Col. 1049D] on this same ground, namely, their lack of origin and succession, addressing them as follows:

“Let them produce the origins of their churches; let them unfold the order of their bishops, running down through succession from the beginning in such a way that their first bishop had as his author and predecessor one of the apostles, or an apostolic man who nevertheless persevered with the apostles.”

For this reason Hegesippus, in Eusebius, Book IV, chapter 22, having undertaken a journey and visited the more distinguished churches, noted two things in them: the succession of bishops descending from apostolic institution, and the purity of doctrine preserved by those same churches. He presents his account in these words:

“In each succession of bishops, and in every city, the same things remain which were preached through the Law, the prophets, and by the Lord.”

He commends the Church of Corinth in the following terms:

“The Church of the Corinthians remained in the right faith until Primus, its first bishop. I conversed with him intimately while I was sailing to Rome.”

[Col. 1050A] After mentioning certain others, when speaking of the church of Jerusalem, he observes that it was called a virgin because, from its first bishop until that time, no one had sat in it who was stained by error:

“They called the Church a virgin up to that time because it had not yet been corrupted by empty speeches.”

Then, while counting the succession and order of its bishops, he adds: “The series preserved in the archives of that Church demonstrates this.”

From this passage and testimony it is gathered that various catalogues existed and were preserved in the archives of the Church of Jerusalem, and that they were produced to demonstrate succession. This sheds light on the statements concerning the synod of Mopsuestia in the case of Theodore, formerly bishop of that city, which was examined at the Fifth Synod, in volume III of the *Councils*, page 526.

For the acts report that John the presbyter and keeper of the sacred treasury, when summoned by the Fathers of the synod to produce the catalogues of the bishops, brought them from the cabinet of the sacred vessels, saying:

“According to the command of your Holiness, I have brought out these diptychs from among the sacred vessels entrusted to my keeping, and I present them for reading. I also have two other parchment quires older than these that are now being read.”

The diptychs were made partly from tablets and partly from writing materials, and John brought out both kinds. The Fathers explain what those various diptychs contained in the following exchange:

“Let the sacred diptychs be read, which record the commemoration of the priests of holy memory of this city of Mopsuestia, from the time when the immaculate and orthodox faith was preached up to the present priest, who died in the thirteenth indiction.”

Thus the successions and series of bishops in each city were religiously preserved, and these were various catalogues, perhaps some recording ordinations and others deaths, as the final words cited from the synod of Mopsuestia make clear. In disputes, recourse was made to them, so that proofs might be drawn from them. Hence, in the comparable controversy concerning the order and succession of the Roman pontiffs, strength is added [Col. 1050C] by the evidence brought forward from the ancient catalogues of the pontiffs.

Line 5.—“He held two ordinations.” A number of ordinations is assigned to Linus, since he is said to have celebrated only two; and because Saint Peter held more, the phrase “through the months of December” was added.

Since the consecration of bishops is joined in one continuous statement with the ordination of presbyters and deacons, so that confusion does not arise, it must be noted that the day and month refer to the presbyters and deacons. The consecration of bishops, however, was not tied to a month but was celebrated on a Sunday in any part of the year.

Accordingly, the punctuation must be understood in this way, as is certainly evident from other passages of the *Pontifical Book*, in which the matter plainly must be explained so. In John VI, the punctuation is expressly given:

“He held an ordination of presbyters and deacons, namely, nine presbyters and two deacons. But he made fifteen bishops in various places.”

The punctuation and the distinction in the consecrations are shown even more clearly under Sergius I:

“He ordained ninety-seven bishops in various provinces. But he held two ordinations in the month of March: eighteen presbyters and four deacons.”

Before these, in the Holstenian manuscript, under Sylvester, page 38, consecrations performed at different times are noted without the name of any month being assigned:

“Seventy-five bishops in various places and at various times in the city of Rome.”

This was stated under Leo II and more distinctly under Constantine, whose ordinations are listed as follows. On the journey to Constantinople that he undertook, he celebrated the consecrations of bishops, concerning which the account says (page 161):

“He held episcopal ordinations on the way there and on the way back, making twelve bishops in various places.”

These ordinations cannot be assigned to any particular month. At the end, however, page 163 states:

“He held one ordination: ten presbyters and two deacons; and in various places, sixty-four bishops.”

And concerning the antipope Constantine:

“The aforesaid Constantine, invader of the Apostolic See, held an ordination of presbyters and deacons: eight presbyters and four deacons; and also, during the course of that year and in one month, eight bishops in various places.”

Moreover, apart from other obvious records, the words of the *Pontifical Book* itself under Zacharias prove that the consecrations of bishops were performed not on Saturday but on Sunday, where it is reported that the consecration of the bishop of Terni was celebrated on a Sunday.

“Fifteen bishops.” The number of bishops consecrated by the pontiffs proves that the ordinations were not performed on a single Saturday, but throughout the period of the pontificate. For in the primitive Church there was an accepted and observed custom that one bishop should be consecrated on a single day.

Thus, among the other crimes charged against Chrysostom as grounds for his deposition, the Synod at the Oak records this: that “in one ordination he created four bishops at the same time.”

The large number of bishops whom the pontiffs regularly ordained, as the *Pontifical Book* records in the Lives of each, could arise both from pontifical and from patriarchal jurisdiction, by which the ordination or approval of bishops depended on them.

There is no room for doubt concerning pontifical authority. Peter, as Chrysostom observes, could, by virtue of the primacy, have enrolled Matthias in the apostolic college without a synod (*Homily III on Acts*):

“Was it not permitted to Peter himself to choose? It was permitted, and indeed most certainly; but he did not do so, lest anyone should think that he was favoring someone.”

For this reason the approval of patriarchs was attributed to the pontiff. When Nectarius was elected patriarch of the imperial city, even though the Council of Constantinople approved him, the pontiff opposed the election; and when Theodosius the Elder saw that the election was being invalidated, he sent legates to request confirmation from Damasus. Boniface I reports this in a letter to the bishops of Epirus, read at a Roman synod, where he writes (in Holstenius’s Roman collection):

“The princeps of most merciful memory, believing that the ordination of Nectarius could not possess validity because it had not come to our attention, sent courtiers from his side together with bishops and regularly requested that a formal document be sent to him from the Roman See, one that would strengthen his priesthood.”

Agapetus, using pontifical authority, deposed Anthimus in Constantinople and ordained Mennas as bishop of Constantinople. The monk Marianus examined these rights, vindicated according to canonical judgment by Agapetus, in a written petition submitted and approved at the Constantinopolitan synod under Mennas (volume II of the *Councils*, page 1194).

The same subject will be discussed again in connection with the Acacian schism under Felix III. That authority to consecrate or confirm the bishops of the same region belonged to the pontiff as patriarch of the West is proved, among other evidence, by Innocent I in his letter to Alexander of Antioch. He attributes this power to the example of the Apostolic See and, because both sees were founded by Peter, concludes:

“Therefore, dearest brother, we think that, just as you ordain metropolitans by your singular authority, so you should allow the other bishops to be created only with your permission and knowledge. In these matters you will rightly observe this arrangement: command by letters that those who are far away be ordained by men who now ordain them solely at their own discretion; but if you consider them nearby, arrange for them to come to the laying on of hands of your Grace. For those whose care is especially entrusted to you ought to receive your principal judgment.”

The pontiff also had a particularly special concern for the urban and suburban churches. From these facts it is clear how the ordinations of several bishops were celebrated by individual earlier pontiffs, even in the primitive Church.

[Note: [Col. 1051D]]

(EX BIN.) Line 4.—“He established that a woman should enter with her head veiled.” What the Apostle Paul established piously, holily, and religiously—namely, that women should enter the temple only with their heads covered and veiled, out of reverence for the angels, who according to Saint Ambrose’s interpretation are priests—the Magdeburgians criticize, either impiously or ignorantly, as having been confirmed by decree by the pontiff Linus. Bellarmine, Book IV *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 4. See Baronius, under the year of Christ 57, no. 84 and following, where he writes beautifully concerning the veiling of women.

(EX LAB.) Line 5.—“He held two ordinations.” These words are absent from C. H.

[Note: [Col. 1052A]]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

We stated above, on page 87, that eleven years, three months, and twelve days of episcopate were attributed to the blessed Linus, and that this was confirmed by the agreement of all the manuscripts. The catalogue of Felix IV and those four manuscripts from Italy, which owe their origin to the genuine records of the Roman Church, all record the same number.

The more ancient catalogue under Liberius does indeed give twelve years, but the consuls listed there expose the error of the added unit: from Saturninus and Scipio in the year of Christ 56 to Capito and Rufus in the year of Christ 67. Thus, of the eight Colbertine manuscripts, four agree with the foregoing witnesses and show that, in accordance with those consuls and with the number of the Italian manuscripts—which agree with them—the four exemplars that counted fifteen or seven instead of eleven must be corrected.

Accordingly, if they are corrected in accordance with the chronology of the consuls expressed in the same catalogues, and also marked in the Ocriculan manuscripts, which correctly assign eleven years, three months, and twelve days of episcopate to blessed Linus, I have observed that the testimony of all the manuscripts agrees with the oldest paintings of the basilicas.

I said that the years of episcopate, not merely those of the supreme pontificate, are counted in this total. This becomes clear from the annalistic chronology of Peter, arranged shortly before at the end of the notes on the first number. There we recorded that, in the year of Christ 56, under the consuls Saturninus and Scipio, Saint Peter returned to the City at the beginning of Nero’s reign—Nero had succeeded his uncle Claudius two years earlier, on 13 October, and, according to Eusebius, Book II of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 22, conducted himself more mildly at the beginning of his reign when Paul’s defense was received—and that Saint Linus was ordained bishop.

We followed the testimony of these manuscripts and catalogues, as well as the most authoritative writers, who are to be consulted in Schelestratius, Dissertation II, chapter 1, and Henschenius in Labbe, volume I of the *General Councils*, exercise 4, no. 31.

That Linus was in Rome while Paul was writing the Second Epistle to Timothy is clear from the greeting addressed to him by name. In the same place the Apostle also mentions Claudia, whom many authors assert was Linus’s mother.

Some also infer from the letter of Ignatius the martyr to the Trallians, section VII, that Linus served the Apostle to the Gentiles in the diaconal order. Others, however, doubt whether that passage was added to the Ignatian letter at a later period, and for that reason the editors list it among the interpolated passages. [Col. 1052D] Cotelerius should be consulted on this matter, volume II, page 66.

If Linus did perform the ministry of a deacon for Paul, this must be regarded as having occurred long before his arrival in Rome under Nero, in the second year of whose reign the Liberian catalogue records Linus’s promotion to the episcopal order, under the consuls Saturninus and Scipio.

Henschenius gives a sufficiently probable reason for this promotion in Exercise IV, no. 31: namely, that when Peter departed for the distant provinces of the West, there might not be a lack of someone to administer in the City the vicarious authority of the Roman bishop. Alternatively, it may have been that, since Linus and Cletus had been marked with the episcopal character and were assisting the Apostle Peter in carrying out his pontifical ministry, the apostolic custom was already being introduced into practice that later found its way among the apostolic canons: namely, that the consecrations of bishops should be completed by the ministry of three bishops whenever a new bishop was to be assigned to a church.

The martyrdom of Saint Linus is assigned by the ancient martyrologies, including the Notkerian, to 23 September. If the year of his martyrdom was the common era year 67, under the consuls Capito and Rufus, as the Liberian catalogue and the *Pontifical Book* explicitly state, and if it occurred in the eleventh year, third month, and twelfth day after he had been ordained bishop, then according to this calculation his consecration fell on 12 June of the common-era year 56, namely on a Saturday as Sunday approached.

But if eleven days are to be read, as in the manuscript of approximately nine hundred years from the Palatine-Vatican Library, previously reported in the fifth work from Schelestratius, then Sunday, 13 June, was the day of his ordination. Nevertheless, it is preferable to retain the earlier number, twelve days, confirmed by as many records as we indicated on page 87.

Nothing prevents us from understanding Linus to have been ordained on Sunday, 13 June, which that year was the octave of Pentecost, since Easter fell on 18 April. For below, in the discussion of Callistus, no. 17, we shall see that the fasts which we call the four Ember seasons were confirmed by that same pontiff and have come down to us from the apostolic age. There they are called the Saturday fast.

He established that the fast should be observed on Saturday three times a year, namely, whenever ordinations were also held. Hence Saint Leo the Great so often commands in his sermons that, after the fast of Wednesday and Friday, a vigil should be kept on Saturday at Saint Peter’s—and indeed according to ancient custom.

For the era of ordinations was reckoned from those Saturday vigils, which, preceded by fasting, opened the sacred mysteries. And although Christian assemblies took place before dawn, as is clear from Pliny’s letter to Trajan, and although the ordinations of bishops were held on Sunday during the offering of the unbloody sacrifice, nevertheless they seemed in some way to belong to the day of those vigils, from which the gathering of the faithful for their celebration had begun.

Thus the second week of June became famous for the Ember fast and for the ordinations of the clergy. In some churches a custom eventually arose [Col. 1053C] of never removing either observance from that week, so that more than once, after the octave of Pentecost, celebrations took place that, according to the most ancient apostolic discipline, should have been performed within the octave—until the vigilance of the pontiffs restored that discipline.

The learned commentator on the Gregorian Sacramentary, Menardus, observes this; I shall soon quote his words. For the present, we can conclude that the chronology and history of the ordination, pontificate, and martyrdom of blessed Linus mutually support one another.

For from the martyrdom recorded in the oldest church tablets on 23 September—just as his burial is marked in the *Pontifical Book* on the same day, the ninth day before the Kalends of October—and from the period of his episcopate, which lasted eleven years, three months, and twelve days, it is gathered that his ordination occurred on the octave of Pentecost. From this ordination, in turn, the tradition descending to us from the apostolic age is confirmed: namely, that the fixed Ember fasts were held within the week of Pentecost, and that the ordinations of the clergy occurred after the Saturday vigils [Col. 1053D] of that same octave.

Menardus must be heard in his commentary on page 107, Book XVII of the Gregorian Sacramentary, concerning the words, “If it should occur after the week of Pentecost”:

“These words,” he says, “are not found in the printed editions or in the other manuscript codices. Nevertheless, they were written according to the custom of those times, when the fast of the fourth month was celebrated in the second week of June; consequently, it often happened that this fast took place after the week of Pentecost, as can be seen in the Council of Mainz under Charlemagne, in which thirty bishops and twenty-five abbots assembled (Canon 34):

‘Likewise, in the second week of June, let there be fasting on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday until the ninth hour.’

This is cited by Burchard, Book II, chapter 14, but in a more abbreviated form, and by the *Micrologus*, chapters 24 and 25, concerning the Observances of the Church. But he seems to understand a different Council of Mainz when he says that it was held under Henry II and attended by twelve bishops. [Col. 1054A]

The same rule was established in the Council of Rouen, held in the year 1072:

‘Likewise, the observance of the four Ember seasons shall be maintained by us in common observance at the appropriate time, according to divine institution: namely, the first week of March, the second of June,’ and so forth, as Ordericus reports in Book IV of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

So much for the practice of those times. Certainly, the older custom was to celebrate this fast in the very week of Pentecost, as is clear from Saint Isidore, Book I *On the Offices of the Church*, chapter 37, and from Pope Saint Leo, Sermons 1, 2, 3, and 4, on the Pentecost fast. It was eventually revived in the Church by the authority of Gregory VII, as the *Micrologus*, chapter 25, teaches, and by Urban II at the Council of Clermont, where the following was established:

‘The second fast shall always be celebrated in the week of Pentecost,’ as Ordericus Vitalis reports in Book IX of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

In former times, the first Ember fast was likewise observed in the first week of March, as can be seen in the same canon of the Council of Mainz cited above:

‘It has been established that the four seasons of the year shall be observed by everyone with fasting, namely, in the first month, the first week,’ and so forth;

and in the Council of Rouen cited above:

‘Let it be observed by us in common observance, namely, in the first week of March.’

But afterward Gregory VII transferred it to the first week of Lent, as the *Micrologus*, chapter 24, teaches; and so it was established in the aforementioned Council of Clermont:

‘At all times, let the first fast of the four seasons be celebrated in the first week of Lent,’ as Ordericus Vitalis reports in the book cited.”

The chronology of the episcopate of blessed Linus is therefore established. His ordination, assigned to the fixed season of fasting during the octave of Pentecost in the year 56, under the consuls Saturninus and Scipio, leads through eleven years, three months, and twelve days to the day of his martyrdom, 23 September of the year 67, under the consuls Capito and Rufus.

Since blessed Peter completed his martyrdom in the year 65, under the consulship of Nerva and Vestinus, on the third day before the Kalends of July, as we demonstrated in the notes on the preceding number, it follows that, of the eleven years, three months, and twelve days of episcopal ministry attributed to Linus, he spent nine years as vicar, or coadjutor, of the Prince of the Apostles while Peter remained alive. During the final two years, with the corresponding months and twenty-five days, he sat as supreme pontiff, the first successor in the chair of the Roman and universal Church.

By this title and in this order he is numbered both in the canon of the liturgy and by the holy Fathers and other writers close to the apostolic age—namely, Irenaeus, Book III, chapter 3, and those from whom Eusebius drew his material in Book III of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 13—as well as by Epiphanius, Optatus, Saint Augustine, and other later writers.

## HISTORICAL NOTES OF THE SAME AUTHOR

Line 4.—“By the command of blessed Peter, he established that a woman should enter the church with her head veiled.”

The command for this discipline is attributed to Peter, and its establishment in the Roman Church to Linus by Peter’s mandate. For this reason Luitprand of Pavia argues that Linus acted at that time as Peter’s vicar in his absence. When, in the case of Cletus, he reports the constitution concerning the number of twenty-five presbyters to be ordained in the City as likewise having been entrusted by Peter, he adds: “From this it is clear that they were his coadjutors, not his successors.”

He should, however, have added this while discussing the promulgation of those decrees.

As for the veiling of women’s heads, Paul established the same rule among the Corinthians in the First Epistle he sent to that church from Asia Minor. This was almost exactly the time when Peter, shortly before returning to the City from his Asian journey—or even from Corinth, which he had visited on his return—left Linus in Rome as his vicar, while Peter himself went to visit the churches of the West.

Nearly all interpreters, following Baronius under the year 57, infer from the context—especially chapter 16, verses 3, 4, and 5—that Paul’s First Epistle to the Corinthians was sent around the year of the common era 57. From these passages it is evident that it was written before Paul went up from Asia to Jerusalem and before he traveled from the coast of Ephesus to Macedonia.

In chapter 11 he commands men to pray and prophesy with uncovered heads, but women with covered heads; and he indicates the mysteries of this rite.

In that same year, 57, when Paul sent this written instruction concerning the veiling of women to the Church of Corinth, Linus was residing in the City and exercising Peter’s vicarious authority. He had been ordained bishop by the Prince of the Apostles in the preceding year, 56, under the consuls Saturninus and Scipio, as we demonstrated shortly before from the Liberian and Felician catalogues and in the *Prolegomena*.

Peter had undertaken to tour the western region of the empire while the early years of Nero’s reign were entirely favorable. Claudius’s edict expelling the Jews from the City had been withdrawn, as Baronius observes in the same place, no. 42; moreover, their king Agrippa had been given four cities, as Josephus reports, *Antiquities*, Book XX, chapter 5, and *The Jewish War*, Book II, chapter 12. Thus the apostles and Christians had complete freedom to frequent the City and the Roman provinces at will, and no one prevented the faithful from assembling freely, both at Rome and at Corinth, or from receiving the discipline of our assemblies.

Therefore, if ever at another time, certainly in this period it was fitting that the laws of Christian discipline should be established by the apostles in our assemblies. What Paul commanded the Corinthians by letter, Peter therefore sanctioned at Rome by a decree promulgated by Linus, ordering women to be veiled when they came to the assemblies of the faithful for prayer and other sacred purposes.

No one should be surprised that this discipline was held in such high regard at the very beginning of the Church that it was counted among the first constitutions of the Apostolic See. For Paul’s Epistle sufficiently indicates how important it was, both for the sake of the mystery and for holiness, that this law should be confirmed with such authority.

Before explaining this, allow me to point out one matter concerning the decrees which the compilers of the Lives enumerate in the *Pontifical Book* as having been issued by Peter and his successors. [Col. 1055C]

I observe that these decrees generally concern two principal subjects, each belonging properly to the care and concern of the supreme pontiff: first, the safeguarding of the integrity of the Catholic faith; and second, the most diligent provision for the ordering of divine worship, both in the sacrifice and in the distribution of grace through it and through the other sacraments.

Both subjects seem to me to shine forth and be discernible in the decrees listed here, so that none of them lacks one or the other. For this reason the judgment of the writers is sufficiently commended: from the many decrees, they selected only a very few to be included in these brief Lives, as more distinguished and more closely corresponding than the rest to the office of the high priest.

Those decrees concerning the sacrifice, and therefore the supreme worship of God, include the regulations instituted by Cletus at Peter’s command concerning the number of presbyters; those of Evaristus concerning the seven deacons; those of Hyginus concerning the grades of the clergy; those of Anicetus concerning worship; and those of Zephyrinus and Caius concerning ordination.

They also include Alexander’s provision that the Passion of the Lord should be inserted into the priests’ prayer; Telesphorus’s decree concerning other prayers of the Mass; the decrees of both Felixes concerning the time for offering the sacrifice and the place where it should be celebrated; the regulations of Sixtus and Soter concerning the vessels of the ministry and their handling; those of Stephen and Zosimus concerning vestments; and those established by Dionysius and Marcellus concerning the division of the titular churches.

To the rules for preserving the faith and administering grace belong the decrees issued by Victor concerning baptism; by Pius concerning the conversion of the Jews; by Sixtus concerning the judgment of bishops; by Anterus, Fabianus, and Eutychianus concerning the acts and burial of martyrs; and by Eusebius, Siricius, and the others concerning the reconciliation of heretics. These matters will be explained in their proper places.

Having thus prefaced these remarks on the general character of the decrees set forth by the writers of the Lives, I turn to the constitution of Linus concerning the veiling of the heads of women who enter the church. I have said that it can be established from the First Epistle of Paul to the Corinthians why the rule requiring women to veil their heads in church was so strongly commended from the beginnings of the Christian faith: both for the sake of modesty and propriety, and also because of its mystery. For the Apostle embraces both reasons in chapter 11, and interpreters detect them especially in verse 10, where he says: “Therefore the woman ought to have authority over her head, because of the angels.”

Whether, by “angels,” he expresses blessed spirits sent to guard us, as some hold with Clement of Alexandria and several Fathers; or priests endowed with angelic ministry in the Church, and therefore called by that name in the Apocalypse, as others prefer with Ambrose; or both—for the term “angels” refers more to offices than to nature—the reason for legislating this custom lacked neither a mystical nor a moral basis. Everyone understands that propriety is served, and the weaker sex more securely protected, in an assembly of all ranks when the head is veiled, as Tertullian demonstrates in his entire book *On the Veiling of Virgins*.

But the age of the nascent Church above all others ought to have taken particular care of this discipline of public propriety, both to provide an example for posterity and to prevent the slanders of contemporaries against Christian assemblies—slanders already stirred up by the pagans, enemies of our sacred rites—as though Christians gathered at their synaxes with utter shamelessness for Thyestean banquets and criminal feasts. The faithful necessarily made extensive use of the ministry of widows and deaconesses, both when admitting sisters and leading them to places separate from men, and when decently covering the women who were approaching the baptismal font; likewise in the crowds attending the agape, in the care of young women, and in other duties collected from the Fathers and councils by Christian Lupus in his *Scholia* on the third chapter of Tertullian’s *On Prescription against Heretics*.

All these matters seemed likely to be managed and arranged more decently by female deaconesses and widows than by ministers and superiors of the opposite sex. Since, therefore, there were so many duties to be performed by women ministers—including duties that the Fathers also reckon among them, such as advising inexperienced women in private conversations and repeating to them whatever they had heard from the catechists, after the example of Priscilla and Aquila (Acts 18)—there was a danger that some women might think that they too had been instituted as participants in the priesthood of the new law.

Not long afterward, indeed, the women of Marcion and the Gnostics, as well as the adherents of the heresies of the Pepuzians and the Collyridians, identified by Saints Irenaeus and Epiphanius and by Tertullian—whose testimonies the aforementioned Lupus brought forward in his notes on chapter 41 of the same work on *Prescription*—dared arrogantly to claim this for themselves. Among them was especially the woman about whom Saint Firmilian wrote to Saint Cyprian:

> “Among the other things by which she had deceived very many, she also frequently dared to do this: by an invocation not lacking in appearance of reverence, she pretended to sanctify bread and to make the Eucharist, and to offer sacrifice to the Lord without the sacrament of the customary prayer. She also baptized many, using the customary and legitimate words of the interrogatory, so that nothing seemed to differ from the evangelical rule.”

Their audacity and insolence were renewed at various times by Quintilla in the Caian heresy, by those Pontic Amazons of whom Saint Jerome speaks, and in later centuries by the Beguines condemned by Clement V. More recently, too, all those who, under Luther’s authority and as members of the sectarians called the “Tremblers,” do not hesitate to usurp publicly in the Church the office of teaching, relying on the monstrous propositions of that heresiarch—reported by Cochlaeus in the place cited by Lupus—which affirm that “Christian women too are truly priests, and consequently that whatever has crawled forth from baptism is truly a pope, bishop, and priest.”

Thus, even in the apostolic age, Simon Magus, that firstborn of Satan, already displayed in the beginning of female arrogance a fertile seed of such presumption. He led about and exhibited his Selene as though she were Ennoia, the first conception of his mind, through whom he would make angels and archangels and even correct the errors of the angels. Baronius explained this at length from Irenaeus under the year 35, no. 20 and following.

The apostles therefore ought all the more forcefully to have resisted this nascent insolence of female pride, already stirred up by Simon, the leader of the heretics, to teach and correct, and shortly afterward exalted by his nearest sectarians to preside, baptize, and offer in priestly fashion. It could more easily have spread among posterity, who would later remember that the Samaritan Simon, architect of such doctrines and impieties, had adhered to the apostles from the beginning and had asked them to grant the Holy Spirit to anyone on whom he laid hands; that he had then been rebuked by Peter and exhorted to repentance, and had commended himself to the apostles’ prayers (Acts 8).

It was important for the faith of contemporaries and posterity that everyone should understand that women were so completely excluded from the priesthood that none of them was permitted “to speak in the Church, nor to teach, nor to baptize, nor to offer, nor to claim for herself any share in a man’s office, much less in a priestly function,” as Septimius Tertullian distinctly recounts in *On the Veiling of Virgins*, chapter 9.

To preserve the authority of this law both in larger churches and in assemblies containing fewer of the faithful, the apostles judged that a concise, ready, and universally visible admonition should be employed in the covering of the head, which would also serve as a safeguard of modesty and chastity. By the veil placed upon their heads, women were reminded that they were subject to another’s authority and would forever have the way closed to the glory of the priesthood, whose rights the Lord had wished to reserve to men, who bear the honor of his image.

Paul clearly indicated this at the beginning of the decree in 1 Corinthians 11:

> “But I would have you know that the head of every man is Christ; the head of the woman is man; and the head of Christ is God. Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head. But every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered dishonors her head.”

And again, in verse 7, he says:

> “A man indeed ought not to cover his head, since he is the image and glory of God; but the woman is the glory of the man. For man is not from woman, but woman from man. Nor was man created for woman, but woman for man. Therefore the woman ought to have authority over her head, because of the angels.”

Accordingly, those Fathers who understand “angels” as the blessed spirits presiding over the prayers of the faithful, as well as those who interpret the term as referring to the angelic ministry of our priests, rightly claim to discern in the Apostle’s decree and words the mystical authority of the sign: in the veiled heads of women, the power denied to them; in the uncovered heads of men, the power granted to them to bear in the priesthood the image and glory of Christ.

For both rites—the veiling of the woman and the man’s appearing before God with uncovered head while praying or prophesying—are directed toward the same confession: that the head of the entire priesthood is placed by its very nature in Christ, since he is the root of holiness, and that it proceeds from Christ. It is directed neither to the angels, whom he did not take hold of for the repetition of his unbloody sacrifice, but only for the ministry of presenting prayers; nor to women, whom he excluded both from the immolation of the sacrifice and from the ministry of offering upon the altar; but solely to men, who were endowed to bear among human beings the image and glory of Christ, the head of the priesthood and the eternal high priest, with the power denied to others to minister, offer, consecrate, and sacrifice.

The dignity of Christ, the divine head, is therefore proclaimed by the tonsure and crown of Christ introduced among men chosen for the priesthood from the age of the apostles and rightly attributed by the laws of Peter, as we shall see below in the case of Anicetus, signifying that the priesthood had been communicated to them; by the uncovered head of other men, demonstrating their ability to receive that power; and by the veiled faces and heads of women, declaring their exclusion from receiving the same power.

Since these are no slight proofs of our confession of Christ, the one mediator between God and human beings—whether when he entered once for all into the holy places, or when he acted with his apostles and priests, so that they might use the authority entrusted to them and denied to others—it was likewise no matter of small importance, but highly worthwhile, that both in Paul’s Epistles and in the decrees issued by Peter through Linus there should be recorded the regulations concerning the veiling of women when they entered the church, which the writers of the Lives commemorate.

I have thought it worthwhile to explain these matters more fully on the occasion of the apostolic decree concerning the veiling of women’s heads while praying in church. There can be no doubt that this decree was issued by the apostles, since it is read in Paul’s Epistle. I have done so not only to clarify the force and reason of the decree, but also so that anyone may infer from it that the apostles instituted mystical rites to be observed by the faithful in public prayers and assemblies, and that these mysteries were not absent even from the veils which, by the apostles’ command, were forbidden to some and assigned to others.

For if even those heretics who count Paul’s Epistles with us among the divinely inspired Scriptures must admit these things, it follows that they can in no way deny that the origin of sacred rites proceeded from the same source from which the Church received the Scriptures. Dodwell therefore applauds himself with excessive confidence in his addition to chapter 6 of Pearson’s dissertation 11, *On the Years of the First Bishops of Rome*, no. 16, believing that he had demonstrated the following:

> “In the time of Clement there was no solemn consecration of virgins by the bishop through the imposition of the veil. In the earliest times of Christianity there were none who professed virginity. Under Clement none were admitted to its public profession, etc. Finally, even afterward, when they had already formed a separate college apart from widows, none were consecrated by the bishop either by the imposition of the veil or by any other solemn rite—not even after a century and a half had elapsed from Clement’s death, when Cyprian wrote.”

What should be thought concerning the state of virgins, their profession, and the rite of receiving the veil in these earliest times of the Church, we shall appropriately examine against the obstinate denials of the sectarians in the case of Soter. For now it is enough to observe that Peter and Paul commanded all women to enter the church and pray with veiled heads; and that in this matter provision was made not only for propriety and for the sanctity of the Christian assembly in the gathering of the two sexes of the faithful, but also that a mystical relation of our faith and hope to Christ’s priesthood might be signified, and that its rights might be asserted as reserved exclusively to men.

The historian Josephus reports that Andronicus, pleading before Ptolemy Philometor, king of Egypt, for the dignity of the temple of Jerusalem against the sanctuary of the Samaritans, won the victory because he demonstrated the authority and sanctity of that earlier temple by arguments drawn from the law and from the uninterrupted succession of the chief priests, among whom the exercise of the priesthood had been preserved. “Beginning,” says Josephus in Book III, chapter 6 of the *Antiquities*, speaking of Andronicus, “by proving from the law the sanctity and religious character of the temple of Jerusalem, he showed through the continuous succession of the high priests the transmission of the priesthood down to his own time … and persuaded the king to decide that the temple of Jerusalem had been founded in accordance with the judgment of Moses.”

The ancient Fathers used this same demonstration against the heresies of their time when contending on behalf of the Roman Church.

> “Let them produce the origins of their churches,” says Tertullian in *On Prescription against Heretics*. “Let them unfold the succession of their bishops, running down in such a series from the beginning that their first bishop had as his author or predecessor one of the apostles, or apostolic men who nevertheless persevered with the apostles … just as the Church of the Romans has Clement ordained by Peter.”

Line 1.—“Roman by nation.” In the older catalogues as well, the native place is recorded for each pontiff. Optatus assumes that this indication was carefully observed and marked as necessary in the primitive age of the Church, in the passage cited above, where he observes that men from every people and nation were raised to the pontificate, and that the election was not restricted to Roman citizens or natives.

For the same reason he attacks the episcopate retained or usurped at Rome by the Donatists, since from Victor of Garba to Macrobius—who in Optatus’s day held the pseudo-episcopate at Rome—all were Africans and had been sent from Africa. Yet men from every people were found to have been chosen from Peter to Siricius, as the surviving catalogues demonstrated. Since the Donatists who came from Africa were exclusively Africans, Optatus addresses them as follows:

> “What is this, that all these Africans and foreigners are successively recognized in that city? Is the deceit not apparent? Is there no faction, which is the mother of schism?”

Saint Augustine raised the same objection, both in the passage cited above and against Cresconius, Book III, chapter 34.

“Of the district of the Vicus Patricius.” The Holstenian manuscript reads better, “of the Vicus.” Festus describes the Vicus Patricius as follows:

> “A street in Rome was called the Patrician Street because patricians lived there, by order of Servius Tullius, so that what they were plotting against him might be crushed from the higher places.”

The location where it formerly stood is identified below under Pius, in these words:

> “At the request of blessed Praxedis, he dedicated the church of the Baths of Novatus in the Vicus Patricius in honor of her sister, Saint Putentiana.”

That church still exists at Rome.]

Because Saint Irenaeus, Ignatius, and Eusebius call this pontiff Anacletus, Baronius, under the year of Christ 93, no. 1, thinks that this resulted solely from the error and defect of Greek writers and copyists—namely, that they wrote “Anacletus” instead of “Cletus.” Deceived by the similarity of the names, just as they confused Marcellus and Marcellinus, and Novatus of Carthage with Novatianus, a Roman by birth, so too, thinking that Cletus and Anacletus were one and the same, they conflated them.

Bellarmin, however, in Book II, chapter 5, *On the Roman Pontiff*, says that there were two Anacleti: one the predecessor of Clement, the other his successor. The former had two names and was called by both Cletus and Anacletus; consequently, he was the same third pontiff who preceded Clement, called Anacletus by the Greeks—Ignatius, Irenaeus, and Eusebius—but Cletus by the Latins, namely Tertullian, Jerome, Damasus, and others.]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES ON THE PONTIFICATE OF SAINT CLEMENT AND SAINT CLETUS

### 1

Why I do not separate the chronology of the two pontificates, those of Saint Clement and Saint Cletus, into two sections divided according to the number of pontiffs, will easily be understood by anyone who observes that, in the ecclesiastical history of the first century after Christ, the periods of the bishops mentioned are so entangled that everyone investigates which of them preceded and which succeeded, while very few seem able to determine the matter.

Let the eminent men of our own age who have treated this question stand for all others: Christian Lupus, in his notes on chapter 32 of Tertullian’s *On Prescription against Heretics*, at the words “Clement ordained by Peter,” and Schelestratius, *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, dissertation 2, chapter 1.

“Various,” says Schelestratius, “are the opinions of the ancients concerning Clement and the other three first pontiffs who succeeded Peter. Some place Clement second in order; others place him third, together with the older catalogue; others place him fourth after Saint Peter, with Jerome. Equally great is the disagreement of the ancients concerning the other three pontiffs who sat after Peter. For Optatus of Milevis, when listing the succession of the first four Roman pontiffs in Book II, places Peter first, and says: ‘Linus succeeded him; Clement succeeded Linus; Anacletus succeeded Clement,’” and so forth.

Saint Augustine says exactly the same in Epistle 165: “Linus succeeded Peter, Clement Linus, Anacletus Clement.” Saint Irenaeus gives a different account in Book III, chapter 3. He lists the order of the pontiffs in this manner: “Peter, Linus, Anacletus, Clement, Evaristus,” and so forth.

Both Pagii should also be consulted, to mention only more recent writers, since they collect numerous testimonies in addition to those produced by Baronius and Bellarmine, who treated the same question in the preceding century.

### 2

A more favorable escape from this labyrinth of questions seems to me to be opened by the method of pontifical chronology that we have adopted—namely, by consulting the more ancient and genuine records of the Roman Church.

The Liberian Catalogue, the most ancient of all, assigns to Peter Linus, to Linus Clement, and to Clement Cletus not merely as successors, but also states under which emperors they sat and under which consuls they marked the first and last years of their pontificates. The consuls are arranged and connected in such a way that the last consuls of a predecessor are followed by the next ones in the order of the fasti, and these are correctly assigned at the beginning of the successor’s tenure.

Linus’s pontificate is completed under the consulship of Capito and Rufus during Nero’s reign, that is, in the year 67 of the common Christian era. Clement, assigned in that catalogue as Linus’s successor, begins his tenure with the consuls of the year 68, Trachalus and Italicus. He is said to have sat under Galba and Vespasian for nine years, eleven months, and twelve days, up to the seventh consulship of Vespasian with his son Titus in his fifth consulship, as we shall examine below.

Cletus follows Clement, beginning with the next consulship, that of Vespasian in his eighth consulship and Titus in his sixth, and lasting six years, two months, and ten days, during the reigns of Vespasian and Titus and the beginning of Domitian’s reign. The last consuls of his tenure are given as Domitian in his ninth consulship and Rufus, in the year of Christ 83.

Anacletus follows him under the next consuls, Domitian in his tenth consulship and Sabinus, in the year of Christ 84. During his twelve years of priesthood he reaches the consulship of Domitian in his seventeenth consulship and Clement, belonging to the year of Christ 95, until Evaristus is substituted for him in the last years of Domitian, marking the first year of his pontificate by the consulship of Valens and Vetus, in the year of Christ 96.

### 3

To prove the truth of this chronology, which proceeds distinguished and ordered by so many marks of emperors and consuls from the year of Nero’s death to the year of Domitian’s death—terms no less certain than the epoch of the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus—we must first collect the sum of the years, months, and days assigned to these three pontiffs, and then measure the interval resulting from the consular fasti and the lives of the Caesars, from the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus, the year of Nero’s death, to the consulship of Valens and Vetus, namely the year of Domitian’s death.

If the two sums are equal, the pontifical era must be judged correctly marked, since no doubt remains concerning the imperial and consular chronology corresponding exactly to it, as coins, inscriptions, and historians abundantly demonstrate.

The consuls will indicate the portions of this interval and total distributed among those pontiffs. If their numerical designations have been corrupted in the copying of manuscripts through a copyist’s error by the addition or subtraction of a unit, they can easily be corrected from the name of the colleague in the consulship and from the preceding and following lists. For it must be presumed that a copyist could more easily err in one numerical designation, or alter one of them, than become confused in expressing so many names of emperors and consuls, whose connections agree both with the parts of the total and with the total itself.

The Catalogue therefore assigns to Clement nine years, eleven months, and twelve days; to Cletus six years, two months, and ten days; and to Anacletus twelve years, ten months, and three days. The total is twenty-eight years, eleven months, and twenty-five days—that is, twenty-nine years less five days.

But if Clement’s months above the full nine years were only two, as the paintings of the Basilica of Saint Paul and nearly all the catalogues and manuscripts record—apart from Bucher’s parchment manuscripts alone, which give eleven months—the total assigned to these three pontiffs would be twenty-eight years and almost three months.

The same interval results from the consular fasti and from the historians, from the year of Nero’s death—when he killed himself on the fourth day before the Ides of July under the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus, in the year of Christ 68—to the year of Domitian’s death, when he was stabbed on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of October under the consulship of Valens and Vetus, in the year of Christ 96.

Since the total period to be divided among these pontiffs is supported at both ends by so many marks of the imperial and consular era, it seems that it must be firmly retained. If some numerical designation has slipped into error in certain manuscripts, while it is correctly expressed in others and agrees exactly with the total and sequence of imperial and consular time, the corrupted numbers of the manuscripts must be restored from the intact numbers of other manuscripts, which correspond neatly to the whole total and to its parts.

### 4

Clement must therefore be regarded as Linus’s successor, both according to the order and according to the testimony of the consular and imperial chronology, as stated in the catalogues of the Liberian and Felician ages, as well as in the *Book of the Pontiffs* and in the Rituals or Lectionaries.

Other testimonies agree with these, cited by Cotelerius in his notes on the *Apostolic Constitutions*, among the *Collectanea of the Holy Fathers*, p. 384, and especially the sepulchral inscription—taken from the Casaurian Chronicle under the year 1103—attached to Saint Clement’s tomb and published by Baluzius in volume V of the *Spicilegium*, p. 475. It reads as follows:

> “Here lies Saint Clement, a disciple of Peter and second after Pope Peter, who by order of the emperor Trajan, with an anchor tied around his neck, was drowned in the sea. Clement is said to have sat during the time of Galba and Vespasian; Cletus during the time of Vespasian and Titus; Anacletus during the time of Domitian.”

Again, Clement is said to have ruled the Church beginning with the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus—the very beginning of Galba’s reign, in the Christian year 68—up to the consulship of Vespasian and Titus, certainly Vespasian in his seventh consulship and Titus in his fifth, in the Christian year 77, since nine years of tenure are assigned to him and the beginning of Cletus’s succession is marked by those same consuls, Vespasian VII and Titus V.

Counting nine full years, two months, and ten days from the day of Saint Linus’s martyrdom, 23 September, under the consulship of Capito and Rufus in the year of Christ 67—the period assigned to Clement by the most ancient paintings at Saint Paul’s—the pontificate of Clement would reach 3 December of the year 76, under the consulship of Vespasian VII and Titus V.

The following Easter, in the year 77, falling under the marked consulship of Vespasian VIII and Titus VI, would belong to Pope Cletus; and its beginning should be entered under those consuls according to the custom of the catalogue. On what day, however, he received the pontificate after Clement’s resignation will be determined from another indication, namely from the total period assigned to Cletus compared with the day of his martyrdom.

The calendars of the Martyrology assign Cletus’s martyrdom to 26 April. The Liberian Catalogue assigns him, in addition to six full years, two months and ten days of pontifical tenure, and places its end under the consulship of Domitian IX and Rufus, in the year of Christ 83.

He therefore must have entered upon the office of Roman pontiff on Sunday, 16 February of the Christian year 77, under the consulship of Vespasian VIII and Titus VI. The see was vacant from Clement’s resignation, 3 December 76, until 16 February 77, for two months and twelve days.

### 5

Godefridus Vendelinus had already long ago concluded, in his commentary on Saint Clement’s Epistles, that Clement resigned the supreme pontificate, and indeed in the year of Christ 77. The distinguished men among the Bollandist associates, with Henschenius, approve and incline toward the same opinion, writing in the apparatus to the pontifical chronology:

> “Godefridus Vendelinus resolves this controversy in his commentary on Saint Clement’s Epistles as follows: In the year 77, when a great dispute had arisen among the faithful at Rome—as later at Corinth—over the honor of the pontificate, Clement, so that he might not seem to have succeeded by Peter’s testament and so that this ambition for primacy might not become a harmful example for posterity, voluntarily resigned the pontificate. Clement himself appears to suggest this in the Epistle to the Corinthians, praised above by Clement of Alexandria and Jerome, where he says in the latter part of the Epistle: ‘If sedition, contention, and schisms have arisen because of me, I will depart; I will withdraw wherever you wish.’”

After prudently considering these points from Vendelinus, Henschenius agrees in no. 41 and concludes as follows:

> “Therefore, when Linus died on 23 September of the year 67, Saint Clement, already ordained bishop by Saint Peter, assumed the administration of the Church and had the next complete year in his pontificate under the consuls designated above, C. Silius Italicus and M. Galerius Trachalus Turpilianus. He governed the Church for nine years, eleven months, and twelve days, up to the year 77; yet the consuls of that year are assigned to Cletus, who was then raised to the pontificate. These consuls are listed above as the emperor Vespasian in his seventh consulship and Titus Caesar in his fifth, who administered the state in the year 76.”

### 6

I think the matter should be understood somewhat differently in bringing Clement’s resignation back to 3 December of the year 76, under the consulship of Vespasian VII and Titus V. I shall assign to the nine years of that same tenure, begun on 24 September of the year 67 after Linus’s martyrdom, only two months and ten days, in agreement with the paintings at Saint Paul’s, rather than eleven months and twelve days with the Liberian Catalogue, and I shall therefore fix its endpoint on 3 December.

With this resignation, thus brought back to that day on the authority of the cited records, I connect Cletus’s succession after two months and thirteen days from the resignation, falling on Sunday—an appropriate day for an episcopal ἐνθρονισμός, or enthronement—16 February of the year 77, under the consulship of Vespasian VIII and Titus VI.

For just as Clement, resisting his original designation and shrinking from undertaking the burden of the whole Church, accepted the honor of assuming the supreme pontificate only later and with reluctance, and obtained permission to defer it to Linus, although he himself had long before been called to that office by the designation of the prince of the apostles, so it is reasonable to believe that the Roman clergy accepted the wishes of one who wished to resign only with greater difficulty and delay. It is even more reasonable to believe that Cletus consented to his own election with still greater reluctance and delay, after mutual prayers had passed back and forth in order to wear down the constancy of both men who were refusing the office.

At length, as the Lenten fast approached, lest the Roman Church be left without a pontiff during the Paschal mysteries celebrated that year on 30 March, Cletus was finally overcome by the entreaties of those who pressed him and undertook the burden on 16 February. This was the first Sunday of Lent in that year, as we would call it, so that he might prepare penitents for baptism and for receiving at Easter the other sacred rites of our religion.

From this day, the reckoning of two months and ten days assigned to Cletus above six full years in the oldest Liberian Catalogue is produced exactly, and agrees with the day and year of his martyrdom recorded in the Church’s calendars, 26 April, under the consulship of Domitian VIII and Rufus, likewise expressed in that catalogue and in the other lists of pontiffs and lectionary books, as I have proposed that readers should observe.

### 7.

I shall gather from the fifth dissertation of the celebrated Henschenius another indication confirming that Clement’s abdication must be assigned to the year 76, when Vespasian was consul for the seventh time and Titus for the fifth. The occasion in question was the exile imposed upon philosophers by Vespasian, who in the year 73, according to Labbe’s chronology, expelled from the city the philosophers who professed Stoic doctrine at the urging of Mucianus, with the exception of Musonius, as is demonstrated by the history of Dio, abridged by Xiphilinus. Petavius referred that expulsion to the same year, 73. “When,” he says, “Helvidius Priscus, son-in-law of Thrasea, a Roman praetor and adherent of the Stoic school, attacked Vespasian, and several Stoics and Cynics, following his example, exercised the same license, Vespasian removed the philosophers from the city, except Musonius; but he banished Hostilius and Demetrius the Cynic to the islands.”

[Col. 1064D] Henschenius considers it likely that on this occasion Cletus too was ordered into exile, whom he supposes at that time to have occupied Peter’s Roman chair, since the professors of our religion were believed by the pagans to be adherents of some especially severe sect, not very different from the Stoic school. With due respect to so great a man, I would more readily apply this to Clement than to Cletus. Clement is remembered as having published several books defending the doctrines of our religion, whereas no one has transmitted that Cletus did so. Therefore, whether philosophers or sophists were being expelled, it ought to be thought that this happened to Clement rather than to Cletus: that he was expelled from Rome under Vespasian as one who was regarded by the worshippers of idols as a philosopher or sophist and accused as a critic of their superstition, while he committed an apology for our faith to writing.

For Mucianus’s severity did not cease with the exile of the philosophers during Vespasian’s reign in the year 73. [Col. 1065A] Dio, abridged by Xiphilinus, reminds us that in the year of Christ 75, when Vespasian was consul for the sixth time and Titus for the fourth, the Temple of Peace was also dedicated with an elaborate display of games. At that time he says that Berenice entered Rome with Agrippa, and then adds:

> “At the same time certain troublesome sophists secretly entered the city. One of them, Diogenes, when he had first come into the theater, which was filled with a great crowd, and had harassed the people with many insults, was beaten with rods. After him came Eras, who, thinking that nothing more serious would happen to him, shouted much more insolently and shamelessly. For this reason his head was cut off.”

Dio, through Xiphilinus and Sylburgius’s translation, records these events as having taken place in the consulship of Vespasian for the sixth time and Titus for the fourth—the date in which both coins and inscriptions demonstrate that the Temple of Peace was dedicated, in the ordinary reckoning of the Christian era, in the year 75.

[Col. 1065B] Concerning Clement, the *Liber Pontificalis* states: “While he was writing many books in his zeal for the faith of the Christian religion, he was crowned with martyrdom.” Jerome, in his catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, reports that Clement was regarded by most Latins as second after the apostle Peter, with Linus alone intervening between the pontificates of the two; and, together with Eusebius, he recognizes the Epistle to the Corinthians written by Clement as very similar in style and meaning to Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews.

The style and meaning of Clement’s works are already discernible when he imitates Paul’s Epistle to the Hebrews. In that epistle the eternal priesthood and kingdom of Christ, and the principality of peace, are extolled with due praises, far surpassing the royal priesthood of Melchizedek, which had been prefigured in him. What words, then, what meanings, and what oracles of our religion would Clement, the Roman pontiff, have been more eager to proclaim in the year 75, while the emperor Vespasian was dedicating the Temple of Peace, than those very scriptural oracles which had been uttered in the divine Scriptures concerning the kingdom and priesthood of Christ the Lord—so that he might arrogantly presume to apply them to himself?

[Col. 1065C] Tacitus certainly testifies to this purpose, and Baronius, under the year 77, numbers 3 and 4, agrees with him: Vespasian lent his ears to flatterers in Judaea, Egypt, and Rome, especially to Josephus, who referred to that Caesar what the prophets had divinely foretold concerning Christ the Lord, the Prince of Peace. Thus the principal reason for erecting and dedicating in Rome the largest Temple of Peace was, “because he had heard,” to use Baronius’s words, “that in the oracles that very king was to be named the Prince of Peace, and that his empire would be extended without limit, and that thereafter there would be no end of peace, as Isaiah says: ‘His name shall be called Prince of Peace; his empire shall be multiplied, and of his peace there shall be no end.’

[Col. 1065D] “Taking these words, as though they had been spoken about himself, from Josephus, who offered them to him, Vespasian erected the most famous temple of all and dedicated it to eternal Peace. For ancient coins show that the façade of the temple’s portico was marked with this title; and an ancient inscription, read at Rome in the Farnese residence, carved upon stone, also records the tribes that contributed money toward the construction of the temple, and has these words written first: *paci aeternae*, ‘to eternal peace.’ We omit what follows, since we have already quoted the same inscription elsewhere. On a silver coin it is likewise written in this form: *paci ae[ter]nae*,” and so forth.

The coins observed by Baronius, showing the Temple of Peace dedicated by Vespasian, are dated to his sixth consulship; another silver coin, cited by Mediobarbus, bears the seventh consulship and the inscription *PACIS EVENTUM COS. VII*—“the outcome of peace, in the seventh consulship.” Accordingly, it is certain that during these years of the Christian era, 75 and 76, when Vespasian held his sixth and seventh consulships, speeches became widespread in the city twisting the prophets’ predictions concerning our Redeemer and God into praise of a profane ruler. Their substance is found in Josephus, the partisan and adherent of that same perverse doctrine, at the end of chapter 12 of Book VII of *The Jewish War*. Josephus testifies that he wrote and delivered these books himself to the emperors Vespasian and Titus, and even records in his *Life* that the emperor Titus ordered the same books, written in his own hand, to be published in the library.

[Col. 1066A] Thus perverse interpretations and distortions of the legitimate meaning of the prophets had become widespread in Rome under Vespasian, both in the speech and writings of the Jews and their priests, such as Josephus, and among the pagans in their conversations and commentaries, as surviving passages in Tacitus and Suetonius, authors of that age, demonstrate. They were reviving the heretical doctrine of the Herodians in order to flatter Vespasian, as Baronius judiciously observes in his *Apparatus* to the *Annals*, numbers 5 and 15.

Clement certainly did not cease confronting these heresies and perverse interpretations, demonstrating to Jews and Gentiles that those prophetic sayings referred to Jesus, the true Christ of the Lord, the Prince of Peace and King of the age to come, and not to the Roman Caesar. Clement certainly did not cease confronting them, demonstrating equally to Jews and Gentiles that those prophetic sayings referred to Christ the Lord.

[Col. 1066B] For this was the duty of the Roman bishop, who taught the universal Church: to oppose the sect and error arising in Rome through the occasion of Jews and pagans flattering Vespasian and perverting the prophetic sayings in order to consolidate heretical opinions. Peter required this office in his epistle.

Therefore, as a sophist, or a malicious philosopher and detractor of the prince whom the others were flattering, Clement may have been ordered to leave Rome and perhaps even at that time to go into exile in Pontus—just as Helvidius Priscus, the city’s praetor, or Hostilius and Demetrius the Cynic had been banished to the islands in the year 73. The patrons of pagan superstition accused him and denounced as attacks upon the emperor the things which, in fulfillment of the duty of our religion, he put forward by voice and writing as the true interpretation of the Scriptures through Christ’s vicar.

[Col. 1066C] If the dignity of this office, which made Clement a participant in Christ’s royal priesthood, caused some new danger to be suspected by the accusers of Christians, then a danger may perhaps have threatened both the pontiff and the entire assembly of the faithful if Clement remained longer in Rome. The pagans, like the Jews, would accuse him of aspiring to kingship, just as they had accused Christ the Lord before Pilate at Jerusalem.

Accordingly, in order that Clement might demonstrate more clearly that he desired nothing mortal and was plotting nothing against the empire while proclaiming Christ’s royal priesthood and exercising its functions in the Roman Church, he judged it preferable—and saw that fuller provision would thereby be made for the safety of the Christian people—to abdicate so great an office, and for the fullness of apostolic power to be transferred to another, perhaps less well known or less exposed to the jealousy of the pagans, whom the clergy would choose as his successor.

[Col. 1066D] All these considerations seem to accord with the events carried out by Vespasian from the year 73 to 76, with the consuls and years assigned to Clement and Cletus in the catalogues, and also with what the holy Fathers say about Clement’s works, their style, meaning, and history. I may therefore hope that these conjectures will receive a commendation entirely similar to that which Baronius, in the passages cited shortly before, did not doubt would result when he wrote at the end of the year 77:

> “Although these matters have been derived by us, as we said above, by conjecture, nevertheless we think that they will not easily be despised by others who consider all the circumstances together with exactness.”

### 8.

Two objections may perhaps be proposed to me, and I confidently trust that I shall not have difficulty resolving them.

The first is this: why, in the canon of the Mass, an autograph of such antiquity and authority, is Cletus placed before Clement, whom I have asserted was given as successor to the one who abdicated?

I would ask all who raise this difficulty to recall that, according to our view and according to the consular and imperial chronology of the catalogues, Cletus was indeed admitted to exercise the office of supreme pontiff in the Church later than Clement, but reached earlier the glory of martyrdom in heaven. For that reason he was entered in the diptychs of the martyrs several years before Clement, who, after his abdication, was tested by the Lord through a long exile and preserved in life until the third year of Trajan, as Jerome testifies in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

[Col. 1067A] In the canon of the Mass we see that the chronological order in which each person departed this life is retained among the classes of martyrs: both in the prayers before the consecration, where the names of Cornelius, Cyprian, Laurence, Chrysogonus, John, and Paul are recited; and after the consecration, where we ask to be associated with John the Forerunner, or Baptist, Stephen, Matthias, Barnabas, Ignatius, Alexander, Marcellinus, and Peter. This is so even though Matthias, by virtue of his apostolic office, and both Stephen the deacon and the others who follow him in priestly rank, ought to be placed before them.

The same reasoning therefore applies to placing Cletus before Clement, since Cletus shed his blood for Christ in the year of Christ 83, when Domitian was consul for the eighth time and Rufus was consul, whereas Clement received the same crown later, around the year of Christ 100. He had held the pontificate from 68 to 77.

[Col. 1067B] The codices of Anastasius, printed by Fabrotus from the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuane libraries, whose words we have given, show another reason for placing Cletus before Clement. You see that Linus and Cletus were consecrated bishops by Blessed Peter much earlier, so that they might assist him in exercising the ministries of the orders in Rome, than Clement was marked by episcopal ordination. Clement, according to the explicit report, was consecrated bishop later—namely, shortly before his martyrdom—by the Prince of the Apostles.

The series expressed in the canon therefore retains the epoch of ordination, mentioning Linus, Cletus, and Clement, while omitting the order of succession, according to which they would have to be listed differently. Nevertheless, I place greater confidence in the first explanation.

### 9.

The second objection will be drawn from the number of twelve years which most codices assign to Pontiff Cletus, although Papebroch’s Belgic codex assigns seven years with us, and the fourth Colbertine extends the period to eight years, while the Liberian catalogue counts only six years.

[Col. 1067C] I could resolve this difficulty without trouble if the number of years, months, and days under Cletus still survived in the pontifical series of the Basilica of Saint Paul, so often praised. Although the entire inscription of Saint Cletus, together with his name and the numbers beneath his image, has been completely destroyed, these figures are nevertheless supplied from the most ancient codex of the Liberian catalogue, which predates the paintings of the Basilica of Saint Paul by an entire century, and the whole matter is settled.

There the numbers I have cited are distinctly read: six years, two months, and ten days, assigned to Cletus. The succession of Cletus after Clement is likewise clearly visible. But, they say, the catalogue of Felix IV and the ancient Italian codices cited above on page 88 assign twelve years to Cletus.

To those who make this objection I reply as follows. Does not the same catalogue of Felix IV express the consuls, and is not the period of seven years to be assigned to Cletus inferred from those consuls? This is plainly stated in Papebroch’s codex g, extended to eight years in the fourth Colbertine codex l, and to nine years in the fifth codex m.

[Col. 1067D] One or the other, therefore, was copied incorrectly in the catalogue of Felix IV and the other codices cited; and one or the other must be corrected—either the names of the consuls on the basis of the number of years, or the number of years on the basis of the names of the consuls.

I ask which kind of scribal error should be presumed and judged the easier. Certainly the error lies in the numbers, since twelve could be written for seven through the alteration of a single element. But how could a careless or drowsy copyist have changed the names of so many consuls, together with those of the preceding and following pontiffs, if he had maintained his attention and faithfully transcribed the numbers of the years?

To mark the names of the consuls in such a way that the last consul of the predecessor is followed by the nearest consul in the successor indicates the consistency of one correctly copying his exemplar, not the carelessness or wandering attention of someone dozing while transcribing.

If an error is therefore much more likely in the numbers than in the names, correction and emendation of the numerical entries from the names—especially on the authority of the older codices, in which the reckoning of the names and numbers agrees—must be preferred to the alternative.

### 10.

[Col. 1068A] Let the sounder rules of properly conducted criticism therefore agree that, where the consuls have been correctly assigned and consistently follow one another in all the codices, we should prefer the numbers in those codices—especially the more ancient ones, such as the Liberian catalogue—that exactly correspond to the names of the consuls.
