I know that the distinguished Henschenius, in his discussion of Cletus and Anacletus in volume V of the *Acta Sanctorum* for May, page 217, preferred to depart from the consuls assigned to Cletus and Clement rather than from the numbers adopted, when he wrote:

> “For I do not think that in this place I am bound to retain the consuls whom the catalogues of the pontiffs assigned to Cletus and Clement. It is credible that their first author, at the beginning of the third century, did not find the consuls assigned to each period of the first century in an earlier source, but fitted the consuls to the calculation of the years attributed to each pontiff and to the order of pontiffs that he had proposed.”

[Col. 1068B] With due respect to so distinguished a writer, I would say that this conjecture of his concerning an arbitrary assignment of consuls made in antiquity is sufficiently refuted both by genuine acts of martyrs and by inscriptions from cemeteries marked with the consulship, which are excavated every day from the martyrs’ crypts near Rome.

He might have remembered Saint Clement, whose consular epoch as placed in the catalogues he questions. Clement himself instituted seven notaries to write those acts of the martyrs, which begin, as is customary with public records, from a chronological indication given by the consulships or by the years of the emperors.

Not to employ more arguments in refuting this assumption, I recommend that the reader kindly review what was published in the preface to the first volume, especially numbers 18 and the following 19.

### 11.

[Col. 1068C] The method of a more reliable criterion therefore requires that, in these codices, the numerical entries for the years be tested and corrected against the names and colleges of the consuls, rather than that the names and colleges of the consuls be transformed and exchanged in accordance with the numerical entries for the years.

I admit that the copyists could err, and that they did in fact err more than once when transcribing the names and colleges of the consuls, especially where a consulship repeated under the emperors with the same colleague had to be distinguished by numerical entries from the nearby lists. This happened in the case of Vespasian and Titus, who began several years together through their shared fasces in the fourth, fifth, and other consulships of Vespasian their father, up to the ninth, always joined with Titus’s second consulship and those following up to his seventh.

I shall grant that a copyist’s negligence could have caused him just as readily to render Vespasian’s eighth consulship with Titus’s sixth instead of Vespasian’s sixth with Titus’s fourth as to assign eight complete years to Cletus when six were to be expressed. The ease of error in copying and altering lies in the numbers in both cases.

[Col. 1068D] Therefore, just as a copyist could easily err in expressing the number, so a critic ought necessarily to hesitate in correcting it unless the consuls of the immediately preceding and following pontiffs indicated, in the nearby entries, not only the true total of years but also the corresponding numbers of repeated consulships. We have these aids for correction and criticism in the cases of Clement and Cletus under discussion, as I shall presently show.

[Col. 1069A] Trachalus and Italicus are the first pair of consuls assigned to Clement. Domitian for the ninth time and Rufus are the last consulship among those numbered under Cletus in all the catalogues and codices that record the colleges of consuls.

From the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus, in the year of Christ 68, to the consulship of Domitian for the ninth time and Rufus, in the year of Christ 83, there are sixteen complete years, including both endpoints. The terminal points of that same total are made certain again by the names of the consuls immediately preceding, at the end of Linus’s episcopate—namely, Capitone and Rufus, in the year of Christ 67—and by the first following consuls in Anacletus’s pontificate, marking its beginning: Domitian for the tenth time and Sabinus, in the year of Christ 84.

Since the total of sixteen years is thus made certain by so many names and must be divided between the two pontiffs, Clement and Cletus, I shall assign nine pairs of consuls to Clement, since the same number of complete years, together with two months and eleven days, is assigned to him in the most ancient paintings of the Basilica of Saint Paul and in all the ancient codices listed above on page 88, except for the single codex a, which increases this total by ten months.

If you begin counting this total of nine years, two months, and eleven days from the consuls assigned to the beginning of Clement’s pontificate, or rather from the preceding 24 September—the day before, 23 September in the year 67, when Linus, his predecessor, suffered martyrdom under the consulship of Capitone and Rufus—you will see that the last consuls to be assigned to Clement’s nine years must be those who marked the year 76 of the common Christian era, namely Vespasian for the seventh time and Titus for the fifth.

[Col. 1069B] For this reason, all the codices mentioned on the same page correctly attribute Cletus’s beginning to these consuls. The end of Clement’s pontificate must therefore be assigned either to these same consuls or to the immediately preceding ones, Vespasian for the sixth time and Titus for the fourth. The latter alternative is contradicted by all the codices and paintings, since it does not complete the nine full years unanimously assigned to Clement by those codices and paintings.

Nor can Clement’s end ever be extended to the consulship of Vespasian for the ninth time and Titus for the seventh, in the year of Christ 79, since Vespasian’s eighth consulship with Titus’s sixth is assigned to Cletus, his successor.

It is therefore plainly evident that the numerical entry in the codex must be corrected at the end of Clement’s pontificate, where Vespasian’s ninth consulship is shown with Titus as colleague, by expressing the consulship from the consular epoch of his successor as Vespasian’s seventh consulship, with Titus for the fifth time as colleague, in the year of Christ 76.

### 12.

[Col. 1069C] Let it therefore be established, on the agreement of documents distinguished by excellence, antiquity, and authority, and in complete concord with the ancient paintings of the Basilica of Saint Paul and the surviving numbers in them, that the chronology of Clement and Cletus is to be arranged as follows.

Clement held the episcopate for nine years, two months, and ten days, from the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus, in the Christian era 68, to the consulship of Vespasian for the seventh time and Titus for the fifth, in the Christian era 76. More precisely: after Linus had suffered martyrdom on 23 September of the year 67, Clement’s period extends from 24 September of that same year, 67, to 3 December of the Christian epoch 76, for nine years, two months, and ten days.

Beginning on 4 December of the year 76, when Clement had abdicated the day before, the see remained vacant until 15 February of the following year, 77. On the next day, namely 16 February, which fell on the first Sunday of Lent at the beginning of the fast, Cletus assumed the Roman pontificate.

Cletus held the episcopate for six years, two months, and ten days, from Sunday, 16 February, in the consulship of Vespasian for the eighth time and Titus for the sixth, in the year of Christ 77, to 26 April, in the consulship of Domitian for the ninth time and Rufus, in the year of Christ 83, when he completed his martyrdom—seventeen years before the death of Clement, his predecessor.

[Col. 1069D] After Clement had abdicated and withdrawn into exile in Pontus, he was preserved until the third year of Trajan, the year of Christ 100, according to Eusebius, Jerome, and others, and then received the crown of martyrdom. Therefore, in the *Liber Pontificalis*, as also in the diptychs and in the canon of the Mass, he is placed after Cletus, his successor in the Roman see but his predecessor in the glory of martyrdom, although in the Liberian catalogue, which presents these pontiffs in succession, he is placed first.

Having established these matters concerning the pontifical chronology of Clement and Cletus, I shall append historical notes on the life of each according to the order of the *Liber Pontificalis*.

## HISTORICAL NOTES OF THE SAME AUTHOR ON THE LIFE OF SAINT CLETUS

[Col. 1070A] **Line 1.—“On the Vicus Patricius in the region.”** It is certain that the Vicus Patricius was not the name of one of the fourteen regions marked out in the city by Augustus’s division, but a part of the fifth region, the Esquiline, as may be gathered from Festus and the other historians and antiquarians.

The biographer, following his usual practice, which I indicated above, now names the part of the region where that pontiff, born into the world at Rome, obtained his birthplace—the pontiff whose life he is describing.

What part of Augustus’s fifth region the Vicus Patricius was can in no way be doubted, as Nardinus observes in Book IV, chapter 3. Festus and the writers mentioned have made sufficiently clear the street, its location, and its name.

It was a lower tract, a valley extending in the manner of a hollow between the Esquiline and Quirinal hills. There the title of Saint Pudentiana—discussed above in Opusculum XV and in the notes to section III of that same work under the letters c and g—was called *in vico Patricii*, or *in vico Patricio*. It was erected in the second century of Christ and dedicated by Pope Saint Pius, as will be shown below in the section on Pius himself, and it still survives.

There also stood the ancient church of Saint Euphemia until the time of Saint Pius V; it had received its name from the same street. This tract extends along the slope of the Esquiline toward Saint Laurence in the Fountain, until it reaches the Subura beneath the slope of Saint Peter in Chains.

Festus asserts that this Vicus Patricius was situated beneath the Esquiline and was so called “because the patricians lived there, by order of King Servius Tullius, so that if they should undertake anything new, they might be crushed from the higher places.”

[Col. 1070B] It is worth noting that Cletus and Clement, who are recorded as the first men born in Rome to be ordained bishops by the Prince of the Apostles himself, lived in these places, where Peter is said to have been received as a guest.

Cletus came from the Vicus Patricius, near the title of Saint Pudentiana, or also of Saint Pudens, her father. Above, in the notes on Saint Peter, I indicated that Pudens may have belonged to the Cornelian family and perhaps have been related to Cornelius, the centurion of the Italian cohort baptized by Peter in Syria; this may be regarded as a sufficiently probable conjecture.

[Col. 1070C] On the other side of the Esquiline, after passing the slope of Saint Peter in Chains, Clement I’s paternal house is said to have been converted into the title which the evidence of mosaics, structures, and writings establishes among the most ancient in the city. It was illustrated by Ciampini in *Ancient Monuments of the Roman Church* and by the canons Piazza and Rondinino in their description and history of the same title, and was preserved through the diligent care of Clement XI, of blessed memory, its magnificent restorer.

Between the two sees distinguished by the birthplaces of Cletus and Clement, almost midway, rises the title of Saint Peter in Chains, or of Eudoxia. Florentius, in his ancient *Martyrology*, gathered in the notes to 1 August that at this place both apostles, Peter and Paul, were accustomed to lodge among the soldiers of Nero’s household.

All these facts confirm the conjectures set out above concerning Peter’s first reception in the Esquiline region. There he formed his earlier and more distinguished disciples according to his own character and by the domestic practice of hospitality, so that they were judged above all others worthy to succeed the great Prince of the Apostles in the pontificate.

[Col. 1070D] **The same line.—“With Aemilianus as his father.”** The cognomen *Aemilianus* indicates that Cletus’s father, having originated among the Aemilian family, passed by adoption into another family. The same thing happened approximately two hundred years earlier to Cornelius Scipio Africanus the Younger, who was called Aemilianus because, having originated in the Aemilian family—namely, from the celebrated Aemilius Paulus, who had triumphed over Macedonia and King Perseus—he was adopted by Publius Scipio, the praetorian son of Africanus the Elder, and transferred into the Cornelian family. Vaillant learnedly observes this concerning coin 138 of the Cornelian family.

I would not dare to conjecture whether Cletus’s father should be regarded as belonging by descent to the Aemilian branch of the Cornelian family. His birthplace in the Vicus Patricius and the origin of the Aemilian family indicated by his father’s cognomen suggest that we should presume nobility of lineage, especially since the consular fasti show that the cognomen *Aemilianus* is found among the Fabii, Fulvii, and Cornelii.

[Col. 1071A] **The same line.—“Twelve years, one month, eleven days.”** Cletus’s dates are sufficiently established in the chronological notes, where I showed from the assigned consuls that preference must be given to the number of six years expressed in the oldest catalogue from the age of Liberius, since the agreement of the codices bearing the same consuls displays this same epoch.

**Line 3.—“From the consulship of Vespasian for the seventh time and Domitian for the fifth.”** In Vespasian the father’s seventh consulship, his eldest son Titus opened the year as ordinary colleague, according to Spartianus’s testimony in the *Life of Hadrian*, who was born in that year, as Panvinius observes, and as the Greek fasti confirm.

Nevertheless, an anonymous writer of the fourth century from the Caesarean library, who is to be read in Norisius after the epochs of the Syro-Macedonians, assigns Domitian as colleague to his father in the seventh ordinary consulship in the catalogue of ordinary consuls. The *Liber Pontificalis* follows his authority.

Panvinius believes that Domitian replaced Titus after the Kalends of July, and that from this arose the substitution of the brother who had been suffect consul for the ordinary consul. The Liberian catalogue, and the catalogue of Felix IV that follows it, as well as the other codices cited on page 88 of the *Prolegomena*, assign Titus as colleague—whom historians and ancient inscriptions likewise show to have proceeded with his father on the Kalends of January in both the sixth and eighth consulships.

[Col. 1071B] **Line 5.—“He ordained thirty-five presbyters in the city of Rome.”** Codices C and B have twenty-five, as do the Casinensis, Vaticanus, Florentinus, one of the Thuani, the first Ocriculensis, the third, and almost all the printed lectionaries, both before and after the editions of Saint Pius V.

That this number of twenty-five presbyters of the Roman city, later called cardinals, was instituted by Cletus at the command of Blessed Peter is an ancient tradition, confirmed through the first three centuries by the examples of several successors. For we shall read below, in number 6 of the life of Evaristus, that the same number of titles was distributed by Evaristus among the twenty-five presbyters ordained by Cletus.

Other pontiffs took care to restore the same number of titular presbyters and titles as soon as the force of persecutions had scattered some of them. This was done by Pope Saint Dionysius under the emperor Gallienus, after the savage persecution of Decius and Valerian, as number 26 will show; and again by Saint Marcellus after the most atrocious persecution of Diocletian and Maximian, as number 31 will explain.

The reader will find this argument treated more fully in a work which I published at Rome fifteen years ago, when I was defending the cause of the baptismal font for the venerable Basilica of Saint Laurence in Damaso, among whose canons I was numbered.

[Col. 1071C] There it was proved by several testimonies that those twenty-five presbyters instituted at Rome by command of the Prince of the Apostles, with an equal number of titles assigned to them, represented a certain image and pattern of the universal Church and of its supreme head—the kind of pattern that the Church of the Jews had obtained before Christ’s birth in the Temple of Jerusalem.

Twenty-four priestly divisions had been established in that same temple for the worship of God, corresponding to the number of the sanctuary’s princes and of the princes of God, as Scripture calls them (1 Chronicles 24). To these was added, under the high priest—who encompassed all the other princes of the sanctuary and all the Levites under his authority—one immediately beneath him, as it were a vicar, who is called *Sagan* by the Hebrews and who held precedence over the rest. He in a certain sense completed the twenty-fifth division.

[Col. 1071D] The Roman Church, therefore, which was to educate all the faithful in the worship of God—the chosen race, the royal priesthood, the holy nation, the people of acquisition—was fittingly organized under twenty-five princes of the sanctuary, established and distributed after the pattern of the former priesthood through an equal number of titles, that is, priestly houses for solemnly conferring baptism, by which this chosen race is born and propagated in Christ.

It corresponded wonderfully to the image of an equal number of priestly divisions prefiguring it in the Old Testament, together with its sacred principate.

Hence we read in Anastasius that Pope Marcellus, when restoring the same titles established by Evaristus at Peter’s designation and weakened by the persecutors, wished them to be regarded as certain dioceses on account of the baptism and penance of those who were converted from paganism.

[Col. 1072A] So great was the force of this first designation of the number, handed down by the Prince of the Apostles, that even in our own times it is preserved intact in the total number of baptismal fonts, even after the number of titles had increased. Pius V sanctioned this after fifteen hundred years, just as Dionysius and Marcellus had judged and restored it as the second and third centuries had passed since Peter’s original designation.

I had brought forward these matters there among many others, all of them pertaining to the question of retaining twenty-five fonts in the city, which was then under discussion. The present place requires us to touch upon certain matters concerning the increased number of titles and cardinals, which show that such institutions were established by Peter’s successors with the same purpose with which the Prince of the Apostles had marked out in Rome—endowed with primacy and authority over the others—the earlier image of the universal Church by opening twenty-five titles and priestly houses.

[Col. 1072B] The reading itself suggests, through the variation of the codices, that the increase in the number of cardinals attached to the titles, and in the total number of presbyters, was consistently directed by the Roman pontiffs toward expressing the principate of the Roman see and Church over the others, and the incorporation and joining together of all of them as though they were the mystical body of Christ under one head.

Thus the codices mentioned read: “He ordained twenty-five presbyters in the city of Rome.” Others, however, give: “He ordained thirty-five presbyters.”

Each reading has its own authority, provided that the periods are distinguished. See also below the notes on Saint Caius. I shall explain.

Moreover, the subsequent restorations carried out by Dionysius and Marcellus leave us no room to doubt that Peter’s institution, and the genuine reading of his command as carried out by Cletus and Evaristus, established twenty-five presbyters and titular churches, requiring the titular houses to be maintained at that same number. These houses were assigned to the presbyters who presided over them as dioceses for the baptism of the faithful, the administration of penance, and the performance of the other Christian sacred rites; they were later called cardinals. During the constant disruptions caused by the persecutions, it was sufficient for the number of these priestly offices to be preserved, so that the image of the sacred principate might be maintained. The same provision had been made for the dignity of the Jewish Church during the captivities, when the priestly lines were carefully preserved together with their proper offices, as we know from the Gospel that they were preserved: it testifies that Zechariah, the father of John, served in the course of Abijah.

Nevertheless, the glory of the house of God had to be displayed more magnificently in the patriarchal basilicas, erected after the passing of three centuries by Constantine, dedicated by Sylvester, and augmented by his successors. They wished, through the sanctuary-princes established by Peter in the titular churches and assigned their ministry by weekly divisions, to exhibit more clearly at the principal basilicas the unity and image of the universal Church, as well as the hierarchy of Christian priesthood at the Roman See.

Thus, just as the total number and shadowy image of the ancient Jewish priesthood, confined within its own boundaries, had been gathered in the twenty-five titular churches, so the breadth of the Christian hierarchy, spread throughout the whole world and gathered under definite sees directed from Rome, was displayed in the patriarchal basilicas. So long as these patriarchal thrones were counted as three—the Roman, Alexandrian, and Antiochene Churches, founded by the authority of Peter—the Roman bishop, together with two assisting bishops (such as we have already seen were assigned to Peter, namely Linus and Cletus), adequately represented this image.

Therefore, even then, besides the twenty-five urban presbyters, successors instructed by the example of the apostles customarily employed auxiliary bishops from the suburban sees: for example, the bishop of Ostia or of Alba; or they ordained a priest in the City who would exercise an apostolic vicariate and, when circumstances and the security of access permitted amid the storms of persecution, appoint a bishop to the neighboring towns. We have observed in the chronological notes that this is established by the consular records: for it often happened that those who had appointed these men as their vicars were subsequently chosen as their successors after their martyrdom. Thus Linus, Cletus, and Clement were vicars of Peter; Evaristus was the vicar of Anacletus; Alexander was the vicar of Evaristus; and many others were appointed vicars and coadjutors who later succeeded to the Roman pontificate, having first exercised their apprenticeship in that distinguished ministry.

It is plausible that, throughout the persecutions, these apostolic assistants were not always taken from bishops of the same city, but were prudently chosen, now from one, now from another of the neighboring sees—one or two whose presence could be interrupted for short periods—so that they could reside with the supreme pontiff without detriment or danger to their own people, while the force of the persecution bore less heavily upon the colony of Ostia, the city of Alba, Silva Candida, the towns of Praeneste, or the Sabine districts.

After the persecutors had finally been removed, we learn that certain bishops from the suburbicarian sees were selected for frequent ministry with the supreme pontiff. For this reason Marcus, the successor nearest to Sylvester and belonging to the period after the end of the persecutions, selected the bishop of Ostia for certain duties in the service of the Roman See, and even endowed him with the right to wear the pallium and increased his privileges by granting him the right to consecrate, and to receive consecration from, the Roman pontiff.

When the peace of the Church finally permitted the bishops nearest to Rome to travel freely, those whom the Roman bishop wished to employ as coadjutors could more frequently remain in Rome without any loss to their own people, assisting him in weightier matters to be handled with his presbytery, as well as in the consecration of bishops and the exercise of other pontifical duties. In the end, the opportunity for certain bishops to remain in the City became so great that nearly as many bishops were able to attend upon the Roman pontiff as there were urban presbyters. Consequently, this group of bishops and presbyters began to coalesce into a single college. Thus bishops were summoned to perform the daily weekly duties in the basilica of the Lateran patriarchate, where the supreme pontiff resided, while cardinal presbyters were assigned to the other basilicas, so that they might perform the sacred rites in the same weekly rotation.

At the Council of Constantinople under Damasus, a fourth patriarch had been added to the three ancient patriarchs—the Roman, Alexandrian, and Antiochene—and had been honored with such precedence that he was regarded as next after the Roman. Shortly afterward, the Council of Chalcedon judged that the bishop of the Church of Jerusalem should be added to their number, so that he then held the fifth place among the patriarchs.

An equal number of basilicas in Rome was considered to represent these patriarchates, and especially the three older ones established by Peter. Panvinius, in *On the Seven Churches of the City*, chapter 1, teaches us that on Sundays three bishops customarily offered the sacred sacrifice in three basilicas. The practice, begun in the fourth century soon after the foundation of those basilicas, is suggested by the rite of psalmody and by the distribution arranged in the same period by Damasus, according to Jerome, through the cycle of the week.

Not long afterward, when the bishop of Constantinople had been raised by the Council of Constantinople to the rank of the patriarchs, and when a fourth basilica had been established at Rome through the magnificent enlargement of the Liberian basilica carried out by Sixtus III, the cardinal presbyters of the twenty-five titular churches could, divided into four groups according to the days of the week, individually perform the sacred rites on each day in each of those basilicas. The total of the three bishops assisting the Roman pontiff together with the twenty-five cardinal presbyters thereby equaled the sum of four sevens, corresponding to the four basilicas and their four weekly rotations.

When the fifth patriarchate of the Christian world was finally declared at the see of Jerusalem around the middle of the fifth century by the Council of Chalcedon, a fifth basilica likewise began to receive a corresponding worship in Rome: the basilica of Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls, representing that see and permanently maintaining in Rome a model of the universal Church. For we read in the *Life of Pope Simplicius*, who began to sit in 467, that, just as in the basilicas of Saints Peter and Paul, a weekly ministry of presbyters had also been established in the Laurentian basilica, so that presbyters might remain there on account of penitents and baptism.

It then became necessary to add seven new priestly offices to the total of twenty-eight, so that there would be thirty-five. How this was accomplished we learn from this same *Pontifical Book*: not only because some manuscripts attribute the later completion of the number of thirty-five ordained presbyters to Cletus, on the authority of Peter, confusing the enlargement of the college with its original designation, but also from the new weekly division of seven bishops and twenty-eight presbyters who formed the same college. The *Pontifical Book* reports this in the *Life of Stephen IV*, where it relates that seven bishops from the neighboring and suburbicarian sees were assigned to the Lateran basilica, to administer there individually, on each day within the weekly cycle, the office of the weekly minister.

I believe this should be understood as follows: the thirty-five priestly offices performed during the week in the five Roman basilicas had previously been carried out partly by the seven neighboring bishops admitted into the college of the Roman presbytery, and partly by the twenty-eight cardinal presbyters belonging to the same number of titular churches in the City. Thus the bishops offered the sacred sacrifice on Sundays, while the presbyters did so on the other weekdays. After Stephen’s decree, the seven bishops performed the sacred rites in the Lateran, while the twenty-eight presbyters performed them in the other four patriarchal basilicas on the several days of the week.

Certainly, since twenty-eight titular churches of the City are counted in the Roman Council under Pope Symmachus at the end of the fifth century, and since this number is shown to have been exactly preserved for several centuries thereafter, it must necessarily be affirmed that, in the fourth or fifth century, three urban titular churches were added to the earlier twenty-five—the twenty-five designated by Peter, instituted by Evaristus, restored by Dionysius, and again reestablished by Marcellus at the beginning of the fourth century.

It is even possible to determine more precisely that the addition of the three titular churches, by which the total of twenty-eight was completed, was the work of the fourth century. In that period, after Marcellus had restored the original twenty-five following his accession to the pontificate in 306, Sylvester, before his death in 335, added the titular church of Equitius to the ancient ones. Marcus, his immediate successor, founded his own church in the Palatine district, which was counted among the Roman titular churches in the fifth-century council under Symmachus. Damasus built and endowed the third of the aforementioned titular churches, still celebrated under the name of Saint Lawrence and his own, beside the Theatre of Pompey.

There, then, is the total of twenty-eight titular churches of the City completed in the fourth century under Damasus. During the pontificate of this same pope, the Council of Constantinople decided that the bishop of that imperial city should be counted with the three ancient patriarchs; indeed, it wished him to be regarded as next in honor to the Roman and placed before the other two, the Alexandrian and Antiochene. Damasus’s predecessor Liberius had opportunely built a basilica which thereafter began to be regarded as the fourth patriarchal basilica, so that in the Roman Church it might represent that fourth patriarchate and restore the complete image of the Christian world.

Damasus therefore had reason to complete the fourth group of seven in the Roman presbytery and the twenty-eight titular churches, so that on each day each patriarchal basilica might have one of the cardinal presbyters performing the sacred rites at its altar, should the bishop assigned to it from the neighboring sees be called away by the care of his flock. Under this arrangement, the twenty-eight priestly offices, distributed among the four basilicas in four groups of seven, occupied all the cardinal presbyters in weekly duties.

That this division of the bishops and presbyters performing sacred rites in the basilicas throughout the cycle of the week is owed to Damasus can be inferred from what Anastasius states in his *Life of Damasus* (no. 54): “He established that psalms should be sung day and night throughout all the churches; he prescribed this for presbyters and bishops, and for monasteries.”

[Col. 1075A] The addition of the fifth patriarchal see to the other four by the Council of Chalcedon persuaded the Roman pontiffs of the following period to establish a fifth group of seven. For it seemed that the precedents required a fifth basilica to be assigned to it in Rome. Since the symbol of universality had rightly been represented by the number seven—among presbyters and urban titular churches as well as among the regional deacons—it seemed appropriate that seven should also be used in selecting bishops from the neighboring towns and colonies, whom we have long seen customarily standing by and assisting the Roman pontiff. The sixth canon of the Council of Nicaea likewise indicates this.

Many infer that this number of bishops was especially commended by the seven Asian churches enumerated by John in the first chapter of the Apocalypse. We gather from Anastasius’s *Life of Siricius* (no. 55) that several of these bishops also customarily celebrated the sacred rites in the principal Roman basilicas on Sundays during the fourth century and sent the *eulogiae*, or the *fermentum*, to the weekly presbyters: “He established that no presbyter should celebrate Mass throughout the whole week unless he received from the designated bishop of the place the consecrated element called the *fermentum*.”

This sign was intended to preserve more carefully and visibly the bond of the presbyters’ communion with the bishop. In that same fourth century Melchiades had ordered it to be observed, shortly before the basilicas were built by his successor Sylvester. Anastasius writes in the latter’s *Life* (no. 33): “He arranged that consecrated offerings should be sent through the churches from the consecration of the bishop; this is called the *fermentum*.”

Altaserra explains these words as follows: “Melchiades decreed that the *fermentum*—that is, fermented bread blessed by the bishop and sent in place of the *eulogia*—should be distributed through the churches as a symbol of communion.” The matter is explained more clearly by the letter of Innocent I to Decentius, which will be cited in its proper place together with Altaserra’s notes on the *Life of Siricius*.

In that letter Innocent reports that on Sunday, in the Roman Church, the bishop’s blessed *fermentum* was customarily sent to the urban titular churches because the presbyters, on account of the people entrusted to them, could not come together with him on that day. It was not to be sent through the parishes—that is, the neighboring dioceses—because the sacraments should not be carried over long distances.

From this we can sufficiently understand why the predecessors of Innocent I among the Roman pontiffs judged that the ministry of neighboring bishops should be used in the patriarchal basilicas on Sundays. Thus the weekly offices of those bishops in the aforementioned basilicas were joined with the offices of the presbyters, performed there on the remaining weekdays. We can also understand why, after the number of patriarchal basilicas was increased by the addition of a fifth after Innocent I, the thirty-five weekly offices were completed by the number of seven bishops together with twenty-eight presbyters.

For this reason, in some manuscripts of Anastasius, the number of thirty-five presbyters entered the account of Cletus’s ordinations, taken in place of the equal total established later from seven bishops and twenty-eight cardinal presbyters.

What I have so far noted concerning the number and increase of the Roman presbytery, and concerning the image of the hierarchy flourishing throughout the whole Church of Christ and visible at Rome, should for the most part be heard as material collected by Cardinal Rasponi in Book I, chapter 3, of *On the Lateran Basilica and Patriarchate*, with no less learning than elegance, and confirmed both by Rasponi himself and by Panvinius through the writings and authority of earlier authorities.

He therefore shows—on the evidence of the *Provinciale* of the Roman Church, produced from the archives of the Apostolic Chamber—that the ancient Roman pontiffs established five greater and more distinguished churches in the City of Rome, which were designated as patriarchal basilicas: namely, the basilica of the Savior at the Lateran; Saint Peter the Apostle in the Vatican; Saint Paul on the Ostian road outside the walls of the City; the Liberian basilica, or that of Pope Sixtus, on the Esquiline, which acquired the names Saint Mary at the Crib and Saint Mary Major; and the basilica of Saints Stephen and Lawrence outside the walls on the Tiburtine road. He then continues:

“Although many reasons are given for why the ancient Roman pontiffs established this arrangement, the chief reason is said to be that these five patriarchal sees were designated in ancient times, for the sake of honor, for the five principal patriarchs of the Christian world: the Lateran for the Roman pontiff, as primary of all the others; Saint Peter’s for the Constantinopolitan; Saint Paul’s for the Alexandrian; Saint Mary Major’s for the Antiochene; and Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls for the Jerusalemite.

“Thus, whenever those patriarchs happened to come to the City, whether for general councils or for other business concerning the Christian religion or their own Churches, and to remain there, each had his own house and his own church as though they were his proper see, situated, in a certain sense, within his own province. It is impossible to say how much dignity and splendor this brought to the Roman Church, which in this way presented the most beautiful image of one truly governing all things and presiding over the entire Christian world. For all four regions of the world, elegantly expressed in four such basilicas—East and West, South and North—seemed to submit themselves to that authority and power.

“This was especially clear from an ancient painting that was once visible in the Lateran patriarchate, where these figures were represented. It is entirely certain, moreover, that among these patriarchal basilicas the principal place was held by the Lateran basilica, which bears the image of the Roman Church. It was the see of the Roman pontiffs, who resided in the patriarchate built beside it for approximately 1,025 years, from Pope Saint Sylvester to Clement V, who transferred the Roman Curia to Avignon in Gaul.

“Furthermore, because the Lateran basilica possessed such dignity and majesty, seven bishops of cities neighboring Rome had been appointed so that on each day of the week, whether the pontiff was present or absent, they might in turn celebrate the divine mysteries upon its principal altar, or at least assist the pontiff when he celebrated on the more solemn days of the year.

“Just as the week has seven days, which recur after completing their cycle, so seven bishops had been chosen to complete the week by celebrating and to perform the ministry properly again when the cycle had come around. This was the principal reason why those seven bishops were called cardinal bishops.

“Their institution is extremely ancient. For in the *Life of Pope Stephen IV*, also called Stephen III, who was created pontiff in the year of salvation 768, the Librarian records the following: ‘He established that every Sunday, by the seven cardinal bishops serving weekly, who observe the solemn rites of Mass in the church of Saint Savior, Mass should be celebrated upon the altar of Saint Peter, and that the Gloria in excelsis Deo should be sung.’”

“Added to this is the authority of Cardinal Damian, who, writing to the cardinal bishops concerning the Lateran basilica, says:

“‘For this reason that church is distinguished by privileges superior to those of all the other churches of the City; nor can it be doubted that it has also been instituted and arranged according to mystical sacraments. To touch briefly on a few points among many: just as the Lateran church is marked by the name of the Savior, who is indeed the head of all the elect, so it is the mother, and in a certain sense the summit and crown, of all the churches throughout the world.

“‘It has seven cardinal bishops, and only they, after the apostolic pontiff, are permitted to approach that holy altar and celebrate the mysteries of divine worship,’” and so forth.

“Among these seven bishops, this office was divided in rotation as follows: Sunday belonged to the bishop of Ostia; the following weekday to the bishop of Silva Candida, who presided over the Leonine City as though it were his own diocese; then to the bishop of Porto, who administered the Trastevere district of the City with episcopal authority; and thereafter to the others, namely the Sabine, Praenestine, Tusculan, and finally Alban bishops.

“All of these sees still exist today, except for the episcopate of Silva Candida, which, because that town became sparsely inhabited, was united by the authority of Callistus II with the Church of Porto. For the same reason, the Church of Ostia was later assisted by Eugene III through the union of Velletri with it.

“In this same Lateran basilica, those who formerly celebrated the divine service and recited the divine offices and canonical hours were the prior and the canons of Saint Augustine. Later these duties were performed by the archpriest and the secular canons, together with the prebendaries, chaplains, clerics, singers, and other ministers whom Pope Boniface VIII substituted after expelling the regular canons, as we shall say below.

“An autograph of a letter of Anastasius IV, dated 1154, exists in the Lateran archive. It contains much concerning the manner of serving the Lateran Church, which must necessarily be related to what we are saying about the celebration by the cardinal bishops. I shall insert here the following passage:

“‘At the suggestion and by the authority of our brothers, the cardinal bishops, we decree that this church, as the principal mother and mistress, shall be entirely free and subject to no one whatever except the Roman pontiff alone; and that those same bishops, with salutary foresight, as our cooperators and vicars, shall provide for the welfare and dignity of that venerable basilica.’

“And a little farther on:

“‘When the bishops are celebrating the solemn rites of Mass there, you shall be present in clerical vestments and shall begin the chant; and you shall always ensure that one of your number is provided as presbyter, one as deacon, one as subdeacon, and one as acolyte.

“‘Furthermore, concerning each of the aforementioned cardinal bishops, who are assigned to the service of the principal altar, we decree that once each week matters of observance of the rule, etc., shall be corrected by them in our stead,’ and so forth.

[Col. 1077B] “But at the other patriarchal churches seven ministers were assigned—not bishops, however, but cardinal presbyters. Together they numbered twenty-eight, for this number is made up of four groups of seven. Since these basilicas were of lesser dignity than the Lateran basilica, which was served by cardinal bishops, they therefore had cardinal presbyters, to whom belonged the twenty-eight titular churches of the City. Concerning these titular churches and the origin of the cardinals, Onuphrius Panvinius wrote accurately and learnedly.”

Although these matters may seem sufficient to illuminate the text of the Librarian and both numbers, twenty-five and thirty-five, recorded in different manuscripts, I do not judge it inappropriate to add a few observations concerning the latest increases in the number of presbyters and cardinal deacons of the Roman Church. It will thereby become more evident that, in this designation of the princes of the sanctuary, just as in the other and more ancient designation, Peter’s successors always followed the same purpose: to present to the faithful, in the Roman pontiff together with his urban presbytery or sacred college, an image of the whole ecclesiastical hierarchy, constituted from those same princes of the sanctuary—cardinal bishops, presbyters, and deacons.

This becomes clear from the papal constitutions, especially the fifteenth of Eugene IV and the fiftieth of Sixtus V, which established the entire number of the Sacred College as seventy members, six of whom were cardinal bishops, fifty presbyters, and fourteen deacons.

Both the Eugenian constitution, which does not define the number, and the Sistine constitution, which determines it in this way, expressly teach that, whatever variety of numbers their predecessors had established according to the needs of the times, this priestly council was intended to display a representation of the chief men of the whole Church: both of that most distinguished assembly of men among the people professing the true worship of God in the Synagogue, when under Moses and his legitimate successors it prefigured Christ’s apostolic Church, and of the hierarchy of the heavenly orders, to which it corresponds on the other side.

In that constitution Sixtus doubled the number of presbyters and deacons instituted by Peter and Cletus, ordering that there should be fifty presbyters and fourteen deacons. He also doubled the number of the three bishops whom the Librarian presents in connection with Peter, making the total number of the entire College seventy. He related this to the equal number of elders chosen by Moses at God’s command to bear with him the burdens of government, so that the truth of our Catholic Church might perpetually correspond to the illustrious figure of the universal Church already prefigured among the Jewish people.

Peter’s purpose therefore remains in the multifaceted discipline never abandoned by his successors: both in displaying the Christian hierarchy, joined and signified through the college of the three orders under its supreme pontiff and head in this Roman Church, and in declaring the symbol of universality, always signified by a mystical number—whether through the twenty-five priestly offices repeated among the presbyters, or through the groups of seven preserved in the weekly divisions, both among the twenty-eight presbyters and among the seven bishops, in the manner described above. The same principle should be regarded as remaining in force even when the number is reduced to six, with the supreme pontiff himself, the head of all, still completing the number seven.

The cardinal deacons likewise do not differ from this symbol: they complete the total of two groups of seven, both long before, as Sixtus reports, and from the time of his Constitution onward.

[Note: Col. 1078C]

Line 4.—“By the command of Blessed Peter he ordained thirty-five presbyters.” Cletus, at the command of Blessed Peter, when he was his fellow bishop and coadjutor, ordained twenty-five presbyters in the city of Rome. During his pontificate the second persecution of the Christians was raised by the emperor Domitian, in which Nereus and Achilleus were exiled and suffered martyrdom. Finally, after the most holy pontiff had sat in the pontificate for twelve years, seven months, and two days, he was crowned with martyrdom by the same Domitian on the sixth day before the Kalends of May [April 26].

[Note: Col. 1078C]

Line 4.—“By the command of Blessed Peter he ordained thirty-five presbyters.” He is said in the *Pontifical Book* to have ordained twenty-five presbyters in the city of Rome by the command of Saint Peter; that is, to have divided the City into the same number of parishes.

[Col. 1059]

### 3

Cletus, a Roman by birth, from the district of the Vicus Patricii, son of Aemilianus, sat for twelve years, one month, and eleven days [Note: Col. 1059: B, seven months, two days.]. He lived during the times of Vespasian and Titus, from the seventh consulship of Vespasian and the fifth of Domitian until the ninth consulship of Domitian and that of Rufus [Note: Col. 1059: B, “the ninth of Domitian and the seventh of Titus, until Trajan and Glabrio.”]. He was crowned with martyrdom. By the command of blessed Peter he ordained thirty-five presbyters in the city of Rome in the month of December [Note: Col. 1059: C, B, twenty-five.]. He was also buried beside the body of Blessed Peter in the Vatican on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, and the episcopate was vacant for twenty days.

### CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS

Cletus: six years, two months, ten days. He lived during the times of Vespasian and Titus, at the beginning of Domitian’s reign, from the consulships of Vespasian VIII and Domitian V until those of Domitian IX and Rufus.

## IV. SAINT CLEMENT. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 93, THE TENTH OF THE EMPEROR DOMITIAN

[Note: Col. 1079]

In Fabrottus, from the Freher manuscript:

No. 4, line 3: B, “Tragalis and Italicus.” Line 4: B, “and of the Christian religion.” Line 13: B, “he made two,” etc.

From the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts:

Line 3: “from the consulship of Tragalis.” The Royal and Mazarin manuscripts have, in the same place, “until the ninth consulship of Vespasian and that of Titus.” “He made seven regions,” line 8. “He governed the pontificate of the Church,” line 9. “The commentary: because the letter written by the same Clement to James, bishop of Jerusalem.” Line 10: “the Church is found more fully.” “Therefore Linus.” Line 13: “two deacons.” Line 14: “fifteen places.” “While he was composing many books in zeal for the Christian faith and religion, he was crowned with martyrdom under Trajan and was buried in Greece on the nineteenth day before the Kalends of December; and the episcopate ceased …”

[Col. 1080]

From another Thuane manuscript:

Line 3: “until the ninth consulship of Vespasian and that of Titus.” Line 5: “he made seven regions and divided them.” Line 6: “might seek out.” Line 8: “he undertook the pontificate of governing the Church.” Line 11: “therefore, for that reason, L.” Line 13: “two deacons.” Line 14: “Trajan III; he was also buried in Greece on the eighth day before the Kalends of December.” Then the episcopate ceased for twenty-one days.

In Holstenius and Schelestratius:

Line 3: Vatican manuscript, two Florentine manuscripts, and the Cassinese manuscript: “Tragalis.” Line 5: the Cassinese manuscript: “and divided.” The same line, in the Florentine manuscripts: “the pontificate of the Church.” Line 14: “Trajan’s third consulship.” This means the third consulship.

[Note: Col. 1079A]

The author of the *Pontifical Book* relates many more things about Clement, drawn from elsewhere than the second catalogue, and he does not conceal this. For what he reports concerning Clement’s pontificate he declares that he took from Clement’s letter to James. Although that letter is spurious, it is nevertheless very ancient and predates Rufinus; by the end of the third century or the beginning of the fourth it was already circulating under Clement’s name.

The material concerning Clement found in the edition of Anastasius appears in Peter in two Florentine manuscripts, the Cassinese manuscript, and likewise in the Mazarin, Thuane, and another manuscript of Marquard Freher.

## NOTES ON THE LIBERIAN CATALOGUE

Clement is placed third and Cletus fourth, though the reason is unknown, since the canon of the Mass presents the tradition of the Roman Church in these words: “Linus, Cletus, Clement.”

The distinguished scholars Henschenius and Papebrochius, in their edition of the catalogue of Felix IV, placed Clement before Cletus. Yet in the manuscript of the Queen of Sweden, which I kept in my possession for several months and from which the first edition of this catalogue was produced by the aforementioned scholars, Cletus appears third in order and Clement fourth. Cletus is likewise placed before Clement in the Colbert manuscript, from which Baluzius wrote to me in his notes: “Cletus is placed before Clement.”

[Note: Col. 1080A]

Line 5.—“He caused seven regions to be divided among faithful notaries of the Church, who diligently and carefully investigated, each in his own region, the acts of the martyrs.” Pope Clement appointed notaries throughout the seven regions of the City to write down the acts of the martyrs and enter them into the records of the Church.

Notaries were writers who wrote with the shorthand signs known especially as *notae*. Martial, Book XIV, epigram 208, writes of them:

“Though words may run, the hand is faster than they:

Before the tongue has completed its work, the right hand has done it.”

They were therefore called notaries because they wrote by means of signs, which are called *σίγλα* (*sigla*), for the sake of speed. Augustine, *On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, chapter 26:

“Of this kind also are the signs which those who have learned them are now properly called notaries.”

The ancients made widespread use of this class of writers. Jerome, in the prologue to his commentary on Isaiah, says:

“We dictate these things; we do not write them. As the hand of the notaries runs, so the discourse runs.”

The same writer says to Alipius and Augustine:

“But if the Lord grants me life, and we have an ample supply of notaries, we shall answer with a few nights of labor.”

And to Augustine:

“In this province we suffer a great shortage of notaries for the Latin language.”

This same class of writers was hired at greater expense. In *Against Vigilantius* Jerome says:

“At least spare your money, with which, when you hire notaries and copyists, you employ both writers and supporters.”

The Roman Church had its own notaries, who recorded the acts of the martyrs. In addition to this passage, Anastasius says in the *Life of Anterus*:

“He diligently sought out the acts of the martyrs through the notaries and deposited them in the Church.”

Their office was also to prepare the Church’s records—that is, all the acts of the Church—including donations, exchanges of Church property, the manumission of the Church’s slaves, and other matters. Anastasius, in the *Life of Julius*, says:

“He established that the record which concerns all things pertaining to the ecclesiastical faith should be collected by the notaries, and that all documents prepared for the Church through the chief of the notaries should be formally authenticated,” and so forth.

There were fourteen regions of the City, which Clement reduced to seven, assigning notaries to each so that they might record the acts of the martyrs. Hence they were called regional notaries. Anastasius, in the *Life of Hadrian*, says:

“Lord Pope Paul ordered him to be made a cleric; appointing him as a regional notary in the Church, he later made him a subdeacon.”

Line 15.—“He was buried in Greece.” Clement, the Roman pontiff, was buried in Greece for the following reason: during Trajan’s persecution he was exiled to Chersonesus, thrown headlong into the sea with an anchor fastened around his neck. His body was later transferred to Rome under Pope Nicholas I. See the *Roman Martyrology*, November 23; Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Martyrs*, chapters 35–36.

[Note: Col. 1081B]

Line 4.—“While he was writing many books.” The compiler of this *Life* inserted several materials drawn from the false writings attributed to Saint Clement. One example concerns his election by Saint Peter, taken from a letter circulated under Clement’s name. Another concerns the many books he is said to have written.

Perhaps, under the name of Clement, the compiler recognized the ten books of the *Recognitions*, in which the fictitious Clement recalls having published other books. In the first book he writes that he published a book *On the True Prophet*; in Book III, one *On the Definition of God*; and in the fifth, another ten books of the *Recognitions*. See Cotelerius, *On the Apostolic Fathers*.

**The same line.—He is crowned with martyrdom.** During the persecution of Domitian, concerning which the very ancient writer Brutus is praised in the Alexandrian Chronicle:

> “Brutus relates that a great number of Christians were carried off and subjected to martyrdom from the fourteenth year of Domitian.”

Thus, in each of the two earlier persecutions stirred up by Nero and Domitian, a great multitude and abundance of martyrs were crowned, as Tacitus had said of the former and Brutus of the latter. This also overturns the recent fiction concerning the small number of martyrs in the primitive Church: although both emperors, after initiating the persecution, did not live long, they nevertheless carried out a great slaughter of Christians; a still greater one was carried out by those who, living for a longer period and burning against Christians as the Christian religion spread everywhere, [Col. 1081D] raged against them. Concerning this Lactantius also writes in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 3, p. 50:

> “After him”—namely, Nero—“after an interval of several years, another tyrant no less arose. While exercising his hated domination, he nevertheless weighed upon the necks of his subjects; he reigned for as long and as securely as possible, until he stretched out his impious hands against God. But after he had been incited by the prompting of demons to persecute the righteous people, then he was delivered into the hands of his enemies and paid the penalty.”

Tertullian observes in *Apology*, chapter 5, that it lasted only a short time:

> “Domitian too had attempted something of Nero’s cruelty; but because he was also merely a man, he easily restrained what he had begun, even restoring those whom he had banished.”

Clement, banished during the violence of the persecution, nevertheless could not benefit from the emperor’s indulgence, since he died a martyr before the proclamation of clemency.

**Line 5.—The notaries.** This is the first mention of the ecclesiastical notaries, who later became famous for recording the acts of councils and preparing other ecclesiastical documents. This was especially the case at Rome, where their importance is shown by the fact that their president, called the *primicerius notariorum*, was a person of the highest dignity; when the see was vacant, the care of the Church was entrusted to him together with the archpriest and archdeacon.

Clement selected seven to write down the acts and deeds of the martyrs, recording their names, tortures, words, and finally the sentence of the judges. The motive for this care was provided by the fabricated accusations of priests and other wicked men against Christians, by which they disseminated Christian teaching as a destructive superstition, along with the other slanders that Tertullian lists and refutes in his *Apologeticus*. Recording the deeds of the martyrs was an appropriate remedy for blunting the insolence of the accusers: from their words and actions, and from the marvelous patience and innocent courage with which they endured torture, the Christian life and the perfection of the religion shone forth.

This institution served the religion exceedingly well, since the acts, carried and read everywhere, [Col. 1082B] increased the splendor of Christianity, so that Christians gloried in the victories that had been recorded as though in a register. Hence Tertullian, in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, urges the faithful to inspect these records:

> “You have your own registers, your own public honors; you have nothing to do with the joys of the world—indeed, you ought to have the opposite.”

Pontius, deacon of Saint Cyprian, speaks of the labors devoted to these public honors when he explains why he wished to write the acts of the holy martyr. At the beginning of his work on Saint Cyprian he says:

> “Since our predecessors bestowed such honor upon members of the common people and catechumens who attained martyrdom, out of reverence for martyrdom itself, that they wrote many things—or, to put it almost more accurately, nearly everything—about their sufferings, so that these accounts reached the knowledge of us who had not yet been born.”

Thus the deeds of all martyrs without distinction were recorded, whether they belonged to the common people or were merely catechumens. These accounts were eagerly read by the faithful, who learned through mutual letters of the more distinguished contests; [Col. 1082C] acts recorded by one Church were transmitted by that Church to a neighboring one, and by the latter to others.

Concerning this practice, the following is read in the encyclical letter of the Church of Smyrna concerning the martyrdom of Saint Polycarp:

> “When you have received these things, we ask you to transmit the letter further to the brothers who are farther away, so that they too may bless the Lord.”

Eusebius also used these records to illuminate his ecclesiastical history, as he himself testifies more than once.

**The same line.—To the faithful.** In choosing the notaries, Clement commends and requires fidelity and sincerity, qualities that were necessary both for strengthening the faith of the faithful and for blunting the accusations fabricated against Christians. That fidelity was especially required of notaries is shown by Cyprian’s Letter 37, written to the clergy of Carthage, in which he praises the deacon and notary Tertullus, whom he calls “most faithful.” Speaking of the services to be rendered to martyrs, whether in prison or gloriously after completing their martyrdom, he writes of Tertullus:

> “Finally, so that we may note the days on which they depart, and celebrate their commemorations among the memorials of the martyrs: although our most faithful and devoted brother Tertullus, in accordance with the exceptional concern and care that he bestows upon the brothers in every service of ministry—and who is not absent even there from the care of their bodies—has written, and continues to write, and informs me of the days on which our blessed brothers in prison pass over to immortality through the glorious outcome of death; and here we celebrate oblations and sacrifices in their memory, which, with the Lord’s protection, we shall soon celebrate together with you.”

In this passage he explains the actual and continual exercise of recording the deeds of the martyrs, expressed in the words “has written, continues to write, and informs.” In former times this duty was most appropriately entrusted to deacons, since their frequent visits to the prisons to relieve the needs of the martyrs provided them with a suitable opportunity to investigate everything [Col. 1083A] and to record their deeds with greater certainty.

Concerning this ancient duty of the deacons, preserved in the Church of Carthage, Cyprian writes in Letter 51:

> “It has always been done by our predecessors that deacons, visiting the prisons, should guide the desires of the martyrs by their counsels and by the precepts of Scripture.”

The author of the *Martyrdom of Saints Felicity and Perpetua*, in the edition of Holstenius, likewise praises Tertius and Pomponius, who ministered to the blessed martyrs in prison. Among other things, the holy women commend them as follows:

> “Those who ministered to us arranged as a reward that, after being released for a few hours, we might be refreshed in a better part of the prison,”

and so forth.

That the Church of Carthage, formed by these same customs, entrusted this care to its archdeacon, and that Saint Cyprian assigned it to Tertullus down to the end of the third century, is declared by the *Acts of Saints Damasus and his Companions*. Although these acts were defiled and interpolated by the Donatists, they are nevertheless considered extremely ancient.

The Donatists produced them in order to fabricate and substantiate accusations against Mensurius, primate of Carthage, and against his then archdeacon Caecilianus. One of the accusations, according to Optatus, p. 103, was this:

> “Finally, when neither Mensurius nor his minister Caecilianus wished to cease from this savage cruelty, while Anulinus the proconsul and the other persecutors were occupied with other business, these blessed martyrs, deprived of bodily nourishment, gradually and at intervals of days yielded to the natural condition under the compulsion of atrocious hunger, and departed with the palm of martyrdom to the starry realms.”

The service that they could not render to the martyrs under the pressure of the Diocletianic persecution, the accusers did not hesitate to turn into a charge against them.

Meanwhile, if the savage persecution prevented the deacons from visiting the prisons, clergy who were present there wrote down the deeds of the martyrs in letters and reported them to the Churches. Eusebius gives several examples, among them a fragment of a letter by Phileas, bishop of Thmuis. He not only took care to send the acts to the Churches but also, for the encouragement of martyrs who were about to enter the final contest, industriously sent the martyrs of Thmuis a letter urging them, by the example of others, to undertake the defense of the faith. In it he describes his own sufferings and those of his companions and exhorts others to confess the faith.

Eusebius adds in Book VIII, chapter 10:

> “These are the words of a true philosopher, a martyr who loved God no less than wisdom. While still confined in custody, before the final sentence of the judge, he wrote them to the brothers of his Church, partly exhorting them to hold fast to piety toward Christ even after his own imminent death.”

Dionysius of Alexandria, whom we shall praise below, acted similarly, as did others. From these acts, once reported to the Churches, the most ancient Martyrologies and Lectionaries were compiled.

If the opinion of some is correct—that Clement wrote the letter delivered to the Corinthians immediately after the death and martyrdom of Saint Paul—it could be inferred that Clement, by his own first example, showed the notaries the model for reporting the illustrious contests of the martyrs to the Churches. For when, in chapter 5, he praises the athletes who had recently lived, no others can be understood except the holy apostles Peter and Paul; and certain women, especially distinguished by the honor of martyrdom, are also mentioned there:

> “To these men”—namely, Peter and Paul—“who lived holy lives, a great multitude of the elect was joined. Having suffered many punishments and tortures for the sake of emulation, they became an excellent example among us. For the sake of emulation, the women Danaids and Dirce endured persecution; after suffering grievous and unspeakable punishments, they completed the steadfast course of faith and, weak in body, received the noble reward of endurance.”

Perhaps he arranged these acts in a special treatise, which later gave some impostor the opportunity to fabricate the *Itinerary of Peter* and the *Acts of Paul*, published under Clement’s name. See Ittigius, *On the Pseudepigrapha*, p. 95.

**Line 7.—Two letters called catholic.** [Col. 1084A] These two letters, which came to light after lying unknown for a long time in libraries after the beginning of the previous century, are called “catholic” by the compiler of Clement’s Acts, in the sense in which that word was used for an authoritative instruction.

The authority of the first is drawn from the Fathers of the earliest age. Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, asserts that it was customarily read at the assembly of the Church on the Lord’s Day. Writing to the Romans, from whom he had received the other letter, he says, according to Eusebius, Book V, chapter 23:

> “Today we have spent the holy Lord’s Day. On it we read your letter, and, continuing to read it always thereafter, we shall be filled with the finest precepts and teachings, just as we have been by that earlier letter written to us by Clement.”

It was regarded in the same way not only by the Church of Corinth but also by the others, as Eusebius testifies in Book III, chapter 16:

> “Clement’s letter, universally received by all with one accord, is altogether outstanding and admirable. He wrote it in the name of the Roman Church to the Church of the Corinthians … We have learned that in most Churches, including our own, it was publicly read in former times and continues to be read.”

He repeats this in chapter 38.

The second letter did not enjoy this estimation or authority. These words, moreover, appear to have been inserted in the *Pontifical Book* long after the Gelasian Decree, in which no mention of either letter occurs. On these matters one should consult the treatise *On the Apostolic Fathers*, published at Amsterdam in 1698 and enriched with annotations by various scholars; it discusses Clement’s letters at great length.

The honor preserved for apostolic men in the primitive Church ensured that their letters would be received and sought out with greater care. Eusebius, Book III, chapter 16, provides a notable testimony to this practice. When the Philippians requested them, Saint Polycarp sent them the letters of Ignatius together with his own and commended their reading. He explains this in these words:

> “We have sent you, as you requested, all the letters of Ignatius that he wrote to me, together with whatever others we were able to find among us. You will be able to derive great benefit from them. For they contain faith, patience, and everything else that contributes to the increase of the worship of our Lord.”

Since these letters are here called by that name and both are called catholic, although the second is rather a fragment of a homily, I am entirely ignorant of where the *Pontifical Book* derived this designation, especially since the Gelasian Decree is completely silent about them. See Morinus, *Biblical Exercises*, from the eighth general council, and Dodwell, *Dissertation on Irenaeus*, p. 53.

**The same line. He undertook the governance of the Church and the pontificate at the command of blessed Peter.** The author of Saint Clement’s Life derives two points from the letter written by Clement himself to Saint James: first, that it was genuinely written by Clement himself; and second, that Saint Peter truly designated Clement as his successor in the pontificate.

But since the letter is false and spurious—it formerly stood prefixed to the spurious acts of Saint Peter—what is inserted here concerning the election of a successor collapses. Two matters should nevertheless be noted. First, it was an ancient opinion that Peter designated Clement as his successor. This was common in Tertullian’s age, when he reports that Clement was ordained by Peter, as will be discussed in the following note.

There are not lacking conjectures concerning how this very ancient tradition may have arisen. It might appear more plausible if the opinion of certain recent writers is correct: they maintain that Clement wrote the First Letter to the Corinthians immediately after the death of Saint Paul. They base this opinion on the bearer of the letter, whom Clement calls Fortunatus, and whom they identify with the person of whom Paul writes in First Corinthians 16:17:

> “I rejoice in the presence of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, because they supplied what was lacking in your communication; for they refreshed both my spirit and yours. Therefore acknowledge such men.”

They suppose that the rivalries which the Apostle’s letter was intended to check continued even after the apostolic admonitions. To calm them, Fortunatus was chosen because Paul’s testimony commended him, [Col. 1085A] as well as because of his own merits, and was sent from Corinth to Rome to report everything to Paul. But when he reached Rome, Paul had already died a martyr, and Fortunatus delivered the letter to Clement. Clement, in fulfillment of the commission he had received, sent the letter to Fortunatus, adding Ephebus and Valerius, whom Clement calls his companions in the embassy at the end of the letter.

Dodwell, who accepts this opinion, thinks that the letter was written in the final years of Nero’s reign. Nor, he supposes, can Clement’s undertaking of the commission—to write, reply, and admonish in Paul’s place, in his own name and that of the Roman Church, as Irenaeus says in Book III, *Against Heresies*, chapter 30, that it was written—be understood otherwise than on the ground that he was pontiff.

The ancient writer Hermas, apparently Clement’s contemporary, assumes that writing to the foreign provinces of the world and reporting the truth belonged to the pontiff. In Book II, Vision 11.3, he receives this command in a vision:

> “You will write two little books and send one to Clement and one to Grapte. Clement will send it to the foreign cities, for this has been entrusted to him. Grapte, however, will admonish the widows and orphans. You will read it in this city”—he means Rome, as the vision indicated—“with the elders who preside over the Church.”

But Isaac Vossius, in his response to the matters criticized by Blondel in his notes on the letters of Ignatius, proves that the letter was written by Clement one or two years before the destruction of Jerusalem. Wendelinus, however, places it during the persecution of Domitian, around the year 95. Consequently, nothing certain can be derived from this conjecture.

The second point that must be carefully noted is that this *Pontifical Book* was compiled from ancient catalogues formerly preserved in the archives of the Roman Church. Some of these indicated elections, others deaths, others ordinations, and others donations made either by rulers, pontiffs, or the faithful. From these was compiled the second, commonly called the ancient and unquestionably reliable catalogue of the Roman pontiffs. The *Pontifical Book* copied its wording, and then one or more persons, by adding material, arranged it into the form and bulk that it now retains.

I believe that most of the additions were first made on separate sheets—or, more likely, in the margin of the *Pontifical Book*. When they later had to be fitted into their proper places, carelessness or the ignorance of copyists sometimes caused a shameful transposition. Hence the reliability of the history often becomes unstable. We shall note this in the case of Felix III, where the additions, restored to their proper places, illuminate the events.

There is no doubt that the additions were made at various times and by different persons, and indeed after the *Pontifical Book* had been published. For the additions concerning donations made by Roman pontiffs in our *Pontifical Book* were composed late. An example is the Life of Saint Damasus: its first part is copied word for word from a manuscript of the archive of the Vatican basilica, from which it was reproduced in the edition of Saint Damasus’s works published at Rome in 1638. Yet that edition does not present the catalogue of donations, although it appears in our text.

Likewise, the complete donation of Constantine is inserted in certain Anastasian manuscripts but omitted in others. Similarly, the present section concerning Clement’s election by Peter, which is omitted from the second catalogue, is added in some manuscripts to the acts of Saint Peter, while in others—as in our text—it is placed among Clement’s acts.

The earlier *Pontifical Book*, which existed under that title in the year 650, did not contain most of these additions. This could be demonstrated from several examples, but it will suffice to mention the passage concerning Anacletus. In certain manuscripts the following words are found:

> “He also wrote two decretal letters full of all wisdom.”

These words appear neither in our manuscripts nor in the others, nor could they have been inserted when the first edition of the *Pontifical Book* was published. They must have been added after the year 800, when these decretal productions of the earlier pontiffs began to be introduced and published by a merchant.

Finally, certain manuscripts contain additions that are rather ornaments belonging to particular nations. That an addition has been made is revealed by the difference in style.

In the Reginensis, Mazarinian, and Thuanean manuscripts, p. 133, the following words appear under Vitalianus:

> “At that time Pope Vitalian sent to Britain Theodore the archbishop and Adrian the abbot, both highly learned men. They enriched the many churches of the English with the fruit of ecclesiastical teaching. Theodore the archbishop described, with marvelous and judicious consideration, the judgments concerning sins—namely, how many years a person ought to do penance for each sin.”

Similarly, under Gregory III, the same manuscripts have the following on p. 180:

> “During his time the province subject to Roman rule was shaken by the impious Lombards, or by their king Liutprand. Coming to Rome, he pitched his tents in the Field of Nero; and after ravaging Campania, he shaved and clothed many Roman nobles in the Lombard fashion. For this reason the man of God, constrained by grief on every side, took the sacred keys from the confession of the blessed apostle Peter and sent them by sea, through his messengers, to Charles, a most prudent man who at that time ruled the kingdom of the Franks. Through Anastasius, a most holy bishop, and Sergius the presbyter, he also asked the aforementioned excellent Charles to free them from such oppression by the Lombards.”

These passages appear to have been excerpted from the *Metz Annalist* and the continuator of Fredegar.

I believe that this present section was added and attached to the second catalogue of the Roman pontiffs during the later and final period before Anastasius, when Greek monks, fleeing to the apostolic see on account of Monothelitism and Iconoclasm, brought to Rome numerous little works that had existed only in Greek. Thus the compiler extracted the material reported here from the spurious letter of Clement to James and did not hesitate to attach it to the acts either of Peter or of Clement.

**Line 8.—Just as the chair had been handed over or entrusted to him by the Lord Jesus Christ.** The compiler of the acts thought it appropriate to insert this section from the spurious letter of Clement in order to demonstrate succession from Peter [Col. 1086C] and the apostolic pedigree in which they gloried as though it were the Church’s token of truth and the prerogative of a chair established in apostolic origin. Perhaps he also wished to confront, on that same ground, the claims of the bishop of Constantinople, who, at the time when this mixture of pseudepigraphical writings was brought from Greece, was claiming primacy on the basis of the privilege of the imperial city.

Anyone who has even tasted, with the first touch of his lips, the ancient customs of the primitive Church knows with certainty that Churches in the earliest period were accustomed to glory in their apostolic origin: either an apostle had established their chair, or had appointed their bishop; from these origins they derived their registers and catalogues.

Tertullian expressed this in *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 32:

> “In this way the apostolic Churches present their registers. Thus the Church of the Smyrnaeans reports Polycarp, consecrated by Saint John; similarly the Church of the Romans reports Clement, ordained by Peter. In the same way the other Churches also display those whom, appointed to the episcopate by the apostles, they possess as branches of apostolic stock. Let the heretics produce something of this kind.”

Saint John Chrysostom explains apostolic designation as a great privilege in Homily 42, volume V, p. 687. He commends the martyr Ignatius also for this reason: Saint Peter entrusted him with the administration, or episcopate, of the Church of Antioch. He adds:

> “Since he succeeded him in the dignity of the Antiochene episcopate.
