For just as, if someone removes a great stone from the foundation, he attempts to set another altogether equal in its place, lest otherwise the whole building weaken and collapse, so, when Peter was about to depart from Antioch, the grace of the Spirit appointed a teacher equal to Peter in his place, lest the building already begun become weaker through contempt for the successor.”

Irenaeus recognizes this succession, by which one ascended to apostolic origin as a token of truth, in Book IV, *Against Heresies*, chapter 44. He commends it as the safer means of finding the truth and urges the faithful, in doubtful matters, to have recourse:

> “to those who possess succession from the apostles, who, together with the succession of the episcopate, received the sure gift of truth according to the Father’s good pleasure; but the others, who depart from the principal succession, wherever they may gather, are to be regarded with suspicion, as heretics and men of evil judgment.”

Optatus uses this argument to attack the Donatists’ efforts against the schismatics and the fanciful Roman episcopate established by the Donatists in the city. In Book I he writes:

> “I see that you are still ignorant of the schism created at Carthage by your leaders. Seek the origin of these matters, and you will find that this judgment was spoken against you when you joined heretics to schismatics. For Caecilianus did not withdraw from the chair of Peter or of Cyprian; rather, Majorinus did, and you sit in his chair, which had no origin before Majorinus.”

Against the Luciferians, who defended another communion outside the Catholic Church in order to show that their fellowship was purer, Jerome opposes these words in *Against the Luciferians*, chapter 9:

> “I shall state briefly and openly the judgment of my mind: we must remain in that Church which, founded by the apostles, continues to this day.”

Moved by this common conviction of the primitive Church, the person who inserted the present addition into the second catalogue believed to be true what he had found in Clement’s spurious letter to James concerning Clement’s election as successor by Saint Peter.

That he was moved by this letter alone to add the passage is shown by two facts. First, he mentions it; second, in the other additions the compiler nowhere praises the source from which he derived an addition, except here, when he says in lines 9 and 10:

> “Nevertheless, in the letter written to James, you will find how the Church was entrusted to him by blessed Peter.”

It is therefore clear that this addition was attached to the acts of Saint Peter by a later hand and at a late date, when such pseudepigraphical productions had been spread throughout Rome and Italy from Greece.

**Line 11.—Therefore Linus and Cletus are recorded before him.** The compiler of the *Pontifical Book* attempts in this way to reconcile the disagreement concerning the order of pontifical succession: namely, that Clement, having been elected as successor, left the see out of a desire for true peace, until Clement, who had been elected, received the see from Cletus.

In the age of Epiphanius there was a celebrated controversy concerning Peter’s immediate successor. Most people thought that Linus and Cletus had not been Peter’s successors or ordinary pontiffs but chorepiscopi, whom he had appointed to govern Rome in his place, especially when he was absent. Others considered them legitimate and ordinary pontiffs.

Following the *Pontifical Book*, Onuphrius writes that while Peter was still alive he appointed two chorepiscopi, Linus and Cletus, in the fourteenth year of his pontificate. Then, shortly before his death, he ordained Clement as his successor.

Epiphanius discusses this opinion in *Against Heresies*, chapter 27, p. 107:

> “Although, for this very reason, other bishops could have been appointed while the apostles—Peter and Paul, that is—were still alive, since they undertook journeys to other cities and regions for the sake of preaching the Gospel, while Rome could not be without a bishop. For Paul reached Spain, and Peter repeatedly traversed Pontus and Bithynia. It could indeed have happened that, after Clement was first appointed, when he fled—if that is what happened, which I say by conjecture rather than by assertion—and after Linus and Cletus had died, each of whom held the episcopate for twelve years, he was finally compelled to assume the pontificate after the death of the apostles Peter and Paul, which occurred in the twelfth year of Nero.”

Epiphanius therefore confirms that this controversy was being debated in his own age, although he does not dare to pronounce judgment on it.

Whether the authors of this opinion discovered it in Clement’s spurious letter or in another more reliable document, Epiphanius does not decide. He does, however, assert that this is beyond doubt: a point that more strongly commends our present account of pontifical succession and the care of the primitive Church in preserving, under special protection, the catalogues of Saint Peter’s successors. For after setting out the series of pontiffs and discussing the disputes concerning the order of succession, he concludes:

> “Let no one be surprised that I have gone through each point with such care. For by these means the truth is continually shown to be certain and accurate.”

Perhaps the ancient authors of this opinion were misled by the apostolic practice, from which the impostor fabricated the letter to James, of ordaining several bishops at once and sending them to the same regions so that they might be available to conduct the ordinations of clergy or bishops.

Thus the Council of Jerusalem sent Paul and Barnabas, bishops, to announce the apostolic commands. Peter likewise judged that Linus, Cletus, and Clement should be ordained for the same duties, just as he had acted at Antioch, where he appointed Evodius and Ignatius. From this arose the story of a successor designated by Peter and also elected.

Tertullian indeed asserts that Clement was ordained by Peter, but not that he was appointed his successor. The same is true at Antioch, where Saint Ignatius is said by Chrysostom to have been ordained, although the constant opinion is that Evodius, not Ignatius, succeeded Peter at Antioch.

The impostor was certainly given the occasion to fabricate the letter; Photius observes as much when he gives the following judgment concerning Clement’s letter to James, in *Bibliotheca*, codices 112–113:

> “This work is neither identical nor from the same author. In some books it is presented as having been sent by the apostle Peter to James; in others, again, as another letter from Clement to James.”

Whether Peter appointed two bishops, either at Rome or at Antioch—one to preside over converts from the Gentiles and the other over those from the Jews, according to what happened between Peter and Paul, so that one evangelized the Jews and the other the Gentiles—is not a matter for discussion here.

Meanwhile, that a bishop ordained by another apostle succeeded to the same chair is shown by the succession of the patriarchs of Alexandria, which reports that Ananias, consecrated bishop by Mark, succeeded that same Mark.

**Note: [Col. 1088C]**

**Line 4.—Many books.** In addition to the letters, he wrote the *Apostolic Constitutions*. He did not compose the *Apostolic Canons*, but wrote in Greek those that had been handed down by the apostles. The *Circuits of Peter*, described in ten books, are rejected among the apocrypha by Gelasius.

**Note: [Col. 1088C]**

## Chronological Notes

I previously set out the chronological notes common to both pontiffs, Clement and Cletus, under number 3, in order to show that blessed Clement exercised the Roman pontificate before blessed Cletus; that Cletus was elevated to the same see only after Clement’s abdication had left Peter’s chair vacant, by the votes of the Roman clergy; and that he held it until he died a martyr under Domitian, several years before Clement’s martyrdom, which was reserved for the third year of Trajan.

For this reason Cletus was entered earlier than Clement in the diptychs of the martyrs and in the canon of the Mass, and in both places is placed before Clement. Nevertheless, in the most ancient succession of the Roman pontiffs—namely, the Liberian Catalogue—he is rightly placed after Clement, since Clement occupied the chair as successor to Peter and Linus and relinquished it before Cletus’s pontificate.

There are examples of such voluntary resignation and of several bishops successively relinquishing office before death, even in other principal sees. Eusebius records one at Jerusalem in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 10. When Narcissus withdrew by flight, Dius was first chosen as his successor, then Germanio, and then Gordius. When Narcissus returned from the wilderness and, at the request of the brothers, was brought back to resume care of the Church he had relinquished, he was almost exhausted by extreme old age—for he was in his one hundred and sixteenth year—and, not without the support of a heavenly vision, obtained relief in the form of Alexander, who had been appointed bishop in his place.

In addition to those chronological notes common to Clement and Cletus, I shall append here the notes proper to Clement alone. They may also illuminate the words of the Librarian under number 4, arranged as follows:

**Line 2.—He sat for nine years, two months, and ten days; and the same line and the following line.—He lived during the times of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus**—for this is how the corrupt reading *of Trajan and Italicus* must be corrected, as we demonstrated with Schelestratius from the more accurate text of the Vatican, Cassinese, and two Florentine manuscripts, with the support also of the ancient Liberian Catalogue published above in the first work’s Prolegomena and appended to this number—**until the eighth consulship of Vespasian and the sixth of Titus.**

I previously showed that the total of nine years, two months, and ten days must be calculated from the immediately preceding consulship of Capitō and Rufus, with which Linus, Clement’s predecessor, ends, to the seventh consulship of Vespasian, [Col. 1089B] by which the end of Clement’s period is marked in the aforementioned Liberian Catalogue. I now confirm and demonstrate this more clearly from an ancient stone of the municipal *Fasti* discovered in the territory of Cassino.

There the reckonings of this nine-year period are recorded according to both magistracies: that is, by the indication of the Roman consuls and by the listing of the magistrates of the four men and of the quinquennial magistrates of the town or colony to which the stone belonged, corresponding year by year to the same total span of time.

From this it will become clear how many genuine documents supported the consular chronology, especially in this part of Italy near Rome, during the age of Liberius, when that most ancient catalogue of the Roman pontiffs was published—before foreign nations, summoned to ruin and devastate Italy, shattered and dispersed these monuments.

This marble tablet, a notable fragment of a larger stone, excavated in the territory of Cassino, had formerly been given as a gift [Col. 1089C] by the most reverend Father, Abbot D. Erasmus [Col. 1090A] Gattola—then prior and librarian of that celebrated monastery, often praised for his outstanding learning and his devotion to antiquarian studies by the distinguished scholars Mabillon and Montfaucon in their Italian journals. As I say, he had given it to the illustrious and most reverend prelate Giovanni Ciampino, when he conducted both of us as guests to the two sacristies of the monastery of Cassino and entertained us with great generosity, Innocent XII then being pope.

The memory of this precious fragment had not faded from me, so that, after the death of that prelate, when his antiquities were dispersed, I diligently sought it out above all others, bought it back, and preserved it, to be added to the more select marbles collected with scholarly care for the elucidation of chronology by the eminent and most reverend Cardinal Alessandro Albani.

From the similarly arranged series of consuls in the inscription published by Gruter, fol. 299, and from another series of the consuls entering upon office at Rome together with the annual officials responsible for the games at Antium, found together with a fragment of the Julian Calendar through the careful efforts and munificent generosity of that same eminent prince six years ago and to be published in due course, we understand that this belongs to the municipal Fasti. These, arranged year by year according to the ordinary consuls, contain the names of the Four Men for the Administration of Justice and of the quinquennial magistrates who served under the emperors Nero, Galba, Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian in the same town or colony.

The first surviving pair of consuls indicated in the fragment mentioned above gives the names of Capito and Rufus, that is, the year 67 of the common Christian era, the thirteenth year of Nero’s reign completed on 13 October, and the fourteenth beginning on the following day. This is clear from the fact that Linus completed his martyrdom on 22 September, as is evident from these same consuls, assigned as the terminus of Linus’s pontificate in the Liberian catalogue.

Here is the stone itself. For clarity, I have appended to the consulships, in Arabic numerals, the number of the years of the common Christian era to which they correspond.

[Col. 1089D] After the consuls of the year 67, Gaius Fonteius Capito and Gaius Julius Rufus, there follow the consuls of the year 68, Silius Italicus and Gaius Valerius Trachalus, who are to be read at Gruter, p. 300, and are correctly assigned in the catalogues at the beginning of the account of Pope Clement. For Clement celebrated his first Easter under these consuls, after succeeding Linus following the latter’s martyrdom on 23 September of the year 67.

Under these same consuls Nero killed himself with his own hand on 9 June, while Galba, who had seized imperial power in Spain, was declared emperor by the Senate. In the following year, 69, the consuls Servius Sulpicius Galba II and Titus Vinius, marked on this marble, entered office on the Kalends of January. They are also read on another marble at Gruter, fol. CLXXXIX, no. 4, in Panvinio’s Fasti, and in Tacitus, *Histories*, book I, as well as in other historians.

“This year,” says Cardinal Norisius in *The Consular Epistle*, p. 47, “had four emperors: Galba, who was killed on 15 January through the treachery of Marcus Salvius Otho; Otho, who, defeated in the battle of Bedriacum, killed himself after completing the third month of his reign; Vespasian, [Col. 1090D] who was hailed emperor by the army on the Kalends of July; and finally Vitellius, who was killed at the end of the year and left the principate to Vespasian alone. The latter ruled for ten years, eight of which he marked in the Fasti by his son Titus as colleague seven times in the consulships”—as Suetonius states in *Vespasian*, chapter 8, and chapter 6 of *The Life of Titus*. “Moreover, although the same consulships are confused and disordered in Cassiodorus and others, Panvinio, following the anonymous author preserved by Cuspinianus like a torchbearer, was the first to arrange them with the greatest accuracy and to confirm them abundantly through inscriptions on coins and stones.”

The anonymous author of Cuspinianus, whom he mentions here, was published by Norisius himself after the *Syromacedonian Epochs*, dissertation 1, on the consular Fasti. There the decade of Vespasian’s reign is displayed with the ordinary consuls as follows:

**Christian Era**

| Year | Consuls | Day of the week and lunar date |
|---|---|---|
| 69 | Galba II and Vinius | Sunday, 15 |
| 70 | Vespasian II and Titus | Monday, 27 |
| 71 | Vespasian III and Nerva | Tuesday, 8 |
| 72, leap year | Vespasian IV and Titus II | Wednesday, 29 |
| 73 | Domitian and Messalinus | Friday, 30 |
| 74 | Vespasian V and Titus III | Saturday, 11 |
| 75 | Vespasian VI and Titus IV | Sunday, 22 |
| 76, leap year | Vespasian VII and Domitian V | Monday, 3 |
| 77 | Vespasian VIII and Titus V | Wednesday, 14 |
| 78 | Commodus and Priscus | Thursday, 25 |
| 79 | Vespasian IX and Titus VI | Friday, 6 |

What Panvinio accomplished through laborious examination of numerous stones and coins is demonstrated in full by a single glance at the Cassino stone, up to the sixth consulship of Vespasian—that is, the year 75 of the Christian era. In that year the sixth year of his reign was completed on the day before the Kalends of July, and his seventh year of tribunician power and imperial rule began on the Kalends of July themselves. In the same sixth consulship, both tribunician powers are combined on the coins: the sixth continuing until 30 June, and the seventh beginning on 1 July.

On the following Kalends of January, in the year 76, while tribunician power VII was still in progress, Vespasian entered his seventh consulship, as the coins, inscriptions, and the anonymous author of the fourth century attest; the designation of a leap year is also correctly attached to this year. The assignment of Titus instead of Domitian as his colleague on the Kalends of January may indeed rightly be censured, and it can be shown that Domitian V, as suffect consul, must be supplied from the Kalends of July, on the testimony of stones and coins.

The year 77 follows, marked by the eighth consulship of Vespasian and the sixth of his colleague Titus, with his brother Domitian VI likewise substituted from the Kalends of July. We stated that in this year, after Clement’s abdication had already taken place in December of the year 76, Cletus assumed the Roman pontificate before the Paschal feasts. Consequently, in the Liberian catalogue, the beginning of Cletus’s pontificate is rightly assigned to the consulship of Vespasian VIII, following the practice of the Paschal chronicles and the reckoning of pontifical years.

Nevertheless, as before, the catalogue errs in assigning Domitian as colleague, unless Domitian is understood as the suffect consul from the Kalends of July. The same is true of the anonymous author preserved by Cuspinianus, who thrusts Domitian in as substitute for Titus, the ordinary consul. The catalogue is, however, more excusably at fault in presenting Domitian as colleague, since Clement’s dismissal occurred near the end of the year 76, when the ordinary consuls, Vespasian the father VII and Titus the son V, had entered office; from the Kalends of July onward, it would therefore find Domitian as colleague of his father.

This Cassino stone therefore demonstrates that the pontiff who began to sit after 28 September, the day commemorated for the martyrdom of Saint Linus, did so under the consulship of Capito and Rufus in the year of Christ 67; and that, before abdicating, he completed nine years, two months, and ten days of his pontificate. He held the see of Peter until 4 December, under the ordinary consulship of Vespasian VII and Titus V, with Domitian V substituted for Titus from the Kalends of July in the year 76.

It likewise shows that his successor, after his abdication, must have marked the beginning of his pontificate at the next Paschal feasts in the year of Christ 77, [Col. 1091D] under the consulship of Vespasian VIII, which the most ancient Liberian catalogue assigns to Cletus as he began his office.

With equal certainty it confirms that the period of those nine years was reckoned under the emperors Galba and Vespasian, and that the rule of Cletus, his successor, is correctly stated in the *Book of the Pontiffs* as occurring under Vespasian and Titus and extending into the three-year period of Domitian’s reign—namely, to 26 April, the date assigned to his martyrdom, under the consulship of Domitian IX and Rufus in the Christian era 83, as we gathered above, p. 35.

Therefore I do not doubt that the genuine reading of the *Pontifical Book*, restored from the Liberian catalogue and the other documents cited, should be given for Clement as follows:

> “He was in office during the times of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus up to Vespasian VII and Titus.”

In the Anastasius manuscripts this is corruptly read:

> “He was in office during the times of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Trajan and Italicus up to Vespasian IX and Titus.”

For Cletus likewise it should be rendered:

> “He was in office during the times of Vespasian [Col. 1092A] and Titus and Domitian, from the consulship of Vespasian VIII and Titus up to the consulship of Domitian IX and Rufus.”

Although the corrupt reading is:

> “He was in office during the times of Vespasian and Titus, from the consulship of Vespasian VII and Domitian V up to the consulship of Domitian IX and Rufus.”

For the context itself makes clear that this pontiff was in office not only during the times of Vespasian and Titus, but also of Domitian, since he reached the consulship of Domitian IX and Rufus.

These are the points I wished to add concerning Clement’s chronology to the earlier notes prefixed to the section on Cletus, in confirmation of what was there established concerning the epoch and succession of both pontiffs.

## HISTORICAL NOTES BY THE SAME AUTHOR

**Line 7.**—“He wrote two epistles, which are called catholic [or canonical].” And below, lines 9 and 10: “Nevertheless, in the epistle written to James, you will find how the Church was entrusted to him by Blessed Peter.”

Jean-Baptiste Cotelier, a Sorbonist associate and [Col. 1092B] royal professor of the Greek language at the Paris academy, who illuminated the works of the holy Fathers who flourished in apostolic times with a celebrated commentary, correctly observed that this passage states the truth concerning Clement’s two epistles and calls both of them catholic—though some readers have *canonical*. Nevertheless, he distinguishes from both of them the epistle circulated under Clement’s name and addressed to James, the brother of the Lord. Concerning this epistle, the *Book of the Pontiffs* gives no judgment, but merely indicates that it contains an account of how the Church was entrusted to him, Clement, by blessed Peter.

Against another biographer of the Roman pontiffs—whose editor at Antwerp in 1642 supposes him to be Luitprand, the deacon of Pavia—Cotelier rightly observes that what is correctly written in this *Pontifical Book* concerning Clement I’s two epistles to the Corinthians has been misunderstood through a very serious error, as though it referred to the fictitious or apocryphal epistles bearing Clement’s name, supposedly addressed to James, the brother of the Lord.

The Christian world received those two epistles of Clement to the Corinthians, as genuine writings, with such devotion and veneration, even in apostolic times, that most churches were accustomed to read the first publicly on Sundays in the assembly of the faithful. Eusebius affirms this in his history in more than one place, namely book III, chapter 16:

> “There is extant an epistle of this Clement written to the Corinthians, truly outstanding and most remarkable. He dictated it as if in the person of the Roman Church, when a dissension had arisen among the Corinthians. It is known that this epistle was publicly read in very many churches, both in ancient times and in our own.”

Then, in book IV, chapter 23, after quoting a letter written by Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, to Soter, who at that time succeeded Clement in the see of Peter, Eusebius adds:

> “In this same epistle he also mentions Clement’s epistle written to the Corinthians, and he testifies in these words that it was customarily read in the church according to ancient practice: ‘Today,’ he says, ‘we have kept the holy Lord’s Day, on which we read your epistle. We shall continue always to read it, just as we read the earlier epistle written to us by Clement, and shall derive abundant benefit from its excellent admonitions and instructions.’”

Such, then, was the discipline of the nascent Church: those holy bishops of the peoples of God regarded the epistles of Peter’s successors as immediately next to the divine Scriptures and decreed that Clement’s writings, just as Soter’s, should be read perpetually on Sundays in the public gathering of the faithful.

With this in mind, Cotelier, while defending the historical reliability of our *Pontifical Book* and censuring the sluggishness of Luitprand’s copyist, supplies the following notes for this passage, which I shall give in his own words:

> “In the *Pontifical Book*, where Clement’s life is discussed, and likewise in the copyists of that work, two epistles of Clement are mentioned, and these are said to be canonical and catholic. [Col. 1093A] The author of the book on the Deeds of the Roman Pontiffs, believed to be Luitprand, understood this as referring to the first two decretal epistles of Clement to James. In my judgment, this is a very serious error. For if the writer of the *Pontifical Book* had had decretal epistles in mind, he would have said not two but five. Such is the case with that *Biographer*—Βιόγραφος—who, with astonishing negligence, after reporting that two catholic epistles were sent by Clement to James, goes on to state what is contained in those two and in the remaining three. Moreover, in the *Pontifical Book* the epistle to James appears to be separated from the two canonical epistles: ‘He wrote two epistles, which are called canonical’; and below: ‘Nevertheless, in the epistle written to James.’”

Thus far Cotelier.

There is no reason for us to be surprised that Clement’s first epistle and his second epistle to the Corinthians were called catholic, and were also regarded by some as canonical. Such was the esteem in which both were held that they are found written immediately after the canonical books in the most ancient Alexandrian manuscript of the sacred Scriptures, which is called that of Thecla. Its script belongs to the fourth century of Christ, as the distinguished Laurentius Zaccagnius demonstrated, with the agreement of learned scholars.

Since the codex belonged to the Alexandrian Church, it was transferred from that see to Constantinople by Cyril Lucaris and sent as a distinguished gift to King Charles I of England. It is preserved in his library in London. Its specimen of handwriting is very similar to that of the most ancient Vatican codex, from which Sixtus V published the Greek edition of the Septuagint through Zannetti’s Roman press in 1587.

Why Clement’s epistles to the Corinthians are placed alongside the canonical books of both Testaments, we shall attempt to investigate shortly below. First, let us offer some selected passages from Cotelier’s *Prolegomena* to the first epistle.

> “Since nearly everything that could be brought forward concerning the epistle written by Blessed Clement in the name of the Roman Church to the Church of the Corinthians has already been handed down partly by the ancients and partly appropriated by more recent writers, by way of preface we shall note only a few points concerning those testimonies of the ancients that might perhaps cause readers some difficulty unless they were explained,” etc.

After raising several questions, especially from statements of Eusebius and Clement of Alexandria that might seem to some to contradict one another, he dispels them as follows:

> “You will remove the contradiction if you say that everyone acknowledged the work—the First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians—as genuine, but that not everyone regarded it as a canonical writing. Concerning the first point, no controversy was raised in antiquity; concerning the second, there was controversy: some placed it outside the canon, while others placed it within, as did the author of the apostolic canons in the final canon, and perhaps also John of Damascus, who places those canons among the sacred Scriptures, together with the bishops who accepted them at Trullo. The most ancient manuscript of the Bible, written by Thecla, provides evidence for this latter opinion, since it presents these two epistles together with the books of the New Testament.”

Saint Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons and martyr long before Eusebius, being a contemporary of Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians, not only praises Clement’s letter to the Corinthians but calls it “most powerful letters.” Father Feuardentius, doctor of theology of the Paris Faculty, explained the reason for this notably excellent designation in his commentary on the passage, p. 240, no. 12 of the Paris edition of 1639, in these words:

> “‘Most powerful letter.’ From this observe that the Roman Church, from the beginning, also exercised its authority in governing the churches of the Greeks. This was so welcome to their bishops that Eusebius writes that the epistle mentioned here was read publicly in many churches, not so much in Clement’s name as in the name of the Roman Church, as he himself remembers, in *History*, book II, chapter 12. Moreover, you will find not insignificant fragments of this epistle [Col. 1094A] in Justin Martyr, *Questions*, 87, to the Orthodox; Clement of Alexandria, book I of the *Stromata*, and books IV and VI; Basil the Great, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 29; Athanasius, *Disputation against Arius* at the Council of Nicaea; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 27; Eusebius, *History*, books III, chapters 16 and 17; and Jerome, book I *Against Jovinian* and his commentaries on chapters 1 and 4 of Ephesians.”

There is another passage of Irenaeus, book III, chapter 3, from which greater light shines upon the expression “power” attributed to Clement’s apostolic letters. There he speaks of the “greater pre-eminence” of the Roman Church, on account of which the other churches must necessarily come to it:

> “The greatest, most ancient, and universally known Church, founded and established at Rome by the two most glorious apostles, Peter and Paul. For to this Church, because of its greater pre-eminence, every Church must necessarily come—that is, the faithful from everywhere.”

When Father Christian Lupus of Ypres, doctor and professor at the University of Louvain, considered these words of Irenaeus in his notes on Tertullian’s *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 36, p. 565, he judged that the following points ought to be observed:

> “He adds that it—the Roman Church—is infallible in doctrine and the guardian and judge of all doctrinal controversies. The primacy and infallibility of the Roman Church are supported by anchors of testimony so firm and ancient that, in addition to Irenaeus and Dionysius as witnesses, Tertullian also joins them, writing in the passage cited: ‘But if you are near Italy, you have Rome, from which authority is available to us also in the matter of established teaching. Happy Church, into which the apostles poured their entire doctrine together with their blood: where Peter was made equal to the Lord’s passion, where Paul was crowned with a death like John’s, where the apostle John, after being plunged into burning oil and suffering no harm, was exiled to an island!’”

When Peter’s successors, as custodians and transmitters, bring forth the whole doctrine of Christ poured out with the blood of the apostles Peter, Paul, and John into the bosom of the Roman Church, they exercise, after the manner of Clement I in his most powerful letter, as witnesses to the traditions of the Fathers, that greater pre-eminence of this Church so often acknowledged by Irenaeus. To it the whole Church must necessarily come—that is, all the faithful from everywhere.

The distinguished doctors of the Paris Faculty of Sacred Theology, Feuardentius and de la Barre, explain this at greater length. I shall not transcribe here Feuardentius’s entire pages, in which he elucidates the privilege of the Roman Church celebrated by Irenaeus in these words, book III, chapter 3:

> “But since it would be a very lengthy task in such a volume to enumerate the successions of all the churches, by indicating the tradition that the greatest, most ancient, and universally known Church, founded and established at Rome by the two most glorious apostles Peter and Paul, has received from the apostles, and the faith announced to humanity, handed down through the successions of bishops even to us, we confound all those who, in whatever way—whether through self-satisfaction, empty glory, blindness, or wrong judgment—gather apart from what is proper. For to this Church, because of its greater pre-eminence, every Church must necessarily come, that is, the faithful from everywhere; in it the tradition that comes from the apostles has always been preserved by those who are everywhere.”

As I say, I shall not transcribe Feuardentius’s entire pages on these words of Irenaeus, in which he clearly demonstrates, by examples gathered from churches, Fathers, and councils throughout the world, in the East and West, that all the faithful of Christ must necessarily come to the primacy and teaching of those seated in the Roman see of Peter.

The other Parisian theologian de la Barre condensed what Feuardentius treats more fully, writing as follows on the indicated passage of Tertullian’s *Prescription against Heretics*, no. 36, p. 82 of the Paris edition:

> “‘From which authority is available to us.’ In matters of faith,” he says, “I have as witnesses all the Fathers of the Church who have always interpreted those words as assigning supreme judgment to the Roman pontiffs: ‘I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven’; ‘Whatever you bind,’ etc.; ‘I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail’; ‘You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church.’”

Augustine, in *Against the Party of Donatus* on the Psalm, volume VI—or rather at the beginning of volume VII—writes:

> “Likewise Chrysostom comments on Psalm 69, homily 26; from various passages in Matthew; Cyprian, book VI, chapter 12, on John; besides these, Theodoret in his epistle to the monks; Cyprian very frequently in epistle 42. Saint Jerome writes to Eustochium about the disagreements of the Western churches, and even about the churches themselves being brought together and summoned to Rome, as does Basil in epistle 52.

> “Saint Athanasius, older than Jerome, together with all the bishops of Egypt, calls Mark the pope of the holy apostolic and universal see in his epistle to Pope Mark; they recognize his holy see as the mother and head [Col. 1095B] of all the churches, and promise that they and all entrusted to them will remain perpetually obedient to it.

> “Saint Augustine, disputing against Julian the Pelagian, teaches that the sole judgment of the Roman Church ought to be sufficient for him; and in sermon 2, *On the Words of the Apostle*, and *Against Cresconius*, book III, chapter 34, he says that an Eastern Catholic would never write to the bishop of Carthage while bypassing the Roman one.

> “Optatus, book I *Against Parmenianus*, in the case of the Donatists, says: ‘The judgment was closed by the sentence of Pope Miltiades.’ The emperors, too, venerate the primacy of the Roman see: Valentinian III in his epistle to the younger Theodosius; the emperor Marcian in his letter to Pope Leo; the emperor Justinian in *Novella* 131. No one doubts that the summit of the supreme pontificate is with the Roman pontiff.

> “At the Council of Chalcedon the voice of all the bishops was that every primacy and chief honor was owed to the Roman bishop. Irenaeus, book III, chapter 3, declared that he had received this by the living voice of the apostles: ‘It would be a lengthy task to enumerate all the successors of the churches. By indicating the faith of the Roman Church, we confound those who gather separately’; and immediately: ‘For to this Church, because of its greater pre-eminence, every Church must necessarily come, that is, the faithful from everywhere.’”

On these words the learned Feuardentius constructed a catalogue of the churches of Gaul, Italy, Spain, England, Scotland, Ireland, Germany, the Goths, Sarmatia, and the Eastern churches, as well as those of Africa—Carthage, Numidia, Mauretania, Hippo—and those of Asia, Arabia, and finally the East: Caesarea, Cappadocia, Phoenicia, Syria, Armenia, Pontus, Galatia, Lydia, Phrygia, Pisidia, Pamphylia, Isauria. All these churches, to conclude in a word, he shows to have referred controversies of faith to Peter’s successors and to have rendered obedience to him with the sacrament of fidelity.

The careful reader may seek the remainder in Albert Pighius, *Hierarchy of the Church*, book IV, chapter 8; Alphonsus the Writer, under the entry “Pope 11”; and Stapleton, *Controversies*, chapter 17, book VI. The same Pighius, *Ratisbon Controversies*, controversy 16; Melchior Canus, book VI of the *Commonplaces*, etc.

I considered these points worth recalling from de la Barre, the abridger of Feuardentius’s fuller work on the cited passage of Saint Irenaeus, in order to explain the force of the expression “greater pre-eminence” as applied to the Roman Church, and of the “most powerful letter” of Saint Clement I to the Corinthians. This must be carefully considered if we are to understand more easily why Clement’s two epistles to the Corinthians, written in the name of the Roman Church, are called catholic by some and thought to belong among the canonical Scriptures, and why, in the most ancient copy of the sacred Bible, they alone are placed after the canonical books of the New Testament.

Thus the *Book of the Pontiffs*, which, in its account of Peter, listed the canonical books of the New Testament as compiled and approved by his authority, selects in Clement’s account, from among the several works attributed to him, the two epistles about which we must now bring our discussion to a close.

[Col. 1096A] To state briefly what I think: since I see that Clement’s First Epistle to the Corinthians was preserved and read in numerous churches, and that in that most ancient biblical codex it was placed after the canonical books together with the second epistle, I suspect that this was a seal by which apostolic tradition confirmed the number of the books of divine Scripture and their approved reading.

This was no different from the practice beginning at the end of the fourth century, when the letters of Pope Damasus began to be attached to the sacred Bibles together with the prologue of Blessed Jerome, as those producing a genuine text of Scripture obeyed the apostolic commands of Damasus. Nor is it different from what is done today after the pontificates of Saint Pius V and Clement VIII, when their letters are prefixed to editions of the approved text, showing that the supreme priest of the Catholic Church hands on to all the faithful those books and that same reading which he himself received from his predecessors, and they from the apostles.

It may be observed that in that first epistle of Clement [Col. 1096B] testimonies and proofs are brought forward from almost every book of the Old Testament, as well as from those parts of the New Testament that had appeared by that time, since the apostle John had not yet written the Gospel or the Apocalypse. The editors of that epistle conclude that it was written either shortly before Jerusalem was conquered by Titus, while the Temple was still standing, or not very long afterward.

Interpreters unanimously testify, together with Jerome, that John published the Gospel and the Apocalypse later: the Gospel after the rise of Cerinthus’s heresy, and the Apocalypse after the fourteenth year of Domitian. Consequently, that epistle, written earlier, could not produce testimonies from these later parts of the New Covenant, which had not yet been published.

From nearly all the remaining canonical books, however, I find passages indicated in the numbers according to Cotelier’s edition, as follows.

### From the books of the Old Testament

[Col. 1096C] Genesis occurs in numbers 4, 6, 9, 10, 17, 20, 32, etc. Exodus in 4, 17, 51. Leviticus is indicated in 32. Numbers in 4, 17, 29, 43, 51. Deuteronomy in 3, 29, 34, 53. Joshua in 12. Judges and Ruth. First and Second Kings in 4; Third and Fourth Kings in 31. Chronicles. First and Second Esdras. Tobit. Judith in 55. Esther in 55. Job in 18, 20, 26, 39, 49, 56. Psalms in 14, 15, 26, 28, 35, 36, 46, 48, 50, 52, 56. Proverbs in 14, 21, 57. Ecclesiastes in 30. [Col. 1096D] Song of Songs and Wisdom in 3, 27. Ecclesiasticus in 9. Isaiah in 3, 8, 13, 14, 16, 34, 50. Jeremiah in 8, 13. Baruch. Ezekiel in 8, 29. Daniel in 45. The Twelve Minor Prophets in 7, 23. Maccabees in 2.

### From the books of the New Testament

Matthew in 27, 46. Mark in 46. Luke in 46. Acts of the Apostles in 18. Paul’s Epistle to the Romans in 30, 35. First to the Corinthians in 13, 24, 34, 47, 40. Second to the Corinthians in 30, 35. To the Ephesians in 46. [Col. 1097A] To the Galatians. To the Philippians in 21. To the Colossians. First to the Thessalonians in 42. Second to the Thessalonians. First to Timothy in 29, 47, 50. Second to Timothy. To Titus. To Philemon. To the Hebrews in 2, 16, 17, 36. First of Peter in 2, 30, 38, 49, 57. Second of Peter in 11, 23. James in 10, 17, 23, 30. Jude. The Apocalypse.

It is therefore clear that in this one epistle of Clement virtually all the canonical books are indicated. For those few whose words it was not necessary to cite for the argument of the epistle—such as [Col. 1097B] the books of Judges, Chronicles, Tobit, Song of Songs, Baruch, and the Epistles to the Galatians, Colossians, Titus, and Philemon, as well as the apostle Jude—are either understood to have been joined with and approved alongside the neighboring books, as in the Jewish Church Baruch was joined with Jeremiah, the Song of Songs with the other Wisdom books, Chronicles with the books of Kings, and Judges with the Heptateuch, and as in the Christian Church the epistles mentioned were joined with the other apostolic writings; or perhaps they too were cited in those parts of Clement’s epistle that are now lost, as the still-open lacunae toward the end indicate; or it was in no way appropriate at that point to produce testimonies from those parts of Scripture, since Blessed Clement knew that they had been sufficiently confirmed by the passages already cited when he issued those letters in the name of the Roman Church.

How much weight the authority of the Roman Church already carried in establishing the canon of Scripture we understand well enough from the Fathers, especially from Blessed Augustine in *Against the Epistle of Manichaeus*, chapters 4 and 5. [Col. 1097C] When asked why he believed the Gospel of Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John but did not believe the pseudo-Gospel of Manichaeus and of the other sectarians, he replied that he accepted the former first of all because it had been handed down to him by the Catholic Church, but rejected the latter, that of Manichaeus, because he had not received it from the Catholic Church. What the Catholic Church was, whose faith he was compelled to accept and to which he was compelled to adhere as the bearer of this most sincere wisdom, he made sufficiently clear when he prefaced the following in chapter 4:

> “The succession of priests extends from the very see of the apostle Peter, to whom the Lord, after his resurrection, entrusted the task of feeding his sheep, down to the present episcopate.”

To this also correspond what he stated in Book II of *On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 8, before the canon had been fully completed through general councils, as Bellarmine observes in *Controversies*, Book I, chapter 10:

> “In the canonical Scriptures, let us follow the authority of the several Catholic Churches; among them, certainly, are those Churches that have deserved to possess apostolic sees and to receive [Col. 1097D] epistles. In the canonical Scriptures, therefore, he will observe this rule: he will place those books that are accepted by all the Catholic Churches before those that some do not accept. Among those that are not accepted by all, he will place those that the more numerous or more authoritative Churches accept before those held by the fewer or less authoritative Churches.”

Thus the books were most safely sought from this Roman Church, which, according to the same testimony, so surpasses the others in authority and primacy; which deserved to possess an apostolic see and apostolic letters; and which therefore had to provide the strongest possible confirmation for those books that it affirmed to be of divine authority and entrusted to its keeping. This was especially so because the historians of the Church remembered that in this Church the letters of Peter, the prince of the apostles, had been given—letters that teach us that the Pauline epistles are to be counted among the other divine Scriptures. Here also the Acts of the Apostles, written by Luke, had been composed; here the Gospel of Mark had been produced with Peter’s approval; here, according to his testimony and answers, the source of all the Gospels had been indicated, through which the sacred oracles and books of the Old Testament as well are opened.

It is therefore not surprising [Col. 1098A] that that prudent cataloguer of both Testaments took care to place in that most ancient fourth-century codex this epistle, given by Clement to the Corinthians in the name of the Roman Church and distinguished above all the others; and that the bishops of so many Churches immediately undertook to have it publicly read as soon as it was issued. No more illustrious document could be offered for the received catalogue of the canonical Scriptures than one demanded by the assertions and usage of the Catholic and apostolic Church, endowed with the greatest authority of all and the principal Church of all, writing in that apostolic age when John the Evangelist was still alive.

We know that by divine providence [Col. 1098B] John himself was brought to Rome toward the end of Domitian’s reign, as Tertullian reports, so that nothing might be lacking to this Roman Church, already the guardian and foremost custodian of the sacred utterance received from Peter and Paul, for the completion of the sacred canon of Scripture, which was soon to be closed with the books of this beloved apostle, who had drunk the streams of the Gospel from the fountain of the Lord’s breast. For, scarcely exiled from Rome to the island of Patmos, he committed both his Gospel and the Apocalypse to writing.

That these final parts of the New Covenant were immediately entrusted to the Roman Church along with the other divine writings may also be inferred from the martyr Justin:

> “When he,” says Jerome in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, “held discussions or lectures in the city of Rome—τὰς διατριβάς (*diatribai*)—and rebuked Crescens the Cynic, who blasphemed much against the Christians, as a glutton, fearful of death, and a follower of luxury and lust, he was finally accused, through that man’s efforts and plotting, of being a Christian, and shed his blood for Christ.”

Among the other writings of the martyr Justin, who held [Col. 1098C] τὰς διατριβάς (*diatribai*, discussions or lectures) at Rome, Jerome lists an interpretation of the Apocalypse:

> “This,” he says, “is interpreted by Justin the martyr and Irenaeus”—the latter, of course, another interpreter after Justin, though of the same century, who, as legate of the Church of Lyons, carried a letter to Rome to Pope Eleutherus.

There are also those who infer that the codex of canonical epistles, mentioned under the name of the Apostle in the epistle of the martyr Ignatius to the Philadelphians, chapter 5, was collected much earlier. Ignatius was an apostolic man who not only stayed at Rome but also suffered martyrdom in the city, according to Jerome, in the eleventh year of Trajan. Thus, if they are correct, that apostolic *Pandect* of the New Testament was present in the Roman Church not merely twenty years before the death of John the Evangelist, but within ten years of John’s falling asleep, if we follow Jerome’s chronology in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, where he assigns it to the beginning of Trajan’s reign.

But concerning the codex of apostolic letters mentioned in Ignatius, [Col. 1098D] judgment may properly be left to others, as Millius, following Grabe, believes (*Prolegomena*). For us it will be sufficient to infer from the martyr Justin and Irenaeus the catalogue of the books of both Testaments in the archives of the Roman Church. Since those two eminent writers and interpreters of the Apocalypse had lived at Rome and possessed such a clear understanding of this final book of the New Testament that they opened to others not merely the outer shell of the letter but also the marrow of the spirit entrusted to them, it is manifest that the complete collection of the Scriptures of both covenants was entrusted to this most eminent of all Churches as soon as it was issued.

For this reason also its authority was sought in distinguishing the divine books, since already, as Tertullian testifies (*On the Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 36), the Roman Church was regarded as one “to which the apostles poured out the whole doctrine together with their blood.” Accordingly, as the passage continues, it “mixes the Law and the Prophets with the evangelical and apostolic writings, and from them derives its faith.”

This is a firmly established maxim, also accepted [Col. 1099A] by Ambrose in Sermon 22 on Psalm 118, when he explains the following words of Song of Songs 7: “New and old things, my beloved, I have kept for you”:

> “I hold,” he says, “all the commandments of the New and Old Testament. The Church alone can say this. No other assembly says it; the Synagogue does not say it, since it holds neither the new according to the letter nor the old according to the spirit. The Manichaean heresy does not say, ‘I have kept the old things for you,’ for it does not accept the prophets. Rightly she is seen as whitened, she who shines with the grace of both Testaments.”

We know that this was also regarded as settled two hundred years before Ambrose by the apostolic man Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, who wrote to Soter, the Roman pontiff, as Eusebius reports in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book IV, chapter 22:

> “Today,” he says, “we have spent the holy Lord’s Day, on which we read your letter. By reading it continually thereafter, just as we read the earlier letter written to us by Clement—and concerning which Eusebius had shortly before reported that, according to ancient custom, it too was regularly read at the solemn assembly of the Church—we shall be filled with the finest instructions and teachings.”

[Col. 1099B] He then adds that, when requested by the brethren, he had written epistles. But certain ministers of the devil had filled them with weeds, deleting some passages and adding others. “Those men,” he says, “will certainly be overtaken by that deadly sentence: ‘Woe to you.’”

It should therefore not seem surprising that certain people attempted to corrupt the Lord’s sacred writings, since they are found to have dared to do the same even in writings of far lower rank.

All these things confirm [Col. 1099C] that, against the treacherous corruptors and falsifiers of the divine books, protection had to be sought from the authority of the apostolic Roman Church, to which the whole teaching of Christ had been poured out together with the apostle’s blood. Consequently, the Churches of Corinth and of the many other places to which they reached undertook to have Clement’s and Soter’s letters read on Sundays in the assembly of the faithful—not only for other reasons, but also so that they might serve as seals and confirmations of the books that, since they were to be regarded as canonical, were employed in the letters of the Roman pontiffs mentioned above to confirm Catholic doctrine.

### Line 7

“By the command of blessed Peter he accepted the Church and undertook the governance of the pontificate.”

The notes of the learned prelate Schelestratius on this number observe that the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* borrowed many things from sources other than the second catalogue. As for what he reports here about Clement’s pontificate, Schelestratius seems to have affirmed that the author took it from Clement’s epistle to James:

> “Although that epistle,” says Schelestratius, “is spurious, it is nevertheless very ancient and predates Rufinus; it was already circulating under Clement’s name from the end of the third century, or the beginning of the fourth.”

The author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* certainly writes that this spurious epistle existed. But it does not appear to me that he trusted it sufficiently rather than the earlier and more truthful documents, or that he was unaware of them. There were older and more reliable documents that reported that Clement had been ordained by the apostle Peter, whom he succeeded in the Roman episcopate.

Such evidence still exists [Col. 1099D] in Tertullian’s *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, cited above with the notes of Sommier, page 30, column 2:

> “Let them produce, then, the origins of their Churches,” and so forth.

After the words:

> “Let their first bishop have had as his author or predecessor someone from the apostles or from apostolic men,”

Tertullian continues:

> “For in this way the apostolic Churches present their records: just as the Church of the Smyrnaeans reports Polycarp as having been consecrated by John, so the Church of the Romans reports Clement as having been ordained by Peter.”

At the beginning, therefore, of the third century, when Tertullian wrote, those older documents still existed from which Septimius drew, before the spurious epistle under Clement’s name to James appeared. Schelestratius acknowledges that this epistle was composed later and circulated around the end of the third century or the beginning of the fourth.

Septimius relied upon those older foundations, and [Col. 1100A] the knowledge then current in the Church concerning Clement’s ordination as bishop and his designation to succeed to the Roman see relied upon them as well. That sincere and more ancient knowledge was nevertheless stuffed with foolish and mendacious additions by that foolishly idle author who compiled and imposed the spurious Acts of Saint Peter, the epistle prefixed under the name of Clement of Rome to James, the disputation with Appion, and the *Itinerary*. These works were rejected along with the apocrypha and condemned not only by Pope Saint Gelasius but much earlier by Athanasius in the *Synopsis* and by Blessed Jerome in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, as everyone knows.

In Anastasius’s text, the conjunction *tamen* (“nevertheless”) seems rather to have the force of an exception, separating the preceding assertion concerning the ordination of blessed Clement and the command added by Saint Peter—that he accept the office of succession even in the governance of the universal Church, if after Peter’s death he should at some time be chosen—from the manner and history of the admission improperly expressed in Clement’s spurious epistle.

Thus I believe that, in the defective style of a barbarous age, the thoughts more obscurely [Col. 1100B] indicated by the writer of the *Life* in Anastasius’s text should be explained as follows:

> “By the command of blessed Peter he accepted the Church and undertook the governance of the pontificate, just as the chair had been handed over or entrusted to Peter by the Lord Jesus Christ.”

That is, Peter commanded Clement, whom he had ordained as pontiff, not merely to bear cheerfully the burden of a bishop charged with announcing the Gospel in whatever Church might be entrusted to him, but also not to refuse, in the Roman see, to undertake the far more laborious administration of the universal Church, with the same breadth of power that he knew had been conferred upon him by Christ the Lord, if after Peter’s death he should be chosen to fill Peter’s chair.

> “Nevertheless,” he says, as if adding an exception, “in Clement’s epistle to James you will find how the Church was entrusted to him by blessed Peter.”

[Col. 1100C] This manner of transferring his own chair, falsely expressed in that condemned epistle and rejected with the other spurious writings by Cotelerius at the end of the second volume, sections 145–147—as though Peter, while still living, had already appointed another Roman bishop, Clement, to preside over the whole Church—is not admitted by the Librarian, but is rejected by him together with us.

Yet, lest the error be too easily admitted on the basis of the preceding truthful information asserted by Tertullian—that Clement had received episcopal ordination through the laying-on of the hands of the apostle Peter, together with the command also to receive the governance of the whole Church if, after Peter’s departure from this life, he should be called to it—the writer of the *Life* judged that the false assertions of Clement’s spurious epistle to James should be separated by the particle *tamen* from the preceding truths, plainly stated on the basis of reliable writings and traditions: namely, that Clement had been ordained bishop by Peter and had received the command not at some time to refuse succession even in the Roman see.

During his own lifetime Peter admitted neither Clement nor anyone else to share that office with him, since he did not wish the Church of Christ to be two-headed, as that spurious epistle of Clement to James makes it by the sections indicated.

[Col. 1100D] I return to the interrupted explanation of the time when Saint Clement was ordained bishop by Blessed Peter. I will not omit to point out that P. Christianus Lupus should be read in his learned notes on the cited chapter 32 of Tertullian’s *On Prescriptions*. After examining various authorities from ancient and recent writers, he concludes as follows:

> “It is certain,” he says, “that Clement was consecrated by Peter, and indeed for succession. Our Septimius expressly asserts this, and his authority cannot easily be refuted.”

There he also raises several questions concerning the time and cause of Clement’s ordination, and whether he was consecrated bishop at the same time as Linus and Cletus, according to Onuphrius in the year 56, or, according to his own view, promoted to the episcopal order in the year 51 of the common Christian era. After indicating the opinions of others, I will explain which view seems preferable to me.

Linus and Cletus were ordained by Peter as assistant and deputy [Col. 1101A] bishops around the year 56, when Peter himself had determined to travel through the western provinces of the empire in order to bring the light of the Gospel to them, as I related above and confirmed with documents in the notes on Saint Peter under Linus.

But since Clement is named as Paul’s fellow-worker in the Epistle to the Philippians, written around the year 60, and shortly before that is listed together with Anacletus among the deacons serving Peter—unless that passage of Ignatius’s Epistle to the Trallians, section 7, is an interpolation, as I discussed above in the notes on Linus, in these words from Cotelerius’s *Interpolated* text, page 66:

> “What, then, are deacons, except imitators of angelic virtues? They offer him a pure and holy ministry, as Saint Stephen did for blessed James, Timothy and Linus for Paul, and Anacletus and Clement for Peter”—

Clement appears to have been not yet consecrated bishop in that same year, 60. His episcopal ordination must therefore be sought between the years 60 and 65.

Vendelinus, in the cited Cotelerius, volume I, page [Col. 1101B] 139, following an anonymous Greek writer on the contests, journeys, life, and death of Peter and Paul, fixes with us the time and cause of the ordination of Linus and Cletus and of Peter’s departure from Rome for the western provinces of the empire, extending the journey even to Britain. He reports that Clement’s ordination took place on Peter’s return from Britain.

Vendelinus’s words are these:

> “After Claudius was removed from life on the third day before the Ides of October, in our year 54, Nero succeeded him. During the first five years of his reign he was a most merciful prince. Under him Peter returned to Rome, but did not spend a stationary life there. Rather, he traveled earnestly and energetically through other provinces of the world and finally penetrated into Britain. While he was absent, lest Rome meanwhile be without a head, he appointed Linus bishop in his place, during the consulship of Nero and Vetus, in our year 55.
>
> “Linus held the see for twelve years—I interpret these as years begun—that is, eleven complete [Col. 1101C] years together with four months and twelve days, the same number of months and days recorded in the Bucherian manuscripts. He therefore ceased to live in our year 66, while Peter was still alive. This is clearly confirmed by the anonymous writer on the contests, journeys, life, and death of Peter and Paul, whom the chaplain of the Earl of Arundel, Pertaeus, brought with him from Greece to England. From this work Patricius Junius cites the following notable passage, in Greek, which I render here in Latin:
>
> “ ‘After Peter had remained in Britain for several days, having enlightened many by the word of grace and established Churches, and after he had also ordained bishops, presbyters, and deacons, he returned to Rome again, having laid hands on them in the twelfth year of Nero—which was our already mentioned year 66. There he found Linus already dead and ordained Clement in his place, although Clement was unwilling and refused the dignity. After persuading him by suitable arguments and exhorting him to trust, he raised him to the chair of the divine utterances, which Linus had held.’
>
> “Baronius also found this journey to Britain from another source, and not long ago it was clearly supported,” and so forth.

[Col. 1101D] In the year 56, then, when Linus and Cletus had thus been promoted to the episcopal order, Peter departed from Rome, at one time for the eastern provinces and at another for the western provinces of the empire, to bring them to the faith. He laid the foundations of Churches and established bishops in many places, especially in the West, including those whom we listed above in the notes of Sommier on number 1, as recorded from the monuments and traditions of those Churches.

That Peter also penetrated into Britain—a journey which Vendelinus recently claims to have been clearly supported—seems to me highly probable during those same years, corresponding to the common Christian era from 60 to 63, from the opportunity for establishing the condition of that province described in Tacitus, *Annals*, Books 14 and 15.

Above, in the notes on number 1, we saw how much assistance Peter received in coming from Syria to Rome and lodging in the city, and likewise his disciples and delegates in carrying the Gospel to the nations through the western provinces of the empire. This resulted from the mobilization of the legions ordered by Gaius, when troops were summoned from every direction for the British expedition. [Col. 1102A] A second mobilization followed shortly under Claudius, and that expedition was successfully completed.

Both expeditions could have transferred there, together with the centurion Cornelius and the other soldiers—especially those of his own Italian cohort or of other cohorts stationed with him in Palestine—as well as with their baptized household members and eyewitnesses of the deeds of Christ the Lord and the apostles, as many heralds of our faith as there were soldiers. Alternatively, they could have had with them soldiers’ companions, messmates, friends, ministers of the New Testament, deacons, and ordained presbyters.

Let us now investigate whether the same opportunity for transmission as far as Britain was available under Nero after the year 60, which was close to the completion of the first five years of his milder reign, in the third consulship of Nero and that of Cornelius Cossus.

In Book XIV of the *Annals*, Tacitus lists Caesennius Paetus and Petronius [Col. 1102B] Turpilianus as consuls for the following year, 61. In that year he relates that Suetonius Paulinus, who governed Britain and was a rival of Corbulo, sought to equal or surpass the achievements of his rival through some notable action against the rebels of the island, after Corbulo had acquired exceptional glory in the preceding year by recovering Armenia.

Yet in that year Suetonius suffered so great a disaster that he learned that seventy thousand citizens and allies had been killed in the colony of Camulodunum, recently founded under Claudius, and in London and the municipium of Verulamium.

The great number of citizens and allies settled in Britain under Claudius makes it sufficiently and abundantly clear how many Roman legionaries or auxiliary allies—some sent from Rome, others summoned from Syria—Peter and the other heralds of the Gospel could have joined, and how many new legates, procurators, legionary prefects, centurions, and their relatives they could have accompanied.

[Col. 1102C] Tacitus mentions that a temple had already been established at Camulodunum for the deified Claudius, together with selected priests. Why, then, should Christians not also have attempted to spread the worship of the true religion?

But let us consider the military forces and legions assigned to Suetonius, as well as those sent afterward following the disaster just mentioned. Paetus Cerialis, legate of the Ninth Legion, commanded it. Suetonius commanded the Fourteenth together with detachments of the Twentieth, and auxiliaries from the neighboring forces—nearly ten thousand armed men. Poenius Postumius, prefect of the camp of the Second Legion, was present with his legion.

> “Caesar increased the forces,” says Tacitus, section 38, “by sending from Germany two thousand legionaries, eight cohorts of auxiliaries, and one thousand cavalrymen.”

Finally, to settle the disagreement between the legate Suetonius and the procurator Julius Classicianus, and “to observe the condition of Britain,” Polyclitus, a freedman, was sent out with great hopes on Nero’s part that through his authority not only could harmony be produced between the legate and the procurator, but the rebellious minds of the barbarians could also be reconciled to peace.

> “Polyclitus did not fail to parade with an enormous retinue, burdensome to Italy and Gaul after crossing the Ocean, and terrifying even to our soldiers.”

[Col. 1102D] Thus, to the regular army serving under Suetonius, this year the freedman of Nero added a huge retinue burdensome to Italy and Gaul and destined to terrify even the Roman soldiers, although the enemy ridiculed him because a commander and an army that had completed a war were obeying a slave.

While Polyclitus, the emperor’s freedman, was leaving Rome in the year 61 with that same enormous retinue, were there not in Rome many Christians from Caesar’s household? In their name, either in that same year or shortly afterward, Paul, writing from Rome, greets the Philippians at the end of his epistle:

> “All the saints greet you, but especially those who are of Caesar’s household.”

Most of the Fathers, interpreters, and ecclesiastical historians judge that this Epistle was written in that very year, 61, or the following year, 62. They likewise assign to this period the Epistles to the Ephesians, the Colossians, and the Second Epistle to Timothy. In the latter, since Paul greets Eubulus, Pudens, Linus, and Claudia by name as people who were with him, I could bring forward [Col. 1103A] the opinion of several writers, especially English ones, who identify this Claudia with the British woman whom they judge to have been the wife of Pudens, praised by Martial in Book IV, epigram 13, entitled “On the Marriage of Pudens and Claudia,” and likewise in Book II, epigram 54, where he praises her and her husband for their appearance and character:

> Claudia, though sprung from the blue-eyed Britons,  
> Why does she possess the heart of the Latin people?  
> What beauty of form! The Italian mothers  
> Can believe her Roman, the Attic mothers their own.  
>   
> May the gods be thanked that, fertile for her holy husband,  
> She has borne as many sons-in-law as he hopes for,  
> And as many daughters-in-law as he hopes for daughters.  
> May she so please the gods that she rejoices in one husband  
> And always rejoices in three children.

They believe that this Pudens fathered Linus, who succeeded Peter as the first of the Roman pontiffs. I will not dwell at length, however, on this British Claudia, whom I consider different from Claudia, the mother of Linus. For in this *Book of the Pontiffs* Linus is said to have been born to a father named Herculanus, not to Pudens.

[Col. 1103B] These things may at least be adduced to show how much intercourse already existed at that time between Romans and the islanders of Britain, after Britain had been added to the empire under Claudius, so that marriages and family alliances were contracted between them. This provided the Romans who professed Christ with a new opportunity to convey to the island presbyters and faithful Christians through whom the Christian religion could be propagated, and to receive into their hospitality the prince of the apostles himself, or those whom he sent to announce the Gospel.

The Greek and Latin Fathers assign to the same years, 61 and 62, after the apostle Paul’s second imprisonment, his journey from Rome to Spain. They may be consulted in Baronius under the year 61, number 2. Among them Jerome writes, in his commentary on Isaiah chapter 11, that Paul was carried in ships belonging to foreigners.

Others, together with Saint Innocent I in his epistle to Decentius, cited shortly before among the notes of C. V. Abbot Sommier on Saint Peter, assert that this journey was undertaken by Peter alone. The father of the *Annals*, however, attempts to reconcile them with the preceding authorities at the place cited.

[Col. 1103C] Whether, therefore, Peter was attached through Christians of Caesar’s household to the retinue of the enormous force that Polyclitus, Nero’s freedman, led into Britain from Italy and Gaul in that year; or whether he was carried with Paul in foreign ships to Spain and from there crossed over to the Britons; or whether he traveled with the legions, cohorts, and centuries that had previously been stationed in Syria and Palestine and were later transferred under Gaius, Claudius, and Nero to the West, and that in this year, both from Germany and from Rome, were sent by the emperor’s command to the islands in support of the Roman garrison in Britain, together with their veterans and centurions, who were eyewitnesses in Palestine of the deeds of the Lord and the apostles—as I previously explained—there was, through these multiple circumstances, a ready opportunity to visit those islanders and the whole western stretch of the empire, just as the eastern stretch, including the regions of Asia Minor and Pontus situated within it.

[Col. 1103D] No one denies that Peter traveled through those regions more than once, as Chrysostom and other Fathers cited by Baronius above affirm. Paul also enumerates in the Second Epistle to Timothy, chapter 4, the disciples who in that same year had gone there or had been sent by him, saying that Crescens had departed for Galatia, while Tychicus had been sent by him to Ephesus.

Since, therefore, the prince of the apostles had so great an opportunity between the years 61 and 64 to undertake a journey to Britain and travel through the whole West, and since the Churches of that region and their records teach us that their first bishops had been consecrated or appointed for them by Peter, I readily accept that Peter went there and afterward returned here to Rome around the year 64. At that time he commanded Clement to allow himself to be promoted to the episcopal rank and consecrated by Peter, and to be designated at some future time as successor even in the Roman see, although Clement resisted this.

[Col. 1104A] Nevertheless, I would not concede that Clement’s ordination by Peter took place after Peter’s return from his western journey and after the death of Linus, since from the documents examined above in the chronological notes on Linus’s section I understand it to be established that Linus survived Peter’s martyrdom. Eusebius expressly testifies to this in Book III, chapter 2, of the *Ecclesiastical History*, as others have observed together with Cotelerius in the notes on the pseudo-Clementine *Constitutions*, Book VII, chapter 46.

I believe that the reason for promoting Clement to the episcopal rank may be traced to the imminent completion of Peter’s martyrdom, divinely revealed to him, as he himself testifies in his second epistle in these words: “Knowing that the laying aside of my tabernacle is swift, even as our Lord Jesus Christ also signified to me.” He not only foresaw this, but had also learned that, after his death, lying teachers would enter, introducing destructive sects. He had learned from the prediction of the divine Teacher that Christ’s apostles, and the true bishops and faithful teachers established by the apostles, would above all be sought out for death. He had also seen this confirmed by the experience of the Herodian persecution, which had arisen in Jerusalem, in which James the apostle, the brother of John, had been killed by the sword, while Peter himself, the chief of the apostles, had been marked for death and was to be brought before the people after Passover, unless an angel had delivered him.

Thus, in the year 64, when the torch of Nero’s persecution had flared up from the savage fire of the city’s conflagration after the fourteenth day before the Kalends of Sextilis—that is, after July 19, the date from which Tacitus, *Histories* XV, section 41, derives the beginning of the fire—and when Nero, in order to suppress the rumor that the fire had been ordered, produced persons whom he accused; and when, under the pretext of that crime, Christians were sought for execution, although they were far removed from our customs, and an immense multitude of them were condemned to the most atrocious death, not so much on account of the charge of arson as from hatred of the human race; blessed Peter, understanding that provision had to be made for Christ’s Church and for its governance through suitable successors, by whose vigilant care the lying teachers and authors of destructive sects might be kept away during the desolation and bereavement that would threaten after his own death and that of Paul—teachers who would rage against souls even more cruelly than Nero himself—formed the plan of presenting to the Roman Church a man whom, among the disciples, he had found more suitable than the others for teaching and steadfast in apostolic doctrine: Clement.

Although he had created Linus and Cletus as bishops and had employed them as especially useful assistants, he nevertheless perceived that, for this very reason, they would be more exposed than others to the blows of persecutors and the snares of informers. Therefore, so that Clement also might be commended to the Church by the prerogative of Peter’s judgment and by the votes of the electors—for Clement had already matured with Linus and Cletus toward an equal or greater hope for the Christian name, although he shrank from the honor of the episcopate—Peter judged that Clement should be consecrated pontiff and instructed not to decline the apostolic succession even in the Roman see, if he were chosen by the judgment of the brethren to occupy it when vacant.

For this is how I interpret the words of the Anastasian text, line 7: “He, at the command of blessed Peter, received the Church and the pontificate to govern, just as the chair had been handed over or entrusted to him by the Lord Jesus Christ,” with reference to the explicit sense of line 11: “For this reason Linus and Cletus are recorded before him, because they had been ordained bishops by the chief of the apostles himself to perform the priestly ministry.”

When Peter ordained them, there was no danger that the universal Church would soon be deprived of Peter, the shepherd of the whole flock of the faithful appointed by the Lord. They could therefore more easily be persuaded to undertake the episcopal burden as a service of the priestly ministry and merely as Peter’s assistants in a vicarious capacity; since Peter was alive and would long remain among the living, the danger of governing the whole Church did not yet threaten them.

But when they were to be ordained to assume the episcopal office upon Peter’s death, which was shortly to follow and had been divinely revealed and plainly attested in writing, I believe that Linus and Cletus would have declined it in the same manner as Clement declined it. For that reason the Apostle judged that Clement had to be given an additional command to accept the episcopal office, not only in order to perform in Peter’s place the greater ministry of the priesthood, but also to assume the governance of the universal Church with the supreme pontificate, when, through those to whom the election belonged, he should be chosen as successor to Peter at his death.

For I scarcely see how the selection of the two—Linus and Cletus—for the ministry, and the designation of the third—Clement—with the command to succeed with the fullness of authority and the transmission of the chair, can be explained in any other way. It is certain from the catalogues and from the assertions of the Fathers that both those men and this one obtained and exercised that rank successively, each after the death of his predecessor.

This explanation also corresponds to the apostolic virtue of those three most holy pontiffs. Since they rightly understood both the greatness of the dignity, which surpassed human measure, and the very heavy burden of the supreme priesthood—men appointed by God and destined to answer to his judgment for the salvation of the whole flock and to render an account to him of all the souls entrusted to them—they feared both to reconcile that sublimity with their own humility and to match that danger with their own weakness.

They therefore had to be encouraged and strengthened gradually so as not to decline the burden. The two were prepared through long practice in exercising vicarious administration under the supreme authority of the chief of the apostles, who alone governed the Roman episcopate as long as he lived. Clement, however, had to be urged by commands even toward succession, if, amid so great a danger to the Church and the divinely foreseen imminent bereavement, he should be summoned to Peter’s chair, although, lacking the previous training in that same vicariate which Linus and Cletus had already administered for so many years, he judged himself less suitable than either of them, far unequal to so lofty a height, and in no way fit to be advanced to it.

The memory of events confirms the explanation given. It is established, by the testimony of all the Fathers and documents, that Linus, not Clement, was Peter’s immediate successor. It is established by the assertion of those same Fathers, confirmed by Clement’s genuine epistle to the Corinthians, that Clement abdicated the pontificate which he had assumed after Linus.
