It is no less evident from the canon of the Mass, from the Fathers, and from the catalogues that Cletus also continued the succession as Roman pontiff.

Therefore it must be clear that each displayed zeal for declining such a great dignity and obedience in accepting it. I believe that this is sufficiently evident in the wording and assertions of this *Book of the Pontiffs*, provided that the natural meaning of the words is retained and the passage is explained accordingly.

Once this interpretation and the chronology of the succession of those three pontiffs—Linus, Clement, and Cletus—are preserved, it becomes clear why Clement’s ordination is rightly reconciled with Peter’s return to Rome shortly before his martyrdom from his western journey, a return also asserted in that Greek anonymous work of Vendelinus. This is why I have composed these observations.

**Line 14.**—“He died a martyr in the third year of Trajan.” Who, then, could doubt that in the *Book of the Pontiffs* the period of Clement’s Roman pontificate is distinguished from the period of his life, prolonged for a long time after his abdication of the supreme priesthood and finally brought to completion by martyrdom?

Line 2 of this entry states that Clement sat in the Roman chair for nine years, twelve months, and ten days, under Galba and Vespasian. Line 14, however, adds that he died a martyr under Trajan; Jerome also testifies to this together with Eusebius.

The author of the *Life* knew perfectly well that between the reign of Vespasian and that of Trajan there intervened two emperors: Titus, who ruled for two years, and Domitian, who held power for nearly three lustra—almost fifteen years. Thus, when he writes that Clement governed the Church for nine years under Galba and Vespasian and survived that nine-year period for at least eighteen years, the number of years from the end of Vespasian’s reign to the third year of Trajan, he must be understood to admit that Clement voluntarily abdicated the supreme pontificate. During that period he had successors in the Roman episcopate which he had relinquished: Cletus under Vespasian and Titus, until Cletus suffered martyrdom under Domitian—which is asserted in the notice concerning Cletus; then Anacletus under the same Domitian for nine years; afterward Evaristus at the end of Domitian’s reign and throughout the succeeding reigns of Nerva and Trajan.

The Librarian reported all these matters coherently and distinctly; before him, the author of the Liberian Catalogue, in the fourth century of Christ, did the same, assigning those emperors to each of the pontiffs mentioned and likewise giving the corresponding pairs of consuls for those periods.

Therefore I cannot sufficiently wonder that, contrary to such a chronology and history—coherent in every respect and confirmed by the testimony of the Fathers and by monuments close in age and place—Eutychius of Egypt, that most unfortunate writer of the tenth century, is summoned. He knew neither his own matters adequately, while in ours he was altogether a stranger and deprived of every support—as though this Egyptian Batricides, a patcher together of old wives’ tales, as he is called among the learned, were a suitable physician for the sick chronology among our writers, as his patrons suppose.

**Line 15.**—“He was buried in Greece.”

Several learned men have written about the place where blessed Clement was exiled, suffered martyrdom, and was buried. Philippus Rondininus, canon of the Church of Faenza, collected their opinions in his work printed at Rome in 1706, *On Saint Clement, Pope and Martyr, and His Basilica in the City of Rome*.

In Book I, chapter 1, no. 11, he reports the notes of Baronius in the *Martyrology* for November 23. Baronius maintains that Cherson, a town of the Tauric Chersonese on the Cimmerian Bosporus, also called Heraclea because it had been a colony of the Heracleans, and made more famous by the exile of Justinian the Younger, was the place celebrated for the exile and martyrdom of the holy pontiff.

From there, he proves from the Acts preserved by Peter de Natalibus that the body of the same martyr was transferred to Rome through the efforts of Saints Methodius and Cyril, who are called the apostles of the Slavs and Moravians, under Hadrian II. Baronius also establishes this in his notes for March 9.

As for the statement by the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* that Clement was buried in Greece—or in Lycia—Baronius considers it a copyist’s error and believes that *Bycia* should be read instead, referring to the marsh named from the Bycus River, which Ptolemy records there in the eighth map of Europe.

“But Heribert Rosweyde” (Rondininus continues, no. 12), “in his notes on the little book of Ado, archbishop of Vienne, concerning the festivals of the holy apostles and of the others who were disciples, or near successors and successors of the apostles, for November 23, embellishing Ado’s work with annotations, writes:

‘Across the Pontus, in the desert adjoining the city of Cherson, Clement was exiled.’ He investigates and discusses, with very learned scrutiny, where Saint Clement, pope, was in fact exiled. He observes that before its last correction the Roman Breviary once read as follows: ‘He was exiled by the emperor Trajan to an island of Lycia,’ whereas later ‘across the Pontus’ was substituted for ‘to an island of Lycia.’

In the Acts preserved by Mombritius, the following is read concerning the island of Lycia: ‘Saint Clement, bishop of the city of Rome, suffered under the emperor Trajan and the governor Aufidianus in the city of Cherson in Lycia, on the ninth day before the Kalends of December.’ This reading is confirmed by a noteworthy parchment codex of the Barberini Library, seen by Rondininus.

Rosweyde more fully establishes his opinion in no. 13, quoting his own words as follows:

‘He will, I hope, pardon me if I attempt to identify the certain place of exile to which Pope Clement was banished—not so much by conjectures as by a reliable indication. I therefore believe that he was banished to the island of Leuce, also called Achillea, near Cherson. If anyone wishes the name Leuce to have been altered afterward into Lycia, I shall not strongly object. I maintain that Pope Clement was sent away to the island of Leuce.’

Thus Rosweyde.

Today Leuce is a small island of European Sarmatia in the Euxine Pontus, opposite the mouth of the Borysthenes River, with a settlement bearing the same name. It was also called Achillea by Pomponius Mela.

Rosweyde proves that this is consistent with an old manuscript of Anastasius concerning the Roman pontiffs, in Clement’s *Life*, where we read: ‘He was also buried in Greece.’ Baronius, as we stated above, erased this passage as corrupt. Rosweyde defends it as sound. This may be seen from the fact that Marius Niger, highly skilled in geography, asserts that even today the island of Leuce is commonly called Graeciaria, a name not far removed from Anastasius’s *Graecia*. Someone might even conjecture that *Graeciaria* should be read there. It may therefore have been called Greece, or Graeciaria, because the Tauric Chersonese, where it is situated, is full of Greek colonies, as Ammianus Marcellinus testifies in Book 22.

Moreover, he argues that this island was Leuce because it was especially suitable for exile and deserted. Thus Arrian, in his *Periplus of the Euxine Pontus*, says: ‘This island is deserted by human beings.’ Ammianus Marcellinus likewise writes in the passage cited: ‘In this Tauric land—that is, in the Chersonese—the island Leuce, without any inhabitants, is dedicated to Achilles.’

Finally, he thinks it was this island because it is entirely rocky and steep with cliffs, as Festus Avienus notes, apart from the Acts, in his description of the world:

> … where hollow rocks  
> open into caves within their recess;  
> where the cliffs gape apart with extended masses  
> and hang beneath a curved vault.

And this is what Rosweyde says about the place of Pope Clement’s exile, both to illuminate the old Breviary and to establish and explain the reading of Anastasius.”

Thus far Rondininus, who rightly observes that Rosweyde vindicates both readings: that of Anastasius and that of the Breviary.

To confirm Rosweyde’s vindication and extend it to the wording of the Acts preserved by Mombritius and of the old Breviary, where they name the island of Lycia, which other authors call Leuce, I shall bring together several documents. They show that almost the same place is indicated by the three descriptions mentioned shortly before: “He was buried in Greece”; “he was exiled to the desert adjoining the city of Cherson”; and “he suffered in the city of Cherson in Lycia.”

These three formulas of description signify the same inhospitable island, Leuce, sacred to Achilles and near the city of Cherson, a colony of the Heracleans. Not far from that city was the river called Leuces by Valerius Flaccus and Lycus by Ptolemy, named after another Lycus River flowing past Heraclea Pontica, the mother-city of that colony of Cherson.

The coastal district there could therefore have acquired the name Lycia among the inhabitants, just as near Troy the Lycian territory is found entirely distinct from the province of Lycia.

Antiquarians celebrate a notable coin of Heraclea Pontica, mentioned by Vaillant and others among the Greek coins of the emperor Gordian the Pious and elucidated by the learned explanations of the distinguished Florentine senator Filippo Buonarroti in his *Select Coins of the Museum of the Most Eminent Cardinal Gaspare de Carpineo*.

The obverse of the coin shows the laureate head of Gordian with the customary inscription:

> Μ. ΑΝΤ. ΓΟΡΔΙΑΝΟϹ ΑΥΓ  
> M. ANTONINUS GORDIANUS AUGUSTUS.

On the reverse are represented a circus, a six-columned temple, a statue of Hercules, and the image of an athlete who has won a victory. The letters read:

> ΗΡΑΚΛΕΩΤΑΝ ΜΑΤΡΟϹ ΑΠΟΙΚΩΝ ΠΟΛΕΩΝ

These are Doric and should be rendered in Latin as:

> HERACLEOTARUM MATRIS COLONIARUM CIVITATUM  
> “Of the cities of the Heracleotans, mother of colonies.”

The most learned interpreter shows that the Heraclea represented on this coin was founded on the banks of the Sangarius and was so near the river Lycus that Eustathius says it was separated from it by only two *jugera*. He confirms from several authors—especially Justin, Pausanias, Apollonius, and Scymnus of Chios—that it was founded by Boeotians and Megarians around the fifty-fifth Olympiad, when Cyrus obtained the Medes.

He reports that it was called Heraclea from Hercules for several reasons; he touches upon the city’s changing fortunes, both prosperous and adverse; and he enumerates the colonies founded by its citizens while it flourished, which are indicated on the coin and also mentioned by Aristotle and listed by name by Strabo.

These colonies are the Chersonesus, or Cherson, of which we are speaking, and Calatis, or Callatia.

In the colonies founded by them, the Heracleans left many traces of the places and names of their homeland. The colony itself, Cherson or Chersonesus, received the name of its metropolis, Heraclea, and was also called Heracleum by Ptolemy, as Cardinal Baronius observes in his notes on the *Martyrology* for November 23, and Baudrand in his *Geographical Lexicon*.

They likewise gave the river flowing along the neighboring shore the name of their native river Lycus, derived from their metropolis; this river is mentioned by Valerius Flaccus together with the Tanais and Hypanis, as the same Baudrand observes:

> “Lyces,” he says, “is a river of European Scythia mentioned by Valerius Flaccus with the Tanais and Hypanis, which Ptolemy calls Lycus.”

A little later, concerning another Lycus flowing past Heraclea Pontica, he writes:

> “Lycus: a river of Paphlagonia according to Pliny, flowing through the interior into the Euxine Pontus near Heraclea Pontica, and mentioned by Ovid, *Letters from Pontus*, Book IV, elegy 10.”

He then repeats under the related name that Lycus of European Sarmatia, previously indicated under the word *Lyces*, and describes its position and its flow into Lake Maeotis. It was sufficiently near the coastal district sacred to the memory of Achilles, with the inhospitable island dedicated to him near Cherson, as may be seen in the *Geographical Map of the Empire of the Ancient Romans*, published at Rome, Paris, and London.

Baudrand’s words are:

> “Lycus: a river of European Scythia according to Ptolemy, flowing into Lake Maeotis between the cities of Cnema and Hygris; it is called Lyces by Flaccus.”

Therefore, whether the island was called Leuce from the Lycus, because it was not far from the river’s mouths; or whether Lycia was the name given by the Heraclean colonists to part of the territory of Cherson, opposite the island of Leuce and the river Lycus—just as the district adjacent to Troy is called Lycian, although it is separated by a vast expanse of land from the province of Lycia in Asia Minor; or whether, just as the coastal part of the Chersonese and the island were called Achillean from the name of Achilles by those same colonists, so the river Lycus was also celebrated in memory of King Lycus, and was found to be called indiscriminately Leuces by the colonies, just as the island was called both Leuce and Lycia—it becomes sufficiently clear from the origin and foundation of these colonies in the Tauric Chersonese by the Heracleans of Pontus, marked both by private investigation among geographers and by public testimony on coins, that the readings of the *Book of the Pontiffs* do not contradict one another or conflict with the readings of the Breviary and the Acts.

The *Book of the Pontiffs* says that Saint Clement was buried in Greece; the Breviary and the Acts record his martyrdom and burial on the island or coastal district of Cherson in Lycia, where the mouths of the Lycus River opened between the Tanais and the Hypanis. The different names of the same place must be understood as Greece and Graeciaria, Lycia and Leuce, the territory near the Lycus or Leuces River, and the Chersonese or Cherson, the colony of the Heracleans established across the Euxine Pontus or lying nearby.

The more rigid critics must therefore restrain their censorious rod. They do not hesitate to consign to fables the accounts found in the Acts and in ancient, genuine documents concerning Clement’s exile across the Pontus; concerning his martyrdom completed at Cherson under Trajan; and concerning the manner of his death by drowning—as though these reports had been drawn from interpolated or fabricated little narratives and the dreams of apocryphal writers.

They admit that the apostle John was exiled by Domitian to Patmos, an island in the Aegean opposite Asia Minor, after learning from Tertullian that John had been immersed at Rome in a vessel of boiling oil for the sake of defending the Christian faith, and that he emerged from it unharmed by divine power.

They admit that philosophers, especially Stoics, were expelled from Rome under Vespasian, Domitian’s father, and exiled to islands; some were even beheaded, as Dio asserts. They are merely afraid to admit that Clement was exiled under Vespasian or Domitian to a place somewhat beyond the Aegean and Patmos, to which John was exiled under that same Domitian.

They doubt only Clement’s drowning under Trajan, as though such things had not occurred even in milder times. Yet they acknowledge the genuine letters of the excellent emperor, who replied to Pliny that among the Christians denounced in Bithynia for refusing to sacrifice to the gods, some ought to be punished. They also regard as truthful the history of Tacitus, Suetonius, and Dio, which relates that under the equally mild emperor Claudius an entire fleet of condemned men—nineteen thousand people—was assigned to death, shipwreck, or burning if they refused to fight, for the sake of a spectacle at the dedication of a public work on Lake Fucinus.

We, considering the ancient monuments of the Church more honorable, assert with Eusebius and Jerome that Clement survived until the beginning of Trajan’s reign. With the *Book of the Pontiffs* and the catalogues, we believe that he left the Roman pontificate under Vespasian, was driven into exile as far as Cherson, and suffered martyrdom there. We believe that his sacred body lay buried there until Saints Methodius and Cyril, bishops called the apostles of the Slavs and Moravians, arranged for its transfer to Rome in the ninth century of Christ, while Nicholas I governed the Church.

There is no need to discuss here the second translation, by which some maintain that the body—or parts of the body—was carried to the island of Piscaria. Although those who assert it assign it to the time of Hadrian II, not even a trace of it is found in the *Book of the Pontiffs*. It therefore requires no treatment in our notes.

The aforementioned Rondininus subjected this alleged translation to mature examination; his work may be consulted for the arguments by which it is refuted. I shall mention one point: in the notes of R. P. Pagi the Younger, which will shortly be quoted for this entry, a new error concerning this translation to Piscaria seems to have arisen under Louis II. Pagius thrusts the island of Piscaria in the Lake of Benacus, in Venetian territory, upon us—an island unknown to our countrymen—in place of the island of Piscaria in the territory of Casauria, on the Aterno River in Abruzzo Citeriore, a province of the Kingdom of Naples. The dispute among the authors examined by Rondininus concerns the transfer of the relics of Saint Clement, pope and martyr, to that latter place.]

[Note: **Column 1109C**

**Line 5.**—“He caused the seven regions to be divided among notaries.” Saint Clement appointed seven notaries, among whom he divided the fourteen regions of the City, so that each might diligently and carefully record the deeds of the martyrs investigated in his respective region. The protonotaries of the Roman See, who are called participating protonotaries—formerly seven, now twelve—preserve their shadow.

**Line 7.**—“He composed two epistles which are called Catholic.” The most holy and learned pontiff wrote, in the name of the Roman Church, a most powerful and weighty epistle by which he quelled the schism of the Corinthians and strengthened their wavering faith. It has nevertheless perished through the injury of time.

This shows that from the beginning the Roman Church also interposed its authority in regulating the churches of the Greeks. Eusebius writes that the epistle bore precisely the same character and style as that which Paul used in his epistle to the Hebrews, *Ecclesiastical History* II.

Noteworthy fragments of this epistle are found in Justin Martyr, *To the Orthodox* 47; Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I, IV, and VI; Basil the Great, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 29; Athanasius, *Disputation against Arius at the Council of Nicaea*; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies* 27; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III, chapters 16 and 37; Jerome, Book I of *Against Jovinianus*, and the shorter commentary and Book IV, chapter 4, on Ephesians; and Irenaeus.

A second epistle is also circulated under his name, which Jerome says was rejected by the ancients. Five other epistles of Clement are extant, concerning the true faith and the proper establishment and governance of the Church, addressed to James, the brother of the Lord and bishop of Jerusalem. The eighty-five canons of the apostles and the eight books of the *Apostolic Constitutions* are likewise attributed to him.]

[Note: **Column 1110A**

**Line 4.**—“Many books.” Those two epistles are proved to be genuine and authentic by the testimony of the ancients who cite them. Saint Irenaeus mentions the first in Book I of *Against Heresies*, chapter 3, as a repository of tradition. Origen, *On First Principles* II, chapter 3; Saint Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* I; Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* III, chapter 38; Saint Jerome, in the catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, under Clement; Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 113; and others likewise praise it.

The second is mentioned by Photius, codex 126, and by Saint Epiphanius, *Heresy* 30, no. 15. From these fragments it may be gathered that the latter epistle contained salutary instructions and an exhortation to a better life, as Photius writes in that passage. Natalis Alexander, in the first century, refutes the arguments brought against those epistles.

Besides these two epistles, five others circulate under Saint Clement’s name. The first two are addressed to James, the brother of the Lord; the third to all bishops, presbyters, and faithful; the fourth to Julius and Julianus; and the fifth to the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

Since all of them are rejected by learned men as spurious, as are the ten books of the *Recognitions*, the *Itinerary of Saint Peter*, the *Disputation of that same apostle with Appion*, and the *Liturgy*, which are attributed to the same Clement, we judge it superfluous and useless to discuss them, since they have already been rejected and condemned by everyone. On these matters the aforementioned Natalis Alexander should be read.

Moreover, all Clement’s works, both genuine and spurious, collected together and illustrated with notes, were published in Greek and Latin by the same Cotelerius in the *Apostolic Fathers*, Paris, 1672, folio.

Here, however, something brief must be said about the *Constitutions* and *Canons of the Apostles*, whose two collections many attribute to Saint Clement. Although both are counted among the apocrypha, the *Canons of the Apostles*, as they are commonly called, are nevertheless filled with a distinctive teaching of the primitive Church.

The *Constitutions*, contained in eight books, were published in 1573 by Carolus Bovius, bishop of Ostuni, who translated them from Greek into Latin. Franciscus Turrianus afterward translated them into Latin and illustrated them with commentaries.

The author of these *Constitutions*, however, is not Clement of Rome. For Eusebius, Book III, chapter 15, and Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, when discussing the writings of Saint Clement, list only one epistle of his, addressed to the Corinthians.

Moreover, Cardinal Humbert, bishop of Silva Candida and legate of Leo IX at Constantinople, replied in these words to Nicetas Pectoratus, who cited certain passages of the *Apostolic Constitutions* against fasting on Saturday:

> “You attempt to establish this from apocryphal books and canons, which the holy Fathers have rejected with equal judgment.”

A little later he adds:

> “Therefore we too, rejecting every apocryphal work, disdain to listen to their fabulous traditions, because they are not like the law of the Lord.”

Nicetas had cited the fifth and seventh books of the *Apostolic Ordinances*, or *Constitutions*. From Humbert’s response, Christian Lupus concludes in Part II, on canon 2 of the Council in Trullo, that the *Constitutions* were apocryphal and that this had been the opinion of the Apostolic See, whose legation Humbert was exercising.

Besides Lupus, Schelestratius should also be read, *Illustrated Antiquities*, Part II, Dissertation II, chapter 2; Natalis Alexander, in the first century; and others who discuss these *Constitutions* at greater length.

As for the collection circulated under Clement’s name, in which he is said to have gathered the eighty-five canons of the apostles into a single body and presented them to the faithful, Marca writes in Book III, chapter 2, no. 5, that it appears to be earlier than the Council of Nicaea but later than the year 258.

The reason for the earlier date is that the emperor Constantine cites the thirteenth canon in his second epistle to Eusebius and the Antiochenes, from which it follows that those canons were known before the Council of Nicaea.

He deduces that they were later than the year 258 because Firmilian, bishop of Caesarea, did not use them to prove the custom that prevailed in the East of rejecting the baptism of heretics, although the canons openly supported that practice.

Canon 45 is worded as follows:

> “We order that a bishop or presbyter who has admitted the baptism or sacrifice of heretics be deposed. For what fellowship is there between Christ and Belial? Or what portion does the faithful have with the unbeliever?”

Canon 46 reads:

> “If a bishop or presbyter baptizes again one who truly possesses baptism, or if he does not baptize one who has been polluted by the impious, let him be deposed, since he mocks the death and cross of the Lord and does not distinguish priests from false priests.”

Since Firmilian, in his epistle to Cyprian, while fighting against the baptism of heretics, attacked the custom praised by Pope Stephen in a sharper style than was proper for a Catholic bishop, and did not cite the aforesaid canons in the year 256 or 257, when he wrote that epistle, it may be inferred from his silence that the apostolic canons were unknown at that time.]

[Column 1111C]

It may be inferred from the most ancient collection of canons—first compiled in the East by the Greeks and in existence before the time of Dionysius Exiguus—that these canons prevailed after the time of the Council of Nicaea, both in the East and in the West, among certain Catholics, although their number met with varying fortunes.

Thus the statement which Pope Gelasius included in the Roman synod of seventy bishops—“The book of the canons of the apostles is apocryphal”—should be understood in a reasonable sense. Apart from the fact that these words are not found in Justellus’s manuscript, it may be said that Pope Gelasius spoke thus because these canons were not collected by the apostles themselves but by others.

Hence Marca, cited above, rightly says in no. 7:

> “There are various classes of apocrypha in the notice of Gelasius, as learned men have observed. For not only the inventions of heretics fall under this designation, but also little works of theologians in which there are certain blemishes.”

We need no other example than the history of Eusebius, which Gelasius counts among the apocrypha, although shortly beforehand he had declared that it should be accepted. He evidently wished to say that these books of histories were mixed with certain blemishes, although, as he says, “because of the singular knowledge of events that contributes to instruction, we do not say that they should be rejected in every respect.”

The same, says the aforementioned Schelestratius in chapter 1, must be said of the *Canons of the Apostles*: they are filled with a distinctive teaching of the primitive Church, although, because of certain blemishes arising elsewhere, Gelasius lists them among the apocrypha.

Nor, Schelestratius continues, were these canons rejected by the ancient Greek or Latin writers, as is evident from the fifty canons that were once universally received and as is confirmed after Gelasius by the collection of Dionysius Exiguus.

After Dionysius came Cresconius, a bishop of some city in Africa—I do not know which—who in his collection enumerates as many as fifty apostolic canons and cites them to support his headings.

Anastasius the Librarian also mentions Pope Stephen IV, or rather III, who decreed in the Lateran synod of 769, in its fourth session:

> “No more of the canons of the apostles put forward by Saint Clement are to be received, except the fifty chapters which the holy Catholic Church of God in Rome has accepted.”

Holstenius published this council. Humbert, the legate of Leo IX, confirms the decision cited from it in his response to the work published by Nicetas, a presbyter and monk, against the Latins:

> “The Fathers count Clement’s book—that is, the *Itinerary of the Apostle Peter*—and the *Canons of the Apostles* among the apocrypha, except for the fifty chapters which they decreed should be added to the orthodox faith.”

And this concerns the Western Church: it did not reject the fifty apostolic canons, but ultimately approved them through pontiffs and synods and received them almost everywhere.

The Eastern Church extended its acceptance of the apostolic canons more broadly. John Scholasticus was the first to insert all eighty-five of them into his collection of fifty titles, as Justellus notes in the preface to volume II of the *Bibliotheca Juris Canonici*. This same John was a presbyter of the Church of Antioch, belonging to the order of the Scholastics; in his preface he says: “The holy disciples and apostles of the Lord issued eighty-five canons through the work of Clement.”

After John’s collection, the Council in Trullo also received and approved them, in canon 2; and after that, the Seventh Ecumenical Council, which in its first session agreed that books both of the canons of the holy apostles and of the holy synods should be brought forward from the library of the patriarchate of Constantinople:

“And the venerable notary of the patriarchate read: The fifty-third canon of the holy apostles [now the fifty-second]: If any presbyter does not receive one who is turning away from sin, but rejects him, let him be deposed,” and so forth.

Alexius Aristinus, a deacon of the Church of Constantinople, counts them up to seventy-seven in his *Synopsis of the Canons*, now published for the first time in volume II of the *Bibliotheca Juris Canonici*. After Aristinus there follows an epitome of the canons by Symeon, the Master and Logothete, in which eighty-two apostolic canons are presented [Col. 1112C]. There also follows the *Synopsis of the Canons* of Arsenius the monk, who adds at chapter 4: “Eighty-five canons of the holy apostles,” and repeatedly presents other apostolic canons, so that it is clear that he accepted eighty-five canons. Long before those collectors, Photius likewise accepted them in his *Nomocanon*, for which he writes in the published preface: “The canons called those of the holy apostles, collected through the work of Clement, number eighty-five.”

From this it can be seen that the Easterners generally accepted all eighty-five canons. In fact, they are found after the decree of Gratian, published by order of Gregory XIII, as well as commonly in all editions of the councils. See further the aforementioned Schelestratius and Natalis Alexander, *Dissertatio de primo saeculo Ecclesiae*. Cotelerius should also be consulted in his notes on the apostolic canons, contained in the second part of the *Works of the Holy Fathers who flourished in apostolic times*.

**Line 15.—“He was buried in Greece,” etc.** His [Col. 1112D] body was transferred to Rome during the pontificate of Hadrian II and thereafter, at the request of Louis Augustus II of that name, carried—with the approval of the same Hadrian II—to the monastery of Casa Aurea, founded by Louis himself on the island of Piscaria, at Lake Benacus, today in Venetian territory, as may be read in volume III of the *Baronian Criticism*.

[Note: [Col. 1112D] Volume I of the *History of Dogma*, p. 122.]

**Line 7.—“He composed two letters.”** One of his letters survives for us, written to the Corinthians. After it had been intercepted and lost for many centuries, it was fortunately discovered about eighty years ago at the end of a biblical codex, whose age is said to reach back to the time of the Council of Nicaea. It is established that this codex was brought from Turkish territory to Charles I, King of Great Britain, as Patritius Junius relates in the preface to the same letter, which he published.

[Col. 1113A] The ancient Fathers praise the aforementioned letter of Clement in lofty terms. They recognize it as the strongest testimony to the authority of the Roman Church: for preserving peace and unity among the faithful, strengthening more firmly those who were wavering in faith, and announcing and impressing more deeply upon their minds the apostolic tradition. Irenaeus uses these very words:

“Under this Clement” (he says in book III, chapter 3, *Against Heresies*), “when no small dissension had arisen among the brethren who were at Corinth, the Church that is at Rome wrote a very powerful letter to the Corinthians, bringing them together into peace, restoring their faith, and announcing the tradition which they had recently received from the apostles.”

Eusebius of Caesarea, who speaks of Clement’s letter in nearly the same terms, adds that in his own time a custom had arisen in many Churches of reading it publicly (*Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 12):

“Only one letter of this Clement is reported, approved by the judgment of all: that celebrated letter, truly illustrious and entirely worthy of admiration, which he wrote, in the person of the Roman Church, to the Church of the Corinthians when a serious and swollen rebellion had already arisen at Corinth. We have learned that in the memory both of the ancients and of our own generation it has been publicly read and used in many Churches.”

He gives a summary of the same letter, especially of the matters there stated concerning the preservation of humility, avoidance of rivalry, the rules of obedience, and reverence toward those who preside over us by divine authority, as they are read in the translation of Patritius Junius, p. 126:

“Let our body, therefore, be preserved in Christ Jesus, and let each person be subject to his neighbor according to the order and dignity in which he has been placed by His grace and favor . . . . The high priest has been assigned his own offices; the priests have been given their proper place, and the Levites have their appointed ministries; the layman is bound by lay precepts. [Col. 1113C] Let each of you, brothers, remain in his own order and station, giving thanks to God with a good conscience and maintaining himself decorously within the limits of his prescribed ministry. To stir up sedition against the presbyters—and this report has spread not only to us but also to those who are more estranged from us and from the faith in mind—remove this from your midst as quickly as possible. For it is better to be found small in Christ’s fold and held in good esteem than to seem superior to others and be cast outside its boundaries.”

After quoting these passages from Clement’s letter, Sommier continues as follows on page 126.

Would that many in the Church of the West today read Clement’s letter as frequently as the Easterners once occupied themselves with its reading! Would that its reading now proceeded with the same success with which it proceeded in ancient times among the Corinthians! They would certainly acquire similar sentiments of veneration toward Clement XI and toward Clement I, whose successor he is. From this they would conclude—just as was established in the age of Irenaeus, from whom we possess such an illustrious testimony—that the Catholic Church has always regarded and employed this as the most excellent remedy for averting and undoing the corruption of morals, and for confounding and removing perverse and false doctrines: namely, that appeal and recourse should be made to that tradition and faith which the Roman Church received from the apostles; that we should hold that this Church, recognized throughout the world from all antiquity as the chief of all Churches and pre-eminent in authority, within whose bosom the purity and integrity of the Christian religion have always shone forth through an unbroken succession of bishops, is necessarily the Church with which every church—that is, all the faithful everywhere—must agree.

“The greatest and most ancient Church,” says Irenaeus (*Against Heresies*, book III, chapter 3), “known to all, founded and established by the two most glorious apostles Peter and Paul, indicates the tradition which it has received from the apostles and the faith announced to humanity, coming down to us through the succession of bishops. By this we confound all those who, in whatever manner—whether through evil self-pleasing, vainglory, blindness, or an evil opinion—gather otherwise than they ought. For with this Church, because of its more powerful primacy, every Church must agree—that is, the faithful everywhere—in which the tradition that comes from the apostles has always been preserved by those who are everywhere.”

Saint Clement had also given the same Corinthians a second letter, of which only some fragments remain. These indicate to us that it contained salutary admonitions for rightly ordering one’s life. Photius, *Bibliotheca*, codex 126:

“There is also a second letter, which likewise contains instruction for a better life.”

See also Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 32, and Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, under Clement. The authority of this second letter is not as certain as that of the former.

In the earlier centuries of the Church, other works were also attributed to Pope Clement, such as the books of the *Recognitions*, or *Acts of Saint Peter*, whose testimony Origen used in volume III of his *Commentary on Genesis*, translated into Latin by Rufinus; the *Apostolic Constitutions*, cited by Saint Epiphanius in heresies 25, 45, 70, and 80, of which we possess several editions today; and the *Clementines*, namely, a collection of letters and other works bearing the name of this Clement. But since some of these are clearly spurious, while others are mutilated and interspersed with errors, we shall not produce them in order to use their testimony to support what I have to say concerning the Holy See.

**Line 14.—“Five bishops in different places.”** The Roman Martyrology, on 11 August, mentions Saint Taurinus, a bishop ordained by Clement. Yvo of Chartres and Baronius also mention other holy bishops who went to Gaul at the command of the same pontiff:

“This man [Clement] sent Fortinus to the people of Lyon, Paul to Narbonne, Gratian to Tours, Julian to Le Mans,” and so forth.

Yvo of Chartres, in the *Chronicle*, in the manuscript cited by Patritius Junius. See Baronius under the year 95, no. 7.]

[Col. 1077]

## 4

Clement, a Roman by nationality, from the district of Caeliomons [Note: [Col. 1077] B: “of Caelius Mons.”], son of Faustinus, sat for nine years, two months, and ten days [Note: [Col. 1077] B: “six months and six days.”]. He lived in the times of Galba and Vespasian [Note: [Col. 1077] B: “Domitian, Nerva, and Trajan.”], from the consulship of Trajan and Italicus until the ninth consulship of Vespasian and Titus [Note: [Col. 1077] B: “of Trajan III and Fronto III.”]. While he was composing many books out of zeal for the Christian religion, he was crowned with martyrdom [Col. 1079]. [Note: [Col. 1079] See Baronius under the year 98.]

He caused the seven districts to be divided among faithful notaries of the Church, so that each of them might diligently and carefully investigate the deeds of the martyrs throughout his own district. He composed two letters, which are called Catholic [Note: [Col. 1079] C: “canonical.” See Baronius under the year 95.]. At the command of blessed Peter, he received the Church and the pontificate to govern it [Note: [Col. 1079] “The pontificate for governing the Church.”], just as the chair had been handed over or entrusted to him by the Lord Jesus Christ. Nevertheless, in the letter written to James, you will find how the Church was entrusted to him by blessed Peter [Note: [Col. 1079] “That in the letter, etc., will be found.” See Baronius under the year 69.]. For this reason Linus and Cletus are written before him, because they had been ordained bishops by the Prince of the Apostles himself to perform the priestly ministry.

He held two ordinations in the month of December: ten presbyters, two deacons, and fifteen bishops in various places. He died a martyr in the third year of Trajan and was also buried in Greece [Note: [Col. 1079] See Baronius, *Martyrology*, 23 November.], on the eighth day before the Kalends of December [Note: [Col. 1079] C: “the ninth day before the Kalends.”], and the episcopate was vacant for twenty-two days [Note: [Col. 1079] B: “for several months and days.”].

### Catalogue under Liberius

Clement, nine years, eleven months, and twelve days. He lived in the times of Galba and Vespasian, from the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus until the seventh consulship of Vespasian and Titus.

## V. SAINT ANACLETUS, IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 103, THE FOURTH YEAR OF THE EMPEROR TRAJAN

[Note: [Col. 1115A]

In Fabrottus, from the Freher codex.

No. 5. Same line: A, twenty-three days; B, twenty-one. Line 2: A, twelve years, ten months, seven days; B, eleven years, one month, seven days. Line 3: AB, “Sabinus.”

From the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuane codices.

Line 2: “in the time of Domitian.” Line 3: “Sabinus.” Line 4: “And he established it, when he had been ordained presbyter by Peter, where the bodies of other bishops might be laid in burial. He also established that a cleric should not grow long hair; he likewise composed two decretal letters full of all wisdom. Under the emperor Domitian he received the glory of martyrdom by beheading, and was buried near the body of blessed Peter, on the third [Mazarin: fourth] day before the Ides.”

Line 1: “He sat nine years, two months, and ten days,” but in Penia another reading is written above: “eleven years, two months, and seven days.” Line 3: “under Domitian X and Sabinus.” Line 4: “Here he constructed a memorial of blessed Peter.” Line 6: “the third day before the Ides of July.”]

[Note: [Col. 1115A]

**Line 4.—“Here he constructed and arranged a memorial of blessed Peter.”** During the persecution itself, Anacletus dedicated a memorial—that is, a sacred building—to blessed Peter. “Memorials” of the apostles and martyrs were the sacred chapels built during the persecution in their memory, so that their memory might be celebrated there.

Optatus of Milevis, book II:

“Finally, if Macrobius is asked where he sits there, can he perhaps say: ‘In the chair of Peter,’ which I do not know whether he has even seen with his eyes, and to whose memorial he does not approach, like a schismatic?”

And shortly afterward:

“Behold, the memorials of the two apostles are present there.”

And below:

“If it seems impious to you, or you regard it as a crime, to have shared in the memorials of the apostles and of all the saints.”

Augustine, on Psalm 44:

“Let the temple of Romulus be shown to me at Rome in as great an honor as I show there the memorial of Peter.”

The same, on Psalm 65:

“It is better that, when the emperor comes to Rome, he should lay aside his diadem and weep at the memorial of the fisherman, than that the fisherman should weep at the memorial of the emperor.”

The same, on Psalm 140:

“The emperor has come to Rome. Where does he hurry—to the temple of the emperor, or to the memorial of the fisherman?”

The same, *City of God*, book XXII, chapter 10:

“But we do not build temples for our martyrs as for gods; rather, we build memorials for them as for dead human beings, whose spirits live with God.”]

[Note: [Col. 1115C]

**Line 4.—“Here he constructed and arranged a memorial of blessed Peter, when he had been made a presbyter by blessed Peter.”** The final words, which also appear in the second catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, suggest the origin and ancient institution of presbyters of the martyrs. Others have touched upon this only briefly; we undertake to explain it in the present observation, while several matters occurring below are illuminated by that explanation.

In the primitive Church, two kinds of men are read of as chosen by Churches and bishops for ministries to be performed for martyrs: deacons, for carrying out the bodily services connected with the martyrs; and presbyters, for the care of their souls and their spiritual [Col. 1116A] salvation.

Concerning the service rendered to martyrs by deacons, and their diligence in carrying out their ministry, there are notable passages among the ancients. Since writers record more about these matters, however, we must pause briefly in order to convey knowledge of the presbyters of the martyrs, with whom this *Liber Pontificalis* is concerned.

The words cited above show that this responsibility belonged to episcopal concern, and that special care was taken in promoting the office. For the *Liber Pontificalis* says that Anacletus constructed a memorial, or tomb, and assigns as the reason for its construction that he had been made a presbyter by Peter.

This presbyteral care, however, was not attached to the order by its original institution, but by an additional deputation. It must be understood as nothing other than an assigned ministry and an office entrusted to a presbyter, particularly for relieving the needs of the martyrs in the Spirit and for providing them with every aid toward salvation and the exercise of their profession of faith.

That the care involved in choosing and appointing a presbyter for the service of the martyrs, specifically in matters concerned with the salvation of souls, was properly episcopal is shown by Cyprian. For this purpose he published a short work, *On the Exhortation to Martyrdom*, prepared at the request of Fortunatus, perhaps a presbyter of the martyrs [Col. 1116C]. At the very beginning of the book he makes clear that it was composed to represent both the bishop’s particular care and the office of the presbyter of the martyrs:

“You desired, dearest Fortunatus, that, since the weight of persecutions and afflictions presses upon us . . . I should compose from the divine Scriptures exhortations for preparing and strengthening the minds of the brethren, by which I might encourage the soldiers of Christ to the heavenly and spiritual contest. Your desire had to be obeyed, since our modest ability, furnished with divine inspiration, should draw forth from the Lord’s commands, as it were, weapons and fortifications for the brethren who are about to fight.”

Cyprian said that it was necessary—whether because of the episcopal burden or because of the obligation of the office entrusted to Fortunatus—to provide weapons and fortifications for those about to fight, so that in the narrow crisis of the contest the soldiers might stand in the battle line with a cheerful and steadfast spirit. He continues by explaining this as follows:

“It is little that we rouse God’s people with the trumpet of our voice, unless we strengthen by divine reading the faith of believers and the virtue dedicated and devoted to God. What, moreover, is more fitting or more important to care and diligence than to prepare by constant exercises, against the darts and arrows of the devil, the people and army divinely entrusted to us and stationed in the heavenly camps? For a soldier cannot be fit for war unless he has first been trained in the field . . . . Nor will one who seeks to gain the athletic crown be crowned in the stadium unless he has first practiced the use and skill of his strength.”

That Cyprian wished to form and instruct the presbyter Fortunatus for the worthy performance of his duties is shown and proved by the very direction of the short work. It is addressed not to the martyrs—although its exhortation is directed to their courageous struggle—but to Fortunatus, because the office of presbyter of the martyrs had been entrusted to him. His special ministry was to equip the martyrs confined in prison and fighting for the faith with spiritual weapons, and to strengthen them through the practice of the virtues [Col. 1117B].

Further proof of the assigned purpose of the work is drawn from the three books of testimonies addressed to Quirinus, which Cyprian elaborated with exactly the same aim, collecting from Scripture the principal passages for the practice of the virtues. He describes the subject of the work transmitted to us as follows:

“On account of the faith and love which you display toward the Lord your God, dearest son, you asked me to extract from the holy Scriptures certain chapters pertaining to the religious discipline of our way of life, in order to instruct you. You sought a concise diligence in divine reading, so that a mind devoted to God might not be wearied by long or numerous volumes of books, but, instructed by a brief compendium of heavenly precepts, might possess a wholesome and great summary for refreshing its memory. And since I owe you a service full of love, I have done what you asked, so that I might labor once and you might not labor continually.”

That Quirinus requested instruction from Saint Cyprian so that he might be made more suitable for carrying out the office of presbyter of the martyrs—and indeed that he diligently performed the office according to the instruction he had received—is declared by the martyrs themselves. They wrote to Cyprian and praised Quirinus, thereby commending both this episcopal care and the office of the designated presbyter of the martyrs (*Letter* 78):

“Those condemned, therefore, together with us, give you, dearest Cyprian, the greatest thanks before God, because by your letters you have refreshed hearts that were suffering . . . . And he has both fulfilled and continued your ministry, our dearest Quirinus.”

Likewise, four bishops, replying to Cyprian in the following letter, declare:

“We have therefore received, dearest brother, what you yourself and Quirinus sent: a sacrifice from every good work.”

Rogatianus was another presbyter of the martyrs. Because of the office he performed among the martyrs, Cyprian, writing to the confessors, calls him “your presbyter.” In his fifth letter to the martyrs he commends him and urges them to follow his counsels:

“That you follow in all things the glorious presbyter Rogatianus, an old man, who by religious virtue and divine favor is making for you the way to the glory of our age. Together with our brother Felicissimus, always calm and sober, he received the assault of the raging people and first prepared a lodging for you in prison. Just as your presbyter, he now also goes before you. Let us pray to the Lord in continual prayers that, as those who have begun are proceeding toward the highest things, so those whom he makes confessors he may make martyrs crowned.”

By this expression he clearly indicates the office and the prerogative of the office when he says, “Just as your presbyter, he now also goes before you”: namely, that outside the prison he served them in the presbyteral office, while in prison he went before them both in the duty of the ministry entrusted to him and in action, standing before them as an exhorter by his own example toward the glorious completion of martyrdom through confession.

In this sense he calls the presbyter Celerinus, who had likewise been endowed with this office and who continued diligently to perform it even while confined in prison, “the overseer of God,” because he not only exercised that presbyteral office but was also a companion of the prisons and punishments (*in the following letter*):

“And now he has been made an overseer of God over them.”

Cyprian considered this office so necessary and dignified that in Letter 37 he wrote to the clergy of Carthage, exhorting them to love suitable ministers for relieving the needs of the martyrs, and declaring that he himself desired to exercise the office and attend the confessors through his own ministry:

“Although I know, dearest brothers, that you have frequently been admonished by my letters to provide every care for those who have confessed the Lord with a glorious voice and are confined in prison, nevertheless I repeatedly press this upon you, lest anything be lacking in the care of those for whom nothing is lacking as regards glory. And would that the condition of my place and rank permitted me to be present myself now, ready and willing, in the solemn ministry, to fulfill every service of love toward our bravest brothers! But let your diligence represent my office and do everything that ought to be done for those whom divine favor has made illustrious in such merits of faith and virtue.”

The holy bishop desired to fulfill every service toward the bravest martyrs through his solemn ministry. Thus the special care of these presbyters, which Saint Cyprian urges and develops throughout the entire letter, was to attend to the spiritual needs of the martyrs.

The duties of the presbyter of the martyrs that we have gathered from Cyprian—for whose complete ecclesiastical observation we are indebted to him—were as follows.

First, to look after the martyrs’ salvation by means of exhortations and sacrifices. The former concern has already been discussed. Regarding the second, the solemn ministry, he observes that it had to be carried out cautiously, lest the persecutors’ hostility be aroused. He writes to the clergy that such caution should be used:

“Therefore consult and take care that this may be carried out more safely with due moderation, so that the presbyters who offer there among the confessors, each with a deacon, may alternate in turn, because a change of persons and a rotation among those who gather together lessens hostility.”

Second, they were to know how to provide the ministries prudently, distinguishing among the confessors: those who were to be crowned, those who had escaped gloriously after receiving the mark upon their bodies, and the exhortations that had to be supplied to each.

Thus he commands the clergy of Carthage to admonish the presbyters of the martyrs (*Letter* 6):

“Let more attentive care also be shown to the glorious confessors. Although I know that many of these have been received through the brothers’ prayers and love, nevertheless, if there are any who lack clothing or food, as I also wrote to you previously while they were still confined in prison, let whatever is necessary be supplied to them—provided only that they know this from you, so that they may be instructed and learn what ecclesiastical discipline has established according to the teaching of the Scriptures: that they must be humble, modest, and peaceful, so that they may preserve the honor of their name, and that those who have been glorious in voice may also be glorious in conduct.”

He notes that instructions and distinct exhortations were to be supplied by the presbyters of the martyrs to the confessors, saying:

“To the glorious”—a name applied to confessors who displayed in a mark or scar the evidence of their confession, and who, because of the stigmata they bore, he decreed were to be honored with more attentive care. By this name Saint Cyprian frequently designates Cornelius the pontiff, who received these stigmata in prison. He rebukes Novatian, however, who repeatedly called himself a glorious confessor without a mark, as may be read in Cornelius’s letter to Cyprian—“to the glorious confessors, I say, instructions are to be supplied, so that they may persevere in what they have begun. But to those who, without a stigma and by the confession of Christ alone, escaped from prison, he commands the presbyters, according to the Gospel and ecclesiastical discipline, to direct admonitions so that they may not become inflated but remain in fear. He shows from the teaching of Scripture that they ought to be humble, peaceful, and modest.”

Salubrious sayings collected by Cyprian occur in the books of testimonies concerning this command. Apollonius, cited above by Eusebius (*Book V*, chapter 18), calls it an injunction of ecclesiastical discipline, against which Themision acted:

“Themision, covered over by splendid greed, did not bear the mark of confession but, after spending a great amount of money, threw off his chains, although for this reason he ought thereafter to have acted more modestly and humbly, presenting himself as a martyr,” and so forth.

From this there arises a third duty of the presbyter of the martyrs, proceeding from the spiritual care they provided to the martyrs: namely, to write down who had completed martyrdom, who were glorious confessors, and who had confessed Christ by voice alone and escaped from prison, so that honors or further exhortations might be supplied to each. There are many Cyprianic letters and observations of other Fathers concerning these matters.

Such was Tertullus, mentioned above, who was chosen by Cyprian to explain all the deeds of the martyrs.

Fourth, if the savagery of the persecutors prohibited access to the confessors—a matter of which Dionysius of Alexandria complains in a letter quoted by Eusebius, book VII, chapter 11, p. 261:

“To this very day the prefect does not cease either to kill with the utmost cruelty some of our people who are brought before him, to tear others apart with tortures, or to wear others down with the squalor and chains of prison, while forbidding anyone to approach them and investigating whether anyone appears to approach”—

then, so that those detained in prison would not be deprived of this presbyteral ministry and the necessary assistance of exhortation, the presbyters of the martyrs fulfilled the same duties through letters secretly sent in.

Such must be considered the exhortation of Tertullian, or the book entitled *To the Martyrs*, which seems to have been published in such circumstances, as is sufficiently understood from the beginning of the short work, where he approaches the matter as follows (*To the Martyrs*, book II):

“Among the bodily nourishment, blessed designated martyrs, which the mistress Mother Church supplies to you from her breasts, and each of the brothers from his own resources, in prison, receive from us something that may also nourish the spirit.”

Here both forms of the Church’s care are expressed: supplying food to the confessors and sharpening their spirit, especially that of those who were nearest to the contest, whom Tertullian designates by his customary title: “blessed designated martyrs.”

He then develops both kinds of care:

“For it does no good for the flesh to be fattened while the spirit hungers. Rather, if anything is weak, let it be cared for; equally, what is weaker must not be neglected. I am not so great that I should address you . . . . Nevertheless, just as not only the trainers and leaders of the most accomplished gladiators but also ordinary and insignificant people exhort them from a distance, so that often suggestions shouted by the crowd itself have proved useful . . .”

Perhaps Tertullian, as a presbyter of Carthage devoted to this ministry, wished, while savage persecution forbade access to the prison, to direct from a distance, as it were to gladiators engaged in combat, the shouted suggestions of exhortation, so that those nearest to the fight would not be deprived of the necessary encouragement.

Moved by the same zeal, Cyprian, when he heard that Rogatianus, the presbyter of the martyrs, had been confined in prison with the others—although he held him in the highest regard and knew that all, after their first contest, were being pressed by the judge’s sentence toward the imminent completion of martyrdom—nevertheless wished through several exhortatory letters to encourage both Rogatianus and the others to courage and endurance.

Thus he speaks of the letters written to those same martyrs (*Letter* 7):

“First of all, I sent letters to you, dearest and bravest brothers, in which I congratulated your faith and virtue with exultant words . . . . Nevertheless, through our common faith and the true and sincere love of our heart toward you, we exhort you: you who have conquered the adversary in this first encounter must hold fast your glory with brave and persevering virtue . . . . You must take care that after these beginnings you also advance to greater things, and that what you have begun to be through fortunate first efforts may be completed in you.”

We find a stricter confinement, by which all access to the martyrs was prohibited, mentioned in the acts of the martyrs, perhaps written by the presbyters themselves. There we read either of the “delicate custody,” as Pontius says in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*, or of the “diligent custody,” as Heraldus states in his notes on Tertullian’s *Apologeticum*, p. 97, and Cujacius observes, book XIV, chapter 16.

Hence, whenever the severity of that confinement was relaxed even slightly, the sacred ministers immediately flocked together to hold spiritual conferences. This seems to be the point of the acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicitas, cited on page 16, when Pudens, the soldier and warden in charge of the prison, somewhat relaxed their former confinement because of their virtue:

“After a few days, Pudens, the soldier, assistant and overseer of the prison, who held us in high regard, began to understand that there was great virtue in us. He admitted many to us, so that both we and they might be refreshed.”

That the presbyters ought to have taken more diligent care in visiting the prisons is taught by Saint Cyprian (*Letter* 5). He sought to moderate the zeal of certain persons who were trying to bring assistance to the designated martyrs, and therefore admonished the clergy of Carthage:

“I also ask that your prudence and diligence not cease in procuring quiet. And although the brothers, out of their love, are eager to meet and visit the good confessors whom divine favor has already made illustrious through glorious beginnings, nevertheless I think this must be done cautiously, not in a crowd or with a multitude gathered together at once, lest hostility be aroused by this very thing and access be denied, so that while we want too much and are insatiable, we lose everything.”

Those whom Tertullian called “blessed designated martyrs” he therefore called good confessors whom divine favor had already made illustrious through glorious beginnings. Opposed to these are those who were false martyrs, concerning whom the same Tertullian says in *To Scapula*, chapter 4:

“Let those who pretend to the sect look to themselves; we ourselves reject them.”

Finally, if the presbyters of the martyrs conducted themselves well in carrying out their ministry, they were promoted to a higher rank. Numidicus, a presbyter who had rendered energetic service, was raised by order of Cyprian to the first rank among the presbyters of the Church of Carthage. Cyprian writes to the Carthaginian clergy in Letter 35:

“Know that you have been admonished and instructed by divine favor that the presbyter Numidicus is to be enrolled among the number of the Carthaginian presbyters and is to sit with us in the clergy, shining with the brightest light of an illustrious confession and exalted by the honor of virtue and faith. By his exhortation he sent before him a great number of martyrs who were killed by stones and flames . . . . and he will be promoted, when God permits, to a higher place.”

No other place remained for him except promotion to the episcopate. Such was the concern Cyprian showed for the presbyter of the martyrs.

To Anacletus, therefore, Peter is credited with assigning this office first: the office which Anacletus fulfilled by burying the sacred remains of bodies and erecting a memorial. For this kind of care was also proper to the presbyter of the martyrs, so that either he himself, or through his command, diligence, or care, the bodies and mangled limbs of the martyrs might be reburied in a suitable place.

Concerning this concern of the presbyters, Dionysius writes in his letter to Domitius and Didymus, when he speaks of the ministers of the Church who had been appointed by the Church for the service of the martyrs. Among others, he praises Eusebius, who, as stated above, watched over this work:

“Eusebius, whom God strengthened and impelled from the beginning, so that he might diligently provide his ministry to confessors held in custody—indeed, strict custody, from which access was denied—and so that he might bury the bodies of those who had completed their course among the blessed martyrs, not without danger to his own head.”

While the Roman clergy were writing to the Church of Carthage during the vacancy of the see, in Saint Cyprian’s Letter 3, and listing the clerical ministers of the martyrs, they specially commended this care in the following words:

“And what is most important: if the bodies of the martyrs or of the others are not buried, great danger threatens those upon whom this work rests. Therefore, whoever among you, in whatever circumstance, brings this work to completion, we are certain that he will be judged a good servant.”

Saint Cyprian also identifies the kinds of martyrs to whom this care should be extended (*Letter* 37):

“That more attentive vigilance and care be shown toward the bodies of all those who, although they have not been tortured, nevertheless depart from the prison by a glorious exit in death.”

These remarks concern the presbyter of the martyrs on the occasion of Anacletus, whom the ancient catalogues present and commend also because, having been appointed a presbyter by Saint Peter, he built a memorial above his sacred remains.]

Line 5.—Or other places where bishops might be deposited for burial. In the second catalogue this passage is read as follows: “Here he constructed and arranged a memorial of blessed Peter, while he had been made presbyter by blessed Peter, where bishops might be deposited.” The *Liber Pontificalis*, however, added the words “or other places,” in order to designate the beginnings of the celebrated Vatican cemetery, where the burned and mangled bodies of the earlier martyrs killed in Nero’s slaughter were deposited, together with those of the pontiffs. These places were intended not only for preserving the bodies, but also for sacred ecclesiastical assemblies held during the persecution. Tertullian recalls this custom in chapter 3 of *To Scapula*, when he reports the cries of the raging populace, which endeavored to deprive Christians of every right of burial, just as it did deprive them of it, and Africa was afflicted with barrenness as a punishment:

> “We must grieve that no city will suffer the shedding of our blood with impunity, since they shouted concerning the plots of our burials: ‘There must be no burial plots; the burial plots themselves did not exist for them, for they did not reap their harvests.’”

From this there arose a custom at other principal sees as well: bishops who succeeded one another were buried near the apostle who had already been deposited there. This is attested by the acts of Saint Peter of Alexandria in the Cambefis edition, where his death is described as follows:

> “When the blessed man had finished his prayers, and had kissed the tomb of the evangelist Mark and of the bishops placed there with him, he returned to the tribunes.”

And shortly afterward:

> “They carried him to the southern side of the sacred church of the evangelist Mark and led him into the valley in which the monuments were situated.”

That sacred assemblies were accustomed to gather in these places is taught by the same acts, when they report the dispute over the burial place of the body of Saint Peter. Some wished him to be buried with the other bishops near Saint Mark, while others preferred another place. The former wanted him buried near the apostle Mark, where he had also lived. This “living together” designates the place where the holy martyr held the sacred assembly.

This practice continued until the time of Gregory III, and among the Roman clergy there was a presbyter appointed to take charge of the burial of the pontiffs. Such was Gregory III. The *Liber Pontificalis*, after saying that he “advanced through the ranks and reached the sacred order of the presbyterate,” immediately adds (p. 173):

> “The Roman men, or rather all the people, from the greatest to the least, suddenly, when his predecessor had departed from this world, violently seized him while he was attending before the bier in the service of his predecessor, and elected him to the order of the pontificate.”

[Note: [Col. 1121D]

**FROM THE SECOND CATALOGUE. Line 4.—“Here he constructed and arranged a memorial of blessed Peter.”** By the memorial of blessed Peter understand a certain structure erected by Anacletus in the Vatican while he was still a presbyter, which ancient usage formerly and more commonly called a church. Thus Augustine too says in *The City of God*, book XXII, chapter 10:

> “We do not build temples for our martyrs, as for gods, but memorials, as for dead human beings whose spirits live with God.”

The ancient theologian Caius, who flourished in the time of Pope Zephyrinus, rightly calls such memorials *trophies*, as Eusebius testifies in book III of his *History*, chapter 24.

**FROM THE LABBE EDITION. Line 7.—“Two ordinations.”** According to Platina, one.]

[Note: [Col. 1122A]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

That Anacletus must be distinguished from his predecessor Cletus, whom several ancient writers, including some of the Fathers, had confused because they were led astray by the similarity of their names—just as Eusebius fused Marcellinus and Marcellus into a single pontiff—was decisively demonstrated by Schelestratius in *Illustrated Antiquities*, dissertation II, chapter 2. He showed that this distinction is strongly confirmed by the documents of the Roman Church, since the homeland, parentage, periods of office, and martyrdom of the two men are entirely different. This can be established from the consuls assigned to each of them in all the catalogues and lectionaries, which agree remarkably on these matters, even though the manuscripts differ in the number of years, months, and days assigned to the same pontiffs.

Since, therefore, all the manuscripts are in such agreement concerning the first and final consulships of Anacletus’s see—namely, from Sabinus, colleague of Domitian in his tenth consulship (A.D. 84), to Clement, colleague of Domitian in his seventeenth consulship (A.D. 95)—and since Cletus’s martyrdom is recorded on April 26, in the consulship of Domitian IX and Rufus (A.D. 83), while Anacletus’s is recorded on July 13, in the consulship of Domitian XVII and Clement (A.D. 95), it follows that the figures for the years, corrupted and varying through the fault of copyists, must be reduced to the true reading corresponding to the assigned consulships.

The year of Saint Cletus’s martyrdom was marked by the consulship of Domitian IX and Rufus (A.D. 83), and the day was April 26. From that date to April 26 of the Christian era A.D. 95, under the consulship of Domitian and Clement, there are twelve complete years. From April 26 to the next consuls, Valens and Vetus, assigned to the Christian era A.D. 96 and the first consuls assigned to Evaristus, thirteen complete years are completed on April 26. From April 26 to July 13, the date assigned to Anacletus’s martyrdom, there follow two months and seventeen days.

From this total of thirteen years, two months, and seventeen days, subtract the twelve years, ten months, and seven days assigned to Anacletus’s see both in the paintings of the Basilica of Saint Paul and in the most ancient catalogues collected in the time of Liberius and Felix IV. Those sources differ from the total by only four days. What remains is four months and ten days, which must be assigned to the vacancy of the see between Cletus’s martyrdom and Anacletus’s episcopal ordination. On this calculation, that ordination fell on Sunday, September 7, of the year A.D. 83.

For if one begins from that date to count the twelve years, ten months, and seven days shown for Anacletus in the paintings of Saint Paul, Anacletus’s martyrdom will correspond to July 13, the day on which he is commemorated, and to the year of Christ A.D. 96, under the consulship of Valens and Vetus, with Evaristus placed first in the catalogues.

The reason for so lengthy a vacancy, extending over four months, can be made sufficiently probable if one considers the condition of the Roman Church at the time when Cletus became a martyr, as well as the circumstances and deeds of the principal men who survived Cletus. When Cletus underwent martyrdom, blessed Clement was still alive. We saw above that he had resigned the Roman pontificate, which he had held for nine years after Linus’s death; and Jerome and other Fathers establish that Clement prolonged his life until the third year of Trajan.

Both Greek and Latin writers relate that Clement was exiled across the Pontus, near Cherson. That he nevertheless came to the aid of the Church in its labors and dangers, when it appealed to him for assistance and counsel, although he had already relinquished the government of the universal Church together with the Roman pontificate, is demonstrated by the letter Clement wrote to the Corinthians in the name of the Roman Church. Vendelinus judges it to have been written during the persecution of Domitian, in the year of Christ A.D. 95—eighteen years after Clement had voluntarily laid down the highest pontificate—so that the hatred of the pagans, already aroused against him, might not be inflamed against the shepherd and bring destruction upon the whole flock.

When, therefore, Cletus died, Clement enjoyed such esteem in the Roman Church, which had been deprived of its shepherd, that it was painful for the Church to see two bishops consecrated by the apostle Peter, Linus and Cletus, consumed by martyrdom, while the third, Clement, still survived. He too had been initiated by the same Prince of the Apostles and had even been designated as Peter’s successor, yet had resigned after nine years of experienced governance. It is credible, therefore, that the Romans were unwilling to proceed to the election of any successor until they had first tested whether Clement could be persuaded to ascend again the cathedra of this Church.

Whoever might have been elected would have been still less willing to proceed without knowing Clement’s mind or awaiting his counsel and encouragement—especially if Clement persisted in his resignation—by which the new elect could be strengthened to undertake the burden of the highest priesthood. Whether Clement was then living across the Pontus or was occupied with other apostolic journeys—for certainly he was far from Rome, consistently withdrawing from the vicinity of the Roman see for the reason mentioned above—the four-month interval should not be considered longer than necessity required.

Clement’s constancy in refusing the office should not have been removed by Cletus’s death in A.D. 83, since the same causes remained in force under Domitian that had compelled him to go into exile in A.D. 76, during the reign of Vespasian his father, and to resign the honor of the supreme pontificate.

I said in the chronological notes to the *Life of Saint Clement*, section 7, that the defense of our doctrines and of the prophecies announcing to Christ the Lord the sovereignty of peace—which the servile flattery of the Jews and pagans had tried to apply to Vespasian when he dedicated the Temple of Peace in A.D. 76—gave Clement an occasion to vindicate the oracles of the Christian faith not only by word but also in writing. For this reason he incurred the hatred of the flatterers and attendants of that prince, as though he were writing curses against the emperor, whom he did not honor with divine honors but affirmed to be utterly different from the Prince of Peace indicated through Isaiah.

I found this in what is commonly called Clement’s Second Epistle, although Vendelinus proved that it should be regarded as the earlier one. It was published by Cotelerius in volume I, p. 140, column 2, together with the other Epistle, and the same letter is mentioned by Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, in Eusebius, book IV, chapter 23. Vendelinus, cited above, found it and thus drew attention to Clement’s careful concern in turning the faithful away from the shameful flattery of Caesar and confirming them in the confession of faith that assigns the sovereignty of peace with Isaiah not to any mortal being, possessing nothing beyond humanity, but to Christ the Lord, the God-man, wondrously uniting divine and human nature in himself.

Speaking of the time when the letter was written, he declares:

> “The time itself indicates a period of profound peace, disturbed by no dangers to the Church, and therefore all the more suited to exhorting people to mutual charity and to fostering peace. To obtain this peace, there should not be found a human being who bestows it, but God, obviously. By these words, unless I am mistaken, Vespasian the emperor is indicated. In our year 75, during his own auspicious consulship, he dedicated the Temple of Eternal Peace, the most beautiful building in the whole world, believing himself to be that Prince of Peace, the Father of the age to come, foretold by Isaiah, whose empire would have no end. Clement therefore teaches that it is not this mortal man, but God, who must be found to bestow eternal peace on his people. This letter, therefore, is earlier than the other, which was sent to Corinth only after twenty years.”

This is Vendelinus’s view: the letter commonly called the Second, but in reality Clement’s earlier letter to the Corinthians, was written in A.D. 75, while the other letter that Clement wrote to the same Corinthians—not in his own name but in the name of the Roman Church—was written in A.D. 95 of the common Christian era.

The period he called “a time of profound peace, disturbed by no dangers to the Church” was that earlier period under the emperor Vespasian, in the Christian year A.D. 75, when the letter in question was written. Yet it soon became turbulent both for Christians and for philosophers and sophists, as I explained above in the chronological notes to the *Life of Clement*, section 7.

For Christians, the cause was the assertion of the sovereignty of peace belonging to Christ God, as Vendelinus discovered in Clement’s letter. For philosophers and sophists, it was the insults hurled against the emperor by certain individuals. Because of these, all persons, both guilty and innocent, were ordered to leave the city; among the obstinate, Hostilius and Demetrius were exiled to the islands, Diogenes was beaten with rods, and Eras was beheaded, as I reported there from Greek and Latin historians.

The same causes, then, that had led to the assertion of Christ the Lord’s sovereignty of peace—causes that could arouse suspicion of revolutionary activity under the emperor Vespasian against Clement, the supreme hierarch of the Church, if he remained in the city, and that we believe providentially drove him into exile and to resign the primacy of the cathedra he held—continued no less forcefully under Domitian. They therefore caused him consistently to refuse the honor of succession after Cletus’s death.

Who could doubt that rumors or suspicions of an attempted empire would likewise have been aroused by Clement, so great a leader and standard-bearer of our religion, if he were once again regarded as first among the bishops and participants in Christ’s royal priesthood, while members of the Flavian family still survived? Public flattery in Rome, mistress of the other nations, bestowed upon them the eternity of empire and the sovereignty of peace—especially since Domitian’s ambition had grown so far beyond his father’s that he wished everywhere to be inscribed and regarded as God and Lord. Perhaps he did this so that the populace would not think anything lacking to make him appear to the Romans heir of his father’s condition and sovereign of peace.
