Therefore, lest Clement’s presence under Domitian revive against the whole urban assembly of the faithful the untimely hatreds that had been avoided and suppressed by the law of exile and by his voluntary resignation of the highest priesthood under Vespasian, he may have judged it better to refrain from returning to Rome and from resuming the cathedra he had already abandoned. Preferring this course, and continuing to exercise the office of an apostolic bishop beyond the solitudes of Pontus, he may have instructed the Roman clergy to proceed to the free election of Cletus’s successor. They did so by elevating Anacletus to the seat of Peter.

Learned men long ago observed signs of this providence and affection in Clement’s letter to the Corinthians, written in the name of the Roman Church. These signs disclose sentiments favoring voluntary exile whenever danger threatened of disturbances arising from the presence of one individual. “If,” he says, “sedition, contention, and schisms have arisen because of me, I will emigrate and depart wherever you wish.” Or, as Epiphanius reports in *Against the Carpocratians*, heresy 27, chapter 6, when he recalls Clement’s resignation: “I withdraw; I depart; let the people of God be firmly established.” He says that he found these words in certain commentaries, as Vendelinus notes on p. 139, column 2 of Cotelerius’s edition. They also occur in the Greek edition of 1544, folio 51:

> Ἀναχωρῶ, ἄπειμι, εὐσαθήτο ὁ λαὸς τοῦ Θεοῦ·  
> “I withdraw; I depart; let the people of God be firmly established.”

These words correspond more aptly to the situation mentioned above: Clement refraining from the highest pontificate and withdrawing from the city of Rome so that the whole Church would not be exposed to danger and persecution because one bishop had resumed a dignity from which he had willingly and voluntarily removed himself only a few years earlier, so that the people of God might be firmly established.

We reserve the remaining matters for the historical notes. We have touched on these points in the chronological notes because it was necessary to determine the periods of these pontiffs. The chronology of Anacletus seems to be assigned as follows.

After Cletus received the crown of martyrdom on April 26, A.D. 83, under the consulship of Domitian IX and Rufus, the see remained vacant for four months and ten days—the result of the double calculation set out at the beginning of these notes—namely, until September 6. During this period Clement’s intention was tested, to discover whether he would again undertake the helm of the whole Church together with the Roman pontificate, although he had previously resigned it.

When Clement consistently refused to return to Rome and again ascend the cathedra of Peter, lest the pagans be given an opportunity to persecute the Christian people as factious if, contrary to the law of exile promulgated against Clement by the emperors, they were to recall him to his homeland—he was well known by reputation and prominent through his writings—and appoint him again as chief of the priesthood, Anacletus was elected Roman pontiff on Saturday, September 6. On the following day, Sunday, September 7, of the same year, A.D. 83, he was consecrated bishop.

He celebrated the first Easter of his pontificate in A.D. 84, under the consulship of Domitian X and Sabinus. He held office from Sunday, September 7, A.D. 83, to July 13, A.D. 96, under the consulship of Valens and Vetus, which is assigned as the beginning of his successor’s term for a reason to be given at the beginning of the notes concerning Evaristus.

Thus his pontificate amounts to twelve years, ten months, and seven days—the period assigned to Anacletus both in the paintings of the Basilica of Saint Paul, in the most ancient catalogues from the age of Liberius and Felix IV, and in several of the Colbertine catalogues published above among the preliminary materials.

For what reason the final consuls assigned to Anacletus are Domitian XVII and Sabinus, corresponding to the Christian year A.D. 95, and why the number eleven years agrees with these in four catalogues derived from the Italian manuscripts of Bergamo, Cava, Farfa, and Lucca, I shall explain in the indicated place, namely at the beginning of the notes to be presented under Evaristus.

## HISTORICAL NOTES OF THE SAME AUTHOR

**Line 2.—“In the time of Domitian, from the tenth consulship of Domitian, etc.”** In the chronological notes I briefly treated several matters from the histories both of Clement and of Anacletus. Those who follow Pearson and Dodwell may perhaps consign them to the realm of fables, disparaging the credibility of both Greek and Latin writers of pontifical history and claiming that they follow more closely the traces of truth, which they imagine they encountered in an entirely unknown author. They do not doubt that Eutychius, the tenth-century Alexandrian writer, drew from this source the material he arranged in his *Annals* concerning the dates and succession of the Roman pontiffs.

They profess to have been moved to this position because they see that Eutychius’s assertions “agree most closely with their own observations, deduced with great labor and diligence from the monuments of history, without a guide and without a companion,” as Pearson candidly admits in Dissertation I, *On the Succession of the First Bishops of Rome in General*. Yet, in judging Eutychius’s *Annals*, he says that he does not greatly dissent from the opinion of Labbe and of the learned men who think that the *Annals* are scarcely worth a penny whenever they disagree with the approved Greek and Latin authors.

Those minds are so disposed that they assert that, from a tenth-century writer whom they suppose to have copied his material from an ancient author wholly unknown both to them and to us, one may safely and ought to recover chronological and historical accounts that differ from all the Greek and Latin writers of ecclesiastical history and chronology. Such minds do not greatly trouble me if they wish to count as fables all that we have labored to collect under the guidance and companionship of Greek and Latin authors.

By Pearson’s own judgment they ought to be led to distrust both Eutychius’s work and their own. The Chester scholar did not value these materials so highly that he published his dissertations during his lifetime; indeed, he did not even complete them. The editors admit in their dedicatory letter that the work was unfinished, although they add that, when it was published posthumously, it was finally brought to completion by Dodwell, the friend of the deceased author.

Let the editors therefore keep the whole of the praise for themselves—no one begrudges it to them, perhaps not even Dodwell himself—if it is praise to boast that they tread the traces of truth in history and chronology without companion or guide, while placing before them both the Egyptian writer Eutychius and his followers as a torch to illuminate their penetration into the affairs of the Roman Church, from an assumed author known to no one, not even by name.

I think that every sensible reader would more readily avoid the tracks of Eutychius, Pearson, and even the editors themselves, in order to pursue historical and chronological truth through known Roman monuments and with reliable authors providing guidance and companionship, authors who point to documents no less ancient than genuine, marked and supported by writers close to them in age, place, and office.

Pearson’s and Dodwell’s theories are sufficiently weakened by their own testimony, with which they close the dissertation cited above, chapter 14, sections 3 and 4. I shall quote Pearson’s words in full, so that the reader’s judgment may determine whether what our method has gathered concerning the pontifical chronology can be overthrown by uncertain documents and authors from which Eutychius, a worthless writer—as all learned opinion supposes—allegedly stitched together his work from the scraps of another person whom no one identifies, or says where or when he lived.

> “Since I considered the common chronology of the Roman pontiffs, especially of the earliest ones, highly suspect, and judged that it ought to be reformed according to the truth of ecclesiastical history, and since I thought that I had accomplished this in some measure through my own industry, I saw that Eutychius’s *Annals* presented another chronology of the earlier pontiffs, differing remarkably from both the Latins and the Greeks, and—what seemed surprising to me—agreeing most closely with my own observations, drawn with great labor and diligence from the monuments of history, without a guide or companion. From whom Eutychius obtained his material I truly do not know. Without doubt he received it from some earlier writer entirely unknown to us, who had woven together the years of the pontiffs with the years of the emperors in the manner of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, but with very great differences from Eusebius, both at the beginning of Linus’s pontificate and in the years of Anacletus. From these misarranged matters, it seems, the principal remaining errors in Eusebius flowed.

> “I am certainly not unaware of what learned men have hitherto thought about the Eutychian *Annals*, and I see that their judgment may rightly be understood from Labbe, who, at the end of the Council of Antioch, notes the following with his customary freedom:

> “‘The very gross and very frequent errors of the Eutychian *Annals*, especially in chronological matters, have produced this result among learned readers: they are scarcely valued at a penny whenever they disagree with Socrates, Sozomen, Evagrius, and other approved Greek and Latin writers.’

> “Nor do I greatly dissent from this judgment. As I showed at length in the *Vindications of Ignatius*, this Batricides was very ignorant of ancient history, and the tenth-century writer cannot himself be compared with the writers of earlier centuries. Yet I do not doubt that he possessed some earlier author on chronology whom he followed. I have therefore judged that this author’s traces must be dug out and followed only in those periods concerning which none of the ancient Greeks or Latins is found to have possessed sufficiently certain knowledge. In sum, strengthened not insignificantly by the authority of this Eutychius, but relying chiefly on my own observations drawn from ancient ecclesiastical history, I thought that the earlier bishops of Rome should be assigned their years in the manner set out in the second dissertation.”

The posthumous editors of Pearson’s work will, I hope, persuade only a few readers that, through such conjectures—from a source assumed to exist in the books of the Arabs and transmitted to Eutychius—the documents of the Roman Church can be overthrown. From its beginning, that Church recorded matters not only in the acts of the martyrs and the reports of notaries, but also, frequently, on the stones of cemeteries: the day and consulship of the burial of martyrs and the faithful.

These documents, transcribed from there and recorded in diptychs, catalogues, and lists of pontiffs depicted in the principal basilicas from the fourth Christian century onward, preserve the pontifical chronology. We have collected it under reliable guides and companions belonging to each age.

When it has been established that Jerome was not guessing when he extended Clement’s life to the third year of Trajan; that Epiphanius was not deceiving us when he reported having found Clement’s resignation in ancient manuscripts; that the canon of the Mass and the martyrologies did not fabricate Cletus and Anacletus as distinct pontiffs; but rather that John Thane, the principal editor of Pearson’s and Dodwell’s posthumous work, was acting foolishly when, in his dedicatory letter, he flattered his patrons and boasted that truth, long driven from the cathedra of Peter, had fled for refuge to the see of Canterbury; when he proclaimed that Dodwell had completed Pearson’s unfinished work according to his own numbering; and when, together with them, he rejected as fables the documents of the ancients recording the beginnings and limits of Cletus and Anacletus under distinct consulships—then the recent defenders of Arabic and Eutychian chronology will also fall. Learned men, together with Labbe, rightly regard these chronologies as worthless.

These defenders are so eager to disperse the periods of the pontiffs mentioned above and to reduce Clement’s years, and so ready to dismiss his exile, deeds, and martyrdom as fables, that they even attempt to destroy the discipline and institutions of the nascent Church, especially with respect to sacred virgins.

They sufficiently destroy themselves with their own weapon when they bring forward foundations so weak for their own position. For, in the final part of the first dissertation, which I have quoted, they themselves provide a sponge to erase the marks and obeli that they had implanted by their own ingenuity in the years and consulships.

But they object that in the Bucherian catalogue the first four pontiffs are listed in this order: Linus, Clement, Cletus, Anacletus. In the later catalogue and in the *Liber Pontificalis*: Linus, Cletus, Clement, Anacletus. In Pseudo-Tertullian: Linus, Cletus, Anacletus, Clement.

When they raise this objection, I first congratulate our chronology: these documents, much older than the Eutychian materials, just like the paintings of Saint Paul, recognize Cletus as distinct from Anacletus, whereas Pearson and Dodwell confused them into a single Anacletus.

Next, I rejoice that they arrange this first tetrad of Roman pontiffs in different ways. If the reason for the difference is sought, it will clearly reveal a twofold testimony of antiquity by which the catalogues are confirmed. One testimony is that of the sacred diptychs, or canon of the Mass, in which names were placed according to the epoch of martyrdom brought to completion by death. The other is the succession of pontiffs, arranged in annalistic books or in pontifical lists according to the order of election and initiation.

The Bucherian catalogue displays the latter order, as is clear from the consulships assigned throughout the catalogues. From this it follows that Clement was elected after Linus’s death.

The canon of the Mass and the later catalogue—which seems to have looked to the same canon and to the lists or diptychs of the martyrs—placed Linus and Cletus, who were killed for Christ before Clement, before Clement, although Clement received the crown of martyrdom later. Pseudo-Tertullian also placed Anacletus before Clement, for the same reason, I think, although the second catalogue places him afterward, and most writers were not sufficiently certain how to calculate the three-year interval between the martyrdoms of the two men.

The canon of the Mass does not mention Anacletus. Instead, after Clement it names only one successor from each succeeding century, for a reason that I shall soon explain.

When they arranged the canon, the supreme pontiffs did not intend to review all the names of their predecessors who had suffered martyrdom, since they wished to preserve suitable brevity. This custom is still rightly retained in our own time both in the canon of the Mass and in the public prayers called the litanies, in which not all the names of the saints are recited, but only a few from each class.

When arranging the canon, therefore, both in the prayers said within the action—or, as some prefer, during the action—and in those immediately following the consecration, they were content, after the three initiated by the apostle Peter, to name one representative from each of the two succeeding centuries.

Thus Xystus was selected from the second century and Cornelius from the third before the consecration. After the consecration, Alexander from the second century and Marcellinus from the third were chosen to be named. No other was added, nor was Telesphorus included, although Dodwell is so certain that Telesphorus was a martyr that he asserts he was the first among the Roman bishops whom he read in ancient writers to have suffered a glorious martyrdom.

It is reasonable to believe that our bishops wished to imitate the examples of the sacred books, especially the Book of Ecclesiasticus. Its author, intending in chapter 44 to praise his glorious ancestors, could have listed many more men distinguished by holiness and deeds, but selected only a few or one from each class: Enoch from the patriarchs before the Flood; Isaac from the descendants of Abraham; Joshua from the judges; and likewise from the remaining classes, prophets, priests, and kings.

The compilers of our canon imitated this example. After selecting a few names from each century, they preferred to include the remaining martyrs—and the whole body of the saints—under a collective designation, namely, “all the saints.” They judged that the succession of pontiffs and martyrs in the Church during those earlier centuries after Christ, at the time when the canon was composed, would be sufficiently indicated if one representative from each century were selected by name from the classes mentioned above.

Let them therefore cease bringing a lawsuit against us over the different number and order of the names found in the catalogues and in the canon. Both arrangements correspond to the distinct purposes of the two books: the pontifical records supplied the periods of election and consecration, while the diptychs of the martyrs supplied the order and date of death and burial. Cardinal Bellarmine also observes this in book II of *On the Mass*, chapter 26: the martyrs are listed in the canon according to the order of their passion, not of their dignity, since Stephen the deacon is placed before the apostle Matthias.

I shall briefly note here, in order to remove the objections raised in Pearson’s posthumous work against the dates and deeds of Clement and of the other neighboring pontiffs, that these matters are not found in writers contemporary with Irenaeus and Cyprian, or at least in writers of the Eusebian age.

Let those subtle investigators of history and chronology remember that, in the inventory of ancient documents of ecclesiastical history—especially of Roman history—there must be many things that Eusebius did not see and that it was not necessary for Ignatius, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, or other writers of their age or of the Eusebian period to mention. They were not writing a history of the bishops of the Roman see, but didactic and apologetic books.

The historical documents of the Roman Church, marked by the blood of the martyrs, may still be seen on the marble tablets sealing their burial compartments. More than once these tablets record, through the consuls, the year, and through the other marks, the month and day of burial for many of the faithful who rest with the martyrs. They are found in inscriptions in the city and in suburban crypts.

There the acts and passions of the martyrs, recorded by the seven notaries instituted by Clement, were not merely recited. Each year, together with sacrifice and prayers, the gathering of the faithful visited these places in memory of the martyrs who had been crowned on the same day and buried in the same place.

“We make offerings for the dead, for their birthdays on the annual day,” wrote Tertullian in *On the Crown of the Soldier*. Cyprian states this even more clearly in book III, letter 6, addressed to his presbyters and deacons, which is letter 37 in Pamelius’s edition:

> “Record the days on which those who were crowned for Christ departed, so that we may celebrate their commemorations among the memorials of the martyrs. Although our most faithful and devoted brother Tertullus, in addition to the other solicitude and care that he exercises toward the brethren in every work of service—for he is not lacking in his care for their bodies—has written and continues to write and inform me of the days on which our blessed brethren pass from prison to immortality through the exit of a glorious death, and on which offerings and sacrifices are celebrated here by us in commemoration of them, which, with the Lord’s protection, we shall soon celebrate with you.”

I referred to this letter in section 18 of the preface to the first volume of Anastasius. If the reader wishes to consult that preface, both at that section and in the following sections up to 32, he will perceive how unjustly the stricter critics, Dodwell and Pearson, reject the chronology, martyrdoms, and many deeds of the earlier Roman pontiffs recorded in fourth-century catalogues from the documents of the Roman Church mentioned above—even though these matters are not mentioned by Eusebius or by writers earlier than Eusebius.

The bishop of Caesarea himself knew very well that not everything had been recorded by Hegesippus, Irenaeus, Clement of Alexandria, and others. For this reason he warns the reader that many things omitted or only briefly treated by writers can be collected and confirmed from Roman inscriptions and cemeteries. He writes as follows in book II of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 25:

> “It is handed down that Paul was beheaded in Rome and Peter was crucified under the same emperor, Nero. This account is abundantly confirmed by the monuments bearing the names of Peter and Paul, which are still visible in the cemeteries of the city of Rome.”

He also shows that this method of confirmation was approved by Caius, a Catholic man who wrote against Proclus, the defender of the Cataphrygians, under Pope Zephyrinus. Caius said:

> “But I can point out the trophies of the apostles. For whether you wish to go to the Vatican or to the Ostian Way, you will encounter the trophies of those who founded that Church.”

7. We therefore rightly use our own sources if we prefer to recover the dates, deeds, and martyrdoms of the Roman pontiffs—committed to writing by the Church’s notaries, engraved on marble, and affixed to the martyrs’ burial niches [Col. 1129C], together with the blood they shed, of which Prudentius is a substantial witness—from our own archives, diptychs, festal calendars, catalogues, basilicas, and inscriptions, founded, adorned, and painted by public care close to the time of the events, rather than fishing them out of Eutychius of Alexandria, a tenth-century writer who followed I know not what more ancient author, posited by Pearson and Dodwell and answering their arguments against the calculations of all Greeks and Latins.

Nor is there any doubt that Hegesippus, Clement of Alexandria, and Eusebius would have acted as we do. In their writings, many events are reported as confirmed by the testimony of a single man whom they had heard or read as having lived close to the apostolic age—such as Eusebius’s accounts of the apostle John (*Ecclesiastical History* III.23 and 28), of the other apostles in the same book, chapter 30, and of Symeon in chapter 32, together with similar examples. They would therefore have admitted with much greater willingness those things that were recorded in the public registers of the Church and supported by the testimony of the ecclesiastical community [Col. 1129D].

“But,” they say, “readings are reported under public authority that were altered in the latest revisions during the previous century. In those revisions the names and dates of Trajan or Hadrian, which had been attached to the same pontiffs in the manuscripts of the earlier period, were deleted and replaced in more recent copies.”

This very fact, however, confirms that the Roman Church never abandoned the practice of correcting later copies of its books against the testimony of an autograph or an older exemplar preserved in its archives, and of comparing them with the writings and traditions of the apostolic age and with more reliable documents. No one can prevent the errors of scribes and copyists from occurring; but recognizing, correcting, and restoring the genuine reading belongs to the Church’s diligence. We pursue that diligence by consulting the more ancient monuments of this Church and the texts issued under public authority, in accordance with the rules established above in *Opusculum* 11, chapter 2 [Col. 1130A].

8. Having examined the prejudiced opinions of Pearson, Dodwell, and their editor, I turn to the period of Anacletus and to the confirmation of its history from Eusebius himself. In Book III, chapter 15, he writes:

> “In the twelfth year of the same reign—that of Domitian—Anencletus, after completing twelve years in the episcopate, left Clement as his successor.”

He makes two assertions. The first is that Anacletus’s twelve-year episcopate coincided with Domitian’s twelfth year; the second is that Clement succeeded Anacletus in the Roman episcopate in Domitian’s twelfth year.

We deny the second assertion, but admit the first, although somewhat differently from Eusebius. For, in agreement with the catalogues and with the paintings of the Pauline basilica, we assign twelve years and, in addition, ten months to Anacletus’s Roman see—and assign them under the reign of Domitian, on which point Eusebius agrees with us. Eusebius, however, aligns the first year of Domitian’s reign, which was A.D. 82, with the beginning of Anacletus’s episcopate; we place the beginning of Anacletus’s episcopate in the third year of Domitian, which was A.D. 84. On this part of our assertion Eusebius disagrees with us.

We think that the error of this historian can be exposed through the names of the consuls, which he misunderstood but which are correctly recorded in the catalogues of our Latin writers. Both years—82 and 84, the first and third years of Domitian—are marked by the ordinary consuls Domitian and Sabinus. In the year 82, Domitian VIII and Titus Flavius Sabinus entered office on the Kalends of January. These consuls are read on ancient stones cited by Panvinius, in the *Fasti*, and in Gruter, folio 68, no. 1. In the year 84, Domitian X and T. Aurelius Sabinus entered office on the Kalends of January; they are read in an ancient inscription cited by Almeloveen in his preface to the *Fasti*, no. 14.

According to Eusebius and our Latin catalogues, Pontiff Anacletus did indeed complete twelve years—full years—under Domitian. The first of these fell in the consulship of [Col. 1130C] Domitian and Sabinus. But the consulship assumed by Eusebius was that of Domitian VIII with the earlier Sabinus, of the Flavian family, in A.D. 82. In our catalogues, however, the consulship of Domitian X with the other Sabinus, of the Aureli­an family, in A.D. 84, is assigned to the first Pascha under Anacletus. A difference of two years arose from the similarity of the names of the two consuls, who are thus listed in the anonymous Bucherian *Fasti*, cited by Norisius and to be consulted after the epochs of the Syro-Macedonians.

We infer that Eusebius was misled by the homonymy of the consuls into a two-year anachronism from the Roman documents. In the Liberian catalogue, the final consuls assigned to Pope Cletus are Domitian IX [Col. 1130D] and Rufus, in A.D. 83, the second year of Domitian’s reign. They are immediately followed by Domitian X and Sabinus, whom our catalogues assign to the beginning of Anacletus’s episcopate as the third year of Domitian’s reign. Since the consulship of Domitian VIII with Sabinus belongs to the first year of the reign, it can never be followed by the third year, marked by the consuls Domitian X and Sabinus.

9. Once Anacletus’s accession is established as 7 September of the year 83, as was explained above in the *Chronological Notes*, no. 1, the twelve years, ten months, and seven days assigned to his see in the Pauline paintings and in the catalogues reach 13 July A.D. 96, in the consulship of Valens and Vetus. The same catalogues assign to those consuls the beginning of Evaristus’s episcopate, thereby correcting Eusebius, who instead of Evaristus gives Clement as Anacletus’s successor.

Eusebius’s error in this second assertion is demonstrated by his own books. In Book III, chapter 2, he writes:

> “After the martyrdom of Paul and Peter, Linus was the first to receive the episcopate of the Roman Church.”

But in chapter 12 he reports that, in the second year of Titus’s reign, Linus handed over the episcopate of the Roman Church to Anacletus, after Linus had administered it for twelve years—obviously counted from Peter’s martyrdom.

Since Eusebius, like everyone else, records Peter’s martyrdom under Nero, marked in all the Church’s calendars as 29 June, he must necessarily place it almost a full year before Nero’s death. Nero killed himself on 11 June A.D. 69, in the consulship of C. Silius Italicus and L. Valerius Trachalus. It must therefore be admitted that Peter and Paul were not put to death later than 29 June A.D. 67.

From that date to the closing part of Titus’s second year, when, according to Eusebius, Anacletus received the Roman episcopate from Linus in A.D. 82—according to the same historian, although he anticipates Anacletus’s beginning by two years through his mistaken identification of the consulship of Sabinus—there are fifteen years. Thus Linus’s twelve-year term cannot fill fifteen ordinary consular years.

Another successor must therefore be sought between Linus and Anacletus in Eusebius, even if the two pontiffs extended their episcopates across the entire twelve-year period from the apostles’ deaths. That period ought instead to have been compressed within the limits of two years, since Linus is regarded as Peter’s coadjutor for nine years and as his successor for approximately two years after Peter’s martyrdom, as was clear from the consuls correctly assigned to him in the catalogues examined above and confirmed in the chronological notes to the *Life of Linus*, no. 2 [Col. 1131B].

10. Once Eusebius’s anachronism has thus been detected, together with its origin in the consulates of Domitian held with the two different Sabini—whether Eusebius himself seized upon the first, or drew an older chronographer into the same error—a new error was added through the information that Clement’s life extended to the third year of Trajan, A.D. 100.

The celebrated name of so great a pontiff, banished for many years into the deserts of Pontus, did not leave the Asians uncertain about the extension of his life or about the postponement of his martyr’s crown to the same period of Trajan. These facts showed that Clement had long survived the first twelve years of Domitian, with which Eusebius chose to close Anacletus’s episcopate. He therefore supposed Clement to have been Anacletus’s successor, even though it was clear that Clement survived for so long afterward.

The error was further confirmed by the ignorance of copyists, who wrongly marked Clement’s beginning by the consulship of Trajan, whereas others correctly expressed it by the true names, Trachalus and Italicus. Trajan’s first consulship, held in A.D. 91, preceded the third year of his reign by nine years—that is, A.D. 100, to which Clement’s martyrdom is assigned.

Eusebius saw from the Church’s documents that Clement had occupied the Roman pontificate for nine years. In the *Fasti* he saw that the year ninth before Clement’s death—assigned to Trajan’s third year—displayed the consul Trajan, whom the copyists had mistakenly written in place of Trachalus, whose consulship marked Clement’s beginning together with his colleague Italicus, as occurs in several copies of Anastasius, whose variant readings we have given under Saint Clement [Col. 1131D].

He supposed that this nine-year period, from A.D. 91 to 100, corresponding to both the consulship marking the beginning of Clement’s see and that marking the end of his life, belonged to Clement’s pontificate. He therefore gave Clement as Anacletus’s successor, from Trajan’s first consulship—the man whom, from the consulship of Trachalus, he ought to have declared the predecessor of Cletus and Anacletus for nine years: Clement, who entered upon the pontificate in the consulship of Trachalus and Italicus in A.D. 68 and laid it down in that of Vespasian IX and Titus VII, as we have explained above from the genuine catalogues.

11. All these matters, carefully considered and compared with one another, sufficiently reveal the origin of the error and anachronism produced by confusing the years of the three pontiffs Clement, Cletus, and Anacletus. They also show that the uncorrupted catalogues preserve the true names of the consuls, the true chronology, and the order of succession of these pontiffs—an order corresponding to the paintings and the most ancient numbers of the pontifical series in the Basilica of Saint Paul and in other Roman monuments, and transmitted into the catalogues of Italian manuscripts more faithfully than into foreign ones.

They therefore confirm us in the necessity of consistently retaining the chronology and sequence of events that we have handed down. They also destroy Pearson’s and Dodwell’s objections against the history of these pontiffs, since those objections arise from a disturbed chronology and a disagreement that are not found in our calculations and monuments.

12. Concerning line 4:

> “Here he constructed and arranged the memorial of blessed Peter, when he had been made a presbyter by blessed Peter, or other places where bishops might be placed for burial.”

Panvinius explains this in Book IV, chapter 4, of *On the Seven Churches*, so that we may understand that Anacletus—whom blessed Peter had ordained as a presbyter while Peter was still in that rank—established a small building or burial chamber in memory of the Prince of the Apostles at the foot of the Vatican hill:

> “Beside the triumphal road, near the Circus of Caius and Nero, at the place where that same apostle had been crucified by Nero’s command with his feet raised upward, etc. The same Anacletus, later made pontiff, established that the other Roman bishops should be buried in that place. Hence Linus, Cletus, Anacletus himself, Xystus, Telesphorus, Hyginus, Pius, Eleutherus, and Victor, holy and blessed pontiffs, are said by Damasus to have been buried in the same place”—that is, by the writers of the Lives that we are explaining.

The Romans so greatly refused to deprive the dead of burial that they generally allowed even those publicly executed to receive that final service through the pious care of their relatives. Thus Pilate, the Roman governor, permitted Joseph of Arimathea, a secret disciple of Christ, to give the divine body of the Master, taken down from the cross, a burial place in a new tomb hewn out of rock, concerning which Isaiah had prophesied: “And his tomb shall be glorious.”

The apostle Peter, foretelling the imminent laying aside of his tabernacle according to what Christ the Lord had revealed to him, had promised in his Second Epistle:

> “But I will take care that you may often have these things after my death, so that you may make them a memorial” (2 Peter 1:15).

He fulfilled his promise. At the very place where he had deposited the tabernacle of his body, he arranged for the Christian people, coming from every nation to these apostolic thresholds, to be gathered by the small building raised by Anacletus, according to the Roman custom of constructing such monuments beside the consular roads. This building later grew into the largest of all basilicas, so that he might often have us after his death and make us mindful of the mysteries of his faith, which he had brought to us as a pledge of salvation and glory.

The outcome proved that these duties of piety had been divinely inspired in the presbyter Anacletus. Once proclaimed pontiff, the fourth among Peter’s successors, he gathered together with the Prince of the Apostles two men who had immediately followed him and who had suffered and been killed at Rome. Clement, however, having been killed and buried for Christ in the regions of Pontus, was brought to Rome only later.

Anacletus himself, added as the fourth in the designation of the burial chamber, drew to himself the other pontiffs who followed, shortly before listed by Panvinius [Col. 1132D]. Caius, a Christian writer at the end of the second century, identified this place on the Triumph­al Way leading to the Vatican. Just as he pointed out the trophies of the apostles on the Ostian Way, so he indicated the tomb, small building, and cemetery of Peter in the Vatican, together with those of the pontiffs who immediately followed him.

Their memory is expressly included in the Roman canon of the Mass. As we shall say below, it is found both in ancient vessels used for the sacrifice and in diptychs—that is, tablets and small lists containing the names to be recited in the sacrifice of the Mass. Since these objects were associated with the same cemeteries where the pontiffs rested, they sufficiently commend the antiquity of the sacred rite and custom, contemporary with the construction of such a building and memorial.

That memorial was raised by Anacletus the presbyter for blessed Peter and enlarged by Anacletus the former presbyter, now Supreme Pontiff, so that it might be attributed jointly to his predecessors Linus, Cletus, and Clement [Col. 1133A]. For this reason he perhaps instituted at that time that their names should be recited in the prayers before the consecration. He thereby displayed a custom that later ages consistently preserved and transmitted to us, not without the authority and suggestion of both Apostles who established this Roman Church—Peter and Paul.

Peter, in his Second Epistle, chapter 3, verse 2, arouses our sincere minds through admonition, so that we may remember our apostles. Paul, however, in chapter 13 of the Epistle to the Hebrews—which Jerome states that most people regard as having been written by Clement of Rome at the dictation of the Apostle—admonishes us in verse 7:

> “Remember your leaders, who spoke the word of God to you; considering the outcome of their way of life, imitate their faith.”

By communing with these men—by considering the outcome of their way of life and imitating their faith—and by venerating their memory, we recite their names.

But the more suitable place for discussing the names of the apostles, pontiffs, and martyrs to be recited in the action of the Mass will come later. Here we stop with the designation and construction by Anacletus of the memorial of blessed Peter in the Vatican.

Simon Stravoltius, a Pole and chief canon of Tarnów, writes as follows about Anacletus in his *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, published together with an *Epitome of the Councils*:

> “He constructed the memorial of blessed Peter—that is, a certain structure of a building, which was later consecrated as a church. He himself was also buried there in peace beside the body of blessed Peter, on 13 July.”

He adds that the same pontiff established by decree the place where, and the witnesses with whom, the sacrifice should be offered. I believe Stravoltius derived this second point from the first decretal epistle attributed to Anacletus. In his notes, however, Binius wisely observed that it should rather be derived from Apostolic Canons 9 and 10.

Although we cannot establish whether those earlier canons were composed by the apostles themselves or by the bishops of the apostolic see who lived closest to the apostolic age—and by Anacletus himself—nevertheless it is certain that the first fifty are extremely ancient [Col. 1133C].

As for regarding Anacletus as the author of the Vatican structure and memorial of Peter, and as the one who designated the place for offering sacrifice to God together with the recitation both of Peter’s own name and of those of the nearby bishops and martyrs resting there with him, this is almost as close to historical certainty as anything could be.

For, as we shall read below in numbers 6 and 7, Evaristus, the pontiff immediately following Anacletus, divided the titles among the presbyters of the city of Rome, and Alexander, his successor, introduced the Passion of the Lord into the priests’ prayers when Masses are celebrated.

There were therefore titles, or fixed places of the Church designated for its assemblies and for the performance of the mysteries, if Evaristus divided these titles. There were priests’ prayers when Masses were celebrated—that is, an order of prayers and sacred rites corresponding to the canon of the Mass, together with the memory of the apostles from whom we received them—if Alexander introduced the Lord’s Passion into those same prayers [Col. 1133D].

And why should these things not have existed? In the same second century in which Evaristus lived, Justin Martyr, and Tertullian a few years later—Tertullian in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, no. 6, and in the *Apology against the Gentiles*, chapter 3, and Justin in *First Apology*, no. 87—describe almost the same order of our assemblies for celebrating and receiving the Eucharistic sacraments that we observe today.

There, too, prayers are mentioned both before and after the offering of bread and wine; then other prayers before the consecration, recited by the one presiding over the brethren, and still others after the consecration, likewise recited by him, while the whole people acclaim “Amen.”

All these things therefore existed, as did a place always regarded as holier than the other titles: the confession of blessed Peter, the trophy and threshold of the apostles. There not only were vigils, psalmody, gatherings before dawn, liturgy, and sacrifice celebrated; ordinations of priests and ministers were also held there [Col. 1134A]. Such ordinations were not customarily performed without sacrifice, according to a tradition continuously preserved and clearly asserted in the sermons of Leo the Great, who summoned the faithful during the four seasons of fasting to keep vigil at Saint Peter on Saturday according to custom.

In view of all this, the statements transmitted here about Anacletus are confirmed: he was the first to construct the Vatican memorial of blessed Peter and to designate a fixed place for the celebration of Christian rites according to the custom received from the apostles and transmitted to us. The great compiler of the *Annals* produced documentary evidence for this under A.D. 57, no. 19 and following.]

[Note: [Col. 1134A]

**Line 1.**—Anacletus, Greek by nationality. Some, whether through a scribal error, the similarity of the names, or some other circumstance, wrongly confuse Anacletus with Cletus, although the two differ greatly in name, parentage, homeland, deeds, year of death, and day of death.

[Col. 1134B] **Line 4.**—“He constructed and arranged the memorial of blessed Peter.” That is, he adorned the site of Peter’s tomb and set it apart from the common people, distinguishing places in the cemeteries and crypts where the martyrs were buried.]

[Note: [Col. 1134B]

As an addition by Fabrotti, from the Regius, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts, among our variant readings.

“Two decretal epistles also, etc.” Three decretal epistles circulate under the name of Pope Anacletus, which scholars judge to be spurious.

The first is addressed to all bishops and the faithful, but is stitched together both from passages of Scripture according to the Vulgate version and from Clement’s Epistles to James, as is clear from the authorities of Rufinus, Damasus, and others. The second is addressed to the bishops of Italy and contains testimonies drawn from Augustine, Hydatius, and Gregory the Great. The third is addressed to all bishops and discusses patriarchs, whose name was unknown in that and the following century. Finally, it contains [Col. 1134C] a testimony from the Roman Council under Gelasius and from other later Fathers.

As for the other decretal epistles of the Roman pontiffs down to Siricius, which the editors of the councils transferred from the collection of Isidore Mercator into their editions, although they were accepted with broad agreement even before the middle of the eleventh century, when they began to be publicly read in the schools—and although from that time not only did the letters of later Roman pontiffs abound in testimonies from them, but the writings of all teachers everywhere resounded with them—nevertheless almost all scholars candidly admit that they are not genuine but spurious. Among them are Peter de Marca, Book III of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, and Schelestratius, Part II of *Illustrated Antiquity*, Dissertation 3.

The same de Marca, cited above, touched upon the arguments proving these letters spurious in chapter 5, section 1.

First, because of the coarseness of their language, foreign to the elegance and polish of the second century in which they are said to have been issued. Second, because of the dissimilarity of style and the identical manner of writing that appears throughout all the letters, so that they seem to have been written by one author rather than by different pontiffs. Third, because of the very frequent use of the Vulgate version of Scripture, which makes it necessary to conclude that they were fabricated after Jerome’s time. Fourth, because they were entirely unknown both to Jerome, who composed a catalogue of ecclesiastical writers, and to Innocent, Leo, and the other pontiffs whose genuine letters have reached us. They were likewise unknown to Dionysius Exiguus, who, while collecting with great zeal and diligence at Rome the decrees of the former bishops of the apostolic see during the reign of the Emperor Justinian, began with Siricius.

Fifth, because of the observation of Antonio Agustín, archbishop of Tarragona, who was the first to note in his annotations on the chapters of Pope Hadrian:

> “The very words of the imperial laws, and the scholia that exist under the name of Anianus on the Theodosian Code, were used in those letters, although the pontiffs to whom the letters are attributed preceded the publication of the Theodosian Code by two or three centuries.”

Antonio Agustín may be consulted in the cited notes, chapters 7, 8, 16, and following [Col. 1135A].

Sixth, because Blondel’s industry has advanced in recent years to the point that he has demonstrated with the greatest precision the very sentences and words from which the letters were composed and the authors from whom they were taken, in his book entitled *Pseudo-Isidore and Turrianus Being Rebuked*. Francis Turrianus had previously published them as genuine under the name of Isidore Mercator.

Seventh, because until the time of Hadrian I no Catholic writer, no Roman pontiff, and no synod had produced any testimony from these letters. Indeed, Photius, in the time of Nicholas I, testified that he had nowhere seen them in the East. Although he accepted their authority, Hincmar, metropolitan of Rheims, appears to support him; for this reason Hincmar more often began with the letters of Pope Siricius and hesitated in the testimonies of the pontiffs who followed Siricius.

Eighth, from Pope Leo IV, who, before Nicholas I, was consulted about these decretals in a letter to the bishops of England and replied that the Apostolic See accepted the regulations:

> “Of the Roman pontiffs Silvester, Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, Gelasius, Hilary, Symmachus, Hormisdas, Simplicius, and Gregory the Younger, which regulations exist in full, and through which bishops judge, and through which bishops are themselves judged.”

Leo IV wrote this around the year 840. He begins not with decretal letters of Clement or Anacletus, but after the statutes of Pope Silvester, with Siricius.

Ninth, from the Vigilian manuscript, which Garzias Loaisa states in the preface to the Councils of Spain was compiled by the monk Vigila in the year 876. Loaisa says that it contains 101 decretal letters but begins with Damasus and ends with Gregory I.

Tenth and finally, from an old manuscript of the canons of the Roman Church, reissued at Mainz in 1525 so that the Church might defend itself against Luther. The title states that this manuscript was transcribed from three very ancient exemplars, yet it displays only decretal letters from Siricius to Gregory the Great.

The arguments brought forward by Turrianus and others who acknowledge these letters as genuine are slight and have been refuted by learned men.

Who fabricated the decretal letters mentioned above under the false name of Isidore Mercator and attributed them to the ancient pontiffs is uncertain. It is known only that Riculph, bishop of Mainz, who flourished around the end of the eighth and beginning of the ninth century, was the first of the Gauls to receive and publish the book of Pseudo-Isidore, brought from Spain into Gaul. Hincmar, metropolitan of Rheims, writes this in his treatise *Against His Nephew*, chapter 54.

From that time arose the veneration of the faithful no less than of the bishops for those decretal letters. Although they are spurious, and although Blondel’s criterion is to be praised for assigning them to ancient pontiffs, they are nevertheless unjustly torn apart by him and by other heretics with excessively harsh language. For, apart from a few additions, they were composed from the sentences and words of the laws, the ancient canons, and the holy Fathers who flourished in the fourth century, as the cited de Marca says.

Moreover, we shall provide the headings of all the pseudonymous letters under each pontiff, lest an uninformed reader suppose that absolutely all the letters of the Roman pontiffs are not genuine. For it is certain that the letters of Saint Cornelius preserved among the works of Saint Cyprian; the letters of Julius I cited by Saint Athanasius in *Apology* 2; the letters of Liberius recorded by Saint Hilary in the *Fragments*; the letter of Damasus to the bishops of Illyricum, which Theodoret copied in Book II, chapter 22, of his *Ecclesiastical History*; other letters of the same pontiff preserved in Saint Jerome; and, finally, all the letters of the ancient pontiffs cited by the holy Fathers or by the early writers of ecclesiastical history are genuine productions of those pontiffs.

“Here under Domitian, etc.” Domitian Augustus initiated the second persecution against the Christians, in the ninety-third year of Christ. It was extremely severe. For in the Alexandrian Chronicle under the year 944 we read that Brutus—one should read *Brutius*, as in Eusebius—

> “reports that a great number of Christians were killed and subjected to martyrdom from the fourteenth year of Domitian.”

It also lasted a long time, as may be read in Baronius’s *Critica* [Col. 1136C]. During its violence, the holy apostle John was banished to the island of Patmos after having been placed at Rome in a vessel of boiling oil. On that island he wrote the divine Apocalypse.

Flavius Clemens also perished in this persecution, immediately after laying down the ordinary consulship that he had held with Domitian in the year 94. Flavia Domitilla, the niece of the same Flavius Clemens, was deported to the island of Pontia. On this persecution, see Eusebius, Book III, chapter 17 and following.]

[Col. 1113]

> [Col. 1113] |

**5. Anacletus**, Greek by nationality, from Athens, son of Antiochus, sat for nine years, two months, and ten days. He lived during the time of Domitian [Note: [Col. 1113] B: Trajan], from the consulship of Domitian [Note: [Col. 1115] C: Sabinus] X to the consulship of Domitian XVII and Clement [Note: [Col. 1115] B: Trajan IV and Articulaeus to Piso and Hasta]. He constructed and arranged the memorial of blessed Peter, having been made a presbyter by blessed Peter, and also established other places where bishops might be buried. He himself was buried [Note: [Col. 1115] CB: in peace] beside the body of blessed Peter, on 13 July.

He conducted two ordinations in the month of December: five presbyters, three deacons, and six bishops for various places. The episcopate then remained vacant for thirteen days.

**CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS**

Anacletus: twelve years, ten months, and three days. He lived during the time of Domitian, from the consulship of Domitian X and Sabinus to that of Domitian XVII and Clement.

## VI. SAINT EVARISTUS. A.D. 112, THE THIRTEENTH YEAR OF THE REIGN OF TRAJAN

[Note: [Col. 1137]

In Fabrotti, from the Freher manuscript.

No. 6, line 4, A and B: nevertheless. Line 6, A: two.

From the Regius, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts:

Line 2: nine years, ten months, two days. Line 4: consuls. “Here he divided the titles.” Line 5: “he ordained deacons who would guard.” Line 6: “on account of zeal for truth.” Mazarin: “by the stylus (written record) of truth.” Lines 7 and 8, number 5: “who was also crowned with martyrdom and buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican.”

In Holstenius and Schelestratius:

Cassinensis and Florentinus: two; nine years. The second Florentinus: ten years. Line 4: “here he divided the titles,” etc. Deusdedit, Book II, chapter 76, cites this passage in his manuscript collection up to “for the testimony of truth.” Line 6: Cassinensis, “he ordained two.” Line 7: six presbyters. The second Florentinus and Cassinensis: seventeen presbyters. Same line: Cassinensis and the second Florentinus, fifteen places. Line 8: Florentinus, “in the Vatican.” Line 9: Vaticanus, sixteen days before the Kalends.]

[Note: [Col. 1137A]

**Line 4.**—“Here he divided the titles in the city of Rome among the presbyters.” Evaristus divided the titles in the city among the presbyters; that is, he assigned presbyters to the individual churches, ordained within them under their title.

The churches were called titles because, when presbyters were ordained, the ordination took place under the title of one of those churches. Ordination did not take place without a title—that is, without enrollment in a particular church in which the ordained man was said to be enrolled under a title. See the canons *Nemo* and *Sanctorum*, Distinction 70; Augustine, *On the Good of Marriage*, chapter 24:

> “Just as, if the ordination of the clergy is performed for the gathering of the people, even if the gathering of the people does not follow, nevertheless the sacrament of ordination remains in those who are ordained.”

Hence a man to be ordained bishop, if he was not yet a presbyter, was first ordained a presbyter under the title of a particular church. Regino, *Chronicle* II:

> “Moreover, in Cologne, Hilduin the abbot was appointed by the king to the episcopal chair, and Franco, bishop of the diocese of Tongeren, had him ordained a presbyter in the Palace at Aachen under the title of Saint Peter of the aforementioned metropolitan church.”

The titles instituted by Evaristus are the cardinal titles—that is, churches assigned to cardinal presbyters. Their number increased over time. Anastasius, in his *Life of Marcellus*:

> “He established twenty-five titles in the city of Rome, as if they were dioceses, for the baptism and penance of the many who were converted from paganism, and for the burial of the martyrs.”

**Line 5.**—“And he established seven deacons to guard the bishop who was preaching, for the stylus (written record) of truth.” By Evaristus’s constitution, seven deacons ought to attend the preaching bishop, so that he might have guards against those laying ambushes and witnesses to the truth of what was preached against its detractors. See the canon *Diaconi*, Distinction 93.

According to a Roman synod held under Gregory, a bishop ought to have clerics in private service, so that he might have witnesses to his manner of life. See the canon *Cura pastoris*, Question 7.

Indeed, according to the constitution of Lucius, a bishop ought everywhere to have around him two presbyters and three deacons “for the ecclesiastical testimony.” See the canon *Jubemus*, *On Consecration*, Distinction 1; Anastasius also discusses this in his *Life of Lucius*.]

[Note: [Col. 1137C]

**Line 5.**—“He established seven deacons.” The pontiff ordered the number and institution so that there would be precisely that many who attended the pontiff’s ministry with special care. The number refers to the apostolic institution of seven deacons; the ministry refers to the special care exercised by the deacons in serving the bishop.

Cornelius mentions the number of deacons in the Roman Church in his letter to Fabius of Antioch, preserved in Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 43, page 244. In listing the clergy, he writes that there were seven deacons and an equal number of subdeacons [Col. 1138A].

That other bishops were given special ministers and deacon-companions is shown by a letter of Dionysius of Alexandria, in which he discusses exile and companions:

> “I went to Aemilianus not alone, but accompanied by Maximus, my fellow presbyter, and by Faustus, Eusebius, and Chremon the deacon.”

The same association is read below when Alexander completed his martyrdom:

> “He was crowned with martyrdom, and with him Eventius the presbyter and Theodorus the deacon.”

Regarding Pontius, the deacon of Saint Cyprian, Jerome writes in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 5:

> “Pontius, Cyprian’s deacon, who endured exile with him until the day of his passion, left an outstanding volume on the life and passion of Cyprian.”

When Novatus usurped the episcopate, he chose the deacon Felicissimus as his companion, according to Cyprian’s Letter 47, where Cyprian writes of Novatus:

> “He is the man who, without my permission or knowledge, appointed Felicissimus, his satellite and deacon, through his own faction and ambition.”

Hence the *Pontifical Book* adds that seven deacons were established at Rome [Col. 1138B] “to guard the bishop.”

Hegesippus speaks of such a deaconal retinue accompanying the Roman bishop when he recounts his pilgrimage to inspect the apostolic Churches:

> “When I came to Rome, I stayed with Anicetus, whose deacon at that time was Eleutherus.”

After Anicetus’s death, Soter succeeded him, and Eleutherus succeeded Soter. From such a retinue of deacons bishops selected those who would carry ecclesiastical documents or announce decrees. Hence decretal letters frequently mention deacons *de latere*, that is, those who served the pontiff’s household.

This designation was considered necessary. Thus the heresiarch Eunomius, first assuming the diaconate in order to dissolve certain arrangements, completed an embassy, according to Philostorgius, Book IV, chapter 8, page 68:

> “When Eunomius heard what had been done by Basil, he went to Antioch, received ordination as a deacon, and was sent as an envoy to Constantius so that he might dissolve the decrees.”

For the sake of the style of truth. In Lucius this diaconal ministry is expressed more clearly [Col. 1138C]: “He prescribed that two presbyters and three deacons should not leave the bishop anywhere, for the sake of ecclesiastical testimony.” For formerly the care entrusted to deacons consisted not only in preserving ecclesiastical documents, but also in directing the records of synods and the letters, so that no falsification or interpolation might occur. Therefore they presided both over their preservation and over their authentication; a genuine and unquestionable compilation was required from them, and documents subscribed by them possessed authority. Optatus, wishing to establish the authenticity of the records of the Council of Cirta, demands proof of their truth and identity from the subscriptions of the deacons (book I, p. 16):

> These men, and the others whom we shall shortly show to have been their leaders [Col. 1139A], after the persecution, in the city of Cirta—for the basilicas had not yet been restored—assembled in the house of Urbanus Carisius on the third day before the Ides of May, as the written testimony of Nundinarius, then a deacon, declares, and as the antiquity of the parchments bears witness. We shall be able to produce them for those who doubt.

Thus, while Meletius of Antioch was preaching, the archdeacon of the Church of Antioch stood beside him as he recited his first sermon to the people. When, contrary to the expectations of the Arians who had promoted his ordination, he began to discuss the consubstantiality of the Word, the archdeacon attempted to cover his mouth, as Sozomen reports (book IV, chapter 27). Likewise, when Eutyches raised doubts about the identity of the first Council of Constantinople under Flavian, Aetius the archdeacon was summoned, as may be seen in the first session of Chalcedon. In the earliest councils, whenever documents, books, or other materials had to be produced, these were demanded and brought forward by deacons. Thus, when the tyrant Bardas, the restorer of Monothelitism [Col. 1139B], burned the acts of the Sixth Synod, the deacon Agatho, who had taken down the acts, repaired the loss, as he testifies in the epilogue added to the acts of that synod in these words:

> I, the sinner and least of all, Agatho, unworthy deacon and librarian of this most holy great Church, and protonotary of the venerable patriarchal secretariat and second chancellor, for approximately thirty-two years, from the time when I was still young, enrolled in the rank of lector, and an unserviceable notary, I served this holy and ecumenical Sixth Synod. I carefully examined in order everything that was done in it, together with Paul, who was archbishop and patriarch of this holy city while he was still a layman and imperial secretary, and with certain others. With my own hand I wrote out all the volumes of the Acts in ecclesiastical letters, purely and neatly. These volumes, sealed in the imperial palace, had been safely deposited together with the decree of faith that had been issued in writing by the holy synod itself. Moreover, I wrote out copies of this decree for the five patriarchal sees [Col. 1139C] in the same manner, having thus been ordered by Constantine of pious memory, who commanded that this be done so that the purity and sincerity of the orthodox faith might not be assailed by any plots.

Deacons, therefore, stood beside the pontiff by virtue of their office, as witnesses, so to speak, of what was being done; and they were present to assist the pontiff in carrying out ecclesiastical business. Accordingly, responsibility for the archives was entrusted to them, the care of conveying letters was assigned to them, and they were ordered to preside over those who recorded the acts in councils, lest falsification creep in. If anything contrary to the canons should occasionally be attempted, it was their task to defend the law by producing the canons. Hilary, Saint Leo’s deacon, vigorously and boldly opposed the tyranny of Dioscorus at the Robber Council of Ephesus, as recorded in the first session of Chalcedon; and Aetius, in the fourth session of Chalcedon, firmly resisted certain recalcitrant monks, as is recorded there (session 4, §16). In response to each of their demands against the canons, he produced the book of canons and brought forward and cited before the council the rules that the obstinate monks had violated, so that their contumacy might be restrained [Col. 1139D] according to the standard of the canons.

[Col. 1139D]

## Notes on Chronology

### (From Binius)

**Line 1.—Evaristus.** Irenaeus (book II, chapter 3), Optatus (*Against Parmenian*, book II), Epiphanius (*Against Heresies*, 26), and Augustine (letter 165) mention this pontiff Evaristus.

**Line 4.—“He divided the titular churches in the city of Rome among the presbyters.”** By “titular churches” understand houses dedicated to divine worship, in which Christians were accustomed to hold assemblies. See the letters of Pope Pius to Justus of Vienne.

### (From Labbe)

**Line 1.—“A Greek by nationality.”** An Antiochene.

## Chronological Notes

In explaining the chronology of the pontiffs one by one, so that we may not be compelled repeatedly to restate the same rules and observations, which apply in the same way to many of them and thus display a consistent method, it will be sufficient to indicate here once for all several principles by which the agreement of the dates and the truth of the documents may be clarified.

In the preface to the preceding volume, numbers 17 and following through 23, I showed that the year and day of the consecration of pontiffs, especially in the Roman Church, were customarily recorded carefully for several reasons. One reason was the example of the priests of the Old Testament, a specimen of which I gave from the sacred Scriptures in the case of Aaron and his son Eleazar. Another was the testimony of the New Covenant, which records for us, in the election of the apostle Matthias (Acts 1), the time between the Lord’s Ascension and Pentecost, when he was enrolled in the college of the apostles. Later generations retained this practice diligently in the other ranks as well, after the canons had provided that those called to the lot of the Lord should serve for a fixed number of years in the lower ministries of the priesthood [Col. 1140B] before being promoted to the higher ones.

To this was added among the Romans an established custom, derived from the very high esteem in which sacred offices were held even among pagans in the worship of their national superstition. Thus the acts and enrollments of their chief pontiffs and of the lesser colleges were engraved on marble tablets, recording the epochs of each and marking the day of the month and the year by the names of the consuls, and sometimes also by the year from the founding of the City. We see this in the tablets of the Arval Brothers, just as on the Capitoline triumphal Fasti we see engraved the days, months, and years of each triumph.

Therefore, among Christians, professors of the true religion and conscious participants in the divine priesthood instituted by Christ the Lord and communicated to the ministers who were chosen—so that it might be shown that a far greater care for sacred things was in force—the regional notaries of the Roman Church, instituted shortly before by Clement, as stated in his number 4, line 5, endeavored to record in registers the epochs of priestly acts and pontificates, no less diligently [Col. 1140C] than the acts of the martyrs. From these records the pontifical catalogues were compiled, mentioned by the holy Fathers, and found to have been extended to their own times under Liberius and his successors.

The practice of the Roman Church, mistress of the others, is confirmed by an almost identical practice observed in the rest of the West and among the Africans. I gave a clear testimony of this from the acts of the Church of Hippo, when Eradius the presbyter was designated by Augustine as its coadjutor and successor in the episcopate, in letter 110 among the letters of the holy Doctor. The record begins by stating the epoch:

> In the consulship of the most glorious Theodosius for the twelfth time and Valentinian Augustus for the second time, on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, when Augustine the bishop had taken his seat together with his fellow bishops Regilianus and Martinianus in the Church of Peace of the districts of Hippo, etc.

Finally, this practice shows the diligent care with which the episcopal era of each prelate and their succession were to be recorded in the registers of the churches; their annual birthday in office was celebrated with appointed prayers to be recited during the sacrifice, commemorating their steadfast life; after death, the day of their consecration was marked in the calendars and Martyrologies, among the Latins as in the case of Ambrose and among the Greeks as in the case of Basil, as well as in many others encountered throughout ecclesiastical history.

We must therefore conclude that the epochs of pontiffs recorded in this way by consulates, or by numbers of years, months, and days in the public monuments established in antiquity among those churches which they themselves adorned by their episcopal seat, should not be altered for trivial reasons, even if a double era is found for them. Rather, one must investigate whether one of these dates can be reconciled with the election and the other with the ordination or succession, which for many reasons was sometimes delayed, as everyone knows in the case of Gregory the Great.

A second principle that we propose for general observation concerns the necessity of appointing an assistant bishop on more than one occasion, a practice that could disturb the epoch of succession unless it were carefully distinguished. It is universally acknowledged that this precautionary arrangement was introduced from the age of the apostles, so that whenever the needs of the Christian people demanded the assistance of a coadjutor, a bishop would be appointed to exercise pontifical functions as vicar in a church that had not yet been deprived of its shepherd.

Almost everyone agrees that Linus and Cletus were ordained in this way by the prince of the apostles, as I observed above in the chronological notes on the Life of Linus. This is also asserted by the author of the *Pontifical Book*, both in number 4 of Clement and in the preceding material, edited from the Regius, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts in volume I, folio 2; and before him by the presbyter Rufinus, or by the person concealed under Rufinus’s name, according to Schelestratius (*Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, p. 136, dissertation 2, chapter 1, §4), in the books of the *Recognitions*. His testimony, also cited by Father Christianus Lupus in his commentary on chapter 32 of Tertullian’s *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, p. 526, is as follows:

> We have received, he says, that Linus and Clement were indeed bishops in the city of Rome before Clement, but while Peter was still alive, so that they might administer the care of the episcopate for him, while he himself fulfilled the office of the apostolate.

Saint Epiphanius, in *Against Heresies* 27, chapter 6, although he states with hesitation rather than assertion that Clement was consecrated bishop by the apostle Peter, nevertheless clearly establishes that there was a legitimate reason why others could be substituted while the apostles were still alive to undertake the care of the Roman episcopate: namely, that Rome could not be left without a bishop when the apostles had to prolong their absence from the City.

> For, he says, even for this reason others could be substituted while the apostles Peter and Paul were still alive, since they undertook journeys to other cities and regions in order to preach the Gospel; but Rome could not be without a bishop. For Paul reached Spain, while Peter repeatedly travelled through Pontus and Bithynia.

Cardinal Baronius, under the year 69, §43, affirms that this is the common opinion of the Latins: namely, that Linus and Cletus, during Peter’s tenure of the see and in his absence, exercised the pontifical office as coadjutors, and that after Peter’s martyrdom they held the supreme pontificate one after the other until their deaths. Clement, although he had been chosen and ordained bishop of the Roman Church by Peter while Peter was still alive, voluntarily relinquished this office, as we mentioned shortly before in the Lives of the individual pontiffs.

In recalling these matters here, I do not wish them to be understood as proof of the succession of these three pontiffs in the Roman see. I mention them for the purpose of showing that this custom was received from the apostolic age: that a very grave cause was considered sufficient for appointing an assistant bishop in a church that had not yet been deprived of its shepherd, especially in a church regarded as one of the chief churches, and specifically in the Roman Church, the first and teacher of all. This could occur if its own bishop foresaw that an unavoidable necessity, directed toward the good of the entire Christian people, would prevent him from remaining present, so that he would be kept for a longer time from personally administering the episcopal care of the City.

This happened more than once during persecutions: either the bishop was compelled to go into exile from the City—as happened under the emperor Claudius, when the Jews were expelled and Peter also had to migrate to Asia—or he was so tightly bound by imprisonment that he could not be present to strengthen the faithful in the greatest danger or to make up the number of sacred ministers, which the cruelty of the persecutors had reduced through numerous executions.

In the Roman see, which embraced the care of the entire Lord’s flock, if the apostolic office called its shepherd elsewhere to preserve the unity of the whole body or to connect the ecclesiastical order with newly enlightened regions, or with regions still to be enlightened, Epiphanius also regarded this as a sufficient reason for assigning a vicar bishop to the Roman Church, following the example of Peter its founder. Peter employed Linus and Cletus as assistants during his absence from the City, when he was called to visit and strengthen the churches founded in Asia, or even to establish new ones throughout the West, as is confirmed by the origins and records of each church [Col. 1142A].

A third principle, deriving from both of the preceding ones, will be this: if it should happen in the Roman see, especially during an intense persecution, that the man appointed as vicar and coadjutor to a pontiff detained in chains or sent into prolonged exile were, after the pontiff’s death, elected as his successor by the votes of the Roman clergy, then two episcopal epochs would have to be recorded—one of ordination and the other of succession. This is what the Church of Hippo recorded in the enrollment of Eradius: by the consulates it marked the epoch of the earlier beginning, namely, the confirmed designation of an assistant in the episcopate; shortly afterward it added a second era for the episcopate of Hippo acquired by Eradius through succession.

Since this is so, it follows that we should not immediately reject the consulates that are found assigned at the beginning of each pontificate in the ancient catalogues of the Roman Church [Col. 1142B], unless it is established that those consulates cannot be reconciled either with the epoch of ordination, when the man was consecrated bishop to exercise the office of vicar under a living pontiff whom he was to assist, or with the era of succession, when the same ordained man, who had been vicar throughout the life of the pontiff who appointed him, was elected by the votes of the clergy as Roman pontiff and successor to the deceased.

Those who are irritated with the writers of pontifical history, because they distinguish the era of vicars from that of succession, should therefore moderate the sharpness with which they condemn them, as though they were searching with feeble ingenuity for a support for a tottering chronology. It is clear from Peter’s own institution that vicars were appointed more than once. The practice of using them is shown not to have become obsolete by the discipline transmitted down to our own time, although six suburban bishops are counted among the cardinals both in antiquity and today. I have already demonstrated that it was customary to record the epochs of ordination and of accession to the see [Col. 1142C]. Who, then, would refuse to recognize in the ancient monuments what no one can deny ought to have been inserted according to the custom of those times?

This is especially so since the appointment of bishops as vicars, without a condition of future succession, introduces nothing contrary to the apostolic laws. The Roman Church carefully avoided such a condition, even though the ease and abuse of designating bishops not merely as assistants but as successors had infiltrated the African churches in Augustine’s time, as the aforementioned acts of the people of Hippo, preserved among the letters of the holy Doctor, make clear.

Once these three principles have been established, it will be easier to proceed toward fixing the dates of the subsequent pontiffs from the genuine documents of the Roman Church. Let us examine Evaristus. The day of his martyrdom is reported by the registers of the Roman Church and by the ancient Martyrologies derived from them under 26 October; the year is given in the catalogues of Liberius and Felix IV as the consulship of Gallus and Bradua [Col. 1142D], or the year of Christ 108. This endpoint is confirmed by the beginning of Alexander’s succession, marked by the consuls Tullus and Palma, belonging to the year of Christ 109.

The same catalogues, the paintings of Saint Paul, and the other documents collected in the *Prolegomena* to this volume, folio 89, assign to Evaristus thirteen years, seven months, and two days of episcopal office. Evaristus’s beginning therefore falls in the year of Christ 95, on 25 March, a day marked and consecrated from antiquity by the Incarnation and Passion of the Lord. This may be seen engraved on the marble chair of Saint Hippolytus, bishop and martyr, excavated from the cemetery of Saint Lawrence outside the walls and published and explained by many authors. We shall reproduce its form in the notes on the Life of Saint Victor.

The consuls marking the year 95 of the common Christian era were Domitian XVII and Clement. These are assigned as the final consuls to Anacletus, his immediate predecessor, just as the beginning of Evaristus’s successor is assigned to the next consuls, Valens [Col. 1143A] and Vetus, in the year of Christ 96. Yet from these consuls to the consulship of Gallus and Bradua there are counted not thirteen years but only twelve.

Therefore, in order that the total of thirteen years may be complete, it must necessarily be asserted that Evaristus was ordained bishop by Anacletus in the year 95, when Easter had been celebrated on Sunday, 29 March, under the consulship of Domitian XVII and Clement, approximately four months before Anacletus himself suffered martyrdom. If Evaristus was ordained bishop in that year, on 25 March, the anniversary of the Lord’s Incarnation and Passion—a date celebrated among Christians even in the time of Saint Hippolytus and Tertullian, since it is attested by the marble and the former’s Paschal cycle and by the latter’s writings, both produced under the Severi—then, from that date to 26 October of the year 108, the total assigned to Evaristus in the genuine and most ancient documents of the Roman Church cited above is exactly thirteen years, seven months, and two days.

Anacletus, shortly afterward sought out for execution, was crowned with martyrdom on 7 July, under the same consuls, Domitian XVII and Clement, who are rightly assigned as the final consuls of his episcopate [Col. 1143B]. Evaristus therefore remained Anacletus’s vicar until that date. He was subsequently elected by the Roman clergy, after Anacletus’s martyrdom, as his successor, and exercised the Roman pontificate in his own name. He celebrated Easter for the first time in the following year, 96, under the consuls Valens and Vetus. These consuls are rightly assigned as the first of his see in the catalogues, since the epoch of the pontifical years is referred to the Paschal season, as I showed above in the chronological notes on Saint Peter.

The author of the prologue to the most ancient catalogue of the Liberian period also expressly warns that he begins counting from that point—namely, from the Lord’s Ascension—in the succession of pontiffs, recording how many years each one presided. Let the following passage from the same chronological notes be repeated:
