> Under the emperor Tiberius Caesar, our Lord Jesus Christ suffered under the consulship of the two Gemini, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April; and after his Ascension the blessed Peter assumed the episcopate. From that time, the succession was arranged: which bishop presided, for how many years, and under which emperor.

[Col. 1143C] If a reason is sought for appointing a bishop as assistant or vicar during the persecution of Domitian, one may assign a reason similar to that which had moved Peter to ordain and appoint Linus when Peter himself was expelled from the City with the Jews under Claudius. One may also assign the other reason which, when Nero was raging against the Christians and had brought Peter close to death, persuaded that apostle to ordain Clement as bishop and recommend him to the Church for election as his successor, even though Linus and Cletus, having already served as vicars, were still alive.

That early period of the Roman Church had to be supported by the institutions of apostolic men who had been closely associated with Peter, the founder of that see. They had to be displayed and, as it were, brought forward publicly as candidates for succession by the head of the sacred senate and recommended by his vote, lest schisms easily arise, as happened at Corinth, where especially the convocation of the assembly of the Church was made difficult and dangerous by the intensity of the persecution.

When Evaristus closed the course of his life in the year of Christ 108, the twelfth year of Trajan, none of the assistant bishops ordained by Peter for the Roman Church was still alive, since the last of the three, Clement, had already died in the third year of Trajan. Anacletus, who had indeed been ordained presbyter by Peter—and perhaps for this reason was elected by the clergy as bishop of the Roman see after Linus, Clement, and Cletus and preferred to the others—ordained Evaristus as bishop and wished to strengthen him with vicarious authority. In this way he displayed him as already trained by a kind of pastoral apprenticeship to feed the flock of the whole Church, so that the Roman clergy might elect him readily and prefer him to the others in the difficult circumstances of those early persecutions.

There were therefore several reasons why Evaristus should be regarded as an ordained bishop and as Anacletus’s vicar in the year 95, before succeeding the dying bishop whom he had assisted. This is asserted by the catalogues, which with remarkable agreement assign to him thirteen complete years [Col. 1144A], although the era of the Roman pontificate that he assumed is customarily referred to the Paschal season of the year 96, duly recorded under the consuls Vetus and Valens in those same catalogues.

## Historical Notes of the Same Author

**Line 4.—“He divided the titular churches in the city of Rome among the presbyters.”** Which titular churches, you ask? The domestic churches of the guests and disciples of Peter and Paul, which they granted for holding assemblies of the faithful and celebrating synaxes.

Consider the domestic church of Prisca and Aquila, which Saint Paul mentions in his Letter to the Romans, chapter 16, verse 3—the Roman titular church still famous among the most ancient ones on the Aventine. Consider also the church of the elder Lucina, likewise a hostess of the apostles, now the title of the first cardinal presbyter; that of Pudens in the Vicus Patricius, where ancient records testify that Paul baptized; and that of Clement at the roots of the Caelian Hill, in the paternal house of that pontiff who, as they relate, succeeded Linus [Col. 1144B].

Add the house of Claudia and those belonging to the household of Caesar, whom the Apostle mentions when writing from the City to the Philippians. Add also the houses of Roman soldiers—whether of those who, after being converted to the faith in Palestine with the evangelical centurion, or baptized by the apostle Peter with Cornelius, centurion of the Italian cohort, were subsequently recalled to Italy with their legion under the emperors Gaius and Claudius; or of those who at Rome, Antioch, in Asia Minor, and Greece had professed Christ through the preaching of the apostles Peter, Paul, and Barnabas and, having returned to the City with their teachers, lived there.

Add those whom Florentius lists in the notes to his ancient Martyrology under the Kalends of August, on the testimony of the very weighty authorities Ambrose, Theodoret, Theophylact, Oecumenius, and Primasius. Recall the Jews whom Paul taught the faith at Rome for two years in his rented lodging (Acts 28:24, 29), where, as the consensus of writers holds, the deaconry of Saint Mary in the Via Lata was later established.

Also include the others who, after the destruction of Jerusalem, were brought by Titus to Rome or recalled under the emperor Nerva and opened domestic churches to the faithful in the Transtiberine district [Col. 1144C]. Finally, the residences of Roman nobles should be added: men born of equestrian rank or even called to Christ from the senatorial order—for Clement, too, was made a martyr of Christ while he was among the consulars under Domitian—who were counted among the brethren under the succeeding emperors Nerva and Trajan. In Trajan’s fourteenth year, so great was the number of Christians flourishing even in the provinces that this is demonstrated by the emperor’s famous letters and by the letters of Pliny, proconsul in Bithynia, letter 93 and following of book X.

Among the first and foremost nobles and Roman citizens worshiping Christ in the City were those equestrian members of Caesar’s household who had openly accepted the word of God when Peter preached, according to Clement of Alexandria and another weighty authority, as Florentius, cited above, indicates in the first volume of the *Library of the Fathers*, at the end of the commentary on the First Epistle of Blessed [Col. 1144D] Peter:

> For there, he says, he not only recalls that preaching but also testifies that Peter, at the request of the Caesareans, gave them the Gospel written by Saint Mark. Mark, Peter’s follower, while Saint Peter was openly preaching the Gospel at Rome before certain Caesarean equestrians and bearing many testimonies to Christ, wrote from these things the Gospel that is called according to Mark, because they earnestly requested him to commit what was being said to memory.

Florentius then adds:

> Since these Caesarean equestrians, for whose benefit the apostle Peter dictated the Gospel, were already very faithful and mature, it is also highly probable that they possessed their own house and church, not far from the Palatine residences.

Since, therefore, the Roman Church had grown in a remarkable way under the pontificate of Evaristus and had an ample supply of citizens’ houses, located in each district of the City; and since the number of twenty-five presbyters, filled at Peter’s command by Cletus, had been approved under Anacletus through ministries extending over many years [Col. 1145A], his successor Evaristus thought that houses, or titular churches, situated in the individual urban districts could safely be entrusted to individual presbyters. This would make it easier for the faithful to assemble for the celebration of synaxes and for frequent participation in the other Christian rites.

The practice followed the very same rite and example as at Jerusalem, where, after three thousand souls had been added in a single day (Acts 2:41, 46), the apostles continued daily with one accord in the temple and, breaking bread from house to house, ate their food with gladness. Acts 5:42 likewise says:

> Every day they did not cease in the temple and from house to house teaching and proclaiming Christ Jesus.

And in Acts 4, many who had been converted to Christ not only offered houses for the celebration of synaxes and the assemblies of the brethren, but also—verse 34—those who owned fields or houses and were devoted to evangelical perfection sold them, brought the proceeds of what they had sold, and laid them at the apostles’ feet. Distribution was made to each according to his need.

These events, which took place within the year after the death of Christ the Lord and the coming of the divine Spirit at Jerusalem, sufficiently demonstrate how many houses and how much growth could be added to the Christian assembly in the City, with the grace of the same Holy Spirit breathing upon it and with Peter himself proclaiming the mighty works of God during the twenty-five years in which he held the Roman chair while alive, and during as many succeeding years and more, up to Evaristus, when his successors governed and propagated this same Church.

**Line 5.—“And he appointed seven deacons, who were to guard the preaching bishop for the sake of the style of truth.”** This number of deacons was assigned to the Roman Church by Peter its founder (above, number 1), just as it had also been established in Jerusalem by the entire apostolic assembly (Acts 6). Likewise, the total of twenty-five presbyters corresponded to an equal number of priestly ministries, counting among the twenty-four others also the place of the one who was chosen as vicar of the supreme pontiff, as was stated above in the historical notes on the Life of Saint Cletus. This reflects the ministry of the Levites in the temple of the Lord, when the Jewish people constituted the Church of God and foreshadowed the Christian Church.

Nevertheless, it was decided to double the number in this primary Church of the New Covenant when it had been greatly enlarged by new accessions. The cardinal presbyters and Roman titular churches, previously numbering twenty-five, were increased to fifty; likewise the cardinal deacons were increased from their number of seven to twice seven, forming the sacred college of the Roman Church together with the six suburban bishops.

The biographer adds that Evaristus decreed that seven deacons should guard the preaching bishop for the sake of the true meaning. In addition to the reasons for the decree explained by Altaserra, the context seems to indicate this purpose: the seven deacons were required to attend the bishop as he preached—that is, all those who at that time were numbered among the Church’s deacons—and specifically “for the sake of the style of truth,” which I interpret as meaning that they were to learn it in the ministry of preaching.

For deacons also had to be trained in this ministry by virtue of their office. The Latin Church gives them this instruction at ordination: “The deacon must minister at the altar, baptize, and preach.” The apostolic Acts sufficiently demonstrate how Stephen the protomartyr and Philip, among the first seven, preached while the apostles were still alive, with how much praise and with how great a harvest of souls.

Therefore, while the pontiff was teaching the people, none of the seven deacons ought to be absent. All were ordered to stand by, like disciples being formed by their teacher for the teaching of truth and its style, so that they might proclaim the word of God to the peoples with equal faith, simplicity, and dignity whenever they themselves were sent to preach at the bishop’s command or at the command of the Holy Spirit through its superiors.

“For how will they hear without a preacher? Or how will they preach unless they are sent?” Therefore the Apostle also instructed Timothy, whom he first ordained as his deacon and then as his presbyter and bishop-assistant, in the Second Epistle, chapter 1, verse 13, when he said:

> Hold to the pattern of sound words that you have heard from me, in faith and in love in Christ Jesus.

[Col. 1146B]

### Note

**Line 4.—“He divided the titular churches in the city of Rome among the presbyters”:** so that each one might be distinguished by the boundaries of his own parish and by the other limits.

**Line 5.—“And he appointed seven deacons, who were to guard the preaching bishop for the sake of the style of truth,”** as witnesses of true doctrine, so that errors might not be imposed by rivals upon the preaching bishop and attributed to him, although he himself had not committed them.

[Col. 1146B]

**Line 4.—“He divided the titular churches in the city of Rome,” etc.** Some attribute to Evaristus the origin of the consecration of churches, but it is much more certain that this was an apostolic institution which passed from the Old Testament to the New and from the apostles to their successors. The Church preserved this rite by the consensus of the entire East and West—unless we accept the view of Cardinal Bona, *On Liturgical Matters*, book I, chapter 20, §3, that this pontiff promulgated in writing what he had received from his predecessors by oral tradition alone.

Or perhaps he added to the ancient ceremonies the rule that basilicas should not be consecrated without the sacrifice of the Mass, as the collectors of the canons report from him. As for the claim made by some that before the empire of Constantine the Great there were no dedications of churches because of fear of persecution, Bona, the authority just cited, believes that this should be understood of public and solemn dedications, not of private ones performed secretly. He discusses the matter at greater length.

On the blessing and dedication of churches, Edmund Martene should also be consulted, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, book II, chapter 13, where he presents several noteworthy details.

[Col. 1135]

> [Col. 1135] |

**6. Evaristus**, a Greek by nationality, the son of a Jew named Juda, from the city of Bethlehem, sat for thirteen years, six months [Note: [Col. 1135] B gives nine years, three months], and two days. He lived in the times of Domitian, Nerva, and Trajan [Note: [Col. 1135] B: “of Trajan and Hadrian”], from the consulship of Valens and Vetus to the consulship of Gallus and Bradua [Note: [Col. 1135] B: “from the consulship of Piso and Hasta to that of Aviola and Pansa”]. He was crowned with martyrdom. [Note: [Col. 1135] See Baronius under the year 112.] He divided the titular churches in the city of Rome among the presbyters and appointed seven deacons, who were to guard the preaching bishop for the sake of the style of truth. He held three ordinations in the month of December: six presbyters, two deacons, and five bishops for various places [Note: [Col. 1135] B: four presbyters, seventeen deacons, fifteen bishops]. He was also buried beside the body of blessed Peter at the Vatican [Note: [Col. 1137] C: “in the Vatican”], on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, and the episcopate was vacant for nineteen days [Note: [Col. 1137] C and B: eighteen].

## Catalogue under Liberius

Evaristus served thirteen years, seven months, and two days. He lived in the final times of Domitian, Nerva, and Trajan, from the consulship of Valens and Verus to that of Gallus and Bradua.

## VII. Saint Alexander in the Year of Christ 121, the Second Year of the Emperor Hadrian

[Col. 1147]

### From Fabrottus, based on the Freher manuscript

Number 7, line 2: B gives 16.

### From the Regius, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts

Number 7, line 2: ten years, seven months, eleven days (Mazarin: two days). “He lived in the time of Trajan, under the consulship of Verus and Hadrian.” “He mixed the Passion of the Lord into the preaching of the priests when Masses are celebrated.” “He established the water of sprinkling.” Line 8: five places. “He was crowned with martyrdom, and with him Eventius the presbyter and Theodotus the deacon; he was buried on the Nomentan Way.” Line 10: twenty-five days.

### From another Thuane manuscript

Line 2: ten years, seven months, twenty-six days; “into the preaching [Col. 1148A] of the priests when Mass is celebrated.” Line 5: Theodolus.

### In Holstenius and Schelestratius

Line 2: the Vatican, Cassinese, and two Florentine manuscripts give ten years and seven months. Line 3: the Florentine, Vatican, and Cassinese manuscripts read “in the preaching.” Line 4: the two Florentine, Vatican, and Cassinese manuscripts read “Theodotus.” Line 9: absent from the second Florentine manuscript, “not far away.”

### In Penia, based on the Cavensis manuscript

Line 2: he sat eight years, seven months, and two days. Line 5: “and Theodorus the deacon,” etc.; “there the water of sprinkling.” Line 8: “He was buried on the Nomentan Way.”

[Col. 1147A]

## Notes on the Text of Anastasius

Regarding Eventius and Theodolus, who attained the palm of martyrdom together with Saint Alexander, the Acts of Alexander report as follows:

> Saint Severina went to the seventh milestone from the city of Rome on the Nomentan Way, to her own estate, and placed Saint Alexander and Saint Eventius in one tomb. But she buried Saint Theodulus in another place.

From this it is clear that the reading should be not Theodorus or Theodotus, but Theodolus, as the second Catalogue has it.

Aelianus and Vetus, under whose consulship Alexander is said to have died, were consuls in the year 116. According to the custom of this Catalogue of Felix IV, Alexander died only in the following year, in which Trajan also died, as the Acts of Alexander testify in these words:

> By the will of God, Trajan died in that same year.

[Col. 1147B]

### Line 3

Here he incorporated the Passion of the Lord into the priests’ prayer when Masses are celebrated. The institution that the memory of Christ’s Passion should be celebrated in the sacrifice of the Mass is not proper to Alexander, but rather to Christ himself, since he commanded the apostles that whenever they did this—that is, whenever they sacrificed—they should do it in his memory: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22). Following these words, Paul says (1 Corinthians 11): “Whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you will proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.” The memory of Christ’s Passion was observed once a year. Augustine, *On the Season*, sermon 144:

> “But since the Passion is read on one day, it is not usually read except according to Matthew. At one time I had wanted the Passion to be read every year according to all the Evangelists as well. It was done; people did not hear what they were accustomed to hearing, and they were disturbed.”

### [Col. 1148A] Line 5

Here he ordained that water for sprinkling, mixed with salt, should be blessed in people’s homes. By Alexander’s ordinance, water blessed with salt ought to be kept not only in the church but also in private houses, according to the canon *Aquam*, *On Consecration*, distinction 8. The use of lustral, or blessed, water in the Church is said by the author of the *Apostolic Constitutions* (book VII, chapter 44) to derive from apostolic institution. Alexander likewise established that it should be kept in the homes of individuals, and not without reason, since the sprinkling of blessed water is effective for repelling demons, averting disasters affecting crops and grain, and avoiding nocturnal terrors.

Marcellus, bishop of Apamea in Syria, drove away a demon by sprinkling blessed water; the demon had been preventing the destruction of Jupiter’s shrine. Theodoret, book V, chapter 21:

> “The demon fled, unable to endure the assault of the water.”

Demons that were attacking a sick man are reported by Peter of Cluny, *On Miracles*, book I, chapter 7, to have been driven away by the sprinkling of blessed water:

> “Therefore, calling out in a loud voice to his companion Olivus to rise, he seized, full of faith, a vessel that happened to be hanging nearby with [Col. 1148B] blessed water, and, confidently sprinkling the consecrated element here and there, he drenched every part of that dwelling.”

And below:

> “When they had been completely expelled—as the sick man, who alone witnessed this, testified—he too was freed from the demons’ assault, and it was demonstrated how effective the sprinkling of salutary water with faith can be in similar circumstances.”

Pope Stephen VI turned away the devastation of locusts ravaging the crops by having blessed water sprinkled throughout the fields. Anastasius, in his Life of that pope:

> “He arose and, blessing water with his own hands, instructed the mansionarii, saying: ‘Take it and distribute it to each person, warning them to go around their fields in the name of the Lord and sprinkle this water over the crops and vineyards, asking God for aid and assistance.’”

Moreover, Anselm, abbot and subsequently elected archbishop of Canterbury and carried off to the Church, was almost lifeless from distress at his election; when blessed water was sprinkled on him and he drank it, he immediately recovered his senses. He himself bears witness in book III, letter 1, to the brothers at Bec:

> “Hearing from afar, they ran up, and when they saw that I was about to lose either my life or my senses, they became afraid. In their fear they sprinkled me with blessed water and offered it to me to drink.”

Blessed water is also beneficial for curing fevers and other illnesses. Gregory of Tours, *On the Glory of the Confessors*, chapter 24:

> “It also frequently cured those suffering from quartan fevers and those whose throats were painful when blessed water was given to them.”

## [Note: [Col. 1149A]]

### Line 1

Concerning the district called *Caput Tauri* (“Head of the Bull”). The name is indeclinable, also in Anastasius II, where the text reads: “Anastasius, a Roman by birth … from the fifth district, Theuma, Caput Tauri.” This district stood on the Palatine Hill, where there was also a bronze bull, concerning which Plutarch writes in *Marius*:

> “After the requested truce had been granted, they dismissed them under oath by the bronze Bull. They say that after the battle this bull was captured and carried into Catulus’s house as a trophy.”

In the fifth district, on the Palatine, stood the house of Catulus, as Pliny records in book XVII, chapter 1:

> “Crassus the orator was among the foremost men of the Roman name. His house was magnificent, but somewhat surpassed on that same Palatine by the house of Quintus Catulus, who defeated the Cimbri together with Gaius Marius.”

Thus the bronze bull was placed in Catulus’s house as a trophy, and from its head it gave its name to the district, which some maintain was also called *Capita Bubula* (“Ox Heads”).

### Line 3

“Here he incorporated the Passion of the Lord into the priests’ prayer.” Some manuscripts read: “into the priests’ preaching.” Those words seem to yield a double meaning.

First, the pontiff may have wished a special mention of Christ’s Passion to be made during the celebration, in accordance with the instruction given by Peter in his First Epistle, chapter 4, verse 1: “Since therefore Christ suffered in the flesh, arm yourselves with the same thought.” In the solemn sacrifice Alexander sought to arouse the courage of the faithful amid the storms of persecution, by the example of the Redeemer who had suffered in the flesh for the salvation of all.

Second—and this seems more probable—the measure may have been intended to counter the perverse teaching of certain heretics who raved that Christ had apparently suffered in the flesh. The writers Irenaeus and Tertullian speak of this heresy of the same century. Irenaeus writes:

> “According to none of the opinions of the heretics has the Word of God become flesh. For if anyone examines all their rules, he will find that among all of them the Word of God is introduced without flesh and impassible, and that Christ, who is above, is presented in this way.”

Tertullian—or the author of the appendix to *On the Prescription of Heretics*—writes of Cerdo and his errors concerning Christ that, among other things, he had raved that Christ denied the substance of flesh, declaring that he existed only in appearance and had not suffered at all, but only as if he had suffered.

Therefore, in the priests’ preaching during the celebration of the divine offices, Alexander decreed that special mention should be made, together with a continual remembrance, of the Passion that Christ had truly endured in his own flesh.

## [Note: [Col. 1149D] (From Bin.)]

### Line 1

Concerning the district called *Caput Tauri*. Since none of the fourteen districts is found among the ancients under this name, Baronius, under the year 121, note 2, thinks that the place was the area near the Palatine, which Suetonius, in *Octavian*, chapter 5, calls *Capita Bubula* (“Ox Heads”). He says that Octavian was born there.

### Line 3

“Here he incorporated the Passion of the Lord into the priests’ prayer.” This should be called something committed to writing and strengthened by Alexander’s decree rather than something newly established by him.

### [Col. 1149D] (From Lab.)

### Line 4

“When Masses are celebrated.” These words are absent from manuscript C. A.

## [Note: [Col. 1149D]]

# Chronological Notes

The date of the martyrdom of Saint Alexander the pope is established from his Acts, vindicated by Schelestratius in dissertation 2, chapter 3, of *Antiquities of the Church*. In those Acts he shows that nothing is found demonstrating that they were written after the age of Honorius and Arcadius.

> “Therefore,” he says in note 12, “the authority of those Acts will always remain: fair-minded judges of historical matters ought to grant such authority to works which, almost twelve hundred years ago—for we should now say thirteen hundred—were copied from more ancient sources.”

From these Acts, then, we learn that Pope Alexander was put to death for Christ by order of the judge Aurelian in the city of Rome on 3 May of the same year in which Trajan died at Selinus in the province of Cilicia, according to Dio; or, as Eusebius reports elsewhere that he had read in the *Chronicle*, at Seleucia in Isauria, on 10 August. Trajan’s death and Hadrian’s adoption occurred under the consuls Niger and Apronianus, in the year of Christ 117.

Therefore it ought not to seem strange if, in a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs written in the age of Charlemagne, an ancient addition in another hand was appended to Alexander’s pontificate— as the aforementioned Schelestratius observes—namely, the brief account “under the emperor Trajan and under Aelius Hadrian [Col. 1150B],” the emperor. From this Baronius took the occasion to alter the ancient reading of the Martyrology, which referred the martyrdom of Saints Alexander the pope and his companions, in accordance with the cited Acts, to the reign of Trajan. He thought that it should instead be postponed to the reign of Hadrian, who was indeed proclaimed emperor in the same year, but at least two months after the death of Saint Alexander.

Bede, Notker, and Ado, however, retain the ancient and genuine reading of those Acts, as Schelestratius notes. The same reading is likewise presented by lectionaries, both manuscript and printed, produced before the Breviary of Saint Pius V.

Since these documents establish the endpoint of Saint Alexander’s mortal life and pontificate as 3 May in the Christian year 117, under the consuls Niger and Apronianus—consuls first assigned to Sixtus, Alexander’s successor—it remains to determine the beginning of his pontificate.

I shall first point out, however, that the catalogues assign to Saint Alexander as his final consuls Aelianus and Vetus—or, more accurately, as they should be identified from the observations in Cardinal Noris’s consular letter, Aelius Lamia and Aelianus Vetus—who belong to the year of Christ 116. The consuls who marked the year 117, in which Alexander suffered martyrdom, are assigned to Sixtus, his successor.

We can easily grasp the reason for this assignment from the method of pontifical and consular chronology, joined in these catalogues to the paschal season. I explained this method above, at the beginning of the chronological notes on Saint Peter and near the end of the chronological note on Saint Evaristus. In both places I observed that pontifical years fixed the beginning of their era at the paschal days, while, in accordance with the Roman civil year and the custom of the priestly colleges, their beginning in the City was reckoned from the birthday festival of the Palilia, or 21 April.

Accordingly, the ordinary consuls who marked the progress of that Julian year from that day, or from the paschal season, are assigned in the catalogues to the pontiff then sitting. The consuls of the immediately preceding year are assigned to his predecessor, who had completed his final day before the paschal season.

Since Sixtus’s election followed Alexander’s death on 3 May by scarcely ten days beyond the Palilia, and since in the year 117 Easter fell on 5 April, within the paschal season, the consuls of the year 117, Niger and Apronianus, are assigned to the beginning of Sixtus’s pontificate. The preceding consuls, Aelius Lamia and Aelianus Vetus of the year 116, close the pontifical era of Saint Alexander.

The determination of the beginning of Alexander’s pontificate may appear somewhat more difficult. But I am confident that it can be collected from the chronological rules previously established in this method.

Alexander’s predecessor Evaristus was crowned with martyrdom on 26 October in the year 108, under the consuls Gallus and Bradua, as we have already seen proved by the documents produced in the *Prolegomena*, folio LXXXIX, and in the notes to his number, page 76. From that day to the day of the martyrdom, or feast day, of Saint Alexander, 3 May in the year 117, there are eight years, six months, and seven days.

The *Liber Pontificalis* and the seventh Colbertine catalogue assign this total, as I shall examine below, after the vacancy of the see has been calculated. But since all the catalogues, the ancient readings, and the paintings of Saint Paul count ten years for Alexander—with the single exception of the Liberian catalogue, which assigns seven—it seems that this ten-year era must be reckoned from Alexander’s ordination to the episcopate. It would therefore fall in the autumn of the year 106.

That was Trajan’s tenth year, when the third persecution had begun to harass Christians, as we have already established from Pliny’s letters to Trajan. There was therefore good reason for Evaristus, following the example of his predecessor Anacletus—who had appointed a vicar-bishop for himself at Rome during Domitian’s persecution, and who had consecrated Clement, the successor of the Prince of the Apostles, during Nero’s persecution—to lay hands on Alexander as well, so that he might ordain him from the presbyterate as his auxiliary bishop and vicar in the City.

Alexander was subsequently summoned by the votes of the clergy to the chair and succession after Evaristus, in the days following Evaristus’s martyrdom, and began a new era of the see he had acquired. This is correctly marked in the Liberian catalogue under the consuls Palma and Tullus, in the year of Christ 109, when the first paschal season of his pontificate was counted for him.

Why, then, does the Liberian catalogue mark seven years and two months, while all the other catalogues and manuscripts assign ten years, and our *Pontifical* gives eight? I think the matter should be determined as follows.

The paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul, the ancient catalogues, and all the lectionary manuscripts unanimously reported ten years, seven months, and two or three days. I suspect that the parchment witnesses mentioned by Bucherius—which were once viewed as the only copies shown to Leunclavius containing the Liberian catalogue, and which survive today only in reproductions—displayed the same numbers.

But perhaps, owing to the damage of age, the letters indicating the years in the line marking Alexander’s era had become less distinct. Consequently, the number seven, belonging to the months, was transferred by the copyist to the place of the years, and the number three, belonging to the days, to the place of the months, while the final unit was retained as though it alone belonged to the days.

There is certainly no easier opportunity for numerical signs to be advanced into the next class, especially since it often happens that in catalogues a writer expresses only the numerical signs X, VII, and III, while indications placed at the beginning of the catalogue distinguish years, months, and days.

Thus, when the parchment had been damaged by age so that the letter X indicating years disappeared, the following sign VII, which indicated months, was entered by the copyist among the numbers of years. The following units III, which ought to have indicated days, were attributed to the months. Or they may have been divided—if perhaps the final unit appeared somewhat farther from the preceding two, as II I—so that the first two were taken as months and the last as a day.

Accordingly, when the autograph parchment read “Alexander X, VII, III,” and the sign X disappeared, the copyist rendered it “Alexander VII, II, I.”

The surviving paintings in the basilica of Saint Paul, however, which clearly display the sign for ten in the place of years and plainly express the three, III, in the sequence of days, while three of the oldest Italian manuscripts retain the number seven for the months between the two totals, together with the catalogue of Felix IV and several others cited above in the *Prolegomena*, show that the genuine reading assigns to Alexander ten years, seven months, and three days from the time when he was promoted to the episcopal order.

The eight years of the Roman see assigned to Alexander by the manuscripts of Anastasius, together with five months and two days, after the nineteen-day vacancy of the see calculated from Evaristus’s death in this section, agrees correctly with the era of both martyrdoms.

For if Evaristus was killed for Christ in the year 108, on 26 October, the day on which he is commemorated, and if the vacancy of the see lasted nineteen days until 14 November, the date assigned to Alexander’s election as Roman pontiff, his *enthronism* (*enthronismus*) could have been completed on the first Sunday of Advent. In that same year this fell on 3 December. From there [Col. 1152A] to 3 May in the year 117, the celebrated day of Alexander’s martyrdom, there elapsed eight years, five months, and two days, if the endpoints of this very total are included.

Thus the basis of both eras in Saint Alexander is established: namely, his ordination to the episcopate and his enthronement in the Roman see. This follows from the credibility, testimony, and agreement of the manuscripts and monuments, if we establish that Blessed Alexander was ordained coadjutor bishop of Saint Evaristus at the beginning of Trajan’s persecution, in the year of Christ 107, on Sunday, 29 September; that after Evaristus was crowned with martyrdom on 26 October in the year 108, Alexander was elected as his successor on 14 November; and that he was placed on the pontifical throne on 3 December of that same year, 108.

For if ten complete years, seven months, and three days are counted from the day of his ordination—as we read in the paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul—the endpoint of the total will be 2 May in the Christian year 117, and the following day, 3 May, will have been the day of his deposition.

The calculations for the other era, from his placement on the Roman pontifical throne on 3 December in the year 108, after the death of his predecessor and his own election—which in Anastasius’s book and in the seventh Colbertine catalogue is marked as eight years, five months, and two days—agree with this interval of time and with the consuls assigned both in the *Pontifical* and in the catalogues and lectionary books.

# Historical Notes of the Same Author

### Line 3

“Here he incorporated the Passion of the Lord into the priests’ prayer when Masses are celebrated.”

The first decrees of the Roman pontiffs concern the principal act of religious worship, namely the sacrifice. Peter attended to the priestly ministry when he promoted Linus and Cletus to the episcopal order (above, no. 4). Cletus established the number of presbyters as twenty-five, following the instruction of the same Peter (no. 30). Evaristus, following the example of the apostles, assigned seven deacons to the bishop as he performed sacred rites with solemn ceremony and administered the word of God (no. 6).

After the grades of the priesthood had thus been arranged, Anacletus designated places suitable for sacrifices and intended for the assemblies of the faithful in the Vatican (no. 5). Evaristus established them in the titular churches (no. 6), retracing the footsteps of his predecessors and of the apostles, who publicly and in their homes broke bread so that the faithful might persevere unanimously in the breaking of bread and in the apostles’ teaching.

Once ministers and places had been established and enumerated, the arrangement of particular prayers to be used in the sacrifice was also ordered by the supreme pontiffs. Christ the Lord, the eternal priest, had already taught the apostles the Lord’s Prayer. In addition, he had commanded that, in his memory, they should do what he himself had done at the supper.

The apostle Paul recounted the same things in First Corinthians, chapter 11: “The Lord Jesus, on the night when he was betrayed, took bread,” and so forth. These words are recited almost verbatim in the canon, not only in our own age but also in the time of Ambrose, in book IV *On the Sacraments*, as Cardinal Bona observed, *On Liturgical Matters*, book II, chapter 13. He also notes that the same things are found in the ancient liturgies attributed to James and Clement.

From the same Apostle they understood that “in every prayer and supplication, with thanksgiving, our petitions should be made known to God” (Philippians 4). Therefore, instructed by salutary commandments and formed by divine institution, they included, together with the petitions of prayer, formulas of thanksgiving in hymns and in the preface, and likewise supplications through the Holy of Holies who is offered, together with the memory of those to whom that sanctifier of all had granted his grace and glory.

The Lord’s Passion had to be mingled with all these things, both through words and sentences drawn from the Gospel and through the sign of the cross—the abbreviated sign of the Passion, frequently employed according to the custom of the nascent Church, which transmitted this tradition to later generations. Tertullian bears witness to it in *On the Crown of the Soldier*:

> “At every advance and movement, whenever we enter or leave, when we put on clothing, when we light our shoes, when we go to the baths, the tables, the lamps, the beds, and the seats, we mark our foreheads with the sign of the cross.”

Tertullian mentions these practices immediately after referring to our cup and bread, of which we suffer something to fall onto the ground through anxiety. These disciplines were interconnected: tradition was their source, custom their confirmation, and faith their guardian.

Alexander incorporated the Lord’s Passion into the priests’ prayers at the offering of the Mass. Certainly, at every advance and movement; certainly, by the tradition, custom, and faith of the apostles and apostolic men whom we enumerate in the canon.

He incorporated it from the Gospel of John, published a few years before Alexander began his pontificate. Hence come the lifting of the eyes (John 17:1), the prayer for those present with him in truth, and for all who would believe in him through their word.

No one can fail to see that in the prayers both before and after the action, the memory, events, and mysteries of the Passion are so mingled in the canon that we know many of them, from Tertullian’s indications, to have been so firmly established by custom and tradition at the end of the second century that they may already then be understood to have been coeval with the Christian faith. Through Alexander’s care and decree, they passed, by the unwritten law of custom, into the written canon.

Therefore, in the sacred Council of Trent, session 22, chapter 4, it is rightly asserted that the canon of the Mass consists of the Lord’s own words, the traditions of the apostles, and the institutions of the holy pontiffs.

### Line 4

“He is crowned with martyrdom, and with him Eventius the presbyter, and so forth.”

The frequently mentioned prelate Schelestratius distinguished and vindicated the genuine Acts of Saint Alexander and his fellow martyrs from the interpolated versions, in volume I of *Antiquities of the Church*, dissertation 2, chapter 30. Their principal features, which must be sampled here, wonderfully illuminate both Alexander’s life and the history of the Christian faith, greatly enlarged in the City by the accession of distinguished men and women.

The antiquity of the Acts is commended by the martyrologies of Bede, Rabanus, and Ado. The first dates to the eighth century and the latter to the ninth; they draw from the same Acts whatever they report concerning the martyrdom of Pope Alexander and his companions in their contest, the presbyters Eventius and Theodulus.

Their antiquity is also commended by the discipline of secrecy observed in them. It is commended by their agreement with chronology, with imperial history, and with the third persecution under Trajan. The Acts relate that Trajan, while staying at Seleucia—when he had undertaken his expedition against the Parthians before the consulship of Pedo, which falls in the year of Christ 115—sent the judge Aurelian.

Aurelian inflicted martyrdom on Hermes, the prefect of the City, and his sister Theodora; on Alexander, the Roman pontiff; on the presbyters Eventius and Theodulus; and on Quirinus, the tribune, and his daughter Balbina. He also caused numerous men baptized by Pope Alexander in prison to be placed in a failing boat, taken farther out to sea, and drowned.

The bodies of those martyrs, their cemeteries, their titular churches, and the very ancient inscriptions still surviving in them support the history. The cemetery of Hermes, prefect of the City, on the Via Salaria at the second milestone from the City, together with its underground chapel, can still be seen. Aringhi records it in book IV, chapter 37, no. 37.

An ancient inscription, an indication of the relics of Hermes, prefect of the City, is preserved by the title of Saint Pudenziana on an engraved stone beneath Gregory VII. The names of Balbina and Theodora are recorded by an older surviving inscription on the pavement of the presbyterium of the diaconia of Saint Mary in Domnica, engraved approximately in the ninth century.

In the same place, in our own age, several bones of Blessed Balbina were found, together with a lead tablet bearing the inscription:

> **CORPUS S. BALBINAE VIRG.**  
> **Body of Saint Balbina, virgin.**

They were enclosed in a marble reliquary placed beneath the principal altar. The matter was also recorded in public documents, when, at the command of the most holy Father Clement XI, the distinguished men Alexander, canon Bonaventura—shortly afterward created bishop of Nazianzus—and Marcus, abbot Boldetti, now canon of Saint Mary in Trastevere, appointed to recognize and care for sacred relics, assembled there. I have explained this more fully in a little work composed on the subject.

The body of Blessed Quirinus, tribune and father of Balbina, was transferred from Rome to the abbess Gepa by Leo IX around the year 1050. The Bollandist scholars establish this from public documents under 30 March, folio 813.

Finally, an ancient inscription carved on the same body’s reliquary, as Aringhi records in book III, chapter 22, confirms that the body of Saint Alexander the pope, together with the martyred presbyters Eventius and Theodulus, was transferred from his cemetery on the Via Nomentana at the seventh milestone into the City, to the title of Saint Sabina, under Eugenius II.

Since it is therefore certain that among the most ancient cemeteries of the suburban district are those made famous by Alexander and his companions, whose bodies were brought there in the second century and subsequently transferred in the ninth, tenth, and eleventh centuries, the Church received remarkable protection from them. Their Acts, and the history of the Roman Church, preserve this protection in such records.

For it is not merely established that a considerable portion of the Roman nobility was converted to the faith under that pontiff—after the consul Clement had already been numbered among its members, and now Hermes, the prefect, with his sister, and Quirinus, the tribune, with his daughter, were added. It is also understood how it happened that the chains which had bound the Prince of the Apostles for Christ, and which the Acts say were given by Balbina, the tribune’s daughter, to Theodora, the prefect’s sister, were preserved by Christians in such a way that, three centuries later, when Eudoxia’s title was erected, they received from them a new name.

A marble figure of a little boat placed before the doors of the diaconia of Saint Mary in Domnica, and renewed there after the ancient model under Leo X, would convey nothing dissimilar if this symbol were referred to the instrument of martyrdom of so many courageous Christians whom the noble virgin Balbina accompanied when they were led to the sea to be drowned.

The Acts report the following concerning the judge Aurelian:

> “At the same time he ordered all the Christians who had been baptized in prison by Pope Alexander to be led to the sea, placed in an old boat, and taken out into the deep. Immediately, after all had been bound hand to hand and stones had been hung around their necks, he ordered that the old, battered, and perforated boat itself be sunk into the depths. With them the virgin of Christ, Balbina, also went, glorifying God,” and so forth.

I discussed these matters more fully in the work mentioned above concerning Saint Balbina’s relics. They had to be touched on briefly here, however, to show that the Librarian’s history of Alexander’s life is supported by documents contemporary with that pontiff, or nearly so, preserved and read through subsequent centuries within the sacred cemeteries and Roman titular churches where the bodies of Saints Alexander, Quirinus, Hermes, Balbina, and Theodora had been deposited, guarded, and laid to rest, and where their memory was annually celebrated by the public veneration of the faithful through sacred rites offered to God over them.

Schelestratius does not deny that some errors entered certain copies of the Acts of Saint Alexander transcribed at a later period. Indeed, he warned that interpolated versions must be distinguished from the genuine ones (dissertation 2, chapter 3, no. 1).

Together with Baronius, he indicates that the judge Aurelian under the empire of Trajan was mistakenly rendered by copyists as the emperor Aurelian. Perhaps, too, the title “count of the two military forces” (*comes utriusque militiae*) was wrongly produced from “Trajan’s companion on the Parthian expedition.” I would not deny that this title became known later than Trajan’s time.

That companions of expeditions nevertheless attended Roman emperors and were honored by that title is demonstrated by public inscriptions dating more than sixty years before Trajan’s reign. The famous monument of Tiberius Plautius Silvanus, still surviving in the Tiburtine territory near the Lucanian bridge, proves this. It is engraved as follows and printed in Gruter’s *Thesaurus*, page 453:

> **TI. PLAVTIO. M. F. … AN. (SILVANO AELIAN.), etc. PR. VRB. LEGAT. ET COMIT I. CLAVDI I. CAESARIS. IN. BRITANNIA. CONSUL I. PROCOS ASIAE. LEGAT. PROPRAET. MOESIAE.**
>
> “To Tiberius Plautius, son of Marcus … Silvanus Aelianus, prefect of the City, legate and companion of Claudius Caesar in Britain, consul, proconsul of Asia, propraetorian legate of Moesia.”

This man, the companion of the emperor Claudius on the British expedition, was promoted through various degrees of office to the prefecture of the City, subsequently sent as legate to Spain, and then recalled to the prefecture of the City.

> **SENATVS. IN. PRAEFECTURA. TRIVMPHALIBVS. ORNAMENTIS. HONORAVIT. AVCTORE. IMP. CAESARE. AVGVSTO VESPASIANO, etc. HVNC. IN. EADEM. PRAEFECTVRA. VRBIS IMP. CAESAR. AVG. VESPASIANVS. ITERVM. COS. FECIT.**
>
> “The Senate honored him, while he held the prefecture, with triumphal ornaments, on the recommendation of the emperor Caesar Augustus Vespasian, etc. In that same prefecture of the City, the emperor Caesar Augustus Vespasian, consul for the second time, made him consul again.”

I have not been reluctant to mention these matters so that we may understand, first, that Schelestratius rightly preserved these details from the harsher criticism directed by Pearson against the credibility of Alexander’s deeds, on page 227 of his posthumous work *On the Series and Succession of the Roman Pontiffs*, concerning the count of the two military forces attributed to Aurelian and the prefecture of the City assigned to Hermes—provided that the genuine Acts are distinguished from the interpolated ones.

Blondel’s criticism is also unsatisfactory: he objects to the immature age assigned in the Acts both to the presbyter Eventius and to Pope Alexander, calling the Acts not merely erroneous but mendacious. He uses the same accusation concerning Aurelian’s commission to exterminate all Christians, as though Pliny’s letters to Trajan and the milder rescripts issued in response to Tiberianus did not exist.

But whoever remembers the age at which men were admitted to the presbyterate or pontificate in that period of the apostolic men will hesitate to pronounce on this matter. Saul is called a young man in the Acts of the Apostles (7:58) when Stephen was being stoned. Yet Pearson, in his posthumous work, recognizes in his Pauline annals, from Acts 13, that this young man, transformed from persecutor into an apostle, was ordained by the laying on of hands with Barnabas ten years later.

Paul speaks of the youth of Timothy, the bishop whom he ordained, in the First Epistle to him, chapter 4, verse 12. In that golden age of the Church’s beginnings, the age of old age was a blameless life; the necessity of a discipline requiring more advanced age in priests had not yet arisen, as it did in later times.

Indeed, when Alexander was elected pontiff, the apostle John had shortly before been thrown into a cauldron of boiling oil at Rome. Jerome affirmed that the Lord had chosen him when he was almost still a boy, in book I *Against Jovinian*. On this matter, however, Baronius should be consulted under the year of Christ 101, notes 8 and 9.

Concerning the thirty years of age assigned in the Acts of Alexander, and the correction of that number, see Schelestratius, dissertation 2, chapter 3, no. 12.

As for Trajan’s moderation in shedding Christian blood more sparingly, no one will deny that there is a great difference between the savage persecutions of Nero and Domitian and the milder persecution of Trajan. Yet everyone will acknowledge from Trajan’s own replies to Pliny’s letters that the third persecution of the Church was carried out under that prince in such a way that those who were denounced under the title of our religion were to be examined and punished with the ultimate penalty.

Therefore, since the Acts are produced as commanding the slaughter of all Christians, either “all” must be understood as referring to all who were denounced and convicted, or the word “all” is an excess belonging to the interpolated Acts.

### Line 5

“Here he ordained that water for sprinkling, mixed with salt, should be blessed in people’s homes.”

Cardinals Baronius and Bona—Baronius under the year of Christ 132, from notes 3–5, and Bona, *On Liturgical Matters*, book I, chapter 20, no. 5—prove from the holy Fathers that the rite of blessing water has been handed down to us from apostolic institution, not merely for administering baptism, but for every use in which the element of water is purified through the invocation of the divine name and sanctified through priestly blessing and prayers.

Accordingly, they teach that Alexander’s decree established an ancient custom. We can understand without great difficulty why the addition of salt should be joined to the blessing and why this water for sprinkling should be kept in people’s homes, if we consider the rite of ablutions established by the Lord under the old Law. The apostles did not reject this rite under the new covenant; rather, they prudently adapted it to the fulfillment of the Scriptures and figures that had preceded the Christian faith.

They moderated the discipline in such a way that, through the frugal use of sprinkling, they would stimulate the mind to purify its affections by Christian dedication, while keeping far away the superstitious and daily washing of the entire body devised by the *hemerobaptists*, as Tertullian and his interpreter de la Barre prudently warned in book *On Prayer*, chapter 12.

Baronius, under the year 57, notes 106 and following, shows that among the Hebrews it was customary not only for the high priest and priests to wash their hands and feet in the bronze basin before entering the sanctuary, as described in Exodus 30, but also for all Jews to worship only with washed hands, as Aristaeus attests.

Baronius thinks that this custom passed from there to Christians of the apostolic age and to succeeding generations:

> “This custom seems to have flowed from Jewish rites. For, as has been said, Aristaeus reports that not only their priests but also the other Jews were accustomed to worship only with washed hands. Writing about the seventy-two interpreters, he says: ‘After greeting the king, they withdrew to their customary places; and, as is the custom of all Jews, having first washed their hands in the sea, they poured out prayers to God.’ A little later he says: ‘I also asked for what reason they washed their hands first when they offered vows. In response to my inquiry, they demonstrated that this was a testimony that they should do nothing improperly, but complete everything piously and reverently, since all actions are performed with the hands, properly referring each one to truth and justice.’”

Baronius adds under note 109:

> “But as regards Christians, not only do the passages we have mentioned teach and the ancient testimonies of ecclesiastical writers confirm that they were accustomed to wash their hands before prayer, in accordance with the Apostle’s instruction (1 Timothy 2): ‘I want men to pray in every place, lifting up pure hands’; for Clement also writes that a Christian should pray after washing (Apostolic Constitutions, book VIII, chapter 58). Tertullian likewise demonstrates this very thing when he says (*On Prayer*, chapter 11): ‘Besides, what point is there in approaching prayer with hands washed but a spirit soiled?’”

He adds several other passages to the same effect from Saint John Chrysostom and other Fathers. He also recalls, under the year 101, note 9, that he had often proved that both the Lord and the apostles had borrowed many things from the legal institution.

I am pleased to pursue Tertullian’s testimony a little further. In it the origin and reason appear for the apostolic custom, and for the decree confirmed by Alexander, that the blessing of water should be completed by the admixture of salt and that it should be kept in the dwellings of the faithful. Tertullian accordingly proceeds to inquire and to give the reason for washing the hands before prayer:

> “When I questioned this scrupulously,” he says, “and sought the reason, I discovered that it was a commemoration of the Lord’s dedication.”

A little later he adds:

> “But we Christians do not merely raise our hands; we also spread them out [Col. 1156D], patterning them on the Lord’s passion; and in praying, we confess Christ.”

From these words it is apparent that, in the second and third centuries, a presbyter investigated and supplied the reason both for washing the hands and for the extension of the hands, a practice long established among Christians when prayers were poured out to God. It is a commemoration of the Lord’s dedication, carried out through the significance and faith of his passion.

Since the Apostle commands us to pray “in every place, lifting up holy hands,” this rite—by which we are to offer a sacrifice of praise in dedication to the Lord—was appropriately derived from the rite instituted by God under the old covenant, namely, the washing of the hands of those making an offering. Yet it was raised to a higher level through invocation of the divine name revealed to us by the Word of God, and sanctified by faith in that same passion and by its merit, in the water of sprinkling. This teaches us to hope for and seek purification—not through the ashes of a heifer mixed with water, as in the legal sacrifices prepared by divine command for the cleansing of the flesh, but through the cross of Christ the Lord and the blood poured out for the purification of the spirit [Col. 1157A].

Since no offering was properly made to God without the addition of salt, as the Lord commanded in Leviticus 2:13—“Whatever sacrifice you offer, you shall season with salt; and you shall not remove the salt of the covenant of your God from your sacrifice; in every offering of yours you shall offer salt”—the apostles and pontiffs, in order to suggest to Christians praying either in church or at home that the dedication of their prayers offered everywhere derives its power from the Lord’s passion, which eminently contains and surpasses all offerings, appropriately judged that salt should be mixed into water and dissolved in it. Through the invocation of the divine name and the sign of Christ’s cross traced over it, the water would express that the ancient offerings had been dissolved in the new covenant, and that this new sprinkling had been raised to a higher level for the purification of the spirit: the sprinkling of the blood and water flowing from Christ’s side. Our consciences would thereby be cleansed much more splendidly, as the Apostle says, than Aaron and the Levites were cleansed by the blood of legal victims and by ashes mixed with water.

This is relevant to the annotation [Col. 1157B] of the Reverend Father Calmet on Leviticus 8:13, “In every offering of yours you shall offer salt,” and on Numbers 8:7 and 19:17, where the rite of lustral water is prescribed. There Calmet brought forward from Philo’s third book *On the Life of Moses*—to which another work by the same Philo, *On Those Who Offer Victims*, may be added—several matters relating to the meaning of such rites among the Hebrews. He also cited further material from Augustine and from Theodoret’s *Questions on Numbers*, which admonishes us to contemplate, in the figure of the legal sprinklings foreshadowing Christ’s death, Christ as the author and source of our purification. The Church took care to enact this very thing in the blessing of water and salt, by which it instituted that we should be sprinkled.

Just as, therefore, Tertullian’s testimony makes clear that the rite of extending the hands during prayer originated among Christians in the apostolic age and signified the Lord’s passion, which we confess and from which we hope to receive, through our Lord Jesus Christ, the power of obtaining things from God in our prayers—for we conclude our prayers by invoking him—so we begin praying from faith in Christ’s passion, sprinkling ourselves with that water. In this rite it appears that we confess and believe that every ancient offering is far surpassed by the commemoration of the Lord’s dedication, that is, of the Passion and sacrifice which the Church received from the apostolic age as something to be properly commemorated through the cross traced over the water and through the prayers of the priests poured over it. Its perpetual sign is preserved both in the public gatherings of Christians and in private homes, just as Pope Alexander commanded, following the authority of this institution, whose origin must be referred to an earlier period, as is gathered from Tertullian and from the other writers cited by Baronius.

It was fitting, moreover, that in Alexander’s time a decree of this kind should be established more firmly. Since his immediate predecessor, Evaristus, had divided the *tituli* among the Roman presbyters—places where the faithful assembled for synaxes and public prayers—it was necessary that the rite of beginning prayer handed down by the forefathers should be observed more carefully in the *tituli* [Col. 1157D]. As the number of the faithful increased under Pope Alexander through the conversion of the Roman nobility, new oratories were founded each day and cemeteries opened where assemblies could be held. These too could not lack the same sign of purification before prayer.

For the more thoroughly preceding stains to be washed away from the minds of the faithful preparing themselves for prayer, faith, hope, and charity had to be aroused in this sprinkling, which Tertullian calls the memory of Christ’s dedication. And, to guard more effectively against their contracting other stains in the future that might corrupt their prayers, it was necessary to invoke the protection of our Redeemer against the evil spirits who envy our happiness and lay snares for us. The priest’s voice and command were to preside properly over the dedication of this water and over the exorcisms, so that by Christ’s power the attacks of spirits rebellious against God might be broken and restrained.

Since all these matters are sufficiently explained by the most ancient rite and practice of blessing and preserving water—both for baptism in the font and for sprinkling in the church courtyards, from the earliest period of the foundation of those churches, whose origin proves them nearly contemporary with the beginning of the Christian religion—there is no reason to dwell longer on Alexander’s decree or on proving its appropriateness. This was especially so at the time when the division of the *tituli* was being completed and the increasing number of Christian churches, growing daily, provided greater opportunity for prayer, whether in the assembly of the entire body of the faithful or in the private retreats of individuals.

**Line 8.**—“He was also buried on the Nomentan Way, where he was beheaded, not far from the city of Rome, at the seventh milestone.” A cemetery was constructed there by the faithful. The distinguished V. C. Boldetti records that in our own age several bodies of holy martyrs were also taken from it, in Book II, chapter 18, page 569, of his *Observations on the Cemeteries*.

[Note: [Col. 1158A]

**Line 3.**—“He introduced the Lord’s passion into the priests’ prayer when Masses are celebrated.” Saint Alexander first added to the sacrifice of the Mass, in memory of Christ’s passion, the words “Who, on the day before he suffered,” up to the words “This is my body.”

**Line 5.**—“He decreed that the water of sprinkling, together with salt, should be blessed in people’s dwellings”—that is, for their purification and for driving out demons.]

[Note: [Col. 1158B]

**Line 3.**—“He introduced the Lord’s passion into the priests’ prayer when Masses are celebrated.” Regarding these words, Peter of Orvieto notes in his unpublished *Scholia* that the phrase there is “of such a blessed passion.” Others likewise commonly write that the prayer “Therefore, remembering, Lord,” which the priest says after the consecration, was instituted by Alexander.

But if the matter concerns precisely the memory of the Passion, whether it is expressed in these words or others, it certainly was not instituted by this holy pontiff, says Cardinal Bona in Book II, chapter 13, no. 3 of *On Liturgical Matters*. Baronius observes this admirably in the year 132, no. 3: we have an explicit command of the Lord concerning this in the Gospels, and Paul provides a clear testimony to the same matter in 1 Corinthians 11, saying: “Whenever you eat this bread and drink this cup, you shall proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes.”

The author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* likewise says that Alexander decreed that blessed water should be kept in people’s dwellings. Baronius proves in the cited place that this practice of blessed water derived from a tradition of the apostles and was established by Alexander’s decree.

When the priest approaches the consecration, he first says this prayer: “Which offering,” and so forth. Then the priest says: “Who, on the day before he suffered, took bread,” and so forth. The same author of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, Walafrid, and others thought that this clause, “Who, on the day before,” and so forth, had been added by Alexander. Alcuin, however, more correctly holds that it was also used by the apostles. On this matter, as well as on the consecration, its form, and its rite, see Bona in the cited place.

Bona also observes in chapter 9, no. 3, that water is mixed with wine in the chalice by Christ’s institution, not, as some incorrectly write, by Alexander’s decree. Alexander is therefore called the author of this mixture because he confirmed in writing, against the errors of heretics, what he had received from the tradition of the Lord and the apostles. Saint Cyprian wrote a lengthy letter on this subject to Caecilius, numbered 63, which Saint Augustine cites in Book IV, chapter 21 of *On Christian Doctrine* [Col. 1158D].

**Line 4.**—“He was crowned with martyrdom.” Eusebius begins the third persecution of the Church in the year 107 of Christ, the tenth year of the Emperor Trajan, in his *Chronicle*, because in that year it greatly intensified and continued until Trajan’s death.

In the year 111, when Pliny the Younger, proconsul of Bithynia, after conducting an inquiry into the Christians, discovered that they were being accused on false charges, he wrote to Trajan in Letter 97 of Book X and reported that they were guilty of no impiety or violation of the laws. He had observed only that, awakened from sleep at first light, they sang hymns to Christ as to a god; for the rest, they avoided adultery, murder, and other such crimes, and did everything according to the prescriptions of the laws. Trajan replied in these words: “They are not to be sought out; but if they are reported and convicted, they are to be punished.”

During that persecution, Simeon, son of Clopas and bishop of Jerusalem, was crucified at the age of 120. Eusebius describes his martyrdom from Hegesippus in Book III, chapter 32. Saint Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, likewise suffered martyrdom, according to the same Book of Eusebius, chapter 36. Both died in the year 116, as may be read in Baronius’s critical notes for the year 107 [Col. 1159A].

This persecution lasted until the tenth year of the Emperor Hadrian, the year 126 of Christ. Hadrian moderated its severity on the occasion of his decennalia. On this matter Eusebius should be read in Book IV, chapter 8, where he reports these things from Saint Justin’s *Apology* addressed to the emperors; in chapter 9 he also presents Hadrian’s letter, ordering that no Christian be punished without a formal charge. Baronius’s critical notes should likewise be consulted.]

[Col. 1145]

>[Col. 1145] **7. Alexander**, a Roman by nation, son of Alexander, from the district of Caput Tauri, occupied the see for eight years, five months, and two days [Note: [Col. 1145] B: 10 years, 5 months, 20 days]. He lived during the reign from Trajan to Helianus [Note: [Col. 1145] B: from the consulships of Aviola and Pansa to those of Catullinus and Aper] and Veterus [Note: [Col. 1145] C: “and the consuls Veterus”]. [Note: [Col. 1145] See Baronius, year 132.]

He introduced the Lord’s passion into the priests’ prayer [Col. 1147] when Masses are celebrated. He was crowned with martyrdom, together with Eventius the presbyter and Theodorus the deacon [Note: [Col. 1147] B: Evenius and Theodulus, presbyters]. [Note: [Col. 1147] See Baronius in the cited place.]

He decreed that water for sprinkling, together with salt, should be blessed in people’s dwellings. He carried out three ordinations during the month of December: six presbyters, two deacons, and five bishops in various places.

He was also buried on the Nomentan Way, where he was beheaded, not far from the city of Rome, at the seventh milestone, on the fifth day before the Nones of May; and the episcopate remained vacant for thirty-five days [Note: [Col. 1147] CB: 25 days].

## CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS

Alexander: seven years, two months, one day. He lived during the reign of Trajan, from the consulship of Palma and Tullus to that of Aelianus and Veterus.

# VIII. SAINT SIXTUS. YEAR OF CHRIST 132; THE THIRTEENTH YEAR OF THE EMPEROR HADRIAN
