[Note: [Col. 1059A]

**Line 3.**—“He decreed that the sacred vessels should not be touched except by ministers.” Sixtus’s decree was that the sacred vessels should not be handled by anyone other than sacred ministers [Col. 1159B], as in the canon *In sancta*, *On Consecration*, distinction 1. According to the Council of Laodicea, canon 21, subdeacons—whose order was not yet sacred—were not permitted to handle sacred vessels. According to the First Council of Braga, canon 28, the same prohibition applied to lectors. In the canons *Non oportet* and *Non licet*, distinction 23, “ministries” means sacred vessels.

Anastasius, in his account of Gregory II, writes: “He also made a marble ambo in the same church and endowed it with various linens and sacred vessels.” The same author, in his account of Urban, writes: “He made all the sacred vessels of silver.”

[Col. 1160B] **Line 4.**—“He decreed that any bishop who had been summoned to the apostolic see and, on returning to his parish, should not be received unless he had letters of greeting from the patriarch to the people, which is a *formata*.”

This is another decree of Sixtus: that a bishop summoned to the apostolic see, on returning to his own church, should not be admitted there without a *formata*, so that it might be clear whether he possessed communion with the apostolic see. *Formatae* were letters by which it was indicated that the bearers of the letters possessed communion with the apostolic see.

Optatus, in Book II, after publishing the succession of the Roman pontiffs from Peter to Siricius, writes:

> “With him the whole world agrees with us, through the exchange of *formatae*, in one fellowship of communion.”

And Augustine writes in Letter 163:

> “He first attempted to assert that his communion existed throughout the whole world. I was asking whether he could give, wherever I wished, the letters of communion that we call *formatae*.”

[Note: [Col. 1161A]

**Line 4.**—“He decreed that anyone who had been summoned to the apostolic see…”

Irenaeus, who lived in the same period, certainly presupposes that this duty of obedience was believed to be current in the second Christian century. He constantly asserts:

> “It is necessary that every church should come together with the Church of Rome, on account of its more powerful principal position.”

The necessity of coming together because of the greater primacy also entails the power of summoning. That churches had recourse to the apostolic see in more serious cases is proved by the mission sent to the pontiff by Irenaeus, commissioned by the bishop and the Church of Lyons, with a letter in which Eusebius writes in Book IV:

> “We have urged our brother and colleague Irenaeus to bring these letters to you. We ask you to hold him in commendation, as one who is zealous for the covenant of Christ.”

At the end of the same century, Tertullian speaks none too obscurely of the summoning of the African churches to the apostolic see when he writes of approaching the apostolic churches for the examination of truth (*On the Prescription of Heretics*, chapter 36):

> “You have Rome, from which authority is available to us also.”

The particle “also” indicates that authoritative judgments were demanded from the remaining churches just as from the African Church. He proves this by the example of certain Asian churches which, in a case concerning the discernment of prophecy, had had recourse to Anicetus and afterward made use of the judgments that issued from him. Tertullian calls these judgments “authorities” in his book *Against Praxeas*.

Thus he writes:

> “For the same man, who at that time was already acknowledging the prophecies of Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla, and on the basis of that acknowledgment was bringing peace to the churches of Asia and Phrygia, by falsely asserting things about them and their churches and defending the authorities of his predecessors, compelled him both to recall the letters of peace already issued and to abandon his purpose of revoking the charisms.”

A witness from the same century is added by Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, who mentions brothers traveling to the apostolic see and being strengthened by the pontiff’s words in the letter sent to the Romans, while praising Soter’s beneficence:

> “Your bishop Soter not only preserved this custom but even increased it, both by supplying gifts destined for the saints and by consoling with gracious words the brothers who arrived from abroad, as a most affectionate father consoles his children.”

That exchanges of letters with provinces distant from the City were frequently maintained by the apostolic see in the same century and the following one is shown by another Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria. Writing to Pope Stephen about the apostolic see’s abundant generosity in assisting the churches, he says in Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 5:

> “All the provinces of Syria, together with Arabia, to which you repeatedly supply what is necessary and to which you have now written letters…”

The subject of Stephen’s letters was that heretics were not to be rebaptized. He sent these letters to all the churches, as the witness of Lérins records in the *First Commonitory*, so that the heresy of those who rebaptized would not spread further and, once that error had been disseminated in the East, contaminate the other churches.

The Roman clergy, during the vacancy of the see, speaks of this solicitude of the apostolic see in sending encyclicals to prevent evils in a letter sent to the clergy of Carthage, preserved by Cyprian in Letter 3:

> “For we do not exhort you in words alone; you will be able to learn from many of us who are coming to you that, with God’s help, we have done and shall do all these things with every solicitude and at the risk of worldly danger, keeping before our eyes the fear of God and eternal punishments rather than fear of men and a brief injury, neither abandoning the brotherhood nor failing to exhort them to stand firm in the faith.”

The sending of these letters and messengers certainly presupposes frequent and continual travel in both directions. Relevant here too is what is observed in Cyprian’s letter to Antonianus, where he writes that certain African bishops, including Pompeius and Stephen, were present at Cornelius’s election, even though the fiercest Decian persecution was then raging (Letter 52):

> “He was made bishop by many of our colleagues who were then present in Rome.”

Letter 41 should also be read, where he speaks of bishops’ arrival before Pope Cornelius and of their return to Africa to announce, through the bishops Caldonianus, Fortunatus, Pompeius, and Stephen, the already defeated case of the schismatics. These men laid out the matter before the full council of all Africa, as Cyprian wrote in his reply:

> “For I myself and many colleagues [Col. 1162B] who had gathered to me awaited the arrival of our colleagues Caldonianus and Fortunatus, whom we had recently sent as envoys to you and to our fellow bishops who had attended your ordination, so that, when they arrived and brought back the truth of what had happened, the wickedness of the opposing party might be broken. Pompeius and Stephen, our colleagues, also arrived; they too, in order to inform us there, produced clear indications and testimonies in keeping with their gravity and fidelity, so that it was no longer necessary to hear those who had come as envoys from Novatian.”

The frequent travel of bishops and faithful, and the letters sent in reply to the churches for the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline by the Roman pontiffs, show that the *Book of the Pontiffs* could record the admission of summonses to the apostolic see and that this practice, already observed through established usage and earlier custom, had been confirmed more firmly by Alexander.

**Line 6.**—“Unless with letters of the patriarch.” This is one of the additions inserted into the second catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, and indeed by a later hand. In Alexander’s own century the designation “patriarch” is not read as a frequent term among the ecclesiastical expressions of Christians—although at this time it was used among the sacred pagan rites of the Egyptians, as is clear from a letter of the Emperor Hadrian—and it is foreign to the usage of ecclesiastical letters during the first three centuries.

Indeed, we think that the interpolator of the second catalogue did not write “patriarch,” but only the letter P, expressing the name of Peter. By this letter, serving as a sign, bishops and the faithful recognized and distinguished canonical letters from others; through it also it became known that the recipient was in Catholic communion when the letter was granted by the apostolic see.

That the addition should be understood in no other way may be inferred from the fact that, in these earlier periods, just as the name “patriarch” was unknown, so there is no trace or testimony that *formatae* letters were marked with that name. Yet it was extremely common for Peter’s name to be placed in letters as a sign, as Atticus of Constantinople observes. He discusses canonical letters and asserts that the aforesaid mark, placed on *formatae* letters by the name of Peter, had been approved by the Council of Nicaea.

Since nowhere is it read that, in the earliest period, the mark of the patriarch’s name was placed on canonical letters, whereas Saint Peter’s name is well attested as having been placed upon them in those times by Atticus, it must therefore be affirmed that the compiler of these acts added only the letter P, meaning Peter; but through the license—or rather the ignorance—of copyists, the letter was explained by the word “patriarch.”

These marks of names, added as symbols to letters, were generally indicated only by their initial letters, as Ferrarius discusses at length in his little work *On Ecclesiastical Letters*, followed by others. It therefore seems credible that Sixtus decreed that henceforth the proper mark of *formatae* letters should be the contracted name of Saint Peter, and that letters sent by these bishops should prove the approved fellowship and communion of the one chair of Peter, as Optatus said above. Through these communicatory letters the bishops displayed their unity with the Church and with the one communion.

Indeed, if synodical or encyclical letters were issued by councils, the pontiff’s name was placed before those of the other bishops, so that this fellowship and the one communion of the chair of Peter might be signified.

We owe this observation to Saint Augustine. In attacking the Donatist Cresconius, who among other arguments claimed that the communion of the whole East with Donatus had been recognized by the Council of Sardica, Augustine notes that the synod writing to Donatus was an assembly of Arians who, in opposition to the gathering of the Catholics at Sardica, had held another assembly in that place. He further concludes from this that it was a false synod, because, if it had observed universal custom, the synod ought either to have placed the name of the true pontiff first or at least to have placed the name of the bishop of the Donatists, whom the Donatists advertised to their followers as the successor of Peter’s chair [Col. 1163B], since this was the established custom.

Cresconius presents his argument, claiming that the Eastern Church had communicated with Donatus at the Council of Sardica (*Against Cresconius*, Book III, chapter 34, page 186):

> “But you say that the Easterners, whom you now admit to be ours, were not unaware of this crime. And to prove this you insert the beginning of the letter of the Council of Sardica, where the name of Donatus, your bishop of Carthage, is found written. You think and assert that this was done because the Easterners who sent these writings from their council were displeased by the betrayal of the traditors, withdrew from communion with them, and therefore communicated with your Donatus.”

Augustine replies to Cresconius:

> “Learn, then, what you do not know. The Council of Sardica was an Arian council, as has long been known and as we have in our hands: it was convened chiefly against Athanasius, the Catholic bishop of Alexandria, who, more sharply than the others, accused and refuted their error, which had arisen in that very city. It is therefore not surprising if those heretics attempted to associate Donatus with themselves, since the Catholic Church condemned them throughout the world. Yet we have the bishops to whom these letters were given, though without the names of their cities. Either there was some Donatus who was not a bishop in Africa, to whose name your people added ‘Carthage,’ or, as I have said, the Eastern heresy attempted to enlist an African. The latter is especially credible because the Catholic East would never write to the bishop of Carthage while omitting the Roman bishop; at the very least, your own bishop ought to have been written in, since you usually send a few of your people from Africa to Rome.”

Nevertheless, Jerome clearly assumes, from established custom, that true communion was indicated by letters sent by a pontiff. During the Antiochene schism he asks Damasus, “With whom ought I to communicate at Antioch?” Then he continues:

> “Meletius, Vitalis, and Paulinus say that they adhere to you… I beseech Your Blessedness… indicate to me by your letters with whom I ought to communicate in Syria.”

Imbued with this conviction, Gratian issued a decree in the year 378 that those who communicated with Damasus should be considered Catholics. When Rufinus obtained a *formata* from Siricius while he was in Rome and was subsequently reproached by Pope Anastasius on account of Origenist doctrine, he produced Siricius’s *formata* as a sign of Catholic communion. Hence Saint Jerome writes in the *Apology against Rufinus*, Book II:

> “You produce the letter of Siricius, who now sleeps in the Lord, and despise the words of Anastasius, who is alive.”

**“Of the people’s greeting.”** Other manuscripts read: “Unless with *formatae* of greeting to the people from the apostolic see.”

Another mark of the *formatae* that pontiffs issued was the sign of the apostolic see’s greeting addressed to the people, in the merit of Saint Peter, whose name was placed on the *formata* as a sign. A *formata* was indeed an indication of communion and a sign of fellowship with the chair of Peter, of which all the faithful boasted.

Optatus reproaches the Donatists, who were deprived of that communion:

> “Will you be able to prove that the chair of Peter is a lie, where our fellowship exists?”

Augustine distinguishes Catholics from Donatists by their fellowship with the chair of Peter (*Against Petilianus*, Book II, chapter 51), the fellowship by which, as he opposed Petilianus the Donatist, Catholics are bound together in Catholic communion, in order to reproach the Donatist schism.

Therefore, when bishops returned from the apostolic see bearing a *formata* and showed it to the people, the pontiff, in Peter’s name, blessed and greeted the people according to Paul’s custom. Optatus teaches in Book III, page 84, that Catholic bishops, and still more pontiffs, were accustomed to greet the people in public gatherings. In this way he attacks Parmenianus, the Donatists, and the schismatic circle of Macrobius:

> “The episcopal discourse is approved by all as clothed in holiness, namely, by a greeting given twice. For a bishop does not begin to say anything to the people unless he has first greeted them in the name of God. Beginnings and endings are alike. Every discourse in the Church begins in the name of God and ends in the name of that same God. Who among you dares to say that Macarius greeted the people in the manner of bishops? Since he neither greeted them before saying anything nor dared to greet them after he had spoken… what is the meaning of your claim that the episcopal college could have been defiled, when you see that Macarius was alien to every episcopal office?”

Since, therefore, the faithful possessed, as a sign of communion, a *formata* obtained from the apostolic see by bishops on their return, and since these same bishops announced it to the people in order to prove their fellowship with the chair of Peter, it was not without purpose for the pontiff to pronounce a greeting to the people, since greeting was an indication of episcopal, and still more of pontifical, office.

This is how the final words of Saint Gregory, Book VII, Letter 29, page 226, addressed to Eulogius, patriarch of Alexandria, are to be understood:

> “We received the blessing of Saint Mark the Evangelist—or rather, what is more truly the blessing of Saint Peter the Apostle—with the sweetness in which it was transmitted, and, offering the greeting of our address…”

And so forth.

From this it becomes clear what greeting letters were like in the earliest centuries, and how highly they were valued and preserved with exceptional care, as the acts of Felix teach. It is read in the Acts that Alfius Caecilianus, who during the persecution of Diocletian had been charged with burning the sacred books, made the following deposition in the proceedings, after Optatus, page 96:

> “Then they sent us to the house of Bishop Felix, so that he might remove the Scriptures from there and they could be burned according to the sacred command. Thus Galatius went with us to the place where we had been accustomed to celebrate prayers. From there we carried away the chair, and the greeting letters, and all the doors were burned according to the sacred command.”

Alfius adds that he denounced these matters to Felix in a letter in which the following words were read:

> “Since Galatius, one of your number, has publicly brought greeting letters out of the basilica.”

Felix, the ordainer of Caecilianus, was prosecuted as guilty of handing over the sacred books because he had allowed the greeting letters to be taken from the chair, where they were kept, by a pagan agent.

To count greeting letters among the sacred books, to preserve them in the episcopal chair, and to turn their seizure into a charge of betrayal presupposes their importance. This esteem could arise from no other source than the fact that these letters, written by the pontiffs, were indications of communion and fellowship with the chair of Peter and, as it were, a sacred pledge of the one faith and communion with the Catholic Church, a definite sign.

**“Which is a *formata*.”** There are various distinctions among *formatae* letters. The person who added this clause wished to designate the marks customarily placed on letters given to bishops returning from the City, so that they would bear the letter P and at the same time carry a greeting to the people from the pontiff. He declares that a letter composed in this manner was a kind of *formata*.

Through these letters, retained during the persecution and sent from one church to another, it was discovered that the churches belonged to the one Church spread throughout the world. Where exchanges of these *formatae* were not found, the people or bishops were understood to be outside the fellowship of this body. Through their assistance, bishops everywhere that the Catholic Church flourished experienced all the duties of communion, fellowship, and hospitality.

Letters of this kind, as I believe, bore a certain sign by which they proved that their recipients were in fellowship with the chair of Peter. This is suggested by Optatus’s words about Damasus:

> “With him the whole world agrees with us through the exchange of *formatae*, in one fellowship of communion.”

Or, as Barthius reads it:

> “The *formatae* of the whole world agree with us through exchange, as in one fellowship of communion.”

Thus a *formata* was an indication of communion and fellowship with the chair of Peter, and consequently with the whole world.

That this *formata* was an indication of communion, so that those deprived of it were not considered to communicate with the churches of the world, is shown by the words of Saint Augustine. From the practice of the Catholic Church regarding the *formata*, which the Donatists lacked, he proves that Fortunius and the Donatists were outside communion (Letter 163):

> “I was asking whether he could give, wherever I wished, the letters of communion that we call *formatae*, and I affirmed what was obvious to everyone: that in this way the question could most easily be brought to an end. If he agreed, I was preparing to have letters sent by you to those churches which we could read in the apostolic authorities as having already been founded at that time.”

I believe these were the letters that we saw above called greeting letters, which bishops preserved in their own chair in the church.

This careful provision by Sixtus, concerning the identity of the *formata* and the marks that had to be added, may have arisen because of the perversity of certain impostors. In order to obtain an abundance of goods, whose plentiful supply they experienced through the hospitality of the faithful, they presented themselves as Christians. By this fraud, disguised as faithful Christians, they went around the houses and churches of the faithful.

Among them was the noteworthy individual about whom the dialogue entitled *The Wanderer*, among Lucian’s dialogues, reports what he had obtained from Christians by this art. It is related there that:

> “Having undertaken a journey, he goes out to wander, believing that sufficient provisions had been stored up for him among the Christians. Wherever he went, they accompanied him, and he lived in complete abundance.”

Mansurius, primate of Carthage, wrote to Secundus of Tigisis. Among other things, citing Saint Augustine in the *Brief Account*, he had the following:

> “Certain criminals were also accused in the same letter, as were debtors to the treasury—people who, taking advantage of the persecution, either wished to escape a life burdened by many debts, or thought they could purge and, as it were, wash away their crimes, or certainly acquire money and enjoy luxuries while in custody through the services of Christians.”

To frustrate such tricks in the future, he could therefore have inserted these marks into the *formatae* letters and barred access to people of this sort by adding this new sign to the *formatae*… [Col. 1165D]

(EX BIN.). Line 5 and 6.—“He would not be received except with the formatae.” It is decreed that bishops summoned to the Roman See should not be received by their own people unless they presented letters of greeting in the form of a *formata*.

(EX LAB.). Line 3.—“Anniculum.” [Read:] “Angulum.”

[Note: [Col. 1165D]]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

In arranging the chronology of Saint Sixtus, there is such agreement among the documents collected from the catalogues and other records edited above in the *Prolegomena*, folio XC, that no one can fail to see that ten years, three months, and twenty-one days must be assigned to him from his episcopal ordination to his martyrdom. All the Italian catalogues uniformly read a decade of years. The foreign catalogues also agree, except for the fourth Colbertine manuscript, in which V could easily have been taken for the sign of ten, X, perhaps because the lower part of the letter X had been worn away in the exemplar from which it was copied; [Col. 1166A] similarly, in the sixth Colbertine manuscript, an accidental stroke of I before the same numeral sign X could have altered the number X to IX; and in the seventh Colbertine manuscript, a stroke, or a similar mark, after the same numeral sign X could have rendered it XI. The Belgian manuscript of Papebroch likewise shows, in the number of months, that a sign for ten years, repeated through the carelessness of a copyist, extended the total of three months to thirteen; for it is not at all credible that the author of the catalogue, after writing ten years X, intended to record thirteen months XIII separately; he would rather have stated eleven years and one month. By the same observation, one or another scribal error is detected and corrected in the Italian catalogues: thus, in the Bergamo manuscript, seven and three months are understood to have been written merely through a bending of the pen in writing the sign of the first unit, VII; when this is removed, other manuscripts number two months; or, when it is taken as the sign for double two, another example gives four, IIII. It is not worth dwelling on these rather minor scribal errors, which are easily recognized [Col. 1166B] and brought into agreement with the other manuscripts and records that assign to Sixtus ten years, three months, and twenty-one days.

It is more important to indicate how the consuls Niger and Apronianus can be reconciled with the beginning of Sixtus’s tenure, and Verus and Ambibulus with its end, since the former belong to the year of Christ 117, while the latter belong to the year 126, only nine years distant from them; whereas the catalogues extend Sixtus’s tenure over a full decade and nearly four months.

We resolve the difficulty with Henschenius by distinguishing Sixtus’s ordination as bishop, future vicar of Alexander while Alexander was imprisoned by the judge Aurelian, from the election of that same Sixtus after his promotion to the Roman See and succession to Alexander, once Alexander had been crowned with martyrdom and departed to heaven on 3 May in the year of Christ 117, during the consulship of Niger and Apronianus. The ten-year era therefore assigned to Sixtus in the catalogues shows that he was ordained bishop—an assistant or vicar to Alexander—ten years, [Col. 1166C] three months, and twenty-one days before he suffered martyrdom in the year of Christ 127, on 3 April, the third day before the Nones of April (on which day this *Pontifical Book* likewise records that he was buried in the Vatican beside the body of blessed Peter). His ordination would therefore have taken place on Sunday, 14 December, in the year 116 of the common Christian era. The consular chronology, however, from which we previously determined that Alexander’s martyrdom occurred on 3 May in the year 117, under the consuls Niger and Apronianus, carried forward to the complete year 126 and its consuls Verus and Ambibulus—the last consuls assigned to Sixtus—and even to 3 April of the following year, 127, whose ordinary consuls were Titianus and Gallicanus, assigned to the beginning of Telesphorus’s tenure, will, according to the method of the catalogue, which relates pontifical years to Easter-time around the Palilia, or birthday of the City, give Sixtus nine years and several months and days. We can determine these more precisely if we accept that the interval between pontificates, or vacancy of the Roman See after Alexander’s death, [Col. 1166D] lasted thirty-five days, precisely the number assigned by the *Pontifical Book* and by the author of the catalogue copied six hundred years ago, which we presented above in the *Prolegomena*, treatise VII, folio 19. On this reckoning, Sixtus’s election, or elevation to the apostolic See, and his ἐνθρονισμός (*enthronement*), would fall on Sunday, 7 June of the aforementioned year 117, and thence to the subsequent martyrdom on 3 April 127. Sixtus would have administered the supreme pontificate for nine years, nine months, and twenty-six days; from his episcopal ordination he would have served ten years, three months, and twenty-one days; and of these he would have served five months and twenty-five days as vicar before his successor was elected and placed in the Roman chair of Peter.

I know that Pearson objects to this vicariate of Sixtus on page 232 of his posthumous work, *Acts of Saint Alexander*, if we wish to regard these as genuine with Henschenius. For in that work, when it is asserted that the matron Severina, after committing the bodies of Pope Saint Alexander and his companions to burial on her estate, “clothed herself [Col. 1167A] in a hair shirt and lay for so long before the thresholds of the saints whom she had buried, until Sixtus the bishop came from the East,” it seems to follow that Sixtus did not perform the office of vicar, since he was absent. Yet from 14 December of the year 115, on which we suppose that Sixtus was ordained bishop and Alexander’s vicar, to 3 May 117, on which Alexander died a martyr and was buried, sixteen months and the remainder elapsed; during that time many things could have occurred that would have required Sixtus, although Alexander’s vicar, to travel to the East, from which Severina would have had to await him after he had been elected by the clergy of Rome to the supreme pontificate. Therefore the *Acts* do not contradict the chronology distributed in this way between Sixtus’s vicariate and pontificate; nor is the credibility of the *Acts* diminished by admitting Sixtus’s absence from Rome while Alexander’s successor was being elected, for Sixtus had been Alexander’s vicar.

## HISTORICAL NOTES OF THE SAME AUTHOR

Line 1.—“From his father Pastor.” The cognomen *Pastor*, [Col. 1167B] common in the second century of Christ, is found in certain inscriptions without the family name being expressed, and indeed during this very period. Saint Pius is said below, no. 11, to have been the brother of Pastor from the city of Aquileia; he is also said to have been called Hermes. See Baronius under the year 159, no. 4. A stone recently excavated from Christian cemeteries bears the following inscription: **PASTORI IN PACE**—“To Pastor, in peace.” We do not know the family names of these Pastors, any more than we know that of Pastor who held the consulship together with L. Papirius Aelianus in the year of Christ 163, although Panvinius judges him to have belonged to the Junian family, while others assign him to the Aurelia family on the basis of an ancient inscription in Cuper’s letter prefixed to Almeloven’s *Fasti*, no. 4.

The same line.—“From the district of the Via Lata.” The seventh region among the Augustan regions is called the Via Lata. A portion of the region extending to the foot of the Quirinal Hill still bears this name; it is carefully described from Varro and Rufus by Nardini, and from it the deaconry of Saint Mary in the Via Lata also takes its name. It should therefore be assigned to the seventh ecclesiastical region. See above in the *Prolegomena*.

Line 2.—“In the time of Hadrian, down to Verus and Ambibulus.” Correctly so, as we have already examined in the chronological notes, in agreement with Eusebius, all the Martyrologies, and the author of the most ancient catalogue, although Pearson does not hesitate to depart from them on page 232, writing:

“Xystus therefore sat from the year of the Lord 101, when Trajan IV and Paetus were consuls, until the year of the Lord 111, when Piso and Rusticus were consuls. Baronius, Petavius, and Labbaeus hold that he died under Antoninus Pius in the year of the Lord 139, an outrageous anachronism. Eusebius and all the Martyrologies report that he died under Hadrian, and indeed, according to the author of the most ancient catalogue, under the consuls Verus and Ambiguus, in the year of the Lord 126.”

Accordingly, retaining with this author of the most ancient catalogue, with Eusebius, and with all the Martyrologies, the martyrdom of Xystus under Hadrian and under the consuls Verus and Ambibulus, we assert that Pearson’s chronology, like the other chronologies he criticizes, must be corrected both for Xystus and for Telesphorus and Hyginus. I shall show this more clearly below, no. 10, where Hyginus and the heresy of Cerdon, which arose while he was seated on the Roman See, will be discussed.

Line 3.—“He decreed that the sacred vessels should not be touched except by ministers.” Thus there were already sacred vessels set apart from other uses and employed solely for the sacrifice. Why should this be doubted, when Saint Epiphanius, in *Against Heresies* 78, and Polycrates, the eighth bishop of Asia after John, testify both in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapter 24, and in Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, to the *petalum*, the frontal plate used by Saints James, the first bishop of Jerusalem, and John the Evangelist? As for Mark the Evangelist, Valesius observes in his notes on the cited passage of Eusebius that the same thing is written by the historian of Mark’s passion.

Moreover, under Zephyrinus, at the end of the second century of Christ with which we are concerned, we shall read below, no. [Col. 1168A] 16, that this pontiff decreed that ministers should carry glass patens into the church before the priests until the bishop celebrated Mass. Some of these have been excavated in the cemeteries of the martyrs and published by Aringhius and Severanus together with Bosio; more recently, they have been illuminated with the finest scholarship by the distinguished senator of Florence, Filippo Buonarroti. From Aringhius I shall present two that contain the name and image of Sixtus. He reported them in book IV of *Subterranean Rome*, chapter 47, page 405. I shall reproduce the first here. Besides Xystus (or Sustus), it also depicts Timothy seated on a chair, and both are crowned by Christ the Lord. Perhaps that Timothy was the presbyter and blood-brother of Novatus, Pudentiana, and Praxedes; Baronius recounts letters exchanged between him and his fellow presbyter Pastor under the year 162, on the occasion of the dedication of the title of Pastor, or Saint Pudentiana, carried out by Pope Pius I in the Baths of Novatus. I shall reserve the second image for illustrating the notes on the life of Saint Damasus, since it depicts him together with Xystus II in almost the same attire in which [Col. 1168B] both are represented in the ancient paintings of the Basilica of Saint Paul.

This first glass bowl, or *patena*, as it was later called by some, thus displays the image of Sixtus, of whom the Librarian asserts that it was decreed that these sacred vessels should not be touched by anyone other than ministers. Here he is called *Sustus*, with the Latin letter V substituted for the Greek Y, just as on the base of the Obelisk at the Flamian Gate one reads the inscription **AIGVPTO** for **AIGYPTO**, and elsewhere we find the names *Sylla* and *Sulla*, *Syria* and *Suria*, written indifferently, as several have noted. Others, failing to observe this, read *Justus* instead of *Sustus*.

[Col. 1169A] Morinus, *On Sacred Ordinations*, part III, exercise XII, chapter 3, no. 8, considering that the touching of sacred vessels had been forbidden to laypeople at the time when, because of the danger posed by persecutions, the faithful were permitted to receive the Lord’s body from a priest, carry it with them, keep it at home, and bring it to their mouths with their own hands—as is plainly established by the letter of Basil the Great to Caesaria Patricia—raises a timely question for clarifying the decree under discussion. He asks why it was not equally permitted to handle the sacred vessels with the same hands with which it was permitted to receive and retain the Lord’s body, which was far more sacred. Basil’s letter clearly shows that this practice had long before been accepted. “The priest,” Basil says, “hands over a particle; the one who receives it holds it with complete freedom and so brings it to his mouth with his own hand.”

In the same letter he first says:

“It is entirely unnecessary to demonstrate that, in times of persecution, when a priest or minister is absent, it is not a serious matter for [Col. 1169B] someone to receive Communion with his own hand. Long practice has confirmed this in reality. For all those who live a solitary life in the deserts, where there is no priest, keep Communion at home and communicate by themselves. In Alexandria and Egypt, moreover, almost every layperson generally has Communion at home and communicates by himself whenever he wishes.”

After Morinus has recited all this from Basil’s letter and confirmed it from other Fathers, both Greek and Latin, he rightly asks in no. 17: “Since, then, that practice of touching Christ’s body was so ancient, widespread, and established, why not also the sacred vessels, the chalice and paten?”

He resolves the question as follows:

“I answer that the two cases are very different. For Christ’s body is a sacrificed thing, and the action by which bread becomes Christ’s body is a sacrifice. But it belongs to the nature of sacrifices—[Col. 1169C] except in the case of a holocaust—that those attending the sacrifice should become participants in it, as is taught in Deuteronomy XII and at the beginning of chapter XVIII, and in Numbers XVIII, verses 9 and 19, as well as elsewhere. Therefore Christ’s body, which is the truth and perfection of all the ancient sacrifices, ought to be shared by all and consequently joined to them.

“Next, Christ’s body, or the sacrament of the Eucharist, is the reality whose figure among the Jews was the Paschal lamb, which each family was obliged to eat. Finally, at the institution of the Mass Christ commands all to receive; consequently, also to touch. It is therefore absolutely necessary for the faithful to touch Christ’s body. Indeed, for this very reason, by the greatest miracle, bread becomes Christ’s body: so that we may touch it, and so that by its contact it may sanctify us and prepare us for immortality.

“The same force of reasoning applies if Christ’s body is considered in the sacrament as the medicine and ἀλεξιφάρμακον (*antidote*) of our souls. In this respect too, [Col. 1169D] contact and participation are altogether necessary.

“But the case of the vessels is entirely different. No necessity has been imposed upon laypeople to handle them; they have nothing in common with the vessels; no usefulness of participation or real union; no relation between figures and reality. Therefore such contact could be forbidden to them. The people participated in the flesh of the sacrifices, yet they were forbidden to touch the sacred vessels. The Levites were appointed to minister the vessels; no ministry of the people was required.

“There are therefore obvious reasons why the touching of the sacred vessels, but not of Christ’s body, was forbidden (XVIII). Yet even if one granted that the two cases were alike—which cannot be granted—in matters belonging to ecclesiastical institution, it cannot be inferred that one thing is forbidden from the prohibition of another. The chief basis of such prohibitions lies in the will and discretion of the one who instituted them. It should be enough that a law was made concerning one, while no law was made concerning the other.”

Thus far Morinus.

[Col. 1170A] I shall gladly add that the Church, conscious of the Lord’s command concerning reception of Christ’s body, and that it should be completed by eating, with contact of the mouth and throat, and by swallowing—without any necessity for contact by the hands, which was reserved to ministers—later decreed, after the dangers of those persecutions had passed and priests were no longer absent from the deserts as Basil had indicated, that the Lord’s body should not thereafter be kept at home by private persons or brought to the mouth with their own hands. In the same way, the Church judged under Sixtus that lay hands should be removed from contact with the sacred vessels by means of a decree, which is not recorded as having been issued before Sixtus.

The abuses of certain faithful people who irreverently handled the holy things they had received—abuses considered in several councils that Morinus indicates in the same place, no. XV—rightly moved the pontiffs to command Christ’s people to be content with the necessary contact of mouth and throat in swallowing and eating the Eucharistic species.

[Col. 1170B] That abuse, however, arose later. In the second century of Christ, with which we are now concerned, and in the third, the discipline testified to by Justin Martyr in his *Apology*, Tertullian in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, and Origen in Homily XIII on Exodus was still vigorous:

“You know,” he says, “those of you who are accustomed to take part in the divine mysteries, that when you receive the Lord’s body, you preserve it with every precaution and reverence, lest any small part fall from it, lest anything of the consecrated gift slip away.”

As long as the vigor and caution of the discipline commended by Origen remained among the Christian people, there was no obstacle to the Eucharist’s being handed over to the hands of those who received and carefully preserved it with reverence. Each of the faithful could diligently protect the portion of the offering entrusted to him, lest any small part fall from it.

But if the sacred vessels in which the offerings were broken and the blood of Christ was kept for distribution to all were entrusted to the care and custody of each member of the Christian people, and to everyone’s hands, the matter would be full of danger. [Col. 1170C] Fragments that fell away, and drops among the chased work of the patens and the relief-work of the chalices, could often be scattered and dispersed if those vessels were rashly and indiscriminately passed through the hands of all who approached. Moreover, it would have to be feared that glass chalices—as we shall see below under Zephyrinus, such as they were at that time—might frequently be broken and the Lord’s blood spilled if the people were permitted indiscriminate contact with the vessels.

Therefore contact with the vessels had to be reserved to ministers, not merely for the sake of the vessels but rather for the sake of securing the Eucharist with the greatest care, so that not even the smallest particle clinging to the vessels might be lost through the inexperience or negligence of the people. There was no such danger from ministers, who had been trained by long experience and by the instructions of the bishop and presbyters to perform these duties properly.

I understand this to be the meaning of Sixtus’s decree from another decree later issued under Soter, forbidding any nun to touch the sacred pallium or to place incense [Col. 1170D] in the holy Church. The same is also clear from the *Life of Urban*: when we read that “he made all the sacred vessels of silver and set up twenty-five silver patens,” it becomes evident that, for the author of the Lives, the sacred vessels were not altar cloths or boxes for incense, but chalices and patens fashioned to contain the Lord’s body. Why, moreover, contact with sacred pallia—which follows the same reasoning as chalices and patens—and also the use of burning incense were forbidden to nuns, I shall try to explain in its proper place in the historical notes on the life of Soter.

Line 6.—“Except with the patriarch’s letter of greeting to the people, which is a *formata*.” That entire phrase—“the patriarch’s greeting to the people, which is a *formata*”—is absent from the Vatican and Florentine manuscripts, as Holstenius and Schelestratus note. The title *patriarch* was assigned to Christian bishops only later, and, according to Thomassinus, first to Leo the Great at the Council of Chalcedon, *On Benefices*, part I, book I, chapter 3, no. 13. He denies that the title originated with the Jewish [Col. 1171A] patriarchs, and much less with the Montanists, whose patriarchs Jerome mentions in Letter 54.

The designation *formata* was also employed later than the age of Sixtus would allow. Therefore either the phrase was inserted, after the time of Leo the Great, to explain the words “with letters,” while the author of the *Life* was copying these decrees from catalogues or other documents; or it was added in some manuscripts of the *Pontifical Book* by later hands as a gloss.

Yet even if the added phrase—“the patriarch’s greeting to the people, which is a *formata*”—is excluded, the force of Sixtus’s decree remains clear: it commands that a bishop summoned to the Roman See should carry letters secured with the seal of the apostolic See when he returned from there to his own parish. Luitprand explains the meaning of this decree as follows:

“He decreed that any bishop afflicted by some adversity might freely appeal to the Roman and apostolic See, and, when summoned there, should not refuse to come; nor should he return from there to his own people without apostolic [Col. 1171B] letters, so that his neighbors might thereby understand how he had settled his own case and that of others there.”

The use of the *formata*, or letter of recommendation, was introduced on the apostles’ example. At the Council of Jerusalem they decided to secure the mission of Paul, Barnabas, Judas, and Silas to the Church of Antioch in such a way that it could distinguish the apostles’ envoys from others who had gone there without legitimate authorization and to whom the apostles had given no commission. The Pauline letters likewise more than once include commendations of those who carried them. At the end of the letter to the Ephesians, Tychicus is commended; in the letter sent to the Colossians, Tychicus and Onesimus are commended.

The addition of a sign also seems to have originated from Paul’s example. Later ages, as Cangius testifies in the *Glossary of Medieval Latin*, and as other learned writers support, wished the *formatae* to be so called from *forma*, or from the type impressed upon them. Paul testifies in the Second Letter to the Thessalonians that he was accustomed to authenticate all his letters with a particular greeting-[Col. 1171C] sign added by his own hand:

“The greeting is in my own hand—Paul’s—which is the sign in every letter. Thus I write: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen.”

The Roman pontiffs, imitating this apostolic custom, became accustomed to mark something similar in their letters, especially those written for more serious causes, which we call consistorial bulls. On the broad sign of the cross—which is a daily indication of salvation and of grace implored from Christ for the faithful—they include a monogram of their name, or the name written out in full; and, in addition, within a circle drawn around the same monogram and the figure of the cross, they inscribe a verse taken from sacred Scripture. Formerly this appeared after the abbreviation rendered “Farewell”; now it comes after the final closing of the letter, corresponding to the greeting mentioned above. Examples of these are frequent among collectors of bulls, both in Ughelli’s *Italia Sacra* and in Mabillon’s *On Diplomatics*, book V. To these may be added the observations of Cotelerius on Apostolic Canon 12, volume II, page 462, in the *Works of the Holy Fathers of the Apostolic Age*.

[Col. 1171D] Reserving these matters for a more appropriate place, I shall add here only a few words about the reason for Sixtus’s decree: that no bishop summoned from the Roman See should be received by his own parish if he returned without apostolic letters. He judged that this was necessary for preserving the unity of the Church under one head and one Catholic doctrine, averting the danger that threatened after the death of the apostles and of the other principal men who had seen Christ the Lord in the flesh.

The danger was this, as Eusebius reported from the books of Hegesippus, a celebrated Christian historian who lived at this same time. His words are given in book III, chapter 32:

“Until these times the Church remained like a certain virgin, whole and uncorrupted; all those [Col. 1172A] who sought to corrupt the rule of the right preaching of the Gospel still lurking in concealment. But after the sacred chorus of the apostles had been extinguished by various kinds of death, and the generation of those men who had been worthy to hear divine Wisdom herself with their own ears had already passed away, then at last a conspiracy of impious error arose through the fraud and malice of false teachers. Since no apostle was any longer alive, they then began, as the saying goes, with uncovered heads, to impose adulterated doctrine against the preaching of the truth.”

Thus wrote Hegesippus.

John the Evangelist, the last surviving apostle, had died under Trajan. Under the same emperor, during the persecution described by Pliny and also by Eusebius—and therefore to be assigned to the end of Evaristus’s tenure and to the pontificate of this very Sixtus whom we are discussing—Symeon, son of Clopas, the second bishop of Jerusalem and a cousin of our Redeemer, consecrated his life to martyrdom at the age of one hundred and twenty.

[Col. 1172B] At that time the license of the heretics, bursting forth from hidden places into the open, openly began to impose adulterated doctrine and to sow weeds in the Gospel field, as though, with those who had seen Christ in the flesh sleeping in Christ, no watchman could be found who was able to distinguish the darnel from the wheat.

What counsel, then, would they take, and what defenses would the guardians of the Lord’s field—and above all Sixtus, who had succeeded Peter in the teaching authority of the chair foremost among the others, for the strengthening of his brethren—set against this? He opposed the emerging disease with precisely the remedy that the apostles and elders had employed in Acts XV against those who came down from Judea to introduce sedition, disturbances, and false doctrines into the Church of Antioch.

They had opposed them with the judgments of a council and presbytery, the decrees of the apostolic college, envoys, and letters, by which they made the authority of those sent clear and commended the truth of the doctrine handed down to those men by the apostles themselves when they were sent back.

Sixtus prepared this same defense, support, [Col. 1172C] and token of doctrine and Catholic unity against the violence and plots of heresies, to be employed in the same way. For he decreed that bishops summoned to the Roman See—which held primacy in the universal Church by the rights handed down to Peter and his successors—should present themselves in such a way that, once their case had been examined and they were to be sent back, they could not be received without apostolic letters. Through these letters it could appropriately be declared, in such important cases, whether their doctrine had been found upright and consonant with the rules of the faith.

Epiphanius also testified that Clement, Peter’s disciple and successor, used encyclical letters against the heresy of Ebion, in these words cited by Cardinal Baronius under the year 74, no. 10:

“The same Clement refuted them—Ebion and his followers—in every respect in the letters that he wrote as encyclicals, which are read in the holy Churches, because his faith and speech have a different character from those things that, under his name, [Col. 1172D] have been corrupted in circulation.”

These, surely, were the traces that the apostle John marked out at the same time in his letters against Menander, Ebion, and other heretics who had come or would come from the same school. Thus he wrote in the First Letter, chapter II, verses 18–19:

“And now many antichrists have arisen; from this we know that it is the last hour. They went out from us, but they were not of us. For if they had been of us, they would certainly have remained with us.”

And in the Second Letter, verses 7–11:

“Many deceivers have gone out into the world, who do not confess that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh. This is the deceiver and the antichrist. See to it that you do not lose what you have accomplished, but that you receive a full reward. Everyone who departs and does not remain in the doctrine of Christ does not have God; whoever remains in the doctrine has both the Father and the Son. If anyone comes to you and does not bring this doctrine, do not receive him into your house, and do not say ‘Hail’ to him. For whoever says ‘Hail’ to him shares in his evil works.”

Since [Col. 1173A] apostolic discipline showed that the communion with the Catholic Church of those legitimately sent out by that Church to proclaim the Gospel of Christ ought to be demonstrated through encyclical letters, and that it was not enough for them once to have belonged to the company gathered with the apostles unless it were clear that they continued and persevered with that company in the doctrine entrusted to it—and otherwise they were neither to be received into the house nor greeted with “Hail”—the prelates of the Churches understood that this requirement had to be enforced much more diligently.

This was especially true of Sixtus, who excelled the others in the Roman See, when under his pontificate the monstrous phenomenon was first heard of: that heresies were being disseminated by men who had obtained or were seeking the episcopate. Their leader, just as Simon had been in the age of the apostles, was Valentinus, who after the apostles’ death came from the school of Simon’s followers—Menander, Ebion, and Basilides. Menander and Basilides claimed to be magicians and philosophers. Valentinus, however, [Col. 1173B] knowing well that these names would not give him sufficient authority among Christians, sought the episcopal dignity, as Tertullian asserts in chapter 4 against him.

The provident pontiff Sixtus therefore saw that a greater danger of seducing the Christian people threatened from those who, since they were regarded by right of the episcopate as successors of the apostles, also possessed the power of teaching among the principal duties of their office, if after obtaining the episcopate they abused the rights of their dignity.

He therefore decreed that bishops summoned to the tribunal of Peter should present themselves in such a way that, after their case had been examined, they could not be received by their own congregations without encyclical letters from the primary See. This was wisely done especially at a time when frequent persecutions made it difficult to assemble bishops in the way the apostles had assembled in council to deal with the disputes that had arisen at Antioch concerning observance of the Law.

Therefore something like dictatorial authority had to be employed—an authority already established by Christ the Lord in Peter’s See—in order to safeguard the [Col. 1173C] unity of the Church and the integrity of the faith, when the greatest danger threatened from bishops turning toward false doctrines and the circumstances of the times did not permit councils of prelates to be convened under the eyes of persecutors, or pastors to be removed from the sheep entrusted to them during that difficult period, when the presence of faithful watchmen was most necessary for congregations placed in danger.

Again, Clement of Alexandria, in book VII of the *Stromata*, teaches that the heresies of Basilides, Valentinus, and Marcion began under Hadrian. He says on page 769:

“Later, around the time of the emperor Hadrian, there were men who devised heresies and continued down to the age of Antoninus the elder: Basilides, although he claims Glaucias as his teacher, whom they themselves boast was Peter’s interpreter. Likewise, they say that Valentinus heard Theodas, who was a companion of Paul. Marcion, since he was born in the same period as these men, lived [Col. 1173D] as an old man among the younger.””

After quoting these words written by Clement, Lupus adds in his scholia on chapter 30 of Tertullian’s *On the Prescription Against Heretics*:

“Saint Clement says in the second place that Basilides, Valentinus, and Marcion were contemporaries and that they all began under the reign of Hadrian. The question is: what did they begin? Life, or heretical preaching? I answer: heretical preaching. For Saint Jerome expressly writes in his eulogy of the illustrious man Agrippa Castor that Basilides preached under the reign of Hadrian.”

A little earlier, on page 479, Lupus had likewise observed from Saint Epiphanius and from the appendix to Tertullian’s *On the Prescription* that Marcion was the degenerate son of a bishop, indeed of a most holy man. He adds that Optatus of Milevis also asserts that Marcion himself was a bishop:

“There are those who think that Marcion was bishop of Sinope under his father Amasenus, bishop and metropolitan of the entire province, and that he appealed to Rome from the synodal judgment by which he had been degraded. [Col. 1174A] They rely upon the passages cited below from Saint Epiphanius.”

He produces the text on page 484, together with various opinions concerning Marcion’s episcopate. But whether Marcion was merely the son of a bishop or was himself also a bishop, since he began to disseminate his heresy under Hadrian, and since Valentinus sought the episcopate on the island of Cyprus, as Father Lupus observes from Saint Philastrius on page 480—where he also proves that under the pontificate of blessed Telesphorus, who immediately succeeded this Sixtus, Valentinus openly raved and preached, according to Justin’s *Apology*, and that Marcion, the disciple of Cerdon, was corrupted and led astray under that same Telesphorus—and since Cerdon himself, according to Saint Irenaeus, book III, chapter 4, at one time made a confession and pretended repentance, and at another returned to his vomit, all these things prove that Sixtus, already discerning that men were being struck down by the breath of heresy and drawn into, or soon to enter, the most sacred order of the episcopate, prudently took precautions through the salutary sanction [Col. 1174B] of that decree: no bishop summoned to judgment before the Roman See and returning from it could be received without encyclical letters providing certain testimony concerning the truth and confession of doctrine consonant with the apostolic dogmas.

It is therefore sufficiently clear from the constitution of the Church under Sixtus I, during the reign of Hadrian—namely, from the history of the heresy that then first dared boldly to intrude among episcopal chairs after the apostles and the disciples who had seen Christ the Lord in the flesh had been removed from mortal life—it is clear, I say, what occasioned and what was the force of Sixtus’s decree. He prudently looked to the preservation of the Church’s unity and the integrity of the faith through letters of this kind, later called *formatae*, which provided certain documents and a token of communion between all bishops and the primary See of Peter, so that on returning to their own congregations they might safely be received by the faithful entrusted to their care.

[Note: [Col. 1174C]]

Line 5.—“Returning to his parish, he would not be received except with the patriarch’s letters.” The holy pontiff Sixtus decreed that bishops summoned to the apostolic See for whatever reason should not, upon returning, be received by their own congregations unless they brought with them letters from the Roman pontiff greeting the people and informing them that the bishops had been cleared or instructed and that their case had been examined.

[Note: [Col. 1174C]

### Line 3.—“He established that the ministries, etc.”

He also established, according to the same *Pontifical Book*, that the sacred vessels were not to be touched by anyone other than sacred ministers. Sixtus prohibited this because both the chalice and the paten were consecrated vessels; for the Roman Order contains the consecration of both, with anointing with chrism and specified prayers. The Council of Laodicea, held about the year 363, later decreed the same thing: canon 21 sanctioned that a subdeacon ought not to touch sacred vessels. The Council of Agde, held under Symmachus in 506, likewise established in canon 66 that unconsecrated ministers ought not to touch the Lord’s vessels. Nevertheless, this permission was granted to subdeacons by the Council of Braga under John III in 563, canon 10:

> “It was decided that none of the readers should be permitted to carry the sacred vessels of the altar, except those who had been ordained subdeacons by the bishop.”

It is also clear from the Roman Order that the same permission was granted to acolytes.

Most writers say that “Holy, holy, holy,” etc., was added by Sixtus to the sacrifice of the Mass. But the fuller *Chronicle of the Ancient Pontiffs* says that Sixtus established only this: when the priest began that hymn, the people too should sing it. Since, however, certain abuses had crept in over time, so that it was said only at solemn Masses, the following canon was issued by the Council of Vaison in 529 to remove that abuse:

> “At all Masses, whether celebrated in the morning, during Lent, or for the commemoration of the dead, ‘Holy, holy, holy’ must always be said in the order in which it is now said at public Masses; for a voice so holy, so sweet, and so desirable, even if it could be sung day and night, could not produce weariness.”

The second part of the hymn—“Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord. Hosanna in the highest”—was sung to Christ the Lord by the crowds during his solemn entry into Jerusalem before the Passion. On the rite and origin of this hymn, Cardinal Bona should be consulted, *On Liturgical Matters*, book II, chapter 10.

### Line 4.—“He established that whoever among the bishops…”

According to the *Pontifical Book*, he decreed that any bishop who had been summoned to the Roman apostolic see, when returning to his own parish, should not be received unless he brought letters of greeting to the people issued by the apostolic see. For the apostolic see gave bishops *formatae*, or letters of communion; through their exchange the whole world remained united in one fellowship of communion, as Saint Optatus of Milevis maintains. With reference to this passage—both in the fuller *Chronicle of the Ancient Pontiffs* and in the *Pontifical Book*—the author of the decretal letters composed the second letter of Sixtus, which concerns the touching of sacred vessels only by ministers and the prohibition against returning without *formatae* letters, as Schelestratius says in his note on Sixtus.

[Col. 1159]

> [Col. 1159] |

**8. Sixtus**, a Roman by nation, son of Pastor, from the district of Via Lata, held the see for ten years, three months, and twenty-one days. [B: ten years, one month, and twenty-two days.] He lived in the time of Hadrian [and Antoninus Pius] until Verus and Anniculus. [B: until Antoninus Augustus and Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, consuls.] He was crowned with martyrdom. He established that the sacred vessels (*ministeria*; variant: *vasa*, “vessels”) should not be touched except by ministers [C: consecrated ministers]. He established that any bishop who had been summoned to the apostolic see [CB: the Roman apostolic see], on returning to his own parish, should not be received except with the patriarch’s letter of greeting to the people, which is a *formata*. [CB: except with *formatae* letters of greeting to the people from the apostolic see. See Baronius under the year 142.] He held three ordinations in the month of December: eleven priests, four deacons [CB: three], and four bishops in various places. He was also buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican on the third day before the Nones of April [CB: the eighth day before the Ides of April], and the episcopate was vacant for two days.

### Catalogue under Liberius

Sixtus: ten years, three months, and twenty-one days. He lived in the time of Hadrian, from the consulship of Niger and Apronianus until the third consulship of Verus and that of Ambibulus.

## IX. SAINT TELESPHORUS. YEAR OF CHRIST 142, THE THIRD YEAR OF ANTONINUS PIUS AS EMPEROR

[Col. 1175]

### From Fabrot, from the Freher manuscript

No. 9, line 10: B reads “two.” In the marginal note: “and bishops in various places, 13.”

### From the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuanus manuscripts

He was crowned with martyrdom and buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican on the fourth day before the Nones of January; and the episcopate was vacant for seven days.”
