### Notes on the Text of Anastasius

In Telesphorus the author of the *Pontifical Book* begins to add several matters that he drew from elsewhere rather than from the second catalogue. Such is the account he adds concerning the prohibition against beginning Mass before the third hour of the day. This follows the system of reckoning the hours customary in Palestine, where the day began at the sixth hour before noon and ended at the sixth hour at noon. Moreover, from the fact that the author of the *Pontifical Book* does not list the consuls—who are absent from the second catalogue but found in the first—it may be inferred that he used not the first catalogue but the second.

### Line 4.—“Since at all times no one presumed to celebrate Mass before the course of the third hour, at which hour our Lord ascended the cross”

The third hour of the day is understood according to the manner of reckoning the hours of the day customary in Palestine, as we noted above. Telesphorus’s decree is especially noteworthy, for it could have had force in the primitive Church, when there was one altar in each church and no more than one Mass was celebrated there per day.

### Notes on the Catalogue of Felix IV

[See the *Prolegomena*.]

**Only at night on the feast of the Lord’s Nativity.** I confess that I do not know where the author of the catalogue derived the claim that, according to the decree of Telesphorus, the angelic hymn—“Glory to God in the highest”—was to be sung only at night on the feast of the Lord’s Nativity. Nevertheless, that it was not recited in the early Church as frequently as it now is at all feasts is evident even from the ancient Sacramentary of Gregory the Great, which was written in the time of Charlemagne and is preserved in the Palatine Vatican Library. At its beginning we read:

> “The ‘Glory to God in the highest’ is also said if the bishop is present, only on Sunday or on feast days; but priests do not say it except on Easter alone.”

### Notes on the Liberian Catalogue

### Line 1.—

In place of “Antoninus Macrinus,” Henschenius and Papebrochius read “Hadrian,” although the manuscript reads as we have printed it here.

### Line 2.—“He established that a fast should be observed for seven weeks before Easter”

The fast of Lent was not first instituted by Telesphorus. It was already recognized as an apostolic institution from apostolic canon 69; rather, it was sanctioned by pontifical law in the canon *Statuimus*, distinction 4. The Fathers acknowledged that the Lenten fast had been instituted by the Lord. Hence Ambrose calls it “the work of our faith” in sermon 33:

> “Last Sunday we said that the first work of our faith is that, throughout the course of these forty days, we should fast with the greatest devotion.”

The same Ambrose complains in sermon 35 that some violated that fast contrary to the Lord’s command:

> “What sort of Christian are you, when the Lord is fasting and you dine? Tell me, I ask you, those of you who dine during Lent: are you not guilty in your consciences when, while the whole people abstains, you alone, contrary to the Lord’s command, devour food?”

The Lenten fast was instituted as an imitation of Christ’s fast. Jerome writes in his commentary on Jonah, chapter 3:

> “The Lord himself, the true Jonah, sent to preach to the world, fasted for forty days; and, leaving us the inheritance of fasting, he prepares our souls under this number for the eating of his body.”

The Lenten fast was arranged over seven weeks. Hence Gregory writes in homily 16 on the Gospels, for the First Sunday of Lent:

> “From the present day until the joys of the Paschal solemnity there are six weeks, comprising forty-two days. When the six Sundays of abstinence are subtracted from these, no more than thirty-six days remain in abstinence.”

### Line 3.—“And Masses should be celebrated at night on the Nativity of the Lord, since at all times no one presumed to celebrate Mass before the course of the third hour, at which hour our Lord ascended the cross”

Telesphorus established that Masses should be celebrated at night on the night of the Lord’s Nativity, since outside that day Masses were not celebrated before the third hour, at which Christ was crucified. See the canon *Nocte sancta*, *On Consecration*, distinction 1.

On the feast of the Lord’s Nativity, Mass is celebrated at night, at cockcrow. The Abbot of Ursperg writes:

> “A certain Roman citizen named Centius, one of the supporters of Henry IV, violently dragged Pope Gregory—namely Gregory VII—from the altar on the feast of the Lord’s Nativity while he was celebrating Mass at cockcrow, grievously wounded him, and imprisoned him in his tower.”

On the day of the Lord’s Nativity, during the Mass celebrated at cockcrow, the emperor Charles IV read the Gospel aloud. Albert of Strasbourg reports this in his *Chronicle*:

> “On the holy day of the Lord’s Nativity the king also received Communion, and at the Mass of cockcrow he read aloud the Gospel, holding an unsheathed sword in his hand: ‘A decree went out from Caesar Augustus.’”

Cockcrow marks midnight, when Christians rose to pray. Augustine writes on Psalm 118:

> “After cockcrow it was customary for there to be a time of prayer.”

Many distinctive practices were introduced in honor of the Lord’s Nativity. First, Mass is celebrated at night. Second, three Masses are celebrated on the same day: the first at midnight, the hour at which Christ was born; the second at dawn, that is, at first light; and the third at the third hour, when public Masses are customarily celebrated. See the Gloss on the canon *Nocte*, chapter *Consuluisti*, *On the Celebration of Masses*.

Third, if the Lord’s Nativity falls on a Friday, it is permitted by general custom to eat meat. Matthew Paris writes under the year 1255:

> “That year the Lord’s Nativity fell on a Friday, and some ate meat out of reverence for Christ, because the Word, having been made flesh, came forth on that day into the light of the world. Hence someone exclaimed in wonder: ‘O honor granted to flesh!’”

Public Masses are celebrated at the third hour, according to the canon *Et hoc*, *On Consecration*, distinction 1, and the Council of Mérida, canon 19, and the Third Council of Orléans, canon 14. I discussed this in *Dissertation*, book VI, chapter 2.

### Line 6.—“And before the sacrifice the angelic hymn should be said, that is, ‘Glory to God in the highest’”

The final part of Telesphorus’s decree is that at the beginning of the sacrifice of the Mass the angelic hymn—namely, “Glory to God in the highest”—should be sung. It was first instituted by Telesphorus that the angelic hymn should be sung at Mass on the feast of the Lord’s Nativity, according to the canon *Nocte sancta*. Later it became customary for the same hymn to be sung always at solemn Masses, including on Maundy Thursday, according to the canon *Porro*, *On Consecration*, distinction 1. Anastasius attributes this to Symmachus in his Life.

### From BIN

#### Line 3.—“He established that a fast should be observed for seven weeks”

The Lenten fast was instituted by the Lord’s apostles and handed down to the universal Church, as is clear from apostolic canon 68. For long before Telesphorus, Ignatius mentioned this Lenten fast in his Letter to the Philippians in these words:

> “Do not despise the Lenten fast, for it contains an example of the Lord’s way of life.”

### From LAB

#### Line 4.—“Since at all times…”

These words are absent from C and H.

## Chronological Notes

Under this pontiff, the paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul—both in the ancient colored mosaic series made under Leo the Great and Galla Placidia, and in the later version of the same period, depicted below by Nicholas III, as I stated in the *Prolegomena*, treatise XI, chapter 3, nos. 3 and 4—clearly demonstrate that eleven years, three months, and twenty-one days must be assigned to blessed Telesphorus.

There is agreement concerning the years among all the catalogues and manuscripts mentioned on the same folio XCI. Only the sixth Colbertine manuscript displays an error in the numeral, substituting VI for XI. Perhaps the copyist was deceived by the customary deterioration of antiquity: as the crossed strokes drawn below the numeral X had faded, he thought that he saw the numeral V in the partly preserved letter X, although the paintings and manuscripts clearly show it intact.

You will understand the remaining errors—minor additions or omissions of one unit in the months—from what I said above concerning Alexander. Therefore, at the foot of the column on Saint Telesphorus in the *Prolegomena*, I collected from all the records that his tenure amounted to eleven years, three months, and twenty-one days.

The day of his martyrdom, 5 January, on which he is commemorated, belongs to the consuls of the year 138, Camerinus and Niger. The preceding consulship, that of Caesar II and Balbinus, shows that Easter was celebrated during the continuing period of Telesphorus’s life; and the first Easter assigned to his successor Hyginus by the catalogue of Felix IV—for the lacuna prevents us from knowing this from the Liberian catalogue—also favors the consuls Niger and Camerinus of the year 138.

Counting backward from 5 January of the year 138 through the eleven full years, three months, and twenty-one days of Telesphorus’s episcopate, we learn that his ordination took place on Sunday, 16 September 126, during the consulship of Verus and Ambibulus, almost six months before Sixtus was crowned with martyrdom. That half-year interval was probably occupied by Sixtus’s vicar and coadjutor, in accordance with a practice frequently used by the Roman pontiffs during persecutions: they conferred episcopal order upon their vicar, for the reasons already indicated in the chronological notes on the Life of Saint Evaristus, no. 2.

The Anastasian codex reports that after Sixtus’s death the apostolic see was vacant for only two days. The following chronology must therefore be assigned to Telesphorus:

- In the year of Christ 126, on Sunday, 16 September, during the consulship of Verus and Ambibulus, he was ordained bishop.

- In the following year, 127, on 5 April, he was elected successor of Sixtus, who had been crowned with martyrdom two days earlier.

- In the year 138, on 5 January, during the consulship of Camerinus and Niger—some call the consul Niger “Magnus”—he was killed for Christ, after spending eleven years, three months, and twenty-one days administering the Roman episcopate: for the first half-year with the vicarial authority conferred upon him by Sixtus, and for the remaining period after Sixtus’s death and his election to the supreme pontificate, as Peter’s successor and Sixtus’s successor in the Roman see.

## Historical Notes of the Same Kind

### Line 1.—“From Anachorite”

No one will deny that there were anchorites in the age of Telesphorus who considers that, according to the Gospel, before the preaching of Christ the Lord, John, his precursor, dwelt in the desert, girded about the loins with a leather belt and satisfying his hunger with locusts and wild honey; he entered the caves of the desert while still a young man.

The Fathers, and with them all Catholics, certainly attribute to his example the origin of the monastic life among Christians. For this reason Saints John Chrysostom and Jerome called him the prince of monks; others praise him with similar commendations. See Baronius under the year of Christ 31, nos. 14 and 15.

Indeed, Christ the Lord himself, our divine teacher, who is the model and standard of every virtue, seems by spending forty days in the desert to have indicated the institution of the solitary life before giving the precepts of the active life. Thus Basil, speaking of the praises of the desert, after commending it on the basis of the examples of Moses, Elijah, Elisha, John the precursor, and the other prophets, raises his discourse still higher and says:

> “And what more should I mention? Since the Savior of all himself visited it at the beginning of his manifestation and deigned to consecrate it by his own dwelling. For after he had washed in the water of baptism with which he was cleansed, as the Evangelist testifies, immediately the Spirit drove him into the desert . . . . The world must acknowledge itself indebted to you, since it knows that God undertook from you to preach and perform wonders.”

It is therefore with good reason that our writers, together with Jerome, Cassian, and others, trace the origin of this institution to the disciples of the evangelist Mark in Alexandria. Philo commended it so highly among the Essenes—that is, in that first Christian Church—that he described its form as plainly anchoritic and not greatly different from the practice of the earliest faithful who lived under the apostles after the coming of the divine Spirit.

Jerome compares these believers in Christ with those same Essenes, converted through Mark’s preaching in Egypt, in his eulogy of Philo:

> “From this it is clear,” he says, “that the first Church of those who believed in Christ was such as monks now appear and desire to be: that nothing should belong privately to anyone, that no one among them should be rich and no one poor, that inheritances should be distributed to the needy, and that they should devote themselves to prayer, psalms, teaching, and continence. Luke also reports that the first believers in Jerusalem were of this kind.”

That a considerable number of Essene ascetics flourished in Judaea in the same apostolic age is clearly shown by Baronius under the year 64. With compelling arguments he proves, against the inventions of the innovators, that most of those whom Josephus praises were Christians converted from the Jewish Essenes, and that they should not be assigned to the antiquity that Pliny and Solinus attribute to them, but rather to the time of Christ the Lord and of Herod the Great, when writers first mention them. Although those writers did not fail to describe the other Jewish sects in earlier periods, they say not a word about these people.

Solinus says that the Essenes inhabited the interior regions of Judaea, were endowed with moral discipline, had withdrawn from the customs of all nations, completely renounced sexual intercourse, knew nothing of money, lived on palm trees, and attracted many people from every nation who hastened to them. Yet no one was admitted unless the confidence of chastity and the merit of innocence accompanied him. For this reason the father of the *Annals* rightly recognized Christians in them, people more easily brought to the faith from the Essene sect than from the other Jewish sects then flourishing.

Thus, whether Telesphorus was a Christian anchorite from among those earlier people in Judaea who professed the evangelical counsels, or from those who lived under the apostles and Mark in Alexandria; or whether he was first an anchorite among the Jewish Essenes, to whom people came from every nation, and, arriving there from Greece in pursuit of a more perfect life, joined himself to them, but soon, having learned more fully about our profession, discovered it in the school of Christ and left the Jewish Essenes—either way he could be said, by the author of the *Pontifical Book*, to have been raised from the condition of an anchorite to the supreme priesthood in this Roman see.

### Line 2.—“He established that a fast should be observed for seven weeks before Easter, etc., and that Masses should be celebrated at night on the Nativity of the Lord, etc.”

Both Cardinal Baronius, under the year 154, no. 2, and Altaserra, in this section of the Anastasian text, observe that the Lenten fast came from apostolic institution. Besides Eusebius, this is attested by several bishops of the second century from Asia, who wrote that they had received the practice by tradition. Eusebius reports them in book V, chapter 24 of his *Ecclesiastical History*. The dispute there concerned not only the day of Easter but also the variety of fasting, each Church claiming to defend its own rites as received from the apostles.

As for the nighttime hours first designated by Telesphorus for celebrating the sacrifice of the Mass—and only on the Nativity of the Lord, as though before that no one had been permitted to anticipate the third hour of the day in celebrating Mass—Cardinal Baronius rightly opposes the custom of gatherings before dawn, which Christians widely practiced long before Telesphorus and which is evident in Pliny’s letter.

He therefore advises that the statements made here about the Lenten fast should be understood in this way: Telesphorus was the first to confirm it by a written law, while it had previously been commendably observed by the Churches as an unwritten tradition, since they professed the observance of apostolic rites.

The indications supplied by the events of that age correspond so closely with the received interpretation and judgment of Baronius and the other authors—that Telesphorus confirmed in writing a custom of apostolic origin—that they guide us toward perceiving the growth of the sacred rites used for the celebration of the principal mysteries. These rites were introduced by the supreme pontiffs as circumstances of time and place required and were prudently arranged in priestly commentaries, entrusted at that time, under the discipline of the secret, to the ministers of sacred things. From these materials, after the Church had obtained peace, the book of the Roman Order was later assembled according to the cycle of the year.

We can understand that these same rites received considerable development in the age of Telesphorus for the annual celebration of the chief mysteries of our religion, if we consider the whole of the three decrees attributed here to Telesphorus and compare them with the testimonies of the Fathers of that age concerning the customs and rites of Christians, insofar as the caution of our more sacred discipline permitted those matters to be discussed openly before unbelievers and catechumens.

These three decrees of Telesphorus therefore show that he should be credited with the celebration and arrangement of the rites rather than with their original institution. The law written by Telesphorus did not introduce into the Church the custom of the Lenten fast, which had already been introduced by the apostles in imitation of Christ the Lord, whose example was always set before them and us as a rule of life. Rather, during the seven weeks constituting Lent, it established a fixed selection of prayers, suitably arranging the clergy and people for the devout celebration of the Paschal mysteries and for the administration of baptism to the new offspring of the Church, after the prior preparation of catechesis and examinations.

Tertullian, a priest who lived near the age of Telesphorus, recalls that these examinations, together with kneeling, vigils, and frequent prayers, already had to be observed by those approaching baptism. He discusses them in the book he wrote on that sacrament.

At that time there were fixed periods for administering more solemn baptism: not only Easter, celebrating the Lord’s Resurrection, and Pentecost, but also the Nativity and Epiphany. These were so closely joined to the Nativity that among the Egyptians both solemnities are said to have been celebrated on the same day. The Latin Church likewise testifies that at Epiphany it commemorates the Lord’s manifestation, Baptism, and the miracle at the wedding.

It followed that Telesphorus would adapt particular rites for the Nativity of the Lord and for Epiphany, suitable for the administration of these mysteries, in the Roman titular churches, which Evaristus had divided among twenty-five priests a few years before him.

Alexander, Evaristus’s immediate successor, as soon as he saw that his predecessor had appointed priests individually over the titular churches, arranged for a written law concerning the daily sacrifice to be given to them. He also provided for the commemoration of the Lord’s Passion, which had been continuously joined to Christ’s original institution and to the apostles’ tradition. Although he knew that both the Passion itself and the formula of certain words belonging to the integrity of the sacrament had always been carefully guarded, he nevertheless instructed the priest, ministers, and people by preliminary prayers and rites that would arouse them to recall more attentively the fearful mysteries of that Passion, as I have explained at length.

By this institution he also ensured that the priests in the titular churches would introduce nothing different from what they saw the bishop preserving in the daily sacred rites according to the apostles’ example.

With equal care and concern, therefore, Telesphorus, after Alexander had prudently provided for the law of the daily sacrifice and its rites in the titular churches, judged that he too ought to act so that, on the occasion of Easter and the Nativity—or Epiphany—when solemn baptism was then administered, the annual sacred celebrations of the principal feasts would attract larger gatherings of the faithful in those same titular churches. Since the titular churches had been instituted especially for administering baptism and penance, as we read explicitly in numbers 11 and 31, Telesphorus established a definite law of rites by which the piety of those who gathered might be more suitably prepared during these celebrations to offer glory to God and to honor him with one spirit and one voice, as the apostles had instructed us.

Alexander’s work was assisted by the completion of the canon of the books of the New Testament, accomplished at the death of the apostle John. Thus Telesphorus could derive the same rites and prayers not only from the books received by himself and his predecessors and by the whole Church over which he presided, but also from tradition.

Since the sacred collection of these books had by then become somewhat more widely known, not only in the Roman Church but also in the more recently founded Churches, it increased Telesphorus’s confidence in asking God for the spirit of counsel, so that, by prescribing fixed readings from both Testaments throughout the seven weeks of the Lenten fast, he might prepare a perfect people for the Lord.

When he saw that this had succeeded well, he also turned to arranging a more solemn celebration of the mysteries of the Lord’s Nativity and ordered that the divine sacrifice be repeated that night. Perhaps he wished to accommodate the influx of the faithful, greatly increased under Alexander by the conversion of the Roman nobility to Christ, and thus to provide a sufficient opportunity for the people to assist at the sacred rites during so great a solemnity.

He is also said to have established that the angelic hymn should be sung that night, in order to recall the past benefits of the peace announced at Christ’s Nativity between God and humanity.

These developments, suitably arranged according to the needs of the times, enabled Telesphorus’s decrees to furnish the ritual books of the Roman Church for the celebration of the Lenten fast and Easter as well as the Nativity of the Lord. The Apology of Justin Martyr and the writings of Tertullian preserve sufficiently clear indications of this.

As regards the rite of solemn fasting during Lent, it is evident, when one compares the rites mentioned by Tertullian and indicated by Justin—rites therefore practiced in the second century of which we are speaking—with those described by Augustine in the fourth century and reduced to order in the Roman Order and the sacramentaries by Gelasius and Gregory the Great in the fifth, sixth, and following centuries, that there is nothing more similar.

Tertullian says, speaking of the solemn Easter celebration:

> “Those who are about to approach baptism ought to pray with frequent prayers, fasts, kneelings, and vigils, etc.”

These are the examinations called *scrutinies* in the ritual books of the Roman Church, especially from the middle week of the seven weeks constituting Lent, and which already constituted it under Telesphorus’s administration of the pontificate according to this decree. From that week, and from the middle Sunday, ancient authors commonly derive the greater fasts. See R. P. D. Martène, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, volume and book I, article II.

From that week and the middle Sunday the Roman Church takes, almost day by day, the Gospel reading from John in its daily sacred rites. This is a perfectly clear indication that the selection was not made before the beginning of the second century, since the beloved apostle committed his Gospel to writing later than the period in which it could previously have been read.

We can also clearly observe in Justin’s First Apology, section 35, that the rites of the scrutinies during these weeks were contemporary with many of the rites that followed them and that we use during Holy Week itself, and that the solemn rites of Good Friday, Holy Saturday, and Easter Day have been handed down to our own age from these sources.

Justin leads the newly baptized from the sacred font to the assembly celebrated with the other faithful and describes the sequence of rites and prayers preserved in his age and that of Telesphorus. It is so composed that one might think he had faithfully transcribed a condensed image of the office of Holy Week in the Roman, Gelasian, Gregorian, and present Orders—unless he had published it before Gelasius, Gregory, and our ritual books had set forth the Order of Mass for the Saturday and Sunday of the Resurrection following the solemn baptismal rite.

He writes:

> “But we, after we have thus washed and purified the person who has believed and given his assent, bring him to those who are called brothers, to the place where they have gathered in order to pray with concentrated minds, both for themselves, for the person who has been enlightened, and for all others everywhere, so that we may be found to be disciples of the truth, genuine practitioners of a good and holy life, and keepers of the commandments, and so that we may obtain eternal salvation.”

R. P. Joachim Perionius, a Benedictine, translates the Greek opening, **Ἡμεῖς δὲ**—“But we”—in this way:

These words correspond entirely to the appointed prayers of the Paschal octave, through which we ask God that those reborn in Christ may retain by their manner of life the sacrament they received through faith. In the same way, the sequence of prayers for oneself, for the neophytes, and for all others everywhere is reported in the collects assigned individually to Good Friday and Holy Saturday by the Roman Order. These prayers ask that Christ grant the gifts of divine grace to the universal Church and its parts, to all others everywhere, and to those who can be called or recalled to the same Church.

Then they proceed from the prayers to the offering:

> “At the end of the prayers, we greet one another with a kiss; then bread is offered to the one who presides over the brethren, together with a cup mixed with water and wine,” etc.

A little later, in section 87, Justin discusses the solemn rite of celebration on feast days more fully:

> “On the day called Sunday all who live in the towns or in the countryside gather in one place, and the memoirs of the apostles and the writings of the prophets are read for as long as the time permits. Then, when the reader has stopped, the one who presides admonishes and exhorts us to imitate the good things that have been read. Then we all rise and pray; and when our prayers have concluded, bread, wine, and water, as I said, are offered. Then the one who holds the first place,” etc.

Anyone who carefully considers both testimonies, that of Justin and that of Tertullian, and reflects that in the period when the discipline of secrecy more sparingly instructed Christians to discuss these matters before unbelievers, Justin nevertheless reported so much about the rites established in the age of Telesphorus and in his own age for the celebration of the Lenten fast that preceded solemn baptism, as well as about the vigils and feasts mentioned above, will easily understand that the decrees reviewed earlier are rightly assigned to this pontiff, although the Lenten fast and the sacred gatherings before dawn had already long flourished, by apostolic institution, before Telesphorus’s priesthood.

We may also suppose that this was the reason why Irenaeus, writing to Victor—as quoted by Eusebius in book V, chapter 23 of his *Ecclesiastical History*—when speaking of the constancy of Victor’s predecessors, the Roman pontiffs, in never separating Easter from Sunday and in not permitting others to observe it otherwise, did not continue his enumeration beyond Sixtus, the immediate predecessor of Telesphorus.

Perhaps the celebration of the rites began, or was first contemplated, under Sixtus; Telesphorus subsequently either perfected it or confirmed it by decree. Irenaeus writes:

> “The presbyters who were appointed before Soter, over the Church which you now govern—I mean Anicetus, Pius, Hyginus, Telesphorus, and Sixtus—although they themselves neither observed this feast on the day on which the bishops of Asia observed it nor permitted those who came after them to observe it in that way,” etc.

From this Pearson further drew a shrewd inference, comparing Anatolius’s words from his Paschal canon, where, concerning the bishops of Asia who celebrated Easter immediately after the fourteenth day of the moon, after the spring equinox, without awaiting Sunday, he writes:

> “Not acquiescing in the authority of certain persons—that is, the successors of Peter and Paul—who taught all the churches in which they had scattered the spiritual seeds of the Gospel that the solemnity of the Resurrection of Christ the Lord could be celebrated only on Sunday.”

It seemed to him that these testimonies could establish that the custom of celebrating Easter on Sunday was not to be attributed to the apostles Peter and Paul, but to certain successors of Peter, whom Irenaeus names individually when, proceeding backward in order, he recalls the predecessors of Soter: Anicetus, Pius, Hyginus, Telesphorus, and Sixtus.

“Therefore,” Pearson inferred, “Xystus, the first bishop established at Rome after the death of Saint John, stabilized the custom of the Roman Church—a custom that no one had dared to establish before Saint John’s death. For this reason he thinks” that when Polycarp urged Anicetus to celebrate on the same day as the disciples of John, Anicetus replied that “he ought to retain the custom of his predecessors,” as we read in Irenaeus’s Letter to Victor in Eusebius:

> “Anicetus,” Pearson adds, “was not asserting any tradition from the apostles in this matter, but only a custom maintained among his predecessors”—namely, the Roman pontiffs Xystus, Telesphorus, and their successors.

But if Anatolius and this more recent writer had wished to consider all the churches founded by Peter’s successors through their preaching in the three patriarchal sees—churches in which Sunday was likewise assigned to the feast of the Resurrection, as was the fiftieth day after it, which also falls on a Sunday and was assigned to the celebration of Pentecost, as all the Eastern and Western calendars of feasts testify, together with the councils, the Fathers, and the author of the Apostolic Constitutions, who is known to have written before the Council of Nicaea—they would certainly have seen, by the unanimous agreement of these authorities, that Sunday was chosen for the consecration of bishops because they knew that the Holy Spirit had descended upon the faithful in the upper room on a similar day. They should therefore have inferred that, before Sixtus and Telesphorus, the custom of celebrating the Christian Passover on Sunday had already prevailed from the apostolic age, together with the Lenten fast, both among the Western churches and among the others throughout Africa, Egypt, Libya, the Asian and Pontic diocese, and Cilicia—regions mentioned in Constantine’s letter in Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book III, chapter 19, and *Ecclesiastical History*, Book V, chapter 23, where several synods add testimony on this matter.

If Telesphorus judged that this custom, observed more consistently than others in the Roman Church, should be adorned with the rite of a more solemn office, as may be gathered from his decree—or Sixtus, as someone has inferred from Irenaeus’s account—Anicetus did not look only to these men, but also to the other earlier pontiffs, whose unshaken custom he proposed equally for observance by himself and by everyone else, as well as the decrees of Sixtus and Telesphorus, when he replied that he ought to retain the custom of his predecessors.

### Line 6.—The Angelic Hymn: “Glory to God in the highest”

The sacred Gospels testify to the antiquity of this hymn, since they report its first part as having been uttered in precisely these words by the heavenly spirits. We also understand that the remaining parts added by the Church are of considerable antiquity from the fact that the hymn is found complete, written in Greek, in the most ancient biblical codex known as that of Thecla, which the distinguished Laurentius Zaccagnius showed to have been written toward the end of the fourth Christian century, as well as in other very ancient copies of the Psalms and Canticles.

Moreover, the Reverend Father Martene observes that it was customary for it to be sung in Greek in the Church of Tours, in *On Ancient Ecclesiastical Discipline in the Celebration of the Divine Offices*, volume IV, chapter 12, no. 20, p. 89. For further information about its antiquity and author, consult Cardinal Bona, *Liturgical Matters*, Book II, chapter 4.

Since this *Pontifical Book* contains several decrees of the Roman pontiffs, to which we append notes in fulfillment of the task undertaken—namely, to illuminate, as far as possible, obscure passages of this book—I think it necessary to set out here, once and for all, matters that generally concern the decrees of pontiffs who occupied the see before Siricius, so that it will not be necessary to repeat the same things in each individual case whenever something requiring notice occurs.

The origin of such decrees might seem obscure to many if their documentary evidence were repeated, or if support were sought from the decretal letters that Bishop Riculfus of Mainz first published under the forged name of Isidore in the eighth Christian century. I shall not propose the decrees of the earlier pontiffs on the basis of these documents, since I know well what learned scholars think of this collection of Pseudo-Isidore, especially two of the brightest lights of ecclesiastical antiquity, Cardinals Baronius and Bona.

It is enough to reproduce the judgment of the latter—which includes the testimony of his colleague—from Book I, chapter 3 of *Liturgical Matters*, in these words:

> “It has long been observed by learned men,” he says, “that their decretal letters up to Siricius are spurious, forged by a certain Spaniard under the name of Isidore—whoever he may have been—toward the end of the seventh century through a pious fraud. They were composed largely from the opinions of ancient canons, even civil laws, and the holy Fathers who flourished in the fourth and fifth centuries, with a shameful anachronism and in almost the same style and rhetorical character. Bishop Riculfus of Mainz first brought them from Spain into Gaul toward the end of the eighth century; from there they were disseminated into other regions and commonly accepted. But eventually the deception was detected, and Baronius, discussing these letters in the year 865, acknowledges their falsity and openly admits it, lest anyone, as he says, should be able to accuse the Roman Church of having fabricated anything of this kind. Their testimonies must therefore be rejected as false and useless, and more certain evidence must be produced from the true and legitimate writings of pontiffs and Fathers.”

I have proposed that the rule of Cardinals Baronius and Bona be followed in selecting material capable of illuminating the decrees of the pontiffs before Siricius. Just as Bona, following Baronius’s example, sets aside the false Isidore and the forged letters and judges that we must abstain from things of uncertain origin and unknown to the immediately succeeding ages, using for the foundation of history only materials drawn from genuine sources—writers of established historical reliability, or works of the Fathers in which such matters are cited—so I believe that I must proceed when explaining the knowledge, origin, occasion, meaning, practice, and other aspects of these decrees, according to what seems appropriate in each case.

## NOTES ON THE LIBERIAN CATALOGUE

### Lines 1–2.—Antonini Macrini

An obvious scribal error in the first catalogue. It should be read, as in the second catalogue, *Antonini et Marci*, that is, of Pius and Marcus Aurelius; their dates are indicated by the consuls listed in the first catalogue.

### Line 2.—Caesare et Albino

Correct to *Caesare H. et Balbino*, on the basis of inscriptions published by Gruterus XXIII, 12, and 445, 10, and by Fabretti, p. 513, inscription no. 180, as well as other similar pottery inscriptions observed at Rome, and all the fasti.

### Note: [Col. 1185C]

#### Line 1.—Telesphorus, Greek by nationality

Saint Telesphorus was Greek, a native of Thurii in Calabria, which was formerly called Magna Graecia and is today Terranova, built among the ruins of Sybaris.

#### Same line.—From an anchorite

Since Telesphorus was the son of an anchorite, it appears that some followers of this holy institution existed in the early Church.

### [Col. 1186A] Line 2.—“He established that the fast should be observed for seven weeks before Easter”

The Lenten fast had already been handed down by the apostles—[as is shown by] Apostolic Canon 6, and Clement, Books V and VII; the *Constitutions of Ignatius*, Letter 4 to the Philippians—but, perhaps neglected by many because of the persecutions, it was restored by a new decree.

### Note: [Col. 1186A]

#### Line 2.—“He established”

Some attribute the institution of the Lenten fast to Telesphorus in Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, under the year of Christ 141, where it reads:

> “Some writers say that the Lenten fast was instituted and commanded by Telesphorus at this time.”

But Arnaldus Pontacus and Josephus Scaliger, in their notes on that *Chronicle*, had already observed that these words are absent from the manuscript copies and were therefore inserted into Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. Rabanus Maurus, Book II of *On the Institution of the Clergy*, chapter 34, and Rupert, abbot of Tuitius, Book IV of *On the Divine Offices*, chapter 9, write the same thing as Eusebius. But it must be said that Rabanus and Rupert were deceived either by the testimony of the *Pontifical Book* or by Eusebius’s already interpolated *Chronicle*, and that the more recent authors are less deserving of belief than Saints Jerome and Leo, as Natalis Alexander states in the second century, dissertation 4, article 3, where he proves that the pre-Paschal fast is more probably asserted to have been received from apostolic tradition.

#### Line 3.—“And on the Nativity of the Lord”

Finally, Anastasius—or the author of the *Pontifical Book*—writes that Telesphorus established that no one should presume to celebrate Mass before the course of the third hour. Amalarius, Book III, chapter 42, and Strabo, chapter 23, report this decree. But they were deceived by Pseudo-Isidore, who rashly forged the decretal letters of the early pontiffs and imposed them on the whole Church as legitimate documents.

“For what,” asks Cardinal Bona, *Liturgical Matters*, Book I, chapter 21, no. 5, “could be more alien to the condition of that age, when Christians hid themselves with the greatest care to evade the swords of raging emperors, than the promulgation of this law, which could in no way be observed?” Tertullian teaches us in *On Flight in Persecution*, and elsewhere, that the faithful gathered at night and in the most secret places for the assembly; he began writing several years after Telesphorus, under the emperor Severus. Indeed, they could not have acted otherwise if they wished both to preserve the dignity of the sacrifice and to secure their own lives.

The more probable and more fitting view, therefore, is that reported by Baronius under the year 382: this fixing of the third hour was sanctioned by Saint Damasus, supposedly on the basis of a prescription of the Nicene canon, although that canon does not exist. Whoever wishes to learn more about these matters should read the cited work of Cardinal Bona.

## [Col. 1175]

### 9

Telesphorus, Greek by nationality and the son of an anchorite, held the see for eleven years, three months, and twenty-two days [Note: [Col. 1175] B: nine months, less three days]. He lived during the times of Antoninus and Marcus [Note: [Col. 1175] B: Antoninus Pius alone, up to the consulship of Glabrio and Verianus]. [Note: [Col. 1175] See Baronius, year 554.]

He established that the fast should be observed for seven weeks before Easter, and that Masses should be celebrated at night on the Nativity of the Lord, whereas at all times [Note: [Col. 1175] CB: “at every other time”] no one presumed to celebrate Mass before the course of the third hour—the hour at which our Lord ascended the cross—and that before the sacrifice the Angelic Hymn should be sung, namely, “GLORY TO GOD IN THE HIGHEST.”

He was crowned with martyrdom. He was buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican, on the fourth day before the Nones of January [Note: [Col. 1175] CB: on the Nones]. He held four ordinations in the month of December [Note: [Col. 1175] CB: bishops, in various places, 132]: twelve priests and eight deacons [Note: [Col. 1175] CB: seven]; and the episcopal see was vacant for four days.

Telesphorus, for eleven years, three months, and three days. He lived during the time of Antoninus Macrinus, from the consulship of Titianus and Gallicanus up to that of Caesar and Albinus.
