## Notes concerning Hyginus, Pius, Anicetus, Soter, and Eleutherius; or Chapter 4 of Dissertation 2 by Schelestratius, in Volume I of *Ecclesiastical Antiquity*, p. 105

### On Pius, Anicetus, Soter, and Eleutherius: In what order and at what times they held the see

1. There is a twofold difficulty concerning the pontificates of Pius, Anicetus, Soter, and Eleutherius. One concerns the order in which Anicetus and Pius should be placed; the other concerns the time during which Soter and Eleutherius held the Roman see.

The first question arose from the testimony of certain ancient catalogues and Fathers, according to which Anicetus is placed before Pius. Thus, in the most ancient catalogue, compiled during the time of Pope Liberius, Anicetus is placed after Hyginus and Pius after Anicetus. Saint Optatus of Milevis, Book II against Parmenianus, and Saint Augustine, Letter 165, appear to have taken this same sequence from this or another catalogue, since they present the succession of the Roman pontiffs in these words: “Hyginus, Anicetus; Anicetus, Pius; Pius, Soter; Soter, Eleutherius.”

The author of the second catalogue, from the time of the emperor Justin, following the older catalogue, places Anicetus before Pius. The same order is preserved in the manuscripts held at Antwerp by the distinguished Daniel Papebrochius, and in the Vatican catalogue written in the ninth century.

The author of the *Pontifical Book* agrees with this order, according to the Mainz edition from the library of Velser, duumvir of Augsburg, and according to the edition of Hannibal Fabrotti in the body of Byzantine history. Several manuscript codices also agree, among them a Vatican manuscript numbered 5269, copied approximately five hundred years ago from another older codex; another is the Thuanean, and a third the Cassinese.

2. Nevertheless, not all manuscripts of Anastasius’s work agree on this matter. There is considerable diversity among them, and several contradict the evidence cited above concerning the order of Anicetus and Pius.

Hannibal Fabrotti noted that in two French manuscripts, the Regian and the Mazarin, Pius is placed before Anicetus. Lucas Holstenius, in his manuscript notes on Anastasius the Librarian, reports the following after the pontificate of Hyginus:

> “In the Florentine manuscripts Pius is placed here, followed by Anicetus; and likewise in the Regian manuscript, namely, the codex now in the Vatican’s Alexandrian Library.”

It is therefore clear that among the Anastasian codices there are some in which Pius is placed before Anicetus—and rightly so, if we follow the consular dates cited by the author of the *Pontifical Book*. He states that Pius held the see from the consulship of Clarus and Severus, which fell in the year 146, whereas Anicetus began with the consulship of Gallicanus and Vetus, which coincided with the year 150. Thus the chronological notation itself shows that Pius must be placed before Anicetus.

Anastasius took this consular notation from the author of the *Pontifical Book*, while that author took it from two older catalogues into which a major error first entered when Anicetus was placed before Pius. After the death of Henschenius, Papebrochius recognized this error. In his *Chronico-Historical Endeavor* he admits that he had long and laboriously turned the matter over in every direction so that the chronology of the older catalogue, derived from the consuls, might correspond to a correct calculation.

> “In such great perplexity,” he says on page 22, “I confess that I remained uncertain for a long time and twisted myself in every direction. At last, however, there occurred to me a conjecture of a doubtful plan which seems not to untie but to cut the knot: the same two pairs of consuls being distributed differently between the two pontiffs, while their names nevertheless remained untouched and Pius was placed before Anicetus, through a slight change made in the most ancient catalogue of all, from which the confusion could have flowed like a spring into all the others.”

He proposes that alteration in his conjecture on page 23. For the consular entries that now appear in the catalogue as follows:

> Anicetus—from the consulship of Gallicanus and Vetus to that of Praesens and Rufinus.  
> Pius—from the consulship of Clarus and Severus to that of the Two Augusti.

He asks permission to reverse them in this way:

> Pius—from the consulship of Clarus and Severus to that of Praesens and Rufinus.  
> Anicetus—from the consulship of Gallicanus and Vetus to that of the Two Augusti.

> “For,” Papebrochius continues, “once this alteration is allowed, I seem to arrange everything in such a way that, with the succession of the pontiffs and their deputies uninterrupted—even between these two and the following Soter—only a few days would suffice for the vacancy of the see, where otherwise an interval of more than six months would be required.”

3. Thus far Papebrochius. To preserve the authority of the older catalogue, he thinks that two errors above all must be corrected. But since that catalogue requires these corrections, everyone can see that it was composed by someone who lacked a more accurate knowledge of the Roman pontiffs.

If one were permitted to alter the Acts in whatever manner one wished, as this learned man sought permission to alter this catalogue, scarcely any spurious document could be found that could not be made plausible. Papebrochius himself recognized this in his *Anamnesis concerning Cletus and Anacletus*, p. 217, where he candidly admits that the first and oldest catalogue is not so reliable on these principles that it can inspire unquestionable confidence once the difficulty concerning Anicetus and Pius has been noticed.

Leaving aside, therefore, matters concerning the authority of the older catalogue, let us turn to the first error that Papebrochius thought should be corrected and show that Pius must be placed before Anicetus. This is the order found in several catalogues from before and after the time of Anastasius the Librarian. Among them are a Vatican catalogue of the eleventh century; another belonging to the once most learned library of Queen Christina of Sweden, from the ninth century; a Palatine-Vatican catalogue of the eighth century; and two Corbeiensis catalogues, one compiled at the beginning of the eighth century and the other in the sixth century under Pope Vigilius.

The authors of these catalogues followed the testimony of Saint Prosper, who in his *Chronicle* placed Pius after Hyginus and Anicetus after Pius, just as Epiphanius presents them in Heresy 27, in these words:

> “Anicetus, who succeeded Pius and the other pontiffs.”

This order was taken from the *Chronicle* and *Ecclesiastical History* of Eusebius Pamphilus. In Book IV, chapter 11, he expressly states:

> “After Hyginus died in the fourth year of his episcopate, Pius assumed the priesthood of the Roman Church.”

And in the same place:

> “When Pius exchanged life for death in the fifteenth year of his episcopate, Anicetus became bishop of that Church.”

Eusebius learned this succession of the Roman pontiffs from those who had been able to see Anicetus and Pius during their lifetimes and who had been in Rome under Anicetus and Eleutherius, the successor of Anicetus.

The first among these was Saint Irenaeus, who was sent to Rome under Eleutherius by the martyrs of Lyons. The second was Hegesippus, who remained in Rome until the time of Anicetus.

Irenaeus’s testimony appears in Book III, chapter 3, where, in his catalogue of the Roman pontiffs, he writes:

> “Hyginus; after him, Pius; after him, Anicetus.”

Hegesippus’s testimony is found in Eusebius, Book IV, chapter 21, where Hegesippus states:

> “When I was in Rome, I remained there until the time of Anicetus, during whose episcopate Eleutherius was still a deacon. Soter succeeded him, and when Soter had died, Eleutherius assumed the episcopal office.”

No clearer testimony could be desired, since it is beyond any reasonable exception. It plainly shows that Soter succeeded Anicetus and consequently that Pius must be placed before Anicetus.

4. Since it is therefore clear from what has been said what must be established concerning the first difficulty—namely, the order in which Pius and Anicetus should be placed in the succession of the Roman pontiffs—we must now address the second difficulty, which concerns the time when Soter and Eleutherius, the successors of Anicetus, held the apostolic see.

As for the years of Pope Soter, nearly all the manuscript and printed catalogues agree. They assign him nine years, together with some months and days.

The most ancient catalogue, written during the time of Pope Liberius, reports that Soter held the see for nine years, three months, and two days. The Vatican catalogue written in the ninth century agrees with it. The Corbeiensis catalogue, compiled under Pope Vigilius, gives the same number of years, two months, and twenty-one days. The Antwerp manuscripts of the sixth century give nine years, three months, and twenty days.

The Palatine-Vatican catalogue of the eighth century states that he held the see for nine years, six months, and twelve days. Other ancient catalogues assign him the same years and months, differing only in changing the twelve days to twenty-one.

The author of the *Pontifical Book* agrees with these figures in three manuscript codices, namely the Florentine, Regian, and Vatican manuscripts. According to their reading, he held the see for nine years, six months, and twenty-one days.

The series of pontiffs painted in the church of Saint Paul approximately five hundred years ago gives nine years, three months, and twenty-one days. Other catalogues do not disagree with it. Thus, according to the common agreement of these catalogues, Soter held the see for nine years.

The catalogue compiled during the time of the emperor Justin differs from this tradition. It assigns Soter eight years, six months, and twenty-one days. Its author followed Saint Prosper’s *Chronicle*, which reads:

> “Soter assumed the episcopate of the Roman Church for eight years.”

Saint Prosper took Soter’s period from Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, where precisely the same words are found.

Eusebius confirms all this in his history, Book V. When he is about to describe the persecution stirred up in Gaul under the son of Antoninus, he begins the preface to that book with these words:

> “Accordingly, when Soter, bishop of the city of Rome, had died after the eighth year of his episcopate, Eleutherus, the twelfth in succession from the apostles, succeeded him. At that time the seventeenth year of the reign of Antoninus Verus was underway. Since at that time a more violent persecution had arisen against our people in certain parts of the world through an incursion of the populace, it is possible to infer from what happened in a single province that almost innumerable martyrs flourished throughout the world.”

And in chapter 1:

> “The region itself is called Gaul. In it two cities above all are celebrated as distinguished and pre-eminent mothers of cities: Lyons and Vienne.”

This is the persecution mentioned by Severus Sulpicius, Book II of *Sacred History*, in these words:

> “Under Aurelius, the son of Antoninus, the fifth persecution was stirred up; and at that time martyrdoms were first seen within Gaul, since the religion of God had been received later beyond the Alps.”

5. The persecution in Gaul therefore occurred during the pontificate of Eleutherius, when Marcus Aurelius was in the seventeenth year of his reign. Saint Pothinus, bishop, and many others suffered in that persecution. The remaining confessors, confined in prisons, reported their martyrdom to the churches of Asia and Phrygia.

The letter of the martyrs of Lyons concerning this matter is preserved in Eusebius, Book V, chapter 2. In it they state that Pothinus, nearly ninety years old, was killed by terrible tortures. Eusebius adds in chapter 5:

> “When Pothinus—some incorrectly read Photinus—was killed in his ninetieth year together with the Gallic martyrs, Irenaeus succeeded him in the episcopate of the Church of Lyons.”

Saint Jerome says the same in his book *On Illustrious Men*, under Irenaeus. He states that:

> “After Pothinus, nearly ninety years old, had been crowned with martyrdom for Christ, Irenaeus was appointed in his place.”

It follows unequivocally that Irenaeus succeeded Pothinus in the see of Lyons during the persecution of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, which began in the seventeenth year of his reign—that is, in the year 177—and ended with his death in the year 180.

Before this, Irenaeus had already been sent from the martyrs of Lyons to Rome to Pope Eleutherius, as is clear from the letter of those same martyrs, which Eusebius reports in Book V, chapter 4. There he testifies that Irenaeus was not yet a bishop but only a priest when he was commended to Eleutherius by the martyrs.

Eusebius’s words are:

> “The same martyrs commended by letter to the aforesaid Eleutherius Irenaeus, who at that time was still a priest of the Church of Lyons.”

And the priest-confessors write in the letter itself:

> “We wish you every good thing, always and in every way, in God, Father Eleutherius. We urged our brother and fellow worker Irenaeus to bring this letter to you.”

6. From these premises it follows that Eleutherius held the Roman see during the persecution of Marcus Aurelius. To make this fit his own calculation, the most eminent Cardinal Baronius judged that several years should be taken away from Soter. Although all ancient writers and catalogues, both manuscript and printed, assign him at least eight or nine years of pontificate, Baronius left him only four years, less twelve days.

Baronius placed the beginning of Soter’s pontificate in the year 175. If he had assigned him eight years, following Eusebius and Saint Prosper, or nine years, following the catalogues and the *Pontifical Book*, Eleutherius would not have begun to reign until 183 or 184.

But when Baronius saw that this conflicted with the testimony of the martyrs of Lyons, he assigned Soter only three years, eleven months, and eighteen days, so that his death could be placed in the year 179 and Irenaeus could have undertaken his embassy to Eleutherius, Soter’s successor, before the death of Marcus Aurelius.

Nevertheless, under the year 179, no. 51, he notes:

> “If anyone should discover a more certain chronology of Soter’s years—provided that Cletus is not removed from the number of the Roman pontiffs and that the genuine testimony of the letters of the martyrs of Lyons is not disregarded—we shall gladly agree.”

Although Baronius himself noted these things, while maintaining the reverence due to him, we have departed from his opinion by establishing a more certain chronology concerning several pontiffs. In their case, either ancient monuments or the testimony of the ancients makes the facts so clear that there is no room for doubt about the time in which they held the pontificate.

We have established this concerning the times of Peter, the prince of the apostles, Clement, and Alexander, who were crowned with martyrdom. We have begun to demonstrate the same concerning the pontificate of Soter, about which it is certain that it could not have extended beyond the seventeenth year of the reign of the emperor Marcus Aurelius, in which the persecution began.

During that persecution, the martyrs of Lyons repeatedly wrote to Pope Eleutherius, as Eusebius testifies in his history, Book V, chapter 1, where he presents their letter, which they entrusted to Saint Irenaeus to deliver to Eleutherius.

7. Concerning the time of Pope Soter, when he suffered martyrdom and left the Roman chair to Eleutherius, the most eminent Cardinal Baronius differs from us only by two years—the same two years by which he continually departs from the true chronology of the early pontiffs.

For this reason he placed all the ecclesiastical events two years later. It was also on this account that he assigned the seventeenth year of the emperor Marcus Aurelius, which coincides with the year 177, to the year 179.

If the seventeenth year of Marcus Aurelius is restored to the year 177 of its era, Baronius will agree with us concerning the time of the persecution in which Soter gained the crown of martyrdom and Eleutherius obtained the Roman chair.

Baronius’s words under the year 179 should be heard. Speaking of the persecution in which the martyrs of Lyons died, he writes in no. 50:

> “That Pope Soter was also taken away in this persecution, the letter of the martyrs of Lyons, written during this same period of persecution to Eleutherius, his successor, necessarily compels us to affirm, although others have assigned him nine years. But since he is found to have held only three ordinations, we may suppose that he did not hold the see for a longer period. Eusebius, however, in his *Chronicle*, under the preceding year—namely, the sixteenth year of the emperor Marcus—places Eleutherius as having been substituted in Soter’s place, but in his history he places this in the seventeenth year itself. Since we believe that he learned this from the letter of the martyrs of Lyons, we readily agree with him; otherwise, in the case of the earlier Roman pontiffs, we cannot agree with him because he omitted Cletus. Thus, in this ambiguous matter, we judge that Soter’s death and Eleutherius’s accession should be deliberately placed at this time, relying not so much on Eusebius himself as on the letters of the holy martyrs of Lyons, who wrote to Eleutherius at this time.”

This is what Baronius says. Following his rule concerning the dates of the pontiffs mentioned above, as derived from the letters of the martyrs of Lyons, we have presented their true chronology.

### Note: [Col. 1192B]

#### Line 4.—“He organized the clergy and distributed the ranks”

The ecclesiastical orders were already distinct from the time of the apostles, and the rank of each had been arranged. Nevertheless, it should be believed that Hyginus added something to the earlier distinction and ordering of the ranks.

### Note: [Col. 1192B]

#### Line 4.—“He organized the clergy and distributed the ranks”

The earlier persecution, before Antoninus, had disrupted the clergy, against which it had raged with especially violent force. Under the emperors Antoninus Pius and Marcus, peace was restored to the Church, as is clear from the rescript addressed to the common people of Asia, preserved in Eusebius, Book IV, chapter 13:

> “Many have reported these matters to me. Following the constitution of my father, I replied to them: If anyone still persists in causing trouble to any of them because he is a Christian, let the accused be acquitted of the charge, even if it is established that he is in fact a Christian; but the accuser himself shall suffer punishment.”

The pontiff therefore, coming to the aid of an order that had been disturbed, organized the clergy and restored it to its former ranks.

For *componere* means to bring a matter back into order, to reform it, and to distribute it more suitably. Cyprian used the word in this sense when the Novatian schism had disturbed the churches, *Letter* 42:

> “They should restore the members of the torn body to the unity of the Catholic Church.”

To distribute ranks means to establish an order based on a certain precedence. Nicholas I wrote in this sense to the emperor Michael, *Letter* 8:

> “For this reason the confessor of Christ, Sylvester, established ranks within the assembly, so that neither a priest against a bishop, nor a deacon against a priest, should bring any accusation.”

At times the word refers to dignity, as when a simple priest is elevated to the presbyterate or to a position of leadership in the Church. Cornelius uses it in this sense in his letter to Fabius, preserved in Eusebius, Book IV, chapter 13:

> “To attain the rank of presbyter.”

Cyprian elevated Numidicus, the presbyter of the martyrs, to the dignity of the presbyterate of the Church of Carthage. Moreover, he says, *Letter* 33:

> “He will be promoted to a higher place.”

And elsewhere:

> “Such a man deserved further ranks and greater advancement in clerical ordination, to be assessed not by his years but by his merits. Meanwhile, however, it seemed best that he should begin with the office of reader.”

That the presbyterate was considered a rank of honor above the priesthood is declared by Pontius in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*:

> “He immediately received both the presbyterate and the priesthood. For who would not believe that all the ranks of honor were suited to such a believing mind?”

That various ranks and distinct ministries also existed in the primitive Church is taught by the acts of Saints Eusebius and Procopius, which are considered to come from the collection of the acts of the martyrs of Eusebius. Concerning the martyr Eusebius, they state, as cited by Valesius in his notes on Eusebius:

> “He performed three ministries of the Church: one in the office of reading; another in interpreting speech from Syriac; and a third in laying on hands against demons.”

### Note: [Col. 1193A]

#### (From BIN.) Line 4.—“He organized the clergy and distributed the ranks”

The hierarchical order of the Catholic Church—which is itself said to be subject to presbyters and deacons [the Latin syntax is anomalous]—is here said to have been organized by Hyginus. This can only be understood to mean that Hyginus added certain things lost through the injuries of time and writers to the ecclesiastical hierarchy already established by Christ the Lord in the apostolic age and confirmed by the holy Fathers who preceded him; or that, through this constitution of his, he illuminated the same things that had been instituted by divine right and confirmed by the Fathers.

#### (From LAB.) Line 1.—“Whose genealogy”

These words are absent from manuscripts C and A.

#### Line 3.—“Veri”

Read *Severi*.

### Note: [Col. 1193B]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES ON THE LIVES OF THE HOLY PONTIFFS HYGINUS, PIUS, ANICETUS, AND SOTER
Students of pontifical chronology are confronted with a formidable difficulty by the order of succession and the duration of the rule of the four pontiffs who follow. The source of the difficulty in establishing both matters arose from lacunae long ago observed in the very ancient Liberian Catalogue by its editor Bucherius, as his own words make clear; these lacunae should be noted in the margin of the first treatise among the Prolegomena to this volume, folio VII. Anicetus is missing here. Eleutherus is missing again. Zephyrinus is likewise missing. Moreover, the consuls are confused and transposed, [Col. 1193C] as are the totals of years, months, and days under Pius and Anicetus, as was indicated in the same Prolegomena; scarcely any traces of the chronology remain to us that do not conflict with one another. Hence we understand why so many ancient writers after Optatus of Milevis, and so many recent historians after Baronius, adopted opinions so numerous and diverse. Schelestratius lists them in *Antiquitates Ecclesiasticae*, volume I, dissertation 2, chapter 4; I arranged for the whole of that discussion to be published after his brief notes on section 10 of St. Hyginus, so that I need not repeat what P. Papebrochius learnedly reported concerning the Historical Knot between the two immediate successors of Hyginus in his *Chronhistorical Attempt*, pages 22–23, or what Pearsonius opposed partly to Blondellus and partly to the supporters of our Anastasius in his posthumous works. If anything remains to be answered among his objections to our chronology, I shall address it. In this difficulty, therefore, the reader will easily judge from what we shall establish here whether the method of Chronotaxis proposed by us in the Prolegomena, and to which we profess to adhere, succeeds in following reliable traces. [Col. 1193D]

Since the series and chronology of the Roman pontiffs have been carried, by the agreement of the Older Catalogue and other documents, down to the end of Telesphorus, under the consulship of Aelius Caesar for the second time and Balbinus, in the year of Christ 137, we must seek the nearest era among his successors in which the same documents and catalogues agree. That era will be the beginning of Soter’s pontificate. Nine years are assigned to him both by the Older Catalogue and by the pictures of St. Paul, as well as by the remaining catalogues and manuscripts reviewed in the series of Roman pontiffs among the Prolegomena—nine years, I say, before the consulship of Severus for the second time and Herennius, in the year of Christ 171. From that point the same catalogues, except the mutilated Liberian one, and the manuscripts begin the fifteen-year pontificate of Eleutherus, which must close under the consulship of Maternus and Bradua, in the year of Christ 185. Therefore, according to these testimonies, Soter’s beginning falls in the year of Christ 162, [Col. 1194A] under the consulship of Rusticus and Aquilinus, whom the catalogue of Felix IV, the *Liber Pontificalis*, and the Ocriculan manuscripts likewise assign to the beginning of Soter’s pontificate.

Thus, from the last year of Telesphorus, A.D. 137, to the first year of Soter, A.D. 162, there are twenty-five intervening years, to be divided among the three pontiffs Hyginus, Pius, and Anicetus. These are listed between Telesphorus and Soter not only by the catalogues and the *Liber Pontificalis*, but also by highly authoritative writers contemporary with those pontiffs, namely Hegesippus and Irenaeus, both of whom lived at Rome around their time and are therefore witnesses to their chronology beyond any reasonable objection.

Irenaeus, book III, chapter 3, writes:

> Ἕπειτα Ὑγῖνος, εἶτα Πῖος, μεθ’ ὅν Ἀνίκητος, διαδεξαμένου τὸν Ἀνίκητον Σωτῆρος.

“Then Hyginus, afterward Pius, after whom Anicetus; Soter succeeded Anicetus.”

And in his letter to Victor he lists the same men in reverse order. Hegesippus too, in Eusebius, book IV, chapter 22, writes as follows:

> Γενόμενος δὲ ἐν Ῥώμῃ, διαδοχὴν ἐποιησάμην μέχρις Ἀνικήτου, οὗν διάκονος ἦν Ἐλέυθερος· καὶ παρὰ Ἀνικήτου διαδέχεται Σωτὴρ, μεθ’ ὅν Ἐλεύθερος·

“But when I came to Rome, I made a succession-list down to Anicetus, whose deacon was Eleutherus; after [Col. 1194B] Anicetus, Soter succeeded, and after him Eleutherus.”

The twenty-five years must therefore be divided among Hyginus, Pius, and Anicetus: the first being the era of Christ 138, under the consulship of Camerinus and Niger, and the last the year of Christ 161, under the consulship of the two Augusti. All the documents assign four years to Hyginus’s Roman see, unanimously adding three months, as I published in the series of Roman pontiffs among the Prolegomena. The catalogue of Felix IV and the *Liber Pontificalis* likewise record Camerinus and Niger as the first consuls of this four-year period; they belong to the year 138. Hyginus’s pontificate therefore extends through the full year 141, whose consuls were Severus and Priscinus.

The *Liber Pontificalis* names Priscus instead of Priscinus, with Orfitus as his colleague, and assigns Severus to the successor Pius, with Clarus as his colleague. [Col. 1194C] But the genuine reading of the consulships belonging to this period can easily be restored from the consistently established number of years, since four years are assigned on both sides. Since the first consuls of Hyginus are Camerinus and Niger, in A.D. 138, according to the catalogue of Felix IV as well as the *Liber Pontificalis*, the fourth consulship marking the end of that pontificate must necessarily be matched with Severus and Priscinus, who mark the year A.D. 141.

Once Hyginus’s four years have thus been assigned, twenty-one years remain from the total of twenty-five, to be divided between Pius and Anicetus, beginning with the consuls of the year 141 and ending with the consuls of the year 162, Rusticus and Aquilinus. Since these consuls establish the beginning of Soter’s pontificate both in the catalogue of Felix IV and in the *Liber Pontificalis* and the Lectionaries, as was reviewed above among the Prolegomena, they leave twenty-one equal consulships—that is, twenty years and one full year—to be divided between Pius and Anicetus, the two pontiffs between Hyginus and Soter whom Irenaeus, living at Rome during their time, lists, as we read from his own account, with Hegesippus as his witness. [Col. 1194D]

The older Italian catalogues, reported among the Prolegomena, divide precisely this twenty-year period between Pius and Anicetus, consistently assigning eight years and three months to one of them, and eleven years and four months to the other. The calculations of the correctly distributed twenty-year period therefore agree in this chronology, which derives most directly from the genuine Roman sources and preserves their native purity.

It remains to show which of the two pontiffs, Pius or Anicetus, who together fill this twenty-year period, received the eight years and three months, so that the other received the remaining eleven years and four months consistently asserted in those Italian catalogues. The pictures of the basilica of St. Paul, together with Irenaeus and Hegesippus, will settle the dispute. Although the names of both pontiffs have fallen away from beside the images, the surviving numbers—three months in the first image and eleven years in the second—sufficiently indicate the pontificate and its era, from which the record was taken and transmitted to those most ancient Italian catalogues, the Bergamese, Farfense, [Col. 1195A] Cavense, and Lucense. They show that Pius rightly claims the first place, with eight years, three months, and the same number of days, while Anicetus holds the later position with eleven years, four months, and twenty-one days. Irenaeus and Hegesippus, both contemporary with them and resident at Rome, testify to the order of succession.

We should therefore credit the providence of Leo the Great for preserving in the basilica the eras of his predecessors in this manner, through the pious care with which it was adorned with mosaics, paintings, and images. With the help and evidence of these monuments, it has been possible to untangle successfully this exceedingly difficult knot of chronology.

Finally, the consulships corresponding to each pontiff must be established. They are indeed expressed in the catalogues, although the still-gaping lacunae in the older Liberian Catalogue gave ignorant and audacious copyists an opportunity to mingle fragments of verses from a damaged exemplar and to displace and rearrange the names of the consuls. Four pairs of consuls are mentioned in these records: Gallicanus and Vetus, whose consulship belongs to the year of Christ 150, and the two Augusti—Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Verus—[Col. 1195B] to whom the year 161 is assigned. Here are the eleven years due to Anicetus, whom Soter rightly succeeded, according to Hegesippus and Irenaeus, under the consulship of Rusticus and Aquilinus in the year 162, correctly assigned by the catalogues and by the Librarian to the beginning of Soter’s pontificate.

The remaining eight years, extending from 141 to 149 and belonging to Pius, show that Rufinus and Quadratus were consuls in the year 142 and marked the beginning of Pius’s pontificate, following the end of Hyginus’s pontificate marked by the consulship of Priscinus and Severus in the year 141. The final consuls closing Pius’s eight-year period in 149 were Orfitus and Priscus. The second catalogue and the Librarian transferred the former pair into the summary of Hyginus, perhaps because in that same year either Hoenius Severus or Orfitus was a suffect consul with Priscinus as colleague. See Gruter, CLXXXII, 4. The periods of these four pontiffs must therefore be arranged as follows.

Hyginus, after the martyrdom of Telesphorus on January 5, held the Roman see from the consulship of Camerinus and Niger in the year of Christ 138 [Col. 1195C] until the consulship of Severus and Priscinus—or Orfitus and Priscinus—in the year 141, for four years.

Pius, from the beginning of the following consulship of Rufinus and Quadratus—for which Rufinus and Praesens of the year 153 were wrongly taken by the copyists to fill a lacuna in the Liberian Catalogue—celebrated his first Easter in the year of Christ 142. He continued in the see until the consulship of Orfitus and Priscus, wrongly transferred to Hyginus’s summary, in the year 149, claiming eight years for himself.

Anicetus, beginning with the consulship of Gallicanus and Vetus, correctly assigned to him in the older catalogue of the Caesarean exemplar apud Schelestratius, page 414, from the year 150, reached the consulship of the two Augusti in the era of Christ 161. The copyists wrongly transferred these consuls to mark the end of Pius’s pontificate, while audaciously attempting to fill the lacuna in the Liberian Catalogue; suppressing Anicetus, they assigned the entire twenty-year period to Pius.

Thus Anicetus receives his eleven years.

[Col. 1195D] Soter, beginning with the consulship of Rusticus and Aquilinus, correctly attributed to him both in the catalogues and by the Librarian and the other manuscripts in the year 162, remained in office until the consulship of Cethegus and Clarus, correctly assigned to him in the full year 170. Thus he completes the eight years of his rule, consistently attributed to him in the pictures, catalogues, and manuscripts.

With the years thus arranged and confirmed by the agreement of the documents, handed down to us from genuine Roman sources, I shall endeavor to elucidate Hyginus’s entire era, expressed with its months and days, in the following notes, which belong specifically to him in this section; I shall do the same in the following sections for each of his successors.

Whether one understands Hyginus’s martyrdom and death, or his burial in the tomb after the martyrdom had been completed on the preceding day, the registers of the Roman Church place it on January 11, in the year 142, as we have proved from the catalogues, when he had completed four years, three months, and eight days of his episcopate. [Col. 1196A] He had therefore been ordained bishop around the beginning of October in the year 137.

September 30 of that year fell on a Sunday. Therefore, if Telesphorus, being near martyrdom because of the persecution that had arisen—he was crowned on January 5 immediately afterward—judged, following the example of his predecessors, that a vicar should be chosen for him, and promoted Hyginus to the episcopate on that day, then the four years, three months, and eight days of Hyginus’s episcopate are rightly reckoned both in the pictures of St. Paul and in the catalogues and other ancient manuscripts of the Roman Church published above among the Prolegomena. That period comprised partly Hyginus’s service as Telesphorus’s vicar for three months and five days, and partly the period of his successor’s rule, after a brief vacancy of the see—four or seven days, according to the duration specified in the *Liber Pontificalis*—for four full years, less one or two days.

Hyginus’s episcopal ordination must therefore be assigned [Col. 1196B] to Sunday, September 30, in the year 137. His election to the Roman pontificate took place on January 10 or 13, 138. His installation on the apostolic throne took place on Sunday, January 14 of the same year, 138. His death or burial occurred on January 11, 142, under the consulship of Rufinus and Quadratus—not Rufinus and Praesens, as the copyists erroneously transcribed from the lacunae of the Liberian Catalogue, and from there into the Librarian’s book under Anicetus. These consuls must rightly be assigned to his successor Pius, elected after Hyginus’s death, since in that same year Pius himself celebrated the first Easter of his pontificate under the same consuls, on April 24, as we have gathered from the documents explained thus far.

From the same documents cited up to this point, I believe that the chronology of Hyginus and his three successors can be regarded as sufficiently established. Nevertheless, we must answer the arguments of those who disagree with us and who, knowing that many writers experienced considerable difficulty in establishing these dates, demand that we examine [Col. 1196C] the testimonies and considerations by which, they assert, they are compelled to adopt a Chronotaxis very different from ours.

Accordingly, Pearsonius and Dodwell, in chapter 8 of their dissertation on the years of the early Roman bishops, professed to restore Hyginus’s era, which has been variously disturbed by chronologists and historians of great reputation, on the basis of Tertullian. Yet although these authors brought no slight assistance to chronological matters in other works, here they are insufficiently consistent with one another and, in my judgment, do not successfully interpret Tertullian. They entangle the chronology in new errors while attempting to free it from the mistakes of others, especially when they follow that Alexandrian Eutychius whom the most learned men have judged to be a writer of no authority.

Among the errors added to those already mentioned I shall certainly include Pearsonius’s assertion, written in number 11 of the dissertation cited:

> “We have seen Telesphorus crowned with martyrdom in the year of the Lord 122. Others say 152. An enormous difference! [Col. 1196D] We declare our opinion to be true and theirs utterly false.”

I likewise consider erroneous another assertion of his at the beginning of chapter 12, where he arranges Hyginus’s dates from his Eutychius as follows:

> “In the sixth year of Hadrian’s reign Eugenius, or Hyginus, was appointed Roman patriarch; after sitting for four years, he died, says Eutychius. He therefore held office from the year of the Lord 122, under the consulship of Agricola and Pansa, until the year of the Lord 126, under the consulship of Verus and Ambiguus. These things seem to me most consistent with the truth and best suited to a correct understanding of the ancient history of the Church.”

Thus Pearsonius. I shall not dwell greatly on the calculations and assertion of Eutychius, whom he follows and whose authority is minimal or nonexistent, as I have already stated. Rather, I greatly value the testimonies of Tertullian, Irenaeus, Cyprian, Jerome, and Epiphanius cited in Pearsonius’s dissertation. Yet I must demonstrate that these testimonies do not support Pearsonius’s opinion, but rather confirm ours and oppose his, [Col. 1197A] agreeing exactly with the calculations of the Chronotaxis that we have set forth from the genuine documents of the Roman Church.

The passage of Tertullian that Pearsonius cites and interprets in defense of the Eutychian chronology and his own—though Dodwell explains and applies it somewhat differently—comes from his account of the origins of the sects of Valentinus, Cerdo, and Marcion, carefully recorded by the ancient Fathers, who were concerned to make clear the character of novelty proper to heresies by establishing the date of their origin.

Tertullian therefore describes the late birth of Marcion’s heresy against the evangelical doctrines in this way, in book I, chapter 19, *Against Marcion*:

> “In the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar, Jesus was pleased to pour forth from heaven the saving Spirit. As for Marcion’s salvation—such as he himself willed it—I have not cared to investigate in what year the dog-star breeze breathed forth from his Pontus. Yet this is certain: he is an Antoninian heretic, impious under Pius. [Col. 1197B] From Tiberius to Antoninus there are approximately 115 years, with half a year and half a month; they place an equal span of time between Christ and Marcion.”

Before Tertullian’s words, Pearsonius set forth the testimonies of Irenaeus and the other Fathers mentioned above, which place the heresies of Valentinus and Cerdo—from whom Marcion drew his own—under Hyginus. Irenaeus, book III, chapter 3 of *Against Heresies*, with Eusebius also noting the point, says:

> “Valentinus came to Rome under Hyginus. Cerdo too, who preceded Marcion, was there under Hyginus.”

Epiphanius, in his *Anacephalaeosis*, concerning Cerdo:

> “He went from Syria to Rome and expounded his doctrine during the time of Hyginus.”

St. Jerome:

> “Under Hyginus, bishop of the city of Rome, Valentinus the heresiarch and Cerdo, the teacher of Marcion, came to Rome.”

St. Cyprian:

> “His teacher Cerdo came to Rome under Hyginus, then bishop, who was the ninth in the city.”

Epiphanius, *Heresy* 42, concerning Marcion:

> “He fled from that same city, Sinope, and went to Rome itself after the death of Hyginus, the Roman bishop.”

And *Heresy* 41, [Col. 1197C] concerning Cerdo:

> “This Cerdo therefore existed in the time of Hyginus, the bishop who held the ninth place in succession from James, Peter, and Paul the apostles.”

Again, from the same Epiphanius, *Heresy* 42, no. 1, Dodwell asserts that during that vacancy of the Roman see which followed Hyginus’s death, Marcion sought not merely communion with the Roman Church but the pontificate itself—τὴν προεδρίαν, “the presidency.” Having been disappointed in both hopes, he then threatened to introduce an everlasting schism when Pius was elected as Hyginus’s successor.

From these testimonies, which Pearsonius produces on behalf of his own position, I therefore affirm that our chronology is established and Pearsonius’s overturned.

Tertullian used the reckoning of 115 years from the fifteenth year of Tiberius to the beginning of Antoninus Pius to demonstrate the late origin of Marcion’s pseudo-gospel, which exhaled its canine breeze from Pontus after that many years had elapsed from the time when the saving Spirit [Col. 1197D] had flowed down from heaven—the Spirit who, at the baptism of Christ the Lord, marked the beginning of his preaching and manifestation in the fifteenth year of Tiberius, as the evangelist Luke testifies.

It is clear that this year corresponds, in our chronology, to the twenty-fifth year of the common Christian era. For I showed in the fourth treatise of the Prolegomena that the year of the Lord’s Passion, under the consulship of the two Gemini, three full years after Christ’s baptism, fell in the year that we count as the twenty-eighth of the common era and the thirty-third of our Redeemer’s age. His birth must be placed five years before the common reckoning, as learned men today agree from the documents produced there, especially since the most eminent Cardinal Norisius explained the coin of Herod the tetrarch preserved at Marseille in the Rigordian Museum and demonstrated that Tiberius’s proconsular authority must be reckoned three years before he succeeded Augustus upon the latter’s death.

Above, in the Prolegomena, we saw that this agrees, through the solar eclipse reported by Dio and corresponding to the astronomical tables, [Col. 1198A] with the thirteenth year of the common Christian era. Tiberius’s proconsular authority must therefore begin in the tenth year of the common era, three years before Augustus’s death. His fifteenth year consequently corresponds to the twenty-fifth year of the Christian era.

If the 115 years mentioned by Tertullian are then counted from Tiberius’s fifteenth year to Antoninus Pius, including both endpoints, the result is the year 139 of the common era. At its beginning, on the Kalends of January, Antoninus, surnamed Pius, was counting the first year of his reign, which had not yet been completed. He had been adopted by Hadrian on February 25 of the year 138, under the consulship of Camerinus and Niger, and succeeded him after four and a half months from that adoption, namely on July 10, under the same consuls.

Thus Tertullian was not counting a full 116 years from that point in Tiberius’s reign to Antoninus, but approximately 115 years and six and a half months. Since he asserts that an equal period elapsed, according to the judgment of all contemporaries, between Christ and Marcion—[Col. 1198B] whom Epiphanius reports to have come to Rome after Hyginus’s death, while the see was still vacant, and to have sought the apostolic chair, according to Dodwell’s interpretation—the period agrees entirely with our pontifical chronology. We place Hyginus’s death at the beginning of the year 142, under the consulship of Rufinus and Quadratus. That year, when it began, completed 116 years after the twenty-fifth year of the common era, namely after the baptism, preaching, and manifestation of Christ the Lord. His crucifixion, corresponding to the twenty-eighth year of the common era and the consulship of the two Gemini, appropriately preceded it by three years.

In Pearsonius’s chronology, however, which moves Hyginus’s death back to the year 122, Tertullian’s total does not fit; it is shortened by a full twenty years unless the words of Septimius are violently distorted. Those words indicate that the endpoint of the reckoning from Christ is the fifteenth year of Tiberius—which establishes the era of the Gospel—to the tenth year of the age of Christ the Lord, the fifth year of the common era. Yet it is certain that this year is not even named in the same book of Tertullian, nor does it have anything in common [Col. 1198C] with either the first or the fifteenth year of Tiberius.

## Historical Notes on the Life of St. Hyginus

**Line 4.—“He organized the clergy and distributed the grades.”** In explaining this text of the Librarian, whose brevity involves some obscurity, most authors have been content merely to observe in general terms that ecclesiastical orders were distinct even in the apostolic age and that each grade had been established. They nevertheless suppose that Hyginus added something to clarify the earlier distinction and the grades of the orders.

But when we attend to the force of the words used by the Librarian, who here and elsewhere mentions that grades were distributed and that the clergy was organized, St. Basil provides a guiding light in his letter to Amphilochius, canon 51, carefully observed by Morinus, *On Sacred Ordinations*, part III, exercise 14, chapter 2, no. 4. From this we may distinguish that Hyginus conferred and distributed to clerics already ordained through the customary institution of the sacrament handed down by Christ the Lord to the apostles [Col. 1198D] certain offices more suitably entrusted to clerics than to the other faithful; these are signified here by the name “grades.”

St. Basil, says Morinus in the place cited, establishes three classes of clerics in canon 51 of his letter to Amphilochius. First are those who are in a grade; then there are two classes of those who are in a ministry, because ministry is twofold. The first is conferred through the laying on of hands; the second is conferred without the laying on of hands.

The canon reads:

> “What has been established against clerics, the canons have promulgated in general terms, ordering that one punishment be decreed for those who have fallen away, namely removal from ministry, whether they happen to be in a grade or persist even in a ministry that is conferred without the laying on of hands: εἴτε ἐν βαθμῷ τυγχάνοιεν, εἴτε καὶ ἀχειροτονήτῳ ὑπερεσίᾳ προσκαρτεροῖεν.”

The same distinction, and something more, can be gathered from canon 2 of the Council of Chalcedon:

> “If any bishop,” and so forth.

Here again you see two things distinguished according to the usage of that period: to ordain, χειροτονεῖν, and ordination, [Col. 1199A] χειροτονία; and to promote, προβάλλεσθαι, and promotion, προβολή.

A bishop, presbyter, and others are χειροτονεῖσθαι, “to be ordained”; but a defensor, an economus, and a paramonarius are distinguished as being promoted. Again, in the same canon the two groups are distinguished, although both are called χειροτονούμενοι, “ordained”—that is, ordained ἐκ τῆς χειροτονίας ἢ προβολῆς, “by ordination or promotion.”

Finally, both groups are subject to the canon, or enrolled in the register of the Church. For this is what it means to be “in the clergy” or “of the clergy,” as can be seen in canon 17 of Nicaea: “Many who are enrolled in the canon,” that is, who are in the clergy; and shortly afterward, “let him be deposed from the clergy and be a stranger to the canon,” which can be said only of clerics.

Therefore, when the Council of Chalcedon says that the defensor, economus, and others are “in the canon,” it thereby enrolls them among the clerics. But they belong to those “who,” as St. Basil says, “receive a ministry conferred without the laying on of hands.”

I judged that Morinus’s entire passage should be transcribed, so that it might become clearer that, besides the powers of the greater and lesser orders, established from the beginning of the Church by Christ the Lord with a sacrament and conferred through definite signs that impart grace for the holy performance of those parts of priestly office that properly constitute the clergy—those called into the Lord’s lot and set apart from others by the imprint of a character—Saints Fathers and councils also recognized other offices, more appropriately entrusted to clerics than to laymen. These offices were not to be conferred through a sacrament, or through that ordination which the Greeks call χειροτονία, and therefore did not in themselves confer grace; rather, they merely assigned a person to a particular ministry, established for the Church’s benefit by order of the bishop or of whoever had authority, namely a man who, through obtaining that office, was enrolled in the Church’s register and counted as belonging to the clergy in the broad sense. In every other respect, the office and ministry were more properly and fittingly conferred upon a man who had already received grace through the sacrament of orders and had had a character impressed upon his soul.

Among these offices of human deputation, distinct from the ministries connected by divine law with the character and seal of the sacramental order conferred upon clerics, Morinus lists from the Council of Chalcedon the defenders of the Church, the steward, and the paramonary. Many other offices and ministries may be added, enumerated by the same Morinus in *The List of Dignities, Offices, and Ministries of the Great Church of Constantinople*, in the same volume, pp. 208 and following: there one reads of the referendary, logothete, commentariensis, first defender, hieromnemon, monitor, teacher, visitor, prefects of ceremonies, and inspectors. Again, in *Exercise* 16, chapters 4 and 5, six principal officials called the exokatakoeloi are mentioned, namely: the great steward, the great sacellarius, the great keeper of the vessels, the chartophylax, the prefect of the sacellum, and the first defender.

Lest anyone think that all these offices were instituted later than Hyginus’s time, so that some of them could not be referred to his age, the authorities of the holy Fathers near the century of Hyginus, indicating some of these offices, should be read in Thomassinus, *On Benefices*, part I, book II, chapters 30 and 34. Saint Cyprian, book III, letter 22, mentions teachers of the hearers. Epiphanius mentions interpreters of languages, both in readings and in sermons. Singers, architects, laborers, custodians of the sacred vestibules, notaries, and custodians of the martyrs’ shrines are frequently read of in the Acts of the martyrs and of the councils.

To these must be added the greater offices, usually entrusted to those initiated into the presbyterate, diaconate, and subdiaconate, such as the ministry of the vicar, or first defender, or archdeacon—not merely for offering the sacrifice or ministering to the celebrant, which belongs to the order, but also for keeping others in the performance of their duties, guarding the Church’s treasury, making charitable distributions, and caring for the sacred furnishings and ecclesiastical patrimony. That this care was necessarily entrusted by the pontiff, about this period of the first and second centuries after Christ, to men distinguished by faith and diligence and marked with the diaconal order, is proved by those distributions sent by the Roman Church—from its very beginnings, indeed—to the many churches established in each city, to needy believers even abroad, to those living far away, and to those condemned to the mines. Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, mentions them in his letter to Pope Soter and the Romans, preserved by Eusebius, book IV, chapter 23:

> “For this has been your custom from the very beginning of the faith: to benefit all the brethren in various ways and to send the necessities of life to very many churches established in each city. In this way you both relieve the poverty of the needy and supply what is necessary to the brethren who labor in the mines. Through these gifts, which you have been accustomed to send from the beginning, you Romans preserve the custom and institution received from your ancestors. Blessed Bishop Soter not only maintained this custom but also increased it: both by abundantly supplying gifts destined for the saints and by consoling with gracious words the brethren who came from abroad, as the most loving father consoles his own children.”

Everyone understands that it was quite impossible accurately to procure, safeguard, distribute, and transmit all these expenses and donations, assigned to so many churches, so many cities, and so many different works, without accountants, custodians, treasurers, and record-keepers. Deacons were generally assigned to direct these officials and keep them to their duties, and one of them was chosen as president so that he could later report to the bishop what he and the others had accomplished and what accounts they had rendered.

We have seen notaries assigned throughout each region to write the Acts of the martyrs, beginning with Clement himself, the disciple of Peter. Fabian assigned seven subdeacons to collect these materials in full, no. 21, and ordered them to supervise the notaries. Shortly before this, Anterus, no. 20, had carefully investigated and deposited in the Church the records of the martyrs. Thus the offices of the scriniarius and chartophylax had already been instituted above the ministry of the notaries.

There must also have been superintendents of construction at the titular churches and cemeteries, from the time when Evaristus divided the titular churches and Pius dedicated them, and from the time when Anacletus, while still a presbyter, built cemeteries and memorials of the martyrs in the Vatican, no. 5, and when Alexander obtained a burial place on the Nomentan Way and Anicetus one on the Appian Way.

As for laborers and gravediggers, whose care for the burial of bodies we know was undertaken even by the pontiffs themselves, just as the apostles cared for Stephen, Fabian for Cornelius (who also ordered many structures to be built throughout the cemeteries, below, no. 21), Stephen for Tertullian, Marcellus for Cyriacus and his companions, Melchiades for Sebastian, and Eutychian alone buried 342 martyrs with his own hand (below, no. 28), I have no doubt that the superintendent was a presbyter. This follows both from the institution of Pope Dionysius, who divided the cemeteries among presbyters just as he did the titular churches, and from Eutychian’s order that the martyrs be buried wearing a dalmatic or purple colobium, with a report on the matter being made to him. It is also supported by the learned notes of the distinguished Bencinius above, no. 5, pp. 62 and following, concerning *Presbyters of the Martyrs*.

These offices, exercised from the beginning of the Roman Church in the distribution of alms, the care of sacred things, hospitality, the archive, the library, letters, *formatae*, construction, cemeteries, and titular churches, necessarily required heads of ministries and masters of offices. Since they were usually taken from the clergy, we say that the Librarian announces them by the designation of their grades.

Nor, from the age of Hyginus onward, do examples and indications of that ordered division of offices ever fail; it was handed down to later generations. Lucius entrusted the prefecture of the sacred patrimony, treasury, and charitable distributions to his deacon Stephen, no. 23; Stephen entrusted it to Sixtus, no. 24; and Sixtus to Laurence, no. 25.

The offices of chartophylax and librarian, or scriniarius, as well as those of secretary and chancellor—called *logothete* by the Greeks—under different names but with the same or nearly the same functions as those which the interpreters had performed for Peter, and the distributors and administrators of the *formatae* for his successors, were retained by subsequent ages. Like the other offices later celebrated in the Roman Order and frequently occurring in the *Book of the Pontiffs*, they are found generally entrusted to clerics.

The office of sacellarius was entrusted by Pope Sergius to Gregory II, then a subdeacon, together with the care of the library, below, no. 77. In no. 71, besides bishops, presbyters, and deacons, several ministers of offices are shown who were customarily admitted to the pontiff’s retinue. The grades named there should also be noted, so that the meaning of the word may be sufficiently clear.

For, describing the journey of Pope Constantine as he set out from Rome for the royal city with a solemn retinue, the Librarian says:

> “There followed him Nicetas, bishop of Silva Candida; Gregory, bishop of Portus; Michael; Paul; George, presbyter; George, deacon; George, *secundicerius*; John, first defender; Cosmas, sacellarius; Sisinnius, nomenclator; Sergius, scriniarius; Dorotheus and Julian, subdeacons; and a few clerics from the other grades of the Church.”

It is therefore clear that among the grades of the Church—that is, among the offices and ministries customarily entrusted to clerics—were counted those higher and greater offices, as well as those immediately below them, such as notaries, chamberlains, and similar positions of considerable dignity. Pontiffs sometimes selected men distinguished by these same offices to undertake royal embassies. Thus, no. 294, Adrian II sent to King Desiderius his envoys Stephen, regional notary and sacellarius, and Paul, chamberlain.

I would not deny that most of the names of the heads of these offices were employed later, after the Church received peace from Constantine and the supreme pontiff and Roman clergy received very extensive gifts, by which support and sustenance could be provided to the individual men exercising these offices in a manner suited to the enlarged ministry. Nevertheless, just as it was necessary to provide the services mentioned above for the administration of the Church’s affairs in every age before Constantine, so there could never have been lacking some ordered succession of offices among those who were available to the Roman pontiff. From this there would be grades even in that ministry which, according to Basil’s distinction, is not conferred by the laying on of hands but entrusted to already ordained clerics and established to relieve the bishop in the care of the sacred patrimony, letters, library, construction, hospitality, and similar concerns, distinct from the priestly ministry of the altar.

The arrangement of these grades is referred to the time of Hyginus, since his predecessors had prepared suitable material for establishing heads of several offices. In the age of Clement and Anacletus, the institution of the notaries and the canon of the sacred books were scarcely being completed, and only the beginnings of an archive and library were appearing. Sixtus’s institution concerning *formatae* to be obtained from the Apostolic See required the appointment and diligent work of a scriniarius. Pius’s generosity toward a titular church he had dedicated, to which he is said to have offered many gifts, no. 11—and likewise toward the other twenty-five titular churches divided by Evaristus—and the increased offerings of the faithful under Alexander, when a large part of the Roman nobility had been converted to the faith, required that a prefect be appointed over the Church’s treasury and sacred distributions, such as Leo the Great identified Laurence as being when he called him “the superintendent of the treasury, who presided not only over the ministry of the sacraments but also over the administration of ecclesiastical property” (*Sermon on the Nativity of Saint Laurence*).

Thus, even before Constantine, there were grades of offices distributed among clerics. By virtue of these, some presided over the administration of temporal goods outside the altar, while at the altar they held another grade and presided over the ministry of the sacraments.

That this discipline was not interrupted in the Roman Church but faithfully preserved and more clearly explained during the tranquillity of peace which, obtained for her by God through Constantine, she enjoys, is shown clearly by past centuries in the books of the Roman Order. Our own age places it before our eyes in the presence of the pontifical throne, in the assembly of the sacred senate, and in the retinue and attendants who sit at the grades of the throne, especially while the pontiff performs the sacred rites.

In the ministry of the sacraments, according to the grades instituted by Christ the Lord, bishops, presbyters, deacons, and the other ministers of the Levitical office, initiated into the greater or lesser orders, take precedence. In this fully completed hierarchy of sacred order, there also stand out grades of ministries naturally distinct from the priestly office but suitably adapted and distributed by the pontiffs among the colleges of this clergy.

For the offices of chancellor, chamberlain, signator, librarian, treasurer, and prefects assigned to sacred revenues are observed among the leaders of the ecclesiastical hierarchy. We also see judges of more serious cases, masters of petitions and letters, and administrators of the sacred patrimony chosen from the clergy, while sacellani and acolytes serve in the celebration of the sacred rites.

Thus, to the grades of the order, given their integrity by Christ the Lord through the institution of the sacrament—which the addition of clergy to other ministries and offices, related in purpose to piety but different in authority, neither adds to nor subtracts from—are joined the grades distributed by Hyginus and conferred upon the clergy, including by his successors.

[Note: [Col. 1202B]

Line 4.—“He organized the clergy and distributed the grades.” Saint Hyginus, as soon as he was appointed pontiff, prudently distributed and distinguished the orders of the clergy by grades, so that in each titular church, or presbytery, some cardinals and some subordinate to the cardinals might minister to the faithful whenever circumstances required it. Concerning the origin of the cardinals, see the same Ciacconius under Hyginus, where he treats the matter more fully.]

[Note: [Col. 1202B]

Line 4.—“He organized the clergy and distributed the grades.” Baronius thinks this should be understood as follows: since those matters belonging to the ecclesiastical hierarchy had already been organized from the time of the apostles, it is reasonable to suppose that Hyginus added only certain elements to the ancient form, or brought the same form into clearer expression.

While Hyginus was seated on the pontifical throne, the heresiarchs Valentinus and Cerdo went to Rome and stirred up great disturbances among the faithful. Marcion, another heresiarch, a Pontic, after being expelled from the Church for incest, went to Rome only after Hyginus had died, as may be gathered from Irenaeus, book I, chapter 28, and Epiphanius, *Heresy* 42, chapter 1. Therefore, since Hyginus passed to the heavenly homeland in the year of Christ 141, on January 10, after having occupied the see for only four years, Marcion’s arrival in Rome must likewise be placed in that year, during the interpontificate.

Philastrius, however, in his *Book on Heresies*, chapter 46, writes that Marcion first taught his errors in Asia and was there refuted by the disciples of the apostle John rather than by John himself, and then came to Rome. But when, during the vacancy of the see, he could not even obtain admission to the Church from the presbyters who, as was customary, were administering it, he returned to Pontus. With greater audacity, he then began to pursue those same errors more vehemently. On these matters Natalis Alexander should be read in his treatment of the second century, where he also discusses the heresies of Valentinus and Cerdo.]

[Col. 1185]

10

Hyginus, a Greek by nationality and formerly a philosopher from Athens, whose genealogy is not found, occupied the see for four years, three months, and eight days [Note: [Col. 1185] A: four years, less two days]. He lived in the times of Verus and Marcus, from the consulship of Magnus and Camerinus to that of Orfitus and Priscus [Note: [Col. 1185] Antoninus Pius, from the consulship of Glabrio and Verianus to that of Silvanus and Augurinus. C: to Orphitus]. He organized the clergy and [Note: [Col. 1185] See Baronius, year 158] distributed the grades. He held three ordinations in the month of December: fifteen presbyters, five deacons, and seven bishops in various places [Note: [Col. 1185] CB: six]. He was also buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican, on the third day before the Ides of January, and the episcopate remained vacant for three days.

[Col. 1187] CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS

From the edition of Bucherius.

Hyginus: twelve years, three months, and six days. He lived in the times of Verus, from the consulship of Gallicanus and Vetus to that of Praesens and Rufinus.

The same from the edition of Schelestratius, corrected against the Caesarean manuscript, etc.

Hyginus: twelve years, three months, and six days. He lived in the times [lacuna].

Notes of Schelestratius on the Liberian Catalogue.

Lacunae are found in the Caesarean manuscript at Hyginus and Anicetus; they can nevertheless be supplied from the second catalogue, since in the time of its author they still existed in the manuscript from which the notices of emperors and consulships may be collected.

Blanchini’s notice on the same Liberian Catalogue and the lacunae indicated in it.

The learned editors of the Liberian Catalogue, Bucherius and Schelestratius, observe that frequent lacunae are found in the same catalogue from Hyginus to Callistus. Schelestratius notes that they can be supplied from the second catalogue, which he appended in his edition and which belongs to the age of Felix IV and Justinian.

In my judgment, however, they are supplied much more successfully both from these monuments and from several passages presented above among the Prolegomena. Bucherius indicated only the signs of the lacunae in the margin; Schelestratius inserted more material in the text itself. To avoid uselessly repeating what has already been printed above in the Prolegomena according to Bucherius’s example, I shall give the position of the lacunae in the context and their supplementation according to my judgment.

The reader will find the proofs of this supplementation below in our chronological notes on Anicetus, section XII. What I shall here add concerning the supplementation of the lacunae in the Liberian Catalogue under Hyginus, I shall also provide for the succeeding pontiffs down to Callistus. Once the lacunae cease, there will be no occasion to supplement the text of the Liberian Catalogue.

Reading of the Catalogue that supplements the Liberian Catalogue and its lacunae, based on the proofs given below in Blanchini’s chronological notes on Anicetus.

Hyginus: four years, three months, and eight days. He lived in the time of Antoninus, from the consulship of Magnus and Camerinus to that of Severus and Priscinus.

XI. SAINT ANICETUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 167, THE FIFTH YEAR OF MARCUS AURELIUS AND LUCIUS VERUS.

[Note: [Col. 1203A]

In Fabrottus, from the Freherian manuscript.

No. 11, line 2: B, 7; line 5: AB, 6; line 6: AB, 8; line 7: B, 19.

From the Royal, Mazarine, and Thuane manuscripts.

In the Royal and Mazarine manuscripts, Pius is placed before Anicetus. Line 1: “from the village of Humisia,” or eleven years, four months, three days. Line 2: Royal: “of Marcus and Severus”; Mazarine: “of Severus and Marcus.” Line 3: “to Rufinus and Priscus.” Here he established that the cleric should [lacuna]. Line 5: eighteen presbyters. Line 6: nine places. Line 7: “who was also crowned with martyrdom and buried in the cemetery” (the manuscript codices consistently have this reading), on the Kalends [or: the fifteenth day before the Kalends] of May. The Mazarine has the twentieth day before the Kalends of May; and the episcopate remained vacant for seventeen days.

From another Thuane manuscript.
