Line 1: Vatican and first Florentine: “Humisa.” Line 2: two Florentine manuscripts: eleven years, four months. Line 4: Cassinese and Florentine: “may nourish.” Line 5: two Florentine manuscripts, Vatican and Cassinese: nineteen presbyters, twelve bishops. Line 7: two Florentine manuscripts, Cassinese and Vatican: seventeen days.]

[Note: [Col. 1203A]

The twelfth Anicetus. From this number, the twelfth of the pontificate, it is clear that the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* placed Pius before Anicetus. For since he makes Hyginus the tenth and Anicetus the twelfth, Pius must have intervened in the ancient codices of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, as Lucas Holstenius attests when he notes: “In the Florentine manuscripts Pius is placed here, and Anicetus follows him.” The same is true of the codex of the Queen of Sweden. It is also noted that in the body of the Byzantine History, after the Lives of the Pontiffs by Anastasius, Pius is placed before Anicetus in the Royal and Mazarine codices.]

[Note: [Col. 1203B]

Line 3.—“He established that the clergy should not grow their hair, according to the Apostle’s command.” The decree of Anicetus is that clerics should not grow their hair, but should shave the top of the head in the shape of a sphere, canon *Prohibere*, distinction 23. From the ancient custom of the Church, clerics were tonsured in the form of a crown.

Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, book IV, chapter 1, writes concerning Theodore, who was ordained by Pope Vitalian and sent to Britain to preach the Gospel:

> “After he had been ordained subdeacon, he waited four months until his crown had grown, so that he could be tonsured in the form of a crown; for he had worn the tonsure, according to the custom of the Easterners, of the holy apostle Paul.”

Nicetius, bishop of Trier, is said to have had a natural crown, with his hair rising in its proper order in a circle. Gregory of Tours, *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17:

> “Accordingly, the holy bishop Nicetius was marked out as a cleric from the very time of his birth. For when he had been brought forth from the womb, his entire head, as is customary with newborn infants, was seen to be bare of hair; but around it there appeared a row of short hairs, so that you might think that the cleric’s crown had been marked out by them.”]

[Note: [Col. 1205A]

(EX BIN.) Line 1.—“Anicetus.” Those who thought that Anicetus should be placed before Pius are most effectively refuted by the testimony of Hegesippus and Irenaeus.

(EX LAB.) Line 4.—“According to the Apostle’s command.” These words are absent from C and H.]

[Note: [Col. 1205A]

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

What must be said concerning the time of Anicetus is known to be so closely connected with the chronology of Pius—especially since their positions were exchanged with one another in certain catalogues and codices of Anastasius—that the examination and observations concerning the epoch of both pontiffs can by no means be separated. Accordingly, what I shall say here under the number of Anicetus, and what I shall reserve for the number of Pius, should be considered to belong to both. Likewise, most of what was set forth above concerning Hyginus is common to both.

The central point of all these observations was that frequent lacunae occur in the text of the Liberian Catalogue according to the codices seen by Cuspinianus and Bucherius. These lacunae, indicated in the margin of Bucherius’s edition from Hyginus to Callistus, I propose to supply here as accurately as possible, so that the supplements correspond exactly both to the style of the catalogue’s author and to the spaces of the lacunae, and especially to the most carefully corrected chronological calculations based on the names of the Caesars and consuls mentioned in the same catalogue.

That there are quite a few lacunae from Hyginus to Callistus is demonstrated both by the suppression of three pontiffs included among them—Anicetus, Eleutherus, and Zephyrinus—which Bucherius noted in the margin of his edition, as we published it at the beginning of the Prolegomena, and by the later edition of Schelestratius, collated with another copy of the Caesarean manuscript.

That the catalogue is complete both before Hyginus and after Callistus is established by the sufficiently exact calculations of the chronology that can be extracted from it by the following method. From Linus to Hyginus, the catalogue counts, beginning with the last consulships of Linus, Capito and Rufus, to the last consulships of Telesphorus, Aelius Caesar II and Balbinus, whose successor was Hyginus, seventy years, six months, and twenty-two days, omitting the period during which the see was vacant.

The years of Clement were nine, two months, and twelve days; of Cletus, six years, two months, and ten days; of Anacletus, twelve years, ten months, and three days; of Evaristus, thirteen years, seven months, and two days; of Alexander, seven years, two months, and one day; of Sixtus, ten years, three months, and twenty-one days; and of Telesphorus, eleven years, three months, and three days. The total is seventy years, six months, and twenty-two days, which corresponds quite closely to the calculations of consular chronology, in which Capito and Rufus are shown to belong to the year 67 of the common Christian era.

If the seventy years collected in this sum are added to that year, the year 137 results, marked by the consulships of Niger and Camerinus. These immediately follow the consulships of Caesar II and Balbinus in the year 137. The surplus year is distributed among the months of an acting administration, compensated by the months and days during which the see was vacant; together they produce this total of time with sufficient approximation.

There is a similar correspondence between the years and epochs from Callistus to Caius, for approximately seventy years, likewise agreeing with consular chronology. This is faithfully collected in the catalogue from the twelve pontifical epochs, as follows: from the first consulships assigned to Callistus, Antoninus and Adventus, which belong to the year of Christ 218, to the last consulships of Eutychianus, Carinus II and Carus, belonging to the year of Christ 283.

Callistus: five years, two months, ten days; Urbanus: eight years, eleven months, twelve days; Pontianus: five years, two months, seven days; Anterus: one month, ten days; Fabianus: fourteen years, one month, ten days; Cornelius: two years, three months, ten days; Lucius: three years, eight months, ten days; Stephen: four years, two months, twenty-one days; Sixtus: two years, eleven months, six days; Dionysius: eight years, two months, four days; Felix: five years, eleven months, twenty-five days; Eutychianus: eight years, eleven months, three days.

The total is sixty-nine years, nine months, and eight days. If seventy years are counted from the year 218, including the endpoints, the year 287 results. The four years by which this total exceeds the consulship of Carinus II and Carus in the year of Christ 283 are assigned to several months of interregnal administration repeated in the epoch of the preceding pontiff. If these are subtracted, pontifical and consular chronology correspond quite closely from Callistus to Eutychianus.

But the total gathered from the epochs of the catalogue from Hyginus to Soter differs from consular chronology by twenty-nine years, although only four of the pontiffs in the catalogue are included: Hyginus, twelve years, three months, six days; Pius, twenty years, four months, twenty-one days; Soter, nine years, three months, two days; Victor, nine years, two months, ten days.

The total is fifty-one years, one month, and nine days. Since it begins with the consulships of Niger and Camerinus in the year of Christ 138, the first assigned to Hyginus, and reaches the consulships of Antoninus III and Adventus, the first assigned to the pontificate of Callistus, which immediately followed that of Victor and belongs to the year of Christ 218, it ought to have filled a period of eighty years. It therefore falls short by a full twenty-nine years unless the lacunae are supplied from elsewhere more successfully.

It is therefore established, both from the suppression of three pontiffs and from the nearly full thirty-year deficit in the consular era when compared with the pontifical catalogue between Callistus and Eutychianus, that numerous lacunae exist in this part of the Liberian Catalogue.

Some ancient copyist of the same catalogue attempted to supply them, but he was very inexperienced both in history and in chronology. For if he had possessed even slight knowledge of either, he certainly would not have left such an enormous gap of twenty-nine years, nor would he have failed to recognize the three pontiffs who had to be restored in their proper places within the lacunae, as is shown by the surviving indications of the preceding and following verses in that part of the catalogue.

How easy it is to identify the lacunae at each place and restore the words belonging in each verse will become clear, as I hope, from a visual comparison of three readings of the same text of the Liberian Catalogue, which I arrange in as many columns. In the middle column I place the text of the Liberian Catalogue with the lacunae not yet supplied. In the column to the reader’s right I present the supplements to the lacunae once added and inserted into the text by that inexperienced copyist of a later age, whose sole surviving copy was preserved and published for us by Bucherius, and which we have already presented from him at the beginning of the Prolegomena. In the column occupying the left-hand position I present the supplements to the same lacunae which, in my judgment, must be restored to the text and to its genuine reading.

I can provide more than one witness for these supplements. The first will be the style of the catalogue’s author, who consistently observes this method from Linus to Urbanus: he appends to the name of each pontiff the years, months, and days of his episcopate; then expresses the names of the emperors who ruled the Roman state at the same time; and finally names the ordinary consuls who marked the first and last Easter seasons of that pontiff’s episcopate.

Apart from these matters, little is added from Linus to Pontianus, except in the case of Pius, where an addition drawn from the apocryphal book of the *Constitutions of Clement* was used to fill a lacuna. This will become evident to anyone who considers the space opened in the lacunae, which the ancient copyist supplies on the right and we supply on the left.

I shall give the remaining witnesses for our reading both from the paintings of the city’s basilicas and the catalogues copied from them, and from ancient catalogues and codices in which the consuls are named. Under each number from Hyginus to Pius, I shall mention in the notes the genuine documents that provide support for our supplement.

In this reading of the Liberian Catalogue, thus restored from Telesphorus to Callistus, where the lacunae were observed, I hope that both critics and chronologists will agree, since nearly every word corresponds to the words, and each verse to its respective verse. For the sake of clarity, the words of the supplements in both the first and third columns are displayed in slanted type, or, as they call it, italic type. What is printed in round letters the reader will find fortunately preserved in its proper place in the text of the catalogue occupying the second column, providing sufficiently clear evidence of the catalogue’s genuine reading.

[Col. 1207]

Critics will ask me why, in the case of Hyginus, I assert by way of example that that copyist, of an ancient yet later age, reconstructed from the lacuna which I suppose in the words of the third line and the following lines—“from the consulship of [lacuna]ni[lacuna]ve[lacuna]ino”—“from the consulship of Gallicanus and Vetus to that of Praesens and Rufinus.” I say that the occasion of the error lay in the selection of the later consuls, since the consul Rufinus’ name marked the beginning of the successor’s period. For he may have thought that the last consuls could rightly be assigned as the same men with whom the successor began his episcopate.

In the Liberian catalogue, after Hyginus’ section, there followed the section of Pius: “Pius, years, etc., in the time of Antoninus, from the consulship of Rufin[lacuna],” whose name was interrupted (as it appears) by a lacuna, removing the final two lines from the end of Pius’ section and as many from the beginning of Anicetus’. The copyist of the catalogue, turned from a transcriber into an abridger, when he found the name of the same Antoninus repeated at the end of the lacuna, from the two distinct sections of Pius and Anicetus forged one section and assigned it to Pius, extending it from the consulship of Rufinus, where Pius had in fact begun, to the consuls called “the two Augusti,” who occurred at the end of Anicetus’ section.

He did something similar in the case of Soter: he confused the worn-away consuls of the age of Antoninus with the consuls assigned to Pope Eleutherus—who was not visible because of the lacuna—under Antoninus and Commodus, when the name of Antoninus occurred [Col. 1208] in the words “in the time of Antoninus,” preserved in Soter’s section. He admitted something similar because of the worn-away line beginning the period of Zephyrinus, together with the preceding lines expressing the names of Victor’s consuls. For, joining the margins of the lacunae from the two distinct sections of Victor and Zephyrinus, he forged one section and assigned it to Victor, with the consuls of his successor, in the words: “from the consulship of Saturninus and Gallus to that of Praesens and Extricatus.”

These are the observations I wished to make in general concerning the lacunae found in the text within these eighty years—from the consulship of Aelius Caesar and Balbinus, in which Telesphorus ends in the year 137, to the consulship of Praesens and Extricatus, in which Zephyrinus ends in the year 217—which were incorrectly compressed into fifty-one years by the unskilled copyist of the catalogue. He nevertheless extended Hyginus’ pontificate to twelve years, contrary to the reckoning of the consular era which he assigns to him, from Gallicanus and Vetus, indicating the year of Christ 150, to Praesens and Rufinus, indicating the year of Christ 153. He also extended Pius’ see through a full twenty-year period, exceeding by a full five years the consular era which he himself assigned to him, from the consuls Clarus and Severus, belonging to the year 146, to the consuls “the two Augusti,” Marcus and Lucius, to be referred to the year of Christ 161.

Now I turn to the section of Anicetus, restored by us to its integrity [Col. 1209A], and to the proper discussion of this number, in order to demonstrate the foundations and appropriate evidence of our restoration. They are as follows.

**Line 1.—“Anicetus, eleven years, four months, three days.”** The surviving numbers, marked in Roman letters beneath his image in the paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul, give Anicetus eleven years, as does the catalogue of Felix IV, together with four months and three days, which have now fallen away from the aforementioned painting but are preserved in the catalogues and in the *Liber Pontificalis*. All the catalogues cited in the *Prolegomena* likewise assign four months, except one of the Italian catalogues and another of the manuscripts outside Italy which, subtracting one unit, expressed three months instead of four wherever the eleven years are found. Those eleven years are the indication of Anicetus’ period, even if his see is exchanged with that of Pius. Two Italian catalogues, those of Cava and Farfa, and several of the Colbertine manuscripts also count three days, agreeing with the catalogue of Felix IV and with the Anastasian text.

[Col. 1209B]

**Line 2.—“He was in the time of Antoninus Pius, from the consulship of Gallicanus and Vetus to that of the two Augusti.”** The catalogue of Felix IV takes the beginning of Anicetus from the consulship of Gallicanus and Vetus, in the year of Christ 150, just as the manuscripts of the *Liber Pontificalis* do. Therefore, if eleven complete years are counted—the number which we have already proved to be assigned to Anicetus in the paintings at Saint Paul and in the catalogues—the endpoint must fall in the consulship of the two Augusti in the year of Christ 161, correctly stated by the Liberian catalogue at the end of that section, which the copyist wrongly confused with the preceding one.

The Florentine manuscript, cited above in the *Prolegomena*, also supports this. There it displayed a catalogue of the bishops of Naples together with the Roman pontiffs and the emperors under whom each had held office, drawn from Paul the Deacon. There the time of Pope Pius is joined with Antoninus and with the beginning of the empire of his sons Marcus and Lucius; whereas the time of Anicetus, Soter, and Eleutherus is joined with Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, Lucius Verus, Commodus, Pertinax, [Col. 1209C] and Severus:

> “Marcus, the fourth bishop of the Neapolitans, held office for twenty-eight years. He was in the time of Hyginus and Pope Pius, and of the emperor Antoninus Pius and his sons. Probus, the fifth bishop of Naples, held office for twenty-four years. He was in the time of Anicetus, Soter, and Pope Eleutherus, and of Antoninus Verus, Lucius Commodus, Aelius Pertinax, or the emperor Severus.”

I mention this catalogue all the more willingly because it arranges the Roman pontiffs so clearly and therefore also restores them to their proper place and time in the lacuna of the Liberian catalogue, according to the order of succession, which is no less clearly asserted by Hegesippus and Irenaeus, who were present with those same pontiffs at Rome.

The total of eleven years, four months, and three days will be established if the beginning of the period is taken from the day of the ordination, Sunday, 15 December of the year 149, with the Sunday letter F—that is, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of January—which opened the year 150, when the consuls Gallicanus and Vetus entered office. For this reason they are marked at his beginning [Col. 1209D] by all the catalogues and manuscripts. The period must then be carried to 17 April of the year 161, when the two Augustan brothers, Marcus and Lucius, were consuls, a day renowned in the Church for his martyrdom. For, with both terminal days included, precisely the same total is obtained.

## HISTORICAL NOTES ON THE SAME SUBJECT

**Line 1.—“A Syrian, from the village of Omisa.”** He perhaps means a village near the city of Amisus, in the region of the Leucosyri, described by Arrian—or, more accurately, by the anonymous Greek author in the *Periplus of the Euxine Sea* among the ancient geographical writers, Oxford edition, vol. III, p. 9:

> “Amisus, a Greek city, a colony of the Athenians, situated by the sea in the region of the Leucosyri, and also a colony of the Phocaeans.”

The same source adds:

> “The river Halys, where it enters the sea, separates the lands and fields of the Sinopeans and Amisenians; but, flowing three hundred stadia distant from Amisus, between the Syrians and Paphlagonians [Col. 1210A], it empties into the Pontus.”

Accordingly, Anicetus could rightly be called a Syrian if he was born in this Pontic region, in a village near Amisus belonging to the Leucosyri, where the Halys separates the Syrians from the Paphlagonians.

From the same Pontic region the heresiarch Marcion had come to Rome, while the apostolic see was vacant after the death of Hyginus, from 11 January until 9 April, when Pius, his successor, was elected by the clergy and assumed the pontificate in the year 142, according to our notes on that number. Pagius assigned to the preceding year the martyrdom of Hyginus, the vacancy of the see, the election of Pius, and Marcion’s arrival.

Saint Epiphanius writes, as Pagius observes:

> “Marcion had first taught his errors in Asia, and there had been refuted by the disciples of the apostle John rather than by John himself; he then came to Rome. But when the see was vacant and the presbyters, who administered the Church according to custom, would not even grant him access to the Church, he returned to Pontus and, growing more presumptuous, began to pursue those same errors with greater vehemence.”

When Anicetus was governing the Church [Col. 1210B], he is inferred to have come again to the City, according to the account of Eusebius, book IV, chapter 14, perhaps presuming that he would find his fellow-countryman more indulgent. Yet he was wholly unable to overcome Anicetus’ unshaken constancy.

Eusebius reports that, during the same period of Anicetus, the blessed Polycarp, hearer of the evangelist John, came to Rome, as is attested by the letter of Irenaeus, because of a certain question that had arisen concerning Easter. The author of the Alexandrian Chronicle also gives the year of Polycarp’s arrival, under the consulship of Tertullus and Sacerdos, in the year of the Christian era 158.

What Polycarp accomplished in the City is taught us by the aforementioned letter of Irenaeus preserved in Eusebius, book IV, chapter 14:

> “In the time of Anicetus, Polycarp came to Rome and brought back to the Church of God many of the heretics mentioned above”—that is, Marcion’s followers.

A little later:

> “When Marcion himself once met Polycarp and said, ‘Recognize us,’ Polycarp is said to have replied, ‘I recognize you as the firstborn of Satan.’”

So religiously did the apostles [Col. 1210C] and their disciples beware of mingling, even in speech, with any of those who adulterated the truth. As Paul also said:

> “Avoid a heretical man after one or two admonitions, knowing that such a person is perverse and sins, being condemned by his own judgment.”

“So far Irenaeus,” says Eusebius.

These testimonies clearly prove that the Roman presbytery, while the see was vacant, and the pontiff Anicetus possessed the same constancy as Polycarp, since they excluded Marcion, obstinate in his heresy, from entrance into the Church and from the fellowship of Catholics.

The distinguished martyr Justin, likewise living at Rome during the same period, as Eusebius testifies in book IV, chapter 16, published books against Marcion. These were commended by Irenaeus, in chapter 18, and received equal praise from Hegesippus in Eusebius, chapter 22, where he touches upon the errors of the Marcionites as arising from the sects of the Jews. Against that same Marcion, Rhodon, a native of Asia but trained at Rome by Tatian [Col. 1210D], wrote several books, as Eusebius says in chapter 13, and fought with the others against Marcion’s heresy.

What Anicetus and Polycarp amicably discussed concerning the controversy over the Paschal rite is likewise recalled by Eusebius in book V, chapter 4, from Irenaeus’ letter to Victor:

> “When the most blessed Polycarp came to Rome in the time of Anicetus, and there was a slight disagreement between them concerning certain other matters, they immediately embraced one another with the kiss of peace, without contending greatly with one another about this question. Anicetus treated Polycarp with honor and, as a mark of respect, granted him the office of consecrating in the Church.”

Nevertheless, Anicetus did not fail to convoke a synod, which Saint Polycarp and ten other bishops attended, if we accept the synodical booklet produced by Pagius under number 3 concerning Anicetus. That synod defined that

> “the dread and saving passion of our Lord Jesus Christ should be mystically celebrated on the holy Parasceve, while the Resurrection, the source of life, should be performed [Col. 1211A] on the solemn and great Sunday.”

But because the distinguished man Henri Valois, in his notes on chapter 23 of book V of Eusebius, expresses some doubt concerning the author of this synodical booklet—whether Anicetus convened the synod or postponed it while awaiting Polycarp’s agreement after he had returned to Asia—it is certain that Anicetus openly replied to Polycarp that he must retain the custom of his predecessors.

Dodwell attempts to infer that this custom was instituted by Xystus, because Irenaeus’ letter mentions among Anicetus’ predecessors only Pius, Hyginus, Telesphorus, and Xystus as having ordered Sunday to be the Paschal day and not permitted their people to assign Easter to another day of the week.

The Romans had received this tradition from the apostle Peter, just as had the Churches of the patriarchates of Antioch and Alexandria and the Pontic Church, as is evident from the letters cited above.

In that letter of Irenaeus, however, the apostolic man could not have gone beyond [Col. 1211B] the age of Xystus in his enumeration, since Polycrates was alleging that John the evangelist had permitted Easter to be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the moon. The predecessors of Xystus could remember the apostle John, who had been at Rome under Domitian.

Moreover, if there was some permission granted by the apostle John, it must certainly be regarded as temporary, arising from the privilege granted to the apostles to postpone abolishing the practice of the legal observances even after the Council of Antioch had been celebrated, according as their prudence judged, in order to win the Jews—as Paul was permitted, for the same reason, to circumcise Timothy.

Therefore, since Irenaeus saw that Victor would have a ready objection—Victor whom he was trying to persuade to tolerate the Asian custom by the example of his predecessors—if he also enumerated those who could have seen the apostle John permitting it, he mentioned only Xystus and the pontiffs who followed him. Their example could not be overturned by the apostolic privilege of John the evangelist’s temporary permission, since John had already died before the pontificate of Xystus [Col. 1211C].

Against this inference, more strongly confined by Irenaeus even to the period of Xystus and his successors, Victor—like Anicetus, who made similar replies to Polycarp’s requests—showed that the contrary custom had been constantly observed by those same predecessors and that he too firmly intended to retain it, requiring its observance from all others who did not possess John’s privilege, which was granted only to apostles.

This is plainly the sense in which the contents of Irenaeus’ synodical letter must be understood, and in which the summary of the acts of the pontiffs mentioned there must be taken. The distinguished theologian Louis Bail, doctor of theology and pro-penitentiary of Paris, long ago saw this, together with the Venerable Bede. In volume II of his *Summa of the Councils*, p. 5, he writes concerning this passage:

> “In this matter I do not concern myself with Polycrates, who may have been driven by party zeal and who conspired with the Jews in celebrating Easter, against the admonition of the supreme shepherd of the Church, whom he ought to have obeyed. Nor does [Col. 1211D] the example of the blessed John excuse him, which he brought forward on his own behalf. For he, as Bede says in book III of the *History*, chapter 25, celebrated Easter on the fourteenth day in order to accommodate himself at the beginning to the Jews converted to the faith, just as the apostle Paul circumcised Timothy the bishop for the same reason. Nevertheless, the blessed Peter established at Rome that Easter should be celebrated on Sunday, and this institution ought to prevail.”

**Line 3.—“He established that the clergy should not grow their hair long, according to the command of the Apostle.”** Two things are asserted here. The first is Anicetus’ decree that the clergy should not grow their hair long; the second is the Apostle’s command, which enjoined the same thing.

The first appears to have been taken by the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* from the second catalogue. The source from which he derived the second assertion, concerning the Apostle’s command, raises a question.

Both assertions are wonderfully illuminated by what Cardinal Baronius learnedly collected from the Fathers under the year of Christ 58, numbers 122 and following, especially from Jerome, Isidore, and Germanus of Constantinople. He confirms there that [Col. 1212A] this custom was maintained not only by the example of Peter but also by Paul and the other apostles and men of the apostolic age. It was borrowed from the Nazirites, so that they might signify that they had embraced exclusively an institution of holier life and dedication to God. They joined to this another symbol, that of the crown, carefully described by Bede and Gregory of Tours; see Altaserra’s notes on this number.

This kind of tonsure is expressed in the most ancient images of the supreme pontiffs in the basilica of Saint Paul, a specimen of which may be found above, at the beginning of the notes, folio 1; likewise in the most ancient mosaics of the churches of the City and in the crypts of the martyrs. From these images Severano and Aringhi faithfully took the representation of the pontiff arranging the sacred veil on a virgin devoted to God, which I shall reproduce under Pope Pius in the next number of the historical notes.

These images and tonsures should be compared with Isidore’s text, cited by Baronius under the year 58, number 123:

> “As for the fact,” says Isidore, “that after [Col. 1212B] the upper part of the head has been shorn, a circular crown is left below, I believe that the priesthood and the kingdom of the Church are represented in this. For among the ancients the tiara was placed on the heads of priests. It was made of linen, rounded like half a sphere; and this was signified in the shorn part of the head. The crown, however, is the breadth of a golden circle that encircles the heads of kings. Thus both signs are expressed on the head of clerics, so that what is written may be fulfilled also through a certain likeness of the body, as the Apostle Peter teaches: ‘You are a holy race, a royal priesthood’ (1 Peter 2:9).
>
> “It is asked why, as among the ancient Nazirites, the hair is not first allowed to grow and then cut. But those who investigate these matters should observe what difference there is between that prophetic veil and this evangelical revelation, of which the Apostle says: ‘When you have turned to Christ, the veil will be removed.’ What the veil placed between the face of Moses and the sight of the children of Israel signified, the hair of the holy men signified in those times. For the Apostle [Col. 1212C] also says that hair is a veil. Therefore the heads of those consecrated to the Lord ought no longer to be veiled with hair, but only to be revealed, because what was hidden in the mystery of prophecy has now been declared in the Gospel.”

Thus far Isidore.

Isidore’s testimony agrees with what I cited above under Linus, number 2, concerning the decree about veiling women’s heads in church. That decree likewise proceeded from the apostles, as Paul’s letters demonstrate, to indicate their exclusion from the Christian priesthood, which Christ the Lord reserved only for men. The Apostle writes in 1 Corinthians, chapter 11:

> “I want you to know that the head of every man is Christ; the head of a woman is man; and the head of Christ is God. Every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head. But every woman praying or prophesying with her head uncovered dishonors her head.”

The remaining matters which Isidore has already explained [Col. 1212D]—concerning the veil of the hair assigned to women for the same reason and concerning the mystical significance of the arrangement of the hair on the head of clerics, preserved and to be preserved according to apostolic tradition—are consistent with both the decree of Linus and that of Anicetus. Both rested upon apostolic institutions and upon the authority of Peter’s discipline, which was especially vigorous in the Roman Church.

They show that, even with regard to these rites governing external worship, provision was made by apostolic care at the origin of the Church. For in the same letter, chapter 14, after Paul had commanded both that women should be veiled and silent and should not teach in the Church, and had regulated the number of those selected to prophesy and interpret, he concludes the chapter by affirming and warning that the commands belong to the Lord and that everything must be done decently and in good order.

Therefore, in prescribing these rites, he does not hesitate to invoke the authority of the Lord, and not merely his own, so that it may be entirely clear why Linus and Anicetus, in confirming these matters as well, affixed pontifical decrees as a new seal to the ancient discipline [Col. 1213A].

**Line 7.—“He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus.”** Anicetus is said to have been the first of the Roman pontiffs buried in this cemetery, which shortly afterward received the name of Callistus from the man who enlarged it.

Henschenius records in the appendix to volume III of the April *Acta Sanctorum*, p. 982, that his relics were later removed from there, and that the removal was recorded in public registers in the year 1590, indiction III, on 16 April, in the fifth year of Pope Sixtus V.

He reports that the head of Saint Anicetus was given to the most serene duke of Bavaria. The body of that pontiff and martyr was obtained from Clement VIII by Duke Angelo d’Altemps on 18 October 1604, as the same Henschenius records in volume II of the April *Acta Sanctorum*, p. 478. The body was brought by the most reverend prelate Don Angelo Rocca, bishop of Tagaste and prefect of the apostolic sacristy, into a chapel magnificently built by the aforementioned duke in his residence. There it is venerated every year by the crowds and devotion [Col. 1213B] of the entire City. This is declared by the inscription carved there, which the often-mentioned canon Boldetti reported in his *Observations on the Cemeteries of the Holy Martyrs*, book III, chapter 14, p. 715:

> **The bones of Anicetus, pope and martyr, were transferred by the authority of Clement VIII from the sand-pit afterward called the cemetery of Callistus. Duke John Angelo d’Altemps dedicated the chapel. In the year of the Lord 1617 he placed the body of the same martyr in the basin that had been the tomb of the emperor Alexander Severus.**

How illustrious this cemetery was made by the frequent gatherings of Christians will have to be considered [Col. 1213C] under Callistus, Urbanus, Stephen, and Xystus II, from the letters of Saint Cyprian.

[Note: [Col. 1213C]

**Line 3.—“He established that the clergy should not grow their hair long, according to the command of the Apostle.”** Namely, so that the Roman Church would not be weakened by bad morals; indeed, this holy pontiff instituted that a cleric should wear at the crown of his head a crown resembling a small sphere. Ciaconius places Pius before Anicetus.]

[Note: [Col. 1214A]

**Line 3.—“He established that the clergy should not grow their hair long.”** During his pontificate, Saint Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna, came to Rome, under the reign of Antoninus Pius, as Eusebius relates in the *Chronicle* and in *History*, book IV, chapter 23. Jerome, Suidas in his entry on Polycarp, Marianus Scotus, Ado in his *Chronicle*, and others also report this.

The year is supplied to us by the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle, who writes under the consulship of Tertullus and Sacerdos, that is, in the year of Christ 158:

> “Polycarp, pontiff of Smyrna, a man worthy of admiration, a hearer of the apostles and appointed bishop by them, still living, came to Rome while Anicetus was pontiff, because of the controversy concerning the time at which Easter should be celebrated.”

Concerning this controversy, Irenaeus should be read in his letter to Pope Victor, a notable fragment of which Eusebius preserved for us in book V of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 24:

> “When the most blessed Polycarp,” he says, “came to Rome in the time of Anicetus, and there was a slight disagreement between them concerning certain other matters [Col. 1214B], they immediately embraced one another with the kiss of peace, without contending greatly with one another about this question,” namely, the day on which Easter should be celebrated, about which he had spoken earlier.

**Line 6.—“He died a martyr.”** The emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus launched the fourth persecution against the Christians, concerning which Eusebius writes both in his *Chronicle* and in the preface to book V of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

During that persecution, Saint Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and disciple of the apostle John, suffered martyrdom with many others on 26 March of the year 169, as Eusebius states in book IV, chapter 15.

Saint Justin, the Christian philosopher, a native of Flavia Neapolis in Syria Palestina, after presenting two apologies in defense of the Christians to the emperors, suffered death for the faith of Christ—indeed in the year 165, if the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle is to be trusted. Eusebius discusses him in the cited chapter 16.

When this persecution spread into Gaul [Col. 1214C], many Christians were killed in the year of Christ 177. Among them the martyrs of Lyon were especially distinguished: Pothinus, bishop of Lyon; Attalus; Alexander the physician; Sanctus the deacon; Maturus; Blandina; Biblis; and Ponticus, a fifteen-year-old boy. Their contests can be read in an excellent account in the letter of the Churches of Vienne and Lyon to the Churches of Asia and Phrygia, preserved by Eusebius in book V, chapter 1 and following.]

[Col. 1203]

## 11

[Note: [Col. 1203] Baronius proves that Pius should be placed before Anicetus under the year 158.]

Anicetus, a Syrian by nation, son of John, from the village of Omisa [Note: [Col. 1203] C: Humisia], held office for nine years, three months, and three days [Note: [Col. 1203] CB: nine years, less three months and seven days]. He was in the time of Severus and Marcus, from the consulship of Gallicanus and Vetus to that of Praesens and Rufinus [Note: [Col. 1203] B: in the time of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, from the consuls Pudens and Orfitus to Severus II and Claudius Pompeianus]. He established that the clergy [Note: [Col. 1203] CB read *clericus*, “a cleric,” in place of *clerus*, “the clergy.”] should not grow their hair long, according to the command of the Apostle [Note: [Col. 1203] 1 Corinthians 11]. He held five ordinations in the month of December: seventeen priests, four deacons, and nine bishops in various places. He also died a martyr and was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the twelfth day before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 1203] the fifteenth day before the Kalends, CB], and the episcopate was vacant for seven days [Note: [Col. 1203] CB: seventeen].

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES ON THE SUPPLEMENT TO THE LIBERIAN CATALOGUE CONCERNING SAINT PIUS

The reading of the Liberian Catalogue is known to have been obstructed by frequent lacunae from Hyginus to Callistus. At times the [Col. 1215B] gaps had consumed only the earlier lines of a section, together with the name of the pontiff and the numbers of years, months, and days which he had spent in the episcopate, as in the cases of Anicetus, Eleutherus, and Zephyrinus. At other times, while the pontiff’s name and the aforementioned numbers remained intact, as well as the indication of the emperor whose reign coincided with those years, the names of the consuls had perished from the parchment. Those names indicated the beginning and end of the period of the pontificate. We observe this in Hyginus, the immediate predecessor of Anicetus; in Soter, the predecessor of Eleutherus; and in Victor, who preceded Zephyrinus.

I presented this to the eye in the number on Anicetus and in its chronological notes, p. 112, when I attempted to restore the genuine [Col. 1216A] reading of the catalogue by setting out three expanded columns. The middle column displayed the catalogue text interrupted by lacunae; the right-hand column displayed the old supplement of the copyist, which, as I believe, supplied the gaps incorrectly; and the left-hand column displayed a supplement that corresponded properly with the extent of the lacunae, the context of the work, the surviving letters, the style of the author [Col. 1216B] of the catalogue, and the true principles of chronology.

That I have called the lacunae supplied by the unskilled copyist erroneous is shown by the matter itself. For once the three readings are placed before the eyes, anyone can easily understand that whenever that copyist encountered the name of an emperor repeated before and after a lacuna, he thought that the two sections of different pontiffs, mutilated by the gap, could be joined as though they belonged to the same pontiff; and he assigned the successor’s consuls to the predecessor pope. Thus he overturned the chronology of both.

[Col. 1217A] This becomes clear in the sections of Soter and Eleutherus. After the name and period of Soter had been preserved in the following form—“Soter, one year, three months, d[ays] [lacuna]9”—when he read “He was in the time of Antoninus and [lacuna],” and likewise found Antoninus and Commodus indicated at the end of the lacuna, he did not notice that, together with the end of Soter’s section, the name and the first two lines of the section of Eleutherus, Soter’s successor, were also concealed in the gap.

The consuls of Eleutherus—*[lacuna]verum, et Herennianum*, that is, Severus and Herennianus, incorrectly rendered by him as Verus and Herennianus—he joined to the earlier part of Soter’s preceding section, as though no lacuna intervened. The nine years which he correctly counted for Soter he then indicated by pairs of consuls separated from one another by fifteen years, the number which belonged to Eleutherus. Those years and consuls belonged to Eleutherus, from Severus and Herennianus in the year of Christ 171 to Maternus and Bradua in the year of Christ 185, whom he incorrectly stated as Paternus and Bradua.

Thus, concealing the lacuna, he wrote:

> “Soter, nine years, three months, two days. He was in the time of Antoninus and Commodus, from the consulship of Verus and Herennianus to that of Paternus and Bradua.”

But he ought to have written:

> “Soter, nine years, three months, twenty-one days. He was in the time of Marcus Antoninus and Commodus, from the consulship of Rusticus and Aquilinus [Col. 1217B] to that of Clarus and Cethegus.
>
> “Eleutherus, fifteen years, three months, five days. He was in the time of Marcus Antoninus and Commodus, from the consulship of Severus and Herennianus to that of Maternus and Baradua.”

The same thing is observed in the faulty contraction of the two periods of Victor and Zephyrinus. To Victor, to whom nine years, two months, and ten days are assigned—although twelve years and ten days are due to him—there are attached pairs of consuls separated by a period twice as long, namely from the consulship of Saturninus and Gallus in the year of Christ 198 to the consuls Praesens and Extricatus in the year of Christ 217.

These consuls, and the total of eighteen years, belong to Zephyrinus, Victor’s successor, through a lacuna hidden in the parchments. The consuls that originally marked Victor’s twelve-year period must first be restored in the lacuna, from Commodus V and Glabrio in the year of Christ 186 to the consuls Lateranus and Rufinus in the year of Christ 197, as I restored them in the supplement to the genuine reading in the left-hand column.

[Col. 1217C] But that old copyist of the catalogue did not stop there, after mingling the periods and sewing together the ends of the fragments of Pius’ and Anicetus’ sections. He saw that a space of approximately four lines still remained vacant in the section of Pius and had to be filled. He therefore borrowed from the apocryphal book of the *Constitutions of Clement*, or from some other source, the little story which he inserted below concerning the book of Hermes and the angel appearing to him in the guise of a shepherd, together with the command concerning the day of Easter, as though these were events connected with the history and office of the pontiff.

He did not observe that this addition had been forced in by him contrary to the style of the author of the Catalogue, which had been preserved in the preceding sections, none of which admitted anything of this kind, nor in the sections immediately following to Pontianus, which likewise display nothing of the sort.

Moreover, when he saw the names of the consuls Gallicanus and Vetus listed in Pius’ section after the words “He was in the time of Antoninus,” he thought that he was permitted to use the same consuls to fill the lacuna in Hyginus’ section, where similar words, “He was in the time of Antoninus,” were likewise read. Perhaps he supposed that they had been transferred improperly [Col. 1217D] from their earlier position to fill the second lacuna by older scribes, or that the author of the Catalogue had repeated them in both places together with the name of Antoninus.

As for the name of the consul Rufinus, which belonged to the beginning of Pius’ period together with his colleague Severus, whose name may have been hidden by the wearing away of the parchment, he regarded it as the final name of Hyginus’ preceding period. In place of Severus, the colleague required by the year 141, which closed Hyginus’ pontificate, he substituted Praesens, the colleague of another Rufinus, who indicates the year 153. The consuls Clarus and Severus, whose traces he thought survived in fragments of the expressions *Clar[lacuna] et. e[lacuna]* (which indicated Clarus and Cethegus), and whom he saw similarly assigned to the time of Antoninus, he likewise thought could readily be recalled to Pius, his predecessor, as though the negligence of scribes had displaced them from their proper place and superimposed them on the lacuna of the successor.

We can scarcely suppose that the text of the Liberian catalogue was corrupted in these seven pontificates—from the end of Telesphorus to the beginning of Callistus [Col. 1218A]—by so many confused transfers of consular names and so many erroneous joinings of lacunae in any other way. From the blessed Peter to Telesphorus, and from Callistus to Liberius, where the catalogue ends, it is almost free from such transfers and lacunae.

I therefore judged that the genuine reading of this section in the Liberian catalogue should be restored by supplying the lacuna as follows:

> “Pius, eight years, three months, three days. He was in the time of Antoninus, from the consulship of Rufinus and Quadratus to that of Orfitus and Priscus.”

I proved shortly above, in the chronological notes on this section, from the older catalogues of Italy compared with the numbers remaining in the basilica of Saint Paul, that eight years, three months, and the same number of days should be assigned to Pius’ Roman pontificate after his election, by which he succeeded Hyginus.

That the consulship of Rufinus and Quadratus in the year 142—the year immediately following the consulship of Severus and Priscinus, which closes Hyginus’ period—belongs to the beginning of this see is testified by the consuls of the year 150, Gallicanus [Col. 1218B] and Vetus. These consuls, after the eight-year period of Pius under discussion, are correctly marked as the beginning of Anicetus’ succession in all the catalogues and manuscripts which I cited both in the notes on his number and in the *Prolegomena* near the end.

The same evidence proves that the final consuls of Pius’ eight-year period are Orfitus and Priscus in the year 149, who immediately precede Gallicanus and Vetus. From the latter consuls, Anicetus’ succession begins according to all the manuscripts and catalogues.]

[Col. 1218B]

### Line 5

“**So that Holy Easter might be celebrated on Sunday.**”

During the time of Pius it was decreed that Easter should always be celebrated on Sunday. This is attributed to Pius in the canon *Nosse*, *De consecratione*, distinction 3. In the time of Pope Victor, a vehement controversy arose concerning the date of Easter. The churches of Asia celebrated Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon, following the example of the Jews, whereas the other churches always celebrated Easter on Sunday, even when it did not fall on that day of the lunar month. Because of this disagreement Victor excluded the churches of Asia from communion. (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book V, chapters 23–24.) Victor also decreed that Easter should always be celebrated on Sunday, in the canon *Celebritatem*, *De consecratione*, distinction 3. Anastasius says of Victor: “He established that Holy Easter should be celebrated on Sunday.”

### Note on line 5

[Column 1218C]

### Line 7

“**He made a decree concerning the Church.**”

Writers of the period, when referring to the sitting of a pontiff, use the word *constitutum*, by which a general decree was indicated. Vopiscus, in his *Life of Probus*, writes: “Perhaps you are surprised that I made an unbearded man tribune contrary to the decree of the deified Hadrian.”

The second catalogue, and the *Liber Pontificalis* when copying it, report indefinitely—both in the account of Pius and in the accounts of the succeeding pontiffs—that a decree concerning the Church was published by each pontiff, but they omit indicating the subject matter of the decree. Therefore, so that the reader may not stumble, its subject must be assigned from the more probable conjectures.

Pius therefore seems to have issued a decree concerning Easter, since the preceding text had said: “During his episcopate Hermes wrote a book in which the command is contained that the angel gave him . . . namely, that Holy Easter should be celebrated on Sunday.”

Unless it is said that what is meant is the decree of Pius praised by Gratian in distinction 2, *De paenitentia*, concerning that negligence of his by which something of the Lord’s blood drips away.

### Line 14

“**He baptized many coming to the faith in the name of the Trinity.**”

This evidently concerns people coming from the Judaizing sects, whose various heresiarchs are listed by Hegesippus, as quoted by Eusebius, book IV, chapter 22:

“From these there also arose the Menandrians, Marcionites, Carpocratians, Valentinians, Basilidians, Saturnilians, and others, who, each separately, introduced their own opinions.”

Most of these either baptized by invoking only the name of Christ or corrupted the Trinitarian formula. The words of the same *Liber Pontificalis* suggest that it is speaking of their reception and baptism: it says that Pius decreed that one coming from the Jewish heresy should be received and baptized.

Cyprian speaks of this Judaizing heresy as still existing in the third century, in his epistolary treatise on the validity of baptism administered under the sole expression of the name of Christ the Lord. Among other things he writes in letter 73:

“But there is no reason for anyone, in order to circumvent Christian truth, to put forward the name of Christ and say: ‘Those baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, wherever or however they were baptized, have obtained the grace of baptism.’”

He refutes this statement at length and asserts the necessity of pronouncing the name of the Trinity in the baptismal formula. Regarding the matter itself, he writes:

“He signifies the Trinity, by whose sacrament the nations are baptized. Does Marcion hold this Trinity? Does he assert the same one whom we also call the Father, the Creator? Does he assert the same one Son, Christ, born of the Virgin Mary, who is the Word made flesh?”

In the time of Theodoret, Marcionites were admitted only through reception of baptism, as he shows by his own example in a letter addressed to the Constantinopolitans (letter 145):

“Long ago I brought forward arguments against those corrupted by the disease of Marcion; and, after they had been convicted, by God’s favor I led more than ten thousand of them to the most holy baptism.”

### Note on line 14

[Column 1219B]

### Line 1

“**Pius.**”

Optatus of Milevis, book II *Against Parmenianus*; Augustine, letter 165; and Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, assert that Anicetus, not Pius, succeeded Hyginus in the pontificate. Nevertheless, the truer and more generally accepted opinion is that Pius must be placed before Pope Anicetus. Thus Eusebius states in the *Chronicle*; Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 27; Nicephorus Callistus, book III, chapter 25; Hegesippus as quoted by Eusebius, book IV, chapter 21; Irenaeus, book III, chapters 2 and 4; Tertullian, book III *Against Marcion*; and Baronius under the year of Christ 158, §3.

### Same line

“**The brother of Pastor.**”

The brother of this pontiff was called Pastor, either because he belonged to the family of Junius Pastor, who held the consulship with Papirius Aelianus in the third year of the emperor Aurelius, or because—which is more probable—the angel announcing on what day Easter should be celebrated appeared to him in the form of a shepherd. See Tertullian, book III, the poem *Against Marcion*, at the end.

### Line 4

“**In which the command is contained.**”

This command is found nowhere in the surviving book of the *Shepherd*.

### Line 6

“**He decreed that a heretic coming from the Jewish heresy should be received and baptized.**”

By “the Jewish heresy” he means here the sect of Cerinthus, so called because it devoted itself above all to observing Hebrew rites. See Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, 28.

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

[Column 1219C]

I had warned in the chronological notes on Hyginus that one must proceed step by step in arranging and defining the periods of the four pontiffs who succeeded one another from Hyginus to Soter. A copyist of a later age had transmitted their order and epochs to us in an example of the older Liberian Catalogue, with its lacunae wrongly filled.

A little earlier, in the entry for Anicetus, I attempted to display these matters more clearly and to complete them by supplying the genuine reading. There I also observed that the order of succession requires Pius to be placed before Anicetus, as several copies of this *Liber Pontificalis* place them. Yet, so as not to alter the earlier editions of Velser and Fabrotti, I considered it sufficient, in order to preserve the rights of true chronology and history, to append—as they prudently did—the succession number 12 to Anicetus’s name at the beginning of his entry, and to add succession number 11 to the name of Pius at the beginning of this entry, although that number had been wrongly transferred to occupy seat 12.

I also promised that, in restoring what I believe to be the genuine reading of the Liberian Catalogue by supplying the lacunae, I would present separately, for each of these pontiffs, the evidence confirming the truth of the restoration belonging to the pontiff discussed in the relevant entry. I have already done this for Anicetus. It remains to be done now for Pius.

We rightly said that the order of succession must be preserved, placing Pius before Anicetus, since Irenaeus and Hegesippus—contemporary witnesses who were present in Rome during those times—give this order. Irenaeus, after carrying out a mission on behalf of the church of Lyons to Pope Eleutherus, who had been Anicetus’s deacon, gives this very order of succession in book III, chapter 3:

“Telesphorus was appointed, and suffered martyrdom gloriously and nobly. Then came Hyginus, then Pius; after him Anicetus held that office. Soter immediately succeeded Anicetus. Eleutherus, twelfth from the apostles, now holds the ministry.”

Hegesippus, who records that he stayed as Anicetus’s guest in the City while Eleutherus was Anicetus’s deacon, marks the same succession in Eusebius, book IV, chapter 21. It has been reproduced above in the same words in Schelestratius’s notes on Saint Hyginus. Prosper in his *Chronicle*, together with several catalogues reviewed there by Schelestratius, §3, makes it impossible today to doubt this order.

Once the order has been established, we proceed to the periods properly assigned to each pontiff. The agreement of the complete manuscripts in listing the last consuls before Hyginus’s pontificate—namely Caesar II and Balbinus, in the year of Christ 137—shows that Hyginus’s beginning fell under the next consuls, 138, Niger and Camerinus. In the text of the Librarian they are designated Magnus and Camerinus, as we read above on page 100. I have adapted the reading of the Catalogue on page 101 accordingly, although I think Niger and Camerinus should be expressed, as I did in restoring the genuine reading on page 112, following the ancient inscriptions that record them in this way.

After the four complete years assigned to Hyginus in his entry by Anastasius and the other documents, both in the *Prolegomena* and in the Notes, Severus and Priscinus close his epoch and open the years of his successor. They entered office in the year 141. From that point a full twenty-year period is counted to the two Augusti, the consuls of the year 161, who mark in all the manuscripts and catalogues the end of the pontificate immediately preceding Soter. By unanimous agreement of those same manuscripts and catalogues, Soter’s seat begins under the next consuls, Rusticus and Aquilinus, in the year 162.

The complete twenty-year period from 141 to 161 must therefore be divided between two pontiffs, the first being Pius and the second Anicetus, according to the order of succession already established by suitable witnesses. The only question remaining is what portion of this twenty-year period should be assigned to Pius and what portion to Anicetus.

The ancient copyist of the Liberian Catalogue easily avoided this investigation by omitting Anicetus, whose name had been erased by a lacuna, although Irenaeus and Hegesippus, together with the other Fathers, catalogues, chronologists, and historians, preserved it intact and did not forget that he was both a pontiff and a martyr of Christ. Our task is to establish the duration of Pius’s period, even though that of Anicetus may appear sufficiently proved.

If the paintings of Saint Paul displayed the complete epochs beneath the images of Pius and Anicetus, merely inspecting them would settle the dispute. But Soter’s epoch—which follows Anicetus—survives intact in the series renewed by Nicholas III after the model of the Leonine series, although the numbers that had been consumed by age had already fallen away in the image of Soter. It is clearly expressed as nine years, three months, and twenty-one days, as I published it in the series of Roman pontiffs in the *Prolegomena*.

In the preceding seat, before Soter—which, as we have said, must be referred to Anicetus—the surviving Leonine series reads eleven years; age has consumed the indications of the months and days. The preceding panel, belonging to Pius, has lost the number of years and days in the Leonine paintings, but preserves the complete middle line, with an indication of three months, marked in this way: “M. III. Ð . . . . .”

From these surviving remains of the numbers, sufficiently clear evidence is supplied by four older catalogues of Italy. In them, the epoch of eleven years is augmented by four months and three days; and to the adjacent epoch, which completes the twenty-year period with eight or nine years, three months are likewise added, belonging to the image of Pius in the paintings of the Leonine period. Three days are also expressed, as we said in the *Prolegomena*.

Since I have sufficiently shown that the numbers in those Italian catalogues were copied from the paintings of the patriarchal basilicas, and since portions of the paintings in the Pauline basilica survive, the Italian catalogues repay this favor to their sources—that is, to the paintings of the Leonine period—by serving to fill their lacunae.

Following their authority, therefore, we may rightly assign to Anicetus, who immediately preceded Soter, eleven years, four months, and three days; and to Pius, who preceded Anicetus, eight or nine years, three months, and three days.

I said “eight or nine years” for Pius because two of the Italian catalogues give eight years, while the other two increase the total by one year. It will now be our task to reconcile both possibilities with the assigned consuls and to weigh the implications of the two versions of Pius’s period, both the eight-year and the nine-year version.

In the *Prolegomena*, in the series of Roman pontiffs, where I collected the more important evidence relevant to establishing the epochs of these two pontiffs, I made several observations.

First, in certain catalogues the epochs of the two pontiffs had been exchanged, an opportunity for this being provided by Optatus of Milevis, who placed Pius after Anicetus, whereas Hegesippus and Irenaeus, contemporary witnesses, placed him before Anicetus.

Second, the oldest catalogue of the Liberian period, mutilated and displaced at this point, indeed omits Anicetus and assigns the entire twenty-year period to Pius, the copyists ineptly filling the lacunae in the manuscript. But in the Caesarean copy of the same catalogue, where the lacuna halted in the numbers, the consuls Gallicanus and Veter—assigned to the beginning of Anicetus’s period—are fortunately displayed.

This single indication is sufficient to guide us in completing both periods. For if the consuls Gallicanus and Veter—or Vetus, as others prefer—in the year 150 mark the beginning of Anicetus’s period, to whom the ancient paintings and the manuscripts alike assign eleven complete years, Soter must necessarily have held office under the consuls of the year 162, Rusticus and Aquilinus. He is assigned those same consuls in the complete catalogues, as well as in the other manuscripts listed in the *Prolegomena*.

It follows, therefore, that the eight pairs of consuls remaining from Severus and Priscinus, who closed Hyginus’s pontificate in the year 141, to the aforementioned Gallicanus and Veter, who opened Anicetus’s seat in the year 150, belong to Pius. For this reason I shall assign him a pontificate of eight years, three months, and three days, according to catalogues once copied from the paintings of those same basilicas, where the remains of this epoch can now clearly be seen in the triad of months, “M. III.”

Nevertheless, on folio 92 I preferred to repeat those same consuls of the year 141, Severus and Priscinus, as the last consuls of Hyginus, and consequently to assign Pius—along with the Bergomensis and Farfensis catalogues—nine years, three months, and three days. The reason is that at the beginning of Pius’s period the catalogues of the age of Liberius and Felix IV, as well as the Librarian, list the consul Severus, although they wrongly give him Clarus as colleague.

That Clarus served as colleague with another Severus, from the Claudian family, who became consul in the year 146, is recorded in several ancient inscriptions. Through the customary carelessness of copyists, Severus, consul in 141 with Priscinus as colleague, was exchanged for Severus, consul in 146 with E-bucius Clarus. Once the consuls have been restored in this way, we can more easily determine the corresponding months and days from the indication of the consuls immediately preceding them at the end of Hyginus’s period and from the total number of years assigned to Pius and Anicetus up to the beginning of Soter.

The days of the two martyrs, recorded in the ecclesiastical calendars, will, I hope, also make this clear and reconcile, if I am not mistaken, the difference between the eight-year and nine-year periods assigned indiscriminately to the same Pius by different catalogues.

The archives of the Roman Church record Pius’s martyrdom, supported by Bede, Usuard, Ado, and other martyrologies, on 11 July. The same witnesses assign Anicetus’s crown to 17 April.

If Anicetus’s blessed death occurred in the year 162—as is clear from the beginning of the period of his successor Soter, marked by the consuls of 162, Rusticus and Aquilinus—and if the epoch of eleven years preserved in the paintings and catalogues also includes four months and three days of that episcopate, as they are assigned to him in the catalogue of Felix IV, then, counting backward eleven years, four months, and three days, we arrive at 15 December 149.

Since that date was a Sunday—the year having the Sunday letter F—it is suitable for his ordination to the episcopate, whether he served as Pius’s vicar, with Pius still living until July of the following year, 150, or whether he was appointed bishop of some recently founded church. For we must admit that those early Roman pontiffs may also have adopted, following the example of the apostles, the practice of temporarily conferring the office of a vicar.

Since it would have been necessary to ordain bishops for various places and then send them away as the establishment of new bishoprics required, it is not unreasonable to believe that they wished, even when no persecution was troubling the Church, to employ priests who were to be ordained—or bishops recently ordained—and retain them for a time in the administration of the city’s episcopate as vicars, as though they were to be trained by experience, before sending them to the sees intended for them.

During this period of apprenticeship, so to speak, if the Roman pontiff happened to die and the clergy of the City elected as his successor the very man who had served as vicar, since he had proved especially suitable in pontifical ministry, that man, once called to govern the universal Church, could appoint another in his place to the church assigned to him but not yet entered. Having been promoted to the Roman Church, in which the care of everyone is united, he would not entirely abandon the church whose governance had been entrusted to him. But this is incidental.

Anicetus’s ordination to the episcopate on Sunday, 15 December 149, therefore agrees exactly with the total of ten years, four months, and three days assigned to him in the catalogue of Felix IV. The Liberian Catalogue lacks this information, because a lacuna occupies the beginning of Anicetus’s period, and the copyist confused and combined into Pius’s single pontificate the two portions of the common twenty-year period.

The same result follows from the paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul, completed by means of the Farfensis and Cavensis catalogues extracted from them, and compared with the day of Anicetus’s martyrdom, 17 April, recorded in the calendars of the Roman Church and in the martyrologies mentioned above.

The calculation is equally compatible with the eight years, three months, and three days assigned to Pius by the Farfensis and Bergomensis catalogues, corresponding to the surviving numbers of the basilica of Saint Paul, from whose paintings we have concluded that they were anciently copied.

For if we begin with the sacred celebration of his anniversary on 11 July in the year 150 and move backward nine full years, three months, and three days, the endpoint of the reckoning, counting both the first and last days, falls on 9 April 141, under the consuls Severus and Priscinus, who are assigned as the last consuls to Hyginus, Pius’s predecessor.

Easter in that year, 141, fell on the following day, 19 April. That day may have been marked by Pius’s episcopal ordination, although the date seems to have been transferred by an excess of one day to the vigil of the preceding day.

“But,” you will say, “Hyginus lived until 11 January of the following year, 142,” as we established shortly before in the chronological notes on his epoch, since he is assigned the Easter season and the final consulship of Severus and Priscinus in the year 141.

I affirm that this very fact caused the same consuls and the same Easter season to be assigned to both men: to Hyginus, celebrating the last Easter of his pontificate under those consuls; and to Pius, deriving the epoch of his episcopal ordination from the Easter day in that same consulship.

Thus all the genuine documents from the archives of the Roman Church are reconciled with one another—documents preserved in the complete catalogues and manuscripts, in the surviving remains of the paintings, in the calendrical tables of the martyrology, and in the diptychs of their churches—if Pius’s and Anicetus’s periods are distinguished by years, months, and days in the way indicated by both groups of manuscripts, whether those assigning a complete eight-year period or those assigning a complete nine-year period to Pius.

Pius was ordained bishop in the year of Christ 141, under the consuls Severus and Priscinus, as Hyginus’s vicar, on Sunday, Easter Day, 10 April.

In the following year, 142, under the consuls Rufinus and Quadratus, Hyginus was crowned with martyrdom on 11 January. Within the third month after his death, Pius was elected Roman pontiff and placed in the Roman see on Sunday, 9 April of that same year, 142.

In the year 149, Pius ordained Anicetus as an assistant bishop, or vicar, on Sunday, 15 December, under the consuls Orphitus and Priscus.

In the year 150, Pius was crowned with martyrdom on 11 July, under the consuls Veter and Gallicanus.

From his episcopal ordination to the day of his martyrdom, Saint Pius’s period amounts to nine years, three months, and three days, the duration assigned to him in the Bergomensis and Farfensis catalogues.

From the succession by which he followed his predecessor Hyginus, however, he held eight years, three months, and three days, assigned to him in the Cavensis and Lucensis catalogues and in Papebrochius’s Belgic catalogue, in order to complete the twenty-year period divided between Pius and Anicetus. These same catalogues assign to one of them eleven years, four months, and three days, and to the other eight years, three months, and the same number of days.

[Column 1223C]

Anicetus was ordained assistant bishop, or vicar, of Pius on Sunday, 15 December, under the consuls Orphitus and Priscus, in the year of Christ 149.

In the year 150, under the consuls Veter and Gallicanus—who are the first consuls assigned to him in the older catalogue, where they are also listed as the last in the words “up to the two Augusti”—he was elected by the Roman clergy two days after Pius’s death and assumed the pontificate on Sunday, 13 July. See the chronological notes on Hyginus and Anicetus.

In the year 161 he completed his martyrdom on 17 April. Therefore the consuls of the year 161, the two Augusti, the brothers Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, are assigned to him as the last consuls, closing the period of eleven years assigned to Anicetus, together with three months and the same number of days, as was established shortly before in the chronological notes on his entry.

## HISTORICAL NOTES OF THE SAME KIND

[Column 1223D]

### Line 1

“**The brother of Pastor.**”

### Line 3

“**During his episcopate Hermes wrote a book in which the command is contained that the angel of the Lord gave him when he came to him in the form of a shepherd, and commanded him that Holy Easter should be celebrated on Sunday.**”

Cardinal Baronius, under the year 159, §12, rightly observes that the book famous among the ancients, entitled the *Shepherd* of Hermas, or Hermes, and cited by Irenaeus, Origen, Clement of Alexandria, Tertullian, and other Fathers, later translated by Rufinus and in our own age published in Greek and Latin by Cotelerius, must be considered entirely different from this commentary of Hermes, which was written while Pius was seated on the pontifical throne.

For in that earlier work the angel’s command concerning the celebration of Easter on Sunday appears nowhere. Moreover, the common opinion—confirmed by Baronius with the strongest arguments—is that the first institution of celebrating Easter on Sunday goes back to the apostles. Although, toward the end of the second century, it became necessary to confront certain Asians who defended a different custom, the decree of Victor confirmed that original institution, as will be said in his entry.

Baronius believes that the author of that first book was Hermas, or Hermes, mentioned by the Apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 16, verse 14, since the work appears to belong to the pontificate of Clement.

The Librarian derived from the second catalogue the account of another Hermes, who, while Pope Pius governed the Church, wrote the angel’s command—given by an angel appearing in the form of a shepherd—concerning the celebration of Easter on Sunday. The second catalogue derived this from the older catalogue of the age of Liberius.

The copyist of that catalogue, rather than its original author, seems to have added this narrative to fill a lacuna, taking it either from the apocryphal book of Clement’s *Constitutions* or from the Acts to be mentioned below, as I reported shortly before in the chronological notes both on the entry for Anastasius and on the catalogue.

Cotelerius judges that the passage should be expunged as an invention and removed, although it is mentioned both in poems by a hidden poet writing under the name of Tertullian and by Bede, Ado, and others.

I shall not enter into controversy about the truth of this second book of Hermes, belonging to the age of Pius, or about the angelic vision and command. I judge that such a dispute is scarcely necessary for pontifical history or for the Easter decree, which is beyond doubt in the age of Victor.

It is enough to note that, when producing this narrative, the Librarian followed the authority of two older catalogues: the complete catalogue under Felix IV and the catalogue interpolated in the Liberian lacunae. He may perhaps also have followed the author of the *Life and Acts of Saint Prudentiana the Virgin*, about whom something will be said shortly below.

Those same catalogues call that Hermes the brother of Pius, and Baronius refers to him under the year 159, §8, the booklet concerning the deeds of Saint Praxedes the virgin and, as he thinks, of her brothers Novatus and Timothy. Others exclude these men from the family line both of Pius and of Praxedes.

After the opinions of such men, it will not be irrelevant to record here what I have observed from the ancient monuments of that age, so that, after examining them as well, the reader’s mind may be better equipped to choose whichever opinion seems more probable.

In that period I find the cognomen Hermes or Herma to have been adopted quite frequently both by Roman citizens and by their freedmen. To pass over the two men named by the Apostle Paul in the same verse—Romans 16:14—Hermas and Hermes, as well as Hermes the prefect either of the City or of a legion or military forces, the father of Balbina, whom I discussed above on page 82 in the historical notes on Saint Alexander, I shall mention here four persons known from inscriptions of the period under discussion, belonging to the Cornelian family.

I have said that it is highly probable that Pudens too belonged to this family—the host of the apostles in the Patrician district—and that Praxedes and Pudentiana, either his daughters or his granddaughters, also belonged to it. In their house Pius consecrated the church mentioned in this entry. This is what I promised to confirm here.

The Capitoline marble inscription, engraved among the city neighborhood magistrates, records three Lucii Cornelii, freedmen of Lucius, under the consulship of L. Ceionius Commodus and Sextus Vettulenus Civica Pompeianus. The last of them, bearing the cognomen Hermes, held the magistracy in the district of Censor, in Region 14, according to Gruter, folio 251. He belongs to the year of Christ 146.

Another marble inscription names Lucius Cornelius Hermes and Gaius Cornelius Hermes. It was excavated three years ago before the Capene Gate, near the Arch of Claudius. I shall quote it here all the more willingly because it contains particularly clear evidence for the age now under discussion and for the pontificate of Pius, through the consulship of the year 141, Servius Salvidienus Orfitus, to whom it assigns Marcus Peducaeus Priscinus as colleague. The same consulship is also indicated on several tiles published by Fabretti.

Although the inscription in Gruter, page 182, no. 4, assigns Titus Hoenius Severus as colleague to that Priscinus, he may perhaps have been a suffect consul. The inscription reads as follows:

[Column 1225]

[Column 1225A]

Lucius Cornelius Hermes sold to Lollia Aprilis the portion of this monument belonging to him. Publius Cornelius Hermes is also listed among the co-opted participants in the rights of the same monument.

We understand that this monument stood near the tombs of the Cornelii on the Appian Way, between the first and second milestones from the City, which Cicero mentions, as I said above, on the evidence of the Caecilian plot acquired for this monument.

The tombs and estates of the Caecilii—for which reason the area received its name—were situated near the second milestone from the City on the Appian Way. This is testified by the surviving tomb of Caecilia Metella, daughter of Quintus Caecilius Creticus, and by the cemetery of Saint Caecilia and her companions, a portion of what is also called the cemetery of Callistus near Saint Sebastian.

From this it seems that the conjecture is not to be rejected which identifies the first Christian cemeteries for us on the estates of the Cornelii. Those who, while the apostles were still alive, had opened their house in Rome to them as a place of hospitality in the Patrician district, near the district of the Cornelii, in the house of Pudens—that is, at the title of Saint Pudentiana—and of Pastor, may also have prepared, for the dead, a burial place and cemetery on their domestic estates. An old inscription of Cornelia Pudentianetis is preserved there; I published it above on folio 11.

For this reason the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way must not be excluded from this reckoning. Priscilla was the mother of Pudens, who lived under Antoninus. On the Salarian Way, in her own cemetery, Pudentiana buried her sister Praxedes, at the house of their father Pudens, long before another Priscilla, in the third century after Christ, at the request of blessed Pope Marcellus, opened another cemetery for Christians on the same Salarian Way, likewise called the cemetery of Priscilla. See Baronius under the years 44, §61; 59, §18; and 159, §8; Aringhi, *Rome Subterranean*, volume II, book IV, chapter 28; and the Acts printed there.

The Vatican crypts and cemetery, where Saint Peter and the pontiffs immediately succeeding him were first buried and where the foundations of this church were laid, should likewise be regarded as not far from the estates of the Cornelii. This is so not only because they lie beside the Cornelian Gate and Way, as I observed in the notes to the topographical description of the cemeteries of the holy martyrs near Rome in the *Prolegomena*, but also because antiquarians report that, besides the tombs of the Cornelii on the Appian Way between the first and second milestones from the City mentioned by Cicero, another tomb belonging to the Cornelian family was also seen not far from the Vatican basilica, between the Mausoleum of Hadrian and the basilica.
