This tomb survived at Saint Mary in Transpontina until it was destroyed by Pope Hadrian VI, as several antiquarians cited by Nardini report, book VII, chapter 13, page 491 of the new edition. It had been constructed in the form of a pyramid with such magnificence that some people commonly took it for the tomb of Africanus.

It is nevertheless established that Africanus had been buried in the earlier tomb of the Cornelii on the Appian Way, where he had also ordered the poet Ennius to be received as an honor.

I am therefore so persuaded that cemeteries for the first Roman pontiffs, the faithful, and the martyrs were excavated on the estates of the Cornelian family—both on the Appian Way near Saint Sebastian and on the Triumphal and Cornelian Ways near Saint Peter—that for this reason I believe blessed Pope Cornelius was credited with having arranged for the body of the chief of the apostles to be brought to the Vatican cemetery from the catacombs of the cemetery of Callistus, where it had once lain.

For if ownership of both estates belonged either to that same Pope Cornelius or to members of his family, he could more safely take up the bones of his most blessed predecessor and bring them, or restore them, to whichever tomb he preferred.

When I consider the inviolable laws of hospitality, so solemnly commended by the divine Teacher to his apostles when he commanded that, once received, they should not move from house to house but remain in the same house (Luke 10)—a passage carefully expounded by Saint Ambrose in book VI on chapters 9 and 10 of Luke, which the Church gives us to read every year during the week of Pentecost—and when I consider every kind of service performed by the first believers for the apostles, the resources laid at their feet, and the centurion Cornelius falling at those same feet and asking, with all his household, that Peter remain with him while he was staying at Caesarea; when I consider also the house of Pudens, the Patrician district, and the Cornelii of Rome, similarly established as a lodging and, so to speak, a nursery of the first pontiffs—I indicated on page 36 that Cletus, the son of Aemilianus, also possessed a Cornelian family connection through the Patrician district, and there I pointed out the sufficiently close relationship of Clement’s house and origin—when, I say, I consider all these things and compare them with Justin’s lodging near the Baths of Novatus, that is, with the house of Pudens and the Cornelii, and with the monuments of those same Cornelii near the more ancient cemeteries of the faithful, I can scarcely restrain myself from concluding that the first fruits of the nations, dedicated and devoted in the person of the centurion Cornelius to Peter, Christ’s vicar, contracted with him and his successors such sacred obligations of hospitality both at Caesarea and at Rome that even after death their deceased host did not forget this token of hospitality.

This is especially so since Peter promised the faithful in his Second Letter, written in the City shortly before his martyrdom, that he would take care that they should often have him even after his death—those whom he had loved so intensely in Christ—once he had laid aside the tent of his body.

Besides these proofs of the constant service and hospitality shown by members of the Cornelian family, both in Palestine and in the City, toward the chief of the apostles and the first believers, the conjecture is also supported to some extent by the cognomina Hermes and Herma, which were equally common in the first and second centuries among the Cornelii and among Roman Christians, especially among those related to the pontiffs born in the City.

For these cognomina indicate that the names were repeatedly shared with relatives, clients, guests, or freedmen, implying some bond of relationship, as antiquarians and historians observed long ago. On this matter see Cardinal Baronius under the year 36, §10 and following; and Saint Jerome, who makes the same judgment concerning the cognomen Paul, adopted by the Apostle to the nations after he had announced the Gospel to the proconsul Sergius Paulus.

In the same way, we see that family names were shared by the emperors themselves as a sign of goodwill, at nearly the same period. Titus honored Josephus, the Jewish historian whom he had captured in the Jewish war at Jerusalem, with the name Flavius, as Josephus himself relates in his book on his life.

If, then, the name Hermes is assigned by the catalogues to the same brother of Pope Pius, who is also said to have been called Pastor and to have been the presbyter of the title of Pudens and Pudentiana, dedicated by Pius in the Baths of Novatus in the Patrician district—a place so full of indications of the Cornelian family—it could have pointed to the hospitable goodwill and service of that family toward the pontiff who dedicated the church and toward his relatives and connections.

But enough of this. What the Librarian states concerning Hermes’s book and his family connection with Pius does not seem to have been written by the author in the Liberian Catalogue. Rather, it appears to have been superimposed upon the lacuna by a copyist of a later age and derived from a highly probable conjecture, either from the apocryphal book of the *Apostolic Constitutions* attributed to Clement or from documents not identified in the Liberian Catalogue, the Felician Catalogue, or the *Liber Pontificalis*.

Line 10 and 13.—Here, at the request of blessed Praxedes, he dedicated a church in the Baths of Novatus, in the Patrician quarter, in honor of her holy sister Potentiana, etc. Indeed, he also dedicated the baptismal font, etc. We read numerous documents concerning the dedication of this titular church, honored before the others in this respect, in Baronius and Panvinius. The latter, in his little work on the seven churches of the City, and the former in his *Annals* under the years 159 and 162, collected from manuscripts and from monuments visible in the church itself numerous testimonies from inscriptions, mosaics, and paintings.

From manuscripts Cardinal Baronius selected letters exchanged both between Pope Pius and Justus of Vienne, and between the presbyter Pastor and his colleague Timothy, together with Timothy’s replies. Yet the letters to Justus of Vienne, although said to have been supplied from the archive of the Church of Vienne, published by Binius together with the councils, and cited by Cardinal Bona in *Liturgical Matters*, book I, chapter 3, can scarcely be produced today as genuine. For in them Pius is made to recall among the presbyters of the Roman Church Eleutherius, who, according to Hegesippus—himself a guest of that same Anicetus in the city of Rome—was serving as deacon under Anicetus, the successor of Pius.

[Col. 1227C]

The letters of Pastor to Timothy, and of Timothy to Pastor, reported by Cardinal Baronius under the year 159, are free from this historical discrepancy. They are contained in the Acts, or Life, of the holy virgins Praxedes and Pudentiana, preserved in old parchment copies kept in more than one archive. Moreover, in a manuscript of this kind kept in the Liberian basilica, the preface placed by the author before the Life indicates that it was compiled from authentic documents. He states that, although he had hesitated to undertake the writing of the Lives of the aforementioned virgins, which he had received in an edited form from the venerable presbyter Pastor and had seen circulating, he was confirmed in his purpose of writing when he discovered that the work of this kind of Life, which had been published under Pastor’s name, had been composed at a later period. This was shown by its opening, taken from the prologue to the Passion of Saint Chrysogonus.

[Col. 1227D]

Therefore, since this author showed himself careful in collating and comparing the documents from which he gathered his history, he should not rashly be rejected among writers of doubtful reliability or counted among the adherents of another’s imposture—unless his assertion is demonstrably contrary to the truth of what happened.

How consistently and how consonantly with truthful documents those Acts, or Lives, were regarded can be gathered both from ancient writers and from more recent ones. Florentinius presents the evidence in his notes on the ancient Martyrology, *Kalends of August*, Exercise 11. He observes that Ado, Notker, and Peter de Natalibus followed the same Acts and abridged them. He himself supplies the complete account on page 703, although he says that he finds it neither in Surius nor anywhere else.

[Col. 1228A]

The same account is also found in our Liberian manuscript, expressed in the same sense but in somewhat different words. It is therefore entirely clear that Florentinius’s copy reproduces the Acts circulating under Pastor’s name, whereas our Liberian manuscript reproduces the Acts written by that anonymous author who collated the work attributed to Pastor with the text of the Passion of Saint Chrysogonus, from which he had discovered that the preface had been taken.

I shall therefore give that account from our Liberian copy, punctuated as follows:

> Accordingly, the glorious virgins Praxedes and Pudentiana, remaining in their own house after their father’s death and devoting themselves diligently and earnestly to pious works, began to sell all their patrimony and distribute it to the poor of Christ. After consulting with the man of God, Pastor, these virgins of Christ decided that they would construct a font in the aforementioned titular church, so that, when the solemnity of Easter arrived, all the gentiles belonging to their household in common might be made Christians by the ministers of the Catholic faith.
>
> [Col. 1228B]
>
> When they reported this to holy Pius, bishop of the principal see, he rejoiced with great joy, so much so that he not only encouraged the undertaking but himself marked out the font with his own hands. When it had been completed with God’s help, the holy virgins Praxedes and Pudentiana summoned their entire household, both from the City and from the suburban estates that had been left to them by their parents, etc.; and on the holy day of Easter ninety-six persons of both sexes were baptized in the aforementioned titular church.
>
> When these matters had been completed in this manner, the Christians began to hold solemn and celebrated assemblies in the same titular church and to devote themselves there to hymns and praises by day and by night. Thus a great multitude of gentiles, delighted by their manner of life, abandoned their ancestral laws and superstitions and converted to the faith of Christ.
>
> On this account the pagans brought a complaint before Antoninus Verus, whom Antoninus [Col. 1228C] Pius, dying in the twenty-second year of his reign, had left as his successor. He immediately promulgated the following edict against the Christians: they were to be permitted only to live in their own dwellings; they were to join themselves to no one among the people of the world; they were to have no permission to buy or sell; nor were they to use the public baths; they were to be content with their dwellings alone, etc.

He continues by narrating that, after another year and a half, the blessed virgin Pudentiana, a virgin of Christ, departed to the Lord. Her body was first cared for at home in the same titular church for twenty-eight days and was then buried in the cemetery of Priscilla, beside her father Pudens, on the Salarian Way.

Meanwhile Praxedes frequently prayed in the titular church together with blessed Pope Pius and Novatus, a distinguished man and the brother of Timothy, the Roman presbyter. It happened that Novatus died within two years and made his brother Timothy and the virgin Praxedes heirs to his property. With their common consent, the Baths of Timothy were surrendered for conversion into a titular church, adorned with the memory of Praxedes and dedicated by that same pontiff.

[Col. 1228D]

> And the virgin Praxedes asked blessed Bishop Pius to dedicate the Baths of Novatus, which were no longer in use, as a church, etc.; and it pleased holy Bishop Pius. He dedicated the church of the Baths of Novatus in the name of blessed Praxedes, the virgin, and established it as a titular church in the city of Rome, in the quarter called Laterica. There also he consecrated a baptistery on the third day before the Ides of May.
>
> At that time blessed Bishop Pius also established that holy Easter should be celebrated only on Sunday, whereas until then it had been celebrated by many on other days. While he was governing the Church, Hermes wrote a book in which it is contained that an angel of the Lord appeared to him in the form of a shepherd, commanding him to proclaim to everyone that henceforth Easter should be celebrated only on Sunday.
>
> Two months later blessed Pius died and was buried at the Vatican, beside the body of blessed Peter the Apostle, on the fifth day before the Ides of July, after governing the Church for eleven years, four months, and twenty-one days.

[Col. 1229A]

Florentinius therefore correctly concludes from this account, and from the other material previously set forth in the notes on the dates of blessed Peter and Linus, that the lodging of the prince of the apostles at the house of Pudens, and the nearby edge of the Esquiline hill beside the quarters of the Praetorian cavalry, were the reason why the first titular churches of the Roman Church were dedicated there and, after fires, demolitions, or persecutions, restored in the same place—where the presence of the apostles Peter and Paul had auspiciously laid the foundations of the priestly City.

We may also observe that the following order of events can be inferred. First, the house of Pudens, which had received Peter under Caius and Claudius, around the time of the final arrival of both apostles in the City, was dedicated to the assembly of Christians. Soon afterward, when the division of the titular churches was carried out by Evaristus at the command of the prince of the apostles, it was honored with the status of a Roman titular church. It was then enlarged, and made more distinguished by the addition and consecration of a baptismal font, when, under Pius, the holy virgins Pudentiana and Praxedes offered it for the more solemn celebration of that sacrament at Easter. The rite had shortly before been established by Telesphorus and was being put into practice; ninety-six members of the virgins’ household approached to receive Christ’s grace in the sacred font.

[Col. 1229B]

After Novatus had been received by God, the Baths of Timothy, likewise offered for a similar use—perhaps so that women might descend separately into the water in one font and men in another—provided the occasion for opening and dedicating there a second nearby titular church in the name of blessed Praxedes. This followed the earlier dedication of the titular church and font in the house of Pudens, under the name of the virgin Pudentiana, or of the presbyter Pastor.

There is one point in the Acts that I think should be corrected; it concerns chronology. I see that the author of this Life, who admits in his preface that he undertook the writing only later, after the publication of the Acts of the martyr Chrysogonus—who had been a confessor of Christ together with the martyr Anastasia at the beginning of the fourth century—seized upon the name Antoninus Verus, that is, Marcus Aurelius, as an opportunity to disturb the chronology. He substituted it for Antoninus Pius, who was then reigning, and brought forward for succession to the empire Lucius Verus, son of Aelius Verus, adopted into the family together with Marcus Aurelius, the son of his wife’s brother. Marcus too was called Verus and, as Caesar, held tribunician power with his adoptive father for fifteen years.

[Col. 1229C]

For otherwise the age and deeds of Pope Pius would not accord with these Antonines. I have shown above that, between the consulships of Rufinus and Quadratus in the year 142 and those of Orfitus and Priscus in the year 149, blessed Pius was Roman pontiff for a full seven years. Antoninus Pius, however, succeeded Hadrian when Camerinus and Niger were consuls, in the year 138; and when he died in 161, he left as his successors his two adopted sons, Marcus and Lucius Verus, who were consuls in that same year. At the time, the twenty-fourth year of tribunician power had begun, as marked on the coins, and he was entering the twenty-third year of his imperial rule. Thus he did not die in the twenty-second year.

[Col. 1229D]

The author’s faulty chronology was confirmed by the transposition of the eras of the two pontiffs Pius and Anicetus, introduced by Optatus of Milevis, whom the author follows. He assigns Pius eleven years, four months, and twenty days—years which I have shown belonged to Anicetus, his successor, according to the order handed down by Irenaeus and Hegesippus, writers contemporary with those events.

Once the sequence of the times has been restored, it follows that when Pope Pius died in the year 150—Antoninus being in the ninth year of his reign and Caesar Marcus Aurelius Verus beginning the fifth year of his tribunician power—only two months had elapsed since the dedication of the titular church of Saint Praxedes and the Baths of Novatus, as the Acts relate. During the eight preceding years of his pontificate, he could therefore have consecrated both the font and the titular church of Saint Pudentiana before Easter of the year 145.

[Col. 1230A]

Hadrian had already died seven years earlier, on the sixth day before the Ides of June, while he was about to complete the twenty-first year of his rule; he had handed the empire to Antoninus Pius, the adoptive father of Marcus and Lucius Verus. The same Acts indicate this, counting five years from the dedication of the titular church and font of Saint Pudentiana to the dedication of Timothy’s Baths and the death of Pope Pius I.

For the peaceful times of Antoninus Pius had brought to Rome and the provinces that fortunate condition of the Church which Justin Martyr, a contemporary of those times, and Tertullian, who followed him shortly afterward, praise in their *Apology*, chapter 6. Lucius Caecilius likewise praises it in his book *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, when they relate that the Church, restored in this way, flourished more splendidly:

> “so that she stretched out her hands toward the East and the West, and there was now no corner of the earth so remote that the religion of God had not penetrated it.”

[Col. 1230B]

The Acts, as reviewed, record the departure from this life of the virgin Praxedes two years after the death of blessed Pius. She therefore died in the year 152 of the Christian era.

If this year indicated by the Acts is accepted, there is no reason for surprise that her father Pudens could have been baptized by the Apostle Paul and have Peter as a guest in his house. Quadratus, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 3, in the *Apology* that he presented to Hadrian then reigning, expressly affirms that some of those who had been healed by Christ the Lord or restored to life had survived into his own time. Hadrian’s rule was separated from those events by at least eighty-eight years from the year of the Lord’s Passion, which we established above as the year 28 of the common era.

The year 152, the last year of Praxedes’ life, was separated by the same interval from the year 65, which we saw marked by the martyrdom of the apostles, when Nerva and Vestinus were consuls. The death of Pudentiana occurred five years earlier. The end of the life of Pudens was much nearer still; the Acts report that he was survived for a long time by both daughters, before Pius dedicated the baptismal font in the same house at their request, around the year 145, as we have inferred from the Acts.

[Col. 1230C]

Therefore, if Quadratus reached Hadrian’s reign in vigorous old age—he who had lived with those healed by Christ the Lord nearly ninety years earlier—then under Antoninus, who succeeded Hadrian after twenty-one years of his rule, the daughters of Pudens could certainly have survived. They were separated by a shorter interval from the death of the apostles, which followed Christ’s death by thirty-seven years. Pudens himself, in whose paternal house the apostles had been honored as guests, could have been baptized by Paul and lived for approximately seventy-five years, into the beginning of Antoninus Pius’s reign.

An ancient painting, still surviving behind the apse of the titular church of Saint Pudentiana, in a chapel opened among the ruins of the Baths of that same house for the use of the faithful at the very dedication of the font under Pius, supports this chronology. Indeed, constant tradition holds that the chapel had been assigned to the same purpose by the apostles Peter and Paul. The painting is explained by a pair of verses, whose antiquity Ciampinus discusses in his explanation of a double sarcophagus depicting the Christian rite of baptism. He considers it to extend beyond the tenth century of the Christian era, although the verses display Leonine rhyme.

[Col. 1230D]

They are as follows:

> *Paulus nascentes plebis natasque Pudentem*  
> *Auxit mactatos hic vivo fonte renatos.*
>
> Paul increased Pudens, the people’s newborn and daughters; here [he increased] those offered and reborn in the living font.
>
> [The exact compressed Latin is preserved because its grammar and the relation of *Pudentem*, *natasque*, and *mactatos* are materially uncertain.]

There are, however, much older monuments that clearly establish the apostolic origin of this most ancient titular church and font, as well as the celebrated dedication under Pius at the request of the holy virgins Praxedes and Pudentiana, when it was assigned to the presbyter Pastor. From this circumstance the titular church received its various names: that of Pudens, that of Pudentiana, and that of Pastor.

To pass over the martyrologies of Bede, Usuard, Ado, and others, since they were drawn from the Acts already cited, the subscriptions of the presbyters of this titular church, preserved in Roman councils from the fifth century onward, demonstrate the same origin and nomenclature. Thus they subscribe the synodal acts under Pope Symmachus:

> Asterius, presbyter of the titular church of Saint Pudens.  
> Justinus, presbyter of the titular church of Saint Pudens.

[Col. 1231A]

In an old inscription carved in marble under Gregory VII, which can still be seen and is reported by Abbot Piazza in *Hierarchia Cardinalis*, page 494, the church is said to have been distinguished by the name of Pastor. In the lists of stations and in the *Book of the Roman Order* it is called Saint Pudentiana, just as it is in the ancient apse mosaic constructed in the time of Siricius and restored by Adrian I. Since the history, origin, and location of the titular church can be perceived in that mosaic, it ought to be counted, together with Baronius and Panvinius, among the principal documents for the matters discussed above.

Although in the new construction of the principal altar the lower part of that mosaic has been concealed, the portion that remains still displays the images and symbols belonging to the history of the titular church.

The view of the Patrician quarter of the ancient City is represented there, at the foot of the Viminal and Esquiline hills. This is shown by the substructure depicted there, which encircles the hill with enormous squared stones. Traces of this encircling wall can still be seen by those proceeding from the titular church of Saint Pudentiana along the side of the Viminal toward the nearby titular church of Saint Lawrence in Panisperna; they have not been entirely destroyed on the left-hand side along the Sixtine Road.

[Col. 1231B]

Magnificent buildings rise upon the substructure on both sides, namely the houses of the patricians, from which the quarter derived its name. According to Festus, Servius Tullius “ordered the patricians to live here below the Esquiline, so that, if they plotted anything new, they might be crushed from the higher ground.”

The magnificence of the buildings represented in this quarter and in the mosaic is also confirmed by an ancient inscription reported by Gruterus, CLXXIIII, 9, and mentioned by Ugonius and others as having been found in this same titular church of Saint Pudentiana, when Cardinal Cajetan was constructing that splendid chapel, counted among the more elegant structures of the City:

> `[lacuna] S. VAL. MESSALA V. C. PRAEFECTVS VRBI [lacuna] SPLENDOREM PVBLICVM IN VICO PATRICIO VICTORIAE ET FIERI ET ORNARI PROCVRABIT.`  
> [Two lacunae occur in the inscription.] Saint Valerius Messala, illustrious man and prefect of the City, arranged for the public splendor in the Patrician quarter for Victory both to be created and adorned.

Among these magnificent buildings there is represented the life-giving sign of the cross, indicating the titular church of Pudens. Beneath it Christ the Lord sits upon a chair, covered in the customary manner with cushions, as upon a throne, and holds an open book in his hand, on which are read the words:

> *Dominus conservator ecclesiae Pudentianae.*  
> The Lord, protector of the Church of Pudentiana.

[Col. 1231C]

This corresponds to another inscription of Pope Siricius, reported in Gruter’s *Appendix*, folio MCLXXII, 7, by Florentinius in the ancient Martyrology under 26 November, and by others:

> *Siricius pia nunc persolvit munera sanctis. / Gratia quo major sit bona martyribus. / Omnipotens DEUS HUNC CONSERVET TEMPORE MULTO / Moenia sanctorum qui nova restituit.*  
> Siricius now fulfills pious gifts to the saints; that his grace may be the greater for the good martyrs. Almighty God, preserve him for a long time, he who restored anew the walls of the saints.

The name of Siricius, the restorer, carved in large letters on marble tablets, still survives. These tablets once enclosed two ambos, or stone pulpits, fashioned from the marbles of the ancient building, as Panvinius records in *On the Seven Churches of the City*, page 266:

> *salvo Siricio episcopo ecclesiae sanctae.*  
> Siricius, bishop of the holy Church, being preserved.

[Col. 1231D]

The nearby marble also preserves the name of the presbyter Leopardus, namely the man whom Innocent, the successor of Siricius after Anastasius, sent to Milan to serve as legate of the Apostolic See together with Crescentius and Maximus at the council convened there in the case of Jovinianus. In letters addressed to blessed Ambrose, Innocent calls Leopardus his brother and fellow presbyter.

Siricius employed this same man—whether as titular presbyter or as superintendent of the building—in overseeing the repair and adornment of this sacred church, when, following the example of his predecessors, he decorated the apse by adding this mosaic work.

Accordingly, around Christ the Lord as he sits and declares himself the protector of the Church of Pudentiana, ten men clad in tunics and cloaks sit on either side. Those nearest the Redeemer’s sides are identified by the names inscribed beneath them as Peter and Paul.

[Col. 1232A]

Before the new ornaments were added to the high altar approximately sixty years ago and concealed those names, the knight Cassianus a Puteo carefully had them copied from the original mosaic and assembled them with the other monuments of sacred antiquity in those precious volumes that now give distinction to the Alban library.

There was also a symbol of a lamb crowned with a halo and of a dove descending upon it from heaven. This was copied 120 years ago by Paolo de Angelis in his manuscript *On the Titular Churches of the Presbyters of the City* in the Liberian archive. It signified baptism, sanctified by Christ the Lord through the grace of the Holy Spirit, descending upon him in the Jordan in a similar form—the same grace that he bestows here in the administration of the sacrament.

The eight men clothed in tunics and cloaks in apostolic fashion, whom some refer to the remaining apostles although they do not complete the number exactly, may perhaps have been intended by the maker of the mosaic to represent the eight immediate successors of Peter, counted from Linus to Telesphorus. Pudens, while still alive, received these men at his house for the sacred mysteries and for the celebration of the assemblies of the faithful.

[Col. 1232B]

Since the Acts cited above place the death of Pudens long before the year 145, that death appears to have preceded the end of Hyginus. For that reason, together with the other bishops received into heaven before Pudens, the image of Hyginus, who was ninth from the apostles, was not represented in the titular church of Pudens.

Two veiled virgins, Praxedes and Pudentiana, each standing beside one of the apostles, crown Peter and Paul with laurel. This was done both in accordance with the ancient custom of honoring guests by crowning them and in accordance with the practice of Christians toward images of Christ the Lord and his saints. The glass roundels found in the cemeteries of the martyrs, together with the icons painted there and visible in the crypts of the faithful in the works of Severanus and Bosio, clearly demonstrate this custom.

For this reason the Apostle, drawing a metaphor from military practice, wrote that a crown of righteousness had been reserved for him by the Lord. On this subject one should especially consult the highly learned interpreter of antiquities, the senator Filippo Buonarroti, in his explanation of plates 15 and following in his celebrated work on the glass roundels and figures excavated in the cemeteries of the holy martyrs around the City.

[Col. 1232C]

The emblems and figures of the mosaic adorning the apse of the titular church are completed by the four animals described in the Apocalypse and bearing the symbols of the Evangelists. These figures appear in most mosaics and paintings of the ancient Church, especially in Rome.

By these documents, therefore, the lodging of the apostles at the house of Pudens, and the frequenting of this titular church by Christian assemblies even before the time of Pius—and much more solemnly after he had properly dedicated the font—are confirmed. The same documents confirm the assertions of the catalogues and of Anastasius concerning the Baths of Novatus, converted by Pius into a church in the Patrician quarter at the request of Praxedes in honor of her sister Pudentiana, and concerning the dedication of the sacred font for the solemn administration of baptism as Easter approached, after Telesphorus had shortly before ordered the same rites to be celebrated during the seven weeks of Lent. Tertullian mentions them; a later age listed them in the ritual books under the name of the scrutinies.

[Col. 1232D]

I may add two observations from the ritual books of the *Roman Order*, which greatly illuminate what has been related about this titular church and the solemn Easter baptism celebrated there.

The first point I propose for observation is that the beginning of the scrutinies is assigned to the day after the station at the titular church of Pudens, or Saint Pudentiana, on the Tuesday of the week after the Third Sunday of Lent. This station was celebrated in the age of Gregory the Great, the restorer of such stations, and has continued to be celebrated in our own time for the eleven hundred years counted from Gregory the Great, with the clergy of the Liberian basilica proceeding solemnly there with a litany.

The purpose was evidently that, while the clergy made supplication at the titular church of Pudens—where that solemn rite had been performed by Pope Pius according to the regulations of Telesphorus—a model for the holy performance of the mysteries might be drawn from the example and memory of the apostles who had been guests there, and of their successors who administered the grace of baptism in that place.

The second point to be observed is the meeting with the regional notary on Holy Easter as the Roman pontiff rode from the Lateran to the Liberian basilica to offer sacrifice to God according to custom. The notary announced the number of those baptized during the preceding night at Saint Mary’s.

[Col. 1233A]

The most ancient Roman Order among those published by Reverend Father Mabillon in volume II of the *Musaeum Italicum* prescribes the following announcement:

> On the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, as he—the Roman pontiff—proceeds to Saint Mary’s, the regional notary stands in the place called Merolanas. This place is on the Esquiline hill, not far from the basilica of Saint Mary Major, where there is the church of Saint Matthew, called at Merolanas, as Mabillon correctly notes.
>
> After greeting the pontiff, the notary says: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, last night at Holy Mary, the Holy Mother of God, this number of male infants and this number of female infants were baptized.”
>
> The pontiff replies: “Thanks be to God.”

[Col. 1233B]

Since, when the pontiff departed from the Lateran patriarchate, the baptisms performed at the other fonts of the City were not reported, but only the fruitfulness in Christ of the Liberian font—which, after the construction of the basilica, stood between the neighboring titular churches of Praxedes and Pudentiana and in some manner took the place of those ancient fonts—one can scarcely suspect any other reason for such a rite than that it was intended to testify to the ancient origin of the solemn Easter baptism celebrated by the primitive Church at the nearby titular church of Pudens.

For just as the holy apostles and Pius had baptized there, so Urban I, whose ancient image is represented behind the apse together with Tiburtius and Valerianus, and likewise Stephen I, were accustomed to baptize there at Easter, as the proper lessons of this Church relate in the feast of the translation of the holy virgins.

[Col. 1233C]

For this same reason, I think, it was established that the pontifical Mass and station on the Sunday of the Resurrection should be celebrated in the aforementioned Liberian basilica rather than at the Lateran or Vatican basilicas. The memory of Pope Pius celebrating the Easter solemnity at the titular church of Pudens and proclaiming there that it should not be celebrated by the faithful outside Sunday prevailed. Thus his successors were drawn not only to the example but also to the place frequented by the apostles, so that the authority of the law might be made more illustrious by the sight of the lodging offered to Peter, the founder of the Roman Church.

Having made these observations in passing, I think it is strongly confirmed that the Librarian’s assertion concerning the dedication of the font and titular church by Pope Pius at the request of the household of Pudens is correct. This occurred on the occasion of the solemn celebration of Easter baptism in the Patrician quarter, where Peter and Paul had made both the Esquiline and Viminal hills more illustrious through catechesis and baptism than Servius Tullius had once done by establishing the residence of the patricians there.

[Col. 1233D]

All the documents agree: the catalogues, manuscripts, mosaics, paintings, and inscriptions concerning this titular church, as well as the monuments preserved in the church itself. To these may be added the response of Justin Martyr, a contemporary of those times, to the prefect of the City, identifying the place of his lodging at these same Baths of Timothy, which were frequented by Christian assemblies. All students of ecclesiastical history, especially under the guidance of the ancient Acts that we have recited, decide this with unanimous agreement.

If we have noted that certain chronological errors in the Acts must be corrected—errors apparently arising from the homonymy of the Antonines, confused by a writer who lived at least two centuries later—this should not seem surprising. Writers otherwise distinguished for careful diligence in investigating the documents of the events they narrated have sometimes suffered what is human, perhaps through a lapse of memory that placed too much confidence in itself, even concerning matters they believed they had thoroughly verified.

I shall give an example from the accurate and celebrated writer Florentinius. In his notes on the Kalends of August, while treating the two titular churches of Pudentiana and Praxedes in a work filled with varied and solid learning, he writes:

[Col. 1234A]

> The two churches of Saint Pudentiana and Saint Praxedes—this one on the Esquiline and the Carinae, the other at the foot of the Viminal hill—contend with one another among writers for priority of antiquity.
>
> Baronius, both in his notes and in his *Annals*, prefers the titular church of Pastor at the Baths of Novatus, or the church of Saint Pudentiana, as the older one. Panvinius, in the final chapter of *On the Seven Churches*, calls it older than all the churches of the City. He also testifies that tradition handed down by the ancestors held that, in the small chapel there adorned with mosaic work, Saint Peter first offered the unbloody sacrifice in Rome.
>
> Yet in the church of Saint Praxedes there is shown, not only on the right as one enters, a wooden altar in the form of a chest on which the prince of the apostles is said to have celebrated Mass, but also on the left a marble inscription asserting its antiquity above that of the other churches:
>
> “In this once most ancient of the churches of the City, in the house of Saint Pudens the senator, father of the holy Novatus and Timothy and of the holy virgins Pudentiana and Praxedes, was the first lodging of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, for the baptism of martyrs and Christians and for Masses and the sacred assembly.
>
> “Beneath the altar lie three thousand bodies of holy martyrs and an abundant quantity of the blood of the saints,” etc.

When I read these statements so confidently published by a celebrated author, I admit that I distrusted my own experience. I had lived in the City for nearly forty years and, during the twelve immediately preceding years, had been a canon of the Liberian basilica. I had repeatedly spent time inspecting both titular churches adjoining the Liberian basilica and their sacred antiquities.

[Col. 1234B]

I had never heard anything in the titular church of blessed Praxedes about a wooden altar or an inscription. Yet I remembered having often seen and read both of them in the titular church of blessed Pudentiana.

Nevertheless, I consulted the deeply religious monks of the Vallombrosian order, inhabitants of Saint Praxedes, and asked them whether they preserved among the sacred relics a wooden altar of blessed Peter or, among the monuments of that church, the inscription reported by Florentinius. They replied that nothing of the kind was preserved there.

[Col. 1234C]

In the other church, however, the titular church of Saint Pudentiana, the inscription is visible to everyone entering on the left, carved in Latin and rendered in Italian on the right. Likewise, beneath the altar table dedicated to blessed Peter, erected in a chapel to the left of those praying before the high altar, a wooden panel is kept. It is said to have been used by that same prince of the apostles while he was performing the sacred rites in the house of Pudens.

I do not wish these remarks to be understood as an attack upon a man who has rendered the most distinguished service to sacred history. Rather, I offer them as a particularly striking example to show that even intelligent and diligent men of our own age have sometimes suffered what is human. Trusting too greatly in their own memory or in that of others, they neglected to examine with their own eyes the monuments of the Roman Church or to verify them by repeated inspection when they undertook to write about those same monuments.

We therefore seem justified in asserting what we have often placed before our eyes and subjected to examination concerning the monuments surviving in the basilicas and titular churches that we have frequented for nearly forty years.

[Col. 1234D]

If the ancient writers of the pontifical succession and chronology in the patriarchal basilicas, and the ancient abridgers or paraphrasts of the Acts who were hurriedly admitted into the archives, had been able to enjoy such prolonged observation, I do not doubt that they would have left to posterity catalogues more thoroughly purified and Acts more completely freed from error.

What they were prevented from doing because necessity compelled them to return quickly to their own places, or because they lacked the power to return to the City, may we be permitted to supply—men nourished in Rome and led for many decades through the embrace of the Roman Church among the crypts of the martyrs, the ancient titular churches, and the basilicas.

May we be permitted to testify to our excellent mother our obedience and gratitude, so that whatever she preserves as evidence of historical truth may not be concealed through our negligence, and may be freed, with the greatest diligence possible, from the blemishes carelessly introduced by writers either of a less cultivated age or of one removed from the subject.

[Col. 1235A]

The occasion now invites us, in connection with the Acts and Life of which we are speaking, describing the purpose by which the holy virgins Praxedes and Pudentiana bound themselves to God in their profession of chastity, and the place of burial that they obtained near their parents in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, to insert in these notes an ancient painting discovered by Aringhi and Bosio in that same cemetery and described and explained in volume II, page 395, of *Subterranean Rome*.

The painting greatly illuminates the rites of the earlier pontiffs in veiling virgins who had vowed perpetual chastity to God. It also displays the seat or cathedra of those pontiffs, their clothing, and the custom of their hair-cutting; these may likewise be seen in their images at the basilica of Saint Paul and in other ancient mosaics entirely consistent with this painting.

I reserve for their proper place matters concerning the clothing and tonsure of the pontiffs. Here I shall briefly set out what concerns the veiling of virgins as they embraced the institution of virginity dedicated to God. In what words could I express this more suitably than those reported by Aringhi in his explanation of the same painting? They are as follows:

[Col. 1235B]

> The aforementioned image, if the matter is carefully examined, represents Praxedes or her sister Pudentiana, both of whom, with the unstained purity of their minds and the firm purpose of their hearts, devoted their virginity to Christ.
>
> But so that the reader, by considering the matter more deeply, may reach the very path of truth, there is presented to the eyes of those looking a standing woman holding a kind of veil in her hand. The pontiff—perhaps blessed Pope Pius himself—seated upon a throne places his hand upon her. Beside him a certain presbyter is likewise represented standing upright: Pastor, if it is permissible for us to interpret the figure in this way.

## Exact inscription and documentary-form register

The following short documentary forms are retained exactly because their spelling, lacunae, or syntax carry evidence beyond the English translation:

- Synodal subscriptions: *Asterius presbyter tituli sancti Pudentis. Justinus presbyter tituli sancti Pudentis.* (“Asterius … Justinus, presbyter[s] of the titular church of Saint Pudens.”)
- Mosaic book: *Dominus conservator ecclesiae Pudentianae* (“The Lord, protector of the Church of Pudentiana”).
- Messala inscription: `[lacuna] S. VAL. MESSALA V. C. PRAEFECTVS VRBI [lacuna] SPLENDOREM PVBLICVM IN VICO PATRICIO VICTORIAE ET FIERI ET ORNARI PROCVRABIT.` The source has one lacuna before the name and another after *VRBI*; *V. C.* abbreviates the honorific translated “illustrious man.”
- Siricius epigram: *Siricius pia nunc persolvit munera sanctis. / Gratia quo major sit bona martyribus. / Omnipotens DEUS HUNC CONSERVET TEMPORE MULTO / Moenia sanctorum qui nova restituit.*
- Ambon inscription: *salvo Siricio episcopo ecclesiae sanctae* (“with Siricius, bishop of the holy Church, preserved/safe”).
- Baptismal verses: *Paulus nascentes plebis natasque Pudentem / Auxit mactatos hic vivo fonte renatos.* The compressed syntax remains uncertain; the translation above does not silently regularize *Pudentem*, *natasque*, or *mactatos*.
- Easter notification: *In nomine Domini nostri Jesu Christi baptizati sunt hesterna nocte in sancta Dei genitrice Maria infantes masculi numero tanti, feminae tantae. … Deo gratias.* (“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, last night in [the church of] holy Mary Mother of God, this many male infants and this many female infants were baptized. … Thanks be to God.”)
- Florentinius’s marble text: *In hac ecclesiarum Urbis vetustissima olim domo S. Pudentis senatoris, patris SS. Novati, et Timothei, et SS. Pudentianae et Praxedis virginum, fuit SS. apostolorum Petri et Pauli hospitium primum ad martyrum et Christianorum baptismum, et ad missas sacramque synaxim. Sub altari jacent tria millia corpora SS. martyrum, et copiosus sanctorum sanguis.* Its complete English meaning is given in the quoted passage above.

## Chronological-name adjudication

The source says that the Life substituted “Antoninus Verus,” meaning Marcus Aurelius, for the reigning Antoninus Pius, while Lucius Verus, son of Aelius Verus, was adopted together with Marcus Aurelius. The parenthetical relative *qui et Verus dictus est, et tribunitiae potestatis annos 15 cum patre Caesar exegit* attaches grammatically to the immediately preceding Marcus Aurelius: “Marcus too was called Verus and, as Caesar, spent fifteen years with his [adoptive] father in tribunician power.” The proposed reassignment of this clause to Lucius was therefore rejected.

## Source column map

- **[Col. 1227C]–[Col. 1229B]** the documentary Acts, the two virgins, the fonts, and the titular churches; **[Col. 1229C]–[Col. 1230A]** the Antonine chronology; **[Col. 1230B]–[Col. 1230D]** Pudens’s family, apostolic chronology, the ancient painting, and its baptismal verses.
- **[Col. 1231A]–[Col. 1232C]** the titles of Pudens, Pudentiana, and Pastor, the Messala and Siricius inscriptions, the apse mosaic, Peter and Paul, the virgins, and the evangelist symbols; **[Col. 1232D]–[Col. 1233C]** the Roman rites of Easter scrutiny, baptism, and station; **[Col. 1233D]–[Col. 1234D]** the converging evidence, Florentinius’s location error, and the author’s repeated inspection; **[Col. 1235A]–[Col. 1235B]** the cemetery painting and the rite of veiling virgins.

I had promised in the notes on Clement that I would here restore what needed to be said about the institution of the vow of perpetual virginity, adopted by devout virgins in the Catholic Church around the beginnings of our religion. Certain unfair assessors of this evangelical counsel have claimed that it belongs to an age other than the one under discussion; consequently, they denied that Pope Clement had veiled the virgin Domitilla. The presbyter Leopardus, whose name we see engraved beneath Pope Siricius in this inscription of Saint Pudentiana, was sent as legate by that same pontiff in the matter of Jovinian, who, through heretical perfidy, was drawing God’s handmaids away from this holy purpose. He and his followers were most unjustly hostile to the Virgin of virgins, their model, and for this reason were condemned both by the supreme pontiff and by the legates at the council, as the synodal letter to Siricius testifies. By his initiative, therefore, he provides us with the occasion to defend the honor of this kind of profession against those who deny it in the age of the apostolic men.

That this is an evangelical counsel, suggested by Christ the Lord to the faithful who aspire to a more perfect life, the Apostle plainly teaches in 1 Corinthians 7: “Concerning virgins I have no commandment of the Lord, but I give counsel, as one who has obtained mercy from the Lord to be faithful”; and in 1 Timothy 1: “Refuse younger widows,” etc.; “for when they have grown wanton against Christ, they desire to marry, bearing condemnation because they have rejected their first faith.” The places produced and explained by the holy Fathers and councils prove that this is the Lord’s counsel, especially that saying of Matthew 19: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.” Chrysostom, Jerome, Augustine, and Epiphanius explain this brilliantly, so that, as Bellarmine shows in *On Monks*, book XI, chapter 27, even heretics cannot deny the meaning and consensus of the Fathers concerning it.

As for the practice of this counsel among the holy faithful of both sexes who lived with Christ the Lord—namely, the most blessed Virgin, his mother; Saint John the Baptist; the apostles; and others stirred by their example toward perfection through the constant profession both of this counsel and of voluntary poverty and obedience—the voice of the Fathers and councils is unanimous. Heretics, however, who refuse to listen to the Church in order to twist the divine Scriptures by the private spirit of their pride and accommodate them to their pleasures, miserably grope in the light shed by others. Most of them nevertheless do not dare deny that, toward the end of the second century and the beginning of the third, the writings of Cyprian, as well as those of Tertullian and others, establish the dedication of virgins. Thus they confine their denials within the limits of the first century after Christ, or little beyond the middle of the second.

When the Essenes in Syria, the disciples of Mark in Egypt, and the adherents of the same profession and their founders are brought against them—those who shortly afterward spread this manner of life throughout the world—they mock themselves and others by denying, at least among women, the vow of chastity and the custom of dedicating women to it through the solemn rite and ministry of pontiffs. Yet Jerome also demonstrates that the monasteries of Egypt and Syria professed the sanctity of an ancient custom, not only for men but also for virgins and widows:

> “It is the custom,” he says in his letter to Sabinian, “in the monasteries of Egypt and Syria that both the virgin and the widow who have vowed themselves to God, renouncing the world and trampling underfoot all the world’s delights, offer their hair to be cut by the mothers of the monasteries. Thereafter they do not go about with their head uncovered, contrary to the Apostle’s command, but with it bound and veiled alike.”

The acts of our virgins and martyrs of the Western Church in the earlier centuries testify to the same thing. And, so that nothing might be lacking for confirming the tradition and example of this holy purpose and rite, the testimony of paintings, expressed by holy martyrs in the crypts of the faithful, repeats the same truth even for those inexperienced in letters. Thus the very walls answer with unmistakable affirmation the brazen inventions of the heretics who deny these things. Nor was more needed to bring the fact plainly to the memory of the faithful of that time, even if they had been uneducated and unfamiliar with letters, since they clearly knew that the pagan pontiffs customarily placed the *flammeum* veil upon their own Vestal Virgins. The profession of virginal chastity therefore appeared worthy of honor even to those who were drawn toward the pursuit of a more perfect life and prepared for it by the light of reason—even though evangelical faith had not yet increased that light—being touched nevertheless by a kind of faint radiance, as Jerome proves learnedly through a lengthy enumeration in book [lacuna] I, *Against Jovinian*.

Therefore, as long as the people of Iconium celebrate their Thecla with Paul; the people of Hierapolis, with Polycrates, the two virgin daughters of Philip mentioned by Eusebius in book III, chapter 21; the people of Aquileia, Dorothea, Euphemia, and Erasma; and we, near the confession of blessed Peter, the virgin Petronilla; and, opposite the Pontine islands on the shore of Anxur, Domitilla, likewise known to Eusebius together with her companion Theodora; on the Viminal and Esquiline hills, Praxedes and Pudentiana; on the Aventine and Caelian hills, Balbina and Theodora—women illustrious in inscriptions, memorials, and tombs—we shall not lack examples of virginity dedicated to God in the first and second centuries of Christ, confirmed by so many genuine documents. Later ages also became illustrious through Cecilia, Eugenia, Agnes, Susanna, Anastasia, and Bibiana.

For these women did not use a different Gospel, which they carried in their hearts, in dedicating their chastity from that used by the earlier women whose examples and footsteps the later ones followed and whose tombs they approached. From the moment our Savior, hanging upon the cross and pouring out his blood, once again dedicated the Virgin Mother standing beneath the cross—as though by a pontifical sprinkling—to be the model of virgins, and entrusted her to the virgin disciple, replacing for the Virgin Mother this very son, adopted in place of her own and loved by him above the others for the honor of virginity, countless virgins arose in imitation of both. They were as numerous as those whom he records in the Apocalypse that he saw around the Lamb on Mount Zion: “These have not been defiled with women, for they are virgins, and they follow the Lamb wherever he goes. These were purchased from among mankind as firstfruits for God and for the Lamb.”

If anyone, amid such abundant light from Scripture and examples, does not see the Christian faith and the calling to pursue the evangelical counsel of virginity, among those who aspired to a more perfect life, brought forth as it were in a twin birth, he will also stop his ears against Jerome, who speaks plainly against Jovinian, the enemy of this counsel, in book I:

> “It is a great act of faith and a great virtue to be the purest temple of God, to offer oneself wholly as a burnt offering to the Lord, and, according to the same Apostle, to be holy in body and spirit. These are the eunuchs who, thinking themselves a dry tree because of their barrenness, hear through Isaiah that a place has been prepared for them in heaven in place of sons and daughters. Their type is Ebed-melech the eunuch in Jeremiah, and that eunuch of Queen Candace in the Acts of the Apostles, who, because of the strength of his faith, obtained the name of man. To these even Clement, the successor of the Apostle Peter, whom the Apostle Paul mentions, writes letters; and he composed almost all his discourse on the purity of virginity. After him came many apostolic men, martyrs, and men distinguished both for holiness and eloquence, whom it is very easy to know from their own writings.”

Thus far Jerome, who, instructed by the sight and experience of nearly all the Churches of East and West, brought the traditions he had received, flowing continuously from the apostolic age to his own, and confirmed them.

Meanwhile, in the inscription of Pudentus, or Pudentiana, dedicated by Pius, and in the cemetery of Priscilla, where the holy virgin was buried with her virgin sister and their parents, we enjoy the sight of evidence expressed in these paintings and mosaics: both in the rite of veiling a virgin, which the cemetery painting displays, and in the wearing of such a garment and veil, especially in the assembly of the Church. We see this garment and veil fittingly and consistently placed upon the heads of both virgins by the mosaicist in their images, represented in the apse of the inscription, adorned by Siricius and restored by Adrian.

[Note: [Col. 1238A]

Line 5.—So that holy Easter might be celebrated on Sunday. While the question concerning the day of Easter was being debated in Asia, Hermes, the brother of Pope Pius, wrote a book entitled *The Shepherd*, as presbyter of the holy Roman Church, the title belonging to his other brother. In it he reports that an angel appearing in the person and dress of a shepherd commanded him to persuade everyone that the feast of Easter ought to be celebrated on Sunday, because on that day Christ the Lord had risen from the dead. And he did so. Moved by this, Pope Pius, after first assembling a council of the clergy in the city, decreed that the Lord’s resurrection should be celebrated on the day called Sunday. This was later confirmed by his successors, the Roman pontiffs. See the following notes of Pagi.]

[Note: [Col. 1238A]

Line 5.—So that holy Easter might be celebrated on Sunday. [Col. 1238B] The earlier opinion is in fact more accurate and more widely accepted. Besides the authors already cited, it is supported by Hegesippus, who came to Rome under Anicetus; by the two Nicephoruses; and finally by all the more recent Latin and Greek writers. A decree concerning the celebration of Easter on Sunday is attributed to this pontiff, but all learned men agree that the decretal letter of Pius from which this is inferred was falsely attributed to him.

Moreover, although that decree is read as having been issued by Pius in the *Chronicle* of Eusebius in these words: “Pius decreed that the Lord’s Resurrection should be celebrated on Sunday, which was afterward confirmed by several pontiffs,” Arnaldus Pontacus nevertheless testifies in his notes that these words are not found in the manuscript copies of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* and must therefore be entirely deleted from it. This is especially clear because Eusebius himself, in book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 23, establishes that such a decree concerning the celebration of Easter on Sunday had been enacted by the apostles. For this reason Joseph Scaliger removed those words from the new edition of the Eusebian *Chronicle* [Col. 1238C].

Yet Gratian, in the chapter *On Consecration*, distinction 2, preserves a decree of Pope Pius concerning penance for one through whose negligence something of the Lord’s blood drips. It is as follows:

> “If, through negligence, something of the Lord’s blood should drip onto the ground, it is to be licked up with the tongue and the board scraped. If there is no board, so that it may not be trampled underfoot, the place is to be scraped away, consumed with fire, and the ashes placed inside the altar; and the priest is to do penance for forty days. If it should drip upon the altar, the minister is to absorb the drop, and do penance for three days. If it should drip upon the altar cloth and the drop reach another part, he is to do penance for four days. If it reach a third part, he is to do penance for nine days. If it reach a fourth part, he is to do penance for twenty days; and the linens touched by the drop are to be washed three times by the minister, with the chalice placed upon them, and the water of the washing is to be taken up and stored beside the altar.”

From this and other decrees concerning the rite and manner of expiating offenses committed against the sacrament of the Eucharist, and of remedying defects occurring in the sacrifice itself, Edmund Martene, in book I of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter 5, article 5, demonstrates how great was the reverence with which the ancients regarded the holy Eucharist. He rightly writes that this reverence ought to hold no minor place among the various considerations by which Christ’s real presence in the Eucharist may be established.

For, he says, if Christians in Tertullian’s time, as Tertullian relates in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3, anxiously suffered whenever anything from the Eucharist fell upon the ground; and if, as Origen relates in homily 13 on Exodus, the faithful believed—and rightly believed—that they were guilty whenever this happened through negligence, what was the cause of such great anxiety? What fault, what crime, made them guilty, and rightly made them guilty, if in the sacrament they had recognized nothing besides bread and wine and a mere figure? They therefore believed that there was something else, and something very great. And what was it? Nothing other than Christ’s real presence in the Eucharist. [Col. 1238D]]

[Note: [Col. 1239A]

Line 7.—“And he made a decree concerning the Church.” During the pontificates just mentioned, after Telesphorus, heretics sprang up everywhere.

> “When the Churches, like brilliant lights,” says Eusebius in book IV, chapter 7 of his *History*, “had spread their splendor throughout the whole world, and faith in our Savior and Lord Jesus Christ flourished greatly among the entire human race, the devil, hater of goodness, enemy of truth, and most bitter perpetual foe of human salvation, turned all his devices and deceptions against the whole Church. Just as previously he had fought against her through external storms of persecution and violent assaults, so now, when those avenues were closed to him, he attempted to attack her by another kind of ambush, using ruined men full of deceits. He strove to devise every path by which these impostors and fraudulent men, cleverly adopting the very name of our religion, might not only plunge the faithful headlong but also wholly turn the ignorant and inexperienced in the faith away from the entrance that lay open to God’s saving Word.”

They boldly disseminated their errors throughout the provinces. But if they came to Rome, since they did not wish to be seen as separated from the communion of this Church, they concealed and disguised their doctrine, whispering it secretly only when witnesses had been removed. If they were exposed, they pretended to make an *exomologesis* and retract it. But when repeated stumbling into the same errors they had shortly before condemned revealed that they had relapsed, they were condemned by the judgment of the pontiffs and expelled from the Church.

The judgments rendered at Rome were followed throughout the provinces. The Montanists, having obtained letters of peace and communion from the Roman see through such deceptions, had been received by the Churches of Asia and Phrygia. But when the fraud of those same heretics was detected, the letters of peace that had already been issued were recalled [Col. 1240A]. Tertullian, one of their own associates, bears witness to the event at the beginning of his work *Against Praxeas*.

To confound heretics and schismatics in the provinces, people had recourse to the holy see of Peter as the arbiter and guardian of doctrine. According to Irenaeus, the common conviction already prevailed that the tradition in the Church which had come from the apostles, together with the proclamation of truth, was preserved here in its native purity and transmitted to all generations through the succession of pontiffs. It was known that Christ the Lord had established this see so that it might be the visible demonstration that one faith and one rule of morals prevailed in the Church.

> “By indicating the faith and tradition of the Church founded at Rome, we confound them, and so forth. Through this order and succession, the tradition in the Church that comes from the apostles, and the proclamation of truth, has reached us. This is the fullest demonstration that the one and same life-giving faith, which has been preserved and transmitted in truth in the Church from the apostles until now, is present.”

Saint Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book III, chapter 3.

That ancient Father who wrote these words had undertaken a mission to the Roman see on behalf of the Church of Lyons, of which he was then a presbyter. Eusebius states in book V of his *History*, chapter 3, that “for this reason he was sent by the people of Lyons to Eleutherus, the Roman pontiff, whom they earnestly begged to establish peace and harmony firmly in the Churches,” where innovators had stirred up schisms and disturbances. Saint Jerome adds that he was sent by the martyrs to seek advice concerning difficult questions. (Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, under Irenaeus.)

These testimonies therefore demonstrate incontrovertibly that from these earliest times the see of Peter was regarded by the Church as the exterminator of heresies. “We confound the evil opinion,” and as the arbiter of the Church’s peace: “Peace and harmony would be established in the Churches.”]

[Col. 1213]

## 12.

Pius, an Italian by nation, son of Rufinus, brother of the Shepherd, from the city of Aquileia, held the see for nineteen years, four months, and three days [Note: [Col. 1213] B: nine years, six months, and fewer than three days]. He lived during the time of Antoninus Pius, from the consulship of Clarus and Severus [Note: [Col. 1213] B: from Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, and Lucius Verus, consuls from Silvanus and Augurinus to Pudens and Orfitus]. [Note: [Col. 1213] See Baronius, year 159.]

During his episcopate Hermes wrote a book containing the command given to him by an angel of the Lord, who came to him in the dress of a shepherd and instructed him that holy Easter should be celebrated on Sunday. Pius established that a heretic coming from the Jewish heresy should be received and baptized; and he issued a decree concerning the Church. He held five ordinations in the month of December: nineteen presbyters [Note: [Col. 1213] C, B: eighteen], twenty-one deacons [Note: [Col. 1213] C: twenty], and twelve bishops in various places [Col. 1215] [Note: [Col. 1215] C, B: fourteen]. He was also buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican on the fifth day before the Ides of July, and the see remained vacant for twelve days. [Note: [Col. 1215] Baronius, year 162.]

At the request of blessed Praxedes, he dedicated the Baths of Novatus in the Vicus Patricius in honor of her sister Saint Potentiana. There he offered many gifts and, frequently offering the sacrifice to the Lord, ministered there. Indeed, he also had a baptismal font constructed, blessed and consecrated it with his own hand, and baptized many who came to the faith in the name of the Trinity.

## XIII. SAINT SOTER. A.D. 175, THE THIRTEENTH YEAR OF THE REIGN OF MARCUS AURELIUS

[Note: [Col. 1241A]

Number 13, line 2: year 15; A, line 7; AB, 11. A: 21 days.

From the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuane codices:

Line 2: three months, 21 days; F: from the time of Saint; line 5: presbyters, 18; Mazarin: 19; deacons: 9; M: 19; line 6: places, 11; line 7: 21 days.

In Penia, from the Cavensis codex:

[Note: [Col. 1241B]

Line 3.—“He established that no nun, etc.” Three manuscript codices read “that no monk.” Yet the reading “nun” is to be retained, since the author took it from the second catalogue and the Palatine-Vatican codex, written in the eighth century, preserves it. It should be noted that in Soter’s time there were nuns, whether they were women who lived together in monasteries and in community under some mother-superior, whom Saint Optatus of Milevis mentions and says existed in Africa in the time of the Donatists, or sacred virgins who lived in their parents’ homes, attended church with the rest of the people, and had a place nearer to the sacred *Bema*, as did the monks of whom Dionysius speaks in his book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*.]

[Note: [Col. 1241B]

Line 3.—“He established that no nun should touch the sacred altar cloth, nor place incense in the [Col. 1241C] holy Church.” Soter decreed that no religious woman should touch the sacred vessels or the sacred altar cloth, or burn incense around the altars: canon *Sacratas*, distinction 23. The same decree was repeated by Boniface I, according to Anastasius in his *Life*.]

[Note: [Col. 1241C]

(From Bin.) Line 1.—Soter: the consolation of afflicted Churches, and, according to Dionysius of Alexandria, a great rewarder of the poor and needy.

Line 3.—“He established that no nun should touch the sacred altar cloth.” Not only nuns but also deaconesses, other laywomen and laymen, and even certain clerics were forbidden contact with the sacred vessels and the corporal. It is probable that the reason for issuing this constitution was that, as Baronius teaches under the year 173, women from the sect of Montanus were involving themselves in sacred functions.

(From Labbé.) Line 6.—“In the cemetery.” Beside the body [Col. 1241D] of blessed Peter. C. H.]
