## Chronological Notes

Soter’s chronology is made sufficiently certain by the documents produced above, both in the chronological sequence of the Roman pontiffs in the *Prolegomena* and in the chronological notes on Hyginus, Pius, and Anicetus. Their sum is as follows.

The consuls of the year 171, Severus II and Herennianus, assigned by all the catalogues and complete codices to the beginning of the episcopate of Eleutherus, his successor, show that the Paschal season around the end of April, from the Ascension of the Lord in that same year, must be assigned to him. To Soter, who attained martyrdom on 22 April, the consuls of the preceding year, Cethegus and Clarus, are rightly assigned as his final consuls.

The agreement of the codices and the mosaics of Saint Paul in counting nine years, three months, and twenty-one days [Col. 1242B] for the see of blessed Soter is as great as the monuments reviewed in the *Prolegomena* demonstrate, and scarcely could greater agreement be expected. For in two or three examples which, following the catalogue of Felix IV, rendered six months in place of three, it is easy to show that a copyist’s negligence caused the error: two preceding units, slightly inclined, were represented as the sign of the numeral five, V.

Therefore, counting backward from the day of his martyrdom, 22 April in the year 171, through nine full years, three months, and twenty-one days, we reach the beginning of Soter’s episcopate, which must be fixed on the Kalends of January, at the beginning of the year 162, when Rusticus and Aquilinus entered the consulship. Whether Soter was ordained bishop on that day, which coincided with the Circumcision of the Lord and the octave of his Nativity, or on the preceding Sunday, the last day of December, it is clear that, according to civil custom—which we still follow in recording the years of Christ’s Nativity—the era of Soter’s pontificate began near the Kalends of January.

[Col. 1242C] The see therefore remained vacant from the day of Anicetus’s martyrdom, which we place in the year 161, on 17 April, until the end of that same year, when the two Augusti were consuls, before Soter’s election.

We can easily suspect the reason for the delayed election from what was previously narrated concerning Pius and Anicetus in the historical notes, as well as from the chronological notes on Hyginus, where we related the following.

The heresiarch Marcion came to Rome while the apostolic see was vacant after the death of Hyginus. Disappointed both in the hope of obtaining communion from the Roman presbytery, by which he had been repulsed, and in the hope of attaining the first see, which he had coveted, he threatened to bring about an eternal schism. Although after a vacancy of three months he saw that Pius had been elected Hyginus’s successor, he remained stubborn in his audacity and drew many from the Catholic faith into his error. Then, returning to Pontus, he turned everything upside down, nor did he meanwhile cease repeatedly to incite and encourage his followers and emissaries in the city. Saint Polycarp, however, on coming to Rome under Anicetus, recalled many of them to the faith, as I mentioned above from Eusebius’s *History* and from the Fathers who were then present at Rome.

It is not surprising that, after Polycarp’s departure from the city and Anicetus’s death, Marcion should have recovered his courage to stir up with all his strength the eternal schism he had previously threatened. For Tertullian, writing in the following century, amply demonstrates that Marcionists and Valentinians, [lacuna] from the same school, continued for a long time to exist. At the beginning of his book *Against the Valentinians*, he says that their college was the most numerous among the heretics, because it consisted largely of apostates from the truth. It was therefore necessary to meet the devices, snares, and violence of so savage a man, who possessed both talent and eloquence, and of so many of his associates, who thought nothing of mixing human and divine matters, as minds commonly do when, as Tertullian warned concerning Valentinus, they are inflamed by presumption of revenge after being aroused by the desire for primacy [Col. 1243A].

The death of Antoninus Pius also increased the occasion for disturbances against the peace of the Church. He died before the Nones of March in that same year, 161, in which Anicetus, condemned in the following month, sealed the faith with his blood. From Anicetus’s martyrdom we may gather that after the death of the very mild emperor Antoninus—who, especially after the tenth year of his reign, had been accustomed to restrain and forbid the ministers and adherents of pagan superstition from persecuting Christians—those ministers sought to exercise freely under the new emperors Marcus and Lucius Verus the power to accuse us: bringing charges, alleging the crime of impiety, as they themselves claimed, and invoking the protection of the Roman laws against us before the magistrates.

The letter written by Marcus Aurelius, then reigning, to the common council of Asia and inserted by Eusebius in book IV, chapter 13 of his *History*, ordered that milder judgments be rendered concerning Christians. Eusebius wrongly attributes it to Antoninus Pius, as Valesius clearly demonstrates from the titles and from the number XV of the tribunician power joined with the third consulship. These titles and numbers belong to Marcus the son, not to Pius the father, who was counting his fifteenth tribunician power and also the seven preceding ones together with his fourth consulship.

The letter itself indicates that persecution had already been stirred up against Christians in Asia and by the governors of several provinces, and that at least some local persecutions had not entirely ceased under Pius. It also indicates that these persecutions had recently grown stronger under the brother Augusti, even if the letter is assumed to have been issued in the fifteenth year of tribunician power, which for Marcus Aurelius ran from 25 February 161—eleven days before Pius’s death—to 25 February 162.

Yet from the title *Armeniacus*, attributed to Marcus Aurelius in that same letter—a title he did not assume until three years later, after defeating Cassius Vologeses, who had occupied Armenia, as coins and inscriptions show—we shall infer that the letter was issued later and bore the number XXV rather than XV for the tribunician power, according to the following number.

In this letter, then, whether issued in the fifteenth year of tribunician power or later, the emperor first declares that several governors of provinces had previously written to his deified father concerning Christians who had been denounced and demanded for execution, asking what should be decided. He then adds: “Many have also reported to me concerning them, and I have replied to them in accordance with the constitution of my father.”

The constitution of his father Antoninus Pius had been: “Such people”—Christians—“are not to be subjected to any punishment unless they should appear to be attempting something against the order of the Roman Empire.” The pagans frustrated Antoninus’s indulgence as though it were temporary and had been removed with his death, since many still sought from Marcus, his successor, permission for accusations to be admitted against Christians.

The manner in which the paternal rescript was confirmed, used, or abused, both by provincial governors and by urban magistrates and the senate, is shown by the martyrdoms both of Justin, who pleaded a capital case before the senate and obtained his illustrious martyrdom within the first five years of the reign of the two brother Augusti under the prefect of the City, Quintus Junius Rusticus—an event which ecclesiastical historians variously assign to the years 163 or 165 of the Christian era—and by the extremely severe outbreaks of persecution that shook Asia.

Eusebius relates these in chapters 13 and 14, when, after Pius had died, Marcus Aurelius Verus—also called Antoninus—his son, succeeded him together with his brother Lucius. At that time, when extremely severe outbreaks of persecution had shaken Asia, Polycarp ended his life through martyrdom.

Here one must wonder that Pearson was so carried away by Eutychian arguments that, in order to reconcile them with the *Life of Anicetus*, he moved the date of Saint Polycarp’s passion back a full twenty years, although Eusebius reports Polycarp’s passion in the *Chronicle* under the seventh year of Marcus Aurelius. Nevertheless, most learned men accept Eusebius’s chronology even after considering the dissertations of Pearson and Dodwell against Valesius. Among them, especially learned is Father Ruinart, who in the *Acts of the Martyrs* no. 6, page 26, assigns Polycarp’s passion more probably to the year 166, after producing and comparing numerous authorities [Col. 1244A].

It would take too long to weigh everything presented in those dissertations with great learning, especially concerning the day of the martyrdom, which according to the *Acts* fell on the Great Sabbath and on 26 March, as well as concerning the year in which the proconsul of Asia, L. Statius Quadratus, was in office. He is named in the Latin edition of those *Acts* and had been consul in the year 142 under Pius.

Some, however, prefer to understand another Statius Quadratus: the father or uncle of T. Numidius Quadratus, who entered the consulship in the year 167 with Lucius Verus Augustus III, while, according to their view, the uncle administered Asia as proconsul in that same year, 167. Relandus, in his *Fasti*, directs readers to the fact that more about him can be found in the distinguished Le Moine’s *Prolegomena to Various Sacred Works*.

As for reconciling the day of the martyrdom with 26 March and the Great Sabbath, Pearson admits in dissertation 2, chapter 29, no. 3, that these two chronological indications in the *Acts* fit extremely well also the year of the Lord 158, the twenty-second year of Antoninus Pius. Yet he excludes that year as the date of the martyrdom because he claims that it cannot at all be combined with Statius Quadratus as proconsul.

But I do not see why Statius Quadratus could not have been sent a second time to the province as proconsul outside the regular allotment. P. Aquius Scaura, in Gruter 360, no. 3, had previously held the province of Cyprus as proconsul, and afterward was, “by decree of the Senate, for a period of five years, having been consul a second time, sent outside the allotment by the authority of Caesar and the Senate to restore the condition of the remainder of the province of Cyprus.”

Nor do I see why, in the year 164, to which I am happy to assign Polycarp’s martyrdom on the evidence of Eusebius, who mentions it around the beginning of the reign of the two brother Augusti, Marcus and Lucius Verus, it should not likewise be possible to assign to Statius Quadratus the proconsulship of Asia outside the regular allotment, perhaps conferred upon him by the authority of Marcus to restore the condition of the province and restrain the disturbances that had arisen there. Nor is there any reason why the two indications of the Paschal lunar fourteenth day cannot both be assigned to that year, when it fell on the Great Sabbath, both according to the true and mean motions of the moon and according to the cycle of Caesar.

I know that in that leap year the Sunday letter B changed to A on 24 February, and that for this reason 26 March, which in an ordinary year would have fallen on Saturday, coincided in that year with Sunday because of the intercalation of the leap day. But since the indication of the day, which in the Greek text of the *Acts* was marked as Xanthicus, is demonstrably corruptly rendered in the Latin translation by both Pearson and the others—when it is written “in the month of April, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May,” although it was said to have to be rendered “in the month of March, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April”—why could it not, according to our view, be rendered “in the month of March, on the eighth day before the Kalends of April”?

Certainly the fourteenth day of the Paschal moon falls on that date. According to both the true and mean motions of the moon, its new moon had preceded it on 12 March before that day was completed; and according to Caesar’s cycle, which we explained from the ancient Farnesian marble nineteen years ago in our book *On the Calendar and Caesar’s Cycle*, it was correctly marked as having been completed on 11 March.

Thus, in that same year, the fourteenth day of the moon coincided with the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April and with the Great Sabbath of the Jews, and would be Easter according to the Paschal custom of the Asians; for us, however, and for the other Churches, Christian Easter was to be celebrated on the following Sunday.

Furthermore, whatever year after Marcus Aurelius had begun his reign with his brother Lucius one may finally assign to the martyrdom of Polycarp—whether the year 164, as I think, or 166, 167, or 169, as the learned men reviewed by Ruinart judge—it is certain that in the letter of the Church of Smyrna concerning that martyrdom, addressed to the Churches of Pontus, one reads that it could already be hoped that blessed Polycarp’s martyrdom had brought the persecution to an end, as though by a kind of seal:

> “We have written to you, brothers, both about the other martyrs and about blessed Polycarp, who by his martyrdom, as though by a kind of seal, brought the persecution to an end.”

Thus both the martyrdom of others and the persecution had preceded it during the earlier years of Marcus Aurelius’s reign, although he, following his father’s example, had written to the provincial governors that “Christians were not to be troubled unless they should appear to be plotting something against the security of the empire.” For the law of that milder rescript remained in force even in the time of Commodus, as Eusebius relates. Yet he also shows that an exception had been prepared to evade the milder character of that rescript, even in the heart of the City and by the Senate itself. For although the senators paid no heed to the still-valid edict of Antoninus, since it had not been revoked, they nevertheless judged according to the old law that Christians, once formally accused, were by no means to be acquitted or released unless they withdrew from their purpose. Consequently, the accusation and threatened punishment of any individual Christian were exposed to the envy and hatred of private persons once he had been summoned before the court. This is strikingly confirmed by the famous example of Apollonius, who was executed by order of the Senate for asserting the Christian faith, while the law prescribing the ultimate penalty for those who accused Christians was still in force.

It is worthwhile to set out here Eusebius’s complete text, *Ecclesiastical History* V.21, excerpted from the Acts of the martyrs that he himself had collected:

> “When Commodus was ruling the Roman Empire, our affairs were in a more tranquil condition, and, by God’s grace, peace embraced all the Churches throughout the world. Meanwhile the saving word of God was drawing very many people from every class of society to the devout worship of the supreme God, so that many of those who excelled in rank and wealth in the city of Rome hastened to obtain salvation together with their entire household and family. But the most hostile demon to all good things, envious by his very nature, could not endure this. Accordingly, he once again armed himself by devising various devices against us. Finally, at Rome he brought to trial a certain Apollonius from among the faithful, who was regarded as outstanding in humane letters and philosophy, having stirred up against him a certain utterly depraved man, who seemed especially suited to such crimes and an apt servant of the demon. But the wretch, having brought his accusation at an inopportune time, was immediately put to death with his legs broken, since the emperor’s edict had established the capital penalty for those who brought such charges; Perennius having pronounced such a sentence against him. The martyr, however, most acceptable to God, after the judge had entreated him with many pleas and had asked him to give an account of his faith before the Senate, was condemned by the Senate to capital punishment after delivering before all an exceedingly elegant speech in defense of his faith. For among them an old law had been enacted that Christians who had once been summoned before the court were not to be released unless they withdrew from their purpose. Moreover, whatever he said in court, whatever he answered to Perennius when questioned, and the speech he delivered in the Senate in defense of our faith—anyone who wishes to know these things may learn them from the accounts of the ancient martyrs’ sufferings collected by us.”

Thus far Eusebius.

I have thought it worthwhile to explain these matters somewhat more fully, both for the sake of chronology and for the sake of history. I see that those who have written about the small number of martyrs according to a prejudice formed by their own inclinations, and who have attempted to deprive the Roman pontiffs, no less than many others throughout the provinces, of that crown of glory in the first and second centuries, generally rely—contrary to the records and traditions of all the Churches—on the laws of the Antonines, which issued milder decrees concerning us but harsher ones against those who accused our brethren. Yet, since these laws had not been revoked, the Senate both issued and followed its earlier decrees whenever distinguished Christians, such as Justin and Apollonius, were again brought before the courts through the machinations of private persons; and it inflicted capital punishment on such men, without opposition from the same emperor who had published milder edicts on behalf of our people. I have therefore judged these observations useful for freeing the times of Anicetus and Soter, and the martyrdoms and crowns of those and other pontiffs of the second century, from such unjust objections by critics.

From this may also be inferred and confirmed certain not implausible conjectures concerning the vacancy of the Roman See, which was prolonged for several months after the martyrdom of Anicetus in that same year 161, when Marcus began to rule with his brother Verus. Besides the followers of Marcion, who were eager to introduce the schism that he had threatened would be brought upon this holy Church forever, the turbulent zeal of the pagans, who after the death of Antoninus Pius were preparing themselves for accusations against Christians, delayed the designation of a successor. For the Roman clergy knew that whoever they elected hastily would be especially exposed to these dangers while the frenzy of the new accusers was still burning; whereas a pontiff whom they placed in the See after the attackers’ efforts to seek the death of the bishops and teachers of the Churches had subsided somewhat would be more safely concealed from the boldness of his enemies and protected from their ambushes.

Nothing, therefore, prevents us from following the evidence of the catalogues and of the other codices and monuments mentioned above, and from concluding that Soter was elected on the last Sunday of the year 161, while the beginning of his pontifical era is to be reckoned from the Kalends of January of the year 162, in the consulship of Rusticus and Aquilinus, as is plainly marked there. Then, after the completion of nine years, three months, and twenty-one days of his pontificate, his martyrdom is to be placed, in agreement with the ecclesiastical tables, in the year 171, on 22 April, the day on which he is commemorated.

## HISTORICAL NOTES BY THE SAME AUTHOR

**Line 2.**—“He was in the time of Severus, from the consulship of Rusticus and Aquilinus to that of Cethegus and Clarus.” The correctly recorded pair of consulships demonstrates the copyist’s error in substituting the name Severus for the names Marcus and Verus, which are distinctly expressed in the second catalogue of the age of Justinian, a catalogue copied by the Librarian.

**Line 3.**—“He decreed that no *monacha* should touch the consecrated cloth or place incense in the holy Church.” I had indicated in the notes on the Apostle’s command, renewed by Linus, concerning the veiling of women in the Church, that the first heresy of Simon—leader of the others—who led Selene about as the *Ennoia* of his own mind, had provided an occasion for guarding the faithful against it and for declaring openly in the assembly of the Church that women were entirely excluded from the priesthood. This was signified by the veil placed upon women’s heads while they prayed, so that they might understand that they were under the authority of a man; whereas men were to pray with uncovered heads, so that they might remember that Christ’s priesthood was reserved to them.

I added that, in imitation of Simon, the heresiarch Marcion and the Gnostics of the period under discussion had taken from this example—namely from Selene and Simon—the practice of assigning various priestly offices to their women; and that these ministries had been usurped by their ambitious women with such arrogance that Firmilian, writing to Saint Cyprian, said that it was evident that one woman belonging to the impious sect had gone so far in her audacity that she

> “frequently pretended to sanctify bread and to perform the Eucharist, and to offer sacrifice to the Lord without the sacrament of the customary prayer.”

The vigilant pastors of the Church, to whom the care of both sheep and lambs has been entrusted in the See of Peter, opposed to the evil arising—or arising again—of the Samaritan Simon in the school of Marcion and his companions an immediate remedy, namely the earliest decrees of apostolic discipline: clerics called by God into the lot of the Christian priesthood were to be distinguished from the others by an external sign upon the head as well. Anicetus accomplished this by again ordering that Peter’s tonsure be worn by clerics, as well as Paul’s.

Anicetus’s successor, Soter, took care to renew the laws excluding from contact with the consecrated ministry all other faithful who had not been called into the Lord’s portion—laws that Sixtus had enacted. The Sixtine law, which had looked either exclusively or chiefly to the care and diligence required in handling sacred things, so that nothing of the offering and consecrated gift, transformed into the body and blood of the Lord, might inadvertently fall away and collapse upon the ground—for this danger was guarded against by reserving contact with the vessels of the consecrated ministry to ministers alone, who by divine institution had been called to the priesthood and were diligently trained for its administration by the pontiffs—had to be strengthened by Soter so that it might also serve to restrain the heresies then arising, the abuse of Marcion, and the audacity of his female associates. For just as Marcion presumed to attain the episcopate, so they presumed to attain the priesthood. Accordingly, every office and priestly ministry, even the lesser ones, had to be forbidden to all women, although they might have been duly dedicated to God by the pontiffs through their profession of religious purity and the title of virginity.

It is clear that this is what is meant by the designation *monacha*—a term introduced later and transferred by the librarians from the phrasing of the second catalogue into this passage, since in the times under discussion such women were called servants of God, virgins consecrated to God, or deaconesses. This is clear both from what was noted above concerning Clement and Pius, where we indicated the custom, originating with the apostles, of dedicating virgins to God, and from what is to be observed below in the Life of Leo the Great, no. 67. There the designation *monacha* is explained as referring to one who, upon the dedication of her virginity, received the blessing of the veil placed upon her head, according to the rite shortly before demonstrated in the case of Pius from an ancient painting discovered in the crypts of the Holy Martyrs in the cemetery of Priscilla:

> “Here he decreed that a *monacha* should not receive the blessing of the veil for her head unless she had been proven in virginity for sixty years.”

**[Col. 1247B]**

**Line 6.**—“Who was also buried in the cemetery of Callistus, on the Appian Way.” This holy pontiff was buried on the Appian Way in the cemetery that he himself built and that was called by his own name, Soter’s Cemetery. After 670 years, Sergius, the second pontiff of that name, transferred him to the Church of Saints Sylvester and Martin in the Mountains, under the title *equitius*, as is clear from an ancient inscription there.

**[Col. 1247C]**

**Line 1.**—“Soter.” Concerning Soter and the Roman Church there is an illustrious testimony from Dionysius, bishop of the Corinthians. Although the Roman Church was extremely wealthy, it relieved the poverty of other Churches through its generosity, and was accustomed to send food and gifts to brethren condemned to the mines or sent into exile. Dionysius says, according to Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* IV.23:

> “Your blessed bishop Soter not only preserved this custom but even increased it: both by abundantly supplying gifts intended for the saints and by consoling, with blessed words, brothers arriving from abroad as a most loving father consoles his own children.”

Saint Dionysius wrote this in his letter to the Romans. Collections were made in the Roman Church for this purpose, and several sermons of Saint Leo the Pope concerning them survive. This praiseworthy custom, instituted from the earliest apostolic times, was also maintained during the final persecution under Diocletian, as Eusebius testifies in Book IV, chapter 23. At that time the Roman Church sent collections of money to Christians condemned to the mines of Palestine and throughout Egypt.

Besides Dionysius of Corinth, Dionysius of Alexandria also speaks of this custom of the Roman Church in his letter to Pope Stephen, which Eusebius quotes in Book VII, chapter 5:

> “All the provinces of Syria,” Dionysius says, “together with Arabia, for which you regularly provide necessities.”

Thus Valesius in his notes on Book IV, chapter 23, of Eusebius. Saint Soter is commemorated on 22 April.

**[Col. 1247D]**

After Sommier, in Book II of his *Dogmatic History of the Holy See*, had reported the testimonies to the dutiful veneration of Saints Polycarp and Irenaeus toward the Holy See of Rome, when they went there to obtain answers from the successors of Peter concerning questions that had arisen about discipline, he adds the following on page 138:

> “Indeed, even in those earlier centuries the Roman pontiffs were regarded as the common fathers of all the faithful, not only in preserving the life of the immortal spirit through Christ’s grace, but also in supplying the necessary supports of temporal life to the body. These supports were withdrawn from an almost countless number of confessors by the persecutors of the Church, when Christ’s faithful were reduced to the utmost poverty. Eusebius of Caesarea, an eyewitness, clearly demonstrates from examples that he himself saw and heard, as well as from those of earlier ages, that they fully correspond to the testimony of Dionysius, bishop of Corinth. Writing to the Roman faithful, Dionysius congratulates them on the custom prevailing among them, perpetually maintained from the origin of that Church, of taking care to transmit every kind of support to all the Churches and of individually supplying the brethren in need, especially those condemned to the mines, with the means of life. The excellent mother, the Roman Church, has always carefully provided this, never failing to observe it from the beginning of its foundation; and blessed Soter, imitating his predecessors, continued to preserve it in such a way that he even added an increase to the benefits of the earlier pontiffs.”

Then he gives the words of Eusebius in the Latin translation of the Ozonius edition:

> “Greatly approving the custom of the Romans, which has been constantly observed down to this persecution now raging in our time, Dionysius writes as follows: ‘Among you this custom has now become established, that you should benefit all the brethren in various ways and send the means of life to the many Churches situated in each city. Thus you plainly relieve not only the poverty of the needy but also assist the brethren who have been condemned to the mines; and through these supports of benevolence, which, as Romans, you have been accustomed to send everywhere from the time when the foundations of your Church were first laid, you diligently observe the custom of the Romans handed down by the Fathers. Your blessed bishop Soter has certainly both carefully preserved this custom until now and increased it wonderfully through his zealous devotion—not only by kindly supplying the resources assigned for the refreshment of the saints, but also by exhorting the brethren who came to him to virtue with blessed and pious speech, as an indulgent and merciful father speaks to his children.’”  
> *(Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History IV.22.)*

After producing these passages from Eusebius’s history, the eminent prelate Sommier adds the following observation in his notes on Soter, rightly selected; it also deserves to be included among observations useful for illustrating Dionysius’s letter:

> “In the portrait of this ancient and holy pontiff we behold the likeness of Clement XI, who today governs us from the same See. His virtue, full of humanity, his exceptional courtesy, his disposition toward generosity, his renowned eloquence, and his admirable ability to win hearts, to command minds, and to inspire piety in those who approach him are already known and recognized as ornaments by all. I learned these things through personal experience; indeed, on the very day on which I commit them to writing, I received word that His Holiness had sent from the papal treasury to Paris a vast sum of money to relieve the needs of that illustrious prince who preferred the honor of the Catholic religion to the royal titles of his birth.”

How gladly, we think, would Dionysius have committed these matters to writing with C. V. Sommier, if he were living among us! For in both princes he would recognize the Roman Church’s chief glory, continued from its origin: in the exile, stripped of his hereditary kingdoms for the sake of the faith, the steadfastness of confessors; in the pontiff, relieving with the customary support of the Roman Church the glorious poverty of a royal guest, the devotion and charity of Soter. In this the most holy Father Innocent XIII fell short in nothing, preserving by his generosity the benefits of his predecessor Clement and the character of the Roman Church.

**[Col. 1239]**

**13. Soter**, a Campanian by nation, son of Concordius, from the city of Fundi, held the See for nine years and three months. **[Note: B gives four years, less twelve days.]** He was in the time of Severus, from the consulship of Rusticus and Aquilinus to that of Cethegus and Clarus. **[Note: B and M: Marcus Aurelius, from the consulship of Aurelius Severus II and Claudius Pompeianus to that of Commodus and Quintillus.]** He decreed that no *monacha* should touch the consecrated cloth or place incense in the holy Church. **[Note: See Baronius, year 179, at the end.]** He held three ordinations in the month of December: eight priests, **[Note: C and B: eighteen,]** nine deacons, and eleven bishops in various places. He was also buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May; and the episcopate remained vacant for twenty-two days. **[Note: C and B: eleven.]**

### Schelestratius’s Notes on the Liberian Catalogue concerning Soter

The lacuna in the older catalogue concerning Soter could be supplied from the Caesarean manuscript, in which we find: “In the time of Antoninus and Commodus, from the consulship of Verus and Herennianus to that of Paternus and Bradua.” But through a copyist’s error this consulship entered the manuscript from elsewhere.

## XIV. SAINT ELEUTHERIUS. YEAR OF CHRIST 179, THE SEVENTEENTH YEAR OF MARCUS AURELIUS’S REIGN

*(Dissertation 2, chapter 4, no. 5.)*

The persecution in Gaul therefore arose during the time of Pope Eleutherius, when Marcus Aurelius was in the seventeenth year of his reign. In that persecution Saint Pothinus, the bishop, and very many others suffered martyrdom. The other confessors, confined in prisons, reported their martyrdom to the Churches of Asia and Phrygia. On this subject there survives the letter of the martyrs of Lyons in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.2, in which it is stated that Pothinus, nearly ninety years old, was killed amid terrible tortures. Eusebius adds in chapter 5:

> “When Pothinus—though some incorrectly read ‘Photinus’—had therefore been killed in his ninetieth year together with the Gallican martyrs, Irenaeus succeeded him in the episcopate of the Church of Lyons.”

Saint Jerome says the same in his book *On Illustrious Men*, in the entry on Irenaeus; for he affirms that, after Pothinus, nearly ninety years old, had been crowned with martyrdom for Christ, Irenaeus was appointed in his place. From these facts it follows altogether that Irenaeus succeeded Pothinus in the See of Lyons during the persecution of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, which began in the seventeenth year of his reign, or in the year 177, and ended with his death in the year 180. Irenaeus had already been sent by the martyrs of Lyons to Rome to Pope Eleutherius, as is clear from the letter of those same martyrs, which Eusebius reports in Book V, chapter 4. There he testifies that Irenaeus was not yet a bishop but only a presbyter when the martyrs commended him to Eleutherius. Eusebius’s words are:

> “But the same martyrs commended by letter to the aforesaid Eleutherius Irenaeus, who at that time was still a presbyter of the Church of Lyons.”

And the presbyter-confessors write in the letter itself:

> “We wish you in all things and always to be well in God, Father Eleutherius. We have urged our brother and fellow-worker Irenaeus to bring this letter to you.”

From these premises it follows that Eleutherius occupied the Roman See during the persecution of Marcus Aurelius. To make the chronology conform to his own calculation, the eminent Cardinal Baronius therefore judged that several years had to be removed from Soter. Although all the ancient writers and catalogues, both manuscript and printed, assign to Soter at least eight or nine years of pontificate, Baronius left him only four years, less twelve days.

Baronius placed the beginning of Soter’s pontificate in the year 175. If, with Eusebius and Saint Prosper, he had assigned him eight years, or, with the catalogues and the *Book of the Pontiffs*, nine years, Eleutherius would not have begun to sit until the year 183 or 184. Seeing that this conflicted with the testimony of the martyrs of Lyons, he assigned Soter only three years, eleven months, and eighteen days, so that his death could be placed in the year 179 and Irenaeus could, before Marcus Aurelius’s death, undertake his embassy to Eleutherius, Soter’s successor. Yet in his note on the year 179, no. 51, he observes:

> “If anyone should discover a more certain chronology of Soter’s years, provided that Cletus is not thereby removed from the number of the Roman pontiffs and the genuine testimony of the letters of the martyrs of Lyons is not disregarded, we shall willingly agree.”

Since Baronius himself made this observation, while preserving the respect due to him, we have departed from his opinion and established a more certain chronology concerning several pontiffs, about whom the ancient monuments or the testimony of the ancients provide such clear evidence that there can be no reasonable doubt about the time during which they held the pontificate. We established this concerning the times of Peter, prince of the apostles, Clement, and Alexander, who were crowned with martyrdom. We have begun to demonstrate the same concerning Soter’s pontificate, of which it is certain that it could not have extended beyond the seventeenth year of the emperor Marcus Aurelius, in which the persecution began. For during that persecution the martyrs of Lyons repeatedly wrote to Pope Eleutherius, as Eusebius testifies in *Ecclesiastical History* V.1, where he presents their letter, which they entrusted to Saint Irenaeus for delivery to Eleutherius.

Moreover, concerning the time when Pope Soter suffered martyrdom and left the Roman Chair to Eleutherius, the eminent Cardinal Baronius differs from us by only two years, by which he constantly deviates from the true chronology of the early pontiffs. He therefore postponed all ecclesiastical events by two years; and this is also why he assigned the seventeenth year of the emperor Marcus Aurelius, which coincides with the year 177, to the year 179. If the seventeenth year of Marcus Aurelius is restored to the year 177 of his era, Baronius will agree with us concerning the time of the persecution in which Soter won the palm of martyrdom and Eleutherius obtained the Roman Chair.

Baronius’s words concerning the year 179 should be heard. When discussing the persecution in which the martyrs of Lyons perished, he writes as follows in no. 50:

> “The letters of the martyrs of Lyons, written at this same time of persecution to Eleutherius, Soter’s successor, necessarily compel us to affirm that Pope Soter was also taken away in this persecution, although others assign him nine years. But since he is found to have performed only three ordinations, we may suppose that he did not sit for a longer period. Eusebius, however, in the *Chronicle*, places Eleutherius as succeeding Soter in the preceding year, namely the sixteenth year of the emperor Marcus, but in his *History* in this very seventeenth year. Since we believe that he learned this from the letters of the martyrs of Lyons, we willingly agree with him, whereas in the other earlier Roman pontificates we cannot agree with him because he omitted Cletus. Thus, in an ambiguous matter, we judge that the death of Soter and the accession of Eleutherius should be deliberately placed at this time, not so much on the basis of Eusebius himself as on the basis of the letters of the holy martyrs of Lyons, who were writing to Eleutherius at that time.”

Thus Baronius. Following his rule concerning the times of the pontiffs mentioned above, based on the letters of the martyrs of Lyons, we have handed down their true chronology.

**Line 3.**—“He received a letter from Lucius, king of Britain.” The Venerable Bede reports the same in Book I, chapter 4, of his *History of the English People*:

> “When Eleutherius, a holy man, presided over the pontificate of the Roman Church, Lucius, king of the Britons, sent him a letter, asking that he be made a Christian through his command; and he soon obtained the fulfillment of his pious request.”

These words entirely agree with the wording of the catalogue and of the *Book of the Pontiffs*.

**[Col. 1252A]**

**Line 5.**—“He decreed that no customary food was to be rejected by Christians.” Like Pius, this pontiff attacks another error of the Judaizers, who maintained a superstitious discrimination among foods. At the same time, other ecclesiastical writers were working with Eleutherius to overthrow this superstition, as Clement of Alexandria does in *The Pedagogue* II.1 and following.

The text says “he decreed,” either because Pius had forbidden this in an earlier decree against the Judaizers, or—and this is more likely—because Eleutherius judged that Paul’s instruction in 1 Corinthians 8 should be published and confirmed. This translation by Eleutherius, when it is certain that Pius did not succeed him, seems to confirm our conjectures concerning the *Book of the Pontiffs*, enlarged by additions that were first entered on loose sheets or in catalogues and subsequently provided the material from which it was compiled. But we leave the investigation of this matter to others; in our notes we follow the order of the book.

**[Col. 1252C]**

**(From the Binian manuscript.) Line 8.**—“He was buried.” Whether he was a martyr or a confessor is uncertain. In the Martyrology he is indeed called a martyr; but that name was also frequently given to confessors, especially to those who had endured some torture for the sake of the faith, as Baronius proves in several notes on the Martyrology.

**(From the Labbe manuscript.) Line 1.**—“Abundius.” Read “Abundantius.”

**[Col. 1252C]**

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

After Soter had won the crown of martyrdom on 22 April in the year 171, Eleutherius was raised to the See of Peter. At the beginning of his pontificate the catalogue of Liberius incorrectly gives the consuls of that same year as Severus II and Herennianus, owing to the loss of the first syllable of *Verus* and the corruption of *Erennianus*. Similarly, among the final consuls assigned to that See, both in the same catalogue and in the second catalogue from the age of Felix IV, as well as in the *Book of the Pontiffs* and other codices reviewed in the *Prolegomena*, folio XCIII, the consuls Paternus and Bradua are corruptly read; and in the printed Lectionaries issued by Luca Antonio Giunta in 1562 they appear even more corruptly as Patrianus and Bradua. Yet they should be called Maternus and Bradua, as they are recorded in several inscriptions: Gruter, CXCII.19; Spon, *Antiquities*, p. 80; Almeloveen, in Cuper’s letter to the *Consular Fasti*, no. 11.

All the catalogues agree in assigning fifteen years of episcopate to Eleutherius. The catalogue of Felix IV adds three months—for the Liberian catalogue is occupied by a lacuna here, as I noted earlier—and the two Colbertine catalogues follow it, although others give six months and Papebrochius’s Belgian catalogue gives four. I consider the latter preferable because it agrees with the Leonine paintings in the Basilica of Saint Paul, as well as in the matter of five days, which are found both there and in the catalogues of Italy and in five of the Colbertine catalogues. I therefore judge that the total period to be assigned to Eleutherius is fifteen years, four months, and five days.

Counting backward from 26 May, the day on which the martyrdom of blessed Eleutherius is commemorated, and from the consuls Maternus and Bradua in the year 185, a period of fifteen years, four months, and five days yields the date of his ordination to the episcopate: Sunday, 22 January of the year 170. This was a full fifteen months before his predecessor Soter was crowned with martyrdom, which occurred, as we said above, on 22 April of the year 171, in the consulship of Severus II and Herennianus.

The Liberian catalogue therefore assigned these consuls, Severus and Herennianus, to the beginning of Eleutherius’s pontifical era because, when the date is calculated from that day according to the reckoning of the pontifical year, the year was renewed by the cataloguers at the Paschal season around the Ascension of the Lord, as the author of the Liberian catalogue expressly states in the Preface:

> “And after his Ascension the most blessed Peter assumed the episcopate. From that time onward it was arranged by succession who each bishop was, how many years he ruled, and under which emperor.”

This was especially so because at Rome the civil practice of reckoning years from the founding of the City, in equal units, was used in the marble fasti—both consular and triumphal—as well as in the priestly colleges for engraving public records on marble. It thus corresponded with our pontifical years, which were arranged according to the institution of that same catalogue. See the observations above in the notes at columns 1020, 1139, and 1149.

There was also another reason for assigning those same consuls to Eleutherius: his ordination to the episcopate must be referred to the month of January, in which the new consuls opened the Julian year, as may be inferred from the day of his martyrdom and from the total number of years, months, and days assigned to him in the catalogues and paintings of the fourth and fifth centuries. It is therefore necessary to recognize Eleutherius as Soter’s vicar during those fifteen months that intervened between 21 January, the Sunday of Eleutherius’s ordination, and 22 April, Soter’s natal day, restored through his martyrdom—a custom sufficiently well established of promoting vicars in Rome during persecutions and other necessities of the Church.

The reign of Marcus Aurelius was by no means free from martyrdoms, although both Antoninus his father and Marcus himself had issued rescripts for the security of Christians, which are discussed in the historical notes on Saint Soter. Since Justin the Christian philosopher, who had pleaded our cause before the emperors and the senate, was condemned to death at Rome in a public trial together with his companions—according to the Alexandrian Chronicle and Baronius, in the year 165, although Ruinartus advises that it should be assigned to 167 (in the *Acts*, p. 42), or, according to Papebrochius’s calculations, to 170—it is not surprising if death was also inflicted at Rome upon Pope Soter.

The governors of the provinces were assailed by the petitions of pagans, by the arts of philosophers and sophists, by the complaints of priests, and by the shouts of the frenzied mob, who invoked dreadful things against us. The apologies of Justin himself, the writings of Tatian, [Col. 1253D] and the letters of the martyrs of Lyons, sent through Irenaeus to Pope Eleutherius—at that time a presbyter—and reported by Eusebius in Book IV, chapter 1 of his *History*, abundantly prove this. Thus, by their importunate demands, they extorted from that same emperor—who ordered milder treatment of us—the power to exercise the sword against the faithful under the pretext of the Christian name. This is clearly shown by the *Acts* of those same martyrs of Lyons and Vienne in Gaul, and by the events and sufferings in Rome, not to mention those in other provinces, such as the martyrdom of Polycarp and his companions in Asia, and that of Ptolemy and his companions in Rome under the urban prefect, which Ruinartus demonstrates should be assigned to the year 166, the fifth consulship of Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus.

Tertullian, in the *Apologeticus* against the pagans, confirms what we are saying when he excludes Marcus Aurelius from the number of those who warred against the Church and mentions his letter, recalling that the thirst in the German campaign was unexpectedly dispelled by rain obtained through the prayers of Christian soldiers. He adds that the emperor, “just as he did not [Col. 1254A] openly remove punishment from such persons [Christians], so in another way he openly published it,” adding a condemnation of the accusers, and indeed one more severe. By this he shows that the emperor, otherwise not hostile to us, indeed even more favorably disposed, did not abolish the penal laws previously enacted against us, even after the benefits received from God through the prayers of Christian soldiers for the preservation of the army, benefits which he had acknowledged before the senate and Roman people. This was sufficient for judges, in the course of their official duties, to exercise at their discretion the power of investigating charges against us.

He did, indeed, devise measures by which accusations and informations against Christians would be made difficult, especially for private enemies, who would face a penalty imposed upon them unless, under the unrepealed laws, they had brought to trial those whom they had caused to be summoned before a public court. When I consider these matters attentively, I seem able to establish with sufficient clarity that, during the first decade of his reign, informations and accusations against Christians were not prohibited, so that provincial governors [Col. 1254B] and urban magistrates exercised the right of the sword against Christians as though they were guilty of violating the religion, according to the practice which Trajan had commanded Pliny, the proconsul of Bithynia, to follow. Tertullian indicates this in *Apology*, chapter 2, and Eusebius in Book III, chapter 27 of his *History*, as Baronius observes under the year 104, nos. 6 and 7.

Tertullian writes:

> “Then Trajan replied that this class of people was certainly not to be sought out, but that those who were brought before the authorities ought to be punished. O judgment confused by necessity! He refuses to have them sought out, as though they were innocent, and orders them to be punished, as though they were guilty. He spares and rages; he ignores and inflicts punishment.”

Trajan’s letter 98 of Book X, among Pliny’s letters, says:

> “You have followed the procedure which you ought to have followed, my Secundus, in investigating the cases of those who were reported to you as Christians. For no general rule can be established that would have the character of a fixed formula. They are not to be sought out; but if they are reported and convicted, they must be punished.”

In reviewing these matters, Eusebius warned what followed from them:

> “After this had been done,” he says, “the fire of persecution, which had pressed upon us with greater violence, [Col. 1254C] seemed to have been extinguished to some extent; yet those who wished to attack us maliciously and deceitfully still had no less opportunity, sometimes setting the people, sometimes the provincial governors, in ambush against our people. Thus, although persecutions did not break out openly and publicly, local persecutions nevertheless flared up in certain provinces, and very many of the faithful underwent the contest of various martyrdoms.”

Again, when explaining the practice observed by Pliny the proconsul and approved by Trajan in his rescript, Eusebius says that it consisted in condemning some and removing others from their rank.

I shall therefore say that, under Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius, these laws, customs, and rescripts of Trajan, which had not been repealed, continued in force until the first decade of Marcus’s reign was ending. Then, in the tenth year, while he was engaged in the German expedition, rain was obtained from heaven through the prayers of the Christians. A celebrated memorial of this event is seen on the spiral column, in which the deeds of that war are carved in relief. Thereafter [Col. 1254D] Marcus ordered that Christians should be treated more mildly, in the letter inserted by Eusebius in Book IV, chapter 13. He abolished the informations which Trajan had permitted by approving Pliny’s practice, and which Antoninus Pius had not abolished, although he had ordered that the harsher laws of Hadrian should remain silent.

It is worthwhile to establish the author and date of this letter reproduced by Eusebius, in order to confirm the history of the pontiffs and martyrs of the second century, which is our present subject. Valesius long ago demonstrated in his learned notes on Eusebius that the historian seriously erred in attributing this same letter to Antoninus Pius, since its inscription clearly shows that it refers to Marcus Aurelius.

> “Eusebius is mistaken,” he says, “in attributing this letter to Antoninus Pius, since it is that of the deified Marcus, as is apparent from the inscription itself. It was written in the first year of his reign, when he himself was consul for the third time.”

He then adds:

> “The author of the Alexandrian Chronicle did indeed notice this error of Eusebius, but wrongly assigned that [Col. 1255A] letter to his tenth year.”

Against Valesius, and with all due respect for so great a man, it must clearly be determined from the inscription of the letter itself—the basis on which he rightly argued that it had been wrongly attributed to Antoninus Pius by both Eusebius and Zonaras—that the letter was written not in the first year of Marcus Aurelius’s reign but in the tenth, and that its title should bear the tribunician-power number XXV, not XV.

Eusebius records the title of the letter as follows:

> “The Emperor Caesar Marcus Aurelius Antoninus Augustus Armeniacus, Pontifex Maximus, holding tribunician power XV, consul III, to the Common Council of Asia,” etc.

The title *Armeniacus*, which the emperor bears in this letter, was not bestowed upon him until after the third year of his reign had already begun, when the tribunician-power number was XVIII, as the coins and inscriptions demonstrate. Nowhere can the cognomen *Armeniacus* be found together with tribunician power XV or XVI. For, while Marcus Aurelius was holding tribunician power XV, Vologaeses, king of the Parthians, after defeating the Roman forces, was devastating Syria, [Col. 1255B] having occupied Armenia. The Parthian war was immediately decreed. The expedition was undertaken by Lucius Verus, and after two years Vologaeses was defeated by Cassius.

From this point Marcus Aurelius began to bear the name *Armeniacus*, together with tribunician power XVIII and the succeeding numbers. Valesius saw that the title *Armeniacus* could not be referred to Pius; I am surprised that he did not observe this in Eusebius. He did not see that the number tribunician power XV was as inconsistent with Marcus’s title *Armeniacus* as the title *Armeniacus* was inconsistent with Pius.

Eusebius knew that Pius had not reached tribunician power XXV, since from XXIV he had held it for only eleven days; accordingly, in the Chronicle he assigns him only twenty-three complete years of imperial rule. Therefore, perhaps, he thought that the first decade should be subtracted from the number XX, which he correctly joined with the title *Armeniacus* in the case of Marcus Aurelius. But the author of the Alexandrian Chronicle, retaining the complete number XXV and recognizing that Marcus had long since acquired the name *Armeniacus*, correctly understood that the letter belonged to the tenth year of his reign and faithfully [Col. 1255C] recorded it.

Our restoration of the number tribunician power XXV is confirmed by the author of the aforementioned Chronicle not only through the title *Armeniacus* but also through the form of the rescript, which bears only the name of Marcus Aurelius and does not add the name of his brother Verus, who had been taken into the partnership of the empire. This name would not have been omitted in the first year of their joint rule, when laws were issued under the title of both brothers. This is shown by the law marked with the date 161, under the same Augusti and consuls, in Book 2 of the *Code*, “On Procurators,” and by another dated to the consuls of the year 162, Rusticus and Aquilinus, in Book 3 of the *Code*, “On Children to Be Supported by Their Parents.”

For when Antoninus Pius died on the Nones of March in the year 161, with Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus as consuls, Marcus so efficiently associated his brother and colleague Verus with the dignity of Augustus that within fourteen days of their father’s death, the Puteolan inscription published by the distinguished Joannes Vignolius at the end of his book *On the Column of Pius*, p. 322, and carved on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, calls both brothers, and both consuls, “Imperators Caesar Augustus,” with tribunician power, etc. [Col. 1255D]

It does not seem probable that Marcus alone would have sent a rescript to the people of Asia when both Augusti were administering justice throughout the world. But in the tenth year of Marcus Aurelius’s reign, when he was holding tribunician power XXV—that is, in the Christian year 171—he alone replied to the Common Council of Asia. For at the end of the year 169, Lucius Verus, reckoning his ninth tribunician power, which was not yet complete, died in midwinter, while Marcus Aurelius was in the course of his twenty-third tribunician power, as the historians report and the coins attest.

In that year 171, therefore, only Marcus is named in the letter. He had lost his brother approximately two years earlier and had not yet taken his son Commodus into the partnership of the empire under the name of Augustus and the title of tribunician power. This was granted only later, namely in the Christian year 175, in the month of August, when Marcus Antoninus, his father, was counting tribunician power XXIX.

Before this rescript of the year 161, accusers could safely report Christians and summon them to trial under that law of tempered severity which the practice of Pliny and Trajan’s approval, not having been repealed, permitted judges to follow. [Col. 1256A] Therefore, when the chronology is carefully weighed and the matters we have cited are restored through genuine documents, it becomes clear why, after the death of Antoninus Pius in the year 161, informations against those who professed the Christian faith revived both in Rome and in the provinces; why in that same year the Roman pontiff Anicetus was crowned with martyrdom on April 17; why Polycarp was martyred in Asia in 164; Justin at Rome in 165 according to the Alexandrian Chronicle, or according to others in 167 or 170; and why in the year 171, on April 21, Soter likewise was killed for Christ.

Marcus Aurelius had scarcely reached the second month of his twenty-fifth tribunician power and had not yet returned to Italy from the German war, where he was still detained. When, later in the same year, while holding tribunician power XXV, he experienced the divine assistance obtained for him through the prayers of the Christians against the Marcomanni, when the army’s thirst was relieved in the summer, he was able to send the letter to the Common Council of Asia and to write to the senate what Eusebius records together with Tertullian.

[Col. 1256B] **HISTORICAL NOTE OF THE SAME AUTHOR.**

**Line 3.—“Here he received a letter from Lucius, king of Britain, asking that he might become a Christian,” etc.**

There is substantial agreement concerning the embassy of King Lucius to Pope Eleutherius and its date among the older writers of that island, as well as among the more recent writers distinguished for their diligence in investigating the antiquities of Britain. They may be consulted in Usserius, *On the British Churches*, p. 29, where he says the following about Marianus Scotus, who followed Bede in connecting the beginning of Eleutherius’s pontificate with the sixteenth year of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus and the consulship of Pollio and Aper:

> “He did not wrongly assign Lucius’s embassy, together with Bede, to the beginning of Eleutherius, and both of these to the consulship of Pollio and Aper.”

Therefore Bede’s dating of the beginning of Eleutherius and of Lucius’s embassy should be understood more broadly, since he equated both with the year 167. Usserius writes this on the following page, where he points out from the *Book of the Pontiffs* that the beginning of Eleutherius fell in [Col. 1256C] the year 171.

It would be lengthy to append entire classes of writers, cited there from several centuries to illuminate the history of King Lucius and the origins of the principal churches of his island, in chapters 3 and following, up to chapter 7, especially the twenty-eight churches—which Bede also counts—which he reviewed on p. 83 from the catalogue of Nennius, copied from the two most ancient Cottonian manuscripts and compared with nine others. They can be read in the same author.

I judge that I shall do something more worthwhile if, while pursuing the spread of the Christian name through those parts of the island of Britain that were not entirely subject to Roman rule, in response to the initiative and efforts of King Lucius, and with Pope Eleutherius laboring and approving his pious prayers, I briefly set out the principal features of the constitution of that province of Britain. It encompassed the greater part of the island during the first three centuries and was later divided into several provinces under Constantine.

I have extracted certain materials from my notebooks, [Col. 1256D] which I had once set aside to illuminate knowledge of the ecclesiastical provinces and which correspond to this second century. These may perhaps shed some light on all the sections of this *Book of the Pontiffs*, in which we read that, almost throughout each of those regions, bishops were established and ordained by that pontiff in various places.

I had therefore observed, together with blessed Leo the Great, that by the plan of divine providence, which gently and powerfully arranges each thing, the size and unity of the Roman Empire, as well as the treaties entered into by Roman rulers with the most distant regions of the earth, had been prepared as a kind of vehicle for carrying the Gospel throughout the world.

> “For the work divinely ordered,” Saint Leo says in Sermon 1, *On the Nativity of the Apostles*, “was especially suited to this: that the universal preaching should quickly find peoples accessible to it, whom the rule of a single state held together.”

When the Lord was born, in accordance with the prophecies of the prophets, while the world of the earth had been established in peace, [Col. 1257A] and during those years of Augustus in which an edict had been promulgated by that same Caesar that the whole world should be registered, the organization of the provinces under one ruler not only prepared an easy approach for the heralds appointed to preach the Gospel; it also began, in the civil ordering of the regions and in the network of towns woven throughout them, to provide a certain model of an ordered and holier government, which Christ the Lord, Prince of Peace, was shortly afterward to entrust to his apostles and their successors in the hierarchy of the Christian episcopate that he was about to establish.

Simon Peter, prince of the apostolic company and the first elected by Christ the Lord to the hierarchy of his Church, already well understood this art of the divine plan before Leo the Great. After the principal sees had been established in the East and West, he added a third in Egypt, so that the vast regions of the South might receive the envoys of Christ, who would extend the boundaries of their authority as far as the Indians and Ethiopians.

Yet, so that all these might understand that the authority of that chair was pre-eminent, the authority [Col. 1257B] which he had endowed with the privilege of his succession in life and at death, as vast as that which the Redeemer of the human race had conferred upon him over all the communities of the faithful, he wished to fix it in the city of Rome, the head of the world, already made the head of the empire spread through Europe, Asia, and Africa. From there he and his successors could more easily send their laws and legations into every region of the earth.

The peace, the organization of the provinces, the census of the citizens, and Augustus’s treaties with the most distant kings served the plan of the divine work—not only these, but also the wars and victories, the roads and divisions of provinces, military expeditions, the establishment of colonies, the transport of legions, the assignment of governors, and almost all the deeds of the Republic and of the Caesars who followed.

Whether Gaius Caligula and Claudius moved against Britain; whether Nero moved against Armenia; whether Vespasian moved against Judaea; whether Trajan moved against Dacia, [Col. 1257C] Parthia, and Mesopotamia; whether Hadrian restored to the barbarians what Trajan had taken from them; whether he himself, and Antoninus after his example, visited the provinces and made the whole empire accessible through frequent journeys; whether they fortified it with Roman legions; whether they even joined seas and islands to the mainland by fleets stationed in Italy in the Upper and Lower Seas, at Ravenna, and at Misenum; whether they strengthened the boundaries of the empire by placing armies in Britain, Cappadocia, Dacia, Germany, Spain, Illyricum, Mauretania, Moesia, Rhaetia, Sarmatia, and Syria—as may be seen on the coins of Hadrian—all these things were preparations, accompaniment, and assistance for carrying the Gospel. They were not arranged by the empty counsel of human beings merely for the uses of temporary life, but were ordered and administered by the command and power of divine wisdom for the glory of Christ and the salvation of the elect. He commands every creature to be ready and to serve this purpose, whether it thinks of doing so or even kicks against the goad.

For [Col. 1257D] how much convenience would the frequent transport of legions from Rome, directed by the supreme head of the Church into whatever distant regions, provide for apostolic missions; and how much convenience would be provided by the almost daily departure of greater and lesser magistrates to the provinces to govern the armies and territories? I touched on this sufficiently above, in connection with the first number, when I considered the utterly wondrous power of divine providence. Choosing the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong, it requires the service of its wisdom’s designs and even derives advantages from the insane and frivolous thoughts of human beings.

This was observed in the case of Gaius Caligula, when he led to the British expedition legions summoned from every direction. Suetonius writes in chapter 46 of that emperor’s *Life*:

> “Having drawn up his army in battle formation on the shore of the Ocean, and arranged his ballistae and other engines, though no one knew or conjectured what he intended to do, he suddenly ordered them to gather shells and fill their helmets and the folds of their garments, calling them the spoils of the Ocean, due to the Capitol and the palace.”

The wisdom [Col. 1258A] of God compelled the vanity of the insane emperor and the absurdity of the Caligulan expeditions—which Tacitus calls the mockery of Gaius in *Histories*, Book IV, chapter 15—to serve it seriously. Through this one joke of human frivolity, it brought from Syria to the Britons many thousands of Roman citizens enrolled in the Fourth, Sixth, and Tenth Legions, which were transported there for this expedition.

Many of these soldiers had been veterans who, fourteen years earlier, had been present at the preaching, miracles, death, and resurrection of Christ the Lord, or who could have witnessed more recently the deeds of his disciples, as eyewitnesses of the wonders and mighty works of God.

Whether they had served with Cornelius, the centurion of the Italian cohort; whether they had served with the other evangelical centurion whose faith the Savior said he had found equaled by none in Israel; whether they had been among the soldiers converted at the Lord’s death, who exclaimed, “Truly this was the Son of God”; whether they had been with Paul, suddenly transformed from persecutor into apostle; or whether they had traveled from Rome to Britain with the Caesarean horsemen mentioned above by Clement of Alexandria and another writer, [Col. 1258B] or with those “of Caesar’s household” who are listed at the end of Paul’s Letter to the Philippians, written from Rome—they could both announce to the Britons what they had seen concerning Christ the Lord and his Church, and transport the Lord’s disciples or the apostles with them into those same provinces.

But I shall discuss more distinctly a little later the illumination of Britain by the light of the Gospel. For now I shall pursue in general the ease with which the Christian faith could be carried into any Roman provinces and into regions near the Roman boundaries, and with which the churches of those regions and provinces could be joined to the head of all, established at the Roman see by the prince of the apostles.

For once Roman citizens had given their allegiance to Christ—especially those born into equestrian or patrician nobility, from whose number praetors, proconsuls, and legates were sent from Rome to the provinces, either annually or for three-year and five-year terms—the Roman pontiff could [Col. 1258C] use this ready opportunity and give them as companions a presbyter, or even a bishop ordained by him, so that he might administer sacred rites to the townspeople and inhabitants of that province, prefecture, and neighboring peoples; expose and purge their ancient errors and newer ones and their sects; and establish and advance the Catholic faith and discipline there.

To encompass everything in a word, he was also given the means of learning every three years about the condition of those churches and the progress of their religion. The same opportunity exists today through the triennial visitations of the holy apostolic thresholds, which bishops are required to make at their consecration, while they strive to inform the Roman pontiff, pastor of the entire flock of the Lord, about the progress of the faithful and to consult him concerning matters relating to divine worship and the eternal salvation of the people entrusted to them in that province.

That the successors of Peter made use of this opportunity can be demonstrated from the earliest episcopal sees, which were generally [Col. 1258D] established where splendid colonies of Roman citizens had been founded, or where the headquarters and camps of Roman armies had been established by Hadrian and Antoninus, or even by earlier emperors or their successors.

I name Hadrian and Antoninus especially because, in this second century, which is our present subject, they completed the original organization of the Roman provinces issued by Augustus and brought it to completion after the additions made under Claudius, Nero, Vespasian, and Trajan.

I. Fraisse, canon of Chartres and author of the booklet *On the Origin of the Churches of Gaul*, decides in chapter 5 that Trier, Lyons, and Vienne should be regarded as the first cities of Gaul to obtain bishops. In the chronological table which he constructed in chapter 10, under the year 68, he reports that Saint Eucharius was given to the people of Trier as bishop in that same year, in which he also thinks that the prince of the apostles was crowned with martyrdom.

In the following year he believes that Saint Crescent was established bishop of Mainz by blessed Linus. [Col. 1259A] He places the beginning of the bishopric of Lyons in the year 140, when it was established through Telesphorus, who also sent Pothinus as bishop, a disciple of Saint Polycarp. In the year 167 he assigns Saint Severus as bishop to the people of Vienne; Severus was called from Persia to announce the Gospel in Gaul.

In these distinguished cities—whether colonies, winter quarters of legions, provincial capitals, or commercial centers—the Roman pontiffs usually established bishops who also possessed the authority of apostolic vicars. The reason for this is given by Celestine I in Letter 13, among the letters edited by Holstenius and reproduced by Schelestratus in his dissertation *On Patriarchal Authority*, chapter 3, p. 41:

> “There are certain faults, not insignificant, which are born in those provinces [through Illyricum] and which, because we are farther away, cannot reach us, or, when all else has been removed, are not conveyed to us as they occurred because of the intervening passage of time. We wish all these matters to be reserved through the intervention of our brother and fellow bishop Rufus [he was bishop of Thessalonica], whose proven experience in all cases and conduct of life is clearly [Col. 1259B] established. Know that our place has been entrusted to him throughout your province, so that, dearest brothers, whatever is being dealt with concerning these cases may be referred to him. Let no one be ordained without his advice; let no one usurp the province entrusted to him without his knowledge; let no one presume to assemble bishops except with his consent. Through him, moreover, let anything that arises be reported to us.”

Celestine was not the first to establish this arrangement. Before him Damasus had already completed it for the reason which the same Schelestratus reports on p. 49: to resist the usurpations of the bishop of Constantinople and to ensure that old Rome possessed the prerogative which, according to the ancient apostolic discipline—as Schelestratus proves from the words of Theodosius in his notes on Leo—had always caused it to preside over all the churches:

> “So that through these provincial bishops established in the major cities the care of the universal Church might flow to the see of Peter, and nothing anywhere might dissent from its head.” [Col. 1259C]

Leo the Great likewise affirms this in Letter 54 to Anastasius of Thessalonica. See the dissertation of Schelestratus cited above.

Although access was easy for the heralds of the Gospel sent to these distinguished colonies, provincial capitals, commercial centers, or towns established near the permanent camps of legions and Roman citizens, episcopal sees were not readily assigned to them unless the organization of the province was known to have occurred in such peaceful circumstances that a sudden change, capable of overturning the condition of the province, could not reasonably be feared.

Therefore, in provinces not yet free from barbarian incursions or from internal disturbances among the native peoples, before the peaceful times of Hadrian and the Antonines, bishops were often sent in the manner of apostolic vicars, directed to that nation in which they could travel wherever necessity summoned them.

But where the peace of the region seemed to promise [Col. 1259D] a lasting provincial settlement, and where there was an opportunity for travel back and forth from the province to Rome and from Rome to the province, and consequently for conferring with the Roman pontiff about the state of those churches, there the Roman pontiff established bishops. From a fixed see and according to an order of succession, they would govern and teach the people entrusted to them in colonies, provincial capitals, and commercial centers.

Accordingly, Innocent I, in his first letter to Decentius, when enumerating the regions under Roman authority throughout the western part of the empire, asserted that this was established and evident:

> “Since it is manifest that throughout all Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Sicily, and the intervening islands, no one has established churches except those whom the venerable apostle Peter or his successors appointed as priests.”

But if a region to be cultivated by evangelical teaching was partly subject to the Romans and partly to friendly or allied kings or peoples of the Romans, it belonged to the [Col. 1260A] providence of the Roman pontiff, before designating a fixed episcopal see there, to ensure that from both sides he obtained confidence that communication and obedience could readily be preserved between those churches and sees and their common mother, Rome.

Thus, even where the temporal dominions of Roman and foreign rulers were distinct, Irenaeus’s principle would remain unshaken:

> “Namely, that every church—and consequently that church, or those churches, which might be established there—ought to come together with this Roman Church because of its principal authority.”

It is therefore not surprising that, although the light of the Gospel spread through the whole world with sufficient speed, episcopal sees were not immediately established everywhere in the first century.

Where an opportunity had not yet arisen for selecting a fixed episcopal see, the practice of ordaining a bishop of that people whose salvation was being promoted was in force. Thomassinus noted this from [Col. 1260B] Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, codex 48, in *On the Ancient and New Discipline of the Church*, Part I, Book I, chapter 54, no. 8:

> “Photius reports in the *Bibliotheca* that Gaius, a most learned and distinguished presbyter of the Roman Church, was ordained under the pontiffs Victor and Zephyrinus ‘a bishop of the nations’—χειροτονηθῆναι ἐθνῶν ἐπίσκοπον, that is, ‘to be ordained bishop of the nations’—and, as though he had been anointed and crowned king, was anointed and crowned as king over that kingdom which he would acquire by power and counsel. In almost the same way the Roman pontiffs consecrated the great majority of the bishops whom they would afterward send to conquer and subject to the yoke of faith those provinces which Innocent I enumerates in his letter.”

I shall mention in passing that, on the occasion of the consecration of this Roman presbyter near the end of the second century as bishop of those nations which he was to win for Christ, there is no reason why Pagius should so vehemently reject [Col. 1260C] the assistant bishops whom we have more than once admitted in this history of the pontiffs during the earlier centuries of the Church. For, besides the example of the prince of the apostles, who appointed Linus, Cletus, and Clement in this manner, it is said that even near the end of the second century Gaius, formerly a Roman presbyter, was ordained bishop of the nations under the pontiffs Victor and Zephyrinus.

That is, he was promoted to the episcopate in order to exercise the authority of an apostolic vicar in some nation, while he was retained in Rome until an opportunity for his mission arose. I think the same thing happened when we recognized that this very Eleutherius, whose life-notes I am appending, was ordained bishop fifteen months before Soter died, according to the date assigned to him.

For, when the times of the Antonines were peaceful and regions allied with Rome or bordering upon Roman territory were being won for Christ, frequent opportunities arose for sending bishops from Rome to instruct those peoples. It was reasonable that the Roman pontiff should test those whom he assigned to apostolic ministry through some experience of government and should train them by a kind of apprenticeship in pastoral office.

This could not be done more easily or safely than by assigning candidates for evangelical missions [Col. 1260D], for several months, to episcopal duties in Rome under delegated authority. It is therefore not surprising if, while a see was temporarily vacant, a bishop promoted in this way— not to fill a definite see, but to form some people in the faith in the manner of an apostolic vicar, and who had consequently exercised the apostolic vicariate for several months before the Roman pontiff—was suddenly chosen as successor by the clergy, who had tested his virtues and prudence under his predecessor.

Nor do I see why V. C. Pagius, both under the year 67, no. 17, and elsewhere, especially under the year 219, should so confidently declare vicariates of this kind during the first three centuries to be fictitious, since he admits the example of the prince of the apostles appointing three vicars for himself in Rome, and since the careful examination of the consular dates which we have undertaken clearly [Col. 1261A] demonstrates that such an arrangement must be admitted more than once, both in the second and in the third century. But enough concerning vicars.
