With these general principles understood—principles relating to the founding of episcopates and the organization of ecclesiastical provinces in the first and second centuries—it is sufficiently clear that the publication of the Gospel in several Roman provinces not yet pacified, or in regions bordering on Roman territory, was not immediately followed by the establishment of episcopal sees.

We must therefore proceed to discover the origin of the older episcopal sees in the British islands, or at least to examine more closely the condition of that Church from the beginnings of the Christian faith in the West to the embassy of King Lucius to Pope Eleutherius.

From that time Tertullian, writing a few years later in his book *Against the Jews*, could assert:

> “The inaccessible places of the Britons, which are beyond the reach of the Romans, have already been subjected to Christ, as have all the boundaries of Spain and the various nations of Gaul.”

Indeed, Justin, approximately fifty years before Tertullian wrote those words, is introduced in the *Dialogue with Trypho* as speaking in this manner:

> “There is not even one race of mortals—whether barbarians, Greeks, or any others, by whatever name they may be called—not even those who live in wagons and tents and lead a pastoral life, among whom prayers and thanksgivings are not offered to the Father and Maker of all things through the name of the crucified Jesus.”

The opportunity for the Gospel to be conveyed to the Britons even by the Apostle Peter and his disciples, I have explained above in the notes to nos. 1 and 4. At that time entire legions of Roman citizens, summoned by Gaius Caligula and Claudius from Syria to the West and occupied for several years in the British expedition, had remained there under Vespasian and Domitian until the end of the first century of the Christian era. [Col. 1261C] They had brought with them a cloud of witnesses from Palestine and Syria to the deeds of Christ and the apostles—events in which those same legions and cohorts had taken part—and many among them had been converted to the faith. Peter, and Peter’s immediate successors, could easily have given them several presbyters, or even bishops, as companions.

Nevertheless, I do not believe that episcopal sees were founded throughout the island so quickly that they can be referred to the first century of Christ. I would more readily believe that the first bishoprics there were established during the second century of redemption, when the condition of the provinces allowed rather more peaceful times. For although the emperor Claudius, after capturing King Caratacus and bringing him to Rome, and after reducing the province to the power of the Roman people, not only filled it with Roman citizens but also led a colony of veterans there—namely Camalodunum in the year 50 of Christ, during the consulship of Gaius Antistius Vetus and Marcus Suillius Rufus—as a support against rebels and for instructing the allies in obedience to the laws, as Tacitus says (*Annals* XII, ch. 32); nevertheless, [Col. 1261D] ten years later, during the consulship of Paetus and Turpilianus, in A.D. 61, near the beginning of Nero’s reign, Queen Irene, seeking to avenge the grave injuries inflicted upon herself and her people by Roman soldiers, and with the Trinovantes stirred to rebellion, fought so manfully against the Roman forces that eighty thousand Roman citizens and allies were slaughtered between Camalodunum, Verulamium, and Londinium, as Tacitus records in the *Annals*, and Dio in his history.

There followed a long succession of reversals and varied dangers of war, even under the emperor Vespasian—these may be read in Tacitus’ *Life of Agricola*, ch. 7—under Cerealis and Frontinus, and likewise under Agricola, sometimes with the nearer islanders and sometimes with those farther away, whom they then called Caledonians and who are now called Scots; these matters are indicated there in chapter 33, under Domitian.

These times, therefore, disturbed by almost continual movements among the Britons—both external movements against Roman aggressors and internal ones among the islanders themselves (for Tacitus also relates in the same place that a petty king of Ireland, expelled by a domestic revolt, had fled to Agricola and had indeed been kindly received, but had been retained by him under the pretext of friendship as an opportunity for war)—seemed less suitable for apostolic prelates to erect episcopal cathedrals there in fixed sees, whether in the territory subject to the Romans or in the remaining regions governed by their own kings.

Once the province had been organized by Hadrian, who, according to Spartianus in his *Life*, “after reforming the soldiers in an exemplary manner, went to Britain, where he corrected many things and was the first to draw a wall for eighty miles, to divide Romans from barbarians, and stationed the British army on that boundary, as ancient coins demonstrate, and equipped a British fleet, as ancient inscriptions attest,” a more favorable age dawned for considering the establishment of fixed episcopal sees.

Antoninus made Hadrian’s peace more stable after suppressing the disturbances that had arisen in Britain through Lollius Urbicus, who defeated the Britons, as Capitolinus states in his *Life* ([Col. 1262A]); coins of every metal published by Vaillantius also bear witness to this. Afterward, following his father’s example, Antoninus drew another turf wall after driving back the barbarians.

When the boundaries between Romans and islanders had thus been sufficiently settled, and hope of a long peace had been strengthened, it seemed opportune for the pontiff of the Apostolic See to respond to the opportunity of establishing bishoprics on the island. This opportunity was offered by that king among the Britons distinguished for piety whom the Latins call Lucius, but whom the British language calls Les, as Ussher reports in chapter 3 of the *British Antiquities*. He had also said on page 20 that the same king was called in Latin *Britwallanorum* in the Saxon Annals of the library formerly belonging to Camden and now Cotton’s; and on page 22 he adds:

> Nor should this be passed over: two very ancient coins have been found in England—one silver coin, which was owned by M. Joseph Holland, and another gold coin, which we saw among the *κοιμήλια* [treasures] of Sir Robert Cotton—marked with the image of a Christian king, as may be inferred from the sign of the cross attached, and with more obscure letters that seemed to denote LVC ([Col. 1262C]).

Certainly all historians who have treated English affairs agree in the tradition received from Bede, Gildas, and other ancient writers of their nation: King Lucius sought from the Roman pontiff Eleutherius that he might instruct his Britons in the Christian sacred rites.

For this reason some say that Timothy, a Roman presbyter and brother of Novatian—and, according to the opinion of some, also the biological brother of the virgins Praxedis and Pudentiana—was sent; others assert that Damianus, or Duvianus, and Fugatius were dispatched. This is stated in a letter attributed to Saint Patrick, as well as in the great Gastonian Table; Ussher and the writers mentioned by Schelestratius in his work *On Patriarchal Authority*, ch. 1, nos. 8 and following, also produce these sources.

Many writers relate that these men were received with such eagerness and treated with such generosity by the most pious king that episcopal sees were also assigned and endowed to them. Ussher reviews a vast number of writers in chapters 4 and 5 ([Col. 1262D]), though he indicates that a selection must be made, since not a few of them are inclined to foist empty popular rumors upon their readers as established histories.

As for King Lucius, the memory of his profession of the Christian faith and of his embassy to Eleutherius for the purpose of preaching that faith to the peoples subject to him is so constant that it is repeated in the Martyrologies of Bede and Ado on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, and likewise in chronicles and annals.

Geoffrey of Monmouth, *History of the Britons* IV, chs. 18 and 19, together with many who follow him, relates that Coilus, son of King Marius and grandson of Arviragus, was brought up at Rome from childhood, taught the customs of the Romans, and, while paying the tribute imposed by them, possessed his kingdom in peace. His son Lucius, he says, was treated no differently from the other Coilus and imitated all his father’s good deeds. When Lucius died without offspring to succeed him ([Col. 1263A]), the Britons revolted from Roman power.

Bale, too, and the Scottish chroniclers cited by Ussher on page 20, where he reports the foregoing, affirm that Lucius the Pious, the only son of Coilus and a supporter of the Roman Empire, ruled the Britons after his father, with both the goodwill and the authority of the Caesar Marcus Antoninus Verus.

It was indeed the Roman custom, as Panvinius noted from Appian (*On the Roman Empire*, p. 25), to appoint kings over several nations when they required nothing further for their rule. Thus Augustus, Gaius, and Claudius assigned kingdoms in Palestine; Nero did so in Armenia; and Trajan, beyond the Euphrates. At this very period of which we are speaking, Lucius Verus, after the Parthian war had been completed in the East, gave kingdoms to kings and entrusted the provinces to be governed to his own companions, as Capitolinus relates in his *Life*. A king of the Quadi appointed by Antoninus is visible on his coins.

To remain in Britain: King Cogidubnus had been given several states, in accordance with the old and long-established custom of the Roman people, “that he might have both the instruments of slavery and kings,” as Tacitus says in the *Life of Agricola*, ch. 14. Tacitus also records that Cogidubnus remained most faithful until his own time.

After the wall had therefore been drawn by Hadrian along the boundaries of Britain, and the rampart renewed by Antoninus, security having been established among the allied kings and the Romans, King Lucius, son of that Coilus who had been educated at Rome and imbued with Roman customs, when he was being called to the Christian religion, sought teachers from Eleutherius, the Roman pontiff, by whom he might be instructed.

Whether he had heard from Christian soldiers serving among the Roman legions of the British army, or from men educated with his father in the City, that the teaching of our faith, which he desired, had proceeded from the apostles and had spread widely throughout the West; or whether, after consulting the teachers of the Christian faith in the neighboring region of Gaul, he had received from Irenaeus the answer that he also committed to writing—that, because of its primacy, the whole Church from everywhere ought to converge upon this Roman see; or whether he had learned something from those same faithful men about retrieving the laws of the worship of the true God from this place, where the chief of the apostles had poured forth the whole teaching together with his blood, for which reason both the Gallican and the Asian Churches could recall embassies undertaken shortly before to Pius and Anicetus, especially at a time when the Marcionites and other heretics were spreading perverse doctrines—in every case, the English agree with writers from neighboring nations that, at the request of King Lucius, ministers of the Gospel were sent by Pope Eleutherius to Britain to imbue the peoples under his rule with the Christian sacraments.

Nor may one doubt that this proceeded successfully, since a few years later Tertullian indicated that the Christian faith had spread so widely and prosperously throughout Greater Britain that it not only flourished within the rampart and boundary of Hadrian and Antoninus—near which Lucius is shown to have ruled by the title given him, “king of the Britwallans,” that is, of the inhabitants of the Valley of Britain, now called Wales or Walles, of which we spoke above from the Anglo-Saxon Annals ([Col. 1263D])—but had also penetrated beyond the Roman boundaries among the Caledonians and Picts during the same period.

For Septimius affirms in ch. 7 *Against the Jews*: “The inaccessible places of Britain, to which the Romans have not reached, have already been subjected to Christ.” Ussher explains this on page 23, ch. 3 of the *Antiquities of the British Church*:

> Beyond that rampart of Hadrian and Antoninus was the part of Britain called Caledonia, embracing most of present-day Scotland. Scottish historians relate that in this region the Christian faith was first received under Victor I—immediate successor of the Eleutherius whom we are discussing—and the emperor Severus. Yet the author of the Annals, written in the Anglo-Saxon language six hundred years ago, refers this very history of Eleutherius and Lucius to the time of Severus, whom he, together with Bede, says obtained the empire in the year of the Lord 189. Nor are there lacking those who believe that Lucius ruled in this part of the island, which the free Britons possessed, and who call Tertullian as witness, since he wrote under the rule of Severus that the inaccessible places of Britain had been subjected to Christ.

Scarcely a hundred years had elapsed after Severus—namely, in the year of Christ 314—when three bishops of Britain signed their names at the Council of Arles (vol. I of the *Gallican Councils*, Paris edition, p. 9), namely:

**Eborius, bishop of the city of Eboracum, province of Britain.**

**Restitutus, bishop of the city of Londinium, of the aforesaid province.**

**Adelfius, bishop of the city of the Colony of the Londinienses; thence Sacerdos, presbyter, Arminius, deacon, etc.**

These three episcopal sees divide the eastern part of the island, subject to the Romans and separated from the western part by the aforementioned wall or rampart of Hadrian and the embankment of Antoninus, at almost equal distances. This boundary ran from Clausentum, the southern port of the island, now Southampton, to Gabrosentum in Northumbria, not far from the mouths of the river Tina, now the Tyne or Tees. There, approximately, the fort of New Castle faces the village of Gatesend, perhaps a corrupted form of Gabrosentum, in the diocese of Durham. The geographical maps also place a wall at this location, separating Scotland from England from ancient times ([Col. 1264B]).

Everything contained between Clausentum and the earlier wall or rampart mentioned above, and between the Germanic Sea washing the eastern part of the island—also separated from Scotland by the course of the other transverse wall near Gabrosentum—constituted, among the Romans down to the reign of the emperor Severus, a single province of Britain. Severus then divided it into two prefectures, as Herodian relates in book III of his *History*. This gave later generations the opportunity to divide ancient Britain into First and Second Britain.

They wish to add a Third and Fourth Britain, which they say Constantine endowed with the name Flavia Caesariensis, as well as a Fifth, which Valentinian called Valentia and which occupies the southern part of Scotland.

This later subdivision of Britain, compared with the subscriptions of the three bishops under Constantine the Great, sufficiently shows that the foundation of those episcopal sees preceded the reign of Severus. For if Britain began to be called Second Britain from the time when Severus divided into two prefectures the single province that had previously been Roman Britain—“dividing the authority over the nation into two governments” [Greek: *Διελὼν εἰς δύο ἡγεμονίας τὴν τοῦ ἔθνους ἐξουσίαν*]—and if Restitutus, bishop of the city of London, which belonged by civil administration to First or Nearer Britain, declares himself to belong to the same province as Eborius, whose see belonged to the other, or Farther Britain, it necessarily follows that the prelates of those sees made no alteration in the constitution of the ecclesiastical province from the time when Britain had been a single province before Severus, while those British sees and that same province were being established.

For they would have said:

**Eborius, bishop of Eboracum, of the province of Farther Britain; Restitutus, bishop of Londinium, of the province of Nearer Britain,**

if the two sees had received this division of Britain at their original establishment. Or they would have written:

**Ebroicus, bishop of Eboracum, of the province of Britain Flavia Maxima Caesariensis.**

**Restitutus, bishop of Londinium, of the province of Nearer Britain.**

**Adelfius, of the city of the Colony of the Londinienses, province of Britain Flavia Caesariensis, [lacuna]**

if the erection of these bishoprics had taken place in the time of Constantine, when the four provinces divided among themselves the single province of Britain that had existed under the Antonines. That the Colony of the Londinienses was Lindum Colonia, Lincoln, will be demonstrated shortly with Thomas Gale.

The subscriptions of the year 314 therefore indicate the origin or foundation of these three episcopal sees, belonging to one and the same province of Britain, and show that their establishment must be referred to the time before the emperor Severus, in the age of King Lucius, whether under the Antonines or under Commodus.

Since the pontificate of Eleutherius extended over part of both reigns, the establishment of those three British sees fits equally well with the time of the first and the second. Several English historians clearly indicate that these sees were not merely designated by Fugatius and Duvianus, bishops ordained by Eleutherius and sent to King Lucius at his request, but were duly completed and brought to an end with the approval of that same Roman pontiff.

Geoffrey of Monmouth, Roger of Wendover, both Matthew Paris and Matthew of Westminster, and likewise the compiler of the history of Rochester—identified by Ussher on page 53, near the beginning of chapter 6—relate that the same Fugatius and Duvianus, whom they call bishops, returned to Rome so that they might obtain from Eleutherius confirmation of what they had established among the Britons. After the confirmation had been given, they returned to Britain accompanied by several others, through whose teaching the British people were soon strengthened in the faith of Christ.

Their names and deeds are found in the book that Gildas entitled *On the Victory of Ambrosius Aurelius* ([Col. 1265B]). Geoffrey of Monmouth assigned these events to the year of grace 184.

If the organization of the provinces of the Roman Empire is considered, and especially that of Britain under the Antonines down to the emperor Severus, perhaps no period could have offered a better opportunity for all these matters to be carried out peacefully: for communicating plans with the Roman pontiff; for obtaining commands from him; for bringing controversies before him, as the Gallican and Asian Churches did; and for convening, by his authority, councils of several bishops, both in the West among the Gauls and in the East among the Palestinians. This will have to be discussed in the following section under Victor, the immediate successor of Eleutherius ([Col. 1266A]).

These serious documents must not be mixed with the imaginary fabrications of later writers—not merely the beginnings, but the monstrosities—of the division of the British Churches and sees. They invent flamines and archflamines established in the cities and bishops and archbishops substituted for them.

These childish fictions were refuted long ago and require no effort from us to reject them, any more than the spurious letters of Pope Eleutherius to King Lucius. Those letters are so remote from the style of their age that, by inspecting only the first line, they can be recognized as the offspring of an incompetent writer abusing his own leisure and that of another.

To establish the condition of the province of Britain under the Roman emperors of the first and second centuries—a matter from which knowledge of the Church’s original constitution cannot be separated—let me bring forward some genuine documents of antiquity. I have extracted them from a larger work that I was preparing to illustrate all the ecclesiastical provinces individually. From the many materials I collected concerning the constitution of Britain, I shall select a few.

Six coins engraved graphically on this plate establish the condition of the province of Britain under the Romans, from Augustus to the emperor Severus. I say “province,” not “provinces,” since Britain had not yet admitted either Severus’ two *ἡγεμονίαι* [governments], Constantine’s four provinces, or Valentinian’s five.

### 1

The first coin, a silver coin of the Tenth Legion among the frequent Antonine issues, excavated in the territory of Maridunum among the Demetae, who formed part of the Silures, is discussed by Thomas Gale in his celebrated little work on the *British Itinerary of Antoninus*, p. 122.

That this legion served in Britain under Ostorius against the Silures and Ordovices is also proved by several bricks or tiles discovered at Conovium—the ruins of Caer Hyn, the older city, later corruptly called Caer Rhyn—three miles from the mouth of the river of the same name, Conovium, now Cowey, opposite the western part of the island called by the ancients Mona and now Anglesey Isle. They were marked with the inscription of the Tenth Legion, **LEG. X**.

Gale records from Josephus’ *Jewish War*, books I and VII, that this legion was transferred from Britain to Palestine under the names Fretensis and Tenth Ferrata (as printed, *decimae Ferratensis*), served under Vespasian against the Jews, and, after Jerusalem had finally been captured, was left there by Titus. Theodosius the Younger found it there when the empire was already collapsing, as he observes from the *Notitia of the Empire*, fol. 92.

### 2

The second coin, one of the silver coins of the emperor Claudius, stamped with a triumphal arch and the words **DE BRITANNIS**, is sufficiently explained by Suetonius, *Life of Claudius*, ch. 17:

> To acquire the distinction of a genuine triumph, he chose Britain above all, since it had not been attempted by anyone after Julius and was then in revolt because deserters had not been returned. Without any battle or bloodshed, within only a few days he received part of the island into submission, returned to Rome in the sixth month after his departure, and celebrated a triumph with the greatest magnificence ([Col. 1267B]).

The Senate and the Roman people erected a distinguished monument to that triumph by raising an arch in the Ninth Region, as the additions of Panvinius to Rufus and Victor confirm. According to Nardini and other antiquarians, a considerable part of that magnificent inscription was discovered on the road leading from the Fountain of Trevi to the nearby Flaminian Way, the Corso, near the area called the Piazza di Sciarra Colonna. We now see it transferred among the chief ornaments of the Barberini palace.

Although several attempts have been made to supply its missing portions, Fabretti seems to have devised the most appropriate restoration in his *Commentary on his Ancient Urbinate Inscriptions*, p. 728. It is presented here in small letters, while whatever remains of the ancient inscription is shown in square characters:

```text
T. CLAVDIO. DRVSI. F. CAESARI

AVG. GERMANICO

PONTIFICI. MAXIMO. TRIB. POTEST. XI.

COS. V. IMP. XXIIII. PATRI. PATRIAE

SENATVS. POPVLVSQVE. ROMANVS. QVOD

REGES. BRITANNICI. PERVLLES. ABSQVE

VLLA. IACTVRA. SVORVM. CAPTIVOS. HABVERIT

GENTESQVE. BARBARAS. VLTRA. OCEANVM

PRIMVS. INDICTO. BELLO. IMPERIO. ADIECERIT
```

“To Tiberius Claudius Caesar Augustus Germanicus, son of Drusus, chief pontiff, tribune of the plebs eleven times, consul five times, imperator twenty-four times, father of his country: the Senate and Roman people, because he first held captive the rebellious kings of the Britons without any loss of his own men and added barbarian peoples beyond the ocean to the empire after war had been declared.”

For Claudius was indeed the first to obtain and subdue them. Tacitus says in the *Life of Agricola*, ch. 13:

> The deified Julius, the first of all the Romans, entered Britain with an army. Although with a successful battle he terrified the inhabitants and gained possession of the shore, he may be seen to have shown it to those who came after rather than handed it over. Claudius was the author of the undertaking: legions and auxiliary forces were transported, Vespasian was associated in the enterprise; peoples were conquered, kings captured, and Vespasian was shown by destiny. Aulus Plautius was the first consular commander, followed soon afterward by Ostorius Scapula, both distinguished in war. The nearer part of Britain was gradually reduced to the form of a province, and colonies of veterans were added. Certain states were given to King Cogidubnus. He remained most faithful down to our own memory, in accordance with the ancient and long-established custom of the Roman people that kings should serve as instruments of slavery ([Col. 1267D]).

We saw above that the legions were first transported by Gaius Caligula, and that Claudius used them seven years later in the British expedition to subdue part of the island. Of these, the Fourth, Fifth, and Tenth had been summoned from the province of Syria, where Augustus had stationed them and Tiberius had retained them. They must therefore have been witnesses of the deeds of Christ the Lord and of the apostles.

God so arranged matters that he had chosen the first fruits of the nations in the centurion Cornelius, so that the transport might thereby be made easier for those who were going to announce the Gospel to the islanders beyond the Ocean, and who would establish themselves with even more secure hospitality and residence in the colonies of veterans.

Suetonius records the following about Vespasian’s deeds in Britain in ch. 4 of his *Life*:

> Under the emperor Claudius, through the favor of Narcissus, he was sent as commander of a legion to Germany; from there he was transferred to Britain, where he fought thirty times against the enemy. He brought two very powerful peoples, more than twenty towns, and the Isle of Wight, lying near Britain, into submission, partly under the command of Aulus Plautius, the consular governor, and partly under Claudius himself ([Col. 1268A]).

Gale demonstrates in his aforementioned work on the *British Itinerary of Antoninus*, Itinerary XII, that Vespasian was placed by Claudius in command of the Second Legion:

```text
A CALLEVA MURIDUNO, ETC.
ISCE LEGVA AVGVSTI. M. P. XV.
```

He teaches that this should be corrected as follows:

```text
ISCA LEGIO II. AVGVSTA
```

This is now Caerleon, called by the Britons *Caer Leon-at-Usk*, that is, “the City of the Legion at the Isca.”

The Second Legion remained here—at London and Richborough—for so long that it was also called the Second British Legion, as Tacitus says in book III, section 44:

> Vespasian, placed in command of it by Claudius because he had distinguished himself in the war there, won the favor of Britain.

In the same book of Tacitus, section 23, the Ninth, Second, and Twentieth Legions are called British.

As for the Twentieth, it came from Lower Germany, where it had been established by Augustus. After Claudius transferred it to Britain, it acquired the name *Victrix*, as Vaillantus collected from ancient historians in his discussion of a coin of Gallienus, where he also places the epithet *Valeria* before it.

An inscription on a stone near the Lucanian Bridge below Tivoli preserves for us the complete record of Aulus Plautius, the consular governor who commanded these legions. Gruter gives it on page 453. I reproduced above the part relating to the British expedition under Claudius.

A lead tablet discovered in the English county of Somerset under Henry VIII also concerns the aforementioned triumph of Claudius over the Britons. Gruter published it from Camden, fol. 238, no. 5:

```text
TI. CLAVDIVS. CAESAR. AVG. P. M.

TRIB. P. VIIII. IMP. XVI. DE BRITAN.
```

For this reason, because he had extended the boundaries of the empire, Claudius enlarged the sacred boundary of the City. We read this in an ancient cippus preserved at Rome near the Cloaca of Saint Lucia, published by the distinguished Fabretti on p. 726 of his *Inscriptions* ([Col. 1268C]) and by Gruter, fol. 196, no. 4.

The colony of veterans led by Claudius into Britain, and the kings defeated by him, are listed by Gale on pp. 91 and 113. There he presents a coin of Cunobelinus, king of the Trinovantes—now Essex and Middlesex—struck at Camalodunum, Walden. The kings of the Trinovantes, attracted by the pleasantness of the site, had established their palace there, and the Romans had led a colony there.

Concerning the king and his sons Caratacus and Togodumnus, defeated by Aulus Plautius, of whom we spoke above, see Dio, book LX, in the third consulship of Claudius, in the year 769 of the City.

A censor of Roman citizens in this same colony is recorded as Gnaeus Munatius, son of Marcus, of the Palatine tribe, Aurelius Bassus, in Gruter, p. 439, no. 5. More correctly, however, he appears in Fabretti, *Inscriptions*, p. 29, where he is called:

```text
CENSOR CIVIVM ROMANORVM COLONIAE VICTRICENSIS
QVAE EST IN BRITANNIA CAMALODVNI
```

“Censor of the Roman citizens of the colony Victrix, which is in Britain, at Camalodunum.”

We saw above from Tacitus, *Annals* XII, section 32, that the establishment of this colony must be assigned to the year 50 of the Christian era, during the consulship of Gaius Antistius and Marcus Suillius ([Col. 1268D]). I have related in the same place the disasters that followed for the Romans under Nero, after the islanders’ affections had been alienated, as well as the victories shortly afterward under Vespasian and the organization and ordering of the province under the succeeding emperors.

### 3–4

The third and fourth bronze coins concern Hadrian. On the first, Britain, an armed province, sits secure after the disturbances had been settled by Hadrian. Spartianus indicates rather than narrates these disturbances, mentioning them briefly as follows:

> He went to Britain with the soldiers converted to excellent discipline, corrected many things there, and was the first to draw a wall for eighty miles, which would divide the barbarians from the Romans.

Shortly afterward, after affairs in Britain had been settled, he presents Hadrian as crossing into Gaul.

Antiquarians generally explain both coins in almost the same words. Among them is the eques Patinus, who appropriately connects the third coin with the restoration of Britain:

> Under Hadrian, he says, the Britons could not be kept under Roman rule. Therefore, having converted the soldiers in the manner of the region—for that is how he reads Spartianus’ passage—he went to Britain, where he corrected many things and first drew a wall for eighty miles, and so forth. To this expedition must be added another coin of larger size, on which the **BRITISH ARMY** is represented by the emperor and the soldiers; and another dedicated to the emperor as **RESTORER OF BRITAIN**. The spear and shield display the arms of the province.

Thus far Patinus.

The poet Florus, in Spartianus, recalled Hadrian’s approach, both for settling the condition of Britain and for maintaining military discipline, in those witty little verses:

> I do not wish to be Caesar,  
> To walk among the Britons,  
> To endure Scythian frosts.

Dio records that Julius Severus was then summoned and sent first as commander to subdue the rebellious Jews in Palestine.

Apart from the land forces in Britain, ancient inscriptions also establish that a British fleet was equipped in the province. Particularly important is the inscription set up at Camerte for M. Maenius, son of Gaius, of the Cornelian tribe, which Reinesius published and illustrated on p. 462, no. 432.

I think it should be displayed here, since Hadrian’s British expedition, the British fleet, and the constitution of the province itself are explained more fully by it than by the historians. It also makes known the Second Flavian Cohort of British cavalry, perhaps established by Vespasian, from which it received the name Flavian, as well as the procuratorship of the province, the office of the imperial agent in the province, and the command of the fleet entrusted to this M. Maenius:

```text
M. MAENIO C. F. COR. AGRIPPAE ET VSIDIO CAMPESTRI
HOSPITI DIVI HADRIANI PATRIS SENATORIS
PRAEF. COH. II. FL. BRITTON. EQVITAT.
ELECTO A DIVO HADRIANO ET MISSO IN EXPEDITIONEM
BRITTANNICAM
TRIB. COH. I. HISPANOR. EQVITAT.
PRAE. ALAE. I. GALLOR. ET PANNONIOR.
CATAPHRACTAE.
PROC. AVG. PRAEF. CLASSIS BRITANNICAE
PROC. PROVINCIAE BRITANNIAE
EQVO PVBLICO
PATRONO MVNICIPI
VICANI CENSORIACENSES CONSECVTI
AB INDVLGENTIA OPTIMI MAXIMIQ.
IMP. ANTONINI AVG. PII.
BENEFICIO. INTERPRETATIONIS EIVS
PRIVILEGIA QVIBVS IN IVRE CIVIVM
AVCTI CONFIRMATIQVE SVNT
D. D. D.
```

“To M. Maenius Agrippa, son of Gaius, of the Cornelian tribe, and to Usidius Campester, guest-friend of the father of the deified Hadrian, a senator; prefect of the Second Flavian Cohort of British Cavalry; chosen by the deified Hadrian and sent on the British expedition; military tribune of the First Cohort of Spanish Cavalry; commander of the First Ala of Gauls and Pannonians, cataphracts; procurator of the emperor; prefect of the British fleet; procurator of the province of Britain; Roman knight; patron of the municipality. The villagers of Censoriacum, having obtained these privileges through the indulgence and beneficence of the best and greatest emperor Antoninus Augustus Pius and through his interpretation, by which they were increased and confirmed in the law of citizenship, dedicated this monument by decree.”

An inscription at Gruter, fol. 493, no. 6, also presents a prefect of the British fleet. In no. 1 there appears Licinius Italicus, legate of the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, and likewise propraetor of the province of Britain, who had served in the Jewish expedition under the deified Hadrian.

### 5

The fifth coin belongs to Antoninus Pius and to the British victory won under his auspices through the legate Lollius Urbicus. Julius Capitolinus relates this in his *Life*:

> He waged many wars through his legates. For he also defeated the Britons through the legate Lollius Urbicus, after a second turf wall had been drawn and the barbarians driven back ([Col. 1269D]).

Vaillantus notes this in his explanation of the coin.

After that victory, which Pausanias also mentions in book VIII, p. 526, as cited by the distinguished senator Bonarroti in his discussion of the large bronze coins of Cardinal Carpineus, p. 49, the Antonines Pius and the Philosopher enjoyed such a peaceful condition of the province that they left us an itinerary by which Britain can be traversed in every direction: from the Boundary, that is, the Wall—or Luguvallium, now Carlisle—to the port of Ritupis, now Stonar, near Dorobernium or Canterbury; from the same Wall to Clausentum, the southern port of the island, now Southampton; and to the western estuaries, where stood Isca of the Second Augustan Legion, now Caerleon; and to Segontium, Caersegont, now Caernarfon, opposite the island of Mona, now Anglesey, in the Irish Sea. Other routes are most carefully set out in the posthumous work of Thomas Gale.

Ptolemy too, celebrated among geographers no less than among astronomers, was able during these same peaceful times to give us the longitude and latitude of several British towns ([Col. 1270A]).

We learn from Dio’s history, book LXXII, that a war broke out under Commodus, and a serious one at that:

> There were, he says, under Commodus certain wars with the barbarians beyond Denmark, and so forth. But the British war was by far the greatest of all. For when the Britons had crossed the wall that lay between them and the Roman camps and had ravaged many places, after killing the Roman commander and the soldiers who had accompanied him, Commodus, terrified by fear, sent Ulpius Marcellus against them. He was a modest and frugal man, brave and magnanimous, and so forth. Marcellus, endowed with such a character, inflicted the greatest and most serious losses upon the barbarians in Britain. After this, Commodus came close to killing him because of his excellence, but nevertheless dismissed him. For Commodus was accustomed, as Lampridius relates, to send to govern the provinces either accomplices in crimes or men recommended by criminals ([Col. 1270B]).

Lampridius acknowledges that the titles “British” and “Imperator for the sixth time” were added to the honors of Commodus because of the deeds of this Marcellus. Yet the historian regarded them as not truly his own, asserting that flatterers had bestowed them, even though they are repeatedly found on coins and inscriptions.

He says that Marcellus was held in such contempt by the Britons that they wished to choose an emperor against him. The occasion for the rumor was provided by that enormous number of Roman soldiers—Dio says there were fifteen hundred—who, after raising a mutiny against Perennis, or Perennius, prefect not so much of the praetorian guard as of the entire empire, since Commodus devoted himself solely to pleasures, were selected from the larger body and came from Britain to Italy without anyone preventing them. From the emperor himself they obtained the execution of Perennis.

The soldiers were indignant because, after the senators had been removed, Perennis appointed men of equestrian rank to command the British war. When the matter was exposed by the legates of the army, he was declared an enemy and handed over to the soldiers to be torn apart, as Lampridius writes ([Col. 1270C]).

### 6

The final coin indicates what was done in Britain under the emperor Severus. It is marked by a double victory, perhaps corresponding to two nations among the islanders defeated by Severus. Dio describes them as follows:

> There are chiefly two peoples of the Britons—he is speaking of those who in his own time lived at the farthest boundaries of the Roman province or even beyond them—the Caledonians and the Maeatae. For the names of the others are generally referred to these. The Maeatae live next to the wall that divides the island into two parts. The Caledonians lie beyond them.

Shortly afterward, having defined the length of the whole island of Britain as 891 miles and its breadth as 189 miles—where it is greatest and where least, 37 miles—he adds:

> A little less than half of this island belongs to us. When Severus wished to bring the whole of it under his power, he entered Caledonia, the southern part of Scotland, and as he passed through it he encountered the greatest difficulties, since he had to cut through forests, and so forth. Nevertheless Severus did not stop until he reached the farthest part of the island, where he carefully observed that the sun’s course, as well as the length of the nights and days, both summer and winter, differed from what it is among us. At last, after being carried through almost the whole hostile land—for because of their weakness they used covered litters for the most part—he returned to his allies, forcing the Britons to make a treaty on the condition that they surrender a considerable part of their territory, and so forth.

> After this, the Britons again revolted. Therefore Severus summoned the soldiers and ordered them to invade their territory and kill everyone whom they encountered. He commanded them to do this in the following verses:

> Let no one escape your hands or the bloody slaughter—  
> Not even the unborn child whom his pregnant mother carries in her womb.

May he escape horrible slaughter. [Col. 1271A] When this had happened, and the Caledonians together with the Maeatae had revolted, he was preparing to conduct the war there in person. But while he was occupied with these matters, he was carried off by illness on the day before the Nones of February.”

Thus far the excerpts of Dio, transmitted by Xiphilinus, who adds at the beginning of Book 77 that, after Severus’s death, his son Antoninus Bassianus began his reign by bringing the war with the enemy to an end, immediately abandoning the region and the fortified places, and then returning to Rome. Spartianus records that Severus died at Eboracum in Britain, “after subduing the peoples who seemed hostile to Britain”; and he relates that “the greatest glory of his reign was Britain, which he fortified by a wall drawn across the island, on both sides as far as the Ocean.”

Since, therefore, there were two boundaries—the first drawn by Hadrian near the meridian line and renewed by Antoninus from the port of Clausentum (Southampton) to Luguvallium (Carlisle), and the other running from west to east, from Luguvallium to Cabrosentum at the mouth of the River Tyne—and since they divided Roman Britain in such a way that the first separated the Maeatae, who lived near those boundaries toward the western part of the island, while the second separated the Caledonians, who lay beyond the other boundary and beyond the Maeatae, Severus carried his victorious arms beyond these boundaries of the rampart and wall. After abolishing the first turf rampart, drawn near the meridian line and henceforth of no use against the barbarians once the Maeatae had been subdued, he more solidly raised a second transverse wall to both ends of the Ocean—that is, where Scotland is separated from modern England—and enclosed within the province of Britain the western part occupied by the Maeatae, as well as the territory granted by the Antonines and Commodus to the Britualanenses, as friendly and allied peoples and kings.

Later writers called this western region, and the part of the island situated beyond Hadrian’s Wall, “Britannia Secunda,” when, under Constantine, Britain was divided into four parts by a new assignment of provinces. Nevertheless, both under Severus and under Caracalla, as previously, there was counted as a single province of Britain whatever territory beyond the turf boundary of Antoninus was acquired toward the west—whether the region had passed to the Romans after the Maeatae were subdued, or whether it had devolved upon them through the territory of Lucius, the allied king who ruled the Britualanenses. He died without offspring, as several of the historians of British annals mentioned above report. Caracalla, however, did not consider it in his interest to include the Caledonians among the peoples of Britain, since they had been sufficiently removed from him by his father’s stronger wall and had not been much sought after by earlier emperors; nor are roads found leading there that carefully measured the remaining part of the island.

I have therefore thought it necessary to sketch the condition of the province of Britain from the emperor Claudius to Severus, so that, from the civil constitution of that island, I might confirm the evidence for Christian worship, which was brought there and successfully propagated within the boundaries of the Roman province during the first century after the arrival of the prince of the apostles in Rome, and which was spread much more extensively in the peaceful times of both Antonines—Pius and the Philosopher—when Lucius, king of the Britualanenses, born of King Coillus, who was exceedingly friendly to the Romans and steadfast beyond all others in his loyalty to them, obtained from Pope Eleutherius, in whose age we are now concerned, that Britons should be more fully instructed in the mysteries of our faith by suitable men sent from Rome. This was no different from the way in which, long before, the Antiochenes had received teachers from the apostles and from the Church of Jerusalem, then the teacher of all the others.

I have shown that, from Claudius to Severus, there was always the greatest facility for sending freely in either direction from Rome to Britain as many heralds of the Gospel as the Roman pontiff might appoint, amid the daily departures of magistrates to govern that province and of legions in their transportations, repeatedly mentioned under the emperors who completed these two centuries under their rule. I have observed that entire legions which had been present in Syria at the events of Christ the Lord and his apostles, and which were transferred from there to Britain under Gaius and Claudius, not only brought a great number of witnesses to those events which had been fulfilled among us, [Col. 1272A] but also may have enabled some of those legions to establish a permanent abode in veterans’ colonies for fellow soldiers of Cornelius the Centurion or of the apostle Paul, who had been converted to the faith in Syria or at Rome. In this way they could foster and extend the practice of the Christian religion, both among the other colonists and among the neighboring islanders.

Nor did those colonies lack an abundance of sacred ministers, who would be sent there by the providence of the bishops of the Roman see as the varying circumstances of the times required. I infer this from the practice of a similar diligence in the neighboring provinces of Gaul and Spain, where assemblies of the faithful were gradually organized through bishops of the nations, or apostolic vicars, and through presbyters and teachers sent there to announce the Gospel, until the opportunity arose to establish definite bishoprics in the principal towns or metropolitan cities of the province, or in Roman colonies founded there.

A similar discipline appears to have been introduced by Mark the Evangelist, Peter’s disciple, into the patriarchate of Alexandria. His successors repeatedly sent teachers and presbyters to the most distant regions of the earth, at the request of envoys from those nations, to announce Christ before definite episcopal sees could be founded there. Thus Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, at the request of envoys from the East, sent Pantaenus—as Saint Jerome reports in *On Illustrious Men*—and he went as far as India for that purpose. Indeed, the foundation of the Church of Antioch had proceeded gradually, following the example of the others: first, brothers dispersed by persecution arrived there and announced Jesus Christ; then Barnabas was sent there from Jerusalem, and took Paul as his companion in the ministry; finally, the prince of the apostles established the episcopal chair in that metropolis of the East, administered it personally for seven full years, and at last handed it over to Euodius and his successors to possess.

When the peaceful condition of the provinces was generally taken into account in assigning episcopal sees, so that definite boundaries—which could not easily be altered—might be assigned to each and retained by successors, it followed that such sees were established especially where Roman colonies, garrisons, and armies, or the seats of allied kings, trading centers, and metropolitan cities of the regions had been founded and had long endured under fixed treaties and established peace. Accordingly, Britain too—whose three bishops we know attended the Council of Arles in the year 314, the most ancient bishops of the entire island whose memory is certain, namely the bishop of Eboracum, the bishop of London, and the bishop of the colony of Lindum—counted them, even under Constantine, as belonging to one and the same ecclesiastical province, as is clear from their subscriptions. The aforementioned sees had by then been established together in a single Roman province during those peaceful times, which belonged to the age of Pope Eleutherius, the Antonines, and King Lucius.

Eboracum is placed first, since Spartianus calls it, by way of distinction, a city. Learned men therefore rightly maintain—as Gale observes on page 20—that it was the metropolis of the whole island. “I take evidence of this also,” he says, “from the fact that in the time of Constantine the Great I see that the district in which Eburacum is situated is called BRITANNIA PRIMA.” That it also possessed, indiscriminately, the status of both a municipium and a colony is shown by the ancient monuments and by the first route of the British itinerary of Antoninus:

**EBVRACVM LEGIO VI. VICTRIX M. P. XVI**  
Eboracum, Sixth Victorious Legion, 16 miles.

A coin of the emperor Severus, recorded by Golzius in the *Thesaurus*, p. 239:

**COL. EBORACVM LEG. VI VICTRIX**  
Colony of Eboracum, Sixth Victorious Legion.

Inscription I, folio 493, in Gruter’s *Thesaurus*, which Cambdenus also reports, and which Gale published in a fuller form in the third line on page 24, shows **M. VERECVNDVM DIOGENEM IIIIII VIRum COLoniae EBORACensis**—Marcus Verecundus Diogenes, one of the four magistrates (*quattuorvir*) of the colony of Eboracum. Panvinius, *Roman Empire*, p. 213. The colony of Eboracum, with the Sixth Victorious Legion, is mentioned by Ptolemy. The colony of Londinum is mentioned by Tacitus in Book 14. Ptolemy’s canon of notable cities follows, recently edited with the greatest accuracy by the distinguished John Hudson in volume 3 of the *Minor Writers of Ancient Geography*, where Eboracum is placed before Londinium. [Col. 1273A]

Regarding the origins and growth of London after the arrival of the Romans, Gale says on page 64:

> “I am now completely uncertain—so may truth love me—what road I should follow in order to find Londinium.”

After noting that Ptolemy places Londinium in Cantium, he continues:

> “It is not easy to believe that Ptolemy wrote this carelessly, since he called Marinus of Tyre to such an exact examination regarding the position of Neomagus and Londinium. I see no other way of resolving this difficulty than to believe that the cradle of the city of London—than which the world now has no equal—must be sought in some Roman station which they established at an early date on the southern bank of the Thames, for the protection of their subjects, after first expelling the Britons from that place. We must seek this station along the military road. A little earlier I showed that this road enters the territory of the Regni of Kent beyond Westminster, at the Thames crossing called the Horse-Ferry.”

He reports that many other remains of antiquity have been found there: numerous Roman coins, mosaic pavements, bricks, and ruins. He adds that the fortress of Cyningston, commonly called Kinton, was located there, where public prisons, public buildings, a fishery, a fishpond, and the meeting point of three military roads—from Durobrivae, Neomagus, and Sulloniacae—indicate a convenient site for a station and one especially cultivated by the Romans.

He therefore holds that Aulus Plautius, the governor, was stationed there with the Roman army beside the River Thames until Claudius, whom he himself had summoned, arrived:

> “Claudius crossed over into Britain,” Dio says, “and proceeded to the forces awaiting him at the Thames; after crossing the river, he engaged the Britons and captured Camalodunum, the royal city of Cunobelinus,” and so forth.

“After that victory over the Trinobantes,” Gale continues,

> “the Romans advanced their forts and garrisons beyond the Thames [Col. 1273C] and gradually pushed the Britons toward the north. From that point onward, the interior regions could be neglected as though they were secure. The colony of Camalodunum was founded; Verulamium was granted the title of municipium; soon London emerged from obscurity in the time of Nero. It was especially famous for its abundance of merchants and supplies, as Tacitus says in Book 14; it was not yet a colony but a prefecture. It also seems to have had a governor’s residence in the village where that famous stone—whether milestone or column of Mercury—stood at the head of the Forum. After surviving many transformations and calamities of the city, it always remained immovable, like the god Terminus.”

It therefore appears from the observations of Gale just quoted and from the testimony of the ancients that, under Nero, London was not yet a colony but a prefecture, and that it gained an opportunity for growth from the destruction of the neighboring colony of Camalodunum, which was so close to its own foundation—we have said that this was carried out by Claudius in the year 50—that only a decade separated the two. Then the queen of the Iceni, sounding the trumpet for the disturbances of Britain, harassed the Romans for so long that in the age of Vespasian and under the rule of his sons Titus and Domitian the condition of the province recovered its former form.

The victories of Hadrian and Antoninus secured complete peace for the Romans on British soil. That period was suitable for restoring the garrisons, establishing the British fleet, and founding or enlarging several colonies. Alcuin assigned first place to Eboracum; Grabe first published him on page 20, where he sings:

> This city Roman hands, with walls and towers high,  
> Founded at first . . . . .  
> That for its leaders the power of the kingdom might be secure,  
> And the glory of the empire, and terror to hostile arms.

But if it was first founded by the Romans “that for its leaders the power might be secure,” and if it became a colony through the transfer there of the veteran soldiers of the Sixth Victorious Legion, this certainly could not have occurred before the reign of Hadrian. For an inscription found in the Roman Forum and published by Gruterus, folio 457, no. 2, presents Marcus Pontius, son of Marcus, of the Pupinian tribe, Laetianus Larcius Sabinus, consul, candidate for the plebeian tribunate of the deified emperor Hadrian, who held several provincial legations and praetorships, and who, under Antoninus Pius, Marcus Aurelius, and Lucius Verus, had been a companion in the expeditions of the German, Armenian, and Parthian wars. This inscription, I say, presents him as military tribune transferring with the Sixth Victorious Legion from Germany to Britain:

**TRIB. MIL. LEG. VI. VICT. CVM. QVA. EX GERM. IN BRITAN. TRANSIIT.**  
Military tribune of the Sixth Victorious Legion, with which he crossed from Germany into Britain.

Since, therefore, the transfer of the Sixth Legion and the colony of Eboracum belongs to the same period as the Antonines, and since the colony of Eboracum was superior in rank to the other colonies of the province of Britain, this shows that the civil and ecclesiastical constitution of the province, as well as the origin of the three oldest episcopal sees founded there, should be assigned to the age of Pope Eleutherius, the Antonines, and King Lucius. It wonderfully confirms what has so far been said concerning the origins of this ecclesiastical province. [Col. 1274B]

It remains to say something about the colony of Lindum [Lincoln], which appears in the subscriptions of the bishops as the third church of that province, and about related matters. For my part, I have nothing further to contribute except to transcribe the equally learned and concise notes of Thomas Gale from page 96:

> “At Lindo [Lin Colne], the Ravenna Anonymous expressly has *Lindum Colonia*. How much light that one added word has shed upon ancient history! We certainly owe him great thanks, because at last we understand the subscription of the Council of Arles: ‘Adelphius, bishop from the city of the colony of Londi,’ undoubtedly for ‘the colony of Lindi.’ Bede almost saw this himself when he called the city *Lindi-Collina*. Ptolemy also called it Lindum. Leland notes in his *Itinerary* that Roman coins are found in the fields north of this city.”

The arrangement of the province, both civil and ecclesiastical, is also commended by the nearly equal division of Britain into three portions through these three colonies and bishoprics: Eboracum, London, and the colony of Lindum. They divide the province into distances sufficiently close to equal, especially if the region beyond the wall restored to the Caledonians by Caracalla is assigned to Eboracum—the region later called the province of Valentia in the *Notitia Dignitatum* under Valentinian.

Certainly, the care of advancing evangelical teaching beyond the wall in the age of Commodus and Severus, and of bringing those places to Christ which Tertullian indicates when he says that the places of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans had then been subjected to Christ, must be considered to have belonged to the bishop of the Church of Eboracum. These matters are more fully understood if some examples are brought forward which we see preserved from the age of the apostles and from the early foundations of episcopal sees.

In founding bishoprics, many arrangements had to be made and taken into account, arrangements that would promote the good both of that particular Church and of the universal Church when a new episcopal see was erected, so that it might not be said of it: “You have multiplied the nation, but you have not increased the joy.”

The first requirement was that definite boundaries be assigned, within which the new pastor would enclose his flock. The second was that, within those same boundaries, the bishop might, through an orderly division, count, know, care for, and govern each of the faithful entrusted to him, both in the city and in the countryside, individually, either personally or through presbyters, so that no one would lack the protections of doctrine and the sacraments prepared for salvation. The third was that the unity of the parts of that Church be carefully preserved, together with the closest bond of unity with the Church, chief and mother of all, established by the Lord through the see of the apostle Peter.

These three conditions and arrangements, necessarily required for the proper founding of new bishoprics, are clearly seen to arise from ancient discipline and are still retained today when one chosen according to the rules of the holy Fathers is consecrated to the dignity of so great an order. He binds himself by oath to visit the thresholds of the apostles every three years and to render an account to Christ’s vicar on earth, the successor of Peter, concerning the condition of his Church, clergy, and the discipline and salvation of the souls entrusted to him. Likewise, in the questions put beforehand by the consecrating bishop, he is asked:

> “Do you wish to teach, both by words and by example, the people over whom you are to be ordained, the things that you understand from the divine Scriptures? Do you wish reverently to receive, teach, and observe the traditions of the orthodox Fathers and the decretal constitutions of the holy and apostolic see? Do you wish to [Col. 1275A] … blessed Peter the apostle,”

and the rest that follows, up to the final question asking “whether he wishes to be affable and merciful toward all who are in need, for the name of the Lord.”

The means and arrangements for fulfilling these promises could not be found equally in every form of government, unless it approached the model of that regime which the apostles had experienced among the people instructed in the true worship of God through Moses and prepared as a figure of the Christian Church.

The surveying of the land and its division among the twelve tribes, the division of each tribe among families and of families among individuals, the designation of priestly cities, the fixed duties of Levites and priests, the registration of citizens in the books of the sanctuary, the assembly of all people summoned on appointed days to the same temple, and the repetition of the divine law from books guarded with the utmost holiness formed minds for preserving the unity of the Church of God, no less than for maintaining a definite and stable order drawn from the faithful collected from every side. They also made it possible for Levites and priests to instruct each of their own people in the doctrine and duties of the divine law, since that civil division made the public benefit of law and priesthood readily and immediately available to every individual citizen.

For this reason it was decided that an episcopal see should be founded at Jerusalem for the nascent Church of Christ before one was founded elsewhere. For many years it was forbidden for Churches independent of that Church of Jerusalem to be founded outside the boundaries of the Jews. In Jerusalem, we know, the council of the new law—the assembly of the apostles, over which Peter presided—had been established, as learned men infer from the account of Apollonius cited above in Eusebius. The purpose was to preserve, together with the unity of the Church, an order of government and a discipline that would make it easy for the bishop to teach the people entrusted to him both in the temple of God and from house to house, following the example of the apostles in Jerusalem.

When, however, the apostles were led from Judaea into the provinces by the divine Spirit, which was destined to fill the whole world with its faithful, they first remained for a time in the synagogues of the Jews, announcing Christ, where there was greater hope of preserving the ancient order and unity. There they demonstrated the connection and harmony of Christ’s doctrine and discipline with the oracles and institutions of the prophets. Then they turned to the Gentiles, who had been in a certain sense tamed by the sight of the ancient Jewish Church. They assigned bishops especially to those peoples among whom some imitation of the Jerusalem polity had introduced into the constitution of the state a rudimentary form of division suitable for the easier exercise of episcopal care, with the diligence that the apostle of the Gentiles said he had shown toward the Ephesians (Acts 20): teaching publicly and from house to house, and for three years, night and day, not ceasing to admonish each of them with tears—the elders of the Church whom he had summoned. In this way he had made them citizens friendly to unity and patient and zealous in preserving order.

The manner in which the apostolic bishops could more easily achieve this in regions subject to the rule of the Roman state, and already arranged by the constitution of that same empire—which had transferred most of its practices from Jewish and Greek examples into its own customs—can be understood by anyone who considers the condition of the city of Rome and of the provinces of the empire under Augustus and the Caesars who followed him, in the first century of Christ and in the second under the Antonines.

The civil arrangement itself and the connections among the parts that constituted the city of Rome, the state, and the empire, especially in colonies and municipia, supplied the bishop and his presbyters with a ready division of the city and countryside to be reduced to an ecclesiastical census. Thus, publicly in the Lord’s house, district by district, and from house to house, bread could be broken for the faithful, just as in the first episcopate of Jerusalem; definite parish boundaries could immediately be assigned to the bishop and definite ones to the presbyters; and the closest bond with the Roman see, the mother and head of all, established by Peter, could be maintained, with easy access and refuge there in more serious cases. The universal Church, thus held together in each of its parts, would become terrifying and impregnable against the attacks of its enemies, like an army arrayed in battle order.

To return to Britain, whose first episcopal foundations are now proposed for elucidation on the occasion of Eleutherius’s sending suitable men to that province: there was an extraordinary ease in assigning duties and boundaries to each bishop from the three oldest sees already mentioned, an ease that seemed to flow naturally from the civil organization of the province itself.

Once appointed—as an example—the bishop of the Eboracenses understood that the same parish boundaries assigned to him together with the city of Eboracum also measured the territory of the colony. In addition, he was instructed to exercise certain rights over the entire province beyond the boundaries of the parish and colony, just as the Roman prefect of Britain, residing at Eboracum, exercised authority over the praetorships of the same province. These rights were later called those of an archbishop or primate.

The bishop of London was assigned the boundaries of the city and prefecture of London. The bishop of Lincoln received a similar assignment, enclosed within the already known boundaries of the territory of that colony. Each bishop, together with his clergy and people, was instructed to preserve a definite order of unity and obedience toward the Roman see and its supreme hierarch, the successor of the apostle Peter.

Since among the Romans it was customary for a definite magistrate to be sent from the emperor in Rome—**CENSITOR CIVIVM ROMANORVM EIVSDEM COLONIAE**, “censor of the Roman citizens of that colony”—and since I mentioned above, from an ancient inscription on page 147, such an official in the British colony of the Victrices at Camalodunum, the same arrangement could be carried out with equal ease in the Christian census of the faithful of that bishopric, since the civil designation everywhere led the bishop along the same boundaries.

Because such arrangements could scarcely be attempted on hostile soil, especially where Romans and islanders were engaged in conflict with varying fortunes—for the boundaries of the bishoprics would have had to change as often as victories on either side followed one another, if episcopal chairs had initially been established anywhere other than in the peaceful parts of the province and according to the fixed order of colonies and municipia already accustomed to them—this is why the most ancient bishoprics of the provinces are found more readily designated and established in metropolitan cities, colonies, municipia, stations, or Roman garrisons. On hostile soil, indeed, the light of our faith was spread by suitable men sent there by the care of the pontiff or of neighboring bishops to teach, but episcopal sees there appear to have been established only later.

To make this discipline clearer, I ask the reader to note that, just as tradition says that Roman presbyters were first sent by Eleutherius to Britain and bishops were later ordained, so too, in the other provinces and foundations of episcopal sees, we read that bishops were often chosen from the Roman presbytery, or at least ordained by the various Roman pontiffs in different places. There were many serious reasons for this discipline, including the following, which should not be counted among the least: it arose from the ease of preserving order both in assigning definite boundaries to individual bishoprics and in maintaining their bond with the principal chair of the whole Church.

The presbyteral titles established in Rome by the successors of the apostle Peter at his command should be regarded as equivalent to dioceses. I mentioned this above in the notes on Cletus and Evaristus, page 77, and we shall read below in Dionysius, no. 26:

> “He divided the Churches among the presbyters, and established cemeteries and parishes as dioceses.”

And more clearly in Marcellus, no. 31:

> “He established twenty-five titles in the city of Rome as though they were dioceses, for the sake of baptism and penance for the many who were converted from paganism, and for the burials of the martyrs.”

What, finally, was this form and rudimentary model of dioceses or parishes—namely, of bishoprics—in the Roman titles? It was such and so extensive that the order and administration of even the most extensive bishopric, no less than its connection with the supreme priest, could be perceived from an inspection of any one Roman title.

Augustus divided the City into fourteen regions, defined by fixed boundaries and spaces. Each region recognized its own districts, and each district its own apartment blocks. This civil division of the regions of the City and of its parts made it easy and clear—as can be discerned from the Capitoline inscription published by Gruterus on page 250, as well as from Rufus and Victor—for the curators, announcers, district magistrates, and other officials appointed to administer each region to know and manage the boundaries assigned to them.

The same division gave the Roman presbyters an equally clear jurisdiction over the definite boundaries assigned to each title. For the regional deacons, the arrangement was especially ready and precise from the circumference and boundaries of the regions: two regions assigned to each deacon contracted the fourteen Augustan regions into seven pontifical ones. Similarly, the known boundaries of the twenty-five districts and apartment blocks assigned by the pontifical division to the presbyters left nothing uncertain or deprived of the care of a particular presbyter.

The system of order that in the civil administration of the City connected district magistrates with the curator and the curator with the prefect of the City was also employed in the ecclesiastical division: notaries were subordinate to regional subdeacons, subdeacons to deacons, and deacons to presbyters. The apartment blocks, districts, their inhabitants, and each of the faithful—whether they were born in Christ through baptism, died, or were restored through the sacrament of grace by penance—recognized their own judge and censor in the cardinal presbyter of the title. Thus they were connected with the bishop, the head of the presbytery and of the universal Church, who acts on earth in the place of Christ.

Who does not see that, just as the organization and unity of the Roman empire provided a vehicle for conveying the Gospel more easily, as we have said, so also the properly constituted division of the City and the organization of the regions with their offices supplied a fully developed method for governing dioceses and parishes? This method was embodied in the administration of the titles and in the urban titles and their presbyters, who were formed by pontifical authority according to this law of order and supplemented by civil custom.

That discipline therefore provided no small compendium of what was required in founding episcopal chairs, assigning boundaries, and preserving the bond with the apostolic see. This was especially so when presbyters from the urban clergy were sent by the Roman pontiff to organize Churches and future bishoprics or provinces—presbyters trained in the administration of the City’s titles as though in the governance of dioceses—or when bishops ordained at Rome, eyewitnesses to this pontifical discipline and sometimes employed for a time in the care of vicariate authority, were granted to peoples and kings who requested them, like veteran commanders of Christ’s detachments and censors of truly Roman citizens, to lead colonies to the heavenly Jerusalem and closely connect them with this earthly metropolis of those same colonies.

If anyone thinks that these matters have been discussed at greater length than the method of notes required for the section on Eleutherius—which presents the requests of King Lucius and Eleutherius’s fatherly care in advancing the Christian religion among the Britons and organizing the Churches of that province—I hope he will forgive an excursion that is neither useless nor unrelated to the method of the Notes on Anastasius. For he will see that the commentary here on the ecclesiastical foundation of the province of Britain has been constructed in such a way that it recognizes not only a model for the Churches of Britain but also for the bishoprics and provinces of the whole West, administered by the supreme hierarch of the Roman see according to the example of the prince of the apostles, whom he succeeded.

Indeed, he may think he sees here a brief image of the Churches of the whole world, since Mark, sent from here to organize the patriarchate of Alexandria in a similar way, and Euodius, sent to administer the see of Antioch in the same manner, connected the provinces of the entire Christian world with the chair of Peter and with the discipline of the Roman Church under the same right and by no different method of government.

I wish the reader to understand what was said above about the double boundary and the walls of Hadrian and Antoninus in the following way: on the western boundary, along the meridian line drawn from Clausentum to Luguvallium, he should not suppose that the emperors raised a continuous wall. Rather, the boundary ran from Clausentum [Southampton] to Isca Flavia [Usk]; from there the river’s course, from its mouth to its source, took the place of a wall as far as Rotunum [Routon]. From there, a wall was again raised to the estuaries near Deva [Chester], and the Ocean, washing the coastal region of western Britain opposite the island of Mona, completed the remaining part of the boundary from the estuaries of Deva to Luguvallium [Carlisle].

There the other boundary begins: namely, a wall running from west to east, from Luguvallium to Gabrosentum, reaching the Ocean at both ends and separating modern Scotland from England. Along the former boundary, drawn approximately on the meridian line, Britannia Prima was later divided from Britannia Secunda and from Flavia Caesariensis under Valentinian, as Gale shows on his map.]

[Note: [Col. 1278B]

**Line 3.**—Here he received a letter from Lucius, king of Britain, asking that he be made a Christian through his command. At the beginning of Eleutherius’s pontificate, Lucius, son of Coillus, king of the Britons in the year of Christ 182 and in the thirteenth year of his reign, wishing to restore the Christian religion that had been extinguished, sent to the apostolic see two prudent and eminent men of his own people, Elvanus and Medianus, with letters. He requested from the pontiff teachers of the Christian religion who could instruct both him and his people in it and baptize them after they had been instructed.

The Christian religion had first been preached in that island by Joseph of Arimathea, who buried Christ’s body. He had arrived there by ship with a large company, whether by chance or by divine plan and God’s will. He and his companions had led many from paganism to piety through the sacred waters and had established a Church. For Gildas, the most ancient writer of that people, testifies that the Britons had embraced the Christian religion from the very beginning of the Gospel’s origin.

Eleutherius, without delay, sent there Fugatius and Damianus, presbyters of the Holy Roman Church, men of outstanding learning and piety, to satisfy the king’s wishes. Thus, through Eleutherius’s efforts, Britain was the first of all the provinces publicly to receive the Gospel. So much so that Tertullian, a contemporary of those times, wrote in his book *Against the Jews* that the places of the Britons inaccessible to the Romans had then been subjected to Christ.

**Line 5.**—So that no customary food might be rejected by Christians. At that time the heresy of the Encratites was gaining strength; it condemned not only marriage but also human foods. Eleutherius therefore decreed that no member of the faithful, out of superstition, should reject any kind of food that people customarily ate.]

[Note: [Col. 1278D]

**Line 3.**—Here he received a letter. At the beginning of his pontificate, Eleutherius received a letter from Lucius, king of Britain, asking him to send ministers and priests of the divine word to Britain, so that they might instruct the people in faith and morals. Accordingly, this holy pontiff sent Fugatius and Damianus, or Donatianus, who initiated the king and others instructed in the Christian religion into the sacred mysteries.

Besides the *Book of the Pontiffs*, we have the testimony of Bede concerning this conversion. In Book 1, chapter 4, of his *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, he says:

> “When the holy man Eleutherius presided over the pontificate of the Roman Church, Lucius, king of the Britons, sent him a letter, begging that through his command he might be made a Christian, and he soon obtained the fulfillment of his pious request.”

Moreover, Baronius, under the year 183, no. 5, proves that in the time of Pope Eleutherius Britain, not yet entirely conquered by the Romans, but with a large part of its population still living beyond the wall, had a king.] 

[Note: [Col. 1279A]

Line 4.—“From Lucius, king of Britain,” etc. Those who call the deed of King Lucius into question, or even deny it (Basnage, *History of the Church*, book VII, chapter 5, no. 4), [Col. 1279B] being led by the conviction that Britain, having been reduced to a province under Claudius, could not at this time have had kings, fail to notice that it was customary among the Romans very often to leave or appoint kings who were bound to them and allied with them over provinces, even provinces brought under their power and subjected to their rule. Examples of this may be seen in Judaea, Armenia, and Britain itself under Nero, as Tacitus records (*Annals*, book XIV), Josephus (*Antiquities*, book XIV, chapter 26, and elsewhere), and Spartianus in his *Life of Hadrian*.

Moreover, it is clear that the whole island was by no means conquered by the Romans; and that the wall extending for eighty thousand paces, constructed by Hadrian, to which his successor Antoninus added a rampart, separated the part obedient to the empire from the remainder, which was under the free rule of the islanders.

Lucius’s kingdom, therefore, could have been situated beyond the wall. Tertullian perhaps speaks of that part of Britain when he asserts that the inaccessible regions of the Britons were inaccessible to the Romans but subject to Christ. But if some more recent writer wished to embellish the event with attributes invented and added on his own initiative, do such additions [Col. 1280B] detract from the credibility of the genuine narratives of the ancients?

[Col. 1249]

14

Eleutherius, a Greek by nation, the son of Abundius, from the town of Nicopolis, sat for fifteen years, six months, and five days [Note: [Col. 1249] B, fifteen years and twenty-three days.]. He lived in the times of Antoninus and Commodus, down to the consulship of Paternus and Bradua [Note: [Col. 1249] B, Marcus Aurelius and Commodus, down to the consulship of Commodus VIII and Pertinax.]. He [Note: [Col. 1249] Baronius, under the year 183.] received a letter from Lucius, king of Britain, asking that he might be made a Christian through his command; and he also confirmed this, that no customary food created by God, which is nevertheless rational and human, should be rejected by Christians, especially by the faithful.

He held three ordinations in the month of December: twelve presbyters, eight deacons, and fifteen bishops in various places. He was also buried beside the body of blessed Peter the Apostle in the Vatican, on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, and the episcopate remained vacant for five days.

Line 4.—“Just as Eleutherius.” The second catalogue reads: “Just as Pius, who, on account of the book of the *Shepherd*, could have commanded that Holy Pascha be celebrated on the Lord’s Day.” In any case, Victor the pope wished this rite, which was not customary among the Asians, to be observed everywhere; and on this account he ordered frequent councils to be held both at Rome and in the provinces of other regions. The author indicates this in his final words, and it entirely agrees with what Eusebius relates on this subject in book V, chapter 23.]

[Note: [Col. 1281B]
