Line 3.—“He decreed that Holy Pascha should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day, just as Eleutherius.” I believe that this paragraph was copied from Bede and inserted by the compiler into the deeds of Victor. In his book *On the Six Ages*, Bede writes: “Victor, having sent letters, decreed that Pascha should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day, just as his predecessor Eleutherius also did.”

I find a similar addition taken from Bede above, under Eleutherius, where I read (*Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book I, chapter 4): “He received a letter from Lucius, king of Britain, asking that he might be made a Christian through his command.” Bede has almost the same words: “When Eleutherius, a holy man, presided over the pontificate of the Roman Church, Lucius, king of the Britons, sent him a letter, beseeching that through his command he might be made a Christian; and he immediately obtained the fulfillment of his pious request,” etc.

I infer that the addition was made by a later hand from codex 39 of the Palatine-Vatican Library, no. 39, which contains very ancient parchment leaves representing these deeds of the pontiffs; there one reads: “Just as Pius.” Moreover, Irenaeus, in his letter to Victor, mentions Pius, not Eleutherius, in connection with this controversy. He says (in Eusebius, book V, chapter 24): “Nor did those presbyters who governed the Church over which you now preside before Soter—I mean Anicetus, Pius, and Hyginus, together with Telesphorus and Sixtus—ever observe it themselves,” etc.

Hence it appears that the addition made by a later hand was taken from Bede, since Bede alone praises Victor and Eleutherius as the authors of those decrees; whereas the most ancient catalogues mention Victor and Pius. The latter must be followed, since they agree with Irenaeus, who, living at that same time, could have known and recorded these decrees more accurately.

Line 4.—“Here he made the following clergy. He is crowned with martyrdom, and he decreed that, when necessity required … he should be baptized.” In the Acts there occurs a remarkable transposition and a disordered sequence of events, which discloses and confirms our conjecture concerning additions and interpolations that must be restored to their proper place. Those words, therefore, “He is crowned with martyrdom,” must be joined to the preceding words, and the text should read: “Here he is crowned with martyrdom. Here he made the following clergy … and he decreed that, when necessity required, etc.”

Apart from the second Florentine and Regal codices, the order of the treatment itself proves the transposition and confirms the restoration that has been made. We have restored, with dots, certain words indicating that some material has been omitted, since we believe that there once existed an order and hierarchy of ministers to be observed in the administration of baptism, which Victor decreed should be retained. The copyist omitted the ranks when he enumerated them, although the words “through the following clergy” plainly indicate that an order established by the pontiff was being specified.

That Victor could have issued this decree because of some circumstance unknown to us is proved by the writer Tertullian, from the same period, in *On Baptism*, chapter 17. He assigns the order to be observed in administering baptism and the distinction among persons, saying:

“Indeed, the right of conferring baptism belongs to the high priest, who is the bishop. Next come the presbyters and deacons, though not without the authority of the bishop, because of the honor due to the Church; when that is preserved, peace is preserved.”

After inserting some remarks about the laity, whom he denies to be the ordinary ministers of baptism, he adds:

“Since these responsibilities belong to superiors, let them not arrogate to themselves the office assigned to bishops—that is, the episcopate. Rivalry is the mother of schisms. The most holy Apostle says that all things are lawful, but not all things are expedient. Let it suffice to make use of this in cases of necessity, wherever the circumstances of place, time, or person compel it. For then the conscience of the one who comes to the aid of another is exempt from blame, when the emergency of the endangered person presses. For he is guilty of the loss of a person if he delays providing what he was freely able to provide.”

The argument, revisited and weighed by Tertullian, shows that in that age there were rivalries concerning the administration of baptism. To suppress them, Victor decreed the following order of clergy, namely, the order to be observed by the senior clergy, setting out a sequence which the negligence of the copyists has concealed. Moreover, that this order was also observed in cases of necessity, when the urgency of time did not prevent assistance from being given, is shown by an event of a somewhat later period, when Novatian was alive.

When he was a presbyter and catechumens were in need of baptism, the deacons did not dare to confer baptism and therefore summoned Novatian, who refused to come. Cornelius lists this among Novatian’s crimes in his letter to Fabius of Antioch, according to Rufinus’s translation:

“For he writes concerning him that, during the persecution, while he was hiding in a certain cell, and the deacons were asking him, as is customary, to assist the catechumens at the point of death,” etc., “he himself, fearing the persecution, refused to undertake that responsibility.”

It was therefore customary, even when catechumens needed assistance, that, if presbyters were present, they should baptize. Since Victor determined the sequence of persons, it must be said that this sequence was omitted, and that there had once been a reason for the determination which moved Victor to issue the decree. See Saint Augustine, *Against Parmenianus*, book II, chapter 13.

Line 10.—“Here he issued a decree.” He repeats at greater length what he had said earlier concerning the decree about the controversy over the day of Pascha. This repetition clearly proves that additions were made either to the second Roman catalogue of the pontiffs or to other sources, and that the compilers generally did not wish to alter them, but later collected them into one account as they found them recorded in the catalogues.

“To the questions of the priests.” This addition explains more fully how Victor’s decree was published: namely, after the letters of the bishops, who, each giving responses to Victor’s questions within his own province, replied unanimously that Pascha was to be celebrated on the Lord’s Day after the fourteenth day of the moon.

Eusebius describes this procedure in book V, chapter 23:

“On this account synods and assemblies of bishops came together. And all, with one accord, delivered the ecclesiastical rule to all the faithful by letters, namely, that the mystery of the Lord’s Resurrection should never be celebrated on any day other than the Lord’s Day, and that only on that day should we observe the ending of the Paschal fasts.”

Concerning the letters sent on that occasion, Eusebius continues:

“There is still extant the letter of the priests who were then assembled in Palestine, presided over by Theophilus of Caesarea in Palestine and Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem. There is also extant another letter of the Roman synod, bearing at its head the name of Bishop Victor. In addition, the letters of the bishops of Pontus are preserved, presided over by Palmas, as the most ancient of them. There is also extant a letter of the churches of Gaul, over which Irenaeus presided. The letters of the churches in the province of Osrhoene and in the cities established in that region are likewise to be seen.”

These letters, collected into a single codex, which was consequently called *encyclical*, still existed in Eusebius’s time, and he briefly described their order. There was another epistolary codex on the same subject, which he mentions there in these words:

“Separately, the letters of Bacchylus, bishop of Corinth, and of many others, are also extant.”

He sets forth their unanimous agreement as follows:

“All of them, expressing the same faith and the same teaching, issued one judgment.”

In this addition the *Liber Pontificalis* corresponds to the order of the cited encyclical codex: Theophilus is placed first, followed by Victor’s synodical letter, as the text reads here: “and having summoned, by letter, Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria”—one must certainly read “of Caesarea,” as Eusebius wrote—“a gathering having been held,” namely, of the synodical letters which they had sent in response to Victor’s inquiry, “so that from the fourteenth moon,” etc.

That these letters were encyclical and declaratory letters, by which bishops in that age clarified emerging questions of faith or discipline according to the tradition preserved and guarded in their own churches, and sent them to neighboring churches, which in turn sent them to others throughout all the churches of the world, is plainly taught by the synodical letter of the Palestinians under Theophilus. It admonishes its readers as follows:

“Take care that copies of our letter be sent throughout all the churches, so that they may not accuse us of a crime who easily lead their souls away from the straight path of truth. We also inform you that Pascha is celebrated at Alexandria on the same day as among us. For letters are carried from us to them and in turn from them to us, so that with one accord and at the same time we may celebrate the most sacred day.”

The particularly specific controversy which arose at that time during Victor’s pontificate, instigated by the Judaizers, concerned those who taught that the observances of the Law were to be combined with the Christian religion as necessary for salvation. They attacked the decree as foreign to the usage of the churches and to the apostolic tradition.

To blunt their accusations, Victor and the other Catholic bishops, assembling in provincial synods, set forth in their synodical letters the established custom of celebration. The first inquiry was undertaken in Palestine, where the apostolic institutions of the churches were still in force and attested the custom held and received from the apostles; this is what they demonstrated in the synodical letter mentioned above.

That the dispute concerned the apostolic tradition and practice preserved down to Victor’s time is clearly suggested by Eusebius. After reporting the synod under Theophilus of Caesarea in Palestine and Narcissus of Jerusalem, who was then subject to Caesarea by metropolitan jurisdiction, he presents the subject of the controversy in these terms:

“After they had discussed in their letters the tradition of the day of Pascha, which had passed down from the apostles to them by continuous succession, they finally used these words at the end of the letter: ‘Take care,’” and the rest quoted above.

This is also gathered from another observation of Eusebius. In listing the synodical letters issued by the bishops, he first praises Palmas, the most ancient bishop and leader of Pontus, as particularly suited to make known the custom of earlier times. Secondly, when reporting Theophilus’s words in the synodical letter, he notes the passage in which Theophilus commends both his own advanced age and the long-disputed question, which he nevertheless says had been resolved by the other bishops according to the received custom of celebrating Pascha on the Sunday following the fourteenth day of the moon:

“I, who am sixty-five years old in the Lord and who have often conferred on these matters with the brothers scattered throughout the whole world …”

This, therefore, is what the *Liber Pontificalis* indicates in its second account of the decree issued by Victor: the predecessors had determined the day; and when the Judaizers attacked the decree as contrary to apostolic usage, Victor, having instructed the Palestinian bishops—and through them the other bishops of the world—summoned or selected Theophilus, since the established custom was already confirmed, and entrusted him with clarifying the tradition. He issued the decree and, once it had been issued, restrained the boldness of the Judaizers. [Col. 1284B] From Victor’s time down to the Council of Nicaea, the bishops and the Church preserved the practice of celebrating Pascha on the Lord’s Day.

“Concerning the Paschal cycle, or also the termination of the fasts.” Eusebius had said in book V, chapter 23, that both controversies had been stirred up under Victor by the Judaizers:

“In those same times a serious controversy arose because all the churches of Asia, relying upon an ancient tradition, judged that the fourteenth day of the moon was the day on which the saving feast of Pascha should be celebrated, on which day the Jews had been commanded to sacrifice the lamb. They also determined that the fasts should be ended on that very moon, whatever day of the week it happened to fall upon; whereas all the other churches throughout the world followed another custom, derived from the tradition of the apostles and still maintained, namely, that the fasts might be broken on no other day than the day of the Lord’s Resurrection.”

The ending of the fasts was the second part of the controversy. Irenaeus expressed this more clearly in his letter to Victor, quoted by Eusebius in book V, chapter 24, page 192:

“For the controversy is not only about the day, but also about the manner of the fast itself. Some think that they should fast for one day only, others for two, and others for more. Some also measure their day by forty continuous hours, reckoning both day and night. This diversity in the observance of the fast was not first known in our own age, but began long ago among our ancestors, who, as may be believed, presiding with less care, handed down to their successors a custom that arose from simplicity and ignorance.”

That Victor settled both controversies is stated by the author of the synodical treatise. After recounting the Roman synod under Victor and the determination of the day, he adds (vol. V of the Councils, p. 1494):

“Nor does he pursue only this matter, but also those things which pertained to this feast; and the members of the synod, gathered together with him in many provinces and regions of the earth, agree unanimously in the same judgment.”

Those words—“he also pursues those things which pertained to this feast”—sufficiently indicate that Victor also established something concerning the rule for ending the fast. Victor decreed that the fast should be extended until the Sabbath before the Lord’s Day, indeed until midnight on the Sabbath, while nevertheless leaving intact the various customs of the peoples who ended the Lenten fast somewhat earlier.

In the following, third century, Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, speaks in his canonical letter, preserved by Beveridge in volume II, part I, received by the Eastern Church and occupying the first place among the canonical letters in his collection of canons, both about the Roman custom and about the diversity of the other churches:

“You sent to me … asking at what hour the fast of Pascha should be ended. For you say that some brothers say that this should be done at cockcrow, while others say that it should be done in the evening. The brothers who are at Rome, they say, await the cockcrow. But concerning those who are here, you said that they do it earlier.”

Dionysius proposes the Roman practice above the others as the one to be followed. He himself states that in the time of Epiphanius the fast was extended in the East until cockcrow, when he discusses superstitious fasting, in the *Ancoratus*:

“Those who are zealous add a second, third, or fourth day; some extend it through the entire week until cockcrow,” etc.

These final words explain that the end of the fasts was generally understood to be at cockcrow on the night of the Sabbath. A *superpositio* in fasting occurred when someone, beyond the ordinary fast, went without food for two or more days. The word occurs in this sense in the Acts of the Martyrs of Numidia, no. 8: “The fasts having been continued in prison by a double *superpositio*.”

That settling disputes about fasts belonged to episcopal responsibility is clearly attested by Tertullian, writing at this very time in his book *On Fasting*: “The bishops are accustomed to prescribe fasts to the whole people.”

Victor, therefore, recognizing the proper end of the fast from the bishops whom he had questioned, declared in his decree what was to be followed, so that they might properly observe the Paschal cycle. Moreover, among the Armenians the custom still continues of ending the fast on the Sabbath evening of the Lord’s Resurrection.]

[Note: [Col. 1285B]

(EX BIN.) Line 11.—“To Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria.” Eusebius, book V of his *History*, chapter 22, testifies that this Theophilus, summoned by Victor to the Roman council, was not the bishop of Alexandria but the metropolitan bishop of Caesarea in Palestine.

Line 13.—“Let Holy Pascha be observed.” He decreed that Pascha was to be celebrated on the Sunday immediately following the fourteenth day of the moon after the spring equinox.

(EX LAB.) Line 11.—“A conference having been held.” The inquiry concerned Pascha, or the first day, with Theophilus.]

[Note: [Col. 1285B]

CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES.

[Col. 1285C] How greatly examination of the original documentary evidence contributes both to the attainment of chronology and to the history of Victor will be shown by the two epochs of Victor and Zephyrinus, which we must examine and establish. It would scarcely be possible to decide anything about them by inspecting the catalogues alone, even where all agree, unless the originals from which the catalogues were copied were consulted and errors in the copies detected.

At the end of Eleutherius, dated by the consulship of Maternus and Bradua, or at the first year of Victor, A.D. 185, all the catalogues and codices agree, just as they do at the end of Zephyrinus, to whom they unanimously assign the consuls of the year 217, Praesens and Extricatus. They assign Eleutherius’s death to May 26 and Zephyrinus’s to August 26. From May 26, 185, to August 26, 217, there are thirty-two complete years and three complete months.

The total period assigned to Victor by the agreement of all the catalogues is ten years, two months, and ten days. [Col. 1285D] One codex only, that of Papebrochius, subtracts a month; and the latest of the Colbertine manuscripts, while preserving the complete two months, subtracts eight days from the total. Accordingly, twenty-two years and twenty days remain for Zephyrinus. Yet the catalogue of Felix IV assigns him seven years, others eight, others nine, and others thirteen, sixteen, seventeen, eighteen, or nineteen years; but no codex reaches twenty years.

If one considers the method of writing the numbers preserved in the basilica of Saint Paul and in certain ancient codices, it becomes sufficiently clear that twelve years and ten days were assigned to Victor’s see, and eighteen years, ten months, and ten days to Zephyrinus. Their total makes thirty-one years, ten months, and ten days, and corresponds exactly to the assigned consulships and to the period of both martyrdoms, allowing only a few days of interregnum after Victor’s death for the election of his successor. I shall explain how I discovered this from the paintings of Saint Paul and the ancient codices.

In the repeatedly described paintings of the pontiffs in the basilica of Saint Paul [Col. 1286A]—a specimen of which I gave above [col. 1001] in a printed figure—the space between the two neighboring pontiffs, between the circles surrounding their images, is filled by a double inscription. The names and periods of those two pontiffs are marked in Roman letters.

The number of years after the pontiff’s name, together with the words “SED AN,” “he sat years,” is generally placed in one line; the months in the line immediately below; and the days in the lowest line. Sometimes, however, a number begun in one line is continued in the following columns because of lack of space.

Thus, in the case of Pope Eusebius, twenty-five days are expressed as follows:

X X V

In the same way, in the case of Mark, twenty-one days are marked:

XX I

And in the case of Anastasius, twenty-six days are placed as follows:

[Col. 1286B]

X XVI

Because copyists failed to notice this, when a number occupied two lines owing to the number of years, they easily read two numbers instead of two parts of a single number, referring the first to the years and the second to the months—especially where no month had to be expressed above the complete years, or no day added above the complete months.

With this observation applied, the totals correspond to the numbers correctly marked and to the consulships likewise correctly expressed. This must be demonstrated in Victor’s case. According to the agreement of the catalogues and other codices, he was assigned, as I explained on page XCIV of the *Prolegomena*, ten years, two months, and ten days.

This cannot at all correspond to the days and years of the martyrdom or death of his predecessor Eleutherius and of Victor himself: Eleutherius is commemorated as having died on May 26, while Victor is celebrated as having been received into heaven on July 28. Therefore two months and ten days cannot be counted between the two termini in addition to complete years, even if Victor is assumed to have been elected on the very day on which Eleutherius died.

The consulships also contradict the assigned decade, since eleven pairs of consuls are counted from Commodus V and Glabrio, A.D. 186, assigned as Victor’s first, to Saturninus and Gallus, A.D. 198, assigned as the first of Zephyrinus. Thus neither the days nor the years agree with Victor’s period, although the codices and catalogues agree so strongly about the numbers.

The Leonine paintings preserve only the sign for ten in the first line, in which part of the number of years was read. The letters of the following lines, where the months and days, if any, were to be marked, are missing. I have no doubt that the sign for two did not follow in the second line, not because it referred to months, of which there were none, but because it belonged to the remaining part of the number twelve, completing the total of the years whose first part was marked in the upper line.

Thus the period should be understood as expressed in this way: [Col. 1286D] the copyist presented it as: “He sat ten years, two months, and ten days.”

Moreover, twelve years and ten days after the end of Eleutherius on May 26, 185, correctly reach the end of Victor on July 28, 197, if one month and twenty-three days of vacancy of the see are assigned between Eleutherius’s death and Victor’s election and ordination on Sunday, July 18, 185. Thus, up to the end of Victor’s life on July 28, 197, the total amounts to twelve years and ten days.

Nevertheless, his first consuls are Saturninus and Gallus, who mark the year 186 and the first Pascha of his pontificate, since in the preceding year, 185, when Maternus and Bradua were consuls, the Paschal season belonged to Eleutherius, who was still alive.

[Col. 1287A] The same corruption of the numbers could have arisen from the codices if the years, months, and days were arranged in adjacent columns, as I have observed in certain ancient exemplars. Their columns are so close that a copyist could easily have taken the number two from one column and moved it into the following one.

I shall give an example. A small amount of space carelessly omitted by a scribe between the decade and the two of Victor’s years could have led copyists into error and provided an occasion for assigning the ten to the column of years and the two to the column of months. They would not have fallen into this error if they had taken care to compare the signs for the years with the consulships recorded in the most ancient catalogue of Liberius. From these it is evident that twelve years must be assigned to Victor and eighteen to Zephyrinus, just as is clear from the natal days of each recorded in the Church’s tables. Nor can two months be assigned to Victor in addition to complete years.

We shall therefore restore the genuine reading of Victor’s period in the codices and paintings by means of the same numerical letters. When these are separated, the reading is corrupted; when joined, it is preserved—provided that, from the consulships named in the Felician catalogue and transferred from it into the librarians’ codices, and also from the recorded natal days of Victor and his predecessor in the ecclesiastical tables, the text is restored as I presented it on page 112 in supplying the gaps in the Liberian catalogue, namely:

Victor sat twelve years and ten days. He lived in the times of Commodus and Severus, from the consulship of Commodus V and Glabrio down to that of Lateranus and Rufinus.

For in the consulship of Maternus and Bradua, in the year 185, when Eleutherius completed his life on May 26, the day on which he is commemorated, the vacancy of the see appears to have continued until about Sunday, July 18, [Col. 1287C] of that same year, when Victor, elected by the clergy as successor, was ordained bishop. He celebrated the first Pascha of his pontificate in the following year, 186, when Commodus V and Glabrio were consuls; these are the first consuls assigned to him according to the Paschal method of the catalogues.

When twelve years and ten days had elapsed after the day of his ordination, if he suffered martyrdom on the same July 28 on which he is commemorated, he reached the consuls of the year 197, Lateranus and Rufinus, whom the catalogues and the codices mentioned above assign to him as his last.

THE SAME AUTHOR’S HISTORICAL NOTES.

Line 2.—“In the times of Helius Pertinax.” Everyone knows from coins and historians that one must read “Helvius Pertinax.” I am pleased to add the testimony of an ancient stone transferred from the hills of Leprignano to the museum of His Eminence Cardinal Alessandro Albani. It establishes the period of his very brief reign—eleven months and twenty-five days—as reckoned by Julius Capitolinus in his *Life*, from the Kalends of January to the fifth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of Falco and Clarus, that is, in the Christian era 193.

The inscription on the base, erected by the Capenates to support a statue of the emperor, is as follows:

**IMP. CAES. P. HELVIO PERTINACI. AVG. COS. II. PONTIFICI MAXIMO. TRIB. POT. P. P. PRINCIPI SEN FORTISSIMO DUCI ET OMNIUM VIR TVTVVM (sic). PRINCIPI CAPENATES. FOEDER PR. C. LICINIO. SPERANDO**

“To the Emperor Caesar Publius Helvius Pertinax Augustus, consul for the second time, chief pontiff, invested with tribunician power, father of his country, a most courageous prince and leader, and prince of all virtues (thus the text): the Capenates [dedicated this] to their prince; the abbreviated formula FOEDER. PR. and the office of C. Licinius Sperandus are uncertain.”

On the right side of the same base the date of the dedication is marked as follows:

[Col. 1288A]

**DEDICATA. XIII. KAL. APRILIS CVR P. SEXTILIO PROSPICIO . . . . MVCIO MVCIANO FALCONE. ET CLARO. COS.**

“Dedicated on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of April, under the care of P. Sextilius Prospicio … Mucianus Falco and Clarus being consuls.”

The distinguished Fabrettus also published it, *Inscriptions*, page 688.

Line 3.—“He decreed that Holy Pascha should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day, just as Eleutherius.” And in line 10: “Here he issued a decree, at the inquiry of the priests, concerning the Paschal cycle, a conference having been held with the presbyters and bishops, and Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, having been summoned”—read “of Caesarea”—“a meeting having been held, so that Holy Pascha might be observed on the Lord’s Day from the fourteenth day of the moon through the twenty-first.”

Victor

In the notes on Anicetus I showed that the tradition and discipline of celebrating Easter on Sunday, established by the apostle Peter in the three patriarchal sees and consistently upheld by his successors, was challenged by certain Asians. They maintained, with Polycarp, that the apostle John had permitted them to celebrate the Christian Passover [Col. 1288B] on the fourteenth day of the moon. When blessed Polycarp came to Rome on account of this controversy and was honorably received by Anicetus, he nevertheless returned to Asia without the matter being settled. Anicetus upheld the custom handed down to him by his predecessors and derived from the apostle Peter, and did not permit it to be observed differently in the West. He did not, however, press Polycarp very strongly concerning John’s temporary permission among the Asians, since he was exercising the apostolic privilege of burying the synagogue with honor.

We learn from the Paschal letters of the Fathers, published by Bucherius in his book *On the Doctrine of Times*—namely, from Anatolius of Alexandria, p. 443, no. 4; Philip, p. 469; and others—that disturbances on this matter arose again not only in Asia but also in Gaul, where some of the same Asians were in dispute with Saint Irenaeus.

The present entry indicates that the law of apostolic custom then prevailing at Rome and accepted in the patriarchates of Alexandria and Antioch was also approved by Pope Eleutherius [Col. 1288C]. By this law it is confirmed that the Paschal day must not be separated from the Sunday immediately following the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month.

The Asians pressed the matter more vigorously under Victor. To make it easier for them to accept, and to commend more sacredly to them, the practice of his predecessors that had been received by the universal Church, Victor summoned the presbyterate and called bishops to a synod. There he not only confirmed by decree the law of custom previously promulgated by his predecessors and then in force in the Roman and universal Church; he also promoted the proper arrangement of Paschal cycles, by which a fixed Paschal day would thereafter be established for many successive years and observed by all the faithful.

Nor was he satisfied with the efforts that Western bishops were devoting to arranging the Paschal matter. He also stirred the zeal of other provinces to contribute, especially wherever there were men trained in all the disciplines necessary for this work. At Victor’s command, the bishop Theophilus of Caesarea convened a council [Col. 1288D]. A fragment of it survives in Bede’s book *On the Vernal Equinox* and in Bucherius’s aforementioned letter of Philip on Easter.

Although the *Liber Pontificalis* records that Theophilus came to Rome in Victor’s time and was present at the Roman council, where it says that the Paschal cycle was discussed, an error of the compiler of the Lives, or of the copyists, caused the name of another Theophilus—bishop of Alexandria—to intrude in place of Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, Victor’s contemporary, who convened the council in Syria. The Alexandrian Theophilus did indeed write learnedly on the Paschal question and extended the nineteen-year cycle to one hundred years, but he lived much later, having dedicated a work to the elder Emperor Theodosius at the end of the fourth century. This is stated in the letter of Dionysius Exiguus on the calculation of Easter, written in the year of Christ 505, in the consulship of Probus, indiction III, as we read in Bucherius’s collection, p. 485.

Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.23 and 25 [Col. 1289A], records that several councils were assembled in the provinces, besides the synod that Victor held at Rome, and that letters of the Fathers from his time were still extant:

“There is still preserved the letter of the priests who were then assembled in Palestine, over whom Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, and Narcissus, bishop of Jerusalem, presided. There is likewise preserved another letter of the Roman synod, at the head of which is placed the name of Victor the bishop. There are also letters of the bishops of Pontus, presided over by Palma, as the oldest among them. A letter of the churches of Gaul is likewise extant, over which Irenaeus presided. Letters of the churches in the province of Osrhoene and in the cities of that region are also seen. Separately, there are letters of Bacchylus, bishop of Corinth, and of many others. All of them, presenting the same faith and the same doctrine, issued one and the same judgment. Such, as I have said, was their decision.”

He had expressed that decision earlier in the same chapter 23 in these words:

“For this reason synods and assemblies of bishops met [Col. 1289B]. And all, with one accord, by letters delivered to all the faithful the ecclesiastical rule: that the mystery of the Lord’s resurrection should never be celebrated on any other day than Sunday, and that only on that day should we observe the end of the Paschal fasts.”

In chapter 25 he quotes words from the letter of the Caesarean synod, attended by Narcissus of Jerusalem, Theophilus of Caesarea, Cassius of Tyre, Clarus of Ptolemais, and other bishops. They testify that the tradition concerning the Paschal day had reached them by continuous transmission from the apostles, and they advise that copies of their letter be sent to all the churches. They also indicate that they agreed with the Alexandrians concerning the day of Easter, since on that account their letters were carried back and forth between them.

The efforts of Victor to uphold apostolic discipline and preserve the unity and peace of the Church—which the obstinacy of the Asians was placing in danger—were advanced in Gaul by Saint Irenaeus in the letter quoted in the same book of Eusebius, chapter 24 [Col. 1289C].

It is also clear that outstanding men of Victor’s generation and of the immediately preceding and following periods labored to organize Paschal cycles. Anatolius of Alexandria, bishop of Laodicea, reports in his short work on the Paschal canon, printed by Bucherius, p. 439, that Origen had published a commentary on this subject at Alexandria, where the studies necessary for such calculations were flourishing.

Anatolius himself was a man of remarkable learning—as Jerome says in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*—in arithmetic, geometry, astronomy, and other disciplines. The magnitude of his genius may be measured from the volume he composed on Easter. He too, working splendidly on the same subject, left us his writings. Dionysius of Alexandria, who flourished under Gallienus, exercised himself in the same field, using the octaeteris, as Cardinal Norisius observes in dissertation 2, *On the Paschal Cycle of the Latins*.

But above all, Bishop Hippolytus illustrates this age by an authentic monument engraved in marble [Col. 1289D]. He composed a sixteen-year cycle by doubling the octaeteris, extending it from the first year of the Emperor Severus Alexander, to which year, as Jerome reports, he had brought his calculations of Easter and his chronological canons.

Although the Church did not use that same cycle, it nevertheless provided the occasion and basis for composing the *enneadecaeteris*, or nineteen-year cycle, which the Church preferred to the others. Moreover, that Hippolytan cycle, engraved in marble and excavated from the crypts of the martyrs near the church of Saint Lawrence Outside the Walls, in the Veran field, was brought into the Vatican Library by Cardinal Marcello Cervini, librarian, who was later raised to the Roman pontificate and retained the name Marcellus II. It may still be seen there, and it exercised the ingenuity of several chronologers who sought to explain it.

I would deprive this entry of a remarkable ornament and an important document of sacred antiquity if I did not insert here an image of that marble and cycle. I had drawn it from the original and published it engraved on copper in my book *On the Calendar and Cycle of Caesar*. There I believe I showed that, from the octagrammic cycle in Caesar’s marble calendar—which accommodates the lunar period with sufficient precision to the Julian years—was derived the method of the doubled octaeteris that constitutes the Hippolytan cycle.

I also showed that from both cycles, the Julian and the Hippolytan, a third cycle could be composed, expressed in 1,184 Gregorian years and repeated whenever necessary. It corresponds exactly to the canons for the celebration of Easter, established most properly both by the Church in the Council of Nicaea and by Gregory XIII in the correction of the calendar, as well as to the very rule recorded in this number in Anastasius’s text: that holy Easter should be observed on Sunday from the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month through the twenty-first day. This method can be understood in expanded and demonstrated form in the short work to which I gave the title *Solution of the Paschal Problem*.

I repeat: I would deprive the history of this entry of an important document if I did not insert that monument. On it, together with Hippolytus’s cycle and canon, is engraved a decree from the first year of the Emperor Alexander. It was constantly proposed to the universal Church by Pius, Eleutherius, Victor, and their Roman successors, and was affirmed during Victor’s time by the agreement of several councils, as we have seen from Eusebius: namely, that the custom and example received from the apostolic age required that Sunday should always be assigned to the celebration of Christian Easter—the Sunday that immediately follows the fourteenth lunar day of the first month—and that the solemn fasts should not be ended before that Sunday.

From this marble it is therefore clear that, even while the heat of persecution was raging, the decree of the Roman pontiffs had been splendidly illustrated in writing and in the councils of the holy Fathers, and that the City possessed genuine documents engraved in marble. Our religion, victorious over time, preserves them intact for posterity.

Let readers draw from this the confidence we ought to place in the records of the times preserved and publicly displayed in the Roman Church after peace had been restored to it. We see that, in so splendid a monument, chronological canons belonging to a single bishop were set forth in writing even in the crypts of the martyrs under Severus Alexander, and that a catalogue of his other works was added.

Blessed Jerome lists them in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. They correspond exactly to the titles of the works inscribed on this marble near the earlier chronological canon, arranged according to the sixteen-year cycles. I explained each of its parts in my dissertation on the cycle of Saint Hippolytus, published in *On the Calendar and Cycle of Caesar* and reprinted in Germany in an edition of the works of that same holy bishop and martyr. I therefore refrain from adding more here concerning the elucidation of that ancient monument, which, after Petavius and Scaliger, you will find further enlarged there by commentaries reprinted in that edition by distinguished men who, through their learning, uphold the honor of our age: Philippus a Turre, while he lived bishop of Adria; Giovanni, abbot of Vignola, distinguished by his services to the Vatican basilica and library [Col. 1290D]; and the Reverend Father Virginius Valsechi, interpreter of sacred literature in the Pisan academy, joined to me by friendship and shared study.

I append, engraved on a double copper plate, an image of the marble seat and statue representing Bishop Hippolytus, with the Greek letters on the two sides of the seat: on one side expressing the chronological canon, and the catalogue of works on the rear curve of the seat; on the other, the Paschal cycle extended into the succeeding years from the first year of Severus Alexander, on the following pages.

Linea 4.—“He created the following clergy.”

The word κλῆρος (*klēros*) is rendered in Latin by Eusebius, book VII, chapter 15, as “rank” or “dignity.” Marinus, having earned the rank of centurion, had a rival who contended that Marinus, as a Christian, was not permitted to assume that dignity, while the rank belonged to him. Thus Valesius renders in Latin what Eusebius expressed in Greek: Αὐτῷ δὲ ἐπιβάλλειν τὸν κλῆρον, “but that the rank belonged to him.”

The words quoted above seem to have been transposed in this entry [Col. 1291A]. Their sense appears to continue with the ordinations listed below: “He performed ordinations,” and so forth. Victor’s section therefore seems to have been assembled by the Librarian from two different catalogues. For the Paschal decrees are mentioned twice in the same section, ordinations are listed twice, and after his martyrdom is expressed once, following the words “He created the following clergy,” new decrees are added, and the discussion returns again to the Paschal question, followed shortly by an account of his burial.

Linea 9.—“Twelve bishops in various places.”

Some count among these the bishops whom Victor is said to have appointed for the Caledonians, or Picts, and the Scots, whom he is said to have arranged to promote the Christian faith throughout the island of Britain beyond the Roman frontier. They interpret in this way the testimony of Tertullian cited above under Eleutherius: namely, that places inaccessible to the Romans throughout Britain had already been opened to the Gospel of Christ.

Scottish historians assert this, and the especially distinguished Hector Boethius committed the following account to writing in book V of his *Scottish History*, near the end, in his discussion of Donald, king of the Scots, and the Christians of this period [Col. 1291B]:

“Christ the Lord, prince and author of peace, had given him such a disposition that he devoted himself to true piety, rejecting the worship of evil demons. For when Severus was emperor, he obtained through envoys from Victor the supreme pontiff—who was the fifteenth to preside over the Church after Peter—that men distinguished in learning and religion should be sent by him to Scotland. There, professing the name of Christ with their children and wives, they would be marked with baptism.

“The Scottish nobility followed the king’s example. Rejecting impiety and embracing the religion of Christ, they were washed in the sacred font. That was the year in which the Scots, by the kindness of the great and good God, were called to and received into the light of true piety by him who was the first of human salvation: the year 203, and so forth.

“Besides these things, Donald was the first of all the Scottish kings, as our annals record, to strike silver and gold coins. On one side he displayed the life-giving cross, on the other the likeness of his head, so that he might transmit to posterity the memory of the Christian piety he had first embraced among the Scottish kings [Col. 1291C].

“At length he died and was buried in land dedicated to Christian burial, with many pious prayers, as is customary, after the priests who then maintained sacred worship among the Scots had persuaded him by their religious and courteous works and by Christian love. At about that time Alexander, who also bore the name Severus, so that he might be held in greater honor, ruled the Roman Empire.

“Our people then first began to cultivate the sacred writings under the instruction of the priests whom Victor the supreme pontiff had sent to the farthest reaches of Albion to spread the doctrine of Christ. Nevertheless, some rites of sacrificing to evil demons remained. King Donald could abolish them by no persuasion, no exhortation of the priests, and no force; nor could Ethodius, who held the rule of the Scots after Donald’s death [Col. 1291D].”

Such is Boethius’s account. Paul Jovius likewise followed him in his description of Scotland and said that Donald “was the first of the Scottish kings to receive the sacred rites of the Christian religion, and the first in Scotland—when goods for human use were purchased in markets and fairs either by exchanges for other goods or with money imported from elsewhere—to strike gold and silver bearing the Scottish mark.”

Baronius, however, wonders in *Annals*, volume V, under the year 429, §2, “that all this was wholly unknown to the older Scottish chronicler Marianus, and completely escaped the notice of Bede, who lived near their time.” Nor are there lacking those who think that the whole history of this conversion must be transferred to Ireland—which was anciently called Scotland. Thomas Bozius’s statement in book VIII, chapter 1, *On the Signs of the Church*, seems not far removed from this view:

“They relate that in Scotland, which at that time was Ireland, the worship of Christ was spread at the same time as in Britain, around the year of salvation 203, while Victor was seated.”

To summarize briefly what I consider nearer to the truth and collected from reliable sources concerning the antiquity of the churches of Scotland, we must first establish the history of the civil domination of those regions which the ancients said were inhabited by Scots. These are the chief points belonging to the history of their civil government; they may be read together with a large body of writers cited by the celebrated Ussher in chapter 15 of his *Antiquities of the British Churches*.

The Reverend Father Michael Alford, also called Griffith, an English Jesuit priest, gathered so much material from this source that he compiled four enormous volumes of *Annals of the British Church*, covering the first five Christian centuries. They were printed after his death at Liège in 1663, and throughout them he frequently cites the historians noted by Ussher.

We said earlier, at col. 1261, that after the defeat of King Caractacus the greater part of the island of Britain had been conquered by the Emperor Claudius and reduced to a Roman province. It was enlarged first by Domitian and then by Hadrian and Antoninus Pius, but did not extend beyond the transverse wall drawn from the Germanic strait to the Irish Sea, from Gabrosentum to Luguvallium [Col. 1292B].

The remaining part of the island, extending northward beyond that wall—what we now call the kingdom of Scotland—was then called Caledonia. It was inhabited by the Picts and by the Britons, who were later succeeded by the Scots from Ireland.

Both peoples, the Picts and the Scots, are said to have been of Scythian origin.

“After the Britons,” says Ussher, “Britain received in its northern part first the Picts, as is thought, from Scythia, and then the Scots from Ireland. Bede’s *Ecclesiastical History* contains the following account of the first arrival of the Picts:

“‘It happened that the nation of the Picts, as is reported, entering the Ocean in a few longships from Scythia, driven by the wind beyond all the shores of Britain, reached Ireland and entered its northern coasts. Finding there the nation of the Scots, they asked to be given settlements for themselves in those regions, but could not obtain their request. Ireland is the largest of all the islands after Britain. It lies to the west of Britain; but just as it is narrower toward the north, so it extends much farther southward beyond Britain’s boundaries, reaching as far as the northern parts of Spain, although a great expanse of sea lies between.

“‘When the Picts reached Ireland by ship, as we have said, they asked that settlements and habitation also be granted to them there. The Scots replied that the island could not contain both peoples, but said: “We can, however, give you sound advice about what you may do. We know that there is another island not far from ours, toward the rising of the sun, which on clearer days we often see from a distance. If you wish to go there, you can make it habitable for yourselves; or, if anyone resists, use us as auxiliaries.”

“‘Thus the Picts went to Britain and began to inhabit the northern parts of the island, for the Britons had occupied the southern regions. Since the Picts had no wives and asked for them from the Scots, the Scots agreed to give them women only on the condition that, whenever the matter came into doubt, they should choose their king from the female royal line rather than the male. This is known to have been observed among the Picts to the present day.’”

The opinion that the Picts mentioned above came from Germanic Scythia is widespread. It is derived from Tacitus’s *Life of his Father-in-Law*: “The tawny hair of the inhabitants of Caledonia and their large limbs proclaim a Germanic origin.”

That Denmark, Sweden, and Norway belong to Germanic Scythia is taught by many testimonies, among them the notable one of Anastasius of Nicaea, question 38 in Hervet’s edition, or question 40 of the Sinaitic edition by Gretserus. The ancients commonly called the whole northern region where the Goths and Danes lived “Scythia.” See also Procopius, book II of *The Gothic War*, pp. 232–233 of the Greek edition, where the island of Scythia, which he calls Thule, includes part of Denmark, Sweden, and Norway. Claudian likewise calls it the abode of the Picts in the *Panegyric on the Fourth Consulship of Honorius*:

“. . . . . soaked with Saxon blood.

“Thule grew hot with the blood of the Picts;

“Ierne, frozen, mourned the heaps of Scots.”

[Col. 1293] [Col. 1295]

“As Ussher explains, this clearly and openly signifies that the Saxon pirates held the Orkneys, the Picts held Thule—whether that was Scandinavia or some other group of northern islands—and the Scots inhabited Ierne. Bede also confirms this concerning Ierne, or our Ireland, in the passage already cited, adding: ‘This is properly the homeland of the Scots, who, having departed from it, added a third nation in Britain to the Britons and Picts.’ The same point is shown, on the sole testimony of the common language, by the Englishman Camden in *Britannia*, p. 12, and by the Scot John Major in book I, chapter 9, *On the Deeds of the Scots*.”

The order of succession of these peoples was therefore as follows. The Britons, who held the southern part of the island and had been reduced by the Romans under the Emperor Claudius to a province, also dominated the northern region, or Caledonia, now called Scotland [Col. 1297B]. Roman arms had reached neither that region under Claudius nor under Domitian.

In Domitian’s time, Juvenal’s fourth satire states:

“When Flavius, now half-dead, was tearing the world apart,

“and Rome was serving bald Nero”—that is, Domitian—

and shows that Arviragus, the father of Marius, ruled the Britons.

“You have the omen,” he says, “of a great and glorious triumph:

“You will capture some king, or Arviragus will fall

“from the British chariot.”

An old scholiast identifies this Arviragus as Arbilas, and ancient coins record the name as ARIVOG.

Several historians report that, during the reign of this Arviragus, or of his son Marius, the Picts, a Scythian people, sailed to Britain. Comparing the dates, they infer that those Scythians were Dacians or Sarmatians who, driven from their homeland by Trajan when he conquered Dacia, arrived there.

The Picts were so called because their bodies were marked with punctures, a custom practiced among them. Pliny, book XXII, chapter 1, states that the Dacians and Sarmatians were accustomed to mark their bodies.

The Scythians, Sarmatians, or Dacians—also called Picts—were therefore carried in longships from the Germanic Sea to the Irish Sea after being expelled by Trajan. When they attempted to occupy the northern part of Ireland, the Scots who inhabited Ireland advised them to seek a settlement in the northern part of Great Britain, promising assistance for that purpose, according to the *Florilegium*. This also happened as they wished.

The Picts therefore gained possession of Albania, the northernmost part of the island of Britain, and first obtained wives from the Scots inhabiting Ireland. They then made peace, friendship, and marriages with the Britons of Caledonia, situated beyond the wall separating Roman Britain from the native Britons—Caledonia, which is also modern Scotland.

This was the first Pictish colony, in which the Picts bore indiscriminately the name of Caledonians [Col. 1297D]. Those Scythians, or Scots, who had already settled in Ireland, or Ierne, and had offered wives to the arriving Picts, crossed into Albion, or Great Britain, and were received among the same Picts as their relatives by marriage.

Thus, under Commodus, when he sought to acquire for himself the title of Britannicus through the conquest of the whole island, they strongly resisted; and when Septimius Severus attempted to extend the Roman frontier to the farthest shores of the island, they opposed him. Together with their related Britons, Caledonians, and Picts, they undertook a common war in defense of their common household gods.

Although the victorious arms of Severus had already occupied the greater part of the island, they were diverted elsewhere by Antoninus Caracalla after his father’s death. He restored to the ancient Britons, Caledonians, Picts, and Scots their former settlements, thereby providing fuel for the new wars under Carausius and Constantius, as may be gathered from Herodian and other writers.

[Col. 1298A]

The sequence of events therefore shows that in the second and third centuries of Christ the northern part of Great Britain beyond the Roman frontier was subject to almost continuous disturbances of war, so that scarcely any opportunity arose for establishing bishoprics there. The rule of the Roman pontiffs, stated above, was consistently observed: episcopal sees were not to be founded prematurely where peace had not yet been secured and the political order of the state consolidated, lest the sees easily collapse.

When the authors cited by the distinguished Father Michael Alford in the *Annals of the British Church*, under the year of Christ 203, report that Codualdus, king of the Caledonians, sent an embassy to the Roman pontiff Victor, following the example of Lucius, who shortly before had sent envoys to Victor’s predecessor Eleutherius, so that Victor might send bishops to his people to establish the worship of the Christian religion among them; and when they report that Paschasius, Dodualdus’s envoy, obtained this from Zephyrinus, Victor’s successor, because Victor had already died; and when a memory of this Paschasius, sent by King Dodualdus to Pope Victor, is said to survive in the Scottish menology on 12 December—I would understand this as meaning that Victor granted a bishop for the people, not yet attached to any particular see, or an apostolic vicar.

It seems more probable, however, that Eleutherius and Victor instructed the bishop of York, already established in Roman Britain, to associate the Caledonians, Maeatae, and all of Albania—that is, the northern part of Great Britain—with the Christian faith through suitable teachers. For the more successful accomplishment of this work, Victor may have extended the rights of the see of York over those peoples.

Presbyters and teachers of Christian law were therefore probably granted by the neighboring bishop and placed under his authority, until, once the condition of the region had been secured and its civil government settled, the time came to establish episcopal sees among those peoples, gathered from Caledonians, Britons, Picts, and Irish.

Although Dempster, in *Apparatus*, book VII, chapter 6, argues from Jordanes that the Church of Limerick was then founded in Ireland as the oldest of the Scottish churches, Ussher overturns the evidence for this. Father Alford appropriately adds an observation that excludes from the Scots themselves the belief in so early a foundation.

He considers the fact that, at the Councils of Basel and Constance, the ambassadors of the king of England disputed very sharply with the ambassadors of the other Western kings, whom they claimed they ought to precede. Since King Lucius of Britain had worshiped Christ earlier than the others, the kings of Britain, successors of Lucius, also claimed that they ought to be preferred to the successors of the other Western kings:

“Why,” he asks, “did the kings of the Scots not at some time fight with the same argument? For in truth, if Dodualdus the Scot—the first of the Scottish kings to be baptized, in this year 203—had pressed the argument more strongly for Scottish preeminence than for Lucius, it would have had greater force. The English differ from the Britons in name, reality, nation, and almost under the whole sky. The Scots occupied our northern region—if the Scots are to be believed—three hundred and thirty years before Christ was born, under Fergus, king of the Scots. Donald is said by the Scots to have come from the same origin, the same blood, and precisely the same name. Why, excluding the English and placing the Gauls and Spaniards behind them, did they not dispute for the first place in the councils and the Roman curia?”

Let others debate the account of Dodualdus and the first place of royal ambassadors. Our concern here is only to investigate the foundation of episcopal sees in that part of the island of Britain, or Albion, then called Caledonia or Albania and now called Scotland.

It is certain that established episcopal sees were founded in that region only later. For why are no bishops from that province found signing the councils of the succeeding ages, when three bishops from Roman Britain, the part of the same island separated by Severus’s wall, are found at the Council of Arles before Nicaea and at the Council of Ariminum after Nicaea?

Why are no bishops mentioned among the Scots, the successors of their ancestors, before Palladius was sent by Celestine, if some had existed under King Dodualdus? Why do the Irish, the ancestors of the Scots, admit none before Patrick?

After weighing the force of the arguments and the testimony of the writers, it is clear from Tertullian that the name of Christ had spread in Great Britain beyond the Roman frontier, among the Caledonians and Picts, into places inaccessible to the Romans. Several historians of Britain affirm that this happened through the agency of Victor and Zephyrinus, the Roman pontiffs. Yet no trace is found of an episcopal see erected there in the second or third century.

It follows that, in accordance with the customary practice of the Apostolic See, the ministries of divine things there—proclamation of the faith and administration of the sacraments to the people—were carried out by presbyters and teachers sent and delegated for that purpose, so that they would be subject to the nearest bishop of York, or would be sent by him at the command of the Apostolic See, until an opportunity arose to establish bishoprics in that part of the island [Col. 1299B].

It is nevertheless useful to draw another conclusion from the long delay in establishing bishoprics among the Caledonians and Picts and their successors, the Scots: namely, that the modern Presbyterian heretics, so numerous in Scotland, vainly seek to derive support for their error from the absence of bishops in that region during the first three centuries of the Christian era. They readily appeal to this absence whenever the question concerns retaining episcopal government in the Church of God according to the institution of Christ the Lord.

I would readily concede that no bishoprics were founded there before the age of Constantine the Great, even if Christian worship had been practiced in that region for more than a hundred years after the time of Severus. It does not, however, follow that those faithful had no bishop over them, or that the presbyters and deacons through whom the doctrine of Christ had reached them and was preserved were not subject to a particular bishop.

During this same age of Severus and his sons, Demetrius, bishop of Alexandria, sent presbyters and teachers as far as the Indians, so that they might proclaim Christ in regions so distant, as Eusebius testifies. Were the presbyters and teachers sent on such an apostolic mission acephalous, without a head? On their return from their missions they rendered an account of their stewardship to the bishop of Alexandria, no differently from the others subject to that Alexandrian Church.

Indeed, they resumed teaching in the schools of catechesis of the same Alexandrian Church. This happened to Pantaenus, whom Demetrius, bishop of that see, granted at the request of the Indian envoys, and whom, after he had returned from instructing the Indians, Demetrius immediately placed over the school of catechesis. The same happened to Origen, who, though not yet a presbyter because of his age, was requested by the ruler of Arabia for the sake of the Gospel; after that mission had been completed, Demetrius declared him, on his return to Alexandria, an instructor in the school of catechesis [Col. 1299D].

A full century after Pantaenus’s Indian mission, Athanasius granted a bishop, Frumentius, to the Indian people, as Rufinus and Socrates, book I, chapter 14, report. Likewise, a century after Origen’s mission to Arabia had passed, Moses the anchorite was ordained bishop by orthodox bishops at the request of the queen of the Saracens, who wanted a teacher of the Christian faith, because the bishop who then occupied the Alexandrian throne and bore the standard of Arian perfidy would not ordain him.

To these examples Thomasin adds, in *On the True Discipline of the Church*, book I, chapter 54, the notable example of Victor, whom we are discussing, and Zephyrinus, mentioned shortly before at col. 126 of these notes. Caius, a most learned and distinguished presbyter of the Roman Church, was first sent and then ordained bishop for the nations, as Photius relates in codex 48.

Thomasin therefore adds:

“Thus, as Prosper testifies, Celestine first ordained Palladius bishop for the Scots—that is, the Irish living in Scotland, as was said earlier [Col. 1300A]. After ordaining a bishop for the Scots, ‘while he endeavored to preserve the Roman island as Catholic, he also made the barbarian land Christian’”—that is, as Thomasin explains, “he expelled the Pelagians from England and the idolaters from Scotland.”

The opportunity to establish bishoprics was therefore awaited and delayed for one or two centuries. In the meantime, this delay did not deprive the peoples called to Christ of the sacraments and ministers, nor did it assign to them presbyters without a head or independent of the jurisdiction of a particular bishop. They were always to be regarded as subject to the successors of the apostles, and therefore under the episcopal hierarchy, so that they might belong to the heavenly Jerusalem, whose twelve gates, admitting its citizens, bear the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb.

This has been said to elucidate both the episcopal ordinations of Victor according to the recension of Caius—who in his time was no less renowned among bishops for the nations than among the presbyters of the Roman Church—and the first episcopal sees of the island of Britain [Col. 1300B]. These were established early in regions where civil affairs had already been settled and a stable political order could be maintained; but they were founded later in places where civil and military affairs were not yet pacified, since it was more suitable for sacred matters to be administered to those peoples by presbyters governed by neighboring bishops, or by bishops for the nations who would receive the law of their ministry from the Roman pontiff and would later report to him when the opportunity arose to establish fixed sees.

[Note: Col. 1300B]

Linea 6.—“Whether in a river, or in the sea, or in springs.”

Among other things, this pontiff established that baptism should universally be celebrated at Easter. But if any necessity arose, or danger of death were imminent, or pagans came to the faith at any time, they could be baptized in any water—whether seawater, rainwater, spring water, or well water.

[Note: Col. 1300C]

### Note on line 10

**“Here he enacted a decree, etc.”** Victor held a synod at which it was decreed that Easter should be celebrated not on the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month, but rather on the Sunday occurring after the fourteenth day of the moon and after the spring equinox, in accordance with the tradition of the apostles, as Eusebius relates in Book V, chapter 23. Fourteen bishops attended the synod, according to the synodical record. The same Theophilus, acting with Victor’s authority, also convened a council at Caesarea in Palestine for the same reason; a fragment of it is preserved by Bede in his work on the spring equinox. Victor’s reasons were, first, that Christians should not communicate with the Jews, the slayers of Christ; second, that there should be one method of celebrating Easter throughout the whole Church, and that the few Easterners who Judaized should yield to all the Westerners and to the greater number of Eastern peoples and bishops who held a different view; and finally, that otherwise the Easterners would sometimes celebrate Easter twice in one year and sometimes never celebrate it. These are the three reasons by which Constantine the Great, in his letter to all the Churches preserved by Eusebius in Book III of the *Life of Constantine*, confirms the justice of this decree after the Council of Nicaea, where Victor’s decree was confirmed.

### Note on column 1300D

Pope Victor made his pontificate illustrious by condemning the heresies that arose in his time and by the care he took to lead all the Churches to celebrate the Easter feast according to a uniform rule.

A certain Theodotus, highly educated in both religious and secular disciplines, although by profession a leatherworker, had wickedly renounced the Christian faith during the persecution. Unable to endure for long the shame with which he was daily overwhelmed, he abandoned Byzantium, his native city, and settled in Rome. His crime soon became widely known, and someone did not fail to reproach him for his apostasy. To avoid the disgrace of being an apostate, he preferred to profess heresy, asserting that when he had renounced Christ he had renounced nothing more than a man. Like heretics generally, he sought support for his error in testimonies of divine Scripture wrongly interpreted according to the inclination of his own intellect. Victor therefore condemned him and excluded him from the communion of the faithful as a corrupter of Catholic doctrine. To defend themselves more obstinately, his followers claimed that they were professing exactly the doctrine of the Roman See handed down by their ancestors, and that they neither published nor taught anything except what had been handed down and received in the Church from the apostle Peter to Victor. They attributed to Zephyrinus the perversion of doctrine and corruption of discipline that they removed from his predecessors.

Orthodox writers of that age, however, exposed the fraud and audacity of such sectarians. Among them one Anonymous writer was especially distinguished. He opposed to their writings the works of the holy Fathers who had lived at the same time, and whom the innovators had selected in defense of their error. With regard to Victor, this Anonymous writer states—according to Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.27—that he is astonished “that they are not ashamed to make such false accusations against Victor, especially when they know with certainty that Victor had forbidden Theodotus the leatherworker—the leader and, as it were, father of this impious and accursed defection from the faith, which denied Christ as God—from Christian communion.”

A few years earlier, “Certain persons were flourishing at Rome, among whom Florinus, deprived of the rank of ecclesiastical presbyter, and Blastus, involved in a similar error, obtained equal authority with him. Irenaeus composed various letters against them: one to Blastus, which he entitled *On Schism*, etc.” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.14, 19). Blastus “secretly wishes to introduce Judaism. For he says that Easter must be kept in no other way than according to the law of Moses, on the fourteenth day of the month” (Tertullian, *On Prescription against Heretics*). These men certainly drew many others away, as though from the embrace of the Church, and brought them over to their opinion (Eusebius V.14).

“Now Florinus and Blastus, who had been enrolled in the catalogue of presbyters, also turned aside to Valentinus’s pernicious sect. They say that the most blessed Irenaeus, grieving over their disease, wrote against Valentinus” (Theodoret, *Heretical Fables* III).

To extinguish the schism that Blastus was raising within the very bosom of the Roman Church, Pope Victor summoned a council in the city. It decreed that the custom preserved by his predecessors should be maintained: the Easter feast was to be celebrated perpetually on the Sunday that first followed the thirteenth day of the moon of March, through the twenty-first day. Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, was summoned to this council. “There was also another decree of the bishops who likewise met at Rome concerning this controversy; it indeed declares that Victor was bishop at that time” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.22). “Victor, bishop of the city of Rome, and Narcissus of Jerusalem, etc., published in writing what seemed probable to them” (the same author, *Chronicle*, under the year 198).

The same Theophilus subsequently convened another council in his metropolitan city. He summoned not only the suffragan bishops of his own see but also bishops from various provinces, at Victor’s command. Victor wished the date of the Easter celebration to be determined and established by a concordant decree in the regions inhabited by the Savior of the world, so that it would be celebrated there in the same way as in the other provinces of the Christian world. This is established by a fragment of the council preserved for us by the venerable Bede:

“Pope Victor, bishop of the city of Rome, sent authority to Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, ordering that a determination be made there concerning the way in which Easter should rightly be celebrated by all Catholic Churches, in the place where the Lord and Savior of the world had lived in the flesh. Having received this authority, the aforesaid bishop summoned all the bishops not only from his own province but also from various regions. When that multitude of priests had assembled, Bishop Theophilus produced the authority sent to him by Pope Victor and showed what task had been entrusted to him,” etc. (*Fragment of the Palestinian Council*, in Bede, *On the Spring Equinox*).

There were also other synods: in Pontus under Palmas; in Gaul under Irenaeus; in Osroene among the neighboring peoples; in Greece under Bacchylus; and in other provinces, all of which unanimously agreed to observe the decree of the Roman See.

“There was likewise another council of the bishops of Pontus, over whom Palmas presided as the most ancient and most revered. Another was held by the Churches of Gaul, governed by Bishop Irenaeus. Another by the Churches inhabiting Osroene and the other cities in that region. Another separately by Bacchylus, bishop of Corinth; and finally many others, almost innumerable, who with one consent and one judgment gave the same decision concerning the observance of that feast” (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.22).

Only Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus, who had gathered a synod of his province after Victor had requested that he summon all the bishops of Asia Minor—showing that all these councils were celebrated by mandate of the Roman pontiff—refused to depart from his custom. He wrote to Victor that it had been established in that council of the Asian bishops that Easter should be celebrated on the fourteenth day of the moon, whichever day of the week it fell upon, for the reasons expressed in the letter he sent him.

“I could mention here,” he says, “the bishops who were present with me in the council, whom, when you requested that I summon them, I diligently summoned. All these observed the fourteenth day of the moon as the day of Easter according to the Gospel’s prescription. They did not depart at all from that institution or custom, but constantly maintained it according to the rule and standard of faith” (Eusebius V.23).

The Roman pontiff, angered by this singular opinion of the Asians, who had even boasted that they were not in the least deterred by his threatening letters, decided to separate them from the body of the Church. In more severe letters addressed to them, he added that he would exclude from the communion of the faithful all who lived in that region.

“I am not at all disturbed by those things which are brought forward against us as threats” (the same source). “Moved by these considerations, Victor, who then presided over the Roman Church, attempted to cut off all the Churches of Asia, together with the neighboring Churches, from the common unity—as though they belonged to another faith and opinion—and, to put it briefly, he attacked them all in letters with great severity, declaring that all the brethren inhabiting that region were to be excluded from communion” (the same source, V.24).

Victor’s severity did not seem appropriate to all the bishops of that age who obeyed his command. Some of them, in letters addressed to him, suggested that since his predecessors had been unwilling to reject the Asians for this reason but had maintained peace with them, it would be better, following the example of his predecessors, for him to treat them more humanely and preserve peace with them. “They therefore strongly urged him to take diligent care for peace, concord, and charity toward his neighbors” (the same source).

The bishops who wrote these things in detail did not sufficiently attend to the reasons that persuaded the head of the Church to act more severely. As long as the question concerned only a discipline that brought such disagreements with it—especially after Saint Polycarp had discussed the matter with Saint Anicetus—the Asian Churches were permitted to use their custom peacefully. But once the Montanists dared to forge from ritual discipline a dogma alien to the Catholic faith, and Blastus took the opportunity to introduce schism, while his followers attempted to establish a universal law from the singular opinion of their own party, the practice appeared intolerable to Victor. He judged himself compelled, by the authority of the supreme pontiff with which he was invested, to suppress it.

He considered this all the more just because the custom of celebrating Easter in the Jewish manner, under another name, could no longer be tolerated as an indulgence granted in memory of the apostle John, who had temporarily allowed it to the Churches over which he presided in Asia in order to win the faithful converted from Judaism to Christ and to bury the synagogue with honor. The occasion for that indulgence had now ceased, as had the reason and motive for the policy.

It must be admitted that the Asians, led by Polycrates, persisted and did not submit to Victor’s judgment. Many of those who had subscribed to the synodical decree together with the pontiff did not approve of denying the sacraments to those who refused to obey the decree. But what follows from this except that the Asians were persuaded that they could persist in the rites handed down to them without danger of schism or incurring the charge of heresy, since the matter concerned only the manner in which discipline was to be observed? The bishops who supported Victor, meanwhile, thought it contrary to the rules of apostolic charity to inflict the harshest penalty of excommunication upon several Churches and separate them from the common Father of Christians over a matter of this kind.

Anyone who, with a more recent writer, dares to infer from this—Maimbourg, *History of the Roman Church*, chapter 8—that “it is clear and evident that neither these Asian and Eastern bishops, nor Saint Irenaeus and the Gallican Church, nor the bishops of other regions who wrote so forcefully to Victor in defense of the freedom of these Eastern Churches, believed the Roman pontiff to be infallible,” goes beyond and wanders outside the bounds of the question.

The Asian bishops were not separated from the Roman Church over any dogma touching faith or morals. Nor did the Westerners, or any of those who on this occasion pleaded in writing or speech, ever say that the Roman pontiff lacked the power to settle such a controversy by a definitive judgment. They complained only about the severity of the punishment, whether Victor actually inflicted it, as some maintain—see Baronius under the year 198—or merely threatened it, as others believe.

Saint Irenaeus, responding in a manner entirely appropriate to the meaning of his own name and showing himself a man devoted to preserving and reconciling peace, then performed the office of mediator (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V.24). The dispute was most rightly pacified by him, says Anatolius, a writer close to those times, published by Bucherius in *The Paschal Canon*, page 445. Victor was induced by Irenaeus’s persuasion to suspend the effects of the excommunication that had been inflicted, as learned authors of our own time demonstrate from Sozomen.

“I think that Victor most wisely dissolved the controversy that had arisen long ago. . . . By common agreement it was decided that, while each celebrated the feast according to his custom, they should not on that account withdraw from mutual communion” (Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* VII.20, cited by Marca, Book III of *On Concord*, chapter 3).

Whatever judgment one finally adopts concerning the character and consequences of that excommunication, we can have no doubt that Victor pronounced a most just judgment in defining the controversy, condemning the Asian discipline as favorable to schism and heresy. The subsequent course of events sufficiently demonstrated this, when even the Council of Nicaea considered it necessary to command the Easterners to conform in this matter to the customs of the Roman Church.

“As for the agreement of all concerning the celebration of the most sacred feast of Easter, know that the controversy undertaken on this matter at your request has been wisely and suitably resolved, so that all the brethren who inhabit the East, and who formerly used to imitate the custom of the Jews in observing that feast, will henceforth celebrate it with united minds by following us Romans and all of you, who from the beginning have maintained the same custom that we have maintained in honoring it” (Synodical Letter of the Council of Nicaea to the Church of Alexandria).

Rufinus says that the Fathers of Nicaea did only this: they proposed to all the Churches the ancient canon issued on this matter, which the Roman Church had established, as indicated in the synodical letter sent to the Church of Alexandria: “Henceforth by following us Romans and all of you,” etc.

Nor is it permissible to suggest, as a certain more recent writer argues in the *Life of Our Holy Pontiff*—Baillet, under 28 July—that those who have been separated from communion with the Roman pontiff may nevertheless be regarded as remaining in communion with other bishops and therefore not separated from the unity of the universal Church.

Firmilian of Cappadocia, whose testimony this recent writer employs, makes no such assertion.
