He merely complains, on the occasion of the disagreement that arose between Pope Stephen and Cyprian, that the Roman pontiff wished to proceed to separate from the unity of the Catholic Church those who, moved by approved reasons, refused to admit the disciplinary practice observed by the Roman Church in certain rites—something, he says, none of his predecessors is reported to have done.

Against the aforementioned author, one must establish and maintain that to be deprived of communion with the Roman See is one and the same thing as to be deprived of communion with the universal Church, since, according to Saint Irenaeus, all the Churches throughout the world must converge upon this Roman Church, their head and the one endowed with pre-eminent authority.

“It is necessary that every Church should come together with the Roman Church, because of its more powerful principal authority.” To remain in communion with the Roman pontiff is, according to Cyprian, the same as to remain in communion with the Catholic Church, since the See of Peter is the first source of priestly unity.

“You also wrote that I should send a copy of the same letter to our colleague Cornelius, so that, laying aside all anxiety, he might now know that he is in communion with himself—that is, with the Catholic Church” (Saint Cyprian, Letter 50, to Antonianus).

“To the chair of Peter and to the principal Church, from which priestly unity arose” (the same author, Letter 59).

Whoever receives the sacred mysteries outside this house profanes them, says Jerome; and whoever neglects to take refuge in this ark chooses to perish in the flood.

“I am joined in communion with the chair of Peter. . . . Whoever eats the lamb outside this house is profane. If anyone is not in Noah’s ark, he will perish when the flood reigns” (Saint Jerome, Letter 57, to Damasus).

That chair, established at Rome by Peter, grants unity to the Church, says Optatus of Milevis in Book II against Parmenianus. It was not granted to the other apostles to transmit this singular privilege to the Churches they founded, and no one may usurp it without incurring the guilt of crime and schism.

“In that one chair—which was conferred upon Rome—unity is preserved by all, lest the other apostles should each defend a separate chair for himself; so that he would already be a schismatic and sinner who set up another chair against the singular chair” (Optatus of Milevis, same work).

No one, Augustine adds, should be unaware that the apostolic See is preferred to and presides over the others by its primacy, and that those excluded from this center of unity are entirely outside the Church and have no part with Jesus Christ, nor live by his life, but are subject to God’s anger and rejection, whatever virtue they may claim for themselves.

“Who does not know that the primacy of the apostolate must be preferred to any episcopate?” (Saint Augustine, Book II of *On Baptism against the Donatists*, chapter 1). “Whoever does not communicate with the unity of the Church is not in the Church” (the same author, *On the Unity of the Church*, chapter 4). “Whoever, therefore, has been separated from this Catholic Church, however laudably he may think he is living, by this one crime—that he is separated from the unity of Christ—will not have life; rather, the wrath of God remains upon him” (the same author, Letter 152).

### [Column 1279]

#### 15

Victor, an African by nation, son of Felix, occupied the see for ten years, two months, and ten days [Note: B: “one month, twenty-eight days.”]. He lived in the time of Aelius Pertinax and Severus, from the fifth consulship of Commodus and that of Glabrio until the consulships of Lateranus and Rufinus [Note: B: “in the time of Commodus and Severus, from the consulships of Commodus Augustus II and Pertinax II until those of Fabian and Mucianus.”]. He decreed that Holy Easter should be celebrated on Sunday, as did Eleutherus [Note: *C, Pius.*]. He established the following orders of clergy. He was crowned with martyrdom. [Note: See Baronius, under the year 198.] He also decreed that, when necessity required it, wherever a person might be found—whether [Note: *whoever of mankind, whether*, CB] in a river, in the sea, or in springs [Note: *in a spring or in a pool*, CB]—provided that his belief had been made manifest through the Christian confession [Note: *declared*, C], anyone coming from paganism could be baptized [Note: *could be made a complete Christian*, CB]. He held three ordinations in the month of December [Note: *two*, CB]: four presbyters, seven deacons, and twelve bishops for various places.

He enacted a decree at the request of the priests concerning the cycle of Easter, after consultation with the presbyters and bishops and after summoning Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria [Note: Baronius, under the year 198, reads “bishop of Caesarea in Palestine”]. A meeting having been held, it was decreed that Holy Easter should be observed on Sunday from the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month [Note: *the thirteenth day of the moon*, C] through the twenty-first.

He was buried beside the body of blessed Peter in the Vatican on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, and the episcopate was vacant for twelve days [Note: *eleven*, CB].

### Note on column 1305B

Lines 3 and 4.—“He decreed that in the presence.” The author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* reads: “in the presence.” Zephyrinus therefore established that ordinations should be performed publicly in the church, as is still observed. The same Zephyrinus is also said to have established that all the priests of that church should stand beside the bishop celebrating—a rite that likewise continues to the present day.

### Note on column 1306B

Lines 3 and 4.—“He decreed that in the presence of all the clergy and faithful laity, whether a Levite or a priest, he should be ordained.” Zephyrinus decreed that the ordinations of presbyters and deacons should take place in the presence of the clergy and people, so that they might be carried out with the counsel of the clergy and the assent and testimony of the people.

The same rule is attributed to Anacletus, canon *Reliqui*, Distinction 67. It is also found in the Council of Carthage IV, canon 22: “A bishop shall not ordain clerics without the counsel of his own clergy, but shall seek the concurrence and testimony of the citizens” (canon *Episcopus*, Distinction 24).

When ordaining clergy, Cyprian imposed this law upon himself in Letter 33 to the presbyters and deacons: “Concerning the ordinations of clerics, beloved brethren, we are accustomed to consult you beforehand and, by common deliberation, weigh the character and merits of each person.”

Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 35, relates that the ordination of Novatian was null and invalid because he had been ordained presbyter against the wishes of the clergy and people.

Jordan, prior of Acre, intended to declare the ordination of Osbern as presbyter for the Church of Trichestana in England invalid, because Osbern had entered the church without Jordan’s consent, against the will and protests of the parishioners, and without observing the solemn order of law and custom of the kingdom. John of Salisbury, Letter 119: “Against Osbert the presbyter concerning the Church of Trichestana, Jordan, prior of Acre, instituted a dispute, saying that he possessed the aforesaid church, which he had entered without the consent of the prior and of another advocate, contrary to the solemn order of law and the custom of the kingdom, against the will and protests of the parishioners.”

### Note on column 1307B

Line 7.—“And thus Masses should be celebrated, except that the bishop’s right should intervene, so that only the clergy should hold [the Eucharist] while all were present, receiving from the bishop’s hand the consecrated crown and handing it over to the presbyter for distribution to the people.”

According to Zephyrinus’s constitution, when the bishop celebrated Mass, he himself distributed the consecrated crown—that is, the sacred Eucharist—to the clergy, and handed the remaining portions to the presbyter, who distributed them to the people. It is the office of the presbyter to hand the sacred Eucharist to the people.

Rural presbyters in a city church, when the bishop or the presbyters of that city are present, may not offer—that is, celebrate Mass—nor give the Eucharist, according to the Council of Neocaesarea, canon 13, and canon *Presbyteri*, Distinction 95. Nevertheless, even when a presbyter is present, a deacon may distribute the Eucharist if necessity requires it, according to the Council of Carthage IV, canon *Praesente*, Distinction 93.

This was the more ancient custom of the Church. Cyprian, *On the Lapsed*: “When the solemn rites had been completed, the deacon began to offer the cup to those present,” etc.

The same is stated by Justin Martyr, *Second Apology*:

“Εὐχαριστίσαντος δὲ τοῦ προεστῶτος, καὶ ἐπευφημήσαντος πάντος τοῦ λαοῦ, οἱ καλουμένοι παρ` ἡμῖν διάκονοι διδόασιν ἑκάστῳ τῶν παρόντων, μεταλαβεῖν ἀπὸ τοῦ ἐυχαριστηθέντος ἄρτου, οἴνου καὶ ὕδατος, καὶ τοῖς οὐ παροῦσι ἀποφέρουσι.”

“But after the presider has completed the thanksgiving and all the people have acclaimed their approval, those called deacons among us distribute to each of those present a portion of the bread, wine, and water over which thanks have been given, and they carry it to those who are absent.”

### Note on column 1307C

Line 5.—“He established a decree concerning the Church, that ministers should carry glass patens before the priests in the church.”

The ministers usually meant by this term are subdeacons. Since they were required to assist either presbyters or deacons in the ministry, they are often called *sequentes*—“those who follow”—in the Roman Order. Amalarius, Book II of *On the Office of the Church*, chapter 11, calls them *subsequentes*, as do Alcuin and many others.

The pontiff therefore decreed that subdeacons should carry glass patens before the priests. After the sacrifice had been completed, the presbyters were to receive the consecrated bread upon these patens and distribute it to the people, as will be explained shortly.

In Zephyrinus’s time the use of glass was widespread, and cups were also made of the same material. His contemporary Tertullian testifies to this in chapter 7 of *On Modesty*, where, attacking the Catholics, he says:

“Let the paintings on your cups come forward, if even in them there will shine through an interpretation of that sheep.”

And shortly afterward, in chapter 10:

“If perhaps the shepherd whom you paint on the cup will lend his support.”

The shepherd is represented in fragile glass and painted upon it, as is clear from the words that follow: “But I, who draw in the Scriptures concerning the shepherd, who cannot be broken.”

The learned Clarissimus Buonarotta discusses with great erudition the use, images, and paintings of ancient glass in his Italian treatise on the glass objects discovered in the cemeteries of Rome, and he includes images of the finds.

The use of glass in celebrating the Eucharistic sacrifice is thought to have been introduced not only for cleanliness but also so that the faithful might display the excellence of the sacrament being performed and signify the majesty of the divine presence. Among many peoples, glass vessels at banquets—especially those that were painted or engraved—were held in the highest esteem. Apuleius expresses this briefly when describing the elements of a ceremonial banquet:

“There was a large number of diners, and, as befitted the foremost woman, the very flower of the city. There were sumptuous foods, couches shining with ivory and woven with golden garments, and large cups, differing in appearance but alike in preciousness. Here was finely engraved glass, there unmarked crystal; elsewhere bright silver, flashing like gold; and amber wonderfully hollowed into cups, so that you might drink” (*Metamorphoses* II, page 52).

Before we leave this note, it will not be useless to observe that although our *Book of the Pontiffs* frequently repeats the expression “he established” or “he made a constitution concerning the Church,” this was not done to magnify pontifical majesty but by virtue of his dignity and Christ’s privilege.

Tertullian himself clearly attests, among other things, the persuasion of the faithful that followed the promulgation of such edicts, in the book he certainly published under Zephyrinus, *On Modesty*, when he had defected from the Church. Speaking of Zephyrinus’s decree granting pardon to those guilty of serious crimes after their penance, he says:

“I hear that an edict has even been published, and indeed a peremptory one: the supreme pontiff, that is, the bishop of bishops, issues the decree: ‘I forgive the sins of adultery and fornication to those who have performed penance.’”

Although he mocks the edict as one issued among the “Psychics”—the opponents of his own rigorism—he nevertheless expresses the condition of the promulgator and, indeed, the common persuasion with which he admits that he himself had previously been imbued:

“This, then, will also be a title against the Psychics, and against the former fellowship of my own opinion with them, so that they may all the more reproach me with fickleness.”

The edicts of the apostolic See were therefore regarded as peremptory, and it is clear from Tertullian and from the other writers cited, and worthy of citation, that the Church at that time received them as such.

### Note on column 1308C

Line 7.—“With the priests standing before him.”

The *Book of the Pontiffs* presents the ancient rite of the pontiff celebrating Mass in the present passage and in the words that follow. It indicates that the presbyters concelebrated with the pontiff who was celebrating and afterward received from him the consecrated [bread] upon the glass patens, to distribute it to the people.

Writing to Decentius of Gubbio, Innocent I speaks of this rite, modified in some respects because of the expansion of religion at Rome:

“Concerning the fermentum, which we send from the Lord’s [sacrifice] to the titular churches, you have wished to consult us unnecessarily, since all our churches are established within the city. Because the presbyters cannot meet with us on that day on account of the people entrusted to them, they receive from us the fermentum prepared by the acolytes, so that they may not consider themselves separated from our communion, especially on that day—that is, Sunday. I do not think this should be done through the parishes, because the sacraments should not be carried far; nor do we send them to the various cemeteries, since the presbyters have the right and permission to prepare them” (chapter 1).

On the assistance of the presbyters and their concelebration with the bishop who is celebrating, see Morinus, *On the Sacrament of Ordination*, exercise VIII, chapter 1, page 188, as well as Lupus, volume III, in his responses to Cerularius’s calumnies against the Latins.

### Note on column 1308D

Lines 7–8.—“Except that the bishop’s right should intervene, so that only the clergy should hold [it].”

I think the passage should be enclosed in parentheses and the text read as follows:

“Thus let Masses be celebrated—except that the bishop’s right should intervene, so that only the clergy should hold [the sacrament] of the sacrificial celebration—while all are present and, from that consecration, taking from the bishop’s hand the consecrated crown; and then the presbyter should receive it for distribution to the people.”

### Note on column 1309A

Line 9.—“The consecrated crown.”

That is, the Eucharistic bread, as it is called by Gregory the Great in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 4: “Then he carried with him two crowns of offerings.” Formerly the Eucharistic loaves were made in the form of a circle, as Constantine Porphyrogenitus observed in Book VII of the *Themes*, title 4, chapter 6: “A piece of bread is said to be made in the form of a circle.”

### Note on column 1309A

Line 5.—“Glass patens.”

Just as it is clear from this passage that glass patens were in use at this time, so other evidence proves that glass, wooden, and silver chalices were also customary in this period. Saint Gregory the Pope writes about the glass chalice in Book I of the *Dialogues*, chapter 7.

### Chronological Notes

In the epoch of Zephyrinus, whether copied from paintings or from manuscripts, the copyists transferred part of the number of years into the place of the months through an error similar to that found above, and transferred the signs for the months into the column of days.

In the oldest paintings of the age of Leo the Great, nineteen years and ten months were recorded in three lines, as can still be recognized by those who examine them closely:

**XVII. II. m X.**

The sign **M**, indicating the months, had been obliterated by the ravages of time, as had the letters preceding these numbers. The copyist therefore could not tell that the ten belonged to the months rather than to the days. He supposed that the three numbers were displayed in separate lines: seventeen years in the first, two months in the second, and ten days in the third. He consequently attributed to Zephyrinus seventeen years, two months, and ten days in the Roman See.

The copyist would not have fallen into this error if he had consulted the catalogues that reckon the epoch of Pope Zephyrinus by the consulates, as we have done in the *Prolegomena*. The first consuls assigned to Zephyrinus are Saturninus and Gallus, marking the year 198 of the common Christian era, according to the agreement of the manuscripts and catalogues. It is therefore understood that he celebrated the first Easter of his pontificate in that same year, on Sunday, 9 April.

The final Easter celebrated under the rule of Pope Zephyrinus, according to the customary style of the catalogues already explained in the note on Saint Peter, is unanimously stated by the catalogues and by the manuscripts that are not mutilated to have occurred under the consuls Praesens and Extricatus. This fell in the year 217, on Sunday, 13 April.

Consular chronology therefore demonstrates that twenty Easters must be assigned to Pope Zephyrinus. These require nineteen full years and several additional months, since this blessed pontiff lived for approximately three and a half months after the day of that last Easter—namely, until 26 July, the anniversary of his martyrdom. That date is marked on an ancient stone of the ninth century, as can be inferred from the form of the letters of that age, by examining it in the portico of the monastery of Saints Stephen and Sylvester in the Campus Martius, now called the title of Saint Sylvester *in Capite*.

Paul I, founder of that monastery, caused a double marble tablet to be engraved when he built an oratory for the monks and placed there the relics of several martyrs whose anniversaries were to be commemorated: on one side the names and anniversaries of the male saints, and on the other those of the female saints, with this title prefixed:

“In the name of the Lord. This is the record of the anniversaries of the saints resting here. In the month of January, on the third day: the anniversary of Saint Antherus, pope, etc.”

I shall defer presenting the complete *Menaion* under Paul I until the discussion turns to the foundation of this monastery and titular church. For now, it will suffice to indicate that the work is close, or nearly contemporary, to his time; and in it one can clearly read that the natal day of Pope and martyr Zephyrinus coincides with 26 July:

[Col. 1310A] **July, the twenty-sixth day.** The natal day of Saints Zephyrinus, pope and martyr, and Tarsicius, martyr.

The twenty Paschal celebrations held for Pope Zephyrinus under the corresponding ordinary consulships demonstrate that the surviving number in the Basilica of Saint Paul beneath his image, continued from the first and second verses, gives nineteen years; while the decade that follows in the next verse signifies ten complete months to be added to the aforesaid number of nineteen years assigned to the same see, with no addition of days.

Moreover, if from 26 July 217—the day that crowned Zephyrinus’s pontificate and life with martyrdom—we reckon backward nineteen years and ten months, the endpoint of the calculation falls on Sunday, 25 September 197, a date suitable for his ordination to the episcopate. Between that date and the martyrdom of his predecessor Victor, which, as established in the preceding section, must be assigned to 28 July of the same year, 196, there intervene nearly two complete months; thus a suitably long vacancy of the Roman see is also included.

I have already said, on the basis of the sequence and names of the consuls—which are less liable to be confused through the carelessness of copyists than numerical signs—that the totals of years in the codices ought to be corrected, since they are frequently exposed to scribal errors; I said this in the notes on Cletus and demonstrated it in the Preface to the first volume by means of the numbers 26 and 32. To these observations, however, it must be added that several councils considered the following precaution especially appropriate for freeing the memory of a definite date from all uncertainty: namely, that the name of the consul should be added in documents attesting the time of each bishop’s ordination. This is a canon of the Council of Milevis, under the consulship of Arcadius and Honorius V, in the year of Christ 402, numbered XCIX in the Greek-Latin codex of the canons of the African Church, where we read:

> It was decided that all who henceforth are ordained by bishops throughout the African provinces should receive from their ordainers letters written by their own hand, containing the consul and the day, so that no dispute might arise concerning dates later or earlier.

The consul’s name is prescribed for indication rather than the emperor’s regnal year when the matter concerns preserving an epoch from the danger of alteration. For a faulty expression of numerical signs can involve a serious corruption even when the years of rulers are being indicated, whereas the expression of consular names can tolerate the deformation of several letters.

In what the Fathers of Milevis prescribe as a duty in episcopal ordinations, they profess to be following an ancient discipline, asserting that they were renewing decrees of earlier councils. Certainly, the names of consuls were commonly added in the Western Churches not only to the dates of bishops’ epochs on their tombs—as I demonstrated from the monuments of the Church of Nola in the Preface to the first volume, no. 26, and could confirm with further examples—but also to distinguish dates in records of lesser importance. At Rome, the Christian cemeteries clearly show how frequent was the practice of adding the consular date not only to the tombs of illustrious men but also to those of ordinary people and even to the burial places of infants.

The dates were recorded with still greater care in the Acts of the martyrs—such as the pontiffs of whom we are speaking—by the regional notaries instituted by Clement, and in the Church registers, both for the ordinations of bishops and for the promotions of clerics of every order, so that from the epoch of their ministry they could advance to a higher rank according to the rules of the Fathers. Above all, the era of a new pontiff was to be indicated by the consul and the day, so that from this it might more easily be judged whether the *formatae*, decrees, and letters sent from there to other Churches were genuine, lest private fraud should pass forged documents off as authentic.

We therefore rightly establish that the numbers of years expressed in the codices must be tested against the consular chronology, and that the epochs of the pontiffs must be restored from it, as we have done for Victor and Zephyrinus. Once restored, they correspond appropriately both to the consulships of the catalogues and to the genuine numbers of the Leonine age, still preserved in the Basilica of Saint Paul.

After the years and months of the pontificate of Saint Zephyrinus have been vindicated, several difficulties concerning the date of his martyrdom, 26 July, must be resolved—difficulties raised by the distinguished scholars Florentinius, Papebrochius, and Pagius. In the Martyrology that its editor Florentinius believes to be Jerome’s, Zephyrinus’s natal day appears to be assigned to 20 December; in the relevant section we read: “At Rome, Zephyrinus the bishop.” In other martyrologies—those of Bede, Usuard, and Ado, to which the Roman Martyrology also agrees—the commemoration of Zephyrinus, pope and martyr, is recorded on 26 August.

[Col. 1311B] Anastasius resolves this latter doubt. He expressly states that Zephyrinus was buried on 26 August in his own cemetery, beside the cemetery of Callistus, on the Appian Way. It was therefore the day of his deposition, not the day of his martyrdom, that was celebrated in that cemetery into which his body was carried. From this, perhaps, the martyrologies just mentioned and the urban clergy derived the practice of celebrating his memory on the day of his deposition rather than on the day of his martyrdom.

Nevertheless, the titular church and monastery of Saints Stephen and Sylvester, when Paul I transferred Zephyrinus’s body from the cemetery of Callistus to that church, restored the memory and celebration of his martyrdom, expressly indicating 26 July as the day of his natal martyrdom. This is declared twice on the same stone: first in the heading stating that it presents a record of “the natal days of the saints resting there,” and again in the repeated word *Natalis* under 20 July: “The natal day of Saints Zephyrinus, pope and martyr, and Tarsicius, martyr.”

I shall not dwell at length on the first difficulty, which arises from the text of the Martyrology believed to be Jerome’s. It does not state whether the memory of that Bishop Zephyrinus falling on 20 December concerns his natal day, ordination, or translation; nor does it assert that this Zephyrinus was bishop of Rome. It says that the holy bishop was commemorated at Rome; he could equally have been a bishop of another Church who, as a visitor in the City, departed to the Lord on that day. His annual memorial of death or deposition could have been honored in some suburban cemetery where he had been buried.

Against the evident testimony of the marble document publicly set up in the eighth century, together with the body of Zephyrinus, pontiff and martyr, expressly recording 26 July as the day of his martyrdom; against the memory of his deposition, celebrated a month later, on 26 August, in his own cemetery; and against the confirmation supplied by the Librarian, by several martyrologies, and by the custom of the Roman Church—which celebrated both memories, of martyrdom and deposition, in distinct places—the objections prompted by three words in a single codex of uncertain date and authorship must be considered entirely weak. Those words do not sufficiently show that they refer to our Zephyrinus.

Finally, Zephyrinus’s epoch agrees not only with the names of the consuls and the numbers of the Leonine age, and with the martyrdom of his immediate predecessor, Pope Victor, but also exactly with the epoch of his successor Callistus, which is clearly established by the agreement of all the documents. We shall explain this in the chronological notes on the following number. Zephyrinus’s nineteen years and ten months in the Roman see are therefore confirmed on every side as having been rightly restored by these indications.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

### Lines 3 and 4

> He established that a Levite or a priest should be ordained in the presence of all the clergy and the faithful laity.

The ancient Ritual, Pontifical, and Sacramentary books recall this old discipline, by which those to be ordained to the grades of the priestly hierarchy were presented before the assembly of the faithful. It should therefore be understood as having been introduced from the beginning of the Christian Church, when it was also in force under the preceding Mosaic law.

Certainly, the preservation of this custom—not only in the time of Gregory the Great but even during the earliest beginnings of the Church—is evident from the Acts of the Apostles, both in the election of Matthias to the apostolate and in the appointment of the first seven deacons for ministry. Thus Paul, the teacher of the nations, intimates to his disciples Timothy and Titus—when he recalls that he left Titus in Crete to appoint presbyters throughout the cities—and, after appointing Timothy bishop of the Ephesians, commands him, in examining the virtues required of those to be ordained to the grades of the Church’s hierarchy, to ensure that they have a good testimony even from those outside the Church (Tit. 1).

For the age of Zephyrinus, with which we are now concerned, at the end of the second and the beginning of the third century, clear evidence survives of this custom continuing without interruption. Saint Cyprian writes in Letter 33:

> In the ordinations of clerics [read: “in ordaining clerics”], dearest brothers, we are accustomed first to consult you, and by common counsel to weigh the conduct and merits of each individual.

Medardus, on page 283 of his learned notes and observations at line 13, folio 236, of the *Sacramentary of Saint Gregory the Pope*, observes that the same point is found in Letter 68 of Saint Cyprian and in Letter 181 of Saint Basil, “where,” he says, “this subject is treated more fully.”

He adds from Lampridius that, in the age of Severus Alexander—whom Zephyrinus’s successor Callistus closely followed—it was so well known and approved that Christian scrutiny of the kind under discussion should precede ordination that the emperor, having borrowed several principles of conduct from Christians, wished to transfer this practice to the election of those who were to govern the provinces. Lampridius writes in his Life of Alexander:

> Whenever he wished to appoint certain men either as governors of provinces or as procurators—that is, financial administrators—he would publish their names, urging the people that, if anyone knew of any crime against them, he should establish it by clear evidence; if he did not establish it, he would incur the penalty of death. He used to say that it was a serious matter that Christians and Jews did in announcing those who were to be ordained priests, but that this was not done with governors of provinces, to whom both the fortunes and the lives of human beings would be entrusted.

“Therefore clerics who are to be ordained must also be ordained publicly,” Medardus concludes after the foregoing discussion, “so that the bishop may openly inquire of the people concerning them, as you see in our manuscript codices, in accordance with the ancient custom that may be noted in the edict of Theophilus, patriarch of Alexandria, canon 6:

> Concerning those who are to be ordained, this shall be the procedure: let everything belonging to the priestly order consent and choose; and let the bishop examine the candidate, or, with the priestly order also consenting, let him ordain him—*χειροτονεῖν ἐν μέσῃ τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ*, ‘to ordain in the midst of the church’—in the presence of the people, while the bishop asks whether the people too can bear witness on his behalf. The ordination must not be performed secretly.”

The public announcements in the consistories of the supreme pontiffs, still observed to this day when episcopal appointments are proposed; and the customary solicitation of the judgment of the Sacred College of Cardinals, formerly announced in the preceding consistory and preceding new creations of priests and deacons of that body, but now individually requested at the very threshold of the creation itself—these are vestiges of the ancient discipline introduced into the Roman Church from the apostolic age and never abolished.

### Line 5

> So that ministers might carry glass patens before the priests into the church.

We can readily conjecture why Zephyrinus ordered glass patens to be carried before the priests rather than wooden or metal ones, if we consider the diligent and anxious care that the priest had to exercise when breaking and dividing the offerings and consecrated gifts, lest any fragments fall away.

For this reason Tertullian, in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, Origen, in Homily 13 on Exodus, and other Fathers cited by the distinguished Edmund Martene in Book I, chapter 5, article 5, of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, commend this practice so strongly.

That care and anxiety of the Catholic Church provide perpetual confirmation of the faith against recent sectarians in confessing the presence of the Lord Christ under the consecrated species. Regarding the reverence due to the sacrifice and the manner of expiating faults occurring in it, the sectarians who now deny these things would readily admit that such constitutions have come down to us from the primitive tradition of the Church if they would reflect even slightly on these words of Tertullian in chapter 3 of *On the Crown of the Soldier*:

> “We anxiously suffer something of our cup and bread to fall upon the ground.”

No less worthy of consideration is what Origen writes in Homily 13 on Exodus:

> You know, those accustomed to attend the divine mysteries, how, when you receive the body of the Lord, you preserve it with every care and reverence, taking care lest any small portion fall from it, lest something of the consecrated gift slip away. For you believe yourselves guilty if anything should fall from it through negligence.

Thus, according to Tertullian, Christians of his time—that is, at the beginning of the third century—suffered with anxiety if anything from the Eucharist fell to the ground; and according to Origen they believed, rightly, that they were guilty if this happened through negligence.

But what, then, was the cause of such great anxiety? What fault or crime would make them guilty, and rightly so, if they had acknowledged nothing in the sacrament beyond bread and wine and a mere figure? They therefore believed that something else, something of great significance, was present. And what could that be except the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist?

Cyril of Jerusalem inspires the same reverence toward the sacred Eucharist in his Fifth Mystagogical Catechesis, where, after the faithful have received the holy bread in their hands, he admonishes them:

> Take care that nothing fall from it. For whatever you lose, you should regard as though you had lost something from one of your own limbs. If someone were to give you gold filings, would you not hold them with great care, taking precautions lest any of them be lost and you suffer a loss? How much more carefully and diligently will you take precautions so that not even a crumb falls from this, which is more precious than gold and precious stones?

These matters will become still clearer from the rite and method of supplying defects occurring in the sacrifice itself, and of expiating faults committed against that divine sacrament—matters that anyone can readily discern in the statutes presented below, and so forth.

Zephyrinus, therefore, appears to have applied himself diligently to this discipline, which anxiously took care that nothing of the offering or consecrated gift should fall to the ground. For this reason he seems to have wished glass patens to be preferred to those made of other materials, to be placed beneath the consecrated species while the Lord’s body was offered in the sacrifice and the gifts beneath which it lies were broken. The transparent material of glass would make even the smallest fragments more visible; and since the entire body of the Lord is confessed to be equally present in each of them, they had to be collected with the utmost attentive care.

It also mattered that, during this period of persecutions, it was often necessary to celebrate the sacred mysteries and distribute the Eucharistic gifts to the faithful in cemetery crypts and other dark, subterranean places. Such glass patens, brought by subdeacons and administered by deacons to the priest celebrating and dividing the gifts among the faithful who approached to partake, would make even the smallest particles that fell conspicuous—especially when, with a light brought near them, these glass vessels were illuminated like panes of glass in windows.

The polished surfaces of the metal vessels we use today provide the same ease in detecting tiny fragments upon them in the open light of sacred buildings. But in the dark recesses into which Christians at that time had to withdraw, there can be no doubt that the transparent nature of glass offered a more convenient means of collecting all the crumbs of the broken species and even the smallest drops that might accidentally have fallen from the chalice, by searching for them on every side with the aid of a light brought near, moved around, and placed beneath them.

I therefore believe that this was why some bishops also chose glass for the chalice used in the sacrifice—not merely from a desire for poverty, but because of this anxious concern, which required that whatever had been changed by consecration into the body and blood of the Lord should be sought out and consumed.

In the fourth letter of Blessed Jerome to Rusticus, the holy bishop Exuperius of Toulouse is praised for many virtues, but especially for his devotion to evangelical poverty. Jerome writes of him:

> No one is richer than he who receives the body of the Lord in a wicker basket and carries the blood in glass.

Cardinal Baronius, in his notes on the Martyrology for 7 August, and Severanus, in Book VI, chapter 18, of *Subterranean Rome*, who recount this example, show that the apostles themselves often used glass chalices, and that many bishops and priests continued to do so for several centuries. They also used, interchangeably, precious chalices made of every kind of richer metal, as we shall show below in the case of Urban.

This continued until the danger of blood being spilled from fragile material—among those who perhaps did not use thicker glass—gave occasion at the Council of Rheims, in the time of Charlemagne, for glass chalices to be entirely removed from the sacrifice. This is recorded in Part III, chapters 44 and 45, of the *Decree*, and in Ivo, Book I.

Baronius should be heard in his notes on 7 August:

> From the times of the apostles, a glass chalice appears to have been in use. Hence Marcion, a heresiarch who lived near those times, himself imitating the Catholic Church and using a glass chalice in his sacrilegious rites, deceived the people by an imposture displayed through magic: the white color of the wine, which appeared externally through the glass, was changed to red by certain illusions.

Besides the decree of the Council of Rheims, a general constitution of Saint Leo IV may be cited. He ordered it to be published throughout all the bishops’ dioceses. It is printed together with the councils under the title of a homily, both in Binius’s edition, volume III, part I, section 2, page 272, and in Labbe’s edition, volume VIII, page 300:

> No one, he says, shall dare to celebrate Mass in a wooden, leaden, or glass chalice.

At the beginning of the same eighth century, we learn from the reply of Alexander, the pseudo-bishop of the Jacobites, that the Egyptians likewise used glass chalices and disks in the sacrifice after the Alexandrian Church had been stripped of the gold and silver vessels it had previously possessed. When monks and laypeople asked him to distribute the customary alms on the Tuesday of Easter week, he excused himself as follows:

> See, brothers, how great has been the plundering of the churches, so much so that, in place of the golden and silver chalices in which the precious blood was offered, we have made glass ones, and sacred disks or patens out of wood.

See also Renaudot, *History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria*, page 193, concerning the year 714.

[Col. 1314D] Among the sacred antiquities of the Church preserved in my possession there remains a portion of a hemispherical glass chalice, approximately the size and shape in which we now commonly fashion sacred silver or gold vessels, which are generally called pyxes and are placed on the altar table for preserving the sacrament of the Eucharist.

That vessel in our collection is made of thick glass. Standing figures of the holy apostles can be seen upon it, with their names carved beside them, in a style of engraving similar to that by which letters and images are displayed in recessed relief on cups made of thicker crystal among the Germans and brought to us.

The barbarous character both of the engraving of the images and of the writing of the names indicates an age around the seventh or eighth century, shortly before the constitution of Leo IV prohibited such chalices. Above the figures of the apostles, separately divided in our fragments by columns forming a portico, the following names are read:

**PETRIUS . . . . ANDREAS, PHILIPPUS.**

[Col. 1315A] The rest are missing. Above each individual column the name of Christ appears, expressed by a Greek monogram and enclosed within a circular ornament.

When these ancient fragments of a glass chalice were brought to me for sale, I heard that they had been excavated on the Aventine Hill, among ancient ecclesiastical ruins near Saint Prisca.

Fragments of ancient glass disks or patens, whose circular diameter exceeds two feet, may be seen in the treasury of His Eminence and Most Reverend Lord Cardinal Gualterius, which is filled with antiquities of every kind.

Other fragments, smaller in size and comparable to our ordinary vessels, decorated with sacred images of saints and inscriptions, have been found throughout the suburban crypts and cemeteries of the martyrs. Besides Aringhius and Severanus in *Subterranean Rome*, they have been published by Fabretti in his *Book of Inscriptions*, folio 539, and most fully by Senator Buonarroti and Canon Boldetti, whom we have often mentioned with praise.

These images and inscriptions generally display the Lord Christ, the Virgin Mother of God—as in Aringhius, volume II, page 589, and Boldetti, page 202—and the holy apostles and martyrs, whose names in particular are recited in the canon of the Mass.

On the fragment of our chalice the names **PETRUS, ANDREAS, PHILIPPUS** are displayed. Boldetti, page 201, has **SIMON, THOMAS, PHILIPPUS**. **PETRUS** and **PAULUS** occur most frequently, as do **STEPHANUS, LAURENTIUS, CORNELIUS, CYPRIANUS, AGNES**, who are listed in the canon as well as on fragments of such glass patens and chalices. Other holy pontiffs and martyrs or confessors, whose names are commemorated in the Roman cemeteries either by deposition or by foundation—such as **CALLISTUS, JULIUS, DAMASUS, SIXTUS, TIMOTHEUS, HIPPOLYTUS, VINCENTIUS**—can be seen with their images in the authors cited.

### Note: [Col. 1315B]

#### Line 5

> So that ministers might carry glass patens before the priests into the church.

Saint Zephyrinus established that the consecration of the divine blood should take place in a glass vessel, not in a wooden one, as had previously been customary. This institution was altered in subsequent times: it was forbidden for the consecration to take place in wood, because of the absorption by which the sacrament is diminished; in glass, because of its fragility; or in bronze, because of the unpleasant taste imparted by it. Instead, it was ordered that the vessel be made of gold, silver, or tin, as appears from the decrees recorded in the Councils of Tribur and Rheims.

### Note: [Col. 1315C]

#### Line 3

> He established, etc.

The author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* asserts that Zephyrinus established that ordinations should be carried out publicly in the church, as is still observed, and furthermore that all the priests of that Church should stand beside the celebrating bishop.

While Zephyrinus was seated on the Roman see, the emperor Severus initiated a persecution against the Christians. During it, Zephyrinus concealed himself in order to provide for his flock. When the persecution had subsided, he emerged from hiding and performed his pontifical duties. Natalis—formerly a confessor, later made bishop of the Theodotian heretics through the corruption of money, but eventually clothed in haircloth and sackcloth and sprinkled with ashes—cast himself suppliantly at Zephyrinus’s feet and made confession of the crime he had committed; Zephyrinus received him.

He condemned Proclus, the celebrated disciple of Montanus, who had been convicted by Caius, a man of outstanding life and learning, of manifest rashness in defending the new prophecy; and he struck all the defenders of the false prophecy, including Tertullian himself, with an anathema.

He received Origen, who had fled for Christ’s sake, humanely and courteously. Eusebius writes in Book VI, chapter 14:

> While Zephyrinus was governing the Roman Church, he writes that he came to the city of Rome, since—as he himself said elsewhere—it had long been his wish to see in person the Roman Church, the most ancient of all.

### Note: [Col. 1315D]

#### Line 1

> Zephyrinus, etc.

The pontificate of Zephyrinus offers us several demonstrations of the supreme authority possessed by the Holy See to proscribe heretics and to absolve them when they repent of their errors.

The vigilance and zeal of this pontiff undoubtedly provoked the slanders of the heterodox of his time, especially the disciples of Theodotus the leather-worker. With the utmost impudence they accused Zephyrinus as a corrupter of the ancient doctrine and went so far as to assert—according to Eusebius, Book V, chapter 27—that Zephyrinus was the first of the Roman pontiffs to hold the doctrine of Christ’s divinity, which the followers of Theodotus impiously denied:

> They assert that the true rule of preaching was preserved intact until the time of Victor, who was the thirteenth bishop of Rome after Peter, but that it was completely corrupted and perverted by Zephyrinus, his successor.

We refuted this notable fraud above, near the beginning of the preceding chapter.

[Col. 1316B] It should here be considered, on the testimony of the ancient Fathers, that Zephyrinus generally triumphed over the heresies of Marcion, Praxeas, Sabellius, Valentinus, and the other sectarians down to the Cataphrygians:

> Marcion, Praxeas, Sabellius, Valentinus, and the others were overcome in their own times by Victorinus of Poitiers, Zephyrinus of Rome, and Tertullian of Carthage, down to the Cataphrygians, and by the other defenders of the Catholic Church.

—Optatus of Milevis, *Against Parmenian*, Book I, near the middle.

As for the Cataphrygians and Montanus, we shall learn from our ancient authors that, after the celebrated debate held at Rome between Caius, a theologian and defender of the Catholic faith, and Proclus, the champion of the Phrygian error, an anathema was pronounced by Pope Zephyrinus against the fanatics (Eusebius, *History*, Book VI, chapter 14; see Saint Jerome on Caius). Tertullian likewise bears witness to this and shows that he too was included among those struck by the same sentence of anathema (Tertullian, *On Fasting*, near the end).

[Col. 1316C] Those recent enemies of the Roman See who, in our own times, have dared to number Pope Zephyrinus among the Montanists have sinned against him with the same injustice as the ancient Theodotians, who attempted to brand him with novelty concerning the doctrine of the divinity of the Lord Christ.

Apart from what we said in chapter 3 in defense of the Roman pontiff—whether that pontiff was Eleutherius or someone else whom Tertullian accuses without naming, as though he had granted letters of communion to the Montanists—the most excellent defense of Zephyrinus is supplied by the distinguished historical testimony concerning his practice and discipline, which was diametrically opposed to the rules of those sectarians in administering penance.

A certain Natalis, distinguished by a confession of the faith made before tyrants, had unfortunately fallen into the heresy of the Theodotians and had even allowed himself to be ordained their bishop. Jesus Christ, unwilling that a man who had been a witness of his sufferings should perish outside his Church, graciously urged him through inner inspirations and frequent apparitions to abandon schism and heresy.

“But when Natalis,” Eusebius continues in *History*, Book V, chapter 28, “neglected such nightly visions, being captivated by the honor of occupying the first place among them and by the desire for shameful profit—which is the ruin of many mortals—he was finally beaten throughout the entire night by holy angels with whips and scourged most severely.

“So, rising at first light, he put on sackcloth, sprinkled himself with ashes, and immediately threw himself with tears at the feet of Bishop Zephyrinus. He fell not only at the feet of the clergy but also at those of the laity, and by his tears moved and shook the merciful Church of Christ herself, who was also merciful.

“After employing many prayers and displaying the welts of the blows he had endured for confessing Christ, he was scarcely at last admitted to communion.”

[Col. 1317A] The discipline then received in the Church, established for the gravest reasons, required that in restoring such offenders to communion—men who had committed serious offenses and had presented a scandal to all the faithful—one should proceed with the utmost caution, even though they humbly sought to be cleansed through the sacrament of penance.

The severity of some had advanced beyond the laws and caution of the Church into such cruelty that they believed forgiveness and remission could not be granted for certain crimes, namely idolatry, homicide, and adultery. They did admit those guilty of such crimes to perform works of penance; nevertheless, they maintained that absolution could not be pronounced for them by the tribunal of the Church, but that remission had to be reserved for God’s judgment in the age to come.

Tertullian, having embraced the sect of Montanus, had fallen into these errors. Accordingly, he raged impotently against the Roman pontiff who governed the Church at that time—believed to have been Zephyrinus—when a decree had proceeded from him granting the benefit of absolution to adulterers and fornicators who performed penance.

> I hear that an edict has even been issued—and indeed a peremptory one. The Supreme Pontiff, the bishop of bishops, says: “I forgive the sins of adultery and fornication.”

From these words of Tertullian we recognize that, from the earliest times of the Church, the Roman bishops were accustomed to be given the title of Supreme Pontiff and Bishop of Bishops. Even if it is argued that this writer, made bolder by his heresy, intended to apply these names to the pope only ironically, the fact and the words together always yield the same conclusion: namely, that the Roman bishop exercised the authority indicated by such titles, an authority that they rightly possessed as having been conferred by the Lord Christ upon Peter and his successors.

[Col. 1305]

## 16

Zephyrinus, a Roman by nation, son of Abundius, sat for seventeen years, two months, and ten days [Note: [Col. 1305] B: eighteen years, eighteen days]. He lived in the times of Antoninus and Severus, from the consulship of Saturninus and Gallicanus to the consulship of Praesens and Striganus [Note: [Col. 1305] B: of Severus, Caracalla, Geta, Macrinus, and Elagabalus, from the consulship of Fabianus and Mucianus to that of Antoninus Augustus II and Sacerdos].

He established that a Levite [Note: [Col. 1305] C: or a cleric] or a priest should be ordained in the presence of all the clergy and the faithful laity. He also issued a regulation concerning the Church, that ministers should carry glass patens before the priests into the church until the bishop celebrated Mass, with the priests standing before him; and thus Masses should be celebrated [Note: [Col. 1305] C: “thus”], except that the bishop’s right was preserved, so that the entire clergy, with all present, should receive from the hand of the bishop the consecrated portion from that consecration and that the presbyter should distribute it to the people.

He held four ordinations in the month of December: nine presbyters [Note: [Col. 1305] C and B: thirteen], seven deacons, and eight bishops in various places [Note: [Col. 1305] C and B: thirteen].

He was also buried in his own cemetery, beside the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, on 26 August, and the episcopate remained vacant for six days.

## XVII. SAINT CALLISTUS. YEAR OF CHRIST 221, THE SECOND YEAR OF ELAGABALUS

### Note: [Col. 1317A]

From Fabrottus, based on the Freher manuscript.

Number 17, line 7: B has fourteen presbyters. On the same line, A has 9; B has thirteen places.

From the Royal, Mazarin, and Thuane manuscripts.

Line 1: “from the district of the city of the Ravennatians”; six years, ten months, ten days. He lived in the times of Antoninus and Alexander, from the consulship of Macrinus and Heliogabalus to that of Praesens and Gallicanus. He established the Saturday fast. Line 6: “across the Tiber, which is called Saint Mary’s.” The Mazarin manuscript has: “which is called Saint Mary’s.” He made another cemetery on the Appian Way, where many priests and martyrs rest. ### Note: [Col. 1319A]

#### Line 9

> He made another cemetery on the Appian Way, where many priests and martyrs rest, which is called the cemetery of Callistus to the present day.

Thus the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* writes, and so too the cemetery is called in our own times; it is frequently mentioned in the Acts of the saints buried there. It should be noted that Callistus is said to have made this cemetery; accordingly, what Burnet observed in his letters on his Italian journey—that the cemeteries are pagan, and that Christians first customarily buried in them only in the fifth century—is not true. See what we shall note below on the Life of Marcellus.

From another Thuane manuscript.

Line 1: “in the city of the Ravennatians.” Line 5: “the prophecy.” Line 8: “He was buried.”

According to Holstenius and Schelestratius.

Line 3: the Cassinese manuscript omits “here he was crowned with martyrdom.” Line 5: the Florentine, Cassinese, and Vatican manuscripts omit “the fourth, seventh, and tenth.” Line 8: the Florentine manuscript has: “He was crowned with martyrdom and buried.”

### Line 4

Here he established a fast on Saturday, for the sake of grain, wine, and oil. Callixtus is said to have been the originator of the Saturday fast; nevertheless, it is more truly to be understood as deriving from apostolic institution and the primitive custom of the Church, in memory of Christ resting in the tomb. Augustine (*Epistle* 86):

> “Saturday follows, the day on which Christ’s flesh rested in the tomb. Hence arose in that imperial city the divergence whereby some—especially the peoples of the East—preferred, in order to signify rest, to relax the fast; while others, because of the humility of the Lord’s death, fasted, as did the Roman Church and certain Churches of the West.”

Ambrose, in his commentary on Romans, chapter 14:

> “For there are some who have decided that flesh is not to be eaten on Wednesday; there are some who observe this on Saturdays; and again there are some who eat from Easter to Pentecost.”

There were diverse customs among the Churches concerning the Saturday fast. The Roman Church observed the Saturday fast, whereas the Milanese Church did not; and Augustine, after consulting blessed Ambrose, wrote that the customs of the Churches should be observed in this matter (*Epistle* 318):

> “When my mother followed me to Milan, she found that the Church did not fast on Saturday. She began to be troubled and uncertain what she should do, while I was unconcerned about such matters; but, for her sake, I consulted the man of blessed memory, Ambrose, on this question. He replied that he could teach me nothing except what he himself did, since, if he knew anything better, he would observe that instead. When I had supposed that, without giving any reason, he wished by his own authority alone to admonish us not to fast on Saturday, he continued and said to me: ‘When I am at Rome, I fast on Saturday; when I am here, I do not fast. So you too should observe the custom of whatever Church you may happen to visit, if you do not wish to cause scandal to anyone or to make anyone a scandal to you.’”

The Saturday fast was also approved by Innocent I. Anastasius, in his life of Innocent:

> “He established that the fast should be observed on Saturday, because on Saturday the Lord was placed in the tomb and his disciples fasted.”

On the Saturday fast, see also Jerome, in Augustine’s *Epistle* 19; Cassian, *Institutes of the Coenobites*, book III, chapter 10; Socrates, book V, chapter 21; and Nicephorus Callistus, book XII, chapter 24.

[Note: [Col. 1319D]

### Lines 3 and 4

“He is crowned with martyrdom.” Concerning the martyrdom of Callixtus, the Roman Martyrology contains the following:

> “At Rome, on the Appian Way, the commemoration of blessed Callixtus, pope and martyr, who, by order of the emperor Alexander, was long tormented by hunger in prison and beaten daily with clubs; finally, having been thrown from the window of the house in which he was being held and plunged into a well, he won the triumph of victory.”

But since the emperor Alexander, according to Lampridius in his life of Alexander, not only did no harm to Christianity but rather promoted it greatly—since he included Christ among the gods, performed religious rites to him in his household shrine in the morning, and, had he not been dissuaded by the responses of the gods, intended to build him a temple; since he took pleasure in Christian morals and proposed Christians as examples for the governors of the provinces to imitate; and since, after expelling the keepers of drinking shops, he granted Christians a public place for holding assemblies, from which, formerly, under Augustus, when Christ was born in Bethlehem, oil had flowed forth, and there permitted a temple consecrated in honor of the Virgin’s childbirth to be erected by Pope Callixtus—in short, since he was so favorably disposed toward Christians, we have thought it more likely that Pope Callixtus was not killed by an express order and decree of the emperor Alexander himself, but rather by the advice and decree of the jurists, especially Ulpian—whom Lactantius Firmianus, in book IV, chapters 11 and 12, shows to have been most hostile to Christians, treating them as sacrilegious—had Callixtus killed.

### Line 8

“Three miles.” Namely, from the city. For according to the law of the Twelve Tables, as Cicero testifies in *On the Laws*, book II, it had been forbidden to bury a dead person within the walls. By this law, therefore, Christians too were compelled to bury their dead outside the walls, unless perhaps someone had secretly removed the body of a martyr—as happened quite often—and buried it in his own house. But under Christian emperors the bones of the saints were transferred into churches. See Baronius, year 226, nos. 7 and 12.

*(From the Labbe edition.)* Line 9: “And he made another cemetery.” These words are absent from C. H.

[Note: [Col. 1320B]

## Chronological Notes

I stated in the *Prolegomena* that the epoch of blessed Callixtus, established through the agreement of the manuscripts and paintings, namely five years, two months, and ten days, corresponds exactly with the epoch of his predecessor Zephyrinus and with the consulships assigned in the Liberian Catalogue—that is, from Antoninus and Adventus (A.D. 218) to Antoninus IV and Alexander (A.D. 222). Of these, the texts of the librarians record only the latter pair, and the Ocriculan manuscripts follow them. How appropriately they agree with the consulships is clear from the five-year period included by them and from the continuous sequence after the consuls of the year 217, Praesens and Extricatus, who were the last during the pontificate of Zephyrinus.

How neatly this also corresponds to the days of his own martyrdom and that of his predecessor I shall explain briefly. Zephyrinus attained the palm of martyrdom on July 26, as I stated could be established from the inscriptional panel in the church of Saint Sylvester in Capite. The see was vacant for six days after his death, as the librarian relates under his entry and as the Lucensian Catalogue, cited above in the *Prolegomena*, agrees. His successor Callixtus was therefore elected on the day after the Kalends of August. Since the Kalends in the year 217 fell on a Friday, as the Sunday letter E demonstrates, the day of election should be regarded as Saturday, August 2, and the day of ordination as the Sunday immediately following, August 3.

Counting five years, two months, and ten days from that date brings the calculation to October 13 of the year 222, on which he completed his martyrdom. On the following day, October 14, the day on which he is commemorated, he was buried in the cemetery of Calepodius, as the librarian records at the end of the entry:

> “He was also buried in the cemetery of Calepodius, on the Via Aurelia, at the third milestone, on the day before the Ides of October.”

The Acts of his martyrdom published by Mombritius do indeed state that his sacred body was carried into the cemetery of Calepodius on that day, but that seventeen days earlier he had been plunged into the well of the house in which he was being held, and that, after rubble had been thrown in, the blessed pontiff died, suffocated and crushed at the same time.

Cardinal Baronius, however, had already noted in the Martyrology, under October 14, that these Acts required some correction. Among other things, the time at which he was removed from the well appears to need correction. The removal, which took place on the day after his martyrdom, was wrongly reported by inexperienced copyists as occurring seventeen days later. The householders could not have been deprived for so long of the necessary use of the well by retaining and decomposing the corpse, since the executioners had been ordered to inflict death on Callixtus, not to make the well unusable for the inhabitants by corrupting it with a corpse. I therefore think that the text should read “on the day after his martyrdom,” not “after seventeen days.”

Accordingly, the martyrdom belongs to October 13, while the removal from the well and the carrying of the body to the cemetery belong to October 14. Thus the period from his ordination to his martyrdom is plainly five years, two months, and ten days, confirmed by the testimony of all the documents, just as these figures are marked in the paintings, manuscripts, and catalogues discussed in the *Prolegomena*.

## Historical Notes

### Line 1

“A Roman by nation, the son of Domitius, from the region of the city of Ravenna.” He is said to have been born of the Domitian family, from the district of the city called the Region of the Ravennates. In the fourteenth Augustan region of the city, called Transtiberim and constituting the sixth ecclesiastical region, antiquarians identify the Gardens of Domitius, placed there by Publicus Victor. In the same region they likewise locate the barracks of the Ravennates, together with Donatus, book III of *On the City of Rome*, page 310, and other authorities.

Callixtus could therefore also have erected, in this place belonging to his own Domitian family, a Roman titular church, which later came to be called indiscriminately the Basilica of Saint Mary in Transtiberim and the Basilica of Callixtus, after its founder. Donatus writes:

> “Beneath the Janiculum there were not only the temporary stations of these Vitellian troops, but also permanent quarters for soldiers established by Augustus, called the camp of the Ravennates—namely, of the soldiers who guarded the fleet stationed at Ravenna for the defense of the upper sea (Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 49). These marines, when they came to the City, had their permanent quarters there, and the place called the Merchants’ Inn, where the church of Saint Mary in Transtiberim now stands, belonged to them or to others. Ecclesiastical records have handed down that oil flowed abundantly from there as far as the river; and the enduring report, together with the marked location beneath the high altar of the church and the ancient inscription *Fons olei*—‘Fountain of Oil’—clearly confirms this. Since maritime expeditions were exceedingly rare under the emperors, while the Ravennate marines were frequently in the City and unfurled the awnings in the theatre, Lampridius writes of Commodus: ‘Thinking this displeasing to the Roman people and to the marine soldiers who unfurled the awnings, Commodus ordered him to be killed.’”

These are the words of Donatus.

An inscription of L. Furius Victor, son of Lucius, of the Palatine tribe, mentions a *missus Ravennatium*, “delegate of the Ravennates,” in Gruter, folio 414, and in Panvinius, *On the City of Rome*, page 172; he is said to have been the procurator, or administrator, of the Great Games on behalf of the Ravennates.

Carlo Piazza, in his *Cardinal Hierarchy*, discussing this titular church on page 367, asserts that Flavius Blondus observed in certain Acts of the holy martyrs that this basilica of Saint Mary in Transtiberim was called the Basilica of the Ravennates. The Acts of Callixtus’s martyrdom, preserved in the manuscripts of Saint Cecilia and in the Vallicellian manuscripts, which the aforementioned Piazza lists on page 561, also testify that blessed Callixtus customarily assembled in the same Transtiberine region, in the house of Pontianus near the barracks of the Ravennates:

> “From that same day Alexander began diligently to seek blessed Callixtus the bishop, and it became known to him that he was in Transtiberim, in the house of Pontianus near the city of the Ravennates.”

In view of these facts, it becomes probable that Pope Callixtus, son of Domitius, offered some portion of his own estates, or of those belonging to his kinsmen, in order to consecrate it to God, establishing a titular church of the Roman presbyter in this part of the City, where it is also said that the prince of the apostles preached Christ to the Jews inhabiting the Transtiberine region. See Baronius under the year 44.

### Lines 9 and 10

“He also made another cemetery on the Appian Way, where many priests and martyrs rest, which is called to this day the cemetery of Callixtus.” Through the burial there of holy pontiffs and martyrs, the cemetery of Callixtus became especially famous after the Vatican cemetery.

Fourth-century writings, published above in the *Prolegomena* and by Bucherius, mention numerous pontiffs and martyrs buried there. Although in the document entitled the *Burial of the Bishops* the oldest of those listed there is Lucius, nevertheless in the neighboring document headed *Burial of the Martyrs* the burial of Fabian in the same cemetery of Callixtus is recorded on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, and on the Ides of August the commemoration of the burial of Pontianus in the cemetery of Callixtus is recorded. Both of these preceded Lucius in martyrdom and pontificate.

Since, therefore, by that time numerous catalogues had already been written around the middle of the fourth century, in which commemorations of those martyrs and pontiffs appeared, instituted long before in these cemeteries; and since the letters of Saint Cyprian cited in the notes on Saint Anacletus, as well as Tertullian in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, show that an older custom had prevailed before the reign of Severus, namely that the memory of martyrs should be commemorated annually with the offering of the divine sacrifice, Burnet argues most unfortunately in his letters concerning his Italian journey, denying that these cemeteries had been assigned to Christian use before the fifth century.

The learned notes of Pagi rightly mark this as a gross error. To refute and overturn it, the daily evidence of Christian inscriptions is sufficient: in these same cemeteries they close the niches of the dead, and direct inspection (*autopsia*, literally “seeing with one’s own eyes”) reveals earlier periods through the consulships inscribed there.

It is truly astonishing that this eyewitness traveler, who undertook so many journeys for the sake of learning and wished to enter and examine these crypts, did not observe—even if only from the testimony of Jerome, which the custodians of that church prudently had inscribed at the very entrance of the cemetery of Callixtus, within the church of Saint Sebastian outside the walls—that the holy doctor affirmed that, when he was a boy staying in Rome for the sake of his studies, as is known to have been at the beginning of the fourth century, he used to visit these sacred places, filled with the burials of martyrs, on Sundays with his contemporaries.

But Burnet, in his voluntary blindness, postponing the centuries in opposition to the evidence of the facts, is not worth the trouble of invoking against him the well-known testimonies of the holy Fathers and the evidence of monuments contemporary with them.

[Note: [Col. 1322B]

### Line 4

“Here he established a fast on Saturday.” Pope Callixtus, amid the great disorders of the time and the excessive luxury of the reign of Heliogabalus, did not in any way depart from his own institution. He established—or rather renewed—the four seasonal fasts formerly imposed upon the Hebrews: the spring, summer, autumn, and winter fasts. From that time onward the ordinations of the sacred orders were arranged according to these seasons, whereas previously this had customarily been done only in the month of December.

### Lines 5 and 6

“Here he built a basilica across the Tiber.” That is, in honor of the Blessed Virgin. It is not, however, believed to have been the church that is now seen to be so famous and spacious, since at that time, because of the frequent persecutions, all chapels were concealed, hidden away, and for the most part underground, rather than being built in open and prominent places.

It may therefore initially have been an oratory or humble chapel serving the ministry of the Christian people, not something intended to provoke the envy of the pagans. Perhaps it was the temple which Christians obtained permission to erect by a rescript of the emperor Alexander Severus, against the tavern-keepers who wished to construct drinking shops on the same site. Alexander declared, as Lampridius writes in his life of Alexander, that it would be better for God to be worshiped there in whatever manner than for the place to be handed over to taverns.

The most devout pontiff Callixtus therefore built this church according to his vows, under the title of the Virgin Mother of God, at the place where, in the time of Augustus, oil burst forth from the earth and flowed abundantly by a great miracle, as a sign of the near coming into the world of Christ, the Redeemer of the human race. The sacred opening from which the oil once sprang still exists, and the earth beneath it remains moist with oil. This was the first temple publicly dedicated to the Virgin.

[Note: [Col. 1322D]

### Line 5

“According to the prophecy.” Antiquity preserves almost nothing for us concerning the pontificate of Callixtus apart from a decree established by him, in accordance with the prophecy, concerning the celebration of a fast three times a year and the offering to God, in thanksgiving, of the fruits of the earth gathered during those seasons—grain, wine, and oil.

It is therefore necessary to recognize that these three fasts are the ones called the four seasonal fasts. The prophecy of which he speaks here is Zechariah, chapter 8, verse 19:

> “The fast of the fourth month, and the fast of the fifth month, and the fast of the seventh month, and the fast of the tenth month shall become for the house of Judah joy.”

[Col. 1317]

## 17

Callixtus, a Roman by nation, the son of Domitius, from the region of the city of the Ravennates [Note: [Col. 1317] C: “of the city of the Ravennates”], sat for six years, two months, and ten days [Note: [Col. 1317] a B: “five years, one month, and twelve days”]. He lived in the time of Macrinus and Heliogabalus, from the consulship of Antoninus and Alexander [Note: [Col. 1317] B: “Heliogabalus and Alexander, from the consulships of Antoninus Augustus II and Sacerdos to Julian and Crispus”]. Here he was crowned with martyrdom.

Here he established that the Saturday fast should be observed three times a year [Note: [Col. 1317] * C B: “four times”], for the sake of grain, wine, and oil [Note: [Col. 1317] “of oil,” C B], according to the prophecy [Note: [Col. 1317] Zechariah 8] of the fourth, seventh [Note: [Col. 1317] * “fifth”], and tenth months.

Here he built a basilica [Note: [Col. 1317] C B: “the Basilica of Saint Mary”] across the Tiber. Here he held five ordinations during the month of December: sixteen priests, four deacons, and eight bishops for various places.

He was also buried in the cemetery of Calepodius, on the Via Aurelia, at the third milestone, on the day before the Ides of October, and he made another cemetery on the Appian Way [Note: [Col. 1317] Baronius, year 26, on the cemeteries], where many priests and martyrs rest, which is called to this day the cemetery of Callixtus. The episcopate was vacant for six days.

## Catalogue under Liberius

Callixtus: five years, two months, and ten days. He lived in the time of Macrinus and Heliogabalus, from the consulship of Antoninus and Adventus to that of Antoninus III and Alexander.
