### Line 2

“Here he made all the sacred vessels of silver.” Urban decreed that the vessels of the Church—the *ministeria*, that is, the sacred vessels—should be of silver.

It is remarkable that Exuperius, bishop of Toulouse, is said to have celebrated the sacrifice in glass, that is, with a glass chalice. Jerome, writing to Rusticus:

> “No one is richer than he who carries the Lord’s body in a wicker basket and his blood in glass.”

Nevertheless, sacred vessels were commonly made of gold or silver. Augustine, on Psalm 113, concerning “the idols of the nations, silver and gold”:

> “But we too possess many instruments and vessels made of such material or metal, for use in celebrating the sacraments; consecrated by that very ministry, they are called holy.”

[Note: [Col. 1323C]

### Line 3

“He was a true confessor.” There were many titles of honor by which martyrs were distinguished for confession and martyrdom, including that of “true confessor.” Great care and investigation were exercised in assigning and granting these titles, perhaps following the preceding careful examination by the priests of the martyrs or by deacons. Through their frequent visits to the prisons they were able to recognize in the martyrs exercises of courage, endurance, and the remaining virtues. Those who were conspicuous for glorious confession were then adorned with the appropriate titles and honored with the praise they deserved as athletes of Christ who had fought manfully in the contest. In this way zeal was aroused among the faithful, so that they might face the struggles of persecution with eager courage.

The institution is ancient. In its encyclical letter concerning the martyrs who had suffered, the Church of Lyons likewise distinguishes true martyrs from others, repeatedly calling them true, most blessed, and most courageous martyrs, while attacking those who had fallen away. Tertullian calls those who, after sentence had been pronounced, were already being led to martyrdom “blessed designated martyrs.” This formula occurs frequently in Cyprian’s letters, especially when he writes of the confessor Paul (*Epistle* 21):

> “While the blessed martyr Paul was still in the body…”

Cyprian sometimes calls the clergy of the confessors “the flourishing clergy.” This appears in the aforementioned letter, where, after writing, “When I too was in such a flourishing confession,” he immediately adds:

> “For I heard that you had received the ministry of the flourishing confessors”; 

and near the end:

> “Those who rejoice in your flourishing confession.”

Lucian was the priest of the martyrs, and therefore Cyprian calls him “the minister of the flourishing ones.” Shortly afterward he says:

> “And now, having been placed over them, the bishop of God recognized the same minister”—perhaps recognizing the ministry he had rendered to the martyrs in prison.

In the same letter he calls the designated martyrs “lords”:

> “Therefore I ask and beseech you through our Lord Jesus Christ to report to your other colleagues, your brothers and mine, my lords, and to ask them that whichever of you is crowned first…” 

At the end he writes:

> “You should know that I have written to you and to my lords, your brothers.”

Thus Lucian writes to Celerinus in Cyprian’s *Epistle* 22, “Lucian to Celerinus the Lord,” addressing a true confessor.

True confessors were distinguished by punishment and torture. Thus Lucian, in reporting the indulgence granted by the martyrs, distinguishes them according to their sufferings, saying:

> “On whose behalf I submit the following names: Bassus, in the stone quarry; Mappalicus, under examination; Fortunio, in prison; Paul, under examination; Fortuna, Victorinus, Victor, Herena, Credula, Herena, Donatus, Firmus, Venustus, Fructus, Julia, Martialis, and Aristo, who, God willing, were killed by hunger in prison.”

Thus the martyrs, glorious through manifold confession, emerged victorious from the contest. Just as in the Olympic games and other athletic competitions the number of victories was recorded, so the contests of martyrdom were recorded and the triumphs won by them.

With this praise Pope Cornelius exalts Maximus and Urbanus in his letter to Fabius of Antioch, writing in Eusebius, book VI, chapter 43:

> “Maximus, a presbyter of our Church, and Urbanus have both already won a distinguished second commendation through the confession of the faith.”

And Cyprian, in *Epistle* 33, speaking of Aurelius the lector, counts among his other praises the fact that he had fought in a double contest, confessed twice, and twice been made glorious by the victory of his confession.

Lactantius uses the expression in the same sense in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*:

> “Nine times you have conquered the adversary by glorious confession.”

In the Passion of Saints Seraphia and Sabina, preserved in Baluze, volume II of the *Miscellany*, page 106, there is mention of a certain Herod, a worker in the mines, who under Vespasian Augustus gave the Romans a “white confession”—that is, an unblemished confession—three times in the city of Rome. In the Acts of Saint Boniface, concerning Aglae, we read:

> “She had therefore three times offered a white confession in Rome, from the position of prefect.”

The confession itself was marked by the title “glorious.” Lactantius writes of it in chapter 1:

> “The Lord has heard your prayers, dearest Donatus, which you pour out before him every hour throughout the day, and those of our other brothers who by their glorious confession have won for themselves an everlasting crown in accordance with the merits of their faith.”

Speaking of the persecution of Diocletian, during which the world was flooded with the sacred blood of martyrs, Severus writes in book II of his *History*:

> “They rushed eagerly into glorious contests, and at that time martyrdoms were sought with much greater desire through glorious deaths.”

In the Acts of the earlier martyrs the expressions “glorious confession,” “glorious deaths,” “glorious contests,” “martyrdoms,” “athletic struggles,” and the like occur frequently.

The diligence with which the Churches, through priests of the martyrs, deacons, and notaries of the martyrs, took care to distinguish those worthy of honor by such titles, and the great antiquity of this concern, is demonstrated by the letter sent by the Church of Lyons to the Churches throughout the world. There true confessors are presented as glorious and crowned martyrs; they are identified as prepared and trained, and distinguished from the false and untested, who failed in the first encounter.

The Acts of Urbanus could honor the pontiff with the title “true confessor,” since he had propagated the Christian name especially in Rome; by his exhortations he had led Valerianus, the bridegroom of the most illustrious virgin Cecilia, and several other noble Romans—including Tiburtius and Maximus, the emperor’s prefect—after their baptism to the crown of martyrdom; and finally, after making a glorious confession with courageous spirit, he himself was crowned as a martyr.

[Note: [Col. 1325D]

### Line 6

“Many were crowned with martyrdom through his exhortations.” He had instructed Valerianus, Tiburtius, and Maximus, together with Saint Cecilia, in the faith; had baptized them; and through his exhortations had fortified them against the stroke of the sword. At last, after himself suffering much for the Church, he too was crowned with martyrdom, having been beheaded, in the year of Christ 233, the tenth year of the emperor Alexander, on May 25.

[Note: [Col. 1325D]

## Chronological Notes

The eight years, eleven months, and twelve days of his episcopate, which according to the agreement of the documents discussed in the *Prolegomena* end during the consulship of Agricola and Clementinus (A.D. 230), must begin earlier than the date indicated by the consulship of Aelianus and Vetus, which marks the year A.D. 223.

Nevertheless, the succession of Urbanus to the apostolic see is correctly assigned to the consulship of Aelianus and Vetus. These consuls immediately followed Antoninus IV—Heliogabalus—and Alexander, under whom the year 222 is marked: the seventh Easter celebrated by Callixtus, after Heliogabalus had died only a few days earlier and Alexander had held the imperial power since the sixth day before the Ides of March.

The author of the Liberian Catalogue, followed by later writers, looks—as I have often stated—to the paschal season when assigning and indicating the years of each pontificate by the consulships. Accordingly, the eight years, eleven months, and twelve days, whose final limit falls during the consulship of Agricola and Clementinus in the year 239, around the burial of blessed Urbanus recorded by the librarian on May 25, must begin in June of the year 221, when he was promoted to the episcopate, whether to act as Callixtus’s vicar in Rome or to be sent to win some people for Christ.

If the day of his ordination is supposed to have been the second Sunday of June, which in the year 221, according to the Sunday letter G, coincided with June 10, then his subsequent martyrdom, after eight years, eleven months, and twelve days, falls on May 23, 230. The *Liber Pontificalis* reports that his sacred body was buried two days later, in these words:

> “He was also buried in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Appian Way, on the eighth day before the Kalends of June.”

From these documents, therefore, we learn that Urbanus received episcopal ordination—whether to act as Callixtus’s vicar or to be appointed bishop of some people or province—on Sunday, June 10, 221.

In the following year, 222, opened by the consulship of Antoninus Heliogabalus IV and Alexander, who succeeded to the empire in March of that same year, Callixtus completed his martyrdom by being plunged into a well on October 13 and was carried into the cemetery of Calepodius on the following day. After the six-day vacancy recorded by the librarian, Urbanus, elected by the clergy, occupied the apostolic throne as his successor on Sunday, October 20, the third Sunday of October, under the Sunday letter F.

He celebrated the first Easter of his pontificate in the following year, A.D. 223, under the consulship of Maximus II and Aelianus, correctly entered in the Liberian Catalogue. His final Easter was in the year 230, under the consulship of Agricola and Clementinus, likewise indicated there and in the other catalogues and manuscripts. Finally, after being crowned with martyrdom on May 23, his body was carried into the cemetery of Callixtus on May 25, the day on which he is commemorated.

## Historical Notes

### Line 2

“Here he made all the sacred vessels of silver and set down twenty-five silver patens.” As for the number twenty-five, it appears to refer to the total number of titular churches. Regarding the material, we said above, in treating Zephyrinus, something about the use of glass patens and the reason for their selection.

Nor was their use entirely abolished even when silver vessels were employed. Even today, for the sacrifice, we generally use glass cruets to present the wine and water, although silver vessels are plentiful, so that it may be more easily distinguished when one or the other species is to be presented to the priest.

I have shown that glass chalices, and even patens, were used at discretion down to the time of Leo IV, until experience established that another material should be used more cautiously, and that pontiff issued a decree on the subject.

In any case, we see silver vessels of the sacred ministry, and still preserve some whose workmanship and engraving are so ancient, as is demonstrated by the elegance of their reliefs, that they must undoubtedly belong to a period before the age of Constantine.

A silver cruet remains in my possession among the sacred treasures preserved there, with which the faithful would present wine or water for the sacrifice. On its exterior surface, in fairly skillfully worked relief, are figures representing Christ the Lord standing among the disciples and changing water into wine at the wedding in Cana of Galilee.

We judge that this Gospel history was appropriately represented on these small vessels from the argument of Cyril that I shall presently cite, by which the faith of those standing by was strengthened in confessing that the conversion of wine into the Lord’s blood is accomplished by the same divine power with which Christ formerly began his signs by changing water into wine, a transformation analogous to this one.

Saint Cyril of Jerusalem certainly arouses the faith of neophytes with the same argument in his fourth *Mystagogical Catechesis*:

> “Formerly he changed water into wine at Cana of Galilee, which has a certain kinship with blood; shall we then consider him unworthy of belief when he has changed wine into blood? At that wedding, where bodies are joined, he performed this miracle beyond everyone’s expectation. Shall we not be much more firmly persuaded that he has also given us his body and blood to enjoy, so that we may receive them with complete certainty as his body and blood? For under the appearance of bread he gives us his body, and under the appearance of wine he gives us his blood, so that when you have received it, you may taste the body and blood of Christ and become a participant in the same body and blood.”

Since the Catholic Church appoints this teaching of Cyril to be recited annually for us on the octave of Corpus Christi, and since earlier believers likewise expressed it in these reliefs, I am pleased to present here the design of a silver vessel engraved in this manner, both to illustrate the text of the librarian and to demonstrate the care of Catholic bishops in awakening and expressing the lights of our faith even in the ornaments of the sacred ministry.

Another silver vessel decorated with a similar design was preserved a few years ago in the museum of the most noble prelate Leo Strozzi, to whom, after his pious death a few days ago, all learned men pay their last respects. I shall not append its image, drawn from the original, since I understand that it has been carried elsewhere.

On it was displayed an image of Christ the Lord handing the keys to blessed Peter and placing them in his mantle, in almost the same type—though with much more elegant sculpture—as is seen on the sarcophagus of Junius Bassus, engraved under the consulship of Eusebius and Hypatius, A.D. 360, and visible in the underground basilica of Saint Peter opposite the altar of the Confession.

Another image of our Redeemer also projects from the same vessel: he is giving sight to a man born blind. In the first figure the power of the priesthood is aptly indicated; in the second, the effect of Christ’s touch.

I have also seen other silver vessels, or fragments of them, marked with other symbols and characters of Christian worship. Tertullian recorded that the image of the Good Shepherd was customarily represented on our chalices. We recognize this, in fact, on patens reproduced by Boldetti in *Observations on the Cemeteries*, page 200, and by Senator Buonarroti in plates V and VI of *Glass Vessels from the Cemeteries*.

On our cruet we likewise contemplate the sheep of the Lord’s flock looking toward the Lamb, offered and slain for our salvation. Chrysostom, the interpreter of the mystery, adds the following question in Homily 60:

> “What shepherd feeds his sheep with his own blood? And why do I say shepherd? There are many mothers who, after the pains of childbirth, hand their children over to other nurses. But he did not endure this; rather, he himself feeds us with his own blood and joins us to himself in every way.”

In another silver vessel, kept in Rome by the distinguished M. Antonius Sabbatinus in his excellent treasury, besides images of Christ the Lord and the apostles, and the little sheep of his flock arranged beneath this Shepherd, doves are visible above, with the sign of a cross attached.

The form and engraving of the vessel seem to indicate that it was used to contain the sacred chrism. The ancient Roman Order, published after Hittorp by Mabillon, page 4, no. 3, shows that the sacred chrism was customarily carried before the pontiff, who solemnly rode to the station, by a station acolyte:

> “One of the station acolytes goes ahead on foot before the bishop’s horse, carrying the sacred chrism in a small flask wrapped in a cloth.”

Both in Sabbatini’s museum and in ours there are still silver spoons, some solid and some perforated: the former for placing incense in the censer, the latter for pouring water drop by drop into the wine during the preparation of the sacrifice.

Cardinal Baronius, under the year 133, no. 1, observes that Gregory of Tours, in *The Glory of the Martyrs*, chapter 38, recorded in writing that silver cruets and vessels of this kind were used for the sacrifice. They were found in the same crypt of the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, where the bodies of the holy martyrs Chrysanthus and Daria had been buried.

Urbanus therefore prepared vessels of the sacred ministry like these, in addition to silver chalices and patens, during the reign of Severus Alexander. The emperor’s well-known favorable disposition toward Christians made the priests’ efforts to acquire such ornaments for divine worship less difficult.

### Line 5

The Acts of Saints Cecilia and Valerian show that even Valerian, a most noble man and the betrothed of Saint Cecilia, and that the vigilant care of Callistus, his predecessor, for the faithful frequenting the Transtiberine district was increased by notable developments under Pope Urban. Their house was ennobled by martyrdom, and at the request of that same Cecilia he dedicated it [Col. 1330B] as a Roman titular church.

If anyone is surprised that, under the rule of Severus Alexander—a prince so favorably disposed toward Christians, as Lampridius demonstrates in his *Life* through several sayings and actions—we should nevertheless admit both the dedication of Christian titular churches and the martyrdoms of those who had offered their houses for the assemblies of the faithful, let him remember that the martyrdoms of Saints Cecilia and her companions under Almachius, prefect of the City, and shortly afterward the passion of Saint Urban the pope, are assigned to about the ninth year of that emperor’s reign. At that time, having undertaken an expedition against the Persians, Alexander departed from Rome in the ninth year of his tribunician power—as the coins demonstrate, bearing *TR. P. VIIII. COS. III. P. P.* and on the reverse the inscription *PROFECTIO AUG. S. C.*—and spent two years in the East.

At that time, however, although the laws of Trajan, Hadrian, and the Antonines had never been revoked, and indeed although more recent laws enacted against us by Caracalla were also in force, informers and judges, stirred up against us, decreed that punishments should be inflicted upon Christians at will while the emperor was absent [Col. 1330C]. The sacrificers of the empty gods opposed the indulgence and equity that the emperor, if present, was ready and inclined to extend toward us.

We therefore may and must reconcile the kindness of the emperor Alexander toward Christians with the truth of the deeds of the holy martyrs who suffered and were crowned under his rule, especially Saints Cecilia, Tiburtius, and Valerian. Baronius treats these deeds more fully in his notes on the Martyrology and in the *Annals*, although his chronology, when compared with the Christian era, differs from ours by two years, as Schelestratius, cited above, observed. Nevertheless, he agrees in assigning those martyrdoms to the ninth year of Alexander’s reign.

Besides the mosaic constructed by Paschal I in the apse of the titular church of Saint Cecilia, where he also expressed in verse that he had discovered and removed the bodies of those martyrs from the cemetery of Callistus and transferred them to this titular church, where they are reverently preserved and venerated, there remains also an ancient painting behind the apse of the titular church of Saint Pudentiana [Col. 1330D], visible in the inner chapel. The surviving wall paintings still display that fountain of Christian baptism established by Pope Pius I, concerning which I treated more fully in the notes on his *Life*, pp. 123–126.

On p. 126, col. 2, I indicated that there remains a painting of the apostles administering baptism to the faithful in the same house of Pudens, reproduced and published by the illustrious bishop Giovanni Ciampini. Nearby, on the adjoining arch, there also remains an image of Pope Saint Urban sending the saints Tiburtius and Valerian ahead to martyrdom, with each of their names written beside them. They are shown under the guidance of that angel, whose promised appearance to Cecilia was the occasion of their conversion.

Thus one sees the angel preceding Tiburtius and Valerian and placing a crown upon the head of the one immediately following him; Pope Urban comes afterward, as the third to receive the crown. In the same place I observed that this painting confirms what is read in the lectionaries of that titular church [Col. 1331A]: namely, that Urban and his successors, especially Blessed Stephen I, following the example of his predecessor Pius and the more ancient practice of the holy apostles, the guests of Saint Pudens, customarily administered solemn baptism at Easter in this same titular church.

### Lines 8–9

In the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Appian Way.

The cemetery of Praetextatus was so close to the cemetery of Callistus that there was an entrance from one into the other. Boldetti makes this observation, together with Bosius in his notes on the *Life of Saint Urban*, in *On the Sacred Cemeteries*, book II, chapter 18, p. 554:

> “As for the cemetery of Praetextatus,” says Bosius, “it was on the Appian Way, and it had a common entrance with the cemetery of Callistus—or rather, it was part of that cemetery.”

The letters of Paschal I likewise indicate that the area was called both that of Praetextatus and that of Sixtus, and also “Saint Cecilia.” It was that section of the crypts beneath the church of Saint Sebastian outside the walls on the Appian Way which still preserves inscriptions carved in marble indicating the places where the bodies of the illustrious martyrs Cecilia and her companions were found.

Panvinio believes that the name Praetextatus was derived from a presbyter bearing that cognomen. That cognomen, however, was made famous above all by two martyrs mentioned by Aringhi in *Underground Rome*, book III, pp. 458 and 476.

The first belongs to the time of Pope Anacletus. From the Acts of Saint Sophia in an ancient codex of Saint Cecilia, Aringhi reports that he was baptized by Anacletus together with the illustrious virgin Lucina, his sister, who had been born with him of royal ancestry.

The martyrdom of the other Praetextatus occurred at the end of the third century under Maximian, on 11 December, as the Martyrology records. Although it cannot be determined with certainty to which of them the name of the cemetery should be attributed, the view seems more probable that derives the name from the earlier Praetextatus, who professed the Christian faith under Pope Anacletus.

For since we read in the Acts of Pope Alexander—who, with only Evaristus intervening, succeeded Anacletus—that Saint Quirinus, tribune and father of Saint Balbina, suffered martyrdom under Hadrian and was buried in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Appian Way, it follows that the name may indeed be referred to the earlier Praetextatus, since he lived before the time of Hadrian. But it cannot be referred to the second Praetextatus, who suffered about 150 years after Hadrian, as the name of a cemetery in which Quirinus was buried under Hadrian and Urban under Severus Alexander; this is impossible if the name was already in use for an entire century before that second Praetextatus was crowned with martyrdom under Maximian.

### Note: [Col. 1332A]

#### Line 5

Valerian, a most noble man, the betrothed of Saint Cecilia.

The most holy Pope Urban brought many people to the faith through the holiness of his life and his singular learning. Among them were Valerian, a most distinguished man and the betrothed of Blessed Cecilia; Tiburtius, the brother of that same Valerian; and Maximus, prefect of the imperial bedchamber. At her encouragement they later endured martyrdom with steadfast courage.

The virgin herself also underwent the same condition in her paternal home, which had already been dedicated to God by Urban at her request. After surviving for three days following three blows inflicted by the executioner, she spoke of the things of God, strengthened those standing by in their confession of Christ’s name, and distributed through Pope Urban to the poor whatever remained of her possessions.

Having thus arranged everything and prayed to God, she completed her martyrdom on 22 November. Pope Urban buried her in the cemetery of Callistus, where Valerian, Tiburtius, and Maximus had first been buried by him. A place in the cemetery was designated for Saint Cecilia; it still stands marked today.

[Col. 1323]

## 18

Urban, a Roman by nationality, son of Pontianus, sat for eight years, eleven months, and twelve days [Note: ann. 6, m. 7, d. 4.]. He made all the sacred furnishings [Note: See Baronius, year 233] of silver and placed twenty-five silver patens. He proved a true confessor during the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus [Note: Of the emperor Alexander, from the consulship of Julianus and Crispinus to that of Pompeianus and Felicianus.]. By his instruction he converted many to baptism and faith, including Valerian [Note: C; also Tiburtius and Valerian.], a most noble man and the betrothed of Saint Cecilia. He brought them even to the palm of martyrdom, and many were crowned with martyrdom through his exhortations.

He held five ordinations in the month of December: nine priests, five deacons, and eight bishops in various places. He was also buried in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Appian Way, on 25 May, and the episcopate was vacant for thirty days.

## CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS

Urban: eight years, eleven months, twelve days. He lived during the reign of Alexander, from the consulship of Maximus and Aelianus to that of Agricola and Clementinus.

# XIX. SAINT ANTERUS, IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 237, THE FIRST YEAR OF THE EMPEROR MAXIMINUS

#### Line 3

He investigated the deeds of the martyrs.

Those Acts of the Martyrs which had been faithfully written down by notaries at the command of Clement, Anterus the pope diligently sought out and deposited in the church, so that they might neither perish nor be corrupted by pagans.

### Note: [Col. 1333A]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

In the year 235, during the consulship of Severus and Quinctianus, when Blessed Pontianus had died on 30 October on the island of Bucina near Sardinia, and news of his death had been brought to Rome, Anterus was elected his successor by the votes of the Roman clergy.

Eusebius, book VI, chapter 29, says:

> “After Pontianus had died, having held the episcopate for six years, Anteros assumed the administration of the Roman Church. After exercising the priesthood for one month, he left Fabianus as his successor.”

The Liberian Catalogue states that Anterus sat for one month and ten days. The Bergomensis and the seventh Colbertinus give one month and seventeen days. The other older Italian catalogues, in the *Prolegomena*, give one month and twelve days, as does the catalogue of Felix IV.

That same Felician Catalogue, however, prefixes eleven years; three Italian manuscripts give twelve years. This addition of years, which is not found in the older catalogue and whose origin will be shown below, is plainly to be deleted on the evidence of the consuls indicated. For no other consuls are mentioned in the period of Anterus than those during whose consulship he died.

“Anteros,” says the writer of the catalogue under Liberius, “one month, ten days. He sleeps on 3 January, during the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus”—that is, in the year 236 of Christ, on 3 January.

In an ancient marble tablet of the titular church of Saint Sylvester, the following is carved at the top:

> In the month of January, on the third day, the anniversary of Saint Anterus the pope.

From that day, 3 January of the year 237, counting backward one month and ten days—the period assigned to him by the most ancient Liberian Catalogue—the date of his ordination falls on Sunday, 22 November 235.

Although Papebrochius accepts this date, I do not see why he concludes from it that the date conflicts with the death of his predecessor Pontianus, if that death is assigned to 30 October of the same year 235, during the consulship of Severus and Quinctianus. There is ample time between 30 October and 22 November for news of Pontianus’s death to have been brought from Sardinia and for a successor to have been elected at Rome.

We assign Anterus’s ordination to 22 November on the testimony of documents that do not differ from the Liberian Catalogue by an entire week, but only by a small number of days—either because of a copyist’s error in writing the number or because Anterus’s accession was traced back to the day of his election, whereas the catalogue seems to derive it from the day of his ordination.

I judge that the addition of eleven years, prefixed in certain codices contrary to the clear testimony of Eusebius, the ancient documents, and the better manuscripts, and suggested by no indication of the consulships, should be attributed to the copyists’ carelessness or to the weakness of their eyesight when they copied numbers from the paintings of basilicas.

The letters that alone survive in the basilica of Saint Paul cannot by themselves establish the suspected error with certainty. The surviving elements of the name are as follows, which I reproduce in square or capital letters:

> ant ERVS S E D A N N I m. 1. et 10.

The remaining letters, here represented in lowercase, were erased by the passage of time. They seem to indicate that Anterus sat for a single month and ten days. But the copyist perhaps interpreted the final syllable *NI*, seen indistinctly on the pavement, as the numeral XI.

The same error could have arisen from the obsolete or badly separated letters of an older codex—for example, if it had been written:

> SED. A N N I. M. I. D. X.

Those who copied it may have taken the abbreviation or sequence in the word *ANNI*, whether gaping or worn away at the second letter N, for the sign of the number twelve, *XII*, just as an eroded sign for *VII* may be mistaken for the duodecimal numeral XII.

Whatever the origin of the error, the addition of years must be removed from the later codices that assign only one month to Anterus, following Eusebius and the most ancient catalogue of the Liberian period. The very context of the section by the Librarian proves this point. Since it states that Anterus held only one ordination, and that only one bishop was ordained during the month of December, no one will suppose that he sat for six or twelve years. Rather, it is understood that he was pope only during the month of December 235, when he ordained that one bishop.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

### Line 3

He sought out the deeds of the martyrs from the notaries and deposited them in the church.

It is so well established that the Acts of the Martyrs were diligently sought out and collected by Anterus that some have for this reason regarded him as the author of the first part of the older catalogue, as Schelestratius observes in the *Prolegomena*. This judgment should nevertheless be understood in the sense that the blessed pope prepared abundant material not only for confirming the catalogue of his predecessors with numerous documents, but also for attaching a history to it, while he collected the Acts and deposited them in the archives of the Church: both those of the former bishops of the Roman see and those of the other martyrs, written down by the notaries established by Clement and subsequently employed by their predecessors in every age.

The image visible among the ancient remains of the cemetery of Callistus—where Anterus was buried—may therefore be referred to him. Aringhi reproduces it in *Underground Rome*, volume I, p. 439. It shows a seated pontiff between two standing ministers—whom I take to be a deacon and subdeacon, or two deacons, according to the practice still observed today and derived from the first age of the Church. Other men kneel before him and address him, while they offer a lectern filled with volumes.

The notaries seem clearly to be represented by these men. During the conversation, one of them extends his hand to point out and indicate that the volumes placed before the pontiff should be deposited on the lectern at his feet.

I arranged for the image to be reproduced and joined with another ancient image taken from the sacred cemeteries, engraved on a glass disk from a fragment of a vessel and published, together with other Christian objects, by the often-mentioned canon Boldetti in his observations on the cemetery of the Holy Martyrs, p. 201, no. 17.

In that image the name and figure of Callistus, wearing the pontifical vestment customary among the apostles, seem to portray the same pontiff from whom the name of this sacred cemetery was taken. His burial, together with that of Anterus and many other pontiffs of the holy Roman see, made the cemetery venerable.

### Line 4

Because of this, he was crowned with martyrdom by the prefect Maximus.

Sulpicius Severus made only a very brief note concerning the persecution of Maximinus, which occurred between the fifth persecution under Severus and the seventh, the savage persecution under Decius. As Pagius observes in the notes cited here, Severus writes that during the thirty-eight years separating the two persecutions the peace of the Church was indeed disturbed by Maximinus, but only in certain churches, where he harassed the clergy.

Eusebius described this same persecution more explicitly. It raged especially against sacred ministers, but was not confined to so small a number of churches or so short a period, although it was not universal. Accordingly, ecclesiastical historians rightly call it the sixth persecution. Eusebius confirms that it lasted three years through several testimonies of Origen, writing in book VI, chapter 28:

> “Meanwhile, after the emperor Alexander, who had ruled for thirteen years, had been killed, Maximinus succeeded him. Inflamed by a bitter hatred against Alexander’s household, in which many were Christians, he initiated a persecution and ordered that only the bishops of the churches, as the authors of evangelical preaching, should be killed. At that time Origen composed a book on martyrdom, which he dedicated to Ambrose and Protoctetus, a presbyter of the Church of Caesarea, because both had undergone no small danger in that persecution.”

Everyone can understand that the persecution raised by Maximinus was no slight one. While the emperor himself was operating in Italy and Germany, it harassed not only the Roman Church and the western churches nearest to it, but also the eastern churches in Palestine.

How much the bloody nature of this savage man delighted in slaughter is sufficiently shown by Capitolinus in his *Life*, where he writes of him:

> “He was so cruel that some called him a Cyclops, others a Busiris, others a Scirron, some a Phalaris, and many a Typhon or Gyges, etc. For he was convinced that the empire could not be retained except by cruelty.”

It is therefore not surprising that Maximus, prefect of the City, obeying the disposition of such a prince, killed Pope Anterus within the second month of his episcopate, which was the fourth year of Maximinus’s reign.

### Line 5

He held one ordination during the month of December, ordaining one bishop.

I have already observed in the chronological notes that this also confirms that Anterus’s pontificate was extremely brief, extending only through the month of December, during which he consecrated one bishop.

For if he had sat for eleven years—as the copyists’ error in certain copies of the catalogues and of this pontifical book wrongly added to his monthly rule—he would certainly have had to ordain several bishops in order to restore the episcopal sees left widowed and desolate by Maximinus. As we have heard from Eusebius, Maximinus made the bishops of the churches the principal target of his persecution.

His immediate predecessor Pontianus consecrated six bishops within five years; his successor Fabianus consecrated eleven within fourteen years; and Cornelius is read to have ordained seven within two years. Pontianus held two ordinations within five years, creating six priests; Fabianus ordained twenty-two priests within fourteen years; Cornelius ordained four priests in two ordinations within two years.

Would Anterus alone, during eleven years and with only one ordination, have supplied no priests or deacons at all to replace the many priests and Levites whom direct persecution was removing? Was he so concerned with collecting the Acts of the Martyrs but negligent about restoring the number of ministers?

Who does not see that Anterus was not lacking in providence, since his diligence produced the sacred martyrial records? But the extremely short period of about forty days, as Eusebius and the most ancient catalogues confirm, offered neither the time nor the necessity for several ordinations.

### Line 6

He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.

It is inferred from the *Life* of Pope Paul I that his sacred body was later removed, together with those of many others buried in that part of the cemetery which Paul noticed to be near collapse. The *Life* says:

> “Therefore, seeing that many places in those same holy cemeteries had been neglected through the extreme decay and carelessness of antiquity and had already been brought near to ruin, he immediately removed the bodies of those saints from the ruined cemeteries themselves. Bringing them into this Roman city with hymns and spiritual songs, he took care that some should be reverently deposited in titular churches, deaconries, or monasteries, and in the other churches.”

The Librarian also relates that in the monastery of Saints Stephen the martyr and pope and Sylvester likewise pope and confessor, and in the church of that monastery—which is now called the titular church of Saint Sylvester in Capite—Paul deposited numerous bodies and relics of saints removed from the cemeteries mentioned.

The church had been begun from its foundations by Stephen III, of that name, the brother of Paul I, in his own house, and completed by Paul. We read of the principal of these relics both in the ancient marble and in the *Hortologium*, which contains the names and feast days of those saints, and in the archives of the monastery and church, which record their subsequent recognitions and reburials in public acts drawn up for the repair of the altars, especially on 30 October 1267 and 13 May 1601. These will be cited in their proper place in the *Life of Paul I*, under the number mentioned above.

At the head of the marble tablet that records the names and feast days of the saints whose principal bodily remains, or most of their bones, are buried there stands Blessed Anterus. Since his feast falls on 3 January, it precedes the feast days of the others in the arrangement of the calendar.

It is recorded as follows:

> In the name of the Lord.  
> This is the register of the feast days  
> of the saints resting here.  
>   
> In the month of January,  
> on the third day, the feast of Saint Anterus the pope, etc.

I have no doubt that, when distributing the sacred relics among the titular churches, deaconries, and monasteries of the City, Saint Paul divided parts of one body among several churches, following the example of Sylvester, who distributed the relics of the holy apostles Peter and Paul among several basilicas.

Thus it happened that other sacred buildings, in their ancient documents, enumerate remaining portions of those saints, even though a large part of them rested here, as that ancient tablet testifies.

I also conclude that the same bodies were first brought to the ancient titular church of Saint Sixtus at the Piscina, since it was closer than the others to the Appian Gate and to the cemeteries of Sixtus, Zephyrinus, and the adjoining cemeteries that threatened to collapse. They were later deposited, at least for the greater part, in the monastery and titular church of Saints Stephen the pope and martyr and Sylvester the pope, constructed by Paul himself, as soon as he had completed that church building.

Ancient marbles at both places mention notable relics of the same saints. On the ancient stone of the titular church of Saint Sixtus at the Piscina, published by Martinelli in *Sacred Rome*, p. 306, and by Carlo Abbot Piazza in *Cardinal Hierarchy*, p. 454, the martyr-popes Zephyrinus, Anterus, and Lucius are listed, together with the other martyrs Calocerus and Parthenius. They are also enumerated on the marble mentioned above belonging to the titular church of Saint Sylvester in Capite.

We must therefore admit that portions of the relics of several saints buried in these titular churches, including specifically Blessed Anterus, were divided among several other titular churches and churches of the City. For a portion of the sacred relics of Pope Anterus is held by the titular church of Saint Praxedes, as is abundantly established by the ancient catalogues carved in marble near the chapel of Saint Zeno.

### Note: [Col. 1336D]

#### Line 1

A Greek by nationality.

Saint Anterus was Greek by nationality, a native of Petilia, a city formerly in Magna Graecia and now in what is called Calabria, situated near Bellicastrum.

[Col. 1331]

## 19. Anterus

[Note: Blessed Anterus should be placed after Pontianus.]

A Greek by nationality, son of Romulus, he sat for twelve years, one month, and twelve days [Note: B: scarcely one month]. He was crowned with martyrdom. He lived during the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus [Note: B: Severus and Quinctianus, and of the emperors Maximinus Augustus and Africanus].

He diligently sought out the Acts of the Martyrs from the notaries and deposited them in the church. Because of this he was crowned with martyrdom by the prefect Maximus.

He held one ordination during the month of December, ordaining one bishop [Note: CB: in the city of Fundi in Campania]. He was also buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, on 3 January, and the episcopate was vacant for thirteen days.

## CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS

Anterus: one month, ten days. He sleeps on 3 January, during the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus.

# XX. SAINT PONTIANUS, IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 233, THE TENTH YEAR OF THE EMPEROR ALEXANDER

### Note: [Col. 1337A]

From Fabrottus, based on the Freher codex.

No. 20, line 3, AB: “Pelignianus.” Line 5: “Afflicted and battered with clubs, he died on 29 October, and in his place [Anterus] was ordained.”

From the Regius, Mazarine, and Thuanean codices.

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

The second Anastasian codex of the library of Saint Mark in Florence, which I examined, correctly places Pontianus before Anterus. The context of the Librarian’s statements in this number concerning Pontianus itself proves that he must be placed first. In line 6 it states that after Pontianus died on 29 October, Anterus was ordained in his place on 30 November.

Pontianus followed Urban, as is shown by the first elements of his name in the paintings of Saint Paul, where the letters *PON* have not yet been erased by time. The Liberian Catalogue proves the same thing both from the continuing succession of pontiffs and from the consuls assigned to the beginning of his period, namely Pompeianus and Felicianus, although the copyist’s ignorance corrupted the second name into Pelignianus.

In the text of Anastasius both consuls are correctly read, under whom Pontianus first celebrated Easter in his pontificate. Since he suffered martyrdom in the year 235, during the consulship of Severus and Quinctianus, on 29 October, according to Anastasius, on the island of Sardinia to which he had been deported, and since the consistent testimony of the codices and catalogues—especially those of Italy cited above in the *Prolegomena*—states that he sat for five years, two months, and the same number of days, it follows that his ordination took place in the year 230, during the consulship of Agricola and Clementinus, on 29 August.

That date properly fell on a Sunday, as shown by the dominical letter C assigned to that year according to the solar cycle. Pope Urban the martyr had died in the same year, on 23 May, as we saw above in his section. An interval of three months must therefore be inserted between Urban’s martyrdom and Pontianus’s ordination.

The Librarian counts only thirty days, perhaps to the election. But it is scarcely credible that two months intervened between the election and the ordination, unless he had been elected in his absence.

No further testimony is available concerning the period during which the see was vacant. We have given sufficiently clear and certain evidence concerning Pontianus’s succession and the duration of his see, assigning him five years, two months, and the same number of days, inclusively, from the Sunday of his ordination, 29 August 230, to 30 October 235, during the consulship of Severus and Quinctianus.

Papebrochius believes that the older catalogue indicates Pontianus’s abdication in exile through the words: “On that same island, he was unbelted on 28 September, and Anterus was ordained in his place.” He does not approve the emendation of the catalogue based on the Librarian’s text, which reads clearly:

> On that same island he died on 29 October, and Anterus was ordained in his place on 30 November.

The second catalogue of Felix IV, from the library of the queen of Sweden and compared with the Colbertine manuscript, agrees with this reading in Schelestratius:

> On that same island, afflicted and battered with clubs, he died on 29 October.

Neither the Librarian nor the catalogues say anything substantial about Pontianus having been unbelted or abdicating.

It is therefore preferable to recognize a copyist’s error in the words “he was unbelted on 28 September,” which should have been rendered more faithfully, as in the catalogue of Felix IV and in the text of Anastasius: “he died on 29 October.” We shall discuss Anterus’s ordination in the following number.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

### Line 4

To the island of Bucina in Sardinia.

Bucina, or Buccina, is a small island adjoining Sardinia on the eastern coast opposite the town of Terranova, formerly called the city of Phannasia, according to Baudrand. The inhabitants call it Isola del Tavolato. It extends for about five miles in length and is two miles wide. Some, says the same Baudrand in his geographical lexicon, identify it with the island called Hermaea by Ptolemy.

The writer mentioned above made the island famous by recording the exile and death there of Saint Pontianus, pope and martyr. It lies on the same parallel as the Pontine Islands, which were likewise made famous by the exile of Domitilla, virgin and martyr, under Domitian, as is clear from Eusebius’s *History*, book III, chapter 14, and by the exile of Pope Silverius under Justinian, according to Liberatus the deacon, who calls Palmaria—one of the Pontine Islands—the island of his deportation.

### Lines 8 and 9

Whom Blessed Fabianus brought by ship with the clergy and buried in the cemetery of Callistus.

Perhaps the writer of Anastasius found here the occasion for corrupting the order between Pontianus and Anterus. For when he read that Fabianus had cared for the body of Pontianus, his predecessor, and had elsewhere wrongly assumed that Anterus had sat for eleven years on the basis of the defective chronology he followed, he may have thought it preferable to make Fabianus succeed Anterus rather than suppose that Anterus had neglected for eleven years to arrange for the relics of Pontianus to be transported from the island of Buccina and deposited among the remains of the holy pontiffs in a Roman cemetery.

But Anterus’s pontificate was extremely brief and did not extend even to two months, as will become clear in the following number. It could not therefore have given him the opportunity to transport from the island adjoining Sardinia to Rome the relics of his recently deceased predecessor, especially during the winter season and while Maximinus’s hatred against Christian bishops was raging.

See the notes on the following number.

### Note: [Col. 1340A]

#### Line 2

He was crowned with martyrdom.

Because of his constant steadfastness in defending the faith, he incurred the intense hatred of the pagan priests. Therefore, having been accused before the emperor Alexander through false denunciations, he was expelled from Rome together with the presbyter Philip and exiled to the island of Sardinia, called Bucinaria. There he obtained the palm of martyrdom.

Ciacconius places Anterus after Pontianus.

S. Pontianus, a Roman by nation, son of Calpurnius, was declared Roman pontiff on 22 June 230. But, as is believed, he was driven into exile by some calumny rather than for the sake of the Christian religion. Together with the presbyter Hippolytus, he was banished by the emperor Alexander to the island of Sardinia, and on 28 September 235 he abdicated the pontificate, after having held it for five years, three months, and seven days. Then, by order of the emperor Maximinus, he was beaten with clubs and completed his martyrdom on 19 November of the same year. His body was later transferred to Rome by Pope Fabian and buried in the cemetery of Callistus. In December he held two ordinations: six presbyters, five deacons, and six bishops for various places. Two decretal letters are attributed to Pontianus; since they are stitched together from passages especially of Gregory the Great and Sixtus, learned men regard them as spurious.

When the emperor Severus died, peace was restored to the Christians, as Sulpicius Severus records. After speaking of Severus’s death, he says: “Then, after an interval of thirty-eight years, there was peace for the Christians, except that in the intervening period Maximinus harassed the clergy of certain churches.” From the year 211, when Severus died, to the year 249, when Decius renewed the seventh persecution, there was an interval of thirty-eight years. Sulpicius speaks so briefly of the persecution raised by the emperor Maximinus because it was not universal but merely local. Firmilianus, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, speaking in a letter to Cyprian about Maximinus’s persecution and the faithful fleeing here and there, says: “There was an opportunity for crossing over, because that persecution had not extended throughout the whole world but had been local.”

In that persecution Pontianus, Roman pontiff, suffered martyrdom, as has already been said. Eusebius should be read, Book VI, chapter 28, where he writes that Maximinus began this persecution, inflamed by intense hatred against the household of the emperor Alexander, in which there were many Christians. He then adds: “At that time Origen composed a book on martyrdom, which he dedicated to Ambrosius and to Prototectus, a presbyter of the Church of Caesarea.” That book of Origen, *Exhortation to Martyrdom*, was published at Basel a few years ago.

[Col. 1337]

## 20

Pontianus, a Roman by nation, son of Calpurnius, held the see for five years, two months, and two days. He was crowned with martyrdom. He lived in the time of Alexander, from the consulship of Pompeianus and Felicianus [Note: [Col. 1337] B, until the consulship of Severus and Quinctianus].

At the same time Pontianus, the bishop, and Hippolytus [Note: [Col. 1337] CB, Philippus], the presbyter, were deported by Alexander into exile in Sardinia, to the island called Bucina, in the consulship of Severus and Quintianus. He died on the third day before the Kalends of November [Note: [Col. 1337] C, the thirteenth day before the Kalends of December; B, 19 November] on that same island, and Anterus was ordained in his place [Note: [Col. 1337] Hence it is clear that Anterus was Pontianus’s successor] on the second day before the Kalends of December. He held two ordinations during the month of December: six presbyters, five deacons, and six bishops for various places. The blessed Fabianus [Note: [Col. 1337] C, Fabianus] brought him back with the clergy by ship and buried him in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way. The episcopate then remained vacant for ten days after his burial [Note: [Col. 1337] C B, thirteen].

### Catalogue under Liberius

Pontianus: five years, two months, and seven days. He lived in the time of Alexander, from the consulship of Pompeianus and Pelignianus. At that time Pontianus the bishop and Hippolytus the presbyter were deported as exiles to the harmful island of Sardinia, in the consulship of Severus and Quintinus. On that island he was stripped of his insignia on the fourth day before the Kalends of October, and Anterus was ordained in his place on the eleventh day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship stated above.
