[Note: [Col. 1341B]

Line 4.—“He divided the regions among the deacons.” Rome, which had been divided into fourteen regions since the time of Clement, had by then been reduced to seven. Notaries, who belonged to the order of lectors, were appointed over each region to record the deeds of the martyrs. Then Fabianus divided deacons among the seven regions of the City, so that they might provide food for the martyrs in custody and teach them what concerned the faith. For it was the duty of the deacons to visit martyrs in prison, distribute provisions to them, and instruct them. Cyprian, [Col. 1343A] Letter 11: “I had indeed believed that the presbyters and deacons who are present there would admonish and instruct us fully concerning the law of the Gospel, as had always been done in the past under our predecessors, so that the deacons, going to the prison, might guide their desires by their counsels and by the precepts of Scripture.” Augustine, in the *Breviculus Collationis*: “The council of nearly seventy bishops held at Carthage against Caecilianus by the Donatists was also read. There they condemned him in his absence because he did not wish to come to them, as one ordained by traditors, and because, when he was a deacon, he was said to have forbidden the bringing of food to martyrs held in custody.”

“And he made seven subdeacons, who would oversee the seven notaries.” So that they might collect the deeds of the martyrs completely, Clement appointed one notary for each of the seven regions of the City, to record the deeds of the martyrs. Fabianus, so that the notaries would not be without witnesses, assigned to them an equal number of subdeacons who would oversee them—that is, observe them—in order that the deeds of the martyrs might be collected completely, that is, with complete fidelity. Hence these subdeacons were called regionarii. Anastasius, in the life of Vigilius: “To oversee means to observe someone.” Gregory, Book VIII, Letter 29: “Let him diligently oversee our brother and fellow bishop Decius.” Quintus Curtius, Book VI: “Thus I oversee the authority which I disdain.” Ambrose, *On the Duties*, Book II, chapter 27: “He was overseeing the agents in affairs.”]

[Note: [Col. 1343B]

Line 4.—“Seven subdeacons.” When the persecution of Domitian was pressing, Clement established seven deacons so that they might preside over the fourteen regions of the City, assigning two to each and entrusting them with special care of the martyrs, especially those confined in prisons. In the seventh and indeed most savage persecution, that of Decius, Fabianus likewise established seven subdeacons who belonged specifically to the Roman Church. Cornelius, Fabianus’s successor, is a witness to this institution and to its continued use in his letter to Fabius, preserved by Eusebius, Book VI, chapter 43, when he lists the Roman clergy and the ministers of that Church: “In it, nevertheless, there were forty-four presbyters, seven deacons, and an equal number of subdeacons; forty-two acolytes; and fifty-two exorcists and lectors together with doorkeepers.”

These, however, seem to have constituted only the Roman clergy in the proper sense, since there were others initiated into the same orders. For although the Church of Carthage consisted of presbyters and deacons, it had outside that body other presbyters who were afterward enrolled, because of their merits, among the presbyters of the Church of Carthage, as we saw above in the case of Numidicus. It is likewise clear from Cyprian himself that Celerinus, also a presbyter of the martyrs, was enrolled within the same order of Carthaginian presbyters because of his repeated glorious confession.

[Col. 1343D] Line 4.—“Who would oversee the seven notaries and collect the deeds of the martyrs completely.” The pontiff’s purpose in choosing the subdeacons is indicated: they had been selected specifically for this duty, so that they might oversee the notaries established by Saint Clement, who recorded the acts of the martyrs, and might collect each deed completely, or with the greatest fidelity.

This precaution was necessary, since from these acts the Church awarded suitable praises not only to confessors bearing the glorious title—which was the provident concern of the bishops—but also to martyrs who had been crowned. At that time there was a particularly pressing need to investigate the true confessors and distinguish them from the rest. For when, on account of the genuine merits of martyrdom or confession, permission was granted to sign petitions of penitents in order to lessen their penalties—a privilege that required a genuine cause of confession, proven endurance, and courage—many invented merits for themselves in order to claim the privilege of signing such petitions.

Saint Cyprian frequently complains about this. By his own example, when he asked martyrs to pray for women who had lapsed, he identifies the true confessors in Letter 21: those who, being in the midst of actual punishment, would grant pardon, as was stated above from Saint Cyprian.

Besides Cyprian’s remarks in the passages cited, there is a celebrated passage in Eusebius concerning the ancient practice of recording the confessions, punishments, and other sufferings of the martyrs, which the notaries collected, and concerning the precedence or assistance established for the subdeacons so that fraud might not intervene. Eusebius commends a letter sent to the churches concerning the martyrdom of Saint Pionius, composed through the careful work of the recorders appointed by the Church. In it he briefly recalls what the notaries generally recorded. Thus he writes in Book IV, chapter 15, page 135:

“Whoever wishes to know each of his confessions, his freedom in speaking before the people and the governors in defense of our faith, his discourses on the instruction of faith, and also his exhortations and invitations to those who had fallen during the persecution; likewise the addresses and consolations which, while he was in prison, he offered to the brethren who visited him; what torments and how many sufferings he endured; the piercings with nails; his marvelous steadfastness in the midst of the fire; and finally the death that followed all those miracles—we refer such persons to the letter composed in fullest detail concerning his martyrdom, which we inserted in its proper order in our work on the ancient martyrs whose passions we collected.”

Through the diligence of these men it came about that the acts of the martyrs reviewed by Eusebius, many of which Lactantius also included in his golden work *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, were preserved down to our own times, as were the registers of depositions, translations, martyrologies, and other similar records. Tertullian’s praise of the churches proves that this had been done from the beginning, as does his statement that they kept such records of their own.

From this institution of Fabianus derives the more genuine origin of those ministers who, by office, were to oversee the notaries recording ecclesiastical acts. Given to the notaries as guardians, they examined the authenticity of the acts so that fraud might not enter even into their transcription.

The use of notaries was also very common in councils and disputations. Thus, in the celebrated conference held at Carthage between Catholics and Donatists, this is listed among the first precautions, Part I, number 10:

“But those who perform the office of recording . . . four ecclesiastical notaries from each side were to stand by in turn. So that their trustworthiness might not waver through any uncertainty, four bishops from each side, selected by the judgment of their own party, were designated beforehand to guard those recorders and notaries with vigilant and careful observation.”

Since they are called ecclesiastical notaries, and that was their proper function, it must also be said that the notaries instituted by Clement had been initiated into some order. In my opinion they were taken from the order of lectors, since Agatho, cited above, asserts in his epilogue that, having been established in the rank of lector, he was entrusted with recording the acts of the Sixth Synod.]

[Note: [Col. 1344D]

Line 2.—“He is crowned with martyrdom.” At the beginning of that most atrocious persecution which the emperor Decius, stirred by anger and envy, initiated.

Line 4.—“He divided the regions among the deacons.” Hence, by virtue of their office, they were called regionary deacons. In the Second Roman Council under Sylvester, chapter 6, they are also required under the name of cardinal deacons.

Line 6.—“The presbyters Moses and Maximus.” Cyprian’s letters to these confessors, and the confessors’ letters to Cyprian, testify that the presbyters and confessors of the Roman Church were miserably afflicted and detained in prison for more than a year. See Cyprian’s Letters 16, 23, 26, and 31.]

[Note: [Col. 1344D]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

In the same consulship in which Anterus’s death is recorded, on 3 January 236—namely, that of Maximinus and Africanus—the beginning of Fabianus is also recorded in the catalogues of Liberius and of Felix IV, as well as in the manuscripts of Anastasius. Fabianus is said to have held the see for fourteen years, one month, and ten days in the Liberian catalogue and in four Colbertine manuscripts (1, 3, 5, and 6); but for thirteen years, one month, and ten days in the Bergomensis, the fourth Colbertine manuscript, and the Leonine paintings of the Basilica of Saint Paul. The catalogues of Cava, Farfa, and Lucca, as well as the second and seventh Colbertine manuscripts, count fourteen years, eleven months, and eleven days. The Lucan catalogue reduces the days to seven.

The names of the consuls from Maximinus and Africanus, in the year of Christ 236, to Decius II and Gratus, in the year of Christ 250, by which Fabianus’s pontificate is measured in the catalogues and manuscripts reviewed, although they seem to require fourteen years, demand no more than the thirteen years indicated by the Leonine paintings, if Fabianus’s ordination to the Roman episcopate is placed on Sunday, 11 December 236, in the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus, and his martyrdom on 20 January 250, in the consulship of Decius II and Gratus. This interval contains exactly thirteen full years, one month, and ten days, correctly marked in the paintings of Saint Paul.

All the more ancient documents of the Roman Church testify that Fabianus’s deposition took place on the same day, 20 January, on which he had suffered martyrdom. The third work from the time of Pope Liberius, published by Bucherius and reprinted by us at the beginning of the *Prolegomena*, presents the depositions of the martyrs according to the sequence of the months. It begins in January with Fabianus’s deposition, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, at the cemetery of Callistus, and Sebastian’s at the Catacombs.

The Liberian catalogue, compared with the Caesarean manuscript in Schelestratius’s edition, reads: “From the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus to that of Decius II and Gratus. He suffered martyrdom on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February.” Although Bucherius’s manuscript, perhaps because its final unit had been worn away, reads the twelfth day before the Kalends of February. The more ancient martyrologies reviewed by Baronius, as well as the one that Florentius calls Jerome’s, assign it to the same day. The ancient sacramentaries, books of passions, and missals likewise agree. Therefore Cardinal Norisius rightly writes near the end of Dissertation III on the Syro-Macedonian eras:

“Decius seized the imperial power in the year of Christ 249, as I have shown from his own rescript (Law II, Book IV of the Code, title 16, concerning actions regarding inheritances, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Aquilinus). In the following year, 250, he was at Rome, where he afflicted Saint Fabianus the pope with martyrdom on 20 January, in the very consulship of Decius II and Gratus, as is read in ancient ecclesiastical monuments. There also he cast Celerinus into prison for the faith of Christ; Saint Cyprian speaks of him in Letter 34 to the Carthaginian clergy.”

## HISTORICAL NOTES

### Line 1.—“Favianus, a Roman by nation, son of Fabius”

Fabianus should be assigned by birth to the lineage of the Fabia gens and, by adoption, received into another distinguished family. This is shown not only by the derivative name Fabianus, from a father named Fabianus, but also by the letter of the Roman clergy sent to Cyprian after Fabianus’s death, in which he is called “a man of most noble memory.” The letter says: “After the death of the man of most noble memory, no bishop had yet been appointed because of the difficulties of the times.”

His nobility of birth may also be inferred from the settled judgment of the clergy, who for specific reasons had judged it appropriate at that time to choose a pontiff from among noble and distinguished men. Eusebius expressly records this, perhaps in order that the respect owed to his lineage might make the bishop less exposed to the attacks of Maximinus’s officials, who persecuted the leaders of the churches above all others.

Yet no one had been thinking of choosing Fabianus as pontiff, as Eusebius relates. He was returning to Rome from the countryside with his household, without considering the episcopate, when a dove suddenly descended from above and settled on his head. The votes of all then turned toward him, and he was placed upon the priestly throne. This does not exclude Fabianus’s noble birth. The common judgment of the brethren had considered that nobility useful to the Church in that election, and heavenly assent confirmed the decision. Heaven caused a noble man who had no such thought to return to Rome with his household, and by the sign of the approaching dove designated him as the best pontiff and, thirteen years later, as a most courageous martyr.

The heavenly sign of this most auspicious event, perceived at the time with the greatest joy and unanimous agreement, pleased later generations as well, so that even today the bishops of the Roman See use the same symbol of the dove flying into the chair.

On an ancient marble discovered within the cemetery of Saints Peter and Marcellinus on the Lavican Way, Bosio found a pontifical chair represented in this fashion, furnished with curtains on either side and bearing the figure of a dove seated upon it and adorned with a halo. Aringhius reproduced it in *Subterranean Rome*, Book IV, chapter 14, and Book VI, chapter 48, recalling Fabianus’s deed there. Consult him and Baronius at the year 238.

### Line 4.—“He divided the regions among the deacons and made seven subdeacons, who would oversee the seven notaries, so that they might collect the deeds of the martyrs completely”

Fabianus pursued with even greater care the acts of the martyrs which Anterus had diligently sought out and through which he had deserved to be associated with those same martyrs, so that they might be secured for the Church.

Following the example of Clement I, Fabianus began with the assignment of the fourteen regions of the City. Clement had divided the regions of Rome, restored to their original integrity after the devastation caused by the two fires of Nero and Vitellius, among seven notaries. This division was preserved under the Antonines and required no new partition. But after another fire under Commodus, in which the Temple of Peace and many of the City’s largest and most beautiful buildings burned, as Herodianus relates, with Dio also bearing witness at the end of Book LXXIII, the regions were repaired again and the entire ground plan of the City was not only restored but publicly engraved on marble pavement in the Temple of the City along the Sacred Way.

The Temple of the City has now been converted into the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian; there the plan of the City was discovered in the previous century and published by Cardinal de Maximis with Bellonius’s notes. Bellonius observed that the engraved trace had been made under the emperors Severus and Caracalla. Fabianus nevertheless continued to assign the seven notaries instituted by Clement to fixed regional boundaries, so that they might write down the acts of the martyrs individually.

For the more diligent execution of this task he appointed an equal number of subdeacons to preside over the notaries. To carry out more effectively the Christian ministry in those same regions, he also divided their general administration among the seven deacons. See what was said near the end of the *Prolegomena*, where I treated more fully the division of the City into Augustus’s fourteen regions and their reduction to seven ecclesiastical regions.

### Line 6.—“And after his passion, etc. At that same time Novatus arrived from Africa, etc.”

These matters will be treated below under Cornelius.

### Line 12.—“He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way”

See the description of the City’s cemeteries in the *Prolegomena*. In this sacred cemetery, made illustrious by Fabianus’s deposition and by the association of so many of his predecessors and successors, His Holiness Clement XI magnificently cultivated the memory of that pontiff and martyr. He built a spacious chapel from its foundations, decorated it with precious marbles, metals, and paintings, and excavated a burial place for the distinguished Albani family beneath the chapel, out of the exceptional devotion of his most pious brother Horatius toward the holy martyrs and the places consecrated by them.

Because Horatius had accumulated there, after the example of the most blessed Germanus, all the other virtues that approached those of that saint, he deserved to be buried there, as he had wished. The heir of both forms of devotion, the eminent and reverend prince Hannibal, Cardinal Albani, chamberlain of the Holy Roman Church, completed the chapel’s decoration with new additions of metalwork. Clement XI ordered the following inscription of his offering to be engraved:

> IN HONOREM S. FABIANI PAPAE ET MART. CVIVS SACRVM CAPVT CVM ALIIS RELIQVIIS IN ALTARI ASSERVATVR CLEMENS XI. PONT. MAX. SACELLVM EXTRVXIT ANNO SALVT. MDCCXII. PONT. XII.
>
> In honour of Saint Fabianus, pope and martyr, whose sacred head, together with other relics, is preserved in the altar, Clement XI, Supreme Pontiff, built this chapel in the year of salvation 1712, the twelfth year of his pontificate.

Since this inscription states that the sacred head of Blessed Fabianus, together with other relics, is preserved in the altar recently constructed, and since the same pontiff did not separate those relics from the head when he found them during the demolition of the old structure, the subject requires us to discuss the translation of the sacred body of blessed Fabianus. This will also illuminate the history of the relics of the other pontiffs who once rested in the cemetery of Callistus and in the parts of the cemeteries or adjoining crypts of Sixtus and Praetextatus, and who were later transferred and divided among several Roman titular churches and deaconries for serious reasons. At times a portion of the holy remains was granted or restored to the same cemeteries, as happened with the head of Saint Fabianus.

When the danger of disaster from the Saracens and of the sacrilegious seizure and plundering of sacred buildings outside the City’s boundaries became imminent—a disaster suffered by the two principal basilicas of Saint Peter in the Vatican and Saint Paul on the Ostian Way under Sergius II, as we shall read below in Anastasius, number 495, in the life of Leo IV, the immediate successor of this same Sergius, whose enlargement of the pomerium and inclusion of the Vatican basilica within the City gave rise to and gave its name to the Leonine City and provided future security for the sacred relics—Sergius II, as the Librarian recounts in his Life, number 491, transferred many bodies of holy pontiffs and martyrs, as well as of others crowned with them, from several cemeteries to the titular church of Equitius, or Saints Sylvester and Martin, over which he himself had presided as presbyter:

> “For the honour of almighty God, he dedicated and placed beneath the sacred altar the body of the most blessed bishop Sylvester, together with the most blessed Fabianus, Stephen, and Soter, martyrs and pontiffs, and likewise the martyr Asterius with his most holy daughter, and Saint Cyriacus, Maurus, Largus, and Smaragdus, together with the pontiffs Anastasius and Innocentius, Saint Quirinus, and Bishop Leo, etc.”

These same names of the saints and their relics are listed on an ancient marble tablet placed, many centuries ago, on the descent to the underground chamber of the same titular church. The barbarity of its lettering reveals its age; I shall reproduce it here in clearer letters:

> + TEMPORIBVS DOMNI SERGII IVNIORIS PP. RECONDITA SVNT IN HOC SAC. ALTARE BEATI SILVESTRI PRAESVLIS CORPVS ET BEATI MARTINI ET BEATISSIMO FABIANO ATQVE STEPHANO ET SOTERE MARTIRIBVS HAC PONTIFICIBVS INSIMVLQVE ASTERIO CVM SANCTISSIMA FILIA EIVS SCTOQVE CIRIACO PAPIA ET MAVRO LARGO ET SMARAGDO TRASONE SISINNIO ATQVE ANASTASIO ET INNOCENTIO PONTIFICIBVS: VNA CVM SCTO QVIRINO AC LEONE EPISCOPIS etc.
>
> In the time of our lord Sergius the younger, pope, there were placed in this sacred altar the body of blessed Sylvester the bishop and of blessed Martin, and of the most blessed Fabianus, Stephen, and Soter, martyrs and pontiffs, together with Asterius and his most holy daughter, and Saint Cyriacus, Papia, and Maurus, Largus, and Smaragdus, Trasus, Sisinnius, and the pontiffs Anastasius and Innocentius, together with Saint Quirinus and Bishop Leo, etc.

It is clear that the bodies of the saints listed here had originally been deposited in different cemeteries. Sylvester was in the cemetery of Priscilla; Fabianus, Stephen, and Soter in that of Callistus; Anastasius and Innocentius were buried at the Ursus Pileatus, as the Librarian asserts in their Lives and as their martyrologies state on their feast days.

On the aforementioned stone of Saint Martin in the Mountains, the cemetery of Priscilla is explicitly named. The body of Blessed Sylvester had been removed from there, thereby adding distinction to the titular church of Equitius, which had been built during his pontificate.

It follows from these documents—the Lives of Anastasius and the stones placed in the titular churches—that several saints’ bodies and relics were transferred by Pope Symmachus. He had built a sacred building so close to the titular church of Equitius that the two merged into a single church and title, and he dedicated it to God under the invocation of Saints Sylvester and Martin (Anastasius, number 80). His successors Hadrian and Sergius II restored the same title.

Other bodies had already been transferred from the cemeteries by Paul I to the title of Saints Sylvester and Dionysius and of Stephen. Portions of still other bodies had been taken by various pontiffs to other titles and were transferred by Sergius II to his former title of Equitius. Conversely, portions of the bodies entombed in the title of Equitius—namely, Saint Sylvester, Saint Fabianus, and Saints Cyriacus, Largus, and Smaragdus, among others—were given, as if by right of compensation, both to the title of Saints Sylvester, Dionysius, and Stephen and to other titles, whose custodians in turn handed over portions of their own relics.

As a result, ancient marble records are also found in the Vatican basilica and in the title of Saint Sixtus at the public pool. They bear the names of the same pontiffs, martyrs, and confessors whose remains were divided among those basilicas and titular churches.

An ancient stone in Saint Sixtus, published by Martinellus in *Sacred Rome*, page 306, mentions Saint Sixtus the pope, Felix the pope, Zephyrinus the pope, Anterus the pope, Lucius the pope, and Soter the pope. A stone discovered in the Vatican basilica near the altar adjacent to the tomb of the emperor Otto II, published by Turrigius in *The Vatican Crypts*, page 18, where it can still be seen, mentions among the pontiffs Lucius, Caius, Zephyrinus, Dionysius, Stephen, and Sylvester as having a portion of their relics there.

An ancient epigram of Saint Damasus, placed in the vestibule of the cemetery of Praetextatus and published by Baronius in volume XII of the *Appendix*, and by Aringhius in volume II of *Subterranean Rome*, page 478, shows that Sixtus II and his companions in martyrdom were buried there together with other pontiffs, among whom Fabianus stands out. The present number is chiefly concerned with him, and he is therefore mentioned in another inscription of Sergius II, quoted by Baronius under the year of Christ 847:

> Nectitur ecce piis Fabiano et compare Xysto,  
> Martyribus, quorum spiritus astra tenet.
>
> Behold, the pious Fabianus is joined with his companion Sixtus,  
> martyrs whose spirits possess the stars.

These documents therefore prove that, in the cemeteries, burial chambers and crypts of these martyrs remained distinguished by the verses of Damasus until the fourth century of Christ.

Later, when Paul I and Sergius II followed the same examples—Blessed Sylvester dividing among several basilicas the sacred bones of the apostles Peter and Paul, and Boniface IV transferring many saints’ bodies from the crypts of the martyrs into the Pantheon, cleansed of superstition and dedicated to God according to Christian rite—they too transferred other saints’ bodies, for serious reasons, to the titular churches and churches of the City.

This was done so that those who visited the crypts to venerate the sacred relics of the martyrs would not be crushed by their collapse, and so that the relics would not fall victim to the injuries of the Saracens, who ravaged the suburban basilicas with sacrilegious plunder. At the same time, care was taken to commend to posterity, by marble inscriptions, records of such translations and divisions. Names were engraved near the altars or represented in mosaic, and images and names of the same saints were added in paint, sometimes with their feast days, so that their annual memory might be celebrated there on the appointed days.

Through this providence of the pontiffs, it came about that in places made illustrious by the burial, translation, or some other event involving those saints, some portion of their remains was left or replaced.

The same occurred with Blessed Fabianus. When his body was transferred to the title of Equitius by Sergius II, a portion, together with the head, was retained or returned to the cemetery of Callistus, which he had formerly shared with Sixtus, Anterus, Stephen, and others. Another portion was granted to the title of Saints Sylvester, Stephen, and Dionysius. Finally, a portion was given to the title of Saint Praxedes, as is testified by an ancient marble tablet within the chapel of Saint Zeno, covered with mosaic work by Pope Paschal I. The appropriate place for citing that tablet will be in the notes to his Life. Baronius mentions it in the *Annals* under year 8; Severanus, *The Seven Churches of Rome*, page 682; Octavius Pancirolius, *The Churches in the Region of the Mountains*, chapter 41; and others who have written about the sacred buildings of Rome.]

[Note: [Col. 1349A]

Line 1.—“Favianus, a Roman by nation.” He was created on 17 January. When all the brethren had assembled in the church for the purpose of choosing a pontiff, and many were considering various illustrious and distinguished men suitable for that office, suddenly a dove flew down from above and settled on Fabianus’s head. Moved by this heavenly sign, the clergy acclaimed him worthy of the pontificate with great enthusiasm and unanimous accord, and without delay seized him and placed him on the pontifical throne. Eusebius bears witness to this in Book IX, chapter 22 of his *History*.]

[Note: [Col. 1349B]

Line 4.—“Who would oversee the seven notaries.” When Saint Clement had formerly appointed seven notaries so that they might rapidly record in abbreviated signs the deeds and sayings of the martyrs, Fabianus, says Baronius, considered that this method of writing was extremely obscure. He therefore placed over the seven notaries an equal number of subdeacons, who would ensure that what had previously been recorded in abbreviated signs was written out completely in letters. Anastasius says that for this reason Fabianus made seven subdeacons who would oversee the seven notaries, so that they might collect the deeds of the martyrs in their entirety.

For many centuries it continued to be the case that only seven deacons served in the Roman Church. Fabianus added to their office the duty of presiding over the fourteen regions of the City, assigning two regions to each, so that they might care for the poor living in them. Hence the name derived from their office, and these deacons were called regionarii.

Fabianus labored to spread the Christian religion and to make the religion he had spread illustrious through buildings. Thus Anastasius also says that Fabianus ordered many buildings to be constructed in the cemeteries. For the tombs of the holy martyrs lay hidden beneath the earth in underground sand-quarries, where the faithful held synaxes, and which thereafter the faithful frequented for the sake of prayer.

He deprived Privatus the heretic of ecclesiastical communion; Privatus had been condemned by an African council of ninety bishops. Finally, the emperor Decius, hostile to the priests of God, put Saint Fabianus to death on 20 January 250, after he had held the see for fourteen years and ten days. Fabianus had carried out five ordinations, appointing twenty-two presbyters and eight deacons, and had also created eleven bishops for various places. He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.]

Eusebius writes in Book VI, chapter 34 of his *History*, and in his *Chronicle*, that the emperor Philip was a Christian together with his son Philip. The Acts of Saint Pontius the Martyr state that Pope Fabian baptized both emperors; Baronius accepted this, as did many distinguished writers after him, among them Petrus Daniel Huetius, bishop of Avranches, in Book I, chapter 3 of his *Origenianorum*. They add to Eusebius and to the author of the Acts of Saint Pontius Paul Orosius, Book VII, chapter 13; Vincent of Lérins, Book *Against the Heresies*, chapter 23; and, before them, Saint Jerome in *On Illustrious Men*, when speaking of Origen.

But the opinion of Baronius’s Annotator, who maintains the opposite, seems more credible. For it is clear from Lactantius—Eusebius’s contemporary and tutor of Crispus, Constantine the Great’s son—in the preface to Book I, chapter 1 of *The Divine Institutes*, that Constantine was the first of the emperors to give his name to Christ:

> “We now begin this work under the auspices of your name, most excellent Emperor Constantine, who, first among the Roman rulers, rejecting their errors, both recognized and honored the majesty of God, who is singular and true.”

The anonymous author of the *Life of Saint Pachomius the Abbot*, who also lived in the fourth century, writes similarly. In its first chapter he says:

> “When the persecution had come to an end, Constantine the Great reigned, the first Christian of the Roman emperors,”

and so forth. Ambrose, in his funeral oration for Theodosius the Great, and Sulpicius Severus, who published two books of his *Sacred History* in the year 400, use almost the same words. So too does Theodoret in Book V, chapter 39, where he rejects the conversion of both Philips in these words:

> “Before the reign of Constantine the Great, all the Roman emperors who existed never ceased to rage against the worshipers of piety.”

Moreover, the silence of pagan authors concerning a new religion adopted by those emperors, together with the agreement of many others—both Christians besides those already mentioned and pagans—who celebrate Constantine as the first among the emperors to profess Christ, rightly and deservedly proves that both Philips were alien to the Christian party. Certainly, if they had professed the faith, it is unlikely that pagan writers would have kept silent about it.

Huetius responds that Philip was initiated into the sacred rites of Christ by Pope Fabian, but secretly, and that he concealed this from the pagans so that his affairs would suffer no harm, since the report that he had abandoned the ancestral religion might perhaps have disturbed them. But this response directly contradicts Eusebius, who writes in his *History* that Philip was publicly admitted into the Church by Babylas, bishop of Antioch, and was made a participant in the prayers after confessing his crimes and being placed among the penitents.

Nor can Huetius say that Eusebius reported this as something heard from an uncertain source because he says, “It is reported.” For if this was what rumor carried, the opposite of Huetius’s opinion is thereby proved: namely, that Philip was not secretly a Christian, but that his conversion was known to everyone.

Furthermore, Baronius and Huetius do not agree about the time when Philip embraced the doctrine of Christ. Baronius says that it happened when Philip celebrated the Secular Games, that is, in the year 247; Huetius, however, places it at the very beginning of his reign, and therefore in the year 244, when Philip was at Antioch. Neither position can be maintained. Not the first, since—as will shortly be shown—Philip celebrated the Secular Games in the manner of pagan emperors. Nor the second, since Huetius himself would then be forced to admit that Philip later returned once again to his vomit, ascending the Capitol and sacrificing victims—both of which he did in the year 247 at the Secular Games. It follows that Philip did not give his name to Christ either at the beginning of his reign or before he celebrated the Secular Games.

Baronius and Huetius appear to have been drawn toward Eusebius’s opinion by the Acts of Saint Pontius the Martyr, later published by Stefano Baluzius from three manuscripts of the Colbert Library in Book II of his *Miscellanies*. But Baronius’s annotator proves that these Acts were written long after Saint Pontius’s martyrdom and were falsely attributed to a contemporary writer. Baronius himself therefore admits that several things contained in them are absent from Mombritius and says that he thinks they were added by someone.

Yet the editions of Baluzius and Bollandus demonstrate that these matters are not only fabulous but also belong to the author of the Acts themselves, rather than to some interpolator. Bollandus likewise published them for 14 May, arranging them according to the authority of the manuscripts. Nothing, therefore, can be extracted from these Acts in support of the present argument.

As for Eusebius, either someone interpolated his *History*, just as Jerome interpolated his *Chronicle*, or else he was deceived by false reports. For in his *Chronicle* he assumes that, at Philip’s celebration of the Secular Games, many things redolent of paganism were performed; this plainly conflicts with the account in Book VI of his *History*.

As for Vincent of Lérins, Cassiodorus, and others who were persuaded that Philip was a Christian, they were led into error by Paul Orosius; and Orosius himself was deceived, as I shall immediately show.

His words in the passage cited are these:

> “In magnificent games, this most august year of all past years—the birthday, that is, of the city of Rome—was celebrated by a Christian emperor. Nor is there any doubt that Philip carried back to Christ and to the Church the grace and honor of so great a devotion, since no author shows that he ascended the Capitol or that victims were sacrificed according to custom.”

For these were the indications of pagan superstition. Thus, because Orosius believed that Philip had omitted from his Secular Games those spectacles that were forbidden to Christians, he persuaded himself and others that Philip was a Christian.

But Orosius is mistaken. Victor, in *On the Caesars*, chapter 28, clearly teaches that victims were sacrificed at Philip’s Secular Games:

> “When victims were being slaughtered according to the law of the pontiffs, in a sow’s womb there appeared the genitals of males and females. The haruspices interpreted this as foretelling the destruction of posterity and that vices would prevail. Emperor Philip, thinking that this would be frustrated, and also because, as he happened to be passing by, he had seen a youth resembling his son, most honorably arranged for the use of a male prostitute to be abolished.”

From this it is evident that at Philip’s Secular Games an extremely impure animal, a sow, was slaughtered, following the example of the emperor Severus, who sacrificed a sow at his own Secular Games, as is clear from his coins.

Eusebius writes similarly in his *Chronicle*, where he says:

> “While the Philips were reigning, the thousandth year of the city of Rome was completed. On account of this solemnity innumerable beasts were killed in the Great Circus, and theatrical Games were celebrated in the Campus Martius for three days and nights, while the people kept vigil.”

These words also imply that Philip ascended the Capitol. For, as Zosimus relates in Book II, after ascending the Capitol and sacrificing the customary victims there, he proceeded to the theater constructed from that point, where Games dedicated to Apollo and Diana were held, as Blondel demonstrates in his book against the primacy of the Church.

Finally, that all the spectacles forbidden to Christians were presented at the Games conducted by Philip is also indicated by Capitolinus in chapter 33 of his *Life of Gordian the Younger*:

> “Under Gordian, there were thirty-two elephants at Rome, twelve of which he himself had sent and Alexander ten; ten elks; ten tigers, and so forth. Philip either contributed or killed all these animals at the Secular Games.”

We know this not only from Christian and pagan writers but also from the coins themselves: Philip changed nothing in the celebration of the Secular Games but preserved everything that had been done on earlier occasions.

Angeloni, on page 308, displays a coin of his on whose reverse is written *SAECULUM NOVUM* (“A New Age”), and a four-column temple with an altar is represented, around which five figures are sacrificing. Spanheim, folio 853, produces another on which *SAECULUM NOVUM* is likewise written, with seven sacrificing figures represented.

Finally, Mediobarbus, in his *Coins of the Emperors*, quotes an inscription on a coin of the elder Philip, which reads:

> *P. M. TR. P. IIII. COSS. P. P.*

That is, “Chief Pontiff, holder of tribunician power for the fourth time, consul, father of the fatherland.” A sacrificing figure at an altar is also shown on it. Philip the elder already held tribunician power for the fourth time in March of the year 247, when the Secular Games were celebrated.

Many other coins remain on which certain traces of the pagan superstition professed by both Philips are visible. I omit them here for the sake of brevity, since from these coins and the authors cited it clearly appears that those emperors were pagans and, consequently, that both Orosius and the others who write the opposite were deceived.

Nor does what Eusebius himself reports in Book VI, chapter 36, oppose our opinion. There, mentioning books composed by Origen, he says:

> “There exists his letter to the emperor Philip and another to his wife Severa.”

From these words Baronius and Huetius infer that Eusebius could easily have understood whether the emperor Philip was truly a Christian. But Eusebius does not assert that he had read those letters. And even if Philip and his wife truly received them, it does not follow any more that they were Christians than that the emperor Antoninus believed the Gospel because Justin the Martyr wrote to him.

Finally, no greater confidence should be placed in Eusebius when he makes the emperor Philip a Christian than in the same Eusebius when, in Book I, chapter 13 of his *History*, he asserts that Abgar, king of Edessa, after hearing of Christ’s miracles, sent letters to Christ and that Christ wrote a letter in reply, promising to send one of his apostles to him. Eusebius says that the apostle Thomas sent Thaddeus, one of the Seventy disciples, to fulfill the Savior’s promise.

For the penitence of the emperor Philip narrated by Eusebius is no less spurious than the two letters—that of Abgar to Jesus and that of Jesus to Abgar—which Pope Gelasius, in his decree concerning apocryphal books, lists among the apocryphal writings.

Nor should greater confidence be placed in Jerome when he speaks of Philip’s conversion than when, in *On Illustrious Men*, he writes concerning Seneca:

> “I would not place him in the catalogue of the saints unless those letters moved me which are read by very many people: the letters of Paul to Seneca and of Seneca to Paul.”

The annotator of Baronius says:

> “The earlier Christians, wholly devoted to advancing our faith and endowed with the greatest candor of mind, often showed themselves too ready to accept whatever favored religion, as countless examples demonstrate.”

I am not unaware that it may be answered that Philip became a Christian after displaying the Secular Games. But this conflicts with the Eusebius cited above, who assumes in his *History* that Philip did penance at Antioch at the very beginning of his reign, while Huetius observes that Philip never afterward went there. It also conflicts with the Acts of Saint Pontius, which say that Philip was converted when he was about to proceed to sacrifice to his gods in celebration of the thousandth year of the City; and finally with Paul Orosius, whose words we have just quoted.

Since this opinion therefore rests on the testimony of no author, it would appear even more absurd than the two preceding opinions. I therefore have no doubt that the baptism of both Philips by Pope Fabian—or by anyone else—is pure fiction.

After the emperor Decius had killed both Philips and been confirmed in the empire, he initiated a very severe persecution toward the end of the year 249. In it Saint Fabian, the Roman pontiff, suffered martyrdom; Saint Agatha also suffered in Sicily.

The Church mourned the lapsing of many of the faithful during that persecution, as is clear from Saint Cyprian in various letters and in his book *On the Lapsed*, which he composed after Decius’s death.

Saint Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria, mentions this persecution in a letter to Fabian, bishop of Antioch, preserved by Eusebius in Book VI, chapter 41. It must nevertheless be observed that the martyrs of whom Dionysius speaks in that letter did not suffer under Decius but under the emperor Philip, specifically in the year 248, when a persecution arose at Alexandria from a popular uprising, such uprisings being frequent in that city.

Serapion, the virgin Apollonia, and the others mentioned in that letter were therefore put to death not under Decius but under Philip, although their martyrdom is recorded under Decius in the martyrologies. This happened because the ancients regarded the persecution raised under Philip and Decius as a single persecution.

In this persecution of Decius, Origen lapsed. This is proved against Baronius and Valesius by Petavius in his *Remarks on Epiphanius* and elsewhere, and by Huetius in Book I of his *Origenianorum*, cited by Pagius in his criticism of Baronius under the year 251.

> “Whether the observations made here by both Pagis against those who, with Eusebius, accept the baptism of both Philips should be preferred to the contrary opinion is left to the judgment of others. They are brought forward here only to show that the Librarian’s silence concerning the conversion of those Augusti to Christ did not occur without the support of serious reasons. For the rest, those who favor their baptism will find the foundations of the opposing opinion in the illustrious Huetius and the other authors cited by Pagius, and in the illustrious Ciampinus, volume I of *Ancient Monuments*, chapter 17, page 145.”

[Note: Column 1352D]

**Line 8.—“From Africa.”** We know that the judgment pronounced in Africa by a council of bishops against the heretic Privatus was confirmed by the authority exercised by this pontiff through his letters:

> “Privatus, an old heretic in the colony of Lambesa, condemned many years ago for numerous and serious offenses by the sentence of ninety bishops, and also most severely censured by the letters of our predecessors Fabian and Donatus—a fact that is not hidden from your conscience.”

So writes Saint Cyprian in Letter 59, Oxford edition.

It is also certain that Origen wrote to him so that he might submit a specimen of his own doctrine and faith to his judgment. Some writers further report that this pontiff, not satisfied with that declaration, wanted Origen to come to the City and clear himself orally before the tribunal of the Holy See of the crimes charged against him.

This must have happened when Origen made his second journey to the City because of Plotinus, who at that time was directing a philosophical school in Rome.

> “Moreover, he writes to Bishop Fabian and to many other heads of Churches concerning his correct and orthodox opinion of the Christian faith.”

Eusebius, *History*, Book VI, chapter 29. See Baronius under the year 248, no. 2; Porphyry, *Life of Plotinus*; Valesius’s notes on Eusebius from the Alexandrian Chronicle; the authority of Saint Chrysostom; Pagius’s criticism in the *Annals of Baronius* under the year 249, no. 6; and Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, no. 16.

[Col. 1341]

## 21

Favianus, a Roman by nationality, son of Favius [Note: [Col. 1341] “Fabius,” CB.], sat fourteen years, ten months, and eleven days [Note: [Col. 1341] B: fifteen years and four days.]. He was crowned with martyrdom. His pontificate extended from the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus to the second consulship of Decius and that of Quadratus [Note: [Col. 1341] B: “Gordian, Philip, and Decius, from the consulships of Maximinus Augustus and Africanus up to Decius and Hetruscus”] [Note: [Col. 1341] C: fourteenth day before the Kalends.]; he suffered on the fourth day before the Kalends of February.

He divided the regions among the deacons and appointed seven subdeacons to supervise the seven notaries, so that they might collect the Acts of the martyrs in full. He also ordered many buildings to be constructed throughout the cemeteries. [Note: [Col. 1341] See Baronius under the same year, 253, p. 421.]

After his passion, the presbyters Moses and Maximus and the deacon Nicostratus were arrested and sent to prison. [Note: [Col. 1341] See Baronius under the year 254.]

At the same time Novatus came from Africa and separated Novatian and certain confessors from the Church, after the presbyter Moses had died in prison, where he had spent eleven months, as had many others. [Note: [Col. 1341] C adds: “and thus many Christians fled.”]

He carried out five ordinations during the month of December: twenty-two presbyters, seven deacons, and eleven bishops in various places.

He was also buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February. The episcopate was vacant for seven days. [Note: [Col. 1341] C: six days. B: “a year and more.”]

## CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS

Fabianus: fourteen years, one month, and ten days. He lived during the reigns of Maximinus, Gordian, and Philip, from the consulship of Maximinus and Africanus until the second consulship of Decius and that of Gratus. He suffered on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February.

He divided the regions among the deacons and ordered many buildings to be constructed throughout the cemeteries. After his passion, the presbyters Moses and Maximus and the deacon Nicostratus were arrested and sent to prison. At that time Novatus came from Africa and separated Novatian and certain confessors from the Church, after Moses had died in prison, where he had spent eleven months and eleven days.

Line 1: “He sat two years, two months, and three days” (the number of days is not supplied in the Mazarine manuscript), “under this episcopate.” Line 4: “who had separated”; Mazarine: “who had separated themselves.” Line 6: “he was expelled.” Line 7: “he wrote concerning Celerinus the lector.” Here the Mazarine manuscript has “concerning Celeimus.” Line 11: “to the shore,” as appears in the writing; someone corrected it in a manuscript. Mazarine: “to the side.” On the same line, B reads: “Peter’s body was received by Blessed Cornelius, bishop, and placed beside the place.” Line 13: “on the Golden Mountain” in the Vatican manuscript. Line 14: “of July”; “at the same time Decius heard that Cornelius had received [a letter] from Blessed Cyprian.” Line 16: “Cornelius, and ordered him to be brought before him.” Line 17: “of the city, in the earth” (M: “in the earth”), “to whom he said: ‘You have decided that you should not consider the gods’” (and in the margin another reading: “that you should not confess the gods”; M: “that you should not confess the gods”; and in the margin another reading: “consider”). Line 18: “or fear threats, and against the Republic.” Line 20: “and not be against the Republic.” Line 22: “to the temple.” Line 23: “and if he did not do it, he should be beheaded. After this, by Decius’s command, [Col. 1355C] he suffered on the third day before the Nones of March, before his passion.”

From another Thuane manuscript.

Line 1: “two years.” Line 4: “the confessors who had been separated from [Col. 1356A] Cornelius.” Line 6: “and there he received the letter sent by Cyprian concerning the confirmation of his martyrdom.” Line 8: “he gave it to the lector-clerk.” Line 10: “First, of Blessed Paul, Blessed Lawrence, and he placed [it].” Line 11: “He received the body of Blessed Peter, Blessed Cornelius, bishop, and placed it.” Line 13: “on the Golden Mountain.” Line 14: “the third day before the Kalends of July; there Decius heard that …” Line 15: “he sent [him] to Centumcellae.” Line 17: “in Tellus II.” Line 18: “so that you should not consider the gods, nor the commands, nor the threats, so that you may act against the Republic.” Line 19: “Cornelius, bishop, said: ‘I have received letters from the crown of the Lord, and not against the Republic, but spiritual counsel.’ Then he ordered his mouth to be beaten with leaded whips.” Line 23: “and if he did not do it, saying, ‘Let him be beheaded.’ This was done; he was also beheaded in the aforementioned place and made a martyr. His body was collected at night by Blessed Lucina with the clergy and buried beside the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, in his own crypt. Therefore, before his passion, he had already entrusted the whole Church to his archdeacon Stephen. He performed the ordinations up to the words ‘seven.’ It continues: ‘the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September,’ and ‘the episcopate was vacant for thirty-five days.’”

In Holstenius and Schelestratius.

Line 1: Florentine manuscripts: “two years, three days,” and thus the Regal manuscript. Line 3–5: “When this had been done, they returned”; the words are taken from the First Catalogue. Line 6: Florentine manuscript: “Centumcellae.” Lines 7–8: Vatican manuscript: “and gave [it] to Celerinus the messenger.” Line 10: Two Florentine manuscripts: “Blessed Lucina received [it] and placed it on her estate on the Ostian Way, beside the place where,” and so forth. The Regal and Vatican manuscripts read likewise. Line 13: All manuscripts: “on the Golden Mountain.” Line 14: Florentine and Regal manuscripts: “the third day before the Kalends of July; afterward he traveled by night to Centumcellae; at the same time,” and so forth. The Vatican manuscript likewise adds this. Line 17: Regal and Florentine manuscripts: “of the Palace, whom he addressed thus, saying: ‘You have decided that you should not consider the gods, nor …’” Line 20: Vatican manuscript: “but rather on account of the redemption of souls.” Line 23: Florentine manuscript: “he should say that he was to be beheaded.” Cassiodorus adds: “Cornelius himself suffered on the third day before the Nones of March. Therefore beforehand,” and so forth. Line 29: Regal and both Florentine manuscripts: “the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October”; the Vatican manuscript reads likewise.

In Penius, from the Cavensis manuscript.

Line 2: “Novatus ordained Novatian outside the Church, and Africanus Nicostratus.” Line 9: “He raised the bodies from the catacombs at night; first, indeed, the body of Blessed Paul. [Col. 1356C] Blessed Lucina, and placed it on her estate on the Ostian Way, beside the place where he was beheaded. Blessed Cornelius, bishop, received the body of Blessed Peter the apostle.” Line 17: “with the prefect of the City, in the interlude, at night before the temple of Pallas; to whom he said thus.”]

[Note: [Col. 1355C]

What is related in the Acts of Cornelius concerning the body of Blessed Peter, which was placed by him beside the place where he was crucified on the Golden Mountain in the Vatican on the third day before the Kalends of July, also indicates the day on which its translation was celebrated by the Roman Church. How it happened that the body of Saint Peter, buried by Anacletus while he was still a presbyter in the Vatican, was again transferred here by Cornelius could have occurred for two reasons.

Either what Gregory the Great relates is true, in Book IV of the *Register of Letters*, Letter 30, to the Empress Constantina: namely, that Easterners carried the bodies away and, while the Romans were pursuing them, placed them at the second milestone from the City in the catacombs, from which place they were transferred by Cornelius.

Or the faithful, discovered in the Vatican crypts, had fled under Pope Callistus to the catacombs with the bodies of Peter and Paul; and there the Roman pontiffs also began to be buried, beginning with Fabian. Thus, at Lucina’s request, Cornelius transferred them to the Vatican, as Onuphrius proves at greater length in his manuscript history.]

[Note: [Col. 1356C]

**Line 9.—“He raised the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul from the catacombs at night.”** It should read *Catacumbis*. This is the place two miles from the City where the bodies of the martyrs were buried in crypts.

Anastasius also speaks of it in his account of Damasus:

> “He built two basilicas, one beside the Theater, to Saint Lawrence, and another on the Ardeatine Way, where he rests in the Catacombs.”

He says likewise in his account of Hadrian:

> “He also built the church of the apostles outside the Appian Gate, at the third milestone, in the place called the Catacombs, where the body of Blessed Sebastian the Martyr rests with others.”

Gregory says the same in Book III, Letter 5:

> “At the second milestone from the City, in the place called the Catacombs.”

This is the place I mentioned.]

[Note: [Col. 1356C]

**Line 17.—“In Tellus, at night, before the temple of Pallas.”** The pontiff Cornelius, while he was in exile at Centumcellae, was presented by the prefect of the City to Decius at night, in Tellus, before the temple of the martyr. The common reading *in interludo* (“in the interlude”) is incorrect.]

[Note: [Col. 1356C]

**Line 20.—“I received letters from the crown of the Lord.”** When Cornelius was questioned by Decius about letters received against the Republic, he answered that he had received letters from the crown of the Lord. The crown of the Lord is the order of the clergy.

The author of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book II, chapter 28, writes concerning presbyters:

> “As the bishop’s counselors and the crown of the Church, for they are the council and the deliberative body of the Church.”

The Greek reads:

> Ὡς σύμβουλοί τοῦ ἐπισκόπου, καὶ τῆς ἐκκλησίας Στεφανος, ἐισί γαρ συνέδριον, καὶ βουλὴ τῆς ἐκκλησίας.

That is:

> “As counselors of the bishop and the crown of the Church, for they are the council and deliberative body of the Church.”

He imitated Paul (*Philippians* 4):

> “My dearly beloved brothers, my joy and my crown; stand firm in the Lord.”]

[Note: [Col. 1357A]

**Line 21.—“Then Decius, full of anger, ordered the mouth of Blessed Cornelius to be beaten with leaded whips.”** *Plumbatae* were a kind of whip furnished at its head with leaden pellets, with which martyrs were beaten. See the Roman Martyrology, 6 June, and Baronius there.]

[Note: [Col. 1357A]

**Line 28.—“His body Blessed Lucina collected at night with the clergy and buried in a crypt.”** During the time of persecution, the bodies of martyrs were buried at night in crypts.

Jerome writes in Book XII, chapter 40 of his commentary on Ezekiel:

> “When I was a boy in Rome and was being educated in the liberal arts, I used to go around on Sundays with others of the same age and purpose to the tombs of the apostles and martyrs, and frequently enter the crypts, which, dug deep beneath the earth, have along both sides of those entering, in the walls, the bodies of the buried.”

Anastasius reports that Blessed Lawrence was buried in a crypt with many other martyrs, in his account of Sixtus II. Ferreolus and Ferrucius were buried in a crypt at Vesontio. Gregory of Tours writes in *On the Miracles of the Martyrs*, chapter 71:

> “Here, in a hidden part of the crypt, lie buried two martyrs, Ferreolus and Ferrucius, as their passion relates.”

The Greeks likewise buried bodies in *hypogaea*, that is, underground places. Petronius writes in the *Satyricon*:

> “When she had carried out her husband, she was not content, after the common custom, to follow the funeral with her hair unbound or to beat her bared breast in the sight of the crowd; she even accompanied the dead man into the burial chamber and, after the body had been placed in a Greek-style underground vault, began to guard it and weep through whole nights and days.”

Christians fleeing martyrdom also hid in crypts. Anastasius writes in his account of Caius:

> “While fleeing the persecution of Diocletian and living in crypts, he was crowned with martyrdom.”]

[Note: [Col. 1357C]

**Line 6.—“He received from Cyprian a letter sent concerning his confirmation …”** The Novatian schism attempted to attack the election of the pontiff through accusations fabricated against Cornelius. The schismatics sent a letter and envoys from him to the African Church.

Cyprian did not receive them. Instead, in the name of the Church, he chose two men, whom he sent to Rome. These men, together with two other African bishops who had taken part in the election, and having been informed by the Roman clergy concerning the legitimacy of Cornelius’s election, returned to Africa with those electing bishops and explained the truth of the matter in the council of the Africans. They proved that Cornelius was the legitimate successor of Fabian and that Novatian, driven by schismatic fury, was usurping the chair of Peter.

Cyprian, in the name of the bishops, sent a letter, which is Letter 45 in the new edition and Letter 42 in Pamelius’s edition. In it he asserts that Cornelius was recognized, and had previously been recognized, by the Africans as the true pontiff, in these words:

> “What was fitting for the servants of God, and especially for just and peaceable priests, dearest brother, we recently sent our colleagues Caldonian and Fortunatus to accomplish: not merely by the persuasion of letters but by their presence and by the counsel of all of you, to strive and labor as much as they could to restore the members of the divided body to the unity of the Catholic Church and to join them in the bond of Christian charity.
>
> “But since the stubborn and unyielding obstinacy of the opposing party refused not only the roots, the bosom, and the embrace of the mother, but also, as discord grew and became more bitter for the worse, appointed a bishop for itself and, against the sacrament once delivered by the divine disposition and against Catholic unity, established outside the Church an adulterous and hostile head, we sent our letter to you after receiving both his letters and those of our colleagues, and after the arrival of our good and very dear colleagues Pompeius and Stephen. They firmly asserted and proved all these things with common sorrow, according as the holiness and truth alike of divine tradition and ecclesiastical institution required.
>
> “Moreover, after making these same matters known throughout our province to each of our colleagues, we ordered our brothers there also to be sent with letters to you. Although our mind and purpose had already been made clear to the brothers and to the entire people there, when, after receiving letters from both sides, we read your letter and announced to the ears of each person the ordination of your episcopate.”

And so forth.

From this event useful ecclesiastical observations are derived.

First, it follows that Cornelius was elected bishop and immediately consecrated before Novatian assumed the pseudo-episcopate. Although the schismatics sent defamatory letters against Cornelius, Cyprian and the bishops of Africa had from that time recognized the legitimacy of Cornelius’s election.

Second, it follows that a Roman council was assembled to dissolve the schism, and that, for its celebration, Caldonian and Fortunatus were chosen as legates in the name of the African Church; they attended the council. Their selection is recorded in the councils that followed. The same number of men from Africa are recorded as having been sent to the Council of Aquileia and to another Roman council under Hilary, from which the conciliar action must be judged.

The very rebuttal shows that a conciliar assembly is expressed in the words:

> “But since the stubborn and unyielding obstinacy of the opposing party …”

These words represent a dispute and a deliberation held in response.

Third, it follows from those words that Novatian was consecrated bishop after the acts of the council:

> “But also, as discord grew and became more bitter for the worse, it appointed a bishop for itself.”

This was the faction of the schismatics. From this and from Cyprian’s subsequent words one may infer the Church’s conviction that it rejected a two-headed authority, as was observed in Peter.

Fourth, the outcome of the Roman council [Col. 1358C] was that all who had been confirmed in the earlier truth concerning the legitimacy of Cornelius’s election publicly pronounced an anathema against the schismatics, and, strengthened by this confirmation, acknowledged him as pontiff. The *Liber Pontificalis* speaks of this subsequent confirmation.

That this confirmation was directed toward removing every doubt through a conciliar act, after weighing the considerations on both sides, Cyprian vividly describes when he adds the reason for the investigation:

> “As for the fact that we desired the letters of our colleagues who were present there at your ordination, we were not forgetting ancient customs or seeking something new. For it would have been enough for you to announce that you had been made a bishop, had there not been an opposing faction whose criminal and factious inventions disturbed the minds and confused the hearts of colleagues and of many brothers alike.
>
> “To put this matter to rest, we judged it necessary that the firm and solid authority of our colleagues who wrote to us from there should be made manifest. They proclaimed, in letters worthy of your conduct, life, and discipline, testimonies concerning you; and they removed every scruple of doubt and disagreement from those who rejoiced in rivalry or in the novelty or perversity of events. In accordance with our counsel and with a wholesome judgment, after weighing the matter, they sincerely and firmly approved your priesthood in the minds of the brothers who were tossed and agitated in this storm.”

When the *Liber Pontificalis* therefore adds that Cornelius received from Cyprian a letter concerning his confirmation, this must be understood in light of Cyprian himself, who sent Cornelius the letter cited by the *Liber Pontificalis* concerning his confirmation and disclosed the reasons for the conciliar investigation: namely, to crush the dissenting faction by a conciliar rebuttal and, through the common agreement of the bishops, to remove every scruple of doubt and disagreement.

Those words—“It would have been enough for you to announce that you had been made a bishop”—prove, according to ancient customs, the longstanding practice adopted by the pontiffs of announcing the pontificate one had assumed. They also prove that this was a prerogative of the Apostolic See and that the customary observances of the bishops followed such an announcement.

**Line 7.—“Which Cyprian wrote in prison.”** Rather, he did not write it while in retreat, since he sent the letter after returning from retreat. Nor could he, while in retreat, have gathered so many of his colleagues to hear the African legates and their fellow bishops, who had both been present at Cornelius’s election in Rome and had attended the Roman council.

Other letters surviving after Letter 45 in the new edition of Cyprian’s works could plainly be added concerning this same subject.

### Lines 7–8.—“And he received [the letter] from Celerinus the lector.”

Celerinus was a presbyter among the martyrs, formerly also a lector, perhaps appointed to record the acts of the martyrs. In conducting these affairs he suffered grievous injuries from the persecutors and was renowned among all for his glorious confession, as Cornelius says in his letter to Fabius, preserved by Eusebius, book VI, chapter 43, page 242:

> “Celerinus, a man who, by God’s mercy, endured with the greatest courage every kind of torture, and who, strengthening the weakness of his body through the steadfastness of his faith, completely defeated the adversary.” [Col. 1359B]

This man, I say, was ensnared by the Novatianist schismatics and joined their party; by his example several confessors likewise wavered in recognizing Cornelius. At length, when the frauds of the schismatics, especially those of Novatian, had been exposed, he acknowledged Cornelius as the legitimate pontiff and stood firmly in Africa as an energetic defender of the truth he had professed.

The pontiff praises him there, together with another man called Sidonius, in these words:

> “When all these men had finally recognized him and had discovered his fraud and cunning, his perjuries and lies, his savagery abhorrent to every form of fellowship, and a certain wolf-like friendship, they returned to the holy Church. In the presence of several bishops, presbyters, and many laymen, they exposed all his tricks and wickedness, which he had long concealed within himself while outwardly submitting for a time; they groaned and grieved that, having been led astray by that fraudulent and malicious beast, they had withdrawn from the Church for some time.” [Col. 1359C]

Celerinus’s return from the schism, therefore, and the zeal he undertook in defending Cornelius’s cause are commended by the *Book of the Pontiffs*, which asserts that Cyprian gave Cornelius a thoroughly reliable letter concerning all these matters. To this should be referred another letter of Cyprian, written to the clergy of Carthage, in which he declares that Celerinus should be elevated to the presbyterate of the Church of Carthage and indicates that his conversion was no obstacle. Letter 32:

> “Now that he is coming to you, most beloved brothers, with so great a manifestation of the Lord’s favor, illustrious through the testimony and miracle of that very man who had persecuted himself [reading uncertain], what else should be done with him than to place him upon the pulpit—that is, upon the tribunal of the Church—so that, elevated by the height of a higher position and conspicuous to the entire people through the distinction of his honor, he may read the Lord’s commandments and Gospel, which he follows courageously and faithfully?”

### Line 14.—“When Decius heard this.”

Under Gallus and Volusianus, Cornelius died a martyr in exile at Centumcellae. Accordingly, what the *Book of the Pontiffs* reports here concerning the martyrdom that followed in the time of Decius seems to be explained as follows: Cornelius was first condemned by Decius to exile, but the holy pontiff later ended his life under the emperors Gallus and Volusianus. [Col. 1359D]

The Decian persecution began with edicts against the clergy, especially the bishops, as can be gathered from these words of Saint Cyprian in Letter 55, where he composed a defense of his own conduct and writes of Cornelius:

> “United with all his colleagues, already approved by his own people during four years in the episcopate, in tranquillity he perceived the discipline; in the storm he was proscribed, with the name of his episcopate attached and added, and was repeatedly demanded before the lion.” [Col. 1360A]

The same Cyprian teaches in Letter 82 that the Decian persecution first harassed the leading members of the clergy. Writing to his successor, he reports that Valerian, in response to a senatorial decree, said that he was renewing the Decian edicts and their principal provisions. Thus the holy bishop relates:

> “Valerian wrote back to the Senate that bishops, presbyters, and deacons were to be immediately punished.”

That is, as soon as they had been identified as holding those orders, they were to be punished with capital penalties according to the edicts promulgated by Decius.

Earlier, Cyprian had described to his successor the storm of persecution that followed against the clergy in these words:

> “The reason why I did not write to you immediately was that all the clergy, placed under the blow of the contest, were prepared, each according to the devotion of his soul, for divine and heavenly glory.”

The persecution consequently became exceedingly savage, when even the places where they had been permitted to perform sacred rites in the cemeteries were taken away from them. This is taught by the account of the exile of Saint Dionysius of Alexandria, where we read that the prefect Aemilianus said:

> “I see that you are ungrateful and foolish, since you do not at all perceive the clemency of the Augusti. Therefore you will not remain in this city, but will be sent into the regions of Libya, to a place called Cephro. I have selected this place by order of our Augusti. You will in no way be permitted, nor will anyone else, to hold assemblies or to enter the places called cemeteries. If anyone is found not to have departed for the place I have ordered, or is discovered in any assembly, he will bring danger upon himself. Appropriate punishment will not be lacking.” [Col. 1360B]

A persecution likewise raged against the Churches from Decius through Valerian—for these alone are counted, even though other emperors ruled between them. Jerome speaks in this way in the *Life of Saint Paul*:

> “Under the persecutors Decius and Valerian, when Cornelius at Rome and Cyprian were condemned to a blessed death, a fierce storm devastated many Churches throughout Egypt and the Thebaid.”

In the ancient Martyrology, on the seventh day before the Kalends of September, we read in the same sense, in Holstenius’s notes on the *Martyrology*:

> “Whom Valentinus ordered to be cast into a sewer during the Decian persecution.” [Col. 1360C]

And in Optatus, book III, page 76:

> “That war is called a persecution which took place under two of those four beasts whom Daniel saw rising from the sea. The first was the Lion. This was the persecution under Decius and Valerian,” and so forth.

Saint Cornelius, therefore, was condemned to exile under Decius and crowned with martyrdom under Gallus and Volusianus. For this reason Saint Cyprian, in Pacianus’s account, writes of Saint Cornelius that he was “often a confessor, often a sufferer.” The celebrated Jerome certainly presupposes that exile was followed by the capital punishment through which he suffered martyrdom, since he says that Cornelius was condemned to a blessed death. Accordingly, our reading is preferable to the opinion of some who maintain that Cornelius was condemned only to exile. [Col. 1360D]

### Line 20.—“From the Lord’s crown”

By “the Lord’s crown,” that is, by the letters of the bishops, whether gathered in synod or scattered throughout the world, this *Book of the Pontiffs* means that all recognized Cornelius as the legitimate pontiff through letters bearing their signatures.

A bishop is called a “crown” by Gregory Nazianzen in his letter to the Bishop of Nyssa, number 2 of the works, page 87, where he writes concerning the death of Basil the Great:

> “For it is grievous to see this solitude of the Church, which has now been stripped of such glory and deprived of such a crown.”

That the term especially designates a gathering of bishops assembled in synod is proved by Orosius in the synod where he presented his case, volume I of the Councils, page 2007:

> “He set forth his case briefly, as far as he could, before your crown.” [Col. 1360D]

At the full Council of Ephesus, session 3, Philip, the legate of the apostolic see, likewise said:

> “From the reading of the acts we have learned what was decreed against Nestorius in your holy council … Now we ask your crown that what was read in your synod may again be read to us.”

And in the *Theodosian Code*, single book, “Concerning Letters”:

> “Since, therefore, the primacy of the apostolic see rests upon the merit of Saint Peter, who is the head of the episcopal crown, and upon the dignity of the Roman city…” [Col. 1361A]

Hence the term is sometimes applied to the Roman pontiff, as in the Roman synod under Hilary, where the bishops say, in the *Cassian Code*, edited by Lupus, page 474:

> “Therefore, offering to your crown the due attentions expressed in the provincial language of our letter, we ask that, in the favor by which you deign to keep the others also in mind in your prayers, you may likewise remember our humility, most blessed Father, venerated by us in Christ with apostolic reverence.”

At other times it is applied to other bishops, as in Jerome, Letter 81:

> “I ask you to greet your crown in my name.”

And in Saint Augustine, Letter 147:

> “Your people adjure you through our crown.” [Col. 1361B]

The expression also occurs in ancient episcopal formulas preserved by Marculf, book I, formula 26:

> “We have sent this present little document to your crown of blessedness.”

Eusebius shows that numerous synods were assembled to recognize Cornelius’s legitimate election, to restrain the assaults of the Novatianists, and that letters were issued by all the bishops and signed by their hands. He testifies that he had seen, concerning this matter, an encyclical volume containing those letters. It is worth recalling this testimony, so that the ancient practice concerning such encyclicals may be more fully illuminated. Book VI, chapter 43:

> “There are still extant letters of Cornelius, bishop of the Romans, sent to Fabius, bishop of the Church of Antioch, in which the proceedings of the Roman synod and the opinions of all the bishops throughout Italy, Africa, and the other provinces and regions are set forth. There are also extant other letters written in Latin by Cyprian and the other bishops who assembled with him in Africa … Attached to these was another letter concerning what had been decreed in the synod, and again another concerning the crimes of Novatus.” [Col. 1361C]

A little later, at the end of the chapter:

> “At the end of the letter he records the number of bishops who, coming together in the city of Rome, condemned the madness of Novatus; he also gives their names and the Church governed by each one. He likewise carefully records the names of those who were not present at Rome but approved the judgment of the others by their letters, together with the names of the cities from which each had sent his letter.”

This was an encyclical volume of letters composed and signed by the bishops of the entire world. It preserved the authentic synodical and individual letters in which each bishop recorded his name, the city where he held the episcopate, and his vote.

The sequence of letters from the entire world, what they contained, and the subject discussed by the episcopal crown contained in that volume are apparent from the letter of the Africans. Cyprian vividly depicts its substance, subject, and number of signatories in another letter addressed to Cornelius, Letter 45.

After recounting the labors undertaken to frustrate the Novatianists’ schemes and to restore those whom the schism had infected, through which he urged all of them to recognize and preserve the root and mother of the Church, he explains how, in addition to the synodical letter from Carthage, other African bishops had also sent letters:

> “But because our province extends more widely—for it includes Numidia and the two adjoining Mauritanias—and lest the schism that had occurred in the city should confuse the minds of those who were absent through uncertainty, it was decided that, after the truth of the matter had been preserved through the bishops and greater authority had been created to confirm your ordination, letters should finally be written by all those established there—as is being done—once every scruple had been removed from individual hearts, so that all our colleagues might unanimously approve you and your communion, that is, the unity and charity of the Catholic Church, and firmly adhere to it.” [Col. 1361D]

> “We rejoice that this happened by divine providence and that our plan advanced wisely. For now both the truth and the dignity of your episcopate have been established in the clearest light and confirmed by the most manifest and firm approval, so that from the replies of our colleagues who sent letters to us from there, all might know the necessary origin and just basis of your ordination, as well as its glorious innocence.”

This is that episcopal crown; this is the encyclical volume through which Cornelius’s ordination remained strengthened, his legitimate election was approved, and the Novatianist schism was blown away.

### “Not against the commonwealth”

Before the emperor Decius, Cornelius had been defamed by the contrivance of the Novatianists, as though he himself, through the earlier Roman synod—in which several bishops and two African legates had participated—and through the Carthaginian synod and the other letters of the bishops throughout the world, were plotting against the empire.

Decius believed this because he had experienced many enemies contending for imperial power and because Christian soldiers were present in the camps, dependent upon the command of a bishop. He therefore turned his fury against Cornelius, whom he could recognize from the bishops’ letters, previously brought to him by the schismatics, as the one acknowledged to be supreme among the bishops. [Col. 1362A]

The following words of Cyprian concerning Cornelius suggest that these events occurred in this way. In Letter 52 he writes:
