> “He sat fearlessly at Rome in the Chair at the time when the tyrant—for by that name he calls Decius because of the emperors he had killed—was threatening the priests of God (that is, the bishops and higher clergy, against whom, as stated above, he had promulgated edicts) with things speakable and unspeakable. He heard with much greater patience and tolerance that a rival emperor was being raised against him than that a priest of God should be established at Rome.”

The words “was threatening with things lawful and unlawful” sufficiently show that Decius really said these or similar things against Saint Cornelius, as they are reported among the deeds of Cornelius.

The suspicious tyrant considered more credible what the Novatianists were fabricating against Saint Cornelius, while synods, assemblies, and letters were being brought from every direction and were represented as conspiracies against the empire. [Col. 1362B]

But how did Decius, who had resolved to destroy the entire higher clergy, spare Novatian and his followers from that same clergy? Cornelius reveals this in his letter to Fabius. After recounting Novatian’s crimes, he states that Novatian was summoned to assist catechumens at the point of death, but, rejecting the presbyterate, said that he was devoting himself to another philosophy and therefore refused to attend to the ministry of the catechumens. Cornelius adds:

> “Rather, seized by anger and indignation, he went away and withdrew. For he replied that he no longer wished to be a presbyter, but was held by a desire for another philosophy.”

Pacianus notes that while Cornelius was suffering—first under Decius and then under Gallus and Volusianus—Novatian lived in safety and was entirely exempt from the edicts published against the clergy.

In refuting the Novatianists’ foolish claims, including the claim that Novatian had possessed the title of a true confessor before Cornelius, Pacianus writes:

> “For as to your belief that Novatian suffered earlier, and your addition that Cyprian said, ‘My adversary has gone before me,’ see how plainly I answer. Novatian never endured martyrdom, nor is that statement heard or read in the words of the most blessed Cyprian. You have his letters, in which he reports that Cornelius, bishop of the City, whom Novatian then envied, resisted hostile rulers, was often a confessor and often afflicted, became a leader to very many confessors and also to many martyrs, and was crowned most gloriously with very many others, while Novatian was still alive and secure. For this reason he had withdrawn from the Church: so that the labor of confession would not press upon him.” [Col. 1362C]

Novatian, therefore, who had invented so many slanders against Saint Cornelius among the faithful, could have denounced him to Decius as a traitor to his country and to imperial majesty, and thus have been the cause of his exile, sufferings, and finally his glorious martyrdom. Cyprian therefore rightly wrote that Saint Cornelius was “often a confessor, often afflicted, and crowned most gloriously with very many others.” [Col. 1362D]

[Note: [Col. 1362D]]

### Line 6.—“He was driven from Centumcellae.”

This place is described splendidly by Pliny the Younger, book VI, Letter 31. Cyprian wrote to Cornelius while he was living there and triumphing over prostrate unbelief. The letter, edition of Pamel, 47, begins:

> “We have learned, dearest brother, of your faith and virtue…” [Col. 1362D]

### Line 17.—“In Interludum”

Correct *Interludum* to *Tellude*. That is, it means “in the temple,” where the Senate was often accustomed to assemble, as is evident from Cicero, Dio, and Livy. See Baronius, year 255, number 6. [Col. 1363A]

### Line 20.—“From the Lord’s crown”

He means the faithful people of Christ, the multitude of the people accustomed to surround the bishop, unless perhaps he intended to signify the crown of martyrdom. Evidence for this interpretation is found in Cyprian’s Letter 56, Pamel’s edition, the most recent letter written to Cornelius. Baronius, year 255, number 79.

## Chronological Notes

Although the pontificate of Blessed Cornelius is illuminated more than any other by both his own letters and those of his contemporary Cyprian, and therefore his date might seem more firmly established than that of others, it is nevertheless entangled in such varied difficulties among the historians and chronologists of our time that they do not agree among themselves either about the year or about the total length of the years. Some conclude that it lasted only one year, together with three months and ten days; others extend it to a full two years or three years. [Col. 1363A]

Some place the beginning of his see in the year 251 of the common Christian era, under the consulship of Decius III and his son Quintus Herennius. Others place it in the preceding consulship of Decius Augustus II and Gratus, in the year of Christ 250; we follow the latter view. Some extend the reign of Decius and, with it, the chair of Cornelius to a later date, postponing the consuls and emperors mentioned by two or three years in the common Christian era, as Pagius and many other chronologists do, contrary to the evident demonstration of the chronology.

Our chronology concerning the see of Cornelius is confirmed by other documents together with the paintings of the Basilica of Saint Paul, documents indicated in their proper place in the series of the Roman pontiffs among the Prolegomena, as well as by the evidence that we shall present here. First, however, one observation may be permitted, which can be displayed more clearly here than it could be explained above in the narrow space of the column assigned to it in the Prolegomena.

In that column I distinguished, according to the usual practice, the letters that still survive from the epoch of Saint Cornelius by capital letters, or majuscules. I indicated letters worn away by age by non-capital letters, or minuscules. The inscription reads:

> + corneLIUS SED  
> AN N I 1. m. III D X [Col. 1363B]

The siglum M, denoting the months, has fallen away; the triad III follows clearly after the lacuna, together with the ten days, denoted by the undamaged letters D X.

Of the two years attributed to Cornelius by Saint Jerome, the Liberian Catalogue, and the other documents mentioned together with the paintings at the place referred to above, only the first unit remains visibly preserved. Time has consumed the second unit, together with the abbreviation for the months. I therefore judged that the lacuna should be supplied by adding the lower-case characters:

> ANN. I I. m III.

Thus the epoch could be read in full:

> “He sat for two years, three months, and ten days.”

The painter’s practice was to arrange the letters in this way also in the other epochs wherever a two-year period had to be expressed:

> EVSEBIVS SED ANN II. M. I. D. XXV.  
> *(folio CII)*

> + MARCVS SED ANN II. M. VIII. DXXI.  
> *(folio CIV)*

With this preliminary statement concerning the authority and condition of the documents on which our chronology rests, I assign, together with Blessed Jerome and the older catalogue, a complete two-year period to the see of Saint Cornelius—which is also said to have had two ordinations in December—and, in addition, three months, distinctly counted in the same catalogue and in the paintings, together with ten days, attested by the testimony of all. [Col. 1363C]

I now proceed to the proofs of this chronology and to dissolving the difficulties that everyone complains have entangled the epoch of Blessed Cornelius.

The beginning of the demonstration must be drawn from assigning the reign of Decius to its proper dates. The sequence of the consulships, the events, and the martyrdom of Cornelius are certainly connected with it, as are the chronological indications confirmed by the letters of Cornelius himself and of Cyprian.

Victor’s *Epitome* clearly teaches that Decius reigned for thirty months:

> “He reigned for thirty months.”

Another Victor, in *On the Caesars*, supports this, writing that after completing two years of reign both Decii—the father and the son—died. Eutropius likewise testifies that both were killed after they had ruled for two years.

During these thirty months in which Decius governed the Roman state, he—who had already been consul before becoming emperor, as is believed, having been suffect consul under Philip, according to the indication in the *Life of Saint Genulphus* cited by Pagius under the year 250, number 11—held two further consulships, both ordinary ones.

The first was his second consulship, with his colleague Maximus Gratus. The second was the consulship he counted as his third, with his elder son Decius, whom coins and inscriptions call Quintus Herennius Etruscus Messius Decius. See Spon, *Miscellanea*, page 273.

The Fasti assign Decius’s second consulship with Gratus to the year 250 of the common Christian era, and all chronologists rightly agree. They likewise generally accept that the third consulship of Decius the father, with his son Decius as colleague, belongs to the year 251 of the Christian era.

No one today disputes the alignment of these consulships with the Christian era, since they are very close to two consulships linked by the strongest possible connection to a fixed year of the Christian era, and also to the other important chronological markers. [Col. 1363D]

The first is the celebrated passage in Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, under the consulship of Ulpius and Pontianus, which is the key to the whole chronology and is shown to belong to the year 238 of the common Christian era.

This is demonstrated both by the total eclipse of the sun, shortly before the boy Gordianus Pius was given the title of Caesar and in the same month in which the two Gordians, father and son, were acclaimed emperors in Africa against Maximinus. The eclipse occurred in the immediately preceding year, 237, and was seen at Rome; Capitolinus records it in the *Life* of Gordianus in such a way that it was thought to be night. According to the astronomical tables, it should be assigned to 12 April of that same year, 237.

It is also demonstrated by the chronological markers of the celebrated epochs given by Censorinus together with the consulship of Ulpius and Pontianus. Under that consulship he counts:

- the Olympiad year 1,014, reckoned from the summer days;
- 991 years from the founding of Rome, reckoned from the Parilia;
- 283 Julian years;
- 265 years from Augustus;
- 268 years of the Alexandrian Augustan era;
- 986 years from Nabonassar;
- 562 years of Philip, reckoned from the death of Alexander the Great.

We, together with all chronologists, therefore assign to that consulship the year 238 of the Christian era. I entirely agree.

I add one point that has hitherto escaped the notice of chronologists: the same Quintus Herennius, son of Decius, who entered upon the ordinary consulship on the Kalends of January in the year 251 together with his father, who was assuming his third consulship on the same day, was also consul suffect in the final months of the preceding year, 250, after Gratus had abdicated, and was the colleague of his father. [Col. 1364A]

Thus, from at least the month of October—I think earlier as well—public documents would have been dated “with Decius Augustus II and Decius Caesar as consuls,” or “with the two Decii as consuls.” From the Kalends of January in the year 251 they would be written:

> “With Imperator Caesar Decius Augustus III and Decius Caesar II as consuls.”

It is equally certain that in that year both Decii died in the thirtieth month of the empire.

The second consulship of Decius the son, joined with the third consulship of his father, is indicated not obscurely in the *Acts of the Martyr Pionius*, dated in the Bollandist edition:

> “With Tertius Messius Quintus Trajanus and Deltius Gratus as second consul.”

It must be understood that the text should read “Decius Gratus as second consul,” since no one mentions a second consulship of another Gratus; nor is the Gratus who had been the colleague of Decius the father in his second consulship called Deltius Gratus; nor does it seem probable that Decius Augustus would have selected the same colleague during the first two years of his reign, a man foreign to his family, while passing over his own children.

In the larger Florentine Fasti, edited by Relandus, the second consulship of Decius the son is clearly recorded as joined with the third consulship of Decius the father in the year 251:

> 250 Δέκιος βʹ, καὶ Γράτος — “Decius for the second time, and Gratus.”  
> 251 Δέκιος τὸ γʹ, καὶ Δέκιος Καῖσαρ τὸ βʹ — “Decius for the third time, and Decius Caesar for the second time.” [Col. 1364B]

That second consulship of Decius the son and Caesar presupposes a first. It must therefore have occurred in the preceding year, when his father began to reign and when he was given the title of Caesar, as is shown by an ancient inscription cited by Sponius, page 273.

In that year he did not hold an ordinary consulship, since Gratus was the colleague of Decius Augustus in his second consulship. This is how the consulship is recorded in the Fasti and in several laws inserted into the Code and collected by Relandus. He must therefore be regarded as a suffect consul after Gratus had held the ordinary consulship for several months with Decius Augustus.

I demonstrate that this suffect consulship of the son was recorded in the acts of the Senate together with the second consulship, which Augustus the father held as an ordinary consul, from the senatorial decree preserved by Trebellius Pollio in his *Valerian*, which is explicitly said to have been issued “with the two Decii as consuls” before the sixth day before the Kalends of November.

Rupertus, in his observations on Besold’s *Historical Synopsis*, page 326, and other writers extend that senatorial decree to the ordinary consulship of both Decii—the third of the father and the corresponding consulship of the son—and make it the final consulship of both.

Rupertus writes:

> “But when were both Decii killed? In November, I think, or December, in the year 1003 from the founding of Rome. Trebellius Pollio, in *Valerian*, book I, section 173, says: ‘With the two Decii as consuls, before the sixth day before the Kalends of November, when the Senate was being held in the Temple of Castor because of the emperor’s letter, etc.’ Therefore Decius was still alive at the end of October,” and so forth.

He rightly concludes that Decius’s life continued through the entire month of October. But he wrongly infers that the death of the Decii occurred before the end of the year in which that senatorial decree was issued. I shall demonstrate this.

Decius the father and his son died in a battle fought near the Tanais against the Scythians, through the treachery and stratagems of Gallus, who succeeded both of them in the empire. They were stuck in the mud of a marsh after the conspirator had deliberately lured both, advancing unwittingly, into the trap.

If the battle and the entrapment in marshy mud occurred in the frozen regions of Scythia, the event certainly cannot have taken place in the year in which the senatorial decree was issued at Rome on the sixth day before the Kalends of November. Neither a battle with the barbarians nor an entrapment of this kind should be assumed at a time that required a marsh not yet bound by frost, so that it could hold men fixed in its mud. [Col. 1364C]

The senatorial decree concerning the appointment of Valerian as censor, of which Pollio speaks, was issued at Rome with the two Decii as consuls on the sixth day before the Kalends of November in the Temple of Castor. It was then carried to Scythia, to the Tanais, according to Zosimus near the end of book I, where Decius was then stationed with his forces, which had not yet been recalled to winter quarters but were drawn up for battle.

Constantine also affirms this in his *Oration to the Assembly of the Saints*, chapter 24:

> “He was struck down in the Scythian fields together with his entire army.”

Let us suppose that, for the copy of the senatorial decree to be carried quickly from Rome to the Tanais, the courier arrived there around the end of November. What follows? Was Decius at that time about to engage in battle with his army deployed in the harshest region of Scythia? Were the barbarians at that time divided into three battle lines, having been summoned by agreement with Gallus to lay an ambush for Decius?

What did Decius do after receiving the Senate’s letter conferring the censorship on Valerian? Trebellius relates it. When Decius received the senatorial decree, he summoned all the courtiers. He was staying in winter quarters, and among the courtiers, as the winter season required, not in the open field and among commanders prepared for battle. [Col. 1364D]

> “He also ordered Valerian himself to be summoned, and in the assembly of the highest men he said: ‘With such a senatorial decree, Valerian, you are fortunate by the judgment of the entire Senate,’” and so forth.

The emperor, overflowing with praise of Valerian and heaping imperial compliments upon him, eloquently extols the judgment of the Senate and the merits of Valerian. Are these the indications of someone proceeding to battle, or of someone sitting peacefully in the palace?

But I ask: how could Decius immediately receive Valerian at the Tanais when he was already about to engage the deployed battle line of the Scythians? Valerian was certainly following military service, as Victor says in *On the Caesars*. In what province he was stationed is not clear. Yet when Zosimus says that Gallus, the successor of the Decii, sent him away to summon the Gallic and German legions, book I, chapter 28, he seems to imply that Valerian was accustomed to remain not far from those regions.

Let us nevertheless suppose that he was sufficiently close to have stood beside Decius on the Kalends of December and to have been advanced by him after the censorship was confirmed.

It remains to suppose that Decius engaged the enemy near the marshes around the Tanais before they had been frozen, advanced unwittingly, became fixed in the mud, and perished with his army in December.

I ask: who could have opened the Kalends of January immediately following, after the third consulship of Decius the father with his son as colleague, to which the senatorial decree is assigned as having been signed “with the two Decii as consuls”? It must have been Trebonianus Gallus Augustus, again consul, and Volusianus Caesar.

So all editors of the Fasti, the inscriptions, and Law 16 of the Code, *Concerning the Management of Affairs*, dated on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, indicate. But in order for Gallus Augustus and Volusianus Caesar to sign the Kalends of January under their own consulship, news of the battle and the deaths of the Decii on the bank of the Tanais had first to reach Rome. [Col. 1365A]

Here, then, another month must be granted to the courier to carry the letters to Rome reporting that, if we suppose the battle occurred in December, the Decii had perished miserably in the engagement with the Scythians. Their bodies were not found; they had not escaped by flight; nor were they seen anywhere. All these facts required an interval of several days after the battle before they could be reported to Rome as established.

Are we to believe that the battle was fought within December, that the bodies of the emperors were sought unsuccessfully, and that a courier sent by the army commanders with letters from the bank of the Tanais reached the City so quickly that within the same month the election of a new emperor could be discussed at Rome, Gallus elected, and the consulship conferred upon him and his son Volusianus before the Kalends of January?

Those who refer the senatorial decree mentioned above to the ordinary consulship of the two Decii, the father’s third consulship, are forced into these narrow confines. They must be caught in an impossible situation, since the twenty-seventh day of October, when the decree was issued at Rome, lies sixty-five days before the Kalends of January, which had to be dated in the name and consulship of Gallus and Volusianus, already shining with imperial dignity. These were the shortest days of the year and the least suitable for battle in the climate of Scythia. [Col. 1365B]

But under the alternative position, which we maintain, the consulship was given as a suffect consulship before October of the year 250 to Decius the son, who held it during the final three months of that year with Decius the father’s second consulship. There is then sufficient time, and a season suitable for the events reported by the historians, both at Rome and in Scythia.

I therefore choose this chronology for the short empire and life of the Decii, lasting thirty months from the attainment of the imperial dignity. It is confirmed by the historians, ancient coins and inscriptions, and other genuine documents of antiquity.

In the year 249 of the Christian era, shortly after the beginning of January, under the consulship of Aemilianus and Aquilinus, Trajan Decius was compelled by the soldiers in Pannonia—where he had been sent to govern and restrain them—to accept the empire. Zosimus writes that he was clothed in purple for this purpose.

Philip Augustus marched against him in the spring, when the season was well advanced, in order to crush him. They met in a battle of annihilation at the beginning of summer, in the Veronese fields, around the month of July. Philip was still reigning on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, as his rescript proves, book VIII of the Code, title 56, *Concerning the Revocation of Gifts*, law 1.

Philip fell after his army had been defeated and destroyed, and at Rome Philip’s son was killed near the Praetorian camp. Decius gained control of affairs and made his son Etruscus Caesar, as Victor says in *On the Caesars*. He immediately sent him ahead into Illyricum and remained for a short time at Rome to dedicate the walls whose construction he had initiated.

In the following year, 250, Decius Augustus entered upon his second consulship on the Kalends of January, with Gratus as his colleague. After several months he made his son, who was stationed in Pannonia, Gratus’s suffect colleague in the consulship, as soon as Decius himself had departed for Pannonia against the Scythians, or Goths, who had invaded Thrace.

Since Decius undertook this expedition as early as he could, as Victor affirms, I infer that he reached the province in the mature spring.

While Decius was absent, Saint Cornelius was elected pope, with the two Decii as consuls, as Cardinal Norisius found written in the ancient ecclesiastical tables, in his *Dissertation on the Epochs of the Syro-Macedonians*, dissertation 3, at the end.

This did not occur in the year 251, but in the year 250, with Decius the father consul for the second time and Decius the son as suffect consul. The father needed only to order Gratus to abdicate upon his arrival, as soon as he himself was in the camp, around the beginning of June. [Col. 1365C]

Nor is it an obstacle if some laws, and even some letters of Pope Cornelius himself, are dated later in that year, after the month of June, under the consulship of Decius and Maximus—that is, Maximus Gratus. Numerous examples teach us that after suffect consuls had entered office, private and public documents were indiscriminately dated under either the ordinary or the suffect consuls.

Suetonius writes that the father of Vespasian was born on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, under the consulship of Quintus Sulpicius Camerinus and Gaius Poppaeus Sabinus, in his *Life of Vespasian*, chapter 2. The surviving marble Capitoline Fasti show that under these ordinary consuls, from the Kalends of July, the suffect consuls Marcus Papius Mut(ilus), son of Marcus and grandson of Marcus, and Quintus Poppaeus Secundus, son of Quintus and grandson of Quintus, entered office.

The dedication of a small shrine in Region XIV, in the Vicus Censorius, is dated on an ancient stone published by Fabretti, *On the Trajanic Column*, page 273, and *Inscriptions*, page 103, now preserved in the Albani Museum:

> “Completed on the fourth day before the Kalends of January, under the suffect consulship of Roscius Aelianus and Claudius Sacerdos, with the tribunician power of Trajan the emperor for the fourth time, and Trajan consul for the third time and designated for the fourth.”

These consuls, who held office for two months, as Norisius calls them in his *Letter on Consuls*, page 99, occupied only the final months of the year of the Christian era 100, as is clear from the attached fourth tribunician power of Trajan. That year had been opened and dated by the ordinary consuls Trajan Augustus III and Fronto—or Frontinus—as Norisius proves in the cited letter, page 62. He also shows from Pliny that in the same year Trajan appointed several pairs of two-month consuls as colleagues. [Col. 1367A]

Sometimes they arranged for both ordinary and suffect consuls to be expressed even in public documents. An example is given by Panvinius in the Fasti under the year 908 from the founding of Rome, or 155 of the Christian era. It is dated:

> “I, Jubentius Celsus, acting in place of the magistrate, signed on the third day before the Nones of November, under the ordinary consulship of Antio Pollio and Opimianus, and under the consulship of Severus and Sabinus.” [Col. 1367B]

Nothing, therefore, prevents either subscription, or both together, from being used for an ordinary or suffect consulship. Nor does anything prevent our understanding that in the month of June Decius the son was made suffect colleague of the ordinary consul Gratus, and that documents and letters were subsequently dated either “with Decius and Gratus as consuls” or “with the two Decii as consuls.” [Col. 1367C]

In the same year, 250, around the end of October, when the two Decii were consuls (the father for the second time and the son as suffect consul), a senatorial decree concerning the conferment of the censorship upon Valerian was issued and signed at Rome on the sixth day before the Kalends of November. Decius received it after it had been sent to him from the City, in Pannonia, where he was then staying. He summoned Valerian and confirmed the honors decreed to him by the Senate in November or December.

The following year, 251, was opened by Decius the father as consul for the third time and Decius the son as consul for the second time, both as ordinary consuls, whether in Pannonia or in the winter quarters of the Scythian camp near the Tanais. “For Gallus, having turned to contriving a revolution,” says Zosimus (Book I), “sent envoys to the barbarians [Col. 1367D], urging them to join the conspiracy against Decius. When they eagerly accepted what had been ordered, and, having been divided into three groups, the first and second lines were cut down or routed by Decius, a few men from the third line unwittingly led Decius into the marsh indicated by Gallus. There, stuck fast in the mud and attacked from every side by the barbarians’ weapons, he perished together with those whom he had with him, since no one at all found an opportunity to escape.” Victor adds: “He was so swallowed up in the marsh’s whirlpool that even his body could not be found.” Another Victor, in his book On the Caesars, adds: “When the Fathers learned of this, they decreed the imperial authority of Augustus to Gallus and Hostilianus, and appointed Volusianus, whom Gallus had begotten, Caesar.”

Thus the purple and the dignity of Augustus were conferred upon Volusianus and Gallus around June of the year 251, when Decius had ruled for approximately thirty months from the first acclamation by the soldiers, according to Victor’s Epitome; and, according to the other Victor’s account On the Caesars, after two full years—namely, from the killing of both Philips, when he had been called Augustus not only by the soldiers but also by the Senate and Roman people at the beginning of summer in the year 249, under the consulship of Aemilianus and Aquilinus. Under that consulship the second law of the fourth book of the Code, under the title “On Hereditary Actions,” is dated the fourteenth day before the Kalends of November.

From this it is possible to understand why St. Jerome, in his book On Ecclesiastical Writers, asserts that St. Cornelius presided over the Church under Gallus and Volusianus: for his pontificate not only extended into their reign, but he held Peter’s see under those same Augusti for more than a full year, as I shall now attempt to show, since the chronology of Decius’ reign has been established by so many documents. To these we should also add the evident testimony produced by the eminent Cardinal Norisius in Dissertation 3 on the Syro-Macedonian Eras, where he confirms Panvinius’ chronology, according to which Decius began his reign in 249 under the consulship of Aemilianus and Aquilinus, although another eminent writer, Baronius, thought the date should be deferred.

“These statements,” he says, “are directed against the opinion of our Panvinius, who is also indicated there in the margin by Baronius. But the chronology of my fellow citizen is certain [Col. 1368B] and cannot be called into question without error. It is of the greatest importance,” Cardinal Norisius says near the end of the aforementioned dissertation, “to assign the beginning of Decius’ principate correctly to its proper year. For since, after seizing the empire, he instituted the persecution against the Christians in which Pope St. Fabianus and other martyrs throughout the Roman world were killed, and since many events also took place at that time in the African Church according to the letters of St. Cyprian, the sequence of events becomes confused in the great annals.”

Having therefore established the epoch of the beginning of the reign both of the Decii in 249 and of Gallus and Volusianus around June of 251, I undertake to reconcile the period of St. Cornelius’ pontificate with the authentic documents of the Roman Church. Among these we count the letters of Cornelius himself and of the Roman clergy, issued together with the letters of Cyprian.

All those documents that are listed by Schelestratius in *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, Dissertation 2 [Col. 1368C], chapter 6, section 7, together with the archives of the Roman Church, confirm that the martyrdom of blessed Pope Cornelius must be assigned to September 14. In his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Jerome states that Cyprian suffered on the same day as Cornelius did at Rome, though not in the same year.

“From this final passage,” says Schelestratius, “we learn not only the place but also the day of Cornelius’ passion. Since Cornelius died as a martyr on the same day as Cyprian, and since all agree that Cyprian suffered on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, it necessarily follows that Cornelius also died for Christ on that day. The day of St. Cyprian’s martyrdom is further attested by the most ancient calendar of the Church of Carthage, edited by the Reverend Father Joannes Mabillon in volume III of the *Analecta*: ‘The eighteenth day before the Kalends of October: holy Cyprian, bishop and martyr of Carthage.’ The *Acts of the Passion of St. Cyprian* agree: ‘The most blessed martyr Cyprian suffered on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.’ On that day, the memory not only of the Lord Cyprian but also of Pope Cornelius is found in the martyrologies. [Col. 1368D] Since, therefore, we know the day of St. Cornelius’ martyrdom to be September 14, just as certainly as the day of St. Cyprian’s passion, we must now investigate the year. Various writers assign different years. Cardinal Baronius postponed it to 255, because he placed the consulships two or three years later. Schelestratius assigns it to 253; Pagius, together with most others, fixes it in 252. I willingly accept this latter opinion of Pagius and those who follow him, to which I am driven by the compelling arguments that will shortly be presented.”

Schelestratius considers two testimonies of Jerome in the cited Dissertation 2, chapter 6, section 4.

“In the *Life of Paul the Hermit* he writes: ‘Under the persecutors Decius and Valerian, at the time when Cornelius at Rome and Cyprian at Carthage were condemned in a blessed shedding of blood, a savage storm devastated many churches throughout Egypt and the Thebaid.’ But in the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Cornelius, he says: ‘He ruled the Church for two years under Gallus and Volusianus.’ In the first passage Jerome appears to assert that Cornelius died under Decius; in the second [Col. 1369A] he expressly affirms that he was crowned with martyrdom under Gallus and Volusianus. These statements will contradict one another unless, in the first passage, you understand the persecution of Decius, which continued under Gallus and Volusianus and is therefore regarded as one and the same persecution with that of Decius.”

Our opinion, however, following Jerome’s traces, joins Valerian with Decius in Cornelius’ condemnation—a reconciliation omitted by Schelestratius—and assigns Cornelius’ pontificate partly to Decius and partly to Gallus and Volusianus. For we have seen that on October 25, 250, when Decius the father was consul for the second time with his son as suffect consul, replacing Gratus, a senatorial decree concerning the conferment of the censorship upon Valerian was issued at Rome and conveyed to Decius, who was then on campaign in Scythia and staying in winter quarters. Valerian was summoned by him, received the credit for the confirmation of his dignity, and was entrusted with the broadest authority. In an assembly, Decius declared it in the following terms, as Trebellius reports:

“You shall be given authority to draft laws. You shall have much to decide concerning the orders. You shall attend to military matters. You shall judge concerning our palace, concerning judges, and concerning the most eminent prefects. Finally, except for the prefect of the City of Rome, the ordinary consuls, the king of sacred rites, and the chief Vestal Virgin—provided that she remains undefiled—you shall pronounce judgment on everything.”

Valerian, therefore, may have returned to the City as censor at the beginning of 251, sent to exercise this extensive authority—as is reasonable to believe—with instructions specifically to punish Cornelius and exact vengeance upon him, no less than upon Julius Valens, who had seized the empire after departing from the City. For, as blessed Cyprian testifies in his letter to Antonianus, Decius “would hear much more patiently and tolerably that a rival ruler, Julius Valens, should be raised up against him than that a priest of God should be established at Rome.”

Valerian, I say, may have been sent by Decius as censor with this authority and these instructions: to drive Cornelius, who had been denounced in the preceding year, 250, into exile at Centumcellae; in 251 and the following year, 252, to summon him from exile to the City; to question him in Decius’ name about the letters delivered to him by Cyprian; to beat him with leaded clubs; and to behead him because he refused to offer impious sacrifice to Mars, as the *Acts* report and the ancient martyrologies and the *Liber Pontificalis* confirm. The sequence and location of his martyrdom will, however, be examined in the historical notes.

Here, where we are investigating the chronological evidence concerning the beginning and glorious completion of his pontificate through martyrdom, we establish the vacancy of the see from Fabianus’ martyrdom on January 20 of the year 250—as was proved in the preceding section—to the election on June 4. By that election the Roman clergy ended a lengthy interregnum through the unanimous election described by Cyprian in these words:

“Cornelius was made bishop by the judgment of God and of his Christ, by the testimony of almost all the clergy, by the vote of the people who were then present.”

Many extend the vacancy of the see over a much longer period [Col. 1369D], postponing Cornelius’ election to June of the year 251, although retaining Fabianus’ martyrdom on January 20, 250, and asserting that the election was prevented for more than a full year, indeed for seventeen whole months. They claim that this must be inferred from four letters, together with four replies, sent back and forth and received between the Roman clergy and Cyprian.

They can, however, be refuted by the act of Cato, who demonstrated the ease of communication between Rome and nearby Carthage by producing from the fold of his toga, in the presence of the Senate, fresh figs that he had arranged to have brought from there. Every day we observe that letters can be brought within a few days—sometimes within a week—from Lilybaeum, the Sicilian promontory from which the harbor of Carthage can be seen. How much more efficient, then, was communication with Sicily and Africa in the flourishing Roman Empire, when compared with our present neglect of maritime affairs, given the daily crossings from the ports of Ostia and Antium; when fleets equipped both for military service and commerce, corporate associations of *scapharii* and *lenuncularii*, the crossing-service of Lucullus, and officials responsible for seagoing ships—whom we find mentioned in ancient inscriptions excavated at the colony of Ostia—could provide the opportunity for departures almost every hour, as is now done in Holland?

Novatus could have arrived from Africa after Fabianus’ death; he could have been present at Cornelius’ peaceful election, before the confessors of Christ had been divided from the rest of the clergy by the foul schism. Thus no necessity compels Papebrochius to depart from the opinion of Henschenius, who determined that the vacancy of the see after Fabianus’ martyrdom lasted less than five months.

For my part, I see no necessity for denying, with the more recent authors listed there by Schelestratius, that before August of the year 250 the letter of the Roman clergy to Cyprian—number 30 among the Pamelian letters—was written. In it they testify that “after the death of the man of most noble memory, Fabianus, a bishop had not yet been appointed because of the difficulties of the times.”

Perhaps one objection might be raised from the fact that the prison-term of Moses and the other confessors had entered its twelfth month before Cornelius’ creation, as the most ancient Liberian Catalogue states in the *Prolegomena*. We can easily answer this if, provided that the number of months in the Catalogue has not been corrupted, Moses’ imprisonment is understood to have been renewed for several months during Decius’ persecution before Fabianus’ death—months that make up the greater part of the number—and for one or two months afterward, which complete the total of eleven months and the same number of days.

For it is established from Caecilius’ *On the Deaths of the Persecutors* that Decius began his persecution immediately upon assuming the empire: “And as though,” he says, “he had been promoted to that supreme dignity for this very purpose, he immediately began to rage against God, so that he might immediately fall.”

Since, therefore, we have seen that the empire was conferred upon Decius shortly after the beginning of the Christian year 249, and that he immediately began to rage against God by persecuting His true worshipers, Moses could also have been committed to prison with his companions eight or nine months before Fabianus’ martyrdom. It is certain from Cyprian’s letters that Christians were being persecuted in Africa at the same time. Indeed, the blessed bishop himself had often been sought for the lion in the arena before Fabianus was put to death at the beginning of 250.

Because Decius was absent from the City, and according to Victor had undertaken his campaign as early as possible, in the mature spring, historians commonly note that the persecution abated somewhat. Thus Cyprian was able to hold councils in May, whereas previously he had been forced to seek hiding places in order to protect both his Church and himself. At that point the Roman clergy also judged that it was sufficiently safe to proceed to an election, since Moses had died in prison after completing eleven months and the same number of days in chains, and Novatus had already arrived in the City from Africa.

After Cornelius’ election had been completed on June 4, as we believe, the fury of the pagan magistrates against the faithful once again followed the impulse of the victorious Decius, who “would hear much more patiently and tolerably that a rival ruler should be raised up against him than that a priest of God should be established at Rome. When, therefore, he heard that this Cornelius was sitting fearlessly in Rome in the priestly chair at a time when the hostile tyrant was threatening the priests of God with threats both speakable and unspeakable,” he ordered him into exile at Centumcellae. There Cornelius received several letters from Cyprian during the declining months of 250, when the year was marked by the ordinary consuls Decius for the second time and Gratus, with Decius’ son as suffect consul from the summer months to the end of the year.

In the final months of that year the censorship was decreed to Valerian at Rome and confirmed by Decius himself in Pannonia or Scythia, together with the extensive authority described above with Trebellius. Through that authority Valerian could judge not only defendants but also judges. Thus, at the beginning of 251, Decius armed against the faithful a man hostile to us in such a way that Valerian was already recognized as destined to prove himself another Decius even in the empire. Jerome therefore rightly writes in the *Life of Paul*: “Under the persecutors Decius and Valerian, Cornelius at Rome and Cyprian at Carthage were condemned in a blessed shedding of blood.”

Cornelius lived in exile at Centumcellae for Christ, “awaiting the executioners of his body and the avengers of the raging tyrant,” as Cyprian says, “resisting the savage edicts and trampling threats, tortures, and punishments beneath the strength of his faith. But the majesty and goodness of the Lord, protecting the priest whom He had chosen to be one, also protected him once he had become one, so that Cornelius later defeated the tyrant, armed and in war, having first conquered him by his priesthood.”

In these words of Cyprian, says Schelestratius, one point above all must be noted: he does not at all testify that Cornelius conquered by his death, but expressly affirms “that through his priesthood—that is, through the patience of a priest—he despised every threat of torture and punishment; and by despising the tyrant, who was afterward defeated by arms and war, he overcame him through the steadfastness of Christian devotion.”

Cornelius also acted fearlessly for the Lord’s flock when, during the period of his exile, he appointed Lucius as his vicar in the City, as I shall show in the next section. He had ordained Lucius bishop toward the end of 250, so that, amid the crisis of the most savage persecution, a bishop would be immediately present to the Roman faithful and would fulfill Cornelius’ duties so diligently that this holy Church would suffer almost no loss from the absence of its own Shepherd.

Meanwhile, at the beginning of 251, Trebonianus Gallus stirred up the Scythians against Decius, while the Italian faction acclaimed Julius Valens and the Macedonian faction Lucius Priscus as emperors. Decius, who had immediately begun to rage against God, immediately fell, as Caecilius observes in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*—although he had crushed both the faction of Priscus and that of Valens. For around June, in the thirtieth month of his reign, “surrounded by barbarians and destroyed together with a large part of his army, he could not even be honored with burial. Stripped and naked, as was fitting for an enemy of God, he lay as food for wild beasts and birds” [Col. 1371C].

Vibius Gallus, Decius’ betrayer, succeeded him and held the empire. According to Zosimus, after dividing the price of his treachery with the barbarians, he fed them with peace and tribute, and returned to Rome. Zosimus writes in Book I, chapter 24:

“At the beginning of the Decian reign, he employed the memory of Decius with honor and goodwill; and he adopted as his own the surviving one of his sons.”

It is therefore not surprising that, imitating Decius’ hostility toward Christians, he drove Pope Cornelius to the desired death for Christ on September 14 of the year 252, when Cornelius had occupied the see for two years, three months, and ten days. We establish this from the surviving paintings of St. Paul, compared with Jerome’s testimony and the more ancient catalogue.

The Liberian Catalogue mentioned above also indicates the consuls of this two-year period, when it says: “from the consuls Decius IV”—which should be read as III—“and Decius II, through Gallus and Volusianus.” The slight error in the number of Decius the father’s consulship, who never reached a fourth, is corrected by the indication of the second consulship attributed to Decius the son and colleague. We have seen this correctly recorded in the larger Florentine Fasti as the father’s third consulship and the son’s second, in the year 251.

Why, then, are the consuls of the years 251 and 252 attributed to Cornelius, while the consuls of the year 250 are not attributed to him, although he spent seven months of his pontificate under them? The explanation is sufficiently clear from the method of the Catalogue, often indicated above, and of the *Liber Pontificalis* compiled from it: they assign consuls to the pontiff who celebrates Easter under them.

In the year 250, when Fabianus became a martyr on January 20 and the see remained vacant through the Easter season, the consuls are not assigned to Cornelius, who was elected after Easter, in June.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

### Line 1.—“Cornelius, a Roman by nationality,” etc.

Blessed Cyprian appends historical notes concerning Cornelius’ first accession to the Roman pontificate, writing in his letter to Antonianus, number 52 in Pamelianus’ edition:

“I now come, dearest brother, to the person of our colleague Cornelius, so that you may know Cornelius more truly with us—not from the lie of malicious and slanderous men, but from the judgment of the Lord God, who made him bishop, and from the testimony of his fellow bishops, whose entire number throughout the world agreed with unanimous concord. For the one who commends our dearest Cornelius to God, to Christ, to His Church, and likewise to all his fellow priests with honorable praise did not suddenly attain the episcopate. Rather, having been promoted through all the ecclesiastical offices and having often rendered himself pleasing to the Lord in divine administrations, he ascended to the sublime height of the priesthood through all the stages of religious service.

“Then he neither sought nor desired the episcopate, nor, like others inflated by the swelling of their arrogance and pride, seized it. Rather, quiet and modest—and such, he says, are those who are divinely chosen for this office—out of respect for the virginal conscience of his character and the humility of his inborn and carefully preserved modesty, he did not use force to become bishop; rather, force was used upon him, so that he was compelled to accept the episcopate.

“He was made bishop by many of our colleagues who were then present in the City of Rome. They sent us letters concerning his ordination that were honorable and praiseworthy and illustrious through the testimony of their commendation. Cornelius was made bishop by the judgment of God and of His Christ, by the testimony of almost all the clergy, by the vote of the people who were then present, and by the college of the ancient priests and good men.

“No one had been made bishop before him, while the place of Fabianus—that is, the place of Peter—and the rank of the priestly chair were vacant. Once that place had been occupied by God’s will and secured by the consent of all of us, whoever should now wish to become bishop must become one outside; he cannot have ecclesiastical ordination if he does not maintain the unity of the Church. Whoever he may be, however much he boasts of himself and claims for himself, he is profane, alien, and outside. Since a second cannot exist after the first, whoever was made after the one who alone ought to be, is no longer a second but nothing.

“Then, after an episcopate received not through ambition or extortion but through the will of God, who makes priests, what strength did he display in the episcopate he had received? What firmness of spirit? What steadfastness of faith? These are things we ought to perceive thoroughly with a simple heart and praise.

“He sat fearlessly in Rome in the priestly chair at a time when the hostile tyrant was threatening the priests of God with threats both speakable and unspeakable, and when he would hear much more patiently and tolerably that a rival ruler should be raised up against him than that a rival priest should be established at Rome.

“Should this man not, dearest brother, be proclaimed with the highest testimony of virtue and faith? Should he not be counted among the glorious confessors and martyrs, since he sat for so long awaiting the executioners of his body and the avengers of the raging tyrant, who would attack Cornelius, resisting the savage edicts and trampling threats, tortures, and punishments beneath the strength of his faith, either with the sword, or by crucifying him, or by burning him with fire, or by tearing his entrails and limbs apart through some unheard-of form of punishment?” [Col. 1372D]

I would have deprived both the life of Cornelius and those of the other pontiffs of the Roman see in this and earlier periods of their chief illumination, commentary, and testimony had I not presented here the complete passage of Cyprian for reading. For in this single testimony of the cited letter, the holiness of blessed Cornelius’ character, his legitimate vocation, his canonical election, and the disciplinary practice of that period are all set forth with exceptional clarity. That practice advanced to the supreme summit of the priesthood those who, out of modesty and the bashfulness of a virginal conscience, shrank from so great a dignity, although they had been gradually tested through all the ecclesiastical offices and had rightly aroused such hope regarding themselves that they had to be compelled by force to accept the episcopate.

Nor does he claim that this was peculiar to Cornelius alone. Rather, he says that it was then common by equal example to the other pontiffs divinely chosen: such, he says, are those who are divinely chosen for this rank. No one can seek a more genuine, distinguished, or secure document concerning the customary election of the pontiffs of the Roman see during this period than the testimony of so great a martyr, who was not only a contemporary of those times but also maintained frequent correspondence with the Roman Church and its apostolic prelates.

The traces of canons and decrees attributed to the pontiffs of the earlier period, or to the period immediately following it, also appear in these letters of Cyprian. Thus it becomes clear that a discipline had already been received in practice which was subsequently confirmed in writing during the century under discussion through decrees of the Roman pontiffs.

For the written law attributed to Caius provides that one should ascend gradually through all the ecclesiastical ranks to the summit of the episcopate (below, section 28). The customs expressed in Cyprian’s letter suggest that this practice had already been received before Cornelius’ election, more than thirty years before the pontificate of Caius:

“Cornelius was made and ordained by several bishops through the judgment of God and of His Christ, the testimony of the clergy, and the vote of the people, while the place of Fabianus—that is, of Peter—and the rank of the priestly chair were vacant.” [Col. 1373B]

How many apostolic canons these words illuminate; what explanation they provide for the prolonged vacancy of the see, when episcopal and priestly colleges could scarcely be held securely and their votes sought; and how great the necessity must have been, in anticipation of the difficulty of a future election after the martyrdom of a pontiff, for a predecessor’s foresight to assign someone a vicarious office, thereby showing the Church, in a certain sense, who should usefully be chosen after him—these points are sufficiently demonstrated by the letter of Cyprian just quoted.

### Line 2.—“Under whose episcopate Novatus ordained Novatian outside the Church, and in Africa Nicostratus.”

You have the history of this event in Cornelius’ letters to Fabius, bishop of Antioch, reported by Eusebius in *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 43. I presented the same account in the Preface to volume I, section 34, and at the same time observed that several decrees of the preceding pontiffs are confirmed by these letters of Cornelius, just as they are by the letters of Cyprian mentioned shortly before. See also the history of Novatus’ schism, abridged in the notes of Pagius and Somier.

### Line 3

By this action, the confessors who had separated themselves from Cornelius together with the presbyter Maximus, who had been with Moses, returned to the Church and became faithful confessors. The more important acts of the persecution of Decius, continued by Valerian, have been snatched from us by that monstrous persecution of Diocletian, which followed it immediately. We therefore consider it necessary to gather fragments from every source, although notable material survives in Cyprian’s letters.

The temporary separation from Cornelius of the presbyter Maximus and the other confessors of Christ who had been imprisoned with him for asserting the faith is shown by the Bibliothecarius to have been corrected by their firm return to the unity of the Church, in which they afterward remained. He mentioned this same presbyter Maximus, the companion of Moses in confession—another [Col. 1373D] Roman presbyter—in the preceding entry on Fabian: after Fabian’s martyrdom, the presbyters Moses and Maximus and the deacon Nicostratus were arrested and sent to prison.

I noted above that this imprisonment of Moses must be understood as having occurred a second time in the year 250, after he had endured imprisonment for several months—perhaps five or six—under Decius in the preceding year; during this second detention he died in prison as a confessor after another half-year. We understand the matter in this way from Cornelius’s letter to Fabius of Antioch, transmitted by Eusebius at the place cited (*Ecclesiastical History*, book VI, chapter 43), where he writes:

> “Maximus, a presbyter of our Church, and Urbanus, both for the confession of our faith, have now for the second time attained distinguished praise.”

The Greek text expresses it more precisely: **δὶς τὴν ὁμολογίας δόξαν ἀρίστην καρπωσάμενοι**, “having twice reaped the most excellent glory from confession.”

They were therefore brought forward for trial again and thrown into prison, where Moses [Col. 1374A] died as a martyr in the eleventh month. The Roman Martyrology commemorates this presbyter Moses on 23 November and praises his constancy both against the Gentiles and against the Novatian heretics.

Accordingly, in agreement with our chronology, we understand that after Fabian had been put to death for Christ in January of the year 250, the see remained vacant until June, when Cornelius was elected Roman pontiff, after Decius had departed from Rome for the Pannonian and Scythian war at the beginning of spring. From Cornelius’s election, Moses spent approximately five months in prison, together with the confessors confined with him, whom Novatus had not yet separated from Cornelius. When Novatus came from Africa during the vacancy of the see, he began stirring up disturbances at the beginning of Cornelius’s episcopate, disapproving the blessed pontiff’s indulgence by which he permitted repentant *lapsi* to return to the Church. This accorded with the decree of the synod he himself had convened around October and with the common judgment of the other bishops expressed in the same letters of Cornelius preserved by Eusebius.

After Moses’s death, [Col. 1374B] the presbyter Maximus and the other confessors of Christ, seduced by the arts and deceptions of the Novatians, withdrew from communion with Cornelius around the end of the year 250 or the beginning of 251. But, by God’s grace, they were brought back to the Church and thereafter adhered firmly to Cornelius, as Eusebius relates from Cornelius’s letter to Fabius—or, as others prefer, Flavianus—of Antioch; the Bibliothecarius makes the same statement in this entry.

Several names of the faithful confessors who returned to Cornelius with Maximus are read in the same letter, namely:

> “Urbanus, Sidonius, and Celerinus, who, groaning and grieving because they had been led by that deceitful and wicked beast to withdraw from the Church for some length of time, submitted themselves once again to Cornelius and to the Church, in the presence of several bishops, presbyters, and laymen.”

Besides those whom Cornelius names individually, we might also gather the names of others from a fragment of ancient marble discovered in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria, when compared with the older Martyrology of the Florentine [Col. 1374C] so often cited, if a somewhat larger portion of that fragment had survived.

On it a prominent chair is visible, placed in the middle, with no one seated upon it. On either side two men sit on lower stools, with cushions beneath them, identified by their proper names. Maximus is read on the right, where a mature-aged man—judged from his neatly trimmed beard, like those represented in images of Hadrian—wearing a tunic and cloak in the Christian manner, raises his right hand. The last joints of two fingers are bent for the act of blessing according to priestly ritual. Thus the image appears to represent the presbyter Maximus seated in the more honorable place in the presbytery near the episcopal chair. On the left sits another man, younger in age, whose name is given as Secundinus.

Several verses had been engraved on this tablet, but only their final syllables survive:

> “. . . TIANAE EJUS . . . . . PTUM EST . . UM . . PICTA EST”

We cannot clearly determine the sense of the inscription from these fragments. [Col. 1374D] The elegant form of the letters shows that the stone was engraved before the end of the third century after Christ, while the art had not yet declined into deterioration—namely, around the time of Cornelius, with whom we are concerned.

For this reason, the monument also appears to furnish a chronological indication connecting it with the presbyter Maximus, who returned to the unity of the Apostolic See and abandoned Novatus and Novatianus. Secundinus, seated with him on the other side of the chair, appears to be the man whom the ancient Martyrologies commemorate, among the martyrs buried on the Via Salaria in the cemetery of Priscilla and belonging to this period, as his companion on 6 August, as Florentinius observes.

That distinguished scholar produces the following entry from the Martyrology of Corbie:

> “On 6 August at Rome: the feast of the holy martyrs Secundinus, Severianus, Carpophorus, Victorinus, and Albinus.  
>   
> And on the Via Salaria toward Ostia: Crescentianus, Sergius, Memmia, Juliana, Cyriacetes, and Smaragdus; Secundinus, Albinus, Victorianus, Faustinus, Donatus, Felix, and Silvanus.”

The oldest little work, written in the time of Damasus and published by us from Bucherius among the *Prolegomena*, lists nearly the same persons, some on 7 August and others on 6 August. [Col. 1375A] Its title is *The Deposit of the Martyrs*. Bucherius noted in the margin that “on the Via Salaria” should be read, as in the Corbie manuscript.

Those martyrs were first buried on the Via Salaria; afterward some of them were transferred by Blessed Marcellus the pope to the estate of Lucina on the Via Ostiensis. See Florentinius’s notes, page 740.

Most of them, however, are recognized as having been later removed from the cemetery of Priscilla by Sergius II and transferred to the *titulus Equitii*, as is shown by an ancient stone still surviving there, on which are read the names of Crescentianus the martyr, Memmia and Juliana, virgins and martyrs, and Cyriaca the widow. At the end the inscription says:

> “These bodies of the saints were transferred from the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria.”

That widow, Cyriaca or Cyriacetes, belonged to the age of Cornelius is shown by her estate in the Campus Veranus, which she offered to the Church for the burial of martyrs under Sixtus II. [Col. 1375B] In it Sixtus was buried with Laurence during the persecution of Valerian—as we shall read shortly after the next entry—during which she herself, dying, received her repose on her own estate but was buried in Priscilla’s cemetery near the Via Salaria. Her relics were later removed by Sergius II and divided between the *titulus Equitii* and the basilica of Saint Laurence outside the walls.

In the same Bucherian work, in the month of July, near the cemetery of Priscilla that it names, the memory of Martialis, Vitalis, and Alexander—six sons of Felicitas—is commemorated in the adjoining cemetery of the Jordanians; and in the cemetery of Maximus the memory of Silanus is commemorated. There it adds:

> “The Novatians stole this Silanus the martyr.”

Bucherius corrects the wording in the margin to “the Novatians,” that is, the Novatianists. This tablet seems to indicate the cemetery of Maximus, since his name and image were excavated near the cemetery of Priscilla on the Via Salaria, one mile from the city, in the vineyard of the most distinguished man Joseph Baptist Sintes, together with several inscriptions indicating Christian burials and marked with the names of the consuls. [Col. 1375C]

He most kindly invited me to visit them in the year 1715 and even wished to donate them to me, so that I might preserve them with the other precious monuments of antiquity collected for the elucidation of the martyrs’ cemeteries and of consular chronology. Bucherius recognizes the cemetery of Maximus from the indication in that little work, in his marginal notes. Since it reads there of Silanus the martyr—perhaps he should be called Silvanus—buried there with his companions, and says that the Novatians stole him, the indications concerning him are strengthened by those connecting him with Secundinus and the others named among the companions in the confession of the presbyter Maximus, who returned to the Catholic Church under Cornelius after the deceptions of Novatus and his followers had been exposed.

As for the possibility that these men wished to steal the body of Silanus or Silvanus, buried in the cemetery of Maximus, we may suspect that they planned to do so either fraudulently to claim the martyr for their faction, having perhaps deceitfully drawn the unwary man into it before he came to his senses, or to deprive the relics of Silanus or Silvanus of the honor due to a martyr. [Col. 1375D] After his return to the Church—or even because, together with Moses, he had remained constant and had never been alienated from it—they may have found him more hostile to them than the others.

Since we are dealing with indications to be gleaned from fragments of letters and history, I have thought it appropriate to present here relics of stones as well, so that they may one day serve to establish a fuller account of these martyrs, should other fragments happen to be excavated from the ruins of the vineyard and the cemetery adjoining it. Joined with the marbles and with the final syllables of the verses already indicated, they might reveal the complete meaning of the inscription.

With the presbyter Moses—whose name I found engraved in elegant Greek letters in the crypts of that same cemetery of Priscilla, though not so near the Sintes vineyard—having been prepared for a blessed end in prison in November of the year 250, and with the temporary withdrawal of his companions to the side of Novatianus [Col. 1376A] joined to the end of that same year, while their return to Cornelius and to the unity of the Church was accomplished in the months preceding Easter of the year 251, everything else proceeds properly up to the martyrdom of Cornelius.

For while Decius was in Pannonia during the summer of the year 250, the rival prince Julius Valens was raised up against him around Rome. Cornelius, the fearless priest of God, meanwhile sat in the priestly chair at Rome, having been elected pontiff, and held a council of bishops concerning the reconciliation of the *lapsi* around October. The persecution in Italy was milder because of Decius’s absence, while the strength and plans of his officials were distracted by the affairs of the rival prince Valens until the end of the year.

Meanwhile, when the year 251 opened in Pannonia, with Decius the father consul for the third time and his son consul for the second time, they were preparing to proceed to the Scythian war. Valerianus was sent to Rome, having been entrusted with the censorship that had shortly before been assigned to him by decree of the Senate. He advanced the persecution of Decius against the Christians together with Maximus, the prefect of the city, in such a way that one and the same [Col. 1376B] persecution came to be regarded as that of Decius, Gallus, Volusianus, and Valerianus.

This was so, first, because under Decius the emperor it was carried out in the year 251 by Valerianus the censor under the emperor’s command, with the great authority conferred upon him which I cited above in the chronological notes from Trebellius; second, because Valerianus continued it—not so much by his own initiative as according to the will of his masters—during the brief reign of Gallus and Volusianus in the year 252; and finally, because in the year 253, when he succeeded them in the empire, Valerianus, having passed from censor to Augustus, did not abandon what had been begun after some interval of time, although at the beginning of his reign he was more lenient toward our people.

From this arose that confusion of the chronology and events of this mixed persecution, in which many acts belonging to Valerianus the emperor are attributed to him when he was still censor, under the commands of Decius and of Gallus and Volusianus, which he shared with Maximus, the prefect of the city. Conversely, acts belonging to Decius, Gallus, and Volusianus are assigned to the period after their deaths, when Valerianus carried them out, as though they had occurred under those earlier [Col. 1376C] emperors through Valerianus’s censorship. This will become clear from the observations that follow.

As for Pope Cornelius—to return to presenting his acts in their proper order—foreseeing that the principal weapons of the persecution of Decius would be armed against the priests of God, he judged that his vicar Lucius ought to be promoted in good time to the episcopal order on the Sunday that fell on the Kalends of December in the year 250. This is established by the epoch of three years, together with the same number of months and days, assigned to his episcopate in the paintings of the Pauline Basilica and in the other documents to be presented in the next entry.

This took place before Valerianus the censor returned to Rome from Decius, carrying harsher commands that would in the future be shared with Maximus, the prefect of the city. After his arrival, Cornelius was ordered into exile at Centumcellae, where he remained fearlessly. By letters sent back and forth to Cyprian, he strengthened the mutual steadfastness of both bishops in the faith.

He remained there, fearless, for the rest of the year 251, awaiting the executioners of his body and the avengers of the raging tyrant. Around June, when both Decii had been killed in the Scythian [Col. 1376D] fields, Trebonianus Gallus was raised to the empire, first by the army and then by the Senate. The Senate declared Hostilianus, the younger son of Decius, who had been left at Rome by his father Decius and created Caesar, Gallus’s colleague in the dignity of Augustus.

At the beginning of his reign, Gallus, as Zosimus relates, “assumed the memory of Decius’s rule with honor and goodwill, and adopted the surviving one of his sons,” namely Hostilianus. Victor, in his book *On the Caesars*, reports that Hostilianus was also granted the title of Augustus by the senators—that is, by the Senate—together with Gallus, while Gallus’s son Volusianus was honored only with the title of Caesar.

Both authors, however, show that Decius’s son Hostilianus did not survive long, and the coins confirm this. He was either killed through the devices of Trebonianus Gallus, as Zosimus writes, or carried off by the plague, as Victor relates. That plague invaded nearly the whole Roman world in the year 252, having arisen in Ethiopia, and devastated it for the following ten years. [Col. 1377A]

Hostilianus could therefore have been alive in the year 252, when Cornelius was summoned from exile at Centumcellae to Rome by Maximus and brought before the tribunal. When Decius—that is, Decius’s son Hostilianus, whom the Acts call Decius—and Maximus the prefect questioned him, he gave the answers recorded in the acts of his martyrdom by Schelestratius in *Antiquitates Ecclesiasticae*, dissertation 2, chapter 6. We shall examine them below in the notes to line 16. Then, having been led to the Temple of Mars on the Via Appia, two miles from the city, and refusing to sacrifice to it, he was beheaded and completed his martyrdom with his companions on 14 September in the year 255.

### Line 8

“Asked by a certain matron Lucina, he lifted the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul from the catacombs [Col. 1377B] at night, etc.”

The first translation of the sacred bodies of Peter and Paul from the place of their martyrdom—where they had initially been buried and where, according to the second-century writer Caius, the apostles’ trophies were indicated—to the catacombs near the cemetery of Callistus must have preceded this second translation, by which the same sacred remains were brought from the catacombs back to their original place of confession under the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus.

Since there is complete silence concerning the first translation, this second one is attributed to Cornelius, although he certainly died as a martyr a full five years before the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus. The account of this translation therefore rightly appeared difficult both to Baronius and to many writers of ecclesiastical history.

I judge it to be one of the anachronisms that shortly before I mentioned as having crept into the abridgers’ accounts of Cornelius’s Acts and into the Lives compiled from them. These anachronisms arose either from gaps in the catalogues or from confusion between the events of the persecution under Decius and Gallus, when Valerianus was censor and Decius’s son, having obtained the title of Augustus with Gallus after his father’s death, was confirmed as Caesar by Gallus together with Volusianus; and the later events under Valerianus as emperor, to whom the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus belongs, and which must also be referred to the pontificate of Sixtus II. See the notes of Pagius on him below, [Col. 1377C] entry 24.

I therefore cannot agree with Pearson, who interprets the translation of the bodies of both apostles from the place of their martyrdom to the catacombs as having taken place under the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, because in the *Depositio Martyrum*, the third of Bucherius’s little works, published among our *Prolegomena*, the burial of Peter in the catacombs and of Paul on the Via Ostiensis is assigned to 29 June, under the same consuls Tuscus and Bassus, belonging to the year 258—six years after Cornelius’s martyrdom.

I readily admit that these sacred bodies were transferred from the place of martyrdom to the catacombs, especially Peter’s, when the persecution of Decius began with his reign, through Cornelius in the year 251, for the reason that Cestriensis records there in Pagius: so that the stations could be held there more safely.

I add something which Cestriensis did not notice: ordinations were customarily held at Peter’s confession in the Vatican, as I demonstrated more fully in the preface to volume I, number 30. The same practice existed at Alexandria, as Liberatus testifies in chapter 20 of his *Brief Account*. The patriarch who succeeded a deceased predecessor kept vigil over his body, placed the dead man’s right hand upon his own head, received the pallium of blessed Mark from the buried man’s hands, placed it around his neck, and was then considered to have taken his seat legitimately.

At Rome, without this handling of the dead man, stations were held in the sacred ordinations near the place of Peter’s confession [Col. 1377D] and the burial of his body, as is clear from the sermons of Leo the Great.

Since Decius was directing the chief blows of his persecution against the priests, as the letters of Cornelius and Cyprian and Eusebius attest, it was necessary to remove those being ordained from the customary place of the station, already sufficiently well known to the pagans under the rule of Alexander.

Nevertheless, because it seemed desirable to preserve the ancient custom of keeping vigil beside the body of the prince of the apostles, who in his second letter had declared that he would diligently ensure that after his death he would have many faithful persons entrusted to him, Cornelius decided to transfer the body of the founder of the Roman Church to the catacombs. There Callistus had already opened a sufficiently spacious and secure cemetery and meeting place for bishops and the Christian people.

Moreover, Cornelius may have possessed an estate belonging to his family [Col. 1378A] on the Via Appia, about two miles from the city, where Cicero records that the ancient tombs of the Cornelii were situated. He may have generously offered it for this purpose, and he could carry out the translation more safely because it was his own property, just as though he were arranging the funeral of one of his own family.

Sixtus II appears to have brought the relics back from the catacombs under the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus: Peter’s to its former place, namely the Vatican, and Paul’s to Lucina’s estate on the Via Ostiensis. After the martyrdom of Pope Stephen, the catacombs could just as readily be recognized as the known place of Christian assembly near the cemetery of Callistus as the station at the Vatican had previously been recognized.

The confusion of these two translations entered the text [Col. 1378B] either through a lacuna, of the sort we observed above in the Liberian catalogue, where the beginnings of one pontificate are joined to the end of another by suppressing the gap; or through a confused understanding of the persecution of Decius the father, Gallus, and Decius’s son Hostilianus under Valerianus the censor, during the reigns of those same Caesars, combined with the later persecution of Valerianus when he was already emperor, as we have often warned must be observed.

### Line 16

“Decius ordered him to be brought with the prefect of the city at night before the Temple of Pallas in the Interlude.”

This passage is taken from the acts of the martyrdom, although it has been somewhat disfigured by an unskilled abridger or copyist. Jo. Petrus Bellorius, the outstanding interpreter of antiquities, restored it to its genuine reading from the remains of ancient Rome, following Nardinus, as he states in the notes to Table XIII of the *Remains of Ancient Rome*.

He observes that on the marble plan of the city, showing Rome under the emperors Severus and Caracalla, two temples are visible near the Temple of Tellus, indicated by the letters **IN TELL**, with the accompanying indication **AEDES . . . . . . .**

He attributes one of them to Minerva, near the Palladian Forum or Forum of Nerva, and confirms this from the Acts of Saint Gordianus, which show that this [Col. 1378C] same place was chosen for his martyrdom by the prefect of the city, Crescentianus.

I shall transcribe Bellorius’s words:

> “Famianus Nardinus, investigating the Temple of Tellus in the Forum of Nerva, noticed Servius’s words on book VIII of the *Aeneid*: ‘The Carinae are buildings made in the manner of the Carinae, which were within the Temple of Tellus.’ He proves that *within* does not mean things located inside the temple, but buildings adjoining the temple, as though beneath the temple, not within it.
>
> “We agree with Nardinus, but with a broader interpretation. We believe that ‘within the Temple of Tellus’ and ‘at Tellus’ are the same and signify the same thing, according to the title on our plan, and refer to the exterior places.
>
> “The Acts of Saint Gordianus sufficiently prove this: ‘Clementianus ordered him to be beheaded before the temple at Tellus, and his body to be thrown before the Temple of Pallas.’
>
> “Anastasius, concerning the holy Cornelius: ‘Yet he ordered him to be brought before him with the prefect of the city in the Interlude.’ Nardinus corrects this to ‘at Tellus.’
>
> “The same Nardinus places the Temple of Tellus at the Forum of Nerva, or Palladium, where the little church of Saint Mary of the Angels now stands on the Via Alexandrina. In antiquity this road extended toward the Carinae and divided the regions of the Sacred Way and the Roman Forum. This road appears on our plan.” [Col. 1378D]

I do not think anyone will oppose Nardinus’s and Bellorius’s correction and interpretation. It is nevertheless useful to add what I indicated shortly before: in the Acts, Decius is represented as ordering that Cornelius be brought before him in the presence of the prefect of the city. He then orders him to be led to Mars and, when he refuses to sacrifice, to be beheaded.

Here “Decius” must be understood as Decius’s son Hostilianus. For this reason the Acts always call him Caesar Decius: his father had created him Caesar before leaving Rome for the Scythian war with his elder son Quintus Herennius, who is also called Decius in coins and inscriptions. Hostilianus was left in Rome, where Victor records that after the death of his father and brother he was elevated to the imperial power of Augustus together with Gallus, by whom he had been adopted.

It was therefore fitting that this young man, conducting judicial proceedings [Col. 1379A] against the Christians in imitation of his father’s example, should summon the prefect of the city to stand beside him at the Forum of Nerva, or Palladian Forum. That judicial proceedings were customarily conducted there, and that tribunals furnished with barriers and railings stood open to those approaching, is shown by the reliefs sculpted on the Arch of the Great Constantine. They display the same forum together with the emperor, judges, and the officers of the curia.
