The images are engraved on bronze plates [Col. 1380A] and are available to us in the book of the learned prelate Jo. Ciampini, *On the Cancellarius*.

We present them here so that the reader may recognize from the images of distinguished men represented there—both on columns and in herms—that the Palladian, or Forum of Nerva, and the neighboring Forum of Trajan are being shown.

> “Constantius the Great standing in the Forum of Trajan, magnificently adorned with herms, columns, and statues of distinguished men, within the railings, together with governors, prefects, and other magistrates adorned with the broad stripe, receiving the petitions of suppliants [lacuna]a[lacuna]at.”
>
> *(At Rome, in the relief of the Arch of Constantine.)*

See the remainder of the Forum, drawn from the same relief, in Ciampini, *On the Vice-Cancellarius*.

### Line 26

“Seven bishops in various places.”

Of these, he himself mentions two in his letter to Fabius of Antioch, preserved by Eusebius. He appointed them in place of an equal number of Novatians who had been deposed, though penitents, since they had been admitted only to lay communion.

### Lines 28–29

“Near the cemetery of Callistus on the Via Appia, on his own estate, etc.”

There he had previously transferred from the Vatican the body of the prince of the apostles. Leo the Great later built a church there, marked with the name of Blessed Cornelius, as will be stated below in his entry. The body of that same pontiff was subsequently removed from there and transferred by Paschal I together with Saints Urbanus, Caecilia, Tiburtius, and Valerianus to the title of Saint Mary across the Tiber, where it rests.

### Note: [Col. 1379B]

#### Line 2

“Under whose episcopate Novatus ordained Novatianus outside the Church.”

Novatus, an African bishop, a deceitful and crafty man, sailed from Africa [Col. 1379C] to Rome and there attempted similar and equivalent things, fomenting dissensions in the Roman Church and tearing away a portion of the people from the clergy. From him, as from a fountain, flowed the origin of all the evils. For it is established that the first schism in the Roman Church was brought about through his agency.

A certain Novatianus, a presbyter of the Holy Roman Church, puffed up by the spirit of ambition, assumed the pontificate at Rome against Cornelius, with the help of Novatus and certain confessors who, at Novatus’s persuasion and through his deceptions, had been deceived after spending a long time in prison and chains for the name of Christ. He spread the report that Pope Cornelius and those who had created him had fallen into heresy.

### Line 17

“In the Interlude.”

It should be read “at Tellus,” or “at Tellure.” The Temple of Tellus, or Telluris, was a place where the Senate often customarily met, as appears from Cicero, *Philosophica* II, and Dio, *Roman History*, book XLIV.

### Note: [Col. 1380B]

#### Line 2

Novatus, a presbyter of Carthage and guilty of the gravest crimes, foreseeing that he would shortly be condemned by the bishops, secretly departed for Rome, where he became the instigator of the Roman presbyter Novatianus in fomenting a schism.

Novatianus had once been possessed by a demon and, when illness threatened, had been baptized in bed. After recovering, he took no care to complete the rites of baptism, nor did he receive the sacrament of Confirmation, which according to ecclesiastical discipline was conferred immediately after baptism.

After some time had passed, he was made a presbyter, the bishop dispensing with him from the ecclesiastical regulations that prohibited the promotion to the clergy of those who had been baptized in bed. Saint Cornelius relates these and many other things about him in his letter to Fabius of Antioch, a fragment of which Eusebius transmits in book VI, chapter 43. There he also explains by what devices Novatianus seized the episcopate.

After becoming an antipope, Novatianus sent legates to Saint Cyprian, [Col. 1380C] bishop of Carthage. Cyprian neither approved his ordination nor communicated with the schismatics.

The chief error of Novatianus and the Novatianists consisted in this: as has already been said, they denied that the Church could show mercy to those who had lapsed during the persecution. They further asserted that the Church could grant pardon for none of the other crimes committed after baptism. They rebaptized those who defected from the Catholics to their sect. They condemned second marriages and permanently excluded bigamists from their communion. In administering baptism, they did not apply anointing with chrism.

Finally, they celebrated Easter either on the fourteenth day of the moon, or on the Sunday immediately following it, or, treating the matter as indifferent, according to the decision established in the Council of Angaris under Pope Siricius. From these points it is clear that the Novatianists joined heresy to schism.

[Col. 1381A] Besides the Roman council convened by Saint Cornelius in October of the year 251 against Novatianus and his followers, mentioned above, another council was assembled by Saint Cyprian at Carthage in May of the year 252. It determined that peace should be granted to the lapsed after full and prolonged penance.

Finally, after the death of Fabius, bishop of Antioch, who had been excessively favorable to the Novatianist party, Demetrianus, his successor, held a synod against Novatianus in the same year 252. The synodical pamphlet mentions it.

Some writers report that another council was convened in Italy against the same antipope under Cornelius. This is found nowhere. The only fact is that, because not a few bishops in Italy had not attended the Roman council, Cornelius separately sought their opinions as well. From this, an Italian council was constructed out of Jerome.

### Note: [Col. 1381B]

#### Line 15

“Letter.”

I will not conceal that considerable weight and importance are added to Cyprian’s words in the indicated letter, not only by Protestants but also by certain Catholic writers. He writes:

> “But what is the reason for coming to Rome and announcing that a pseudo-bishop has been made against the bishops? Either they approve what they have done and persist in their crime, or, if they disapprove and withdraw, they know where to return. For since it has been established for all of us, and is equally fair and just, that each person’s case should be heard there where the crime was committed, and since a portion of the flock has been assigned to each shepherd for each one to rule and govern, rendering an account of his conduct to God, those over whom we preside ought certainly not to run about, nor by their crafty and deceitful rashness to shatter the harmonious concord of the bishops; rather, they should conduct their case there where they can have both their accusers and witnesses of their crime. [Col. 1381C] Unless, perhaps, the authority of the bishops established in Africa, who have already judged them and recently condemned their conscience, bound by many snares of offenses, by the severity of their judgment, seems lesser to a few desperate and lost men.
>
> “Their case has already been heard; judgment has already been pronounced against them. It is not consistent with the dignity of priests that the decision should be criticized with the fickleness and inconstancy of a changeable mind.”

Some Protestants take pleasure in these words as deserving the greatest attention because, they say, Saint Cyprian indicates to the pope that he has nothing in common with affairs overseas and that the Roman See ought not to involve itself in them.

Some Catholics, however, consider that Cyprian complains in his letter to the Roman pontiff about an appeal to this see as though it were a mode of proceeding established contrary to the rules. (Fleury, *Ecclesiastical History*, book VII, no. 8.) Others infer from this occasion that in the earlier centuries of the Church ecclesiastical judgments were customarily rendered “by the synod of each province with the authority of the metropolitan, so that it was not permitted to appeal from a judgment delivered in a provincial [Col. 1381D] synod.” (De Marca, *On the Concord*, book VII, chapter 1, no. 2.)

The Protestants are answered by denying that Cyprian says in this letter, or indicates to the Roman pontiff, that he ought not to involve himself in affairs overseas. On the contrary, in addition to what he had written in earlier letters or discourses, he goes on in this very letter to say what we shall hear concerning the authority of the Holy See. He calls the chair of Peter in this same letter the principal Church, from which priestly unity arose and is maintained in the others.

These would certainly be empty and imaginary titles if the right of this holy see to involve itself in the affairs of particular Churches were denied. Many of those Churches, at every period, have attempted too strongly to withdraw themselves from the Roman Church’s primacy [Col. 1382A] and to dissolve or break that bond of unity.

It is clear that the holy bishop is attacking the insolence of his enemies, who, although struck by the thunderbolt of anathema because of their notorious crimes, dare to sail to the chair of Peter and to the principal Church, to which treachery cannot gain access. Indeed, to use such expressions is rather to acknowledge and confess jurisdiction than to reject or evade it.

When he asks why they sail to Rome, he sufficiently indicates that he does not hold the view that nothing concerning the Africans belongs to the Roman See. I ask the reader to recall what we brought forward in the preceding chapter. The argument instead maintains what the following words demonstrate: he wishes to show the uselessness of their subterfuge, whether they persist in their crime, which requires no further proof, or repent, which is better demonstrated in Africa, where the scandal that was committed ought to be repaired by an open display of repentance.

As for what he adds concerning the place where their case should be examined, their condemnation, the authority of the African bishops [Col. 1382B] by whom they had been judged, and the gravity of their sentence, which should not be overturned for trivial reasons unworthy of priestly constancy, this is very far from being a protest or exception, as though he were asserting that the Holy See had no right to decide anything concerning the Africans.

He is explaining to Pope Cornelius the proper order to be observed in conducting affairs. He warns the pontiff about the notorious reputation of such criminals and about their detected plan, so that Cornelius might guard against granting anything too indulgently to these fraudulent petitioners, who had no other reason for going to Rome than to circumvent and take advantage of those who had not previously known or recognized them. Otherwise, the majesty and gravity of priestly judgment might appear to have been weakened.

As for the observations of those Catholics who create difficulties over appeals from outside the provinces to the Roman See, the question is whether this should be called an appeal to the Holy See, and whether it is what St. Cyprian complains about to Pope Cornelius as an abnormal procedure. It might rather be regarded as a pre-emption of the case than as an appeal, since Fortunatus fled to Rome so that he might there be received as the legitimate bishop of the Church of Carthage, without his case first having been examined according to the canons in Africa, where certainly he would not have dared to contend in a just judgment.

Whatever the precise characterization, the reasoning of the observations is sufficiently ambiguous. It is important to understand clearly whether the author of the observations means to affirm that every appeal from African bishops and councils to the Roman See must be judged an abnormal or irregular proceeding, of which St. Cyprian complained; or whether he contends only that this particular appeal should be judged to have been lodged by Fortunatus contrary to the rules of ecclesiastical law.

Those who bring this particular event to judgment will readily affirm that the appeal of Fortunatus and his fellow-members was alien to the order of law—whether they were seeking restoration in full to all the matters judged against them in Africa and confirmed at Rome, where Privatus had been deposed from the episcopate, after having recently carried out Fortunatus’s false ordination, and where he had previously been rejected and expelled from the Church by Pope Fabian; and where Novatus and the other rebels, accomplices and agents of that schism, had been struck with anathema by Cornelius himself—or whether the matter concerned only Fortunatus’s ordination, a crime especially detestable, in defense of which not even those utterly depraved satellites would have dared to seek judgment from the African bishops, who had long known their audacity and shamelessness.

In his letter to Cornelius, St. Cyprian overturns the machinations of this perverse faction in both of the proposed schemes. But to assert that Cyprian meant, in general, that every appeal from the African Churches to Rome should be regarded as abnormal and irregular—that is precisely what we must neither think nor declare, even though the particular disgracefulness of the crime committed might have pressed him more strongly than was proper toward touching, in a manner, upon the general thesis.

This limitation concerning the class of cases must necessarily be inferred from what the holy bishop explicitly expressed in hundreds of places concerning the supreme dignity of the Roman See. He certainly could not have imagined that dignity, or represented it, as an empty title lacking any solid force or substance of authority.

I shall make one further point, concerning the third class of writers mentioned earlier: even if we grant that in the earlier centuries of the Church the rights of the Holy See could not always attain their full and free exercise among all the provinces of the world then clothed in the Christian faith, because of the obstacles created by persecutions and by other impediments that would naturally arise in establishing a matter of such importance, what, I ask, follows from this?

> So great was the labor of founding the Roman people.

Nevertheless, nothing reveals itself as more clearly or firmly established than those primordial and original rights of the Roman chair and jurisdiction. Let the oracles of the divine Scriptures be consulted, and the books of the ancient Fathers, guardians of the most ancient tradition, preserving this deposit for us: it will be evident that no power on earth possesses a more evident and solemn warrant from the word and law of God than the power granted in this way to the Holy See of which we speak.

Moreover, the explanation and clarification of the rights divinely attributed to this august see must be sought in the occasions presented and in the Church’s opportunities and necessities. From these it is possible to recognize more fully the very broad extent of those rights.

St. Cyprian undoubtedly recognized in the Roman see of Peter the principles from which all those rights of primacy and prerogative derive, rights continuously possessed and exercised by that see in the succeeding centuries. Yet he could have thought that ecclesiastical judgments ought to be defined and concluded in the same provinces in which the accusations had arisen, just as he believed that no baptism whatsoever administered by any group of heretics was valid.

But was what seemed to Cyprian in this way therefore consonant with the truth? Did universal practice give the force of law to the particular African practice, so that Cyprian might assert it in his own province? Certainly not. Ecumenical councils, consulted on both questions, exposed the Catholic truth in the full light, as well as the rights of the Church that had perhaps not been sufficiently known or expressed by the martyr Cyprian.

Those councils recognized and admitted the right of appeal to the Holy See as one of the attributes attached to this supreme dignity and power, just as they recognized its inviolable fidelity in guarding the deposit of faith through their decrees concerning the validity of baptism when properly administered by heretics. This will become clear in its proper place, in the discussion of the pontiffs that immediately follows.

[Column 1353]

## 22

### Cornelius

Cornelius, a Roman by nationality, son of Castinus, held the see for three years, two months, and ten days. [Note: B: “less than two years, in the time of Decius, Gallus, and Volusian, from the consulships of Decius III and Gratus II to Gallus and Volusian II.”] He was crowned with martyrdom. [Note: See Baronius, year 254.] During his episcopate Novatus ordained Novatian outside the Church, and in Africa, Nicostratus. After this, the confessors who had separated from Cornelius, together with the presbyter Maximus, who had been with Moses, returned to the Church and became faithful confessors. [Note: See Baronius, year 256.]

Afterward the bishop Cornelius was expelled at Centumcellae [Note: “Centumcellas”], and there he received a letter concerning his confirmation, sent by Cyprian—a letter which Cyprian had written in prison and which Cornelius received from Celerinus the lector. [Note: C gives: “which he gave to Celerinus the lector.”]

In his time, at the request of a certain matron, Lucina, he removed by night from the Catacombs the bodies of the apostles Peter and Paul. Blessed Lucina first placed the body of blessed Paul on her estate beside the Ostian Way, at the place where he had been beheaded. But blessed Cornelius the bishop took the body of the blessed apostle Peter and placed it beside the place where he had been crucified, among the bodies of the holy bishops, in the temple of Apollo on the Golden Mount, in the Vatican, beside Nero’s palace, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July. [Note: Baronius, at the cited year, proves that this occurred under the emperor Volusian.]

After this, at the same time, Decius learned that he had received a letter from blessed Cyprian, bishop of Carthage. He sent to Centumcellae [Note: C: “Centumcellas”] and brought blessed Cornelius back. He nevertheless ordered him to be presented before the prefect of the city at the *interludus* [Note: CB: “Tellude”], by night, before the temple of Pallas. He said to him:

“Have you decided that you will fear neither the gods, nor the commands of the emperors, nor our threats, so that you receive and send letters against the commonwealth?”

Bishop Cornelius replied:

“I received letters from the Lord’s crown” [Note: B: “crown,” that is, from the faithful], “not against the commonwealth, but rather a particular” [Note: C: “spiritual”] “counsel for the redemption of souls.”

Then Decius, filled with anger, ordered the mouth of blessed Cornelius to be beaten with leaded scourges, and commanded him to be led before the temple of Mars to worship. If he did not do so, he said: “Let him be beheaded.” [Note: C has “if he should not do so.” See Baronius, year 255, at the end.]

Afterward—that is, on the third day before the Nones of March, already before his passion—he handed over all the goods of the Church to his archdeacon Stephen. He carried out two ordinations in the month of December: four presbyters, four deacons, and seven bishops in various places.

He too was beheaded in the place mentioned above and became a martyr. Blessed Lucina gathered his body by night with the clergy and buried it in a crypt beside the cemetery of Callistus, on the Appian Way, on her estate, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September. [Note: 18; C.] The episcopate then remained vacant for thirty-five days.

### Catalogue under Liberius

Cornelius: two years, three months, and ten days, from the consulships of Decius IV and Decius II to those of Gallus and Volusian II. During his episcopate Novatus ordained Novatian outside the Church in the city of Rome, and Nicostratus in Africa. After this, the confessors who had separated from Cornelius, together with the presbyter Maximus, who had been with Moses, returned to the Church. Afterward, having been expelled at Centumcellae, he received there a glorious dormition.

### [Note: Column 1385A]

#### Line 7.—“He granted power over the whole Church to his archdeacon Stephen.”

As Lucius was proceeding to martyrdom, he gave to his archdeacon Stephen authority over all the Church’s affairs. The archdeacon was the guardian and administrator of the Church’s property. Hence Jerome, writing to Evagrius, requires diligence in an archdeacon: “Let the deacons choose from among themselves one whom they know to be diligent, and let them call him archdeacon.” Sidonius imitates him in Book IV, Letter 25: “At first a lector, then, after the passage of toil and time, an archdeacon, in which rank or ministry he was retained for a long time because of his diligence.”

Stephen likewise, the immediate successor of Lucius, before his martyrdom entrusted all the vessels of the Church and the treasury of ecclesiastical money to his archdeacon Sixtus, as Anastasius says in his account of Stephen: “He entrusted all the vessels of the Church to his archdeacon Sixtus, and the treasury of money.”

Cornelius had done the same earlier, as Anastasius says: “Already before his passion he handed over all the goods of the Church to his archdeacon Stephen.” Sixtus II had Lawrence as his archdeacon and fellow-competitor in martyrdom. Hence, when Sixtus was hastening to martyrdom, Lawrence said to him, according to Ambrose, *On Duties* I.41: “Why, holy priest, are you hastening without a deacon?”

### [Note: Column 1385B]

#### Line 4.—“He ordered that two presbyters ... should not leave the bishop.”

A memory of this ancient custom is preserved by the previously cited Dionysius of Alexandria, who in his letter mentions a presbyter-companion when he was proceeding into exile under the pressure of the Decian edicts. The accepted custom long continued among the patriarchs of the East.

Epiphanius of Constantinople, in volume III of the Councils, p. 1036, elected in the year 520 among the legates sent by Hormisdas, is praised in these terms: “Heraclianus, the most reverend presbyter of the holy Great Church, and the cohabitant of the aforesaid most holy archbishop and patriarch Epiphanius.”

#### Line 6.—“He too was beheaded by Valerian on the third day before the Nones of March.”

Saint Lucius suffered many things, both under the Decian edicts and at the hands of the Novatians, who had not laid aside any of their former anger, conceived against pontiffs and Catholics. He was first punished with exile, as the *Liber Pontificalis* had earlier stated, and indeed at the beginning of his pontificate. That he was released from exile and returned unharmed is suggested by the words of St. Cyprian, who wrote to the pontiff:

“And recently, dearest brother, we rejoiced with you, when divine favor established you, in the doubled honor of the administration of your Church, as both confessor and priest.”

He calls the honor “doubled”: the honor of the confession made and that of the pontificate, in accordance with the observations made above. Concerning his present safety he writes:

“But now also we rejoice no less for you, for your companions, and for the whole brotherhood, because the Lord’s kindly and generous protection has brought you back again, with the same glory and the praises belonging to you, to your own people.”

From the honor of confession and from the martyrdom of his predecessor Cornelius, St. Cyprian then infers both the perversity of the Novatian schismatics and the certainty of succession in both cases, indicating that those same schismatics were, as it were, the first authors of the Decian persecution:

“We have understood, dearest brother, and with the full light of our heart we clearly perceive, the saving and holy counsels of the divine majesty: whence the sudden persecution recently arose there; whence secular power suddenly burst forth against the Church of Christ, against blessed Cornelius the bishop and martyr, and against all of you; so that, to confound heretics and blunt their force, the Lord might show what the Church was, who was its one bishop chosen by divine ordination, and who were the presbyters joined with the bishop in priestly honor.”

Indeed, until the time of Valerian, while the fury of persecution raged against the clergy, the Novatians remained unharmed. They continued to retain pontiffs in their schism, and bishops who survived down to the time of Pope Celestine, as Socrates testifies in Book VII, chapter 11, when they were forbidden to have them publicly.

The respite lasted only a short time. The earlier edicts were again strengthened against Christians, especially against the clergy. Dionysius of Alexandria announced this to Hermammon in the following words, preserved by Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 1:

“Nor did Gallus understand the guilt of Decius, nor perceive what had finally destroyed him. Rather, he stumbled against the same stone placed before his eyes. When his empire was in a prosperous condition and everything was proceeding according to his wishes, he persecuted holy men who were offering prayers to God for his peace and safety.”

The renewed persecution was caused by the plague that followed. It devastated the whole world, as Orosius writes in Book VII, chapter 14, and the emperor Hostilianus is listed by Victor among those who died from the pestilential disease. To avert the plague, vows and sacrifices were prescribed to Apollo by the priests of the nations—hence, as may be seen on coins of this period, the inscription “To Apollo the Savior.” By imperial edict the priests of the nations ordered these rites to be performed by everyone. The peoples, stirred up by those priests, demanded in the circus the slaughter of the Christians, whom they believed to be the authors of all evils because they refused to offer impious sacrifices to Apollo.

Cyprian writes of this popular demand in Letter 55, saying that he himself was demanded for the lions by the public cries of the crowds:

“Even in these very days, when I wrote this letter to you, because of the sacrifices that the people were ordered by the promulgated edict to celebrate, I was again demanded for the lions in the circus by the cry of the crowds.”

On this occasion, then, Lucius suffered persecution a second time and brought his life and labors to an end in glorious martyrdom. Whether he was condemned to exile or to capital punishment, writers debate. The *Liber Pontificalis* says that he was punished with capital punishment, which seems more credible, since he should be regarded as the first victim of the renewed persecution.

#### Line 7.—“He granted power over the whole Church to his archdeacon Stephen.”

Concerning the same Stephen, it had likewise said of Cornelius: “Already before his passion he handed over all the goods of the Church to his archdeacon Stephen.” Thus two things are said to have been entrusted to the pontiff’s archdeacon: authority over the whole Church and all the goods of the Church.

From this comes the truer origin of the authority and dignity of the archdiaconate of the apostolic see, which for a long time was an exceptionally great dignity and, when the see was vacant, retained primary responsibility for that same Church.

St. Jerome confirms us concerning this dignity when, in his commentary on Ezekiel 48, he says that those who did not know the humility of their state grew swollen beyond presbyters and estimated dignity not by merit but by wealth.

Even in the year 1097, at the time of the Council of Bari, they continued in this dignity. St. Anselm, because of the excellence of his learning, was ordered to sit before the supreme pontiff and was raised to the apostolic assembly; he was ordered to sit beside the Roman archdeacon, who, as William of Malmesbury says in his account of this council, customarily sat before the pope.

We shall discuss in its proper place how, when the see was vacant, the care of the Church and supreme guardianship of ecclesiastical goods were entrusted to the archdeacon, whose associates were the archpriest and the primicerius.

In both places he is called “his archdeacon” because he adhered perpetually to the pontiff’s side. A similar personal deacon was present among the patriarchs of the East. Such was Athanasius, who, while performing the office of deacon of Alexandria, is called the perpetual assessor of the holy patriarch of Alexandria.

Thus the Alexandrian synod, convened in the year 340, testifies in its synodical letter, where it describes the devices of the Arians. Among other things, concerning Arius, it says:

“Since Alexander, on account of his devotion to Christ, did not receive the impious man, they hated Athanasius, then a deacon, because they carefully observed that he was constantly with Alexander and highly valued by him. And since they had already experienced his devotion to Christ in the Council of Nicaea, where he had spoken with great freedom against the impiety of the Arians, they burned with the most intense hatred.”

Moreover, when Euphemius was expelled under the tyranny of the emperor Anastasius and Macedonius was substituted for him, the archdeacon was first removed before the deposition, according to Theophanes:

“Macedonius, having promised to bind himself by an oath, went to Euphemius in the baptistery, after first ordering the archdeacon to be carried away from his shoulders; then, meeting Euphemius in the private dress of a priest ...”

Among the goods of the Church entrusted to the archdeacon’s custody, the preservation of ecclesiastical documents held a particular place. Prudentius clearly observes this when he introduces the prefect urging Vincent of Zaragoza, the archdeacon, to hand over all the books of the Church entrusted to his care, in *The Crown of Martyrs*, hymn 5, p. 165:

> If such hardness of heart  
> Maintains its stubbornness,  
> So that you loathe to touch  
> Our cushion with your hand,  
> At least uncover the hidden pages  
> And disclose the open books,  
> So that the sect, sowing a little,  
> May be burned in righteous fires.

When the second Council of Constantinople was summoned under Flavian at the request of Eutyches, in order to verify and examine whether the earlier Acts had been corrupted and whether some writings had been secretly removed, Aetius, the Constantinopolitan archdeacon, to whom the integrity of the Acts had been entrusted by virtue of his office, made the following protest, as recorded in the first session of Chalcedon:

“Since, some time ago, when the documents were still with us, Asterius, the presbyter and notary who is with us and acts with us, went down and took away all our documents, both the drafts and the authentic copies; and it has now been two or three months, and we have none of these things. Therefore, if anything is altered or said hereafter, this shows that we are free from responsibility for the present matter.”

Similar examples occur everywhere in the Acts of the Eastern councils.

### [Note: Column 1387C]

#### Line 3.—“He was sent into exile.”

He went into exile twice on account of his confession of the faith: once with Cornelius and once after he had already obtained the pontificate, as is clear from Cyprian’s Letter 58 written to him.

#### Line 9.—“Bishops.”

Among them was Melanius, bishop of Rouen, renowned for his holiness. See Baronius in the notes to the *Roman Martyrology*, 28 October.

### [Note: Column 1387D]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

#### Lines 1–2

The portraits of St. Paul assign to Lucius three years, three months, and three days. These numbers, however, are preserved more completely and appear more clearly from this pontificate through those of the succeeding pontiffs down to St. Innocent I. The agreement of the catalogues with them is therefore greater. Thus in Lucius only the Liberian exemplar, although agreeing with the others in years, adds five months to the number of months—perhaps because the copyist of the manuscript, not noticing the first and last strokes of the obliterated abbreviation M, the sign for months, wrote V. III instead of copying M. III.

In the number of days, it rendered X for III, although all the catalogues, like the portraits, preserve the number III. The defect of worn writing is evident in that old exemplar which the copyist had before his eyes in the period of the pontificate of Pope Lucius.

The agreement of all the other manuscripts conveniently remedies the defect of one codex and shows that, together with the original of the Leonine-era portraits, the reading must consistently be: three years, three months, three days.

The martyrdom of Lucius, recorded on 3 March, is reported in the catalogues not only in the manuscripts but also in an ancient marble inscription of the eighth century at the Roman title-churches of Saints Stephen and Sylvester, and in the catalogue of the burials of the Roman pontiffs from the time of Pope Liberius, published above from Bucherius in the prolegomena. As in the *Liber Pontificalis*, it is assigned to the consulship of Valerian and Gallienus. Yet the numbers of their consulships are incorrectly given as III and II, since in the following section of the same catalogues these same consuls conclude the period of Stephen, Lucius’s successor.

We therefore understand without doubt that Lucius must be assigned to the second consulship of Valerian and Gallienus. Those consuls belong to the year of Christ 254, although the carelessness of copyists wrote Valerian the father’s third consulship instead of his second, and made a similar error in writing the name of Gallienus, for which they incorrectly inserted “Gallicanus,” as the aforementioned Bucherius long ago noted.

Counting backward from 3 March of the year 254 by three years, three months, and three days, we arrive at the ordination of blessed Lucius to the episcopal rank on Sunday, 30 November of the year 250—almost six months after blessed Cornelius had been raised to the Roman pontificate in June of that same year, as I proved in the preceding number.

We therefore do not doubt that Lucius was appointed Cornelius’s vicar, since the presence of a bishop-vicar was required during the time of the fiercest persecution whenever Cornelius, as happened, was driven into exile. The pontiff’s prudent care also required that every avenue be blocked against the schemes of Novatus and Novatian, who sought to seize the primacy of the Roman see, by choosing for the dignity of papal vicar a bishop of proven virtue whom the Church would have ready to administer every priestly office.

The necessity of a bishop-vicar is further confirmed by the fact that Lucius himself was driven into exile and afterward returned unharmed by the will of God. The persecution of Decius and of Valerian raged against the priests of God—Valerian first being censor under Decius and later, after Gallus and Volusian, his successor in the empire—as is clear from the letters of St. Cyprian and from a homily of St. Leo the Great.

In Cyprian’s Letter 52 to Antonianus, in Pamelius’s edition, he says of the persecutor Decius:

“When the tyrant, hostile to the priests of God, threatened things lawful and unlawful ...”

St. Leo the Great, in his sermon on the feast of St. Lawrence, writes of the persecution first begun under Decius and then renewed under Valerian:

“When the fury of the pagan authorities raged against Christ’s choicest members, and especially attacked those who belonged to the priestly order,” and so forth.

The priests of God, in the face of the persecution of the clergy, not only remained fearless in their sees but also provided the clergy and people with vigorous leaders, especially when they themselves were expelled from Rome, so that their deputies might perform their duties courageously against both the rage of the pagans and the treachery of the schismatics.

This need for vigilance often led the Roman pontiffs—Cornelius, Lucius, and Stephen—to promote their own vicars to the episcopal rank in that difficult time, as we shall examine in each case. Lucius therefore administered the Roman Church in the capacity of vicar, as the life of Cornelius makes clear.

After Cornelius’s martyrdom, Lucius, elected as his successor from the office of vicar, was elected in the year 252, on Sunday, 17 October. Since the *Liber Pontificalis* says that the vacancy of the see lasted thirty-six days, his pontificate extended to 3 March of the year 254, during the second consulship of Augustus Valerian and Augustus Gallienus, when he won the palm of martyrdom. From the death of Cornelius, he held the Roman see for one year, four months, and fifteen days, counting from the thirty-fifth day after Cornelius’s death.

From his ordination, however, he exercised the episcopate for three years, three months, and three days, as all the documents unanimously attest, as may be seen in the prolegomena.

Eusebius and Prosper, as Schelestratius notes at the end of chapter 6 of dissertation 2 of *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, assign Lucius a pontificate of eight months, perhaps because they did not count the time of his exile. During that period he himself also ordained Stephen, the archdeacon, as bishop-vicar, as we shall see in the following number.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

#### Lines 1–2.—“Three years, eight months, three days.”

I stated in the chronological notes that the number of months in the Liberian catalogue’s exemplar, which differs from the others, must, on the testimony of those other sources and of the portraits of the Leonine era, be reduced to three.

#### Line 3.—“Valerian III and Gallicanus.”

There I proved that the reading of the consulship must be restored and that the consuls Valerian II and Gallienus must be given.

#### Line 4.—“He ordered that two presbyters and three deacons should not leave the bishop anywhere, for the sake of ecclesiastical testimony.”

Above, in number 6 concerning Evaristus, we saw that a company of seven deacons was assigned to a bishop preaching, for the sake of the style of truth. Here, wherever the bishop was acting, at least two presbyters and three deacons were appointed as his inseparable companions, for the sake of ecclesiastical testimony. This was explained in the notes of Altaserra, Bencinus, and myself; consult them from columns 1137 to 1146.

#### Line 6.—“He was beheaded on the second day before the Nones of March.”

As he was proceeding to his passion, he granted authority over the whole Church to his archdeacon Stephen. The same was done by Cornelius, unless this section was transferred from Lucius’s life into Cornelius’s life. Anyone could readily suspect this from the added indication of the same day in number 23 concerning Cornelius, line 23:

“After this, that is, on the third day before the Nones of March, already before his passion, he handed over all the goods of the Church to his archdeacon Stephen.”

For the third day before the Nones of March was the day on which Lucius proceeded to martyrdom, as is asserted here and as the Church’s records attest. Cornelius, however, was led to his passion on 14 September, as I observed in his life from Jerome and other writers and documents.

Nevertheless, Cornelius too could have had Stephen as his archdeacon, and Stephen could also have served Lucius, while Cornelius entrusted him with a different authority—namely, authority over the Church’s temporal goods. I shall explain this more fully in the chronological notes concerning Stephen.

#### Line 8.—“He carried out two ordinations in the month of December.”

These words indicate that the Roman pontiff Lucius presided over the Church for more than a full year, since he held two ordinations in the month of December.

Our chronology is therefore confirmed. According to the text of the Librarian, after Cornelius’s death, with thirty-five days assigned to the vacancy of the see, the first ordination held by Lucius as Roman pontiff falls in December of the same year, 252, counting from 14 September, the day on which Cornelius won the palm of martyrdom by being beheaded, to 19 October, when Lucius, previously the vicar, was elected Cornelius’s successor. The second ordination falls in December of the year 253, and Lucius’s martyrdom falls on the third day before the Nones of March in the year 254.

Thus, from his ordination to the episcopate—which must be assigned to Sunday, the Kalends of December in the year 250, when he was appointed vicar by Cornelius—his episcopate amounts to three years, three months, and the same number of days, as I demonstrated in the chronological notes.

### [Note: Column 1390A]

#### Line 1.—“Lucius, a Tuscan by nationality.”

Eusebius, *History* VII.2; Optatus of Milevis, Book II *Against Parmenianus*; St. Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, in the *Chronicle*; St. Augustine, Letter 163; and St. Cyprian in his letter to the same Lucius, worthy of so great a man, all report his succession to the pontifical see immediately after Cornelius.

### [Note: Column 1390A]

#### Line 3.—“He was sent into exile; afterward, etc.”

He was immediately driven into exile by the persecutions, but was restored to his Church very soon, by God’s gift. The African Church, which had written to him concerning his election and exile, did not fail to send him letters also concerning his return.

After announcing the joy common among the Roman faithful at the restoration of their pontiff, and the wishes of the Africans, who desired to increase the force of that joy by enjoying his presence, the letter declares that the African bishops were sending representatives to him. These representatives would bear letters testifying that they came to share with the Romans not only the joy but also the service of charity, and that they were interpreters of the faithful obedience which the bishops from overseas, together with their peoples, rendered to him.

The letters also state that, since the devil’s cunning attacked the orthodox only because he already held the heretics and schismatics under his power, God permitted that evil spirit to raise up persecutors. By attacking Catholics alone and leaving the sectarians in peaceful repose, those persecutors served, even against their will, God’s purpose: that the true Church might thereby be recognized, to the shame of the innovators.

This is an exceptionally excellent testimony to the steadfast faith continually asserted throughout the Church of God concerning the pre-eminence of this Roman see. Even those who were stirred up to destroy it served at every moment to confirm its authority:

“For us, then, I and my colleagues and the whole brotherhood send these letters to you through representatives, dearest brother, and, presenting our joy to you in writing, we set forth the faithful services of charity ... whence secular power suddenly burst forth, so that, to confound heretics and blunt their force, the Lord might show what the Church is, who is its one bishop chosen by divine ordination, who are the presbyters joined with the bishop in priestly honor, who is the united and true people of Christ, bound together by the charity of the Lord’s flock; who are those whom the enemy attacks; and, on the other hand, those whom the devil spares as his own.” (Cyprian, Letter 71.)

## 23. Lucius, a Tuscan by nationality

[Note: CB: “a Roman by nationality, son of Porphyrius”], from the city of Lucca, son of Lucinus, held the see for three years, eight months, and three days. [Note: B: “two years less.”] He was crowned with martyrdom.

He lived during the time of Gallus and Volusian, up to the third consulship of Valerian and the consulship of Gallicanus. [Notes: B: “from the consulships of Gallus and Volusian to those of Valerian and Gallienus.” C: “the second”; C: “Gallienus in the consulship.”] [Note: See Baronius, years 255 and 257.]

He was sent into exile, but afterward, by the will of God, returned unharmed to the Church. He ordered that in every place two presbyters and three deacons should not leave the bishop, for the sake of ecclesiastical testimony.

He too was beheaded by Valerian on the third day before the Nones of March. [Note: CB: “the fourth day before the Nones.”]

As he was proceeding to his passion, he granted authority over the whole Church to his archdeacon Stephen. He carried out two ordinations in the month of December: four presbyters, four deacons, and three bishops in various places. [Note: CB: “seven.”]

He too was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, and the episcopate remained vacant for thirty-five days.

### Catalogue under Liberius

Lucius: three years, eight months, and ten days. He lived during the time of Gallus and Volusian, up to the third consulship of Valerian and the second consulship of Gallienus. He was in exile and afterward, by the will of God, returned unharmed to the Church. He died on the third day before the Nones of March, under the consuls mentioned above.
