### [Editorial Apparatus]

Line 1. In Reg. and Flor. sec., “Jovius”; in the two Florentine manuscripts and Reg., “seven years, five months, two days.” Lines 4–10: the words “in his time … was beheaded” are absent from the Vatican manuscripts, the two Florentine manuscripts, and Reg. Line 10: “that they should use vestments”; “that” is absent in Vat., which reads “in a consecrated garment.” Florent. retains “that” but reads “should not use.” The Florentine manuscript adds at the end: “and the presbyters presided from the consulship of Maximus and Glabrio II until that of Tuscus and Bassus, and from the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus until the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, at which time there was the greatest persecution under Decius.” Florent. adds: “which is soon repeated in the entry on Sixtus as well.”

At Penia, from the Cavensis manuscript.

Line 6: “two bishops, Honorius and Castus, and three deacons, Xistus, Dionysius, and Gaius.” In the same place: “etc.” Line 9: “he himself alone.”

### [Note: Col. 1391B]

Line 4. “In his time, etc.” The material contained in this note of B is absent from several manuscript codices, as Luca Holstenius noted in the margin. It nevertheless seems certain that the earlier words concerning his return from exile entered this passage from the Acts of Lucius. I confess that I do not know from where the rest was taken by the person who interpolated the *Book of the Pontiffs* at this point. I could not find it in his Acts as presented in Vatican manuscript 5771. Indeed, in that manuscript it is instead reported that Stephen was beheaded in the cemetery of Callistus, at his own episcopal seat.

### [Note: Col. 1391B]

Line 10. “He established that priests and Levites should not use sacred garments in daily use, except only in church.” Stephen forbade presbyters and deacons to wear sacred vestments in ordinary daily use. [Col. 1391C] The Vandals are mentioned in this connection because they made garments for themselves from sacred hangings and vestments. Sigebert, under the year 451: “When the Vandals were raging in Africa, while they were burning the divine books in this manner, they made garments for themselves from the sacred hangings and vestments.” Victor of Utica, *On the Vandal Persecution*, charges Proculus, an envoy of Genseric, king of the Vandals, with making shirts and trousers for himself from altar hangings.

### [Note: Col. 1391C]

Line 4. “In his time he was deported into exile; afterward, by the will of God, he returned unharmed to the Church.” Stephen was elected amid the very fervor of the edicts confirmed by Gallus and Volusianus, perhaps also while the Novatians were pleading their case; by order of the emperors he was sent into exile with the rest of the clergy. But when Valerian assumed the imperial power, whether through the customary clemency by which those especially who had been punished with exile were recalled by newly elected emperors, or through some inclination toward the Christians, Stephen then [Col. 1392B] returned free.

Dionysius speaks of the cessation of this persecution in his letter, preserved by Eusebius, book VII, chapter 1, when he reports both the common sufferings, the things the Christians endured, and the peace that followed:

> “After these things came war and famine, which indeed we endured together with the pagans. The evils that afflicted us we alone endured. But the evils that they inflicted upon one another, and that they themselves suffered, we also bore a share of. Yet once again that peace delighted us, which Christ granted to us alone.”

Eusebius, book VII, chapter 10, in describing the beginning of the reign of the emperor Valerian, commends his benevolence toward Christians in these words:

> “He was gentle and kindly toward the servants of God. For none of the preceding rulers—not even those who are said to have openly professed Christianity—embraced our people with such humanity and benevolence as he displayed at the beginning of his reign. His entire household abounded in devout people and seemed to be a church of God.”

Meanwhile, [Col. 1392C] one must observe that the *Book of the Pontiffs* customarily records repeated confessions by the pontiffs in connection with the Novatian schism, in order by this title also to demonstrate the legitimate succession in the chair of Peter, while the Novatians, the authors of the persecutions, remained secure without any conspicuous proof of confession of faith, whereas the distinguished pontiffs and the other faithful were harassed by the savage storm of the persecutors.

Lines 7 and 8. “There, in the prison at the Arch of Stella, he held a synod, etc.” Perhaps the place was indicated in this way because of a sign or some other accident. Nor did the confinement of the prison prevent the bishops from holding a synod. Indeed, the very severity of Decian edicts, which particularly persecuted the higher clergy, may have provided the occasion for its celebration. Several bishops could have met with Pope Stephen—those whom the tranquility previously granted to the Church had gathered in Rome, or those who, being presbyters of Rome, were confined in the same prison.

In this sense Cyprian wrote at the same time, in Letter 82:

> “What, then, it is fitting for us to observe hereafter, before the proconsul delivers judgment against me concerning the confession of the name of God, we shall arrange together, with the Lord instructing us.”

Thus also Saint Peter of Alexandria, at the end of his life, made a similar arrangement, as the Acts published by Combefisius and cited above report. The *Book of the Pontiffs* teaches that pontiffs were accustomed, at least at the end of life, to give a general instruction to the archdeacon, in the entries on Cornelius, Lucius, and Sixtus II. Thus Liberius, when he was about to be deported into exile, summoned the clergy and appointed Damasus as his vicar, commending him in the *Life of Damasus* in these words:

> “You have as your vicar your brother and fellow presbyter Damasus, a most faithful man and adorned with every virtue. You publicly praise his prudence and steadfastness; therefore, with him going before you after God, use him in all your ways.”

Alternatively, we may say that Saint Stephen did not hold a synod in an ordinary and criminal prison, but in a crypt, where he was hiding because of the persecution that had arisen; this *Book of the Pontiffs* certainly designates as a voluntary prison. Perhaps it derived this account from the Acts of Saint Stephen in Surius, which testify that “in the crypts he continually celebrated Masses and councils as a martyr, and there his head was cut off.”

### [Note: Col. 1393B]

Line 3. “Valerian III.” Baronius proves that this is erroneous under the year of Christ 260, number 2. For in Valerian’s fourth consulship, the more accurately revised Acts of Saint Stephen were recorded.

### CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

The principal catalogues published in the *Prolegomena* are understood to agree with the paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul. For the ancient Liberian catalogue agrees with the other older Italian catalogues in its years and months, once the copyist’s error has been removed: the copyist inadvertently added the sign for ten to the Farfensis alone and subtracted one from the Cavensis alone. The number of days in the Bergomatis was corrupted into eleven instead of fifteen, because the final stroke of the numeral for five had been worn away, while the copyist of the Liberian catalogue had doubled the numeral sign. The Italian witnesses otherwise give fifteen days, in agreement with the Leonine paintings.

These agree entirely with the Belgian catalogue of Papebrochius, two of the Colbertine witnesses, and the fourth Ocriculensis codex, all of which retain the same epoch, which follows from the paintings of Saint Paul and from the Liberian and Italian catalogues: namely, four years, two months, and fifteen days.

The day of the martyrdom and burial of blessed Stephen is recorded in the Liberian-era document cited above and published in the *Prolegomena*, column 972 onward from Bucherius, as well as in the Church archives and in the *Book of the Pontiffs*, on 3 August: “On the fourth day before the Nones of August, Stephen at Callistus.” The consuls expressly given in the Liberian catalogue, Valerian III and Gallienus II, indicate the year 255 of the common Christian era; the numbers of the consulships were written at the end of the predecessor’s entry. But just as I noted that the reading there should be “Valerian II and Gallienus,” so here I affirm that it should be written “Valerian IV and Gallienus III,” so as to indicate the year 257. I shall prove this in the following section from the pontificate of Sixtus, compared with the Acts and the proconsular dates of the martyrdom of Saint Cyprian, as well as from Cyprian’s letters.

Starting, then, from 3 August of the year 257 and reckoning backward four years, two months, and fifteen days, we arrive at the day of the ordination of blessed Stephen. He was promoted to the episcopate by Saint Pope Lucius, whose archdeacon he was, in order to exercise a vicarious administration in Rome while Pope Lucius himself was driven into exile.

It must nevertheless be noted that Stephen’s first appointment as archdeacon is narrated in different terms from his second appointment by Lucius. In the first election, Cornelius entrusted Stephen with all the goods of the Church; in the second, Lucius entrusted him with all the power of the Church. It is [Col. 1394A] indicated clearly enough that Cornelius entrusted to the archdeacon Stephen the vessels, wealth, and temporal goods of the Church, to be distributed as alms to the poor and to relieve their need—just as Stephen himself is said to have given Sixtus, his archdeacon, authority over all the vessels of the Church, or the treasury, as stated above in the text.

Lucius, however, who had promoted that same Stephen from the archdiaconate to the episcopal order in May of the year 253, as may be inferred from the chronology, gave him authority over the whole Church, so that he might be at once archdeacon in the distribution of the Church’s property and vicarious bishop in supplying the functions of priestly office during Lucius’s absence or detention, when he had been ordered into exile.

The confusion that entered either the Acts of the seventh persecution, extending from Decius to Valerian, or the abridgers of the Acts relating to that same persecution under the briefly reigning emperors Decius, Gallus, Volusianus, and Aemilianus, wrongly assigned to the day of blessed Lucius’s progress toward martyrdom this delegation of vicarious power, by which Stephen was taken from the archdiaconate and appointed assistant bishop. It should instead be assigned to the period of that same exile mentioned in the letters of blessed Cyprian.

This should not seem surprising: the abridgers of the Acts, living at a distant time, could fall into such confusion. For Orosius, book VII, chapter 14, when discussing these same times—separated from his own by no more than about 140 years—wrongly confuses Gallus with Hostilianus, as Pagius noted in his criticism of Baronius under the year 252, number 14.

As Lucius was about to depart from Rome into a brief exile—although Pagius rightly refuses to reduce it to a period of six months, as Pearson attempts without justification to infer from the adverb “recently,” which Cyprian also used to denote a period of three years, as Pagius observes under the year 252, number 17—around the summer or late spring [Col. 1394C] of the year 253, he marked the archdeacon Stephen with the episcopal character and granted him authority to govern the Roman Church in his absence under the title of vicar.

At nearly the same time that Lucius was being driven into exile, news arrived from Pannonia that Aemilianus, commander of the Moesian frontier, had been acclaimed emperor by that army. Trebonianus Gallus marched against him from Rome and, engaging him in battle at Interamna, was slain. Under the emperor Aemilianus, that local persecution, which Gallus had not interrupted at Rome, began to proceed more mildly.

Aemilianus’s brief reign, however—barely lasting three or four months through the summer of 253—gave way to the rule of Valerian. Indeed, this occurred in the year 253 of the Christian era, before autumn, as shown by a coin of the Aegaeans in Cilicia struck under Aemilianus and bearing the era ΘqΣ (299), which can be seen in the Corrarian Museum and which Vaillant published in his second edition.

For the Aegaean era begins in the autumn of the year 706 from the foundation of Rome, under the consulship of Calenus and Vatinius. It is established that Caesar, passing from Syria through Cilicia, conferred many benefits on the cities of that province, as Hirtius testifies. The Aegaeans, who commemorated the founding of their city by Alexander the Great and used the Macedonian era beginning in autumn, thereafter reckoned their years from this benefaction of Caesar. Their year 299 corresponds to the summer months of the year 253 of the common Christian era.

Valerian’s reign followed Aemilianus’s four-month rule beginning in September, as Lydiatus correctly establishes. This is confirmed by coins struck by those same Aegaeans of Cilicia for the new Augustus Valerian, bearing the letter T, indicating the three-hundredth year of the previously mentioned era, which at that time began in autumn.

How great was Valerian’s humanity and benevolence toward the Christians at the beginning of his reign is testified by Dionysius’s letter to Hermammon, which is to be read in Eusebius, *History*, book VII, chapter 10. This benevolence, however, was of no practical benefit to our Christians: no law was enacted for their relief, and the prohibition imposed by the earlier emperors was not abolished. Magistrates accustomed under Decius to inflict the most extreme punishments upon us were able, under the still unrepealed laws of the Antonine emperors, to condemn Pope Lucius and many martyrs to death once they had been denounced. See above, in the notes to the Life of Soter, columns 1241–1248.

At Rome, greater severity was to be expected from the magistrates. Valerius Maximus had been prefect of the city in the year 252 and is mentioned in the Acts of Pope Cornelius. In this year 253, the year in which we say that Lucius was exiled, he held the ordinary consulship; and in the following year, 254, he again administered the prefecture of the city at the beginning of Valerian’s reign. He had been prefect of the city under the censor, and his colleague in pronouncing the capital sentence against Cornelius, as the Acts of Cornelius’s passion demonstrate.

It is futile, however, to attack the credibility of the Acts on the basis of an apparent anachronism in their description of Cornelius’s martyrdom at Rome, [Col. 1395B] since the chronological discrepancies are dissolved by the observations already presented, and the events of the martyrdom are confirmed by the documents brought forward by Schelestratius, *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, dissertation 2, chapter 6, number 7.

The chronology of the times and the history therefore agrees with the figures of the principal catalogues and with the paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul, if we say that Stephen, Lucius’s archdeacon, was ordained bishop in order to supply his functions when Lucius was about to depart into exile, under the consulship of Volusianus II and Maximus—although the Liberian catalogue corruptly gives “Maximinus”—on Sunday, Pentecost, 23 May, according to the total number of days in the Bergomatis catalogue; or on Sunday, the Ascension, 23 May, according to the Liberian catalogue, which counts twenty-one days; or on the eighth day after the Ascension and the third before Pentecost, according to the other catalogues, which give Stephen’s episcopate as lasting fifteen days beyond four years and two months.

In the year 254, under the consulship of Valerian Augustus II and Gallienus, Lucius was crowned with martyrdom on 3 March. After the see had remained vacant for thirty-five days, according to the *Book of the Pontiffs*, Stephen was chosen from his position as vicar to succeed Lucius and ascended the Roman chair on Sunday of the Passion, 9 April, so that he might celebrate the Paschal festivals, which that year fell on 23 April.

In the next consulship, that of Valerian III and Gallienus II, in the year 255 of Christ, Stephen appointed Sixtus as vicar. Sixtus later succeeded him, as we shall show in his own entry.

Finally, in the year 257, under the consulship of Valerian IV and Gallienus III, Stephen, seated in his own episcopal see at the Catacombs, in the cemetery of Callistus, was beheaded on 2 August. According to the better authorities, he had completed four years, two months, and fifteen days from his episcopal ordination; according to the Bergomatis catalogue, eleven days; and according to the Liberian catalogue, twenty-one days. He had spent most of these years and months partly as Lucius’s vicar and partly as his successor, as we have explained.

I know that Pagius, in his criticism of Baronius, attacks these vicariates on nearly every page dealing with these years, although Papebrochius and many writers on pontifical history accept them. Yet Pagius merely presents bare assertions and pronounces with a sort of dictatorial authority:

> “Papebrochius is not to be heeded; the vicariates are fictitious. Lucius’s life could extend to 4 March of the year 254; Pearson is to be preferred,”

and with Pearson he dares to guess, although no suitable witness asserts it, that “the entire pontificate of Lucius consisted of five months and ten days from his ordination.” Thus confidently he writes under the year 252, number 12.

With due respect to the learned man, however, I maintain that the vicariates were both customary and ought to be accepted; that Papebrochius, who asserts them, should be heeded; that Lucius’s life should be extended to 3 March of the year 253; and that Pearson, who maintains otherwise without any suitable witnesses, should be rejected.

As for the vicariates, I ask Pagius to answer the arguments so often proposed and here to be repeated, strengthened by additional proofs and examples. Pagius readily accepts a vicariate under the apostle Peter, to whom he assigns Linus as vicar for several years in the year 65, number 2. Thus, in the first century, under the very prince of the apostles and founder of the Roman see, the use of vicars was established.

He must acknowledge that the use of vicars continued within the bounds of the Western patriarchate even in the fourth century, since Augustine demonstrates its use by his own example. Indeed, he shows by his own action that an abuse had crept into the Church of Hippo beyond the limits of legitimate usage: the election of vicar bishops with future succession. This happened in his own case, when Valerius chose him as assistant and when he himself took Heraclius as an assistant. He ordered this to be entered in the public records of the Church by the notaries in Letter 110, which I cited above in the notes to Saint Cletus and Evaristus.

The Roman Church, mistress of all, neither practiced this abuse of choosing an assistant bishop during the life of the bishop with future succession, nor tolerated it in others. But it did admit the legitimate use of appointing a vicar without the right of succession, for the benefit of the Church, even to perform pontifical functions, especially when persecution was pressing. It retained this practice also in times of peace, for the gravest reasons, and transmitted it to later ages, as we too experience.

It is truly astonishing that so learned a man should have been so hostile to vicar bishops in the second and third centuries—although the continuity of the practice is established when the dates of the episcopates are carefully considered—while he is forced to admit that in the first and fourth centuries of Christ, and afterward, the same custom of appointing and employing a vicar bishop existed even within the territory of this Roman, or Western, patriarchate wherever necessity, or an advantage closely approaching necessity, so advised.

I now add that Pagius was compelled by the letters of blessed Cyprian to admit vicar bishops even in the third century and at this very time of Cornelius, Lucius, and Stephen, of whom we are speaking, even within the territory of the Western patriarchate, which certainly included the African Church.

For, along with Baronius under the year 254, number 36, and in his own work under the year 250, number 17, he readily acknowledges that the bishops Caldonianus and Herculanus, Cyprian’s colleagues, together with the presbyter Numidicus—whom Cyprian had recently added to the clergy of Carthage—were sent to Carthage by Saint Cyprian while he was in exile. They were “appointed, together with Rogatianus, as vicars to perform his functions, so that they might meet the needs of the brethren at their expense, and also distinguish their ages and merits, etc.” He also admits that Cyprian wrote to these vicars of his in Letter 41, number 37 in Pamelianus, instructing them to excommunicate Felicissimus, etc.

Here, then, even in the third century, we find bishops employed as vicars and colleagues by Bishop Cyprian to perform pastoral functions in his diocese in his name. Cyprian calls them vicars, and Pagius is compelled to call them so. He may object that they were rather judges delegated for particular acts. I reply that this is precisely what the office of a vicar entails: a person delegated by a bishop, at his pleasure, to perform those acts which the delegating bishop himself would perform by his own right in his own diocese, whether acts of jurisdiction or of order, insofar as the delegate is capable of them, for as long as the delegation of the vicar continues.

For we recognize no other kind of vicars during the lifetime of a pontiff than those delegated with such powers, without any agreement or right of succession. It often happened, nevertheless, that the clergy chose as successors the very men who had been assistants and delegated vicars by their predecessor, since they had learned by experience their prudence in government and their virtues worthy of a bishop.

The same thing occurred in several Churches of this Western patriarchate, when assistants were promoted to succession by the votes of the clergy after the bishop’s death—assistants who had been sent by the Roman Church to help him or had been added by the bishop himself.

The Church of Milan offered a distinguished example in the fourth century in Ambrose and Simplicianus. [Col. 1397A]

> “For this Roman presbyter, a man of outstanding learning and proven integrity, as Spondanus, Baronius’s abridger, briefly summarized under the year 374, number 3, was sent by Pope Damasus to take charge of his new office—namely, the episcopate of Milan, which Ambrose, formerly a catechumen, assumed as bishop within eight days—with such a fortunate outcome that the catechumen was immediately transformed into a bishop and the disciple into a teacher of the Church, and that he joined the monastic life with the duties and offices of the clergy in the administration of the episcopate.”

Although Damasus sent this assistant of Ambrose, and more than a vicar—namely, a teacher and director—with episcopal character, without any agreement or law of succession, the Church of Milan, after long experience of his worth, nevertheless chose this same man as Ambrose’s successor and its bishop after Ambrose’s death.

There is therefore no reason for Pagius to be angry, from the first to the fourth century, at admitting vicars of the Roman pontiffs. He sees them accepted, appointed, and delegated in so many examples throughout the Western patriarchate, properly and beneficially, to assist in governing that Church and to act in its name.

Finally, from the example of Ambrose and Simplicianus, in addition to the practice of vicars, the reader will, I hope, gather confirmation of the opinion I mentioned above in the notes to the Life of Saint Eleutherius, column 1252: namely, that a custom was established by right whereby, for the benefit and advancement of the Christian people, presbyters were chosen and sent from the urban clergy by the Roman pontiff to the Churches of the provinces, either promoted to those episcopates or sent to form bishops there in the discipline of the Roman Church.

As for the vicariate of blessed Stephen, the Life of Saint Pope Lucius contains clear testimony in the letters sent by Cyprian and cited above in Sommier’s notes to Lucius. There Saint Martyr Cyprian expressly names Stephen first as the vicar and then as the successor of the blessed martyrs Cornelius and Lucius: he who became their vicar and successor. He combines the titles “vicar” and “successor.”

But enough concerning vicars, and concerning the chronology of blessed Stephen and the neighboring pontiffs.

### HISTORICAL NOTES

Line 2. “He is crowned with martyrdom.” In Baronius’s *Annals* one may see that the Acts of this martyrdom were received by both the Latin and the Greek Church; their authenticity is defended by Schelestratius, *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, dissertation 2, chapter 7, numbers 2–5.

From Firmilianus’s letter to Cyprian—number 75 in Pamelianus’s edition—we learn that when the letter was written, as winter was approaching, about twenty-two years after the death of Severus Alexander, whose murder occurred on 18 March 235, that is, around autumn of the year 256, Stephen was still seated as Roman pontiff. According to the Acts mentioned above, he died as a martyr, beheaded at his own episcopal seat, on the fourth day before the Nones of August, under the consulship of Valerian IV and Gallienus III, that is, in the year 257 of the common Christian era.

The text, however, reads: “He was in the time of Valerian, Gallicanus, and Maximus, until Valerian III and Gallicanus II.” The reading from the Acts must be corrected by restoring the words “in the time of Valerian and Gallienus,” and it must be fully restored from the Liberian catalogue as follows:

“He was in the time of Valerian and Gallienus, from the consulship of Volusianus and Maximus”—that is, the year of his ordination to the episcopate in order to exercise a vicarious administration in Rome, the year 253 of Christ—“until Valerian IV and Gallienus III,” the year 257 of Christ, in which he died as a martyr, as I explained in the chronological notes.

The era of his pontificate may nevertheless also be derived from the consulship of Valerian II and Gallienus. Under these emperors, when Lucius died on the third day before the Nones of March, his successor Stephen celebrated the first Easter of his administration under the same consuls, in the year 254 of Christ.

Line 4. “In his time he was deported into exile.” [Col. 1398A] From this we understand why Sixtus II was ordained bishop by Stephen to carry out the office of vicar, according to the customary rule mentioned so often.

Indeed, while Glabrio and Maximus II were holding the consulship in the year 256, Stephen seems to have endured a brief exile, since at that time investigations were being conducted against several people whom he had baptized and whom Stephen followed into martyrdom the following year with his own crown.

The pagans seized upon the occasion for their investigations, as we may suspect, from the councils held on questions concerning baptism. See the notes on these matters.

Line 5. “He was sent into prison with nine presbyters, two bishops, Honorius and Castus, and three deacons, Xistus, Dionysius, and Gaius, etc.” Above, in the entry on Lucius, we read the decree that two presbyters and three deacons should not abandon the bishop anywhere. From the capture of his companions together with the pontiff, we learn that this discipline was preserved under Stephen.

According to the custom introduced under Decius, the persecution was directed chiefly against the clergy, [Col. 1398B] as the rescript of Valerian to the senate shows. Saint Cyprian cites it in his letter to his successor, number 82 in Pamelianus’s edition:

> “Valerian sent a rescript to the senate”—in the year 258, after he had departed from Rome and reached Antioch—“that bishops, presbyters, and deacons should be punished; senators, distinguished men, and Roman knights, however, were to lose their rank and also be stripped of their property.”

See the elder Pagius under the year 257 and the younger Pagius in the entry on Stephen, number 8.

Line 7. “There, in prison, he held a synod.” This was with the bishops, presbyters, and deacons detained with him. Several other councils were held concerning the question of the baptism of heretics. Their history is clarified by the *Annals* of Baronius, the elder Pagius, and other ecclesiastical historians.

Line 8. “All the vessels of the Church.” This follows the custom of his predecessors, Cornelius and Stephen, which was also preserved by their successors.

### Line 10.—

He established that priests and Levites, etc., should not use sacred vestments in daily life. That the use of sacred vestments [Col. 1398C], and their distinction from ordinary clothing, was introduced from the beginning of the Church is demonstrated by those things which the apostles drew from the divine institutions of the Old Testament as figures of the New, and handed down to the Church.

They relate that the *petalum*, or golden plate, was customarily worn by the apostles James and John as a badge of priesthood: Eusebius, *History*, book V, chapter 24; Polycrates, bishop of the Asians, in his letter to Victor; Jerome, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; Epiphanius, in the heresy of the Nazarenes and in *Against Heresies* 78; and Rufinus—authors noted by Valesius in his notes on Eusebius. Valesius also adds that the same thing was handed down concerning Mark the Evangelist by the writer of his *Passion*.

I have explained more fully elsewhere that this plate, or *petalum*, was fitted to the forehead and bound around with a ribbon or band, which the ancient Latins expressed by the name *mitra*, and which is now used in the consecration of bishops. I did so in a short work on the sacred vestments of Christian priesthood, composed some years ago on the occasion of transferring [Col. 1398D] the body of Saint Leo the Great, but not yet published.

Sacred ministries, therefore, were already in use among Christians. Thus we read, in no. 8, that Sixtus I of that name commanded that consecrated vessels should not be touched except by ministers. From the decree of Soter we likewise know—above, no. 13—that consecrated cloths were used in the ministry among the faithful, and that even consecrated virgins were forbidden to touch them there.

The Church had drawn from the institutions of the ancient Law the admonition that Levites and priests approaching the divine service should come in a purer kind of external clothing, so that they might bring with them thoughts and intentions undefiled by any earthly stain, but almost heavenly ones (Philo, *On Monarchy*, book II). Likewise, as Jerome testifies, the washing of the hands signifies the purification of works, so that the word of God may be fulfilled in them (book II of his commentary on Matthew, chapter 5).

For this reason sacred interpreters also observe that the washing of the feet was performed by Christ the Lord before the sacred mysteries that he was instituting, even though the apostles had just come from the [Col. 1399A] Paschal supper of the ancient institution. To that supper they were required to come girded in a particular manner and holding staffs in their hands, to signify the Lord’s passage.

Since it was customary to approach the banquets of honorable men dressed in white—as in the evangelical parable in Matthew, chapter 22—not without reason and with considerable significance those examples, together with the admonitions of the institutions and the care owed to cleanliness, were also suggested in the laws governing clothing.

That Christians newly raised from the baptismal font were to be clothed in white by solemn rite, from the beginnings of the Church down to our own times, is taught by the Acts of the Martyrs and the Sacramentaries, as well as by the very name of the Paschal week, which in the ancient expression we call *in albis*, “in white garments.”

Recent and ancient writers explain the same practice, including Venantius Fortunatus, Paulinus, and others cited by René Laurent de la Barre in his commentaries on Tertullian’s *On the Crown of the Soldier*. There the Carthaginian presbyter, enumerating traditions not yet committed to writing, which we defend solely by the protection of tradition and without any written [Col. 1399B] instrument, begins with the sacred ceremonies already received by the Church in the rite of solemn baptism:

> “To begin with baptism: water is approached,” etc.

The sacred text of the Apocalypse also supports this tradition, displaying the companions of the Lamb in white garments.

It must therefore be acknowledged that, from the beginning of the Church, those initiated into Christian priesthood prepared themselves for divine service with a special form of dress, separated from daily use. At that time the Church had also instituted that laypeople and infants approaching entry into the Church through the sacrament of baptism should be adorned with a white robe.

Some derive even this practice from the example of the Lord: when, after the typical supper and before the institution of the Eucharist, he proceeded to wash the feet, he put aside his garments and wished to take up a towel, girding himself with an ornament prepared not only for cleanliness but for cleansing and wiping, as a symbol of ministry.

For this reason our subdeacons too, who are assigned to cleanse the vessels of the sacrifice, are prescribed to carry a small cloth in the left hand, according to the ancient *Roman Order* [Col. 1399C] VI in Mabillon; and in no. 35 of this *Book of the Pontifical*, linen cloths (*pallae linostimae*) are mentioned as being used on the left by deacons.

We have already seen above the glass patens and silver vessels intended for sacrificial use. Why not vestments as well, since this had been commanded by the Lord long before for the high priest, priests, and Levites of the Mosaic Church? Indeed, we know that even the gentiles adopted it by imitation and transferred it to their own priesthoods.

Among the Syrians, according to their ancestral rite, a magnificent ornament was used for the worship of the sun. Herodian censures its excessive luxury in book V of his account of Elagabalus, when he relates that, on his first arrival from Syria in Italy, that young prince brought it with him:

> “He celebrated the worship of the ancestral deity to whom he had been dedicated with superfluous dances” (and we know from the divine writings that these were wrongly transferred to the profane superstitions of the nations, although they had been properly used by the most religious king David before the ark of the Lord), “adopting a luxurious dress, woven with purple, and adorned with gold, necklaces, [Col. 1399D] and bracelets; he also wore crowns made in the manner of a tiara, decorated with gold and precious stones, and had a form midway between a Phoenician robe and Median attire.”

On an ancient gem, which I would compare with the most precious objects, we see elegantly expressed in relief the bust of Elagabalus, the natural colors of the gem having been skillfully accommodated by the artist. This gem is preserved in the museum of the most distinguished and learned prelate M. Ant. Ansidaeus, who, after rendering outstanding service in both the more severe and the more elegant disciplines through various stages of office, was serving as assessor in the supreme tribunal of the Sacred Inquisition.

From this we can gather the form of the Phoenician robe described by Herodian. If it is compared with the pontifical *cappa*, as it is called—the kind we displayed above, in the case of Pope Pius, from an ancient painting in the Christian cemetery among the martyrs’ crypts, no. 12, together with Aringhius, and the kind still customary among bishops, as also among the other priests and ministers who sing in the choir—[Col. 1400A] we can readily gather and conjecture that it was once composed of the Levites’ ephod and the priestly tiara, or head-covering, sewn together into a single garment. It was transferred from Palestine and Syria by the first founders of the Church into other regions and handed over to the ministers of the sanctuary.

But there will be a more suitable occasion elsewhere to discuss the origin and form of sacred vestments. Here it is enough to recognize that sacred vestments were distinguished and separated from ordinary ones, so that, in the age with which we are concerned, Christian priests and ministers approached divine service equipped with certain cloths, garments, and ornaments reserved exclusively for sacred actions—even if those cloths, garments, and ornaments did not differ greatly in form from the clothing, coverings, and adornments customarily used for other purposes by the same peoples among whom they lived.

Who would say that the consecrated cloths so often mentioned in the preceding sections were indiscriminately used for other purposes, when even consecrated virgins were forbidden to touch them?

I have already mentioned, together with Liberatus in chapter 20 of the *Breviary*, that, according to the ancient institution of the Alexandrian Church, the successor bishop was accustomed to receive the pallium of blessed Mark the Evangelist [Col. 1400B] from the body of his predecessor bishop with his own hands and to place it around his own neck. Who would dare to confuse such a sacred pallium with the everyday pallia of philosophers and Christians?

No one will deny that the frontal plate of the same evangelist Mark, as well as those used by the apostles John and James and described shortly before with Eusebius, Jerome, and Epiphanius, were made sacred to God by those same bishops through some sign of dedication and invocation of the divine name.

Tertullian traces back to traditions contemporary with the origin of the Church our custom of touching the forehead with the sign of the cross at every advance and promotion, at every entrance and exit, in dressing, putting on shoes, bathing, meals, lamps, beds, seats—in every activity through which our way of life is exercised.

By this sign of our dedication, which encompasses the more important mysteries of our [Col. 1400C] faith, we devote every act of our life to God. In the consecration of altars and churches we use chrism, impressed with this sign upon the altar table and upon the walls.

For this reason coins struck by Constantine the Great display it impressed upon the altar—coins of the kind we preserve among our treasures. From this period, that is, from the age of Sylvester, dates the use of stone altars and the public liberty of Christian worship.

Already then, and from the apostolic age—the source from which Tertullian rightly derives the authority of custom and tradition—we preserve the impress of the Lord’s cross on sandals, cloths, stoles, pallia, coverings, plates, and the mitres of priests. This sign, sprinkled and consecrated by the blood of the spotless Lamb for the salvation of all, was not placed only upon our foreheads; that venerable sign is also found on the very instruments of the priesthood, often joined with other symbols of the Good Shepherd and of Christ the Lord performing signs, especially on the small vessels [Col. 1400D] made to contain the material of the sacrifice or to preserve the sacred chrism, and on such ministerial vessels, metal and glass chalices and patens as those described above in the section on Urbanus.

> “Let them see where lies the authority of the custom about which we are now especially inquiring,” says Tertullian in *On the Crown of the Soldier*, p. 334 of de la Barre’s edition. “Moreover, when it is asked why anything is observed, it is meanwhile established that it is observed.”

These signs are marks of things properly consecrated to God by Christian bishops. Just as they appear throughout the sacred furnishings, stores, and vessels of the Church—which, in these same sections, we read were entrusted by the bishop to the archdeacons—so they also appear on vestments. We are therefore compelled to regard and call these vestments sacred and to recognize them as separated from common use in the age of Stephen, who by his decree confirmed that ancient custom which he had received by tradition from his predecessors.

### Line 13.—

He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus. From there his sacred body was removed by Saint Paul I [Col. 1401A] together with the body of his successor Dionysius, when Paul established in his own buildings at the Campus Martius the *titulus* of Saints Stephen and Dionysius, otherwise called Saints Stephen and Sylvester. There he founded a monastery for monks and transferred the relics of both pontiffs and martyrs; they are preserved there, as is clear from the documents indicated above at the end of the notes on Blessed Anterus, which will be explained more fully below in the notes on the Life of Blessed Paul I.

We also stated in the earlier notes on Anterus that portions of those same relics, deposited there by Paul I, were transferred by Sergius II to the *titulus* called Saints Sylvester and Martin in the Mountains, or the *titulus* of Equitius. This is testified by an ancient marble tablet affixed there, at the descent from the steps of the presbytery to the hypogeum and underground church, which has been illuminated by the scholarly labors of several writers.

### Note: [Col. 1401A]

### Line 2.—

He was crowned with martyrdom. When the emperor Valerian [Col. 1401B], aware of what was happening, sent soldiers and had blessed Stephen arrested and led to the temple of Mars, where he was to be punished by beheading if he refused to sacrifice to the idol, the most blessed pontiff poured out a prayer to the Lord. Suddenly the shrine and the idol were struck from heaven and collapsed for the most part with a tremendous crash.

Then the terrified soldiers fled, leaving Stephen alone. Accompanied by his people, he withdrew to the cemetery of Lucina nearby. There, after again exhorting his companions to endure martyrdom, he offered sacrifice to Almighty God.

When Valerian heard this, he again sent soldiers to capture him. They found him offering sacrifice to God. Undaunted, steadfast, and fearless, he completed the mysteries he had begun and was beheaded in the same place before the altar, in his own seat, on the fourth day before the Nones of August, in the year 260.

There was then great mourning among the Christians because they had been deprived of so great a shepherd. They buried his body together with the very seat, sprinkled with his [Col. 1401C] blood, in the same crypt, which is in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, three miles from the City.

### Note: [Col. 1401C]

### Line 7.—

He held a synod. Protestants, and even some Catholics, believe that Stephen, by condemning the practice of Cyprian and the African bishops, as well as that of Firmilian and the Easterners, concerning the rebaptism of heretics, fell into extreme error and decreed that the baptism of all heretics—even if it had not been administered according to the Church’s customary and solemn form and rite—was valid and legitimate, and therefore was not to be repeated.

But this opinion is wholly improbable. For if Stephen had fallen into error, the whole Church in those times would have been in error. All the bishops, whether they supported Cyprian’s opinion or Stephen’s, were involved; yet, even according to the Protestants’ own hypothesis, both opinions were erroneous.

Moreover, Cyprian, in the cited letter to Pompeius, testifies that Stephen regarded the baptism of heretics [Col. 1401D] as valid because of the force and efficacy of the evangelical words by which it is conferred. Stephen, therefore, always supposed that baptism had to be conferred with evangelical words in order to be valid.

On this matter Schelestratius should be reread, part II of *Illustrated Antiquity*, dissertation 1, article 2, where he demonstrates at length that the entire question between Stephen and Cyprian concerned the baptism of heretics, on the supposition that they conferred it in the name of Christ, or of the Trinity.

### Note: [Col. 1401D]

### Line 7.—

He held a synod. The falling away of many Christians of every rank and condition during the persecutions had compelled the Church, under the preceding pontiffs, to prescribe rules for penitents by which they might expiate the crime they had committed and guard against relapse.

The faithful who possessed no ecclesiastical ministry or other public office and who had sacrificed to idols were to be deprived of the benefit of absolution and excluded from [Col. 1402A] communion until they had undergone the more rigorous trials of prolonged penance. Clerics, however, who had fallen into the same crime were compelled to undergo deposition, without hope of being restored to their own offices; the only result they could obtain from the penance they undertook was admission to lay communion.

All who were moved by the spirit of true repentance were bound by and obeyed these rules. Hypocrites, however, and those who were dissipated by worldly desires applied themselves to nothing more diligently than evading those same rules.

The restoration of peace to the Church—or, more accurately, its period of calm—at the beginning of Valerian’s reign and the pontificate of Blessed Stephen gave many who had been falsely reduced to the order of penitents an opportunity to assume rebellious attitudes. Some did so openly and publicly; others added frauds and schemes to evade the justice of the bishops or to abuse their clemency.

A certain Fortunatianus from Africa belonged to the first class. Although he had been deposed from the episcopate and Epictetus had been substituted in his place, he nevertheless [Col. 1402B] did not cease exercising the pontifical functions, to the great scandal of the faithful.

Cyprian opposed this evil by his authority, writing to that new bishop and to his people that they should no longer permit such a thing to be attempted, but should ensure that the Church’s rules were observed and should hold separated from the communion of the faithful those who transgressed those same rules.

Basilides and Martial, however—the former bishop of León and the latter bishop of Astorga, both deposed from the episcopate in Spain—fled to Stephen, the Roman pontiff, so that by his authority the rigor of the law, to which they had been compelled by the force of their provincial bishops to submit, might be relaxed in their favor.

They were heard at Rome and returned to their province with a favorable rescript. Since their case, however, had not been examined in adversarial judgment before the Roman See, but they had merely presented whatever account they wished in the absence of their accusers and with no one opposing their statements, the Churches of Spain judged that they should not be received [Col. 1402C] until they had obtained the support of the other Churches.

They therefore turned to the neighboring African Churches to consult them concerning so serious a matter, since Cyprian had secured for those Churches such a reputation for learning and discipline. They sent the bishops Felix and Sabinus, who had been substituted in the place of the others, together with letters and other documents concerning what had been done in the matter.

It was discovered that Basilides and Martial had rightly been deposed according to the decrees of blessed Pope Cornelius, which had been received throughout the universal Church. The Africans declared that those decrees had to be adhered to all the more firmly because these restless men, by adding apostasy to the charge of deceit and circumvention, had extorted an underhand concession from Stephen after fraudulently leading him toward clemency. This is clear from Cyprian’s letter 67, where he writes:

> “A validly completed ordination cannot be rescinded because Basilides, after his crimes had been exposed and his conscience had been laid bare even by his own confession, [Col. 1402D] went to Rome and deceived Stephen, our colleague, who was far away and ignorant of what had been done and of the concealed truth. The point is that Basilides’ crimes were not so much abolished as multiplied, since to his former sins was added the crime of deceit and circumvention. For the one who was carelessly deceived is not as culpable as the one who deceitfully practiced deception. … Nor could deceit have benefited Martial. … especially since long before this our colleague Cornelius, a peaceful and just priest, together with us and with all the bishops established throughout the whole world, had decreed that such men could indeed be admitted to perform penance, but were to be prohibited from ordination to the clergy and from priestly honor—a decision which the Lord had also honored by granting him martyrdom.”

Enemies of the Roman See and envious detractors of its authority make useless use of this response of the Africans to the Spanish bishops.

First, this [Col. 1403A] response proves nothing at all against the right and custom of appealing and coming from every part of the world to the Roman See to obtain justice or grace, since this supreme See has always been the dispenser of both.

Indeed—and this is the second point—the response itself presupposes that the right of appealing and fleeing to the tribunal of the Roman See was known and accepted by all. It notes that the distance did not prevent an appeal from being made to that same See: Stephen was far away.

Third, the response in fact asserts that the distance was the reason why the frauds fabricated by the apostates more easily deceived Stephen: “he deceived him, who was far away.” Yet, when it reproves the pontiff’s negligence in proceeding to a sentence of absolution without full knowledge of the facts, saying that he was ignorant of the truth, it does not deny that the judge who pronounced the sentence possessed competent authority.

Fourth, it also demonstrates that Stephen’s legitimate power was acknowledged. [Col. 1403B] He is accused only of negligence: “the one who was carelessly deceived is not so culpable”; the petitioner, however, is marked by the crime of a maliciously presented falsehood: “the one who deceitfully practiced deception.”

Fifth, the meaning of these letters is finally confirmed by the fact that they describe whatever Basilides obtained from Stephen as *obreptitious*. This term, taken from the subtleties of the jurists, signifies a quality attributed to letters or rescripts obtained from a legitimate judge concerning a favor, right, or concession by circumventing that same judge through concealment of the truth, whose expression would have been necessary for the validity of the rescript obtained.

This very point is expressed word for word in the letter of the Africans: “He deceived him, who was ignorant of the concealed truth; the one who was circumvented, who deceitfully practiced deception.”

There is, however, an outstanding demonstration from these responses of Saint Cyprian and the bishops of the African province to the Spaniards that excludes every doubt concerning the supreme authority of the Holy See. I say, an outstanding demonstration of authority exercised is found in Cyprian’s own [Col. 1403C] request directed to Pope Stephen, asking him to apply that same authority in a matter of equal weight and of very similar character, which had recently arisen in Gaul.

Marcianus, bishop of Arles, professed that he had joined the party of Novatian both in its heretical doctrine and in its communion of schism. The bishops of the neighboring provinces who had written to the Roman See about this matter also communicated it to the Church of Carthage in another letter addressed to Bishop Cyprian.

The sequence of events makes clear that they wrote to Blessed Cyprian because his reputation and the testimony of his esteem at the Roman See were well known. Cyprian therefore wrote to Pope Stephen in these terms (letter 68):

> “You ought to write a very full letter,” etc.

These words require no commentary to demonstrate the authority of the Roman See asserted in them: in defining doctrines of faith; in discipline and in confirming the custom received in the administration of the sacraments; in exercising the right of ecclesiastical government; and in necessarily selecting suitable means for preserving order and traditions.

We cannot, however, deny that the African Church at that time suffered a certain eclipse [Col. 1403D], when it attempted to claim for itself a particular light as though it were its own. In the particular Churches there is no such light other than that which the Sun of justice, Christ the Lord, loved and chose to spread over the universal Church, shining from the Roman See upon the others as from the center of the Christian world.

> “In the West the Sun of justice rises. You are the light of the world.”  
> Saint Jerome, letter 57.

The presumption of the African Church must therefore be considered as an occasion capable of producing a disturbance not unlike that which the poets imagine would be produced by the moon if it attempted to usurp the place of the sun and, with the order of nature disturbed, appointed itself arbiter of the world’s daylight:

[Col. 1404A]

> “Phoebe, opposing her brother,  
> will go forth, indignant at driving her chariot through the slanting sphere,  
> and will demand the day for herself; and the whole universe,  
> its bonds torn apart, will disturb the order of the world.”  
> Lucan, *Pharsalia*, book I, verse 77.

The whole matter came down to this. The Africans maintained that the baptism of heretics was null and invalid, regardless of the form and rite in which it was administered.

The evil became widespread, and it was said to have originated in the East. Perhaps it happened there that the baptism of certain heretics was not immediately rejected because they did not confer it according to the legitimate form; later, however, every kind of baptism administered by heretics was indiscriminately rejected under the false belief that had crept [Col. 1404B] in that no sacrament could exist outside the Catholic Church.

Dionysius of Alexandria, quoted by Eusebius, *History*, book VII, chapter 6, says:

> “It was not only the bishops in Africa who introduced this practice of rebaptizing heretics, but also, long before the memory of those bishops, their predecessors in Churches attended by very large numbers of people, and in synods of the brethren held both at Iconium and at Synnada and in many other places, this was decreed.”

The practice had become established in Africa before blessed Cyprian. He testifies that it had been defined in a provincial council under Agrippinus, the predecessor of the Donatus to whom Saint Cyprian succeeded:

> “This too Agrippinus, a man of blessed memory, established and confirmed after careful examination by a common council, together with his fellow bishops who at that time governed the Church of God in the province of Africa and Numidia.”  
> Saint Cyprian, letter 71.

Whatever, then, may have been the origin of the error and the evil, this much is perfectly clear: under the pontificate of Pope Stephen, two bishops no less distinguished for the holiness of their lives than for the dignity of the sees they held—namely, Saint Cyprian, primate of Africa, and Firmilian, metropolitan of Cappadocia—declared themselves proponents of this practice and opinion. [Col. 1404C]

Each of them convened synods in the provinces subject to him and communicated to Pope Stephen the decrees issued by those synods.

The African synod wrote to Pope Stephen in letter 74 among the Cyprianic letters:

> “We had especially to write and confer with your gravity and wisdom about that matter which concerns both priestly authority and the unity and dignity of the Catholic Church, which derive equally from the ordering of the divine dispensation: namely, that those who have been baptized outside, outside the Church, and defiled among heretics and schismatics by the pollution of profane water, ought to be baptized when they come to us and to the Church, which is one. For it is not enough to lay hands upon them to receive the Holy Spirit unless they also receive the baptism [Col. 1404D] of the Church. …
>
> “We have brought these matters to your conscience, dearest brother, both for the sake of our common honor and out of simple affection, believing that, in accordance with your religion and the truth of your faith, you too will approve what is both religious and true.
>
> “Nevertheless, we know that some people do not wish to abandon what they have once absorbed and do not easily change their position; but, while preserving the bond of peace and concord among colleagues, retain certain practices which they have once adopted among themselves. In this matter we neither use force against anyone nor impose a law,” etc.

And Firmilianus, in letter 75 preserved by Saint Cyprian, says:

> “Many of us gathered together at Iconium and confirmed with the greatest care that every baptism whatsoever performed outside the Church must be rejected.”

In response to these letters, Stephen wrote to the Easterners, stating that he would remove from the communion of the faithful Helenus, Firmilian, and all the bishops of Cilicia, [Col. 1405A] Cappadocia, Galatia, and the neighboring peoples, wherever heretics rebaptized.

Saint Dionysius, reporting this in Eusebius, book VII, chapter 4, asserts that the teaching and salutary admonitions of that pope, in the letters he sent to the Churches of Syria and Arabia, had brought them very great assistance:

> “You have always been of great assistance to all Syria and Arabia through your teaching and counsel; and even now you have written letters to them.”

According to these responses, bishops were sent as envoys of the Africans and Asians to that same Pope Stephen, as some writers have related. This is clearly understood from the context of Firmilian’s letter to Saint Cyprian, namely letter 75, and from the testimony of Blessed Jerome in the *Dialogue Against Lucifer*, so that they might give an account of the decrees issued concerning the matter.

But he did not admit them even to a conversation, as Firmilian complains. In his letter to Saint Cyprian, letter 74 among the Cyprianic letters, Stephen declared that no baptism of heretics was to be repeated:

> “If, therefore, anyone comes to us from any heresy whatsoever, let nothing be innovated except what has been handed down: that hands be laid upon him for penance.”

It would have been greatly to be desired that the Asians and Africans had kept before their [Col. 1405B] eyes the opinions of their ancestors concerning the tradition of which the See of Peter is the guardian, opinions sufficiently explained among the Asians by Irenaeus and among the Africans by Tertullian, witnesses from their own lands.

The first of these, Irenaeus, declares that, to prevent corruption of doctrine [Col. 1405C] and refute errors, the true sons of the Church have recourse to that tradition and faith which the Roman Church, the greatest and most ancient, known to all because it was founded and established by the apostles Peter and Paul, preserved entire and unchanged. It had received this tradition from the apostles through the succession of bishops extending down to us, together with the principal authority by which it is distinguished. Since it is necessary for Churches and faithful everywhere to have recourse to it and to assemble around it because of its more powerful pre-eminence [Col. 1405D] (Irenaeus, *Against Heresies*, book III, chapter 3; whose words we already gave above in the notes on Saint Clement), the African Tertullian adds:

> “We have Rome, from which authority will also be available to us. Happy is the Church into which the apostles poured out their entire teaching together with their blood!”  
> Tertullian, *On the Prescription Against Heretics*, near the end.

The Asians and Africans were less unfortunate in this respect: they believed that the question which had arisen between them and Stephen concerned not doctrine but discipline and the administration of the Church, as both sides themselves declared.

Firmilian complains that Stephen decreed that those should be separated from the unity of the universal Church who, for just reasons, believed that certain customs particular to the Roman Church ought not to be received by them, since those customs concerned discipline alone. None of Stephen’s predecessors, he says, had judged that those who refused to follow similar institutions should be excluded:

> “As in very many other provinces also, many things vary according to the diversity of places and peoples; yet on that account no one has ever departed from the peace and unity of the Catholic Church. This is what Stephen has now dared to do, breaking against you the peace which all his predecessors had always preserved with you in mutual love and honor.”  
> Firmilian’s letter, in Cyprian, 75.

The African synods, however, had protested that they imposed a law upon no one, but believed that each person was free, while preserving peace with the others, to follow his own custom:

> “In this matter we neither use force against anyone nor impose a law.”  
> Cyprian, letter 72.

> “We judge no one, nor do we remove anyone from the right of communion if he holds a different opinion.”  
> Council of Carthage, *On the Baptism of Heretics*.

The enemies of the Roman See therefore transfer this ancient dispute unjustly in order to lend authority to the new dissensions by which they themselves disturb the Church.

Did not the outcome prove that Pope Stephen had proposed the [Col. 1406A] rule of truth and faith when he set forth the tradition of the Apostolic See? The Asian and African Churches obeyed once they recognized that their custom was burdened with the fault of novelty, while they discovered that the practice of the Holy See was commended by the excellence of its earliest antiquity and was therefore legitimate.

A great deal of investigation was certainly required to disentangle the sequence of events and place it in the proper light. Hence Saint Augustine, attempting to excuse Saint Cyprian after asserting that the blessed martyr had not departed from the unity of the Church, adds that no plenary council had yet pronounced judgment on the matter:

> “For in those times, before the judgment of a plenary council had confirmed by the agreement of the whole Church what ought to be held in this matter, it seemed right to him, together with nearly eighty fellow bishops of the African Churches, that every person who had been baptized outside the communion of the Catholic Church ought to be baptized again upon coming to the Church.”

Saint Augustine indicates [Col. 1406B] that Cyprian held the opinion that the dispute at that time concerned discipline alone. That is, since the question belonged to the class of matters that did not touch doctrine, each province was free to conform to its own customs until solemn examination determined which custom was ancient and legitimate.

Let us carefully take heed lest we suppose that the holy bishop of Hippo, while excusing the bishop of Carthage and affirming that a plenary council had been necessary to settle the controversy, was thereby pronouncing anything against the authority of the holy see in deciding controversies—an authority which he recognized so clearly, as we shall explain in its proper place. For, in this connection, he declares that even plenary councils themselves were often corrected by later ones in particular cases, without injury to the authority of either, which remained wholly intact. In the same sense, therefore, he could say that, in such cases, even plenary councils could recall for examination matters defined by [Col. 1406C] the holy see, without overturning its rights.

According to the blessed Doctor’s judgment, those cases concerned matters that were hidden and obscure, which the progress of time and experience brought to light:

> “Who, then, does not know,” he says, “that plenary councils themselves are often corrected by later ones, when some experience of events reveals what had been closed and makes known what had remained hidden?” (Ibid., book II, chapter 3.)

The matter under dispute must be reckoned among those cases. Stephen referred his decree concerning the baptism of heretics—which he forbade to be repeated—to tradition: “Let nothing be innovated except what has been handed down.” He meant tradition as Augustine then understood it: so entangled and obscure that its evident meaning could not seem fully established except by convening a plenary council—indeed, so obscure that, according to the holy Doctor, even plenary councils could correct one another concerning its clarity. For the matter was considered to be of such a nature that it could not be fully defined in a plenary council [Col. 1406D] before it had been thoroughly discussed and sifted through many particular debates and conferences of bishops.

> “For how,” he says, “could this matter, wrapped in such clouds of dispute, have been brought to the clear illumination and confirmation of a plenary council, unless it had first been examined at length throughout the regions of the world in many debates and conferences of bishops here and there, so that it might be established?” (Ibid., chapter 4.)

This clearly shows that the assistance of a general council which Augustine required in the matter chiefly under examination concerned, in his view, the sphere of discipline relating to ecclesiastical administration. In that sphere he asserts that even plenary councils could correct earlier councils by later ones without mutual injury or the overthrow of rights.

This becomes still clearer if we consider the matter from the perspective and in the light in which Augustine places it, and listen to him as he treats it thoroughly. He says that nothing was brought against Saint Cyprian except a custom—certainly a genuine one—whose proofs of truth, however, were not produced. This custom had been called into question before Cyprian by Agrippinus, one of his predecessors, in a council of several African bishops. Had these doubts and questions not preceded him, Cyprian would not have dared to reason against the assertion of that custom.

In a case of such obscurity, after weighing what was brought forward on both sides—on the one hand, what Cyprian himself saw concerning the custom, so strong and widespread; and on the other, what he found established in his own Church by the authority of the council held under Agrippinus—he grew weary of the labor of a more extensive investigation and, rather than undertake a further examination, preferred to follow closely in the footsteps of his predecessors.

> “But because,” Augustine says (ibid., chapter 8), “at that time there were only those who opposed the custom to him, he did not wish to yield to a custom that was indeed true but had not yet been asserted. Yet unless Agrippinus had earlier attempted, together with some of his fellow bishops throughout Africa, to argue for that custom even by the decisions of councils, this man would not at least have dared to reason against it. But, disturbed in so obscure a question, and seeing everywhere a universal and firmly established custom, he rather restrained himself . . . . . But when he had received the authority of the preceding council held under Agrippinus, wearied as he was, he preferred to defend the position of his predecessors as an established finding rather than labor further in investigating it.”

We shall therefore conclude that, in the judgment of the blessed Cyprian, the question did not appear to him to concern a dogma of faith, since he did not wish to separate himself from communion with those who held opinions different from his own. He certainly ought to have done so if he had judged them heretics. According to Saint Augustine’s view, however, the matter was so obscure—because of the admixture of elements in the proceedings—that it could be fully uncovered only through the benefit of time; it required trials and investigations that called for the assistance of a plenary council in order to complete the inquiry precisely. What had to be demonstrated was the universality of the custom: that is, whether such a practice and disciplinary arrangement ought to be regarded as conforming to the traditions [Col. 1407C] of all the Churches. Nothing at all can yet be seen here [Col. 1408A] in which the enemies of the Apostolic See could take such great delight.

As for those who, while preserving the obedience they owe, appear to be drawn by a taste for disputation and to seek occasions for arguing about the authority of that See, they must carefully beware lest, by setting before themselves the image of achieving what they believe the saints achieved, they deceive both themselves and the Church under a false appearance of imitation. They must also consider with blessed Ambrose that even the saints were not everywhere masters of complete perfection; and since they possessed the same corrupt nature as we do, they too could be subject to weakness.

> “They were not of a nature superior to ours, but more observant; they were not ignorant of vices, but corrected them. If envy even scorched the saints, how much more must we beware lest it inflame sinners?” (Saint Ambrose, *On Joseph*.)

> “No correction of this opinion, however, is found. Nevertheless, it is not unreasonable to think of such a man that he did correct it; and perhaps this was suppressed by those who took excessive pleasure in that error and did not wish to be deprived of such a patronage.” (Saint Augustine, Letter 48, to Vincent.)

They should also attentively consider these words of Vincent of Lérins, whose truth has been continually confirmed and made evident by the experiences of every subsequent age: namely, that Pope Stephen’s zeal shone above the firmness of the other bishops who resisted innovation to the same extent that he was raised above them by the dignity of his chair; and that, at the conclusion of this matter, what ordinarily occurs in similar cases was likewise seen: antiquity prevailed and innovation was rejected.

> “Then Stephen, of blessed memory, bishop of the Apostolic See, resisted together with his other colleagues, but above all the rest—deeming it worthy, as I think, that if he surpassed all the others in devotion to the faith, he should likewise surpass them in the authority of his position . . . . What, then, was the outcome of the whole matter? What indeed, except the customary and usual one? Antiquity was retained, and innovation was rejected.” (Saint Vincent of Lérins, *Against Heresies*, chapter 9.)

[Col. 1389]

## 24

Stephen, a Roman by nationality, son of Julius, held the see for four years, two months, and ten days [Note: [Col. 1389] B: three years, three months, and twenty-two days]. He was crowned with martyrdom. He lived in the times of Valerian and Gallienus [Note: [Col. 1389] B: Volusianus, Valerian, and Gallienus, from the consulships of Valerian and Gallienus to those of Valerian IV and Gallienus III], and of Maximus, up to the third consulship of Valerian and the second of Gallienus [Note: [Col. 1389] C: the fourth consulship of Valerian and the third of Gallienus].

[In his own time he was carried into exile; afterward, by God’s will, he returned unharmed to the Church. Thirty-four days later he was arrested by Maximian and sent to prison with nine presbyters and two bishops, Honorius and Castus, and three deacons, Xistus, Dionysius, and Gaius. There in prison, at the Arch of Stella, he held a synod [Col. 1391] and handed over all the vessels of the Church, or the treasury, to his archdeacon Xistus. After six days he came out under guard and was himself beheaded together with them.]

He decreed that priests and Levites should not use sacred vestments in daily life, but only in the church. He held two ordinations in the month of December: seven presbyters [Note: [Col. 1391] CB: six], five deacons, and three bishops in various places. He was also buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, on the fourth day before the Nones of August. The episcopate remained vacant for twenty-two days.

### CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS

Stephen: four years, two months, and twenty-one days. He lived in the times of Valerian and Gallienus, from the consulship of Volusianus and Maximus up to the third consulship of Valerian and the second of Gallienus.

## XXV. SAINT SIXTUS II. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 260, IN THE SIXTH YEAR OF THE EMPERORS VALERIAN AND GALLIENUS
