Line 9.—“And after the passion of blessed Xistus, on the third day blessed Laurence, his archdeacon, also suffered.” Blessed Laurence was Xistus’s archdeacon. As Xistus was hastening toward martyrdom, Laurence, himself yearning for martyrdom, addressed him in the words reported by Ambrose, *On Duties*, book I, chapter 41: “Why are you hastening, holy priest, without your deacon?” etc. Having obtained what he desired, he suffered martyrdom six days later.]

[Note: [Col. 1409B]

Line 2.—“He lived in the times of Valerian and Decius, at which time there was a very great persecution.” While Sixtus was serving in the clerical ministry under Decius, he distinguished himself, together with the rest of the clergy, by the merit of a true confessor, as is stated below: “At that time blessed Sixtus was being pressed under Decius by a most savage persecution.” Both emperors raging against the pontiff are indicated: Decius by the earlier edicts issued against the clergy, and Valerian by renewing the edicts and the persecution. The persecution of Decius and Valerian is regarded as one and the same persecution, even though other emperors ruled in the interval. Hence Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 4, when speaking of the beginnings of the persecution that followed under Diocletian, writes:

> “For then the devil, who had received power over this world, as though he had first begun to awaken from a very deep sleep, and after that interval of time which followed the persecution of Decius and Valerian, was still secretly and covertly plotting against the Church.”

Here he treats it as one and the same persecution, beginning with Decius and ending with Valerian. Lactantius says similarly, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 5:

> “Not long afterward Valerian also, seized by a fury not unlike that of Decius, of which I had spoken, stretched out impious hands against God and shed much righteous blood, although for only a short time.”

He says that Valerian pursued the faithful with a fury not unlike that of Decius, in order to show that the limits of the Decian persecution should be reckoned from the death of Valerian, who judged that the persecution of the higher clergy should be continued under the same Decian edicts.

Line 1.—“Because he despised Valerian’s commands.” We have seen above that, under Gallus and Volusianus, sacrifices to Apollo had been imposed. Likewise, under Valerian, other sacrifices were imposed upon the peoples. Macrianus gave Valerian the occasion to change his policy and harass the Christians. Initiated into the Egyptian rites, Macrianus enjoyed the highest favor with Valerian. When he saw that the emperor was anxious about the outcome of the impending Persian war, he promised victory and a secure empire if Valerian would be initiated into the rites of Isis.

> “He ordered him to perform initiations, impure and detestable magic rites, and abominable sacrifices,” as Eusebius writes, book VII, chapter 10.

Macrianus obtained such power with Valerian that he was entrusted with the functions of the empire while the emperor led the army against the Persians. This is clear from Pollio, who says that Valerian informed the senate of the vicariate of imperial power entrusted to Macrianus in these words:

> “Conscript Fathers, while waging the Persian war, I have entrusted the entire republic to Macrianus.”

Apuleius describes the forms of these initiations at greater length in books II and XII of the *Metamorphoses*. At Macrianus’s urging, therefore, Valerian wished to publish these new ceremonies in other edicts, in order to secure a fortunate and auspicious outcome for the war. The words of the ancient *Passion of Saint Cyprian* should be understood as referring to these edicts. They read, at the beginning of the works of Saint Cyprian:

> “The most sacred emperors Valerian and Gallienus deigned to send me a letter in which they ordered that those who do not observe the Roman religion should recognize the Roman ceremonies.”

That is, the ceremonies which, at Macrianus’s urging, he had decreed should be performed in a special way through initiation. The command was directed to bishops and presbyters, as appears from the following:

> “They deigned to write to me not only concerning bishops, but also concerning presbyters.”

The same command indicates that every place of prayer had been taken away from Christians in these words:

> “They also ordered that assemblies should not be held in any places and that they should not enter cemeteries. Therefore, if anyone should fail to observe this salutary command, let him be punished by death.”

We have seen above that the same orders were communicated to Dionysius of Alexandria. The Egyptian initiations, commonly called Isiac, were numerous and varied; Apuleius recounts their principal features in the books cited above. That these were especially promoted is shown by the following words of the *Passion of Cyprian*:

> “The most sacred emperors ordered that the rites be performed.”

This final verb designates the jumble of rites practiced in the Isiac ceremonies. In this sense, the sentence of capital punishment issued by the proconsul speaks of “the sect of their ceremonies.” It continues:

> “You have lived for a long time with a sacrilegious mind; you have gathered to yourself many men of an impious conspiracy; you have set yourself up as an enemy of the Roman gods and sacred laws; nor could the devout and most sacred princes, Valerian and Gallienus Augustus, and Valerian the most noble Caesar, recall you to the sect of their ceremonies.”

Here the Roman gods are distinguished from the sect of ceremonies established by the emperors and claimed by them. These ceremonies were none other than the Egyptian initiations. The same ceremonies were proposed to Sixtus, which the *Liber Pontificalis* expressed under the name of Valerian’s commands. When the holy pontiff abhorred these commands, the *Liber Pontificalis* continues, he was condemned to capital punishment.

[Col. 1411B] Line 5.—“He was beheaded.” Those among the bishops and presbyters who refused to perform the initiations imposed upon them were punished by capital sentence, as appears from the *Passion* cited above, in which Saint Cyprian became a martyr. That this was the ordinary punishment for those who resisted the edicts is inferred from the same *Passion*, which says that the faithful standing by at Cyprian’s death cried out that they too should suffer the same capital punishment with him:

> “After this sentence, the crowd of brothers said: ‘Let us too be beheaded with him.’”

Line 7.—“And the presbyters presided.” During a vacancy of the pontifical see, as had occurred under Fabian, the presbyters and deacons are said to have presided and, having undertaken the care of the Church, to have displayed universal concern, especially in the matter of the lapsed, by sending letters and exhortations to restrain the excessive freedom of certain persons in admitting the lapsed.

Among these, they admonished Cyprian concerning this controversy, and also because, during the fervor of the persecution, when the congregations needed greater assistance, he had left them and was still lying concealed in retreat. For these matters he sent a letter to the presbyters and deacons residing at Rome in the new edition, no. 20, where he explains the reason for his retreat and what he had done for the lapsed, the confessors, and the martyrs. He also adds that he had informed the same Roman clergy about all his actions:

> “What I have done is told you by the letters sent according to circumstances—thirteen in number—which I have transmitted to you.”

What he did in those thirteen letters, and which letters they were, John of Chester identifies in the *Cyprianic Annals*, for the year 256, sections 11 and 12.

What the care of the presbyters and deacons was, in the bishop’s absence and also after his death, is shown by Cyprian’s letters to the presbyters and deacons of the Church of Carthage during his retreat. The fact that the presbyters are mentioned here while the deacons are omitted, although the greater responsibility—at least for the external administration of the Church’s goods—belonged especially to the archdeacon, seems to me to have occurred because the archdeacon Laurence was martyred together with Sixtus, along with six other deacons: Felix and Agapitus, Januarius and Magnus, Vincentius and Stephen, as the *Liber Pontificalis* says. Consequently, it noted that only the presbyters presided, because the others had suffered martyrdom with Sixtus.

Line 8.—“At which time.” This passage is corrupt through the customary transposition of scribes. The words above should therefore perhaps be restored, with better sense, as follows:

> “He lived in the times of Valerian and Decius, at which time there was a very great persecution. At that time blessed Sixtus was attacked under Decius by a most savage persecution. At the same time”—that is, during the great persecution—“he was arrested by Valerian,” etc.

The circumstances of the time support this restoration, namely the time when the Catholics were striving to demonstrate against the Novatians: first, that the schismatics had been responsible for the Decian persecution; second, that the higher clergy had been harassed in the Decian persecution, while the Novatians lived secure and unharmed; and third, that Cornelius and his successors were distinguished by many glorious confessions. To show that Sixtus too had been such a man, the author of the *Gesta* therefore left a note that he had been harassed by Decius in that most savage persecution.

Pacianus shows in his letters that the Catholics charged the Novatians with the inglorious fickleness of their own people in those most savage persecutions, since neither Novatian nor his followers were recorded as having endured anything for confessing the faith throughout that entire period. Pacianus likewise exposes the later Novatian fabrication based on corrupted letters of Cyprian, by which they attempted to prove that Novatian had been a true confessor.

The argument from repeated confession, then customarily used as a token of virtue, is established by Cyprian’s letters written in the cause of Cornelius against the schismatics. In them he magnifies this mark of confession in order to demonstrate both Cornelius’s legitimate election and the ambition of the schismatic Novatian. Thus Cornelius, in the name of the Roman synod, censures Novatian for refusing to assist catechumens in the danger of persecution and for fleeing the struggles of persecution.

The *Liber Pontificalis*, therefore, wished to indicate that, throughout the whole period of the Decian persecution, Sixtus had been harassed both under Decius and under Valerian, when he completed his martyrdom in glorious combat. The same pattern is observed in the cases of Urban, Cornelius, Stephen, and Lucius.

Line 16.—“Cyriacetes.” The word occurs under Sylvester, where we read:

> “In the same place there was the property of a certain devout woman, Cyriacetes, which the treasury had seized during the time of persecution.”

This was a devout woman who, when the Decian persecution was pressing heavily, had suffered the loss of her property, in accordance with the tyrant’s edicts. Cyprian writes of these edicts in the letter to Successus cited above, when he sets forth their principal provisions:

> “Matrons, their property having been confiscated, are banished into exile . . . . But the prefects in the City also press this persecution daily, so that if anyone is brought before them, he may be punished and his property claimed for the treasury.”

These properties, adjudicated to the treasury during the persecution, were later, when Constantine granted peace to the Churches, assigned by him as endowments for churches and the poor. Eusebius discusses this at length, as does the *Liber Pontificalis* below.

On the small estate that remained, therefore, the holy woman prepared a place for the burial of martyrs. Why Sixtus was not placed, like his predecessors, near the memorial of the Apostles is easy to answer: access to the cemeteries had been prohibited by Valerian’s later edict, as noted above.

For the same reason, Sixtus had transferred the bodies of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul to the place of Saint Fabian, so that they might be guarded more safely and so that, if the persecution grew fiercer even against the cemeteries, it would not consign the sacred relics to the fire. Therefore, what the *Liber Pontificalis* reports under Cornelius concerning such a translation should be assigned to Sixtus, and the text should be corrected.

This also confirms our conjecture concerning the additions and the manner in which they were made in the *Liber Pontificalis*. That the translation occurred in the time of Sixtus is proved by the list of the depositions of the martyrs preserved by Bucherius, where we read:

> “On the third day before the Kalends of July, Peter in the catacombs, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus.”

That consulship belongs to the year 258, when Sixtus was alive, not to the time of Cornelius.]

[Note: [Col. 1412D]

Line 5.—“He was beheaded.” It is established by the testimony of Saint Cyprian that he was killed in the same cemetery in which he had violated the law of the emperor Valerian prohibiting access to the cemeteries. Whether the pontiff Sixtus died by beheading or crucifixion is disputed. Prudentius alone, in hymn 2, says that he was fastened to a cross, in these verses:

> “Now Sixtus, fastened to the cross,  
> seeing Laurence weeping  
> beneath the very trunk of the cross,” etc.

Nevertheless, several testimonies establish that he was beheaded in the cemetery mentioned above.]

[Note: [Col. 1413A]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

The most ancient Liberian catalogue, four Italian catalogues together with the Belgian catalogue of Papebrochius, and four Ocriculan manuscripts unanimously assign to Pontiff Sixtus two years, eleven months, and six days, as is clearly shown in the Leonine paintings, although some of the Colbert manuscripts vary in the number of days. Accordingly, the duration of his episcopate should be regarded as extending to almost a full three years, beyond the reach of serious doubt.

The day of his martyrdom is as clearly established as that of his deacon Laurence. As Sixtus was being led to execution, he foretold to Laurence: “After three days you shall follow me, the priest and Levite,” as appears from the Acts, confirmed by the testimony of the holy Fathers. The martyrdom of Sixtus II is therefore recorded by the unanimous evidence of the calendars on the day of August that is also given in the depositions of the martyrs, written in the age of Liberius (in the *Prolegomena*, cols. 975 ff.), in these words:

> “In the month of August, on the eighth day before the Ides: Sixtus in the cemeteries of Callistus and Praetextatus, Agapitus, and Felicissimus.”

The most ancient calendar of the Church of Carthage agrees:

> “On the eighth day before the Ides of August, Saint Xystus, bishop and martyr, at Rome; on the fourth day before the Ides of August, Saint Laurence.”

Blessed Cyprian, shortly before his own martyrdom, which he completed with great courage in the same year as Sixtus, received from Rome the news of his colleague’s recent coronation, on September 14. The deacon Pontius writes in his *Life*:

> “The news had already arrived from Rome concerning Xistus, the good and peaceful priest and therefore most blessed martyr. The executioner was expected at any moment, coming to strike the neck of the most holy victim devoted to God, and so all those days were spent in the daily expectation of death. Then, behold, by order of the proconsul, he was brought to his gardens,” etc.

The Acts of the martyrdom state that Saint Cyprian was arrested on the Ides of September, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus . . . . . and that on the following day, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, he was brought before the judge in the morning and condemned to beheading. The other ancient records agree with this; they may be read in Schelestratius, dissertation II, chapter 7, no. 8.

Thus, counting backward from the sixth day of August in the year 258, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, by the two years, eleven months, and six days assigned to Sixtus’s episcopate, his ordination falls on September 2, a Sunday in the year 255, when he was appointed as Stephen’s vicar by his predecessor, as I indicated in the preceding entry, in the consulship of Valerian III and Gallienus II.

The Liberian catalogue says that his episcopate began in the following consulship, that of Maximus II and Glabrio, marking the year 256. During Stephen’s exile, Sixtus had apparently celebrated the first Paschal festivals of his vicariate, while the emperor Valerian persecuted the clergy more harshly than the other Christians, as is clear from Saint Cyprian’s Letter 82 to Successus:

> “Valerian has written back to the senate that bishops, presbyters, and deacons are to be punished immediately.”

He adds below:

> “You should know that Xystus was punished in the cemetery on the eighth day before the Ides of August, and Quartus with him.”

Since Xystus completed his martyrdom on that day in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, the see remained vacant for nearly a full year, namely until the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus. This is attested by the author of the Liberian catalogue in these words:

> “He suffered on the eighth day before the Ides of August . . . . . . from the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus until the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus.”

Schelestratius states that Henschenius correctly supplied the lacuna. Henschenius arranged the supplement as follows:

> “He suffered on the eighth day before the Ides of August, and the presbyters presided from the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus until the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus.”

In support of the supplement Schelestratius offered the following:

> “And the presbyters presided, etc. For while the older catalogue still existed intact, eleven hundred years ago, the author of the second catalogue read this under Xystus: ‘And the presbyters presided from the consulship of Maximus and Gravion II up to Tuscus and Bassus, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August.’”

> “What the author of the second catalogue has under Xystus,” Schelestratius continues, “is also reported by the author of the *Liber Pontificalis* and Anastasius the Librarian, according to the authority of the most ancient Florentine manuscript. Its reading appears in the manuscript notes of Luca Holstenius under the pontificate of Stephen in these words: ‘And the presbyters presided from the consulship of Maximus and Glabrio II up to Tuscus and Bassus, from the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus up to the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August.’”

Here one can see a double error committed by Anastasius: first, he reports under Stephen’s pontificate what he ought to have reported under Xystus’s; second, he confuses the consulships and claims that the presbyters of the Church presided from the consulship of Maximus and Glabrio II, in the year 256, when Stephen was still pontiff, until the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August in the year 258, when Xystus was still alive under the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus.

On the eighth day before the Ides of August, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, Xystus was first crowned with martyrdom, as is clear from what has been said above. Hence the older catalogue is entirely correct in saying that the presbyters presided over the Church after Xystus’s death from the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus [Col. 1414B] until the seventeenth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus, when Dionysius succeeded Xystus.

Nothing remains to be added to Schelestratius’s learned observations except that a third difference should be noted between the copyist of the catalogue and the author of Anastasius’s text: the number of the second consulship is joined to the name of Glabrio, although it is assigned to Maximus, his colleague, in book XV of the *Fideicommissa*, in the *Fasti* of Cassiodorus, and in the Alexandrian chronicle.

Other laws cited by Relandus, and an inscription published by Fabretti on page 723, formerly in the house of Count Bigazzini and now in that of Count Bolognetti, near the title of the distinguished church of Saint Mark, assign the repeated consulship to neither man by number. It is inscribed as follows:

> DEDIC. IDID. NOV. MAXIMO. ET GLABRIONE COS. CVRA. AGENTIBVS. AELIO. ACHILLA, etc.
>
> “Dedicated on the Ides of November, in the consulship of Maximus and Glabrio, under the supervision of Aelius Achilla, etc.”

We are therefore confirmed in the method often commended above: in transmitted manuscripts, it is preferable to correct the numbers according to the names of the consuls rather than the names according to the numbers, and to test both against genuine and ancient documents close in date to the consuls whom they enumerate.

The chronology of Xystus therefore remains consistent with itself. It assigns him two years, eleven months, and six days of episcopate, a period partly spent as Stephen’s vicar and partly as his successor. As vicar, he served from the day of his ordination to the episcopate, September 2 of the year 255, which fell on a Sunday, until Stephen’s death on August 2, 257. As successor, he served from the twenty-second day after his predecessor’s martyrdom, since the *Liber Pontificalis* says that the see was vacant for that number of days, namely until Sunday, August 29 of the same year, 257.

The interpolated Acts of the same martyrdom then relate that Sixtus was elected to the Roman see after the death of blessed Stephen, in these words, quoted by Baronius under the year 259 and by Schelestratius, dissertation II, chapter 7, no. 4:

> “When the Christian Church had assembled, they ordained Sixtus bishop in the place of blessed Stephen, bishop and martyr of Christ, on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, etc., under the consulship of Valerian and Gallienus.”

In other Vatican manuscripts the wording is more explicit:

> “They ordained in the place of blessed Stephen Sixtus, a Greek by nationality and an Athenian by origin, bishop on the ninth day before the Kalends of September, in the consulship of Valerian IV and Gallienus II.”

Schelestratius corrects Gallienus II to Gallienus III. The word “ordained” must also be corrected or interpreted to mean that, when the Church had assembled, the votes of the clergy elected—or rather elevated—Sixtus, who had long since been ordained bishop, to the See of Peter, so that he might occupy it in his own right by succession. The vicariate had been administered by command of his predecessor from the preceding year.

Then, in the year immediately following that election, 258, on the sixth day of August, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, he was led to martyrdom. Beforehand he foretold to Laurence, his archdeacon, that the latter would receive an equal crown after three days [Col. 1415A], just as Sixtus himself was receiving it. In that same month of August the news of his martyrdom reached Cyprian, who likewise became his companion in the palm of martyrdom and celebrated him in letters, as we have mentioned.

## HISTORICAL NOTES
### Line 2

“Now he lived in the times of Valerian and Decius.” This chronological period, which is lacking in certain manuscripts, was confused by some abbreviator insufficiently experienced or diligent, on the basis of interpolated—or less accurately understood—Acts, as Schelestratius warned. For when the emperor Decius appointed Valerian censor, with that exceedingly broad authority, scarcely granted to any private citizen, which I have described; and when Valerian, not long afterward chosen emperor from the office of censor, made Decius’s son Augustus, while the persecution begun by Decius the father continued and was prolonged by his successors Gallus and Volusianus, but was renewed with greater severity by Valerian himself as emperor, the similarity of the periods and the repetition of the name “Decius” under Valerian—whether as censor or as Augustus—gave later ages, less concerned to arrange distinctly the chronology and genealogy of the emperors, an opportunity to mix all these things together recklessly.

It could also have happened that the writer of the passion and Acts of Saints Sixtus and Laurence began from the persecution of Decius, the origin of these joined persecutions, since under that persecution edicts against the clergy in particular began to be promulgated. By their force Sixtus, not yet pope, was reported once, and others with him escaped, while the law of the Antonines was still in force, according to which Christians were to be spared on the first denunciation.

But after denunciations were repeated, on the occasion of the rescript issued by Valerian, now emperor, against the clergy in imitation of Decius and sent to the senate—by which it was ordered that bishops, priests, and deacons should immediately suffer punishment—Sixtus, Laurence, and their companions at Rome, and Cyprian with others at Carthage, were compelled to undergo the death sentence. Cyprian relates this in Letter 52, above, column 1413.

Thus the things which the writer of the Acts had thought should be repeated as beginning with that first denunciation under Decius, in order to proceed to the second denunciation under Valerian, were ineptly confused by some unskilled abbreviator of a later age; and he presented Decius and Valerian to us as though they had been colleagues in the empire at the same time, ordering Sixtus, Laurence, and their companions to be brought before their tribunal at the same place in the Forum of Nerva, at the Temple of Tellus [*in tellure*], where Pope Cornelius and Gordian had been brought to be put to death. He did not reckon it important to separate from one another those emperors whom matching edicts joined in their zeal to persecute the ministers of sacred things, who had been harassed almost continuously during the eight years that elapsed between the laws of Decius and Valerian. But there is no need to discuss the causes of the error at greater length.

It is enough that genuine Acts existed in the time of Ambrose, from which the holy Doctor copied the same words that are read in the principal account of the contest of Sixtus and Laurence, even in the interpolated Acts used by Anastasius. The same passion, and a large part of the Acts, were celebrated in verse by Prudentius in the *Peristephanon*, only about 150 years after the martyrdom of Sixtus and Laurence. There, concerning the three days foretold by Sixtus—from his own passion and death to the passion and death of Saint Laurence—we read the following verses, which are found in prose in the Acts as words foretold by Pope Sixtus to Laurence, who was grieving that Sixtus, about to suffer death for Christ, would leave his deacon behind:

> Do not, at my departure,  
> Pour forth your grief in sorrowful tears.  
> I go first, brother; you also  
> Will follow after three days.  
>   
> The bishop’s final voice,  
> Foretelling glory,  
> Deceived in nothing; for the foretold day  
> Granted the palm.

The chronology, therefore, and the genuineness of the Acts should be regarded as sufficiently confirmed by the Acts and by the testimonies of the holy Fathers considered thus far.

### [Column 1416A] Line 12

“And the Roman doorkeeper.” And, in line 14: “And the aforesaid deacons were buried in the Coemeterium of Praetextatus.” Each passage in this number ought here to be illuminated by an outstanding discovery made on this very day, 27 April, in the cemetery of Praetextatus, while we were sending these observations to the press. In that cemetery the blood of the martyrs, still visible in its own crusts filling the glass, confirms what the Roman pontiffs ordered to be preserved concerning the depositions of the martyrs during the persecutions, and what their successors consistently retained concerning the relics of those martyrs, which were to be venerated and most carefully guarded.

But the publication of that noble monument must be reserved for a more suitable place, namely, in the historical notes on the number of Blessed Eutychianus, which the reader will be able to consult.]

### Note: [Column 1416A]

#### Line 10

“And Blessed Laurence, his archdeacon, suffered.” Three days after the martyrdom of Sixtus, namely, on the fourth day before the Ides of August, a Saturday, Laurence himself—the chief of the deacons, or rather the archdeacon, or archilevite—underwent a famous contest, as a most illustrious athlete of the faith. After various and exceedingly savage tortures, he was placed upon an iron gridiron and roasted by fire. Having obtained the distinguished crown of martyrdom, he triumphed over the perfidy of his persecutors with truly admirable courage of spirit, receiving, in accordance with his name, a laurel crown.

Ambrose celebrates the contest of this outstanding martyr in Book I of *De Officiis*, chapter 41, and Book I, chapter 28, as well as in Sermons 1 and 71 and Letter 1 of Book II. Augustine does so in *Tractate 27 on John* and in Book I; Isidore in the Missal and Breviary; Bernard in his sermon on the *Song of Songs* and in the sermon on Saint Andrew; Pope Leo in a sermon; and Prudentius expressed it most gracefully in verse in the *Peristephanon*. There are also many others whom it would take too long to enumerate.

#### Line 12

“Here he held two ordinations.” This is an error. For Blessed Sixtus held one ordination, not two, in which he appointed two bishops in different places, and in the city of Rome four priests and seven deacons, in the month of December.]

### Note: [Column 1416C]

His deeds during his pontificate are unknown to us. Pearson, in the *Cyprianic Annals*, observes only this from the *Calendar of the Depositons of the Martyrs*: Saint Sixtus transferred the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul to the Catacombs, so that stations might be held there more safely, as the fury of the persecution grew fiercer day by day.

For, he says, the *Calendar of the Depositions of the Martyrs* contains the following: “On the third day before the Kalends of July, Peter in the Catacombs and Paul on the Ostian Way, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus.” This consulship belongs to the year 258, in which Sixtus occupied the see until 6 August. The passage concerns the transfer of the bodies of Saints Peter and Paul.

The *Liber Pontificalis*, changing the pope—as it often does—put Cornelius in place of Sixtus; and from there Pseudo-Isidore inserted the same story into a fictitious letter of Cornelius. It therefore appears that Sixtus, not Cornelius, transferred to the Catacombs these trophies which, according to Caius, who wrote around the year 200 of Christ, were at that time preserved in the Vatican.]

### Note: [Column 1416D]

Under the episcopate of Sixtus II, who succeeded Stephen, the Roman see received splendid testimony from the Alexandrian Church, governed by Bishop Dionysius, of the obedience and due veneration owed to its supreme authority. Dionysius wrote a second letter concerning baptism to Sixtus. After first explaining the controversy concerning the baptism of heretics, and the earlier letter which he himself had sent to Stephen, Sixtus’s predecessor, on behalf of bishops who wished the baptism thus administered to be repeated, he asks Sixtus to consider carefully the gravity of the matter. He is clearly speaking of the excommunication which Stephen had threatened, so that he might plead with him on behalf of those who merely followed decrees issued in the greatest councils of bishops:

> “Therefore grasp the gravity of the matter with attentive reflection. For decrees were made, as I hear, in the greatest councils of bishops . . . . . And in order that I might plead with him [Stephen] on behalf of all these bishops, I wrote a letter.”  
> —Dionysius of Alexandria, in Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VII, chapter 4.

In the same letter the holy bishop announces to the Roman see the heresy of Sabellius, which was then beginning to arise. He informs Pope Sixtus that this impious doctrine, which had arisen in Ptolemais in the Pentapolis, was a fabric of blasphemies against God the Father; that it also contained many false doctrines against the Son; and that it led its hearers to obliterate their confession of the divine Spirit.

Reliable evidence of this matter had been brought to him by letters sent to him by many people and by faithful persons who came to him for discussion. Therefore, by God’s permission, he had written certain letters in order to expose more precisely the hiding places of the error: “Copies of these,” he says, “I have sent to you.” —Ibid., chapter 5.

He also sent another letter to Sixtus, asking him to write back what he ought to do lest he fall into error concerning a request made to him by a certain faithful person regarding the repetition of baptism. This man had received baptism from heretics who did not observe the Catholic rites in that sacrament; and, even with tears, he repeatedly insisted—not merely with prayers—that he should be washed with a pure ablution by which he might obtain grace and be enrolled as a son of the Church.

Dionysius adds that he had not dared to attempt this, since the man who had made the request had already been in communion with the faithful for a long time and had already participated in the holy mysteries. Yet he had still been unable to provide consolation to the afflicted man or tranquility to his wavering mind:

> “Truly, brother, since a case of this sort has been brought before me, and since I fear that I may fall into error, I seek counsel and earnestly request your opinion. A certain brother from our community,” etc.  
> —Ibid., chapter 8.

### [Column 1418A]

Protestants, as though applauding themselves, presume and boast that these letters sent to the Roman pontiff are nothing other than fraternal consultations; that they differ in no significant way from other letters commonly sent to other bishops; and that it therefore cannot be concluded that submission to the Roman pontiff is signified in them, since submission is not demonstrated in the other cases.

But those who think this way about these letters must, through voluntary blindness, deprive themselves of the use of their eyes, lest they see what openly reveals itself in them: namely, that the bishop of the Alexandrian see, which is next in dignity to the Roman see, recognizes Pope Sixtus as his superior and as one who grants rights to all the Churches.

He approaches him as a suppliant on behalf of a large part of the bishops of the East; informs him of heresies that have arisen in his own patriarchate; sends him the writings which he had prepared to refute them; and finally has recourse to his providence and authority in order to obtain a rule to follow in resolving a matter which he did not dare to judge by his own unaided judgment.

### [Column 1418B]

Sixtus was about to exercise this supreme authority against the Millenarians, a kind of heretic recently arisen in Egypt. They taught that, after a thousand years, the saints would reign with Christ the Lord upon earth and enjoy bodily delights and every pleasure. But a sudden persecution anticipated the action he was preparing and allowed no time for the case to be resolved.

“This supreme priest of God,” says Maximus of Turin in Homily 2 on the feast of Saint Laurence, “was attacked by pagan fury, so that, with the ecclesiastical limbs severed from so powerful a head—as though the protection of heavenly defense had been removed—the bloody persecutor might invade.”

We shall see that what Sixtus was planning was completed by his successor Dionysius.]

### [Column 1407]

## 25

Sixtus, a Greek by nationality, formerly a philosopher, occupied the see for two years, eleven months, and six days [Note: [Column 1407] B: one year, less eight days]. He was crowned with martyrdom.

“He lived in the times of Valerian and Decius” [Note: [Column 1407] B: Valerian and Gallienus, from the consulship of Valerian for the fourth time and Gallienus for the third, to Memmius, Tuscus, and Bassus], when there was a very great persecution.

At that time he was seized by Valerian and brought to sacrifice to demons. Because he despised Valerian’s commands, he was beheaded, and with him six other deacons: Felicissimus [Note: [Column 1407] Roman Martyrology, 6 August], Agapitus, Januarius, Magnus, Vincentius, and Stephen, on the sixth day before the Ides of August [Note: [Column 1407] C: the eighth].

The priests presided from the consulship of Maximus and Ravio [Note: [Column 1407] C: Glabrio] up to the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August [Note: [Column 1407] C: the fourteenth]. At that time Blessed Sixtus was accused during the fiercest persecution under Decius.

After the passion of Blessed Sixtus, on the third day, Blessed Laurence, his archdeacon, suffered; also Claudius the subdeacon, Severus the priest, Crescentius the lector, and Romanus the doorkeeper, on the fourth day before the Ides of August. [Note: [Column 1407] Baronius, under the year of the Lord 261.]

He held two ordinations during the month of December [Note: [Column 1407] B: one]: four priests, seven deacons, and two bishops in different places.

He was buried in the cemetery of Callixtus on the Appian Way. For the aforesaid deacons were buried in the cemetery of Praetextatus on the Appian Way, on the eighth day before the Ides of August.

Blessed Laurence, however, was buried on the Tiburtine Way, in the cemetery of Cyriaca, in the field of Veranus, in a crypt, with many other martyrs, on the fourth day before the Ides of August. The episcopate then remained vacant for thirty-five days.

## Catalogue under Liberius

Sixtus: two years, eleven months, six days. He began in the consulship of Maximus and Glabrio and continued until Tuscus and Bassus; he suffered on the eighth day before the Ides of August . . . from the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus until the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus.

### Note: [Column 1419B]

#### Lines 4–5

“He divided churches among the priests, and established cemeteries and parishes as dioceses.” Evaristus was the first, according to Anastasius himself, to divide the *tituli*, that is, the churches, in the city. Later, after the condition of the Churches had been disturbed by the devastation of various persecutions and by the prolonged vacancy of the churches, peace was finally restored to the Church by Gallienus. The parishes were again divided—or, more accurately, restored—by Dionysius, first in the city and then in the provinces, as is clear from the complete letter of Dionysius to Severus, bishop of Córdoba, part of which survives in canon “Churches,” 13, question 1, and in the chapter “Pastoral Care,” concerning acts performed by a superior without the consent of the chapter. I discussed this more fully in Dissertation, Book V, chapter 4.]

### Note: [Column 1419B]

#### Lines 4–5

“He divided churches among the priests, and established cemeteries and parishes as dioceses.” This organization of the Churches, or their reform into a better condition and form, took place toward the end of Dionysius’s episcopate, when Valerian had been captured in war with the Persians and Gallienus moderated the persecution. Gallienus issued public rescripts, granted indulgence, and ordered that the sacred places be restored to the bishops.

Eusebius reports both actions in Book VII, chapter 13:

> “But when Valerian had not long afterward been captured by the barbarians and reduced to slavery, his son Gallienus, possessing the empire alone, conducted himself more moderately. By sending edicts, he brought to an end the persecution that had been stirred up against our people; and, so that the leaders of our religion might henceforth carry out their office in safety, he issued the following rescript:
>
> ‘The Emperor Caesar Licinius Gallienus, pious, fortunate, Augustus, to Dionysius, Pinnas, Demetrius, and the other bishops. We order that the benefit of our indulgence be extended throughout the whole world, so that all may withdraw from the religious places. Therefore you too may make use of the form of our rescript, so that no one may henceforth cause you trouble. Moreover, what you are permitted to carry out has already been granted by me long ago. Accordingly, Aurelius Cyrenius, procurator of the imperial treasury, shall follow the form of the rescript issued by us.’”

Dionysius could therefore, by Gallienus’s indulgence, restore, divide, and reform into their former arrangement all the churches of the Christians that had been plundered by the pagans during the persecution of Decius. For Dionysius should not be regarded as the author of the division of the churches, since priests had previously been established in the sacred places and those presiding over the city’s *tituli* had performed the sacred rites. Rather, he restored and organized the confused order produced by the Decian persecution.

#### Churches

That churches had multiplied throughout the Christian world, that they existed in the individual cities of the empire, and that they were places enclosed by buildings and dedicated to divine worship is presupposed by Gallienus’s rescript, when it orders that all should withdraw from the religious places which the pagans had occupied under the edict of Decius and that those places should be restored to the bishops.

That they had been dedicated to divine worship—that is, to the celebration of sacred ministries, with every profane use strictly prohibited—is attested by the emperor Valerian in Vopiscus. The superstitious emperor censures the senate for neglecting the examination of the Sibylline books, as though the senate were in a Christian church, where such an examination was forbidden. Thus the emperor says:

> “I am amazed, Conscript Fathers, that you have hesitated so long to open the Sibylline books, as though you were deliberating in a Christian church and not in the temple of all the gods.”

He contrasts the Christian church with a pagan temple and considers the place so religious in the eyes of Christians that every action not sacred was prohibited. Thus the churches were Christian places, or sacred buildings for celebrating the mysteries of religion.

That altars existed in them is demonstrated by an event that occurred during the reign of Gallienus himself, reported by Eusebius concerning Theotecnus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, in Book VII, chapter 10:

> “When Theotecnus, the bishop of the city, had come out of the praetorium, [a man] approached him and, drawing him away into a lengthy conversation, took him by the hand and led him to the church. When he had stood him beside the altar inside, he drew back his cloak for a moment and showed him the sword with which he was girded; then he placed before him, on the other side, the book of the sacred Gospels, ordering him to choose which of the two he preferred.”

This passage indicates that there were altars and that sacred books and similar objects proper to Christian churches were kept there.

That, shortly before the persecution of Decius, there had been spacious places publicly maintained and regarded as religious is clearly demonstrated by the response of the emperor Alexander, reported by Lampridius:

> “When the Christians had occupied a certain place that had been public, and the innkeepers claimed that it belonged to them . . . . . he wrote back that it was better for God to be worshiped in whatever manner than for it to be handed over to the innkeepers.”

Gallienus had said in his edict, addressed particularly to Pope Dionysius, that Dionysius himself should insist upon recovering the churches that had been taken away. Following this precedent, when Paul of Samosata appealed to Aurelian concerning the church of Antioch, Aurelian entrusted the matter to the pope, according to Eusebius, Book VII, chapter 30.

Eusebius, recounting the deeds of that heresiarch after the council held against him, says that although Paul had been deposed, “he was unwilling by any means to leave the house of the Church.” When the emperor Aurelian was appealed to, “he judged the matter most correctly, ordering that the house be handed over to those to whom the leaders of the Christian religion in Italy and the bishop of Rome should write. In this way the man mentioned above was expelled from the church with the greatest disgrace by secular authority.”

From that time Eusebius calls the buildings “ancient,” though after Gallienus’s edicts they were enlarged into a more imposing mass. This further strengthens the evidence for the early existence of ancient churches throughout the empire.

When describing the immediately subsequent period and the abundant benefits resulting from Gallienus’s rescripts, Eusebius observes in Book VIII, chapter 1:

> “Who could adequately describe the countless crowd of people who daily took refuge in the faith of Christ? Who could describe the number of churches in the individual cities, or the splendid gatherings of the peoples in the sacred buildings? As a result, no longer content with the ancient buildings, they began to construct spacious churches from their foundations in every city. As these buildings grew with the passage of time and daily advanced toward greater size and excellence, neither envy nor the malice of the demon could ever wear them down or bewitch them, nor could human plots prevent them.”

And concerning their frequency throughout the empire he says below:

> “It was possible to see churches gathered in every city, the very numerous assemblies of Christians, and the customary assemblies held there.””

#### Cemeteries

These were underground places, also called by another name, [Column 1421A] Catacombs, where Christians were buried and where sacred mysteries were celebrated during the persecutions.

Decius first deprived the bishops of the churches. Since the faithful then assembled in the cemeteries, Valerian also barred access to the cemeteries, as stated above. When the churches were restored, permission was granted to visit the cemeteries, which Dionysius also divided, so that Masses could be celebrated beside the birthplaces—or anniversaries—of the martyrs, where their bodies had been laid to rest.

When Diocletian began the persecution, he did not begin with the churches but with the prohibition of meetings in the cemeteries. Eusebius says:

> “While he attempted everything possible to destroy the peace, he first began, under some pretext or other, to prevent our people from attending the meetings that customarily took place in the cemeteries.”

That the cemeteries were also restored to the bishops by Gallienus’s law was taught by the same Eusebius cited above, who adds:

> “There is also another decree of the same emperor, issued to other bishops, by which he permitted them to recover the sites of their cemeteries.”

#### Parishes

Among Latin Fathers the word *parish* (*paroecia*) is used chiefly in two ways: sometimes for an entire diocese, as in Augustine, Letter 261; sometimes for an individual church.

This latter meaning is the more ancient. It is used by Apollonius, the opponent of the Cataphrygians, when speaking of the false Alexander in Eusebius, Book V, chapter 18, question 145, at the end:

> “The church—Greek: μαρτυρία (*martyria*, ‘testimony’ or ‘witness’)—of the place from which he originated did not receive him, because he practiced robbery.”

Thus the Roman priests were assigned churches either in the city or outside the city, together with cemeteries and parishes, in such a way that each one, possessing a particular territory for exercising his duties, governed those places as though they were particular dioceses.

That in the period close to Dionysius there were forty basilicas in Rome, even before the time of Constantine, is proved by an important passage of Optatus in Book II. Refuting the false primacy of the Donatists, which they boasted of possessing at Rome, and speaking of Victor, the first schismatic bishop of the Donatists at Rome, he uses among his other arguments the fact that, although there were then forty basilicas, each governed by its own priests, the Donatists had neither possessed nor been able to occupy any of them.

Thus Optatus writes:

> “For the few who had no place in which to assemble within the forty and more basilicas were not to be called a flock and a people.”

By this authority he demonstrates not only the existence of basilicas before the peace and liberty granted to the Church through Constantine, but also the existence of ministers appointed over the basilicas to govern them. Since they were governed by their own rectors, the schismatics could not occupy any of them.]

### Note: [Column 1421C]

#### Lines 4–5

“In the consulship of Claudius and Paternus.” From the synodical letter of the Council of Antioch, written to the emperor Aurelian in the second year of his reign, which is the year of Christ 271, it is entirely clear that Dionysius was still alive at that time. Therefore he cannot be said to have died in the consulship of Claudius and Paternus, since these consuls are recorded in the fasti under the year of Christ 270. —Baronius, at the place cited, number 21.
