### Note: [Column 1421D]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

The Liberian Catalogue preserves for us, in the names of the consuls, the complete chronological period of the years of the holy Pope Dionysius, which the deteriorated painting had presented mutilated to the copyists of the Italian catalogues.

For unless it named the consuls of the year 259, Aemilianus and Bassus, both in the preceding period, where it related that, while the see was vacant, the Church had been administered by priests under those same consuls, and in the present number, to mark the beginning of the see of Pope Dionysius; and unless it subsequently stated that the pontiff had occupied the see until the consulship of Claudius and Paternus, who, three days after his death, were to open the year 269, we could scarcely understand how, from the nine years corresponding to this period—which the copyist had perhaps written out completely with the same letters, VIIII—only the final two letters, “II,” could have survived after the preceding letters had been worn away and appeared to indicate the number two.

The same thing happened to the copyists of the four catalogues of Italy, as well as to the four Colbertine catalogues and that of Papebrochius, listed in the *Prolegomena*. Since the preceding letters had already become faint and barely distinguishable, the Catalogue of Felix IV retained V from VIIII; the second Colbertine retained VII; the third retained VI. It must therefore be suspected that even in the paintings of one or another basilica, apart from the Pauline basilica, in which a period of nine years had been marked in the customary Roman fashion by the letters VIIII, the eyes of viewers at a distance were deceived by the deterioration of the paint in the units following the five. One person saw only the five, V; another saw VI; another VII.

The catalogues of Italy were more successful in agreeing on the number three for the months and seven for the days. Only the Cavensis catalogue removes the final unit, whereas in the basilica of Saint Paul the complete seven is preserved by the clearly visible letters D. VII.

The date of the deposition of Saint Dionysius is assigned to the sixth day before the Kalends of January by the archives of the Roman Church, together with the Bibliothecarius, and by the catalogue of the depositions of the bishops of the city composed in the Liberian age, cited above in the *Prolegomena*.

A catalogue of the same age, in the same place, shows that the feast of Pope Dionysius belonged to the preceding day, the seventh day before the Kalends of January, in the year 269, which was to be opened by the consuls Claudius and Paternus—unless the number “VII Kalends” was accidentally increased by one unit.

Therefore, if the number in the Liberian Catalogue is assumed to be uncorrupted, the commemoration of Pope Saint Dionysius, which in the ancient stone so often praised, at the title of Saint Sylvester in Capite—or of Saints Stephen and Dionysius—is assigned to the sixth day before the Kalends of January, must refer to his deposition.

Accordingly, the ordination of Dionysius should be assigned to Sunday, 29 September 259, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus; and his departure to the Lord should be placed on 26 December 268, after nine years, three months, and seven days spent in governing the Church of Christ from the see of Peter.

His sacred body should be regarded as having been deposited in the cemetery of Callixtus on the day immediately following his death, namely, 27 December of that same year, 268. It was kept in that cemetery until Paul I transferred it to the monastery and oratory which he had built in the title of Saints Stephen and Sylvester—or Dionysius—in the Campus Martius. The marble tablet there mentioned, together with the public documents of the archive of that monastery, bears witness to this.

### [Column 1422D] HISTORICAL NOTES

#### Line 4

“He divided churches among the priests and established cemeteries, etc.” The churches of the city had already been divided by the preceding pontiffs. Evaristus, number 6, says: “He divided the *tituli* among the priests in the city of Rome.”

“But it must be considered,” Baronius says under the year 270, number 17, “that the parishes were distinguished by their own boundaries and divided among the priests not first by Pope Dionysius, but by other Roman pontiffs who preceded him. Yet when, during the persecution of Valerian, as has been said, the priests had been torn away from the churches and all the Christians had also been forbidden to assemble in the cemeteries, after that impediment had been removed and Gallienus had restored peace to the Church and granted free permission to visit the cemeteries, many of the priests of those churches having died by martyrdom, it was Dionysius’s task to divide those churches again, distribute them according to their proper order, and assign cemeteries to each.” 

[Column 1423A] Binius agrees with Baronius in his notes on the second letter attributed to Dionysius. His words may be seen shortly before, in the notes of Binius and Labbe on this number.

#### Line 5

“He established parishes as dioceses.” In his *Glossary of Medieval Latin*, under the word *diocese*, Cangius, when producing this text of Anastasius, reads: “And he established parishes and dioceses.”

Before resolving this point, one must observe the threefold meaning of the word *diocese*, as the same learned man explains with precision.

> “*Diocese*—Greek: Διοίκησις, *dioikēsis*—was the name given to the prefecture of several provinces. Balsamon, in canon 9 of the Council of Chalcedon, says: Διοίκησις δὲ ἔστιν ἡ πολλὰς ἐπαρχίας ἔχουσα ἐν ἑαυτῇ: ‘A diocese is that which contains many provinces within itself.’ These dioceses are frequently mentioned in the Theodosian and Justinian Codes, and sometimes, in Marcellinus’s ancient book of provinces, are called *districts*, etc. Each diocese, which comprised several provinces, had its own metropolitan cities. The individual provinces were governed by counts and vicars; several together were governed by the praetorian prefect.”

This concerns the first meaning. He then continues:

> “In particular, provinces were called dioceses, over which metropolitans or archbishops presided, as in canon 28 of the Council of Chalcedon.”

He assigns to this meaning the dioceses of which he thinks Anastasius is speaking here. For this reason he adds the passage from the present number and cites places in other authors that reflect the same usage, especially Gilbert, bishop of Luni, who asserts, concerning ecclesiastical usage and the archbishop: “His church is called a diocese.”

Then he adds:

> “Later, however, the districts of bishops were abusively called dioceses, although they are commonly designated by their proper name, parishes.”

Finally, he supplies this third meaning of the word:

> “*Diocese*, *parish*. William Brito, in the *Vocabulary*: ‘A diocese properly is the territory and government of a baptismal church.’ The Council of Agde, canon 54, and the Council of Epaon, canon 8: ‘When a priest holds a diocese, he shall draw up a document in the name of the church concerning the things he has acquired.’”

He adds several further testimonies from other councils and writers in which the same meaning is expressed by the word *diocese*.

It therefore appears to be the learned man’s opinion that Pope Dionysius established archbishoprics. Yet the origin of archbishoprics is shown to be much earlier by many writers, especially by Schelestratius in Part II of the *Illustrated Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, Dissertation 4, chapter 4.

It is also preferable to quote here what Schelestratius argued in chapter 4, numbers 1 and following, of his dissertation *On Patriarchal and Metropolitan Authority against the Dean of London*. There he explains the first canon established by the Fathers of the Council of Arles, together with their words to Pope Sylvester, restored to the genuine reading by Cardinal Petronius and Francis, archbishop of Rouen:

> “It was also decided that these matters, according to ancient custom, should be communicated by you, who hold the greater dioceses, and especially through you to everyone.”

The observations made by Schelestratius in explaining the clause “who hold the greater dioceses” can greatly illuminate this text of the Bibliothecarius concerning Dionysius. Therefore, what he wrote at the cited place, from number 1 through number 4, must be reproduced in full.

“Among the various monuments of antiquity that serve to establish the patriarchal authority of the Roman pontiff over the whole of the West, what the Fathers of the First Council of Arles committed to the memory of posterity is not to be disregarded. For when they had assembled from Gaul, Spain, Britain, Africa, and Italy, at the very beginning of the Church’s flourishing, they enacted twenty-two canons. In the first they dealt with the observance of Easter everywhere on one day and at one time, and they added that, concerning this matter, Pope Sylvester ought, according to custom, to send letters to everyone. From this canon it may be inferred that the Fathers of Arles referred their decree concerning the date of Easter to Sylvester, just as it is clear from their synodal letter to the same pontiff that they referred the other canons to him also. In that letter they expressly write: “It was also decided that, before [the sentence is incomplete in the source], it should especially be communicated to all through you, who hold the greater dioceses.” [Col. 1424A]

Learned men have often noted that this passage is not complete, but that some words are missing from it. They have therefore applied their industry and diligence to restoring it, as we demonstrated in Part II of *Antiquity Illustrated*, Dissertation 1, chapter 7, article 4, where we presented the following emendation by Cardinal Peronius and Francis, Archbishop of Rouen: “It was also decided that these matters, according to ancient custom, should be communicated by you—who hold the greater dioceses—and especially through you to everyone.” The two most learned men correct two things in the passage mentioned: one is the adverb *antequam* (“before”), and the other concerns the words *per te* (“through you”). They thereby indicate that the question concerns only those words in the passage that were either corrupted or omitted, and not the other words that seemed correctly written. But we now see that our author thinks otherwise, since he considers even those words that are demonstrably correctly written to require correction. [Col. 1424B] For on page 83 he asserts that the Fathers of Arles truly said that the Pope possessed a greater diocese, where he alters the words *qui majores dioeceses tenes* (“who hold the greater dioceses”) and substitutes the singular noun *dioecesis* (“diocese”) for *dioeceses* (“dioceses”), contrary to the evidence of the synodal letter.

“The variation of a single word might indeed seem insignificant, unless it changed the entire meaning and overturned the authority of the Roman patriarch over several dioceses of the Roman Empire, an authority acknowledged by the Fathers of the Council of Arles. To confirm this truth, it must be recalled that in the Empire the term *diocese* was formerly customarily used for a territory comprising several provinces. Thus the ancient account of the Empire, written before the time of Arcadius and Honorius, reports five dioceses under the prefect of the praetorium of the East: the East, Egypt, Asia, Pontus, and Thrace; two dioceses under the prefect of the praetorium of Illyricum: Macedonia and Dacia; three under the prefect of the praetorium of Italy: Italy, Illyricum, and Africa; and finally, under the prefect of the praetorium of Gaul, three dioceses: Spain, the Seven Provinces, and the Britains. [Col. 1424C] It is therefore clear that the Roman Empire, distributed among four praetorian prefectures, was divided into thirteen dioceses, five of which belonged to the East and the remainder to the West.

“Whether the Fathers of Arles had this description of the Empire before their eyes, or whether they learned elsewhere of the dioceses, they wrote from a Western council to Sylvester, the patriarch of the West: “You who hold the greater dioceses.” They intended thereby to signify that he had been placed over not one diocese but several dioceses—indeed, over all those contained within the boundaries of the West. Since this is so, who does not see that this very point could have displeased our author and given him an occasion to alter the text? Since this single testimony of the Fathers of Arles overturns his view concerning the restriction of the boundaries of the Roman patriarchate, he perhaps wished, in order to weaken the force of the argument, to read *diocese* in the singular instead of *dioceses* in the plural. Thus the man who, presiding over several dioceses, extended his patriarchal authority as far as Britain would be confined within the boundaries of a single Italian diocese, possessing authority over it alone. [Col. 1424D]

“That this is what our author attempted to impose upon the council’s text by altering it is sufficiently indicated by the fact that, when he again mentions the synodal letter of the Fathers of Arles, he says: “As for the words ‘greater dioceses,’ it is doubtful whether Constantine had divided the Empire into dioceses at the time of the Council of Arles; and it is more probable that this had not even been done at the time of Nicaea, since there mention is made only of provinces, not of dioceses. If this is true, the words in that passage are corrupt, just as it is certain that they were corrupt elsewhere. Moreover, even if the passage is admitted to be complete, nothing follows from it except that the Roman bishop had a diocese of greater extent than the other Western bishops—a claim that is not denied.”

“Here our author explains his mind clearly. [Col. 1425A] In order somehow to prove the corruption of the text, he adduces several arguments in support of his reading, which must now be examined. First, he indicates that the Empire had been divided into dioceses under Constantine the Great before the time of Arcadius and Honorius, but suggests that this division may have occurred only after the Council of Nicaea, so that the Fathers of Arles could not have mentioned greater dioceses: “It is doubtful,” he says, “whether Constantine divided the Empire into dioceses at the time of the Council of Arles; and it is more probable that this had not even been done at the time of Nicaea, since there mention is made only of provinces, not of dioceses.”

“Yet our author is seriously mistaken, and adds error to error. In speaking thus, he shows that he has not read through the Acts produced at the time of the Council of Nicaea. There exists, in fact, Constantine’s letter concerning the celebration of Easter on one day throughout the entire world, which he wrote at the time of the Council of Nicaea. In it he not only mentions various provinces under the name of a single region, but expressly speaks of the Pontic and Asian diocese: *Ἀσιανὴν τε διοίκησιν, καὶ Ποντικὴν*—“the Asian and Pontic diocese.” What could be clearer? What more explicit? What more unmistakable could have been written by Constantine the Great? It is therefore certain that dioceses existed in the Empire at the time of the Council of Nicaea. This exposes our author’s ignorance and proves that he was gravely mistaken on this matter. [Col. 1425B]

“Second, he says that it is uncertain when Constantine divided the Empire into dioceses. This has nothing to do with the question, since dioceses existed in the Empire under the four praetorian prefectures even before that division, and the Fathers of Arles could therefore have used the name of dioceses in their own time, as no one has hitherto called that usage into question. They attribute dioceses to Sylvester; therefore dioceses existed in the Empire at that time, and the Fathers expressed the extent of patriarchal jurisdiction by that name.

“Onuphrius Panvinius, reporting the division of the provinces that existed under the Emperor Hadrian, places among his headings one concerning the provinces of Italy, under which he states: [Col. 1425C] “There were seventeen provinces, or dioceses, in Italy and its islands.” Although I do not know the source from which he recognized that the provinces were then called dioceses, I have no doubt that he found this statement, like all the others presented there, in ancient monuments. Let us therefore suppose that, from the time of Hadrian himself, the name *diocese* was also applied to provinces. No one can deny that the provinces were smaller dioceses in relation to the greater dioceses of which Sextus Rufus spoke when he wrote that seven provinces had been established in the diocese of Macedonia, and of which Constantine the Great speaks in his letter to the Churches when, at the time of the Council of Nicaea, he recalls the Pontic and Asian diocese.

“Thus, to indicate what they intended to signify, the Fathers of Arles contrasted greater dioceses with smaller ones, and wrote that the greater dioceses were held by Saint Sylvester. Sylvester therefore held dioceses when the Council of Arles was celebrated. He was consequently placed not merely over a few provinces, which constituted smaller dioceses, but over several extensive territories, which constituted greater dioceses; and in them he possessed patriarchal authority.” [Col. 1425D]

With these points established from Schelestratius, since it is clear that Sylvester held the greater dioceses according to ancient custom, it must also be acknowledged that his predecessors, from whom that ancient custom was transmitted to Sylvester’s time, likewise held several provinces comprising those same regions of the Empire. Victor could not have threatened the Asian bishops with the judgment of the supreme see unless he had held the Asian diocese by some authority of the highest priesthood. Nor could he have instructed the metropolitan of Caesarea, established in the region or diocese of Syria, to convene a synod from the neighboring provinces concerning the date of Easter, unless the same region of the Eastern diocese had also been embraced by some authority of the highest pontificate.

Since it is therefore certain that, in the third sense of the word, dioceses—meaning bishoprics or parishes—were established from the origin of the Church by the apostles; [Col. 1426A] and that, in the second, metropolitan sense, dioceses were founded in that same apostolic age—for Paul had left Titus in Crete as metropolitan and primate of the whole island, so that he might appoint presbyters in each city; and since, in the first sense of dioceses, it is evident that the institution of the three patriarchates established in those regions belongs to the Prince of the Apostles, the founder of the three principal sees of Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch—it follows that Dionysius should not be called the first institutor of dioceses in any of the three senses of the word.

Nor does Anastasius assert this. His words are preserved by the manuscripts in such a way that they must be understood of the urban titular churches, endowed with a font and territory by his predecessors and restored by him after the persecutions of Decius and Valerian, when he distributed among the presbyters the same urban titles and suburban cemeteries, as the common reading itself demonstrates: “Here he divided the churches, cemeteries, and parishes among the presbyters and established dioceses.” [Col. 1426B]

The meaning of the words is perceived even more clearly in the somewhat more explicit expression used in the section concerning Marcellus. When he restored the cemeteries that had been destroyed and the twenty-five Roman titular churches that had been violently shaken and disrupted during the persecution of Diocletian, it says: “He established cemeteries on the Salarian Way, and established twenty-five titular churches in the city of Rome as dioceses, for the sake of the baptism and penance of the many who were being converted from paganism, and for the burial of the martyrs.”

The adverb *quasi* (“as if” or “as it were”) placed before the expression, and the phrase *propter baptismum* (“for the sake of baptism”) attached to the word *dioceses*, greatly illuminate both passages. They show that, through the assignment of fonts and the urban territories of the titular churches, a certain likeness to dioceses in the third sense—namely, episcopal parishes—was introduced into those same titular churches of the presbyter-cardinals. I reserve this explanation for the section on Marcellus, where it will arise more appropriately, although I have already anticipated something of it in the earlier notes and observations on no. 3 of Saint Cletus, col. 1061 and following. [Col. 1426C]

Before leaving this subject, I think I shall do something worthwhile if I explain somewhat more clearly here what I presented above in the cited column, in the notes to the Life of Cletus. There I was attempting to illuminate Anastasius’s text concerning the institution of the twenty-five presbyteral titular churches of the city of Rome, introduced by the clergy at the command of blessed Peter and restored and enlarged by his successors, as well as concerning the subsequent distribution of these titular churches for the performance of weekly services in the patriarchal basilicas of the City after those basilicas had been erected.

For the brevity with which Anastasius drew upon the catalogues, and the multitude of events that we compressed into a narrow space on that page, so that we might append observations rather than complete treatises, could produce some obscurity unless we took advantage of the present opportunity to clarify especially what we explained there concerning the number and ministry of the patriarchal basilicas of Rome, distributed among the seven presbyter-cardinals or titular presbyters, and concerning the weekly offices and rotations gradually increased according to the changing discipline of the times. [Col. 1426D]

Innocent III, that illustrious pontiff who among the Roman pontiffs was distinguished by learning and holiness, the most faithful interpreter of the sacred rites and mystical meanings established by his predecessors in the Roman Church, and likewise a most wise legislator—in the letter *Register* XV, no. 154, cited by Thomassinus in Part I of *The Old and New Discipline*, book I, chapter 15, no. 2—indicated that the Roman Church, as the head and mother of the others, presents such an image of the Catholic Church that it is an illustrious representation of that throne and seat of God and of the Lamb which the Apostle John saw and described in the Apocalypse.

The words of Innocent are these:

“‘In the midst of the throne and around the throne were four living creatures full of eyes, and so forth.’ This throne is understood as the Roman Church, which is called the apostolic see. [Col. 1427A] It is indeed the seat of the Lamb, the seat of him who lives forever and ever. In the midst of it, as daughters in their mother’s lap, sit the four patriarchal Churches; and around it they stand, as attendants in service.”

What Innocent recalled here he had received from his predecessors. Through their efforts he saw—and we still see—that in many Roman basilicas and in many titular churches this same image of the seat of God and of the Lamb had therefore been represented, together with the four mystical figures of the living creatures. These creatures draw along the chariot of the Lord’s glory when it must advance among foreign nations, and surround the throne of God and of the Lamb in honorific service when the majesty of the Lord, before whom all prostrate themselves at the seat of his glory, awaits their adoration.

Thus the whole community of Churches bearing the Catholic name is symbolically depicted: it has been widely propagated throughout every region of the world by the bishops of the patriarchal sees, and gathered and consolidated by those same bishops under the patriarchal throne of Peter, established at Rome as the chief of all, for the unanimous worship and faith of God. It is fittingly articulated into the structure of the body of Christ through the hierarchical governance of the priesthood, with its several communities of the faithful and their prelates arranged by cities, provinces, and dioceses—that is, by bishops, archbishops, primates, and patriarchs—under one supreme pontiff who occupies in this Roman see the succession and place of Peter, Prince of the Apostles. [Col. 1427B]

This unity and ordered connection of the parts of the Catholic Church under one visible head, which is rightly numbered among the articles of the apostolic creed as necessary for the complete expression of our faith, also rightly moved the pontiffs to make it perceptible to the eyes of the faithful: both in the figures mentioned by Innocent and in the appearance of the sacred buildings and the arrangements of those buildings by which the wise architect, the Apostle Peter, wished this most holy tabernacle of God among human beings—the Roman Church—to be constituted.

Whether, therefore, the twenty-five titular churches were founded from the beginning so that all the priestly courses visible at Jerusalem under the ancient priesthood might be recognized here as established more enduringly and more sacredly; or whether, after peace had been restored to the Church, basilicas were also erected in addition to the twenty-five Roman titular churches, so as to reproduce the image of the patriarchal thrones, as Innocent indicates and Cardinal Raspon confirms on the testimony of another cardinal, much more ancient—Saint Peter Damian—and on other documents cited above in the notes to the Life of Saint Cletus, the intention of all the successors was the same as that understood to have belonged to the Prince of the Apostles when he instructed Cletus to establish twenty-five presbyters in the City: namely, to display the ordered primacy of the entire Christian priesthood under several bishops, acknowledging the primacy of one supreme pontiff, who would strengthen the brethren and govern all those called to share in his care by the excellence of his authority. [Col. 1427C]

A single symbol of universality, derived from the courses of the ancient Mosaic priesthood, was not used exclusively to display this image. It was especially suitable at the Church’s emergence. Since for several years the Church was gathered from Jews alone, and then, after the vision of Cornelius, also from the Gentiles, it was appropriate at that time to use the sign of the twenty-four priestly courses, with a twenty-fifth added for the pontifical vicar. That age still vividly and intensely retained the memory and presence of the ancient priesthood.

Meanwhile, once the Synagogue had been honorably buried, other mystical numbers expressing universality remained in the Churches founded by the apostles, especially the number seven, made famous by the Apocalypse of John: both in the Asian diocese, with its seven Churches under the see of Ephesus, which Paul had entrusted to Timothy, and in the symbol of the same number of lampstands and the same number of spirits of God standing before the throne, expressed in that same book. [Col. 1427D]

The Roman pontiffs also decided to employ this symbol in arranging their titular churches, in order to present an image of the universal Church and to express the synod of the whole Christian priesthood in adorning the throne of the Roman Church as the seat of the Lamb. [Col. 1428A]

Just as, therefore, the bishops of the Empire’s smaller dioceses—or provinces—recognized from among their number someone endowed with a superior right, established by the apostles to preside over the others and to convene and order the assembly of the bishops of the same province, so in the Roman titular churches, designated for this reason as dioceses, it was decided that presbyter-cardinals should preside. The other presbyters assigned as assistants to the same titular church would obey them, so that they might administer the sacred rites in the homes of the faithful or in the nearby cemeteries assigned to the boundaries of the titular churches.

Again, just as those smaller dioceses—whether provinces or regions—were constituted under the arrangement that, besides them, the Empire recognized greater dioceses, assigned in civil administration sometimes to more and sometimes to fewer praetorian prefects, so Peter had founded in the ecclesiastical hierarchy two greater diocesan sees, Alexandria and Antioch, next in dignity to Rome and, by the extent of their authority, embracing the prelates of several provinces. It seemed fitting to display an image of these also, distinct from the titular churches, in the divisions of the Roman Church. The opportunity for presenting such an image arose when the larger basilicas were erected by Constantine.

Yet this was not the work of one pontiff or of one century, just as defining the number of patriarchs of the Christian world was not the care of a single pontiff. [Col. 1428B]

The pattern of greater and lesser dioceses was sufficiently displayed under Dionysius, with whom we are concerned, by the titular churches that he repaired, and likewise under Marcellus. After the persecutions just mentioned, each of these pontiffs restored the number of twenty-five titular presbyters—in which the universality of the priesthood shone forth through the total number of its courses—and divided the titular churches and cemeteries among particular presbyters, in the partition already described, with twenty-five titular presbyters serving as though they were the bishops of dioceses. [Col. 1428C]

When larger basilicas were constructed by Constantine, those greater dioceses could conveniently be represented and figuratively displayed in those basilicas. The lesser dioceses of provinces or cities—for eventually the name *diocese* was also applied to individual cities—could be represented by the Roman titular churches, which exercised certain rights in their daughter Churches, as they are called. The greater dioceses, however, could be represented figuratively by the patriarchal basilicas.

It therefore seemed that this image could be presented through the number seven, frequently used in Scripture as an indication of universality, according to the opinion of Augustine, Gregory in Homily 33 on the Gospels, and other Fathers, and also appropriately corresponding to the weekly rotations. Accordingly, seven presbyter-cardinals from the titular churches were individually assigned to the great basilicas that represented the patriarchates. They signified elegantly that the lesser dioceses of cities and provinces were gathered and closely joined by the patriarchs under one head of the whole Catholic Church, which all recognized in the Roman patriarch, as the successor of Peter, Prince of the Apostles, in this same episcopate that he had made the primacy of the Church. [Col. 1428D]

Nor would I say that these weekly rotations of the titular presbyters in the same basilicas were certainly instituted in the very century in which the Constantinian basilicas were founded. Nor would I say that four or five basilicas were initially endowed with this number of seven titular ministers, so as to correspond to the figure of the same number of patriarchal sees in the Christian world.

I know how firmly the Roman pontiffs resisted, in both the fourth and fifth centuries of the Christian era, the efforts of the bishops of Constantinople to be counted either on an equal footing or in a position superior to the other patriarchs. The letters of Damasus and of Leo the Great are sufficiently well known and celebrated. They assert the ancient rights of the three patriarchal sees—Rome, Alexandria, and Antioch—and restrain the usurpation of the bishops of Constantinople, who sought to displace the Alexandrian and Antiochene bishops so that they might gradually creep toward occupying the primacy of the entire Catholic Church and place themselves ahead of the Roman pontiff. [Col. 1429A]

Yet this final ambition did not invade the minds of those bishops who held the see of Constantinople in the time of Damasus and shortly thereafter. Among them was Saint John Chrysostom, who was certainly most obedient to the see of Peter and far removed from encouraging any spark of ambition. When he was accused of attempting to exercise another’s jurisdiction, because he had either ordained or deposed bishops of the Antiochene, Pontic, or Asian diocese, he was thinking nothing of invading the primacy of the universal Church or overturning the original hierarchy and the constitution of the patriarchal thrones of the Antiochene and Alexandrian dioceses.

Thomassinus treats and explains these matters at greater length in Part I of *The Old and New Discipline*, book I, chapter 10. [Col. 1429B] At the beginning of that chapter he shows that, by canon 7 of the Council of Nicaea, a precedence of honor had been decreed for the bishop of Jerusalem, while the rights of the metropolitan of Caesarea, to whom Jerusalem was subject, were preserved. He acknowledges that this honor was increased by the Nicaean Fathers and by the Council of Chalcedon through a new right, with the legates of the apostolic see consenting; nor was the decree rescinded by Leo the Great (chapter 12, no. 7). From that time Jerusalem began to be counted among the patriarchates, rather than merely among the exarchates or metropolitan sees.

He likewise shows that, following this example requested by the Council of Nicaea—which had acknowledged and decreed dignity for the bishop of Aelia, that is, Jerusalem—the clergy of Constantinople arranged for honorary decrees to be issued at the council held in the imperial city under Damasus against Macedonius. These decrees attributed primacy or exarchate to the bishops of that Church, as in canon 3: “The bishop of Constantinople shall have the primacy of honor, *τὰ πρεσβεία τῆς τιμῆς*—‘the privileges of honor’—after the Roman bishop, because it is New Rome.”

Although the apostolic see did not ratify the acts of that council except in the matters it had properly decided against Macedonius, and did not accept the canons concerning the ordering of the patriarchal sees, it nevertheless firmly and consistently persisted, both in that century and in the following ones, in defending the ancient discipline and the jurisdiction of the principal sees after Rome—namely, Alexandria and Antioch. For while it acknowledged their honor, it also recognized that the Byzantine clergy were striving to appropriate the rights of another’s authority.

Nevertheless, it is clear that the Roman see did not refuse to allow an honorary precedence to be granted to the bishops of that imperial city. Thus Paschasinus, the legate of the Pope, complained at the Council of Chalcedon that at the false council of Ephesus only fifth place had been given to Flavian of Constantinople, although he ought to have held first place after the legates of the apostolic see, as Anatolius actually obtained at Chalcedon. [Col. 1429C]

Thomassinus summarizes the matter in no. 19 of chapter 10:

“Nor will I deny that, after the Council of Chalcedon, the bishops of Constantinople always possessed certain privileges of no slight importance, with the Roman pontiff’s consent. They always sat before the patriarch of Antioch and the patriarch of Alexandria. At the Council of Chalcedon, Paschasinus, the Pope’s legate, complained that at the false council of Ephesus only fifth place had been assigned to Flavian, archbishop of Constantinople, although first place after the legates of the apostolic see was owed to him, and was in fact obtained by Anatolius at the very Council of Chalcedon. Thus there can no longer be any doubt that his successors always retained the same place.” [Col. 1429D]

The invasion of ordinary jurisdiction into the provinces of others was therefore rightly condemned by Leo the Great and the other Roman pontiffs in the case of the bishops of Constantinople. On the other hand, they did not prevent an honorary appearance of primacy, in name only, among the other metropolitans—or even of exarchate—from being granted to them with indulgence.

Damasus, or the successors of Damasus, could therefore allow one of the Roman basilicas—which represented the type of such principal sees [Col. 1430A] and which, as Innocent III describes them, displayed “the four patriarchal Churches residing as daughters in the lap of the Roman see, the mother of all, and standing around it as attendants in service”—to represent Byzantium, which had been raised by the councils to a new honor with the express or tacit consent of the Roman see.

The councils themselves—the Constantinopolitan, Ephesian, and Chalcedonian councils—that explicitly decreed new honors for the bishops of Jerusalem and Constantinople testified that these canons would receive force from the will of the Roman pontiff. In the manner of suppliants, they humbly offered prayers to him so that he might consent to them: “We ask that you honor our judgment with your decrees; and just as we have added our agreement to the head in good things, so may your eminence complete for your sons what is fitting.”

Thus the letters sent by the Council of Chalcedon to Pope Leo were at once most dutiful and most reverent, filled with proofs of singular respect. They proclaimed Leo himself the head of the Church and of the council, as Thomassinus aptly observes in chapter 11, no. 15:

“‘You presided as the head over the members,’ they say, ‘with the apostolic light shining among you and spreading its rays even to the Church of Constantinople, because without envy you have been accustomed to enrich your household by sharing in your goods.’” [Col. 1430B]

Therefore, as long as, under Damasus or his immediate successors, the bishops of the imperial city chosen by Constantine as the seat of the Eastern Empire attempted nothing against the firmness of the Nicaean canons or against the ancient privileges of the earlier patriarchs and exarchs, but desired only to be counted, under the consent of the Roman pontiff, with the other greater dioceses by an honorary title and by a place in the assembly close to the Roman legates, it did not seem incongruous for the figure of a daughter honored in this way by the pontiff of ancient Rome, the head of the whole Church, to be dedicated to it, like the other metropolises of the greater dioceses, in one of the basilicas of the City.

Whether that basilica was from the beginning the Laurentian basilica outside the walls, or the Liberian, or even the Vatican [Col. 1430C]—for the Lateran is said to represent the Roman and the Pauline the Alexandrian basilica—makes no difference. Nor does this conflict with the constancy of the Roman pontiffs, who preserved intact, according to the Nicaean canons, the rights of the jurisdiction and authority of the two patriarchal sees instituted by the Apostle Peter, which he placed immediately after Rome above all others.

This is the sense in which the remarks I proposed in my notes to the Life of Cletus should be understood. After the foundation of the larger basilicas had been completed in the fourth century under Liberius, the immediate predecessor of Damasus, when the greater ecclesiastical dioceses had been defined as three original patriarchates together with two more recent ones added by honorary title, making five in all, five basilicas of the Roman episcopate, established in and around the City, likewise represented the universality of the Christian priesthood, which was orderly gathered under Peter’s primacy and comprised all the prelates who governed Churches founded throughout the regions of the world.

Whether Damasus accomplished this when he adjusted the offices of divine worship and the rite of psalmody by weekly rotations in the same recently founded basilicas [Col. 1430D], and enacted that rule for bishops, presbyters, and monasteries (below, no. 54); or whether it was the successors of Damasus—especially those who are said to have instituted weekly rotations of seven bishops from the neighboring regions of the City in the basilica of the Savior at the Lateran, already famous from the time of Stephen IV in the eighth century; or whether it was Simplicius, who is said in the fifth century to have established weekly rotations of presbyters at the three basilicas then situated outside the walls of the City, namely Saint Peter the Apostle, Saint Paul the Apostle, and Saint Lawrence the Martyr, selecting ministers from the first, third, sixth, and seventh of the seven ecclesiastical regions of the City to perform the same offices (as below, no. 48); this one conclusion always follows: the universality of the priesthood spread throughout the entire Christian world was mystically represented at the Roman see in the titular churches and basilicas of the City.

These structures expressed the greater dioceses of the individual patriarchs, and, immediately beneath them, those of exarchs, metropolitans, and bishops, all joined in a hierarchical bond to the successor of Peter. To him, therefore, the Fathers of Arles wrote—as Cardinal Peronius and the Archbishop of Arles observe in Schelestratius—“you who hold the greater dioceses.” Thomassinus observes that this point shines forth especially in chapter 8, no. 14, of Part I and book I of *The Old and New Discipline*: the first see, that of Sylvester, to whom the Fathers of Arles were writing, exercised an unalterable jurisdiction over all the other patriarchs. [Col. 1431A]

I have therefore thought it worthwhile to explain these matters somewhat more clearly, both so that what was obscure in the notes to Cletus, because of the compression of numerous events, might become clear, and so that the passage of the Bibliothecarius concerning Dionysius might be illuminated. It asserts that, in the division he carried out of the churches and cemeteries of the City among the presbyters, Dionysius established parishes, or Roman titular churches, as dioceses. Likewise, the section concerning Marcellus, after the second terrible persecution under Diocletian, expresses more clearly that this pontiff established twenty-five titular churches in the city of Rome “as dioceses.” He did this so that, in the figure of their number, government, and arrangement, the greater dioceses and ecclesiastical provinces might be displayed as gathered and mutually connected under one head, the supreme priest, in such a way as to exhibit the unity and harmony of the whole body and the flow of authority from the head to the members—like the oil that descends from the head of Aaron to the edge of his garment.

The following reasons, among others, were present to Dionysius for making such a connection and ordered unity of the ecclesiastical hierarchy evident to the eyes. First, Novatus had attempted to introduce a schism into the Roman Church. He had come from Africa nine years before Dionysius himself was elected Roman pontiff; and throughout nearly that entire nine-year period Novatian, the antipope, having been intruded by the machinations of that same Novatus, had—as Eusebius reports from the letter of Saint Cornelius to Saint Cyprian (*Ecclesiastical History* VI.43)—not only raised his own sectarians in the city, but had also sent letters of communion to Dionysius of Alexandria [Col. 1431C], to numerous Eastern bishops, and to the Churches, hoping to draw over to his party both the bishop of that greater diocese and many Easterners. They, however, sufficiently careful to preserve the unity of the Catholic Church, rejected the rash letters of the schismatic and remained most closely united with Cornelius, the legitimate bishop of the Roman see, and after his martyrdom with the other successors of this apostolic chair—Lucius, Stephen, and Sixtus—clinging to the Rock cast by Christ the Lord as the foundation of his Church.

He also sent envoys to the African Churches, from which Novatus, the leader of the schism, had come in order to seduce and have himself ordained by him. Through the prudent care of Saint Cyprian, however, these envoys were promptly driven away and deprived of the communion of the faithful in several councils, as their synodal letters to Cornelius testify—letters of which Cyprian makes mention. Thus you may read the whole history arranged suitably in Baronius under the year 254.

While these things were being carried out in the provinces through Novatian’s letters and envoys, for the purpose of ravaging the whole Church of God by propagating the schism and separating it from the See of Peter, what Novatian himself was striving to introduce at Rome, into this citadel of religion, as a source of disturbances and divisions, is clearly attested by Pope Cornelius, who wrote about it to Cyprian. Having summoned his followers to his sacrilegious gatherings for the offering, “after distributing to each his portion of the sacrament, and proceeding onward, he compelled the wretched men, in place of a blessing and thanksgiving, to swear an oath; and taking hold with both his hands of the hands of the recipient, he did not release him until he had bound him by this oath (I shall use his own words): ‘Swear to me by the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ that you will never desert me or return to Cornelius.’”

Thus all the efforts of the schism, then arising for the first time, were directed toward dissolving the firm structure of the Christian body [Col. 1432A] which, joined to the Head established in the Roman See, displayed the several bonds suitably arranged and the influx of grace, beauty, and strength, both in the city and in the provinces.

Against this impious trumpet-call of separation—which Michael had once caused to be heard in heaven by rebellious spirits against God, and which the schismatics, the worst imitators of those rebellious spirits, were now renewing around the earthly seat of the Lamb—the immediate successors of Cornelius could oppose no more effective remedy than to pursue the work of preserving and guarding unity throughout the universal Church. They therefore professed their concern to root and signify that unity more deeply in this very see, with the symbol of the whole Church represented in its own divisions and priestly functions.

The first author of the schism had attempted, by separating the titular churches from Cornelius, the bishop of the city, to prepare the way for separating the provinces and dioceses from the metropolis of the Christian name, established through the See of Peter. “Let,” they said, “the audacity of the cunning deceiver be blunted by the symbol of unity: let the closer bond of the city’s titular churches with their bishop be signified and displayed, thereby showing the bond of the hierarchy of Christian priesthood with the prince of the apostolic order established by the Lord [Col. 1432B].

“Let the Roman titular churches represent the one episcopate of the Catholic Church, distributed among several bishops under one supreme Priest. Let the titular churches be arranged like dioceses beneath the throne of the Fisherman, to display the seat of God and the Lamb on earth, wherever the world extends, under the one Vicar of Christ who grants rights to all.”

Dionysius therefore wished the type of the Christian dioceses to be recognized in the Roman titular churches. Marcellus approved the type, after the recent persecution of Diocletian, restoring those same titular churches in such a way that they were, as it were, dioceses. His successors approved it as well, exercising public worship of God under Constantine the Great and the other Christian emperors a few years after Marcellus.

For, in order to show that the Roman titular churches and basilicas represented the unity of the Church, they also marked upon their walls images of the entire assembly of the priestly elders [Col. 1432C], prostrate before the seat of God and the Lamb, offering to him the offerings and prayers of the saints, together with that new song which clearly explains the mystery in John’s Apocalypse:

> “You redeemed us by your blood  
> from every tribe and tongue,  
> and people and nation,  
> and made us for our God a kingdom and PRIESTS”  
> (*Revelation* 5:9).

Thus these elders prostrated themselves, sang, and testified with a united voice that they had been made for our God a kingdom and priests from every tribe, tongue, people, and nation. For this reason they had been depicted in the preceding chapter seated in as many seats and thrones before the principal seat of the Lamb, and crowned:

> “Around the throne were twenty-four seats; and upon the thrones were twenty-four elders, clothed in white garments, and on their heads were golden crowns.”

Whoever he may have been—whether Sylvester, in the foundation of the three principal basilicas; Damasus, after their number had been increased, in the arrangement of the psalmody; or, in the following century, Simplicius, who established or restored the weekly turns of the priests in certain principal basilicas—each subscribed to the mystical symbol and institution of the preceding pontiffs [Col. 1432D].

For he judged that another sign of universality, namely the number seven, ought to be employed in each basilica: a group chosen from the titular priests of the city, and in the Lateran from bishops, so that the ordered hierarchy of the whole priesthood in the universal Church might be fully represented. The patriarchal thrones contain the parishes—that is, the episcopates preserving their particular order in relation to their metropolitans, exarchs, and patriarchs; and the exarchs and patriarchs themselves acknowledge that they are arranged beneath the one Head of the Church, holding Peter’s primacy throughout the universal Church by the hereditary right of the Roman See. To this See the prince of the apostles, by the power received from Christ the Lord, was commanded to preside over the others, to strengthen his brothers, and to feed the sheep and lambs [Col. 1433A].

This, then, is what we judge to have been instituted by Dionysius and Marcellus: that they arranged and restored the twenty-five titular churches of the Roman presbyterate, or parishes, so that they might be like dioceses. This symbol of the unity of the ecclesiastical hierarchy, impressed after the erection of the basilicas by Sylvester, Damasus, Simplicius, and their successors, was gradually made more conspicuous by assigning the same titular priests to administer sacred rites in the basilicas by weekly turns, and by the number seven, expressing the appearance of a complete assembly. Innocent III aptly explained this, reminding us that among the figures of the Apocalypse the Roman Church is set before us by the same example as the seat of God and the Lamb, and that the things Evangelist John saw in the midst of and around the seat are represented there:

> “This seat signifies the Roman Church, which is called the Apostolic See. Indeed, it is the seat of the Lamb, the seat of the One who lives forever and ever. In its midst, as daughters in a mother’s lap, they sit; and around it, as maidservants in attendance, stand the four patriarchal Churches.”

For a fuller illustration of these matters, one could also cite the rites instituted by the ancient pontiffs in the Roman Order and preserved in our own age with the observance that is fitting [Col. 1433B]: namely, that when the Roman pontiff sits upon his throne and solemnly exercises the office of supreme hierarch of the Church, patriarchs, primates, bishops, and prelates of the orders serving in the Church of God attend and assist him. Above all, the bishops, priests, and cardinal deacons of the Roman Church not only attend and assist him, but also render obedience by kissing the hand covered with gold-embroidered cloth. This was done to testify to that unity, under Peter’s successor, of the entire body of the Church, which the sacred college of bishops, priests, and cardinal deacons of the Roman Church represents together with the basilicas, titular churches, and deaconries of that same Roman Church.

I believe, however, that the words of the Bibliothecary have been sufficiently explained by what has been observed above.

[Note: [Col. 1433B]

**Line 1.**—“Dionysius, formerly a monk, whose parentage we have been unable to discover.” Saint Dionysius, of obscure origin, was a Greek monk—or rather an anchorite, since at some time he had lived a solitary life—from Thurii, a city of Calabria formerly called Magna Graecia. He was chosen from the monastic state to become a priest of the Roman Church, as Jerome testifies in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Dionysius of Alexandria.

**Lines 4 and 5.**—“He divided the churches among the priests.” As soon as Dionysius became pontiff, he divided the churches and cemeteries in the city of Rome among the Roman priests; outside the city he distributed parishes and dioceses, so that each person might remain within his own boundaries and limits and no one might interfere in another’s administration.]

[Note: [Col. 1433C]

At the end of the notes on Sixtus II and the history of his pontificate, the notes concerning the completion of the matters then begun and completed under Dionysius had been promised. They are as follows.

The pontificate of Saint Dionysius, the successor of Sixtus, is made illustrious by the judgment delivered by this pontiff in the case between the people of Pentapolis and Dionysius of Alexandria; by the condemnation of Sabellius and Paul of Samosata and of other heretics, whose errors this blessed pontiff proscribed by his authority and refuted by his teaching.

Although Dionysius of Alexandria had brought the heresy of Sabellius before the Holy See during the preceding pontificate, and had himself fought against that same arch-heretic in his own writings, he nevertheless learned that such errors had spread astonishingly through Pentapolis, the province of his patriarchate in which they had arisen, and that certain bishops had already been infected by those pestilential doctrines:

> “Their speculations had become so powerful that scarcely any longer was the Son of God preached in the Churches”

—as Saint Athanasius reports in *On the Opinion of Dionysius*.

“When Dionysius learned of the matter, since those Churches belonged to his care, he sent envoys to draw the authors of those teachings away from their depraved opinions. But when they did not relent from their foolishness and proceeded more shamelessly in impiety, he was compelled to write a letter of this kind in order to blunt their wickedness … and to charge them with expressions that sounded in a human and humble way concerning the Savior, so that they might be restrained by the human aspects of his nature from saying that the Son was the Father, and so that an easier path might be laid open for them to believe in the divinity of the Son … When, therefore, he had been informed about the Pentapolitans, he wrote this letter, as I have said, out of zeal for religion, against the heresy of Sabellius to Ammonius and Euphranor. Certain brothers from the Church, however, who held the correct view but had not questioned him in order to learn in what manner he had written, went up to Rome and there accused him before Dionysius, the Roman bishop of the same name.

> “There, when certain men accused the Alexandrian bishop before the Roman bishop, alleging that he said that the Son was a work and not consubstantial with the Father, the Roman synod took the matter grievously; and the Roman bishop wrote to his namesake, communicating the judgment of all, and he immediately began preparing his defense,”

and so forth. (The same Athanasius, *On the Synods*.)

The Roman pontiff Dionysius therefore ordered the Alexandrian to explain his opinion more clearly. This bishop, the prelate of the second see in the Catholic Church, obeyed the Roman bishop as his superior without delay, and requested that the charges be communicated to him so that he might present his defense before him. He asked the Roman prelate to indicate the charges made against him. (Athanasius, *On the Opinion of Dionysius*.)

Whatever Protestants may add in their anti-histories of the Church, it is openly and plainly evident that the case of a bishop from overseas was brought before the tribunal of the Holy See according to the established order of jurisdiction; and that this case concerned not a bishop of an inferior bench, but the bishop who holds the second place after the Roman bishop in the universal Church, whose head is the Roman prelate.

That bishop was far from refusing to appear before this tribunal in order to give an account. On the contrary, once the articles on which he had been accused had been communicated to him, he immediately produced his defenses, asserting that the errors attributed to him were calumnies fabricated in Satan’s workshop.

> “After receiving these charges, he produced a work under the title *Refutation and Apology*, in which he rebuked the criminal workshop of the enemies of Christ and demonstrated how they had stirred up this infamy against him.”

The same Athanasius says this in the same place. He gave his treatise the title *Refutation and Apology*, and wrote to the Roman bishop in these words:

> “I also wrote in another letter, in which I show that the charge brought against me is false—namely, that I say Christ is not consubstantial with God. For although I say that I have not found this term, nor read it anywhere in the sacred Scriptures, nevertheless the principles which we have retained do not differ from this opinion … and, as I said, I cannot produce the letter because of the circumstances of the times. If I were sending you the wording, I would much more gladly send the entire copy; and when I obtain it, I shall not omit to do so.”

(The same author, *On the Synods* and *On the Account of the Nicene Synod*.)

We understand Eusebius of Caesarea and Saint Jerome to be speaking of this very defense or apology when they state that four books were composed by Dionysius of Alexandria against Sabellius and dedicated to Dionysius, who was bishop of Rome. (Saint Jerome, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under Dionysius.)

The outcome of the affair, according to Blessed Athanasius, was that the accused defended his case so excellently that he underwent none of the punishments customarily inflicted upon heretics as soon as their impious doctrines have been proved:

> “Nor did he depart from the Church by defending heresy, but he fell asleep in it with piety … If he had not given an account of his writings, there is no doubt that he would have suffered the same things as they did.”

(The same author, *On the Opinion of Dionysius*.)

Pope Dionysius not only condemned the heresies then arising by the authority of his see, but also supplied the Church, through the teaching of his writings, with weapons for defeating future heresies, especially Arianism and the enemies of Christ’s divinity.

Saint Athanasius, who bears witness to this, preserved for us a fragment of those writings, in which the opposing blasphemies of the Sabellians and Marcionites are equally condemned:

> “Rightly, then, I should speak against those who divide, cut apart, and destroy the most reverend proclamation of the Church of God—those who divide the monarchy into three powers, three substances, and three divinities. For I hear that among you there are certain teachers of the divine word who profess this opinion and who, so to speak, fight diametrically against the teachings of Sabellius. He, with blasphemy, says that the Son is the Father and the Father the Son; but these, in a certain sense, establish three gods, while dividing the holy unity into three substances foreign to one another and mutually separated.

> “For the Word of God must be united with the God of all, and the Holy Spirit must abide and dwell in him; and the Holy Trinity must be brought to completion and grow together into one God, almighty and God of all things, as into its summit and principle.

> “The vain-speaking doctrine of Marcion established a division and separation of the monarchy into three principalities. But this is a diabolical institution, not that of the true disciples of Christ and of those who accept the Savior’s teachings. For just as they clearly know from the sacred Scriptures that the Trinity is preached, so they in no way acknowledge three gods to be introduced anywhere by the Old or New Testament.”

(Athanasius, *In the Decree of the Nicene Synod*.)

The same pontiff likewise condemned Paul of Samosata, bishop of Antioch. Several authorities establish this from the testimony of Saint Athanasius (*On the Synods*). This arch-heretic taught that Jesus Christ possessed only human nature and that his blood in the Eucharist was corruptible. (Eusebius, *History* VII.22; and Saint Dionysius, *Letter against Paul of Samosata*.)

Thus Christ the Lord was believed to be present in the Eucharist in those ancient times of the Church, whereas recent sectarians deny him. Paul abjured his errors in the first council held for that purpose in his Church of Antioch. But when it became clear that he had done so deceptively, a second synod assembled there and deposed him.

> “All the bishops and pastors who had been summoned to the aforesaid council jointly composed a single letter to Dionysius, bishop of Rome, and to Maximus, who administered the Church of Alexandria, addressing them by name; and they sent copies of it to all the provinces.”

(Eusebius, *History* VII.24.)

Paul refused to surrender the episcopal house to his successor appointed in his place and therefore sent petitions to the emperor Aurelian, asking that he be compelled to do so. Although this prince was a pagan, he delivered a judgment that was plainly proper, thereby confirming the supreme authority which the Roman Church and its pontiff had always possessed among Christians:

> “For he ordered that the Church’s house be granted to those to whom the bishops of Italy and of the city of Rome indicated by letter that it ought to be granted.”

(Eusebius, same place.)

As Eusebius observes, this was therefore a most holy decree: he decreed most holily—that is, entirely in harmony with the laws of our holy religion and exactly suited to the character of the most perfect justice.]

[Col. 1417]

## 26

Dionysius, formerly a monk, whose parentage we have been unable to discover, occupied the see for two years, three months, and seven days [Note: [Col. 1417] B, eleven years, three months, fourteen days.]. He lived in the time of Gallienus, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus, until the seventh day before the Kalends of January, in the consulship of Claudius and Paternus [Note: [Col. 1417] B, and from the consulship of Valerian and Claudius Aurelianus, from the consulship of Fuscus and Bassus to Aurelian Augustus and Bassus.]. He divided the churches and cemeteries among the priests, and established parishes and dioceses [Note: [Col. 1417] C, and dioceses.]. He held two ordinations during the month of December: twelve priests, six deacons, and eight bishops in various places [Note: [Col. 1417] C B, seven.]. He was also buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January; and the episcopate was vacant for five days.

### CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS

Dionysius: eight years, two months, four days. He lived in the time of Gallienus, from the eleventh day before the Kalends of August, in the consulship of Aemilianus and Bassus, until the seventh day before the Kalends of January, under the consuls Claudius and Paternus.

## XXVII. SAINT FELIX. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 272, THE SECOND YEAR OF THE EMPEROR AURELIAN

[Note: [Col. 1435C]

Line 1: “but four years, three months, twenty-five days.” “He lived in the time of Aurelian.” Line 4: “above the memorials of the martyrs.”
