According to Penius, from the Cavensis codex.

Line 1: “but two years, ten months, twenty-five days; he was crowned by martyrdom.” “He lived in the time of Claudius and Aurelian.” Lines 4 and 5: “to celebrate Mass.” Line 7: “where he was also buried, on the third day before the Kalends of June, at the second milestone from the city of Rome; and the episcopate was vacant for five days.”]

[Note: [Col. 1437A]

**Line 4.**—“Masses were celebrated above the tombs of the martyrs.” Other readings have: “above the memorials of the martyrs.” The tombs, either because of the inscriptions and signs of martyrdom or because the martyrs’ bones had been placed there, were called “memorials of the martyrs.” I think that Canon 34 of Elvira arose from this constitution of Felix: that no candle be lit in cemeteries, for the spirits of the saints must not be disturbed. The pagans would thereby discover from the light of the candle the places where the martyrs had been buried, and from that indication would overthrow their tombs. Since this was not permitted in the time of Diocletian, I believe that the bones of the martyrs then began to be placed in other locations beneath altars, and that from this arose the Church’s practice of consecrating altars with the relics of the martyrs, which are buried beneath them by the consecrating bishop.]

[Note: [Col. 1437A]

**Line 4.**—“He established that Masses be celebrated above the tombs of the martyrs.” Oratories or altars were built above the tombs of the martyrs in their memory. Augustine, *Against Faustus* XX.22:

> “The Christian people celebrates the memorials of the martyrs with religious solemnity, both to stir up imitation and to be joined to their merits and aided by their prayers; yet in such a way that we establish altars not to any of the martyrs, but to the God of the martyrs, although in the memorials of the martyrs,” etc.

These places were called *martyria* (Council of Chalcedon, canon 8):

> Greek: Οἱ κληρικοί τῶν πτωχείων, καὶ μοναστηρίων, καὶ μαρτυρίων, ὑπὸ τὴν ἐξουσίαν τῶν ἐν ἐκάστῃ πόλει ἐπισκόπων διαμενέτωσαν·  
> “Let the clergy of the poorhouses, monasteries, and martyria remain under the authority of the bishops in each city.”

(Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 103, concerning the abbot Innocent):

> Greek: Εἰσῆλθεν εἰς τὸ μαρτύριον ἑαυτοῦ, ὁ οἰκοδομήκει αὐτὸς, ἐν ᾧ κατέκειτο λείψανα τοῦ θείου Ιωάννου τοῦ Βαπτιστοῦ.  
> “He entered his own martyrium, which he himself had built, in which the relics of the divine John the Baptist lay.”

He entered his own martyrium, which he himself had built, in which the relics of Saint John the Baptist had been placed. (Jerome, *Life of Hilarion*.)

> “They reported that the reason for concealing it, in accordance with the command of Antony, was to prevent Pergamius, who was the richest man in those regions, from taking the holy body to his estate and building a martyrium.”

By the constitution of Theodosius it was permitted that, wherever one of the saints had been buried, a martyrium—so called—might be built there in his honor (Book VII of the Theodosian Code, *On the Violation of Tombs*).

Hence the priests appointed in the oratories of the martyrs for the sake of the worship of the martyrs were called *martyrarii* (“martyr-shrine priests”) (Council of Orléans II, canon 13):

> “Let abbots, martyrarii, recluses, or priests not presume to issue letters.”

Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of the Martyrs* II.46:

> “At that time, after the death of Proserius the martyrarius, the city deacon of this basilica was appointed its sacristan.”

What the constitution of Felix permitted—namely, that Masses be celebrated over the tombs of the martyrs—is to be understood of Masses celebrated in oratories built in memory of the martyrs, in which their relics or entire bodies had been placed.]

[Note: [Col. 1437D]

**Line 2.**—“He was crowned by martyrdom.” That Felix received the crown of martyrdom on the third day before the Kalends of July in the year 275 is indicated, in addition to the authority of the *Book of the Pontiffs*, by his letter to Maximus, bishop of Alexandria, the successor of Dionysius, a fragment of which survives in the acts of the Council of Chalcedon. In that fragment of the letter, however, the day and year are missing. See Blanchini’s following notes.

**Line 4.**—“He established.” This decree was not first instituted by Pope Felix; for long before Felix’s time the Church claimed such an institution, and most appropriately according to sacred Scripture—Revelation, chapter 7—where the tombs of the martyrs are called altars.]

[Note: [Col. 1438A]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

The Liberian catalogue preserves Felix’s period intact both in its numerical indications and in its consular dating. The catalogue of Felix IV, the *Book of the Pontiffs*, and the Ocriculan codices likewise provide the full consular dating, although it is somewhat corrupted in the numbers, as is clear from the comparison of the documents which we reviewed in the *Prolegomena*.

The beginning of Pope Felix’s pontificate should be fixed on 3 January of the year 269, which was opened by the consulship of Claudius and Paternus—a date that fell on a Sunday—since the vacancy of the see after the death of Dionysius lasted five days, as this same *Book of the Pontiffs* testifies.

The Liberian catalogue counts five complete years of this pontificate, eleven months, and twenty-five days. Felix’s death is therefore referred to 29 December of the year 274, under the consuls Aurelian for the second time and Capitolinus. These are the consuls which both the catalogues and the Bibliothecary and the Ocriculan codices assign to the final period of Felix’s life.

The paintings of Saint Paul, after Felix’s name, display only the final preserved letter. In the second verse, however, they preserve the letter N from the syllable *an[n]orum*, “of years,” and in the third the abbreviation M, indicating months. All the numbers have disappeared.

When the Italian catalogues were copied from these same paintings, the numbers must already have been faint. Instead of the abbreviation V, which was to be written for five years, the copyist’s eyes, deceived into thinking that they saw the sign for two, present it to his mind—and to ours—as the number II. This error could easily have arisen when looking from the floor of the church at that height and distance, if the colors and strokes of the letter V had faded at their lowest junction into the form II.

In the months likewise, the unit which followed the sign X for ten in the Liberian catalogue, if it was less distinct, provided an occasion for recording ten months instead of eleven. The names of the consuls, preserved in so many codices, and the day of election, placed on the fifth day after the death of the predecessor, together with the day of deposition, are equally certain from the ancient and genuine documents which will soon be produced; they do not allow us to doubt the integrity of the epoch defined in the Liberian catalogue in these words:

> “Felix, etc. He sat five years, eleven months, twenty-five days.”

I said that the day of deposition is established by genuine and very ancient documents. For in the work cited among the *Prolegomena*, written during the lifetime of Liberius, the depositions of Felix and Callistus are recorded on the third day before the Kalends of January; several martyrologies and lectionary codices support this reading.

Our Bibliothecary—or rather his copyist—must therefore be corrected. Through the error of a single letter he wrongly wrote the third day before the Kalends of June, that is, 30 May, whereas the work of the fourth century cited above among the *Prolegomena* correctly had the third day before the Kalends of January, that is, 30 December. This gave later writers an opening to transfer the commemoration of Felix from the true day of his deposition, 30 December, to 30 May, as Bede, Usuard, and Ado did in their martyrologies.

When the *Prolegomena* was being committed to the press, I observed that the catalogue of Felix IV and two Colbertine manuscripts (h and m, page c.) counted four years for Felix, coming closest to the period of five years indicated by the consuls if one endpoint was excluded, while most of the other catalogues expressed two years and differed still more widely from the Liberian catalogue. Since all the numbers had disappeared from the paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul, I thought it safer to follow the Felician catalogue.

After more careful consideration, however, the consular lists recorded for Felix—both in the Liberian and Felician catalogues and in the Bibliothecary and the other codices—indicated that the Liberian catalogue was the oldest of all, since it assigns five years, eleven months, and twenty-five days: namely, from the day of his ordination, 3 January, which was also a Sunday in the year 269, under Claudius and Paternus, to 30 December 274, under Aurelian for the second time and Capitolinus.

The Italian catalogues c, d, e, and f, the Belgian catalogue g, the Colbertine manuscripts l and n, and the Ocriculan codices, which display only two years, appear instead to have arisen from the faulty transcription of an ancient copyist, who distorted the number five, V, into the number two, II, by separating the lower strokes of the numeral.

Accordingly, in the *Pontifical and Consular Chronology* printed at the end of the *Prolegomena*, I followed the epoch of the Liberian catalogue and judged that the other catalogues and codices should be corrected in accordance with it, as the consular calculations demonstrate.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

**Line 4.**—“He established that Masses be celebrated over the tombs of the martyrs.” Cardinal Bona illustrates this institution and its causes with numerous testimonies of the holy Fathers and writers contemporary with them, as well as with examples from the Roman Church and others (*Liturgical Matters* I.19.5).

Regarding the institution itself, he records from Prudentius that it was observed at the tomb of Saint Hippolytus the martyr, namely the one who had suffered together with Blessed Laurence under Valerian:

> “That table, giver of the sacrament, likewise a faithful guardian set beside its martyr,  
> preserves the bones for the hope of the eternal Judge,  
> and also feeds the people of the Tiber with holy food.”

From Blessed Paulinus, in the ninth birthday poem of Saint Felix, he likewise shows that the same practice was observed at the shrine of the holy apostles:

> “The entire altar looks out through windows toward heaven,  
> beneath which the bodies of the saints have their dwelling within.  
> For the apostolic ashes, placed beneath the heavenly table,  
> return among the sacred offerings of holy dust  
> a peaceful fragrance breathing toward Christ.”

From Ambrose he also teaches that, according to Roman custom, a basilica was dedicated through the relics of the martyrs brought to the altar.

[Col. 1439C] As for the reasons, above all he advances the reason derived from the article of faith by which we profess the communion of the saints in the Creed:

> “Nevertheless, the most ancient custom, received everywhere, dictates that the relics of the martyrs be used in the consecration of altars. John saw their souls beneath the altar of God in heaven, in chapter 6 of the Apocalypse. This veneration of the martyrs arose from that article of faith by which we believe and confess the communion of the saints.
>
> “The faithful, therefore, in order to profess this by their action, gathered for prayer and participation in the divine mysteries in those places where the saints’ remains had been placed, so that in this way, insofar as the condition of the dead permits, they might communicate with them. For through those remains the Church triumphant is represented, which thus in some manner communicates with the Church militant and takes part in our sacrifice.
>
> “Although the remains and bones of the saints, in the absence of the soul, lack sensation, they nevertheless refer to the soul which is in heaven; and within them there is a certain seed of resurrection and eternity.”

Therefore Jerome, in the same place, mockingly rebukes the impious inference of Vigilantius, who had dared to attack the worship of the martyrs:

> “Then the Roman bishop does wrong, who offers sacrifices to the Lord over the venerable ashes of the dead Peter and Paul, according to us, but according to you merely worthless dust, and regards their tombs as Christ’s altars.”

With no less appropriateness, he adds other observances in support of the reason just given, writing at the end of the same chapter:

> “For this reason also the Fathers of the ancient Church were accustomed to bury orthodox bishops beneath an altar, so that sacrifices and ordinations might be performed with them. They considered the communion of the living bishop with his deceased predecessor necessary for preserving the unity of the faith and indicating legitimate succession.
>
> “A trace of this custom appears in the conference held at Carthage between the Catholics and Donatists in the time of Innocent I, at the first hearing, chapter 204. There Donatus, bishop of Sitifis, said: ‘He ordained a priest above the body of a Catholic bishop, and, God willing, a bishop will be ordained there.’”

This is cited there by the most learned cardinal. One might add to it the ancient custom of the Alexandrian prelates, which Thomassinus, from Liberatus, records in *A Brief Account*, chapter 20, and in *The Old and New Discipline*, part I, book II, chapter 54, section 2:

> “It was the custom that the man who was to succeed a deceased bishop should keep the night vigil over his body, place the deceased man’s right hand upon his own head, and, after the body had been committed to the earth, be clothed with the pallium of blessed Mark and thus ascend the throne of Mark. It is the custom at Alexandria that the man who succeeds the deceased should keep vigil over the body of the dead man, place his right hand upon his own head, and, after he has been buried, receive with his own hands the pallium of blessed Mark around his neck; then he may legitimately sit.”

Although this practice of placing the predecessor’s hand upon the head of the succeeding pontiff did not prevail in the Roman Church, it is nevertheless established that ordinations were generally carried out near the body of blessed Peter, as may be gathered from the sermons of Leo the Great, who summoned the people and clergy on the day of ordination to keep vigil at Saint Peter’s.

Hence we explain the origin of the suspicion that the body of the same apostle was transferred from the Vatican to the Catacombs. During the persecution of Decius and Valerian, which especially attacked the clergy, the place at the Vatican assigned for the assembly at the ashes of blessed Peter had become so celebrated that it exposed the clergy and Christians who would go there for ordination to the danger of the persecutors.

When Gallienus’s campaign against us had subsequently been relaxed, the apostle’s body could readily have been returned to its former place. There, in accordance with the established continuity of the preceding rites, ordinations could again be celebrated as usual near the body of the prince of the apostles. From him that power of preserving and reconciling the unity of the Church was transmitted to his successors, as we have already explained in the case of Dionysius.

## Line 6, 7.—

Here he built a basilica on the Via Aurelia, where he was also buried, at the second milestone from the city of Rome. Bosius and Severanus, among those whom Schelestratius cites (in the notes on this number), wrote that they had diligently investigated the church and cemetery of Saint Felix, but had searched in vain at a place too near the City—namely, at the title of Saint Pancratius, situated only half a mile from the City gate. It is now understood from Opusculum XVI, stated in the Prolegomena, col. 375 and following, when compared with the site of the cemetery of Saints Processus and Martinianus, recently discovered by the distinguished Canon Boldetti on the Via Aurelia, at the second milestone from the City in the vineyard of the Reverend Fathers of Christian Doctrine, not far from the vineyard of the most illustrious prelate Mapheus Farsetti, Venetian patrician. A second entrance to this cemetery opens toward the suburban estate of Saint Pius V, commonly called Il Casaletto di Pio quinto. For this distance corresponds to that nearby church and cemetery marked by the name of both Felixes and indicated by these words: “In the other church, Processus and Martinianus; and in the third, the two Felixes.” Concerning the place recently discovered, and the cemetery of Saints Processus and Martinianus at the second milestone from the City, see the aforementioned Boldetti, *On Sacred Cemeteries*, book II, chapter 18, p. 539.

### Note: [Col. 1440D]

**Line 4.—** Here he established that Masses should be celebrated over the tombs of the martyrs. The Church claims such an institution for herself from a time long before the age of Pope Felix, and this is supported also by the testimony of divine Scripture. For the book of Revelation, chapter VI, says: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain because of the Word of God and because of the testimony which they held,” etc. This clearly demonstrates that the altars were the tombs of martyrs. This custom always continued in the Church, and Greek and Latin interpreters alike agree in it; they likewise affirm that the tomb of the martyrs was an altar and that sacrifices were accustomed to be offered upon it. Felix, therefore, seems not so much to have established this decree for the first time as to have renewed an ancient practice. Hence altars and shrines are not consecrated without the relics of martyrs.

### Note: [Col. 1441A]

**The Ninth Persecution of the Church.**

Aurelian was made emperor in the year 270 and was well disposed toward the Christians. Against Paul of Samosata, condemned by a later synod of Antioch as the author of a new heresy, he issued an edict. “But as time went on,” says Eusebius, book VII, chapter 30, “he began, through the counsels of certain persons, to be moved to think differently about us, so that he might stir up persecution against our people.” Although it was brief, having been launched by Aurelian near the end of his life, it nevertheless produced a great number of martyrs. On this, see the Annotator of Baronius under the year 272.

### Note: [Col. 1441A]

Pope Felix wrote a letter against the heresies of Sabellius and Paul of Samosata to Maximus, bishop, and to the clergy of Alexandria. The Council of Ephesus and the Council of Chalcedon preserved for us, together with its title, a fragment of this letter, which they use to confirm the faith of the Church against the heresies condemned by him. It reads as follows:

“From the letter of Felix, most holy bishop of Rome and martyr, to Maximus, bishop, and the clergy of Alexandria. Concerning the Incarnation of the Word and the faith, we believe in our Lord Jesus Christ, born from the Virgin Mary, that he himself is the eternal Son and Word of God, and not a man assumed by God so that he would be another apart from him. For the Son of God did not assume a man so that he might exist as another distinct from himself; but, being perfect God, he at the same time became perfect man, incarnate from the Virgin.” (*Council of Ephesus*, part II, act 1; likewise in the *Council of Chalcedon*, act 1.) See also Saint Cyril to the Alexandrians, in the *Apology*, and Vincent of Lérins, *Against Heresies*, chapter 42.

**Line 4.—** Here he established that Masses should be celebrated over the tombs of the martyrs. This custom derives from apostolic tradition, as we learn from what John records in Revelation, chapter VI: “I saw beneath the altar of God the souls of those who had been slain because of the Word of God and because of the testimony which they held.”

[Col. 1435]

### 27

Felix, a Roman by nation, son of Constantius, occupied the see for two years, ten months, and twenty-five days [**Note:** [Col. 1435] B: two years, five months, and one day]. He was crowned with martyrdom. He lived in the time of Claudius Aurelianus, from the consulship of Claudius and Paternus to the consulship of Aurelianus and Capitolinus [**Note:** [Col. 1435] B: from the consulship of Aurelianus and Bassus to that of Aurelianus II, on 4 July, and Capitolinus]. He established that Masses should be celebrated over the tombs of the martyrs. He held two ordinations in the month of December: nine priests, two deacons [**Note:** [Col. 1435] CB: five], and five bishops in various places. He built a basilica on the Via Aurelia, where he was also buried, at the second milestone from the city of Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of June; and the episcopal see was vacant for five days.

## Catalogue under Liberius

Felix: five years, eleven months, and twenty-five days. He lived in the time of Claudius and Aurelianus, from the consulship of Claudius and Paternus to the consulship of Aurelianus II and Capitolinus.

## XXVIII. SAINT EUTYCHIANUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 275, THE FIFTH YEAR OF THE EMPEROR AURELIANUS

### Note: [Col. 1441C]

Line 1: “from Maximus, bishop of the city of Luna; he occupied the see for one year and one day.” Line 3: “the second of December, and Carinus consul,” in the Mazarine; “the second Carus and Carinus consul,” in the other. “He established.” Line 8: “to his own notice, so that it might be made public.” Line 10: “nine, who was also crowned with martyrdom and buried.” Line 12: “eight days.”

Line 3: “in the consulship of Aurelianus.” Line 5: “that beans and grapes be blessed.” Line 6: “he buried with his own hands.” Line 8: “so that this might be made public to his own knowledge.” Line 10: “and crowned with martyrdom.” Lines 11 and 12: “and the episcopate was vacant for eight days.”

[Col. 1442C] In Holstenius and Schelestratius.

Line 2: “Florentius II and Cassianus, one year, one month, and one day.” Line 4: In the Vatican manuscript, “he commanded that they be blessed,” with *ut* deleted; according to Florentius and Cassianus alike, the words “he buried without a dalmatic” are absent from the Vatican manuscript. Line 7: “his own,” in Florentius and Cassianus. Line 8: “he ordained three in succession,” in Florentius.
