Line 2: he occupied the see for eight years, ten months, and four days. Line 3: “from the consulship of Aurelianus III and Marcellinus.” Line 5: “that beans and grapes be blessed. In the times mentioned above, he buried 242 martyrs with his own hand in various places.” Line 6: “so that anyone from the assembly of the faithful” (the copyist added *de*, or omitted the number); “the episcopate was vacant for eight days.”

### Note: [Col. 1443A]

**Line 4.—** Here he established that only beans and grapes should be blessed as produce upon the altar. It was an apostolic institution that new produce and fresh grapes should be offered upon the altar as first fruits of the harvest and blessed by the priests, and that neither honey nor milk nor anything else should be offered except grapes and fresh produce. This is found in Apostolic Canon 3; the Council of Carthage, canon 40; the Sixth Synod in Trullo, canons 28 and 57; the canon beginning “We have learned,” *On Consecration*, distinction 1; and the *Apostolic Constitutions*, book VIII, chapter 46.

From this arose among the Greeks the custom that the patriarch of Constantinople should bless produce and fresh grapes on the feast of the Assumption of the Blessed Mary in the sacred church of Blachernae, as Balsamon testifies in his commentary on the aforementioned Apostolic Canon 3; and among the Latins, the custom that grapes should be blessed on the feast of the Lord’s Saint Sixtus, according to the Gloss on the aforementioned canon beginning “We have learned.” Eutychianus, therefore, should not be called the author of this institution but rather its restorer.

Baronius’s conjecture is also highly probable: that Eutychianus renewed this institution in opposition to the error of the Manichaeans, who believed that wine was the gall of the princes of darkness and considered it sacrilegious to taste wine, as Augustine testifies, *On the Morals of the Manichaeans*, chapter 26, and likewise in *Against Faustus*, book XX, chapter 12.

**Line 6.—** He established that no one who buried a martyr should bury him in any manner without a dalmatic or purple colobium. Eutychianus decreed that no martyr should be buried without a dalmatic or purple colobium. This was established for the honor of the martyrs, since the dalmatic was the common garment of bishops and deacons. Augustine, *Questions on the Old Testament*, chapter 46: “As though deacons today were not clothed in dalmatics, just as bishops are.” And Pontius the Deacon, in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*, in Surius, September 14: “After he had removed his dalmatic and handed it over to the deacons, he stood in his linen garment.”

When the dalmatic of Paschasius the deacon was placed upon his bier, it immediately became illustrious through miracles. Gregory, *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 40: “When this man had died in the time of Symmachus, bishop of the apostolic see, a demon-possessed man touched his dalmatic, which had been placed over the bier, and was immediately healed.”

Martyrs were buried with a dalmatic or purple colobium. The colobium was a tunic without sleeves, like a dalmatic, having a small purple patch sewn onto it; this was a sign of the warfare of Christ. Dorotheus, *Doctrine* 1:

> “Our colobium also has a purple sign. What does the purple sign mean? Everyone who serves as a soldier for the king has purple on his cloak.”

Pachomius the abbot placed hoods (*cucullae*) upon the brothers of Tabennisi, marked with the sign of a purple cross. Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 38:

> “He ordered purple crosses to be put upon them; he ordered hoods bearing a purple cross to be placed upon them.”

### Note: [Col. 1443D]

**Line 5.—** In his own time he buried martyrs with his own hand in various places. The persecution of Decius, which forbade Christians access to the cemeteries, may have been the reason that the bodies of the martyrs lay without due honor. Later, therefore, when the basilicas had been restored and the parishes had been distributed, the pontiff solemnly transferred and deposited the relics of the martyrs.

But if the matter is traced further back, since the *Liber Pontificalis* describes not only the deeds of the pontificate but also what preceded them, these words seem to indicate that during the persecution of Decius Eutychianus, while serving in the office either of priest or of deacon of the martyrs, buried the celebrated martyrs. This seems to be indicated by the words explaining that Eutychianus performed these things in his own times, or throughout the various periods of his offices—namely, by burying the celebrated bodies of the martyrs.

That the *Liber Pontificalis* is there designating an ecclesiastical office is also inferred from its observation that he performed this work of piety with his own hand. The office of burying the martyrs and caring for their memorials, relics, and similar matters properly belonged to the priest of the martyrs, as is shown above by the example of Anacletus, who erected a memorial to the apostles. This institution and office had been entrusted to priests of the martyrs because it was useful, indeed necessary, that they should report to the bishops the acts of virtue and the true signs of martyrdom that had preceded the death. The bishops could then either confer the title of confessor upon those who had deserved it or decree veneration for those crowned after completing their martyrdom. In this way the cause of the martyrdom, the number of martyrs, and their illustrious struggles would become more certainly known.

This was especially important because, at that time, the abundance of genuine martyrs was considered a sign of the true Church. Thus Montanus, a disciple of Saint Cyprian, mocking heretical depravity, uses this argument and challenges heretics to understand the truth from the abundance of martyrs in the Church. An ancient anonymous writer quoted by Eusebius, book V, chapter 16 at the end, while attacking the heretics of his time with equal zeal, says this about their practices:

> “When, after being convicted in everything I have set forth above, they have nothing to answer, they attempt to flee to the martyrs, claiming that they have many martyrs. For the followers of other heresies also proclaim that they have very many martyrs. The first, certainly, who follow the heresy of Marcion … say that they have very many martyrs of Christ.”

Therefore, so that true confessors and crowned martyrs might be recognized, it was necessary—and it belonged to the prudent care of the bishops—to choose zealous inspectors from among the priests, who would determine from the acts and deeds of the martyrs whether they were worthy to be honored with that distinction.

Apollonius, cited above in his refutation of the Cataphrygian heresy, presupposes such an examination. Describing their practices, he says that they boasted of their martyrs and, from this, of the true Church. Rebuking them, he writes:

> “We shall show that those whom they call prophets and martyrs collected money not only from the rich but also from beggars, orphans, and widows. The deeds of a prophet must be examined like fruit.”

Regarding the examination of a certain Alexander among them, who claimed to be a martyr, Apollonius adds:

> “As for Alexander, so that the truth may become known to all who desire to know it: he was tried at Ephesus by Aemilius Frontinus, proconsul of Asia, not because of the name of Christ but because of the robberies he had committed, since he had already deserted the faith. Afterwards, having falsely claimed the name of Christ, he was released after deceiving the faithful by his words. The Church of the place from which he came did not even receive him.”

For how could the Churches and the faithful determine who should be honored with the customary titles unless there were priests to examine the deeds? This task, therefore, had been entrusted to appointed men who examined the deeds of confessors and martyrs, reported them to the bishops, and then made public the honors to be conferred.

No others could have performed this duty except those closest to the ministry of the martyrs—certainly the priests and deacons of the martyrs. To them, by virtue of their offices, belonged the responsibility of consigning the bodies of the martyrs to burial and marking them with signs for purposes of veneration. This must be admitted, since the identity of the martyr had to be clearly established for the proper honoring of the relics.

When Caecilianus the archdeacon did not find such signs while Lucilla was kissing the bones of someone, he forbade her communion, according to Optatus. The names and times of martyrdom attached to the tombs as indications are also shown by an incident concerning Martin, praised by Severus, when he discovered that the people were frequenting a tomb concerning which it was not certainly known whether it was that of a martyr. Thus Sulpicius writes in the *Life of Saint Martin*:

> “Martin, not rashly trusting uncertain claims, asked those who were older than the priests or clergy to show him the name of the martyr or the time of his passion.”

From the priests, I say, whose concern this was, and through their diligence, there have come down to us the records of the deposition, burial, and feast days of the martyrs, as well as other material from which the Martyrologies were compiled.

To make the matter clear by testimony, there is an ancient register indicating where each of the Roman pontiffs rests—we gave it above. And at the beginning of the ancient Calendar of the Church of Carthage, published by Mabillon, it is explained from what the work was compiled. *Analecta*, volume III, says:

> “Here are contained the birth-days of the martyrs and the depositions of the bishops, whose anniversaries the Church of Carthage celebrates.”

Sozomen likewise praises the fact that each Church possessed such separate registers according to the most ancient institutions, when he speaks of the cities of Palestine, Constantia and Gaza, book V, chapter 3:

> “Each has its own bishop separately, its own clergy, its own feast days of its martyrs, and commemorations of the bishops who presided over them.”

Eutychianus’s diligence, therefore, in burying the martyrs with his own hand indicates that he did this on the occasion of the persecution of Decius, which raged during his time. When cemeteries and catacombs had been forbidden, the deacon or priest of the martyrs buried the bodies of the martyrs wherever he could, so that they would not be deprived of that honor.

**Line 6.—** “He who established that whoever among the faithful buried a martyr … should nevertheless make it known to him.” This decree confirms the preceding observation: namely, that the pontiff, while performing the office of a priest of the martyrs, personally cared for the bodies of the martyrs and, to prevent fraud, attached the customary signs. The words signify that through this care the identity of the martyrs and their relics might be verified.

On the same occasion he decreed that, whatever their rank or condition, those faithful who were then seeking out the relics of martyrs with special devotion and keeping them in their homes should report them to the pontiff, together with the honor paid to them, so that he might know whether they were genuine martyrs, recognizable by the signs and tokens that had been used.

Eutychianus may have judged that this precaution was necessary when, after the indulgence of Gallienus had restored the Churches and cemeteries, the bodies of the martyrs were reburied beneath altars for the celebration of solemn Masses, as his predecessor Felix had established by decree.

Another custom had also become widespread: the faithful kept the relics of martyrs in private houses and offered prayers to God before them, invoking the martyrs as mediators. From the beginning of this century, in order to increase the glory of confessors, bishops granted remissions of the penalties due for sins to penitents who brought petitions for the prayers of martyrs, with those petitions signed by the confessors themselves. Indeed, when martyrs had been designated, people hastened to them, standing before God after their crown, to obtain pardon for their crimes and true repentance.

Examples of this survive in the Cyprianic letters, especially Letters 21 and 26, which should be read. In them Cyprian himself seeks, both for himself and for others, the intercessions of crowned martyrs.

That the faithful were accustomed to build domestic oratories in which they deposited the bodies of martyrs that they had sought out, so that they might have them as intercessors with God for sins committed, is taught by the Acts of Saint Boniface the martyr, who died a martyr only a few years later. Aglaes and Boniface, resolving to abandon their former impurity, decided that the bodies of martyrs should be sought out and, once found, kept within their household, after constructing an oratory for that purpose.

Thus Aglaes encourages Boniface to travel toward the East, where the beginnings of the persecution of Diocletian were then occurring, according to the Holstenian edition, p. 8:

> “Go, therefore, to those regions and bring us relics—that is, the bodies of the holy martyrs—so that, by serving and ministering to them, and by building worthy houses of prayer for them, we may be saved through their holy sufferings, both we and many others.”

Eutychianus may also have been moved by the insolent faction of the Novatians then active, as well as by the disorderly mass of Cataphrygians, Marcionites, and similar wicked men. When they saw Catholics presenting the glorious struggles of the martyrs as the token of the true Church, they too boasted of their own martyrs, as was explained above from the anonymous writer and Apollonius quoted by Eusebius.

Moreover, since the bodies of martyrs were purchased from the agents of the persecutors with money, and impostors fabricated relics, Eutychianus decreed that information concerning buried martyrs should be reported to the bishops, so that, after the signs had been examined, it might be determined who the genuine martyrs were and honor could safely be given to them.

The diligence of the Churches and bishops in weighing the martyrs’ former way of life, the circumstances of their martyrdom, and the causes of their completed martyrdom was most careful and at the same time most ancient. All these matters are found to have been considered and examined with balanced judgment.

In an age closer to the apostolic period, the Churches worked zealously on behalf of this diligence. In crowned martyrs they examined whether they had been trained and prepared or untrained. An outstanding document on this subject survives in the letter of the Church of Lyons, addressed to all the Christian Churches, in Eusebius, book V, chapter 1.

A few passages may be cited to illuminate the argument. Describing the crowd of confessors detained in prison and explaining how the unprepared failed in the struggle while those trained in the faith persevered in their confession, the letter clarifies the meaning of the terms as follows:

> “From that point the others also began to be recognized and distinguished. The first martyrs, who with the greatest eagerness of spirit made that solemn confession of the martyrs, were indeed ready and prepared. But those who were unprepared and untrained, and who did not yet possess firm strength to withstand the onset of so great a struggle, were then plainly revealed.”

The signs of a trained and prepared martyr are described in Attalus:

> “Attalus … was strongly demanded by the people for punishment, as a man of great renown. Prepared for the contest, he came forward, relying upon the conscience of his right actions; for he had been thoroughly trained in the discipline of the Christians and had always stood among us as a witness to the truth.”

It was necessary to exercise caution in weighing the cause of the punishment, since even those who had denied Christ were sometimes condemned to death. Hence the bishops needed to be circumspect in distinguishing among those killed which were confessors and which were outsiders to the faith.

The Church of Lyons declares this in the following words:

> “All those who immediately upon their first arrest denied the faith were also thrown into prison and endured the same things as the other martyrs. Their denial of the faith did them no good at that time. But those who confessed themselves to be what they truly were—that is, Christians—were thrown into chains, with no other crime charged against them. These, however, were subsequently detained as murderers and criminals, enduring punishment twice as severe as the others. The joy of martyrdom, the hope of promised blessedness, love for Christ, and the Spirit of God the Father refreshed the former. But the conscience of the latter was grievously numbed, so that while they were being slaughtered they could easily be distinguished from the others by their very expression and appearance.”

The remaining signs of the trained and untrained are to be read there, p. 166 and following.

Before the encyclical of Lyons, the Church of Smyrna, in another encyclical, likewise demonstrated through the example of the martyr Polycarp—Eusebius, book IV, chapter 15—which martyrs should be regarded as evangelical. It distinguished those who voluntarily offered themselves to death and persecution from those who, persevering in the practice of virtue, awaited arrest.

This caution too was considered necessary, since many of those who voluntarily offered themselves denied the faith, as the Church demonstrated in that case. It therefore presented Polycarp as a true martyr worthy of praise and imitation: he did not offer himself voluntarily, but, after being arrested, displayed the signs of Christian fortitude in the struggle.

Thus, from a fragment preserved by Valesius in his notes on Eusebius, pp. 69 and 73, they present him to the faithful as an example:

> “He was not only an outstanding teacher but also a supreme martyr. Everyone strives to imitate his martyrdom, since it agreed with the Gospel of Christ.”

That bishops took this consideration into account when honoring martyrs is shown by Mansurius, primate of Carthage and predecessor of Caecilianus. He forbade those who had offered themselves to the persecutors to be honored as martyrs. This is read in the *Brevic.*, col. 3, chapter 14, in the new collection of councils by Baluzius, p. 327, where the letter of Mansurius is quoted:

> “It was also read in the same letters that Mansurius disapproved of those who offered themselves to persecution without having been arrested and voluntarily declared that they possessed Scriptures which they would not hand over, although no one had asked them for them; and he forbade Christians to honor them.”

Earlier, when the proconsul was inquiring about the priests of the Church of Carthage, Saint Cyprian answered, as recorded in his Life:

> “Since discipline forbids anyone to offer himself voluntarily, and since this also displeases your judgment, they ought not to offer themselves, but, when sought out by you, they should be found.”

Saint Augustine commends this discipline, confirmed by Cyprian’s own testimony, in *Against the Letter of Gaudentius*, when he writes:

> “The blessed Cyprian, instructed by these sacred writings, said in his confession that discipline forbids anyone to offer himself.”

The subdeacons of the Church of Carthage, imbued with the same ancient discipline, were questioned during the persecution of Diocletian and ordered to hand over the sacred books. They answered that responsibility for them belonged to the readers. When the judges insisted that they name the readers, they replied—in the *Acts of Turgatius and Felix*, after Optatus, p. 94:

> “We are not betrayers.”

Cyprian imparted this discipline to the clergy in his final exhortatory letter. Among the other instructions was this:

> “No one should voluntarily offer himself to the pagans. But one who has been arrested and handed over ought to speak, since the Lord, who desires us to confess rather than rashly to profess, is present within us and speaks at that hour.”

Another matter observed in venerating martyrs was that they should not thrust themselves voluntarily into certain death. Hence Eusebius, narrating in book VIII, chapter 14, the deed of a Christian woman whom Maxentius was attempting to violate, says:

> “Entering a chamber and seeing that she had been left alone, she drove a sword into her breast.”

Concerning these words, an ancient Greek scholiast noted, in Valesius’s notes on Eusebius, p. 170:

> “How does this man admire women who killed themselves, and yet the judgment of the Church does not place among the number of martyrs those who became their own executioners? To anticipate death out of fear of punishment is a matter of cowardice rather than courage. But she places among the martyrs those who, because of their confession of Christ, judged that nothing was to be feared and were prepared with cheerful spirit to endure whatever tortures the ingenious cunning of tyrants and demons might inflict upon them.”

Saint Augustine discusses this matter at length. Thus the Council of Elvira forbids the honoring of those whom pagan fury delivered to destruction because they had publicly destroyed idols. Lactantius likewise mocks, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 13, a Christian who publicly tore down the edicts of Diocletian posted against the Christians, although Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 5, declares that the deed was inspired by an excessive fervor of faith. Optatus repeats further details concerning these signs in book III, p. 77.

These, therefore, were the considerations that led Eutychianus to decree that every faithful person who sought out and buried relics should report the matter to the bishop, so that the honor of martyrdom would not be conferred without examination and the identity of the relics could be verified.

**Line 7.—** “Without a dalmatic … he should in no way bury him.” He decrees that a certain token be added for the honoring of martyrs: a definite kind of clothing, which the faithful were to place upon them when depositing the sacred pledges in domestic oratories.

Thus the servants of Aglaes, when they saw Boniface the martyr, according to Holstenius in the Acts of Saint Boniface, p. 22:

> “They received the body of the holy martyr, anointed it with spices, wrapped it in precious linens, and placed it in one of the baskets.”

### Note: [Col. 1447D]

**Line 2.—** “He lived in the time of Aurelianus.” He governed the pontifical see not only in the time of Aurelianus but also in the times of Tacitus, Florianus, Probus, and finally Numerianus, as is clear from the beginning and end of his pontificate.

**Line 4.—** “Here he established fruits, beans, and grapes.” The custom of blessing created things in the Church is extremely ancient and was practiced from the time of the apostles, as is clear from Apostolic Canons 2, 3, and others.

**Line 7.—** “Dalmatic.” A dalmatic is a tunic without sleeves, formerly in use. See the notes of Baronius on the *Roman Martyrology*, May 31, letter B.

### Note: [Col. 1448A]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

The dates preserved for the epoch of Saint Eutychianus, both at the basilica of Saint Paul and in the catalogues of Italy copied from it in ancient times, as well as in the Liberian catalogue and in several Colbert manuscripts cited above in the Prolegomena, correspond fully to the names of the consuls stated both in the catalogues of Liberius and Felix and in the *Liber Pontificalis*.

In the Liberian catalogue, one error of the copyists must be corrected. It also entered the other catalogues and even the paintings: namely, the separation of the unit from the number of months and its transfer to the place of the days. It should have been written: “The deposition of Eutychianus,” in the age of Liberius, is recorded above in the Prolegomena on the sixth day before the Ides of December.

The consuls named by the catalogues and by the Librarian as the last consuls under Eutychianus are Carus II and Carinus, indicating the year 283. The first consuls assigned to him, however, are Aurelianus IV and Marcellinus, introducing the year 275. The third day of that year—which was the sixth day after Felix’s death, after whom, according to the preceding entry, line 8, the see is said to have been vacant for five days—fell on a Sunday and corresponds appropriately to Eutychianus’s ordination.

From that date to 6 December of the year 283, when Carus II and Carinus were consuls and he departed this life victorious, there are counted eight years, eleven months, and three days. The documents cited above report that two days later, namely on 8 December, the sacred body of the blessed pontiff was deposited in the cemetery of Callistus.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

**Line 6.—** “He established that whoever among the faithful buried a martyr should in no way bury him without a dalmatic or purple colobium, but should nevertheless make this known to him.”

While advancing the care of vindicating the martyrs, the cautious pontiff prudently ordered that certain signs of martyrdom be added at their deposition. He commanded that a colobium or dalmatic be used to wrap the martyrs—not just any garment, but a purple one. The Church also commonly called them “the purple-clad” in the hymn of All Saints:

> “You purple-clad martyrs.”

Before this decree of Eutychianus, Christians had been accustomed to bury the sacred bodies of martyrs with linens spattered with their blood. Some were deliberately placed there while the martyr was being tortured, so that the blood might flow onto them, as the deacon Pontius carefully described in the Acts of the martyrdom of Saint Cyprian. Others were used to absorb blood spilled upon the ground, as the well-known verses of Prudentius concerning the martyrdom of Saint Hippolytus show, verse 141:

> “With little cloths the thirsty sands are dried,  
> lest any trace of dew remain upon the stained dust.  
> And if blood, still warm from the fresh spray,  
> clings to the stakes, the pressed sponge gathers it all.”

And in the hymn of Saint Vincent:

> “Many stain a linen garment  
> with the blood that drips,  
> so that they may preserve at home  
> a sacred protection for their descendants.”

A portion of the linens was generally placed in the martyr’s tomb itself, as numerous examples show; these may be read in the observations of the often-mentioned Canon Boldetti on the cemeteries, book I, chapter 37.

This is especially evident in the case of Saint Cecilia, discovered by Pope Paschal I with garments spattered with blood. The same pontiff speaks as follows:

> “There too we found the linens with which her most sacred body had been wiped of the wounds that the executioner had cruelly inflicted with three blows; they had been rolled together and were full of blood.”

The wrapping of linen soaked with blood, which he says he found around the martyr’s head and deposited in her little tomb, should also be remembered; see p. 183. A rather large glass flask was found there as well. Blood had flowed from it during the opening, and when the flask fell upon the martyr’s feet, it had coagulated there into clearly visible crusts. Another small vessel of blood had also, according to custom, been placed on the outside of the little tomb, to show, as I think, that the martyr had been vindicated.

There is also another reason why an open vessel filled with the martyr’s blood was placed on the outside of the little tomb, and more frequently there than in the inner receptacle, usually excavated in the tufa in these Roman cemeteries. That reason is suggested to me by the verses of Prudentius quoted shortly before:

> “Many stain a linen garment  
> with the blood that drips,  
> so that they may preserve at home  
> a sacred protection for their descendants.”

The faithful were already seeking the relics of the martyrs as sacred protection and as a pledge of their intercession with God. They knew from what had been revealed to John in the Apocalypse, chapters 8 and 9, how powerful were the voices of those slain for the Word of God, who awaited and demanded vengeance for the blood poured out for God—both for themselves and for their brethren—by merit of Christ’s blood, through whom they confessed themselves redeemed. They knew that they had been told to rest for a short time, until the number of their fellow servants who were to be killed as they had been was complete. Then these too were to be numbered with those above, who had washed their robes in the blood of the Lamb, ruled by that same Lamb, and placed around his throne in the glory of eternal life.

In seeking out the martyrs’ relics, their faith and hope in God were kindled by the sight of this example and by the pledge of the intercession of their brethren who had shed their blood for Christ. Yet the hope of a glorious resurrection, to be obtained through Christ’s blood by souls and bodies reunited once more, was also nourished and declared among those same faithful by their careful burial of the bodies and their preservation under guard in a sealed repository. What more suitable method, then, could have been devised for collecting the bodies of the martyrs and preserving them as testimony to the resurrection, which we await, relying on divine hope, while at the same time distributing among the faithful those protections and pledges of intercession that the sight and veneration of the martyrs in their relics provide? Certainly no method more ready could have been found than that ingeniously devised by the faithful themselves: namely, to place externally on the repository—where the bodies of the martyrs, vindicated by the bishop with the assistance of ministers whom he had delegated and appointed to supervise the faithful notaries in these duties, had been laid—a vessel filled with the martyr’s blood.

Without diminishing the intact relics resting in the repository, the faithful could dip linen cloths, or *brandea*, as they were later called, into the open external vessel, then take them home soaked with the martyr’s blood and preserve them as protection for themselves and their descendants, as Prudentius affirms in that poem.

This custom must also be examined in the *Acts of Saint Susanna, Virgin and Martyr, and of Pope Caius and Martyr*, which will be cited from the Reverend Father Becillius below, in the notes to line 12 of the next number. It was advantageous in this way to provide both for the piety and for the safety of the faithful. The bishops sometimes saw them expose themselves to the danger of combat even when they had not been provoked, whenever, during the martyrs’ actual torture, they placed linen cloths there to be sprinkled with blood and then withdrew and carried them away. They therefore judged that the faithful should be helped to obtain the desired blood by this safer form of devotion. Thus, in the crypts, without being observed, they could collect the blood poured out for Christ in the externally placed vessel, which was open to the devotion of their fellow believers.

This sequence of events may also be gathered from other verses of Prudentius, as well as from an ancient custom affirmed by Saint Gregory the Great when he wrote to the empress Constantina and refused to send her the relics of the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, while not refusing *brandea*. Prudentius’s poems, which testify to the reasons we have indicated—namely, that the sight of the relics of the holy martyrs should arouse Christian faith and hope, and that pardon should be sought through the intercession of those whom, as servants of God, they venerated in their relics, as though in instruments employed by their souls to endure their sufferings courageously for Christ—are especially those with which he concludes his hymn in praise of Saint Vincent the martyr:

> Be present now, and receive  
> The suppliant voices of those praying;  
> As an effective advocate for our guilt,  
> Plead before the Father’s throne.
>
> Through you, through that prison,  
> The increase of your honor;  
> Through bonds, flames, and claws,  
> Through the prison stake;
>
> Through that earthenware fragment,  
> By which your glory grew;  
> Through which your trembling descendants  
> Kiss your little bed:
>
> Have mercy on our prayers,  
> So that Christ, appeased toward his own,  
> May incline his gracious ear  
> And not reckon all our offenses,
>
> If with mouth and heart  
> We duly venerate the solemn day;  
> If, amid the joy of your footprints,  
> We prostrate ourselves;
>
> Glide down here for a little while,  
> Bringing Christ’s favor,  
> So that our burdened senses may feel  
> The relief of indulgence.
>
> Thus no delay remains  
> But that the noble spirit  
> May take up the awakened flesh,  
> Having achieved equal valor,
>
> So that the flesh, which shared its labors  
> And endured the common danger,  
> May also be co-heir  
> Of glory throughout all ages.

With nearly the same intention of arousing our hope and faith, he concludes the hymn while singing of the holy martyrs of Zaragoza:

> This crowd, placed beneath the everlasting altar,  
> Prays for pardon for our failings—  
> The multitude whom the creator of the noble  
> Purple-robed ones preserves.
>
> With devout tears, grant that we may wash  
> The grooves of the marble beneath which  
> Hope is covered, so that I may release  
> The bonds of my restraints.
>
> Prostrate yourself wholly, noble city,  
> With me upon the holy tombs; then soon  
> You will follow, entirely, the souls and limbs  
> Rising again.

Here, then, is the value of enclosing and sealing the relics in order to assert the hope of resurrection, while at the same time placing blood in an external and open vessel, so that linen cloths might be sprinkled with it and carried home by devout petitioners as pledges of protection for our prayers. This custom of distributing *brandea* after they had been brought into contact with the confession of blessed Peter and with those of other martyrs was preserved in the time of Gregory the Great and in the following centuries. It is still preserved in our own time in the church of Saint Cecilia, where veils brought into contact with that sacred tomb are prepared and distributed in order to lift minds toward God, and to inspire faith in the resurrection, hope of glory, confidence in the martyrs’ intercession, and the obtaining of pardon through Christ the Lord by venerating those who proved themselves worthy members of his mystical body. In this way they suggest that a similar outcome has also been pledged to us, if we imitate those whom we honor.

It follows from what has been said that some vessels still retain a clearly visible crust of blood. In these cases the faithful did not quickly draw out all the blood with their cloths, but left it for a period of time, allowing it to dry into a crust firmly adhering to the glass. Other vessels, from which the faithful succeeded in drawing out the blood through their eager attendance, were able to preserve for later generations only a thin trace of blood, or none at all. Once the liquid portion of the blood had been absorbed by the cloths, contact with the *brandea*, even though it no longer absorbed moisture, still aroused a religious feeling and a devotion of no lesser kind.

For this reason blessed Gregory the Great, in his letter to the empress Constantina (*Book III, Letter 30*, Roman edition), rightly testified that it was the custom of the Romans, when people requested relics of the martyrs, to give them *brandea*. These were placed in a small box and set beside the repositories enclosing the bodies of the martyrs—indeed, these blood-filled vessels adhere to such repositories—and were sent as sanctuaries without touching the martyr’s body.

> “Let the most tranquil lady know,” he says, “that it is not the custom of the Romans, when they give relics of the saints, to presume to touch anything from the body. Rather, only a *brandeum* is placed in a small box and set beside the most sacred bodies of the saints. When it has been removed, it is deposited with due veneration in the church that is to be dedicated.”

Among the Greeks, he says, the custom of dividing portions of the same martyr’s body was adopted earlier; the Roman Church practiced this custom less frequently before Gregory and accepted it later. We have learned that under Sylvester I the bones of the apostles Peter and Paul were divided in equal portions between their two principal basilicas. This was done for a reasonable and weighty cause: namely, so as not to separate those who had been joined in the foundation of the Roman Church both in life and in death.

For the rest, the Romans under Gregory the Great still reluctantly tolerated frequent translations and divisions of bodily relics. Later they admitted them more freely, both to protect the martyrs’ remains from the injuries of the Saracens and heretics and to adorn new churches consecrated to God, whose number was increasing daily, with the protection of the martyrs pledged by these tokens. *Brandea* and linen cloths, dipped into these vessels coated with a bloody crust and then removed, or applied to the martyr’s adjoining repository, were distributed among the faithful as tokens of their common faith, of the hope of resurrection, and of the communion of the militant Church with the triumphant Church. This practice existed long before Gregory and Leo the Great, as is clear from the *Acts of Saint Cyprian* and of other martyrs.

The same fact is demonstrated by these vessels, which served, as it were, by substitution in place of the division of relics. When the blood was still fresh and could be absorbed from the outpouring by linen cloths, and when it had congealed into a crust, the same *brandea* acquired something of the nature of relics through contact with blood poured out for Christ. They were brought into contact with the blood and body and distributed to those who requested them, who would taste them with religious kisses and preserve them for themselves and their families as a sacred amulet and protection.

This is what I wished to note in order to elucidate the decree of Eutychianus and the custom of the Roman Church of placing the blood shed for Christ by officially vindicated martyrs. When I call the blessed martyrs “vindicated,” I mean that this was done with the bishop’s knowledge, in accordance with this very decree of Eutychianus. The decree required, in addition to the custom concerning *brandea*, that the matter be brought before the pope’s tribunal, so that genuine martyrs might be distinguished from false ones and from other faithful who had not attained the glory of martyrdom.

That Eutychianus added to the earlier custom of placing blood in the repositories of martyrs a rule requiring the use of a purple *colobium* to clothe the martyrs’ bodies when they were carried out and buried should be considered neither superfluous nor unrelated to the matter of vindication. When tyrants inflicted death on blessed martyrs through various punishments, they were not always killed by the shedding of blood—for example, when they were drowned in a river or the sea, consumed by fire, killed by hunger, cold, the noose, poison, or similar forms of death. In such cases the test of blood could not be used to demonstrate the vindication of their martyrdom.

Eutychianus therefore ordered that the bodies of the martyrs be clothed in a purple *colobium*, or a *dalmatica* of the same color, once the circumstances of the martyrdom and the circumstances of the martyr’s burial had first been brought before the bishop’s tribunal. After the case had been examined, if the person was proved to have been a martyr, the common signs of martyrdom were to be placed upon him or her—namely, a purple *dalmatica*, or *colobium*.

This was also observed in the western provinces far from Rome. For Rudolph, the abbot, testifies that a *colobium*, or purple *dalmatica*, was placed over the military cloak of Saint Gereon, commander of the Theban Legion. We recognize this garment from Rudolph’s description, reported by Surius under 24 November and reproduced in Boldetti’s observations on the cemeteries, page 301:

> “After eight hundred and several more years from the martyrdom of the Thebans”—which occurred under Diocletian and Maximian, a few years after the decree of Pope Eutychianus under discussion—“a large body was found dressed in a military cloak of purple color. This garment, proper to him, hung down on both sides to just below his knees by about three fingers, a not ignoble kind of mantle. Over it he had another, shorter garment, unknown indeed by name but recognizable by its silk thread and its noble purple color.”

Since the *chlamys* is the outer garment of soldiers, placed over all the others, the garment that touched the *chlamys* and is described as shorter than it was either a *colobium* or a *dalmatica*, apparently used to cover the martyr in accordance with the recent laws established by Pope Eutychianus.

For this reason a sign of the Lord’s cross is also described as having been sewn onto or woven over it in gold embroidery:

> “Upon his chest a sign of the Lord’s cross was found, made of gold embroidery, as could be observed from the sparks of gold metal shining through it.”

The martyr’s own garments are said to have been found stained with congealed blood dried upon them in crusts:

> “All his garments were therefore carefully collected, heavy with thick but dried blood.”

All these facts confirm the careful concern undertaken by the Roman pontiffs for the vindication of the martyrs. They appointed notaries to record their acts, subdeacons to collect them, and regional deacons and priests of the martyrs to perform specified duties toward them. They also prescribed careful treatment of their clothing, as well as of the bodily relics, establishing a definite type of garment in which they were to be wrapped when buried, so that the notaries might enter into their records the particular signs of their martyrdom, confirmed by the testimonies of the whole Church.

When these matters had been presented to the bishop’s knowledge, permission was given for external vessels filled with the martyr’s blood to be placed there by the ministers responsible for the burial. Priests and deacons are known to have been placed in charge of them, so that everything might be carried out in due order. To these vessels, once the martyr had been vindicated, the faithful could devoutly apply their *brandea* at will, either to stain them with blood that had not yet dried or, through contact with the bloody crust, to give them the efficacy of stirring believers’ faith and hope in God. Thus, through that martyr’s intercession, they might obtain from Christ the Lord what the woman in the Gospel obtained through the merit of faith by touching the Lord’s garment (Mark 5), and what the shadow of passing Peter conferred on the sick (Acts 5). And, what is more excellent, they might understand that the preserved *brandea*, when devoutly kissed, recalled to them the example of Christian fortitude as a household monitor.

The supreme pontiffs judged that the fellow believers of the martyrs should not be deprived of this consolation. They had carefully arranged that the sacred bodies be deposited, that the blood be collected with sponges and linen cloths, that the repositories be sealed with cement, and that they be adorned with signs of martyrdom, which the notaries were to enter into the records. This becomes clear from the combined testimonies of Cyprian and Prudentius, to which Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, and others may be added, as well as from the letter of Gregory the Great mentioned above. That letter testifies to the custom maintained by the Roman Church of distributing the martyrs’ relics neither rashly nor indiscriminately. The decree of Eutychianus, mentioned by the Librarian, provided the opportunity to illustrate this custom.

I would wrong the history both of this number and of the preceding ones if I did not present here a remarkable document concerning the matters so far discussed, especially concerning the custom and reasons for placing the martyrs’ blood in open vessels fitted externally to their repositories by the cement workers. I had promised to do so at the end of the historical notes on the entry concerning blessed Sixtus II.

While those notes on blessed Sixtus II were being sent to the press, it fortunately happened that, when we were taken to inspect the cemetery of Callistus and Praetextatus on the Appian Way in the company of the most serene Bavarian prince Theodore, elected bishop of Regensburg, we were guided by the often-mentioned distinguished man Marco Antonio Boldetti, canon and custodian of the sacred relics. There we found a glass saucer painted, as was customary, with figures in gold—the figures being drawn with a stylus on gold leaf between the two glass plates of which the base of the vessel consists—and generously sprinkled with the martyrs’ blood. The crusts adhering to it and the blood-red color plainly visible when light was brought near it clearly demonstrate this.

Through the pious patronage of so great a prince, who, following the august footsteps of the most serene electoral house—the firmest bulwark of the Catholic religion in Germany—strives with such zeal toward the other virtues worthy of so great a vocation, we were enabled to obtain this monument. Among the other sights of the City that he wished to have set before him for contemplation in this church, the mother and teacher of all others, was the sight of the crypts of the holy martyrs. He had learned that this sight had been especially pleasing and useful for fostering piety to his most serene princely brothers, who were equally devoted to the matter, when they visited Rome.

Thus, when we devoutly entered the indicated cemetery of Callistus and Praetextatus on 27 April of the present year, 1723, it happened that we saw fragments of a glass saucer, discovered there by the excavators near a martyr’s repository, as is customary. Joined together, these fragments display figures and letters, reproduced here in a copper engraving. I also arranged for the lost fragment to be represented by dotted lines and for the portion covered by the bloody crust to be shown in the figure. When turned toward the rays of the sun or toward a candle, it reveals its natural redness.

At the top is the image of the Good Shepherd from the Gospel, whom Tertullian, in *On Modesty*, chapter 10, says was customarily painted on the chalices of Christians. He is shown carrying a sheep on his neck, with a little sheep or lamb standing on either side at the Shepherd’s feet and looking toward him. The holy apostles Peter and Paul are also shown seated on chairs placed on either side. The second figure is intact, and the name Paul can be distinctly recognized.

The image of the Good Shepherd in the surviving fragments is sufficiently clear and resembles those already published by the distinguished senator Buonarroti in his *Observations on the Glass Plates of the Cemeteries*, plate 1, no. 1; plate 4, no. 2; and plate 6, no. 2; and by Canon Boldetti, page 200, plate 1, nos. 10 and 11. It also resembles the paintings still visible in this very cemetery, which Aringhi formerly drew in chamber 1 of this cemetery, plate 2, page 531, and in another, plate 3, page 573. The images of the holy apostles and the two chairs on which they sit are likewise very similar to those represented in this cemetery by Aringhi, plate 1 of chamber 1.

Paul sits on the left of the Good Shepherd. We understand that Peter was placed on the right, although the fragment of this glass saucer on which he was represented has fallen away, perhaps broken by the excavators through carelessness during the digging.

Below those three sacred images, as though under their protection, two other larger figures appear, representing a man and a woman from the chest upward and indicating noble birth. In the man this is shown by the broad purple stripe (*laticlave*) running over the toga and across the chest; in the woman, by the elaborate, almost Phrygian borders of the *stola* in which she is clothed.

The letters expressing the man’s name, together with a convivial acclamation or Christian *agape*, which frequently occurs on similar vessels and is explained learnedly by the distinguished senator Buonarroti in the observations cited above, plate 14, no. 3, page 95, leave no doubt that this man was a Roman:

> DIGNITAS AMICORVM ROMANE PIE. ZESES. CYM. TVA. . . . . . NE
>
> “O pious Roman, ornament of your friends, may you live with your . . . ne.”

The final portion may perhaps have been *Euphrosyne*, *Irene*, or another name ending in a similar syllable. It is therefore entirely clear that this saucer was a gift from the *agape*—perhaps even a wedding *agape*—of that Roman, a noble Christian man represented there with his bride.

I would not dare to assert that this is the famous Roman martyr and porter whom the Librarian says was a companion in martyrdom of blessed Sixtus II and of his deacons, and was buried in this very cemetery of Praetextatus, where we found the glass sprinkled with blood. Other Christians of the same name also flourished under Pope Sixtus II, including the Roman soldier baptized by blessed Laurence and sent ahead to receive the palm on the day before Laurence’s feast, when the martyrdom of the Roman is commemorated. Moreover, determining this would contribute little to the clarification of these notes.

It will, however, contribute greatly to demonstrate the example of blood collected and placed in these glass saucers, adorned with the tokens of Christian belief. For it thereby becomes clear, first, that this custom belongs to the period of the persecutions; and second, why blood collected in open vessels was placed externally on the repository where the martyr had been buried: namely, to satisfy the vows and custom of the faithful, who carried away linen cloths and *brandea* soaked with the martyr’s blood, or at least dedicated through contact with his blood, as protection and as a pledge of the martyrs’ intercession. This is attested by the poems of Prudentius. It was also intended that the memory of the faith, hope, and charity exercised by the martyr, as well as an incentive to imitation and a support for steadfastness, should be preserved among later generations.

It is useful to confirm this custom by the deed and words of blessed Saturus the martyr, which are to be read among the acts of Saints Perpetua and Felicity. They were first published at Rome by Lucas Holstenius and later at Paris by Lucas D’Achery in the *Sincere and Selected Acts of the Martyrs*. In number 21 of the second edition, Saturus, condemned to the beasts with his companions, is exposed to a leopard. Attacked by its bite, he is drenched in so much blood that the watching crowd cries out: “Saved and washed, saved and washed!” He is handed over half alive to the soldier Pudens, to be guarded until he is killed at the end of the spectacle.

Saturus turns to Pudens, whom he saw moved by the martyrs’ steadfastness and inclining toward professing the Christian faith with them:

> “Remember my faith,” he says, “and do not let these things disturb you, but let them strengthen you.”

Then he has the ring removed from Pudens’s finger and given to him. He brings it not merely close to his wound but immerses it in the wound, so that it may be thoroughly stained with blood. He returns it to Pudens in this bloody condition, leaving him an inheritance of the pledge and a memorial of the blood. Then, having been joined to his companion by the kiss of peace in the Christian manner, he is killed for Christ.

**Glass saucers decorated with sacred images painted in gold and sprinkled with the blood of the holy martyrs, found affixed externally to their tombs**

I. In the cemetery of Callistus and Praetextatus  
II. In the cemetery of Saint Agnes

The whole matter is presented more vividly in the words of the acts. Since they were written by Vibia Perpetua herself, a companion in martyrdom, I think they should be reproduced here, both for clarity concerning the events and for evidence of the custom.

> **XXI.** Likewise, at another gate Saturus was exhorting the soldier Pudens, saying: “I am certainly present, as I promised and foretold; until now I have felt none of the beasts. And now believe with all your heart. Behold, I am going out there, and with a single bite of the leopard I shall be consumed.” Immediately, at the end of the spectacle, he was exposed to the leopard and was drenched with so much blood from a single bite that, as he returned, the crowd cried out in testimony to a second baptism: “Saved and washed, saved and washed!” Clearly he was saved, since he had been glorified by this spectacle.
>
> Then he said to the soldier Pudens: “Farewell, and remember my faith; do not let these things disturb you, but let them strengthen you.” At the same time he asked for the little ring from his finger, immersed it in his wound, and returned it to him, leaving him an inheritance of the pledge and a memorial of the blood. From that point, already lifeless, he was thrown down with the others for the customary killing.

The Reverend Father Ruinart, in his edition, aptly adds this note:

> “Why, then, do the heretics complain that we religiously preserve the relics of the saints? Was that ring, stained with a martyr’s blood, to be thrown away?”

Anyone, therefore, who compares these acts and sayings of the martyrs with the writings of Prudentius, and with the vessels and saucers discovered filled with a bloody crust and firmly attached with cement to the outer side of the repository, which was closed on every side and preserved the martyr’s body, will understand that such vessels were placed there under the bishop’s supervision—that is, after a legitimate examination and vindication of the martyrdom—as testimony to the faith and memorial of the blood poured out for Christ; namely, for the vindication and confirmation of the martyrdom courageously endured by that servant of God; and as a pledge of his protection, to be carried away by the faithful after they had dipped into it linen cloths, *brandea*, rings, or similar treasures to be kept at home and handed down to their descendants.

For this reason Eutychianus, in the decree mentioned in this section, not only ordered that the martyr be buried in purple clothing, but also ordered that he be informed of the rite observed at the burial of each martyr. This information, however, was to be communicated to him through public report.

[Note: [Col. 1457A]]

**Lines 1 and 2.** “He sat for eight years.” Eusebius is mistaken when he reports that Eutychianus sat only eight months, or that he did not complete ten months. For five ordinations took place in December and could not have occurred within less than five years. We should therefore rather accept those who assign eight years and several months to his pontificate, among them Panvinio and Cardinal Baronius. The consular reckonings also support them, and the fact may be gathered indirectly from the ancient ecclesiastical tables.

**Line 4.** “He established that only beans and grapes were to be blessed among the produce placed upon the altar.” This was intended to oppose more strongly the errors of the Manichaeans, who said that created things had arisen from an evil principle and declared them accursed. Eutychianus, by contrast, blessed and sanctified them by his word, and wished them to be offered by the faithful upon the altar and blessed by the priest with thanksgiving. This practice was ancient and continued in the Church, so that Eutychianus should not be regarded as the first to establish it, but rather as having strengthened it again by his decree.

**Line 6.** “He established that none of the faithful who buried a martyr should bury him without a *dalmatica* or purple *colobium*.” The *dalmatica* was a sleeveless garment, and the *colobium* also lacked sleeves and resembled the garment now called the bishops’ *mozzetta*. Later, however, the Christian people exceeded the limits of this decree under the pretext of religion, so that not only the bodies of holy martyrs but also those of sacred ministers were covered with a *dalmatica*, as is clear from the testimony of Saint Gregory the pope in the *Register*, book VI, chapter 48. He himself subsequently prohibited this so completely in another decree that he even forbade the bodies of Roman pontiffs, when being carried for burial, to be covered with *dalmaticas*.

[Note: [Col. 1458A]]

**Line 6.** “That whoever among the faithful buried a martyr should under no circumstances do so without a purple *dalmatica* or *colobium*”—that is, a sleeveless tunic. This was established as an honor. But when the same honor was extended to pontiffs and even to deacons, as Saint Gregory indicates in *Dialogues*, book IV, chapter 40, he enacted by his decree in book IV, letter 44, that the bier on which the body of a Roman pontiff was carried for burial should not be covered with *dalmaticas*.

The body of Saint Eutychianus was taken back to his homeland, Luna, and is now found and honored at Sarzana, a neighboring city in the Genoese territory, which succeeded the completely deserted and destroyed city of Luna in cathedral dignity. Eutychianus, after holding five ordinations in December, ordained fourteen priests, five deacons, and nine bishops in various places. He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way. Two decretal letters are attributed to him: the first to all the bishops established throughout the province of Baetica, the second to the bishops of Sicily. They are spurious, since they quote passages of later pontiffs in full and contain many other indications of forgery.

[Note: [Col. 1458B]]

**Line 4.** “He established that only beans and grapes were to be blessed among the produce placed upon the altar.” This decree, confirming an ancient tradition concerning the same practice of the Church, was undoubtedly issued on account of the heresy of the Manichaeans, which was then emerging. It rested upon the error that the universe had two principles, entirely independent even of one another, according to their doctrine: the good and the evil.

They asserted that the Good was the author of light and, according to their view, of the creatures formed from it. They called the Evil the prince of darkness and claimed that he had produced the things associated with it, such as the earth and the fruits of the earth. The heresiarch Manes had drawn this teaching from the Magi, the philosophers of Persia, among whom he had been raised and in whose school he had long remained, as we have shown in the *Dogmatic History of Religion*, book II, in the chapter on the origin of idolatry.

[Col. 1441]

## 28

Eutychianus, a Tuscan by nationality, son of Marinus, from the city of Luna, sat for eight years, ten months, and four days [Note: [Col. 1441] B, eight years and several months]. He lived in the time of Aurelian, from the third consulship of Aurelian and the consulship of Marcellinus until the Ides of December, when Carus was consul for the second time and Carinus was consul [Note: [Col. 1441] B, of Tacitus, Probus, and Carus, from the consulships of Aurelian and Capitolinus to those of Carus and Carinus]. He established that only beans and grapes were to be blessed among the produce placed upon the altar. [Note: [Col. 1441] Baron. under A.D. 104.] During his pontificate he personally buried 342 martyrs in various places. [Note: [Col. 1441] Baron., same place.] He established that whoever among the faithful buried a martyr should under no circumstances bury him without a purple *dalmatica* or *colobium*, and that this should nevertheless be reported to his knowledge. He held five ordinations during the month of December: fourteen priests, five deacons, and nine bishops in various places. He was crowned with martyrdom. He was also buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, and the episcopate ceased for perhaps eight days before the Kalends [Note: [Col. 1441] C B, nine].

[Col. 1441] **CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS**

Eutychianus: eight years, eleven months, and three days. He lived in the time of Aurelian III and Marcellinus, until the fourth day before the Ides of December, when Carus was consul for the second time and Carinus was consul.
