In the same line, the Florentine and Cassinese codices read “Gavinus.” Line 13: The Cassinese and Vatican read “of March.”

**In Penius, from the Cavensis codex**

Line 1: “Caius, a Dalmatian by nationality, descended from the family of the emperor Diocletian, son of Caius, sat eleven years, four months, and nine days. He lived in the time of Carus and Carinus from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January” (a later hand has superscribed “the fourth day before the Kalends”) “from the second consulship of Carus and Carinus.” Line 9: “He is crowned with martyrdom after nine years.” Line 11: “with his brother Gavinus.” Lines 13 and 14: “on the Appian Way, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May, and the episcopate ceased for eleven days.”

[Note: [Col. 1459B]]

**Line 11.** “Who after the eleventh year was crowned with martyrdom with his brother Gavinianus on account of the daughter of the priest Gavinius, named Susanna.” Thus, after the eleventh year of his pontificate, Caius was crowned with martyrdom together with his brother Gabinus, or Gavinianus, on account of the latter’s daughter Susanna, Caius’s niece, whom Diocletian was requesting for his son. Because she refused the marriage, Pope Caius was crowned with martyrdom together with her father Gabinus, as is clear from the acts of blessed Susanna, which Henschenius assigns to 22 April.

[Note: [Col. 1459B]

Linea 5.—He established that all ordinations in the Church should proceed in the following sequence, so that anyone deemed worthy to be a bishop would first be ordained as doorkeeper, lector, exorcist, acolyte (*sequens*), subdeacon, deacon, presbyter, and thereafter bishop. By Caius’s constitution, episcopal ordinations by skipping grades were forbidden—that is, no one was to be ordained bishop unless he had first received each individual order, as stated in canon *Illud*, distinction 77; and accordingly, by the constitutions of Sylvester, Zosimus, and Siricius, it is forbidden for anyone to attain the episcopate unless he has spent prescribed periods in each order, according to Anastasius under Sylvester, Sigebert under the year 387, canon *In singulis*, canon *Quicunque*, the same distinction, and canon *Monachos*, question 16, distinction 1.

That John reached the episcopate of Chalon through these grades is attested by Sidonius, Book IV, Letter 25:

> “First he was a lector here, then a minister of the altar, and this from childhood; afterward, as his labors and years progressed, he became archdeacon. In that rank or ministry he was retained for a long time because of his diligence; for a long while his dignity could not be increased, lest his authority be released. Nevertheless, they consecrated him as already a priest of the second order and made him their colleague.”

Hence Cato, a presbyter elected to the episcopate of Clermont after Gallus, took pride in having reached the episcopate through every grade. Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book IV, chapter 6, records:

> “For I also received the very grades of the clergy through the canonical institution. I was a lector for ten years; I was devoted to the office of subdeacon for five years, and to that of deacon for fifteen years; now I have possessed the honor of presbyter for twenty years. What remains for me now except to receive the episcopate, which faithful service has earned?”

Hence Tertullian condemns the sudden ordinations of bishops that took place among heretics, *On the Prescription against Heretics*:

> “Their ordinations are rash, light, and unstable: now they appoint neophytes, now men entangled in worldly affairs, now your apostates, so that they may bind them by glory, since they cannot by truth. Nowhere is advancement easier than in the camp of rebels, where simply to be there is to deserve office. Thus one man is bishop today and another tomorrow; today a deacon who is a lector tomorrow; today a presbyter who is a layman tomorrow. For they even impose priestly functions upon laymen.”

[Note: [Col. 1460B]

**Linea 8.—“He, fleeing.”** Not out of cowardice or fear, but by a salutary withdrawal, caring for the needs of the faithful at the beginning of the Diocletian persecution. In this way, when the Decian persecution began, Saint Cyprian by his withdrawal commended the ancient discipline. Pontius writes of him:

> “Do you wish to know that that withdrawal was not fear? I shall excuse nothing else: afterward he himself suffered, and he would certainly have avoided that suffering in accordance with custom if he had also avoided it earlier. Yet it was fear—a just fear, to be sure—which feared offending the Lord; a fear that preferred to obey God’s commands rather than to be crowned … He had to be one who could apply the healing of heavenly medicine according to the nature of the wound—to cut for a time or to soothe men wounded and struck by the enemy’s varied and destructive art; a man preserved whose spiritual temper, among his other gifts, was such that amid the surging waves of clashing schisms he could steer the Church along the middle course with a balanced step.”

After the middle of the second century, a serious controversy arose among the Fathers concerning flight and withdrawal during persecution, and Tertullian has a work on the subject. The stricter writers disapprove of flight, and some appeared to cast blame upon Cyprian, as the letter sent by the Roman clergy to the clergy of Carthage seems to imply—the Roman see being vacant because of the martyrdom of Saint Fabian. Cyprian wrote several letters to dispel this charge, especially one addressed to the Roman clergy, where, in chapter 15, he says:

> “For, as the Lord’s commands instruct us, when the first onset of the disturbance had arisen, and the people had repeatedly demanded me with a violent outcry, thinking not so much of my own safety as of the public peace of the brethren, I withdrew for a time, lest through my shameless presence the sedition that had begun should be provoked still further, and so forth.”

The same discipline was observed when Valerian published the Decian edicts against bishops and against the more distinguished members of the lay order, proscribing their property. When the holy bishop had returned from exile and heard that he was to be brought before the proconsul at Utica, he withdrew, so that he might receive martyrdom not at Utica but in his own see. In his final letter to the clergy of Carthage he explained this intention. Thus he disclosed the reason for his later withdrawal:

> “When it had been reported to us … that officers had been sent to take me to Utica, and when the advice of my dearest companions persuaded me to withdraw for a time from our gardens, I consented because a just reason intervened: it is fitting that a bishop should confess the Lord in the city over whose Church he presides, and that the entire people should be honored by the confession of their present ruler … Otherwise the honor of our Church, so glorious, will be mutilated if I, a bishop placed over another Church, after receiving at Utica a sentence concerning confession, should then depart to the Lord as a martyr.”

For similar reasons Pope Caius may have been moved to withdraw in order to assist the Church.

**The persecution of Diocletian.** This persecution, from which the famous Diocletian era derives its beginning, did not commence until after Caius’s death; nor did Diocletian stir up persecution against the Church by edicts before the year 304, and even then its beginnings were in the East. Yet the Diocletian persecution appears to have to be counted as twofold: the first was particular and was not promulgated by any edict; the second was official and was proclaimed throughout the empire by edicts.

The first should be assigned to the tenth year of Diocletian’s reign, the year 294. At that time, as Eusebius says in the *Chronicle*:

> “Diocletian was the first to order that he be worshiped as a god and that jewels be inserted into his clothing and footwear, whereas before him all emperors were saluted in the manner of judges and had nothing more than a purple cloak distinguishing them from private persons.”

Eutropius says something similar of Diocletian’s character in Book V, page 226:

> “He was the first in the Roman Empire to introduce more of the form of royal custom than of Roman liberty, and he ordered that he be worshiped, whereas before him all were merely saluted. He inserted jeweled ornaments into clothing and footwear. Previously, the insignia of imperial office consisted only in the purple cloak; the rest was common.”

On that occasion, when the people in their customary manner followed the new god with flattery, while Christians condemned the madness of popular superstition, either the emperor himself, or his courtiers and judges, began to persecute the Christians whom they saw resisting and withdrawing from these sacrifices, in order to gratify the proud emperor who desired divine honors. It was customary at these imperial festivals to compel everyone to sacrifice. The judges, seeking the favor of the rulers, raged against those who resisted.

Thus Saint Marcellus the centurion, when he was compelled to take part in those celebrations, boldly resisted, as he confessed before the judges:

> “On the twelfth day before the Kalends of August, when you celebrated the festival of your emperor, I replied publicly: ‘I am a Christian.’”

It is clear that the judges began promoting these sacrifices and raging against those who resisted at the emperor’s vicennalia, when written edicts of persecution were being published. In the acts of Saint Procopius, fragments of which Valesius inserted in his notes on Eusebius, page 172, we read:

> “Then he decided upon other arguments, so that he might sacrifice even to kings. But the holy martyr of God, scorning his speech, said: ‘Homer’s verse says: It is not good to have many masters.’ … When he heard this, as though he had uttered an ill-omened statement about kings, he was led to execution by order of the judge.”

That Diocletian was inclined both to hear and to do such things is shown by an event reported by Lactantius in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, which occurred in the year 298:

> “While he was in the eastern regions, and, because of his fear, was examining future events, he sacrificed animals and sought what was to come in their livers. Then certain servants who knew the Lord, while they stood beside him as he sacrificed, placed upon their foreheads the immortal sign—that is, the cross, an epithet Lactantius frequently uses in the same work. When this was done, the demons were driven away and the rites were thrown into confusion. The haruspices were alarmed and could not see the customary signs in the entrails; and, as though the sacrifice had not been favorable, they sacrificed repeatedly. Yet the slaughtered victims still revealed nothing, until Tayas, the chief of the haruspices, whether by suspicion or by sight, said that the rites were not answering because profane men were taking part in divine matters. Then, raging with anger, he ordered not only those who were serving at the rites but everyone in the palace to sacrifice, and commanded that those who refused should be punished with blows. He also sent letters to the commanders ordering that even the soldiers be compelled to these abominable sacrifices, and that those who did not obey be discharged from military service.”

The custom then prevailing could therefore have driven the judges to flatter the insane prince, who claimed divine honors for himself, by raging against the Christians. Thus the beginnings of the persecutions were laid; and this, I think, is what the *Liber Pontificalis* means here: for these reasons Caius was compelled to withdraw.

**Linea 9.—“He is crowned with martyrdom in the ninth year.”** Additions made to the sequence of the deeds can plainly be detected; later hands, drawing them either from catalogues, martyrologies, or the acts of the saints, inserted them into the catalogue commonly attributed to Damasus. In that same sequence of deeds it says:

> “He sat for eleven years, four months, and nine days”;

and afterward:

> “He, fleeing the persecution of Diocletian by living in the crypts, is crowned with martyrdom in the ninth year.”

Finally, it repeats the cause of his martyrdom on account of Saint Susanna:

> “He, after the eleventh year, is crowned with martyrdom together with his brother Gavinianus, because of Susanna, the daughter of the presbyter Gabinus.”

Here additions collected from various acts are revealed. The first belongs to the ancient catalogue and agrees with the catalogue of the Queen of Sweden published by Schelestratius and Papebrochius. The second addition appears to have been taken from the queen’s ancient martyrology, where, from Holstenius, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May, it is read in the notes on the martyrs, page 67:

> “At Rome, the passion of Saint Caius the pope, who, after governing the Church for eleven years, four months, and twelve days, was crowned with martyrdom under the emperor Diocletian, together with his brother Gabinus.”

The third addition appears to have been cobbled together from the acts of Saint Susanna, whose identity learned men dispute. Nevertheless, the earlier chronology, drawn from the ancient catalogues, seems to be retained.

[Col. 1462D] **Linea 12.—“Because of Susanna, the daughter of the presbyter Gavinus.”** If this circumstance of Saint Caius’s martyrdom, taken from the acts of Saint Susanna, is true, it must be said that he was crowned with martyrdom by Maximian, who was hostile to Caius. The pontiff could have undertaken Saint Susanna’s protection; for when she had dedicated her virginity to God, it belonged to him, in virtue of his episcopal office, to assume responsibility for her defense. In support of Saint Cyprian’s earlier withdrawal, Pontius invokes this consideration, among others:

> “Who would restrain virgins with the appropriate discipline of chastity and with a manner of life worthy of holiness, as though with the reins of the Lord’s teaching?”

The letter of Saint Ambrose to his sister is relevant here, where this episcopal vigilance is examined.

**“He is crowned with martyrdom.”** In the catalogue of the Queen of Sweden he is said to have died as a confessor, not as a martyr. This agrees with the ancient little registers, since he is not placed in the register of the deposition of martyrs but in that of the deposition of bishops. In these registers the Churches most carefully distinguished depositions and martyrdoms; at the same time, with equal care, they distinguished the titles by which confessors, honored by a flourishing and glorious confession, were distinguished from designated martyrs and crowned martyrs.

Pontius provides testimony for this matter in the *Life of Saint Cyprian*. To prove that Saint Cyprian was the first among the bishops of Carthage to be ennobled by martyrdom, he derives this from the register, writing:

> “When his passion had been completed, it was revealed that Cyprian, who had been an example of every good thing, was also the first in Africa to receive priestly crowns; for he had also begun to be such a man before others after the apostles. From him the order of the episcopate at Carthage is likewise counted, and no one, although among the good and the priests, is ever recorded to have gone to suffering, even though devotion continually dedicated to God is reckoned as martyrdom among holy men. Cyprian, however, advanced to the Lord’s perfect crown by completing his course, so that in the very city in which he had lived in this manner and had done many noble things, he might also be the first to adorn the insignia of the heavenly priesthood with glorious blood.”

But if either Caius or others whose completed martyrdom is doubtful are called martyrs, this can be understood in the sense in which Pontius said:

> “Although devotion continually dedicated to God is reckoned as martyrdom among holy men.”

For anyone who professed the faith before judges through a true confession, or contended for the faith within the confines of prisons, was called by the title of martyr, as often happened with Cyprian.]

[Note: [Col. 1463B]

**Linea 8.—“He, fleeing the persecution of Diocletian.”** That these hiding places of Caius occurred after the martyrdom of Saint Sebastian and his companions—namely, around the year 286—is demonstrated by the highly authoritative acts of that same martyr. They state quite plainly that Sebastian, together with his other companions, was instructed by Caius in the faith and was afterward baptized.

[Col. 1463C] **(FROM THE DRAFT.) Linea 7.—“Subdeacon.”** This word is merely a gloss on *ἀκόλουθος* (*akólouthos*, “acolyte,” literally “one who follows”).]

[Note: [Col. 1463C]

**CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES.**

In the case of Caius, the figures in the manuscripts and paintings agree with the interval confirmed by the consuls, both in the catalogues and in the text of the Librarian, as well as in the other books indicated on folio CI among the *Prolegomena*, provided that what we shall soon say about the consuls is taken into account. For both in the basilica of Saint Paul and in the other documents reproduced there, eleven years, four months, and nine days are read.

Only the Liberian catalogue gives twelve years, beginning from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January—that is, 17 December—when Carus was consul for the second time and Carinus was consul, namely in the year 283. This is truly the date from which the reckoning must begin, since eight days afterward follow—other manuscripts of Anastasius read nine days—after the death, or deposition, of Eutychianus, which is placed in the preceding section of the Liberian catalogue on the sixth day before the Ides of December, that is, on 8 December.

The *Liber Pontificalis* has the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January. Nevertheless, this should be corrected from the Liberian catalogue, which gives the sixteenth day before the Kalends. Since 17 December in the year 283 fell on the Saturday of the Ember Days, when vigils were customarily held for the ordination of presbyters and deacons, the continuation into Sunday, 18 December, on which Caius was ordained bishop, gave rise to confusion between the vigil of the ordination and the day itself.

Among some writers, the chronology of the succession was also disturbed by several months added to the vacancy of the see after Caius’s death—whether he was crowned with martyrdom or was deposited on 22 April of the year 295. They extended the interregnum through the remainder of that year until the ninth day before the Kalends of January, when the consuls of the year 296, Diocletian for the sixth time and Maximian, were to enter office. I infer this from the following era.

From Schelestratius we shall see that Marcellinus suffered on 16 March, when Diocletian was consul for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth, in the common era of Christ 304. This is also indicated by the catalogue of the Queen of Sweden, published by the same Schelestratius and reproduced by us in the *Prolegomena*, when we observed that the total of 276 years from the Passion of the Lord recorded there had been correctly calculated. For, from the year 28 of the common era—which we determine to be the year in which the Passion of the Lord began on 25 March in the garden and was completed on the 26th on Mount Calvary, a Friday, following Victorius of Aquitaine, page XIII of the *Prolegomena*—to the same days, 25 and 26 March, in the year 304, exactly 276 years are counted.

Therefore, counting backward from 16 March, the day on which Marcellinus received the crown of martyrdom—as we shall establish with Schelestratius in the next entry—by eight years, two months, and twenty-five days, the period assigned to that see by the paintings of Saint Paul and by the older catalogues of Italy, we arrive at Marcellinus’s ordination to the episcopate on Sunday, 22 December 295.

The death of his predecessor, which preceded it on the date indicated, the tenth day before the Kalends of May, on which either his martyrdom or his deposition at the cemetery of Callistus is commemorated—as the writings of the Liberian period testify in the *Prolegomena* published above, folio IX—shows that the vacancy of the see continued until 21 December of that same year, that is, twelve days before the Kalends of January, which would be opened by Diocletian for the thirteenth time and Maximian, in the year 296 of the common era.

If these nearly equal testimonies are accepted, it is established that the eleven years, four months, and nine days expressed in the Pauline paintings and in the other catalogues exactly measure the duration of Caius’s see, while the Liberian catalogue adds to this total eight months of vacancy of the see, together with the three months that followed, up to Easter of the year 296, marked by the consulship of Diocletian for the sixth time and Maximian. Thus the authority of both calculations is preserved, provided that the calculations are understood as completed and that the period of vacancy before the election of Marcellinus, Caius’s successor, is charged to Caius in the Liberian catalogue. The correctness and chronological markers of that period will become clear in the next entry.

**HISTORICAL NOTES.**

**Linea 6.—“So that he would be doorkeeper, lector, etc.”** This sevenfold division of the orders is read in the letter of Pope Cornelius preserved by Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 43. There he also enumerates in the Roman clergy forty-four presbyters, seven deacons, an equal number of subdeacons, forty-two acolytes, and forty-two exorcists and lectors together with doorkeepers. I presented this portion of the letter in the Preface to volume I, no. 35.

**Linea 8.—“He divided the regions among the deacons.”** The number of fourteen regions of the City established by the emperor Augustus was reduced to seven in the ecclesiastical division and assigned to an equal number of deacons, as I explained more fully in the *Prolegomena* to this volume, treatise XV.

[Col. 1464D] **Linea 12.—“Because of Susanna, the daughter of the presbyter Gavinus, crowned with martyrdom,” etc.** Caesar Becillus of Urbino, a presbyter of the Congregation of the Oratory of Rome, published and illustrated with notes the *Acts of Saints Caius the Pope and Martyr and Susanna the Virgin and Martyr with Their Companions* in the year 1628. The following passage occurs there and sheds considerable light on the decree of Saint Eutychian mentioned shortly before, as well as on the origin of the title of Saints Susanna and Caius, page 39:

> “Then the emperor Diocletian Augustus ordered that she be punished by the sword there, within her own house beside the house of Caius the bishop. When struck, Susanna gave up her spirit beside her own house. When the Augusta Severina heard this, she came joyfully by night, gathered the body of Saint Susanna the martyr, wiped away with her own garment the blood that she had shed in that same place, and placed it in a silver casket in her palace, where she did not cease to pray day and night at secret intervals. She herself adorned the body of Saint Susanna with linen cloths and spices, and placed it beside the bodies of the saints in the cemetery of Alexander, and so forth. From that same day Blessed Caius the bishop began to enter the same house where she had been struck with the sword, and to offer sacrifice to the Lord his God for the commemoration of Blessed Susanna before the people, because the house of Blessed Gabinus the presbyter adjoined the house of Blessed Caius the bishop. From that time—for this was a sign among Christians—a station was assigned to the two houses, and this continues to the present day. This took place at Rome in the sixth region, beside the Street of Mamurius, before the Forum of Sallust, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns with the Father and the Holy Spirit forever and ever. Amen.”

The subscriptions of the presbyters at the Roman council under Symmachus made both titles—that of Saint Susanna and that of Saint Caius—famous in the fifth century: Asellus, presbyter of the title of Saint Susanna; Agatho, presbyter of the title of Saint Susanna; Benedictus, presbyter of the title of Saint Caius; Severus, presbyter of the title of Saint Caius.

Of these titles, the one bearing Saint Susanna’s name never ceased to be counted among the presbyteral churches of Rome. From the evidence of the station transferred there, Carolus Piazza inferred that, after the title of Caius had collapsed through age, the church of the Four Holy Crowned Ones was first substituted for it; see the *Hierarchia Cardinalis*, page 533. He then shows that Pope Callistus III substituted the title of Saint Callistus. Urban VIII, however, assigned the ancient church of Saint Caius, which he had restored from its foundations, to the monastery of sacred virgins known as the Barberini, which he had likewise magnificently built, restoring the station as well, although he did not remove the right of the Roman title from the church of Saint Callistus.

**Linea 13.—“He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way.”** That some portion of Saint Caius’s relics was once removed from there is attested by an ancient stone placed in the hypogeum of the Vatican basilica and taken from the very ancient chapel of John VIII. Among the other names of saints whose relics were kept there, the following are carved:

> “Saint Lucius, pope; Saint Caius, pope; Zephyrinus, pope.”

Or at least it must be acknowledged that his blood and *brandea*—relic cloths—were placed there according to the ancient custom.

Becillus reports in his notes on the acts of Saint Caius, page 95, that the entire body was found in the cemetery of Callistus in the year 1622 under Gregory XV. A small tablet bearing the name of the pontiff, inscribed with the letters **CAIO PP.**, was found with it, together with the sign of a palm and a monogram of Christ the Lord. Becillus also asserts that in the same place, together with the sacred bones, the pope’s ring and coins of Diocletian, under whom he had suffered, were found. He says that a letter of Stephen Cerqua reported that no part of the body was missing.

I would nevertheless have preferred that an expert in anatomy had been employed in examining the sacred bones, as was done by order of His Holiness Clement XI when the relics of Saint Balbina were examined, having been found beneath the high altar of the deaconry of Saint Mary in Domnica, and when the sacred body of Saint Leo the Great was inspected during its most recent translation.

For if that martyr Caius identified by Becillus was Pope Caius rather than Caius the administrator or Caius who held a praetorian office—which could equally have been indicated by the same initials **PP.**—it would have been established that those relics of Pope Caius, mentioned on the marble of John VIII’s chapel, indicated blood and linen cloths, since it is said to have been established from the bones that no part of the same skeleton was missing from the body that he describes.

It must certainly be presumed that the relics of Caius **PP.** mentioned on the Vatican stone, together with the remains of Saints Lucius and Zephyrinus, the pontiffs, belong to Pope Caius, his companion in dignity and martyrdom. They may either have been cut off and preserved by order of Severina, who was collecting the blood-relics of Saint Susanna while the martyr’s body was being carried to the cemetery, or have been removed by one of John VIII’s predecessors during the restoration of the cemetery of Callistus and carried to the Vatican basilica. In either case, their standing is established: they are relics attributed to the martyr and belong to him named Caius PP.]

[Note: [Col. 1465D]

**Linea 5.—“He established that the ordinations,” etc.** [Col. 1466A] Caius distinguished the orders in the Church, by which, as by certain grades, ascent and access to the episcopate were made possible. These were the doorkeeper, lector, exorcist, acolyte, subdeacon, deacon, presbyter, and bishop.

This should by no means be understood to mean that he himself was the first to institute the rule that anyone ascending to the highest grade should climb to the lofty summit of the priesthood through the grades of the lower orders. For it is established that the hierarchy in the Church had already been fixed in apostolic times and that this order had been received by usage. Rather, Caius’s decree on this matter appears to have been that no one should be promoted to the episcopal throne unless he had ministered in each of the lower orders.

**Linea 12.—“Because of Susanna, the daughter of the presbyter Gavinus.”** Pope Caius had a blood brother named Gabinus, who in the vigor of youth had taken a wife, by whom he had a daughter named Susanna. After his wife’s death, he lived a celibate life and raised his daughter with a most holy Christian education. Because of his outstanding piety and learning, he deserved promotion to the presbyterate; he had published a defense of the Christian religion against the pagans.

When the emperor Diocletian Augustus had declared Galerius Maximian Caesar and made him his partner in the empire, and since Diocletian had no male offspring, he wished to bind Galerius by a closer bond of marriage and betrothed to him the virgin Susanna, because he had no nearer female relative of his own family. The consent of Gabinus, of her uncle Pope Caius, and of the girl herself was sought. She rejected the marriage, although it was an imperial one, saying that she did not wish to defile Christ’s bridal chamber with any mortal marriage.

At last Susanna could be softened by no promises or blandishments, nor frightened by threats. Because of her steadfast profession of faith, Diocletian, her pagan kinsman, ordered her to be secretly beheaded within her father’s house.

From the day on which Susanna was struck down, Pope Caius continually offered sacrifice for her commemoration. The house of Pope Caius was joined to the dwelling of Saint Susanna and of her father Gabinus. Hence it came about that a station of Christians was established in those two houses near the Quirinal, before the Forum of Sallust, and that a church between the two houses was built and erected as the title of a cardinal presbyter. It was customarily called the church of Saints Gabinus and Susanna, “between the two houses.”

Afterward Gabinus was arrested, committed to prison, beaten with whips, and completed his martyrdom by decapitation after his daughter Susanna and before his brother Caius.]

[Note: [Col. 1466C]

**Linea 5.—“He established that all ordinations in the Church should proceed in this way.”** If anyone, etc., so that he would be doorkeeper, lector, exorcist, etc. The clerical hierarchy owes its institution to our Lord Jesus Christ, as has been demonstrated in the dogmatic *History of Religion*. The various orders composing it were not all conferred simultaneously at the foundation of the Church. Rather, ministers were created gradually, as necessity required that their ministries in the worship of sacred things be distinguished and separated.

Jesus Christ himself wished to create the supreme pontiff, the first bishops, and the first presbyters. The apostles, having received authority from him, created the first deacons. The bishops, successors of the apostles, created the other subordinate ministers with the same authority when, as the number of the faithful in the Churches increased, it became necessary to entrust their duties to a larger number of people, as the proper conduct of divine worship and the edification and support of the Christian people required.

At the election of Pope Cornelius, around the middle of the third century, his letter to Fabius of Antioch, reproduced in the notes on that entry from Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 35, shows that all the orders of the Christian hierarchy had already been distributed in the Roman Church.

Accordingly, we understand Caius’s constitution not to contain the institution or new creation of any of these orders. [Col. 1467A] It commands only that no one be promoted to the higher priestly offices and duties of the clergy unless he proceeds gradually from the lower order to the next higher order in the sequence of those that form the ecclesiastical hierarchy.] [Col. 1468A]

[Col. 1457]

**29**

Caius, a Dalmatian by nationality and descended through his father Caius from the family of the emperor Diocletian, held the see for eleven years, four months, and nine days [Note: [Col. 1457] B, twelve years, four months, and five days]. He lived during the reigns of Carus and Carinus [Note: [Col. 1457] B, Carinus, Numerian, Diocletian, and Maximian, up to the consulship of Diocletian for the sixth time and Constantius], from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of January, from the consulship of Carus for the second time and Carinus, until the tenth day before the Kalends of May, when Diocletian was consul for the fourth time [Note: [Col. 1457] C, the sixth time] and Constantius for the second time.

He established that ordinations [Note: [Col. 1457] C B, orders] in the Church should proceed in this way [Note: [Col. 1457] Baron. under the year of the Lord 296]: if anyone were deemed worthy to be a bishop, he should first be ordained doorkeeper, lector, exorcist, acolyte [*sequens*; Note: [Col. 1457] C, acolyte], subdeacon, deacon, and presbyter, and thereafter bishop.

He divided the regions among the deacons. He, fleeing the persecution of Diocletian by living in the crypts, was crowned with martyrdom in the ninth year. He held four ordinations in the month of December: twenty-five presbyters, eight deacons, and five bishops in various places. After the eleventh year, he was crowned with martyrdom together with his brother Gavinianus [Note: [Col. 1457] C, Gabinius and Gabinus], because of Susanna, the daughter of the presbyter Gavinus [Note: [Col. 1457] C, Gaoinus; see Baronius at the cited place]. He too was buried in the cemetery of Callistus on the Appian Way, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May. The episcopate was vacant for eleven days.

**CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS**

Caius: twelve years, four months, and seven days. He lived during the reigns of Carus and Carinus I, from the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, when Carus was consul for the second time and Carinus was consul, until the tenth day before the Kalends of May, when Diocletian was consul for the sixth time and Constantius for the second time.

**XXX. SAINT MARCELLINUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 296, DIOCLETIAN AND MAXIMIAN 13.**

**Linea 6.—“For this reason Marcellinus himself was led to sacrifice,” etc.** The author of the *Liber Pontificalis* says the same.
