Although these acts appear spurious in other respects, they do not seem to depart from the truth concerning Marcellinus’s fall, as Onuphrius Panvinius shows in his *Ecclesiastical History*, which is preserved in manuscript in the Vatican Library.]

### Line 16.—

In the crypt beside the body of Saint Crescenton. From this passage it is clear that the holy martyrs were buried in crypts. This is so unquestionably true that no doubt on the matter can exist, since it is also established that Christians lived in crypts during the time of persecution and performed there every kind of Christian act of piety. Hence the author of this catalogue says of Caius: “that he fled the persecution of Diocletian by living in crypts.” Pope Stephen was beheaded in the Catacombs, in the place where he was preparing himself to offer the sacrifice, as his Acts relate.

Concerning Sixtus, Saint Cyprian reports in his letter to Successus: “Know that Sixtus was executed in the cemetery, on the eighth day before the Ides of August.” Concerning Blessed Laurence, the author of this catalogue says under Sixtus II: “But Blessed [Col. 1469C] Laurence was buried on the Tiburtine Way, in the Veranus estate, in a crypt with many other martyrs.”

Concerning the martyr Alexander, his ancient inscription, found in the cemetery of Callistus, reads:

> “Alexander is not dead, but lives above the stars, and his body rests in this tomb. He completed his life under the emperor Antoninus, who, when he foresaw that he would greatly precede him in benefaction, repaid gratitude with hatred. For, bending his knees, he is led to punishments in order to sacrifice to the true God. O unhappy times, in which, amid sacred rites and vows, we cannot be saved even in caves,” etc.

### Line 19.—

“And the episcopate ceased for seven years, six months, and twenty-five days, while Diocletian was persecuting the Christians.” The second catalogue reads: “six years”; the most ancient catalogue, “four years.” Cardinal Baronius does not admit even a single year in which the see was vacant. In this matter Onuphrius Panvinius agrees with him; together with the consensus of more recent writers, Panvinius shows that Marcellinus died in the same year in which Diocletian laid down the purple. From this it follows that the episcopate could not have remained vacant for seven, six, or four years while Diocletian was persecuting the Christians, but that the persecution ceased in the same year in which Marcellinus died, giving the Roman clergy the opportunity to substitute Marcellus in his place. Marcellus held the pontificate for more than a year, as his Acts testify: “in the stable, after serving for many years, clothed in a haircloth garment, he breathed out his spirit on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of September.”

### Note: [Col. 1469D]

#### Line 11.—

“And after this event the holy bodies lay in the open, as an example to Christians, for thirty-six days, by order of Diocletian.” The bodies of the martyrs lay unburied in the forum, as an example to Christians—that is, so that Christians might be moved to apostasy by this spectacle—by order of Diocletian, as a punishment intended for public example. Anastasius, under Theodore, says:

> “When Isaac saw the head of Maurice, he rejoiced and had it placed on a stake in the circus at Ravenna, as an example to many.”

At the same time, during the persecution of Maximian, the bodies of the martyrs were exposed unburied to beasts and birds, and guards were appointed to prevent their burial [Col. 1470B] (Eusebius, Book VIII, chapter 19). Among the Greeks, the bodies of the condemned remained unburied (Quintus Curtius, Book VIII, chapter 2):

> “The Macedonians declared that Clitus had been justly killed, and would also have forbidden his burial, had not the king ordered him to be buried.”

Among the Romans the same custom existed even in the punishment of soldiers. Tacitus, *Annals*, Book I:

> “The bodies were thrown outside the rampart for display.”

Nevertheless, a constitution of Diocletian does not forbid condemned persons to be handed over for burial (*Obnoxios*, Code, *On Religious Matters and Funeral Expenses*). At Constantinople there was a place called Polagium, designated for the burial of the condemned; Cedrenus mentions it under Constantine Copronymus: τάφον καταδίκων, “a tomb of the condemned.”

Even in the time of Decius it was not forbidden to hand over the bodies of martyrs for burial, and responsibility for burying the bodies of martyrs belonged to the *copiatae*, or laborers (Cyprian, Letter 3):

> “And what is most serious is that, if the bodies of martyrs or of others are not buried, great danger threatens those upon whom this duty rests.”

When Tarquinius Priscus was constructing the sewers of the City through the labor of the plebs, and citizens, wearied by the work, were killing themselves, he restrained them from taking their own lives by a new kind of punishment: he fastened the bodies of the dead to crosses so that they might be viewed by the citizens and at the same time torn apart by beasts and birds (Pliny, Book XXXVI, chapter 15) [Col. 1470C].

### Note: [Col. 1470C]

#### Line 4.—

“There was a great persecution at that time.” This persecution is rightly called great, since three emperors, with equal cruelty and monstrous savagery, carried out a slaughter of Christians for many years. Learned men discuss its date and beginnings in their notes on Lactantius’ *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. The *Pontifical Book* likewise calls it great, because under these emperors the earlier beginnings that had appeared during the decennalia burst forth with great force against the Christian religion.

Three periods must in fact be distinguished. The first occurred during the decennalia, when Diocletian claimed divine honors for himself and, as is credible, the clergy resisted; the first disturbance then broke out against them, during which Caius was compelled to establish a retreat in the crypts [Col. 1470D]. The second disturbance occurred in the year 298 against Christian soldiers, who were not punished by death but by the removal of their military belts, according to Lactantius. The persecution properly so called, begun through the publication of edicts—and here called great—started during the vicennalia celebrated in the year 303.

It was instituted gradually: first against the Palatines and soldiers, according to the same Lactantius, chapter 15, page 99; then against the clergy, as he says in the same chapter 15:

> “The presbyters and ministers were arrested and condemned to confession without any trial, and were led away with all their households.”

#### Line 5.—

“So that within thirty days seventeen thousand persons . . . might be crowned.” The number of martyrs killed throughout the provinces of the Empire is given as an indication of the greatness of the persecution. The implacable hatred and most stubborn obstinacy of the mother of Galerius Maximianus—who, driven by madness, was planning to put an end to the Christian religion—show that the slaughter could have been carried out within a month of the publication of the edicts.

To this must be added the same stubborn purpose of the three emperors, Diocletian, Maximian, and Galerius Maximianus. If one also considers their evil idols, their depraved morals, and their private plans for destroying the Christians, lest the Christians favor Constantius, who was operating in Gaul and whose power they had good reason to fear, these circumstances, taken together, will readily persuade us that matters unfolded as they are reported in the Acts of Marcellinus, and that the stated number of martyrs corresponds to the emperors’ cruelty.

If one further adds the charge of arson imposed on Christians in the edicts—as though they were plotting to kill the emperors—the slaughter that followed becomes still more certain. After describing the hatred of Galerius’ mother, raging against the Christians, and the imperial edicts that followed, Lactantius adds:

> “But Caesar—namely Galerius—not content with the terms of the edict, prepared to attack Diocletian in another way. For, in order to drive him toward the purpose of the most cruel persecution, he set fire to the palace through secret agents. When part of it had burned, the Christians were accused as public enemies, and, amid immense hatred, the name of the Christians burned together with the palace. It was alleged that, after deliberation with the eunuchs, they had plotted the destruction of the emperors, and that the two emperors had almost been burned alive in their own house.”

These calumnies, sharpened by the priests of the pagan nations, who were fostering the superstitious zeal of Galerius’ mother, could not fail to stir up the idolatrous cities, intensify the judges’ savagery, and drive Diocletian to destroy the faithful utterly. Lactantius testifies that this is what happened, adding shortly afterward:

> “But Diocletian, who always wished to appear clever and intelligent, suspected nothing; yet, inflamed with anger, he immediately ordered all his own people to be tortured. He himself sat by and roasted the innocent in the fire. Likewise all the judges, and finally all the officials who were masters in the palace, tortured them after being given authority. They competed to see who would discover something first. Nothing was found anywhere, nor did he allow the anger of the foolish old man to die down. But after fifteen days had passed, he planned another fire; it was detected more quickly, yet no author appeared. Then Caesar, having prepared his departure in the middle of winter, burst forth, declaring on that same day that he was fleeing lest he be burned alive.”

Thus Galerius, sharpening his mother’s orders and his own evil disposition against the Christians, strengthened the persecution, advanced the most savage slaughter, and himself carried it out together with Diocletian. This makes the number of those killed as martyrs certain and indisputable. Lactantius therefore continues:

> “The emperor was now raging not only against his household but against everyone . . . People of every sex and age were dragged away to be burned. They were not taken singly, since the multitude was so great that they were surrounded in groups by the fire . . . The whole earth was afflicted . . . and from east to west three most savage beasts were raging.”

Eusebius gives the same account, saying:

> “It is impossible to say how many and how great were the martyrs of Christ whom one could see everywhere, in every place and city,”

and he compares the slaughter to civil disturbances, when the killing of human beings is most frequent:

> “They polluted the provinces under their rule by slaughtering worshipers of God, both men and women, as though in a kind of civil war.”

Both writers were still alive when the tyrants were unleashing the fury of their persecutions. Severus likewise says:

> “The world was never exhausted by wars more completely; nor did we ever conquer in a greater triumph than when we could not be conquered by ten years of slaughter.”

#### Line 8.—

“By Diocletian himself . . . they were beheaded.” Not by Diocletian, but by his judges, since in the year in which the martyrdom occurred Diocletian was away from Rome. What is said here about the fall of Marcellinus appears to have been added and supplemented from certain Acts fabricated by the skill of the Donatists. The person who forged them, failing to notice the chronological indication, inserted a false account of Diocletian’s actions against Marcellinus [Col. 1472A].

For Diocletian, scarcely after the opening celebrations of the Roman vicennalia, departed in the very winter, and in the month of May, when the martyrdom occurred, was far from the City. Lactantius reports this as follows—perhaps being present at Rome at the time. After relating the edicts of persecution first published in the city of Nicomedia, he adds:

> “After this crime had been committed, Diocletian, when prosperity had already departed from him, immediately proceeded to Rome to celebrate there the day of the vicennalia, which was to fall on the twelfth day before the Kalends of December. When those solemnities had been celebrated, unable to endure the freedom of the Roman people, impatient and sick in spirit, he burst out of the City as the Kalends of January approached, on which a new consulship was being assigned to him. He could not endure thirteen days, so that the consul might take office at Rome rather than at Ravenna. He therefore departed in winter; battered by bitter cold and beaten by rains, he contracted a slight but persistent illness. Afflicted throughout the entire journey, he was carried mostly in a litter. Thus, after the summer had passed, he reached Nicomedia by way of the bank of the Striga [Col. 1472B], as the illness, now severe, began to rise.”

Since this circumstance was not noticed by the compiler of the account of Marcellinus’ fall, the entire credibility of the Acts collapses. The Donatists were attempting through these fragments to defend their own cause, as can be seen in the Conference of Carthage, and Saint Augustine often points this out while refuting them.

The Donatists were laboring to prove that the episcopate had fallen away through Marcellinus, in order to weaken the sentences later issued against them by the pontiffs. In the same way, they accused Felix, the ordainer of Caecilian, of the crime of handing over the sacred books, so that they might show his ordination invalid on that ground. Perhaps they also wished to strengthen the Roman pseudo-episcopate established by the Donatists, as though they themselves had restored it after Marcellinus’ fall, while they boasted that the true Church existed among them, immaculate and undefiled.

#### Line 19.—

“The episcopate ceased.” The vacancy of the Roman see was prolonged because of the severity of the persecution and became still longer because of Galerius’ further machinations [Col. 1472C]. For Galerius’ mother, scarcely satisfied by so many Christian deaths and by the most bitter slaughter of the innocent throughout the world, believing the persecutors too slow, kept stirring up her son against the Christians without respite.

They seized upon an opportunity: Galerius advanced the matter by his customary deceptions, taking advantage of rebellions stirred up against the emperors by certain tyrants who were aspiring to imperial power. Bishops and clergy were accused as the authors of seditions, and the persecution consequently intensified. The priests of the pagan nations advised that the Christian religion could easily and completely be uprooted if the bishops and sacred books were removed from the midst of society.

New edicts against the clergy were therefore published, and a dreadful assault was made upon the sacred books. This produced the multitude of those who handed them over, which, according to Optatus, gave occasion to the Donatist schism.

Our conjecture is strengthened by the words of Eusebius, who narrates the sequence of this persecution. After recounting the Nicomedian edicts and the slaughter of human beings that followed, he says in Book VIII, chapter 6:

> “These things were done at Nicomedia at the very beginning of the persecution.” [Col. 1472D]

He then adds:

> “A little later, when some attempted to seize imperial power in the region of Melitene in Armenia and others in Syria, an imperial edict was published ordering that all rulers of the churches everywhere should be bound and thrown into prison. The spectacle of what happened afterward surpassed every power of description, since an innumerable multitude of people everywhere was handed over to custody. The prisons, formerly assigned to murderers and plunderers of tombs, were then filled with bishops, presbyters, deacons, readers, and exorcists, so that no room remained for those who had been condemned for crimes.”

I believe that these machinations were introduced by Galerius, in whom ambition and desire for imperial power and domination without a colleague had taken root. Lactantius seems to indicate this when, after recounting the disturbances that had been stirred up, he observes that Galerius “had recently clashed with the old Maximianus and terrified him by imposing the fear of civil arms” [Col. 1473A].

This more urgent persecution of the clergy was intended to destroy the religion by removing the leaders of the Christian people. It had to be directed especially against Rome, since they knew very well that, because of his greater authority among Christians, supreme jurisdiction belonged to the Roman bishop. The emperor’s agents therefore devoted every effort to preventing the election of a pontiff, hoping that everything else would easily collapse if no supreme bishop were elected.

Thus Decius, as was noted above from Cyprian, sought to destroy Cornelius as pontiff. During this same first decade of Diocletian’s persecution, when the tyrant Maxentius was at Rome and was of the same character and perversity, he also wished to restrain Marcellus, his successor, so that Marcellus would deny that he was a bishop, as will be read below under Marcellus. From this cause, therefore, it happened that the election of a successor was delayed after the martyrdom of Marcellinus.

### Note: [Col. 1473B]

#### Line 6.—

“Marcellinus himself was led away to sacrifice, so that he might offer incense, and he did so.” Although by several arguments—see Baronius, year 302, no. 96 and following—it can probably be shown that this story of Marcellinus’ offering incense is entirely refutable and an interpolation, nevertheless we think that one should not easily depart from the view that has hitherto been accepted by common agreement and found in the ancient ecclesiastical records.

Marcellinus therefore sinned by sacrificing to idols, induced by fear of death to act against the confession of faith. Thus, by his external act, he appeared to have denied the faith. Yet inwardly he believed nothing against the faith and taught nothing of the sort; therefore he could not have been a heretic or unbeliever. His repentance, carried out shortly afterward, his voluntary resignation of the pontificate, and the martyrdom he undertook for the faith provide the clearest evidence of this. See Augustine, *On the Uniqueness of Baptism against Petilianus*, and Bellarmine, *On the Roman Pontiff*, Book IV [Col. 1473C], chapter 9.

#### Line 14.—

“In a bright chamber.” See Baronius’ notes on Marcellinus in the *Martyrology.*

### Chronological Notes

I indicated in the Prolegomena, folio CI, and in the preceding number, that Marcellinus’s see was fixed at eight years, two months, and twenty-five days in both the paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul and the principal catalogues and other manuscripts; I also showed that this period corresponds exactly to the consuls named, if his episcopal ordination is fixed on Sunday, 22 December 295, so that its end falls on 16 March 304, to which date I said it remained to show that his martyrdom must be referred. This was done by the illustrious prelate Schelestratius, Dissertation 2, chapter 8, no. 6. He first shows that, according to both ancient and recent writers, Marcellinus suffered under the ninth consulship of Diocletian and the eighth of Maximian [Col. 1473D]—that is, in the year 304, Diocletian’s last year:

> “On this point,” he says, “modern writers agree so fully that those who often differ among themselves in the chronology of the earlier pontiffs hold one and the same view concerning the time when Marcellinus died. Onuphrius Panvinius and Antonius Augustinus, Cardinals Baronius and Bellarmine, Dionysius Petavius, and Philippus Labbeus attest the matter; all of them place Marcellinus’s death in the year 304. Labbeus adds the date 26 April, the very day on which the commemoration of Marcellinus is celebrated in the martyrologies of Bede, Rabanus, Notker, Ado, and Usuard. Yet it must be observed that Diocletian and Maximian laid down the purple on the first day of April in that same year. One must therefore either say that Marcellinus died before the first day of April, or that he died in 303, not 304. To solve this difficulty, one should note the words of the Venerable Bede, who testifies that after his death Marcellinus lay unburied for thirty-six days in the manuscript, or thirty-five in the printed edition [Col. 1474A], and was afterwards buried on the Salarian Way. It may therefore be that the martyrologies recorded not the day of his death but that of his burial; and Bede suggests that this happened when he writes, under 26 April, ‘The deposition of Saint Marcellinus, pope,’ as the above-mentioned most ancient manuscript reads, although the printed edition has *natale* [birthday or feast-day]. Thus the day of deposition was 26 April, since he had suffered on 16 March while Diocletian was still reigning; and Marcellinus’s martyrdom can therefore rightly be placed under him. And, since no further question can remain concerning the proof of these points, there is no reason to dwell longer upon them.”

Concerning the day and year on which Diocletian and Maximian laid down the purple, Idatius is explicit in Scaliger’s edition, as Schelestratius observes, quoting his words: “In the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII, Diocletian and Maximian laid down the purple and became private persons on the day of the Kalends of April.” Rupert likewise observes this in Besold’s *Historical Synopsis*, p. 362 [Col. 1474B], writing: “When Diocletian and the elder Maximian abdicated, likewise on the Kalends of April, as Idacius writes (not on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, as Golzius and Onuphrius reported),” etc. Zonaras, *History*, Book II, chapter 7, likewise testifies to the year, namely the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII.

Some, with Baluzius (*Notes on Lactantius, On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, p. 389 of volume II of the *Miscellanea*), wrongly interpret a passage of Zosimus as though Zosimus had written that the interval from the secular games celebrated by L. Septimius Severus under the consulship of Libo and Cilo (A.D. 204) to the aforesaid consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII amounted to one hundred and one years. Zosimus’s text should be rendered thus: “For from the consulship of Cilo and Libo, in which Severus exhibited the secular games, to that of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII, διέδραμεν εἷς ἐνιαυτὸς πρὸς τοῖς ἑκατόν: one year beyond a hundred had elapsed.” Its sense is that, from the Palilia of the year 204, under the consulship of Cilo and Libo, to the Palilia of the year 304, under the consulship of Diocletian IX and [Col. 1474C] Maximian VIII, after one hundred years had been completed on the day of the Palilia, the first year after the completed century was running from that day. Contrary to the testimony of both writers, Baluzius and Hervart therefore wrongly defer Diocletian’s abdication to the year 305 and to the day of the Kalends of May. Schelestratius’s assertion is indeed established: Idatius places their abdication on the Kalends of April in 304, under the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII.

To Schelestratius’s learned observations one further point may be added. From the documents which he produced, the fifth verse in Bucher’s Little Work II, printed above among the Prolegomena, where the depositions of bishops—that is, of the supreme pontiffs—are listed, must be corrected. The fifth verse of that work reads: “On the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February, [the deposition] of Marcellinus in Priscilla’s [cemetery].” The indications of place and time require that the name be restored as Pope Marcellus, whose final syllable was added by a copyist [Col. 1474D], and that XVII, not XVIII, days before the Kalends of February be read, the final unit having likewise been added. For on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February the martyrdom and deposition of Pope Marcellus occur at the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way in every martyrology; while Marcellinus’s death has been shown to agree with 16 March, and his deposition with 26 April, the day on which he is commemorated.

Having set forth these points to establish the day of Saint Marcellinus’s martyrdom, I return to the year—not in order to repeat the argument and show again that it belongs to A.D. 304, under Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII, which Schelestratius observes is confirmed by the agreement of all ancient and recent writers, but in order to consider the reckoning of the total preserved in the old manuscript catalogue of the Queen of Sweden, observed by Schelestratius and cited by me among the documents concerning Marcellinus’s see in the Prolegomena, col. 23. It remarkably confirms the same year, and indeed our entire papal chronology hitherto explained [Col. 1475A]. That codex reads: “From the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ to the see of the most blessed Pope Marcellinus there are 276 years, 9 months.” I said that this total of years agrees exactly with the chronology of Victorius of Aquitaine and with ours, which is set forth in Little Work IV and in the notes on the Liberian Catalogue: “The Passion of the Lord, and the consulship of the two Gemini, belong to the twenty-eighth year of the common Christian era and to the thirty-third year of the age of Christ the Lord; it began on Thursday, 25 March, in the garden of Gethsemane, and was completed on the cross on the immediately following Friday, 26 March.”

For if the twenty-eighth running year of the Christian era at the Passion is increased by the stated total of 276 years, one arrives at 26 March of the running year 304 of the common Christian era. I now add that it ought to read: “From the Passion of our Lord Jesus Christ to the see of the most blessed Pope Marcellinus there are 276 years, *min. d.* 9” [Col. 1475B]—that is, nine days less. Since it has been shown that the end of Blessed Marcellinus’s see was marked by his martyrdom on 16 March, it follows that, to complete 276 whole years from the Passion of the Lord, nine days after 16 March 304 are lacking—the day which put a blessed end to the see of Marcellinus, both pontiff and martyr.

### On the Vacancy of the See after Marcellinus’s Death

In verse 20, after the martyrdom of Blessed Marcellinus, the Anastasius codex reports that the Roman see was vacant for seven years, six months, and twenty-five days while Diocletian was persecuting the Christians. Schelestratius notes that Diocletian laid down the purple a few days after Marcellinus’s death, and bestowed it upon Daia on the Kalends of May. Diocletian bestowed upon him his purple, of which he divested himself—so L. Caecilius writes in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, no. 19—and became Diocles again. The author of the Catalogue, writing in the age of Liberius, states that the episcopate ceased for four years, six months, and twenty-five days. The catalogue under Justin has six years, six months, and twenty-five days. Other sixth-century manuscripts have: “and the episcopate ceased for seven years, five months, and twenty-five days.” This diversity of readings shows that the passage in the Bibliothecarius and the catalogues has been badly mangled by copyists. If an autograph copy of that most ancient Liberian catalogue survived, I think it would scarcely be found to read otherwise than: “the episcopate ceased until Maximian Augustus (Daia), for two months and five days.” For we have seen that the purple which Diocletian was putting off when he abdicated the empire was bestowed on this Maximian Daia on the Kalends of May. I shall show that on Sunday, 21 May of that same month, the Roman clergy elected and ordained Marcellus, Marcellinus’s successor, in the same year, 304. This is shown by Marcellus’s era still visible in the Leonine paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul, where one reads *SEDIT ANN. V, MENS. VII ...*, supplemented in the Farfa Catalogue, which also reads twenty-five days. For if these times are compared with the certain date of his martyrdom [Col. 1475D]—namely 16 January, after the tenth consulship of Maximian, that is, A.D. 310, as will be established in the account of Marcellus—it is clearly shown that Marcellus’s ordination and installation in the Roman see must be referred to Sunday, 21 May 304. That day was two months and five days after the martyrdom of his predecessor Marcellinus, completed on 16 March of the same year, as I showed shortly before with Schelestratius; and it began the five years, seven months, and twenty-five days attributed to his see in the Pauline paintings, insofar as they survive in the preserved number of years and months, and fully expressed in the Farfa Catalogue, which faithfully retained the number of twenty-five days as well. For this total is calculated exactly from 21 May 304 to 16 January 310. Since, then, the chronological arguments agree exactly both with the epoch of his predecessor and with the day of martyrdom completed by Blessed Marcellus, in the number of years, months, and days entered in the genuine documents of the Roman Church, there is no doubt [Col. 1476A] that, through copyists’ error, the vacancy of the see after Marcellinus’s death—which was denoted by two months and five days until the beginning of the imperial rule transferred to Maximian Daia in the same month of May by Diocletian, perhaps in these or similar words, *ET CESS. EPISC. VSQVE AD MAX. AVG. MENS. II. D. V.*, that is, “and the episcopate ceased until Maximian Augustus, two months, five days”—was extended into several years, months, and days, variously transcribed in corrupt copies.

Cardinal Baronius (as Schelestratius observes, Dissertation 2, chapter 8, no. 7), Onuphrius Panvinius in his manuscript *Ecclesiastical History*, and virtually all authors of our age who have illustrated papal history or chronology, after consulting the documents produced here—to which I think I have added no little in these observations—now establish that the vacancy of the see after Marcellinus’s death was not merely not extended beyond the limits of that same year, but ended immediately after the imperial insignia had been conferred upon Maximian and the empire had been abdicated by Diocletian, followed happily by the Roman clergy’s election of Marcellus [Col. 1476B]. Panvinius thought that Marcellus was elected on the fifth day before the Kalends of July, since he saw five years, six months, and twenty-one days assigned to his see. We place his ordination thirty-four days earlier, because in the paintings of Saint Paul we see five years and seven months, and in the Farfa Catalogue twenty-five days also, fully preserved in addition to the same years and months.

What reason led certain copyists of the catalogues, and the Bibliothecarius himself, to add to the vacancy of the see after Marcellinus the years which they took from his successor Marcellus, I shall attempt to show in the chronological notes on the immediately following epoch of that Marcellus.

### Historical Notes

#### Line 7.—

“Which he did,” etc., “and led by repentance,” [Col. 1476C] etc.; and Line 14: “On the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla, in a bright chamber, which he himself had prepared, repenting, while he was being led to execution in the crypt beside Saint Crescenton.” This passage, which is not read in the Acts of the Council of Sinuessa nor in the Acts of the martyrdom of the blessed pontiff Marcellinus, published with the alleged council from Isidore Mercator in Binius, but is read in this *Liber Pontificalis* and in the second catalogue, which is referred to the age of Pope Felix IV and the Emperor Justinian, indicates that it was drawn from a different source than those fictitious Acts, or the corrupt medley stuffed into Mercator. Therefore, if older Acts existed which mentioned repentance, one may infer that the fall and repentance of that blessed pontiff, though unknown to Augustine, ought to be regarded as consonant with the truth.

But on more attentive consideration of this text of the Bibliothecarius and of the second catalogue, and of the variant readings on the same text noted by the editors, I think a wholly different conclusion must be drawn: namely, that the origin of the assertion of a fall, entirely unknown in the fourth and fifth centuries, flowed from a corrupt variation of one word in an abridgment of the genuine Acts of Blessed Marcellinus. The repentance there asserted should be referred not to Marcellinus—whom I would judge more plausibly to have been immune from a fall and innocent—but to those penitents whom Marcellinus had resolved to cleanse from impious incense-offering and its apostasy, and to admit to penance at the Paschal feasts together with the neophytes approaching to receive the grace of baptism.

I shall explain the matter more clearly if the variant readings are repeated from volume I of this edition, in the verse of the present number which reads: “He buried [him] on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla, in a bright chamber, which he himself had prepared, repenting, while he was being led to execution in the crypt.” Other codices read, “which he himself had ordered, repenting.” Velserus observes that the manuscripts of the Suprian Collection of Councils and the Baronian copies read, “which Saint Peter himself had ordered” [Col. 1477A]. We thus understand that the passage was corrupted from Acts differently abridged. Since the indicated copies mention Saint Peter as directing the choice of this place—or, according to other codices, as preparing it in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way—and since repentance is signified, I think it should read: “which Saint Peter himself also had prepared for the penitents, while he was being led to execution in the crypt,” etc. I shall now explain how both Saint Peter and Pope Marcellinus prepared a place for penitents in the same crypt of the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, where Marcellinus was buried after his martyrdom.

It must be repeated that the martyrdom of Pope Saint Marcellinus occurred around 16 March, as I demonstrated above in the chronological Notes, whereas his burial was delayed by thirty-six days—or even forty—during which, on the persecutors’ orders, his body lay unburied, as the Librarian recorded from the Acts. This must be reconciled with 26 April, the day on which he is commemorated. In that same year of Christ 304, Easter was to be celebrated on 9 April. Therefore, during those days [Col. 1477B] when Marcellinus was brought before Diocletian’s tribunal—plainly after the Kalends of March, when the emperor, not yet fully recovered from a long illness, had first allowed himself to be seen, as we understand from L. Caecilius on *The Deaths of the Persecutors*, a contemporary witness—he had to consider at what safer place he might, when the Easter feast arrived, administer baptism in the customary manner to catechumens amid the heat of persecution.

That celebrated place at the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way was offered to him. Earlier documents stated that there the prince of the apostles had baptized people; the place was also called the Ostrian Cemetery. It was, I say, a celebrated place, and during persecutions it could appear safe to visit. This is established by the Acts of Pope Liberius. When Liberius, sought by Constantius Augustus and by the Arians for execution, had withdrawn outside the city into the crypts on the Salarian Way as Easter approached, the Acts show that he convened his presbytery and deliberated with the clergy about administering baptism there [Col. 1477C], with Damasus, then a presbyter and Liberius’s vicar, advising this above all others.

The crypt of that Ostrian cemetery was so extensive—being part of the cemetery of Priscilla, as may be seen in Aringhius’s *Roma subterranea*, volume II, book IV, chapter 31—and so capable of accommodating a gathering crowd of the faithful, that the same Acts of Liberius say that five thousand people were baptized there at a single Easter. There was also reason for assigning Marcellinus such a spacious place for assembling the presbytery, or even for gathering a synod of bishops from at least the neighboring Churches, so that by common agreement it might be decided what was to be done at the approaching Easter concerning the administration of penance to the lapsed during those same days of Holy Week, which by custom were appointed both for conferring baptism on catechumens and for reconciling public penitents, especially those who, overcome by torture or terror, had fallen away from the worship of the Christian faith.

This council [Col. 1477D], according to the judgment of more expert scholars, was assembled in the crypt, with Marcellinus, the Roman pontiff, present and presiding—not, as some suppose, in the Cleopatrian crypt near Sinuessa, a place wholly unknown to antiquity, where he could not, amid the heat of persecution, have approached and assembled two or three hundred bishops within fifteen days, as anyone prudent can easily understand; nor for the purpose of receiving penance from Marcellinus as an innocent man, wholly removed from the crime of impiety, as Saint Augustine, cited by Cardinal Baronius, observes. See Baronius, under the year 302, no. 96.

Rather, it was for the administration of penance, through the indulgence of the Church and by Pope Marcellinus, and in accordance with the discipline recently confirmed under Cornelius, to the lapsed—laypeople and clergy alike, indeed even priests and bishops—some of whom, during that monstrous persecution, are known to have offered incense or handed over the sacred books, as is clear from the testimony of Caecilius Lactantius and other writers.

Whether there was among these someone named Marcellinus who, repentant of the crime he had committed and clothed in sackcloth, presented himself at the council, thereby giving later generations an occasion for attributing the crime and penance of another to the Roman pontiff Marcellinus; or whether Pope Marcellinus himself, having experienced the vicissitudes of human weakness, succumbed during the persecution and was restored by the divine grace of Christ while, through a public confession, he sought to obtain pardon from God through the Church in the sacrament of penance—although Cardinal Baronius, weighing the arguments on both sides, strongly sets forth the grounds for asserting his innocence, supported by Augustine’s testimony and not attacked by Petilianus, the patron of the Donatists, except through calumnies shared by Marcellus, Melchiades, and Silvester, who are known to have been free from the alleged crime—I do not dare go beyond the limits established by Baronius. I shall be content to do what belongs to the duty of our commentary and observations: namely, to indicate how little force there is in the expression, or clause, [Col. 1478B] “which he himself had prepared, as a penitent.” Perhaps this was carelessly copied from another version reading, “which he himself had prepared for penitents,” and may have provided an occasion for attributing another person’s crime and penance to our pontiff Marcellinus.

Accordingly, as Easter approached, Pope Marcellinus had prepared this cemetery, famous among the faithful because the prince of the apostles had administered baptism there to many people. While he was the guest of Pudens and Priscilla on their suburban estate, just as, when circumstances permitted, he had opened the saving bath of Christ’s baptism in the city itself, near the Esquiline, he assembled the presbytery in good time and perhaps also a council of the bishops nearest to Rome. He prescribed regulations for the penance of the lapsed who were to be admitted to the peace of the Church at the approaching Easter, according to the needs of each individual.

While he was making these preparations, he was discovered by the persecutors, brought before Diocletian’s tribunal, and condemned to the ultimate punishment. He bravely suffered death for Christ around [Col. 1478C] 16 or 19 March, together with the companions mentioned by the Librarian and by the author of the *Catalogus*. After the bodies of the martyrs had lain unburied in the forum, by the emperor’s command and as an example to Christians, for thirty-six or forty days—during which Diocletian abdicated on the Kalends of April and then withdrew from the city, after his colleague Maximian Herculius had likewise resigned the imperial power on 21 April, the day of the Palilia—the city prefect and the new emperors, willingly accepting, as one may reasonably believe, the purification of the forum on the birthday of the city and of their own rule, silently permitted Marcellus to gather the remains of the slain and place them in an underground burial chamber in the cemetery of Priscilla, or at least did not forbid it.

From the indicated designation of the place, from the name of Peter mentioned in certain manuscripts, from the proximity of the Easter feast, and from the ancient discipline of the Church recently confirmed under Cornelius on the occasion of disputes with the African Church concerning the lapsed, we seem able to reconstruct this sequence of events with greater security, insofar as one may conjecture from the concise indication supplied by the compilers of abbreviated catalogues.

The enemies of the Roman Church, especially those who lent their support to the Donatist heresy, vainly attempted to cast the accusation of offering incense and handing over the sacred books upon our most holy pontiffs Marcellinus, Marcellus, Melchiades, and Silvester, as Augustine testifies. When, during the fourth and fifth centuries, their accusations had run aground and they could not advance the calumny, which Augustine and the Church’s public reputation had sufficiently dispelled, it seemed that, a century later, after the Acts had been transformed, Marcellinus should be represented as having lapsed and done penance at a council of two or three hundred bishops. He would have had to be said to have assembled them within a few days between the Kalends and Ides of March, during the persecution of the Church, although the 318 Fathers had gathered at Nicaea much more slowly, even though the emperor permitted them to use publicly stationed horses for the journey, as Eusebius testifies in book III, chapter 6, of *The Life of Constantine* [Col. 1479A].

This three-hundred-member council is said to have been held without difficulty in the Cleopatrian crypt, known to no geographers or ecclesiastical historians; and Marcellinus alone, from so great a number of Fathers, is summoned before the emperor’s tribunal. I fear that these circumstances, so inconsistent with the conditions of those times, have been built upon a single scribal error, carelessly admitted by incompetent copyists of the Acts, when they altered the words that were read in the Acts or catalogues: “He was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla, in a bright chamber, which he himself had prepared for penitents,” although others maintained that one should read, “which Saint Peter himself had prepared,” as Binius noted in the variant readings.

But, affirming nothing rashly, whether he himself, as a penitent, prepared the chamber or prepared it for other penitents, I set limits to conjecture and willingly remain within Baronius’s bounds. From this cemetery of Priscilla, the body of blessed Pope and martyr Marcellinus, together with many others distinguished in the Church’s calendars—namely Marcellus, Priscilla, Praxedes, Pudentiana, and Saint Leo IV—was transferred into the city by Pope Leo IV, first to the title of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs. Later the sacred relics were divided among the other churches of the city. Our Liberian basilica received the venerable head and arm of blessed Marcellinus, which are preserved there with the greatest devotion.]

[Note: [Col. 1479B]

Line 1.—Marcellinus, a Roman by nationality. Among the Greeks there was confusion in the names, since they thought Marcellinus and Marcellus were the same person. Thus Eusebius, in the *Chronicle* and in *History*, book VI, chapter 16, passing over Marcellus, lists only Marcellinus. The other writers seem to have followed this error, such as Nicephorus Callistus, *History*, book VI, chapter 34, and Nicephorus the bishop in his *Chronicle*. The Latins, however, did not do so: Optatus of Milevis, *Against Parmenianus*, Saint Augustine, letter 175, and others consistently distinguish the two: “After Caius, Marcellinus; after Marcellinus, Marcellus.”

Line 6.—“For this reason Marcellinus himself was also led to sacrifice, so that he might offer incense, and he did so.” It is not surprising if the pontiff Marcellinus, yielding to the tyrannical instruments of coercion, terrified and afraid, while retaining faith in Christ in his heart, denied it outwardly; coming to himself, he recognized and lamented his sin. For this reason a synod of 180 bishops, thirty presbyters, and three deacons assembled at Sinuessa in Campania, now commonly called Sessa. Marcellinus came to it disheveled, clothed in sackcloth and with his head sprinkled with ashes. There, with abundant tears, he publicly and openly confessed the gravity of the sin he had committed.

Yet none of them dared pronounce a sentence against him or condemn him, since they all said that Peter had sinned in much the same way and had washed away his sin by weeping. But all, having given a distinguished testimony to the supreme pontifical dignity, cried out with one voice: “Judge your case by your own mouth, not by our judgment, [Col. 1479D] for, as they say, you will be justified by yourself, or condemned by your own mouth.” For “the first see is judged by no one.”

Nevertheless, at the same synod those presbyters and deacons were condemned who had accompanied him as far as the temple of Vesta, then abandoned him, and, coming to the church, accused him as though they had seen him do what they suspected. Marcellinus’s penance is recorded in the first volume of the Councils and has been handed down by Gratian in the *Decretals*. Augustine, in *On the Sole Baptism against Petilianus*, chapter 16, and *Against the Letter of Petilianus*, book II, chapter 92, denies that Marcellinus offered incense, while Petilianus could establish nothing of the kind. Eusebius, book V, chapter 26, knows nothing of his lapse, but only of his martyrdom.

Nevertheless, since the opinion that Marcellinus had lapsed was spread abroad by everyone’s testimony and believed through universal agreement, and since it was received without any controversy in the ancient martyrologies both of the Roman Church and of other authors, as well as in the Roman Breviary, and was retained and confirmed by the letter of Pope Nicholas I to Michael, emperor of Constantinople, one must in no way depart from it merely because it was unknown to others.

Line 13.—“Marcellus the presbyter collected the bodies at night,” namely at the command of the apostle Peter, who appeared to him in a dream.]

[Note: [Col. 1480A]

Line 7.—“And he did so; and after a few days, moved to penance, etc.” The lapse said to have occurred in Pope Marcellinus clearly reveals human weakness and the stain of the will in individuals; nevertheless, it implies no prejudice against the gifts of the apostolic see or the authority of the pontiff.

Concerning the lapse attributed to Marcellinus, Nicholas I writes thus to the emperor of Constantinople, Michael:

“During the time of the emperors Diocletian and Maximian, Marcellinus, bishop of the city of Rome, who afterward became a distinguished martyr, was so compelled by the pagans that, entering their temple, he threw grains of incense upon the coals. For this reason, after a council of numerous bishops had been assembled and an inquiry had been held, that same pontiff confessed that he had done this. Yet none of them dared pronounce a sentence against him, since they all repeatedly told him: ‘Judge your case by your own mouth, not by our judgment.’ And again: ‘Do not be heard in our judgment, but gather your case into your own bosom.’ And again they said: ‘The first see is judged by no one.’”

The council of which this letter speaks is the council of Sinuessa. From its Acts Nicholas derived what he reports concerning Marcellinus. The Roman Breviary likewise confirms that the Roman Church recognizes the truth of this history.

Yet, unmoved by these considerations, many recent writers reject the same history, especially for the following reasons: first, because the ancient writers nearest to those times who spoke about Marcellinus report nothing of the kind concerning him; second, because Eusebius makes no mention whatever of the event; and third, because Theodoret attaches to this pontiff a eulogy as though he had attained the greatest glory during the persecution, describing him as “a man made illustrious by great glory during the times of persecution” (book I, chapter 3; see Eusebius, book II, chapter 12).

They observe that the Donatist Petilianus really did wish to bring forward something similar concerning Marcellinus and some of his presbyters, but that Saint Augustine declares it to be an entirely incredible calumny:

“Why, then, is it now necessary for us to clear away the crimes alleged by him against the bishops of the Roman Church, whom he attacked with incredible calumnies? Marcellinus and his presbyters, Melchiades, Marcellus, and Silvester, are accused by him of handing over the divine books and of offering incense. But are they for that reason also convicted? Or are they shown to have been convicted by any firm documentary evidence? He says that they were criminal and sacrilegious; I reply that they were innocent,” etc. (Saint Augustine, *On the Sole Baptism against Petilianus*, chapter 16.)

They also reject the alleged history connected with the council of Sinuessa, arguing that it was a spurious council, since they say that Sinuessa is an imaginary place, of which not even a trace has yet been found in any sacred or secular writer. They add that it is incredible that Marcellinus, while the most savage persecution of all was raging, could have summoned three hundred bishops to a council, etc.

After weighing the arguments on both sides, which Cardinal Baronius and many others after him have collected, the distinguished Sommier finally concludes his observations as follows.

But whoever ultimately accepts either opinion concerning the historical event will understand that nothing in religion’s doctrine is thereby impaired. That doctrine does not teach that its ministers are impeccable in the particular conduct of their own actions; it teaches instead that those same ministers are animated and sustained by the divine Spirit in the government of the universal Church. One must distinguish what belongs to a person’s private character from what pertains to the public office. Augustine writes against Petilianus, chapter 16:

“Whatever Marcellinus, Marcellus, Silvester, Melchiades, Mensurius, Caecilianus, and the others may have been, against whom the Donatists bring whatever they wish in their own defense, does not prejudice the Catholic Church, spread throughout the whole world. We are crowned in no way by their innocence; in no way are we condemned by their iniquity. If they were good, they were cleansed like grain in the threshing floor of the Catholic Church; if they were evil, they were crushed like straw in the threshing floor of the Catholic Church.”

Thus the action of Marcellinus, who is said to have been compelled by the violence of tyrants and struck by fear of death and punishment to offer incense to idols, brings no stain upon the authority or rights of the holy see. As a private individual, he was a man who committed a crime against the confession of faith [Col. 1482A] through an act of idolatry. But it will never be said that he brought forward the authority of his see to establish or approve the worship of idols, or that he himself was personally a heretic, or taught anything contrary to the doctrines of religion.

Indeed, those who assert his lapse also assert his speedy penance: “After a few days, moved to penance, etc.” Those who say that he could not be condemned by the Fathers of the council of Sinuessa nevertheless say that he condemned himself: “I cannot remain in the priestly order . . . Yet Bishop Marcellinus was condemned by his own judgment.” (*Council of Sinuessa*, at the end.)

He was afterward crowned with martyrdom. As he proceeded to his passion, he adjured the presbyter Marcellus not to carry out Diocletian’s commands. He is venerated as a saint, his memory is recorded in the ancient Calendar, and he appears in the martyrologies of the Roman Church.]

[Col. 1467]

>[Col. 1467] |

30. Marcellinus, a Roman by nationality, son of Projectus, held the see for eight years [Note: [Col. 1467] B: eight years, fewer seven days], eleven months, and twenty-two days. He lived during the reigns of Diocletian and Maximian [Note: [Col. 1467] B: of the emperors Constantius and Galerius, from the consulship of Diocletian VI and Constantius to that of Diocletian VIII and Maximian VIII], from the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Diocletian VI and Constantine [Note: [Col. 1467] C: Constantius] XI, until Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII. At that time there was a great persecution, so that within thirty days seventeen thousand Christians of both sexes were crowned with martyrdom throughout the various provinces [Note: [Col. 1467] Baronius, at the place cited, refutes this history from page 739 onward].

For this reason Marcellinus himself was led to sacrifice, so that he might offer incense, and he did so. After a few days, moved to penance, he was beheaded by that same Diocletian [Note: [Col. 1467] Maximian] for the faith of Christ, together with Claudius, Cyrinus, and Antoninus, and they were crowned with martyrdom. As blessed Marcellinus proceeded to his passion, he adjured the presbyter Marcellus not to carry out Diocletian’s commands [Note: [Col. 1467] CB: “He was beheaded and crowned with martyrdom; as he proceeded to his passion, he adjured Marcellus.”]

After this event, the holy bodies lay in the street for thirty-six days, by Diocletian’s command and as an example to Christians. Then the presbyter Marcellus collected the bodies at night, together with presbyters and deacons, with hymns, and buried them on the Salarian Way in the cemetery of Priscilla, in a bright chamber that remains open to this day, which he himself had prepared [Note: [Col. 1467] Ipsi: “Saint Peter himself had ordered it”; CB] as a penitent, while he was being dragged to execution in the crypt beside the body of Saint Crescention, on the seventh day before the Kalends of May. [Note: [Col. 1467] Baronius, under the year of the Lord 304, no. 790 of the 1594 Vallicellana edition, refutes this.]

He also carried out two ordinations in the month of December: four presbyters, two deacons, and five bishops in various places. From that day the episcopate ceased for seven years, six months, and twenty-five days [Note: [Col. 1467] Baronius: only six months and twenty-four days], while Diocletian persecuted the Christians.

**CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS**

Marcellinus: eight years, three months, and twenty-five days. He lived during the reigns of Diocletian and Maximian, from the day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Diocletian VI and Constantius II, until the consulship of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII. At that time there was a persecution, and the episcopate ceased for seven years, six months, and twenty-five days.

## XXXI. SAINT MARCELLUS. IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 304, THE TENTH YEAR OF CONSTANTIUS AND GALERIUS
