Lines 11–12.—“He was condemned to the *catabulum*.” Marcellus was condemned by Maxentius to the *catabulum*. The *catabulum* [Col. 1483C] in the city was a stable for animals used to transport public loads. Anastasius mentions it below in three places.

Line 12.—“While he served for many days in the *catabulum*.” And shortly afterward, line 14: “They dug him out of the *catabulum*.” Again, line 19: “And he ordered planks to be spread again in the same Church, so that the animals gathered in the *catabulum* might stand there.” Papias says: “A *catabulum* is an enclosure for animals, where something is thrown over them from above.” Hence the *Catabulenses* were so called, those who served in the *catabulum* as a punishment. Concerning them, see book 9 of the Theodosian Code, *On Bakers and Catabulenses*, and Cassiodorus, *Variae*, book III, letter 16, and book IV, letter 47.

The *catabulum* is the royal stable, to which martyrs were accustomed to be condemned. Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 22: “Ὅπως τὲ βασιλικῶν ἵππων ἐνόχους παραστίσει, παταδίκασεν”—“He condemned him as responsible for the care of the royal horses.” Cedrenus, in his account of Nicephorus: “Ἀπό γενικῶν, καὶ ἁπελθὼν ἐν τῷ καταβολιῳ”—“From the general [service], and having departed into the *katabolion*.” Platina ineptly calls it a *catabulum*. Cujacius, *Observationes*, 16.5.]

[Note: [Col. 1483D]

Line 5.—“He established titular churches in the city.” The Diocletianic persecution, an imitator of the Decian persecution, assigned all sacred places, including the cemeteries themselves, to the imperial treasury. It did so with such extensive and thorough destruction that Constantius, although he was in Gaul and restrained the judges from the violence of the persecutions, nevertheless could not prevent the devastation of the churches, as Lactantius testifies in *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*, chapter 15:

“Constantius, lest he appear to dissent from the commands of his predecessors, allowed the meeting places—that is, the walls that could be restored—to be demolished; but he preserved unharmed the true temple of God, which is in human beings.”

Therefore, in houses and, as I think, in the private oratories mentioned above, which were more convenient places where the bodies of martyrs were kept, he consecrated other titular churches. While he was arranging these matters, he was arrested by the emperor, as is stated shortly afterward: “Here he was confined and held because he was organizing the Church.” After he had assigned another title where day and night they confessed the Lord Jesus Christ with hymns and prayers, as the text immediately adds, the purpose of the expelled pontiff was renewed.

Accordingly, this new institution of titular churches should not be considered the first introduction of churches into the city. Rather, after the sacred places and basilicas existing in the city had been confiscated for the treasury, as was proved above, Marcellus introduced a new substitution of oratories existing in private houses. These were consecrated as titular churches, or churches, with presbyters placed in charge of them, insofar as the circumstances of the persecution permitted.

Line 6.—“For the sake of baptism.” Since the churches had been destroyed in this persecution, as Lactantius had said, and oratories had been substituted among private homes where these oratories existed, he granted them the ability to baptize, so that he might provide for the needs of the faithful and of others who were being converted. He specifically appointed domestic oratories, choosing them especially so that they might be regarded as churches. Hence Lucina offered her own house.

Whether the power granted to these titular churches to administer baptism was ordinary remains open to debate, since formerly such ministries were celebrated only in a church directed by a bishop, and this was still observed in the time of Zosimus. It should therefore be regarded as an extraordinary concession, since the condition of the churches, destroyed or assigned to the imperial treasury, required Marcellus to dispense from the earlier discipline.

“And for the penance of many.” This should not be understood only of sacramental absolution, but also of the assignment of the lapsed to perform acts of penance, so that, after completing them, they might be reconciled to the churches. There were many lapses during the persecution, whose loss Optatus laments in book I. To assist them, he also granted presbyters the power of reconciliation, which had formerly been reserved to the bishop and was not granted to presbyters except in a case of necessity by episcopal concession, as is found in the code of the canons of the African Church, where the first volume of the Councils, page 870, reads:

“Bishop Aurelius said: If anyone is in danger and asks to be reconciled to the divine altars, and the bishop is absent, the presbyter must certainly consult the bishop and, by his command, reconcile the person in danger.”

At that time the discipline imposed on the lapsed was extremely strict, especially upon those called *traditores*. Thus, in the Acts of the martyrs Donatus and his companions, the faithful were repeatedly admonished, after Optatus’s work, page 102:

“If anyone communicates with the *traditores*, he shall have no share with us in the heavenly kingdom.”

Line 7.—“And for the burials of the martyrs.” Since he entrusted presbyters with responsibility for the burial of the martyrs and assigned titular churches to them, this strengthens the conjecture made above concerning Eutychianus: that a presbyter retained responsibility for burying the bodies of martyrs.

During this Diocletianic persecution, Christians were forbidden to bury the bodies of martyrs, and the penalty was confiscation of their property. For below it is said that Saint Marcellus was crowned with martyrdom: “Blessed Lucina collected him and buried him”; and it is added: “Lucina, however, was condemned to confiscation.” Hence the number of gravediggers multiplied in each Church. In the register of each Church, where the number of clergy was recorded, gravediggers are also listed.

Indeed, the Acts of Felix show that there were many such persons in the African Church during this persecution. The register is given by Optatus, page 92, as follows:

“While Paul was bishop, with Montanus and Victor, Deusdedit and Memorius as presbyters; with Mars present together with Helias the deacon; Marculius, Catulinus, Silvanus, and Carosus as subdeacons; Januarius, Maralcus, Fructuosus, Migginus, Saturninus, Victorius, and the other gravediggers.”

The author of the *Treatise on the Seven Orders of the Church*, addressed to Rufinus and included among the works of Saint Jerome, discusses their office. This precaution was necessary because the cemeteries of the Christians had been assigned to the imperial treasury. Marcellus established these titular churches as if they were dioceses, following the arrangement that Dionysius had decreed for the restoration of the basilicas; with the same purpose Marcellus substituted private oratories.

Line 9.—“Here he was confined and held because he was organizing the Church, having been arrested by Maxentius.” The punctuation should be as follows: “Here he was confined . . . because he was organizing the Church. Arrested by Maxentius, etc.” Thus the catalogues of Holstenius and Schelestratius. Stephen uses the same construction and punctuation:

“During his time he was deported into exile; afterward, by God’s will, he returned safely to the Church. And thirty-four days later he was arrested by Maximian and sent into prison.”

Besides the arguments already given, the necessity of this punctuation is also proved by the practice then in use: the glorious confessions of martyrs were recorded, as was proved above. The weight of repeated confession is revealed by Pontius’s words, when he defends Cyprian’s withdrawal:

“Who would raise up such great martyrs by the exhortation of divine speech? Who, finally, would animate with the encouragement of the heavenly trumpet so many confessors, marked on their foreheads with a second inscription and preserved alive as an example of martyrdom?”

Thus the *Liber Pontificalis* records three glorious confessions of Marcellus.

The first, as seems credible, Marcellus endured when, while the see was vacant, he assumed responsibility for the Church in accordance with Marcellinus’s command. When he saw the basilicas and cemeteries being assigned to the imperial treasury, he organized twenty-five titular churches and was then arrested for the first time and punished with exile. This earlier passion is expressed in the words:

“Here he was confined and held [Col. 1485D] because he was organizing the Church.”

This occurred when the Diocletianic persecution, begun at the start of the preceding year, had scattered the Church, and he had assumed responsibility for it at the command of his predecessor.

The second confession took place under Maxentius, who came to Rome in 306 while Marcellus was pontiff. The following words refer to it:

“Arrested by Maxentius so that he might deny that he was a bishop.”

At that time new edicts had been issued against bishops, as we saw above.

The third is described in these words:

“When Maxentius heard this, he sent for blessed Marcellus and arrested him again.”

The particle “again” urges us to distinguish these three events, for it indicates that Maxentius raged against Saint Marcellus on two occasions. The first confession, however, took place before Maxentius’s arrival in Rome, at the command of the judges who had condemned Marcellinus to death, while Marcellus was still a presbyter.

The compiler of the Acts thought it necessary to record these events in order to show that Marcellus was a true confessor before his pontificate and during his pontificate, and afterward a crowned martyr [Col. 1486A]. This was intended to answer the calumnies of the Donatists, who slandered Marcellinus, Marcellus, Eusebius, Melchiades, and Silvester as having been illegitimately ordained, either because they had lapsed or because they had been ordained by lapsed men. Their purpose was to persuade populations entangled in schism that the Roman Church had defected and to represent the Roman pseudo-episcopate usurped by those men as legitimate, so that the credulous people might submit to it and reject the judgments issued against them by the apostolic see.

For this reason Saint Damasus wished the following brief inscription to be recorded on the tombstone:

> A truthful ruler, who foretold to the wretched  
> That the lapsed should mourn their crimes,  
> He was a bitter enemy to all his foes.  
> Hence fury, hence hatred followed, discord and quarrels,  
> Sedition and slaughter; the bonds of peace were broken  
> Because of another’s crime, who denied Christ in peace,  
> Expelled from his homeland by the savagery of the tyrant.  
> Damasus wished briefly to relate these facts as established,
the merit of Marcellus, so that the people might be able to recognize it. [Col. 1486B] These statements mentioned above confirm this. For, in order to show that Marcellus had not fallen away, but rather had foretold that all who had fallen would bitterly lament the crimes of apostasy, betrayal, and the rest, brought about by the cruelty and savagery of the persecutors, Damasus therefore placed the earlier verses. These matters coincide with the establishment of the titular churches, which he organized so that the many who had fallen might perform penance. Moreover, at the time when these events were taking place, he had been driven from the borders of his homeland by the tyrant’s savagery.

When the exile occurred, and while he was a presbyter administering the Church during the vacancy of the see and proclaiming penance to those who had fallen, appointing presbyters to impose it, Damasus wished by this to show that, even before his pontificate, Marcellus had been concerned with the penance of those who had fallen. For at that time, namely in the year 305, the Council of Cirta was held. At that council forgiveness was granted to those who had fallen through a too-hasty indulgence, and the decree concerning fallen bishops laid the earlier foundations of the schism of the Donatists, as Optatus observed, book II, p. 16. [Col. 1486C] In that council Victor of Garba is listed among the first authors of the decree; shortly thereafter he became the first Donatist bishop at Rome and the founder of the Donatist pseudo-episcopate at Rome. And when Damasus states that evil came from those who had fallen, he plainly indicates the schism of the Donatists, from which those evils spread and disturbed the African and neighboring churches.

Damasus declares that these matters were known, and that he had placed them on the tombstone of Saint Marcellus in order to dispel the calumnies imposed upon the holy pontiff by the Donatists. Saint Augustine teaches that, in the time of Damasus and afterward, the Donatists were accustomed to make these frivolous accusations against the pontiffs and to level such calumnies against them. Against Petilianus he writes:

> “What need is there now for us to clear away the crimes charged by him against the bishops of the Roman Church, whom he has attacked with incredible calumnies? Marcellinus, and his presbyters Melchiades and Marcellus, and Sylvester, are accused by him of the crime of betraying the divine books and of offering incense. But are they thereby convicted, or are they shown to have been convicted by the firm evidence of any documents? He says that they were criminals and sacrilegious; I reply that they were innocent. Why should I labor to prove my defense, when he has not even attempted, however slightly, to prove his accusation?” [Col. 1486D]

From this point onward, where a more reliable preservation of the Acts of the pontiffs is found and the scribes’ negligence has not reversed the order, important evidence is offered for illuminating sacred history.

### Line 13.—“All his clergy came and bought him out of the Catabulum.”

The gathering of all the clergy to ransom Marcellus during the fiercest period of persecution—which was then raging especially against the clergy—will not seem incredible if Maxentius’ character is considered. For although he rivaled Galerius in equal cruelty toward all Christians, nevertheless, out of fear of Constantine, who in the year 306, after the death of his father Constantius, was Caesar, he thought that the persecution should be moderated, lest Constantine’s army be increased [Col. 1487A] by Christian soldiers.

At the beginning of his imperial rule he therefore presented himself as favorable to Christians, according to Eusebius, book VIII, chapter 14:

> “Maxentius, who seized tyranny at Rome, at first pretended to profess our faith, in order to follow that custom and flatter the Roman people. Accordingly, he ordered his subjects to desist from persecuting the Christians, displaying a false appearance of piety, so that he might seem much more benevolent and humane than the earlier emperors. But as time went on, he by no means showed himself in reality to be such as he had been expected to become.”

He could therefore permit the lesser clergy a certain freedom, so that they would not be subject to the edicts already promulgated and could publicly ransom the bodies of martyrs. Moreover, that violence was inflicted upon the bodies of martyrs in this monstrous period, and that Christians were granted the ability to bury them only when money intervened, is taught by the aforementioned Acts of Saint Boniface, who was killed at Nicomedia at the very beginning of Diocletian’s persecution. They describe the concern of his companions, who were searching for Boniface and found that, contrary to expectation, he had suffered martyrdom. Since the body of the holy martyr had lain unburied from the second day after his martyrdom was completed,

> “he said to the official: ‘This is the man whom we were seeking; we ask you to give him to us.’ He replied to them: ‘I cannot give you his body for nothing.’ But they gave him five hundred solidi and received the body of the holy martyr.”]

### [Note: [Col. 1487B]]

**Line 5.—“Cemeteries, etc.”** What had formerly been prohibited by the law of the Twelve Tables—as Cicero testifies in book II of *On the Laws*—namely, that the bodies of the dead should not be buried within the City, was granted to the Roman Church through the favor of Maxentius, so that the bodies of Christian martyrs might be buried within the walls. (Baronius, year 309, no. 4.)

**Lines 11–12.—“He was condemned to the catabulum.”** That is, to feed the emperors’ horses.

**Line 19.—“Planks.”** As Festus explains, *plancae* are flat boards.]**

### [Note: [Col. 1487C]]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

It fits well with pontifical chronology that the epoch of the see of Saint Marcellus, at least in the number of years and months, has been preserved in the Leonine paintings of the Basilica of Saint Paul, with only the final part of the verse missing, in which the number of days followed after the sign indicating them. Of the four most ancient catalogues of Italy, which I suppose were copied from those paintings, the Farfense has preserved all the parts of the epoch intact, namely five years, seven months, and twenty-five days. In the Cavense catalogue one month is lacking, and a four-day discrepancy is evident: the copyists, perhaps because the final part of the numeral five had been worn away, apparently thought that the number was not twenty-five but twenty-one, which they assigned to it.

In the Liberian Catalogue a similar error or abrasion retained only one year from the complete five-year period and removed the entire sign for five from the total number of days, [Col. 1487D] leaving the two tens, twenty, which preceded it. See the *Prolegomena*, where, in the eleventh line before the end of the page, in both columns, you should correct the text to read “after the consulships of Diocletian X and Maximian VII, in the year of Christ 309”; and in column 2 you should read as follows: “. . . . . . . pairs of consuls.”

From the second year after the consulship of Maximian (Herculius) X and Maximian (Daza) VII, the common Christian era 310, to the consulship of . . . .

I have shown above, in the notes concerning the vacancy of the see after Marcellinus, that the reading of the Farfense catalogue, being entirely intact, is to be preferred to the others. For it is certain that on 16 January in the year 310 of the common Christian era, which was designated “the second year after the consulship of Valerius Maximian X and Galerius Maximian VII,” Blessed Marcellus completed his martyrdom. And since it is established that Sunday fell on 21 May in the year 304, during the opening of which month Diocletian had already abdicated the empire, the interval between these two endpoints—five years, seven months, and twenty-five days—corresponds exactly to the period asserted by the Farfense manuscript and, insofar as they survive, by the paintings at Saint Paul’s. It also agrees with the consuls indicated in the fourth-century catalogue under Liberius.

To make this clearer, the sequence of consuls from the year 304, when the elder Augusti Diocletian and Maximian abdicated, to the year 314, the beginning of the see of Saint Sylvester, must be set out. During this ten-year period, when in the year 306 Constantius Chlorus, Augustus and consul for the sixth time, died at York on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, and was succeeded by his son Constantine, Maxentius was acclaimed at Rome by the Praetorian soldiers. Moreover, Galerius Maximian created Severus Caesar Augustus in the East, as Pagius proves from the book of Lactantius, *On the Deaths of the Persecutors*. He adds, in his *Hypatic Disputation*, chapter 13, p. 242:

> “Since, therefore, the empire was governed for six years by several Augusti who were at odds with one another, there were some ordinary consuls in Italy, where Maxentius ruled, and others in the rest of the Roman world. Since these were not set out separately by the compilers of the Fasti, the chronological situation is rendered somewhat obscure during this period. Therefore, the Fasti for the following six years must be divided into two parts: in the later column the consuls designated by Maxentius, and in the earlier column those designated by the others, are to be displayed.”

This is what Pagius says. Relandus, drawing from Pagius, condensed that six-year period into a shorter list, which I shall copy here, preceded by the preceding three-year period, as it is read in the fourth-century work on the Urban Prefects published by Bucherius.

[Col. 1488D] Once this sequence of consuls has been set out and established, we can investigate the cause of the error admitted in the catalogues, which remove several years from Marcellus’ pontificate and assign them to an imaginary vacancy of the see after the death of Marcellinus. They had seen that the final year of the pontificate of Marcellinus was marked by the ninth consulship of Diocletian and the eighth of his colleague Maximian Herculius, [Col. 1489A] at the time when the persecution took place. They had seen that the same Maximian Herculius held his ninth consulship in the year 307 and, immediately afterward, his tenth in the year 308, so that the year 307 was indicated by the words “Maximian nine times,” and the year 308 by “Maximian ten times.”

They had also read that Marcellus, the successor of Marcellinus, began his pontificate after the elder Augusti Diocletian and Maximian had withdrawn from imperial power. Since this Maximian continued not only to be Augustus but also to serve as ordinary consul, and marked the years 307 and 308, they assumed that the beginning of Marcellus’ see had to be postponed until Maximian Herculius no longer appeared in the Fasti either as Augustus or as consul. This first occurred in the year 309, which was designated throughout the Roman world outside Italy as the year after Maximian’s tenth consulship.

They therefore regarded the four-year period extending from 304 to 308, during which they observed that Maximian Herculius still presided over Roman affairs and gave his name to the Fasti, as a period foreign to the pontificate of Marcellus, whom they knew to have been elected after the joint abdication of the elder Augusti Diocletian and Maximian. Since the author or interpolator of the Liberian Catalogue attributed this four-year period to the vacancy of the Roman see, it followed that the single year remaining from Marcellus’ five-year pontificate, together with seven months and twenty or twenty-five days, had to be assigned to Marcellus. This is what he did, asserting that Marcellus had sat for one year, seven months, and twenty days; other readings have twenty-five.

The cause of the error, therefore, was the multiplicity of Eastern and Western consuls, the differing designation used in Italy and outside Italy, and the repeated abdication and resumption of the rank of Augustus by Maximian. He had first abdicated in the year 304, laying aside the purple at Milan before the tenth day before the Kalends of May, but resumed it twice before the end of that year. Later, after again relinquishing imperial power and regretting what he had done, he attempted a third return while Massilia was under siege. There he was captured and forced to die in the year 310, according to Hydatius and Victor in the *Epitome*.

[Col. 1489C] The cause of the error admitted in shortening Marcellus’ five-year period having thus been detected, and the greater part of it having apparently been assigned to the vacancy of the see after his predecessor by the person who filled the gaps in the older catalogue—for the editor Bucherius also recognizes a lacuna at the end of the section on Marcellinus and indicates it in the marginal notes—and after the truth of the epoch marked in the paintings of Saint Paul and in the oldest Italian catalogues copied from them has been weighed according to the measure of the consulships, we assign to Blessed Marcellus the period from Sunday, 21 May in the year of Christ 304, when Diocletian was consul for the ninth time and Maximian for the eighth, when Marcellus was ordained bishop of Rome, until 16 January of the year 310, the beginning of the second year after the tenth consulship of the elder Maximian and the seventh of Maximian Galerius, while at Rome Maxentius alone was consul for the third time, when Marcellus became a martyr: five years, seven months, and twenty-five days.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

[Col. 1489D] **Line 4.—“He asked a certain matron named Priscilla and made a cemetery on the Salarian Way.”** The distinguished writers of earlier times, together with Baronius in the *Martyrology* on 16 January and in the *Annals*, and together with Aringhius in *Subterranean Rome*, book IV, chapter 28, noted that there were three very distinguished women known by the name Priscilla.

The first appears in the sacred writings, namely in Acts of the Apostles, chapter XVIII; the other two appear in the Acts of the martyrs. The first was the wife of Aquila, with whom Paul lodged. She is mentioned by the same apostle in 1 Corinthians, chapter XVI; 2 Timothy, the final chapter; and Romans, chapter XVI. She is recorded in the *Martyrology* on the eighth day before the Ides of July.

The second Priscilla was a noble matron, the wife of Punicus and mother of the senator Pudens, with whom, as we have said, the apostles were guests in the Patrician district. There the titular church of Pudentiana, the daughter of that same Pudens, still survives today; she was also called Pastoris. Priscilla was buried on the Salarian Way with her husband. We have said in the life of Pius, in the second century of Christ, that both daughters, Praxedes and [Col. 1490A] Pudentiana, were brought there and buried with her.

From what has been related above concerning the depositions and the Acts of the saints, we learn that the older cemetery on the Salarian Way was named after this second Priscilla, the mother of those virgins. We have also related that the site was selected on her suburban estate, near the Ostrian crypts. Ancient monuments testify that the Prince of the Apostles once baptized there, not far from the bank of the Anio, which crossed the Salarian Way at that point and shortly afterward flowed into the Tiber.

The third Priscilla, no less distinguished, is the woman whom the Acts of that same pontiff and, following them, the Librarian present as a contemporary of Pope Marcellus. At Marcellus’ request she added her own cemetery to the cemetery of the older Priscilla.

The reason for this addition and enlargement can easily be understood from what was said concerning Marcellinus. Since the place had been chosen because of its religious character—it had been frequented by blessed Peter, among others, for administering baptism, and by later martyrs—and since it appeared sufficiently safe and sufficiently spacious for celebrating the assemblies of the faithful and convening the clergy, blessed Marcellinus had decided to celebrate the coming Easter there in the year 304, though his martyrdom came first. It pleased the presbyter Marcellus, who had charge of his burial, as soon as it was permitted, to collect the relics of the man who had been killed for Christ and lay in the Forum. Shortly afterward he himself was elected Marcellinus’ successor in the apostolic see. It pleased him, I say, to awaken the piety of this third Priscilla so that she would enlarge, with new additions, so celebrated a cemetery.

The undertaking was carried out with such success that not only Marcellus but also the pontiffs Sylvester, Liberius, and Siricius, besides countless other faithful, were buried there. Indeed, Liberius, while still alive, found such an open and spacious area in that cemetery, enriched by additions from the third Priscilla—who, as the more recent of three women bearing the same name, seems to have been called Novella to distinguish her from the elder and younger Priscilla—that the Acts of Liberius, read in Aringhius, book IV, chapter 30, [Col. 1490C] record that, on one Easter, more than four thousand faithful of both sexes were baptized by Saint Liberius in the adjoining parts of the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, where it took the name of Novella and Ostriana.

Thus the Ostrian cemetery was not far from the cemetery of Noella, or Novella, where the apostle Peter had baptized. The words of the Acts are:

> “At that same time, after taking counsel, Bishop Liberius baptized there four thousand twelve persons of both sexes, because not only Romans but also the Romans’ neighbors desired to be baptized by him.”

The desire of the neighboring people to receive the sacraments from the supreme pontiff Liberius is confirmed by the celebrated inscription of a pious woman, discovered among the Christian inscriptions of the church of Spoleto and reported by Gruterus, folio ML VII, no. 6. She boasts that she received the sacrament of confirmation from Pope Liberius:

> **D. P. PICENTIAE LEGITIMAE NEOPHYTAE DIE. V. KAL. SEPT. CONSIGNATAE A LIBERIO PAPA FL. HOSPITIVS MARITVS VXORI BENEMERENTI DVPLICEM SARCOPHAGVM CVM TITVLO HOC LOCO . . . O . E . . . I. POSVIT etc.**
>
> “To D. P. Picentia, a legitimate neophyte, confirmed by Pope Liberius on the fifth day before the Kalends of September. Flavius Hospitius, her husband, placed in this place a double sarcophagus with this inscription for his well-deserving wife . . .”

To return to the Acts of Liberius: their author had said shortly before that Liberius had taken his seat in the cemetery of Novella and had gathered the urban clergy there, so that by common counsel it might be decided where baptism should be administered during the approaching Paschal feast to those chosen to be reborn in Christ. He then continues:

> “Then Liberius began publicly to rebuke Constantius . . . Therefore Constantius, being exceedingly angry, ordered him to be carried outside the city as though into exile; and he lived three miles outside the city in the cemetery called Novella on the Salarian Way, etc.
>
> “At that same time, as the solemnity of Easter approached, at which all desired to be reborn in Christ, Liberius, the bishop of the City, summoned all the Catholic ecclesiastical orders. Sitting in the cemetery mentioned above, he began to speak as follows: ‘Days of tribulation and distress have arisen, dearest brothers. In them the ship of Peter, shaken by rising winds, fears shipwreck as though Christ were asleep, etc. It is therefore necessary that we awaken the Lord with our cries, etc.
>
> “‘Meanwhile, brothers, I cannot be present with you bodily. You have as your vicar a brother and fellow presbyter, Damasus, a man of complete fidelity and adorned with every virtue, whose prudence and steadfastness you publicly praise to me. With him going before you, use him, after God, in all your ways. As for baptism, decide what must be done and determine where it should be celebrated, since the Paschal solemnity is near and many desire to be baptized.’
>
> “The presbyter Dionysius replied: ‘Holy and innocent bishop, prepare the chrism in the name of the one whom you publicly proclaim, and we shall celebrate the baptism.’
>
> “Damasus, the vicar, replied: ‘We may be certain that the Lord will not abandon his people, with whom he promised that he would remain until the end of the world. Provide us now with the means to celebrate Easter. I speak humbly: we cannot relieve you of the burden that you carry, since you do not know where you should baptize. Did not John baptize in the desert? Our fathers also passed through the middle of the sea as a type of baptism. In rivers and marshes, too, especially when necessity demands it, baptism may properly be administered.’
>
> “Liberius, the bishop, received this speech with joy, so that he wept for joy. When he heard the divine counsel from the mouth of blessed Damasus, whom he himself had chosen as his vicar, he turned to him and said: ‘You shall be greater than the ministers, like the one who instituted baptism.’ And concerning him he said to the clergy: ‘Let the one who is your lesser become greater, and the one who humbles himself shall be exalted.’
>
> “For while he was pontiff, he prophesied that blessed Damasus would one day be raised to the summit of the apostolic see through the preeminence of humility and vigilance.”

After these words, it was decided that baptism should be administered at the approaching Easter in the nearby Ostrian cemetery, where the apostle Peter had baptized. There, it is said, four thousand people of both sexes received the grace of the saving bath.

I thought it necessary, together with Aringhius, to set out this entire passage from the Acts under Liberius in order to establish several points, some of which he himself also noted. First, he observes that the cemetery of Novella, located at the third milestone from the City on the Salarian Way, was part of the cemetery of Priscilla, which stood on that same road at an equal distance from the City’s boundary.

Second, Roman pontiffs during times of persecution were accustomed to withdraw with the faithful into the crypts of cemeteries to perform sacred rites, especially to administer the sacraments of baptism and the Eucharist to large numbers of people.

I shall add a third point: in accordance with the custom of the Roman pontiffs, a vicar was elected when they foresaw that they would be unable to present themselves to the assembly of the faithful, especially for the Paschal rites, whether because they had been sent into exile by persecutors or because some other necessity had forced them to depart.

The fourth point is that, since hiding places had to be sought during persecutions, both for councils and for the cautious celebration of assemblies, a place suitable for gathering was sought—one spacious enough and thought to be secure.

This, then, is how I understand why Marcellinus presumed that the site on the Salarian Way at Priscilla would be suitable.

Before Zephyrinus, Roman pontiffs generally held ordinations in the Vatican cemetery, and when they had completed their lives they were buried there near Saint Peter. But as the prominence of the site became somewhat more evident to the pagans under the Antonines, who treated us with greater mildness, it became too widely known and exposed during the persecution under the emperor Severus.

Therefore Zephyrinus and Callistus opened new cemeteries and martyrial assembly places on the Appian Way, situated almost directly opposite the Triumphal Way on which the Vatican cemetery lay. Urbanus, Pontianus, Cornelius, and Stephen held assemblies and sometimes administered baptism there.

We also read above, in no. 22, that during this period the bodies of the holy apostles Peter and Paul were brought to this cemetery. I have interpreted this as having been done so that, according to custom, ordinations might be held wherever the body of the Prince of the Apostles was preserved.

But when Fabianus had ordered many structures to be built throughout the cemeteries, as the Librarian states in his account, he seems to have made the catacombs and the martyrial assembly places in the cemetery of Callistus too well known. Under Cornelius and Stephen, his immediate successors, knowledge of the Callistan cemetery at the catacombs became so widespread that Stephen himself was discovered by the persecutors’ agents celebrating the solemn rites of the mysteries there, and his head was cut off while he sat in his chair, which had been established in those same crypts.

New hiding places and safer refuges therefore had to be sought by Stephen’s successors under Decius and Valerian. At that time, in the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus—that is, in the very year of the martyrdom courageously endured by Stephen in the catacombs—we read that the bodies of the holy apostles were returned to their former places: Peter’s to the Vatican, and Paul’s to the Ostian Way.

Other cemeteries farther removed from these were also opened. For we read that Laurence was buried in the cemetery of Cyriaca in the Veran field (above, no. 25). Felix, on the Aurelia at the second milestone, where he is also said to have built a basilica, buried 342 martyrs with his own hand at various places during his pontificate (no. 28). The expression “at various places” is not superfluous there, since it indicates the various cemeteries and refuges sought by the holy pontiffs during that uninterrupted succession of persecutions, which would have exposed the faithful too greatly if they had frequented only the better-known sites.

Finally, when the storms raised by Diocletian invaded the Church with their overwhelming waves, it was appropriate to designate a new harbor and station from the old one, in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way. This lay far from both of the better-known cemeteries—the Vatican on the Triumphal Way and the cemetery of Callistus and its neighboring sites on the Appian Way—and was chosen by Marcellinus and Marcellus for the safer celebration of assemblies of the faithful and the administration of the Paschal sacraments.

The proximity of the Ostrian crypts also recommended it. They lay not far from the banks of both the Anio and the Tiber, where people remembered that Peter had once baptized. Thus that site seemed more suitable than the others for the condition of the Church at that time. It was separated from the Callistan crypts by the entire diameter of the City and its suburbs, and from the Vatican by nearly equal distances involving both river and city, while nevertheless retaining the memory of Peter’s footsteps.

This, therefore, seems to have moved Marcellinus and Marcellus to prefer the indicated site on the Salarian Way and to encourage the third Priscilla, or Novella, to offer her estate to the Church. It lay near the cemetery of the older Priscilla and was intended for safer assemblies of Christians, especially at Easter, when those who had fallen were to be admitted to penance and neophytes to baptism.

### Lines 4–5.—“He made a cemetery on the Salarian Way and established twenty-five titular churches in the City, as though dioceses, for the baptism and penance of the many who were being converted from paganism, and for the burial of martyrs.”

From the notes recently given concerning the designation of the cemetery of Priscilla, it can sufficiently be understood what should be thought about the restoration by Marcellus of the number of twenty-five titular churches in the City and about their establishment in the image of dioceses. We seem to have explained this more clearly in the notes on Dionysius, no. 26.

Decius had been displeased that a priest had been established at Rome. Decius’ son and Valerian were displeased that letters were being received from bishops concerning the crown of the Lord. Therefore, both they and the succeeding Augusti, down to Diocletian, directed harsher edicts against the clergy, as possessors of Christ’s royal priesthood.

Nevertheless, the fearless Roman pontiffs did not cease to sit in office, following the example of Cornelius and Stephen, nor did they cease to restore the number of titular churches and to organize an image of the royal priesthood that they exercised in the see of Peter. They therefore consistently restored the Roman titular churches and raised their number to the full total of twenty-five, which had been established by Peter their founder, in order to signify through this type and head of the Church militant the universality of the Christian priesthood.

They obeyed both evangelical commands equally: humbly seeking safer hiding places for the flock entrusted to them, lest they be blamed for attacking and provoking the wolves through their boldness, as though relying on human hope; and at the same time protecting and preserving not only the Lord’s flock but also the folds and sheepfold entrusted to them for containing and ordering it when it was attacked by wolves, lest they be accused by the Prince of Shepherds as deserters from their station.

With this priestly steadfastness Marcellus persisted against Maxentius while seeking new and safer retreats in the crypts of Priscilla against the persecutors. He completed the number of titular churches while cautiously avoiding public assemblies. He set forth the Church’s hierarchy among the faithful while protecting them from the anger and snares of informers by placing them under the shelter of hiding places.

By God’s grace he received the reward of both virtues.

> “For,” as the Librarian continues in this passage, “he was constrained and arrested because he was organizing the Church. He was seized by Maxentius so that he might deny that he was a bishop and humble himself before the sacrifices of demons.”

Having already exercised sufficient humble caution by not provoking the persecutors, he displayed the steadfastness of a priest when he was arrested by them.

> “For he always despised and mocked the words and commands of Maxentius. He was condemned to the catabulum, where he did not cease to serve the Lord with prayers and fasts.”

The steadfastness of the priest stirred the piety and courage of the widow Lucina to offer her house so that it might be dedicated as a Roman titular church. Maxentius impiously designated a stable as a Christian titular church:

> “He ordered planks to be spread again in the same church, so that the animals gathered in the catabulum might stand there and blessed Marcellus might serve them.”

The fearless Christian pontiff, equally for Christ, assumed the role both of shepherd and of cattleman. The tyrant added a garment of haircloth to the tortures he inflicted, and Marcellus died clothed in sackcloth.

By this steadfastness he protected the Roman titular church that he had dedicated. Today, victorious, he possesses it, and through the presence and patronage of his sacred body, transferred into it from the cemetery of Priscilla, he makes it illustrious.

The Librarian rightly reported that, during this final persecution of Diocletian, the number of twenty-five titular churches in the City was steadfastly maintained, a number that Peter had ordered to be designated at the foundation of this Church. He describes them as organized like dioceses, so that it may be clear that throughout the first three centuries of persecution, no less than during the peace of the Church brought shortly afterward by Constantine the Great, the character of the royal priesthood, together with its universality and unity, was clearly preserved in this Roman see and its episcopate. See our notes on Dionysius, no. 26.]

### [Note: [Col. 1493D]]

**Lines 11–12.—“He was condemned to the catabulum.”** The *catabulum*, or *cacabulum*, was a place for keeping and maintaining public beasts of burden.

**Line 19.—“Planks were spread.”** The impious tyrant ordered the most holy pontiff to be brought into the church consecrated by him in Lucina’s house but profaned by beasts, so that he might care for them by spreading straw, allowing the animals to rest more comfortably. An ancient copy reads this way, not “planks.”

**Line 23.—“Lucina was condemned by proscription.”** Since she had given her property to the Church, she seems to have suffered this judgment of proscription; for the imperial edict forbade such an act. Constantine the Great abolished this law in his legislation *Concerning Bishops and Clergy.*]

### [Note: [Col. 1494A]]

Saint Marcellus, a Roman by birth, son of Benedictus, was named pontiff and ordained after an interval of three years, eight months, and three days between pontificates, in the three hundred and eighth year, on 27 June, which was a Sunday. He held the see for one year, six months, and twenty days; for he died on 16 January of the three hundred and tenth year, as is taught by the *Liber Pontificalis*, the genuine Hieronymian *Martyrology*, the authentic *Martyrology of Bede*, and the Sacramentaries of Gelasius and Gregory.

Pope Damasus is said to be the author of his epitaph, which survives in Baronius. From it it is inferred that Marcellus was driven into exile by Maxentius. Although Maxentius put an end to the persecution at the beginning of his reign, he afterward omitted no kind of impiety or lust, as Eusebius reports in book VIII, chapter 14, until he was defeated by Constantine the Great almost three years after the death of Saint Marcellus.

The author of the *Liber Pontificalis* writes that Marcellus established twenty-five titular churches, or parish churches, at Rome, for the administration of baptism and penance and for the burial of martyrs. He adds that in December he ordained twenty-six presbyters and two deacons, and more than twenty bishops in various places, and that he was buried in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way.

Although some infer, from the fact that Eusebius does not mention Marcellus in his *Chronicle*, that he was not distinct from Marcellinus, it nevertheless seems certain from what was said above concerning Marcellinus that the two were separate and distinct pontiffs.]

### [Note: [Col. 1494C]]

The peace which Maxentius allowed Christians to enjoy in the City at the beginning of his reign gave Marcellus an opportunity to advance the affairs of the Church with ardent zeal and vigilant freedom. To him is attributed the establishment or restoration of “twenty-five titular churches in the city of Rome, as though dioceses, for the baptism and penance of many who were converted from paganism, and for the burial of martyrs.” Ciaconius enumerates these titles, etc.

Marcellus’ care was equally directed to the observance of the penitential canons by those who had fallen during the persecution. But the same indolence that had led them to deny the faith kept them from undertaking salutary penance. They conspired against the holy pontiff and stirred up seditions and dissensions among the faithful; rushing through these into attempting and perpetrating every extreme, they filled the Church with slaughter to such an extent that they everywhere butchered all whom they found outside their faction. Without examining the facts of the case, the tyrant Maxentius ordered the pontiff into exile.

We owe this account of the events to Pope Damasus, who briefly embraced all these matters in the sepulchral inscription which he composed for Marcellus, brought again to light when Baronius was engaged in writing the *Ecclesiastical Annals*:

> The truth-speaking ruler, who foretold that the fallen,
> 
> wretched men, would bitterly lament their crimes, became a bitter enemy to them all.
> 
> Hence rage, hence hatred: discord and quarrels follow;
> 
> sedition, slaughter: the bonds of peace are dissolved.
> 
> Because of the crime of another, who in time of peace denied Christ,
> 
> he was driven from the borders of his homeland by the tyrant’s savagery.
> 
> These things briefly. Damasus wished to report what had been ascertained,
> 
> so that the people might be able to recognize Marcellus’ merit.

][Col. 1481]

[Col. 1481] 31. Marcellus, a Roman by nationality, son of Benedictus, from the district of the Via Lata, held the see for five years, six months, and twenty-one days. He lived in the times of Constantius, Galerius, and Maxentius, from the fourth consulship of Maxentius and the consulship of Maximus until the consulship [Note: [Col. 1481] B, one month and twenty-five days; and of the emperor Constantine, from the consulships of Diocletian IX and Maximian VIII to those of Maxentius and Maximus. Baronius, under A.D. 309, at the beginning.] He requested a certain matron named Priscilla, and established cemeteries on the Salarian Way. In the city of Rome he established twenty-five titular churches, as though dioceses, for the baptism and penance of the many who were being converted from paganism, and for the burial of martyrs. He ordained twenty-six [Note: [Col. 1481] C B, twenty-five.] presbyters in the city of Rome during the month of December, two deacons, and twenty-one bishops for various places.

He was harassed and arrested because he was organizing the Church. Maxentius seized him so that he might deny that he was a bishop and humble himself before sacrifices to demons. But Marcellus continually despised and mocked the words and commands of Maxentius, and was condemned to the *catabulum* [Note: [Col. 1481] *Catabulum*, that is, a stable for beasts of burden]. While he served there for many days, he did not cease serving the Lord in the *catabulum* with prayers and fasts. In the ninth month all his clergy came by night and purchased him [Note: [Col. 1481] C B, “by night”] out of the *catabulum*.

A certain matron named Lucina, who had lived with her husband Marcus for fifteen years and had been a widow for nineteen years, received the blessed Marcellus. She dedicated her house, under the title of the blessed Marcellus, where day and night they confessed the Lord Jesus Christ with hymns and prayers. When Maxentius heard this, he sent men and again seized the blessed Marcellus. He ordered boards [Note: [Col. 1481] “flat boards,” according to Festus] to be spread throughout the same church, so that the animals gathered from the *catabulum* might stand there and the blessed Marcellus might serve them. At length he died naked, clothed in a hair shirt, while serving the animals.

The blessed Lucina gathered his body and buried it in the cemetery of Priscilla on the Salarian Way, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of February. The episcopate was vacant for twenty days. [Note: [Col. 1481] Baronius, under A.D. 309.] Lucina, however, was condemned to confiscation of her property.

[Col. 1495]

## CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS

Marcellus: one year, six months, and twenty days. He lived in the time of Maxentius, from the consulship of Maximian Herculius X and Maximian Galerius VII until after their consulship X and VII.

## XXXII. SAINT EUSEBIUS. A.D. 309, THE FOURTH YEAR OF CONSTANTINE

Line 2.—In his time the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ was found [Col. 1495B] on the fifth day before the Nones of May, and Judas, also called Cyriacus, was baptized. Abbo of Fleury says, in his account of Eusebius, that the Cross was found by Judas, who was afterward baptized. The author of the second catalogue likewise indicates this, and Gregory of Tours recounts the story in Book I, chapter 34, where he is speaking of the time of Constantine: “In his time the venerable wood of the Lord’s Cross was found through the efforts of his mother Helena, Judas the Jew having revealed it; after his baptism he was called Quiriacus.” The author of the second catalogue agrees entirely with this, and Gregory of Tours perhaps took the account from it. Baronius and Onuphrius Panvinius, together with Pope Gelasius, however, deny the truth of this story; Gelasius calls it a novel revelation.]

Line 4.—“He found heretics in the city of Rome, whom he truly reconciled through the laying on of hands.” The reconciliation of public penitents and converted heretics belongs to the bishop and is performed through the laying on of hands: canon *In capite*, distinction 50; canon *Quamvis*, distinction 68; canon *Si iubet*, question 6, canon 26. Anastasius, in his account of Sylvester, says: “He decreed that a repentant Arian presbyter should not be received except by the bishop of the designated place.” The same was decreed by Siricius. Anastasius, in his own Life; Sigebert, under A.D. 387.]

[Note: [Col. 1496A]

Line 2.—“In his time the cross of the Lord was found.” This too must be judged an addition arising from the copyists’ carelessness, one that ought to be inserted among the deeds of Saint Sylvester. For Helena, the mother of Constantine, found it. To place this event at Jerusalem in this period was untimely, since Syria was being oppressed by the tyranny of Maximinus and shaken by the storm of persecution; moreover, Macarius, under whose episcopate the discovery is said to have occurred, was not yet bishop of Jerusalem, and Maximinus, raging against the Christians, could not willingly have permitted the solemn discovery of the Cross. These facts prove that, in the additions made to the *Liber Pontificalis* and inserted in their proper places, the book was subject to the carelessness or ignorance of certain copyists. Likewise, in the deeds of Marcellinus, certain Anastasius manuscripts contain words whose handwriting clearly belongs to an account of Sylvester, where the Council of Nicaea is discussed, as we shall explain in its proper place.]

[Note: [Col. 1496B]

Line 2.—“In his time the cross [Col. 1496C] of the Lord was found.” Since at this time neither Helena, the mother of Constantine, nor the emperor Constantine her son had yet embraced the Christian religion, and since, by the nearly unanimous agreement of the most ancient writers, the Lord’s Cross is said to have been found only after the Council of Nicaea had been celebrated, what this author of the *Liber Pontificalis* asserts—that the Lord’s Cross was found under Pope Eusebius—is very far from the truth. (Baronius, A.D. 311, no. 41.)]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

The Liberian catalogue assigns Eusebius a brief pontificate of four months and sixteen days. Since it distinctly records both termini—namely, from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May to the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September—it shows that its reading is not internally consistent. From 18 April to 17 August there are scarcely four complete months. The deposition of the same Callistus on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, on which he is commemorated, is clearly read with the other depositions of the Roman pontiffs in fourth-century manuscripts edited by Bucherius (see our Prolegomena). This does not conflict with the date of death given as 17 August in Book I, that is, in the Liberian catalogue reproduced from the same manuscripts.

If Marcellus’s successor had been elected four months and sixteen days after Marcellus—crowned with martyrdom on 16 January—then before 17 August the date of his election would have fallen on a Saturday, the first day of April in Holy Week, while the following Monday, 2 April, would have been Easter Sunday. It seems highly probable that, during the persecution of Maximian, continued in the city by Maxentius, the faithful took care that the Roman clergy should elect a pontiff on that day for the celebration of the Paschal mysteries.

Eusebius, who had already been ordained bishop two years earlier and had served in the name of a vicar as Marcellus’s deputy while Marcellus was detained in the *catabulum*, as I shall soon demonstrate, seemed the most suitable person immediately to occupy the apostolic see. That Eusebius had received episcopal ordination two years earlier is shown by the total of two years, two months, and twenty-five days assigned to him in the paintings of Saint Paul and in most of the catalogues listed in the Prolegomena, together with the consular era that I shall examine shortly.

His ordination is correctly placed on Sunday, Pentecost, 21 May—or, more precisely, on 23 May, during the Pentecost triduum—of the year 308. From that date, the two years, two months, and twenty-five days recorded in the Leonine paintings and catalogues correspond exactly [Col. 1497C] with the date of death established from the Liberian Catalogue, 17 August A.D. 310.

As for the consulships, in the Prolegomena, folio CII, column 2, the verses from the ninth to the twelfth before the end of the column, where it read:

| Consular pairs | Christian era |
|---|---:|
| From the second year after the consulships of Maximian VII and Diocletian X | 309 |
| to after the consulships of Diocletian X and Maximian VII, with Maxentius consul III | 310 |

should read:

| Consular pairs | Christian era |
|---|---:|
| From the consulships of Maximian VII and Diocletian X | 308 |
| to the second year after the consulships of Diocletian X and Maximian VII, that is, with Maxentius III alone | 310 |

For the last consulship of Eusebius’s life is known from the first one assigned to his immediate successor Melchiades. The Liberian Catalogue assigns Melchiades Maximian VIII alone; and the work on the City Prefects of the same fourth century, published with the others by Bucherius, explains that this is the year of the Christian era [Col. 1497D] 311, in which Maximian VIII alone is read as consul—though the month of September belongs to Rufinus and Eusebius, more correctly Rufius Volusianus and Eusebius.

If the consuls of the year 311 are first assigned to Melchiades, who celebrated his first Roman Easter under them, then the last consuls belonging to his predecessor Eusebius must be those immediately preceding them, namely, the consuls of A.D. 310. The year 310 is designated by this heading: “Again, after the consulship of Maximian X and Maximian VII”—in the provinces—or “with Maxentius III alone”—at Rome.

Outside Italy, throughout the Roman world, this year was preceded by two years in which Maximian the elder was consul for the tenth time and Maximian the younger for the seventh; within Italy, however, Maxentius and Romulus were consuls in A.D. 308. Therefore Eusebius’s episcopal ordination must be referred to Sunday, 23 May of that year, 308. It cannot have been an ordination to the Roman episcopate, since Marcellus was still alive in the *catabulum* and prolonged his life through a long martyrdom until 16 January A.D. 310, as was proved in his entry [Col. 1498A]. Eusebius was therefore ordained as a vicar, following the example of his predecessors, to carry out episcopal ministries in Marcellus’s place, until, after Marcellus had attained the crown of martyrdom, Eusebius was elected successor by the votes of the Roman clergy as the Paschal feast of A.D. 310 approached, on the first day of April.

Thus the Liberian catalogue correctly begins to count his defined tenure as four months and sixteen days, up to 17 August, the day of his death. The others, however, count Eusebius’s episcopal era from his ordination—namely, from Pentecost Sunday, 21 May A.D. 308, or from the completion of the Pentecost triduum, 23 May. From either date, the period counted to 17 August, the day of his death on earth and his birth into heaven, is exactly two years, two months, and twenty-five days.]

[Note: [Col. 1498A]

## HISTORICAL NOTES

Line 2.—“In his time the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ was found on the fifth day before the Nones of May.” This epitome, taken from the second catalogue, contains an anachronism that the Librarian copied in good faith and inserted under Eusebius, since the discovery of the Lord’s Cross occurred under Sylvester, as everyone, following Baronius, gathers from the testimonies of the ancient Fathers.

The author of the second catalogue, however, substituted the discovery of the Lord’s Cross for the appearance of its heavenly sign, which was shown to Constantine before he fought against Maxentius. This appearance would properly fit the pontificate of Eusebius if Pope Eusebius had survived until the beginning of Constantine’s reign and had spent six years in the pontificate, as that same author of the second catalogue assigns to him, contrary to the testimony of the others. The Librarian, nevertheless, did not think that author should be followed, counting only two years for Eusebius’s episcopate.

During that disturbance of the times—which, after Constantius’s death in 306, was produced over the following six years by so many Augusti at odds with one another, and by the different consuls designated in Italy and outside Italy, as I have shown in the chronological notes on Marcellus—it should not seem surprising that a sixth-century writer fell into a chronological error of one or another year when harmonizing with the consulships the date of the apparition of the Cross represented to Constantine. The reason is that this author extended Eusebius’s pontificate to six years.

We learn from another Eusebius, namely Eusebius of Caesarea, that Constantine first saw the vision in the year 311. For Constantine obtained victory in the year 312, on the sixth day before the Kalends of November, when Maxentius was drowned at the Milvian Bridge. Against Maxentius, historians report that Constantine had been conducting an annual military expedition for several engagements; see Pagi under A.D. 312, no. 4.

Constantine told Eusebius that he had seen that heavenly sign before undertaking the annual expedition against Maxentius. As soon as he resolved to invoke God’s aid, following his father’s example, in order to free the city from the tyrant’s oppression, he perceived that God’s aid was favorable to him. He then began his preparations for war by constructing the Labarum, into which he inserted the divine name of Christ and the sign of the Cross that had been shown to him, as we read in Eusebius, *Life of Constantine*, Book I, chapters 33 and following.

In the Latin Church, the memory of this apparition was recalled on the same day, 3 May, on which fell the feast of the discovery of the Lord’s Cross, found at Jerusalem by Helena Augusta much later—namely, after the celebration of the Council of Nicaea. In the lessons of the first Nocturn of this feast, as used in old books of the divine offices before Saint Pius V, that earlier apparition is narrated; the story of the Lord’s Cross, found by Blessed Helena, is reserved for the second Nocturn and is to be read from Saint Ambrose’s *On the Death of Theodosius*.

It is worth presenting those same lessons here as they are printed in the Roman Breviary from the press of Lucius Antonius Junta in the year 1562:

> “In the two hundred and thirty-sixth year from the destruction of the Temple and the overthrow of Jerusalem by Vespasian and his son Titus, while the most devout and serene Augustus Constantine was reigning, in the sixth year of his reign a great host of barbarians gathered for war against the Romans under the leadership of Maxentius. At that time Constantine had not yet received the sign of the Lord’s Cross. His heart, however, placed its confidence in the Lord. On that same night a radiant man appeared to him, saying: ‘Constantine, do not fear; but look up to heaven and see the sign of victory.’ Awakening from sleep, he saw in the eastern part of the sky the sign of the Cross shining with fiery brightness. Terrified by the sight, he saw angels standing beside him and saying: ‘Constantine, in this sign you will conquer,’” etc.

Florentinius notes in his ancient Martyrology that the Greeks refer this apparition to 18 August, the discovery of the Cross to 3 May, and its Exaltation to 14 September.

Since the offices of our Roman rite commemorated both stories on the feast of the discovery, the author of the second catalogue, under the date of the earlier event, confused it with the later one. Since he referred both to the beginning of Constantine’s expedition against Maxentius—which must be placed in the year 311, before the six-year period from the death of Constantine’s father Constantius had yet elapsed—he assigned the event to the time of Pope Eusebius, whom he believed to have spent six years in the pontificate under Constantine.

The Librarian, placing excessive confidence in this faulty assertion of the catalogue, transferred it into Eusebius’s life and retained the confusion between the history of the discovery of the Cross by Blessed Helena and the history of the first apparition, which he thought could be moved back to the two years preceding the victory over Maxentius reported by Constantine.]

[Note: [Col. 1499A]

Line 7.—“In the cemetery of Callistus, in the crypt on the Appian Way.” Ciaconius and Pancirolius testify that he still rests there in the treasures preserved in the sacred places of the Roman Church. They also observe that, of all the Roman pontiffs buried in that cemetery, only Eutychianus and Eusebius now remain there, while the others were transferred into the city lest their relics suffer injury from the barbarians.

Since, however, the title church of Saints Sylvester and Dionysius possesses portions of the relics of Saint Eusebius the pope, as is confirmed by records of that monastery’s archive signed on 30 October 1267, and since Pancirolus likewise mentions other portions, preserved in the title church of Saint Laurence in Formoso, or “in Panisperna,” it is clear that these venerable bones too, like those of the others, were preserved by his successors and carried into the city during the barbarian incursions. They were subsequently divided: some were granted to the urban churches mentioned above, while others were brought to Saint Sebastian outside the walls, just as we said concerning the relics of Blessed Fabian the pope in his notes.]

[Note: [Col. 1499C]

Line 2.—“In his time the cross [Col. 1500A] of our Lord Jesus Christ was found.” There is no way to explain how Christ’s Cross could have been found during Eusebius’s pontificate, since Constantine then possessed no authority in Syria, which was being oppressed by the extraordinary tyranny of Maximinus. Moreover, Rufinus, Book I, chapters 7 and 8; Theodoret, Book I, chapter 18; Sozomen, Book II, chapters 1 and 2; and Socrates, Book I, chapter 17, report that this happened approximately twenty years after the Council of Nicaea, which better accords with the facts.

Line 4.—“He found heretics in the city of Rome.” That is, Donatists, whom, as penitents, he reconciled to the Catholic Church solely through the laying on of hands.]

[Note: [Col. 1500A]

Line 2.—Saint Eusebius, a Greek by nationality and the son of a physician, obtained the pontificate on 5 February, which was a Sunday in the year 310, after the see had been vacant for twenty days, as the *Liber Pontificalis* and the ancient *Chronicle of the Popes* by Auctius report. These works nevertheless falsely say that the Lord’s Cross was found under Eusebius’s pontificate, since the ancient authors establish that the discovery of the Lord’s Cross did not occur before the time of the Council of Nicaea.

Concerning the discovery after that council, the following is read at the end of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, according to Pontacus’s edition: “Helena, the mother of Constantine, instructed by divine visions, found at Jerusalem the most blessed sign of the Cross, on which the salvation of the world hung.” Although these words are not found in most manuscript copies of Eusebius, they are nevertheless read in several others and in earlier editions. Indeed, this discovery is reported in almost the same words by Sulpicius Severus, Idacius, Ado, and others; by Rufinus, Book VI, chapter 8; by Ambrose, *On the Death of Theodosius*; by Sozomen, Book II, chapter 1; by Theodoret, Book I, chapter 18; and by many others cited by Arnoldus Pontacus in his notes on this passage of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*. In all these authors the discovery is referred to the time of the Council of Nicaea.

Moreover, it cannot reasonably be said that Helena, Constantine’s mother, found the Lord’s Cross at Jerusalem under Pope Eusebius, since Constantine then possessed no authority in Syria, which was under the tyranny of Maximinus. Nor did Constantine yet fully believe in Christ; he did so with the greatest fervor only after the vision of the Cross in heaven, which occurred in the year 312. At this time, therefore, he had not yet embraced the Christian religion, nor had his mother Helena.

Finally, under Eusebius’s pontificate Macarius was not yet bishop of Jerusalem. He assumed responsibility for that Church only in the year 312, yet the discovery of the holy Cross is supposed to have taken place under him.]

[Col. 1495]

32. Eusebius, a Greek by nationality, son of a physician, held the see for two years, one month, and twenty-five days [Note: [Col. 1495] B, seven months and sixteen days]. He lived in the time of Constantine [Note: from the consulships of Maxentius IV and Maximus to those of Galerius Maximianus VIII and Licinius] [Note: [Col. 1495] B denies this]. In his time the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ was found on the fifth day before the Nones of May, and Judas, also called Cyriacus, was baptized. He [Note: [Col. 1495] B C, “the discoverer of the Cross”] found heretics in the city of Rome, whom he truly reconciled through the laying on of hands. He held one ordination in the month of December: thirteen presbyters, three deacons, and fourteen bishops for various places. He was also buried in the cemetery of Callistus, in the crypt on the Appian Way, on the sixth day before the Nones of October [Note: [Col. 1495] B, the fourth day before the Nones or the fourth day before the Kalends], and the episcopate was vacant for seven days.

[Col. 1495] ## CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS

Eusebius: four months and sixteen days, from the fourteenth day before the Kalends of May until the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September.

## XXXIII. SAINT MELCHIADES. A.D. 311, THE SIXTH YEAR OF CONSTANTINE
