[Note: [Col. 1501B]

Line 6.—“Consecrated . . . which is called *fermentum*.” Because of the discipline of secrecy, the Eucharist is called *fermentum* in this passage, as we demonstrated in the dissertation published on the subject. For the pontiffs were accustomed to send the Eucharist to bishops and presbyters coming to the city, as Saint Irenaeus testifies in Eusebius, Book V, chapter 24.]

[Note: [Col. 1501B]

Line 6.—“He caused consecrated offerings to be sent through the churches from the consecration of the bishop, which is called *fermentum*.” Melchiades decreed that *fermentum*, that is, blessed leavened bread sent by the bishop in place of a *eulogia*, should be sent through the churches as a symbol of communion. On this subject see Anastasius below, in his account of Siricius.]

[Note: [Col. 1501B]

Line 6.—“He caused consecrated offerings to be sent through [Col. 1501C] the churches.” Such a solemn consecration throughout the churches of the city, and the still more solemn sending of the Eucharist, while the ninth year of the persecution was still in progress and the churches were assigned to the treasury under the earlier edicts, did not seem consistent with the circumstances of the times and the events recounted.

The narrative of the *Liber Pontificalis*, however, agrees perfectly with the special indulgence that Maxentius extended at Rome, as also in Africa, to Christians—more truly, out of fear—following Constantine’s example. When Constantine assumed power in the year 307, “he did nothing before restoring the Christians to the worship and service of their God. This was the first enactment establishing the holy religion” (the same work, chapter 34, from Lactantius).

Christian soldiers stripped of their military belts by Diocletian’s edict had filled Constantine’s army in great numbers. Seeing the walls of Rome filled with Christians, Maxentius, concealing his cruelty, according to Eusebius, lest they defect to Constantine, decreed by public edict that the churches in Rome should be restored to the Christians.

That all ecclesiastical properties were restored to the Roman clergy, and that Melchiades selected deacons to recover them, is shown by the acts reproduced in the famous Carthaginian conference, chapters 12 and 13, and by Saint Augustine in the book written after the conference. In that work he refutes the accusations that the Donatists brought against Melchiades. One of them was that, among the other deacons, he selected Strato, who was accused of betrayal, to recover those places:

> “They also recited other proceedings in which Melchiades was said to have sent deacons with letters from the emperor Maxentius and the praetorian prefect to the praetor of the City, so that he might recover the places that had been taken from the Christians during the persecution. Since no crime of Melchiades appeared there at all, they added to the earlier proceedings concerning the betrayal that the traitor Strato had been named.””

In the brief record of the same conference those places are called sacred and ecclesiastical. Thus it says:

> “When, even in these proceedings, no crime of Melchiades appeared either to the judge or to the Catholic advocates, the Donatists said that Strato the deacon, whom Melchiades had sent with others to recover the ecclesiastical properties, had been named in the earlier proceedings as a traitor. They therefore wished to stain Melchiades also with the crime of delivery, because he employed that deacon without degrading him. They further said that, during their persecution, Melchiades was the third bishop after the one who held office when the delivery occurred.”

When he reports the Catholics’ reply, he likewise recalls that the ecclesiastical properties had been restored and recovered by Melchiades, saying:

> “Even if it should be proved—which will certainly not be proved—that the same deacon Strato had committed betrayal and was afterward sent by Melchiades with other deacons to recover the ecclesiastical places,” Melchiades would not thereby immediately be stained with this crime. The persecution might have kept him far away, so that he knew nothing whatever of the matter, and he might have regarded as innocent a man whom no one had demonstrated to be guilty by accusing him.”

The restoration of the basilicas was therefore made public by Maxentius before the year 311. In the following year Constantine defeated the tyrant, thereby giving Melchiades an opportunity to restore the basilicas to their former use, especially for the celebration of Masses and the transportation of the Eucharist through the churches.

For this reason the *Liber Pontificalis* deliberately says *he caused* this to be done, rather than using the word *he decreed*, indicating that the practice introduced was not new but a restoration of an earlier custom.

That Maxentius adapted himself to the circumstances and ceased the persecution because of fear, not from conviction, is suggested by the other indulgence proclaimed to the African churches. When he heard that Alexander the Tyrant was plotting new schemes in Africa and seizing power against Maxentius, he immediately sent peace to the churches of Africa, moderated the storm of persecution, and ordered that Christians be granted liberty. Optatus, Book I, says of this:

> “The storm of persecution was brought to an end and concluded. By God’s command, when Maxentius sent an indulgence, liberty was restored to the Christians.”

He goes on to report that the sacred places were also restored.]

[Note: [Col. 1502D]

Line 7.—“Which is called *fermentum*.” This expression strengthens the conjectures of Schelestratius, who proves in his book *On the Discipline of Secrecy* that the Eucharist was called by the title *fermentum*, not to indicate its material—as though it were leavened rather than unleavened bread—but to explain the Eucharistic bread.

The preceding sequence of words concerns the consecration of the Eucharistic bread, as is evident in itself. The *Liber Pontificalis*, in order to indicate what was consecrated by the bishop, adds, “which is called *fermentum*,” as though it were saying: Because solemn celebrations could not be conducted in the private oratories during the persecution, Melchiades, after Maxentius’s edict restored the churches, renewed the original institution by which the Eucharist was consecrated by the bishop in the presence of the presbyters. The consecrated bread given to them, called *fermentum* among the faithful, signified the Eucharist, so that, when they carried it to the churches, they might distribute it to the people.]

[Note: [Col. 1503B]

Line 6.—“He caused consecrated offerings to be sent through the churches from the consecration of the bishop, which is called *fermentum*.” The passage is certainly obscure, but it should be explained as follows: Pope Melchiades instituted that leavened bread, offered by the people or by presbyters and consecrated by bishops, should be received by the presbyters of the individual titular churches or parishes as a symbol of Catholic unity and communion—not merely by the presbyters themselves, but also, at a fixed time, distributed to the other faithful under their care who had not communicated in the most sacred Eucharist.

(FROM LABBÉ.) Line 7.—“Which is explained as *fermentum*.” The passage appears to be corrupt.]

[Note: [Col. 1503C]

## CHRONOLOGICAL NOTES

Melchiades’s era, defined as three years, seven months, and seven days, is confirmed by the paintings preserved intact in the basilica of Saint Paul. These agree exactly with most of the catalogues listed above in the Prolegomena. It is also confirmed by the consuls correctly assigned in the Liberian catalogue, and by those that must be restored in the second catalogue and in Anastasius’s text, where the carelessness and incompetence of copyists expressed and deformed the consuls of those years, which had naturally become confused.

The relevant date is from Maximian VII alone, which was in the month of September under Rufius Volusianus—for that is how that Italian consul must be named, not Rufinus Volusianus, as I noted above and shall demonstrate in the chronological notes on Sylvester—[Col. 1503D] namely, from the year of Christ 311, when Melchiades first celebrated Easter after the death of his predecessor Eusebius on 17 August 310, until the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus in the year 314, on 10 January, the day of Melchiades’s death.

This is likewise declared in the catalogues of Liberius and Felix IV, and on an eighth-century stone set in the portico of the title church of Saint Sylvester in Capite. After the words:

> “In the name of the Lord, this is the record of the birthdays of the saints resting here,”

the second verse for the month of January reads:

> “On the tenth day of that month: the birth of Saint Meltiades, pope and martyr.”

If, therefore, we move backward from 10 January of the year 314, under the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus, by the three years, seven months, and seven days of the era recorded in the paintings of the Pauline basilica from the age of Leo the Great, we arrive at the date of his ordination to the episcopate, 4 June of the year 310, which was a Sunday.

The catalogues of Liberius and Felix IV, apart from the same three years, count six months and thirteen days, since they derive the era from the sixth day before the Nones of July, which was likewise a Sunday suitable for an ordination, no less than 4 June, as the calculations derived from the Pauline paintings indicate.

For the Liberian catalogue reads:

> “Meltiades: three years, six months, and eight days, from the sixth day before the Nones of July, from the consulship of Maximian VII alone—which was in September under Volusianus and Rufinus—until the third day before the Ides of January, under the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus.”

Whether, therefore, Melchiades was ordained bishop on 4 June 310 and completed three years, seven months, and seven days, or received ordination on 2 July of the same year and his episcopate is counted as three years, six months, and eight days, the endpoint of his life falls equally on 10 January 314.

It will also be clear that he served as vicar from the day of his ordination until Eusebius’s death, which occurred in the same year, 310, under Maxentius, on 18 August. He was elected successor several days after Eusebius’s martyrdom, both according to the era of the Liberian catalogue and according to the epoch of the paintings in the basilica of Saint Paul; the two dates are separated by only four weeks.

In the year 312, when Constantine Augustus II and Licinius Augustus II were consuls, before Maxentius was defeated by Constantine in October and thrown into the Tiber, Melchiades ordained Sylvester. Maxentius was then harassing the Christians with savage persecution, indeed surrendering the city to as many tyrants as there were soldiers, as Cardinal Baronius proves under A.D. 312, numbers 8 and 9. Melchiades appointed Sylvester his necessary assistant and vicar amid so severe a persecution on Sunday, 10 February, as I shall explain in the following entry.

Melchiades therefore served as Eusebius’s vicar from 4 June, or 2 July, of the year 310 until approximately the end of August of that same year. He was then elected successor and served as Roman pontiff until 10 January 314.]

[Note: [Col. 1504B]

## HISTORICAL NOTES

[Col. 1504C] Line 3.—“He decreed that no faithful person should fast under any circumstances on Sunday or on Thursday, because, etc.” The interpreters of the papal lives ask, and still consider it insufficiently explained, what the pagan fasts on Sunday and Thursday were that Melchiades is said here to have forbidden Christians, lest our chaste fasts, instituted by Christ the Lord and the apostles as a sign of true religion, be confused with those superstitious fasts impiously devoted to the worship of demons.

They have clearly demonstrated that, against the calumnies of the sectarians of our own age, there is a great difference between the superstitious fasts devised and prescribed by Montanus and his Paraclete, and our own legitimate fasts, introduced and practiced both in Lent and throughout the year, especially by those who, according to the approved rules of the Fathers, profess the holiness of a penitential life. On this subject see Baronius under A.D. 173, no. 28.]

Yet a clearer explanation is still needed to illuminate Melchiades’ precaution and decree: he feared that our fasts might be thought to have proceeded from pagan rites if they were celebrated on Sunday or Thursday. The matter, unless I am mistaken, is explained by the words that immediately follow, namely: “And Manichaeans were found in the City by the same man.” Cardinal Baronius, under the year 372, observes from St Jerome’s Letter 22 that at Rome the superstitious fast of the Manichaean sect of Manes was turned into a reproach against Christian fasters: “so that anyone whom they saw pale and sorrowful they called wretched and a Manichaean.” He had already stated there that the Manichaeans had also been proscribed by Diocletian’s law long before this slander was directed against the faithful living at Rome—that is, while Melchiades was alive, though he had not yet been advanced to Peter’s chair. Thus Manichaeans were already in the City at that time, and Melchiades rightly took precautions lest our lawful and holy fasts provide an opportunity for the slander of those who would interpret them contrary to the institution and practice of our people, as though they had been borrowed from the superstitious abstinence of the Manichaeans.

[Col. 1505A] But the earlier question again presses upon us and demands that we explain what the abstinence of the Manichaeans had in common with the superstitious fasts of the pagans, so that Melchiades, as though foreseeing the future slander, had to take precautions by a decree excluding Sunday and Thursday from the solemn fast of Catholics, lest they be thought to fast according to Manichaean institutions.

A discussion of Archelaus the bishop against Manes, the founder of that sect, opportunely supplies the reason for the precaution then necessary. It had recently been printed in a collection of monuments of the Greek and Latin Church, issued for the first time with learned observations by Laurentius Zaccagnius, “who deservedly earned the prefecture of the Vatican Library through his learning and comprehensive expertise in ecclesiastical scholarship.” The distinguished writer of our own age, Philippus a Turre, bishop of Adria—himself also to be numbered among the foremost and most learned prelates of our century—applies this eulogy to that eminent man.

In his *Dissertation on Mithras*, chapter 5, page 207, he concluded from the account of Archelaus’ disputation against Manes that this Persian, Manes by name, from Corbicio, having become devoted to that barbarous philosophy which flourished among his countrymen, had learned the errors of Zoroaster and the Magi: namely, the worship of the sun, the rebirth of souls, the two principles of the world, the good and evil spirit, and other such monstrous errors. He undertook to wrap these together and mingle them with distorted rites and teachings carefully gathered from Christian books, so that he might construct new heresies out of earlier ones.

Above all, he was tenacious of his ancestral superstition and professed the worship of fire and the sun; he also wished to be initiated into the sacred rites of Mithras. Accordingly Bishop Archelaus addresses him as follows:

> “Barbarian priest of Mithras and fellow-player, you worship only the Sun, Mithras, the illuminator and confidant of the mystical places, as you suppose; that is what you play among them (as Zaccagnius renders it), or ‘player’ (as the Bishop of Adria thinks it should be read)—and, like an accomplished mime, you perform the mysteries.”

[Col. 1505C] The aforesaid Bishop of Adria then adds:

> “Thus for Archelaus, Manes is a mime and player who, under the forms of wild beasts and in the manner of an actor, performed the mysteries of Mithras; hence he was also called his fellow-player. Since the subject is Manes, I shall add a conjecture. Plutarch, in *On Isis and Osiris*, p. 369, relates that the Persian Magi, following the doctrine of Zoroaster, established two gods opposed to one another, Oromazes and Arimanius, one of whom bestowed evil things and the other good things; and that between them Mithras was worshipped as an intermediary, which is why they called him μεσέτην (*mesetēn*), that is, mediator or intermediary. Did not the wicked doctrine of Manes concerning two principles, one good and the other evil, flow from the priests of Mithras—a doctrine first taught by Scythianus and then by Terebinthus, from whose books Manes himself drew it? Certainly Mithra, that mediator-god, is the same as the wall which Manes presented as an intermediary between good and evil; concerning this, see Archelaus’ aforementioned disputation, p. 39. Moreover, Epiphanius, *Heresy* 68, on the Manichaeans, no. 3, reports that Terebinthus, or Buddha, had spoken with the attendants and priests of Mithras about two principles.”

The learned prelate adds a description of the rite by which the priests of Mithras put on the figures of animals. They were purified by a superstitious washing, in order to suggest to their spectators the transmigration of souls, together with the errors of both heretics and pagans, which were transmitted to the followers of Manes through the worshippers of Mithras and the Sun, and mingled by sacrilegious imitation with Christian rites. For he writes as follows:

> “But I return to the initiations of Mithras, which were completed by an impious rite of mysteries. For, in imitation of the sacraments of the holy Christian religion, they were trained to receive the sacred things by initiatory rites arranged in stages according to a profane form of augury. Nor would I dare describe them otherwise than in the very words of Tertullian, *Against the Prescription of Heretics*, chapter 40: ‘The devil himself also baptizes certain persons—of course those who believe and are his faithful—and promises the cleansing of sins through the washing’”—

> “(He also recalls, in the book *On Baptism*, chapter 5, that initiates were admitted through a washing.) ‘And, if I still remember correctly, Mithras marks his soldiers on their foreheads there, celebrates the offering of bread, presents an image of resurrection, and, under the sword, crowns them with a wreath.’”

To give the image of the Eucharist a more vivid resemblance, bread and a cup of water were placed before them, with certain words added, as Justin Martyr reports, *Apology* 2, p. 98, Paris edition of 1615, by G. L.

Leaving aside, however, those matters that concern the sacrilegious imitation of the sacraments, we must hasten to the practices by which the worshippers of Mithras—and among them the Manichaeans, together with the founder of their own sect, who had been initiated into the sacred rites of Mithras and was its idol-priest and temple-attendant (*aedituus*; printed “eudio”)“—acted in such a way that Melchiades had to take precautions by decree, lest our fasts appear to agree with their abstinences.

St Gregory Nazianzen, *Oration* 3 against Julian, p. 77, volume I, Paris edition of 1630, asserts:

> “Tortures, and appropriate or even mystical burnings, were employed in the rites of Mithras.”

The Bishop of Adria confirms this on page 211 from Suidas and Porphyry, but illustrates it more clearly from Nonnus and from Bishop Nicetas:

> “Nonnus—not Elias of Crete, as Barthius incorrectly cites him in his note on the passage of Statius at the end of Book I of the *Thebaid*, ‘O guest mindful of hospitality’—enumerates eighty stages of torment by which those who were initiated into the sacred rites of Mithras had to be tested. Bishop Nicetas, cited by the same Nazianzen, gives a more explicit account in these words: ‘At the very beginning of the probation they torment them for fifty whole days; then they beat them with scourges for two days; thereafter they immerse them in snow for twenty days.’”

But in the Greek codex of the Laurentian Library, written seven hundred years ago and translated into Latin by the distinguished V. C. Montfaucon, the eighty stages are presented to us as follows, on page 212:

> “There are certain initiations into the mysteries of Mithras, especially among the Chaldaeans. Those who were initiated into the mysteries of Mithras were accustomed to be tested by certain tortures, as though by stages: first they were subjected to a milder kind of punishment, and afterward to a harsher one. For example, at first they afflicted the initiates with hunger for fifty days; and if they endured this steadfastly, they ordered them to be beaten for two days, and thereafter subjected each of them to the same kind of punishment for twenty-eight days; and in this manner, if those who were initiated endured all the tortures and bore them patiently, only then were they taught the more advanced mysteries.”

> “If you add up the number of the tests—namely, fifty days of hunger, two of scourging, and the repetition of the same kind of punishment for another twenty-eight days—you will discover Nonnus’ eighty stages,” and so forth.

The aforementioned prelate concludes these observations by remarking:

> “Mithras, or the Sun, is the ruler of earthly fire, which he preserves and nourishes, as the ancients, especially the Persians, believed. It is therefore not surprising that they transferred the worship of that same fire to its ruler and preserver, namely the Sun or Mithras.”

He also observes from Augustine that the Manichaeans were accustomed to profane all the Christian sacraments through their superstitious mysteries, and that from their leader Manes, who had been initiated into the sacred rites of Mithras, they had also derived this blasphemy: that they thought Christ the Lord was the Sun, or Mithras.

> “Indeed,” he says on page 211, “the Manichaeans, whose wicked leader we have seen to be devoted to Mithras, thought that the Sun, who is Mithras, was Christ himself, as Augustine testifies in his *Tractate on John*, chapter 8, tractate 34, p. 534.”

[Col. 1506D] These passages had to be transcribed in full so that we might understand how prudently Melchiades had to take precautions through his decrees lest the discipline of Christian fasting degenerate, or be thought to have arisen from and incline toward the superstitious fasts of the Mithraists. Among whom Manes had been enrolled, he had handed down errors and superstitions to his Manichaean followers, who by his example had been made, from players and mimes of Mithras, players and mimes of Christ’s sacraments, confusing Christ with the Sun and Mithras.

[Col. 1507A] It is also clear why, at this time close to Manes—who had lived under Probus and Aurelian during Melchiades’ lifetime, although before Melchiades became pontiff—the Manichaean heresy, creeping like a cancer, had to be driven out at the beginning of Melchiades’ pontificate once it had been detected. His pontifical law confirmed the ancient discipline: solemn fasts were not to be performed on Sundays, even during the seven weeks of Lent, which Telesphorus had reduced from tradition to written law; nor was Thursday to be included in the fasts prescribed outside Lent, in the four seasons of the year, for those being initiated, as we read above in the notice concerning Callistus.

For the first fifty stages of the Mithraic probation consisted of an equal number of days of continuous abstinence during seven weeks. “For fifty whole days they torment them with hunger,” says Nicetas in the passage cited by Nazianzen. The seven weeks of our fast, handed down by the apostles after the Lord’s example and firmly established by Telesphorus in written law, could have appeared to be those first fifty stages of the Mithraic probation, especially if that institution, having been adopted from Manes, a worshipper of the Sun, were also practiced by the Manichaeans, who impiously worshipped the Sun, confused with Christ the Lord.

[Col. 1507B] What more immediate remedy could Melchiades oppose to this danger of wicked persuasion and confusion than one he applied as soon as he discovered Manichaeans in the City? He judged that a decree of the ancient apostolic discipline had to be set against it, separating the chaste rite and its purpose from the superstitious inventions of the Mithraists and Manichaeans.

“Let the seven weeks of our fast,” he says, “never be thought to be seven weeks corresponding to the fifty days of probation devised or deformed by the Mithraists.” For the days of fasting properly dedicated to God by Christian pontiffs under the examples of the Lord and the prophets are forty. The seven Sundays beginning each week are not counted with them. Since they preserve the memory of Christ’s Resurrection in every weekly cycle, it is wrong to assign them to a fast commemorating the Passion.

Similarly, the other solemn fast handed down by the Fathers and committed to writing by Callistus for each of the four seasons of the year, so that each season might separately be consecrated to the giver of all good things, is contained in Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. These days are specifically assigned to the Lord’s Passion because its decision to hand him over occurred on Wednesday, his death on Friday, and his burial on Saturday. Thursday, however, is not included in these established fasts according to ancestral custom; for the evening of that day, when the Passion began in the garden, is referred according to ancestral practice and divine law to the Friday that follows.

“Let us therefore,” says Melchiades, “avoid even in these matters novelty and confusion with profane worship, or the occasion of a false persuasion that might easily arise among the pagans from the continuous three-day sequence of fasting and vigils celebrated in their secular sacred observances—that is, in their superstitions—and adapted to the fables of their empty gods.

“Let that unbroken pattern of fasting be maintained on the weekdays assigned to us by the Fathers. By these it may be clearly demonstrated that the institutions of our custom have nothing in common with the worship of the Sun and Mithras, or with the Manichaeans’ Christ confused with the Sun. In the form of our fast, we worship only God, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, creator with the Father and the Spirit of the Sun, heaven, earth, all things, and the seasons. We profess that this Christ, having suffered in the flesh for us, displayed these fasts beforehand by his example and dedicated them by the merit of his Passion.”

[Col. 1507D] Thus the danger of confusing the Christian Catholic and true doctrine with the perversion of the Manichaeans and pagans having been removed, Melchiades prudently preserved the chaste discipline of fasting as he had received it from his predecessors, and recorded in it an open profession of our faith, so that it would always be recognized as diametrically opposed to pagan superstitions and to the deceitful transformation of the corrupted faith of the Manichaeans.

Therefore the Librarian rightly numbered among the decrees of the Roman pontiffs this solemn declaration concerning the fasts enjoined upon all Christians. For private abstinences—undertaken by individual believers at their discretion and according to their needs solely for the sake of penance, not of mystery—are governed by another rule.

This applies either when Eleutherius opposed the heresies of Basilides and Carpocrates, who established two principles of things, good and evil, and counted them among the gods, while also inventing the transmigration of souls, and therefore superstitiously abstained from certain foods and living creatures, which they referred through those doctrines to the Creator of evil, or to the evil principle; he then promulgated a law permitting every edible thing to be used indiscriminately in common, as we read above in number 14.

Or it applies when Melchiades decreed that the solemn fasts of the Church should not be deformed or altered from the ancient institution: Sunday was excluded from that number even during Lent, and Thursday was removed, during the four seasons of the year, from the three-day fast always to be offered to God. This was done just as public prayers are dedicated to God by lawful pontiffs, through the faith exercised in memory of the Passion and Resurrection of Christ the Lord.

[Col. 1508B] If this prudent care of Melchiades had not preceded, what confusion do we think would have arisen from the imagined agreement of Catholics with the divergent worship of the Manichaeans and Mithraists? The mere similarity of the time assigned to fasting—seven weeks among Catholics, while the Mithraists prescribed fifty days of hunger to worshippers of the Sun—would gradually, by Jerome’s time, scarcely a full century removed from Melchiades, have encouraged the practice of counting among the Manichaeans, worshippers of the Sun and Mithras, all those whom they saw pale and emaciated from fasting, together with their leader who wickedly attached the name of Christ to the same Sun.

The reason for the decree enacted under Melchiades and the cause for inserting it immediately after the Manichaean sect was discovered in the City are therefore evident. Hence, in the Librarian’s text, the passage concerning the Mithraists is contained in one and the same period, introduced by the causal particle *because*, where we read:

> “He established that no believer should in any way fast on Sunday or on Thursday, because the pagans celebrated these days as a sacred fast.”

The other cause, referring to the Manichaeans, who had learned their superstitions from the pagan Mithraists, is then given immediately after the comma, perhaps without being separated from the same period, in the words that follow, thus conceived:

> “And Manichaeans were found in the city of Rome by the same man.”

[Note: [Col. 1508C]

Line 6.—“He caused consecrated offerings to be sent through the churches from the bishop’s consecration,” which is explained by *fermentum*. During his pontificate Miltiades discovered that many heretical Donatists were hiding in Rome. Therefore, so that they might be recognized and distinguished from Catholics, and the diseased flock from the healthy, he instituted blessed leavened bread, which, as a symbol of communion, was distributed by the bishop to all the parish priests; they in turn distributed it on appointed days to the faithful assigned to them.

It was called *fermentum* to distinguish it from unleavened bread, from which the Eucharist was customarily made. It was called a sacrament because it had been sanctified by episcopal blessing. This rite remains inviolate among the Greeks.]

[Note: [Col. 1508D]

The schism of the Donatists, whose beginning almost everyone, together with Baronius, dates to the year 306, in fact began only in the year 312, after peace had been restored to the African Church by Maxentius:

> “The storm of persecution,” says Optatus, Book I against Parmenianus, “has been completed and brought to an end. At God’s command, when Maxentius granted pardon, freedom was restored to the Christians. Botrus and Celeusius, as is said, wishing to have themselves ordained at Carthage, arranged that, in the absence of the Numidians, only the neighboring bishops should be summoned to celebrate the ordination at Carthage. Then, by the vote of the entire people, Caecilianus was elected, and, when Bishop Felix of Aptunga laid hands upon him, he was ordained,” and so forth.

The persecution in Africa, however, ended only in the year 312, as Baronius’ Annotator proves. When Botrus and Celeusius saw that they had been disappointed in their hope, they began to conspire against Caecilianus, who had been ordained bishop of Carthage. They enlisted Lucilla, a woman of great power who was hostile to Caecilianus, as well as the elders of the Catholic people, to whom Mensurius, Caecilianus’ predecessor, had entrusted the Church’s ornaments. They also arranged for the bishops of Numidia—who considered it a considerable injury that they had not been summoned to Caecilianus’ ordination—to come together at Carthage.

Seventy of them assembled. Since Caecilianus, though summoned, had refused to come, they condemned him in his absence, bringing two charges against him. First, that he had been ordained by traditors; and second, that while he was a deacon he had forbidden food to be brought to martyrs held in custody. After this they ordained Majorinus as bishop in Caecilianus’ place, for the favor of Lucilla, in whose household he was employed.

This was the beginning of the schism of the Donatists, so called from Donatus, bishop of Casis Nigris, the ordainer of Majorinus. Augustine writes in his *Brief Account of the Third Conference* and in the *Book of Reconsiderations* that Donatus had created the schism at Carthage while Caecilianus was still a deacon, and that he was afterward convicted of that crime in the Roman synod held under Melchiades. But because the schism burst forth more violently at Caecilianus’ ordination, its beginning is taken from that ordination.

The schismatics wrote pamphlets against Caecilianus and appealed to Anulinus, proconsul of Africa, asking him to send them to Constantine, who was then residing in Gaul, and requesting that he order judges to be appointed from Gaul. After reading the Donatists’ pamphlets, the emperor replied somewhat angrily, as Optatus of Milevis reports:

> “You ask me for judgment in this world, when I myself await the judgment of Christ.”

Nevertheless, he appointed as judges Maternus of Agrippina, [Col. 1509C] Rheticus of Augustodunum, and Marinus of Arles, bishops who, together with Pope Melchiades and other Italian bishops whom he himself was to select, would judge Caecilianus’ case.

A synod was assembled at Rome on 2 October, a Friday, and therefore in the year of Christ 313, in the house of Fausta in the Lateran. Melchiades presided; the three bishops named above and fifteen Italians sat with him.

Sentence was passed against Donatus of Casis Nigris with the unanimous support of all:

> “Because he confessed that he had rebaptized and laid hands upon bishops who had fallen, which is foreign to the Church. The witnesses brought forward by Donatus confessed that they had nothing to say against Caecilianus. Caecilianus was pronounced innocent by the judgment of all those mentioned above, including the judgment of Miltiades, by which the case was closed in these words: ‘Since it has been established that Caecilianus has not been accused, according to his own profession, by those who came with Donatus, and since it has not been established that he was convicted by Donatus on any point, I rightly judge that he must be retained in his ecclesiastical communion with his status unimpaired.’”

These matters are reported by Optatus of Milevis, Book I against Parmenianus. He omitted the other part of the sentence, namely, the condemnation of Donatus and the reception of the bishops belonging to Majorinus’ party.

The presbyter Marcus, later Roman pontiff after the death of St Sylvester, attended this synod, as may be seen in Valesius’ notes on Book X, chapter 8, of Eusebius, and in Baronius’ *Critical Notes* under the year 313.

It is said that the Donatists, after being condemned, appealed from the sentence of the council’s bishops to the emperor, and that Constantine, when he heard of it, said:

> “O rabid audacity of madness! They have lodged an appeal, as is customary in cases involving pagans.”

Scholars dispute whether this appeal to the emperor was made at this Roman council or at the Council of Arles under Sylvester.

Moreover, Donatus of Casis Nigris confessed that he had rebaptized and laid hands upon bishops who had fallen because the schism of the Donatists had developed into a heresy whose principal errors were these.

First, they contended that baptism conferred outside the Church was invalid. Since they confined the Church within their own sect, they therefore rebaptized Catholics whom they had deceived and entangled in their schism.

Second, they asserted that the Church in the other regions of the world had perished through the contagion of traditors and communion with wicked men, and that it had remained in Africa only in the party of Donatus. For this reason they laid hands anew upon bishops who had fallen.

Third, they called the Catholic Church a prostitute, as St Augustine reports in his *Sermon on the Proceedings with Emeritus*. Whoever desires more information about the schism of the Donatists should read the dissertation on it published by Henri Valesius and appended to his edition of Eusebius.]

[Note: [Col. 1510A]

Line 2.—“From the consulship of Maxentius IX.” When persecution in Africa had ended around the year 311, the bishops of the province of Carthage were free to assemble in that metropolis to elect a successor to Bishop Mensurius.

Some part of the history of the African Church is inserted here because it is connected with the history of the Roman See. Caecilianus, therefore, a deacon of the Church of Carthage, was canonically elected and consecrated bishop by the votes of the clergy, with the consent of the whole people.

Against this man, lawfully elected and duly consecrated, a faction of seditious men, led partly by ambition and partly by greed, rose up so boldly that it refused to acknowledge him as bishop. They summoned to Carthage several bishops of Numidia and the neighboring regions—seventy in number—who were resentful that they had not been called to the election.

These men, gathered as though for a council, declared Caecilianus’ ordination invalid when he refused to appear before their assembly, and substituted Majorinus in his place. They subsequently sent letters to all the African Churches, urging them to withdraw from communion with Caecilianus and defect to Majorinus, whom they had promoted. Such was the origin of the Donatist schism.

But two great bishops of the African Church, namely Optatus of Milevis and Augustine, who wrote a full century after that sedition—which had not yet been completely quieted but continued into their own age—testify that this was constantly the sign and identifying mark by which the schismatics and heretics were always detected: namely, that they had withdrawn and separated themselves from union with the Roman Church.

> “Seek the origin of these events, and you will find that I have pronounced this judgment against you when you joined heretics with schismatics. For Caecilianus did not go out from Majorinus, his grandfather, but Majorinus from Caecilianus. Nor did Caecilianus withdraw from the chair of Peter or of Cyprian, but Majorinus did—the chair in which you sit, which had no origin before that Majorinus.”  
> *(Optatus of Milevis, against Parmenianus, Book I.)*

[Col. 1510D]

> “Caecilianus could have disregarded the multitude of conspirators and enemies, since he saw that he was joined by letters of communion both to the Roman Church—in which the primacy of the Apostolic Chair has always flourished—and to all the lands from which the Gospel came to Africa itself. He would have been ready to plead his case if his adversaries attempted to estrange those Churches from him.”  
> *(St Augustine, Letter 162.)*

This matter was in fact referred to Pope Melchiades, the successor of Eusebius, after that change in affairs which, for the good of religion, God had happily brought about through Constantine’s accession to imperial power.

For this prince, strengthened by the victory divinely granted to him under the sign of the life-giving cross, seen by himself and by the entire army in the heavens, and confirmed in the disposition of mind he had toward Christians, immediately began to declare it through edicts granting the free exercise of our religion and the restoration of all property to those who professed it.

Afterward he interposed the authority of his imperial dignity to settle the Church’s internal disturbances, professing himself the protector of the same holy laws.

When he was therefore informed of the seditious movements raised in Africa by the Donatists, he ordered the magistrates whom he had appointed in that province to suppress them. In letters to Caecilianus, the legitimate bishop of the Church of Carthage, he informed him that his ministers would not fail to assist him whenever he requested their help.

Since he was certain that the schismatics would ask that their case against Caecilianus be decided by judges from overseas, the emperor, not daring to judge the bishop’s case himself—as St Augustine observes in Letter 166—delegated it to the bishops for examination and resolution. He wrote to Pope Melchiades concerning it as follows:

> “Constantine Augustus sends greetings to Miltiades, bishop of Rome, and to Marcus. Since several letters of this kind have been sent to me by Anulinus, the distinguished proconsul of Africa, in which it is evident that Caecilianus, bishop of the city of Carthage, is accused on many counts by certain fellow bishops of his who were ordained in Africa, it troubles me that in these provinces, which divine providence has of its own accord and freely subjected to my rule, and in those places where crowds of people constantly gather, not only should the multitude turn toward worse things and be divided by dissensions, but the bishops themselves should also exercise discord among themselves.

> “It has seemed good to me that Caecilianus should cross by ship to Rome with ten bishops who appear to accuse him and ten others whom he himself considers necessary for the adjudication of his case, so that he may be heard before you, and also before your colleagues Reticius, Maternus, and Marinus, whom I have ordered to hasten to Rome for this purpose, as the most holy law of God, as you know, requires.

> “And so that you may have the fullest and most accurate knowledge of all these matters, I have sent copies of the letters dispatched to me by Anulinus, together with my own letter, to your aforementioned colleagues. When your dignity has read them, you will carefully weigh how and by what method the matter mentioned above may be diligently and justly settled, and finally resolved according to the prescriptions of law.

> “For it is not hidden from you that I attach such reverence to the holy and Catholic Church that I wish you to leave no general schism and no discord anywhere at all. May the supreme majesty of the great God preserve you, most honored men, for many years.”  
> *(Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, Book X, chapter 55.)*

When the men of both parties had arrived at Rome, where the three bishops of Gaul mentioned in Constantine’s letter were also present, together with fifteen other bishops from Italy, a council was held under the authority of Pope Melchiades.

> “With Melchiades, bishop of the Apostolic See, presiding. Reticius took part as a judge with the others.”  
> *(St Augustine, Book I against Julian, chapter 2.)*

> “They assembled in the house of Fausta in the Lateran, in the third consulship of Constantine and the third of Licinius, on the sixth day before the Nones of October, a Friday.”  
> *(Optatus of Milevis, Book I, and elsewhere.)*

> “Caecilianus was pronounced innocent by the judgment of all those mentioned above, including the judgment of Miltiades, by which the case was closed in these words: ‘Since it has been established that Caecilianus has not been accused, according to his own declaration, by those who came with Donatus, and since it has not been established that he was convicted by Donatus on any point, I judge that he should rightly be retained in his ecclesiastical communion with his status unimpaired.’”  
> *(Optatus, against Parmenianus, Book I.)*

> “What was the final sentence pronounced by that blessed man Melchiades? How innocent, how complete, how prudent, and how peaceful it was! He did not dare remove from his college the fellow bishops against whom nothing had been established. He censured Donatus alone, whom he had found to be the chief author of all the evil, yet granted the others a free choice of recovering their health. He was ready to send letters of communion even to those who were known to have been ordained by Majorinus, so that wherever there were two bishops, whom dissension had made two, the one who had been ordained first should be confirmed, while another people should be provided for the other to govern, and so forth. O excellent man! O son of Christian peace, and father of the Christian people!”  
> *(St Augustine, Letter 163.)*]

[Col. 1499]

>[Col. 1499] |

**33. Miltiades.** [B: Melchiades.] An African by nationality, he sat for three years, seven months, and twelve days, from the Nones of July in the ninth consulship of Maxentius until the eleventh consulship of Maximus, which was in the month of September, when Volusianus and Rufinus were consuls. [B: two years, two months, and seven days.] [B: from the consulship of Galerius Maximianus VIII and Licinius to that of Constantine III and Licinius II.]

He established that no believer should fast in any way on Sunday or Thursday, because the pagans celebrated these days as a kind of sacred fast. And Manichaeans were found in the City by the same man.

He caused consecrated offerings to be sent through the churches from the bishop’s consecration; this is called *fermentum*. [See Baronius under the year of the Lord 313.]

He held one ordination in the month of December: seven priests [C B: six], five deacons, and twelve bishops in various places. [Col. 1501] He was buried in the cemetery of Callistus, on the Appian Way, in the crypt, on the third day before the Ides of December; and the episcopate was vacant for sixteen days.

**CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS.**

Miltiades: three years, six months, and eight days, from the sixth day before the Nones of July, in the sole consulship of Maximianus VIII—which was in September, when Volusianus and Rufinus were consuls—until the third day before the Ides of January, when Volusianus and Anianus were consuls.

### Number 34

Here Constantine the emperor, on the fourth day after his baptism, granted a privilege of the Roman Church to the pontiff, so that throughout the Roman world they should regard him as its head, just as everyone regards a judge as king. Among other things, the privilege reads as follows:

“We have judged it useful, together with all our satraps, the entire senate, the nobles also, and all the Roman people subject to imperial rule, that, just as Blessed Peter appears to have been constituted on earth as the vicar of the Son of God, so also the pontiffs of that prince of the apostles should possess from us and from our empire a principality and power greater than the mildness of our earthly imperial serenity appears to have granted; choosing for ourselves that same prince of the apostles, or his vicars, as firm patrons before God.

“And just as ours is the earthly imperial power, so we have decreed that his most holy Roman Church be reverently honored, and that the most sacred see of Blessed Peter be gloriously exalted above our empire [Col. 1529C] and earthly throne. We grant it power, dignity, strength, and imperial honor, and we decree as follows: we sanction that it hold primacy over the four sees—Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem, and Constantinople—and also over all the Churches of God throughout the entire world; and that the pontiff who at any time presides over that most holy Roman Church be higher than all the priests of the whole world. By his judgment, whatever must be arranged for the worship of God, the Christian faith, or the preservation of order shall be determined.

“And within the churches of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, for the continual maintenance of the lights, we have granted estates and landed properties, enriched them with various goods, and through our imperial sacred authority, both in the East and in the West, and also in the northern [M: ‘or also in the northern’] and southern regions—namely, in Judaea, Greece, Asia, Thrace, [Col. 1529D] Africa, and Italy, and in our various islands—we have granted them possessions from our generosity, on the definite condition that everything be administered through the hands of our most blessed father Silvester, supreme pontiff, and his successors. Moreover, we now hand over to Blessed Silvester and all his successors the Lateran palace of our empire.

“Then the diadem, namely the crown of our head and name, together with the Phrygium, and also the shoulder-cloth, namely the band which customarily surrounds the imperial neck; furthermore, the purple cloak and scarlet tunic, and all the imperial garments, as well as the dignity of those who preside over the imperial cavalry. We also confer on him the imperial scepters, together with all the standards and banners, as well as the various imperial ornaments, the entire procession of imperial majesty, and the glory of our power.

“We decree that the most reverend clerics of various orders serving that most holy Roman Church shall possess that summit of singular power and excellence [Col. 1530A] with which the glory of our most extensive senate appears to be adorned—that is, that they be made patricians and consuls. We also proclaim that they be adorned with the other imperial dignities. And just as the imperial soldiery is adorned, so we decree that the clergy of the holy Roman Church be adorned; and just as imperial power is arranged through various offices—namely, chamberlains, doorkeepers, and all chamberlains—so we wish the holy Roman Church to be decorated.

“And so that pontifical dignity may shine forth most fully, we decree also that the clerics of the same holy Roman Church may ride horses decorated with saddlecloths and linens, that is, with the purest white color; and just as our senate uses footwear with socks, so let them be made splendid with white linen, and thus let heavenly things, like earthly things, be adorned for the praise of God.

“Above all, we grant Blessed Silvester and his successors permission, by our command, to clericalize whoever he wishes, after peaceful deliberation [M: ‘after appeased counsel’], and to enroll him among the number of religious clerics; let no human being presume arrogantly to oppose this.

“We have therefore decreed also that he and his successors should use the diadem, namely the crown which we have granted him from our head, made of the purest gold and precious gems, in honor of Blessed Peter. But that most blessed pope, over the clerical crown which he wears for the glory of Blessed Peter, did not allow himself to use that crown of gold.

“We placed upon his most sacred head, with our own hands, the Phrygium, which by its gleaming whiteness signifies the glorious resurrection of the Lord; and, holding the bridle of his horse, we performed for him, in reverence for Blessed Peter, the office of stable-master. We decree that all his successors may use this Phrygium individually in their processions, in imitation of our empire.

“Therefore, so that the pontifical summit may not be diminished but may be adorned with greater glory and power than the dignity of an earthly empire, behold, we hand over and leave to the most blessed pontiff and universal pope Silvester our palace, the city of Rome, and all the provinces, places, and cities of Italy and the western regions; and by a pragmatic constitution we decree that they be administered by him and his successors, and we grant them to remain under the jurisdiction of the holy Roman Church.

“Therefore we have considered it fitting that our empire and the power of our kingdom be transferred to the eastern regions; that a city be built in the province of Byzantium, in the most suitable place, in our name; and that our empire be established there, since where the heavenly emperor has constituted the principality of the priests and the head of the Christian religion, it is not right for an earthly emperor to exercise authority.

“All these things which we establish and confirm through this imperial sacred decree and through our other divine decrees, we decide shall remain unimpaired and unshaken until the end of the world. Therefore, before the living God who commanded us to reign, and before his fearful judgment, we adjure all our future successors, emperors, and all the nobles, satraps, the most extensive senate, [Col. 1530D] and the whole people throughout the world, now and hereafter, not in any way to violate these things or overturn any part of them.

“But if anyone—which we do not believe—should prove in this matter to be a violator or despiser, let him be bound by earthly condemnations, and let him feel the holy princes of God, the apostles Peter and Paul, opposing him both in the present life and in the future; and let him be burned in the lower hell with the devil and perish with all the impious.

“Strengthening the document of this imperial decree with our own hands, we placed it upon the venerable body of Blessed Peter. Given at Rome, on the third day before the Kalends of April, in the fourth consulship of Flavius Constantine Augustus and the fourth consulship of Gallicanus.”

## Note: [Col. 1539]

### No. 34, line 5

“Constantine Augustus was baptized.” There is indeed a serious dispute among scholars concerning the place and person who baptized Constantine. On the basis of Eusebius, Jerome, Ambrose, and other Fathers, some maintain that he was baptized at the end of his life by Eusebius of Nicomedia. Nevertheless, the common and ancient tradition of the Roman Church holds that he was baptized at Rome by Saint Silvester. The *Book of the Pontiffs* presents that tradition here, and learned it from the second catalogue, whose author perhaps drew it from older acts preserved in the archive of the apostolic see.

### No. 35, line 1

“Here he issued a decree concerning the whole Church.” The author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* does not explain what this decree was. Since peace had been restored to the churches under Silvester, however, and many things during the persecutions had either been unable to be established or could not be observed, the circumstances of the time required him, as “bishop of bishops,” to use Tertullian’s words, or as “Father of the Christian people,” to speak with Augustine, to regulate the rites and the collapsed discipline of the Church [Col. 1539D]. There is no reason to doubt that he did so.

### Line 18

“Here he established that if anyone wished to serve or advance in the Church, he should be a reader,” etc. One of Silvester’s decrees concerning the whole Church may be identified as the rule reportedly issued concerning the various intervals for ordination: a reader was to have twenty years of age; an exorcist was to be appointed after thirty days; an acolyte after five years; a subdeacon after five years from receiving the acolyte’s office; a deacon after five years; and a presbyter after three years. All the orders are listed except that of doorkeeper, who perhaps is understood under the name “guardian of the martyrs.” For in ancient times churches were called *martyria*, so that doorkeepers could also have been called guardians of the martyrs deposited in the churches.

### No. 36, line 48

“The holy font where Augustus Constantine was baptized.” The words of the Greek writer Theophanes are especially notable, agreeing with the *Book of the Pontiffs*: “The great Constantine was baptized at Rome by Silvester, together with his son Crispus, as the inhabitants of old Rome preserve the baptistery to this very day as testimony and proof that, after the death of the tyrants, he was baptized at Rome by Silvester.”

In manuscript M. 833 of the Palatine Library there is an inscription at the font of Saint John, followed by these words: “This place, once heaped with the squalor of a filthy tomb, was adorned and dedicated through the expense and zeal of Christ’s servant Hilary, bishop, with the Lord’s help, after so great a mass of ruins had been removed as the height now visible, as an offering to Christ the Lord.” This is clear evidence that the font existed there from Constantine’s time; it is still called Constantine’s baptistery.

### No. 38, line 2

“Whose small coffin he deposited with the body of Saint Peter,” etc. The small coffin mentioned here is a chest or repository in which the relics of Saint Peter had been placed. Pliny, speaking of someone whose body could not be cremated, says: “They report that he could not be cremated with the rest of the body, and that he was placed in a coffin, in a temple.”

The chest or repository containing the relics of Blessed Peter was therefore said by a Roman canon of Saint Peter, in a book [lacuna], concerning the Vatican basilica, to have been of silver, and to have been enclosed by Constantine in the altar: “He enclosed, he says, the silver coffin containing the most holy body, closed on every side with bronze and Cyprian bronze, which is immovable” [Col. 1540D]. Instead of “with bronze and Cyprian bronze,” the author of the *Book of the Pontiffs* more correctly reads: “with Cyprian bronze.”

Moreover, a bronze urn still exists beneath the altar of Saint Peter in the Vatican basilica. Perhaps Otto IV, who reigned in the time of Innocent III, ordered it to be renewed; for, if I remember correctly, I read the names of the emperor Otto and Innocent III engraved on it.

## Note: [Col. 1540D]

### No. 34, line 4

“Here he was in exile on Mount Soracte.” Silvester hid on Mount Soracte while fleeing Constantine’s persecution. Mount Soracte is near the City. Pliny, book II, chapter 93: “And Soracte, in a tract near the City.” The same author, book VII, chapter 2: “Not far from the city of Rome, in the territory of the Falisci, there are a few families called Hirpi. At their annual sacrifice, held for Apollo on Mount Soracte, they walk over burning wood without being burned.”

### Line 8

“Here in the city of Rome he built a church on the estate of one of his presbyters, who was called Equitius; he established it as a Roman titular church beside the Baths of Domitian, and it is called the titular church of Equitius to this day.”

Evaristus was the first in the City to divide the titular churches—that is, the parish churches—among the presbyters. As the number of the faithful increased, Marcellus established twenty-five titular churches in the City. After peace was restored to the Church, the pontiffs gradually increased the number of the City’s titular churches. Silvester established the titular church of Equitius, named after the presbyter Equitius, on whose estate it was built.

### Line 14

“Two silver *amae*, each weighing ten pounds.” *Hamae* are vessels from which vinegar or water is poured to extinguish fires: see book 5, section “Sciendum,” of the *Digest*, concerning the office of the prefect of the watch; and the law “Quaesitum,” section “Acetum,” concerning the equipment of a legacy; and Pliny, book III, letter 33.

In ecclesiastical usage, *amae* are vessels from which wine or water is poured into the chalice for the sacrifice of the Mass. Anastasius, in his life of Benedict III: “One *ama* of the purest silver, weighing ten pounds.” The Roman Order: “Silver *amae*, the cantatorium, and the other golden and silver vessels.” Hence the diminutive *amulae*. Anastasius, in his life of Gregory III: “In the oratory, two pairs of gilded *amulae*.” The same author, in his life of Hadrian I: “He offered one offering-*amula*, weighing sixty-seven pounds” [Col. 1541B]. The use of *hamae* and *hamulae* is clearly indicated by the Roman Order: “Silver *amulae*, prepared for pouring wines.”

### Line 15

“A silver chrismal paten enclosed in gold, weighing five pounds.” The chrism paten is the paten on which chrism was placed, prepared for ordinations or baptism. It is called “enclosed in gold” because it was enclosed in a golden case for safekeeping. A paten is an open vessel in which the sacred body of Christ is placed.

Anastasius, in his life of Nicholas I: “The emperor Michael sent a paten of the purest gold, with various precious stones, white, green, and hyacinth-colored.” Hence the paten is joined to the chalice. Ditmarus, book 6: “And from the same metal he gave a great chalice together with a paten and a tube.”

### Lines 15–16

“Ten crowned *pharae*, each weighing eight pounds.” A *pharus* is a larger kind of lamp, candlestick, or lantern, named metaphorically after the Pharos of Alexandria, which gave light at night to those sailing. Anastasius, below, at this passage: “A *pharus* of the purest gold; likewise, a *pharus-cantherus* of the purest gold before the altar, in which genuine nard oil burns.”

And again: “A silver *pharus-cantherus* with one hundred and twenty dolphins.” The same author, in his life of Hadrian: “He also made a larger *pharus* in the same church of Blessed Peter, in the form of a cross, hanging before the presbytery and containing 1,365 candles.” The same author, in his life of Benedict III: “He made a silver *pharus-cantherus*, standing on four feet, in which a lamp and candles were placed beside the reading stand, with marvelous workmanship.”

Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book III, chapter 31: “He also made a *pharus* with twelve towers attached externally, six [in number], and thirty-six lamps.” Walafrid Strabo, *Life of Saint Gall*, book II, chapter 34, in Surius, volume V: “The *pharus* that hung before the altar of Saint Gall, for lighting the lamps.”

The text says “oil of genuine nard,” that is, faithful or genuine and precious, as in Mark 14, “genuine nard” (*nardou pistikou*). Jerome, on Matthew, book IV, chapter 26: “Genuine nard, that is, true and without deceit” [Col. 1541D]. Sometimes *cantherus* is joined to *pharus*; it is a kind of vessel on which the *pharus* is placed.

### No. 35, line 8

“And that the chrism be prepared by the bishop.” The consecration of chrism belongs to the episcopal order, according to the fourth canon of the Roman synod held under Silvester. It is forbidden to presbyters and assigned to bishops alone, as was confirmed by the Second Council of Carthage, canon 3, and the Third Council of Carthage, canon 68; by the canon “Si iubet” and the following canon, in distinction 26, question 6.

Jerome, on Zephaniah: “The priests also who baptize, invoke the coming of the Lord at the Eucharist, make the oil of chrism, lay on hands, instruct catechumens, and appoint levites and other priests.” Frodoard, in his *Chronicle* under the year 967, concerning Adalbero, bishop of Laon: “Finally, at Rheims, on the Kalends of April, he was ordained bishop, on the holy day of Palm Sunday; then, returning to Laon, he consecrated the sacred chrism according to ecclesiastical custom,” etc.

### Line 9

“And he gave the bishops the privilege of signing those who had been baptized, because of heretical persuasion.” The signing, or confirmation, of the baptized belongs to the episcopal order and pertains only to bishops, according to the Roman synod held under Silvester. This is confirmed by the canon “Presbyteri” and the following canon, concerning consecration, distinction 4; and by the canons “De his,” “Manus,” “Novissime,” and those that follow, concerning consecration, distinction 5.

Jerome, *To the Luciferians*: “I do not deny that this is the custom of the churches: that the bishop should hasten to those who in distant lesser towns have been baptized by presbyters and deacons, in order to lay hands on them in invocation of the Holy Spirit.”

### Line 10

“Here he also established that the presbyter should anoint the baptized person with chrism after he had been lifted from the water, because of the possibility of death.” Chrismation, or anointing, of the baptized was instituted by Silvester because of the possibility of death—that is, because of the frequent cases in which the newly baptized died. See Vicecomes, *On Baptism*, book V, chapter 3.

### Line 11

“Here he established that no layman should dare to bring a charge against a cleric,” etc. According to canon 14 of the Roman synod held under Silvester, laymen are not admitted as witnesses or accusers against a bishop: canon “Nullus,” 2, question 7, and canon “Testimonium,” 11, question 1, because very many are violently hostile to them; see the canons “Laicos” and “Laici,” 2, question 7.

### Line 12

“Here he established that deacons should wear the dalmatic in the church, and that their left side should be covered with a linen cloak,” etc. Silvester established that the deacons of the Roman Church should wear dalmatics inside the church. Others were forbidden to use the dalmatic except by privilege, as in the case of the people of Arles, canon “Communis,” distinction 23, or on certain days, canon “De Jejunio,” distinction 76.

The dalmatic is a sleeveless tunic worn by deacons. Augustine, *Questions on the Old Testament*, chapter 46: “As if deacons today were not clothed in dalmatics like bishops.” Ammianus, book XXIV: “A certain man named Maras wore a woven breast-tunic without sleeves, which Christians call a deacon’s garment.”

To the dalmatic is added on the left, as part of clerical dress, the linen cloak called *linostinum*: a linen garment, white, or *mappula*, used by the deacons of the Roman Church; see the canons “Diaconus” and “Illud,” distinction 93. This is the *orarium* that deacons wear on the left shoulder, canon “Unum orarium,” distinction 25.

### Line 14

“Here he established that no cleric should enter the court for any cause, nor plead before a girded judge, except in the Church.” The Roman synod under Silvester forbids any cleric to plead before a girded judge—that is, a civil judge—canon “Nullus clericus,” question 1.

“Girded judges” are all magistrates who possess full sovereign authority, who possessed the right of the belt and sword. Gregory Nazianzen, letter 46 to Africanus: “Whether he exercises bloodless authority, or authority with sword and belt” (*kan tēn anaimakton archēn, kan tēn meta psiphous kai telamōnos*).

Hence “girded” is opposed to “ungirded”: judges actively holding office are opposed to those who have completed their magistracy. Sidonius, book V, letter 7: “To the girded, laws; to the ungirded, privileges.” Julius established the same rule; Anastasius, in his life, says: “He issued a decree that no cleric should conduct any case publicly except in the Church.”

### Line 15

“Here he established that the sacrifice of the altar should not be celebrated on silk or dyed cloth, but only on linen produced from earthly flax.” The Roman synod under Silvester decreed that the sacrifice of the Mass should not be celebrated on silk or dyed cloth, but only on linen, canon “Consulto,” concerning consecration, distinction 1.

Linen clothing was the distinctive garment of priests. James the Nazarene used only a linen cloak; concerning him Matthew says: “The young man fled, leaving behind the linen cloth with which he was clothed.” Hence the white garment is called the sacred vestment of clerics. Paul the Deacon, *Life of the Emeritensian Fathers*, chapter 6: “Therefore, on the Lord’s Day, when he was going into the atrium with many sons of the Church, as is customary, the archdeacon with the clergy in white garments,” etc.

### Line 20

“A subdeacon for five years, a guardian of the martyrs for five years.” “Guardian of the martyrs” was not the name of a particular grade or ecclesiastical order, but an office of subdeacons. Fabian established seven subdeacons in the City, who were placed over an equal number of notaries assigned to the City’s seven regions, so that the acts of the martyrs might be written out accurately—that is, faithfully—as is observed from Anastasius’s account of Fabian.

Their duty was also to guard the martyrs, supply them with food in prison, bury the bodies of the dead, and prevent the bodies of those buried from being carried away. Alternatively, guardians of the martyrs were chosen from the order of subdeacons after they had performed the office of subdeacon for five years; their service lasted five years before advancement to the diaconate was permitted.

### No. 36, line 2

“An ornamental silver pediment of beaten silver.” The Constantinian basilica was adorned with a silver pediment. Pagan temples were customarily provided with a *fastigium*, that is, a gable or summit, for ornament. Arnobius, book I *Against the Pagans*: “Temples raised for cats, scarabs, and little bulls were lifted high by lofty gables.”

It was likewise customary among Christians to place pediments on sacred buildings. Anastasius testifies to this concerning the Constantinian basilica here and below, in his account of Sixtus III: “Valentinian, at the request of Bishop Sixtus, made a silver pediment in the Constantinian basilica, which had been taken away by the barbarians.”

The pediment of this basilica was made of *batutile* silver—that is, silver cast or beaten into sheets, produced by striking the metal. The word derives from the Latin *batuere*, “to strike.” Plautus, in the *Casina*: “With which your face may be beaten.” Suetonius, in *Caligula*, chapter 32: “Beating a gladiator from the training school with wooden swords.” And chapter 54: “He was beating him with weapons of war.”

Anastasius uses the same word below in this passage: “Seven altars of beaten silver.” Imperial buildings also had pediments. Florus, book IV, chapter 2: “All honors were heaped upon one prince: images around the temples, a crown distinguished by rays in the theater, a raised platform in the senate-house, a pediment in the house, and tables in heaven.” Ambrose, on Psalm 118: “It does not shine like the starry summits of roofs, which are well covered and fortified.”

### Line 9

“With Alabandan gems in the eyes.” Alabandan gems are those obtained from the city of Alabanda in Caria, not far from the Maeander River. Pliny, book XXXVII, chapter 2: “Alabandan crystals.” The same author, chapter 7 of the same book: “Alabandan carbuncles.” Anastasius, in his account of Gregory IV: “Twenty larger Alabandan gems.”

### Line 10

“Of hammered silver.” *Dolaticum* silver is hammered or beaten silver.

### Line 13

“The chamber of the basilica from *trimme* gold.” The chamber—that is, the vaulted ceiling—of the Constantinian basilica was paneled with *trimme* gold, that is, gold beaten into thin plates. Anastasius uses the word in the same sense here: “He also made the chamber of the basilica shining with *trimme* gold.” See Bulenger, *On the Roman Pontiff*, book II, chapter 67.

### Line 17

“A single cup adorned with coral metal, enclosed on every side with green and hyacinth-colored gems set in gold.” A *scyphus*, which is a type of drinking vessel, is said to be enclosed in gold because the gems are set into gold. Paul, in the law “Pediculis,” section 1, concerning legacies of gold and silver: “Gems set in gold are counted as part of the gold.”

Hence *inclusores* were called the goldsmiths who set gems in gold. Jerome, book V on Jeremiah: “We must understand ‘craftsmen,’ ‘setters,’ interpreters of the law, and teachers; or craftsmen and setters of gold and gems, an art most highly valued among barbarian nations.” Augustine, *On the Wonders of Sacred Scripture*, book II, chapter 29: “For soldiers, craftsmen, and setters.”

Anastasius uses the word in the same sense below in this passage: “Seven bronze-gilt candlesticks of silver, enclosed with the prophets’ seals.” And above: “A chrismal paten enclosed in gold.”

Conversely, *exclusores* are those who remove gems—that is, examine or test silver. Augustine, *On the Spirit and the Letter*, chapter 11: “Hence certain silversmiths are also called *exclusores*. Hence also the saying in the Psalms: ‘And let those who have been tested in silver be brought forth.’” The same author, on the Psalms: “Therefore, in the art of silversmithing, they are also called *exclusores*, that is, those who, by a certain separation of the mass, bring things forth into their proper form.”

### Line 33

“Fifty silver *cantherae-cerostratae* in the body of the basilica.” *Cantherae-cerostratae*—for this is how the reading should be, or simply *cerostratae*—are vessels in which candles or lamps are placed. Anastasius, in his account of Vigilius: “Two larger gilded silver *cerostratae*, which stand to this day before the body of the blessed apostle Peter.” Anastasius, in his account of Honorius: “He also made two pairs of larger silver *cerostratae*, which stand before the body of the blessed apostle Peter.” The same author, in his account of Leo III: “He made larger, revolving, relief-work *cerostratae* of the purest silver.”

Oil burned in *cantherae*; candles and lamps burned in *pharae*. Bulenger, *On the Roman Pontiff*, book II, chapter 6: “Incense was also placed in the *cantherae* for the purpose of fumigation.” Anastasius, in his account of Benedict III: “A chased *cantherus*, into which incense is placed.”

### Line 34

“Three *metretae* of the purest silver, each holding ten *medimni*, etc.” A *metreta* is a measure of liquids, such as wine or oil, containing ten *medimni*. A *medimnus* contains six *modii*.

The *medimnae* are mentioned in John, chapter 2: “There were six stone water-jars standing there according to the purification of the Jews, each holding two or three *metretae*” (*ēsan de ekei hydriai lithinai hex keimenai kata ton katharismon tōn Ioudaiōn chōrou sai ana metrētas duo ē treis*).

It is reasonable to believe that Constantine dedicated vessels of this kind for holding oil for the lamps of the Church. *Metretae* were customarily offered because they were used in the Church, as below in this passage: “Two silver *metretae*, weighing two hundred pounds.” And below in the same place: “A golden *metreton*, weighing 150 pounds and holding three *medimni*.”

### Line 35.—

Seven brass-gilt candelabra before the altars, with their silver ornamentation, enclosed with seals of the prophets.

Candelabra of brass-gilt were customarily ornamented with *sigilla*, that is, with figures of the apostles and prophets. Anastasius below, at this passage, says: “He also made brass-gilt candelabra, ten feet in height, four of them enclosed with silver seals. Forty brass-gilt *cerostrata*, enclosed and stamped with silver.” *Sigilla* are small figures. Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 41: “Having worshiped the gods and prostrated himself before their seals.” Garments also were customarily woven with seals or little images; hence they are called *vestes sigillatae*, “stamped garments,” in book 11 of the *Theodosian Code*, *On Stage Performers*. We shall say more about this below, in its proper place.

### Line 45.—

Two *thymiamateria* of the purest gold.

Constantine offered two *thymiamateria*, that is, censers, for burning incense before the altar. *Thymiamaterium* comes from the Greek θυμιατήριον (*thymiaterion*). Anastasius shows its use in his account of Sergius: “He made a large golden thymiaterion, with columns and a lid, which he hung before three golden images of the blessed apostle Peter; in it incense, and the fragrance of sweet odor, is more abundantly offered to almighty God on feast days, while the solemn rites of Mass are being celebrated.”

The very ancient ecclesiastical rite of burning incense is commended by Evagrius, book IV, chapter 7:

> Θυμιατήριον ἐξητήσατο, καὶ πάντα τὸν χρόνον ἐν ᾧ καθειστήκεισαν ἐπιθυμιάσας, ἐπὶ γῆς ἑαυτὸν ῥίπτει, προσευχαῖς τε καὶ λιταῖς τὸν θεὸν ἱλεούμενος.

“He asks for a censer and, having burned incense throughout the whole time during which they remained standing together in the choir, throws himself upon the ground, seeking to appease God with prayers and supplications.”

### Line 47.—

The holy font where Augustus Constantine was baptized by that same bishop, Sylvester.

When persecution had ceased, baptisteries were established in churches for the administration of baptism. They called them “fonts” because, from the beginning, baptism was administered in fonts. This font in which Constantine was baptized was made of *metallum*, that is, of porphyry marble, as is added immediately afterward: “The holy font itself, of porphyry marble, covered within on every side, and outside and above, and, so far as the water reaches, with the purest silver.”

Here *metallum* means marble, as also in book *Item si fundi*, section *Sed si haec*, in the *Digest*, *On Usufruct*; and in book 3, final section, *On the Property of Those under Guardianship or Curatorship*. Spartianus, in his *Life of Pescennius Niger*:

> He bears the name Niger; we ourselves fashioned him black,  
> So that the marbles might agree with your form.

Cassiodorus, *Variae* 2.7: “Let fallen stones after the ruins adorn something, provided that it is clearly demonstrated to you by sound reasoning that the marbles themselves have fallen from public places.”

### Line 53.—

But a *myxum* of asbestos tow.

A *myxum* is the wick of a lamp. Anastasius, in his account of Hilary: “A golden lamp with ten light-wicks.” In common usage, *mèche*; among the ancients, *ellychnium*. Pliny, book XXIII, chapter 4: “Wicks are made from the grape, of exceptional brightness.”

### Line 53.—

In the basin of the baptistery font, a lamb of the purest gold pouring out water.

In the basin of the Constantinian baptistery font there was a golden lamb, pouring from its mouth water intended for the baptism of infants. A *labrum* is a kind of vessel in which infants are accustomed to be washed, as though from *lavabrum*. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XX, chapter 6.

Here the *labrum* of the baptismal font is a basin containing water prepared for baptism; elsewhere a porphyry *labrum* is a marble vessel in which the body of a dead person is placed. Ambrose, letter 34: “Here there is a most beautiful porphyry basin, and one especially suitable for such uses; for Maximianus, the associate of Diocletian, was likewise buried in it.” Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book II, chapter 9: “Otto II, returning to Rome, died at that same time and was buried in a porphyry basin in the atrium of the church of the blessed apostle Peter, on the left as one enters the paradise of that church.”

*Labra* are also washing-basins in which linen cloths are washed, book *Lines*, in the *Digest*, *On the Action for Partition*. Elsewhere *labra* are the edges of fields. Servius, on Virgil’s *Eclogue* 5: “The wild vine, because it grows on the margins of the earth, is called *labrusca*, from *labra* and the extremities of fields.”

### Number 38, line 18.—

One paten of the purest gold, with a tower and a dove.

Constantine offered a golden paten with a tower and a dove, for the safekeeping of the Body of Christ. The holy Eucharist was customarily placed, for safekeeping, in a little tower of gold or silver, upon which rested a golden or silver dove.

Besides this passage, Anastasius, in his account of Innocent I: “A silver tower with a paten and a gilded dove, weighing thirty pounds.” The same, in his account of Hilary: “A silver tower with dolphins, weighing sixty pounds, and a golden dove weighing two pounds.”

Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 72: “But another man, not fearing to trample upon the holy tomb, while seeking to strike down the golden dove—”

Fortunatus celebrated in verse, book III, chapter 23, a tower cast from gold by Felix, bishop of Bourges, for preserving the Eucharist.
