Gregory of Tours also mentions this tower, *On the Miracles of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 86: “And the deacon, having received the tower in which the sacrament of the Lord’s Body was kept, began to carry it toward the door.”

Above the little tower in which the Body of Christ was kept hung a golden dove, the sign of the Holy Spirit. This is what John Chrysostom understands in *Homily* 31, addressed to the people of Antioch, when he says that the Lord’s Body is placed upon the altar not wrapped in swaddling clothes, as formerly when it was in the cradle, but clothed with the Holy Spirit.

### Line 21.—

A golden crown before the Body, where there is a *pharocantharus* with fifty dolphins.

Constantine offered a golden crown before the Body of blessed Peter. Crowns hung before the altar and the tomb of blessed Peter. Anastasius, in his account of Sergius: “He ordered the *canthari* and crowns that had from ancient times hung before the sacred altar and the confession of the blessed apostle Peter to be taken down.”

Golden crowns were customarily offered to God because Christ alone reigns and commands. Emperors themselves were accustomed to dedicate their crowns. Leo, son of Copronymus, perished miserably, not without divine vengeance, because he removed and publicly wore the crown of Heraclius that had been dedicated in the Great Church; Cedrenus relates this in his *Life*.

Crowns were also dedicated in honor of martyrs. Augustine, letter 205: “That garland, however, which is more than that forum, is the crown of martyrdom by which he ended his bodily life.” And below: “Because he did not end his life by the sword, such a person does not possess the golden crown that is given as a sign of martyrdom.” Paulinus, *On the Life of Saint Martin*, book VI:

> He snatched away the holy crown with grasping right hand,  
> Which, because of the joined merit of the saint, was fitting.

### Number 42, line 1.—

At the same time he built a basilica of the holy martyr Agnes at the request of his daughter Constantia, and a baptistery in the same place.

The baptistery was at the threshold of the church. Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of Saint Martin*, book II, chapter 6: “He came to the holy basilica; for many days he had lain at that door which, beside the baptistery, opens an exit at midday.”

### Number 43, line 2.—

Above the cemetery of the crypt.

An *arenarium* is a cemetery where martyrs were buried, because it was generally situated in sandy places. Innocent III, book II, letter 140: “The church of Saint Julian, with its houses, cells, crypts, vineyards, and cemeteries.” Anastasius himself, in his account of Theodore: “At that time the bodies of the holy martyrs Primus and Felician were revealed; they had been buried in a cemetery on the Nomentan Way.”

Elsewhere cemeteries are called *areae*, burial grounds. Tertullian, *To Scapula*: “Likewise under the governor Hilarianus, when they shouted about the burial grounds of our people, ‘There are no burial grounds,’ their burial grounds did not exist.”

### Line 3.—

In that place he constructed an apse and adorned it with porphyry marbles.

Constantine founded in the city the basilica of Saint Lawrence the martyr and placed the martyr’s body in it, in a crypt; above it he constructed an apse adorned with porphyry marbles.

An *absis* or *absida* is a structure that was customarily placed over the tombs of martyrs in the form of an apse. Anastasius, in his account of Honorius, concerning the church of the blessed martyr Agnes: “He made the apse of that basilica from mosaic.” Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book III, chapter 27: “Moreover, he sends legates to Constantinople to bring craftsmen skilled in mosaic and squared-stone work, so that others might compose the apse, arch, and vestibule of the greater church in mosaic.”

The apse was a structure adorned with marble, situated in the middle of the basilica, in which the bishop’s seat stood. Anastasius, in his account of Benedict III: “And with a sudden assault, lions of the utmost ferocity climbed the apse in which the bishops, singing psalms with the clergy, were seated.”

Usually the apse was marble-clad, that is, covered with marble slabs, and vaulted, that is, arched. Paulinus, letter 11 to Severus: “He brightens the apse, marble-clad on floor and walls, with a chamber illumined by mosaic.” Cassian, *Conferences* 24.6: “If anyone, wishing to close the vault of an apse high above, continually draws around it the line of that most delicate center.”

The apse was elevated and was reached by steps. Augustine, letter 203: “The honor of this age passes away; ambition passes away. At the future judgment of Christ there will be neither stepped apses nor veiled chairs, and so forth.” Leo of Ostia, book I of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, chapter 19: “Then, in the middle of the apse of that basilica, to which one ascends by eight steps, he established an altar in honor of the Lord the Savior.”

I say that a summit in the form of an apse was customarily placed over the tombs of the saints. Tetricus, son and successor of Gregory, bishop of Langres, placed an apse over Gregory’s tomb. Gregory of Tours, *On the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7:

> When the blessed bishop had been buried in a corner of the basilica, Saint Tetricus, his son and successor, laid the foundations before the altar of the basilica; and, having raised it, constructed an apse with marvelous workmanship and vaulted it over. When it had been vaulted and the wall broken through, he built an arch. When this work had been completed and adorned, he dug a chamber in the middle of the apse, wishing to transfer the body of the blessed Father there; and he summoned priests and abbots for that service—

The apse was enclosed by railings. This is what Anastasius says immediately afterward: “And he adorned the railings with the purest silver.” The tombs of martyrs were customarily surrounded by railings. Augustine, *City of God*, book XXII, chapter 8: “Easter also came, and on that Sunday morning, when a great crowd was already present, the same young man, praying, held the railings of the holy place where the martyrdom was.” Gregory of Tours, *On the Miracles of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 28: “This tomb, placed beneath the altar, is considered very rare; but whoever desires to pray approaches the tomb after the railings enclosing that place have been opened.”

### Line 6.—

And before that place, in the crypt, he placed a lamp of the purest gold, with ten wicks.

Constantine placed a golden lamp before the tomb of blessed Lawrence the martyr. Lamps and lights were accustomed to burn before the tombs of martyrs and holy confessors.

It is said that before the tomb of the apostle Thomas at Edessa in Syria an everlasting light burned, without fuel of oil or pitch. Gregory of Tours relates this, *On the Miracles of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 32:

> For a lamp placed and lit there before the place of his burial shines perpetually, day and night, by divine command, receiving from no fuel of oil or pitch—

Before the tomb of Felix of Nola the martyr there hung a lamp. The same Gregory of Tours, book I, chapter 104: “Against the wall of this little chamber, where the blessed body rests enclosed in a tomb, there clings a portico hanging from above; in it a lamp suspended by a cord was accustomed to provide light for the place.”

Constantine also offered twelve silver lamps before the body of blessed Lawrence the martyr. Anastasius says below at this passage: “Before the body of the blessed martyr Lawrence, a silver-clad representation of his Passion, adorned with seals, together with silver *bimyx* lamps”—read *byssinis* in place of *bymixis*. A *bimyx* lamp is one that has two wicks (*deux mèches*). Anastasius, in his account of Leo III: “He made two large cast, embossed, double-wicked lamps.”

### Line 16.—

In the same place, the property of a certain religious woman named Cyriacetes, which the treasury had seized during the persecution.

The property of martyrs was confiscated into the imperial treasury. Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 54: “Origen, also called Adamantius, when persecution against the Christians was stirred up in the tenth year of Severus Pertinax, was left with six brothers and his widowed mother in poverty, after his father Leonides had been crowned with the martyrdom of Christ; for the treasury had seized the family property because of his confession of Christ.”

### Number 44, line 1.—

At the same time Constantine made a basilica for the most blessed martyrs Marcellinus, the presbyter, and Peter, the exorcist, *inter duas lauros*, and a mausoleum where his most blessed mother, Helena Augusta, was buried in a porphyry sarcophagus, on the Lavican Way, three miles from the city of Rome.

*Inter duas Lauros*, “Between the Two Laurels,” was the name of a place on the Lavican Way, three miles from the City, near which Constantine built the basilica of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter. Tertullian reports that Severus was besieged there by those who belonged to the party of Cassius, Niger, and Albinus, *Apology*, chapter 35:

> Whence Cassius, Niger, and Albinus; whence those who besiege Caesar *between the two laurels*; whence those who exercise their skill in strangling his throat; whence those who, armed, burst into the palace?

### Line 18.—

Twenty silver ministerial chalices, each weighing three pounds.

Some chalices were smaller and intended for the service of the altar sacrifice; hence they were called *ministeriales*, “ministerial,” as here and below: “Ten ministerial chalices, each weighing three pounds.” And below: “Fifteen ministerial chalices, each weighing two pounds.” Likewise, in the account of Mark: “Three silver ministerial chalices, each weighing two pounds.” In the account of Damasus: “Five silver ministerial chalices, each weighing three pounds.”

Chalices with a *syphon* were chalices with a tube for administering the Blood of Christ. Conrad, in the *Chronicle of Mainz*: “There were five silver-gilt tubes for communicating.” Ditmarus, book VI: “And he gave a large chalice of the same metal, together with a paten and a tube.”

Other chalices were larger and hung for ornamental purposes from arches or beams. Anastasius, in his account of Leo III: “He made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Paul eleven large chalices cast from silver, hanging on the great arch, and forty others hanging between the greater columns, on the right and left.” And below, in the same account: “He also made in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter large chalices of the purest silver, resting upon the silver beams.” And below: “He also made chalices cast from silver, sixty-four in number, hanging between the greater columns on the right and left of the basilica.”

Nor should it be omitted that chalices used for communicating were called *communicales*, “communion chalices”: “He made communion chalices of the purest silver for each district, to precede the stations, carried by the hands of the acolytes.”

There were also chalices that were placed around the altar for ornament. Anastasius, in his account of Leo IV: “He also offered to the blessed apostle Peter silver chalices that rest around the altar, sixteen in number, weighing so many pounds.” They were also called *ministeria*, “vessels for the service.” Anastasius, in his account of Hadrian I: “Likewise, he made a paten and chalice in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, from the purest gold, for the daily rites.”

Other chalices were larger and had handles, for ornament. Anastasius, in his account of Leo III: “And a larger chalice with gems and two handles, weighing fifty-eight pounds,” and so forth. The same, in the same account: “He offered a larger cast chalice with a tube, weighing thirty-seven pounds.”

### Line 25.—

The island of Sardinia, with all the estates belonging to it.

Constantine offered the island of Sardinia as a dowry to the basilica of the holy martyrs Marcellinus and Peter, which he had founded, for the Church. From that time Sardinia was under the jurisdiction and ownership of the Roman Church; concerning this, see the chapter *Si diligenti*, *On Prescription*, and the chapter *Ea te*, *On Oaths*, where I discussed it.

### Number 45, line 7.—

One distinctive silver chrismal paten, weighing ten pounds.

A chrismal paten is a vessel in which chrism is kept, intended for the anointing of the baptized. The Synod of Auxerre calls it a *chrismarium*, canon 6: “Let presbyters request chrism, but with a chrism-vessel and linen cloth, as the relics of the saints are customarily carried.” Anastasius calls vessels for chrism *patenae*, in his account of Innocent: “Two patens for chrism, each weighing four pounds.” Optatus of Milevis, *Against the Donatists*, book II, calls it a chrism flask: “They also threw the chrism flask through the window so that it might be broken.”

### Line 8.—

A silver basin for baptism.

The basin for baptism is a *hydria* containing blessed water for baptism.

### Line 16.—

A silver embossed chalice.

An embossed (*anaglyphus*) chalice is chased, that is, engraved with figures or seals. Embossed vessels are chased vessels, engraved with figures or seals. Anastasius, in his account of Hadrian: “An engraved embossed cross.” The same, in his account of Innocent: “An embossed silver cup.” The same, in his account of Leo III: “And also an engraved, embossed cross of the purest gold, hanging in the *pergula* before the altar.”

The *pergula* was an exedra before the altar, in which sacred gifts were displayed. See Cujas, *Observationes* 11.13.

### Number 48, line 6.—

He also constructed an aqueduct-channel (*forma*) over a distance of eight miles.

*Formae* are built channels through which water is conducted, as here and in books I, VIII, and IX of the *Theodosian Code*, *On Aqueducts*: the Aqua Augusta, the Aqua Claudia, in books VIII and IX; the Aqua Sabathena, mentioned by Anastasius below in his account of Honorius, and in that of Hadrian I; and Trajan’s aqueduct, in Anastasius’s account of Felix.

Sidonius celebrates the aqueducts of the City among its notable works, book I, letter 5: “Among these things Rome also became visible to my sight; and I seemed destined to drink down not only its aqueducts but even its naval battle basins.”

---

### [Note: Column 1548D]

### Number 34, line 10.—

He established these gifts.

The splendor of the vessels was increased by Sylvester, and such use existed in the primitive Church. Among other evidence, this is demonstrated by the inventory of sacred vessels entrusted by Mansurius Primus of Carthage to the elders of the Church, when he saw the churches being plundered under the edicts issued by Diocletian, as reported by Optatus, book I:

> For the churches possessed very many ornaments of gold and silver, which he could neither bury in the earth nor carry away with him. He entrusted them to faithful elders, making a written record, which he is said to have given to a certain old woman, so that, if he himself did not return, once peace had been restored to the Christians, that old woman would hand it over to the person whom she found seated in the episcopal chair. He departed after stating the reason; he was ordered to return but could not reach Carthage. The storm of persecution was brought to an end and concluded.

After Optatus, page 92. In the acts of the examination of Caecilianus and Felix, the inventory of ornaments is described as follows:

> Two golden chalices; likewise six silver chalices; one small silver vessel; seven silver lamps; two *cereofalta* [candle-holders]; short bronze candlesticks with their lamps, seven [in number]; likewise eleven bronze lamps with their chains.

During that same century, once freedom had been granted to the churches, the value of their ornaments increased. Hence among the other accusations brought against Chrysostom at the Synod of the Oak, as reported by Photius, codex 59, page 54: “That he had sold off a great quantity of precious objects.”

The abundance of such wealth in the churches of heretical communities during this and the following centuries must also be noted in its proper place. Such were the churches of the heretics in the age of Justin and Justinian; Justinian, after seizing them from the heretics, assigned them to the churches of the Catholics.

In a letter of Pelagius I to Childebert, king of the Franks, there is a fragment of a letter from Vigilius to Justinian, in which we read:

> These things happened in this manner: when your most merciful father, the emperor, had overthrown all the heresies that, up to his reign, had possessed at Constantinople their own bishops and churches, with great revenues and a variety of vessels, and had taken away their basilicas, revenues, and all their other possessions, he handed them over to the Catholics.

From Sylvester onward, the *Liber Pontificalis* undertakes to insert, in the acts of each pope, the gifts given to the churches either by princes, by the faithful, or by the supreme pontiffs themselves. I think that this material was added or enlarged at a later hand, especially in the time of Charlemagne. For many words occur that clearly came from the Lombard people. Thus the ancient life of Saint Damasus, preserved in the archive of the Vatican basilica, does not contain an inventory of gifts; yet an inventory transcribed from that same manuscript is appended to the life in the *Liber Pontificalis*.

The author and compiler took this material from the archives of the Apostolic See, where individual donations were recorded. From the same period onward, donations made to other churches throughout the world are also recorded in ancient charters. Mabillon and others, who collected these unpublished materials, provide examples of them.

### Line 14.—

*Amas.*

The meaning of the word varies. In book 3 of the *Digest*, *On the Office of the Prefect of the Watch*, we read: “It must be understood that the prefect of the watch ought to keep watch throughout the whole night and go about wearing shoes, with hooks and axes.” In the *Life of Saints Perpetua and Felicity*, in Holstenius, page 8: “There were swords, lances, hooks, machetes.” In that passage the word denotes an iron implement, while the *Acts* add: “Every kind of iron tool was fixed in the hiding places of the staircase.”

In these acts of the pontiffs, however, *ama* and *amula* occur frequently and must be understood as sacred implements suitable for holding liquids, as the following words make clear: “Golden *amae* … each holding three *medimni*.” Hence Papias: “*Amula*: a wine vessel.”

When the Eucharistic sacrifice was celebrated, the people, as the Roman Ordo says, in volume X of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, page 3, gave their offerings—that is, bread and wine—and offered them with white cloths, first the men and then the women; finally the priests and deacons offered, but only bread, and this before the altar.

The faithful carried the wine in *amulae*, which the subdeacons poured into *amae*, according to the same Ordo:

> Then the subdeacon comes, carrying on his right arm the paten and on his left the chalice into which the people’s *amulae* are received. Immediately, when the pontiff receives the offerings of the people, the archdeacon receives the *amulae* behind him and pours them into the larger chalice, which the subdeacon holds; an acolyte follows him with a cup over the chasuble, into which the filled chalice is poured.

When wine was offered to the pontiff for consecration, it was clarified by being strained through a filter, whenever the quality of the wine offered required it. Thus the Ordo says:

> When the altar has been prepared, the archdeacon takes the pontiff’s *amula* from the regional subdeacon who presents the offerings and pours it through a filter into the chalice.

It was a solemn custom to clarify wines at banquets, as Apuleius expresses it when describing the preparations for a banquet, book IX, page 290:

> But the modest wife immediately prepares a sumptuous dinner, clarifies the precious wines, seasons the fresh dishes with *tucceta* [prepared relishes], and lavishly sets the table—

Thus *ama* and *amula* seem to be distinguished in this way: *amulae* were small wine flasks, whereas *amae* were larger vessels for holding the wines offered, which were afterward clarified through a filter and placed in the chalice.

That *amae* were very large vessels is shown by the measure of their capacity given above. According to Pollux, a *medimnus* was a vessel containing one hundred and eight pounds. There were several *amae*, because wine was used not only for the sacrifice but also to feed the poor faithful. Hence at the stations, when the generosity of the faithful was greater, several *amae* were carried, as is read below in the account of Gregory IV: “The pontiff himself made six silver *amae*, which preceded all the stations.”

The practice of using golden flasks continued in later times, especially those carried for pouring wine into the chalice for consecration. Thus an anonymous poet concerning the bishops of York:

> He ordered a large flask to be made of refined gold,  
> Of no small weight, with which the priest would pour the wines  
> Into the chalice while celebrating the solemn sacred rites.

From this the number, variety, and use of the *amae* and *amulae* are evident; they are repeatedly mentioned in the acts of the succeeding pontiffs.

### Line 17.—

*Canthara cerostata.*

First the use of these vessels must be examined, and then the variety encountered in the *Liber Pontificalis*. A *cantharus* is a kind of cup proper to Bacchus, as Valerius Maximus says, book III, chapter 6:

> After his triumph over Jugurtha, and over the Cimbri and Teutons, Marius always drank from *canthari*, because Father Liber, said to have led his celebrated triumph from Asia, was accustomed to use this type of cup.

The *cantharus* and *cantharulus* were named from their larger or smaller form. The vessel was therefore larger than ordinary cups, as befitted Bacchus.

Among the pagan peoples, the *cantharus* was among the vessels of temples, and was placed before the couches of the gods. Apuleius, book IX, page 276, while describing the priests of the gods wandering through the cities and recounting their deeds, speaks of the theft by rogues of a golden *cantharus* from a temple:

> And, repeatedly pressed by insistent speech, they quickly produce the golden *cantharus*; they produce that evidence of their crime, which they had secretly stolen from the very couches of the Mother of the Gods, under the pretense of the solemn rites they had publicly performed, and, as though they could escape the punishment for so great a crime, had crossed the boundary of the city in silent departure while the light was still uncertain.

He then introduces the rogues excusing the theft:

> “Behold,” they say, “the cruelty of an unworthy affair! How many innocent men are endangered! For the sake of a single *cantharus*, which the Mother of the Gods offered as a hospitable gift to her sister, the Syrian goddess, you wish to expose innocent priests of religion to danger.”

After these and similar idle speeches had been fruitlessly suppressed, the pagans led them back and immediately confined them in the Tullianum; then, after the *cantharus* and the image itself that they had been carrying had been returned and consecrated as an offering in the temple,—

From this passage it is clear that the *cantharus* was a vessel placed before the statue of the Mother of the Gods, and indeed in the more sacred inner chambers of the temple, where the priests performed the sacred rites; it was set before the very couches of the goddess and then deposited with the other gifts in the treasury. The inner chambers had given the impostors an opportunity to seize the *cantharus* safely.

That it was a vessel for holding liquids is shown by the same Apuleius below; it was, moreover, a cup of imposing size. He describes it as being offered to him while he was in the form of an ass, at the command of his wealthy master:

> “Ho there,” he says, “boy, mix that golden *cantharus* carefully with mulsum, and bring it to my parasite.”

Thus *canthari* were adopted in Christian churches for holding liquids, but were assigned to sustaining light, using more precious materials such as balsam, nard oil, wax, or similar substances suited to burning.

The vessel is found called *cantharus cerostratus*, *pharus cantharus*, or simply *cantharus*. It may have been called *cerostratus* from its tessellated form and workmanship; it was called *pharus* because a lamp was placed above it, so that the oil and candles might burn. Thus below: “A *pharus cantharus* of the purest gold before the altar, in which nard oil burns … where candles burn with genuine nard oil.”

Salmasius should be consulted in his *Exercitationes*, and Pliny, page 163. Here *canthara* is used because in the time of the Lombards it was very common for masculine nouns in the plural to end and be pronounced with *-ra*. This establishes the period of these additions.

### *Fundum.*

The compiler continues to report the estates given to the churches. These must be considered very ancient, on the basis of the notable passage preserved in the little book of Faustinus and Marcellinus, presented to the elder Theodosius, where, speaking of the basilicas of the Catholics, they say:

> Let them have basilicas flashing with gold and clothed in the splendor of precious marbles, or raised with the magnificence of columns; let them have estates stretching far and wide.

Thus, already by the maturity of the fourth century, extensive estates had been assigned to the basilicas. Most of these came to the churches from the possessions of Christians and from estates confiscated to the treasury during the persecutions.

Magnificence, whether in vessels or in estates and annual revenues given to the churches, also shone forth among many heretical communities. Such were the churches of the heretics in the age of Justin and Justinian; after seizing them from the heretics, those emperors assigned them to the churches of the Catholics.

In a letter of Pelagius I to Childebert, king of the Franks, there is a fragment of a letter from Vigilius to Justinian, in which we read:

> These things happened in this way: when your most merciful father, the emperor, had overthrown all the heresies that, until his reign, had possessed at Constantinople their own bishops and churches, with great revenues and a variety of vessels, and had taken away their basilicas, revenues, and all their other possessions, he handed them over to the Catholics.

Among these, the Arian community was counted for the power of its wealth; down to the time of Justinian it surpassed the others in the magnificence of its estates and ornaments. Justinian claimed these for the treasury, as Procopius, an eyewitness, testifies in his *Secret History*, page 51:

> In the temples of those whom they call heretics, and especially in those in which the sect of Arius was celebrated, wealth was stored up in a quantity plainly beyond what anyone could believe. For neither the entire Senate nor any other part of the Roman Empire, especially, could be compared with those shrines in riches. All their sacred furnishings were of gold and silver and precious stones, in wealth and abundance beyond measure; their houses and villages were exceedingly rich; their estates were scattered throughout the world, together with every other kind of wealth possessed by mortals, since no ruler had ever inflicted any trouble upon them. Indeed, many men of orthodox opinion, through the opportunity provided by their occupations and institutions, received from them the necessities of life. The property of these temples, therefore, was publicly confiscated as booty by the emperor Justinian.

Enriched by these estates, the Vatican basilica always shone forth; it possessed patrimonies throughout the world. After the Lombards, the Iconoclasts laid hands upon them, as may be seen in a letter of Hadrian preserved in the acts of the Second Session of the Seventh Synod, and in another letter addressed to Charlemagne, in which he urges him to recover what had been taken away. There he also explains from where those possessions had come:

> These possessions were granted to the blessed apostle Peter and to the holy and apostolic Church of God in the regions of Tuscany, Spoleto, and Benevento by various emperors, patricians, and other God-fearing persons, for the reward of their souls and the remission of their sins; and they were seized and carried away over a period of years by the impious nation of the Lombards.

The *Liber Pontificalis* below, in its account of Severinus, explains how the goods and revenues were to be expended, when the treasury of the Church was seized by the exarch.

### Number 35, line 1.—

Here he established a regulation concerning the whole Church.

The *Liber Pontificalis* has omitted to indicate the subject matter of the regulation. Perhaps after Constantine’s conversion he issued general decrees for the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline, especially concerning the lapse of many during the decade of the great persecution under Diocletian.

That these matters concerned the whole world, and that the general decrees so called were directed by the pontiffs through the individual provinces, is suggested by the records both of others and of the pontiffs who lived during this very century.

For the Council of Arles decreed that its decisions were to be announced to the provinces of the Catholic world only through Sylvester. The Synod of Sardica likewise sent a letter to Julius, which it judged should be directed to the other bishops of the world; and the previously cited Saint Augustine thought that an encyclical should not be sent to the other bishops before the Roman pontiff had first been consulted.

When the emperor Valens, who had promoted heresies, had died, Gratian, wishing to have a formula of faith followed by everyone, asked Damasus for one. Damasus issued a doctrinal statement to which (1) Meletius of Antioch subscribed at the Synod of Antioch, together with the other Eastern bishops (no. 157), and to which the Ecumenical Synod of Constantinople itself also subscribed. Theodosius repeated this action under Siricius, as must be noted in its proper place.

Siricius likewise recalls a decree issued by Liberius against rebaptizing heretics, and calls it a general decree published throughout the provinces. Thus he writes in his decretal letter to Himerius, volume I of the Councils, page 848:

> At the very beginning of your letter you indicated that many baptized by the impious Arians were hastening to the Catholic faith, and that some of our brothers wished to baptize them again. This is not permitted, since both the Apostle forbids it and the canons oppose it; and, after the Council of Rimini had been annulled, the general decrees sent to the provinces by my predecessor of venerable memory, Liberius, prohibit it.

He then boldly declares that obedience must be expected. In the decretals, chapters 8 and 15:

> What all the churches must follow after this, and what they must avoid, we decree by a general pronouncement.

And below:

> Although no one is free to be ignorant of the statutes of the Apostolic See or of the venerable definitions of the canons.

When Constantius tried to compel Liberius to violate his earlier decrees, Liberius replied resolutely:

> I have never established my own decrees, but apostolic ones, so that they might always be confirmed and observed. Following the order and custom of the ancestors, I have allowed nothing to be added to the episcopate of the city of Rome and nothing to be taken away.

And Innocent I, confirming the general decree of Siricius concerning celibacy, unhesitatingly asserts that these matters may be ignored by no one. Thus he writes to Exsuperius, chapter 1, volume I of the Councils, page 1003:

> For if it should be shown that that rule of ecclesiastical life and discipline which was sent by Bishop Siricius to the provinces did not reach certain persons, forgiveness for their ignorance will be granted to them, so that from then on they may begin to abstain. But if some are found to have known the rule of life sent by Siricius and yet not immediately to have cast away the desires of lust, they must by every means be removed.

### Line 3

“Whose handwritten document was circulated.” Namely, the Nicene Creed was sent directly to the bishops of the whole world who had not attended the council, so that they might subscribe to it and the agreement of the entire world might be represented. This practice—that conciliar decrees should be received by everyone after their promulgation—seems to have been introduced by the apostles, who, after the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15), sent Paul, Barnabas, Judas, and Silas, chosen for this purpose, to announce to the brethren the synodal decree issued at that assembly. Hence, at the end of the chapter, it is said of Paul: “He went throughout Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches and instructing them to observe the commandments of the apostles and elders.”

This was a most widely accepted practice during the first three centuries, as has repeatedly been observed in the preceding notes. But before the Nicene Synod, when Alexander, Patriarch of Alexandria, and Hosius had condemned the blasphemies that Arius was beginning to utter and had approved the use of the word *homoousion* (“of the same substance”), they announced the decrees by an encyclical letter and sought the votes of absent bishops. Philostorgius reports this in his *History* (book I, title 7, p. 6):

“Even before the Nicene Synod, when Alexander, bishop of Alexandria, while staying at Nicomedia, encountered Hosius of Corduba and five bishops who were with him, they agreed by synodal votes that the Son should be proclaimed consubstantial with the Father and that Arius should be condemned.”

There exists an Alexandrian synodal letter which, after recounting Arius’s impious efforts and the judgment of the synod, addresses the bishops of the world concerning subscription in these words (*Councils*, vol. I, before the Council of Nicaea):

“These men, then, dearest brothers, who agree with us in the faith, reject together with us and join your votes against their insane presumption—not otherwise than our other colleagues, who are distressed by this affair, who sent me letters written against them, and who subscribed to the pamphlet issued against them. I have sent all these to you through my son Appion, the deacon: first, the letters of our colleagues throughout Egypt and the Thebaid; then those of the inhabitants of Libya, the Pentapolis, Syria, Lycia, Pamphylia, Asia, Cappadocia, and the other regions adjoining these. Following their example, I am convinced that you likewise will send us letters. And although many other remedies have been applied for healing those who have been wounded by this error, this remedy too has been devised for treating the people deceived by them: when they understand the agreement of our colleagues, they will, under the authority of those colleagues, eventually return to repentance.”

The votes, letters, and episcopal subscriptions are called a kind of healing, employed by the Church to display agreement, so that opposing errors might be dispelled by the assent of pastors and teachers who professed the same doctrine. Weighing the force of this argument, the heresiarch Arius, when he first vomited forth his impiety from his wicked mouth, tried to extort similar episcopal subscriptions. Alexander therefore announced to the people and to others, lest they be deceived, that these subscriptions had been fraudulently extorted by the heresiarch (ibid.).

Accordingly, after issuing its decree, the Nicene Synod followed the same practice: it notified the other bishops established throughout the world who had not been present at the council and requested their subscriptions. Philostorgius, an Eunomian sectarian and adherent of Arius’s perfidy, does not deny that the agreement of the remaining bishops was obtained; but, concealing the matter in the customary manner, he asserts that they were deceived (*ibid.*, no. 9):

“He admits that all agreed with the Nicene formula of faith … and that the remaining company was led over to the synod.”

After their fall, the bishops of Ariminum, realizing that they had been deceived by the Arians’ craft, all subscribed an encyclical letter addressed to the whole world and recanted, as Liberius reports in his letter to the Easterners (letter 11):

“Almost all those bishops who assembled at Ariminum, and who at that time either, enticed by deceitful allurements or compelled by force, departed from the faith, have now returned to sound judgment. They have pronounced an anathema upon the formula of faith issued by the bishops convened at Ariminum, subscribed to the Catholic and apostolic faith confirmed at Nicaea, and now communicate with us as one body.”

(Fragment 2, p. 1319.)

Among the fragments of the lost historical work of Saint Hilary there is a letter from the bishops of Italy to the Illyrians, who were still held in error, ensnared by the frauds of Ursacius and Valens. To expose the fraud to them, they sent the formulas subscribed by other bishops, so that they might either follow their examples or be declared separated from the assembly of the others:

“We rightly rescind the decrees of the Council of Ariminum, corrupted by the evasion of certain persons. We have also judged that copies of them should be sent, so that no disagreement might appear either in retaining the faith or in refuting the Council of Ariminum. Therefore, whoever wishes to share in our unanimity, whoever desires to possess with us an indivisible peace, should hasten to approve what we judge and unambiguously send the subscription to the faith mentioned by us and the rescission of the Council of Ariminum.”

A form of the subscriptions was therefore circulated, so that no variation would occur in their issuance, as is shown by the action of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage. At the plenary council convened against the Pelagians, he thus decreed the form that was to be preserved by those absent:

“Let your Reverence know how each one of you ought to subscribe, whether you are among those whose subscriptions are already contained in the synodal acts, or among those who were unable to attend that plenary council of all Africa.”

There was no opportunity to refuse subscription except at the risk and under the reproach of contumacy. Thus Faustus, bishop of Riez, while urging the Predestinarian Lucidus to subscribe to the six anathemas already subscribed by the other bishops, threatens him as follows:

“But if you wish to send it with your subscription … by that very silence you will openly prove that you still persist in error.”

A book was therefore compiled containing these letters, subscriptions, or votes; some examples of it have been given above. In this same century, in the case of Marcellus, who had previously been condemned before the Council of Sardica, the subscriptions and votes are said to have been gathered into one volume, according to the synodal letter of the Council of Sardica, which the Arians convened (*Councils*, vol. I, p. 739):

“For there exists a book of judgments written against him by the bishops; and in that book those who are now with Marcellus and favor him also subscribed the judgment with their own hands.”

In the archives of the churches such subscriptions were preserved with the greatest care. Thus an ancient codex of the Vatican Library, published by Holstenius in the *Roman Collection*, testifies that the subscriptions of the Antiochene bishops, authenticated in the volume of Damasus, were preserved in the archives of the Apostolic See.

### “Another 208 weak men, who set forth the complete faith”

This assigns the number of bishops who, detained by some impediment, were unable to attend the celebration of the Nicene Synod. A catalogue of those who subscribed, compiled from them, is found in Gelasius of Cyzicus, *On the Acts of Nicaea*, book II, the final chapter, with the heading:

“Catalogue of the holy bishops through whom the holy and universal Synod, convened at Nicaea, sent to all the churches of God throughout the whole world the things established by them through the Holy Spirit.”

This resolves the controversy concerning the number of bishops who are counted as present at a council after its celebration, although it is certain that far fewer attended the actual proceedings. The Fathers at Ephesus are said to have numbered about six thousand, although only two hundred were present; and the bishops at Chalcedon are said to have numbered twelve hundred, although only six hundred and thirty were in attendance. That excessive number must be understood of bishops both present and absent who had nevertheless subscribed to the article of faith either before the celebration or afterward.

Once this explanation has been carefully considered, the statement of Dalmatius, the most holy archimandrite, is easily clarified. Hearing of the losses inflicted by the Nestorians upon the faith and increasing day by day, and learning that Theodosius had been surrounded by courtiers and had become hostile to the Ephesian Fathers, Dalmatius approached him and undertook their defense. In his *Apology* (in Deltan, p. 408), addressing the emperor, he said:

“Moreover, on behalf of the other side—that is, the Cyrillian side—I said publicly: would he prefer to hear six thousand bishops, or only one man, and that one impious? I called those six thousand who live under the authority of the most holy metropolitan bishops.”

For Saint Cyril, after the two Alexandrian synods and before the celebration of the Council of Ephesus, had sent a synodal letter to the metropolitans, and Nestorius was condemned by unanimous votes. Here Saint Dalmatius praises the number of those who had approved the Ephesian decree (*Councils*, vol. II, p. 439).

At the full Council of Chalcedon, in act 4, when Bishop Cecropius heard the evasions of ten Egyptian bishops who had stubbornly supported Dioscorus to that point and refused to subscribe to the dogmatic letter of Saint Leo, he addressed the Fathers as follows:

“This universal council is greater than the Egyptian region and more worthy of belief; nor is it just that ten heretics should be heard while twelve hundred bishops are disregarded.”

Although only six hundred and thirty were present, the remaining number was represented by the metropolitans who, having been established throughout the provinces before the celebration, had already subscribed to the letter, as is read shortly afterward in the same action:

“The letter of the blessed Archbishop Leo was sent to the metropolitans everywhere, and it was subscribed. Thus, what had appeared appropriate to the most holy bishops who were present was brought forward and subscribed.”

This was an established practice and a common conviction. Hence the Eastern schismatics under John of Antioch at Ephesus, separating themselves from the legitimate council, boasted that they numbered two hundred, although scarcely twenty-two of them are found subscribed in the decree (in the Cassinian synodal collection, chapter 129, p. 266). In the synodal letter in which they announced to their followers the condemnation of Cyril and Memnon, they boldly asserted:

“Nearly two hundred in Egypt agreed to the condemnation”—namely, the condemnation of Saint Cyril—“although only twenty-two are read as having subscribed to that condemnation.”

(Ibid., chapter 149, p. 303.)

Thus Alexander, although present at the deposition, did not hesitate to write to Theodoret, recalling the decree of deposition issued by the pseudo-synod of Ephesus against Saint Cyril, when Alexander himself was then united with the schismatics. He wrote that Cyril’s deposition had been subscribed by nearly two hundred bishops, because the schismatic metropolitans had extorted approval from their suffragans.

This seems to be how Saint Augustine is to be understood in book IV against Cresconius, chapter 6, where, discussing the condemnation of Primianus, he writes:

“The first was what was done at Carthage by forty-three, by which Primianus was condemned beforehand. The second was what your bishops, one hundred or more, then decreed at Cabarsussum, by which he was condemned more fully and completely.”

He repeats this number of bishops of the Council of Cabarsussum in his book *To the Donatists after the Conference*, chapters 4 and 22. Nevertheless, in the synodal letter preserved by Baluze, after fifty-three episcopal subscriptions have been listed, the following is added (*New Collection of Councils*, p. 96):

“Fifty-three in all.”

It must therefore be explained that the number of one hundred or more asserted by Saint Augustine refers to subscriptions made to the synodal letter at the council, together with the other subscriptions added to that same synodal letter by bishops to whom the synodal letter had been announced outside the council. Since the number was once carefully preserved in a subscription register, the compiler of the acts could derive and record the number he cited from that register.

### Line 4

“They condemned Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius, or their followers.”

Photinus began disseminating a heresy far removed from the faith of the Council of Nicaea. Nevertheless, his name is inserted twice—here and again in the subsequent Roman Synod, where Silvester is said to have condemned Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius once more. This, however, is not to be understood as referring to the person, but to their heresy, which had already been sufficiently overthrown by the exposition of the Nicene faith.

The synodal booklet expressed this as follows:

“The holy synod set forth the divine discipline of the faith against every heresy: namely, that of Arius, Sabellius, Photinus, Paul of Samosata, Manes, Valentinus, Marcion, and those who share their opinions.”

That is, the Nicene Synod, illuminating the mystery of the Incarnation in clearer terms, also anticipated, struck down, and condemned Photinus.

This is the explanation of a learned writer in a treatise against the Nestorians and Eutychians. Its author is identified as Anastasius Sinaita, and it was published by Jacob Gretzer. Speaking of the decree of the Nicene Synod and of the persons condemned, he writes:

“It also condemned the heresy of Photinus, which said that Christ had the beginning of both his divinity and his humanity from Mary, and that, according to his uncreated divinity, he did not precede the ages.”

He deliberately says, “It also condemned the heresy of Photinus,” in order to indicate that the person of Photinus was not proscribed by the decree that preceded him.

This expression is very ancient for the fourth Christian century. It is used in the aforementioned letter of the bishops of Italy to the Illyrians, who, discussing the fall of the bishops of Ariminum, explain how Photinus, who was then pouring forth his errors, had also been proscribed through the Nicene Synod (in Stilar, fragment 2, p. 1355):

“Therefore, dearest brothers, accept our one and the same judgment, confirmed by a single subscription, while preserving the decrees of the Nicene formulation against Arius and Sabellius, of whose heresy Photinus is condemned as a partial heir.”

Photinus received the worst inheritance from Arius and increased his blasphemies; hence he is condemned in Arius and together with Arius.

It was also in this sense that the Ephesian pseudo-synod of the schismatics inserted the condemnation of Photinus into its decree condemning Cyril. After the schismatics had first recited the Nicene formula, they added the following (*Councils*, vol. I, p. 1538):

“This is the faith which the Fathers set forth, first of all against Arius, who blasphemed and said that the Son of God was a creature; then against every heresy of Sabellius, Photinus, Paul of Samosata, Manes, Valentinus, and Marcion; and against every heresy that rose up against the Catholic Church. These too were condemned by those bishops who, numbering three hundred and eighteen, once assembled in the city of Nicaea.”

### Number 36, line 8

“Holding ribs with crosses.”

The carrying of ribs as an angelic ministry is wholly unusual and inappropriate. It happened through the carelessness of copyists that *ribs* was substituted for *crowns*. For within the crowns a cross had been placed, in the very form in which Constantine had arranged for it to be represented on military standards, as Eusebius testifies. In recounting the vision in his *Life of Constantine*, he adds concerning the crown and the saving sign that was placed upon it:

“Then, summoning the craftsmen in gold and precious stones, he sat among them and described the appearance of the sign in words; he ordered them to reproduce its likeness in gold and jewels … It was a kind of long spear covered with gold … At the very top of the spear a crown had been fastened, woven of gems and gold. In this was the sign of the saving name.”

I therefore believe that Constantine offered these votive crowns. Traces of crowns enclosing a cross are found in Rome; Baronius gives an example under the year 377, in the epitaph of Jovina. The *Cassinian Chronicle*, book III, chapter 73, says:

“Carrying a gilded silver crown adorned with precious stones, bearing six crosses.”

See Ciampini, *On Mosaic Work*.

It could also be said that the autograph of the book read, “holding spears with crosses,” with the initial letters altered through the ignorance of the copyists. Since he had obtained victory through such spears bearing the saving sign, it is credible that he placed the same or similar ones there as a memorial of his victories.

Concerning such military spears and their use, among others Apuleius speaks when describing a soldier placing a military spear among his baggage:

“But he had also carefully set up a very long spear, conspicuous because of its hostile appearance, not at that time for the sake of military discipline, but to terrify unfortunate travelers, upon the highest and most elevated heap of baggage, arranged like an army.”

### Line 14

“Seven silver altars”—that is, service tables assigned to the sacred vessels and to the duties of the ministers according to the ancient practice, by which, when the bishop celebrated at the altar—which was generally one altar, where the sacrifice was offered—the remaining choir of ministers stood nearby.

Hence tables are frequently mentioned in the *Roman Ordinal* and the *Roman Diurnum*. They designated places for receiving the sacred vessels, of which there was a varied and multifaceted number, as is evident from this *Life*, when the same vessels are listed as placed in the individual churches.

Since, at the time of the sacrifice, the ministers were assigned to carry various and distinct vessels, each group had its own tables from which it took and to which it returned the sacred vessels. These altars, therefore, seem to be understood as tables arranged around the altar of sacrifice, not as the altar of sacrifice itself, which was one in the primitive Church.

### Line 16

“Seven golden bowls.”

The bowls accompanied the sacred chalices, and both are listed in the ritual books. Their use was for clarifying or filtering the wine; this was especially the duty of certain clerics, particularly the deacons. Hence, as I believe, there were on a separate table basins, small basins, a strainer, and bowls.

The *Roman Ordinal* says:

“But the subdeacon follows the archdeacon with the empty chalice. While the pontiff receives the offerings of the people, the archdeacon receives the small basins behind him and pours them into the larger chalice, which the subdeacon holds; the subdeacon is followed by one carrying the bowl, into which the filled chalice is poured.”

### Lines 35 and 36

“Seven brass-gilt candelabra before the altars, which are, etc.”

The number seven is taken from the Old and New Testaments. The practice existed before Constantine; in the cited *Acts of Felix*, seven silver lamps are listed. It was a special prerogative of the Roman pontiff, as the *Roman Ordinal* says when it describes the order of the ministers attending the pontiff as he celebrates:

“Acolytes carrying seven lighted candle-bearing stands proceed before the pontiff outside the church and as far as the choir.”

Likewise, four shining candelabra are said to signify the four Gospels, as is stated below:

“Four candelabra according to the number of the Gospels.”

### Line 37

“Enclosed with the seals of the prophets,” or “adorned with images of the prophets.”

At that time work decorated with figures in relief was in use and held in high esteem. Festus explains that *sigillatum* indicates a sculpted image:

“Certain figures are called signs, which are also sculpted; and cups too, in which there are likenesses, are fashioned with figures in relief.”

Cicero discusses the value of such work in *Against Verres* 6, when Verres complains that “a vessel of this kind, which had been left to him by his father and ancestors and which he was accustomed to use on festival days and when guests arrived,” had been taken from him.

He adds shortly afterward:

“He placed before him a dish on which there were excellent figures in relief. As soon as Verres saw it, he did not hesitate to take from the guest table that distinguished image of the household and hospitable gods.”

But “nevertheless, as I had said earlier concerning his abstinence, after the figures had been torn away, he returned the silver without any avarice.”

Thus *sigillatum* seems to have been used when small figures were inserted into another metal. Tertullian calls these *sigillaria*, objects kept in the home in which sculpted images of the gods were found:

“Moreover, since the nations do the same, they sit down after worshiping their little images.”

Constantine therefore inserted sculpted figures into the candelabra and adorned the candelabra with them. Hence they are called images enclosed within them, or, as the *Liber Pontificalis* says, “closed in.”

Speaking below of the ornaments of the basilica of Saint Agnes, it lists:

“Forty brass-gilt candle-bearing stands, enclosed and decorated with silver figures.”

And concerning the body of Saint Lawrence, adorned with such work:

“Before the body of the blessed martyr Lawrence, the representation of his passion was enclosed in silver and decorated with figures in relief.”

It immediately explains the technique of this figured work:

“He made it from porphyry-colored metal with sculpted figures.”

Such is the celebrated Isiac Table, which is preserved in the royal archives at Turin as a distinguished monument of antiquity. On these figures the sacred histories of the New Testament were represented. Thus we read on page 42:

“He made brass-gilt candelabra … with silver figures of the Acts of the Apostles.”

That is, they displayed the history of the Acts of the Apostles.

### Number 44, line 7

“A crown.”

Crowns were commonly placed either around the altar or in the middle of the church. They were either votive or intended to support lights. Votive crowns have been discussed above. Concerning those intended for lights, called *pharales*, we read below under Sixtus III that he made “a silver *phara* crown before the altar.” Shortly afterward:

“Thirty-four silver *pharal* crowns.”

Because they held abundant lights, crowns were called *pharales*, as were the *cantharus* and similar objects. Nor did all these items exhaust the altar treasury of the basilicas; until the ninth century, such vessels and other objects were among the most frequent donations (chapter 26, question 177).

Thus in the *Cassinian Chronicle*, when the prince Sicenulf is described as plundering the monastery of Cassino, it reports that he took what Charles and the other kings had given:

“The first time he took, in chalices, patens, crowns, crosses, *phalae*, small basins, *bochi*, and clasps, one hundred and thirty pounds of the purest gold,” etc.

The same custom was current among pagan peoples, as appears from Vitruvius, book VIII, who says:

“When Hieco, after his successful deeds, had placed a golden votive crown to the immortal gods in a certain shrine,” etc.

Livy, book II, writes:

“The dictator placed in the Capitol, from public money and by order of the people, a golden crown weighing a pound as a gift of the Forum.”

Other writers also mention this. One reads in an ancient inscription preserved in the episcopal palace at Praeneste that one hundred crowns were dedicated to Fortuna Primigenia:

“In the custom of his vows,

as the number increased, he dedicates one hundred crowns,

honoring the images of Fortune and the altars of Apollo.”

The use of votive offerings is frequently recorded in inscriptions and writers.

[Note: Column 1558B]

### Number 34, line 4

“He was in exile here on Mount Soracte.”

Apart from his own acts, the fact that Silvester was exiled from Rome because he feared the emperor’s cruelty is probably indicated by Zosimus, book II, and Sozomen, book I, chapter 5. They relate that Constantine, seeking expiation for his crime, consulted not the Roman pontiff but a foreigner—namely, Hosius, bishop of Corduba.

### Line 5

“He baptized Constantine Augustus.”

That Constantine was baptized in the year of Christ 324, during the third consulship of Crispus and Constantine, is demonstrated most clearly by the Roman council celebrated under those consuls.

The claim of Eusebius Pamphilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine, in book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapters 61 and 62—that Constantine, at the end of his life, many years after the Council of Nicaea, was baptized in the suburbs of Nicomedia by Eusebius of Nicomedia, the foremost leader of the Arians, and departed this life—is an impious fiction entirely alien to the Catholic Church. It was devised for the benefit of the Arian emperor Constantius by the standard-bearer of the Arians, as Jerome calls him in the *Chronicle*.

For Eusebius repeatedly contradicts himself, since in many places he regards Constantine as Catholic and most devout. The Greeks included Constantine among the saints in their *Menologion*.

### Line 6

“Whom the Lord cured of leprosy.”

Constantius, Constantine’s son, earnestly desired that the story according to which his father had been struck with leprosy because of the atrocious crimes he had committed should be completely obliterated. I therefore suppose that Eusebius, acting more as a flatterer than as a historian, just as he falsely and deceitfully related that the emperor received baptism at the end of his life, deliberately suppressed the story of the leprosy so that the fictions he had written might please the son.

### Line 10

“Where he also established these gifts.”

What follows confirms that it is not unlawful for the Church to possess goods contributed for the worship and honor of God and for the support of the ministers.

### Number 35, line 8

“For the chrism to be prepared by the bishop.”

By Christ’s institution it was established that the bishop alone should be the minister who blesses the chrism. See Bellarmine, book II, *On Confirmation*, chapters 5 and 6, and book IV, *On the Roman Pontiff*, chapter 8.

### Lines 10 and 11

“He also established this: that the presbyter should anoint the baptized.”

This is to be understood not of the sacramental anointing with chrism on the forehead, but of the ceremonial anointing performed on the crown of the head of the person being baptized in a solemn baptism. Hugo of Saint Victor confirms this in book II, *On the Sacraments*, page 7, chapter 3.

### Line 16

“That the sacrifice of the altar should not be on silk.”

This constitution of Pope Silvester confirms what had been established by his predecessor Eusebius: that the consecration of the Lord’s body should take place upon a certain consecrated linen cloth, not silk.

By common agreement and custom, as testified by Bede and Burchard, this was received in the Church and confirmed by the Council of Rheims, chapter 3. In canon “Sacratas,” distinction 24, it is called the sacred cloth, because it is like the pallium and garment of Christ upon the altar.

It is more commonly called the corporal, either because it represents the shroud in which Christ’s body was wrapped, or because the Lord’s body is placed upon it. See Alcuin, Durandus, and many others who wrote on the divine offices.

### Number 36, line 52

“Where balsam burns on the days of Easter.”

Balsam is an oil of the highest value. The extremely extravagant emperor Heliogabalus used it in lamps, as Lampridius writes in his *Life of Heliogabalus*. Constantine is found to have applied it to the worship of the sacred religion. See Baronius, year 312, no. 36.

### Number 38, line 15

“Three golden chalices, etc.”

The vessels and ornaments of the basilica of Saint Peter that follow are the very same objects which, eighty-six years later, when Rome was captured by Alaric, were hidden with the Holy Virgin. When they were discovered, they astonished the Goths by their size, beauty, weight, and variety, as Orosius relates in book VII, chapter 39. By divine providence, they were restored by the Goths with honor to the same basilica. See Baronius, year 312, no. 64.

### Number 40, line 1

“He built a basilica for the blessed Apostle Paul.”

When the basilica of Paul was built, at the place where his body had been laid between the Ostian Way and the Tiber, it could not be constructed with the broad spaces that were appropriate because of the narrowness of the intervening site. The emperor Valentinian the Younger, however, extended it beyond that road and made it very spacious. See Baronius, year 324, no. 66.

### Number 41, line 1

“At the same time Constantine Augustus built a basilica in the Sessorian palace.”

The fact that this basilica was built after the discovery of the cross in the year of Christ 326, with a fragment of the cross placed there in the most devout worship, clearly demonstrates the point.

But why, I ask, in the Sessorian atrium, beside the temple of Venus and Cupid? Clearly so that he might justly avenge the monstrous crime committed by the pagans out of hatred for the cross. At holy Golgotha, on the rock of the cross—as Saint Jerome testifies in letter 13—an immodest statue of Venus had been placed, and the very place, so greatly illuminated by the title of the cross, had been called by them the Venus shrine.

For this reason, the temple of Venus, which was more famous than the others in Rome, seemed worthy to be overthrown with disgrace and to yield to the most holy cross, which, after trampling upon immodesty, shone with the splendor of every virtue. Baronius, year 324, no. 105.

### Number 42, line 1

“At the same time he built a basilica for the holy martyr Agnes at the request of Constantia.”

It is certain that he built this basilica at the request of Constantine’s daughter, Constantia; the time, however, is uncertain. For it is not established when both the emperor’s sister and daughter were baptized.

### Number 43, line 1

“A basilica for the blessed Lawrence.”

Here Baronius notes that the places where the bodies of the martyrs were laid were called, according to ancient custom, *confessiones* and were magnificently adorned. The relics of the bodies themselves, formerly kept in cemeteries and underground recesses, began to be honored and venerated after basilicas were erected above them and decorated with gold and silver.

[Note: Column 1559D]

## Chronological Notes

The epoch of Saint Silvester, which seems to differ by a full two years in the Liberian Catalogue, where twenty-one years are counted, agrees exactly with the other evidence and with the paintings of the basilica of Saint Paul, which display twenty-two years. The same is true of the preceding epoch of Melchiades, if one distinguishes the time of his ordination to the episcopate and the vicariate conferred upon him during the persecution from the time of his election and succession to the Roman see after the death of Melchiades, as I explained beforehand in the *Prolegomena*.

We know from a work of that same century, in which it is stated that Silvester was received into heaven, published in the *Prolegomena* from Bucherius, and supported by all the archives of the Church, that Silvester was buried at Priscilla’s on the day before the Kalends of January.

The Liberian Catalogue, published above in the *Prolegomena* from that same century, explicitly records the date as 31 December in the Christian era, when Constantius and Albinus were completing their consulship in the year 335.

The retreat into earlier time by the twenty-three years, ten months, and twenty days attributed to him in the Leonine numerals of the basilica of Saint Paul, which have been preserved with complete integrity, shows that the day of his ordination was a Sunday: in February of the year 312, as is established by the *Life of Melchiades*, from whom he was appointed vicar during the height of the persecution under Maxentius, following the example of his predecessors.

The two Colbertine catalogues, the first and the third, shorten this total by a full week; others reduce it by two days in the following abbreviated form. I do not dwell on them, since the number of days is clear from the original model of the paintings. All the catalogues, both Italian and foreign, as well as Felicianus himself, accurately give twenty-three years and ten months.

The consuls at the time of the ordination are sufficiently indicated by the same Catalogue of Felix IV, together with our Librarian, when it states that the beginning must be reckoned from the time of Constantine and Volusianus.

Constantine Augustus was proceeding as ordinary consul for the second time outside Italy on the Kalends of January in the year 312. Among the Eastern consuls, reckoned from the preceding September, the first was Rufius Volusianus with his colleague Eusebius. This is testified by a work of that same fourth century concerning the urban prefects, published by Bucherius together with the other materials. There we read under the year 311:

“The consuls whom the lords our Augusti shall have appointed. From the month of September it was done under Rufinus and Eusebius.”

The names must be Rufius Volusianus and Eusebius, as Schelestratius proves from an ancient inscription formerly preserved in the Capitol. In it he observes that Rufius Albinus, *vir clarissimus*, ordinary consul, is called the son of Rufius Volusianus, twice ordinary consul. Panvinius also records this in the *Fasti*, in the following form:

> The Senate and People of Rome [honored] Ceionius Rufius Albinus, a man of senatorial rank, philosopher, son of Rufius Volusianus, consul, and [lacuna], because his independence after the Caesarian age—that is, 380 and [lacuna] years—[the damaged text is syntactically incomplete]. Flavius Magnus Ianuarius, a man of senatorial rank, curator of statues, decreed [this].

Schelestratius indicates that it was read as “the son of the twice ordinary consul,” and in the fourth line as “380 and one years.” Whichever way it is read, the father of Ceionius Rufius was the consul Rufius Volusianus, who, with half a year of his term not yet completed, was holding the consulship in the Eastern Empire when Silvester was ordained bishop on 10 February of the common year 312. In the West, Constantine Augustus II and Licinius II were consuls from the Kalends of January.

Therefore the Catalogue of Felix IV and the *Liber Pontificalis* record this epoch of the ordination of blessed Silvester to the episcopate under the names of Constantine and Volusianus.

The consulship from which Silvester’s Roman pontificate began after the death of Melchiades, when he was elected as successor after serving as vicar, is called the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus—namely, the year 314, when Volusianus entered upon the consulship again with Anianus. The day fell on the day before the Kalends of February, that is, on a Sunday, when Silvester ascended the Apostolic See.

He then held it for twenty-one years and eleven full months, until 31 December, the final day of the year 335 and of the consulship of Constantius and Albinus, when he also brought his mortal life and pontificate to an end.

The paintings of Saint Paul correctly count from the day of his episcopal consecration, 10 February of the year 312, twenty-three years, ten months, and twenty days. The first and third Colbertine catalogues differ by a single week in dating Silvester’s consecration, assigning it instead to 17 February, likewise a Sunday, and giving him twenty-three years, ten months, and thirteen days.

Nevertheless, on the basis of the rules of critical evaluation already established in the *Prolegomena*, we prefer the number given by the Pauline basilica on the Ostian Way.

Schelestratius observes from the inscription of Ceionius Rufius Albinus, who was ordinary consul with Flavius Constantine in the same year 335, at the end of which Saint Silvester most devoutly concluded his life and pontificate, that 381 Julian years were counted from the Caesarian era to that consul.

That many years are indeed obtained if the 46 years preceding the common Christian era are added to the 335 years of the common Christian era—counting the very year that is called the year of confusion, which Caesar extended to 445 days.

But if the number of 380 years expressed on the marble is retained, it agrees exactly with the interval between the first year of the new Julian arrangement, year 45 before the Christian era, and the consulship of Ceionius Rufius Albinus.

And since the observations of others and our own concerning pontifical chronology have reached this point, and since they endeavor to refer that chronology carefully to the consular fasti and to the Caesarian period, so that the advance may be more secure once the indication of the boundary has been established from which the beginning of the reckoning can be made certain, it seems appropriate here to demonstrate the definite characteristics of the Julian year from which the beginning of the Caesarian periods before the common era of Christ is to be derived.

For although all chronologists agree about the first Julian year, which, by Caesar’s new arrangement, the dictator, consisted of 365 or 366 days—placing it so that it occupies the position 45 before the beginning of the common era of Christ and contains the new moon on the very Kalends of January—they nevertheless differ in assigning to it Caesar’s fourth or fifth consulship. It is very important to clarify this distinctly, lest the sequence of the consuls, through the Julian years both preceding and following, be displaced from its proper position. For us, moreover, this examination is especially necessary, since in the pontifical and consular chronology prefaced by notes at the end of the Prolegomena to this volume, we begin with these Caesarian periods and consulships, and indicate the exact characteristics of eclipses and other celestial movements marked by those same years and consulships, so that they may make certain the measure of time asserted by us there.

To save space, I shall transcribe only chapters 3 and 4 from a still unpublished little work to which I gave the title *On the Restoration of the Times of the Christian Era*. I had prepared it for publication at some future time, I hope, in order to furnish that part of the chronology with its demonstrations. The title of chapter 4 will also show how correctly, with Schelestratius and nearly all chronologists, we retain the first year of the new arrangement of the Julian calendar, consisting of 366 days—for it is a leap year—and marked by the new moon on the very Kalends of January, in position 45 before the beginning of the common era of Christ. We assign Caesar’s fifth consulship to that same year, in which Caesar’s death must also be placed, on the Ides of March, according to our calculations.

The year that Caesar placed before this one, I call the year explained through the full 445 days, which historians therefore report as having been called the “year of confusion.” Of these 445 days, the final 365 constitute proleptic Julian year 46 before the Christian era. I say that Caesar’s fourth consulship must be assigned to that year. The remaining 80 days—the part of that same year of confusion preceding the 365 days that constituted year 46, the proleptic Julian year, before the common era of Christ—I say belonged likewise to Caesar’s fourth consulship and at the same time to his third dictatorship. This will become evident in the course of chapter 4 from the genuine testimony of the *Fasti* preserved to this day on the Capitoline marbles. I shall append that chapter here, preceded by chapter 3 of the same work and likewise inserting it here.

## From the chronological work *On the Restoration of the Times of the Christian Era*

### Chapter III

Documents are presented concerning the lunisolar movements and eclipses of both luminaries, relating to proleptic Julian years 50 and 51 before the common era of Christ, and to the Roman civil years and the consuls assigned to those years in the Capitoline *Fasti* and in Roman history.

Let no one object to the extension of our criterion of time to the Julian years 50 before the common era of Christ, proposed in the present chapter, as though it might seem that the beginning of the Julian years ought to be placed five years later. Julius Caesar the dictator began the first year of his new arrangement on those Kalends of January on which the true and mean new moon occurred—namely, 45 complete years before those Kalends of January from which the common era of Christ takes its beginning. Of those 45 years, the first and last, as well as every fourth year counted from the first complete year, are leap years.

Accordingly, when those Kalends of January began the first year of the new Julian arrangement, the true new moon occurred at 14 hours and 43 minutes after noon in Paris, which is 15 hours and 26 minutes after noon in Rome. The mean new moon occurred at 8:00 p.m. in Paris, which is 8:41 p.m. in Rome, at the beginning of year 45, Julian, before the common era of Christ. This is inferred from the astronomical tables most accurately published by D. de la Hire and corresponding with the observed results of celestial phenomena with the greatest precision.

[Col. 1563] Mean longitude of the Sun: 9° 7′ 38″ 50‴.  
Mean longitude of the Moon: 9° 4′ 53″ 43‴.  
Mean distance of the Moon from the Sun: 0° 2′ 45″ 7‴.

[Col. 1564] True longitude of the Sun: 9° 8′ 36″ 42‴.  
True longitude of the Moon: 9° 2′ 51″ 3‴.  
True distance of the Moon from the Sun: 0° 5′ 45″ 39‴.

There remain until the mean conjunction 5 hours and 24 minutes; until the true conjunction, 11 hours 45 minutes. Therefore the mean new moon occurred on the Kalends of January, at the beginning of the first year of the new Julian arrangement—which is year 45 before the common era of Christ—at 5:24 p.m. in Paris and 6:06 p.m. in Rome. The true new moon occurred at 11:35 p.m. in Paris and 12:17 p.m. in Rome.

[Col. 1563A] Let another Julian five-year period be prefixed to these 45 Julian years running from Caesar’s new arrangement to the beginning of the Christian era. We shall reckon it proleptically as five times 365 days, with the addition of one leap year; that is, let 1,826 days be assumed immediately preceding the first Kalends of January of the Julian calendar, which contain the mean and true new moon, as recently calculated from the tables. Those 1,826 days will constitute five Julian years, four common and one leap year.

This assumption derogates nothing from the truth. For we do not assert that the Romans used Julian years five years before Caesar’s arrangement; rather, we seek to assign the events of the 1,826 days before the Julian era so distinctly that, within that number of days, we can demonstrate individually, from the position the days would have occupied in the year of the Julian calendar, the position occupied both by human events and by observed celestial movements reported by historians, together with the events in the distribution of those same days through the civil year then prevailing, which differed from the Julian year, whether in the City, in the provinces of the Roman Empire, or under foreign rule.

The appendix, therefore, of this proleptic five-year period—prefixed to the beginning of the Julian era, which initiates the basis of the reckoning at the indicated interval of 50 years before the common era of Christ—is made especially notable and precisely defined by two solar eclipses observed at Rome. One is preceded by 300 days, since the eclipse falls on 7 March of proleptic Julian year 51 before the Christian epoch; the other eclipse itself occurs 233 days after its Kalends of January, which would be 21 August of Julian year 50 before the common era of Christ.

Thus the certain characteristic and mark of the fiftieth year of the Julian calendar, assumed proleptically before the Christian era, leaves no room for doubt about the true distance of that time from our own age, since it is confirmed by the movements of the Moon and Sun observed in those two eclipses, which correspond to no other time than the one indicated.

And if, between the observation of the two eclipses, something occurred at Rome or in the provinces, reported by historians under those consuls whose Kalends of January and magistracy they state to have preceded one eclipse and been followed by the other, we can no longer doubt the true distance of those consuls and of the civil year marked by them from our own age and from the beginning of the common era of Christ. This, we say, makes the epoch so marked illustrious through the observed celestial movements, which define the certain distance of the indicated time.

A nearly total solar eclipse, visible at Rome shortly after sunrise, occurred on the day that would be 2 August in proleptically assumed Julian year 50 before the common era of Christ. In the preceding year—which would have been Julian year 51 before the Christian era—a central and annular solar eclipse, visible at Rome, occurred at noon on 7 March, according to the astronomical tables.

This very observation of the eclipses, at least one of which was total at Rome, is found described in Dio and assigned to that same year, which Roman history makes more memorable than others, both for its disastrous and famous beginning of the civil wars and because the consuls in that year were C. Claudius Marcellus and L. Cornelius Lentulus, followed soon by the first dictatorship of C. Julius Caesar, which made the year still more illustrious. Their names, together with the dictator’s, are marked on the Capitoline marbles and assigned to the same civil year then used at Rome as follows:

> C. CLAVDIVS M. F. M. N. MARCELLVS  
> L. CORNELIVS LENTVLVS  
> EODEM ANNO C. IVLIVS C. F. C. N. CAESAR DIC  
> TATOR

Under these consuls Dio, book 43, records the mark of the total solar eclipse and the beginning of the civil war.
