He also does not omit to assert that another solar eclipse had been observed in the immediately preceding year, and that popular superstition regarded both eclipses as among the signs and portents that befell Rome, as indications, so to speak, of these calamities.

His words, on page 159 of Leunclavius’s Greek-Latin edition, are as follows, while he is speaking of Pompey the Great approaching Dyrrachium:

> Εὐθὺς γε κατέρων εἰς τὸ Δυρράχιον ἔμαθεν, ὅτι οὐ καλῶς ἀπάλλαξε etc.

“Immediately upon arriving at Dyrrachium, he learned, under an evil omen, that he had left his native land. For during the voyage itself several soldiers were struck dead by lightning, etc.”

These portents befell Pompey. But other portents

> TOTI VBBI EO ANNO AC PAVLO ANTE EVENERVNT

“befell the whole city in that year and shortly before.”

In enumerating the events that occurred in the City during that year and shortly before it, Dio also records solar obscurations. For, he says, “in the City itself wolves and owls appeared in great numbers, and frequent earthquakes occurred with bellowings; fire was carried from the western part of the sky toward the east; another fire shook both other buildings and the temple of Quirinus; and

> ὅ τε ἥλιος ΣΥΜΠΑΣ ἘΞΕΛΙΠΕ

‘the whole Sun suffered an eclipse.’”

The scepter of Jupiter and the helmet of Mars, deposited in the Capitol, as well as the columns on which the laws were inscribed, were struck from heaven. Among the prodigies popularly believed to have been seen at Rome, he records a total solar eclipse—namely, that of the year whose Kalends of January, at the beginning of book 43, he says were marked by the names of the consuls then entering office, Cornelius Lentulus and C. Claudius—and shortly before it, since in the preceding year another nearly total solar eclipse, namely a central and annular eclipse, had been seen in the City on the day corresponding to 7 March of proleptic Julian year 51 before the common era of Christ.

Lucan, book 1, agrees with Dio. He described the hour of the eclipse at midday in Rome, while also recounting the other prodigies mentioned by Dio, singing thus in verse 540:

> The Titan himself, when he carried his head through the middle of heaven,  
> Hid his blazing chariot in black darkness;  
> He wrapped the world in shadows and forced the nations  
> To despair of daylight. Such a night, when the Sun fled from the eastern skies,  
> The Mycenaeans endured in the time of Thyestes.

The consuls who opened this year of the civil wars, “in which year also and shortly before those prodigies occurred,” according to Dio, are likewise reported by Caesar in his *Commentaries*, book 1 of the *Civil Wars*, as Cornelius Lentulus and Claudius Marcellus.

When these men fled from Rome, while Caesar, after defeating Pompey, was making for Spain and was staying at Massilia, he learned that he had been named dictator by M. Lepidus. Therefore, when he returned to Rome and entered upon the magistracy—which is also memorable to us, since at that time he granted Roman citizenship to our Transpadane Gauls—he abdicated the dictatorship within eleven days, according to Plutarch.

Since, then, the consuls and the dictatorship of that year from which the beginnings of the civil wars burst forth are established by so many documents of contemporary writers and of those who transcribed them from contemporary sources, nothing could demonstrate more clearly that this year and the consulship of Claudius and Marcellus correspond to proleptic Julian year 50 before the common era of Christ than the agreement of the celestial movements observed at that time: the total solar eclipse seen shortly before at midday in Rome, and the other solar eclipse likewise seen in the City during the same year. These movements, evident from the eclipses, correspond to none of the neighboring years except those indicated.

To preserve the order of the times, the eclipse that most immediately preceded that same year 50 before the Christian era must first be presented. It fell on 7 March of proleptic Julian year 51 reckoned with reference to that era. Its calculation, gathered from the tables of D. de la Hire, is to be set down here. It shows that on that day the Sun, situated on the Roman meridian, was so covered by the interposition of the lunar globe that the centers of the two luminaries were separated from one another by only one minute.

If the Moon’s anomalistic movement had been slightly smaller, the Moon’s diameter would have appeared larger than the Sun’s and would have hidden the entire solar disk. But the eclipse must have been annular, since the solar disk was seen under an angle slightly greater—namely, one minute and 57 seconds—than the Moon’s diameter; therefore it exceeded the circumference of the lunar globe by a narrow margin of one minute.

This eclipse corresponds to the more reliable tables of all astronomers. Its calculation is easier than most at Rome, since the luminaries were found there at the time of true conjunction. For that reason its diagram can be presented most concisely from a table of the angle of the ecliptic with the meridian, as the calculation and Figure 1 here show.

[Col. 1565] Calculation of the ecliptic new moon observed at Rome at 0 hours 8 minutes after noon in proleptic Julian year 51 before the common era of Christ, on 7 March: a central and annular eclipse. The roots, or epochs, of the mean movements of the Sun and Moon at noon on the Kalends of January of the first Julian year—that is, 45 before the common era of Christ—at the Paris meridian, from the tables of D. de la Hire.

**SE**, the ecliptic.  
**MLN**, the Moon’s path.  
**S**, the center of the Sun at 14° 4′ 53″ Pisces, at 0:08 p.m. in Rome.  
**L**, the center of the Moon at 14° 4′ 53″ Pisces, at 0:08 p.m. in Rome, in its orbit.  
**LS**, the parallax of 0° 40′ 9″, lowering the Moon’s center from L to S and producing there a central and annular eclipse of the Sun, in Julian Scaligerian period year 4663, on 7 March, 51 proleptic years before the common era of Christ.

[Col. 1567A] A second solar eclipse follows, visible at Rome and in several provinces under Roman rule, shortly after sunrise on 21 August, in Julian proleptic year 50 before the common era of Christ, under the consulship of C. Claudius Marcellus and L. Cornelius Lentulus.

We give its calculation from the usual tables of D. de la Hire, together with a diagram in a condensed form from our ecliptic pantometer. In it one can observe that at Rome, at the sixth hour, the Moon intercepted approximately three digits of the Sun’s diameter. At that time the angle **ASE**—the azimuth **AS** with the ecliptic **SE**—was 22 degrees, and the parallax **II** lowered the Moon’s center from L to H by 59 minutes, while the Sun occupied point S at 24° 22′ Leo. The Moon, however, was at L, at 23° 15′ of the same sign.

On the African coast opposite Italy and Greece, around Tripoli and Cyrene, at the same hour the angle **ASL** was only six degrees; that is, **MSE**, likewise alternate and equal to **SLT** in the Moon’s azimuth, brings the centers of the luminaries closer together. There an eclipse of nine or ten digits occurs; and, as one proceeds through Africa toward the summer tropic, a central eclipse occurs around upper Thebes and the neighboring region of Ethiopia and inner Libya.

But lest anyone doubt the exact agreement of D. de la Hire’s tables with the movements of the heavens from the age of C. Julius Caesar to our own, it is worthwhile to compare the central eclipse of the indicated proleptic Julian year 51 before the common era of Christ, observed at Rome at midday on 7 March, with the partial eclipse observed at Rome in the year of the Christian era 1718, on 2 March Gregorian style—that is, 19 February Julian style—at 7 hours after midnight, at the beginning of Ash Wednesday. In that eclipse we observed that one and one-quarter digits of the solar disk had been intercepted.

The complete agreement of the tables with the observed movements throughout the 1,768 years that elapsed between the two eclipses will be clearly apparent. For the Sun’s position on the ecliptic at noon on that day is calculated from the tables as 11° 35′ 30″ Pisces, where it was also found by exact observation.

Although I could not observe the Sun on the meridian on 2 March, on the following day, 3 March, I was able to observe both limbs of the Sun approaching the meridian and the passage of Sirius to the same meridian plane, at the equinoctial hours 7:39:00 after the Sun. From Sirius’s right ascension, 98° 17′, the Sun’s right ascension was calculated as 343° 57′. This showed the Sun’s position in the zodiac to be 12° 36′ Pisces on the 3rd and, on the immediately preceding day, 11° 36′, exactly as nearly obtained from the tables.

The Moon’s latitude, longitude, diameter, and parallax at the indicated hour—7 after midnight—at Rome were such as is shown by the obscuration of one digit and a quarter that we observed at the same time through a telescope. The image of the Sun was captured on paper placed at right angles to the axis of the optical tube, in a room darkened in the customary manner. During that observation we also noted that points **a** and **b** on the circumference of the solar disk, intersected by the Moon’s limb, fell respectively at 5° and 60° from azimuth **cd**, which cuts the solar circumference at **c**, according to the method of observation set out below by us in chapter 4 of this same work, *On the Restoration of the Times*.

Claudius Marcellus and L. Cornelius Lentulus.

The roots of the movements of the Sun and Moon, referred to the Parisian noon on the Kalends of January of year 51 before the common era of Christ, excerpted above from the tables of D. de la Hire.

[Col. 1567B] The true conjunction of the luminaries therefore occurred at 24° 27′ 26″ Leo, at 7:22 p.m. Paris time, which was 8:04 after midnight in Rome.

At 6:00 after midnight in Rome, which is 6:00 before noon, let the diagram of the eclipse be constructed. The Sun was at S, 24° 22′ 28″ Leo, at a distance from the zenith **GM**. The Moon was at L, 23° 15′ Leo, at a distance of 78° 30′ from the zenith. [Col. 1568B] The Moon’s parallax at that altitude was 0° 59′.

**ASE**, the angle of the Sun’s azimuth with the ecliptic, 22°. Therefore, at Rome, the Moon’s center appeared at H in its azimuth **HL**, lowered by 59 minutes through parallax, as the figure shows.

[Col. 1569] In upper Thebes and in Cyrenaica, situated in inner Libya beneath the Tropic of Cancer, where the angle **ASL** is small and where the Sun’s azimuth **SA** nearly coincides with the line of the ecliptic **SE**, the whole parallax of the Moon passes into longitude and lowers it along the line **LS**. Thus, on the parallel of the summer tropic, at a point approximately 15° east of the Roman meridian, at the same hour—6 before noon at Rome, 5 there—the Moon, elevated about 25° above the horizon, displayed its center at M by the parallax **LM** of 52 minutes. And where the Roman meridian intersects the parallel of the tropic in Africa, the parallax **SL**, at the same hour, displayed the Moon’s center at S and concealed the entire solar disk from the peoples situated on that same parallel and meridian.

[Col. 1571] Calculation of the solar eclipse of one digit and one-quarter observed at Rome in 1718, on Ash Wednesday, 2 March Gregorian style, or 19 February Julian style.

[Col. 1571B] It is therefore established that the tables agree faithfully with the eclipses observed from Caesar’s age to our own, being so closely connected that over an interval of nearly eighteen centuries they are found to differ by not even two or three minutes in indicating the position of the luminaries, and agree altogether in the magnitude of the eclipses.

Accordingly, among the evidence for the chronology assigned to these eighteen centuries, we rightly give the foremost place to this celestial testimony, which demonstrates with such precision and fidelity the years, days, and hours of the observed eclipses.

Let the annual nail of proleptic Julian year 50 before the common era of Christ therefore be fixed on the Kalends of January, between the two demonstrated solar eclipses, in such a way that it is separated from the earlier one by 300 days—the number counted from 7 March to the following 1 January—and precedes the later one by 233 days, the number that elapses from the Kalends of January to the immediately following 21 August in a common Julian year, such as proleptic year 50 before the common era of Christ.

Let it likewise be established that the consuls C. Claudius Marcellus and L. Cornelius Lentulus belong to that year 50 before the common era of Christ. Dio connects them with the indication of those same eclipses: the first occurring immediately before their consulship, and the second within the annual period of their magistracy.

But on what days of the lunar year, displaced from its position and then used by the Romans, the days of the proleptic Julian year are to be matched during this five-year period prefixed to the first year of the Julian arrangement, year 45 before the common era of Christ, I shall endeavor to show from Hirtius’s commentaries, from the *Ephemeris*, and from the position of the Moon recorded there.

### Chapter IV of the same work *On the Restoration of the Times of the Christian Era*

In this chapter a demonstration is presented of years 45 and 46 before the common era of Christ.

First it is shown that, in the series of common years extended proleptically before the common era of Christ, the first Julian year of the new arrangement established by Caesar the dictator—consisting of 365 days in the non-leap triennium and 366 days in the fourth, leap year—was the year that began with the new moon on the Kalends of January and occupied the position 45 before the beginning of the common era of Christ. [Col. 1572B] It must be marked by Caesar’s fifth consulship on the Kalends of January, and by his assassination on the Ides of March.

Next it is shown that, before this first year of the new Julian arrangement, occupying position 45 before the common era, Caesar placed the year called the year of confusion, consisting of 445 days. The final 365 of those days constitute proleptic year 46 before the common era of Christ, which year must be marked by the fourth consulship of Julius Caesar. The remaining 80 days preceding proleptic year 46 and included in the year of confusion are likewise shown to have been marked by Caesar’s fourth consulship and by his third and fourth dictatorships.

We must proceed to demonstrate year 45 before the common era of Christ, which is to be regarded as the first of the Julian years arranged by Caesar the dictator. The Kalends themselves, bearing the true and mean new moon, demonstrate this.

The celebrated men Paulus of Middelburg, bishop of Fossombrone, in his *Paulina*, and Cardinal Henry Noris, at the beginning of his dissertation on the Latin Paschal cycle, together with Langius, book 1, chapter 12, *On the Years of Christ*, cited by me in my dissertation *On Caesar’s Calendar and Cycle*, observed that Caesar selected as the day he would call the Kalends of January of his new arrangement the day that contained the new moon, so that he might regulate the civil year and sacrifices according to measurements based on the Moon, as Macrobius testifies in the *Saturnalia*, book 1, chapter 14.

The head of the year and of the cycle, expressed through the sequence of eight letters and properly marked on the ancient autograph marble inscriptions of that same calendar, establishes the same Kalends and the same new moon that all the astronomical tables display at the beginning of Julian year 45—and indeed a leap year—before the common era of Christ.

From the tables of D. de la Hire we gave above, in chapter 3 of this volume, the calculation of this conjunction and of the mean and true new moon.

[Col. 1572D] The mean conjunction occurred at 5:25 p.m. in Paris, which is 6:06 p.m. in Rome. The true conjunction occurred at 14:45 in Paris, which was 15:26 in Rome.

[Col. 1573A] The consular *Fasti*, in the surviving autograph fragments, preserve for us an entire five-year sequence from the consuls already mentioned, Marcellus and Lentulus, who mark the year 50 before the common era of Christ, through the year 45. They arrange the names of the consuls as follows in the five-year sequence of the *Fasti*. I shall place Arabic numerals in the margin, counting the proleptic Julian years before the common era of Christ corresponding to their ordinary consuls.

[Col. 1573]

**50** C. Claudius, son of Marcus, grandson of Marcus, Marcellus | L. Cornelius Lentulus

**49** C. Julius, son of Gaius, grandson of Gaius, Caesar II | P. Servilius

**48** Q. Fufius, son of Quintus, grandson of Gaius, Calenus | P. Vatinius

**47** C. Julius, son of Gaius, grandson of Gaius, Caesar III | M. Aemilius

**46** C. Julius, son of Gaius, grandson of Gaius, Caesar IV | Without a colleague

This is to be regarded as the year of confusion, consisting of 445 days, as I shall show from Hirtius.

**45** C. Julius, son of Gaius, grandson of Gaius, Caesar V | M. Antonius

This is the first year of the Julian arrangement, consisting of 366 days and marked by the new moon on the Kalends of January.

[Col. 1573A] The celebrated parchment manuscripts of the Vienna Library, produced by Bucherius and elucidated by Cardinal Noris, preserve the same sequence of consuls after the epochs of the Syro-Macedonians. They are the work of the fourth century after Christ, as Bucherius indicates and Noris confirms.

### Years of the City and Years of the Cycle

[Col. 1573B]

705, 75 | Marcellus II and Cruscello  
706, 76 | Julius Caesar and Isauricus  
707, 77 | Caesar and Vatinius  
708, 78 | Caesar III and Lepidus  
709, 79 | Caesar IV and alone  
710, 80 | Caesar V and Antoninus

The year of the new Julian arrangement opened on the day of the new moon by the consuls Caesar V and Antonius is therefore year 45 before the common era of Christ. For no year during Caesar’s lifetime and while he governed—or oppressed—the republic, other than this fifth year beginning with the Kalends of January of proleptic year 50, which must necessarily be assigned to the consuls Marcellus and Lentulus by the evidence of the eclipses, placed the conjunction of the luminaries on the Kalends of January of a Julian year.

I shall now undertake to show that the year immediately preceding this one, which Caesar alone marked as consul for the fourth time, was the year called the year of confusion and consisted of 445 days. I shall do this the more willingly because it is our purpose to pursue the restoration of the times, namely, to assign events to the times at which they occurred, from the narratives of contemporary and trustworthy writers.

Several chronologists, and indeed very distinguished ones, have judged otherwise concerning this year of Caesar’s fourth consulship, which I believe I shall demonstrate to have consisted of 445 days. They assert that it was itself the first Julian year, defined as 365 days.

I shall condense what I explained at greater length in the exposition of the *Fasti*, in order to show that from the Kalends of January to its end 445 days must necessarily be counted, with both endpoints included.

Censorinus, *On the Birthday*, chapter 8, is an authoritative witness concerning the number of days completing the year of confusion. He also explains how this was accomplished through two intercalations.

The lunar year used by the Romans consisted of 354 days. To bring its reckoning into agreement with the Sun, an intercalary month called Merkedonius, consisting of 23 days, was inserted from time to time after the month of February, according to the instructions of the pontiffs.

In the year of confusion Caesar, besides the intercalary Merkedonius placed in that location, added two months totaling 68 days between November and December. [Col. 1574B] The total number of days was therefore 445.

Censorinus’s words are:

> The error had gone so far that C. Caesar, as Pontifex Maximus, during his third consulship and that of M. Aemilius Lepidus, inserted two intercalary months of 67 days between the months of November and December, in order to correct the accumulated discrepancy. For he had already intercalated 23 days in February and had made that year consist of 445 days, while also taking precautions for the future so that the error would not recur.

Macrobius assigns 444 days to the year of confusion, book 1, chapter 14, writing as follows:

> Therefore C. Caesar, about to begin the new arrangement, used up all the days that could still produce confusion. As a result, the final year of confusion extended to 444 days.

I attach no importance to the difference of one day in the year of confusion. But I wish to point out that the occasion for assigning the year of confusion to Caesar’s third consulship, with M. Aemilius Lepidus as his colleague, was taken from Censorinus’s words without, as I think, sufficient consideration.

From Censorinus it can be gathered that the decree ordering the use of that double intercalation was established during the consulship of those men. But I do not see that Censorinus’s words imply that the intercalation decreed was inserted in that same year. On the contrary, according to the customary practice of magistracies, it is reasonable to interpret the matter as meaning that the law for removing the confusion was announced during that consulship for the following year.

But conjecture is unnecessary where a demonstration is available from a contemporary writer, and one who was Caesar’s constant companion, Aulus Hirtius. In his book on the Spanish War undertaken by Caesar the dictator in his third dictatorship and designated for his fourth, as he writes at the beginning of the book, he includes not only a history but also an *Ephemeris* of that same year.

Before proceeding, however, it must be noted that Caesar’s third dictatorship is connected in the Capitoline marbles with the year in which Caesar proceeded to his third consulship. Thus we read on the stone still preserved in the Capitol, as published by Marlianus, Aldus, Panvinius, Gruterus, and others, following the consuls Q. Furius Calenus and P. Vatinius:

[Col. 1573]

> C. IVLIVS C. F. C. N. CAESAR III. | M. Aemilius  
> C. IVLIVS C. F. C. N. CAESAR III. | Dictator  
> M. AEMILIUS M. F. Q. N. LEPIDVS | Master of the horse  
> EODEM ANNO | |  
> C. IVLIVS C. F. C. N. CAESAR IIII. | WITHOUT COLLEAGUE

[Col. 1573D] Dio likewise connects these offices in book 43 of his *History*, which he begins as follows:

> In the following year he held both the dictatorship and the consulship for the third time, with M. Lepidus as his colleague.

The Capitoline stone also adds the connection of the fourth consulship with Caesar’s continuing third dictatorship, and indeed in the same year. From this it follows that the date of the renewed dictatorship was different from the date of the renewed consulship. Otherwise the same third dictatorship could not be connected with both the third and fourth consulships.

We have shown elsewhere that the epoch of Caesar’s annual dictatorship was renewed around the month of Quinctilis, when that magistracy had been decreed to him for ten years during the same month, while, after the war in Africa had been completed, he was preparing to return to Italy. Dio and other historians testify to this.

For after setting sail from Africa on the Ides of June, he reached Sardinia on the third day; from there, boarding ships on the seventh day before the Kalends of Quinctilis, he arrived at the city of Rome on the twenty-eighth day. Fran. Fabricius, in his *History of Marcus Tullius Cicero Arranged by Individual Years*, p. 210, accurately gathers these dates from Hirtius and other historians.

The epoch of the consulship, however, which according to ancestral custom ought to have been referred to the Kalends of January, began after the decree of the ten-year dictatorship to be transferred to the year of that same dictatorship from the month of Quinctilis, as though the year belonged to the dictatorship rather than to the consulship.

These observations, briefly drawn from many matters collected and explained by us at greater length in the restoration of the *Fasti* for this year, should suffice to indicate how the marble *Fasti* can be reconciled with the historians, whom even chronologists of the highest standing suspected of disagreeing with them.

Now we return to completing the demonstration of the year of confusion from Hirtius’s *Ephemeris*.

Distinguished men among the chronologists therefore suppose that the year of confusion, which Caesar arranged to extend through the full 444 or 445 days, fell in the year marked by his third consulship and third dictatorship. They suppose that the year immediately following it, in which Caesar held the fourth consulship alone, without a colleague, and spent most of the year on the Spanish expedition, was the first Julian year of the new arrangement, consisting of 365 or 366 days, and that it must be regarded as year 45 before the common era of Christ.

I affirm that Hirtius’s *Ephemeris* contradicts both assertions, as do the celestial movements recorded in it.

I maintain that the year marked by Caesar’s third consulship and third dictatorship, after he departed victorious from Africa, was the year in which, four days after his triumph, having passed numerous laws recorded by Dio in book 43, p. 226 of H. L.’s edition, he also enacted, among other measures, the correction of the calendar to be applied in the following year, when he himself would open the new year in his fourth consulship.

In the Capitoline marble *Fasti*, in that same year marked by the numbers of Caesar’s third consulship and third dictatorship, we read that Q. Fabius Maximus, son of Quintus, grandson of Quintus, entered office as suffect consul, and that, when he died in office, C. Caninius Rebilus, son of Gaius, grandson of Gaius, was substituted in his place.

Dio reports this in book 43, p. 236: Caninius was appointed on the final day of the year for only a few hours and completed his consulship, as Cicero also confirms. Therefore, as Sigonius observes in the *Fasti*, Cicero’s festive saying, which others report together with Macrobius, book 2, as having been uttered about P. Vatinius, is more appropriately assigned to Caninius.

After that day, which thus brought to a close, within a few hours, the year marked by Caninius’s consulship, there follows, on the Kalends of January, the year inscribed as the fourth consulship of Caesar, which he held without a colleague. This year, unlike the others, was called the Year of Confusion. Suetonius, chapter 30, asserts that fifteen months were counted in it: in addition to the customary twelve, three intercalary months were added—one Mercedonius of twenty-three days between February and March, and two others, each of thirty-four days, between November and December, as Censorinus records, affirming that the total number of days counted in that year was 445. After the day that closed this number, on the last day of December, the new year of the Julian arrangement began; Caesar, as consul for the fifth time, opened it on the Kalends of January. I therefore affirm that the beginning of the forty-fifth year before the common era of Christ occurred on the day of the new moon and of the new Julian arrangement, and that in this same year Caesar was murdered by the conspirators in the Curia of Pompey on the Ides of March.

Our demonstration from Hirtius is as follows. Hirtius, Caesar’s companion in the Spanish expedition, writes that Caesar, traveling by forced marches from Rome, and arranging various matters along the way, proceeded to besiege Ategua. He then received the Corduban envoys who approached him, took possession of the town by surrender on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, and was acclaimed imperator. He reviews the events of several days; then he says that the deserters reported that, on the third day before the Nones of March, there had been great fear, and that Atius Varus was in command around the forts. “On that day,” he says, “Pompey moved his camp and took up position in an olive grove near Hispalis. Before Caesar departed for the same place, the moon was seen at approximately the sixth hour.”

Therefore, on the day before the Nones of March, or on the night preceding the Nones of March, the moon was above the horizon at the sixth hour of the night—that is, at midnight.

I oppose the opinion of those chronologists who think that this year, distinguished by Caesar’s Spanish expedition and his fourth consulship, should be placed forty-five years before the common era of Christ, and that it was the first Julian year, completed in 365 or 366 days. Their view is contradicted by Hirtius and by the movements of the moon. For if that year was the forty-fifth Julian year before the common era of Christ, the first of the new arrangement, and if it began with the new moon on the Kalends of January, then the moon must have descended below the horizon on March 6 before the sixth hour of the night. For the moon illuminated on the Kalends of January shows that it was renewed on the Kalends of March; and from the Kalends of March to the night preceding the Nones, within five days, before it had yet approached quadrature, the moon would have descended below the horizon earlier than the sixth hour could be counted.

The calculation demonstrates that on that day and at that hour the sun had traversed the fourteenth degree of Pisces, while the moon was at the twenty-sixth degree of Taurus. The twenty-sixth degree of Taurus reaches the western horizon at Hispalis approximately five hours after the fourteenth degree of Pisces. Therefore, not only could the moon not have been seen when the sixth hour of the night was nearly being counted on that day indicated by Hirtius, but it had also ceased to be visible within the fifth hour; nor could it have shone opportunely for Caesar when he moved his camp.

Our view, however, which makes the Year of Confusion—the year extended by Caesar to 445 days—coincide with his fourth consulship and with the Spanish expedition, agrees remarkably with the moon’s being visible around the sixth hour on the night preceding the Nones of March, as Hirtius indicates. For we maintain, on the authority of Dio, Censorinus, and Macrobius, that the Year of Confusion was arranged so that twenty-three days of Mercedonius were inserted between February and March; sixty-eight days, counted as two extraordinary intercalary months, were inserted in that year between November and December; and the remaining months followed the practice introduced by Tarquinius. According to Censorinus, from March through December there were six hollow months of twenty-nine days and four full months of thirty-one days; January had twenty-nine days and February twenty-eight. Their total completes the 355 days owed to the year of Tarquinius, which the Romans followed until Caesar’s reform.

The days to be counted, therefore, from the day before the Nones of March to the end of that March are twenty-five; April has twenty-nine, May thirty-one, June twenty-nine, July thirty-one, August twenty-nine, September twenty-nine, October thirty-one, November twenty-nine, the two intercalary months sixty-eight, and December twenty-nine. The total number of days is 360.

We therefore know that 360 days intervened in this Year of Confusion from the day before the Nones of March to the end of the year, and to the Kalends of January of the immediately following year, which was to be the first year of the Julian arrangement and was to carry the new moon on the very day of the Kalends, beginning the Julian solar year forty-five years before the common era of Christ. This corresponds to Julian Scaliger’s Period 4669, the twenty-first solar cycle, the fourteenth lunar cycle, and the dominical letter CB, since the year was a leap year.

We need no laborious calculation to determine whether the moon could have been seen above the horizon around the sixth hour of the night—that is, around midnight—on the day before the Nones of March in that same Year of Confusion. Of the 360 days, 18 hours, and 45 minutes remaining until the hour of the new moon on the Kalends of January, which Caesar had fashioned together with the beginning of his era and the Kalends, after twelve mean lunations—namely, 354 days, 8 hours, and 48 minutes—have been subtracted, there remain 6 days, 9 hours, and 57 minutes of the old lunation.

The Nones of March in the Year of Confusion were therefore illuminated by the moon’s last quarter, which had occurred only approximately twenty-three hours before that day. Thus, at the sixth hour of the night—which for the Romans was midnight—the moon’s light would have appeared so close to the eastern horizon that it could have been seen shortly afterward, before the seventh hour, and could have served as a torch for Caesar as he moved his camp, just as Hirtius observed. For the remainder of the night it also provided Caesar’s troops with the greatest possible ease of advance. Moreover, it removed the danger that the darkness of the gloomy night had brought upon the Pompeians, who had shortly before been deceived when Caesar’s cavalry passed through their defenses and was admitted into Corduba, as Caesar had wished. The force of the storm that had arisen had produced such darkness that each soldier could scarcely distinguish the man nearest to him. Hirtius reports this on page 32 of the Aldine edition.

We can also gather from the sequence of events carried out by Caesar before the Nones of March in that same year, when he departed for Spain, that a month of Mercedonius consisting of twenty-three days was intercalated between February and March, and consequently that this was the year we call the Year of Confusion, extended to 445 days.

Appian of Alexandria, a contemporary writer, relates in book II of the *Civil Wars* that Caesar departed from Rome for Spain while holding his fourth consulship (*τέταρτον ὑπατεύων*, “serving as consul for the fourth time”), and reached his men after twenty-seven days, having traversed a long route with a very large army. Dio, however, is witness that Caesar had only a very small number of companions on this rapid journey, in book XLIII, page 229: “Meanwhile Caesar reached Spain with a few men, etc., for he had left the greater part of his soldiers behind.”

The speed of Caesar’s journey must therefore be referred to his passage through Italy and through the provinces of Gaul devoted to him, which he traversed within twenty-seven days. But once he had reached the borders of Spain, where most people favored Pompey’s cause—especially throughout inland Spain, which had joined itself to Pompey, as Dio states in the passage cited—Caesar, Appian says, brought his soldiers into battle more slowly. Nearly the whole extent of Further and Nearer Spain still remained for him to traverse before he could proceed from Tarraconensis to the borders of Baetica and arrive at the siege of Corduba and Hispalis.

If we follow Hirtius and Dio, a swift courier bringing the news of Caesar’s victory at Munda to Rome in the following month required thirty-three days. For it is established from Hirtius that the battle of Munda, and Caesar’s victory there, occurred on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April, that is, March 17, and that the message sent from there reached Rome on the day before the Palilia, that is, April 20. If at least seven days were required for the courier to traverse the Spanish territory—as we may allow twenty-seven days for the remaining journey from the Spanish borders to Rome—then Caesar, leading an army for the most part through hostile territory, must have required considerably more time.

Let us therefore suppose that Caesar, after the Kalends of January, on which he ordered the consular fasces of his fourth consulship to be carried before him in Rome, immediately devoted himself on the following day to the journey to Spain. He would have reached the borders of Tarraconensis on January 28. When he arrived there, “he informed his legates Quintus Pedius and Quintus Fabius Maximus of his arrival, and ordered them to send him the cavalry they had raised for him from the province,” says Hirtius. Several days must have been spent in sending the letters and receiving the replies with the cavalry. Once Caesar had been informed that the reinforcement had arrived, he led the army from there toward the Baetis. If this was done as rapidly as possible—for Appian writes that he brought the soldiers out more slowly—the troops would reach Caesar within ten or fifteen days.

At that point it was first necessary to remove Gnaeus Pompey from the siege of Ulla. For this reason Caesar himself advanced to attack Corduba. On the journey, “when he had come to the river Baetis,” in Hirtius’s words, “and was unable to cross because of the river’s depth, he threw down baskets filled with stones; after thus constructing a bridge, he led the troops across to the camp in three divisions.”

Meanwhile Gnaeus Pompey, summoned by letters from his brother, moved from Ulla to Corduba and placed his camp opposite Caesar’s. Both sides undertook works to seize the bridge: “from this contest,” Hirtius says, “minor daily battles arose, so that now one side, now the other, withdrew victorious.”

Everyone can see that, after the month of January had been spent in the rapid advance toward Spain and at least half of February in assembling and leading the troops to the Baetis, the remainder of the month was consumed by these daily skirmishes. After this, Caesar spent several days trying to draw the enemy into open country. At last he advanced to besiege Ategua. Hirtius counts ten days of that siege, reporting the events of each day individually. After the tenth and final day, he says: “Thus, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, the imperator took possession of the town.”

A single month of February does not contain as many days as are required to complete this count. Nevertheless, Caesar and Pompey had accomplished all these things before the eleventh day before the Kalends of March. Who, then, cannot see that, after January and February, an intercalary month of Mercedonius was also inserted into this year before the Kalends of March?

From the eleventh day before the Kalends of March—which was the fourteenth day of that Mercedonius—Hirtius’s *Ephemeris* enumerates the following eight days individually, and only then reaches March. The historian writes:

“In the following period, when our men were carelessly dispersed in the work, it was reported by deserters that on the third day before the Nones of March a battle was taking place at Soritia, etc. On that day Pompey moved his camp and took up position in an olive grove near Hispalis. Before Caesar departed for the same place, the moon was seen at approximately the sixth hour.”

Either I am mistaken, or no demonstration of the time is more evident than this: that the year is shown by so many indications of celestial movements, and by such a quantity and reckoning of nearly every individual day, to have contained a month of Mercedonius before the Kalends of March and two extraordinary intercalary months, totaling sixty-eight days, between November and December. Only thus do we arrive, after the year of Caesar’s fourth consulship and fourth dictatorship had been extended to 445 days, at the Kalends of January of the new Julian arrangement, forty-five complete Julian years before the common era of Christ, with both the true and mean new moon appearing to us on the very day on which the first Julian year began, as we explained above.

I have thought it necessary to transcribe these two sections from my *Opusculum de Reparatione temporum*, not only to illuminate that chronological summary which Schelestratius aptly derived from the consulship of Ceionius Rufus Albinus and from his Capitolian inscription—an inscription that, for this very consulship, which closed the pontificate of Silvester on the final day of the year, counts 380 years, or 380 and 1, after the Caesarian period—but also to provide support for the whole chronology contained in the notes of this volume, from the Caesarian period to the end of the mortal life of blessed Silvester.

The entire extent and measurement of that period seems to me to be confirmed on every side by the most certain documents available in chronological matters: namely, demonstrations from celestial movements, which in the eclipses cited plainly require this span of time; inscriptions on stones; writings of contemporaries belonging to the same age; and the agreement of learned men numbered among the more authoritative historians and chronologists.

Having therefore established these two temporal boundaries for this volume, let us close its chronological notes together with the *Life of Silvester* and the Peace of the Church. In the next volume, if God grants it, we shall attempt, with equal certainty and clarity, to determine both the total span of time and the lives of the individual pontiffs according to our ability, once it has become clear that these matters have not displeased the learned.

## HISTORICAL NOTES

**Line 4.**—He was in exile on Mount Soracte, shaken by the persecution of Constantine, and later, returning in glory, baptized Constantine Augustus.

I might be thought to be laboring over what has already been done if I wished to touch upon the question, previously discussed by many distinguished authors, concerning the baptism of Constantine the Great. One may consult two full pages on each side in Baronius, who argues in favor of the baptism administered to him at Rome by Silvester, as the Librarian asserts together with the second catalogue from the age of Justinian; and in the authors who oppose Baronius, indicated by Pagius in the *Critica* and by the other Pagius in the notes to this entry. Thinking that Eusebius should be followed, the latter declares that the grace of baptism was conferred upon Constantine at Nicomedia.

The matter is full of difficulties. The *Acts of Silvester*, which favor a Roman baptism, are condemned by everyone and are themselves presented by Baronius as interpolated and stuffed with inept additions. Eusebius’s history, which supports the case for a baptism at Nicomedia, is dismissed as having been composed by an author devoted to the Arians and bent toward the character of the Arian prince Constantius. Even the testimony of more reliable writers is said to have been corrupted in the names by copyists. Such is the case with Athanasius’s work *On the Synods*, which was set against Baronius; its defenders, however, reply that in Athanasius’s manuscripts one ought to read *Constantena*, not *Constantinum*. See Pagius in the *Critica* on Baronius, year 324, no. 5. There one will also find that the supporters of both opinions interpret the words of Ambrose and Jerome—words sufficiently clear for neither side—as favoring their respective position. Numerous passages in the works of Zosimus, Socrates, and Sozomen are likewise called into question, both by Baronius, who carefully examined them, and by those who wrote after Baronius.

Critics presume that no equal testimony can be set against Eusebius, a writer of Constantine’s age who lived in his company and makes this assertion, from interpolated *Acts* composed later by Latins according to the Roman point of view. Yet, by good fortune for history, the *Chronography* of John Malalas, an Antiochene writer composed in the sixth century under Justinian, came to light not long ago. It presents the history of the baptism administered at Rome to Constantine the Great by Pope Silvester without any inserted additions. And, what must be judged equally significant, it also presents the account of what happened at Nicomedia near the end of Constantine’s life in an unadorned form. Nor did Malalas fabricate it on his own authority; rather, he faithfully copied it from an older chronographer named Nestorianus. The *Chronicle* called Alexandrian also mentions him, as Vossius observes in *On Greek Historians*.

Thus, at the beginning of book XIII of his *Chronography*, after recounting the vision of the cross and the victory won by the great Constantine under its auspices, the Antiochene writer Malalas records the victorious prince’s entry into the city of Rome and the law he issued that Christian churches should be opened everywhere.

“Then,” he says, “after he had fasted and had been instructed in the rudiments of the Christian religion, he himself was baptized together with his mother Helena by Silvester, the Roman bishop. All his relatives and friends were also baptized, as was an immense multitude of other Romans. Thus the emperor Constantine became a Christian.”

He then enumerates the deeds of that same prince: the magistracies he established; the prefects of the praetorium appointed by him from among Christians for the East; the provinces he organized; Constantinople, which he founded and adorned; other cities that he restored; the city of Helenopolis, founded in his mother’s name; and the province of Helenopontus, which received its name from her.

He then adds:

“Not long afterward”—that is, after these cities and provinces had been established—“the emperor Constantine, having traveled to Nicomedia in Bithynia, fell ill. After he had lain sick for six days, he died in a suburb of that same city called Achyron, not far from the city, before he had brought to completion that magnificent work, reckoned among the wonders of the world, namely, the construction of the church of Antioch. He died at the age of sixty years and three months, as the most wise chronographer Nestorianus has handed down to memory. He also described in his *Chronicle* the deeds of the aforementioned emperors.”

We therefore possess a witness sufficiently close to Constantine, neither attached to Eusebius nor to the Western Latin writers, who records without inserted additions the history of the baptism received by Constantine, Helena, and their relatives in the city of Rome, administered by Pope Silvester. He also records Constantine’s death at Nicomedia, after his mother Helena had long since died, and after the city and province had received the names Helenopolis and Helenopontus.

I have called him a witness sufficiently close to Constantine because he lived in the fifth century and extended his history to the year 474 of the Christian era, the year of the death of Leo the Younger, as Malalas himself testifies at the end of book XII, a point noted by Cardinal Norisius in *On the Syro-Macedonian Eras*, page 174 of the Leipzig edition.

I hope this testimony will be received more willingly if I demonstrate that, from this bare and brief account of the chronographer, it is possible to reconcile the assertions of our Latin writers concerning the baptism administered at Rome by Silvester, together with the laying on of hands, with the sacrament of confirmation conferred upon the emperor Constantine by Eusebius, bishop of Nicomedia, near the end of his life, when the solemn baptism was to be administered on the very eve of Pentecost—not to Constantine, who had already been baptized at Rome, but to many who had been converted to the Christian faith.

I therefore say that, from the chronographer preserved for us by Malalas and from the testimonies of other writers produced on both sides in the celebrated question concerning the place and time of Constantine’s baptism, the following may be gathered. This prince, divinely called to the light of the true faith by the heavenly sign of the cross and by the victory won against Maxentius, after he entered Rome as victor in the year 312, began to consider professing the Christian religion. He immediately arranged for its rudiments to be taught to him by priests summoned to him for that purpose, as the Nestorian chronographer clearly relates through Malalas, in agreement with Eusebius in book I, chapters 32 and 42, of the *Life of Constantine*.

Indeed, in chapter 32 Eusebius relates that Constantine, following the first vision of the cross and the appearance of Christ the Lord, before he led out his standards against Maxentius, “resolved to worship no other God except the one whom he had seen. For this reason he summoned priests to himself, men instructed in the mysteries of that secret teaching. From them he learned the Christian catechesis and received instruction concerning the unity of God, the coming of Christ, its causes, and his triumph over death, which had been shown to him beforehand in the sign of the cross. When he had compared that heavenly vision with the interpretation of the priests’ words, he was confirmed in mind, holding it certain that the knowledge of these things had been imparted to him by God himself. From then on he began to devote himself to the reading of the divine books; and, having taken priests of God as his companions and advisers, he judged that the God whom he had seen was to be worshiped with every form of devotion.”

The Greek text reads: **τὸν ὀφθέντα Θεὸν πάσαις δεῖν ᾤετο θεραπείαις τιμᾷν**, “he judged that the God whom he had seen ought to be honored with every form of worship.”

“After this, fortified by the good hope that he had placed in Him, he undertook to extinguish the fire of tyrannical fury.”

The expedition and victory against Maxentius in the year 312 follow.

In chapter 42 of the same book, where Eusebius continues his account of the events of the following years, he mentions bishops and other ministers of God summoned by Constantine. He says that they were not merely admitted to his table but were taken with him wherever he traveled, and that he sat among them in synods, as he states in chapter 44. This occurred before he celebrated his decennalia, which falls in the year 316, as he says in chapter 48.

The emperor did not cease to use this company of priests of God, which had remained at his side for an entire decade from that first apparition, even according to Eusebius’s testimony, until his quindecennalia, which must be assigned to the year 321. For Eusebius, who in his *Chronicle* records the persecution of Licinius in the year 320, when Christians were expelled from the palace, states in book II, chapter 3, of the *Life of Constantine* that, because of that persecution and to suppress the tyrannical oppression raised against the faithful, the pious prince Constantine undertook war against Licinius.

He relates that the expedition began under these auspices in chapter 4:

“And since he understood that he needed prayers more than ever before, he took the priests of God with him, judging that they ought to be present and to accompany him as the best guardians of his soul.”

As this second five-year period passed, during which Constantine, largely free from war, organized the western provinces recovered from Licinius after the earlier victory celebrated in his decennalia, he was sufficiently instructed in the mysteries of our religion through the divine Scriptures, which he eagerly read and which were explained to him daily by the ministers of God whom he had made his table companions and advisers.

Who can believe that a prince who had already resolved that the God whom God himself had enjoined upon humankind ought to be worshiped with every form of devotion, as Eusebius says, and who had understood from the servants and ministers of God over a decade that the first and necessary means to eternal salvation is that we be duly washed in baptism administered into Christ’s death, and be made from enemies of God into adopted sons and coheirs of Christ—who, I say, can believe that the pious prince did anything other than what Malalas reports from the ancient and illustrious chronographer Nestorianus: namely, that baptism was received, administered by Pope Silvester, both by Constantine Augustus and by his mother Helena, as well as by their relatives, household members, and friends?

It follows that the other matter related by the same historian, and confirmed by the very walls, also occurred: basilicas were erected everywhere in the chief cities of the empire, especially at Rome and in the region immediately around the city, and in Syria.

Constantine had wished to receive the sacrament of baptism with solemn rites in the river Jordan, the place chosen by our Savior to provide us an example and to indicate the symbol of another baptism instituted by him, when he wished to be baptized by John the Forerunner, in order to sanctify John’s baptism, as Saint Ambrose transmits in his commentary on chapter I of Luke’s Gospel.

The emperor, near death, offered testimony to this desire that he had previously cherished in the address he delivered to the bishops summoned by him, as Eusebius narrates in book IV, chapter 62, of the *Life of Constantine*. The address occurred in the year 338 of the common era, when, after celebrating Easter at Constantinople with the other faithful, as chapter 60 relates, Constantine departed for Helenopolis and began to fall ill in Bithynia.

“There, after spending a long time in the temple of the martyrs, he offered supplications and prayers to God. When he felt that the final day of his life was already approaching, he at last thought that the time had come to expiate the sins of his entire life. Firmly believing that whatever he had sinned as a human being could be completely wiped away by the efficacy of the mysterious words and the saving washing, he fell prostrate on the ground with bended knee and humbly asked God for pardon, confessing his sins in the very shrine of the martyrs, where he first deserved to receive the laying on of hands together with solemn prayer.”

Many think that this testimony of Eusebius overturns the history of the baptism administered at Rome to Constantine Augustus by Silvester and is believed to establish the opinion of those who are convinced—and try to persuade others to maintain with them—that the emperor received baptism at Nicomedia at the end of his life.

For Eusebius adds at the passage cited:

“From there he went down to the suburbs of Nicomedia, summoned the bishops, and addressed them as follows,” and so forth.

He explains the pious desire I mentioned earlier, which Constantine had once cherished: to receive the saving sign in the river Jordan. But, by God’s providence, the solemn ceremonies had to be performed there where Constantine then was, namely, in the suburb of Nicomedia. The bishops did not delay carrying this out.

“For the pious prince, having been granted the divine sign”—**θείας σφραγῖδος ἀξιούμενος**, “being deemed worthy of the divine seal”—“was clothed in white and royal garments radiant like light, and reclined upon a brilliantly white bed. For the few days he survived thereafter, until Pentecost Sunday, he no longer wished to touch purple, and on that day he died peacefully in Christ.”

Yet when I carefully weigh these testimonies of Eusebius, a view very different from theirs remains with me. Eusebius does not appear to contradict Nestorianus and Malalas, who clearly relate that baptism was administered at Rome. Nor does he speak here of baptism, but of two sacraments of the Church distinct from the washing of baptism, although one of them is called the perfection of baptism—namely, confirmation—and the other a kind of second baptism, or a second plank for escaping shipwreck—namely, penance.

These two sacraments, suitable for those already initiated through baptism—namely, the sacrament of confirmation and the sacrament of penance—seem, if I understand correctly, to be indicated by Eusebius in the words quoted. Indeed, Constantine himself seems in that address to the bishops to indicate the reason for postponing his reception of the sacrament of confirmation until that day, and in a certain sense to excuse the delay as arising from a reasonable cause. He signified that, from his first conversion to Christ, a desire had arisen in him to receive the washing of regeneration in the place where Christ the Lord, by his example and power, had sanctified the waters of the Jordan.

A religious prince is seized by the pious desire to receive the sacrament of baptism in the Jordan as soon as he has heard from Silvester and the other priests, from the Gospel history, that there the voice of the Father was heard proclaiming the beloved Son of the Father, through whom we are adopted; that there the divine Spirit appeared visibly over him in the form of a dove, in whom we cry together, “Abba, Father.”

But Silvester would not have failed in the duty of a provident shepherd by explaining to the faithful Constantine that he could indulge this devotional desire wherever no danger to eternal salvation arose from delay, but that those things which the Lord’s command had declared necessary for salvation could neither be delayed nor ought to be delayed.

Silvester would have shown the prince that the sacrament of baptism, necessary for salvation, must be diligently sought wherever suitable catechesis had instructed the mind of the adult recipient so that he might receive it devoutly. He could point to the example of Philip the deacon, who baptized the eunuch of Queen Candace on the road, and of the apostle Peter, who immediately ordered water to be brought and at once baptized Cornelius and his companions, who believed in Christ so fully that they spoke in tongues.

He would have shown that it would be a sacrilege fraught with danger to delay the reception of divine grace on the pretext of receiving the saving washing in that river where the memory of Christ’s deeds might intensify devotion, while the soul remained soiled and exposed to sin.

The reception of the other sign, if he wished it, could indeed be postponed until that place where, through the sacrament of confirmation, we are anointed as athletes of Christ. If the prince desired this, with hope of obtaining more abundant grace from that disposition through the second sacrament of the Christian profession—by which we are strengthened in the grace already received through baptism and obtain the gifts of the divine Spirit and the sevenfold virtue—Silvester would not have opposed the pious wish of Augustus, once he had secured the central matter through the reception of the first grace of baptism.

There were also examples among the apostles of their sending bishops to confer the sign of confirmation upon those who had long before become Christians through baptism. And, as a matter of episcopal prudence, the sacrament of chrism was not always administered immediately to adults emerging from the baptismal washing; rather, time was sometimes granted for increasing the grace already received through exercises of virtue, so that those thus prepared might obtain more abundantly what was given in confirmation.

The pious desire of Constantine, converted to Christ, should therefore be granted in that respect which would postpone confirmation until his arrival at the Jordan, with the hope that his mind might be prepared to receive the gifts of the Spirit more abundantly, provided that the other part of the counsel did not falter—namely, that the grace necessary for salvation should be sought without delay through the reception of baptism.

Instructed by these teachings, Constantine asked Silvester for baptism and obtained it without any delay after suitable catechesis. Silvester did not dissent from the postponement of confirmation, which he judged could, in accordance with the prince’s wish and with benefit, be deferred until Constantine’s arrival in Palestine and at the bank of the Jordan.

Constantine seems to me to have indicated this justification of the postponed confirmation to the bishops summoned to him, as Eusebius relates, when he was seized by illness while making his way to Palestine. In my judgment, that was where the emperor was hastening when he stopped at Nicomedia. When illness overtook him and he foresaw that he would not reach Palestine, he did not wish to depart this life without being fortified by the other sign of Christ, by which we are confirmed.

For the Greeks likewise call the sacrament of confirmation the **θεία σφραγίς**, “the divine seal,” and here Eusebius is speaking of it. Likewise, among them and among us chrism, a gift of baptism, is called the divine seal.

I therefore maintain that Eusebius does not oppose the account of Nestorianus and Malalas concerning the baptism received by Constantine at Rome; rather, he opposes interpreters who approach Eusebius’s words with preconceived judgments. I say that Eusebius presents Constantine as confirmed, not baptized, at Nicomedia: he had already been washed in the saving baptism of Christ at Rome by Silvester.

He certainly received the divine seal—**θεῖαν σφραγῖδα**—at Nicomedia, since he was prevented from reaching Palestine and the waters of the Jordan, where he had long desired to receive the gifts of the Holy Spirit through the anointing of chrism. He was confirmed by a bishop officiating at Nicomedia—not, however, by Eusebius, the Arian bishop of Nicomedia, but by that one among the Catholic bishops whom the pious emperor, by appointment of Pope Silvester, took with him as a father and guide of his life after he had been baptized at Rome by Silvester.

This was no different from the way in which the holy presbyter Simplicianus was sent from Rome to Milan to guide blessed Ambrose in episcopal government and ecclesiastical discipline, by delegation of the holy pontiff Damasus, immediately after Ambrose, previously a catechumen, had been elected to the episcopate of that church, as I observed elsewhere together with Cardinal Baronius under the year 374, when I was discussing the practice of bishops’ employing vicars in the fourth century of Christ.

I have already demonstrated from Eusebius that Constantine brought several bishops with him in his entourage, both so that he might draw from them, through daily exposition of the sacred books, instruction in the precepts of the divine law, and so that he might more readily establish in newly added regions [Col. 1584A], enlarged by Constantine’s victories, those whom the supreme pontiff had designated to instruct the peoples in the faith. From the authorities cited I have proved that he was by no means baptized by an Arian. Nor does anyone record that Constantine received any other sacraments from the Arians, except for those defective testimonies which the Arians distorted from Eusebius in favor of Constantius, his son, as I indicated above and as has already been stated in the notes of Labbe inserted under this number.

Before confirmation, however, since he was an adult, he had to be cleansed by another sacrament, which we metaphorically call a second washing—namely, the sacrament of penance; indeed, Saint Augustine also calls it the “daily washing,” as Morinus notes, *De Poenitentia*, book V, chapter 31, no. 15 and following. That this rite had properly preceded Constantine’s reception of confirmation is declared so clearly by Eusebius’s words that no room for doubt remains for those who consider them attentively.

For what does Eusebius record Constantine having done “when he felt that the last day of his life was already approaching and judged that the time had come when he should [Col. 1584B] expiate the sins of his entire life”? He aroused the whole force of his own faith and ours, “firmly believing that whatever he had sinned in human life was entirely to be erased by the efficacy of the mysterious words and by the salutary washing.” He reflected upon this and, with his assent to the faith renewed, steadfastly held that, by the power imparted by Christ the Lord to the sacraments instituted by him, those two sacraments—called by our theologians the sacraments of the dead, namely baptism and penance—were capable of utterly removing all the sins of life: the one being administered through the efficacy of the mysterious words, and the other through the efficacy of the mysterious words together with the salutary washing.

And since Christ forbade the salutary washing of baptism to be repeated, while he graciously permitted the healing of the mysterious words—or the spiritual washing of penance—to be renewed and applied, according to the needs of the faithful, both seven times and seventy times seven, Constantine, understanding that this alone remained available to him, since he had long before been baptized, duly received it at Nicomedia for the expiation of all the sins of his life. Thus [Col. 1584C] cleansed, he could approach the sacrament of chrism, which, as we indicated with Eusebius, he had postponed in the hope of receiving it on the banks of the Jordan. Therefore “he fell prostrate upon the ground with bent knee, humbly asking pardon from God and confessing his sins in the very place of martyrdom.”

None of this concerns baptism; everything concerns the sacrament of penance. The same is true of the administration of the sacrament that follows: “In that place he first deserved to receive the laying on of hands with solemn prayer.” No one is unaware that among the ancient rites of the administration of penance, especially public penance, the laying on of hands was included: priests placed their hands upon the head of the penitents with a solemn outpouring of prayers.

Morinus clearly teaches that, after the Novatian heresy, this apostolic discipline was restored, especially for penitents of the third station, which they call *substratio*. See Morinus, *De Poenitentia*, book VI, chapter 8, and book IX, chapter 9. There, on the basis of testimonies of the Fathers of the third and fourth centuries and even of canons older than the [Col. 1584D] Council of Nicaea, he confirms the practice which Eusebius’s text here indicates Constantine observed.

The emperor, eager for eternal salvation, wished to imitate and undergo a certain form of public penance, and, once cleansed, to approach the sacrament of Confirmation, whose postponement has been explained, so that he might be fortified as he hastened toward the final struggle of life. There were indeed reasons why he should ask that the errors of his entire life be erased through such a public reception of penance. Perhaps he regarded as requiring healing by something more than a private rite of penance—by a public confession before the Church—the murder of his innocent son Crispus, as well as deeds of this kind which he seemed to himself to have committed either rashly, seized by anger, or impetuously driven by the goad of jealousy, hastening toward vengeance rather than judgment.

The pagan writer Zosimus, book II, chapter 29, records that the prince regarded the gravity of his offenses in such a way that he adds a slander [Col. 1585A] against his penance, writing that Constantine attempted to cleanse the sins of his entire life through the pagan purifications called *lustricae*. Since none of the priests of the gods was willing to provide these purifications for him, Zosimus says that, on the advice of an Egyptian, he arranged to seek them among the Christians.

The twenty full years which the emperor had already spent with Christian bishops and other priests sufficiently refute the slander of a writer hostile no less to the Christian name than to the prince who asserted and advanced the Christian faith. During that time he conferred with them daily concerning the manner of divine worship and its mysteries. He therefore could not have been unaware that the remedy of the sacrament of penance had been prepared by the mercy of Christ for those who sinned after receiving baptism and lamented their faults.

Although Zosimus’s slander thus imagines that the Christian emperor sought false and detestable remedies, it nevertheless suggests that the pious prince had aroused within himself a true and severe judgment upon his life.

[Col. 1585B] It is therefore not surprising that Zosimus, with equal shamelessness, slandered the public confession of the penitent prince as a pagan superstition, and that later Arians attempted, by a different slander, to draw it over to their own side. Zosimus was not ashamed to invent that the pious prince, eager to abolish his crime, had turned to the *taurobolia* and other such impious purifications, seeking them from the initiates of demons. This crime was afterward actually committed by Julian, the most impious apostate, with whom Zosimus, as with a fellow initiate, sang in harmony.

The Arians likewise were not ashamed to turn Constantine’s true penance into a false repetition of baptism, in order to please his impious son Constantius. They thought that Constantius, drawn into their heresy, would more willingly approach the sacrilegious reception of baptism administered by the Arians if he should see and believe that he himself, following his father’s example, ought to repeat it.

What, then, Eusebius of Caesarea wrote—whether concerning the mystical washing of penance [Col. 1585C] received by Constantine at Nicomedia, or concerning Constantine’s confession of the crimes committed during his life—was that Christ the Lord had instituted in the sacraments two purifications: one to be repeated through the mysterious words, namely in the absolution of the confessing and penitent person; the other not to be repeated, through word and washing, in baptism. They distorted this into a false repetition of baptism attributed to Constantine the father, so that they might persuade Constantius the son to undertake a genuine and sacrilegious repetition, or boast that the practice they themselves were already administering had been derived from the authority of this superior example.

I see that some writers are so convinced of the Arians’ frauds that they suspect this very passage of Eusebius to have been deliberately mutilated by them in book III of *The Life of Constantine*, chapter 7. Pagius the Younger, following Peter de Marca, held this opinion in the *Breviary of the Deeds of Saint Sylvester*, no. 21, p. 77. Gelasius of Cyzicus, however, in book II of his *History of the Council of Nicaea*, chapter 5, declares that he transcribed from the indicated passage and [Col. 1585D] chapter of Eusebius the following words, which are now missing from Eusebius:

> “For Hosius himself, distinguished among the Spaniards for the renown of his name and reputation, who held the place of Sylvester, bishop of great Rome, was present at that assembly together with the Roman priests Victor and Vincent and many others.”

Moreover, Pagius the Younger doubts whether the text of Eusebius has been interpolated in other places as well. For in the *Life of Saint Fabian*, no. 4, after suspecting that many fabulous elements had been added to the Acts of Saint Pontius, he turns to the text of Eusebius, about which he writes as follows:

> “As for Eusebius, either his History was interpolated by someone, just as his Chronicle was by Jerome, or at any rate he was deceived by false reports. For in the Chronicle he assumes that, at the celebration of Philip’s secular games, many things redolent of paganism were performed; this plainly conflicts with the narrative of the sixth book of his History, where”—namely, in book VI, chapter 36—“he asserts that Philip was a Christian. Jerome drew this from Eusebius in [Col. 1586A] his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the section on Origen, writing as follows: ‘Who does not know that, when requested, he came to Antioch to Mamaea, the mother of the emperor Alexander, a religious woman, and was received with the highest honor, and that he wrote letters to the emperor Philip, who was the first of the Roman emperors to be a Christian, and to his mother—letters which exist to this day?’”

Pagius adds:

> “As for Vincent of Lérins, Cassiodorus, and the others who were convinced that Philip was a Christian, they were led into error by Paulus Orosius, who himself was deceived, as I shall immediately show,” and so forth.

If these things are true, I do not see why certain critics cited by Cave should be surprised that, in the decree of Pope Gelasius, the History of Eusebius is listed among the apocrypha. It was not placed in that category because they thought that most of what Eusebius reported was alien to the truth or had not been written by Eusebius. Rather, there was a legitimate reason to doubt whether something had been inserted into the genuine text of Eusebius’s History by Arians or [Col. 1586B] Donatists, since these authors mutter that both of Eusebius’s works had been interpolated, namely both the *Chronicle* and the *History*.

But as for corruption of the Eusebian text, at least in this part of the History of the Life of Constantine, which was produced just above by advocates of the Nicomedian baptism, I myself make no complaint; indeed, I do not even suspect it. I complain only of the prejudiced interpretation and distortion of the same statement. The occasion for this was, as Pagius noted concerning Orosius, the use of a transferred expression or metaphor according to the discipline of the secret teaching, which prevailed in that age whenever the sacraments were being discussed. Eusebius’s statements concerning Constantine’s reception of the salutary washing of penance—administered to the prince confessing the sins of his entire life through mysterious words and the laying on of hands with solemn prayer by priests—were carelessly referred to baptism. Likewise, the divine seal mentioned by Eusebius and conferred upon Constantine by the bishop of Nicomedia was interpreted as baptism, although it must be understood as chrism, or the sacrament [Col. 1586C] of Confirmation.

I believe I can demonstrate that Eusebius’s statement must be interpreted in this way. Unless it is explained thus, one would have to admit that Eusebius in the *History of the Life of Constantine* contradicts himself in writing elsewhere, both in the *Chronicle* and in the *Ecclesiastical History*. In the latter he asserts, in book VI, chapter 34, that the emperor Philip was a Christian. He states the same thing in the *Chronicle*, under the first year of Philip’s reign, the fourth year of the 255th Olympiad, writing:

> “Philip makes his son Philip his partner in the kingdom, and was the first of all the Roman emperors to be a Christian.”

Since Eusebius reports this both in his *Ecclesiastical History* and in his *Chronicle*, how could he write in the aforementioned book IV of the *Life of Constantine*, chapters 61 and 62, about the sacraments received at Nicomedia and then add these words?

> “Thus Constantine alone among all the emperors who ever existed was reborn and renewed in the martyries of Christ, and, endowed with the divine [Col. 1586D] seal, rejoiced in spirit; he was renewed and filled with divine light.”

If these words mean nothing but baptism, how could Constantine alone among the emperors have been endowed with the divine seal, if, nearly a whole century before Constantine, Philip had been the first of the Roman emperors to be baptized and made a Christian, according to Eusebius? The historian contradicts himself if in both places he is speaking only of the seal of baptism.

But if we understand the divine seal—*θείαν σφραγῖδα*—and the “perfect safeguard” (*τέλειον φυλακτήριον*) conferred upon him at Nicomedia as the sacrament of Confirmation, preceded by the sacrament of penance—which, according to the historian, the emperor Philip is not said to have performed—then the two statements of Eusebius are reconciled. Philip was the first among the Roman emperors, in Eusebius’s account, to become a Christian through baptism; and Constantine the Great was the only emperor, up to Eusebius’s own age, to have publicly professed penance according to the Christian rite, to have been cleansed in that sacrament through the mysterious words of the priests, and to have received from the bishop, through the sacrament of Confirmation, the gifts of the Holy [Col. 1587A] Spirit: the divine seal, *θείαν σφραγῖδα*, and the perfect protection of the soul, *τέλειον φυλακτήριον*.

Here one should add the notes of the learned Hugo Menard in his *Sacramentary of Saint Gregory the Great*, especially pp. 129 and 110. While proving there that the power and rite of administering chrism had been handed down by the apostles to bishops, just as the apostles themselves had received them from Christ the Lord, he writes:

> “Indeed, it is shown that this practice existed in the time of the apostles, as is well known from the history which Eusebius reports from Clement of Alexandria in book III of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 17. There, concerning a certain bishop who had baptized a young man entrusted to him by Saint John the Apostle, he writes: *ὡς τὸ τέλειον αὐτῷ φυλακτήριον ἐπιστήσας τὴν σφραγῖδα τοῦ Κυρίου*—that is, ‘having sealed him with the seal of the Lord as a perfect safeguard of his soul.’ This can be understood in no other way than of chrismation, which, because it is performed in the form of a cross upon the forehead, as will be said later, is rightly called the seal of the Lord. Likewise, in the *Epitome of the Life of Saint [Col. 1587B] Athanasius* in Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, no. 258: *τούτους ἐπιχρίσας διὰ τῆς ἐκ Χριστῷ σφραγῖδος ἐτελέμοσεν*—that is, ‘having anointed them with Christ’s seal, he confirmed them.’ For the passage concerns those boys baptized by Athanasius when he was still a boy, to whom Saint Alexander the pontiff afterward administered the sacrament of Confirmation.”

See him at the cited place, and observe the same phrase that he uses in the *Life of Athanasius*, just as Eusebius uses it of Constantine’s chrism. In the *Life of Cyprian*, the deacon Pontius describes those confessors of Christ who had been confirmed with chrism as marked with a second inscription, the mark of their foreheads. See above Bencini’s notes on Marcellus, line 9: “Thus around.”

Nothing, therefore, is discordant or contradictory in the texts of Eusebius when they are understood in this way. Nor do the accounts preserved by the clearest testimonies of the Nestorian chronicler, transmitted in Malalas and written in the century immediately following the time in which Eusebius wrote, conflict with them. Those testimonies explicitly state that Constantine was baptized in the city of Rome [Col. 1587C] together with his mother Helena and with several members of his household and friends.

Once Constantine’s and his mother Helena’s baptism in the city of Rome is admitted, the whole chronology and history of Eusebius proceeds correctly. It would certainly be thrown into confusion if what has thus far been explained concerning the penance and chrism received at Nicomedia were distorted into an account of baptism there.

As for Helena Augusta, Constantine’s mother, the Nestorian testifies that she was baptized together with her son. She certainly could not have postponed receiving the sacrament of baptism until the year 338, the year of Constantine’s death, since long before that she had departed to the Lord, full of merits. Eusebius himself describes her dying in the presence of and attended by her son Constantine—plainly at Rome, where her tomb near the cemetery of Saints Peter and Marcellinus is preserved in the Lateran patriarchate and is described by the illustrious Ciampini, together with the mausoleum constructed for her by Constantine three miles from the city on the Via Labicana.
