The Bibliothecary confirms this below, in no. 43 of this *Life of Sylvester*, with testimonies of the ancients, also [Col. 1587D] considered by Valesius in his notes on book V, chapter 47, of Eusebius’s *Life of Constantine.

See Ciampini, *On the Sacred Buildings Constructed by Constantine the Great*, chapter 8. This was after Helena, already advanced in age, had undertaken—as Eusebius reports in book III, chapter 42—a sacred pilgrimage to Jerusalem. There she fulfilled all the duties of Christian piety, praying and searching for the instruments of our redemption, and also set forth magnificent examples of generosity by erecting churches to God at royal expense. Returning from that pilgrimage, she lived for a long time afterward in the city of Rome, while the imperial city of Constantinople was not yet completed.

The same chronicler copied by Malalas, writing in the century immediately following Constantine, explicitly reports that this pilgrimage and search for the Lord’s cross were undertaken by his mother at Constantine’s urging. He says in book XIII, p. 5 of the Oxford edition:

> “The same emperor Constantine sent his mother, the lady [Col. 1588A] Helena, to Jerusalem to seek the venerable cross. From that time onward the affairs of the Christians grew better day by day.”

The restoration of Byzantium under the consuls Gallicanus and Symmachus, in the year of Christ 330, follows next—eight years before Constantine’s death. Jerome agrees with this in his continuation of Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, adding, under the following year, A.D. 331, the dedication of the same city:

> “Constantinople is dedicated amid the near desolation of almost all the cities.”

This corresponds perfectly with the age assigned by Eusebius in book III, chapter 46, of the *Life of Constantine*: Helena was nearly eighty when she died shortly before the year of Christ 330, namely around the year 327, as Sigonius likewise concludes in the passage cited by Ciampini. This is so if, ten years later—namely, in the year 338—the age of her son Constantine the Great at his death is said to have been sixty, or three years more, according to the *Epitome* of Victor, unless that number three referred not to years but to months, as the Nestorian asserts in Malalas.

[Col. 1588B] Since Helena, the Augusta and mother, died at Rome around the year 328, a veteran and honored veteran of the army of the Christian faith, with her most pious son Constantine standing beside her and embracing her hands, according to Eusebius’s narrative—and since she had brought back from Jerusalem, at the urging of that same son, the pledges and instruments of our redemption—and since, according to the chronology of the Nestorian and Malalas, baptism had been received jointly by mother and son, it must be affirmed that Eusebius’s text concerning the sacraments received by the same emperor at Nicomedia in the year 338, a few days before his death, cannot in any way be understood of baptism. It must concern penance and Confirmation administered to him, since he had been baptized in Rome by Pope Sylvester in the Lateran palace approximately fifteen years earlier, or even eighteen or twenty years earlier. Only the sacrament of Confirmation had been postponed, so that [Col. 1588C] he might gratify his pious desire to receive that seal of Christian profession on the banks of the Jordan, if the opportunity arose to visit that region, made holier by the presence of Christ the Lord, to which he had sent his devout mother.

If anyone seeks examples of the postponement of Confirmation among adults during that period, he must find a reason corresponding to Constantine’s decision. I know that adults generally used to be confirmed by a bishop, whether they had recently been baptized by priests or by the bishop himself. Nevertheless, there were certain reasons why the sacrament of Confirmation could be postponed for those cleansed by baptism.

The canons of Laodicea under the same Sylvester whom we are discussing, as well as the letters of Cyprian written a full century before Sylvester, declare that those who had received baptism because of illness or some other necessity, by an abbreviated sacramental rite—as in the case of the eunuch of Candace, baptized by the deacon Philip on the road—were, once they had recovered or been freed from that necessity, required to learn and recite the Apostles’ Creed and to approach the sacrament of Confirmation administered by the bishop. See canons 47 and 48:

> “Those who have been baptized must, after baptism, also become participants in the heavenly chrism and in the kingdom of Christ,” and so forth.

For, following the ancient practice of the apostles and tradition, the Church had observed and [Col. 1588D] continues to observe this, as is clear from a letter of blessed Cyprian, in which it is written:

> “It is also necessary that the one who has been baptized be anointed, so that, having received chrism—that is, anointing—he may be anointed as Christ’s own and may have Christ’s grace within him.”

This sealing with chrism was so closely joined to the baptism of an adult that the African bishops derived from it the cause of their error, supposing that among heretics there was no true baptism because among them there was no anointing. Cornelius and Sixtus condemned this error, while retaining the tradition of chrism and the discipline of the rites which Cyprian lists there: the blessing of the font, the questioning of the catechumen, and the other solemn ceremonies of baptism.

Once Sylvester understood that the reception of chrism could nevertheless be deferred according to the availability of the bishop, the appropriate opportunity, or the pious desire and progress of the recipient, as circumstances permitted, nothing prevented him from graciously allowing Constantine, who desired to receive the heavenly seal, *θείαν σφραγῖδα*, on the banks of the [Col. 1589A] Jordan, to postpone it in the hope of further progress.

Yet, tenacious of discipline, he took care that no anointing should be omitted even when a priest administered baptism. To preserve the mystery, he established that the priest should anoint the baptized person with chrism after he had been lifted from the water, a matter that will occur in the following section.

Moreover, Saint Jerome gives us a sufficiently clear account of the Church’s discipline, current in his own age and in that of Sylvester, concerning the administration of chrism—not always immediately after baptism, but sometimes after an interval, for various reasonable causes—in his *Dialogue Against the Luciferians*. There the Orthodox speaker [Col. 1589B] declares:

> “It is the custom of the churches that, when those who have been baptized by priests and deacons in small towns far away are concerned, the bishop should travel to them in order to lay on hands for the invocation of the Holy Spirit.”

A little later, explaining the same point more fully, he teaches:

> “This observance derives from the authority that, after the Lord’s ascension, the Holy Spirit descended upon the apostles, so that, in the Church, one who has been baptized may not receive the Holy Spirit except through the hands of the bishop—in the sacrament of Confirmation—which we maintain is bestowed in true baptism. Hence it follows that, without chrism and the bishop’s authorization, neither priest nor deacon has the right to baptize; although, when necessity compels, we know that even laypeople are frequently permitted to do so.”

He therefore says that it can happen that those baptized in villages, towns, or more remote places by priests and deacons die, or “fall asleep,” before the bishop visits them. Hence it is clear that the sacrament of chrism was not accustomed to be conferred immediately after baptism even upon all adults, but was postponed according to varying circumstances, as is still done today. In the same way, the Holy Spirit’s being given in the Acts of the Apostles several days after the Lord’s ascension showed the Church this discipline: that the conferral of chrism, or the sacrament of Confirmation, should be adjusted according to the suitability of place and time, together with the other duties to be performed by the bishop or the causes for postponement approved by him.

[Col. 1589C] It should therefore not seem surprising if blessed Sylvester followed the same discipline in reserving Constantine’s Confirmation for a more suitable place and time, since he knew that this practice had been handed down by the Holy Spirit to the apostles at the beginning of the Church.

Thus the whole of what has been said stands in agreement with the legitimate sense of Eusebius’s History and *Chronicle* concerning the life, age, and baptism of blessed Helena and Constantine. It is reconciled with the chronology and narrative of the Nestorian and Malalas, as well as with the text of the Bibliothecary, all of whom assert that the pious emperor was baptized by Pope Sylvester in the city of Rome at the Lateran.

But if the phrase used by Eusebius concerning the washing of penance and the seal of Confirmation gave the Arians an opportunity to transform his statement, this should not be blamed on the historian but on those who abused his history in defense of error. That abuse was unwisely imposed [Col. 1589D] upon later generations when they accepted the illegitimate distortion of plagiarists in place of the writer’s correct meaning.

In this history, especially, it was not difficult for such a distortion to be imposed upon later generations, since the work had been troubled by so many devices of heretics. To them is attributed the change of the name Constantius to Constantine in Athanasius’s text *On the Synods*, as well as the passages of Ambrose, Zosimus, and Socrates being called into question and examined by Baronius, as I noted from Pagius at the beginning of the historical notes on this number.

A similar transformation of the meaning may be suspected in the Acts of Sylvester. There, together with the genuine baptism administered by him to Helena and Constantine, a cure of leprosy was introduced. This cure, I believe, was mentioned in the genuine Acts, but with a meaning very different from that found in the transformed version.

From the customary phrase by which the stains of the mind marked by the guilt of sin are usually expressed under the name of leprosy, I strongly suspect that the bodily disease of elephantiasis, or [Col. 1590A] leprosy, was unwisely added to Constantine. The metaphor was drawn from Scripture. The custom of using this figurative expression in Scripture to signify sins, when the distinction between one leprosy and another is referred to the office of the priest, was so familiar in the age of Sylvester and Constantine that ecclesiastical writers commonly adopted it even when formulating the canons of councils.

This becomes clear to readers of canon 17 of the Council of Ancyra under Sylvester, composed and rendered into Latin as follows:

> “Those who have lived irrationally and have polluted others with the leprosy of a branded crime, the holy synod commanded to pray among those who are endangered by an unclean spirit.”

It was therefore the leprosy of crimes, not bodily leprosy, from which the sincere documents described by the author of the second catalogue—and with him the Bibliothecary in this number—presented Constantine as cleansed, when they asserted that Constantine Augustus had been baptized by Pope Sylvester, “whom the Lord cured of leprosy through baptism.”

[Col. 1590B] It is highly probable that the un-interpolated Acts of Sylvester contained nothing beyond these words. The author of the second catalogue added nothing to them, nor did the Bibliothecary, faithfully transcribing a phrase widely used throughout that age, including in the canon of the Council of Ancyra.

The ancient discipline of secrecy, which took care to speak cautiously when treating the mysteries of the sacraments and to conceal the more sacred doctrines of the faithful from profane eyes, had become accustomed to using such transferred expressions—expressions found in the divine Scriptures—so freely that it employed them everywhere as proper expressions, or as equivalent to proper expressions, and sometimes as more convenient for conveying a meaning, in accordance with the instruction of blessed Augustine in his books *On Christian Doctrine*.

These doctrines, enclosed in figures and transferred expressions, were afterward explained distinctly to the faithful by priests instructed in the mysteries of the secret teaching. Eusebius himself teaches that Constantine employed such men from the very beginning of his conversion.

In later times, however, mystical and metaphorical expressions were sometimes substituted for the use of [Col. 1590C] proper terms for the sake of brevity. This offered readers, especially in a later age, an opportunity to interpret them on their own initiative and to derive foolish narratives from an ignorance of the force of a figurative expression, which had been used by the first writer in a sense entirely different from that understood by some later copyist. Such a copyist then dared to elevate himself into the author of a marvelous history unknown to others, marketing his inventions or attaching them to the narratives of the ancients. Thus, in some manuscripts, the number of three thousand infants cruelly slaughtered to prepare a bath for Constantine’s leprosy is found added; a more careful concern for posterity judged that this should be removed from the corrected manuscripts.

I therefore suspect that something similar was fabricated by some simpler craftsman of a later age from the phrase and metaphor of leprosy cleansed through baptism in the history of Constantine. I also suspect that the older addition—which less successful interpreters of Eusebian history, or perhaps Arian enthusiasts and its corruptors, took care [Col. 1590D] to fabricate in favor of their fellow Constantius concerning the Nicomedian baptism—arose from the opportunity provided by Eusebius’s metaphor. In speaking of Constantine, Eusebius expressed the cleansing of the spirit through *exomologesis*, or penance, by the name of washing, and the sacrament of Confirmation by the word common to it and to baptism, namely the divine seal, *θείας σφραγῖδος*.

Nor will the advocates of the Nicomedian baptism gain anything from the words of Eusebius’s *Chronicle* in Jerome’s addition. Jerome, translating not his own *Chronicle* but that of Eusebius into Latin, and extending it beyond Constantine’s Vicennalia—where Eusebius’s *Chronicle* ended—rendered, from the history of the same author, the metaphor of the salutary washing in exactly the same words, if he believed that the statement concerned the sacrament of penance. Or, if he supposed that baptism had been administered according to an abbreviated and private rite, as baptism was administered to those [Col. 1591A] confined to bed by illness, he supplied the solemn rites of baptism; this still occurs today, for a reasonable cause, in the case of certain great princes’ royal households. In that sense he thought Eusebius had spoken.

For the rest, Scaliger observes that, in this passage of Jerome supplementing Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, the history of the baptism received by Constantine was written differently by Gelasius of Cyzicus, a writer of the fifth century, in the account preserved by Photius. Gelasius does not assert that Constantine the Great was baptized by an Arian bishop, such as Eusebius of Nicomedia was, stained as he was by that corruption, but by an orthodox bishop.

Indeed, if his words are carefully weighed, they also indicate that Eusebius of Caesarea understood the pious emperor to have obtained remission of sins at the end of his life through the washing we have described—the mystical washing of penance—by the mysterious words of the sacrament pronounced by an orthodox prelate, not by a heretic.

For when Eusebius reports that Constantine was accustomed to have bishops in his household entourage, since, at the beginning of his approach to the faith in Rome, he had arranged to receive from them daily expositions of divine law, he had at hand a Catholic prelate from whom [Col. 1591B] he could receive the remission of sins according to the Catholic rite, as well as the sacraments of Confirmation.

Therefore that Gelasius of Cyzicus clearly declared and reported him cleansed:

> *ὀρθοδόξου μυσταγωγήσαντος, καὶ τελέσαντος, ἀλλ’ οὐχ ὡς τίσιν ἔδοξε, τῶν αἱρετικῶν τινὸς χειραπτήσαντος*—

> “An orthodox priest, administering the sacred rite and completing it, not—as some have reported—some heretic laying hands upon him.”

The final words especially are, among the Greeks, proper to the sacrament of Penance, as we explained above with Morinus. Gelasius also adds the reason for the postponed rite, namely the same reason that we derived from Eusebius of Caesarea: Constantine had greatly desired to be baptized in the Jordan itself, although Gelasius appears to be speaking of baptism rather than of the spiritual washing of penance.

Nevertheless, the Nestorian, a writer of the same period and older than Photius, most clearly testifies in Malalas that the grace of baptism had been conferred upon Constantine, Helena, and all their household through the ministry of Pope Sylvester in the city of Rome, just as the Bibliothecary retained it in this number.

[Col. 1591C] Line 17.—The Valerian estate, etc., yielding 80 solidi.

In each of the following sections of the *Life of Silvester*, the Librarian’s principal concern is to enumerate the gifts offered by Constantine to God, so that they might be assigned by patrimonial right to this holy Roman Church and to its bishop, the successor of Peter, as sacred possessions to be retained and administered under the entire authority of the Supreme Pontificate by Silvester and his legitimate successors. Therefore, so that we may not linger over the individual sections with a tedious and sufficiently superfluous investigation of the locations, names, revenues, and various changes of the individual estates, I think it useful to append here a general observation concerning their total value and the uninterrupted continuation of the patrimonial rights arising from this offering of Constantine the Great. These rights were granted with full authority to the father of the whole Christian commonwealth, to be retained and vindicated by him both by patrimonial right and by another, superior right deriving from the divine laws, according to which sacred possessions are to be administered, possessed, retained, vindicated, and recovered by the supreme priest of God whenever sacrilegious usurpers occupy them.

I shall be content here to touch briefly upon their total value and to reserve for the notes to be appended to the *Lives of the pontiffs of the eighth and ninth centuries* a comparison of this total with the annual payment of three and a half talents, which the successors of the emperors paid in its place, under the name of the Sacred Patrimony, after the barbarians had invaded several provinces in which these patrimonies had been established by Constantine. In its proper place we shall also demonstrate that approximately the same amount was exacted by the Roman pontiffs from Robert Guiscard and from the princes who succeeded him in both Sicilies, and was assigned to them under fiduciary law by the direct lord—namely, the Roman and universal bishop and supreme priest—once they had consolidated the patrimonial rights transferred to those provinces, together with the power freely to exercise the right of vindicating them, into the public father’s patrimony, from whose duty of administration and payment rebellious sons had fallen away.

A more careful treatment of these rights should be reserved for illustration in its appropriate places. Nicolaus Alamannus has performed this task brilliantly in his most learned book *On the Lateran Walls*, on the occasion of explaining the mosaic of Leo III that remains in the Lateran patriarchium; we shall also provide it in the *Life of that same pontiff*. Here we shall merely collect the total annual revenue of those estates which Constantine offered, in the name of the Patrimony, through the hands of Pope Silvester to God and to the supreme priest, the vicar of Christ on earth. When we collect from each section of this *Life* the names of the estates and the total annual payment received individually from those estates, the following catalogue results.

If to this total of solidi we add the annual commodities exacted from those same provinces where these patrimonies had been established, to be paid to the Roman Church—namely, balsam, nard oil, pistachio oil, cyprine oil, spices, storax, bundles of paper, cleaned papyrus, *racana*, and flax—they are known to come very close to 35,000 solidi, the amount which Nicephorus and Theophanes stated the provincial governors had customarily paid each year before Leo the Isaurian.

That the rectors appointed by the Roman pontiff to collect these revenues from the patrimonies in the nearer regions of Italy, including or adjoining them—namely Calabria and Sicily—is clear from the letters of Gregory the Great addressed to those same rectors, as well as from the letter of Nicholas to the emperor Michael, produced by Alamannus on page 169 of the aforementioned book *On the Lateran Walls*.

We can easily compare the total of 35,000 gold solidi with the gold and silver coins of our own age, once the weight and value of the solidus have been established from the ancient weights of that age, which are preserved in treasuries and marked with definite signs indicating the corresponding number of solidi. I possess a bronze weight of unquestionable antiquity, square in shape, of the sort that can also be seen engraved among the treasures of the Museum of St. Geneviève in Paris and in Spon’s *Miscellanies*. Inscribed upon this weight of ours are the letters **SOL. XII**, indicating that it contains twelve gold solidi in one ounce and three quarters, which is the weight of this bronze standard and assay-weight.

There are four Spanish gold coins in a single ounce of those which we commonly call *doppie*, so called because each contains the double of a solidus—that is, two gold écus, or two gold florins, or two gold ducats. For one Spanish *doppia* weighs one quarter of an ounce. Therefore, twelve Constantinian-era solidi, to which period that weight belongs, are equal to fourteen of our gold écus—also called ducats or florins from the type of a ducat or flower impressed upon them—or to seven Spanish or Italian coins called *doppie*.

Thus we find that a total of 12,000 solidi contains 1,000 weights equal to our assay-weight, namely 1,750 ounces of gold. This total multiplied by three, producing 36,000 solidi, likewise contains 5,250 ounces of gold and 21,000 Spanish coins called *doppie*, which amount to 42,000 gold florins, or gold pieces. After deducting one thirty-sixth, the result is 35,000 solidi, represented by 20,417 gold coins called *doppie*, or approximately 40,000 gold ducats. If a tenth, to be spent on the officials of collection—the bankers or money-changers—is deducted, there remain approximately those 35,000 [gold ducats], to be paid annually in the name of the patrimonies into the apostolic treasury of the Roman Church. They are 17,000 gold coins called *doppie*, or 4,250 ounces of gold.

The calculation of Theophanes, as he writes in Nicephorus and as Alamannus observes on page 170, comes to the same result: 350 pounds of gold are the total of the three and a half talents of gold which the emperors paid annually to the Roman Church. These payments—indeed, according to Theophanes’ wording, **ἔκπαλας**, “from ancient times”—were called the patrimonies of the holy chief apostles who are venerated in ancient Rome. In 350 pounds there are 4,200 ounces.

In ancient times the emperors customarily paid these sums after the eastern barbarians had harassed the provinces following the reign of Theodosius the Great and had made the administration of the patrimonies difficult in Syria, Egypt, Africa, and other regions and provinces of the Roman Empire. For the pious concern of the Augusti, mindful of their territories and prompting the Church’s defender to protect its possessions, had undertaken such guardianship; and, having agreed with the Roman pontiffs upon an annual payment corresponding to the revenue of the patrimonies indicated above in the offerings of Constantine the Great, they fulfilled their promise by paying each year, according to Theophanes, 350 pounds of gold to the Roman Church through the governors of those provinces.

It appears that, by agreement with the Roman Church and for easier collection, the patrimonies established in Syria, Egypt, Crete, and Africa were replaced by nearer patrimonies, which are mentioned in the letter of Nicholas to Michael and in other records of the ninth century: namely, the Calabrian, Sicilian, Beneventan, Salernitan, Neapolitan, and those of both Upper and Lower Calabria and of Sicily. The Eastern emperors were obliged to make these payments to the supreme pontiffs, as Alamannus observes on page 167: “Adrian I warned the emperor Constantine under the law concerning the recovery of what had been exacted, and threatened him with proscription if he did not restore the patrimonies.”

At the appropriate place we shall see that approximately the same annual payment of 350 pounds of gold arose from the census imposed by the Roman pontiffs upon Robert Guiscard and his successors, when, under fiduciary right, they transferred to them dominion over those same provinces. The transfer of the patrimonial rights to these provinces also provided the occasion for freely exercising the power of vindicating them.

For it will be evident from the tax imposed at twelve Pavia denarii per jugerum of land—a payment which Robert undertook in 1059 to make annually to Nicholas II, Roman pontiff, and to his successors in the first investiture, as it is read in Baronius’s *Annals* and Labbe’s *Councils—that a sum very nearly equal to 35,000 gold solidi, payable from the Constantinian patrimonies, can be calculated if the method of the royal tithe is applied to the area of both Calabrias and Sicily. This method was recently devised by the celebrated marshal D. Vauban and adopted by the Most Christian King throughout all the boundaries of his kingdom as especially useful both for the treasury and for the welfare of his subjects. The matter could be demonstrated by a calculation of no great difficulty. But, so that I may not prolong the notes to this section, I shall reserve it for more careful treatment in a more suitable place, in the *Lives of the pontiffs of the eighth and ninth centuries.

[Note: [Col. 1594D]

**Section 34, line 5.—“Constantine baptized.”** Concerning Constantine’s baptism, received at Rome in the year of Christ 323, the eleventh year of Pope Silvester and the eighteenth of Constantine’s reign, there are certain and indubitable testimonies. The Roman Council convened at Rome under Pope Silvester testifies to it at its beginning; so do Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, book II, chapter 31; Hincmar in the *Life of St. Remigius*; the *Acts of Silvester*; Pope Adrian IV; the Second Council of Nicaea; volume II of the *Decretal Letters*; Nicholas I, Roman pontiff, in his letter to Michael, emperor of Constantinople, in which he commemorates the God-fearing Augusti who exalted the Church of God, and especially the Roman Church: Constantine the Great, Constans, the elder Theodosius, and Valentinian. [Col. 1595A] Nicephorus, *History*, chapter 3; Cardinal Baronius, volume III; and very many others.

Therefore the imposture of Eusebius, the standard-bearer of the Arians, is exposed. To curry favor with the Arian emperor Constantius, he fabricated the fiction that Constantine had been baptized at Nicomedia by an Arian bishop, wishing to brand him with that stigma, flatter the son, comply with his wishes, and appear to have softened his errors by supporting them with lies according to the standard of his father.

**Section 35, lines 1 and 2.—“A council was held,” etc.** Under the emperor Constantine the Great, a certain Alexandrian presbyter named Arius arose, attempting to teach that the Son of God had been made from nothing in time, was entirely a creature, and was of a substance different from that of the Father. Had this teaching not been promptly dispersed, it would have penetrated the hearts and minds of many like a cancer, as Optatus of Milevis relates in book IV.

The eastern synod against Arius and his followers was postponed until the following year after the council held by Silvester and Constantine, so that the wounds inflicted might be treated more closely. Accordingly, a synod was summoned at Nicaea, the metropolis of Bithynia, to which 318 bishops from the whole world assembled. It began on 14 June and continued until 25 August in the year 325, the eleventh year of Pope Silvester and the twentieth of the emperor Constantine.

To this council Hosius, bishop of Corduba, and Victor and Vincentius, presbyters of the city of Rome, were sent as legates by Blessed Pope Silvester. They presided in the same synod in his place, and, when all had assembled in the great church, a complete and orthodox faith was written and explained. The emperor Constantine, with the greatest piety, embraced the decrees of the Fathers.

Meanwhile, while the decrees were being subscribed, the bishops Chrysanthus and Musonius died. Therefore the remaining Fathers approached their tomb and entreated them to be willing to subscribe to the decrees as well. Leaving written and sealed copies upon their coffins and keeping vigil there throughout the night, they opened them in the morning, broke the seals that had been placed upon them, and discovered the subscriptions of the two bishops who were sleeping in death, as Gregory Nazianzen and Nicephorus testify.

**Section 36, line 2.—“The Basilica of Constantine.”** To this basilica, called Constantinian after his name—although usage established that it should rather be called Lateran—he most generously gave exceedingly rich gifts and revenues, as to the principal papal see. They amounted, to speak in ordinary terms, to a total of 2,285,867 gold pieces. This total is correctly obtained by converting the pounds of silver into their value in gold and reckoning each solidus at the price of four gold pieces.

Annual revenues were assigned to the same basilica and to the adjoining baptistery, which he magnificently constructed, from estates, villas, and farms, amounting to 77,856 crowned gold pieces. Among these revenues were 200 pounds of balsam, an oil of the highest value, which was paid back at twice its value in silver, as Pliny attests in book XII, chapter 25. Gregory the Great calls this oil “the oil of the Holy Cross” in book VII, letter 43. Constantine first transferred it to sacred religious use, so that it might provide the light used at the celebration of Easter and on other occasions.

**Section 37, line 1.—“The gift of the baptistery fountain.”** At the same place in his Lateran palace where he had been baptized, the emperor Constantine later constructed a baptistery with the greatest splendor and magnificently adorned it, so that a perpetual monument of his regeneration might remain as a memorial of the sacred event. While he himself was being washed in the sacred laver, a divine light appeared there in a visible sign, flashing with heavenly brilliance; and Christ seemed to extend a hand to him. Christ not only washed away the filth of his soul but immediately freed him from the contagion of leprosy, with scales falling from his whole body.

**Section 38, lines 1 and 2.—“Constantine did,” etc.** After Constantine had been baptized, on the eighth day he came forth, having laid aside his white garments, purified, cleansed, and unharmed, and presented himself publicly for the people to see. Although before his baptism he had appeared wavering, thereafter he showed himself in everything and before everyone, especially the pagans, as a most perfect Christian, and declared himself exceedingly zealous in propagating the Christian faith.

To give thanks to God for the benefit of the purification of soul and body, he went with Blessed Pope Silvester to the confession of St. Peter. After pouring out prayers there, he laid aside the diadem from his head, removed his imperial garments, took a mattock, and was the first to open the ground for laying the foundations, so that he might establish a new basilica under the title of the Apostle Peter. Also, because of the number of the twelve apostles, he carried twelve baskets full of earth upon his shoulders.

**Section 42, line 1.—“He built the basilica of the holy martyr Agnes at the request of his daughter Constantia.”** She had been healed of leprosy through the prayers of that same virgin, and was baptized there by St. Silvester. In that same place she perpetually vowed and preserved her virginity.

**Section 43, line 17.—“Of a certain religious woman, Cyriaca.”** This Cyriaca was a widow and martyr. During the persecution of Valerian, after devoting herself and all her possessions to the service of the saints, she built this cemetery in her own name, in which she buried the body of the blessed martyr Lawrence. Therefore her goods were confiscated and, from the imperial treasury, restored by the emperor Constantine to that same cemetery.

**Section 44, line 26.—“Yielding 1,120 solidi.”** The solidi referred to here as gold coins were half-ounce coins, each weighing four of our gold pieces. The same weight was the gold shekel among the Hebrews and the *stater* among the Greeks.]

## 34

Silvester, a Roman by nationality and the son of Rufinus, occupied the see for twenty-three years, ten months, and twelve days [Note: [Col. 1511] B: twenty-one years, ten months, and one day.]. [Note: [Col. 1511] B: from the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus to that of Constantius and Albinus.] He lived during the time of Constantine and Volusianus, from the day of the Kalends of February to the day of the Kalends of January, when Constantius and Volusianus were consuls. [Note: [Col. 1511] See Baronius under the year 324.]

He was in exile on Mount Soracte, shaken by the persecution of Constantine; afterward, returning with glory, he baptized Constantine Augustus, whom the Lord healed from leprosy through baptism. Having first fled that persecution, he is known to have been in exile.

He built in the city of Rome a church on the estate of one of his own presbyters, who was called Equitius. He established it as a Roman title-church beside the Baths of Domitian; to the present day it is called the Title of Equitius. There he established the following gifts: a silver paten weighing twenty pounds, and a gift from Augustus Constantine. He also gave two silver bowls, each weighing ten pounds; a gold chalice weighing two pounds; five ministerial chalices, each weighing two pounds;

[Col. 1513] two silver vessels, each weighing ten pounds; a silver chrismal paten enclosed in gold [Note: [Col. 1513] C: closed.], weighing five pounds; ten crowned *pharae* [Note: [Col. 1513] C: *pharoi*.], each weighing eight pounds; twenty bronze *pharae*, each weighing ten pounds; twelve bronze, wax-coated *canthara*, each weighing thirty pounds; the Valerian estate in the Sabine territory, yielding 80 solidi [Note: [Col. 1513] C: 40]; the Statian estate in the Sabine territory, yielding 55 solidi; the estate of Duas Casas in the Sabine territory, yielding 40 solidi; the Percilian estate in the Sabine territory, yielding 20 solidi; the Corbitan estate in the territory of Cora, yielding 40 solidi [Note: [Col. 1513] C: 60]; a house in the City with the bathhouse in the Sicininian district, yielding 85 solidi; a garden within the city of Rome in the district of Adduoframantes [Note: [Col. 1513] “ad duos adamantes,” “at the two diamonds.”], yielding 15 solidi; a house in the Roffean district [Note: [Col. 1513] C: Orphean.] within the City, yielding 58 solidi and a tremis [Note: [Col. 1513] C: a tremissis.].

## CATALOGUE UNDER LIBERIUS

Silvester served for twenty-one years and eleven months. He lived during the time of Constantine, from the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus, from the day before the Kalends of February until the day before the Kalends of January, when Constantine and Albinus were consuls.

## 35

He issued a decree concerning the whole Church. During his pontificate, with his consent, the council was also held at Nicaea in Bithynia [Note: [Col. 1513] C: the First Council of Nicaea.]. Three hundred and eighteen Catholic bishops assembled, and their written document was circulated; another 208, who were weak, also set forth the complete, holy, catholic, and spotless faith, and condemned Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius, or their followers.

In the city of Rome he himself, with the emperor’s approval, assembled 277 bishops and again condemned Calixtus, Arius, Photinus, and Sabellius. He decreed that a repentant Arian presbyter should not be received unless the bishop of the designated place [Note: [Col. 1513] C: should designate him.]. He decreed that the chrism should be prepared by a bishop and granted bishops the privilege of signing those who had been baptized because of heretical persuasion.

He also decreed that a presbyter should anoint with chrism the baptized person raised from the water, because of the risk of death in the interval.

He decreed that no layman should dare to bring a charge against a cleric.

He decreed that deacons should wear the dalmatic in church and that their left shoulder should be covered with a linen cloak [Note: [Col. 1513] “A linen cloak.”].

He decreed that no cleric should enter the curia for any reason or plead a case before a girded judge, except in church.

He decreed that the sacrifice of the altar should not be celebrated on silk or dyed cloth, but only on linen produced from earthly flax. Just as our Lord Jesus Christ was buried in a clean linen shroud, so the Mass should be celebrated.

He decreed that if anyone desired to serve or advance in the Church, he should be a lector and should have thirty years of age [Note: [Col. 1513] C: thirty years as doorkeeper, thirty as lector.]; an exorcist, thirty days; an acolyte, thirty-five years [Note: [Col. 1513] five years, C.]; a subdeacon, five years; a guardian of the martyrs, five years [Note: [Col. 1513] seven years, C.]; a deacon, thirty-seven years; and a presbyter, three years. He was to be proven in every respect, possess a good testimony even from those outside, be the husband of one wife, and have a wife blessed by a priest.

Thus he was to ascend to the order of the episcopate, invading no one’s greater or prior position, but acknowledging with modesty the order of time. The votive wishes [Note: [Col. 1513] vows.] of all the clergy were to be acceptable, with no cleric or member of the faithful at all objecting.

He held seven ordinations of presbyters and deacons in the month of December [Note: [Col. 1513] C: seven.]: forty-two presbyters, thirty-seven deacons, and, at various times and in different places in the city of Rome, seventy-five bishops [Note: [Col. 1513] 65, C.].

Likewise, the estate of Sponsas, on the Lavican Way, yielding 262 solidi; below the city of Laurentum [Note: [Col. 1521] Lorentum], the estate of Patras, yielding 120 solidi; below the city of Nepete, the estate of Anglesis, yielding 150 solidi; below the aforesaid city, the estate of Terega, yielding 140 solidi; below the aforesaid city of Falerii, the estate of Hercules, which had been given to Augustus Constantine and which Augustus offered to the church of Jerusalem, yielding 140 solidi; likewise below the city of Falerii, the estate of Nimphas, yielding 115 solidi; below the city of Juder, the estate of Angulas, yielding 153 solidi.

## 42

[Note: [Col. 1521] See Baronius, in the place cited.] At the same time he built the basilica of the holy martyr Agnes at the request of his daughter Constantia, and a baptistery at the same place, where her sister Constantia was also baptized with the daughter of Augustus by Bishop Sylvester. There he established the following gift: a paten of very pure gold weighing 20 pounds; a golden chalice weighing 10 pounds; a crown—a pharus cantharus with 30 dolphins—of very pure gold, weighing 15 pounds; two silver patens, each weighing 20 pounds; five silver chalices, each weighing 10 pounds; 30 silver phara-can thara vessels, each weighing 8 pounds; 40 bronze-gilt phara-can thara vessels.

Forty bronze-gilt cerostrata, enclosed in silver and stamped with seals. A lamp of very pure gold, with twelve lamps [Note: [Col. 1521] lanterns], above the font, weighing 15 pounds; and a gift for annual income around the city of Fidenae, yielding 160 solidi every year [Note: [Col. 1521] C: a field]. Along the Salarian Way, below Pavetina, the whole field of Saint Agnes, yielding 105 solidi; the field of Mucius, yielding 80 solidi; the estate of Vicopiso, yielding 250 solidi; the field of Caculas [Note: [Col. 1521] C: Casulas], yielding 100 solidi.

## 43

[Note: [Col. 1521] See Baronius, in the place cited.] At the same time Constantine Augustus built a basilica for the blessed martyr Laurence on the Tiburtine Way, in the Veranian field above the Arenarium crypt, extending to the body of Blessed Laurence the martyr, where he constructed a stairway for ascent and descent.

At that place he built an apse and adorned it with porphyry marble. From the upper part he enclosed it with silver and adorned the railings with very pure silver; they weighed 1,000 pounds. Before that place in the crypt he placed a lamp of very pure gold with ten lamps [Note: [Col. 1521] C: lanterns], weighing 30 pounds; a silver crown with 50 dolphins, weighing 30 pounds; and two bronze candelabra, ten feet high, each weighing 300 pounds.

Before the body of the blessed martyr Laurence he placed a depiction of his Passion, enclosed in silver and decorated with seals, together with silver byssine lamps, each weighing 15 pounds. The gift which he offered was: a golden paten weighing 20 pounds; two silver patens, each weighing 30 pounds; a cup of very pure gold weighing [Col. 1523] 15 pounds; two silver cups, each weighing 10 pounds; ten silver ministerial chalices, each weighing 20 pounds; two silver ewers weighing 10 pounds; thirty silver phara vessels, each weighing 15 pounds; a golden metreta weighing 150 pounds and holding three medimni.

At the same place, the estate of a certain religious woman, Cyriacetes, which the treasury had seized during the persecution: the Veranian estate, yielding 140 solidi; the estate of Aqua Turia, on its side, yielding 153 solidi; the estate of Augustus in Sabine territory, yielding 120 solidi in the name of the Christians; the estate of Sufuratae, yielding 66 solidi; the estate of Micinae of Augustus, yielding 150 solidi; the estate of Thermulae, yielding 60 solidi; the estate of Aranae, yielding 70 solidi; the estate of Septimitius, yielding 130 solidi.

## 44

[Note: [Col. 1523] See Baronius, in the place cited.] At the same time Augustus Constantine built a basilica for the most blessed martyrs Marcellinus, the presbyter, and Peter, the exorcist, between the Two Laurels, together with a mausoleum where his most blessed mother, Helena Augusta, was buried in a porphyry sarcophagus, on the Lavican Way, at the third milestone from the city of Rome.

At that place, both out of love for his mother and in veneration of the saints, he placed the offerings of his vow: a paten of very pure gold weighing 35 pounds; four silver candelabra enclosed in gold, twelve feet high, each weighing 200 pounds; a crown of very pure gold, namely a phara-can thara vessel with 120 dolphins, weighing 30 pounds; three golden chalices, each weighing 10 pounds, set with green and hyacinth-colored gems; two golden ewers, each weighing 11 pounds; and an altar of very pure silver weighing 200 pounds.

Before the tomb of Blessed Helena Augusta he made, of porphyry metal and carved with seals, twenty silver phara-can thara vessels of very pure silver, each weighing 20 pounds.

Likewise, in the basilica of the saints Peter and Marcellinus, the gift which he gave was as follows: an altar of very pure silver weighing 200 pounds; two patens of very pure gold, each weighing 15 pounds; two silver patens, each weighing 15 pounds; a large golden cup weighing 20 pounds, on which the name of the Augusta is inscribed; five silver cups, each weighing 12 pounds; twenty silver ministerial chalices, each weighing 3 pounds; four silver ewers, each weighing 15 pounds; every year, 900 pounds of genuine nard oil, 100 pounds of balsam, and 100 pounds of spices and incense before the bodies of the saints Marcellinus and Peter.

The Laurentian estate beside the aqueduct [Note: [Col. 1523] C: Formian], with its bathhouse, and the entire field from the Foforritan Gate [Note: [Col. 1523] all the fields from the Sessorian Gate], by the travel road as far as the Latin Way, to Mount Albius [Note: [Col. 1523] and as far as Mount Galbius]. Mount Galbius itself, the estate of Augusta Helena, yielding 1,120 solidi.

The island of Sardinia, with all the estates belonging to it, yielding 1,024 solidi; the island of Mosenum, with the estates belonging to it, yielding 810 solidi; the island of Attitia and Mount Argentarius [Note: [Col. 1523] with Mount Argentarius], yielding 600 solidi. An estate in Sabine territory called the Two Houses, below Mount Lucretius, yielding 200 solidi.

## 45

[Note: [Col. 1523] See Baronius, in the place cited.] At the same time Constantine, at the suggestion of Sylvester, built a basilica in the city of Ostia, beside the harbor of the city of Rome, for the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul and Saint John the Baptist. There he also offered the following gift: a silver paten weighing 30 pounds; ten silver chalices, each weighing 5 pounds; two silver ewers, each weighing 10 pounds; thirty silver phara vessels, each weighing 5 pounds; two silver cups, each weighing 9 pounds; a separate silver chrismal paten weighing 10 pounds; a silver basin for baptism weighing 20 pounds; the island called Assis [Col. 1525], in the territory of Portus and Ostia [Note: [Col. 1525] C: which lies between Portus and Ostia], with all the maritime estates as far as the sun’s finger, yielding 300 solidi; the estate of the Greeks in Ardeatine territory, yielding 80 solidi; the estate of Quiritus in Ostian territory, yielding 311 solidi; the estate of Balneolum in Ostian territory, yielding 42 solidi; the estate of Nunsula, yielding 30 solidi.

Likewise, what Gallicanus offered to the basilica of the aforesaid saints Peter and Paul and John the Baptist was: a silver crown with dolphins, weighing 20 pounds; a silver embossed chalice weighing 15 pounds; a silver ewer weighing 18 pounds; the Millian estate in Sabine territory, yielding 115 solidi and a tremissis [Note: [Col. 1525] C: a tremissis]; the Picturas estate in Veliternian territory, yielding 43 solidi; the estate of Surus on the Claudian Way, in Veientine territory, yielding 56 solidi; and the Gargilian estate in Suessan territory, yielding 655 solidi.

## 46

[Note: [Col. 1525] See Baronius, in the place cited.] At the same time Augustus Constantine built a basilica in the city of Albanum, namely one of Saint John the Baptist, where he also placed the following gift: a silver paten weighing 30 pounds; a gilded silver cup weighing 12 pounds; ten ministerial chalices, each weighing 3 pounds; two silver ewers, each weighing 20 pounds; the estate of Lake Turnus [Note: [Col. 1525] C: Laurentina], with the adjoining plains, yielding 40 solidi; the estate of Molas, yielding 50 solidi; the Alban estate, with the Alban Lake, yielding 250 solidi; the Mucius estate, yielding 170 solidi.

All the abandoned buildings or houses within the city of Albanum he offered as a gift to the holy Constantinian Church [Note: [Col. 1525] Perhaps: Constantine]. The estates of Horti, yielding 20 solidi; the estate of Tiberius Caesar, yielding 80 solidi; the estate of Maritana, yielding 50 solidi; the Nemus estate, yielding 280 solidi; the estate of Armatianus in Caranus territory, yielding 150 solidi; the Statilian estate, yielding 70 solidi; and the Median estate, yielding 30 solidi.

## 47

[Note: [Col. 1525] See Baronius, in the place cited.] At the same time the most blessed Constantine Augustus built within the city of Capua a basilica of the Apostles, which he named Constantinian. There he placed these gifts: two silver patens, each weighing 20 pounds; three silver cups, each weighing 8 pounds; fifteen ministerial chalices, each weighing 2 pounds; two silver ewers, each weighing 10 pounds; bronze candelabra ten feet high, each weighing 180 pounds; and thirty silver phara-can thara vessels.

The gift which he offered was: an estate in Menturnian territory; the Statilian estate, yielding 315 solidi; an estate in Cajetan territory [Note: [Col. 1525] C: Gaetan], yielding 85 solidi; the Paternus estate in Suessan territory, yielding 150 solidi; an estate called Ad Centum in Capuan territory, yielding 60 solidi; an estate in the same Suessan territory, Gauronica, yielding 40 solidi; and the estate of Leo, yielding 40 solidi.

## 48

[Note: [Col. 1525] See Baronius, in the place cited.] At the same time the most blessed Constantine Augustus built a basilica in the city of Naples, to which he also offered these gifts: two silver patens, each weighing 25 pounds; two silver cups, each weighing 10 pounds; fifteen ministerial chalices, each weighing 2 pounds; two silver ewers, each weighing 15 pounds; twenty silver phara vessels, each weighing 8 pounds; and twenty bronze phara vessels, each weighing 10 pounds.

He also constructed an aqueduct over a distance of eight miles. He likewise built a forum in the same city and offered this gift: the estate of Machari [Col. 1527], yielding 150 solidi; the estate of Cymbrana, yielding 105 solidi; the estate of Hyrclina [Note: [Col. 1527] C: Sclinum], yielding 108 solidi; the estate of Affilae, yielding 150 solidi; the estate of Ninfilae, yielding 90 solidi; the island with its fortress, yielding 80 solidi.

Here Sylvester carried out six ordinations during the month of December: 42 presbyters, 26 deacons, and 65 bishops for various places [Note: [Col. 1527] B: elsewhere, 36]. Here he was buried on the Salarian Way, in the cemetery of Priscilla, at the third milestone from the city of Rome, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January [Note: [Col. 1527] C: the day before]. He truly rested as a Catholic and confessor, and the episcopate remained vacant for fifteen days.
